## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library**, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III: a chronological reprint of all extant monuments of Catholic tradition through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, compared with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost care; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the addition of all works discovered after the very ample editions completed during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following either individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly distributed throughout the text, and likewise with headings at the upper margin of each page marking its subject matter; enlarged with works both doubtful and apocryphal which nevertheless possess some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two copious general indexes: one an index of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers wrote upon any topic may be seen at a glance; the other an index of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented upon particular texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in which places in their works.

A most accurate edition, easily to be preferred to all others, if one weighs: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the completeness of the correction, both the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the whole course of the work, the low price, and, above all, this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time brought together in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series**, in which are issued the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin.—The 260 volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,300 francs; the 130 volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for 800 francs.—The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, Western as well as Eastern; the latter, however, are provided in it only in Latin translation.

# The Complete Works of the Venerable Gerhoh, Provost of Reichersberg

[Col. 0009]

## Continuation of the Exposition on the Psalms (G)\*

### Psalm LXIV, or Book on the Corrupt State of the Church, addressed to Pope Eugenius III

*(Baluze published this exposition of Psalm LXIV separately in his* Miscellanies, *and Gallandius did so after him. When Dom Bernard Pez placed Gerhoh’s complete work before the public, he restored it after the exposition of Psalm LXIII, in its proper place. There is no reason for us to depart from his arrangement; nevertheless, we follow Gallandius’s text,* Vet. Patr. Biblioth. *XIV, 549.)*

### Gerhoh’s letter to Henry, Cardinal Priest

[Note: [Col. 0009B] This letter was extracted by the Rev. Father Bernard Pez from a Reichersberg codex. We give its variant readings. It begins: “Brother G. of Reichersberg offers devout prayers together with faithful service to Henry, venerable cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church” [Col. 0010B]. “For a long time I have earnestly desired to see the holy Roman Church adorned without spot or wrinkle. For not …”]

[Col. 0009A] **I.** Psalm sixty-four concerns two cities opposed to one another, namely Jerusalem and Babylon, and their citizens likewise opposed to one another. When, in the time of Pope Eugenius, we discussed at length their mixture and distinction, we then used this very psalm as our subject and presented it to that pontiff of blessed memory for his reading. Our purpose was that the Roman curia—which, as Peter testifies, is the Church gathered in Babylon [1 Pet. 5:13], Rome being figuratively indicated by the name Babylon—that curia, I say, might attend to itself and endeavour to show itself, together with the whole Church which it ought to govern, distinct from Babylonian confusion, without spot and wrinkle.

[Col. 0009B] For even the fact that it is now called the Roman curia, whereas formerly it was called the Roman Church, does not seem free from a spot. For, if the ancient writings of the Roman pontiffs are examined, nowhere is this name, *curia*, found as a designation of [Col. 0010A] the most holy Roman Church. It is more rightly called Church than curia, because the name *curia*, as has been said before us, derives from *cruor*, “blood,” or from *curae*, “cares,” as someone says:

> The curia, mother of cares and nurse of evils,  
> Makes the unjust equal to the just, the dishonourable to the honourable.

**II.** But may such a spot and wrinkle as is denoted by the name *curia* be far from the most holy Roman Church! That name may not implausibly be applied to those who wear soft garments and dwell in kings’ houses, and to all judges who cooperate in judicial bloodshed for the punishment of evildoers. Thus it was appropriately suited of old to the Roman senate, when, under belted judges, emperors, dictators, and consuls, it claimed dominion not only over the city but also over the world.

But since the imperial seat has now become apostolic—while Antiochus and Remus yield Peter the throne of the kingdom, and Emperor Constantine also withdraws from old Rome to the new city which [Col. 0011A] he named Constantinople after himself—it is not without reason that, in the city of Rome, the name Church ought to be preferred to the name curia. For those who now make themselves senators there, although they have authority to handle and judge civil cases and legal disputes without bloodshed, as blessed Peter teaches in the ordination of Clement, nevertheless their judgments fall far short of the weightier affairs of city and world. These belong to the Roman pontiff, or to his vicars like Linus and Cletus, faithfully cooperating with him as with blessed Peter; and likewise to the Roman emperor, or his vicar, the prefect of the city. In respect of his office, the prefect looks to both, namely to the lord pope, to whom he does homage, and to the lord emperor, from whom he receives [Col. 0011B] the insignia of his authority: namely, the drawn sword.

**III.** For just as those whose business it is to lead an army into the field are suitably invested by a standard, so by long custom the prefect of the City is not improperly recognized as invested by emperors with a sword drawn against the city’s evildoers. Thus those who, taking an unlawful sword, rashly usurp vengeance involving blood may perish by the lawful sword. The prefect of the City, however, lawfully uses the sword bestowed on him from above for the punishment of evils and the praise of good men when by it he serves both the lord pope and the lord emperor, to honour priesthood and empire, having promised and sworn fidelity to each and preserving between them such a distinction as exists between the two great lights which God so created and ordered that one should rule the day and the other the night.

[Col. 0011C] For spiritual matters, over which the lord pope presides, are compared to the day; temporal matters, over which the lord emperor presides, to the night. Behold the two lights, and behold here the two swords: lights, because the judgments of the Lord are true and justified in themselves; swords, because vengeance must be carried out upon those who refuse to obey the Lord’s true judgments, justified in themselves. They are true, lest the judge be deceived in distinguishing good and evil, just and unjust; they are justified, so that evil may be rejected and good chosen by regard for justice alone, without the seeking of gifts and without respect of persons—whether this be done through the judge [Col. 0011D] who holds the spiritual sword or through him who does not bear the material sword without cause. For gifts blind even the eyes of the wise, and respect of persons sometimes perverts judgment. A perverted judgment, or one bought by gifts, has no force before God, even if no human being dares to say to the judge, “Why do you act thus?”

**IV.** Hence that saying in Isaiah: “Woe to you who turn [Col. 0012A] judgment into wormwood” (Amos 5:7). And in the Apocalypse: “The name of the star which fell from heaven is called Wormwood” (Rev. 8:11). Since the juice of wormwood, when taken, forces vomiting, judgment is rightly compared to wormwood when it is justly and piously rejected by the devout and righteous. The name of the star is likewise called Wormwood when, beneath the brilliance of justice, judgment is rendered unjust; as though wine were mixed with gall, which Christ, having tasted in his Passion, would not drink. Therefore it is no wonder that his servants refuse to drink judgment mixed with the gall of iniquity, which, like wormwood, causes vomiting.

Although one oppressed by the perversity of such judgment may not dare openly to condemn it, especially when all perverse judges love gifts and pursue [Col. 0012B] rewards, the person who understands and loves truth nevertheless dares at least to approve truth itself in his heart. He is like that blessed Joseph who did not consent to the judges judging Christ unjustly. With the same Joseph he also dares to bury Christ, when he silently reveres in his heart truth as though buried, confident that that same truth will at some time rise again and say: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18)—in priesthood and kingdom, in spiritual and temporal matters.

**V.** Concerning their distinction we have discoursed as best we could in the following treatise on the psalm mentioned above. We first offered it to Pope [Col. 0012C] Eugenius of blessed memory, and now offer it again to you, Henry, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church, as a gift.

[Note: [Col. 0011D] The Reichersberg codex adds: “Not as gold and silver, for it belongs to great princes to offer gold, silver, and precious stones for adorning the high priest’s ephod or breastpiece. May our writings, whatever their quality, at least be in the tabernacle of the Lord as wood by which the fire of the altar is fed, according to the command of the Law: [Col. 0012D] ‘The fire upon the altar shall always burn; the priest shall feed it by laying wood upon it each morning, day by day.’ Finally, the fire of charity upon the altar of the faithful heart must be fed, as by wood, with devout exhortations, so that, even if it grows cold in many because iniquity abounds, it may at least remain in a few elect persons.”]

For, because we have perceived you to be inflamed with zeal for God’s house, we desire, through God’s grace inspiring you, that you may be set more greatly aflame with that fire which the Lord Jesus sent into the earth and earnestly wished to be kindled. “I came,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will but that it should burn?” (Luke 12:49). This is the fire of which the Law says: “This fire shall always be upon the altar; the priest shall feed it by laying wood upon it each morning, day by day” (Lev. 6:12).

Therefore, although princes bring great gifts for the service of the tabernacle—gold, silver, and precious stones, to adorn either altar, breastpiece, or ephod—let us poor people at least offer wood [Col. 0012D] to feed the holy fire, and goats’ hair to cover the tabernacle. We desire our little works, whatever their quality, to be such that the fire of charity may be nourished by them as by cedarwood, and that the covering of repentance, as though woven from goats’ hair, may advance the increase of that blessedness of which it is said: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31:1). Receive then this small gift [Col. 0013A] from the hand of our poverty, since we have scarcely any gold or silver, lest we be found altogether transgressors of the command concerning which the Law of the Lord says: “You shall not appear empty before the presence of the Lord your God” [Col. 0014A] (Exod. 34:20).

# Psalm LXIV

[Col. 0013]

**I.** “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, and to you shall a vow be paid in Jerusalem.” In this psalm, by a third recapitulation, there is now a return to the summit of hope—that is, to the end of the age, when, having received our bodies again, we shall set out for the heavenly homeland. It bears the following title: “Unto the end. [Col. 0013B] A psalm of David. A song of Jeremiah and Haggai, concerning the word of pilgrimage, when they began to set out.”

Its sense is this: this psalm belongs to David the prophet, contemplating the end, that is, the last age. I say it is a psalm, a song—that is, the joy and gladness—of Jeremiah and Haggai, and of all the faithful. Jeremiah means “exalted of the Lord”; Haggai, “solemn” or “sublime.” Both foretold the future pilgrimage of the Jewish people and their return to their homeland. Haggai was also present at that return. Both understood that the pilgrimage of the faithful which takes place in this life, and the return which will occur at last, were signified by it.

By these two, moreover, all faithful people are signified. For as, beneath the figure of that pilgrimage, they more especially lamented this spiritual exile, [Col. 0013C] so in the joy of that return they rejoiced chiefly in spiritual deliverance. Jeremiah, indeed, having suffered and been afflicted more than the others, is beyond doubt also more gladdened than the others; and, truly in accordance with his name, he is conspicuously exalted in the kingdom of heaven. For he was appointed over nations and kingdoms to pluck up, destroy, overthrow, and scatter, and to build and plant; he suffered many adversities in this office, was greatly humbled, and was expressly planted together with Christ’s Passion. Yet by Jeremiah himself, though he is preeminent, the less perfect and those of middling attainments are signified; by Haggai, who was present at the return, the perfect, who not only know themselves to be pilgrims but, according to the Apostle, already have their citizenship [Col. 0013D] in heaven. There, in accordance with the name Haggai, they keep festival and, while on earth’s pilgrimage, already taste beforehand the joys of their heavenly homeland.

**II.** So too in the Gospel: when the Lord says to Peter, “Follow me” (John 21:19), but of John, “Thus I will that he remain” (ibid., 22), the life of those of middling attainments, labouring well in good action, is signified by the prince of the apostles; and by John, the life of the perfect, resting as it were upon Jesus’ breast in the repose of contemplation, and tasting beforehand in this pilgrimage the sweetness of everlasting life. Yet it is certain that both Peter and John were perfected in both forms of life.

Blessed John, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast at supper, is indeed greatly to be honoured. [Col. 0014A] Yet, above the other apostles, authority was given to the prince of the apostles—chiefly established, like Jeremiah, over nations and kingdoms—to strengthen the brethren and overthrow the gates of hell, so that the everlasting gates might be raised: the gates of Zion, which the Lord loves [Col. 0014B] above all the tabernacles of Jacob. Longing to enter them with Jeremiah and Haggai, the pilgrim citizens of that same Zion cry continually, with the cry of mouth and heart: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, and to you shall a vow be paid in Jerusalem”—understand, the heavenly Jerusalem. And, lest any of them should be absent there, they pray in fear and hope: “Hear us, O God, our Saviour, the hope of all the ends of the earth, and of those far off upon the sea,” and the rest.

**III.** The history is known: Jeremiah both foretold and saw the captivity of the Jews in Babylon. He also prophesied that they would return after seventy years. In that captivity there were prophets in Babylon, among whom were Ezekiel and Haggai. When the seventy years had been completed, Cyrus king of the Persians permitted them to return to Jerusalem; Haggai was with them, [Col. 0014C] and the temple was restored.

But because these things happened to them as a figure, we must understand that spiritually there are two cities: one of evil persons, which began from Cain; the other, which began from Abel. The former’s citizens are made by cupidity, the latter’s by charity. Both are intermixed in body, not in desire; for so long as we are in the body, this city, like that one, is on pilgrimage away from the Lord. The cause of this pilgrimage was the word spoken to the first parents: “You shall be as gods” (Gen. 3). This is not unfittingly called the word of pilgrimage, because it is the cause of the universal pilgrimage in which we are held captive. Yet the person who begins to love begins to depart toward the homeland, so that at last, fully placed at the right hand, he may be separated.

[Col. 0014D] **IV.** Nor is it without significance that they return from pilgrimage after seventy years. For this number denotes the time of the present life, in which the people were especially held in confusion before the Advent; from it they began to return through Christ, who was born in the seventy-seventh generation. Therefore this song concerning return is consolation in exile, lest anyone despair on hearing that return is certain, and through whom it comes, and what riches belong to those who return. First, the prophet affirms the return and prays; secondly, he describes the praises of God at the words: “The hope of all the ends of the earth, and of those far off upon the sea.”

**V.** Therefore, concerning this return, the prophet sings in the voice of those returning and says: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion.” O righteous God, by whose just judgment we are in pilgrimage under the Babylonian king, but we trust that we shall at last return to our homeland, namely the heavenly Jerusalem. [Col. 0015A] We who remain in the Church and walk now by faith are beginning to set out for it. Praise is fitting for you: for you, not for the demons who are the gods of the nations. Praise is fitting—that is, praise with song. Where? In Zion, that is, in the Church. According to the condition or movement of pilgrimage, in which it now walks by faith, it is called Zion, meaning “watching” or “contemplation”; but according to the condition of eternity toward which it tends, it is called Jerusalem, meaning “vision of peace.” For then it shall see face to face what it now sees through a mirror, and by seeing through a mirror is called Zion—that is, contemplation.

In this Zion, praise is fitting for you, the true God, from the citizens of that city. For even if one of them should be in [Col. 0015B] Babylon’s furnace, in consequence of bodily distress and human contempt, nevertheless, because in spirit he contemplates spiritual and heavenly things, he fittingly sings the hymn of the three boys. He is neither induced to worship the golden image—that is, to pursue avarice—nor is he fatally burned by Babylonian fire, which is the utterly disgraceful lust of impurity.

Conversely, if some Babylonian citizen, devoted to the love of worldly glory or desire, or to both, and especially a slave of avarice, which is idolatry, should be in Zion—that is, in the Church now present and on pilgrimage—whether honoured with ecclesiastical dignities or cloaked in the appearance of holiness as a citizen of Jerusalem, praise to you, the true God, is not fitting in a single person or [Col. 0015C] a congregation marked by such confusion. For praise is not beautiful or precious in the mouth of a sinner, especially when he seeks in divine service what is his own rather than what belongs to Jesus Christ; this is to worship the golden image.

**VI.** For this reason, in the fasts of the four seasons, in which singers of hymns are advanced to sacred orders, the hymn of the three boys is appended after their contempt for the golden image and their conquest of the furnace’s fire. Those to be ordained are thereby instructed that, even though they are called and regarded as citizens of Jerusalem, it is not fitting for them to sing a hymn to the true God or minister at the holy altar unless they have first despised the golden idol of deadly avarice and conquered or extinguished in themselves the pitchy and sulphurous fire of lust. [Col. 0015D] The king of Babylon nourishes this fire; the king of Jerusalem abominates and hates it. It does not burn the boys of the Lord, protected by the Holy Spirit as by a wind of dew; rather, it burns the Chaldean servants of the king, who feed it instead of quenching it.

The three boys, that is, all who purely worship the triune God in unity, do not feed this fire within themselves. They extinguish it by fasts, vigils, prayers, and other spiritual exercises. And when it has been quenched—or when it is absent, as sometimes happens to old men; or at least when it does no harm, though it naturally inheres in the law of the members, as happens to young men, who, although they feel fleshly desires within themselves, do not follow them or make their members weapons of iniquity—when they serve God’s law with the mind and resist the carnal law of the members [Col. 0016A] in the Holy Spirit, as under the blowing wind of dew; then at last, the Apostle assuring them that there is no condemnation for those who do not walk according to the flesh, and that a crown is owed as to lawful contestants to those who live in the flesh but do not wage war according to the flesh, let them approach, when the Lord calls them, to receive sacred orders and sing hymns to God. For praise is fitting for you, O God, in such a Zion, which possesses such citizens even in the midst of Babylon, in the midst of a crooked nation. But far more fully and perfectly a vow shall be paid to you in that Jerusalem above, wholly free from every Babylonian confusion, which is our mother.

**VII.** Not everyone possesses that perfection of the three boys [Col. 0016B] enabling them to sing a hymn in a strange land. Thus they also say: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a strange land?” (Ps. 136:4). But in Jerusalem a vow shall be paid to you by all Jerusalem’s citizens, when human flesh—which is now a strange, corruptible land, burdening the soul by its corruption even when it is wholly intent upon spiritual and heavenly things—shall in the elect have become altogether incorruptible and incapable of suffering.

Now indeed, although spiritual men, inspired and refreshed by the blowing wind of dew, sing the Lord’s hymn in a strange land, even they frequently hang their instruments upon the willows in the midst of Babylon. Those who are weak, still inferior in the struggle of the flesh, wholly fall silent from the exultant song of hymns; sitting beside the rivers of Babylon, [Col. 0016C] they find it sweet to weep, feeding upon their own tears while eating the bread of sorrow. Therefore, as they make their way in mind toward the heavenly Jerusalem and set its remembrance at the beginning of their joy, they vow praises and thanksgivings which they will at last fulfil and pay in Jerusalem.

**VIII.** But because, before we arrive at that Jerusalem, we are now beginning to set out; and because, when the captivity of Zion is converted, as though captivity had been loosened and the Babylonian fire quenched by the blood of martyrs, we see another Babylon—that is, Rome—changed into the city of Zion and rejoice: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion,” that is, in the Catholic Church, established by the faith of Peter the apostle and taught through [Col. 0016D] the apostles and apostolic men, as it were through Jeremiah and Haggai.

For Peter the apostle, when the Lord looked upon him, wept bitterly, like Jeremiah in his lamentations; and he teaches Jerusalem’s pilgrim citizens to sow in tears what shall afterwards be reaped in exultation. Paul the apostle is joined with him, like another Haggai, whose name means “solemn” or “sublime.” For, caught up to the third heaven, he was solemnly and sublimely glorified by the greatness of his revelations, and, as a vessel of election, is truly worthy to be glorified.

Or, because Jeremiah was crushed by manifold sufferings and finally crowned by martyrdom, the white-robed host of martyrs may be signified by him. By Haggai, however, we may understand the company of confessors resting in peace, in the conversion of Zion’s captivity made as though consoled, [Col. 0017A] and enjoying the assistance of kings for the building of churches.

**IX.** For as Jerusalem was rebuilt through Haggai and the other prophets of that time when Cyrus loosened the captivity, so, when Emperor Constantine granted peace to God’s holy Church, the kingdom of Babylon having as it were already been destroyed, the gates of Zion were rebuilt and made firm by imperial and pontifical decrees as by bolts and bars. The foulest Nero, who, like another Nebuchadnezzar, had first set up idolatry as a golden image in the second Babylon, together with his successors, the torturers of Christ’s martyrs who increased the fires of the furnace (sic), had already been judged. [Col. 0017B] Thus some of these, humbled to repentance, ate grass like an ox and acknowledged that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men. Others, luxuriating and tyrannizing in excessive security with Belshazzar, lost their kingdom and perished with their lives.

The acts of the martyrs testify that some torturers and senators in the city of Rome, as in Babylon, were humbled beneath the yoke of Christian law; while others were handed over to the devil both visibly and invisibly, and deprived together of kingdom and life. Accordingly, some having been condemned and others converted, the name of that Babylon was also changed, so that the city might more rightly now be called Zion than Babylon. Thus the instruments formerly hung up there are now taken up for songs.

[Col. 0017C] **X.** For when the Christian faith was still stationed in battle-array and, as someone says:

> [lacuna] troubled by a rustic mode of life,  
> Bare in shoulders, unshorn in hair, with arms uncovered,  
> Fighting, and mindful neither of weapons nor of armour,  
> But with a strong heart and uncovered limbs  
> Challenging the dangers of a mad war that must be broken—

there was no leisure for the pontiffs of the apostolic see to adorn the worship of faith as it is now adorned, and crowned with glory and honour in the altar’s ministry. Now instruments resound, and singers are equipped for singing, especially in monasteries secured by the decrees and privileges of the Roman pontiffs. Therefore, while these now strike the lyres [Col. 0017D] in the house of the Lord, praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion—that is, in the Roman Church. Its name has been changed from Babylon to Zion through apostolic faith, and its foundations are now upon the holy mountains.

**XI.** The holy ministries of the priestly office, adorned with spiritual songs and hymns, are fitting for you in that Zion. For example, one Roman pontiff decreed that psalms should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice; another added the *Glory in the Highest*; another, *Holy, holy, holy*; another, *Lamb of God*, to the sacred office. The pontiffs of that same Roman Church also inserted certain solemn prayers together with festal songs and hymns, especially on the chief solemnities. In their vigils [Col. 0018A] Jeremiah the mourner goes before, as it were, fasting, keeping watch, and weeping before the Lord who made us. Then, on the feast days, that solemn Haggai is present, he who was personally present at the return from Babylon to Jerusalem.

Thus every eminent solemnity—for example, the Paschal festival—by its songs and hymns as it were presents to us, after Babylon has been left behind, a vision of heavenly peace and joy. For at so great a feast, preceded by the Lenten lamentations, vigils, and fasts, the heavenly angelic host now rejoices, and the divine mysteries rejoice, for those who begin to journey upward and, rising again with Christ, savour the things above. When these things have been fittingly ordered and Babylon’s citizens excluded from them, praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion. And this hymn [Col. 0018B] is preparation for the vow which shall one day be paid perfectly in Jerusalem.

**XII.** But, O God, is praise fitting for you in Zion when it is forbidden by the leaders of that same Zion? By their decretal edicts they forbid ecclesiastical offices and benefices to clerics who are manifestly incestuous with Nicholas the fornicator, and who, with Judas the wicked merchant or Simon Magus, trade shamefully and commit robbery in God’s house. Yet, protected also by material weapons, they are found more savage than Judas, who, reproved by his own conscience, said: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27:4); and than Simon Magus, who, cursed by the apostle Peter, said to Peter and the other apostles: “Pray to the Lord for me, that none of the things which you have said may come upon [Col. 0018C] me” (Acts 8:24).

But these malicious persons are neither humbled when their own conscience rebukes them, nor do they patiently endure rebuke from any zealot for truth. Rather, they persecute and hate such people, and expose them to be butchered and killed by their soldiers. What, then, do these men intend, or what does the Babylonian prince of this world intend through them, except to destroy the city of Zion and rebuild Babylon?

**XIII.** For when the Roman empire, like a furnace, burned with Babylonian fire against worshippers of the Trinity, tormenting by diverse tortures those who scorned the golden image—that is, idolatry, especially avarice—Rome was then not without reason figuratively called Babylon by the apostle Peter. “The Church gathered in Babylon,” he says, “greets you” (1 Pet. 5:13). [Col. 0018D] But once the fire of persecution had been cooled and extinguished in the Roman empire, now bowed to faith in Christ, Rome itself, the city of cities, is rightly called Zion, as has already been said.

Thereafter no place ought to be allowed within it for Babylonian tyranny or confusion, since it is the court of chastity, the seat of justice, and the refuge of canonical and monastic religion. Its cloisters are regularly arranged and defended on every side by reasonable privileges as though by ramparts, so that singers may freely repeat hymns from the songs of Zion within them, in accordance with: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion.”

XIV. Here I wish to pause a little; and, interrupting for a moment the course of the exposition [Col. 0019A], to turn against those who must be refuted—those who destroy the walls of Jerusalem and, so far as lies in their power, strive to build the walls of Babylon. Do they not separate what God has joined, or confuse into one what he himself has separated and distinguished, raising high the walls of Babylon—that is, of confusion? They also strive to make the Roman Empire Babylonian; and, what is worse, they wish the Christian kingdom to be pagan. Or rather, by mixing together two opposing things, they restore the kingdom of Babylon and revive that kingdom concerning which the Lord complains through the prophet Jeremiah: “Israel is a scattered flock; lions have devoured it” (Jer. X, 21). The king of Assyria first devoured it; this last one, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, stripped it to the bones [Col. 0019B].

Truly, rulers—lions in their bestial ferocity—have devoured the Lord’s flock. The king of Assyria first devoured it, either because the first ruler of the Assyrians—that is, of the Jews who directed themselves—devoured it when Pilate, their tetrarch, killed Christ and his flock of disciples was scattered; or because, when the Jews themselves incited him, King Herod laid hands upon certain members of the Church in order to afflict them. Then the remaining lions, from Nero to Diocletian, through the ten universal persecutions, so devoured and scattered the Lord’s flock that the beast dreadful to Daniel, with ten horns, had already raged in each persecution by means of its individual horns and had been sated with the blood of the saints beyond all telling.

And because in the final persecution, while Diocletian and Maximian tyrannized, the Church was harassed for ten years: whether you understand the ten horns of the cruel beast—that is, the Roman Empire—as the ten universal persecutions or as the ten years of the final persecution, gladly acknowledge that from that time the beast was humbled. Like an ox eating hay and recognizing the manger of its Lord, it was moistened by the dew of heaven: that is, when Emperor Constantine was baptized—not, as heretics contend, by the Arian heretic Eusebius, but, as Catholics hold, by Sylvester, the Catholic bishop of Rome.

XV. For I remember that, when I was in the city of Rome, an adversary of God’s Church, a certain legal advocate, objected to me that Emperor Constantine’s privileges favorable to ecclesiastical liberty were invalid, because he had either been baptized or rebaptized in the Arian heresy, as the Tripartite History appears to suggest. Against this we then argued in part, and we remain prepared to argue and prove that, just as in ancient Babylon the edicts commending the God of Daniel were valid [Note: [Col. 0019D] Perhaps a typographical error for *commendantia*, “commending.”], although promulgated by a pagan emperor—whether when Nebuchadnezzar glorified the Son of God manifested to him in the furnace, or when, after Daniel had explained his dream, he exalted Daniel himself above all the princes of Babylon and magnified in praise Daniel’s God and the God of the three youths; and when afterward, cast out from the kingdom and restored again to it [Col. 0020A], he confessed that God rules over human beings—so much more must imperial privileges or edicts in the second Babylon, issued by emperors glorifying God and exalting his servants above all princes of the earthly realm, be considered valid insofar as they are found consonant with prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic teachings, even if the emperors’ lives are not in every respect to be approved.

XVI. For if Cyrus, king of the Persians, is praised by divine testimony and is called by the prophet the Lord’s Christ, not because he possessed sound faith or lived justly—for he was a pagan—but because by an imperial edict he first released the captivity of God’s people, permitting the citizens of Zion to return to sing hymns in Zion: how is Emperor Constantine not to be praised [Col. 0020B], who first among Roman emperors protected the Church’s liberty by public edicts, so that God’s servants might freely serve God in psalms, hymns, and songs of Zion?

Until his time this had been done in the city of Rome—that other Babylon—in crypts and other hiding places, as though in silence, with their instruments hung up in the midst of Babylon. But from that time, when by his help the walls of Jerusalem were built, the true God is sacrificed to in magnificent churches, while chosen singers, trained in the songs of Zion, rejoice aloud. What wise and understanding person, seeing this, would not venerate the work of divine mercy, whatever faith or manner of life may be attributed to the man through whom God performed such things?

XVII. [Col. 0020C] We read of excellent writings and edicts of pagan kings—Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes—promulgated for rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem. We do not judge them to be rejected because of those rulers’ unbelief; rather, because of the divine mercy by whose inspiration they proceeded, we ought to love and venerate them, especially because, remitting certain things and granting others from the public treasury, they gave assistance to God’s servants rebuilding the house of God and the walls of Jerusalem after the captivity of God’s people had been released.

We also read and venerate the good letters of King Ahasuerus, contrary to the earlier wicked letters issued at the counsel of Haman the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews; and we praise them. How then should we not praise the edicts of Constantine and other emperors favoring the peace of the Church, whatever may have been the state of their faith and conduct? Certainly, in Ecclesiastical History, as Eusebius narrates, the faith and piety of Prince Constantine are praised. If afterward, as is read in the Tripartite History, he departed from this and was baptized or rebaptized by the Arian Eusebius, the fault belongs to him himself and nevertheless does not invalidate his good writings [Col. 0020D].

Thus David’s fault, though it greatly harmed him, could not invalidate his good writings. So too we retain Solomon’s good and holy writings, although we know that the latter part of his old age was grievously defiled by luxury and idolatry. We likewise receive with the highest authority the prophecy of Balaam, a diviner who loved the wages of iniquity, because it is found consonant with sacred Scripture [Col. 0021A], weighing not who said it but what was said.

XVIII. Therefore, let Emperor Constantine in his final days have been an adherent of whatever sect, having, as is reported, abandoned the Catholic faith for which he had labored at the Council of Nicaea—something I by no means believe. For even his sons Constantine and Constans, successors to their father’s faith, are commended by two witnesses, two olive trees, and two lampstands, namely John and Paul, to the reproach of Julian the Apostate; and they are declared to have been Catholics, steadfast in Catholic faith and good conduct, translated from an earthly kingdom to a heavenly one.

Let their father Constantine then have been stained in respect of faith by the Arian plague, against which he had previously fought praiseworthily, as Cassian asserts [Col. 0021B], whose heretical opinion is noted and rejected not only in the excessive praise of the Tripartite History but also in his other writings, although we retain his writings on the Lives of the Fathers—only those approved by the distinguished man Jerome. For the rest are apocryphal and, as the most learned teacher Prosper observes, rejected for their heretical teaching. Yet certain works are found corrected by Prosper himself.

Whatever, then, may be the proper acceptance or rejection of the Tripartite History’s account of Constantine’s baptism, this has nothing to do with weakening his edicts, promulgated for the Catholic faith in defense of God’s holy Church and confirmed among the other imperial writings by apostolic teachers.

XIX. Hence in the Ecclesiastical Acts one reads among other things [Col. 0021C]:

> “Finally, kings, governors, and magistrates not only bestowed adjacent properties, but throughout the kingdoms of the earth gave their own possessions as well, so that the needy, who possessed nothing in the world, might be supported; churches might be built and restored; and provisions might be supplied without want for those who duly serve God and his Church, and for his servants. Among these, the most religious man Constantine, the first openly to embrace the faith of truth, granted throughout the world to those living in his empire permission not only to become Christians, but also ordained that churches should be built and estates bestowed. Finally, the aforesaid prince himself established immense gifts and the construction of the church of the first see of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles [Col. 0021D], to such an extent that he left the imperial seat, over which the Roman rulers presided, and granted it for the benefit of blessed Peter and his successors.”

Let the adversary hear that Emperor Constantine is called “a most religious man” in the ecclesiastical acts, and that his enactment is praised not because it was his, but because it was just and reasonable. Nor does the statement of jurists that public property cannot be acquired by prescription conflict with so praiseworthy a constitution, since, rightly understood, that statement establishes that what belongs to public law cannot be reduced to private ownership. Finally, property given to the Church by the state remains public: it is devoted to the public service of the highest King, not claimed as private property.

XX. [Col. 0022A] Many praiseworthy examples of such transfer are found not only in the holy Church, but also among an unholy and pagan people. Let us read the deeds of pagan kings in the books of Maccabees, and we shall find Jerusalem, because sins required it, repeatedly miserably humbled and trampled by the nations; yet, once God was propitiated, greatly honored by kings of the nations and enriched from public funds. For when the holy city was inhabited in complete peace and its laws also most carefully observed, the kings of the nations themselves held in highest veneration the holy place. Later, after God’s laws had been despised and it had been profaned and dishonored, we read that it was restored again through the triumphant wars of the Maccabees, adorned with golden crowns, and, after the kings of the nations had been greatly humbled, magnificently honored by their gifts [Col. 0022B].

Similar to this is what occurred after the victorious conflicts of the martyrs: kingdoms were brought low, and through the pious Prince Constantine imperial walls and estates were transferred to Christ’s service, while the liberty to build and enrich churches was confirmed by public edicts.

XXI. After Constantine, his successors in empire and piety—Catholic kings and emperors—confirmed the same liberty of God’s holy Church: namely Constantine the Younger and Constans, Valentinian, Arcadius and Honorius, Charles and Louis. Their imperial enactments concerning ecclesiastical liberty are at hand; by them the privileges of ecclesiastical immunity and liberty, promulgated both by themselves and their predecessors, are declared altogether reasonable and inviolable [Col. 0022C].

Thus Arcadius and Honorius say among other things:

> “Whatever has been established at different times by our forefathers concerning the most holy churches, we command to remain inviolate and uncorrupted. Therefore let nothing be altered from their privileges; let protection be afforded to all who serve the churches. For in our times we desire rather that reverence be increased than that anything formerly granted be changed.”

Valentinian likewise decreed:

> “We decree that all whom it is established are guardians of churches and serve the holy places in religious duties shall suffer no annoyance from any encroachment.”

XXII. [Col. 0022D] We could collect many similar passages from the laws and edicts of emperors and kings. But we possess stronger defenses in the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, which by the unanswerable authority of their apostolate defend the liberty and immunity of ecclesiastical estates and of all that churches possess. By these decrees those who defraud, ravage, or alienate ecclesiastical property are struck with the dart of anathema and declared sacrilegious.

But if some doubt arises for you from the Ecclesiastical Acts, because the Ecclesiastical History seems in certain matters to differ from the Tripartite History concerning what is written in each about Emperor Constantine: set aside the diversity of manuscripts, which variously treat Constantine’s baptism but nevertheless attest one and the same piety of the aforesaid prince [Col. 0023A]; look, I ask you, to the Roman pontiffs, who unanimously agree in attesting the same truth.

And if you seek arguments still stronger, have recourse to the immovable foundation of evangelical, apostolic, and prophetic testimonies. In them you plainly find approval that kings, princes, and other rich persons of this world may lawfully and beneficially honor God’s holy Church with generous liberality; and, by offering gold from their treasures to Christ reigning in it, adorn his cradles—that is, the communal dwellings of those who serve him. In the same way holy martyrs, by offering myrrh, and holy confessors, by offering incense, adorn the same cradle according to what befits their respective orders: while the relics of martyrs placed there shine with powers and miracles, assist by their merits those who serve there, and the teaching of confessors forms holy character, while their prayers lend aid to the ox and ass recognizing the manger of their Lord [Col. 0023B].

XXIII. And because this manger of the Lord ought to be filled not only with the food of angels but also with the hay of animals, let the rich of this world bring together this hay, making friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when they fail they may be received by them into eternal dwellings. For the attainment of these, kings themselves should offer royal buildings, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “In the haunts where dragons formerly dwelt, there shall spring up the green growth of reed and rush” (Isa. XXXV).

We see this fulfilled also literally [Col. 0023C], for we behold not only temples of idols but even palaces of emperors and kings transformed into churches and dwellings of those who serve God. Let the round church of Saint Mary in the city of Rome be an example for us. Built for demons, it is now dedicated in honor of the most blessed Virgin Mary and all the saints. Likewise, the Lateran Palace, formerly imperial and now priestly, plainly represents the truth of this prophecy: “In the haunts where dragons formerly dwelt, there shall spring up the green growth of reed and rush.”

Likewise, in monasteries built with the help of the rich, reeds and rushes fill what were, as it were, dragons’ dens: when the tongue of teachers, like the reed of a swiftly writing scribe [Col. 0023D], firmly sets down the word of God; and the faith of hearers, like a flourishing rush rooted not upon the rock of pride but in the valley of humility, preserves the word spoken to it lest it perish. So too baskets woven from rushes preserve the fragments of the five loaves lest they perish. And Mary, queen of the humble and foremost example of humility, kept all the words entrusted to her faith, pondering them in her heart, until she committed them to the reeds of the apostles and the Gospels—those worthily speaking and writing of such matters, which did not befit the female sex.

XXIV. Something almost similar occurs in regular monasteries. As infirm and female persons pray, while strong and virile persons [perhaps *viris* or *virilibus*, “men” or “virile persons”] manfully and courageously attest the word of God in writing or speech, reeds and rushes—the strong and the weak, the eloquent and the silent—cooperate with one another [Col. 0024A]. This especially delights the observer and lover of God’s wonders when it occurs in haunts where dragons formerly dwelt—as in royal palaces or ancient temples of demons, according to the examples above of Saint Mary’s round church and the Lateran Palace.

Let the bleary eyes of the envious be tormented by this spectacle; but I shall delight in the Lord who works such things, and with unclouded eyes behold God lying in every such manger, in the midst of two animals, ox and ass, as though in the midst of reed and rush. For the ox, a clean animal fit for sacrifices, chewing the cud and treading out grain, aptly signifies the choir of learned persons devoted to the ministry of the word [Col. 0024B], whose tongues are compared with swiftly writing reeds. The ass, a simple beast of burden, no less fittingly signifies the flock of the simple: for example, lay brothers, devout sisters, or other faithful persons, who have hearts altogether ready to bear, so far as they can, the burden of obedience; and who, in that charity which bears all things and endures all things, like Issachar the strong ass, set their shoulder to bear and endure everything.

XXV. Who that considers these things does not see that Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi? For since Caesar was emperor and Philip tetrarch, those names suitably prefigure the power of Christ, which was to advance so far in the world that emperors and all other rulers, both greater and lesser, would bend their necks to him [Col. 0024C]. Thus the ancient Jesus, also called Joshua, placed the necks of five kings beneath the feet of his leaders, while the sun prolonged the day until such victory was completed.

Do you suppose it was without mystery that Peter was told not elsewhere but in such a place: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 19)? The Lord could have said this to Peter elsewhere [Col. 0024D], but he wished to show that Caesars, tetrarchs, and all other rulers of this world must either be broken or bent by the primacy of apostolic dignity.

Blessed are those found capable of bending: Prince Constantine, and after him Arcadius and Honorius, Valentinian, Gratian, Charles, and pious Louis, together with all others like them, able to turn from evil to good. But wretched are those who, refusing to bend, deserved to be broken: Nero, Decius, and others who tyrannized in paganism; and some afterward worse than they in Christianity, such as the Arian Constantius and Julian the Apostate, together with other kings favoring the mad heresy opposed to God’s Church; or those in modern times who sold spiritual gifts which they did not possess, or rather pretended to sell them, in appointments of bishops, abbots, provosts, and chaplains—not for God’s pleasure, but for their own—seeking Simonian profit in everything [Col. 0025A].

XXVI. For wicked and simoniacal kings, and other rulers agreeing with them, wished either to confer bishoprics and other ecclesiastical dignities according to their own will without any canonical election, or to have elections in which they themselves held sovereign sway. They relied on the fact that, according to the canons, the consent of the *honorati*—the dignitaries—must be sought and admitted in episcopal elections.

I recall that this question of admitting and requiring the assent of each city’s *honorati* in the election of a bishop is treated at length in the letter of Chuonrad, archbishop of Salzburg of blessed memory, to Norbert, the learned archbishop of Magdeburg [Col. 0025B]. That author had wished even powerful rulers, or kings who administered the commonwealth, to be included among the *honorati* of each city. The authority of the sacred canons altogether opposes this.

Thus, in the Seventh Ecumenical Synod, held by the five patriarchs with 350 Fathers under Pope Hadrian, chapter three reads:

> “Every election of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon made by rulers remains void, according to the rule which says: If any bishop uses secular powers to obtain a church through them, let him be deposed and separated, together with all who communicate with him.”

Likewise, in the Council of Antioch:

> “If any presbyter [Col. 0025C] or deacon obtains the Church of the Lord by secular rank, let him be deposed, and his ordainer cut off in every way from communion; and let him be under anathema, like Simon Magus at the hands of Peter.”

From the synod of Pope Symmachus with 218 bishops:

> “It has not pleased us that laypersons should have any authority to determine anything in the Church; theirs remains the necessity of obeying, not the authority of commanding.”

The Eighth Synod, chapter 11:

> “Agreeing with earlier councils, this holy and universal synod has defined, decreed, and lawfully promulgated that promotions and consecrations of bishops are to take place by the election and decree of clerics and by the college of bishops; that no lay ruler or powerful person is to insert himself into the election or promotion of a patriarch [Col. 0025D], metropolitan, or any bishop, lest disorderly and unsuitable contention or confusion arise from this. Especially since it is fitting that none of those in authority, or any other laypersons, possess any power in such matters, but that they keep silence and attend to themselves until the election of the future bishop duly receives its completion from the college of the Church. But if any layperson is invited by the Church to deliberate and cooperate, he may, if he wishes, comply respectfully with those summoning him. For in this way the Church lawfully promotes a worthy man for its own salvation. But whoever, whether a secular ruler, a powerful person, or a layperson of another rank, attempts to act against the common, harmonious, and canonical election of the ecclesiastical order, let him be anathema until he obeys and consents to what the Church has shown itself to will concerning the election and ordination of its own bishop.”

The canons of Paris:

> “If anyone, with excessive rashness, presumes to attain the summit of this honor through royal appointment, he shall by no means deserve to be received by the provincial bishops of that place, who know him to have been improperly ordained. If any of his fellow provincials presumes to receive him against these prohibitions, let him be separated from all his brethren and removed from the charity of them all” [Col. 0026A].

XXVII. By rules of this kind promulgated concerning the promotion of bishops, the coercive power of kings, princes, and other powerful laypersons is excluded from episcopal elections and promotions, although the assent of each city’s *honorati* is rightly sought [Col. 0026B]. To this is added a new decree of Pope Innocent, commanding that election be made by the canons according to the counsel of religious persons.

When all this is carefully weighed, four distinctions are found in a canonical election. Spiritual and religious men are to give counsel; canons are to elect; the people are to petition; dignitaries are to give assent. Yet if, when the counsel of religious fathers, the election of clerics, and the petition of the people have converged in one, they refuse to give assent, the election is not thereby invalid if it is otherwise canonical. For neither kings nor dignitaries possess any power to annul it; rather, as Pope Symmachus says, they have the necessity of obeying.

Rightly, then, as God, when fashioning the world in the beginning, made heaven and earth, so in fashioning the new creation he first forms what is heavenly and spiritual, and afterward what is earthly and bodily. Thus, once a bishop has been spiritually elected and established, the assent of the laity follows, together with that royal grant through which the king or emperor must invest the bishop already appointed, when there is no further dispute whatever concerning his election or promotion [Col. 0026C].

XXVIII. For if disagreement concerning an election is evident, the judgment of spiritual judges is rightly awaited in such matters, so that, once the elect person has been confirmed, the royal grant may take place. Nevertheless, things long ago given to churches ought already to be reckoned ecclesiastical possessions, though they are to be held with fitting service toward the king, not bestowed upon or taken from churches at his pleasure as though anew [Col. 0026D].

Kings and princes obstinately persisting in such wickedness as to wish ecclesiastical goods, or the regalia themselves, to be disposed of according to their own pleasure have in part been broken, while others have been humbled to obedience to the apostolic see. Thus we could now rejoice in the things said and done, as those who come from Babylon to Jerusalem go into the house of the Lord, if we did not see Babylon rebuilt by certain persons—that is, the confusion by which the king of Babylon, the devil, in these last days strips the Lord’s flock to the bones, as Jeremiah laments: “Israel is a scattered flock; lions have devoured it. The king of Assyria first devoured it; this last one, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, stripped it to the bones” (Jer. L, 17).

XXIX. [Col. 0027A] For what is it for the Lord’s flock to be stripped to the bones, except for it to be so bewitched that it is led into error, if possible—even the elect, who are compared with bones bearing flesh—and, because sins require it, joined to the number of those who are reckoned citizens of Babylon rather than of Jerusalem?

For example, among the clergy are those who, though highly educated, are nevertheless called and indeed are *Acephali* (“headless ones”); and, as Isidore says, are likened to hippocentaurs, neither horses nor human beings, representing in themselves a mixed and confused kind. Observing neither clerical nor lay discipline, because they are called clerics or canons, though they are a synagogue of Satan, they wish according to their own whim partly to usurp ecclesiastical honors for themselves and partly to confer them on persons like themselves, or even worse. Some of them occupy the chief dignities and sees in the Church, and oppress the citizens of Jerusalem all the more heavily because they serve the king of Babylon all the more freely within Jerusalem itself [Col. 0027B], mingling secular with spiritual matters and confusing everything so thoroughly that, if you saw such a person, you could not judge his profession either from his dress or from his conduct.

Likewise, among the laity you can scarcely find anyone in the military order content with his own wages, that is, those belonging to secular military service, so that they do not possess tithes assigned by divine ordinance to spiritual rather than secular warfare. Thus they too, confused as though from a different kind, are citizens of Babylon: separating what God has joined and joining what he has separated. The chief contrivers of this confusion are bishops who foster such clergy [Col. 0027C] and grant such benefices to laypersons; and rulers who hold the same things in their powerful hands, thereby serving not God but the king of Babylon. For the king of Babylon loves such confusions, so that spiritual and secular things, mingled together, may in some fashion represent the ancient chaos, when the earth was still void and empty and darkness was upon the deep.

XXX. But lest such confusion of things should endure forever, the Spirit of God was borne over the waters, in order to bring forth distinct forms from so great a confusion of things and distinguish them from one another by their proper character. Much more graciously now he is borne over the waters of baptism, that from them he may bring to light whatever beauty and delight there was [Col. 0027D]. Therefore, before making anything, the eternal wisdom of God delighted in itself, playing upon the circle of the earth and finding its delight in being with the children of men.

This same Wisdom, speaking in these last days to human beings in its own flesh and dwelling with them, distinguished among themselves the people with whom it dwelt: speaking in one manner to its disciples on the mountain and in another to the crowds in the plain. It thus showed that the chosen followers of its discipleship were to be separated from the crowds of men and joined to it upon the mountain of a higher manner of life.

Mindful of this divine institution, blessed Peter says at the ordination of Clement:

> “You must live irreproachably and strive with the utmost zeal to cast aside all the occupations of this life, lest you become a surety [Col. 0028A], lest you become an advocate in lawsuits, and lest you be found at all entangled in any occupation arising from worldly business. For Christ does not wish today to ordain you a judge or investigator of secular affairs, lest, choked by present human cares, you be unable to devote yourself to the word of God and to separate the good from the evil according to the rule of truth.”

Likewise:

> “Just as it is a crime of impiety for priests, neglecting study of the word, to take up secular concerns, so it is a sin for every layperson unless they faithfully give one another assistance also in matters belonging to the use of common life.”

And Paul, teacher of the nations, says: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II, 4).

Likewise: “Every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed for human beings in those things which pertain to God” (Heb. V, 1) [Col. 0028B]. “In those things,” he says, “which pertain to God”; not in those which pertain to the world.

XXXI. These salutary admonitions of apostolic teaching must certainly not be understood in such a way that they conflict with the Apostle’s statements in which he asserts that he and those like him possess authority even to judge angels, and much more secular matters. Likewise: “The spiritual person judges all things, and is judged by no one” (I Cor. II, 15).

Therefore let the spiritual person judge all things, especially those entrusted to his care, even secular matters—yet in such a way that he does not become entangled in secular business. For it is one thing to judge secular matters justly; it is another to entangle oneself in them. A bishop has authority to judge secular judgments and judges [Col. 0028C], knowing how to reject evil and choose good, knowing how, according to the law, to distinguish leprosy from non-leprosy, holy from unholy. But some judgments and affairs a spiritual person sitting in Moses’ seat can administer himself; others he ought to entrust to prudent laypersons, especially those concerning the punishment of evildoers, against whom the armed minister and girded judge do not bear the sword without cause.

No one ought presumptuously to take that sword, lest one who takes the sword perish by the sword. But when ecclesiastical authority directs secular authority and sometimes restrains it, sometimes spurs it on, let the nations thus be judged by the saints, so that, while those officials rule justly, the hand and tongue of the priest may remain clean from the business of blood [Col. 0028D]. For blood shed by a girded judge, though appointed by a bishop, is not to be imputed to the bishop, provided that he does not allow that judge unrestricted power or violence contrary to justice.

XXXII. Thus we read that Roman pontiffs excommunicated and removed certain kings or princes because of their uselessness or wickedness, appointed others in their place, and required that those whom they advanced should pursue the enemies of Church or kingdom with the avenging sword, not only by their institution but even by their command.

Certainly, when wars of this kind are undertaken in defense of one’s country or the Church, and the priestly trumpet sounds in harmony with the prince’s proclamation, the priestly tongue must so restrain itself [Col. 0029A] that it does not appear to involve itself even in the deaths of enemies. So we read of blessed Gregory: when he helped Roman soldiers in defending the City against the Lombards with ecclesiastical money, as though he were their treasurer, and encouraged them with priestly teaching as a standard-bearer of justice, he nevertheless took care to avoid involvement in the deaths of those Lombards. He spared even the enemies themselves, neither making war nor ordering war made except insofar as necessity required for repelling injury or defending city and country.

Hence, when enemies hasten toward the city, he advises pressing them from behind or resisting them face to face. But when they remain at peace and do not harm the Church, he by no means teaches that war should be made upon them, although their hostile wickedness was known [Col. 0029B].

Thus, when he had been accused before the Emperor Maurice, who was wholly hostile to him, of having kept Malchus, bishop and administrator of his patrimony, so long in custody for payment of rents that he died, he wrote to Sabinian, his deacon at Constantinople:

> “There is one thing which you should briefly represent to our most serene lords: if I, their servant, had wished to involve myself even in the death of the Lombards, the Lombard people today would have neither king, nor dukes, nor counts, but would be divided in utter confusion. But because I fear God, I dread to involve myself in the death of any human being. This Bishop Malchus, however, was neither in custody nor under any affliction; but on the day when he pleaded his case and was condemned, without my knowledge he was brought by the notary Boniface into his house, where he dined and was honored by him, and during the night was suddenly found dead” [Col. 0029C].

XXXIII. How cruel it seemed to this most holy teacher that, at a bishop’s command, someone should be punished in such a way as to bring about the cause of death through that very punishment is clear from what he writes, among other things, to John, bishop of Calliopolis:

> “Suspend for two months from the solemn celebration of Mass our brother and fellow bishop Andrew, bishop of Tarentum, because he caused Matricula to be beaten with rods. Although we do not believe that she died eight months afterward as a result, nevertheless, because he caused her to be afflicted in this way contrary to the rule of her profession, let this very disgrace instruct him as to how he may conduct himself henceforth” [Col. 0029D].

XXXIV. Let those bishops hear these things who of their own accord and contrary to justice frequently wage wars, stir up conflicts, and often command even innocent persons to be mutilated and cruelly treated to death; who confuse in one person the office of soldier and priest, and administer at once the dignity of count and pontiff; who threaten swords against enemies who are not acting tyrannically but humbly seek what belongs to peace and favor, and command that they be killed or maimed. Would that they ordered them to be taken alive and guarded themselves against being responsible for their deaths! For if such men, refusing to allow themselves to be captured, were killed by the bishops’ soldiers, they might be covered by some cloak of excuse, however thin, [Col. 0030A] so as not to appear murderers. But now certain bishops tyrannize so greatly that they sometimes expose even innocent and spiritual persons to their soldiers’ swords. We hunger and thirst for this justice: that spiritual judgments and affairs be conducted by spiritual persons, and secular matters by secular persons, lest the boundaries established by the Fathers be disregarded. If such jurisdictions were distinctly ordered in Christ’s Church, the king of Babylon—the prince of darkness and confusion—would be wholly confounded and excluded; he who now glories in abounding, through the wicked mixture and confusion of affairs, in sons and daughters multiplied beyond the number of the sons and daughters of Jerusalem.

XXXV. I pity the daughters of Babylon—those wretched women falsely called religious. If they had either been spiritually wed to Christ [Col. 0030B] by a vow of continence, or had been married in the secular state before taking a vow, they could have been daughters of Jerusalem, or among the sixty queens and eighty concubines who behold King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his espousal. But now, though professing holiness, they are excessively attached to the world; they are rightly called daughters of Babylon and confusion. They must be separated from the daughters of Jerusalem, not merely, like foolish virgins, at the Bridegroom’s final coming, but even now be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that their spirit may be saved. Thus, recently at the Council of Reims, you, Pope Eugenius, ordered concerning such women that they should even be deprived of Christian burial unless they amend their lives in communities according to the Rule [Col. 0030C] of blessed Benedict or of Saint Augustine, renounce private property, and live in common.

Certain bishops are not watchful enough in carrying out this decree. Yet the daughters of Babylon themselves murmur among themselves, saying: “What reason is there that regular observance should now be imposed against our will upon us women, established and maintained in some cloister, yet not bound by the vow of any rule—since we customarily defer the vow of a rule until the weariness of old age?” When I answer them, “Because you are in a monastery and use support assigned to those who live under a rule,” they reply: “Do not likewise the canons of episcopal churches live from support assigned to those who live under a rule? Yet they themselves observe no rule whatever, not even that relaxed rule which they say was proposed or imposed upon them by Louis. Although it commands them to live together in their cloisters and does not allow them to sleep outside their dormitories except for an unavoidable cause, this is not done: rather, each one goes about freely and sleeps wherever he wishes. Why then is forbidden to us women what is tolerated among men consecrated to God, when not even their aforementioned rule permits it to them?”

XXXVI. Thus the wretched daughters of Babylon murmur against the sons of that same Babylon—would that they were so small that they could be seized and dashed against the rock! The successors of Peter, clinging to the Rock, have labored with great concern to restrain such persons—for example, by commanding that neither bishops nor clerics should offend the eyes of those who ought to find in them an example and pattern, whether through excess, indecency, variety of colors, slashing of garments, or a tonsure [Col. 0031A] calculated to attract notice. Rather, by their conduct they should condemn faults and display a love of innocence, as the dignity of the clerical order requires.

A splendid saying: “As the dignity of the clerical order requires!” Lest it be understood feebly, the dignity of the clerical order must be weighed, not by the frivolous judgment of common opinion but according to divine law. For the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Take the Levites from among the children of Israel, and you shall purify them according to this rite: they shall be sprinkled with water of purification, and they shall shave all the hair of their flesh. [Col. 0031B] And when they have washed their garments and have been cleansed, they shall take bulls from the herd,” etc. (Num. VIII, 8).

“He says, ‘They shall shave all the hair of their flesh.’” The hairs of the flesh are thoughts of the old life, as blessed Pope Gregory says: we cut them from the mind in such a way that we are troubled by no grief at their loss. The hairs of the flesh are every superfluity of human corruption. For the Levite is so called because he is “taken up.”

XXXVII. Therefore the Levites must shave all the hairs of the flesh, because one who is taken up for divine service ought to appear before God’s eyes cleansed from every thought of the flesh. Let the mind not produce unlawful thoughts and make the fair appearance of the soul ugly, as though darkened by hairs. Yet, however greatly, as we have said, the virtue of holy conduct [Col. 0031C] may have raised someone, there still grows from the old life something which he must endure. Therefore the Levites’ hairs were commanded to be shaved, not plucked out. For when the hairs are shaved, their roots remain in the flesh and grow again in order to be cut again: superfluous thoughts must indeed be cut away with great diligence, but cannot be wholly eradicated. For the flesh always produces superfluities, which the spirit must always cut back with the blade of watchful concern. But we perceive these matters within ourselves more subtly when we penetrate the heights of contemplation.

Yet no one can attain this perfection of purity or beauty unless he has first shaved from his mind, with the razor of divine love, all worldly possessions. Accordingly our Lord, who came not to abolish [Col. 0031D] the law but to fulfil it, says to the rich young man, so that this law also of the Levites may be fulfilled by those whom he has taken up: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor; and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21). And afterward: “And everyone who has left house or brothers” (ibid., 29), and the rest.

XXXVIII. Moses also proves in Deuteronomy that this is indeed the shaving of the Levites, when in the blessings of Levi he says: “He who said to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you’; and to his brothers, ‘I do not recognize them’; and they did not know their own children. These have kept your word and preserved your covenant; they have kept your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel” (Deut. XXXIII, 9). Moses himself shows here, I say, that the sons of Levi ought spiritually to be shaved, when he immediately adds there: “Placing incense in your wrath, and a burnt offering upon your altar” (ibid.).

And here, when he had said, “Let them be sprinkled with water of purification, and let them shave all the hair of their flesh” (Num. VIII, 7), he immediately adds: “And when they have washed their garments and been cleansed, they shall take a bull from the herd, and its libation, fine flour mingled with oil. But you shall take another bull from the herd for sin; and you shall bring the Levites before the tabernacle of the covenant, having summoned the whole multitude of the children of Israel. And when the Levites stand before the Lord, the children of Israel shall lay their hands upon them, and Aaron shall offer the Levites as an offering before the Lord from the children of Israel, that they may serve in his ministry. The Levites likewise shall lay their hands [Col. 0032B] upon the heads of the bulls,” etc. (ibid. 7, 12).

What does it mean that Levites sprinkled with water and shaved, cleansed after their garments have been washed, touch before the Lord one bull for a burnt offering and another for sin, laying their hands upon their heads, after—or at the same time as—the children of Israel have laid their hands upon the Levites? What, I say, does this mean, except that men of a spiritual vocation, cleansed from their own vices and shorn of all worldly possessions and concerns, should devote themselves solely to that for which they were taken up: namely, to place incense in the Lord’s wrath and a burnt offering upon his altar—that is, to intercede for the sins of the peoples? For the children of Israel lay their hands upon the Levites, who receive tithes from them; and the Levites lay their hands upon the heads of the bulls, of which, he says, “you shall make one [Col. 0032C] for sin and the other a burnt offering,” when men of the spiritual order take upon themselves the sins of secular persons, from whose alms they live, and strive, by sacrifices of prayers offered before the Lord, to press them down and overcome them unto their remission or pardon.

Because this must be done with great earnestness, its accomplishment is recalled at the end of the chapter by a threefold repetition: “And Moses and Aaron and the whole multitude of the children of Israel did concerning the Levites what the Lord had commanded Moses” (ibid., 20). Then: “And they were purified and washed their garments,” etc. (ibid., 21). And a third time: “As the Lord had commanded Moses concerning the Levites, so it was done” (ibid., 22).

[Col. 0032D] XXXIX. And indeed it was done concerning the Levites as the Lord commanded: first, those ministers of the old and carnal sacrifices were purified and shaved literally; then, under the new lawgiver who bestowed blessing, the sons of Aaron the true priest—that is, Christ’s apostles, the first and chief ministers of the new sacrifice—were purified and shaved spiritually. But just as, in the Babylonian captivity, when wicked presbyters judged wickedly, iniquity came forth from the elders who seemed to rule the people, because the command given through Moses concerning the purification of the Levites was neglected; so now, as though the king of Babylon tyrannized and God’s people were captive, iniquity comes forth from the elders who seemed to rule the people, because the purification and shaving of the Levites established through Christ has been neglected—except for a very few Levites. Following the example of the three youths and the prophet Daniel, these make themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven and are accounted worthy and fit to sing a hymn to God, behold visions of the heavenly kingdom, and judge shameless elders.

Judgment against presbyters of this kind, who behaved shamefully with the daughters of Israel and lay in wait also for daughters of Judah resembling Susanna, began to be pursued more rigorously from the time when divine offices and ecclesiastical benefices were forbidden them, as though Daniel presided in every chaste and just bishop of the apostolic see. But since the whole Babylonian captivity has not yet been ended nor the return to Jerusalem completed, we still sit weeping by the rivers of Babylon and, awaiting greater remedies for this confusion, sing with Jeremiah and Haggai: “To you is fitting a hymn, O God, in Zion, and to you shall a vow be paid in Jerusalem.”

LX. What greater remedies do we await and seek? Namely these: that, just as at the return of God’s people from captivity the singers, priests, and Nethinim were most carefully registered by their tribes and families, and those were excluded from the priesthood who could not show their genealogy from the records, so it may now be done, in answer to Jeremiah’s prayer: “Turn us, O God, to yourself, and we shall be turned; renew our days as from the beginning” (Lam. V, 21).

For if we look back to the beginning of the Church’s birth, we shall find bright and serene days in ecclesiastical orders: so that some, as bishops in place of the apostles; others, as priests in place of the seventy disciples; and others, as deacons with Stephen, rightly followed the leaders and princes of their vocation, as though carefully preserving the line of their genealogy. Whoever departed from this line, like Judas the traitor and most wicked trader, Nicholas the fornicator, or Simon the perverse merchant, was immediately exposed and cast out from the sacerdotal and Levitical order. The Levitical order was kept in its purity under a definite rule or a synodal law requiring life together, following the example of Christ’s disciples. By first dwelling together, they prefigured the form of cenobitic life, worshipping God with one heart and one soul; afterward, scattered through the several regions of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, [Col. 0033D] Asia, and Bithynia, they lived holy lives in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, holding fast the word of life and shining like lights in this world.

By this manner of life of the scattered holy brethren is fashioned the life of God’s ministers: those who hold fast the word of life and who, by divine ordination, are scattered in the midst of a crooked nation in order to shine among them as lights in this world.
