XLI. Read in the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke, the primitive rule of cenobitic life: “The multitude of believers,” he says, “was of one heart and one soul in God,” etc. (Acts IV, 32). Read the epistles sent by the prince of the apostles to brethren living in dispersion, as though they were the first decretal rules which all councils framing decrees of the saints must keep before their eyes, so that such brethren may be trained in every holiness. Thus the apostle Peter says: “I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly desires, which war against the soul, maintaining good conduct among the Gentiles,” etc. (I Pet. II, 11–12).

Likewise: “I exhort the elders, I who am a fellow elder and witness of Christ’s sufferings, and also a sharer in the glory to be revealed: feed the flock of God which is among you, exercising oversight not under compulsion but freely according to God; not for the sake of shameful gain but willingly; not lording it over the clergy, but becoming from the heart an example to the flock. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you shall receive the unfading crown of glory” (I Pet. V, 1–4).

[Col. 0034B] Likewise: “Applying all care, supply in your faith virtue; and in virtue knowledge; and in knowledge self-restraint; and in self-restraint patience; and in patience godliness; and in godliness love of the brethren; and in love of the brethren charity. For if these things are present in you and abound, they will not leave you idle or fruitless in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever does not have these things is blind and groping with his hand, having fallen into forgetfulness of the cleansing of his former sins. Therefore, brethren, strive all the more to make your calling and election sure through good works. For by doing these things you shall never sin; for thus an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ shall be abundantly supplied to you” (II Pet. I, 5–11).

Likewise: “As each has received grace, administer it to one another as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. If anyone speaks, let it be as the utterances of God; if anyone ministers, let it be according to the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be honored through Jesus Christ our Lord” (I Pet. IV, 10–11).

XLII. Although these apostolic sayings and exhortations concern the whole Church, yet because they were sent to brethren living in dispersion, as strangers and pilgrims dwelling among the nations, they especially instruct those whose purpose and office are to live piously among the impious and to instruct them. [Col. 0034D] Those who depart from this purpose, following the way of Balaam of Bosor, who loved the wages of iniquity but received rebuke for his madness from the dumb beast of burden, are, as blessed Peter says, springs without water and mists driven by storms, for whom the blackness of darkness is reserved. Speaking proud words of vanity, they entice through the fleshly desires of licentiousness those who have only just escaped, those living in error; promising them freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption. “For by whom a person is overcome, by him he is also enslaved” (II Pet. II, 19), and the rest.

Certainly, through these apostolic teachings we are warned not only whom to follow but whom to avoid, lest, led astray by the error of fools, we fall from our own steadfastness, whether we live in community or in dispersion. For we have firm rules for both modes of life: first and principally in the acts and sayings of the apostles; then in the examples and rules of the Fathers who imitated them. Indeed, all who rightly established rules of cenobitic life made the account in Acts of the Apostles concerning the multitude of believers who had one heart and one soul in God and called nothing their own the hinge of their teaching—for example Basil, Augustine, and Benedict, in whose Rules the life of a community is rightly ordered.

XLIII. But the Roman pontiffs and other orthodox Fathers, who instructed clerics living in dispersion by decretal or synodal ordinances, set forth the apostolic epistles as the primitive and principal rules and laws of the city of Jerusalem at the beginning of its joy, and taught nothing discordant from them. For Pope Urban, martyr and the sixteenth from blessed Peter, declares in his decrees that clerical communities maintained a common life according to the Acts of the Apostles from the beginning of the Church’s birth. Pope Innocent II, of blessed memory, also recalls this in one of his letters, whose rescript follows:

“INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother CONRAD, Archbishop of Salzburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Divine Scripture teaches us much concerning the dignity and excellence of the life of canons, and much could be said to show that the life of canons is the apostolic life. For the apostles, despising all things, lived this life with the Lord; and after the Ascension, living this life with the multitude of believers, whose soul was one and whose heart was one, they left it to posterity to be maintained by their example. Urban, martyr and pontiff, took care to recall this in his decrees for the instruction of the faithful, saying: ‘We know that you are not ignorant that the common life has hitherto flourished among good Christians and still flourishes by the grace of God, especially among those chosen for the Lord’s portion—that is, clerics—as is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers was of one heart [Col. 0035D] and one soul” (Acts IV, 32).’

“Saint Jerome, in his letters, gave form to this life, ordered by the rules of blessed Augustine. Armed, therefore, with their authorities and those of others, we judge that, when the Spirit of the Lord inspires and sustains it, to observe the canonical life is of no less merit than to preserve the monastic profession through perseverance in that same Spirit. Therefore we recall that it was established by the decrees of our predecessors that no one of canonical profession, after he has placed upon his head the honor in God’s stead, should dare, from any impulse of levity or under pretext of a stricter religious life, to depart from the cloister without the permission of the prelate and community.

“Following in their footsteps, by apostolic authority we forbid the fulfillment of what certain brethren in the cloister of Berchtesgaden have sought, in vain presumption, to undertake for the fortification of their order. We command them to render to God what they have vowed and, with the Lord’s help, diligently to observe the Rule of blessed Augustine which they have professed. If you should perhaps find them lax and lacking fervor in its observance, we exhort your brotherhood, according to the wisdom given you by God, strictly to admonish them—as pertains to you—to preserve their profession and order and obey the commands of the Rule. Given at the Lateran, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April [16 March].”

XLIV. Therefore, since we recognize, instructed by apostolic writings and formed by divine institution, a twofold manner of life for clerics—either living in community in common, or living under discipline in dispersion—and observing either cenobitic rules or synodal rules, which we call canons: who but the king of Babylon and confusion devised a third, excessively confused and Babylonian class of clerics, mingling secular and clerical life alike into a kind of intermediate state? They neither devote themselves in community to singing hymns with the fittingness of “To you is fitting a hymn, O God, in Zion,” nor, in dispersion, wage ordered warfare against fleshly desires which war against the soul.

The holy Fathers before us liken these men to hippocentaurs, who are neither horses nor men, a “mixed race and a two-formed offspring,” as the poet says, because they are recognized as followers of no definite religious order.

> [Note: [Col. 0035] Perhaps “the poet.” VIRGIL, *Aeneid* VI, 25, has this verse.]

[Col. 0036C] Some of these are unbound and wandering. As Isidore says, they are embraced only by a shameful and vagrant life, because they are constrained under the Lord’s yoke by no bond of a prudent institution. They are as if free, having freedom as a cloak for military service—not as servants of God but as servants of Mammon. For the sake of gain or luxury they change places; or, worse, occupy several places contrary to synodal prohibitions. These command that no wandering cleric may serve at the altar or live from the altar before canonical stability has been confirmed by letters of recommendation and his own confession. They also forbid one person to be instituted in two or more churches: for example, to be a canon in a cathedral see and a parish priest in the countryside; or to occupy an intermediate position between parish priest and bishop, such as was recently both described and proscribed at the Council of Reims by apostolic decree through you, Pope Eugenius. For certain persons fraudulently grant the title of parish priest to their hired substitutes, while they themselves establish themselves under bishops and above such parish priests, occupying an intermediate position so that they may devour the flock rather than care for it, and lay it waste rather than feed it.

XLV. To attack or overcome these men is exceedingly laborious, because, seeking their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ, they hold the citadel in Jerusalem and, as is read in the books of Maccabees, “became a great devil in Israel.” They are a great wound to chastity and leaders of the remaining foreigners in harassing the holy city, so much so that Jerusalem is deserted by its citizens through the oppression of such men and inhabited by Gentiles, according to the words: “O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem a watch-post for fruit. They have given the corpses of your servants to the beasts of the earth,” etc. (Ps. LXXVIII [79], 1–2).

But one day vengeance for the blood of God’s servants shall be made known among the nations, and the groaning of prisoners in chains shall enter into God’s presence. For just as, after Simon the high priest had been exalted, those in the citadel were first shut in and then expelled, so, God consenting, it shall happen to these men. For this is written: “Those who were in the citadel of Jerusalem were forbidden to go out into the country or to enter it, to buy or sell; and they suffered extreme hunger, and many of them perished of famine. They cried to Simon to receive pledges of peace, and he granted it to them, expelled them from there, and cleansed the citadel from its pollutions. And they entered it on the twenty-third day of the second month, in the one hundred and seventy-first year, with praise, palm branches, harps, cymbals, lyres, hymns, and songs, because the great enemy had been crushed out of Israel. And he established that these days should be celebrated every year with rejoicing. He fortified the mountain of the temple beside the citadel, and he himself lived there with those who were with him” (I Macc. XIII, 49, 53).

XLVI. Is not this deed like the fact that irregular canons, although stationed in the citadel, are forbidden by the decrees of Roman pontiffs to buy and sell churches [Col. 0037C] in the country? Because of this they hunger greatly—not like those blessed persons who hunger and thirst for justice, but like those who burn with avarice. The acceptable time will come, will come, when they are cast out from the citadel, first when each cathedral church has been cleansed in particular; then universally at the final winnowing. Nor will the defenses or missiles by which they have long sheltered in the citadel avail them.

For in their rule, not ordered according to the apostles, they have certain reasonable chapters, or very strong defenses, by which their manner of life is defended as though it were canonical. And truly, if they lived according to the materials assembled there from treatises of the holy Fathers, their life could rightly be called—and would be—canonical. But the small leaven mixed in there corrupts the entire mass: namely, that which was introduced not from the writings of the Fathers but from elsewhere, and which destroys the holy sanctions set down there. It is as if, after first setting out the king’s lawful edicts, they send an embassy after him with other edicts, indeed contrary ones, saying: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke XIX, 14).

For while the earlier edicts forbid them private ownership and private dwellings, those later and wholly apocryphal provisions allow such things. This is not with the discernment by which blessed Gregory permits adequate support outside communities to clerics who remain outside sacred orders and have entered lawful marriages, while they diligently attend to psalmody and live under the Christian rule that forbids unlawful things; rather, it is with the confusion by which King Antiochus wrote to his kingdom that all the people should be one. Therefore among them there is no distinction between sacred and profane, and little distinction between priests and laity—unless perhaps they are distinguished by this: clerics deviate more than laypeople, apart from a very few among them sufficiently sensible to understand and grieve that they observe not even that confused rule except in its basest part. For they neglect the things there taught by the saints as most holy, and retain only what some unknown person permits concerning private property and private dwellings.

XLVII. Must this rule, then, either be observed so that it may be pure and consonant with the saints, or, if it cannot be observed, wholly removed? For from it comes a confusion like that which once arose from the already mentioned decree of King Antiochus, by which he wrote to his whole kingdom that all the people should be one. If they retained only their own possessions, as they are there permitted to do—and no one is compelled to surrender these unless bound by a vow or purpose of a stricter life—this might in some fashion be tolerated, provided that they held the property of the Church, as the sacred canons command, not as private possessions but in common. Nor should they, in the manner of the sons of Eli (I Sam. II), divide raw among themselves, to be carried to private lodgings frequented by little women, the flesh that ought to be cooked in the common cauldron at Shiloh and eaten within the holy precincts.

Certainly, to cut away private property entirely from such communities and allow them no private residences at all would be to lay the axe to the root of the evil tree, rather than merely cut off its branches. In this cutting-off of branches those labor in vain who, while allowing private property and private residences, attempt to remove superfluity and the blemish of secular pomp from garments, and vices from conduct. For as long as the root of property and the practice of private dwellings are not uprooted, however much labor any diligent cultivator may expend in cutting off the useless branches of the Lord’s vineyard, other equally useless branches will sprout from the vicious root. For if, even in cloisters canonically ordered without private property, vices and even crimes can scarcely be cut away by the vigilant care of superiors, how much less can this be done where the absence of fraternal witness, the secrecy of a private dwelling, the slipperiness of youth, leisure joined with abundance, the attentiveness of cooks, and the service of a household all concur?

XLVIII. But such persons object to us that neither are the vicious wholly absent among us, nor the virtuous among them. Would that, just as perhaps one vicious person among us is overborne by the multitude of the diligent, so that he either changes within or departs outside, among them some diligent person were not overborne by the multitude of vicious persons—or even driven out by the fury of persecution! For who among them, knowing the vices of others and attacking them with brotherly zeal, avoiding and rebuking them, could live with such men securely—let alone have peace with them? “You came in as a stranger,” they say; “did you come in to judge?” (Gen. XIX, 9). They use the greatest violence against him, so that for anyone wishing to save his soul nothing remains except to flee from the midst of such persons, not to remain anywhere in the whole surrounding region, but to save himself upon the mountain of a higher profession.

Yet I see one means of conquering this city of letters, accessible to every true Caleb and every commander of the Lord’s hosts appointed according to God’s heart, by which such *Cariatharbei* may gradually be conquered and exterminated without the land being reduced to desolation. It is this: that an edict issue from the throne of God, who desires to make all things new, and from those whose office on earth is to represent Christ; or that any bishop divinely inspired should firmly resolve in his heart that, when one of those men dies, he will not appoint another like him in his place. Instead, retaining the prebends and ecclesiastical benefices in his own hand, he should meanwhile distribute them to the poor as alms until enough prebends have been liberated to support six, ten, or however many canons living under a rule in some nearby chapel. As those evil vinedressers die off one by one, he may then introduce these lawful heirs into the Lord’s inheritance.

Let the action already taken in one church of Saint Maurice in Burgundy suffice as an example. Canons having been introduced there, some of the former clerics still survive, apparently receiving their stipends outside [Col. 0039C] the community. These Burgundians, however, were not sinners beyond all other clerics living secular lives. Rather, divine judgment set an example in them and showed those desiring to imitate it how this should be done everywhere in comparable cases and can be done without difficulty.

XLIX. How much I am moved to say against arrangements of this kind and Babylonian confusions! Once these are removed, “To you is fitting a hymn, O God, in Zion”—a hymn now blasphemed by the harlot Babylon, drunk, as the Apocalypse says, “with the blood of the saints” (Rev. XVII, 6). For, transforming the Lord’s grace into licentiousness, she revels in banquets richly supplied with dishes and cups from the substance of the saints, while shameless women are mingled among the banqueters.

[Col. 0039D] They scarcely restrain their hands from the sacrilege by which Belshazzar, king of Babylon, drinking and making his concubines drink from sacred vessels, incurred God’s wrath—a wrath made known to him by the fingers of a hand writing on the wall, as holy Daniel interpreted it (Dan. V). And would that something of this kind might be written against these banqueters, by which God’s wrath might be made known to them! Perhaps he is more angered because they eat and drink unworthily the sacrament of his body and blood than he would be if, following King Belshazzar’s example, they drank wine from sacred vessels and abstained from the sacrament of the altar, lest they cause scandal among God’s people.

For when wholly unlettered laypeople see clerics of this sort boldly ministering at the altar—while, as they minister, or joyfully sing in melodious voices hymns from the songs of Zion, [Col. 0040A] their women stand beside them like wretched daughters of Babylon—then, with iniquity thus having gone forth from the clerics and elders who seem to rule the people, we behold a pitiable spectacle: in your midst, Jerusalem, a people almost wholly Babylonian.

L. How then is praise fitting for you, O God, in Zion, when its people are a people of Gomorrah or Babylon, without teachers and guides of righteousness? For these, “who seemed to rule the people” (Dan. XIII), have almost “all turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII, 3; Rom. III, 12). Even those to whom, like Cherubim, the flaming sword was given to guard the way of the tree of life (Gen. III), though they ought [Col. 0040B] openly to bar manifest criminals and forbid them access to the Lord’s table until adequate satisfaction has been made, indiscriminately offer the fruit of the tree of life to all who approach, even though they are manifest criminals—the fruit which they ought to deny to such persons. “Therefore among” us “there are many weak and sickly, and many sleep” (I Cor. XI, 30). And because this Babylonian confusion concerns no one more than idle and negligent rulers, therefore, by God’s just judgment, contention has been poured out upon both secular and spiritual princes, and has made them wander in a trackless place and not in the way: while spiritual persons delight to entangle themselves in secular business, and secular persons dare to meddle in spiritual causes. This confusion indeed makes the body of the whole Church languish, and causes its members to dissent [Col. 0040C] against one another: as though the eyes should say to the feet and hands, “We have no need of your works”; and the hands or feet to the eyes, “You are not necessary to us.” For spiritual persons, who, like eyes, ought to direct hands for working or fighting and feet for walking, are held captive under Babylonian kings and princes in such a way that it is said to them: “Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion” (Ps. XIII, 6, 3). “Sing us a hymn,” they say, “not against us, by restraining our evil desires, but by speaking things pleasing to us. Yet a hymn from the songs of Zion, because we do not wish to seem princes of Babylon, but of Zion. We wish to hear heavenly teaching—but in order to accomplish, not obstruct, our own will.”

[Col. 0040D] LI. Such was the case when King Herod sent for and assembled all the chief priests and scribes of the people, and inquired of them where Christ was to be born; as though he said, “Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion.” And would that they had been such men as to answer his malicious inquiry thus: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” (Ibid., 4.) How shall we betray heavenly mysteries to you, a foreigner who wishes to kill the true King? Likewise his other son, Herod, heir to his father’s impiety, also wished to hear a hymn from the songs of Zion from the mouth of John the Baptist, whom he feared and gladly heard, until John began to sing things troublesome to him, saying: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark VI, 18). John was indeed singing a hymn from [Col. 0041A] the songs of Zion, not one that Herod or Herodias wished or found welcome. Similarly, that king and high priest of Zion himself wished to hear a hymn from the songs of Zion, having long desired to see Jesus and rejoicing that Pilate had sent him to him. But Jesus, judging it unworthy to cast pearls before swine, kept silent before him and performed no sign; he preferred to be despised rather than honored by him and his soldiers. For then it was his time to be silent. But after he rose from the dead, wherever it was time to speak, speaking himself in his disciples, he did not keep the truth silent before kings and governors, giving his own a mouth and wisdom which all their adversaries could not resist. As they lawfully sang, and sounded like sacred trumpets around Jericho, the walls of the accursed city fell, with Joshua, the true leader, bringing them into a land flowing with milk and honey; by whose public edict cursed was declared to be whoever rebuilt Jericho.

LII. Yet behold: certain persons dare to rebuild the accursed city which persecutes the messengers of Joshua—indeed, the apostles of Jesus Christ—although the house of Rahab alone, namely the holy Church, was excepted from the destruction of that city. As worldly structures fall, this house itself grows, both in the building up of morals and of walls, into a holy temple in the Lord: “In whom,” as the Apostle says, “every building, being joined together, grows” (Eph. II, 21); it does not diminish. The eyes of the faithful are fed by the spectacle of this fact throughout the world, and certainly [Col. 0041C] more clearly in the city of Rome, when imperial palaces and other wondrous buildings of the rich there present the ruin of Jericho, while ecclesiastical buildings, increasing day by day and glittering with gilded images, plainly show by the daily increase and adornment alike of morals and walls, as it were, the saved house of Rahab—namely, the holy Church, made firm by the faith and name of Peter. Thus in our days the Lateran church, the church of Holy Cross, and the church of Saint Mary the New have increased and advanced both in religious life and in the outward enlargement of their walls. The house of the blessed apostle Paul, restored through Gregory VII, now shines in monastic religious life, in which we also see the monastery of the Holy Four Crowned Martyrs and that of Saint Anastasius [Col. 0041D] flourishing, together with other churches and monasteries religiously ordered in the city of Rome. Therefore we grieve not without cause that, even now, in the house of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we see the abomination of desolation standing—fortifications and other instruments of war having even been placed on the height of the sanctuary above the body of blessed Peter. Although we do not dare to judge this evil, nevertheless we judge without doubt that it is from evil: namely, from the evil of those who, by the malice of their rebellion, compel such things to be done.

LIII. Here I am compelled to recall a certain judgment of blessed Augustine, who says among other things in the book *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*: “Why then was the sentence given that he who takes the sword shall perish by the sword? Unless because no one, except an avenger, is permitted to kill anyone with the sword. But to the apostle Peter was permitted only so much as would create fear, not as would kill. Having heard this, he learned not to strike again.” The same writer, to Publiola: “Those who are repelled by some terror from doing evil may perhaps themselves also receive some benefit.” Since Saint Augustine says these things concerning the evangelical sense and apostolic example, we believe lawful those practices which, as we have heard, are customary in the neighborhood of the Saracens: arms are collected in the high towers of churches or monasteries, and barbarians are frightened by their display, even through spiritual men, lest they invade holy places—places which they would boldly invade if they knew them to be furnished with no defensive equipment. I do not think this should be rashly condemned, because it is plainly done under the compulsion of extreme [Col. 0042B] necessity: thus at times clerics or monks also appear there on the walls in armor or bearing shields, not with an intention of injuring anyone, but of frightening enemies and in whatever way repelling them from attacking holy places. When they sometimes cast darts or stones down from above to drive the enemy farther away, an irregular action indeed occurs; yet, in order to avoid a greater danger and inspire terror in barbarians, it is rightly to be tolerated, provided every intention of killing anyone is utterly absent. This is not lawful for men of a spiritual vocation to do: they ought to prefer being killed to killing, however much they may by the display of arms or armed men keep enemies from harming them.

LIV. But if such armament is provided by duly constituted authority, nothing disorderly is done in this. [Col. 0042C] For the apostle Paul also, when he had foreseen plots against himself, obtained through the tribune of Roman authority the protection of arms. If enemies thirsting for his death and blood had fallen upon that protection, he would not have been guilty of homicide; rather, the vengeance due to them would have befallen them, and their blood would have been upon their own heads, since the guilt of their death would be imputed not to others but to themselves. The protection of arms which was then granted by legitimate authority to one ecclesiastical person is now recognized as granted to the universal Church: namely, that she may have, from the kingdom conferred upon her, armed ministers against her enemies. If, while these defend the Church or accompany a bishop for his protection and assist what is right, killings happen through them, [Col. 0042D] the bishop is no more a murderer than the apostle Paul would have been a murderer if, during his escort, one of his enemies had fallen slain. But if a bishop misuses his ministers for evil business, he is certainly made a murderer if anyone is killed by them in such service; just as kings, dukes, and counts become murderers if, without judgment and justice, they kill men or cause them to be killed. For the same reason, certain ecclesiastical towers among Christians are fortified with arms and defensive works; if enemies of the Church are harmed through these, their blood will be upon themselves, because their own iniquity alone and eagerness to do harm drive them to such acts.

[Col. 0043A] LV. The case is different when constituted authority, ignorant or forgetful of its ordination, persecutes the Church; and different when she is oppressed outwardly by pagans or inwardly by domestic enemies. Legitimate authority must either be directed to obedience to its ordination by the word of teaching, or, if it cannot be directed, broken by the word of excommunication—while the unity of the Church is preserved, even as a kingdom disobedient to God is divided, as happened in Saul, in whose kingdom faithful David succeeded. But external assaults from outsiders, because they cannot be removed by the word of teaching—for the Church has no power to judge those outside—must rightly be repelled by human forces through arms, and at the same time by divine forces through prayers, according to both civil and imperial law. When these two laws [Col. 0043B] agree in defense of the Church, with princes rightly ordered and citizens well at peace, the Church easily withstands external attacks, whether of pagans or excommunicated persons. Finally, when one of the two laws is violated, the Church is in great danger, unless either imperial law, defending her, restrains the rioting citizens, or the unanimity of the citizens restrains tyrannizing princes, as ecclesiastical histories relate has often happened. Yet greater dangers threaten the Church when internal wars harass her, and princes and citizens alike join together against the Lord and against his Christ. In such a danger the sea must be struck as it were with Moses’ rod, that is, the pastoral rod, so that it may be divided into divisions, struck and rent by the word of teaching. Thus the apostle Paul, hard pressed by the unanimity of his persecutors, by the word of teaching caused Pharisees and Sadducees to disagree with one another, so that he might cross without danger as through a divided sea; namely, with the Pharisees acting for him against the Sadducees, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles.

LVI. We remember that something similar has happened more than once in the city of Rome, when the Roman people were divided against themselves, with one party of the faithful restraining the unfaithful, while priestly assistance cooperated. But if the Church pursued these rebels more orderly, as an army arrayed in battle, Jericho or Babylon would not be rebuilt by them—as is apparent at Rome in the Capitoline building, once destroyed and now rebuilt against the house [Col. 0043D] of God, against the house of Rahab. Rather, the wisdom and strength of the Church would shine in the conflict: wisdom in clerics teaching rightly, and strength in soldiers obedient to their teaching, expending their powers for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good, and destroying every height that raises itself against the knowledge of God. This safeguard, however, would be maintained in the Lord’s camp: a cleric, even a bishop, who did not teach rightly would be deposed and another would receive his bishopric; and a soldier, even a prince, disobedient to sound teaching and unwilling to yield, like Saul, would be struck by the dart of anathema, and another substituted for him, like David. Finally, in every war and discord among soldiers or citizens, either one party is just and the other unjust, or both are found unjust. [Col. 0044A] Priestly teaching ought to disclose the truth of this matter, and no wars should be undertaken without its judgment. Justice having thus been made manifest, the just party should be encouraged by priestly trumpets and strengthened, before and for battle, even by communion in the Lord’s body; for this bread strengthens the heart of man when someone prepares himself for combat in defense of justice or of the Church. The unjust party, resisting it and refusing to assent to a covenant of just peace, ought to be anathematized and humiliated even by the denial of Christian burial.

LVII. But now, when city fights against city, kingdom against kingdom, and prince against prince without just wars being undertaken, the body [Col. 0044B] of the Lord is given to both parties without delay or examination of the causes, as though Christ were divided and could be present in parties so divided and opposed. Surely he ought to be denied either to one party or to both, and should in no way be given to anyone openly fighting against justice, lest perhaps, through the carelessness of priests, when he is thus handed over into the hands of evident sinners, righteous wrath be stirred against priests who again hand him over with Judas. In such great thirst and hunger for so great a justice, hunger itself compels us to lick even a few small crumbs.

LVIII. Therefore I relate a just and honorable deed which laudably occurred in the land of Hungary, a barbarous land scarcely subject, even in name, to the dominion of Christian princes. When the king of that land, more than a year ago, was preparing for war against the king of the Greeks, he held counsel with the bishops [Col. 0044C] of that land before the campaign. Like learned men, they examined the cause of the war with the greatest care and found that the treaty of peace had first been violated on the Hungarian side. They remembered the prophecy saying: “Shall he who breaks a covenant escape?” (Ezek. XVII, 15). Instructed by this prophecy, they prophesied that, if the king fought contrary to the right of the treaty and the covenant of peace, he would by no means triumph and would lack God’s aid. On hearing this, the king, though fierce and barbarous, nevertheless called off the campaign and repaired, on his own side, the covenant that had been broken.

LIX. How much more, then, would the violence of princes or captains who rage against one another in the Roman Empire and lay many churches waste be restrained in the Church of the saints, if the judgment of bishops who know how to reject evil and choose good agreed as one. Indeed, so that there might not be, nor could there be, schism among them, one is set over all, to whom it was said: “Strengthen your brethren” (Luke XXII, 32). If he strengthened any judgment of bishops consonant with the justice of the kingdom of God, even though contrary to the kings of this world, there would be no king in the Church who would dare—or, if he dared, be able—to overturn it. Moreover, if he who possesses the power and authority to strengthen the rest became the leader in every just judgment communicated to bishops by letters, who could overturn it? For he is established like another Jeremiah not only over churches but also over kingdoms, to pluck up [Col. 0045A] and destroy, to ruin and overthrow, to build and plant. Thus we find profane and simoniacal kings uprooted by apostolic authority, with the grace of God cooperating—a grace which often confounds the strong through the weak things of this world, choosing the low-born and despised in order to instruct and destroy the great. I think that the apostle Paul intended this very point when he wrote to the disciples: “If anyone does not obey our word by this letter, note that person; yet do not consider him an enemy, but correct him as a brother” (II Thess. III, 14). “If anyone,” he says, “does not obey”—excluding neither bishop nor prince nor rich man, so that he should not be corrected and instructed even by the least brethren: first, in a spirit of gentleness, to humbly resume the obedience neglected or interrupted. [Col. 0045B] If he refused to resume it, Paul testified that he stood ready to punish every disobedience: “Every,” he says, even that “of bishops and princes, when,” he says, “your obedience has first been fulfilled” (II Cor. X, 6)—understand: in fraternal admonition.

LX. For those who sin openly must first be admonished, even kings, and bishops still more, so that by the example of King David they may correct their evil deeds, rather than, by the example of Herod, slaughter their admonishers. He is, as it were, a beheader of the herald who, refusing to yield to warnings, blocks the path of the voice crying in the wilderness. And would that only kings like Herod did this, and not also pontiffs imitating Caiaphas! For the Scriptures must be fulfilled, in which this was foretold [Col. 0045C] and prefigured: not only the beast but also the false prophet opposes the truth. Hence every Pharaoh has his magicians, every Nebuchadnezzar his diviners, every Herod scribes who agree with him, from whom he asks how or where he may persecute Christ, or how he may find an opportunity to behead his heralds, that he may take away their voice even if he does not kill them bodily. This is a kind of beheading and killing of Christ’s witnesses.

LXI. In Daniel four beasts, greedy for human blood, are seen fighting among themselves; by these four were signified the bloodthirsty kingdoms of Babylon, Persia or Media, Macedonia or Greece, and Rome. When these beasts have altogether been removed, the Son of Man is seen in a cloud, to whom kingdom and honor are given; for to Christ is given the rule and honor of the kingdom, most especially in human form, in which he has also been given authority to judge because he is the Son of Man. Therefore the ministers of his kingdom delight in human gentleness rather than beastly cruelty, in accordance with the exhortations not of false prophets but of holy prophets, to whom holy priesthood has been given in Christ’s kingdom—a priesthood so unstained by and remote from the shedding of blood that sacred canons exclude from priestly ministry one who, while ever serving as a soldier, has killed a man, however justly, or who has cooperated, either by urging or by serving, in a judgment of blood with a judge who killed, however justly. Accordingly Pope Innocent, writing to Felix, bishop [Col. 0046A] of Nocera, says: “The classes have been specified from which persons cannot come to the clergy: namely, if a believer has served as a soldier; if a believer has conducted lawsuits, that is, has brought suits; if a believer has held an administrative office.” Sacred canons also instruct those already advanced in priesthood in precautions concerning such matters. For in the decretal letter of Pope Nicholas to King Charles we read: “What you have put forward is clearly very reprehensible: you say that the greater part of the men, bishops, are detained day and night with your other faithful men against maritime pirates, and that for this reason bishops are prevented from coming. Yet soldiers of Christ ought to serve God, and soldiers of the world the world, as it is written: ‘No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs’ (II Tim. [Col. 0046B] II, 4). If soldiers of the world devote themselves to military service, what concern is it of bishops and soldiers of Christ except that they should give themselves to prayers?” From the Council of Lleida, chapter 1: “Concerning clerics placed under the necessity of siege, it is decreed that those who minister at the altar, deliver Christ’s body and blood, or handle vessels assigned to sacred office, must abstain from every human blood, even that of an enemy. If they kill, they shall be deprived of office and communion; after they have been received back following two years’ penance, promotion shall be denied them.” From the Council of Toledo, chapter 44: “Clerics who are found to have willingly taken arms in any sedition, or to be taking them, shall lose their rank of order and be confined to a monastery for penance.” From the Council of Toledo, chapter 7: “Those by whom the sacraments [Col. 0046C] of the Lord are to be handled may not conduct a judgment of blood. Therefore the excesses of such persons must be sternly forbidden, lest, moved by impulses of indiscreet presumption, they dare either to conduct by their own sentence a matter punishable by death, or personally inflict any mutilation of limbs upon any persons, or order it personally to be inflicted. If anyone forgetful of these commands does such a thing to servants of his church or to any persons whatsoever, he shall be deprived both of the honor and place of his conferred order, and bound in the prison-house of perpetual condemnation. Nevertheless, communion is not to be denied to him when he departs this life, because of the mercy of the Lord, who does not will the death of the sinner but that he [Col. 0046D] be converted and live.” From the Council of Toledo, chapter 30: “Princes often entrust their affairs concerning persons liable for offenses against majesty to priests. Since priests have been chosen by Christ for the ministry of salvation, they should consent to act as judges with kings only where remission of punishment is promised under oath, not where a sentence of peril is prepared. Therefore, if any priest, contrary to this common resolution, acts as an examiner in cases involving the perils of others, let him be guilty of shed blood before Christ and before the Church, and let him lose his own rank.”

LXII. Warned by such saving precepts and instructed by apostolic teaching, we desire bishops and the other ministers of the altar to remain removed from judgments and business involving blood, except insofar as the office of teaching [Col. 0047A] and commanding requires: that is, so that secular judges may be instructed and bound by spiritual persons who judge all things, to judge rightly and exercise their authority for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. But that a judgment of blood should issue from the lips of a priest, which preserve knowledge, and from the mouth from which the law of the Lord is required—this is exceedingly reprehensible. Accordingly, the imperial powers and dignities themselves granted to churches—for example, duchies, counties, and the like—ought to be administered by lay persons bound to those same churches by fealty, so that neither lips nor hands by which Christ’s body must be consecrated may be defiled by judgment or business involving blood, however just the shedding of that blood may be. For this purpose, just as in the kingdom of Antichrist the beast and the false prophet cooperate in evil, so that the mystery of iniquity may be concealed beneath a certain appearance of just order—while Pilate the beast condemns to death none other than the one whom Caiaphas prophesies should justly be killed—so in Christ’s kingdom royal power and priestly dignity cooperate in good. Thus every David has his Nathan to hear, every Hezekiah is guided by the Isaiah contemporary with him, every Josiah is mourned by his Jeremiah, and every Zerubbabel serves under Jesus the high priest; the appropriate distinction between the two powers being maintained, as the rules of the Fathers teach, rightly distinguishing both dignities.

[Col. 0047C] LXIII. Although we could offer many passages concerning this, for the present let one decree of Pope Nicholas suffice. He says among other things: “When the truth has been reached, neither did the emperor thereafter seize the rights of pontificate for himself, nor did the pontiff usurp the imperial name. For the same mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, by distinct offices and distinct dignities so separated the functions of the two powers—wishing each to be raised on high through its own healing humility, not to be plunged again into hell by human pride—that Christian emperors should need pontiffs for eternal life, and pontiffs should use imperial laws only for the course of temporal affairs; so that spiritual action might remain apart from carnal incursions, [Col. 0047D] and one serving God might not entangle himself in secular affairs, while conversely the other might not appear to preside over divine matters.” Likewise: “Finally, how those who are permitted to preside only over human affairs and not divine ones dare to judge those through whom divine matters are ministered, we do not understand at all.” Since Pope Nicholas says these things, we affirm in agreement with him that one who ought to preside over earthly things only in the administration of secular affairs ought not to entangle himself in spiritual affairs; and conversely, the spiritual judge ought to give himself to divine things, yet without entanglement of his spirit should govern even kings and emperors by teaching—how much more lesser powers.

[Col. 0048A] LXIV. But they very often wish to rule and refuse to be taught; indeed, they kill witnesses to the truth. Even some who are shepherds only in name and outward appearance, but inwardly ravening wolves, and who, contrary to the teaching of Peter the chief shepherd and apostle, lord it over the clergy, kill witnesses to the truth. Imitating Herod, they first imprison those who rebuke them within the confines of silence, lest they be publicly reproved by them; then, insofar as lies in their power, they kill them altogether by beheading. They take precautions, as they suppose, against the guilt of homicide, but they do not escape the crime of witness-killing. For it is one thing to kill a human being, another to kill a witness. A man kills a human being when he takes away his life; but he kills a witness when he cuts off that person’s ability to bear witness and to read, with the intention that he may have, as it were, liberty to commit unlawful deeds with impunity, [Col. 0048B] no one rebuking or contradicting him. Yet, just as Herod feared John, knowing him to be a just and holy man, and did many things when he heard him, guarded him, and gladly heard him; so these men pretend to hear gladly the very persons whom they fear, imprison, and kill. For they utterly refuse to hear their voices crying in the wilderness, neither in deserts, mountains, caves, or caverns of the earth—much less in the houses of a king feasting luxuriously, and at the very banquets where they discuss the death of John. They grieve that he still lives in the spirit and power of Elijah, and therefore contrive to extinguish him in just and holy men. But will the word once gone forth from the mouth of the Lord therefore return to him empty? [Col. 0048C] No. It will accomplish whatever he wills and prosper in the things for which he sent it. For as in the creation of the world he spoke and they were made, he commanded and they were created, so, remaining with the elect until the consummation of the age, he speaks and they come to pass. Because few believe this, it is said: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?” (Luke XVIII, 8.) For almost all see the boiling pot, with the north wind blowing; but only faithful persons, and few of them, see together with Jeremiah the watching rod, which shows that the Lord watches over his word in order to perform it. He proceeds prosperously and reigns so as to accomplish all that he intends, and no one can withstand [Col. 0048D] his giant course.

LXV. Here I weigh two opposing intentions. For the boiling pot signifies the malicious purpose of the devil or Antichrist, by which he intends to throw all things into confusion, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error, blinded by the smoke of this pot. Against this the Lord intends that all flesh may be saved through the shortening of the evil days; for unless they were shortened, as he himself says, all flesh would not be saved, but for the elect’s sake, he says, they will be shortened. Therefore not only the elect themselves, strong and perfect, but also the frail and weak, designated by the name “flesh,” will be saved; so that he may say of the perfect: “This now is bone of my bones” (Gen. II, 23), and then add concerning imperfect human beings who nevertheless have good will, [Col. 0049A] “and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. II, 23). Thus, “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion,” in order that what is sung in the same hymn may happen, where it says: “All flesh shall come to you.” For there will not fail in the holy Church persons like Jeremiah and Haggai—though weak and poor—through whom the strong things of this world will be confounded, those things which, as far as they can, prevent all flesh from coming to you and all flesh from being saved. Jeremiah and Haggai prophesy this in this hymn; and Jesus the high priest, in the bishop of the apostolic see, is known to support them by praying, exhorting, sending letters, and framing synodal decrees. Thus every Catholic and religious person, however poor and insignificant, is encouraged against wrongdoers, however great, by the authority of Peter, against whom these gates of hell cannot prevail. Likewise, in every Catholic prince sent by God and confirmed by the authority of the apostolic see for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good, that Zerubbabel, leader of the people returning from exile according to the word of the Lord, is conspicuous, as it is written: “And the word of the Lord came a second time to Haggai on the twenty-fourth of the month, saying: Speak to Zerubbabel, leader of Judah, saying: I will shake heaven and earth together; I will overthrow the throne of kingdoms and all the strength of the kingdom of the nations; I will overthrow the chariot and its rider, and horses and their riders shall come down, each by the sword of his brother. On that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, my servant, says the Lord, and [Col. 0049C] make you like a signet ring, because I have chosen you, says the Lord of hosts” (Hag. II, 21–24). It should be noted that he prophesies the overthrow of the throne of kingdoms before he sets in place the leader beloved and chosen by him.

LXVI. In the same way, if any king or prince, admonished by priestly command as it were through Samuel to strike the ungodly, destroy the Amalekites, and strike King Agag, the enemy of the people of Israel, should spare such persons contrary to the priestly command—or, what is worse, dare to foster God’s enemies and persecute his friends—such a man is rightly deprived of the power which he misuses, so that the kingdom is divided from him. This is especially so if he himself dares to rend the priestly or prophetic mantle [Col. 0049D] by diminishing the right and honor of the Church. This belongs to the adornment of priestly preeminence, which shines clearly in that return from Babylonian captivity to Jerusalem, according to this hymn, “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion.” For once the throne of kingdoms had been overthrown among the Jewish people—first, when the kings of Israel, worshippers of golden calves because of their separation from the house of David, or rather because of idolatry, were destroyed and expelled from God’s kingdom; then, when the kings of Judah too were brought to an end in the Babylonian deportation, with some of them laudably crowned in the kingdom of heaven, David, Hezekiah, and Josiah being chief among them—from that time, as has already been said, the throne of kingdoms having been overthrown and the royal title wholly removed, Zerubbabel, although born of the royal tribe, was promoted not [Col. 0050A] as king but as leader. His successors were not kings but leaders, until that time when, after the scepter had been taken from Judah, even the leader had to be removed from his loins, as the foreigner Herod came in as king. He was born of an Idumaean father and Arabian mother; and therefore, while he reigned—or rather tyrannized—it was fitting that he should be born king of whom the patriarch Jacob had long before foretold: “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes to whom it is laid up; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10). Thus, when the secular dignity of the Jewish kings had already then been somewhat reduced to leaders, as the citizens of Jerusalem began to return from their exile, the priesthood—previously religious indeed, but somewhat depressed under kings, as the Book of Kings indicates; for example, where Elijah is read to have suffered the persecution of king and queen in Israel, and Zechariah in Judah to have been stoned between the temple and altar by the king’s command (Luke XI, 51)—is read to have been increasingly exalted and glorified above their leaders and their rule, and honored with royal crowns, according to that passage in the prophet: “You shall take,” says the Lord, “silver and gold, and place them upon the head of Jesus, son of Josedec, the high priest” (Zech. VI, 11). On this the illustrious Jerome says: “Crowns are placed upon Jesus, son of Josedec, the high priest, because through each of our virtues the Lord is crowned; indeed, when we are crowned through the virtue of repentance, the Savior receives crowns in each individual.”

[Col. 0050C] LXVII. Since, then, Jesus Christ our Lord is the same King and Priest, crowned with glory and honour, nevertheless his priestly dignity is more especially crowned whenever someone returns from Babylonian wickedness to Jerusalem through repentance. For it is clear that there the royal eminence in some manner failed, when the king of Babylon usurps sovereignty either in the Church or in any soul formerly faithful. Therefore, when his yoke has been made rotten from before the anointing-oil through repentance—which belongs to the priestly office—crowns are rightly placed upon Jesus the high priest.

A type of this is recognized as having gone before in Jesus the high priest; and at the same time this was prefigured: that, when idolatrous, schismatic, and undisciplined kingdoms, bent beneath the burden until their own pride should fail, had declined, the priestly dignity was to be more greatly glorified and crowned. Thus even the office of stirrup-holder is to be rendered to the Roman pontiff by kings and emperors. This renews, that is, the ancient miracles in which Joseph is seen exalted in Pharaoh’s chariot, Daniel adorned with royal purple, and Mordecai carried upon the royal horse. These spectacles indeed now delight the kindly observer—kings having been partly removed and partly humbled through the diminution of their realm, while the priesthood is exalted—but they torment the envious.

That the envious person may be tormented still more, and the devout eye more greatly delighted, perhaps, just as before Christ’s first advent kings were removed and leaders ruled until he himself came, so before his second advent, through the stone cut from the mountain without hands, the whole golden image of kingdoms will be shattered insofar as it is found contrary to the divine kingdom. In secular dignity there will succeed a power of lesser name, great kingdoms being reduced to tetrarchies or even smaller portions, lest they be able to oppress churches or ecclesiastical persons, defended by the patronage of the high priest—the president of the apostolic see—crowned and exalted above all kingdoms, and by the privileges of apostolic primacy.

LXVIII. Whose eye now, unless it is wicked or bleary—open rather for envy than for sight—does not see these things partly fulfilled, so that every kindly observer may rightly have no doubt concerning their fulfilment when he sees so many things fulfilled according as they are expressed in the Scriptures of truth? Who does not look with reverence upon Peter the apostle, the high priest—or rather, upon Jesus Christ the supreme priest in him—crowned with as many golden crowns as are the kingdoms over which he established him? “Behold,” he says, “I have set thee over nations and over kingdoms, that thou mayest root up and destroy, and waste and scatter, and build and plant” (Jer. 1:10).

Thus the illustrious prince of the holy senate of apostles is ruler of the world and governor of kingdoms, regulating the conduct and life of the churches which are everywhere faithful through apostolic teaching. Antiochus and Remus yield to thee, Peter, the throne of sovereignty. When such things are proclaimed in churches with melodious voices, and sacred solemnities sing hymns from the songs of Zion in royal praises to the glory of the apostles, but especially of the prince of the apostles—“To thee praise is due, O God, in Zion”—then deeds correspond to words, and the divine mighty works which resound in words shine forth in realities and are displayed even to the eyes, so that we may sing the hymn, saying: “As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of our God, in his holy mountain” (Ps. 47:9).

For this reason we desire that God’s wonders, which we declare in hymns and psalms and other spiritual songs, should also be made visible to the eyes through an effect of things worthy of them, lest the nations should ever say: “Where is their God? My tears became my bread day and night, while it was daily said to me: Where is thy God?” (Ps. 41:4). Miserable are those who say this, for they do not know that those to whom they say it are blessed: since, while these envy and do not see, the God of gods shall be seen by them in Zion. Therefore to thee praise is due, O God, in Zion, in whose streets the sick are to be laid, so that, when Peter the apostle comes in the glory of his primacy, at least his shadow may overshadow some one of them, and they may be delivered from their infirmities—lest the nations should say, “Where is their God?” when they see their infirmities healed.

LXIX. Look upon, O prince of the apostles, the streets of this city, full of the beds and pallets of the sick. Look—or rather, obtain for us that look with which the Lord looked upon thee, so that, wounded, thou mightest weep bitterly, still languishing under a great infirmity. From this thou wast so healed and strengthened that thou no longer fearedst Rome, mistress of the world—thou who, in thy infirmity, hadst feared the maidservant of a priest.

Now draw after thee the bishops, thy successors in the apostolic see—indeed, also us sheep entrusted to thee—so that we may all run after the fragrance of thy ointments, under thee and in Christ, ruler of all kingdoms and governor of all churches.

LXX. But someone will say: How can kingdoms be ruled, or churches governed, through the prince of the apostles when they do not obey the pontiff of the apostolic see? To this, according to my capacity and without prejudice to my betters, I, the least of men, reply.

The prudence of ecclesiastical government shines conspicuously in that discernment whereby the ruler of the Church “eats butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. 7:15). By butter, which is the accumulated fatness of spoiled milk, may be understood corruption of morals, by which one, having grown fat, sleek, and swollen, forsakes God his maker and withdraws from God his saviour. But by honey, which, separated from the waxen thickness of the comb, is at once sweet and pure, is understood purity of sweet morals.

For although honey and milk beneath the bride’s tongue, or in a land flowing with milk and honey, or again on that day when the mountains shall drip sweetness and the hills shall flow with milk and honey, agree well together—where milk signifies love of neighbour and honey love of God—yet butter, which is the excrement of spoiled milk, not inappropriately signifies, as has been said, corruption of morals, just as sweet and pure honey signifies purity of morals.

Since this is so, the ruler of the Church, and Emmanuel dwelling in him, eats butter and honey when, diligently investigating, he searches out the evils and goods in the Church entrusted to him, that he may know to reject evil and choose good. We are not now speaking of hidden evils, which no prelate is to judge unless either a lawful accuser is found or a corrupt opinion is defended with obstinate determination.

But concerning manifest evils, even when no one accuses or testifies—or, what is worse, when a foolish and senseless people approves them—the judgment of the judge who rejects them must be pressed upon his hearers even against their will, whether by sermon or by letters, with such stern warning that not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, or rashly share food or greeting with them after prohibition, may know, and be compelled to know, that they are held under equal condemnation. To the angels of such churches, corrupted by the leaven of this butter, it must be announced in apostolic letters that, unless they correct evils so certain and open, or, if they cannot correct them, exclude them—or, if to exclude them they lack power because they wish to avoid slaughter, condemn them in justice and, with discriminating protest, carry them as a cart laden with hay carries its load with creaking—they must recognize that they themselves are to be excluded or deposed, Christ moving their lampstand, he who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands.

[Col. 0053A] LXXI. The seven golden lampstands are the seven churches; and by the number seven is understood the universality of all churches. They are to be visited by apostolic letters in such a manner that in one place, as though by the voice of thunder, the teaching and sect of the Nicolaitans may be rebuked in the incest of clerics; elsewhere, the teaching of Balaam, the hired prophet, in the sect of hirelings; elsewhere, the wickedness of Jezebel, tyrannizing and killing God’s prophets, in tyrants who persecute righteous men like Elijah; elsewhere, the particular slothfulness of the angels themselves—whether they have abandoned their first love, or have a living name in their offices but are dead in evil works, or are lukewarm and, unless they repent, to be vomited from God’s mouth.

Likewise, if we look to the Epistles of the apostle Paul, we see, from his example, that churches are to be rebuked by apostolic letters: that they should not take food with one who is called a brother and is a fornicator or greedy; that they should withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly; that if anyone does not obey the apostolic word sent by letter, they should mark him and rebuke him as a brother; and that, if he refuses amendment after rebuke, they should beware of him as an enemy. For the caution required among such people, he says: “See how carefully you walk, not as unwise but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5:15). And lest anyone should think that in evil days he ought to redeem time for himself by consenting to evils in any way, he says: “Put away evil from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5:13).

Thus, showing that even because of one fornicator the whole lump is corrupted, as it were through a little leaven, he says: “Purge out the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump” (ibid.). In respect of this manifest evil, he did not await anyone’s accusation or testimony, but only the outcry of public notoriety, of which he says: “It is altogether reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles” (ibid.). Nor does he threaten that man alone, but the whole Church that tolerates him, with the rod, unless the man who committed this evil is removed from their midst and delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.

LXXII. It would take long to show, point by point from the apostolic epistles, how the ruler of the Church ought, after the example of the apostles, to eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good. As an example in this matter for the pontiffs of the apostolic see to imitate, let blessed Pope Gregory suffice. He ate butter and honey with such diligence that, pressed by concern for all the churches, he wrote unsolicited letters regarding many matters reported to him only by rumour. How earnestly in these he rejected evil and chose good is attested by his letters, voluntarily sent to pontiffs, kings, and other ecclesiastical persons, though no one sometimes requested them; public report demanded them, or some truthful reporter had brought the matter to his ears.

Hence it was customary for him to say at the opening of certain letters: “It has been reported to us,” or, “It has come to us.” Thus he writes to the Roman defensor:

> “It has been reported to us that our most reverend brother Basil, bishop, is occupied in lawsuits as though he were one of the laity, and uselessly serves in the courts. Since this both makes him contemptible and destroys priestly reverence, as soon as thy Experience has received this command, compel him by strict execution to return, so that, with thee pressing the matter there, he may not be permitted to remain five days under any excuse. For if thou permit him by any means to stay there longer, thou wilt begin to be held guilty with him before us.”

Likewise, to Anthemios the subdeacon:

> “It has come to us that Priminius, bishop of the city of Amalfi, is not content to reside in his church, but wanders abroad through various places. Seeing this, others do not remain in the fortress either, but, following his example, choose rather to live abroad. And because those who do this rather invite enemies to plunder them, we therefore command thee by this authority not to cease warning the aforesaid bishop, that he may not presume to do this henceforth, but may reside in his church according to priestly custom. If perchance thou learnest that he is not corrected after thy warning, thou shalt assign him to a monastery and take every care to inform us, so that thou mayest learn again from our direction what thou oughtest to do.”

Likewise, among other matters, he writes thus to Secundus, servant of God:

> “Rouse Bishop Marianus, thy brother, with such words as thou canst, for I suspect that he has fallen asleep. Certain persons came to me, among them some old beggars. I questioned them about what they had received and from whom, and they reported individually how much had been given them even on their journey. When I carefully asked concerning the aforesaid brother what he had given them, they answered that they had asked him, but received nothing from him—not even bread for the road, which that church had always customarily given to everyone. For they said: ‘He answered us, saying: I have nothing that I can give you.’ And I wonder whether one who has clothes has nothing to give the poor. Tell him, therefore, to change his mind with his place; let him not think that reading and prayer alone suffice for him; let him not make it his concern to sit apart and not bear fruit by his hand; but let him have a generous hand, come to the aid of those in need, and regard another’s want as his own. For if he does not so act, he bears the empty title of bishop.”

[Col. 0054D] LXXIII. Many of his letters are found in this manner, sent voluntarily and without anyone requesting them, by which evils are rejected and goods chosen. You see, therefore, kindly observers, how this saint contended for the law of his God; how, eating butter and honey, he searched out evils and goods from every quarter, and knew and laboured to reject evil and choose good; without awaiting accusations or testimony in matters manifest and in whatever manner made known to him. Certainly, if this saint were alive now, in these last days and dangerous times, he would have many evils to rebuke—evils committed so openly that they require no judicial procedure of accusation or testimony.

LXXIV. If, therefore, apostolic letters are sent concerning the rejection of these things, and religious men are also written to, instructing them that, if anyone does not obey the word sent by letter, they are to mark him according to the teaching of the apostle Paul, then, with God’s grace favouring, many things will be corrected which are now freely done, though evil and shameful—not only in secret but even openly—and are even regarded as good though they are evil, because there is no one to reject them.

We could point with the finger and identify by plain name certain evils to be rejected, rooted up, destroyed, and scattered; and, contrariwise, certain goods to be chosen, planted, and built. But we leave it in all these matters to apostolic vigilance—pressed by concern for all the churches and charged with the governance of all kingdoms—to eat butter and honey, that it may know to reject evil and choose good. Let it know, namely, how in the priesthood to reject the frivolous, not purified and shaven according to God’s law, choosing good men well purified and content with God as their inheritance. Let it likewise know how in the realm to reject unjust rulers and choose good men divinely sent for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good.

Let it know, I say, how to reject some by excluding them altogether while preserving ecclesiastical peace; how to forbid others, because of open wickedness, from ministry at the altar or from communion in the Lord’s body and blood, yet to tolerate them within the Church’s fellowship for the sake of peace, on this road of pilgrimage by which we journey from Babylonian captivity to Zion, or Jerusalem. There the chief senators, with their King, in the final winnowing, after all evils have been rejected, will choose every good thing.

LXXV. Therefore, the more carefully shameful evils are now rejected by the governors of churches and goods fitting for the good are chosen, the more fittingly praise is due to thee, O God, in Zion, and the more worthily shall a vow be rendered to thee in Jerusalem. Since this is hastened more by prayer than by argument, after this ample digression in support of our position let us return to the interrupted exposition and prayer of the psalm.

For in this exposition we intend nothing more than, by gathering the Fathers’ meanings into this little rustic work, as into a basket—a vessel, as it is said, for manure—to stir up ourselves and those who will read what we write, insofar as God’s favour enables us, to the same affection of praise and prayer which the words of the psalms contain, together with the Fathers’ expositions upon them. Accordingly, we frequently assume the personae of David, Idithun, Asaph, or others who speak in the psalms, so that we may express their affections more forcefully.

In this psalm, therefore, having assumed the person of Jeremiah, or Haggai, or both, let us pray with those who pray, praise with those who praise, and vow the vows to be rendered in Jerusalem while on this pilgrimage. But thou, Lord, to whom vows of praise are to be rendered in our homeland, hear my prayer now upon the way; for if thou hearest—or rather, because thou wilt hear—unto thee shall all flesh come. For unless the evil days were shortened, as thou sayest, no flesh would be saved. But for the elect’s sake, as thou dost promise—and I, Jeremiah and Haggai, assured by thy promise, pray—the evil days shall be shortened. When they are shortened, all flesh shall come to thee: that is, people of every kind—poor and rich, learned and unlearned, children and old people, Jews and Gentiles, men and women—who are often denoted by the name “flesh,” as in: “He gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of flesh, but of God” (John 1:72). Likewise: “This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2:23).

LXXVI. Therefore, in order that what is written may be fulfilled—“The two shall be one flesh” (ibid.)—the bridegroom and bride, the head and members, all flesh shall undoubtedly come to thee. This means not only that flesh which is certainly to be saved when the evil days are shortened, namely, flesh predestined to salvation, however frail and weak it may be; but also that flesh which shall not be saved shall then come to thee as judge, when, as it is written, every valley shall be filled, every mountain and hill brought low, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.

Therefore, what I, Haggai, say—“Unto thee shall all flesh come”—is partly prophecy and partly prayer. It is prophecy insofar as all flesh will come to thee as judge; but it is prayer insofar as the elect may not be led astray during the shortened days of captivity, and that, as they return by the straight way from captivity to Zion, all flesh, even the frail, may be saved under their leadership, as it were through Jeremiah and Haggai—yet adhering to the elect and strong through obedience and charity, and beginning their journey together with them.

LXXVII. In the Hebrew it reads: “May all flesh come unto thee.” Therefore I, Jeremiah or Haggai, about to recite a prayer in God’s presence and desiring that it be heard effectually, preface it with another prayer, saying: “Hear my prayer” (Ps. 38:13). Once this preparatory prayer for the prayer that follows has thus been set first, as though a vigil preceded the feast day with lamenting Jeremiah, the prayer is then uttered as though festively with Haggai: at the end the Psalmist sings, “I pray that all flesh may come unto thee.”

For because thou willest all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth, in agreement with thy will I rightly pray that all flesh—that is, every human being—may come to thee, and that in thee, the seed of Abraham, all tribes of the earth may be blessed. This does not mean that all human beings shall be saved or blessed, for not all possess the promises made to Abraham; rather, all tribes means some persons from every tribe of the earth, so that there is no respect of persons, since in every nation everyone who fears God and works righteousness is accepted by him.

LXXVIII. Thus do we pray, we who, now beginning to journey, tend toward the end where the God of gods shall be seen in Zion, where praise is due to thee, O God, in Zion. Yet we are not heard as quickly as we would wish. Why? Because the words of the wicked have prevailed against us.

The first wicked ones were the serpent, Adam, and Eve. Among them were forged the words that effectively caused our pilgrimage, when the devil, speaking through the serpent, said to the wicked parents of humankind: “Eat, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:5). Our parents, too credulous of these words, became covetous, proud, and curious. For through their desire to eat forbidden food entered the lust of the flesh; through their desire for likeness to God, pride of mind; through their desire to know good and evil, the vice of curiosity entered.

And indeed, before these words of the wicked—that is, the word of pilgrimage—there had gone forth from God’s mouth the word of blessing, by which it was said to our parents: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28). Made fruitful by this word, they possessed the power to bear only blessed children, who would remain in the blessed homeland. But after the sin came the words of pilgrimage, when God said to Eve: “I will multiply thy afflictions and thy conceptions” (Gen. 3:16), as though he said: Beyond the number of blessed children I shall multiply thy conceptions, so that thou mayest bear far more children of curse than of blessing. Thus even the blessed children are pilgrims and, as it were, captives among the cursed until that separation of the two, when, as the cursed rule in the cursed land and oppress the blessed children unjustly, it shall be said: “Depart, ye cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41); while to the blessed children who wander in the cursed land and labour amid the words of the wicked prevailing against them, it shall then be said: “Come, ye blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., 34).

Joined to their number by faith and hope, because amid the words of the wicked prevailing against us we lament with Jeremiah by groaning rather than delight in them through perverse assent, we make this very complaint: that the words of the wicked have prevailed against us. Thus we, the children of blessing, although possessing the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit and desiring to return to our heavenly homeland, nevertheless groan within ourselves, seeing the wicked law in our members resisting the righteous, holy, and good law of the mind. Since this wicked law holds us captive in the law of sin and death, we rightly complain that the words of the wicked have prevailed against us.

[Col. 0057D] LXXIX. The words of very many wicked persons, greatly multiplied beyond our number, have prevailed against us few. The words of the rich, powerful, proud, and perverse have prevailed against us poor, weak, humble persons, converted to thee, O God, and ready to return from the midst of Babylon to Jerusalem. Since, then, our faces are turned toward thee, as of persons going to Jerusalem, Babylon having been left behind our backs, thou, rising up, wilt have mercy on us citizens of Zion, and thou wilt be propitious toward the impieties that we committed in Babylon.

For as we return from captivity to our homeland, Jesus the high priest intercedes for us at thy right hand, and he himself, the perfect offering, has become the propitiation for our sins. Therefore, through thy incarnate Word it shall come about that the words of the wicked which prevailed against us in Babylon, when we begin our departure from there, will no longer be able to prevail. They do not then sound before our eyes and face, but whisper as it were behind our back, and mutter dimly, like speech from the ground.

If, therefore, we call blessed those who, setting aside the Babylonians’ words, begin to journey at the sound of the prophetic trumpet sounding through the mouth of Jeremiah or Haggai, much more blessed is he whom thou hast chosen and received, and who, having been received, dwells in thy courts.

LXXX. Blessed above all his companions is the man whom thou, the Word of God, hast so received and wonderfully united to thyself in one person that the words of the wicked could never prevail against him. For he is “the blessed man who hath not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. 1:1).

Truly blessed is the man chosen from among thousands, whom thou, God the Father, didst choose and make God: certainly not an adopted God, but true God, thy natural Son—not by conversion of the Godhead into flesh, but by the assumption of humanity into God.

> [Note: [Col. 0057D] This is perhaps faulty through a printer’s carelessness. Restore it thus, according to the Athanasian Creed: “not by conversion of the Godhead into flesh, but by the assumption of humanity into God” [Col. 0058D].]
