For thou didst not merely choose him from the mass of perdition at his conception, or earlier in thy predestination, but didst also receive him in glory into the session at thy right hand, as he himself says: “Thou hast held my right hand, and hast guided me in thy will, and hast received me with glory” (Ps. 72:24). Blessed is the man whom thou hast thus chosen and received as high priest, most necessary for thy pilgrim people, just as Jesus, that ancient figurative high priest, was once necessary. He is read to have been crowned with golden crowns as a type of this true priest and king, as we briefly noted above.

LXXXI. Blessed also, after him and in him and through him, is the person whom thou hast chosen from the world and received into some ministry of salvation, both his own and that of others. Since he works this excellent work with thee—and without him thou, Father, dost nothing, because he is thy hand working with thee and in thee all that thou dost—whatever thou dost, he likewise does. Rightly and truly he says to those chosen by thee and by himself: “Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you and appointed you, that ye should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15:16). Likewise: “If ye were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but because ye are not of the world, and I have chosen you from the world, therefore the world hates them” (ibid., 19).

Blessed is the person whom thou hast thus chosen from the world, so that for this very reason he endured the world’s hatred: for thou hast chosen and received him, not for an evil work, nor for a time only to remain in thy courts, but for a good work enduring for ever, because he shall dwell in thy courts. “The servant does not remain in the house for ever; the son remains for ever.” Therefore the evil servant, received temporarily for some necessary work, looking back and going back, shall not dwell in thy courts into which thou hadst received him; but the son shall dwell in thy courts as a lawful heir. And we who journey from Babylon to Zion become heirs indeed of God and co-heirs of Christ; and thus through him who is our head we shall be filled.

LXXXII–IV. Blessed indeed is he who, chosen and received by thee, shall dwell in thy courts. Yet in the courts themselves there is not fullness of blessedness. For though our feet standing in thy courts, O Jerusalem, are blessed, nevertheless only those who dwell in thy house, O Lord, are completely blessed, where they shall praise thee for ages of ages.

Here we begin our journey rejoicing in the things said to us: “We shall go into the house of the Lord”; and Jesus the high priest provides many refreshment provisions for us as we travel. But when we arrive, then we shall be filled utterly with the good things of thy house, O God. The gifts of his house are ineffable, whether the house itself is understood as human nature assumed into God, or as the chosen portion of angels, or even as the whole holy universal Church. This house is also a temple—not any ordinary temple, but a wonderful one; not wonderful in artificial, handmade structures adorned with gold, silver, or precious stone, but wonderful in equity.

Do not be surprised that I have called that temple wonderful in equity: it is wholly free from iniquity and resplendent with the highest equity. For if you consider the temple not made with hands, namely the Lord’s body, there is no iniquity in it; rather, its equity is sufficient and more than sufficient to abolish all our iniquities.

[Col. 0059C] LXXXV. For what could be more just or equitable than that the slave should return to the liberty he lost, when the Son voluntarily underwent servile punishments for the slave’s iniquity? What could be more just or equitable than that the unjust robber should lose the right and dominion he had over sinful man, when he laid violent hands upon a man wholly without sin and giving thanks to God his Father in supreme equity?

Indeed, this was humanity’s greatest iniquity: though created good by God, humanity offered its Creator absolutely no thanks; indeed, stripped naked by its own fault and left half-dead beneath inflicted wounds, it did not even possess the means by which to give thanks. For to give due thanks for a benefit is to be wholly devoted to one’s benefactor in respect of all that one has received, striving to render back in service nothing less than one received in benefit. If one renders less, the gift offered is not acceptable in God’s balance of equity because of such fraud or iniquity.

It is clear, however, that the first parents, created good and enriched with paradisal goods, gave no thanks to God. Ungrateful to their benefactor, they succumbed, sold without payment to his enemy. Thus distorted from the rule of equity, they begot children of iniquity, children of curse, children of wrath. None of these was fit to give thanks to God, all being hindered by the original sin of paternal ingratitude. Hence, amid all the proclamations of patriarchs and prophets, although the voice of praise, confession, exultation, and salvation often sounds in the tabernacles of the righteous, nowhere sounds the voice of thanksgiving except in this temple of wonderful equity.

LXXXVI. Before Christ, indeed, none of the saints is recorded as having given thanks to God, because they knew themselves unequal to it. But he was the first: one man giving thanks to God the Father on behalf of all his people, as is read in the Gospel—first when he satisfied a great multitude from a few loaves; then when he raised Lazarus; finally, when, taking bread, he gave thanks, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “This is my body,” etc. (Matt. 26:26).

And what was his whole life in the world except a thanksgiving worthy of God? Does not human nature, employed by the Most High and advanced to the highest in the Son of God, even now give thanks to the supreme Trinity? Moreover, through him and in him, he gave his disciples power there to give thanks to God the Father, saying: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19), that is, do what I have done by my example and with my help, while I work in you and through you.

Behold the high priest wholly without iniquity; himself the offering sufficient to abolish every iniquity; himself the temple wonderful in equity. In him alone an equitable thanksgiving is rendered to God without the fraud of iniquity, because all that was granted by God to humanity assumed was wholly bestowed in divine service as a holocaust of most sweet savour and as a sacrifice of fullest thanksgiving—something that no one before him could accomplish.

One of the chief elect says: “What shall I render unto the Lord for all that he hath rendered unto me?” (Ps. 115:12). And when he found within himself nothing worthy to render in return for God’s gifts, he says: “I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord” (ibid., 13): that is, I shall await and faithfully invoke him who, though innocent, will drink the cup of suffering and by the saving offering of his flesh and blood will make satisfaction to the Father with perfect thanksgiving.

LXXXVII. This too has now been granted to the Church in him and through him. When she offers this very sacrifice in this very temple, it is her customary act to give thanks, so that it is “worthy and just, equitable and saving,” in highest equity, in the balance of equity and justice. In this balance, “Would that my sins and the calamity which I suffer were weighed,” says holy Job (Job 62), desiring this temple wonderful in equity and within it the balance of justice. In that balance, by the two scales of the arms of the cross—that is, of justice and mercy—the weight of human calamity appears, as though heavier than the sand of the sea, than all the sins of all human beings who sacrifice in this temple.

For the calamity of a shameful death in the person of God incarnate—who suffered without any iniquity of his own because of our iniquities—immeasurably outweighs, in the scale of mercy, our sins in the scale of justice. Thus the scale of mercy, appearing heavier than the sand of the sea through the weight of such calamity and descending as far as hell to despoil it, shall in judgment exalt above the scale of justice with so vehement an exaltation that, when the sins of believers have been shaken from it into the depths of the sea, there shall be a wonderful spectacle of divine mercy and equity. Pharaoh is submerged by the judgment of equity because in his eagerness to harm he dared pursue those departing from him and fleeing to that protector who was merciful in the pillar of cloud and just in the pillar of fire, guilty of no iniquity, and himself the temple wonderful in equity. Therefore in him there is the safest refuge from every iniquity.

LXXXVIII. Holy, therefore, is your temple, [Col. 0061B] wondrous in equity: holiness abounds in itself, so that it is rightly called the Holy of Holies; and its equity is directed toward the Father, or rather toward the divinity of the whole Trinity, to whom, by giving thanks perfectly, it preserved wondrous equity. Thus it did not inflict unjust violence upon the unjust enemy, but overcame him by equity, when it judicially took away what had been granted from one who was unlawfully invading what had not been granted.

There is also in this temple, not made by hands, an equity that is wondrous and impenetrable to any reasoning: for during the time when this lawful heir of the heavenly kingdom was a little child, differing in nothing from a servant in the likeness of sinful flesh, he so emptied himself and made himself equal to his least servants that he washed their feet; and, being reckoned among the wicked, he did not resent this injustice, but gave thanks to the Father, [Col. 0061C] the author of all equity, and praised his justice, while at the same time excusing some of the wicked on account of ignorance, saying: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you” (John 17:25). Again: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Who would not marvel and at the same time venerate, amid such an abundance of iniquity, this praise of the paternal justice which judges all things in highest equity? What human being, when judged by a human being, if judged so unjustly and so unjustly reckoned with the wicked, would praise the equity of a judge who arranged—or, by not preventing, permitted—such things? Absolutely no one. But this God-man humbles himself thus beneath divine judgment, as though he differed in nothing from a servant; [Col. 0061D] nor did he deem equality with God a thing to be seized, so long as, humbled in the form of a servant and made equal to servants, and reckoned with the wicked, he humbly bore for them the punishment due to wicked servants. Therefore God also exalted him; and, granting him the name above every name, made him equal to himself in highest glory, so that every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father—both according to that nature which we believe was exalted in him and endowed with the highest name, and according to that nature which from eternity was most high.

LXXXIX. For human nature, assumed into God the Son of God, [Col. 0062A] although during the time of assumed mortality it was made a little lower than the angels, and although it was far below God even while in God, nevertheless has, beneath God, lesser glory, but in God and with God absolutely the same glory: all power in heaven and on earth having been given to it, which God himself, the Son of God, eternally possessed in his divinity together with God his Father, but received in his humanity in time. It remains indeed lesser than the Father according to the nature of humanity, but is not lesser according to the divine power and glory granted to its humanity.

Is not, in this elevation of humanity to the heights, the equity as rational as it is wondrous? Since he voluntarily humbled himself, was reckoned with the wicked, and was made equal to them in punishment for the glory of God the Father, [Col. 0062B] it was given, by the just judgment of equity, to human nature so humbled to ascend to the place where the Son of God himself had formerly been, most high with the most high Father—thus fulfilling the irony, or prophecy, once spoken: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us” (Gen. 3:22).

XC. What was a most severe irony against the old Adam was the sweetest prophecy concerning the new Adam. Of him God the Father can truly say: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us”; that is, he has been made equal to us in glory, knowing good and evil as one of us knows them, powerful to execute judgment as one of us is powerful. Hence, just as all living creatures were brought to the old Adam so that he might see what he would call them—for whatever Adam called each living creature, that was its name—so all things are to be brought to this Adam for judgment, that he may see what he calls them, according to the discernment [Note: [Col. 0061D] Perhaps a typographical error for “knowledge” (*scientiam*).] of good and evil, by which he most perfectly knows how to reject evil and choose good, with equity preserved in all things. For he is the temple wondrous in equity, not differing in the brightness granted to him from the highest divinity dwelling in him.

Thus “the stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This was done by the Lord, and it is wondrous in our eyes.” It is wondrous especially in that equity by which the natural essence of this stone or temple—remaining in itself indestructible and lesser than the divinity—was advanced beyond itself as far as equality [Col. 0062D] with the glory of the divine being dwelling in it, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “In whom dwells all the fullness of the divinity bodily. And you,” he says, “are made full in him” (Col. 2:9–10). Accordingly, we who sing here say: “We shall be filled with the good things of your house; holy is your temple, wondrous in equity” (Ps. 64:5).

Truly wondrous was the equity by which God the Father said to the man who is the Son of God: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1). This is the same as saying: “Reign with me in equality with me.” This was said to him according to his human nature, because according to it dominion and honor were given to him, not partially but universally; [Col. 0063A] as he himself testifies concerning himself: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18).

“As waters are hardened into the likeness of a stone, so the lowest things are made equal to the highest.” For just as water, without its substance or quantity of substance perishing, but with only the quality by which it flowed passing into solidity, is hardened into the likeness of a stone, and a thing previously liquid is made equal in hardness to a thing naturally hard; so fragile man, assumed into God without the loss of his substance, first ascended locally above the heavens of heavens toward the east—that is, beyond the choirs of all heavenly powers—as far as the Word personally united to him.

XCI. Here it should be noted that the text does not say “to the rising” or “to what will rise,” but “to the east” (*ad orientem*). For that ineffable generation is not considered according to past and future: the Son is generated by the Father in an everlasting present. Yet this should also be understood locally, because he ascended above the firmament of heaven, and this toward the eastern quarter. For the statement “as far as the east,” that is, “as far as the Word personally united to him,” is not made with reference to place, but to the transformation of human nature; and by such a transformation we too, according to the Apostle, shall be transformed in our measure.

Yet it was not transformed in such a way that, through mutability of nature, the substance of flesh passed into the substance of that East; rather, by the equity of divine judgment, to the man humbled unto the death of the cross for the glorification of the Father [Col. 0063C] was added the magnificence of paternal glory, while the essence of the human condition was not taken away. Passibility was absorbed; impassibility was added. Weakness passed into strength, mortality into eternity, so that the man who had formerly been lower than the angels might be equal to God the Father in glory. And this is what is wondrous in eternity.

XCII. Therefore, as we both marvel at and venerate this temple wondrous in equity, whose name also is “Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9:6), some small ray of the reason for this equity shines forth—a reason which I ought not withhold from my fellow servants. Since all things were created without labor through Christ’s divinity, but restored with much labor through his humanity, and since the work of restoration is certainly better than the work of creation, the equity of divine judgment required that the humanity in Christ, though naturally lesser than the divinity, should nevertheless be made equal to it in glory and in every brightness, because of the more excellent works accomplished through his labor and humiliation.

Thus, after saying, “I have glorified you upon the earth; I have finished the work which you gave me to do” (John 17:4), he added, as though demanding also the reward due by the judgment of equity: “And now, Father, glorify me with yourself by the glory which I had with you before the world was” (ibid., 5). By these words, as Hilary interprets them, the brightness of the eternal Word is sought for the flesh: so that he who was and is lesser than the Father according to the condition of humanity may no longer [Col. 0064A] be lesser according to the glorification of that same humanity. Hence the aforementioned Hilary says in his book *On the Trinity*: “The Father, being about to glorify the Son, is greater; but the Son when glorified is not lesser.”

Accordingly, what Athanasius says—“Lesser than the Father according to humanity”—must be referred to nature, not to glory; or at least to that time when he was lower even than the angels, not to that time when, crowned with glory and honor and set over the works of the Father’s hands, he is now inferior to none in glory, as has been abundantly demonstrated in the first part of this work by the most authoritative testimonies of the Fathers.

XCIII. There is yet another wondrous equity, which the brightness and charity of this same temple itself set before the eyes of those who look upon it. Since in the redemption of the human race a temple was given for a temple—not made by hands for what was made by hands; undefiled and holy for what was defiled and profaned—one thing would not have been given for another unless what was purchased was as precious as the price given for it. Thus that holy temple is also wondrous in equity in this respect, the equal charity of that which was sold and that which was redeemed being preserved.

In wonder at this admirable equity, the living stones of the redeemed temple itself sing aloud, as though with Haggai, in festive celebration: “O inestimable love of charity: to redeem a servant, you delivered up your Son.” Let us now be content, on this way of pilgrimage, to have said these few things about this temple by wondering at it rather than explaining it. Its entrance, closed to worldly philosophy [Col. 0064C] but now partly opened to Catholic faith and to be opened fully in the future, is not to be stormed by undisciplined questions, but knocked upon with humble and reverent prayers.

Therefore, Christ, you who are this holy temple, wondrous in equity—both the doorkeeper of the temple itself and its door—hear us, that, our iniquities forgiven, we may merit to enter after being freed from the king of Babylon: O God of our salvation, hope of all the ends of the earth, and of those far out at sea.

## PART TWO

XCIV. Hear us as we knock and faithfully pray that all flesh may come to you. Hear the hymn which is fitting for you, O God, in Zion: not in that small and narrow Zion [Col. 0064D] which occupied a modest part of Judaea, but in that great city which is established as the joy of the whole earth, since you, its king, reign everywhere. You are the hope of all the ends of the earth—not only of Judaea, as the carnal judge desires; nor only of Africa, as Donatus desired; nor of any private sect, as those desire who say, “Behold, here,” or, “Behold, there”—but of all the ends of the earth. Thus all flesh may come to you, not only the continent (those living in sexual continence), but also the married, though they are at the ends of the earth or far out at sea.

For just as the queen of Ethiopia came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, so the universal Church, chosen and gathered from Jews and Gentiles, will come to you, the true Solomon, from the ends of the earth, namely by putting an end [Col. 0065A] to earthly vices and desires. Or, literally, you are the hope of all the ends of the earth, as the sound of the apostles goes forth into all the earth and their words reach the boundaries of the world, so that there are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard, even at the farthest ends of the earth and far out at sea—whether literally, on sea islands far removed from the habitation of other people; or because the sea of this age, bitter with cares, troubled by temptations, and stormy, driven by malignant spirits as by contrary winds, in which fish devour fish, rightly describes lovers of this world tumultuously contending among themselves as being far out at sea from the city of Zion and Jerusalem, the vision of peace.

Yet for them also, if they repent worthily and through you, Jesus, the great priest, seek to find grace in Zion, there is hope of obtaining mercy in you, because you are the one who prepares the mountains in your strength.

XCV. For you make preachers like Jeremiah and Haggai—small and humble in themselves—lofty and immovable in your strength, not their own. They themselves confess this, saying: “We have such confidence through Christ toward God; not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us capable ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the spirit. For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life. But if the ministry of death, engraved in letters upon stones, was in glory, so that [Col. 0065C] the children of Israel could not look steadily upon Moses’ face because of the glory of his countenance, which is being abolished, how shall the ministry of the Spirit not be still more in glory? If the ministry of condemnation is glory, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory” (2 Cor. 3:4–9).

Likewise, in the present hymn we may say: If the ministry of return to earthly Jerusalem was in glory, so that its chief administrator, Jesus the great priest, was, at the Lord’s command, crowned with golden crowns and, his filthy garments having been removed, is read to have been adorned with precious changes of clothing, how shall the ministry of return to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is above and is our free mother, not be in glory? Indeed, if the ministry of that return deserved to be honored with crowns and changes of clothing, much more ought those to be crowned with glory and honor who, in the new priesthood, stand before the Lord, sacrificing a living sacrifice and rebuking the Satan who opposes them.

XCVI. For just as Satan then stood against Jesus in order to oppose him, so now Satan is known to stand in those who resist the truth. When the Word of the Lord rebukes him, he departs and falls backward, just as those fell backward to whom the true Jesus, now about to sacrifice himself on the cross and already on the point of being sacrificed in his supper, said: “Whom do you seek?” They said to him: “Jesus of Nazareth.” When he answered them, “I am he” (John 18:4–5), struck by the thunderbolt of this word, they fell to the ground.

Those, therefore, who could not bear the brightness of the eternal sun while it was still [Col. 0066A] beneath the cloud of mortality, but fell to the earth when struck by it—how will they now bear his face, shining clearly like the sun in its strength? When, transfigured on the mountain, he showed himself thus to a few disciples, even they could not have endured him unless by that same power by which they were terrified they had also been strengthened. And John, in the Apocalypse, when he saw the same face of Jesus shining like the sun in its strength, fell at his feet as though dead. “And he placed,” he says, “his right hand upon me, saying: Do not be afraid. I am the first and the last, and I was dead, and behold, I am living for ages, and I have the keys of death and of hell” (Rev. 1:17–18).

Thus, Lord Jesus, you prepare the mountains in your strength, saying to each of them, “Do not be afraid.” In this saying is the bestowal of steadfast courage. But in saying, “I am the first and the last, and I was dead, and behold, I am living for ages, and I have the keys of death and hell,” you show yourself girded with power, by which you prevail to do whatsoever you will. For you live for ages with that life by which you are able to give life to all your members, and you have the keys of death and hell, by which you are able powerfully to imprison death and hell—namely, the devil, inventor of death, and the dark people in whom, as in hell, the devil and death have a place exceedingly broad and deep, though by no means quiet. For you trouble the deep of the sea—that is, you trouble the exceedingly bitter people—not merely at its surface, as with a gentle wind, but in its depths, as though shaking its waves from the very bottom [Col. 0066C] of the abyss.

XCVII. Another text reads: “Girded about with your might.” This can be understood after the likeness of a king surrounded on every side by his soldiers. For you are the King of glory, the Lord of the hosts surrounding you; fighting through these same hosts, you are mighty in battle—not only in land battle, by which you moved the earth and troubled it, but also in naval battle, by which you trouble the depth of the sea.

For there was, as it were, a land battle in the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon, where an image as it were of gold was set up, when Rome, the head of the Roman empire, like another Babylon, defended idolatry by issuing harsh decrees and kindling the furnace of persecution. But now that churches and monasteries have been built like ships making their way beyond [Col. 0066D] the sea to the land of promise, contrary winds rise, nor are pirate vessels full of robbers lacking: that is, perverse conventicles. As these struggle against one another, the sea is troubled and the sound of its waves increases, until you, awakened by the prayers of the Church, command the winds and the sea. Now, because sins demand it, you trouble the deep while sleeping in the ship, and permit the sound of its waves for this purpose: that you may quickly be awakened by disciples praying more attentively, and that, when you rebuke the winds and sea, there may be a great calm.

XCVIII. Alternatively: You trouble the depth of the sea by stirring the depths of human hearts, either that they may follow or that they may persecute [Col. 0067A] your elect; and you raise and calm the sound of its waves as you will. Men waste away through terror at the sound of the sea and the waves; but when your disciples see these things happen, they look to you and lift up their heads, because the redemption promised them by you draws near. They will lift up their heads—that is, they will gladden their hearts—knowing that after a brief tempest there will follow the tranquility of eternal rest.

Another translation reads: “Who will endure its sound?” That is, who will bear that commotion? Truly, no one by human strength, but many by your strength: you who prepare mountains in your strength—lofty mountains which the wondrous swellings of the sea cannot cross, immovable mountains of which you say to the sea, “Thus far you shall come, and here you shall break your swelling waves” (Job 38:11).

For idol-worshipping nations, and even false Christians, serving the creature rather than the Creator, mammon rather than you, the true God, behold the immovability and loftiness of the towers of the holy city founded on holy mountains. To this city the blessed citizens, returning from Babylon, have now begun to advance and will someday happily arrive. From such a sight some nations will be troubled by servile fear, as King Herod and all Jerusalem with him were troubled when the king of this city was born and made known to the eastern kings; others by filial fear, as the apostles were troubled and terrified, thinking after the resurrection of this king that they saw not a resurrected body but only a spirit. [Col. 0067C]

XCIX. For the cause of disturbance is no small one when this king is thought to be present to his disciples only spiritually, and not also bodily. Their disturbance is fittingly relieved when Jesus the great priest offers himself not only to be seen but also to be touched, visibly and bodily crowned with glory and honor in Catholic priests and in the other beloved and chosen, whose filthy garments have been taken away through true repentance and who have received clean changes of clothing. Likewise, he is seen conspicuous in good leaders resembling Zerubbabel. This is no small consolation to those rightly troubled, and an increase of disturbance to those wrongly troubled.

C. For the nations will be troubled and fear in different ways. First, they will fear servilely; then those among them who believe will fear your name filially and chastely—those who inhabit the boundaries of the earth, that is, not only those nearby but also those situated at the furthest ends of the earth—when the apostles’ sound goes forth into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world; or when, through their successors, the Gospel is preached throughout the whole world as far as the earth’s end.

They will be troubled, I say, by your signs: first by miracles, then by the illustrious and notable deeds of virtues which they will observe in your elect, whom you will make so perfect that the departures of morning and evening will be delightful to them. [Col. 0068A] Since prosperity is signified by morning and adversity by evening, they will be so undisturbed that, amid alternating changes of circumstance, the passing of morning prosperity into evening adversities will be delightful to them: in the one they will find consolation in this pilgrimage, and in the other exercise for their progress.

Thus, while morning repeatedly passes into evening and, conversely, evening into morning, neither condition will displease them; rather, they will give thanks in all things, especially when they perceive, O God, that by your ordering their Sabbath evening does not grow dark into an obscure night, but brightens into the first day of the Sabbath. Far removed is that night of which blessed Job prays: “Let it not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months; but let it be solitary and unworthy of praise. Let a dark whirlwind possess that night; let it await light and not see it, nor the rising of the dawning dawn” (Job 3:6–7, 9). Thus there shall be no passing from that night into morning, for it will not see the rising of the dawning dawn.

CI. Such a night was Judas the betrayer’s. Of him it is written that, after he had received the morsel from Christ’s hand, Satan entered into him, and he went out immediately. And it was night. From this excessively dark night there was no passage for him into morning light, because he did not practice fruitful repentance, although moved by repentance he returned the ill-gotten silver, saying: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27:4). This repentance was too late and unworthy of praise, because it concerned not so much the sin committed as the frustration of his plan.

For just as his forerunner Ahithophel hanged himself with a noose, tortured by a grievous conscience, because, through the frustration of his counsel, he foresaw that David would reign—the David whose kingdom and glory he had envied—so Judas, the most wicked merchant, envying Christ’s kingdom and glory and hating the devout judgment of the faithful disciples, by which his plan was shown to be foolish because none of them agreed with him, acted likewise. Yet, after the example of Hushai the Archite, the apostle Peter denied Christ, the true David, not in heart but with his mouth, just as that Hushai denied David before Absalom.

Certainly, just as Hushai’s denial arose from David’s prudent counsel—David having through him foretold that Ahithophel’s counsel would be frustrated—so Peter’s denial of Christ himself was permitted by prudent counsel, not only to show the prince of the apostles what he was, since he had very rashly boasted that he would never deny him, but also so that through Peter Judas’s counsel might be frustrated. For because of the denial Peter, thought not to be a friend of the true David, escaped the danger of premature death; yet afterward he glorified him by a glorious death and, not merely by his life but also by his preaching, destroyed Judas’s foolish counsel, which had refused to let Christ reign.

CII. Here it should be noted that Judas’s sin, devised in profound malice and wholly nocturnal and dark, found no passage into the serenity of morning light. Peter’s fault, however, was like an evening mist [Col. 0069A] mingled with both light and darkness: he denied with his tongue the Christ whom he loved in his heart, sinning from frailty rather than malice. It undoubtedly found a passage from evening into morning when, after the cock’s crow, with daylight already approaching, he wept bitterly.

Likewise, the morning of Peter, girding himself and presuming too much upon himself, was not as bright as the morning of Lucifer, who rose excessively early, because Lucifer gloried in his own light, not in the Lord or for the Lord, but against the Lord. Such glorying and presumption arose from hatred of the Creator. Peter’s presumption, however, sprang from the root of love—not yet indeed fully brought to perfection unto the brightness of day, but like morning still mingled with darkness.

Yet there was for Peter an outcome from this morning, [Col. 0069B] and a delightful consummation of that love, reaching such meridian brightness of daylight that, conscious of it, he confidently answered his master, who asked him three times whether he loved him: “Lord, you know that I love you” (John 21:16). I think that the soul which loves in this way cries to its beloved through that very love: “Tell me where you feed, where you lie down at noon” (Song 1:6). Therefore Peter, loving thus, is also told: “Feed my lambs”; again, “feed my sheep” (John 21:17).

In feeding them, the issue of morning and evening was delightful to Peter: while resting at noon, and now, as evening approached, keeping watch and laboring against the wolves. This evening labor, or even the heat of noon, though it at times weighed upon him, nevertheless had a delightful outcome.

CIII. Hence another shepherd of sheep, tested and exercised by the frequent alternation of morning and evening, delighted by the outcome of such changes, says: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). This delight is truly praiseworthy. Whoever is not delighted to depart from such things is easily captured by earthly gains, since he is not delighted by the promise or expectation of heavenly gain. If the mind delights in this as it ought, it is neither lifted up by the morning of prosperity nor broken by the evening of adversity; nor is it itself changed amid such changes, having its heart fixed there where true joy is.

Accordingly, we pray that amid the changes of this world our hearts may be fixed there [Col. 0069D] where true joys are. For where a person’s treasure is, there also the person’s heart delights. Delight in transitory goods and temporal pleasures is cheap and unstable; but delight in spiritual pleasures and eternal goods is precious, never cloying, and ever enduring—such goods as righteousness, wisdom, charity, kindness, and the other gifts of this kind, which delight blessed souls now in part but there fully, where delights at your right hand, O God, will remain unto an endless end.

For these delights will not be drawn from that well whose water those who gladly drink will thirst for again, especially there where the rich man thirsted, who, asking for a drop of water, could not obtain it. For his delight had passed into the left hand, and the delight at your right hand did not belong to him.

CIV. All this delight proceeds from the fact that you, Lord, for whom hymn is fitting in Zion, having been born in her, “visited the earth and made it drunk.” You visited the blessed earth, of which it is said elsewhere: “You have blessed, Lord, your land” (Ps. 84:1). You visited by your own coming this blessed earth, set apart from the accursed earth which brings forth thorns and thistles: made flesh in a virgin womb, the blessed flower springing from the blessed earth, the fruit of a blessed womb.

Recognizing this, the angel said: “Blessed are you among women.” And holy Elizabeth likewise said: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1:42). Long ago you had visited barren women—for example Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, and the mother of Samson, or Samuel, [Col. 0070B] or Solomon, and finally the mother of John the Baptist, than whom none greater has arisen among those born of women. These seven mothers had formerly been barren; when you visited them, they bore great men: namely Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and the other illustrious men already named.

And behold, one greater than Solomon, or Samson, or any one of those men is here: the son of the Virgin, in whom the blessed Lord God of Israel visited and accomplished the redemption of his people. For although the fruitfulness of the aforesaid barren mothers came from the gift of divine visitation, nevertheless the words, “You visited the earth and made it drunk,” suit none of them. The earth of virginal flesh alone is distinguished by the prerogative of a singular visitation. Not cultivated by the plough of a man’s operation, but visited through the angel Gabriel, cherished by the Holy Spirit, and overshadowed by the power of the Most High, it conceived the Son of God.

Therefore, by a singular visitation, you, Lord—for whom hymn is fitting, O God, in Zion—visited this earth of the city of Zion and made it drunk: namely, with the dew or rain of the Holy Spirit, as that eminent friend of this bride had long beforehand desired and foretold: “Drop down, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth open and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness spring up with him” (Isa. 45:8). Magnificently, therefore, Lord, you visited the earth and wonderfully made it drunk, giving drink from the torrent of your delight to her who was separated from the accursed earth that brings forth thorns and thistles, in order that she might bring forth the Savior.

CV. After this earth gave its fruit, the blessed fruit, in accordance with that oracle of the Gospel greeting, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1:42), that same fruit was threshed through the passion, sown anew in the earth through death, and died in the earth. From it much fruit sprang forth, in accordance with the words: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit” (John 12:24).

By this abundant fruit you multiplied to enrich her, because the honor of the Son will in large measure be ascribed to the mother, when she herself, as queen, will rule in the kingdom of her Son. For you, Lord, who in dying fell into the earth, rising from [Col. 0071A] the dead brought forth much fruit, because “ascending on high, you led captivity captive; you gave gifts to men” (Eph. 4:8). Through these gifts you again visited the earth and made it drunk, so that your disciples were thought to be full of new wine. You so made them drunk with your Spirit and estranged them from themselves that their earthly substance, made drunk from heaven, became wholly heavenly.

After you had thus visited the earth and made it drunk, those who had first been earthly became heavenly: “the heavens declared the glory of God” (Ps. 18:1). You also sent them like rain-bearing clouds over the whole earth, which you visited and made drunk with their teachings: the holy Church spread through the world, made drunk by the splendid cup of your passion, forgetting what lies behind and stretching [Col. 0071B] itself toward what lies ahead. In these things you multiplied to enrich her, because you endowed her with gifts of manifold grace, which came to her in this order.

CVI. First: “The river of God is filled with waters.” That is, the former people, bounded by the banks of the commandments of the Law, whose channel was almost dried up because its stream of blessing was scanty. Yet its blessing was in the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven above, because Esau, detained and occupied with hunting flesh, was nourished almost solely by promises and expectations of carnal and earthly goods. Indeed, even the apostles chosen from that people, in their beginnings, thought carnally about the kingdom of God.

That people, I say, in the few called from it, is called and is the river of God. For Isaiah reproaches the rest, like stagnant waters, saying: “Because you have come forth from the waters of Judah” (Isa. 48:1): that is, you are the seed of Judah only according to the flow of the flesh, not according to the fruit of faith. For according to the baseness of your conduct, you are the seed of Canaan and not of Judah, because your father is an Amorite and your mother a Hittite.

Therefore, while these persons, like muddy waters, rightly dry up and fail, the river of God is filled with waters in the true Israelites. One such was he of whom the very fountain of this river said: “Behold, a true Israelite, in whom there is no guile” (John 1:47). Such were all the apostles except Judas, who had come forth from the waters of Judah, wholly estranged from the nobility of its faith.

[Col. 0071D] CVII. Therefore, with waters of this kind rejected as putrid and bitter, the river of God was filled with pure and sweet waters when, as the apostles sat together in one upper room, “there suddenly came from heaven a sound as of a mighty rushing spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:2). Once they had thus been given drink, so that food might not be lacking in abundance, you prepared their food: having drunk the water of saving wisdom, they had an understanding of the truth which was to be fulfilled, and they also saw the manifest result of that truth once fulfilled, as though it were solid bread. Nor did this happen by chance, since the preparation of that food by which the elect are fed is such that first, purified and refreshed by the water of wisdom, they understand what they ought to ask or desire; then they ask for and receive the manifest effects of the things understood, [Col. 0072A] as the bread of life and understanding. Thus a good understanding is for them saving water and drink, while its manifest effect is their food.

Some unbelievers oppose this preparation and say: “For he struck the rock and waters flowed, and torrents overflowed; can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people?” (Ps. 77:20). That is to say: Since Christ’s side was struck and waters of wisdom flowed from that side of the temple, filling believers’ hearts with understanding so that they know what ought to be requested or done, will he add to this gift of understanding the gift of effective accomplishment? Because the word of God runs swiftly through the mouths of teachers or the pens of scribes writing swiftly, will obedience follow with the same [Col. 0072B] speed with which understanding has gone before? Truly, he foretold that it would be so, who elsewhere says: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. 17:47). Wonderful is the speed of obedience that accompanies hearing! For obedience to the commanded work does not follow after the hearing of the ear; rather, “at the hearing,” he says, “of the ear they obeyed me.”

CVIII. Then there is added, accordingly, concerning those who are slow and lame travelers, who have the foot of understanding sound and strong, but carry the foot of disobedience weak and halting: “Foreign sons have lied to me; foreign sons have grown old, and have limped from their paths” (ibid., 46). Without doubt theirs is that murmuring in which it is said: “For he struck the rock [Col. 0072C] and waters flowed, and torrents overflowed; can he give bread also, or prepare a table for his people?” (Ps. 77:20). These people hear the word but delay obeying. They hear the signal by which they are summoned to the Church, but delay coming. That is to say: Because it is easy for masters to command, will it likewise be easy for disciples to keep their commands? They hear the inward counsel of the Holy Spirit, by which he suggests that something should be done, but delay consenting. Therefore the Lord heard and delayed. He heard their petition, but delayed answering it. He heard their groaning in tribulations, but delayed delivering them from these. He heard the enemies’ insults against them, but delayed vengeance and defense.

[Col. 0072D] For this is certainly understood of teaching: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and from his belly shall flow living waters” (John 7:37). Likewise: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give him shall not thirst again; but the water that I give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:13).

CIX. The river of God was filled with waters from a living vein of this kind when the Holy Spirit, coming in tongues, taught the apostles and filled their hearts with understanding. Since they promptly and willingly assented to the truth understood, and were as though filled with new wine, you promptly and willingly prepared their food: namely, the perfect work and the good effect of good understanding, concerning which you may say: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (ibid., 34). For in the disciples there was obedience [Col. 0073A] without delay, through which it was ready at hand for God to give bread and prepare a table for his people; just as, on the contrary, the same speaker, in his apostle, has at hand the power to avenge every disobedience.

CX. Therefore, when Peter had already been given drink through understanding and hungered for the result, it was said from heaven: “Slay and eat” (Acts 11:7). A table was prepared before him, full of many kinds of food, on which were land animals and birds of heaven, because active and contemplative persons from among the Gentiles were to be converted, were to belong to the Church of God, and were to pass into Peter’s body through obedience rendered without delay—such obedience as Peter first found in the house of Cornelius, the centurion from among the Gentiles, and such as the venerable Father Saint Benedict commends in his Rule.

“The first,” he says, “degree of humility [Col. 0073B] is obedience without delay. This befits those who consider nothing dearer to themselves than Christ, whether because of fear of hell or the glory of eternal life. As soon as something has been commanded by a superior, as if commanded by God himself, they know no delay in doing it. Of these the Lord says: ‘At the hearing of the ear they obeyed me’ (Ps. 17:45). And again the Lord says: ‘He who hears you hears me’ (Luke 10:16). Such persons, therefore, immediately leaving what is their own and abandoning their own will, with hands at once freed and leaving unfinished what they were doing, follow the commanding voice with the foot of obedience close at hand. As though in one moment, the command previously given by the master and the completed work of the disciple are both jointly accomplished with the swiftness of the fear of God, [Col. 0073C] in those upon whom rests the love of advancing toward eternal life. Therefore they take up the narrow way. Hence the Lord says: ‘Narrow is the way that leads to life’ (Matt. 7:14), so that, not living by their own judgment or obeying their own desires and pleasures, but walking under another’s judgment and command, dwelling in monasteries, they desire to have an abbot set over them. Beyond doubt, such persons imitate that saying of the Lord in which he says: ‘I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father’ (John 6:38).

“But this very obedience will then be acceptable to God and pleasing to men if what is commanded is carried out neither sluggishly, nor tardily, nor hesitantly, nor with murmuring or a reluctant reply; for the obedience rendered to superiors [Col. 0073D] is rendered to God. For he himself said: ‘He who hears you hears me’ (Luke 10:16). It must also be rendered by disciples with a good disposition, because ‘God loves a cheerful giver’ (2 Cor. 9:7). For if a disciple obeys in a bad spirit, and murmurs not only with his mouth but also in his heart, even though he fulfills the command, it will no longer be acceptable to God, who looks upon the heart of the murmurer. He obtains no reward for such a deed; indeed, he incurs the punishment of murmurers unless he corrects himself by making satisfaction.”

CXI. Moreover, in the Rule of Blessed Augustine, where it is said, “Let the superior be obeyed as a father,” the same obedience is commended, though in very few words—not to be rendered with servile sluggishness and lack of devotion, as from sadness and necessity, but with the gladness [Col. 0074A] of filial love. “Let the superior,” he says, “be obeyed as a father,” so that the one who obeys may be drawn to obedience more by filial love than by servile fear; and so that the one obeyed, though both are necessary, may nevertheless prefer to be loved rather than feared—loved as a father, not feared as a master. For he who, though by rank is called and is a superior before men, nevertheless is laid beneath even the feet of his subjects before God through fear, will regard himself as blessed not through ruling power but through serving love.

In superiors of this kind—followers of the apostolic life and successors of the apostles after them—the river of God was filled with waters, as has above been explained concerning the apostles themselves. And you, O God, prepared their food as you did that of the apostles: first giving them sound understanding as drink, [Col. 0074B] then a real effect as solid food.

CXII. Or again, the river of God was filled with waters when the word of Truth was believed in the Scriptures. And you, O God, prepared the food of believers by giving them the life-giving refreshment of your body and blood, denied to all unbelievers; for the preparation of that food is such that it must first be believed, and then received. For it is fitting that only believers be told: “Take and eat: this is my body” (Matt. 26:26).

CXIII. “Make its streams drunk.” When the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul in God, and their dispersal among the nations had not yet occurred, but all the disciples were together in the same place and nearly all shared the same purpose of holy life, there was as yet no division of God’s river into many streams; rather, all the fullness of its waters was together. For that is properly called the river of God whose source and origin is found to be God himself, who alone is the author and founder of the kind of life the apostles maintained, and to whom it is said: “Lord, with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10). The fountain is with God the fountain: God Christ is with the Father. Yet there are not two fountains, but one fountain, just as there are not two gods but one God. The Spirit of both, proceeding from there like a vein consubstantial with each, invisibly penetrated the apostles’ breasts; and thus the river of God was filled with waters while they were still gathered together in the confined place of Judea, when, as [Col. 0074D] was said, all the disciples were together in the same place under the undivided holy purpose of one common life.

Then, with the dispersal of the disciples, as though one river had been drawn out into many streams, some disciples delighted in being entirely solitary; their discipline produced monks. Others were retained by the task of teaching and governing the Church; their institution flourished among clergy religiously ordered to a common life. A distinction like that of one river into many streams also arose among the multitude converted from the Gentiles to faith: some were restricted to the purpose of continence, as though preserving the water of their devotion in utter purity within the narrowness of their banks; others were released to lawful marriage, like waters running over level ground and therefore [Col. 0075A] indeed drawing mud along, yet holding to the origin of their source. Accordingly, they are to be counted among its streams. Thus, formerly, when the Jordan was divided for Jesus’ crossing, the portion which held to the source retained the name of stream; but those which, cut off from their spring origin, flowed into the Dead Sea, when their channel was wholly dried up, lost the name of stream and themselves perished and failed as though they had not existed; and by their failure they opened a way for the people of God.

CXIV. For, as is read in the book of Joshua, when he himself crossed the middle of the channel of the Jordan with the ark of the covenant, the upper waters, raised up like a mountain, could be seen far away, while the lower waters, flowing downward and failing, vanished altogether; later the upper waters descended into the place thus emptied [Col. 0075B] by them. So may all sects of the ungodly perish and come to nothing like running water—sects which, because of the name of Christianity and the sacrament of baptism, seem to be waters of the Jordan, although they have been severed from the vein of the fountain of this name. May they perish and fail, and by their failure open a way for the people of God; and may they leave their channel empty through their failure and departure for the true Jordanian waters that depend upon their source.

Among the other sects that are to perish—as, thanks be to God, many already have perished—may that sect of clerics also perish and come to nothing, which the holy Fathers, in their descriptions, call acephali, that is, “headless.” From this it may be understood that even a life without a head does not altogether lack limbs. Their wandering and dissolute manner of life is found nowhere in all the rules derived from the fountain or river of evangelical or apostolic teaching, since they live neither according to the canons nor observe the rules of cenobitic life derived from the fountain or river of God filled with waters.

But so that the force of this river may gladden the city of God unto the end of the age, do you, fountain of this most pure light, make its streams drunk, so that no want may exist, either through lack of persons or lack of virtues, in every way of life ordered according to evangelical and apostolic rules, even in the life of married people disposed according to the law of divine justice. Make its streams drunk, so that first the life of those who [Col. 0075D] abstain from wine in which is debauchery—that is, from every alluring vanity of this world—may be intoxicated with better wine, which fills it with the Holy Spirit, according to the Apostle’s words: “Do not,” he says, “be drunk with wine, in which is debauchery; but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to God in your hearts” (Eph. 5:18).

CXV. Therefore, because praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, make those who sing psalms and hymns so drunk that they lack no grace while awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, the great priest, who restores his people from captivity and rebuilds his holy temple, burned by the Chaldean fire of avarice and lust. But because [Col. 0076A] the life of the continent cannot be uniform in all who profess it, “multiply its offspring,” so that whoever can receive it may receive virginal holiness with the Blessed Virgin Mary and her guardian, John the Evangelist. Whoever cannot receive this, after committing public sins, may receive penitential continence with Matthew the Evangelist and Mary Magdalene.

Multiply also the offspring of this same life in this respect: let there be many regular monasteries, of one purity and holiness indeed, yet, owing to the distribution of manifold grace, let their observance be differentiated in various ways and by many modes. This is according to what is read of Joseph, clothed in one long robe prepared for him by his father, which was nevertheless not of one color but embroidered in many colors, that is, distinguished by various colors. Thus may the beautiful and comely queen stand beside the king, more beautiful than the sons of men, adorned indeed with one golden garment, yet clothed about with golden fringes. That is, according to the differing condition or custom of various churches and even persons, let whoever can receive it receive and maintain a rigor imitable only by few and strong persons; whoever cannot receive it, let that person receive the discriminating concession tolerable even for children or women—such as existed in the primitive Church, ordered with such discernment that religion itself was bearable not only for strong men but also for fragile women.

And in it was Stephen, full of grace and strength, but he ministered to feminine frailty. Those [Col. 0076C] who were greater devoted themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word; those who were lesser busied themselves with the frequent service necessary to the present life. All alike, greater and lesser, were of one heart and one soul in God, and none of them either possessed or called anything his own. Yet distribution was not made equally to all, because all were not equally able; rather, it was made to each according to what each needed—that is, to one more and to another less, according as was necessary for each. Thus the weak were not forced by the strong toward stricter things beyond their strength, nor were the strong drawn by the weak toward looser things suitable only for the feeble. Thus the river of the Lord was filled with waters, so that no one among them lacked even temporal assistance.

[Col. 0076D] CXVI. The same fullness is now desired for its streams when it is said: “Make its streams drunk; multiply its offspring,” so that no grace may be lacking to those who follow a stricter life and chastely pursue the discipline established by the holy apostles and derived from the supreme fountain of purity. But because not all receive this saying—so as, on leaving Sodom, immediately to hasten upward to the heights of the mountain—it is granted to the weak to remain in little and modest Zoar, because they possess slight strength and are not fit to ascend the mountain of the Lord or stand in his holy place. There the innocent in hands and clean of heart ascends, joined in the sixth degree of the eight beatitudes to those blessed persons who shall see God because they are pure in heart.

Let these others be content with the lower and lesser degrees of the beatitudes: namely, “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” “blessed are the meek,” “blessed are those who mourn,” “blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness,” “blessed are the merciful,” because the life of married persons must be cleansed and purified through works of mercy; so that those who use this world may be as though they did not use it, and those who have wives may be as though they had none. “I desire,” says the Apostle, “that younger women marry and bear children” (1 Tim. 5:14). Likewise: “Let each man have his own wife and each woman her own husband” (Eph. 5:33), namely in order to avoid fornication and to beget offspring.

CXVII. Watered by teachings of this kind as by certain drops, the fruitful earth will rejoice, being so adjacent to the river of God filled with waters that, even if it cannot be made drunk among its streams, it nevertheless rejoices and bears fruit in its drops. For from the well-ordered life of married persons comes the offspring of blessed and well-disciplined sons or daughters, and the fruit of good works. Let these drops descend upon the earth and make it fruitful. “Drop down, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth open and bring forth the Savior” (Isa. 45:8). Let it open by assenting to sound teaching, and bring forth the Savior Christ by showing in its fruits the power of God and the wisdom of God. Let this same power and wisdom of God descend like rain upon the fleece and like drops falling upon the earth, so that by such rain the fleece of virginal purpose may be filled, and the fruitful earth of married persons [Col. 0077C] may rejoice in its drops.

It is praiseworthy in this respect: although it does not wholly abstain from wine in which is debauchery, as virginity is entirely separated from such wine, still in its fruit is found choice grain and wine bringing forth virgins, while a blessed people is born from lawful marriage. Such was the man sent from God, Blessed John, born from lawful marriage, drinking neither wine nor strong drink and eating nothing unclean. Because many rejoiced at his birth, the fruitful earth itself also rejoiced that this choice grain would be the cause of such great joy.

CXVIII. Do you wish to hear what voice of exultation and joy sounded in that land? “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished redemption for his people” (Luke 1:68), said the boy’s father. And, turning directly to the boy himself: “You,” he said, “child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (ibid., 16). He certainly remembered the angelic promise by which it had been said: “He himself shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to prepare a perfect people for the Lord” (ibid., 17). The mother rejoiced, and her neighbors rejoiced with her, so that the saying of the angel might be proved true: “And many shall rejoice at his birth” (ibid., 14).

It was a delightful spectacle to see, in one house, the river of God filled with waters, while the son was still filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb; its streams made drunk, while both parents, through the merits of the child born to them, reveal hidden things; and the earth rejoicing in its drops, while the neighbors rejoiced with the rejoicing parents. [Col. 0078A] At the first coming into the world of the Son of God, building for himself the house of a forerunner, one herald sufficed in the narrow land of Judea. But now, before the second coming, by whose illumination Antichrist, the chief prince of Babylon, is to be destroyed and the temple destroyed by him rebuilt, I think one herald will not suffice. Rather, so that every word may stand in the mouth of two witnesses, two witnesses, two olive trees, two lampstands, and two lamps burning and shining are required to drive away the darkness sown by Antichrist and scattered throughout the whole world.

CXIX. The great and holy Fathers say various things concerning these two witnesses and heralds of the second coming. For many, of whom Blessed Gregory is foremost, maintain that Elijah and Enoch will come bodily, fight Antichrist, and be bodily killed by him. Others, of whom the eminent Jerome is foremost, interpret Moses and Elijah as the two witnesses already designated, who appeared with the Lord on the mountain. Malachi names them expressly, saying: “Remember the law of Moses my servant, which I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel, statutes and judgments. Behold, I shall send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes; and he shall turn the heart of fathers toward their children, and the heart of children toward their fathers, lest perhaps I come and strike the earth with anathema” (Mal. 4:4–6).

Treating this passage, Blessed Jerome says among other things: “After Moses, whose commandments we have taught must especially be observed, he says that Elijah is to be [Col. 0078C] sent. In Moses he signifies the Law; in Elijah, prophecy, as Abraham says to a certain rich man clothed in purple: ‘They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them’ (Luke 16:29). And the Lord and Savior, transfigured on the mountain, has Moses and Elijah in white garments speaking with him; they also told him what he was to suffer in Jerusalem. For the Law and the whole choir of prophets proclaim Christ’s passion.

“Therefore, before the day of the Lord comes and the Lord strikes the earth with anathema—or utterly or suddenly, as the Septuagint translated; for this is what ἄρδην means—the Lord will send in Elijah, whose name means ‘my God’ and who is from the town of Thesbi, a name signifying conversion and repentance, the whole choir [Col. 0078D] of prophets, to turn the heart of the fathers—that is, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets—toward their children, so that their descendants may believe in the Lord and Savior, in whom they too believed. For Abraham saw the day of the Lord and rejoiced. Or, the heart of the Father toward the son—that is, the heart of God toward everyone who has received the Spirit of adoption—and the heart of children toward their fathers, so that Jews and Christians, who now differ among themselves, may agree in an equal devotion to Christ. Hence it is said to the apostles, who handed down the seed of the Gospel throughout the whole world: ‘Sons have been born to you in place of your fathers’ (Ps. 44:17).

“For unless Elijah first turns the heart of fathers toward children and the heart of children toward their fathers before the great and terrible day comes—great for the saints, terrible for sinners—the true and just Judge will strike with anathema not the heavens nor those who dwell in heaven, but the earth, that is, those who do earthly works. Jews and Judaizing heretics think that their Elijah will come and restore all things. Hence in the Gospel a question is put to Christ: Why is it that ‘the Pharisees say Elijah is to come?’ (Matt. 11:14). To them he replied: ‘Elijah indeed will come; but if you believe, he has already come,’ understanding John in Elijah.”

CXX. Since Saint Jerome says these things, it is not incredible, once the Jewish interpretation has been rejected, that Moses and Elijah are the Law and prophecy. These have now been carefully expounded and set before every congregation of the whole Church; whoever does not obey them will not believe, even if [Col. 0079B] someone rises from the dead. Nor will they believe if Elijah comes bodily, as Jews and Judaizers think; nor if Enoch and Elijah—who, as Blessed Gregory says, deferred death but did not escape it—appear visibly so as, fighting Antichrist and enduring his tyranny, to pay the debt of death, as many expect. Those who do not hear Moses and the prophets will not believe them: those who despise Catholic teachers speaking in the spirit and power of Moses and Elijah; who reject and refuse to follow those rising from the town of Thesbi, which means conversion or repentance, and summoning others to conversion and repentance by their example.

These persons, finally, do not sit by the rivers of Babylon and breathe forth their captivity in weeping; rather, immersed in those same rivers like fish, they do not care about rebuilding the nest of the holy city and temple. Yet those who, like little birds, sit above Babylon’s rivers seek their nest, continually singing: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, and to you shall a vow be paid in Jerusalem. Hear my prayer.” Therefore, as they begin to set out, lest heralds or forerunners be lacking—men like Moses and Elijah, or Haggai and Jeremiah, or, according to another interpretation, Enoch and Elijah, speaking and acting in their spirit and power—the river of God is filled with waters in entirely spiritual men. And so that, multiplied, they may abound, earth made fruitful by the drops of the same river will rejoice, according to the grace of that blessing stated [Col. 0079D] in the beginning: “Let the earth bring forth green grass, yielding seed, and fruit-bearing trees according to their kind” (Gen. 1:11).

There is no mention in this declaration either of thorns or thistles, with which the earth was cursed after sin, when God said: “When you cultivate the earth, it shall not yield its fruits; but it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:18). The fruitful earth, polluted by the sin of the first parent Adam through the word of exile whispered by the devil through the serpent, will not rejoice in shoots of that kind. For from the time it was said to the woman, “I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions” (ibid., 16), the offspring of vipers—wicked children, children of wrath, children of hell—have so multiplied [Col. 0080A] that the small number of the elect was alien amid their multitude. In bringing them forth, the earth of woman’s condition was nearly barren: with sorrows and conceptions of evil children multiplied, that cursed feminine earth willingly brought them forth like thorns and thistles, nearly barren of good and fertile in evil shoots, until that [lacuna; see note]—“of your goodness, and your fields shall be filled with abundance.” [Note: [Col. 0079] Something seems to be missing through a printing defect. Perhaps one should read: “until that: You will bless the crown of the year, etc.”]

CXXI. The year of goodness is that in which appeared the goodness and loving-kindness of God our Savior, who saved us not by works of righteousness which we performed, but according to his mercy, through the washing of regeneration and renewal, though we had been lost through the foulness of generation and the guilt of the ancient [Col. 0080B] transgression. Thus even the holy man, though anticipated by the blessing of sweetness by which God had blessed the first parents before sin, saying, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:22), nevertheless complains: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. 50:7).

But because, as God revealed, he knew the uncertain and hidden things of God’s wisdom, he did not fail to know that he had come into the world from the blessing rather than the curse pronounced upon the woman, in order to abolish the stains of carnal conception and generation. He therefore prophesies to himself the washing of regeneration, saying: “You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me and I shall be made whiter than snow” (ibid., 9). Therefore, although this man was born before the year of goodness, he nevertheless shows that he belongs to this fruitful year, whose whole crown throughout the circuit of its revolution is blessed and filled with plentiful fruits of abundance, according as it is written: “The threshing of the harvest shall overtake the vintage, and the treader of grapes the sower of seed” (Lev. 26:5).

That is to say: There will be such abundance of harvest to be gathered into the Lord’s barns that, considering the multitude of crops, the Lord must be asked to send—or thrust out—many laborers into the great harvest. While they reap and thresh, the work of reaping and threshing will, because of the excessive abundance of grain, be prolonged until the vintage, in which the treader of the abundant grapes, long occupied, will overtake the sower of seed preparing another harvest. Finally, when the year of goodness has ended and returned into itself, all tares that must be tolerated until that harvest will be gathered.

CXXII. Behold, the crown of this year will thus be blessed, so that throughout its entire circuit abundance overflows: now of reapers and threshers, now of vintagers and grape-treaders, and again of sowers, without interruption of this most joyful husbandry. The time of the first harvest is understood to be that in which the lord of the harvest said to the first reapers: “Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest” (John 4:35). Likewise: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore ask the lord of the harvest [Col. 0081A] to send laborers into his harvest” (Matt. 9:37–38).

For then the time was at hand for the conversion not only of the multitude of believers from among the Jews, who were to be of one heart and one soul, but also of the multitude of Gentiles seeking living waters. On the occasion of the conversion of a single Samaritan woman and of citizens from that city coming to him, the lord of the harvest spoke these words. In such firstfruits he then contemplated the entire harvest of the Gentiles as though ripe for reaping, calling his disciples to the same contemplation. He said to them: “Do you not say, ‘There are still four months, and harvest comes’?” (John 4:35, 38). As though rejecting that saying, he said: “Lift up your eyes and see the fields, because they are already white for harvest. I sent you to reap that for which you have not labored. Others labored, and you have entered into their labors.”

For many kings and prophets wished to see what was granted to the apostles to see, and did not see it. Yet, holding the plow of long-suffering expectation, they indeed overtook the reaper, because they fixed the eyes of their faith and hope upon his coming; and, seeing his day, they rejoiced, greeting it from afar. Thus the prophecy was fulfilled through them: “The plowman shall overtake the reaper” (Amos 9:13). Yet they did not themselves enter into the harvest, because their days were swifter than a runner, as holy Job laments.

John the Baptist too, the last herald, who even with bodily hands clasped him in baptizing—the soldier clasping the king, the servant the Lord—nevertheless showed that it was denied him to walk after Christ with the holy apostles and other suitable reapers, and to carry his sandals in the field full of grain, whose fragrance the patriarch Jacob had sensed from afar. But neither he nor anyone who preceded Christ’s death saw that grain multiplied which, not yet fallen into the ground, had not died; and which the blessed eyes of the first apostles saw bring forth much fruit, as the number of believers multiplied and extended to the ends of the earth. Though this had been promised to Abraham himself, it was not shown to his eyes in present reality, because the year of goodness had not yet come, whose whole crown, [Col. 0081D] whose entire circuit, is full of abundant fruits.

CXXIII. Thus the apostolic reapers, entering into others’ labors, gathered multitudes of Gentiles into the Lord’s barns. And while they were still gathering sheaves in such a harvest, the vintage overtook them, and Nero, the first treader of grapes, crushed the choice clusters Peter and Paul, then the rest, ready and ripe for the winepresses of suffering. So, after him, as persecution became frequent, the treader of grapes was not lacking until he overtook the sower of seed. For after the dreadful contests of the martyrs, when holy confessors and teachers had multiplied throughout the whole world, through explanations of both Testaments brought to light, he who sows went out to sow his seed. And indeed he sowed good seed [Col. 0082A] in his field.

But while the guardians of the same field slept, an enemy sowed tares over the wheat and went away. Yet where tares become overwhelmingly strong, choke the wheat, and strive to occupy the Lord’s field by themselves, there is no reason why they should be spared, as there is where both grow together and care must be taken lest, in uprooting the tares, the wheat mingled among them also be uprooted. Thus very many sects and perverse teachings have been uprooted and condemned by synodal judgment for this reason: wheat could not grow together with them.

But the sect of clerics living under no rule, whether synodal or cenobitic, is found to have been pruned many times by the apostolic sickle since the time for pruning arrived, because the excessiveness of dress and other disorders are cut away from such persons by apostolic decrees. Yet unless it is wholly uprooted and that utterly unauthentic rule in which they glory is entirely condemned, the good seed of holy rules and paternal traditions is choked. What necessity, finally, is there for clergy in the principal and mother churches to profess that they will observe a rule forged in the king’s court? Since, while mixed with the sound teachings of the Fathers, it has been corrupted by the small leaven of royal concession—like wine mixed with gall, which the Lord tasted and would not drink—it must without doubt be rejected and deprived of its name, lest that be called a canonical rule which is found contrary to the sacred canons and is, moreover, wholly condemned beforehand in the decrees of Pope Urban.

[Col. 0082C] CXXIV. Since this distinguished martyr, by apostolic authority, lays down in his decrees a rule concerning the goods of the Church, according to which they are evidently to be administered—namely, for clerics living the common life and for other poor persons—royal and lay authority has no standing whatever to enact anything contrary. For, as Pope Symmachus affirms in his decrees, “No authority whatsoever is ever found to have been assigned to laypersons, however religious, in disposing of ecclesiastical matters.” Thus that Emperor Louis, as he is said to have been, may have been pious both in name and in fact, who allowed the goods assigned to those living the common life and to the poor in each mother church to be distributed to the rich, who possessed abundance of their own.

Of greater weight for me is the apostolic authority, clearly enough expressed in the decrees of Pope and martyr Urban concerning church property, [Col. 0082D] and established under threat of condemnation in such a way that it is lawful for no one—not merely for laypersons, but not even for bishops—to decree anything contrary to his ordinances. Indeed, against those who deal otherwise than he prescribes with the aforementioned goods of the Church, he threatens the judgment of Ananias and Sapphira with so grave a burden of condemnation that what they suffered bodily for withholding such goods, their followers may suffer in the soul—a death more to be feared than bodily death.
