For, after confirming the common life among clergy in mother churches, preserved from the time of the apostles down to his own time and, he affirms, to be preserved in them for all future ages, he pronounces a judgment concerning church goods to be observed in every church and altered in no royal court. “The goods,” he says, “of the individual parishes were and are, until now, under the authority of bishops, who hold the place of the apostles; and they ought always to be so in future times. From these goods bishops and their faithful stewards must supply all necessities, as best they can, to all who wish to live the common life, so that none among them may be found in need. [Col. 0083A] For these goods are called the offerings of the faithful, because they are offered to the Lord. Therefore they must not be turned to uses other than ecclesiastical ones and those of the aforementioned Christian brethren or of the needy; for they are the vows of the faithful and the price of sins, and have been delivered to the Lord for carrying out the aforesaid work. But if anyone—may it not be so!—acts otherwise, let him beware lest he incur the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira and become guilty of sacrilege.”

CXXV. In these words of Saint Urban, a law for ecclesiastical support is established from the chief example of the Acts of the Apostles: according to this law, those who are willing and able to serve must receive the support of their service. But since not all receive this word, so that those counted among the clergy may voluntarily embrace the purpose of common life and continence—and that purpose must not be imposed upon anyone through violent and unjust exactions—apostolic discernment also makes allowance for such weaker persons. Thus blessed Pope Gregory, writing to Augustine, bishop of the English, after assigning the rule of common life, established by the holy apostles under Christ’s authorship, to clergy living in a community, and commending it to the aforesaid bishop for observance with the clerics dwelling with him, added this also concerning clerics of a lower rank:

“If there are any clerics outside the sacred orders who cannot remain continent, they ought to take wives and receive their stipends externally. And because we know it is written concerning those same portions of which we have spoken, that distribution was made to each according to his need, provision and care must also be taken concerning their support. They are to be kept under an ecclesiastical rule, so that they may live with good morals, apply themselves diligently to the singing of psalms, and, with God as their author, preserve heart, tongue, and body from every unlawful thing.” [Col. 0083B]

It should be noted that Saint Gregory says married clerics must be kept not under a canonical or apostolic rule, but under an ecclesiastical rule, which he summarizes briefly: “Let them,” he says, “live with good morals, apply themselves diligently to the singing of psalms, and, with God as their author, preserve heart, tongue, and body from every unlawful thing.” Where clerics of this kind are formed by a Christian rule and receive suitable support externally, outside communities, the community gathered into one is not thrown into the confusion found in King Louis’s rule. Although it contains many most holy institutions of common life, it is confused in this respect: private and personal dwellings are permitted to the very clerics for whom monasteries or cloisters are there ordained.

What is this but a contradiction in terms, so that one thing is destroyed by the other? Thus, when one says “a dead animal,” by the addition of “dead” to “animal,” the animal is understood to have been destroyed by that qualification. For if it is dead, it is not an animal, since “animal” is the name of a living thing. Likewise, when, after a cloister has been arranged with its gates and guards, a private and personal house is left to the inhabitants of that cloister and granted through a kind of supposedly pious indulgence by a pious king, the whole cloistered arrangement is confused and corrupted. It is as though a little poison were added to much wine, so that the “woe” of eternal condemnation may be drunk more sweetly—a woe which Scripture indicates when it says: “Woe to the sinner who enters the land by two ways!” (Ecclus. 2:14). [Col. 0084A]

CXXVI. Do not those walk by two ways who, under the permission of such a rule, accept the institutions of a community together with the indulgence of a private home? Another blameworthy feature of the aforesaid rule is that, in its first chapter, evangelical exhortations to the highest perfection—such as, “Go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21), and others like them—are assigned to monks alone; while clerics, no less than other Christians, are at the same time instructed indiscriminately, through certain lower requirements, in obligations commonly binding upon all baptized in Christ.

Such teachings are surely more fittingly made in a royal court than in the apostolic see. For, just as King Antiochus wrote throughout his kingdom that all the people should be one people, so King Louis—excepting monks alone—joins the clergy to the people, and either himself writes, or approves another of his clerical chaplains writing, throughout his whole realm, that the people should be one people, and that it should become, “as is the people, so is the priest.” [Col. 0084B]

The commandments of the Law, therefore, are better than those of the king. For in the Law the tribe of Levi is read to have been wholly separated from the other tribes and deprived of earthly inheritance. And the giver of blessing under the New Law wished and taught that the ministers of his word and stewards of the mysteries of God should be separated not only from the people of common Christianity, but also from the body committed to the spiritual and monastic purpose: namely, so that not all monks become clerics, but only some among them are chosen and separated, by a certain prerogative, to live more holily than the rest.

[Col. 0084D] CXXVII. Therefore the Apostle Paul, set apart for the Gospel of God, glories in the Lord that he, together with Barnabas, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, was set apart for the work of evangelizing—not only from the lax purpose of those living secular lives and using marriage, but also from the strict and almost monastic institution of those living the common life. For while the disciples were ministering and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13:2).

Accordingly, every teaching that joins what God has separated, or separates what he himself has joined—such as the institution of the aforesaid king, which separates clerics from monks in the pursuit of holiness, though God has joined them and, with regard to priestly office, exalted the former above the latter; and which joins clerics to the people, though the divine word distinguishes them from it, as upright two-footed shepherds from a four-footed flock bent down toward the ground, as clouds flying on high from the earth lying below and thirsting for rain from the high clouds—every such teaching, I say, resembles not the river whose rushing gladdens David’s city, but troubled water. As is read in the Apocalypse, the dragon sent it from his mouth like a river after the woman who bore a male child destined to rule all nations, in order to sweep her away with the river. But “the earth opened its mouth and swallowed up the river, helping the woman” (Apoc. 12:16). [Col. 0085A]

Thus the mouths of teachers who establish the true faith have been opened not only to swallow heretical teaching; the mouth of the earth has also more than once been opened to swallow the aforesaid rule, likened to muddy water. Yet its river has not wholly been swallowed up, branded with manifest condemnation, or rejected as it ought to be rejected: like a sacrifice that, although rightly offered, is not rightly divided, but excessively confused—since in the observance of holiness clerics are distinguished from monks, yet are joined in an excessively confused way to the people whom they must govern.

CXXVIII. Pope Urban II, writing more rightly concerning the canonical order, both offered and divided more rightly for regular clerics in this manner:

“We who, though unworthy, sit in Peter’s place, ought to correct what is wrong, establish what is right, and arrange matters to be arranged throughout the whole Church according to the judgment of the inward Judge, so that our judgment may proceed from his countenance and our eyes may behold equity. [Col. 0085B] Therefore we give thanks to almighty God, whose mercy is better than lives, because you are those who renew the worthy life of the holy Fathers and, by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, revive the institutions of apostolic discipline, which arose at the beginning of the holy Church but, as the Church grew, had now almost perished.

“For from the beginning of the holy Church two forms of life have been established for her children: one by which the weakness of the infirm is sustained, the other by which the blessed strength of the stronger is perfected; one remaining in little Zoar, the other ascending to the heights of the mountain; one redeeming daily sins by tears and alms, the other acquiring eternal merits by daily earnest striving. Those who hold the lower way use earthly goods; those who follow the higher despise and abandon earthly goods. This latter way, which turns aside from earthly things, is divided into two portions, nearly of one and the same purpose: that is, canons and monks. The latter of these, through divine mercy, is now sufficiently widespread and shines throughout the whole world. The former, however, as the fervor of the faithful has cooled, has now almost entirely disappeared. [Col. 0085C]

“This was instituted by Urban, martyr and pontiff; this Augustine ordered by his rules; this Jerome shaped by his letters; this Gregory commanded Augustine, archbishop of the English, to establish. Therefore it is to be judged no less meritorious to raise up this primitive life of the Church, with the Spirit of the Lord inspiring and sustaining it, than to preserve, through the perseverance of the same Spirit, the flourishing religious life of monks.”

CXXIX. Since in these words of the Roman pontiff the whole Church is most carefully described as distinguished according to its orders, nowhere in it is included the life of clerics living according to King Louis’s rule—or rather, violating that same rule in its more important institutions. Thus unjust judges, joined to the rock, have been swallowed up: those who deform the order of clergy, anciently well formed and firmly founded upon the rock. Let us therefore drink from the spiritual rock that follows us, in the most pure teaching of the Apostle Peter and his successors; and let us beware of drinking from the muddy river which the dragon sent from his mouth in every seduction of destructive teaching. Such a river is found [Col. 0086A] not only in the errors of heretics that stain the sincerity of faith, but also in the teachings of secular men that disturb the purity of Christian conduct by a corrupt confusion—separating what God has joined or joining what he has separated.

For since it is written, “Moses and Aaron are among his priests” (Ps. 98:6), when the Lord was transfigured upon the mountain Moses may suitably signify the order of clerics, and Elijah, the first solitary man, the sacred order of monks. Christ, author of both orders, joined these two with himself on the height of one mountain; and he clearly expressed both in himself, since, fasting in the wilderness, he was like a monk in silence, and afterward, teaching daily in the Temple, he was like a pontiff.

[Col. 0086C] CXXX. Speaking of these two orders in a letter sent to the people of Vercelli, the distinguished teacher Ambrose says among other things:

“Who can doubt that these two are preeminent in the more earnest devotion of Christians: the offices of clerics and the institutions of monks? The former are trained in affability, moral conduct, and discipline; the latter in abstinence and endurance. The former is, as it were, in the theater; the latter in seclusion. The former is seen; the latter is hidden. Therefore the good athlete says: ‘We have been made a spectacle to this world, and to angels and to men’ (1 Cor. 4:9). He was indeed worthy to be watched by angels as he wrestled, so as to attain the prize; as he contended so as to establish on earth the life of angels, and refute in heaven the wickedness of angels. For he wrestled with spiritual wickednesses. Rightly did the world watch him, that the world might imitate him.

“The former life is in the arena; the latter in a cave. The former contends against the confusion of the world; the latter against the appetite of the flesh. The former subdues bodily pleasures; the latter flees them. The former is more gracious; the latter safer. The former governs itself; the latter restrains itself. Yet each denies itself, in order to become Christ’s, because it was said to the perfect: ‘Whoever wishes to come after me,’” etc. (Matt. 16:24). [Col. 0086D]

Do you see how blessed Ambrose, by his teaching, forms both the clerical and monastic orders for the summit of perfection? This is not done by that royal rule, fashioned in the houses of kings and contrary to apostolic teaching, as the preceding testimonies of Pope Urban and Saint Ambrose show. Pope Paschal, too, of blessed memory, rightly opened his mouth against the aforesaid rule in the treatise which he confirmed for the canons of Saint Mary in Portu. Its first chapter is as follows:

[Col. 0087A] CXXXI. “No one of sound judgment doubts that the order of clerics holds in the Church the place of the tribe of Levi, and observes the rights and carries out the offices of apostolic dignity. Hence it is certain that they ought to imitate the rules and lives of Levites and apostles, whose place they are known to hold, whose dignity they possess, and whose offices they perform. For whatever law is laid upon Levites and whatever rule is given to apostles by the Lord, the same is without doubt prescribed to Catholic clerics, who fulfill their functions, down to the end of the world.

“Indeed, what is forbidden to Levites while they still walk in the shadow—how can it be granted to us, who now stand in the truth, when we read that many things were allowed them which are undoubtedly forbidden to us? Thus the Lord says to Aaron, his sons, and the other Levites: ‘You shall possess nothing in the land of the children of Israel, nor shall you have a portion among them. For I am your portion and inheritance in the midst of the children of Israel’ (Num. 18:20). And shortly afterward follows: ‘I have given all the tithes of Israel to the sons of Levi as a possession, in return for the ministry by which they serve me in the tabernacle of the covenant.’ And, concerning the same, after a few words: ‘They shall possess nothing else, being content with the offering of tithes, which I have set apart for their use and necessities’ (ibid., 18:23–24). [Col. 0087B]

“And these things belong to the Old Testament. But in the New Testament let us hear what he said to everyone wishing to adhere to the perfection of his discipleship: ‘If you wish to be perfect, go and sell everything that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me’ (Matt. 19:21); and elsewhere: ‘Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple’ (Luke 14:33). And in another place, when he sent them out to preach, he forbade them, saying: ‘Do not possess gold or silver’ (Matt. 10:9).

“Peter clearly showed that he had fulfilled this when he said: ‘Silver and gold I do not have’ (Acts 3:6). The same Peter testifies that the other apostles did this too, when, on behalf of himself and his fellow disciples, he asks the Lord: ‘Lord, behold, we have left everything and followed you. What then shall be ours?’ (Matt. 19:27). To him—and in him, to all who do the same—the Lord replies: ‘Truly I say to you, that you who have left everything and followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. [Col. 0087C] And everyone who has left house, or father, or mother, or brothers, or sisters, or fields for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life’ (Matt. 19:28–29).

“These commandments were given to Levites and to apostles. One rule and the same law are prescribed to both; possession is removed from both, and earthly wealth forbidden. Who, then, are bound by this other than clerics, who hold the place of the Lord’s Levites and Christ’s disciples, fulfill their ministry, discharge their functions, and possess their orders?

“For the observance and perpetual fulfillment of this command God ordained that the price of sins, the vows and offerings of the faithful, firstfruits and tithes of goods, should be given to their churches. Thus those devoted to divine worship, stripped of private means, might have a permanently appointed support by which to live, serve the Church, supply the needs of the poor, and more diligently fulfill every ministry of their order, never separating themselves from these duties for any reason or necessity, nor attending to secular affairs. [Col. 0088A]

“From this it is plainly shown that it will be unlawful for clerics who serve Christ both to hold earthly property and to take ecclesiastical goods; to possess an inheritance in the world and receive an ecclesiastical portion. To confirm this judgment, the Apostle’s words are fitting: ‘No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has proved himself’ (2 Tim. 2:4). And Solomon’s words: ‘Woe to the sinner who enters the land by two ways’ (Ecclus. 2:14).

“Therefore whoever wishes to follow Christ’s discipleship must renounce secular affairs; and whoever, once made sacred, has begun to live from sacred things is commanded henceforth to use sacred things for his living. But lest we seem alone in holding this view concerning the life and rule of Catholic clerics, let other witnesses also agree with us: men most devout and richly learned—namely Jerome, Augustine, and Prosper. Let us hear what they have said or understood on this matter.

“Jerome, writing to Nepotian on the life and morals of clerics, says among other things: ‘Let the cleric who serves Christ’s Church first interpret his own title, and, having stated the definition of his name, strive to be what he is called. For if κλῆρος (*klēros*) in Greek is called *sors* [“lot” or “portion”] in Latin, clerics are so named either because they belong to the Lord’s portion, or because the Lord himself is their lot—that is, their portion. [Col. 0088B] Since either the cleric himself is the Lord’s portion or has the Lord as his portion, he ought to show himself such that he both possesses the Lord and is possessed by the Lord. He who possesses the Lord and says with the Prophet, “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. 72:26), can have nothing apart from the Lord. For if he has anything else besides the Lord, the Lord will not be his portion. For example, if he has gold, silver, possessions, or various furnishings, the Lord does not deign to become his portion together with those portions.

“‘But if I am the Lord’s portion and the measuring-line of his inheritance, I receive no portion among the other tribes; rather, like a Levite and priest, I live on tithes, and, serving the altar, am sustained by the altar’s offering. Having food and clothing, I shall be content with these, and naked I shall follow the naked cross.’”

And, after a few words, he writes to the same man in the same letter: “How can clerics be managers and stewards of other persons’ houses and estates, when they are commanded to disdain their own possessions?” Thus far Jerome.

Augustine, in the nineteenth chapter of his book *On the Words of the Lord*, writes as follows: “Tax collectors also came to John to be baptized by him and said to him, ‘Teacher, what shall we do?’ But he said to them, ‘Demand nothing more than what has been appointed for you.’ And after a few words: Soldiers too asked him, ‘What shall we do?’ John said to them, ‘Extort no one, make no false accusation, but be content with your pay’ (Luke 3:12–14). [Col. 0088C] Here every person who serves as a soldier ought now to recognize himself. For Scripture does not speak only of those soldiers held in armed service; whoever wears the belt of his service is enrolled as a soldier of his rank. Therefore this judgment may be applied, for example, to soldiers, protectors, all governors, and whoever receives publicly assigned support: if he seeks more, he is condemned by John’s judgment as an extortioner and oppressor.”

And a little later he adds: “The Catholic cleric also is bound by this judgment. For if he is not content with the support which, at the Lord’s command, he receives from the altar, but engages in commerce, sells intercessions, eagerly accepts widows’ gifts—such a man appears more a trader than a cleric,” etc.

So that his deeds might speak more than his tongue, Augustine established in the bishop’s own house a monastery of clerics, where no one was permitted to have anything private, as he himself testifies: “I wished to have in this bishop’s house a monastery of clerics. See how we live. No one is permitted to possess anything private in our community. But perhaps some do possess something? No one is permitted to do so. If any do it, they do what is not permitted.” [Col. 0089A] Thus Augustine.

But let us now hear what blessed Prosper thought on this matter: “Therefore,” he says, “let the person whom the ambition of possessing delights possess God, who possesses all that he created, with an unencumbered mind; and in him he will have whatever he desires to possess in a holy manner. But since no one possesses God unless he is possessed by him, let him first be God’s possession, and God will become for him both possessor and portion.”

And a little later he adds: “What more does one seek for whom his Creator becomes all things? Or what is sufficient for him, to whom he himself is not sufficient?” And, after a few words in the same chapter: “Who, to whom God deigns to be a possession, seeks anything else? Or who does not, because of love for him, despise all things thought great? Therefore whoever wishes to possess God should renounce the world, so that God may be his blessed possession; for so long as he does not abandon what is his own, he serves the world whose goods he retains. And certainly he cannot serve the world and God at the same time.

“Thus God wished his worshippers to renounce all things for which the world is loved, so that, once worldly desire has been excluded, divine charity may increase or be perfected in them. And therefore he ordained that tithes, firstfruits of crops, firstborn animals, sacrifices for sin, and vows which God commanded to be offered to himself should be distributed to priests and ministers, so that, with the most devout people providing for them, they might serve their Creator and Shepherd more freely.” [Col. 0089B] Thus far Prosper.

Now then, let these statements concerning renouncing one’s own possessions suffice. But, dearest brothers, the Lord clearly shows in the Gospel that you must also renounce your own wills, saying: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and follow me. Whoever wishes to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses it for my sake will find it” (Matt. 16:24–25). And elsewhere: “I have come not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). Elsewhere holy Scripture teaches us: “My son, turn away from your own desires” (Ecclus. 18:30). For, as is said elsewhere, “Will has punishment; necessity produces a crown.” And in another place it is commanded: “Do not go after your own desires” (ibid.). Let those who follow them hear what is said of them through the Prophet: “They have become corrupt and abominable in their pleasures” (Ps. 13:1).

Accordingly, the same Prophet, assuming the voice of prelates, writes: “He has subjected peoples to us, and nations beneath our feet” (Ps. 46:4). [Col. 0090A] Warned by these examples, brothers, let us not refuse to be subject to others for God’s sake. Rather, having utterly renounced our own wills, let us carry out Christ’s will under another’s judgment—yet one that is spiritual and discerning.

That in every canonical congregation one person ought to be chosen to preside over the rest is required both by ecclesiastical practice, divinely inspired, and plainly shown in both the Old and New Testaments: for the Lord set Moses, and after Moses Joshua, over all the children of Israel; Aaron over the other Levites; and Peter over the other disciples. What kind of person the superior ought to be is clearly shown by the Lord’s threefold question and Peter’s threefold answer. For when the care of feeding the sheep is entrusted to him, the Lord asks Peter three times whether he loves him, Peter answers three times that he loves him, and the Lord three times commands him to feed them.

Let us therefore see how a threefold love ought to be present in those who are chosen. He has a threefold love who believes and loves God and the things of God in his mind; confesses and preaches them with his voice; and imitates and keeps them in his works. The inquiry is threefold when, as we ought, we investigate, foresee, and examine whether the candidate possesses this threefold love. If fitting speech and action outwardly show the faith and love of the heart, the threefold answer has now satisfied the threefold inquiry. [Col. 0090B]

The care of feeding the flock is also rightly imposed upon such a man three times, because whoever undertakes to feed the sheep must provide for them through the continual watchfulness of his heart, admonish and defend them through the office of speech, and always draw them toward Christ through the examples of his actions. Therefore he rightly receives the care of feeding the flock who inwardly possesses full faith and love in his mind; outwardly, through speech, has complete knowledge and ability to admonish, freely rebuke, and wisely exhort; and in action keeps and follows whatever he says.

No one, moreover, ought to be rejected from this office because of any fault if he has already made satisfaction; for after Peter’s sorrowful satisfaction for his threefold denial, since threefold love was evident in him, the feeding of the flock was imposed upon him by the Lord. This form of threefold love, therefore, dearest brothers, prefigured in the first shepherd by none other than Christ, must be looked for in those to be chosen—not only in leaders, but in every person to be placed over others in the Church.” [Col. 0090C] Thus far the words of Pope Paschal.

CXXXII. To this writing, established and approved at the apostolic see, there subscribed first Pope Paschal, then the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, whose names are recorded: Crescentius, bishop of Sabina; Peter, bishop of Porto; Cono, bishop of Palestrina; Vitalis, bishop of Albano; Boniface, cardinal of Saint Mark; Deusdedit, cardinal of Saint Lawrence; Desiderius, cardinal of Saint Praxedes; Guido, cardinal of Saint Balbina; Peter, cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian; Peter, cardinal of Saint Adrian; Rossemannus, deacon of Saint George; Comes, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro; Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, who afterward became pope and was called Innocent; and John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Lucy. [Col. 0091A]

CXXXIII. Since these matters stand thus, if this apostolic teaching, intended for only one congregation, had been universally proclaimed, much muddy water emitted from the dragon’s mouth might thereby have been swallowed up. There is no slight lacuna in that rule, often noted and, God willing, still to be more fully noted and branded. For this rule, if I am not mistaken, is a kind of overflow drawn or issuing from that great river Euphrates, in which there is a certain mixture of pure and muddy Babylonian waters.

For what is purer than the fact that, in the collection of patristic sentences prefixed to this rule, common life is very clearly set forth? In it suitable support, according to each person’s need, is ordained only for those whom necessity or choice has made poor; and the steward of those supports is commended as one who, as Prosper says, either distributed all his goods to the poor or added them to the property of the Church. What, I ask, is purer than this most salutary precept, wholly consonant with apostolic teaching? [Col. 0091B]

But what is more muddy than the leaven of the Sadducees, with which is filled that chapter of the same rule that commands equal stipends to be given in one and the same community to persons who abound in riches through possessing much of their own and to persons who are poor because they possess little or nothing? Yet, as the aforementioned Prosper says: “To give to one who has is nothing other than to waste, because what the Church possesses ought to be held in common with those who have nothing.” Certainly a great waste—and an institution pleasing to the son of perdition, though he has not yet been revealed—is recognized when goods owed to the poor are given to the rich and the pattern of apostolic teaching is not observed, since an equal portion is commanded to be given to rich and poor alike.

Such equality in distribution must not be admitted even among true poor persons of Christ living in a community, because food and clothing should not be bestowed equally upon all when not all have equal capacity. Therefore, having carefully considered each individual, the utmost distinction must be made in such matters according to each person’s need. Since these things are so, God’s wrath from heaven is rightly believed someday to be revealed against the teaching of this rule, and the vial filled with God’s wrath more fully poured out, of which the Apocalypse says: “And the sixth angel poured out his vial upon that great river Euphrates, and dried up its water, so that a way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun. And I saw three unclean spirits like frogs come forth from the mouth of the dragon, from the mouth of the beast, and from the mouth of the false prophet” (Apoc. 16:12–13). [Col. 0092A]

[Col. 0092B] CXXXIV. We read that the seven angels poured out seven vials full of God’s wrath after the sounding of the seven trumpets by the seven angels. While the trumpets sound, we find great plagues; but when the vials are poured out, greater and final plagues, to which it is fitting to apply the words: “A fire is kindled in my wrath, burning even to the depths of hell.”

Therefore, when the sixth angel sounded the trumpet, the four angels bound at the great river Euphrates were released, and there was a plague that afflicted God’s people through the four chief kingdoms of the world, under which Israel or Judah was afflicted by God’s judgment. That was not among the final plagues in which the wrath of God is consummated, because it delivered not souls but bodies to such angels—that is, to earthly kingdoms.

CXXXV. But here the vial of God’s wrath is poured upon that river, not in order that such angels may be released, but that its water might be dried up and a way prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun. Thus the vial of God’s wrath is poured into the river’s water. Consequently, this water must be understood as something to which God’s wrath may reasonably be said to be due. Otherwise, since the preceding vials have condemned sea, rivers, and springs of water into blood, why does the river Euphrates deserve a vial of its own, unless some particular evil is signified by the water of this river among the other evils done under the sun?

There is an evil whose condemnation is not found in the preceding vials poured out by the five angels, but is reserved for the sixth angel. It is rightly understood to be signified here, first by the water of that river, and then by the three unclean spirits creeping forth like frogs. This evil is plainly threefold, and its parts are the tricks of magicians, the inventions of philosophers, and the fictions of poets. [Col. 0092C] Their profound malice and muddy verbosity are suitably signified by the waters of the Euphrates, because the Euphrates is Babylon’s river and, flowing through it, is divided into many branches. By its very name also, in Scripture, it commonly signifies the whole generation of the wicked, opposed to the generation of the righteous: the city of the devil opposed to the city of God. For Babylon is interpreted as “confusion.”

[Col. 0093A] **CXXXVI.** Therefore, after bowls have been poured out upon the rivers and springs of waters, this one is poured out upon the Euphrates as well. For when tyrants or impious kings, together with the nations subject to them—designated by the names of sea, rivers, and waters—have incurred condemnation for themselves, wrath is due also to those who drove them mad and increased their error by empty words, indeed by writings malicious, deceitful, fabulous, and wholly false, or, worse still, mingling truth and falsehood: as the aforesaid rule is in large measure likened both to the paradisal and to the Babylonian river Euphrates.

For just as the river Euphrates, drawing the stream of its origin from the fountain of Paradise and adulterated by many foreign waters, flows through the midst of Babylon, being numbered among those waters [Col. 0093B] of which the captive citizens of Jerusalem say: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept” (Ps. 137:1); so the teaching of heretics often draws certain testimonies from the fountain of truth, cunningly mingles falsehood with them, so that water of this kind tastes fit to drink not so much for captive citizens of Jerusalem as for citizens of Babylon.

Likewise, the rule of which we speak, having proceeded from the king’s court, contains within its composition many sound teachings of the Fathers, drawn from the sayings of orthodox Fathers and suitably shaping the common life according to the doctrine of the apostles. Yet, alongside these preceding materials, certain adulterated elements have been mixed in. Through I know not what courtly composers, who mingle falsehoods with truths, evils with goods, [Col. 0093C] and teach things contrary to the former, the purity of what preceded has been so infected and disturbed that this water is no more drinkable for true citizens of Jerusalem—because of the vanity mixed into it—than are the writings of philosophers, poets, or even heretics, which contain many truths mingled with falsehoods.

For if, by God’s just judgment, the bowl full of God’s wrath is poured out not only upon the earth, by which earthly persons are denoted; and upon the sea, by which bitter persons are denoted; and upon rivers, by which sensual or furious persons are denoted; and upon the throne of the beast, by which liars are denoted; but also upon the sun, by which persons of distinction are denoted, who, because of an outward display of piety, seem worthy of heaven—if, I say, the bowl of God’s wrath is poured even upon persons so illustrious and exalted, according to what is elsewhere written: “Contempt was poured out upon princes; and he caused them to wander in a trackless place, and not in a way” (Ps. 107:40)—and therefore God’s wrath is rightly revealed from heaven even against the impiety of such persons—then it ought not seem strange that the river Euphrates is not spared. Though it came forth from Paradise, it has gathered no small amount of mud from Babylon’s streets, especially in teachings written to please Babylon’s citizens or rulers. Therefore God’s wrath from heaven must rightly be revealed against such teachings, so that they may be judged heretical, apocryphal, pestilential, or deadly, and not thought fit to be numbered among authentic and sound writings.

**CXXXVII.** A sound writing, especially one bearing the name of a rule, ought to contain nothing foul [Col. 0094A] or crooked, lest it lead those who follow it not so much into the straight way as into a perverse one. Such is the aforesaid rule: it does not rightly rule anyone, and therefore is unworthy of the name “rule.” The reason why one is now compelled to argue so strongly against it is that certain canons, professing the common life according to the rule of blessed Augustine, are attracted by the insertion of a discourse of blessed Augustine and thus accept this same rule in such a way that they have it recited in their assemblies as though it were authentic and untouched by any admixture of error, without observing that in many respects it is contrary to apostolic teaching.

Accordingly, if it pleases apostolic discernment that this courtly writing be retained in the mother churches as the canonical rule for clerics, its crooked features should first be made straight, so that courtly edicts may be made consonant with apostolic edicts concerning the life of clerics: the perverse portions being cut out, and the remainder canonized by apostolic authority. For what reason is there that the larger and more numerous congregations of clerics should profess a courtly rule never canonized by any authority of the Apostolic See, when there are many most straightforward writings of orthodox Fathers which, because of their rectitude, may be treated as a rule both for forming the life of clerics living in a congregation under prelates and for those who live outside such communities yet intend to live rightly according to the canons under the governance of bishops? What exceeds these two kinds of clerics is from evil; and, according to Isidore’s affirmation, it is to be counted neither among religious clerics [Col. 0094C] nor among Catholic laity.

**CXXXVIII.** And, to return our attention to Babylon’s river Euphrates: with the exception of a very few, such clerics do not, like birds mindful of their nest—which is Jerusalem—in the beginning of their joy sit weeping by Babylon’s rivers. Rather, immersed in those same waters like fish, they play in them in such a manner that they never consider flying back to that nest of Jerusalem’s common dwelling, in which the first children of the Church, like good fledglings, had one heart and one soul in God, and none of them called anything his own.

Apart, then, from the few, as has been said, whose mind is set upon conversion and return to Jerusalem, most of them, despising the waters of Siloam that flow quietly, [Col. 0094D] love Babylon’s rivers and turbid waters more—waters which, God willing, are to be wholly dried up by the bowl of the sixth angel.

**CXXXIX.** Since the seventh and final bowl, full of God’s wrath, will pour out the wrath of judgment into the air—that is, upon the aerial powers, namely the demons and all their accomplices—it is not without reason that this sixth bowl of the sixth angel, drying up the waters of the Euphrates, is believed to precede the final judgment, according to what was said: “that the way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun” (Rev. 16:12). For these kings, indeed, the way to judgment will be smoother, even now in this present life, in proportion as they see the Babylonian waters more fully dried up; and we see those waters, apart from a few pools, already for the most part annihilated.

[Col. 0095A] Before God’s wrath was revealed from heaven against waters of this kind through the Gospel of Christ, holy kings could not cross them—namely, those who were princes or authors of the Scriptures of truth. They are rightly said to have come from the rising of the sun, because they did not come or speak from themselves, but received illumination from the Godhead enabling them to say what they said. These kings could not cross those waters; with the single Hebrew tongue they could not meet the eloquent Greeks and the learned Latin grammarians, rhetoricians, dialecticians, and so many tragic, comic, and satirical poets.

For the river of God had not yet been filled with waters; its streams had not yet been made drunk by the Spirit of truth; and Babylon’s rivers still flowed out in fullest abundance and filled their channels. Most famous among them was that great river Euphrates, coming forth from Paradise and enlarged by many other waters. For many fabulous falsehoods, intermingled with certain sayings of truth, sounded forth in such a way that the voices of Babylon’s many waters descending into the sea of this world produced wonderful swellings of the sea, while the Lord, wonderful on high, had not yet appeared, nor were his testimonies credible to a world driven mad and bewitched by so many lies, made drunk by so many waters of Babylon’s river.

**CXL.** But when that Spirit of truth came to convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment, then, indeed, by this very conviction he caused the waters [Col. 0095C] of so great and mighty a river to dry up. For he made the wisdom of this world foolish. When God’s wisdom went forth and supplied the reason for what seemed God’s foolishness, as the Apostle said, “We preach Jesus Christ crucified: to Jews a stumbling-block, to Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1:23), then, by comparison with him, what had hitherto seemed grand and profound appeared foolish and dry.

John fittingly indicates, in his own person, how cheap, detestable, and contemptible that worldly wisdom was, or appeared, in the eyes of those illuminated by truth, when he says: “And I saw three unclean spirits, like frogs, coming forth from the mouth of the dragon, from the mouth of the beast, and from the mouth of the false prophet” (Rev. 16:13). [Col. 0095D] He calls them unclean spirits: that is, the schools, as it were, of magical, poetic, and philosophical wisdom and knowledge, which the unclean spirit of this world—opposed to the Holy Spirit—inspired.

For magicians especially enlisted unclean spirits as patrons for themselves by some, I know not what, unhappy compact. Poets, under respectable names, petitioned those same unclean spirits to inspire them, sacrilegiously presuming to call them gods when they are demons. And the spirit that inspired philosophers was likewise undoubtedly unclean. Does not the Apostle say of them: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and they became vain in their thoughts” (Rom. 1:21)?

**CXLI.** See to what degree of uncleanness they became vain: serving the creature rather than [Col. 0096A] the Creator, they were therefore delivered over to passions of dishonor, to the desires of their hearts, and to uncleanness. They are therefore rightly called unclean spirits. By the name “dragon,” moreover, the devil is rightly understood to be indicated; and by the designation “beast,” the bestial kingdom of the devil is here rightly signified. In Daniel, for example, four principal kingdoms of the world are signified by four beasts: the Babylonian, Persian or Median, Macedonian, and Roman.

Thus the first spirit came forth from the dragon’s mouth, because human curiosity learned the magical art from intercourse with the devil. The next spirit came forth from the beast’s mouth, because the baseness of the human mind, flattering the bestial kingdom of this world, sang in fabulous chants that earthly human kings had been translated into gods, heaven, and the circles of the stars through poetic inventions. The philosophical profession too proved to be a false prophet, for it referred the filthy extravagances ascribed to the gods—for example, Jupiter’s adulteries, the jealousy of Juno, his sister and wife, Venus’s prostitution, and the like—to the elements of the world. It sought, by contrived allegorical interpretations, to give a respectable appearance to things concerning their gods of which people might already be ashamed.

Such an interpreter was truly a false prophet, because he prophesied from his own heart and vainly consoled human shame by adorning divine adulteries with invented and useless mysteries, while nevertheless remaining one who served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen. “I saw,” he says, “three unclean spirits coming forth from the mouth of the dragon, [Col. 0096C] the mouth of the beast, and the mouth of the false prophet.” He adds further: “Like frogs” (Rev. 16:13).

Frogs, of course, are both unclean and ugly, small and, as it were, talkative. Living in mud, they take away peace by croaking importunately and with something like chattering. It is therefore an apt comparison when those who appear great and eloquent to themselves are compared to, or said to resemble, frogs: for example, poets who think themselves to utter great things. Yet all their material is fabulous mud, and their greatness is mere inflation.

**CXLII.** Therefore, because their knowledge, though nonexistent, puffs itself up against the knowledge of God, the story from Aesop’s fable fittingly suits their spirit: a frog, trying by puffing itself up to stretch itself [Col. 0096D] to the size of an ox, vainly strains its skin and finally bursts by puffing itself beyond its strength. Where now are those grandiloquent persons who exalted themselves against the true greatness of God’s knowledge? “Their memory has perished with a noise, but the Lord endures forever” (Ps. 9:8). Who believes the verbosity of those men? Indeed, who does not laugh when reading or hearing their shameful theologies?

Furthermore, magicians—whose leaders in Egypt, Jannes and Mambres, by their incantations brought forth frogs before Pharaoh in opposition to Moses and Aaron, and could proceed no further—are rightly said to have the form of frogs, so that they may resemble those frogs which they made in opposition to God, beyond which their feats could accomplish nothing. The Apostle likewise testifies that, as Jannes [Col. 0097A] and Mambres opposed Moses, so now corrupt-minded people, reprobate in mind, oppose the truth: “But,” he says, “they shall proceed no further; for their folly has been made manifest, as theirs also was” (2 Tim. 3:7).

They shall not proceed, I say, beyond the point to which those others proceeded, who, after producing frogs, could not make further signs resembling Moses’ signs. Thus some lawyers, legal scholars, sophists, or dialecticians of this age—or rather heretics, speaking sophistically and therefore hateful—fight against the divine law, as though against Moses, and against the lawful and truly Levitical priesthood, as though against Aaron. Favoring Pharaoh’s kingdom against God’s kingdom, they will not proceed further when, in their chattering, they are equated with talkative frogs croaking in the mud. For their folly, made manifest and refuted by Holy Scripture, will clearly show that the talkativeness of such persons resisting truth and suppressing God’s truth in unrighteousness was not inspired by the Holy Spirit but concocted through malignant and unclean spirits.

For they hold the truth of sound doctrine captive, as it were, surrounding it with their falsehood so puffed up through evil spirits that a great appearance of truth and image of goodness is found in it.

**CXLIII.** Such falsehoods cannot be refuted without a great battle among the combatants, like that which the martyrs endured against idolatrous tyrants and the high priests of temples; like that which holy confessors nevertheless endured against heretics and kings [Col. 0097C] favoring them in evil; and like the great conflict which, most recently in these days, religious men endured—and still endure—against simoniacal, hired, incestuous, wandering, vagabond, dissolute, roving, or, worse still, irregularly assembled clerics in the time of Pope Gregory VII. Seven wicked spirits in openly evil persons, and seven others still more wicked in persons falsely good, fight against those truly good and harass them with importunate talkativeness.

Therefore, when John had said that he saw unclean spirits coming forth from the dragon’s mouth and the false prophet’s mouth, he added, “like frogs,” and further said: “For they are spirits of demons, performing signs, and they go forth to the kings of the whole earth to gather them for battle on the great day of Almighty God” (Rev. 16:14). Truly, I say, I would call them unclean, for they are spirits of demons. Since their doctrines are in fact opposed to truth, no one can doubt that all their grandness—or rather, their inflation—is an inspiration of demons. “And they go forth,” he says, “to the kings of the whole earth, to gather them for battle.”

**CXLIV.** The first to do this, as Holy Scripture recounts, were the aforesaid sorcerers Jannes and Mambres. The spirit of deception that was in them went forth to Egypt’s king, and, through confidence in signs that appeared similar to signs of God’s power, increased his folly so that, fighting against God on Israel’s account, he dared to wage war. In the same or a similar manner, other [Col. 0098A] sorcerers, poets, and philosophers gathered the kings of the whole earth—not into one place, certainly, but into one and the same state of most evil will—in order that they might fight against the Lord. Forestalled by the high estimation in which those persons were held, the kings of the earth might despise or neglect to value highly the miracles performed by the Lord’s servants, or to admire the wisdom they preached, because those others had likewise become accustomed to performing wonders and to speaking magnificently as wise persons.

**CXLV.** The likeness of all those who thus, as the Apostle complains, suppress God’s truth in unrighteousness appeared in the kingdom once divided within David’s house. There King Jeroboam, by a devised scheme, made golden calves and established festivals resembling God’s festivals. The apparently divine reverence shown to golden calves was meant to hold the people bewitched by such worship, lest they seek the true God in Jerusalem or return to the lawful kingdom of David’s house.

This deceiver, sinning in this way against the Holy Spirit in opposition to his own conscience and condemned by his own judgment, was held worthy of no forgiveness. Yet the people deceived by him were in great part recalled to repentance through the holy prophets. Among them the chief was the one who prophesied and cried out against the aforesaid Jeroboam as he stood and sacrificed at the altar; and the altar was split in two, and its ashes were poured out.

Nearly similar to this is the case of heresiarchs or schismatics who, condemned now by their own judgment and sinning against the Holy Spirit not through ignorance but [Col. 0098C] through malice, have no remedy of repentance. Yet those deceived by them are sometimes corrected, especially when the sacrifices of such heretics or schismatics are blown away as though they were ashes and are shown to be offensive to God.

**CXLVI.** We are taught, by the example of that prophet who was deceived by another prophet and, after eating forbidden food, is said to have been handed over to a lion to be killed, how cautiously the witnesses of this truth ought to abstain from forbidden things: lest, after an interdict, they eat food with persons of this kind and thus be deceived by them. True prophets must therefore beware false prophets, lest, deceived by their seduction, they share in forbidden things and fall into the mouth of the lion who prowls about seeking someone to devour. Yet the lion has no power to devour true and good prophets, even when, by God’s hidden but not unjust judgment, he is permitted power to bite or kill them.

For the aforesaid prophet, because he did not reject the deception of the lying prophet, was given to the lion to be killed, but not to be devoured; and it is believed that by this very death he was cleansed. Hence the lion that had killed him while God was angry, when God was appeased guarded the corpse of the slain man and his ass, touching neither.

Sometimes, when some simoniac is raised by lay violence to the Apostolic See or to another chair of Moses, being intruded or imposed above someone Catholic who was regularly elected and promoted, controversies of this kind have arisen. In them the powerful Egyptians and tyrants were greatly led astray, because within their party they had clerics strongly trained in letters and gloried against the Church in the identity of sacraments, as though in a likeness of signs, though they themselves were outside the Church. They did not attend, or were unwilling to attend, to the fact that although outside the Church there may be a place for a true sacrament, there is no place for a true sacrifice except in the holy Catholic Church, as blessed Augustine maintains.

**CXLVII.** In the time of the schismatic Peter Leo, when his supporters, together with him, had been excommunicated and greatly gloried in the identity of the sacraments, both among themselves and in comparison with their excommunicator, Pope Innocent of blessed memory, I was then at the Roman curia and was compelled to collect many authorities from the Scriptures of truth. By them it was plainly shown that sacraments celebrated according to the Church’s rite, whether outside or within, are inviolable; but that in sacraments celebrated outside, the Spirit of Christ works no more than the finger of God worked in the signs of the Egyptian magicians—a finger which in the end, by their own confession, shone forth in the signs of Moses and Aaron.

Thus, in that debate of mine, with the support then given me by the venerable Walter, archbishop of Ravenna, of blessed memory, the following statement of Pope Pelagius prevailed among many opinions:

> “The very word *schism*, which is Greek, means a division; but division cannot exist in unity. Therefore they do not share in unity. They have made themselves parties; and, having separated themselves from that which is one—to speak now in the words of the Apostle Jude—they do not have the Spirit. From all this it follows that, because they are not one in unity, because they wished to exist in a part, and because they do not have the Spirit, they cannot possess the sacrifice of Christ’s body.”

We then assembled many truthful testimonies of the Fathers to this effect. By these it was demonstrated—and, through the efforts of Eimeric, then chancellor, approved—that offices of the Mass celebrated outside the Church, though they possess sacramental signs similar to the signs of Catholics, are nevertheless void and empty, since they possess neither the Holy Spirit nor the body of Christ.

> **[Note: Col. 0099D]** If sacraments celebrated according to the Church’s rite even outside the Church are inviolable, as Gerhoh himself conceded shortly above, it is scarcely intelligible how Christ’s body is not possessed in a sacrifice performed outside, especially since sacrament and sacrifice are celebrated in one and the same act. Accordingly, these statements must either be understood of those who, through a defect of ordination, lack priesthood in heresy, or be understood as referring to the fruit of the sacrifice itself—which certainly is nonexistent for a heretic offering sacrifice on behalf of heretics. The same must be said proportionately of the sacrifice of an evil priest on behalf of hired clerics, and so forth.]

Yet the enemies of truth have fought—and do not cease even now to fight—against this truth. [Col. 0099D] Many of them, being married, concubinary, or hired clerics, sacrifice even though under interdict. And because the cathedral clerics of great congregations are the employers and protectors of such hired clerics, the battle they raise is not light. They have fought, therefore, and do not cease to fight, persecuting all who wish to live piously in Christ; but to their own harm, because, gathered for battle in this manner, they shall be gathered for judgment.

Therefore, after saying here [Col. 0100A] that they were gathered for battle, he adds: “for the great day of the Almighty” (ibid.). For the great day of the Almighty will be the day of judgment, undoubtedly great, as the Prophet says: “Near is the great day of the Lord, near and very swift. Bitter is the sound of the day of the Lord. The mighty man shall be troubled there” (Zeph. 1:14), and so forth.

**CXLVIII.** “Near,” he says; and it is true. For even if some delay seems to have occurred from the time when he prophesied until that great day of the Almighty, death and the end of this present life are certainly near to each individual, and no one knows when they will come. Therefore he says immediately: “Behold, I come like a thief” (Rev. 16:15). The evil servant says in his heart: “God delays his coming.” But the Lord says: “Behold, I am present; I come quickly” (ibid.); and he adds, “like a thief,” that is, dreadful to those who are negligent and asleep.

For he deigned to apply to himself the comparison of a thief when, after giving his servants the command to watch—“because,” he says, “you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come” (Matt. 24:44)—he said: “But know this: if the master of the household knew at what hour the thief would come, he would surely watch and would not allow his house to be broken into” (Luke 12:39). With the same intention and for the same reason as when he says there, “Let your loins be girded; blessed are those servants whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching” (ibid., 35), he immediately adds here also: “Blessed is the one who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame” (Rev. 16:15).

[Col. 0100C] **CXLIX.** The Almighty inserted this concerning his great day because it had been promised that the kings of the earth would be gathered for battle in the place called in Hebrew *Hermagedon*. Whom did he gather there? Surely kings, because this account of a gathering began to be written concerning kings. Yet the kings here are diverse—indeed opposed and contrary. Of good kings it had already been said that a way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun; but of evil kings it was added: “And they go forth to the kings of the whole earth, to gather them for battle” (ibid., 14).

Which of these kings, then, did he gather in the place called in Hebrew *Hermagedon*, or who gathered them in such a place? For he had not introduced any single person, nor did he expressly distinguish whether he gathered the evil [Col. 0100D] or the good. Therefore one may say that the gathering of good and evil persons is here foreshadowed, that gathering of which we know that, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, not kings alone but also all nations will be gathered before him for that marvelous battle. For there the marvelous and dreadful end of the battle between good and evil has been appointed.

That condition is rightly designated by the name here given, [Col. 0101A] *Hermagedon*. For it is interpreted “rising again unto the things before,” or “a rounded mountain.” It rightly signifies that gathering in which the holy kings who came from the rising of the sun shall rise again unto the things before and shall sit in judgment; while evil kings, like a rounded mountain, shall be lifted up with their prince the devil. For then this will truly be said to this mountain: “Lift yourself up and cast yourself” (Matt. 21:21), no longer into the sea but into the depth of Gehenna.

Now, before that great day comes, on which all holy kings shall universally rise again unto the things before, those same kings who in their own time stretch forth toward the things before and forget what lies behind rise unto the things before. This pleasing spectacle, as it is broadly manifest through God’s grace, especially delights good eyes and torments evil eyes in the successors of blessed Peter.

**CL.** When Roman pontiffs grant privileges to churches founded, or to be founded, upon the rock, they especially confirm by the authority of Peter, prince of the apostles, those institutions which they judge to accord with the foundation of the primitive Church. Therefore, if those courtly institutions in the frequently noted rule, later than apostolic institutions, are brought forward in the Apostolic See to be weighed alongside the earlier and better institutions, there is no doubt that the former will there be approved and that these later institutions, contrary to the former, must wholly be rejected.

For even though these later materials include some things taken from the earlier ones and mixed into the aforesaid rule, necessity nevertheless demands that it be cauterized by a certain burning of condemnation and dried up like water from Babylon’s river. Thus a way may be prepared for kings from the rising of the sun in the mother churches overtaken by this flood of water. Or, if this cannot be done once and all at the same time, that tortuous rule should at least be shown to be Babylonian water, likened to the river Euphrates—a Babylonian pool intermingled with paradisal waters; it must therefore be avoided, lest, because good sayings of the Fathers are gathered together in it, that which wholly opposes them be received as well.

For, to omit other matters, there is there a sermon of blessed Augustine saying: “No one is permitted to possess anything private in our fellowship. Those who do so, do what is not permitted.” Then, as though by a certain royal piety, as they call it, it is there permitted that private property and a private house may be possessed contrary to the foregoing teaching of blessed Augustine. The holy Apostolic See does not accept this concession, as is plainly evident from what was said above by Pope Urban and martyr, likewise Pope Urban II, and Pope Paschal.

Likewise, the Roman pontiffs Nicholas and Alexander, commanding as though with one voice, decreed that clerics in sacred orders, obeying the ordinances of the Fathers concerning continence, should live together, eat together, and sleep together near the churches to which they are ordained, as religious persons ought. Nor do they permit them private dwellings—dwellings granted by blessed Pope Gregory only to married clerics, and wholly forbidden to those living chastely in a congregation, since they afford much occasion [Col. 0102A] for wickedness and shameful conduct.

It is not surprising that pious King Louis did not fully consider or guard against this in his rule. For authority to strengthen the brethren was given not to a king or emperor, but to Peter the fisherman, when the Lord said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:18).

**CLI.** Among the gates of hell—which, according to the Fathers’ exposition, we understand to be wicked doctrines or tyrannical violence—we may not unreasonably count the wicked teaching of the aforementioned courtly rule, all the more dangerous because its pestilential poisons lie more secretly concealed, coated with the honey of many salutary doctrines. For the royal concession, by which house is joined to house and field coupled to field, is opposed to and intermixed with the sound institutions of the holy Fathers.

For if, according to the Prophet’s teaching, woe is pronounced against those who join a secular house or field to a secular house or field through the covetousness of avarice, how much more against those who, contrary to the prohibitions of divine law, dare to add to the house or field of their own property, from which they possess sufficient abundance for themselves, a house or field from which the poor, who possess nothing, ought to live while serving God without impediment?

At one time it might have been doubted whether this rule should be reckoned among the gates of hell, when honorable conduct and at least some kind of shadow of canonical religious life existed under it in many churches, owing to certain established and customary forms of cloistered life. These were like the bars of that gate, so long as they remained customary. But now, with those bars cast away, the doors wholly open, and no barrier delaying anyone, people live luxuriously and excessively irreligiously in private houses, neglecting cloistered dwellings; God’s grace is turned into licentiousness, and the wage of sacred warfare is used in the devil’s service.

For even those who sometimes use a common dormitory and refectory, and who at times remain in their own private rooms whenever and as long as they please, find the gates of hell open to them in such alternation. Would that, when these gates have been removed, the heavenly and everlasting gates might be lifted up: namely, regular and truly cenobitic disciplines, without any pretence or admixture of any leaven whatsoever!

**CLII.** Since the sacred Gospel teaches that three leavens are to be avoided—the leaven of the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Herod—in well-ordered cloisters neither the phylacteries of the Pharisees, displaying excessive rigor, find favor; nor the lax dissipation of the Sadducees, in which there is no preparation worthy of resurrection; nor Herodian domination, in which pride reigns with cruelty.

For, according to the theologian John, everything in this world is either the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, or the pride of life; and in the latter is the desire to dominate in this age. Of these three desires, the desire of the eyes is present in phylacteries, magnificent fringes, and the other displays of the Pharisees. [Col. 0103A] The desire of the flesh rules in the feasts and other luxurious excesses of the Sadducees, who have no hope whatever of resurrection. The desire to dominate in this age tyrannizes ambitious persons, those who rule in this world, or, worse still, those who rule even among the clergy.

In contrast, good and religious persons live soberly against the leaven of the Sadducees, justly against that of the Pharisees, and piously against that of Herod in this world, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Since his kindness and humanity appeared, blessing has been prepared for the crown of the year of his goodness, and his fields are filled with abundance. The good seed is multiplied in the children of the kingdom, all the more abundantly as the seed of the children of Gehenna, oversown by the enemy, and tolerated until the near approach of the final harvest while both shoots were still tender, is now, where this can be done without harm to the wheat, more cautiously and diligently separated from the wheat by the harvesting angels.

The harvesters of the first harvest in this year of goodness, as stated above, were the apostles, brought by the Lord into the labors of others. The harvesters of this final harvest, now under discussion, will be angels, according to the Gospel’s declaration: the Lord teaches that the field is the world, the good seed the children of the kingdom, the tares the children of Gehenna, and the harvesters angels. Through them the tares must first be gathered into bundles to be burned, and afterward the wheat gathered into [Col. 0103C] the Lord’s barn.

**CLIII.** It is believed that all these things will be fulfilled in manifest effect at the final winnowing, in great power, through angels, exactly as has been said. Nevertheless, because “the lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7), it is not unreasonable to believe and hope that such things are even now, before the end of the age, partly accomplished through certain angelic ministries of priests. By eloquent writings, wicked morals, like tares bound into bundles, are shown to be punishable by hellfire; and good morals, like grains of the wheat harvest, are shown to deserve reward with a heavenly recompense.

This is clearly found in the moral books of blessed Pope Gregory. Knowing how to reprove evil [Col. 0103D] and choose good, he diligently guarded against confusing the vices and virtues of conduct, carefully distinguishing them from one another in speech and writing. For he was an angel of the Lord of hosts, prudently arraying armies of morals and virtues against the phalanxes of vices.

CLIV. Likewise the remaining Catholic shepherds and teachers are shown to be reaping angels: either, as we have already said, by separating vices and virtues as tares and wheat; or by distinguishing the children of Gehenna from the children of the kingdom in such a way that anyone hearing their sermons or reading their writings may clearly recognize whether evil is found in any rank among Catholics—whether monks or clerics serving God in such a manner that they deserve to dwell in the eternal tabernacles; or laypersons who so obey those serving in this way, and make good use of the mammon of unrighteousness, that, when they fail, they may be received into eternal tabernacles by those whom they have made their friends through obedience and good works. For “he who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward.”

But in receiving a prophet, one must beware of a false prophet; in receiving a righteous person, one must beware of false righteousness. Therefore the diligence of reapers is necessary, separating tares from grains, lest evils be received as goods and false things as true. For since we are now speaking of two orders, namely clerics and monks, whom it benefits the rich of this world to make friends by means of unrighteous mammon—receiving a prophet in a cleric and a righteous person in a monk—lest anyone be deceived under the false name of prophet or righteous person: some clerics and monks are found so branded and so deprived of the name of prophets or righteous persons that no one but a fool should receive them in the name of prophet or righteous person.

CLV. Blessed Benedict, in his Rule, identifies four kinds of monks. Two of these he approves under the name of the righteous: namely, cenobites, serving under a Rule and an abbot; and anchorites or hermits, delighting in solitude and enjoying continual prayer. But he altogether rejects two utterly wretched kinds of monks: Sarabaites, living disorderly without rule or abbot; and wandering monks, roaming through various places. Who, then, would think that these men, rejected by so great a reaper, should be reckoned or received under the name of the righteous? Alms given to such persons are wasted, once their manner of life is known to be deprived of the name of righteousness.

Likewise, among the clergy there are designated kinds to be received in the name of prophets: namely, those living in common according to the praiseworthy example of Christ’s disciples, who were of one heart and one soul in God, and none of them said that anything was his own; or those who govern themselves and the people in the Church according to the canons, neither overstepping nor permitting others to overstep the boundaries established by the Fathers, and who, after the fashion of watchmen, anticipate the assaults of approaching enemies. To each of these it is said: “Cry aloud, do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins” [Col. 0104D] (Isa. 58:1). Again: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion. Raise your voice with strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem. Raise it; do not fear” (Isa. 40:9).

These are the watchmen set upon the walls of Jerusalem, that they may not be silent by day or night. These are the seven angels with seven trumpets, or seven bowls, shown in the Apocalypse. These are the seven stars of the seven Churches, and the seven golden lampstands with seven lamps burning and shining before the Lord. But smoking flax in a false priesthood has many forms: namely, false clerics who are acephalous, simoniacs, hirelings, Nicolaitans, and members of irregular conventicles. When their folly is manifest, to receive them in the name of prophets is folly—especially those expressly proscribed, such as manifestly incestuous persons and hirelings repeatedly forbidden by the Apostolic See.

Moreover, those who employ them, since they too make God’s house a house of trade, are not to be received in the name of prophets. Rather, they must be reproved and warned; and if, once rebuked, they do not come to their senses and do not separate themselves from this leaven of commerce, the employers themselves are to be judged with their hirelings by an equal sentence, and, as public transgressors of the canons, publicly reproved and avoided.

CLVI. Here I should like certain bishops and abbots to be warned, who under the name of parish priests conceal the foulness of their hirelings. For a hireling is a caretaker of the people or minister of the altar who, receiving less than the canonical portion, pays an illicit tribute to his employer out of his service, by undue subjection. Blessed Pope Gregory openly condemns this form of simony, together with that committed by a gift from the hand or by a gift from the tongue.

But if, with the bishop’s permission, an abbot has charge of a church, he may place there one of his own brethren. Since this man is bound by cenobitic religious discipline, no canonical portion is to be assigned to him from tithes and offerings; rather, concerning him there should be maintained that apostolic distribution by which there was given to each according as each had need. But those who are not under cloistered rule, though they are under the rule of the canons—whether placed in parish churches by a bishop, abbot, or provost—must there be supported according to the canons, because “the laborer is worthy of his food and his wages.”

If he remits this wage to his appointing authority for the purpose that the latter may somehow not so much feed as steal, slaughter, and destroy the sheep—because he cares more for his shameful gain than for the sheep—it is no wonder if the sheep do not follow him but flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers. Nor do such persons furnish any basis whatever for imagining in themselves that perfection for which the Apostle, preaching the Gospel without charge, is much to be admired and imitated by few—especially now that churches have been established, along with the pay of ecclesiastical service, for establishing which the Apostle had labored without charge.

Accordingly, the undue subjection of clerics of this sort, who labor for another’s profit and sometimes murmur at the very fact that they are defrauded of the stipend due to their labor—while, before their eyes and to their resentment, others who labor little or not at all feast and grow rich—is to be called disordered hiring rather than ordered institution.

CLVII. Indeed, the already noted form of simony is utterly detestable in inferior persons, since they are subject to their own proper condemnation. But for bishops who ordain clerics, a great danger threatens the holy Church of God. Pope Nicholas judges that whoever permits himself to be ordained by one whom he does not doubt is a simoniac is to undergo, together with his ordainer, a like sentence of condemnation: that both be deposed, do penance, and remain deprived of their own rank [Col. 0106A].

Yet I do not think that a judgment on this matter should be hastily pronounced; rather, the Apostolic See should be consulted as to whether the aforesaid compact or practice of hiring ought to be designated by the name of the simoniacal pestilence, or called by a milder name—although the writings of blessed Pope Gregory, carefully examined, sufficiently show under what name such transactions ought to be classified.

But lest we seem to prejudice the judges of the Church, it is fitting first to seek counsel from Peter’s successor concerning such matters, without exposing persons, so that their reputation may be spared while caution is provided for. Perhaps, on hearing that such practices are disapproved at the Apostolic See and marked with the branding-iron of simoniacal perversity, they may endeavor quickly to correct themselves before their persons are exposed. Let them know that they may perhaps escape the heretical stigma of simony if they prefer, by repentance, to guard against what has been wrongly done in future rather than, by defending themselves and persecuting their monitors, to increase their wrongdoing.

For just as blessed Peter, not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel and by his dissimulation compelling certain people to Judaize, was rebuked in this matter by the least of the apostles, and yet, because he graciously received admonition and correction, is judged worthy of praise and his authority is not rejected because of such a transgression: so likewise, if any bishop errs in matters which he does not perceive to be done simoniacally, and when rebuked loves the one reproving him and corrects himself where he ought, I think that he is not to be compared with the enemy who sows tares over the field, nor condemned with him, but counted among the husbandmen; nor is he to perish miserably with the wicked, if he does not persecute the Son of God in his members, assents to sound admonitions, loves true grains, and endures tares. By contrast, evil husbandmen love and foster tares and grievously endure grain.

CLVIII. Certainly, I think it should not be omitted here that the following custom is sufficiently tolerable: certain religious abbots and provosts administer the parishes belonging to their monasteries themselves, and assume as their assistants in this ministry no others except either brethren of their own, regularly formed, or learned clerics bound to them in obedience at least according to the discipline of the canons. Thus such men are not free either to depart from them or to live loosely under them contrary to synodal rules.

Those who are bound in this way are not to be called hirelings, but helpers serving the altar and living from the altar, bearing, under a worthy master and in a worthy manner, the yoke of obedience—cenobitic indeed, but also synodal. If, having food and clothing from their ministry, they are content with these, seeking not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ, and use the property of the Church for no purpose except his service, they may be counted among the good husbandmen. They are not in the order of the apostles who left all things, but in the order of the imperfect who cleave to the perfect, obey them as best they can, and assist them in cultivating the Lord’s field.

For true grains are known by the distinction of their fruits: one brings forth thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, another a hundredfold [Col. 0107A]. Many teachers laboring in the Lord’s harvest explain this in such a way as to indicate that these fruits are to be understood as found in the upright married life of spouses, in the chastity of widows or continent persons who are not virgins, and in the perfect holiness of virgins. For no one outside these three kinds of persons living soberly, righteously, and piously can be saved at all. The chosen grains of these three kinds are nourished amid the tares themselves, which must be endured in their time and removed in their time.
