The Gospel teaching plainly instructs us how this ought to take place.

CLIX. For the householder himself, the sower of the good seed, who says, “Lest perhaps, while gathering the tares, you root up the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest” [Col. 0107B] (Matt. 13), is himself the king of the kingdom of heaven—that is, of the present Church or congregation of saints. In it, tares are mingled with the good seed: that is, the children of wickedness, whom the devil has oversown, are mingled with the children of the kingdom until the harvest, that is, until the consummation of the age.

He commands that they be tolerated when he says, “Let both grow together until the harvest,” although very often they blossom sooner and grow higher, so that they attain the highest honors in ecclesiastical ranks. For the mixture of the wicked does no harm to the good, who unwillingly endure them for a time before the harvest because they cannot correct them. Therefore, what he was rightly about to command, and as was fitting for a teacher, he himself first did: he admitted Judas into that number of saints to whom he gave authority to cast out unclean spirits and cure every disease and every infirmity. Thus you may know that the gifts of God reach those who receive them with faith, even if the person through whom they receive them is such as Judas also was.

CLX. Yet it must be understood that after, as Luke writes, Satan entered into him, and he went away and spoke with the chief priests and magistrates about how he might hand him over to them, and they rejoiced and agreed to give him money, and he promised: he no longer exercised that apostolic authority either in casting out unclean spirits or in healing diseases and infirmities. For on the following day, while dining, he was identified as the traitor by the dipped morsel, and immediately went out; and before the Jews hanged upon the cross him whom he had betrayed, he himself hanged himself with a noose.

Nor should we suppose that the true apostles of Christ were of such sluggish patience that, after he had been identified, they could have continued to communicate with him as before if he had not gone out. We say this so that we may not think that the tares which the enemy has oversown upon the good seed ought to be tolerated without discernment of circumstances or times, or that communion with them causes no harm. While Judas was still a hidden thief, and God Christ alone knew this, it did no harm to the apostles that he was joined with them in communion or apostolic authority. But when his most wicked iniquity came forth in action, so that he entered into a bargain of betrayal and murder with the enemies of his Lord and master; when Christ the man made this known to human beings, does reason permit us to suppose that thereafter faithful people could without fault associate in any communion with that devil?

Thus, so long as any children of wickedness, however much harm they do to Christ’s kingdom, nevertheless act under the appearance of good and are covered by the Christian name, while God alone knows what they are, they must be tolerated. But once Christ, who speaks in the Church, has marked them by manifest and proven deed with the name they deserve, neither reason nor the rule of truth permits us even to take food with such persons.

CLXI. Thus the son of the slave woman was tolerated in Abraham’s house together with the son of the free woman until his malice was exposed by evident persecution. When this was seen, the free woman said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” [Col. 0108B] (Gal. 4). “And as then he who was according to the flesh persecuted him who was according to the Spirit, so also now.”

For the apostolic rule of common life, described by the evangelist Luke, has now, thanks be to God, after a long barrenness produced an elect and noble offspring: namely, the regular clergy, heir of all that the Church possesses, offered to God and his saints as the pay of spiritual warfare. Seeing him, the evil tenants say to themselves, thinking wrongly: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance” (Matt. 21). Again: “Behold, the dreamer who accuses his brothers before their father of a most wicked charge. Come, let us kill him and see what his dreams will profit him” [Col. 0108C] (Gen. 37)—dreams by which he declares that our sheaves must be set below his sheaf.

For he holds in contempt the divine offices forbidden to us, as he says, because of the most wicked crimes of simony or open adultery; and, as he says, he esteems beyond measure his own “reasonable service” and that of persons like himself in the divine offices more highly than is right. “Come,” they say, “let us kill him and see what his dreams will profit him.” As though the prohibitions or commands of the Apostolic See ought to be regarded as empty and vain dreams. These are indeed so firm and binding that, when they shut heaven, neither dew nor rain descends except according to the word of their mouth, to whom judicial authority was given in blessed Peter. We could demonstrate many of their prohibitions as closures of heaven, but it is enough here to recall one.

CLXII. GREGORY [Note: [Col. 0107D] Gregory VII], bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, OTTO, bishop of Constance: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“The urgency of your messengers, who wished to return quickly, did not permit us to inform your brotherhood in due order of the decisions made in the Roman synod. Nevertheless, we judged that the following must necessarily be written to you. In accordance with the authority of the holy Fathers, we have pronounced in that synod that those who, through the simoniacal heresy—that is, through the intervention of payment—have been promoted to any rank or office of sacred orders are henceforth to have no place of ministry in the holy Church [Col. 0109A].

“Those also who obtain churches by the giving of money are to lose them altogether; and henceforth no one may be allowed to sell or buy them. Nor should those who lie in the crime of fornication celebrate Masses or minister at the altar according to the lower orders. We have also decreed that, if they are contemptuous of our constitutions—or rather, of the constitutions of the holy Fathers—the people are in no way to receive their offices, so that those who are not corrected for love of God and the dignity of their office may come to their senses through worldly shame and the rebuke of the people.

“Let your brotherhood therefore strive to show itself our fellow-worker in these matters, and to root these crimes utterly out of your churches, so that you may obtain with God the merit of a good shepherd and the Roman Church may rejoice in you as a good brother and diligent fellow-worker.”

CLXIII. Great hostility from their transgressors threatens those who keep these prohibitions and others like them, especially from persons holding high places and offices in the Church. Therefore, when persecution of this kind makes clear which side inflicts and which endures unjust violence, it is fitting that the person who, like the son of the slave woman and as a true schismatic, ought to be cast out should indeed be cast out. He no longer lays snares with Judas the still-hidden thief, but rages with the same Judas, now exposed, against the good through manifest schemes of fury and tyranny; in malignant hatred he persecutes not only those whom he knows, but even those whom he supposes, to be good. Though he himself is darnel, he does not permit good seed to grow with him in the same field. If he bore it with him equably in the same field, he too should be borne.

For example, if, whenever some cleric of an irregular community died or was justly deposed, those remaining allowed another to succeed in the vacant place—a man who had left his own possessions and lived in a cloister—until, as the children of Hannah increased, the children of Peninnah wholly failed, while “the barren woman bore many and she who had many children became weak”: then such persons, bearing such conditions, might be tolerated, receiving their stipends outwardly; even if they lacked sacred orders, entering lawful marriages and living under a Christian rule, keeping, as blessed Gregory says, by God’s help, heart, tongue, and body from unlawful things [Col. 0109D].

Nor are any among those living in this manner judged to be tares, except persons who do not love the holier purpose of those better persons who live in common. Those who lack this in themselves but love it in others make the goods of others their own by loving them. But those who do not endure the good—or those whom they regard as good—are certainly not themselves to be endured.

CLXIV. How tares are to be recognized, endured, or removed, blessed Augustine, one of the chosen reapers, explains to the clergy in his book *Questions on the Gospels*, saying:

“Heretics are rightly understood to be tares among the wheat, because they are mingled with the good not by fellowship in one Church or one faith, but by fellowship in the Christian name alone. Thus those who are evil within the same faith are to be counted rather as chaff than as tares. The difference between heretics and evil Catholics is this: heretics believe false things, but the latter, while believing true things, do not live as they believe.

“It is also customary to ask how schismatics differ from heretics; and this distinction is found: schismatics are not made by a different faith, but by a fellowship once shared and then broken. Whoever believes something false concerning God, or concerning any part of teaching pertaining to the edification of faith—not with the restraint of one hesitating in inquiry, but with the unshaken conviction of one believing, indeed disagreeing by the opinion and error of one who thinks he knows—is a heretic, and is outward in mind, although he may seem bodily to be within.

“For the Church bears many such persons, because they do not defend the falsehood of their opinion so as to draw an attentive multitude after them. But if they do so, then they are expelled. Again, whoever envies the good so as to seek opportunities for excluding or degrading them, or is ready, if his crimes are alleged or exposed, to defend them in such a way as even to contemplate stirring up separations or disturbances of conventicles—such a person is already a schismatic, cut off in heart from unity, even though, because opportunities have not been found or his deeds have been concealed, he may be joined to the sacrament of the Church by bodily association [Col. 0110B].

“Accordingly, those alone are rightly counted evil Catholics who, although they preach truths pertaining to the teaching of faith, and, if they happen not to know something but think it ought to be investigated, examine it with piety preserved and without prejudice to truth; and who love and honor, so far as they can, the good or those they think good; nevertheless live shamefully and wickedly contrary to the manner of life which they believe ought to be followed. Such persons, even if exposed or accused, and for the discipline of the Church and the sake of their salvation corrected or suspended from communion, by no means think that they ought to withdraw themselves from Catholic communion; wherever they are permitted, they seek an opportunity for satisfaction. Sometimes through repentance they become wheat; sometimes under the name of penitents they live as they formerly did, or much less so, and some even more so. Yet in no way do they depart from Catholic unity; and if death overtakes them, they are counted as chaff until the end. This they themselves also believe. For if they believe otherwise and hold it unshakably, they must already be numbered among heretics.

“Good Catholics are those who both follow the whole faith and possess good morals. With respect to the teaching of faith, if they have anything to investigate, they investigate in such a manner that dangerous contention is absent, whether for those investigating, for the person with whom they inquire, or for those listening to the discussion. If they have anything to teach, they teach it so that customary and established matters are conveyed as safely, confidently, and gently as possible; but unfamiliar matters, even if they have grasped them with the clearest manifestation of truth, are put forward as matters for inquiry rather than command or assertion, because of the weakness of the hearer.

“For if some truth has such weight that it exceeds the strength of the learner, it must be suspended so that it may stretch one who is growing, not laid upon him so as to crush one who is little [Col. 0111A]. Hence comes the saying: ‘When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?’ (Luke 18:8.) Sometimes it must also be concealed, but with encouraging hope, so that despair may not make people colder but desire more capable. Hence the saying: ‘I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now’ (John 16:12).

“But with respect to morals, this is well and briefly said: one must either struggle with the love of temporal goods so that it does not conquer; or it must be tamed and subjected so that, when it begins to rise, it may easily be repelled; or it must be so extinguished that it moves one in no respect at all. Hence it comes about that some undergo death for truth bravely, others with equanimity, others willingly. These are the three kinds of fruit of fertile ground: thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold [Col. 0111B]. In one of these kinds a person must be found at the time of death, if he intends rightly to depart from this life.”

CLXV. With Saint Augustine saying these things, good, better, and best ground, distinguished by thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit, is easily recognized. If anyone wishes to distinguish more numerous classes of persons to be saved by means of the foregoing threefold distinction, or likewise by that threefold division in which two are shown in a bed, two in a field, and two at a mill, one of whom is taken and the other left, we refer him to the volumes of the aforesaid Father. In them we find excellent and specific works concerning every kind of person to be saved.

For the instruction of married life he wrote most clearly the book *On the Good of Marriage*; for the education of widows in chastity, *On the Good of Widowhood*; for bringing virgins to the completion of perfection, *On Virginity*; and for the formation of soldiers and princes, *To the Count*. Moreover, for the instruction of monks he wrote *On the Work of Monks*. Concerning the life of clerics he wrote a rule concise in expression, rich in meaning, and entirely consonant with the teaching and life of the apostles.

Therefore, when I consider this teacher’s books, separately composed concerning the distinct orders of the Church, I weigh them as certain sheaves which he is to bring with the joy of a reaper before the Lord of the harvest. Likewise, the most lucid writings of blessed Pope Gregory are certain splendid rules concerning every order of the whole Church. In his book *Pastoral Care* he instructs the clergy; in his *Dialogues*, through the life of Father Benedict which he describes, he instructs the monastic order; and in his homilies, letters, and moral writings he teaches the whole Christian people, according to the care of all the Churches entrusted to him [Col. 0111D].

CLXVI. The teachings of the aforesaid and other orthodox Fathers are therefore certain most upright rules for directing our feet into the way of peace. Those who depart from them must necessarily be healed by the medicine of repentance. Yet false repentances must be avoided—false repentances which the reapers of our time, the Roman pontiffs Gregory VII and Pope Innocent II, have so expelled from the Lord’s field and bound into bundles for burning that those who weigh their writings and prohibitions can plainly recognize that false repentance has no more power against actual sin than false baptism against original sin.

Since this is so, we are rightly moved and grieved when we see in God’s Church some persons excommunicated or under interdict admitted, through false repentance—or, worse, through none at all—to communion in the Lord’s body as laypersons, or, worse still, as Levites. It is as though the flaming sword set to guard the way of the tree of life had been so completely extinguished in our days that access to it lay open to those abusing the tree of the knowledge of good and evil and covering their shameful parts, or, worse still, even defending their manifest sins. In this present storm we see many, with Herod or Herodias, daring what is unlawful, and few, with John, rebuking such things.

CLXVII. And, to take examples from the good: many kings and princes sin after the example of King David, but few are corrected after his example. Many pontiffs and priests fall after Peter’s example, but few rise again after his example. Many merely animal persons, not having the Spirit and living altogether disorderly, using no rule either of cenobitic or even of Christian religion, visibly separate themselves from Christ’s body so that they display in themselves not even the appearance of any good member; yet they communicate with that same body merely sacramentally, no one forbidding them, or, worse still, offer and dispense that same body [Col. 0112C].

Hence even some unlearned persons now not without reason ask that a faithful person be found among the stewards; and few are able—or do—say with the Apostle: “Let a man so account of us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” (1 Cor. 4:1). Again: “In all things let us show ourselves as ministers of God, so that our ministry may not be blamed” (2 Cor. 6:4). Many such persons demand merely by swords and clubs, threats and terrors, that their ministry not be blamed, though it is blameworthy in the sight of God and of human beings.

CLXVIII. Therefore, now that human counsel and assistance fail, “Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation.” For in you alone is our confidence: that you will send and cast out laborers into your harvest; send volunteers and even drive out the unwilling—those whom you know to be suitable laborers. We desire all prelates of all Churches, and especially the bishops, cardinals, and legates of the Apostolic See, to be such persons, so that through them whatever is wrongly done by others may be corrected.

Send, Lord Jesus, your angels into your harvest, who will gather out of your kingdom all scandals and from your fields all tares, among which no small one is that often-noted rule whose evil shrubs occupy the more fertile places in its fields. Thus, as the prophet Amos laments, “the summit of Carmel is dried up, and the lovely places of the shepherds mourn” [Col. 0113A]. For he says: “The Lord shall roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem shall give forth his voice. And the lovely places of the shepherds mourned, and the summit of Carmel was dried up” (Amos 1:2).

CLXIX. Therefore not only is a hymn fitting for you, O God, in Zion, but also a roar from Zion. For just as a hymn is the voice of exultation in the tabernacles of the righteous, citizens of the holy city Zion or Jerusalem, so a roar is a voice of terror, as from the mouth of a lion in terrible judgments upon the lovely places of the shepherds and upon Carmel’s summit.

Formerly the God of majesty thundered over the lovely places of the shepherds and over Carmel’s summit, when the Jewish priests gloried in the precious and beautiful Temple and said, “The Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord is this” [Col. 0113B] (Jer. 7:4). In response, the voice of the Lord breaking the cedars—that is, humbling the falsely glorious—rebuked them for their lying words. Since they were robbing within God’s Temple, that building was no longer to be called a temple but a den of thieves; and by God’s just judgment, when the king of Babylon came, all the beautiful things of the Temple were to be laid waste.

Carmel’s summit—that is, the pride of the Jews who vainly gloried in their knowledge of circumcision, for this is what “Carmel” signifies—was to be humbled and dried up by the withdrawal of rain. And this happened: first through the first Babylon, and second through the second Babylon, Rome. The Jews were taken captive and all their beautiful things laid waste. Since the clouds do not rain down the shower of grace upon Carmel—the name of which, because it is interpreted “knowledge of circumcision,” indicates the whole worship of Jewish religion—Carmel itself is rightly compared to the mountains of Gilboa, because neither dew nor the rain of heavenly grace comes upon Jewish observances, however beautiful and glorious they may be through their knowledge of law and circumcision.

Thus the lovely places of the shepherds, in which God was not well pleased, rightly mourned; and Carmel’s summit was rightly dried up, being deprived of heavenly dew and rain. What was said of false Jews, children only according to the flesh and not through faith or imitation, against the glory of those who vainly gloried in the lovely places of the shepherds and in Carmel’s summit, the Spirit undoubtedly now says also to the Churches. In them the worship of walls is beautiful and shines with much gold, while the condition of minds is found neglected and filthy [Col. 0113D].

CLXX. Carmel’s dried-up summit is also demonstrated when it may truly be said to the angel of any Church raised upon the summit of episcopal eminence: “You have left your first love” (Rev. 2:4); or, “Because you are lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you out” (Rev. 3:16); or, “You have a name that you live, but you are dead” (ibid., 3:1); or, “You do not know that you are wretched and miserable, blind and naked” (ibid., 3:17). What do these sayings addressed against the angels of the Churches signify except Carmel’s summit dried up?

But when each such person is told, “Repent” (ibid., 3:19), hope of both forgiveness and grace is given, so that, moistened anew by the dew and rain of grace, Carmel’s summit may be drenched with the upper and lower watering, bud forth, and produce fruits worthy of repentance: in place of the nettle of lust, the myrtle of chastity; and in place of the *saliunca* [a plant signifying sloth], the fir tree of the contemplative and active life together. Both are signified in the fir tree, which stands upon the earth but rises upward in its growth, so that its rooting below and height above may teach us, while despising earthly things, to possess them only in use, and, contemplating heavenly things, to burn with holy desire.

CLXXI. Therefore, once such nettles and *saliuncae* have been removed—such as uncultivated ground produces, ground never turned by the plough of any cenobitic or at least Christian rule according to the Fathers’ sound instruction—you who curse the fig tree beautiful only in leaves and without fruit, namely the malignant Synagogue, pompous in outward appearance and empty of virtues, will bless the crown of the year of your goodness by granting fertility after much barrenness. And when your blessing has thus been poured out, your fields, hitherto uncultivated but now well cultivated, will be filled with abundance fully sufficient to fill the Lord’s barns with the plenty of that final harvest, in which all tares are to be removed.

Your fields—that is, human beings filled with the equity of justice—will be filled with the abundance of good works. And while the lovely places of the shepherds, discussed above, mourn, by contrast the lovely places of the desert will grow fat. For, once the Jews and their like have been rejected—those who have an appearance of piety and are therefore beautiful, but deny its power and are therefore contemptible—the poor receive the Gospel, not only from among the Jews but also from among the Gentiles: contemptible to the world, but beautiful to God, who sees hearts [Col. 0114C].

Such persons, deserted and forsaken by the world, grow fat inwardly before God. Each of them says to him: “May my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. 62:6). By contrast, to others it is said: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Luke 13:35). Although outwardly they may be made fat, rich, and enlarged by abundance of temporal goods, they lack the fatness of fatted calves. When, though under interdict and deserted by the Holy Spirit, they offer and eat it merely sacramentally, they become guilty of his body and blood, not participants in its fatness.

CLXXII. By this very richness the beauties of the desert will grow rich [Col. 0114D], when the poor, abandoning this world and abandoned by it, worthily sacrifice or eat the Lord’s body, through which they become partakers of the Holy Spirit, who is the richness of the fatted calf. But those who set themselves apart as merely natural persons, having not the Spirit, although they continually sacrifice or communicate, fast from this richness by which, as has been said, the beauties of the desert will grow rich and the hills will gird themselves with exultation. In this beautiful desert, or in these fields filled with abundance, the hills may be understood as those who, because they humble themselves, shall be exalted; and in that very exaltation they shall then exult in glory before those reclining together, when each of them will be told: “Friend, come up higher” (Luke 14:10). The dried summit of Carmel, as we have partly shown above [Col. 0115A], is very unlike these hills, rejoicing and exulting amid the multitude of sweetness that intoxicates them. For these, insofar as their spirit cleaves to God and becomes one with him, are inwardly filled with exultation; but insofar as their body of humility shall be conformed to the body of his glory, they shall also be girded outwardly with exultation.

CLXXIII. And since some among such persons become teachers of rational flocks, they are called hills because of the prerogative of grace, and rams because of the flocks committed to them. They shall indeed be girded with the aforesaid exultation together with the other hills, but shall be clothed above the rest, so that each may say with the prophet: “I will rejoice greatly in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God. For he has clothed [Col. 0115B] me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in the covering of righteousness, like a bridegroom adorned with a crown and like a bride adorned with her jewels” (Isa. 61:10). In the name of bridegroom, consider the fatherly affection of devotion; in that of bride, the motherly affection. A double adornment is deservedly due to such affection, most fitting both for bridegroom and bride. And the hills shall abound with grain. The “mountains” indeed “shall leap like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock” (Ps. 113:4); then the hills shall be girded with exultation, and the rams shall be clothed with that same exultation as with a wedding garment. But valleys lower than such hills—that is, those holy and humble in heart, endowed with no ecclesiastical dignity—shall abound in the grain of spiritual virtues [Col. 0115C], such as the Apostle enumerates when he says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control, chastity” (Gal. 5:22). Abounding in fruits of this sort, they shall not be silent from praise or thanksgiving, by which they shall cry out—not against the Lord, as blasphemers, the arrogant, and murmurers do, or as those who boast of their own merits and utter other things better left unsaid. That is not to abound in grain, but to bring forth thorns and briars.

CLXXIV. Therefore both hills and valleys, both prelates and subjects, shall cry out, continually praying to God and praising him, or giving him thanks. Against the word of exile, which was the cause of their long captivity, they shall cry out by preaching the word of salvation [Col. 0115D], which shall be the effective cause of their return. Sold by that former word, they sat beside the rivers of Babylon, not singing but weeping, because they could not sing a hymn from the songs of Zion in a foreign land. Redeemed by this word, and now established in spirit in the heavenly Jerusalem, thereafter also to be transferred there in body, they take up the instruments once hung aside and celebrate the hymn from the songs of Zion all the more solemnly as, withdrawing from Babylon, they enter more readily through the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem.

CLXXV. For since it is written, “Enter his gates with confession, his courts with hymns,” these people returned from Babylon stand in the courts of Jerusalem. For they shall utter the hymn which they would not utter if they were outside those courts. They shall utter a hymn—not such as it was fitting for a few, suited to such martyrdom, to utter in the furnace of fire [Col. 0116A] in the midst of Babylon, for example under the persecution of the most foul and wicked Nero—but the hymn of which it was said at the beginning of this chief song among the songs of Zion: “A hymn is fitting for you, O God, in Zion.” What is that hymn, unless, after the destruction of all the Babylonian kings, of whom Antichrist shall be the last, and after the rebuilding of the city Jerusalem, it is the exultant song expressed in the last seven psalms? There the universal Church, or any ecclesiastical person delivered from the evil sword, whether in hope or, better still, in reality, so exults in Christ her king that not only the three children, or most mighty men, but even the daughters of Zion exult in their king, greatly opposed to the king of Babylon. Of the king of Babylon Daniel says: “Whomever he wished he killed; whomever he wished he struck; whomever he wished he exalted; whomever he wished he humbled” (Dan. 5:19). “Whomever he wished,” he says—not whomever he ought.

CLXXVI. Therefore the daughters of Zion exult in their king, who says: “I came not to do my own will, but that of the Father who sent me” (John 6:38); because he exalts no one, however closely related in the flesh, except insofar as the cause of justice requires. He rejects his Jewish brethren when guilt is present, and strikes or humbles no one whom faith and humility commend. Thus neither does he exclude from the glory prepared for the saints Gentiles who are found worthy in other respects. Accordingly, he is the king of righteousness [Col. 0116C], worthy of glory and honour, worthy of the hymn of Zion’s citizens: “A hymn is fitting for you, O God, in Zion.” For young men and virgins shall utter the hymn, the younger with the elder, the little ones with the great, singing unanimously: Glory to the Father, whose temple is wonderful in righteousness; glory to the Son, who is himself the temple; glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that richness by which the beauties of the desert shall grow rich. Glory to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the one and triune God, both in the temple wonderful in righteousness and in the fields filled with abundance. Let priests and Levites glorify him in the temple by a wonderful observance of justice: when, as mediators among the people, they neither turn aside to unjust judgments, nor defraud God by proclaiming his righteousness less than they ought, nor defraud the people by rebuking their sins less than is fitting [Col. 0116D]. Likewise, in the fields filled with abundance, let the whole Christian people glorify him, bringing him glory and honour in the fruits of righteousness or of worthy repentance. Amen, amen, amen.

## Letter of Pope Eugenius III to Gerhoh, approving the work described above

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son G., provost of Reichersberg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have graciously received the writings of your devotion, and from examining them have plainly recognized the fervour of your religious commitment. For your heart has grown warm within you, and in your meditation a fire burns brightly. Your utterance, too, is powerfully aflame. Therefore, because we know that, out of zeal for charity, you burn against the worst innovations and also against the disturbances [Col. 0117A] which arise against the Church of God and ecclesiastical persons, we rejoice with paternal affection and commend your devotion in the Lord. Yet because it is good to begin, but much better to complete, we exhort your love in the Lord [Col. 0118A] to persevere firmly in your good purpose. For we love your person with paternal charity as a learned and religious man, and desire, insofar as we can according to God, to honour and support you.

## GERHOH’S LETTER TO EBERHARD, ARCHBISHOP OF SALZBURG

[Col. 0117]

To his most serene lord and father E., archbishop of the venerable Church of Juvavum, brother G. of Reichersberg, his devoted servant: prayers together with the obedience of faith.

I now offer for the inspection of your dovelike and eagle-like eyes a portion of my exposition of the Psalms which you have not yet seen: dovelike because of the simplicity of devotion; eagle-like because of the sharpness of subtle discernment. But I care little for the eyes of ravens that judge my writings malignantly, provided that they please the eyes of the Beloved and of the beloved: of the Beloved, “whose eyes are like doves washed with milk, dwelling beside full streams”; of the beloved, “whose eyes are doves,” apart from what lies hidden within. Therefore, dearest Father in the Lord, deign to read through the little work of your little son and servant; and if anything in it offends you, tell me. By God’s mercy, I shall without doubt either correct it or fortify it with a reasonable defence.

## PART SEVEN

[Col. 0117]

## THE PROLOGUE OF GERHOH BEGINS

[Col. 0117B] In the last psalm of the preceding part, addressed to the Apostolic See, we digressed more fully than the exposition of the psalm required, while we tried, by God’s favour, faithfully and sufficiently to set before apostolic ears the disorders which we see and lament occurring in the Church of God. We believed and hoped that from the throne of apostolic rule there would proceed, through Pope Eugenius of holy memory, lightnings, voices, and thunderings against the manifold monsters of errors and prodigies of disorder. And, thanks be to God, in urging these things we found him a willing, learned, and attentive hearer, when the exposition of the said psalm was presented to him through our person, and when he also heard from our lips, in an exhortation by living voice, what we had written [Col. 0117C]. But we did not find the effect desirable to our affection, because that blessed man was already then weighed down, like another Elijah, by the persecutions of the Roman people, as by the vexations of an impious Jezebel; or, like another Jonah, battered by storms. Death was more desirable to him than life, so that he said with Elijah: “It is enough for me, Lord; take away my life” [Col. 0118B] (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19:4); or with Jonah: “Death is better for me than life” (Jonah 4:3).

How acceptable to him the urging of our littleness was is undoubtedly indicated by the fact that he afterward appointed our humble person to sow the seeds of ecclesiastical faith and discipline in two great kingdoms, namely those of the Hungarians and the Ruthenians. We could not, however, go there because of the hostility of the king of Hungary, whom we had formerly rebuked and who was angry with us on that account. Therefore, avoiding the bloody hands of that man as of another Herod or Pharaoh, we could not carry out the ministry of legation laid upon us, because our writings sent into Hungary had touched upon the aforesaid Herodian cruelty [Col. 0118C]. Thus, after the mission of legation assigned to our person by Pope Eugenius had been delayed and removed, he died a blessed death, leaving among us—indeed, throughout the whole holy Church—a sweet memory of his fervour and good will. Many grieved that after him there was not found in the Apostolic See [Col. 0119A] one like him who would preserve the law of the Most High, as the letters and deeds of his successor, Pope Anastasius, an old and infirm man, attest. Of these matters we must not now speak individually, since no human being ought to judge the successors of Peter, whether they wield the sword and walk upon the sea with him, or tremble among the ministers of death and are endangered in the storm with him. Yet, concerning our insignificant person, we say this: when Pope Eugenius, like another Elijah, was taken up on high, and we did not see another Elisha, as it were, appointed in his place, we were so dismayed that we imposed silence upon our mouth [Col. 0120A], almost entirely ceasing the work on the Psalms which we had begun, content with the study of prayer and reading. But now, because Pope Adrian—[Note: [Col. 0119] Nicholas Breakspear, an Englishman from the College of Cardinals, called Adrian IV, in the year 1154.]—who succeeded Anastasius possesses something of the spirit of Pope Eugenius, or rather of the spirit of the Apostle Peter, indeed also of the spirit of Christ himself, so as to love those whom he believes or knows to be good and to support those who contend for the law of their God, we have, as it were, awakened from the sleep of sorrow, and give an opening to this seventh part through the resurrection of joy that had for a time been lulled to sleep, beginning with Psalm 65, entitled “Of the Resurrection.”

## PSALM 65

[Col. 0119]

[Col. 0119B] “Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his name,” etc. This psalm and the two that follow it in succession look toward the shining face of Moses, drawing their material from it by deriving a mystical meaning from the letter of the Law. For this present psalm draws its material from the place where it is written in the book of Numbers: “And it came to pass on the day when Moses completed the tabernacle, and raised it up, anointed and sanctified it with all its vessels, likewise the altar and its vessels, that the princes of Israel and heads of families offered gifts before the Lord: six covered wagons with twelve oxen, etc.” (Num. 7:3). It was not without the signification of a great mystery that, once the tabernacle had been completed and raised up at the Lord’s command, the individual leaders, on individual days, offered gifts at the dedication of the altar, and all their gifts were the same, as the Lord commanded. Thus on the first day Naasson son of Aminadab, from the tribe of Judah, offered his offering: a silver dish weighing one hundred and thirty shekels; a silver bowl weighing seventy shekels according to the sanctuary weight; both filled with fine flour mixed with oil for sacrifice; a golden mortar weighing one hundred and twenty gold shekels, full of incense; a bull, a ram, and a year-old lamb for a burnt offering; a goat for sin; and, for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five goats, and five year-old lambs. Likewise, each leader of the remaining tribes, each on his own day, offered gifts of the same [Col. 0119D] quantity and value. All offered equal gifts, and Moses’ pen is not wearied by saying the same things twelve times, for each of the twelve tribes, in the same words and with the same full syllables.

What does this mean, except that a great mystery is concealed here also beneath the letter of the Law? Therefore we look also to him in whom are hidden all the treasures [Col. 0120B] of wisdom and knowledge, who fulfilled the Law in himself, as he says: “Do not think that I came to abolish the Law; I came not to abolish but to fulfil” (Matt. 5:17). Certainly, in fulfilling even this part of the Law, he called to himself those whom he wished to come up the mountain; and they came to him, and he made twelve to be with him, that he might send them to preach, and gave them authority to heal infirmities and cast out demons. “And when,” says Mark, “his own people heard, they went out to seize him; for they were saying, ‘He has gone mad’” (Mark 3:21). But that truly and uniquely blessed man had not gone mad; rather, his delight was in the Law of the Lord, and on his Law he meditated day and night, since he was himself the sanctuary of the whole Law. Then [Col. 0120C] he meditated upon fulfilling the Law: that is, according to the mystery of this present Law, upon appointing leaders of twelve spiritual camps. Looking to this also, he says elsewhere to the same Apostles: “Amen I say to you that you who have left all things and followed me, in the kingdom, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, shall also sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). For Peter had said to him: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you. What then shall there be for us?” (ibid., v. 27). He honoured them greatly, marked out for them great honour and a great reward, when he answered them thus. For he intends it to be understood that he himself is the Lord of the heavenly tabernacle, but that they will be the leaders [Col. 0120D] of the tribes of the Lord, of whom the Psalmist, after saying, “Jerusalem, which is built as a city whose participation is in unity,” immediately added: “For thither the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, a testimony to Israel, to give thanks to the name of the Lord” (Ps. 121:3); and that what was commanded to those twelve leaders of the sons of Israel to do or offer bodily [Col. 0121A] would be fulfilled spiritually by these or through them. For when was this heavenly tabernacle, after the pattern of which Moses made this tabernacle, raised up, anointed, and sanctified with all its vessels? Certainly when Jesus Christ, Son of God and high priest of the tabernacle, shed his blood, by which, in granting forgiveness of sins, he anointed and sanctified the whole Church, insofar as it had been gathered from the beginning of the world. Immediately afterward these leaders offered oxen and wagons to carry the tabernacle or the sanctuary of the tabernacle, when they undertook to have the faith of the patriarchs and prophets preached throughout the whole world. In this way they themselves are the wagons, they themselves the guides, they themselves the bearers of the Church.

[Col. 0121B] Each offered a silver dish weighing one hundred and thirty shekels. This number, composed of a hundred and thirty, rightly signifies faith in the one God and three persons. They also offered a silver bowl weighing seventy shekels. This number, composed of ten and seven, denotes the evangelical grace of the sevenfold Holy Spirit and true knowledge of the Law, whose commandments are ten. They also offered a golden mortar weighing one hundred and thirty gold shekels, filled with incense: that is, they proclaimed in harmonious voice Christ, the Son of God, whose body conceived of the Virgin was golden, an immaculate body containing in itself all the precious incense of pure prayer, and was crushed for us by the passion of death. These things they offered [Col. 0121C]; these things each proclaimed for the praise and glory of God on his own day, that is, each according to the measure of grace or revelation which he received from God, from the one and same Lord, the Holy Spirit. Some indeed drew more people to faith, others fewer. But all preached the same thing in the same Spirit and with the same mind, just as those tribal leaders had some more and some fewer thousands of their tribe under their hand, but all offered equal gifts, all the same vessels. Those leaders offered fine flour in vessels—visible flour mixed with visible oil; but these proclaimed the spirit of the Law hidden in the letter, the true and invisible fine flour, the true and life-giving food of believing souls.

[Col. 0121D] Nevertheless, they offered a bull, a ram, and a year-old lamb for a burnt offering, a goat for sin, and, in the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five goats, and five year-old lambs. These, I say, our leaders each offered. For while preaching to others, lest they themselves should become reprobate, they afflicted themselves and exposed themselves to sufferings. For they are those of whom each says in the psalm which we are now considering: “And my mouth spoke in my tribulation; I will offer you fat burnt offerings with the incense of rams; I will offer you oxen with goats.” For this whole psalm is the voice of these leaders, as though each of them said: Even when placed in tribulation, I shall preach to others [Col. 0122A], that by my example they too may be led to the same end; and meanwhile here I shall offer you fat burnt offerings—that is, myself, made a fat burnt offering, wholly consumed by the inward fire of charity—with rams, oxen, and goats burned up: every resistance, every self-exaltation, every foulness of the vices of flesh and spirit. For this is why there are five rams, five lambs, and five goats: namely, because the flesh indulges itself, when permitted, in the five senses. This accords with our meaning.

### Title

(V. 1). **FOR THE END: A SONG, A PSALM OF THE RESURRECTION.** For this title sends attentive hearers forward to the end, when, once the building of the heavenly tabernacle is complete [Col. 0122B], that tabernacle must be dedicated by the universal resurrection. It is now constructed from day to day, until, with all its columns and boards and its entire structure complete, the day of dedication shines forth. This is understood as the day of universal resurrection, whose dawn already spreads over heaven, while the saints who are thereafter to rise bodily now rise spiritually, having been planted together not only in the likeness of Christ’s death through the fat burnt offerings and the other sacrifices noted in this psalm, but also in the likeness of his resurrection, as they make joyful noise and give glory to his praise. He both displayed in himself the firstfruits of resurrection, rising from the dead while many bodies of saints rose with him, and promised the glory of that same resurrection not only [Col. 0122C] to those chosen from Judaea, but also to those called from the multitude of the Gentiles from all the earth. Therefore it is said:

“Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth.” Make a joyful noise to God, so that your praise may be a song; and so that it may be the song of a psalm, “sing a psalm to his name.” This is the universal song of universal hope: that all of us who shall rise may make joyful noise. Therefore this psalm says universally: “Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth. Sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise,” etc.

Yet it also sings to the oft-mentioned combatant, teaching in what order he ought to hope and in what manner he must set his hope in liberating grace. “If,” he says, [Col. 0122D] “I looked upon iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear.” It is as though he said: If I, who ought to fight against the law which is in my members, loved and willingly looked upon the iniquity of those members, the Lord will not hear me silently, so as by his grace to free me from this body of death. For he says *I looked upon* in place of *I loved*, because we more frequently turn our eyes toward that which we love. Therefore God heard, because, as I have said above, “my mouth spoke in my tribulation”: I confessed in my misery, namely in the resistance of the flesh, and said: “I will offer you fat burnt offerings with incense of rams; I will offer you oxen with goats.” By rams he intends every resistance of the flesh; by oxen, self-exaltation; by goats, every foulness of evil works [Col. 0123A]. He says that he offers all these when he punishes them by confessing and repenting.

This undoubtedly belongs to the song of resurrection, because in acting thus he rises by the first resurrection, which is that of the soul. The Jews hoped from the righteousness of the Law for temporal goods and for themselves alone the resurrection to a blessed life, though in it they understood no goods or delights other than earthly ones. Hence they could not answer the Sadducees’ question about the woman’s seven husbands, being ignorant of Christ’s solution: “They shall neither marry nor be given in marriage” (Matt. 22:30); for succession is not necessary where there shall be no departure through death. Against their presumption and pride, this psalm shows that Gentiles also have been called through faith to that same hope of resurrection [Col. 0123B], so that our whole attention may be fixed where Christ, the firstfruits of those rising, has gone before. Hence it is called “a song of resurrection for the end,” that is, exultation over the future resurrection through Christ; and it is also called a psalm because on account of this we are exhorted to do good works.

With this hope, therefore, the Church first exhorts all to rejoice in the resurrection of Christ, who gives life. Second, she invites beginners to consider the works of God, so that one faith may unite those who await one reward; in expounding those works of God, she openly says that the Gentiles shall rise while the Jews are rejected, at the words: “Come and see the works of the Lord.” Third, she exhorts the Gentiles to bless our God because, although he tests us by tribulations [Col. 0123C], he nevertheless leads us to the kingdom: “Bless, O nations, our God.” Fourth, she exhorts no longer the untrained but the devout, by the example of her liberation, to place fuller confidence in the Lord: “Come and hear, and I will tell, all you who fear God.” Therefore, as has been said, in this song of resurrection, in this solemn celebration of the universal dedication of the tabernacle which God, not man, established, let not Judaea alone but all the earth make joyful noise, as the holy Apostles invite the whole earth to this feast of dedication and say:

### Verse 2. “Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth.”

You five earthborn peoples and sons of men, gathered together as one—the rich and poor, Jew and Greek, barbarian and Scythian, male and female alike—make joyful noise for the joy of this [Col. 0123D] dedication, namely for the feast of resurrection. Make joyful noise in your hearts, rejoicing magnificently, so that our joy may be full and so wonderful that it can neither be concealed by silence nor explained in speech. Yet lest such inward jubilation of heart should remain hidden and fail to build outwardly by displaying itself in good works to God’s glory—though not displaying itself in ostentation for boasting—

“Sing a psalm”: that is, do good works, not to spread your own name but for the name of him who called us out of darkness into his wonderful light and placed us in his tabernacle; or rather, who made you yourselves his tabernacle. In it, throughout all the days in which he now wages war and overcomes his enemies from you and within you, he prepares for you the feast of the future dedication [Col. 0124A]. It shall then be completed, when every enemy has been defeated and the last trumpet shall sound—not now summoning his soldiers to battle, but awakening them to rise: “For that trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Cor. 15:52), that is, wholly sanctified and dedicated—we who now wage good warfare in this tabernacle and who are ourselves God’s tabernacle, of which it is elsewhere said: “Behold the tabernacle of God with human beings; and he shall dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself with them shall be their God” (Rev. 21:3). Then, in that dedication, God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes; death shall be no more, neither mourning nor crying nor pain shall be any more, but everlasting jubilation. Therefore, in order that you may come prepared and trained to [Col. 0124B] that everlasting jubilation, even now make joyful noise and sing a psalm to his name by doing good.

Nor are you to claim glory for yourselves from this; rather, give glory to his name, not to your own effort, as the Jews do, who attribute righteousness to their merits and begrudge grace to the Gentiles. If one must glory, though indeed it is not expedient, let no one glory in his own strength, but in the Lord, who chose the weak things of the world and the things that are not, in order to confound the strong and destroy the things that are, so that no flesh may glory before him. He resists the proud but gives grace to the humble; he casts down the mighty from their throne and exalts the humble. Hence it is greatly to be feared that he may withdraw from the humble person the grace he has given when that person grows proud even of grace itself. For it is not human power but the divine that works in us both to will and to accomplish according to good will. Therefore it is greatly to be feared that, if we wish to attribute a divine work to human power, grace may be withdrawn. Thus it happened to the Jews, who, when they said, “We see,” became blind. Thus it happened to the philosophers of this world, who, professing themselves wise, became fools. Thus everyone who thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself; nor does the severity of divine judgment spare those who vainly glory in any rank or nobility of birth. For if God did not spare the natural branches of the olive tree, lifted up too far beyond their measure, how would he spare branches of the wild olive grafted contrary to nature into such an olive tree, if they grow luxuriantly in vain glory [Col. 0124D]? See then the goodness and severity of God: goodness toward those grafted into the olive tree, who, making joyful noise and singing well, give glory not to themselves but to his name throughout all the earth; but severity toward those who, amid God’s gifts, glorified not God but themselves and boasted in their own strength, and deserved to be cut off. Therefore, although I first said “Make a joyful noise,” which pertains to joy, lest perhaps someone exult without trembling—since elsewhere it has been said, “Serve the Lord in fear, and exult before him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11)—I now say:

### Verse 3. “Say to God: How terrible are your works, O Lord!”

You yourselves, who make joyful noise to God with exultation over some gift bestowed on you in reality or in hope, at the same time, in the trembling and fear of his dreadful judgment [Col. 0125A], say to God himself: “How terrible are your works, O Lord!” Who can fully weigh how terrible your works are, O Lord, when you rejected your Jewish kinsmen and laid waste, as enemies—indeed, truly as hostile enemies—the children of your friends, the patriarchs?

You did this, certainly, by just judgment, because “in the multitude of your power your enemies shall lie to you,” though born from your friends. It was not enough for them to have lied many times amid the multitude of your power—for example, when they said that you cast out demons by Beelzebub, and, “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9:16). Instead, still further, to crown their wickedness, amid the great multitude of your power, when you had risen from the dead and raised many [Col. 0125B] bodies of saints, they bought from the soldiers who guarded your tomb such a lie that it remains and shall remain spread among their descendants until the end of the age. By this very lie all Jews are blinded, except for the few remnants who, according to the prophecies of the prophets, are to be saved and have been saved. Thus iniquity not only lied to itself then, but they also shall lie to you with a lie harmful not to you but to them, who love that lie; while those remnants are delivered from it by you, the Truth, who set them free. “For I too am an Israelite” (Rom. 11:1), says the Apostle when treating of the remnants, partly saved and partly to be saved, counting himself also among such remnants. And indeed in all your works the multitude of power is recognized, because you performed works which no other performed: namely, not as the other saints performed miracles by an imparted power, obtained through prayer, but acting authoritatively in the multitude and fullness of your own power. Thus you commanded the winds and sea, and they obeyed; commanded demons to be silent or depart, and they obeyed; commanded the dead to rise, and they obeyed. That centurion recognized this multitude of your power, who said to you: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only speak the word, and my boy shall be healed.” “Speak,” he says, “the word” [Col. 0125C]—that is, not a supplicatory but a commanding word—and my boy shall be healed. And to demonstrate by human reasoning also that he had spoken truly, he added: “For I too am a man set under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it” (Matt. 8:8–9). Therefore, he says, “Only speak the word, and my servant shall be healed.” In all such wonderful works of yours, the multitude of your own power abounded in you. Hence when, amid such deeds, you poured out prayers—as in the raising of Lazarus—you did this solely as an example, necessary not for yourself but for us. For in the multitude of your power you did all things whatsoever you wished. Chief among them was this: having authority to lay down your life and take it up again by your own power, in the multitude of your power [Col. 0126A] you rose and caused others to rise with you; and in yourself you consecrated the firstfruits of those who sleep, who likewise are to be raised in the multitude of your power. Truly, you not only rose in the multitude of your power, but also raised them in that same power. For death shall no longer have dominion over you; and it is most faithfully believed of those who rose as a testimony to your resurrection already accomplished and ours still to come that they did not return thereafter to their tombs, but have already received the twofold robe. The same is also thought, by a pious opinion though not asserted with certain assurance, concerning the most blessed Virgin Mary: namely, that, glorified, she has already received the twofold robe not only in her soul but also in her spirit. Her body, it is reported, was indeed buried by the holy Apostles according to human custom [Col. 0126B], but was afterward not found in the tomb, just as the Lord’s body was not found in the tomb after his burial.

Nor is it surprising that, in the multitude of your power by which you are faithfully believed to have raised your mother’s virginal body, your enemies should lie to you, since even in the multitude of unquestioned power by which you consecrated anew the divine temple of your own flesh, folded in a three-day burial and then raised up, your enemies lie to you. You yourself commended this wondrous work of power by your own testimony, saying: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will rebuild it” (John 2:19). Again: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights” (Matt. 12:40) [Col. 0126C]. Yet your enemies, denying nonetheless that this temple of your body was rebuilt or consecrated anew, will lie to you, so that this very lie may result in honor for you, not for them. The members of a man’s household sometimes so lie about him that his glory is diminished through their lie; but your glory is thereby magnified all the more, because your enemies shall lie to you in the multitude of your power. For had your lying enemies not been believed concerning you, you would not have been crucified. [Note: [Col. 0125] Perhaps: “For if the enemies lying concerning you had not been believed, you would not have been crucified.”] For if the rulers had known you in the multitude of your power, they would not have crucified you. If you had not been lifted up on the cross, you would not draw all things to yourself; nor could you, the grain of wheat, be multiplied through the faith of the peoples unless you had been put to death by the falsehood of the judgments.

Therefore your enemies were believed as they lied concerning you and called you a deceiver or a magician, so that power might be perfected in weakness; indeed, so that the multitude of our weakness might be swallowed up in the multitude of your power, and our death might die through your death, according to the saying: “O death, I will be your death.” Likewise, while other heretics and false speakers still lie concerning you, the truth of your sayings shines forth more clearly, as the orthodox defend the doctrine of your truth in the multitude of power. “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel,” says the Apostle, “for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Rom. 1:10). Yet the Jew, unbelieving and contradicting your Gospel, will lie to you [Col. 0127A], because he is unwilling to see in it the multitude of your power, but prefers to envy the salvation of the Gentiles. Therefore, that through further envy he may see that by which he is tormented:

**VERSE 4.** “Let all the earth worship you and sing psalms to you.”

Because the branches of the natural olive tree have been broken off, let branches of the wild olive be grafted in their place and bear fruit worthy of the richness of the root. Abraham, the chief root of the olive tree, “saw three and worshipped one” (Gen. 18:2–3). But these fleshly sons of Abraham refuse to do Abraham’s works, because they refuse to worship you as the true God; indeed, they seek to kill you. Abraham did not do this. Abraham, their father, rejoiced to see your day; he saw it and was glad. But they both saw and hated both you and your Father. Therefore, when these have been rejected and the Gentiles substituted in their place, let the Church, spread throughout the whole world, be enlarged; and thus let all the earth—that is, the whole Church in every land—worship you, fear you, love you, and follow you, so that, while it continually walks in your footsteps, it may deserve, under your guidance, to reach the heavenly promises.

Let it worship you as Truth, and in you, the Truth, worship the true Father; for “true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4:23). Since the Holy Spirit gives them life and sanctifies them, while you, the Truth, illuminate them, they love him with a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith; and in him they love his only-begotten Son—you, born from the Father before the beginning of all ages and begotten from a virgin mother at the end of the ages [Col. 0127C]. Therefore, equally with your Father, who is true God, let all the earth—that is, the whole Church—worship you, true God and also true man, consubstantial with both Father and mother, together with the Father: believing with the heart unto righteousness and confessing with the mouth unto salvation. Let it sing psalms to you by works befitting faith. And lest the boastful display of one’s own name should creep in during such work, let it declare the psalm of all good action and ascribe it to your name, not its own.

Here the Hebrews insert *Selah*, and we have *Diapsalma*. *Selah* means “Always,” because praise must always be sung to the Lord’s name. *Diapsalma*, a division in the psalm, indicates that the speakers change here. For the apostrophe that had been made is turned toward addressing the worshippers themselves [Col. 0127D], of whom he had spoken as though they were absent.

**VERSE 5.** “Come,” he says, “and see the works of God.”

Some manuscripts have: “Let all the earth worship; let it sing a psalm to your name, O Most High.” This is the same as saying: Although your enemies, lying to you amid the multitude of your power, deny that you are the Most High because they see you as the lowliest of men, reckoned among the wicked, nevertheless, beyond all genuine contradiction, you, the Son of the Most High, are with him and in him one Most High, equally with your Father worthy of worship. O Most High, because of your ever-most-high divinity, and because of your humanity, crowned and exalted with the glory and honor of divinity beyond measure [Col. 0128A]—unlike the other saints, however exalted in glory they may be, none of whom is called the Most High. For example, Peter, the chief of the apostles, is greatly honored; and after him, or together with him, your other friends are greatly honored. Yet among all of them none is a Most High comparable to you. O Most High, not only in your lofty divinity but also in your ineffably exalted humanity.

Thus the stone which the liars, fabricating their lies, rejected was exalted and made the head of the corner—the Most High; and this is wonderful in our eyes. Come, then, you Gentiles seeking the truth rejected by the lying Jews, and behold this wonderful spectacle with a single eye.

On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says in a homily [Note: [Col. 0127D] Book I, Homily 4 on the Gospels]:

> “We must carefully understand that in everything we do we should always fear the hidden counsels of the almighty Lord, lest, while our mind, poured outward, does not withdraw itself from its pleasure, the dreadful Judge inwardly ordain adverse things against it. The Psalmist, seeing this well, says: ‘Come and see the works of God, how terrible he is in his counsels over the children of men.’ He saw, therefore, that one person is mercifully called and another is rejected by the demands of justice; and because the Lord disposes some things by sparing and others by anger, he was awestruck at what he could not penetrate. And seeing him not only unsearchable but also inflexible, he declared him terrible in his counsels.”

Come, therefore, by believing, and see by understanding; for unless you believe, you shall not understand. See the works of the Lord, for this Son of Man is the Lord, and he alone does great wonders, because together with the Father and the Holy Spirit he alone is most high, most present and most hidden, most merciful and most just; and therefore terrible in his counsels over the children of men. Among them, by his most hidden counsel, he hardens whom he wills and has mercy on whom he wills, discerning whom he shall harden and whom he shall soften, or whom he shall make firm out of what is fluid and slippery. This, indeed, he is accustomed to do.

**VERSE 6.** “Who turned the sea into dry land.”

That is, he turns the bitter, turbulent, stormy hearts of the Gentiles to the firmness of faith and the dryness of chastity. Such dry land thirsts for the rain of heavenly grace, and, watered from above [Col. 0128D], bears the fruit of holiness. Those who have been turned into dry land have not yet escaped the river of passing mortality, in which, after the manner of a river, wave comes upon wave: some things arrive, some pass away, and others that will pass succeed them. But those who believe in Christ are neither choked nor drowned beneath this river, for in this river they shall pass over on foot, as once the children of Israel crossed dry-shod through the midst of the Jordan, with the ark of God going before and opening a way in the middle of the river.

Those who came in chariots and on horses pursued with Pharaoh the people of God crossing the Red Sea on foot, and were overwhelmed in the midst of the waves [Col. 0129A]. But the children of Israel crossed on foot, without the chariot of pride or the horse of wantonness. So now, in the river of surging mortality, each pedestrian—that is, each humble person—crosses more readily than if, lifted up in Egyptian horses or chariots, he were borne by the vehicles of pride.

There is indeed some sadness in this passage, while a person does not know whether he will reach the shore of eternal stability. But when we reach it, there we shall rejoice in him who, as formerly he turned the Red Sea into dry land and made a way for his people, and as he divided the streams of the Jordan, so now through baptism brings his people across, drowning the spiritual Pharaoh with all his retinue; and brings across the streams of passing mortality those who walk with the foot of humility, not leaping with the foot of pride, concerning which it is elsewhere said: “Let not the foot of pride come against me” (Ps. 35:12). But that foot of pride will come if we rejoice in ourselves or in the vanity of this world, and not in the Lord. Therefore we shall rejoice in him, and in no one but him.

**VERSE 7.** “Who rules in his power forever.”

Our power is not eternal for us, since we fell into sin, the opposite of power, and from sin gained punishment, being filled with many miseries from which we cannot be delivered except through him who rules in his power forever. For if we share in his power, we shall be strong in him—not by our own power, but by his. He, however, is strong not by another’s power but by his own proper power, whether his enemies will or no, lying to him amid the multitude of his power [Col. 0129C]. Since the Jews, through their lies, deny that multitude of power, few chosen and diminished remnants from among them having been saved while the rest are blinded and hardened, “his eyes look upon the Gentiles.” His apostles, who are the eyes of his body, say thus: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). Thereupon the Jews, filled with jealous envy, murmur and provoke God by their murmurings; and therefore those who provoke him “shall not be exalted in themselves,” that is, so long as they have confidence in themselves and their own merits or fleshly observances. Therefore let them cease to glory or put confidence [Col. 0129D] in themselves, and together with the Gentiles acknowledge their own weakness. When they have recognized it, they may obtain healing, as the Gentiles do.

*Diapsalma.*—**VERSE 8.** “Bless, O Gentiles, our God, and make heard the voice of his praise.”

The Jews, who envy the grace granted to the Gentiles and thereby provoke God, have deservedly been rejected because of their perversity. But you Gentiles receive blessing in the seed of Abraham, according to God’s promise to Abraham himself: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). Therefore you too, Gentiles, bless God, by whom you are blessed; and make heard to your neighbors, whom you love for his sake, the voice of praise—not your own, but his, by whose grace we are what we are. Bless God by loving him with all your heart, all your soul, and all your strength [Col. 0130A], and by loving your neighbors as yourselves. Make the voice of his praise heard by them, so that, hearing this voice through you, they too may love God by your example with all their heart, soul, and strength.

Though the voice of his praise resounds everywhere in the Scriptures of truth, that particular voice of his praise was heard at his baptism and at his transfiguration, when the Father said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 17:5). Therefore hear, and at the same time make heard, before kings and rulers, the voice of his praise, that this man may be acknowledged as God, the Son of God, according to the voice of his praise. He may also be recognized as true God because he has performed in me, David—or in me, any penitent person; for example, in me, the apostle Peter—such things as no one can perform except God alone. What are these things? Namely these:

**VERSE 9.** “He has set my soul unto life, and has not given my feet to be moved.”

Certainly he who set my soul unto life gave testimony by doing so that he truly is God. My soul was set unto death when I, Peter, denied the Lord three times, or when I presumed beyond measure. But he set it unto life by looking upon me and, by that look, causing me to weep bitterly. Again, when he asked me a third time whether I loved him and enabled me truthfully to confess my love for him a third time, then also he set my soul unto life, which had been set unto death by my threefold denial.

[Col. 0130C] Each of the other leaders among the twelve can likewise give thanks to him who set his soul unto life and did not permit his feet to be moved. Surely this thanksgiving resembles the offering made by the leaders of the twelve tribes when the tabernacle was completed and raised up: on the day of its dedication they offered twelve oxen to convey the tabernacle. These twelve oxen are those who bore the tabernacle of God from Judea to the Gentiles on ox-like feet, judicious and strong, so that each of them might give thanks to him who did not permit his feet to be moved. Let us compare individual things with individual things.

Those leaders offered twelve oxen for transporting the tabernacle. These leaders became twelve oxen, and their leadership was greatly strengthened to support the living tabernacle, of which they were not merely guides from Judea to the Gentiles, but also pillars and foundations; for the whole construction of this tabernacle rests upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets. Those leaders offered twelve silver bowls and twelve silver basins; these leaders say in this psalm:

**VERSES 10 AND 11.** “For you have tested us, O God; you have examined us by fire, as silver is examined.”

Thus, tested and examined silver, they are found comparable to silver bowls and basins—so much better than those ancient ones as they are ministers and heralds of a better covenant and dispensers of a better libation [Col. 0131A]. Those men offered twelve golden mortars full of incense; these sing and say: “You brought us into a snare; you laid tribulations upon our back; you set men over our heads. We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment.” This is the same as though they said: Through the tribulations imposed on us and through most humble subjection even to wicked men, raised over our heads in Moses’ chair, we have been planted together with your passion, O Christ the King, and made like you as in a golden mortar.

We are also full of incense, either because we have passed through the fire of temptation or because we burn with the fire of love. As that fire melts our hardness and tears become our bread day and night, we are led through this kind of water into refreshment [Col. 0131B], holding firmly that “if we have been made one with the likeness of Christ’s death, we shall likewise be one with his resurrection. If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (Rom. 6:5). Although we now weep among the blessed mourners, afterward, having received consolation, we shall laugh. For you, Truth, do not deceive us when you say: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5). Again: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21). Again: “Blessed are you when men hate you and when they separate you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil because of the Son of Man. Rejoice and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven” (Luke 6:22–23). Thus we have passed through fire and water, and you have brought us into refreshment, while we hold, partly in hope and partly in reality, the most certain consolation from your promises.

What was meant by the leaders’ offering an ox, a ram, a yearling lamb for a burnt offering, a goat for sin, and, for a sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five goats, and five yearling lambs, has been explained above in the prologue of this psalm—as also how it applies to the apostles, leaders of the New Testament, and to their followers, each of whom says in the present song:

**VERSES 13, 14, AND 15.** “I shall enter your house with burnt offerings; I shall render to you my vows, which my lips have distinguished, and which my mouth has spoken in my tribulation. I shall offer you fat burnt offerings with the incense of rams; I shall offer you oxen with goats.”

Someone may ask: Why do you offer all these things? Namely, because my God, in whom I rejoice in this psalm and whom I urge others to praise joyfully, has set my soul unto life and has not given my feet to be moved. He has set my soul unto life by the first resurrection, raising it from the death of sin to the life of faith and righteousness; for “the righteous lives by faith” (Gal. 3:11). Moreover, he has made firm, and has not allowed to be moved, my feet from that firmness of hope, because I am certain that he is able to preserve my deposit until that day. By the second resurrection he will give life also to my mortal body, conforming it to the body of his glory, so that the dedication of this tabernacle may be complete. Throughout all the days in which I now serve, I wait until that transformation comes [Col. 0132A]: namely, that solemn dedication and sanctification of the whole tabernacle which is the Catholic Church.

And from what do I hope this, my God? Namely from the fact that you have tested us and not rejected us by the fire of tribulation, temptation, or love. By this fire you have examined us as silver is examined: silver is not turned into ashes by fire, as wood, hay, and stubble are, but is purified when all dross and filth are consumed, so that it becomes workable. Nor does it break, but is spread out by the repeated blows of hammers, whereas impure silver that has not been well smelted, tested, or examined breaks beneath hammer blows. In good order, therefore, you first examined us as silver is examined by the fire of love, which does not permit the torments of tribulation to be felt or seem burdensome; and then, after we were thus examined and tested, you brought us into a snare by the voluntary vow of a holier purpose, persuaded in us through your inspiration. Hence Wisdom says to each of us: “You are ensnared by your own words” (Prov. 6:2).

After you had thus ensnared us, inspiring such a vow in us, you then laid tribulations on our backs, when we were compelled to obey the harsh commands of men whom you set over our heads, raising over us teachers who imposed heavy burdens and were wholly unwilling to move them with their finger. Yet we bore those commands where we understood them not to be contrary to your commands, and thereby obeyed you when you said: “The scribes and Pharisees sit upon Moses’ seat. Therefore do all things that they tell you, but do not act according to their works” (Matt. 23:2–3) [Col. 0132C].

But we were more greatly afflicted when we resisted evil commands, displeasing to you, of the men set over our heads, saying: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29)—however highly they may be raised above other persons in spiritual or worldly authority—if they command what is contrary to divine commands. Even when we willingly obeyed good men placed over us as our head, as we ought, we were not free from the distress of tribulation, because on the narrow way of strict and righteous obedience, diabolical and human assaults are not lacking. The devil wishes, either by himself or through others, wholly to block our way, or at least somehow to delay it. Thus in many ways you laid tribulations upon our backs when you set men over our heads: whether they commanded rightly or wrongly, we endured many tribulations in the way of righteousness, and were sometimes tested by torments, sometimes also by enticements.
