**VERSE 4.** Let the peoples confess to you, O God; let all the peoples confess to you. First, let them confess their sins to you, each saying: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you” (Luke 15:21). Then, that the harmony may become clear, let them confess you with unceasing—indeed continual—praises: for you are good, for your mercy endures forever. The order is good, because “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, then confession with the mouth is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). By believing with the heart, therefore, as we have pursued in the first part of this Psalm, let us first know your way in the earth, your salvation among all nations. Then, as we are instructed in this second part, let the peoples confess to you, O God, both their sins and your praise.

Nor should this be done by the people of one land alone; rather, let all peoples confess to you, so that the Church may not be confined merely to Judaea, to some other single corner of one land, or to the division of some sect, but may be spread through every land and all nations, with the oil of gladness poured out.

[Col. 0158A] **VERSE 5.** Let the nations rejoice and exult. Behold the hymn and song fittingly joined to the foregoing confessions. For those who have now confessed do not fear judgment, since you, Christ, are their advocate: you are accustomed not to condemn confessed sinners but to set them free. You are at once the judge who will judge those who confess with equity in the future judgment, and now you direct the nations on earth in the way of equity, so that there may be persons on whom you can afterwards have mercy in the judgment of equity.

It is therefore a great consolation that you, who judge peoples with equity, now direct nations on earth before judgment. Hence that equity of your judgment is not greatly to be feared by those nations especially whom you now direct upon earth and cause to rejoice and exult under your rule. Therefore let peoples and nations rejoice in the glad and joyful movement of the mind, and exult in the disciplined gesture of the body, because you judge peoples with equity in the future examination, and, that they may be able to bear the judgment of equity, you now direct the nations with the bridle of discipline upon the earth of their present pilgrimage.

For as you once directed your people in a desert land, in a place of terror and vast solitude, giving them a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night to go before them and show them the way, so that they could not go astray, so now you direct the nations called to faith, both in the day of prosperity and the night of adversity. Now, like a pillar of cloud, you draw them after you by the gentle enticements of mercy, O Christ—who, covered by the cloud of human flesh, are the Savior of human nature. Now, like a pillar of fire, you illumine [Col. 0158C] and at the same time inflame those whom you lead through the night: amid adversities you make them shining and burning, shining through knowledge of truth and burning through love of virtue. Therefore, again and again, let the peoples confess to you, O God.

The third part, in which all peoples are again urged to rejoice and confess, not only for the benefits already stated but also for those added below, begins when it says:

### Verses 6 and 7

Let the peoples acknowledge you, O God; let all the peoples acknowledge you, because the earth, formerly cursed and assigned to thorns and thistles, has now yielded its fruit: when the virginal earth, made fruitful by the Holy Spirit and wholly exempted from the curse, yielded its fruit—the blessed fruit of whom it was said: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1:42). This blessed fruit, promised to Abraham, has now been sent and given to all nations, so that in that blessed fruit of the blessed earth all tribes of the earth may be blessed, and that they too may produce their fruit—some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, some a hundredfold—according to the distribution of gifts bestowed upon them.

Thus it shall come about that this insensible earth also, formerly cursed and made barren because of human sins, sprinkled with the Lord’s blessing, shall yield its fruit: now abounding in grain, now in oil, now in wine, according as it has been apportioned by God. For, as among human beings, so also in enriching lands, he employs a distributive measure as he wills, so that one may need another, and thus, through benefits mutually exchanged on either side, the fruit of charity may increase more and more, both among different lands and among the distinct conditions of humankind.

Otherwise: Let the peoples acknowledge you, O God; let all the peoples acknowledge you. Let spiritual peoples, stirred by the fruit of spiritual desires and abundantly enriched with those same fruits, acknowledge you and praise your name, because the earth—whether Holy Scripture, or the holy Church, or the Lord’s flesh—having as it were died by falling into the earth and multiplied by rising again, has yielded its fruit. This acknowledgment may be called complete when not one iota of the Scripture of truth remains unfulfilled; when none of the assembly of the righteous, which is the Church or the unity of the elect, is lacking; and when neither the Lord’s body nor even one of its members remains unglorified.

This acknowledgment grows day by day as the fruit of this holy threefold earth grows, until, when the entire fruit has been gathered into the barns of heaven, it may most truly be said: The earth has yielded its fruit according to the spiritual desire of spiritual peoples.

But since it has been said, “Let all the peoples acknowledge you,” animal or natural peoples also, from whose number spiritual persons are chosen, must themselves, according to their natural understanding, be aided by the fruits of the insensible earth. When abundantly enriched with those fruits and fruitful toward the poor through almsgiving from them, let them acknowledge that such an earth too has yielded its fruit, to the praise of your mercy, O God: your mercy which, through a favorable climate, makes this earth fruitful also and removes the curse by which, because of the sin of the first Adam, the earth was cursed and consigned to barrenness, through the overflowing grace and blessing of the second Adam.

For just as the curse then abounded, so that the feminine earth, sown by marital intercourse, did not yield its fruits in the swift sprouting forth of the elect, but produced the thorns and thistles of the ungodly, with sufferings multiplied and conceptions excessively increased; and, moreover, this insensible earth itself, withholding its fruit, spontaneously produced thorns and thistles: so, through Christ, the blessed fruit of the virginal womb, blessing overflows, so that the generation of the saints may be multiplied and even the earth which we tread may yield its fruit so abundantly that all peoples, both carnal and spiritual, may acknowledge that the earth has yielded its fruit.

Moreover, the curse also abounded in this respect: the earth of the human heart, which receives the good seed—that is, the word of God—did not yield fruits suited to this seed, namely holy thoughts, except through labor and sweat; but, at the demand of the desert of the first Adam, it spontaneously germinated perverse or useless thoughts. Yet through the second Adam, when the heavens abundantly send down dew from above and the clouds rain the Just One, since the Lord thus gives his goodness, the earth too yields its fruit: the human heart becomes flourishing in holy meditations and fruitful in holy works. And because all this proceeds not from human power but from divine blessing:

### Verse 8

May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us. May God the Father bless us; may God the Son, who by assuming our flesh became ours, bless us—for a Son has been given to us, a child has been born to us. May God the Holy Spirit bless us. And, with this threefold blessing of the triune one God poured out upon us, may we at once love and fear him, so that, while fear is joined to love amid benefits received, grace once accepted may be guarded more carefully.

Otherwise: May God, our God, bless us. And however great the blessing poured out upon us, because we are uncertain of our end, let all the ends of the earth fear him, since none of us knows whether he himself is worthy of hatred or love before the end comes. When it comes, all the ends of the earth shall fear him. But lest they then fear with the punitive fear with which even demons fear and tremble, let all the ends of the earth now fear with healing fear, so that those whom love of righteousness does not restrain from sin may at least be curbed by fear.

Otherwise: May God, our God, bless us believers; may God bless us with the twofold blessing of mind and body, contemplation and action, or of twofold love. But may he so terrify unbelievers who refuse to receive blessing that they may fear him and be compelled to fear. Let there be no one throughout all the ends of the earth who hides himself from his heat, without either rejoicing and exulting upon receiving blessing, or fearing, terrified by the judgment with which you judge peoples, according to the saying: “Let all the ends of the earth fear him.” He says “him,” not “them,” although he has named God three times.

On this passage blessed Gregory says:

> “David, in order to show the Trinity as God, the Author of all things, said: ‘May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us.’ And lest, in naming God a third time, he should be thought to have spoken of three gods, he immediately added, indicating the unity of that same Trinity: ‘And let all the ends of the earth fear him.’ For by adding not ‘them’ but ‘him,’ he showed that the three which he had named are one. Hence Isaiah also, when he disclosed praise of the unity of the Trinity, voicing the Seraphim, said: ‘Holy, holy, holy’ (Isa. 6:3). And lest, by naming ‘holy’ a third time, he should seem to divide the unity of the divine substance, he added: ‘The Lord God of Sabaoth’ [Hosts] (ibid.). Therefore, by adding not ‘Lords gods’ but ‘the Lord God,’ he indicated that what he had three times called holy is one. Thus Paul too, in order to show the operation of the holy Trinity, said: ‘Of him, and through him, and in him are all things’ (Rom. 11:36); and he indicated the unity of that same Trinity when he immediately added: ‘To him be glory for ages of ages’ (ibid.). For by adding not ‘to them’ but ‘to him,’ he made known that what he had above said three times was one by nature and three according to persons.”

[Note: Col. 0159D, Gregory, *Morals*, Book XXIX, chap. 31.]

To these Three, to this One, be glory always and everywhere. Amen.

Glory to the Father, who causes his countenance—that is, his natural Son—to be impressed upon us adopted children. Glory to the Son, the countenance of the Father impressed upon us who are adopted. Glory to the Holy Spirit, the mercy of the Father and the light of his countenance, of which elsewhere it is said: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4:7). Glory to the one and triune God, our merciful one, our blesser, and our illuminator, to whom we say: “May God have mercy on us and bless us; may he make his countenance shine upon us and have mercy on us.” May he glory in us as children blessed and enlightened through his mercy. May we glory in him as our most merciful blesser and illuminator. So be it, so be it, so be it. Amen, amen, amen.

## Psalm LXVII

[Col. 0161]

“Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; and let those who hate him flee before his face.”

It is written in the book of Numbers: “Whenever the ark was lifted up, Moses said: ‘Arise, O Lord, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee before your face.’ And when it was set down, he said: ‘Return, O Lord, to the multitude of the host of Israel’” (Num. 10:35–36).

When the cloud was lifted and the leaders moved the camp, Moses, persevering in contemplation of its archetype which the Lord had shown him—as Scripture, frequently repeating this, testifies—said: “Arise, O Lord,” or, “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered.” For this psalm, whose beginning is, “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; and let those who hate him flee before his face,” has from this its beginning and its heavenly cause or subject matter.

Whither is God to arise? Surely to that place to which the lifted cloud signifies that he will arise. The prophetic Spirit in the Psalmist investigated what this meant: that, when the cloud was lifted, the leaders moved the camp and set out. “You ascended on high,” he says, “you led captivity captive; you received gifts among men.” And then, continuing in the mystical meaning of this passage, he says: “They saw your goings, O God—the goings of my God, my king, who is in the sanctuary. The leaders went before, joined with those who sang psalms, in the midst of maidens playing tambourines. There is little Benjamin in an ecstasy of mind; the leaders of Judah, their rulers; the leaders of Zebulun, the leaders of Naphtali.”

A third apostle comes forward and, with the whole veil removed, more plainly declares with unveiled face what the lifting of the cloud is, who the leaders of the camp are, what the ascent on high is, and what the gifts among men are. “To each one of us,” he says, “grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Therefore he says: ‘Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.’ And he himself gave some to be apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, and others pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ” (Eph. 4:7–12).

Therefore let God arise—that is, let Christ ascend on high—and through these leaders who, when the cloud of his flesh has been lifted, set out as those sent to us: through apostles, evangelists, prophets, teachers, and pastors; through these, I say, leaders of Judah, Zebulun, and Naphtali, who are beautiful in faith, strong in hope, and enlarged in charity, among whom is little Benjamin in ecstasy of mind, namely Paul, the least of the apostles, caught up to the third heaven—let his enemies be scattered, and let those who hate him flee before his face. This both has happened, is happening, and shall happen until the end of the age, unto the completed victory.

“But when the ark was set down, Moses said: ‘Return, O Lord, to the multitude of the host of Israel’” (Num. 10:36). This too shall surely happen when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in. Then the Lord will return to that carnal Israel, so that a remnant from them may be saved.

It should be noted that in this psalm the often-mentioned warrior, fighting between hope and fear against the law of his members, finds many things with which to fight, strike, scourge, crush, and burn the enemy. “Let God arise,” he says, “and let his enemies be scattered; and let those who hate him flee before his face. As smoke vanishes, let them vanish; as wax melts before fire, so let sinners perish before God,” and so forth. These faithfully spoken words are accompanied by swift effect; and, as though God were arising, those who hate him flee: malignant spirits with their suggestions, vanishing as smoke and melting as wax before fire.

And lest the soldier of God perhaps despair if, acting incautiously, he has suffered something, or has been wounded by some sin, he afterwards hears the Holy Spirit say to him: “God is in his holy place; God makes those who are of one manner dwell in a house. He brings forth prisoners in strength, likewise those who provoke him, who dwell in tombs.” This has indeed happened among all nations, so that there is no reason for one prisoner to despair—one who dwells even in a tomb, however much he may deserve comparison with Lazarus, stinking and four days dead.

But the title of this psalm is:

### Verse 1

**For the end: a psalm of David’s song.**

Here the subject is the exaltation of Christ the head, or of the Church and its members, and the overthrow of enemies here and hereafter, with the purpose of frightening the wicked and gladdening the good. Hence both in the title and in the psalm he repeatedly exhorts us to exult in mind and deed. First, he briefly touches upon what he later explains at greater length: namely, Christ’s exaltation, the overthrow of enemies, and the grace and joy of the good here and in the future. Secondly, concerning the word of the Gospel: “O God, when you went forth.” Thirdly, concerning the gifts of the ascending Christ: “When the heavenly one distinguishes kings.” Fourthly, concerning works—namely the crushing of enemies, the conversions of some, and martyrdoms of both sexes—at: “Our God is a God who saves.” Fifthly, he prays and affirms that what has been begun may be strengthened, and, that this may happen, destroys heretics, at: “In the churches bless God the Lord.” Sixthly, he says that he who ascended will come in order to strengthen the saints, at: “Sing psalms to God, who ascends.”

The title of the psalm may be explained thus: “For the end: a psalm of David’s song”; that is, this treatment of joy is to be attributed to David the prophet, looking to the end—that is, to Christ, who is the end of the law unto righteousness, and who, “having loved his own, loved them unto the end” (John 13:1), by dying for them, rising again, ascending, sending the Paraclete Spirit, and through that Spirit building and glorifying the holy Church after scattering its enemies.

David the psalmist, foreseeing and desiring all these things to come, himself sings psalms and invites others to sing in what follows, saying: “Sing psalms to God, who ascends above the heavens of heavens toward the east.” Observing, however, that Moses and the people of Israel, about to fight against hostile nations, raised the ark of the covenant while saying, “Arise, O Lord, and let your enemies be scattered,” he fashioned the manner of his speech from this. Christ was signified by that ark, in whom, as in the two tables of the covenant, are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God; through him Israel was victorious even then. He desires Christ to be exalted through glorious resurrection and wondrous ascension for the overthrow of enemies, saying from the innermost affection of his heart:

### Verse 2

Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered. He who, dying on the cross and lying in the tomb, appeared true man, let him arise from the dead in such brightness of his divinity, in order that he may appear true God, that his enemies, unable to endure it, may be scattered and those who hate him may flee before his face. Those very people who stood before him as he hung on the cross, mocking him and saying, “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matt. 27:42), now flee before the face of the risen one. First they are terrified by the flashing appearance of the angelic vision at the tomb; then by the Lord’s own glorification, with the Holy Spirit proceeding from his countenance in fire, both inflaming and illuminating his apostolic friends, but burning the Jewish and other malign enemies because of envy and blinding them because of pride.

Therefore, he who died as man may arise as God, since he is at once man and God—not two, however, but one Christ. Let God arise, I say, and let his enemies be scattered. He confidently desired what he knew beforehand would happen. Now, indeed, what he desired has happened in part. Christ rose, and the Jews were scattered throughout all nations. They are yet to be scattered more fully together with his other enemies—pagans, heretics, and false Christians—who shall universally be scattered at the final judgment.

Even now they are scattered in particular, and the more so as the testimonies of the Lord’s resurrection have been made exceedingly credible through the splendors of saints, and through signs, powers, and many wonders testifying that he who died as man because of our offenses also rose as God because of our justification. For since Christ’s resurrection is the efficient cause of our justification, as the rising sun is the efficient cause of day, as long as—or whenever—our justification does not shine, we sit like women lamenting at the tomb of the buried Lord; desiring his resurrection to take place in us, we say: “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered.”

For although, having died and been buried once in his own body, he rose again, nevertheless he is again crucified, exposed to contempt, and buried whenever truth—which is himself—is oppressed, despised, and, by the evil custom of falsehood, is held enclosed as though by a great stone rolled over it in the tomb of silence: Christ the truth, as though never to rise again. This happens when falsehood prevails so greatly through false Christians, false clerics, monks, bishops, other judges, and also false penitents that it is thought to be truth. Against these evils we rightly desire with the prophet that God may arise and his enemies be scattered.

Let Christ arise in true Christians justified by his resurrection, and let false Christians, his enemies, be scattered. Let Truth himself arise in his members, whether truly innocent or truly penitent, and let his enemies be scattered—those neither truly innocent nor truly penitent. Let Justice himself arise in those righteous through innocence or justified through repentance, and let his enemies be scattered: the unjust and the enemies of justice. Let them be scattered, not insofar as they are human beings, God’s handiwork, but insofar as they are wicked and enemies of God. Thus Saul the enemy was scattered so that he became Paul the friend; and many enemies made friends show in themselves the fulfillment of what is said later: “The tongue of your dogs from among enemies,” because from enemies of God they became dogs of God, barking well and keeping vigilant watch in guarding the house or flock.

But those who, though enemies, refused to be scattered well were scattered and destroyed badly, to their own harm, according to the saying: “He will miserably destroy those wicked men” (Matt. 21:41).

Since, therefore, there is a twofold scattering and destruction of God’s enemies, let us continually say, desiring the former, which is for good, and prophesying the latter, which is for evil, in the Prophet’s words: “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; and let those who hate him flee.” That is, let stubborn enemies, who hate the righteous one, flee before his face, struck by the splendor of justice; let those who hate goodness flee before his face, driven out like bats by the splendor of goodness. Let foolish and malignant persons who hate wisdom flee before his face, from the splendor of wisdom shining everywhere, so that, even if they flee, they do not escape his face, but are caught in their own craftiness.

Let those who hate truth and piety flee, yet not escape, without being entangled, like fish of the sea, in the rules and disciplines of true piety and pious truth as though in nets, so that either they may become devout, or, remaining ungodly—may it not be so!—they may have no power to harm or to traverse the paths of the sea. Let them flee, not by changing place but by changing mind, because there is no place of flight open from east, west, or desert mountains: God is himself the judge, present everywhere, and his judgment cannot in any way be avoided except by fleeing from his wrath to his mercy.

Such flight does not occur by local bodily movement, but by the spiritual movement of the mind, when his angry countenance is feared and therefore iniquity is avoided. Thus let those who hate him flee before his face, weeping over past sins and taking care henceforth to avoid sins deserving tears, so that in him—from himself angry to himself appeased—they may find the safest refuge.

When he comes and appears in the clouds, of which he says: “Amen I say to you, you shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and majesty” (Matt. 24:30), then, from his flashing face shining everywhere in the saints as in the purest mirrors, when he the sun of righteousness appears in whitest clouds, let dark clouds flee before his majesty. And because then there will be a desire to flee but no place at all to escape, I explain what I have said—“let them flee”—by adding:

### Verse 3

As smoke vanishes, let them vanish. Smoke vanishes in two ways: either lifted upward or consumed by the magnitude of the rising flame. Therefore let these people also vanish in the loftiness of their minds, so that they cannot accomplish the evil they desire but disappear in their wicked attempts. Or certainly, as smoke vanishes when flame rises, so, on considering the flame of Gehenna—where their fire shall not be quenched and their worm shall not die—let their smoky wickedness vanish, either now through true repentance, which we pray for, or then at judgment through punishment, which we prophesy.

And as wax melts before fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God. When candles burn, wax melts and perishes before fire, and by its own loss makes light for sound eyes. But our God is a consuming fire: consuming sins, which he did not make, and illuminating rational creatures, whom he did make, so that sinners may perish while human beings, provided they consent to be saved, may be saved.

So be it, so be it: let it happen as has been foreordained, that, before the face of God manifesting himself and by fiery power illuminating the good through knowledge of truth and inflaming them through love of virtue, sinners—not human beings—may perish, and by the example of their own destruction may display light and an example to others, so that, instructed by the pit of destruction, they may beware for themselves. Or let them perish as wax melts before fire: namely, let them here melt in tears of repentance, their hardness dissolving before the burning of a good will grieving over past sin and gladly avoiding future sin. By this true repentance let the unjust become righteous, and many from the number of sinners shall be joined to the number of saints, while the impenitent, perishing badly, are removed. Let these, therefore, be separated and handed over to the penal prison, lest they be able to disturb the unity of the righteous.

### Verse 4

Let the righteous feast and exult in the presence of God. Let the righteous—either glorified through innocence or purified through true repentance—feast at the wedding banquet, arrayed in the wedding garment; and let them know that the bridegroom has said to them: “Eat, friends, and drink; be intoxicated, beloved” (Song 5:1). Therefore let them not tremble when the king enters to inspect those reclining at table. Rather, let them exult in the presence of that same king and their God, conscious that they possess the wedding garment, understood as love of God and neighbor. Whoever has it shall not be cast forth from God’s presence into the outer darkness, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth; but shall remain within, in God’s presence, seeing God himself in that blessed and everlasting vision in which the blessed, pure in heart, see him.

Therefore let them exult, not in the eyes of men by boastingly displaying their righteousness, but in the sight of God, who without error sees every good thing they have and attributes it to his own grace. On the sure and unfailing testimony of this God, whose Spirit bears witness to their spirit that they are children of God, let them exult in his presence—not as formerly, serving him in fear and exulting before him with trembling, when perfect charity had not yet cast out fear—but let them delight in a joy which will never end for them, just as their charity will never fail.

Conscious of this charity, and with fear cast out, let them rejoice, feast, and exult in God’s presence; and, with the sting of punitive fear wholly removed while holy and chaste fear remains, let them delight in joy. But to you, beloved of God, who now hold the pledge of that great joy to be consummated in the future because you love God and neighbor, I now turn in direct address, as though I, David—or I, whatever psalmist—were present, and say to you:

### Verse 5

Sing to God; sing a psalm to his name; make a way for him who ascends above the setting.

Sing to God with the single intention of goodness; sing a psalm to his name by good action. Sing to God, inwardly seeking his glory in all things; and, so that your neighbors may see your good works and glorify God, sing psalms to his name by acting well. And if anyone attributes such a psalm to your own name, contradict him and sing the psalm to God’s name, attributing the good work to him alone who alone works all things in all people, for the glory of his name and the manifestation of his goodness.

Peter and John were going up to the temple at the ninth hour of prayer. This was singing to God. And a man lame from his mother’s womb heard them say: “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6). Then the lame man leapt up, walked, and entered with them. This was singing a psalm in the Lord’s name. Hence Peter did not say, “Rise and walk in my name,” but, “In the name,” he said, “of Jesus Christ, rise and walk.” Afterwards, when the people saw the lame man walking and praising God—not Peter or John—the apostles perceived that the people were assigning to them the glory for so great a miracle. They said: “Why do you look at us, as though by our own power or piety we had made this man walk? The God of our fathers has glorified his Son, and through faith in his name has given him this perfect healing in the presence of you all” (Acts 3:12–13, 16). Thus to refer a divine work to the glory of the name was to sing a psalm to his name.

And you also, through whom God works good things until the end of the age, if at any time you are tempted to glory silently or openly in these things as though they had been done by your own power or piety, sing the psalm to his name in such a way that you proclaim not your own name, but his, as the name to be glorified. Otherwise, by seeking, seizing, or voluntarily accepting glory offered to you—glory owed to God, not to yourselves—you will be fraudulent servants: rightly making the offering, indeed, but not rightly distributing it. For you act well, but do not glory well when you arrogate to yourselves the glory of a good work.

The angel divided more rightly when he said: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). “Glory,” he says, “to God; peace to human beings,” so that it may be understood that God alone is to be glorified through all things and in all things, he who grants peace to people of good will. Let them therefore be content with the peace offered them and leave glory to God, lest, if they usurp unconceded glory, they lose the peace granted them.

You especially should be warned of this precaution, you to whom this psalm of song is assigned, since singers, teachers, and workers of righteousness alike have been chosen and appointed for this purpose: that in the spirit and power of Elijah or John the Forerunner you may prepare the Lord’s way by rebuking wicked kings and other rulers, preparing a perfect people, and making crooked things straight and rough things into level paths.

Indeed, we little ones, together with little David, are neither fit nor worthy for these tasks. Yet in this psalm of song, applauding your virtue with affection, we sing and say to you, heralds and forerunners of the Lord: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting; the Lord is his name.” By your preaching make the hearts of hearers straight from crookedness and smooth from roughness. At the same time preserve your own hearts in every purity, so that they may be ready and welcome for the coming Lord, not merely for walking in them but also for dwelling in them, as he himself says: “For I shall dwell in them and walk among them; and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people” (2 Cor. 6:16).

Therefore make a way for him who is to walk in the Church, a pilgrim on earth, although he reigns in heaven exalted above all things. For he is the one who ascends above the setting, when he recovered the fall of his own body in death through glorious resurrection and wondrous ascension. Or he ascends above the setting because, in us, the old life falls and dies, while the new life receives him as he comes.

Otherwise: This visible sun, tending from the winter solstice toward the summer solstice, daily rises above its setting, because from day to day it rises higher than it had set on the preceding day, as by its progressive course it approaches from the winter signs toward the summer ones. Likewise Christ, the sun of righteousness, emptied himself from the height and summer-like summit of the Father’s exaltedness—where, together with the most high Father, he always had an eternal station—down to the weakness of human frailty. Found humble and little as a man, as though at the winter solstice, born of a woman around the winter season, when the sun goes down no farther in order to rise to the place where it was before, he who was “full of grace and truth” (John 1:15) thereafter advanced “in age and wisdom and grace before God and men” (Luke 2:25). Already then, as it were after the winter solstice, he began to ascend above the setting.

For he appeared to set as many times as, in suffering human things, he ceased to emit the rays of his divinity. Yet over such a setting he always rose more brightly, because his weakness appeared stronger than human beings. For example, laid in a manger as a weak infant, he was as if at sunset; but, when the star led the Magi to him and they worshipped him with mystical gifts, he ascended above the setting by the splendor of his divinity shining in their hearts with so much greater and more wondrous brightness as power was not diminished in weakness but rather perfected—indeed, shown to have been perfect from eternity.

Likewise, that he was nourished at a woman’s breasts was for that eternal sun a kind of setting. Yet above this setting he rose when angels sang to him, “Glory to God in the highest”; or rather, in that he, while sucking at a woman’s breast, had himself filled it from heaven, in a heavenly manner, while his mother’s virginal integrity remained intact, he ascended above the setting.

Again: He came to a carnal wedding as a man, which was for him a setting; but there he ascended above the setting by making wine from water. In that miracle, showing himself to be God after the humility which had gone before as at sunset, he revealed his glory as a flashing sunrise following and rising above the setting.

Thus the eastern splendor of the Son of God is always preceded by the western humility of that same Son of Man. For as the sun does not come to sunrise except through sunset, nor ever rises in the east unless it first goes down in the west, so the merit of preceding humility is always the gateway to subsequent glory: “For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

Therefore, as has been said, the humility of the one and same Son of Man always precedes the glory of the Son of God. This can readily be recognized in nearly everything that he did or deigned to suffer on earth, willingly intent upon the work of our salvation. Born of a woman, as has been said, he was nourished at virginal breasts; wrapped in swaddling clothes, he is praised by angels singing, “Glory to God in the highest”; laid in the narrowness of a manger, he is declared in the breadth of heaven by the shining star; brought to the temple as though a sinner, he is proclaimed by Simeon as the true light; coming among sinners to the baptism of his servant, he is revealed as the Holy of holies by the voice of the Father and the Holy Spirit appearing over him in visible form; he endures the deceits of the tempter, and immediately angels approach and minister to him.

He suffered hunger as man, yet as God satisfied five thousand from five loaves and two fishes. Weary on the road, he asked water from a Samaritan woman, but immediately offered her living water, which whoever drinks shall never thirst. He fled the stones of his pursuers, lest they inflict upon him a death he had not ordained; and immediately he restored life to Lazarus, dead four days. Thus Christ, the sun of righteousness, always humbled before glory, ascended above the setting, so that the Christian may learn to ascend in the same way.

The sons of Zebedee, as though passing over such a setting, wished to ascend by asking through their mother that one might sit at Christ’s right hand and the other at his left in his kingdom. But he recalled them to order, teaching that before the glory of such an ascent they must drink the cup of suffering (Matt. 20:21).

At last, lest we be reproached like the Pharisees and [Col. 0169B] Sadducees, who seek a sign from heaven and yet refuse to discern the signs of the times, let us follow the course of the Sun of righteousness, as he makes his glowing descent toward setting and thereafter rises above the setting. Was not that descent of his to the setting of death radiant, which the Church celebrates on Palm Sunday by solemnly commemorating his coming to the place of his foreknown passion and now-imminent death? But this Sun shone far more brightly in rising above the setting, when, on the third day, very early in the morning, the sun having already risen, the night of sorrow was driven away and that day of joy dawned, of which it is sung: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice in it” (Ps. 117:24).

On this setting and rising of his, blessed [Col. 0169C] Pope Gregory, discoursing in a homily [Note: [Col. 0169D] Homily 17, on the Gospels], says: “The Lord rose above the setting, because from the very place where he set in his passion, he showed forth his greater glory by rising again. That is, he rose above the setting because, by rising again, he trampled down the death which he endured. Therefore he says: ‘Make a way for him who rises above the setting’—that is, by faith provide a path in your hearts for the risen Lord. Certainly we make a way for him who rises above the setting when we preach his glory to believing minds, so that he himself, coming afterward, may enlighten them by the presence of his love.” Hence it is said to John by the Spirit: “You shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke 1:76). For whoever, by preaching, cleanses the hearts of hearers from the filth of vices prepares a way for the Wisdom that is coming.

It should certainly be noted that, having once passed beyond the setting of death, Christ, the Sun of righteousness, will not set again in such a manner; for he dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him. Yet in his body, which is the Church, that alternation continues in which the same Sun knows his setting and his rising: now when the darkness of temptations, errors, or persecutions gains strength against the Church or against an ecclesiastical person; now when these are calmed or mitigated, and the faithful rejoice in length of days and prosperously carry on their work [Col. 0170A]. Of this alternation it is elsewhere said: “You have appointed darkness, and night has come; in it all the beasts of the forest shall pass through. The young lions roar, that they may seize prey and seek their food from God”; and afterward: “The sun has risen, and they have gathered together and shall lie down in their dens. Man shall go forth to his work and to his labour until evening” (Ps. 103:20–23).

This alternation will not cease until that sunrise of the eighth day, made bright by the universal resurrection, in which the righteous shall shine like the sun; in which the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun; when the body of our lowliness shall be re-formed in the likeness of the body of Christ’s glory. Henceforth the Spirit says that they may rest from their labours of the night. For night shall be no more, nor crying [Col. 0170B], nor mourning, nor pain, because the former things have passed away—when the saints laboured for their Lord and were planted together with him in the setting of his passion, sharing with him in death, so that they might be planted together also with him as he rises and rises again and ascends into heaven.

Therefore, since there is no other way by which one comes to him, or by which he comes to us, except humility and obedience, foreshown in his setting and death, you whose office is to teach, make a way for him who rises above the setting. Prepare your own hearts and those of others to imitate his setting, through the merit of humility and obedience, likened to the setting of the sun. For as the sun comes from its setting to its rising, so everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted; and whoever obeys the commandments out of love [Col. 0170C] will feel within himself the steps of that Lord coming to him, who rises above the setting. “If anyone,” he says, “loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

And lest it perhaps be uncertain to you that these things can be done by him, I tell you: the Lord is his name. There are many who are called lords, whether in heaven or on earth, but improperly so, because the power of ruling neither subsists in them nor comes from themselves. Hence in heaven the dominions worship him from whom they have the power to rule; and on earth the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, giving it to whomever he wills, and, when he wills, taking away the breath [Col. 0170D] of princes.

But he who rises above the setting—who for us human beings and for our salvation humbled himself in the form of a servant even to the setting of death—has now transcended every servile ministry. And just as he then emptied himself before his lord, when, in the form and office of a servant, he said: “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matt. 20:28), so now, since he has risen above the setting, rising from the dead with his servile form hidden in God, he shows himself as Lord in heaven and on earth. Thus he says: “All power has been given to me [Col. 0171A] in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18).

Truly, therefore, and properly, the name Lord belongs to him, who not only always had and has, in his divinity, together with the almighty Father and the Holy Spirit, indivisible power to rule through all things and over all things, but also attests that this same power has been given to his humanity. For when he says that all power in heaven and on earth has been given to him, this cannot fittingly be referred to his divinity, which always possessed this power, but is most fittingly referred to his humanity, which received it in time. Thus in every respect the name Lord truly and properly belongs to him who always possessed in his divinity this name above every name of all lords, and who, by the Father’s gift, received the same name in his humanity. For because he humbled himself [Col. 0171B], becoming obedient to the Father unto death—even death on a cross—“therefore God exalted him and gave him a name” which is not to be counted among the names of many lords, but “which is above every name” (Phil. 2:9), so that, just as according to his divinity he is rightly called and is Lord of all, so likewise in his humanity, glorified by that same name above every name, he may be called and held to be Lord of all; and nothing may be able to resist his dominion, but rather “at his name every knee may bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:11). Therefore, the Lord is his name.

[Col. 0171C] And because this Lord is such and so great that to serve him is to reign, you who serve him by making a way for him, if perhaps you find tribulation and sorrow in your service, do not be distressed; do not lose heart. Rather, counting it all joy when you fall into diverse temptations, rejoice before him in the service of so great a Lord. Rejoice, not before human beings, who are often deceived when they look upon the servants of that Lord as though sorrowful and do not know that they are always rejoicing. Therefore rejoice rather before him, who cannot be deceived, than before human beings: rejoicing in hope inwardly, where God sees you enduring tribulation, so that those who see you may glorify your Father who is in heaven. “But whoever he may be, he who troubles you shall bear the judgment [Col. 0171D]” (Gal. 5:10), just as that Achan was troubled who had troubled Israel by presumptuously taking forbidden things when Jericho, the city under anathema, fell. For Joshua had said to him: “Because you have troubled us, may the Lord trouble you this day” (Josh. 7:25). Once this sentence had been pronounced, he was stoned by the people.

So indeed those who trouble you while you fight in the army of the true Jesus, who is conquering this whole world set in evil and under anathema, shall be troubled. They shall be troubled, I say, by his face. By whose face?

**VERSE 6.** *Father of orphans and judge of widows.*

Orphans are those for whom the world and the devil, father of the wicked, have died—the sort of persons to whom it is said: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father [Col. 0172A]” (John 8:44). This father begets sons and daughters from worldly desire, as from a mother suited to him, desiring to do the wishes of such a father and such a mother. From the number of such persons the Catholic Church is gathered, to which it is said: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king shall desire your beauty” (Ps. 44:11–12). Those who willingly and obediently hear this voice become orphans: their evil father has died for them, and their mother, desire, has been extinguished; and they find a better Father, who is truly and rightly called the Father of orphans and Judge of widows, because in fatherly kindness he cherishes souls bereft of an evil father.

He also protects them as widows, since error—their husband, indeed their adulterer—has died, he judging [Col. 0172B] who says to the Samaritan woman: “You have spoken well in saying, ‘I have no husband’; for you have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband” (John 4:17–18). Similarly, every faithful soul had five husbands so long as it could and ought to be directed under the rule of the five senses—namely, in childhood. But when it has reached years of discernment, unless it marries the true Bridegroom, Jesus Christ—or rather, if adulterous error lies with it—it can use the Samaritan woman’s words, saying: “Lord, I have no husband.” And the Lord, approving such a confession of truth and sin, can answer it: “You have spoken well in saying, ‘I have no husband’; for you have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband. This you have spoken truly.”

Such a confession pleases that Father of orphans [Col. 0172C], Judge and Defender of such widows, who confess their former error—as that Samaritan woman did. Rebuked by the Lord because he whom she had had after five husbands was not her husband, she said: “Lord, I see that you are a prophet” (John 1:21). This was to yield to him who rebuked her and to recognize herself as a widow rather than a wife, a sinner rather than one lawfully joined, in accordance with such a prophecy, by which the things she had done had been told her. She therefore left her water-jar and became an apostle to her city, announcing Jesus to her fellow citizens—that widow deprived of five husbands and rebuked concerning the one whom she had not lawfully had.

Those become like her who, after the rule of the five senses—which, as stated, was legitimate in its proper time—are joined to perverse understanding [Col. 0172D] as to an adulterer, and afterward, rebuked through the teaching of truth, humbly yield to the truth that rebukes them and draw others into the same thing as far as they can: that they too may hear the truth, recognize their Savior, and seek his protection as widows. But those who trouble such widows, who have God as protector and judge, shall themselves certainly be troubled by the face of that Father of orphans and Judge of widows. They shall be troubled either now unto repentance or hereafter unto condemnation.

By what shall they be troubled? By his face, that is, by his manifest knowledge, which is denoted by “face,” because in the face lies the knowledge and recognition of every person. “The Lord shall be known when he executes judgments” (Ps. 9:17): either now, distinguishing his own from those who are not his by their differing manner of life [Col. 0173A], or hereafter by a differing sentence. And from this knowledge some shall be troubled, through your teaching, unto their amendment—you who make a way for him who rises above the setting.

Rejoice before him over this good fruit of your labour: for not only from the aforesaid orphans and widows, but also from evildoers troubled unto repentance, is a house of one manner built, in which God has a place of rest; and in this his holy place

**VERSE 7.** *God dwells,* and causes to dwell not just anyone, but those who are of one mind, willingly observing the discipline of one manner of life. For not all who are in the house, in which vessels of dishonour are found along with vessels of honour, are, or can truthfully be called [Col. 0173B], God’s holy place; but only those who are of one mind, thinking one thing, being wise in the same thing, speaking the same thing, and remaining in the same rule that directs toward the one thing necessary. These are his holy place and a temple dedicated and consecrated to his name—not through the merit of their own virtue or piety, but through his gratuitous grace, he who brings out prisoners in strength, likewise those who provoke him, who dwell in tombs.

Indeed, many such persons were among those who are now loosed from the bonds of sins and brought out from the tombs of their crimes, and have become the house of God and his holy place. Therefore the salvation of those who are likewise bound, dead, and buried is not yet to be despaired of. For God, dwelling in his holy place and never ceasing to work his work, himself, until [Col. 0173C] the complete consummation of his house, which the true Solomon builds for himself, creates living stones from the dead, that he may unite them in himself, the cornerstone, and make them of one mind. Therefore I, not David, do not say in words of past time, “who brought out,” but in the present: “who brings out prisoners.” For he continually brings out prisoners; every day he looses those in fetters—that is, those entangled in venial sins, which press in daily and must likewise be mourned daily. Therefore every day we must say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). Nor do we say this in vain if we forgive from the heart. For he who said, “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6:37), is true. Under this same covenant, by forgiving their debtors [Col. 0173D], he brings out prisoners, forgiving them venial debts, such as commonly creep in through ignorance or frailty against the devout will of a good purpose.

Likewise he brings out those who provoke him, because he does not deny pardon even to those who sin wilfully, stir up his anger against themselves, and, so far as lies in them, exasperate his gentleness—provided that he finds them ready for repentance. Among such persons are some who, buried in the habit of sinning, now stink like Lazarus four days dead. Even such as these, who dwell in tombs, the merciful Lord, calling them forth to confession of sin, raises to life, while the contemplative and active persons in the holy Church, like Martha and Mary, weep and pray for them.

Those who are bound wish indeed to walk, but [Col. 0174A] cannot. But those who provoke him, placed in the deep, despise. Still more, those who stink in the deep tomb of a perverse habit not only despise but do not even attend to their salvation. The Savior brings such bound and dead persons, when they yield to calling grace, from perdition to salvation. And he does this in his strength, by which he reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly. Or he does it in the strength by which, after multiplied weaknesses, he makes them strong for a good work, so that, now striving stoutly against sin even unto blood, they may prove fulfilled in themselves the Apostle’s saying: “Where iniquity abounded, grace superabounded” (Rom. 5:20).

Some, brought thus out of tombs, recovered so greatly from weakness [Col. 0174B] and became so strong in battle that, fighting in the battle-line of the ordered camps—which is the Church of God, enlarged by such persons—they overthrew the camps of strangers.

A *diapsalma* is inserted here, distinguishing what has been said from what must be said. This is quite fitting, because up to this point the Psalmist has briefly touched upon matters which he will subsequently explain more fully, beginning thus:

**VERSE 8.** *O God, when you went forth in the sight of your people, when you passed through the wilderness.*

**VERSE 9.** *The earth was moved; for the heavens distilled before the face of the God of Sinai.*

In these words past history is recalled in such a way that future grace is simultaneously proclaimed, as follows: Truly, O God, you shall bring out prisoners in strength; and the preceding examples prove that this shall be so. For when, at Israel’s departure from Egypt, you went forth, bringing out your prisoners from Pharaoh’s bonds, and went before your people in a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night, the earth was moved by the greatness of your strength. For the earthly Egyptians, recognizing your strength in such great wonders, were disturbed and moved, so that, with the waves of the Red Sea threatening them on every side, they said: “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them against us” (Exod. 14:25).

And when the princes of the Philistines heard of this miracle of your strength, “they were troubled”; likewise “the princes of Edom, and the mighty men of Moab, were seized with trembling; all the inhabitants of Canaan grew rigid,” when “fear and dread fell upon them through the greatness of your arm [Col. 0174D]” (Exod. 15:15–16), hearing then that you, O God, went forth before your people, bringing them out with a mighty hand and an uplifted arm. Therefore, when in such great strength you, O God, not only went forth from Egypt but also passed through the wilderness, for forty years near to that generation which you had thus brought out, truly the earth was moved, and the earthly hearts of the nations were shaken because of the wonders shown there.

“For the heavens distilled before the face of the God of Sinai, before the face of the God of Israel”; or, as another translation has it: “Mount Sinai [smoked] before the face of God”—the word “smoked” being understood—when Moses ascended it and the Lord descended upon it. The heavens distilled because, while the Lord spoke to Moses from heaven, the words of commandments and judgments descended like drops of dew or rain [Col. 0175A]. Or the heavens distilled when manna rained upon them from heaven before the face of the God of Sinai, because the Law was given on Mount Sinai.

For Sinai is interpreted “temptation,” which accords well with the Law given there, a Law given to the ancient people for testing, according to the Lord’s word: “That I may test him, whether he will walk in my law or not” (Exod. 16:4). Or because, when the commandment came, sin revived, with temptations consequently becoming more frequent; for that stiff-necked people always strove after what was forbidden, just as the first human being desired more the tree of knowledge forbidden to him than every tree of Paradise granted to him. Therefore, while the heavens thus distilled,

**VERSES 10 AND 11.** *You shall set apart a voluntary rain* [Col. 0175B]—then, according to the letter: *And you shall set it apart still in the Spirit for your inheritance*, that is, for the people whom you chose as your inheritance. I say a voluntary rain, that is, a gratuitous rain: you set it apart for your inheritance, because “you have not done thus for every nation, and you have not made your judgments known to any nation on earth” as you have to that people, your inheritance, whom for this very reason we call blessed, saying: “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he chose for his inheritance” (Ps. 32:12).

Nevertheless, because the Law was not given that could give life, because it brought nothing to perfection—indeed, it was weakened through the flesh, made unbearable through fleshly ceremonies, whose “yoke,” Peter says, “neither we nor our fathers were able to bear” (Acts 15:10)—that inheritance itself, namely the nation belonging to your worship [Col. 0175C], was weakened in the many undisciplined persons whose bodies were strewn in the wilderness. But you perfected it in the few who were disciplined—for example, in Joshua and Caleb and the others brought into the Land of Promise. In it, like your animals, dwelt those who endeavoured, in whatever manner, to bear the yoke of the Law.

Behold, in these words of the letter we have sought and found the literal sense, so far as we could with God’s help. But because it is less fitting to say concerning that nation weakened by transgression of the Law, “But you perfected it”—since that wicked and perverse generation was struck down rather than perfected, so much so that even Moses and Aaron, embittered by its murmurings, were struck with temporal death and forbidden entrance [Col. 0175D] into the Land of Promise—it is better and more fitting that all these things be expounded and understood spiritually. The wording itself indicates this: the future tenses prophesy a future mystery rather than narrate a past history, when it says: “O God, when you go forth before your people, when you pass through the wilderness, you shall set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance.”

That words of past tense are also inserted is not unusual for prophets, who often foretell future things as though narrating past ones; as there: “They dug my hands and feet; they counted all my bones. They divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots for my clothing” (Ps. 21:18–19). Therefore, just as there Christ, speaking in the Prophet, laments as past events things that were future for him when these words were written, so here [Col. 0176A], when the Prophet said, “The earth was moved, for the heavens distilled, and it was weakened, but you perfected it,” and the rest in this manner, a prophetic declaration of future things is woven in words as though of past history.

Let us then say: O God, who bring out prisoners, and likewise those who provoke you, who dwell in tombs, you work this deed of your power especially when you go forth before your people. For you were as though hidden within the wilderness when you had not yet gone forth for the salvation of your people. But going forth from the Father through the mystery of your holy incarnation, you worked salvation [Col. 0176B] in the midst of the earth before your people, born of Abraham’s stock and beloved by your Father because, through you, one was to be born and go forth from the rod of Jesse.

That people, your special possession, had you before its eyes in hope, as one to be born from itself. But after you went forth truly in the manifestation of the incarnation, it had you before its eyes in actuality. For those to whom you were promised and sent observed and beheld you; they tested and saw your works, such as no one else had done. If they had not seen them, they would not have had sin; but now they have both seen and hated both you and your Father. Therefore, leaving their house desolate—which had formerly been inhabited by you—you passed over to another wilderness, henceforth to be inhabited by you, according to that prophetic saying: “The wilderness [Col. 0176C] and pathless land shall rejoice, and the solitude shall exult and blossom like a lily. It shall bud and blossom and shall exult joyfully and praising” (Isa. 35:1–2). Why? Because the glory of Lebanon has been given to it.

Lebanon, a boundary of Judaea on one side, signifies the Jewish people, whose glory was transferred to the Gentiles, formerly wilderness and pathless land, when, after they had rejected the word of God—to whom it had been promised and sent—the apostles passed over to the Gentiles. Thus the Apostle Paul said: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but because you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). Then the earth was moved: earthly people were stirred, some to obey the apostles, others to persecute them and their followers.

Nor is it strange [Col. 0176D] that the earth was so variously moved. For the heavens—that is, the apostles—did not distil uniformly in one language, but, speaking in varied languages, distilled the mighty works of God variously: proclaiming wrath to some and mercy to others, according to the differing disposition of their hearers. Thus the heavens, declaring the glory of God, distilled—not from themselves, however, but from the face of God speaking through them and dwelling in them.

Another translation has: “Mount Sinai [smoked] before the face of God,” or “distilled.” The mountain is the same thing as the heavens. Nor should it trouble us that “heavens” is said in the plural and “mountain” in the singular to signify the same thing, since elsewhere, after it has been said in the plural, “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:2), the same is repeated in the singular [Col. 0177A] under the name “firmament.” It is understood either as one heaven because of the one faith, or as many heavens because of the divisions of graces.

These heavens distilled not from their own power but before the face of the God of Sinai—namely, he who gave the Law on Mount Sinai, which is interpreted “temptation”—and before the face of the God of Israel, who came to fulfil that same Law through the blessing by which he blesses the true Israel, changing the name Jacob into Israel. For he who gave the Law on Mount Sinai—a Law which does not deliver amid the temptations which it provokes, but terrifies like a pedagogue—will also give the blessing which delivers and changes the name Jacob, struggling in temptation, into the name Israel. Thus such a wrestler shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be his name, when, by angelic or divine touch, the sinew of his thigh withers [Col. 0177B] through the chastity bestowed from above. This could not be fully given through the Law, which increases temptations, but is given through the voluntary rain of divine grace, which extinguishes temptations.

Mount Sinai distilled this rain: both because the Law prefigured grace, and because the Apostle Paul, a pupil of that same Law, preached to the Gentiles the grace which was not empty in him. Or likewise the other apostles, pupils of the Law, as heavens declaring the glory of God, distilled upon the earth—that is, they preached prudently and distinctly. For they did not say everything to everyone; rather, speaking differently to the weak, differently to the strong, differently to the old, differently to the young, differently to the healthy, and differently to the sick, they distilled in manifold ways according to the various kinds of people. Nor was it a scanty dropping, but so abundant [Col. 0177C] that, as they distilled, it became a universal rain—not only in Judaea, but throughout the whole earth.

And indeed it was a universal rain, by which God rains upon the righteous and the unrighteous; nevertheless, you shall set it apart by producing diverse effects from it, when the whole earth, watered by it, yields its fruit in some persons but remains barren in others. Worse still, it not only fails to produce the fruit proper to the nobility of the seed or rain, but, although carefully cultivated, produces thorns and thistles. Therefore I say of this your earth, this your inheritance, that it was weakened in regard to those who did not produce good fruit; but you perfected it in regard to those who, keeping the word of God in a good and excellent heart, bear fruit in patience. Your inheritance was weakened in stony, thorny, and trodden ground; but you perfected it in good ground bearing fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold.

Thirtyfold is in married persons living in discipline; sixtyfold in those who, after marriage or fornication, live chastely in continence; a hundredfold in virgins who know no defilement of the marriage-bed and therefore, in the regard of holy souls, have a hundredfold fruit. Alternatively, we recognize thirtyfold fruit in faith in the Trinity, sixtyfold in perfection of action, and a hundredfold in purity of contemplation. By these fruits, distinguished from one another and set apart from one another, it is proved that you, O God, shall set apart a voluntary rain for your inheritance.

[Col. 0178A] And that inheritance was weakened—that is, it acknowledged that of itself it could do no good. But you perfected it. For “power is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9), when one who fails in oneself advances in God’s power; and, having in oneself the answer of death, grows strong in God, who raises the dead, gives life, and exalts those who humble themselves.

Alternatively: Your inheritance, O God, was weakened as sin abounded; but you perfected it, because “where iniquity and transgression abounded, grace superabounded” (Rom. 5:20). Your inheritance was weakened because, while the Law displayed but did not heal the wounds of those under it, “their weaknesses were multiplied” (Ps. 15:4)—that is, their many weaknesses appeared. But you perfected it [Col. 0178B]—either the Law or the inheritance—because you came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil and perfect it, and to strengthen those who are heirs of your kingdom and promises so that, after their weaknesses had multiplied, under grace they might hasten to perfect the work of their own salvation, which could not be perfected under the Law, since it brought nothing to perfection.

Rightly, therefore, is it said of you, O God, that both your Law and your inheritance were weakened, but you perfected it and will perfect it until full consummation, setting apart for it a voluntary rain—that is, the gratuitous rain of the new Law, of which it is said: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth, that we might be some firstfruits of his creation” (Jas. 1:18). God the Father willingly begot us by the word of truth, adopting us as sons; but you, O God the Son, perfected and perfect us [Col. 0178C] by sending forth, as a voluntary rain, your Spirit, who blows where he wills and, distributing his grace to each as he wills, sets apart the voluntary rain of his gifts for your inheritance: making some prophets, others apostles, others evangelists, others pastors and teachers. As these feed your flock, your animals shall dwell in that same inheritance of yours which, acknowledging that it can do no good of itself and having in itself the answer of death, was weakened; but you perfected it, making it grow strong from that very weakness, in which power advances rather than fails. For the strength of the mind is perfected in the weakness of the flesh, and the strength of grace is sought and gained in the weakness of the Law.

[Col. 0178D] Alternatively: Your inheritance, the people whom you chose as your inheritance, was weakened because its outward human being is corrupted; but you perfected it because, through your work, its inward human being is renewed day by day. “For when I am weak,” says the Apostle, “then I am stronger and powerful” (2 Cor. 12:10). Thus in your inheritance strength of mind is virtue, while weakness of flesh is the safeguard of virtue.

The Hebrew truth has: “O God, when you went forth before the people and walked through the wilderness, the earth was shaken and the heavens distilled before the face of the God of Israel. You raised up a voluntary rain, O God; you strengthened your inheritance when it was weary.” It follows:

*Your animals shall dwell in it.* You set apart the rain of grace for your inheritance, and in that inheritance—or [Col. 0179A] grace—your animals shall dwell, animals joined together into one, of whom your inheritance itself consists. Thus the Church itself consists of many ecclesiastical persons dwelling in the Church; thus the Bride herself consists of brides who go to meet the Bridegroom and the Bride. Therefore your animals, tame and accustomed to the yoke of discipline—namely, the meek and humble, your poor in spirit—shall dwell in your inheritance, so that they themselves may be your inheritance.

Alternatively: *Your animals shall dwell in it*—in the grace of the voluntary rain which you set apart for your inheritance, to whom you also say: “Remain in my love” (John 15:9), as though you were saying: Dwell in my grace; make use of my voluntary rain. And indeed you rain upon the righteous and the unrighteous, offering salvation to all [Col. 0179B]. Nevertheless, you have prepared in sweetness the taste of grace only for your inheritance—your inheritance, I say, which is poor, that is, which attributes nothing good to its own powers or merits. Or poor with that poverty of which you say in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3).

Thus you have prepared in sweetness for your poor inheritance. What, or how great, are the good things which you have prepared for it? I, David, neither say nor can say; for neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart, what you have prepared for those who love you. Yet I say that you have prepared ineffable goods, which cannot be felt or understood, in a sweetness which can be felt—and is well felt—when the word of truth is heard and kept not from fear of punishment but from sweet love of righteousness [Col. 0179C]. Nor is it strange that this word tastes sweet, because sweet and upright is the

**VERSE 12.** *Lord, who will give the word to those who proclaim the Gospel,* according to that promise: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict” (Luke 21:15). Therefore a word shall be given to the preachers who proclaim the Gospel, by which the animals may be fed. It shall be given, I say, with great power, as it is written: “With great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord” (Acts 4:33). Thus until the end of the age the Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the Gospel with great power.

Some manuscripts have “great power,” so that you may understand that great power is given to those who sincerely proclaim the word of God out of the sole [Col. 0179D] love of truth: either steadfastness in good conduct, or also that efficacy by which the word runs mightily, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that follow. Do not wonder that I said that the Lord gives either the word with great power to those who proclaim the Gospel, or great power. For he is able to give great power, who is
### Verse 13

The King of the powers is beloved, beloved. For by him the heavens and the powers of heaven are governed. Hence elsewhere he is also called “the Lord of powers, the King of glory” (Ps. 23:10), because he, the King of his powers, gloriously rules the host of heavenly powers. But where he ought to have said “his own,” the Psalmist says “beloved, beloved,” following the usage of the ancient Scripture. Thus it is written: “Moses did as the Lord commanded Moses” [Col. 0180A] (Exod. 39:1). The Apostle followed this manner of speaking when, speaking of this same beloved one, he says: “Who was predestined Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ” (Rom. 1:4). For instead of saying “from his own dead,” he said “of Jesus Christ.” Likewise here, instead of saying, “The Lord Jesus is King of his own powers,” it is said, “King of the powers of the beloved, beloved.” For he is the one to whom the Father speaks: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

He is called beloved twice, just as in the Song of Songs he is twice declared beautiful by the bride, who says to him: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely” (Gen. 39:6). She was not content to say “beautiful” once, [Col. 0180B] unless she also added “comely,” indicating by that repetition the preeminence of his beauty. Or certainly, in each substance of the beloved she expressed a beauty worthy of all admiration: in the one, that of glorious Divinity; in the other, that of glorified humanity. Because of this double beauty he is now likewise called beloved twice, when it says: “King of the powers of the beloved, beloved.” Or it is because the Father loves him according to each nature: according to the divine nature, possessing all things with him eternally; and he also gave him, according to his assumed humanity, to be King of all powers—not only earthly, but also heavenly. Hence the beloved himself says: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18).

Therefore he is the King of glory, ruling powers [Col. 0180C] in heaven and on earth: in heaven, ruling the powers of heaven; on earth, ruling those of whom the Apostle says: “God has set in the Church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers, then gifts of healings, helps, governments” (1 Cor. 12:28). By “powers” understand the virtuous: angels in heaven and chosen persons in the Church. Since Christ, ruling both, is loved by both, he is rightly proclaimed beloved twice in this respect also, when it says: “King of the powers of the beloved, beloved.”

Yet the Father may be understood by “King,” and the Son by “beloved,” so that it may be read thus: “The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the Gospel with great power.” Which Lord? The King—the Father of the King—to whom elsewhere it is said: “O God, give your judgment [Col. 0180D] to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71:2). This King, holding the undivided kingdom of the entire monarchy with his Son the King, is King of the powers of his beloved Son, since both the angelic powers and those through whom the apostles and the other rulers of the Church work equally belong to Father and Son, the Son himself testifying and saying: “All mine are yours, and yours are mine” (John 17:10).

Therefore, when it says, “The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the Gospel with great power,” let the King of powers be understood as God the Father. For the angelic or apostolic powers which are given by him are also ruled by him. And since these powers belong to the Father who loves the Son, they are also those of the beloved Son—beloved, beloved: that is, greatly beloved; or beloved by God the Father and likewise beloved by human beings, as it is said: [Col. 0181A] “Beloved by God and by men, whose memory is in blessing” (Ecclus. 45:1). Yet not all manuscripts have this repetition, “beloved, beloved.”

In the Hebrew truth we have it thus: “The kings of armies shall be allied, allied, and the beauty of the house shall divide the spoils.” The sense is: the kings of armies—that is, the rulers of the Churches—shall be united, so that they may think the same thing, believing in their hearts unto righteousness, and say the same thing, confessing with their mouths unto salvation. Therefore they shall be united, and again united, so that they may think and say the same thing.

Nevertheless, the very King of the powers, beloved, beloved—who gives them the word to proclaim with great power, beloved in a double love, beloved, beloved, in thinking the same thing—since he himself is the very beauty of the house, will give [Col. 0181B] them also to divide the spoils for the beauty of the house. For, in order to make the comeliness and beauty of the house more illustrious, they shall divide the spoils with rejoicing, “as victors rejoice when the prey has been taken, when they divide the spoils” (Isa. 9:3).

Finally, when the strong armed devil guarded his courtyard—that is, this whole world lying in evil—all that he possessed was at peace. But when one stronger than he comes upon him, as we pray when we say, “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered,” he will take away all his weapons and distribute his spoils. Since the King of powers will perform this work of power through powerful ministers from the first coming of his beloved Son until the second coming of that same beloved one—or rather, since the very power [Col. 0181C] of the beloved Son of God, the beloved Son of Man, works in his ministers—we rightly maintain that he will give them to divide the spoils for the beauty of the house.

For it contributes to the adornment of the house’s beauty that the spoils taken from the strong armed man by one stronger are divided, when from them Christ makes some apostles, others prophets, others evangelists, others pastors and teachers, for the building up of his house, which is the Church. Thus it contributes to the beauty of the house that the spoils are divided, since the Church is thereby made beautiful: distinguished into various orders and adorned also with the various charisms of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit distributing to each as he wills. “For as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually [Col. 0181D] members one of another” (Rom. 12:4–5).—“If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? And if the whole body were hearing, where would smelling be? The hands cannot say to the feet, nor the feet to the hands: You are not necessary to us; nor is there any member at all in the body which does not need another, since even the weaker members are more necessary” (1 Cor. 12:17 ff.).

Therefore, with the members distinguished in the holy Church, the spoils are rightly divided, so that those which seem more ignoble may be found surrounded with greater honor. Otherwise, ugliness would be brought upon the beauty of God’s house if the rightly offered spoils were not also rightly divided, both in the universal house, which is the whole Church, and in every particular Church ordered by the ecclesiastical disciplines of the canons [Col. 0182A] or by the monastic rules of the Fathers.

For if distributors of ecclesiastical or cloistered goods and offices do not rightly divide the money entrusted to them, and confer dignities on the unworthy, they bring great ugliness upon the beauty of God’s house. By contrast, as the Church now sings in the Holy Spirit, they are admonished to divide the spoils for the beauty of the house—that is, to divide the spoils so that adornment may thereby accrue to the house’s beauty.
