And indeed the spoils must be divided according to the distinction of ranks, dignities, and offices in the holy Church of God. You who are the spoils must not labor to seek or obtain them, be anxious about them, or make others anxious concerning them. Do not rise before daylight, but rise after you have sat down.

Hear what Christ says to his disciples: “Sit,” [Col. 0182B] he says, “here and watch with me”; and he adds: “Sleep now and rest” (Matt. 26:38, 45). These commands are not contrary when he says “Watch” and then adds “Sleep,” because the bride knows how to observe both at once, saying: “I sleep, but my heart watches” (Song 5:2). No one can watch while sleeping, or sleep while watching, unless, after the example of the patriarch Jacob, he puts a stone beneath his head: that is, unless he rests his mind upon him who is the cornerstone and the greatest ornament of the house’s beauty. His spoils are most rightly divided among those who rest upon him in sleep and, after a little sleep, hear from him: “Rise, let us go” (Matt. 26:46).

To those who have first been lulled to sleep by contempt for the world, and then stirred up to work with Christ’s Gospel—as Jacob awoke from sweet sleep in which he had seen angels ascending and descending—it is fitting, when awake, to set up as a memorial through praises and teachings the stone placed beneath their heads. This is so, however, only if the King of powers, beloved, beloved, in dividing the spoils for the beauty of the house, has assumed them for that office in which they ought to be not only praisers but preachers. Otherwise, they should be content merely to praise and magnify his name and, like her who says, “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior” (Luke 1:46–47), should not arrogate to themselves the authority of any dignity among spoils already divided or yet to be divided. Rather, they should sleep and rest, and not rashly and presumptuously thrust themselves [Col. 0182D] into the labors and anxieties of pastoral care.

Such sleep and rest delighted Peter when, having tasted the sweetness of the vision on the mountain, he said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17:4). Luke also relates that he and the sons of Zebedee fell asleep there, weighed down by sweet sleep. O good sleep! O delight of sleep, which makes a person weighty with a praiseworthy gravity, of which it is said: “I will praise you among a weighty people!” (Ps. 84:18). By contrast, those who excessively seek spoils altogether unfitting for them are carried about by blameworthy lightness. They haunt courts, seek people’s favor, gather little gifts for inferiors and presents to be given to superiors, and greet people with excessive zeal and deceit, almost like entertainers [Col. 0183A] who flatter each person appropriately. Chief among them is a certain Gnatho, presented by the comic poet as having trained himself to say:

> If someone says no, I say no; if he says yes, I say yes.  
> —Terence, *Eunuch*, Act II, Scene II

Thus those who are in royal houses and seek secular dignities, or—what is much more dangerous—even spiritual responsibilities, clothe themselves in the soft coverings of flattery. If they were wise, they would flee those responsibilities; yet by courtly and inquisitive maneuvering they seek them, and sleep is snatched from their eyes because they are too anxious for tomorrow.

By contrast, you who know how sweet is the shade beneath which the bride rests, rest with her and hear her saying: “As an apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is [Col. 0183B] my beloved among the sons. Under his shade, whom I desired, I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song 2:3). Invited by the bride’s example to sit down, you too who labor and are burdened—now at last weary and exhausted by biting cares—sit beneath the shade of him who says to you: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29).

Under this shade, in this rest, sleep—not just anywhere, but between the two *cleri*. Sleep, I say, and rest with great hope of great benefit for yourselves, because:

### Verse 14

“If you sleep between the two *cleri*, the wings of the silvered dove, and the hind parts of her back in the yellow gleam of gold.”

On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says:

> [Note: [Col. 0183D] In St. Paterius, *Exposition of the Old and New Testament*, Book XI, ch. 139.]
>
> “In the Latin language we call *cleri* ‘lots.’ Our sleeping is to rest from wrongful action. And because the elect, who restrain themselves from the disturbance caused by the perverse, abandon earthly things and desire heavenly ones, undoubtedly sleep between the two lots: for, fleeing temporal things and desiring eternal rewards, they rest from perverse deeds. For in mind they fly to the heights, and therefore they are called wings. They are rightly described as the wings of the silvered dove. The silvered dove is the holy Church, which shines with the light of open preaching. Yet this dove is silvered in her wings, but [Col. 0183D] the hind parts of her back shine in the appearance of gold, because the holy Church is now bright through the tongues of preachers; but in the reward which follows she is adorned, no longer with the gleam of silver but with the radiance of gold. For when she comes to those invisible goods and attains those heavenly gifts which eye has not seen nor ear heard, she will no longer need the speech of preaching. She is beautiful only in the appearance of gold in her hind parts, because in what she receives she shines solely with the splendor of brightness.”

May these extracts from the words of blessed Gregory instruct us morally.

But according to the sense of blessed Augustine, [Note: [Col. 0184D] In the *Exposition of the Psalms*, on this passage.] he calls the two Testaments *cleri*, not because *clerus* is the name of a testament. For *cleros* is Greek, and in Latin means “lot.” Hence *cleronomia* means inheritance, following the custom of the ancients, who divided inheritances among their sons by lot; Joshua also is read to have done this in the distribution of the promised land. It is more correct, however, to understand that the Lord permitted rather than commanded the promised land to be divided by lot. For whatever he commanded cannot be changed, as in the saying: “You shall love the Lord your God,” and so forth (Deut. 6:5). But things permitted because of hardness of heart—such as the bill of divorce and lots—were allowed only during the period when they were permitted.

The apostles also used this permission in choosing Matthias before the coming of the Holy Spirit. Once more fully instructed by him, they are never afterward read to have used lots, [Col. 0184B] which the holy Fathers later prohibited, once the holy Gospel shone forth, as pagan practices hostile to the Christian religion. Yet the word “lot” remains, according to ancient usage, in designating either inheritances which were divided by lot or testaments by which inheritances were secured: the term being transferred from what effects something to what is effected, or conversely. For inheritance was effected by testaments and lots; and again, inheritance was the reason for casting lots in order to divide it, and for writing testaments in order to secure it. Thus the term for lots is transferred to signify inheritance, and again from inheritance to signify a testament. Grammarians call this figure [Col. 0184C] metonymy.

In this sense, we may understand the *cleri* in the present passage either as signifying the two Testaments, by which is confirmed the double inheritance of the promises of the life which now is and of that which is to come; or as signifying those inheritances themselves, confirmed by the aforesaid Testaments and indicated by the Greek name *cleros*. Hence also a cleric is one taken into the lot or inheritance of the Lord, so that he is called—and is—the Lord’s inheritance, and the Lord his inheritance, as the Lord says: “You shall give no inheritance to the sons of Levi, for I shall be their inheritance” (Num. 18:20).

Let us therefore first call the two *cleri* the two Testaments. What their middle is, we learn from Solomon’s teaching. After he had described a couch supported by silver columns, with its ascent of purple and its reclining-place of gold, he added: “He paved its middle with love, because of the daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 3:10). There you have the silver columns; here, the wings of the silvered dove: in both places, purity and the brightness of eloquence are signified. There likewise you have a golden reclining-place; here, the hind parts of the dove’s back in the pale gleam of gold: in both expressions the radiance of eternal Wisdom is signified. There you have, “He paved its middle with love”; here, “If you sleep between the two *cleri*.” In both places understand by “middle” love, which is the middle of all the Scriptures signified by the couch, because all the testimonies of both Testaments hang from it as from [Col. 0185A] a central stem, as Truth says: “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:49).

Likewise, in the description of the dove having silvered wings and a golden back, understand the middle in such a way that you avoid the corner. Notice that the Lord opens the mouth of the righteous in the midst of the Church, but he does not hear those praying in the corners of the streets. Jesus therefore stood in the midst of his disciples so that, as their eyes were fixed upon him, he might commend to them the commandment of love, the middle: a commandment which is not to be observed in the corner of one sect, but in the full universality of the whole Church; it is set before all, suffices for all to attain eternal life, and by the binding force of this love, as though from many members, one dove is made.

Here it should be observed that he did not say “between the *cleri*,” according to Latin usage, but “between the two middle *cleri*,” according to Greek usage. Where we say, “Between me and you,” the Greeks more explicitly say, “Between my middle and yours,” wishing to signify a certain agreement of things which Latin usage does not express. Thus, when God says to Abraham, “There shall be a covenant between me and you” (Gen. 17:2), and to Noah, “There shall be a sign between me and the earth” (Gen. 9:13), the Greeks, in order to express agreement, use “between my middle and yours” in order to make the agreement clearer.

Therefore, when the Psalmist says here not “between the *cleri*” but “between the two middle *cleri*,” [Col. 0185C] he expressed an agreement of realities which cannot endure without love in the middle. Since this love is patient and kind, does not envy, is not puffed up, is not provoked, thinks no evil, does not rejoice over wrongdoing but rejoices together with truth—and, what is more pertinent to the present passage, is not ambitious and does not seek its own—it makes, as it were, in the quietest leisure, a fitting place for that sleep of which it is said here: “If you sleep between the two middle *cleri*, the wings of the silvered dove.”

You therefore who have labored by walking about in a circuit, as it is said, “The wicked walk in a circuit,” come to the middle of the two *cleri* by keeping love, which is the central marrow of the two Testaments. For thus the word is given to you who proclaim the Gospel with power: if you firmly hold both the authority of the two Testaments [Col. 0185D] and the love commended by the two Testaments. If, in love’s most peaceful chamber, you sleep by despising the temporal goods promised in the Old Testament and patiently awaiting the eternal goods promised in the New, then, sleeping and resting in peace together between the two middle *cleri*, you will be the silvered wings of the dove of which it is said: “My dove is one” (Song 6:8).

This dove is lifted through you as through silvered wings, when she is aided either by your prayers, harmonizing with divine speech, or instructed by your preaching. For “the words of the Lord are chaste words, silver tried by fire” (Ps. 11:7), and nothing ought to be prayed or preached except according to the rule of these words. [Col. 0186A] When the sons of Zebedee asked that one might sit at the right hand and the other at the left in the kingdom of God, they indeed had wings of prayer, but not silvered wings, not bright with the splendor of divine words—rather, wings contrary to those words. For no authority of divine speech teaches that there are seats at the left hand in the kingdom of God, unless perhaps the present Church is called the kingdom of God; for in it the good and the evil, the spiritual and the secular, rule under the Christian name, as though it had seats at the right and left.

But God’s saints occupy seats in the present Church, as on his left hand, in two ways: either authority to govern is given them, so that they sit with princes and hold the throne of glory; or their previously marked-out glory is so increased that they rest in it as in a most soft seat and live for themselves. But the sons of Zebedee had in view not the seats of the Church militant, but those of the same Church reigning, when they sought a seat with Christ. Therefore it was said to them: “You do not know what you ask” (Matt. 20:22). As though he said: You have wings of prayer, indeed, but they are not silvered by divine speech. Therefore they were directed to the rule of divine speech, so that they might learn that the cup of suffering must first be drunk, and afterward they must sit in the kingdom only at the right hand, not at the left. For there will be no left hand there.

Still more is the word necessary to those who proclaim the Gospel with great power, so that they may have wings of teaching marked with the silver of divine words, lest they presume to teach [Col. 0186C] anything except what they have learned between the two middle *cleri*: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s?” (Ps. 54:7)—silvered wings. Who will teach me, in proclaiming the Gospel, to speak to people in such a way that all the utterances of my heart and mouth may in every respect be conformed to the chaste words of the Lord, likened to refined silver, according to the saying: “If anyone speaks, let it be as the words of God” (1 Pet. 4:11). Again: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20).

Another interpretation: The Lord will give power to those who proclaim the word of the Gospel, if you teachers—who are the silvered wings of the dove—sleep between the two middle *cleri*: that is, if in meditation, prayer, and teaching you do not fall away from that middle which will never fail, [Col. 0186D] because love, the central marrow of the two Testaments, will never fail.

Another interpretation: O you who are divided as spoils for the beauty of the house, do not seek positions or offices higher than those assigned to you: namely, so that one who is an archdeacon may not seek to become a bishop, or one who is a bishop seek to become an archbishop, and similarly in other cases. Be content with the places and offices through which you have been variously assigned, the Holy Spirit distributing to each as he wills, for the adornment of the beauty of God’s house. Let each of you sit, rest, and, supported on either side by the two *cleri* as upon his bed, sleep—unless perhaps he who invited him says: “Go up higher” (Luke 14:10).

Sleeping and resting in this way between the two middle *cleri*, you will receive the grace to be wings [Col. 0187A] of the dove, since through you—whether praying in secret and in chambers, or publicly proclaiming the word with great power and upon the housetops—the one Church, God’s dove, is adorned and exalted. And you yourselves, humbling yourselves beneath the mighty hand of God as you sleep, will in due time fly upward like wings of the dove, “for everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14).

Another interpretation: You preachers who proclaim the word with great power, who are the wings of the dove—that is, of the Church flying upward and seeking the things above—if you sleep between the two middle *cleri*, will be silvered wings in the front parts of the dove, that is, in the condition or flight of the present Church. But the hind parts of her back, in the future state after the resurrection, will shine for you in the pale brightness of gold. Just as in [Col. 0187B] Solomon’s days, when gold abounded greatly in Jerusalem, silver was of no value, so then, when the radiance of angelic wisdom or divine love shines above all things, silvered wings will not be needed through the brightness of doctrinal eloquence. By means of these the Church, like a dove, flies, with the roots of those wings fixed in the hind parts of her back.

For her back is love, in which, having taken up the burden of God’s commandments, she bears all things and endures all things. The hind parts of her back are that future and supercelestial brightness in which the love that begins here will be perfected. In this love the pale or greenish gleam of gold will be seen, because then, through the splendor of wisdom shining through all things and in all things, when God will be all in all, the God of gods will be seen in Zion face to face, as he is. No one will need to be taught then by the ringing of silver speech, or awakened like a camp by silver trumpets, as was ordained in the law of Moses. For then all, from the greatest to the least, without anyone showing them, will themselves see the Sun of righteousness; and the battle-order of God’s camps, now militant and needing trumpets, will be entirely dissolved. When Israel departed from Egypt, God’s camps were traveling and arrayed for battle, and it was commanded that silver trumpets be made, which the priests would sound either when they held a solemn feast or when the camp had to be moved for battle.

Indeed, in this pilgrimage, while we flee from Egypt and from the authority of the invisible Pharaoh, [Col. 0187D] such silver trumpets are necessary. Through the Lord’s sacraments, as through a festal meal, fitting worship is offered, with the sound of the two Testaments—or two silver trumpets—in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs fitting for the same feast, and by singers white with silver brightness and resonant with its ringing. Likewise, as wars now threaten us on every side, we are necessarily stirred by the same silver trumpets to battle; for example, as the Apostle teaches, so that, “armed with the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left” (2 Cor. 6:7), we may be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. “For our struggle is not only against flesh and blood,” but, more dangerously, “against the rulers of this world, the governors of this darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12).

These are priestly, sacred, hammered silver trumpets. At their blast Jericho, the city of this world, which persecutes Jesus’ messengers and refuses to receive him, will fall. The one who says, “Cry aloud, do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isa. 58:1), desires such a blast. Through all these necessary ministries of silver trumpets or wings, the one Church, God’s dove, is now adorned and aided in her front parts. But the hind parts of her back, shining in the pale brightness of gold in the future life—when tongues will cease, prophecies will be abolished, knowledge will be destroyed, when that which is perfect comes [Col. 0188B] and that which is partial is abolished—will not need silvered wings to be lifted upward. For once exalted on high, the elect will always be with the Lord. Nor will they need silver trumpets, either to praise the Lord at the festal meal or to be stirred and encouraged in battle to defeat adversaries. For then there will be peace, eternal Sabbath, and the most blessed leisure of complete happiness: the ministry of the sacraments and offices which we now use will cease, and every fear of wars will be entirely removed.

Since this repose of such great joy, reserved for the hind parts of the dove, will be everlasting, the Hebrew rightly inserts here “for ever,” where we have *Diapsalma*, a sign of a division between what has already been said and what remains to be said. For, two parts of the psalm having now been completed, the third part begins, concerning the gifts of Christ ascending, in this manner: “If you sleep between the two middle *cleri*, you shall be wings,” or, “the wings of the dove shall be silvered for you, and the hind parts of her back in the pale brightness of gold,” as set forth above.

But perhaps you say in your beds, and thoughts rise in your hearts in this way: How long must we sleep thus? To this I say: You must sleep, sit, and rest in the city with Christ’s disciples until you are clothed with power from on high. This was magnificently accomplished when “there came suddenly from heaven a sound of a rushing mighty spirit, and it filled the whole house where the disciples were sitting” (Acts 2:2), [Col. 0188D] as though sleeping between the two middle *cleri*. By distinguishing them from other people, he also made them kings and rulers over the one Church, the dove. In a similar way, therefore, we must now sit, rest, and as it were sleep in the upper room of spiritual discipline,

### Verse 15

“While the heavenly one”—that is, Christ, exalted into heaven at the right hand of the Father—“distinguishes.” What does he distinguish? Kings: that is, those set over the Church, distributed and distinguished by various dignities, the Spirit distributing to each as he wills, so that some are prophets, others apostles, others evangelists, others pastors and teachers. In order that they may indeed be fit for their offices, they will be whitened like snow in Selmon. “Like snow”: that is, through the forgiveness of sins they will be whitened in the likeness of naturally white snow. And this is not by their own merits, [Col. 0189A] but in Selmon.

*Selmon* is interpreted “shade” and signifies grace, of which the angel said to Mary: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). And the bride says in the Song of Songs: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons. Under his shade, whom I had desired, I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song 2:3). Again, elsewhere it is said: “He will overshadow you with his shoulders, and under his wings you shall hope” (Ps. 90:4). Therefore grace is called shade, because it protects the flesh from the heat of carnal desires and cools the mind from the flame of spiritual vices, such as anger, pride, and envy.

Shade is produced by light and a body. Likewise grace is produced by Word and flesh. For the Word is light and flesh is body. The Word came to the flesh, light to body, [Col. 0189B] so that the Word became flesh and God became man. Since he protects those who believe in him from evils by the shade of his grace, and cherishes them in good things, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, protects them from a kite, and warms them with her own heat, he is rightly called *Selmon*, that is, “shade.”

But lest anyone suppose that this mountain is to be compared with other mountains, I, David the prophet, tell you that this mountain is:

### Verse 16

“The mountain of God, a fat mountain,” or, as another translation has it, “a fertile mountain; a curdled mountain, a fat mountain.” This mountain, according to Daniel’s vision, grew from a little stone in height and length so that by its magnitude it fills the whole world (Dan. 2:35). For a little child was born to us, like a small stone [Col. 0189C] cut without hands from the mountain, or mass, of the human race: separated from sinners by divine operation alone and made higher than the heavens. For he is rightly called the Son not only of the immaculate Virgin, but also of God the Father Most High, so that he too is believed to be Most High together with his Father. Yet the Father Most High and the Son of the Most High, himself Most High, are not two Most Highs, just as the Father God and the Son God are not two gods.

Therefore this mountain is rightly called the mountain of God, to whom was given the name above every name, so that he is called the mountain of God by excellence, just as he is called Son by excellence. For God adopted the other sons of God, but begot this one: not only eternally, as the radiance of his paternal glory and the image of his substance, God consubstantial with himself, God; but also temporally at the end of the ages, he begot this same one through the working of his love, so that a virgin might conceive him and bring forth true God and perfect man, a giant of two substances, consubstantial with God the Father and with his virgin mother.

Therefore, because in the Virgin’s womb, through the working of the Father’s love and the mother’s faith, there occurred a coalescence of the paternal seed—which is the Word of God, God—and the maternal seed, which was the matter from which the new human being was formed, that which was born from her is rightly called Holy, as the angel testifies. It is not called holy in just any way, but the Holy of holies, whose holiness is not accidental, as it is in other saints, to whom it was given first to exist and afterwards to be holy. But this one, holy from eternity in his Divinity [Col. 0190A] and conceived in his humanity by the Holy Spirit, received, at the same time as he received that he should be man, that he should be holy; and as God he is holy equally with his Father and with the Holy Spirit, the Father’s love by whom he was conceived. Of him the angel says to his mother: “For he shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke 1:32). Truly great is the Lord, whose greatness has no end.

Likewise, a mountain of God, a fat mountain, whose richness has no end. For the richness of this mountain is the fullness of the Godhead dwelling in it. Although the flesh of Christ is inhabited by the Son alone, united to him in such a way that the flesh, the soul, and the Word are one Son of God, nevertheless the Father and the Holy Spirit, being one with the Word, so inhabit the Word’s flesh that they never depart from it. [Col. 0190B] Truly, then, it is a fat mountain, whose richness is the fullness of the supreme Trinity. Truly it is proclaimed a curdled or cheese-like mountain, because the Word made flesh, like bread dipped in milk, nourishes little children until they advance so far as to be able, according to their capacity, to receive something of the richness of this mountain. It is now called “fat” a second time, so that there may be no doubt that it is full both according to the humanity united to the Word and according to the nature of the Word himself, through the Holy Spirit, who is the richness of the eternal Godhead.

Wonderful is the coagulation of this cheese-like mountain: formed from diverse natures curdled into one, it cannot in any way be dissolved, just as the strap of his sandals cannot be untied. Indeed, [Col. 0190C] the acts or sufferings predicated of this mountain are in some measure distinguished according to the properties of the natures. Thus, for example, it is said that death happened for a time to Christ’s flesh alone, when on the cross he gave up the spirit, which he also received again at the resurrection. Likewise, sorrow could belong to the soul alone, on account of which he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38). Eternity too is attributed to the Godhead alone, of which he says: “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58), and: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14).

Nevertheless, the coagulation of these different natures—the human flesh, the human spirit, and the eternal Word—into one person has been made in such a way that the man assumed into God may truly be called eternal, and God united to the man may rightly be proclaimed crucified and [Col. 0190D] dead. Hence he did not say, “My Godhead was before Abraham,” but: “Before Abraham,” he says, “I am.” And the Apostle declares that the Lord of glory was crucified, so that you may perceive from this, in our Lord Jesus Christ as in a coagulated mountain, the inseparable union of the divided natures—especially after the rebuilding or resurrection of that temple not made with hands, which the Jews had dissolved by death. By this, this temple was so strengthened, this mountain so curdled, that it can no longer be dissolved or separated.

For whatever is separated after the union is separated either actually or intellectually. Actually, as Christ’s soul was separated from his body while the body lay in the tomb and his soul either triumphed in hell or rejoiced in [Col. 0191A] paradise, as he himself had said to the thief: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Intellectually, as he likewise says: “The flesh profits nothing” (John 6:64)—that is, flesh understood without the spirit, as it had been understood by those who said: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (ibid., 53).

And indeed the flesh then in question was full of both spirits, namely the human and the divine; but in their understanding it was so separated from the Spirit that it was thought to be offered to them to eat as though it were the dead flesh of a beast, when it was said to them: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). By separating Christ’s flesh from the Spirit through an understanding as it were lean, they believed it would be distributed to those who ate it as though it were itself lean. But that abundant mountain, that fat mountain, which even in the blessing of Asher is called “fat bread, providing delights for kings” (Gen. 49:20), and which in the Gospel parable is called the fatted calf, did not offer his flesh to his own to be eaten as though it were lean flesh separated from the richness of the Spirit either in actuality or in understanding.

Therefore he says: “It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:64): flesh understood as they understood it profits nothing. Accordingly, Christ himself indicated a better understanding of his flesh when, as though explaining his earlier words, he added: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so he who eats me shall live because of me.” Note the comparison. “As,” [Col. 0191C] he says, “the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father,” so likewise “he who eats me shall live because of me.” He had said before: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.” Afterwards he adds: “He who eats me shall live because of me” (ibid., 54, 58), so that you may plainly understand that by the flesh of Christ named here, Christ in the flesh is signified, because the Word was made flesh. Therefore, just as the living Father gives the one begotten of himself to have life in himself, so the living flesh of Christ—or rather the living Christ—gives eternal life to one who worthily eats him.

Let new disputants, then, depart far from the schools of the Church, separating by a perverse understanding what God has joined together, while they preach something other than Christ in the flesh as the flesh of Christ. [Col. 0191D]

But we preach the Word made flesh without any change in himself, like a coagulated and cheese-like mountain: so that one who worthily eats Christ’s flesh cannot fail to eat the life remaining in that flesh itself; and one who worthily understands the flesh of the Word recognizes in the flesh the Word, as the inseparable richness of that flesh. To indicate this, the Evangelist preferred to say, “The Word was made flesh” (John 1:14), rather than, “The Word put on flesh.” A garment put on by someone can be taken off and laid aside actually, and can be separated intellectually from the wearer, as we separate a line or colour from a body by thought alone, although it exists nowhere else but [Col. 0192A] in that body. For such is not the union between wearer and garment, or between a bodily accident and the body, that it cannot be separated either in actuality or in thought.

But Christ, perfect God and likewise perfect man, is divided by no actual or intellectual divorce, because his two natures have been so coagulated into one person, into one electrum, into one Emmanuel, into one mountain, that everyone who dissolves Jesus by separating them through a perverse understanding is declared by the Apostle John to be Antichrist. “Every spirit,” he says, “that dissolves Jesus is not from God; and this is that of which you have heard, that Antichrist is coming” (1 John 4:3). And already it is in the world, because many of his forerunners separately discuss the soul, separately the flesh, separately [Col. 0192B] Christ’s Godhead, through undisciplined and foolish questions. “Christ’s body,” they say, “was in the tomb, not Christ. Likewise, Christ’s soul was in hell, not Christ; Christ’s Godhead is everywhere, not Christ.”

Far sounder is the confession of the Catholic faith, in which we confess that Christ was crucified, died, was buried, descended to hell, rose on the third day, and afterwards ascended into heaven, whence he will come to judge the living and the dead; and that now, before his coming, he is with his own unto the end of the age.

Animated by this faith, when the blessed martyr Anastasia was asked by a judge where Christ was, she replied: “In heaven at the right hand of the Father, and on earth everywhere are his saints.” We confess all this of whole Christ. Although he was enclosed in the tomb through his body alone, and was present through his soul alone to holy souls in hell or paradise, nevertheless he worked wholly in both places: in the tomb preserving his body so that it might not see corruption, but rather might raise from corruption many bodies of saints rising with him; and in hell or paradise governing his Spirit and making it reign, so that the hostile powers said: “Who is this King of glory?” To them the answer was given: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle; the Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (Ps. 23:8). You hear that both the good angels and the evil do not dissolve Christ, the coagulated mountain, but recognize the King of glory in his soul alone. [Col. 0192D]

Likewise Mary Magdalene recognized him in his body alone, saying: “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him” (John 20:13). Why, then, do you dissolve him, arguing that his flesh, soul, or Godhead is so separate that, according to your sense, flesh understood in this way profits nothing, as though it were lean and deprived of that richness of which it is here said: “A mountain of God, a fat mountain”? Do you not yourself see through the eyes alone, hear through the ears alone, walk through the feet alone, smell through the nostrils alone, taste through the palate alone, understand through the mind alone, and remember through memory alone—yet do you not deny that you do all these things in such a way that they are truly ascribed to your whole person?

How much more, then, does that person, [Col. 0193A] coagulated from two natures in such a way that he is consubstantial with God the Father through his Godhead and with human beings through his humanity, experience himself as acting wholly in whatever he does according to either nature? Hence there was such richness in his human acts that eyes smeared with his spittle were clothed with light, the tongue of a mute person was freed when touched, leprosy fled at his touch, the dead were raised by his voice, and the waves of the sea and the winds were calmed at his command. Hence too his flesh, when eaten, gives life, because in that flesh is the Spirit who gives life, without whom, as he himself says, flesh profits nothing. Those who thought it was to be eaten without the Spirit could not taste its richness, as though their throats were choked by lean flesh. Therefore they went back.

So too those of whom some said that he was John the Baptist and others Jeremiah or Elijah had not tasted in him that richness which tasted sweet to Peter saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Therefore they are rebuked by the prophetic Spirit, while Peter is praised by Christ himself. For it is said to them:

**VERSE 17.** Why do you look with suspicion upon coagulated mountains, as though they were the mountain in which God has been pleased to dwell? Thus some manuscripts have it: “Why do you look with suspicion upon coagulated mountains, [at] the mountain in which God has been pleased to dwell?” As though it were said: Why do you human beings so err concerning the Son of Man as to suppose Elijah, Jeremiah, or any of the prophets comparable with him? They too indeed [Col. 0193C] are great and coagulated mountains, because to their human nature was added the grace of the prophetic Spirit. But incomparably surpassing them is the supereminent mountain which is the mountain of God, a mountain fat with that ointment with which Peter recognized him, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16).

Peter recognized the mountain and ascended the mountain; and he himself became a great mountain when it was said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (ibid., 18). But far beyond, indeed infinitely above, the summit of this mountain and of all other mountains rises the mountain in which God the Father was pleased to dwell, to whom he also says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). Therefore the Father is pleased to dwell in him in his own person, while through that Mediator he dwells in other holy mountains. Or the mountain is the man assumed into God, in whom God the Word has been pleased to dwell, not in any manner whatsoever, but unto the end.

For the Lord, the Word of God, will dwell in him unto the end, unto final perfection: that is, not only by essence, whose majesty is undoubtedly present everywhere; or by grace, through which he is withdrawn from some and made present to others; but through personal union, so that the man inhabited by God the Word and God inhabiting that man are one person existing from two and in two natures. This person is properly called both Son of God and Son of Man, because he who is incorporeally begotten of the Father, as a good mind begets good understanding, was also conceived and born bodily from a virgin through the Holy Spirit, the Father’s love at work. He remained God the Word of God, which he always was, but began to be a bodily temple of God, finally inhabited by God, which he had not been before; he remained the Father’s understanding, Word, and reason, as he was, but was inscribed upon the skin of a human body, which he had not been before; he remained the intellectual Word of the Father, but was made a Word not only visible and audible but also touchable, according to that of the Apostle John: “That which we have seen and heard, which our hands have handled concerning the Word of life—and the life was manifested” (1 John 1:1–2).

Hence too, when the Apostle had said: “In whom dwells all the fullness of the Godhead” (Col. 2:9), he added, “bodily,” because the Word was made flesh [Col. 0194B] and through his flesh dwelt bodily in us. For as God, reconciling the world to himself in Christ, dwelt unto the end, so Christ himself will dwell with and in his elect unto the end, of which it is said: “I have seen an end of every perfection” (Ps. 118:96), according as he himself promised, saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). Or he will dwell unto the end by bringing them to behold himself, who is the beginning and end of all things. Or he will dwell in them unto the end, so that whatever good they are or do, they may refer it to no other final cause than himself, who is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

And because the Lord will dwell in them, from this they become chariots of God, carrying God who governs them, as the old man Simeon carried the child, while the child governed the old man. By governing them thus, he brings them to the end appointed for them, of which the Apostle says: “Christ the firstfruits; then those who are Christ’s; then the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father” (1 Cor. 15:23–24).

**VERSE 18.** This chariot is not of one kind, as, for example, having martyrs only, confessors only, or adherents of just one other order; rather, it is manifold with ten thousands. Thus you should understand a finite number set for an infinite one, signifying perfection, which is customarily indicated by ten and by a thousand. Therefore the ten thousands are all those chosen and perfected for this purpose: that, proclaiming the Word of God with great power, they carry God himself to the hearts of believers. [Col. 0194D]

Because they do this not from sadness or necessity but with spontaneous and devout cheerfulness, these chariots are “thousands rejoicing”: for, rejoicing in hope and patient in tribulation, although they sometimes become as though sorrowful, nevertheless always rejoicing, they delight in him whom they carry, whose chariots they are and are called. Among the ancients, chariots were vehicles of triumphant and ruling kings or princes. It may seem drawn from this comparison that they are called chariots of God, in which God triumphs—God adapting himself, the Word of God, to human speech—since the triumphal chariots of kings, adorned with gold, were said to serve as decoration for the triumphal procession.

Such, by like chariots, were Elijah and Elisha, each of whom was called the chariot of Israel and its driver. What kind of chariot Elijah was may be recognized in the fiery chariot in which he was taken up. Of him it is said in the Praises of the Fathers: “In those days Elijah the prophet arose, and his word was like fire and burned like a torch” (Sir. 48:1). Whoever rightly weighs the reasons fittingly reveres the zeal of the Lord, like the fire of a torch burning so vehemently, kindled so strongly in Elijah, God’s chariot, Israel’s chariot, that in one day that true Prophet put to death eight hundred and fifty false prophets. O perfect hatred and holy flame of good zeal, whose worth the heavens testified to by withholding rain at his command and then again giving the earth the benefit of rain; and, even more, by sending a fiery chariot with fiery horses to raise up the victorious veteran and mighty friend of the Lord of all! [Col. 0195B]

From so great and astonishing a glorification of Elijah, let every champion of truth and lover of justice take an example and conceive hope: he shall not lack a reward if, made a chariot of the Word of God, he fights against falsehood welcomed by false prophets and hated by true prophets. For true prophets, to kill false prophets after the example of Elijah, is to refute them by striking them with the sword of truth. This will be most necessary at the end of the age, when false prophets multiply, calling good evil and evil good. Therefore Truth foretells that Elijah will come before the great and manifest day of the Lord arrives. “Elijah,” he says, “will come and restore all things” (Matt. 17:11). The opinion of very many teachers concerning him is that he will come with Enoch near the end of the age and, they say, [Col. 0195C] will pay under the persecution of Antichrist the common debt of death which he did not escape but postponed.

But Jerome, not the least among illustrious men, seems to think otherwise at the end of the prophet Malachi, where the Lord says: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes” (Mal. 4:5). For, after some remarks, he says: “We have said these things about Elijah, following the teachers, although there are also many among our own who believe that he will come literally and restore. But when the Lord was questioned by the apostles about the coming of Elijah, he answered: ‘Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wished’” (Mark 9:12), wishing John to be understood in Elijah. Therefore he subsequently added: “If you are willing to receive it, John himself is Elijah who is to come” (Matt. 11:14).

In saying these things, he certainly indicates his agreement with other teachers who understand Elijah’s coming not according to the letter but according to the Spirit. Moreover, in saying, “Although there are also many among our own who believe that he will come literally and restore all things, and pay the debt of death,” he sufficiently indicates that he wishes Elijah to be already freed from the necessity of death. If this is so, then it is truly great, magnificent, and highly praiseworthy among glorious men what the Lord has wrought in him by his magnificence. For if he still awaits death, one may judge that he has attained less blessedness than other saints, who, having laid aside every corruption of mortality, have been freed from a great debt and a heavy burden. For expectation of death undoubtedly entails punishment; and therefore all those may be called more blessed for whom there is no fear of death and a sure hope of the glory of the resurrection. More magnificently, then, has God dealt with Elijah and blessed Enoch if they did not postpone death but escaped it, if, translated while alive, they have no torment of prolonged anxiety or expectation concerning death.

But concerning these and other secrets of divine miracles, about which diverse views are held by different persons without harm to the faith, anyone may, without prejudice to those who think differently, agree with whom he wishes as he wishes, provided the Catholic faith—as has been said—is preserved. Against it, no person’s authority or subtlety is to be accepted. It is not contrary to the faith whether Elijah is thought to be coming bodily in his own person or whether someone is worthy to be called, in Elijah’s spirit and power, the chariot of Israel and its driver—as Elijah himself and his disciple Elisha were both called chariots of Israel. The former was called so when he was taken upward in a chariot; the latter when, already near death, he was likewise called the chariot of Israel by the king of Israel. [Col. 0196B]

Who knows whether God may turn and forgive the sins of those who repent near the end of the age, and leave behind them a blessing as copious and abundant as, in the last days, he knows how to make iniquity abound when the love of many grows cold—and as, when iniquity abounds among the very wicked, he knows how to make love grow cold among the good?

Indeed, Elijah when taken up obtained for Elisha a double [Col. 0196C] spirit, because of the increase of the twofold sin to be overcome by him in both Judah and Israel. But now iniquity has so multiplied, while the love of many grows cold, that a single or double spirit of Elijah is not enough against it; one or two chariots of Israel are not enough against the innumerable chariots of Pharaoh, against the infinite armies of Antichrist, who will reign after Pharaoh’s example and at last be submerged in the abyss of hell.

Therefore, for the consolation of Israel endangered in its departure from Egypt while Antichrist pursues, God’s chariot is well promised as manifold with ten thousands. You are to understand that not merely one or two persons will be raised up in the spirit and power of Israel’s chariot, the fiery chariot such as Elijah was, but so great an army that each of the faithful who has eyes to see may say with Elisha: “There are more with us than with them” (4 Kgs. 6:16). Finally, while we contend against spiritual wickednesses and fleshly desires that wage war against the soul, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are with us. The heavenly hosts, sent for the service of our salvation, are with us. Thousands of saints who have already obtained triumph over flesh and blood and every devilish wickedness are with us. God’s chariot, manifold with ten thousands, is with us.

And lest you think that all whom that chariot contains are comprehended within this finite number of ten thousands, I add the infinite number by affirming that there are in it thousands rejoicing, so that through a definite number [Col. 0197A] you may understand an infinite army of many thousands serving God and continually sending prayers like fiery darts against the devil and Antichrist. These are the thousands rejoicing: that is, fighting not from sadness but in joy, rejoicing in the hope of victory, and therefore preserving patience in tribulation.

Whence comes this to them? Certainly not from themselves, but from the Lord, because the Lord is in holy Sinai. Or, in holy Sinai. Sinai, or Sinay, is a mountain in Arabia, on which the Law of Moses was given. The interpretation of this name suits the command given there, because Sinai is interpreted “command,” and the Apostle says: “The law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good” (Rom. 7:12). The Lord is in holy Sinai—that is, [Col. 0197B] in the holy command—because the life-giving Spirit is in the killing letter. “For the letter kills,” merely instructing and making sin known; “but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6), giving the will and power to accomplish good. For “love,” which is the fullness of the Law, is poured out “in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). That you might send him from on high, O Christ,

**VERSE 19.** You ascended on high. And before you ascended on high, descending into hell you took captivity there as spoils, like a conqueror. Then you received gifts in human beings, gifts which you had first received in yourself: your and the Father’s Godhead bestowing them, and your humanity receiving them. And indeed you received the Spirit in yourself [Col. 0197C] not by measure; but in human beings, your members, you received these gifts by the measure of each member, knowing how to divide the spoils through the distribution of gifts of the Spirit.

Alternatively: the Lord is in Sinai—that is, he is present with his own in temptation, in holiness. And from this, those very thousands rejoicing will have joy: because the Lord is present with them in Sinai, that is, in temptation, preserving them in the holy purpose of holiness and enabling them to consider it all joy when they fall into various temptations, knowing that “blessed is the man who endures temptation, because when he has been proved he shall receive the crown of life” (Jas. 1:12). Thus, because of this complete joy which endures even amid various temptations in every holy person, they are thousands rejoicing, because the Lord is in [Col. 0197D] Sinai in the holy person. They possess this inviolable devotion to holiness amid temptations through the grace bestowed upon them because you, Christ, ascended on high to the right hand of the Father.

But before you ascended, you took captivity—that is, you conquered death, which held captives. Or you took captive for good those human beings whom the devil had wickedly made captive, and placed them beneath the light yoke. Of such a capture it was said to Peter: “From now on you will be catching human beings” (Luke 5:10). This is the blessed captivity which you, Christ, took; and afterwards you received gifts in human beings—that is, you received human beings themselves as a gift after your triumph. Or you received in human beings, your members, [Col. 0198A] the very gifts which you gave. Hence the Apostle, expounding this verse with apostolic authority, altered the words and said: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Eph. 4:8).

This is to say: ascending on high, the Son of God—eternally most high in his Godhead, but exalted in his humanity as far as the confession of God the Father—led captivity captive: that is, many chosen persons liberated from hell, of whom several rose bodily with him in order to be true witnesses of his resurrection. In them, before his death, the flesh had held the spirit captive under the law of sin and death, which fought against the law of the mind. But after the resurrection, the flesh itself was made captive by the spirit, so that those whose bodies had risen with the Lord might be wholly spiritual and like the blessed angels.

Therefore captivity was taken captive in those in whom the law of the members, swallowed up by the law of the mind reigning in God and with God, could no longer resist that law of the mind. This will be reserved as a reward for all the elect who now, consenting to the law of the mind for good, resist the law of the flesh. And then, when what is mortal has been swallowed up by life, when death has been swallowed up in victory, this blessed captivity of captivity will be completed—a completion which could never occur in human beings unless Christ, ascending on high, had given gifts to human beings.

On this passage the blessed Pope Gregory says:

> **[Note: Col. 0197D, Book II, Homily 29 on the Gospels.]** “What is declared by these words of the Prophet if not the Lord’s ascension? For, ascending on high, he led captivity captive, because by the power of his incorruption he swallowed up our corruption. And he gave gifts to human beings because, having sent the Spirit from above, he granted to one the word of knowledge, to another the word of wisdom, to another the working of powers, to another the grace of healings, to another kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of words. He gave gifts to human beings when, through his grace, their power increased in the world.” [Col. 0198C]

Therefore he gave the gifts of the Holy Spirit to human beings, sending him as he had promised when he said: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16:7). Likewise: “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14:16). Behold: in that the Father sends, [Col. 0198D] the Son also sends; it is clear that this Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, proceeds from both—proceeds, I say, not departs, because neither is the Son separated from the Father by being born of the Father, nor does the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both, depart from that from which he proceeds. For these three are one: one essence, one form, one nature, one God, one almighty, one immeasurable, one eternal. Therefore, when the Spirit is given to human beings, the whole Trinity dwells in them through him, though some do not believe this. But by the gift of the Holy Spirit many of them who believe become chariots of God.

For those who do not believe that the Lord God dwells in them [Col. 0199A] become believers by his gratuitous gift, and experience in themselves that what is said is true: “Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them” (Rev. 21:3). Likewise: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). From such persons, whom God himself inhabits, or who dwell in the aid of the Most High, that manifold chariot of God with ten thousands is woven together. In it, he triumphs, proceeds prosperously against Pharaoh’s chariots, and reigns.

Therefore, favouring his triumphal procession, let us say day by day—that is, continually:

**VERSE 20.** Blessed be the Lord in his chariot, exalted above all heavens. Blessed day by day, or from day to day—that is, continually. Or, as the Hebrew truth has it: “through each day.” Let heaven and earth, sea and all things that are in them bless him, because he has triumphed through all and above all: dyeing the earth purple with his blood, walking upon the sea and calming its waves, penetrating the heights of heaven. So that we may eagerly follow him on his prosperous course, God, the author of our salvations, will make our way prosperous—preparing chariots and, triumphing in those chariots, making captivity captive—not on one day only, but daily; not only in his single resurrection or ascension, which occurred on one day, but also in the glorification of those of his own who rise with him and sit with him in heaven. This occurs daily until all God’s chariots have been completed and all Pharaoh’s chariots cast into the abyss, and we meet in the four-horse chariot of the Gospel as a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness. God, the author of our salvations, will make our way prosperous for the completion of such a course.

What a prosperous way is, to be sought in all movements and actions, the Apostle Paul indicates when writing to the Romans in this manner: “For God, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, is my witness that without ceasing I make mention of you in my prayers, entreating that somehow at last I may one day have a prosperous journey, in the will of God, to come to you.” Why? “That,” he says, “I may impart to you some spiritual grace to strengthen you; that is, that I may be comforted together with you through the faith which is mutual, yours and mine.” Likewise: “That I may have some [Col. 0199D] fruit among you, as also among the other nations” (Rom. 1:9 ff.).

From these apostolic sayings it is gathered that a prosperous journey is one arranged in God’s will and fruitful for human beings. Therefore God, the author of our salvations, having said to his apostles, his chosen chariots and foremost drivers of his chariots, “I have appointed you that you may go,” added, lest their journey should not be prosperous, “and bear fruit”; and, lest that fruit of the journey be thought transient, he joined: “and that your fruit may remain” (John 15:16). Thus may God, the author of our salvations, make our way prosperous, so that in all our movements nothing may occur which is not pleasing to the will of divine goodness and fruitful both for us and for other people—especially for those to whom [Col. 0200A] we are debtors, wise and foolish alike—whether we bear much fruit or little. Thus, when the evil branches have been cut off by the hand of the best husbandman, the whole vineyard of God, the author of our salvations, may be fruitful with saving fruit; and may our fruit remain, not in ourselves or in our own powers, which are exceedingly weak, but in God, the author of our salvations.

The three parts of the psalm having now been completed, the fourth follows, in which it is shown what comes from the aforesaid gifts of God: namely, the crushing of enemies, the conversions of some, and the martyrdoms of believers of both sexes. A diapsalma is inserted here; among the Hebrews it is *Selah*, which is interpreted “always,” because this prosperity in the saving fruits mentioned above ought to be desired so that it may remain always. [Col. 0200B] And this is believed possible because:

**VERSE 21.** Our God is a God of saving. For “the Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save” (Luke 9:56). Our God, I say, who assumed our nature, is a God of saving, to whom we rightly say: “Our salvation is in your hand, Lord” (Gen. 47:25). Here grace is highly commended, since our salvation is proclaimed to rest not in our own power but in God’s, so that whoever glories may glory not in himself but in the Lord.

You therefore say to me: Why then do the good die bodily just as the evil do? Or why are the evil themselves destroyed by the death both of soul and body and made far from salvation, though they believe and confess God the Saviour, saying that our God is a God of saving? Lest, speaking thus, you wonder and become indignant at human mortality or death, hear that “of the Lord, the Lord, are the issues from death.” “Of the Lord, the Lord”—that is, according to the twofold nature of his person, ruling everywhere both in heaven and on earth.

Of the Lord, I say, who committed no sin and therefore was in no way subject to the necessity of dying either in body or spirit, as Adam was, to whom it was said: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17). Of such a Lord, ruler of life and death, the only departure from this life was by death: namely, through death accepted not by necessity but voluntarily, so that when, in his [Col. 0200D] person, an issue from death is seen, the fear of death may be removed from his servants, to whom he says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28).

Alternatively, so that you may know that our God is a God of saving, observe him saving his servants, whose Lord he is by creation, because he created them, and also Lord by redemption, because he transferred them from the dominion of the devil—from the slavery, that is, of the invisible Pharaoh—to his own possession, “that, delivered from the hand of our enemies without fear, we may serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days” (Luke 1:74–75). Of such a Lord is the issue from death: because he himself came forth from bodily death through his resurrection, and opened for those who believe in him [Col. 0201A] an exit from the death of both body and soul, when by dying he destroyed the death of the soul and by rising restored the life of bodies.

**Verse 22.** “Nevertheless God will crush the heads of his enemies.” That is to say: although our God is a God who saves, yet he will not save all alike; rather, he will crush the heads of his enemies with a twofold crushing or breaking: humbling some unto repentance, and sending others, who refuse to repent, into Gehenna. And although by crushing all his enemies he will make them the footstool of his feet, nevertheless he will especially crush the heads of his enemies—that is, either their leaders, who hold the primacy of wickedness among them, [Col. 0201B] or their pride and authority. Thus the pride and authority of the Jews, tyrants, and heretics has perished, since Christ’s authority reigns supreme everywhere, and no one now dares openly to contradict or resist it.

But because the cunning devices of false Christians, who pass from vice to vice and persevere in their chosen courses, are still vigorous, so that with Elijah we may say, “The fornications of Jezebel still prevail” (4 Kings 9:22), the Lord will also crush this hairy crown of those who walk in their offences. By “hairy crown” we may understand the subtleties of empty questions or thoughts. For there are some who seek out such petty grounds for accusation that they seem, by crafty subtlety, even to scrutinize hairs themselves; and their foolish, devious thought, unless it is checked and broken, leads them into sin. But the Lord, where and when it pleases him, will crush such a hairy crown of those walking in their offences. He will assuredly crush the hard-hearted, who refuse to bend, as elsewhere it is read: “The Lord has broken kings in the day of his wrath” (Ps. 109:5). But those whom he finds pliable and capable of conversion, he himself will convert. How do you know this? Namely from the fact that the Lord, who cannot lie because he is Truth, spoke thus:

**Verse 23.** “From Bashan I will convert,” or, “I will turn into the depths of the sea.” Bashan is interpreted “confusion” or “dryness”; by this name are signified those who are ashamed of their sins and, poor and dry, desire the voluntary rain [Col. 0201D]. Of these the Lord said, “I will convert, I will convert,” or, “I will turn,” because he converts such persons to himself, and himself turns toward such persons.

Some manuscripts have, “I will convert in the depth of the sea,” that is: I will also convert those who, through the enormity of many crimes, are so dulled in the depths of vices as though set in the depths of the sea beneath great, bitter waves of the sea. Jonah, placed in the belly of the whale, foreshadowed such persons; crying to God from depths of this sort, he said: “Your waves passed over me, and I said: I am cast out from before your eyes. The abyss surrounded me, and the sea covered my head. The bars of the earth shut me in. Do you think that I shall see your holy temple? [Col. 0202A] But you will raise my life from corruption” (Jonah 2:4 ff.). The Lord heard him thus praying in the depths of the sea and delivered him from the whale’s belly. Thus he still hears those who cry to him from the depths, so that what the Lord himself said may be fulfilled: “From Bashan I will convert; I will convert in the depth of the sea.” Or, as other manuscripts have it: “I will turn into the depths of the sea,” that is, even to deliver those who seem most utterly desperate, because they themselves are called “the depths of the sea” on account of the depth of their bitterness. Such a man was King Manasseh, when, despising the true God and becoming an idolater, he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood up to its mouth; but later, being taken to Babylon, he did penance in that captivity and cried to God as if from the depths of the sea, and the Lord converted him from Bashan [Col. 0202B]. For Babylon, like Bashan, signifies by its name the confusion of this world. Babylon itself may be called “the depths of the sea,” since Isaiah, intending to speak against Babylon, gives the heading, “The burden of the desert of the sea” (Isa. 21:1), and afterwards adds: “Babylon has become a wonder to me” (ibid., v. 4). Again: “Babylon is fallen, is fallen” (ibid., v. 9). By these sayings, “the burden of the desert of the sea” and “the burden of Babylon” are shown to signify one and the same thing, though he treats each separately: first the burden of Babylon, afterwards the burden of the desert of the sea. Therefore, those whom the Lord converts from Bashan, he rescues by converting them from Babylon, or from the depths of the sea.

In the Hebrew it is read thus: “The Lord said: From Bashan I will convert; I will convert from the depths of the sea” [Col. 0202C]. Hence it is evident that the Latin translator, translating from the Greek and ignorant of the Hebrew truth, either erred or used the accusative case in place of the ablative; so that, when he ought to have said, “I will convert from the depth of the sea,” he said, “into the depths of the sea.” Therefore the faulty usage has prevailed that it is sung, “I will convert into the depths of the sea,” although both the Hebrew truth disagrees and the more correct manuscripts have, “I will convert in the depth of the sea,” that is, those who are in the depths of the sea. But where it is read, “I will turn,” “into the depths of the sea” is correct. For the Lord also turns at times to deliver those who are, as it were, the depths of the sea: exceedingly turbulent and bitter, and wholly alienated from the light which illumines the surface of the sea [Col. 0202D], because of their exceedingly deep and turbulent wickedness. There could scarcely be confidence concerning the conversion of such persons, except that the Lord, who is not accustomed to lie, said: “From Bashan I will convert in the depths of the sea,” or, “from the depths of the sea,” or, “I will turn into the depths of the sea.” And it should be observed that those to be converted are not people who glory in their wickedness or seem to themselves full and satisfied, but those who, in accordance with the meaning of the name Bashan—“confusion” or “dryness”—are ashamed of their sins in repenting, and are dry in hungering and thirsting after righteousness. For lack of it they pant, always attending to their own dryness, which cannot bear fruit of itself unless it receives voluntary rain from above. It follows:

[Col. 0203A] **Verse 24.** “That your foot may be dipped in blood; the tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him.” In these words the Prophet turns to the Lord as though present and addresses him, as if he said: O Lord, with the hearing of my inward ear I heard you speaking: “From Bashan I will convert from the depths of the sea.” And you, Truth, truly spoke truth, because you will so convert whomsoever you will that your foot may be dipped in blood; that is, they themselves may become your foot by bearing the Gospel, bearing you, the incarnate Word, exalting you, their head, by their good sayings, and carrying you around the world even unto bloodshed. Thus, having been converted from enemies, they become the tongue of your dogs—not of those dogs of whom the Apostle says, “Beware,” he says, “of dogs” (Phil. 3:2), who are alien dogs—but of your [Col. 0203B] dogs, faithful to you, barking to guard your house and gladly eating of the crumbs of your table. Therefore I do not say merely “dogs,” but add “your”; nor do I mention their teeth, by which wounds are made, but praise the tongue by which sores and wounds are licked and healed, according to what is written of Lazarus: “Dogs came and licked his sores” (Luke 16:21).

This tongue of dogs is good; an ancient mystery also commends it, where it is read that Gideon, leader of Israel, after dismissing the rest, led to victorious battle only those who lapped water with their tongues like dogs. Their number, increased to three hundred, denotes the sacrament of the cross on account of the letter T, which signifies three hundred and represents the cross in its form. By its victorious banner all triumph who preserve in deed the faith of the Holy Trinity, and in word as it were by hand and tongue. Just as those three hundred fellow-soldiers of Gideon, casting water to their mouths with the hand and lapping it with the tongue after the manner of dogs, beautifully prefigured those who, exercising themselves in the Scriptures both in deed and word, drink the waters of wisdom (Judg. 7:5) [Col. 0203C]. This indeed occurs more wonderfully when evil enemies of God become good dogs of God—from him, namely, whose enemies they had first been and whose friends they afterwards became; from no other source than from him.

What remarkable swiftness of apostrophes! First he spoke to the hearers about the Lord, saying: “The Lord said: From Bashan I will convert; I will convert into the depths of the sea”; and immediately, turning to the Lord himself, he speaks as if to one present, saying: “that your foot may be dipped in blood, the tongue of your dogs from enemies.” Then, turning again to the hearers so that they may not wonder how it happened that those who had formerly been enemies of God are now called his dogs, he announces that this happened from him, lest anyone glory in free choice or in personal strength; rather, “let him who glories glory in the Lord,” because salvation is from him and not from elsewhere—he who also says: “I am the salvation of the people.”

In the Hebrew truth it is read thus: “That your foot may tread in blood; the tongue of your dogs, from enemies [Col. 0204A], from yourself.” Therefore, for the second person placed in Hebrew, the Latin interpreter gives the third person, telling the hearers that this whole good of enemies converted comes from God himself. And again, turning toward God, he speaks to him as though present, saying:

**Verse 25.** “They have seen your goings, O God.” And again, turning to the hearers, he says of God: “The goings of my God, my King, who is in the holy place.” On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0203D] Book XX of the *Morals*, ch. 6]:

> “What are called dogs in this place but holy teachers, who became guardians of the faithful in holy Church? Since, intent upon their Lord in watchings by day and night, they cried aloud, they gave, so to speak, great barkings of preaching. For some [Col. 0204B], recalled from the worship of idols, became preachers of God. Therefore the tongue of the dogs of the Church came forth from enemies, because the Lord made converted Gentiles preachers also. Hence the slowness of the Jews, who refused to speak for God, is rebuked by the Prophet’s reproach: ‘Dumb dogs, unable to bark.’”

If anyone doubts and asks why these dogs were not at all afraid in their barking even amid the dangers of their sufferings, let this be known: they were stirred by your examples, O Christ, because they saw your goings—or “the goings of you, O God,” if *tui* is taken as a genitive. First the apostles saw them, to whom it was said: “Blessed are the eyes which see what you see” (Luke 10:23); afterwards, following the apostles, your dogs also, converted from the Gentile enemies, [Col. 0204C] saw your steps—or your goings: namely, how, entering this world for truth and justice, for obedience to the Father, and to plant the faith of truth throughout the whole world, doing and teaching good things, you endured many evils from evil men. They first saw your goings by which you entered on the way of holy obedience through the humility of the Incarnation, coming forth from the hidden place of heaven and entering this world, as you said: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16:28). Then again they saw your goings by which, leaving the world and going to the Father, it pleased you to suffer insults, and thus to enter your glory through insults and reproaches. They saw, I say, such goings [Col. 0204D] of yours; and, stirred by your examples, they too, striving to enter through the narrow gate of your imitation, chose to cling to your footsteps.

In a moral sense also, whoever perceives within himself that the disordered movements of a wandering mind are restrained by remembrance of God’s judgments sees, as it were, the steps of the Lord walking within him. The Lord directs his goings toward the mind: first the steps of intention, then those of action, so that his invisible entering may become known through outward good works. And of those who see these things and therefore love and glorify the author of such works, our Father who is in heaven, it may also be said that they have seen the goings of my God, my King, who is [Col. 0205A] in every holy person doing good, or in every holy work, without whom nothing is powerful, nothing holy.

But if you, hearers, wish to know of whose goings I, David, speak, I announce to you great joy which shall be to all people, because I speak of the goings of my God, my King, who is in the holy place: my God, who is creator of all things; and my King, who governs all created things by preserving the natures of things, condemning vices, and glorifying virtues. He dispenses to natures the permanence of being; to vices, the measure of punishment, whether corrective or destructive; and to virtues, glory. Such is the rule of my King, who is in the holy place, because God’s Word, who governs all things, is in the holy Father, as the Son himself said when entering the world: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10). Or he is in his holy body, born of the holy Virgin, conceived through the Holy Spirit, and therefore, principally and uniquely, holy above all holy things, so that he is rightly called the Holy of Holies. Therefore the angel said to Mary: “The holy thing that shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35) [Col. 0205B]. Of this holy body it is elsewhere said to the Father: “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10). Since in this holy body all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, I rightly speak of my God, my King, who is in the holy place; for though the whole Trinity fully dwells in that holy body, nevertheless the Word, to whom that body is personally united through a rational soul, is in a special manner—indeed, beyond every manner—in that holy body. Therefore, in accordance with the angel’s proclamation, that holy one is properly and truly called the Son of God; for God gave him the Holy Spirit not by measure.

Furthermore, my God and King, the Son of God, is in the holy place—that is, in his holy temple, which is the Church—so that nothing holy is found outside it. And because, as was said above in this very psalm, God in his holy place makes people of one manner dwell unanimously in a house, wherever in any house there is found this unanimity of one manner, one love, one religion, and one discipline, there without doubt is the blessed [Col. 0205D] presence of my God, my King, who is in the holy fellowship of spiritual brethren of this sort. He creates and rules this his chariot invisibly through himself, but visibly through you as his vicars. Although this chariot is manifold with ten thousands because of the diversity of persons or charisms, nevertheless, because it is unanimous in love, in one faith, and in one hope—having one spirit, one body, one heart, and one soul in God—this holy chariot of God is rightly spoken of in the singular number as manifold, both simple and manifold: manifold because of the diversities of charisms, which the Spirit apportions to each as he wills; simple because of the one prize toward which the whole course of such chariots tends. Although many are to receive it, whom the foreknowledge of my God, my King, ordained and whose predestination prepared them, nevertheless because of the unity of hearts tending to one and the same goal, it is rightly and truly said that “one receives the prize” (1 Cor. 9:24) [Col. 0206A].

Moreover, it is beyond doubt that although no saint is holy as the Lord is holy, still in each holy member of his, however small, however despised and neglected by human beings—as Lazarus was—my King and my God, who is in every holy person, is himself present. Therefore he will say: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40). Again, calling a little child before himself, he said: “If anyone receives one such little child in my name, he receives me” (Matt. 18:5). Since this is the statement not of a prophet nor of an apostle, though we must of course wholly believe those who speak in the Spirit of truth, but of my God himself, my King, who is in the holy place, it ought to be received with much greater gratitude; and from the truthful declaration of my God, my King himself, his presence in each of his holy ones, however small, must in no way be doubted.

How much more, then, is he himself present in those princes whom this same King of mine appointed princes over all the earth, ruling them in his power? And when their rule has thus been greatly strengthened:

**Verse 26.** “These princes went before” the other followers of my God, my King, because, just as they were the first with blessed eyes to see the goings of my God, my King, so they were also the first, entering after him on the way of obedience, to precede others who would follow their examples. Hence [Col. 0206C] it is no wonder that the tongue of God’s dogs was formed from enemies by him and strengthened even unto bloodshed; since, trained not only by the examples of my God, my King himself, but also by those of his princes and fortified by their authority, it was able, through his favouring grace, to overcome adversities.

Therefore the princes, first to see the goings of my God, my King, and first and alone to enter after him, went before others; but they did not arrive at him alone. For while they went before upon the way of righteousness, on the narrow path of obedience, many believed through them; and they learned not only to sing psalms on the ten-stringed psaltery—that is, according to the Law of Moses spiritually understood—but also to beat the tambourine of the Gospel: men with women, young men and virgins, old men with the younger; Jews first and Greeks afterwards; while the chariot of God, manifold with ten thousands, ran to the very end of the earth [Col. 0206D].
