Therefore I, David, announcing future things as though past in the spirit of prophecy, recount as something accomplished—and indicate as something truly accomplished daily in the mouths of those who sing psalms in the churches—that these princes, the chief and foremost triumphant soldiers in the battle line of Christ, my God and my King, are joined to those who sing psalms, glorifying God with strings and instruments of good works, in the midst of young women playing tambourines. For, even literally, the female sex is not excluded from this choir of psalm-singers, while they exercise themselves in good works, nor from those who play tambourines, while they restrain themselves from desires for evil works. In their midst these princes are placed, carrying out an honourable ministry like pillars and supporting the entire house, as it is elsewhere said: “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in my temple” (Rev. 3:12) [Col. 0207A]. Again: “In the midst of the Church he will open his mouth” (Ecclus. 15:5). Again, the Lord himself, the Prince of these princes, says of himself: “But I am among you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27). Therefore, when these princes are said to be in the midst of young women, the honourable ministry by which they observe the command and example of Christ, the Prince of princes, is signified. For when he had ministered to his disciples by washing their feet, he said to them: “I have given you an example, that you also should do likewise” (John 13:15).

Young women may also be called the Churches newly converted to God, or fragile persons newly converted to God. They play the tambourine praiseworthily when, as though their skin had been dried and stretched, they crucify their flesh with its vices and desires, stretching the sinews of all their members on the wood of the Lord’s cross. Each young woman desires to comprehend, with all the saints, what is the breadth, length, height, and depth of the cross: in the breadth of love, perseverance in long-suffering; in the depth, faith and fear; in the height, hope and continual desire for things above [Col. 0207B].

*Diapsalma.* The fifth part begins, in which the strengthening of this good undertaking is treated as follows:

**Verse 27.** “In the churches bless God.” Above we recalled that the Lord said: “From Bashan I will convert,” and we have shown the efficacy of this saying in many ways: namely, in the tongue of dogs formed from enemies converted and strengthened even to the shedding of blood, in which the feet of evangelists were dipped; then in the princes preceding these dogs; then in the choir of psalm-singers and young women who play tambourines. But so that these great goods may grow from day to day and not fail, you princes, you good dogs, you choirs of psalm-singers and tambourine players, bless God not in the synagogues of the Jews, not in the conventicles of heretics or schismatics, not in sects of perdition, but in the churches. Do not glory as though you had not received the gifts of grace which you possess; rather, in thanksgivings bless God the Father and the Lord the Son, from whom both proceeds into you that Spirit who helps your weakness, so that you may be found praiseworthy [Col. 0207D] princes, psalm-singers, tambourine players, or some other member of the Church, not by strength of your own but by his.

Since strong princes are in the midst of young women who play tambourines, it is quite clear that there is no discord among the Church’s members: neither the greatest despise the least, nor the least envy the greatest. The eyes do not say to the feet, “You are not necessary to us.” For just as the many members of a single human body, not performing the same function, are ruled by one soul so that there may be no schism in the body, so also in the churches there is one Spirit, proceeding from Father and Son, among the different orders—for example, prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, virgins, innocents, penitents, the continent, married persons, prelates, subjects, clerics, monks, and widows. This Spirit gives life to all the members of the Church and distinguishes many churches within the one Catholic Church according to the diversity of charisms. In all these, God the Lord, God the Father, and the Lord the Son are blessed through the operation of the Spirit of both; those who are merely natural persons, lacking this Spirit—indeed separating themselves from this Spirit and from his temple—though they bless with their mouths, blaspheme by their conduct and deeds. Therefore, you psalm-singers and tambourine players, do not sing psalms or beat tambourines in just any assemblies, but in holy churches, in ecclesiastical orders and gatherings instructed by ecclesiastical discipline [Col. 0208A].

And lest you be deceived in choosing and recognizing such churches, acknowledge as true churches only those which have flowed from the fountains of Israel. For the apostles, who established churches throughout the world, were themselves fountains of Israel, because they were chosen from the people of Israel so that living waters might first flow from their bellies to water the primitive Church, and then to plant and water the many churches among the Gentiles. Afterwards there succeeded cisterns that cannot hold water—that is, teachings dissenting from apostolic doctrines. Among these we may also count that rule for clerics composed not in the Church but in a royal court. In its instructions for communities of clerics it first presents most sacred teachings of common life, as though drawn from the fountains of Israel, by which cenobitic discipline is rightly formed; but afterwards, by indulging certain things contrary to them as though from foul water, it corrupts all the earlier draughts drawn from the fountains of Israel [Col. 0208B].

For among other sound teachings of the Fathers, there are read there also sermons of blessed Augustine, in which, after citing the reading from the Acts of the Apostles that tells how the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and that no one called anything his own [Col. 0208C], that blessed Father adds his own statements, likewise derived from the fountains of Israel. By them the cenobitic life of clerics living according to the pattern drawn from the Acts of the Apostles, as though from the fountains of Israel, is most fittingly regulated. For among other things he says: “No one in our fellowship is permitted to have anything of his own; if any do, they do what is not permitted.” Although these and similar cups of sound doctrine drawn from the fountains of Israel are gathered together in that rule, I do not know from what deadly cistern there is drawn the provision that, after many prohibitions of private property, property itself is granted to professed adherents of the same rule, and that, after workshops suitable for common life within the cloister have been arranged, private and individual dwellings are also allowed—as though the basest rag were sewn onto a precious garment [Col. 0208D].

But let it be so: let them remain as they wish. We do not condemn them all, since among them we recognize some, though few, as so disciplined that, though they possess private property, they possess it as though not possessing it, and strive to follow moral discipline. To me they resemble persons running swiftly but outside the path appointed for their course, because they do not keep the rule [Col. 0209A] prescribed for their manner of life. Although wise themselves, they willingly—or too patiently—tolerate fools in their community; though chaste themselves, they patiently tolerate the prohibited ministries of priests, deacons, and subdeacons who are manifestly incestuous. And though they themselves seem to live orderly lives, they do not withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly, as **Verse 28**, “Benjamin, a young man,” exhorts.

Indeed, although he says, “Do not share in the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather rebuke them,” they share in such things and do not rebuke them at all. Nor do they consider it safe to violate the ancient proverb, “Laws are silent amid arms,” because undisciplined brethren, surrounded on every side by their kindred and armed clients, impose silence by terror upon those who ought to rebuke them [Col. 0209B]. We know of wounds inflicted and murders perpetrated on this account, as happened in the Church of Halberstadt, where one of the brethren was killed in the refectory by soldiers of the provost because he had spoken against the provost concerning a certain disorder.

Therefore, rejecting synagogues of Satan of this kind, in which the small number of good persons is overwhelmed by the multitude of evil persons, the Holy Spirit rightly and safely advises those who desire to bless God purely in this psalm, saying: “In the churches bless God the Lord.” In churches, I say, founded upon the rock of apostolic discipline and watered by their teachings as by fountains of Israel. In such churches bless God. For there apostolic doctrine is preserved, spread especially among the Gentiles through the Apostle Paul, teacher of the Gentiles. Since he is read to have been born from the tribe of Benjamin, I say that there was Benjamin, a young man, who was called last of all the apostles and is also remembered in Acts as a young man, where the false witnesses standing against Stephen are said to have laid their garments “at the feet of a young man named Saul” (Acts 7:58) [Col. 0209C]. He was named from Saul, the impious king, as though *Benoni*, that is, “son of sorrow.” Later he was surnamed Paul—that is, “humble” and “small”—after the proconsul Paul whom he converted, and was fittingly called Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand.” Although called last, he was nevertheless notably numbered among the fountains of Israel, when it is said here: “There is Benjamin, a young man, in an excess of mind”—that is, amid the mental astonishment of all who said: “Is not this he who came for this purpose, to destroy this name?” (Acts 9:21). Or it may mean the astonishment and fearfulness of his own mind when, struck down by the Lord on the road, he was made fearful and stunned. Afterwards he was also in an excess of mind, that is, in ecstasy, when, not knowing whether he was in the body or outside the body, he was caught up into the third heaven and heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to speak [Col. 0209D].

Although this man alone is called Teacher of the Gentiles, nevertheless, wherever he established in the churches choirs of psalm-singers and young women playing tambourines, there too, whether in spirit or in body, other princes of the peoples were present with him: namely, the princes of Judah, their leaders—that is, those who are in those churches; the princes of Zebulun; and the princes of Naphtali [Col. 0210A]. He mentions these tribes because perhaps apostles came from them. Yet, since no certain account in any authoritative Scripture records from what tribe each apostle came—as the Apostle Paul himself states that he was born from Benjamin—it seems preferable to attend here, through the names of the other tribes, to what is derived from their interpretation and is most fittingly applied to all the apostles and their followers, apostolic men. For Judah is interpreted “confession,” Zebulun “dwelling of strength,” and Naphtali “my breadth.” All these suit the princes of the churches, and especially the holy martyrs after the apostles. For in martyrdom the first virtue is not to deny but to confess the Catholic and apostolic faith; if any adversity is inflicted for its sake, strength is taken up. Then, when adversities are ended, breadth follows as a reward, not only in the future life but also frequently in this life, as he experienced who said to God: “In tribulation you have enlarged me” (Ps. 4:2) [Col. 0210B].

Alternatively: the princes of Judah, the first confessors, are the holy apostles, whose sound of confession went out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world. The princes of Zebulun are the order of holy martyrs, who, struggling in confession of the Catholic faith even unto countless deaths, gave their bodies to punishments for God, fighting bravely and defeating by their strength and endurance the monstrous enormity of idolatry. The princes of Naphtali are holy pastors and teachers, who, living in the peace of a Church enlarged after the tribulation of martyrdom, as leaders of the Lord’s flocks keep the wolfish rage of heretics away from Christ’s sheepfolds, watch over doctrine, and govern God’s household with gentle tranquillity [Col. 0210C].

This order of confession, strength, and enlargement is observed not only in martyrdom or in the three orders just mentioned, but in every upright undertaking of any religious way of life. At its beginning is made the profession of some holy discipline, not according to new inventions of beginners, but as the princes of Judah, their leaders, established in ancient times—for example, the Apostle Peter, and after him blessed Augustine, leaders of clerics; John the Baptist, the solitary one, and after him blessed Benedict, leaders of monks. Therefore, once such a profession has been made, as though Judah had gone before, Zebulun follows, called “dwelling of strength,” because strength is necessary lest those who have entered the narrow way grow weary in the temptations and tribulations by which beginners are tested and trained [Col. 0210D]. But once they have been tested and trained, because the Lord’s yoke becomes sweet and his burden light, when the way of God’s commandments and counsels, begun upon a narrow path, is run with willing devotion through the very habit of living well, Naphtali is joined to Zebulun. Naphtali is interpreted “breadth,” and there the faithful runner learns to sing: “I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118:32) [Col. 0211A]. Again: “When I called upon you, you heard me, O God; in tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. 4:2).

Benjamin the young man is fittingly joined by the princes of the tribe of Judah and of the other tribes: that is, Paul the Apostle, now carried beyond himself in mind toward God, now sober-minded toward the Gentiles of whom he was the teacher. For Paul himself, unwilling to stand alone in his teaching, went up to Jerusalem to Peter and the other apostles, and laid before them the Gospel which he preached among the Gentiles, lest perhaps he should be running, or had run, in vain, if his teaching should be found to differ from theirs. [Col. 0211B] Therefore those who seemed to be pillars gave to him and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship, so that they might preach the Gospel among the Gentiles in the same way as the others preached it among the circumcised (Gal. II, 9).

This young man, though the least of the apostles both by his own declaration and by the apostles’ reckoning, yet by labouring more than them all was so made equal to the Prince of the Apostles that these two, like two olive trees and two lampstands, illuminate the Church with an equal grace of splendour. At its summit, as the light of the Gentiles, both together hold the city of Rome, like two eyes in the head; there their bodies are not separated, just as their merits are believed to be equal in heaven. There, then, is Benjamin the young man; [Col. 0211C] and with him the prince of Judah, Peter, who by his chief confession confessed Christ, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI, 16), and who, after his threefold denial, was cleansed and enlightened by a threefold confession of divine love.

But because Peter, Prince of the Apostles, confessed Christ as the Son of God not only for himself but also for his fellow disciples, they too may together with him be called princes of Judah, their leaders. After them, and from that time onward, those receive the faith of the same confession and pursue a manner of life suited to that faith: with such strength in work as the name Zebulun requires, and with such breadth of charity as the name Naphtali requires. For by these three tribal names—Judah, Zebulun, and Naphtali—is expressed faith working through love [Col. 0211D], which that young Benjamin strongly commends in his epistles and which all apostolic teaching plainly conveys. Thus Judah’s confession consists in faith; Zebulun’s strength is recognized in work, together with hope, which is made firm by the good conscience resulting from good work; while the breadth denoted by the name of the princes of Naphtali is the commandment of charity. If by it we love one another as Christ also loved us, extending even to love for enemies, we too shall be enlarged—even if not princes of Naphtali, yet followers of those princes who offered us examples of this faith working through love.

Indeed, through his teaching and example, Christ himself demonstrates this love; and we shall be not so much servants as friends, “because the servant does not know [Col. 0212A] what his master does” (John XV, 15). Knowing that such commands of faith, hope, and love, shown to us through the Son of God, can be fulfilled not by human but by divine power, we turn with complete devotion to his Father and say to him:

**VERSE 29. Command, O God, thy strength.** O God the Father, since thou knowest that in us there is no strength for doing what thou commandest or counselest, command thy strength—that is, thy Son, who is thy strength by nature and the strength of thy people by grace. For from the time when this thy strength was made weak in the hands of thine enemies, the strength of thy friends increased: through him they became strong from weakness and mighty in battle, because they possessed faith. The ancients believed in thy strength that was to be weakened by the Incarnation; the new people believe in that same strength weakened by the Passion; in both there remains the one faith through which they conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, and obtained promises.

Human beings could not have performed these illustrious deeds of power by human capacities unless thou, O God, hadst commanded thy strength—whether, as said, thy Son, or the Holy Spirit—to do such things in them and through them as none can do without thy power. For thy Spirit too is thy power: he is called the power of the Most High, and is understood as the power proceeding from thy Son, “because power went out from him and healed them all” (Luke VI, 19). He also strengthened the apostles, the princes of Judah, the princes of Zebulun, and the princes of Naphtali; for they were weak and feeble until they were clothed with power from on high.

How much more weak are we, the frail troop of young women—or, [Col. 0212C] as the Hebrew has it, “maidens playing tambourines”—for playing the tambourine rightly, unless by thy power we are strengthened to do it as we ought, according to the examples of the aforesaid princes, first weak but afterwards strengthened in thy power. Therefore, so that we too, acknowledging our weakness, may will and be able to do what thou commandest, and so that the willing, ardent in affection, and the ability, shining forth in action, may be for thy glory and not our own: be not content merely to instruct us by a letter which thereby kills, but command thy strength—which enlightens every human being coming into this world—to enlighten us and at the same time assist us, so that what we know must be done through its illumination, we may also do through the aid of thy Spirit and his. Thus we speak, turned toward God the Father.

And because everyone who confesses the Father also confesses the Son, we turn also to the Son and say: **Confirm this, O God, which thou hast wrought in us.** For thou, the Word made flesh in our nature and dwelling among us, hast wrought many wonders in us, which we pray thee to confirm in us. For example, this was the beginning of thy signs, by which, to reveal thy glory, thou madest wine from water. Confirm in us this same work, which thou didst in us and for our sake, so that we too, corruptible and like water enclosed in mortal skins—that is, weak bodies, excessively prone to decay—may become wine to be preserved from corruption in new skins [Col. 0213A], so that “incorruption,” which does not permit decay or putrefaction, may keep us from decaying; for, as it is read elsewhere, incorruption “makes one near to God” (Wisdom VI, 20).

Likewise, thou gavest sight to the blind, cleansed lepers, healed a multitude of sick persons, cured those afflicted by unclean spirits, raised the dead, and—no less a deed than these—made the poor blessed by preaching the Gospel to them, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” and so forth (Matt. V, 3). This same eminent work of thy wonders, which thou didst in us by thy bodily presence, now that thou hast been exalted to heaven, confirm in us: enlightening our blindness in body and in soul; driving away leprosy of flesh, and still more of mind; strengthening us, prone to sin and weak in doing good, in the power of good will and action; driving far from us, by the grace of thy holy and gracious Spirit, [Col. 0213B] the unclean and malignant spirits, suggesters of unclean and malignant thoughts; and casting them, with their own swine given to them, into the abyss from which they may never again emerge to afflict us.

Raise us also, who are dead in sins and in the penalties of sins, together with thee who hast risen from the dead; and, now free from the death of souls and later to be freed also from the mortality and death of bodies, gladden us with Paschal joys, so that our joy may be full. Work and confirm in us that poverty of spirit, to which thou dost promise the kingdom of heaven, which thou hast wrought in thy disciples—the princes of Judah, the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali. [Col. 0213C] Work, I say, all these things, that we may make progress to the end. Confirm these same things, that we may never fail.

**Otherwise:** “Command, O God, thy strength,” that is, Christ—understand: that he be made known to humankind through the aforesaid princes. Or, “command thy strength,” that is, thy strong ones, to proclaim thee among the Gentiles. And lest their preaching be in vain, confirm what thou hast wrought in us by giving firm faith through hearing them. Or confirm, by thy grace ever cooperating and by confirming their word with the accompanying signs of miracles and good works, the doctrines of those princes, which must be proclaimed to the end of the age and to the ends of the earth; so that unbelievers may be converted through marvellous signs, and those already made believers may deserve to be strengthened ever more through good works.

**Otherwise:** Confirm this, O God, among the Gentiles, which thou hast wrought in us Jews, beginning

**VERSE 30. From thy temple which is in Jerusalem:** that is, may thy grace flow from the converted Jews or the apostles, through their ministry, from thy temple which is in Jerusalem, as the prophetic eyes saw water proceeding from the right side of the temple as far as the Dead Sea (Ezek. XLVII). Thy temple, whether the Lord’s body or the primitive Church incorporated into it, is now in the Jerusalem which is above. But we Gentiles, who are the Dead Sea, ask for the living water proceeding from this temple, that by it we may be made alive and confirmed in holy life.

[Col. 0214A] We do not ask this in vain. For when they have been confirmed by the water of the Holy Spirit proceeding from thy temple, all kings of the earth will offer thee gifts—that is, all who govern their earthliness well. Or, they are kings of the earth literally, or spiritual kings, whom the heavenly one distinguishes above the dove adorned with silvered wings and with the pallor of gold. All these kings will offer thee gifts nowhere but in thy temple, and from nowhere but from thy temple; for from Christ they receive what in Christ they offer to thee, God the Father. Outside his temple, outside his body and Church, thou wilt accept no sacrifice. Therefore the kings will offer thee gifts both acceptable in thy temple and received from thy temple.

For what good do we possess which we have not received from him and in him? Or what that is not good have we received from him and with him? Hear young Benjamin on this point: “He,” he says, “who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all—how shall he not also, with him, have given us all things?” Therefore, from thy gifts kings shall offer thee gifts of devoted service: in good works and conduct, in the sacrifice of the altar, in devout praises, in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, in holy discipline and sound teaching.

Because very many will raise a beastly roar against this, lest their voices prevail beyond measure,

**VERSE 31. Rebuke the beasts of the reed.** The beasts of the reed are called heretics because, like beasts, they sometimes harm through lack of understanding and sometimes, by perversely interpreting Holy Scripture, corrupt it; Scripture is signified by the reed. The ancients wrote with a reed, and therefore Holy Scripture is suitably understood by “reed.” Unbelievers mock it, such as those who put a reed in Christ’s hand as a sceptre of derision. Yet he received it in earnest, knowing that by it he would strike poisonous creatures and write the names of his own in the book of life, and the names of unbelievers on the earth, as it is written: “Those who depart from thee shall be written in the earth” (Jer. XVII, 13). Likewise: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous” (Ps. LXVIII, 29). Thus Christ rightly received the reed in order to write the names of the righteous in heaven, possessing in himself the authority of all Holy Scripture. [Col. 0214D] But since the beasts raise their clamour against it, it is rightly said to him—or to God his Father—now: “Rebuke the beasts of the reed,” namely, heretical corruptors of truth, so far as lies in them. For truth itself cannot be corrupted in itself.

By the name “reed” are also rightly signified all unstable persons, moved by every wind of doctrine. Among them heretics and all those who strive to teach novelty rather than truth are especially influential, because such hearers “will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, and shall be turned to fables” (II Tim. IV, 4). Therefore, whether I, David the prophet, foreseeing these things, or I, the Psalmist, presently observing these evils as they press upon us, joined with the other singers amid the maidens playing tambourines, say to thee, author and lover of the doctrine expressed in the Scripture of truth: Rebuke the beasts of the reed by sending the Spirit of truth, who, through the mouths not only of the aforesaid princes and kings who serve thee and offer gifts to thee, but also through the songs of thy tambourine-players, may convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment.

Rebuke, I say, the beasts of the reed, the depravers of the Scriptures of truth. And certainly it is necessary that thou rebuke these most evil beasts, for among them are fat bulls, armed with fat necks and dreadful horns of earthly power. They are especially terrifying to those who are easily deceived and resemble cows in this respect: they willingly admit these bulls, conceive pain from them, and give birth to iniquity. These same persons are both beasts and bulls: [Col. 0215B] beasts because of cruelty, bulls because of the stiff-neckedness of pride. Their herd is among the cows of the peoples—that is, among those who are deceived and can readily be seduced, whom the Apostle, because of their excessive weakness of understanding, calls “little women,” saying: “Of this sort are they who enter into houses and lead captive little women” (II Tim. III, 6). Those who lead captive the little women are the bulls; they themselves entice the cows.

Yet this will not be permitted by God without a beneficial purpose, but so that they may bring forth those who are tested by silver—that is, so that those tested in the sayings of God may become manifest. *Excludant* (“they may bring forth”) is used properly in the sense of “make stand out,” because goldsmiths too are called *exclusores*, those who bring out from a confused mass the form of each beautiful image previously hidden in that mass. So too the few expound meanings in the Scriptures, known to the understanding of few and stored under the seal of faith; and, as it were, by bringing them forth, they cause them to be brought to birth for the multitude, when heretics standing in opposition compel them to do so.

For while the Church enjoys peace, all holy persons skilled in letters strive to devote themselves only to prayer and good works. They keep watch reverently before the sanctuary of heavenly mysteries; they do not knock at its door and fear even to look into or enter its inner parts, unless the importunity of opponents compels them and the necessity of replying presses them—especially when questions are raised about the highest secret of the supreme Trinity or the deepest mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation. To such questions answers must be given not so much from human subtlety as from divine authority, by those tested by silver—that is, trained in the divine word.

**Otherwise:** The herd of bulls is among the cows of the peoples for this purpose: that from those same cows they may bring forth—that is, separate—those tested by silver, namely, those fit to teach the chaste words of God, which are “silver tried by fire, purified from the earth sevenfold” (Ps. XI, 7).

Some manuscripts have: “among the cows of buffaloes,” which does not differ in meaning, since buffaloes are wild, untamed oxen and are not accustomed to bear the yoke. And among a herd of such buffaloes the cows are more wanton than among domestic oxen. [Col. 0216A] Thus in crowds of undisciplined people wantonness reigns; it is removed from the people of the Lord and the sheep of his pasture by the rod of discipline, when the sweet yoke of God is imposed through the instruction of Holy Scripture not only on oxen or buffaloes, but also on cows—that is, on those who are especially wanton among the wanton.

For thus, by the Lord’s ordinance through Moses, oxen drew in the wilderness carts carrying gilded tablets, silver or bronze bases, columns, bars, curtains, and all the furnishings of the tabernacle. Thus too, in the book of Kings, cows are read to have drawn the ark of God. They are also said to have been nursing; with their calves shut up at home, they gave lowing from their inmost being, yet did not turn back their necks as they drew God’s ark, but went straight on the road to Beth-shemesh, which means “house of the sun” (I Kings VI, 12).

Do we not see these wonders now fulfilled in the holy Church, when not only men but women too, not only the strong but the weak as well, bear the Lord’s yoke in ecclesiastical service, journeying toward the land of promise and the house of the true Sun, where Christ is at the right hand of God the Father? These women, in what is more wonderful in them than in men, have compassion, as it were, on their calves shut up at home, but do not return to nurse them. Thus religious persons, even of the female sex, do not turn aside from the course of religion once begun because of affection for children or relatives; as they proceed along it, bearing the ark of the Lord—that is, Christ by faith in their hearts—they press on toward the eternal house of the eternal Sun. There they may clearly see Christ himself, the Sun of righteousness, whom now [Col. 0216C] they bear and do not see, and in that vision rejoice eternally, according to the promise of the Apostle Peter: “Though you do not now see him, you believe; but you shall exult with unspeakable joy, receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls” (I Pet. I, 8–9).

This is not promised to the cows of the peoples or buffaloes, nor to the herd of bulls, while such wanton cows persist in their stiff-neckedness or wantonness. For such bulls and cows are not accustomed to bear the yoke of holy obedience; indeed, what is worse, they strive, so far as they can, to attack and disturb those who proceed in orderly fashion beneath the yoke of discipline.

[Col. 0216D] But although they attack them, lest they perhaps overcome them as they wish, O Lord, who art strong and mighty in battle, scatter the nations that desire wars, because they strive not for correction but for contention. I, David, call heretics “nations,” either because of the kinds of sects, in which a succession of evil transmission, like a family genealogy, confirms error; or because they live as Gentiles do, going after dumb idols wherever they are led. For what are the doctrines of heretics—false indeed, but plausible—except certain images of true doctrine? They are led to such images either by diabolical persuasion or by a vain desire for their own glory. For a heretic is one who, especially from desire for his own glory and pre-eminence, either invents or follows new opinions. Whoever believes such people is deceived by a kind of image of truth.

But a heretic differs from a schismatic in this: a heretic attacks and attempts to corrupt the unity of Holy Scripture; whereas a schismatic labours to tear apart the unity of Catholic peace. We may therefore fittingly understand, as already said, heretics to be denoted by the beasts of the reed; and by the nations that desire wars, schismatics or any restless persons who delight in disputes, form sects, sow discord among brothers, disturb the harmony of unanimity, and strive to break the bond of peace and charity. They always desire wars because in settled peace they cannot practise their wickedness. A fitting retribution is certainly wished for them both at the beginning of the Psalm—that, when God arises, such enemies of his may be scattered—and here, where God is told: “Scatter the nations that desire wars.” For because they strive to scatter the unanimity of brotherly peace, it is rightly prayed that they themselves be scattered. When these evildoers are scattered, that is sometimes not an evil even for them; and this scattering of evils always works together for good to the good.

For just as it was beneficial for the Red Sea to be divided, so that a path might lie open for Israel fleeing the Egyptians and making for the promised land, so for the good not only their own concord but also the discord of the wicked is always good. This discord will sometimes be useful even to the wicked and become an occasion for correction; at other times it will be useless, as for those of whom it is said: “They were scattered, and were not pierced with compunction” (Ps. XXXIV, 16). [Col. 0217C] But here is prayed for a beneficial scattering of God’s enemies, followed by either their own conversion to good or at least that of others who outstrip them in goodness. This I, David, proclaim prophetically, saying:

**VERSE 33. Envoys shall come from Egypt; Ethiopia shall anticipate his hands unto God.** For when the unbelieving Jews were scattered and reckoned among the Gentiles, the natural branch having, as it were, been broken off, the wild olive was grafted in. From their offence came the salvation of the Gentiles: when they were blinded, the Gentiles were enlightened; and when the full number of the Gentiles has entered, the remnant of Israel shall be saved. This shall be fulfilled in the following order: “Envoys shall come from Egypt; Ethiopia shall hasten her hands unto God.”

As was foretold, so it was done. First envoys came into Egypt, namely, the apostles sent throughout the whole world. Then envoys came also from Egypt—that is, from the darkness of the Gentiles—such as Saint Dionysius and blessed Augustine. All these are understood as envoys, heralds of reconciliation. Hence the Apostle says: “We perform an embassy for Christ, and as though God were exhorting through us, we beseech you for Christ: be reconciled to God” (II Cor. V, 20). Envoys of this kind have come and will come until the whole fullness of the Gentiles enters.

They shall come not empty, but bringing gifts from Egypt to Christ, just as formerly gifts were brought to King Solomon by the envoys of many kingdoms, and especially from Egypt, from which he had taken Pharaoh’s daughter as his wife. She indeed, summoned and sought through the envoys of King Solomon himself, came to him; for envoys came both into Egypt and from Egypt, making fitting preparations for the arrival of this daughter of Pharaoh. But the queen of Ethiopia, coming from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, anticipated such envoys and invitations. This queen came of her own accord, unbidden, to Jerusalem with a great retinue, bringing limitless gold, precious gems, and many spices borne on camels.

Thus envoys have come and will come from Egypt to Christ, the true Solomon, the peaceful King, acting as envoys to him on behalf of Pharaoh’s invisible daughter—that is, the Gentile people whom he is to espouse. These envoys say to her: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline thy ear, and the King shall desire thy beauty” (Ps. XLIV, 11). But the Ethiopian queen—that is, that multitude of Gentiles which recognizes itself as more deeply blackened by sins—fearing the enormity of its crimes, does not await the one who calls, or the envoys of the caller, or his drawing hands, as she says, “Draw me after thee” (Song I, 3). Rather, by its spontaneous coming it shall anticipate his hands: like Zacchaeus, running ahead and climbing the sycamore tree—that is, the wood of the cross—in order, if possible, to see him before being seen in its blackness.

Thus, as her type, the sinful woman came to him unbidden, approaching from behind as though desiring to see and touch him while fearing to be seen: eager to see, yet fearful of being seen. Likewise, as her figure, like a bundle of first-fruits from the Gentiles, the Canaanite woman came freely and unbidden through the apostles or other envoys, driven by her misery. Hence she cried out: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is grievously afflicted by a demon” (Matt. XV, 22). Therefore, whoever you are whose daughter—that is, either your own soul or one entrusted to you—is afflicted by a demon through diverse passions of temptations or tribulations, run freely to the physician, anticipating his face in confession, so that this too may fittingly apply to you: “Ethiopia shall anticipate his hands unto God.”

How shall it anticipate them? By voluntary conversion and the renewing and whitening of its old, black life—yet itself secretly first anticipated by God in predestination or by the most merciful prompting of the Holy Spirit. Hence it is also said: “His mercy shall anticipate me” (Ps. LVIII, 11). But which hands of God shall Ethiopia anticipate? Certainly his conquering and avenging hands. Fearing and avoiding their blows, it comes freely to surrender, awaiting no envoys but sending an embassy and asking for terms of peace while he is still far away. Though he comes with twenty thousand—that is, to exact an account of our thoughts and actions—even if we meet him armed with ten thousand—that is, good deeds—we cannot resist, because our army is surpassed twofold by his.

What then remains, except that Ethiopia—that is, the soul blackened by sins—should anticipate his hands by forestalling his face with confession and fitting amendment for sins [Col. 0219A], lest it fall into the hands that strike and avenge? Those who begin their flight too late—namely, in winter or on the Sabbath—cannot escape these hands. To such persons it is said at the beginning of the Psalm: “Let those who hate him flee from before his face.” They shall indeed flee, but they shall not escape, because they cannot avoid the light which their bleary eyes hate. Then God’s enemies shall flee from his face, from which they would not wish to be seen and which they do not find sweet to behold; but they shall escape neither his gaze nor his hand. Ethiopia, knowing this beforehand now, while there is time to flee, anticipates his avenging hands by fleeing not from him, like enemies, but to him, so that from enemies they may become friends. Therefore it anticipates his hands unto God, cleaving to him by faith.

[Col. 0219B] **Otherwise:** “Ethiopia shall anticipate his hands,” namely, Ethiopia’s hands. This reference may be understood from the Greek, where the relative pronoun found here is feminine in gender, so that “it shall anticipate his hands” means the same as “it shall anticipate its hands,” as though it said: “its own hands.” In this phrase, hands are properly understood as good works, which arise from faith working through love, and sometimes from faith which justifies without works. The sense is: Ethiopia shall anticipate its hands unto God—that is, before it works, it shall believe God. Therefore its justification is attributed rather to faith inwardly inspired by grace than to external action, as is said to the sinful woman: “Thy faith has saved thee” (Luke VII, 50). When this faith goes before, good action follows according to one’s ability. Otherwise faith would be dead, if it were able to work but unwilling to do so. Thus, just as it is praiseworthy that faith should precede working hands, so it is wholly blameworthy if someone refuses to do what sound faith believes he ought to do.

**Otherwise:** The envoys from Egypt are the apostles from the Synagogue, which was in darkness. Ethiopia—that is, the Gentile world blackened in sins—shall anticipate the hands, that is, the works, of Egypt, that is, of the Synagogue, unto God, that is, for God’s honour. For the Gentile people first received and believed the word of faith.

There is yet another reading: “Ethiopia shall hasten to give hands unto God.” The comparison here is drawn from the defeated, who, laying down their arms, hasten to give their hands to the victors [Col. 0219D] lest they be killed. Where the text says, “Ethiopia shall anticipate his hands,” some make a pause here, and then, as though beginning anew, read: “Unto God, kingdoms of the earth, sing.” But we attach *Deo* (“unto God”) to the preceding words, as the truer copies do, and say: “Ethiopia shall anticipate his hands unto God,” that is, by turning itself to God.

On this passage Saint Pope Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0219D] Book XVIII of the *Morals*, ch. 52]:

> “The prophet David, seeing that the Lord would come to redeem Judaea, but that the Gentile world would believe first and Judaea would afterwards follow—as it is written, ‘Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved’—says: ‘Ethiopia shall anticipate his hands unto God’; that is, before Judaea should believe, the Gentile world, blackened by sins, would offer itself to the almighty Lord to be saved. Let us therefore give thanks to the only Son of the supreme Father, we who, gathered from the Gentile world and flooded with his light, have even preceded Judaea itself in faith, so that what is written might be fulfilled: ‘Ethiopia shall anticipate his hands unto God.’ We were black by the deserving of unbelief; but, receiving the brightness of grace, we have preceded even the Synagogue itself, through whose offspring we were called to the grace of God.”

It follows:

**VERSE 33. Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God.** As though it said: For benefits already bestowed, not only in the narrow Jewish kingdom but throughout the whole world, kingdoms of the earth—that is, every race of humankind, all rulers of all kingdoms, denoted by the two kingdoms of Egypt and Ethiopia, where the whole is signified by a part—sing to God with purity of mind, and make melody to the Lord through good works.

*Diapsalma, sixth section.* Sing to God, Christ, equally with God the Father, because he is

**VERSE 34. He who descends and ascends to the Father.** He ascends, namely, insofar as the assumed humanity has been advanced to the highest glory of the Godhead. For insofar as he is God, naturally equal to God the Father, there was nothing higher to which he could ascend. But he ascended above the heavens of heavens—that is, above all heavens—to the right hand of the Father. He calls the higher creatures “heavens of heavens”; above them ascended he who, with all creatures made subject to himself, sat at the Father’s right hand upon the highest throne of paternal majesty [Col. 0220C], that is, amid the better goods which the Word has always possessed with the Father and which humanity received without measure. Thus he ascended to the East—that is, to the brightness of the Word united to him.

I do not say “to the rising” or “to one who will rise,” because the divine generation of the Word has neither past nor future, but an eternal and unchanging present. Accordingly, the Son of God is called “the one rising from on high” (Luke I, 78): from the Father, while he who was to rise, and now has risen or been born, from a lowly mother. Formerly he was proclaimed as one to be born from the Virgin; now he is announced as born from her. But his generation from the Father lacks beginning and end; and therefore, in respect of that generation, he is not called one who has risen or will rise, but “the one rising.” And from where does he rise? From on high, namely the Father. Hence he is rightly called “Son of the Most High” (Luke I, 28), not by adoption but by generation.

**Otherwise:** He ascended to the east—that is, literally, toward the eastern region, in the sight of his disciples. Or, he ascended from the east—that is, from Jerusalem, situated in the east—where he locally ascended from the Mount of Olives; he ascended non-locally to the spiritual Mount of Olives when he caused his humanity to sit with his Father, the Father of mercies—signified by the Mount of Olives—upon the throne of majesty, in the fullness of the glory of the supreme Godhead. He had not yet ascended to this mountain in the faith of the woman to whom the angel said: “Woman, whom do you seek? The living among the dead?” (Luke XXIV, 5.) Jesus himself also said to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John XX, 17). As if he said: In your faith, by which you believe that I have been removed from the tomb, I have not yet ascended to my Father; I have not yet ascended to the Mount of Olives above the heavens of heavens.

Finally, the ascent of the assumed humanity above the heavens of heavens—that is, above the highest orders of angels—was from the Mount of Olives, because the Father of mercies gave it to him, as he himself says: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matt. XI, 27). From that Father was surely given to the man the name of God, which is above every name: namely, that the man should be called God, not as many gods are by adoption, but as the Son of the Most High by generation. For it was also given to the man that he should be the Son of the Most High; and this, without doubt, was for him to ascend invisibly and non-locally to the Mount of Olives. From him it was also given that he should locally ascend from the Mount of Olives above the heavens of heavens to the east.

That power in his human nature is divine is clear from this: behold, he shall give his voice, a voice of power. Behold, I say, because it will be evident at the Second Coming. I, David, see as if present that he who, like a lamb before its shearer, was silent without uttering a sound, shall at the last judgment give a voice not of weakness but of power—a voice by which the dead shall be raised, the ungodly judged, and the good transformed. [Col. 0221C] Even at his first coming he made his voice to be a voice of power. For when he said in his humanity, “Lazarus, come forth” (John XI, 43), divine power worked in the human voice. Likewise, in his other human sayings the splendour of divine power shone forth: when he said to the leper, “Be cleansed,” he was cleansed; when he said to the blind man, “Look,” he immediately saw; when he said to the dead man, “Young man, I say to thee, arise,” he arose. Even to this day he gives his voice a voice of power, working through his word in the offices of his ministers works of such power that thanksgiving and glory are always due to him for them. Therefore:

[Col. 0222A] **VERSE 35. Give glory to God**, to Christ, in his voice of power—both working now in the Church and at the end judging all things and separating the good from among the wicked. Then, when the ungodly have been cast into hell, his magnificence shall be manifest over Israel—that is, over the good worthy of the vision of God—because those whom he called and justified he shall then magnify. And his power shall be in the clouds, because above the other elect those shall then shine in the glory of power who, like clouds flying, carried voluntary rain far and wide, flashing with miracles and, by prayers and merits, helping and sheltering their inferiors. But lest anyone take some other meaning from the name “clouds,” I shall speak more plainly:

**VERSE 36.** God is wonderful in his saints: God, I say, is the God of Israel—that is, especially of those who will then be Israel, namely pure in heart, and therefore will see God as he is. And indeed, in the clouds and in the foremost saints he will bestow a surpassing magnificence. Yet he will also give strength in the resurrection to his humble people, and to those saints who faithfully obey it and preserve the bond of charity: so that what was sown in weakness may rise in power. He will further give that people, hitherto weak in itself, the strength of impassibility which he himself possesses in the body of his glory, to which the body of our lowliness will be conformed through the grace of his mercy. Therefore blessed is God in these his gifts, and holy in all his works. Or again: from that time God will be seen as blessed in his glory; and, wonderful in the saints, he will be wonderfully glorified by them, as each and all say eternally: Blessed be God.

Glory to the Father, the Lord, who will give great power to those who proclaim the Gospel. Glory to the Son, namely to the Word itself which is proclaimed. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is the power of both, given as gifts to human beings. Or: Glory to the Father, lover of the Beloved; glory to the Son, beloved of his loving Father; glory to the Holy Spirit, the love of both. Glory to the one and triune God from eternity and unto eternity, in heaven above and on earth below, so that heaven and earth may always everywhere be filled with his glory, while this praise resounds: Blessed be God.

## PSALM LXVIII

[Col. 0221]

[Col. 0221D] “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even unto my soul.” That combatant who, in the first fifty, was strengthened through faith, now in this second fifty—as has often been said—fights in the hope of victory. In this psalm he is clearly instructed how, battling lawfully, he may fight not as one beating the air, but striking the enemy himself with continual prayers as with most keen darts. For Christ himself, our Head, is introduced here as the chief leader of the battle, as though at the forefront of the camp, praying thus for his own outward tribulations in the manner in which he desires each of his own to pray for inward temptations: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even unto my soul. I am fixed in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance. I have come into the depth of the sea, and the tempest has overwhelmed me.” For by praying these words and the rest, he indicates that he gives his own, endangered amid vices, an example of prayer, when he says: “Let the poor see and rejoice; seek God, and your soul shall live. For the Lord has heard the poor, and has not despised his prisoners” [Ps. 68:33–34]. Accordingly this psalm fittingly bears the title:

**(VERSE 1.) UNTO THE END, FOR THOSE WHO SHALL BE CHANGED: A PSALM OF DAVID.**

Its sense is this: this psalm treats of those who are to be changed into conformity with Christ, so that they may go unto the end—that is, unto complete perfection. Although “man born of a woman, living for a short time, who comes forth like a flower and is crushed, and flees like a shadow and never remains in the same state” [Job 14:1–2], undergoes varied and manifold changes, there are nevertheless two principal changes.

The first is that by which, when Adam sinned, human nature, corrupted in him through sin, was changed from the good state in which it was created into a worse state by a miserable change, because in him all sinned and in him also died. But, just as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ. The other change is that by which believers are changed from evil to good and advance from good to better unto the end. For this reason this psalm is entitled, “For those who shall be changed unto the end”; and that end is Christ, “the end unto righteousness for everyone that believes” [Rom. 10:4]—the end of consummation, an end beyond which nothing is to be sought. For he himself, the end and final cause of combatants, will crown the victorious with infinite glory when, their contest ended, he changes them unto the end.

The beginning of this change is when, in the present mortal condition, souls are changed from vices to virtues. Its end will be then, when what the Apostle says is fulfilled: [Col. 0223C] “For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” [1 Cor. 15:52]. This change wrought by the right hand of the Most High does not belong to the goats set at the left hand, but to those who can say with the Apostle: “But our commonwealth is in heaven, whence also we await the Lord Jesus Christ, who will refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” [Phil. 3:20–21].

The efficient cause of this change is Christ’s own passion. Through it he both passed himself and made us pass from this world to the Father, from fear to security, from death to life, from corruption to incorruption, from earth to heaven—from which he himself descended in order to raise those who had fallen. This passing-over was called in Hebrew *Pascha* [Passover], and was accomplished in the Passion, which in Greek is *πάσχειν* (*paschein*, “to suffer”). Therefore this psalm is assigned to David—that is, to Christ—for those who will thus be changed unto Christ the end. It is one of four psalms that treat more fully of the Passion and Resurrection. The first is: “My God, my God, look upon me”; the second: “Judge, O Lord, those who wrong me”; the third: “Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise my supplication”; the fourth is this one now before us, in which, as in the others treating of the Passion, a sorrowful beginning and a joyful end are found.

First, Christ, crying out over his own tribulation and that of his people, prays to be saved, recounting that he suffers many things while paying what he did not seize and bearing undeserved penalties. Second, he prays that those for whom he suffers may not be disappointed in their hope, adding how great are the things he bears and with what patience he bears them, at: “O God, thou knowest my foolishness.” Third, he asks that he and his people may be delivered from the mire of the world. Again, he recalls what he suffers at: “But as for me, my prayer is unto thee, O Lord.” Fourth, he prophesies what is to come upon his enemies at: “Let their table before them become a snare.” Fifth, he sets forth the joyful end of the Passion and exhorts the faithful to praise; this is his purpose at: “I am poor and sorrowful; thy salvation, O God, has upheld me.” In this psalm the whole Christ speaks, now in his own voice and now in the voice of his members, crying to God his Father:

[Col. 0224B] **VERSE 2. “Save me, O God.”** Behold, I, Christ, am the grain of mustard seed: small in the form of a servant, cast into the garden and liable to be trodden underfoot. I, whom the unbelieving Jews despise because I am to become a great herb—indeed, a most lofty tree—cry out among those who afflict and trample me: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even unto my soul.” “The many waters are many peoples” [Rev. 17:15], because, as wave follows wave, one generation passes and another arrives. But this evil and adulterous generation, this wicked and perverse generation of the Jews, ever surging with the motions of avarice, pride, envy, and the other fluctuating vices, is rightly compared to turbid and bitter waters. They have entered even unto my soul, because they prevailed [Col. 0224C] not only to seize, bind, and strike me, but even to take away my soul.

Although I have said, “No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down and take it up again” [John 10:17–18], nevertheless, in order to express the malice of the Jewish temptation by which they cried, “He is guilty of death” [Matt. 26:66], and again, “We have a law, and according to our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” [John 19:7], I rightly say that the waters entered even unto my soul in order to take it away. For what I suffered by my own will they, in their malice, judged bitter and grievous to me—like the gall and vinegar which they offered me in my Passion. My disciples later tasted this also when the same persons gave it to them; and all who desire to live piously will have to taste it, as evils assail them, until the end of the age.

Therefore, transforming into myself my little ones who will be endangered in turbid waters, I cry also for their salvation. The voice of my blood crying from the earth requires this before the Father and the whole heavenly court: that those for whom I laid down my soul may not be allowed to be so overwhelmed or choked in the waters of temptations or tribulations as were overwhelmed and choked those who utterly failed in such waters by loving their souls too much in this world. “For he who loves his soul in this world shall lose it.” Conversely, “he who hates his soul in this world keeps it unto eternal life” [John 12:25].

For the sake of preserving such souls unto eternal life, I, Christ, endured—not by necessity but by voluntary will—the waters entering even unto my soul: not so that it might be torn from me against my will, as the souls of the thieves were torn away when their legs were broken, but so that it might be voluntarily laid down and commended into the hands of the Father. In short, so that I, the immortal God, might be able to die.

**VERSE 3.** “I am fixed in the mire of the deep”: that is, I assumed a human being formed from mire. Certainly, if I had assumed such a human being as I had created him, I would have been fixed in mire, but not in the mire of the deep. But now, because I, the immortal God, assumed mortal man so that I might taste death for mortals, I rightly say that I am fixed [Col. 0225B] in the mire of the deep, “and there is no substance”: both because, having become mortal, I came even unto death, which is not a substance; and because the profound iniquity of the Jews, which is not a substance, prevailed against me.

For just as nakedness in a body and baldness on a head are not some substance but a deprivation of substance, so sin in the soul, and the punishment of sin—death in the body—are not substances, but, as it were, a certain annihilation of substance. Certainly I, Christ, was not annihilated by sin, because I had neither original nor actual sin; and therefore my substance remained intact, adorned with every beauty of virtue. The younger son did not preserve his substance in this way when, having gone into a far country, he dissipated it by living luxuriously with prostitutes.

Yet because many of such people will be changed by confession and repentance, I transform their complaints into myself and say: “I am fixed in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance”—that is, there is no power of the flesh to escape death, which is not a substance but the destruction of substance.

Or, because *substance* is commonly understood as riches, “there is no substance for me,” because I am needy and poor, impoverished to such an extent that, stripped even of my garment and hanging naked upon the cross, I atoned for the nakedness of the man who, going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers; they also stripped him, inflicted wounds on him, and departed, leaving him half-dead. Thus it follows shortly afterward: “I am poor and sorrowful,” because I, the Samaritan, have taken upon myself the sufferings of that wounded and despoiled man. I became his neighbour by taking upon myself his nature, not his fault: his nature, which truly is substance; not his fault, which is not substance. Yet because I pay its penalty with many scourges as though I myself had sinned, I say in the voice of my people that “I am fixed in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance.”

For as long as one of my least ones is fixed in the mire of the deep through iniquity, which is not substance, I declare myself fixed in the mire of the deep—that is, in mire which has no firm bottom on which the foot may stand, because of sin, which is not substance but nothing.

The Hebrew truth agrees with this sense, reading: “I am fixed in the mire of the deep, and I cannot stand,” which is the same as saying: “I cannot stand in the deep, which has no bottom,” because sin itself is not something solid but nothing. It is not a substance sustaining any form that clothes itself; nor is it form, but deformity; it is not something, but nothing; it is not clothing, but nakedness. Hence Adam knew himself naked after committing sin. And would that what he learned through the experience of misery he had recognized again through the satisfaction of repentance! But he came to nothing, like water running down from the height of righteousness into the depth of iniquity, which is not substance because it was not made by God through the Word.

For all things that are something were made through him, and without him was made nothing. Through him were made all creatures, all substances, all forms, and everything composed of substances and forms; and these praise the Lord as their maker. Not that all things possess understanding to praise, but because all things, when rightly contemplated and considered, produce praise in rational spirits, so that every spirit praises the Lord, Creator of all, when it considers the beauty of creation. Their essence, order, and usefulness commend the triune God: from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things.

Among all those things praising God, iniquity has no place, because it is not a substance created through the Word, nor a form of substance, but deformity—just as blindness in an eye is not its form but deformity. It was not created through the Word; human perversity made it. Hence it does not praise [Col. 0226C] God, whom all created things praise—not only heavenly things, but earthly things also, down to the lowest creeping creatures. Therefore man, mute in the praises of God and fallen into iniquity, is fixed in the mire of the deep, “and there is no substance,” especially when he consents to iniquity and sin reigns in him.

But in order that this kingdom might cease, and righteousness reign in those who will be changed, while they do not consent to the iniquity by which they feel themselves tempted, I, Christ, “have come into the depth of the sea, and the tempest has overwhelmed me.” I came voluntarily into the depth of the sea—that is, into the profundity of this age, where my people were suffering shipwreck—and the tempest of Jewish persecution overwhelmed me. I came, the Angel of great counsel, descending into the water, namely visiting the Jewish nation when I took flesh from their lineage. But when I descended, the water was stirred, and there arose a great disturbance of those who surged, raged, raised storms, and cried: “Crucify, crucify him” [John 19:6]. Such a tempest overwhelmed me because, amid the waves of such sedition, I suffered death and, like another Jonah, was swallowed by the whale for three days and three nights.

Someone may say: Why, Lord, did you not tell the Jews raging against you that you were the Messiah promised to them and sent to save them? Perhaps—indeed certainly—if they had recognized you, they would never have crucified you, the Lord of glory. To this I, Christ, reply:

**VERSE 3.** “I laboured crying out; my throat became hoarse.” I laboured crying out and preaching that I, the Son of God and Son of Man, had come to seek and save that which had perished, attesting by divine works that I was the Son of God the Father. Thus I said: “If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, even though you do not wish to believe me, believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I in the Father” [John 10:37–38]. In crying out thus I laboured, as elsewhere I say: “I laboured in enduring” [Isa. 1:14].

But what does the Almighty mean by saying, “I laboured,” he to whom nothing is hard or impossible? It is this which blessed Gregory says:

> [Note: [Col. 0227D] Homily 8 on Ezekiel.]

The Prophet speaks, in the person of the Redeemer, concerning those who still live perversely: the Lord does not labour by enduring, for no weariness can touch the power of his divinity; but, speaking in the language of his humanity, he calls his own patience toward us “labour.”

Again, concerning his saying, “My throat became hoarse,” we do not read that this literally happened. Yet, as regards those by whom he was neither heard nor understood, he spoke hoarsely. Thus they said: “Who can hear him?” [John 6:61]. Again: “He has a demon and is mad; why do you listen to him?” [John 10:20]. Nor are they excusable for saying such things, because they did not lack the capacity to hear or understand him, but the will, according to the saying: “He was unwilling to understand, that he might do good” [Ps. 35:4].

Among such hearers, therefore, “my throat became hoarse”; or, as the Hebrew reads, “my throat was exasperated,” because I, Christ, laboured in vain in preaching to evil hearers who hated me so greatly that they blinded me, the true Samson, as though shorn and made bald in the place of Calvary—or rather extinguished all my bodily senses—so that all my limbs, stretched out upon the cross, were deprived of their functions, while neither the ears had power to hear nor the eyes power to see in the dead and lifeless body.

But, putting the part for the whole, I complain concerning the eyes alone and say: “My eyes have failed while I hope in my God”—that is, while I await divine mercy like another weak human being and do not exercise power. What a marvellous sight: that sight should fail by which Jesus, seeing the crowds, went up the mountain to give the precepts of the New Testament; by which, seeing Peter [Col. 0227D] and Andrew, he called them; by which, seeing a man sitting at the tax-office, he called him and made him an evangelist; by which, seeing the city, he wept over it; by which, seeing the sisters weeping, he himself wept; by which, seeing the tables of the money-changers in the Temple, he was moved with great zeal against unjust commerce; by which, seeing the crowds, he had compassion upon them because they were distressed like sheep without a shepherd; by which, looking up, he saw Zacchaeus; by which also, when he had lifted up his eyes, he saw a great multitude coming to him; and by which at last, seeing his mother and the disciple beside the cross, he was moved with filial devotion toward his mother and brotherly devotion toward the disciple, saying to his mother, “Behold thy son,” and to the disciple, “Behold thy mother.”

For Christ’s bodily sight radiated something divine beyond all speech, and therefore exercised now the affection of justice, now that of mercy. Among these acts, this especially delights: that, seeing the disciple, Jesus said to him, “Behold thy mother.” For this sight reaches from end to end mightily and disposes all things sweetly, so that everyone who becomes Christ’s disciple by hearing and keeping the word of God becomes his brother, sister, and mother; and consequently holy Mary becomes mother also to such a brother. Standing beside the cross in great travail at the death of her only-begotten Son, she gave birth to many children, whom that same Only-Begotten adopted as brothers; and, showing each of them to his mother, he says to her: “Behold thy son.”

[Col. 0228B] Would that you too, Lord Jesus, looking upon me with kindly eyes, might say concerning me to your mother, the mother of mercy: “Woman, behold thy son.” For anyone upon whom you do not look with such eyes is neither your brother nor the son of your mother. With these eyes you looked upon Simon when you said to him: “You are the son of Joanna; you shall be called Cephas” [John 1:42; Vulgate: Jona]. With these eyes you looked upon the sinful woman, to whom you said: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.” By continual prayers we desire that you turn these your eyes toward us and never turn them away from us—for example, when we say: “O Lord, look upon thy servants and upon thy works”; again, “Look, O Lord, from thy sanctuary”; again, “See, O Lord, our affliction”; again, “Look, O Lord, from thy holy seat”; and other such words, by which, O Lord, we invoke upon ourselves the kindly gaze of your eyes.

Is it not therefore marvellous and at the same time pitiable that your bodily eyes, radiant with divine mercy, should have failed even for a time? Like open windows, they admitted into this world, hitherto dark, the light of divine mercy. The sun of this world could not endure to see the failing of these lights in the head of Christ, the Sun of righteousness; when they failed, it too failed, so that darkness came over the land from the sixth hour to the ninth. At that hour Christ’s death, being completed, brought light even into infernal darkness. At the same time, by the resurrection hastened on the third day, he restored the spiritual eyes—that is, the apostles—which had failed even while he was dying, illuminating them with the bright light of faith. They had failed so utterly that all were offended in him, abandoned him, fled, and scarcely retained within themselves small remnants of faith and hope.

Hence comes the saying: “But we hoped that he would redeem Israel” [Luke 24:21]. It should indeed be noted that, when they say *we hoped*, using the imperfect tense of a past verb, they intimate that their hope had not wholly failed, because an action denoted by such a verb is understood not to be entirely past. Therefore I, Christ, say: “My eyes have failed,” namely my disciples, “while I hope in my God”—that is, while they hope in my God. For this reason their outward eyes also were kept from recognizing me, though they still hoped and said, “But we hoped,” as though saying: We had a hope which we have not completely laid aside. Such eyes of mine, loving me, failed for a time and were reduced to a very small number. On the other hand:

**VERSE 5.** “They who hate me without cause are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.” Perhaps it seems ambiguous whom I earlier called waters, mire, and the depth of the sea. Therefore I say more clearly: “They who hate me without cause.” For they themselves are the turbid water, the mire of the deep, and the depth of the sea. In short, by hating me they were like a bitter sea. But because they did this gratuitously and without any cause, they may be called the depth of the sea, because their high and profound wickedness, stirred by the north wind, was raised up against me when those who hated me without cause were multiplied beyond the hairs of my head. They were innumerable in number and in a certain way comparable to hairs in insensibility.

For they neither grieved nor felt when, by crucifying me in the place of Calvary, they were deservedly shorn away from me. I am the Head worthy of better hairs, of which my Bride says in the Song of Songs: “His locks are like branches of palm trees, black as a raven” [Song 5:11]. These are my elect, clinging to me their Head: first the apostles, and after them all who would believe through them and cleave to me. Though they are many, those who hate me without cause are multiplied beyond their number. Moreover, in order that the latter may be multiplied still more, some are added from the number of my disciples, such as Judas—falsely a disciple but truly a devil—whom many will imitate in a similar apostasy.

And if they were merely many and weak, the evil would somehow be bearable. But now they are both multiplied beyond the hairs of my head, and strengthened—these my enemies who persecuted me unjustly, that is, by hating me without cause. This is the glory of the Passion in me and in my martyrs: it is not to be assessed by the bitterness of the punishment but by the goodness of the cause, because punishment does not make martyrdom praiseworthy, but its cause does—especially when someone suffers innocently, as I did, “paying what I did not seize.”

The devil seized in heaven, arrogating to himself what was not his when he boasted that he was like the Most High. For this reason he rightly paid the penalty, cast down from on high and bound with the cords of hell; and he is yet to be bound still more in hell at the coming of the final judgment. Adam also seized in paradise when, at the devil’s persuasion—“You shall be as gods”—he desired likeness to God by yielding to the deceived woman. Thus he and all his posterity rightly paid the penalty, expelled from paradise and exposed to many miseries in the exile of this world.

But I did not consider it robbery to be equal with God. For although I considered myself equal with God, this neither was nor is robbery, but nature; because, being the natural Son of God, equally with God the Father I too am the most high God. Yet, when my enemies said, “Let him be crucified, because he made himself the Son of God” [John 19:7], I was then paying what I had not seized. For I was punished for this very reason, that I had called myself the Son of God—as though I had borne false witness, and as though I had usurped by robbery the name of the Son of God, falsely arrogating to myself likeness or equality with God.

Certainly the devil and Adam had committed this robbery, but I had not. For in the divine nature, together with God the Father, I the Son of God eternally possess one divinity, equal glory, and coeternal majesty; and in the human nature in which I emptied myself, I received in grace the whole glory which I have always possessed in the divine nature. I received it, I did not seize it: I received it from God the Father giving it; I did not seize it against the Father’s will. Hence I said: “All things have been given over to me by the Father” [Matt. 11:27]; again: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” [Matt. 28:18].

For God did not give the Spirit by measure to me, the man conceived of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. She was at once virgin and bride: virgin, namely, knowing no man; but bride, made fruitful by the love of my Father and thus brought into the storehouses of God the Father, just as lawful brides are brought into their husbands’ possessions by matrimonial right. Therefore I, born from such a bride as lawful heir, did not consider it robbery that I called myself the Son of God. For the angel, testifying to this very thing, said to the virgin that she would bear me, the Son: “That holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God” [Luke 1:35].

And because I myself confessed this—that I was the Son of God—I was judged foolish and paid penalties as though a false witness, as though a thief and usurper of a name foreign to me; while in the eyes of the wise of this world I appeared a foolish and senseless man, and in the eyes of those who considered themselves righteous and despised others I was judged a sinful man. For they said to Pilate: “If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have delivered him to thee” [John 18:30]. Thus unjust judges judged me foolish and sinful. But:

**VERSE 6. “O God, thou knowest my foolishness, and my offences are not hidden from thee.” — Second part.**

“O God, thou knowest my foolishness,” namely because, for the sake of foolish people who are to be changed unto wisdom, I took upon myself the cause of the foolish; “and my offences,” that is, those of my people, which I assumed, not committed—these thou knowest. In this also thou knowest my foolishness: through the Spirit of knowledge thou makest known that my foolishness is wiser than men. Hence the Apostle, instructed by this knowledge, says: “We preach Christ crucified, indeed a stumbling-block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God; because the weakness of God is stronger than men, and the foolishness of God is wiser than men” [1 Cor. 1:23–25].

Thus, Father, not only dost thou know, but thou makest others know my foolishness: foolish in the eyes of fools, yet, in thine eyes and in the eyes of thine own, to be preferred above all the wisdom of this world. For by it that ancient serpent, wiser than all the animals of the earth, was deceived. Therefore, my Father, thou knowest—that is, approvest and ordainest—my foolishness, namely the death of the cross. Although it appears to foolish people a great folly, because, since I was proclaimed almighty, it seemed unfitting that I should redeem the human race with so great labour when I could have done so by a word alone, yet thou knowest and ordainest this as a work of great wisdom.

Further, “my offences are not hidden from thee.” Offences were indeed alleged against me by the Jews, who said: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” [John 9:16]. For on the Sabbath I anointed and healed the eyes of the man born blind; likewise, after healing a paralytic on the Sabbath, I commanded him to take up and carry his bed and go home; and on the Sabbath I said to another man with a withered hand: “Stretch out thy hand” [Mark 3:5]. Again, on the Sabbath I raised up and healed the bent woman, and performed other works on the Sabbath which were thought to be forbidden by the law. Not knowing that I was Lord even of the Sabbath, they reproved such good works as the greatest offences.

But these offences of mine are not hidden from thee, Father. After the first Adam committed the offence of transgression, he hid himself from thy face among the trees of paradise because he was ashamed for thee to see the ugliness of his sin. Therefore he made himself a girdle of fig leaves in some fashion to cover his shame. But I, the second Adam, do not flee from thy presence because of my offences, Father, since those offences are not hidden from thee—that is, they are altogether worthy of thy gaze and pleasing to thee, as being full of every beauty.

I too sometimes tried to demonstrate this by reason to my rivals who condemned such offences. For example, I said: “Many good works have I done among you; for which of them do you wish to stone me?” [John 10:32]. Again: “If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because I made the whole man sound on the Sabbath?” [John 7:23]. But they passed these things by with deaf ears and judged me a transgressor of the law because of the offences just mentioned and the like.
