Yet, since these are honourable and good works, they are not hidden, nor ought they to be hidden, from thee, Father; rather, they should be offered to thy sight and to that of the entire heavenly court as acceptable sacrifices.

By these may my offences—that is, those of my people—be abolished. These are truly my offences, not committed by me, but imputed by thee, Father, to me who take the place of all my people and die for them; as one of my people confesses, saying: “Behold, we saw him without form or beauty, and the Lord placed upon him the iniquities of us all; the chastisement of our peace was upon him” [Isa. 53:2 ff.]. A wonderful thing: the innocent Son is chastised and disciplined for the sins of servants, yet not unwillingly, since he himself voluntarily took up the cause of the servants and was offered to discipline for them, because he willed it and the Lord himself bore the sins of his servants. What could be more honourable or more beautiful than this mercy?

[Col. 0232A] Therefore I, the second Adam, do not hide myself or my offences as the first did. Rather, having suffered exalted upon the cross outside the gate for my beloved ones, I desire that my offences be visible before thee, O God, and before the holy angels and every creature in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. As regards my own person, they are marked by no ugliness; as regards my people who believe in me, they have been blotted out by my blood.

For if the children of Israel could be cleansed and freed from Egypt by the blood of the Paschal lamb, how much more do I, the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, purify by my blood those whom I know must be fortified by the same blood placed upon the lintels and both doorposts of their houses. My faithful ones, the true Hebrews who are to pass out of this world, do not place my blood upon one doorpost only, merely partaking orally of the sacrament. Rather, what they receive with their mouth, as though anointing one doorpost, they also place upon the doorpost of the heart, when with devout mind they resolve to be conformed to my Passion by denying themselves, taking up their cross, and following me. Thus, having become partners in the Passion, they may also be found partners in the Resurrection and consolation.

This, indeed, I signified to my disciples by giving them the remnants of fish and honeycomb after my Resurrection: namely, that with most certain hope they might await healing in my kingdom through the honey of eternal sweetness, and might also be nourished in their present pilgrimage by certain remnants of delights—only those, that is, who are conformed to me suffering and to my roasted fish, so as to crucify their flesh with its vices and desires. They also await this honey-flowing sweetness who are conformed to me roasted and suffering in this respect: that they endure adversities for righteousness’ sake.

Lest the expectation of these people be disappointed in its hope, I pray for them—not for the world, because the world has not known thee, righteous Father, but these have known thee as Father, because they have received me, thy Son. For whoever has the Son has the Father, just as whoever denies the Son denies the Father. Therefore I pray that, because they have received me:

**VERSE 7. “Let not those who wait for thee be ashamed in me, O Lord, Lord of hosts.”** Let not those who wait for thee, O Lord of hosts, in me and through me—working works of power before my death, and to complete those same works of power by the glory of my Resurrection and Ascension—be ashamed in me. This would happen if those who expected great works of power in me, and desired to see what many kings and prophets desired to see but did not see because they did not have me present in the flesh, should not see me even though they have me present.

For if people said to them, “Where is your God? Where is he who said to you: ‘You believe in God; believe also in me’” [John 14:1], they would rightly be ashamed if they could not demonstrate by works of power that I am the true God. But I pray thee, O Lord of hosts: through me, raised from death and exalted to heaven, perform splendid works of power, so that, when they are manifested in the world, those who wait for thee, O Lord of hosts, may not be ashamed in me, expecting thee according to my promises to work in them.

For I said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: if you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you” [John 16:23]. Again: “He who believes in me shall do the works that I do; and he shall do greater works than these, because I go to the Father. And whatever you ask the Father in my name, this I will do” [John 14:12–13].

Unbelieving in promises of this kind from me, they do not await you, O Lord of powers, to perform or grant any powers in my name. But those who believe in me and will believe until the end of the age await you, Father, Lord of powers, always to work through me such great powers that enemies may never have leisure to exult, nor to insult my friends, as though they were [Col. 0233B] without God in this world; since you, Lord of powers, are in me and I in them, performing through me in them works of power, by which they may be joined to the angelic powers, of whom you are Lord, O Lord of powers. This I promised to my own before my death; this I ask in my death with a loud cry: that they who, trusting my promises, await you as Lord of all universally, and especially as Lord of powers, may be glorified by your so working in them works of power that they may not be ashamed, inwardly bereft of virtues and exposed to vices, having lost the hidden treasure in the field of a good conscience.

I ask also that they may not be confounded outwardly by enemies insulting and reproaching them beyond measure, [Col. 0233C] because, as though worshippers of a crucified and dead God, they themselves have become like dead men, lying and stinking before his tomb, having lost the fragrance of a good reputation. Rather, let the enemies, unwilling that I should live, terrified by the sight of angels and made like dead men—indeed, truly dead in their souls—so lie and stink that others may be corrected by their example, and that even some of them, compelled by their own stench, may be converted. But let my friends, who with the blessed women seek you, O Lord of powers, carrying to my tomb spices of holy and precious conduct, not be confounded concerning me; for such men seek you, God of Israel, God of all in general, God of those who see God in particular: that is, those who see me crucified do not doubt that they see the living God—God of Israel, you the Father in me the Son, and [Col. 0233D] me the Son in you my Father, and in us both the Spirit belonging to us both. Therefore let such friends of mine not be confounded by the taunts of the wicked over me as I die, but let them be glorified by good conduct, like fragrant spices; and let my angels say to them: “Do not be afraid.” Why? “For you seek Jesus” (Matt. 28:5), who is eternal salvation to those who seek him purely.

I, Christ, ask all these things, rightly to be heard both because of my dignity—for I am the great priest and in my days pleased God the Father, who also said of me: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17)—and also because of my many and great merits, by which I have merited great glory not only for myself, who have always been worthy of glory, but for my servants and friends, who by [Col. 0234A] my merit are to be delivered from every reproach. For, briefly gathering into one all that I endured for their deliverance, I desire the court of the heavenly and earthly Church now to be attentive in your presence, while I recount my merit and request the reward. I speak of a merit not small:

**VERSE 8.** “For for your sake I have endured reproach; shame has covered my face,” and so forth, as far as: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”

With these words concerning the Lord’s Passion, almost the whole bundle of myrrh has, as it were, been gathered together—the bundle which must always rest between the breasts of the bride, lest she ever forget what her bridegroom suffered for her. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear the bridegroom recounting his sufferings.

“Let not those who seek you,” he says, “be confounded concerning me, [Col. 0234B] O God of Israel: for I, delivered into the hands of enemies for them, endured reproach,” so that men said to me: “Behold, a gluttonous man and a drinker of wine, the carpenter’s son, a friend of publicans; he has a demon, and by Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Matt. 11:19). Thus I, Christ, endured manifold reproach. It is thereby precious, worthy of praise and of great reward, because I endured this not for my own faults but for your sake, God the Father, having become obedient to you in proclaiming the truth, to bear witness to which I came into the world by your command, as I said to Pilate: “For this I was born, that I should bear witness to the truth” (John 18:37).

Thus, bearing witness to truth—calling good good and evil evil, light light and darkness darkness—by your command and in obedience to you, Father, I endured reproach for your sake from liars who called good evil and evil good, and who resisted me, the Truth, so fiercely that shame covered my face, when they spoke against me to my face and when I did not turn my face away from those who rebuked and spat upon me.

[Col. 0234C] Nor indeed is it surprising that shame covered my face, because human nature is so constituted that amid reproaches, even false ones, it is suffused with blushes, and the face of a good person is, as it were, covered. This too is a special beauty of that beloved of mine, to whom I, her bridegroom, say: “Your cheek is like a fragment of pomegranate, apart from that which lies hidden within” (Song 4:3). For it is not a great beauty for cheeks to be suffused with blushes amid reproaches when consciousness of sin lies within the heart. But when, apart from that which lies hidden within, a blush suffuses the translucent skin of the face so completely that such shame covers the face, it is a praiseworthy beauty and a sign of a good and tender conscience, opposed to that woman of whom it is said: “You have acquired the brow of a harlot; you do not know how to blush” (Jer. 3:3).

The latter, by contrast, though she has within herself cause rightly to blush, hardened in evil does not know how to blush. My bride, however, though free of the offense of conscience which lies hidden within, nonetheless amid reproaches, even false ones, has cheeks like a fragment of pomegranate. This kind of fruit, when whole, smells sweet and is red; but when broken it delights far more both by the fragrance of its sweet odor and by the beauty of its redness. Thus surely my beloved, made like me her beloved, having nothing within that deserves shame because of the single eye of her heart, which makes the whole body bright, is lovely in a blooming face like the rind of a pomegranate when no reproaches tear at her. But amid revilers she resembles a fragment of that same fruit, redder and more sweetly scented, yet apart from that which lies hidden within. Therefore it is not surprising that shame covered my face with a blush of modesty amid reproaches, though false, for human nature is so constituted—a nature in whose flesh and blood I, the Son of God, shared in every natural property that can be understood without sin.

[Col. 0235A] And this is what I mean when I say, “Apart from that which lies hidden within,” since every sin, insofar as it is sin, lies hidden and wishes to lie hidden, being a work of darkness; for which reason “everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3:20). But I, wholly light, the whole light from light, when I came into the world and rebuked works of darkness, endured reproach for your sake, Father, who imposed upon me such a work of light. Thus, though free from the defect of human nature which lies hidden within, I nevertheless suffered shame in my face from the good and tender constitution of human nature itself, just as I truly suffered sorrow in my mind; and therefore I say that shame covered my face.

Another translation has: “Irreverence covered my face.”—Irreverence is not being ashamed, a kind of good boldness, such as the Apostle had when he said: “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel” (Rom. 1:16). [Col. 0235C] We ought to have this boldness or irreverence among those to whom Christ is displeasing, so that, when they reproach us for worshipping one who died, we may not blush as though shameless. Or else, the irreverence of the wicked, who showed me no reverence but treated me irreverently in many ways, covered my face. For literally they also veiled my face, thereby displaying their malice: they wished the splendor of my face, I who am the sun of righteousness, to be covered rather than revealed. Hence this visible sun also hid its face from them.

Moreover, from that time onward they themselves had a veil over their hearts, and shame truly covered those whose irreverence covered my face. They could no more bear the brightness of my countenance [Col. 0235D] than their fathers of old could bear the brightness of Moses’ face. And certainly it is not surprising that shame covered my face when I, poor and despised among the rich and honored, deprived of every human testimony, was compelled to bear witness about myself while they mocked me and cried: “Behold, you have heard the blasphemy” (Matt. 26:65). For they judged words of truth snatched from my mouth to be blasphemy, condemning me far more cruelly—though I was their brother according to the flesh—than their fathers of old condemned Joseph when they said: “Behold, the dreamer; come, let us kill him” (Gen. 37:19). For “Behold, you have heard the blasphemy” truly sounds more cruel than “Behold, the dreamer”; and it was more tolerable for him to be sold into slavery than for me to be sold to death: he to serve, I to die; he because of dreams, I, as they alleged, because of blasphemies. “It is not for a good work,” they say, “that we stone you, but for blasphemy, because you, though a man, make yourself God” (John 10:33). Therefore I more greatly—

**VERSE 9.** “I have become a stranger to my Jewish brothers, and an alien to the sons of my mother, the Synagogue.”

For among those seller-brothers descended from their father Jacob, none was a son of the same mother Rachel, because Benjamin, Joseph’s brother by the same mother, was absent. But in my sale, my brothers from the Synagogue, born of the same mother as I, joined to themselves my disciple, as it were a son of Rachel—that is, one trained in the disciplines of a most holy life—[Col. 0236B] to accomplish the crime of betrayal. Betrayed not to serve but, as I have said, to die, I became a stranger to my brothers, those very sellers, by descending into Egypt; yet I was not, as they desired, to perish there, but rather to rule throughout the land of Egypt, as I plundered hell, as though lower Egypt, and subjected this world, as though upper Egypt, to the laws of my discipline after defeating the armed strong man.

I am the true Joseph, who, just as that ancient Joseph had come to be hated by his brothers not only because of his dreams but because he had accused them before their father of a very wicked crime, so I too came to be hated by these brothers of mine not only because of my good teaching but because of their criminal life, which I frequently rebuked, [Col. 0236C] saying, for example: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe every herb and neglect the weightier matters of the law—justice and mercy and faith; who outwardly appear clean to men like whitewashed tombs, but within are full of every filth and uncleanness; who, having the key of knowledge, shut the kingdom of heaven, neither entering yourselves nor allowing others to enter” (Matt. 23:23 ff.).

By speaking such things, as an accuser of my brothers, I became a stranger to my very brothers. Yet I was especially burdensome to them because, disputing against their greed, overturning their tables and seats in the Temple, and driving them from the Temple with a whip made of cords, I declared that they were robbers, saying: “It is written that my house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations; but you have made it a den of robbers” (Matt. 21:13). Yet this was said and done by me in such a way—and indeed must be done in this way until the end of the age—that evil merchants may be driven out of your house, my Father, and that the Spirit of truth may rebuke those committing robbery in it.

**VERSE 10.** “For zeal for your house has consumed me” in my own person, and will consume me in my chosen members until that last judgment, when my house, or the house of my Father—the holy Church—will be fully cleansed, after robbers and all the wicked have been driven out by the great scourge of judgment, woven from the cords of sins and crimes. Although these are abominable everywhere, they are especially [Col. 0237A] detestable in the temple of God: namely, in the life that professes religious discipline, which stands out in the entire Church as the Temple did in the city of Jerusalem.

Therefore, although throughout the whole holy Church I detest evils that are done, and, seeing the city, have cause to weep over it when it does not know the time of its visitation, yet I am more deeply moved in consecrated persons, dedicated in the place of the Temple to the office of holiness, when I see evil commerce and most wicked robberies being carried on by them and among them. When these are rebuked by me or by my people in true reproaches, drawn from good zeal in the spirit of truth, false reproaches are returned; for those reproved for their sins cast darts of reproach upon their reprovers, as I experienced in myself: “For the reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me.”

[Col. 0237B] I rightly say, “of those who reproached you,” because whoever dishonors one sent dishonors the sender. For just as I say to those whom I send: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16), so also those who either honor me, the Son sent by you the Father, with glory, or dishonor me with reproaches and injuries, do to you what they do to me. Indeed, whatever good or evil they do to one of my least ones, they do to me and to you; and therefore, reproaching me, they reproach you. But because you are impassible and most high, their reproaches could not touch you. Upon me, however, who was made capable of suffering, both reproaches and other injuries fell and oppressed me unto death.

Likewise, after my death, enemies oppressed my disciples by persecuting me in them. Indeed, long ago they maltreated my prophets who foretold my coming and required the fruit of the vineyard entrusted to those evil tenants; and they cast many reproaches upon them—or rather upon you, who sent them—when they beat one and stoned another. Finally, when you said, “They will reverence my Son,” and sent me, “the greater reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me” (Matt. 21:37), more than upon your other messengers.

[Col. 0237C] Their fathers once said mockingly to your servant Moses in the wilderness: “Have you really brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey? Do you also mean to put out our eyes?” (Num. 16:14). Again: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Ps. 77:19). So too, now, they said reproachfully to me hanging on the cross: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matt. 27:42). Again: “Ha! You who destroy the Temple of God and rebuild it in three days” (Mark 15:29). These and other reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me. They mocked me thus; but I prayed:

**VERSE 11.** “And I covered my soul with fasting.” My hunger and thirst was that they might pass by faith in me into my body; but because they refused to believe, they left me, as it were, empty and fasting. Thus, when I said upon the cross, “I thirst,” they did not offer me what I thirsted for—namely, the new wine which I was to drink in my kingdom through the devotion of faith—but wine mixed with gall and myrrh, exceedingly bitter, like their own hearts. Therefore I would not drink such wine, and preferred to fast rather than receive into my body a drink so embittered, signifying by this that those who are bitter and corrupted by the gall of impiety are to be rejected and alienated from my body.

Yet, that even such persons may in some measure become sweet, my Apostle says to them among other things: “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, clamor, and blasphemy be removed from among you, with all malice” (Eph. 4:31). When they are thus changed and sweetened, I drink them; but those who stubbornly remain bitter I reject, and I fast from their taste, just as I fasted on the cross and covered my soul with fasting as with a certain [Col. 0238B] cloak of sorrow.

Or certainly I then covered my soul in this respect: I did not exert its powers in taking vengeance on my enemies, though I could have done so. For in the body then weak and frail, according to my own will, the most powerful soul lay hidden and did not exert its strength, as it did when stripped of flesh, plundering hell, destroying the Egyptians, and enriching the Hebrews. Finally, while it was still the hour and power of darkness, I preserved patience and showed that it must be preserved, postponing and concealing power.

And this very fact—that I presented myself as weak in order to gain the weak—became a reproach to me. This reproach was increased also by that blasphemous thief, who said to me: “If you can do anything, save yourself and us” (Luke 23:39). [Col. 0238C] But I did not have this weakness by either divine or human nature. My divinity, which shook the earth as evidence of its strength, could not be weakened. Nor, since it was without fault, was my humanity under any legal obligation to suffer punishments, the chief of which is human weakness, imposed on account of the sin of the first parent when he received a garment of skins as a token of his mortality. Since I was free from sin, I ought rightly to have been free from that mortality, so that the man whom I, the Word, put on might be like a soft garment and a robe of gladness. Yet I did this in order to deliver mortals from the death of soul and body.

**VERSE 12.** “I made my garment sackcloth,” voluntarily accepting the mortality of the flesh as the roughness of sackcloth. In it I, innocent for the guilty, performed penance, not only fasting forty days in the wilderness, but also bearing other hard and harsh things in my flesh. With my divinity hidden, I set this before those raging against me, so that by the sin committed against me I might condemn sin. In it also, as in a mourning garment, I wept over the sinful city. I also wept for Lazarus when dead, and was sorrowful unto death, through which, after this sackcloth or sacred garment had been torn apart, I would exult with joy in glorified flesh—I, Jesus the great priest. As a type of this, it is written that Jesus the great priest, after filthy garments had been removed from him, was clothed in change of garments, adorned with a clean turban, and crowned with golden crowns (Zech. 3:4–5).

[Col. 0239A] I even wished the crucifiers of my body, who were sackcloth to me—that is, harsh—to be my garment, when I prayed for them, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23:24).

Thus, doing good and suffering evil for them, I became to them an object of mocking proverb—that is, a likeness for reproach and curse—so that, when cursing anyone, they might say: “May you be that man’s disciple” (John 9:28), that is, may it happen to you as it happened to that crucified man reckoned among the wicked. And indeed such a curse is truly not a blessing. Yet by saying these and similar things they made true the parables spoken concerning me and them; for example: “A certain man planted a vineyard,” and so forth, as far as, “They will reverence [Col. 0239B] my son” (Luke 20:9 ff.). For what was said there figuratively concerning evil tenants killing the son, they literally fulfilled by crucifying me outside the gate, just as the son in the parable is said to be killed outside the vineyard.

Again, when in another parable I was signified by the slain fatted calf, they too, though unknowingly, fulfilled that parable, for by crucifying me they killed me and thus prepared a great feast for the prodigal son returning to his father—although envy, marked in the same parable in the elder son, torments them. Having therefore become to them a parable, I spoke to them in parables. Hence I said to my disciples: “To you it has been given to know the mystery [Col. 0239C] of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables, that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand” (Luke 8:10).

But when they understood my parables less than they ought, they did not reverently ask me about them, as did the disciples who, humbly asking, were given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; rather:

**VERSE 13.** “Those who sat in the gate spoke against me”—men who seemed to themselves wise, according to the ancient custom by which judges used to sit in city gates to judge the cases of those entering, as is read in Ruth, where the case of Boaz was judged by those sitting in the gate (Ruth 4:1 ff.). This was done so that each city might remain peaceful and undisturbed, since anyone entering the city who had some dispute would be dealt with by the wise men sitting at the gate and would have no cause for complaint within the city. Yet, while the wise sat together in the gate, diligent curiosity brought together people of different kinds, carrying various parables there and back.

Therefore, if it happened at the gate of the city of Jerusalem, which did not recognize in me the fulfilled time of its visitation—if, I say, it happened that some simpler persons entering or leaving spoke well of me, some saying that he is good, others saying, No, but he deceives the crowds—then those who sat in the gate as judges and wise men, possessing the key of knowledge, spoke against me. They contradicted those who called me good and, by their supposedly authoritative judgment, favored those who called me a deceiver, [Col. 0240A] just as they themselves said to Pilate: “Lord, we remember that that deceiver said, ‘After three days I shall rise again’” (Matt. 27:63).

Because my Passion was like a matter of common talk, Cleophas said: “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known the things done there in these days?” (Luke 24:18). It is as though he said: You may be ignorant because you are a stranger; but the crowds assembled for the feast from one region, together with the city’s inhabitants, know what has been done in it during these days. Thus, as I said, the greater men spoke against me, and the lesser men also sang against me—those who drank wine while assembling in taverns, where amid frequent and excessive drinking mockery of me was common, especially on that Passover night. Then, after the paschal lamb, intoxicated with much wine, having received me from the betrayer, they kept watch from evening until morning throughout the night, mocking me first in Annas’s house and afterwards in Caiaphas’s house. Thus, from the undigested wine which they had drunk more freely than usual at the Paschal supper, they belched loudly between words into my face.

[Col. 0240B] Therefore I say: “Those who drank wine sang against me,” gravest irony calling “psalmody” their clamorous talkativeness, by which they mocked me all night. They ought rather then to have sung psalms in thanksgiving to God, because this was the night that despoiled the Egyptians and enriched the Hebrew fathers of these very men. They themselves would surely have been enriched far more blessedly if they had received and eaten me, the true Lamb, with reverence—not with the old leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

Otherwise: Those who, turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine, gave me vinegar to drink, spoke against me. But those who drank sweet wine at my supper, and who will also drink that new wine in my kingdom with all who drink the same wine now in pilgrimage and will drink it later in my kingdom, sang of me; for such persons honor me by acceptable works and glorify me in songs of spiritual psalmody.

Otherwise: “Those who drank wine sang against me,” because it was not enough for them that I was, as Jeremiah laments, “their song” (Lam. 3:63), [Col. 0240D] when they sang mockingly about me in my absence; they also did the same to me in my presence. This they did especially on that night, when they not only cast insulting words into my face but also continually dishonored my very face with spittle, mingling many slaps and blows. Such work of their hands, interwoven with abusive words, was to them like a kind of psalmody—indeed, more delightful than psalmody performed on a ten-stringed psaltery.

These were the men marked by the prophet Amos when he said: “They drank wine in bowls; like David they thought themselves to possess instruments of song, and they suffered nothing over the ruin of Joseph” (Amos 6:6). For I was the true Joseph, sold for a sandal, as Amos likewise complains (2:6), because the thirty denarii among those high priests, entering the house of God in pomp, were scarcely the price of a sandal—just as the twenty pieces of silver formerly given by the Ishmaelites for Joseph to his eleven brothers were scarcely the price of a sandal when divided among them individually.

[Col. 0241A] And when those brothers saw the anguish of his soul as he begged them, they did not hear him, nor did they suffer anything over the ruin of that Joseph. Similarly, when these men saw my anguish, they had no compassion whatever for me, the true Joseph. Yet, thinking themselves to possess instruments of song like David, they sang against me, that is, against me, because they appropriated the words of Holy Scripture against me; for example, saying: “We have a law, and according to our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:7).

Thus my enemies sang against me: that is, they fulfilled in me the psalms written concerning my Passion. For in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink, as is written in this present psalm; and they themselves fulfilled the other proclamations of my Passion inserted in Davidic psalms. Yet when they saw the anguish of my soul, when, as another psalm says, “My spirit was in anguish within me” (Ps. 142:4), they suffered nothing—that is, they had no compassion in my sufferings and afflictions, nor in those of my disciples, who deeply sympathized with me. My mother too, pierced by the sword of sorrow, stood with the beloved disciple beside my cross in that pitiable spectacle, by which my enemies were not [Col. 0241C] moved to pity.

**VERSE 14. THIRD AND FOURTH PARTS.** “But I direct my prayer to you, O Lord: O God, it is the time of favor.”

In the face of the evils recounted above, Christ sets forth prayer on his own behalf, so that we may learn from his example to oppose to insults, quarrels, and abuse not quarrels but prayers. It is as though he said: They spoke against me, as has been stated; but I directed my prayer to you, O Lord, even for them, saying: O God, it is the time of favor which you foretold through another prophet, saying: “In an acceptable time I have heard you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you” (Isa. 49:8). Behold, now is the acceptable time, the time of favor; behold, now is the fullness of time, in which I, your Son, have come, I of whom you said: “This is [Col. 0241D] my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

Since therefore it is the time of favor, in which I, the grain falling into the earth, must now die and bear fruit, hear me in the multitude of your mercy, in the truth of your salvation. Let the multitude of your mercy abound where misery abounded.

There is, moreover, a twofold misery in the people for whom I suffer: namely, misery in sins and in punishments. To drive away this great misery, hear me, the Son, in the multitude of your mercy—you, the Father, me the righteous man, God the Father acting justly—so that I may not only be delivered from the punishments which, though undeservedly, I willingly endure, paying what I did not take; but so that my people, for whom I make this payment, may be freed alike from sins and punishments. And let all this be done in the truth of your salvation: that is, in that salvation which you, who are truthful, promised me, so that you may be justified in your words by which you promised me salvation, both long ago in the prophets and recently in open voices.

[Col. 0242A] Long ago indeed, speaking to the fathers in many portions and many ways through the prophets, you promised and prefigured for me the perfect salvation of resurrection, attesting not ambiguously but truly that, just as the first Adam through disobedience fell into many miseries, so I, the second Adam, through obedience proven in sufferings and death, would utterly escape every misery and obtain every glory for myself and my own; so that, as all die in that Adam, so all may be made alive in me.

As figures of this truth, Joseph received dominion over all Egypt not before but after his sale and imprisonment. Moses, first exposed as a little child to death in water, was afterwards found to be a great leader when he divided and reunited the waters of the sea, freed his brothers, and overwhelmed their enemies. Jephthah, first rejected and expelled by his brothers, was afterwards raised up as leader over his brothers and fellow-tribesmen and made glorious by a noble triumph. Samson, dishonored after his hair was cut, blinded and made weak, afterwards proved strong by shaking the pillars of the house, because in dying he killed more enemies than while living, and made the heap of the collapsing building a glorious tomb for himself.

[Col. 0242B] And behold, one greater than Joseph is here. For I am God and man; he was merely man. He was sold into slavery; I, to death. He was sent into prison; I descend into hell. Therefore, Father, hear me in the truth of your salvation, so that, as he, in the shadow of truth then still to come, lived among the nations and ruled throughout Egypt, so I, the Truth, may now be heard in the truth of your salvation, receiving dominion over the whole world. Let it thereby appear even to those who sold me that all power in heaven and on earth has been given to me.

With my Passion now imminent, I asked this, saying: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself” (John 17:5). Again: “Glorify your Son, and your Son will glorify you” (ibid., 1). Thus, when I asked for the brightness of divine glory and power for the humanity I had assumed, you answered: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John 12:28). Therefore, that you may be justified in your words and appear truthful in your promises, hear me in the truth [Col. 0242D] of your promised salvation and glory—not only in the singularity of that mercy by which I am named and am Son of Man and Son of God, not deeming equality with God the Father to be robbery, since you begot me as your own Son by your love, which is the Holy Spirit, making the Virgin the mother of your Son; but also in the multitude of your mercy, by which you willed me to be firstborn among many adopted brothers, who need the multitude of your mercy. Such was the thief who confessed me on the cross and is saved in the multitude of your mercy, so that by such an example faith and hope may be granted to others to obtain the same multitude of mercy.

And because many need this multitude of mercy—indeed, because Scripture has enclosed all under [Col. 0243A] sin, so that the salvation of believers may be accomplished not from the merit of justice but from the multitude of mercy—hear me, Father, in the multitude of your mercy. As none of my people is free from great misery, so let great mercy proceed to all from this Passion of mine in the truth of your salvation: while I truly and effectively rule throughout the land of Egypt; while my brothers, together with me, make good use of Egypt’s riches; while I, repaying them good for evil, love them inwardly; and while they, following my example, do the same by forgiving debts in the multitude of misery. Thus may the same measure of mercy be measured back to them; may no sin turn out to their harm; but may all things work together for their good, in the truth of salvation that will remain forever.

Just as it turned out not for evil but for good to Joseph’s brothers that, by selling him, they had sinned against heaven and against their father Jacob, so may true repentance for sins committed against me the Son and you the Father be granted to all whom you foreordained as my brothers, and through this repentance full mercy. For whoever sins against the Holy Spirit—as Judas did, knowingly and willingly doing evil by selling me, the true Joseph—will be guilty of an eternal offense.

[Col. 0243B] Likewise, the world, set in wickedness and hardened in wickedness, will be guilty of an eternal offense. Therefore I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you gave me out of the world: that all may come to me, the true Joseph, and, receiving from me the grain necessary for them and obeying me as I rule everywhere, may live and not be consumed by the famine which will oppress the world set in wickedness. Rather, let them be in the truth of your salvation, saying: “Our salvation is in your hand, O Lord; let your mercy look upon us, that we may serve you securely” (Gen. 47:25).

Again, because I am greater than Moses and am in greater peril in the waters—for now the waters have entered even to my soul, I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me—whereas he, having been taken from the water and adopted as a son by Pharaoh’s daughter, when at last grown up, caused the horse and rider pursuing him to be drowned in the sea rather than being himself drowned in it: rightly I ask, Father, that in the multitude of your mercy you now hear me, as you then heard him, and at the cry of his prayer drowned all Pharaoh’s chariots [Col. 0243D] in the sea, while providing a way for your people, of whom he was leader. Therefore now hear me, I beseech you, as leader of your people whom you have given me, in the multitude of your mercy, so that the multitude of your people and mine may be delivered from the oppressions and persecutions of the invisible Pharaoh, and may enjoy the good things in the truth of your salvation, both on the road of pilgrimage and in the land of promise. For a certain shadow of your salvation was displayed to that people: you gave them from heaven bread possessing every delight and every pleasing flavour; you brought waters forth from the rock for them; you glorified them through frequent victories. Yet because in these gifts of yours there was not truth but a shadow of salvation, they provoked you in the wilderness, and very many of them perished by various deaths. [Col. 0244A] But I, the truth, desire to be heard in the truth of salvation, so that those whom you gave me, Father, to lead through water and blood out of Egypt into the true land of promise, may truly be saved, as the apostles were saved, being as it were the seed-bed of the twelve tribes; and none of them perished except the son of perdition. Thus, with the exception of the sons of perdition, whose wickedness of perverse intention is obstinate, may they be preserved in the truth of your salvation, following me as leader and fleeing the invisible Pharaoh.

Likewise, as Jephthah in the shadow was first rejected by his brothers and afterwards, having delivered his nation, was raised up as its ruler, so that there was peace for his people during his days: so now, after I have been rejected by my Jewish brethren, let it come to pass in the truth of salvation that, [Col. 0244B] while I rule, neither a foreign nor a domestic enemy may be able to oppress those subject to me. For in his time neither the foreign sons of Ammon nor the domestic sons of Ephraim, once crushed by him, could thereafter prevail, while he ruled, against the Gileadites, Jephthah’s fellow-tribesmen, of whom he was ruler—just as I, Christ, am named and am ruler of all Christians who preserve this name in the truth of salvation.

May the salvation prefigured in shadow through Samson likewise now come to pass in the truth of salvation: when every engine hostile to me and mine falls, may my tomb become glorious from the very heap of such a ruin. For, shaken by fear and love of my strength as by two arms, the heights of this world will fall, [Col. 0244C] so that from this ruin my victory and glory may shine forth; and in this way my tomb may be glorious, while my body, which is the Church, rests in humility among the rich and proud of the world, their generosity consoling it and their power protecting it, though it was formerly harassed by their wickedness. Thus may the Church, extended throughout the world, make for herself monasteries from riches and buildings formerly worldly, as certain glorious tombs in which my members may rest, so that in this manner also may be fulfilled what is written of me: “The nations shall seek him, and his tomb shall be glorious” (Isa. XI. 10). In another translation it says: “And his name shall be glorious.” Therefore, God the Father, let both my tomb and my name be glorious [Col. 0244D] in the truth of salvation through such a triumph: my enemies falling either through repentance, which I pray for, or through punishment, which I promise by just judgment; and my members enjoying blessed rest, now living peacefully and after death rejoicing in everlasting peace.

Good tombs are religious monasteries and holy churches, in which the bodies of saints are buried in peace and those least ones rest, of whom Christ will say at judgment: “As long as you did it to one of these least of my brethren, you did it to me” (Matt. XXV. 40). Therefore, while such persons, living in concord and receiving the necessities of body and soul from the alms of the rich, keep watch at the tombs of martyrs buried beneath God’s altar, a tomb is prepared for both the living and the dead members of Christ from the ruins [Col. 0245A] of worldly height. The true Samson humbles his enemies and makes many of them friends, so that among such persons and in such places he delights to rest as in a most beautiful tomb, or as in a flowering bed, which his bride points out to him, saying: “Our bed is flowering; the beams of our houses are cedar, our ceilings cypress” (Cant. I. 15–16).

By these words religious communities are certainly described, in which praiseworthy persons of diverse virtues, beloved by both bridegroom and bride, are signified: some under the name of flowers, others of beams, others of ceilings. By this the Holy Spirit signifies that it is pleasant for bridegroom and bride to rest upon so flowering a bed, in houses so richly adorned. Hence the bridegroom himself, the true Samson, when by his death he had shaken the whole fabric of the world with a great earthquake and darkening of the sun, [Col. 0245B] chose to have a tomb in a garden, showing even thereby that it is fitting for himself and his members to rest in a flowering place: namely, where holy religion, pure and undefiled, flourishes, made secure through the keeping of discipline as a garden is usually fortified by a wall or hedge against the assaults of worldly tumult and the snares of malignant spirits. Thus the Lord’s tomb will indeed be glorious, because it is found placed not in a street but in a flowering garden.

On the contrary, there is a great complaint concerning the last times in the Apocalypse, because the bodies of slain saints are not allowed to be placed in tombs, but “will lie in the streets” (Apoc. [Col. 0245C] XI. 8). We plainly see this occur where holy places dedicated to saints’ relics are so profaned that everything is found to be like muddy streets, since ecclesiastical religion is no more observed in them than in streets. Against these evils I, Christ, pray with vehement cry in the present psalm, to be heard because of my reverence: “In the multitude of your mercy hear me, God the Father, in the truth of your salvation,” so that the salvation which beforehand proceeded as a shadow of truth through Moses, Joshua, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson, and other deliverers, thus called by name—when, in response to the Israelites crying to you, you sent such deliverers to free them—may now be fulfilled in truth through the sacrifice of my passion recounted in this psalm.

[Col. 0245D] I fittingly join mercy to truth in this prayer, in which I, the truth, ask to be heard, because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV. 10). With these as with two feet he walks in his house, which is the rational elect creature. In order to build two walls into one, through mercy he forgives human sins, and through truth fulfils the promises which, speaking through angels and prophets, he foretold. Thus, having invoked and recalled mercy and truth together, I ask to be heard not in a small or scant measure of mercy, nor in a shadow of salvation, as the saving forerunners who announced me were heard before me, but in the multitude of mercy and in the truth of salvation. For I am truly called Saviour of the world, not merely of the one Jewish people, as the angel explained the meaning of this name, Jesus, saying: “For he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. I. 21). Praying for this salvation, I say:

**VERSE 15.** “Deliver me from the mud, that I may not be stuck fast.” Or, as another translation has it: “that I may not cling.” Deliver me, the head, from the mud of misery, which I endure to deliver my members, paying what I did not steal. Deliver me, that I may not be fixed or cling longer than is expedient in the mud or slime in which I am fixed, having willingly become mortal. Deliver me from this mud and slime through the glory of the resurrection, glorifying my flesh. Or deliver me from the impious Jews and people like them: muddy through uncleanness and impious through wickedness; or muddy and slimy through love [Col. 0246B] of evil, and impious through hatred of good. Therefore I say: “Deliver me from those who hate me,” who hate both me and mine with profound hatred. They must therefore be compared to deep waters, such as the waters of the Red Sea before Moses. Therefore, as you then delivered him with the people accompanying him, so deliver me with my people—not in shadow, as you delivered him, but in the truth of your salvation.

**VERSE 16.** “Let not the storm of water overwhelm me,” as Pharaoh was overwhelmed with his army. Let not the stormy sedition of the Jews engulf me; though it afflicts me according to the passibility of the flesh, in which I am weak and fixed in the slime of the deep, yet, because the spirit is willing, let this storm not so overwhelm [Col. 0246C] me or let its depth not swallow me up that I may be swallowed by the sorrow by which my soul is sorrowful even unto death.

Alternatively: Let not the depth of hell, into which I am about to descend, swallow me up so as to hold me there; rather, with the pains of hell loosed and my own who await me there delivered, let it be impossible for me to be held by that depth. Nor let the pit of the infernal deep press its mouth over me, as it was accustomed to press it over all people before my coming. Rather, as I triumph there, let the gates of hell be lifted up before my face, and let none of them prevail against me.

Alternatively: “Deliver me,” that is, my people, from the mud of sin and misery, so that, even if the flesh is weakened in such things by sensation, [Col. 0246D] the Spirit may not be stuck fast or cling through consenting to temptation or through impatience in misery. Rather, through good patience may they possess their souls free from consent to sin and from impatience under sufferings—indeed, liberated and delivered through me, the Saviour. I ask this delivery and liberation for them, saying: “Deliver me from the mud of temptation, that I may not be stuck fast through the mind’s consent,” though I am bodily fixed in the slime of the deep. “Deliver me from those who hate me,” lest I become impatient against them, “and from the deep waters”—that is, from those temptations which, by a gentle inundation, dissolve the ground of firm purpose and draw it into the deep.

Likewise, let that kind of temptation not harm me or mine which does not wash gently over us but rushes in violently, even carrying rocks from their place, as it is said in Job [Col. 0247A] that the earth is gradually consumed by inundation, “and the rock is moved from its place” (Job XIV. 18). By this saying these two kinds of temptations are signified. Let neither, I say, the gentler nor the graver temptation harm mine. Against the one I ask help, namely that they not be drawn into the deep waters; and against the greater and stronger, I ask stronger help, saying: “Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor let the deep swallow me up, nor let the pit press its mouth over me.” The pit is the same as the depth of human wickedness. If anyone falls there, he falls into a depth where he is also held if he closes his mouth against confession of sin. But if he confesses his sins and cries out, he escapes from the depths. If, however, when he has come into the depth, he despises it, the pit closes its mouth [Col. 0247B] over him; he is dead, and what is said in Solomon is fulfilled in him: “From the dead, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes.”

On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0247D] *Moralium*, Book XXVI, ch. 36]:

> Everyone who abandons the way of life and casts himself down into the darkness of sins plunges himself, as it were, into a pit or ditch. But if, through long persistence in wrongdoing, he is also oppressed by the habit of wickedness, so that he can no longer rise to higher things, he is, as it were, constricted by the narrow mouth of a pit. Thus David prays under the figure of sinners, saying: “Let not the storm of water overwhelm me.” For one whose evil deed’s wickedness has shaken him from good stability has, as it were, been carried away by a storm of water. But if habit has not yet prevailed, it has not overwhelmed him. [Col. 0247C] He has already fallen into the pit who has done what the divine law forbids. But if a long habit does not yet weigh him down, the pit has by no means constricted its mouth. Thus he comes out all the more easily, the less tightly he is constricted by habit.
>
> For there is a kind of more confined narrowness: to wish to rise from oppressive evil habit and yet be unable; already to tend upward in one’s desires, yet still remain in weak things in one’s action; to go before in heart but not follow in deed; and to endure oneself as one’s own contradiction. But when the soul thus striving is aided by the hand of elevating grace, it reaches from the narrow mouth into breadth, because, difficulties conquered, it performs the good works it beholds. The prophet David had seen the confinement of the narrow mouth when he said: “You have saved my soul from necessities, and have not shut me up into the hands of the enemy.” He recalls that he has been saved into the greatest breadth when he adds: “You have set my feet in a spacious place.” [Col. 0247D] Feet are established in a spacious place when we tend toward fitting goods and are hindered by no difficulty. We proceed, as it were, through an open place wherever we will, because no obstacles of difficulty confine us.

Having first offered prayer against many dangers, he prays that the prayer itself may be heard, saying:

**VERSE 17.** “Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is kind.”—Hear me, Christ, O Father [Col. 0248A] of mercies, for your mercy is kind. I do not put forward merit, because I speak in the person of the members, none of whom has merit worthy of being heard. Therefore I, the Christian, say in words fitting for me, because I am not worthy to be heard on account of my merits: “Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is kind.” Christ suffered for me, whom you, Father, sent—not because I, lost in Adam, deserved him, but because your mercy is kind. For “the kindness and humanity of our Saviour,” your Son, “appeared, not from works of righteousness which we had done, but according to his,” and your, “mercy” (Tit. III. 4–5). Since it was kind in promising and sending this Saviour, it is much more kind now [Col. 0248B] toward us, his members, for whom he offered himself as a sacrifice of sweet savour.

Hence another translation has: “Hear me, for your mercy is sweet”—namely because of the sacrifice of the Lord’s passion, a sacrifice of sweet savour. Although offered once, it has nevertheless been and is to be repeatedly recited in this psalm and in the other divinely inspired Scriptures; it has been and is to be repeated in the sacrament of the altar and presented to the heavenly court, likewise as a sweet savour. Mercy is therefore sweet both because of the sweet savour already recalled and continuously to be recalled, and because of the pressure of tribulations or temptations. For as bread is sweet, so consolation is sweet to the afflicted [Col. 0248C] and deliverance to the tempted. For you, God, mercifully permit or even cause tribulation; yet you do not withdraw nourishment, but stir desire. Thus, as cold [perhaps read: heat] is sweet to one who is chilled and drink to one who thirsts, so mercy will be sweeter to one suffering misery.

Therefore I too, David—or I, a penitent human being born of woman, living for a short time and filled with many miseries—seek a multitude of mercy, saying: “Hear me, Lord.” I do not say “that your mercy may be sweet,” but “because your mercy is sweet” to me, scourged and distressed by so many miseries that I need your many mercies also for my consolation. Therefore I say: “According to the multitude of your compassions look upon me”—not upon my sins, so great is their multitude that, if you look at them, justice requiring it, [Col. 0248D] you will reject me. To prevent this, “turn your face from my sins” (Ps. L. 11), and do not look upon them, lest you be provoked to just vengeance against me. But look upon me, filled inwardly and surrounded outwardly by many miseries, according to the multitude of your mercy in affection and your compassions in effect. And although I have deserved by my sins that you turn your face away from me, nevertheless:

**VERSE 18.** “Do not turn your face away from your child,” who both prayed on the cross for transgressors that they might not perish, and now intercedes in heaven for the same persons that they may not perish. For the voice of his blood crying to you [Col. 0249A] from the earth is heard while the Church sings in this psalm and in the other psalms commemorating his passion. Therefore you, Father of mercies, do not turn your face away from your child, chosen from thousands, who alone is fit to appease you for us your servants and to be heard for his reverence, of whom you say in Isaiah: “Behold my chosen child, whom I have chosen; I have put my Spirit upon him” (Isa. XLII. 1).

The first man, earthly and from the earth, did not receive your Spirit, which he was to receive after his obedience was perfected, unless the malignant spirit had forestalled him through disobedience. But this your child, conceived of the Holy Spirit and made obedient to you, Father, rightly and truly says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. XVI. 1). How then could you turn [Col. 0249B] your face away from him who has your Spirit upon him? What I, David, say—“Do not turn your face away from your child”—is partly prophecy and partly prayer. It is prophecy concerning the head; concerning me and the other members of this same servant, it is a prayer, or claim, because by the Son’s obedience we seek the Father’s face as though by a certain right, not only praying but also claiming, saying: “Do not turn your face away from your servant.”

In the Hebrew it reads: “Do not hide your face from your slave.” The sense is the same. For he who for our sake was born a child to us also emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, being found not only in appearance as a man but also in punishment as a robber, [Col. 0249C] reckoned among the lawless in order to free the lawless. Therefore, Father, do not in turn hide your face from this servant; preserve those for whom he prayed, saying: “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil” (John XVII. 15). For he said this not for the apostles alone, but for those who would believe through their word. Of these I, a penitent, am one—now a child, that is, humble, humbled by scourges, and, like a slave deserving many blows, scourged with many tribulations. Amid these tribulations I cry to you rather than murmur against you, and now sing: “Because I am troubled, hear me swiftly.” Hear me swiftly, I say. For consolation ought not to be delayed, because I am troubled both in body and soul. But my greater concern is for my soul. Therefore [Col. 0249D] I say:

**VERSE 19.** “Attend to my soul and deliver it because of my enemies”—either to convert them, which I desire, or to confound and weaken them, which, agreeing with justice, I approve. It should be noted that there are two deliverances. One is hidden and is effected for the saints themselves, as the seven Maccabean brothers were delivered when they were bodily put to death by exceeding torments together with their mother, who urged them to choose death for God’s laws rather than life against them. There is also an open deliverance of saints, effected in order to convert or punish enemies: thus when the three boys were delivered from the fire, Nebuchadnezzar, converted, proclaimed their God whom he had despised; and when Daniel was delivered from the lions’ den, his enemies were handed over to the same lions to be devoured.

Therefore what I, David, say—“Attend to my soul and deliver it”—belongs to the hidden deliverance, which is not manifest to the eyes of the foolish. But what I say, “Deliver me because of my enemies,” belongs to open deliverance. Thus I, the true David, first delivered in soul, immediately entered paradise and brought into it the soul of the thief, to whom I said: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII. 43). But this deliverance of my soul alone did not benefit my enemies. Therefore, when my body was visibly raised into heaven in the Ascension and the Holy Spirit was sent down in fiery tongues, and apostles formerly unlearned began thenceforth to speak in various tongues, so that [Col. 0250B] their sound went forth into all the earth, my bodily deliverance was revealed and my enemies were partly confounded and partly converted.

Blessed Pope Gregory says on this passage in Job [Note: [Col. 0249D] *Moralium*, Book XXVI, ch. 18]:

> It often happens that righteous people, overtaken by tribulation, receive heavenly consolation even in time, though they do not seek it for temporal reasons. They desire to be saved not for themselves but for the salvation of their adversaries, so that, while almighty God delivers them from immense dangers by some holy miracle, he may make his power known even to their persecutors and thereby redeem their adversaries unto eternity by that through which he saves his own temporally. Hence the Psalmist, taking up the voice of martyrs, says: “Deliver me because of my enemies.” As though he said: “For my own sake, indeed, I do not seek deliverance from temporal tribulation; but I desire deliverance for the sake of my adversaries, so that, while my life is seen to be saved miraculously, the hardness of my enemies may be converted by the very sight of the miracles.”
>
> For just as the Lord often saves the lives of his people in time for the conversion of enemies, so he often does not hear their voices for the condemnation of persecutors, so that the latter may accumulate their guilt precisely by that in which they wickedly rejoice that they have prevailed. For those who despise invisible things can sometimes be moved by visible miracles. But when, in the case of the righteous, no visible miracle is commonly done, it is because their adversaries do not deserve to be enlightened invisibly. It follows:

**VERSE 20.** “You know my reproach, my confusion [Col. 0250D] and my shame.” I ask to be manifestly delivered and rescued because of my enemies, without specifying from what. There is no need, since I speak to you, God of knowledge, who knows all things, to whom thoughts are prepared and before whom all things are bare. Therefore you, who know all, also know my reproach, my confusion, and my shame, from all of which I ask to be manifestly delivered because of my enemies. They reproach me, Christ, because I am a carpenter’s son; because I, who saved others, could not save myself. They shame me with spittle, slaps, and blows, mocking me; they also add a false show of reverence by greeting me as king with bent knee, [Col. 0251A] crowning me with thorns, giving me a reed for a sceptre, and clothing me with a scarlet cloak as though it were royal purple. In all these things was false reverence and true dishonour.

Hence “dishonour” stands in the Hebrew where we have “reverence,” or “shame,” as some manuscripts read. Reproach is what an enemy casts up; confusion is what gnaws the conscience, which could not exist in Christ, in whom there was no fault; shame is what makes an honourable countenance blush even at false accusations. This could exist in Christ, and must be believed to have existed, especially when he, poor among rich enemies, bore witness concerning himself and heard them contradict him and say: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true” (John VIII. 13). [Col. 0251B] As they said these things, there was indeed shame in his face, as though at the charge of false testimony; yet the truth of that testimony was then hidden, reserved to be revealed in its own time.

But now, after the truth of that testimony has been declared through the Holy Spirit, of whom he said, “He will bear witness concerning me” (John XV. 26), and through the apostles testifying in Jerusalem, throughout Judaea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth—when Christians are reproached with the name of Christ as though it were empty and signified no genuine power, for the strong, such as Paul, it is neither confusion nor shame but glory. Hence he says: “I am not ashamed of the Gospel” (Rom. I. 16), and: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI. 14).

But when it was objected to certain persons that they had killed Christ, they were pricked in their evil conscience and wholesomely confounded, so that any one of them could say to God: “You know my reproach and my confusion.” Others also believe but are ashamed to confess and fear reproaches. Since they are members of Christ, though weak ones, they should be believed to be helped by this very prayer of Christ, in which, transfiguring their reproach, confusion, and shame into himself, he prays to the Father, saying: “You know my reproach,” that is, that of my members; “and my confusion,” that is, that of my members; “and my reverence or shame,” that is, that of my members. For strengthening them, I endured reproach, confusion, and shame, so that by my example and help my own might learn likewise to bear the same things—which enemies [Col. 0251D] do not know, and therefore are unwilling to amend.

But you, Father, who know all things and know from whom and for whom I endure such things, know that:

**VERSE 21.** “All who trouble me are before your sight.” Some do not know what they are doing, and for them I pray even on the cross, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke XXIII. 34). But some know that I am your Son, the heir of the vineyards, which they wickedly possess, and say among themselves: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him” (Matt. XXI. 38). For such persons I, Christ, do not pray, because for those who sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of truth there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation and a fire of zeal that will consume the adversaries. I do not say sinners, but adversaries. [Col. 0252A] For all have sinned and need the glory of God; they are justified freely through gratuitous grace, who have received and receive me as Lord of the vineyard. But those who do not cease to oppose me, and in their obstinacy trouble me in myself or even in my members, while you, my Father, look on, are surely worthy of your righteous wrath of indignation and the fire of zeal which will consume adversaries provoking you, Father, in your sight.

For all who trouble me are before your sight, devising reproaches and miseries against me; yet not without my knowledge or against my will, because my heart awaited reproach and misery, ardently desiring to eat this Passover, by which I was to pass from this world to you, Father, and to drink the cup that you, most merciful Father, gave me. Although it was presented to me through the bloodstained hands [Col. 0252B] of the impious, it was for the accomplishment of the supreme effect of loving-kindness: to die for the impious, when scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person. But I chose to endure reproaches, misery, and finally death for the impious, that they might become pious; and therefore I did not avoid reproach and misery, but awaited them. Nor do I merely say, “I awaited,” but “my heart awaited,” so that the voluntary desire of my expectation may be understood, in accordance with the prophetic word said concerning me: “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. LIII. 7). For though my flesh was weak, my spirit was willing and my heart was voluntary in enduring reproach and misery.

Yet this misery may more truly be ascribed to those who crucified me than to me who was crucified; for mercy rather than misery is fitting for me, because I mercifully prayed for my miserable crucifiers, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke XXIII. 34). My soul was sorrowful even unto death, moved by bowels of mercy, also for those who knew that I was the Lord of the vineyard and nevertheless presumed to kill me in order to have my inheritance. Therefore, seeing the city, I wept over it when it did not see; but I saw its misery, which it had deserved because it did not know the time of its visitation. Since it would not weep, I wept all the more and was sorrowful.

“And I looked for one to grieve with me, and there was none”: among all those tenants knowingly sinning against me, [Col. 0252D] not one grieved with me. Rather, rejoicing in most evil things, they happily carried out their intended crime. I too, persisting in my purpose, willingly endured the reproach of the cross—already imminently present—which my heart had awaited as future, sorrowful indeed not for the cup offered to me but for the impiety of those offering it; and “I looked for one to grieve with me, and there was none.” For even if my disciples were sorrowful and the women lamented and wept over me, they were not sorrowful with me, because their sorrow was carnal: sorrow at the loss of the present life which they loved in me. They did not yet understand so fully that by my death they would be given life that they could either rejoice in my death, by which I was to pass to the Father, [Col. 0253A] or be so sorrowful as I was for the frenzied persons who had rushed against me, their physician.

Even my mother, whose soul was pierced by the sword of sorrow when she saw me fastened to the cross, had sorrow like a woman in childbirth; yet in every respect her sorrow was not like mine, nor was that of the apostles—though their sorrow, because it was praiseworthy, was to be turned into joy. The sorrow of my mother and of the apostles, though devout, was nevertheless far subordinate to my sorrow: they grieved at the injuries done to me, whereas I grieved at the enemies who injured me. For I had wished, like a hen gathering her chicks under her wings, to gather them; but they would not. Like a physician, I freely offered saving remedies to those who were sick; but they were ungrateful for such gifts and, like madmen endowed with evil strength, rushed upon me, their physician. In that hour of darkness there was none to console me by recognizing his illness and accepting the medicinal drink which I, the physician, had prepared for them from my flesh and blood. They refused to drink it, but rejected it as bitter, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John VI. 53). Again they say: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (ibid. 61). Thus they rejected my saving food and drink, and repaying me evil for good:

**VERSE 22.** “They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” For when I sought them as sweet and savoury food, they made themselves gall-like; [Col. 0253C] and in my thirst—that is, where I thirsted for them—they made themselves most bitter. In the literal sense also, according to John, the Lord’s passion was completed when, after he had said, “I thirst,” one of the soldiers offered his mouth a sponge full of vinegar, set upon a reed and surrounded with hyssop. And when he had received the vinegar, he said: “It is finished” (John XIX. 30). Matthew also relates: “Wine mixed with gall was given to him by soldiers to drink” (Matt. XXVII. 34). But when he had tasted it, he would not drink.

Here it should be observed that the wine mixed with gall according to Matthew, or with myrrh according to Mark, offered by the soldiers before he was raised upon the cross, [Col. 0253D] he tasted but would not drink; but after he had been raised on the cross he received the vinegar set about with hyssop. By this is signified that he does not reject those who repent bitterly of their bitterness and possess humility, marked by hyssop: he does not despise a contrite and humbled heart, and he eats ashes like bread when he incorporates penitents into his body just as he does the innocent.

But those double-minded persons signified by wine mixed with myrrh or gall or both are not acceptable to him. One of these—and chief among them—was Judas, the worst merchant. Saying, “I have sinned,” he offered wine, as it were, in confession of sin; but this wine was mixed in him with the gall of bitterness and the myrrh of impiety, because he confessed his sin not to Christ himself [Col. 0254A] or to his apostles in hope of pardon, but like another Cain, to the Scribes and Pharisees, his partners in the same crime, despairing of forgiveness.

Simon Magus also asked Peter and the other apostles to pray for him; because he did not do this sincerely, he was like one offering wine mixed with gall, and heard from Peter the apostle, among other things: “I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity” (Acts VIII. 23). Therefore the Lord rightly tasted but would not drink wine mixed with gall or myrrh, because he does not receive those who are double-minded and feign repentance. Yet he is recorded as having received vinegar offered him with hyssop placed around it, because the bitterness of repentance in the sponge of a contrite and humbled heart pleases him. Such was the repentance of Peter, [Col. 0254B] weeping bitterly, who truly, as one of the good soldiers, offered Christ thirsting a drink of his repentance, tempered by his tears and not embittered with gall. Christ himself shows elsewhere that he receives such a drink, saying: “I tempered my drink with weeping” (Ps. CI. 10).

It should certainly be observed that he is said to have drunk vinegar from a sponge, not from a cup. Whoever drinks from a sponge takes part and leaves part in the sponge. So too Christ does not receive every repentance, though offered with a simple heart, but only that which he judges fruitful. Hence it is not said: “Do repentance,” but: “Bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke III. 8). Whoever does not bear these according to his ability, though he offers vinegar in the bitterness of grief, nevertheless does not offer what is acceptable to him who desires fruit worthy of repentance. Such vinegar was offered by that vineyard which was turned into the bitterness of a strange vine: it was expected to yield grapes, but yielded thorns. For the crown of thorns also mocked Christ’s kingship.

The wording of the Psalm here seems to differ from that of the holy Gospel. For in the Gospel gall is said to have been given, not in food, but in drink. Therefore this must rather be understood mystically. In this the fact fits well that it does not say, “They gave gall as food,” but “they gave gall into food,” so that the wording of the Psalm too may agree with that of the Gospel. For the Lord had already received food: he had eaten the Passover with his disciples [Col. 0254D], where he had also administered the sacrament of his body and blood. This food is both sacrament and reality, and the power of the unity of members and head in the body of Christ, which is the Church. Speaking of it, the Apostle says: “Though many, we are one bread, one body” (1 Cor. 10:17). Into this food, then, so sweet and savoury, the persecutors of the Lord cast gall and vinegar when he did not find them sad with him, or consoling him—indeed, when they made him sad and, worst of all, rejoiced in their own sorrow and in the sorrow of those belonging to him. They were, of course, unaware that their joy was to be turned into mourning, and the sorrow of his people into joy; and Christ himself, after the resurrection, allowed them, for the cleansing of Jewish gall, to eat with him from a honeycomb [Col. 0255A]. But now those who despise Christ seated in heaven, sinning more grievously than the Jews who crucified him while he walked on earth, cast gall and vinegar into the food when they introduce into the Church the scandal of evil drinking, whether as sinners or as heretics. The Lord tasted the bitter cup, teaching us also by this sacrament to taste—that is, to endure—such people; but he did not drink, because such people cannot be received into Christ’s body. Thus this is mystically foretold just as it was mystically accomplished in the Passion. For these I, Christ, pray: for some that they may be bent, for others that they may be broken, saying:

**VERSE 23. Let their table become a snare before them.** They prepared before me my table, at which I had resolved to complete the Paschal supper, [Col. 0255B] as I knew, as a snare for me, because while they were plotting, the hand of him who betrayed me was with me at the table, so that through that hand I might be caught and ensnared. Let there therefore be a just recompense for them: let their table, namely sacred Scripture, set before them—that is, placed within their knowledge—for the Paschal feast, by which their passage was to be prepared from Egypt through the Red Sea, namely from this world through baptism into the land of promise, be turned for them into a snare before their very eyes. Thus, as though swallowed alive, seeing their own iniquity and at the same time their misery, they persist in that very letter of Moses which they read, while it accuses them, as I told them with my own mouth: “Moses accuses you; for he wrote of me, and you do not believe him” (John 5:45–47). Let therefore the very letter of the Law become a snare to those who wish from it to ensnare others by abusing the Scriptures of truth to confirm their own error. This is done not only by the Jews, but by all heretics and other perverse teachers. Lest they be able to pervert others as they wish, I desire that they fall ensnared in their own snares, and receive this as the recompense of their voluntary error: because they have not received, or refuse to receive, the love of truth, let an operation of error be sent to them, and let them believe a lie. Yet it was fitting that the word of God should first be preached to them, to confirm the promises of the Fathers, to whom this had been promised. But since they rejected and still reject it, my apostles shall turn to the Gentiles, to the rejection of the Jews and [Col. 0255D] to their scandal—that is, their stumbling-block—when, like another Esau, grievously saddened, they stumble because the Gentiles are blessed after they themselves have been supplanted. At first, indeed, these evils shall happen to them knowingly. But because they refuse to use their knowledge well, and, though having eyes, refuse to see and instead choose to envy:

**VERSE 24. Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see.** Let them be sent, that is, into outer darkness because they love inner darkness. Therefore, since they refuse to possess the light of a good conscience by seeing and loving me, Christ, the Sun of righteousness, let them lose the brightness of their good repute, according to which they were called sons of Abraham, or even [Col. 0256A] sons of God Most High; and let it be recognized by all that they are of their father the devil, whose desires they wish to perform.

Blessed Pope Gregory, touching on this passage in Job, says: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bend their back for ever.” [Note: [Col. 0255D] *Pastoral Care*, Part I, ch. 1.] “The Prophet announces this concerning the reprobate, not with the mind of one wishing it, but by the mystery of prophecy. For the eyes are those who, placed in the very face of highest honour, have undertaken the office of providing for the way. Those who adhere to them thereafter are rightly called backs. He says therefore: ‘Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bend their back for ever.’ It is as though he said: ‘Let those who preside over the actions of human life, as over paths that must be provided for, lack the light of truth, [Col. 0256B] so that the subjects who follow them, bent beneath the burdens of their iniquities, may lose their upright standing.’” [Note: [Col. 0256D] The same, *Morals*, Book XXV, ch. 16.] “We know beyond doubt that this happened in Judaea when, at the very coming of our Redeemer, the crowd of Pharisees and priests closed the eyes of their minds against the true light, and the people, walking by the examples of their leaders, wandered in the darkness of unbelief.”

The Prophet, then, spoke prophetically what he foresaw would happen. But Christ, who endured these things in his presence, does not, like a prophet, foretell future events; rather, as judge, he pronounces just sentences against the wrongs unjustly inflicted upon him, before the Father and the whole heavenly court, through his own mouth [Col. 0256C]. He also speaks through the mouth of the Church which sings the Psalm, in which he himself too is believed to sing, according as he himself says elsewhere: “I will give thanks to you among the peoples, O Lord; I will sing a psalm to you among the nations” (Ps. 56:10). He speaks, I say, Christ himself, against the Jews, his enemies, and against others like them, who offer him wine mixed with gall: that is, who administer or receive the purest and holiest sacraments unworthily, and, in administering them, seek what is their own, since in all that they do in divine offices they think not of the Lord’s interests but of their own profit.
