Do not those offer wine mixed with gall who, though forbidden on account of manifest incest and simoniacal gains, as concubinary or hired priests, nevertheless presume to sacrifice? Likewise, those who harbour in their heart hatred or the bitterness of any mortal sin, when they presume to offer prayers or sacrifices to God, offer wine mixed with gall. By that sacrifice they do not appease God but offend him, especially if, warned and rebuked, they refuse to amend themselves and persist obstinately in their wickedness. Against these, in this Psalm, Christ the just judge says: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bend their back for ever.” That is, let their prelates, who glory that they are wise and clear-sighted, because they are wise in order to do evil and know how to defend their deeds when reproved, lose their sharpness of reason and light of knowledge, lest they be able to lead others into error [Col. 0257A], but may understand that they need a guide. “And bend their back also for ever”: let their followers not stand erect in pride, but be bent and humbled, either unto repentance—which I will by mercy—or unto punishment—which I endure by just judgment. And let this always be so, according to what I say: “Bend their back for ever,” so that in the penitent humility may remain everlasting, and in the impenitent humiliation likewise everlasting; so that, neither in the former, bent by the virtue of humility, nor in the latter, bent beneath the weight of humiliation, may there be any occasion for self-exaltation.

Otherwise: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bend their back for ever.” It is written: “The eyes of the wise are in his head, but the eyes of fools [Col. 0257B] are at the ends of the earth” (Eccl. 2:14; Prov. 17:24). The eyes of the wise are in his head because they are directed to Christ, who is the head of all good things, and also the head and beginning of all creatures, as he himself says: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:25); and of whom Moses says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). To that head and beginning, I say, the wise person’s eyes are directed, so that from that source they may have right wisdom, from which they have being. But the eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth, because they think only earthly things and refuse to think what is above. Since it is more advantageous for them to have no understanding than to understand badly—so that they may rather be likened to irrational beasts than be accounted intelligent and wise—let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see [Col. 0257C]. Thus, when the subtlety of knowledge in which they glory has been lost or blunted within, in the inner person, let them also outwardly be humbled, their back bent in the outward person, their abasement bearing witness to the blindness of the inner person. For the face not inappropriately signifies the inner person, and the back the outer person, because in the former the likeness and image of the divine countenance is expressed, so that the latter may be led by its governance and be directed after it, as the back follows the face. When the eyes of the inner person have been darkened, it follows that the bearing of the outer person too is deformed. Thus King Nebuchadnezzar, once deprived of understanding, was also bent in body and ate grass like an ox for seven years, humbled by this beastly deformity, until his pride was healed and he acknowledged that the Most High ruled [Col. 0257D] in the kingdom of men. So also now let the pride of those who exalt themselves against discipline divinely instituted be brought low, so that their eyes may be darkened, that they may not see, and their back may be bent for ever. “For ever,” I say, so long as they remain what they now are. For if they are changed and made humble, this curse does not touch them; rather, the blessedness of the humble belongs to them, according to the saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). But those of whom it is elsewhere said, “Forget not the voices of your enemies; the pride of those who hate you rises continually” (Ps. 73:23), let them be bent continually, so that this imprecation may be manifest in them, which I, Christ, utter to you, righteous Father, through the mouth of the Psalm-singing [Col. 0258A] Church: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bend their back for ever,” so that always bent and never upright, they may not be able to oppress the good as they wish.

And because they are comparable in wickedness to the Egyptians who once oppressed and hated the children of Israel, or even are worse than they, let them also be compared with them in punishment. Concerning those Egyptians you said to Moses: “Stretch out your hand over Egypt, and let there be darkness in Egypt so thick that it can be felt”; and it was so (Exod. 10:21). For during three days horrible darkness lay over all the Egyptians: their eyes were darkened, not because sight itself had been extinguished in them, but because dense gloom surrounded them on every side, so that none of them could see [Col. 0258B] his brother or move from the place in which he was. So let the sight of these people too, who hate the children of Israel and look upon the good with an evil eye—or rather look down upon them—be impeded in length and breadth. Though they possess sharpness of reason, let them nevertheless, surrounded by the dense gloom of folly, be unable to move as they wish or to advance the evils they devise. Again, the Sodomites who wished to break into the house of righteous Lot were struck with blindness so that they could not find the door (Gen. 19:11). Thus let these people too, resembling the Sodomites in uncleanness and wickedness, who wish to break into and disturb the house of the righteous, of which it is written, “In the house of the righteous there is much strength” (Prov. 15:6), be struck with blindness so that they cannot find the door, finding no entrance to disturb any righteous person. [Col. 0258C] May they never find Christ himself either, who says, “I am the door” (John 10:9), since, filled with Sodomitic impiety, they seek him not faithfully but faithlessly. Again, soldiers sent by the king of Syria to capture the prophet Elisha are said to have been struck with blindness (4 Kings 6:18), so that, not knowing where they were going, they entered Samaria, the city of the king of Israel. Yet the king of Israel, though they had been sent to harm him, was forbidden by Elisha to harm them. So let these people also, prepared to harm the good, be struck with a beneficial blindness and conquered in goodness by the good themselves, just as those Syrians, overcome by Elisha’s kindness, did not again come into the land of Israel to harm anyone. So beneficial was it, both to Syrians and Israelites, that the enemies’ eyes were darkened for a time through the prophet’s prayer [Col. 0258D]. Therefore let this prayer be uttered with a twofold beneficial purpose: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bend their back for ever,” so that the enemies of the Church, robbed of the cunning of their minds, may always have bodies incapable of harming others or even themselves, and backs always bent—provided, however, that their pride rises continually. This is for restraining or extinguishing that pride, lest it rise beyond measure.

**VERSE 25. Pour out your wrath.** I do not say, “Let it trickle out little by little,” but: “Pour it out abundantly, like a great river, upon them,” so that your wrath may overwhelm them. This is known to have happened when the Roman army devastated the Jews and, like an overflowing river [Col. 0259A], overthrew all their walls, so that no stone was left upon another. This was an evident manifestation of your wrath, O God, just Judge. Although you are not angry every day, yet you are sometimes angry, though with a tranquil mind; and henceforth you are more angry when you hide your wrath from sinners. Therefore I say, “Pour out your wrath,” lest, concealed within, it grow and become fury; for anger grows into fury when gentle correction does not amend the sinner. Indeed, O God, for those whom the very present scourges change and correct, there is a most hidden flight from your wrath that presently scourges them to your mercy. But the person made worse by these scourges will at last, when the present life has ended, be seized by inescapable fury. Therefore, because I speak here of the irreformably wicked [Col. 0259B], I set anger and fury together, saying: “Pour out upon them your wrath, and let the fury of your wrath seize them,” so that those who stubbornly oppose truth and justice may be tormented alike by temporal and eternal punishments. By contrast, one who is truly penitent and sings penitential psalms, desiring to escape both wrath and fury, continually says: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your wrath, nor correct me in your fury” (Ps. 6:2); or, as the usage of another translation has it: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, nor correct me in your wrath.”

For there is no small difference between your wrath and your fury, O God, just Judge: for “when you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Hab. 3:2), and in wrath you will be mindful of mercy; but in your fury [Col. 0259C] there is no remembrance of mercy. We have an example of both in two of your past judgments which we read. When, in your wrath, you judged the man who sinned at the devil’s persuasion and expelled him from paradise, you remembered mercy: you forbade him to eat from the tree of life. For if the sinner had eaten its fruit and thereby obtained life forever, no way back to your mercy would have remained open to him, because he would have been, like the devil, unhappily immortal and immortally unhappy; for the eternity of one living miserably forever would have been a miserable eternity and eternal misery. From that misery your mercy, God the Father, then preserved him. But your fury, judging the devil in heaven and casting him down thence like lightning, remembered no mercy [Col. 0259D] toward that proud being, exalted in sins by pride alone and not tripped up by any inward frailty or outward temptation, as frail man was deceived and overthrown by him. Since, then, it is very grievous, O God, to be corrected in your wrath after the likeness of Adam the transgressor, but utterly damnable to be reproved by you in your fury after the likeness of Satan falling like lightning from heaven: the penitent person desires to escape both evils. But the devil and his members store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and revelation of your righteous judgment, O God. Wrath stored up and, as it were, heaped together rightly receives the name of fury, which admits no mercy at all, because it seizes impenitent sinners so that no place of escape lies open [Col. 0260A] from east or west or from the desert mountains. For God is judge: scarcely can anyone escape his wrath, but the fury of his wrath no one can escape in any way. Therefore I, Christ—or I, David, singing here—not by the wish of one desiring it, but by a just judgment allow both to come upon the impenitent, namely wrath and fury, saying to you, God the Father: “Pour out upon them your wrath, and let the fury of your wrath seize them.” Long ago, foretelling the future in words of the past tense, you said: “A fire is kindled in my fury, and it shall burn to the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. 32:22). Let this fury of your wrath seize them, so that, because they themselves refuse to understand in order to do good, they may at least be unable to hinder those who wish to do good.

[Col. 0260B] Otherwise: “Pour out upon them your wrath” through hidden punishments of souls, in contrast to what I desire for myself and mine when I ask for hidden deliverance, saying: “Attend to my soul and deliver it.” Likewise, just as I desire visible deliverance for my own when I say, “Rescue me because of my enemies,” so let visible fury of your wrath seize enemies hardened in their wickedness, so that others may fear when sinners are rebuked before all and likewise punished before all with manifest punishments proportionate to their guilt.

For since, while pretending to the people that they sought to preserve their place and nation, they crucified me, the Lord of place and nation, it is fitting that:

**VERSE 26. Let their habitation be desolate, and let there be none to dwell in their tents.** This occurred when the Romans came and took away their place and nation. Thus, while the Romans—although unbelievers—were fighting for God, the Jews, having lost the Temple and been deprived of the homes of the illustrious and holy city of Jerusalem, became wanderers and fugitives over the earth like another Cain, which opened its mouth and received Christ’s blood from their hands. And now, while believing Romans likewise fight for God under the authority of apostolic governance, let false Christians, and especially false clerics trafficking in the house of the Lord, be driven from the Temple by the Lord’s scourge, the Lord saying to them: “Behold, your house will be left desolate to you” (Luke 13:35). Thus let their habitation be desolate, and in their tents [Col. 0260D]—that is, their private dwellings—let there be none to dwell, lest, in their bedrooms and debaucheries, they have leisure to serve the devil, though they wish to serve God.

Otherwise: let their habitation in which they dwell bodily, namely the very Temple which they frequent for gain, and their private tents which they inhabit in the affection of their minds—whereas, conversely, they ought to dwell in the Temple in the affection of their minds and to dwell only bodily in their own private houses—be taken from them while the Romans are fighting, so that both their habitation may become deserted by them and no one of their number may dwell in their tents. Let the royal Temple and the royal and holy city be taken from them and given to a nation producing its fruits. We see this partly fulfilled: not only Jews have been cast out [Col. 0261A] from the Temple of the Lord, but clerics resembling Jews have likewise been expelled and religious worshippers of God brought in to take their place. But because this Psalm is entitled, “For the end, for those who shall be changed,” the words of this Psalm require the end of all consummation, so that what is requested in this Psalm, sung by Christ, may be fulfilled wholly at the end when it says, “Let their habitation be desolate, and let there be none to dwell in their tents”: namely, when the holy Temple, profaned and polluted by the spiritual Antiochus, has been purified. It cannot be purified unless the Jews and those like the Jews who crucify Christ have been cast out, and true observers of the true religion have been brought in. Nor is it surprising that I, Christ, naturally merciful, judge these wicked people so severely, in agreement with your just judgment, righteous Father—a judgment in which wisdom is justified by her children against these foolish and evil people who hate her, wisdom being indignant by a most just judgment.

**VERSE 27. For they persecuted him whom you struck, and added to the pain of my wounds.** You, Father, struck him—for you scourge every son whom you receive—and you made this sufficiently evident in me when you did not spare your own Son, whom you struck with mortality and other miseries, the punishments of iniquity, in order to redeem adopted sons, although I committed no iniquity. Him, then, whom you struck in this way, with the good intention of you who struck and of me who endured, they persecuted with evil intention, pressing Pilate that I might be crucified and that I, Lord of the vineyard, might be cruelly killed after being cast out of my vineyard. Afterwards, pursuing my apostles from city to city, they persecuted me most cruelly in my members, killing and crucifying some of them, stoning them, and scourging them in their synagogues, “so that upon them may come all righteous blood that has been shed, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, whom they killed between the Temple and the altar” (Matt. 23:35).

But in every shedding of righteous blood, this was the chief pain of my wounds: the enemies of truth could not be moved by the wounds either of me or of those who loved me toward the love of truth, though they saw that I and my beloved loved truth [Col. 0261D] even unto death, wounds, and every kind of torment. Though martyrs and witnesses to truth, imitators of my death—which I endured for truth, having been born for this purpose, to bear witness to the truth—could be killed, they could not be bent. They also added to the pain of my wounds in this: after my death they said to Pilate, “Lord, we remember that that deceiver said, ‘After three days I shall rise again’; command therefore that the tomb be guarded,” and so forth (Matt. 27:63–64). Thus, in persecuting me, they inflicted wounds not only upon me living, but even when I was buried they called me a deceiver. They sealed the stone with guards, whom afterward they bought with abundant money to bear false witness, abusing the treasures of the Temple against me, the Lord of the Temple. Some still imitate them [Col. 0262A]: by persecuting me in my own, they wound me with sword or harsh speech—their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword—and they also add to the pain of wounds, whether mine or my people’s, by abusing ecclesiastical goods to perpetrate evils, purchasing for themselves armed force to accomplish their wickedness. Therefore, because they thus add evils to evils, you, righteous Father and Judge:

**VERSE 28. Add iniquity to their iniquity.** Their iniquity persuades them unjustly to kill a just man, chiefly because he was opposed to their works. Upon this iniquity another was added: that they should kill the Son of God. You, Father, added this, for you sent me—whom they had killed in your messengers and servants—to be killed also by them, and permitted me to be killed. I, obedient to your will, approve this insofar as it concerns your intention, Father; but I disapprove it insofar as it concerns their intention, because they persecuted me, whom you struck, and added to the pain of my wounds by adding iniquity to iniquity, so that when I had been killed through iniquity they might likewise possess my inheritance through iniquity. Add iniquity therefore to iniquity in punishing, as you added it by permitting it to be done: so that, since I, the Lord of the vineyard, have been taken from them by equity because of iniquity, their inheritance too may likewise be taken from them by equity because of iniquity, to be entrusted to better husbandmen.

And let those who stubbornly wish to establish their own righteousness, which is from the Law, not enter into your righteousness, which is from faith. For the righteousness of faith, like a mistress, can bring one into the kingdom—or rather is itself the kingdom—as is elsewhere said: “The kingdom of God is not food or drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.” But the righteousness of the Law, like a handmaid, is to be cast out of the kingdom of God together with its followers, according to the saying: “Cast out the handmaid and her son.”

And because many, deceived by this false righteousness, think that they are written in the book of the living—that is, of the righteous:

**VERSE 29. Let them be blotted out of the book of the living**, once the truth has been disclosed that the righteous lives by faith, provided that faith itself is not dead, but lives and works through love—not by the works of legal ceremonies, but by what those ceremonies signify: for example, offering [Col. 0262D] chastity in place of a turtledove, simplicity in place of a dove, innocence together with patience in place of a lamb, and the other good works of faith working through love. Those who lack these, or, worse, do the contrary, let them be blotted out of the book of the righteous, who live by faith working through love, lest they be called or thought righteous, as they themselves think that they possess eternal life through knowledge of the Scriptures without observance of them. Therefore I, Christ, said to the Jews who glory in knowledge of the Law, and still say to those like them: “Search the Scriptures, in which you think that you have eternal life” (John 5:39). So long as they think that they have eternal life in the Scriptures, they are, in their own judgment, written in the book of life. But let this false opinion be taken away from them, so that they may understand that they are not [Col. 0263A] written in the book of life, since they do not keep the commandments of life. For if those who are written in the book of life, which is the knowledge of my foreknowledge, were written there, they would never be blotted out. Those whom I foreknew with my Father to be conformed to me, the new man created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth, will be planted together in the likeness both of my death and of my resurrection; and, themselves inscribed in me, the eternal Word inscribed in the garment of assumed humanity, they can never be blotted out of the book of life—which book, or life, I am.

Nevertheless, among those who are thought to be enrolled—because from me, Christ, they are called Christians; from me, righteousness, righteous; from me, wisdom, wise—many shall be blotted out when their iniquities are disclosed, either now or at the final judgment, and they are recognized to be foolish, unjust, and members of the devil himself or of Antichrist [Col. 0263B]. I pray that this may happen as soon as possible, to humble them and amend some from their number or through their example, lest only then they fall from my side, who think they will sit with me in judgment, or from my right hand, who think they will be placed with the lambs at the right hand and not with the goats at the left, when neither they nor others can be amended by their fall. Let them rather now be blotted out of the book of the living and fall from the number of judges, so that, their wickedness uncovered, judicial power may be taken from them; let there be no judges in the Church except those for whom a seat has been prepared by my Father, such as those to whom I said: “You who have followed me shall sit upon seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). Those, then, who will also judge angels, should now judge secular matters, so that none of my faithful people who has a dispute may be compelled to be judged before the unrighteous rather than the saints. Let my powerful enemies be cast down from the judicial seat and the humble exalted. This is now being done in particular cases; but at the end, as this Psalm is entitled “For the end,” it must be fulfilled altogether, when all who are truly unrighteous and falsely named righteous shall universally be blotted out of the book of the living. To blot some out of the book of the living is nothing other than for it to be made manifest at the divine judgment that they were never enrolled therein. Therefore, as though explaining what I said, “Let them be blotted out,” I add: “and let them not be written with the righteous,” so that those whom false righteousness pretended were written in the book of life may be shown by the truth of righteousness never to have been written in it [Col. 0263D].

Otherwise: Let them be blotted out from among the living—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—of whom God is said to be God, he who is not God of the dead but of the living. For all live who have been justified by the faith of these Fathers, just as “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15:6). Let those who oppose their faith be removed from their fellowship and not be written with the righteous Fathers of the New Testament, namely the apostles, whose faith and teaching they likewise oppose.

Otherwise: Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, which is divine foreknowledge—not because they are utterly unknown there, since God foreknows every future thing, evil as well as good—but in such a way that they are not written with the righteous: that is, they are not found among those inscribed there as righteous, but among the wicked, likewise inscribed and foreknown there for damnation, just as the righteous are foreknown for salvation. For foreknowledge embraces all, both evil and good; but predestination concerns all and only the good [Col. 0264A].

Otherwise: So long as heretics, or any followers of some perverse sect, have a name that they live when they are dead, like the angel of the Church of Sardis, to whom it was said: “You have a name that you live, but you are dead” (Rev. 3:1), they do more harm through true perversity—provoking God’s wrath against themselves and others while holding an ecclesiastical office—than they do good through feigned holiness, putting themselves forward as though they were good examples. Let them therefore be blotted out of the book of the living, first so that they may know that they are dead, repent, and [Col. 0264B] strengthen the remaining things which were about to die in them or through them. But if they obstinately remain in the worst death of sins, while yet retaining a name that they live, then lest others be deceived by such pretence, while I, Christ, judge of living and dead, diligently exercise my office in the Church, let such deceivers be blotted out of the book of the living. Thus, just as their hearts do not live by the faith through which the righteous person lives, so their names too may not live in the world, but may be recognized as dead. And as unclean carcasses are not to be eaten but cast away, so let their names—whether they are called bishops, clerics, Christians by the universal name, or rulers of the people, such as kings and princes of the world—be worthy of every rejection, with holy Church judging. But let the names of those whose hearts live in heaven live in the world; they can say with the Apostle: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Again: “And now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

### Verse 30

“I am poor and sorrowful; your salvation, O God, has upheld me.” The fifth part, in which the dispensation of the Incarnation and the fruits of the Passion are set forth. It is as though Christ himself were asked: Why will all these curses come upon this generation, which is to be erased from the book of the living? To those who say this, I, Christ, answer: precisely because I am poor and sorrowful.

For the wicked and accursed tenants deserved this because, casting me, the Lord of the vineyard, outside the vineyard, they deprived me of my inheritance, saying: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance” (Matt. 21:38). This purpose of the Jews was partly fulfilled by themselves and is partly fulfilled daily by their successors. For what they said, “Come, let us kill him,” has already been done; but what they added, “We shall have his inheritance,” they could not accomplish, because the Romans came and took away their place and nation, lest they should retain the inheritance they had seized.

But their followers—bishops sitting upon the chair of Moses, and clerics possessing holy places as though by inheritance—who also say, “Let us possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance” (Ps. 82:13), make me poor in my members. In them they neither feed me when hungry, nor give me drink when thirsty, nor clothe me when naked, nor receive me as a stranger, nor visit me when sick or imprisoned. Indeed, what is worse, they transfer the prices of sins, the patrimonies of the poor, the ransoms of souls, and the offerings of the faithful to luxury. They surpass the disgrace of that young man who, living luxuriously, squandered his substance with harlots.

For when the people of the nations, still walking in the darkness of ignorance, lived luxuriously in the passion of desire—as the nations that do not know God still do—they squandered not the possessions of the poor in their luxuries, but their own. These persons, however, worse than pagans, enriched beyond measure from the goods of the poor, live luxuriously. But I, Christ, who, though rich, became poor in order to enrich my least ones, am oppressed by extreme poverty in these same needy, distressed, afflicted persons. For behold, sinners, abounding in this world, have obtained riches that are the patrimonies of my poor. For the potter’s field—the holy land—is the field of blood, bought with the price of my blood for the burial of strangers, who have no abiding city here but seek the city to come.

But behold: while these sinners, abounding in this world and occupying almost all the field bought with the price of my blood, scarcely can my strangers and poor find burial and rest for their bodies in that very holy land which belongs to them by inheritance. Thus long ago the holy patriarch Abraham, while the Canaanites possessed the holy land promised to him and his seed and made his inheritance by promise, scarcely obtained in it a cave and the right of burial in it, by a price paid to Ephron. His name is interpreted “useless dust,” because it was to be thus: the impious, like dust which the wind casts away, would eventually be scattered by the judicial winnowing-fan, yet would occupy the holy land and act wickedly in the land of the saints, according to the saying of the prophet: “In the land of uprightness he has dealt unjustly, and he shall not see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. 26:10). For the impious shall be taken away, lest he see the glory of the Lord.

Such people are sometimes scarcely induced by payment to grant the holy children of Abraham some cave in the holy land they occupy; sometimes, indeed, they cannot be induced even by costly gifts to tolerate those who possess the right of burial beside them. Rather, they expel them from their territories and persecute them from city to city, so that every righteous blood shed by the unrighteous may come upon them.

Amid these things I, Christ, am poor and sorrowful with a twofold sorrow. I grieve with more than maternal affection for the wicked who are to perish miserably, because I wished, like a hen weakly brooding over her chicks, to gather them, and they were unwilling. And I grieve for my least ones and poor, needy and distressed, in whom I hunger and thirst, am naked and a stranger, sick and in prison; I have many causes for sorrow both from the abundance of enemies and from the excessive want of my poor.

But amid these straits of poverty and sorrow, this is a consolation to me and mine: your salvation, O God, has upheld me. Your salvation—of which I said above, “Hear me in the truth of your salvation”—has upheld me, Christ, in my own person, so that I am not only saved in myself, but also the salvation of the people who believe in me; for whoever believes in me shall be saved, but whoever does not believe shall be condemned.

Likewise: Your salvation, O God, has upheld me, David, or any humble and penitent person following my example, so that I may first hear my Savior say to me, languishing and lying upon the pallet of weak flesh: “Rise and walk” (Matt. 9:5); likewise, “Take up your pallet and go to your house” (Mark 2:11). Therefore I, Christ, in myself and in my members—

### Verse 31

“I will praise the name of God who saves me,” whether he gives or takes away the things outside me. For I say, praising his name: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has come to pass: blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

I shall make such praise frequently, not with grief brought on by outward things taken away, but with a song of joy over the inalienable gladness of salvation and hope, which no one shall take from me. For I also, Christ—whose soul was sorrowful unto death in the Passion, and who was poor and sorrowful before death—now, death’s rule having been conquered, enjoy everlasting joy. And all who are mine, though at times sorrowful in circumstance, nevertheless rejoicing in hope, are patient in tribulation and humble amid prosperity, so that neither adverse things which test them break them nor favorable things which console them exalt them. For, having now entered by hope into their Lord’s joy, into which they shall afterwards enter in reality, they find it sweet, amid adversities soon to end, not so much to weep as to sing, knowing that, planted together in the likeness of my Passion, they shall also share my Resurrection.

Therefore in them, amid both adversity and prosperity, “I will praise the name of God with a song,” rejoicing, that is, in the treasure of a good conscience, as in oil stored in the vessels of their hearts. “And I will magnify him with praise,” with the lamps of good works burning and shining before men, so that they may see their good works and glorify the Father of lights and author of those shining works. Thus, while I praise God with a song and magnify him with praise, the sacrifice of praise shall honor God.

### Verse 32

“And it shall please God more than a young bullock producing horns and hoofs,” such as was offered in the Law for the sin of a priest or of the multitude; for to God the sacrifice of praise with devotion of heart is more pleasing than the sacrifice of a brute animal.

Nor without reason were irrational animals sought for sacrifice to God, since by them were prefigured rational human beings to be sacrificed and sanctified to God: for example, the innocent in lambs, the obedient in oxen. A bullock producing horns and hoofs, although not yet fit for the yoke, which signifies perfect obedience, nevertheless, while with its horns it tosses its adversaries and with its hoofs stirs the earth—being hot with the ardor of youth and in some sense impatient—it gives confidence to those feeding it that such a bullock may become a strong ox, fit to bear the yoke.

[Col. 0267A] Such a bullock, producing horns and hoofs, was Moses in Egypt, when still a young man he struck an Egyptian quarrelling with a Hebrew, as though with the horns of just vengeance. He also stirred the ground as though with hoofs when, on the next day, he urged two Hebrews striving with one another toward brotherly peace, saying: “Brothers, why do you wrong one another?” (Acts 7:26).

And indeed God was pleased with this sort of bullock, producing horns and hoofs. Yet more than this young bullock producing horns and hoofs, he was pleased with the same bullock when it had become a great ox, brought back into Egypt in the cords of obedience at the Lord’s sending. Joined to his brother Aaron as to another ox, Moses performed such great tillage throughout Egypt that the seed of God’s word scattered there in the hearts of hearers wrought a great judgment: not one Egyptian struck as though by calf’s horns, nor one Hebrew thus freed, but, through the mature gravity of an ox, the whole land of Egypt ploughed and the entire Hebrew people liberated from it.

Hence this ox, as though with a mighty lowing, praised God with a song and magnified him with praise, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. 15:1). This song of praise pleased God more than the young bullock which Moses himself had represented when, moved by zeal for justice, he struck one Egyptian—not bound to do this by the tightened cord of obedience or the yoke of the Lord’s command—as, when commanded by the Lord, he divided the sea, through whose midst he led God’s people while Pharaoh and his army were drowned.

I too, Christ, as a bullock producing horns and hoofs, stirred the earth as though with hoofs when, still twelve years old, sitting among the teachers in the Temple, I made them attentive by my questions, so that they were astonished at my wisdom and answers. Since they themselves were earthly, they were thereby stirred to meditate upon heavenly things. Thus through many parables I stirred their earthly minds to seek truth.

At times also I tossed my brutish adversaries with horns, openly rebuking them without parables; for example, when I overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves, saying to them: “It is written: My house is a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of robbers” (Luke 19:46). Likewise: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who tithe mint and dill and every herb, and pass over the weightier matters of the Law—mercy, justice, and faith” (Matt. 23:23).

In saying such things and performing wonderful works, I was likened to a young bullock producing horns and hoofs. I do not say, “having horns,” but “producing” them; because, while horns grow, they increase day by day, just as I, while still a young bullock, advanced in wisdom, age, and grace before God and men.

Likewise, another of my young bullocks producing horns and hoofs was the youth named Saul. He grew stronger and stronger, and the little horns by which, while still breathing threats and slaughter against my disciples, he had formerly abused, he was then using rightly against my enemies. Many bullocks in this manner toss adversaries with their horns and stir the earth with their hoofs, by casting down the adversaries of truth and urging those who think earthly thoughts toward the understanding of heavenly things.

And indeed such a bullock pleases God, to whom all good things are pleasing. Yet more than a young bullock producing horns and hoofs, God is pleased with that ox-like maturity by which the Lord’s easy yoke is gently borne and God is praised in a song of joy, in such peace that neither an adversary needs to be tossed nor a sluggard stirred. This peace belongs to people of good will gathered into one, for whom it is good and pleasant to dwell together in unity. But this peace cannot be full and perfect in this pilgrimage: here it must be begun, and in God’s future kingdom it shall be completed.

In that kingdom I, Christ, having already won the triumph, exalted beyond the choirs of angels, death conquered and crowned with glory and honor, shall no longer be called a young bullock still to be sacrificed, for death shall no longer have dominion over me, but a lion or an eagle. I shall praise the name of God with a song and magnify him with praise.

I shall praise and magnify him in myself, who am a “joyful psaltery” in spirit, “with a harp” (Ps. 80:3) of flesh mortified in the Passion but glorified in the Resurrection. I shall praise him in the angels; I shall praise him in the churches. I shall confess among the nations and sing psalms among the peoples, while I make them sing, confess, and praise—those whom I shall unite to myself through faith, hope, and charity. And this sacrifice of praise in me and mine shall please God more than a young bullock producing horns and hoofs.

Certainly such a sacrifice is not that of the poor but of the rich; not of the weak but of the strong—such as Moses when he struck the Egyptian, Peter when he struck the servant of the chief priests, and Stephen, full of the tenderness and richness of a calf and also of the strength of horns that toss even strong bulls. But “the sacrifice of praise shall honor me” (Ps. 94:23), and my Father: a sacrifice which both poor and rich, weak and strong, can offer. Indeed, it is more acceptable from the hands of the poor and weak when, following the example of that poor widow who put all her livelihood into the offering-box, they spend all that they live by, know, and are able to do in praise of God’s name, reserving nothing of themselves for themselves and never separating their own will from the divine will, but subjecting themselves and all that is theirs to God’s obedience.

### Verse 33

“Let the poor see and rejoice.” For even if they cannot offer bullocks, let them now be poor in spirit; if they praise God in their poverty, they will please God more than a young bullock producing horns and hoofs.

Let the poor, therefore, rejoice, because the offering is now placed not in resources but in the mind, where the poor person is equal to the rich. Let the poor, to whom good news is proclaimed by these sayings, believe them—chiefly, indeed solely, those who remain poor, whether by lacking riches or by not setting their hearts upon abundance, and who do not exalt themselves at all either for their abundance of passing possessions or their store of virtues.

You poor, therefore, keep watch over your poverty in such a manner that, if you belch forth any signs of pride, the bread of life may not be denied you. It shall be given to those who seek, ask, and knock perseveringly, but shall be denied to those who boast in their own strength. Seek God, the bread of life, the life-giving bread, and your soul shall live by him. “He who eats this bread shall live forever” (John 6:59). Seek this bread, O poor, and your soul shall live.

Examples are not lacking for the assertion which I, the Psalmist—or I, Christ, in my Passion, reckoned with the poor, indeed even with the wicked—make. In my poverty I prayed and was heard by the Father, who is always ready to hear the poor crying to him. This is made clear from what follows:

### Verse 34

“For the Lord has heard the poor, and has not despised his prisoners.” He heard our fathers, the children of Israel, crying to him as poor in the land of Egypt, and he did not despise them, prisoners under Pharaoh’s power. Prisoners, I say, under an alien lordship, but nevertheless his servants through faith.

For there are prisoners who are not his—namely demons, dragged from heavenly brightness and held bound in the dark air by the cords of hell until the last judgment, when they are to be thrust into the prison of lower hell. The Lord will not free them, because they are not his prisoners. Unlike those who, when I, Christ, descended into hell, cried to me: “You have come, O Desired One, whom we awaited in darkness, to lead forth tonight the bound from their prison-cells.”

The Lord certainly did not despise these his prisoners. As he once sent Moses to free the children of Israel from Egyptian darkness, so now, at the end of the ages, he sent me to free his prisoners—not only from the darkness of infernal punishments, but, a still greater cause of joy, from two chains, those of sins and punishments. As a sign of this, Peter too, one of my prisoners, was “bound with two chains” (Acts 12:5–6) in the prison of the enemy, the wicked Herod. But because prayer was made by the Church to God for him, the Lord heard the poor and did not despise his prisoner: his prisoner, because he was imprisoned for him; his prisoner, because he hoped in him, trusting that he would not abandon him in chains until he brought him the scepter of the kingdom and power over those who oppressed him.

Moreover, because *Herod* is interpreted “of skin,” by which name the devil is fittingly signified, through whose contrivance it came about that the human race, first stripped of the robe of innocence, had to be clothed in garments of skin. These signify the frailty of human mortality, since garments of skin are made only from the skins of dead animals.

Thus in Peter, captured under Herod’s power, is rightly understood the Church strengthened by Peter’s faith, or any faithful person constrained by the bonds of human mortality. For her, while she is thus a pilgrim on earth under the power of this world’s prince and labors in the bonds of miserable flesh, the heavenly Church—free from these bonds in the angels and delivered in the souls of the just—prays earnestly. It is as when prayer was made by the Church to God for Peter bound in prison.

The soldiers of this Herod signify demons and wicked human beings. From their hands and custody all good people, alike to blessed Peter in faith, shall be delivered, so that each of them, released from this life’s prison-house, may rejoice with blessed Peter, saying: “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the Jewish people” (Acts 12:11).

By the people of the faithless Jews may be understood the multitude of demons who confess Christ, the Son of God. For, as we have in the Gospel, demons rebuked by his command and compelled to come out confessed him to be the Son of God; “but he, rebuking them, did not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ” (Luke 4:41).

The expectation of these Jews—that is, of the demons—is great concerning every faithful and righteous person. Their prince, the devil, promises them that after Passover, that is, after the passing of this mortal life, he will bring such a person out for them to afflict and mock. Against them the righteous person who lives by faith prays in another psalm: “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, I trust in you: let me not be put to shame, nor let my enemies mock me” (Ps. 24:1–3).

The power of such prayer therefore obtains from God that he does not despise his prisoners, but delivers them from the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the Jewish people. With blessed Peter he sometimes honors them in this present life; but much more and more perfectly he makes them glad in eternal life, so that their joy may be full and no one may take their joy from them. Concerning these most abundant benefits of God’s grace:

### Verse 35

“Let the heavens and the earth praise him, the sea and every creeping thing in them.” Let the heavens praise him by declaring God’s glory: first the angels, then the apostles, holy martyrs and confessors, and all the perfect who, according to heaven’s height, are raised above the earth. Let the earth praise him, that is, the Church of believing Jews; and the sea, that is, the Church gathered from the nations, which surrounds Judea everywhere as the sea surrounds land.

Let the stars, the ground, and the sea rejoice, and let every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth bend at Jesus’ name. Let heaven exult with praises; let earth resound with joys. Let the angelic host of heaven now exult, let the divine mysteries exult, and let the saving trumpet sound for the victory of the supreme King. Let the earth rejoice, irradiated by such splendors; illuminated by the brightness of the eternal King, may it perceive that the darkness of the whole world has been removed.

Let mother Church also rejoice, adorned with the splendors of so great a light, while the Lord hears the poor and does not despise his prisoners, saving on earth and in the sea his living creatures animated by the spirit of life: not only walking creatures, by which active persons are signified; or flying creatures, by which contemplative persons are signified; but also creeping things, by which weak and imperfect persons are signified, as though clinging to the earth and abominable in monstrous forms.

[Col. 0271A] Of all these it was said to Peter: “Slay, slay, and eat” (Acts 10:13), so that holy mother Church, strengthened by Peter’s faith and founded upon the rock which is Christ, may receive even such persons into her body. Therefore let not only the heavens and birds beneath the heavens praise him, but also the earth, the sea, and every creeping thing in them.

### Verse 36

“For God will save Zion,” that is, the Church increased by creeping things also gathered into one. God, eternally just and holy, temporally justifies and sanctifies the earth, the sea, and every creeping thing in them, and in this way will save Zion with everlasting salvation. From such persons, polished by the hammer of temptations and tribulations, the cities of Judah shall be built—that is, the churches of Christ, born from the tribe of Judah, in whom all the cities of Judah ought to believe unto righteousness and confess unto salvation.

The whole Church is one city of Judah, of which the bride says: “I will rise and go about the city; I will seek him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:2). Likewise: “The watchmen who keep the city found me” (Song 3:3). But this one city has many narrow lanes and many broad streets, because, passing through narrow and broad ways, it contains many persons distinguished by diverse ranks and vocations.

Therefore they shall dwell there not as guests and strangers in pilgrimage, but as fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household, abiding steadfastly: not only the great, but also little ones likened to creeping things. And they shall acquire Zion by inheritance—or, when they reach the heavenly Jerusalem, they shall acquire it by inheritance—being adopted from servants into sons, so that they may indeed be heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ. Hence the Apostle: “If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. 3:29). Likewise: “If sons, then heirs” (Rom. 8:17), namely of the heavenly city, of which it is here said: “They shall acquire it by inheritance,” or, as some manuscripts have, “They shall acquire the inheritance.”

Nor shall only sons, who are perfect, possess it; even servants, although imperfect—of whom it is said, “Your eyes saw my imperfection, and all shall be written in your book” (Ps. 138:16)—shall possess it. And, what is more remarkable, even—

### Verse 37

“His servants’ seed shall possess it.” Since the imperfect may be understood under “servants,” and under “the seed of God’s servants” even weaker persons among the imperfect, all of them shall possess by inheritance the land of the living, liberated through Christ’s Passion, which has been recounted in this psalm, from the land of the dying—if only they love his name. He says: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14:15). And lest you should be ignorant of what the commandments are: “This,” he says, “I command you: that you love one another” (John 15:17).

These commandments are not burdensome to one who is willing, though they seem burdensome to one unwilling. They are not burdensome but light and pleasant to those who love the Lord of this city and inheritance and its citizens. Therefore, at the conclusion of this psalm, I, David the prophet, exhort you: because God first loved you with that charity than which no one has greater, you also should love his name and the citizens of his city, and, according to your ability, defend the rights, laws, and discipline of his city. Where ability is lacking, let willingness not be absent, for to will much is to love.

Hence peace belongs to people of good will, that is, of true love, which is twofold: love for the Lord of the eternal city and for its citizens. For no others shall be its citizens except those who love the Lord’s name and the beauty of his house. Therefore let this psalm end here, in the Lord’s name: those who love his name shall dwell in that city which he who was born in it, the Most High, founded. He who was born and suffered in it as a little one, the same Most High founded it, laying its foundations upon holy and lofty mountains; he himself became the mountain of mountains, the summit of the mountains, the foundation of foundations bearing the entire edifice.

Glory to God the Father, to whom God the Son, made man, speaks in this psalm: “Save me, O God,” etc. Glory to God the Son, Jesus Christ, who thus prays for himself and his members, to be delivered and saved from the storm. Glory to God the Holy Spirit, who is that love and salvation by which God shall save Zion, and by which whoever loves his name shall dwell in it. As glory belonged to him in the beginning, in his glorious predestination—“Glorious things have been said of you, city of God”—so in the fulfillment of predestination let glory be his now and always and unto ages of ages. Amen.

## Psalm 69

[Col. 0271D] “O God, attend to my help.” This psalm, like the preceding one, is sung in the person of Christ for the instruction of every faithful person, so that he too may pray and labor in hope whenever he is wearied by various temptations from enemies seeking his life. Its title is:

### Verse 1

**“Unto the end, a psalm of David, in remembrance because the Lord saved him.”**

“Christ is the end unto righteousness for everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). Likewise David is Christ, to whom the words of this psalm are directed as to the end, as to their final cause. Whoever prays here is understood as the head for his members: King David for himself and his soldiers; the good shepherd for his sheep, partly saved and partly still to be saved.

Hence is added: “In remembrance because the Lord saved him,” that is, in consideration of the fact that the Lord saved him. This remembrance occurs in two ways. Either, remembering our sins, we fear the coming judgment, as in Psalm 37, which is sung “in remembrance of the Sabbath”; or, retaining the promised goods in memory, we conceive confidence concerning our salvation, which is to be completed unto the end. This is the sense here, as is shown by the addition, “because the Lord saved him.”

For it was fitting that, after Christ our head had in the preceding psalm narrated his Passion and added words concerning the hope of the Resurrection—in the voices and cries of his own person, and in the power of his blood crying from the earth, that is, from the holy Church which opened its mouth in confession of faith and received him from the murderous hands of the Jews—he should now, in this following psalm, set forth in the voices and cries of his members their sufferings, and at the same time join to them the hope of their resurrection and deliverance. For example, at the psalm’s end it is said: “Be my helper and my deliverer, O Lord; do not delay.”

Thus this is the voice of the afflicted, struggling and endangered with Christ amid sufferings and temptations, yet trusting in their head: both martyrs and other righteous persons who, because of their love for truth—which does not rejoice in iniquity—are afflicted and saddened when truth and justice themselves are oppressed by liars and wicked persons. Such was the affliction of Lot, a lover of righteousness, among the Sodomites, who, as the apostle Peter says, “afflicted the soul of the righteous man by their wicked deeds” (2 Pet. 2:8). Of people like these the prophet says: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom” (Isa. 3:9).

For such persons are not ashamed when, on the forehead where Christ’s sign had been impressed, they bear the mark of the beast, that is, Antichrist. Therefore it is prayed that they may be converted and ashamed; for so long as they are not ashamed, they themselves, evil and shameless in their wickedness, afflict and persecute the good. The devil, the many-formed traitor, who is a lion in his assault and a dragon in his snares, stirs up this persecution against the righteous.

Accordingly, in the first part of the psalm prayer is made against the violences of the lion, where it is said: “Let those who desire evils for me be confounded and ashamed”; and against the snares of the softly hissing dragon, where it is said: “Let those who say to me, ‘Aha, aha!’ be turned back immediately, ashamed.” In the second part, however, the good are admonished to exult and rejoice: God both helps them as they fight in the contest and eventually crowns them as victors delivered from the contest. The intention of the singer is also plain in the words: “Let all who seek you exult and rejoice in you.”

Thus Christ himself, afflicted, cries out for his own and in his own. The often-mentioned combatant also cries out amid temptations and tribulations, he who fights throughout this fiftyfold sequence against the law of the members.

### Verse 2

“God,” he says, “attend to my help.” O God, who sees and knows all things, attend to my help, knowing and seeing that I can do nothing by human strength: neither against the law of the members opposing the law of my mind and at times leading me captive under the law of sin and death, nor against the violence or deceit of evil angels and human beings.

Therefore you, who shine by the splendor of your divinity even in the darkness—although the darkness does not comprehend you, because you see even those who do not see you—now, in the time of conflict, attend to my help in your good will, as you know and will, having mercy on me endangered in this protracted struggle. If you delay too long in helping, I cannot endure or stand. Therefore I say, O Lord: “Hasten to help me.”

O Lord, ruler of heaven and earth, against whose sovereign power nothing can resist, hasten to help me. Come swiftly, O Father, to aid me, Christ your Son, laboring and afflicted in my members, as I said to Saul: “Why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4), although I suffered no persecution in myself, but in my members. For as long as one of my least ones is afflicted, I, though now incapable of suffering, sympathize with these least ones of mine. Therefore I do not say, “Attend to the help of mine,” but “Attend to my help”; nor do I say, “Hasten to help mine,” but “Hasten to help me.”

Alternatively: I, David—that is, any penitent like David—unable to resist the tyranny of Saul, that is, sin reigning or seeking to reign in my mortal body, flee to you, O God, saying: “God, attend to my help; O Lord, hasten to help me.” The devil, chief over death, with his followers, intends to destroy me; but you attend to helping me. Attend, O God, because of the goodness of your divinity; hasten, O Lord, because of the invincible power of your lordship, to help me, lest I be pierced by sin’s sting as by Saul’s spear, or ever fall into his hands or those of his followers.

### Verse 3

Rather, “let those who persecute me be confounded, and let me not be confounded; let them be terrified, and let me not be terrified” (Jer. 17:18). Let them be confounded, ashamed that they began the tower of pride when they cannot finish it. Let them be confounded by the division of their tongues, so that they cease from building the tower raised against you, O Lord and God, who attend and hasten to help the poor, one of whom I am, as I shall say at the end of this psalm: “But I am needy and poor; O God, help me.”

Let them be confounded, troubled by their perversity and hindered in their attempts; and let them revere in fear, lest punishment follow the injury done to justice. Through fear of this punishment, let them become ashamed by accusing their own sins—those who formerly, by defending them or boasting in them, were glorious in their own eyes. Let them be confounded and revere: confounded at their frustrated evil designs, and revering those whom their evil designs have exercised and crowned.

Thus Joseph’s brothers are read to have been clothed with both shame and reverence: shame with respect to their frustrated evil designs, and reverence with respect to the good which came from them when God turned to good what they had intended for evil. Thus, ashamed by the accusation of conscience, they said: “We suffer these things deservedly, because we sinned against our brother” (Gen. 42:21); and, revering their brother’s power, they bowed to the ground, showing him reverence. So may all my enemies—whether enemies of me, Christ, or of any poor and needy person—be clothed with shame and reverence. Let those who seek to take my life by death in a time of openly raging persecution be confounded and revere.

### Verse 4

“Let those who desire evils for me also be turned backward and ashamed,” in a time of peace, when they do not dare openly display the evils that they hold in their will against me.

Let them be turned backward, so that those who live by their own judgment and refuse to follow the footsteps of the saints, but as though go before those whose teaching they despise, may no longer go before but follow, living not by their own counsel but by that of the saints.

Let them be turned backward, like that blessed woman who, ashamed and blushing for her sins, came from behind and washed with tears the feet of him by whom she herself was to be washed (Matt. 9:20). Or like the woman with the flow of blood, *haimorroousa* (αἱμοῤῥοοῦσα), who, after vainly spending all her substance on false physicians, afterwards approached the true physician from behind and touched the fringe of his garment (Matt. 14:36). Or let them be converted backward, as was said to Peter: “Follow me”; or as was said universally: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (ibid., 16:24).

Alternatively: Let them turn backward, as Mary in the garden turned backward and saw Jesus standing—whom she had supposed not to be standing alive, but lying dead. Let them turn backward by reflecting on ancient days and eternal years, in which Jesus existed before he came into the world; and let them know that he ascended bodily to that place where he was before in his divinity. Otherwise it will be said to them: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father”—that is, in relation to your scant faith, by which you seek me by night upon the bed of the sepulchre. For now that I have entered the palace of my kingdom, I am not so confined within the narrowness of a single place that I cannot be at once in heaven and on earth even by bodily presence, as the salvation of those for whom my humanity [Col. 0275D] was assumed, by virginal conception, into the person of my divinity requires; and this humanity has now, through the glory of the resurrection, been assumed into the glory of that same divinity. Hence my body also has this glory: assumed into heaven and not abandoning heavenly things, it fills earthly altars throughout the Church extended over the whole world. Therefore, let those who seek me in the sepulchre of one place in such a manner that I cannot be bodily present in several places at one and the same time turn backward; and, with me as teacher, let them learn that I have not yet ascended to my Father for them. Let them go also to my brothers and learn from them what this means: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (Job XX, 17).

Certainly, for the man assumed into the Son of God—that is, so that he may be the Son of God—to ascend to [Col. 0276A] his Father is nothing other than to enter into the glory of his Father; nor, for the man assumed into God—that is, so that he may be God—to ascend to his God is anything other than to be glorified with that glory which God possessed eternally in his divinity. Let those who do not yet believe these things turn backward with Mary and learn what they still do not know concerning the glory of the Lord’s ascension.

Let them also turn backward, as those fell backward who seized me to put me to death—those in whom, against me and mine, though the power to harm is lacking, there is nevertheless the will of obstinate malice, who wish evil to me. Let such persons turn backward through humiliation, since they never wish to fall upon their faces through voluntary humility. Therefore let them first fall backward through at least a compelled [Col. 0276B] humiliation, so that, humbled in this way, they may learn not to blaspheme, not to be puffed up, not to exalt themselves; but may freely grow accustomed to humble themselves beneath the mighty hand of God, so as to deserve to be exalted in the time of visitation.

Note the different periods in the Church. At first there was the assault of persecuting tyrants, whence he said above: “Those who seek my life.” But now, open persecution having ceased, there remains the ill will of those who devise evil. Hence here he says: “Those who wish,” or “those who devise evil against me.” Again, it must be noted that there are two kinds of persecutors: those who revile and those who flatter; and the tongue of the flatterer persecutes more than the sword of the persecutor. For both reviling and praise are fire: as gold is tested by fire, so the hearer is tested by reviling and praise [Col. 0276C].

Therefore blessed is the person who, lest he enter the furnace of this fire, is heard while praying not to enter—or be led into—temptation; so fully delivered from this evil that he is not tempted in such matters by remaining unmoved among revilers and praisers, not going in the counsel either of sinners, of those who frighten, or of those who flatter. Such a person, as though outside the furnace, does not feel the burning fire of the king of Babylon.

But suppose he enters—or is led into—this fire, namely by feeling the blaze of a burning tongue when he is tempted by praise or reproach. Let him nevertheless beware of being so bent or broken by either that he departs from the straightness of truth and justice. Rather, with the three youths in the midst of the furnace, let him praise God and pray, invoking his help; and God will make the midst of the furnace for him like a wind blowing with dew.

King Herod, touched by this fire, when the people shouted measured praises to him, did not give honor to God, taking delight in being praised himself rather than God. Therefore, struck by an angel, he rotted and died swarming with worms. Dangerous, then, is the fire of the reviling tongue, after the manner of those who seek my life, who wish and devise evil against me.

But much more dangerous is the fire of the flattering tongue, after the manner of those who say to me, “Well done, well done.” Therefore, praying against those who seek my life, or who wish and devise evil against me, I did indeed say: “Let them be confounded and ashamed; let them turn backward”; but I did not immediately add “at once,” because among revilers patience is sometimes exercised, pride checked, and guilt cleansed away [Col. 0277A].

King David experienced this, when he was at one time cursed by a wicked servant. Yet he did not regard the accumulated insult, because he foresaw grace. Hence he forbade anyone to restrain the reviler, reckoning curses as gain: “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah?” he said. And he added: “The Lord has sent him to curse David” (2 Sam. 16:10). O truly a man after God’s heart: on hearing the reviler, he did not at once allow silence to be imposed upon him, but judged that anger should be directed against the one taking vengeance rather than against the one reproaching him. Indeed, he was after God’s heart, for he carried in his own heart a judgment from God’s heart. A cursing tongue raged, while he considered what God was doing in secret. The voice of the reviler was in his ears, and his spirit inclined itself toward blessing [Col. 0277B].

Was God in the mouth of the blasphemer? Far from it! Rather, God used him to humble David. Nor was this hidden from the Prophet, to whom God had revealed the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom. Therefore in another psalm he says: “It is good for me that you have humbled me, that I may learn your ordinances” (Ps. 118:71 [119:71]). And here, praying that such revilers may turn backward, he did not immediately add “at once,” desiring to be humbled through such people before they turn backward, because humiliation is the way to humility in the heart of the faithful person who says: “It is good for me, Lord, that you have humbled me, that I may learn your ordinances.”

Do you see that humility justifies us? I said humility, not humiliation. How many are humiliated who are not humble! Some are humiliated with resentment [Col. 0277C], bearing it indignantly when reproached or troubled in other ways. Others bear these things patiently; others willingly. The first are guilty, the second innocent, the last righteous. Yet innocence too is a portion of righteousness, but its perfection is found in the humble person. But one who can say, “It is good for me, because you have humbled me,” is truly humble. The unwilling sufferer cannot say it, still less the one who murmurs. We do not promise grace to either because he is humiliated, although these two are indeed far apart: one possesses his soul in patience, the other perishes in murmuring. But although one escapes wrath, neither earns grace, because God gives grace not to the humiliated but to the humble. Therefore may true and sincere humility be established in me, your servant, O my God [Col. 0277D].

VERSE 5. Let all who seek you exult and rejoice in you. Seeing good works in me, let them glorify not me but you—they who seek you, having first been sought by you. For you first sought them, and descended in order to carry the lost sheep. Therefore, with the adversaries confounded and turned away, let all who seek you exult and rejoice in you—in you through whom those who were once darkness have become light—those who love your salvation, your Son, by whom and in whom alone salvation exists. Therefore, loving him, let them always say: “Let the Lord be magnified.”

Whoever among them says from his whole heart, “My soul magnifies the Lord” (Luke 1:46), does not thereby cause him to grow in himself through praises; for he is the Sun of righteousness, without any deficiency or increase. But while we advance by praising him and are enlightened more and more from day to day, we are magnified in him and he in us. Desiring this, we pray that the Lord may always be magnified by multiplying and magnifying such servants as may fittingly call him Lord and friend, and to whom he may say: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15) [Col. 0278A].

For those deserve to be called friends not who fear slavishly, but who love your salvation with filial love. Should not he be loved who first loved us?—who calls the sinner, justifies the confessor, directs the one living righteously, and glorifies the one who perseveres? For those whom he calls, he also justifies; and those whom he justifies, he also magnifies, removing them from vices and enriching them with virtues.

VERSE 6. But I am needy and poor beyond all whom I know to be needy and poor. For even if [Col. 0278B] there is anyone in humankind poorer than I, I do not know him, just as I know my own poverty: “I am the man who sees my poverty” (Lam. 3:1). These words of Jeremiah lamenting and confessing his poverty also suit me, David the penitent, because I too, a man who sees my poverty, confess that I am needy and poor. My conscience testifies that my need is so great, in that I lack many things, and my poverty so great, in that I do not possess the things I need, that by my own judgment I find myself poorer than all the poor whom I know in this world. Among the poor invited to God’s supper, I scarcely dare, and only with trembling, claim the last place for myself, because I am needier and poorer than all the guests invited [Col. 0278C].

For it is not mine to judge that those outside are poor, since from the abundance of their riches they excuse themselves from coming to the supper, whether by buying a farm, buying five yoke of oxen, or indeed marrying a wife. The supper is prepared only for the needy and poor, among whom I am one. Although I know that I am invited with the other poor, I do not know whether I am chosen. And although in my mind I consent to God’s law, I nevertheless do not obey perfectly in all things, because I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin and death. Therefore, unhappy man that I am, needy and poor in this body of death, I need a helper most strong, wise, and kind against the enemies who seek my life, who wish and devise evil [Col. 0278D] against me, who say to me, “Well done, well done.”

I continually say: “God, help me; you are my helper and my deliverer. O Lord, do not delay.” As at the beginning, so at the end of the psalm the subject is God’s assistance, so that the golden meaning of this psalm may be like a circle returning upon itself—a circle by which, as by a bracelet, the jaw of Leviathan is pierced. His members are those who seek my life and devise evil against me, who say to me, “Well done, well done,” so that they may devour me and incorporate me into themselves. And they would do so unless, by divine help, I found an escape from their mouth.

So the circle of divine help placed in the nostrils of the king of Assyria will frustrate the cunning of his counsels, so that he is caught as a fool and brought back by the way by which he came. For he came against me, David, through envy in order to harm me, but he will be brought back to greater envy when he sees all his schemes, aimed at my evil, through the constantly invoked divine help, to have resulted in such great and evident goods for me that, as they shine forth and demonstrate that God has attended to help me and hastened to assist me, those who wish evil to me may be confounded and turn backward; and those who say to me, “Well done, well done,” may immediately turn away [Col. 0279A].

Let them, I say, turn away blushing at once, because by their flatteries, saying to me, “Well done, well done,” they wished to build in me a tower of pride; but they could not finish it, since God attended to help me and hastened to assist me. When they perceived this, they immediately turned away.

Yet there is not immediately an end either of temptations or of tribulations, as long as I, David—I, penitent and humble like David—am still mortal and sold under sin, filled with many miseries, not knowing whether I am worthy of hatred or love; though I trust in the help of the Most High, I nevertheless regard the frailty of my weak body with suspicion. For though the spirit is willing, the flesh is weak and needs help most strong and continual. Therefore I say: “God, help me.” And rightly do I say it, because I have hope in no other but you, who are my helper in the conflict, that I may conquer, and my deliverer from the conflict, that I may freely serve you alone—to whom to serve is to reign and to be free. Conversely, whoever does not serve you becomes the slave of as many masters as he has vices [Col. 0279B].

[Col. 0279C] Therefore I rightly flee from vices as from most cruel masters to you, my God, because you are my helper and my deliverer, O Lord; only do not delay. That is, in my expectation, increase my patience together with the desire for your coming, your consolation, your help, and your deliverance. For if I await through patience what I hope for, I shall be like those people waiting for their lord when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him at once.

But if I am impatient, while the bridegroom delays, I may, drowsing or sleeping, be deprived of that blessedness by which those servants are blessed whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching. Or certainly—what must more greatly be both feared and guarded against—I may, from excessive weariness at the delay, look backward like Lot’s wife. She was changed into a pillar of salt for this purpose: that she might season me, lest, becoming tasteless and foolish, I look backward or return in heart to Egypt [Col. 0280A]. I may become like those who, wearied with excessive tedium, remembered the Egyptian pots and meats and sought luxuries on the way which they should patiently and long-sufferingly have awaited, promised and reserved for them in their homeland.

They were heard, indeed, but to their harm; for while the food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God rose against them and killed their stoutest. Many other evils also befell them because of their impatience, which should not be recalled in this psalm entitled “for the memorial of salvation.” These things, however, are recalled so that, through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures, we may always possess enduring hope—content with the goods and provisions for the journey while on the way, and awaiting greater things in the homeland—lest the delay of the times, which the Father has put in his own power, seem so long or tedious that, broken by weariness, we fail on the way [Col. 0280B].

But who is sufficient for these things? Is not the flesh weak even when the spirit is willing? Therefore, O my God, both at the beginning of the psalm, that you may hasten to help me, and now at its end, I pray: “O Lord, do not delay.” For unless the evil days are shortened by your swift help, no flesh will be saved. Yet I do not cast my prayers down before your face on the ground of my own justifications; rather, on account of your many mercies, I ask you to hasten to my help and not to delay, having heard the prayers of your Church crying to you and saying: “God, attend to help me.” Again: “Do not delay for your own sake, O God; incline your ear and behold our tribulation” [Col. 0280C]. Again: “Return, my beloved; be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of Bethel” (Song 2:17), leaping and running swiftly. Rejoice as a giant to run your course to help me; do not delay in running and coming to the aid of me, poor and needy, for my consolation and for your glorification.

Glory to God the Father, who attends to help me. Glory to the Son, the Lord who hastens to assist me. Glory to the Holy Spirit, the Lord, my helper and deliverer, because, as the apostle Paul says, “The Spirit helps our weakness” (Rom. 8:26); and, “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17). Glory to the one and triune God, who attends to deliver from evils and to help in good things. Amen.

## PSALM LXX

[Col. 0279]

[Col. 0279D] “In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be confounded.” The words of this psalm are plainly the words of the often-mentioned warrior, set in battle, retaining hope and professing hope. “In you, O Lord, I have hoped,” he says, “let me never be confounded.” And thereafter: “For you are my patience, O Lord; O Lord, my hope from my youth” [Col. 0280D]. Again: “But I will always hope, and will add to all your praise.”

Certainly, in the words, “My God, deliver me from the hand of the sinner and from the hand of the one acting against the law and of the unjust,” the devil is readily understood, at whose prompting that discord takes place whereby the law of sin [Col. 0281A] in the members resists the law of the mind. Indeed, the chief singer and foremost teacher of this prayer is Christ himself, the head and leader of those who contend lawfully. He prays that he may here be delivered from the hand of the Jewish people acting against the law, and of the unjust Roman empire, by that same justice or divinity whereby he is able also to deliver those who are tempted. Finally, its title is as follows:

VERSE 1. A PSALM OF DAVID, OF THE SONS OF JONADAB AND OF THE FIRST CAPTIVES.

And the sense is this: This psalm is Christ’s, because in this psalm he both speaks and speaks about himself. It is also of the sons of Jonadab, because here the Lord speaks about them, the sons who were captives first. Hence it is also called “of the first captives.” Jonadab is appropriately added here both in respect to the matter and to the interpretation of the name [Col. 0281B].

In respect to the matter: just as Jonadab the priest commanded his sons to abstain from wine and to live in tents, so our Lord forbids his faithful ones temporal pleasure and admonishes them to regard themselves as strangers and sojourners in this life and to seek the life to come. In respect to the interpretation of the name: Jonadab is interpreted “the Lord’s willing one.” This interpretation fittingly belongs to our Lord, who above all others obeyed God the Father especially and uniquely, even unto death. In this psalm he prays, namely in order that, as has already been said, he may teach his children by his example to pray.

In the literal sense, this is the Jonadab commended by Jeremiah, who commanded his sons not to drink wine [Col. 0281C] and to dwell not in houses but in tents (Jer. 35:6–7).
