Understanding that the Lord had commanded children to obey their parents in what is good, they kept the holy command; on account of this God blessed them for their obedience, setting them before his disobedient people and reproaching that people by their example. Jeremiah, in commending this, did so while urging the people of Israel to prepare themselves for captivity and not resist God’s will. For the Jews, having despised God’s law, were destined for a first, second, and third captivity, that they might be corrected. Before the first came, it was foretold through the Prophet.

Therefore the title of this psalm seems to have been drawn from this. Accordingly, after saying, “Of the sons of Jonadab,” it added, “And of those who were led away captive first.” Certainly not because the sons of Jonadab were led away captive, but because they were set in opposition to those about to be taken captive. They were set before them so that they might understand that they were to be taken captive because they had not obeyed God, as the sons of Jonadab had obeyed their father. And the children of Israel were indeed taken captive first, second, and third; but the psalm says nothing about these [Col. 0281D].

Thus, from this comparison with the sons of Jonadab obedient to their father, every disobedience is rather condemned: by it we are taken captive in the law of sin which is in our members, and by the disobedience of Adam, in whom all sinned, we are first made captive. Therefore we are first captive through the first man and redeemed through the second, because the first man is earthly, from the earth, and we are like him; the second is heavenly, and by him we are freed. Or we are first captive in this world, from which escape is possible, and second in hell, from which escape is impossible. Or [Col. 0282A], because what is animal comes first and then what is spiritual, he calls us first captives because we are taken captive by vices before becoming sons of Jonadab—that is, of Christ, the willing one—who, by obeying God the Father willingly, freed us, who of ourselves are nothing but evil, from this body of death through his grace, by whose mercy we are whatever we are.

So great a grace, then, is commended to us in this psalm almost syllable by syllable, with the purpose that we may place our entire hope in the Lord, not in our own strength; and that we may not imitate the contumacious captive sons, but the obedient sons of Jonadab.

It should also be considered in the obedience of the sons of Jonadab that their father imposed upon them a command not imposed by God: namely, not to drink wine or live in cities, but outside in tents [Col. 0282B]. Hence, when the Chaldeans’ siege was imminent and they were compelled to remain in the city, they regarded this very thing as a first captivity for themselves. Thus they seem to be called the first captives in the title of this psalm, where it says: “A psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab and of the first captives.”

Indeed, their captivity was prior to that captivity in which, after Jerusalem was destroyed, the Jews were led into Babylon. These sons of Jonadab were not led there; for, after the leaders and warriors had been partly slain and partly carried away into Babylon, the poor of the land were left in Judea. Since the sons of Jonadab belonged to their number, they too remained in Judea. Thus they were released from that captivity in which they had first been taken captive, when they had been compelled to dwell in the city contrary to their father’s command and their own choice; yet, although wine was offered them, they refused to drink it contrary to their father’s command. On this account God declares them blessed through the prophet Jeremiah, who rebukes the Jews for refusing to obey the divine command when these men had obeyed a human command [Col. 0282C].

Let the meek hear these things and rejoice—those who imitate the sons of Jonadab in obeying their prelates when they prohibit certain things which God has not prohibited, such as drinking wine or living amid the crowds of cities. Did not the holy Fathers Basil, Augustine, Benedict, and the others who established rules for cenobitic life set down certain such [Col. 0282D] ordinances concerning abstinence, maintaining silence, and other regular disciplines? Therefore those who observe such statutes deserve, together with the sons of Jonadab, the sons of Rechab, to be blessed. And because they are poor in spirit, although the first captivity weighs upon them, in which they see another law in their members resisting the law of their mind and taking them captive in the law of sin and death while they unwillingly experience the pleasures of the flesh, nevertheless they do not enter the second captivity, since they do not consent to these pleasures; for they are commanded not to drink wine, in which is debauchery.

Therefore they will not go into Babylon, but will receive the blessing, being wholly free from the second captivity, which is consent to sin, and soon to be freed also from the first, according as each of them says: “Unhappy man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Rom. 7:24–25) [Col. 0283A]. In longing for this liberation, soon to be hastened by the grace of God through Jesus Christ, each one of them sings, saying:

“In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be confounded.” First, David, singing in the person of all the sons of Jonadab, asks to be delivered outwardly and filled with praise. Second, he asks that the same be preserved for him in old age, at the words: “Do not cast me off in the time of old age.” Third, he gives thanks for this grace at the words: “O God, who is like you?”

Let Israel now speak—let him speak who has already been redeemed in hope and is still to be redeemed in reality. Let him say, I say: “In you, O Lord, I have hoped.” I, Jonadab, the Lord’s willing one, the priest who freely stand before God the Father, offering myself upon the altar of the cross; I who, for my own whom you gave me, Father, sanctified and sacrificed myself, that they too might be holy in truth—I have hoped in you that I shall not be confounded forever. That is, I shall never be confounded, as are those who are not heard in their good prayers, or even those heard in evil petitions. For I, having died once in order to exhaust the sins of many, asked you, Father, for life for those whom you gave me, that they might be sanctified in me and through me. In this petition I hope—indeed, I know—that I shall never be confounded, but shall be heard for the salvation of my own who cleave to me forever [Col. 0283B].

Alternatively: I, David; I, the penitent; I, a true son [Col. 0283C] of Jonadab—that is, a willing imitator of Christ, who is willingly sanctified and sacrificed on the cross—although I am oppressed by the first captivity, while willing is present to me but I do not find the power to accomplish it, because I cannot overcome by my own strength another law contrary to the law of my mind: nevertheless, in you, O Lord, I have hoped and hope that I shall not be confounded forever.

Even if for a time I am found confounded in Adam because of sin, having no fruit in those things of which I am now ashamed, I am confounded not with the confusion that brings sin—when someone foolishly blushes to confess and amend sin—but with the confusion that brings glory, when the person who was not ashamed to commit shameful acts, now confounded by repentance, is not ashamed to confess and amend those same acts. Such confusion is very beneficial for the sons of Jonadab in the first captivity. In that captivity I too, David, one of the sons of Jonadab, confounded when the prophet Nathan rebuked me, hope that I shall not be confounded forever [Col. 0283D].

But I hope not in myself but in you, O Lord; not in my own strength and mercy but in yours. For the prophet Nathan, rebuking the sins of the sons of Jonadab, is not lacking as long as the word of God is an adversary on the way, lest it accuse us in the homeland; it opposes us in the first captivity in order to free us from the second. Since I consent to the law that is good when it rebukes me on the way, and therefore delight in it with my mind, I hope that I shall not be confounded forever. Rather, delivered from confusion and crucified to the world, I may be able to glory with that chief son of Jonadab who, glorying in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, said: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20) [Col. 0284A]. Again: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). Therefore far be it from me to glory in my own righteousness; instead, grant that I may glory in your righteousness, O Lord, to whom I also say:

VERSE 2. In your righteousness deliver me—that is, through the faith by which I believe that you justify the ungodly, which faith is reckoned as righteousness. This righteousness is yours, given by you, not mine; if I establish my own righteousness, I am not subject to your righteousness. Therefore I say: “In your righteousness deliver me,” so that you may be justified in your words, so that you may be found just and true in promising grace to the person who confesses and repents and refuses to drink that wine in which is debauchery—grace prefigured in the sons of Jonadab, who were delivered both from the first captivity, lest they who were accustomed to dwell in tents should suffer too long a siege in the city, and from the second, lest they should be led with the other Jews into Babylon [Col. 0284B].

It is indeed a work of mercy that you call the sinner to repentance; but it is a work not of mercy alone—indeed, also of your justice—that you deliver one now repentant and crying to you from the depths of the evil of the first captivity. Therefore I, now repentant, now unwilling with the sons of Jonadab to drink wine in which is debauchery, now grieving over the law of sin taking me captive and consenting to your law, say: “In your righteousness deliver me from the captivity of that law,” so that, freed from sin and made servant to you, my lawful Lord, I may now have fruit unto sanctification and await eternal life as the end.

[Col. 0284C] And because I am sick and cannot raise my cry to you, the Most High, do you incline your ear to me, left half-alive as I lie by the robbers who wounded and stripped me. Incline your ear in such a way that, drawing near, you may bind my wounds and save me by pouring in both oil and wine: namely, the twofold gift of the Holy Spirit, one for the remission of sins, the other for the bestowal of virtues. Thus, the apostles were, as it were, anointed with oil on the day of the resurrection, when the Lord said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 20:22–23). And on the day of Pentecost, as though made drunk with wine, they were even called full of new wine because of the power of the Holy Spirit inflaming and inebriating them, in demonstration of the salvation given and sent to them through oil and wine—that is, through the twofold gift of the Holy Spirit, as has been said.

Thus, hearing that many sick persons had been healed and saved, I too, hoping in you as the true physician, seek salvation, saying: “Incline your ear and save me.” And, lest I lose the salvation once received while I am set among enemies:

VERSE 3. Be to me a protecting God. For just as I could not create myself so that I might exist, nor save myself so that I might be well, so neither can I defend myself so as to remain safe. Therefore I flee to you, asking that you be to me a house of refuge, or a fortified place; or, as the Hebrew truth has it: “Be to me a strong rock, a mighty dwelling-place.” You who were a terror to Adam when he fled, now be a refuge for the sons of Jonadab: whoever flees there is safe, because it is so high that he need not fear enemies from below [Col. 0285A].

Be to me a fortified place. Like David’s tower, built with battlements, from which hang a thousand shields, all the armor of the mighty. Be to me a fortified place, so that, as you made me to exist from nothing in such a way that I cannot cease to exist, so likewise you may make me, weak and sick, so sound that the salvation given me by you may not be losable—a salvation by which you give a human being well-being, freeing him from the first captivity. For one who has existence from you the Creator cannot cease to exist, however greatly he may be oppressed by the misery of either the first or the second captivity. Therefore, as I possess being from you the Creator without loss, so may I possess from you the Deliverer, under you the Protector, well-being and blessed being without loss: save me, because you are the salvation of your people, and in salvation protect and preserve me. For you are my strength against temptations and tribulations which engulf the sons of the first Adam in this first captivity and grievously assail also the sons of Jonadab, that is, of the second Adam [Col. 0285B]. Lest I, David—I, penitent—I, son of Jonadab—be engulfed by them, you are my refuge, my God. You who are my God and Creator are likewise my refuge through the mystery of your incarnation, an unconquerable strength for the sons of Jonadab who keep their father’s commands.

VERSE 4. You, my God, deliver me from the hand of the sinner, and from the hand of the one acting against the law and of the unjust. Deliver me, Christ, the true Jonadab, from the hand of the pagan sinner who does not have the law, so that the persecution of idolatrous Gentile tyrants may cease; and from the hand of the one acting against the law and of the unjust—namely, the carnal Jew and false Christian, who indeed has the law and yet acts against the law. Hence he is judged unjust; sinning through the law, he is judged through the law. So too the pagan is unjust, who sins without the law, is judged, and will perish without the law. From both, my God, deliver me, lest I be incorporated or conformed to such persons.

Deliver me—I say what I said above and now repeat the same prayer because of the twofold deliverance so necessary to me: first, lest the pleasure of sin bite me; second, lest consent to sin against God’s law wholly kill me. Therefore I say: “Deliver me from the hand of the sinner and from the hand of the one acting against the law,” lest either the pleasure of sin, resisting the law of my mind, wound me, or consent put me to death [Col. 0285D].

Moreover, deliver me from the hand of the unjust, universally from every unjust thing, whether angel, human being, or any unjust thing such as anger, pride, envy of the mind, and lust of the flesh; lest any such member of the unjust be able, by its own hand and power, to oppress me and strip me of my innocence or—what is equally dangerous—of my wisdom, which I possess not from myself but from you.

VERSE 5. For you are my patience, in which, if I persevere amid temptations like another Job, I know that I shall not be confounded, because patience produces tested character, tested character hope, and hope does not confound. Thus hope is born of patience; and in turn greater patience arises from hope, while those rejoicing in hope will, from the joy of hope itself, be more patient in tribulation [Col. 0286A]. But all this good comes to me from you, not from me, O my God, because you are my patience, O Lord, in tribulation or temptation; and likewise you, O Lord, are my hope that through you I may be delivered from that tribulation and temptation.

This hope of mine began in my youth, an age suited to warfare; and it began in me then, when, infancy and childhood having passed, I took up the arms of faith, hope, and charity, about to fight against the devil and the flesh. In order that I might be fit to take them up, before I took them up I was anticipated by your mercy, whereby:

VERSE 6. In you I was strengthened from the womb, before I knew how to hope. First conceived by the initial rudiment of faith in the womb of the Church, and then born, as it were, [Col. 0286B] from my mother’s belly through water and the Spirit, I was not weakened in faith; rather, nourished with the milk of spiritual sustenance, I received an increase of youthful strength. Hence my song is always in you. I have never had, nor shall I ever have, hope in another; but my song is always in you. Even if at some time I had song or delight in someone else, henceforth it shall not be except in you, the true God, my most strong helper, because, hoping in you, loving and proclaiming your ordinances—

VERSE 7. I have become a wonder to many. You have been and, as I hope, will be a strong helper to me until the end; and therefore my song is always in you, my strong helper, both while I walk by faith and when I shall see by sight. Lest this vow of mine to render song now [Col. 0286C] and always and unto ages of ages be rendered void and empty, but may be full both in the affection of devotion and in the effect of consummation, I ask:

VERS. 8. Let my mouth be filled with praise, that I may sing of your glory, of your greatness all the day long. Let my mouth, I say, be filled with praise in such a way that, from the depths of my heart to the lips of my mouth, the fullness of your grace, O God—poured into my heart and diffused upon my lips—may magnify you with loving devotion, lest I be found like the people of whom you say: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13). The lips of such a people were not filled with your praise, but were, as it were, sprinkled externally while the heart within was empty and far from God. But I say: Let my mouth be filled with praise through grace poured into my heart, springing thence [Col. 0286D] and spread upon my lips, just as one of yours is recorded as being full of grace and power, full of the Holy Spirit and faith; and such grace overflowed in his lips that his adversaries could not “resist the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke” (Acts 6:8, 10).

Thus, with your grace overflowing from the depths of my heart even to my mouth, let that mouth itself be filled with your praise, that I may sing of your glory. Glory is praise celebrated by the mouths of many. Let me sing such glory, having as companions in it a multitude of good people; although they are few in comparison with the wicked, nevertheless, because the wicked themselves “shall come to nothing like water running down” (Ps. 57:8), this glory is and shall be for all God’s saints: praise celebrated by their mouths shall be glorious and likewise beautiful. Conversely, [Col. 0287A] “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sir. 15:9), even if it is loud, since to God’s ears it is burdensome. Hence he says: “Take away from me the tumult of your songs; I will not hear the melody of your lyre” (Amos 5:23). Lest this be said to me as one praising you unworthily, I ask that my mouth be so perfectly filled with your praise that I may fittingly sing your glory: your greatness all the day long.

“All the day long,” that is, both when you comfort me by cherishing me through prosperity and when you correct me through adversities by rebuking me: may I sing your glory and your greatness, by which you made me from non-being so that I might be some creature; and, when I existed, protected and advanced me so that I might become a new creature. Again, when I had sinned, you forgave me; when converted, you helped me; and for my perseverance you prepared a crown, which is laid up [Col. 0287B] for me with you in the greatness of your mercy. For under the single name of your greatness I embrace many of your benefits, praising and singing your greatness all the day long. “For great are your judgments, O Lord, and your words beyond telling” (Wis. 17:1). Great is your power, by which you can do whatsoever you will. Great is your wisdom, by which you know all things and no thought is hidden from you. Great is your mercy, by which you have mercy on all and hate none of the things you have made. All these are great in you—or rather, all these are in you one immeasurable greatness, and are not other than you—according to what is said: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power; and there is no number of his wisdom” (Ps. 146:5), and “there is no end of his greatness” (Ps. 144:3). Therefore you alone perform great wonders by great power, [Col. 0287C] which neither grows old nor fails, as human strength both grows old and fails.

Therefore I, a wretched and mortal man, subject to age and failure, flee to you and say to you, who remain forever:

VERS. 9. Do not cast me off in the time of old age. The second part, concerning the grace necessary in the time of old age, begins thus. Do not, I say, cast me off in the time of old age, frustrating my expectation—an expectation by which my hope, existing from my youth, made me hope that you would not cast me off in the time of old age. This hope of mine was laid up in my bosom like a pledge and earnest given from above. Therefore, because hope does not disappoint, I demand, as though due, the reward of hope, saying: Do not cast me off in the time of old age.

The time of youth is when someone, presuming upon his own strength, girds himself and walks where he will, saying: “In my abundance I shall never be moved” (Vulgate: “my”; Ps. 29:7). Or: “Even if I must die, I will never be scandalized” (Matt. 26:33, 35). But this youth quickly fails, and such old age and failure of human strength follow it that this youthful person, overtaken by premature old age, is compelled to say: “O Lord, in your favor you gave strength to my beauty; you turned your face away from me, and I was troubled” (Ps. 29:8). The late complaint drawn from another psalm after that disturbance is here forestalled when it is said: Do not cast me off in the time of old age. This is the time when my strength fails, when shaken patience grows weak, when [Col. 0288A] the temptation of the devil or of the flesh becomes stronger than we can endure. Then do not cast me off or abandon me, faithful God; but with the temptation also make a way out, that I may be able to endure it. For human strength, wearied out, needs all the more to be strengthened by the Spirit of the Lord helping our weakness, the more it has experienced that weakness itself.

It is also said that Christ had an old age—not of sin, but of punishment—on account of which antiquity or old age he became weak, a portent to many, mocked on the cross, where our old man was crucified together with him; so that, just as he received weakness from us, we may receive strength from him. Since he was tempted in all things, he can also aid those who are tempted. As the true Jonadab, voluntarily offered for the salvation of his children or members, [Col. 0288B] he is rightly understood to intercede with the Father for those same weak persons in this manner: “My strength has been weakened in the hands of my enemies; how much more will the strength of my little children be weakened in the hands of their enemies whenever, in the first captivity—which they have from their first parent—wine to drink, in which is licentiousness, is set before them, while temptation of the flesh grows strong and human strength fails?” Therefore, when my strength fails—that is, the strength of my own—do not abandon me, that is, my own, in the hands of my enemies, who are thereby to be feared all the more.

VERS. 10 and 11. For my enemies have spoken against me, and those who watched my soul took counsel together, saying: “God has forsaken him,” etc. My enemies, who watched my soul with the purpose of tripping me up, took counsel—that is, they spoke deliberately—and made the counsel itself one, so that, like a bundle undivided and therefore heavy to carry, it might oppress more heavily. Hear, O Lord, the voices of my adversaries, who took counsel together, saying: “God has forsaken him; pursue him and seize him, for there is none to rescue him.” They said this because they saw me worn out by calamities, weighed down by bodily weakness, bound by various necessities, and possessing from myself and in myself no strength whatever to resist so many evils, so many vices, so many miseries pressing upon me from every side. Therefore they say: “God has forsaken him.” The God whom he preaches, whom [Col. 0288D] he glorifies, has himself forsaken him, as he himself testifies when he says: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46).

But to their harm they think me forsaken by God; yet that very evil works for good to others, namely, to those who are called saints according to his purpose. For if they had known, they would never have crucified me, the Lord of glory. If I had not been crucified, lost man would not be saved, who could be redeemed by no price but my blood. Not knowing this—for they were ignorant of God’s mysteries—they cried: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 26:66): “Pursue him and seize him.” Pursue him as slow; seize him as weak, for there is none to rescue one seized, bound, and fastened to the cross. Thus they deliberated concerning me, the true Jonadab, just as [Col. 0289A] they judged concerning my children: namely, that they had been forsaken by God when they were exposed to excessive temptations or tribulations. But you, O God, who know all good and evil things and will good alone, being supremely provident and gracious—

VERS. 12. Do not be far from me, as you seem to be when you delay to come to your servants. Hasten through the bestowal of aid, most necessary precisely when adversaries are insulting. Do not be far from me by delaying to help and deliver me from imminent calamities. And lest I be exposed to still graver things, O God, my God, come to my aid, helping me by your regard as you helped Peter: because you looked upon him, he wept bitterly and deserved to be made blessed by that consolation of which it is said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” [Col. 0289B] (Matt. 5:5). Again: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21).

Formerly, when Pharaoh’s chariots drew near your people as they departed from Egypt, you came to the aid of that people of yours: “you looked upon the camp of the Egyptians” (Exod. 14:24), and they were carried into the deep like lead in mighty waters. So now look upon the camp of demons and vices, or of vicious men, so that they may be carried into such a depth of your judgments that your people, delivered by your regard, may be permitted to sing over it the song of Moses, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord,” etc. (Exod. 15:1). Thus look to the help of me and my own, O God the Father, appeased through my obedience, an obedience greater [Col. 0289C] than the obedience of Jonadab’s sons. For they, obeying their father, would not drink wine; but I, obeying you, Father, tasted wine mixed with gall, or wine mixed with myrrh, and drank vinegar, both in my own person and in the persons of my martyrs, of my confessors who chastise their flesh, and of others who bear, for my sake, galling and bitter reproaches among my enemies who slander my soul. For them I pray, saying:

Let those who slander my soul be confounded and fail. Those who slander my soul—that is, my life—by saying, for example, “A gluttonous man, a drinker of wine,” and other false reproaches of this kind, let them be confounded in their slanders against the one who justifies and magnifies my soul, that is, my life: justifying it [Col. 0289D] by freedom from sins and magnifying it by the brightness of virtues. Unable to bear its splendor, let these slanderers of my soul be confounded, either unto repentance, if they sin against me through ignorance or weakness, or unto punishment correcting others, if their sin is so unto death that one should not pray for its forgiveness—which happens when there is sin against the Holy Spirit. Thus, however they sin, let them be confounded when they see the reproaches of their slanders proved false, while you help me and I patiently bear and endure all things in charity, which suffers and never fails, and in hope, which does not disappoint. But those who are so wicked that they have no hope of good from me, let them be confounded by the evidence of the good things that shall shine forth in me; and let them fail, [Col. 0290A] their material for slander being removed, just as fire fails when wood is taken away. Let those who slander my soul, or the souls of my own, fail. Let them be confounded because of their sins and fail in their perverse powers. Let them be confounded, blushing that they wished evil; and even if they persist in wishing it, let them fail in strength, lest they prevail in doing what they wish.

Some manuscripts have: “Let those who engage my soul fail,” that is, those who wage war with my soul in order to provoke it to resist God—which is to wage war against God himself. This is what those do who do not consent to divine judgments when they experience adversities befalling the good and prosperity the wicked. Job’s wife provoked holy Job to undertake such a war, saying: “Do you still remain [Col. 0290B] in your simplicity? Bless God and die.” But he, keeping peace with God and commending his judgments, though hard upon himself, said: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things? In all these things Job did not sin with his lips, nor did he speak any foolish thing against God” (Job 2:9–10), avoiding the engagement of a most dangerous war. For from the moment someone resists you, almighty God, your implacable wrath is kindled; and the wisest person avoids it who humbly acquiesces in your judgments, blaming not you but himself and asking forgiveness. The soul also engages in ruinous warfare if it hates those from whom it suffers evils.

[Col. 0290C] The Hebrew truth has: “Let the adversaries of my soul be confounded and consumed.” Three captains of fifty were sent against Elijah by the impious king of Israel, a worshipper of Beelzebub. Two of them, with their fifties, were consumed when Elijah said: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and devour you and your fifty” (4 Kings 1:10–12). The third captain of fifty was not consumed because, humbly disposed, he was confounded and sought mercy rather than provoking wrath. And while witnesses of truth are still fighting against Beelzebub, it is promised that they are lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth; and if anyone wishes to harm them, fire will come forth from their mouths and devour their enemies. For each of them says what we have in the present psalm: “Let [Col. 0290D] the adversaries of my soul be confounded and consumed.” Let them be consumed by heavenly fire. For “our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24). Let the adversaries of my soul be consumed by the fire of most ardent prayer or by the just sentence of excommunication—not that they may not exist at all, but that they may not be adversaries, nor be able to oppose or slander my soul. So Elijah’s opponents slandered and opposed him when, as he stood upon the mountain, they said to him: “Man of God, the king commands that you come down” (4 Kings 9:11 [probably 1:9, OCR uncertainty]). For those who drag down, or desire to drag down, a soul from the height of its profession, from the summit of holy conduct, to the low affairs of the ruler of this world—as though by royal authority, saying to any saint stationed upon the mountain’s summit, “Man of God, the king commands: come down”—are themselves worthy [Col. 0291A] that fire issuing from the mouths of the saints should devour them. This is what is desired here when it is said: “Let the adversaries, or the slanderers, of my soul be confounded and consumed,” or “fail.”

Let those who seek evils for me be covered with confusion and shame. Although they may not themselves inflict those evils, nevertheless they seek and desire that evils may happen to me, sometimes knowing and sometimes not knowing what they do, like Job’s wife, already mentioned, and Tobias’s wife, who said to him: “Where are your acts of righteousness?” (Tob. 2:16–22). Seeing the Lord’s help upon me, let such people be covered with confusion and shame as with a veil and covering, by which their sins may be covered, as it is said elsewhere: “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31:1). For they do not know [Col. 0291B] what they do when they seek to cast me, as another Job or Tobias, into despair of divine consolation, and thus seek to throw down my soul from the height of hope into the pit of despair.

VERS. 14. But I shall always hope in God, saying with blessed Job: “Even if he kills me, I shall hope in him” (Job 13:15). Let Satan be permitted to tempt or buffet me, to deprive me of riches, to afflict me with diseases or with a grievous ulcer—which is the perverse desire of the flesh—yet I shall always hope for divine help and consolation, so long as I neither murmur amid adversities nor consent to corrupt enticements. As at the beginning of the psalm, speaking of the past, I said: “In you, O Lord, I have hoped”; so now, speaking of the future, I say: “But I shall hope in you,” that is, I shall persevere in my hope.

And because hope does not disappoint, when the good things hoped for arrive, I shall add to all your praise. Your praise, God the Father, was great in the creation, distinction, ordering, and governance of all things. But I, Christ—I, the true Jonadab—voluntarily obedient to you, Father, and instructing my children in holy obedience, shall add to all your praise when you are recognized as praiseworthy not only for the establishment of the world but also for its restoration through my voluntary obedience and the glory due to such obedience. Thus one of Jonadab’s sons says of me: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto [Col. 0291D] death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:8 ff.). Praise of this confession did not exist before the Law or under the Law. But I, Christ—I, Jonadab—shall add this praise beyond all praise that came before my advent.

Alternatively: You, O God the righteous judge, were worthy of all praise for the justice by which, whether before the Law or under the Law, you punished sins. But beyond all this praise of yours shall be added the praise of your mercy, when throughout the whole world it is proclaimed that you do not despise the poor or abhor the sinner. You did not abhor the confessing thief, the weeping sinful woman, the pleading Canaanite woman, the woman caught in adultery, the one sitting at the tax-office, the pleading publican, the denying disciple, the persecutor of disciples, or your very crucifiers. When you are praised for these and other similar works of your grace, there is a great addition of praise beyond all the praise by which you were praised among the ancient people. The Synagogue praised you for temporal benefits, which passed away with time: for example, because you brought the children of Israel out of Egypt with mighty hand and uplifted arm; because you divided the Red Sea for them into divisions; because you gave manna; because, after exterminating the Canaanites, you brought your people into their land. [Col. 0292B] But I, the Church, shall add beyond all this praise thanksgiving for these same benefits spiritually fulfilled in me: for example, because I have been led out of the darkness of ignorance, Christ’s human conduct going before me as a pillar of cloud and the divine illumination of miracles as a pillar of fire; because the Father gives me the true bread of angels from heaven in the most holy mystery of the altar; because, already brought in through hope and yet to be brought in through reality, I enter the kingdom of heaven, from which the bands of proud angels have been cast out. Giving thanks for such things, I shall add beyond all your praise. Nor shall I praise only within myself, but shall instruct my neighbors toward the same praise.

VERS. 15. My mouth shall declare your righteousness, [Col. 0292C] your salvation all the day long. My mouth shall declare your righteousness, namely Christ, who “was made for us by God wisdom and righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30). Therefore I do not boastfully proclaim, with the Pharisee, my own righteousness which comes from the law of works, saying: “I thank you, God, that I am not like other men—robbers, unjust, adulterers” (Luke 18:11). Rather, I proclaim that righteousness which is none other than your salvation: your Son, Creator at the beginning of the world and made its Savior at the end of the ages. My mouth shall declare this salvation of yours all the day long. The whole day is understood together with its night, because night serves day, not day night. Therefore I shall praise all the day long, that is, at every time, in prosperity [Col. 0292D] and adversity alike. For the night, by which adversities are signified, is included with the day, because in the good conduct of good people day does not serve night, but night serves day: the exercise of holiness is not undertaken for bodily advantage, but rather whatever is done in the body contributes and profits toward the exercise of holiness. We do not evangelize in order to eat—that would make day serve night—but we eat in order to evangelize and to be strong and ready for other spiritual exercises. This makes night serve day and pass into the name of day, when “night shall be illuminated as day” (Ps. 138:12), and bodily exercise, or the prudent care of the body itself—which is useful for a little—serves the ministry of godliness, which is profitable for all things and has promises of the life that now is and of that which is to come [Col. 0293A].

Alternatively: My mouth shall declare that the righteousness by which I am righteous is yours, the righteousness that comes from faith, not mine, which comes from the Law.

Because I did not know legal learning: I, the Church, did not know—that is, I did not approve—the killing letter as able to profit me for justification. For the Law without grace is merely letter, giving life to no dead person, just as Elisha’s staff, laid upon the dead man, did not restore him to life. Therefore the great Prophet who was to come into the world came, and through him God visited his people. This great Prophet contracted his greatness to the wretchedness of a little dead body; and, setting aside the staff and burden of the Law—“which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear,” says Peter (Acts 15:10)—he himself visited his people: a servant from the Lord, poor from the rich, flesh from the Word; nor did he disdain to become Son of Man from the Son of God. Eternal, yet he was born to us as a child; great, yet he was given to us as a little one; Creator, yet he became Savior; and he who made me became salvation to me, the Church.

Judea also had certain saviors, for the children of Israel repeatedly cried to God because of their oppressors, and he sent them saviors and champions to deliver them from the slaughter inflicted by ravagers: for example, Gideon, Samson, and others like them. These were called saviors, though far unequal and far inferior to that Jesus, that Savior, whose name the angel explains: “For he shall save his people from their sins” [Col. 0293C] (Matt. 1:21). Yet they were sent before him as the letter of the Law before the Spirit, as the staff laid upon the dead man before the Prophet’s arrival; and they were unable to interpret their own names, for those names were empty. The staff was laid upon the dead man, but there was neither voice nor perception, because it was a staff, neither possessing life in itself nor able to give life. For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly come from the Law. But the Scripture of the Law shut all things under sin, and the staff of the Law could not give life to the dead. At last the great Prophet who had sent the staff came down, and immediately saved his people from their sins, thereby proving himself to be the one of whom it was said: “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” [Col. 0293D] (Luke 7:49). Surely he is the one who says: “I am the salvation of the people.” Now there is voice; now there is perception; and it becomes clear that he does not bear an empty name like the former ones. Salvation poured in is felt, and the benefit is not kept silent. Within is perception; without is voice. Hear the voice of the dead man raised: “I shall add,” he says, “to all your praise. My mouth shall declare your righteousness, your salvation all the day long, because I did not know legal learning to have profited me; I did not feel through it the grace of the Spirit poured in.” Therefore I did not know legal learning; that is, I rejected those who boast in the letter that does not give life and recoil from grace, knowing that the Law without grace is a killing letter—taking life from the living, much less bestowing it upon the dead.

For the Law, having five books, convicted the guilty, just as the pool having five porticoes held the sick within those [Col. 0294A] porticoes, in which it did not heal them, because the Scripture of the Law had shut all things under sin (John 5:2 ff.). But the angel came down, and one was healed, because Christ, humbled and made under the Law, gave life to the Law itself, previously dead—indeed, deadly—joining the life-giving Spirit to the killing letter through the ineffable mystery of his Passion. In order that this might be accomplished, the water was stirred: a great storm of Jewish persecution against the angel who had descended to save the Jewish people itself was raised. That people was like shifting water, yielding to every wind of error and unwilling to receive the solid truth offered to it. Thus that water was stirred even to the submersion of the angel himself, on which account he says: “Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even unto my soul” [Col. 0294B] (Ps. 68:1). Thus the angel died in that storm, and one was healed, because through Christ’s death no one is healed who is separated from the unity of faith in God and of love for God and neighbor alike which must be maintained—such as those of whom it is said: “Sensual persons, separating themselves, not having the Spirit” (Jude 19).

The passage may also be connected thus:

VERS. 16. Because I did not know legal learning, I shall enter into the powers of the Lord; that is, because I placed no confidence of salvation in the ceremonies of the Law, therefore I shall enter into the powers of the Lord—that is, I shall receive and keep Christ’s sacraments. Because the Law, weakened through the flesh, brought nothing to perfection and could give life to no one, [Col. 0294C] I shall enter into the powers of the Lord, knowing that Christ’s powerful and mightily saving sacraments do not rest upon human strength, but on the power of the Lord himself. He is rightly preached as the strong Lord, the Lord mighty in battle, who also has authority on earth to forgive sins through the life-giving sacraments of his death, resurrection, and ascension. For we were baptized into his death so that, as he rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life, having been brought into the powers of the Lord; or, as it is read in Hebrew, “into the strength of the Lord.” For it is no small strength or power bestowed upon me that that great man—the prophet mighty in deed and word—descending from the height of heaven deigned to visit me, although I am ashes and dust; to pity one dead; to bend down to one lying prostrate; to contract himself; to make himself equal to one small; to share with a blind person the light of his own eyes; to loosen a mute mouth with the kiss of his own mouth; and to strengthen weak hands by the touch of his own hands [Col. 0294D].

I sweetly chew over these things, and my inward parts are filled, my interior is made fat, and all my bones put forth praise. He bestowed this once upon the whole world; every day each of us feels it enacted within ourselves: namely, that light of understanding is given to the heart, a word of edification to the mouth, and a work of righteousness to the hands. He gives faithful perception, useful endurance, and effective accomplishment. This is the threefold cord, which is not easily broken: surely strong for drawing souls out of the prison [Col. 0295A] of the devil and drawing them with you and after you to the heavenly kingdoms, if you rightly understand, worthily speak, and confirm it by your manner of life.

He touched my eyes with his own, adorning the brow of the inner person with bright lights, namely faith and understanding; he joined his mouth to mine and impressed upon one dead the sign of peace. Therefore let not only the bride boast—now altogether beautiful, now brought into the bridal chamber, now enjoying sweet rest in Abraham’s bosom, betrothed by the ring of faith in the patriarchs and prophets, crowned in many kings and righteous persons—that the Bridegroom deemed her worthy to receive the kiss of his mouth and raised up Abraham’s seed from her own flesh. He also kissed me, the Church from the Gentiles, because, while we were still sinners, the Son, God’s righteousness, reconciled us dead persons to God the Father.

Let not the elder son boast that, holding [Col. 0295B] the letter of the Law, he has never transgressed the Father’s command and therefore ought alone to be heir in the paternal house. For I, the younger son—I, the people of the Gentiles—who dwelt in darkness, saw a great light; I saw the mercy of the most merciful Father toward me, being graciously admitted to his kiss, clothed at his command in the first robe, adorned with the ring of faith, and shod for the readiness of the Gospel of peace. I heard his gracious rejoicing as he said to my elder brother: “You ought, son, to rejoice, because your brother was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:32). For I was dead, but I came to life through the kiss of the most merciful Father, who applied his mouth to mine, again breathing into my face the breath [Col. 0295C] of life, holier than at first. For at first he created me as a living soul; the second time he re-formed me as a life-giving spirit. He adorned me with the ring of faith, taught my hands for battle and my fingers for war, fortified my feet with evangelical footwear, giving me power and strength to tread upon serpents and scorpions and every power of the enemy; and, greater than these, giving all who have received or shall receive him until the end of the age power to become children of God—those who believe in his name, who do not remain under the legal learning of the Law but, with grace assisting, enter into the powers of the Lord, knowing by certain experience how great is the difference between the killing letter and the life-giving Spirit, between shadow and reality, between figure and truth. For “the Law” of the killing letter “was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” [Col. 0295D] (John 1:17).

Therefore the Synagogue, which knew only the legal learning of the Law, rejected grace and wished to enter into the powers of the Lord. Hence the saying: “We know that God spoke to Moses, but this man—we do not know where he is from” (John 9:29). Again they say to the man born blind who had been enlightened: “You may be that man’s disciple, but we are Moses’ disciples” (John 9:28). Again: “We have a law, and according to our law he ought to die” (John 19:7). Thus, glorying in legal learning, it would not enter into the powers of the Lord. But I, the Church from the Gentiles, because I did not know the legal learning of the Law, [Col. 0296A] shall enter into the powers of the Lord, gladly receiving Christ’s Gospel.

Another translation has: “Because I knew commerce, I shall enter into the powers of the Lord.” There is praiseworthy commerce, of which it is said: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant” (Matt. 13:45), and of which the master of the household says to his servants: “Conduct business until I come” (Luke 19:13). For it is good that temporal goods should be given and bodily services performed for spiritual gains. Carnal Jews did not know this commerce, since they served God only for temporal things while observing the letter of the Law. This was bad commerce: in legal promises—for example, abundance of grain, wine, and oil—they understood nothing beyond what the letter sounded, which, on the surface of its wording alone, promised them temporal things.

Indeed, this commerce—serving God in Judaism only for temporal things—was perverse; and such commerce remains perverse in Christianity. Merchants of this kind are driven from the Temple by the Lord’s scourge, nor can any such person enter into the powers of the Lord, since they have been cast outside the Temple and are wholly alienated from the power of divine virtue. Peter says to Simon Magus: “You have neither part nor lot in this matter, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money” (Acts 8:21, 20). By this saying the intention of that most wicked commerce is rebuked: Simon intended to possess God’s gift as though it were his own, so that, once bought, he could [Col. 0296C] sell it whenever he wished.

The Gospel merchant, however, is not blameworthy because, having found a precious pearl, he gave all that he had and bought it. He seeks merchants of this kind who says: “Go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21). To such people he says: “Conduct business until I come” (Luke 19:13), so that—because *negotium* is said as though “denying leisure” (*negans otium*), or as though “not leisure” (*nec otium*)—no place may be left for idleness in God’s household. Of this commerce it is by no means said: “Because I did not know commerce, I shall enter into the powers of the Lord.” For unless you know and practice this evangelical commerce, by which earthly things are spent for heavenly gain, temporal things for eternal, and bodily things for spiritual, you will not [Col. 0296D] enter into the powers of the Lord—provided that one has the age and means to conduct such business; this qualification is stated because of infants and those naturally lacking reason.

Moreover, that Judaic or Simonian trafficking, by which spiritual things and exercises of divine worship—such as fasting, prayer, or the administration of any ecclesiastical office—are undertaken for some earthly gain, whether profit, human favour, or praise, shuts the entrance into the kingdom, into the powers of the Lord, and into the bridegroom’s chamber. Therefore the door was shut to the foolish virgins because they went to those who sell oil—that is, the favour of flatterers. Likewise, concerning those who do all their works in order to be seen by men, Truth says: “For they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 5, 16). It is shameful commerce to give gold for [Col. 0297A] mud: that is, fasting, prayer, or another such thing in exchange for human favour or earthly profit.

Hence such traders, after the manner of commercial merchants, set a magnificent value upon all that is theirs and depreciate what belongs to others beyond measure, like the man who said: “I fast twice in the week; I give tithes of all that I possess” (Luke XVIII, 12). But he had first said, “I am not as other men,” in order to show that his own merits surpassed those of others, just as market-merchants, in the art of trade, prefer their own goods to the goods of others. Yet this is not a fault of the art, but of the people who misuse the art, which is not evil in itself if it is practised without lies and frauds. Since this can in no way, or scarcely at all, be done—especially by people who seek what is their own—penitents are not without reason forbidden to engage in trade, as they are forbidden to serve as soldiers. Yet a perfect person may engage in trade or serve as a soldier without damnation, provided especially that the precaution be observed of doing to no other person what one would not wish done to oneself.

Such merchants, then, may also enter into the powers of the Lord either by committing no fraud or by restoring what has been fraudulently taken, following the example of Zacchaeus—even if not, like him, fourfold, at least according to their ability. But Judaic, as has been said, or Simonian trafficking closes the entrance into the powers of the Lord. Simon Magus, while remaining in the gall of bitterness, could enter the font of baptism, or the temple of the Lord, and could even receive the body of the Lord; but because he recognized and approved that most evil trafficking [Col. 0297C] thereafter named after him, he could not enter into the powers of the Lord through visible sacraments.

Thus many traders like him even to this day, seeking principally or solely their own interests in ecclesiastical offices, will not enter into the powers of the Lord. For although they have an appearance of godliness, they deny its power. And it is certain that, without the power of godliness, all sacraments are as empty and dead as a body without a soul.

For this reason holy Church, gathered from the sons of Jonadab—that is, of Christ the willing one—obedient to that Father, and not drinking wine contrary to his command, wine in which is excess, but content with the wine that gladdens the heart of man; dwelling in tents, which are the dwellings of pilgrims or [Col. 0297D] soldiers, such as churches, monasteries, or hospices of holy persons living holily—such a Church, I say, in her chaste children who are pilgrims and soldiers in this world and obedient to the Father, rightly and truly says: “Because I have not known trafficking, I shall enter into the powers of the Lord.” Having not merely an appearance of godliness but also the power of godliness, she says, for example, that she abides in Christ and walks as he walked—not in her own power, but in his, who “gave power to become the sons of God to all who received him, to those who believe in his name” (John I, 12). Believing, they shall enter into the powers of the Lord, placing no confidence in the powers of the human soul or of the corruptible body, which weighs down and depresses the soul’s own powers, so that its [Col. 0298A] memory most readily falls into forgetfulness, its reason into error, and its will into lukewarmness, unless it is helped by the power of divine mercy.

The translations seem to disagree, since one has “literature” and the other “trafficking.” Yet, if attention is given, they do not differ greatly. For the Prophet, seeing that the law understood literally was of no benefit, says: “I have not known literature”; that is, I have not approved placing the hope of salvation in the law understood according to the letter, because the letter of the law does not cure the disease of concupiscence, but the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord does. Therefore, “I shall enter into the powers of the Lord”; that is, into the spiritual sense, which powerfully gives life to the one whom the letter kills.

That translation which reads, “I have not [Col. 0298B] known trafficking,” does not depart far from the same sense. For the law understood literally instructed the people only carnally and taught them to savour nothing but earthly things, according to the saying: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the earth” (Isa. I, 19). It therefore made such interpreters traders, that is, occupied in the pursuit of temporal goods. But the Prophet, embracing the liberty of the Spirit that breaks the bonds of this commerce, says: “I have not known trafficking”; that is, a law thus understood does not please me, so as to entangle me in the transactions of carnal observances imposed until the time of correction, and then especially useless or even damnable when they are performed for any worldly advantage, such as the favour of human praise or favour, or temporal gain.

Therefore I, a son of Jonadab—the willing Christ, willingly obedient to the Father—and I, introduced through willing obedience into the powers of the Lord, am free, indeed freed by grace, from such traffickings.

“Lord, I will remember thy righteousness alone”: that righteousness which is not from the law of ceremonies handed down in the letter of the law, nor from the powers of free will, which needs a liberator. Since we belong to the number of the former captives, as was explained above, “I will remember thy righteousness alone”: that righteousness which is not from law but from faith, for those who believe in thee, who justifiest the ungodly. In this righteousness nothing can be ascribed to human power, because divine mercy alone awakens the will in the believer’s heart by sowing [Col. 0298D] good thoughts, assists good actions, and kindles good affections—sufficient in themselves for justification where perhaps time and opportunity to do good are lacking.

Since, therefore, this righteousness has from thee, O God, its beginning, progress, and completion, it must be ascribed to thee alone; and therefore, “I will remember thy righteousness alone.” And that I might understand this, thou—

**VERSE 17.** O God, “hast taught me from my youth, and until now I will proclaim thy wonders.” Thou hast taught me to understand that the righteousness of faith is thine and comes from thee, who inspirest faith and also breathest into it the right willing by which it works through love, giving right understanding and consent to what is right, so that all who are justified and made right by thee may be upright in heart. Thus hast thou taught me, [Col. 0299A] because whatever righteousness or uprightness I possess, I possess from thee. “For what hast thou, O man, that thou hast not received? And if thou hast received it, why dost thou glory as though thou hadst not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7).

I read and understand this Scripture: that I have no good from myself, but many evils, among which are also the sins of my youth—whether according to the age of human life, or according to the first beginnings of faith, when, presumptuously in youthful fashion, I girded myself and walked where I wished. Therefore thou hast taught me from my youth, so that, instructed by my own dangers, I might learn not to presume upon myself; taught by the example of him who, as often as he presumed upon his own strength, so often, being left to his weakness, denied his Master.

And when I was younger, I girded myself and walked where I wished, through self-chosen presumption aiming [Col. 0299B] at the greatest goods while wholly insufficient even for the least—as I later proved by much experience. By that experience thou, O God, hast taught me from my youth until now.

Again and again, even after faith has been received and long exercised, it is necessary for me to be taught, lest, if thou cease to teach, I become foolish and fail to understand what I lack. For divine instruction is not like human instruction. A man teaches another man, for example, agriculture, carpentry, or something else of that kind; and once he is trained, when his instructor leaves him, the trained man works by himself, without the instructor, as well as he did—or perhaps better—whether in farming, building a house, or another task that he learned from his master. He knows and can work even without his master.

You find the same thing also in miracles wrought through men: the dead raised by Elijah and Elisha lived without them after they had departed. Lazarus likewise, raised by the God-man, could live bodily when Christ who raised him had departed from him. So too the one who plants and the one who waters, once their work is done, rejoice that the work they visibly performed no longer needs their help—provided God is present, invisibly giving the increase. If he withdraws his hand, their work cannot remain.

For as this visible sun makes day upon earth by illuminating the air with its radiance through its presence; and when it is absent through setting, the day which it made upon earth fails and is not restored unless the sun rises again over the earth and once more by its presence illuminates the spaces [Col. 0299D] of ether and air beneath it: so the Sun of righteousness, though he is everywhere and nowhere absent, is nevertheless nowhere present locally. Now by his grace he displays his presence, most greatly enlightening rational creation: in the elect angels, likened to the purest ether; and in human souls still clothed with flesh, likened to dense and cloudy air. He makes the day of which it may be said: “This is the day which the Lord hath made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. CXVII, 24).

But if he withdraws grace, this day will certainly fail and will never be renewed unless the Sun of righteousness again deigns, through grace restored, to display his presence. Elisha, when his teacher Elijah left him, not only did not fail, but even advanced when his master’s spirit was doubled in him. But thou, O God, who hast taught [Col. 0300A] me from my youth until now—if thou abandon me even for a moment, thou knowest that I shall utterly fail. For since thou art the life of my soul, as the soul itself is the life of my body, just as, when the soul is withdrawn, all the body’s harmony is dissolved, so that neither the eyes see, nor the ears hear, nor the other limbs perform their functions; so, if thou forsake me and cease to justify my soul, it will be unrighteous. Unless thou enlighten it by thy presence, it will be dark; unless thou give it life, it will be dead. For its living soberly, righteously, godly, and wisely is not its nature, but thy wonder: thou alone dost these wonders above nature.

Therefore, Lord, in these things I will remember thy righteousness alone, thou who workest the same wonders, so that thou mayest be justified in thy words, through which thou hast promised such wonders—thou who canst not lie. Therefore in all such things accomplished with me from my youth I shall not boast of my merits, but shall proclaim thy wonders—I, the ecclesiastical person, or I, the universal Church. And because I know that such wonders fail if thou withdrawest grace, I give thanks for the past and, praying for the future, say:

**VERSES 18 AND 19.** “O God, forsake me not unto old age and oldness.” I, the Church, had youthful strength when, brought forth through the Gospel by the preaching of the apostles and other apostolic men, and nourished and strengthened not only with milk but also with solid food, I fought vigorously in martyrdom against tyrants. My old age followed that youth when the grey hairs of my understanding shone in confessors who commended the right faith by the word [Col. 0300C] of sound doctrine and by the habits of mature discipline.

I still await oldness, now soon approaching, or plainly, behold, already present: dangerous times in which, with iniquity abounding and the love of many growing cold, fervour of faith remains among a few elect persons. Even they, perhaps, if possible, would be led into error unless the days of that most evil oldness were shortened. And if even those counted among the elect must be feared for, lest they be led into error through lying signs—that is, sacraments possessing indeed an appearance of godliness but denying its power—then surely the word of Truth is true when it declares that, unless those days are shortened, no flesh will be saved. For the weak, frail, and easily deceived within the Church are called “flesh,” just as the strong are called “bones.”

Both belong to Christ’s body, of which Adam said in figure: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. II, 23). As if the second Adam said: In my body, and formed from my body, I have not only strong persons but also frail ones—both predestined with me and chosen in me before the foundation of the world. For one of those elect says: “As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and spotless before him in love” (Eph. I, 4).

This I know, I the Catholic Church, gathered from the sons of Jonadab: strong in my youth, mature in my old age, and in oldness destined to suffer many infirmities—and perhaps already suffering them in part—according to the saying: “And if by reason of strength they be eighty years, yet their labour and sorrow are more” (Ps. LXXXIX, 10).

Having therefore already suffered many and great labours and sorrows, I fear still more and greater ones in decrepit old age, exposed to many failures and sighs. Therefore I say—indeed I beseech thee—my God, who hast taught me from youth until now: forsake me not unto old age and oldness.

Thou art the true Jonadab, willing in all the good things thou hast done for the instruction of thy children and in the evils thou hast endured; promising thy children many good things, thou hast said among thy other promises: “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. XVIII, 20). That is: in youth, near the beginnings of the Church; in old age, about its middle; and in oldness, when the Church is to be ended and brought to completion.

Therefore I confidently ask for that good which I hold from thee thyself, its truthful promiser. I say this that thou mayest be justified in thy words, that thou mayest appear righteous and true, and that thy prophets, who believed and prophesied such things, may be found faithful, righteous, and true: be with us unto the consummation of the age. Be with me, my God, who hast taught me from my youth until now; and, O God, forsake me not unto old age and oldness. Forsake not the strong, who are bone of my bones, nor the weak, who are flesh of my flesh.

Remember thy word, which thou wast about to say—“I am with you”—by first saying: “Behold, I.” “Behold,” thou sayest, “I am with you all [Col. 0301C] days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. XVIII, 20). In saying, “Behold, I,” thou hast promised two things more desirable than gold and precious stone: namely, an evidence demonstrable to all through the demonstrative adverb, and a presence not shadowy but substantial through the likewise demonstrative and substantial noun.

Formerly thou wast present to thy people in the pillar of fire and cloud and in other shadowy figures. I do not now seek such a presence of thee, but one altogether substantial and demonstrative, so that what thou hast said may be true: “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age”; and so that we, glorying in this truth, may say: “Behold the Lamb of God, who taketh away the sins [Col. 0301D] of the world” (John I, 29). Likewise: “Behold my God, and I will honour him; the God of my father, and I will exalt him” (Exod. XV, 2).

And let the nations no longer say: “Where is their God?”—the God of Christians, whose being among the saints is doubted when the holy man fails, when truths have been diminished among the children of men, as though among no one the truth of the divine promises remained. Yet the evidence of those promises is promised without doubt even to the Church in oldness. I ask this, I the Church, or I the ecclesiastical person, saying: “O God, forsake me not unto old age and oldness,” so that, as my youth shone in the strength of faith’s courage and my old age in the maturity of hope, so the final period of my old age, called oldness, may shine in the mercy of the word. Thus greater mercy was reserved for Job’s latter end than for his beginning, since Satan’s temptations had by then been altogether overcome.

Thus, once the violence of tyrants has been overcome through martyrs, and the fraudulence of heretics through confessors, let the craftiness of false brethren finally be overcome through good brethren, truly faithful and prudent, lest the Church’s oldness be mocked because she lacks a faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord may appoint over his household to give them their measure of wheat—most necessary in the time of oldness, when there will be famine and the flight of Elijah, with excessive drought threatening and the wickedness and filth of Jezebel reigning.

Overcoming every peril until that final time, be to me a protecting God and a fortified place, as was explained above [Col. 0302B] near the beginning of the psalm, which can be compared to my youth. This, therefore, I ask: that, having become to me a fortified place and a house of refuge, giving me at the beginning of faith strength to act manfully, thou mayest not forsake me in the time of oldness when my strength fails, but mayest unfailingly help me strongly to the end.

“Until I proclaim thine arm to every generation that is to come, thy power and thy righteousness, O God, unto the highest things which thou hast done, thy great deeds.” Amid these vicissitudes of events and times, in which one generation passes and another comes, like wave following wave, may the generation of the upright who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob, not fail—until I, the Church, through this generation, concerning which I hold the promise that it shall not pass away until all things are accomplished, proclaim thine arm to every generation that is to come, whether good or evil, so that none may hide himself from the heat of this sun. In it the true Jonadab set his tent, commanding his sons also to dwell in tents, as pilgrims and soldiers after the example of their father, the true Jonadab, truly willing to obey God his Father.

Through these sons, who shall remain until the end of the age, may I proclaim thine arm everywhere, preaching that by the strength of thine arm thou hast scattered my enemies; that thou hast shown might in thine arm when thou hast scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts, put down the mighty from their seat, and exalted the humble. Thus may I proclaim thine arm as ruling in the past, ruling in the present, and destined to rule in the future, to every [Col. 0302D] generation that is to come; because thine arm, thy Son, through whom thou workest mighty deeds, will always resist the proud and give grace to the humble.

Thus may I also proclaim thy power, by which thou art able both to harden whom thou wilt and to have mercy on whom thou wilt; and thy righteousness, without which thou doest neither of these things—for all that thou doest, thou doest powerfully and justly, so that none can accuse thee of acting unjustly, whether in hardening those whom thou hardenest or in having mercy upon those to whom thou hast mercy.

This thy powerful righteousness and righteous power, O God, reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly: from end to end, from the worm to the angel, from the lowest abyss to the highest things of heaven—unto the highest things. For thou hast done great deeds not only on [Col. 0303A] earth but also in heaven: casting the proud devil out of heaven, and exalting there the human being who is ashes and dust, not merely unto the high ranks of heavenly powers, with which all the members of the Church, even the lowest, are to be associated, provided that they are in unfeigned love, but even unto those highest things which the Father possesses in his majesty. At his right hand human nature has been placed in Christ, as Pope Leo says: “It was joined in glory upon the throne of him to whose nature it was united in the Son.”

In this also I shall proclaim thy power and righteousness, O God, unto the highest things in which thou hast done wonders: whether a human being is found powerful and righteous among the weak, or an angel among the highest, this power and righteousness belongs neither to human nor angelic nature, but to thee. It must be ascribed to thee alone, to whom I also said above: “Lord, I will remember thy righteousness alone.”

Since these things are so, O God, who is like thee? Certainly none: for by thy own power thou art what thou art and canst do what thou canst do; all other things have from thee their being, whatever they are, and their power, whatever they can do. Not considering this, Lucifer in heaven presumed to prefer himself above the other angels, who shared his nature and companionship, as though he were, or could become, like the Most High. But in his fall he learned—or rather, we learn through it—that he who, by falling, became like the serpent is not like thee, O God.

And the devil, entering that serpent as a vessel fit and suitable for himself, persuaded the first human beings perversely to desire likeness to God, saying: “You shall be like [Col. 0303C] gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III, 5). Thus they too, cast out of paradise and taught by manifold misery, learned that the devil was a false promiser and that he was the true teacher who says: “O God, who is like thee?”

No one, therefore, is like thee by his own power; but some are made like thee by the gift of thy grace. For in this valley of tears, from which we cry to thee, “O God, who is like thee?” thou makest some like thyself according to the measure of thy gift. Otherwise man would have been made in vain in thine image and likeness, if all human beings perished in the far country of dissimilarity from thee. But it is not so: the lost drachma is sought, and in it the obliterated beauty is restored; the lost sheep is found and borne back upon the shepherd’s shoulders; the prodigal son is received when he returns to his father. Finally, the bright likeness of thy countenance, O God, is promised to all who love their enemies and, as far as they can, do them good, in likeness of thee, who makest thy sun rise upon good and evil, and rainest upon just and unjust.

By this way of holy love, obedience, and devotion, the likeness of God will be obtained—a likeness which neither the angel in heaven could obtain through self-exaltation nor man in paradise through disobedience. Therefore we must return by another way to our own country; when we arrive there, we shall be like God and shall see him as he is. For we must return there through humility and obedience, having fallen from there through pride [Col. 0304A] and disobedience, so that what we cannot be by nature, we may be by grace: namely, like God, abiding in him and with him, and continually drinking from him, as from an inexhaustible fountain, the grace and glory of this likeness.

For whoever thinks himself to be or to be able to do anything through himself or from himself, though he neither is nor can do anything from himself, deceives himself. For to be or to have power in that manner belongs only to the divine nature, which alone is above all things and by itself can do and knows all things, needing no external helper. Whoever, therefore, whether human or angelic, claims such power or knowledge for himself from himself, perversely desiring the likeness of the Most High, will fall into the pit of dissimilarity: either, like the devil, to be left there, or, like man, to be drawn back thence with long ropes of tribulations.

Those who are not chastised with human beings, as demons are not, will at last be sent with the demons into the abyss, to be tormented with them in eternal fire. But those predestined to eternal life, lest they be sent into the abyss of everlasting perdition, are scourged with very many tribulations and, willing or unwilling, are compelled toward the way of holy humility. That this is so, both I the Church and I the ecclesiastical person have learned by many experiences. For, O God—

**VERSE 20.** “How many tribulations, many and evil, hast thou shown me! And, turning, thou hast given me life, and hast brought me back again from the abysses of the earth!” To me, seeking to become like thee, the Most High, through the self-exaltation of the first human being—who would not be held as a servant under a command, in order that, ruled by no one, he might become like God—to such a one as I was, lest I should remain so, thou hast shown how many tribulations were due to such great self-exaltation or disobedience. This is plainly evident in the first parent of the former captives. For because he broke the command, he himself was first taken captive, and his descendants were taken captive with him before they were born.

How many great and evil tribulations this captivity contains cannot be told; nor can it be told how unlike God—blessed and untouched by every tribulation—man is in these afflictions, being afflicted and captive. Therefore, rather than attempting to describe what cannot be described, I am compelled to cry out in certain wonder: “O God, who is like thee? How many tribulations, many and evil, hast thou shown me!”—many in quantity, evil in harmful quality.

These many and evil tribulations thou hast not merely sent in order to punish for guilt; thou hast also shown them in order to instruct for discipline. The one was a work of justice, the other of mercy, and therefore both joined together, wine with oil, benefited me when wounded. For through these two, turning to me—thou who through the fault of pride hadst been turned away from me—thou gavest me life, lest I should remain in everlasting death with the devil, the ruler of death; and thou hast brought me back again from the abysses of the earth. Thou, great Prophet, turning to me when dead, hast done through thyself what could not be done through thy staff: made man and stooped down to my littleness, thou hast given me life.

[Col. 0305A] And this was the manner of my vivification: thou hast brought me back again from the abysses of the earth. As it is one thing for man to be created and another to be recreated, so it is one thing for him to be led forth and another to be brought back from the abyss of the earth. He was created once, and this divine operation has no repetition and can have none, because one created from nothing does not thereafter return wholly to nothing, so that he could again be created from nothing. Yet, though made from nothing, he tends through natural defect toward nothingness—although he cannot wholly be nothing—so that a person once created needs to be recreated many times by the constant, indeed continual, aid of divine mercy.

Likewise man was once led forth from the abysses of the earth, in which he lay hidden, when, still hidden beneath the waters of the abyss, the earth was without form and void, and darkness was upon the abyss. Then, by divine operation, when the waters [Col. 0305B] of the abyss had been gathered into one place, the earth, the material from which man was to be formed, was brought forth from the abysses themselves. This divine operation has no repetition, because there will be no further confusion of things such as existed at the beginning of the world.

But mortal man, brought forth from beneath the waters of the abyss and being ashes and dust, raised himself excessively beyond his proper measure when, in pride, he presumed to desire likeness to his Creator, the most high Spirit, believing the deceiver who said: “You shall be like gods” (Gen. III, 5). Therefore he deserved to hear: “Thou art earth, and unto earth thou shalt go” (Gen.
