III, 19), because the equity of divine judgment demanded that, since he had exalted himself above heaven, he should be humbled under heaven by many blows until he returned to the earth from which he had been taken. This is accomplished by bodily death, which is owed to every human being begotten from Adam through concupiscence.

But in the one man conceived without carnal concupiscence through the working of the Holy Spirit and born of a virgin, the earth of the human race was restored to such dignity that bodily death had no claim upon him, in whom there was no death of the soul; for he had neither original nor actual sin. Yet he willingly accepted undeserved death and willingly descended into the abyss of hell: dead indeed in body, but free among the dead from death of the soul.

Therefore let no one say, “Who descended into the abyss?” For “that is to bring Christ back from the dead,” says the Apostle (Rom. X, 7). He alone descended there free; yet he did not return alone, because he brought many back from there with him. Many of them also rose bodily with him from the abysses of the earth—that is, from the tombs—and entered the holy city and appeared to many, just as dry land appeared at the beginning when the abysses had been removed. This was one bringing-back from the abysses.

But the bringing-back from the abysses and depths that are in the pit of misery of souls is repeated in the first resurrection through the sacraments of faith. Those who, having been raised in it, persevere, live. Over them the second death has no power: the final condemnation of the wicked and their casting into the abyss, when the Judge says: “Go into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41). For them there is no bringing-back from the pit of the abyss, from the depth of hell, from the pit of misery, because there is no change for those who remain in their wickedness without repentance.

But for human beings predestined to life—who either preserve innocence after baptism or bring forth fruits worthy of repentance before death—the final bringing-back from the abysses will be the resurrection of bodies, not into a judgment of condemnation, since “the judgments of God” are “a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV, 7), but into the glory of that transformation in which, although we all rise, we shall not all be changed. For “all the dead shall indeed rise incorruptible,” that is, perfectly whole as regards the integrity of their members, “but we shall not all be changed” (I Cor. XV, 51), says the Apostle concerning himself and those like him. For, having then been freed from the abysses of the earth, they will not be overwhelmed or submerged in the pit of eternal misery through thy judgments, O God, which are a great abyss. From these, as has now been said, thou hast brought me back by the third repeated bringing-back.

Thus, I say, thou hast brought me back, I the universal Church, so that, recalling this in thanksgiving, I may worthily add this praise beyond every praise of thee. For although it is great and worthy of every praise that thou didst once lead me forth from the abysses of the earth in the first formation of things, yet in doing this thou didst not labour. For thou didst say, “Let this or that be,” and it was so. Neither then, in speaking or doing, didst thou labour, O Father, who didst utter a good Word; nor was it laborious for thee, the Son, who art the Father’s Word, to be begotten from the heart of the Begetter in a birth not painful but eternally joyful; nor was it laborious for thee, the Holy Spirit, who then didst move over the waters of the abyss, to move over them in such a way that man might be led forth from those dark abysses of waters by the operation of the whole Trinity.

But now thou, Son of God, one Person in the Trinity, in order that I the Church might be led forth a third time from the abysses of the earth, as has been said, having become man, didst labour greatly: enduring a long earthly life in mortal flesh; contradiction in teaching, as though thou wert a deceiver; disparagement in miracles, as though thou didst them by the prince of demons; mockery in eating and drinking, as though thou wert a glutton and wine-drinker; and finally spitting, blows, scourges, a garment of derision, a crown of thorns, the cross, and on the cross submission to the most shameful of deaths. Through all these things thou hast brought me back again from the abysses of the earth.

Therefore, beyond all the praise of that leading-forth by which, without labour, thou didst lead me forth from the abysses of the earth in the beginning, I shall add and exalt this praise: that thou hast brought me back again from the abysses of the earth through many labours and sufferings. Thus those who despise these restorations incur a greater guilt of ingratitude; and for those who acknowledge them as is fitting, they furnish greater matter and a more compelling reason for thanksgiving—not only for those universal repeated restorations from the abysses which, as has been shown, have a fixed number, but also for the individual and particular ones, which have no number.

For since the righteous person falls seven times in a day and rises again, and since forgiveness of sins is promised seventy times seven to one who sins and repents—and this forgiveness is nothing other than a bringing-back repeatedly from the abysses of the earth—who can count [Col. 0307A] how often, and in how many repeated instances of this restoration, thou, O God—

**VERSE 21.** “Hast multiplied thy magnificence, and, turning, hast comforted me.” For through diverse and many kinds of scourging and consolation thou, in willing love, bringest thy sons of Jonadab back from the abysses of sins whenever they fall into them and cry to thee from the depths. Thus everyone brought back from the abysses of the earth, not only through universal but also through particular restorations, has reason continually to say to thee in thanksgiving: “Thou hast multiplied thy magnificence, and, turning, hast comforted me.”

Thou hast multiplied thy magnificence in scourges, because “many are the scourges of the sinner,” and in many ways thou scourgest every son whom thou receivest. Yet because, when thou hast been angry, thou rememberest mercy, making lightning into rain through that mercy, thou hast, as it were, turned from severity to gentleness and comforted me. Thou hast not allowed me so to be swallowed up amid scourges by excessive sorrow that despair of salvation might creep in; rather, even amid scourges, rejoicing in hope, I may through hope of salvation obtain the reality itself.

That this has happened to me, a son of Jonadab willingly humbled under scourges and willingly made captive through obedience to fatherly discipline, is evident from the fact that confession of sin, accusing myself, and thanksgiving, praising thee, God, continually resound in the devotion of my heart, where thou hearest, and frequently in the ear, where human beings hear.

**VERSE 22.** For I too will confess to you, O God, your truth upon instruments of psalmody—this is the confession of one who praises; [Col. 0307C] and I will sing psalms to you on the lyre, O Holy One of Israel—this is the confession of the penitent, chastising and crucifying his flesh with its vices and desires, to the glory of the Holy One of Israel, who sacrificed himself upon the cross for his own, that they too might be holy in truth, singing psalms and playing the lyre in all holiness. For the psaltery, the vessel or instrument for psalm-singing which gives forth sound from above, signifies the Spirit which is from above, which has already risen in hope and savours the things above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God. The lyre, however, resounds from below, signifying the body chastised and fitted for the praises of God: a body which indeed took its origin from the earth, but in the resurrection to come will receive heavenly and angelic impassibility [Col. 0307D] in glory so much greater as it is now more fully exercised in divine service, by singing well and acting rightly; because a good psalm is a good work, and “it is good to confess to the Lord, and to sing to your name, O Most High” (Ps. XCI, 2).

Therefore I will confess to you, O God, your truth upon instruments of psalmody, knowing this: that the words or songs of psalms are like silver or golden vessels of truth, containing and preserving wine and the oil of charity. For this reason, whether upon the psaltery sounding from above, through the pursuit of holy contemplation, or upon the lyre sounding from below, through the pursuit of good action, I will sing psalms to you, O God, upon instruments of psalmody filled with the oil of gladness. I shall do this not by bearing the cross under compulsion, but by willingly sacrificing the free offerings of my mouth; and [Col. 0308A] while sacrificing, rejoicing in that gladness which you, O God, love; because:

**VERSE 23.** My lips shall rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed. My lips shall rejoice while I sing psalms with the spirit; my soul shall rejoice while I sing psalms also with the understanding. For to sing only with the spirit, while the understanding remains without fruit, is altogether useless. To sing with the spirit is to utter from memory the words of the psalms; but to sing with the understanding is to apprehend in the mind the life-giving meaning of the words. That meaning is then sweeter to the taste of the soul which you have redeemed, O Lord, when, in singing psalms, it meditates upon the mysteries of its redemption. Thus, for example, when it sings: “Man ate the bread of angels,” it should understand that bread, not by following the bran of the letter, but the fine flour of the Spirit: [Col. 0308B] not the bread which Moses gave, nor that which Moses ate with the people. For the eating of that bread, though it nourished the flesh, was not sufficient for the redemption of the soul; rather, it is the bread signified by the Father, in which he gave life to the world, and by which he feeds angels immortal­ly.

Since the Jews do not do this, following the killing letter and not the life-giving Spirit, what they offer while singing psalms is contemptible; and rightly it is said to them through the prophet: “You offer polluted bread upon my altar” (Mal. I, 7). Therefore, that my soul, which you have redeemed, O Lord, by bringing it back again from the depths of the earth, may be able to rejoice, I shall not be satisfied merely to observe externally, in the instruments of psalmody, a silver brightness or a kind of golden radiance. Rather, I shall taste the wine which gladdens the heart of man [Col. 0308C] and the oil of gladness stored within those very vessels; and I shall see that you are sweet, O Lord, you who have brought me back again from the depths of the earth.

Paul himself, the vessel of election, had received a taste of this sweetness in the vessels of psalmody. Exhorting us to the same and warning us against contrary things, he said: “Do not be drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Holy Spirit” (Eph. V, 18). And, as though we might wonder from what vessels we could draw the Holy Spirit, this kindly teacher, displaying the vessels and, as it were, offering them with his hand, added: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody”—not indeed always openly before men, but—“in your hearts [Col. 0308D] to the Lord” (ibid., 19).

In the hope of this filling—indeed, assisted by the reality of that filling itself, insofar as you grant it—I shall sing psalms to you upon instruments of psalmody, offering my heart to you as an instrument of singing. I shall sing in order to be filled, and I shall be filled in order to sing to you, O Lord. I shall sing, I say, and as I sing shall be filled according to my capacity; when filled, I too shall become a vessel among the vessels of psalmody, full of the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and from the vessels of psalmody the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill me. For “the spirit of life” is “in these wheels” (Ezek. I, 20): in the vessels of psalms, fashioned and turned by the fingers and hand of God.

But what if I am too sluggish an animal to be raised together with these wheels when they are lifted from the earth, and to go wherever the wheels go, [Col. 0309A] so that, singing with the spirit, I may always sing also with the understanding, and that what is uttered by the mouth may always be held in the heart? This is the lawful manner of singing psalms, and one always to be desired by us. But if we strive and do not accomplish it, attempt it and fall back, do we therefore return from the vessels of psalmody fruitless and empty, since the Apostle testifies that the understanding of those who sing only in spirit and with the tongue is without fruit? Yet the word of the angel consoles me: “Peace to men of good will” (Luke II, 14). Likewise, the voice of the Psalmist says: “The thought of man shall confess to you, and the remnant of thought shall keep festival for you” (Ps. LXXV, 11). For what is that thought of man which confesses to God, if not the principal intention of pleasing God and confessing him through psalm-singing? [Col. 0309B] Unless this had been left to us by God as a seed even in psalm-singing, when harmful or vain thoughts at times rush upon us, we should have been as Sodom, and been made like Gomorrah.

Now therefore, while God accepts this principal intention of pleasing and confessing him—of whom the Psalmist says, “At midnight,” he says, “I rose to confess to you because of the judgments of your righteousness” (Ps. CXVIII, 62)—and while I repel, or unwillingly endure, the incursions of other thoughts, the remnant of this principal thought, left to us by God, shall keep festival for you. For the end of the one singing psalms and confessing to you shall be better than the beginning, because you have brought me back again from the depths of the earth. First, I confess again that I have been brought back in my soul, which you have redeemed; [Col. 0309C] second, again in my body, whose firstfruits in you, O Christ—in those who rose with you—already shine in heaven, brought back again from the depths of the earth. Therefore, when I have sung to you, not only shall my soul rejoice, which you redeemed and gave life by your death;

**VERSE 24.** But also my tongue shall meditate all day upon your righteousness. The outward tongue is an instrument for speaking, not for meditating. But when that which is uttered by the mouth is held in the heart, the tongue of flesh itself also becomes an instrument of good meditation. Therefore I do not say, “My tongue shall speak,” but I say, “It shall meditate upon your righteousness.” For in that repeated return from the depths of the earth, understood in [Col. 0309D] the blessed resurrection of the flesh, the tongue of flesh itself, together with all bodily members, shall become so spiritual that I should more rightly say of it that it will meditate upon your righteousness than say that it will speak. For vocal speech shall not be needed there, where tongues shall cease, where prophecies shall be abolished, where, without a monitor, O Lord, I shall remember your righteousness alone; where my tongue shall meditate all day—that is, in eternity, without end—upon your righteousness.

All day, I say, without the terror of night; for there shall be no night there. All day, I say, in great serenity and security, which neither is nor can be here among those who seek evil against me; but it shall then be complete, when those who seek evil against me have been confounded and put to shame. For they shall be confounded and troubled by horrible fear, [Col. 0310A] and, as though with reverence—although far too late—shall marvel at the suddenness of unexpected salvation, seeing that inestimable good things have come to me, when they always sought evil against me. Then there shall be for the saints a place of secure rejoicing, when the ungodly, confounded in the divine judgment and cast down into the depths of the earth, shall no longer be permitted to rule.

Then there shall be only the voice of rejoicing and salvation in the tabernacles of the righteous reigning with Christ; but not so in the tabernacles of those still fighting, where the voices of those singing psalms with rejoicing are frequently interrupted by the groans of those weeping and grieving. For to whom, still weighed down by the burden of flesh, does the oil of gladness so overflow in the vessels of psalmody that he is not sometimes compelled to groan over the emptiness of those very vessels—and, what is worse, their emptiness [Col. 0310B] together with their scarcity? For it is a miserable house where there are many vessels for wine or oil, but they contain neither wine nor oil. Yet most miserable is that house in which not even vessels capable of holding wine or oil are found.

So, certainly, where psalmody is disciplined—for example, where singers chant: “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity, like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which descends upon the edge of his garment” (Ps. CXXXII, 12)—yet the ointment itself or the pleasantness of brethren dwelling together in unity is absent, the vessels of psalmody may indeed appear beautiful, but they are empty and void. Thus, before we were first brought forth from the depths of the earth, the earth itself was empty and void, [Col. 0310C] not yet adorned, that is, with any fruit of grain, wine, and oil.

Likewise, when someone sings psalms to God: “I am yours; save me, for I have sought your ordinances” (Ps. CXVIII, 94), yet is himself a servant of Mammon, a servant of as many masters as he has vices, and has never sought to be justified from those vices so as to be able truly to say to God, “I have sought your ordinances”—is not this vessel of psalmody, even if it makes a ringing sound in the mouth like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal, empty of inward sweetness and of that truth concerning which one who sings well says: “I will confess to you, O God, your truth upon instruments of psalmody”? But where not even the outward discipline of psalm-singing is observed, the house is most miserable, having within it no vessels even empty ones, much less [Col. 0310D] full ones.

The household of such a house needs the maternal diligence and solicitude of teaching such as was found in that widow who, having been one of the wives of the prophets, came after her husband’s death to Elisha the prophet, the greatest prophet in his day, and said to him: “Your servant, my husband, is dead; and behold, the creditor has come to take my two sons to serve him.” And he said: “What do you wish me to do for you? What have you in your house?” And she said: “Your handmaid has nothing in my house except a little oil with which I may anoint myself.” And he said: “Go and ask your neighbours for many empty vessels; and shut the door of your house upon yourself and your children; and when you are inside, pour into all the vessels, and when they are full, remove them” (IV [Col. 0311A] Kings IV, 1 ff.). And so it happened: the little oil was poured into all the vessels, and the vessels were filled, so that the prophet said: “Go, sell it, and pay your creditor; but you and your sons shall live on the remainder” (ibid., 7).

Without prejudice, certainly, to the more sacred and mystical sense in which that widow signifies the universal Church, according to an allegory long known and expounded by the Fathers, the sweetness of moral instruction breathes here. For every soul that believes the words of the prophets, being as it were one of the wives of the prophets, rightly has recourse to that great Prophet who, having once died and become the death of death, and having been raised after the dominion of death was destroyed, dies no more, and death shall have no more dominion over him. The soul rightly laments its poverty to him when the spirit of prophecy or psalmody, which was its husband, has died; [Col. 0311B] and it has two sons subject to it, namely the active and contemplative modes of life. But, their father having died—that is, the spirit having been extinguished—they are so impoverished that that most wicked creditor, the devil, from whom the coin of sin was given to man, desires to take them to serve himself.

For just as the Apostle joins these two things, “fervent in spirit, serving the Lord” (Rom. XII, 11), so conversely these two are joined: the spirit extinguished, lukewarmness, and slavery to the devil. Since the Lord threatens that those who are lukewarm and refuse to grow warm again will be cast out of his mouth unless they repent, what remains for them if they persist in their lukewarmness, except that the roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour, should incorporate into himself these animal men, [Col. 0311C] who do not have the Spirit and thereby separate themselves from the body of the Lord? What hope of consolation, then, is there in such desolation? Surely that hope which is conceived from the mouth and words of the prophet teaching: “Gather not a few empty vessels” (IV Kings IV, 3), vessels to be sought from neighbours.

For, lest examples be sought from afar, neighbouring and disciplined monasteries, sufficiently furnished with vessels of psalmody, ought to be set before slothful disciples for imitation by every father or mother of a household. From them they should seek not a few vessels: that is, they should apply themselves to a similar discipline of psalm-singing and of living well according to the Scriptures. Even if such vessels are empty among those who sing with spirit and understanding or do good works but not from devotion, nevertheless, [Col. 0311D] in the gathering of children who remain obediently with their mother in a closed house and offer her vessels, the oil increases and the small becomes great, if only there is one soul among the wives of the prophets which pours oil into the vessels according to its ability by attending to the meaning of the Psalms.

Let the house therefore be shut, lest the children, being undisciplined, may wander about. Let the door be shut, so that each of the children and sons of the Church, with the door closed, may pray to his Father; and, praying, may gladden his mother, that is, the congregation in which he has been nourished. For just as the universal Church is mother of each of her members, so every congregation worthy to be numbered among the wives of the prophets is rightly called the mother of each whom it nourishes and whom it desires to be free from the creditor’s service.

[Col. 0312A] This further increases consolation: in a disciplined and regularly enclosed house, our mother which is above, who is free, is accustomed to dwell with her sons as they sing psalms in order and offer her vessels. For from her come the “princes joined with those who sing psalms in the midst of maidens playing timbrels” (Ps. LXVII, 26), namely the holy angels, in whose presence I shall sing psalms to you, O God. For I too will confess to you upon instruments of psalmody, setting before the sight of the heavenly mother the psalms themselves and the songs of psalms as vessels fashioned by the hand of the Craftsman: sometimes full, sometimes half-full, sometimes empty. Those which are full of the wine or oil of joy, may you deign to preserve; those which are half-full or empty, I ask may be filled, at least [Col. 0312B] through the remnant of thought which shall keep festival for you.

It would indeed be good, and most desirable, if the firstfruits of thoughts were offered in the vessels of psalmody, so that the vessels themselves might be found full; so that not one word in a psalm might be empty, but that throughout the whole psalm, from beginning to end, one might sing intelligently, such that the understanding of the words might have savour upon the palate of the mind. But which mortal can boast that he sings so intelligently that, from the beginning of the psalm to the end, the firstfruits of his thoughts have savour together with all the remaining words of psalmody uttered with their full meaning? If anyone sings so intelligently, he is great before the Lord and venerable before men, though imitable by few. It goes well with me if I am granted to keep festival [Col. 0312C] through the remnant of thoughts.

The remnants of food left over by those who have eaten are small in comparison with the food of which they are remnants. Thus, in comparison with one who sings psalms wholly intelligently, my understanding is like a small remnant, keeping festival in a few thoughts. In these is that little oil with which I may anoint myself; and I hope that, distributed among empty vessels, it can be increased by the blessing of the great Prophet, so that it may suffice not only for me, sick or infirm, for healing anointing, but also for my children who bring me vessels—that is, those who sing psalms with me in discipline—for complete deliverance from the creditor and sufficient support for a sober, righteous, and godly life, in which there may be:

Glory to the Father for sobriety, to the Son for righteousness, [Col. 0312D] to the Holy Spirit for piety: as this glory was in the beginning predestined to remain in the sons of Jonadab, to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, unto all ages. Amen. For the sobriety of the sons of Jonadab is marked by the fact that they did not drink wine; their righteousness, by the fact that, in obedience imposed upon them, they lived in tents outside the cities; their piety, by the fact that they devoutly observed all this, devoutly commanded to them by their father, not from sadness or necessity, but from the gladness which God loves. To him, as has been said, may there always and everywhere be glory for this sobriety, righteousness, and piety: as it was in the beginning predestined and ordained before the ages of the world. Amen.

## PSALM LXXI

[Col. 0313]

[Col. 0313A] “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son.” In this psalm, by a fourth recapitulation, we are now recalled to the height of our hope, when it is said: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son,” and so forth. What it says—“give”—has already been accomplished in the first coming. For “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22). Yet that judgment will take place at the second coming, when this King, according to the truth of the Gospel, shall sit upon the throne of his majesty and all nations shall be gathered before him. There is fear in this, because he shall judge in righteousness; but hope also, because he shall spare the poor and needy, and shall save the souls of the poor. This psalm bears the following title:

**VERSE 1. A PSALM OF DAVID CONCERNING SOLOMON.**

[Col. 0313B] David, I say, the prophet looking toward Christ, who is the true Solomon, the true peaceful one. For he established peace between God and men, between the angelic and human creation, between Jews and Gentiles. Of this peace the present psalm says: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace.” Salem means “peace,” whence Solomon is named, that is, “peaceful.” By this name the ancient Solomon was named in figure, but Christ in truth. For, overthrowing idolatry among the Gentiles and abolishing among the Jews the law of commandments, by which they abhorred one another, he made both peoples one in faith, through which he reconciled them also to God.

He added peace upon peace, because after the peace of reconciliation [Col. 0313C] he gives the peace of immortality, as he himself says of each in the Gospel: “I give you my peace; I leave you peace” (John XIV, 27).

This psalm is directed to commend this Solomon, that is, Christ; and, as the fourth recapitulation, it displays both his natures. First it prays that judgment may be given to the Son in the future, and through him peace may first be given to the people. Second, it declares what it has prayed, adding concerning his eternity at the words: “He shall judge the poor of the people.” Third, it says who and what manner of one is to come, and with what great reverence he shall reign, at: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece.” Fourth, how he is useful, at: “For he shall deliver the poor man from the mighty.” Fifth, concerning his honour and ours through him, at: “And he shall live, and there shall be given to him of the gold of Arabia.” Sixth, it makes its intention clear and exhorts us to praise, that those blessed in him may bless him, at: [Col. 0313D] “May his name be blessed for ever.” Seventh, the prophet himself praises him at: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel.”

The prophet foresees that, although now the whole Trinity, God, judges secretly, in the future nevertheless the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son—not because he did not possess it in the one Godhead together with the Son, but so that it might be manifest in the man who is to come. What, therefore, he foresaw, he prays for, saying:

[Col. 0314A] **VERSE 2.** O God the Father, give your judgment to Christ the King, because he is the Son of Man. For insofar as he is your Son, he possesses eternally, equally with you, O Father, the power of judging. But because this your Son is also the Son of Man and became man by assuming manhood, give to this assumed man alone the power visibly to execute judgment which the whole Trinity shall invisibly execute. Indeed, there is no authority except from you, who sometimes cause a hypocrite to reign because of the sins of the people, and permit unjust men to rule over the just—justly, so far as you are concerned, but unjustly, so far as they are concerned, because what you ordain justly they pursue unjustly, abusing the authority given them. So Pilate unjustly judged the King, the son of a king; and other such judges unjustly judge the just servants of the same King.

Therefore, lest such judges, who exercise judgment without righteousness, should have freedom to rule against the just as they wish, you, the Judge of all, who in tranquillity and great majesty order all things by judgments always just—even though the righteousness of those judgments is sometimes hidden—you, I say, Judge of all, give your judgment to the King: namely, to the man anointed king with such an anointing of your mercy as was prefigured in the anointing of Solomon, king and son of a king—my own son, that is, because I, David the king, begot him and intended him to reign on my throne in peace, all assaults of enemies being everywhere calmed. So you also, O God the Father, with the enemies of peace everywhere humbled and subdued, give your judgment to the King, the son of the King, whom you, the King, begotten of yourself, [Col. 0314C] have so anointed above his companions that he is holy not only in his divinity consubstantial with you, but also, sanctified by himself in his anointed humanity, fit not only to rule and judge all things invisibly with you, but also visibly through himself and his members.

Therefore, when he sits on the throne of his majesty to judge the world by fire, those judges also shall sit with him who, despising the world, followed him. Nor will they be judges only in that final judgment, but earlier too, by the authority given them to bind and loose. Whenever that authority is usurped by the son of iniquity, the son of perdition—that is, Antichrist and his members—judgment is indeed exercised, but without righteousness.

[Col. 0314D] Therefore, that this power of judging unjustly may be exterminated from your kingdom, you righteous Judge, give your judgment to the King and your righteousness to the king’s son, so that there may be no judgment without righteousness in your kingdom. I mean righteousness not of the law, which is from works, but yours, which is from faith: the righteousness which justifies those who believe in him who justifies the ungodly. For the just man lives by faith, and without it there is no true righteousness; hence there is no life either, because, as has been said, “the just man lives by faith” (Rom. I, 17).

The righteousness of faith was therefore prefigured in that anointing of Solomon with which Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anointed him. Zadok means “righteous,” and Nathan, “he gave” or “giving.” By these names is signified that righteousness which does not come from men through works of the law, but is given from above through faith, the sacraments of faith, and works fitting to them, according to grace; by which every good gift and every perfect donation is from above and from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change nor shadow of turning.

You, therefore, Father of lights, with whom there is no change, who have immutably ordained that your Son shall reign in the assumed man, take care lest, Solomon being displaced, Adonijah reign, who says in his heart: “I will reign” (III Kings I, 5). By this saying ambition is indicated; or, what is worse, Absalom, the open persecutor. Let both be exterminated, and, with Bathsheba—that is, the holy Church—intervening, let full authority be given to Solomon alone to maintain so great a peace that he and his friends may without disturbance enjoy the delights contained in his songs, which because of their excellence are called the Song of Songs, just as, for a similar reason, he himself, the true Solomon, is called King of kings, Lord of lords, and Holy of holies.

Although he is the lawful King, as the Son of the eternal King—your Son, O God the Father, who rule all things—yet, to teach that no one ought to usurp the office of governance (for no one rightly takes honour to himself, but is called by God, as Aaron was), he too, though the King’s Son, reverently awaits the Father’s voice saying: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance and the ends of the earth for your possession. You shall rule them with a rod of iron” (Ps. II, 8–9). This voice of the King and Father, disposing that his Son should reign and saying, “You shall rule them with a rod of iron,” is sought in this psalm directed to Solomon, when those singing are made to say: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son.”

Give judgment and righteousness to the man assumed into the person of your Son, so that, having authority on earth to forgive sins, he may justify ungodly persons and penitent sinners by forgiving those sins; condemn the impenitent or falsely penitent; and cast down the mighty who have presumptuously seized a throne through ambition. Thus Solomon deposed his brother Adonijah, who sought the kingdom by requesting Abishag the Shunammite in marriage. Solomon judged that Adonijah had spoken against his own life in such a way that, by his desired marriage to the queen, the kingdom also was being sought for him. For he said to his mother: “Why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask the kingdom for him also” (III Kings II, 22). Thus, when the fraud of wicked ambition was discovered, the king ordered the plotter against his kingdom to be killed.

Likewise, when fraud was discovered between the two harlots, he ordered the living child to be given to the one who was its mother. He also ordered Shimei, who cursed him and was not content with the terms of repentance assigned to him, to be killed. He exercised many other just judgments, as a figure of the true peaceful Son of God. Singing in reference to Solomon, both in his members and in his own person, I ask you, almighty Father, that judgment may be given to him, so that he may judge your people in righteousness and your poor in true judgment—that is, just judgment.

I mean your poor: those made poor in your Spirit, that is, humble, according to the saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V, 3). Let him judge these poor as judges and soldiers worthy of his kingdom, saying to them: “Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke VI, 20). But that these poor may freely judge and fight in Solomon’s kingdom, and reign with him and under him, let him himself execute judgment and vengeance against the ambitious disturbers of his kingdom: humbling those like Adonijah; distinguishing from true mothers the harlots who kill their children—first distinguishing the Synagogue from the holy Church, then condemning in the Church every perverse sect as a harlot and murderer of her own children; and consigning to death, unless they truly repent, blasphemers like Shimei, allies of Absalom—indeed, servants of Antichrist, persecutors of Christ, blasphemers of the true Solomon. This is what it is for you, O God, to judge your people in righteousness and your poor in judgment.

By saying “your judgment,” “your righteousness,” “your people,” and “your poor,” I show that all things of his are yours, and what is yours is his, as he himself says to you, Father: “All mine are yours, and all yours are mine” (John XVII, 10). All these things were indeed given to the Son from eternity; nevertheless, they shall be given to him because he is the Son of Man, so that in the man they may be openly manifested [Col. 0316C] which, before the assumption of manhood, were secretly given to him as the eternal Son of the eternal King. Conceived by the Holy Spirit and born a man from man, he became the Son of Man and began to have human members both in his singular body, which is exalted above all things in the glory of the Father, and in his great body, which is the holy Church. Among these, some are great like mountains, some small like hills, and some least of all, comparable to plains or valleys.

And because in the kingdom of the peaceful Solomon nothing is more acceptable than peace itself, which surpasses all understanding and unites heavenly and earthly things so that both become one kingdom wholly at peace, the peaceful King himself first said to the mountains, the apostles, on the triumphant day of his resurrection: “Peace be to you” (John XX, 26). Let those mountains receive peace, the wall of enmity having been destroyed by the inestimable price of his blood and death. Let them, I say, receive peace, reconciled to God; he also placed in them the word of reconciliation, that they might know that they received peace not only to preserve for themselves but also to confer upon the people. Therefore I say: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people,” so that they may have not only remission of sins—which is true peace—and reconciliation with God, but also: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them,” among the people. This occurred when the true Solomon stood in the midst of the disciples and said to them: “Peace be to you.” In saying this he truly kissed them with the kiss of his mouth. [Col. 0317A] For he breathed upon them also, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX, 22).

But for the complete pacification of his kingdom, it was not enough that the mountains alone should receive the Holy Spirit from him by such a kiss, so long desired in the Song of Songs. The beautiful feet of those preaching peace also had to be directed into the way of peace, to give knowledge of salvation to his people. “Therefore he said to them again: ‘Peace be to you,’ and added: ‘As the Father has sent me, I also send you’” (John XX, 21 [printed “XXVI, 21”]). It was as if he said: “As the Father sent me to give peace to you mountains, so I send you to give peace to the people; not because you are authors of so great a gift and grace, but so that the people may regard you as my ministers and stewards of sacred mysteries, according to the measure of my gift. Consequently, let no one be puffed up or boast against another, saying, ‘I am of Paul, I of Apollos, I of Cephas, but I of Christ’ (I Cor. I, 12). For all are to be named neither Paulinians from Paul nor Apollinians from Apollos, but Christians from me, Christ—whether baptized, confirmed, ordained, or consecrated through whatever minister.”

To make this known to the people is to give peace to the people, so that there may be no occasion of schism in my peaceful kingdom, to which I, the true Solomon, “give peace” and “leave peace” (John XIV, 27). For I give you mountains my peace to preserve; I also leave you peace to teach among the people, as is desired in the psalm where it says: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people.” Let the people themselves, receiving peace from the mountains, say in thanksgiving: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me” (Ps. CXX, 1). But because the mountains themselves are neither creators nor authors of this peace and help, let them add consequently: “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (ibid., 2). He is therefore the author of every grace, both in earthly and visible benefits and in heavenly and invisible fruits: giving earthly goods to his people for use, but heavenly goods for enjoyment. For the fruits of the Spirit are charity, joy, peace, and other such gifts, which remain now and unto eternity, and are therefore better than those which will pass away with this present life.

[Col. 0317D] Among all gifts, however, peace—which is also called charity—is pre-eminent in the kingdom, or bridal chamber, of Solomon. He loves that one queen, that one dove, his perfect and chosen one, more than sixty queens: that is, other virtues which are to be loved after that one virtue. Therefore let the mountains principally receive peace to bring and offer it to the people; then let the hills receive righteousness likewise to proclaim it to the people, because the kingdom of the true Solomon “is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. XIV, 17).

The hills, less than the mountains, are the disciples of the apostles, ministers after them of peace and righteousness. The mountains first received peace because what they believed when Christ preached before the coming of the Holy Spirit, they fully understood when that same Spirit came and filled their hearts with understanding; and in this understanding they preserved peace. For then they disagreed neither with the Scriptures nor with one another in their understanding of the truth. This appears from the fact that the apostles themselves concordantly preached peace to the people of the Gentiles and confirmed from the Scriptures that this ought to be done.

But their disciples, like hills smaller than mountains, were not in agreement in this teaching until, enlightened by the eternal mountains, they received this faith: that God is not the God of Jews only, but also of Gentiles. When this faith had been instilled, the hills received righteousness, because the just man lives by faith, and there is no true righteousness without apostolic faith. By that faith the holy Church is taught to be not confined among the Jews [Col. 0318B] but expanded among all nations so extensively that it is rightly called Catholic, that is, universal, because through her extension in every direction the name of the Lord is wonderful in all the earth, not in Judea alone or in any particular sect found divided from the universal Church.

Those, therefore, who understand and love with the apostles the hidden mysteries of sacred Scripture are like mountains, higher than the dark water which is in the clouds of the air, and have peace with God and among themselves. But those who believe the teaching of such persons and obey their commands are like hills beneath the clouds: they do not understand the obscure letter, but are justified by faith together with obedience.

Alternatively: Let the mountains receive peace for the people, not only through his own mouth, when the true Solomon says, “Peace [Col. 0318C] be with you,” but also through the mouths of bishops who say in his stead, “Peace be with you.” Likewise, when Catholic priests say, “The Lord be with you,” or, “May the peace of the Lord always be with you,” let the mountains—that is, all rulers of peoples who hold an exalted station—receive the peace necessary for the people; and let the hills, those holding lesser offices, the leading ministers of both secular and spiritual government, receive righteousness, so that both the course of the world may be directed peacefully in Solomon’s kingdom and the holy Church may rejoice in tranquil devotion.

Alternatively: Let the mountains receive peace for the people, that they may preserve among the people the peace of unity and the bond of concord. For this ought to be the chief vigilance of the highest princes in the Church: lest, by ruling the clergy proudly [Col. 0318D] and abusing their authority, they cause schisms among the people subject to Solomon. Let the hills also receive righteousness by presiding over and taking precedence over fields and valleys in such a way that they do not cease obediently to be subject to their superiors—namely, the mountains—and above all to the Mountain of mountains, the King of kings, the true Solomon. No one whatsoever is to be obeyed against his command; to obey him is true righteousness, not only in those things which he himself commanded, but also through those of whom he says: “He who hears you hears me; he who rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10:16). For through these his vicars, judging justly,

VERSE 5. “He will judge the poor of the people, and save the children of the poor, and humble the slanderer.” The second part, in which the fruit of the preceding prayer is affirmed. [Col. 0319A] It is as though he said: Behold, what I desired I now see in the spirit; what I hoped for I now hold in the certainty of faith, which is a sure proof of things not visible to bodily eyes, though they are manifest to the eyes of faith. For I asked that judgment be given to King Solomon, the King’s Son, and my prayer has been heard. For he, having been given all power in heaven and on earth, will judge the poor of the people and save the children of the poor.

The Christian people in Solomon’s kingdom, before his final judgment, are so mixed together that there are among them rich persons, to whom it is said: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation” (Luke 6:24); and poor persons, of whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3). But now in particular, and universally at the final judgment, he himself, the just Judge, [Col. 0319B] will judge the poor of the people, separating them from the rich, so that those alone may receive the kingdom of heaven promised to such persons, while the rich are excluded, who are now filled but will later hunger, now laugh but will later weep and mourn.

He will therefore judge the poor of the people, making them alone heirs of the kingdom promised to the poor, since even here they begin to reign by governing their flesh and all things subject to them—for a king is so named from ruling, or acting rightly—and in the future they shall reign more fully. Here they reign after the manner of David, the renowned warrior, while they do not permit sin to reign in their mortal body so as to obey depraved desires, which wage war against the soul. But in the future they will reign more fully after the manner of Solomon, the peaceful King, [Col. 0319C] when there neither will be nor can be sin in their then immortal and impassible body, because then these poor of the people will be like the angels of God. Thus will the true Solomon judge the poor of the people, to whom, speaking on the mountain as to the perfect, opening his mouth in a great proclamation, he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3).

“And he will save the children of the poor”: that is, the lesser children of the greater poor, yet imitators according to their ability. Speaking to them on a level place in a more moderate proclamation, he said: “Blessed are you poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke 6:20). Indeed, both on the mountain and in the plain he was not speaking to different disciples; yet the very difference of the places marks a distinction between the perfect [Col. 0319D] and the less perfect poor, as between great fathers and their little children.

At the beginning of the newborn Church, when the Lord sat upon the mountain and summoned those who followed him to the height of supreme perfection, his disciples came to him as members of his household, as perfect persons, as eager persons manfully seeking ever loftier pursuits of virtue. But now, as if descending from the mountain, Jesus stands in a level place, condescending to the little children and imitators of the apostles, in order to save these children of the poor, namely, of the apostles. Since they were born as sons to be fathers of the Church and were therefore to be appointed princes over all the earth, the true Solomon will honour them and save them in his kingdom; and through them he will humble the slanderer, [Col. 0320A] because he will choose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and things base and despised, in order to destroy the things that are.

The slanderer is the devil, who through slander detracts from the good and strives, insofar as God permits, to cast them down; as he said concerning the man who was simple, upright, and feared God: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” (Job 1:9). But the true Solomon, both in his own person—as man—worshipping God freely, obeying his Father unto death, and drawing others by his example to the same freely imitated obedience, so humbles the slanderer that his lie, by which he slanders the good life of good people, is made manifest. He is indeed the accuser of the brethren and the slanderer, accusing them before [Col. 0320B] God day and night—that is, in prosperity and adversity. Thus he slandered and accused blessed Job in prosperity, claiming that he did not worship God freely; likewise, in adversity, through the mouths of his slanderous friends and wife. Above all, through Elihu’s mouth, he detracted from Job’s perfection by many subtleties. But when all these were disproved through Job’s own mouth, and especially through the mouth of God speaking for him, the slanderer was humbled and refuted. The outstanding virtue of the man who was simple, upright, and feared God was displayed: amid prosperity he was humble, amid adversity secure; armed on the right and on the left with the weapons of righteousness, he was neither corrupted by riches into self-exaltation nor driven by misery into impatience.

[Col. 0320C] More fully, however, and more perfectly, this slanderer was humbled—and will be humbled to the end—in that man who is simple and upright, who is not only man but also God, Son of Man and Son of God. First his ministers, the Jews, were proved false: in slander they called him a deceiver, a magician, an evildoer, said that he had a demon and was mad. Then the pagans were proved false, who slanderously preferred created gods to God the Creator, destructive gods to God the Saviour; likewise heretics, who detracted from his glory; and finally false brethren, counterfeit Christians, who confess him in words but deny him in deeds.

When all these have been proved false and refuted, he will humble the slanderer through the poor of the people, whom he judges, distinguishing them far from the people gathered in the level place, by the summit [Col. 0320D] of holy contemplation; and through the children of the poor, whom he saves within that very people. They remain indeed in the level place with the people, but are distinguished from the people in this: that Solomon’s discourse is addressed to them principally and especially when he says, “Blessed are you poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke 6:20). For just as, seated on the mountain, he opens his mouth to the poor whom he judges worthy of such height, so that they may hear great things loftily expressed; so, standing in the plain, he raises his eyes and directs them especially toward the children of the poor, that they may plainly understand what they hear.

Therefore through these two kinds of poor—those who contemplate on the mountain the true Solomon seated and transfigured, and those who stand in the plain, labour while standing, and cooperate with the standing Solomon, as one of them says: “For this [Col. 0321A] I labour, even unto bonds” (2 Tim. 2:7); and to a faithful disciple, “Cooperate,” he says, “with the Gospel of Christ” (2 Tim. 1:8)—through these two kinds of poor, I say, those free for the word and those labouring in the word, the true Solomon will humble the slanderer, the devil and Antichrist. Both will be greatly confounded when they see the poor apostles and the children of the poor, namely their imitators, as judges of the world and true lights of the world, shining forth in judicial power and miracles—or, what is more excellent, in the prerogative of their character. In them King Solomon himself will accomplish his work: a wonderful work, a glorious work, by which, exalting humble poor persons and casting down proud mighty ones, he will humble the slanderer in all his members throughout all the days which shall be formed by the rising and setting [Col. 0321B] of the sun, unto the consummation of the age.

VERSE 6. “And while doing this, he will endure with the sun and before the moon, through generations of generations.” For as days are formed by the rising and setting of the sun, and night is sometimes illuminated as day by the brightness of the moon, when the moon is full, but at other times part of the night is darkened when its light has waned, and in this work the two luminaries remain until the end of time through the succession of generations orderly following generations, so that the service of these two lights is never lacking to any time: so Solomon himself, the King of righteousness and true Sun, will adorn all times through generations of generations, now forming days by the manifestation of his brightness, [Col. 0321C] now creating nights and forming darkness by its concealment, unto the consummation of the age. Thus, while the world endures, the Christian religion, constantly to be exercised amid the prosperities of day and adversities of night, will never fail; nor will it ever lack, in the day of prosperity, the solar light which is the splendour of glory in the true Solomon, or, in the night of adversity, the lunar light which is the brightness of his way of life.

For the conduct of this Solomon in mortal and passible flesh, set before our eyes amid adversities, shows the paths of life and patience, so that we may not fear “the terror by night” or “the business that walks in darkness.” But his transfiguration upon the mountain, when his face shone as the sun, or rather his glorification upon the high throne of paternal majesty, set before our eyes, makes the glory of the world and the flower of the flesh seem worthless to us by comparison in the time of prosperity, [Col. 0321D] so that we may never be wounded “by the arrow flying by day” or “by the noonday demon,” while the desirable vision of this brightness is continually present to the eyes of faith and hope, just as the presence of the sun will never be absent for the forming of days.

But because, for the creation of nights, the presence of the shining moon is sometimes withdrawn, it was rightly said prophetically that Solomon “will endure with the sun”: he will always be present to his Church, made peaceful through himself, the peaceful King, just as the visible sun is always present to the days formed by its presence. It was rightly and suitably said, therefore, “He will endure [Col. 0322A] with the sun,” because of the apt likeness between him and the sun; but it could not be said, “He will endure with the moon,” because the analogy with the moon is so defective that a great dissimilarity intervenes. The moon often leaves nocturnal darkness when it is absent or obscured, and sometimes undergoes eclipse. Christ’s human conduct, however, abiding before the eyes of faith like a moon made perfect for ever, always by the display of its brightness causes night to be illumined like day.

Therefore that Solomon who is said to endure with the sun because of the fitting correspondence of the likeness, is said to endure before the moon because the brightness which he showed even in his human works, and the patience he showed amid adversities, also remain. This, like a perfect moon, will endure for ever; for “the patience of the poor shall not perish for ever”—I mean those of whom it has already been said that he will judge the poor of the people and save the children of the poor.

Alternatively: “He will endure with the sun and before the moon,” that is, with times and before times, distinguished by the sun and moon. “Through generations of generations”: because, while one generation passes and another comes, he continually displays his name, praiseworthy and bright from the sun’s rising to its setting, like the sun and more than the moon. The sun, continually bright in itself, signifies God the Father; the sun’s radiance, God begotten from God, namely the Son. Although he is the radiance of glory and the image of his substance, yet, in order to effect the cleansing of sins, he was seen for a time to be darkened in his passion, [Col. 0322C] as the visible sun also testified by its own darkening when he died.

But when, overcoming death by his resurrection, he ascended above the setting and, “the sun having now risen” (Mark 16:2, 9), appeared to his disciples shining with great brightness, he plainly showed, through the power given him in heaven and on earth, that he himself is the radiance of the sun, the Son of the eternal Father; and that together with his Father, who is the eternal Sun, he may likewise be called the Sun of righteousness, now that his body has been glorified. This body, indeed, could during the time of assumed, perishable mortality be called a lunar body; but now, since it has put on the beauty of divine glory, it is believed to be a solar body, in some measure assimilated to the visible sun in this respect: that, as in the solar body [Col. 0322D] the whole force of ethereal fire has its source, so in the Lord’s body “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily,” and from it he dispenses rays of graces through generations of generations—that is, to those reborn and transferred from the first generation into the second.

The first generations are those by which we are begotten mortally; but the generations of generations are those by which the Church regenerates persons born unto death unto salvation. Therefore, because this sun imparts his brightness not to all who are begotten, but only to those who are reborn, he is rightly said to endure “in the generation of generation,” or “through generations of generations,” or “for the age of the age,” as some manuscripts have it.

Likewise, as this sun, equally constituted from heavenly and earthly elements, retaining brightness from the heavenly and solidity from the earthly, holding the middle place of the ether and the middle place among the planets, is balanced in the space midway between heaven and earth—neither soaring upward nor sinking downward, but preserving the rights of both its natures by being poised, as stated, in the middle, according to the physical principle of weights—so the Lord Jesus, a giant of twofold substance, is rightly established as mediator of God and human beings. [Col. 0323A] In himself he joins and reconciles heavenly and earthly things; he illumines heavenly things, warms, enlightens, and gives life by his heat to earthly things; he is present to heavenly things and not absent from earthly things. He “rejoices like a giant to run his course,” poised in the middle of the universe for the benefit of heavenly and earthly things; and none can hide from his heat. Thus he endures with the sun and before the moon through generations of generations.

[Col. 0323B] The Hebrew truth has: “And they shall fear thee, as long as the sun endures and beyond the moon, in generation after generation.” That is: when the slanderer has been humbled beneath the feet of your poor, to whom you give power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon every power of the enemy, these poor themselves will not be exalted because of this victory. Rather, though bold in you, they will be fearful in themselves, conscious of their own frailty; they will fear you as long as the sun exists and beyond the moon, through generation after generation—that is, throughout all the time in which sun and moon perform their courses in service for the use of generations that pass away and succeed one another.

THIRD PART. VERSE 6. “He will descend like rain upon a fleece, and like drops dripping upon the earth.” [Col. 0323C] The order is artificial. For the future judgment of the King was first mentioned, and now his birth, which precedes it, is added. This order, as has been said, is artificial, opposed to the natural order. Natural order is when what was done first is narrated first, and what was done later, later. Artificial order, however, is when what was done later is anticipated in the narrative and what was done first is subsequently attached. Thus, in this place, after the King’s judgment has been narrated, someone might ask: How will his coming take place, or how will his kingdom begin? The answer is: He will not come in a great and strong wind breaking rocks; he will not come in earthquake or fire, but “in the whisper of a gentle breeze” (3 Kings 19:12), as was said to Elijah.

A wind breaking rocks did indeed precede his coming, in the captivity of the ten tribes of Israel; but the Lord was not in the wind, because the time of his coming had not yet arrived. [Col. 0323D] An earthquake likewise preceded it, in the captivity of King Jehoiakim, when Jerusalem was plundered; but the Lord was not in the earthquake. Fire too preceded it, when, after King Zedekiah had been taken captive, the city of Jerusalem was burned and devastated by Chaldean fire in the Babylonian deportation. But the Lord was neither in the earthquake nor in the fire, because his coming was deferred until the Virgin was to be breathed upon by the Holy Spirit through the angelic annunciation, as by the whisper of a gentle breeze, and made fruitful as though a wind of dew were blowing. This I, David, foretell when I say: “He will descend like rain upon a fleece, and like drops dripping upon the earth.”

Recognize his first coming by this apt comparison. For at his second coming he will come in a wind breaking rocks, because “with the breath of his lips he will slay the wicked” (Isa. 11:4), whom, as the Apostle says, “the Lord Jesus will slay with the Spirit of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2:8). He will also come in an earthquake, because he will shake not only the earth but heaven also: “For the powers of the heavens will be shaken” (Luke 21:26). He will come also in fire, because “a fire will blaze before him, and a mighty tempest around him” (Ps. 49:3). Had he come at his first advent in such a manner, who could have endured him? He did not so come into the Virgin, consecrated for divine childbearing.

But how will he descend into the Virgin who is to bear the only-begotten Son of God, and descend into the Church [Col. 0324B] which is to bear many children through the grace of regeneration? He descended and will descend like rain upon a fleece and like drops dripping upon the earth. As rain descends noiselessly into wool, so God gently entered the Virgin by hidden power. Wool is not broken by receiving and yielding water; so the Virgin, conceiving and bearing the Son, remained incorrupt and intact. Similarly the mother Church, made fruitful by the Word of God, bears children of God while remaining incorrupt, because her bridegroom, the Word of God, comes to her as lightly as drops of dew, gently dripping without noise upon the earth.

A sign of this was once shown to Gideon. When he was about to fight the Midianites, he asked that, if he were to gain victory, a fleece laid upon the threshing-floor might be filled with dew while the floor remained dry; and so it happened. For the same reason he then asked that the floor be moistened by dew and that the fleece laid upon it be found dry; and this too happened. Mystically, the wet fleece is Judaea, which, sprinkled with the dew of heavenly teaching through the Law and the prophets, worshipped one God. Into this fleece the Son of God descended like rain, because by his grace he assumed flesh from Judaea in the Virgin. He chose disciples from there while the threshing-floor of the whole world remained dry, because the clouds had been forbidden to rain upon this floor. Hence: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. 10:5).

But when the Jews rejected from themselves this rain of grace, the fleece of blinded Judaea remained dry; and then drops [Col. 0324D] of grace descended upon the earth, the formerly dry threshing-floor of the Gentiles. Judaea is aptly designated by the name of fleece: as fleece is taken from a sheep, so it was to be stripped of the authority of teaching; or because, as fleece holds water, Judaea held teaching without fruit. But the threshing-floor watered by rain will sprout and blossom. So too the calling of the Gentiles, watered by the word, will sprout, blossom, and rejoice with glad praise, because to it have been given the glory of Lebanon, the splendour of Carmel and Sharon. For the younger son, clothed in Esau’s exceedingly fine garments, breathes from the very fragrance of those garments an odour in which the eternal Father delights, saying: “Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27:27).

Do you wish to hear what are the shoots of this full field, irrigated by drops of heavenly dew after a long drought, which delight King Solomon? Surely they are these:

VERSE 7. “In his days righteousness shall arise, and an abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away, or lifted up, or removed”—all of which expressions concern the same meaning. For the holy Church is now beautiful as the moon, which even at its full does not lack a blemish; and from the state in which it now exists it must be taken away, removed, or lifted up, so that what is said of it may be fulfilled: “chosen as the sun” (Song 6:9). This will happen when what is mortal puts on immortality and that brightness in which the body of our lowliness is hoped to be conformed to the body of his glory, of which it was said above: “He will endure with the sun.”

But now, before the moon is so lifted up, having borrowed its light from the sun, through the benefit of that same sun which warms the earth watered with drops by its heat, [Col. 0325B] righteousness will arise in his days—the righteousness which is through faith. For the righteous person lives by faith, reconciled to God through that very faith, so that there may be peace between God and man; between spirit and flesh; between the Church in the immortal angels and the spirits of the righteous reigning in the Lord—or, what is greater, dying for the Lord—and the Church sojourning in mortal human beings.

Thus righteousness and peace will arise, so that even with a small measure of righteousness there may be an abundance of peace, when there will be peace for people of good will, even if the good effects of that good will are lacking. Such good will is a small righteousness compared with the righteousness which not only burns in the affection of hearts but also shines in the effect of works. There will therefore be an abundance of peace, because this peace begins amid wars but will be so consummated after the wars that, once death, the final enemy, has been destroyed, there will thereafter be no disturbance in the monarchy of Solomon, the peaceful King, whose kingdom is wholly at peace.

Before that occurs, he will rule in the midst of his enemies; and, in order to bring peace to completion,

VERSE 8. “He will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth.” By ruling in this way he will extend his kingdom beyond the narrow boundaries of the land of Judaea, from sea to sea—that is, everywhere in the world encircled by the great sea. He will begin this work of extension from the river and carry it to the ends of the earth, [Col. 0325D] because, being baptized in the river Jordan, with the Holy Spirit appearing above him and the Father’s voice sounding from above, he was revealed to be the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit. From there his teaching began to spread. After his resurrection he also gave the apostles the rule of baptizing, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). Thus, as the doctrine of his baptism ran forth, his kingdom, which is the Church, was extended from the river to the ends of the earth. This will appear in its parts. For:

VERSES 9, 10, AND 11. “Before him the Ethiopians will fall down; the kings of Tarshish, the kings of Arabia and Saba, and the other kings [Col. 0326A] of the earth will worship him; and consequently, when the dominion of this world has been bowed in all kings, all nations subject to kings will serve him.” Friends will serve by loving, seeking, and savouring the things above. But his enemies will lick the earth, savouring and loving earthly things after the manner of the serpent, to which it was said, “You shall eat earth.” Or they will lick the earth—that is, they will love earthly teachers, on whose authority they contradict the divine utterances.

On this passage blessed Gregory says in Job [Note: [Col. 0325D] Book XX of the *Morals*, ch. 14]:

> “It pleases me to consider what was said through the Psalmist: ‘His enemies will lick the earth.’ There are two kinds of persons who serve ambition: one, namely, always uses the flatteries of speech for avarice; the other openly aims at plunder by force. [Col. 0326B] For when we crush something external by strenuous effort, we gnaw it. But it is licked when what cannot easily be eaten is tasted by the applied gentleness of the tongue. Therefore all who live perversely, even under the appearance of faith, who desire what belongs to others but cannot seize what they desire, attempt to draw away their coveted things by smooth speeches and, as it were, by a soft sweetness. What else do they do but lick the earth? What they cannot take by force, they seek to remove by the softness of their tongue. But those who in this world are supported by some power, and who desire another’s possessions, disdain to flatter deceitfully, because they can accomplish by unjust force what they wish. What they desire they do not lick, but gnaw, because with the strength of their power they destroy the life of their neighbours as though by the effort of their teeth.” [Col. 0326C]

Alternatively: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands will offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Saba will bring presents.” These lands delight the nostrils with different scents, and signify the world strewn with various delights. But those who subject these enticements to strict discipline may be called kings of Arabia and Saba; and such people gladly serve King Solomon.

Alternatively: Tarshish is interpreted “exploration of joy”; Arabia, “low” or “of the plain”; Saba, “incense” or “conversion.” These names signify that contemplatives exploring eternal joys, humble converts, and those kindled by the fire which the Lord sent upon the earth, while both living well themselves and governing others toward good living, bring gifts to Solomon as kings. Kings who are also tyrants, when they afflict saints and make martyrs, serve God even unwillingly and bring him gifts, since the true Solomon uses wicked ministers piously, so that all things work together for good to those called saints according to his purpose.

The islands also are those who exclude from themselves the surrounding vices of the world. Such persons offer gifts when in holy devotion they perform good works and ascribe these not to their own praise but to divine praise. The Ethiopians too—either those who are farthest away by their geographical situation, or, by the meaning of their blackness, the foulest sinners—will fall down before him, [Col. 0327A] worshipping him. Thus may the Church, enlarged from such a number and humbled before him, represent that Ethiopian queen who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom.

For Solomon’s wisdom is heard not only from the mouth of the wise, but also from the mouth of infants and nursing children, when the great King, the peaceful King, makes the tongues of infants eloquent. The kings of the earth worship him—kings such as were once themselves worshipped and honoured with sacrifices, as Augustus was, to whom a famous poet says in flattery:

> O Meliboeus, a god has granted us this leisure.
>
> For he will always be a god to me; often a tender lamb
>
> From our folds shall stain his altar.  
> —Virgil, *Eclogues* I.6

Likewise Flaccus says to the same man:

> To you, present among us, we bestow mature honours,
>
> And set up altars by which men must swear through your divinity.

[Col. 0327B] Nor do the divine Scriptures lack examples of such presumption. In the kingdom of the Egyptians Pharaoh, and in the kingdom of the Babylonians Nebuchadnezzar, set themselves above the true God; and in the kingdom of the Persians Haman, although second after the king, nevertheless wished to be worshipped as a god. So in the kingdom of the Greeks King Antiochus arrogated divine honour to himself. So in the Roman empire the already mentioned Augustus was not afraid to be worshipped as a god. In his time this Solomon, the peaceful King, was born; and was honoured even in this way and shown to be King of peace, because at his birth there was peace throughout the whole world—a peace Augustus falsely claimed for his own achievement, though it came from him at whose birth the angelic [Col. 0327C] voice was heard saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

All kings rightly ought to worship him as the author of peace, and nations, though they have earthly masters, ought to serve him as supreme Lord. And this is done by persons of every nation and language under heaven: all nations, though not every individual of every nation. There is no nation from which some have not been converted to worship this King. And rightly so:

VERSES 12 AND 13. “For he will deliver the poor from the mighty.” From this saying the fourth part begins, showing what benefit there is for those who worship. There is indeed very great benefit and great fruit for true worshippers who venerate this King: for he will deliver the poor person from the mighty one—the poor in spirit from the prince of this world, who, as a mighty and strong armed man, guarded his court until the coming of this King. Coming upon him as one stronger, he will conquer him and deliver from his power the poor person—not just any poor person, but one for whom there was no helper.

For the poor in spirit—that is, the humble—are found even among the holy angels, who do not need to be delivered from this mighty one. They themselves are stronger in good than he is in evil, and their power, having God as helper, far surpasses his power, which has only an imagined appearance of strength, while it is weak against God, strong and mighty in battle, and against his angels, made strong and mighty by his help. [Col. 0328A] But the poor person who had no helper was the human being who, going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, from Paradise into this world, fell among robbers; they stripped him, inflicted wounds upon him, and departed, leaving him half dead. He had no helper while priest and Levite passed by, because neither the Levitical priesthood nor the ministry of the Law benefited, or could benefit, him toward healing or salvation.

This poor person, therefore, for whom there was no helper, is delivered by this peaceful King, King and physician alike: he pours oil and wine into his wounds, leads him into an inn defended by the enclosures of ecclesiastical discipline, and cares for him. Because he is an expert physician, he will not spare the disease he removes, nor spare the putrid flesh he cuts away; but while doing these things, he will spare the poor person and the needy, saving nature and blotting out nature’s fault. Thus, while he blots out the faults of souls, he will save the souls of the poor, not imputing to them the sin for whose abolition he will give himself as the price. For by the price of his blood,

VERSE 14. “He will redeem their souls from usuries and iniquity.” Future punishments are called “usuries,” because more bitterness will be found in eternal punishments than sweetness was found in temporal sin. For example, a person, from a brief desire for vengeance, kills and destroys only the body of his enemy by homicide; as a consequence, his own soul and body will be destroyed and tortured eternally in Gehenna, unless he repents before death. Likewise, whoever commits an act of fornication is, through a shameful and brief pleasure, bound by the eternal guilt of that act, though the act itself has already passed, [Col. 0328C] unless help is given by that King who, redeeming the souls of the poor from usuries and iniquity, will save them.

Alternatively: Sin, whether original or another sin, which is the cause of other sins subsequently following it, is properly called “iniquity” by antonomasia: a general name becomes specific because of eminence. Thus, although there are many poets, among the Latins the name “poet” belongs especially to Virgil alone because of his excellence in poetry. Similarly, although the name “apostle” is common to many, it was given to the Apostle Paul, because of his preeminence in his many labours, as though it were proper and distinctive; so that when “the Apostle” is said absolutely, Paul alone is understood.

Therefore the sin that is the cause of subsequent sins is rightly called “iniquity” because of its eminence, although every sin is iniquity and every iniquity sin. Such iniquity, preceding subsequent sins as a coin its interest, is rightly compared to Pharaoh’s firstborn, or to the other firstborn of Egypt, whom God first struck—from human being to beast—in order thereafter to strike the whole army of Egypt. So original sin, in the kingdom of this Solomon, is first destroyed as though Pharaoh’s firstborn; then the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world removes actual sins as a kind of interest upon that sin. He does this not by the letter of the Law, which points out sins, but by the power of grace, which freely [Col. 0329A] delivers from all evils, likewise freely assists toward every good necessary for salvation, and again freely strengthens and preserves in the good that has been begun.

All this is to be delivered and redeemed from iniquity together with the usuries of that iniquity: those who have his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads, so that they may truly be named after Christ and be Christians, truly be named and be children of God the eternal Father.
