Though this name may seem contemptible to the world lying in wickedness, it is honourable before Christ himself, from whom they are named Christians, and before God the Father, who has sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, crying, “Abba, Father,” so that they are sons because they have the Spirit of the Son.

Or his name—that of the King—will be honourable before them as they give thanks for his benefits; and chief among these is the certain fact that the King himself has redeemed their souls by his death from usuries and iniquity. Even unbelieving Jews and pagans believe that he died; but they do not believe what follows:

VERSE 15. And he shall live. But we believe, and therefore we speak, that the true Solomon, who once died to drain away the sins of many, now lives; and that the life of humankind rose with him, fulfilling the prophecy which said: “And he shall live. For in that he died to sin, he died once; but in that he lives, he lives unto God. He died for our offences and rose again for our justification” (Rom. VI, 10). He died so that we too might die to sin; [Col. 0329C] he rose and lives so that we too may walk in newness of life. He lives, having been raised from the dead, and death shall no longer have dominion over him, so that, although his members are burdened with sin, sin may nevertheless not rule or reign in their body, though mortal, while they await the glory to come—when sin shall neither exist nor be able to exist in their immortal body.

It is a great consolation to soldiers endangered amid many kinds of death that their King shall live. Thus one of these soldiers, and a chief one, consoling himself, says among other things: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth,” and so on, down to: “this hope of mine is laid up [Col. 0329D] in my bosom” (Job XIX, 25). It is a great consolation to the dying that he for whom, or in whom, they die shall live eternally. If we die with him, we shall also live with him and possess his riches together with him. For this Solomon is rich, and in him are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God.

To make the greatness of his riches manifest, there shall be given to him gold from Arabia. By Arabia the Gentile world is understood, the whole being signified by the name of a part in which precious gold occurs. By Arabian gold itself is signified the wisdom of the philosophers of this age: for example, Platonic or Aristotelian teaching, or the science of numbers comprehended by the characters and figures of Arabic numerals, [Col. 0330A] much cultivated among the Arabs and, as some maintain, first discovered there. Not all such Arabian gold is offered to Solomon, because not all secular learning is approved in the divine Scriptures; rather, it is received in part and rejected in part. Therefore it was not said, “Gold shall be given to him,” but, “There shall be given to him *of* the gold of Arabia”; for whatever is found in secular books suited to the instruction of sound learning and the building up of a good life, this the soldiers of Solomon take as though from unjust possessors and offer to him, when they thereby either adorn or fortify the teaching of faith or morals. Thus Egypt is despoiled; thus the righteous took, and still take, the spoils of the ungodly; thus the foreign woman, with her hair shaved and her nails cut, passes into marriage with an Israelite, when [Col. 0330B] the wise teaching of secular masters—its useless parts cut away, like hair and nails lacking vital blood—is interwoven with divine utterances, so that the vessels of the imperial table at Solomon’s banquet may shine as though made of Arabian gold.

“And they shall worship continually by virtue of what comes from him.” They shall worship the Son of the King as they worship his eternal Father. And the very fact that they worship him they have from him, since he taught them the prayer by which they may either pray to him or even worship him. “When you stand,” he says, “to pray, say: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name,” and so on, down to “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. VI, 9). Thus they shall pray to and worship him, having from him the pattern for praying to and worshipping the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0330C] in both; for in this Lord’s Prayer the whole Trinity is understood under the name of the Father, as in: “One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all, who is blessed for ever” (Eph. IV, 6).

For when it is said, “God, Father of all,” or “Our Father,” that universal fatherhood of grace is understood, by which the one triune God is shown to be Father of many sons: he who is above all, through all, and in us all, since all things are from him, through him, and in him. But when the eternal Father is named, in the singular, as Father of the eternal Son, that natural fatherhood is indicated, in which he has the eternal only-begotten Son alone. Therefore, when this Solomon, the Son of the King, says: “My [Col. 0330D] Father works until now, and I work” (John V, 7); and again, “My Father—what he has given me—is greater than all” (John X, 29), that singular fatherhood is expressed through the possessive term *my*. From it the Only-begotten rightly declares himself equal to his Father, because whatever the Father does, the Son also does in like manner. For the Father gave him authority to execute judgment, as is requested at the beginning of the psalm: “Give thy judgment, O God, to the King, and thy righteousness to the King’s Son; to judge thy people in righteousness, and thy poor in judgment.” But when he teaches us, in praying or worshipping, to say, “Our Father, who art in heaven,” the entire Trinity is understood by the name “Father.” This Trinity is worshipped “in heaven,” that is, dwelling in pure spirits; [Col. 0331A] and in its one person, which is the Son, human nature also, having been assumed into him, is rightly worshipped.

Yet this worship does not depart from the rule which says: “Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve” (Deut. VI, 13).

But if Photinus objects that it is a kind of idolatry to worship a creature as God, because he does not allow Christ to be worshipped, considering him a mere man, I think no authority can defend me better than that which I have from Christ himself. For while he still lived as a mortal among mortals, he was worshipped by mortals and did not refuse it; indeed, he granted grace to those who worshipped him. For example, to a leper worshipping him and saying, “Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean” (Matt. VIII, 2), he granted [Col. 0331B] the cleansing that he requested. Likewise the kings coming from the East, though he lay in a cradle, nevertheless fell down and “worshipped him” (Matt. II, 11); by their gifts they testified that he was man, King, and God, and therefore rightly to be worshipped. In the worship of Christ, neither the man is to be separated from God nor God from the man.

Therefore, as we showed far above in another psalm, the Synod of Ephesus rightly condemned under anathema not only those who taught that the man assumed by the Word of God was not to be worshipped, but also those who asserted that the man was to be co-worshipped with the Word. For one simple worship is due to the God-Man, because the Word made flesh gave to his flesh an undivided sharing in his own worship. Hence the Fathers of the Council of Ephesus, over which [Col. 0331C] Cyril, Patriarch of Alexandria, presided, say among other things:

> “If anyone dares to say that the assumed man is co-worshipped with God the Word, and co-glorified, and called God as though one were another alongside the other—for the addition of one syllable, namely *co*, compels this meaning—and does not rather worship Emmanuel with one reverence and render one veneration to him, according as the Word became flesh: let him be anathema.”

Therefore the words, “They shall worship continually by virtue of what comes from him,” must be understood in this way: we are to believe and confess that King Solomon is worshipped not only in his divinity, but also in his humanity, with one altogether identical worship and veneration. For although [Col. 0331D] Christ exists from two natures and in two natures, yet, with the abiding reality of the natures preserved, there is one glory of both natures, in which both have become one.

Jerome, commenting on Jeremiah (XVII, 5), explains the words, “Cursed is the man who trusts in man,” and says among other things:

> “If every man who trusts in man is cursed, but Paul of Samosata and Photinus, although they preach the Saviour as holy and excelling all in virtues, nevertheless confess him to be merely man, then those who put their hope in man will be cursed. But if it is objected to us that we also believe in him who says, ‘But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth which I heard from God; this Abraham did not do; you do the works [Col. 0332A] of your father,’ we shall answer with the apostolic saying: ‘Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer.’ Finally, the same Apostle writes at the beginning of his Epistle to the Galatians: ‘Paul, an apostle—not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead—and all the brethren who are with me.’ For if death has been swallowed up in victory, why should not the lowliness of the flesh, assumed for human salvation, have passed into the majesty of divinity, so as to make both one, and so that we worship not the creature but the Creator, who is blessed for ever?”

As the illustrious Jerome says these things, our assertion agrees with his in every respect: we confess that the God-Man is to be worshipped with simple [Col. 0332B] worship, according to the words, “And they shall worship continually by virtue of what comes from him.” They shall worship him, and this they have from him, because the branch has no life except from the vine, nor does a member live without the head. Therefore, the members continually receive from him the capacity to worship the head—in him they always live, and without him they can do nothing. From him they continually and unceasingly receive the power to pray and worship. “Continually,” that is, at every time and without interruption, they shall pray and worship. But when the course of temporality is ended, throughout the entire day of eternity they shall bless him.

Other manuscripts read: “They shall pray for him.” What is it to pray for him but to pray either to attain him, or that he may be multiplied and magnified in his members? Or distinguish the text thus: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabs and of Sheba shall bring presents, and shall worship”; then add afterwards: “From him they shall continually bless him throughout the day.” This means: in themselves they have causes and material for prayer or weeping continually before him; but from him they shall receive causes and material by which to bless him throughout the day. Among the not least causes for praising or blessing him is this:

VERSE 16. There shall be a firm foundation in the earth upon the tops of the mountains; its fruit shall be exalted above Lebanon, and they shall blossom from the city like the grass of the earth.

We read that a firmament was made in the midst of the waters while the earth was still void and empty. This was a work of the primary creation. We see this heaven [Col. 0332D] adorned with stars, a beautiful and marvellous work, made through the Word not yet incarnate. But far more marvellous and venerable is the fact that the Word itself was incarnate and shall be a firmament in the earth once void and empty.

“There shall be a firm foundation in the earth,” because man ate the bread of angels, and this bread, strengthening the heart of man, shall be a firmament in the earth—so much more beautiful than that heavenly firmament as it has inherited a name more excellent than it. For he who called that ethereal heaven a firmament because by a fixed distinction it divides waters from waters, he himself, setting a firmament in the earth, gave it the name which is above every name, and gave it authority to execute judgment, so that it might divide waters from waters: his people from the people that are not his. For “many waters [Col. 0333A] are many peoples” (Rev. XVII, 15).

But among these waters, some remain upon the solidity of the firmament in such a manner that they are found like the man who built his house upon a firm rock—“and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4). Others refuse to rely upon this firmament, this firm rock; yet they will by no means be able to resist its ordinances. Therefore they are held fast beneath it as beneath a firmament, and cannot raise themselves above it, however great the storms by which they are shaken; just as swelling waves rise to heaven but are nevertheless unable to be raised above the heavens.

For the purpose of distinguishing and restraining these waters in their order, there shall be a firmament in the earth, which is no longer void and empty; for upon the tops of the mountains its fruit shall be exalted above Lebanon, and they shall blossom [Col. 0333B] from the city like the grass of the earth.

The earth is the Church; the firmament is faith or canonical Scripture. The mountains are the elect, of whom elsewhere it is said: “Her foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI, 1). The tops of the mountains are either the eminence of virtues in the saints or the authority of faith and the Scriptures. The fruit upon the tops of the mountains is charity, which the Apostle calls “a more excellent way” and “above all, the bond of perfection” (I Cor. XII, 31; Col. III, 14). This is the fruit of which it was said to the mountains themselves: “I have chosen you out of this world, that you should go and bear fruit, and that [Col. 0333C] your fruit should remain” (John XV, 16). “These things I command you, that you love one another” (ibid., XV, 17). Again: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John XIII, 34). Again: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John XII [sic]).

This fruit, which never falls away, is not only exalted but superexalted—that is, greatly exalted—above Lebanon. Lebanon means “whiteness” and sometimes signifies the brightness of virtues, sometimes the splendour of secular dignities. But however Lebanon is understood here, the fruit of charity is exalted above it, for charity surpasses not only carnal things but also the spiritual gifts of God. For although faith and hope are great gifts, charity is greater than these.

[Col. 0333D] “And they shall blossom from the city like the grass of the earth.” There are two cities: one of God, whose name is Jerusalem; the other of the devil, whose name is Babylon. The saying, “And they shall blossom from the city,” may be understood of either.

Concerning the city of God, read it thus: Truly its fruit—that is, the fruit of the earth in which the firmament shall be—shall be superexalted above Lebanon. For those who belong to the city of God, which is the Church, shall blossom most delightfully like the fruitful grass of the earth, like the grass of grain. In Genesis grain is called grass, where we read: “Let the earth bring forth every tree and every grass” (Gen. I, 11). Grain is included under grass, because after these words nothing further was added concerning grain.

But the city of this world is that of which Genesis says (Gen. IV, 17) that Cain built a city; its glory is like the flower of grass. Concerning it, read thus: Truly above Lebanon—that is, above secular brightness—is the fruit of the earth whose firmament is the Lord. For it is fruit abiding for eternity. But in secular brightness those who belong to the city shall indeed blossom, though vainly, like the grass of the earth, because in that city “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is as the flower of grass” (Isa. XL, 6). For as grass withers and its flower falls, so worldly glory quickly fails. But the fruit of that earth in which Solomon, the peaceful King, shall reign shall remain eternally. Therefore:

VERSE 17. Let his name be blessed for ages, that is, eternally, because it bestows fruit eternally; and his name is from eternity and unto eternity, because his name endures before the sun. Times are distinguished by the course of the sun, and therefore times are rightly understood by the sun. His name, and the reality signified by his name, is therefore before the sun: he is eternal and precedes the sun not in time but in eternity—not in time as yesterday precedes today or today tomorrow, but in eternity, as the Creator precedes the creature which was begun at some time and, when it was unformed, given form.

Let his name be blessed. And lest that blessing be solitary, all tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him. I do not say “in them,” as though in many, but “in him,” as in one: in him who is the seed of Abraham, to whom it was said in the promise, “And in thy seed shall all the tribes of the earth be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18). As was promised, so it shall be until the end of the age. For not the twelve tribes of Israel alone, but all tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him. Therefore [Col. 0334C] all nations from every tribe shall magnify him: that is, they shall believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation.

I said, “They shall magnify”; and I, David, magnifying him and setting forth to others a pattern for magnifying him, pour forth in his praise—in praise of my Son according to the flesh, the eternal King, Solomon the peaceful King—a hymn from the songs of Zion, brief in wording and great in meaning, saying:

VERSE 18. Blessed be the Lord God of Israel—that is, of all who strive to be Israel—who alone works wonders by his own power, whether he works them himself or through others: works which none other performs, because none acts without him. Although he says, “The Father abiding in me, he does the works” (John XIV, 10), nevertheless [Col. 0334D] without him, who is the hand, arm, power, and wisdom of the Father, neither does the Father do anything, nor the Spirit of the Father, who is also his Spirit; for the works of the supreme Trinity are undivided.

He therefore works wonders alone, but not in solitude, because the man assumed into the Word, which is of one essence with the Father and the Holy Spirit, works by the power, authority, and majesty of the whole Trinity. Therefore let him be blessed:

VERSE 19. And let the name of his majesty be blessed for ever, and the whole earth shall be filled with his majesty. Let it be, let it be.

In the Hebrew it reads: “And blessed be the name of his glory for ever, and the whole earth shall be filled with his glory: Amen, amen.” Blessed eternally is he whom I have inherited with an eternal name. The eternal Father gives [Col. 0335A] him “the name which is above every name” (Phil. II, 9), so that he may be called and be, above all things, God blessed for ever. And because this name of his glory or majesty is eternal, let it be blessed eternally.

“And the whole earth shall be filled with his majesty”: namely, the majesty of Solomon. Or the whole earth shall be filled with the majesty and glory of his name, because not only in heaven but also on earth “his dominion shall be multiplied” (Isa. IX, 7). When he, the peaceful King, reigns, there shall be no end of peace, after all enemies of peace have at last been cast out from his kingdom. This occurs daily in part; but when he sits upon the throne of his Majesty, then it shall be fulfilled universally.

“Let it be, let it be.” Let it now be in part, and then universally. Let it now be according as is necessary for the consolation of the way; [Col. 0335B] let it then be for the full joy worthy of the heavenly homeland. Or, “Let it be,” said once, may be the subscription of the Prince who speaks; said again, it may be the assent of the multitude standing by and concurring, saying, “Let it be,” or “Amen.” To say it once in singing is a sign of wishing; to say it twice is a sign of vehement desire.

Let us therefore all say, “Let it be, let it be,” or “Amen, amen,” ardently desiring to see King Solomon not only in the diadem with which his mother crowned him—crowning him with a crown of thorns, by which was signified the Church gathered from sinners, male and female, and fitted to Christ in the form of a crown—but also in the diadem with which his Father crowned him on account of the suffering of death, crowning him with glory and honour and establishing him upon the throne of everlasting glory. Concerning that throne we pray: May he rule all things subject to him, so that the whole earth may be filled with his majesty and glory.

Glory to the eternal Father-King, giving judgment to his Son the King. Glory to the Son himself, the King, the true Solomon, making [Col. 0336B] peace throughout his whole kingdom. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is the peace of all who serve and minister in warfare under this Solomon; and, more abundantly, this Spirit shall be the peace of those same persons reigning with him in heaven. Let it be, let it be: Amen, amen.

## PSALM LXXII

[Col. 0335]

[Col. 0335B] How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart. In the preceding psalm there was a cry to the King, the Father of the King, that judgment might be given to the King, the King’s Son. By that judgment the people of God shall at last be judged in such righteousness [Col. 0335C] that no good person shall fare badly and no bad person shall fare well: no good person shall have anything from which to grieve, nor any bad person anything from which to rejoice.

But before that judgment is accomplished, the oft-mentioned combatant sometimes fails and falls somewhat from his hope, seeing many sinners enjoy a certain peace amid evil, while the righteous are wearied by adversities. Yet afterwards he repents of this error. This man, thus corrected, speaks in the following—that is, the seventy-second—psalm:

> “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart. But my feet were almost moved; my steps almost slipped, because I was jealous when I saw the peace of the ungodly.”

And then:

> “If I said, ‘I will speak thus,’ behold, I have rejected the generation [Col. 0335D] of thy children.”

“If,” he says, “I said or related this”—indeed, “if I should say this: ‘How does God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High?’” and so forth—“behold, I have rejected the generation of thy children”: that is, I should then stand opposed to the authority of all the saints.

For those who say these or similar things are marked by the foregoing title: “The praises of David, son of Jesse, have failed” (Ps. LXXI, 20). “Son of Jesse,” he says: that is, in those over whom David, son of Jesse, reigned, and in all who imitate them through excessive love of earthly or carnal things, praises have failed when they speak thus—when, unless they possess an abundance of temporal goods, they cease to praise God. What then? “But for me,” he says, “it is good to cleave to God; to place my hope in the Lord God.” For true praise begins to be offered by spiritual persons through love of heavenly things and contempt for earthly things. Let us now unfold the title more clearly, which runs as follows:

VERSE 1. The praises, or hymns, of David, the son of Jesse, have failed.  
[Note: [Col. 0335D] In the Vulgate edition the title is: “A Psalm of Asaph.” The preceding words are the final verse, namely the twentieth, of the preceding Psalm [Col. 0336D] LXXI; yet there the Vulgate does not contain the words “or hymns.”] A Psalm of Asaph.

Contrary to his usual practice, he adds “the son of Jesse,” signifying carnal praise by carnal descent. For the Israelite people used to praise God for temporal benefits, as the histories relate: they sang when the Egyptians were drowned; they sang when often fed in the wilderness; they sang when victorious over enemies; and they sang when they received the kingdom in Jerusalem. But when such prosperities failed because of their sins, the hymns of David likewise failed—not, I say, of the Son of God, but of the son of Jesse, who possessed a temporal kingdom in Jerusalem. That is, the hymns which were offered for temporal things failed. For when temporal things failed, some did not praise God, because he seemed perverse to them in giving prosperity to the wicked and adversity to the good.

Yet there were some among the same people who profited from their very loss. For when the things which they had regarded as great failed, they were compelled to seek things which would never fail. They understood that, just as fruit is hidden in the root, so his promises had lain hidden in ancient figures. For the New Testament was in the Old, but concealed—just as Christ was in David and Abraham. Thus the title is “A Psalm of Asaph,” that is, of the faithful synagogue, which, though for earthly things, nevertheless worshipped God devoutly, asking those things from him alone, [Col. 0337A] not from demons as the nations did.

But when Asaph saw blasphemers abound in the very things for which he served God, he began to waver, not knowing what lay hidden in those figures, as if there were no better thing which God could give. Yet this Asaph was admonished, through the removal of these things, to seek what he did not share in common with the wicked; he turns his purpose so that, though temporal things fail, there may nevertheless be a hymn for eternal things.

A hymn contains three elements: it is praise, of God, and with song. Praise contains confession, and the gladness of the song contains the affection of one who loves. For unless one sings gladly, it is not a hymn; one who does not love does not sing.

First Asaph describes the happiness of the wicked and, repenting, recalls that he was deceived by jealousy. Secondly, setting out his own error and that of others concerning the prosperity of the wicked, he says that he and they were brought back from it to a better counsel—namely, to consider the final end of the ungodly—at the words, “Therefore he shall turn.” Thirdly, he discloses the cause of the prosperity and punishment of the wicked, and his own deliverance from it, at the words, “Nevertheless.” Fourthly, he reproves himself for envying earthly things and seeks heavenly things, at the words, “For what [Col. 0337B] have I?” Therefore, so that he may be more readily believed as one who has experienced it, Asaph himself, who had erred, chastising himself and reflecting on what God reserves for his own after temporal things have been taken away, says:

VERSE 2. How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart. “Israel,” meaning “a man seeing God” or “a prince with God,” is understood as one who, having bright and pure eyes, delights to behold the eternal light of truth, righteousness, wisdom, goodness, and eternity. For light is sweet to pure and healthy eyes, while it is a punishment to diseased eyes.

Thus that Israel who, in everything done under the sun, seeks the Sun of righteousness as in mirrors, seeing all things ordered justly, delights in the vision of justice itself as a prince with God and as the friend of the bridegroom. This applies even to things which seem to the crooked not to be done rightly, although all things are done rightly, as supreme justice, supreme wisdom, supreme goodness, and power decree and order them. Reaching mightily from end to end, they dispose all things sweetly, so that all things work together for good to those upright in heart, who have pure and healthy eyes. Hence, with the delight of the inward man, delighting in the law of God, they approve God’s goodness even in things which wicked persons, judging wrongly, criticize as though they were done unjustly and without just order.

For example, people of good will sometimes suffer such great misery that, crippled in limb and scanty in resources, they cannot show the fruit of their good will by good works; and, on the other hand, they see persons malignant in heart and harmful in deed flourishing in this world’s prosperity. Then, like blind people unable to see in such matters the light of divine justice—chastening the good through hardship, testing them as gold in the furnace of tribulation, blinding and rejecting the wicked through prosperity—they break out into undisciplined murmuring, as though either God did not exist, or had no care for all things, or as though all things, or at least some things, happened by chance and good things thus came to the wicked or bad things to the good.

Finally, blind persons fail to consider that the bonds of this world possess real harshness, false pleasantness, certain pain, uncertain pleasure, hard labour, fearful rest, a condition full of misery, and an empty hope of blessedness. Those who are themselves not upright in heart put neck, hands, and feet into these bonds when they love false and deceiving riches, and do not judge their works fruitful unless present and temporal gain results from them.

Whoever is obstinate in this error perishes; whoever is not obstinate comes to his senses and, repenting of his error and instructing others lest they similarly err, says: How good is the God of Israel; how gracious, how sweet! To whom? To those who are upright in heart, whose heart is not bent [Col. 0338B] toward disordered desires for earthly things, but who possess earthly things for necessary use, not for the misuse of desire, and seek with their whole heart the things above.

And because temporal things are common to good and bad alike, they do not regard them as a great good when they abound, nor set their heart upon them while they abound, lest perhaps, when they flow away, they too flow away with them. Thus, when God in his goodness wishes such good people to lack them, they lack them without sorrow, since they had not clung to them in love. Their patience in lacking them is greater in proportion as the human will has been most rightly conformed in all things to the divine will, so that it is not crooked but straight, not bent down toward the lower regions of earth but raised upward. O how good is the God of Israel to such persons—he who appears perverse to the perverse!

Therefore, when others’ wandering steps have slipped away in a trackless place and not in the way, their feet have been moved altogether, so that they fall backward by remaining in their sin.

VERSE 2. But my feet, though not altogether, were almost moved; and my steps, though not altogether, almost slipped. That is, I felt the feet of my mind’s choice moved somewhat, though not as far as a fall. For free choice itself performs, as it were, the office of feet, by which the settled will disposes itself to go. Steps are the very acts by which the will accomplishes what it has determined. Such steps of mine were almost moved outside the way of righteousness. I say “almost,” not “entirely,” because although with difficulty, I remained within the bounds of equity, so as not to approve the suggestion of error. Nor is it remarkable that I, Asaph, was grievously tempted:

VERSE 3. Because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners—the temporal peace for which I served God, not yet understanding that God did not come to send this peace, but a sword. For before the Saviour’s coming, the good warfare had not yet been sent to break the evil peace. Therefore, seeing temporal peace, which I considered especially desirable, abound among sinners, I was stirred by great jealousy and almost strayed from the way of equity. I now grieve that this once happened to me; grieving, I confess it; and, singing as though a penitential psalm, I say: How good is the God of Israel to those upright in heart. But my feet were almost moved; my steps almost slipped, because I was jealous when I saw peace among sinners.

On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says in his commentary on Job:  
[Note: [Col. 0339D] *Morals on Job*, Book VI, chapter 6.]

> “When weak persons see the wicked flourish, they are troubled; disturbed inwardly by the prosperity of sinners, they stagger within in the steps of their minds. The Psalmist therefore took on their appearance when he said: ‘But my feet were almost moved’ (Ps. LXXII, 2). But when the strong behold their glory, they immediately consider what punishment follows after death, and in deep inward reflection despise the proud, who outwardly swell with the empty display of vain exaltation. Hence concerning this contempt of the perfect it is said through blessed Job: ‘I saw the fool firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty.’ To curse the beauty of the fool is to judge his glory in light of his contemplated condemnation; for he is overwhelmed all the more terribly in torments the higher he is raised in sins. What is exalted passes away; what is punished remains. Because he was honoured on the journey, he shall be condemned at its end; and, as though through pleasant meadows, he comes to prison who hastens through life’s prosperities toward destruction.”

Thus fools run through temporal prosperity to eternal condemnation, as though with their eyes closed, hurling themselves into fire.

VERSE 4. Because there is no regard for their death: neither does God’s mercy look upon them as they hasten to death—for of such persons it is said, “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. VIII, 21)—nor do they themselves look back or reflect that, now dead [Col. 0339C] in soul, they will die in body. They are sunk in forgetfulness of God and of themselves, in a deep sleep from which they do not awaken even amid blows, because there is no firm effect in their chastisement.

For though their wounds are putrid in their peace and prosperity and ought to have been cut by a forceful incision, there is no firm effect in their chastisement. The wound of their foul and inveterate sin is indeed deep; but the wound of the healing incision is not impressed with a firmness proportionate to the deep corruption. Therefore, because there is no regard of God’s mercy for healing their death—or, as it is read in the Hebrew, because they have not reflected on their death—and because there is no firm effect in their chastisement, such that the scourging correction might endure until amendment, therefore:

VERSE 5. They are not in the labour of men, because God has given [Col. 0339D] them over to the desires of their heart, so that those who are in filth may become still filthier—like a sick man to whom the physician, seeing that the disease is incurable, forbids nothing.

Alternatively: “There is no regard for their death,” for which some manuscripts read, “There is no turning aside toward their death”; that is, they do not die soon, but live long, and are not struck by a passing blow. Rather, there is firmness in their chastisement: that is, their scourge is firm, not temporal but eternal. Therefore they are not now in the labour of men, because they are reserved for the punishments of demons. For to such people it shall be said: “Depart from me, ye cursed, into eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil [Col. 0340A] and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

Thus it turns to their harm that they are not scourged with human beings for amendment, since they are to be tormented with demons in eternal condemnation. They do not lack necessities or fall ill, like the beggar Lazarus; rather, they feast splendidly every day, clothed in purple and fine linen. Like kings, they rule in purple, because the kings of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them; and, adorned like pontiffs with twisted linen, they claim priestly honour for themselves, though they are worthy neither of imperial rule, signified by purple, nor of priesthood, signified by fine linen. Yet they are honoured as though worthy and fit, though they are ministers of Satan clothed in outward honour while inwardly ravening wolves.

When they commit unlawful acts, no one rebukes them: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, [Col. 0340B] and the unrighteous is blessed” (Ps. X, 3). And because things succeed so prosperously for them that nothing resists their perverse desires,
### Verse 6

Therefore pride held them fast. I do not say, “They became proud”—though that itself is a grave evil, even when one is proud of good things through vain glory—but how much more execrable is that pride which arises from evil, when someone glories in wickedness because he is powerful in iniquity? Such utterly detestable pride held them like captive slaves, because “everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:44). Accordingly, he is held captive by sin, entangled in the cords of sins—not like the man who, grieving that he is thus held captive, cries with the Apostle: “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” [Col. 0340C] (Rom. 7:24); or as elsewhere it is read: “The cords of sinners have entangled me, and I have not forgotten your law” (Ps. 118:61).

I say, not in this way did pride hold these men captive, so that they might desire to be freed and cry to God for their deliverance. For they are so covered with the iniquity by which they wrong their neighbour, and with the impiety by which they blaspheme against God, that not even their head or mouth is free to cry out or to draw in the Spirit of truth, as did the man who said: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. 118:131). But these are so covered by voluntary iniquity and impiety that neither do they themselves see, nor are they seen by others.

I do not say that they are clothed like a bride “arrayed round about with variety,” [Col. 0340D] for in such a garment the whole face remains free and under its own control, so that she may see and herself be seen. Rather, I say that they are covered with iniquity and impiety as with a double garment and a twofold covering, under which they can neither be seen nor see.

They do not see themselves naked, as did those first parents, whose eyes were opened for this purpose: that they might see that of which, ashamed, they should blush. Nor are they seen by others, because though inwardly miserable, outwardly they are thought blessed by those who called blessed the people “to whom these things belong”—the things in which these men abound, namely worldly riches. Fattened, grown sleek, and swollen by these, they not only inwardly love iniquity—“he who loves it hates his own soul”—but also outwardly display it [Col. 0341A] to the injury of their neighbour. For it is as though overflowing from within to without.

### Verse 7

Their iniquity came forth, not from the necessity of misfortune, as happens when someone steals under compulsion of need or poverty, but as though from fatness: that is, from the mere pleasure of sinning. Having hearts made fat, and displaying this sort of grossness through evil works, they have gone beyond in the desire of their heart.

They have passed from vice to vice; or they have boldly crossed the ancient boundaries of the Fathers. Or they have exceeded the limits of habitual sinners when they went in their own inventions, committing new crimes hitherto unheard of. Or they have passed beyond the limits of common humanity, so as not to acknowledge themselves equal by nature to other human beings, although rich and poor alike possess together the natural gifts of God—for example, that they are equally rational human beings.

But these men, disregarding their equality with the poor, as though forgetting themselves go beyond themselves. They commit—not merely those sins to which some necessity seems to impel a person or human weakness to draw him—but go beyond into the desire, not of God, but of their own heart; so that, from the deepest inclination of free choice, intent on their own desires, they not only commit sins but even love them. This, however, does not happen to them suddenly; rather,

### Verse 8

They have thought and spoken wickedness. They have thought it by the inward deliberation of the mind. Nor did this seem sufficient to them; they also spoke outwardly, teaching others the wickedness conceived within. They spoke [Col. 0341C] not secretly but “on high,” that is, openly, with many hearing them.

They would sin less if not pretence but fear kept the movement of evil desire within the confines of thought; for pretended righteousness is a double iniquity. Moreover, he who publishes crimes conceived in thought sins in two ways: in one, he injures his conscience; in the other, his reputation. Both are greatly necessary for a person: he must have a good conscience for his own salvation, and a good reputation for the edification of his neighbour. If he loves that neighbour as himself, he undoubtedly takes care not to scandalize him by an evil example. But if he rightly loves himself, he strives to keep his conscience clean before God, who is witness.

For one who intends evil merely by his inward intention makes God alone, the searcher of hearts, a witness; and therefore he must say to God: “Against you alone have I sinned, and done evil before you” (Ps. 50:6). But one who displays evil thoughts outwardly in speech or even in deed offends neighbours who hear or see these things, contrary to the saying: “Giving no offence to anyone” (2 Cor. 6:3). Therefore, impious toward God because of a defiled conscience and cruel toward his neighbour because of a neglected reputation, if he comes to his senses he must say: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you” (Luke 15:18).

“Against heaven”: that is, against the saints, who are heaven, who have been offended and grieved by seeing or hearing of my sins. “Before you”: inwardly in the heart, devising many evil thoughts while you look on. Thus these men ought to confess that they have sinned against heaven. But they,

### Verse 9

Set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue [Col. 0342A] went over the earth. They set their mouth against heaven by reproaching the good and holy, who are heaven, in whom God dwells, who says: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66:1). Hence when the soul of a righteous person, which is the seat of wisdom, is insulted by evil people, heaven, the throne of God, is struck by such insults, and he who sits in it is dishonoured.

Nor is it enough for them thus to dishonour God in his heaven, in his throne. They add sin to sin, and their tongue passes—even often has passed—beyond heaven, as far as blaspheming God himself, the God of heaven. Astonishing presumption! Their tongue passed beyond heaven when it was on earth, when it was earthly; it ought to have been content with the limits of which it is elsewhere said: “He who is of the earth speaks of the earth” (John 3:33).

From such presumption heretics have often arisen. Though rooted in the earth, loving not heavenly but earthly things, they have nevertheless dared to teach about heavenly things which they did not learn with truth as their teacher, but themselves fabricated from their own heart. Many still imitate them. Though they are natural persons, not receiving the things of the Spirit of God, educated in secular learning, they proceed from that wisdom which is earthly, natural, and demonic to pronounce judgement on heavenly things. Yet they remain upon the earth, far removed from those who set their minds on things above, not on things upon the earth.

Persons of this sort may indeed roll forth frothing words from the Scriptures of truth with bursting cheeks, but the very Spirit of truth, who teaches Christ’s disciples all truth, [Col. 0342C] is far from these disciples of Antichrist. For the heart of Christ’s disciples is in heaven, where Christ sits at the right hand of God; but the heart of these disciples—or forerunners—of Antichrist is upon the earth, where their treasure is: “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Matt. 6:21). Thus their madness is all the more astonishing: though their heart is on earth, their tongue passes from earthly matters to the discussion of heavenly matters. Would that their life passed there together with their tongue, so that the conversation of those who dispute concerning heaven might be in heaven!

Alternatively: by their own judgement their tongue has passed beyond earth, as though to heavenly things; but in reality it is on earth and speaks from the earth, according to Isaiah: “You shall be brought low; [Col. 0342D] you shall speak from the earth; your voice shall be like that of a python, and your speech shall whisper from the dust” (Isa. 29:4). For when the spiritual person—who judges all things and is himself judged by no one—examines the sayings or writings of such people, he often finds there his own things, as though stolen, and takes them up for the purpose of discourse. But what is properly their own, since “when they speak a lie, they speak from their own resources,” the spiritual person rejects as the voice of a python whispering from the earth.

## Second Part

### Verse 10

Therefore my people will be converted here. In the preceding part Asaph said three things: namely, the peace of the wicked; the evils that result from that peace; and that, through jealousy of this peace, he began to waver and go astray. Now, in this second part, he explains how he began [Col. 0343A] to err, and how, considering the evils that arise from the peace of sinners, he came to his senses.

“Therefore,” he says, “my people will be converted here.” My people, worthy of my name—which is Asaph—will therefore be converted here, that is, in the present life, because they do not have the peace of sinners but are continually chastised for their sins. Those men, however, “will not be chastised with men.” Therefore they will not be converted here as human beings are converted, but will be condemned there as demons, where there will be no place for fruitful repentance.

Alternatively: “Therefore my people will turn hither,” that is, to a diligent consideration of what is discussed here. For since many evils are seen to arise from the peace of the wicked, my people will therefore turn hither, or here, to provide for themselves and guard against such great evils.

[Col. 0343B] The Hebrew truth reads: “Therefore his people will turn here.” But some translations have “hither,” and some “here.” The meaning is the same. We may also say thus: My people here—that is, seeing with me, in the same zeal, the evils arising from the prosperity of the wicked—will turn to seek out the truth. And whereas those who desert truth “will not halve their days,” full days will be found in those who love and seek it.

In sacred Scripture fullness of time or days is always taken in a good sense. Hence: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4). And of Abraham, or of any other holy man, it is written that he died “full of days” (Gen. 25:8). And: “The time was fulfilled for Elizabeth to give birth” (Luke 1:57). And “the days were fulfilled” for Mary “to give birth to her firstborn Son” (Luke 2:6–7).

Conversely, empty days, vain days, or half-days—days only half full—are evil days. For if King Hezekiah said: “In the middle of my days I shall go to the gates of hell” (Isa. 38:10), then, if the gates of hell are to be feared in the middle of one’s days because days that are half full, as it were, were not worthy of the reward of blessedness, the wise king wept and by his weeping and prayers obtained full days. What then is to be thought of days entirely empty, spent idly or even harmfully, except that they not only send one to the gates of hell but bury one in hell’s depths? Hence that rich man is said to have been “buried in hell” (Luke 16:22), [Col. 0343D] whose days were empty of good fruit; or, if they contained anything good, did not bring it to fullness—indeed, he lost it because he was rewarded here, as he who said judged: “Son, remember that you received your good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke 16:25).

Lazarus indeed had full days and lost nothing of the fullness of his days when prosperity flowed to him; rather, amid adversities he advanced day by day until the fullness of his days. Lest venial and daily sins diminish this fullness, he received evils for them in his life. Thus full days will be found in those who, worn down by scourges, are converted here and purified in this life through adversities. Before they fully grasped this knowledge, however, they hesitated and thought within themselves:

### Verse 11

How does God know, and is there knowledge in the Most High? It should be known that, just as the sick become more feverish and sweat more when health is near, so the more violently a soul is tossed by the storm of some question, the more swiftly it reaches the harbour of understanding truth. Therefore, though dangerously and almost blasphemously, they said in order to arrive at truth: “Is there knowledge in the Most High?” They did not affirmatively say, “God knows nothing, and there is no knowledge in the Most High.” Rather, hesitating as in a matter obscure, they say: “Is there knowledge in the Most High?”—that is, Is there knowledge in the Most High?

Once it is accepted that there truly is knowledge in the Most High, another question still remains: how does God know? They anticipate this by asking: “How does God know?” Does he know through himself, or through angels acting as messengers? Far be it that God, who knows all past, present, and future things, should learn anything through angels, as though it had previously been unknown to him. He knows all things, therefore, in himself and through himself, although he wills to employ the ministry of angels, necessary not for himself but for human beings predestined to salvation. For, as the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?” [Col. 0344B] (Heb. 1:14). He says “for them,” not “for him”: for those, that is, whom they assist and who are entrusted to them, not for him who sent them. For without them he himself knows all things and can do everything that he wills.

Yet Asaph still asks and says: “How does God know?” Does he know all things in such a way that he also has care for everything he knows, although his Apostle says: “Does God care for oxen?” (1 Cor. 9:9); or does he know all things in such a way that he has no care for some things? The response is: God knows all things in such a way that he also has care for all things.

For when the Apostle denies that God’s care for four-footed oxen was the reason this was stated and commanded in the Law—that the mouth of an ox treading grain should not be muzzled—and transfers the name of oxen to preachers threshing the grain of the Word, this is to be understood as follows: it was not out of concern for irrational oxen that God put and prescribed this in the Law, but for rational oxen, one of whom was the Apostle himself. Hence he said: “Does he not say this for our sake?” Certainly it must be understood that God’s concern was not for four-footed oxen, such that he gave the command in the Law for their sake that the mouth of an ox treading grain should not be muzzled. Rather, beneath the covering of the letter he provided for the future, lest the wages due to those preaching the Gospel be thought to be withheld, since the one evangelized by the Word ought rather to share all good things with the one who instructs him. “The labourer is worthy of his food.”

But in another respect, as regards God’s universal providence, God’s care extends not only to large oxen but also to small sparrows, not one of which falls upon the ground without the Father. He brings about and orders all that happens, and is accustomed so to bring about good things and order evil things that throughout the commonwealth of his dominion, from the heights of heaven to the lowest depths of things, nothing occurs which is not either commanded or permitted by him, in a most fitting order evident even in the lowest things. [Col. 0345A]

For who clothes the grass of the field so that even Solomon in all his glory was not so clothed or covered, if not he himself? Who causes thorns and thistles, cursed because of the sin of the first human being, to spring from the earth, if not he? Who gives the cock knowledge to distinguish the hours of the night, if not he? Finally, who administers everything that takes place among created things, if not the Creator himself? If he entirely withdrew himself from created things, every creature would return to nothing, because what was made from nothing could not subsist without its Maker.

God did not make creation as an artisan makes a chest. When the artisan departs, the chest does not cease to exist because of his departure. But if God, the artisan and maker of all things, withdrew himself, nothing whatever could subsist of itself among things; just as the day does not subsist when the sun, which creates it by its presence, withdraws itself. This must be understood still more of righteousness alone: righteousness is created in human beings by the sole spiritual presence of God, and when he withdraws and is absent because of injustices, the night of unrighteousness comes on, since the Sun of righteousness is absent—not by a local or essential departure, but by the withdrawal of his grace, according as he who knows all things knows to whom and in what manner he should be present or absent.

We now have how—or rather, how without measure, without limit, beyond every manner and measure—God knows all things. This was the question: “How does God know?” But if this is so, and if there is in the Most High such immeasurable knowledge [Col. 0345C] that he knows, cares for, administers, and orders all things, whence is this confusion in the world: that sinners, abounding in this age, have acquired riches? For

### Verse 12

Behold, it is sufficiently evident and demonstrable to all that many are sinners and yet, abounding in this age, have acquired riches; whereas many righteous people are needy, straitened, and afflicted, of whom the world is not worthy. Those are sinners and abound in this age; these are holy and needy. Those acquired riches, even other people’s riches, through unjust violence; these, I do not say could acquire what belonged to others, but could not even retain what was their own, for the more anyone withdrew from iniquity, the more exposed he became to plunder.

A great opposition, a great contradiction: to be a sinner and abound in riches; to be righteous and lack necessities; for the former to feast sumptuously every day, while the latter cannot obtain even the crumbs falling from his table; for the former to enjoy health, while the latter languishes in prolonged illness; for one serving mammon to flourish in prosperity, while one serving God grieves, oppressed by various adversities.

Since these things are so disordered in the great commonwealth, how does God know, and how can he be believed to know them, if he neither punishes the perverse nor consoles the pious and those devoted to him? He appears an unjust judge who, knowing the wicked, does not punish them; he would be more excusable if he neither knew them nor punished them. But now, since it is established that God knows all things and that there is knowledge in the Most High, a greater question—or rather complaint—has arisen for me, Asaph. For while I was still serving God for temporal things, and one serving demons abounded more in these things, I was troubled and spoke thus; this I thought within myself:

### Verses 13 and 14

Therefore in vain have I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent. Therefore, I say, if God is either ignorant or unjust, I, Asaph, have justified my heart in vain—that is, fruitlessly—by the purity of holy thought, and washed my hands among the innocent by the righteousness of good action. In vain I was scourged all day, since the virtue of patience profits me nothing; and in vain was my chastisement “in the mornings,” since I did not come late or in the evening to serve the Creator, like some who are lazy, but was hired in the morning, early at dawn, to work and bear the burden and heat of the day.

Asaph does not say this as an affirmation but as an estimate, which appears more clearly in the Hebrew, where it reads: “Is it then in vain that I cleansed my heart and washed my hands in innocence, and was scourged all day, and my rebuke was in the mornings? And I said: If I should speak thus, behold, I have forsaken the generation of your children.” It follows:

### Verse 15

If I should speak thus, behold, I have rejected the nation of your children. The order of the words is: I was saying, “I will speak thus,” not content merely to think this within myself: that God was ignorant or unjust, and that therefore he was served in vain, whether he were ignorant or did not care, and consequently did not reward service offered to him.

As I entertained such thoughts, there was a most grievous weariness upon me, so that no breath would have remained in me had not the authority of the righteous and holy persons, who did not agree with my judgment, occurred to me and come to my aid. Therefore I said: “If I should speak thus, behold, I have rejected the nation of your children.” For the authority of the holy Fathers is contrary to me; they teach that God is neither ignorant nor unjust, as certain erring people have thought.

Once their error is destroyed, this truth is established on the authority of God’s holy children: since God knows all things, there is knowledge in the Most High; and because he has care for all things, no good or evil person will go unrewarded under his judgement. The good receive evils in this life and the evil likewise receive good things, solely according to those merits which must be recompensed in this life. For those to whom eternal rewards, whether good or evil, are due: good things are reserved for the good and evil things for the evil in the life to come, so that after the final judgement no good person may fare badly and no evil person well.

Thus, O God, teaches the nation of your children, which I rejected and forsook if I speak otherwise or say something other than they do. By speaking thus to myself, I checked the onset of error, lest what had defiled my conscience by wicked hesitation should also corrupt others by most wicked teaching. Corrected, therefore, so as to yield to the authority of my elders and believe their teaching, after accepting belief in sound doctrine I strove, by the ladder of faith, to understand the pure truth of this question: why, namely, prosperity smiles upon the wicked in this life, while adversity often afflicts the righteous so greatly that the righteous person is sometimes compelled to cry out and say: “My soul is weary of my life” (Job 10:1). Likewise: “Alas [Col. 0347A] for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. 119:5).

### Verse 16

And I reflected, in order that I might know by understanding what I had already received through faith and must hold: but this is labour before me. To know this fully is labour before me. It is difficult in view of the things before me—that is, present things, which lie before our eyes—among which I cannot discern the reason for so great a mystery, because they stand before me like a wall set against me.

I confess that, overcome by the teaching of the Fathers, I cannot but believe what I know that they believed. But to know by reason or understanding this very thing which I believe is labour before me; to know it in this life is altogether impossible for me. But it is not labour before God, because no word is impossible before God. Therefore, if I too should be before God, I believe that I shall pass beyond the wall of this question by the help of him who alone opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens, that sanctuary in which what is now obscure will clearly be seen.

Therefore I do not say absolutely that to know this is labour before me; but I add:

### Verse 17

Until I enter into the sanctuary of God, and there understand their end. Meanwhile, let it suffice me to know my ignorance, which is the first step toward full knowledge. In this prudent ignorance I shall be wisely unknowing and wisely untaught, content with faith alone. Faith does not ordinarily burst in, but reverently knocks at the door of its friend, until he rises and opens to me what had hitherto been shut, and I, when he opens, enter into the sanctuary of God: namely, the secret of holy contemplation, hidden from the wicked but set forth for the good in the Scriptures of truth.

Or, I shall enter into the sanctuary of God, which is Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge of God.” To enter that sanctuary is nothing other than to be incorporated into his members and made alive and enlightened by his Spirit; whoever does not have that Spirit is not his.

Therefore, enlightened by his Spirit and instructed concerning the end of good and evil persons, I shall understand at their end that God was foreknowing of future things: when he predestined eternal good things for the good and preordained eternal evils for the evil, while likewise recompensing both in the present life for their small good and evil merits. Thus we read that the rich man who asked for a drop of water heard from Father Abraham: “Son, remember that you received your good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things” [Col. 0347D] (Luke 16:25). Thus, brought into the sanctuary of God, I shall know as I am known—not in part, as now I see through a mirror and in an enigma.

### Verse 18

Nevertheless, even now, standing before the sanctuary and reverently knocking concerning this question of the prosperity of the wicked, I have learned something that I did not know before: namely, that you, O God, have set [these things] for them because of deceits. You cast them down while they were being raised up.

Third part, in which the aforesaid Asaph sets forth in part [Col. 0348A] the cause of the prosperity of the wicked and his own deliverance, saying: “Nevertheless, because of deceits you have set [these things] for them.” Because of the deceits which they devise against others in acquiring earthly things, they too will be caught in deceits and snares. For “those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil, and many harmful desires which plunge people into destruction” (1 Tim. 6:9).

The Hebrew truth has: “Nevertheless, you have set them in a slippery place.” The meaning is the same. For the riches set before them because of deceits are a slippery place, in which, established by love, they cannot stand, as those stand who love true riches. Hence Saint Pope Gregory says [Note: Col. 0347, Homily 15 on the Gospels]: “If you truly desire, brothers, to be rich, love true riches.” He likewise says in Job [Note: Col. 0347, Book 32 of the *Moralia*, chapter 9, and *Pastoral Rule*, part 3, chapter 26]:

> “When the reprobate do not repay right works with divine works, when they abandon themselves entirely here and give themselves up to abounding prosperities, from the source by which they advance outwardly [Col. 0348B] they fall away from inward things. Hence the rich man, tormented in hell, is told: ‘You received your good things in your lifetime.’ Therefore the wicked man received good things here so that he might receive evil things more fully there, since he had not here been converted even by good things. He therefore does not say, ‘You cast them down after they had been raised up,’ but, ‘while they were being raised up,’ because this very thing is an inward casting down for the proud: that false glory happens to raise them outwardly. For by the ordering of divine judgement, their fault is not one thing and their punishment another; rather, their fault itself is turned into their punishment. Thus, when they are raised up by the arrogance of pride, their very apparent outward advancement is truly an inward fall.”

The prophet says: “Woe to you who plunder: will you not yourself also be plundered?” [Col. 0348C] (Isa. 33:1). For one who makes a prey of a human being becomes the devil’s prey. Similarly, here we may say: Woe to you who ensnare and deceive others by deceit: will you not yourself be ensnared and deceived by deceit? For the very love of temporal things takes away eternal things—the temporal things which deceitful people deceitfully take from others.

Therefore, by a just judgement, you, O God, knowing all contrivances of deceit—hidden from human beings but manifest to you—have, because of their deceits, set before deceitful persons those riches acquired by deceit as a trap, by which they may be caught and cast down. For you cast them down not only after they have been raised up, but while they are being raised up, in the likeness of a wheel which, while it is lifted at the rear, is cast down at the front. Thus these also, while raised in outward things, are hurled down from a height in inward things. Where? Into the deep pit of everlasting desolation, which Truth threatens when it says: “Woe to you rich, for you have your consolation; woe to you who now laugh, for you will mourn and weep; woe to you who are full, for you will hunger” [Col. 0348D] (Luke 6:24–25).

Great indeed will be the desolation of those who lose the temporal things they loved and do not obtain the eternal good things they neglected. Therefore I, Asaph—I, the faithful congregation—understanding at their end the great danger and outcome, am compelled by the magnitude of so great an error to cry out:

### Verses 19 and 20

How have they become a desolation! I say this not as a question but in amazement, as Jeremiah likewise says: “How does the city, once full of people, sit alone!” (Lam. 1:1). For it is indeed a great desolation for a city full of people to be laid waste, so that all its citizens are driven out, captured, or killed, and it is reduced to solitude. We read that this happened at the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, first by the first Babylon, and second by the second; for Rome too is called Babylon in the Epistle of the Apostle Peter, who, being at Rome, says: “The Church gathered in Babylon greets you” (1 Pet. 5:13).

Therefore, just as the murderers of prophets, sages, scribes, and Christ himself were handed over to the Babylonians or Romans and, devastated by them, became a desolation, so at the end of those who hate prophets and wise persons eternal desolation will come. To me, Asaph, this is as certain to occur as if I already saw it done. Therefore I state in words of the past rather than future tense what I know will happen at the end.

I say, then: How have they become a desolation—that is, how are they desolated, having lost their possessions in death, which came suddenly, so that they quickly failed? And because their end and dying are shared with the good, he adds the point in which they differ: “They perished.” Why? Because of their iniquity. How? “Like the dream of those who awake,” or, “awaking.”

A poor man lies down and dreams that he has riches, treasures, honours, and things of this sort. But what he seems to possess with closed eyes, he does not possess with opened eyes. Thus also the wicked, when they awaken by dying from this life in which they sleep as blind persons, will find nothing but misery. Truly so. For, O Lord, and so forth.

The city of the wicked, which Cain built, is earthly. In it they have removed the image of God from themselves and erected their own images or likenesses: one has become a lion through ferocity, another a bird through frivolity, another a swine through the filth of lust, another an ass through sluggishness, and so forth. They have also regarded temporal happiness as happiness; yet this is not true happiness but its image, that is, its likeness.

Therefore every such image which is theirs—that is, which they themselves made—you, O Lord, will reduce to nothing in your city, the heavenly Jerusalem. For even here, in the portion of your city still on pilgrimage, you reduce their image to nothing: you make those who have put away the oldness of sins walk in newness of life [Col. 0349D] and become conformed to you, O Christ, who are the connatural image of the Father, to whom all the adopted children of the same Father must be conformed. “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. 8:29).

Just as any metal melted in fire loses the forms it previously had while its nature remains, and takes on the form of the fire itself, so in your city, Jerusalem above, which is free, all its citizens, delivered from this pilgrimage in which we are and set aflame by the fire of your love, will be conformed to the image of your Son. Since you are a fire consuming rust and refining gold, and since your Son—coeternal and consubstantial fire with you—is the radiance of glory [Col. 0350A] and the exact image of your substance, those set ablaze by the love of you and of your Son, which is the Holy Spirit, cannot be unlike you.

“For now we are children of God, but what we shall be has not yet appeared. But when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:5), says John, that chief lover and citizen of that city in which you will reduce to nothing the image of those who hate you, and glorify the image of your Son in the adopted children whom you will set aflame. Nor is it surprising that you will then set them aflame, when you will be clearly seen face to face.

### Verses 21 and 22

For even now my heart has been set aflame, ever since I entered, by the insight of the mind and the steps of faith, into the sanctuary of God, and understood at the end what I could not understand at the beginning. My heart is now inflamed with zeal for righteousness, thanks be to God. But before, when I envied sinners on seeing the peace of sinners, my heart was inflamed with the zeal of folly: I grievously envied rich evildoers, saw good people in poverty, and grieved over this.

But now my heart is inflamed with a better zeal, since I emulate both good and evil persons with God’s emulation: desiring that the former may always increase from good to better, and that the latter may be changed from evil to good. For I know from a domestic proof that this is possible for God, through whose grace my kidneys (renes) also have been changed. When the moderated—or extinguished—carnal pleasure which ruled in my kidneys gave way to a better delight, that delight succeeded of which it is elsewhere said: “Delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart” (Ps. 36:4). Likewise: “Delights are at your right hand for ever” [Col. 0350C] (Ps. 15:11).

But before, when I delighted in temporal goods and envied those who possessed them, I was reduced to nothing by envy and foolish emulation. For “even if I have prophecy and know all mysteries, but do not have love”—which “does not envy” and “is kind”—“I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2). How much more, wasting away with the zeal of malignant emulation, was I reduced to nothing when I did not even have knowledge of my own sin—a profound ignorance comparable to the stupidity of irrational beasts? Therefore I confess my sin and my ignorance, saying: “I was reduced to nothing, and I did not know.”

[Col. 0350D] **VERSE 23.** *I became like a beast.* For I know that, just as “man, though he was in honour, did not understand” that honour itself, “he was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13, 21), so a man, when he is in sin and does not understand sin itself, is compared to beasts—especially when, loving earthly things and neglecting heavenly ones, he does not walk upright as a human being, but proceeds with downcast face like cattle. Thus I became like a beast by desiring earthly things alone, though I sought them neither from demons nor from the idols of the nations, but from the true God. Therefore I say: *And I am always with you.* For however great my desire for earthly things may have been, I nevertheless sought them only from you, the true God, worshipping you alone; and in this respect I have always been and shall be with you.

I was with you in the time of [Col. 0351A] ignorance, when, in order to obtain such things, I thought that you ought to be worshipped, while invisible and eternal goods were despised. Much more from now on shall I be with you, knowing that in your worship heavenly things must be sought first and principally; and all these things will be added, which will be necessary to those who serve you. Therefore, *I am always with you*—a resolution that I purpose most firmly to maintain, not by my own strength, which is none at all, since in this too I have been reduced to nothing, so that I know that without you I can do nothing—but by the help of your power and grace. I have sure proof of this: from the time when I became like a beast, gentle and submissive in bearing your burdens, so that in this obedience I may always be with you, you—

**VERSE 24.** *You held my right hand*, that is, [Col. 0351B] my works; and in your gratuitous will you guided me, and with glory you received me—that is, you will yet receive me. For because of the great certainty of future things, I state a future event with a verb of past time. For I know that the one whose right hand you held when, seeing the violent wind and fearing that I would sink, I cried to you, and whom you guided in your gratuitous will, unanticipated by any merits—for this one you will finally receive with glory into your kingdom.

Therefore what I believe and hope will occur, I announce as though it were past and already accomplished, in the prophetic manner. Thus, “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21:18) was said of my future Passion, just as this is said of my future glory. For I sing and speak in Asaph, because I am that Christ, [Col. 0351C] that David whose praises shall not fail, nor ever have failed—even when the praises of David, son of Jesse according to the flesh, of the people carnally born from Jesse, did fail.

Therefore this saying principally applies to me: *I became like a beast before you, and I am always with you. You held my right hand, and in your will you guided me, and with glory you received me.* For, though I was in the form of God, I did not consider equality with God my Father a thing to be seized; but I emptied myself, taking the form of a beast, in order to carry that half-dead man whose neighbour I made myself by showing mercy to him. And indeed I was sent for this purpose by you, Father. Yet I am always with you, and you with me; and you have not left me alone, because I have done and always do what is pleasing to you—God mighty equally [Col. 0351D] with you—because I and you, Father, are one.

I could therefore have resisted my crucifiers; but you, Father, so held my right hand and guided me in your will that I had to say: “Father, not my will but yours be done” (Luke 22:42). And because, while you held my right hand—that is, while you directed my good and divine works—I obeyed your will, therefore, when obedience had at last been completed, you received and assumed me with glory into the throne of your majesty, giving me the name above every name, so that I could say: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18).

At first, indeed, you received me at my conception—that is, you received my human nature to be united to your Word. And certainly there was great glory in this reception, than which [Col. 0352A] there is none greater; but this glory was hidden, until through the glorious resurrection, wondrous ascension, and outpouring of the Holy Spirit it was plainly manifested that I had to suffer and thus, through the disgrace of the Passion, enter into my glory. Therefore, although my right hand, which is the power of my divinity, could have defended my left hand—that is, my humanity, exposed to so many miseries and indignities—you held my right hand, or the hand of my right side, that is, the power of my divinity, by which I could have snatched myself from the hands of my enemies and cast them down into hell—those before whom, when I had said only once, “I am he,” “they went backward and fell to the ground” (John 18:6).

Unless therefore you, Father, had held my right hand [Col. 0352B] by whose power I made them fall to the ground, I could by that same power have made them fall into the abyss. But you held my hand bound by the bond of obedience, and in your will guided me from heaven into the virgin’s womb, from the womb into the world, from the world into hell, from hell again into the world; and then you assumed me with glory into heaven, to reign with you in humanity now glorified, as from eternity I reigned with you in the eternal glory of my divinity.

In the Hebrew it reads: *My heart was constricted and my reins were loosened. And I was foolish and ignorant; I became like a beast before you; and I was always with you, and you held the hand of my right side. You will guide me into your counsel, and afterwards you will receive me in glory* [Ps. 72:21–24]. In these words there clearly resounds both confession of sins committed, thanksgiving for the virtues of grace freely bestowed, and certain expectation of future goods.

For when I, Asaph, say, *My heart was constricted*, it is the same as saying, *I did not have charity*. Charity’s broad commandment, received in the heart, enlarges the heart itself; a heart constricted by envy and evil zeal cannot at the same time be enlarged in charity, or, as we said above, set aflame. I therefore confess that my heart was constricted through envy, as leather is sometimes shrunk by excessive dryness. And *my reins were loosened*, because carnal pleasure, restrained by no bridle, though the heart was constricted through wickedness, overflowed [Col. 0352D] through loosened reins in delights. For I was without that righteousness which is the belt of the loins, and without that faith which is the girdle of the reins.

Thus I was in great danger: dry in heart, dissolute in flesh; and, understanding this very thing, reduced to nothing, foolish and ignorant, I became like a beast. I give thanks to you, Lord, who, binding me with hook and bridle, made me from a foolish and untamed beast so gentle that I might always be with you, from the time when you held the hand of my right side—that is, my good works, which belong to the right side, just as evil works belong to the left. You held me in your right hand, sustaining me, lest, when I began to sink, I should sink entirely while walking toward you upon the sea, where I would have walked in peril had you not held my right hand and led me to the harbour of salvation; and from [Col. 0353A] the harbour to a wholly firm shore, where no danger is thereafter to be feared. This I prophesy of what will happen to me in the Spirit of truth, saying: *You will guide me into your counsel, and afterwards you will receive me in glory.*

God’s counsel is like a desired harbour for those fleeing this great and wide sea: for example, virginity, voluntary poverty, and devout obedience to the Fathers in all things and in every respect, even unto death. All these and similar institutions of an arduous life receive, as into a certain harbour, those fleeing the stormy waves of this world, which at times overwhelm persons devoted only to the vessel of the commandments.
