From this harbour one easily comes to the shore of eternal stability, where eternal glory is found.

This I, Asaph, confidently promise myself through your help, O God: that you [Col. 0353B] will guide me into your counsel, so that I may gladly and obediently hear you proposing not only saving commandments but also the most saving counsels of perfection; and afterwards you will receive me in glory, when the virtue of obedience has been completed and preserved unto death. Like the ladder shown to the patriarch Jacob, this virtue rests upon the earth through observance of the commandments, but is raised to heaven through observance of the counsels, as Truth says: “Sell what you have, and give to the poor; and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21).

**VERSE 25.** *For what have I in heaven?* What good, and how great a good, is laid up in heaven for me, who obey not only divine commandments but also counsels, and therefore have treasure in heaven?

From this point, the fourth part of the psalm rebukes the former folly by which earthly things were preferred to heavenly by those who praised God and thought that he should be praised only, or chiefly, for bodily safety and the prosperity or abundance of temporal possessions. Such praises did not wholly fail among God’s people before our Lord, King of all ages, came and, by the things he suffered, confirmed us, lest we be scandalized when we see the wicked prosper and the good unjustly oppressed.

For what righteous person, seeing Justice itself crucified by those “whose iniquity came forth as if from fat,” who “were not in the labour of men, nor were they scourged with men”—what righteous person, I say, when something similar [Col. 0353D] happens to him, would now say, “Therefore in vain have I made my heart righteous and washed my hands among the innocent”? For if he spoke thus, behold, he would reject the generation of God’s children—indeed, the Passion itself of God’s natural Son.

Therefore, fittingly, on Palm Sunday the adopted children, justified or to be justified through that naturally righteous and good Son, sing in remembrance of him who was scourged and crucified: *How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart!* Thus instructed by this song, may we praise God even amid adversities, and may our feet—that is, our reason and judgment—not be moved when we see the peace of sinners. Nor, even when we can, should we avenge ourselves; rather, let us reserve vengeance for God, who is just and merciful, and who holds our hand precisely when he says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. [Col. 0354A] 32:35). Thus he held the hand of his Son at the time of the Passion, lest he then avenge himself, giving us an example that we too should act in this way and possess our souls in patience; because “tribulation works patience; and patience, proven character; and proven character, hope” (Rom. 5:3–4), by which we may hope for heavenly, not earthly, things.

*For what have I in heaven? And what have I desired from you upon earth?* I do not state definitively: “This or that good is laid up for me in heaven.” Rather, indicating in an undefined way that highest reward which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which has not entered the human heart, I, Asaph, cry out in great wonder: *For what have I in heaven?* What? That is: how much? How great? How [Col. 0354B] inestimable is the reward prepared for me in heaven if I love God? For he will give himself to those who love him; and this is an inestimable reward. You, O God, prepared this for those who love you; and therefore I foolishly desired something else in place of you. What a cheap exchange: to seize mud instead of gold, earth instead of heaven, a passing creature instead of the Creator himself! *For what have I in heaven?* Something great that cannot be expressed in words; it can be obtained, but it cannot be estimated.

Conversely, what did I desire from you upon earth? The delights of pleasures? They are short, and they send people into eternal punishments. For like putrefaction they generate worms that gnaw the conscience and will not die eternally, because neither their fire will be quenched nor their worm [Col. 0354C] die; and at the judgment it will be said to them: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). What did I desire upon earth? Suppose it was the glory of this world. But oh, how empty and deceptive is glory, which, like the flower of grass, quickly falls and plunges its lovers into eternal confusion!

When I consider one by one and all together the things that I desired upon earth, I find that I pursued nothing but a shadow, like the dog of which fables tell: carrying a piece of meat in its mouth while crossing water by a wooden path, it saw in the water the shadow of the meat; grasping at the shadow, it lost the real meat. Thus I too, desiring false and shadowy goods upon earth, lost the true goods; nor can I recover them at all unless I truly repent and do the opposite of those deeds [Col. 0354D] of which I repent. Now the first degree of repentance is to cease from evil; the second is to advance in good. Therefore:

**VERSE 26.** *My flesh and my heart have failed.* My flesh has failed, afflicted by the chastisements of repentance, so that it is weakened for evil works. My heart also has ceased from the habit and study of thinking vain and useless things. If such thoughts sometimes strike the eyes of memory, they nevertheless do not reach the heart’s voluntary approval, because its deepest recesses are occupied with better desires.

For *God is the God of my heart, and God is my portion for ever*. That is to say: God possesses my heart, and I, in return, possess him. *God of my heart*—understand, “is its possessor”; and *my portion*—that is, my possession—is God, not merely for an hour while I rejoice [Col. 0355A] or exult in this light, but for ever. “God of my heart” is said with the same force as “God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob,” because, though Creator of all in general, he is especially not only their Creator but also their lover. So too he is known as not only Creator but lover of my heart, because he himself is in return loved by my heart above all creatures. Hence, glorying humbly not in myself but in him, I say: *God is the God of my heart, and God is my portion for ever.*

This is fittingly said by Asaph—that is, by the assembly of those who are admitted to the clergy in such a way that they have no inheritance or property of their own upon earth, but the Lord is their portion and inheritance, and they too are the Lord’s portion and inheritance. Thus it is written in the law of the Lord: “You shall not give an inheritance to the sons of Levi; I, the Lord, shall be their inheritance” (Num. 18:20).

Therefore, although it is fitting for every true Christian to say, *God is the God of my heart, and God is my portion for ever*, it applies especially to those who have no inheritance upon earth and do not wish to have one, and to whom God himself deigns to become an inheritance. Thus they can confidently say: *God is the God of my heart, and God is my portion for ever.* Behold what I have in heaven! Let others choose other things: God is my portion. Let the younger son seek the share that falls to him and go into a far country; but I, having now returned from the far country to my father, ask for no inheritance beyond him. Henceforth he himself shall be my inheritance; he himself, the God of my heart, shall be its cultivator, indweller, and [Col. 0355C] possessor for ever; and God himself shall be my portion for ever, from whom I shall no longer depart into a far country. For:

**VERSE 27.** *Behold, those who remove themselves far from you shall perish*—understand: unless they repent. This must be understood in many of God’s threats, as in: “Everyone who takes the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:53)—understand: unless he repents. Those who remove themselves far from you shall perish—not those who at one time removed themselves far from you and afterwards came to their senses, as I, Asaph, removed from you, became like a beast. Yet I did not withdraw too far from you, since I sought from you alone the temporal things themselves which I loved.

But at last, knowing that, just as such things are to be sought only from you, so too they are to be desired only for your sake—just as, for example, a seafaring pilgrim seeks a ship solely in order to reach the homeland which he loves—I chose not merely to be with you in asking these things from you rather than from the idols of the nations, but also always to be with you, saying, *And I am always with you*: namely, loving you alone chiefly, and after you, or in you, whatever helps me attain you.

Therefore I said, *I am always with you.* But from that time you too have always been with me. For you held my right hand, guided me in your will, and received me with glory. What was explained above need not be expounded again.

[Col. 0356A] Therefore, as I say and firmly resolve that I may always be with you, you have held me and guided me in your will. But those who remove themselves far from you shall perish, as many such persons have already perished. For you have destroyed everyone who commits fornication away from you, worshipping idols or loving something other than you, against you, and more than you. This is great fornication, when you alone—or at least you chiefly—ought to be loved with a chaste love, by which those who love you freely possess all things in you alone. For all things suitable and useful for such a pursuit will be added to those who seek you first and principally—prosperities, to support such people, or adversities, to exercise them. Hence those who depart from you and consider this beneficial to themselves are foolish.

[Col. 0356B] **VERSE 28.** *But it is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in God, that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion.* It is good for me to cling to God through faith; likewise, it is good to place my hope in the Lord God, lest faith be without hope. But above all goods it is good to possess such charity that I myself praise you, God, and declare all your praises to others in the gates of the daughter of Zion; for it is the business and earnest desire of a true lover to praise what he loves and draw fellow-lovers to it.

Alternatively: for me to cling to God—that is, to see him face to face—is the highest good. Meanwhile, while this cannot yet be, it is good for me to place my hope in God, so that he may nourish me with the milk of faith and hope [Col. 0356C] for the vision of the reality itself. Perhaps I am delayed from entering the long-desired city, in which you will reduce the images of enemies to nothing, so that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion, or in the courts of the daughter of Zion.

By the gates or courts of the heavenly Zion—that is, of the Church that beholds God—are understood the holy exercises of the pilgrim Church, which direct people toward those structures of the heavenly court that no eye has seen, no ear heard, and no human heart comprehended. Outside such gates or courts, by which the whole Church is surrounded and united, every praise is empty. Therefore I have resolved to declare all your praises, O God, not outside but in the courts or gates of the daughter of Zion—that is, of the pilgrim Church, which is the daughter of the Church [Col. 0356D] already reigning. For she who is above is free: she is our mother, whose noble daughter is the Church labouring on earth, joined to her by the bond of maternal love from that side, and filial love from this.

Glory to God the Father of Israel, who is good to the upright in heart. Glory to God the Son, whose right hand the Father held, whom he guided in his will and assumed with glory. Glory to the Holy Spirit, the true and living God, who is that will of the Father in which the Father himself guided the Son, voluntarily obedient in his humanity, for the salvation of humankind. Amen.

# PSALM LXXIII

[Col. 0357]

[Col. 0357A] **VERSE 1.** *Why, O God, have you cast us off unto the end?* The title of this psalm is:

## UNDERSTANDING OF ASAPH

Those who have understanding, and sing wisely, set forth questions in this psalm, saying: “Why, O God, have you cast us off unto the end? Has your wrath been inflamed against the sheep of your pasture?” and so on. Although they set forth questions of this kind, they do not do so in doubt, but with concern for the salvation and instruction of others. Their questions first engage attention; then, taught by the solutions, their hearers may applaud God’s just judgment and not be saddened by the tribulation of the faithful, but rejoice in hope, knowing that by suffering hard and harsh things they will attain glory.

Asaph means “synagogue,” which, although it is an assembly of any persons whatever, is properly said of the people of Israel. To this people the Old Testament was given, containing three things: commandments, promises, and sacraments. Some commandments were moral, such as “You shall not kill”; others figurative, such as circumcision on the eighth day. The promises were temporal, such as the fertile land of Canaan and temporal kingship. But in these figurative commandments and promises other, spiritual things were promised; thus the commandments and promises themselves were sacraments of realities hidden within them.

Besides these sacraments of figurative commandments and promises, there were other sacraments, as in the sale of Joseph and similar events. And just as the first man was earthly, from the earth, while the second was heavenly, from heaven, so to that people, which bore the image of the earthly man, there first had to be promised what is animate—that is, temporal things; then, to those bearing the image of the heavenly man, that which is spiritual—that is, eternal things. Therefore God, desiring a people trained in temporal things to become spiritual, took temporal things away from them and gave them abundantly to the wicked, to teach by this that, although given by God, they were not truly good.

Here the synagogue was divided into good and evil persons. The good were those who first hesitated when they saw the peace of sinners, but afterwards turned away from this and sought God alone, as the preceding psalm contains. To these the New Testament was given, which likewise contains three things: commandments, promises, and sacraments. Yet the moral commandments are the same as those in the Old Testament, whereas the figurative commandments are not the same. The promises and sacraments are not the same either. For there, as stated, temporal things were promised; here, eternal things. It is also evident that the sacraments differ: there they promise the Saviour; here they possess the Saviour. In it salvation is now promised; in the future it will be given. Those, therefore, were sacraments of things now present; these, of things future. For those promise the Saviour; these, salvation. This is the understanding of Asaph—that is, of the faithful synagogue.

[Col. 0358A] Finally, because what is possessed need not be promised, since truth has now come, the figurative institutions have been removed, such as the kingdom, priesthood, temple, circumcision, and the like. Here the wicked—the other part of the synagogue—not attending to the heavenly things promised to the mature, but fearing the loss of earthly things received in childhood, killed Christ who had given them. Therefore they lost those things, and were themselves killed. To show that the time also disclosed the cause, after forty-two years had passed, at the very feast at which they killed the Lord, they suffered under Titus and Vespasian and the city was overthrown. Asaph laments this in this psalm.

This lament is called the *Understanding of Asaph* because, while he mourns the cause of an irreparable overthrow, he understands it: namely, that a person, abandoning earthly things and the Old Testament, should cease to be animate and, made spiritual in the New Testament, await heavenly things. This is the purpose of the psalm.

The method is as follows. First, mourning the irreparable destruction, he prays that at least the remnant may be saved, recalling when and how the Jews, provoking God, were destroyed. Second, when the signs have been destroyed, he shows the reality itself: namely, Christ’s coming and salvation everywhere through him, at “*But God*.” Third, he prays that God may spare the repentant and profitably punish Roman pride, at “*Remember*.” This is the first psalm of lamentation, concerning the final captivity inflicted by Titus. Two further psalms of lamentation follow: namely, “*O God, the nations have come*,” and “*By the rivers*.”

Consider, moreover, how great was the breadth of mercy in the Prophet: he mourned in prosperity a disaster long to come, no differently than Jeremiah, who wept when he saw the captivity. This manner of speaking is full of charity, by which we are taught to weep with those who weep. Therefore the overthrow of the lamented city is described so that the hardness of the Jews might be frightened even by calamities.

Therefore, prophesying the captivity, he speaks in the person of the faithful synagogue: “O God, you cast off your people, as you have often cast us off, and destroyed us; you were angry, and had mercy on us. By alternating these, you showed your people both hard and pleasant things: through hard things giving those who fear you a sign, that they might flee before the bow; through pleasant things—such as peace and abundance of temporal possessions—urging them to desire eternal things more than these. For just as, through hard temporal things, which nature itself teaches must be fled, a sign is given to those who fear you, that they may flee before the bow, so through pleasant temporal things, which nature itself advises us to desire, a sign is given to those who love you, that they may desire eternally pleasant eternal things.

“For if people labour with great expenditure and difficulty to escape or avoid temporal illnesses, how much more should they labour to escape and avoid eternal punishments? Again: if bodily, temporal health, which finally, whether we wish it or not, must be cut off by death—and against death no art of medicine prevails—is loved and preserved with great care, how much greater care must be expended for the health of the soul, which will not die? Therefore you often showed your people now hardships, now prosperity in turn, because by these you trained them. But now I see harsh things alone lasting unto the end, since you cast off your people unto the end.”

Seeing and wondering at this, I, Asaph, say with grief and groaning:

“Why, O God, have you cast us off unto the end? You have indeed cast off your people by a just judgment, yet a hidden one, from yourself and from your protection. Therefore I, Asaph, understanding that you are just, do not murmur against your justice in striking; but I inquire into what is hidden: namely, for what reason it is just that you cast off your people not for a brief time, to be chastened and quickly freed, as you often freed them from the hands of the nations that ruled them—for example, through Gideon, Samson, Samuel, King David, and the other saviours and defenders.

“But now you have cast them off unto the end, because they are cast off until the end of the age; and then not all will be converted, but, according to the Prophet, only a remnant—that is, fewer out of many. For where the Apostle says, ‘When the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved’ (Rom. 11:25–26), one must understand: all Israel preordained to life, lest Isaiah, the greatest of the prophets, and the Apostle himself, teacher of the nations, seem to teach contrary things.

“You also cast some of them off unto the end in such a way that, instructed by your scourges, you sent and compelled them unto the end—that is, into Christ, who is ‘the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes’ (Rom. 10:4), who is the beginning and the end, Alpha and Omega, the origin and consummation of things. This was manifestly fulfilled in the Apostle Paul, whom, striking with the evident blow of blindness, you cast off from the synagogue of Satan—blind and without understanding—to the understanding of Asaph, whose title shines forth in this psalm. For he is Asaph, that is, the faithful synagogue, whose understanding in the legal commandments and ceremonies wholly tends toward Christ, whom faithful Asaph recognizes as the end of every consummation.”

[Col. 0359D] There is no complaint, then, concerning those who were thus cast off unto the end of consummation and perfection and, abandoning the figure, held fast the truth. The complaint concerns those cast off unto the end of failure, so completely that they failed not only inwardly—dying in their souls—but also outwardly: in body, some killed, some captive and scattered, stripped of every observance both legal and evangelical; having neither temple nor priesthood nor altar according to the Law or according to the Gospel. Thus they are wholly devastated and desolate unto the end, after the final captivity inflicted by Titus and Vespasian, who came like two bears from the forest of the Roman Empire and scattered the foolish boys who mocked the true Elisha.

In this it appears that you were not simply and briefly angry as before, but *your fury was angry*. I do not say separately, “You were angry” or “You were furious,” but I say, “Your fury was angry,” so that by this doubling the greatness alike of your wrath and fury may be shown. And this was not against enemies but against the sheep of your pasture, since it is in some sense natural to punish more sparingly those who were once members of one’s household. I, Asaph, do not reproach your judgment in this; but, sympathizing with my neighbours, I complain in wonder, saying: “Why have you done this? Why have you brought such fury and wrath upon the sheep once of your pasture? Did you not say that, ‘when you are angry, you will remember mercy’? (Hab. 3:2). Therefore, lest in this wrath you forget mercy or forget to have pity, O God:

**VERSE 2.** *Remember your congregation, which [Col. 0360B] you have possessed from the beginning*, so that you, merciful judge, may attend more to your customary benefits than to the faults of sheep who do not acknowledge you as their shepherd. Remember, I say, the congregation which you did not gather at the end of the ages, as you gathered the nations, but possessed from the beginning. For when from the beginning of the world, through many ages, you allowed all nations to go their own ways, you set this generation apart from the evil generation of Cain the fratricide—a generation from which you, God made man, willed to be born. Upon it you placed the seal of circumcision and the yoke of the Law. For it you appointed patriarchs, judges, kings, and prophets, because you deigned to possess it under the bridle of your discipline, while in some manner neglecting the other nations and hiring no labourers from among them into your vineyard until this eleventh hour, when the end of the world is believed to be near.

Moreover, you not only possessed this people of yours from the beginning, separating it from the people not yours by the sign of circumcision and many other things—for example, by looking favourably upon their sacrifices and offerings as those of the generation of Abel, while not looking favourably upon those of others, as the generation of Cain, although offering rightly, yet not dividing rightly. But later, when they sinned by selling their innocent brother, and consequently came to Egypt under the pressure of famine, so as to be reduced there to slavery because they had sold their brother into slavery, you remembered the faithful fathers—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—had mercy on the children, and by sending the rod redeemed the rod.

[Col. 0360D] For the rod of Moses, by which, working signs, you redeemed your people, signified this very people of yours. That people too was in some sense your rod, because through it you scourged many nations: when Pharaoh himself and his house were scourged with great plagues because he had taken Abraham’s wife into his house; and later another Pharaoh was scourged with greater plagues through and because of this people of yours, likened to Moses’ rod. With that rod also you expelled twelve nations from the holy land promised to your saints.

But in what respect was this nation likened to Moses’ rod? Namely, because just as Moses’ rod, at first straight, then appeared twisted in the form of a serpent, and afterwards, once the dragon’s form was laid aside, was found again straight in Moses’ hand, so your nation was upright in its ancient righteous persons and patriarchs, in Moses’ hand, as long as it kept the Law given through him and faithfully awaited Christ, promised in the Law. But when it denied him, it was turned into a serpent so twisted that Moses flees—or rather, Moses himself accuses this people, in whom they hope and whose words they read continually, but in vain, because his letter, without the Spirit, kills them, bringing them death. That death is signified by the serpent, because it came upon humankind through the serpent—indeed, through the devil speaking in the serpent.

But it will come to pass at the end that Moses, as it were by the tail, will seize at least the remnant of this people, which near the end of the age will recognize Christ as prefigured and promised in the Law of Moses; and then it will return to its former state.

[Col. 0361B] For, to pass over the sacrifices, offerings, and other legal observances by which Christ was prefigured in many and various ways, he is found to be manifestly prefigured in this very rod of Moses, now under discussion. He is also the flourishing “rod of strength” “in the splendors of the saints” (Ps. 110 [Vulgate 109], 2–3), which the Lord therefore sent forth, that he might rule in the midst of his enemies, as Moses’ rod ruled in the midst of the Egyptians. This is the rod of which Jeremiah says: “I see a watching rod”; and the Lord, explaining this of himself, says: “You have seen well, because I watch over my word” (Jer. 1:11–12). This is the rod concerning which the Lord said to Moses, when he sought a sign by which it might be believed that he had been sent by him:

> “What are you holding in your hand?” And Moses said: “A rod.” And the Lord said: “Throw it on the ground.” When he had thrown it down, it was changed into a serpent; and Moses was terrified and fled. And the Lord said to him: “Take hold of its tail.” And he took hold of it, and it became again a rod as it had been before” (Exod. 4:2–4).

Mystically, death is understood through the serpent that urged death, and Christ through the rod. Therefore the rod becoming a serpent is Christ dying. He is the bronze serpent raised up in the wilderness; those bitten by serpents were healed by looking at it, because those who believe in Christ dead are saved. Moses was frightened when he saw the serpent and fled, because the disciples feared when they saw the Passion and withdrew from their former hope. The serpent was changed back into a rod because Christ returned [Col. 0361C] from death to life. Moses grasped the tail without fear because, once they knew the resurrection, the disciples believed firmly.

When his flesh blossomed again, like the rod of Moses or Aaron, it bore such fruits that by its power the Egyptians are despoiled and the Hebrews enriched; hell is despoiled and paradise enriched; through the water of baptism the invisible Pharaoh is drowned with his armies and attendants—that is, vices and demons. And God’s people rejoice, singing to the Lord, who has been gloriously honored: he cast horse and rider into the sea—drowning the rider, the devil, but freeing the horse from his hand, namely the human race that believes in him, purified by the sacrament of baptism and, in this respect also, made like the rod of Moses now under consideration.

For, as commentators on this passage have said before us, the rod of Moses signifies the uprightness of the human race in which it was created. For God made man upright, but man himself entangled himself in innumerable questions. Thus the rod, falling to the ground, was changed into a serpent, which moves by the winding coils of its body. So too, enticed by the devil through the hissing serpent, man fell from the stability and uprightness in which he had been created into the wretchedness of this mortal and unstable life. Burdened by the death of the soul and the mortality of the body, he cannot walk upright, but proceeds in the manner of a serpent upon his breast: unable to raise heavenward the rational faculty he possesses, he presses it down to earth; he desires earthly things alone, or chiefly; and, after the likeness [Col. 0362A] of the serpent, he eats earth when he savors earthly things.

But the serpent, returning by its tail to Moses’ hand, becomes a rod, because at the end of the age, which is understood through the tail, man, returning to the Lord’s hand by the resurrection, will receive his original uprightness. This transformation by the right hand of the Most High began with Christ’s resurrection; it will be completed in the elect at the final resurrection. Then all human beings will rise incorruptible, but only the elect will be so transformed that they rejoice to have received more through grace than they lost through sin.

For then will be fulfilled what was prefigured in Israel’s departure from Egypt and prophesied in these words: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance.” That is: you restored in the human race the uprightness of its former stability. This is expressed in the past tense because it is most certainly hoped for as future. Nor without reason: for we already possess the firstfruits of that universal harvest in Christ’s resurrection, together with those whose bodies rose with him, redeemed from hell by the blood of the true paschal lamb—as once those who were the rod of your inheritance were redeemed from Egypt by the blood of the figurative lamb, as explained above.

But, far more excellently, O God, the rod of your inheritance is those whom you have now redeemed by calling them out of darkness into your marvelous light. The first and chief of them were the apostles, chosen from that congregation which you possessed from the beginning. They are indeed the rod of the entire Church gathered from the nations, which [Col. 0362B] is your inheritance, according to the saying: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2:8). Again: “Behold, sons are the inheritance of the Lord, the fruit of the womb a reward” (Ps. 127 [Vulgate 126]:3).

The apostles, I say, are the straight rod of that inheritance, by which the inheritance itself—the mountain of Zion—is governed; for by their teaching the Church is governed and shines like the sun and moon: like the sun in the perfect, like the moon in the imperfect. Therefore they are rightly and properly called the rod of your inheritance, the new Church from among the nations.

Hence it is wonderful and, at the same time, exceedingly pitiable that that people from which this rod came forth should be so rejected that, until the end, your wrathful fury does not permit its scattered members to be gathered, its outcasts to be brought back, its broken members to be bound up—though you are the shepherd who says: “Behold, I myself will seek my sheep; I will bring back what was cast out, and I will bind up what was broken” (Ezek. 34:11, 16).

Otherwise: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance,” that is, the rod which is your inheritance, given to you by your Father, as you say: “They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word” (John 17:6). Should not this straight and flowering rod, this fruitful inheritance most acceptable to you, move you to mercy toward that nation from which this rod came forth and through which this inheritance was received?

Thus, concerning the new Church, it may be read that it is the inheritance whose rod is the discipline of apostolic government, by which the whole Church is governed. Yet the addition, “Mount Zion [Col. 0362C] in which you dwelt,” or “of Mount Zion in which you dwelt,” directs us especially to another interpretation. By this past-tense verb we are compelled to understand not the new Church, in which God now dwells, but that ancient one in which he formerly dwelt through legal institutions prefiguring and promising Christ, so that it was rightly called Mount Zion.

Let us therefore say: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance,” used intransitively, means: You redeemed your ancient people, likened to Moses’ rod. When it came forth from Egypt and entered the land of promise, you afflicted peoples by chastising them and drove them out, bringing into their place this people of yours, this rod of yours, this inheritance of yours. Hence it is written: “A blessed people, to whom the Lord of hosts gave blessing, saying: You are the work of my hands, my inheritance, Israel” (Isa. 19:25). This rod, your inheritance, is Mount Zion, in which you dwelt. Hence in the Hebrew it is read: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance, Mount Zion in which you dwelt.”

But the addition found in certain manuscripts, “in it,” is superfluous. For what need is there, when it is said “Mount Zion in which you dwelt,” to add “in it”? Unless perhaps we should understand the doubling of the expression—“in which” and “in it”—as a confirmation of this matter, insofar as it concerns the elect of that Hebrew nation, or Mount Zion, chief among whom are the patriarchs and prophets. In that mountain he dwelt through figurative observances, and in it he will dwell through the manifestation of truth.

For although Abraham was circumcised figuratively, nevertheless he rejoiced to see Christ’s day—that is, the light of the truth that was to follow—and he saw it and rejoiced. Therefore he and those like him among that people were Mount Zion, in which you then dwelt through figures and in which you still dwell through the truth that duly succeeds the figures, as day succeeds night. Seeing that day, Father Abraham rejoiced; and now, having seen it, he rejoices more than the other faithful of that people. Their faith intercedes with God for its now-devastated people, just as the ruler of the synagogue interceded with Christ for his dead daughter.

But as that daughter was not raised before the woman suffering from an issue of blood was healed by touching the fringe of his garment, and only after her healing was the dead daughter raised, so that nation, like the synagogue ruler’s daughter, will not be raised until after the fullness of the nations has been healed of the flow of idolatry, when its remnant is converted. This is what Asaph—the congregation of the faithful of that people—longs for and asks in the preceding part of this psalm with groanings that cannot be uttered, saying: “Why have you rejected us unto the end? Has your fury grown angry against the sheep of your pasture? You redeemed the rod of your inheritance, Mount Zion in which you dwelt—in it.”

From this point he seeks judgment and vengeance against the enemies: corrective for some, destructive for others, saying:

**VERSE 3.** “Lift up your hands against their pride unto the end.” You indeed, O God of vengeances, have already “humbled the proud one like one wounded, and in the strength of your arm scattered my enemies” (Ps. 89 [Vulgate 88]:11). But since they still act proudly against you, lift up your hands against their pride; let your right hand be exalted, so that, as by a mighty stroke hurled from on high, their pride may be struck “unto the end”—that is, may have an end.

“Lift up your hands”: exercise your lofty power in breaking the pride of those proud men—namely, the Gentile Roman soldiers by whom your holy city was overthrown. Lift them up, I say, unto an end: partly an end of falling away and partly an end of perfection. Thus some of them may fall away, so as no longer to prevail against your inheritance, your people whom they afflicted; while others may so fall away from their malice and pride that, converted and humbled, they do not fall away to the end of destruction, but advance to the end of perfection and consummation, that is, to Christ. This was fulfilled in part, because the Romans themselves either acknowledged Christ and thus arrived at a good end, or stubbornly denied him and fell away to an evil end. Examples of both are abundantly found in ecclesiastical history.

The very history of the overthrow by which the holy city was destroyed—O God, how many lamentable things it contains! How greatly did the enemy act wickedly in the sanctuary! Who can enumerate how many and how great evils the idolatrous Gentile people maliciously wrought in the sanctuary? Who can estimate in thought or set forth in words how many and how horrible evils the unclean world, set in wickedness, maliciously wrought in the holy place, and therefore worked maliciously? If this had happened in the field where Abel, the first righteous man, was killed by his malicious brother, it might be judged detestable. But now, how greatly did the enemy act wickedly in the holy place—in the holy city, in his holy temple, in the very sanctuary, where they ought to have worshiped the Godhead, which they made into, indeed reduced to, something like a watchman’s hut in an orchard, and destroyed.

And whereas evil deeds are ordinarily followed by repentance and the humbling sting of conscience, these men were not merely un-humbled after their fury had been satisfied, but moreover:

**VERSES 4–5.** “Those who hate you gloried against you in the midst of your festival”—namely, while the paschal feast was being celebrated. On that feast day, by a just judgment, vengeance came upon those who had killed Christ, despite their own resolution: “Not on the feast day, lest perhaps there be an uproar among the people” (Matt. 26:5). It was therefore justly ordered that they should pay on the feast day for a crime committed on the feast day. Yet that this should be done by those who hate you is most pitiable, and all the more detestable because they arrogated victory to themselves. That victory had been accomplished not by their own power but by your permission and your just judgment; nevertheless they gloried in the midst of your festival, amid many sacrileges committed there by those who hate you, where formerly sacrifice had been offered to you by those who loved you.

They gloried not only in their proud hearts; but, in order that this very boasting might be evident, “they set up their signs as signs, and they did not recognize [them] as at the outgoing above.” The Romans had their signs upon the standards which they displayed in wars and triumphs—eagles, dragons, and other images. Such signs they set over gates, at an exit or along a road, when enemies had been conquered; and, in order that they might be more conspicuous, they placed them “above,” that is, in a lofty position.

“They set up their signs”—signs which I, Asaph, in my grief of mind call “signs” a second time—so that you, O God, who have thus rejected us, may, at the sight of these signs, be moved to mercy toward us and to vengeance against them. This is especially so because they committed such great sacrileges “and did not recognize.” None among them said: “I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 51 [Vulgate 50]:3), because they did not recognize—that is, they refused to acknowledge that they had sinned. Or, they did not recognize this as coming from God. Or, they did not recognize “as at the going forth from above”: that is, they did not recognize that their power proceeded from above, from God, since they could have had no authority whatever against the holy city unless it had been given them from above.

Otherwise: “They set up their signs above”—understand, above the building of the city, which was the very temple of the Lord—upon or in which they set up their statues or other signs with such great irreverence, as though at the junctions of roads or in public streets.

**VERSE 6.** “They cut down its doors”—that is, the doors of the temple, on whose adornment formerly the greatest care had been lavished—with axes, without any reverence, as though they were cutting timber in a forest fit for no use except burning. They did all this “together,” that is, united in conspiracy and in the same will. What marvelous force of prophecy! The temple had not yet been built, and behold, David prophesied its overthrow. It follows: “With axe and hatchet they brought it down”—its city and it; and because of grief he does not specify whose city or which thing. Great objects are cut with an axe, smaller ones with a hatchet. By this he signifies that the city was devastated so utterly that even every lesser thing was thrown down.

**VERSE 7.** “They burned with fire” what they could not cut down: “your sanctuary,” not that which is in heaven but that which is on earth. For they could not [destroy] that which was in heaven. Or “to the ground”: that is, they cast down even the roofs to the earth. “They defiled with sacrilege the tabernacle of your name,” which Solomon had first built for your name. They did this because:

**VERSE 8.** The Romans “said in their heart,” all their kindred together; they said, I say: “Let us make all feast days cease from the earth.” That is: Let us root out this people, so that they may not celebrate a feast for God and so that the glory of the Lord’s name may not be on earth. Asaph, speaking in his own person, adds “of God,” for they would not have called God the one whose temple they were overthrowing.

**VERSE 9.** “We have not seen our signs.” Behold Asaph’s understanding. For these foretold evils are a lesson to him. He understands that, because the reality has come, the signs of figures cease. Hence he says, “We have not seen,” as though to say: Everything has been utterly overthrown, because we do not see the signs which we are accustomed to see—our signs; that is, nowhere is there a priest, a victim, or things of this sort, which are ordinarily signs of the thing to come. There is now no prophet to foretell the day or year of our restoration, as is customary in other captivities. “And God will no longer know us,” that is, will no longer restore us.

Or it is said reproachfully: “Have we not seen our signs?” Certainly we saw them, but did not understand. Truly we saw them, because in the fact that there is no prophet, the anointing also has now ceased, since the Holy of Holies has come; and he will no longer “know,” that is, no one henceforth will prophesy that he is to come, because he has already come.

**VERSE 10.** “How long?”—the sick man left behind, who preferred to strike the physician rather than to be healed by him, cries: “How long, O God, will the enemy, the Gentile people, reproach there?” And as though he suddenly recognized how long, he adds: “The adversary provokes your name unto the end.” As though to say: for as long as the Jewish adversary provokes your name, which he will do until the end of the age. Therefore rebuke him in wrath, and so at the end, grasping the tail and returning to the kingdom, he will acknowledge Christ. Or this will be “unto the end”: it will apply not to the grain but to the chaff.

**VERSE 11.** “Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand from the midst of your bosom unto the end?” This directs us to the other sign which, after the sign of the rod, the Lord gave Moses, saying: “Put your hand into your bosom; and he put it in. He said again: Bring it out. And he brought it out, and it was found leprous. He said again: Put it back into your bosom; and he put it back, and it returned to its color” (Exod. 4:6–7).

Moses’ hand is the people Israel, God’s people, which, sent forth, became unclean. Lamenting this, Asaph says: “Why do you turn away your hand”—that is, your right hand; understand, the Jews—“from the midst of your bosom?” How long will you not take your hand back? As though to say: Take it back into your bosom, that, recognizing the Savior, it may return to its color, at least at the end.

Or, when they saw the overthrow, the Jews said in anger—not merely a few, but all their kindred together, that is, all said these things: “Let us make [the feasts] cease,” and so forth—that is, let us reject the law which did not deliver us. Nor have we seen the signs which used to be given to our fathers when a few defeated many. Fools! As though to say: ought what is customarily granted to the devout to have been granted to the guilty? Again, these are words of the despairing: “There is now no prophet to comfort us,” as there once was in adversities. He supplied these despairing utterances of the Jews lest God’s seeming severity in not hearing Asaph, when he prayed for those whom God holds in punishment because of the sin of their impenitence, should appear to be cruelty. “How long?” As though to say: they said this; but how long will you endure the reproaches of the Jews? He did not say this because he wished them to perish, but to be changed for the better.

**SECOND PART. VERSE 12.** “But God.” Behold Asaph’s understanding, after the destruction of the signs, concerning the reality itself: namely, the salvation of the nations accomplished at Christ’s coming while the Jews were blinded. As though to say: We cry out without understanding: “There is now no prophet,” and so forth. But God, Christ, who is our King—King, I say, not in time but before the ages, who was the Word in the beginning—while blind Israel is for a time abandoned, has wrought the salvation of the world, teaching everywhere on earth that eternal, not earthly, things must be sought.

But because in Judaea, which is called the middle of the earth, and likewise in the virgin’s womb, as though in the middle of the earth, God became man, he wished it to be noted not only what he did and where, but also from where and how he began, when he said: “In the midst of the earth.” Behold, blindness has happened to Israel so that the fullness of the nations may enter and so all Israel may be saved. [The phrase “If it did not precede or follows” is textually uncertain.] He goes on to tell how he acted; and, turning to him, says:

**VERSE 13.** “You established the sea in your power.” He alludes to the event in which the water of the Red Sea stood fixed on both sides, so that a dry path lay through it. The sea signifies the nations surrounding Judaea as the sea surrounds land. Having removed the flood of idolatry, you established them in your power—that is, you made them firm for yourself, that they might be solid earth thirsting for your rain. “You crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters”: that is, you destroyed the pride of the demons when, through the waters of baptism, you set free the nations that had been possessed by them. Literally, the leaders of the Egyptians were drowned; they were dragons desiring to devour.

**VERSE 14.** “You broke the heads,” or “the head,” “of the dragon,” namely Leviathan, the prince of demons, because you weakened the beginning of sin, which is pride, and which Eve—that is, the Church—is commanded to avoid or guard against. “And you gave that dragon as food to the peoples of Ethiopia.”

It is read in Exodus (32:20) that Moses, angered, burned the molten calf and ground it into powder, scattered it in water, and gave the children of Israel drink from it. It is also read in Exodus (7:12) that Aaron’s rod, which Moses had taken, turned into a serpent and devoured the rods of the magicians that had become dragons. Mystically, the children of Israel and the rod signify the first apostles who believed from the Jewish people, among whom was Peter, to whom, when reptiles were shown, it was said: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13).

Therefore the children of Israel ate the calf, Aaron’s rod ate the magicians’ rods, and Peter ate the reptiles, when the nations—which were at once, typologically, the calf, the magicians’ rods, and the reptiles, that is, the body of the devil—by believing through the apostles passed into the body of Christ. The Church itself from the nations, which had been a people of Ethiopians, that is, black through sins, was made white through its conversion. The devil himself is its food, but differently from Christ. For Christ is food for the nations, in whom they may be consummated; but the devil is food whom they consume.

Yet this consumption occurs gradually. Thus Moses first burned the calf, so that its form might be destroyed; then he ground it, so that it might gradually be consumed by the people in drink. Likewise, the nations that are converted destroy the devil’s form in fire when, through love of God, they abstain from every appearance of evil; then they grind it when they gradually abandon evils; and finally they drink it when, perfected, they consume it wholly.

The devil is also food for peoples when even those who worship him accuse and rebuke him so greatly that an angry Jew or Gentile calls his servant “Satan,” thus cursing the devil, as though biting him for food. Or, while the devil tempts, he is food for the saints. By this temptation the saints advance as by food: made martyrs through his schemes, they attain what they desire. Or the devil is given as food to Ethiopian peoples unwilling to be converted, so that they may delight in him. It follows:

**VERSE 15.** “You broke open”—that is, opened so that they might flow—“springs and torrents.” Spring and torrent have the same signification. The spring is the word of preaching, which because of its abundance is called a torrent, that is, a river. Or, among the good, the word is called an unfailing spring, in whom there is made “a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:14); but among the wicked, who do not so possess the word as to live well, it is called a torrent, because as a torrent runs with force but dries up in summer, so the wicked who receive the word are not silent while they flow, but fail in the summer of temptation.

Yet he fittingly says concerning both: “You broke open,” because through both God waters the earth. “You dried up,” as though to say: You made the springs of God’s word flow, but you dried up “the rivers of Ethan.” Ethan means “strong.” The sense is: You rendered useless the doctrines of the Gentiles, the astrologers, and the Jews, who are strong in self-confidence.

Or the whole concerns sinners. For they too are springs, whose evils flowed continually; and torrents, whose evils were sudden and violent. He calls both rivers which usually flow from Ethan, that is, from the strong devil. But God broke them away and divided them from their source, the devil, so that they would no longer flow from him. He even dried them up completely, forgiving their sins together with them and overthrowing the devil’s counsels.

Blessed Gregory says concerning this passage:

> [Note: [Col. 0367D] Book XXXIII of the *Moralia*, chap. 10.] “Ethan is interpreted ‘strong.’ And who is this but he of whom Truth says in the Gospel: ‘No one can enter the house of the strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man’? Therefore the Lord broke open springs and torrents when he opened streams of truth in the hearts of his apostles. Of these it is said again through another prophet: ‘You shall draw waters with joy from the springs of the Savior.’ For we go thirsting to their teaching and carry back the little vessels of our hearts filled with truth. But, while his springs flowed forth, he dried up Ethan’s rivers when he withered the teaching of the strong and evil spirit by the striking ray of his truth.”

It follows:

**VERSES 16–17.** “The day is yours,” etc. Day, sun, and summer signify the perfect; night and dawn, or moon and spring, signify the imperfect. Yet they signify them in different ways, according to the differing qualities of things.

The perfect are called “day” because, being spiritual, they judge all things; they are called “sun” because of the wisdom in which they abide and which they speak among the perfect, of whom it is said: “Day utters speech to day” (Ps. 19 [Vulgate 18]:3), namely the Word which was in the beginning with God. In this they persevere, according to the saying: “The righteous man remains as the sun” (Ecclus. 27:12). They are also called “summer” because they are fervent in spirit.

Conversely, the imperfect are called “night” because, being carnal, they cannot receive the wisdom of the Word. Hence the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal” (1 Cor. 3:1). Of these it is said: “Night shows knowledge to night” (Ps. 19 [Vulgate 18]:3), namely, that the Word was made flesh and matters of this historical kind. They are called “dawn,” as those beginning; or “moon,” because they change, according to the saying: “The fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. 27:12). They are also called “spring,” because they are new in faith and temperate in gentleness.

Therefore, lest anyone boast as though he had not received, he says: “The day, sun, and summer are yours; likewise the night, dawn or moon, and spring.” Truly so: for you made them, so that you “formed” them—that is, literally, made them from nothing. In restoration too you formed them, because first you gave grace, and then grace for grace. In giving grace, you made all the boundaries of the earth—that is, you caused each person to have his own gift, one in this manner and another in that. Or he calls the apostles and prophets “boundaries,” because as boundaries distinguish fields, so they distinguish the ordinances of faith. Or all this may be understood historically.

**THIRD PART. VERSE 18.** “Remember this.” Behold the end toward which he has been recounting mighty deeds: that God may spare the Jews. As though to say: You have wrought salvation thus in others; you also, Lord, remember this. He does not add whose; but it may be referred to those whom he had said literally that God formed. Hence some add: “your creature,” so that the Jews are understood here. This prayer has already begun to be fulfilled. For although branches were broken off, the root nevertheless remains, and some of the broken branches have returned.

The one praying recalls their fault and says: “The enemy,” that is, the Jewish people, “the foolish people”—for at that time Asaph was without understanding—“reproached,” that is, uttered reproaches against you, O Lord: “This man is a sinner, a glutton, a friend of tax collectors,” and things of this kind. By such words it provoked or embittered your name against itself, and by deeds stirred it up.

**VERSE 19.** “Do not deliver.” As though to say: Asaph without understanding thus reproached you; but I, Asaph understanding, pray: “Do not deliver to the beasts,” whose dragon-heads you previously broke—that is, do not deliver to the devil and his angels the soul that confesses its sins to you, nor the souls of your poor, who, unlike before, do not set up their own righteousness as riches. Do not forget them, but grant the benefits of grace by which they may tend toward Christ, the end—or at least toward the end of the age.

**VERSE 20.** “Look upon the covenant,” not indeed the old one, which promised earthly things, but yours—the new one, which promises the kingdom of heaven, concerning which you said in promise: “I will complete the New Covenant” (Heb. 8:8; Jer. 31:31). The sense is: The remnant of Israel will be saved, not through its own merits, for it has none. This is clear from the fact that those who are darkened—that is, who dwell blinded in the houses of earth, delighting in earthly things—have been filled with iniquities.

Hearts also are houses, in which the blessed who are pure in heart, and who shall see God, gladly dwell. But those who seek earthly things there will not see him. Why? Because they are filled with earth—that is, with the dust of earthly things, which, when loved, blinds the eyes of the mind and heart. Hence he adds: “who are darkened.” All this comes from dwelling in houses of iniquity—that is, from having wicked hearts. Or: they “are filled with thorns,” that is, thorns of iniquity; they “are darkened upon the earth,” having darkened you and yours by persecutions.

**VERSE 21.** “Let him not be turned away.” Orators commonly do this: they substitute one person for another, putting what is pleasing in place of what is hateful, so that the love due to the devout may temper hatred toward the obstinate. He therefore says: Let the one “confounded”—whom his own pride confounds, since he attributes what he has received so completely to his own powers and merits, a confusion not belonging to the humble—that one, I say, once his pride has been removed, made humble and grateful, not be turned away from you. For the poor and needy, that is, only those humble in spirit, not others, will praise your name: confessing their sins and longing for eternal things.

Behold Asaph, now understanding, shakes off the earthly promises of the Old Testament. But because he has not yet received the heavenly things promised him in the New, he seems to be abandoned and endures the reproaches of those who say: “Where is your God?” Therefore he cries:

**VERSE 22.** “Arise.” As though to say: You are despised by Jews on earth and by false Christians while you sit in heaven; yet I believed what I did not see. Therefore arise and judge your cause, so that I may receive the crown you promised, while they receive confusion—either here, that they may be converted, or in the future, that they may be condemned. Though he ought to have said “my cause,” he says “your cause,” making his own cause the cause of the judge, that he may move him more effectively by disclosing the nature of the affair. For what sort of affair is it when, in insulting Asaph by saying, “Where is your God?”, they also speak evil of God himself?

Hence it follows: “Remember the reproaches”—I do not say mine, but yours—namely, those coming from the foolish person, and this “all day,” that is, continuously. For Christ is still insulted, and vessels of wrath will not be lacking until the end of the age. He says this so that the very continuity may stir the patience of the forbearing judge. He repeats the prayer.

**VERSE 23.** “Do not forget”—to crush the blasphemous voices of your enemies. Or, “Do not forget”—to hear the voices of those praying to you. “The pride of those who hate you,” namely the Romans who gloried while acting wickedly in the sanctuary, or generally those who say: “Where is your God?”, “rises,” or, as other manuscripts read, “may rise always to you.” This indeed occurs because you either punish or correct them. Note that he placed last the pride which God especially abhors, so that it might be especially preserved in memory.

These remarks on this psalm, following the expositions of the Fathers, so confine Asaph’s understanding to the devastation of the man-made temple, accomplished in vengeance for Christ’s blood, that there is scarcely any mention of that final devastation signified through it, which is to occur at the end of the world.

But we, mindful of Chuno, bishop of Regensburg, of blessed memory, who carefully discussed this psalm with us and intelligently investigated Asaph’s understanding on the occasion of a certain revelation—in which a religious person had seen, according to this psalm, the final judgment being carried out against the abuses of our own time—shall not hesitate to set forth once more, in brief, what then pleased us and what, at his request, we then wrote.

The vision was as follows. God, judge of all, was seen seated on high upon the throne of judgment, with the senate of the heavenly court seated with him and the host of heaven standing on either side. Before the tribunal stood the multitude of the whole world awaiting judgment. There was silence among all, full of unutterable fear and trembling, each reckoning with himself his own deeds, while thoughts mutually accused or even defended them. They awaited the sentence of judgment to proceed from the throne; monks also stood there, awaiting judgment with very great trembling.

Then, behold, intercessory voices were heard in the words of this psalm: the choir of holy angels and martyrs especially appeased the judge’s wrath toward the monks, crying loudly: “Why, O God, have you rejected us unto the end? Has your fury grown angry against the sheep of your pasture?” When that cry had ended, the judge appeared appeased toward all who, cleaving to the pastures of Scripture, had been nourished and delighted like pious sheep by their savor.

The saints further prayed for those who, from childhood, from their parents, or voluntarily, had been dedicated to God and had remained in holy religious life, saying: “Remember your congregation, which you possessed from the beginning.” At this saying the judge was appeased toward these also.

They likewise interceded for those who had advanced so far that they could govern others in the discipline of the Lord by the rod of correction: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance.” Concerning those also who had grown in such a life to the summit of a loftier height and strength, it was said: “Mount Zion, in which you dwelt—in it.”

When, by the voices of the saints, the judge had been appeased toward those for whom prayer had been made, at last the voices both of those prayed for and of the entire multitude of saints were heard, demanding judgment upon the ungodly and saying: “Lift up your hands against their pride unto the end. How greatly has the enemy acted wickedly in the sanctuary.” And so, with the psalm chanted aloud to its end, judgment was also carried out upon the ungodly according to its tenor.

But let each take these matters as he wishes. We, however, relying more upon the Scriptures of truth than upon dreams, shall, as we began, briefly pursue Asaph’s understanding of the final judgment. Yet even in that vision itself we cannot dismiss as mere empty dreams what is set forth according to the Scriptures of truth concerning that meaning which concerns the final judgment, prefigured, I judge, by the judgment carried out through the Romans. For Asaph’s understanding of the judgment signified is nobler than that of the judgment signifying, just as the Apostle’s understanding of the two Testaments figured by two women was nobler than his understanding of the women themselves. “It is written,” he says, “that Abraham had two sons, one by the bondwoman and one by the free woman; these things are spoken allegorically. For these are the two Testaments” (Gal. 4:22, 24). And we say that what is written concerning the destruction of the holy city and the overthrow of the temple consecrated to God is spoken allegorically, and directs the understanding of wisely psalmodizing Asaph toward that final destruction in which judgment shall begin at the sanctuary and be completed, not in the conflagration of one city or one temple, but of the whole world: there, not Jews alone under captivity, nor Romans alone who captured and oppressed them, shall be judged, but all nations persecuting the Church of God and violating the temple of God within the Church itself. For the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are. Therefore, if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3:17). Speaking sharply against fornicators who violate God’s temple in themselves, the Apostle says: “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit? But whoever violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (ibid., vv. 16–17). Here one must understand: unless he repents. For the Apostle himself reconciles that notable fornicator whom he had handed over to Satan when the man’s repentance had been received. Although he says, “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. 13:4), nevertheless he who, by true repentance, ceases to be a fornicator or adulterer will escape the judgment prepared for fornicators and adulterers in that final judgment to which Asaph’s understanding directs us, mentioning “the end” five times in this psalm. First he says, “Why, O God, hast thou cast us off unto the end?” Second, “Lift up thy hands against their pride unto the end.” Third, “The adversary provokes thy name unto the end.” Fourth, “Why dost thou turn away thy hand and thy right hand from the midst of thy bosom unto the end?” Fifth, “Forget not unto the end the souls of thy poor.”

With these preliminaries, let Asaph sing; let the undefiled mother Church sing, seeking judgment—indeed, singing of mercy and judgment: mercy, namely, promised before the end to the merciful, to be given at the end and to remain without end; but judgment, without mercy, to come upon those who showed no mercy toward God’s holy Church, which they laid waste more cruelly than Roman commanders or soldiers laid waste Jerusalem. They killed the bodies of the ungodly with swords; these kill the souls of the godly by evil examples. They scattered insensible stones, leaving not one stone upon another which they did not destroy; these scatter living stones, so far as lies within them, leaving not one stone upon another, when through diverse heresies they strive to destroy the truth of the one faith, and through schisms the Church’s unanimity. For, as has been said before us, a heretic is one who does not follow catholic truth; a schismatic is one who does not embrace catholic peace. Therefore the heretic attacks the doctrine of faith; the schismatic, the discipline of charity. The one strives to corrupt the purity of faith, the other the purity of morals, while both, trampling underfoot the traditions of the Fathers, depart from the way of truth and peace and tear apart God’s holy Church—like the two bears that came out of the wood and tore apart the Hebrew boys who mocked Elisha, or like the two rulers, Titus and Vespasian, who came from the forest of Roman imperial power and devastated those who mocked Christ. Would that these men too persecuted Christ’s mockers alone and allowed Christ’s lovers to live! But they persecute the latter more particularly, and strive to draw them away from the purity of Christian discipline. Therefore Asaph sings for those who suffer these persecutions and against those who persecute them, clearly understanding that the former shall at last be delivered and the latter at last condemned.

And because even the good and faithful will be troubled when the dreadful countenance of the Judge appears, when even the powers of heaven shall be shaken, Asaph first appeases the Judge on their behalf—that is, the holy and faithful congregation, somehow secure in and for itself, since it shall judge with the Judge himself, yet deeply anxious for the weak who need pardon: “Why, O God, hast thou cast them off?” They are those who elsewhere say, “O God, thou hast cast us off and destroyed us” (Ps. 59:3). Why hast thou cast them off, when they are faithful persons of good will? Hast thou cast off such persons so that they are cast away from thee unto the end—that is, eternally? Has thy wrath been so angered that thou wouldst destroy the righteous with the ungodly, the lamb with the wolf, and in judgment spare not even those who are the sheep of thy pasture, to whom the Scriptures have tasted sweetly—sheep which, if any had strayed, were carried back upon thy shoulders to thy pasture and there delighted in the same pastures unto death, so that they may worthily be called the sheep of thy pasture? Shall thy wrath rage so that thou destroyest even such sheep together with wolves? Far be this from thee, who, when thou art angry, wilt remember mercy! (Hab. 3:2).

Therefore in this mercy remember thy congregation, which thou hast possessed from the beginning: that is, those who from their earliest years remained steadfast in the resolve and practice of holy religion. Though inferior to the perfect, they are nevertheless subject to them; and thou hast redeemed the latter in such a way that, by the power of thy redemption, thou hast made them the rod of thy inheritance, by which thou rulest thy inheritance—that is, the Church—as with a rod of direction, a rod of iron never damnably bent away from the straightness of justice. Some from the number of such persons have grown in the office of governance through an increase of virtues, so that they became Mount Zion, wherein thou hast dwelt and which thou hast set before others like a watchtower for their protection. Oughtest thou not, then, to spare such subjects of good will, as has been said, and such prelates likened to the straight rod and to Mount Zion? Therefore spare them for the contrition and humility of their hearts, since thou dost not despise a contrite and humbled heart, and since thou givest grace to the humble who do not defend their sins but confess them in repentance.

But because thou resistest the proud: “Lift up thy hands against their pride unto the end”—against those whose pride lasted unto the end, because before the end they refused to be converted or humbled on account of the wickedness implanted within them, a wickedness not only concealed in desire but also manifest in deed. For, O God, how greatly has the enemy acted wickedly in the holy place, and “they who hate thee have gloried in the midst of thy solemnity.” How greatly, how horribly, has the enemy acted wickedly in the holy place! An enemy from within: such as Judas, the most wicked merchant and thief of the Lord’s money-bags; such as Simon Magus or the impure Nicolas. Such an enemy, I say, has committed such great wickedness that I am compelled to cry out with indignation mingled with astonishment: How greatly has such an enemy acted wickedly—how wickedly has he worked and devised evil—in the holy place! Judas’s theft, indeed, would have been less detestable in a private matter, since it might by legal right be restored twofold, or certainly fourfold by the example of Zacchaeus. But to commit fraud in a holy matter, in a consecrated thing given to Christ, the Holy of Holies, is the crime of manifest sacrilege. Likewise, Simoniacal trafficking is the more detestable because it takes place in a holy place, when it turns thy house, O Lord—the house which holiness befits, namely the house of prayer—into a den of thieves; and this is sin against the Holy Spirit. Likewise, the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which God hates, would be less hateful if they were not done in a holy place. But they are done in a holy place when, from what is holy and owed as support for holy uses, such abuse is made that women of shameful conduct, entering God’s holy house in pomp, are supported from that from which the continent and those serving God in chastity ought to live. It is surely great audacity in those who act wickedly to distribute or receive Christ’s body, which is holy, in the sacred office of clerical ministry, while refusing to live holily—indeed, while wishing to glory in an unholy manner of life, in matters over which each ought rather to humble himself than to glory. Yet these men, adding sin to sin, as they have sinned wickedly in the holy place, so they have proudly loved their sin in their hearts and, moreover, have gloried with their mouths—those who hate thee. For they hate the truth that rebukes their perversities; that truth is thou. Foolish and wicked men hate wisdom, which thou art; they hate justice, charity, and every light of virtue, which thou art. And just as one who does evil hates the light, so I truly say that those hate thee who are the light of the world—that is, thee; whoever follows thee does not walk in darkness. And because, for these iniquities, they would not be ashamed or blush in the light, they “gloried in malice, mighty in iniquity.” Where did they glory? “In the midst of thy solemnity”: for example, at the Paschal feast, which is the solemnity of solemnities, or at some other such celebration. There they displayed themselves and their women clothed in garments embroidered with gold and wrapped in varied adornment, not hiding such things in corners but making them a public and open spectacle in the midst of the solemn assembly.

“They set up their own signs as signs.” Finally, although they refused holiness, they nevertheless set up signs of holiness in shaving, in tonsure, and in the clerical form of dress. Yet these were so corrupted that they might more aptly be called their own signs than thy signs, O God, because thereby they sought not thy glory but their own, and seized not thy gains but theirs. “And they did not know”: that is, they refused to acknowledge their sin during their lifetime, just as, when life ends, willingly or unwillingly, they shall know it. In this they resemble their forerunner Judas, an apostle in name but in truth a devil. Though Christ repeatedly rebuked him, he did not acknowledge his sin throughout all the time he lived with Christ; but at last, in his end, he acknowledged it, saying, “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27:4). He acknowledged this sin, committed exceedingly wickedly against the Most High, because he had so exalted himself above Christ, who is highest of all, magnifying his treachery against him so as to sell him as though he were his own slave. The Simoniacs likewise incur the guilt of this sin when they sell the Holy Spirit, who with the Father and the Son is the one supreme God. To recognize this sin only at one’s end is late repentance; and then, far too late, will be thrown away the silver wickedly given or received, which may not be put into the treasury, because God does not accept such repentance for such a sin.

Nor is it surprising, since as long as they could, they served the devil in the house of the Lord and destroyed that house itself, so that they did not spare even its doors, fashioned for the house’s ornament or defense. For as though in a forest of wild timber fit for no use, they irreverently cut down its doors, united in the same undertaking—or into the same thing, that is, into one heap, one pile, or stack of wood beneath which shall be placed the fire that will burn with such wood and shall not be extinguished. For they so annulled and confused the rules according to which each person is to be admitted to the clergy or to a sacred order that by and according to them no one, or scarcely anyone, enters either the episcopate or another sacred ministry to be performed in the house of God. For with axe and hatchet they cast it down, so that it may be called not so much a house as a ruin, having been cast down by axe and hatchet. The axe, the greater instrument, and the hatchet, the lesser instrument, for damaging wood, suggest this: the enemies of the Lord, through greater and lesser expenditures, labouring for their own gain and for the fulfillment of luxury, destroyed the greater and lesser ornaments of the Church. Thus they provoked thee, O God—not in thyself, since thou art untroubled, but in thy saints who possess zeal for justice. While they afflicted those saints by their perversities, “they set thy sanctuary on fire,” because the zeal of thy house, like fire, consumed those who are called, and are, thy sanctuary in the Church. For as a sanctuary surpasses the other buildings in a city, so these surpass the people in the Church because of the merit of their holiness and religion. They set such a sanctuary on fire “upon the earth”: that is, in those elect and holy persons who still live as pilgrims upon the earth. Those, however, who have been lifted from earth to heaven now rest in peace, in utter tranquillity. Thy sanctuary, O God, which by reason of the integrity and perfection of its holiness they could not defile, they set on fire, as has been said. But “the tabernacle of thy name,” which was less firm and could be moved from place to place, they defiled when they drew holy persons of lesser perfection, though nevertheless soldiers in thy service, into consent with their wickedness “upon the earth”: that is, for the sake of gaining some earthly advantage or avoiding some earthly disadvantage. Loving earth more than heaven, they departed from justice; and by their silence, their excessive patience, or their humility, they furnished strength to the enemies of justice, for which they ought to have fought bravely, since they themselves were the tabernacle of thy name.

“They said in their heart,” that is, they thought this—their whole kindred together—for example: Moses chose his brother Aaron as high priest. Thus even now brother chooses brother and kinsman kinsman, so that they may dwell and sing together as one: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity”; and this is, for them, to keep a feast day (Ps. 132:1). But we, who do not wish to dwell together as one, “let us cause all God’s feast days to cease from the earth”: that is, let us remove from the earth the remembrance of feast days. The wicked said this among themselves, reasoning wrongly in their hearts; and in their thoughts they became guilty of the deed, even though they could not bring their thoughts to completion in action. For feast days shall remain unto the end of the age, according to the promise of Truth, which says: “Amen, I say to you, this generation shall not pass away until all these things are accomplished” (Matt. 25:34); and again: “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation” (Matt. 28:20). By these sayings he signifies that there will never be lacking in the world, until the end of the age, persons worthy of God’s abiding with them.

Mocking such persons, the wicked say among other things: “We have not seen our signs; there is now no prophet, and he will no longer know us.” As if they said: Therefore you, who by your own judgment are called, and are, either the sanctuary or the tabernacle of God, are alone wise, as you suppose, and know the sacramental signs, which, as you judge, among you are whole, valid, and full of the efficacy of power and salvation. But we “have not seen our signs,” since by your judgment we are blind; and now there is no prophet among us, as you suppose, since you assign prophecy and the other charisms of the Holy Spirit to yourselves alone; and God will know us no longer, because we are considered such persons as those to whom, at the judgment, the righteous Judge must say: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Luke 13:27). Are not the same sacramental signs found among us as among you? Is not any educated, learned person, and teacher of others, a prophet among us? Will not God know us also, just as he knows you—and indeed more so, because in this world we are richer and more honourable than you, we hold chairs from which we possess authority even to judge you, we exact tithes from your labours, and among us are many badges of rank through which we can be shown to be known by God more than you?

How long, O God, will the enemy—heretic, schismatic, Simoniac, Nicolaitan, and false Christian, opponent of Christian discipline—reproach thee by saying these and similar things? How long does this adversary provoke thy name? I think, unto the end—that is, unto age of ages—for as long as the world endures, Cain will persecute Abel chiefly because Abel’s gifts and sacrifices are accepted by God, while Cain’s are not worthy of the divine regard.
