For although he offers rightly, he nevertheless does not divide rightly: he gives what is his to God, but himself to the devil, turning away from virtues and pursuing vices. Such men do not permit thy people, O Lord, to sacrifice to thee in peace except under a strong hand. Why, then, dost thou turn away thy hand from the midst of thy bosom—that is, thy hand drawn forth from thy secret place and displayed in such a manner that, through terror of it, either the converted may attain the end of consummation or the unconverted may fail into the end of destruction? For thou, O God, art a fire consuming gold and destroying lead.

But God, our king before the ages, has worked salvation in the midst of the earth. I indeed, Asaph, seek vengeance against the enemies of the Church; but God the king, more ready to rule than to avenge, acts patiently, willing that none should perish but that all should turn to repentance. Therefore he worked salvation not in a hidden corner but in the midst of the earth, as was explained above, lest anyone who wished to know should be unaware. For Jerusalem, where by dying and rising again he worked the salvation of humankind, lies in the midst of the earth; and in it the work of salvation was not shut up or concealed. Rather, “the law went forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3), his witnesses beginning from Judaea and ranging to the furthest end of the earth, since “their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the earth” (Rom. 10:18).

While they preached everywhere and performed many signs, thou, O God, “didst strengthen the sea by thy power”: for, having seen the powers of miracles, the world—formerly bitter and unstable—was established in faith in thy name. While they also baptized, thou didst crush the heads of the dragons in the waters of baptism, drowning there the Egyptians, that is, demons and vices. Thou didst also break the heads of the dragon, namely, the prince of demons, like Pharaoh king of the Egyptians, who had raised up seven heads—that is, the capital sins—which, once broken, he cannot raise again. For when the law under which sin held dominion had ceased, grace succeeded; and by grace’s gift sin is easily overcome, namely when the dragon’s heads are broken. Thou gavest him as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians. Let no one hear or note me as though I were teaching something new concerning how this occurs. Let us rather hear the distinguished man Jerome, who says among other things in his sermon on the Paschal Lamb:

> “Let us not suppose that this lamb can be eaten everywhere. We are commanded to eat it in one house, lest we suppose that the lamb may be sacrificed outside the Church. From this it is clear that Jews, heretics, and all assemblies of perverse doctrines, because they do not eat in the Church, eat not the flesh of the Lamb but of the dragon, who was given as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians. But we eat the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”

With Saint Jerome saying this, and we holding sentiments consonant with his, we may affirm that their wine is the gall of dragons: those who, seeking their own interests in the divine sacrifice and office, eat and drink judgment upon themselves. For they offer rightly indeed, but do not divide rightly, when through faith without works, which is dead, or through a wholly false faith, they separate themselves from the communion of the holy Church, setting themselves apart as natural persons who do not have the Spirit. For although the sacraments are inviolable in themselves, they nevertheless work death for those who do not receive good well, as though they were the dragon’s gall; as in the example of Judas the apostate, who, by receiving the morsel—not being good and not receiving it well—gave the devil a place within himself.

“Thou didst break open fountains and torrents,” so that the rush of the river might gladden the city of God through saving doctrine. “Thou didst dry up the rivers of Ethan,” nullifying the false doctrine of heretics. “The day is thine, and the night is thine; thou hast made the dawn and the sun. Thou hast made all the boundaries of the earth; summer and spring, thou hast fashioned them,” as was explained above.

Thou who hast done all these things, remember this. What? Namely, this poor and needy person and the soul confessing thee, as is gathered from what follows; but to stir up the Judge, this is prefaced: “The enemy hath reproached the Lord, and the foolish people hath provoked thy name” (Matt. 27:43), chattering foolish reproaches and mocking words against the Lord’s glory and the honour of his name; for example: If he is the true Son of God, let him free himself from our hands; or, if this man is the Lord’s servant, as he professes himself to be, let him free himself from our hands, from the teeth of beasts. Therefore, O Lord, do not deliver to beasts the soul that confesses thee, and do not forget unto the end the souls of thy poor; rather, deliver them before the end. And that thou mayest do this more swiftly: “Look upon thy testament,” the New Testament written in thy blood. Look upon the title placed above thy cross, in which thou art named Jesus and King of the Jews—that is, ruler, not deranger, of those confessing thee. Therefore, although thy indignation against sinners is just, distinguish the obstinate, who sin obstinately, from the humble poor who offend through weakness or ignorance. Those who remain proud unto the end and stubbornly love and defend their sins—I, Asaph, at justice’s prompting, grant and judge that they ought to be delivered by thee, the righteous Judge, to beasts: the infernal beasts, of whom elsewhere thou sayest, “I will send upon them the teeth of beasts, with the fury of those that draw along the earth and of serpents” (Deut. 24:32). But far be it from thee, King of the Jews—that is, King of those who confess thee—to deliver to these beasts souls that confess thee, both accusing themselves by confession in their sins and praising thee by confession for thy gifts. Even if for a time thou deliverest some such persons to beasts, as thou didst deliver blessed Job, who confessed thee, to Satan to be tormented in his body, nevertheless receive their souls as thou didst receive his, saying to Satan: “Behold, he is in thy hand; but preserve his life” (Job 2:6). Thus, even now, preserving the souls of thy poor, do not forget them unto the end, just as thou didst not forget his soul unto the end, whom thou deliveredst from the hand of the beast before the end. Deliver them, I say, not so that beasts may never afflict them; for the servant is not greater than his lord, who was tortured by such beasts even unto death. But deliver them so that the beasts may not injure those whom they afflict—thy poor, who, even if they sin, do so not from obstinacy but from the misery of frailty and ignorance. For they are filled with many miseries, so that each of them experiences in himself the truth of the saying: “Man born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” (Job 14:1). Because, then, they are filled with miseries, they ought to be pitied. And this too increases their misery: they are darkened by the earthly houses of iniquities—that is, by dwelling in houses of clay which, like crypts, admit little light from above and foster darkness. They are darkened in these earthly houses, which are also called houses of iniquities because bodies are more prone to committing iniquities than to pursuing virtues, especially in houses of iniquity—namely, when houses of prayer are made dens of thieves, which may truly be called houses of iniquity. In such houses of iniquity the proud and insolent are honoured, while every humble person is dishonoured, the poor person is shamed, and the needy is left destitute, as the Church’s resources are dissipated in abuse serving pride.

Therefore, turned away by human beings like the stone which the builders rejected and cast aside, let this humble, shamed person not, I pray, be turned away by thee, the merciful and righteous Judge. It befits thee to console and exalt in thy house, where there are many dwelling places, those rejected by human beings in houses of iniquity. Therefore not kings and righteous persons alone, enriched with great virtues, but also the poor and needy shall praise thy name there, knowing themselves saved more by thy name, by which thou art called Saviour, than by their own merit.

Therefore, when the humble and poor of whom we have spoken have been set apart from the storm of judgment—those who now confess their sins and afterward shall praise thy name—delay judgment no longer. Rather, arise, O God, and judge thy cause throughout the whole Church, as thou didst judge thy cause in the city of Jerusalem, first separating from it thy poor, the disciples of the apostles, who, forewarned by divine revelation, withdrew to the kingdom of Agrippa, where they were safe from the Roman devastation. Arise, I pray, and judge thy cause against Simon, the perverse trafficker; against Judas, the betrayer; against Nicolas, the fornicator. These three wicked men, standard-bearers of the wicked, afflict the whole Church just as, during the siege, three wicked and seditious leaders afflicted Jerusalem: John, Eleazar, and Simon. As Josephus reports, while the Romans attacked the city from outside, they tyrannized it more severely and cruelly within, especially by the Sicarii slaughtering such a multitude of the mixed population that the extreme stench from the rotting corpses oppressed a people wasting away from hunger and simultaneously worn down by terror. For outside the sword of the Romans devastated; inside was the terror of the Sicarii. Then thou didst judge thy cause against them, so that they were ruined by factions, since, rejecting thee, they had chosen the seditious Barabbas. And now judge thy cause against those who, rejecting thee in thy least ones, exalt in the Church men like Barabbas. And that thou mayest not delay vengeance, remember thy reproaches, which come from the foolish person all day long. For whatever reproach they heap upon one of thy least ones, they heap upon thee. “Forget not the voices of thine enemies,” for example, loudly crying, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). Similar is what their followers now say: We have no law or rule but Caesar’s. This they certainly say, trampling underfoot apostolic and synodal rules and preferring perverse customs to truth; and that is great pride. And the pride of those who hate thee, the truth, “ascends continually,” because, just as proud men of old proposed to build a tower in the plain of Shinar whose summit should reach to heaven, so these have a detestable boldness in their pride against thee, and, so far as lies within them, a boundless boldness. Therefore, O righteous Judge, confuse their tongues, with which they intend to devise their lies, so that, even if they have an everlasting desire to be proud, they may not attain its effect.

Glory to the Father, who gave this judgment to the Son. Glory to the Son himself, who judged the city of Jerusalem and who shall yet judge the whole Church; for those who are outside and do not believe have already been judged. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who shall protect in the righteous judgment the poor in spirit of whom it was said, “The poor and needy shall praise thy name.” Amen.

## PSALM LXXIV

[Col. 0381]

[Col. 0381A] “We will confess to thee, O God; we will confess, and we will call upon thy name,” etc. This psalm benefits the attentive reader and the warrior who repeatedly struggles against the law of sin. It establishes the strongest consolation of hope: that he shall at some time reach the triumph which, once attained, will enable him to urge others, still sluggish in resisting sin, likewise to resist. For it belongs to persons whose spirits have been well strengthened and consolidated by good hope to say to the wicked: “Do not act wickedly,” and to transgressors: “Do not exalt the horn; do not lift up your horn on high,” etc. These utterances belong principally to Christ our Head. For no one other than he can say: “When I receive the time, I will judge justices”; “I have established its pillars”; and “I will break all the horns of sinners.” Hence the title fittingly reads:

[Col. 0381B] **VERSE 1.** “Unto the end: Destroy not; a psalm of Asaph, a song.” Its sense is: O Asaph—that is, the unbelieving congregation of the Jews—do not corrupt anything in this psalm by expounding it wrongly or attributing it to anyone other than Christ. Yet when he says in the plural, “We will confess,” “We will call upon,” and “We will recount,” the Head declares that he speaks in common with his members. Therefore the whole Christ speaks here; and first there is set forth the song of resounding confession, by which the humble person is strengthened in hope. Secondly, the proud person is terrified by remembrance of God’s judgments, where it says: “When I receive the time, I will judge justices.” And because, in expounding the Psalms up to this point, we have made many digressions while responding here and there to the various objections of hostile opponents, and have therefore extended this work at length, with God’s help we shall henceforth strive to run through the psalms not so much by expounding as by singing them, pressing toward the end, as this psalm and many others are entitled “unto the end.”

**VERSE 2.** “We will confess to thee, O God; we will confess, and we will call upon thy name. We will recount thy wonders.” The repetition of confession is confirmation, as in the Gospel, “Amen, amen,” and at the end of certain psalms, “so be it, so be it”; and Pharaoh’s dream, Joseph taught, was confirmed by its very repetition (Gen. 41). Therefore it is not enough for us to confess our sins once in contrition of heart; rather, we repeat the same confession in humility of heart, because a contrite heart, O God, does not please thee unless it is also humbled. A contrite heart grieves over sins committed; a humbled heart willingly guards against committing them. Therefore we shall confess to thee, O God, with a contrite heart, and again we shall confess with a humbled heart, knowing that one without the other does not please thee at all.

Alternatively: We shall confess to thee, O God, a merciful forgiver, not an earthly and cruelly avenging judge. We shall confess that we have sinned against thee, as is said elsewhere: “Against thee only have I sinned” (Ps. 50:6), so that, if thou alone forgivest, no one else ought rightly to inflict punishments, since “blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. 31:2). For who can exact debts which thou, O Lord—to whom alone they are owed—forgivest to those who confess? Therefore in this hope of pardon we shall confess to thee, O God, our sins, accusing ourselves. We shall also confess thy gifts, praising and glorifying thee, so that confession may be twofold: both of our ungodliness and of thy godliness, whereby thou dost long endure sinners and, when thou wilt, call those same persons to repentance. For thou didst not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance. Inflamed by its ardour, they continually say: “We will confess to thee, O God, and we will confess, and we will call upon thy name. We will recount thy wonders.” The order is good. First we shall confess our sins so as to cleanse our hearts, which were created as clean vessels but were afterward defiled by sins. When, through confession, they have been cleansed and emptied of the contagion of filth, so that they may be filled with those goods of which it is elsewhere said, “He has filled the hungry with good things” (Luke 1:53), then rightly we shall call upon thy name, so that thou mayest deign to dwell in us: strengthening our weak things, kindling our cold things, illuminating our dark things, and filling our empty things. Then, pouring forth a good word from the abundance of the heart, we shall recount thy wonders. For we shall not preach ourselves or seek our own glory, but recount the glory of thy name; and by those very virtues which thou shalt work in us, we shall bear witness, so that those who see our good works may glorify their giver and author, from whom we received them—though we are beggars, who received these things freely and can preserve them by no power of our own. Accordingly, we shall be judged more severely than if we had not received them, unless we make the due profit from thy money, O God. For he says:

**VERSE 3.** “When I receive the time, I will judge justices.” That is to say: Although I, the Son of God, eternally have, equally with my Father, the power to judge all things, yet because, when the fullness of time came, I was made temporal and mortal, made of a woman, made under the law, less than the Father—indeed, less even than the angels—and humbled myself, being found in appearance as a man, I came not to judge the world but to be judged in the world. Thus I rightly await that time which the Father has placed in his own power—a power that is also mine, because he and I are one. Therefore, not only from the Father but also from myself giving, I shall receive in human form the time of judgment which I have always possessed in divine form. When I receive it, then I shall judge justices. When I, though eternal, received according to my humanity the time for being born, dying, and rising again, I still deferred judgment. But when I receive—that is, when I show that I have always possessed in divinity, and have received in humanity, the time for judging—then I, unjustly judged, shall judge justly.

Or I, the Head, together with my elect members who have been unjustly judged in this world, will judge this world justly, without mercy; for it also judged me and mine without mercy, sometimes under the pretext of a certain justice, as was thought, as in: “We have a law, and according to our law he ought to die” (John 19:7). Again: “If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18:30). By saying such things they fabricated certain justices for themselves; and, before I had received the time to contradict or judge them, I kept the time for silence. [Col. 0383B] But when I receive the time for speaking, then I shall judge their false justices, openly showing that every false justice is truly injustice. But because a justice which is not justice now appears as justice and often deceives human judgments, I, the true Judge, who cannot be deceived, shall judge justices: I shall uncover what is covered; I shall reveal what is hidden—especially in those who cloak themselves in a certain appearance of justice while being slaves of injustice. Though they pretend to serve God, they serve mammon rather, since they consider gain to be godliness and neglect true godliness, the appearance of which nevertheless they put forward while denying its power. I shall then judge the justices of such persons, for I shall not be deceived in judging. For concerning those who are outside and do not [Col. 0383C] believe, it is clear that they have already been judged, since those whose sins are manifest, going beforehand to judgment, are already judged by the sentence which follows:

**VERSE 4.** *The earth has melted, and all who dwell in it.* Just as lovers of heavenly things are called “heavens,” as in: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:2), so lovers of earthly goods are called “earth,” as here: *the earth has melted.* And, as though you asked what this earth is, it is explained by what follows: *and all who dwell in it.* But those whose citizenship is in heaven are pillars chosen from the earth and raised aloft. For although the earth has melted away through diverse desires, I nevertheless set up pillars upon which certain earth-born people might lean [Col. 0383D] and stand. Yet even the pillars wavered for a while, because some even among the disciples doubted the resurrection of bodies. But I, raised from death, confirmed those very pillars by the example of my resurrection, adding also the testimony of many saints, whose bodies rose with me and appeared to many.

Otherwise: the earth, formerly bound fast by winter cold, melted when the south wind blew and became fit for seeds. So, when I judged the false justices of the Jews and visited by the Holy Spirit the earthly hearts of the Gentiles confessing their sins, the earth and all who dwell in it melted—that is, the holy Church was planted and spread throughout the whole world. In order that it might stand firmly and not be moved by any [Col. 0384A] impulse, I confirmed its pillars, namely the apostles, giving them the Spirit of truth in every kind of language, speaking through their mouths.

**VERSE 5.** *I said to the wicked: Do not act wickedly.* While they stood in paradise I had said that they should not become wicked by transgressing obedience to the command; but by yielding to the serpent’s deception they became wicked and crooked, made like that same serpent by which they were deceived. Therefore their children, conceived in iniquities, are themselves wicked. To these wicked persons I, Christ, a man conceived without iniquity, spoke through myself, through my apostles, and through the Holy Spirit given to them. What did I say? *Do not act wickedly;* do not love or increase the iniquity that is in you. Thus [Col. 0384B] I spoke. But they neither heard me while standing, so that they might not fall, nor while lying down, so that they might rise; rather, they sinned still more, because, abandoning my warnings, they knowingly did wrong. Yet I did not abandon them; rather, to those sinning I said: *Do not exalt the horn* by pridefully sinning against men, as the Pharisees did by despising others.

**VERSE 6.** *Do not lift up your horn on high* by pride against God himself, as Adam did when he cast his blame back upon him, saying: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3:12). Thus he lifted high the horn of his pride, so as to judge the utterly just God the author of his iniquity. Many of his children still [Col. 0384C] imitate him, attributing their sins either to the necessity of divine foreknowledge, or to the configurations of stars formed by God, or to the frailty of flesh created by God and joined to a rational spirit. Thus they exalt the horn of pride even to the injury of God Most High, whom they judge unjust because he punishes sins of which they consider him to be the author; or they judge God unjust because, under his ordering, they see good people afflicted and wicked people prospering. Sometimes it does not suffice them to think this unjustly in their hearts unless they also utter it with their mouths, to their own destruction and that of others. By contrast, “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10): namely, that God is just and that there is no iniquity in him. Therefore I said to such people: Do not speak iniquity against [Col. 0384D] God, because “evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33), and the judgment of condemnation will greatly increase through the corruption of very many. Fear also the guilt itself of a heart that thinks and approves such things, for God is Judge: the secrets of the heart are manifest to him, and there is no refuge from his wrath apart from him. This is proved point by point:

**VERSES 7–8.** For neither from east to west, nor from west to east, nor from desert mountains to other cultivated mountains—indeed, nowhere at all—is there a place of escape, because God is Judge: he is not confined to place; he is everywhere and absent nowhere; he contains all places and is himself not contained by place. He works in the east so that the sun rises there; [Col. 0385A] in the west, so that it sets there; and in the desert mountains, so that the sun never approaches them. For, properly speaking, “desert mountains” are those situated beneath the Arctic and Antarctic poles, where the earth is always numb with icy cold and never becomes warm enough through the sun’s benefit to be habitable. These two extreme portions of the whole earth cannot be inhabited because of the excess of cold, just as the middle region, called the torrid zone, cannot be inhabited because of the excess of heat, since the sun’s burning is always over it and never reaches those regions. Therefore the mountains located there are rightly called desert, since they are uncultivable and wholly uninhabitable. It is reported that mountains of this sort contain places of punishment of excessive cold, just as Mount Etna in Sicily is said to contain [Col. 0385B] places of punishment of excessive heat. Certainly both kinds of mountains are desert: both those uninhabitable because of excessive cold and those uninhabitable because of intolerable heat and burning.

Yet if any are assigned to punishment in them, to be tormented by cold or heat, or punished by both—as is read in Job: “Let them pass from snowy waters to excessive heat” (Job 24:19)—after judgment has been rendered they have no escape whatever from these desert mountains. They could now escape before judgment if they obediently heard the voice behind them warning and saying: *Do not act wickedly; do not exalt the horn; do not lift up your horn on high; do not speak iniquity against God.* For neither from east nor west nor from desert mountains—understand, “escape is open”—[Col. 0385C] because God is Judge.

In the spiritual sense, however, the east may signify the good, whom the Sun of righteousness illuminates; the west, the wicked, among whom that same Sun of righteousness sets and, as it were, dies, though it rises upon the good. After judgment there will be no place of escape from either group, because a great chasm will have been fixed between the two, so that no one can cross either from here to there or from there to here, because God is Judge, whose judgment, being just, will be as irreproachable as it is unchangeable.

The desert mountains may also fittingly signify demons, who under the figure of the mountains of Gilboa are cursed, so that neither dew nor rain comes upon them. These uncultivated, cold, and dark mountains are rightly denoted by the name [Col. 0385D] Gilboa, which is interpreted “devouring” or “running down,” because their prince is the devil himself, who devours the poor in secret and has ministers cooperating in that devouring, partly secretly and partly openly. For they too, at his prompting, devour the poor. Hence comes this complaint: “They devour my people as bread for food” (Ps. 13:4). Again: “They eat the sins of my people” (Hos. 4:8). The Savior drives out with a whip these persons who commit robbery in God’s house and make spoil from the people. The Holy Spirit himself curses those who trade in God’s house and sin against the Holy Spirit through the Simoniac heresy, so that neither the dew nor rain of his grace comes upon them or upon their sacrifices, because there the shield of the mighty has been cast away, the shield [Col. 0386A] of Saul, as though he had not been anointed with oil.

The Prophet said too little in saying that this shield had been cast away. We find more in the Apostle: namely, that there the shield of the mighty, the shield of Saul—that is, Christ—was not only cast away but also slain, as though he had not been anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions. These aforementioned devourers not only cast him away, but, by unworthily eating his body, so far as lies in them, kill him; hence they become guilty of his body and blood. But those who do not cast away the shield of the mighty, the shield of Saul—that is, Christ, the protector of the mighty who surround and guard his bed—indeed, who are themselves counted among the company of these mighty ones who hold swords because of terrors by night, are far from Mount Gilboa and strangers to this name which, as [Col. 0386B] has been said, means “devouring” or “running down.” For they do not devour God’s people as bread for food, nor will they come to nothing as water running down and not returning to its source comes to nothing, because in running down it wholly fails away. All who are puffed up through the vice of pride and separated from God, the source of virtues, become like this. Against this the humble person says: “But for me it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord” (Ps. 72:28).

Such a person, like a valley well watered by rain, is distinguished from the desert mountains before judgment, because Christ himself, the lily of the valleys, will be found in that valley; and such valleys will abound in grain and bear fruit in patience: either the hundredfold fruit of virginity, or the sixtyfold fruit of chastity, or the thirtyfold fruit of the marriage union and the honorable, undefiled bed [Col. 0386C]. Those who, at the end of their lives, are found outside these fruits and without true repentance are counted among the desert mountains. After this life’s end and the judgment fixed upon them, no escape is open to them from those mountains, because God most carefully distinguishes between fruitful valleys and desert mountains.

**VERSE 9.** *This one he humbles, and this one he exalts.* He humbles the one who exalts himself, and exalts the one who humbles himself. “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

**VERSE 10.** *For a cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of pure wine mixed.* The cup is used for a measure, because God’s judgment is administered by measure, so that with the measure in which each person has measured, it is measured back to him. And as much as each person has drunk from the Lord’s cup, sharing in his passion, so much will he also share in his resurrection, with the further abundance of eternity added; for as the generous rewarder of good things, he will give into their bosom not merely a good and just measure but an overflowing one. Likewise, whoever drinks from the cup of demons will also drink with them the drink of condemnation. For both that cup and this are in the Lord’s hand: one is full of pure wine, to be drunk new in the kingdom of God, sincere and unmixed; the other has its lees not emptied by repentance and confession. All sinners of the earth—that is, lovers of earthly desire—will drink from these lees: whether those [Col. 0387A] who buy five yoke of oxen and plough the land, or those who buy an estate and pursue earthly riches, or those who take a wife and place earthly pleasures before heavenly delights.

Otherwise: the cup is all Scripture divinely inspired and administered according to the measure of Christ’s gift. This cup contains unmixed wine, mixed wine, and lees. What is its unmixed wine? Moral precepts, for example: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole strength, and your neighbor as yourself” (Mark 12:28). Heavenly promises also are unmixed wine, in which eternal goods alone are promised, as in: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3); and: “Blessed are the pure in heart, [Col. 0387B] for they shall see God” (ibid., 8).

Figurative precepts, however—such as where the Law commands the Sabbath to be kept and the Gospel commands the face to be washed or the head to be anointed—may be regarded as mixed wine, because a spiritual meaning lies hidden in figurative words and things. Figurative promises likewise, for example those promising a land flowing with milk and honey, are also counted as mixed wine, because they contain together a promise of heavenly and earthly things. In the Gospel too, where the Lord says: “You will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29), the promise is mixed. For in the number one hundred is signified the perfection granted to the saints in this age, even “with persecutions,” as Mark says (Mark 10:30), while the promise pledges provisions for the journey together with an eternal [Col. 0387C] reward.

But where there is such a threat of evil as has no good mixed into it, as in the Law—“A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it will burn to the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. 32:2)—and in the Gospel—“Then the King will say to those at his left: Depart, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41)—there are exceedingly troubled lees, which all and only the sinners of the earth will drink: those in whom no desire for heavenly things is found mixed with their earthly desires.

Finally, where mixed desires, good and evil, are found, there too one must drink from the mixed cup, as the Judge himself determines: either the purgatorial torment of a tolerable evil, or the rewarding refreshment of a tolerable good. A tolerable evil or good means that which has not stirred up many human complaints against itself. But “all who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus,” not content with mediocre goods, stretch themselves toward better goods, so that they must suffer persecution from those unlike them, who, so far as lies in their power, either hinder or delay their good endeavors (2 Tim. 3:12). And because this cup, full of unmixed wine, mixed wine, and lees, is in the Lord’s hand, he will, as he knows best, incline from this to that—that is, tempering one with the other—so that his mercy is neither judgment without mercy nor mercy without judgment, because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10).

Otherwise: “He will incline from this,” the proud Jew, “to this,” namely to this humble Gentile. For there is to some extent a spiritual sense in this. Nevertheless its lees have not been emptied, because the lees of carnal sacraments remained among the Jews. Moreover, the lees of eternal damnation have been reserved for them—except for the remnant, who will at last drink the mixed cup by receiving the Old Testament together with the New, spiritually understood. But now neither Jews nor Manicheans drink the mixed cup, because the former do not receive the New Testament, nor the latter the Old. We Christians, however, drink the mixed cup because we receive both Testaments.

In our prayers too we drink unmixed wine when we ask only for heavenly things, as in: “May your kingdom come” (Luke 11:3); mixed wine when we ask for heavenly and earthly things together, as in: “Give us this day our daily bread” (ibid., 3). [Col. 0388B] But those drink the lees who ask for and desire only earthly advantages. All sinners of the earth will drink these lees through the appetite of carnal and earthly desire. When it abounds in them, they become drunk and rejoice in the worst things; when such things are lacking, they become sad, complain, and sometimes blaspheme.

**VERSE 10.** *But I will sing to the God of Jacob.* I, Christ, in myself and in my faithful ones, without corrupting the title of this song, which began from confession so that it may also end in confession, will sing to the God of Jacob. I will proclaim for ever—that is, always—and sing or chant psalms to the God of Jacob: the God of the younger people, which, after supplanting the elder, received the blessing promised to Abraham’s seed, concerning which the title says: *Do not destroy.* For such a blessing is indeed unmixed wine; but it is corrupted if the leaven of human praise is mixed with it, or some profit of earthly gain. Even if this gain should abound, “do not set your heart upon it” (Ps. 61:11), says the Spirit to the churches, so that every lover of God’s kingdom may desire to be blessed with Jacob by heavenly blessing, to whom it was said: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27:27), and not by an earthly blessing, such as Esau received when his father said: “Your blessing shall be in the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above” (Gen. 27:39–40).

This blessing, sounding only of earthly advantage, has no fragrance but stench. The elder was content with it, though he had raised against his younger brother [Col. 0388D] horns of pride and condemnation. Hence he wept with a great cry when he heard from his father: “I have made him your lord, and have subjected all his brothers to his service” (Gen. 27:37). What finally came to pass? The horns of that envious man were broken, and the horns of simple Jacob were exalted. For it is recorded that, when David and his descendants reigned—David who was anointed with the prophet’s horn—Edom was humbled and made tributary, not only to David but also to the other kings descended from Jacob. In this manner I am the true David, in whose house the horn of salvation has been raised.

**VERSE 11.** *I will break all the horns of sinners, and the horns of the righteous shall be exalted.* The horns of those who do not obey me when I say, *Do not exalt the horn; do not lift your horn on high*—[Col. 0389A] the horns, I say, of those persons, that is, their powers—I shall break utterly, according to the title of this psalm, *unto the end.* For I myself shall be the end of evil horns, so that they may be annihilated, and of good horns, so that they may be brought to perfection. Therefore the horns of the righteous shall be exalted, because [Col. 0390A] his horns are none other than my gifts.

Glory to the Father, to whom we say: “We will confess to you, O God.” Glory to the Son, who says: “When I receive the time, I will judge justices,” and, “I will break all the horns of sinners.” Glory to the Holy Spirit, whose gifts are the horns of the righteous to be exalted for ever. Amen.

## PART EIGHT

[Col. 0389]

## THE PROLOGUE OF GERHOH BEGINS

[Col. 0389B] What are you doing, my soul? Why are you sad, and why do you trouble me? You are sad over an unfinished work because, in expounding the Psalms, you have failed as though midway through the road—partly from bodily weakness, partly from that weariness in which you sleep excessively because the bridegroom delays. Had he come to you swiftly—indeed, had he been here with you—you would not have died, nor lain buried, as it were, for three days, doing nothing vital; or, worse still, already stinking like a corpse four days dead. This is why you are sad, my soul, and why you trouble me.

But hope in God. For the Lord, seeing the sisters weeping and praying for you, has already restored to you in part the health of your body. At their prayers he is also able to lighten the weariness that weighs upon you, making his statutes songs for you in the place of your pilgrimage [Col. 0389C], as those sisters beloved in God themselves ask. They still thirst and hunger for expositions of the Psalms, according to that saying of Wisdom: “Those who eat me will still hunger, and those who drink me will still thirst” (Ecclus. 24:29).

I had wished to satisfy their thirst and hunger by reading the volumes on the Psalms composed by the holy Fathers, or even through the glosses of the masters extracted from those very volumes. But they press me, opportunely and inopportunely, that, if not by a full exposition—as I had hitherto attempted—then at least by a certain brief survey I should run through the Psalms that remain, so that, even if not by expounding, at least as though by singing, I may reach that end where it is said: “Let every spirit praise the Lord” (Ps. 150:6).

Therefore be present, O Spirit of all spirits, most strong and at the same time most sweet, ordering all things strongly and sweetly, so that, with you directing my feet into the way of peace, I may run without stumbling through this long undertaking [Col. 0390C] to the desired prize; and, having received it, my spirit may praise the Lord among the spirits and souls of the righteous.

## PSALM 75

[Col. 0389]

[Col. 0389D] *God is known in Judah; in Israel his name is great.* This psalm now treats, in its fifth recapitulation, of the end of all things: the end which we both fear in hoping and hope for in fearing. “God,” he says, “is known in Judah; in Israel his name is great; and his place has been made in peace.” And afterward: “You caused judgment to be heard from heaven; the earth trembled and was still, when God arose in judgment, to save all the meek of the earth,” and so forth. He spoke prophetically in the past tense instead of the future: *you caused to be heard* for *you will cause to be heard.*

Certainly, in saying, “You caused judgment to be heard from heaven; the earth trembled and was still,” there is cause for immense fear. It is as though he said: The earth—that is, the ungodly lovers of earth—will tremble and be still, because they will cease doing evil. For the great Judge will restrain them by saying: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” [Col. 0390D] (Matt. 25:41). But in saying, “to save all the meek of the earth,” he greatly animates the hope of the meek. It is as though he said: Rising in judgment, he will save the meek, who do not defend their sins but redeem them by alms, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

The title of this psalm is as follows:

**(VERSE 1.) UNTO THE END, AMONG PRAISES, A PSALM OF ASAPH, A SONG TO THE ASSYRIANS.**

“Assyrian” is interpreted “one who directs,” and here signifies the Jews who pridefully direct themselves on account of Abrahamic descent or the works of the Law, thinking it sufficient that they are carnal Judah and carnal Israel. Against their pride the psalm says that God is known in that which is truly Judah, and his name is great in that which is truly Israel. Judah signifies confession of sins; Israel, interpreted “one seeing God” or “one striving uprightly with God,” signifies the man who contends against the assaults of vices—the kind of man already often discussed. Furthermore, what follows—“and his place has been made in peace”—designates the state of which the Apostle says: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Rom. 7:24). For truly there God broke the powers: the bow, shield, sword, and war.

The first part shows that the names of glory—Judah, Israel, Zion, and Salem—have been transferred away from those Jews, who are more rightly called Assyrians than Jews either because of the pride by which they direct themselves, establishing [Col. 0391B] their own righteousness and not submitting to God’s righteousness, or because of the extreme cruelty by which they persecute the Church, just as the Assyrians once persecuted the Synagogue. The second part shows what Christ does with those from whom, and to whom, he transferred these names, at: “You shine wondrously from the eternal mountains.” The third makes known its intention by exhorting the devout to fulfil vows, at: “For the thought of man shall confess to you,” and so forth.

Therefore let the undefiled mother Church, rightly to be called Judah because of her confession both of her own iniquity and of divine mercy, sing psalms. Let her sing, I say, and say:

**VERSE 2.** *God is known in Judah.* In the literal sense, Judah was the portion of the promised land, divided among the twelve tribes, which fell by lot to the tribe of Judah. From that tribe came kings, princes, and leaders among God’s people, down to Herod the foreigner. In his reign, when the sceptre had already been removed from Judah and the ruler from his loins, Christ was born. Those who confessed him—as Peter did when he said to him, “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16)—are rightly counted as Jews, that is, confessors, because of their confession of the truth. But those who denied him, saying, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15), are called not Jews but Assyrians, according to Daniel: “And his people, who are to deny him, shall not be his people” (Dan. 9:26). Therefore a people denying him is not his people, nor is it in Judah—that is, in confession—and hence in it there is no knowledge [Col. 0391D] of God. But in true Judah, which is the holy Church confessing faith in Christ, God is known by that knowledge which flesh and blood did not reveal, but the heavenly Father.

Therefore God is known in the apostles and martyrs; God is known in confessors; God is known in true Christians. But in those who deny God by words, deeds, or both, God is not known *in* them, even if he is known *to* them. For to those who, when they knew God, glorified him or gave thanks, God was known in both senses; but he was not known in them in the manner in which he is known in true Jews. Of such the Apostle says: “If all prophesy, and an unbeliever or uninstructed person enters, he is convicted by all, and so he will fall on his face, declaring that God is truly in you” (1 Cor. 14:24–25). Thus in such Jews, or in such a Judah, God is known: manifest both to them and in them, because in them and through them he speaks the most faithful words of confession, the Lord himself working with them and confirming the word by signs that followed—[Col. 0392A] sometimes signs of miracles (Mark 16:20), but always signs of pious works—so that their doctrine may truly be confession, since with the heart they believe unto righteousness and with the mouth confess unto salvation (Rom. 10:10).

For this is to confess: to acknowledge with the mouth what one holds in the heart. If you teach things which you do not hold through faith working by love, you speak, but do not confess. Consequently your speech itself is not confession, nor is it Judah in which God is known, even though God may in some fashion be known to you by the knowledge by which even demons know him and tremble (Jas. 2:19). Therefore God is known in true confession, attested by the power of faith and the signs of works.

And because through the true confession of faith one comes to the clear vision of the very truth believed—God rewarding the merit of faith with the prize of understanding—the person called a Jew because of his confession of faith is rightly called Israel because of the clear vision of good understanding. Israel is interpreted “a man seeing God,” and in this Israel his name is great. Why is this so? Clearly because such a person, in order truly to obtain the name Israel and to be truly an Israelite in whom there is no guile, wrestles with God, continually saying to him: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Gen. 32:26). That this wrestling is performed through prayers and tears in temptations is indicated by the prophet Hosea, speaking thus of Jacob: [Col. 0392C] “He prevailed over the angel; he wept and entreated him” (Hos. 12:4).

So you too, if you wrestle by prayers and tears against the law of sin which is in your members and opposes the law of your mind, and persevere in the struggle until, through assisting grace, you obtain victory, will see God your Savior and be able to say: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved” (Gen. 32:30). For the good vision of the Savior and Deliverer is known in the evident experience itself of deliverance and salvation. From this vision Israel is rightly named “the man seeing God,” or “a prince with God.” In this Israel God’s name is great, because through such an Israel God himself, who glorifies him, appears exceedingly great, exceedingly renowned, and illustrious—just as a physician appears great in one who is visibly healed by him of leprosy or another grave infirmity. Thus, having recovered health—or rather, having received the health he did not possess—the person can wrestle mightily with the strong physician, not letting him go until the final completion of his health, continually repeating in a manner: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” Such is what this wrestler says elsewhere: “May God have mercy on us and bless us” (Ps. 66:1). Again: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us” (ibid., 7–8).

Certainly that person is very blessed who, forestalled by blessings of sweetness, through observance of virginal integrity feels no struggle, or only a slight one, of the flesh opposing the mind. Yet “where iniquity abounded,” [Col. 0393A] grace often “abounded still more” (Rom. 5:20), so that, through a most strenuous struggle and the winning of Israel’s name, the greatness of God’s name shines more clearly in the fruits of repentance—by which he delivers and saves even such persons—than in the innocence of certain persons who do not need repentance. But if these too repent, lamenting the sins of thoughts as the others lament sins of deeds, then both innocent and penitent, both righteous and tax collectors, will have peace with God. Nor will either despise or judge the other, just as the holy Virgin Mary is at peace with Mary the sinner in the kingdom of peace: both give thanks to God, the former because, through the Holy Spirit’s overshadowing, she has been preserved from evils; the latter because, through that same Spirit’s cleansing, she has been delivered from evils.

[Col. 0393B] It should certainly be known that “peace” is named in many ways. One peace is God’s gift; another peace is God’s very essence. Of the former it is said to God: “Give us peace.” Again: “Give peace, Lord, in our days.” But of the latter it is said: “The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4:7). From this surpassing peace, as from an inexhaustible fountain, every good peace should be believed to flow.

I say “good peace,” because there is also an evil peace, which the Lord did not come to bring, but against which he sent a sword. Good peace flows from him, for unless the peace of the universe were administered by him, the whole creation, deprived of peace and contrary to itself within itself, would be destroyed and reduced to nothing. This universal peace flowing from God has a manifold distinction, which has been treated before us as follows:

The peace of the body is the ordered balance of the parts or elements composing the body.  
The peace of the irrational soul is the ordered repose of its appetites.  
The peace of the rational soul is the ordered harmony of knowledge and action.  
The peace of body and soul is the ordered life and health of the living creature.  
The peace of mortal man and God is ordered obedience, in faith, under the eternal law.  
The peace of human beings is ordered concord in good will.  
The peace of a household is the ordered concord of those dwelling in it, in commanding and obeying.  
The peace of a city is the ordered concord of citizens, in commanding and obeying.  
The peace of the heavenly city is the most perfectly ordered and harmonious fellowship of enjoying God and one another in God.  
The peace of all things is the tranquillity of order.

Order, moreover, is the arrangement which assigns to each its own place among things alike and unlike; [Col. 0393D] and it comes only from God. Hence the Apostle: “Those things which are, are ordered by God. Therefore those who resist authority acquire condemnation for themselves” (Rom. 13:2). I mean lawful authority, not tyranny. For just as those resisting lawful authority acquire condemnation for themselves, so the blessed martyrs who resisted tyranny were crowned, because they would not have peace with the enemies of peace. Hence John and Paul said to Terentianus: “If Julian is your lord, have peace with him; for us there is no other Lord but the Lord Jesus Christ.” They were entirely right to reject peace with one who opposed Christ.

For he is our peace, who made both one; and, after destroying by his death the wall of enmity, when raised [Col. 0394A] from death he invoked peace upon his own, saying: “Peace be with you” (John 20:19). Before his death he had also said to them: “I leave peace to you; I give you my peace” (John 14:27). Again: “I have spoken these things to you so that you may have peace in me” (John 16:33). You are to have peace not merely in any fashion, but *in me*: that is, truthful in me who am truth, wise in me who am wisdom, walking in me who am the way, and tending toward me as your homeland, you may use my peace as provision for the journey and enjoy me as supreme peace.

Peace for the journey is that you love one another—not in any manner whatever, but “as I have loved you”; that is, love one another in me for the end for which you are loved by me. Without this love you cannot have the true peace which, at my birth, was announced by the angel saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). The author of peace loves this peace.

**VERSE 3.** *And his place has been made in this peace,* because God, who is peace and unity, is not in the division of minds. Therefore his place has been made in peace, because he who is not confined to place is his own place and exists in himself. Hence those who reject peace repel from themselves God, who is peace. For his place has been made in peace; or, as it is read in Hebrew: “And his tabernacle is in Jerusalem,” which is the same thing. For Salem means “peace,” and Jerusalem “vision of peace.” God dwells there, for he is peace and loves peace. Whoever disputes against God does not possess this peace; and one surely disputes against God if what pleases God displeases him, or conversely if what displeases God pleases him. In such a person God has no place.

[Col. 0394C] Some manuscripts read: “His shelter is in Salem.” By this expression it is signified that the power of the Most High overshadows the peaceful mind, so that he may rest in it who says: “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2.) In the peace of such a soul his place is made, he who visits souls of this kind. Yet he does not dwell in those whom he visits even in this way, unless they join to the peace which they maintain that zeal by which, through faith in invisible goods, they press on toward the vision of those same goods: namely, by forgetting what lies behind and continually stretching themselves toward what lies before, so that they desire through hope to obtain what they now hold through faith, in such a way that vision succeeds faith as fruit, abiding forever, succeeds the falling flower. For now faith and hope remain [Col. 0394D] as flowers destined to fall; but charity, which will be perfected in the vision of the things believed and hoped for, never fails, because this is the fruit of which it is said: “And may your fruit remain” (John 15:16). This is the fire of which it is said: “The Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31:9). Finally, in Zion—that is, in that contemplation in which truth is now seen through a mirror and in an enigma—there is felt, however small it may be, a fire of love by which that same truth is loved. But in Jerusalem—that is, in that clear vision in which God will be seen face to face—there will be a furnace of most perfect love, admitting no coldness or sluggishness. But now, while we dwell in Zion and contemplate God through an enigma, all is well with us if the aforesaid fire, lest it be wholly extinguished, is increased day by day by suitable fuel, according to the commandment of the Law which says: “This fire shall always be upon the altar; the priest shall feed it by laying wood upon it every morning, day by day” (Lev. 6:12).

Would that the things we write might be suitable kindling for feeding this fire upon the altar of the heart, like wood carried into the house of the Lord! For we do not dare compare ourselves to those princes who offered gold and precious stones for adorning either the altar, the breastpiece, or the ephod. And would that we might at least offer goats’ hair for weaving the tabernacle’s haircloth covering, or, as we have said, wood for feeding the holy fire in the hearts of readers! [Col. 0395B] If they are innocent, they need, like the altar of incense, burning coals to diffuse the fragrance of the sweetest odour, so that through the teachings and examples of holy charity they may be kindled and shine. Let them be kindled before God and shine before human beings. But if they are penitents, they need a haircloth covering, so that their sins may be covered by fruits worthy of repentance. This is what we intend when, in our writings, we weave together exhortations and examples of holiness or repentance for readers to behold and contemplate. For in such contemplation dwells he of whom we sing here: “And his dwelling is in Zion,” that is, in those who, forgetting what lies behind, stretch themselves toward what lies before.

[Col. 0395C] Observe the order and meaning. Judah—that is, confession—is placed first; Israel follows, because one must first confess sins, and remission follows pure confession. In that remission God is tasted and seen, according to the saying: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9). Peace follows, because once the wall of enmities has been cast down through remission—that wall built from original and actual sins, which separated humanity from God—there is now peace for the person of good will. Last comes Zion, that is, the watchtower, by which contemplation of the Divinity is here initiated in some manner through a mirror; when it is consummated in eternity, nothing further will be desired.

VERSE 4. “There he broke”: that is, God undoubtedly will break the powers opposed to his own power, [Col. 0395D] because there will not be a time of war there, but a time of peace; not a time of business, but a time of rest. Accordingly, there he will break—and in those who have arrived there, he has already broken—evil powers: namely, the bow, that is, the deceits of those lying in wait, who wound travellers unexpectedly. Of these it is said elsewhere: “They bent the bow, a bitter thing, that they might shoot the blameless in secret” (Ps. 63:4–5). Again: “The teeth of the children of men are weapons and arrows” (Ps. 56:5). There also he has broken, or will break, the shield, that is, every instrument of defence; for it will not be needed there, where they will no longer be trained for battle. He will also break the sword, with which fighting is done at close quarters, as with the bow from afar, because there will be no one there to attack anyone either from afar or nearby. Some manuscripts read: “There he broke the powers of bows,” which has the same meaning.

Diapsalm. VERSE 5. “You illuminate wondrously from the eternal mountains.” On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says in Job:

> [Note: [Col. 0395D] Moral. Book 27, ch. 10.] One who cannot contemplate the rising sun looks upon the mountains illumined by its rays, and thereby perceives that the sun has risen. Therefore God enlightens us from the eternal mountains, because through the life of the preceding Fathers, which we admire, he illumines us with the ray of his brightness.

Behold, we are kindled in zeal for devotion and charity toward the Lord; but in this devotion and charity we are better formed by contemplating these mountains. What is more devout than Peter? What dearer than John? The former, through devotion, did not fear to tread the fluid backs of the sea (Matt. 4); the latter, through love, both rested upon the breast of our Creator himself and, having come to the refreshment of a bodily meal, received spiritual nourishment from the bosom of the Redeemer (John 21). But since we have said that the mountains signify the life of the preceding Fathers, it is necessary that we bring forward, still further, examples even of the earlier Fathers.

Behold, when we desire through obedience to submit ourselves to heavenly commands, we are aided by considering the footsteps of the ancient Fathers. For what was more obedient than Abraham, who at one word of the Lord left kindred and country, and, in order to gain an eternal inheritance, did not shrink from striking down the very one whom he had received as heir when already an old man and almost at the point of death? (Gen. 22.) When [Col. 0396C] we endeavour to acquire the virtue of patience, we behold examples of those who went before. For what was more patient than Isaac, who carries the wood, asks about the burnt offering, and shortly afterward is bound and says nothing, is laid upon the altar and does not resist? What, then, can be called more patient than this man, who is led as though for consolation and asks questions, is bound to be struck down and is silent, asks questions while he is to offer a burnt offering, and is silent while he is to be offered as a burnt offering?

When we strive to gird ourselves for the endurance of labours, we are instructed by the examples of those before us. For what was more laborious than Jacob, who for a long time rendered servile labour to Laban, his kinsman by family relationship, and fulfilled the role of a servant in order to enjoy the rewards of an heir? When we strive to ascend the height of self-control and chastity, we are raised by the examples of our predecessors. [Col. 0396D] For what was more chaste than Joseph, who, even when captive, could not be pressed under the yoke of lust at the desire of his wanton mistress? (Gen. 39.) He was indeed a slave to human beings, but against the ruling wickedness he remained free even in slavery.

When we desire to be filled with meekness, we are helped by the examples of those who went before. For what was more meek than Moses, who endured the rebellion of the people entrusted to him and yet prayed to the angry Lord for his persecutors, exposing himself to the divine wrath on their behalf, because in his holy breast charity is kindled even by persecution? When we strive to form steadfastness of mind against the adversities of the world, we are strengthened by considering those who went before. What was more steadfast than Joshua, [Col. 0397A] who, sent to investigate the character of the peoples, was frightened neither by the greatness of their stature nor by the multitude of their number? (Josh. 10.) Thus he also overthrew in battle the very peoples whom he had not feared while scouting them.

When we endeavour to attain the summit of kindness, we are instructed by the examples of those who went before. For what was more kindly than Samuel, who, removed from the office of ruling the people, humbly sought a successor for himself, anointed as king the man he had found, soon endured his anointed successor as a persecutor, feared lest he should be killed by him, and yet prayed that the Lord might not be angry with him? (1 Sam. 12.) For when he was sent, he said: “Saul will hear, and he will kill me” (1 Sam. 16). And Truth himself says to him: “How long will you mourn for Saul, when I have rejected him?” What, therefore, could be called more kindly than this man, who did not wish the man by whom he feared he would be killed to be divinely struck down?

When we strive toward the height of piety and humility, we are raised by the examples of those before us. What could be called more merciful or more humble than David, who received insults from a reprobate king in return for victory, who bravely rescued the Israelite people from the enemy’s hand, yet fled like a weak man lest he should die? He recognized both himself as chosen by divine judgment and his persecutor as reprobate (2 Sam. 16), and yet subjected himself to that persecutor again and again in the humility of making amends. He took away his persecutor’s spear, cut off the hem of his cloak, and immediately hastened to the summit of the mountain; and at one and the same time he showed that he had the power to kill him and begged that he might not be killed. (1 Sam. 20.) Hence it is said of preachers through the prophet: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” [Col. 0397C]

Therefore, in all that we spiritually desire, we are formed by the examples of those who went before. For, spread over us in the manner of clouds, the lives of the Fathers cover us, so that we may be watered for the fruit of fruitful growth. And just as, looking at heaven, we first see clouds, so we behold the admirable deeds of the good and afterward penetrate by experience those things which are heavenly.

Some manuscripts read: “You illuminate wondrously,” which is connected to what precedes in this way: “God is known in Judah,” namely because he illuminates. For the rising sun is recognized because it first illumines high mountains, and then its brightness descends from the mountains into the valleys. So you, God, first illumine the mountains; then, from the illuminated mountains, you illumine [Col. 0397D] the valleys, because through consideration of the foremost saints, who are the eternal mountains, the poor, meek, and humble in heart, who are the valleys, are illumined by the light and warmth of eternity—by knowledge and love poured out together. The mountains themselves do not have, nor will they give, light from themselves; but you, the true light, “enlightening every person coming into this world” (John 1:9), send forth your light and truth through them and from them. This your “light came into the world,” but “human beings loved darkness rather than light, because their works were evil” (John 3:19).

But because this connection of this reading with what precedes may be rejected on account of the intervening Diapsalm, let us say instead that in the Diapsalm itself there is an apostrophe addressed to God in this manner: I, Asaph—that is, the assembly of the faithful—have thus far spoken about God and shown how sweet he is in Judah, Israel, and Zion. But now, wishing to show how terrible he is to those enemies, namely the Assyrians mentioned in the title, I turn myself to God and say: “You illuminate wondrously from the eternal mountains.” These mountains are opposed to those mountains treated in the preceding psalm. Hence those mountains are called deserted, but these eternal. All these mountains are illumined and thereby magnified, so that they are rightly called eternal mountains. For “those whom God foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, those whom he predestined he also called; those whom he called he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom. 8:29–30). Therefore, magnified now in God’s predestination, which is fixed immovably and eternally, they are rightly called great and eternal mountains. You, God, illumine them by justifying them, so that there is no one who can hide himself from the radiance of this light, because this light also shines in darkness, but the darkness did not comprehend it. It is as though one said: You, Sun of righteousness, pour the rays of your light not only into clear eyes but also into bleary eyes; but bleary eyes do not comprehend it—indeed, they are disturbed by it all the more. This is what follows:

VERSE 6. “All the foolish of heart were troubled.” When you, Sun of righteousness, illumined the world from the eternal mountains, or from certain inextinguishable lamps, [Col. 0398C] such as John, of whom it was said, “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35)—illumined, namely, in order that he might bear witness to the light—all the meek and humble of heart rejoiced. But all the foolish of heart were troubled by the brightness of the light, like owls or bats unable to bear the light. Therefore, fleeing to the darkness friendly to them, they delighted in dens and shameless acts and slept their own sleep. I deliberately call it *their own* sleep: the sleep of those who keep watch for themselves, sleep for themselves, and live for themselves, while in all that they do they direct their heart to their own gain, their own glory, and their own pleasure, seeking what is their own and not what is Jesus Christ’s.

Alternatively: the wicked sleep their own sleep, and the good theirs, [Col. 0398D] because the good too sleep to sins and to the world, to which all who live to God are also dead. But the wicked sleep to God and are dead, those who live to themselves and to this world. They are not improperly called “men of riches,” because they do not possess riches as masters, but are possessed by them as slaves. In contrast, it is said elsewhere: “A man’s own riches are the redemption of his soul” (Prov. 13:8). Thus Zacchaeus, by giving his own riches to the poor, distributed them as their master. The slave-like men of riches do not act thus. Lulled by the love of riches, they are not so much rich through possessing riches as through dreaming that they possess them: falsely rich and truly poor, because after the death of the body, when awakened from their sleep, they will find nothing in their hands.

On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says in Job:

> [Note: [Col. 0399D] Moral. Book 18, ch. 18.] In order that the rich may find something in their hands after their own death, they are told before death in whose hands they should place their riches: “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity,” he says, “so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9). Therefore, when the rich man has slept, he finds nothing in his hands. For he would have taken his possessions with him when he died if, while alive, he had taken them to himself at the cry of one who asked. For all earthly things which we lose by keeping, we preserve by giving; our inheritance, when retained, is lost, but when distributed it remains. We cannot endure with our possessions as their masters, because either we leave them by dying, or they leave us while we live, as it were, by perishing. Therefore we must act so that we compel things destined utterly to perish to pass into a reward that does not perish.

[Col. 0399B] For the rich man sleeps and finds nothing—nothing, plainly, of the things he held. Yet the guilt incurred through those things is taken with him from here, although the things for which the guilt was committed are left here. Let him then go now, swell with the goods he has received, lift himself above others, and boast that he has what his neighbour does not have. A time will come when he awakens, and then he will know how empty was that which he held in sleep. It often happens that a poor man, while sleeping, sees himself rich in a dream; he lifts up his heart over those same possessions, rejoices that he has what he did not possess, and even seeks to despise those by whom he had grieved to be despised. But suddenly awakening, he grieves that he has awakened, since in the meantime, even while asleep, he held the image of riches. For at once he groans under the weight of poverty when he is pressed by the constraints of his want, and all the more grievously because, for a very brief time, he had been rich only emptily.

So, indeed, are the rich of this world, who swell with the possessions received and do not know how to do good from their abundance: like sleepers, they are rich. But when they awake, they find their poverty, because they carry nothing with them to that judgment which remains. And the more highly they are now exalted for a brief time, the more grievously they will groan against themselves forever. For, as Wisdom testifies, at the time of their condemnation they are reported to say: “What did pride profit us, and what did the boasting of riches bring us? All these things passed away like a shadow and like a messenger running by.” Thus, now that the things they held have been lost, they recognize that they were worthless and fleeting, though while they were present they seemed both great and lasting to their foolish lovers. Too late the rich man opened his eyes when he saw Lazarus at rest—the Lazarus whom he scorned to see lying before his gate. There he understood what he had refused to do here, and in his condemnation he was compelled to recognize what he had lost when he did not acknowledge his needy neighbour. For when the body falls asleep in death, then the soul wakes to true knowledge. Thus the rich man sleeps and opens his eyes: when he dies with the flesh, his soul is compelled to see what it had scorned to see. Then it perceives that what it held was nothing; then it finds itself empty, though it had rejoiced above other human beings in being full of possessions.

[Col. 0400A] Alternatively: “Men of riches,” namely the avaricious, “slept their sleep”; that is, they will sleep among those of whom it is said elsewhere: “Like the wounded, sleeping and cast away in graves, whom you remember no more, and they are thrust away from your hand” (Ps. 87:6). Yet not only men of riches will sleep in this way, but also the proud, whose exaltation is customarily indicated by their being called riders of horses. The kings of the Assyrians and Egyptians were accustomed to boast excessively in their multitude of such riders. Hence Rabshakeh, messenger of the king of Assyria, exultantly taunted King Hezekiah: “And now surrender yourself to my lord, and I will give you two thousand horses, if from then on you can provide riders for them” (Isa. 36:8). Thus Pharaoh, pursuing God’s people with chariots and horsemen, was drowned in the deep on account of his pride. This is a fitting punishment for pride, just as exaltation is the reward of humility, because “everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

There is, moreover, a mode of speech called *sarcasm*, that is, hostile mockery, in which more is indicated by saying less, as here:

VERSE 7. “At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, those who mounted horses slumbered.” This trope is as though one said of someone sent into sulphurous fire that he had been sent to a bath. Thus in the Apocalypse the Lord threatens Jezebel, saying: “I will cast her onto a bed” (Rev. 2:22), meaning: I will cast you into hell, where not so much she herself as her wickedness, by which she had troubled the earth, may rest. So in this very psalm it is said: “The earth trembled and was still.” Similarly, the rebuke and slumber here marked under hostile mockery imply a meaning greater than the words themselves can convey.

For although God’s rebuke is sometimes made by words alone, as where he rebuked King Abimelech, saying: “Behold, you shall die because of the wife whom you took; restore the wife to her husband, and he shall pray for you, because he is a prophet” (Gen. 20:3, 7); and although he more than once rebuked kings, saying: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets” (Ps. 104:15), he rebuked the aforementioned riders of horses—the Assyrians and Egyptians—more by deeds than by words.

Thus he rebuked, or reproved, the Assyrian riders of horses in such a manner that, after the aforementioned boast which Rabshakeh spewed forth against the meek and humbled Jews, in one night the angel of the Lord struck down in the Assyrian camp one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the horse-riders in whose multitude the king had gloried. Thus the king of Assyria returned in disgrace to his own land and, while praying in the temple of his god, was killed by his own sons (4 Kings 19:35). Likewise Pharaoh, with his army: though rebuked by words and plagues, he did not yield to God who rebuked him, but instead hardened and weighed down his heart, like one sleeping and unwilling, though awake, to listen meekly to the rebuker. At last he was so rebuked by you, O God of Jacob—God of the lesser, younger, and humbler people—that, willing or unwilling, he would thus slumber; rather, stupefied by eternal death, he perished, cast down into that depth of the abyss where are those wounded sleepers “whom you remember no more, and who are thrust away from your hand.”

Thus it is hostile mockery when it is said: “At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, those who mounted horses slumbered,” because they were rebuked not merely in some slight way but most powerfully, as an example to those who, being similarly proud, must repeatedly be rebuked—now in particular cases, but universally on the day of judgment. Nor did they merely slumber; plunged into the deep sleep of eternal death, they fell into the abyss, and the depths covered them. They went down into the depths of the sea as an example of the destruction of all who oppose and exalt themselves against God. Their chief is he who opposes and “exalts himself above everything that is called God or is worshipped,” whom “the Lord Jesus will slay with the spirit of his mouth,” rebuking him and destroying him by the brightness of his coming (2 Thess. 2:4, 8).

He is the king of the Assyrians to whom this song is entitled: those who make themselves straight and refuse to be subject to God’s righteousness, not only in Judaism but also in Christianity. For Assyrians, as has already been said repeatedly, are called “those who direct themselves”; under this name the proud are aptly denoted—filled with knowledge that puffs up, not with charity that builds up. Hence they endure no yoke of discipline or lawful teaching, by which their will—straight and self-directed, as they suppose—might be bent or broken. This is why they are called Assyrians, that is, self-directing persons.

But when God rises in judgment to save all the meek—that is, the humble and gentle, who bear the Lord’s yoke in holy obedience—then these Assyrians, together with their king Antichrist, will be rebuked by the harvesting angels as those earlier Assyrians were rebuked by the smiting angel. They will no longer be riders of horses, because they will have no subjects over whom to rule. Only he will rule who alone is the legitimate rider of horses, to whom it is said elsewhere: “You shall ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3:8); he is also seen in the Apocalypse “upon a white horse” (Rev. 6:2), and in Zechariah upon a “red horse” (Zech. 1:8), because all those subject to him will be found either white through innocence or ruddy through martyrdom, just as he himself, the Beloved, is white and ruddy.

That there are two kinds of martyrdom by which the cup of the Lord’s passion is drunk is demonstrated by the two sons of Zebedee. Although both were told: “You shall indeed drink my cup” (Matt. 20:23), it is clear that one of them, James, died by martyrdom, while the other, John, completed a long old age in peace after a long exercise of many tribulations. This was for him like martyrdom, and is to be held as an example by those to whom that cup is offered not so much through tyrannical cruelty as through diabolical wickedness, to be detested and overcome either in themselves or in others. In this conflict, the reasonable and persevering vigilance of charity—which patiently bears all things, endures all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and never fails—is reckoned as martyrdom.

Thus all the Lord’s horses will be either white or ruddy, or both, like John the Baptist and the other elect, blessed by a double lot: white through innocence, ruddy through martyrdom, as their rider and ruler is white and ruddy. But the horses of the Assyrians, as likewise seen in the Apocalypse, are red, black, or pale, and are to be condemned together with their riders. They are red not with their own blood but with another’s, because their feet are swift to shed blood; their chief representatives were those who, at the bidding either of the devil or of some evil ruler, killed martyrs. They are black through falsehood, as contrary to truth as black is opposed to white; their chief representatives were heretics, who at the prompting either of the father of lies himself or of some heresiarch endeavoured to attack the truth of the Catholic faith. They are pale, those who waste away through envy, not looking with upright or kindly eyes upon the prosperity or peace of those who serve God.
