Their chief representatives are those who either corrupt monasteries from within by evil conversations, being enemies of a man’s own household, or attack them from without through open persecutions. To all Assyrians of this kind, and to their horses—

[Col. 0402C] VERSE 8. “You are terrible, you who will ride upon your horses.” For they ride upon other people’s horses: that is, they lord it over subjects who in no right belong to them. But you ride upon your own horses, whom you created, whom, when they had been lost, you redeemed, and whom you also received from your Father in order that they might be yours. To him you say: “They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word” (John 17:6). They are yours even in this respect: they strive to do your will, not their own; and in doing it, they seek your glory, not theirs. Because you say to each one of them, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17), while feeding your sheep, not their own, they consider your profit, not their own; so that each of them may truly say what one such horse said: “For me,” he says, “to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21). Again: “I seek not what is useful to me, but what is useful to the many” (1 Cor. 10:33).

Upon such horses, moderated by the bit of your fear and the bridle of your love, you are terrible as you make war against the horses of the Assyrians and their riders. For the holy angels too are your horses, whom you showed to Elisha and his servant in the form of fiery horses, such as had carried Elijah up into heaven. Likewise, holy human beings are your horses, as we have already shown above. Riding upon them, you, the king of unconquerable rule and ever-glorious conqueror of hostile dominion, restrain opposing powers and powerfully overthrow hostile wickedness. Thus truly you are terrible. To foreshadow your terror, your angel struck, as has been said, the Assyrian camp, so that from this it may be understood that no one can resist you, the Angel of great counsel; because you are “terrible in counsels above the children of men” (Ps. 65:5), you bring to effect whatever you have immovably decreed, with no one resisting or able to resist.

For who will resist you? That is, which of the Assyrians against whom this psalm is sung will resist you by his own powers? Certainly none. For although you may seem to spare and to conceal your wrath as long as any Assyrian does not resist you by glorying in wickedness or defending his sins against your rebukes, nevertheless, once he has cast aside or neglected fear of your name, becomes proud in sins, resists you like a rider on a horse, and repels your reproofs by proudly defending his sin, from that point your wrath becomes intolerable to him.

This happened to proud Saul when, rebuked by Samuel, he repelled the word of God, presumed to defend his sin, and to insult his own rebuker by tearing his cloak. From that point your wrath, O God, raging against him, could not be appeased even by the lamentations of the prophet himself, to whom you answered: “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have cast him away from reigning over Israel?” (1 Sam. 16:1.) But where resistance to you is not of this kind, your wrath, however great, can be appeased, as it was appeased in David. When Nathan the prophet rebuked him, David did not resist, but humbly yielded, saying: “I have sinned.” By these three syllables of one word the wrath of the whole Trinity was appeased, because that confession of sin came from a humble and contrite heart.

Saul, however, after likewise saying “I have sinned,” only after some elaborate words wickedly devised to make excuses for sins, added: “But now honour me before the elders of the people” (1 Sam. 15:30). This statement makes sufficiently clear that in such a confession he sought vain honour, human honour, rather than divine grace. Accordingly, he is shown to have been more Assyrian than Jew; and so the wrath threatened against him was not turned away or softened. Therefore those like him in sin will be like him in punishment, not only in that brief punishment by which he perished on Mount Gilboa, but also in that eternal punishment to which he passed from the brief one. For these too will indeed die shortly in the body, [Col. 0403D] but from that point will be punished eternally, and from then on your wrath will endure.

Therefore, lest that day should arrive unexpectedly—the day of wrath, the day of calamity and misery, in which your wrath will then be, and will thereafter endure—it has been foretold in many ways, because you, speaking “in many portions and in many ways” through the prophets,

VERSE 9. “Made judgment heard from heaven.” From heaven—that is, from any heavenly oracle—you made judgment heard whenever you resolved to judge some city or kingdom, giving an opportunity to repent and escape your wrath, so that those who did not fear your judgment when they heard it might be subject to your judgment without excuse.

Thus, when you were about to judge the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, you made judgment heard through the angels speaking with Abraham and lodging with Lot, his relative. Having heard it, Lot was delivered with his household; but his sons-in-law, to whom he seemed to be speaking in jest, and who therefore would not leave with him the city destined to perish, perished without excuse. Thus too, when you were about to judge the kingdom of the Egyptians, you made judgment heard from heaven, speaking through Moses your servant as through a heavenly oracle. You also made judgment heard from heaven to the Ninevites through the prophet Jonah, giving them time and opportunity for repentance. Therefore they will rise in judgment and condemn the evil, perverse, and adulterous generation which refused to believe and repent upon hearing from heaven—that is, from Christ—the judgment concerning its condemnation and conversion. Remaining unrepentant, it suffered from the Romans a most cruel judgment of humiliation, and it is to be tormented with demons forever, so that it not only experienced temporal wrath then, but will also experience everlasting wrath from then on.

[Col. 0404B] You made this judgment, appointed against that generation because its sins required it, heard from heaven through many prophets; but finally through your only-begotten Son you made the same judgment heard in a clear proclamation. For he did not speak obscurely or in an enigma, as the earlier prophets did, so that he could not easily be understood; rather, “seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: Days shall come upon you, and they shall surround you, hem you in on every side, and cast you to the ground, because you did not know the time of your visitation” (Luke 19:41, 44).

Therefore a harsher judgment is due to those who did not believe this announcement than to the Ninevites who believed Jonah, since one greater than Jonah is here: the foreteller both of that particular judgment by which Jerusalem was condemned and of the universal judgment in which this same great Prophet will appear terrible. For he who was judged unjustly, meek as a lamb and not opening his mouth, “will then speak to them in his wrath and trouble them in his fury” (Ps. 2:5): those worse than the Ninevites, whether Jews or Greeks, who did not believe him and did not repent. For there is no distinction, because those who sinned under the Law will be judged by the Law, and those who sinned without the Law will perish without the Law.

Likewise, in this time of grace preceding the wrath of judgment, whoever does not draw near to the one who grants pardon will be brought before the avenger; those who receive a rule for right conduct will be judged by that rule, and those who do not receive it will perish without a rule. “Will perish,” however, sounds graver than “will be judged,” because among those who perish without law or rule, none at all will be saved. But among those who will be judged by the Law or rule, when the Judge himself judges and distinguishes who has carefully kept the Law or rule received and who has not, some will be saved and some will perish.

Hence the saying: “Two will be in one bed: one will be taken and the other left. Two will be at the mill: one will be taken and the other left. Two will be in the field: one will be taken and the other left” (Luke 17:34–35). For all these had received lawful rules: either to rest with Daniel in the bed of contemplation, or to grind with holy Job at the mill of married life, or, with Noah, to plant vineyards in the field of prelacy, sow and harvest crops, and carry out the other duties entrusted to their rank in a manner worthy of that rank. Thus it was said to one of them: “Behold, I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, that you may uproot and destroy, ruin and scatter, build and plant” (Jer. 1:10).

Therefore those who have the Law will be judged by the Law: one, that is, the keeper of the Law, will be taken, and the other, the transgressor of the Law, will be left. But those who hold no law at all, living dissolutely without the yoke of all discipline and without the profession of any ecclesiastical order, will all perish together. Among them there will be no such discriminating judgment in which one is taken and another left; rather, as has been said, all will perish without law and without distinction. Of that universal judgment it is said here: “The earth trembled and was still.”

**VERSE 10. When God rises up in judgment.** By these words, in the prophetic manner of the past tense, a future event is announced, as there: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21:18). For what is most certainly to happen may already be narrated as though past. And it is most certainly to happen that, just as the earth trembled when God rose from the tomb, and his enemies became as dead men while his friends, the apostles, were as those comforted—for the most wicked Jews were grieved even to death when they heard and learned of his resurrection, whom they had killed, whereas the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord—so also, and far more greatly, when God rises up in judgment to save all the meek of the earth, or, as elsewhere it is read, “to rebuke with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth,” since no one will be rebuked on the day of judgment on behalf of the meek of heaven, who are angels—when, I say, he thus rises up, the earth will tremble and be still.

Truly, on that dreadful day, when heaven and earth are to be shaken, the earth itself will tremble, and all lovers of earthly things will tremble. In that very trembling they will be disturbed by horrible fear; and they will marvel at the suddenness of the unlooked-for salvation of those who will then rejoice when they see the Lord, whose glory they shall behold as that of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth. Lest the wicked person should see this glory—he who is here denoted by the name of the trembling earth—he shall be taken away in his trembling and cast into hell, where he shall fall silent and be at rest, according to the saying: “And the wicked shall be silent in darkness” (1 Kings 2:9).

For then their tongues, tortured by the fires of hell, will cease to utter useless and criminal words; then, with hands and feet bound in outer darkness, they will be still. As we mentioned above, this is said tropologically by the figure called sarcasm, with hostile mockery: for they will not rest from their labors as those are said to rest of whom we read: “From henceforth, says the Spirit, that they may rest from their labors; for their works follow them” (Rev. 14:13). Rather, they will rest in such a way that, exposed beyond all repose to the eternal torments of body and soul, and with hands bound, they will no longer be able by evil deeds to unsettle or disturb the rest of the saints. This rest will be granted to them when God rises up in judgment to save all the meek of the earth, according to the saying: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4). Again: “But the meek shall inherit the earth and delight in an abundance of peace” (Ps. 36:11). To them on that day it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

For God will then rise up in judgment for a twofold reason: namely, to save all the meek of the earth by calling them into the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world, and to send the wicked into eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. Thus his kingdom will be wholly prepared for the good angels and human beings alone, gathered there, while all evil angels and human beings are cast out and thrown into the fire prepared for the devil.

**[Diapsalma. VERSE 11.] For the thought of man shall confess to you.** The third part, in which the devout are exhorted to pay their vows, may be connected with what precedes in this way: We attentive hearers have heard that in your judgment, O God, the meek of the earth shall be saved. And we believe that this happens neither without merit nor through burdensome merit, because the thought of a person meditating upon good is reckoned by you as merit, although that thought itself does not arise except from your gift. Therefore that very thought shall confess to you: either by confessing sins for your good pleasure, or by recalling your gifts with thanksgiving for your glory.

The intervening *Diapsalma*, however, seems rather to press us to take the connective conjunction as referring to what follows rather than what precedes, in this way: “For the thought of man shall confess to you, and the remnant of thought shall keep festival to you,” O God, who are known in Judah. Therefore I, Asaph—that is, the faithful congregation—invite hearers to your worship, which is not as burdensome as it was under the Law, whose “yoke” was unbearable, “which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear,” as the apostle Peter says (Acts 15:10). But now, since under the gentle yoke good thought alone, where there is no opportunity for action, shall confess to you, O God, I invite, as many as I can, to receive this gentle yoke, saying:

**VERSE 12. Make vows and render them to the Lord your God, all you who round about him bring gifts.** Heavy was the yoke of the Law, under which mortal sins were punished by death, while lesser sins were expiated either by retaliation—for example, repaying eye for eye and tooth for tooth—or by offering goats, rams, bulls, and similar things. But now “the thought of man shall confess to you.” If, O human being, you think with sorrow that you have sinned, and desire henceforth to beware, wondering what you should offer God for your sin, know that this very thought is received as a great sacrifice. It is, before him to whom every will speaks and from whom no secret is hidden, a clear confession.

Such a thought is like the offering of firstborn animals that are clean, or of firstfruits from crops and other produce. We lawfully offer these firstfruits when, at the beginning of some good purpose or vow, we disapprove and accuse our past evils, according to the saying: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17). But after this beginning, after these firstfruits, God also requires the remnant: namely, that you should add a good end to the good beginning of a virtuous life. For in your thought the conception of a holy vow is like a holocaust of a firstborn creature, or like two loaves of firstfruits, while you renounce evil works and prepare your intention for good ones.

As a figure of this, God required under the Law offerings of firstborn creatures and firstfruits. But in the sacrifice of firstborn creatures he required nothing female, but only what was male: “For every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Luke 2:23). And in the offering of firstfruits he required from every household of Israel two loaves made from two tenths of fine flour, so that you may know that, in the very beginning of your vows, nothing feminine, nothing unstable, soft, or lax is acceptable to God; nothing is to be offered to the divine sight except what is pure, perfect, sincere, and like the cleanest fine flour.

Nor is it without significance that two loaves of firstfruits had to be offered from two tenths of fine flour. For in every devout and religious vow the perfection of twofold love is required. This twofold perfection was represented by the two tenths of fine flour, since perfection is customarily signified by the number ten, which is also called the second unity. Thus it is indicated that the sacrifice of our tithes is acceptable only in unity, because God is not in the division of minds.

These loaves of firstfruits do indeed please God and make peace with God at the beginning of religious vows; but the remnant of the same loaves is accepted much more when good vows are consummated with a good end. For just as the remnants collected from five or seven loaves were greater than the loaves themselves, and therefore offered a greater subject for praise in the remnants than in the loaves themselves, so it is said here: “For the thought of man,” which is the first conception of a vow, “shall confess to you; and the remnant of thought,” by which the consummation of a virtuous life is understood, “shall keep festival to you.”

Just as the vigil of any feast, because of the fast joined to it, does not possess full joy, so the beginnings of religious life, because of the penitence for past evils joined to them, do not possess full gladness. But when perfect love has cast out fear, then the remnant of thought shall keep festival to you, O God. For when a person senses that he has been freed from evils and confirmed in goods, then, remembering the evils in which he was and at the same time tasting the goods he has received, he celebrates a feast day in thanksgiving to his deliverer. He now has his fruit unto sanctification, and awaits from God’s promise eternal life as his end.

Such were those to whom the apostle Paul said: “For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness; but now, having been freed from sin and made slaves to God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Rom. 6:20, 22). Observe that the outstanding Teacher, speaking to those already freed from sin, reminds them of that sin itself, so that in the day of present blessings they may not forget past evils, but may possess remnants of their thoughts as material for thanksgiving toward their deliverer—to whom such remnants shall keep festival.

Thus the Apostle himself, remembering what he had been, says in thanksgiving: “I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an injurious man; but I obtained mercy” (1 Tim. 1:13). David likewise, intent upon the feast day, says: “I know my iniquity, and my sin is always against me,” or “before me” (Ps. 50:5). Again: “I will declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin” (Ps. 37:19). Such continual remembrance of past sins is a feast day before God. So we must act.

Otherwise, we despise other sinners as unworthy; and so, mounting horses with the Assyrians, we deserve to be crushed under God’s rebuke so that we fall asleep. We must beware lest this happen. Therefore, that your thought may confess to the Lord, make vows—not only of what you already owe, but also of what you did not owe before the vow. And that the remnant of thought may keep festival, render what you have vowed, not forgetting what you were before the vow.

When I say, “Make vows,” understand both commandment and counsel: commandment in those things which you necessarily owe even if you do not vow them, such as faith, hope, charity, and what is joined to them—not to kill, not to commit adultery, not to steal, and so on—without which there is no salvation. Even if one does not vow these things, yet if one wishes to be saved, one must perform them. But because necessity unaccompanied by devout will is less praiseworthy, vow the very thing that is necessary, so that it may also be voluntary, and that you may be able to say to God: “I will sacrifice to you freely” (Ps. 53:8). Then you will no longer be called servants, but friends and children, like those to whom it was said: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15).

But, says Truth in the Gospel, “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to do” (Luke 17:10). Therefore, if you wish not to be reckoned among unprofitable servants but to be called most dearly beloved children, do not be content with keeping the commandments. In addition, accept counsel by vowing and keeping things concerning which you have no commandment. For example, the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7:25). Again, to leave everything and follow Christ naked is not commanded to you, but counseled, as the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

Those who thus receive, together with the commandment necessary for salvation, the counsel of perfection also—vowing and rendering beyond the necessary debt the voluntary holocaust of perfection, so that they may be like shorn sheep, “all bearing twin offspring,” as is written in the Song of Songs (4:2)—have sufficiently and obediently heard the voice exhorting them and saying: “Make vows and render them to the Lord your God.”

One must certainly know that what one was free to do or not to do before a vow, one will not be free to omit after a vow. In matters of this kind, liberty is permitted in making the resolve, but necessity is imposed in fulfilling what has been promised. For not merely breaking a vow, but even willing to break it, is altogether damnable according to the Apostle’s judgment. Concerning widows devoted to God, he judges not that they incur condemnation by marrying, but by wishing to marry, because “they have made void their first faith” (1 Tim. 5:12). But if a vow broken in will alone is condemned, how much more certain is the condemnation of transgression when it is not merely intended in will but actually committed in deed?

Therefore make vows and render them: if you vow, render, lest by making void the pledged faith of your vow you incur condemnation. Certainly, before a vow you are not required to cut yourselves off from lawful and permitted things, such as marriage and the possession of private property, provided that hitherto you have lived in such a way as not criminally to exceed in unlawful and forbidden matters. But anyone conscious of having sinned criminally in unlawful matters must, in order to produce fruits worthy of repentance, not only make a vow but fulfill it: he must restrain himself from lawful things in proportion to the manner and extent of the iniquity committed. The measure and extent of satisfaction ought to correspond to it, insofar as one’s capacity permits.

Hence the Apostle says to such persons: “For as you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. 6:19). By saying, “As then, so now,” he requires equality—not an equality to be measured by length of time, but by the earnestness of one’s efforts. Earnestness, when fulfilled in a short time, accomplishes many periods of time; thus the repentance of one hour opened paradise to the confessing thief, though it had been closed to him by his long practice of theft.

Whether, therefore, you make vows from necessity or, more praiseworthily, from voluntary freedom, it is altogether necessary that you fulfill what you have vowed—unless perhaps you have made foolish vows, which, by correcting the folly itself, you ought rather to break than to keep. To guard against such vows, it is first said: “For the thought of man shall confess to you, and the remnant of thought shall keep festival to you”; then it is added: “Make vows and render them,” so that with prudent thought you may deliberate what ought to be vowed and what ought not.

“Make vows,” he says, “and render them.” To whom? “To the Lord your God,” who is known in Judah, not to the gods of the nations, who are demons or mute idols.

It has now been shown both what you ought to vow and to whom you ought to vow. The order now requires that I indicate who you yourselves are who ought to make vows: namely, “all who round about him bring,” or “bring,” gifts. Who are those round about him? Surely the humble, who look toward the central point of truth just as a circle drawn evenly round a center has no angle. The proud riders of horses, who are called Assyrians in this psalm, possess the angles of some particularism or hypocrisy, and strive to draw truth—which is central and common to all who seek it—aside by saying: “Behold, here,” or “behold, there” (Luke 17:21).

But humble lovers of truth stand around it in such a way that they hold it in common and do not draw it into the angles of any particularism. Hence “Jesus stood in the midst” of such persons “and said to them: Peace be to you” (Luke 24:36). He stood, I say, in the midst of the disciples, not in a corner, so that all who were around him might worship him in common and receive without distinction the peace invoked upon them by him.

Not so heretics; not so hypocrites; not so the various sects which glory excessively in the singularity of their observances or teachings, praying, as it were, in corners and at the head of every street. They in some sense shun human eyes, yet desire to be seen. Such persons, I say, are not around Jesus as his disciples were. In the midst of them he stood bodily for an hour; and spiritually he stood and stands, not for an hour but now and eternally. They are round about him here as devout ministers and there as tireless praisers, as is declared by the beautiful vision in the Apocalypse, where the Lamb is seen in the midst of the four living creatures (Rev. 5:6).

Moreover, all the angels stood round about him, so that you may know that among neither blessed human beings nor angels is the rounded wholeness of community disturbed or disfigured by angular particularism. Some saints have also understood the little child whom Jesus set in the midst of the disciples as an example of humility, saying: “Unless you become like this little child, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3)—this child, I say—as either Jesus himself, who was in their midst, as he says: “But I am in the midst of you as one who ministers” (Luke 22:27), or as the Holy Spirit, whom Jesus placed in the midst of the disciples, that is, in their hearts, because the heart’s place is the middle of the living creature.

Therefore, all of you who, in the likeness of the disciples of truth, are round about him and bring him gifts—namely, whatever services of devotion—make vows to him of these things and still more, and, when you have vowed them, render them. Thus you will please him in both respects: by the devotion of the vow and by the fulfillment of the deed. You will be children of Israel, of whom it was said above: “In Israel his name is great.”

For just as Israel pleased God more because, when he awoke from the sleep in which he saw the Lord leaning upon the ladder, he “made a vow” to him and later fulfilled it (Gen. 28:20), so you too will please him more if, after the ladder has been shown to you—that is, the form of life whose summit touches heaven—you make a vow, as he did, to offer tithes and peace-offerings and to serve him alone. Preparing himself to serve him, Jacob said: “The Lord shall be my God, and this stone which I have set up as a pillar shall be called the house of God”; and trembling he said: “How dreadful is this place!” (Gen. 28:21–22, 17).

And I say to you: “Make vows to the Lord, dreadful among all the kings of the earth.” Jacob, who was also called Israel, is the first among all the ancient and faithful patriarchs recorded as having made a vow. Therefore he is rightly set forth as an example to all true Israelites, in whom there is no deceit, in making vows to God. Hence, when it was said of Nathanael, “Behold, a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit,” after a few intervening words there is immediately added: “Because I saw you under the fig tree, you believe; you shall see greater things than these.” And it is added: “You shall see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1:47, 50–51).

Do not these words most delightfully recall that dream of Jacob, also called Israel, in which he saw a ladder whose top reached to heaven? On its highest rung, leaning upon the ladder itself, the Lord was seen by the true Israel, the one truly seeing God; and from there he heard God speaking to him: “The land on which you sleep I will give to you and to your seed after you” (Gen. 28:13). But that Jacob, unlike those who “slumbered at your rebuke, O God of Jacob,” did not sleep oppressed by deep slumber, nor did he doze under the pressure of sleep; rather, he awoke. And when he awoke, he made a vow which he also fulfilled.

You, therefore, who desire to be called and to be children of Israel, in whom the name of God is great, and who struggle with that Jacob against Edom, against flesh and blood: behold the ladder of perfect consummation, upon which angels are known to have ascended and descended. Or, to speak more plainly, behold that ladder upon which saints, made angels from among human beings, have now ascended and now descended through teaching and life.

For he ascended in preaching who said: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). He descended also, saying: “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.). Again, the same person had ascended in life when he had left all his possessions and followed Jesus; but at that same Lord’s command he was compelled to descend and undertake the care first of his immaculate mother, then of the holy Church of God, which he governed in Asia—now drawing her toward heavenly things through the love of God, now instructing her in earthly matters through love of neighbor—ascending and descending, that is, upon that highest ladder of perfection which had been shown to him.

Looking, then, upon this ladder, make vows and render them; with Jacob make vows of tithes and peace-offerings. Every elect and perfect person is rightly called a tenth and a tithe. Thus it is written in the second book of Maccabees (5:27): “But Judas Maccabeus, who had been a tenth, withdrew into a desert place.” For it was itself an indication of perfection that at the time he fled into the desert when no one in Jerusalem was free to sacrifice to God, since the Lord’s temple had already been defiled by the filth of idolatry under the impious king Antiochus, and transgressors of the Law held the temple with the sacrilegious Jason, who tyrannized in the holy place through a priesthood purchased from the king.

By tithes, therefore, is understood the purpose of perfection, which is proposed, not imposed. It is proposed to those who are willing, where it is said: “If you wish to be perfect, sell what you have,” and so forth (Matt. 19:21). It is not imposed upon those unwilling to do so, especially upon those to whom this place is too dreadful, since there they tremble with fear where there is no fear. Peter displayed their figure when he said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8). Such persons, as though in confusion, have no counsel: they are dying and fear life; they fear to undertake the ways of the stricter life, yet do not fear to slumber and lie in the laziness of their own bodies.

If such a person hears the Lord saying to him, “Do not fear; from now on you shall catch men” (ibid., 10), he will understand—with evil terror changed into good—that the Lord, or the place, is to be feared as dreadful in such a way that one flees not from him but to him. Peter also understood this. Although he said, “Depart from me, Lord,” he nevertheless remained with the Lord, by whom he was made a fisher of men; and he instructed those whom he caught in that perfection which he had at first dreaded.

The patriarch Jacob likewise first called dreadful the place where he had seen the ladder reaching to heaven; yet afterward he called that place Bethel, that is, “house of God.” There he set up as a pillar the stone upon which he had poured oil, signifying that the hardness of truth and justice must be softened by the oil of divine compassion and mercy—especially for those who reverence God’s house, either by duly offering peace-offerings there or by devoutly obeying those who offer them.

Nevertheless, what Jacob said remains true: “This place is dreadful” (Gen. 28:17). Likewise it remains true that this Lord is dreadful, “who takes away the spirit of princes.” And truly dreadful is the place where the vow of perfection is begun; dreadful is the Lord to whom the vow is made. He is indeed dreadful, but to beginners and to those who serve under the fear of avoiding punishment. For the way of perfection must be begun by a narrow path; but for those who go forward and advance day by day, when fear has at last been cast out, it is widened through the broad commandment of charity, so that everyone who walks in it may say: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118:32).

To whom is this said? To the dreadful God, who terrifies by threats not those hard of heart, such as Pharaoh or the Assyrian riders of horses, who were not terrified by his threats and therefore did not awaken at his rebuke but slept; rather, he is dreadful to the humble and meek. Yet they are not humble persons whom he found humble, but those whom he himself made humble: he, the dreadful one, who by his terror takes away the spirit of princes, so that those formerly puffed up with a great spirit and inflated as though by wind may become poor in spirit.

Alternatively: he takes away the spirit of princes, whether evil or good, through bodily death. Or he takes away the spirit of princes in order to put in his own, according to the saying: “You shall take away their spirit, and they shall fail and return to their dust. Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103:29–30). Therefore he who is dreadful among the kings of the earth must be served with fear and rejoiced in with trembling.

I do not say “among the earth,” which cannot now be terrified, though at last, terrified, it will tremble and be still; but “among the kings of the earth,” who rule their bodies. Though these bodies are heavy and earthly, they reduce them to the service of the Spirit who serves God and seeks and desires heavenly things alone.

Glory to the Father, known in carnal Judah. Glory to the Son, known in spiritual Judah, whose name is great in Israel. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that light which you, O God, illuminate wonderfully from the eternal mountains. Glory to the one and triune God, known in Judah—that is, in the Church. Amen.

## PSALM 76

**[Col. 0413B] I cried to the Lord with my voice.** In the preceding psalm, the future judgment was considered, where you, O God, will be dreadful, and who shall withstand you? Therefore, because there God will destroy those who resist and save all the meek of the earth, fear and hope are fitting for human beings who are to stand there. By these two, as by two millstones, the humble heart is ground, so that it may be contrite and humbled, which God will not despise. He will attend to its prayers, and may deign to assist it in its struggle against the law of sin implanted in the members of the flesh, on the day of tribulation and in the hour of temptation, while it is striving, praying, or crying out.

Such a combatant, placed between hope and fear, is introduced here singing and saying: “I cried to the Lord with my voice; I cried to God with my voice, and he attended to me. In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands.” And afterward: “I was exercised, and my spirit failed.” “In the very exercise,” he says, “my eyes anticipated the watches”: that is, I labored more than others, and yet I failed. Hence I was troubled, grieving on account of that very failure; and I did not speak, I did not become angry against God because the fruit of my labor failed or was delayed. And I said: “Will God cast off forever, or will he no longer add that he may be favorable again?” In saying these things and the rest, he plainly struggles between fear and hope: now indeed he fails in fear, but then comforts that very failure with good hope.

This psalm has in its title *for Idithun*, which is interpreted “one who leaps over”: that is, for good will and right intention, by which, setting all things aside, one desires God alone. “My soul refused,” he says, “to be comforted; I remembered God and was delighted.” The title is:

**VERSE 1. UNTO THE END, FOR IDITHUN, A PSALM OF ASAPH.**

It has often been said that *Idithun* means “leaping over them,” and *Asaph*, “congregation.” This psalm is attributed to this Asaph, in which the faithful congregation itself, by its example, commands us to trample the enticements of the world and leap over to Christ, beyond whom there is nothing, and who is sufficient because he is God with the Father. Philip, leaping over, sought him and said: “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:8). He thought that the Son must be leapt over and that the Father must thus be found beyond or outside the Son. But the Son instructed him that the Father was in the Son and was not to be sought or shown otherwise than in him: “He who sees me,” he says, “sees the Father” (ibid., 9). Therefore Idithun should know that he is not to leap beyond the Son in order to see the Father, since “he who sees the Son sees the Father.”

First, he says that, leaving all things aside, he sought God. Second, he recounts with how great a labor of deliberation he sought whether he was to be redeemed: at the words, “My eyes anticipated the watches.” Third, he sets out what he found through deliberation: namely, redemption for Israel through Christ; at the words, “And I said: Now I have begun.” Fourth, he pursues the things Christ did when he came to redeem, at the words, “The waters saw you.”

Carefully distinguish what this one who leaps over relates that he sought; how he sought; under what necessity; when; where; and with what result. For in a few words he does not so much explain as enfold these matters, because the word does not so much form speech as burst forth, when from the abundance and fullness of his heart he thus sounds aloud:

**VERSE 2. I cried to the Lord with my voice; I cried to God with my voice, and he attended to me.** By this repetition—when I say, “With my voice,” and again, “With my voice”—I signify the intensity of great desire, by which even in silence I cried out, as it was said to the silent Moses: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. 14:15). I cried: that is, I desired with vehement desire, so that by the importunate force, as it were, of a loud voice, my most powerful desire might obtain from the Lord, the ruler of all, and God, the creator of all, as many loaves as I needed.

Indeed, because to me, leaping over all things, everything was a cry to him who is Lord and God above all things, that I might taste that true bread containing every delight, I did not cry in vain. For he to whom I cried heard me and attended to me. For one cries to that which one chiefly desires in one’s cry. Therefore of some who cry out without desiring God it is said: “They cried to the Lord, and he did not hear them” (Ps. 17:42). Again, of these and others like them it is said: “They did not call upon God” (Ps. 52:6). For each person calls upon in prayer that which, while praying, he desires to obtain.

I, Idithun, leaping over all things that were beneath God, cried to the Lord and to God himself, not in any manner whatever, but with my own voice. He cries to the Lord with a voice not his own but another’s who does not present himself to him as a servant. To such persons he says: “Why do you call me, Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46). Again: “Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father shall enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21).

But I, Idithun or Asaph, cried to the Lord with my own voice, because I faithfully presented myself as a faithful servant to him whom I called Lord. I acknowledged myself to be the creature of him whom I called God. I endeavored through love to be the son of him whom I had been the servant through fear. But the person who calls Lord one whose servant he does not wish to be, or Father one whose son he does not wish to be, or master one whose disciple he does not wish to be, cries, if indeed he cries at all, with a voice not his own but another’s.

For not everyone who prays cries out in praying, but only one who vehemently desires what he prays for. This occurs especially when some great tribulation presses upon him, as happened to me, whom the intensity of tribulation stirred to pray or cry out. The law of sin pursued me: it was in my members, or also in the members of others. In the former, a domestic enemy; in the latter, a foreign enemy attacked me, so that I had conflicts without and fears within.

But I know that no foreign enemy, human or devil, can harm me unless the domestic enemy consents to him. For example, the woman, another man’s wife, whom David saw outwardly, would have done him no harm had inward lust not been inflamed to desire her. Hence Truth does not judge guilty the person who sees a woman, unless he sees her “to desire her”; concerning this it judges that “he has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). Likewise, the servant-girl of the priest, by questioning the apostle Peter, would have done him no harm if the fear of death had not inwardly shaken that pillar.

This, therefore, is the day of tribulation, in which conflicts without and fears within trouble a person more by day than by night; more when prosperity smiles than when adversity wearies; more through the noonday demon than through the terror of the night; more when Satan’s angel, tempting or striking with fists, transforms himself into an angel of light than when he appears as he is, an angel of night and prince of darkness.

Therefore this day or night of tribulation is the whole duration of this mortal life: day in comparison with the unbelieving children of night and darkness, among whom the faithful, holding fast the word of life, shine as lights in this world; but night in comparison with the holy angels and holy souls reigning in heaven with Christ, the sun of righteousness. Compared with them, however holy they may be, those clothed with flesh can be called night while they live in this region of the shadow of death. This, finally, is their complaint: “For you have humbled us in a place of affliction, and the shadow of death has covered us” (Ps. 43:20).

Who is wise and will understand these things? For the fool understands affliction or tribulation only as that produced by adversity: for example, prison, hunger, fever, poverty, and other evident losses and burdens. Against each of these he seeks fitting relief: release from the confinement of prison, food against hunger, health against fever or other diseases, riches against poverty, and advantages opposite to any other hardships.

But the righteous and wise person, leaping over all these things—whether comforts or discomforts—accounts all of them as tribulation so long as he does not possess the highest and eternal consolation. God, the supreme comforter, promises this consolation to those who love him above all things and leap over all things to him, saying through the prophet: “As a mother comforts her children, so will I comfort you” (Isa. 66:13); again: “Comfort, comfort my people, says your God” (Isa. 40:1). Therefore I, Idithun, leaping over all things placed beneath God—
### Verse 3

**“In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands, and in the night before him—or toward him—and I was not deceived.”**

In these few words, attentive hearers, you may observe when and under what necessity I sought God: namely, in the day of tribulation and in the night. You also have how I sought him: namely, with my hands—either outstretched in prayer or exercised in good works; better still, in both ways. And that you may know with what result I sought him, I tell you [Col. 0416C] that I was not deceived; indeed, I obtained what I asked for.

Do you wish to know where I sought him? Toward him, or before him, doing good with the right hand while the left does not know. “Toward him” is said as though one said “before him” or “in his presence.” Thus elsewhere it is said: “My sin is always before me, or in my presence” (Ps. 50:5 [Vulgate]), as if to say: I set my sin before my face through continual remembrance and acknowledgment; I do not cast it behind my back through negligence or forgetfulness.

So too he stretches out his hands toward God, or before God, who seeks God alone as witness of his prayer or work, and asks from him nothing but God himself, or what may profit him in attaining God. He knows [Col. 0416D] that the One who sees in secret will reward him, before whose face he continually offers himself to be examined and rewarded. In this he is not deceived, because he is first examined and afterwards rewarded. He is examined by temptations; when he has been proved in them, he will receive the crown of life as his reward.

But the very examination of temptation is harder when, in our affliction, temporal consolation is offered in place of eternal consolation. He is easily deceived by it who does not leap over all temporal things in seeking eternal things alone. But I, Idithun—I who leap over them—was not deceived, because I found what I sought and received what I asked, more abundantly either in hope or in actuality, because, for the sake of that one thing which I sought, I refused to accept other consolations, though they were continually offered to me. [Col. 0417A] If I had accepted them in place of that one thing, I should have been deceived, like those to whom it will be said on the Day of Judgment: “You have received your reward” (Matt. 6:5)—namely, human praise or favor, or some other passing gain found in temporal things which pass away with time.

### Verse 4

**“My soul refused to be comforted.”**

For, either patiently doing without these things when absent, or wisely using them when present, I sought eternal goods alone. In spirit and soul I leapt over all temporal things, admitting from earthly and weak things only what was necessary and expedient for the uses of the weak and fragile body.

Therefore I do not say, “My body refused to be comforted in such things,” because bodily food and clothing are necessary to the mortal body. Yet these should be admitted [Col. 0417B] for support, not for corruption; they should not be wickedly embraced, but bravely leapt over. Thus, mercifully helped by temporal aids, we may confidently seek eternal things; and our expectation of future things may become firmer and more ardent through receiving present gifts.

Otherwise, we may be tempted as our fathers were tempted in the wilderness. Having eagerly desired flesh and been abundantly filled with it in the desert, they neither gave thanks to God their giver nor raised themselves through temporal comforts to seek eternal things. Therefore, “while the food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God rose against them and slew their well-fed men” (Ps. 77:30–31 [Vulgate]).

A similar evil would have happened to the children of Israel returning from Babylon, had not the prophet Zechariah instructed them. For, after they had been afflicted by a long captivity and, through God’s mercy and by permission of Cyrus king of Persia, had come to Jerusalem and seen the walls of the Temple restored, they thought that they need no longer mourn, since their consolation seemed complete. They sent to Zechariah the prophet, saying: “Must I mourn in the fifth month, or must I sanctify myself, as I have done already for many years?” And, he says, “the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Speak to all the people of the land and to the priests, saying: When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months throughout these seventy years, did you fast a fast for me? And when you ate and drank, did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?” (Zech. 7:3–4).

[Col. 0417D] Truly, the understanding of those who asked such a question was undoubtedly imperfect. Since they saw or heard that the Temple had been built, they believed that no cause remained for mourning and fasting. Their question plainly shows that, intent on temporal and visible things, they felt little or no concern for eternal and invisible goods.

They remembered that in the fifth month Jerusalem and the Temple had been overthrown and the people taken captive; that in the seventh month Gedaliah was killed by Ishmael and the remnant of the people scattered; and that for this reason they fasted and mourned every year. But they gave insufficient thought to that universal captivity by which the human race was made captive away from God in Adam; neither did they greatly long for [Col. 0418A] the coming of the Deliverer, which was still delayed, nor did they think that they ought to mourn and fast on account of these things.

If, keeping these reasons before their eyes, they had fasted and mourned, the Lord would never have answered them in this manner: “Speak to all the people of the land and to the priests, saying: Did you fast a fast for me? And when you ate and drank, did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?”

Daniel, fasting, received a very different answer, because he had proposed very different reasons for fasting. “Daniel,” says the angel Gabriel, “I have now gone out to teach you, that you may understand. From the beginning of your prayers the word went forth. But I have come to tell you, because you are a man of desires. Therefore attend to the word and understand the vision. Seventy weeks have been shortened upon your people,” etc. (Dan. 9:23–24).

Certainly, he fasted a fast for the Lord, because, as a man of desires, he desired the things of the Lord: not merely that the city and handmade Temple should be rebuilt, but, what is far greater and incomparably better, that transgression should be brought to completion, sin should come to an end, iniquity should be blotted out, everlasting righteousness should be brought in, vision and prophecy should be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies should be anointed.

Therefore, since the one and same Lord both says here through the prophet, “Did you fast a fast for me?”—with the implied answer, “No”—and, “When [Col. 0418C] you ate and drank, did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?”—with the implied answer, “Yes”—and elsewhere says through the Apostle: “He who eats, eats for the Lord; and he who does not eat, does not eat for the Lord” (Rom. 14:6), we must clearly and diligently distinguish between the man who, when he does not eat, does not eat for the Lord—that is, when he fasts, fasts for the Lord—and the man who, when he does not eat or fasts, does not abstain or fast for the Lord but for himself. Likewise, we must distinguish between the man who, when he eats, eats for the Lord and the man who, when he eats, eats not for the Lord but for himself.

Surely, the person who fasts or abstains from food in order, through this labor of penitence, to make satisfaction to almighty [Col. 0418D] God for his sins and receive the fruit of eternal life, fasts a fast for the Lord and does not eat for the Lord. But the person who fasts or abstains in order either to escape temporal punishment, as Ahab did, or to receive passing praise, as any hypocrite does, fasts not for the Lord but for himself; he abstains not for the Lord but for himself.

Likewise, the man who eats in order that he may be able to do the Lord’s work—such as he wishes his apostles or evangelists to be, saying: “Eating and drinking, for the laborer is worthy of his hire” (Luke 10:7)—eats for the Lord. Conversely, the person who works, even though it is a holy work, even God’s work, only in order that he may eat, works not for the Lord but for himself, and eats for himself. Moreover, if he refuses to work and yet eats, [Col. 0419A] he eats not for the Lord but for himself.

Let him therefore say, “Did you fast a fast for me?” and let the answer be understood: “No”; because you did not fast for the kingdom of God; you did not fast in order that you might deserve to recover, at the coming of the seed promised to Abraham—that is, Christ—the heavenly city which you lost in Adam. Let him say, I repeat, “Did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?” and let the answer be: “Yes”; because you did not eat in order to perform God’s work, so that, sustained by provisions for the journey, you might reach the homeland or kingdom of God.

But now let us hear what the Lord finally answered when questioned about fasting after these things. “And the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: The fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall be to the house of Judah joy and gladness and splendid solemnities. Only love truth and peace, says the Lord of hosts” (Zech. 8:18–19).

To the question asked above by Sherezer and Regem-melech through their messengers—whether they ought to fast and mourn in the fifth month, or, after the Temple had been built, to end the fast and put aside mourning—the Lord gave this answer through the prophet, after setting forth many things that they should do and hope for. They had asked about one fast only, that of the fifth month; but the Lord, answering, also declared his judgment concerning the other fasts: the fast of the fourth [Col. 0419C] month, of the fifth, of the seventh, and of the tenth.

The fast of the fourth month—called July among the Latins—was held on the seventeenth day of that month, when Moses cast down and broke the tablets of the Law on Mount Sinai and, according to Jeremiah, the walls of the city were first breached. In the fifth month, which we call August, when an uprising arose among the people because of the scouts sent into the Holy Land, they were commanded not to go up, but to wander for forty years at great cost far from the Holy Land, so that, except Caleb and Joshua, all should fall in the wilderness. In this month also the Temple at Jerusalem was burned and destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, and the people were led into captivity.

In the seventh month, which we call October, Gedaliah was killed and the tribe of Judah and the remnant at Jerusalem were scattered. In the tenth month, called January among us, Ezekiel, while in captivity, heard that the Temple had been overthrown in the fifth month, as we learn fully from that prophet himself.

They rightly fasted for these sad and mournful causes, but they did not know how to fast. Indeed, they wished one of these fasts—the fast of the fifth month—to be observed no longer, because they saw that the captivity had been ended and the Temple rebuilt. Yet the Lord wished the fast to be observed, not merely until the Temple was rebuilt, but until sin should be blotted out and transgression come to an end. This is what he says: “The fast of the fourth, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, [Col. 0420A] and the fast of the tenth shall be to the house of Judah joy and gladness and splendid solemnities.”

It is as though he said: Until now you have asked for nothing while fasting sorrowfully for sorrowful causes. Ask, that your joy may be full: namely, not fasting with sadness, as gloomy hypocrites fast; not, I say, with sadness, but with joy, according to the saying: “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face” (Matt. 6:17). Anoint your head—that is, your mind—with the oil of gladness, so that your fast may be turned into joy and gladness and splendid solemnities.

For there is a splendid solemnity where there is a joyful and pure intention, sustained by most eager expectation; where there is full joy, not in beholding the handmade Temple, which shall not be in [Col. 0420B] the heavenly Jerusalem, as John says: “I saw no temple in it” (Rev. 21:22), but in beholding the unmade Temple, concerning which John likewise says: “For the Lord is its temple, and the Lamb” (ibid.). There is full joy and everlasting gladness; there is the splendid solemnity which, even during this pilgrimage, is preceded by splendid solemn observances, to which the four fasts called the Ember Days are assigned.

Finally, while the Synagogue fasted on account of the sad causes already mentioned and now past, the Church appointed the fasts of the Ember Days with reference to splendid solemnities always to come as the year turns, and to be fulfilled in the eternal solemnity: the spring fast before Easter; the summer fast, which could not fittingly be held before Pentecost during the fifty days, when it is a season of rejoicing and feasting on unleavened bread in that week of the splendid festival of the Paraclete’s coming; the autumn fast in September; and the winter fast in December before the feast of the Lord’s Nativity.

This feast is fittingly preceded by a double fast, just as the night of that feast is adorned by a double sacrifice because of Christ’s two generations: one from the Father, the other from the Mother. To his generation from the Father belongs what is sung in the first Mass: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; this day I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7); likewise: “In the splendors of the saints, from the womb before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 109:3 [Vulgate]).

But his generation from Mary is touched upon more clearly in the Gospel: “She bore her firstborn Son” (Luke 2:7). Christ is indeed proclaimed by the Apostle to be “the firstborn of every creature” chiefly in accordance with the divine generation by which he was born from the Father before the ages, rather than that according to which he was born from his mother at the end of the ages. Yet in this latter respect he too is called firstborn—not firstborn of every creature, but firstborn of the dead, who are to be raised from death through him.

But this belongs to the feast of his resurrection, since he himself first rose from the dead, the firstborn of the dead and the firstfruits of those who sleep. Very many of them rose with him and appeared to many, so that it might thereby be established that he is not only the firstborn of every creature according to the eternity of his Divinity, but also [Col. 0421A] the firstborn among many brethren according to the temporality of his humanity. In that humanity he is the blessed one who comes in the name of the Lord, as is sung in the second Mass, in which the eternal Word of God, made temporal, is commemorated, the shepherds saying: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this Word which has been made” (Luke 2:15).

In the public Mass, however, both generations are commemorated together, especially in the Gospel. What is written, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:1), touches upon his eternal generation; and what follows, “The Word was made flesh” (ibid., 14), reveals his temporal generation, by which “a child has been born to us and a son has been given to us” (Isa. 9:6).

It is therefore no wonder [Col. 0421B] that two Ember Days fasts, as we have said, precede this feast adorned by the twofold generation of the ever-existing Son of God. For although, in this pilgrimage, the citizens of that heavenly Jerusalem receive some small consolation because, when Babylonian captivity has been relaxed through forgiveness of sins, visible monasteries or temples are built under leaders like Zerubbabel, or priests not unequal to Jesus the high priest, where those serving God devote themselves to worship and keep solemn feasts; nevertheless, all these temporal consolations must be leapt over. We should use them justly and soberly, as though they were ships, and hasten to enter that rest of eternal blessedness where there is full joy, everlasting gladness, and splendid solemnity.

Let us know that the temporal consolations of riches have been granted not to the rational soul but to the mortal and fragile body. Therefore that rich man was foolish who said to his soul: “Soul, you have many goods for many years; eat, drink, rest.” God rightly said to one who spoke thus: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and whose will be the things you have prepared?” (Luke 12:19–20). Truly, that man was foolish whose soul clung to such things as though it would find rest in them, though all are unstable and perishable.

Therefore, thoughtful hearers, listen to what this Idithun says concerning his soul, which leaps over all these temporal things as not its own, as not pertaining to it. “My soul,” he says, “refused to be comforted”—as though he said: Although the body’s frailty needs support through temporal comforts, my soul nevertheless refuses to be comforted in them, delighting in greater things: namely, eternal delights sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, and eternal riches more desirable than much gold and precious stone.

For who can explain how sweetly wisdom tastes to the wise soul, and how greatly are the delights in your right hand, O God, delightful—your left hand containing riches and glory? Therefore, “Let your left hand be under my head, and let your right hand embrace me.” By “head” the heart is surely understood, according to the saying: “Lift up your heads” (Luke 21:28), that is, gladden your hearts. Therefore let your left hand be under my head, so that my heart may, through its desire, surpass all [Col. 0422A] temporal things; and let your right hand embrace me, so that my heart itself may continually delight in heavenly things alone. For the delights in your left hand are either none or slight and momentary; but “the delights in your right hand are unto the end” (Ps. 15:11 [Vulgate]), an end without end.

Although no mortal is granted an abundance of these delights in this life, even their memory alone nourishes and refreshes the mind. This I, Idithun, have experienced in myself, because:

### Verse 4

**“I remembered God and was delighted; I was exercised, and my spirit failed.”**

On this passage blessed Gregory says in his *Morals on Job*:

> [Note: [Col. 0421D] Book XVIII of the *Morals*, chapter 41.] Holy men admit into their minds no grace of consolation from the present life. For the rich of this world, when they are commonly affected by weariness of mind, are accustomed to look upon the temporal goods they have received and so soften their sorrow. When they feel themselves touched by some sadness, they look at their horses, contemplate their vessels of gold and silver, go about their estates; and, willingly drawing their eyes through these temporal things, they overcome the sadness that has arisen in their soul. Therefore Truth says to them in the Gospel: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation.” But the holy man who grieves because he has fallen away from eternal things receives no consolation from temporal things, saying: “I refused to comfort my soul.” As if he plainly said: Since I do not grieve over the loss of temporal things, I cannot possibly comfort my soul through their abundance. To him, as though we who hear these things said, “What then do you seek, since you refuse to be comforted in the things that belong to the world?” he immediately added: “I remembered God and was delighted.” As if he plainly said: Neither the abundance of earthly things refreshes me, but even the memory alone of my Creator, whom I am not yet able to see, delights me.

The same author, in the same work:

> [Note: [Col. 0422D] Book XXII of the *Morals*, chapter 18.] “I was exercised, and my spirit failed” for a little while. What is this “my spirit,” except the spirit of man, namely the spirit of self-exaltation? Since we advance toward the love of God through the hidden grace of a measure bestowed from above, the more strength from the Spirit of God grows daily in us, the more our own spirit fails. Because this spirit of error is not suddenly and utterly cut off from us, it is rightly said to have failed “for a little while.” But we then fully advance in God when we have utterly failed in ourselves.

[Col. 0422D] Alternatively: “I remembered God and was delighted” in his goodness, “because he is good, because his mercy is forever” (Ps. 135:1 [Vulgate]); because he has mercy on all and hates none of the things he has made, overlooking human sins for the sake of repentance; and because his mercies are over all his works. Although his creation and the works of his hands delighted me, above all things his own loving-kindness and mercy delighted me.

Yet, knowing that truth and the severity of justice are inseparable companions of that same most merciful mercy, I was exercised in investigating the most merciful, most just, and most wise judgments of this justice. Why should the consideration of the sweet and upright Lord not delight my memory [Col. 0423A] and at the same time exercise it?

Is it not sweet that the mercy of the Lord is from everlasting and unto everlasting upon those who fear him? Is it not sweet that God’s purpose stands, that the decree of peace stands over those who fear him—overlooking their evils and rewarding their goods, so that in a wonderful manner not only good things but even evil things work together for their good?

But again, it is exceedingly terrible to fall into the hands of that justice, from whose eternal judgment proceeds the most hidden and severe scrutiny of the Judge, watching over the ungodly who are eternally to be condemned, terrible in his counsels over the children of men foreknown for evil. Therefore he neither washes away their evils nor desires their good; moreover, he hardens their hearts lest perhaps they grieve, come to their senses, turn, and he heal them. [Col. 0423B] And this is not without a certain and eternal reason—a reason known to be more fearful in proportion as it is known to be more immovably fixed in eternity.

Meditating on these things concerning God, who is sweet and upright, I was delighted and exercised: delighted in beholding his goodness, exercised in beholding his severity. And because I could not investigate the eternal causes of either matter, my spirit failed: my reason failed; my intellect failed, unable to perceive the profound secret of this matter. In wonder at it I was compelled to cry: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33).

Great indeed is the depth of wisdom and knowledge by which God orders all things sweetly, reaching strongly from end to end: ordering and disposing all things, from the highest angel to the lowest worm, from the summit of things to their depths, from primordial causes to final causes, assigning to every creature weight, measure, and number. In considering these things my spirit failed, because they are incomprehensible; but faith advanced, because they are worthy of reverence, desirable not only to know but even to seek.

Here a *diapsalma* is inserted, and the second part is thus joined to the first: “I, Idithun, said, because my spirit failed.” But lest anyone think that I was negligent, lukewarm, or lazy in my exercise, let him know that I not only observed the common vigils with others, but:

### Verse 5

**“My eyes anticipated the watches of others.”**

For I accustomed both my bodily eyes, by which colors are distinguished, to night vigils in the search for truth or in praises of divine goodness; and the eyes of my mind, by which good morals are distinguished from evil as white from black, I endeavored always to keep awake, anticipating in this pursuit other equally earnest seekers.

And because I could not fully understand what I sought, I was troubled in my heart. Yet I set a guard upon my mouth and did not speak—neither foolishly murmuring against God nor rashly affirming what I did not understand. I knew that concerning an ineffable matter it is safer to be cautiously silent than carelessly to speak. Therefore I did not speak about that wherein I was troubled within myself.

At times I was also troubled by persons speaking against me, [Col. 0424A] and I did not speak, lest, being too occupied in replying, I should become increasingly disturbed in thoughts which I wished to keep free, because I had occupied them with better things.

### Verse 6

**“For I considered the ancient days, and held eternal years in my mind.”**

The ancient days are the old days of the present life, in which man grows old; days in which everything mutable becomes old and ages and is near to destruction. Into these days man fell when he sinned—he who had been created for eternal days and years. I considered those ancient days, compared the eternal years, in which there is no change, with them; and, considering and despising those ancient days, I held these eternal years in my mind.

### Verse 7

**“And in the night I meditated with my heart.”**

[Col. 0424B] I meditated upon the ancient days, upon the unfailing years which I lost in Adam, and how they might be recovered through the second Adam, promised long ago to the ancient fathers. I meditated, I say, with my heart, inwardly and in secret, finding outside no safe ears to which I could entrust my secret meditations. Therefore I exercised myself only inwardly, within myself; or, as another translation has it: “I chattered.”

To chatter inwardly, where God alone hears, is to exercise oneself in the spirit: the noise of this world does not mingle with one chattering in holy meditations, especially if what follows is done: “And I swept,” or “I brushed,” as another manuscript has it; “I winnowed”; or, as the Hebrew truth has it, “I searched my spirit.”

For what is it to sweep the spirit except, by good intention as by a broom, to cleanse away the filth of invading fantasies? Or what is it to sweep or winnow the spirit except, by the vigilance of that same intention, as it were by sweeping and searching, to make in the rational spirit a hollow or trench of humility, after every dust of earthliness has been winnowed out and cast away?

Strictly speaking, we call a *scobs* the excavation made by a boring tool or plough; accordingly, in a moral sense *scobs* may be called the confession and drawing out of hidden sins. It is elicited, as if by the drill or plough of sound doctrine, so that the sinner, convicted of his sin, may show outwardly in confession what he had formerly concealed. And it is indeed praiseworthy when someone confesses his sin after another rebukes him. But I, [Col. 0424D] Idithun—or I, Asaph—did not wait for a voice rebuking me from outside, because I myself swept my spirit within.

Observe the leaps by which I leapt over things. First, in the day of tribulation, as though leaping over all earthly consolations, I sought God. But when my spirit failed in seeking him, I sprang back to my mind and committed the eternal years to memory there. Still contemplating the End of which the title of the Psalm speaks, I considered these things within myself.

### Verse 8

**“Will God cast off for ever?”**

He cast off for a time when he said: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return”; likewise: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken” (Gen. 3:19). But will he cast off forever?

And he who sleeps, will he not add that he may rise again? Will not he who ordained that men should die through one man’s disobedience also raise men to life through one man’s obedience? Or will he not add, so that he may be more pleased still?

God was pleased with himself when he saw the individual things that he had made, and each was good. But when he saw them all together, he was more pleased with himself in them, because they were very good. Each individual thing was good; all together they were very good. But sin occurred, which did not please God and in which God was not pleased with himself, since he was not the author of sin. Therefore, because of man’s sin, God was justly angry and could not be appeased until another man was born, upon seeing whom the Most High Father could say: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

For if every craftsman rightly takes pleasure in himself because of some excellent work completed by himself, although he is not himself the author of the material from which he worked, how much more rightly does God the Father take pleasure in himself in a work created and completed by himself? I, Idithun, leaping over other works, awaited such a work, in which God, pleased with himself, might also be appeased from his wrath through it: namely, being reconciled to men who were by nature children of wrath through the one Son of Man, full of grace and truth.

The Hebrew truth agrees with this interpretation, where it reads: “Therefore will the Lord cast off forever, and will he not be reconciled again?” In place of this the Latin translator put: “Will God cast off forever, and will he not add, that he may be more pleased still?” But *complacatior* (“more appeased”) would be more usual than *complacitior* (“more pleased”) for the Hebrew verb, which means “will be reconciled,” because being reconciled and being appeased are the same in meaning.

We know that God was angry with the first parents because of sin, but was appeased before the Law by Abel’s sacrifice and the devout services of other righteous persons. Thus he promised to Abraham the patriarch that a seed from his flesh would come, by which he would become more appeased—or, as we said above, more pleased. Seeing this seed, forgetful of wrath and mindful of loving-kindness, remembering his mercy as he had spoken to our fathers, God would be appeased toward men, or pleased with himself, so as to say: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

[Col. 0425D] Awaiting this, I—David, or Asaph, or Idithun—sweeping, trenching, or searching my spirit, made trusting by divine promises, said within myself: “Will God cast off forever, or will he not add, that he may be more pleased still?” Will he, already appeased and reconciled to such an extent that he promised the holy seed with an oath to the fathers, not add further so that he may become still more pleased or appeased, by accomplishing what he promised?

### Verse 9

**“Or will he cut off his mercy,”** begun by so many promises and confirmed also by the oaths which he swore in the good pleasure of his grace?

Those to whom he swore in his wrath that they should not enter into his rest could not enter it, being hindered by the wrath in which the oath had been sworn against them. But will those to whom it was sworn that they should enter it—those blessed in the seed of Abraham, to whom he swore by himself, or in the seed of David, to whom he also swore—not enter into the rest of promised and sworn blessing?

“In your seed,” he says, “all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). Again, after the offering of his son, it was said to the same father Abraham: “Because you have done this thing and have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake, blessing I will bless you, and I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven” (Gen. 22:16–17).

Since it is impossible for God speaking to lie, who would suppose that God swearing lies? For, as the Apostle says, he further “interposed an oath” (Heb. 9:17 [citation as printed]) in his promises, swearing by himself because he had no greater by whom he could swear, in order that through two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have the strongest consolation. We hold him as promiser and debtor, and may confidently say to him: “That you may be justified in your words” and promises “and never be found unjust or false” (Ps. 50:6 [Vulgate]): do all that you spoke to our fathers concerning the blessing of all tribes of the earth in Abraham’s seed.

Thus I, Idithun, speaking within myself and, by searching my spirit, strengthened in faith and hope, said among other things: Will God cast off forever those to whom he has promised such great goods? Or will he not add [Col. 0426C] so that he who, now somewhat appeased and reconciled, made so many promises of mercy to the children of wrath may be more pleased—or more appeased—still? Or will he at last cut off his mercy, which he surely began when, in wrath mindful of mercy, he promised that he would establish enmity between the serpent and the woman, saying: “I will place enmities between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed: she shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. 3:15)?

With these words mercy toward wretched human beings was first begun, to be fulfilled at the end of the ages. Will he then cut off his mercy forever, whose faithful promises are expected to be fulfilled at the End? Will he cut off his mercy—mercy which is to proceed from generation to generation and remain forever—so that it may truly be sung of him: “And his mercy is from generation to generations upon those who fear him” (Luke 1:50)?

VERS. 10. Or will God forget to show mercy—God, whose own property is always to have mercy and to spare his creature, to whom it is truly said: “You have mercy on all, Lord, and hate none of the things which you have made” (Wis. 11:24–25)? Will the fountain of inexhaustible mercy be dried up when the drought of misery threatens? The brook could dry up for blessed Elijah, because that brook had no spring of flowing water. For a brook properly means water rushing downward, collected from rain or melting snow; and therefore it quickly fails [Col. 0427A] and comes to nothing, being water that runs down and does not return, unlike all rivers, which return through hidden channels to the place from which they flow, so as to flow again. Can the current of a river proceeding from the inexhaustible fountain of mercy—and therefore making glad the city of God—be dried up in this way, since it cannot be cut off or severed, as Holofernes, the general of the king of Assyria, caused the water-supply to be cut off from the children of Israel when Bethulia was besieged? (Judith 7:6.) Not so, not so will the ungodly be able to cut off, nor will they have power to bring it about that God himself should cut off, the current of the river which makes glad the city of God, flowing from the true promises of mercy. God will not so forget those promises as to cease to show mercy, or to restrain his mercies in anger. He has indeed been provoked and angered by many [Col. 0427B] human sins, so that he might become more and more wrathful, forget mercy, and restrain his mercies in anger. But if he did this, he would not be shown true, but false, in his words. Since, however, it cannot happen that truth should be found lying, will God forget to show mercy, or restrain his mercies in his anger? Far be it. Rather, he will restrain his anger in mercy: when he has been angry, he will remember mercy and be propitious to those to whom he promised mercy.
