VERS. 11. And I said: Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High. Here a *diapsalma* is inserted, distinguishing what has been said from what is to be said. For I, Idithun, who long laboured in anxious deliberation, have now begun to attain what I sought. Or: now I have begun to understand what previously [Col. 0427C] I could not grasp: namely, that in God, whose proper work is to have mercy and whose alien work is to be angry, anger is changed into mercy rather than mercy into anger. And this change is the work of the right hand of the Most High, because the Son of the Most High was humbled and made incarnate for this purpose: that he might be “the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world,” as the Apostle says (1 John 2:2). Through him, therefore, wrath will cease and mercy will work—a mercy prefigured by many ancient works and wonders. Of these works of the Lord,

VERS. 12. I was mindful in time past, lest, when forgetfulness came upon me, ingratitude should come with it; for where ingratitude occurs, there can be no thanksgiving for [Col. 0427D] past benefits, and thus the way to future benefits is closed by ingratitude. Lest this should happen to me, I was mindful of the Lord’s past works, which were signs of things to come: as the sacrifice of a lamb by Abel, and of a ram by Abraham, signified the sacrifice of him who was prophesied to be led “as a sheep to the slaughter”; and by Noah’s ark, guided and preserved in the flood, was signified the Church, to be guided and saved by Christ amid the waves of worldly temptations. Yet I was mindful not only, with thanksgiving, of such works of God, but much more I held in memory at the same time the greater works of God prefigured by those lesser works. For the latter were more worthy of remembrance and more wondrous. Thus I call those old things simply “works”; but I call these new things “wonders,” speaking [Col. 0428A] in the exercise of my spirit and saying: “For I shall be mindful from the beginning of your wonders.” As though it were said: It is evident from this that I was rightly mindful of past works, because through their signification and reminder I shall be mindful of your other works, O God, which are more wonderful. For example: it is more wondrous that the invisible Pharaoh with his army should be drowned in baptism than that the visible Pharaoh was submerged in the Red Sea. Likewise, it was sufficiently wonderful that bread from heaven was given to the people brought through the sea; but it is more wonderful that the true bread from heaven is given to the Christian people purified through the waters of baptism. For that bread was neither living nor able to give life to those who ate it; but this bread is living—indeed, it is life—and gives life to those who eat it, as he himself says: “He who [Col. 0428B] eats me shall live because of me” (John 6:58).

Of such wonders of God, predestined from the beginning and prefigured by wondrous works, I shall always be mindful, because in the remembrance of such things faith is nourished, hope is stirred, and charity is delighted. And therefore I shall not merely remember, but:

VERS. 13. I shall meditate on all your works, constantly investigating what you intended when you did this and that, whereby, by displaying your power, wisdom, or goodness, you made your might known among the peoples. I shall indeed meditate on your works in thanksgiving. But lest even this thanksgiving of mine be fruitless to me, I shall be watchful for myself and shall exercise myself in your inventions—that is, in the precepts of righteousness, by which [Col. 0428C] you are found by those who seek you; or in those things which you discovered, you who found every way of knowledge and prudence and gave it to Jacob your servant and Israel your beloved. In these your discoveries, therefore, I shall exercise myself by reading, meditating, learning, teaching, and—what is more efficacious—by doing, praying, and dwelling upon your praises. Among these praises I am accustomed continually to say:

VERS. 14. O God, your way is in the holy place; what god is great like our God? Instead of our reading, “And I shall exercise myself in your inventions,” another translation has: “And I shall speak of your affections.” Behold, the third way of speaking. For first I spoke idly outside, and my spirit failed; nor did I benefit myself or another, because there were no hearers who were either well-disposed or attentive, or even teachable or learned. Secondly, I spoke within, in my spirit, searching it (*scobendo*), or digging it out (*scrobendo*), or exercising it, and I profited, because I usefully deliberated within myself concerning the inquiry into truth. Thirdly, I now speak not with myself but above myself, rejoicing not in myself but in God, exulting in his works and wonders, and in this tasting beforehand the divine affections.

For just as earthly things have their own affections, delighting outwardly either the eyes, as spectacles do, or the ears, as stories do, or the taste, as banquets do, so likewise one who passes beyond all these things, mindful of God and delighting in him, meditates continually upon him and has inward affections from him. Thus, when this visible world is regarded, and the Creator’s power, wisdom, and goodness are sought and found in the creature, he is found nowhere displeasing but pleasing through all things; stronger than all strong things, more beautiful than all beautiful things, sweeter than all sweet things, being the fountain and origin of all strength, beauty, and sweetness. From this there arises in the soul of the contemplator a great affection, so that he finds it sweet to speak in the praises of God and continually says: “O God, your way is in the holy place; what god is great like our God?” What does this mean? O God, your way, by which you come to human beings or by which human beings come to you, is in your Holy One—that is, in your Son, whom you sanctified and sent into the world. He is the Holy of holies; he justifies, sanctifies, and magnifies those who cleave to him; he “was made for us,” as the Apostle says, “wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30), [Col. 0429B] and salvation is in no other. “For no other name under heaven has been given to human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

Therefore those who trust in the gods of the nations are deceived, because those gods can profit them in nothing; indeed, they destroy their souls, “for the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 95:5)—he who is our God. Therefore, in praise of this our God, let us say: “What god is great like our God?” God, the Creator of all, has become our Saviour. By ruling all, he is God and Lord of all; but by saving us, he is our God, and the God of all who believe in him. Acknowledging his greatness, although he was born little for the good, we rightly magnify him, saying:

[Col. 0429C] VERS. 15. You are the God who works wonders—both by healing the sick in body and by justifying the ungodly in soul. Your servants also work wonders, indeed, but with you working in them and through them. But you work wonders alone, by your own power—the power by which you made, without their aid, those very persons who work wonders. If I were to say, “You are the God who worked wonders,” it might seem that I was speaking only of those ancient wonders which you performed long ago. But now, when I say, “You are the God who works wonders,” it is clear that I speak of those wonders which you perform now and do not cease to perform until the end of the age. Long ago, for forty years, you rained manna; now, throughout the entire time of the Church’s pilgrimage in the desert of this world, you rain down the true bread from heaven, possessing [Col. 0429D] every delight and every flavour of sweetness. Such wonders you alone perform, requiring no strength from another for them. For without human power you made human beings powerful, through whom you performed wonders.

Through them you made your power known among the peoples. Truly your power, not theirs, as they themselves acknowledge when they say: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113:1). Again, when one of them had said, “I have laboured more than all,” lest this seem attributable to his own strength, he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

Alternatively: You made your power known among the peoples, O God the Father, by making known your Son, who is your power [Col. 0430A] and wisdom: power, through which you made all things from nothing; wisdom, through which you govern the things created; or power which cannot be conquered, wisdom which cannot be deceived. The evident proof of this unconquered power is what follows: “You made your power known among the peoples”—that is, you made known your very Son, your power, by this fact:

VERS. 16. You redeemed your people by your arm, in that same Son of yours. In figure, the lamb sacrificed delivered the ancient people from Egypt; and in his own person, his sacrifice delivered and redeemed his people from hell. For just as Pharaoh could be struck by ten plagues, yet your people could not be delivered from his dominion [Col. 0430B] unless the typological lamb was sacrificed, so the devil could be struck by the ten commandments of the Law; nevertheless, the people of the saints, held captive in death, could not be delivered from his dominion unless you, the true Lamb, were sacrificed. With our foreheads marked by your blood, we shall be free from the sword of the smiter.

Therefore you delivered your people magnificently of old—the children of Jacob and Joseph; but now you deliver your people far more magnificently: the children of Jacob, that is, the elect from Jacob’s stock, and the children of Joseph, that is, the elect from among the nations. As regards the historical sense, it would have been enough to say, “the children of Jacob,” among whom the children of Joseph are included, since Joseph was Jacob’s son. But the distinction between the children of Jacob and Joseph is not idle. For by the children [Col. 0430C] of Jacob, or Israel, believing Jews are rightly understood: those who derive their lineage from him not only according to the flesh but also according to faith. Although Joseph was one of them, because he was sold by his brothers and, after many afflictions, was exalted among foreign nations, he is quite suitably distinguished from the children of Jacob; and, having been made prince of the nations, he is fittingly named separately from the children of Jacob who sold him.

Mystically, moreover, this same Joseph signifies Christ, who, sold by the Jews, was carried from his own land, as it were, into the Egypt of the nations. There he was first afflicted and humbled in the persecutions of the martyrs, then glorified and exalted to reign. And [Col. 0430D] thus it is read: “All nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71:11). Again: “Those who reviled you shall come to you, and shall worship the footsteps of your feet” (Isa. 60:14). These, then, are the children of Joseph, for whom he provides as a merciful father lest they perish by famine, and who cry to him: “Our salvation is in your hand, Lord; let your mercy look upon us” (Gen. 47:25). When these are joined to the children of Jacob, God’s people is increased in accordance with the name Joseph, which is interpreted “increase.”

*Diapsalma.* Here begins the FOURTH PART, in which the very manner of redemption by which God’s people was delivered is explained.

VERS. 17. The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you, and were afraid. We are compelled here to understand rational waters, which could see and fear. For although elemental water felt the power of its Creator—whether when, withdrawing at his command, it supplied a dry path on the bed of the sea and the Jordan, or when it offered itself to the Son of God to be walked upon—yet it was not capable of the fear of God. Hence the rational waters are rightly understood, of which it is said here: “The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you, and were afraid.” In the Apocalypse, many waters are said to be many peoples. These waters, therefore, saw you, O God: they saw—that is, they understood you—through the divine works which, having formerly performed in your servants in many portions and in many ways, you finally performed in your incarnate Son, as he himself says: “The Father abiding in me, he himself does the works” (John 14:10). In such divine works the waters—that is, some peoples from among the Jews—saw, that is, understood you; and again the waters—that is, many peoples from among the nations—saw you. They saw you and were afraid, according to what is written: “Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, ‘A great prophet has arisen among us’” (Luke 7:16). Again: “But when the crowds saw it, they were afraid and glorified God, who had given such power to human beings” (Matt. 9:8).

The waters were afraid, but the depths were troubled, because rulers deeper in wickedness, both among Jews and among the nations, when they saw the people’s faith, were troubled. Some were troubled toward repentance: for a great multitude of priests from among the Jews obeyed the faith, and many rulers of the nations, following the faith of the people, were beneficially troubled and imitated the crowds [Col. 0431C] of believers. But certain rulers of both peoples, deep in wickedness like an abyss, were stirred greatly toward evil and, not following but persecuting the people’s faith, became troubled. Hence:

VERS. 18. The multitude of the sound of the waters: for the various devotions of the peoples resound like a stormy sea—in groaning and confession of sins, in thanksgiving, and in continual praises of God—while, on the other hand, the blasphemies of the ungodly resound, and human beings wither “from the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves” (Luke 21:25). And indeed a confused and tumultuous sound was heard from the waters, that is, from the peoples; but the clouds gave forth a voice: a rational voice, a voice of gladness, a voice of exultation. Unlike the sound of waters, it was not confused, [Col. 0431D] but melodious and distinguished, as though by musical harmonies, and contained nothing confused in itself, although it was heard far and wide from the clouds like great thunders. For then, through the clouds—that is, through lofty and bright preachers—the seven thunders uttered their voices.

For although the prophetic writings had been produced under the inspiration of the sevenfold Spirit of God, they had until then appeared like thunders possessing little or no intelligible meaning, striking terror into their hearers with a tumultuous sound. But then the clouds gave forth a voice, when the prophetic and legal writings were shown by holy interpreters to be full of reason. Hence Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: “It is written, he says, in the book of Psalms: ‘Let their dwelling place become desolate, and let there be none to dwell in their tents’” (Acts 1:20); [Col. 0432A] again: “Let his days be few, and let another receive his episcopate” (ibid.). When this thunder of prophecy sounded in Judaea, those who heard might have been frightened, not knowing to what that threat was directed, because in that sound there was no full or certain distinctness of meaning: the water was still dark in the clouds of the air, and knowledge was hidden in the prophets. But when Peter expounded the aforementioned prophetic denunciation as concerning Judas the traitor and his accomplices, the clouds gave forth an evidently intelligible voice. So it happened also in the other prophecies: in accordance with their predictions, truth, previously hidden, was made manifest throughout the whole world.

For your arrows pass through—that is, your apostles, who were like “arrows in the hand of the mighty one” (Ps. [Col. 0432B] 126:4), passed from the narrowness of Judaea into the breadth of the nations. We Gentiles walk in the light of these arrows when we hold their teachings. Your arrows pass through also when your commandments, sent forth through them, do not remain in the ears but penetrate as far as the heart. Or they pass through the deaf and hardened ears of those unwilling to hear, so that, when one who “did not wish to understand, that he might do good” is left behind, another who has ears to hear may hear. Thus it came to pass that:

VERS. 19. The voice of your thunder was plainly heard in the wheel. The voice of thunder—that is, the threat of the coming judgment—was heard in the wheel, that is, in the world. And because testimony confirmed not only by hearing but also by sight is commonly regarded as established, your lightnings shone upon the world. “Wheel” and “world” signify the same thing here, and one explains the other. Thus, after it has first been said that the voice of thunder was heard in the wheel, it is consequently added that the lightnings shone upon the world, so that you may know that in the wheel, which is the world, the rain-bearing clouds, going about it, thundered by commandments and flashed by miracles.

The rains of these clouds are arrows which pass through, watering the earth and wounding it. For they water good ground, so that it bears fruit with patience—thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold; but they shoot and strike with lightning bad ground: stony, thorny, and trodden down, fit for no fruit. For the same word of apostolic teaching, according to the different hearers, is rain, a lightning-arrow, a flash of lightning, and thunder.

Because of these things heard and seen, the earth was moved and trembled. It was moved by fear, it trembled with horror; because “it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31). The earth, namely Judaea, loving earthly things alone, was moved when it heard evangelical preaching, in which earthly riches are not promised as they were in the Law of Moses, but the distress of the poor man covered with sores is praised and the rich man’s daily feast is condemned. Therefore, when it is said, “Blessed are you poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke 6:20), and, “Woe to you rich, for you have received your consolation” (Luke 6:24), the Synagogue, desirous of earthly riches and for this reason called “earth,” [Col. 0433A] was, unsurprisingly, moved and trembled because of this new and unfamiliar teaching.

Finally, their teachers, the scribes and Pharisees, “called blessed the people to whom these things belong,” namely, “their storehouses full, pouring forth from one thing into another; their sheep fruitful, abundant in their offspring; their oxen fat” (Ps. 143:13–14), and other like incentives and instruments of greed. But the new teachers declared blessed the poor, the meek, those who mourn, those who suffer persecution for righteousness while hungering and thirsting for righteousness. Because of such unfamiliar teaching, therefore, the earth was moved and trembled—partly toward repentance and conversion, partly toward indignation and persecution of those who preached such things—to such a degree that, rejecting the word of God, they drove them from their borders and compelled them to pass to the nations, as from land into a stormy and wave-tossed sea. At that time this was difficult and dangerous, especially when the tempest of persecution began to be stirred up by the Roman Empire, whose official Pilate had killed Christ, and whose other official, King Herod, had already laid hands on some of the Church in order to kill them.

In that storm the ship of the Church was in grave danger: Peter, its chief helmsman, was imprisoned, and James, the brother of John, was killed. In such a commotion the earth was troubled, so that this deed of Herod pleased the earthly Jews. Therefore mountains were transferred from the earth thus troubled into the heart of the sea—that is, into the depth of exceedingly bitter, false, and turbid paganism. In that sea, as it were, the greater fish devours the lesser; in that sea are creeping things without number, small animals with great ones. Yet because there your ships, O God, shall pass through,

VERS. 20. Your way was and is in the sea, and your paths in many waters. For just as you walked invisibly upon the sea and gave the apostle Peter power to do the same, so now you walk invisibly and cause your ministers to walk upon the troubled hearts of the nations. These hearts offer themselves to be trodden underfoot by you and by your feet, so beautiful and prepared for proclaiming the Gospel, so that the tracks of truth may be formed in them through the ways of commandments and the paths of counsels. By forbidding sins, indeed, they make rough places into level ways; but by counselling arduous virtues—such as continence, virginity, and voluntary poverty—they form paths, not in all the waters of this entire sea, because “not all receive this word” (Matt. 19:11), namely, these most arduous counsels, but in many waters. For although the perfect are few in comparison with the evil or imperfect, nevertheless they are many in their own number: those who have not been defiled with women and who walk in white, whether among virgins, among the continent, or indeed among martyrs who have washed their robes white in the blood of the Lamb, drinking the cup of the Lord in either open or hidden martyrdom, as the two sons of Zebedee drank that same cup differently.

For though it was said to both: “You shall indeed drink my cup” (Matt. 20:23), nevertheless James alone is expressly recorded as having suffered and been beheaded. For him, it was to drink the Lord’s cup in a brief martyrdom, when he was compelled to die although he still wished to live. But John, worn out by long labours, while he desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ, was compelled against his will to live, in order to strengthen believers in the faith and defeat faithless heretics. Therefore, while among the perfect one is girded and led where he does not wish, that he may be compelled to live, and another that he may be compelled to die, your paths, O God, though narrow, will be not among a few but in many waters. And your paths will not be known, because the end for which each person walks in them, and which of those walking in them is worthy of love or hatred, is hidden from human knowledge—even from those who now walk well but do not know the end.

That your tracks, O God, are not known arises partly from this: upon hearts that are too hard they are not deeply impressed; but upon those that are too soft, such as water, though impressed, they are quickly erased. For these are those “who believe for a time and in time of temptation fall away” (Luke 8:13). But those who do not even believe for a time do not receive your tracks, like hard and stony ground. Such were the Jews among whom you taught and performed miracles, seeking to impress your tracks upon them. But they did not receive your tracks, as it is written: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11). Therefore your tracks will be known neither by them nor in them: they will not be known by them because they were blinded; they will not be known in them because they were hardened. This is all the more astonishing and detestable because your power, so remarkably displayed to that special people, has become known among the peoples of the nations—especially in that:

VERS. 21. You led your people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron. You led them from Egypt through the desert, through a land of horror and vast desolation, not merely in any fashion but like sheep—although very many of them were not innocent and simple sheep, but wanton goats to be placed on the left. Therefore I do not say, “You led them as true lambs or sheep,” but “like sheep”: they presented the appearance of sheep, while inwardly they were goats or even ravening wolves. Such were those who, raging with bestial fury against the authority of their shepherds, were swallowed up by the earth and consumed by fire; and those who perished from serpents because of their murmurings, and who were struck down in the wilderness by various other disasters. Yet because you preserved their children and multiplied them so that they became a great people, it is rightly said to you in thanksgiving: “You led your people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron.”

Through these leaders of your people and their names, their mystical deeds are commended. For Moses is interpreted “taken up,” because Pharaoh’s daughter took him up from the waters; Aaron, however, means “mountain of strength.” By their eminent strength they made a way in the sea for the children of Israel, as a figure of Christ’s baptism, through which the faithful people was to be delivered. That people also excels in the honour of being taken up and chosen, and stands firm in the stability of faith like an immovable mountain. [Col. 0435A] To this is added that Moses and Aaron, foremost among God’s priests, were figures of the new priesthood, through whose ministry God’s people is delivered from the power of the invisible Pharaoh and will be brought into the land of promise. Therefore that people is deservedly blamed and [Col. 0436A] charged with ingratitude, since for such great benefits it owed thanksgiving.

Glory to the exalted Father, and to the Son, the right hand of the Most High, and to the Holy Spirit, who is that delight in which I was mindful of God and was delighted. To the one and triune God be glory and thanksgiving. Amen.

PSALM LXXVII.

[Col. 0435]

[Col. 0435B] “Give heed, my people, to my law.” This psalm sets before the aforesaid combatant the magnificent works of God for meditation: “Give heed,” it says, “my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth,” and so forth. This is plainly directed usefully toward strengthening hope, as it says: “Children who shall be born shall arise and tell it to their children,” immediately adding, “that they may put their hope in God.” For continual meditation upon the works of God is of great value to one struggling in the contest.

Observe, however, that this whole exposition is parabolic, as the Prophet himself testifies: “I shall open my mouth in parables,” he says; and what is said historically in these words is to be understood spiritually. For the words of the whole psalm, sounding of past events, signified future mysteries of Christ: namely Christ himself and the things which now belong to the Church of Christ. Title:

(VERS. 1.) A PSALM OF UNDERSTANDING FOR ASAPH.

This psalm recounts the things divinely done among the ancient people, the benefits God bestowed upon them, and the punishments he inflicted upon the ungrateful. In it the grace of the New Testament is made manifest, and it intends to warn the new people—in whose figure those things were done for the ancients—not to provoke against itself a more grievous wrath of God by ingratitude for his benefits. This intention is evident where it says, “That they may not become as their fathers,” and so forth. The Apostle also teaches this when he says: “These things were written for our correction” (1 Cor. 10:11).

[Col. 0435D] In the title and first two verses, by making a prologue, he first renders his hearers attentive because of the greatness of the matter. Secondly, under a general statement he gathers together what he will later recount at length: namely, God’s benefits, the provocations of the Jews, and their punishments—at “How great things we have heard.” Thirdly, recalling what God did for them in Egypt, he relates what he did in the sea and in the wilderness, and how they provoked him—at “Before their fathers.” Fourthly, he tells how God, postponing punishment, gave them what they desired—at “Therefore the Lord heard.” Fifthly, he explains their punishments, their feigned conversion from fear of punishment, and yet the judgment of God tempered through mercy—at “While their food was still.” Sixthly, he enumerates the plagues inflicted upon Egypt for their sake, comparing with those benefits their wickedness, which he sets forth at “How often.” Seventhly, he tells how God led them, after bringing them out of slavery, into the land of promise, and how there they again offended—[Col. 0436B] at “And he led forth his people like sheep.” Eighthly, he treats of their punishment in the land of promise and how he turned it back upon those by whom he punished them—at “The Lord heard.” Ninthly, he tells from which tribe he chose a king, whom he chose, and in what place he established the kingdom—at “And he rejected.”

Christ speaks throughout: first in the person of the Head, so that the reverence of those who follow may increase; then in the person of Asaph, that is, of the faithful Synagogue, which reproaches evildoers. It must be understood, however, that the things narrated are to be understood not only as figures but also inwardly, in reality. Hence they are called parables and propositions, and the title contains words of understanding—an understanding which Asaph alone did not possess, though it lay beneath the veil of figures destined to be revealed in reality in the fullness of time. Hence the Apostle says: “They ate the same spiritual food” (1 Cor. 10:37). The food was indeed the same then, but the same in signification, not in spirit: the same Christ, figured in the rock for them, manifested in flesh for us.

This must be explained thus: “Here is the understanding for Asaph.” For *understanding* is in the genitive, while *Asaph* is in the dative, as is evident from the Greek articles; and the sense is: These are the words of understanding—that is, of the understanding given to this Asaph, not to one man only, but to the congregation of God’s people, to which we too are gathered from the nations. Although, however, just as then “God was not well pleased with all of them” (1 Cor. 10:5), so neither now is he pleased with all these, nevertheless the Lord neither now nor then cries out and warns without fruit, saying not to one person but to many: “O my people, give heed to my law”—that is, behold with the heart the reality itself which is veiled in figures. And he adds how: “Incline your ear”—that is, attend and understand humbly—“to the words of my mouth.”

It is not David’s law or David’s people; rather, assuming the person of him through whom he spoke, he speaks by the authority of the one whose inspiration filled him. We see this happen daily in the Church, if we look attentively. For the reader, standing in the midst of the people, cries out: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” and so forth (Matt. 22:32). He certainly does not say that he himself is truly God; yet in saying it he does not abandon the rule of truth, because by his voice he asserts the lordship of the one to whom he renders the service of reading. Thus the writers of sacred speech, because they are filled with the Holy Spirit and drawn above themselves, become, as it were, outside themselves, and so utter judgments about themselves as though about others.

[Col. 0437A] “Give heed, my people, to my law.” My people, whom I made peculiar and special by separating you from the multitude of nations and delivering you from the power of Pharaoh, give heed to my law given to you in the wilderness through Moses. Attend to the great things figured in small deeds, lest you be ungrateful to me, who first delivered you from the power of visible Pharaoh and then, what is more, from the Egypt of infernal darkness, after overcoming the prince of darkness by the sacrifice of the true, real Lamb. Give heed, you whom I found in hell: though resting in Abraham’s bosom, you nevertheless lacked that light enjoyed by the holy angels. Give heed, because you were delivered freely, by gratuitous grace and not by the righteousness of the Law, lest you be ungrateful for so great a grace.

But give yet greater heed to my law, you upon whom I did not lay the burden of the ancient Law, but set before you a new law written not on tablets of stone but on tablets of hearts by my finger: that is, by giving the Holy Spirit, who may teach you all truth and announce to you the things to come. Give heed in my ancient and new sayings to the pure truth, which you cannot grasp or savour except through pure and true humility. For as rain coming from heaven flows down from the hills and gathers itself in the valleys, so truth leaves proud hearts and rests in the humble. “Upon whom,” he says, “shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who fears my words?” Therefore incline your ear [Col. 0437C] to the words of my mouth. Incline the ear of your heart through faith, believing the words of my mouth, the words of eternal life, so that, while some go back and cannot bear the words of my mouth as though they were hard, you may humbly reverence even what you do not yet understand and, from the savour of faith, say: “You have the words of eternal life; and to whom shall we go from you?” (John 6:69). Otherwise, if you think lofty thoughts and do not consent to humble things, you will not attain the understanding of Asaph. For Asaph—that is, the faithful congregation—through faith tends toward understanding, knowing that the sharpness of reason is very weak for examining the parabolic propositions of my words. For except for the few to whom it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, I shall speak to the rest in parables, so that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand.

### Verse 2

“I will therefore open my mouth in parables; I will utter propositions from the beginning of the age.” The Evangelist Matthew confirms that this was spoken in the person of Christ, saying: “Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables, and without parables he spoke nothing to them, so that what had been spoken through the Prophet might be fulfilled: ‘I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world’” (Matt. 13:34–35).

It should certainly be observed that, although the Evangelist says, “I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world,” in place of what the Psalm has, “I will utter propositions from the beginning,” we should not understand here parabolically only those things which God performed among his people from the beginning, when he separated that people from the nations by the sign of [Col. 0438A] circumcision, but also those things which he performed from the beginning of the age, or from the foundation of the world. The Hebrew truth agrees with this sense, reading: “I will open my mouth in parables, ancient riddles.”

For example, in the people who, though possessing the bread of angels containing every delight, were not content with it but, indeed, despising it, craved flesh, Adam is rightly understood: in him all sinned, when that father of all humanity despised the tree of life granted to him and desired rather the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which had been forbidden him. From that time, as Jesus says in a certain parable, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers” (Luke 10:30). For he went down by relishing lofty things and perversely desiring inwardly the likeness of God. [Col. 0438B] Therefore, when outwardly tempted through the robbery of the serpent and the woman, he could not stand. For “there fell those who work iniquity; they were cast out and could not stand” (Ps. 35:13): the parents of the human race. And in them all their posterity fell, descending by the same road through the concupiscence of the flesh, so that neither priest nor Levite was excepted—that is, each descended by that same way.

But a certain Samaritan, travelling, though not by the same way—for, having been born into the world without the concupiscence of the flesh, he was free alike from original and actual guilt—came to the aid of the stripped and wounded man. He had been stripped of accidental goods, which could be taken from him, such as innocence and obedience; he had been wounded in natural goods, such as memory, reason, and will. He was not wholly [Col. 0438C] deprived of these; nevertheless, since they were injured and wounded, he was so weakened that forgetfulness oppresses his memory of God, ignorance of truth his reason, and evil concupiscence his will. Nor is there a remedy by which he can be healed, unless that aforesaid Samaritan pours oil and wine into his wounds and undertakes his care.

Before this Samaritan came, however, so that the wounded man himself might recognize his wounds, the priest and Levite of the ancient law went before him: the law itself did not heal, but displayed the wounds themselves. In that law, O how great were the things he commanded our fathers to make known to their children, so that the generation to come might know them!

### Second Part

Up to this point God has spoken in his own person, instructing Asaph. Now Asaph himself speaks—that is, the congregation possessing understanding, as signified by the title [Col. 0438D] of the Psalm.

### Verses 3–4

“How great,” he says, “are the things we have heard; how many and how magnificent are those things which we heard in the Old Testament and recognized in the New as fulfilled just as they had been foretold by fitting heralds. For our fathers too knew these things by divine revelation and faithfully related them to us, their children: first Moses, then the faithful prophets.”

Though the wonderful works of God which they recounted were hidden from unbelievers, they were not hidden from their children—not children in a carnal generation, but in the generation to come, namely the spiritual generation, “who were born not of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:13). So too were their fathers, to whom, because the word of God came and was believed by them, it was granted to hear: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High’” (Ps. 81:6).

Therefore, the things announced to those fathers were not hidden from their children, because the fathers themselves were recounting the praises of the Lord—that is, his praiseworthy deeds, such as the creation of heaven and earth and of all visible and invisible creatures. They also recounted his powers, by which he governs mightily what he has created and orders all things sweetly, so that those who consider his kingdom rightly praise and love him because he powerfully made from nothing what he wisely governs in the course of nature—such as the daily revolution of the firmament and the return of rivers to their source.

Moreover, they declared that he should especially be praised, loved, and feared, recounting the wonders which he performed contrary to ordinary usage: for example, dividing the Red Sea, providing his people a dry path through its midst, raining bread from heaven, and bringing water out of a rock. These and similar wonders he not only foretold truthfully, but also performed effectually. And through these wonders:

### Verse 5

“He raised up a testimony in Jacob, and established a law in Israel.”

Jacob, who is also called Israel, signifies parabolically, through the difference of his names, a difference among the children begotten from him. For by Jacob the less perfect are signified, but by Israel the perfect. Thus the same Jacob is recorded as having limped after his thigh was touched by an angel—his one foot weakened and the other sound (Gen. 32:25, 31). This event was a parable of a greater reality, which we now see fulfilled in his race: part of it blinded and part enlightened. Thus the name Israel properly belongs only to those who have been enlightened, such as that one to whom the great angel who had touched Jacob’s thigh, having taken flesh from him, said: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47).

Likewise, those to whom he said, “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending above the Son of Man” (John 1:51), were true Israelites, because they knew the Word of God as God and saw him manifested in their flesh. “This mystery is great,” says the Apostle: “he was manifested in the flesh, preached to the world, appeared to angels, and was taken up [Col. 0439D] in glory” (1 Tim. 3:16).

He raised up the testimony of so great a mystery in Jacob when Jacob, seeing angels ascending and descending upon the ladder, which signified Christ, understood the sacrament of so great a vision. Therefore, as a sign of the Christ to come, he anointed the stone placed beneath his head, pouring oil upon it. He also set it up as a pillar, foreknowing that the little stone, anointed with the oil of gladness above its companions, would thus be raised and exalted, and would become a great and lofty mountain.

Whenever this testimony had become almost entirely dead, he raised it up in Jacob whenever he raised prophets among his people, whose cries awakened Jacob from sleep. Finally, according to Moses’ prophecy, he raised up from Jacob’s seed a prophet to whom Moses himself bears witness: “Every soul that does not listen to that prophet shall perish from his people” (Acts 3:23). This is the limping of Jacob: those who do not listen to that prophet, although Israelites according to the flesh, do not belong to that Israel of whom it is said here: “And he established a law in Israel.”

For although blindness has happened in part to Israel, nevertheless the great Prophet raised up in Israel established a law in that very Israel, because from that nation the Apostles and many others were chosen. In their hearts he established his law, written by his finger—not upon tablets of stone, hard and senseless, but upon the intellectual tablets of rational minds.

Lest knowledge of this law should remain confined to the narrow bounds of the Jewish nation alone, he made the Apostles themselves, chosen from that nation, to be fathers and teachers also of those children whom he came to gather into one from all nations, though they had been scattered far and wide. He raised up the testimony of this matter in Jacob so powerfully that even that foot of his which had limped, according to the words, “Foreign sons have lied to me; foreign sons have grown old and have limped from their paths” (Ps. 17:46), that limping foot, I say, bears testimony to this truth.

For Caiaphas, the high priest in the year in which Christ was crucified, prophesied, saying: “It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John 11:50). “But,” says John, “he did not say this of himself; rather, because he was high priest that year, he prophesied [Col. 0440C] that Jesus was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but in order to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (ibid., 51–52).

Therefore no one should doubt this truth, whose testimony God, who does not lie, raised up in Jacob and concerning which he established a law in Israel. To testify to his promise, both Jacob and Israel, both the perverse and the good, cooperate: what Caiaphas prophesied, the holy Evangelist confirmed concerning the testimony raised up in Jacob and the law established in Israel. In that law, O how great were the things he commanded our fathers to make known to their children,

### Verse 6

“So that the generation to come might know.”

For he gave the ancient fathers many commands involving mystical observances which they either did not understand themselves or, even if they knew them, did not make known to their contemporaries that they knew them; a veil still lay over the brightness of Moses’ face, while those contemporaries desired temporal and carnal goods and cared little or nothing for heavenly things. Yet these heavenly things were entrusted under a veil to the ancient fathers, so that they might make them known to their children—that is, to those who receive and succeed to their fathers’ faith. These alone are rightly and truly called children of Abraham and of the other faithful fathers.

For those who, rejecting this faith, refused to receive Christ, the seed of Abraham, deserved rightly to hear from Christ himself, Abraham’s seed: “You are of your father the devil, and you desire to do your father’s desires” (John 8:44); likewise, “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham. You do the works of your father” (John 8:39, 41). What works? “He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44).

Thus those who imitate that ancient murderer by killing Christ or Christians are proved truly to be his children. Worst among them were the Jews, stained with the blood of Christ and the saints, who, having heard or known the truth, did not stand in it but held the truth captive in falsehood. Chief among these were the heresiarchs, condemned by their own judgment, since they erred more through malice than ignorance and sent others into error. False Christians succeed them, likewise children of that murderous father because of murderous hatreds, since “whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). When they do not stand in the truth of Christian profession, doing things contrary to their name with diabolical obstinacy, they are shown to be children of that father of whom Truth says: “He did not stand in the truth.”

Therefore only lovers of truth and observers of fraternal charity show themselves to be children of Abraham and of the other faithful Fathers, of whom it is said here: “How great were the things he commanded our fathers to make known to their children, so that the generation to come might know”—that generation which the crooked and adulterous generation refused to know. Let the generation chosen from among the nations, while the Jews are blinded, know the mystery alike of grace and truth. For it is a judgment of truth that branches of the natural olive tree are cut off, and a gift of grace that branches of the wild olive are grafted into the olive tree and made sharers in its richness. To them belongs what follows: [Col. 0441C] “The children who will be born shall arise and tell it to their children.”

### Verse 7

“So that they may place their hope in God, not forget the works of God, and seek his commandments.”

The earlier children, born according to the flesh and desiring only carnal things, refused to arise to seek and set their minds upon heavenly things. But the children who are born of water and the Spirit, moved by the same Spirit through whom they have been reborn, shall arise by seeking and setting their minds upon things above. And not content with their own salvation alone, they shall tell their children, so that they too, having their hearts above, may place their hope in God—not in works of the law, as the Jews did, nor in idols, as the pagans did.

They must not forget God’s works, whether by boasting of their own good works and arrogating them to themselves, though they are nothing except from God, or by doing evil works which God forbids. Rather, always mindful of God, they should fear and love him and seek his commandments—not only in order to understand them, but in order to perform what they understand, because “understanding is good for those who do it” (Ps. 111:10). They should seek, I say, his commandments: by his illumination they are understood, and by his help they are fulfilled. These things the children regenerated through grace must diligently seek,

### Verse 8

“Lest they become like their fathers, a crooked and provoking generation.”

That is, like the Jews, who were a crooked generation because they refused to receive truth, and provoking because, beyond all other bitterness, they strove to provoke their Savior, present among them, with blasphemies and insults, and at last condemned him to a most shameful death.

Therefore this crooked and perverse generation—that generation, I say, which did not set its heart straight so as to correct its mistaken understanding and direct its distorted will toward the straight will of God—did not do what all who are upright in heart, that is, upright in will, strive to do. They subject their own will in every respect to the divine will, striving to imitate him who said: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (Luke 22:42).

The only uprightness of the human will is that it should be directed in all things toward what pleases the divine will. Thus he rightly directed his heart who said: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (Acts 9:6). This was Saul, whose heart had formerly been crooked, but who afterward straightened it by submitting it to the will of God. But the crooked generation [Col. 0442B] did not set its heart straight, willing what God did not will and refusing what God did will. This is the great strength of rational will in angel or human being.

For because “the word of the Lord is upright” (Ps. 33:4), the created will must be lifted up and directed to its uprightness. This the crooked generation does not do, because it does not receive the upright word of the Lord. Why? Because it does not desire it even of itself, with nature as its guide: “the natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14). Nor is that person’s spirit entrusted to God together with God.

The human spirit, left to itself, is weak for doing good, because it cannot even will—or, what is less, think—anything good without God’s help. It must therefore entrust and commit itself to God, as did the one who said: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he, the righteous Judge, is able to keep my deposit until that day” (2 Tim. 1:12). “I know whom I have believed,” he says—that is, I have committed my spirit as a precious deposit. “And I am certain that he is able,” and so forth.

He entrusted his spirit to God, and his spirit was entrusted to God together with God: he believed that he could not do righteousness without God but could do it with God, because it is written, “All things are possible to one who believes” (Mark 9:22). Such was, and in this manner entrusted to God was, the spirit of the one who said: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4:13). Likewise: “Through Christ we have such confidence toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:3–5).

Very different is the crooked generation, which did not set its heart straight and whose spirit was not entrusted to God, nor is with God. For just as the one who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit with him, so a human spirit rebellious against the Lord is separated from the Lord, though he is present everywhere, just as one who is blinded is separated from light, however near it may be.

The Hebrew truth reads: “A turning-aside and provoking generation; a generation which did not prepare its heart, and whose spirit did not believe God.” For one is far from God who, even if he believes God, nevertheless does not believe *in* God. Much farther indeed from God departs one who does not even believe God, whether he promises good things or threatens evil things. But the one who believes God may advance by the steps of faith so as also to believe in God: that is, believing, to love him to whom he believes, thirsting and seeking no other reward of faith than God himself.

Such faith has grace, which not only forgives sins but also causes the human spirit to cooperate with it in good works. To express this, the Septuagint translators, whose translation we use, said, in place of “His spirit did not believe God,” which is what the Hebrew truth has, “His spirit was not entrusted with God.” That is, it did not possess the faith which, through hope and charity as mediators, obtains what the law commands; but it wished to be justified, as it were, by works of the law. This follows:

### Verse 9

“The sons of Ephraim, aiming and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle.”

By the sons of Ephraim more than by another tribe, he intended to signify the whole Jewish nation by a part, because Ephraim was Joseph’s younger son, upon whom the patriarch Jacob laid his right hand in blessing and set him before his elder brother Manasseh. This tribe, severed and divided from the house of David, worshiped idols instead of the true God, reverencing with divine worship the golden calves made by Jeroboam and also adoring Baal.

Therefore this tribe is especially blamed here because, though foremost in blessing, it became most contemptible in conduct. On account of the idolatry already mentioned, it was wholly rejected; nor was its captivity, in which it was carried away to Assyria, relieved, whereas Judah’s captivity was relieved after seventy years. Thus it is said later: “He did not choose the tribe of Ephraim, but chose the tribe of Judah.” So “the last shall be first, and the first last” (Matt. 19:30): Ephraim the younger was set before Manasseh the elder, yet his precedence did not endure, because he went backward on the day of battle.

Let the lesser one set before the greater fear, lest he who did not spare the natural branches should not spare others either, should he find them unfruitful. In the same figure righteous Abel was set before his elder brother; Isaac before Ishmael; Jacob before Esau; Perez before Zerah; David before his elder brothers; and the publican before the Pharisee—that is, the Christian people before the Jewish people. The latter, pursuing the righteousness of the law, did not attain to the law of righteousness, because, “aiming and shooting the bow, they turned back on the day of battle.”

For like men practising before battle, they bent the bow of their own strength and, as if shooting arrows from that same bow in vain, said to Moses: “All that the Lord our God has spoken we will do” (Exod. 24:7). They turned back on the day of battle because, in the time of temptation, they withdrew and killed the prophet whom Moses had commanded them to obey.

On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says in his work on Job:

> **[Note: Col. 0443. In St. Paterius, *Exposition of Sacred Scripture from the Books of St. Gregory*, book XI, chapter 103.]**
>
> Often we who seem to be teachers preach, instruct hearers, and arm others by speaking; but we ourselves refuse to go into the contest of labors, as it is written: “The sons of Ephraim, bending the bow and shooting their arrows, turned back on the day [Col. 0444A] of battle.” Ephraim is interpreted “fruitfulness.” And what fruitfulness is such or so holy as the tongue of teachers? While it sows words, it multiplies fruits of souls. When we prepare to teach and seek the meaning of sacred Scripture, we bend the bow. When we utter words of correction, we shoot arrows.
>
> For “bow” is sometimes used in sacred discourse to mean sacred Scripture itself, which consists, as it were, of horn and string from the two Testaments. The Old Testament is represented by the horn because of its hardness; the New, brought about when the Lord was incarnate, is signified by the string. And as the string is drawn, the horn is bent, because when the New Testament is examined, the Old is inclined away from the hardness of the letter and bent toward spiritual understanding, since its rigor is not retained in hardness.
>
> The arrows are these very words which teachers utter. Thus the Prophet rightly says also of holy teachers entering among the Gentiles: “They shall enter there with arrows and a bow.” Therefore, when we weigh the sayings of sacred Scripture, we bend the bow; when we give words of instruction, we shoot arrows. But we turn back on the day of battle, because we sometimes refuse to undergo toil in struggles against vices.

Figuratively, “aiming and shooting the bow” is said in the sense of “aiming the bow and shooting missiles,” namely, from the bow. Therefore some manuscripts read: “The sons of Ephraim, aiming and shooting with a bow,” or “with bows.” The sense is clear: having aimed the bow and shot arrows from it before battle, they turned back on the day of battle—or, as the Hebrew reads, “they turned their backs on the day of battle.” How do you prove this? By the fact that:

### Verse 10

“They did not keep God’s covenant,” comprehended in the Ten Commandments, “and they refused to walk in his law”—not because they were unable, but because they were unwilling.

This is not speaking of the law of Moses, which consists almost wholly of ceremonial observances and sacrifices. Moses instituted these after the guilt incurred by the calf, not because God commanded but because he permitted it, in order to call a people accustomed to Egyptian sacrifices away from idolatry by sacrifices that figured the truth. Rather, it is speaking of the law and covenant of God, established before the guilt of the calf by words to Abraham and also written for Moses.

Thus the lawgiver himself, distinguishing God’s law from the ceremonial law, affirms that the former was written in the Ten Commandments by God’s finger. He never said this of the ceremonial law, nor ought he to have said it, since he knew it to be temporary. And when the Apostle says, “This I say: a covenant confirmed by God is not nullified by the law that came four hundred and thirty years later, so as to annul the promise” (Gal. 3:17), he immediately adds: “Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made; it was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (ibid., 19).

He says that the ceremonial law was ordained not by the hand or finger of God, but “by the hand of the mediator,” Moses, while asserting that the covenant was confirmed by God. Conversely, Moses said that the commandments of life were written by God’s finger, while he said nothing of the kind about sacrifices or the observance of solemn festivals.

Therefore, not only where Moses repeatedly speaks of unleavened bread and gives law concerning annual festivals, but wherever certain institutions are given to that people through the hand of the same mediator, institutions without which the covenant confirmed by God with Abraham stood, they must be understood not as commands but as permissions, on account of transgressions, as the Apostle most truly says. They were certain bonds imposed because of transgressions, so that, while the people were occupied with the rite of such sacrifices or festivals, they would not be free to stray from their God into their own inventions [Col. 0445B] and unlawful idolatrous worship.

Accordingly, God himself speaks through the Prophet to those trusting in such things: “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh. For I did not speak with your fathers, nor command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices; but this word I commanded them, saying: ‘Hear my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people; and walk in every way that I command you, that it may be well with you’” (Jer. 7:21–23).

“I did not speak,” he says—that is, “I did not command.” For whatever Moses commanded of such things as though from my mouth, he commanded not because I commanded it, but because I permitted it. And in David: “Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 50:13), with many similar sayings.

Therefore, when the Jews are blamed here because they did not keep God’s covenant and would not walk in his law, covenant or law must be understood in this way, lest anyone suppose that they are rebuked because they neglected those sacrifices concerning which God himself says in another Psalm: “Hear, my people, and I will speak, O Israel; and I will testify to you: I am your God. I will not rebuke you concerning sacrifices” (Ps. 50:7–8).

Rather, they are rightly rebuked for the transgression of faith by which Abraham believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. For they despised, denied, and—what is worse—killed Christ, whose day Abraham saw in the Spirit and rejoiced, but whom they themselves saw in the flesh. Calling down his blood upon their descendants, they cried: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25).

Why, then, did they hate him in this manner? Because they refused to walk in his law. For he came not to abolish but to fulfill the law comprehended in the Ten Commandments. For example, the command spoken to the ancients, “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20:13), he did not abolish but fulfilled when he forbade anger, from which murder proceeds. Likewise, “You shall not commit adultery” (ibid., 14), he did not abolish but fulfilled and confirmed when he forbade looking at a woman in order to lust after her. Likewise, “You shall not swear falsely” (Matt. 5:33), he did not abolish but confirmed when he forbade his disciples to swear at all. Thus he did not weaken but confirmed the other commandments of his law.

[Col. 0446A] Here the objection is raised that observance of the Sabbath, included among the Ten Commandments, is rejected in evangelical teaching, in which God’s law seems partly abolished. But one should know that, in commanding observance of the Sabbath, God directed the person to remember that day on which he rested from his works, so that, following God’s own example, a human being might hope for rest after the completion of his works. Thus, when the Apostle said, “Therefore a sabbath-rest remains for the people of God” (Heb. 4:9), he added: “Let us hasten to enter that rest, lest anyone fall into the same example of unbelief” (Heb. 4:11). He had previously stated that certain persons did not enter into rest because of their unbelief, and that God was recorded as swearing in his wrath that they would not enter his rest.

Therefore, when he says in the law, “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. 20:8), it is as though he says: In all your works, direct yourself to this end, that when your works are completed you may enter God’s rest. The words that follow indicate this meaning: “For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth and all things that are in them, and rested on the seventh day; and he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it” (ibid., 11). This is the sabbath-rest which, as the Apostle affirms, remains for the people of God.

For God’s lack of concern for carnal sabbath observance is understood from Isaiah’s words: “My soul hates your new moons and Sabbaths; they have become burdensome to me; I am weary of bearing them” (Isa. 1:13–14). He added the reason, saying: “For your hands are full of blood.” Therefore, the Christian people, rejecting the Sabbath polluted by the blood of Christ and the righteous whom the Jews killed, should sanctify the Sabbath day—or rather celebrate the day sanctified by God in such a way that, in all their works, they hope only for eternal rest as their reward. For that rest is the sanctified day which has shone upon us and of which it is said: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. 118:24). Likewise: “Proclaim day from day” (Ps. 96:2), that is, the Son from the Father.

For he is the true light enlightening every human being coming into this world. By his illumination, the souls of the righteous now rest as though in a holy Sabbath, awaiting the eighth day of their resurrection. We too should await and hope for it, once our good works have been completed—as though they were the creatures of six days—in the six works of mercy through which that rest is prepared. To it those will be called who hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

The expectation of this rest and Sabbath, in which souls stripped of their bodies rest, is indeed blessed. But the solemnity will be greater when, as though at the Paschal full moon, the evening of the Sabbath grows bright into the first day of the week. For when the full number of the Gentiles has entered and all the remnant of Israel has been saved, so that no elect person predestined to rest is lacking from the Church—which is signified by the full and perfect Paschal moon—then there shall be the eighth day and truly the solemnity of solemnities. It will be begun on the eighth day by the Lord’s resurrection and completed at the end, when all members are raised together with their head, Christ.

Since the Spirit will from then onward say to them, “that they may rest from their labors,” the Church more rightly celebrates the eighth day made glorious by the Lord’s resurrection than the seventh day darkened by the Jews’ crime. For on the next day, after the Preparation—that is, on the Sabbath—they came to Pilate, asserting that Jesus was a deceiver and asking that the tomb be guarded. Let the Jews, then, have their Sabbath polluted by their own crime. But Christians, knowing that Christ himself is the day sanctified by the Father, as he himself says, “whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world” (John 10:36), should continually observe his festival, not merely commemorating his past resurrection but also awaiting their own future resurrection.

Thus they shall truly fulfill the law saying, “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. 20:8), because the same Christ who now shines as Sabbath to souls resting in him will shine and be more fully glorious to them on the eighth day through the resurrection of their bodies, according as we await the Lord Jesus himself, who will transform the body of our lowliness so that it may be conformed to the body of his glory.

Abraham received the covenant of this day when he rejoiced to see him: he saw and rejoiced. This covenant the sons of Ephraim did not keep, who saw Christ and hated him, as he himself says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father, so that the saying written in their law may be fulfilled: ‘They hated me without cause’” (John 15:22, 24–25).

Why did they hate him in this manner? Because they refused to walk in his law—not through ignorance or weakness, but through malice, disparaging his obedience. To this malice they added ingratitude, because:

### Verses 11–12

“They forgot his benefits and his wonders which he showed them”—not only by doing many good works among them while present in the flesh, works such as no one else performed, but also long before he was revealed, when he performed wonders before their fathers in the land of Egypt, [Col. 0447D] in the field of Tanis.

### Third Part

The order is artistic. For first he recounts the events of the Exodus, then the plagues of Egypt, which he nevertheless mentions briefly when he says, “He performed wonders before their fathers”—not only before the evil fathers, of whom it has already been said, “lest they become like their fathers, a crooked and provoking generation,” but also before good fathers, such as Moses and Aaron, and before them Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Since the one who sent Moses wished to call himself the God of these fathers, those wonders in Egypt were also performed before them, present in the Spirit. For God is not God of the dead but of the living: all those live to him who said to Moses, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14). Likewise: “I am the God of Abraham, the God [Col. 0448A] of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (ibid., 15), signifying nature in the one designation and grace in the other.

For what is “he who is”? It is natural to him that being and being something are not different things—for example, for him, to be and to be good or powerful are the same. This is not so for other creatures, for whom being and being something are different: for example, for a human being or an angel, it is one thing to exist and another to be good or powerful, just as it is one thing for a body to exist and another to be something. Likewise, the goodness by which he is good is nothing other than what he himself is; the truth by which he is true is nothing other than what he himself is; the wisdom by which he is wise is nothing other than what he himself is; the life by which he lives is nothing other than what he himself is.

To be something—that is, to be of a certain quantity or quality, large or small, black or white—is different from simply being. Every composite thing is thus constituted: for it, being and being something are different. But God, who is simple, does not have one thing as what he is and another as that by which he is. For in him, being and being God, good, just, or anything else are not different things. In a human being, humanity, by which the person is human, is one thing and the human person another; but in God, the divinity by which he is God is nothing other than God himself.

Likewise, the goodness by which he is good is nothing other than himself; the truth by which he is true is nothing other than himself; the wisdom by which he is wise is nothing other than himself; and the life by which he lives is nothing other than himself. Therefore he rightly says: “I am who I am. Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: ‘He Who Is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14). This alone is his name of nature.

But his name of grace is this: that he who is and needs nothing else in order to be deigns to be called the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, the God of the Hebrews—of those who have no being except from him, nor any good or blessed being except with him and in him.

Accordingly, before these fathers who lived in him, he himself worked wonders in the land of Egypt: wonderful consolations for the Hebrews through mercy, and wonderful torments for the Egyptians through justice. He subdued them not by bears and lions, but by frogs, gnats, flies, locusts, and caterpillars, which fought on his behalf against their pride; he did not deign to humble them by an angelic or human army, except that in the final plague their firstborn were struck by an angel. I, Asaph, say that these plagues, these wonders, were wrought in the land of Egypt; and, that they may be more clearly known from the particular name of the province, I recall that they were wrought in the plain of Tanis. Tanis, or Taphnis, is a city of Egypt, where, as in the other places of Egypt, the plagues occurred—not secretly or in a corner, but in the plain, that is, openly. But since these matters are expressed through parables and propositions, as the beginning of the psalm teaches, their mystical meaning must be sought.

Egypt, therefore, which is interpreted “darkness and tribulation,” is the world. Tanis means “a humble command,” so that the plain of Tanis is the level ground of the humble command. Before the Fathers of the New Testament the Lord set forth this humble command, saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI.29). Before those who first received this command, and through them, he worked wonders; and he wonderfully exalted them, [Col. 0449A] making them princes over all the earth and finally transferring them into angelic and heavenly glory. Thus their followers may place their hope in God, knowing from their example that everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted, and, from the example of the Egyptians, that everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled. For those also were exceedingly honoured who, after the example of Moses and Aaron, became friends of God by resisting the invisible Pharaoh; and the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob—the God of the Hebrews—plunged their enemies into the sea, indeed into hell: that is, the God of apostles, martyrs, and confessors, and of all who pass from the darkness of worldly blindness into the wonderful light promised and reserved for such persons in the land of promise. Truth himself says: “He who follows me [Col. 0449B] does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John VIII.12).

For by Abraham, who obeyed God saying, “Go forth from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. XII.1), the order of the apostles is rightly understood; it was first to obey Christ teaching that followers of perfection must leave all things and follow him alone. Hence Peter says: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. XIX.27). By Isaac, who consented to be slain by his father’s sword as a sacrificial victim of a holocaust, the company of martyrs is understood. By Jacob, the husband of Rachel and Leah, the choir of confessors, devoted to contemplation and teaching, is suitably represented, when the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob is named and invoked. But when he is called the God of the Hebrews—which means “those who pass over”—all those are fittingly signified [Col. 0449C] who cross through Egyptian darkness by the Red Sea into God’s wonderful light. Thus “God of the Hebrews” is equivalent to saying, “God of the righteous who pass from the darkness of ignorance to the light of Wisdom,” which says: “Pass over to me, all you who desire me, and be filled with my generations” (Ecclus. XXIV.26). It follows:

**VERSE 13.** “He divided the sea and led them through, and made the waters stand as in a wineskin.” The history is well known; but since it has been set forth parabolically, let us pass over the outer shell of the letter, familiar as it is, and seek the kernel of its mystical sense. The Red Sea is baptism reddened by Christ’s blood, through which a passage was prepared for the people of God fleeing Egypt; there too the invisible Pharaoh and all his army are drowned. Tropologically also, the waters of carnal desire are as though in a wineskin when the slippery desires of the wicked, finding no effect in action, are compressed under the carnal heart. They are divinely restrained when the invisible Pharaoh is renounced, so that one may arrive at the promised reward of God’s glory as at the land of promise.

**VERSE 14.** “And he led them by a cloud by day, and throughout the night by the illumination of fire.” The pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night, showing the way in the wilderness to the ancient people, was indeed a great spectacle; but far greater in the eyes of believers is the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection. Through it God incarnate, [Col. 0450A] by the cloud of his humanity, overshadows or cools them against the heat of the sun, which dries up seed cast upon rocky ground, and which also burns the flower of grass through evil inducements; and by the fire of his Divinity he illuminates and inflames them against the darkness of ignorance and the cold of wickedness, by whose excessive abundance the charity of many grows cold. Christ as man led his faithful people in the cloud by day, and the same Christ as God led them throughout the night in the illumination of fire, so that he does not permit them to stray from the way of truth either in the day of prosperity or in the night of adversity.

**VERSE 15.** “He divided the rock in the wilderness and gave them abundant drink as from the deep.” Observe the miracles in opposites. To the people journeying through the deep in the midst of the sea he provided a dry path; in deserted [Col. 0450B] land, trackless and waterless, he brought water from the rock for people and beasts to drink, abundantly as from the deep.

**VERSE 16.** “And he brought forth water from the rock and made waters flow like rivers.” Wherever they went, the rock followed them—not because the rock moved from its place, but because the water flowing from the rock followed them. Someone expressed the mystery of this miracle rather elegantly in verse:

> Twice the leader and prophet strikes the flint with his rod;  
> The leader’s two strokes are the two timbers of the cross.  
> From the rock a fountain is given to the people without measure;  
> From the Lord’s body abundant salvation comes to humankind.

For the struck rock is Christ crucified, from whose right side came clean, living water. Whoever drinks it will have within himself a fountain of water springing up into [Col. 0450C] eternal life. This we say of the Spirit, whom those believing in him receive. That Spirit, to be sure, was signified by the visible water which issued from the right side of the temple—that is, from the body of Christ. For Christ had, as it were, two sides: the left, according to the time of weakness and mortality; the right, according to the time of his humanity’s glorification. No water came forth from his left side, because the Spirit had not been given while Jesus was not yet glorified. But his right side poured forth waters for the salvation of his people, because, crowned with the glory and honour of resurrection, on the very day of his resurrection and glorification he breathed upon the apostles, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose [Col. 0450D] sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John XX.23).

Likewise, crowned with the diadem of his ascension, he poured forth the water of the Holy Spirit in such abundance that the apostles and disciples, having drunk from it, were thought drunk and were said to be full of new wine. For such is this water that it truly produces a certain sober drunkenness in those who drink it, in the manner in which the Apostle teaches that it should be drunk: “Do not,” he says, “be drunk with wine, in which is debauchery; but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing to the Lord in your hearts” (Eph. V.18–19). Psalms, hymns, and the other spiritual songs are like silver and golden vessels containing the drink of salvation. We drink from them as often as we sing psalms not only with the spirit [Col. 0451A] but also with the mind, following the example of him who said: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (I Cor. XIV.15). This is to sing psalms truly and wisely: when the mind understands what is either uttered by the mouth or pondered in the spirit by meditation alone.

For “spirit” here means that faculty of the soul by which we turn over in our mind things read or heard, retaining them in memory. But the mind is fruitless unless the belly of memory, in which such things have been accumulated, has within it a fire and heat that cook these matters, as it were, like raw food. While the stomach of the mind thus burns and is hot with holy desires during psalm-singing, chanting, or meditation, the whole inner person grows fat from this, as though sucking honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone.

But the phrase, “He gave them abundant drink as from [Col. 0451B] the deep, and he brought forth waters like rivers,” signifies the abundance of grace flowing with the rush of a river from this rock and making glad the whole city of God. There the strong drink and the simple are watered like beasts, when “day pours forth speech to day, and night declares knowledge to night” (Ps. XVIII.3), and wine is given to the strong while milk is given to little ones. Where? In the wilderness, the desert, the solitude: to those who journey there and flee Egypt, that is, who sincerely renounce this unclean world and thirst more for the most limpid waters issuing from the rock of the desert than for the muddy waters of poetic and philosophical teaching—or, worse still, heretical teaching—which are “stolen waters,” appearing “sweeter” to fools than the water of wisdom (Prov. IX.17).
