[Col. 0451C] **VERSE 17.** “And they continued to sin against him.” Before they received water from the rock, they tested God by murmuring; and although they had seen so many wonders in crossing the sea and in the bringing forth of water from the rock, they nevertheless, still not believing in God’s power, tested God in the waterless place—that is, in dryness. For it is a most grievous sin not to believe in God’s power. On account of it the Spirit of truth also reproves the world concerning sin, especially the sin of unbelief, since from this sin, as from an evil root, the shoots of all other sins spring forth. Through faithlessness the life of those who neither believe nor hope in God perishes, whereas, on the contrary, “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. I.17).

Therefore, through the sin of unbelief, by which they doubted God’s power when they said, “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” they provoked him to anger. The anger aroused by their provocations was so great that he was angry also with Moses and Aaron over this matter, at the water of Contradiction, which he brought forth from the rock by a repeated miracle for the second time. For the first time, as is read in Exodus, when they had moved their camp from the wilderness of Sin and came to the place called Rephidim, the struck rock gave water (Exod. XVII.6): this was when, as has already been said, “he divided the rock in the wilderness and gave them abundant drink as from the deep.” The second time, as is read in the book of Numbers, when they were in the wilderness of Sin, in the place called Kadesh, water again failed. There Moses sinned by doubting and the others had despaired; nevertheless, when Moses struck the rock twice, [Col. 0452A] water was given, which was called the Water of Contradiction (Num. XX.11).

All these things, however, happened to them figuratively. The fact that water brought forth from the rock at the first stroke was not called the Water of Contradiction, because Moses did not doubt there, whereas in the second case, where he doubted, the water that came forth from the rock struck twice was called Contradiction, indicates that Moses, one and the same man, represented believers in one place and unbelievers in another. When he confidently brought water from the rock, he represented the apostles and the other faithful who believe without doubt in Christ saying: “The water that I shall give—whoever drinks of it shall never thirst” (John IV.13); and, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John VII.37–38). But when, like an unbeliever, [Col. 0452B] he said, “Can I bring forth water for you from this rock?” (Num. XX.10), he represented the scribes and Pharisees crucifying Christ, and, as it were, striking him twice with the two timbers of the cross, yet not at all believing that living waters would come forth from the temple of his body.

Unbelievers still imitate these people, crucifying Christ again when they handle his sacraments unworthily and refuse to drink the waters of his teaching and wisdom, instead contradicting them by word or deed. Moses and Aaron, though in themselves friends of God, were nevertheless rebuked in their figure, God saying: “Because you did not believe me, so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring this people into the land which I swore to their fathers” [Col. 0452C] (Num. XX.12). These friends of God are certainly not doubted to have been brought with the other faithful into the true land of promise, the paradise of rejoicing. Yet they did not enter that figurative land of promise, the Holy Spirit thereby signifying that rebels and unbelievers shall not enter into the Lord’s rest—the people to whom he swore in his anger, saying: “If they enter into my rest” (Ps. XCIV.11). For by righteous judgment he swore in anger against them because they provoked the Most High to anger in the waterless place—that is, in the dryness of their hearts rather than of the place—and, not asking for water, provoked God’s anger with distrust. Yet in the same faithlessness

**VERSE 18.** “They tested God in their hearts, that [Col. 0452D] by murmuring they might ask food for their souls.” By “souls” temporal life is signified, as in: “He who loses his soul for my sake shall find it” (Matt. X.39). Therefore these murmurers sought temporal rather than spiritual food, prefiguring perverse petitioners, who often murmur against God in their prayers and requests unless they obtain temporal rather than eternal goods. They do not believe that, if they served God by seeking first and principally the kingdom of God, all these things would be added to them. Nor was it enough for them to test God in their hearts by evil thinking; from the abundance of the heart they added the sin of speech to the sin of thought.

**VERSE 19.** “And they spoke wickedly concerning God.” For [Col. 0453A] they said distrustfully: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? He has indeed given water from the rock like rivers. We see this miracle; nevertheless, we know that water often flows from veins in rocks without a miracle. But who would for that reason believe that bread can be given in an utterly uncultivated wilderness, when it exceeds the limits of natural possibility that a table of abundant refreshment should be prepared in the wilderness—not for one person, but for so great and so numerous a people, accustomed to be satiated in Egypt?” Thus we speak in amazement and doubt:

**VERSE 20.** “For he struck the rock, and the waters flowed, and the torrents overflowed. Can he also give bread or prepare a table for his people?” The order of this psalm is not the same as that in which the holy and truthful history was composed through Moses. There events are narrated in the same order in which they happened: bread is first recorded as having been given to those who asked, and water afterward as having been produced from the struck rock. But here the sequence has been reversed thus: “He divided the rock in the wilderness and gave them abundant drink as from the deep; and he brought water from the rock, and made waters flow like rivers.” Once this has been stated first, the following is added: “And they continued to sin against him.” In what respect? They said: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? For he struck the rock and the waters flowed, and torrents overflowed. Can he also give bread or prepare a table for his people?” By saying this, the passage plainly seems to make the waters flowing and torrents overflowing from the struck rock earlier, [Col. 0453C] while “he commanded the clouds above, opened the gates of heaven, rained manna upon them to eat, and gave them the bread of heaven” comes later.

Why is this so? Clearly because he speaks in parables, as he stated at the beginning of the psalm: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak propositions from the beginning.” Lest the solution or interpretation of these parables should be difficult, the Apostle, after saying, “They drank from the spiritual rock which followed them,” immediately added: “Now the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X.4). This saying was like a single ray of sunlight cast through a window which dispersed the darkness of an entire house, enabling us plainly to see that in these parables we should understand another rock and another water flowing from the rock.

The Lord also, when the Jews said to him, “Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat’” (John VI.31), immediately contradicted them, answering: “Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven” (John VI.32). It was not he who gave it in the past, as you say; it is this one who gives it in the present. Speaking thus, Truth showed that the true bread signified in this psalm was that whose testimony the Jews, opponents of truth, had misused; but the bread which they remembered their fathers to have eaten according to the historical account was figurative and not true. They had wrongly fitted the parable of this psalm, uttered in a spiritual sense, to the literal sense of the history. Therefore, with manifold authority—[Col. 0454A] namely, Asaph’s testimony here speaking in parables; the faith of the Apostle saying, “All these things happened to them in a figure” (I Cor. X.11); and the truth of Christ, who in the Gospel declares himself to be the true bread—let us faithfully understand in the striking of the rock the Lord’s passion, and in the abundance of bread descending with dew upon the camp his body, which we receive from the holy altar. Thus we may show that the order of this parable rests on the truth of the matter, and that the reversal has not occurred in this parable without reason, contrary to the letter of the Law.

But someone may say: “Even if the dividing of the rock signified Christ’s passion, and manna Christ’s table prepared for our salvation, historical events still ought not to have been reversed, so that the Prophet first says the rock was struck and waters flowed, and afterward that the clouds above were commanded and manna rained upon them for food. For before the burden of the cross struck the Lord Jesus Christ, he himself opened the gates of heaven by his word and rained this manna.” To this I say: the Lord did not do this in himself before his passion, but at the very moment of his passion. He had already been sold; he was already being betrayed; his soul was already sorrowful unto death; the hour was already at hand in which he was afraid and sad, was in agony, and prayed while sweating drops of blood; because the certainty of his imminent death was before him, he already said that he was not in the world. Hence this too should be noted: although elsewhere he had commended this bread—that is, the necessary eating of himself—by saying, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John VI.54), he nowhere showed how this could or should be done except in that hour in which he was betrayed, in which, as has been said, he was agonizing in the distress of his passion. Why? Because the work of his passion is the reality and power of the sacrament, by which the substance of bread and wine is transformed for us into the reality of his body and blood. Hence the Apostle says: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (I Cor. XI.26).

[Col. 0454D] Moreover, no one can be unaware that each person must be invited first to faith in the Lord’s passion, and then to participation in this bread: that is, one must first be baptized into his death before being admitted to the holy altar to partake of his flesh and blood. The Prophet therefore rightly reverses the historical acts in this way: the rock is first said to have been divided so that waters might flow; afterward the gates of heaven are opened so that man may be fed with the bread of angels.

Again someone may say: “Since the Apostle says of the fathers, ‘They all ate the same spiritual food, and they all drank the same spiritual drink’ (I Cor. X.3–4), how does Christ say, when speaking to the Jews, ‘Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven’?” We answer: when the Apostle says, “the same food” (John VI.32), the wording in no way indicates that he wished us to understand, “the same as ours.” Indeed, great Fathers before us have understood this reference implicitly. But, as has been said by someone concerning another matter, although the greatness of their authority, holiness, and wisdom may overwhelm us, we are guided more by the evangelical authority of Christ than by the arguments of any eloquence. Reason does not allow figure and reality to be the same. The Apostle said concerning this and the other things that happened: “All things happened to them in a figure” (I Cor. X.11).

Accordingly, when he says “all” and “all,” and then makes a distinction by saying, “But God was not well pleased with many of them, for they were overthrown in the wilderness” (I Cor. X.5), it is plainly understood as though he had said: “All ate one food, and all drank one spiritual drink”—that is, food and drink produced not by a natural process but by spiritual power—and yet not all entered that land of promise. This was a figure of us: although we all partake of the same sacrament of Christ’s body, we shall not all be admitted alike into that land of the living, whether we have lived well or badly. Therefore, what Truth says, denying it of the past but affirming it of the present—“Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven” (John VI.32)—and what the Apostle of truth says—“They all [Col. 0455C] ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink” (I Cor. X.4)—are manifestly shown by reason not to be inconsistent or contrary.

Now, intending to say something concerning the mystery of this bread, let us consider the letter of the history, which is as follows: “Behold, I shall rain breads from heaven upon you. Let the people go out and gather what is sufficient for each day” (Exod. XVI.4). “I shall rain upon you,” he says. In accord with this word the Prophet says: “He commanded the clouds above, opened the gates of heaven, and rained manna upon them to eat.” And, indicating what he means by manna, he immediately adds: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels.” Who is this bread of heaven, this bread of angels? Does an angel in heaven feed on that bread which those people gathered, like coriander seed, and ground in a mill or pounded in a mortar? The bread of heaven, the bread of angels, is therefore he who says in his Gospel: “I am the living bread who came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever” (John VI.51–52). For he is the nourishment and life of the angelic nature: the angels desire to look upon him. The angel who despised doing this fell and became the devil. He suffers the perpetual hunger of this bread; he is always pale, and death follows him.

The Prophet’s exclamation and amazement are therefore fitting: because, once the gates of heaven had been opened, man ate the bread of angels! [Col. 0456A] How did this happen? It happened because “he commanded the clouds above and opened the gates of heaven”: that is, he foreshadowed this to the apostles and also to the prophets, concerning whom Scripture says, “dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. XVII.12), that is, hidden knowledge in the prophets. Then, through himself, he opened the gates of heaven formerly closed to humankind, having dissolved in his flesh the ancient enmities. Thus he joined heavenly things to earthly things—that is, he associated human beings with angels—so that they might feed on the same bread of heaven: the angels in the manifest sight of Divinity, while those still on earth receive it in the sacrament of godliness, of which the Apostle says: “Great is the sacrament of godliness, which was manifested in flesh, justified in spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the nations, believed in by the world, and taken up in glory” (I Tim. III.16).

Here, indeed, “bread of heaven” and “bread of angels” are spoken in the singular; there, however, “I shall rain breads upon you” is said in the plural. Yet you should not suppose any discrepancy. For here too it is subsequently said in the plural: “He sent them foods in abundance.” Christ, or Christ’s one body, is bread according to himself; nevertheless, according to local churches and the persons who offer or receive it, you rightly speak in the plural of innumerable foods or breads. The very word “rained,” which both Scriptures use—God saying in the former, “Behold, I shall rain,” and the latter saying, “He rained manna upon them to eat”—signifies the same abundance prepared everywhere in the world for all, great and small. Thus the great Prophet says of himself: “You have prepared a table before [Col. 0456C] me”; and of us, though least among all: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and those who seek the Lord shall praise him; their hearts shall live for ever and ever” (Ps. XXI.27). It follows:

**VERSE 21.** “Therefore the Lord heard and delayed.” **FOURTH PART**, in which it is narrated that God, delaying punishment, first gave what they requested, although they asked while murmuring and testing him, and afterward punished the murmurers and testers. He did not immediately punish those who murmured, but delayed the penalty. Yet first he heard them by granting their request, lest he seem unable to give; and after he gave what they sought, fire was kindled in Jacob and anger rose up in Israel. Do you wish to know in what he heard them [Col. 0456D] and what anger he delayed? He heard them, namely, in this:

**VERSES 23, 24, 25.** “He commanded the clouds above, opened the gates of heaven, and rained manna upon them to eat; and he gave them bread of heaven, not gained by human labour.” It was great grace that man ate the bread of angels: namely, the sign of the bread of angels called manna, which means, “What is this?” The Jewish people at first did not know what it was. Likewise, people wonderingly ask concerning Christ’s body what it is or how it can come to be. To those who inquire devoutly, the truth of this matter is disclosed; but to unbelievers it remains wholly hidden.

It follows: “He sent them foods in abundance.” For he sent them not only manna but also other foods [Col. 0457A] in an abundance they could not consume. How did he send them?

**VERSE 26.** “He brought the south wind from the upper heaven,” so that it might blow near the camp, “and he brought in the south-west wind,” not by a chance movement of the breeze but by his power.

**VERSES 27, 28, 29, 30.** “And in this power, through warm southern winds, he rained flesh upon them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea”—that is, quails. So that there might be no difficulty in catching them, they fell in the midst of their camp, flying two cubits above the ground around their tents. The Lord is read to have given these quails twice to check their murmuring: first in the wilderness of Sin, then in the wilderness of Paran, a place called the Graves of Craving because of the plague which occurred there. For after they ate the flesh they craved and were exceedingly filled—indeed, to nausea—and their desire had thus brought them so far that they were not deprived of what they desired, they were immediately punished and very many of them killed. “For while the food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose against them and killed their fat ones.”

It should certainly be noted that, when in the wilderness of Sin they asked food for their souls, although they spoke wickedly of God, saying, “Can God give bread or prepare a table for his people?”, they were nevertheless not punished; rather, though they asked only for bread, God freely gave them quails as well. But here, namely in the wilderness of Paran, because they possessed the bread of heaven [Col. 0457C] and despised it, burning without any necessity with a craving for flesh, they were punished most severely. These things, therefore, like the rest that happened to them, “were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (I Cor. X.11), so that, even if we ask God for necessary provisions to use, we may nevertheless beware of craving superfluities to abuse. The Apostle James instructs us in this caution, saying: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask badly, that you may spend it upon your desires” (Jas. IV.3).

Mystically, by the south wind and the south-west wind—southern and warm winds—are understood teachers bright in understanding and fervent in charity. When they blow in heaven, great hearers fly like clouds; but for the nourishment of little ones [Col. 0457D] on earth they are sometimes brought down from heaven, like him who said: “I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons; I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (I Cor. III.1–2). Thus the eternal Shepherd feeds the small faith of those who do not test but believe, through the fleshly tongue, uttering signs of sounds that pass through the air like clean winged creatures. It is lawful and salutary to feed upon them when the south wind blows, signifying the Holy Spirit, by whose breath the words spoken “are spirit and life” (John VI.64), and are useful like clean winged creatures to those who eat them.

But the word of heretics and all perverse doctrines which fly, when the north wind—that is, the malignant spirit—blows, upon the wings of secular eloquence, are unclean birds forbidden to the people of God by the Law. For example: “You shall not eat the eagle, the griffin, the kite, and the vulture according to its kind, nor anything of the raven kind. The hoopoe also, the bat, and everything among birds that goes upon four feet shall be abominable to you; and whoever touches their carcasses shall be defiled and unclean until evening” (Lev. XI.13 ff.). What, moreover, are the words of heretics except unclean birds of their kind? Whoever touches their carcasses, even by assenting for a little while to their meaning, shall be unclean until evening: that is, until repentance, by which the heat of sin grows cool, and the sinner who had seemed bright to himself in his own eyes grows dark.

The words too of teachers in the Church who seek what is their own are likened to birds of prey, such as the eagle and kite; or to creatures walking on more than four feet upon earth, because they seek and desire earthly things alone; or to nocturnal birds, fleeing the light like the bat; or to creatures gladly lying in wait upon dung like the hoopoe, a bird that gladly feeds on human excrement. In such birds forbidden by the divine Law, it is indicated how the words of wicked teachers, and principally of heretics, must be avoided, when there is added what we have already expounded as we could: “Whoever touches their carcasses shall be defiled and unclean until evening.”

Clean birds, however—that is, the words of sound teaching—although they may seem comparable to dust because of lowliness, or to the sand of the sea because of its bitter taste, according to the words, “He rained flesh upon them like dust and winged birds like the sand of the sea,” are nevertheless precious and savoury to the faithful people.

The eating of flesh given before manna may also signify the use of carnal ceremonies permitted to God’s people before the bread of angels descended. Thus Moses’ words, “In the evening you shall eat flesh, and in the morning bread to satiety” (Exod. XVI.12), may be understood as though he said: “Carnal observances shall be permitted to you before the true bread from heaven descends.” But their craving for flesh after tasting the bread which possesses “every delight and every sweetness of flavour” (Wis. XVI.20)—when the flesh was still in their mouths and God’s anger rose against them—prefigured the Jews who, after Christ’s coming and after tasting his teaching, went backward either into Judaism, despising evangelical teaching and seeking the customary rite of the Law, or indeed those who, after receiving the life-giving sacrament of angelic bread, do not love the spiritual life of angels but live carnally like beasts. They will then be weighed down by a greater mass of condemnation when they are not deprived of their desire.

“While the food was still in their mouths,” etc. **Fifth part**, in which the author treats of their punishments, their feigned conversions through fear of punishments, and yet God’s judgment tempered by mercy. Two points were previously stated: “He heard and delayed.” Having explained how God heard them by not depriving them of their desire, he explains how the punishment which he delayed came upon them, in this way: “While the food was still in the mouths of those who spoke wickedly against God.”

**VERSE 31.** “And the anger of God rose against them.” I rightly say “rose,” not “descended,” because “a flame consumed sinners” (Ps. CV.18), and it is natural for flame to rise, not descend. This anger and this flame killed sinners dying in their sin, and hindered Israel’s chosen ones, so that they could not benefit or assist through human and paternal affection those with whom God was angry. It truly hindered them so greatly that Moses himself, foremost among the chosen, almost despaired because of their murmurings. Hence, doubting, he said: “Can we bring forth water for you from this rock?” (Num. XX.10). Because of this doubt, although he was chosen, he was nevertheless hindered—or, as some manuscripts read, “fettered”—from entering or bringing others into the land of promise.

The Hebrew truth has: “And he bent down the chosen of Israel.” This truly happened, and we still see it happen. For when the wicked are divinely corrected by pestilence, hail, sterility, or another plague, the good too, along with the impious who are scourged as an example of justice, are bowed down—that is, humbled as an example of patience—under the same punishments. They are also fettered and hindered by the excess of sinners, so that their prayers cannot avail to appease God’s anger, since they themselves are few, while those provoking that same anger are many.

### Verse 32

In all these things—whether softened by benefits or corrected by punishments—they still sinned. In what respect? Namely, in that they persisted in their wickedness, as it is written: “Let the one who is filthy become filthy still, and let the one who does harm do harm still” (Rev. 22:11). For this is to sin still: that past sins do not suffice a sinner unless he voluntarily adds others besides. Thus they still sinned and did not believe in his wonders. This sin—namely, unbelief—is especially blameworthy, since the Spirit of truth convicts the world “concerning sin and righteousness and judgment. Concerning sin indeed, because they do not believe” in Christ (John 16:8–9), [Col. 0459D] who performed many wonders, just as their fathers did not believe in the wonders of God.

### Verse 33

Therefore their days failed away in vanity, and their years in haste. For just as the days of those walking in truth advance, so the days of those walking in vanity fail away. As one born dead is said to have been born in vain, so “the widow who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:6), and lives in vain. Since this is established concerning a widow on the Apostle’s testimony, it may much more be affirmed concerning men luxuriating in pleasures: the days of such persons have failed, and still fail, in vanity. If, abandoning vanity, they believed in truth and clung to it by believing, they could gain eternal years. Conversely, “men of blood and deceit,” full of wickedness and very far from [Col. 0460A] truth through deception, “shall not halve their days” (Ps. 54:24), being separated from that fountain of truth to whom it is truly said: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101:28).

### Verse 34

“When he slew them, they sought him.” They did not seek him before punishment out of love, but amid punishment out of fear. Hence it is clear that their conversion, or return, by which they returned and came early to him while some of them were being slain, was not genuine but feigned. For it was not the slain who sought him, but those who remained. What is said of one people as though of one body is this: “When he slew them, they sought him,” although not the dead but the living sought him.

Terrified by fear of slaughter, they returned in words of mouth, not of heart, and came early [Col. 0460B] to him—like laborers hired, or rather compelled, for work at the first hour. They seemed to begin well at daybreak when they said: “All that the Lord has commanded, we will do” (Exod. 19:8). But once daybreak had passed, unable to endure the burden and heat of the day, they failed and did not remain in the service begun in the morning until evening, as did that blessed laborer of whom it is elsewhere said: “Man goes forth to his work, and to his labor until evening” (Ps. 103:23): that is, he carries a good work through to completion. But those “who believe for a time and in a time of temptation fall away” (Luke 8:13) come to God, as it were, at daybreak, but do not reach the full day.

Perhaps you ask how these people came to [Col. 0460C] him. Did they approach him, who is everywhere, by walking on foot, or in chariots, horses, ships, or other vehicles of this sort? No: they came by a movement of the heart, by which alone one approaches God or withdraws from him. Thus they came to him in this respect:

### Verses 35, 36, 37

They remembered, compelled by evils, that God is their helper, and God Most High their redeemer: helper, of course, in good things; redeemer, from evils. And they loved him with their mouth, not with their heart—foolishly failing to consider that all secrets are naked and open before him. And with their tongue, by which they said, “All that God has spoken, we will do” (Exod. 19:8), they lied to him. But their heart [Col. 0460D] was not right, because they were not upright in heart; rather, it was distorted from the rectitude of God’s justice. Nor was it right in God, because it was not with him. For they did not seek God for God’s sake.

Hence it follows: “Nor were they counted faithful in his covenant,” because they did not keep the commandments as they had promised, and sought temporal rather than eternal goods—goods promised in that covenant, as also in the new covenant, although there under the veil of figures and here without a veil. Those are like them who now, in God’s service, praise God with their lips while their hearts are far from him, seeking especially, or only, temporal goods. They differ from pagans only in this: pagans seek such goods from false gods, while these ask not true goods from the true God—not in order that they may thereafter serve the true God, but that they may spend them upon their own vanities. [Col. 0461A] Therefore they should not even be said to worship God, because in serving him they do not seek him. For everyone worships what he loves above all else, and for the attainment of which he willingly or patiently does or suffers what he believes advantageous to attaining that which, among all things, he loves above all.

### Verse 38

“But he is merciful, and he will be propitious to their sins.” By lying to God and not being found faithful in his covenant, they provoked God’s wrath against themselves; they angered him by their perversities. But he, whose proper nature is always to show mercy and to spare, was not merely merciful, I say, but is merciful with eternal mercy: “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. 135:1). And so that the same mercy which is his in disposition may appear [Col. 0461B] in manifest effect, “he will be propitious to their sins.”

This is apparent in that “he will not destroy them,” according to what God says elsewhere: “Showed me concerning my enemies: do not kill them” (Ps. 58:12). Although he slew some of them when, “as he slew them, they sought him,” nevertheless he will not destroy them altogether. For a remnant will be saved from them; on account of that remnant, which was to be born from them, he will not utterly destroy them, as he had said to Moses in Exodus: “Leave me, that I may destroy them and make you into a great nation” (Deut. 9:14).

But when Moses prayed, he was abundant in turning away his wrath—not in the sense that he had no wrath, but in that he did not kindle all his wrath. For when he is angry, he remembers mercy: he makes his sun rise upon the righteous [Col. 0461C] and the unrighteous; he also rained manna upon the wicked as well as the upright. And although some branches were broken off, he nevertheless preserved the root of that people, from which the holy apostles sprang; and the rest, through their preaching, were converted from the number of those who killed Christ. For very many of those who, while unbelieving, shed blood, afterward drank it as believers.

Nor did he spare them only for the sake of the future remnant, but also because:

### Verse 39

“He remembered that they are flesh: a spirit going and not returning.” The human spirit goes into death and does not return to the body in this world. Thus the phrase “a spirit going and not returning” is a brief description of death: the body dies [Col. 0461D] and, unless another raises it, will never rise again.

The death of the soul is similar. For the human spirit, although it may sometimes be ready for good, because the flesh is weak and weighs it down, is always prone to sin; nor does it return by itself. Thus it is said in Proverbs concerning the way of iniquity: “All who walk in it shall not return” (Prov. 2:19)—not because they cannot return in any way, but because they have no power to return by themselves, since grace alone brings back those whom the good Shepherd, seeking what was lost, carries home upon his shoulders.

On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says:

> **[Note: Col. 0461D, Book IV of the *Moralia*, ch. 3.]** Almighty God, just as he was able to make good things from nothing, so, when he willed, through the mystery of his incarnation he restored good things that had been lost. He made two creatures capable of understanding him: the angelic and the human. Pride struck both and broke them from the state of their inborn uprightness. But one had a covering of flesh; the other bore nothing weak from flesh. For an angel is spirit alone, whereas a human being is spirit and flesh. Therefore the Creator, in his mercy, had to bring back to himself for redemption the one which, in committing sin, is known to have had something arising from weakness; and he had to cast away the apostate angel all the more deeply because, when he fell from the strength to persevere, he bore nothing weak from flesh. Hence the Psalmist rightly, when speaking of the merciful Redeemer, also stated the very cause of mercy, saying: “And he remembered that [Col. 0462A] they are flesh.” It is as though he said: Because he saw their weakness, he was unwilling to punish their sins with strict severity.
>
> There is yet another reason why fallen humanity ought to be restored, while the spirit of pride could not be restored. The angel fell through his own malice; humanity, however, was overthrown by another.

Accordingly, it was fitting that the one who fell when another tempted him should be restored with another’s help. But the one who, without any tempter, fell through voluntary pride ought also, without anyone’s help, to rise again—if he could. Since he cannot, he too, no less than a human being—indeed more than a human being—may be called “a spirit going and not returning,” in accordance with what Truth says to him: “Go, Satan” (Matt. 16:23). He was not told, “Return,” as the faithful soul, God’s bride, is told in the Song of Songs: “Return, return, Shulammite; return, return, that we may behold you” (Song 6:12).

That spirit therefore goes and will never return, because that spiritual Pharaoh is obstinate and hardened in his sin. Human beings obstinate in their sins are like this spirit that goes and does not return. Although they sometimes appear to return—as Pharaoh at one time allowed God’s people to go and at another forbade it—they are not to be said to return in truth if they refuse to stand in truth. So too that lying spirit “did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44); he is a liar and the father of the lie which he first devised.

Those who belong to his party imitate him, such as those who loved God with their mouth and lied to him with their tongue, concerning whom he elsewhere complains: “Foreign children have lied to me; foreign children have grown old and limped from their paths” (Ps. 17:46). [Col. 0462D] Their limping was so great that, in indignation and astonishment at their perversity together, one is moved to cry out:

### Verses 40, 41

“How often they provoked him in the wilderness!” Not only in the ways described above, but also in many other ways they repeatedly provoked him in the wilderness.

### Part Six, in which he compares their evils with God’s benefits

For, intending to speak of the plagues brought upon Egypt on their account, he recalls that they forgot God and tested him in many ways, by which they provoked him to take away the good things [Col. 0463A] he had given them in the wilderness, where, deprived of human aid, they were more in need of divine help. They stirred him to wrath so that he might bring evils upon them in the waterless place, where they ought rather to have feared him than murmured against his judgments and lied to him.

But they did not turn to him with a sincere will when they said: “All that the Lord has spoken, we will do” (Exod. 19:8). In saying this they lied, as is clear from the fact that they tested God by distrustfully and murmuringly asking for what they desired; and, upon receiving what they desired, proved ungrateful. Thus they provoked the Holy One of Israel: that is, God, whom the true Israel sanctifies and who sanctifies the true Israel.

Wonderful ingratitude! Neither God’s present benefits shown to them in the wilderness could move them to give thanks, [Col. 0463B] nor did past benefits remain in their memory, although they had recently been wrought magnificently against great dangers, when God delivered them with a mighty hand and uplifted arm. But they:

### Verse 42

“Did not remember his hand stretched out against Pharaoh’s hand on the day when he redeemed them from the hand of the oppressor.” God’s power and Pharaoh’s power are both described by the one word “hand,” when it is said: “They did not remember his hand on the day when he redeemed them from the hand of the oppressor.” Yet there is no comparison between the strength of the two hands, because the hand of the deliverer prevailed over the hand of the oppressor. This ought to have remained in the memory of those delivered. But they did not remember his hand on the day when he redeemed them from the hand of the oppressor by such wonders, which were signs and prodigies surpassing other wonders. For:

### Verse 43

“He set his signs in Egypt,” like impressions of a seal stamped upon the hard hearts of the Jews, “and his prodigies in the field of Tanis”: that is, greater miracles, which are called *prodigies*, as it were *porrodicia* (“foretelling”), because they indicate great things to come.

So afterward he was to act in the universal Egypt against the invisible Pharaoh, whom he chastised by the ten commandments of the given Law as by ten plagues, and whom he finally defeated by the sacrifice of the paschal lamb. “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7). He is the true Lamb who took away the sins of the world, who by dying defeated our death and by rising restored life.

He placed certain signs of such great matters in [Col. 0463D] Egypt, which he crushed by ten plagues, and in the field of Tanis, one of the chief cities of Egypt. Greater miracles were displayed in its field, and, because of the greatness of their significance, they were called prodigies. The name *Tanis*, interpreted in Latin, means “lowly commandment,” by which we are instructed, in this world—in the broad field of this Egyptian city, where God performs many wonders—to humble ourselves beneath his commandment so that we may be exalted eternally. “For everyone who humbles himself” in this field “will be exalted” in the land of promise; whereas “he who exalts himself,” like Pharaoh and his army against God and his people, “will be humbled” (Luke 14:11), no longer into the depths of the Red Sea but into the depths of hell, unless he repents.

[Col. 0464A]

### Verse 44

“And he turned their rivers into blood.” Here he begins to recount the plagues brought upon Egypt for their deliverance. He omits three: gnats, sores, and darkness. He adds three others not read in Exodus: blight, frost, and fire. Nor is it surprising if one who said, “I will open my mouth in parables,” does not preserve the historical sequence in every respect, because he chiefly strives to convey the spiritual meaning.

Beginning, therefore, with the first plague, he says: “And he turned their rivers into blood, and their rains”—that is, rainwater, whether gathered in cisterns or sought in dug pits, because the Egyptians dug and found blood instead of water. Truly the Lord is just in his judgments. Since they killed the Hebrew males by casting them into the river, it was just that their waters should be turned into blood, so that men of blood might be punished in the element in which they perpetrated the bloody murder of so many little ones.

This first plague began with water turned to blood; the last took place in the water of the Red Sea, which drowned their army and chariots, just as they had drowned the Hebrew children. They had killed only male children in the river, preserving the women; and only males perished in the sea, while the women were kept at home. For the same measure in which they had measured had to be measured back to them.

### Verses 45, 46, 47, 48

“He also sent among them the *coenomyia*, which is called the dog-fly, because *cynos* means ‘dog,’ and it devoured them; and he sent the frog, and it destroyed them. And he gave their fruits, which grew [Col. 0464C] without cultivation, to blight.” This is not in Exodus. “And their labors to the locust”: that is, he gave their crops to the locust. “And he killed their vines with hail”; and likewise he killed their mulberry trees with frost, which differs greatly from hail. This also is not in Exodus. Likewise, “he gave their cattle to hail”; this is recorded there. And likewise, “he gave their possessions to fire,” though Exodus does not say that anything was burned, but only that hail and fire mingled together were carried in the lightning.

“He did not spare their souls from death,” with which he enclosed their cattle in death. He compares human beings to cattle, because, when they do not act according to reason, they are comparable to cattle. “And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt,” and also “the firstfruits of all their labor”: that is, every consolation of their life, in the tents of Ham, not in the land of Goshen, where the Jews were.

Mystically, just as water changed into wine signifies history, or the moral sense, being changed into its spiritual meaning, or a people changed for the better, so water turned into blood—by which flesh is understood—signifies understanding spiritual things carnally. The *coenomyia* signifies dog-like conduct: failure to honor parents or superiors. The frog signifies empty talkativeness and chattering amid muddy thoughts in heretics. Blight, which others have interpreted as rust, harms secretly like a burrowing animal; it is compared with a vice that is difficult to detect, such as excessive confidence in oneself. A harmful breeze works secretly in fruits and harms them. So too, in conduct, hidden pride is difficult to detect when someone thinks himself [Col. 0465A] to be something although he is nothing.

The locust, which harms with its mouth and devours crops, is malice that corrodes the reputation of good by detraction. Hail is violent injustice, taking others’ goods by theft and robbery—things by which the thief or robber himself is more thoroughly devastated. Frost is dark foolishness, by which, as though through night-time cold, love for one’s neighbor freezes. Fire is great anger, from which homicide also arises; or it is greed, which lays waste and consumes possessions—that is, the state of the mind.

In those figurative plagues the cattle died, because people signified by cattle, and made like them through concupiscence, perish through the loss of chastity. That generative desire through which offspring are produced is common to us with cattle and livestock, beasts and birds. To yield to it and voluntarily serve its lustful impulses in acts of shame is the sin of unchastity; but to restrain it under the governance of reason is the virtue of chastity. Feeling this in his flesh, the chaste person cries with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24).

The unchaste person, therefore, desires its movement even before it arises, according to the saying: “They lusted after lust in the wilderness” (Ps. 105:14); and after it arises, he serves to satisfy its desire, himself made a slave of that shamefulness by which he has been enticed and conquered. No one is freed, or can be free, from this slavery of sin except through the grace of that man who alone was born free among the dead. Conceived without fleshly concupiscence and born without sin, and therefore alone free from sin, he alone is able [Col. 0465C] to give freedom to those born in slavery, so that they may now bear the fruit of holiness and finally receive eternal life.

It should certainly be observed that the firstborn of the Egyptians were killed by God’s judgment, whereas the firstborn of the Hebrews were sanctified. For every male opening the womb was called holy to the Lord, and was either taken for the Lord’s service, redeemed by a price, or killed so that it might not be put to ordinary use. All these things happened figuratively and were written for our instruction, lest we be Egyptians, whose firstborn must be killed, rather than Hebrews, whose firstborn must be sanctified.

The prince of the Egyptians, who is also called the prince of this world, was a liar from the beginning and the father of the lie which he conceived and brought forth. He must be punished so that his firstborn—his lie, by which he said, “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14)—may be utterly destroyed, and that, cast down from the throne of desired exaltation, he may be plunged into the abyss with his chariots in the lower hell, convicted of falsely boasting that he was like the Most High.

Likewise, all his accomplices, who themselves have brought forth the firstborn crimes of pride, must be destroyed with their firstborn: either beneficially and voluntarily humbled unto repentance, in accordance with the saying, “Overthrow the wicked, and they shall not be” (Prov. 12:7); or unwillingly, as though dragged down by the ropes of hell from the height of pride into the depth of destruction.

But the male firstborn in Israel which opens the womb is rightly understood as humility, opposed to pride. As a holy firstborn it is placed first among the virtues where it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.” This firstborn is sanctified when it is added: “For theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). Did not this holy male firstborn, called holy to the Lord, open the womb of the closed Virgin? Because the Lord regarded her humility, she conceived a male without a male: “A woman,” as Jeremiah says, “shall encompass a man” [Col. 0466A] without a man’s agency (Jer. 31:22).

Likewise, does not the whole Church, or every faithful soul in which the Lord finds the humility he loves, become the mother of God? Her womb is opened, so that by believing she may conceive the seed of the eternal Word and by speaking and teaching may give birth. Does not eternal Truth incarnate itself affirm what we say? “Whoever,” he says, “does the will of my Father, he is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12:50).

How good a firstborn is holy humility: a foundation first laid and firmly established in the hearts of the poor in spirit through the holy fear of the Lord, which endures for ages of ages! Holy humility is indeed a good and stable foundation of the virtues. If it totters, the gathering of virtues is nothing but ruin. This, therefore, is the firstborn worthy to be sanctified in Israel. Conversely, the vice of pride—the firstborn of Pharaoh, who from the beginning exalted himself against God—is detestable not only in the invisible Pharaoh himself, but also in all Egyptians who favor him, [Col. 0466C] whose firstborn are killed when truth triumphs everywhere through the humble and poor in spirit, takes every understanding captive into the obedience of Christ, and destroys every height opposing and exalting itself against the knowledge of Christ, who teaches humility and says: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:20).

At present, indeed, some firstborn of Egypt are killed individually, and the firstborn of Israel are sanctified. But in that judgment, in which the prince of this world with the entire army of his Egyptians will be submerged in the abyss, not even one of those who, exalted against God, persecute the children of Israel [Col. 0466D] will remain without being cast into the abyss. Then the children of Israel will be completely liberated, when everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted.

But before this final plague of the Egyptians, they are greatly condemned by that first plague through which everything they draw from the waters of Holy Scripture is turned into blood for them. For truth understood by them will not help them, but will stand as testimony against them: they do not draw from it help toward living well, which they certainly do not wish to do; rather, they are convicted as wicked servants who, knowing their master’s will and not doing it, deserve to be beaten with many blows.

They also find the cisterns which they dig for themselves through secular philosophy filled with blood, because, understanding the Creator through creation, they choose rather to serve the creature than [Col. 0467A] the Creator, loving created things more than their Maker, who is blessed forever. Conversely, for the children of Israel dwelling in the land of Goshen—that is, those approaching truth, for *Goshen* is interpreted “approaching”—water is changed not into blood but rather into wine, which gladdens and stirs up in those who drink it that joy of which it is said: “You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Savior” (Isa. 12:3).

The same distinction is preserved in the other plagues: they harm the Egyptians alone, while for the Hebrews—that is, all the elect who love God—all things work together for good, just as the calamities of the Egyptians worked for the good of the Israelites. Seeing these things, they were stirred to praise God, while Moses sang before them, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea. The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation” (Exod. 15:1–2).

For the righteous Lord, like an almighty warrior, punished the wicked in order to instruct his servants, especially in that:

### Verse 49

“He sent upon them the wrath of his indignation—indignation, tribulation, and a sending forth through evil angels.” There is wrath mingled with divine mercy, as it is said: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Hab. 3:2), or, “In wrath you will remember mercy.” But this wrath is greatly intensified when indignation, tribulation, and a sending through evil angels are joined to it.

First, God is angry with one sinning not through frailty or ignorance, but through pride. Then he is indignant with one who loves his iniquities and covers them with an Adamic girdle. But after a sin has been rebuked, if the person does not acknowledge it but defends it, God sends tribulation through evil angels. Yet no tribulation is more dangerous than that flattering temptation by which the sinner is handed over to a reprobate mind, through which, stripped of God’s protection, he falls headlong into that depth of destruction of which the Wise Man says: “When the sinner comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3).

It is not surprising that the good God uses evil angels either for the destruction of the perverse, as is clear in the Egyptians; or for the testing of the good, as is clear in Job; or for their humiliation, as is evident in Paul. For a good person also uses a bad servant well, whether to discipline fellow servants [Col. 0467D] or to serve his children. Finally, as a good or bad person uses visible matter—earth, water, air, and fire—in his own manner, not only in necessary matters but also in superfluous, playful, and artistic works, so good and evil angels use creatures according to the authority possessed by each. Their authority is greater than that of human beings, and greater in good angels than in evil ones; yet they use creatures according to God’s will.

It must be understood, however, that the devil has power over the wicked as over his own flock, unless he is prohibited by a higher authority; over the good he has power only when permitted. So a person drives his own flock where he wishes, as he wishes, asking no permission, though a stronger power sometimes prevents him even from doing this. But concerning another’s flock, in order to do what he wishes, he waits for authority to be given to him by its owner. [Col. 0468A] Thus Satan, although he envied Job’s prosperity exceedingly, did not dare to touch either Job himself or what belonged to him until authority was granted him by the Lord.

And the true Job says to Pilate, Satan’s minister: “You would have no power at all against me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). “And an angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him” (Luke 22:43), so that from this it may be clear that good angels will never be absent from the good; indeed, they will be especially present when the good themselves are tempted by evil angels through assaults of either tribulations or suggestions—provided that tribulation produces patience and the evil suggestion is not accepted by consent.

But we do not concede that people are afflicted by good angels: both because we find no such thing in Scripture [Col. 0468B] and because we read that they are sent “in the ministry of salvation for those who shall inherit salvation” (Heb. 1:14). On behalf of such persons, and at times to avenge and protect them, the good angels themselves destroy the wicked evilly. Thus, when Lot, though righteous, was badly oppressed by evil people, they first struck his oppressors with blindness, so that they could not find the door, and then destroyed the wicked evilly, as they deserved, along with their perverse city (Gen. 19:11).

And because, as Jeremiah laments, the sin of the city of Jerusalem was heavier and greater than the sin of the Sodomites (Lam. 4:6), the Jews were rightly blinded as well, so that they cannot find in their own Law him who says: “I am the door” (John 10:9). Their city likewise perished in miserable [Col. 0468C] destruction, burned by the Romans; their bodies were killed by famine or sword, and their souls were dragged into hell, according to the saying: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn unto the lowest hell” (Deut. 32:22).

The universal judgment also will be carried out in a similar manner. Those who, after the fashion of the Sodomites or Jerusalemites, zealously oppose the truth, oppress righteous monitors when rebuked by them, and refuse to listen, will themselves be blinded by divine judgment and will by no means find the door—that is, an opportunity to injure the good. Or, what is worse, failing to find him who says, “I am the door,” while attempting to climb up by another way they will fall, to be enveloped in the final conflagration of the whole world and destroyed like the Sodomites mentioned above, unless through true repentance [Col. 0468D] they leave the city destined for destruction and are saved, after the example of the aforementioned Lot, either in little Zoar by keeping the commandments of righteousness, or on the mountain by keeping the counsels of perfection. Lot left Sodom and preserved himself first in Zoar and afterwards on the mountain.

Thus the apostles also left the city of Jerusalem that was destined for destruction and were saved, following not only the commandments of righteousness but also the counsels of the perfect life. But for those to whom it is not enough to be wicked, who moreover persecute those fleeing their company—as the Egyptians did, pursuing the Hebrews who fled from them—the statement made by Asaph concerning God in this psalm is appropriate:

### Verse 50

“He made a way for the path of his wrath; he did not spare their souls from death.” The path of God’s wrath was hidden equity: he could, if he had wished, have punished the wicked Egyptians for the wickedness of their will alone. For this path, formerly narrow and understood by few, he made a level and broad road, sufficiently evident, when he permitted them to fall into open crimes, so that the justice of the punisher also might become open. By its verdict, just as they did not spare the Hebrew children whom they killed in the river, so he, the righteous Judge, did not spare their souls from death—the death that precedes bodily death.

For they were crushed with a double destruction: not only did their bodies perish as hail devastated them, the angel struck them, and finally the Red Sea overwhelmed them; but, worse for them, their souls also, deprived of the life which is God and consequently dead, were thrust into hell. The abyss of hell swallowed [Col. 0469B] them, just as the abyss covered their bodies descending into the deep like stone and lead in mighty waters. Pharaoh’s hardened and weighed-down heart is rightly compared to stone and lead; with it his army, corresponding in hardness, was deservedly cast into the abyss. This serves as an example to those who, found like them in the sin of hating and persecuting God’s servants, will also be like them in punishment, God not sparing their souls from death, just as in Egypt he “did not spare their souls from death,” whose cattle he also enclosed in death.

### Verse 51

“And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt,” concerning whose striking enough has already been said above. “The firstfruits of all their labor”: namely, the chief products of the earth, as is read in Exodus, because the early fruits were ravaged by hail, while the late fruits were neither harmed nor capable of being harmed, “because they were late” (Exod. 9:32).

Similar to this is the fact that the sins of some persons go before them to judgment: because they are manifest, they are also punished by manifest judgment in this life and, as it were, struck by hail when the heavens thunder, flash, and thunderbolt from above, casting down hailstones—the sentence of condemnation—so that others may fear. But the sins of those whose sins follow after them, being late, as it were, because they are committed secretly, are not struck by the hail of human sentence. Rather, they are pasture for the Egyptians until the abyss of God’s judgments comes upon them, of which it is elsewhere said: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35:7).

He calls the tents of the Egyptians “the tents of Ham,” because the Egyptians descended from the stock of Ham. Although Ham in his own person had been free, just as Shem was free, from whom the Hebrews were descended—and although Ham’s son Canaan was assigned to servitude by the curse of father Noah—his servile condition is now indicated when devastation of the firstfruits for the liberation of the Hebrew people is said to have occurred in the tents of Ham. This people was blessed in its father Shem and further enriched with blessings in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

### Verse 52

“And he took away his people like sheep.”

### Part Seven, in which, after recalling the plagues sent upon the Egyptians, the liberation of the Hebrews is recounted in this manner:

“And he took away his people like sheep, [Col. 0470A] and led them through the wilderness like a flock.”

### Vv. 53–54. “And he led them forth in hope, and they did not fear; and the sea covered their enemies. And he brought them to the mountain of his holiness, the mountain which his right hand acquired. And he drove nations out before them, and by lot allotted them the land with a measuring-line of distribution.”

The historical narrative is clear and needs little exposition. Although it recounts the magnificent miracles of God, who delivered his people and brought them into the land of promise, where, though they had previously been very few in number, they greatly multiplied after their adversaries had been driven out and expanded into a kingdom: nevertheless, unless greater things are understood and shown to be intended than the letter conveys when it speaks of the mountain of holiness, upon which the temple was founded by Solomon, the mountain acquired by his right hand, and the other promises understood literally, the rulers of this world—kings more powerful than the Hebrew kings, especially the Romans, who ruled the world to such an extent [Col. 0470B] that, at the time when Christ, King of the Jews, was born, the whole world was registered in order to pay them tribute—could have mocked at the proclamation of the power of such a most high King. For they knew that they had occupied kingdoms broader than the kingdom of the Jews, which, like the other kingdoms, had also been reduced to Roman power.

But behold, one greater than Solomon is here: he builds for himself a house from living and chosen stones, namely the holy Church, founded upon himself, the mountain of holiness [Col. 0470C]; and he says: “Upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. 16:18). This rock is “the stone cut from the mountain without hands” (Dan. 2:34), which also grew into a great mountain when the kingdoms of this world were bent down—indeed, shattered—according to Daniel’s vision. For neither the golden kingdom of Babylon, nor the silver kingdom of the Persians, nor the bronze kingdom of the Greeks, nor the iron kingdom of the Romans could or can prevent the King of kings and Lord of lords from reigning.

For by reigning and ruling he took away like sheep his people, who awaited him in Egyptian—indeed, infernal—darkness, after the invisible Pharaoh had there been defeated and drowned by his blood, together with the water flowing from his side. He also took them, like sheep, from the lion’s mouth: this strong-handed David, who killed the lion itself [Col. 0470D], and led them as a flock, making one fold from diverse sheep joined together—namely, Gentiles and Jews believing in him. He himself, the good shepherd, leads them as a flock in the wilderness of this age, where he feeds them with the bread of angels.

Already in great part he has truly brought them in, but all in hope, to the mountain of his holiness. There, on the day of his Passion, he first placed the repentant thief—like a sheep snatched from the wolf’s mouth—joining him to the ninety-nine sheep, that is, to the choirs of angels. By that Passion, when he was lifted up from the earth, he draws all his own to himself upon the mountain acquired by his right hand. For from his right side he sent forth waters with blood, by which the invisible Pharaoh and his army are overwhelmed, and [Col. 0471A] all those predestined to life are delivered. For them he prepared eternal dwelling-places in his Father’s house, from which he drove out the nations—that is, the evil spirits ruling the nations. Once these had been driven out before his people, he allotted them the land by a measuring-line of distribution: since both now the one and same Spirit works in them, distributing to each as he wills, and in the future he will distinguish the dwelling-places of heavenly life by a measuring-line of distribution, so that, as star differs from star in glory, so it may be in the resurrection of the dead, who are the tribes of Israel—that is, those who see God.

### V. 55. “And he caused them to dwell in the tents of the nations,”

in two ways. For even now the land of nations living as Gentiles and worshipping demons has in large measure been transferred to the use of those who live piously [Col. 0471B] and worship the true God. And in heaven, from which evil spirits were cast out, chosen human beings will possess their dwellings, as is now said: “And he caused the tribes of Israel to dwell in their tents.” Who, then, is like the Lord in strength—he who even now conquers his enemies and rescues his own from the hand of the stronger, and who formerly delivered the children of Israel from Pharaoh’s hand, conferring many benefits upon them? Yet they were ungrateful for those benefits.

### Vv. 56–57. “They tempted and provoked God, though he was most high; and they did not keep his testimonies,”

that is, his law. “And they turned away from God and did not keep the covenant, just as their fathers did not keep that which they had pledged, saying: ‘Whatever God commands us, we shall do’” (Exod. 19:8).

Up to this point he has spoken of different persons as though they were the same, according to the rule which Tyconius places among his seven rules and which is called that concerning the mixed body of the Lord: when different persons are treated as though they were one body, or members of one body. Thus above it was said, “When he slew them, they sought him,” although it was not those slain but the survivors of that same people who sought him. So too, when he says that they were led out of Egypt and brought into the mountain of holiness, he uses the same rule, speaking of different persons as though they were the same: those who came out of Egypt and those who entered the land of promise. For when all but two of the former had died in the wilderness, their children were brought by Joshua [Col. 0471D] into the land promised to their fathers. God had promised that he would bring them into the land flowing with milk and honey, which he had sworn to give to their fathers’ seed; for example, when he said to Abraham: “To your seed I shall give this land” (Gen. 12:7).

Therefore, since those born in the wilderness were Abraham’s seed no less than those who came out of Egypt, the truth of the promise could not be nullified by the death of those to whom, while in Egypt, the possession of the land formerly promised to their fathers had been promised. For those born from them filled their fathers’ places and equally belonged to the seed of Abraham, to whom the promise had been made.

Moreover, this promise is confirmed in Abraham’s seed, which is Christ, who is heir of that promise first in himself and then [Col. 0472A] in his members. For it was not said without purpose to believers: “Therefore you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise,” since there is one seed of Abraham, “which is Christ” (Gal. 3:29). Hence it was not said, “In seeds,” as though in many, but as though in one: “And to your seed,” he says, “I shall give this land, and in your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gal. 3:16, 8).

Thus the promise was made to Abraham’s seed while it was still mixed together in Egypt: that they should be brought into the land promised to their fathers. But only those were heirs of the promise who were found faithful with faithful Abraham, and who are called children of promise, not of flesh. For those who were Abraham’s children according to flesh alone, such as Ishmael, are not reckoned in the [Col. 0472B] seed, but are carnal Israel. Isaiah rebukes them, saying: “You who came forth from the waters of Judah” (Isa. 48:1), that is, you are descended from Judah not according to the power of faith, but according to the flow of flesh.

Yet speech is sometimes framed concerning these carnal persons, mixed into the body of the spiritual, as though it were addressed to or concerned with the same persons, when what is said must be understood of different persons. This pertains to the Song of Songs: “I am dark and beautiful, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon” (Song 1:4). For she did not say, “I was dark, like the tents of Kedar, and I am beautiful, like the skins of Solomon,” but said that she was both, on account of the temporal unity of good and bad fish within one net. The tents [Col. 0472C] of Kedar belong to Ishmael, who was not an heir with the son of the free woman.

Accordingly, when God says of the good part, “I shall lead the blind in a way which they did not know, and they shall tread the path which they did not know; and I shall make darkness light before them, and crooked things straight. These words I shall do, and I shall not forsake them” (Isa. 42:16), he immediately says of the other part, which is mixed with the good: “But they themselves turned backward” (ibid., 17), as though he were speaking of those of whom he had been speaking. Yet they will not always remain in the one net. For he is that servant mentioned in the Gospel whose Lord, when he comes, “will cut him in two and assign his portion with the hypocrites” (Matt. 24:51).

Likewise, when it is said here, “He took away his people like sheep and brought them into the mountain of his holiness,” different persons [Col. 0472D] are treated as though they were the same, since the fathers were one group and the children another. But now, where it says, “They turned away and did not keep the covenant, just as their fathers,” it separates what it had previously joined, speaking distinctly of children who imitate their evil parents in evil: in that they turned away from God and did not keep the covenant as their fathers had not kept it. The fathers, indeed, are understood to be those who provoked God in the wilderness; the children are those who, after being brought into the land of promise, imitated their evil fathers.

For each person is to be judged the child of such parents as he resembles; thus only those who hold Abraham’s faith are rightly called Abraham’s children. Hence Truth says: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham”; and adds: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” [Col. 0473A] (John 8:44). Therefore murmurers are children of murmurers, resembling their fathers in this: that “they were turned into a crooked bow.” A crooked bow is one which readily slackens, or which does not shoot from afar but turns its arrows back upon itself.

Some manuscripts have, “into a perverse bow.” Explaining this, blessed Pope Gregory says:

> [Note: [Col. 0473D] *Morals*, book 27, chapter 46.] A perverse bow strikes the very person by whom it is drawn, etc. Hence, through the arrogance of their speech, they are like a perverse bow in their sayings, because, while they speak words against pride, they fix arrows in their own authors. Therefore the utmost care must be taken lest wisdom received, while illuminating the darkness of ignorance, remove the light of humility, and so cease to be wisdom: though it shine with the power of eloquence, it nevertheless obscures the speaker’s heart with the veil of pride [Col. 0473B]. For some goods are highest goods, while others are intermediate goods, such as prophecy, teaching, the power of healings, and so forth. These are so placed in either direction that sometimes the eternal homeland, but at other times earthly glory, is sought through them alone. We therefore call these powers intermediate, because we incline them toward whatever the mind desires; once they have been received, the mind can use them just as it can use earthly riches. For through earthly riches some grow proud in the display of glory, while others perform works of mercy toward their needy neighbors. Thus, when outward praise is sought through teaching and prophecy, it is as though the summit of earthly glory were sought through bodily riches. But when teaching and prophecy are employed for winning souls, it is as though riches received were bestowed upon needy brothers. Since, therefore, the incautious mind often exults in what it receives and is drawn away from the giver’s hand, vigilant provision must ensure that vices are first subdued and gifts afterward retained under watchful care. For if the mind carelessly abandons itself in them, it is not advanced to life through them, but is rejected as though rewarded for former labors. Hence it comes about that a gift received, when assumed for the use of passing praise, is not a virtue because it serves vice. For since humility is the origin of virtue, that virtue truly springs up in us which endures in its own root—that is, humility. If it is cut off from that root, it withers, because it loses the life-giving moisture of charity, which is found in lowly places.

Let these words of blessed Gregory concerning the crooked and perverse bow shape the moral sense.

[Col. 0473D] These words can fittingly be applied also to those who, though trained by good teachers in sound learning of both Testaments, strike their teachers by the very knowledge through which they ought to have assisted them: they are like a perverse bow striking the one who draws it. Historically, however, the perverse intention of those who perversely raised themselves against God their Creator and diverted the worship owed to him toward idols was likened to a crooked bow. Hence the Hebrew text reads: “They were bent like a useless bow, and they provoked him at their high places and stirred him to jealousy with their carved images.” The same meaning appears in what our manuscripts have:

[Col. 0474A]

### V. 58. “They provoked him to anger on their hills, and with their carved images they provoked him to jealousy.”

For they were accustomed to place their idols upon hills and mountains in order to venerate them. Hence they are often rebuked by the prophets because they sacrificed at high places; and their kings are severely censured when it is said of any one of them: “Yet he did not remove the high places”; or, what was worse: “He sacrificed at the high places.” On high places and hills of this sort they provoked to anger God, who is by nature gentle, and with their carved images they provoked him to jealousy—that is, indignation. Or, according to other manuscripts: “With their carved images they were jealous of him,” while they bestowed his honor upon foreign gods. This was especially charged against King Jeroboam, who ordained that sacrifices and festivals should be offered to idols in imitation of the sacrifices and festivals instituted for the true God.

Mystically, we set idols upon hills in proud thoughts when we consent to them, or, worse still, serve them also in deed; and, being vicious, we worship Venus if lustful, Mars if enraged, or the other monstrous forms of such vices.

### Vv. 59–61. “The Lord heard and rejected.”

THE EIGHTH PART, concerning vengeance in the land of promise. It is as though he said: They provoked God. God heard this and rejected Israel; and in rejecting them he reduced those who sinned exceedingly to utter nothingness. When he rejected them, those who had been what they were through his help were reduced to nothingness.

They were truly reduced to nothingness. For because of the idolatry by which they served the creature rather than the Creator, even the priests of that time, Hophni and Phinehas, greedily snatching raw sacrificial flesh from unwilling persons and sleeping with the women before the entrance of the tabernacle (1 Sam. 2:12 ff.), he rejected the tabernacle itself, which was at Shiloh. I mean his tabernacle, once beloved by him, where he dwelt not in walls but in people. For God, who is spirit, does not dwell in buildings made by hands, but in rational spirits; hence those who worship him must worship in spirit. Yet he wishes to have structures made by hands, whether temples or tabernacles, in which he may be served by people in whose minds he dwells through faith working by love. But if this faith and love [Col. 0474D] have been extinguished in people, he cares little for the walls of temples, however beautiful and costly they may be.

Thus he abandons heretics who tear themselves away from the unity of the Church, who are denoted by Shiloh, which is interpreted “rupture” or “separation,” and whose bodies and minds he had formerly inhabited through faith.

He likewise utterly rejects greedy and shameless priests such as Hophni and Phinehas. Even if they are not to be slain with the material sword as those were—that is, Eli’s sons—he declares that they are to be slain by the sword of the word and casts them out from the fellowship of the saints, just as he cast them out when “he delivered their strength into captivity and their beauty into the hand of the enemy.” By their strength and [Col. 0475A] beauty he means the ark of the covenant, through which they seemed invincible and in which, foolishly, they took pleasure. In this they were deceived: they thought that God sat upon the cherubim made of molten gold and placed on the ark, although the thrones or cherubim in which God dwells and sits, according to the words, “You who sit upon the cherubim, show yourself before Ephraim” (Ps. 79:2–3), are angelic spirits. They are called thrones or seats because eternal Wisdom rests in them, disposing all things sweetly and judging mightily.

Nevertheless, it was a great reproach to Israel that the visible ark, though made by human hands, was delivered into the hands of enemies because of the people’s sins, and especially because of the sins of priests who, under the pretext of divine service, served their own greed—which is idolatry—and [Col. 0475B] neglected their reputation to such a degree that people spoke disparagingly of God’s sacrifice because of their shameful conduct. Because their father, the priest Eli, did not rebuke them worthily, he too did not escape God’s vengeance when his sons were killed in battle. For, on hearing the news of his sons’ death and of the ark’s capture, he fell backward from his seat, broke his neck, and died. Phinehas’s wife also, near her time of giving birth, hearing that her husband had died, bent over in grief and gave birth; and so she died (1 Sam. 4:19).

Blessed Gregory says on this passage:

> [Note: [Col. 0475D] *Pastoral Rule*, part 4.] “Strength and beauty are delivered into captivity, into the hand of the enemy, when the ancient enemy gains mastery over a deceived mind through pride in a good work. This pride in virtue, although it does not wholly overcome, nevertheless often in some degree tempts even the minds of the elect. But when it is abandoned, the abandoned person is recalled to fear. Thus David again says: ‘I said in my abundance: I shall never be moved’ (Ps. 29:7). But because he swelled with confidence in his own strength, shortly afterward he added what he endured: ‘You turned your face away from me, and I was troubled’ (ibid., 8). It is as though he said openly: ‘I believed myself strong amid my virtues, but, abandoned, I learned how great my weakness was.’ Again he says: ‘I have sworn and determined to keep the judgments of your righteousness’ (Ps. 118:106). But because it was not in his own strength to remain in the observance that he had sworn, he immediately found his weakness when troubled. Therefore he suddenly turned to prayer, saying: ‘I have been utterly humbled; give me life according to [Col. 0475D] your word’” (ibid., 107).

### V. 62. “And he shut up his people to the sword,”

because thirty thousand of the people fell in one day; “and he rejected his inheritance”—the inheritance which, from among all nations, he had chosen as a people peculiarly his own, and to which he says: “Israel is my inheritance.” He rejected it, taking no care to defend it from slaughter by enemies. For:

### V. 63. “Fire consumed their young men,”
