that is, the anger and fury of their enemies, themselves burning like fire in their rage, consumed their strongest men. The terror of the enemy was so great that their virgins did not mourn according to the funeral custom: neither did the virgins mourn for the killing of the men, nor did the men mourn for the virgins exposed as the enemies’ spoil, since fear of the enemy terrified them on every side [Col. 0476A].

### V. 64. “Their priests too, Hophni and Phinehas” (1 Sam. 4:19), “fell by the sword, and their widows were not mourned,”

because in so great a disturbance there was no opportunity to render the customary honor to funerals through lamentation.

So too the wicked, rebels against God, when at times they are handed over into the devil’s power, are hemmed in for the slaying of the soul by temptations rising up everywhere like Philistines. For the fire of evil desire consumes the young and the strong. Priests also, resembling the aforesaid priests, fall by the sword of their own mouth, being condemned by their own words: either because, like heretics, they teach wrongly, or because, like false prophets and false apostles, they live badly while teaching rightly; or again like the scribes and Pharisees, to whom the Lord says: “How can you speak good things when you are evil?” (Matt. 12:34).

Do you wish to hear by what sword of the word such people were slain or are to be slain? “Well,” he says, “did Isaiah the prophet prophesy of you, saying: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me’” (Matt. 15:7–8). Who says this? Truth and Life, so that you may know that hearts far removed from this true Life are dead, according to what Life itself says: “But their heart is far from me.”

Virgins in body but not in spirit, exposed to corruption, are not to be lamented amid such an abundance of iniquity. For it is more tolerable for them to be corrupted by that shamefulness [Col. 0476C], which is often followed by the shame of repentance, than to persist in that folly while retaining bodily virginity, for which the foolish virgins, having no oil in their vessels, will be condemned.

Virgins are also not lamented and widows not mourned in this sense: when people fall from so lofty a purpose, there sometimes befalls them an obstinacy of mind by which their hardened and impeded minds neither grieve for their own loss nor give others confidence that tears can fruitfully be shed on their behalf. For they are not, like Lazarus, friends—male or female—of Truth; nor do they have sisters or any debtors weeping and interceding for them. Rather, they belong to the number of those of whom Truth says: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. 8:22).

### V. 65. “And the Lord awoke as one sleeping.”

[Col. 0476D] Here Asaph shows that punishment was turned back upon their adversaries. The Lord seemed to be sleeping while he allowed them to be so afflicted, just as he now seems to sleep while he gives his own into the hands of those who hate them, whether to be purified or condemned. The Lord, I say—ruling even in the midst of his enemies—at length awoke at a twofold cry: that of Samuel and the other faithful people of that time, though few; and that of the enemies, glorying and laughing against him and his people, and treating his ark improperly because they placed it in the temple of the false god Dagon.

Those people are certainly resembled by those who, as enemies of the Church, in a manner join the ark of the covenant—that is, the body of Christ—to a false god: while continuing in some mortal sin which they cherish more than God and worship as God, they presume to receive the holy body. Therefore, just as the Lord then awoke like a mighty man exhilarated with wine—that is, in the manner of a person acting more vigorously when, having drunk much wine and fallen asleep, he is suddenly awakened by the cry of household members or enemies—so, I say, when the Lord was then aroused:

### V. 66. “He struck his enemies in their hinder parts,”

so that their buttocks protruded; that is, he manifested the wound by which he had struck them in the more private part of their buttocks (1 Sam. 5). So now too he is aroused against those like them and first strikes them in the more secret part of their sexual members, so that, handed over to a reprobate mind [Col. 0477B], they do things unfitting—indeed, contrary to nature. And since they are not ashamed even of these things, he makes their shameful parts protrude through manifest deeds of impurity. Therefore, just as he gave everlasting reproach to those who had placed God’s ark in Dagon’s temple, so too he gives these people an everlasting reproach, never to be erased unless they amend themselves through true repentance and, abandoning incontinence, maintain pure continence.

This means offering golden “anuses” in place of disfigured anuses: the example of the Philistines, who offered golden anuses for the healing of the wound by which, struck in the more private part of their buttocks, they had shameful anuses for so long. At last, warned by their satraps, they offered golden anuses according to the number of the cities in which this plague had occurred (1 Sam. 5:6 ff.) [Col. 0477C].

Those wise satraps are persons who exhort others to renounce impurity and to devote themselves to the preservation of purity, saying with the Apostle: “For just as you presented your members as slaves to impurity and to iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. 6:19). This is the same as saying: Just as you displayed anuses disfigured through impurity, so now strive to have golden anuses—that is, clean ones—through devotion to continence and fruitful repentance.

Likewise, mice swarm over the fields when, because of sins committed against the ark of God, thieves and robbers arise, robbing either spiritually or bodily, and like mice devastating the crops either of the Scriptures or even of the lands (1 Sam. 5:6). But golden mice are offered in place of fleshly mice when such persons, converted to the purity of faith—which, as the Apostle Peter affirms, is “much more precious” than “gold” (1 Pet. 1:7)—do what is good toward all, but especially toward the members of the household of faith. That faith, as has been said, more precious than gold, makes satisfaction before God for the former sin of error [Col. 0477D].

Alternatively: the punishment by which the Lord struck them in their hinder parts signifies that those who ought to stretch forward toward what lies ahead but look back toward what lies behind will be punished in Gehenna after this life. As the Apostle says, they ought to reckon such things “as dung” (Phil. 3:8). For those who receive God’s Testament in such a way that they do not put off their old vanity are like those Philistines [Col. 0478A] who placed the ark of the testament beside Dagon’s idol. Yet, just as Dagon fell though they did not wish it and grieved over it, so the old things also fall: for the hay of the flesh has withered and the flower of its glory has fallen. But the ark—that is, the secret word of God—remains forever; or the secret contained in the ark is the kingdom of heaven, where the word of God remains, as is elsewhere said: “Forever, O Lord, your word remains in heaven; your truth unto age after age” (Ps. 118:89–90).

Thus, yes, those who love what lies behind will be tormented by it in everlasting reproach, just as he gave everlasting reproach to those whose punishment differed from other punishments for sin, for an increase of shame: because no one was punished in this manner.

### Vv. 67–68. “And he rejected Joseph’s tabernacle.”

[Col. 0478B] THE NINTH PART, concerning the establishment of the kingdom. It is as though he said: Those among whom God’s ark was captured, mistreated, and placed beside an idol were punished deservedly. But the Hebrews to whom the ark was restored were exalted—yet not all of them. For God rejected Joseph’s tabernacle and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim. But he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loved.

He did not say that he rejected the tribe of Reuben, the firstborn, and the others who seem deservedly rejected because Jacob condemned their sins; or Benjamin, from whom Saul had recently been rejected. Rather, he named those who seemed eminent: Joseph, who, sold wickedly, was exalted for righteousness and fed his brothers and father; and Ephraim, whom his grandfather’s greater blessing set above the elder brother. Through these names of conspicuous merit we understand that the whole old people was rejected and the tribe of Judah chosen—not on account of Judah’s merits, for Joseph was better, but because Christ came from Judah.

Scripture thus testifies that Christ’s new people was preferred to the old people. Accordingly, we understand Mount Zion as the Church, which contemplates what is to come rather than earthly things. Thus the narrative proceeds from the beginning of the election of the Hebrew people to Christ. It signifies him parabolically under the names of Judah and David, from whom he also descended according to the flesh and by whom he was magnificently prefigured. For the fact that Judah was blessed more splendidly than the rest in the blessings of the twelve patriarchs delivered by Jacob and Moses pertains to Christ, who is God blessed above all [Col. 0478D]. And the fact that David, though the least among his brothers, was chosen as king prefigured Christ’s kingdom. This parabolic narrative contains, as if in a brief painted panel, the development of that kingdom in the present passage, where it says: “He rejected Joseph’s tabernacle and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim.”

Explaining this, the Apostle says: “Consider your calling: not many powerful, not many wise, not many noble were called; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and the weak things to confound the strong, and the ignoble and despised things, and things that are not, in order to destroy the things that are” (1 Cor. 1:26–28).

Truly, at the beginning of his kingdom, God, desiring in Christ to reconcile the world to himself, did not choose the powerful, as Joseph was ruler of all Egypt; nor those excelling in rank or riches, as Ephraim did, who, through the prerogative of riches and crops and through the greater multiplication of his lineage in offspring, was preferred to Manasseh, his firstborn brother [Col. 0479A]. He did not choose such people. Rather, he chose the tribe of Judah—that is, sinners confessing their sins, such as Matthew the tax collector. For Judah means “confessing.” By this name those who refused to confess either that they were sinners or that Christ was the Son of God showed themselves unworthy.

Peter confessed him: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16); and therefore he is honored by the name of Judah and, like the other Judah, is blessed above his brother-apostles, when he is told: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” [Col. 0479B] (ibid., 18). Of the former it was said: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Gen. 49:8). To the latter it was said: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Of the former it was said: “Judah, lion’s whelp, you have lain down at rest like a lion” (Ps. 16:12). To the latter it was signified by what death he would glorify God: namely, dying on the cross with his hands stretched out, girded by another. Thus Peter too, himself a lion and a lion’s whelp, was made like Christ—a lion and a lion’s whelp—in death.

Does Peter not have the strength of a lion, strengthened by God in Christ, so that the gates of hell may not prevail against him? But what was said of Judah, “Your brothers shall worship you” (Gen. 49:8), far surpasses Peter’s person and pertains particularly to Christ alone, the one man among human beings to be worshipped.

The name Judah, that is, “confessing,” suits not Peter alone, who confessed the rock, but all God’s elect, through whom the heart believes unto righteousness and confession is made with the mouth unto salvation. Therefore God chose the tribe of Judah from the mass of the reprobate and made this tribe Mount Zion—that is, the Church which contemplates what is to come and, despising visible things, knows that visible things are temporal, but invisible things eternal [Col. 0479C].

### V. 69. “And he built his sanctuary like a unicorn in the land which he founded for ages.”

Literally, God once built for himself, through King Solomon, a temple in the land of promise. He founded that land by a most firm promise, establishing it as an inheritance for Abraham’s seed. He built the temple like a unicorn—or rather, truly as a unicorn—because of the one horn of the altar, of which it is elsewhere said: “Appoint a solemn day in the thickly crowded place, even to the horn of the altar” (Ps. 117:27).

For the Jews, to whom it was said, “You shall worship before this altar” (2 Chron. 32:12), were not permitted to multiply altars; but in one temple, before one altar of incense, they were commanded to worship one God. To those worshipping him he was, and is, the horn of strength, against which no force of opposing strength prevails. Hence the kings of Israel and Judah who multiplied altars for themselves and worshipped idols outside the temple, having lost true strength as though their horn had been lost, are often recorded as having succumbed to enemies, both visible and invisible [Col. 0480A].

Still more wonderfully did those perish who, though they were unicorns—that is, professing the worship of one God—made the unique temple of God a den of robbers by committing robbery in it against the only-begotten Son of the one God. Therefore he says: “Deliver me, Lord, from the lion’s mouth, and my lowliness from the horns of unicorns” (Ps. 21:22).

Nevertheless, the temple itself was called the *sanctificium* (“holy place”); the Hebrew text has “sanctuary” in its place, because by it was signified the Lord’s body, which was to be destroyed by Jewish impiety and rebuilt after three days by divine power. That body was indeed a holy place or sanctuary, never to be corrupted by any violation, as it is written: “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10) [Col. 0480B].

This sanctuary—namely, the heavenly sanctuary—was then built upon the earth which he founded for ever, when “Wisdom built herself a house” (Prov. 9:1), supported upon seven heavenly pillars. Although it was fashioned upon earth from virginal flesh, it was nevertheless made higher than the heavens, not only because of the loftiness of the seven pillars—the heavenly choirs, far surpassing all else—upon which this house rests, but also because of that celebration of its dedication, by which, rebuilt and glorified after three days, it was made, as the Apostle declares, higher than the heavens. In this also he built his sanctuary upon the earth which he founded for ever: he sent the Holy Spirit from heaven to sanctify the primitive Church gathered from the stones of the Jewish land [Col. 0480C]. Like a unicorn he built it, because he united those stones so that the multitude of believers might be of one heart and one soul, seeking that one thing of which he elsewhere says: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:4).

One of these aforesaid stones also says: “But one thing: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I shall pursue the prize” (Phil. 3:13–14). Again, urging his disciples to attain that one prize which only one receives, he says: “So run that you may obtain it” (1 Cor. 9:24). Again, “one Lord, one faith, one hope, one baptism, one body” (Eph. 4:5–6) are commended by him, lest there be schism in the one body, enlivened by one Spirit and strengthened by one horn [Col. 0480D]. This horn, surely, is none other than the one God and Father of all, who is above all and in all the chosen stones joined together by one love. Does not Peter also, writing to the primitive Church, show that it was built in this manner, so as to be God’s holy place or sanctuary? “But you,” he says, “are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession, that you may proclaim the mighty acts of him who called you out of darkness into his marvellous light” (1 Pet. 2:9). But because he also had other stones which were not of this sanctuary—namely, sheep which were not of this fold—he called them for this purpose also: that, when these too had been brought in, there might be one sanctuary, one fold [Col. 0481A].

**VERSE 70.** “And he chose David his servant”—that is, the shepherd of a very few sheep in Judaea—that he might be set as a light to the nations, gathering them into his fold. This was thus accomplished through David his servant, that is, through the Son, born in the flesh from David and humbled in the form of a servant. Though in the form of God he was not a servant but Lord, from David he took the form of a servant. In this too he was likened to David: as David was taken from flocks of sheep to reign over men, so he was transferred from the Jews to the nations, as it were from few sheep to many. This was not in his own person, in which he did not bodily pass over to the nations; and in which he testified that he had been sent only “to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 10:6) [Col. 0481B]. Yet in the assembly of the apostles, in whom he himself spoke and acted, he passed from the Jews to the nations—not merely in any fashion, but having been taken from behind those with young.

For in Judaea there had been sheep not barren but, indeed, distinguished by twin offspring: lovers of perfection, not content merely to observe the commandment of righteous conduct, but further adding the observance of the counsel of perfection. Such sheep, shorn—that is, stripped of their own possessions and made, as it were, naked—came up from the washing of baptism, with Peter baptizing: three thousand in one day, and another five thousand. When they had been gathered into one, they were of one heart, and none of them called anything his own. When these were scattered through the regions of Samaria, Cappadocia, and Bithynia, since they were good and fruitful sheep, there too rams producing offspring were not lacking: that is, perfect teachers, lovers and instructors of perfection [Col. 0481C]. These are they to whom Peter, shepherd of the sheep, writes: “I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder: feed the flock which is among you, not under compulsion but willingly, nor for the sake of shameful gain; and when the chief Shepherd appears, you shall receive the unfading crown of glory” (1 Pet. 5:1 ff.).

Therefore, while these good rams, as it were, were producing good sheep, and the true David, shepherd of the sheep—who also spoke in Peter, shepherd of the sheep—governed both, namely the procreating rams and the sheep truly brought forth, this true David himself was taken from behind those producing offspring.

**VERSE 71.** “To feed Jacob his servant among the nations” [Col. 0481D], that is, good persons of the active life, diligently occupied in frequent service, such as was shown in Martha’s ministry; “and Israel his inheritance,” that is, contemplatives, blessed in part by the better portion and still to be made fully blessed. This better portion is the eternal inheritance to be given not outside them but within them. Hence those who are to be enriched, or have been enriched, with such an inheritance are rightly called God’s inheritance. So too in this parable, when it says, “He fed Israel his inheritance”; and elsewhere, where he says: “You are the work of my hands, Israel my inheritance” (Isa. 19:25). Again, the Lord says in the Law: “You shall not give the sons of Levi an inheritance, for I shall be their inheritance” (Num. 20:18).

Those, therefore, whose inheritance God is are themselves also God’s inheritance: holy with the Holy One, chosen with the Chosen One [Col. 0482A]. God chose them indeed as an inheritance for himself, as is elsewhere said: “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he chose as his inheritance” (Ps. 32:12). Thus the true David, God’s servant according to the form of assumed humanity, and nevertheless the omnipotent Lord—not only in the eternal form of God, but also in the now glorified form of man, exalted to the throne of the Father’s kingdom—himself feeds Jacob his servant and Israel his inheritance, invisibly through himself and visibly through his own ministers. The Apostle bears witness: “The grace of the Saviour appeared to all men, instructing us that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and piously in this age” (Tit. 2:11–12): soberly, with respect to the order of the continent; [Col. 0482B] justly, with respect to the order of rulers who live justly and judge justly; piously, with respect to the order of married persons serving God through works of piety by constant almsgiving. Thus they may be Jacob, God’s servant, just as virgins and other continent persons, because of the better portion which they chose, are called and are God’s inheritance, as was shown above. It follows:

**VERSE 72.** “And he fed them in the innocence of his heart, and led them by the understandings of his hands.” It would indeed seem more fitting if it were said: “He fed them in innocence of hands and in understandings of heart,” because those who harm do so with their hands, while all who understand do so with their heart. Yet innocence of hands is rightly ascribed to the heart, so that one may understand that innocence is not perfect unless it proceeds from the heart. The true David truly possessed this innocence, who above all was innocent in hands and pure in heart, because, conceived and born without sin, “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22) [Col. 0482C]; no seedbed of sin was in his heart.

Likewise, understanding, which properly belongs to the heart, is rightly attributed to his hands, which elsewhere are called “golden, full of hyacinths” (Song 5:14), because his deeds shine like golden letters: they nourish not only the gaze of one looking, but also the understanding of one reading. For example, with five loaves he satisfied five thousand men. This divine work, accomplished by divine and golden hands, delights the sight when viewed simply [Col. 0482D], but nourishes the understanding when interpreted mystically. For who other than the true and supremely good shepherd David, who alone has the key of David, has in this very parabolic text which we are handling unlocked those matters inserted from the five books of Moses? He is the one who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens. Not only did he open the Psalms of David, by which he daily feeds his sheep while they sing psalms, giving them to sing wisely; he alone was found worthy also to open the whole book of the entire Old Testament, shut with seven seals, and to loose its seals, because he himself, the good shepherd, was slain for his sheep and was not held by death, but rose—the good shepherd, now never again to die.

Therefore he who fed his sheep before his death in the innocence of his heart and led them by the understandings of his hands [Col. 0483A], for example saying, “Do you know what I have done to you? I, the Lord and Teacher, have given you an example, that you also should do likewise” (John 13:12, 15), now likewise, death having been conquered, feeds his flock still more through the Holy Spirit sent from heaven. The Spirit teaches all truth, clearly displaying the understandings of his hands—that is, of his works—which showed by their examples the way of salvation along which he leads his sheep.

In the Hebrew it reads: “He fed them in the simplicity of his heart, and by the prudence of his hands he was their guide” [Col. 0484A]. Therefore he is shepherd, commander of soldiers, teacher, and guide: the simple and prudent shepherd, the true David, who, as a prudent commander, requires prudence in his soldiers and says to them: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16).

Glory to the Father of this David. Glory to his Son, this David. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is the abundance of pasture for this shepherd David. Amen.

## PSALM 78

[Col. 0483]

[Col. 0483B] “O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance.” When the seventy-seventh psalm had been completed, the following psalm, namely the seventy-eighth, ought to have been expounded, were it not that the night is now drawing near in which no one can work. Therefore, making a leap from here to Psalm 118—which we previously expounded, insofar as we could with God’s help—we then continued the exposition to the end of the Psalter; but now, since the power of darkness is imminent, we are compelled to cease exposition. Yet, lest we seem to have passed over the intervening psalms untouched through negligence, we here give the reason.

The spiritual Antiochus now reigns. By his tyrannical violence the Church is so oppressed, the temple of God so violated, profaned, and polluted, while the danger of schism grows exceedingly grave [Col. 0483C], that there is abundant occasion for singing—or rather for lamenting and weeping—according to the words of this psalm: “O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have polluted your holy temple.” For through the nations—that is, people living as Gentiles—the name of God is blasphemed, when such persons are free to trade in God’s temple and to fornicate around God’s temple. We read that this happened in the days of the Maccabees, when Antiochus sold the priesthood first to Jason and then to Menelaus, and when shameless women thrust themselves into the holy place and the finest young men were placed in brothels.

Asaph, to whom this psalm is ascribed, seems to bewail this desolation [Col. 0483D]. For it has the title, “A Psalm of Asaph.” But it befits the same Asaph—that is, the congregation singing unto the end—to lament still more this abomination of desolation which we now see impending as the end of the world approaches: the spiritual Antiochus reigns and profanes God’s temple, while none, or few, like the Maccabees resist him; men wither from fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world. For it is written in the book of Maccabees: “But there came an attack of evils, most grievous and oppressive to all. For the temple was full of debauchery and feasting, and of those consorting with harlots; women freely intruded themselves into the sacred precincts, bringing in things which were unlawful. The altar too was full of forbidden things prohibited by the laws. Nor were Sabbaths observed, nor were the ancestral feast-days kept; nor did anyone simply confess himself to be a Jew” (1 Macc. 6:3 ff.) [Col. 0484B].

All these things, if there were leisure to expound them, could be applied sufficiently to this stormy age. Yet the evils which then occurred through Antiochus are far surpassed by the evils which now occur in the temple of God, which is the Church: the sanctuary of God is profaned through manifold transgression of old and new laws, and through the abomination of desolation [Col. 0484C]. Considering this, Asaph—that is, the congregation of the faithful—cries out: “O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have polluted your holy temple,” and so forth.

Since I, a little one, have begun to resist these evils in writings and speech, behold, I have been exposed to persecution, because I am compelled to flee from the place entrusted to me. Consequently, I cannot, as I have done until now, attend to the exposition of the psalms which remain, nor pursue all the sections by which the psalms are divided. Yet, lest the division of these sections remain wholly unknown, we take care to sketch briefly each psalm from here to Psalm 118, as though kissing the heads of the psalms [Col. 0484D] and indicating their intentions in summary. In the first of them, which we now have before us, Asaph recounts in mournful declamation the tribulations of the saints, in order to show that they occur for the benefit of the faithful, so that they may be strengthened and not despair in any struggle of inward or outward temptations. They know and hope without doubt that the cry and groaning of the fettered, who say, “Lord, do not deal with us according to our sins,” and so on to the end, shall enter into God’s presence.

“Let your mercies,” they say, “quickly come before us,” lest, if you delay in showing mercy to some prodigal son returning to you, the elder brother—the accuser of the younger brother—should come and hinder compassion [Col. 0485A].

The elder brother is the devil: a brother because he was created by our Father God just as man was, but elder because he was created before man. Or he is called elder because envy makes old the person whom it devastates: he is tormented by the salvation of his received brother. Thus the elder brother Esau too was tormented by the blessing of his younger brother Jacob, as a type of the Jewish people wasting away through envy at the Gentile people’s reception. Thus every envious man, or angel ready to harm the prodigal son compelled by tribulations to return to you, his Father—or adorned by the counsel of his mother, grace, with Esau’s very good and fragrant garments. But you, Father of mercies and God of all consolation, hasten to do us good, saying to your servants: “Bring forth the first robe quickly” (Luke 15:22)—quickly, I say, before the elder brother comes. We have no answer to his reproaches, because we have become exceedingly poor [Col. 0485B], impoverished above all because the nations have entered into your inheritance and have polluted your holy temple, and so forth.

Certainly, for every faithful person his own vices are barbarian nations which have polluted God’s holy temple—that is, our body—as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Cor. 3:16). Therefore, resisting and striving, as has often been said, against sin, they rightly say in this psalm: “Help us, O God our Saviour,” and so forth.

Because in the treatises of teachers who expound the Psalms, the opinions of the holy Fathers Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome, Cassiodorus, Remigius, and Saint Hilary are frequently introduced, and nearly all modern expositions are woven from them; whereas the sayings of Saint Gregory the pope are nowhere, or only rarely, introduced into expositions or new glosses: we, as we have done hitherto, shall join his sayings to our own. Since they are moral sayings, shaping good conduct, they greatly assist and instruct the combatant who, in this middle group of fifty psalms, struggles like another Jacob against vices of conduct [Col. 0486A]. At the end of the psalm a joyful victory is laid up for him, like a crown of righteousness for a just and good contest. For, as though the contest had been completed and the race finished, although not yet in actuality, nevertheless in the hope of victory the faithful combatants rejoice, saying: “But we, your people and the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you for ever; from generation to generation we shall proclaim your praise.” Truly we shall proclaim your praise, not our own, because not by our power but by yours have we fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith. Therefore glory, praise, and honour are due—not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name—through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## EDITOR’S NOTICE

[Col. 0485]

Thus far Gerhoh, who in the Reichersberg manuscripts appended no other exposition of the succeeding psalms down to Psalm 118 than a very brief explanation of the titles by which the individual psalms are marked, together with an explanation of one verse and then another, composed from the sayings of Saint Gregory the Great. Therefore, lest readers should lack in this commentary a continuous exposition of the individual psalms, it has seemed fitting, according to custom, to fill the gap from Honorius of Autun. We shall return to Gerhoh when we reach Psalm 118.

## PART NINE

[Col. 0485]

## PSALM 78

[Col. 0485C] “O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance,” etc. The end of the preceding psalm recounts David’s true building of the temple; this one laments the violation of that same temple. For as Antiochus polluted the temple in Jerusalem under the Maccabees, so Julian the Apostate or the herd of heretics profaned the Church, the temple of Christ [Col. 0486C]. Three psalms are written in lamentation for this same temple. The first is “Why, O God?” in which the overthrow of the Church, Christ’s temple, by persecutors is lamented as the overthrow of that temple by the Romans. The second is “O God, the nations have entered,” in which the violation of this temple by heretics is lamented as was that temple’s violation by Antiochus and the nations [Col. 0487A]. The third is “By the rivers of Babylon,” in which the destruction of this temple under Antichrist is bewailed as was that temple’s destruction under Nebuchadnezzar. There is also another mystery: the preceding psalm recounted that Christ chose the tribe of Judah, which will occur in the time of Antichrist; this psalm recounts how great evils it will suffer for the faith of Christ.

This psalm is placed in the seventy-eighth position. That number is divided into six times twelve, with six remaining, which mystically signify perfection for us. By twelve is understood the teaching of the apostles; by six, the perfection of the righteous, who suffer persecution for righteousness and are brought to the eight beatitudes. Its title is:

**VERSE 1. A PSALM OF ASAPH.**

[Col. 0487B] That is: thus praise is attributed to the perfect faithful of the Jewish people, who deal in this psalm with the tribulation which they perceive to have been inflicted upon them, because they instructed faithful Asaph in the spiritual understanding; as it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that preachers suffered great persecution (Acts 13:50). Or faithful Asaph speaks here before Christ’s coming—that is, the prophets and other perfect persons in God’s people, foreseeing in the Spirit the persecution of the Church, which was signified by the persecution carried out in Jerusalem under Antiochus.

The subject of the psalm is the affliction of the Church under heretics who violate God’s temple, concerning whom the preceding psalm said much. Its purpose is to show that the tribulation of the faithful is for their benefit and to the harm of those who afflict them. The words seem borrowed from the histories of the Maccabees, where the nations polluted God’s temple and shed the blood of the righteous like water. It signifies that heretics profaned the Church, the temple of the living God, and shed much Catholic blood. The first part is “O God, the nations have entered,” in which the Church’s miseries are recalled. The second is “How long, O Lord?” in which the faithful pray for divine aid against adversaries [Col. 0487C]. The third is “The vengeance of [the] blood,” in which the righteous call down God’s vengeance upon the ungodly. Asaph—that is, the faithful people—speaks here under the person of Mattathias.

“O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance.” This happened under the Maccabees, when Antiochus and other nations entered Judaea, God’s inheritance, and polluted God’s temple, because they set an idol in it and sacrificed there to demons. “They made Jerusalem into a watch-hut for fruit”: that is, as a fruit-keeper’s hut remains deserted after the fruit has been gathered, so they made Jerusalem deserted, its inhabitants having been killed [Col. 0487D].

**VERSE 2.** “They gave the dead bodies of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth”: that is, they did not permit the slain to be buried, but cast them out to be devoured by birds and beasts.

**VERSE 3.** “They shed their blood like water around Jerusalem.” Just as water that is poured out is reckoned as nothing, so they reckoned as nothing the shedding of their blood; as they did to Eleazar and the seven Maccabees with their mother and many others [Col. 0488A]. “And there was none to bury them,” because there were so many that they could not be buried, and even the survivors did not dare to bury them because of their enemies. Hence this verse too, “They shed,” is introduced into the history of the Maccabees for the same reason, so that there can be no doubt that the whole psalm was written from it (2 Macc. 1:8). This continues the preceding psalm, where it is read that fire consumed their young men and their virgins, and that because of their multitude they were not lamented. Mattathias and the Maccabees, seeing such great evils, cry:

**VERSE 4.** “We have become a reproach to our neighbours, mockery and derision to those around us.” In Antiochus’s time the Jews were a reproach to all nations, who reproached them for the rite of the Law, mocked those they captured, and derided captives [Col. 0488B].

In a similar manner this happened to the Church under Julian the Apostate, or under the heretic Constans. Groaning, it says: “O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance.” God’s inheritance is the Church, called to the inheritance of the kingdom, of which it was written in the preceding psalm: “Feed Israel your inheritance.” The nations entered into this inheritance when heretics living as Gentiles, together with Jews and pagans, rushed into God’s Church like wolves among sheep and cruelly persecuted Christians. “They made Jerusalem into a watch-hut for fruit”: that is, they made the Church desolate, as fruit-watch shelters are abandoned once the fruit has passed away. For the faithful who remained—some others having been polluted by unbelief and others killed—were like a deserted hut, deprived of the comfort and fellowship of those who had either been slain or polluted [Col. 0488C].

But when the Church seemed deserted to the nations or heretics, then the spirits of the martyrs passed to the heavenly table, like a very abundant and sweet array from the Lord’s garden. “They gave the dead bodies,” that is, the corpses of your servants, “as food to the birds of heaven; they gave the flesh of your saints as food to the beasts of earth.” Had he said only “to birds and beasts,” that would have sufficed; but he added “of heaven” and “of earth” to indicate their intention. For when the spirits of the martyrs had passed like fruit to their cultivator, and the unbelievers daily heard the faithful promise the restoration of their bodies, they scattered the martyrs’ limbs in fragments through air and over earth [Col. 0488D], as though thereby to show that what Christians maintained could not happen, since the bodies had evidently been devoured by birds and beasts. They burned some bodies with fire and scattered their ashes in water, as though they could not rise from there.

“They shed their blood like water around Jerusalem”—that is, throughout the whole world, as cheaply as water is poured out. “And there was none to bury them,” either because of fear of the persecutors, or because so many were slain that the living were insufficient to bury them. In many places the bodies of the saints lay unburied for a long time, until religious persons somehow stole them away for burial. The Church suffered greater persecution from heretics than from pagans or Jews. When many had been slain, the survivors cry: “We have become a reproach to our neighbours” [Col. 0489A]. We are treated so disgracefully that we have become a reproach to neighbours already wishing to come to the faith, because we are mockery and derision to the unbelievers around us. Mattathias speaks for the Maccabees.

**VERSE 5.** “How long, O Lord, will you be angry with the Jewish people that worships you, permitting it to be afflicted by the savagery of the pagans? Will you do this unto the end,” that is, until the destruction of the whole people? “How long will your zeal burn like fire?” Zeal was shown when Phinehas killed a Jew in fornication. Zeal was shown when Mattathias killed a Jew sacrificing to idols. Zeal is called emulation or indignation. This zeal burns like fire when God delivered the Jews to the nations to be killed for idolatry. You have exacted sufficient vengeance upon us; now:

**VERSE 6.** “Pour out your wrath upon the nations which have not known you” [Col. 0489B]. Send indignation upon the adversaries who afflict us and do not worship you as abundantly as you have sent it in many ways upon us who worship you. “Pour out your wrath upon the nations”: you pour your wrath upon us here—that is, a hidden vengeance—but in the future pour it out, that is, exercise manifest and utter vengeance, upon those living as Gentiles, “who have not known you,” that is, have not believed in you; “and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name,” that is, upon lands and many regions which have not worshipped your name, which is Christ Jesus. Therefore pour out wrath upon them:

**VERSE 7.** “For they have devoured Jacob.” That is, they polluted certain supplanters of vices striving for your faith; they led them into their own error and devoured them as food into the body of perdition [Col. 0489C]. Moreover, they desolated his place, because they prevented others from coming to the faith. But literally, the places of the faithful were desolated when their assemblies were destroyed and they themselves were oppressed by persecutors. And because we know that you avenge guilt in us and allow nothing to go unpunished, we pray:

**VERSE 8.** “Do not remember our former iniquities,” that is, sins inherited from parents or committed through ignorance or youth. May your mercies quickly come before us, so that we may will what is good; and strengthen our free choice so that we may persevere in good. Or: may the effect of your mercies swiftly come before us before failure comes first, because we have become exceedingly poor, oppressed by original and actual evils and deprived of the goods of paradise and of the world. Against these evils:

**VERSE 9.** “Help us, O God our Saviour” [Col. 0489D], also to overcome our enemies, so that we may make them conform to us. “And for the glory of your name, O Lord, deliver us” from persecutors, so that we may glory in the Christian name. “And be gracious to our sins for your name’s sake”: you who brought tribulation upon us because of sins, be gracious to us who are afflicted for your name’s sake, because we suffer all these things for that name, since we are called Christians. Deliver us:

**VERSE 10.** “Lest perhaps the nations say: Where is their God?”—the one whom they say they have as helper and defender. “See, now they do what we want and command!” Be gracious to us, and let this grace become known among the nations before our eyes, so that you subject to us those who wish to subject us to themselves [Col. 0490A]. Do not delay until after our death, but do this before our bodily eyes, so that we may see it in our lifetime. Mattathias speaks for the Maccabees.

“Vindicate the blood of your servants which has been shed.” Another translation reads thus. The blood of the seven Maccabees and of many others was shed for the Lord’s Law. The Lord vindicated it when he destroyed Antiochus by a cruel death and destroyed his people by wars.

**VERSE 11.** “Let the groaning of the fettered enter into your presence,” that is, of those placed in captivity [Col. 0490B]. For they had captured many and cast them into chains; their groaning entered into God’s presence, because through Judas and his brothers he punished their adversaries. “According to the greatness of your arm, possess the children of those put to death”: that is, those whom they kill and thereby make our children, possess according to your power as your own inheritance, so that you no longer permit them to depart from you.

**VERSE 12.** “And repay to our neighbours sevenfold into their bosom their reproach”: that is, into their inward being; “their reproach,” I mean, the reproach inflicted by them: “with which they reproached you, O Lord,” supposing that you were wiped from the earth in your servants [Col. 0490C]. For, converted to the faith, they suffered much inward grief that they had ever reproached God or the saints; and they reproached themselves seven times as much as previously they had reproached Christ or his people whom they persecuted.

**VERSE 13.** “But we”—whom they persecuted—“your people and the sheep of your pasture,” whom you fed with the bread of life and understanding, “will give thanks to you for ever”: that is, we shall praise you in heart, mouth, and deed eternally. “From generation to generation” [Note: [Col. 0489D] Vulgate: “unto generation and generation.”], that is, as long as generation succeeds generation, “we shall proclaim your praise” to others, so that they too may praise you, both here and in the life to come.

Otherwise: “Let the vengeance of the blood of your servants be made known among the nations,” that is, in the time of Christians let it become known to all nations that you will avenge the blood of the martyrs [Col. 0490D]. This has now happened, because persecutors have been subjected to the Christian religion, while others were destroyed. “Let the groaning of the fettered enter into your presence”: those whom the mortal body weighs down, who groan under its burden, desiring to be clothed over with the dwelling from heaven, so that mortality may be swallowed up by life. “According to the greatness of your inheritance, possess the children of those put to death.” Fettered for Christ’s name, they endured most grievous persecutions; and, placed amid those very sufferings, they prayed for the Church, lest their blood be fruitless for later generations. The children of those put to death are those who suffered for Christ after the example of the martyrs. The Lord possessed them according to the greatness of his arm [Col. 0491A] when he subjected persecutors to the sovereignty of the Christian name.

“And repay our neighbours sevenfold into their bosom.” This is said not as a curse, but as a prophecy. They call neighbours heretics or false brethren, established in the same religion and worship, but attacking the Church either by depraved conduct or by perverse doctrine. He will repay them sevenfold reproach into their bosom when he punishes them with every kind of punishment in everlasting disgrace. Then he will repay them with the reproach with which they reproached the Lord by evil living or perverse teaching, when he says: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41) [Col. 0492A]. They indeed shall go into eternal punishment; but us, your people and sheep of your pasture, place at your right hand, to whom you will say: “Come, blessed of my Father”; “we will give thanks to you for ever” (ibid., 34), that is, we shall praise you without end.

## PSALM 79

[Col. 0491]

[Col. 0491B] “Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel,” etc., etc. The preceding psalm recounted the calamity which the Church endured from heretics; this one recounts the disaster which the Synagogue suffered from adversaries. Its title is:

**(VERSE 1.) UNTO THE END, FOR THOSE WHO ARE CHANGED, A TESTIMONY OF ASAPH; A PSALM FOR THE ASSYRIANS.**  
[Note: [Col. 0491] Vulgate: “Unto the end, for those who shall be changed, a testimony of Asaph.”]

That is: this hymn tends toward the end, Christ, for those who are changed from Jews into Christians, from a carnal into a spiritual understanding. This psalm is a testimony of Asaph, that is, of the faithful Synagogue, for the Assyrians—that is, for Jews still unbelieving, who consider themselves righteous and upright in the Law. For “Assyrians” is interpreted “those who direct.” Here it testifies that the Jews were destroyed because they did not believe in Christ, and that Jewish Christians escaped destruction because they received faith in Christ [Col. 0491C]. Finally, this testimony confesses both Christ and the vine: that is, the head and the body, king and people, shepherd and flock, and the entire mystery of all Scriptures.

The subject of the psalm is the prayer of the faithful Synagogue for Christ’s coming, and the Church’s prayer for his second coming. Its purpose is that we should pray God to convert us here, and at some time to show us his face face-to-face, as he is. It is divided into three parts, because the Synagogue is described as having been destroyed three times: by the Babylonians, by the Greeks, and by the Romans. The first part is “Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel,” in which Christ’s first and second comings are desired. The second is “You brought a vine out of Egypt,” in which the Church’s expansion is recalled. The third is “O Lord God of hosts, restore us,” in which the visitation of the Church is requested.

This psalm is seventy-ninth in order and signifies the faithful who, after the captivity of this world, will come to fellowship with the nine orders of angels. The psalm’s words seem drawn from the prayer of the Maccabees, who prayed that Christ might by his coming deliver them from Antiochus and from the oppression of adversaries, just as Moses delivered their fathers from Pharaoh and Egyptian affliction. It is the voice of Asaph—that is, of the prophets—for the conversion of the Jewish people in the time of the apostles [Col. 0492B], and the voice of the primitive Church for their conversion after the destruction of the Jews. This conversion occurs daily, and especially in the time of Antichrist.

VERS. 2. Give heed, you who rule Israel. *Is* means “man,” *ra* “seeing,” and *el* “God.” Thus Israel is called “the man who sees God.” Here, by Israel are denoted the angels, who always behold the face of the Father. O King of heaven, who rule the angels, give heed to come to us human beings on earth. You, I say, who lead Joseph like a sheep—that is, who led through the wilderness from Egypt the people descended from Joseph and his brothers, as a shepherd leads sheep to good pasture—come, rescue us, and establish us in a place of safety. The name Joseph is used for the people because he is read to have been, as it were, a prince among that people [Col. 0492C], and it is also used for its signification. You who sit above the cherubim, reveal yourself.

VERS. 3. Before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. Cherubim and seraphim are the highest orders of angels. Christ sits above the cherubim: he is exalted at the Father’s right hand above every principality and power, and above every name named in heaven or on earth. *Cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge”; Ephraim, “fruitfulness”; Benjamin, “son of the right hand”; Manasseh, “forgetfulness.” All these names are set down solely for their signification. For by them the three orders of the Church are denoted: by Ephraim, teachers making others fruitful in faith; by Benjamin, the continent, who are sons of the right hand—that is, imitators of Christ, to be set at his right hand [Col. 0492D]; by Manasseh, married persons, who forget the works and pomps of the devil and follow Christ’s commands. Thus it is said: You who sit above the cherubim, reveal yourself before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh; that is, as you are known in heavenly creatures and rest in them, so make yourself known to those who are in the Church—teachers, the continent, and married persons—that you may rest in them.

Something literal is indicated in these names. Saul, the first king, reigned in Israel from the tribe of Benjamin; and Paul, teacher of the world, was to come from this tribe [Col. 0493A]. When the kingdom was divided into Judah and Israel, Jeroboam, from Ephraim, was the first king to rule in Israel; Ephraim was preferred in Jacob’s blessing. Gideon, a leader in Israel, was from Manasseh; by the sign of the fleece he prefigured the Virgin’s childbirth, and by his wondrous battle foreshadowed Christ’s battle. Hence by Benjamin is understood the primitive Church from the Jewish people, in which Christ first reigned. By Ephraim is understood the Church from the Gentiles, fruitful in faith, in which Christ likewise reigned. Its name is placed first here because it too was preferred in the blessing, and because the Gentile people was preferred by Christ to the Jewish people. By Manasseh is expressed the Church still to believe from among the Jews, which now lies hidden, as though in forgetfulness, but which will yet, like Gideon, engage in fierce battle [Col. 0493B] with Antichrist. Christ, give heed to all these and appear to them.

And in order to do this, awaken your power and come to save us, as Moses saved them. When an event performed symbolically has not yet come to pass, it seems, as it were, asleep; but when that which it signifies occurs, it seems, as it were, awakened. It was God’s power that brought the people out of Egypt and drowned their enemies; and this signifies the salvation of the righteous and the condemnation of the wicked. This apparently sleeping event was awakened when Christ brought the righteous out of hell and plunged the demons into the lake of fire. And because your power, O Christ, was asleep upon the cross while you suffered from weakness, awaken your power now and come to judge, that you may save us and destroy our enemies [Col. 0493C], as you did at the Red Sea. And that this may happen:

VERS. 4. O God, turn us from crooked works to good works, from vices to virtues; and show us your face: reveal yourself to us, as you promised; and we shall be saved from the enemies of mind and body by eternal salvation.

VERS. 5. Lord, God of powers, turn us—that is, you who are Lord and creator of the angels. How long will you be angry over the prayer of your servant? That is: how long, in anger, do you defer what your servants pray for? As if he said: Show yourself quickly. By this is indicated the longing of the saints in tribulation. If the showing of his face is mercy, then delay is truly wrath—the kind of wrath that is in God [Col. 0493D]. This continues the passage read above: “How long, O Lord, will you be angry?” Rightly do we pray to be rescued quickly. For:

VERS. 6. You will feed us with the bread of tears; that is, you permit us here to be afflicted by disasters and miseries, as the fathers were in Egypt. The bread of tears is a life full of sorrows. Especially the righteous live here in toil and suffering. And you will give us drink in tears. Human frailty is sustained by food and drink. By these two is understood that the entire life of the righteous is spent in mourning, groaning, and tears. Yet this is in measure, because labor is apportioned by God according to their strength. The strong are set to bear greater labor, as Lawrence and the other martyrs; the weak, lesser labor, as the confessors.

[Col. 0494A] VERS. 7. You have made us an object of contradiction to our neighbors. Christians were contradicted both by Jews and Gentiles, as it is written: “It is known that this sect is everywhere spoken against” (Acts XVIII, 19–22). Hence it was said also of the Head himself: “This one is set as a sign that shall be contradicted” (Luke II, 34). Therefore Asaph—that is, the primitive Church from the Jews—says: You have made us an object of contradiction to our neighbors, because the Jews, their neighbors, who were unbelievers, such as the Pharisees, contradicted their teaching, as they are read to have done to Paul and Barnabas (Acts XIII). And our enemies, namely the pagans, mocked us: that is, they derided us, saying, “You worship a dead man who was crucified.” The Church from the Gentiles likewise says: You have made us an object of contradiction to the heretics, our neighbors in the same worship of Christ [Col. 0494B], who contradict our faith and assail our teaching; and our enemies, Jews and pagans, mocked us because we worshipped a man condemned with thieves and held differing views within his faith. This verse continues the one: “We have become a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those round about us.” This is understood literally of the Maccabees, whom the Gentiles contradicted and derided for the worship of God. It follows:

VERS. 8. God of powers, turn us, because we continually feed on tears of affliction as food and drink, and Jews, pagans, and heretics contradict us. O God, who gives powers, creator of angels, turn us from earthly things to heavenly, and show the face [Col. 0494C] of your divinity, which you will reveal to your elect, as to Moses; and we shall be saved from the evils that we suffer. And because labor is performed for six days, the Church’s labor is here mystically described in six verses.

VERS. 9. You transplanted a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. This passage continues that which reads: “He removed his people like sheep and led them like a flock in the wilderness, and brought them into the mountain of his sanctification; and you drove out nations before them” (Ps. LXXVII, 52–54). A vine is so called from vines. God brought the vine—that is, the Hebrew nation, from which the gathering of prophets and other faithful persons arose—out of Egypt with great miracles; and, having expelled the nations, namely the Amorites, Hittites, Jebusites, and all the rest, planted it as a wondrous [Col. 0494D] cultivator.

VERS. 10. You were the guide of its journey before it, because you went before them in a pillar of fire and cloud and fed them as they pleased. And you planted its roots: that is, you established their fathers, brought into that inheritance; and it filled the promised land with a numerous offspring.

VERS. 11. Its shadow covered the mountains: that is, its habitation occupied not only the plains but also the highlands. And its branches covered the cedars of God. Vines are called shrubs when they climb trees. The shrubs covered the cedars because many occupied Mount Lebanon, where the cedars are.

VERS. 12. It stretched its branches as far as the sea [Col. 0495A]; that is, it brought forth believers from the sea of all nations. And its shoots as far as the river: that is, it propagated many from the Jews through faith. For by the river is understood Judaea, in which is the Jordan, where baptism began; but by the sea, Gentile life, which has always been in the bitterness of unbelief. Or, it stretched shoots from the river to the sea, when it spread the children of regeneration, beginning from the baptism of the Jordan, in every direction as far as the ocean. After these benefits bestowed upon the Church follow the misfortunes which it incurred through the vices of certain persons.

VERS. 13. Why have you destroyed its hedge? The hedge of Christ’s vine, that is, of the Church, is sacred Scripture, by which it is firmly fortified on every side. God destroyed this hedge when, because of the fault of the faithful, he permitted sacred Scripture [Col. 0495B] to be corrupted by heretics. And therefore all who pass along the way gather its grapes: that is, when Scripture has been overthrown by heretics, even those who do not believe in Christ trample the Church. For when it began to be defamed by heretics, it immediately began also to be attacked by the Gentiles. Hence follows:

VERS. 14. The boar from the forest has laid it waste, because the Roman Empire, from among the Gentiles, devastated it by persecutions. And the solitary wild beast has fed upon it, because Antichrist, uniquely savage, will consume it as grass by various torments. Or the uniquely savage boar is the devil, who is from the forest—that is, from the way of uncultivated thoughts—who laid waste the Church by casting many into heresies and diverse errors [Col. 0495C]. He fed upon it by devouring those fattened in various vices. The prayer of the righteous follows:

VERS. 15. God of powers, that is, of angels, turn from wrath to mercy. Look down from heaven—that is, from Christ—and see: that is, make yourself seen through your heaven, namely through your Son, and behold the misery, plundering, and trampling of your vine; and visit this vine, upon which you have bestowed so many benefits. Visit the Church by freeing it from heretics and persecutors. Visit the Synagogue by giving it faith and good works.

VERS. 16. And perfect it—that is, the Church—in virtues, which your right hand, that is Christ [Col. 0495D], your Son, planted through himself and through the apostles. And upon the son, [Note: [Col. 0495D] Vulgate: “the Son of man.”] whom you have strengthened for yourself: that is, perfect it, founded upon Christ your Son, whom you have strengthened for yourself in all virtues, that is, for your honor. If you perfect it, then:

VERS. 17. Burned with fire and dug up by the rebuke of your countenance: that is, sins committed through desire and fear will perish in them through the preaching of your Son. For every sin is committed either through desire or fear, while someone either desires to obtain something or fears that another may inflict harm upon him. The burning of fire is the heat of desire. The digging up of the vine is fear penetrating the depths of the soul. The rebuke is [Col. 0496A] evangelical preaching. The countenance of God is Christ, who is the image of God. Therefore, if God the Father, the cultivator, cleanses his vine from vices and perfects it in virtues, then all sins committed through desire and fear will perish through Christ’s evangelical preaching, and the cleansed branches will bear abundant fruit. And because this is the first testimony of Asaph “for those changed,” this is understood as the prayer of Jews who have been converted, for those still to be converted and to be changed from unbelief to faith in Christ: God of powers, how long are you turned away from the Israelite people? Turn to it; look upon it through Christ, who is the heaven of heavens; and behold it with mercy, making it see you through faith. Visit this vine, that is, the Synagogue brought out of Egypt by you and once planted in the promised land [Col. 0496B], but now destroyed. Visit it through Elijah and Enoch, and perfect it, which you began to dig in Abraham and the patriarchs, which your right hand—that is, your operation—planted in the prophets. Perfect it upon the Son whom you have strengthened for yourself, Jesus Christ, who is Abraham’s seed, in whom all nations shall be blessed, the firm foundation of the house to be built. In this vine, burned with fire and dug up by the rebuke of your countenance, they shall perish: those from the same nation who, inflamed by the fire of impiety and undermined by evil conduct, refused to believe in Christ shall perish at Christ’s rebuke in the future judgment, when he says: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 41). But that you may visit this vine:

[Col. 0496C] VERS. 18. Let your hand—that is, your power—be upon the man of your right hand, that is, upon Christ your Son, and upon the son of man, namely of the Virgin, whom you have strengthened for yourself by signs and wonders—that is, for your honor—that you may raise him from the dead and all these things may be done through him. And when we have been turned to him:

VERS. 19. We shall not depart from you, as we formerly did when we turned aside to idolatry. You will give us life from the death of the soul through the death of your Son, and we shall call upon your name, which is Father, through the Son. Therefore:

VERS. 20. Lord, God of powers, turn us from unbelief to faith; show your face, and make us [Col. 0496D] understand Christ, who is your face; and through him we shall be saved in eternal life.

The prayer of the Church: Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand and upon the son of man, whom you have strengthened for yourself. God’s hand is his operation. The man of the right hand is the Son of God sitting at his right hand. The son of man is the Son of Mary. From this is taken the frequent expression in the Gospel, “Son of man,” that is, Son of the Virgin. Thus it is said: Let your hand—that is, let your power—be, God the Father, upon Christ, the Son of man received at your right hand, whom you have strengthened as Son for yourself by the Holy Spirit, that he may come in your majesty to judgment [Col. 0497A] and gather fruit from his vine. And we shall no longer depart from you, straying from the true way through vices, as we formerly did. You will give us life by raising us from death, and we shall call upon your name by praising your majesty: Lord, God of powers, turn us from mortality to immortality, and show us your face as you show it to the angels [Col. 0498A]; and thus we shall be saved, when you are all things in all.

This verse is called an intercalary verse, and it is now repeated for the third time, because all these things are accomplished through the Trinity, when the three orders of the Church are taken up into heaven.

## PSALM LXXX

[Col. 0497]

[Col. 0497B] Rejoice in God our helper. This psalm appears to be sung for victory. For in the preceding psalms the King was addressed in complaint that enemies had invaded his inheritance and devastated his vine; and it is understood that he crushed them in war. But here the victors rejoice in their King and helper, and acclaim God and the conqueror. Hence the words of the psalm seem drawn from the Maccabees, who, after Antiochus and the Gentiles had been defeated, blessed the Lord in hymns because he had given them victory. It signifies that faithful Jews will acclaim the Lord after they triumph over Antichrist and the persecutors. This psalm is connected with the preceding one in that the former treated of the vine, while this one is entitled concerning winepresses. A winepress pertains to a vine. It should be noted [Col. 0497C] in all the psalms that what follows is always connected with what precedes, either through the title or through the text. The title is:

(VERS. 1.) UNTO THE END, FOR THE WINEPRESSES; THE FIFTH DAY OF THE SABBATH; A PSALM OF ASAPH. [Note: [Col. 0495] Vulgate: “Unto the end, for the winepresses. A psalm for Asaph himself.”]

The end is Christ, in whom all things shall be consummated. A winepress is a place of treading, in which grapes are pressed, wine is poured into storehouses, and grape-berries are thrown to pigs. It signifies the Church, in which the righteous are heavily pressed by the wicked; but the righteous are brought as sweet wine to the table of the heavenly King, while the impious, like dregs, are cast to pigs—that is, to demons. It is said “for the winepresses” in the plural because there are two Churches: one from the Jews, the other from the Gentiles. The fifth day [Col. 0497D] of the Sabbath is Thursday, on which God produced birds and fish from water, lifted birds into the air, and left fish in the depths. It signifies that Christ raises some of the baptized to the heights and casts others down to the depths. A psalm is a work of God: that is, a song made in praise of God. Asaph is called the Synagogue, which means the Lord’s congregation. Thus the title is expounded: This hymn of the Lord’s congregation tends toward the end, that is, Christ who consummates all things. It is a song for the winepresses, that is, the Churches oppressed here by the wicked, considering what was done on the fifth day of the Sabbath: for as God raised to the heights birds created from water and submerged fish in the waves, so he will raise those oppressed in the Church to heaven and condemn the wicked to Tartarus.

[Col. 0498B] The subject of the psalm is the rejoicing of those liberated for victory. Its purpose is that, as conquerors of vices, we may acclaim God, so that we may be filled by him with the bread of life and the honey of eternal sweetness. This psalm is divided by two *diapsalmata* into three sections, because the two Churches are divided into three orders, namely virgins, widows, and married persons, who through the two commandments of love, in faith in the Trinity, shall attain heavenly things. In the first part praise is sung to the King by those who have been freed. In the second, the King addresses the people. In the third, the recompense of friends and enemies is set forth.

This psalm is the eightieth, produced by multiplying ten and eight; for eight tens or ten eights make the sum of that number. It signifies that those who fight armed with the ten commandments shall arrive at the eight beatitudes. Note that in this decade the King addresses the people three times. First, where he says: “When I receive the appointed time, I shall judge its just judgments” (Ps. LXXIV, 3). Second, where he says: “Attend, my people, to my law” (Ps. LXXVII, 1). Third, in this psalm, where he says: “Hear, my people, and I will speak.” In the first place he promises just judgment as judge; in the second he sets forth the law to the people as King; in the third, as rewarder, he will give a worthy recompense to observers of the law and punishment to its despisers. It is the voice of priests exhorting the liberated or victorious to praise the King.

VERS. 2. Rejoice in God our helper. O congregation [Col. 0498D] of the Lord, sing joyfully to the King who helped us overcome our enemies and delivered us from their cruelty. Acclaim the God of Jacob, that is, our wrestler. For Jacob, who wrestled with the angel, stands for the wrestler. The Lord loved Jacob and hated Esau; and Jacob is the younger son, whom the elder serves. He signifies the Christian people, whom the Jewish people, by God’s agency, now serves. The Lord loves this supplanter of vices and hates the other because of unbelief. Therefore you who are Jacob, acclaim God with voice and praise him in heart as one who fights for you, in this manner:

VERS. 3. Take up the psalm and give the timbrel, the pleasant psaltery with the lyre. By the psalm is understood heavenly teaching; by the timbrel, which is stretched skin, affliction of the flesh, such as fasting; by the psaltery, which sounds from above, heavenly commands; by the lyre, which sounds from below, good works [Col. 0499A]. That is to say: eagerly receive heavenly teaching as food; offer almsgiving and fasts; in the contemplative life sing spiritual hymns joyfully to God; in the active life persist in good works. With these weapons you fought and conquered; with these instruments you ought to celebrate your victory. Also sound the trumpet as a sign of victory: that is, preach to others in praise of Christ the victor. This is what he says:

VERS. 4. Sound the trumpet at the new moon. The new moon is the *neomenia*, or the Kalends. The Hebrews count months from the new moon, which the priests observe; when it is first seen, they sound trumpets and by this signal announce the feast to the people. Three festivals are written in the Law: Passover, Pentecost, and Scenopegia. Passover was the feast on which they passed out of Egypt, celebrated in spring. Pentecost was the feast on which they received the Law from the Lord on the fiftieth day after their departure, celebrated in summer. Scenopegia was the Feast of Tabernacles, held in autumn in September: before this feast they fasted for ten days until evening, and from the first day of the seventh month sounded the trumpet, then celebrated Scenopegia. After the Temple was built, a fourth solemnity was added, called *encaenia*, that is, Dedication, held in winter. According to [Col. 0499C] this custom the Church still observes the fasts of the Four Seasons. By fasting is expressed Christians’ battle against the battle-lines of vices. The ten days of fasting are the ten commandments, which are our weapons. The trumpet’s blast is the voice of prayer or preaching; the seven days in the seventh month are the seven gifts in the sevenfold Spirit. The festival following the fast is the future joy promised to us. The new moon is the Church, daily renewed from its old life through Christ, the new sun. In it those sound the trumpet who preach in the Church what we have already said. It follows:

On the notable day of your solemnity: that is, at Passover, when Christ was sacrificed for us and we passed from unbelief to faith. At Pentecost, that is, on the fiftieth day after the Resurrection, we received through the Holy Spirit the law of love. On this day those sound the trumpet who announce this grace to the redeemed. The Feast of Tabernacles is when we rise after a fall and renew by repentance our bodies, the soul’s tabernacles. For there will be rejoicing among the angels over the repentant. Hence fasting and the trumpet blast precede this feast, because repentance is accepted through fasts and prayers. The Dedication of the Temple signifies that feast at which Christ will dedicate the Church, his temple, in the glory of the resurrection. At these feasts we sound the trumpet when we preach these things to the people.

It should be noted that we are commanded to praise God with musical instruments. The ancients used these arts in sacrifices; hence we too use organs in the divine offices. The whole Church is God’s organ; the elect are sweet-sounding pipes. They are also a lyre, resounding to God with the heart. For just as various pipes or different strings in song seem discordant, yet all are harmonious in concord, so the lives of saints seem discordant among themselves: one gladly prays, another weeps continually; one fasts, another keeps more vigils; yet all sound together in one charity. Music is an art of heavenly discipline, whose first division is harmonic, rhythmic, and metric; its second division is percussive, as cymbals; stringed, as the lyre; wind-blown, as organs. Its third division is into seven symphonies; its fourth into fifteen tones. Through this art many miracles are read to have occurred, both in secular and divine [Col. 0500B] books: for example, the evil spirit was expelled from Saul by this art, and the walls of Jericho fell through the sound of this art. Therefore, instructed in this art, we set divine words to melody in this praise, such as hymns and the rest, and we serve God with instruments of this art, such as organs, cymbals, and bells, because we know that psalms were uttered by musical instruments.

VERS. 5. For it is a commandment in Israel. It is commanded among the people Israel that these solemnities be properly observed. And judgment has been given to the God of Jacob—that is, to the God of Christians—to crown the celebrants of these solemnities and condemn those who despise them.

VERS. 6. He established that as a testimony in Joseph when [Col. 0500C] he went out of the land of Egypt: he heard a language he did not know. Joseph did not leave but entered the land of Egypt, and there he heard a language he did not know. But by Joseph, who was a prince in Egypt, is understood the whole people descended from his stock. When it went out of Egypt, it heard a language it did not know, when it heard God speaking the ten commandments on the mountain. Therefore God established that testimony in Joseph: the unknown language which he heard from heaven through angels, when he also sounded trumpets as a sign, as he gave the commandments of the Law and sounded trumpets for this signification.

VERS. 7. He turned his back away from burdens; his hands served in baskets. Joseph is not read to have carried burdens or served with baskets. But afterward the people Israel carried heavy loads of stones to build houses for Pharaoh; its hands served in baskets while, sweating in mud and brick, they carried these materials in baskets. God turned its back away from those burdens when he delivered it from Pharaoh’s slavery. Joseph means “increase” and is Christ, because as Joseph, sold into Egypt, was exalted after tribulations, so Christ, passing to the Gentiles, was glorified in the Church after the sufferings of the martyrs. This Church is called “increase” because “the children of the desolate are more numerous than of her who has a husband” (Isa. LIV, 1). Therefore Joseph’s leaving Egypt—that is, the people multiplied through Joseph—passed through the Red Sea because the Church’s people, leaving its old life through baptism consecrated by Christ’s blood [Col. 0501A], heard a language it had not known: that is, it received mysteries it had not known. He established the covenant in this Joseph when he taught the Gospel to this people. It heard a language it had not known when it heard the apostles speaking in various and unknown tongues; and it heard the commandment, “Love your enemies” (Luke VI, 27), which it had previously not known. By this language he turned its back away from burdens: that is, he turned it from the vices that burdened the soul. Truly it bore burdens, for its hands served in baskets: as those people served in mud and brick to build cities for Pharaoh, so these people filled themselves by filthy deeds to build the devil’s city, Babylon. Here the person of God is introduced speaking thus: O Joseph, observe what you heard through the unknown [Col. 0501B] language, because:

VERS. 8. In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you, etc. The people Israel called upon God in Egypt’s tribulation, and the Lord delivered it through Moses. He heard it in the secrecy of the storm when, with Pharaoh pursuing it with his army and a severe tempest, as it were, threatening, he rescued the people crying out in the hidden place of the heart through fear of the pursuing enemies. I tested you at the water of contradiction. This occurred where he tested it with thirst and brought water from the rock to the murmuring people, when Moses and Aaron offended God and therefore did not enter the promised land (Num. XX, 10 ff.). The Lord delivers the Christian people calling on God in tribulation when he rescues it from any affliction or forgives its sins when it is in the sorrow of repentance. He hears it in the secrecy of the storm when he rescues it from hidden temptation. He tests it at the water of contradiction when, among a people opposing its good life, he tests it as a grape pressed in the winepress or as gold in the furnace.

*Diapsalma.* Here the King addresses both peoples, of the good and the evil:

VERS. 9–10. Hear, my people, and I will testify to you: Israel, if you hear me, there shall be no new god in you, nor shall you worship a foreign god. These words are taken from the Law, where the Lord said: “Hear, Israel: your God is one; you shall not make a graven image; you shall not worship another god besides me. For I am the Lord [Col. 0501D] your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Deut. V, 6 ff.; VI, 4). O my people, hear through faith—that is, obey what I command you—and I will testify to you: that is, I swear to you that I shall fulfill what I promise you. O Israel, seeing God through Scripture, if you hear me in the Scriptures, if you obey my teaching, there shall be—that is, let there not be—in you a new god, and you shall not worship a foreign god; and I shall reward you, because I shall fill your mouth with every sweetness. And I am able to do this.

VERS. 11. For I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt: that is, from unbelief to faith. A new god is one made in time; the not-new God abides eternally forever. Note that he did not say “before you,” as though it were an image brought in from outside, but “in you”: namely, in your heart, in the image of your imagination, in the deception of your error.
