A person makes a new god within himself who fashions God by imagining him in the heart as a glorious king. A person worships a foreign god who proclaims the Son lesser than the Father, or the Holy Spirit a creature. All heretics worship a foreign god because they preach about God what is foreign to God. Yet a new god will be to everyone who worships the belly as god. God is to be worshipped, through whom we have been brought out of the Egypt of diabolical slavery into life. He who is truth, wholly present everywhere, says here to his worshipper: Enlarge your mouth, and I shall fill it—that is, enlarge the mouth of your heart like the young of birds, and I shall satisfy it. Desire virtues, and I shall give them to you. I commanded this people and promised it these things.

[Col. 0502B] VERS. 12. But my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not heed me. My people according to the mystery of faith did not hear my voice, because it did not obey my commands; and Israel, namely the instructed, did not heed my teaching. Therefore, in anger:

VERS. 13. I dismissed them according to the desires of their heart. At first I restrained them, lest they bring eternal death upon themselves. But after they despised my words, I dismissed them to go headlong into the abyss. Therefore they shall go in their own devices: that is, they shall fulfill the desires that they devised for their own destruction. To the utterly miserable, it seems to be God’s benefit when they are allowed to fulfill their own wishes; they do not know that it is God’s anger and inward [Col. 0502C] vengeance, as it is written: “God gave them over to their desires, to impurity” (Rom. I, 24), that they may be judged according to their works. For the more they sinned, the more grievously they shall be condemned. Because I am merciful, I shall receive them: this is the meaning of what follows, if they have returned.

VERS. 14–15. If my people had heard me, doing what I commanded it; if Israel had walked in my ways, that is, in my commandments: perhaps—that is, easily—I would have humbled their enemies, that is, I would have subdued demons, the proud enemies of souls; and I would have laid my hand, that is, my power, upon those who afflicted them—that is, upon the vices and sins inwardly afflicting them—taking them away lest they afflict them. “Perhaps” is said because he foreknew that they would not be converted. It is the likeness of an affectionate father who lets his stubborn son do what he wishes in wickedness, yet afterward, complaining to his friends, says that he would receive him if he came to his senses. This is drawn from the Jews, who, having rejected God’s Law, were handed over to their enemies.

*Diapsalma.* The voice of Asaph, the King’s spokesman, follows. The King gave commands to the people and promised rewards, and they promised that they would do everything; but:

VERS. 16. The enemies of the Lord lied to him. Everyone who is a friend of this world is made an enemy of God. Those who do not fulfill what they promised God in baptism become God’s enemies, because they lie about what they promised to do and return like dogs to their vomit. And their time shall be in the age: that is, in [Col. 0503A] this time and in this age they do what they will; in the other age, in an instant they go down to hell. But when they have done what they desired, after this their time shall be for ages: namely, a time of eternal punishment, when it shall be said to them: “Go into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 41), where “their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. LXVI, 14; Mark IX, 43, 45, 47). Thus we are accustomed to say: “Tomorrow will be your time,” that is, tomorrow you shall pay for whatever you have sinned. Or their “time,” that is, their failing, shall be eternal and without end. And who are these enemies? Those whom:

VERS. 17. He fed from the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock: that is, whom he made partakers of his sacraments. This is drawn from the history in which he rained manna upon them and brought water from the rock. By this is understood that the bread of heaven, which possessed every delight, naturally tasted, like the finest wheat, sweet; and that water brought from the rock changed its flavor for the pleasure of its drinkers. For elsewhere it is written concerning this rock: “That he might suck honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone” (Deut. XXXII, 13). To one it tasted like honey, to another like oil or wine. By the fat of wheat is understood the body of the Lord, by which the elect are refreshed. By honey from the rock is understood the sweetness of the Holy Spirit. Or honey from the rock is wisdom flowing from Christ. For it seems a great sweetness when one can solve riddles set before him. The King will condemn his enemies who lied to him; [Col. 0503C] but he will satisfy his friends with wheaten food and honeyed drink—that is, he will fill them with every sweetness of complete joy.

[Col. 0504A] Note the order of the eighth decade, which pertains to the grace of the New Testament. In the first psalm the power and justice of the new King, sent by God to the Jews, are described. In the second, his unusual practice is described, for which he is blamed: because he exalts his enemies with riches and honours, while he constricts his friends with poverty and oppression. In the third, the wondrous equity of his judgment is related, because he punishes the wicked by means of the wicked, just as he crushed the Jews by the Romans. In the fourth, he is praised by the people for his judgments. In the fifth, the King’s dwelling in Zion and Jerusalem is recalled. In the sixth, the human race makes its complaint before the King concerning its expulsion from the inheritance of Paradise. In the seventh, the King sets forth a law for the people, by which it may recover its inheritance; and Asaph, the King’s spokesman, recounts the benefits which he bestowed upon the fathers, [Col. 0504B] to whom, once delivered from affliction, he restored their lost inheritance. For Shem first inhabited the land of Canaan; but after the division of tongues, the descendants of Ham drove out the inhabitants of that land and possessed it. The Lord expelled them through the Hebrews, his proper heirs, and restored the inheritance taken away by force. In the eighth, a grave lament is made before the King concerning his inheritance overrun by enemies: its inhabitants slain, the royal city plundered, and the country laid waste. In the ninth, there is again a complaint concerning the vineyard ruined by enemies, which the King had planted with great care. When the King has justly judged all these matters, in the tenth the people hasten together for the solemn celebration of victory, with trumpets sounding; there they acclaim the King with instruments and [Col. 0504C] timbrels, are refreshed by the King with grain and honey, and, rejoicing, receive back their lost inheritance, flowing with milk and honey.

## PSALM LXXXI

[Col. 0503]

[Col. 0503C] “God stood in the synagogue of gods,” etc. Nine orders of angels are found in the Scriptures; and this is the ninth decade, in which much is written concerning the sons of God, or angels, and eternal blessedness. For it treats of him who is God and man, through whom human beings are joined to angels. [Col. 0503D] This psalm is the eighty-first, a number distinguished by eight, ten, and one. By eight is understood the blessedness of the resurrection; by ten, the recompense of labour; by one, the joy of eternal life, that “one thing necessary” (Luke 10:42). Therefore this number is assigned to this psalm, because all who faithfully believe that Christ is God and man receive him himself as the reward of life in the resurrection.

The subject of the psalm is God’s intercourse with humanity. Its purpose is that we may believe the crucified Christ to be God, so that we may be named, and may be, sons of God or gods. Its title is:

**(VERSE) 1. A PSALM OF ASAPH.**

That is, this praise of God is from the faithful people to the unfaithful [Col. 0504C] people, that they may know Christ to be God. The words are taken from the Law, where priests, who are called gods, are commanded to judge the people justly; and it looks to the chief priests, who judged Christ unjustly. It is divided by two *diapsalmata* into [Col. 0504D] three sections, because through the two Testaments the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—are converted to faith in Christ. In the first section Christ as God and man is described; in the second, the iniquity and ignorance of the Jews are blamed; in the third, the deification of the righteous, the casting down of the wicked, and Christ’s inheritance among all nations are recalled.

The voice is that of Asaph, that is, of the faithful:

“God stood in the synagogue of gods.” The synagogue of gods is the assembly of the righteous. Priests and prophets anointed with oil are called gods, as is written in the Law: “You shall not speak ill of the gods” (Exod. 22:28), that is, of priests. And Moses is told: “I have made you a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1). Not angels but human beings are called gods, because God assumed a human being, not an angel. Hence, when certain angels wished to be called gods, [Col. 0505A] they were condemned by the highest God.

Therefore God stood in the synagogue of gods when God, dwelling in Christ among human beings, remained among the apostles and priests. For *stood* is often used in the sense of *remained*. We now say, “He stood in that city for a year,” that is, he remained or lived there. “But in the midst he judges gods.” The prophetic gods preceded Christ; the apostolic gods followed him. He himself was in the midst, as the central point, joining both groups in himself—he who is God over all, blessed for ever. Here he judges gods, that is, distinguishes them, because by the gifts of the Holy Spirit he set the apostles apart from the priests of the Law. He also distinguished gods when he gave knowledge to one, wisdom to another, prophecy to another, and another grace to another. But he judged the gods, namely the chief priests, [Col. 0505B] saying:

**VERSE 2. “How long will you judge unjustly?”**

It was an unjust judgment when they deemed mint, rue, and dill to be offerings required, while neglecting God’s justice. They judged unjustly when they decreed that prophets sent by God should be killed. It was iniquity when they judged that the Son of the Father, sent to the vineyard, should be killed, so that they themselves might possess his inheritance.

“How long do you accept the persons of sinners?” The Law commanded that they should not show regard for persons in judgment, but judge all people justly. Yet they acquitted the rich and oppressed the poor. “How long?” means: how long will you do these things? They did this to such a degree when they accepted the person of Barabbas the robber and condemned the person of innocent Christ, [Col. 0505C]

**VERSE 3. “Judge for the needy and the orphan.” *Diapsalma*.**

Christ was needy, having nowhere to lay his head, because though he was rich, he became poor for our sake. He was likewise an orphan, because in heaven he had no mother and on earth lacked a father. For him, O priests, judge according to his justice, and do not condemn him: “Vindicate the humble and the poor.” Christ, exalted in heaven, became humble on earth; rich in heaven, poor on earth. You peoples, vindicate him in judgment and do not declare him guilty.

It may also be understood thus: let judges judge justly for the needy and orphan, and vindicate the humble—that is, the despised—and the poor in his cause. And you rulers,

[Col. 0505D]

**VERSE 4. “Rescue the poor.”**

Rescue poor Christ, seized by the raging Jews; deliver the needy one from the hand of the sinner—that is, from Pilate’s hand, by which he was unjustly condemned to death. This must be done for all good persons: that they rescue the poor, Christ’s member, from oppressions, and deliver the needy from the ungodly. It follows:

**VERSE 5. “They did not know, nor did they understand.”**

That is, the scribes and Pharisees did not know Christ to be God, nor did they understand the Law written concerning him. “They walk in darkness,” that is, they persist in blindness until they extinguish the eternal light by death. Had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. Since they did this, “all the foundations of the earth shall be moved.” For when he who was crucified expired, the whole earth was shaken and trembled.

[Col. 0506A] Alternatively: “All the foundations of the earth shall be moved,” because the rulers of the earth will be converted to faith in Christ with fidelity.

*Diapsalma.* Christ, crucified in the weakness of the flesh and rising in the power of God, stood in the midst of the disciples—that is, the apostles—saying:

**VERSE 6. “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.”**

He expressed this meaning in other words when he said: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20:23). For forgiving sins is an office of God.

The question is asked: when did he say to the apostles, “You are gods”? Certainly when he called them his friends and brothers. Christ is God; therefore his brothers are gods and sons [Col. 0506B] of the Most High, that is, of the Father. But Christ is God by nature; they are gods by grace. He is the Son of God by nature; they are adopted sons by grace, heirs of the kingdom, and co-heirs with Christ. Christ, born God from the Father, was made human; they, born human, were made gods.

**VERSE 7. “But you, chief priests, shall die like men.”**

Here he distinguished gods from gods: the apostles from the priests. Another translation has: “You shall die like Adam.” That is: I appointed that you should be gods, and I came in the flesh so that all of you might be sons of the Most High and heirs of God’s kingdom; but you, deceived through malice, shall die like Adam, who was deceived by the devil. Or: like human beings, namely carnal people, you shall die in sins by eternal death, because you are unwilling [Col. 0506C] to know me, life.

“And you shall fall like one of the princes.” There were ten orders in heaven, each with its own prince. The more worthy order fell, and a multitude of angels collapsed with it, as it is written: “The dragon drew down with his tail a third part of the stars to the earth” (Rev. 12:4). Therefore, just as the prince of demons fell from heaven, so you chief priests shall fall from the glory by which you were called gods. And just as the devil, their prince, when he fell voluntarily, was not deceived by anyone else, so Caiaphas and the other rulers did not kill the Lord because another deceived them, but voluntarily. Therefore they shall fall from God’s glory into the depths of hell.

The voice of Asaph—that is, of the faithful—follows, because they refuse to be converted:

**VERSE 8. “Arise, O God; judge the earth.”**

You who, unjustly judged, lay in the tomb as a human being: arise in judgment as God; judge earthly people and blind the Jews. For when they have been blinded, you shall inherit among all nations: that is, instead of one faithful people, you shall possess all nations through faith. Above, the settlers complained that the inheritance—the kingdom of Judea—had been overrun by nations. This inheritance is now restored to him manifoldly, when all nations are possessed by him.

[Col. 0506D] Alternatively: God, arising, shall judge the earth when Christ, God and man, in judgment condemns earthly persons—that is, lovers of earthly things—and shall inherit among all nations when he calls the righteous from every nation to the inheritance of the kingdom, whom he himself shall possess for ever.

## PSALM LXXXII

[Col. 0507]

[Col. 0507A] “O God, who shall be like you?” etc. This psalm deals with the destruction of enemies. In the preceding psalms the Church said that the King’s inheritance had been laid waste, his vineyard ruined, and possession of all nations restored to him anew. This psalm considers who laid waste or attacks his inheritance and vineyard, what reward they have received or will yet receive. And just as the preceding psalm described Christ, God and man, together with his body—that is, the elect—so this psalm treats of Antichrist together with his body, that is, with all the reprobate. All of them will strive to take away the Church, Christ’s inheritance and vineyard; for this they shall finally perish.

This is the eighty-second psalm, a number [Col. 0507B] divided into forty and forty, and into two. Forty signifies repentance; two, love. This number is therefore attached to the psalm because both peoples, Jewish and Gentile, who attack the Church, God’s inheritance, and refuse repentance, shall be condemned; while the Christian people, possessing the twofold love, shall be saved. The title of the psalm is:

**(VERSE 1.) A SONG OF A PSALM OF ASAPH.**

“A song of a psalm” is one expression: it is the song which the choir begins and the instruments follow or accompany. It signifies joy of mind concerning eternal things, joined with good works. This song belongs to Asaph, that is, to the faithful assembly from among the Jews, which sings to God with spiritual joy concerning the overthrow of the Church’s [Col. 0507C] enemies and the reward of the faithful.

The subject of the psalm is the invaders of Christ’s inheritance. Its purpose is to urge us to avoid the pursuits of such persons, so that we may be counted in the Lord’s inheritance. The words are taken partly from the book of Judges, partly from the book of Kings, where it is written that many nations invaded, ravaged, and oppressed the nation of the Hebrews. This signifies that Jews, pagans, heretics, and false Christians attack, scatter, oppress, and plunder Christ’s Church.

It is divided into two parts. The first begins, “O God, who is like,” in which it is said how Antichrist with his body rages against the Church, hastening to ruin Christ’s vineyard. The second is “Make them like Midian,” in which it is written how God overthrows him with his followers. The voice is that of Asaph, that is, of the faithful assembly:

**VERSE 2. “O God, who shall be like you?”**

Antichrist wishes not only to be like God, but even “exalts himself above everything that is called God or is worshipped as God” (2 Thess. 2:4). But, O Christ, true God, who [Col. 0508A] shall be like you in judgment? No one. Here many seem to be like you because they sin with impunity. But a time will come when it will appear that they were not like you here, when they undergo punishments which they cannot ward off, because they made themselves like you.

And then, Lord, do not be silent in vengeance—you who are now silent in patience, “overlooking human sins for the sake of repentance” (Wisdom 11:24). Take vengeance, and do not be restrained, O God, from vengeance. He who now patiently endures the wickedness of the wicked will then not be restrained—that is, will not for ever withhold their punishment.

Set your power against them,

**VERSE 3. “For behold, your enemies”**—Jews, pagans, heretics, false Christians—“have made a tumult”; they have assembled a great army and sounded the trumpet. “And those who hate you,” that is, all these who hate you, “have lifted up the head”: they have raised Antichrist as king and worshipped him as God. The Lord’s enemies make a tumult when they preach evil; those who hate him lift up the head when they raise their mind in pride.

[Col. 0508B]

**VERSES 4–5. “They have devised a malicious plan against your people.”**

Your assembled enemies have devised a malicious plan against your Christian people. “And they have taken counsel against your saints,” considering how to destroy them. They said: “Come, let us destroy them from being a nation, and let the name of Israel be remembered no more.” That is: let us rush together upon Christians and remove them from the human race, so that there may no longer be remembrance of the Christian name upon earth. For Israel means the faithful, who are Abraham’s seed. Resist them,

[Col. 0508C]

**VERSE 6. “For they have taken counsel with one accord.”**

That is, many are united and will be united in thought against us. “Together they have made a covenant against you”: that is, they have concluded a pact against your people, binding themselves by a promise to persecute them. And who made this agreement? Eleven nations attacking the Church under the guardianship of the twelve apostles. By nations I mean those living in a Gentile manner, namely:

**VERSES 7–9. “The tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites; Moab and the Hagarites; Gebal and Ammon and Amalek; the foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre. Assur also came with them; they became a help to the sons of Lot.”**

These nations formerly devastated the Hebrew people, [Col. 0508D] and signify those who daily devastate the Christian people. David met them with an army, killed seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen, and returned victorious with great spoil; for Christ casts down the Church’s enemies in their vices, and brings spoil from them when he converts them to the pursuit of virtues.

“The tents of the Edomites” are the multitude of earthly-minded persons. Esau was called Edom; hence they are called Edomites, which means “earthly,” and they signify those who savour only earthly things, such as the Jews. Ishmael was Abraham’s son by Hagar. Ishmaelites are interpreted as “obedient to themselves”; they are false Christians who obey their own pleasures. Moab was Lot’s son by his daughter, and his name means “from the father” or “from the law.” He signifies those whose father is the devil, who reject the Lord’s law—that is, his commands—and wish to establish their own ordinances.

The Hagarites are named from Hagar; the name means “strangers,” and they are heretics who estrange themselves from the Church’s body through their heresy. Gebal was a king of the eastern peoples, and his name means “vain valley.” He signifies hypocrites who, through fasting and other means, pretend to be religious so as to acquire for themselves a reputation for religion. They are deadly within the Church, because [Col. 0509B] when they utter an erroneous judgment, it is quickly believed because of the holiness thought to be in them.

Ammon was Lot’s son by his other daughter, and means “troubled people.” These are teachers of heretics, who make others troubled by their unclean teaching, though they were formerly clear while holding the right faith. Amalek was the son of Eliphaz, son of Esau, and means “licking the earth.” He signifies those who, established in the Church, covet worldly riches and honours, as though some blessedness were in them. They are very harmful, because by their example and exhortation they sometimes teach others to desire earthly things.

The foreigners are Philistines, named from the city of Philisthiim, which is also called Ascalon. They are called foreigners because they were more alien from the Jews than all others and persecuted them. Philistines, moreover, are interpreted as “falling by drink,” and signify the lustful, who, drunk with the foulness of lust, fall into destruction.

[Col. 0509C] Tyre is a city founded by Sidon, son of Canaan. In Hebrew it is *Sor*, named from a certain fish; it means “straitness” or “tribulation,” and signifies unbelievers. They dwell in Tyre when they seek to inflict straitness and tribulation upon the faithful; or they dwell in *Sor*, that is, in distress of soul.

Assur was Nimrod’s son; from him came the Assyrians, among whom Nebuchadnezzar reigned, who led an army against the Lord’s people. Assur means “directing,” and is understood as the devil directing the wicked toward destruction. He came with them, that is, he inspires them to persecute God’s Church. By saying “with them,” the text indicates their free will: they persecute not under compulsion but voluntarily.

[Col. 0509D] All these “became a help to the sons of Lot,” that is, they assist demons in the Church’s destruction. Lot was the son of Haran, Abraham’s brother, and his name is interpreted “turning aside.” He signifies the prince of demons, who voluntarily turned aside from God’s grace. His sons are the other demons, his imitators, who attempt to destroy the Church, though they cannot do so except through the service of certain people.

Having described the eleven nations gathered against the Church, he goes on to their seven leaders: Midian, Sisera, Jabin, Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna, who formerly sought to destroy the Hebrew nation. They signify those who now [Col. 0510A] attempt to destroy God’s Church. But as those men were defeated by a woman, namely the prophetess Deborah or Jael, so these will be crushed by God’s wisdom. Their condemnation is written here:

**VERSE 10. “Make them like Midian.”**

The history referred to is as follows. The children of Israel, having forsaken the Lord, served Baal; and the Lord handed them over to Midian, Amalek, and Gebal of the Ishmaelites from the east. Like the sand of the sea, they filled the land as they ravaged Israel. Gideon met them with three hundred men; attacking the enemy in the middle of the night, he terrified their camp with the blare of trumpets and the crashing of jars so thoroughly that they all killed one another with mutual wounds. The survivors scattered in flight toward the Jordan (Judges 7). Their Midianite leaders, Oreb and Zeeb, were captured by Ephraim [Col. 0510B] and struck down with another one hundred and twenty thousand warriors. Zebah and Zalmunna, said to have been the first to tame horses, fled across the Jordan with another fifteen thousand, and there were killed.

Do thus to these men: let them fall by their own swords. And do to them as to Sisera, and as to Jabin at the brook Kishon. Another history is referred to, as follows. The children of Israel worshipped idols, and the Lord delivered them into the hand of Jabin, king of Assur. With five hundred scythed chariots he oppressed Israel, and they served him for twenty years. But Barak, judge of Israel, taking ten thousand fighters, came with Deborah to Mount Tabor. Then Sisera, commander of King Jabin’s army, pitched camp at the brook Kishon with nine hundred chariots. [Col. 0510C] Barak descended against him; the chariots were terrified by the Lord, Barak pursued them, and destroyed them. Sisera, however, fleeing on foot, came to Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, and to Galilee [sic]. [Note: [Col. 0509D] So the manuscript.] She received him, hid him in an inner chamber, and drove a nail through his temples as he slept. But the children of Israel pursued the rest at Endor, a large village south of Mount Tabor, and destroyed them (Judges 4).

As they perished, so may the Church’s enemies perish. “Make them,” that is, you shall make them, “like Midian.” Midian means “turning aside” or “abandoning judgment,” and signifies those who turn aside from God’s commandments, abandon just judgment, and do not fear the coming judgment. And [make them] like Sisera, whose name means “vision of a horse” or “exclusion of joy,” and who signifies persons occupied with wars and disputes, excluding joy from themselves through discord. Like Jabin, whose name means “understanding,” and who signifies philosophers trusting in their own wisdom rather than in the Lord’s grace. Or Jabin is interpreted “wise in his generation,” and signifies those who wisely gather gold and silver, etc.

[Col. 0510D] “At the brook Kishon,” whose name means “hardness”: that is, such people exist in an abundance of wickedness of heart. And therefore:

**VERSE 11. “They perished at Endor.”**

Endor means “fountain of generation,” because those who remain in carnal generation and do not care for the regeneration that leads to life shall perish. He used “fountain” because generation proceeds from generation. Since they are destined for destruction and do no good in this life, why does God permit them to live? This is not without benefit, because “they became like dung of the earth”: that is, they will be like manure, which is itself unclean and most worthless, yet, spread upon the earth, makes it fertile. Thus they, vile and filthy in themselves, make God’s Church fruitful by bringing tribulation upon it. Thus you will deal with them in the future, and unbelievers shall perish. But in this life:

[Col. 0511A]

**VERSES 12–13. “Make their leaders”**—namely, teachers of heretics, false Christians, and unbelievers—“like Oreb,” whose name means “a hole,” in which a serpent dwells and from which it hisses. Oreb signifies heretics, who are the hole of the ancient serpent: through them it hisses, and hiding in them, stings others with some error. And [make them] “like Zeeb,” which means “wolf,” and signifies unbelievers who lie in wait daily, seize God’s flock, and draw it into their own body. And [make them] like “Zebah,” whose name means “a wolf’s victim”: these are false Christians, who make themselves the devil’s victim by sinning. And [make them] like Zalmunna, which means “consummation”: these are Jews consummated in vices. As all those men are to be made thus, so make all the Church’s enemies, and all their leaders, who said: “Let us possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance,” that is, let us seize God’s Church as heirs do.

[Col. 0511B]

**VERSE 14. “My God, make them like a wheel.”**

That is, make them like a wheel. Make them fall forward and rise behind, as a wheel does. The things before are eternal; the things behind are temporal. They fall in the things before—that is, the better things—who desire them. “And make them like chaff before the face of the wind”: that is, make them powerless, so that they readily yield to every evil suggestion. Thus you will make them in this life; but in the future you will make them thus:

[Col. 0511C]

**VERSES 15–16. “As fire burns a forest, and as flame burns mountains, so shall you pursue them in your tempest, and trouble them in your wrath.”**

That is, you shall thus convict them in your judgment, in which there will be a tempest—that is, a winnowing which separates grain from chaff. And you shall thus trouble them in your wrath, that is, in your vengeance, namely in punishment itself: as fire pursues while burning a forest, and as it pursues while laying waste mountains. Fire has greater force on a mountain, where the wind has greater power, than in a forest set in a valley. Therefore, to indicate a great persecution, [Col. 0512A] he says, “and as flame burning mountains.” God’s tempest consists of the good angels, who do in judgment what a tempest does in the air. Therefore Scripture says that the Lord will come, and judgment, “in a mighty tempest” (Ps. 49:3). A prayer for their conversion follows.

**VERSE 17. “Fill their faces with shame.”**

That is, fill the faces of some with confusion in this life: let them be thoroughly ashamed because they persecuted your sanctuary. “And they shall seek your name, O Lord,” seeking to establish what they previously sought to destroy. But those whose faces are not filled with shame here shall at last:

**VERSES 18–19. “Be ashamed.”**

That is, let them have confusion for all their sins, “and be troubled for ever and ever”: let them grieve eternally, be confounded before angels and human beings, and perish with demons, so that they may know that your name is Lord, because they were unwilling to know you here as Lord, as Father. And let them know that you alone are Most High over all the earth: that is, you alone are most powerful in the whole world. This shall be the recompense of the Lord’s enemies, who now destroy his inheritance: they shall be delivered into outer darkness, when people will seek death and not find it. Then the Lord’s friends shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and groaning shall flee away.

[Col. 0512C] It should be noted that Holy Scripture speaks in many ways through likenesses: sometimes through Hebrew names, as especially in this psalm; sometimes through stones, as in Ezekiel, where it says: “Every precious stone was your covering: jasper, onyx, beryl, etc.” (Ezek. 28:13); sometimes through trees, as in the book of Wisdom, where it says: “Like a cedar in Lebanon, and like a cypress on Mount Zion” (Ecclus. 24:17); sometimes through places, as in Tobit: “Jerusalem, you shall shine with splendid light” (Tob. 13:13); sometimes through beasts, as there: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and shall trample the lion and dragon” (Ps. 90:13); sometimes through birds, as there: “I became like a pelican and like a sparrow” (Ps. 101:7); sometimes through herbs, as there: “Like a grain of mustard seed” (Matt. 13:31; 17:19). And you will find many things of this kind.

## PSALM LXXXIII

[Col. 0511]

[Col. 0511D] “How beloved are your tabernacles,” etc. The preceding psalm sang of the retribution of the wicked; this one sings of the reward of the righteous. It is the eighty-third in order. Eight signifies resurrection, six is the number of reward, and three signifies the Trinity; this number indicates that the elect in the resurrection [Col. 0512D] receive the reward of life in the Trinity. Its title is:

**(VERSE 1.) UNTO THE END, FOR THE WINEPRESSES: A PSALM FOR THE SONS OF KORAH.**

The end toward which the saints strive is the joy of eternal life. The winepresses, in which grapes or olive berries [Col. 0513A] are pressed, are the Churches, in which the elect are grievously afflicted by the reprobate. But as wine or oil is strained into storehouses and the grape pomace or olive-dregs are cast out, so the righteous are received from the pressures of the world into eternal tabernacles, while the wicked are shut up in savage Tartarus.

Korah means “baldness”; the sons of Korah are imitators of Christ crucified at the place of Calvary. This psalm—that is, this metrical praise of God—is assigned to the sons of Korah, that is, to imitators of Christ amid the pressures of the world. This praise is sung “for the winepresses,” that is, for Churches oppressed by the wicked and striving toward the end, that is, eternal joy.

Note that the title “For the Winepresses” occurs only in three psalms: namely, the eighth, the eightieth, and the eighty-third. The eighth signifies Christ’s resurrection; the eightieth, our resurrection; the third, the vision of the Trinity. The eighth is assigned to David, whose name means “strong of hand,” because Christ, strong in battle, conquered death in the resurrection. The eightieth is entitled for Asaph, whose name means “assembly,” because it signifies our assembly in resurrection in him. The eighty-third is assigned to Korah, whose name means “bald,” signifying Christ, because after the resurrection we shall see Christ, crucified at Calvary, in the glory of the Trinity.

The subject of the psalm is the saints’ longing for future blessedness. Its purpose is to show that the pressures of the present life are necessary for attaining the blessedness of the heavenly homeland. The words are taken from David himself, who, after the tabernacle of the Lord made by [Col. 0513C] Moses, made another, supplied resources for the work of the temple, and was forbidden to build it himself. This signifies that the faithful people make the Church a tabernacle for the Lord, and expend good works in building the temple in heaven, in which they will praise God for ever and ever.

It is divided into three parts, because the threefold order of the Church—virgins, widows, and married persons—is gathered to the vision of the Trinity in the house of God. The first part is, “How beloved are your tabernacles,” in which the everlasting praise of the righteous in the Lord’s house is described. The second is, “Blessed is the man whose help is from you,” in which the vision of God is expressed. The third is, “Protector,” in which the day of eternity, in which grace and glory are found, is recalled. The voice is that of the sons [Col. 0513D] of Korah, that is, of the perfect who long for eternal joys.

**VERSES 2–3. “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts.”**

Our tabernacles, in which we serve as soldiers under our King, are our bodies, in which we are pressed as grapes in winepresses. But the Lord’s tabernacles are eternal joys, in which his soldiers enjoy immeasurable gladness. O Lord of the heavenly hosts, our tabernacles are despised, because they are full of mourning, sorrow, and pressure; your tabernacles are greatly beloved, because they are full of joy and gladness. Therefore “my soul desires and fails for the courts of the Lord.”

God’s house is called a court because of its vastness, so great that one person does not have less because of another—a condition unlike this world, where the more one person has, the less another has. My soul greatly desires to enter these courts and fails, not away from them but into them, as a grape, by being pressed, ceases to be what it was and flows into the Lord’s vessels—something it could not do while it was a grape. This indicates that the soldiers of the eternal King, who are here in the labour of military service, desire to be with the Lord in rest. Hence follows: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.” That is, my reason and carnality—that is, my sensual nature—desire with rejoicing to go to the living God, that is, to that immortality and impassibility which are in God. This belongs to the perfect, when sensuality already agrees with reason and desires the same thing, namely eternal things. Or: my soul and body desire to see God in eternal life, where [Col. 0514B] they may rejoice eternally, though here they groan amid pressures.

**VERSE 4. “For the sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest for herself, where she may place her young.”**

The sparrow does not dwell in woods but nests on the walls of houses. Having found a suitable place, it rejoices greatly, because it hopes to be safe from the snares of birds of prey. The turtledove, however, does not seek a house as the sparrow does, but makes its nest in a secluded place out of certain small materials.

The soul is understood by the sparrow: it desires to have a dwelling in the heavenly house, where it may be secure from the snares of demons and the pressures of evils. By the turtledove, which joins itself to only one mate, is understood the body, subject to the soul’s reason; through vigils, fasts, and almsgiving it builds itself a nest, where [Col. 0514C] it may place its young, that is, good works. The heart, like a sparrow, finds a house; the flesh, like a turtledove, finds a nest where it may place its young. A house is built as if for eternity; a nest is gathered for a time. With the heart we think of God, like a sparrow flying to its house; with the flesh we perform good works.

The house is charity; the nest, the catholic faith. The sparrow finds a house when the soul raises charity, which is God, toward an eternal dwelling. The turtledove builds itself a nest in which to place its young when the body stores good works in the catholic faith. What house and what nest are these? “Your altars, O Lord of hosts.” Or, just as the preceding verse reads, “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts,” so it should be read: “How beloved are your altars, [Col. 0514D] O Lord of hosts.” This figure is called *apodosis* [manuscript: *aposini*], that is, “from the common,” when what precedes corresponds to what follows.

God’s altars are Christ’s human flesh and rational soul, upon which the sacrifices of the faithful are daily offered. In them we shall have eternal dwellings and feast at heavenly banquets upon these tables, because he is the Lord of hosts, that is, of angels; our King, ruling us in virtues while we serve against the battle-lines of vices; and our God, who created us subject to himself and will reward us with eternal goods. Of these it continues:

**VERSE 5. “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord.”**

God’s house is the heavenly Jerusalem, in which are the vision of God, every kind of glory, and complete joy. Those [Col. 0515A] who dwell in this house are blessed, because every hardship is absent from them and every good thing flows to them according to their desire. And what do they do there? “For ever and ever [Vulgate: for ages of ages] they shall praise you.” This will be our whole occupation, without cessation. There is great stability there, and the immortality itself of our body is held in contemplation of God. There will be eternal love and an unfailing beauty; therefore praise also will be without end, because that blessedness will be everlasting. No one shall attain this blessedness except by God’s help. Therefore it follows:

VERSICLES 6–7. Blessed is the man whose help is from you. That is, only the man whom you help in this life will be blessed. And let him ascend there by the steps of ascent in the valley of tears. Hence it adds: He has set in order the ascents [Col. 0515B] in his heart in the valley of tears; that is, that man is placed in the valley of tears, namely in the lowliness of body and soul, where there are tears, that is, many miseries. By free choice and by grace he has resolved within himself to ascend from this valley through the steps of the virtues. He resolved it, but could not accomplish it unless God helped: for example, he may resolve to distribute all his substance to the poor or to enter a monastery; but in no way will he be able to fulfil it except through assisting grace. This world is the valley; heaven is the mountain. The world is a valley of tears, full of miseries; the mountain is the height of joys. The ascents from the valley to the mountain are the steps of the virtues. That man is in the place in which he was set, that is, in the pilgrimage of this world, which he deserved by sinning in the first man [Col. 0515C]. Or, it is the place which God appointed when he gave man understanding that he is set in the depths, so that he may grieve to be here and desire to depart from here. Or, one must ascend to the place which God appointed, in which we shall see face to face what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man. And he explains how help is from him:

VERSE 8. For the lawgiver will give a blessing. The lawgiver is Christ. The law is the commandments of charity; the blessing is assisting grace. Therefore he who gave the law will also give the blessing; for he who established the commandments will also give grace to fulfil them, and to those who fulfil the law he will give the blessing of the eternal inheritance [Col. 0515D], when he says: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34). Sustained by this hope and helped by God’s grace, they will go from strength to strength, ascending on the ladder of charity by the steps of virtues, to the place which the Lord appointed, where there is every kind of glory and full joy. Thus at last the God of gods will be seen by them in Zion: that is, they will see face to face in the heavenly Zion the God of Christians. For a ladder of charity is, as it were, raised from the valley of the world to heaven, when the Apostle describes the more excellent way of knowledge, into which, as it were, the various steps of virtues are inserted when it is said: “Charity is patient, is kind” (1 Cor. 13:4), and so forth. Those who walk upwards through these steps will see God in Zion, that is, in heavenly contemplation. For when the necessity of mortality is ended [Col. 0516A], Christ, God as he is with God, the Word with the Father, will appear to the pure in heart.

Otherwise: God, who gave the Law through Moses, was seen in Zion when Christ appeared in Jerusalem, where he had lodging in Zion. Since, as I have said, such is the blessedness which the saints will have in the heights, where they shall see God himself, he prays, because of his excessive desire for it, that he may see him in Zion.

VERSE 9. O Lord, God of hosts, hear my prayer. You who are Lord over things and God, creator of all hosts, grant effect to my prayer, that I may see you in Zion. Give ear, O God of Jacob. You who are the God of those who labour, receive in your omnipotence [Col. 0516B] my prayer, so that you may make me Israel out of Jacob. Jacob are those who wage war here in the pilgrim Church, struggling against vices; Israel are those who behold God in glory in the reigning Church.

VERSE 10. Our protector against vices, look upon us as we labour in battle, and make yourself seen by us, O God. And because, on account of sins, you are unwilling to look upon us, who are ugly, look upon the face of your Christ, that is, upon the beauty of your Son. We set before you the merits of your Son, who for us was made beautiful and comely; therefore it is just that you look upon us mercifully and bring us to behold you. Why do you so greatly desire to come into the courts of the Lord? For this reason:

[Col. 0516C] VERSE 11. Because one day in your courts is better than thousands. The one day is eternity, which is better than thousands of days in this life, because it is darkened by no storm, scorched by no heat, and ended by no evening. And because that day is better than thousands: I chose to be cast down in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners. For my part, I chose rather to be least in God’s house than lord in the transitory dwellings of sinners. Note that he said “to dwell,” although tents are temporary, because even if he were granted to dwell there so as to live until the end of the world, he would nevertheless choose to be lesser in the house of God rather than first in the tents of sinners. And with what confidence do you seek [Col. 0516D] that day? With this:

VERSE 12. Because God loves mercy and truth; that is, he himself is merciful and true in his promises. He loves mercy because he first comes to my aid. He loves truth in order to give the believer what he promised. In the Hebrew it reads: “For the Lord God is sun and shield.” For through the illumination of his mercy he becomes for us the sun of righteousness; faithfully fulfilling his promises, he crowns us with the shield of his good will. The Lord will give us grace and glory: grace, that we may do good works; glory, that we may receive the crown of life. This is to say: I, who am pressed here in the winepress as a grape, chose, before the riches and honours of the world, to dwell—or to be cast down—in the house of God, where one day is better than thousands, because through the mercy [Col. 0517A] and truth of Christ eternal glory will be given freely.

VERSE 13. He will not deprive of good things those who walk in innocence; that is, he will not take eternal goods away from those who persevere here in innocence until the end. And since God will not take eternal goods from them, no one else will take their joy from them. These goods are reached through hope. Hence it follows: O Lord of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in you. That is: O Lord of hosts, those who hope in you will go from strength to strength. This man is blessed because in this way he will attain supreme blessedness.

## PSALM LXXXIV

[Col. 0517]

[Col. 0517A] “You have blessed, O Lord, your land,” etc. In the preceding psalm the soldiers of the King, hemmed in by enemies in the tent, desire to approach the commander’s tents [Col. 0517B]. In this psalm, having entered the Lord’s inheritance, they joyfully give thanks. This is the eighty-fourth psalm, that is, seven times twelve. By seven eternal rest is expressed; by twelve, perfection. It signifies that all the perfect, following the teaching of the twelve apostles through the sevenfold Spirit, shall enter into the rest of the Lord. Its title is:

(VERSE 1.) UNTO THE END, FOR THE SONS OF KORAH: A PSALM.

That is: this praise, sung to imitators of Christ, is directed toward Christ. Christ is the end of our labour; for we labour in order to reach him. Korah means “bald,” and he is the one whom the Jews mocked as Elisha was mocked by boys, when he was crucified on Mount Calvary [Col. 0517C]. Those who believe in this bald one, that is, in Christ, and imitate him, are his sons. “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12). This psalm is sung to them, and they themselves will be possessors of the Lord’s inheritance.

The subject of the psalm is the praise of those who have possessed the Lord’s inheritance. Its purpose is that we may give thanks for the benefits bestowed, in order that we may receive his inheritance. Its words are drawn from the people who, after captivity, received back their inheritance; and it signifies the human race, which, after diabolical captivity, received through Christ the inheritance of paradise. It is divided by two *diapsalmata* into three sections, because through the two commandments of charity one comes to the vision of the Trinity. [Col. 0517D] In the first section there is thanksgiving for God’s benefits; in the second, the enlivening of the human race and the manifestation of God; in the third, the peace restored to human beings is mentioned. It is the voice of those rejoicing in possession of the Lord’s inheritance.

VERSE 2. You have blessed, O Lord, your land. God’s land is the Church. It was accursed while it worshipped idols and produced the thorns and briars of sins. The Lord blessed it when he sent his Son into the land, who released it from the curse; watered by the rain of blessing and the font of baptism, it brought forth the fruits of good works. The comparison is with one who recovers land long uncultivated and lost, and then cultivates it with every care. And he says how he blessed it [Col. 0518A]: You have turned away the captivity of Jacob. This is drawn from the return of the captive people from Babylon [Col. 0518B]. By Jacob is understood the faithful people, captive to the devil amid the confusion of sins. The Lord turned away its captivity when he freed it by the death of his Son. Through whose death:

VERSE 3. You have forgiven the iniquity of your people. You remitted the debt, and through faith made your people a people that was not formerly yours. And in baptism you covered all their original and actual sins. The comparison is with those who are covered over in the sea and escape, rejoicing when delivered. And after satisfaction has been made to you by your Son for humankind:

VERSE 4. You have softened all your wrath; that is, you have lightened every punishment deserved. All God’s wrath consisted in the penalties of sin: mortality, susceptibility to suffering, and every torment. He has now softened these for believers, though he has not wholly removed them; he has lightened them by the hope of future glory. But in the future he will take every pain away from his own. You have turned away from the wrath of your indignation. The wrath of God’s indignation—or fury, as another translation has it—is eternal damnation. God turned away from this wrath when, through Christ, he remitted to humankind Adam’s debt and rescued it from eternal damnation. Note the six benefits of God, expressed by the figure of *homoeoteleuton* [Codex: *omoeoteleuton*], which gives similar endings to many words: *benedixisti*, *avertisti*, *remisisti*, *operuisti*, *mitigasti*. You blessed, O Lord Jesus, the land by being born. You turned away captivity by preaching. You forgave iniquity by dying. You covered sins by rising again. You softened wrath by giving the Holy Spirit. You turned our nature away from fury by leading it to heaven, and will yet turn it away [Col. 0518D] by rescuing it from damnation at the judgment.

*Diapsalma.* Since, after the inheritance had been recovered through the Mediator’s death, many would sin and thus lose again the restored inheritance, they now pray:

VERSE 5. Convert us, O God our Saviour: you who saved us on the cross, turn us from our sins to repentance, from falling to pardon; and make defenders of the Church out of persecutors, preachers out of blasphemers, disciples out of opponents. And turn your wrath away from us, lest in anger at the judgment you take from your own the inheritance restored through the cross and received through faith and works. And because God chastises many in this life for sins, it adds:

[Col. 0519A] VERSES 6–7. Will you be angry with us for ever? That is: if here you chastise us as sons with fatherly affection, will you, angry, condemn us for ever as rebellious slaves and deprive us of the inheritance? You will not. Or will you extend your wrath from generation to generation, punishing us for the sins of our parents or our children for our offences? You will not. “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son; but each shall bear his own burden” (Ezek. 18:20). God’s wrath is his vengeance. Through that wrath we are mortal: in this flesh we bear the torture of pains, the bond of death, and the snares of temptations. This wrath extended from Adam’s generation to Christ’s generation, in whom all shall be made alive, just as in Adam all die. [Col. 0519B] Will you extend this wrath from this generation, which is in this world, into that generation which is to come after the resurrection, so that there we suffer such things as we suffer here? It will not be so. For you, O God, turned away from us because of sins, and turned toward us because of Christ, will enliven us in soul through baptism or repentance; and your people will rejoice in you, though it rejoiced in itself to its own harm. It wished to have joy from itself, and found mourning in itself. Now, because God is all its joy, it rejoices in him alone.

Otherwise: you, O God, turned from wrath to mercy, will enliven—that is, raise—us in the resurrection; and your people, which were here, will rejoice in the things that are in you: immortality and impassibility. [Col. 0519C] Therefore:

VERSE 8. Show us, O Lord, your mercy; that is, in this life show yourself merciful by forgiving our sins; and in the future show how mercifully you have saved us. There grant us to embrace and possess your salvation, that is, Christ your Son, and to enjoy the gift of eternal glory. Grant that we may know and see your Christ, not as the Jews saw and crucified him, but as the angels see and rejoice.

*Diapsalma.* After this prayer the Prophet, withdrawing himself from the tumult of the world and turning to himself, and from himself to him whose voice he heard inwardly, as it were tumultuously resisting the restlessness of this life, the soul weighed down by the corruptible body, and the mind depressed by earthly habitation and occupied with many thoughts, says:

VERSE 9. I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me, that is, the Holy Spirit. By this authority is given to the book: God spoke it through a man; he does not speak to outward ears, but speaks by inspiration to the inward person. I will hear, as a servant, what the Lord commands; and understand, as a son, what God speaks to my heart. And because he was carried from earthly to heavenly things, he tells what the King spoke to him: For he will speak peace to his people; that is, he promises his own eternal peace and rest, so that they may no longer be disturbed by any fear. The voice of God is peace: God calls those oppressed in winepresses [Col. 0520A] to peace. In the sons of God, the sons of Korah, imitators of Christ, there will be pure peace for all who love him, all who see him, all who are filled with God, when God shall be all in all: peace itself, full and perfect. He speaks this to his people, and over his saints, that is, over those living holy lives in that people, and to those who turn to the heart, that is, penitents who turn from deadly things to thoughts of salvation, as the prodigal son, returning to himself from the swine, thought of his father. The Lord spoke peace to his people when Christ, true peace, was born. Hence the angels immediately announced peace to people of good will. He spoke peace over his saints when, rising from the dead, he said to the apostles: “Peace be with you” (Luke 24:36). He spoke peace to those [Col. 0520B] who turn to the heart when, after the nations had turned from the devil to the Creator, he gave them forgiveness of sins and his grace. Although he saves all, he will not come bodily to all.

VERSE 10. Yet his salvation is near to those who fear him. He will dwell among the Jews and be preached among the nations. Christ will be salvation to all who fear God. No one is far from God by regions, but by affections. Whoever loves God is near; whoever hates him is far. He will offer himself to all alike. So that glory may dwell in our land, that is, in the Church. Glory already dwells in our land through Christ, because the Roman empire rules under the Christian religion. Glory dwells in our land [Col. 0520C] because in the future the King of glory will reign without end in the Church, the land of the living. Glory will also dwell in our land when immortality and impassibility dwell for ever in our flesh. Through what will that peace and glory come? Through this:

VERSE 11. Mercy and truth have met each other; that is, God has so had mercy on human beings as he promised through the prophets. The mercy of redemption and the truth of promise jointly come to meet humankind.

Otherwise, mercy among the nations and truth among the Jews met each other through the mediator, the Lord Jesus Christ, who made both one. Or they will meet in the future; that is, mercy [Col. 0520D] and truth will agree together in God.

Righteousness and peace have kissed; that is, whoever does righteousness will find peace. Or righteousness is the remission of sins, while peace is love of God and neighbour, both of which have been found for human beings through Christ.

Otherwise: the glory of our land will be given because mercy and truth will meet each other in judgment, that is, agree together: mercy, which will admit those on the right into the joy of their Lord; truth, which will cast those on the left into the fire. Then righteousness and peace will kiss each other, because the righteous will be received into the peace and grace of God the Father through the Son. All this will happen because:

VERSE 12. Truth has sprung from the earth: that is, Christ, through whom all the Father’s promises are fulfilled, was born of the Virgin Mary. And righteousness has looked down from heaven [Col. 0521A]: that is, the Word of God, through whom sinners are justified and all things are justly ordered, proceeded from the Father, who is the heaven of heavens.

Otherwise: truth springs from the earth when confession of sins is offered from earthly persons; righteousness looks down from heaven when forgiveness of sins is granted through the heaven of heavens. But the fact that truth—that is, confession—springs from us happens by grace. Hence it adds:

VERSE 13. For the Lord will give kindness; that is, through his grace he will inspire us to confess our sins. And our land will give its fruit; that is, the Virgin Mary will bear God and man.

VERSE 14. Righteousness will walk before him; that is, the righteous will advance in good fruit toward [Col. 0522A] his good pleasure. And the Lord will set his footsteps in the way; that is, he will set his footprints in those who are a way to others by acting and teaching. He will walk with them, that is, he will help them to act well. Or the righteous will place their works in the way, that is, in conformity with Christ, who is the way leading to himself, life and truth.

This psalm is connected with the preceding one in that there it is sung: “God loves mercy and truth”; but here: “Mercy and truth have met each other.” There: “The Lord will give grace and glory,” that is, so that glory may dwell in our land. This psalm is sung at the Nativity of the Lord because there the truth of Christ springs from the virgin earth.

## PSALM LXXXV

[Col. 0521]

[Col. 0521B] “Incline, O Lord, your ear.” The title of this psalm is:

A PRAYER OF DAVID HIMSELF.

That is: the prayer indicated by these words is attributed to the true David, the Lord Jesus Christ. Only two psalms bear the inscription “a prayer of David himself,” namely the sixteenth and this one, because there are two Churches, one from the Jews and the other from the nations, which are called Christ’s body. Their head is described here; sometimes he himself prays in his members, and sometimes the members pray through the head. He prays for us as our priest; he prays in us as our head; he is prayed to by us as our God. For he is God from God and man among human beings: with God, hearing; with human beings, praying. And because in the preceding [Col. 0521C] psalm mention was made of peace, which is the kingdom of heaven, this psalm rightly follows, in which prayer is made for deliverance from the lower hell. This is the eighty-fifth psalm. Moses was eighty years old when he went down into Egypt to lead out the people, to whom he gave the Law of five books; this signifies Christ, who in this eighty-fifth psalm is written to have descended into hell in order to lead out the people of five ages.

The subject of the psalm is Christ’s prayer for the Church, or the Church’s prayer in Christ its head. Its purpose is to instruct us in prayer, through which we must attain the eternal inheritance. Its words are taken from David himself, against whom wicked persons rose up and the assembly of the powerful—namely Saul, Absalom, and others—sought his life; but the Lord helped him and gave him dominion. It signifies Christ, against whom wicked Jews rose up and the assembly of chief priests sought to destroy his life, but whom the Lord helped in the Passion and gave dominion in the Resurrection.

It is divided into three parts because Christ’s body is divided into three orders [Col. 0522B]: teachers, celibates, and married persons. The first part is “Incline, O Lord,” in which the proper prayer of the head is written. The second is “Lead me, O Lord,” in which the head’s prayer is expressed. The third is “O God, the wicked,” in which Christ’s Passion and Resurrection are touched upon. In this psalm now the head, now the body speaks. The voice of the Church:

VERSE 1. Incline, O Lord, your ear, and hear me. One inclines one’s ear to the weak in order to hear their voice. The human race lay weak in the pit of misery and the valley of tears; to it God, the good physician, inclined the ear of mercy and heard the voice crying thus: For I am needy and poor. Needy because I lost the riches of paradise; [Col. 0522C] poor because I wasted away in want and weakness. The compassionate physician heard this voice when he sent his Son to bring help, as the preceding psalm related: for he raised the fallen one from the mire, carried the wounded one on his own shoulders, washed him in the bath of baptism, clothed him in the first robe which he had lost in paradise, gave him his own name, and enrolled him as an heir of the kingdom. The voice of Christ:

VERSE 2. Preserve my soul, for I am holy. O Father! At your command I descended into the pit of misery; I lifted fallen humankind from the mud of filth; I myself remained without the stains of sin; in this holiness I preserved my soul. Sometimes in the psalms the weak member speaks, as there: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak” (Ps. [Col. 0522D] 6:3). Sometimes the member made whole through Christ the sanctified head speaks, as here: Preserve my soul, for I am holy—namely through baptism and your body. The voice of the member:

Save your servant, O my God, who hopes in you. You redeemed me: I acknowledge you as Lord and profess myself your servant. You created me: I confess you as my God, and I hope in you alone. Save [Col. 0523A] one obedient to you and hoping in you. The voice of the member set in sorrow:

VERSES 3–4. Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I have cried to you all day: that is, continuously or at every time. God mercifully delivers from tribulation the one who continuously prays to him. Gladden the soul of your servant, set in the bitterness of repentance, through pardon; for to you, O Lord, I will lift up [Vulgate: “I have lifted up”] my soul with good intention, which lay in carnal pleasure. Now I delight in you,

VERSE 5. Because you, O Lord, are sweet and gentle, and of much mercy, and abundant in mercy—or, as another translation reads: “to all who call upon you.” You are sweet because you are sweetness itself, taking away sorrow, gladdening souls, and giving virtues. You are gentle because you patiently endure sinners and do not immediately punish them. You are abundant in mercy in pardoning sins through repentance. You are of much mercy to all who call upon you—and to no others. Whoever calls upon God for money, rank, or vengeance upon enemies does not call upon God, but upon the thing he desires to obtain. But to all who pray to you that you may not punish them for their sins, but patiently bear with them, forgive them, and afterwards enable them to act well, you are gentle, sweet, and merciful. The voice of the member set in tribulation:

VERSES 6–7. Give ear, O Lord, to my prayer; that is, mercifully hear what I ask. And attend to the voice of my petition; that is, understand what I ask. Prayer concerns present things; supplication, future things. [Col. 0523C] Hear me praying for both. For in the day of my tribulation I cried to you, because you heard me: that is, in the time of affliction you heard me because I cried to you, desiring to depart from tribulation and to attain you, who are eternal rest. The whole time of this life is a day of tribulation. There is no day on which the righteous are not troubled, because “while we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:6). If the homeland is sweet, pilgrimage is bitter; if pilgrimage is bitter, tribulation lasts all day. Therefore one must cry out all day, that we may be delivered. The voice of the member delivered and rejoicing in deliverance:

VERSE 8. There is none like you among the gods, O Lord. Among the gods of the nations, or among gods made by you, none is like you. [Col. 0523D] And there is none according to your works. No one can do such things as you do: you justify the ungodly and free the oppressed. The voice of the Church’s priests:

VERSE 9. All the nations whom you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord. The Lord made Adam and Eve the source of all nations, from which source all nations flowed. Therefore he made all nations. Thus all will come to their Creator, not with their feet but by faith and religion; abandoning idols, they will worship before you, O Lord, within themselves and in accordance with your good pleasure. And they will glorify your name, that is, praise you by good works. And rightly:

VERSE 10. For you are great, that is, mighty, and doing whatsoever wonders you will—unlike others.

For you alone are God by nature; the others are gods by the choice of the nations [Col. 0524A] or by your appointment. The voice of the whole body:

VERSE 11. Lead me, O Lord, in your way. I run to you from all nations: lead me, O Christ, in your way, that is, in faith in and knowledge of your Son, who is for us the way to you, life; and I shall walk in your truth, that is, in the precepts and ordinances of Christ, who is truth. Let my heart rejoice as it walks in the way, so that it may fear your name, O Lord, by keeping your commandments.

In the Hebrew it reads: “Make my heart one, that it may fear your name.” That is: it was divided among the desires of the world; make it one in your love and affection. The voice of the people delivered from hell:

VERSE 12. I will confess to you, O Lord my God, with [Col. 0524B] all my heart; that is, I will praise you with all my soul, you who are my Lord and God. And I will glorify your name for ever: that is, I will sing the glory of your name both here and in the future. And rightly:

VERSE 13. For your mercy is great upon me, who led me into refreshment; and you have delivered my soul from the lower hell.

The question is what the lower hell is. The upper hell is mortality, which is in the body; the lower hell is the death of the soul, which is an inner death and is therefore called the lower hell.

Otherwise: there is a certain heavenly dwelling of angels, where there is life of ineffable joys, immortality and incorruptibility, where all things endure according to God’s gift [Col. 0524C] and grace: that is the upper part of things. Accordingly, as that is upper, so this is earthly, where there is flesh and blood, corruption, birth and mortality, succession and passing away, changeability and instability, fears, desires, uncertain joy, fragile hope, perishable substance; and this part of things is hell. But again, below this hell—that is, below this portion of hell—there is another lower place to which the dead go, from which God willed to rescue our souls, even by sending his Son there. For the Son of God was sent to free from both these hells in every respect. He was sent to this hell by being born; to that one by dying.

There is also another opinion. Perhaps among the dead there is a lower region, to which are consigned the ungodly who have sinned most greatly, where the rich man, as he was tormented, lifted his eyes to see Abraham. But he could not have seen by lifting his eyes unless the latter were above and he below. Therefore perhaps between these two hells—one in which the souls of the righteous rested, the other in which the souls of the wicked were tormented—this man rejoices that God delivered his soul from the lower hell: that is, from such sins as could lead him to the torments of the lower hell. He says by what means God rescued his soul from hell, namely through Christ’s death. This is what follows. The voice of Christ:

VERSES 14–15. O God, the wicked—that is, the Jews—rose up against me and seized me; and the assembly of the powerful, that is, the gathering of the chief priests, sought to destroy my soul. And they did not set you before their eyes, but killed me, your Son. But you, Lord God, merciful and compassionate Father, patient, of much mercy, and true, look upon me, the man assumed by you, and through me free lost humankind. And have mercy on me by giving humankind immortality through me, who underwent death for it. Give your dominion to your servant, that is, give power to your beloved, that I may destroy the devil’s rule and rescue souls from it. And save from death me, the son of your handmaid Mary. This the man says literally.

VERSE 16. Perform for me a sign for good: that I may rise again, not for evil, by coming down from the cross. For in the former lies the restoration of the human race; in the latter, vain clamour. Perform such a sign that my enemies, the Jews [Col. 0525B], who hate me may see it and be confounded, that is, be ashamed, because you, O Lord, helped me by raising me from the dead, whom they thought you had abandoned; and you comforted me in sorrow, because through me you brought souls out of hell into joys.

It should be noted that he calls the Father by seven names, and by each word defines the Father’s majesty. He is Lord of all, God the creator of all, compassionate because he shows mercy to every creature; merciful because the nature of the Godhead is always loving; patient because he endures sinners; of much mercy because he invites conversion; true because he will fulfil all his promises. Although these things are said of the Father, they are nevertheless without doubt likewise present in the Son and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0525C]. The Father performed the sign of Jonah with the Son, because just as the fish vomited Jonah out on the third day [Col. 0526A], so hell gave this one back after three days. He gave him dominion because he committed all judgment to him and exalted him above all things. Thus he himself says: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18). Those who hate him were confounded because the Jews were slain by the Romans. This can also be understood of the Church. The voice of the martyrs:

O God, the wicked rose against me: that is, persecutors afflicted me; and the assembly of the Jews sought my soul, that is, my life, in order to destroy it. And they did not set you before their eyes: that is, they did not believe you to be God, but rather killed me, your people who believe in you, with elaborately devised punishments. But you, O Lord, look upon me, how I suffer for you; and have mercy on me, delivering me from [Col. 0526B] eternal torment. Give your dominion, which the ungodly now have, those who cruelly torment us, to your servant, that is, the Christian people. And save, here and in the future, the son of your handmaid, that is, the people of your Church. The voice of that Church follows: Perform for me a sign for good. God performed a sign with the Church because he subjected beneath her feet the Roman empire which persecuted her. This was a sign for good, because it believed in Christ, the supreme emperor. The Jews who hated her saw this and were confounded because they were expelled from the cities; for the Lord helped the Church in persecutions and comforted her by giving peace and promising glory in the future. This psalm is sung at the Epiphany of the Lord because there Christ is worshipped as God by the nations.

## PSALM LXXXVI

[Col. 0525]

[Col. 0525C] “Its foundations are in the holy mountains,” etc. In the preceding psalm mention was made of God’s tent and house; in this psalm the city of God, into which the elect are brought, is described. This is the eighty-sixth psalm, which is twelve times seven, plus three. Twelve signifies the apostles, princes of this city [Col. 0525D]; seven, those wise men filled with the sevenfold Spirit, teachers of this city; three, all the faithful citizens of this city who worship the Trinity. The title of the psalm is:

(VERSE 1.) FOR THE SONS OF KORAH: A PSALM OF A SONG.

That is: this hymn was composed out of great joy and set before all the faithful. A psalm is said to come from the psaltery; a song is uttered by the mouth. A psalm relates to the hands, that is, to action; a song to contemplation. The sons of Korah are the sons of the resurrection.

The subject of the psalm is the city of God. The psalm “Great is the Lord” also describes the city of God; but that one concerns the great city Jerusalem, while this one is issued, as it were, from the tower of Zion set within the city. Its purpose is to exhort us to become citizens of this city through faith and works.

It is distinguished by two *diapsalmata* into three sections, because the inhabitants of this city are divided into three orders—teachers, celibates, and married persons—who are governed by the law of twofold love. In the first part [Col. 0526D] the city itself is praised; in the second its inhabitants are declared blessed; in the third the joy of its citizens is mentioned. The words are taken from the situation of Jerusalem, set on a mountain, to which Babylonians, Tyrians, Ethiopians, and other peoples gathered and in which they had joy; and it signifies the Church established upon the mountain Christ, into which peoples of all nations have come together and in which they will have eternal joy. The voice of the Holy Spirit:

His foundations are upon the holy mountains. This “his” is not joined to the words found in the book, but to those things which the writer of the book inwardly saw in the Spirit. For, caught outside himself, he beheld in the Spirit the city of God; and, wishing to tell this also to others, he burst forth in great joy, saying: “His foundations are upon the holy mountains”; that is, glorious is that city which I saw within: its foundations are upon the holy mountains. The Church is called a city by analogy, because just as citizens gather in a city, so the faithful of the Church are united in one faith. The foundation of this city is Christ, the cornerstone joining in himself two walls, Jews and Gentiles. The builder and founder of this city is God, and it is founded upon the two Testaments. Its foundations are upon the holy mountains, that is, upon the prophets and apostles, upon whose teaching the Church is founded, as it is written: “Upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2:20). He therefore said “holy,” because there are also the mountains of a shipwrecking sea, against which unwary sailors have often struck: these are heretics and philosophers, adversaries of this city.

He states what the name of this city is:

**VERSE 2.** The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob. This city is called Zion in the present life, meaning “watchtower of life”; in the future it will be called Jerusalem, that is, “vision of peace,” or “the Lord there.” The gates of this city are the apostles or teachers, through whom we enter the kingdom of God. Its door is Christ, through whom we shall enter into life. The tabernacles of Jacob are the saints of the former people, serving under the figures of this city. Therefore the Lord loves the gates of Zion—that is, the apostles, the gates of the city that watches for things to come—above the tabernacles of Jacob, that is, more than all the saints of the former people, whether prophets or any others serving under the shadow.

[Col. 0527C] Alternatively: the gates of Zion are faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues which are in that city; they are the heavenly gates of the higher Zion, beholding the face of God. These the Lord loves above the tabernacles of Jacob, that is, above all the observances of the former people, by which that city—everlasting and ever heavenly in peace—was signified.

Alternatively: Zion is the gathering of the saints in heavenly glory. The tabernacles of Jacob are the present warfare of the righteous, because here they fight by struggling against vices. That spiritual Zion is said to be loved above this, because it is declared that in it there is nothing of confusion, nothing of disturbance. The comparison is drawn from a city situated upon a mountain and fortified both by its site and by its construction.

[Col. 0527D] **VERSE 3.** Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God, by the Holy Spirit. And what are they? Namely these: that in it there shall be princes, unlearned persons, country people, poor fishermen; and that Babylonian, Philistine, Tyrian, and Ethiopian citizens shall be in it. The following concerns these:

*Diapsalma.* **VERSE 4.** I shall remember Rahab and Babylon, who know me. By Rahab prostitutes are understood; by Babylon, tax collectors; for, having become citizens in this city, they go before the Jews into the kingdom of God. Rahab was the prostitute who received the spies of Joshua son of Nun; she alone, together with her household, was saved when Jericho fell. Rahab means “breadth” or “pride,” and signifies the Gentile world, which was travelling to destruction by the broad and attractive road of vices, and was proud in philosophy or in imperial rule. It received the apostles of Jesus; and, when the world collapses through the trumpets of angels, it shall be saved with its own—that is, with Christians—just as Rahab is read to have been saved when Jericho fell through the trumpets of the priests. For it abandoned the broad road and took up the narrow way leading into this city; it laid aside the swelling of pride and, made humble, deserved to be a citizen in this city, just as that Rahab deserved to be joined to the people of God and enrolled in Christ’s genealogy.
