Babylon was the capital of the Assyrians. It was built by Queen Semiramis, wife of King Ninus, from unbaked bricks and bitumen; it was destroyed by Cyrus and Darius. Its circuit was sixty stadia. It is said of it that it was wonderful that it could be built by human beings, but more wonderful that it could be destroyed. Babylon means “confusion,” because there long ago human languages were confused; and it signifies this world, in which its lovers are confounded in various ways. Those who, ashamed of their sins, began to dwell with Rahab in this city, and deserved to know and serve the king of this city (Josh. 2 and 6), are intended. The sense, then, is: I shall remember by granting virtues and glory those Gentiles who prostituted themselves with their idols, who were ashamed of their sins, who now dwell in this city through faith, and who know me through the sacraments.

Behold, the foreigners, and Tyre, and the Ethiopian people: these were there. The foreigners are the Philistines, whose name means “falling through drink”; they are drunken and lustful persons alienated from the kingdom of God. Tyre means “narrowness,” and signifies persecutors who afflict the Church. Ethiopians are called “black,” and signify sinners blackened by sins. All these were enemies of this city, but, subdued by Christ the King, they became its devoted citizens. All these things were made glorious through the King born in it, God and man. This is what follows:

**VERSE 5.** Shall Zion say: “Man and man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her”? That is, a man will be born in that city, and he himself founded that same city in the first creation, because he who is man is also God Most High—that is, most powerful. He founded it in this respect: he made materially those from whom this city would be built spiritually.

The verse is construed thus: O Zion, will any human being say this? “The city was built, and a man was born in it; and he who was born founded it; and although he is man, he is the Most High”? Hardly anyone will dare to proclaim this, for it will appear incredible and impossible.

Another translation has: “Mother Zion shall say: ‘Man.’” The sense is: the Synagogue, which is the mother of Zion—that is, of the Church—will say of Christ, “He is only a man”; but Zion says, “He is the Most High.” How are these things known?

**VERSE 6.** The Lord recounted them in the writings of the peoples—[Note: [Col. 0527D] The Vulgate has “will recount” (*narrabit*).]—that is, in the Law and the Prophets, writings intended for the benefit of the peoples; and in the writings of the rulers, that is, of those apostles who were rulers in it as long as they lived, taught such things, and left writings behind them. Holy Scripture belongs to all peoples, because almost everyone understands it; secular literature belongs to few, because few understand it. What Plato wrote, scarcely three people understand. Philosophers shut the way of truth to people when they wrapped their opinions in obscure language; the apostles opened it to the world in plain words. A great thing has occurred in this city—great joy, great gladness! Therefore, having gathered together every joy, he concludes:

*Diapsalma.* **VERSE 7.** As the dwelling-place of all who rejoice is in you. The dwelling-place of all in you, O city of God, will not be that of mourners, but like that of those who rejoice in this life—indeed, who truly rejoice in the life to come. Here we are worn down in tabernacles; in that heavenly city our dwelling will be joy alone. There will be no groaning of those who long for something, but the joy of those who possess and enjoy it. For he whom we sigh for will be present: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). There will be no task for us there except to praise God and enjoy God. We shall be dwelt in and shall dwell. All things will be subjected to him, so that God may be all in all. What, then, will it be? As far as human speech could express it, he said: “As the dwelling-place of all who rejoice is in you.” Why “as of those who rejoice”? Because he found no other comparison than one known to human beings here.

This psalm also concerns the soul. The city of God is the faithful soul, whose foundations—that is, the beginnings of good conduct—are upon the holy mountains, that is, in the life and teachings of the saints. This city is called Zion, that is, “watchtower of life.” The Lord loves its gates. The gates of this Zion through which the soul enters are faith and baptism. The gates through which it goes out are action and love. The tabernacles of Jacob are the carnal understanding and traditions of the Jews. Glorious things have been spoken of this city, because it is built from virtues as from stones, and because it is joined to Christ the Emperor as a bride. The Lord remembers it because it has turned to him from Rahab and Babylon—that is, from the breadth of vices, the pride of worldly glory, and the confusion of sins. Foreigners, Tyrians, and Ethiopians dwell in this city, because former shameful things remain in its thought, things which alienated it from God; hence it has narrowness and the dread of fear. After this Christ is born in it, that is, virtue or a good work in imitation of Christ; and the Most High himself founded it in virtues. And he will make known to it his will in the writings of the peoples, that is, in the sufferings of martyrs and the lives of saints; and in the writings of the rulers, that is, of apostles and prophets. And he will tell it this: that its dwelling will be like that of all who rejoice, because Christ, King of virtues, will reign forever in this city, and he is perfect joy.

The feast of Saint Mary sings this psalm, because she gave birth to Christ, God and man.

## PSALM LXXXVII

[Col. 0529]

[Col. 0529C] “O Lord, God of my salvation,” etc. This psalm concerns Christ’s passion, death, burial, and descent into hell. Soldiers labouring in tents, having heard of the glory found in the city of the emperor, burned with intense desire to leave the camp, enter that city, and enjoy immeasurable joy. A contest is appointed for them; and because it is necessary to enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations, they are told that the entrance into this city is tribulation, just as it was first necessary for Christ their King to suffer and thus enter that glory, in which, as they suffer with him, they too shall reign with him.

Lest they fail in the contest, the contest of Christ their King is set before them in this psalm; and after the struggle a crown is promised to the victors, because “no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). The lawful contest was as follows: two naked men, anointed with oil, wrestled together. If one fell beneath the other, he was not immediately defeated; but if, having been thrown down repeatedly, he altogether withdrew from the contest, he was defeated and delivered into the victor’s service, while the victor was crowned with a laurel. Such is the contest between Christians and demons. [Col. 0530C] The demons are naked; Christians are anointed with oil. If anyone, at the prompting of the devil, falls into some sin, he will not immediately become the devil’s slave, provided that through repentance he restores his strength and rises boldly against the adversary. But if he entirely abandons the purpose of resisting sin, he will undergo the dominion of the one who conquers him and will be deprived of the crown. Whoever perseveres in the contest until the end will receive the crown of life.

This is the eighty-seventh psalm, which is nine times nine, plus six. By the number nine the joy of the angels is expressed; by six, the labour of those who struggle here. This number indicates that those who fight against vices for Christ will receive the joys of angels in the glorious city. The title of the psalm is:

**(VERSE 1.) A SONG OF A PSALM, FOR THE SONS OF KORAH, UNTO THE END, FOR MELECH [Note: [Col. 0529D] The Vulgate has *Maheleth* and “of Ethan the Ezrahite.”] TO ANSWER, AN UNDERSTANDING OF EMAN THE ISRAELITE.**

A song is the joy of contemplation. A psalm is the pursuit of good action. The sons of Korah are martyrs, imitators of Christ crucified on Calvary. The end is perseverance. Melech [Maheleth] means “choir,” understood as the choir of martyrs. “To answer” has understood: “to instruments,” or “to another who sings first,” because when a precentor sings first, the responding choir answers him. Where “understanding” is placed, it signifies that the text should be understood spiritually. Eman was one of the skilled singers to whom David gave this psalm to sing; and he is called his brother, signifying Christ, who became the brother of that choir by making martyrs sons of God. The addition “Israelite” signifies that they will see God.

Another translation has: “Eman the Ezrahite.” Eman means “receiving”; Ezrahite, “native-born” or “eastern.” It signifies Christ’s martyrs fighting in the camp, who received from the Lord the power to suffer for him; they are not strangers and sojourners, but native-born inhabitants of the city of God—that is, citizens and members of God’s household—and are called eastern from him who is called the East, just as Christians are named from Christ. Thus the title is explained: This song of a psalm—that is, the gladness of good action—is set before the sons of Korah, that is, imitators of Christ’s passion, so that they may contend unto the end for the crown of righteousness. The song is “for Melech [Maheleth],” that is, for harmony in answering—understand, to Christ: namely, just as Christ sang first through his passion, so the choir of martyrs may answer through suffering, if it desires to reign with him in the glorious city. And because the song is “an understanding of Eman the Israelite,” this means that it directs the understanding toward Christ, the brother of those who see God. Or the understanding of this song is ascribed to Eman the Ezrahite, that is, to the people who have received from the Lord the privilege of being native inhabitants of the city of God.

The subject of the psalm is Christ’s humiliation in his passion, death, and descent. Its purpose is to urge us, by Christ’s example, to walk the narrow way if we wish to enter the city of God. The words appear to have been taken from Joseph’s history: his brothers placed him in a pit in the wilderness; his acquaintances became far away and made him an abomination to themselves; he was handed over by them to the Ishmaelites and did not escape from them. But it signifies Christ, whom his brothers—that is, his disciples—placed in the tomb, while his acquaintances, namely the Jews, made him an abomination to themselves upon the cross; betrayed by Judas to the Pharisees, he did not escape from them.

[Col. 0531D] It has three parts. The first is, “O Lord, God of salvation,” in which the calamities of Christ’s passion are described; the second, “Will you work wonders for the dead?” in which six questions are set forth negatively; the third, “But I have cried to you, O Lord,” in which are added the miseries of the Church, which is Christ’s body. The voice of Christ in the form of a servant:

**VERSE 2.** O Lord, God of my salvation: O Word, Son of God, who are Lord of all, who in me, a human being, assumed the form of a servant—you, God, who created me, God, I say, of my salvation, that is, giving salvation to humanity through me—in the day I cried, that is, in the brightness which I possess with you I preached to the peoples; and in the night, that is, amid the darkness of the Jews; and this before you, that is, according to your good pleasure. Or he cried before God by day and night, because he prayed in the sight of God in prosperity and adversity.

Alternatively: he cried in the day when, upon the cross, he sang the psalm, “My God, my God, look upon me,” as it is written: *Eloi, Eloi*, that is, “My God, my God,” etc. (Mark 15:34). He cried in the night when on the Mount of Olives he said: “Father, if you will, take this cup away from me” (Luke 22:42). And this was before God because he alone knows with what intention he did this. “I cried”:

**VERSE 3.** Let my prayer enter into your sight; incline your ear to my petition. The entrance of his prayer into God’s sight is the reception of his flesh, in which he prayed for human salvation. The inclining of God’s ear is the merciful hearing by which he raised fallen humanity from the mire to heavenly things. Hear me:

**VERSE 4.** For my soul is filled with evils: with the sins of the perishing people, or with anxieties caused by the sufferings of the flesh. And my life drew near to hell, because I die through suffering, and thus shall go to hell. I shall truly die, for behold, already:

**VERSES 5–6.** I have been counted with those who go down into the pit: that is, I have been condemned with thieves who descend to hell because of their deserts. I have become like a man without help: that is, they regard me as a man who has neither friend nor neighbour to avenge his death. Or they torment me thus because they judge me to be a sinner abandoned by you, one who after death will descend to hell with other sinners—though I am free from sin among the dead. For others, death is the penalty of sin; for me it is voluntary and the cause of human salvation. And because I am free from sin among those dead in sins, I shall not be held by death in punishments. I have also become like the wounded who sleep in tombs. Thus I was slain by their wounds, like thieves wounded, killed, and thrown into graves for their crimes.

Or I have been counted by them like those wounded in soul by shameful deeds, sleeping in tombs—that is, lying at rest, buried in the habit of sins—or like those who die in crimes and, like the rich man, are buried in hell. You no longer remember them in order to redeem them through me; and they have been driven away from my hand, that is, from the salvation which you work through me, your hand. Wounded and slain,

**VERSE 7.** They placed me in the pit, that is, in the tomb; and also in the lower pit, that is, my soul in hell: in dark places and in the shadow of death, that is, “into a dark land, covered with the gloom of death, where there is no order but everlasting horror dwells” (Job 10:21–22). Or by their estimation they placed me in the lower pit, that is, in the deepest calamity, judging me the most wretched of all people, since I was condemned to the most shameful death, namely the punishment of the cross. And so they placed me in darkness, that is, among thieves darkened by sins, and in the shadow of death, that is, among imitators of the devil. Death is the devil; the shadow of death is the wicked who imitate the devil as a shadow imitates a body. They formed such an estimate of me because:

**VERSE 8.** Your wrath has been established upon me. The wrath of God was avenging punishment raging with many penalties against the human race. This wrath was established upon Christ when he handed him over to a horrible death for the sins of all. And you brought all your waves over me, that is, all the sufferings which you foretold in the prophets. Or the Jews regard me as though you had brought every kind of punishment upon me for my own crimes.

**VERSE 9.** You have made those who knew me far from me—that is, his apostles and kinsmen who followed him from Galilee, all of whom fled when they abandoned him. They made me an abomination to themselves, because, seeing me so treated, they abhorred me as utterly wicked, so much so that some denied knowing me on oath. Or the Jews made me an abomination to themselves when, in abhorrence, they condemned me to the punishment of the cross. I was handed over by the Jews to the Gentiles, and I did not leave Pilate’s custody, confined as an accused person; or, handed over to death, I did not escape by showing myself to be God. And therefore:

**VERSE 10.** My eyes grew weak through want. The body of Christ is the Church. In this body the eyes are the apostles, leading it from darkness to the light of life. The light of these eyes was the Sun of righteousness. When he lay hidden here under the cloud of flesh and did not show himself to be God in his passion, the eyes grew weak through the lack of their light, because they doubted his power. Some even denied that he was God, and some said: “We had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21); but this implies, “We have been deceived, because he died like another human being, abandoned by everyone.” I cried to you, O Lord, saying: *Eloi, Eloi*; or I cried for them: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). All day I stretched out my hands to you, that is, throughout my life I directed my works to you.

**VERSE 11.** Will you work wonders for the dead? Therefore I prayed that they might not die in sins, because for those dead in sins you do not work wonders with them, either to free them from the punishments of hell or now to raise them with the righteous.

[Col. 0533D] Alternatively: while I hung upon the cross, the sun was darkened, darkness came over the whole earth, rocks were split, the veil of the temple was divided, the earth shook, and it cast forth the dead. You performed these wonders for the living—that is, for those who perceived them—who, converted to faith by what they saw, said: “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Mark 15:39). But will you perform these wonders for those dead in sins—that is, for those who do not perceive—who, with hardened hearts, such as Caiaphas and the Pharisees, see these things and do not believe, indeed even place guards at the tomb? You will not. Or will physicians raise them, and will they confess you? The apostles were physicians of souls, instructed by the heavenly Physician, who healed wounds inflicted upon souls with the ointments of the Holy Spirit. Will these physicians raise the scribes and Pharisees, dead in sins, whom the supreme Physician did not raise from the death of the soul; and, once raised, will they confess—that is, praise—the Lord? Certainly not. For such “dead persons will not praise you, O Lord” (Ps. 113:17).

**VERSE 12.** Will anyone in the grave declare your mercy, and your truth in destruction? Christ is the mercy of God, because through him human misery is removed; he is likewise God’s truth, because through him heavenly things are restored. No one in the grave will declare this mercy and truth to another, nor will anyone placed in destruction—that is, in hell—remember it, for the pain of immense torments takes away thought of God.

Alternatively: the sinning soul is dead; its tomb is the body or an evil habit, in which it lies buried and stinks. Destruction is despair. Those therefore established in the habit of sins or in despair do not seek God’s mercy and truth; they do not believe that the world has been saved in mercy or that judgment will come in truth.

**VERSE 13.** Will your wonders be known in the darkness, and your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness? He calls the prison-houses of hell “darkness.” The land of forgetfulness is hell, because those placed there have forgotten God, and God has forgotten them in respect of mercy. In those places God’s wonders and righteousness will not be known, because no one declares them there. The unbelieving are likewise darkness, in whom God’s wonders will not be known because, hardened, they will not turn to repentance. The Jews are the land of forgetfulness, because on account of earthly things they have forgotten God. In them Christ, the righteousness of God, is not known, because he is not sought. All this was said so that his soul might not be left in hell but might rise swiftly, in order that God’s praise could be known through his benefits. You, Father, will not work wonders for the dead except through me, nor will physicians raise them except through me.

**VERSE 14.** But I cried to you, O Lord, that you might raise me, so that through me you may work wonders for the dead: receiving some from hell, raising some in body, and justifying some in soul. For “many bodies of the saints arose and appeared to many” (Matt. 27:52); and through me the physician-apostles may raise the dead, some bodily and many spiritually, so that they may confess you. I prayed, and in the morning my prayer will come before you: that is, you will glorify me by my resurrection in the morning. He adds how he prayed:

**VERSE 15.** Why, Lord, do you reject my prayer, by which I prayed, “Let this cup pass from me” (Luke 22:42)? Why do you turn your face away from me, as from Adam, and not look upon me to deliver me?

This is also said in the person of the Church, which is Christ’s body. The unbelievers will not know your wonders; the Jews forget you; and I, namely the people faithful to you, have cried to you alone with devotion, in word and deed, that I may obtain you. “In the morning my prayer will come before you”: in the light of virtues my prayer comes before your judgment. And although I have prayed for what is good, why, Lord, do you reject my prayer and turn your face away from me? When saints ask for what is not beneficial to them, as Paul did, God rejects their prayer because he does not grant them what is not useful. He seems to turn his face away when he does not rescue them from tribulation, as with Lawrence, because he has purposed to give them eternal joys. Christ’s voice continues: Because you turn your face away from me, Father, therefore:

**VERSE 16.** I am poor, having no comfort or help; and I have been in labours from my youth—from the time of the assumed flesh, or from the thirtieth year of my age, when I began to preach. But, raised up on the cross, I was humbled in the tomb and troubled in death.

**VERSE 17.** Your angers—that is, the avenging punishments of sin—passed over me when they struck me with scourges as though I were guilty; and your terrors troubled me, that is, the dreadful sufferings which I preached that you would inflict upon the wicked were poured out upon me on the cross.

**VERSE 18.** The Jews surrounded me like water, that is, like waves of persecution. Throughout the whole day of the Preparation, from morning until evening, they laboured for his death. The Pharisees together with the priests, Pilate with the rulers and peoples, surrounded me.

**VERSE 19.** You have removed friend and neighbour far from me, that is, the apostles and kinsmen; and you have removed all my other acquaintances from my misery. And because they saw me deprived of every aid, they killed me as utterly wretched. From there, descending into hell, he bound the strong man, bore away his spoils in triumph, rose in the morning, and thus the King of eternal glory entered into his glory. All this is written as a pattern for the saints, because if the King of glory entered the city only through the entrance of tribulation, neither can they enter except through tribulation.

## PSALM LXXXVIII

[Col. 0535]

[Col. 0535B] “I will sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord,” through generations, etc. Since Christ had to suffer, the preceding psalm foretells his abasement; but since he also had to rise from the dead and thus enter into his glory, this psalm is numbered eighty-eight, a number formed by multiplication of eleven and eight. For eleven times eight makes the total of this number. As ten signifies the Law, so eleven signifies transgression of the Law. Eight suggests resurrection. This number therefore signifies that the human race, dead through transgression of God’s Law, rises in soul through Christ and, in the final resurrection, receives the joy of the eight beatitudes. Its title is:

**(VERSE 1.) AN UNDERSTANDING OF ETHAN THE ISRAELITE.**

Ethan was a skilled musician, and David therefore entrusted this psalm to him for recitation. Ethan means “strong,” and signifies the people of martyrs, strong in persecutions, who are Israelites, that is, those who will see God. Another translation has “Ethan the Ezrahite,” meaning “the strong native-born man.” Thus this psalm—that is, this praise of God—is an understanding of Ethan the Israelite, or the Ezrahite: that is, of the strong people of martyrs who will see God and were native-born inhabitants of the city of God.

The subject of the psalm is Christ’s exaltation. Its purpose is to call to mind for us the glory of eternal life, urging us through Christ’s praises to hasten toward it. Its words are drawn from the history in which God found David according to his own heart, anointed him with holy oil, made him king over the people, and promised the kingdom to Solomon. But it signifies Christ, whom the Father found according to his own heart, in whom he was well pleased, whom he anointed with the oil of gladness in the Holy Spirit, and appointed King of the Church; he will give him, the truly peaceable one, the kingdom to come, when he will reign forever in heavenly glory in the Church.

It is divided by five *diapsalmata* into six sections. By five is signified the Jewish people established under the Pentateuch; by six, the faithful people serving under the six works of the Gospel, who are subject to the Lord Christ. In the first part God’s mercy and truth are commended; in the second, Christ’s unique magnificence and the glory of the saints in his name are proclaimed; in the third, the benefits bestowed by God upon the Lord’s human nature are narrated; in the fourth, the overthrow of Christ’s enemies’ kingdom is recalled in praise of him; in the fifth, the reconciliation of the Jews with Christ is indicated; and in the sixth, the recompense of the wicked is declared. The voice of the faithful people:

**VERSE 2.** I will sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord. The Lord’s mercies are many: illumination, forgiveness, righteousness, advancement, perseverance, and finally reward. I will sing of all these for ever, that is, here and in the future I will praise you, God, for them. From generation to generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth: that is, among the Jewish people and the Gentiles; or, as long as one generation succeeds another, I will proclaim with my mouth—the instrument by which confession is made unto salvation—the truth of God in Christ, whom I believe in my heart unto righteousness.

**VERSE 3.** For you said through the prophets: Mercy shall be built up for ever in the heavens. The heavens are the apostles, who will reign in heaven. In them God’s mercy has been built by the Holy Spirit and will remain for ever. Your truth will be prepared in them—that is, Christ, God’s truth, will be preached through them to others. And you said this:

**VERSE 4.** I have established a covenant with my chosen ones: that is, I gave the precepts of the New Testament to the apostles whom I chose. And you said: I have sworn to David my servant—that is, I have firmly promised Christ, born of David and obedient to me in all things:

**VERSE 5.** For ever I will establish your seed: that is, I will make Christians, your followers, endure for ever. And I will build your throne from generation to generation: that is, I will build the Church from living stones, in which you, the King, will then sit for ever.

*Diapsalma.* Christ’s royal power follows and is exalted with many praises. What precedes is referred to the Father; what follows, to the Son.

**VERSE 6.** The heavens will confess your wonders, O Lord. The heavens—that is, the apostles, in whom mercy has been built through Christ’s Gospel and truth prepared through the Holy Spirit—will confess your wonders, O Lord: that is, they will praise the signs which you, Christ, will perform. Indeed, they will preach your truth in the Church of the saints—that is, your true promises and signs—in the congregation of the saints; and they will proclaim that no one is like you.

**VERSE 7.** For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Here the Trinity is introduced, so that all this praise may be understood of the Trinity. The clouds are the prophets, from whom the rain of life had flowed. Who among them was equal to the Lord the Father? No one. Or who will be like the Lord the Son among the sons of God—that is, the apostles, who are God’s adopted sons and co-heirs of his kingdom? No one.

**VERSE 8.** God, who is glorified in the council of the saints—namely the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who is proclaimed in the apostolic congregation as worthy of worship and equal to the Father and the Son. For the Lord Jesus Christ with the Father and the Holy Spirit subsists in one omnipotence, great and terrible—or “fearful,” as another translation has it—above all who are around him. Christ lived in Judaea, and all nations were around him. Therefore he is mighty and to be feared above all nations. Or he is mighty in signs and terrible in judgments above the apostles and all saints who are around him—that is, who are near him through innocence.

The Hebrew has: “God, illustrious in the secret counsel of the saints, exceedingly [mighty] and terrible to all who are around him.” Christ’s power is known only to the saints, who know his fearful judgments and cry out to him:

**VERSE 9.** O Lord God of hosts, who is like you? You are Lord of all and God of the angels: who among angels or human beings is like you in power and strength? You are mighty, O Lord, in signs and wonders; and your truth is around you, that is, the Church, in whose midst you are, to which you have displayed through the heavens, the apostles, all the things that are true which you promised through the clouds, the prophets. He then states what signs he performs mightily:

**VERSE 10.** You rule the power of the sea, and you calm the movement of its waves. This is drawn from the history in which he calmed the Red Sea for the passage of his people. The sea signifies the age, troubled by many errors, whose powers Christ rules. The movements of the waves are the temptations of persecutions, which Christ calms so that the raging storm may not overwhelm his servants; he does not wholly remove them, lest he take the crown away from martyrs.

**VERSE 11.** You humbled the proud one as one wounded; with the arm of your strength you scattered your enemies. This is drawn from Pharaoh’s history: God wounded and humbled the proud Pharaoh with flies, frogs, and other vermin; he scattered his Egyptian enemies when he immersed them in the sea’s waves. The proud one is the devil, who, wounded by the nails of Christ’s cross, was humbled in the loss of his spoils. Therefore he said, “as one wounded,” because he was struck with pain in his mind, not in flesh, which he does not possess. Thus he who proudly wished to be worshipped as God by all peoples was humbled by Christ when he lost those who had been his kingdom. “With the arm of your strength you scattered your enemies”: that is, in your mighty power you scattered the Jews throughout the whole world.

### Verses 12–14

Yours are the heavens, and yours is the earth; you founded the world and its fullness; you created the north wind and the sea. These words are drawn from the creation of the world, since in Christ all things were created, whether in heaven or on earth, visible and invisible. The heavens are the apostles, who belong to Christ and were made radiant in virtues by him. The earth is the Church converted from the Jews, cultivated by the plough of the Gospel. It now belongs to Christ because it worships him and has transformed the legal ordinances into sacrifice. The world is the whole circuit of Churches converted from every nation; its fullness [Col. 0538C] is all the elect gathered into the Church of the Gentiles. He himself founded this Church in faith and baptism, and taught it, through love and active works, to build itself as a tower toward heaven. The north wind is a harsh wind and signifies Antichrist; the sea is his turbulent persecution. You created these—that is, you prepared them for a crown for your elect. Or: “You created the north wind and the sea,” that is, you ordered the devil and his members, because you made their works fruitful for your saints. For whatever the devil accomplishes through himself and his own, all turns to the benefit of the saints; thus both he himself and evil persons are proved necessary.

And because you made all things, Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name. Tabor is a mountain in Galilee near Nazareth, on which Christ taught the eight beatitudes. [Col. 0538D] Hermon is a small mountain in Judea near the Jordan, onto which the Lord went up after his baptism, when the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove. Tabor means “coming light”; Hermon, “his anathema.” By Tabor is understood the Church from the Jews, into which the true light came from heaven; illuminated by it, that Church itself became a coming light to the people of the Gentiles, who sat in the darkness of unbelief and the shadow of death. For from the primitive Church the light of truth came to the Gentiles. By Hermon is signified the Church from the Gentiles, which anathematizes the north wind—that is, the devil and his works. Therefore Tabor and Hermon, that is, believers from Jews and Gentiles, shall rejoice in the Christian name, because they have escaped the north wind and the sea—that is, the devil, Antichrist, and the persecution of the wicked. [Col. 0539A] Your arm is with power: that is, you readily restrain the savagery of the ungodly, because whatever you will, you accomplish mightily. Their prayer follows:

“Let your hand be strengthened”: that is, in judgment let your action against your adversaries be made firm, so that you may crush into the depths those whom you now endure to trample upon your own people. “And let your right hand be exalted”: that is, let the number of the predestined, who are to be placed at the right hand, be glorified, because

### Verse 15

Righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne. Christ’s throne is the Church, in which he shall rest, through which he shall judge the world, and in which the King shall reign for ever. The preparation of this throne is righteousness and judgment, because through the righteousness which it has done here it will be judged worthy of the kingdom, while an unrighteous people will be separated from it in judgment as chaff from grain. Thus righteousness and judgment are the preparation [Col. 0539B] of the throne, because holy equity shall be revealed in judgment, the true Judge shall be displayed, and the ministries of angels shall be seen, by whom the evil are divided from the good. Meanwhile mercy and truth shall go before your face: mercy, by which you spare those who turn back; truth, by which you restore what was promised.

### Verse 16

Blessed is the people that knows jubilation. He did not say, “that sings,” but “that knows jubilation.” For jubilation is an abundant exultation of the mind which cannot be expressed in words. Blessed, therefore, shall be those who here rejoice before God for his benefits, because they shall rejoice eternally. Of their joy it follows: “Lord, they shall walk in the light of your countenance”: that is, here they shall dwell in the illumination of the Holy Spirit and persevere in the brightness of your thought; and afterwards they shall see you face to face. [Col. 0539C]

### Verse 17

And in your name they shall rejoice all day: that is, throughout the whole time of this life they shall rejoice in the Christian name; and in that entire future day, which has no evening, they shall rejoice because they followed your name in righteousness. And then they shall be exalted in your righteousness in heavenly glory, because here they were humbled in penitence. For it is your righteousness to exalt the humble and cast down the proud. Truly they shall be exalted:

### Verse 18

For you are the glory of their strength. For the virtues which you gave them here, you yourself shall be their joy, glory, and blessedness. They shall have glory from no other thing than from you, in whose vision all saints shall rejoice. And in your good pleasure our horn shall be exalted. The horn is the strength of the saints, by which [Col. 0539D] they overcome vices and sins. The horn also signifies the kingdom of the righteous, who reign in heavenly places. This horn shall be exalted in God’s good pleasure, because the virtue of the saints, accomplished in God’s will, shall be raised in the kingdom on high. This is so:

### Verse 19

Because ours is the taking up by the Lord, and by the Holy One of Israel, our King: that is, our Creator and Governor, sanctifying us and making us Israel—that is, those who see God—took up our flesh and raised it above the angels into heavenly glory. Or, he took us up from mortality, from ignorance into light, from this world into eternal joy. There follows the manifold grace bestowed by the Divinity upon the human being whom it assumed.

[Col. 0540A] **Diapsalm. Verse 20.** Then you spoke in vision to your saints—that is, in revelation to the prophets. There are three kinds of vision: bodily vision, by which we see bodily things; spiritual vision, by which we conceive in the spirit images of bodily things; and intellectual vision, by which we understand the realities of things as they are. The Lord spoke to the prophets in spiritual vision when he appeared to them in an assumed form, or showed them figurative forms, as to Ezekiel, Daniel, and John in the Apocalypse. And because the prophets alone saw these things, they were called “seers.” He spoke to them in intellectual vision when, filling their minds with inward inspiration, he showed them things to come, as he did to David. After you revealed to me all these things which you said concerning Christ, you then also spoke [to] your other saints, namely Samuel, [Col. 0540B] Nathan, and Gad, in vision, or dreams, or inward inspiration, and said: “I have placed help in the mighty one”: that is, the help which I intend to give the human race I shall lay upon a mighty one—that is, I shall help through the Mighty One.

Another translation reads: “Upon the mighty one”—that is, upon Christ, who shall be a helper to the oppressed—I shall place [him] over the mighty devil, so that he may oppress him. He speaks of the future as though it were already past because of its immutable certainty: what is future can change, so that it may not occur; what is past cannot change so as not to have happened. “And I have exalted one chosen from my people”: that is, I shall exalt one chosen from the Israelite people by signs and powers, and I shall exalt him at my right hand above every name. Whom did I choose? David—that is, Christ—strong against [Col. 0540C] demons and desired by angels. I sought this chosen one in the patriarchs and prophets. And:

### Verse 21

I found David my servant: namely, Christ, obedient to me, born from David’s stock; in divinity he is David, “the beloved,” and in humanity he is a servant, serving my will. Having found him according to my heart, I anointed him with my holy oil as king and priest by spiritual grace, that he might offer sacrifice for them and rule in virtues. From the whole human race I shall choose him—that is, I shall assume him for this office—because he alone shall please me, upon whom I shall lay this office, through whom I shall help the human race rise from its misery. I shall exalt him as king and priest and establish in him the help of the human race. These words are taken from Samuel, when he anointed David [Col. 0540D] king. This chosen one shall free and help the oppressed people.

### Verse 22

For my hand shall help him: that is, my Son, through whom I made all things, personally united to him, shall help him restore the human race. And my arm shall strengthen him: that is, the Word united with him shall make him firm, lest he yield. Therefore:

### Verse 23

The enemy shall gain nothing against him: that is, the devil, tempting him, shall not prevail or draw him away from obedience. And the son of iniquity shall not continue to harm him: that is, Judas the betrayer, the devil’s son, shall harm him no further. Beforehand he seemed to harm him when he delivered him over to sufferings and death. But after God’s right hand exalted him, he shall not continue to harm him, because “he dies no more; death shall have no more dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9). [Col. 0541A]

### Verse 24

And I shall cut down his enemies before his face: that is, I shall confound the Jews before him by the sword of his word. For they often departed from him defeated and confounded. And those who hate him—namely demons—I shall turn to flight. For they often fled before him, saying: “Why have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matt. 8:29). These words are drawn from the history in which David’s enemies Saul and Absalom were killed and others put to flight. So the Jews, Christ’s enemies, were killed by the Romans, and demons were driven from the Gentiles.

### Verse 25

And my truth and my mercy shall be with him. Truth in preaching, because he shall speak what he heard from me; mercy in healing, because he shall heal the sick in mind and body alike. Or, my truth is with him because through him I shall fulfill all that I foretold through the prophets. My mercy is with him because I shall free human beings from misery. And in my name his horn shall be exalted: that is, the strength of his holiness—or rather, that of the Church redeemed by his blood—shall advance in my praise, attributing it to me, not to itself. [Col. 0541B]

### Verse 26

And I shall place his hand upon the sea: that is, his works in the world. And his right hand upon the rivers: that is, I shall establish his power over the princes of the age. For as rivers flow into the sea, so greedy persons slip into the bitterness of this age. Yet all these kinds of people shall be subject to Christ, because

### Verse 27

He himself shall call upon me: “You are my Father, my God, and the sustainer of my salvation.” My Father, because you begot me equal to yourself; my God, because you created me lesser than yourself; the sustainer of my salvation, because you received me as a human being into yourself for the salvation of the human race. He himself shall say these things to me. [Col. 0541C]

### Verse 28

And I, the Father, shall make him the firstborn. I shall show the world that he is my firstborn, equal to me; and I shall make him the firstborn of the dead by raising him from death. I shall make him higher than the kings of the earth, exalting him above the heavens and subjecting to him every kingdom of the world.

### Verse 29

For ever I shall preserve my mercy for him—namely, this mercy, that he should be higher than the kings of the earth—and my covenant with him shall be faithful: that is, my pact, which I made with the fathers, shall be faithful to him, because he shall rule all nations for ever. [Col. 0541D]

### Verse 30

And I shall establish his seed for age upon age: that is, I shall make Christians, sprung from his name, endure eternally. And his throne shall be as the days of heaven: that is, I shall make the Church equal to the angels in heaven, who shine with eternal brightness, illuminated by the Sun of righteousness.

Alternatively: just as a certain heavenly order is called a throne because of its excellence, so the chaste are called God’s throne, in whom he sits more familiarly because of purity of heart. I shall make them like the days of angels: that is, I shall place in them the same knowledge that is in the angels.

[Col. 0542A] Alternatively: a throne is a royal seat and signifies the power of the future judgment, which must be carried out with such truth that it shines before all saints with heavenly brightness.

### Verse 31

But if his children forsake my law, etc. Christ is the bridegroom; the Church, the bride. Their children are all Christians regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit. If these forsake my law—that is, if they reject solemn observances and fasts instituted by me or by my own—and do not walk in my judgments—that is, if they do not judge justly—

### Verse 32

If they profane my righteousnesses—that is, if they detest the canonical censures appointed through my servants for sinners—and do not keep my commandments written in the Decalogue of the Law, I shall not reject them or leave them in perdition, but:

[Col. 0542B] **Verse 33.** I shall visit their iniquities with a rod—that is, with gentle correction—and their sins with stripes—that is, with harsh scourges. Note: subjects forsake God’s law; prelates despise just judgments; priests regard righteousnesses as things to be profaned; rulers do not keep the commandments. The Lord visits their iniquities with a rod when he takes from them outward goods which they loved while despising God, whether by thieves, enemies, fire, or pestilence. He visits their sins with stripes when he chastises them with bodily affliction, or hands them over to enemies for diverse tortures or death, as he often did to Christians in persecution.

Note also that transgressors trample the four principal virtues. For forsakers of the Law despise prudence; those who forget judgments, fortitude; profaners of righteousnesses, justice; transgressors of commandments, temperance. Such children of his I shall correct with scourges:

### Verse 34

But I shall not scatter my mercy away from him: that is, if they repent, I shall mercifully forgive them and shall not take from them the kingdom promised through Christ. Some refer this to Solomon, saying that the Lord scourged him here when he took the kingdom from his son, but did not scatter mercy away from him because he delivered him from hell with the other righteous.

There is therefore a question concerning Solomon: was he saved, though he worshipped idols? But it should be known that Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine—three qualified witnesses—prove that he was saved. Jerome says: “Although Solomon sinned, nevertheless he did penance by writing the Proverbs, where he says: ‘At the last I did penance and looked back, that I might choose discipline.’” The Hebrews say that this book is the repentance of Solomon. Ambrose, in the *Apology of David*, says: “What shall I say about David? And what about holy Solomon, who, as the Jewish populace supposed that he had come in place of Christ, lest he seem to be above human beings, fell by divine prompting?” And David is not called holy, because everyone knows that he is holy. He calls Solomon holy in order to remove our doubt about his repentance. Is it to be believed that Solomon, wisest of men, thought there was any benefit in idols? Rather, because he was wasting away in pleasures, lest they be diminished by the grief of women, [Col. 0543A] he worshipped idols. Again Jerome says: “The Hebrews say that Solomon was dragged five times through the streets of Jerusalem as an act of penance. Coming into the Temple which he himself had built, he gave rods to the experts in the Law, that he might be beaten by them. By common counsel they said that they would not lay hands upon the Lord’s anointed. Therefore, dismissed by them, he deposed himself from the kingdom.”

Having said these things briefly, let us return to the subject. “I shall not take mercy away from David here,” that is, from Christ or his members, “nor shall I do harm in my truth”: that is, in the future judgment, where truth shall be fulfilled, I shall not inflict punishments.

### Verse 35

Nor shall I profane my covenant: that is, I shall not make my promise accursed. And what proceeds from my lips I shall not make void: that is, I shall not make empty what I speak through my prophets. I promised forgiveness to sinners; I shall fulfill it for those who turn back. I correct those who turn away by adversities, because:

### Verses 36–37

Once I have sworn by my holy one: that is, I have not merely promised but have also sworn by my holy one, namely by the Lord’s human nature, or by my holiness; and this once, that is, inviolably. This is what I swore: that his seed—that is, the acquired people—shall remain for ever. For the Lord knows those who are his. And if I should lie to David—that is, Christ—understand: I should not be God. For falsehood and God, who is truth, are contraries. And just as God is unchangeable, so his oath shall be unchangeable. [Col. 0543C] God’s oath was the firm decree that he would restore the human race through Christ.

### Verse 38

And his throne shall be as the sun before me. This continues what was said above: “I shall establish his seed for age upon age, and his throne as the days of heaven.” God’s throne is the Church. In the resurrection it shall shine like the sun. I also swore that all who are his seats shall in the future be in my presence, seeing me face to face, bright and burning like the sun, perfectly knowing and perfectly loving—and this according to the soul. In body they shall be like the moon when it is full; and so they shall remain eternally, not again failing in corruption as the moon does. For the righteous shall shine spiritually like the sun in the kingdom of the Father, not bodily like this sun which shines from heaven upon good and evil alike. Finally, “like the sun,” he says—not before the eyes of human beings, not before the sight of flesh, not before mortals, but before my sight. But his throne shall be perfected like the moon, full for ever: that is, the Church shall be perfect in soul and body. “Like the sun before me” was said of the soul, because none but God sees the mind; “like the full moon for ever” was said of the body, because the flesh shall be incorruptible in the resurrection of the dead. And David—that is, Christ, established bodily in heaven—shall be the faithful witness of this fact: faithful, that is, true and making faith firm. You spoke all these things to your saints concerning David. But lest this be understood carnally of David the king rather than [Col. 0544A] of Christ, there follows the destruction of David’s kingdom, because Christ’s kingdom shall be eternal.

**Diapsalm. The voice of David.** Through the prophets you promised me prosperity; through your holy one you swore good things to me:

### Verse 39

But you rejected and despised; you deferred your Christ. Just as the Jewish people is understood through Jacob, so the kingdom of Israel is understood through David. Therefore God rejected David’s kingdom when he took it away from Solomon’s son; he despised it when he gave it to Solomon’s servant. And because he fulfilled his promises neither in David nor in Solomon, he deferred his Christ, in whom he would fulfill all things. He also rejected David’s kingdom when he allowed the kingdom of Israel to be destroyed by enemies. He despised David’s kingdom when he did not prevent the kingdom [Col. 0544B] of Judah from being overthrown by the Babylonians. For David reigned over Judah and all Israel. He deferred sending his Christ to help them until the fullness of time should come. When it came:

### Verse 40

You overthrew the covenant of your servant: that is, the covenant which you promised David and Solomon you turned wholly toward Christ, and in him fulfilled all things. You profaned his sanctuary on earth: that is, you permitted the holy Temple in Jerusalem to be polluted by the Gentiles or entirely destroyed. Jewish sacred ordinances have been profaned throughout the whole earth. Kingdom, altar, sacrifice, and priesthood have been overthrown; taken from the Jews, they have been transferred to the Christian people.

[Col. 0544C] **Verse 41.** You destroyed all his hedges, or “walls,” as another translation has it. For all the walls were destroyed by the Romans. But his hedges were also the Holy Scriptures, which surrounded him as walls surround a vineyard. These have been destroyed in their carnal interpretation and converted into a spiritual understanding. You made his stronghold a terror: namely Jerusalem, the metropolis, or other cities or fortifications in which they had greatest confidence, when they collapsed under the siege of enemies. Note that, by the figure of *homoeoteleuton*, the words are turned with similar letter-endings: *repulisti, despexisti, distulisti, evertisti, profanasti, destruxisti, posuisti*—“you rejected, despised, deferred, overthrew, profaned, destroyed, made”—and they signify diverse calamities inflicted upon one people.

### Verse 42

All who pass along the way plundered him. That is, all nations passing through this life plundered David’s kingdom, namely Israel, fragments of which are among all nations. For it is said of them: “They shall be portions for foxes” (Ps. 62:11). He became a reproach to his neighbours: that is, to all nations surrounding the Jewish people. [Col. 0544D]

### Verse 43

You exalted the right hand of those who oppressed him. The power of the Romans was exalted, who oppressed the Jews. You made all his enemies rejoice. They rejoiced when, victorious over them, they celebrated triumph.

### Verse 44

You turned away the help of his sword. Few were formerly accustomed to fight and overthrow many, as the Maccabees did; but afterwards many were overthrown by few, because you did not help him in war. For by its own deserving that people was conquered, captured, alienated from its kingdom, scattered, and lost that land for which it killed the Lord. [Col. 0545A]

### Verse 45

You destroyed him from cleansing: that is, from the priesthood through which they were accustomed to be cleansed from sins by legal sacrifices. Or, “from cleansing,” that is, from faith which cleanses hearts, you destroyed him. And you dashed his throne to the ground: that is, you annihilated the throne of the kingdom. Because they refused to have Christ as king and chose Caesar—indeed, Barabbas—they deserved, while the devil ruled them, no longer to have any ruler from their own people.

### Verse 46

You shortened the days of his time. He thought that he would reign for ever if he killed Christ. But in a short time he lost both place and nation. [Col. 0545B] You drenched him with confusion, because, reduced to slavery, he was covered with everlasting disgrace.

In the Hebrew it reads: “You covered him with perpetual dishonour.” Thus the temporal kingdom of David was destroyed. Its spiritual restoration follows. **Diapsalm. Again, the voice of David:**

### Verse 47

How long shall your wrath burn like fire? If blindness has happened in part to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, will you always be angry with your people and consume it in vengeance as fire consumes wood? Why are not at least the remnant saved?

### Verse 48

Remember what my substance is: that is, remember Christ, begotten from my substance. If the Jews have failed, my substance has not failed. The Virgin Mary was born from that people; Christ’s flesh came from the virgin, and that flesh was not sinful but cleansing of sins. Therefore, although you rightly forget the Jews because of unbelief, remember him whom I foresee in the Spirit as bearing the substance of my flesh, and have mercy on them by saving them through grace. Did you indeed establish all the children of men in vain? That is, did you make so many people without purpose? Or can you despise those whom you made?

### Verse 49

Who is the person who shall live and not see death? No one. For Elijah and Enoch, who now live, shall yet die. Or who shall rescue his soul from the hand of hell? No one. This is to say: all the children of men seem to have been established in vain, because all die through the guilt of one man [Col. 0545D] and all descend to hell through the merit of their parents—except Christ alone, born from my substance, who lives and shall not die for ever, who alone rescued his soul from the hand of hell, because he never sinned. Yet it is clear that all were not established in vain, because this mighty one can save the living and free his own from there. Therefore, when at the end of time the Jews are reconciled to Christ and united to our faith through Elijah and Enoch, the persecution of Antichrist shall blaze up, and he shall afflict them beyond measure. Therefore, in their affliction they shall cry to the Lord:

**Diapsalm. Verse 50.** Where are your ancient mercies, Lord, as you swore to David in your truth? You swore to David that Christ would be born from the fruit of his womb and would mercifully save the people; and this you truly fulfilled. You also promised that through him peace, rest, and a land flowing with milk and honey would be given to us. Where are these promises? Behold, every evil has seized us.

### Verse 51

Remember, Lord, the reproach of your servants, which I have borne in my bosom, from many nations. The order of the words is: “Remember the reproach of your servants from many nations, which I have borne in my bosom.” Many nations reproached God’s servants because they worshipped one who had died. The Christian people bore this reproach in its bosom, because it grieved in the secret affection of its mind, not daring to answer idolaters. What was that reproach?

### Verse 52

With which your enemies reproached you, Lord; with which they reproached the change of your Christ. Christ’s change was this: that he who was mortal became immortal, passible became impassible, and one rejected by human beings was exalted above angels. But because this took place through death, the Jews and pagans, God’s enemies, reproached Christ’s worshippers, saying: “You worship one who died, and you venerate one crucified.” And because they themselves refused to turn from unbelief to faith, the change of Christ—and of those who were converted—was displeasing to them. The Lord shall remember this reproach, because he shall eternally condemn all persecutors and all enemies of the Church and exalt the faithful in everlasting glory. Therefore the righteous cry aloud:

### Verse 53

Blessed be the Lord for ever, who [Col. 0546C] raised up the fallen tabernacle of David. Let it be, let it be. In the Hebrew it is: “Amen, amen.”

This is also referred to the person of Christ. The voice of the apostles: “God, you promised Christ many sublime things. But you rejected him from this promise and despised him in the Passion; you deferred recognition of your Christ. Therefore they await Antichrist. For when they saw him suffer such weakness, they did not believe him to be the Christ, whom they expected to be immortal. You overthrew the covenant of your servant. You seem to have overthrown and violated every promise which you made concerning him and his own, though you promised that we should reign with him. You profaned his sanctuary on earth: you permit him to be treated in the manner of profane persons while he was on earth. You destroyed [Col. 0546D] all his hedges: namely, the words of the Law and Prophets, by which he was held fast. Or you permit the teachers of the sanctuary to be killed, who fortified others against heretics and every adversity by their teaching and consolation. You made his stronghold a terror: you made us, who surrounded him while he taught the crowds, a cause of fear; or you make the prelates, who are the stronghold of faith and holiness, a cause of fear, so that, seeing them treated in this way, people fear to confess themselves Christians. All who pass along the way plundered him: those who pierced his body—the way of life—with nails or a spear plundered his garments. Or all unbelievers who pass by Christ, the Way, and do not believe in him, plunder his members by subjecting the Church to diverse punishments. He became a reproach to his neighbours, [Col. 0547A] the Jews and chief priests, who said: ‘Ha! You who destroy the temple of God, come down now from the cross’ (Matt. 27:40). Or, the Church became a reproach to those who were just about to convert. You exalted the right hand of those who oppressed him when you humbled him unto death; or you raised the power of the persecutors of the Church by giving them authority to afflict it. You made all his enemies rejoice: Pilate with the Gentiles and Jews; or you made pagans, Jews, and heretics rejoice in the killing of Christians. You turned away the help of his sword, when the word of his preaching did not prevail among the Jews; or you turned away from the Church the help of the Word, so that it could not conquer others as it had done. And you did not help him in battle, namely in the conflict of the Passion; or you did not help the Church [Col. 0547B] in tribulation so that it might not suffer. You destroyed him from cleansing, because his garments were stained with blood because of his sins when he was reckoned among the wicked; or you destroy the Church from cleansing when you permit it to be killed solely for holiness; or you do so that, in the blood shed, they may be cleansed from sins. And you dashed his throne to the ground: the souls of the saints, upon whom he rested, were troubled by his death; or you dash the Church, Christ’s throne, but in that part in which it is earth—that is, its body, not its soul. You shortened the days of his time so that he might return more quickly to the Father; or you shorten the days of the Church so that it may quickly pass from the evils of the world to joy. You drenched him with confusion when there was mockery and derision among all peoples in persecution.” Here he has expressly expounded the Passion of Christ and of the Church, his body.

The Church, succeeding the apostles, says: “How long, Lord, do you turn away utterly? Shall your wrath burn like fire?” That is: how long will you be angry, so as not to call him back from death?

Alternatively: “To what measure shall your turning away from the Church extend? Shall it be complete? No.” Or: “Your vengeance shall burn like fire, which purifies gold and consumes wood.”

“Remember what my substance is.” I have no substance of life except in him whom I await to return from Tartarus.

[Col. 0547D] Alternatively: “Remember how worthy is that substance which is to come forth from me, and, at last, [Col. 0548A] through his merits have mercy on your servants, whose own merits do not suffice for salvation.”

“Did you indeed establish all the children of men in vain?” But you established them not vainly, but truly in hope of resurrection; how much more ought you to raise your Son?

Alternatively: “Did you establish all people in vain?” No. If God does not have mercy on the good, then truly all people would have been made without cause and for no use, which would be unfitting. But because you made them not in vain but for your glory, and because my substance is worthy, have mercy and save.

“Who is the person who shall live and not see death? Shall he rescue his soul from the hand of hell?” I know that no fleshly human being escapes death or saves his soul from hell; [Col. 0548B] but I know that God lay hidden beneath the covering of flesh, one whom death and hell ought not to retain. “Where are your ancient mercies, Lord, as you swore to David in your truth,” if he were not to be raised here?

Alternatively: this man, who shall live in such a way as not to die, will first rescue his soul from the power of hell and afterwards live immortally. Where are your mercies, arranged from ancient time? They are in him as you swore to David in your truth, as you firmly promised David, the temporal king, through yourself, who are true.

“Remember, Lord, the reproach of your servants,” who await him, “which I have borne in my bosom, from many nations,” which I have gathered as if into a bosom in the one household of faith. “With which your enemies, Lord—the Jews, Pharisees, and Sadducees—reproached the change of your Christ,” when, changing from them to the Gentiles, he said: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:38).

Alternatively: recompense your own because of the reproach which they patiently endure, inflicted not by a few but by many nations, and which they conceal within themselves—the reproach, I say, with which your enemies, Lord, Jews and pagans, reproach them: namely, the death of your Son. But we Christians, because of the transformation accomplished by his death, say: “Blessed be the Lord for ever”: that is, Christ the Lord is to be exalted above all things for ever. “Let it be, let it be.”

The third book ends with honour to the Trinity. This psalm is sung at the Nativity of the Lord because it says that Christ is born as firstborn from the Father.

## Psalm LXXXIX: On the Condition of Man

[Col. 0547]

[Col. 0547D] “O God, you have become a refuge to us,” etc. The Holy Spirit begins the fourth book with prayer, a number suited to the Church gathered from the four regions of the world under the four Gospels. It also suits the human being, who consists of four elements, whose condition is discussed here and who is saved through prayer. [Col. 0548D] Hearing that the King entered into his glory only through a narrow gate and that they too must take up the narrow path leading there, the soldiers call upon the Lord as their refuge, that entrance into the heavenly city may at least be opened to them through labour and suffering. This psalm stands in the eighty-ninth place because, in the resurrection—signified by the number eight—humanity is joined to the nine orders of angels. In the preceding psalm it is said: “Who is the person who shall live and not see death?” But in this one it is written that a human being passes like grass and lives for a brief time. Its title is:

### (Verse 1.) A PRAYER OF MOSES, THE MAN OF GOD

Why is this psalm attributed to Moses when he did not compose it? It should be understood that Hebrew names are sometimes placed in psalms solely for their interpretation, as Jacob and Israel are; sometimes because of a resemblance in some respect, as Moses is here. Moses wrote about the beginning of the human race, how heaven and earth were made, and the condition of humanity—how the human being was made. And this [Col. 0549B] psalm speaks of the condition of humanity: what the human being is and why he or she was born. Therefore, the one who wrote in Genesis concerning the human condition is now also introduced by the Holy Spirit as discussing what the human being is. The ancients were accustomed to introduce the persons of their forebears, whom they made speak in their books for the sake of authority, as Plato introduces Socrates and Cicero makes Cato and Scipio debate. Moses was also minister of the Old Testament and prophet of the New. Moses means “drawn from water,” and signifies the Hebrew people drawn from the Red Sea, insofar as he was minister of the old Law. No less does he signify the Christian people taken from the water of baptism, insofar as he was prophet of the new Law. He is presented here in the person of both. This, then, is a psalm concerning the prayer of Moses, the man of God: that is, of the Christian people, who, in the water of baptism, having put off the old human being, became the new human being of God, serving God not under compulsion but willingly.

The subject of the psalm is the condition of the human race. Its purpose is to show that the salvation of humankind is accomplished through Christ, though it had perished through Adam; and to urge us, through prayer, to turn to Christ if we wish to return to the glory we have lost. The words received are understood of Moses’ prayer on the mountain while Joshua fought Amalek, by which the Lord became their refuge and through him they gained the triumph of victory. It signifies, moreover, that the faithful people ought to fight the devil with the weapons of prayer [Col. 0549D], flee to the Lord, and through him attain the victor’s palm.

The psalm is divided into three sections, because the time of the righteous has three periods: the patriarchs before the Law, the prophets under the Law, and the apostles and their followers under grace are recorded as having pleased the Lord. The first section is, “Lord, you have been a refuge,” in which God’s eternity is shown. The second, “Do not turn man away into lowliness,” indicates the brevity of human life. The third, “Make your right hand known,” expresses Christ’s incarnation and humankind’s salvation. It is the voice of the faithful people addressing Christ:

“Lord, you have become a refuge for us Christians,” whom the Jews refused to acknowledge as their Lord. He who always existed in divinity became humanity’s refuge [Col. 0550A] when he began to exist as man; just as a coin is always a coin, but becomes a price when something is bought with it. Or he became a refuge when he became man. For “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Whoever seeks refuge flees either heat, a beast, or an enemy. We burn with the heat of vices; the beast, the devil, pursues us; hostile, perverse, and malicious people oppress us. Let us seek the Lord as refuge, where we shall find refreshment for our souls and a safe asylum against every adversity.

“From generation to generation,” or “from offspring to offspring,” as another translation has it: that is, from the old generation and the new generation. Or, “from generation,” from the time when the human race began to be begotten, “and offspring,” until the end of the age. Or, you became a refuge “from generation [Col. 0550B] to generation”: from the time of Abraham, when you were promised; from the time when you were sent in the flesh; and from the generation in which you will judge the world. You became a refuge, and yet you have always been God. For:

**VERSE 2.** “Before the mountains were made, or the earth and the world were formed, from age and unto age you are God.” Since God exists not only before the earth, but before heaven and before every bodily and spiritual creature, what great thing is proclaimed in saying that he existed before the mountains? Yet every rational creature is distinguished by this difference: by the mountains the loftiness of angels is expressed, and by the earth the lowliness of human beings.

Note that he said that the mountains were *made*, but that the earth was *formed* [Col. 0550C], because angels were made from nothing; the earth was formed from unformed matter; and human beings were formed from earth. You indeed became a [refuge] for us, but “from age unto age,” that is, from eternity into eternity, you are God: before all things without beginning, and remaining without end. Note that he did not say, “From age you were, and unto age you will be,” but “You are,” which belongs properly to the Word of God, who has neither past nor future but is always present. Hence it is said to Moses, “I am who I am”; and again, “He who is has sent me” (Exod. 3:14). O Lord, who are before all things and yet became a refuge for us, I pray:

**VERSE 3.** “Do not turn man away from you any further,” neither here nor in the future, when he has been cast down into lowliness [Col. 0550D], that is, into the abasement brought about by the fault of the first parent. This is what is prayed in the Lord’s Prayer: “Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13). “And you said: Return, children of men.” *And* is used in place of *because*. From the time of Abel you have always said: O you children of men, who have turned away from me because of your sins, return to me by faith and repentance. You said this because:

**VERSE 4.** “For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed.” We seek refuge in you, who are always the same, because—alas—we have come from eternal years to these passing ones, in which, even if someone has lived a thousand years, it is like yesterday, which has already passed. “And like a watch in the night,” which is a fourth part of the night. There are four watches of the night [Col. 0551A], each marked off by three hours. Hence the Gospel says, “If he comes in the second watch or in the third” (Luke 12:38); and again, “In the fourth watch of the night he came to them” (Matt. 14:25). These watches were observed by those who stayed in military camps. Therefore, if a person lived a thousand years, once they had passed it would be like one guard-duty, that is, one watch of the night. He used the watch of the night because a person lives here amid the anxiety of toil, like sentries in camp. And since a thousand years of this life are like a day that has passed, or one watch of the night, their years are therefore reckoned as nothing.

**VERSE 5.** The years of mortals are reckoned as nothing, because before they come they do not yet exist, and when they have come they will no longer exist. They do not come in order to be present [Col. 0551B], but in order not to be. For where is all the time we have lived? Where is that which we still must live? Thus a thousand years, or the entire time of the age, is like a point of time, reckoned as nothing in comparison with that eternity which is before the Lord’s eyes, that is, in God’s present vision. And since this wretched life is lived for so brief a time, you said: “Return, children of men,” from temporality to eternity, from mutable life to me, the immutable one.

The mutability of humankind follows. I prayed, “Do not turn man away into lowliness,” that is, into the world’s desire, which is so brief; but:

**VERSE 6.** “In the morning, let him pass away like grass; in the morning let him flourish and pass away; in the evening let him fall, grow hard, and wither”—understand, *man* [Col. 0551C]. Morning is childhood, which is fragile and tender like grass. Again, morning is youth, which flourishes in its pursuits as grass flowers before bearing fruit. Evening is old age, because at the setting of life’s light a person falls into death, then grows hard in the corpse, and withers into dust.

This, then, is what he says: since human life here is so brief, let childhood rise as the morning of a day and quickly pass away like grass; let youth burn like noon and pass away like a flower; let old age decline toward its setting as evening, and thus fall into death, grow hard into a corpse, and wither into dust, so that it may flower again in the resurrection and thus be able to live in eternity. By these comparisons, namely morning and evening, mutability is indicated; by grass and flowers, the brevity of human life [Col. 0551D]. These things have happened to us because:

**VERSE 7.** “For we have failed away in your anger,” that is, in your vengeance, by which you avenge in us our first parent’s transgression through hunger, thirst, old age, and death. “And in your wrath we have been troubled,” that is, by fear of the future judgment because of our daily sins. Or: we have failed in weakness; we have been troubled by death. And rightly are we troubled. For you:

**VERSE 8.** “Have set our iniquities before your sight,” that is, you have observed them; you have carefully marked them all and not overlooked them. You have also set our “age,” that is, our life, “in the light of your countenance.” Or, as the Hebrew has it: “Our negligences in the light of your countenance.” That is, you have taken notice of everything [Col. 0552A] we have done. For all our hidden things lie open to your eyes. Iniquity is the act of sin; negligence is disobedience to a command. God notices and punishes both. Therefore we have been troubled. And therefore also:

**VERSE 9.** “For all our days have failed away, and in your anger we have failed.” At first, the days of humankind in paradise were eternal. Afterwards, some people’s days in this world were nearly a thousand years, as Methuselah’s; some were nine hundred, as Adam’s; some eight hundred or seven hundred. All these days failed away: for after the originally eternal days were lost, and afterwards life had been reduced from a thousand years, then from nine hundred, or six hundred, or three hundred, or even a hundred, human life was at last contracted to scarcely eighty or seventy years [Col. 0552B]. Thus we have failed from our former state in your anger. Moreover, in this exceedingly brief time we are filled with many miseries, crushed by many hardships and tribulations.

“Our years shall meditate like a spider”: that is, throughout our life we devise works like a spider’s—useless and of no avail—such as gathering riches and building great houses, which are lost through some slight event and, if not earlier, will be abandoned in death. Just as a spider is always running about, weaving a fragile web and easily losing the work it has completed with such effort, whether through a gust of wind, a small stone, or some other slight cause. This failure is in the soul.

**VERSE 10.** “The days of our years are seventy years in them”: that is, the days of our life are seventy years [Col. 0552C]. “But if in strengths,” that is, if we live longer with sound strength, our years will be eighty; “and their excess is toil and pain”: that is, whatever we live beyond these will be toil and pain. For though a person lives at every time amid toil and pain, nevertheless in old age whatever one does is done with great effort; and one is continually in pain from coughing, fevers, or some infirmity. These failures are in the body.

Moreover, since one person of seventy is weak in strength whereas another of eighty is still very vigorous, this number is better understood spiritually. For here it is multiplied through seven, eight, and ten, and is pregnant with marvelous mysteries [Col. 0552D]. Seven times ten is seventy, and eight times ten is eighty. Seven represents the Old Law because of Sabbath observance; in it the Ten Commandments show the twofold love through three and seven. Eight exalts the Gospel because of the eighth day of the Lord’s incarnation; its observers receive the tenfold number of life. Therefore we live in these years if through both laws we seek God as our refuge.

Likewise, seventy signifies the active life; eighty, the contemplative life. We are in the seventy years while we serve our neighbors in the active life. We move in the powerful eighty while in the contemplative life we associate through spiritual things. Whoever passes beyond these and seeks something more finds toil and pain: toil [Col. 0553A] in the present, and pain in the future. Seven and eight make fifteen; seventy and eighty are fifteen tens, making one hundred and fifty—the number of psalms contained in this book. This number signifies that, through the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer, having received the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, we must ascend from the valley of tears by the ladder of love, set in the heart with fifteen steps, to the eight beatitudes. There the hundredth sheep, in the fiftieth year of eternal jubilee, will receive the joy and gladness, or the glory, of the eternal inheritance. Those who strive beyond this number find toil and pain.

“We have failed in your anger”; therefore we are in toil and pain, because gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be corrected [Col. 0553B]. In the Law there was severity, which justice imposed on sinners; in the Gospel, gentleness, which grace grants to penitents. Therefore, because the gentleness of the Gospel has come upon the severity of the Law, we are corrected by adversities, labours, and pains, like sons by a loving father. For “whom the Lord loves he corrects; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). Thus he delivers us from the coming wrath, concerning which it is added:

**VERSES 11–12.** “Who knows the power of your anger?” That is, who knows the vengeance which you will exercise in judgment upon those who refused to receive discipline here and remained incorrigible in wickedness?
