Or who then, because of your fear, can number your wrath, when the heavens will pass away with great force and the elements will be dissolved by the heat of fire; when a fiery storm will be your chariot, which will burn your enemies round about; when heaven will be folded like a book and rolled up like a tent; when the pit of the abyss will be opened, and the devil, the torturer, will be present with all his torments?

To deliver us from this wrath, make your right hand known in such a way—that is, make your Son known to us through faith and love—that we may know his power and fear his future judgment. And thus make us wise, instructed in heart, so that we may possess fear and love: that we may fear our evils and love you for your own sake, since you are the supreme good.

Otherwise: this is drawn from the right hand of Moses, which he brought forth leprous from his bosom [Col. 0553D] (Exod. 4:6), signifying that Christ, coming forth from the bosom of the Father, appeared in the world as though leprous. “Make your right hand known”: that is, send the Son hidden in your bosom and thus make him known to us in the flesh. “And those bound in heart in wisdom.” Thus another translation reads. The prophets were bound in heart in wisdom, because their writings are certain bindings of meanings. Make them known to us, so that we may plainly understand what they foretold under shadow concerning your Son.

Otherwise: make your right hand, that is, Christ your arm, known in such a way that, imitating his sufferings, we may hope for heavenly things. And make known those instructed in heart in wisdom—that is, those taught in understanding by the Holy Spirit [Col. 0554A]—so that they may despise temporal things and seek heavenly things even through the adversities of the world. In this way Christ truly became known to the world: he granted this strength through the Holy Spirit to his worshippers, so that they would abandon earthly things and seek eternal things through sufferings. This the apostles and martyrs did, and monks and many faithful people still do, praying for others and saying:

**VERSE 13.** “Return, O Lord—how long? And be entreated concerning your servants.” You are justly angry with us; you afflict us with toil and pain; you do not make your right hand known. But return, O Lord, from your anger, for as long as pleases you—that is, upon whomsoever you will—and be open to entreaty, looking upon your servants. Another translation has: “A little while,” that is, turn away the pain for a little while, lest we fail under toil. But, set amid toil, they joyfully cry out in hope of future goods:

**VERSES 14–15.** “We have been filled in the morning with your mercy.” Morning is the beginning of eternity, shining forth after judgment. In it we shall be filled with your mercy: namely immortality, impassibility, and every blessedness. “And therefore we rejoiced and delighted in all our days.” Now, in the watch of the night, we spend our years in toil and pain; and prophecy has been kindled for us like a lamp in a dark place, until the day of eternity dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts—or rather Christ, the sun of righteousness [Col. 0554C]. Then, on that morning, the righteous will be filled with the good for which they now hunger and thirst. Those whose days now fail away will then see good days: eternal days refreshing them with exultation and delight in every good.

During those days without interruption by night, we shall rejoice in the body, which will shine like the sun, and delight in the soul, which will be equal to the angels. “We rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us”: that is, we shall always rejoice with the angels for the humiliation which you gave us here. “And we shall rejoice for the years in which we saw evils”: that is, the tribulations which you gave us for a time will become a cause of everlasting joy. While still placed in evil days, let us say:

**VERSE 16.** “Look upon your servants and upon your works”: that is, mercifully look upon those obedient to your commands, who through grace are your works. For “we are his workmanship,” not only in Adam but also “created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Eph. 2:10) [Col. 0554D]. “And direct their children,” that is, their followers, that they may be upright in heart.

**VERSE 17.** “And may the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us”: that is, may the sign of the cross of Christ our God be upon us, defending us from dangers to soul and body. Or, may the brightness of Christ’s divinity be in our mind. Or, may the holiness of his life be in our memory. “And direct the works of our hands over us,” so that through them we may seek not earthly things but those above. “And direct the work of our hands”: that is, direct whatever we do toward the end of love, so that at the end of life we may deserve to rejoice through all days in those eternal goods.

## PSALM 90. On the temptations of the devil.

[Col. 0555]

[Col. 0555A] “He who dwells in the help of the Most High,” etc. This psalm concerns the temptation of the faithful, who groan in this pilgrimage and do not remain here but seek the city to come. It is joined here to the preceding psalm in that the former tells those longing for their homeland that the Lord has become a refuge, whereas this one tells those groaning in temptation: “You have made the Most High your refuge.” That one discusses the brevity of those who serve here in warfare; this one treats the eternity of those who reign with the Lord.

This is the ninetieth psalm, which is ten multiplied nine times. Nine corresponds to the nine orders of angels; ten to the elect human beings who labour here in Christ’s vineyard for the denarius of life. This number signifies that the faithful who endure temptation here will be blessed, because they will receive the crown of life when they are equal to the angels. Its title is:

## PRAISE: A SONG OF DAVID.

That is: this hymn is the joyful praise of the faithful people against the temptations of the strong-handed one. Its subject is the fourfold temptation of the faithful. Its purpose is to instruct us to resist temptations. The words received are thought to derive from Moses’ address to the people, where he says that “one would pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight” (Deut. 32:30); that angels guarded him in all his ways; that they went before him in a pillar of cloud and fire; that he called upon God, who delivered him from tribulation and glorified him in the promised land [Col. 0555C].

It signifies Christ, from whose side a thousand and ten thousand at his right hand will fall; to whom angels ministered; whom the Father heard when he called for humankind; and whom he glorified at his right hand. It also signifies the faithful people who cry to the Lord in tribulation, and whom he hears, delivers from evils, and fills also with good things. After the people of God, through Moses praying on the mountain with outstretched hands and through Joshua son of Nun fighting, defeated Amalek, they endured many temptations. From these the Lord delivered them and led them into the promised land. So the Christian people, after defeating the devil through Christ praying on the height of the cross with outstretched hands and through the true Jesus fighting, endured many temptations in the world from persecutors [Col. 0555D] and heretics. From these the Lord delivered them and glorified them in heaven. Hence in the preceding psalm prayer is intended; in this one temptation is mentioned.

And Christ, the head of the faithful, after fasting endured in the wilderness the temptations from the devil, the head of the wicked; he patiently overcame them through Scripture and taught us to overcome them in the same manner [Col. 0556A]. For when a faithful person resolves to do something good, the devil immediately tempts him to turn aside; he must conquer him through the Lord.

This psalm is divided into four parts, because four temptations are noted in it. The first part is, “He who dwells in the help,” in which the dwelling of the faithful in God, and their deliverance from demons and evil people, are expressed. The second is, “With his shoulders,” in which God’s threefold defense and fourfold temptation are set forth. The third is, “A thousand shall fall at your side,” in which are shown the apostasy of hypocrites, Christ’s glory, the guardianship of angels, and the trampling-down of demons. The fourth is, “Because he has hoped in me,” in which are declared the deliverance and eternal glorification of the faithful. It is the voice of the Holy Spirit, under the person of teachers addressing the people as Moses did [Col. 0556B].

**VERSE 1.** “He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide in the protection of the God of heaven.” God my Father is called “Most High,” because among the three persons he is named first, not in dignity but in order; and because from him is the Son by generation and the Holy Spirit by procession. The Son is called “help,” because through him the Father aided the human race, as was said above: “I have placed help in one who is mighty.” The God of heaven is called omnipotent, in distinction from the gods of the Gentiles, of whom some were said to be gods of earth, others gods of sea or fire.

Angels too are called heavens by analogy: as the heavens are elevated above earth, so they are exalted above all bodily things, not in place [Col. 0556C] but in dignity, for they are unlocalized. Likewise the righteous are called heavens by analogy, because in spiritual things they are raised above carnal things as heaven above earth: their soul is heaven and their body earth. Holy Scripture is heaven: its lofty allegory is heaven, while history is earth. The God of this heaven is the Holy Spirit, who composed Holy Scripture; from this heaven he thunders in preaching, rains in teaching, flashes in miracles, and gleams in signs.

Therefore the faithful people, who dwell by faith in Christ, sent by the Most High Father as help to humankind, and who abide in the protection of the God of heaven—that is, in the illumination of the Holy Spirit, author of Holy Scripture, protecting them from temptation—shall:

**VERSE 2.** Say to the Lord with voice and heart: “You are my protector, [Col. 0556D] who received me as the prodigal son returning from the swine, washed me in the bath of baptism, and refreshed me at the banquet of your body. And you are my refuge, because I fled to you from idolatry; because you are my God, who created me by nature and recreated me by grace.”

Here the Trinity is expressed twice. In “help,” the Son is marked; in “Most High,” the Father; in “God of heaven,” the Holy Spirit [Col. 0557A]; and in “Lord,” unity is shown. Again, in “protector” the Son is indicated, who took humanity up into himself; in “refuge,” the Holy Spirit, to whom souls flee from sins; and in “my God,” the Father, who created all things. But do not let the transposed order of the persons trouble you, because all are equal.

Otherwise: he who dwells here in faith, doing good works aided by God, will abide hereafter in the protection of the God of heaven—that is, in the fortress of the heavenly city—and will say joyfully to the Lord: “You are my protector, who received me from the world into heaven; you are my refuge from the evils of the world, my sweet refreshment, my God.”

The speech of the teachers concerning deliverance from hunters and human harshness follows. Because God is a refuge, I will hope in him, not in myself or [Col. 0557B] in the children of men. Passing beyond myself, I shall go out to him in hope:

**VERSE 3.** “For he himself, not another, will deliver me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word.” The snares of hunters are the traps of demons, who hunt souls. Snares are cupidity, avarice, carnal desire, and the like, which entangle souls; from these the Lord delivers his own. The harsh word is the reproach of adversaries, the insult of enemies, the curse of neighbours. From this the Lord delivers the one who hopes in him, tempering every harsh thing for him with eternal sweetness.

The voice of the prophets to the believing people follows, recalling God’s threefold defenses and four kinds of temptation. The defenses [Col. 0557C] are God’s shoulders, wings, and shield; the temptations are nocturnal fear, the arrow flying by day, the business that walks in darkness, and the noonday demon.

**VERSE 4.** “With his shoulders he will overshadow you.” That is, O faithful people: carried upon his shoulders from the valley to the mountain, from Babylon to the Church, he will shelter you from the burning of vices by giving faith. Christ’s shoulders are his sufferings, in which, as on certain shoulders, he bore our weaknesses and infirmities. For when the good shepherd had sought with great labour for the lost sheep and at last found it among wolves, he carried it on his shoulders—that is, on his scapulae of suffering—back to the flock of angels. He overshadowed it when he refreshed the human race, rescued from the burning of hell, with the shaded coolness of paradise [Col. 0557D]. It follows:

“And under his wings you shall hope”: that is, sheltered under his protection, you will hope that he will give you future goods. He uses “feathers” for “wings.” Christ’s wings are the arms of the cross. He spread out these wings, gathered peoples, and bore them on the shoulders, that is, the scapulae, of his suffering. And just as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings from the seizure of kites, so he gathered flocks beneath the wings of the cross from the seizure of demons. The wings, indeed, are the two Testaments, or the two commandments of love, which raise souls to heaven. Or God’s feathers are the exhortations of the prophets, which lead the faithful to the heights of heaven.

**VERSE 5.** “His truth will surround you with a shield”: that is, his truth which is in you—namely faith, knowledge [Col. 0558A], and love—will surround you on every side like a shield. The shield is Christ’s humanity; his truth, his divinity. Truth will surround the faithful with a shield when divinity, through humanity, fortifies them against the devil’s temptations as against the missiles of enemies. Protected by this threefold defense, you will not fear the four temptations. The first is the hidden attack of demons; the second, the manifest disturbance caused by neighbours; the third, the deceitful persuasion of heretics; the fourth, the tribulation of persecutors. Of these it is added: “You will not fear the nocturnal terror.”

**VERSE 6.** “The arrow flying by day; the business walking in darkness; the assault and the noonday demon.” Nocturnal terror is the hidden suggestion of demons leading to the night of hell and the fear of torments. The arrow flying by day is trouble inflicted by neighbours, which wounds the heart like an arrow but swiftly passes by. The business walking in darkness is a scheme plotting evil in secret. By this is indicated the intricate doctrine of heretics, which wanders through darkened hearts in order to deceive. The assault is a hostile attack; the noonday demon is burning persecution incited by the devil. By noon, indeed, the hot cruelty of the impious is expressed; by the demon, their malicious envy [Col. 0558B].

Another translation has: “From ruin.” *Ruina* (“collapse”) is so called as though “returning to the depths.” Ruin is where a people falls together, whether in body or soul. In body, as in war; in soul, as in the theatre. In war, when the conflict is waged not for justice but for human glory and the people fall together, as happened to Apollonius with the Maccabees and to Catiline with the Romans. In the theatre, however, the people flock together for a cruel spectacle, as they did at the killing of the Lord, or when they assemble for theatrical entertainments [Col. 0558C].

Otherwise: two temptations are light and two are grave. One is light in secret, such as the suggestion of jesting; this is the nocturnal terror. Another is light openly, such as frequent conversation; this is the arrow flying by day. Likewise, one is grave in secret, such as the thought of fornication; this is the business walking in darkness. The other is grave openly, such as association with evil people; this is the noonday demon.

Some simple people believe that some demons are nocturnal, others diurnal, and others noonday demons: nocturnal demons, who can harm more by night than by day; diurnal demons, who can harm more by day than by night; noonday demons, who can harm more at noon than at other hours. But they are altogether mistaken. Demons can by no means harm more at night than by day, or more at noon than at another time [Col. 0558D]; they can harm only when people yield to their temptations. They can merely urge people toward evil; they cannot compel anyone to sin apart from that person’s own will. But, as has often been said, this book is spiritual and speaks spiritually to spiritual people through the likenesses conceived by the Spirit, because it speaks not to the outward but to the inward person.

The speech of the teachers to Christ follows, concerning those who yield to temptations [Col. 0559A] and depart from him by doing evil.

**VERSE 7.** “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” The side is called *latus* because it lies hidden beneath the arm. Those adhering more familiarly to rulers in counsel are called their “side.” Hence even today, when we request judges from an emperor or king, we say: “Send from your side,” that is, one of your trusted intimate friends. Christ’s side is the multitude of the righteous judging with him. A thousand fall from this side: namely the leaders of heretics, or evil prelates in the Church, who promise themselves that they will sit as judges with Christ. Judas clung as it were to Christ’s side when, as his intimate companion and a future judge of the world, he was hidden among the apostles. He fell from Christ’s side when he departed from Christ’s intimate apostles. Those who said, “This saying is hard” (John 6:61), fell from his side when they departed from him. Therefore prelates who, overcome by temptations, fall from Christ’s intimacy will not be judges at the judgment; but, fallen from his side—that is, from the choir of judges—they will incur punishment as persons judged [Col. 0559B].

“And ten thousand at your right hand.” Many reckon themselves righteous and expect to be placed at Christ’s right hand in judgment, such as heretics and false Christians, especially those called “the bearded,” who are proud of their long beard and loose clothing and despise all secular people, considering themselves better than most. These will fall from his right hand when, at judgment, he says to them: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I never knew you” (Luke 13:27). Hence follows: “But they shall not approach you,” because, while they place hope in their own merits, they do not resort to the remedies of repentance, and therefore will be far from the Lord. “A thousand” and “ten thousand” use a finite number for an infinite one, because innumerable persons will be found both among prelates and among subjects.

Another translation has: “But he shall not approach you,” namely any of those who deceitfully promise themselves the kingdom of God. Or, temptation will not approach you. For although Christ was tempted in every respect in likeness to us, yet without sin, all his temptation was outward and not inward: his mind was never moved to anger as ours is, nor did he feel any stirring of desire in the flesh. Hypocrites lay claim to the rewards of the righteous.

[Col. 0559D] **VERSE 8.** “Yet with your eyes you will consider”: that is, you will discern whom you should justly set at the right or at the left. God’s eyes are discernment and justice, by which he distinguishes hypocrites from true Christians and repays each with just rewards. Hence it is added: “And you will see the retribution of sinners.” They themselves, while living wickedly, promise themselves future goods; but you see what punishments will be repaid for their deeds.

These things can also be understood of the people who will not fear nocturnal terror and the other things that follow. “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” By the side the left is understood; by the left, adversity; by the right, prosperity. A thousand fall at your side when many who attack you through adversities are defeated and withdraw. Ten thousand fall at your right hand [Col. 0560A]: those who attack you through prosperities will be defeated by you. That he places the greater number on the right indicates that temptations in prosperity are greater than those in adversity. “But it shall not approach you,” in the sense of consent leading to action. “Yet with your eyes you will consider”: that is, with reason you will understand that it is dishonourable to be overcome in temptations and shameful to sin. “And you will see the retribution of sinners”: that is, in your mind you will foresee the future punishments of sinners.

The voice of the faithful people follows, commending their hope and Christ’s glory.

**VERSE 9.** “For you, O Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge.” The sinful people will not approach you; but I, who do not yield to temptations, approach you in conduct and life, because [Col. 0560B] you, O Lord, are my hope; their hope is earthly. Because you, Lord, have made the Most High your refuge—that is, you have transferred assumed humanity to the right hand of the Father. You are my hope, so that I too, as your body, may reach you, my head. And because you sit on high:

**VERSE 10.** “No evil will approach you”: namely, no evil person or adversity will reach you. “And no scourge will approach your tent”: that is, no misfortune will harm your body. The guardianship of angels follows. No evil will touch you:

**VERSES 11–12.** “For he has commanded his angels concerning you”—namely that Most High—“to guard you in all your ways,” that is, to minister to you in all things. “They will bear you in their hands”: that is, they will be present with you in your works [Col. 0560C], “lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone,” that is, lest you sin against the Law. The foot of the mind is its affection. The Law, however, was written on tablets of stone. He strikes his foot against a stone who disregards the Law written on stone. There can be no doubt that angels guarded the Lord’s human nature in all his ways and continually supported him in his activity; to him, as their Lord, they ministered, as it is written (Matt. 4:11). Hence the devil too, when he tempted him, cited this passage as testimony. Concerning the devil’s trampling-down it is added:

**VERSE 13.** “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample down the lion and the dragon.” The asp is the devil when he strikes secretly; the basilisk when he openly spreads poisons; the lion when he persecutes the innocent; the dragon when he devours the negligent. He tempted the Lord as a dragon; he attacked him in the Passion as a lion; but, trampled by him, he fled. By the four kinds of beasts are signified four classes of demons: namely principalities and powers, rulers of darkness, and spiritual forces of the wickedness of vices [Col. 0560D]. Thus all were trampled down by Christ, beneath whose feet they cried: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matt. 8:29). He also granted his disciples power to trample them down, saying: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and upon all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19). Hence it is again written: “God will crush Satan beneath your feet” (Rom. 16:20).

[Col. 0561A] Alternatively: the asp is a kind of serpent that does not tolerate the enchanter, but stops its ears with its tail so as not to hear him; its venom is so powerful that it kills before it can be felt. The basilisk, called in Latin the *regulus* (“little king”), destroys every living creature by its breath, but is itself killed by the weasel. The lion is the strongest of beasts; the dragon the largest of serpents, enemy of the chaste animal, the elephant. The cause of this enmity is that the dragon’s venom boils with the greatest heat, whereas the elephant’s blood is exceedingly cold. Therefore the dragon wishes to temper its heat with the elephant’s cold blood. The asp, killing by venom, is death slaughtering all things. The basilisk, destroying all things by its breath, is sin killing souls. The lion, terrifying all beasts, is Antichrist, [Col. 0561B] striking terror into all nations. The dragon, enemy of the chaste animal, is the devil, enemy of the Son of the Virgin. Christ therefore walked upon the asp and basilisk when he overcame sin and death; he will trample down the lion and dragon when, at the judgment, he casts Antichrist and the devil into the lake of fire.

This whole passage may also be referred to the people victorious over vices, who say to God: “I reject earthly things; from you I hope for heavenly things: for you are my hope, O Lord.” The divine voice answers them: “You have made the Most High your refuge.” Therefore evil, which has been prepared for the wicked, shall not approach you. And the scourge—that is, vengeance—shall not come near you, where you shall be in the joy of [Col. 0561C] your Lord. “For he has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may guard you in all your ways.” There is no doubt that every righteous person, both in prosperity and adversity, is guarded by God’s angels, as it is written: “Their angels always behold the face of my Father” (Matt. 18:10). And elsewhere: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:14). “They shall bear you up in their hands,” that is, they shall assist you in good works, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone—that is, lest you sin against Christ’s law. For Christ is “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence” (Rom. 9:33), against whom the Jews stumbled when, building upon sins, they rejected him. He strikes his foot against this stone who despises love [Col. 0561D] of God and of neighbour. Whoever falls upon this stone shall be broken, because whoever does not believe in Christ shall be cut off from the Church. But upon whomever it falls, it shall crush him: that is, whomever it finds in sins, it shall condemn at the judgment.

Angels are called messengers, and are understood to mean the teachers of the Church, [Col. 0562A] who announce heavenly things to God’s people. God commanded these teachers to guard the faithful in all their ways by preaching good conduct, and to bear them in their hands when they provide them an example of good action, lest they stumble against the Lord’s law, written upon stone. Therefore you, O people guarded by angels, shall walk upon the asp and basilisk—that is, you shall overcome sins and vices that bring about death; and you shall trample down the lion and dragon—that is, the devil raging openly in his members or secretly suggesting evil things.

God’s promise follows. Above it was said, “I shall hope in him”; therefore he now says:

**VERSE 14.** “Because he shall hope [Vulgate: *has hoped*] in me, I shall deliver him from evils; I shall protect him in good things, because he has known my name,” which is Lord. [Col. 0562B] He has made himself my servant by acting well; in these good things I shall protect him, preserving his rewards.

**VERSE 15.** “He shall cry to me,” or, as another translation has it, “He shall call upon me”—understand, in temptation—“and I shall hear him,” protecting him from overthrow. “I am with him in tribulation,” as I was with Joseph, lest he fail; and at last I shall deliver him from every disturbance and glorify him with immortality and impassibility.

**VERSE 16.** “With length of days I shall satisfy him,” that is, with long and unfailing life; “and I shall show him my salvation,” that is, I shall show him my Son as he is, equal to me, so that he may always see him face to face. Likewise the Son himself promised his lovers: “He who loves me, I shall love him, and [Col. 0562C] I shall manifest myself to him” (John 14:21).

For this reason the Church sings this psalm at Compline: that angels may guard her from the terror of the night.

Observe the order of the ninth decade, corresponding to the nine orders of angels. The first psalm concerns the sons of God made gods and established as heirs of God’s kingdom; the second, the invaders of God’s inheritance, disinherited from that inheritance; the third, the house of God and its inhabitants praising God for ever; the fourth, the thanksgiving and joy of those who have deserved to enjoy peace and glory; the fifth, the prayer of those who remain here in exile; the sixth, the glorious city of God and its citizens rejoicing therein; the seventh, the narrow gate of this city, through which the King of Glory himself entered into his glory and showed his soldiers how to enter through it; the eighth, the immeasurable glory of the King and the joy of his soldiers; the ninth, the shortness of those fighting here; the tenth, the eternity of those reigning there.

## PSALM XCI. On the Praise of God’s Works

[Col. 0561]

[Col. 0561D] “It is good to give thanks to the Lord,” etc. The Holy Spirit begins the tenth decade with praise and rest, [Col. 0562D] because in the rest of eternal praise the denarius of life shall be given to the saints. The preceding decade ends in [Col. 0563A] the promise of eternity; this one begins in confession of divine praise. Its title is:

**(VERSE 1.) A PSALM OF A SONG FOR THE SABBATH DAY.**

That is: in this hymn are contained the work and the reward, which shall be future rest and the knowledge of God. Sabbath is called “rest,” because on that day God rested from all the works which he created during six days. On this day Christ also rested in the tomb from all the works which he performed in the world; he shall give rest to our souls in the heavenly kingdom when our bodies have rested in the tomb. By “psalm” is understood the activity of the active life; by “song,” the rejoicing of the contemplative life; by “day,” the brightness of eternal life; and by “Sabbath,” perpetual rest. The sense is: this psalm [Col. 0563B] sings that the righteous shall receive everlasting rest in eternal brightness for the praise of God and for the work of this life.

It is placed here as the ninety-first in order. In ninety, the Trinity occurs three times; in the unit, unity is shown. This number signifies that the reward of the saints shall be God himself, who is worshipped as Three and One.

The subject of the psalm is the praise of God’s works. Note that rest is written in the title and God’s work in the text of the psalm, because rest shall be given for work. Its purpose is to exhort us to good action, so that we may have rest from our works after this age. Its words seem to have been taken from Moses, [Col. 0563C] to whom God showed his mighty works on the mountain, and who also wrote them down. It signifies the Church, to whom God made his wonderful works known and whose understanding he opened, that she might understand the Scriptures.

It is divided into three parts, because the Church is divided into three orders: virgins, married persons, and widows. The first part is, “It is good to give thanks,” in which God’s work is commended; the second, “When sinners have sprung up,” in which the destruction of the wicked is treated; the third, “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree,” in which the splendour of the righteous is recalled. It is the voice of the Church praising God for his wonderful work.

**VERSE 2.** “It is good to give thanks to the Lord, and to sing psalms to your name, O Most High.” At the beginning of this praise the Trinity is set forth: in “Lord,” the Holy Spirit; in “your name,” the Son; and in “Most High,” the Father is expressed. Yet the order among the persons is often changed so that their equality may be understood. Confession belongs to contemplation; psalmody to action. It is good—that is, most useful—in the contemplative life to give thanks to the Lord, that is, to praise God; and in the active life to sing psalms to the name of the Most High, that is, to perform a good work in honour of God’s name, doing so with this intention:

**VERSE 3.** “To proclaim your mercy in the morning, through the night.” Note that throughout almost this whole book mercy and truth are joined, because through God’s mercy the world is saved; through his truth it shall be judged. By “morning” prosperity is understood; by “night,” adversity. It is therefore good in prosperity [Col. 0564A] to announce to others God’s mercy: how he saved the world, how he restored fallen humanity, how mercifully he endures our errors, and how kindly he forgives sins to those who turn back. And in adversity it is good to announce to neighbours God’s truth, by which he shall yet judge the world, assigning rewards to the righteous and punishments to the unrighteous; and to proclaim that he here chastens his own mercifully by adversities, so that there he may receive them as sons into their inheritance. It is good to sing these things

**VERSE 4.** “Upon a ten-stringed instrument, upon the psaltery, with a song upon the harp”: that is, in the performance of the law, which consists of the ten commandments as though stretched across ten strings; and this not with sadness, but with humility, cheerfulness, and mortification of the flesh. The psaltery, sounding from above, is heavenly [Col. 0564B] teaching, which commands us to do good works. This psaltery has ten strings because of the Decalogue of the law. Note that this is the tenth decade, which sounds sweetly as though it were the tenth string. The harp, which gives sound from below, is the chastisement of the flesh, singing praise to Christ. Thus the psaltery denotes the divine work of those living the contemplative life; the harp, the distinction of those serving in the active life. This song ought to be sung, because:

**VERSE 5.** “You have delighted me, O Lord, in your creation, and I shall exult in the works of your hands.” By “creation” is understood every invisible creature, such as angels and powers; by “works,” every visible creature, such as heaven, earth, and human beings. Or by God’s “creation” is understood Christ’s incarnation; by the works of his hands, the restoration of humanity through Christ’s mighty deeds.

Alternatively: God’s creation is that a human being is justified from injustice, believes Christ to be God and man, hopes for and loves heavenly things; the works of his hands are that through these good things he works diligently. Or creation is the Church, God’s new creature; the works of Christ’s hands are his miracles. In all these things there is great delight for one who considers them, and immense exultation for the faithful soul. Therefore, rejoicing in wonder, it cries:

**VERSE 6.** “How greatly magnified are your works, O Lord!” Truly, God’s works are to be proclaimed as exceedingly magnificent: not only that he created the heavenly orders of angels, the lights and gems of heaven, the sea, lands, [Col. 0564D] human beings, beasts, birds, and fish; but also that he created certain tiny things [perhaps *minuscule*], such as bees and ants, flies and gnats; and that he daily performs marvellous and astounding acts, bringing forth from small seeds such crops and enormous trees. Hence follows: “Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep.” They are indeed exceedingly deep: he brought all things forth from nothing, and arranged them into so many kinds of things, and those kinds into so many species. Yet these works of God are also wonderful: the wicked flourish here, while the righteous are oppressed; the children of good persons often die unregenerate, while the children of unbelievers are frequently reborn and led into joys. Truly your thoughts are deep, and your judgments are a great abyss.

**VERSE 7.** “The foolish man shall not know, nor shall the fool [Col. 0565A] understand these things.” The unwise person is one empty of wisdom but full of cunning. The fool, however, is one who understands neither divine nor human matters. Unwisdom belongs to clerics; folly to laypeople. The unwise person shall not know these judgments, nor shall the fool understand them.

**VERSE 8.** “When sinners spring up like grass”—that is, when they flourish in prosperity like the flower of grass, which quickly falls—and when all who work iniquity appear glorious and famous on earth, it is “that they may perish for ever and ever,” that is, perish eternally. The wicked flourish here like grass, which is here today and tomorrow cast into the oven.

**VERSES 9–10.** “But you, O Lord, are the Most High for ever”—understand, you shall remain. “For behold, your enemies, O Lord,” the Jews; “for behold, your enemies,” the pagans, “shall perish”; and all heretics and evil Catholics, who work iniquity, shall be scattered, like chaff from grain by the winnowing-fan [manuscript: *ventilantibus*, “those winnowing”] of righteous judgment.

**VERSE 11.** And when they have been delivered to unquenchable fire, then “my horn shall be exalted like that of a unicorn,” that is, the strength which I possessed against vices, [and] I shall be crowned in Christ’s kingdom. For by “horn” strength or kingdom is understood. The unicorn is an untameable beast having one horn; to capture it, a virgin is placed before it, and, reclining in her lap, it is captured. Christ was like a unicorn, unconquerable by demons; his one horn is the eternal kingdom, which is one and must be weighed or considered. He reclined [Col. 0565C] in the lap of his virgin mother, and was captured and killed by the Jews. Therefore, as his kingdom is exalted, so the glory of my kingdom shall be raised on high. “And my old age shall be in abundant mercy,” that is, my final state after death shall be in abundant mercy.

The Church has its ages. Its infancy was the time before the Flood, when Abel and the other righteous persons flourished; its childhood was Abraham’s time, when the patriarchs flourished; its adolescence was Moses’ time, when the fathers were joined to the law; its youth was David’s time, when the prophets brought forth writings; its maturity was Christ’s time, when the apostles and martyrs bore the greatest fruit; its old age is the time of Antichrist, when the Jewish people, joined to the multitude of the faithful, shall bear abundant fruit, for which it shall soon receive a hundredfold [Col. 0565D] return.

**VERSE 12.** “And then my eye looked down and looked upon my enemies”: that is, I, the Church, then placed at your right hand, shall see at your left hand, in punishments, [Col. 0566A] all my adversaries and persecutors, now rising against me, and the heretics or Jews acting maliciously against me—that is, doing malicious things. “My ear heard” them groaning and saying: “These are those whom we once held in derision and as an example of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end dishonourable. Behold how they are counted among the sons of God” (Wisdom 5:3–4)—that is, among the angels! The wicked shall wither like grass.

**VERSE 13.** “But the righteous shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall multiply like a cedar of Lebanon.” The palm tree is thorny below, very beautiful above, and always flourishing. So too the multitude of the righteous is bristling here on earth with tribulations, but above is beautiful with great splendour [Col. 0566B] and flourishes with everlasting glory. The palm is called, as it were, *pacis alma* (“nourishing of peace”), because it is an emblem of peace and victory. It was formerly given to victors, that they might always flourish in honours. Hence John saw Christ’s soldiers victorious over their enemies, with palms in their hands. The cedar is a very tall, decay-proof tree on Mount Lebanon, abundant in branches. So the Church, now white in faith—for this is the meaning of “Lebanon”—lofty in contemplation, incorruptible in works, and abundant in virtues, shall in the future be beautiful in glory and abundant in gifts of body and soul: in the body, immortality, impassibility, agility, and ease; in the soul, wisdom and love.

The Church is compared to a tree because the primitive Church rose up as though it were a root, and the Church from the Gentiles as though it were a trunk; it produced the fruit of righteousness in its season, and its branches are all the elect, who are

**VERSE 14.** “Planted in the house of the Lord”: that is, rooted in God’s Church by faith and action, they shall finally flourish in the courts of our God; that is, in the likeness of angels they shall shine with heavenly glory. Or the house of the Lord is the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the fellowship of all the elect in the vision of God. The courts of God are the various dwelling places, that is, the various rewards according to merits.

**VERSES 15–16.** “They shall still multiply in fruitful old age,” these branches—that is, the saints shall be innumerable at the end of the age. And they shall be patient in suffering when they endure the persecution of Antichrist, in order that they may announce this [Col. 0566D] to others: “For the Lord our God is upright,” who grants eternal joys to those who suffer persecution for righteousness; “and there is no iniquity in him,” who shall give eternal punishments to persecutors and all the ungodly.

## PSALM XCII. On the Foundation of the Church

[Col. 0565]

[Col. 0565D] “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with majesty,” etc. The preceding psalm sang generally of God’s works; this one sings specifically of the earth. The former prefigured those works which [Col. 0566D] Christ performed before the Passion; the latter, those which he performed after the Resurrection. This psalm places its calculation in the fortieth position and expounds to us a great mystery. [Col. 0567A] For there are ninety, which are seven times twelve plus nine. Seven denotes eternal rest; twelve, apostolic teaching; nine, the fellowship of angels. Therefore this number signifies that the elect are brought through the teaching of the apostles to eternal rest and equality with angels. The psalm’s title is:

**A PRAISE OF A SONG [Note: [Col. 0567D] The Vulgate adds: “Of David himself.”] OF DAVID, ON THE DAY BEFORE THE SABBATH, WHEN THE EARTH WAS FOUNDED.**

On the third day the earth is read to have been made. But the day before the Sabbath is the sixth day. Hence it is clear that this title is to be understood not of the earth but of the Church. On the sixth day humanity was made, and in the sixth age redeemed; in that age the Church, the land of the living, was founded. This age is like the day before the Sabbath, that is, before the [Col. 0567B] future rest after this age. From Adam to Christ there was, as it were, night, because ignorance and death reigned. The sixth age is like a day, in which the true light appeared, preceding the Sabbath—that is, eternal rest. On that day he established the earth, that is, the Church, by the Holy Spirit, preparing it for perpetual rest. Or the day before the Sabbath was the Preparation, when the earth—that is, the Church fashioned from Christ’s side—was founded. Therefore the praise of this song is sung to David, that is, to Christ, desired by angels, for the work which he performed before the Sabbath—that is, in the time before the joy of future rest—when the earth, namely the Church, was founded by him.

The subject is the instruction of God’s house, which is the Church. [Col. 0567C] Its purpose is that we may be adorned with virtue, if we wish to enter the rest of the Lord’s house. The words are transferred from the construction of the Temple or tabernacle, and signify the building up of the Church, God’s house. It is varied through seven topics of demonstrative argument. The first topic is from beauty; the second, from strength; the third, from works; the fourth, from power; the fifth, from the praises of the whole universe; the sixth, from the truth of the sayings; the seventh, from the praise of the house itself, which house is supported by seven columns and illuminated by seven lamps. The Jews rejected him, saying: “We will not have this man to reign over us” (Luke 19:14). It is the voice of the Church praising God for her foundation.

**VERSE 1.** The Lord himself reigned from the wood, because [Col. 0567D] he overcame the devil through the cross. Therefore, death having been conquered, he reigns over all things. Nor are the insignia lacking; for “he has clothed himself with majesty,” that is, he clothed himself in the apostles as in a diadem and purple robe. “He has clothed himself with strength” when he surrounded himself with the army of martyrs; and he girded himself, as it were with arms, with the preaching of confessors.

Another translation has: “He girded himself with power,” because surrounded by the angelic multitude he returned to the Father; but first he established the Church. “For he established the world, which shall not be moved.” By “earth” is understood the Church first founded in Judaea; by “world,” the Church of the Gentiles established throughout the whole world. Christ founded it by the Holy Spirit [Col. 0568A] and made it firm; before the Passion he established it as earth by preaching. This is what is written in the title: “When the earth was founded.” Christ is the wise architect, both God and man. Inasmuch as he is God, he created for the Father in heaven an eternal city not made with hands; and inasmuch as he is man, he built for him on earth a house of living stones. He founded this house when he chose the apostles, instituted baptism, and taught the Gospel of the kingdom. But in the Passion of the builder, its foundations were shaken by the great storm of Jewish persecution. Meanwhile, he himself fell asleep in the little boat of the cross; awakening from death, he calmed the waves of disturbance, made firm the shaken house, ascended into heaven, and sent the Holy Spirit. He so firmly established the founded earth and world [Col. 0568B] that it shall no longer be moved, until the house is transferred into the city. Now he turns his words to Christ himself.

**VERSE 2.** “Your throne has been prepared from then.” Christ’s throne, in the house founded by faith and made firm by love, is the purity of the perfect, in whom the King and Judge sits, governs the house, and drives enemies away from it. This throne was prepared from then—that is, adorned with virtues—from the time when the house or earth was founded by the Holy Spirit. But because some thought that Christ began from the Virgin and had not existed before, it is added: “You are from everlasting.” In Hebrew it reads: “Your throne is firm from then; from eternity you are.” It does not say, “You were,” because eternity has no “was” or “will be,” but is eternal being. [Col. 0568C] After “your throne has been prepared”:

**VERSE 3.** “The rivers lifted up, O Lord; the rivers lifted up their voice.” This is drawn from the rivers of Paradise. In Paradise is a spring from which four rivers flow, watering the whole Paradise. Paradise is the Church; the spring is Christ; the rivers are the Evangelists or apostles. The fountain of life, the source of rivers, lifted up his voice when he said: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). The rivers flowing from him lifted up their voice when Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice: “Repent, and be converted, and be baptized, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3:19). “Rivers” is said twice because of the Evangelists and apostles, or because of teachers taken from each people. A river came from that [Col. 0568D] spring with great force and filled those rivers when the Spirit, like a torrent, filled the apostles. From this torrent those rivers overflowed and, with uplifted voice, watered the whole world.

But against those divine rivers other, diabolical rivers lifted up waves—or “poured forth whirlpools,” as another translation has it—namely philosophers and heretics with their heresies, or rulers with their persecutions, in order to carry believers away or overwhelm those who resisted. And this:

**VERSE 4.** “From the voices of many waters,” that is, because of the voices of many preachings. This is drawn from the Flood, when rivers of many waters overflowed and submerged everything. Here heresies [Col. 0569A] and persecutions raged exceedingly and threw everything into confusion. Then the swellings of the sea became marvellous: that is, the threats and terrors of paganism, rising like storms against the teaching of the apostles and opposing it with extraordinary tortures. The comparison is with the sea, which, stirred by winds, raises storms. So the rulers of the nations, stirred by the persuasions of demons, aroused persecution against the preachers. Yet they accomplished nothing, because the Lord, wonderful on high, restrained the waves foaming with cruelty and subjected kings and powers to faith. Thus:

**VERSE 5.** “Your testimonies”—namely, the preachings of the apostles testifying that you are God—“have become exceedingly credible” through the signs and miracles that followed. Therefore holiness befits your house, O Lord: your house [Col. 0569B] founded by you and adorned by the apostles with holy instruction, “for length of days,” that is, for eternity. All the righteous sanctify this house, dedicating themselves to God as a temple by holy habits and acts. This holiness shall remain for length of days, because it makes them reign in God’s house—that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem—for ever. Therefore the Church sings this psalm at Lauds on Sundays and feast days, because Christ rose in the morning and, reigning throughout the world, established the Church as his throne or house; and the saints shall rise on the last morning and reign with him for ever.

This psalm may also be referred to Christ’s incarnation. The Lord, who reigned among the Hebrews, “clothed himself with majesty”: that is, he clothed himself in human flesh, clean from every defilement, as in a breastplate. The Lord clothed himself with strength, in order to bind the strong man. And he girded himself with power as with arms, [Col. 0570A] in order to fight his adversaries. “For he established the world.” The earth is the Virgin Mary; the world is the Lord’s body taken from the Virgin, perfected in virtues. God made this world firm when he united divinity to flesh, so that God and man might be one person. It shall not be moved from good to evil. “Your throne, O God, was prepared from then.” God’s throne was the humanity in which he sat while reconciling the world to himself. This throne was prepared from the time when it was conceived in the womb by the Holy Spirit. But you, O Christ, did not then begin, for you are God from everlasting.

“The rivers lifted up, O Lord; the rivers lifted up their voice”: that is, after you, the fountain of life, came up from the River Jordan, the apostles filled by you preached throughout all Judaea that you are God born of a virgin. “The rivers lifted up their waves from the voices of many waters”: that is, the scribes and Pharisees, filled from the fountain of the law, opposed them and denied that you are God. “The marvellous swellings of the sea” are the persecutions of the pagan people, namely Pilate and his soldiers, who killed the innocent Christ. “Wonderful on high” means the Lord on the cross, who prayed for his crucifiers, though he could have plunged them into the abyss with one word. Your testimonies, set forth from the law and prophets, became exceedingly credible when you appeared in flesh among human beings and underwent death for human beings, as you had foretold through them. Holiness befits your house—namely, the body in which you dwelt among us—for length of days, O Lord, because [Col. 0570C] you raised that holy body into heaven, where it shall reign for ever.

## PSALM XCIII. On the Oppressors of the Church

[Col. 0569]

[Col. 0569D] “The Lord God of vengeances,” etc. This psalm is directed against those who attack the house of God, founded by him, and oppress his inheritance by perverse conduct. Its title is:

**A PRAISE OF A SONG [Note: [Col. 0569D] Vulgate: “A Psalm of David himself,” etc.] OF DAVID, ON THE FOURTH DAY OF THE SABBATH.**

The fourth day of the Sabbath is Wednesday, on which the lights of heaven were created. Heaven is the Church, whose lights are teachers shining amid a crooked and perverse nation. In the fourth age of the world, as on the fourth day of the Sabbath, the prophets shone like stars in the night of ignorance, but did not drive away the darkness. Then the apostles shone like sun and moon, and drove the darkness far away. After them other teachers—Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and very many others—illuminated the house of God with great brilliance. Therefore the praise of this song is sung to David, Christ, “strong of hand and desirable,” to signify the thing which was made [Col. 0570D] on the fourth day of the Sabbath: namely, the lights of heaven, that is, the teachers of the Church.

Note that the preceding psalm concerned the founded earth and the rivers by which it was watered; this one, the lights by which it was illuminated. That one concerned the builders of God’s house; this one, its defenders. That one, persecutors; this one, blasphemers of the Church. That one, the King’s kingdom; this one, his judgment.

Alternatively: this praise of song belongs to David—that is, the faithful people—which exists on the fourth day of the Sabbath, that is, in observance of both Testaments. The fourth day of the Sabbath is in the middle of the week, with three preceding days and three following days. By the three preceding days is understood the Old Testament, in which were those who possessed faith in the Trinity. By the three following days is understood the New Testament, in which are those who [Col. 0571A] likewise believe in the Trinity. Therefore Christians are on the fourth day of the Sabbath—that is, in the middle of the two Testaments—because they observe both: the Old according to its signification, the New according to its truth. This is also indicated by the number itself. For one, two, three, and four make ten, because the four Gospels are contained in the Decalogue of the law, and the ten commandments are fulfilled in the four Gospels. Moreover, four arranged angularly form the shape of a cross; likewise the letter X, which denotes ten in numerals, displays the shape of a cross, because both the old and the new law are fulfilled through the Crucified One. Therefore numbers, letters, and the form of the world proclaim him, and all things worship him.

This psalm is the ninety-third, which is nine times ten and three. The ten denotes life’s reward; nine, fellowship with angels; three, the vision of the Trinity. [Col. 0571B] This number therefore signifies that the illuminators and defenders of God’s house shall possess reward, equality with angels, and the vision of the Trinity, when those who are learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many unto righteousness as stars unto everlasting eternities. Hence these three psalms are entitled by the Sabbath, because the elect are proclaimed as destined to possess eternal rest in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The subject of the psalm is the oppression of the Church by importunate people. Many think that God does not know human sins because he does not punish them at once, and they oppress with impunity the part of Christians that has been condemned. The purpose of this psalm is therefore to show both that God [Col. 0571C] knows hidden things and that he does not yet punish sinners, and that he swiftly comes to the aid of the oppressed. Its words are taken partly from the song of Moses, where he says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. 32:35); and elsewhere, “A nation without counsel and without prudence” (ibid., v. 28). They are taken partly from the history in which Gentile peoples humbled the Lord’s people and oppressed his inheritance. It signifies that vengeance against the foolish and unwise belongs to Christ; that persecutors humbled the Christian people and heretics oppressed God’s inheritance; and that at the judgment the Lord shall repay vengeance upon the enemies of the Church and be merciful to his people.

It is divided into three parts, because God’s house is strengthened by faith, hope, [Col. 0571D] and charity. The first part is, “The God of vengeances,” in which it is written how adversaries attack God’s house. The second is, “Understand, you foolish,” in which it is stated how the Holy Spirit resists them with severe rebukes, while strengthening the inhabitants with gentle consolations. The third is, “Who shall rise up for me?” in which mention is made of the battle of God’s people against those who work iniquity, who finally glory in victory, saying: “The Lord has become my refuge, and my God my helper; he shall repay my enemies their iniquity, and in their malice shall destroy them.” It is the voice of teachers arming the faithful people against blasphemers.

**VERSE 1.** “The God of vengeances, the Lord; the God of vengeances has acted freely.” At the outset the Trinity is expressed when vengeance [Col. 0572A] for the Church is ascribed: in “God,” the Father; in “Lord,” the Son; and in “God,” the Holy Spirit are understood. This God shall avenge the Church upon her adversaries. For he is the God of vengeances, the creator of all things, who said: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay them.” And because he is Lord of all, in the future he shall punish the guilt of the servants of his adversaries. And because the wicked exceedingly afflict the righteous, they cry to one another:

**VERSE 2.** “Exalt yourself”—that is, appear in your majesty—“you who judge the earth,” that is, who shall judge all inhabitants of the earth. “Render recompense to the proud,” that is, to those who pride themselves on their evils; and take vengeance on those who crucified you and daily torment us. And because those sinning with impunity blaspheme God, as though he does not know human deeds because he does not punish them immediately, [Col. 0572B] those afflicted by them cry out:

**VERSE 3.** “How long shall sinners, O Lord, how long shall sinners glory?” That is: how long do you defer judgment? How long do you allow the ungodly to glory in their evil deeds, and delay avenging your injury and ours? Behold, you see that they not only glory in wickedness, but also:

**VERSE 4.** “They utter”—that is, announce to others—“and speak iniquity.” All who work injustice speak, so that others may imitate them. That is, they not only do evil, but also draw others into consenting to evil, now by counsel and now by insult; and they wish to be praised for this and considered great because of it. What iniquity do they speak? That:

**VERSE 5.** “They have humbled your people, O Lord.” [Col. 0572C] What injustice, indeed, do they speak? That “they have afflicted your inheritance.” Pagans often boasted to their companions how they had subjected the Christian people to contempt through various tortures, and how they had oppressed the Church, God’s inheritance, by outlawing it, destroying it, carrying it into captivity, insulting it, and blaspheming it. Nor was this enough; further:

**VERSE 6.** “They have slain the widow and the stranger, and murdered the fatherless,” whose advocate you are. This happened literally among both peoples: they killed them in order to possess their goods, because they had no help.

**VERSE 7.** “And they said: The Lord shall not see what we do, nor shall the God of Jacob understand what we think.” [Col. 0572D] The God of Jacob is called the God of the Christian people, which is set above the Jews just as Jacob was set above Esau. There are also many in the Church who think that God is ignorant of such matters because he does not punish them. The Holy Spirit rebukes them, saying:

**VERSE 8.** “Understand, you unwise among the people”: that is, you unlearned clerics among God’s people, perceive that these things happen by God’s providence and not by chance, as you say; “and you fools, become wise at last”: that is, you brutish laypeople, know that all things proceed from God’s judgment and do not happen accidentally, as you suppose. Understand and be wise concerning what I say:

VERS. 9–10. He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? Must one suppose that he who gave hearing to others does not himself hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not observe? [Col. 0573A] Must one suppose that he who gave sight does not himself see? Or he who rebukes the nations through his Scriptures, and chastens them in this life by imposing penance, will he not himself rebuke in the future—that is, will he not punish sinners? Or he who teaches humanity knowledge, by giving understanding of good and evil, does he not himself know human deeds? Rather, he hears and sees, and at last will rebuke, and possesses knowledge. For unless this were so, he could never give what he did not possess. He rebukes some—the learned—by giving them the Scripture itself to read; others, that is, the laity, he rebukes through those skilled in the Scriptures.

VERS. 11. The Lord knows not only deeds but also the thoughts of human beings, because they are vain; that is, he knows not only good thoughts but vain ones as well. Having refuted blasphemers, fools, and senseless persons, he comforts the understanding [Col. 0573B] and the wise.

VERS. 12. Blessed is the person whom you instruct, O Lord, by scourging him here with tribulations, and whom you teach from your law to understand this: that those who endure scourges here will be blessed in the future, while wretched are those whom no adversities chastise. Blessed is the person whom you scourge here, O Lord.

VERS. 13. That you may give him relief from evil days; that is, that you may grant him gentle refreshment in the future, in good days, after he has endured hardships here in evil days. He calls them evil days because evil things are done in them; these will cease when in the future you grant relief to the chastised person. Until a pit is dug for the sinner: that is, until he is led down into the precipice of death, and, when Christ’s pit of burial is dug, [Col. 0573C] his soul is buried in hell like that of the rich man. Thus not fools, but those taught by God’s law, understand that persons instructed by scourges will find rest for their souls; sinners, however, glorying in their sins, will fall into the deep pit of the abyss.

VERS. 14–15. For the Lord will not reject his people from the kingdom at the judgment—those whom here, as a loving Father, he instructed by scourges for the inheritance; and he will not abandon this inheritance, namely, his people, in tribulation—until justice is turned into judgment; that is, until Christ the just judge turns from patience to judgment, to render to each according to his works. Or, until the justice of those who have been instructed is turned into judgment, so that those who were oppressed here may be judges there. And who are beside it? That is, who will reign [Col. 0573D] with that justice? All the upright in heart: that is, all who will what God wills. Those are not upright in heart who either murmur at scourges or blaspheme God for his judgments, as though he were unjust in instructing the just here by scourges and not punishing the unjust. These will not reign with justice, but will fall into the pit of the abyss. But those who rejoice in God’s scourges and for whom God’s judgments are pleasing—these are upright in heart, that is, just; and therefore Christians will always be beside justice.

There follows the voice of the people dwelling in the house of God and hastening to the contest against adversaries:

VERS. 16. Who will rise up for me against evildoers? I rise from sloth to fight against malignant demons, so that at last I may be with that justice. [Col. 0574A] Who will rise with me, to fight in the battle-line? This is to say: Soldiers of Christ, rise up; fight for eternal glory, because “our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers” (Eph. 6:12), that is, against demons. Therefore let us take up the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, the breastplate of justice, and the sword of God’s word, and let us stand firm bravely for the crown. Armed with these weapons, I shall rise against them. Which of you will rise with me? Or who will stand with me in the battle-line against those who work iniquity? This is the voice of teachers to the faithful. Those who, through fear or favour, do not oppose wrongdoers are as though lying down; those who for no consideration cease to oppose them are those who rise up. Yet they stand in the battle-line if they persevere to the end [Col. 0574B] in zeal for God. But because this battle is fought not by human strength but by God’s help, it is accordingly added:

VERS. 17. Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell. That is: while demons cunningly persuaded, heretics mocked, pagans and Jews taunted, and false Christians slandered, I almost consented; and thereby my soul almost dwelt in the hell of vices, just as theirs will afterwards go into the hell of punishments—except that the Lord helped me to resist them and to persist in a good purpose. Or: having come into the hell of vices, my soul would almost have dwelt there, unless the Lord had helped me so that it might not remain there. Why did the Lord help you? Because of confession. For:

[Col. 0574C] VERS. 18. If I said, “My foot has been moved,” that is, if I confessed to the Lord what I often did, saying: “Lord, my affection has moved from good toward consent to evil,” your mercy, O Lord, helped me, lest I fall away from good. And I not only confessed, but also grieved that I had sinned; therefore:

VERS. 19. According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations made my soul glad. That is, in proportion to the many ways in which I grieved in my heart over the movement of my foot, your mercies gladdened my soul. For in the measure in which a person grieves over sins, God forgives those sins; and this forgiveness is consolation for sorrow. This too is great consolation: that the penitent person will not dwell in hell [Col. 0574D] but will reign with Christ, justice; whereas the impenitent will not be with you, O Christ.

VERS. 20. Shall the throne of iniquity cleave to you? As the soul of the just person is the seat of wisdom, so the soul of the unjust person is the seat of the devil. That seat does not cleave to you, because you do not sit in it, but in me, who have become your seat through justice. Do those in whom iniquity reigns cleave to you—here according to good will, or in the future according to glory? No: because you give a commandment, and in it require the endurance of pain, which you would not do if the throne of iniquity cleaved to you. This is what he says: “You fashion labour in the commandment,” that is, you temper pain in the observance of your commandment according to the measure of each person’s strength.

Alternatively: “You fashion labour in the commandment,” that is, [Col. 0575A] you make labour part of the commandment, because you desire your commandment to be observed with diligent effort; and you would not do this if the throne of iniquity cleaved to you. And who are the thrones of iniquity? Those who:

VERS. 21. Lie in wait for the soul of the just person: that is, they frequently desire to seize the soul, that is, the life, of the just, so as to draw him into consent to evil, or to strip him of his possessions, or to take away his life. Christ took captive the souls of the saints, but not *against* their souls. “Against the soul” means contrary to the soul’s salvation. And when they cannot take it captive, they will condemn innocent blood: that is, they will kill an innocent body, shedding guiltless blood by condemning it. The soldiers of Christ, who rose up to battle against the malignant ones and stood in the battle-line against the unjust—whose [Col. 0575B] souls the wicked, the seats of iniquity, lay in wait for and whose blood they condemned—returning in victory to the king, cry aloud:

VERS. 22. The Lord has become my refuge. [Col. 0576A] That is, when I suffered the fiery darts of the evil one and despaired of my own strength, I fled to Christ, who is Lord of all and God of the faithful. This God of mine became the help of my hope: that is, he helped me through fighting to attain what I had hoped for through loving. To me as victor he will render the crown of justice; but he will clothe my enemies with confusion.

VERS. 23. And he will repay them their iniquity, because he will send them into the place of torments; and in their malice he will destroy them—that is, he will destroy them in soul and body because of their malice. Christ the avenger, the just judge, will destroy them—he who is the Lord our God, the God of Christians, the God of vengeances. You fools and senseless persons suppose that God does not know human evils because he does not immediately condemn sinners; at the judgment he will punish the wicked, [Col. 0576B] when he destroys all whom he finds in malice, saying: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41)—may God avert this from us.

## PSALM XCIV. On the invitation of the peoples

[Col. 0575]

[Col. 0575C] “Come, let us exult in the Lord,” etc. This psalm concerns the calling of Gentiles and Jews to the grace of faith, or of fallen believers to repentance. It is spoken to those called to the wedding feast, so that they may come from the pit of misery to the joys of heaven, and from labour in the vineyard to the Lord’s rest, where they may enter God’s banquet with the angels; lest, through negligence, they remain on the journey like the Jews in the wilderness, who did not enter the promised land because of unbelief. The three preceding psalms bear the superscription “Sabbath,” which means rest; in them it is written that the just, flourishing like a palm tree through faith in the Trinity, ought to enter the Lord’s rest. But in this psalm God swears that those who lie in wait for the soul of the just and condemn innocent blood shall not enter his rest.

[Col. 0575D] This psalm is placed ninety-fourth in order, a number divisible into forty, fifty, and four. Forty signifies repentance; fifty, joy; four, the Church gathered from the four regions of the world. This number indicates that peoples gathered to faith from the four quarters of the world come through repentance to everlasting joy. The title of the psalm is:

**A PRAISE-SONG OF DAVID.**  
[Note: [Col. 0575D] The Vulgate: “Of David himself.”]

That is: this praise of the faithful people is sung joyfully to Christ, noble and delightful to behold. Its subject is the calling of the people to the Lord’s rest. Its intention is to admonish the fallen to repentance, so that they may enter the Lord’s rest. Its words are taken from the history in which the Hebrews were called out of Egypt to the land flowing with milk and honey, although almost all of them were struck down in the wilderness because they offended God. It signifies that many are called to the kingdom of God, but few are chosen because of evil works.

It is divided into two parts, because a twofold calling is described here. The first part is, “Come, let us exult in the Lord,” in which both callings are contained; the second, “Today, if [you hear] his voice,” in which God’s admonition is introduced. The voice of the apostles to the Gentile people:

VERS. 1. Come, let us exult in the Lord. O Gentiles, who are far from Jerusalem, the city, dwelling in Babylon, the city of the devil: come from unbelief to faith, from the devil who persuades to Christ the Saviour. Let us exult in the Lord: that is, let us joyfully do good in honour of God the Father, who is Lord of all. Let us make joyful noise to God our Saviour: that is, let us praise Christ, our true God and Saviour, with a pure [Col. 0576D] mind. Exultation pertains to action; jubilation to contemplation. The Hebrew reads: “Let us make joyful noise to our rock, Jesus.” The rock is Christ, the true Jesus, to whom we make joyful noise.

VERS. 2. Let us come before his face in confession: that is, let us anticipate the coming of his presence in praise. Or, let us anticipate his judgment through confession of sins. The Hebrew reads: “Let us come before his face in thanksgiving.” The Lord’s first coming was, as it were, his back, when he appeared hidden in the form of a servant; his second will be, as it were, his face, when God appears manifest to all. Let us anticipate this with praise and repentance. And in psalms let us make joyful noise to him: that is, with good works let us make jubilation to him. A psalm belongs to the activity of the active life; jubilation belongs [Col. 0577A] to the praise of the contemplative life. That is, let us praise him through action and contemplation. “Let us make joyful noise to him” must be joined to the following three verses. Let us make joyful noise to him:

VERS. 3. For the Lord is a great God, and a great King above all gods: that is, this great God is a powerful God above all gods, that is, above Moses and all the saints; a great Lord above all lords; and a great King above all kings chosen as gods by human beings. Therefore let us also make joyful noise to him:

VERS. 4. Because the ends of the earth are in his hand: that is, all the boundaries of the earth are in his power, from which he made one priestly kingdom, the Church; and the heights of the mountains are his: that is, he subjected the powers of princes to his dominion. Another translation adds more: “For the Lord will not reject his people.” This is joined to the previous psalm, where the same is written: “Make joyful noise to God, and you shall be his people.” He does not reject this people from the kingdom because he redeemed it with his blood. Therefore let us likewise make joyful noise to him:

VERS. 5. For the sea is his, and he made it. In Genesis it is written that God made heaven and earth, but it is silent concerning the sea. Hence some heretics said that the waters were not created but coeternal with God. Therefore the Spirit who through Moses said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), added through David: “The sea is his, and he made it.” And he who there said, “Let the waters be gathered into one place and let the dry land appear” (ibid., 9), himself says here: “His hands founded the dry land.” The sea is the Gentile world. It belongs to the Lord by his power, and he made it in the first creation. And his hands formed dry land out of the sea: that is, his works made the Church beautiful out of what was formless. It is called dry land by comparison, because, just as the earth thirsts for rain, so the Church thirsts for justice or the rain of teaching, that it may bring forth fruit to be stored in the heavenly granary. This whole passage is drawn from the creation of the world and signifies the creation of the Church from formless matter. There follows the voice of Elijah and Enoch, or of other preachers, to the Jewish people: O Jews, who are far from God’s kingdom, scattered throughout the world:

[Col. 0577D] VERS. 6. Come from faithlessness to faith, from Antichrist to Christ. And because he is true God, let us worship him and fall bodily before him, asking forgiveness because we have despised him so long. And let us weep for our sins before God, who made us in the creation of the world and remade us in his passion:

VERS. 7. For he is the Lord our God, and we are the people of his pasture, because he fed us in the wilderness; and we are the sheep of his hand, that is, of his working, because, like a shepherd, he provides us with necessities. He did not say, “the sheep of his pasture and the people of his hand,” which would seem more fitting, but “the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand,” because it is said of those sheep to whom the shepherd himself speaks: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and I give them eternal life” [Col. 0578A] (John 10:27–28). And elsewhere: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved and will find pasture” (ibid., 9). The shepherd himself is the gate of life. Through this gate these sheep will enter and find the pasture of eternal satisfaction. There follows the voice of the Holy Spirit to the synagogue of the Jews:

VERS. 8. Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts. “Today” is used in four ways: of eternity, of temporality, of a human lifetime, and of the present day. Of eternity, as in: “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7), that is, in eternity I have begotten you equal to myself. Of temporality, as here: “Today, if you hear his voice,” that is, as long as this world lasts. Of a human lifetime, as Moses says: “I testify to you today” (Deut. 32:46), that is, as long as [Col. 0578B] you live, I declare to you that you will perish if you act wickedly. Of the present day, as when we say: “Give us this day our daily bread.” The six ages of the world are as the six days of the age. Today—that is, on this sixth day—if you hear from the very mouth of Christ, our shepherd, the voice which on previous days you heard through Moses and the prophets, do not harden your hearts. Scripture also commonly sets forth two days: the day of death, from Adam to Christ; and the day of life, from Christ’s time to the end of the world. Again, one is the day of wrath, the other the day of grace. You sheep, who on the previous day heard the shepherd’s voice through the law and hardened your hearts—today, that is, in this time of grace, if you hear his voice in the Gospel—do not harden your hearts; that is, do not be unbelieving.

[Col. 0578C] VERS. 9. As in the provocation, according to the day of testing in the wilderness: that is, as your fathers were unbelieving on the former day in the wilderness, where your fathers tested me concerning meat and water brought forth from the rock. They tested me and found me powerful, and saw my works, when I rained manna and flesh upon them and poured water out of the rock. Those who imitate the wicked are called children of the wicked, as is said to the Jews: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44). And because they tested me and did not believe:

VERS. 10. For forty years I was offended with that generation: that is, as long as they were in the wilderness, I was angry with them; and I said to Moses: “They always err in heart.” At times they wandered bodily, because they travelled through the wilderness for forty [Col. 0578D] years, though they should have travelled it in forty days; they always wandered in heart because they did not believe God.

Another translation reads: “For forty years I was near to this generation.” There are two generations, one of the good and the other of the wicked. The generation of the good began with Abel, and that of the wicked with Cain, and both continue to the end of the age. Four times ten is forty. By four are signified the four parts of the world; ten indicates perfection. Thus forty years signify the whole time of the age, in which the generation of the wicked always errs in heart and with which God is offended.
