Or: he was near to their mouth, far from their heart; they continually embitter him by their evil customs, just as those in the wilderness tested him with their murmurings. To these he always says [Col. 0579A] through Scripture: “They err in heart,” that is, seriously, knowingly, or deliberately.

VERS. 11. And these did not know my ways: that is, such persons, for whom I performed my works for forty years and of whom I said, “They always err in heart,” did not understand my ways, namely faith and action. Therefore I do to them as I swore in my wrath: if they enter my rest, I cease to be. To your unbelieving fathers I swore—that is, being angry because of their unbelief, I firmly threatened—that if they entered the promised land, then I would not be God. God calls that land his rest because the people brought into it by him rested in peace, having previously laboured on the journey. The history is well known: when the people approached the promised land, they sent ahead scouts, who returned and caused the people to murmur against the Lord, saying that the land was indeed good, but was defended by fortified cities and by powerful, tall men, who would devour them and their children like bread if they entered their borders (Num. 13). Hence the terrified people began to cry out in mourning: “Would that the Lord strike us here! Would that he not bring us into that land!” Angry with them, the Lord [Col. 0580A] swore that he would do to them just as they had said, and that they would never enter the promised land. All of them were struck down in the wilderness, and only two entered, together with a multitude of the children of Israel. As the Lord, appeased, swore to Abraham that he would give to his seed—that is, to believers—the land flowing with milk and honey, so, angry, he swore to unbelievers that they would never enter his rest, that is, eternal life. Those who were struck down in the wilderness are the many called who refused to come; the two who entered are the active and contemplative, who, animated by twofold love, will enter the Lord’s rest. Hence this entire psalm can also be the voice of teachers exhorting the fallen to come from error to truth, worship the true God rather than make a god of the belly, fall down before God, do penance [Col. 0580B] for their errors, weep for their sins before the Lord, and not harden their hearts at his voice, lest, like the Jews, they fail to enter his rest.

Therefore this psalm is sung in the night offices, because through it the just are summoned to praise God, while the fallen are invited to repentance and satisfaction.

## PSALM XCV

[Col. 0579]

[Col. 0579C] (VERS. 1.) “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord,” etc. In this psalm those who were invited to the Lord’s rest in the preceding psalm are exhorted to praise God. Its title is:

**WHEN THE HOUSE WAS BEING BUILT AFTER THE CAPTIVITY, A SONG OF DAVID.**

VERS. 1. Christ, the supreme craftsman, constructed in heaven a city out of translucent stones, that is, angels; a portion of them fell in apostasy. Then he built in paradise a house out of living stones, that is, human beings. The enemy destroyed this house when he seduced the human race out of paradise. But the craftsman, not abandoning his work, came into the world and brought together the scattered stones into one, gathering the scattered children of God into one faith. He built the house again [Col. 0579D] when, after the devil’s captivity, he established the Church. Thus this is a song of David—that is, of Christ, desirable to behold—namely a song about him, made by craftsmen, that is, preachers, for living stones, that is, chosen human beings, when the house of God, the Church, was being built through their preaching after the devil’s captivity.

The words of the title are taken from the rebuilding accomplished after the captivity under Zerubbabel the prince and Jesus the high priest. In David’s time, moreover, the temple had not yet even been begun; after David’s death it was built by Solomon, then four hundred years later destroyed by the king of Babylon, and after seventy years rebuilt by Jesus the priest and others. [Col. 0580C] It is therefore evident that nothing is said here about that temple, but about the one destroyed by the devil and rebuilt by Jesus Christ from living stones.

This psalm occupies the ninety-fifth place. Ninety, in which three is repeated three times, expresses the people from the Gentiles converted to faith in the Trinity; five signifies the people converted from the Pentateuch of the Law. This number indicates that the house of God is built from these two walls. The subject of the psalm is the Gentiles called from streets and lanes to the Lord’s rest. Its purpose is to urge us to praise God, that we may deserve to be built together with the elect in his house. Its words are taken from priests singing to God in the temple [Col. 0580D] and from peoples sacrificing there; they signify the priests of the Church offering themselves as a living sacrifice to God.

It is divided into two parts, because the Church is divided into the learned and the laity, or because the house of God is constructed from two peoples. The first part is, “Sing to the Lord,” containing the praise of the priests; the second, “Bring to the Lord,” containing the offering of the peoples. The voice of the Holy Spirit calling to the Lord’s rest:

“Sing to the Lord a new song.” “Sing” is said three times, and “to the Lord” is placed three times, because the three orders of the Church—teachers, the continent, and the married—called from Asia, Africa, and Europe, exhort to praise of the Trinity. [Col. 0581A] Sing to the Lord Father, sing to the Lord Son, sing to the Lord Holy Spirit a new song: that is, joyfully fulfil, in honour of God, the new commandment of love. The old song was observance of the Old Testament; the new song is fulfilment of the Gospel. Whoever puts off the old person with his deeds and puts on the new person according to truth and justice sings the new song: that is, let such a person love not only friends in God but enemies also for God’s sake, abandon all possessions, and seek God alone. Sing to the Lord, all the earth: that is, praise the Lord, all who dwell upon the earth.

VERS. 2. Sing to the Lord by a good life, and bless his name: that is, attribute what is good not to yourselves but to him. This is said generally to all. Now he addresses the teachers specifically:

VERS. 3. Announce his salvation from day to day: that is, preach Christ the Saviour without interruption, from day to day, that is, from the Old Testament into the New. The prophets, writers of the Old Testament, were days that foretold the rising of the eternal sun of justice. The apostles, writers of the New Testament, were days that preached that the eternal sun had shone and had set for our salvation. By this song of love, this blessing of praise, and this proclamation of preaching, the building of God’s house is constructed and grows.

Another translation reads: “Proclaim well his salvation from day to day”; that is, preach the Son from the Father in catholic fashion. [Col. 0581C] And as though the workers asked, “Where do you command your house to be built? Where do you wish it to grow?” he points out the place among the Gentiles: “Declare his glory among the nations,” that is, preach his divinity in the midst of the Gentiles. By Christ’s salvation his humanity is understood; by glory, his divinity. O builders of the house, teach among the Gentiles that Christ is God and man, and proclaim among all peoples his wonders: that he was born of a virgin; tempted by the devil; gave sight to the blind, walking to the lame, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, and life to the dead; redeemed humanity by his death; rose from the dead; ascended with our flesh into heaven; and gave the Holy Spirit in knowledge of all languages. And [Col. 0581D] proclaim this:

VERS. 4. For the Lord is great: that is, powerful above all lords, and exceedingly praiseworthy, beyond what a human being can praise or understand. He is terrible above all gods: that is, above all angels considered gods by the Gentiles; or above all saints made gods by him, such as Moses—terrible to sinners. This is joined to the preceding psalm, where it is written: “For the Lord is a great God,” etc. Or, he is to be feared above all beings chosen as gods by human beings.

VERS. 5. For all the gods of the Gentiles are demons: that is, they are not gods but demons. For when idols gave answers, the demon himself spoke in them. Here the thorns of superstition are uprooted, filth is cleared away, the house is built, its mass rises within the house, and the stones brought to the building grow. The demons that impeded the building of this house have been cast out; but the Lord made the heavens, namely angels, apostles, and other saints, to support this house like pillars. And who will be in this house? Those who confess, that is, praise God; beautiful in virtues, holy in life, and magnificent in works. This is what follows:

VERS. 6. Confession and beauty are before him; holiness and magnificence are in his sanctuary. Confession consists of those who confess God with the mouth. Beauty consists of [Col. 0582B] those who believe in him with the heart. These will be before him because they behold him with the mind. Holiness consists of those who live chastely. Magnificence consists of those who perform good works. These will be in his sanctuary: that is, they will reign with those whom he has sanctified. Thus confession and beauty belong to the contemplative life; holiness and magnificence to the active life. God’s house is built from such stones. Once the house has been built, they are admonished to offer sacrifices in it to the Lord.

VERS. 7–8. Bring to the Lord, countries of the Gentiles; bring to the Lord glory and honour. Bring to the Lord glory to his name. The preceding action represented the clergy praising God in the Church; this following passage signifies the people offering gifts in the Church. Therefore, just as it previously said “sing” three times, so now it repeats “bring” three times, that the threefold order of the Church may offer itself to God in soul and body. After the human race was divided into seventy-two languages, the Gentiles were divided into a hundred countries. The Hebrew reads: “Families of peoples.” O countries of the Gentiles, that is, all peoples of the nations, bring glory to the Lord Father, believing him to be the creator of all; bring honour to the Lord Son, believing him equal to the Father and redeemer of humankind; bring glory to the Lord Holy Spirit, believing him to be your sanctifier. And bring this to his name: that is, work well in honour of God’s name, which is Lord. Or glorify the Trinity in heart and mouth, and honour it in deed.

Take sacrifices—not goats or calves, but prepare yourselves as a living sacrifice for martyrdom; [Col. 0582D] or sacrifice a contrite spirit and broken heart, and so enter his courts, that is, conformity with the apostles and prophets. The house is the Church; its courts are the prophets and apostles. Through these courts lies entry to God’s house. Those enter these courts who live by their example. Once the sacrifices have been offered:

VERS. 9. Worship the Lord in his holy court: that is, worship him in the unity of the Catholic Church. He said “courts” on account of the many preachers, but “court” on account of the one faith. Those who offer sacrifices and worship the Lord will enter this house; but those attached to earthly love depart. Therefore it follows: “Let all the earth be moved at his face,” that is, all lovers of earthly things are removed from his presence. Or, let all the earth be moved from unbelief to faith, from wicked works to good works, from silence to confession, and from persecution to martyrdom. And you who have been converted:

VERS. 10. Say among the Gentiles that the Lord has reigned from the wood: that is, teach among the Gentiles that the Lord Jesus has gained the kingdom through faith and subjected the world to himself.

Another translation reads: “Say among the nations that the Lord has reigned from the wood”—understand, the wood of the cross. For after the cross he reigned throughout the world. Death hung upon the tree in paradise; life hung upon the wood of the cross, restoring those dead through sin to the tree of life and the Father’s kingdom. Christ’s passion is understood through the cross. When we worship the cross, we worship Christ’s passion—indeed, the one [Col. 0583B] crucified for us. He truly reigns: “For he has set right the world, which shall not be moved.” This is joined to the passage where it is written: “For he established the circle of the earth”; for in that title the earth is founded, in this one the house is built, and in the text of both psalms the reign of the craftsman is proclaimed. He corrected the world, which had been twisted by unbelief and wrongly made circular: that is, he made it straight and bent it through unity of faith and love into the circle of the eternal crown. It will no longer be moved from faith to idolatry, or from uprightness to the distortion of injustice.

Observe that first the house is built; then it is dedicated with sacrifices; it is sanctified on the wood of the cross; then the world is surrounded by the walls of the court; finally, the faithful people are separated from the unbelieving people. Therefore it adds: “He will judge peoples in equity,” that is, the good and evil in justice. Another translation reads: “And the nations in his wrath”: that is, he will judge the peoples of the faithful in equity unto eternal life and the unbelieving nations in his wrath unto eternal punishment. The built house has praisers from heaven, earth, and sea; its dowry is fields and trees. This is what follows:

VERS. 11. Let the heavens rejoice, that is, the angels restored through human beings; and let the earth exult, that is, the Church to be raised from earthly things to heavenly ones.

[Col. 0584A] Alternatively: Let the heavens rejoice, that is, the apostles; and let the earth exult, that is, Judaea watered by them.

Let the sea be moved, that is, the Gentile world from the bitterness of unbelief to the sweetness of truth; and its fullness, that is, all who dwell in it.

Alternatively: Let the heavens rejoice, that is, the just, at the equity by which they will be judged unto life; and let the earth exult, that is, sinners, at the repentance by which they will be saved. Let the sea be moved: that is, let those bitter in vices grieve, together with all the wicked who dwell in them, because they will be condemned to punishment in God’s wrath.

VERS. 12. The fields will rejoice, that is, those flourishing in God’s virtues, and everything in them, that is, all virtues and good actions, through which they will receive eternal rewards in the future. Then, when the Jews rejoice, [Col. 0584B] all the trees of the forests will exult: that is, all the nations that have always been uncultivated. The trees of forests are those fit not for building but for fire. The forest was the Gentile world; the trees, Gentiles; the olive tree, Judaea; the branches, Jews. The branches were broken off, and wild olive shoots were grafted in; they grew into huge cedar and cypress trees fit for building God’s house. Therefore they exult:

VERS. 13. Before the face [Vulgate: *From the face*] of the Lord, because he comes; because he comes to judge the earth, that is, all who dwell on the earth. He said “he comes” twice because first he came to be judged and afterwards he comes to judge. Or: he comes to reward, and he comes to condemn the wicked. Then the just, placed in the structure of the house, will exult in the manifestation of the vision [Col. 0584C] of God and in the judgment which he will then make. For he will judge the circle of the earth in equity: that is, he will reward in justice, according to their works, believers made circular in virtues; and he will judge peoples in his truth: that is, he will condemn sinners according to their merits. And then let the heavens rejoice and the earth exult, because they will be invited into the glory of the children of God.

Sunday feasts claim this psalm for themselves, because in it living stones sing the wonders of the Lord, the cornerstone.

## PSALM XCVI. On the praise of the Gentiles

[Col. 0583]

[Col. 0583D] “The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult,” etc. This psalm takes its subject from the end of the preceding one. In that psalm judgment is mentioned; in this, the manner in which it occurs is described. In the former is the exhortation of the Holy Spirit; in the latter, the praise of the Gentiles coming to God’s house. And because through Christ’s first coming the Gentiles were built into God’s house, and through his second coming they will enter the Lord’s rest, both comings of Christ are set forth in this psalm: the first, in which idolatry [Col. 0584D] is destroyed; the second, in which the Church will be rewarded. This psalm is placed ninety-sixth in order, a number divisible into twelve times eight, because through the judgment of the twelve apostles the Church is brought into the Lord’s house unto the eight beatitudes. The title is:

(VERS. 1.) **A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN THE EARTH WAS RESTORED TO HIM.**  
[Note: [Col. 0583] Vulgate: “For David, when his land was restored.”]

David, a man of war, fighting against the nations round about, subdued them and reduced them to his power, and recovered the land which they had unjustly possessed. David, whose name means “strong of hand,” is Christ, who by strength conquered the strong one, the devil, and the world by the cross; who recovered his land—that is, his flesh—in the resurrection; who overcame all the surrounding nations through the apostles; and who brought all the earth under his dominion. Therefore this psalm is sung to David, that is, to Christ in his mighty conflict, when his land—that is, his flesh—was restored to him in the resurrection. Or Judea, which had been lost in his Passion, was restored to him after his Ascension, when, after the Holy Spirit had been sent and the apostles were preaching, three thousand were converted to the Lord in one day (Acts 2:41), and five thousand on another (ibid. 4:4). Or the land was restored to him when the Gentile world was restored to him in place of Judea.

[Col. 0585B] The subject of the psalm is the praise of the Gentiles concerning both advents of Christ. Its purpose is to show Christ’s advent in the Incarnation, the destruction of idolatry, the building of the Church into God’s house, and to exhort us to hate evil and love Christ, so that we may reign with him. Its words are taken from the history in which cloud and darkness appeared on Mount Sinai, when the whole mountain smoked like a burning fire, lightning flashed, thunder roared, those worshipping the calf were put to shame, and the daughters of Judah rejoiced. It signifies that in the Church the cloud of Christ’s humanity and the darkness of his Deity appeared; the fire of the Holy Spirit shone forth; the lightnings of signs flashed; the thunders of preachings sounded; idolaters were confounded; and the souls of those confessing God rejoiced, because Christ, the true light, rose for the righteous and upright in heart as eternal gladness. It also indicates the Day of Judgment, when darkness and fire will go before Christ’s face and consume his enemies, while eternal light will rise for the righteous and enduring gladness for the upright in heart.

The psalm is divided into two parts because it describes the two advents of Christ, or the two peoples to be judged. One part begins, “The Lord has reigned,” in which both advents of Christ are expressed; the other, “Zion heard and was glad,” in which the Church’s glory is set forth. It is the voice of the Gentiles praising God:

“The Lord has reigned”: he who stood before Pilate in the form of a servant, hung condemned with thieves upon the cross, and lay dead in the tomb, himself rose again and reigned as Lord of all, destroyed idols, and subjected the world to himself. Therefore let the earth rejoice, which has been snatched from the devil’s dominion and restored to its true Lord. Let the many islands rejoice, which have deserved to have Christ as king. By “earth” is understood the primitive Church from Judea, which rejoiced in Christ’s kingdom. By “many islands” are meant the churches of the Gentiles, set amid the sea of persecutions, which rejoiced in the kingdom of the eternal King. Through whom did he obtain the kingdom and conquer earth and islands? Through clouds, that is, through the apostles.

[Col. 0586A] **VERSE 2.** “Cloud and darkness are round about him.” The clouds are the prophets; the darkness is the obscurity of the Law. These are around him—that is, around the Church, which is, as it were, about him, while he stands in its midst. These clouds and darkness overshadowed the Church when the Law and prophecies made Christ known to it. The apostles too were clouds, who filled the restored earth with doctrine. The darkness was the wise, who, understanding lofty matters, disclosed them to the Church. The cloud also is the Lord’s body, in which the Sun of righteousness lay hidden; the darkness is the hidden Deity, which did not appear to fleshly eyes. “Righteousness and judgment are the correction of his throne.” Christ’s throne is the Church, in which he sits and reigns as king. Its correctors are righteous judges. And after this throne has been corrected by wise rulers and righteous judges, Christ the King will sit in it. But:

**VERSE 3.** “Fire shall go before him, and shall set his enemies round about him aflame.” This happened when the Holy Spirit appeared and set all the nations round about, which had been hostile to him, on fire with love for him. The fire of the Holy Spirit went before through faith and the remission of sins; but the Lord in them [Note: [Col. 0585D] Something is lacking.] wrought miracles, and then inflamed his enemies with love and enlightened them with knowledge. And then:

**VERSES 4–5.** “His lightnings shone upon the world”: that is, miracles became bright to the whole earth. Lightnings and thunders are said to arise from the collision of clouds, as fire is struck from a rubbed stone. When the Lord reigned, clouds and darkness arose, from which lightnings and thunders proceeded. Prophets and apostles, the clouds, collide when they are compared by teachers. From them thunders resound—that is, preachings which terrify hearts. From them lightnings flash—that is, sayings which enlighten minds. It should be noted that in the psalms the earth is often called the “world,” because geometers describe its form as round; and this signifies that the Church, God’s earth, is gathered into the circle of the eternal crown. “It saw and was moved”: that is, the nations submitted to eternal faith and, warmed by the fire which went before his face, were changed into another form, like wax. “Before the face of the Lord all the earth”—understand, “melted like wax,” liquefied by the fire of the Holy Spirit and changed into another religion.

In the Hebrew it reads: “Before the face of the Lord, all the earth.” Christ the Lord Jesus is Lord of the whole earth: he first made all things, then remade all things. The earth was moved at the sight of the lightnings, because:

**VERSE 6.** “The heavens declared his righteousness”: that is, the apostles preached the Gospel and that the world is justified through him; and thus all peoples saw his glory—that is, all nations recognized God incarnate for humankind and human nature exalted through him.

**VERSE 7.** “Let all who worship carved images be confounded, and those who glory in their idols.” Carved images are those carved from stone or wood; idols are those cast from bronze or any metal. Let those who worship these as God be confounded, and those who glory in them as though able to grant them favors, while refusing to worship Christ, the true God, whom the angels worship. To him they turn and, in exceeding joy, sing:

**VERSE 8.** “Worship him, all his angels.” Satan’s angels wished to be worshipped by human beings as gods. But God’s angels did not allow human beings wishing to worship them—namely Joshua and John—to do so; rather, they taught them to worship God the Creator. Those who desire equality with angels ought to imitate them. Zion heard this faith of the Gentiles—that is, the Church from Jerusalem—and rejoiced. For when “the apostles and the Church which was at Jerusalem heard that Samaria—that is, the Gentile world—had received the word of God, they rejoiced” (Acts 8:14). And the daughters of Judah—that is, faithful souls from among the Jews—rejoiced because of your judgments, Lord: because you are not a respecter of persons, but judged idolaters worthy to be received into your kingdom. And they rejoice because the Gentiles believe this:

**VERSE 9.** “For you, Lord, are most high over all the earth”: that is, you are most powerful over all nations. And because they believe that you are exceedingly exalted at God’s right hand above all those whom they falsely worshipped as gods, the apostles and faithful address the Gentiles:

**VERSES 10–11.** “You who love the Lord, hate evil.” Some Jews who had become Christians wanted the converted Gentiles to observe the Law of Moses and circumcision. The apostles told them not to lay upon them a heavy yoke which neither they nor their fathers could bear. They wrote to the Gentiles that they should abstain from fornication, things sacrificed to idols, blood, and strangled meat, and so be saved (Acts 15). This is what they say here in equivalent terms: You who have believed from among the Gentiles and love the Lord Jesus, do not love evil. And if you suffer bodily adversities for Christ, do not be concerned, because “the Lord guards the souls of his saints,” lest they fail in tribulation. “He will deliver them from the hand of sinners”—that is, from the hand of persecutors—and lead them to joys. Or, from the hand of the sinner—that is, from the devil’s power—he will deliver them. Therefore rejoice, because:

**VERSE 12.** “Light has risen for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart.” Christ is the true light of souls and the joy of angels. This light appeared to the righteous when Christ was made known by faith to a people justified from sins, and promised eternal gladness to those who live uprightly. Therefore:

**VERSE 13.** “Rejoice, righteous ones, in the Lord,” in whom is supreme joy, “and give thanks to the remembrance of his holiness”: that is, praise him because he remembered to sanctify you from idols and join you with the saints in heaven. This concerns the first advent; now something must also be said concerning the second advent.

[Note: [Col. 0587D] Another exposition of the same psalm.]

**VERSE 1.** The Lord Jesus will reign in the Father’s glory, and he himself, the King, will sit as judge at the judgment. Therefore let the earth rejoice—that is, the Church called from earthly things to heavenly. [Col. 0588A] Therefore also let the many islands rejoice—that is, all churches rescued from the sea of this age.

**VERSE 2.** “Cloud and darkness are round about him”: that is, a mighty storm. “Righteousness and judgment are the correction of his throne.” Nothing is corrected unless it previously appeared crooked. It appeared crooked that the wicked flourish here while the good are oppressed. This will be corrected by righteousness at the judgment, because the good will be judged to joys and the wicked to punishments.

**VERSE 3.** “Fire shall go before him,” as it is written: “A river of fire went forth before his face,” which will set the world ablaze and rise fifteen cubits higher than the height of all mountains. Of this it is written: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and shall burn even unto the lowest parts of hell” (Deut. 32:22). “And it shall set his enemies round about him aflame,” because it will burn up his adversaries.

**VERSE 4.** “His lightnings shone upon the world”: that is, then dreadful thunders will shake the world and terrifying lightnings will split the earth. He used the past tense for the future because of its certainty: the future can change, but the past in no way can. “The earth saw and was moved”: that is, when the earth sees such things, it will be terrified and tremble; and immediately it will be changed into pitch and burning sulphur, and will destroy the wicked from itself. Then:

**VERSE 5.** “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord, before the face of the Lord all the earth,” when the heavens shall pass away with great violence and the elements shall be dissolved by the heat of fire. [Col. 0588C] He therefore said twice, “before the face of the Lord,” because he will appear in his humanity to the unjust, and in his Deity to the righteous. Then there will be a fearful expectation and fiery zeal that will consume the adversaries of truth.

**VERSE 6.** “The heavens declared his righteousness”: that is, the very heavens, dissolved by fire, will show God’s just judgment; “and all peoples shall see his glory”—that is, the judge’s power. “Every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him” (Rev. 1:7). Then:

**VERSE 7.** “Let all who worship carved images be confounded”: that is, those who worshipped idols and those who now glory in their images. And not only pagans who were idolaters, but also Jews and heretics who worship an imaginary god, when they transform the incomprehensible God in their hearts into the image of a human being or of some other thing. So too false Christians, who worship the god Belly, will then go into confusion.

**VERSE 8.** “Worship him, all his angels”: that is, at that judgment all his angels will worship him as the true God. Zion—that is, the Church then contemplating life—heard this and rejoiced. And the daughters of Judah—that is, the souls of those confessing and praising God—rejoiced because of your judgments, Lord: because you judged the oppressed to glory and the oppressors to punishment. Then they will recognize:

**VERSE 9.** “For you, Lord, are most high over all the earth”: that is, you are the supreme Lord of all; “exceedingly exalted above all gods”: that is, raised by singular power above all powers of angels and saints. Therefore now:

**VERSES 10–11.** “You who love the Lord”—that is, who worship him—“hate evil,” because it is not enough not to do evil unless one also hates it. Thus you will be holy, and then hope for life, because “the Lord guards the souls of his saints” from evil; “from the hand of sinners”—that is, of demons—he will deliver them at the judgment. [Col. 0590A] Then light will rise for the righteous: another light, far better and greater than this light; and eternal gladness for the upright in heart; while the wicked will be cast into outer darkness. Therefore:

**VERSE 12.** “Rejoice, righteous ones,” because you are in the Lord, in whom you enjoy the highest joy; “and give thanks to the remembrance of his holiness”: that is, always praise him because he remembered to sanctify you.

Therefore the feasts of the Lord celebrate this psalm, because it proclaims Christ’s mighty works.

## PSALM XCVII

[Col. 0589]

[Col. 0589B] “Sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done wondrous things,” etc. In another psalm the Holy Spirit exhorted the Gentiles, called to praise God in his rest, with “Sing”; in this psalm he admonishes the Jews, likewise invited to praise God in his rest, with “Sing.” The title of the psalm is:

**(VERSE 1.) A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF.**

That is: This praise is sung to the faithful Jewish people, strong of hand, amid the persecution of Antichrist. This psalm is the ninety-seventh. Ninety is nine times ten. In nine is the fellowship of angels; in ten, the Old Testament because of the Decalogue of the Law; in seven, the New Testament is expressed because of the sevenfold Spirit. This number therefore signifies [Col. 0589C] that the people converted from the Law to the Gospel will possess the perfection of life in the company of angels through the Holy Spirit.

The subject of the psalm is the people converted from the Law to the grace of the Gospel. Its purpose is to admonish those converted from error to persist in praises of the truth, which they know renders to each according to the righteousness of his works. The words are taken from priests and Levites who praised God in the tabernacles or temple with musical instruments; they signify those who praise God in the Church with voice and good action.

It is divided into two parts, because it treats of the praise of God and of human beings. One part begins, “Sing to the Lord,” and sings Christ’s mighty works; the other, “Make a joyful noise to the Lord,” and celebrates the people’s praises. It is the voice of the Holy Spirit, or of Elijah and Enoch, exhorting the Jews invited to God’s rest to praise God:

“Sing to the Lord a new song.” This psalm is joined to the one written concerning the Gentiles, because at the end of the world the Synagogue will be joined to the Church from the Gentiles. Therefore it begins likewise, because it indicates that the two walls coming from opposite directions are to be joined in the one cornerstone, Christ Jesus. O Jews, who have hitherto persisted in oldness and at last have put on newness in Christ, who now bear the new name of the Christian religion, sing to the Lord a new song of Gospel observance. Jews sing a new song when they observe the new precepts of the Gospel. And you ought rightly to sing, because “he has done wondrous things.” What things? “His right hand and his holy arm have saved [Vulgate: will save] for him.” Christ is God’s right hand, because through him he made all things; he is his arm, because through him he sustains all things. By “right hand” work is understood, and by “arm,” strength. This right hand saved for himself when he restored his work that had perished, which he had created in his own image. In this holy and strong arm, touched by blood, he saved for himself when he bound the strong armed man and distributed the spoils taken from him. These are the wonders that he did: not only that he gave sight to the blind, cleansed lepers, and raised the dead, but also that by his death he raised the human race from death.

**VERSE 2.** “The Lord has made known his salvation”: [Col. 0590C] that is, the Father manifested his Son to the Jews, through whom he saves all; “in the sight of the nations he revealed his righteousness”: that is, he made his Son known to the knowledge of the Gentiles, through whom he justifies the world. Christ is called God’s salvation because through him the world is saved; therefore he is righteousness, because the world is judged through him. In the Hebrew it is written: “To his man.” He did not say, “he showed,” but “he made known.” Adam knew him, who prophesied concerning him: “A man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Matt. 19:3). Abel also knew him, who offered a lamb; Seth knew him, who invoked him; Noah knew him, who saved every kind in the ark; Abraham knew him, who offered his son. But because afterward [Col. 0590D] the world forgot him when it worshipped idols, the Lord made his Jesus known when he sent the Word in flesh to the Jews and revealed righteousness to the Gentiles when he justified them through faith in him. Why did he reveal him to the Gentiles? Because of mercy. Why did he make him known to the Jews? Because of truth—that is, his promise.

**VERSE 3.** “For he remembered his mercy”: that is, at last he was mindful to have mercy on the Gentiles, whom he had seemed almost to have forgotten for so long. “And [he remembered] his truth”: that is, the promise made to the house of Israel, namely what he promised Abraham: that in his seed all nations would be blessed.

Another translation has: “He remembered his mercy to Jacob, and his truth to the house of Israel.” The Lord seemed to have forgotten the Jews when he permitted them to be blinded in unbelief. But after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, the Lord, remembering his mercy, will have mercy on Jacob, and Israel will be saved. He says “Jacob” because of the multitude; “Israel” because of the teachers of the Law. After all Israel has been saved, then all the ends of the earth saw the salvation of our God—that is, all who inhabit the boundaries of the earth. Therefore:

**VERSE 4.** “Make a joyful noise to the Lord, all the earth”: that is, all who inhabit the earth, with inward joy. Sing to him with cheerfulness of voice, rejoice in spirit, and make melody in deed. This figure is called *homoeoteleuton*, where different words end in similar sounds, as *jubilate, cantate, exsultate, psallite*—“make a joyful noise, sing, rejoice, make melody.”

[Col. 0591B] **VERSES 5–6.** “Make melody to the Lord with the harp, with harp and psalmody; with beaten trumpets and the sound of the horn.” They are commanded to praise God with four musical instruments—harp, psaltery, trumpet, and horn—because the life of the righteous is perfected by four virtues: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. The harp, which sounds from the lower part, is the active life, ministering to neighbors in bodily matters; it belongs to justice. Therefore he mentioned the harp twice, because there is a justice which renders each person his due, and a justice which gives God what is due to him. The psaltery, which sounds from the upper part, is the contemplative life, which praises God in spiritual things; it serves prudence. The beaten trumpet, struck with hammers from silver, is the life of teachers, made fit for the sound of preaching by the hammering of tribulation; it accords with temperance. The horn stands for kingship or strength. The horn trumpet is the life of rulers, raised by power above others, just as a growing horn lifts itself above flesh; it concerns fortitude. Therefore they make melody to the Lord on the harp who serve their neighbors for the Lord in the active life. Again, those sound praises on the harp who chastise their flesh for the Lord. They rejoice in the voice of psalmody—that is, on the psaltery—who praise God in the contemplative life and preach good things to others. Those sound praises on beaten trumpets who preach God amid tribulations. Those sing to God with the sound of the horn trumpet who, fighting against vices by voice and deed, defend their neighbors from evils. With these instruments, O Jews, praise God if you wish to reign with him. “Make a joyful noise before the King, the Lord”: that is, praise God because by faith you behold him who is King and Lord of all. Therefore:

**VERSE 7.** “Let the sea be moved, and its fullness”: that is, let the Law and legal observances be moved from a carnal to a spiritual understanding. Let also the inhabited world and its inhabitants be moved from evil works to repentance, so that they may be able to meet Christ as he comes. Or let the inhabited world be moved—that is, changed into a better state—and let the people who inhabit it be changed into equality with God’s angels. This passage is joined to that which reads: “Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult; let the sea be moved, and its fullness; the fields shall rejoice, and all things that are in them” (Ps. 95:11–12), because the Jews will be joined with the Gentiles in faith in Christ. Let the sea be moved—that is, sinners bitter with vices—before the face of the Lord.

**VERSES 8–9.** “The rivers shall clap their hands together.” The rivers are the wise, filled from the fountain of life and flowing in doctrine to others. They clap their hands together when, preaching together, they perform good work. For to clap hands is to do a good work cheerfully. “The mountains rejoiced [Vulgate: shall rejoice] before the Lord”: that is, the leaders among the Jews will rejoice in the knowledge of God and because he comes to judge the earth—that is, the good and evil for earthly deeds. For after the persecution of Antichrist and the conversion of the Jews, the Lord will come to judgment, and “will judge the inhabited world in righteousness”: that is, he will justly reward those who were made from earth, yet have become a world—that is, perfect, formed into the circuit of the eternal crown; “and the peoples in equity”: namely, he will condemn false Christians, heretics, and unbelievers according to equity.

Therefore this psalm is sung on the feasts of the Lord, because it proclaims in many ways the power of the Lord.

## PSALM XCVIII

[Col. 0591]

[Col. 0591D] “The Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry,” etc. The preceding psalm contains the Holy Spirit’s exhortation; this one contains the Jews’ praise. In the other psalm, “The Lord has reigned,” the called Gentiles praise God; in this psalm, Jews invited to faith rejoice in Christ. The title of the psalm is:

**VERSE 1. A PSALM [Note: [Col. 0591D] The Vulgate adds: “Of David himself.”] OF DAVID.**

That is: This praise is sung to Christ, the desired one, by a faithful and strong people. This psalm is the ninety-eighth, which is seven times fourteen. By seven, the fullness of time is expressed; by ten, the Decalogue of the Law; by four, the observance of the four Gospels. It signifies that, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, the Israelite people will pass from the Law to the Gospel and thus be saved.

Otherwise: By seven, rest is indicated; by fourteen, Christ’s generation, because his genealogy is woven through three sets of fourteen generations, and God is read to have rested on the seventh day. This number signifies [Col. 0593A] that the Jews, generated from him through faith in Christ, will enter eternal rest.

The subject of the psalm is the praise of Jews converted to faith. Its purpose is to show that Christ is God and Lord of all, and most worthy of praise. The words seem taken from the praise of Levites singing to God in the temple, and signify the praise of Jews rejoicing to God in the Church.

It is divided into two parts because Christ’s humanity and Deity are proclaimed in it. One part begins, “The Lord has reigned,” in which Christ’s royal honor is expressed; the other, “Exalt,” in which his humanity is declared worthy of worship. It is the voice of Jews praising God for his benefits:

“The Lord has reigned.” Three psalms have the same beginning: “The Lord has reigned, he is clothed with majesty”; “The Lord has reigned, let the earth rejoice”; “The Lord has reigned, let the peoples be angry.” They seem to proceed backwards. For he ought first to have placed, “The Lord has reigned, let the peoples be angry”; then, “The Lord has reigned, let the earth rejoice”; and last, “The Lord has reigned, he is clothed with majesty.” But, as has often been said, this book is spiritual and follows its own order, always beginning with what is greater and completing its words with what is lower. It begins with kingship, which is chief among things; kings are clothed with majesty and strength, whence come rejoicing for themselves and their friends, followed by the anger of the envious. The Lord chose the Hebrew people from the world and reigned among them; he clothed himself with majesty because he surrounded himself with patriarchs and prophets as with a precious garment; he clothed himself with strength because he girded himself with judges and kings as with splendid weapons. Then he chose the Gentiles and reigned among them; therefore the earth rejoices and all the islands of the sea are glad. The whole earth is like an island, being surrounded on every side by ocean. Moreover, churches are called islands because, placed among bitter waters, they are battered here and there by the waves of tribulations. He will yet convert the Jewish nation and establish his kingdom within it; then the peoples subject to Antichrist will be angry. Therefore this psalm begins as the other does, because it announces that the Jews are to be joined with the Gentiles in Christ’s praise. The Lord who conquered death, redeemed the world, subdued the Gentiles, and subjected his Jewish enemies to faith—he reigns in all. “Let the peoples be angry”: this is said mockingly. Let peoples be angry at Christ’s kingdom, though they can do no harm, because whether willing or unwilling he reigns everywhere—he to whom the faithless once said, “We will not have this man reign over us” (Luke 19:14), but whom they now worship as subjects. That Lord reigns who sits above the Cherubim—that is, above every height of the angels. This points to Christ, who, ascending into heaven, is exalted above every order of angels at the right hand of God the Father. For the Cherubim are among the highest orders of angels, and the name is interpreted “fullness of knowledge”; it signifies those full of love, whom he set beneath himself especially as a throne, in whom he rests. Or: You, Lord, who sit above the Cherubim—that is, reign in the righteous—let the earth be moved: that is, let those who desire earthly things, such as Julian and others of that kind, be indignant as much as they wish. At the kingdom of the eternal Christ, by which he will reign in faithful Jews and Gentiles, unbelieving peoples under Antichrist become angry and the whole earth is shaken in persecution. But faithful Jews say: What concern is lacking?

**VERSE 2.** The Lord Jesus, who was in Zion—that is, in Jerusalem—is himself great, that is, exceedingly powerful; and high above all angry and shaken peoples. He is able to restrain them and raise us up, humble them and exalt us. Now they turn to him, saying: Let these peoples, angry against you and subdued, 

**VERSES 3–4.** “Confess your great name”: that is, praise your name, which is “Lord,” as we also say that it is great above every name and able to do all that it wills, because it is terrible to sinners in judgment and holy—that is, pleasant—to the righteous. “And the honor of the King loves judgment”: that is, that King who reigns everywhere is honored because he condemns the wicked and rewards the righteous. Or the confession of Christ the King requires this judgment: that each person accuse himself concerning sins and condemn them through repentance; then honor his name by doing good works. “You have prepared directions”: that is, you, Lord, prepared correction and amendment for them. “You have executed judgment and righteousness in Jacob,” because you justly blinded that people and now have enlightened it by grace. Likewise, if those hardened by righteousness are converted, you will receive them by grace. Therefore:

[Col. 0594C] **VERSE 5.** “Exalt the Lord our God”: that is, O peoples, do not be angry, but receive God’s kingdom and believe him to be exalted above all things, the true God and our Lord. “And worship his footstool”: that is, the Lord’s body, because it is holy—that is, innocent and filled with the abundance of every virtue. By the feet is understood the stability of the Deity; by the footstool, the humanity upon which God sat and walked among human beings. Note that they are commanded to exalt God and worship the footstool, because whoever worships Christ’s humanity will be exalted by his Deity. It is the voice of believing Jews to unbelievers: Worship Christ, the footstool of Deity, because:

[Col. 0594D] **VERSE 6.** Moses the lawgiver, mediator between God and human beings, god to Pharaoh and leader of the people, worshipped him and sacrificed to him. Samuel also, the greatest of the prophets and anointer of kings, worshipped him and invoked him. Worship and invoke him, because Moses and Aaron among his priests invoked him—not another—and Samuel among those who invoke his name invoked him. These fathers are introduced because of their greater authority, and because they alone are recorded to have prayed for enemies, so that, following their example, they may invoke God for enemies and know that they will be heard. Moses means “assumption”; Aaron, “mountain of strength”; Samuel, “his name is God.” Christ is understood: assumed from the Word of God, he is the mountain of strength for the Church, his name is God, and he is to be worshipped. Our fathers [Col. 0595A] invoked the Lord, and he heard them, did whatever they asked of him, and:

**VERSES 7–8.** “He spoke to them in the pillar of cloud.” A pillar of cloud went before the Hebrews. In it God appeared to the people, and from it he gave commands. A pillar is placed in a house for strength and adornment, and the building is supported by it. Christ’s humanity is the pillar of cloud, by which the structure of the Church is sustained and God’s house is excellently adorned. In this pillar God spoke to the people of the faithful, because “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). God spoke formerly through the pillar of cloud to the fathers, or through Christ to the faithful; and they kept his testimonies—that is, they believed his promises—and observed the commandment which he gave them, [Col. 0595B] namely the commandment of love, of which he said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 15:12). They kept this commandment when they prayed even for enemies, like Moses and Samuel; and you, Lord our God—not another—heard them praying for enemies. God, you were gracious to them, remitting sins and sparing the guilty because of their prayers, and “taking vengeance upon all their inventions”: that is, punishing their sins. An invention is the presumption of an unprecedented deed. God did not punish the Gentiles for sins because he left them to the fires of Gehenna; but he always punished the presumptions of the Hebrews, because he purified them for life. For God chastises every son whom he receives; but those whom he does not care to correct, he neglects. Therefore:

**VERSE 9.** “Exalt the Lord our God”: that is, worship the God of our fathers, exalted above all things; “and worship at his holy mountain”: that is, in his body touched by blood and worshipped by the fathers, because that mountain is holy, sanctifying all who believe in it. He himself is the Lord our God: God is man, and therefore he is to be invoked and worshipped by all. He saves those who invoke him and condemns those who do not worship him.

It should be noted that in the psalms verses are often written which are similar in words but different in meaning, just as gems of the same color but different kinds are set in royal ornament. The feasts of the Lord also frequently use this psalm, because it proclaims Christ’s deeds.

## PSALM XCIX

[Col. 0595]

[Col. 0595C] “Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth,” etc. This psalm concerns the praise of the whole Church. Its title is:

**(VERSE 1.) A PSALM OF CONFESSION.**

That is, of praise. In Hebrew it reads: “A song in thanksgiving.” For in this psalm the Church praises God and gives thanks because the Synagogue, joined to it in faith, sings together with Christ. This psalm is the ninety-ninth, and this number indicates that those who praise God in faith in the Trinity are joined with the angels in heaven.

Its subject is the Church’s praise. Its purpose is to exhort the faithful to praise Christ if they desire to be made equal to angels. It is divided into two parts because the Church is divided into two peoples. One part begins, “Make a joyful noise to the Lord,” in which the praise of the Church of the Gentiles is sung; the other begins, “his people,” in which the praise of the Church from the Jews is set forth. The words are taken from the singers of the temple, who signify those praising Christ in the Church and who will praise him for ever and ever in the world to come. It is the voice of teachers to the Church from the Gentiles:

**VERSE 2.** “Make a joyful noise to the Lord [Vulgate: to God], all the earth.” O faithful, who have assembled from all the earth to faith in Christ, make joyful noise to the true Lord—that is, give thanks in all things with gladness of mind. And, rescued from the devil’s dominion, serve this Lord with gladness—that is, do good works cheerfully. Joyful noise pertains to contemplation; service pertains to action. “Enter before his presence with exultation”: that is, do not rejoice in outward things, but enter the inner chamber and exult before God in spiritual things.

**VERSE 3.** Know that the Lord Jesus himself is God, not another. He made us first bodily, and secondly spiritually in the new creation; and we did not make ourselves. The Father as a farmer sowed; the mother as earth received the seed; God gave the increase. Since he himself is creator, he is rightly praised by the creature. There follows the teachers’ admonition to the Church from the Jews: Not only you faithful from the Gentiles, but also you from the Jews, who have become by faith his people—and he is our King—and the sheep of his pasture, namely of Holy Scripture or of paradise; and he is our shepherd,
**VERS. 4–5.** Enter through his gates, namely faith and baptism, with confession of sins or of praise; and [Col. 0596D] enter into his courts, namely the prophets and apostles, imitating them in abundant love. In hymns confess him—that is, give him thanks for all things and ascribe everything to him. Praise his name, because the Lord is gracious; and do not shun this out of servile fear, but hunger for it in chaste fear. For the Lord is gracious, not harsh or bitter, but gracious to those who hunger. His mercy endures for ever. It will not fail those who have been converted and praise him, but remains always entire. And his truth endures from generation to generation: that is, the truth of his promises is fulfilled in the generation reborn through faith, and will be fulfilled in the generation of those who rise again. In this generation [Col. 0597A] forgiveness of sins will be given; in that generation, incorruption of bodies and equality with angels will be given.

[Col. 0598A] Therefore this psalm is sung at Lauds after “The Lord has reigned,” because, after Christ reigned from the wood of the cross, the whole earth raised a joyful shout to him.

## PSALM 100. Concerning Judgment.

[Col. 0597]

[Col. 0597B] “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord,” etc. The fiftieth psalm sings of repentance, but this hundredth psalm of mercy, because those who have brought forth the hundredfold fruit of repentance will receive the reward of life at the judgment. This psalm is fittingly placed after the preceding one, in which the Church’s thanksgiving for the conversion of the Jews is written, because immediately after the Jews’ faith the last judgment will follow. It is counted in the hundredth place because, at the judgment, the hundredth sheep is joined to the heavenly flock through the mercy of the loving shepherd. The title of the psalm is:

**(VERS. 1–2.) A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF.**

That is: thus the praise of good works is attributed to Christ himself, the victorious judge, delightful in aspect. Its subject is the merits of the Church to be rewarded at judgment. Its purpose is to urge us to turn away from evil and do good, that we may be able to find mercy at judgment. The words are drawn from David’s rule, who governed the kingdom of Israel well, hated the wicked, and loved the good; and this signifies the rule of Christ, who governs the Church well, hates the wicked, and loves the good.

It has two divisions, because the Church’s conduct has two parts: namely, avoiding evil and doing good. The first part is, “Mercy and judgment,” in which seven things to be avoided are noted; the other is, “My eyes,” in which six things to be done are mentioned. The voice is that of the Church:

“I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.” Mercy concerning the present and judgment concerning the future are sung. O Lord, Trinity, with joy I shall proclaim [Col. 0597D] to others the mercy which must be ascribed to you, which you show here to penitents, and the judgment which you display in those remaining in hardness of heart. For to the former you will give joys, to the latter punishments. “I will make music, and understand in the undefiled way”: that is, because you are a righteous judge, I shall do good by abstaining from evil. Singing belongs to contemplation; making music, to action. The undefiled way is innocence. True innocence is that which harms neither itself nor another, since “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6). And no one sins first against another rather than against himself. In this way I shall make music by doing good, and I shall understand when you come to me—that is, when you reward me.

Otherwise: I shall make music and be innocent, and shall understand that you will render rewards for this. O Bridegroom, when will you come to me, to lead me, your bride, out of Babylon and bring me into the city Jerusalem? He now explains the undefiled way.

[Col. 0598B] “I walked in the innocence of my heart”: that is, I abstained not only from a depraved action but also from an evil thought of the heart. And this was “in the midst of my house,” that is, publicly among all who dwell in the house of the Church. From this point he enumerates the merits for which he hopes for heavenly things. First he sets out seven things all must avoid; then six things all must do. The things to be avoided are these: imitation of an unjust deed, transgression of the law, murmuring, malice, detraction, pride, and covetousness. This is what he says:

**VERS. 3–4.** “I did not set an unjust thing before my eyes”: that is, I did not set before the eyes of my heart doing evil, nor of imitating those who do it, nor of consenting to those who do it. “I hated those committing transgressions.” I hated parents, relatives, and friends [Col. 0598C] transgressing your law—not the persons, however, but their errors. “A perverse heart did not cleave to me”: that is, the evil will of one who murmurs, or someone’s perverse counsel, found nothing in me agreeing with itself. Murmurers and contrivers of perverse counsels were not my companions. “I did not know the malicious person departing from me”: that is, one maliciously departing from my purpose I avoided as though I did not recognize him. Or: I so abhorred a heretic departing from me with a corrupt doctrine and acting maliciously that I treated him as unknown.

**VERS. 5.** “The one secretly slandering his neighbour, him I persecuted”: that is, one who disparaged his brother in secret and sowed discord, I attacked as an enemy. The slanderer sins more grievously than the fornicator: the latter kills himself alone, but the former kills both himself and his neighbour. [Col. 0598D] The wicked must not only be avoided, that they may be put to shame; they must also be pursued, that they may be corrected.

In the Hebrew it reads: “I killed him,” because slanderers are slain by the sword of their own tongue.

“With a proud eye and an insatiable heart, I did not eat with him”: that is, I did not eat with the proud and the covetous. Every proud or covetous person is envious, because, while wishing to appear alone powerful or rich, he is tormented by others’ goods and fed by others’ evils. I did not enter into the banquet of envy with such persons; indeed, I so detested them that I would not tolerate them at my table. Hence Scripture commands us not even to take food with such a person (1 Cor. 5:11). Pride is especially marked in the eyes, because the proud, who think themselves worthier than others, are said even to look down upon others. Covetousness, however, is attributed to the heart, because a heart empty of God is not satisfied with perishing things. These two vices are more notable than the rest because they are worse than all others. For “pride is the beginning [Col. 0599A] of every sin” (Ecclus. 10:15), and “covetousness is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:20). Through the former an angel fell from heaven; through the latter man fell from paradise. From these two, as from the devil’s fountains, all evils proceed and drag the wretched into torments. All these things which have been mentioned must not merely be avoided; they must also be hated and pursued.

There follow six things to be done: faithfulness, chastity, humility, preaching, holy conduct, and opposition to the wicked. Of these he adds:

**VERS. 6.** “My eyes are upon the faithful of the earth, that they may sit with me”: that is, my attention was not upon the noble and rich of this world, in order to set them over your people, but upon the faithful of the Church, that I might appoint them as prelates and rulers, to sit with me in judgment and judge [Col. 0599B] your people justly. “The one walking in the undefiled way, he ministered to me”: that is, I appointed not unchaste persons, but chaste and innocent ministers of the altar.

**VERS. 7.** “He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house”: that is, those sinning openly and defending it proudly did not remain publicly with me in communion, because I excluded them from the sacraments and from the house of the Church; but the humble and obedient were my fellow-citizens. “He who speaks iniquity did not stand upright before my eyes”: that is, a flatterer desiring to please by wicked words did not direct himself toward what pleased me. Or, vain talkers did not please my eyes so as to be my messengers, namely preachers and persuaders of good things.

[Col. 0599C] **VERS. 8.** “In the morning I killed all sinners of the earth”: that is, in good works, which are a kind of morning of the eternal day, I killed every sin of my earthliness; and by my example I destroyed all who sin and seek only earthly things. “That I might destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity”: that is, I assailed the wicked in word and deed, that I might convert them from iniquity to righteousness, or wholly separate them from the Church.

These things also suit Christ the Judge: “My eyes are upon the faithful of the earth, that they may sit with me”; that is, I chose the apostles and other faithful persons from the earth, that they might sit with me as judges at the judgment. “The one walking in the undefiled way, he ministered to me”: that is, my undefiled ministers [Col. 0600A] will be there where I am. Those who stain themselves with impurity do not minister to Christ; those who seek what is their own do not serve Christ, and therefore will not be with Christ. “He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house.” No one who performs evil works descending from pride will dwell in my heavenly house, Jerusalem. “He who speaks iniquity did not stand upright before my eyes”: that is, not only those doing evil, but also those speaking wickedly, will not be before me—that is, they will not see my face. “In the morning I killed all sinners of the earth.” The present life is like night; eternal life is like day, whose morning is the day of judgment. In that morning the Lord will kill with the sword of his mouth all sinners of the earth—that is, those desiring earthly things—saying, [Col. 0600B] “Depart from me, all workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:27). “That I might destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity.” Then he will separate goats from sheep, tares from wheat, chaff from grain, and will cast them from the city of heavenly Jerusalem and from the company of the saints, with the devil and his angels, into eternal fire.

Observe the order of the tenth decade, which pertains to the number ten of life. The first psalm sings of Christ’s works, which he performed while in the flesh before his passion, when he planted palms and cedars for building the house. Its title mentions the Sabbath, on which he rested from his works. The second psalm recounts Christ’s deeds after the resurrection, when he founded the earth for the building of the house, and the fountain of life rose up as rivers to water [Col. 0600C] it. In the third, its lights are formed and its inhabitants arranged. In the fourth, Gentiles and Jews are called to Christ’s rest in his house. In the fifth, the Gentiles who have been called are exhorted to praise Christ the Maker, and the house is built of them as though of living stones. In the sixth, the Gentiles now built into the Lord’s house resound with praises, whereby they restore to Christ the earth lost in paradise. In the seventh, the Jews are invited and exhorted to Christ’s praise, and are built together with the Gentiles in God’s house. In the eighth, the Jews voice praises to Christ. In the ninth, the whole Church rejoices in thanksgiving to him. In the tenth, Christ separates the wicked from his house and rewards the good according to their merits.

## PSALM 101.

[Col. 0599]

[Col. 0599D] “Lord, hear my prayer,” etc. This is one of the seven penitential psalms, in which the remission of the sevenfold Spirit is marked. It is placed fifth because Christ’s passion is described in it, through whose five wounds humankind receives remission from sins. The first penitential psalm is assigned to the Spirit of fear; the second, to the Spirit of piety; the third, to the Spirit of knowledge; the fourth, to the Spirit of fortitude; this fifth, to the Spirit of counsel, because through Christ, the Angel of great counsel, [Col. 0600D] the human race is delivered from death, as is recounted in this psalm. It is aptly placed after that first psalm in which judgment is described, because through repentance a human being escapes the sentence of judgment. It is well suited to penitents, because it commands that ashes be eaten as bread and drink mingled with weeping. This is the hundred-and-first psalm—that is, ten times ten and one—and signifies that to those who fulfil the ten commandments of the law is promised [Col. 0601A] the number ten of life, which is the one God. The title of the psalm is:

**VERS. 1. A PRAYER OF THE POOR MAN, WHEN HE HAS BEEN DISTRESSED AND HAS POURED OUT HIS SUPPLICATION BEFORE THE LORD.**

> [Note: [Col. 0601] Vulgate: “has poured out his supplication in the presence of the Lord.”]

That is: it is the prayer of the Lord Jesus, who, though rich in the glory of the Father, became poor for us—that is, mortal and passible. It is, I say, a prayer offered when he was distressed: when he grieved over the perdition of the human race and poured out his supplication before the Lord, his Father, on the Mount of Olives, when, having become sorrowful unto death, he prayed more earnestly in agony and his sweat ran down to the ground like blood.

The subject is the misery of the human race and Christ’s prayer or passion for it. The purpose is to show that humanity is saved by Christ’s grace alone, and to exhort us to prayer and repentance. The words are taken [Col. 0601B] from Adam, whose bone adhered to flesh when God built his rib into a woman and supplied flesh in its place. This signifies that the power of God—namely, the Word made flesh—adhered to flesh and built the Church from his own body.

This psalm is divided into three parts, because three kinds of persons are marked in it under the figure of three birds. The first part is, “Lord, hear,” in which the prayer of a penitent is set forth. The second, “I am struck down like grass,” bewails the misery of the human race. The third, “But you, O Lord,” explains humanity’s restoration through Christ. The voice is that of the human race in Christ. The misery of the whole human race is here lamented, that the Judge may be moved to mercy; and the building of [Col. 0601C] heavenly Zion from living stones is celebrated. Since Christ is one of humankind, he speaks for all human beings. He is judge, advocate, mediator, and reconciler of the world:

**VERS. 2.** “Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you.” The human race prayed anxiously through Christ on the mountain, and through him cried out upon the cross: O Lord Father, hear my prayer, which I, as man, pour forth for the human race that is distressed in misery; and let my cry come to you, that it may be delivered from misery. Prayer is petition, even with little inward intent. Thus Moses is told, “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. 14:15), although he is recorded as having said nothing. Christ prayed for humankind on the Mount of Olives; on the cross he cried out for them.

[Col. 0601D] **VERS. 3.** “Do not turn your face away from me,” your Son praying, as you turned it away from Adam when he sinned. The face of God is knowledge of him. In paradise man in some manner saw God’s face, because he had a very great knowledge of him. When Adam sinned, God turned his face away from them, because he withdrew from him the knowledge of himself. Therefore he now prays that God may restore this knowledge to those believing in him. “On whatever day I am troubled, incline your ear to me.” The human race prays this in Christ. From the time humanity fell from paradise, it has been in tribulation every day. Therefore it must call upon God every day because of tribulation, that he may incline the ear of mercy to it. The comparison is with a physician bending toward a sick person unable to raise his [Col. 0602A] voice. God inclined his ear to humanity when Christ humbled himself to death upon the cross. “On whatever day I call upon you, hear me speedily.” On the day of his passion Christ called upon the Father for human salvation, and he heard him speedily by restoring humankind through him. Hear me:

**VERS. 4.** “For my days have failed like smoke.” This is the voice of the human race in Christ. Humanity’s days in paradise were eternal; in this world they became unstable like smoke. For as smoke rises on high and vanishes, so the time of human life, growing from childhood into youth, thence into old age, and thence declining toward death, comes to an end. “And my bones have dried up like a frying-pan.” The bones of the soul are rationality and free choice, which after sin were so weakened in humanity as a frying-pan loses its strength when its juices are extracted. Hence another translation has: “They have been crushed as in a frying-pan.” Rationality dried up because it lost the sharpness it formerly possessed; free choice dried up because it no longer has the ease it formerly had. Literally, too, bones stripped of marrow dry up in the tomb, just as a frying-pan dries out when its fat has been drawn off. This happened because:

**VERS. 5.** “I was struck down like grass, and my heart dried up.” All flesh is grass, and from it Christ took a human body. Therefore he was struck down like grass—that is, like another human being—by sufferings. As grass flourishes for a time and, once cut by the sickle, quickly dries up, so humanity flourishes [Col. 0602C] for a short time, languishes when struck by sickness, and, cut down by death, its heart dries up because it loses sense and understanding. Why then did this happen? “Because I forgot to eat my bread.” The bread of the soul is the commandment of life. God gave bread to humanity to eat when he set before it the commandment of life to keep. For when he said, “Keep this, lest you die,” it was equivalent to saying, “Eat this bread, that you may live.” Humanity forgot to eat this bread of its own when it was not diligent to keep the Lord’s commandment: forgetting the commandment, it touched what was forbidden; forgetting to eat bread, it drank poison. Hence its heart was struck and dried like grass. Christ put on this grass and changed it into bread; he restored the human being struck by the serpent and dried up by death. [Col. 0602D] It follows:

**VERS. 6.** “At the sound of my groaning, my bone adhered to my flesh.” The voice of human groaning was the devil’s voice, which said, “Eat, and you shall be like gods.” Because humanity heard this voice, it fell into the groaning of pain and death. “Bone” signifies masculine strength; “flesh,” feminine weakness. At the sound of groaning, bone adhered to flesh when, through the devil’s persuasion, the man consented to the woman. For Eve was made from Adam’s bone, and flesh was restored in its place. This bone adhered to flesh when, expelled from paradise, he joined himself to the woman through concupiscence. Had they remained in paradise, they would have begotten children without concupiscence, pain, or defilement. But because they heard [Col. 0603A] the devil’s voice, they unite through concupiscence in animal fashion, give birth in pain and groaning, rear their offspring like the young of beasts, and return to the earth in pain and groaning by dying.

This is also Christ’s voice: “At the sound of my groaning, my bone adhered to my flesh.” Christ’s bone was his divinity, which adhered to flesh when the Word put on flesh because of the sound of the human race’s groaning as it cried to God in misery. Bone also adhered to flesh when strong Christ joined himself to the Church.

**VERS. 7–8.** “I became like a pelican of the wilderness.” The pelican is a large Egyptian bird, like a stork, always emaciated by its natural leanness. There are two kinds: one always remains in pools and feeds on fish, and in Latin is called an *onocrotalus*; the other is always in the wilderness, and its food consists of venomous [Col. 0603B] creatures—serpents, crocodiles, and lizards. This bird is said to kill its young, mourn for them during three days, and on the third day wound itself and revive its offspring by sprinkling them with its own blood. It is called the pelican “of the wilderness” to distinguish it from the one that remains in pools. Christ became like this bird because he alone was born of a virgin and, as it were, ate poisonous creatures when he received sinners into his body. He raised up as though slain offspring by the sprinkling of his blood, when he gave life through the shedding of his own blood to human beings dead in sins.

“I became like a *nycticorax* in a dwelling-place.” *Nycte* means “night,” *corax* “raven”; *nycticorax* means “night-raven.” Some call it a horned owl (*bubo*), others an owl (*noctua*); it loves only darkness. Christ [Col. 0603C] became like this bird, namely blackened by his sufferings as a sinner, loving darkness—that is, sinners—not that they might remain darkness, but that they might become light—that is, righteous persons. A dwelling-place is where, once the house has been destroyed, only the walls remain. Hence the Hebrew reads: “Among ruins,” where the night-raven dwells. The dwelling-place was the Jewish people, inwardly destroyed by a throng of demons. In this dwelling Christ became like a *nycticorax*, because he was accounted a sinner in the hearts of the Jews. The *nycticorax* flies only at night, and Christ delivers sinners only through death. Or, he became like a *nycticorax* in a dwelling-place when I slept, troubled, in the tomb.

Then I awoke, because I rose from death, and became like a solitary sparrow upon the roof. A sparrow separates itself from other [Col. 0603D] birds and lives upon the roof of a house, or in lofty and firm places. The house is the world; the roof is heaven. Christ became like a solitary sparrow on the roof because God-Man alone dwells in heaven. In the Hebrew it is: “like a solitary bird.” Christ was a pelican of the wilderness, alone born of a virgin and alone living without sin; a *nycticorax* in a dwelling-place, dead in the tomb; a solitary sparrow on the roof, the only human being in heaven.

The three kinds of birds also signify three kinds of human beings. The pelican of the wilderness is the believing people from among the Gentiles. Gentile life was like a wilderness because it was inhabited by no holy person. The *nycticorax* is the people converted from among the Jews, who were a dwelling-place of demons. The sparrow is the people who, from among Christians, [Col. 0604A] turn to the contemplative life and fly in mind to the roof of heaven, where, separated from the world’s activities, they dwell in solitude. Before I poured out my blood like a pelican for my children:

**VERS. 9.** “All day long my enemies reproached me”: that is, throughout the whole time of my life the Jews reproached me, calling me a carpenter’s son, demon-possessed, and a friend of tax collectors. Or, throughout the day of the passion my enemies reproached me, while all day they mocked me with blows and spittings and taunted me on the cross. “And those who formerly praised me, saying, ‘We know that you are truthful,’ swore against me” (Matt. 22:16), when, having assembled the council, they condemned me to death. This was because:

**VERS. 10.** “I ate ashes as though bread”: that is, I incorporated sinners into myself as though they were righteous. [Col. 0604B] “And I mingled my cup [Vulgate: drink] with weeping”: that is, I mingled good persons with those for whom one had to weep, and drank sinners as though they were righteous. Therefore those reproaching him said, “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (Luke 15:2). The comparison is taken from places where wine is perhaps mixed with water. By ashes are understood sinners repenting in ashes and sackcloth. For sinful man was told, “You are ashes, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19). Bread signifies those hungering for righteousness; the cup, those thirsting for life; weeping, those lamenting their sins. Christ ate ashes as bread when he joined penitents to those hungering for righteousness; he tempered his drink with weeping when he mingled those mourning their sins with those thirsting for life.

[Col. 0604C] Otherwise: drink is taken inwardly; weeping is expressed outwardly. Christ mingled his cup with weeping in his passion when he drew the Gentiles into himself as a sweet drink and cast out the Jews as weeping. Literally, too, he tempered drink with weeping when the impious offered him, as he thirsted, vinegar mixed with gall. This came about:

**VERS. 11.** “Because of the face of your anger and indignation”: that is, because of the presence of your vengeance and severe punishment, which I endured on Adam’s account. Passibility and mortality, which are punishments for sin, are called God’s anger and indignation. This anger of God remains upon one who does not believe in Christ, through whom God’s anger is taken away and the immortality of the kingdom will be given. Because of your anger I suffered many punishments in the pit of misery: “For, lifting me up, you dashed [Col. 0604D] me down”; that is, you lifted me up through free choice and dashed me down through the judgment of justice.

This again is the voice of the human race in Christ. God raised humanity above all animals by reason and understanding. But because, though placed in honour, it did not understand, he dashed it down into misery. For just as none of the animals has this honour, so none has this misery. Humanity alone, after the many miseries of this life, is thrust after death into avenging flames. Therefore the foregoing also fit a penitent, whose bones dried like a frying-pan because, on account of guilt, he forgot to eat his bread, and whose bone adhered to his flesh at the sound of groaning—namely, so that [Col. 0605A] through fasts and weeping his bones may be visible beneath his flesh; and therefore, through excessive emaciation, he became like a pelican; through black and dirty clothing signifying the blackness of sins, like a night-raven; and through solitary wandering, like a sparrow. His enemies—that is, the impenitent or demons—reproach him all day because he eats ashes as bread and mingles his cup with weeping; because he created his anger and indignation, but dashed him down because of guilt, when he submerged him beneath every punishment.
