The voice of Christ follows: On account of this, Father, you lifted me up upon the cross and dashed me down in death.

**VERS. 12.** “My days declined like a shadow”: that is, they became passing and unstable like a shadow. This is Christ’s own voice concerning himself and his followers. [Col. 0605B] Above was Adam’s voice concerning himself and his descendants: “My days have failed like smoke; I was struck down like grass, and my heart dried up.” My days are like shadow or smoke because I lived for a short time. And I, whom you, God, assumed into yourself, dried up like grass because, consumed by sufferings, I withered in death for the sake of humanity, whom I grieved to see dry up in death like grass.

**VERS. 13.** “But you, O Lord, remain for ever”: that is, your days endure always, and you are able to lead us to them. “And thus your memorial shall be from generation to generation”: that is, your mercy, by which they remember you, or by which you remember them, will be in this life and in the other—namely, among Zion and the Gentiles. Or, your memorial will be in the generation of the Jews [Col. 0605C] and in the generation of the Gentiles.

**VERS. 14.** “You, arising, will have mercy upon Zion.” God seemed to lie down when the people of Zion worshipped idols. Then he seemed to arise when he sent them his Son, the true God. Then he had mercy upon Zion when he first chose the Church from the Jewish people and bestowed faith and virtues upon it. You will arise in me and have mercy on Zion, because it is the time to have mercy on her, because the time of grace has come in which you will have mercy upon her. Of this time it is written: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4). For what purpose? To redeem Zion—that is, those who were under the law. Zion will be built as an inhabited city:

**VERS. 15.** “For her stones pleased your servants”: that is, the prophets pleased your servants, [Col. 0605D] the apostles, builders of Zion—living stones built into it—whom they understood to have foretold this building. Through these stones preaching was promised; from them proceeded the instruction of the Gospel; through their proclamation Christ, the cornerstone, was recognized. Therefore they will have mercy upon her earth, namely the builders, because from earth they made heaven. From that earth came one wall: so many thousands of believers laying the price of their possessions at the apostles’ feet. Another wall follows, coming from the Gentiles.

**VERS. 16.** “And the Gentiles shall fear your name, O Lord,” you who are the cornerstone, joining in yourself the two walls coming from opposite directions. The Gentiles shall fear—that is, venerate—your name, which is Lord. [Col. 0606A] Or: they will venerate me, your Son, who am your name. “And all the kings of the earth [shall fear] your glory”: that is, all rulers will venerate you as glorious. And thus the walls will meet in the cornerstone:

**VERS. 17.** “For the Lord has built Zion in powers”: Come, living stones; run to the structure, not to ruin; Zion is being built; the ark is being built—beware the flood. Once Zion has been built, he who was first seen in his weakness will be seen in his glory. Another translation reads, “in his majesty,” that is, in the power of his divinity. And for what reason did he build this house? Because:

**VERS. 18.** “He regarded the prayer of the humble.” The patriarchs, prophets, and other humble fathers of old prayed to God that he would build in the world the house built in paradise [Col. 0606B] but destroyed by the devil, and would restore through it the city fallen in heaven. God therefore regarded the prayer of the humble when he sent his Son into the world, who bound the people of the faithful together into one Church. “And he did not despise their petition,” because he fulfilled their desire by promising humanity equality with angels.

**VERS. 19.** “Let these things be written for another generation”: namely, let these benefits—prayer, passion, faith, forgiveness, building, and hearing—be held in remembrance in the other generation, which, having been lost, became other. Let this generation, built into God’s house, always keep these things before its eyes. “And the people who shall be created shall praise the Lord”: that is, the Christian people, dead [Col. 0606C] in sins, new in virtues, created out of idolatry and changed into another observance, will praise the Lord for the benefits mentioned above.

**VERS. 20.** “For he looked down from his holy height”: that is, through me, holy in body and exalted in divinity, he looked upon the misery of humankind. “The Lord looked from heaven upon earth”: that is, through me, being heaven, he looked mercifully upon earthly people.

**VERS. 21.** “That he might hear the groaning of the fettered”: that is, that he might free those who groan from the bonds of sins, and release from sins “the children of the slain”—that is, the Gentiles, imitators of the slain Adam and Eve, who were the killers of the whole human race. The groaning fettered ones were the Jews; the children of the slain were the pagans. In [Col. 0606D] Hebrew it is written: “the children of death,” that is, that he might free the devil’s children from sins.

**VERS. 22–23.** “That they may declare the name of the Lord in Zion,” that is, in the Church, “and his praise,” finally in heavenly Jerusalem, “when peoples and kings gather together as one”: that is, they declare the Lord’s name in Zion in order that peoples and kings may come together into the unity of faith, to serve the Lord.

**VERS. 24.** “He answered him in the way of his strength”: that is, the gathering of peoples and kings in Zion answered the Lord Father in the way of his strength, namely in imitation of his Son, who is the way of his strength. For the Word, the power of God, entered among human beings through Jesus Christ and by this way brought back the wandering to life.

Otherwise: Jerusalem, or its praise—that is, the Church [Col. 0607A] called from the whole world—answered Christ in the way of his strength because, as Christ did, so it walked in virtues. Its voice follows here:

“Make known to me the fewness of my days”: that is, the Church, set in the way of strength, answered, saying: Tell me when these few days and the consummation of the age will end, and eternal years come. And it is said to her: “The Gospel will be preached among all nations, and then the end will come” (Matt. 24:14). Literally also the Lord answered Jerusalem in the way of strength when he approached his passion and the people received him with palms. When he heard the people’s song in it, he answered and made known to it the fewness of its days, saying: “Days shall come when your enemies will surround you and cast [Col. 0607B] you and your children within you to the ground, and will not leave in you one stone upon another” (Luke 19:43–44).

The words which follow to the end of the psalm are those of the other generation and of the new-created people, released from fetters, which gathers in Zion and sings praise concerning eternity.

**VERS. 25.** “Do not call me back in the middle of my days”: that is, do not withdraw me from your years, I who am placed in the middle of days. Two parts considered together are each one half, although one is greater and the other lesser, as when one day is compared with a hundred years. The eternal years are one half; the days of this life are the other half. In one half—that is, the temporal—humanity exists; in the other—that is, the eternal—God exists. Therefore it follows: “Your years are from generation [Col. 0607C] to generation,” that is, from the present generation into the future.

Otherwise: do not call me back, by abandoning me to fall again into error, as I stretch from my temporal half—that is, from the fewness of my days—toward your eternal half; rather, help me and draw me as I reach toward eternity. Otherwise: when half my life has been completed, do not call me out of the world uncorrected and imperfect; but permit me to live the whole time you have appointed, as you did Hezekiah, so that, corrected concerning the past and perfected in good works, I may attain to the perfect man, to your years, which are eternal.

**VERS. 26.** “In the beginning, you, O Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.” This is drawn from the new creation of the world, where it is written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). The Beginning is Christ, in whom God made heaven, earth, and all things, as it is written: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). And as there was there a beginning of the world, so here there is a beginning of the new creation—that is, the Church. In this beginning you, Lord God the Father, founded the earth when you established the Church [Col. 0608A] in Christ. “And the heavens are the works of your hands”: that is, the apostles formed through the working of the Holy Spirit.

**VERS. 27.** “They themselves shall perish,” because they will die according to the body. The visible heavens also shall perish, because “heaven and earth shall pass away” (Matt. 24:35); but you remain always in one state.

Since it is said here that the heavens shall perish, the question arises how another Scripture can say, “The earth stands for ever” (Eccles. 1:4), and again, “Every creature of God remains for ever.” One must understand that the form of things will perish; their substance itself remains for ever.

And all of them shall grow old like a garment. The heavens are like the garment of the world: in their present form they fail through age and antiquity. And like a covering [Col. 0608B] you will change them, and they shall be changed. Heaven is the covering of the earth, which shall be rolled up like a tent. But when the judgment has been completed, the heavens shall be changed into another form, because the Lord will then make a new heaven and a new earth; and the moon shall possess the glory of the sun, and the sun the light of seven days. The bodies of the saints are the garments of their souls. Therefore all the saints shall grow old like a garment: that is, the bodies of all shall first fail through old age, and at last through dissolution—likened to a garment which is worn away until it is reduced to nothing. Bodies also are the covering of souls, in which, being covered, they are not seen. Afterwards you will change them from this dissolution like a covering, so that they, who were previously souls, may attain equality with the angels. The heavens—that is, the saints—shall thus be changed:

[Col. 0608C] **VERSE 28.** But you are the very same as you were when you made the world from nothing; you have not grown old, and you are first before all things and last after all things, because you are ever new. And your years shall not fail: that is, your eternity remains forever. You are unchangeable and invariable because eternal; and those whom you made heavens out of earth, you will make eternal.

**VERSE 29.** The children of your servants shall dwell: that is, Christians, the children of the apostles, whom they begot through the Gospel, shall possess those unfailing years of yours, dwelling in the everlasting kingdom, where joy is eternal and security never to be ended. And their seed shall be directed for ages: that is, other Christians begotten from them shall be guided into eternity.

[Col. 0608D] Otherwise: Your years are eternal, and in those years the children of your servants shall dwell; that is, your servants, through children—that is, through good works—shall possess those years, and their seed shall be directed for ever: that is, they shall reap in joy the fruits which they send before them. See what the Son of God accomplished by praying: he brought the human race to eternity.

## PSALM CII. On the blessing of the primitive Church

[Col. 0607]

[Col. 0607D] “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me,” etc. In the preceding psalm the restoration of fallen humanity is sung; in this one, the praise of humanity restored is sung. The subject of this psalm is the blessing of the primitive Church. [Col. 0609A] Its purpose is to exhort people to bless God for the benefits bestowed above. Its title is:

**(VERSE 1.) A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF.**  
[Note: [Col. 0609D] The Vulgate only: “Of David himself.”]

That is: thus praise is sung to Christ—that is, to the noble one, desirable in appearance to the faithful people, mighty in hand against vices. The words of the psalm were taken from David himself, who blessed the Lord for the benefits bestowed upon him, signifying the faithful people, who continually bless the Lord for his benefits.

This psalm occupies the one hundred and second place. The number one hundred expresses perfection; two expresses twofold love, since those truly bless God who are full of love, and these shall have perfect joy. It is divided into three parts, because angelic, human, and inanimate creation are invited to the praise of [Col. 0609B] God. The first part is, “Bless, O my soul,” in which six benefits are recalled: forgiveness of iniquity, healing of infirmity, redemption from destruction, crowning with mercy, fulfillment of good desire, and renewal like that of an eagle. The second part is, “The Lord who performs mercies,” in which the washing away of the punishments of sin and the glorification of the Redeemer are expressed. The third part is, “Bless the Lord,” in which both heavenly and earthly creation are admonished to bless God. It is the voice of the primitive Church exhorting itself to the praise of God.

“Bless the Lord, O my soul”: that is, O my soul, praise the Lord with inward praise. “And let all that is within me bless his holy name.” [Col. 0609C] The name of the Father is the Son, as he himself says: “Father, I have made your name manifest to men” (John 6:6). In a human being there are lungs, stomach, and intestines. These are not exhorted to bless, because it is not the outward but the inward person who speaks here. “All that is within me,” that is, all the powers of my soul—reason, sensuality, sensibility, vegetative power—should bless his holy, venerable, adorable name. As though it said: O soul, redeemed by the Lord from destruction, praise the Lord through all your powers. Because of excessive gladness it repeats:

**VERSE 2.** “Bless the Lord, O my soul.” The spirit speaks to the soul. For there are two principal powers of the soul: one by which it understands spiritual things, which is called spirit; the other by which it gives life to the body, which is called soul. The preceding verse belongs to the spirit, [Col. 0609D] whose inner parts are virtues; but this belongs to the soul, which governs the bodily senses and often turns them to contrary uses. As though rationality said to sensuality: O soul—that is, sensuality—which now is mine, that is, has become subject to my authority, though formerly you were under the devil’s yoke, beneath the burden of sin: bless the Lord, that is, exalt, praise, and bless the Lord in intention, heart, and deed. And do not forget all his recompenses, because he repays you good for evil. Do not consign to oblivion that for your sake he became poor, that he might make you rich; that, free, he was bound, that he might free you from bonds; that, innocent, he was scourged, that he might rescue you from punishments; that the Lord of glory was condemned with thieves, that he might free you, condemned, from torment. [Col. 0610A] Six benefits follow, and “Bless” must be joined to each one: Bless the Lord,

**VERSE 3.** “Who forgives all your iniquities”: that is, who is merciful toward all your sins, original and actual, venial and mortal. Bless him who heals all your infirmities: that is, who heals all your sicknesses and pains. The comparison is drawn from a sick person: when the infirmity has been driven out, weakness and pain still remain until he wholly recovers. Thus, after sins have been forgiven, there still remain the tinder of sin, its remembrance, and weakness arising from past evil habit. He heals all these by habituating one to good works. Bless the Lord,

**VERSE 4.** “Who redeems your life from destruction”: that is, who, having given a price, redeems your soul into the life [Col. 0610B] of the body from hell, where destruction is always present, so that you may live not in punishments but in rest. He says “redeems” in the present tense, although redemption was accomplished once for all, because daily through the sacrifice of his body he redeems souls from the destruction of death. Bless the Lord, who crowns you in mercy: that is, who will crown you, the conqueror of vices, with glory—a victory which was not from yourself but from mercy, that is, from the conception of mercy, and from acts of compassion, that is, in the bestowal of mercy. When you are crowned, this too is grace: grace for grace. Mercy is that Christ came to the exile; compassion, that he redeemed the slave; mercy, that he helps one fighting against vices to conquer; compassion, that he rewards the victor. Bless the Lord.

[Col. 0610C] **VERSE 5.** “Who satisfies your desire with good things”: that is, he shall so fill your desire, existing among good things, with every good that you will say, “It is enough; I seek no further.” Such is that good which will not become wearisome: it is always desired, and desire is always fulfilled. In this good your youth shall be renewed like an eagle’s: that is, with old age removed you shall be new; with corruption removed, incorruptible.

Natural philosophers relate that an eagle’s beak continually grows in old age, so that it cannot take food; and, when it has already been weakened by extreme emaciation, it approaches a rock and, striking against it, breaks the beak. Then, taking food without hindrance, it recovers as much vigor as it formerly possessed. By this the human being [Col. 0610D] is likened to the eagle: burdened by the weight of sins, he does not seek to eat the heavenly bread until he turns to the rock—that is, Christ—and the body of sin is destroyed; and, having put off the old person, he is renewed in the spirit of his mind and eats the bread of heaven. Another thing is reported of the eagle. When it grows old, it flies upward against the sun; when its wings have been burned, it falls into a fountain, and, emerging from it, grows young. So the person born in sins, if he falls upon Christ, the sun of righteousness, and is immersed in the fountain of baptism, will come forth new, as he was in paradise. Likewise, in the resurrection, when the old age of corruption has been put off, he will be a new person, shining like the sun and equal to the angels. From this point he begins to prove [Col. 0611A] that the punishments of sin which now reign—namely hunger, thirst, toil, pain, susceptibility to suffering, and mortality—will be removed, and immortality and impassibility bestowed. Those truly converted to Christ will be renewed, because:

**VERSE 6.** “The Lord performs mercies”: here forgiving sins, in the future removing the punishments of sin, and rendering judgment for all who suffer injury, because in the future he will condemn by just judgment those who inflict injury here, and reward those who suffer it. The righteous suffer injury because here they are afflicted with the punishments of sin along with the unrighteous. To these the Lord performs mercies, when the merciful obtain mercy. And he will render them judgment when he brings them to joy, while judging the ungodly to punishment. But someone says: Many who do not know how to do good will perish unjustly. [Col. 0611B] Against this it is said: They are without excuse, who are able to know but refuse to know the ways of the Lord. Now the Lord

**VERSE 7.** “Made his ways known to Moses”: that is, he commanded Moses to write his precepts, which he willed to become known to all. And he made his wills known to the children of Israel through the law and the prophets, through whom all people could learn what ought to be avoided and what ought to be done. And why did he not immediately punish those who despised them? Because:

**VERSE 8.** “The Lord is compassionate and merciful”: that is, the Lord, compassionate in bestowing acts of pity, merciful in nature, long-suffering as he patiently waits for sinners and does not punish them, and greatly merciful beyond what a human being can conceive. Therefore he does not will [Col. 0611C] the death of the sinner, but that he should be converted and live.

**VERSE 9.** “He will not be angry for ever, nor threaten to eternity.” Here he is angry at our evils; therefore we are afflicted by the punishments of sin, namely hunger, thirst, and others, and here he threatens sinners with the punishment of Gehenna. But he will not be angry forever, because the punishment of sin, called his anger, will be removed in the future; and since then no one will sin, he will threaten no one. For such things the Lord should be blessed.

**VERSE 10.** “He has not dealt with us according to our sins,” original or venial, “nor repaid us according to our iniquities,” actual or mortal. Every sin dishonors God. Therefore every sin deserves punishment. He has not assigned [Col. 0611D] us the punishments owed according to our sins; rather, according to unmerited mercy he has given glory.

**VERSE 11.** “For according to the height of heaven above the earth he has strengthened his mercy upon those who fear him”: that is, just as heaven protects the earth on every side, encloses it within itself, and leaves no part without protection, so mercy protects those who fear him. Upon those who fear him, not upon others, he made his mercy strong after the manner of the height of heaven above the earth; that is, by as much as heaven is worthier than earth, by so much through his mercy he has made us worthier than we were. For we were muddy and foul, and he made us clean.

**VERSE 12.** “As far as east is from west, so far has he made us distant from what we were.” And he has made [Col. 0612A] our iniquities as far from us as east is from west—that is, as far as the light of the sun is from the west, that is, from darkness. For those who were formerly darkness in sins and wandered in the darkness of ignorance have become light in the Lord, and Christ the light has risen in them. Nothing can be farther away than that which does not exist. Or, he has removed our iniquities from us as far as the east—that is, heaven, where joy always rises—is from the west—that is, hell, where there is always setting and destruction.

**VERSE 13.** “As a father has compassion on his children, the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him”: that is, just as a father corrects his son lest he lose his inheritance for some superfluous matters, so the Lord corrects those who fear him in many ways lest they lose their inheritance. Note three comparisons: [Col. 0612B] the height of heaven, the rising of the sun, and a father’s affection, because he has established us in heaven equal to angels, shining as the brightness of the sun, heirs of God the Father. Therefore, as a father, he scourges us here and does not abandon us.

**VERSE 14.** “For he knew our formation”: that is, our creation, and from how frail a material we were created. Here some say that the devil fell irrecoverably because, unlike man, he did not have the material of flesh through which to sin. What formation? This: “He remembered that we are dust”: that is, because we were made from dust. Or, we are susceptible to the wind of suggestion and unable to resist the powers of the air, comparable to grass in our brevity. For:

**VERSE 15.** “Man is like grass.” In what respect? In [Col. 0612C] his days. “His days shall blossom like a flower of the field.” The days of a human being are brief and quickly fail, just as grass cut by a scythe quickly fails; and just as a flower withers and fails more quickly than other things, so a human being quickly falls into decay. Or, a person according to the flesh is like grass; his days—that is, purity of mind—shall blossom like a flower of the field, that is, like a flower it is changeable. Therefore he said “a flower of the field,” not of the plain, because a field is arable and fruitful land, in which cut grasses dry more quickly than those of a meadow or forest, which, uncut, last longer. Truly, a human being is like grass.

**VERSE 16.** “For the spirit that is in him shall pass away”: that is, he shall die and shall not remain in the form [Col. 0612D] in which he was before, but shall wither like a flower. And because some say that after a hundred years the soul returns to the body, he says: “And it shall no longer know its place”: that is, it shall no longer know the body in which it was, so as to have to return. Truly we are dust, because the spirit that is in a person will lightly pass, at the Lord’s command, into sin; and it will not remain in one sin, but fall from vice into vice, and it will no longer know its place—that is, its former state, its former dignity, where it was before—and will not recover it by itself, unless through grace. For the spirit is one that goes and does not return. A human being shall not remain;

**VERSE 17.** “But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity”: that is, it remains before the ages and shall remain unto eternity upon those who fear him, to protect them or restore [Col. 0613A] the fallen. This protective “upon” means that, from the first righteous person to the last, the mercy of God protects those who love him. Here there will be mercy, and in the future reward. For “his righteousness is upon children’s children”: that is, the Lord’s equity shall be for the recompense of righteous works. For our works are our children. Righteous people are children of God; their children are good works, for which they shall receive rewards. But that recompense shall not be for all, but:

**VERSE 18.** “For those who keep his covenant,” that is, his commandment; or for those who observe his precepts, this recompense shall remain upon children’s children—that is, throughout all generations. And for those who are mindful of his commandments, not for vanity, not for human favor, but in order to do them. [Col. 0613B] For it profits nothing to know the psalter and sing the psalms unless good works follow. Those who keep the commandments he will raise into heaven. For:

**VERSE 19.** “The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven.” In three ways he has prepared his throne through virtues in the saints, so that through them he may judge those who do not keep the commandments. Or, the Lord has prepared his throne in heaven because he will appoint the Church, his throne, in heaven with the angels. And then his kingdom shall rule over all, good and evil alike. Or, the Church, his kingdom, shall rule over all things that are Christ’s when it is set over all the Lord’s goods. The praise of the angels follows from the fellowship of the righteous:

**VERSE 20.** “Bless the Lord, all his angels,” [Col. 0613C] that is, O heavenly creatures, do what you do: fulfill the wills of God, observing his commandments. “Mighty in strength”—understand, the Lord’s strength, not wickedness, as in the devil—“doing his word,” that is, fulfilling his command, “in order to hear the voice of his words,” that is, in order that you may make the voice of his words heard by all.

Otherwise: Angels are called messengers, and the apostles are understood: mighty through Christ’s power in miracles, doing his word—that is, fulfilling his precepts—[Col. 0614A] in order to make others hear the preaching of his words, that is, his commandments. Therefore he calls preachers angels, because no one will ever be saved unless he is like one of the orders of angels.

**VERSE 21.** “Bless the Lord, all his powers”: that is, all the angels through whom he performs mighty works. In the Hebrew it reads: “All his host,” and all the orders of angels are understood. They are called powers because they persevere strongly in their station and do not yield as the devil did. “Bless the Lord, his ministers, who do his will.” There is no need to speak a word, because they see God’s will better than anyone sees another’s face. By angels the principal orders are understood; by powers, the highest orders; by ministers, angels sent to human beings or [Col. 0614B] their guardians are indicated. All good angels are God’s ministers: some in that they are sent to human beings; some in that they command and teach others what they are to do. Yet all serve in the commonwealth of the eternal Emperor, either in person or through others. And not angels alone, but also:

**VERSE 22.** “Bless the Lord, all his works,” heavenly and earthly, who created you from nothing and distinguished you in so wondrous a manner by genus and species. Yet you will change all things into the glory of the children of God. Following their example, “in every place of his dominion, bless the Lord, O my soul.” God’s dominion is in every creature. Therefore, O creature of the Lord, praise your Creator; whether in every place of earth or heaven, bless, O my soul, his dominion—that is, his power—who will reform [Col. 0614C] the body of our humility, conformed to the body of his glory. He made a beginning with blessing and ends with blessing, because all praise is sung at the end.

It should be known that the hymn of the three youths, namely *Benedicite*, drew its subject matter from this psalm. The feast of the angels likewise claims this psalm for itself, because this very choir invites them to praise God.

## PSALM CIII

[Col. 0613]

[Col. 0613D] “Bless the Lord, O my soul. O Lord my God, you are exceedingly magnified,” etc. Just as the preceding psalm is ascribed to the primitive Church, so this one is ascribed to the Church from the Gentiles. Here it is placed in the one hundred and third position. In the number one hundred jubilee is found twice; in the number three the faith of the Trinity is expressed. This number indicates that the Church, because of faith in the Trinity, receives everlasting joy in body and soul. Its title is:

**A PSALM [Note: [Col. 0613D] The Vulgate omits: “A Psalm.”] OF DAVID HIMSELF.**

The preceding psalm had this title also, because both Churches sang to Christ in one faith. This hymn is sung to Christ, desirable to the people and mighty against vices. [Col. 0614D] The subject of the psalm is the blessing of the Church from the Gentiles. Its purpose is to exhort the faithful to bless God for the benefits described in the psalm “Lord, hear,” [*Domine, exaudi*]. The words are taken from Genesis, where the new creation of the world is written, and it signifies the Church, which is called a new creation, whose creation is expressed here physically through praise of the whole creation.

This psalm is divided into three parts, because in it a threefold praise is sung. The first part is, “Bless the Lord, O my soul,” in which God is praised for heaven, earth, and all things that are in them. The second is, “This great sea,” in which praise is sung concerning the sea and all things [Col. 0615A] that are in it. The third is, “I will sing to the Lord,” in which God is praised by the microcosm—that is, the lesser world, namely the human being. First let us examine the literal sense, then discuss the allegory. It is the voice of the Church from the Gentiles exhorting itself to the praise of God.

“Bless the Lord, O my soul,” for such benefits, for so many and great gifts of his graces.

Now it turns its words toward God, the giver of good things: “O Lord my God,” whom I serve as Lord and worship as God, “you are exceedingly magnified,” among angels, among human beings, and in all creation—you who are great before every creature in the essence of your majesty. “You have put on confession and beauty.” First it wishes to praise him for heavenly creation. God was, as it were, [Col. 0615B] naked while, before all visible and invisible things, he remained alone in eternity; he put on a beautiful garment when he brought forth from his hidden treasury the multitude of angels, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. They at once burst forth in confession of praise for their creation when, as it is written, “the morning stars praised him, and all the sons of God shouted with a great voice” (Job 38:7). Because of their unceasing praise they are called confession; because of their incomparable beauty, beauty.

Note that the twenty-two verses up to the division of the psalm are expounded by most beautiful allusions through the figure of parable, which occurs when things unlike one another in kind are compared.

[Col. 0615C] **VERSE 2.** “Clothed with light as with a garment.” God, as it were, clothed himself in light when he said that light should shine out of darkness. For he said: “Let light be made, and it was made” (Gen. 1:3–4). With each verse one must repeat: “You are exceedingly magnified.” “Stretching out heaven like a skin,” when he said: “Let there be a firmament,” which “he called heaven.” This is stretched out above the earth in the manner of a skin, because as skin covers all the limbs, so the encompassing circuit of heaven encloses the creatures; hence it is also called the covering of the earth. Some say that heaven is round in the manner of a sphere, as is written elsewhere: “He bent heaven like a vault.”

**VERSE 3.** “Who cover its upper parts with waters,” that is, [Col. 0615D] those of heaven: for above it is covered with waters. For God placed it in the midst of the waters so that it might divide waters from waters. Hence it is said: “Waters that are above the heavens, praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148:4). Mists are suspended above the firmament so as to temper the lower fiery element. “Who make the cloud your ascent.” Clouds are waters suspended in the air, drawn up from sea and rivers by the movement of the air. Here he addresses the incarnate Lord, who made a cloud his ascent when he ascended into heaven. For, with hands raised, he was borne into heaven, and a cloud received him from their eyes. “Who walk upon the wings of the winds.” Wind is air set in motion and agitated, namely waves of air. The wings of the wind were his swiftness, surpassing the swiftness of winds, [Col. 0616A] by which he transcended the agility of angels.

**VERSE 4.** “Who make your angels spirits.” Angels are heavenly spirits, whom he makes his messengers when he sends them to human beings. Angel is the name of an office, not of a nature. The name of their nature is spirit; that of their office, angel; just as “man” is the name of a nature and “soldier” of an office; “male” a name of nature and “herald” of office. Through their ministry all things in the world are ordered. “And your ministers a burning fire.” Angels have often been seen, such as those who carried Elijah away or appeared around Elisha. Thus the angel appeared to Moses in the flame of the bush, or on Mount Sinai in burning fire. He makes them his ministers when through them he burns others. Or this concerns evil angels, who are a burning fire: he makes them his ministers when he commands them to punish the reprobate. Here he begins to praise him for earthly creation:

[Col. 0616B] **VERSE 5.** “Who founded the earth upon its stability.” Some think that the earth is supported by some foundation. But philosophers say that it is upheld by the four winds. Against them Scripture says: “He suspended the earth upon nothing” (Job 62:7). For in the middle of the world it is balanced equally, as a centre in a circle, and founded upon its stability alone. “It shall not be moved for ever and ever,” so as to fall downward, because, placed in immovable firmness, it stands forever.

**VERSE 6.** “The deep is its garment, its covering.” The whole mass of waters spread everywhere through seas, rivers, and hidden caverns is together called by the one name “deep”; it is like a garment around the earth, [Col. 0616C] encircling it with the ocean as with a robe [manuscript: *verbo*, uncertain], just as our body is outwardly covered with a cloak. “The waters shall stand above the mountains.” This is said concerning the Flood, when the waters passed over the highest mountains and covered them fifteen cubits higher.

**VERSE 7.** “At your rebuke they shall flee.” At God’s command the waters, moving and returning over the face of the earth, subsided and withdrew into their proper channel. “At the voice of your thunder they shall be afraid.” Thunder is the crash of clouds. For winds enclosed in clouds, striving to burst out, resound with a great rumbling, as a struck bladder makes a sound. When the clouds collide, they strike out fire, called lightning, just as stones ground together emit fire. [Col. 0616D] At the voice of thunder the waters are afraid because, after thunder, they flow out of the clouds, as it is written: “He made lightnings into rain” (Ps. 134:7).

**VERSE 8.** “The mountains rise, and the plains descend into the place which you founded for them.” When the waters withdrew in the Flood, high mountains and low plains appeared as they had been founded in the beginning, though they had previously been covered by waters. The earth too was clothed with the deep like a garment when, newly created, it lay wholly hidden beneath the waters and darkness was upon the face of the deep. The waters stood above the mountains because they reached as far as the firmament, which is read to have been placed between the waters. They fled at God’s rebuke when they were gathered into one place. When dry land appeared, the mountains then rose and the plains descended [Col. 0617A] into the place God founded for them, whether upward or downward. This seems rather to have been said concerning mountains of the sea, when the waves swell like mountains and again subside into the flatness of a plain. And they do this in the place appointed to them, which they never exceed even when storms are swelling.

**VERSE 9.** “You set a limit which they shall not pass”: namely, the seas never go beyond the shores; nor shall the waters return to cover the earth, as they did formerly, either at the beginning of the world or in the Flood. And why? Because they fear the voice of his thunder: that is, they obey his command.

**VERSE 10.** “Who send forth springs in the valleys.” Valleys are places situated between mountains. In them springs burst from the earth, from which rivers flow; and thus waters pass through the midst of mountains to the sea, return whence they came, and again return to their former place, so as to flow anew. From these waters:

[Col. 0617B] **VERSE 11.** “All the beasts of the field shall drink,” because they cannot drink from the sea. “Beasts of the field” means all wild animals that feed not on flesh but on the fruits of the earth, such as deer. “The wild asses shall wait in their thirst.” The onager is a wild ass of remarkable size, stupid and very untamed. Africa produces it. Since it fears other wild beasts, it endures thirst for a long time. At the equinox it brays twelve times by night and the same number by day, so that the equinox can be recognized even by its voice. Each male presides over herds of females; they are rivals in lust and bite off the genitals of newborn male foals, so their mothers guard them.

[Col. 0617C] **VERSE 12.** “Above them the birds of heaven shall dwell.” Birds of heaven are those which wander without fixed nesting places. They dwell above mountains and springs so as to obtain from them either food or drink. “From the midst of the rocks they shall give forth a voice,” because they sing from the crags and rejoice before the Creator.

**VERSE 13.** “Watering the mountains from your upper regions.” The upper regions of the mountains are clouds, from which the mountains are watered. Above certain mountains there are also deep lakes full of fish. “The earth shall be satisfied with the fruit of your works”: that is, the earth is filled with diverse fruits when it is satisfied with waters.

**VERSES 14–15.** “Bringing forth grass for cattle, and herbage [Col. 0617D] for the service of humankind.” Grass properly means what grows in a meadow and feeds cattle; herbage is what grows in crops and feeds human beings. “That you may bring bread out of the earth, and wine may gladden the human heart, that the face may be made cheerful with oil, and bread may strengthen the human heart.” That is, you water mountains with waters that they may bring food to beasts; you satisfy the earth with waters that it may bring forth grass for cattle and crop-herbage for people. You bring bread out of it, by which you feed the human being, your special flock. From it you bring wine, which gladdens the human heart. From it you bring oil, by which an anointed face is made cheerful. Herbage produces bread, which strengthens the human heart wearied by labor. The earth brought forth all these fruits when God said: “Let the earth bring forth green herbage,” etc. (Gen. 1:11).

[Col. 0618A] **VERSE 16.** “The trees of the field shall be satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon, which he planted.” Trees of the field are called elms, willows, plane trees, and other fruitless trees. Cedars are tall trees on Mount Lebanon, fragrant and imperishable, which serpents avoid. Because of their dignity he adds: “Which he planted,” as it is written of paradise: “The Lord God planted a paradise of delight” (Gen. 2:8). Therefore the trees of the field—that is, all fruitless trees—are satisfied with waters, that they may bring forth leaves suitable for food for animals; fruit-bearing trees may produce apples for people; and cedars may serve for buildings.

**VERSE 17.** “There the sparrows shall make their nests.” All small birds are called sparrows. They make nests in branches or hollows of trees in order to obtain food there or escape the snares of bird-catchers and the attacks of predatory birds. [Col. 0618B] “The home of the herodii is their leader.” The *herodius* is the greatest of all birds, which defeats and eats the eagle. It is also called the coot, which always stays in ponds. This bird is of immense size, resembling a duck not in bodily comparison but in habits. Because of its size, this bird is called the leader of sparrows. Or rather, the home of the *herodius* is their leader. The leader of the *herodius* is the sea, from which birds were produced.

**VERSE 18.** “The high mountains are for deer; the rock is a refuge for hedgehogs.” The deer kills and eats serpents, sheds its horns and hair, and grows young again. The *herinacius* is an animal no larger than an *ericius* (hedgehog), resembling a mouse and a bear, plentiful in Palestine and always dwelling in rocky caverns and holes in the ground. He placed these two animals before all others. Swift animals flee hunters to the mountains, like timid deer; hedgehogs flee into caverns. [Col. 0618C] He has praised God concerning living creatures and their food. He now wishes to praise him concerning the seasons.

**VERSE 19.** “He made the moon for the times” of Passover, Pentecost, and certain other festivals, as it is written: “God made two lights and set in them signs and seasons, that they might divide night and day” (Gen. 1:14 ff.). Times are marked especially by the moon because it is closer to the earth. The ocean imitates it in all things: as it increases, the ocean increases; as it wanes, the ocean wanes. Yet the moon does not increase or decrease in its body, but in its light, because it has no light of its own but receives it from the sun. [Col. 0618D] The sun is so called because it alone shines by day. “The sun knew its setting,” because from its rising it always moves toward its setting; from there it returns beneath the earth to the rising, directing its course through darkness, as some say. Or, as others prefer, it shines beneath the earth at night in the same way as it shines above the earth by day. How great it is is clear here, since it fills the whole world with heat and brightness.

**VERSE 20.** “You set darkness, and night came to be.” Darkness is so called because it holds shadow. Darkness is not a substance but the absence of light: for example, when the sun is beneath the earth, darkness falls from the earth’s shadow. God set this darkness; he did not create it, when he divided light from darkness, and night came to be when God called the light day and the darkness night. This alternation of time was made so that a person who labors throughout [Col. 0619A] the day may rest at night; or so that beasts, which remain in their dens all day, may freely come out by night to feed. “In it all the beasts of the forest shall pass through.” Beasts of the forest are those that feed on flesh, such as lions, and are called wild beasts from their ferocity. They wander more in the night in search of food, because by day they hide in the recesses of forests from the snares of hunters and dogs. They shall also pass through at night.

**VERSE 21.** “The young lions roaring to seize some beast for food seek their food from God,” because they can seize none unless he permits it. For he created some beasts so that they might be food for others. They are called *catuli* (“young ones”) because they are keen in the sense of smell. He mentioned lion cubs because of their preeminence and because these beasts rage more fiercely. When they roar, all beasts are terrified. Yet lions themselves fear the crowing of cocks and the noise of wheels.

[Col. 0619B] **VERSES 22–23.** “The sun has risen, and they have gathered together, and shall lie down in their dens.” When the night has passed and the sun risen, the lion cubs and other wild beasts gather together and hide in caves and dens. Then, without fear of beasts, a person will go out to his work and to his labor until evening; then he will go to bed, while the beasts go out to feed. “Work” is said of something quickly completed, such as a building; “labor” is a daily activity, such as agriculture. Having considered all these things, the Church cries out:

### Verse 24

How magnificent are your works, O Lord! [Col. 0619C] For whoever surveys in mind the whole universe—the earth, sea, and heaven—and sees all things beautifully arranged and ordered, all distributed according to kinds, sustained by seeds, changed through succession, and moving through their seasons, cries out in wonder: “How magnificent are your works, O Lord!” You have made all things in wisdom; you made nothing superfluous, but arranged everything in number, measure, and weight. Truly, all the works of the Lord are full of wisdom. We see that the ant knows when winter is coming and stores food for itself. We see that a gnat or flea, though so tiny, has eyes, a belly, nostrils, feet, and every member just as we do, just as we see the great beast, the elephant, possesses them. Likewise we see how the bee [Col. 0619D] makes wax; and all these things are judged worthy of admiration and full of wisdom. The earth has been filled with your possession: that is, the whole earth has been occupied by all these things according to your ordering. Having praised God for the heavenly and earthly creation, he now begins also to praise him for the sea.

### Verse 25

This sea, great and broad of hands. The sea is called *mare* from moving to and fro, because it continually goes and returns. It is called “broad of hands” because it has, as it were, outspread hands and receives all things into itself. “Broad of hands” means a wide place for activity. The comparison is with a spacious country in which one can work without hindrance. The great sea, whether the ocean or another sea which divides the earth into three parts, is called great and broad because [Col. 0620A] the whole earth, in comparison with it, is like a small island. There are creeping things without number: innumerable fishes, both greater and smaller, which plunge into the deep and draw life from that place from which, if a human being falls into it, he dies; and they themselves die if they come onto land. There also are small animals with great ones: that is, little fish and great whales whose bodies are equal to mountains.

### Verse 26

There ships pass through. It is very wonderful that a ship, loaded with many weights, runs over swelling waves, carries people above visible death, and leads them through so many dangers from beasts and storms to their homeland. There too is this dragon which you formed to be played with. The Jews say that God made a great dragon called Leviathan [Col. 0620B], which is in the sea; and when, as they say, the ocean recedes, the dragon turns about. It was made to be played with, because, while it devours a multitude of fish, they escape through its open jaw and thus mock their devourer. Of it is written: “Great dragon, who dwell in many waters” (Ezek. 29:3). Some say that it was the first fish created by God and is still alive. In Scripture it is variously used figuratively as “dragon,” “Leviathan,” and “whale.”

### Verses 27–28

All things await you, that you may give them food in due season: namely creeping things, small and great animals, the dragon itself, and your possession. Some fish live on other fish; others, as is reported, take their nourishment from the dew of heaven. Therefore he said, “in due season,” because that dew descends at a fixed time, just as [Col. 0620C] the earth produces fruit at a fixed time. When you give food to those animals, or that dew to the fish, they gather it. When you open your hand to give, all will be filled with goodness—that is, with refreshment.

### Verse 29

But when you turn away your face, they will be troubled: that is, when you do not give food, they will waste away with hunger. You will take away their spirit, and they will fail—that is, they will die—and return to their dust: that is, they will be dissolved into earth.

### Verses 30–31

You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created: that is, they will be created again, being given life through the Spirit. And you will renew the face of the earth—in human beings, animals, offspring, and fruits. From all these things may there be glory to the Lord for ever; the Lord will rejoice [Col. 0620D] in his works—that is, all the works of the Lord rejoice in the glory of the Lord.

### Verse 32

He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble. An earthquake has often occurred as a sign, as when the Lord died or when he rose again; at both times the earth shook. He touches the mountains, and they smoke. This is said of Mount Sinai, which entirely smoked when the Lord descended upon it. Many mountains also breathe out flame and smoke, as Etna does, so that people, frightened by evils, may come to their senses. Mountains likewise smoke while they give off moisture which, drawn up by the breath of the air, gathers into clouds; and from these the mountains and the plains of the earth are again watered. For all these things, I—the Church chosen by him—

### Verse 33

Will sing to the Lord during my life; I will make psalmody [Col. 0621A] to my God as long as I am in this life. I will sing in the contemplative life; I will make psalmody by acting rightly in the active life.

### Verse 34

May my speech be pleasing to him: that is, may my praise for his benefits be acceptable to him. But I shall delight not in creatures, but in the Lord, in whom is true delight; for delight in a creature passes away, while that delight remains.

### Verse 35

May sinners fail from the earth, and the wicked, so that they are no longer wicked but righteous.

Although the Creator’s praise is great in all creatures, nevertheless everything already said in this psalm has been introduced only by way of likeness. For this book is spiritual, and speaks spiritually to spiritual persons through likenesses. It does not recount past events, but foretells future ones; from past things it takes only words [Col. 0621B] which were shadows of things to come. This psalm says that God is worthy to be praised because he made heaven and earth, the sea, and all their adornment; and by these allusions and likenesses it suggests that, if he is to be praised and blessed for the first creation, then he is especially so for the second—that is, for the re-creation and salvation of the human race—and for its magnificence. For if he acted magnificently in creation, much more did he do so in re-creation, as is said: “O God, who wonderfully created the human being, and more wonderfully re-formed him.” Afterwards it says through whom—namely, through the apostles—he accomplished that re-creation; against them the waters rose up, wishing to overwhelm them, until the Lord rebuked them and thus restrained them. The voice of the Church:

[Col. 0621C]

### Verse 1

Bless the Lord, O my soul. Soul, now belonging to me, bless the Lord by whom you have been redeemed. Whatever you think, whatever you say, whatever you do, let it belong to his praise. The soul, exhorted by the Spirit, turns to God with intense longing, saying: “O Lord my God, you are exceedingly magnified!” The whole Church is in Christ. Therefore the human being speaks here: O Christ, you who are ruler and are held to be my great God among Jews and Gentiles. And rightly so, because you have clothed yourself with confession and beauty: from idolaters you made persons confessing you; from those foul in sins, persons beautiful in virtues; and you clothed yourself with them as with a precious garment.

### Verse 2

Clothed with light as with a garment, dwelling in inaccessible light in the adornment of the Father’s glory; [Col. 0621D] and those who were darkness became light in you, with whom you are surrounded as with a garment. The righteous are called light because by word and deed they offer others the light of wisdom, as it is written: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). They are therefore called God’s garments because they are the adornment of the Church, which is Christ’s body. You made them light through heaven—that is, by opening Scripture to them—stretching out heaven like a skin. Heaven is so called from concealing, because heavenly things are concealed from us in it. In this book, “heaven” is sometimes understood as God the Father, as in: “The heaven of heaven” (Ps. 113:16); sometimes as Christ, as in: “God looked down from heaven” (Ps. 13:1); [Col. 0622A] sometimes as the Church, as in: “The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven” (Ps. 102:19); sometimes as sacred Scripture, as here: “stretching out heaven like a skin.” It is called heaven because many mysteries are concealed in it. He stretched out this heaven, formerly folded up like a skin, when he opened to the Church sacred Scripture wrapped in many mysteries. For just as in a stretched skin there are no folds and nothing is hidden there, but everything lies open, so the writings of the prophets, expounded to believers through the Holy Spirit, lie open. Or, just as a skin is stretched so that a tent may be made from it for protection, so he opened sacred Scripture to them in order to protect them against the attacks of heretics and against vices. A skin also, since it comes only from dead animals, signifies mortality. [Col. 0622B] After their sin, garments of skin were made for the first parents, signifying that they had fallen into mortality. Thus God stretches out heaven like a skin when he makes Scripture resound to the Church as widely as he made its writers known to the world. For the prophets and apostles, the writers of Scripture, were mortal; but after death, stretched out, they resounded more widely. They were not as well known while living as they later became through miracles and writings. Judaea alone had the prophets alive; all nations had them dead. They were stretched out after death because they were expounded by the apostles.

### Verse 3

You cover its upper parts with waters: that is, you cover the surface of Scripture, which is the letter, with waters—that is, with deep and obscure allegory. Or the upper parts of heaven are the more excellent commandments of Scripture. These [Col. 0622C] you cover with surpassing charity, which is in the waters—that is, in spiritual gifts. Of its flow it is written: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). He said “waters” because there are two commandments of love. It is called water because it washes away filth, covering a multitude of sins, and quenches the thirst for righteousness through the flowing streams of Scripture. For the excellence of Scripture there is a certain ascent for believers, of which he adds: “You make the cloud your ascent”: that is, you place among the people apostolic preachers, raining down the shower of doctrine, through whom an ascent to you may be made, as they ascend to understanding through Scripture understood by their teaching.

Here he begins to declare his magnificence until [Col. 0622D] the end of the psalm. “You are exceedingly magnified” must be joined to every verse. “You walk upon the wings of the winds”: that is, your word runs to hearts more swiftly than the wind flies. The Lord also ascends to heaven through clouds when the Church, his body, ascends through teachers to the understanding of Scripture. Or, just as he first ascended in himself through a cloud, so he will still ascend to heaven in his members through clouds, as it is written: “We shall be caught up in clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:16). By winds are understood angelic spirits; by wings, the swiftness of their understanding. The Lord walks upon the wings of the winds, for he surpasses every understanding of heavenly spirits, [Col. 0623A] because they will never understand so much concerning God that he does not still exceed the swiftness of their understanding. By winds souls are also understood, and by wings the virtues through which they are raised to heavenly things; all these consist in the two wings, namely love of God and neighbor. For “on these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets” (Matt. 22:40). Therefore he walks upon the wings of the winds because he surpasses the swiftness of the love of spiritual persons, loving them more than they love him.

### Verse 4

You make your angels spirits: that is, you make spiritual persons messengers of your word; and your ministers a burning fire: that is, burning with the flame of charity, consuming in others the filth of sins and setting others ablaze with love.

[Col. 0623B]

### Verse 5

You founded the earth upon its own stability: that is, the Church upon faith in Christ, who is its firm rock and its stability. Upon this foundation it shall not be moved for ever and ever: that is, it shall not fall eternally. This house is assailed by the storms of persecutions; but, established upon a firm foundation, it is not overthrown.

### Verse 6

The abyss is the garment with which it is clothed. The abyss is the multitude of evil persons, deep in the counsels of vices. It is an obstacle to the saints as a garment is to one at work. Waters will stand above the mountains because the tribulations and punishments of evil persons will have power over the bodies of preachers. For the flood of persecution covered the earth—that is, the Church—like an abyss, so that not even [Col. 0623C] the great mountains themselves—that is, the lofty preachers—appeared. For while martyrs were being killed, Christians fled everywhere, and even the apostles hid themselves. But how long will the waters stand? Only for a little while. For:

### Verse 7

At your rebuke they will flee. Christ’s rebuke through the preachers was this: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2). At this rebuke the waters fled when the persecutions withdrew from their oppression of the Church. At the voice of your thunder they will be afraid. Christ’s thundering voice was: Unless you repent, you will go into the fire of Gehenna. At that voice the raging waves feared, when Constantine and other tyrants turned from persecution to Christ. And those waves—

[Col. 0623D]

### Verse 8

Ascend the mountains and descend the plains, because persecutors often raised themselves up in pride through threats and terrors, but descended humbly into the Christian rite and began to defend the Church which they had formerly attacked. And how far do they ascend? To the place which you founded for them: that is, to the limit up to which you permit them to rage. For:

### Verse 9

You have set a boundary which they will not cross: that is, they will be unable to do more harm than you judge necessary and know to be necessary for the Church. But once converted to you, they will not turn back to cover the earth: that is, to persecute and destroy the Church. When the flood withdrew, the mountains appeared because, once [Col. 0624A] persecution had ceased, the apostles, the mountains of the Church, stood forth prominently, having previously lain hidden as though depressed. For they began to be venerated by emperors, and the eminence of the mountains became visible, through whom salvation came to the human race.

Alternatively: once peace was restored to the Church, councils were held and it was established how prelates and subjects should conduct themselves, though they had previously been indiscriminately mixed together. Then the mountains ascend—that is, the prelates to the position of prelacy—and the plains descend—that is, the subjects to the place of subjection—to the place which you founded for them: that is, as you arranged through your people in councils. You have set a boundary which they will not cross: so that a layperson may not usurp for himself the office of a cleric, nor a cleric claim for himself the office of a priest, nor a priest that of a bishop, nor a bishop that of the Apostolic See; and therefore they will not turn back [Col. 0624B] to cover the earth—that is, to throw the Church into confusion. Therefore, once the Church’s condition has been ordered in this way, you are exceedingly magnified.

### Verse 10

You send forth springs into the valleys: that is, through teachers you send the doctrine of the apostles, like a spring that refreshes and cools, to the humble. Or the valleys were humble teachers, such as Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory, in whom God sent forth springs, with which he satisfied his earth when through them he expounded sacred Scripture to us. And then waters—that is, doctrines—will pass between the mountains: through them, in the shared harmony of apostles and prophets, they will go to others. As those taught, so these taught—not as heretics, who formerly disturbed the Church’s order. Concerning those springs and waters:

[Col. 0624C]

### Verse 11

All the beasts of the field will drink. A field is arable land, and it signifies the Gentiles, ploughed by the plough of the Gospel and by the oxen, the preachers, and sown with the seed of the word. Its beasts were Gentiles living beast-like lives. They all drank living water from the springs of the Savior when they drew sound doctrine from Catholic preachers. Wild asses will await in their thirst. The wild ass is a large and untamed animal, signifying secular rulers. They will drink from those springs and still await drinking with great desire, remaining in their thirst: that is, always thirsting to hear the word of doctrine, as Charlemagne and others did.

Alternatively: by beasts are understood married persons; by wild asses, continent persons who endure thirst. The beasts drink [Col. 0624D] from those waters when married people are told: “Husbands, love your wives” (Eph. 5:25), and again: “Let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband. Let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the woman to her husband” (1 Cor. 7:2–3). Wild asses drink from them when continent persons are told: “Not all receive this word; let the one who is able to receive it receive it” (Matt. 19:11–12): that is, let those who are continent remain so. They await in their thirst when they restrain their members from lust and mortify the desires of the flesh. Wild asses also signify the wise of this world, who waited in their thirst—that is, burned with eagerness for life—because the wiser they had formerly been in the world, the more fervent they became, once converted, in God’s service, as Ambrose and Augustine did.

[Col. 0625A]

### Verse 12

Above them the birds of heaven will dwell. The birds are spiritual persons, flying in mind to the heights, enjoying the free air and rejoicing in the serenity of heaven, dwelling above mountains and valleys, above springs and waters. They live among mountains through contemplation, among valleys through humility, and are satisfied by the springs of Scripture and flowing streams of doctrine. Or the birds of heaven are virgins whose minds dwell in heaven; they will dwell above them—that is, above beasts and wild asses—because they surpass the merits of married persons and widows, as it is written: “I shall give them a named place” before other saints “in the kingdom of the Father.”

From the midst of the rocks they will give voice. The rock was Christ; the rocks were the apostles. Birds remain among rocks because spiritual persons live in the doctrine of the apostles. [Col. 0625B] They give voice from the midst of the rocks when they preach from the apostles’ writings. These birds rest in the mountains—that is, in the apostles and prophets—and utter a sweet voice. The birds sound; the rocks resound. Spiritual persons dispute; the answering Scriptures agree. Just as Christians are called from Christ, so saints are called rocks from the rock, because they cling to Christ the rock. “From the midst of the rocks” means from the common harmony of the saints. You who send forth springs into the valleys,

### Verse 13

Watering the mountains from your upper regions: that is, teaching the apostles from the prophets, who were above the apostles not in life but in time. Some manuscripts have: “from your upper regions,” that is, watering the apostolic mountains from your better gifts of the Holy Spirit. In the Hebrew it reads: “from the upper chambers of God”: that is, [Col. 0625C] the apostles were watered from the secrets of heaven through the Holy Spirit, as Peter, who saw a vessel descending from heaven, and Paul, who was caught up to the third heaven and heard God’s mysteries in paradise. Water flows from the upper regions into the mountains, from the mountains into the valleys; and so the earth—that is, the Church—will be satisfied from the fruit of your works, being filled with good works. These will be the fruits of those mountains and springs; and their preaching and doctrine are your works. But the earth is satisfied,

### Verse 14

Producing grass for beasts of burden: that is, giving temporal sustenance to its prelates, who are God’s beasts of burden and, under the Lord’s yoke, carry him to others through preaching. And it produces plants for the service [Col. 0625D] of human beings: that is, bodily food, ministering to preachers who serve people by preaching. This happens when laypeople give bishops and priests tithes, so that, being supported from them, they may devote themselves to prayer and the ordering of the Church.

Note that spiritual persons are called the beasts of burden of secular persons because by word and example they carry them to heavenly things. They are also their servants because they serve them in spiritual matters. Secular persons therefore ought to provide their spiritual prelates with necessities, so that they may attend to God’s service without anxiety. These temporal things are called grass and plants in comparison with the spiritual things bestowed upon them. Prelates, however, ought to show themselves servants, not lords, to the faithful, as it is written: “Whoever is greater among you [Col. 0626A] shall be your minister, and whoever is first among you shall be servant of all” (Matt. 20:26–27); not like foolish prelates, who regard the household of the Church as their own servants. For what purpose does the earth produce grass for the beasts of burden? “That you may bring forth bread from the earth”: that is, that you may bring forth from the beasts of burden—that is, from the prelates, who are earth cultivated by the Scriptures—the doctrine that refreshes the soul. The subject earth therefore provides bodily support so that it may receive from the ruling earth—that is, from God’s beasts of burden—the bread of life, namely preaching.

### Verse 15

And that wine may be drawn from it, which makes the heart of a human being glad. For other animals are bent toward the earth and obedient to the belly. “That he may make the face glad with oil”: that is, that through the laying on of hands they may receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as occurs in confirmation. This [Col. 0626B] oil makes the face glad because the Holy Spirit gladdens the mind by his gifts and charisms. The comparison is with people who, anointed with oil, appear externally shining and beautiful. So those anointed by the Holy Spirit shine inwardly. And that they may receive from the prelates the bread of the altar—that is, Christ’s body—which bread strengthens not a human being’s stomach but heart: that is, it strengthens the rational soul in the gifts of the Holy Spirit. This bread is consecrated by priests. But for one whose heart has not been cleansed through the Holy Spirit, it condemns and weakens rather than refreshes. Those who receive worthily, however, it sanctifies in the soul by giving virtues; it sanctifies them in the body by keeping them in good works; and finally restores the body itself to immortality. Note the sacraments of the Church [Col. 0626C] signified in bread, wine, and oil, because bread is baked in fire, while wine and oil are pressed in the winepress; and the Church is afflicted by the fire of tribulation and the pressure of persecution. First, bread is brought forth from the earth when the doctrine of the letter is offered by the Church’s prelates to catechumens or unlearned persons. Next, wine is brought forth when the doctrine of allegory is presented to the baptized or the learned. Next, oil is brought forth when the believer is made glad by spiritual gifts. Finally, he is strengthened by Christ’s body in the gifts bestowed. The lower earth produces grass for beasts of burden; the higher earth brings forth bread, wine, and oil for peoples; and from these charisms

### Verse 16

The trees of the field will be filled: that is, Jews, Gentiles, and evil Christians formerly unfruitful, but now fields—that is, humbled. And the cedars will be filled by these things: [Col. 0626D] that is, lofty rulers, elevated in nobility and wealth and exalted in sins, but now cedars of Lebanon—that is, whitened and made beautiful by virtues—which the Lord planted in the Church through faith, hope, and charity. Christ’s wine and oil reached senators, nobles, and kings. But for what purpose did he plant the cedars? That sparrows might nest beneath them. Hence it follows:

### Verse 17

There sparrows will make their nests. The Lord planted cedars and sparrows nest beneath them when monks, clerics, or any religious persons construct cells under the authority of rulers and dwell under their protection. Such persons are supported by the rich just as a nest is supported by branches. The house of the heron is their leader: that is, rich persons furnish the poor with an example. The heron is a bird of prey and signifies the powerful of the world, eager for temporal possessions. [Col. 0627A] When, through love of the heavenly homeland, they distribute their wealth to the poor and, stripped naked, follow the naked cross, they construct for themselves through devout works a dwelling of heavenly conduct. Truly they become leaders of sparrows in the pursuit of spiritual life. Therefore the house of the heron is their leader, because the virtue of an illustrious rich person who has been converted—his contempt for the world and love of God—provides an incentive for the poor. For when persons of moderate station see the powerful converted, they themselves turn more quickly and boldly. The heron surpasses the eagle eager for plunder; and they too will overcome the devil, who lies in wait for souls.

Another translation has: “The house of the coot is their leader.” The coot is a large bird which always remains in waters, and signifies wise people who are always occupied [Col. 0627B] with the streams of Scripture. They are God’s house, and Christ is their leader. Sparrows nest under cedars and live under the heron’s leadership. And what of the deer?

### Verse 18

The high mountains are a refuge for deer. The high mountains are sublime commandments and lofty virtues. They become a refuge for deer—that is, spiritual persons passing through the thickets of the world—when they turn aside from the heat of vices. These deer devour serpents when, through prayer or counsel, they strangle the sins of others. What hope is there for hedgehogs? The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs. The rock is Christ. The hedgehog is an animal like an urchin, bristly, thorny, covered everywhere with spines and prickles, very timid, and dwelling in rocky places. It signifies burdened sinners, [Col. 0627C] fearing the mass of thorns—the punishments of Gehenna’s fire—for whom Christ’s mercy is a refuge, so that they may escape the eternal fire. Concerning these trees, cedars, deer, and hedgehogs:

### Verse 19

He made the moon for seasons: that is, the Church, which will endure eternally. Although many rage against it, it will nonetheless remain through all times. Or he made it according to the pattern of the seasons, because as long as the Church exists, seasons comparable to the moon will exist: at one time failing in certain people, at another rising again in certain people. Its seasons are peace and persecution. In a time of peace it appears to grow; in a time of persecution, to diminish. It is illuminated by the sun—that is, by Christ. This sun knew its setting, because Christ, the sun of righteousness, knew [Col. 0627D] the hour of his death, saying: “The Son of Man will be delivered to the Gentiles, and they will kill him” (Matt. 17:21–22). He made the moon so that it might approach the sun and receive light from it. But it is not illuminated by him unless it imitates the setting of the sun—that is, Christ’s death. The moon, the Church, suffers diminution when the sun’s light—that is, Christ’s grace—is withdrawn. But the sun knew his setting: that is, he knows well why he withdraws his grace for a time—lest they become proud because of their virtues, and so that they may recognize their own frailty. When the sun of righteousness set, certain darknesses arose among the apostles, as their hope failed; for at first he had seemed to them great and the Redeemer of all. Hence it follows:

### Verse 20

You set darkness, and night came to be: that is, you caused blindness in Israel, and thus your [Col. 0628A] death came to be. Or, at your setting, O sun of righteousness, darknesses of disturbance arose in the hours of the day—that is, in the apostles—and night came to be: that is, great despair. For Peter denied; Thomas doubted; and the others said: “We had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21); but in this we were deceived. And in that very night all the beasts of the forest will pass through: that is, all demons, who are called beasts because of their savagery and of the forest because they dwell in hidden places. They will pass through that Church with temptations and suggestions. Just as certain animals go out by night and seek food for themselves, but flee when the light comes and hide in caves, so, at the Lord’s death, demons went forth in that darkness and sought food for themselves; but when [Col. 0628B] the sun came—that is, when Christ rose again—they fled and hid in the places where they had formerly dwelt. What are those beasts?

### Verse 21

The lion cubs: that is, lesser demons together with the greater ones, roaring—that is, raging—in order to seize food for themselves. For “the roaring lion goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8), as it is written: “His food is choice” (Hab. 1:16). Yet he does not dare seize anyone unless the Lord permits it. For the Lord knows whom and when he ought to permit to him. Some are seized for testing, as Peter and Job; some for final ruin, as Judas. Peter was in the devil’s jaws and was rescued; Judas, however, was incorporated into him. Christ the sun set [Col. 0628C] in death, night came to be, and in that night demons went out and obtained food for themselves; but, when the sun came, they fled. Now:

### Verse 22

The sun arose—that is, he rose again—and the demons gathered together into one and will be placed in their dens: that is, among Jews and Gentiles, where they had formerly lain. But when they had been driven away:

### Verse 23

The human being will go forth to his work. That human being whose head is in heaven—that is, the Church—will go forth to good pursuits and to his activity—that is, to the exercises of virtues—until evening: that is, until the end of life, or until the coming of Antichrist, for then the Church will be in evening and at its setting. For it will not prevail as much then as it does now. After the Lord’s resurrection, the apostles, laborers in the Lord’s vineyard, went forth to [Col. 0628D] their work—that is, to preaching—and drove the beasts from the vineyard, that is, demons from the Church of the Gentiles; and they cultivated it with virtues. After them other teachers went forth to their activity—that is, to the building up of the Church—and still others after them, until evening: that is, until the end of the world.

Alternatively: when the sun sets, the moon fails, because when Christ withdraws his grace, the Church fails in virtues. Then darknesses will arise—that is, errors and heresies—and night will come to be: that is, unbelief. In it all the beasts of the forest will pass through: that is, all devils who are in unbelievers; like a forest in hidden places, they run through every temptation in order to deceive. And not only the greater ones, but also the lion cubs—the lesser ones—roaring and fierce like a lion, will pass through in order to seize [Col. 0629A] the faithful; and they seek food from God for themselves, though they can deceive no one unless they are permitted, as in Job’s case. Just as among angels some are more excellent, such as archangels, and others of lower rank, such as angels, so among demons some are of greater malice and others of lesser. Hence it is written: “Our struggle is against principalities, powers, and rulers of darkness” (Eph. 6:12). After the night of temptation, the sun rises because the light of grace will return; the one who has fallen will repent, and all beasts and sins will flee, and he will become such as he was before. And they are gathered together: that is, they will cease from him and will be placed in their dens—that is, they will rest from persecuting him. Then, through the rising of the sun of righteousness, the human being, now rational, will go forth from thought to good work, which [Col. 0629B] will be his own—that is, fitting—and he will go forth to his continual activity until evening: namely, until his own end, or until the end of the world, when there will be such persecution that no one will go forth—that is, no one will dare openly to do good.
