The difference between *opus* (“work”) and *operatio* (“activity”) is that work is for an hour, while activity is continual work. You are exceedingly magnified, you who made this and these things, who illumined the failing moon by your rising and drove away all the beasts of the forest. Therefore I rightly cry out:

### Verse 24

How magnificent are your works, O Lord! That is, they are exceedingly magnificent and glorious. Nor is it surprising. For you made all things in wisdom—that is, in the Son. You performed all things wisely, rationally, and with great counsel: the things I have said concerning your setting, the Church’s failure, preaching, and the other matters explained above. The earth has been filled with your possession: that is, the whole earth has been filled with the Church, which is your possession. Or the earth has been filled with faith, charity, and other virtues, which are your possession, and this happened through your rising. Or the earth—that is, Judaea—has been filled with your possession: namely, with faithful persons and, especially at the end of the world, with faith and good works through which you possess it. And not only the earth, but also:

### Verse 25

This sea—that is, the Gentile world, bitter in its habits—will be filled with your possession. It is great because it is deep in vices; broad—that is, wide and suited for hands at work, as one calls a house or country spacious. We call the Gentile [Col. 0629D] people spacious from east to west, where work will not fail those who labor. Judaea was not spacious; therefore it is deserted to laborers. Before your possession comes to be in the sea, there are creeping things without number: that is, innumerable demons creeping into human hearts through hidden temptations. Small animals with great ones: that is, small and great demons are there to stir up storms in the sea. Yet:

### Verse 26

There ships pass through: that is, preachers carrying Christ through preaching to human hearts; or the Churches pass through the storms and tempests of temptations, their helmsman being Christ upon the wood of his cross.

Note: the sea is the world; storms are temptations; [Col. 0630A] winds are demons; tempests are persecutions; the ship is the Church; the tree is the cross; the sail is faith; the yards are works; the sailors are apostles and teachers; the helmsman is Christ; the favorable wind is the Holy Spirit; the harbor is the end of the world; the homeland is eternal life. In that sea there are not only small animals but also the greatest dragon and prince of demons, of whom enough has been heard, where he dwells. You formed him to be played with: that is, you ordained him such that the faithful might mock him. When he devours certain persons through evil works, such as David, Peter, and Mary, they escape through his jaw, pierced by the bracelet of Christ’s mercy, when they flee to repentance; and thus they mock him. Or you formed the dragon to be played with by it—that is, by the Church-ship passing through the sea. And he is deceived, because he is mocked by angels [Col. 0630B] or by saints. God created a good angel, but the devil himself, through pride and malice, made himself deformed; the Creator formed him again well when he ordained him for the benefit of the Church. For he is useful to the saints whom he tests with temptations, as Job, or whom he cleanses through adversities, as David.

### Verse 27

All things await you, that you may give them food in due season: the creeping things, the animals, and the dragon himself. For they cannot harm unless you permit it. Therefore he says, “in due season,” because they can tempt no one unless permitted by God, as is written concerning Job; nor can any human being do good unless inspired by God.

### Verse 28

When you give to them, they will gather—that is, when you permit it and give them power, they will gather prey and consume the obstinate. When you open your hand—that is, when you reveal your Son and your power—all things that were previously diverse will be filled with goodness, that is, with virtues. “All things,” that is, all believers who are to be saved. The food of the dragon and creeping things is earth, that is, sinners; the food of the possession, that is, of the Church, is goodness, that is, Christ.

### Verse 29

But when you turn away your face—that is, the presence of grace—then they will be troubled by promptings and temptations. You will take away their spirit, namely the spirit of pride, and they will cease from their wickedness; and they will return to their dust—that is, recognizing that they are dust, they will turn to repentance. And then [Col. 0630D]

### Verse 30

You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created in goodness; and thus you will renew the face of the earth—that is, the mind of earthly persons—so that it may attend to heavenly things, whereas it formerly attended to earthly things.

Otherwise: in that great sea there will be creeping things without number—that is, in this world, innumerable temptations. Small animals together with great ones—that is, soldiers together with princes—will be persecutors. There ships will pass through—that is, nevertheless the Churches will pass over to the shore, that is, to Christ. There will be this dragon, Antichrist, full of malice and deceit, whom you formed for him to be mocked; for, when he thinks that he will reign as God throughout the ages, he will first lose the Jews converted to faith in Christ; then he will perish through himself, and those oppressed by him [Col. 0631A] will mock him.

All things await you, that you may give them food in due season: that is, all await the time when you will permit them to rage against the saints, whom they may devour as food. When you give them power, they will gather them for slaughter and torture. When you open your hand—that is, when you reveal your Son to some, such as the Jews—all things will be filled with goodness; that is, all those persons will be filled with good works and virtues. But when you turn away your face—that is, when you withdraw grace and help—they will be troubled by the persecution of Antichrist. You will take away their spirit, and they will fail—that is, they will die—and return to their dust, that is, they will decay. They will not be able to die before God permits them to be killed. But death will not harm them, because you will send forth your Spirit, consubstantial with you, [Col. 0631B] and through him they will be created—that is, they will rise again. And you will renew the face of the earth: that is, you will make a new earth, and human beings immortal, shining like the sun. Therefore:

### Verse 31

Let the glory of the Lord be for ever, because they themselves will then be glorious in the Lord eternally, and the Lord’s glory will always be in them. The Lord will rejoice in his works. The righteous are the Lord’s works. They will then rejoice in the Lord, and the Lord in them.

### Verse 32

He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble: that is, he who now looks upon the Church in mercy and makes it fear punishment for its sins, as he looked upon Peter when he wept bitterly. He touches the mountains and they smoke: that is, he who now touches prelates fallen through some crime with adversities, and they smoke through tearful repentance, as David did. By “earth” are understood subjects; by “mountains,” prelates.

Or, on the Day of Judgment he looks upon the earth—that is, earthly persons—when he says, “I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and the other things that follow. And he makes it tremble when he says, “Go into eternal fire.” Then likewise he touches the mountains, and they smoke: that is, he will touch proud kings and princes with a penal sentence, saying, “Depart from me with the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41) [Col. 0632A]. Then they will smoke, because they will burn in eternal fire. Literally, too, the earth will begin to tremble at the judgment when it feels the dead rising from it. Then the mountains will smoke, because the flame will rise fifteen cubits above them. Or the mountains that are touched will smoke—those who will be saved through fire. For many of the elect will fear on that day and will be purified by fear. For all these benefits:

### Verse 33

I will sing to the Lord in my life. I will make melody to my God while I exist: that is, in good works I will sing to the Lord until the end of the world, the end of my life. And I pray that:

### Verse 34

My speech may be pleasing to him; that is, that what I utter with my mouth may be acceptable to him. Sinners and wicked persons delight in earthly things; but I will delight [Col. 0632B] in the Lord—that is, I will take pleasure in those things which are in the Lord. And I pray, Lord, that:

### Verse 35

Sinners may fail from the earth—that is, from the earthly things in which they delight; and may the wicked cease from wickedness, so that they are no longer wicked. Sinners are those who sin against themselves; the wicked are those who sin against their neighbours. For all these things, bless the Lord, O my soul.

Both psalms began in a similar manner and ended in a similar manner, because both Churches were begun by Christ’s blessing and are likewise to be consummated in Christ’s blessing. In the first blessing, calling, he said: “Come to me, all who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). In the second blessing, calling, he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc. (Matt. 25:34).

[Col. 0632C] This psalm is sung on the feast of the Holy Spirit because through him the Church is renewed in virtues, and through him it is made alive in the resurrection. Note that in the psalms the state of the Church is frequently described in one way and then another, because the Church’s condition is often recorded as having changed: now persecution presses; now heretical perversity compels; now the faction of schismatics forces; now tranquil peace smiles upon it. According to each period, the Holy Spirit varied his style, to whom all future things are present.

## Psalm 104. On the benefits bestowed upon God’s people

[Col. 0631]

[Col. 0631D] “Give thanks to the Lord, and call upon his name,” etc.

The first psalm of this decade sings of Christ’s benefits bestowed upon the human race. The second and third sing the particular praise of each Church for benefits received; and as reward for that praise, eternal life is promised in this psalm. This psalm, therefore, is composed concerning both peoples, namely the Hebrew and the Christian. The letter speaks of the old people; the interpretation indicates the new people. For each people is joined, as it were, as a twin wall in Christ Jesus, the cornerstone; and each is built through faith in Christ into the heavenly house [Col. 0632D]. What the one believes to have happened, the other believed would happen.

The psalm’s purpose is to prove by the old example that, just as God gave the land promised to the fathers, so he will give the life promised to the faithful.

The subject of the psalm is the seed of Abraham and the children of Jacob: that is, believers in both peoples who imitate Abraham’s faith. The Holy Spirit speaks concerning and to them, exhorting them to praise God; and he gives the reason why he is to be praised: because he performed wonders, namely, he promised them and gave them the land of Canaan. [Col. 0633A] So he has promised us an eternal inheritance and will give it, if we are imitators of Abraham. Indeed, he has already given it through the Son and through faith, namely as an earnest. True faith is the earnest of that land, and afterward he will give it in reality.

Next, through many particulars, he recounts how he fulfilled the promise in them, so that we may be more certain of that eternal inheritance. For if he gave them that land, then he will give us that which was signified by it. The intention is that, through the exhortation of this praise, we may imitate them so as to attain and seek the land of the living.

This psalm is the one hundred and fourth, which is thirteen times eight. The number three signifies faith in the Trinity; ten, observance of the law’s Decalogue; eight, the reward of future blessedness. Thus this number indicates that, for faith in the Trinity, through observance of the law in action, eightfold blessedness will be given as recompense. The title:

## Alleluia

That is, “Praise God.” *Allelu* means “praise,” and *ia* means “God”; this is one of the ten Hebrew names, and the word is exhortatory, as when we say, “concerning the praise of God.” Twenty psalms bear the title *Alleluia*, and this is the first, because the Decalogue, observed both spiritually and actually, leads to everlasting joy.

The Decalogue says: “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20:13). We observe this spiritually if we do not hate our neighbour, because “he who hates his brother is a murderer” (John 3:15). We fulfil it actually if we kill no one either by hand or by counsel. [Col. 0633C] Again it is written: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:13). We fulfil this spiritually if we do not desire another’s wife, because “whoever looks upon a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). We observe it actually if we do not violate our neighbour’s spouse. So the remaining commandments are to be understood.

Wherever such a title is found, it shows that joyful praise and exultant gladness follow in the psalm. For if praise is contained in the title, it is especially so in the psalm, which consists wholly of praise.

The words of the psalm are taken from the history in which God promised the land of promise to the ancient people and fulfilled this promise for their descendants. It signifies that [Col. 0633D] the land of the living, which God promised to the Christian people, he fulfilled for his children—that is, through good works.

It is divided into seven parts because the promised inheritance is received through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

The first part is, “Give thanks to the Lord,” in which the faithful are exhorted to praise God.

The second is, “Remember,” in which the three supreme patriarchs are put forward under the figure of faith in the Trinity, and eternal life, the reward of faith, is promised.

The third is, “And he called for a famine,” in which Joseph’s sale into Egypt and the people’s salvation through him are narrated under the signification of Christ, the Saviour sold for the people.

The fourth is, “And Israel entered,” in which Jacob’s descent into Egypt and the oppression of God’s people are recounted; and the descent of the ancient people into hell [Col. 0634A] and the affliction of the Christian people by the enemies of the Church are prefigured.

The fifth is, “He sent Moses,” in which Moses’ mission into Egypt and the Egyptian people’s being struck by ten plagues are recalled; and Christ’s mission into the world and spiritual punishment are signified.

The sixth is, “And he brought them out with silver,” in which the people’s departure from Egypt and the greatness of benefits on the journey are related; and the Christian people’s departure from idolatry and the multitude of God’s benefits in the Christian religion are set forth.

The seventh is, “And he brought out his people,” in which possession of the promised land is written of, and reception of the inheritance of the eternally promised land is expressed.

It is the voice of the Holy Spirit exhorting the faithful to the praise of God:

### Verse 1

Give thanks to the Lord, and call upon [Col. 0634B] his name. O seed of Abraham—that is, imitators of Abraham’s faith—and O children of Jacob—that is, children of the wrestler, and of Christ through imitation—give thanks to the Lord; that is, praise the Lord. And afterward call upon his name: that is, call his name into yourselves, submitting yourselves to him as servants and creatures, so that you may be true Christians from Christ’s name. Give thanks, because he will hear the one confessing who calls upon him.

And do not praise him only among yourselves, but also proclaim his works among the nations: that is, among all people generally living, both Jews and Gentiles, preach that he has made you people who give thanks. Or: confess your sins to the Lord, and after confession call upon his name. For the right order is that we first confess our sins and then call upon the Lord. Give thanks, therefore, namely:

[Col. 0634C] ### Verse 2

Sing to him: that is, praise him with mouth and heart; and make melody to him: that is, do good works. Song belongs to contemplation, but psalmody to action. Recount all his wonders, whether the governance of the world or the conversion of the people. Praise in such a way that you yourselves may be praiseworthy—that is, that you may thereby receive praise—and attribute that praise within yourselves to him. Psalmody:

### Verse 3

Glory in his holy name, attributing praise to him, or by living holy lives in the Christian name. And do this with joy. Let the heart of those who seek the Lord—not gold—now rejoice. Therefore, because the heart of those who seek the Lord will rejoice:

### Verse 4

Seek the Lord through good works and through reading Holy Scripture, and be strengthened through knowledge of the Scriptures. Seek his face continually: that is, his knowledge and presence. If he is always sought, when is he possessed? “Always,” I say, for as long as you live, or always, here and in the future. But how will he be sought in the future when he will be seen? He will be possessed and sought as one always to be loved, because he will never become wearisome; rather, he will always be sought as one to be loved and desired more deeply. It is as if someone possessed an object of love yet continually sought it in love, longing not to lose it.

Or: seek the Lord—that is, the Lord’s grace, namely forgiveness of sins—through faith; and be strengthened in hope. Seek his face continually—that is, his presence—through love by means of Scripture. The face of God is used for presence or knowledge, as the face of wind [Col. 0635A] or fire. By what shall we seek? By his wonders.

### Verse 5

Remember his wonders which he has done. Up to this point the Holy Spirit has kindled the faithful to praise of the high Divinity; now, accommodating himself to weak minds through words they can grasp, he descends. Since you are not sufficient to seek the nature of the Godhead, do at least what you can: remember his wonders, which he did in himself—that he was born of a virgin, that he died and rose again. Attend also to the prodigies he did in others—that he brought the children of Israel through the Red Sea, and such things—and attend to the judgments of his mouth: that is, commandments which, if unfulfilled, condemn and judge all, and which he spoke with his own mouth. Or “judgments” means the commandments which he judges ought to be done. Remember, I say, you who are:

[Col. 0635B] ### Verse 6

The seed of Abraham his servant: that is, imitators of Abraham’s faith, servants of the Lord in their works; you who believe as accomplished what he believed was to come; who believe that you are saved through Christ—that is, by imitation of Christ—as he himself believed; who believe that an eternal inheritance will be given you, as he believed; and who are children of Jacob—that is, children of the wrestler by imitation, who bought the birthright with a dish of lentils. So you too buy heavenly things in exchange for earthly things, and thus you will be his elect.

By Abraham faith is understood; by Jacob, action. Through faith they will be servants of the Lord; through action, his elect. Only believers are reckoned in the seed of Abraham, who are blessed through Christ, the seed of Abraham.

Or these words are spoken to Abraham’s children according to the flesh, who became servants of God. And because they were born from Abraham, after “children of Abraham” he added “children of Jacob” [Codex: “children of Jacob”], lest he seem to be speaking of others. Truly he is to be praised by you. For:

### Verse 7

He is the Lord, who rules over all, and God, creator of all, and also our restorer—not newly so—whose judgments are throughout the whole earth, because he alone possesses dominion everywhere. He, I say:

### Verse 8

Remembered his covenant: that is, the new promise signified through the Old Testament, namely the new life through which the eternal inheritance is promised. The covenant, I say, is to endure for an age—that is, for eternity. And he remembered his word—that is, the faith [Col. 0635D] through which that heavenly inheritance is given to us. This is the word which he commanded when he said: “If you do this, you will have eternal life.” And to whom did he command it? To a thousand generations—that is, to the perfect. For that inheritance will be given to the perfect, whom the number one thousand signifies.

Or, “to a thousand generations” means all generations of the world. For after the Flood the world was divided into one hundred homelands and into a thousand generations, that is, into all successions of generations. For the children of promise observe the command to live by faith, being born and living, and dying and passing away, until every generation is ended.

### Verse 9

Which covenant, understand, he arranged to give to him and to others when speaking to Abraham; and he remembered his oath: that is, the promise of the land, made with an oath, pertaining to Isaac—that is, to legitimate sons, not to the sons of a concubine.

### Verse 10

And he established that covenant. For whom? For Jacob, setting it as a command: that is, he gave the covenant under a condition: “If you keep my commandments, I will give you that inheritance.” And he established that covenant. For whom? For Israel, the leader, as an eternal covenant: that is, as a heavenly inheritance.

The covenant addressed to Abraham was: “To your seed I will give this land” (Gen. 12:7). The oath addressed to Isaac was given when his father offered him: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord: because you have done this thing and have not spared your son, I will bless you, and in your seed all nations will be blessed” (Gen. 22:16–18). Likewise Isaac said after Abraham’s death: “This land [Col. 0636B] which I promised Abraham your father I will give to you, and in your seed all nations will be blessed.” In the same way he said to Jacob: “This land which I promised to your grandfather Abraham I will give to you, and in your seed all nations will be blessed.”

He made this covenant a command when he gave that people the law: if they kept it, he would give them the land promised to the fathers; if they did not keep it, he would give them nothing. And he established it for Israel as an eternal covenant, because he wished spiritual persons to understand that this promise signified eternal life, which will be given only to those who keep God’s commandments.

Jacob is the name of birth; Israel, of blessing. By Jacob the ancient people is understood; by Israel, the Christian people. Therefore he promised this to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, so that through it you might have knowledge of eternal life and keep his commandments—that is, live well—so that through this understood covenant you might be able to come to eternal life. Which he arranged for Abraham:

### Verse 11

Saying: “To you I will give the land of Canaan.” These are the words of God making the promise. The Holy Spirit continues: “The measuring-line of your inheritance”: that is, he promised himself the land of Canaan, which Joshua son of Nun distributed to you as an inheritance by measuring-line, signifying the future inheritance which the true Jesus will distribute to each according to merits.

Abraham was in the land of the Chaldeans, and the Lord commanded him to leave it and come into the land of Canaan; and he promised to give this land to his seed. Yet Abraham was then in that same land of Canaan when God promised it to him, and he did not give him even a footstep. Therefore Abraham understood that eternal life was promised to him through this land.

It is recorded that Shem first inhabited this land after the Flood. Later the children of Canaan, having expelled the descendants of Shem, dwelt there in their place; from them the land was called Canaan. God later restored this land of Canaan to the children of Israel, born from Shem’s lineage: he did not give it as a new gift, but restored it as their own inheritance, long ago taken away by force. This signifies that God will not newly give to humankind the inheritance of Paradise, the land of the living, but will restore what was once possessed and wickedly lost.

The name Canaan is also meant to signify this, for it means “humility,” because that land is the land of the humble. By Canaan, whom Noah consigned to servitude, is understood servile fear, which perfect love casts out, because “the servant does not remain in the house for ever; but the son,” who loves, “remains for ever” (John 8:35). [Col. 0637A]

Histories relate that Abraham was thrown by the Chaldeans into fire because he refused to worship fire; but the Lord delivered him from it. Haran, however, his brother and Lot’s father, died in the fire. Hence the Lord said to him: “I am the God who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans” (Gen. 15:7). For *Ur* means “fire.” From there he led him into the land of Canaan because he faithfully worshipped him. And, so that he might give him that land, he did not allow anyone to harm them.

### Verse 12

When they were few in number. They could have been a thousand and still few in number. Therefore he added: “and when they were very few.” Moreover, when they were inhabitants of that land—that is, guests, not natives—and anyone might have injured them. An inhabitant is called one who cultivates another’s land; a native, one born there.

### Verse 13

And, since they were strangers, they passed from nation to nation, from place to place: from Chaldea to Mesopotamia, thence to the land of Canaan, thence into Egypt; and from kingdom to another people—that is, from kingdom to kingdom—which was a great danger. In that land there were seven nations, through whom they passed as strangers and guests. And:

### Verse 14

He did not allow anyone to harm them. And when famine pressed, they descended from that kingdom into Egypt, another people. On another occasion they went to Gerar, and he rebuked [Col. 0637C] kings on their behalf. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, took Abraham’s Sarah because of her beauty (Gen. 20 and 26); on another occasion Abimelech, king of Gerar, took her. The Lord rebuked both until each restored her to her husband. He rebuked another king on behalf of Rebekah and Isaac; he rebuked Laban on behalf of Jacob. He scourged and rebuked certain persons in dreams, saying:

### Verse 15

“Do not touch my christs,” that is, my anointed patriarchs; “and do not act maliciously against my prophets,” that is, do not behave wickedly, or be wicked.

It is asked how they are called “christs,” that is, anointed ones, since priestly anointing began with Aaron and royal anointing with Samuel. They are called christs because they believed that Christ would be born from them; they were anointed with invisible oil. It is also handed down that firstborn sons were anxious to be blessed and anointed by their fathers, as Jacob was by Isaac; these were to possess greater power than the others and to be heirs, and this dignity was called the birthright. Hence Jacob said to Esau: “Sell me your birthright” (Gen. 25:31).

It is also asked how the patriarchs were called prophets. For the Lord said of Abraham: “He is my prophet, and he will pray for you” (Gen. 20:7). Their deeds were prophecy of future things. Abraham’s offering of his son was prophecy of Christ, whom the Father offered for us. Isaac’s receiving Rebekah from Mesopotamia was prophecy of Christ, who received the Church from among the Gentiles. Jacob’s receiving Leah and Rachel was prophecy of Christ, who loved the active [Col. 0638A] and contemplative life. These things have been said according to the letter; a few things must be said concerning allegory.

First it should be noted that the righteous are called by four names: the seed of Abraham, servants of God, children of Jacob, and elect of God, because they are called from the four parts of the world into the eternal covenant of the four Gospels. They are Abraham’s seed through faith; God’s servants through action; Jacob’s children through endurance of labour; God’s elect through perseverance. Thus Abraham’s seed are believers; God’s servants are those who do good; Jacob’s children are those who struggle against vices; the elect are heirs of the kingdom through virtues.

Therefore, you who are the seed of Abraham and you who are God’s servants, praise the Lord by faith and action. And you who are children of Jacob and God’s elect, seek his face continually through hope and love. Remember his deeds and commandments, so that you may proclaim his deeds and fulfil his commandments. For he himself, the Lord God, remembered you, and fulfilled for you what he promised Abraham and the patriarchs, when he sent his Word in the flesh, redeemed the human race through him, established the Gospel as an eternal covenant promising eternal life, gave in addition the helping Holy Spirit, and promised an eternal inheritance to the keepers of the covenant.

This inheritance was promised to the three patriarchs, through whom the Trinity is expressed. Abraham signifies the Father; Isaac, the Son; Jacob, the Holy Spirit. Their names themselves also suggest this. For Abraham means “high father” or “father of many nations”; Isaac, “joy”; Jacob [Col. 0638C] or Israel, “prince with God.” Therefore in the Old Testament he named these three especially, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:15). Likewise the Son in the New Testament especially named the same three, saying: “Many will come from east and west”—that is, from the whole world—“and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8:11): that is, in eternal life, the promised inheritance.

This inheritance is acquired through three virtues, which are figured by these three patriarchs: faith by Abraham, who believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness; hope by Isaac, concerning whom his father believed against hope in hope; and love by Jacob, who served for love of his wives.

These three also signify three orders of the Church. Abraham signifies teachers; Isaac, the continent; Jacob, the married. They are distinguished in the one Catholic Church, to which it is promised: “To you I will give the land of Canaan,” that is, the land of humility—for Canaan means “humility”—namely the heavenly inheritance, which is acquired through humility. “The measuring-line of your inheritance”: that is, the inheritance which will be given by a measuring-line, that is, by measure, as it is written: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2); and there each will receive what he has deserved.

The Lord promised this inheritance. And how will it be given? By multiplying the Church through many tribulations and labours. For when believers were few in number and very few, and inhabitants of this Church, because “we do not have here a lasting city, but seek the future one” (Heb. 13:14) [Col. 0639A], and passed from one nation to another in preaching, and from the kingdom of the devil to another kingdom, the kingdom of God, and when another people, formerly the devil’s, became God’s people, he did not allow anyone to harm them. Although people afflicted them with beatings, they did not do much harm, because in many cases the hand was withered. And he rebuked kings on their behalf, saying: “Do not touch my christs,” that is, Christians anointed with oil and chrism; “and do not act maliciously against my prophets,” that is, against preachers.

Let us return to the history. He says how the Lord brought the patriarchs out of that land and afterward brought their descendants back into it:

### Verse 16

And he called for famine upon the land: that is, because of the people’s sins, he commanded famine to prevail in the world for seven years. And he broke every support of bread: that is, he destroyed every kind of grain, which is human support and strength, as is recorded when the children of Israel went down into Egypt to buy grain (Gen. 42:3). Famine is nothing other than destruction brought on by want of food. And as disease is often cured by medicine, so famine is in some way cured by nourishment. Compelled by this famine, the fathers went down from the land of Canaan into Egypt. But the Lord:

### Verse 17

Sent before them a man: that is, one acting manfully. What man? Joseph. How did he send him? He was sold as a slave though free. Certainly, when this happened it was the brothers’ sin, and yet God sent Joseph into Egypt. This is a great and most necessary matter to consider: how God makes good use of people’s evil deeds, just as they, in turn, make evil use of God’s good works. The Egyptians purchased Joseph, sold by his brothers, and:

### Verse 18

They humbled him in his fetters: that is, they afflicted him by binding his feet in shackles. Iron passed through his soul: that is, he was bound with an iron chain. Or, iron passed through his soul: that is, the fierce temptation of the woman, or the harsh tribulation of prison; and this continued until:

### Verse 19

His word came: that is, until the interpretation of the dream concerning the king’s cupbearer and baker came to pass. The story is well known: Jacob loved Joseph above his other sons; therefore, because of his brothers’ hatred, Joseph was sold into Egypt. A certain official bought him and, finding him faithful, put him over his affairs. Since he was handsome, his mistress desired his embrace; he refused this wickedness. Therefore she accused him, and he was shut in prison, bound with shackles and chain. In prison he explained their dreams to two of the king’s officials, and it happened as he said (Gen. 41). Yet he did not do this from himself; the utterance of the Lord kindled him—that is, the Holy Spirit showed it to him, the Spirit who afterward appeared in tongues of fire. When the king learned this:

### Verse 20

The king sent and released him from the shackles. What king? The ruler of peoples, who could do this; [Col. 0640A] and he dismissed him from prison as a free man. And he did something still greater.

### Verse 21

He appointed him lord of his house, namely of the court or household, and ruler of all his possession, that is, of the whole kingdom of Egypt. For what purpose?

### Verse 22

That he might instruct his princes concerning the condition of the kingdom, make himself king [the reading is materially uncertain], and teach his elders—that is, the priests—the wisdom of interpretation.

It is recorded that Abraham was an expert astrologer and taught astronomy in Chaldea. Coming to Egypt in the time of famine, he taught the Egyptians the same art. Later Joseph, more fully instructed in this art, instructed the priests of Egypt. This is indicated where Joseph is said to have declared: “Do you not know that no one is like me in the art of divination?” (Gen. 44:15). Thus these two lands, Chaldea and Egypt, excelled other nations in astronomy.

Let us return to the allegory:

“And he called for famine upon the land”: that is, the Lord permitted emptiness of mind and blindness to come into the hearts of earthly persons. “And he broke every support of bread”: that is, he destroyed all the doctrine of philosophers, which seemed firm. Afterwards he sent preachers, and through them scattered the food of God’s word among the peoples.

But he sent before them a man: that is, before the apostles, Christ acting manfully. And as Joseph, by the counsel of Judah, one of the twelve patriarchs, was sold for thirty silver pieces, so Christ, by the counsel of Judas, one of the twelve apostles, [Col. 0640C] was handed over for thirty silver pieces. And as Joseph descended into Egypt and prepared a place there for his own, so Christ ascended into heaven to prepare a place for his own. Joseph prepared a homeland for his brothers in prison; Christ prepared eternal life for believers on the cross.

And first they humbled his feet in shackles: that is, the Jews afflicted Christ’s humanity when he was bound. Iron passed through his soul: that is, nails and spear passed through his life. Or iron—that is, grievous tribulation—passed through his soul when he said, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38), until his word—that is, the Father’s—came and caused him to rise again. Then the utterance of the Lord—that is, the divinity of the Word united to him—kindled him by making the Lord’s man rise again.

King and God the Father sent his angel, who rolled away the stone and loosened Christ’s burial cloth; and the Father released him from death. What king? The ruler of peoples—that is, the Lord of angels—and he sent him forth from hell immortal and incapable of suffering. He appointed him Lord of his house, that is, of the Church, which is the house of the living God; and ruler of all his possession, that is, of all those whom he drew away from the devil’s power and who became God’s possession. That he might instruct the princes of his house, namely the apostles, as himself through imitation, so that they might imitate him according to their capacity; and that he might teach his elders, namely priests advanced in character, the wisdom of correcting and admonishing others.

Christ instructed the princes of God’s house, namely the apostles, as himself, saying: “All [Col. 0641A] that I heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). “As the Father loved me, I also loved you” (ibid., 9); so you too love one another. He taught his elders, namely the chief priests, doctors of the law, and scribes, wisdom, saying: “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him” (John 6:44). “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Let us repeat the literal sense. Jacob, hearing that Joseph was alive and that he reigned in Egypt:

### Verse 23

And Israel entered into Egypt, and Jacob was a resident in the land of Ham. Jacob was named by his parents; the name means “supplanter,” because at birth he held Esau’s foot in his hand. He was named Israel by the angel with whom he wrestled; the name means “seeing God,” because he saw the Lord in the angel. The Lord afterward appeared to him and named him Israel, doubtless because formerly he had seen the Lord standing upon the ladder when he beheld angels ascending and descending.

Egypt is named after a king of that name. It is also called the land of Ham, after Noah’s son, who first inhabited it. A resident is one who comes from elsewhere and cultivates a foreign land. Israel entered Egypt with all his family and possessions, and the Egyptian king gave him the land of Goshen, rich in pastures, on Joseph’s account. Thus Jacob was a resident in the land of Ham, that is, in Egypt. Jacob died, and Joseph, and all his brothers.

### Verse 24

And God increased his people exceedingly: that is, he multiplied the children of the patriarchs greatly. And he strengthened them over their enemies in power and wealth [Col. 0641C], but still more afterwards, when by the mighty hand of God, through signs and wonders, they became feared and honoured.

### Verse 25

He turned their heart so that they hated his people. Is God a lover of sinners? Does he turn human hearts toward doing evil? Far from it! Rather, this is that wondrous goodness of God by which he makes good use even of evil angels or human beings. For although they are evil through their own fault, he brings good out of their evil. Envy is hatred of another’s happiness. Since the Egyptians envied the Hebrews because they flourished in wealth and glory, God, as it were, turned the Egyptians’ heart toward hatred when he increased the Hebrews’ glory and riches. And so that they might deal deceitfully with his servants—that is, they caused them to labor [Col. 0641D] under a pretext. For they said that bricks were necessary for the construction of the kingdom; but this was deceit, because they did it in order to oppress them. They killed the male infants in the river and spared the females. Let us consider the allegory.

Christ taught the elders wisdom, and Israel entered Egypt: that is, one who sees God in the mind descended into tribulation, or entered in mind into the darkness of this life and considered it to be nothing; and therefore Jacob—that is, “the struggler”—was a sojourner in the land of Ham, that is, in the land of the raging one. For Ham is interpreted as “raging.” And he greatly increased his people in number and strengthened them with constancy, courage, and knowledge above their enemies. Although Nero killed Peter and Decius killed Lawrence, each was nevertheless stronger than his killer. [Col. 0642A] He turned their heart—that is, he allowed the hearts of tyrants to be turned, so that they hated his Christian people, oppressed them, and that heretics and philosophers might deal deceitfully with his servants. For heretics practiced many deceits and deceptions against the saints.

Let us return to the literal sense. Here the embassy of Moses and the ten plagues are recounted; they are also set forth in Psalm seventy-eight [seventy-seven], namely, “Give ear.” But there they are described under one meaning, here under another. Their historical order is not preserved, because this book follows not the order of events but of mysteries. Therefore it changes some above, and here includes some which it did not mention there, namely darkness and gnats. It sets down sores neither here nor there, because it intends only correspondences. The Egyptians oppressed [Col. 0642B] the Hebrews, and God delivered them.

### Verse 26

He sent Moses, his servant, useful to him, to Pharaoh; and Aaron himself, whom he chose—that is, a man of great holiness, whom he loved especially—he sent with him. In the Hebrew and Greek it reads, “whom he chose for himself,” not “himself.” Just as he formerly sent Joseph to provide them a place, so now he sent Moses and Aaron, who would lead them out from there.

### Verse 27

He placed in them the words of his signs: that is, effective messages through signs; and of his wonders in the land of Ham, that is, in Egypt. As the words which we speak are signs of the things about which we speak, so those signs were words of future things. The signs were that he changed the rod into a dragon and water [Col. 0642C] into blood; but the wonders were that the earth suddenly produced frogs or that a dreadful chaos covered the land.

### Verse 28

He sent darkness into Egypt and darkened the peoples. This was the ninth plague, though it is placed first here. But this author does not follow the order of bodily events, but of spiritual ones. For he writes about spiritual matters and merely takes words from bodily similitudes. In Egypt darkness was indeed made for three days so dense that it could be felt by touch. But where the children of Israel were, there was light; and this was a great wonder. And he did not embitter his words against those two, Moses and Aaron: for it happened as he foretold. Or: he did not embitter his words against the Hebrews—that is, he did not speak harshly to them, although they [Col. 0642D] embittered him by their unbelief. For while they were in Egypt, they were unbelieving both toward his words and his signs.

### Verse 29

He changed their waters, those of the Egyptians, into blood, because they had killed the Hebrew infants in the water. And he killed their fish in the river. This was the first plague.

### Verse 30

And their land, which formerly yielded grain, now produced frogs—not only in the huts of the poor, but even in the inner rooms, that is, in the bedchambers of their kings, that is, their rulers. Some manuscripts have: “Their land produced frogs.” The Hebrew has: “Their land swarmed with frogs.”

### Verse 31

He spoke—that is, he willed it—and there came the *cynomia*, that is, the dog-fly; for *cynos* means “dog”; or *coenomyia*, that is, a fly of every kind. And there came gnats, [Col. 0643A] that is, mosquitoes with a fiery sting, throughout all their borders, that is, throughout the whole land.

### Verse 32

He made their rains hail. Since it is not usually rainy in Egypt, he now gave them hail instead of rain, and consuming fire in their land, that is, lightning.

### Verse 33

And by hail and lightning he struck their vines and their fig trees, that is, their fruit-bearing trees. And he shattered the trees of their territory, that is, he shattered the unfruitful trees in their borders.

### Verses 34–35

He spoke—that is, he willed it—and there came locust and *bruchus* [caterpillar], without number. The locust ate every blade of grass in their land, that is, every crop; and the *bruchus* ate every fruit of their land, [Col. 0643B] that is, all the trees. Or, the locust devoured the fodder of beasts of burden, and the *bruchus* that of human beings.

### Verse 36

And finally he struck every firstborn in their land: that is, he struck all the firstborn of human beings, from the firstborn in Pharaoh’s house to the son of the handmaid; and he struck the first fruits of all their labor, that is, the firstborn of animals, which are nourished by labor.

Let us seek the allegory. Moses was sent into Egypt and delivered those oppressed by Pharaoh; Christ was sent into the world and rescued those oppressed by the devil, or led captives out from hell. He sent Moses and Aaron—that is, the Law and the priesthood, that is, lawgivers and preachers, whom he chose from others, as Paul. And he placed in them the words of his signs, [Col. 0643C] that is, words followed by lesser signs, such as the healing of the blind; and of his wonders, that is, greater signs, such as the raising of the dead, to be displayed in the land of Ham, that is, the land of the raging one. And he sent darkness, that is, blindness, upon the Jews and heretics, and darkened them in secular philosophy. When preachers began to expound the hidden mysteries of Scripture, then divine Scripture was opened and secular learning was closed. And he did not embitter his words: that is, his hard and harsh sayings were not frustrated—“Leave the world”—because they left it. Soon heresies arose.

And God changed their waters into blood: that is, the teachings of heretics into the shedding of the blood of their own soul and of others—that is, into [Col. 0643D] the destruction of faith, which is the blood of the soul. He did this for the testing of the faithful. And he killed—that is, he permitted their fish to be killed: namely, their wandering disciples, flying from one opinion to another. And their land produced frogs: that is, they who are earthly produced philosophical wordiness, not only among lesser persons but even in the private chambers of their kings—that is, philosophical verbosity pleased rulers such as Julian. He spoke, and permitted it, and there came *cynomyia*, that is, dog-like habits, namely luxury and shamelessness; gnats, that is, dialectical doctrine, which stings and blinds many throughout all their territory.

And he made their rains—that is, the teaching of those heretics—hail, [Col. 0644A] that is, something shaking and crushing themselves. And he made consuming fire, that is, the incitement of the flesh, in the land, that is, in their hearts. For it is said that heretics are more licentious than others. And he struck their vines, that is, their greater virtues, and their fig trees, that is, their lesser ones; and he shattered the trees of their territory, that is, he permitted every good work which was in them to be destroyed. He spoke—that is, he permitted it—and there came the locust, that is, open destroyers, and the *bruchus*, that is, secret detractors, beyond number; for heresies are innumerable. And they ate every blade of grass in their land and every fruit of their land: that is, rulers and detractors took from the faithful whatever temporal goods they possessed, and thus were taking from them the prescribed minor sins [reading uncertain], which grass [Col. 0644B] and stubble signify. And he struck every firstborn in their land: that is, he struck faith, which is primary in a human being, among those heretics; and he struck the first fruits of all their labor, that is, all their remaining virtues and doctrine, in which they trusted. Let us return to the literal sense.

Here follow seven benefits divinely bestowed upon the ancient people: abundance of money, bodily health, the protection of a cloud, nourishment from birds, satisfaction with heavenly bread, water brought forth from the rock, and the gift of the land of the nations. The Lord afflicted the persecutors of the Hebrews with so many plagues, as has been said.

### Verse 37

And he brought them, the Hebrews, out of Egypt with silver and gold, which the Egyptians had lent them as though they would return. And he brought them out in such prosperity [Col. 0644C] that there was no sick person among their tribes. This was a great benefit: in that emergency of departure, no one was ill. Therefore the Lord commanded the Hebrews to despoil the Egyptians, because they were greedy and did not reward the laboring Hebrews. Thus, having received payment for their labor, they departed, just as workers in a vineyard, after receiving their appointed rewards, return home.

### Verse 38

Egypt rejoiced at their departure from the Red Sea, after Pharaoh and his whole army had been drowned, because fear of them had fallen upon the Egyptians remaining behind: they feared that the Hebrews might return to the land and crush their remnant with great ease. Then came about what he said above: “He strengthened him above his enemies.” Moreover, the Egyptians were greatly [Col. 0644D] distressed that they did not recover the gold and silver vessels and precious garments lent to the Hebrews. Then:

### Verse 39

He spread out a cloud—that is, he sent a cloud spread out for their protection, to protect them by day from rain and heat—and fire, to give them light by night, lest they shrink from the darkness of the wilderness. And in the wilderness they murmured against the Lord, saying, “We shall return to the pots of meat,” and the sweeter things.

### Verse 40

They asked for meat, and quail came. Therefore he gave them birds, that is, *quasquilas* [quails; Note: [Col. 0643D] Codex Gemnicensis: *quaquilas*], not quadrupeds; the birds are wholesome and more savory; and he satisfied them with bread from heaven, which is manna. Afterwards:

### Verse 41

[Col. 0645A] He split the rock with a rod, not with iron, and waters flowed, which they and their beasts drank. Streams went through dry ground: that is, they went with them through the whole wilderness as far as the land of promise, as it is written: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them” (1 Cor. 10:4), that is, from the accompanying rock—namely, water brought forth from the rock. Therefore he bestowed these benefits upon them,

### Verse 42

because he remembered his holy word: that is, his certain and firm promise, which he gave when speaking to Abraham, his servant, that is, one obedient to him, when he said: “To your seed I will give this land” (Gen. 12:7). From this it is clear that the children of Israel possessed that land not for their own merits, but for the fulfillment of God’s promise; indeed, nearly all of them fell in the wilderness because of their own merits. Let us return [Col. 0645B] to the allegory.

God sent the foregoing tribulations upon the persecutors of the faithful and brought his own out from among them with silver, that is, with the brightness of speech, and gold, that is, with knowledge. Or, when the world has been struck in many ways, the souls of the righteous are led out in the silver of brilliant confession and the gold of shining purity, every weakness of sin having been removed. Hence it adds: “There was no sick person among their tribes.” For when the saints depart from this life, the Lord removes every pain and illness from them, and they depart with great joy. And at their departure—that is, their passing from this life—Egypt rejoiced: that is, darkness, namely those who are dark, rejoiced at the departure of light because there is no light to rebuke darkness. “For everyone who does evil hates the light” [Col. 0645C] (John 3:20).

He spread out the cloud—that is, the holy body of the Lord, cooling them in its protection—and fire, namely the Holy Spirit, enlightening them, to give them light by night: that is, to illumine them throughout this entire life, which is compared to night. They asked, and quail came: that is, they asked for virtues, which like feathers raise one to heavenly things and satisfy the mind, and they came to them; and he satisfied them with bread from heaven, that is, with his body or heavenly doctrine. He split the rock: that is, he caused them to understand that the rock had been split, namely Christ in his Passion by the lance; and from that splitting waters flowed, that is, manifold grace—baptism, redemption, sacred Scripture. For when Christ’s side was opened, blood and water came out. And then streams went through dry ground: that is, preachers went among the nations, which were dry of every dew of mercy. [Col. 0646A] And therefore he bestowed all these things upon his own, because he remembered his holy word: that is, his firm promise, which he gave to Abraham his servant, namely that he promised to give an eternal inheritance to Abraham’s imitators.

The literal sense must again be taken up. Here he says how he brought Abraham’s seed into the promised land. The Lord fed the Hebrews in the wilderness with heavenly nourishment.

### Verse 43

And from that wilderness he brought out his people, obedient to him, in outward exultation, such as Joshua and Caleb; and his chosen ones, namely the worthier, in inward joy; and he brought them into the land which he had formerly promised to the patriarchs.

### Verse 44

And he gave them the territories of the nations, and not empty ones, but they possessed the labors of the peoples. For just as [Col. 0646B] they had formerly despoiled the Egyptians, so they took gold, silver, and garments from these nations. For harsh slavery he gave them the gold and silver of the Egyptians; for prolonged wandering, the territories of the nations; for a long journey, the labors of the peoples. For what purpose did he give them these earthly goods?

### Verse 45

That they might keep his ordinances, that is, commandments which justify, and seek his law, in order to understand it spiritually. Therefore the Lord gives these goods to the saints: so that, not being hindered by acquiring necessities, they may devote themselves to prayer and reading; or that they may keep his ordinances and seek his law, understanding that God is not to be worshiped for earthly things but for himself. For these earthly things given by God, we ought to give thanks; and we ought to worship him, possessing him for his own sake. The allegory must be considered.

[Col. 0646C] The Lord promised eternal life to the faithful and led his people out of the world—that is, those obedient to him—so that they might exult in good works; and his chosen ones, that is, the more perfect, such as Martin and Benedict, in great joy from a good conscience. Exultation belongs to the body; joy pertains to the soul. But first he gave them the territories of the nations, so that they might acquire them by their preaching; and they possessed the labors of the peoples, that is, they drew the disciples of philosophers into their own school. For what purpose? That they might keep his ordinances, that is, commandments which justify, and seek his law spiritually. At the end of this psalm *Alleluia* is placed, by which the praise of joy is expressed, because those who perform the Lord’s commandments will enter the Lord’s promised inheritance, where they will possess joy and gladness.

## Psalm 105. On the praise of the Church drawn from the nations

[Col. 0645]

[Col. 0645D] “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is for ever,” etc. This psalm occupies the one hundred and fifth place. This number rises from the unit and, increasing by the decade, reaches fourteen and makes up the sum of this number: [Col. 0646D] for example, when you name one, add one; when you name two, add two, and there are three; when you name three, add three, and there are six; when you name four, add four, and there are ten; and so continue to fourteen, and there will be one hundred and five. The number four [Col. 0647A] expresses the New Testament; ten, the Old Testament. This number also signifies that observers of both Testaments receive a hundredfold reward.

The subject of this psalm is the less perfect converts from the Jews. The Holy Spirit speaks of them, warning them to confess their sins, praise God, perform penance, and remember certain wonders and benefits which he bestowed upon their fathers; yet they provoked him and were therefore punished. In this punishment, the Lord’s mercy was not absent from those who were to be saved. And just as mercy was not absent from them, so it will not be lacking in all who confess their sins, praise God, and do penance. The preceding psalm [Col. 0647B] spoke of the imitators of Abraham; this one speaks of peoples who provoke God. The former recounted the benefits which the Lord bestowed upon that people; this one recounts the evils which the ungrateful people returned even for benefits. Its purpose is to exhort us to love of God, who is able to punish and able to show mercy. Its title is:

## Alleluia

That is, “Praise God.” Jerome says that wherever two *Alleluia*s are placed, one belongs to the preceding psalm and the other to the following one. Augustine, however, says that both belong to the following psalm, because of the praise of both peoples. But Jerome is more to be followed, because of his knowledge of the Hebrew language.

The words of the psalm are taken from the history in which the children [Col. 0647C] of Israel, after many benefits from God, offended God in many ways; consequently some were punished, while others, converted to repentance, were saved. It signifies that many Christians, after many gifts of grace, offend God in many ways; of these he condemns the hardened but saves the penitent.

This psalm is divided into six parts, because God’s praise is in the number six, just as the world was completed in six days. The first part is, “Give thanks to the Lord,” in which are contained a confession of praise and prayer. The second is, “We have sinned,” in which is written the confession of sins and the offense of the fathers, whom he delivered from Egypt and saved in the Red Sea. The third part is, “They acted quickly,” in which three offenses and an equal number of punishments [Col. 0647D] of the Jews are set forth: namely, that when they desired meat, the wrath of God consumed them while they were full; that, when they rebelled against Moses, some were swallowed by the earth and some consumed by fire; and that, when they worshiped the calf, they were killed. The fourth part is, “They regarded the desirable land as nothing,” in which again follow three provocations and three corresponding punishments: they did not believe God’s promises and therefore did not enter the promised land; they murmured because of the words of the spies and therefore died, perishing in captivity; and they sacrificed to Baal-peor and therefore were killed. The fifth part is, “They provoked him at the waters of contradiction,” in which four crimes of the Jews are related: namely, that because of scarcity of water they contradicted the Lord and Moses; that, after [Col. 0648A] entering the land, they did not destroy the nations as the Lord commanded; that they served their carved images; and that they sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons, on account of which they are said to have been handed over to the nations. The sixth part is, “Save us, O Lord,” in which are contained the prayer of converts and praise of God.

The great deeds of this psalm attest the sacraments of the whole redemption of humankind. For we are rescued from the Egyptians when, through the divine gift, we are freed from works of the devil. We cross the Red Sea when we receive the sacraments of baptism. We are fed in the wilderness while, amid the solitude of the world, we are satisfied by the abundance of good things. We shall be brought to the promised land when, by the gift of heavenly [Col. 0648B] mercy, we enter that blessed homeland. It is the voice of the Holy Spirit exhorting converted but fallen Jews to repentance:

### Verse 1

Give thanks to the Lord. You who believed from among the Jews and have fallen: do not despair in your sins; do not lose heart; do not imitate your parents who provoked God, but imitate the penitent and confess to the Lord original and actual sins. Accuse yourselves and do penance, lest he himself punish you; for he is able to punish. Confess to him, and he will not put you to shame, for he is good—not immediately punishing, but waiting—and he rains upon the righteous and the unrighteous. He is goodness essentially, and therefore wishes good to all. After confession, implore mercy, because his mercy is for ever. [Col. 0648C] There is in him a certain hidden power by which he forgives sins to all who show his mercy. And that mercy remains for ever—that is, as long as the course of this life endures. For afterward it will not be necessary, where repentance will not be fruitful. For “who shall confess to you in hell?” (Ps. 6:6). Or, his mercy remains for ever—that is, eternally—because even after this life the saints, made immortal and incapable of suffering, could not continue to exist except by the Lord’s mercy. After sins have been forgiven, speak of the Lord’s powers: that is, preach to all that he is able to forgive, and make all his praises known to others, that is, his commandments, by which he is praised and you will be blessed.

### Verse 2

For who will speak of the Lord’s powers, which he shows in justifying the ungodly who repent? Or who will make known all his praises, that is, commandments for his praise? Commandments are called praises because, when they are fulfilled, a person is praised. Having completed repentance, remain in righteousness, because:

### Verse 3

[Col. 0648D] Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times. One keeps judgment who judges rightly; one does righteousness who acts rightly. Judgment belongs to faith; righteousness to work. Blessed, therefore, will be those who preserve faith in judgment and do righteousness in deed, and this at every time—that is, from when they begin until life ends. For “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

[Col. 0649A] Note: he sets forth five things for attaining blessedness: confessing sins, speaking the Lord’s powers, declaring his praises, keeping judgment, and doing righteousness.

Alternatively: blessed are those who keep judgment—that is, who understand the future judgment, what evil or good they will receive there, and forestall it by confession and repentance, lest the Lord punish them. Or those who preserve discernment regarding what must be done and what omitted, judge and accuse their sins here, punish them in themselves, lest they be punished in the future, and do good at every hour. After the Holy Spirit’s admonition follows the prayer of the penitent:

### Verse 4

Remember us, O Lord, etc. We remember one who is absent or in exile; we visit one who is present or sick. [Col. 0649B] We were absent from the vision of God and the fellowship of angels, exiled in this world; and the Lord remembered us: he sent his Son to us, who by his presence visited those sick persons left half-dead by robbers. As then, so now: Remember us, O Lord, in the favor of your people, that is, in your Son, who was well pleasing to you beyond all your people. Or: remember us, O Lord, that we may be among the people pleasing to you. God seems forgetful when he allows a person to fall from vice into vice. He remembers when he calls one back from sin and summons one to repentance. Remember us, who by sinning have gone far away from you, and visit us by inward inspiration in your salvation, that is, in your Son, who is the Savior of all. Or, “in your salvation,” that is, in that salvation [Col. 0649C] by which you visit others in the Holy Spirit. As often as a person remembers sins, grieves, groans, and is pierced with tears, so often the Lord visits that person. Visit us, who are weak. For what purpose?

### Verse 5

To see the goodness of your chosen ones. Visit us and advance us for this purpose: to see the goodness of your chosen ones, that is, to understand the good things which you confer upon your chosen ones. Or: to see the goodness of your chosen ones, that is, to understand the virtues and good works which the chosen possess here. And visit us also for this purpose: to rejoice in the joy of your nation, that is, advance us so that we may rejoice with the kind of joy in which your nation rejoices, which exults in preserved innocence; so that you also may be praised by us with your inheritance, [Col. 0649D] that is, with the righteous, who are your inheritance. Or, that you may be praised with your inheritance—that is, among your inheritance—when we say, “Holy, holy, holy.” Or, that you may be praised with your inheritance: that is, that both you be praised here and the human person be praised.

Note that the penitent pray for four things: that God remember them by calling them back from sins; then visit them by inspiring repentance; that they see the good things of the chosen; and that they rejoice in the joy of the righteous. The joy of God’s nation is the supreme, true, unchangeable, and beatifying good, which is God himself; to see him is to praise him, and to rejoice is to praise him. After their prayer follows their confession:

### Verses 6–7

We have sinned with our fathers: that is, just as our fathers acted unjustly against God in so many and such great ways, so we have committed iniquity against our neighbor. We did not understand your wonders, and we did not keep your works of mercy in memory, as did our fathers, who in Egypt did not understand spiritually the wonders which they saw performed bodily; and they did not remember the multitude of your mercies, that is, your manifold mercy, by which you visited them in exile, scourged their enemies, and freed them from distress. Two things commend bestowed benefits: understanding and memory; both were lacking through unbelief. And they provoked him when going up to the Red Sea. That is: after being delivered from Egypt by the Lord’s hand, they at once provoked God to anger when they reached the Red Sea. For, seeing the Egyptian army pursuing them, they distrusted God’s help [Col. 0650B] and murmured, saying: “Were there no tombs in Egypt, that we should act here in the wilderness?” (Exod. 14:11). He said “going up” because departure from Egypt in whatever direction is an ascent, and the region in which the Red Sea lies is higher than Egypt. He calls it the Red Sea to distinguish it from the sea which is not red, or because in that sea they were delivered from enemies. That Red Sea is not naturally red, but takes this color from red earth. For the soil of that region is red. The Lord could have led them out by another route, but he wished to lead them by the Red Sea so that the faithful might understand that they are someday to be brought through baptism, reddened with blood, to the promised inheritance. Note that they confess their own sins under those of their fathers, because, just as those sinned bodily, so these sinned spiritually. And although they provoked God to anger by murmuring, nevertheless:

### Verse 8

[Col. 0650C] He saved them, not because of them but for the glorification of his own name. For what purpose? To make his power known. Thus, to reveal how powerful he is. And how did he save them?

### Verse 9

He rebuked the Red Sea. Just as a powerful person might rebuke a servant not to obstruct anyone, so he rebuked the sea not to hinder them in their flight; and it was dried up. And he led them through the depths as through the wilderness: that is, they crossed on such dry feet as if they were in a place where water had never been. Or, he led them through the sea as he later led them through the wilderness.

### Verse 10

And so he saved them from the hand of those who hated them, that is, from the power of the Egyptians, who hated them because of the spoiling; and he redeemed them from the hand of enemies, that is, from the power of Pharaoh and all the overseers who had ruled over them in their labors. He said “redeemed” because it already prefigured the redemption of the human race by Christ’s blood. He adds how he saved them:

### Verse 11

[Col. 0650D] Water covered those afflicting them, so completely that not one of them remained to report it. And this signified that in baptism all sins are forgiven.

### Verse 12

And then they believed his words: that is, only then did they first believe true what he had promised them, namely that he would deliver them. And they praised his praise, [Col. 0651A] because they were victorious: that is, in a praiseworthy deed they praised him. Or, as another translation has it: “And they sang his praise,” saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified” (Exod. 15:1), etc. And they offered this praise

### Verse 13

quickly: that is, they praised him for a brief time, and afterward forgot his works—that is, they consigned his benefits to oblivion. They did not wait for his counsel: that is, they did not patiently await his plan. God’s counsel was that they should enter the land of promise in this manner and that; but, impatient, they wished to be there without any labor or delay, as the common saying goes: “A shrewd man wants to eat fish, but does not want to work for them.” They forgot God’s works performed in Egypt and at the Red Sea.

### Verse 14

[Col. 0651B] And they desired a desire in the wilderness: that is, they desired a desirable thing, namely the fish of Egypt and pots of meat. This is a manner of speaking like our saying, “He served this service,” or “he led such a life.” And they tempted God in the waterless place: that is, from distrust they asked for water in the wilderness. Having entered from the Red Sea, they came into the desert. There the provisions which they had brought from Egypt failed them, and the whole multitude murmured for food and drink; Moses and others who were better asked God to give these things to them.

### Verse 15

And he gave them their request, namely water from the rock, and sent abundance into their souls: that is, he gave them manna and the flesh of birds in sufficient quantity. By “souls” he means desires: [Col. 0651C] that is, as much as they wished. Here they murmured against God, and he endured patiently; but afterward they murmured against their leaders, Moses and Aaron, and he did not endure it.

### Verse 16

And after these things they provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the Lord’s holy one: that is, the Lord’s chosen one or the Lord’s priest. For those anointed with oil were called holy.

It is asked why he did not call Moses holy but called Aaron holy. No one doubted Moses’ holiness, but Aaron’s holiness was doubted because he made an idol for the people. Therefore, in order to remove this doubt for us, he calls him holy, as he said above: “He sent Moses and Aaron, whom he chose,” namely Aaron himself, or for himself. But since [Col. 0651D] the children of Israel often provoked Moses and Aaron, he specifies the provocation of which he speaks: namely, in the camp. This happened as follows. After the Law had been received, the tabernacle and ark made, and the priesthood instituted by God, when they had come into the wilderness, Korah, one of the leaders among the priests, and Dathan and Abiram, leaders of the people, rose against Moses and Aaron with fifty men. They said that the Lord had not chosen Aaron as high priest, but that Moses had appointed him in order to exalt his own family. When Moses sent for them to come to the camp, they refused, saying: “Is it not enough for you that you deceived us by leading us out of an excellent land and bringing us into these worst places, unless you also rule over us? Do you also wish [Col. 0652A] to gouge out our eyes?” (Num. 16:13–14). Therefore, when the Lord was angry, the earth swallowed them alive, with their houses, tents, and all their possessions. This is what it says:

### Verses 17–18

The earth opened and swallowed Dathan and Abiram, and, coming over the assembly—that is, Abiram’s household—it covered them. And fire blazed in their synagogue. For fire went out from the Lord, namely from the pillar of fire, and burned those fifty men who had agreed with them. Hence it adds: Flame burned the sinners. A flame is so called from the lash of sparks. Over their destruction the people murmured, whom fire again consumed; but when Aaron prayed and offered incense for them, the fire ceased. To remove weariness from the reader, let us add the allegory.

[Col. 0652B] Egypt, which is interpreted as “darkness” or “tribulation,” is this world, covered with the darkness of vices and the tribulation of evils. Pharaoh, which is interpreted as “destroyer,” king of the Egyptians, is the devil, who destroys virtues and good works, king among the darkened in sins. The people oppressed by harsh slavery are the faithful people constrained under the devil’s yoke. Moses, who delivered the people from Pharaoh’s power through signs, is Christ, who rescued the faithful people from the devil’s dominion through miracles. The Red Sea, through which the people are led out, is baptism bathed in Christ’s blood, through which the people are saved. The enemies pursuing the fleeing Hebrews are demons pursuing those who flee the world. The wilderness, through which those delivered journey laboriously to their homeland, is the Christian religion, deserted by demons and unbelievers; through it the redeemed strive with much labor toward the homeland of paradise. In the wilderness those people are fed with bread from heaven and water from the rock; on God’s way these people feed upon Christ’s body, the living bread, and his blood. The promised land, which Jesus son of Nun apportions to that people, is the land of the living, which Jesus Christ distributes to the faithful according to the merits of each.

Thus let the faithful, rescued through him from the yoke of Pharaoh the devil and from the Egypt of unbelief, but again subjected to enemies—namely vices and sins—return in repentance to their task, saying: “We have sinned with our fathers.” The fathers of the wicked are the wicked whom they have begotten by evil example [Col. 0652D]. Hence it is said: “You are from your father the devil,” that is, from Cain, “(John 8:44),” who because of envy was called a devil and was a murderer from the beginning. Sinners are the children of sinners whom they imitate. We have sinned with such fathers, because we have lived wickedly after their example. We have acted unjustly, because we have rejected your law. We have committed iniquity, because we have harmed our neighbours. Our fathers, from whom we have been begotten through imitation of evil, being in the Egypt of unbelief, did not understand your works: that you created the angels for eternal glory, and, after they fell from glory, purposed to repair their fall through human beings; while you restored humanity’s fall through your Son. They did not remember the multitude of your mercy: that you did not spare your only-begotten Son, but delivered him to death for human salvation and rescued them from death. And they provoked God by ascending in pride into the sea—that is, into cruelty—into the Red Sea, that is, into persecution reddened with the blood of the saints. Here “sea” denotes the storm of persecution. Yet he saved these people when they turned to the faith for the sake of his name, that is, for the sake of the Son, who is the Father’s name; or for the sake of the Christian name, so as to make known his power—that he alone has power to justify the ungodly.

And he rebuked the Red Sea, that is, he commanded persecution to cease. And it was dried up, because the savage storm of the age dried up when the fountain of life came. And he led them through the depths as through a desert: that is, he led the faithful placed [Col. 0653B] amid the deep counsels of pagans and heretics so safely on the path of the Christian religion as if they were in a desert, that is, in no danger. And he saved them from the hand of those who hated them: in body, from the power of persecutors and heretics; in soul, from the power of demons and sinners. And he redeemed them by Christ’s blood from the hand of the enemy, that is, from the devil’s power. And water covered those who afflicted them: that is, the water of baptism washed away the unbelievers who formerly afflicted the faithful; not one of them remained an unbeliever. This occurred when Constantine believed. Or, the water of baptism or of tears covered all iniquities which afflicted souls, and not one sin among these remained undeletable. And they believed in his words, namely the Gospel promises, and praised his praise—that is, through his praiseworthy deeds they praised him. Yet some quickly rendered this praise and ceased from praising. And immediately they forgot his works: that he endured slaps, spittle, scourges, and the death of the cross for them, and that he rescued them from the hands of their enemies. They did not await his counsel—that is, they did not patiently await God’s counsel that through many tribulations they should enter the kingdom of God, as Christ went before them. Or, through evil works they lost baptismal grace: “And they lusted with lust in the desert.” The wicked are a desert, because those who desert God’s commandments become deserted by grace. In this desert they lusted with lust, that is, for worldly glory. And they tempted God in the waterless place [Col. 0653D], that is, being themselves waterless, for dry of the Spirit’s watering, they tempted God by seeking riches and worldly honours, though they doubted that he would give them. And he gave them their request, namely worldly riches and dignities, and sent fullness into their souls: that is, he gave them an abundance of all things which they desired. And they provoked Moses and Aaron in the camp, that is, the law and the priesthood in the churches. By transgressing God’s law they provoke it; the priests exasperate them and separate them from the camps when they excommunicate them from the churches. Once they had been cast out of the Church, the earth was opened, because then it will be plain to all how earthly-minded people, despising God, eagerly pursue earthly things. This earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram: that is, earthly desires absorb heretics and schismatics; afterwards they descend alive—that is, knowingly—to hell, who, divided from Christ’s Church, make an erring congregation for themselves.
