And fire blazed in their synagogue, that is, the heat of lust in their assembly, and the eternal flame burned sinners dead in sins. Or, those consenting with them will burn in eternal fire. Let us again consider the literal sense.

**VERSE 19.** “And they made a calf in Horeb.” The order is wholly inverted. For he often places before what happened later, and often places after what happened earlier; and he does this because of a definite mystery. For he does not narrate past events, but foretells future ones. He takes words from past events and weaves together future events. Therefore he most carefully preserves not the order of history, but that of prophecy. [Col. 0654B] They made the calf in Horeb before the earth swallowed Korah with his followers, as happened thus. While Moses stood with the Lord on the mountain for forty days and Aaron remained with the multitude in the valley, the people, thinking that Moses had been consumed by fire, asked Aaron to make them a god to go before them into Egypt. Struck with fear, Aaron ordered them all to bring him gold, from which he caused a calf to be cast. Worshipping it and sacrificing a victim to it, the children of Israel said: “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of Egypt” (Exod. 32:4). Learning this through the Lord’s disclosure, Moses hastily descended from the mountain, broke in anger the tablets written by God, cut the calf into pieces, burned it with fire, scattered it in water, and gave it to the people to drink. [Col. 0654C] Because of this sin, twenty-three thousand of the people were killed.

Since this happened on Mount Sinai, it is asked how it can here be said to have occurred on Mount Horeb. In ancient times that mountain was called Horeb. But after Moses saw the burning bush there, or received the law there, he named it Sinai, which means “bush” or “commandment.”

Again, it is asked why the children of Israel made for God the form of an ox rather than of a human being. In this they imitated the custom of the Egyptians, who worship the ox Apis. Apis was a king of Egypt; after his death he was called Serapis and was considered a robber. He possessed an ox of a single colour, but having on its side a mark like the moon. [Col. 0654D] After a long time, one very like it appeared in Egypt. Therefore it seemed that their god Apis had appeared in an ox, and for this reason they began to worship it.

**VERSE 20.** “And they changed their glory into the likeness of a calf,” as has been said: a calf, I say, eating grass. This is said to reproach those who worshipped not a living ox, nor even a dead one, but rather a senseless image. By this the devil is shown, who devoured them away from the worship of God and incorporated them into himself.

**VERSES 21–22.** They forgot God, who saved them from all dangers: that God who did great things in Egypt, when he humbled the Egyptians by signs and exalted the Hebrews; and who worked wonders in the land [Col. 0655A] of Ham—that is, Egypt, so called from Ham the son of Noah—when he struck the enemies of his people with plagues and kept his own unharmed; and who did terrible things in the Red Sea, when he drowned Pharaoh with all his people and brought his own out of danger.

**VERSE 23.** And then the Lord said—that is, he purposed—to destroy them, saying to Moses: “I see that this people is stiff-necked; let me alone, that I may destroy them and wipe them from the earth” (Exod. 32:9–10). And he would have done this, if Moses, his chosen one, had not stood in the breaking before him, saying: “Forgive the people this offence, or blot me out of the book which you have written” (Exod. 32:31–32). “Breaking” pertains to earthenware vessels. They were vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, and the Lord’s anger intended to break their bodies with some plague as pots, and to consign their souls to fires. But Moses stood before him, praying amid the breaking; that is, he exposed himself to God’s wrath in that danger.

In the Hebrew it is written: “If Moses, his chosen one, had not stood more worthily before him.” By this it is shown that, through the prayers of the righteous, punishment is suspended from sinners. For what purpose did Moses stand? To turn away his wrath, lest he destroy them—that is, to remove God’s vengeance from them, lest he kill them. Let us return to allegory.

Oreb or Horeb means “Calvary.” Those who, forgetting God in Horeb, worshipped the calf signify those who, on Calvary, denying Christ, chose Barabbas—that is, the devil. Mount Sinai, high and lofty, is Christ, the foundation of the city of God. The fire which [Col. 0655C] burned on the mountain is the Holy Spirit, who filled Christ and illumines the city of God, namely the Church. The blast of trumpets is the cry of preachers. The burning lamps are saints shining by example. Moses with the Lord on the burning mountain is the law in lofty understanding, fervent in the Spirit. The law is written by the finger of God on two tablets, because every commandment of God is set forth in the two precepts of charity through the Holy Spirit. Aaron holds the multitude, and the priesthood governs the people. The golden calf is the body of the devil, because as an ox labours upon the earth, so the devil’s members continually toil in earthly things. It is cast from gold, because through worldly wisdom the multitude of the wicked is established in avarice, which is proclaimed to be the service of idols. They make the calf in Horeb because they set up an idol in God’s place [Col. 0655D], when they worship gold instead of God. Moses descends from the mountain to the crowds because the law, bending down from lofty understanding, extends the killing letter to carnal people. He broke the tablets and cut the calf into pieces, because when the law is broken open by interpreters, its spiritual meaning springs forth; this meaning, through preachers, crushes the devil’s body. The calf is burned by fire, scattered in water, and given to the people as drink, because the fire of the Holy Spirit consumed the sins of those whom it kindled in its love; the priestly order immersed them in the water of baptism, and the faithful people incorporate them into themselves as though as drink. Those who fell slain are those who perished in idolatry. But those who worshipped the carved image are heretics, who fashion God in their heart as the image of a human being and, deceived, worship this as God. Of them it is rightly added: “And they changed their glory into the likeness of a calf eating grass.” God is the glory of souls. Therefore heretics changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of corruptible man; just as their fathers—the erring ones—changed not God’s glory but their own into the likeness of the calf, that is, of the devil, who eats grass like an ox when he consumes the wicked as fire consumes wood.

They forgot God, Christ, who saved them from death, who did great things in Egypt—that is, many signs in Judaea, veiled by the darkness of unbelief—and who worked wonders in the land of Ham, that is, among the Gentiles, the raging land. For Ham means “raging,” and the Gentile world [Col. 0656B] was raging in idolatry; there Christ performed many wonders through his preachers. Or Ham is hell, the land of the raging devil, in which he did wonders by binding the devil and snatching away his spoils. And he did terrible things in the Red Sea, that is, in persecution, when he cast down persecutors and crowned martyrs. Or, in baptism he drowned sins and made vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath. And he said that he would destroy them—that is, he willed to destroy such people—and would have done so if Moses, his chosen one, had not stood in the breaking before him: that is, if the people observing the law had not exposed themselves to danger in prayer. “To turn away his wrath, lest he destroy them.” Because of their prayers he spared them. For the chosen turn God’s wrath from a sinning people and, by their prayers, stay the judge’s hand from an impending punishment; and they often convert by praying those whom they cannot convert by preaching.

The literal sense must again be consulted. Our fathers provoked God when they worshipped the calf; moreover, they provoked him when

**VERSE 24.** “They treated the desirable land as nothing.” The history is touched upon here. When they had approached the promised land, they sent scouts ahead. On returning, these terrified the people by saying that giants inhabited that land, and that if they entered it with their sons and wives, the giants would devour them. Hearing this, all were disturbed, wept, and counted the desirable land as nothing. This is the land which they had long desired to see and enter; now [Col. 0656D] they began to loathe and flee it, saying: “Let us appoint a leader for ourselves and return to Egypt.” And though Joshua and Caleb consoled them, promising them victory from the Lord,

**VERSE 25.** they did not believe his word, that is, God’s promise, and murmured in their tents, saying: “Would that we had died in Egypt and not in this wilderness!” Therefore the angry Lord swore that none of them should enter that land except the two who had followed him. Moved by repentance, they then said that they were ready to go up against their enemies. The Lord commanded them not to go up, lest they be defeated and fall before their enemies; but they did not heed the Lord’s voice. Instead, darkened in mind, they went armed up the mountain, and the Canaanites whom they encountered [Col. 0657A] killed them all. The remainder, who survived, returned with Moses and the Ark into the wilderness. Here four crimes are briefly set forth: they rejected the excellent land promised to their fathers and freely offered to them; they did not believe God’s word; they murmured against God; and finally, they did not obey his voice, and therefore perished. Thus the unbelievers who entered the wilderness with Moses provoked God in many ways.

**VERSE 26.** And he lifted up his hand, that is, his power, over them, to cast them down in the desert. For the bodies of all were laid low in the wilderness: some were consumed by fire, some perished by serpents.

**VERSE 27.** And he again lifted up his hand to cast down [Col. 0657B] their seed among the nations: that is, to kill their children among Gentile nations and scatter them as captives through many regions.

The allegory must be considered. Those who have fallen from the Church into paganism and heresy counted the desirable land as nothing—that is, paradise, the land of the living, which is greatly to be desired by the saints—because they loved earthly things instead. They did not believe his word, that is, the Son of God, who promised glory to the righteous and threatened punishment to the unjust. And they murmured in their tents, that is, in their bodies, which are tents of the soul, whether because of drought, rain, or some plague brought upon humanity by God’s judgment; this is a grave sin. For murmurers will perish by the bites of demons, as those people perished through poisonous [Col. 0657C] serpents. And when sacred Scripture or teachers called them back to repentance, they did not heed God’s voice but persisted in obstinacy. And he lifted his hand over them—that is, he delayed the vengeance hanging over them, to punish them more severely later through excommunication. Or, he lifted up his hand, that is, his power, over them. For what purpose? To cast them down in the desert: that is, since they themselves were a desert because they had abandoned truth, he decreed to condemn them in this error. And to cast down their seed among the nations—that is, to hand over their works and teaching, or their imitators, to demons, and to scatter them in the regions: that is, to destroy them, scattered among vices, in the prisons of hell. The literal sense [Col. 0657D] must be resumed.

**VERSE 28.** “And they were initiated to Baal-peor.” The history is as follows. When they had defeated Kings Sihon and Og and approached the land of Midian, King Balak, terrified at their arrival, sent for Balaam the priest, promising him very many gifts if by cursing he would turn the people away from his kingdom. But Balaam, filled with the divine Spirit, blessed the people of Israel and foretold many things about Christ and the Church in prophecy. Among other things he uttered these words: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel” (Num. 24:17), who will subject all kingdoms to himself. Afterwards, conquered by avarice, he gave counsel that the girls of the Midianites, adorned with gold and jewels, should go out to meet the people carrying the image of Priapus and entice them into prostitution and idolatry [Col. 0658A], knowing that the Lord would kill them for these things. Thus the children of Israel, overcome by lust, had intercourse with the girls and were initiated to Baal-peor—that is, consecrated; that is, they devoted themselves to serve the idol Baal, as it was worshipped on Mount Peor. Beel, Baal, Baalim, and Belial are the same. This likewise is a name derived from Belus, the father of Ninus, who founded the city of Nineveh. After Belus’s death, his son made a statue and image of him and commanded the people subject to himself to worship it. Priapus was a certain man expelled from the city of Lampsacus because of the size of his male member. After death he was made the god of gardens. Newly married people were especially accustomed to sacrifice to him. He was worshipped on Mount Peor, which means “disgrace.” The children of Israel sacrificed to this idol because of their love for the girls, [Col. 0658B] and ate sacrifices of the dead. For Belus, Priapus, Jupiter, and others considered gods were humans who were dead in soul and body; they themselves ate the sacrifices offered to them with a certain veneration.

**VERSE 29.** And they provoked him by their inventions, that is, by those rites which the Gentiles invented for themselves and which the Lord did not give. In this way, by their deeds, they provoked God. Therefore destruction was multiplied among them, because more than twenty thousand were killed.

**VERSE 30.** And when the destruction was so great, Phinehas the priest stood before the Lord and appeased him from this plague. This Phinehas was [the son] of Eleazar, son of Aaron, who [Col. 0658C] stood firm because he did not mingle with the Midianites. Seeing a Jew entering a tent with a Midianite woman for fornication, he grieved; entering the tent after him, he pierced them both with a dagger, and the shaking—that is, destruction, or God’s agitation—ceased.

**VERSE 31.** And it was reckoned to him for righteousness, that is, for justification, because he did this out of zeal for God and not hatred: in that present generation, because the priesthood was given to him; and in the future generation, because the dignity of the priesthood was established for his descendants. And this was for ever, because his reward was laid up eternally. This indicates that judges do not sin when they punish the wicked; indeed, they receive the reward of righteousness if they do this from zeal for God.

The allegory must be sought. Those apostatizing from the Church [Col. 0658D] were initiated to Baal-peor, that is, to the idol of disgrace: they consecrated themselves to an idol devoted to lust, when they wholly made themselves subject to the demon of uncleanness, dishonouring their bodies in themselves, males committing shameful acts with males. And they ate sacrifices of the dead: that is, they received sacrifices offered by heretics and excommunicated persons, who were dead in soul. And they provoked God by their inventions, that is, by diverse errors invented by themselves—or rather, inspired by the devil. Therefore destruction was multiplied among them: that is, their condemnation became manifold. And Phinehas stood—that is, the Church’s priestly order stood in good works—and appeased God by the saving sacrifice for sinners; and the shaking ceased, that is, God’s vengeance ceased from destroying them. And it was reckoned [Col. 0659A] to him for righteousness, because God reckons it as a reward of righteousness to his chosen ones that they pray for those who err, so that they may recover their senses from the devil’s snares: from the generation of this life and the future generation in the resurrection, and for ever, that is, with the angels unto the age. Phinehas means “sparing the mouth,” because the priestly order causes Christ, who is the mouth of God, to spare sinners. Let the literal sense again be brought into the middle.

**VERSE 32.** “And they provoked him at the water of contradiction.” This happened before they sacrificed to Baal-peor. When they were suffering a shortage of water, they contradicted the Lord and Moses, declaring that they would no longer obey unless he gave them water. The Lord gave them water from the rock. It was therefore called the water of contradiction, because they publicly contradicted the Lord and Moses. [Col. 0659B] And Moses was troubled, not on his own account but on theirs,

**VERSE 33.** because they embittered his spirit: that is, Moses was disturbed because of the Jews, because they exasperated him by evil words. And because he was sorrowful, he therefore made a distinction with his lips—that is, in this miracle he used language different from that used in the other miracles he had done earlier. Before, he said confidently: “Whatever you wish, God will give you.” But now, disturbed by them, he said with distrust: “Can we bring water for you out of this rock?” (Num. 20:10). And although he had previously brought water from the rock, he now struck the rock twice with his rod in doubt; and the water flowed out and flowed with them throughout the entire journey. Because of this fault neither he nor Aaron entered the promised land. For he blasphemed God by doubting his power. Let the allegory be examined.

Moses in this passage bore the figure of the Jewish people, who did not believe that the rock was God himself; and therefore fastened him to the two pieces of wood of the cross. From his side waters flowed, through which the nations were saved. But because the Jewish people remained unbelieving, it did not deserve to enter the Lord’s inheritance.

Otherwise: the water of contradiction is baptism, in which the devil and his works are renounced. Those who apostatized from the faith provoked God at this water when, like a dog returning to its vomit, they returned to the works of the devil which they had already renounced. And Moses was troubled [Col. 0659D] because of them: that is, the faithful people taken up from the water of baptism was grieved because of them. For Moses is said to mean “drawn from water.” Because of heretics or evil Christians, God’s chosen people was disturbed, because through wicked conduct and perverse doctrine they embittered the spirit—that is, grieved its soul. And he made a distinction with his lips: that is, he prayed distinctly for evil Catholics, distinctly for heretics, and distinctly for the good.

Let the literal sense be recalled. Not only in the above-mentioned ways did our fathers provoke God in the wilderness, but also after they entered the promised land.

**VERSE 34.** They did not destroy the nations which the Lord had commanded them utterly to destroy; instead, they spared [Col. 0660A] them, and afterwards suffered unceasing persecution from them.

**VERSES 35–36.** And they mingled with the nations through intermarriage and learned their works, that is, their rites; they served their carved images, that is, they worshipped idols; and this became a stumbling block to them, that is, an offence and loss, because the Lord therefore allowed them to suffer many evils. They did evil by worshipping idols; but they did worse still, because

**VERSES 37–38.** they sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons, in order to appease their gods by shedding their blood. Pagans, and especially magicians, used to sacrifice little children to their gods and receive responses through their blood. For the soul of the slain person—or rather, an unclean spirit in that person’s form—appeared there and answered the questioner’s inquiries, as is read of Simon and Julian the Apostate. The Jews imitated this practice with their own children. Although the ancient history does not recount this, the Holy Spirit speaking in the Psalms must nevertheless be believed. They worshipped demons and shed innocent blood. Whose? The blood of their sons and their daughters, whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan. They spared that nation and became its imitators. He shows that they committed three monstrous crimes in one deed: murder, because they shed innocent blood; parricide, because they slaughtered their sons and daughters; and sacrilege, because they sacrificed them to idols. And it must always be connected with that passage: “And they provoked.” Note, indeed, throughout this psalm, that [Col. 0660C] those provoking God did not enter the promised land. Some were struck down by a cruel death, such as the murmurers who died from serpents; some died a common death, such as Aaron and Moses, who could not enter because of unbelief. But those who entered and provoked God by idolatry were delivered to enemies. They killed their own children, and the land was slain [Vulgate: “and the land was defiled”] in their blood—that is, blood shed or to be shed is understood. “The land was slain,” that is, they themselves were slain. For when they shed their children’s blood, they killed themselves in soul; and he has put the container for that which it contains, a figure of metonymy. Those are wrong who say: “It was defiled by the land.” For the Hebrew reads: [Col. 0660D] “The land was slain.” Or, “the land was slain,” that is, their bodies, “in bloods,” that is, in the pollution of lust.

**VERSE 39.** And it was defiled by their works: that is, the promised land was soiled through their deeds. And they committed fornication in their inventions: departing from God, the true husband, they fornicated with alien gods by sacrificing to idols. “In their inventions,” that is, by acting according to their own institutions against God’s ordinances. Another translation has: “In their pursuits.” Another: “In their pleasures.”

The allegory is recounted. Those who contradict at the water—that is, who renounced the devil at baptism and afterwards subjected themselves to his service—did not destroy the nations which the Lord commanded them to destroy: that is, [Col. 0661A] they did not abandon the vices and sins which the Lord commanded them to abandon. And they mingled by consent and will among the nations, that is, by living among pagan practices. And they learned their works, that is, the rites and pursuits of the wicked. And they served their carved images because they followed magicians, diviners, soothsayers, astrologers, and those possessed by Python spirits (*pythones*), observing omens and dreams. This became a stumbling block to them, that is, an offence, because many were corrupted by their wicked example and they themselves were rejected by God. *Scandalum* means “a thing on the left.” And they sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons. By sons we understand spiritual pursuits, by daughters secular pursuits: that is, all studies which they had either in divine or in secular books they turned through vices into the service of demons. “For everyone [Col. 0661B] who commits sin is a slave of sin” (1 John 3:4). And they shed innocent blood: that is, they destroyed the souls of the simple by wicked example. What blood? That of their sons and daughters—that is, their dependents, or those who became their offspring through evil imitation. How did they destroy these? They sacrificed them to the carved images of Canaan. By Canaan, who through Noah was consigned to slavery and cursing, is understood the people given over to the service of sins and cursed by the Judge among those on the left at judgment. Its carved images are those dead in body and soul whose examples people follow, such as Hector, Achilles, Catiline, Jugurtha, Alexander, or Simon Magus. Therefore those sacrifice sons and daughters to the carved images of Canaan who recount these persons’ deeds to the people as examples or sing of such matters to instruct others by them. For they serve idols who venerate such persons in this way. And the land was slain in bloods: that is, their incorporeal temples of the Holy Spirit were corrupted by pollutions. And it was defiled by their unclean works, and they committed fornication in their inventions, that is, in Sodomitic crimes. God is the husband of the soul; those who desert him and join themselves to demons through wicked desires are fornicators and adulterers and will be one with them, just as the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit with him. We must return to the literal sense.

**VERSE 40.** And the Lord was wrathful in fury against his people: that is, he was moved with vehement anger on account of such deeds [Col. 0661D] in that people, which ought to have been his in the observance of the law and worship of the one God. And he abhorred his inheritance: that is, he disinherited from the inheritance promised to their fathers those whom he had cultivated as someone cultivates an inheritance. Or, he seemed to abhor his inheritance through the tribulations and afflictions which were among them, yet he reserved some so that they might be his inheritance.

**VERSE 41.** And he delivered them into the hands of nations, namely Philistines, Midianites, and others; and those whom they served in their idols, who hated them, ruled over them. It is a very grievous thing for a human being to be delivered into the enemy’s power.

**VERSE 42.** And when they had been delivered to these, their enemies afflicted them, oppressing them with servitude, as the Egyptians had once done, [Col. 0662A] or exacting tribute from them. And they were humbled beneath their hands: that is, they were afflicted under their power. For humiliation is affliction. They afflicted them by prisons, chains, beatings, and many other means. And the Lord

**VERSE 43.** often delivered them: now through Jephthah, now through Gideon, now through Deborah, now through Samson, or through other judges, and finally through kings. On the contrary, they provoked him in their counsel—understand: earthly counsel, not beneficial to them. Their counsel was to fulfil their own wills, not the Lord’s commands. And therefore they were humbled, that is, afflicted by their iniquities.

**VERSES 44–45.** And he saw when they were afflicted: that is, the Lord had mercy because they were troubled, and he heard [Col. 0662B] their prayer. And he remembered his covenant. For these three reasons he again delivered them: because he saw their tribulation, heard their prayer, and remembered his covenant. For he promised Abraham that he would give that land to his seed. And because he remembered this covenant, he fulfilled it as he had promised. This verse is joined to the passage where it is written in the previous psalm: “For he remembered his holy word, which he had spoken to Abraham his servant.” And he repented according to the multitude of his mercies: that is, according to human perception, he changed the tribulation which he was about to bring upon them, in accordance with the abundance of his mercy. *Paenitentia* (“repentance”) is said to derive from *poena* (“punishment”) and *teneo* (“I hold”). For one who repents grieves that he has done something, and thus punishment holds him.

[Col. 0662C] Since God is unchangeable and is affected by no punishment or pain, how is he said to have repented, as in: “It repents me that I made humankind” (Gen. 6:6), and: “It repents me that I anointed Saul as king” (1 Sam. 15:11)? But it must be understood that Scripture speaks according to our manner. As he is said to be angry when he severely punishes human sins, so he is said to repent when he changes adversities inflicted on sinners into prosperity. For that over which we repent, we wish to change. He is said, as it were, to have repented of making humankind when he purposed to change the human race through baptism just as through the flood. He is said, as it were, to have repented of anointing Saul king when he wished to change the kingdom through Christ just as through David. So now he repented [Col. 0662D] when he changed the affliction of the people. Repentance therefore pertains to us, not to God, who does not change. For from eternity he ordained everything that was to occur; yet he willed to be entreated through tribulations so that it might occur.

**VERSE 46.** And he gave them unto mercies: that is, he surrounded them with manifold mercy in the sight of all who had taken them captive—that is, openly before all who had formerly ruled them.

We must return to allegory. Because of fornications and uncleannesses, the Lord was wrathful in fury against his people, chastising them by famine, pestilence, and sword. And he abhorred his inheritance: that is, because of many shameful acts he disinherited them from the inheritance promised to the faithful. He calls them his people because of baptism, his inheritance because of their observance of Christianity. And he delivered them into the hands of nations: that is, he allowed them to fall under demons’ power. For God is then angry when he allows a person to do what that person wishes, because the devil immediately subjugates the person to himself. Hence it follows: “And those who hated them ruled over them”; that is, demons and vices, which hate their souls, immediately rule over them. And their enemies afflicted them, visible enemies outwardly and invisible enemies inwardly; and they were humbled beneath their hands, that is, severely afflicted under their powers. And then he often delivered them; but they provoked him in their counsel, which they had in order to fulfil their own desires, and they were humbled in their iniquities, that is, afflicted in their lusts. And he sees when they were afflicted [Col. 0663B], that is, he mercifully regarded their tribulation. And he heard their prayer, because he immediately said to those who called upon him: “Behold, I am here.” And he remembered his covenant, by which he promised pardon to those who repent, saying: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 33:11); and again: “At whatever hour you turn and groan, you shall be saved” (ibid., 12).

And he repented according to the multitude of his mercies: that is, having pity on them, he gave them repentance and changed their sorrow into joy. And he gave them unto mercies: those formerly wrapped in misery he now wrapped in mercies, giving chastity to one, humility to another, love to another, grace to others [Col. 0663C], in the sight of all—that is, openly before the demons that had formerly caught them in the snares of vices. Note that the preceding psalm contains twenty benefits of God bestowed upon the fathers [Col. 0664A]; this one contains an equal number of crimes committed by the faithless. The prayer of those converted follows: as you once saved our fathers from enemies, so

**VERSE 47.** save us, Lord Jesus Christ, who are our God; and gather us into one faith from the nations among which we have been scattered. The Jews have been scattered through all nations.

Alternatively: Save us, O Lord our God, from sins and enemies; and gather us, scattered among the nations through vices—that is, separate us from demons and from all who live wickedly—so that we may confess your holy name, that is, praise you in accordance with your holy name. And thus in the future may we glory in your praise, that is, because of the praise offered here to you by us. For by praising God here we shall exult in eternal glory. Their praise follows:

**VERSE 48.** Blessed be the Lord God of Israel. Gather us in love, that we may confess, saying thus: May the Lord, who is redeemer, and the God of Israel, who makes men see God, be blessed—that is, exalted and glorious—in the very fact that he makes us Israel, beginning from this present age and continuing into the age to come, ever glorious. And all the people, of circumcision and uncircumcision, shall say: “So be it, so be it,” that is, “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel.”

In the Hebrew it is written: “Amen, amen, Alleluia,” that is, “Praise the Lord, all of you.” It began with praise and ended in praise, because the penitence of those who confess is the praise of God, and God’s forgiveness is the joy of human beings. Here ends the fourth book, consecrated to the four Gospels or the four virtues.

## PSALM 106. On the Praise of the Church from among the Gentiles

[Col. 0663]

[Col. 0663C] **VERSE 1.** “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever. Let those redeemed [by the Lord] say,” etc. The Holy Spirit begins the fifth book with praise [Col. 0663D] and also brings it to completion in praise, because those who spiritually observe the Pentateuch of the Law will praise God with the angels unto ages of ages. These three psalms begin in the same manner, because the three regions of the world, or the three orders of the Church, sing the Trinity in like manner.

The first, in the person of both peoples, sings of Christ’s coming; and after this it sings of the benefits bestowed upon believers, which God granted bodily to the ancient people and spiritually to the new. The second, in the person of the Church from the Jews, sings in confession of the evils which the faithless people repaid to the Lord before Christ’s coming and afterward through misguided belief. The third, in the person of the Church from among the Gentiles, sings joyfully [Col. 0664C] how the merciful one redeemed captive servants from the enemy’s hand and how the good shepherd gathered scattered sheep from many regions into one fold.

[Col. 0664D] This is the one hundred and sixth psalm. By the hundred is denoted perfection; by the six, activity. This number therefore signifies that those who devoutly fulfil the six works of the Gospel receive a hundredfold reward in the future. The title of the psalm is:

**ALLELUIA, ALLELUIA.**

[Note: [Col. 0663D] The Vulgate omits the second *Alleluia*.]

Jerome says that wherever *Alleluia* is placed twice, one is the ending of the preceding psalm and the other the title of the following psalm. Augustine, however, says that both belong to the following psalm on account of the two peoples: one belongs to the Jews, the other to the Gentiles.

The subject of the psalm is four temptations and four mercies of the Lord. The first temptation is general unbelief; the second, a more constraining evil habit; the third, still more, acedia; the fourth belongs only to prelates, and occurs in two ways: either when the subject people behaves without discipline, or when it persecutes even the prelate himself. Because of these four dangers, the verse “And they cried to God” is given four times. And because God’s mercy comes to their aid as often, the verse “Let them give thanks to the Lord” occurs four times. These are called intercalary verses, because just as the sixth day before the Kalends is inserted twice, so a verse repeated more than once is inserted among the psalms. Or they are called intercalary as though placed in the middle of the path, that is, set in the course of the song.

The intention is to exhort us to thanksgiving for [Col. 0665B] these benefits bestowed. The words are taken from the people delivered from Egypt but suffering many evils from the nations under the judges; they signify the Christian people redeemed through Christ but suffering many and varied evils from persecutors and heretics. For under the judges some, through fear of enemies, wandered in the wilderness, hungry and thirsty; others sat captive in darkness, bound in prison with chains; others were weakened by a long sickness and drew near to the gates of death; others were gravely endangered upon the sea and amid waves. Christians also suffered these same things under persecutors, and the Lord delivered them from them all.

The psalm is divided into five parts, because praise is rendered to God by our five senses; and each [Col. 0665C] part is marked off by the word “Let them give thanks.” In the first, those redeemed by the Lord are exhorted to praise God. In the second, the Gentiles give thanks because they have been satisfied by grace and released from the bonds of sins. In the third, the nations recount that bronze gates and iron bars were shattered and that they themselves were snatched from the way of wickedness. In the fourth, priests offer sacrifice to the Lord for his benefits and proclaim God’s wonders. In the fifth, the Church gives thanks to God because he has granted such great benefits to the human race.

It is the voice of the Holy Spirit exhorting the faithful from among the Gentiles to God’s praise: O all you redeemed by the Lord and gathered from the regions,

“Give thanks to the Lord,” that is, offer to the Lord the praise of confession, to the Son, “for he is good,” that is, pleasant, gracious, sweet [Col. 0665D]: as agreeable food is to the hungry, so the Lord is sweet to those who know him. And therefore give thanks, “for his mercy is forever,” that is, his mercy bestowed upon you will endure forever. He has set forth God’s goodness and mercy. But because it is difficult to treat of God’s natural goodness, he passes it over and begins to treat mercy in its parts. In overflowing joy he turns to the third person, saying:

**VERSE 2.** “Let those redeemed by the Lord say,” namely, captive servants redeemed by the merciful Lord should say, “For he is good; for his mercy is forever”: those whom he redeemed by his precious blood from the enemy’s hand, that is, from the devil’s power. There are certain animals, such as sea-shells, which, closed within themselves, clasp firmly and do not let go unless the shell is broken and they are violently separated from it. But if oil is poured in, it immediately loosens, and what had been tightly closed is dispersed and divided into parts. So Christ’s blood dissolved the most hardened hand of the devil, which enclosed and constricted the human race within itself; he poured it forth as it were the oil of mercy and freed us from it. “And he gathered them from the regions.” This is connected with the place where it is written: “That he might cast down their seed among the nations, and scatter them among the regions” (Ps. 105:27); and with: “Save us” (ibid., 47); and: “Gather us from among the nations.” For as sheep scattered among the nations, he gathered them through the apostles from the regions, taken into [Col. 0666B] the unity of faith from the four quarters of the world, namely,

**VERSE 3.** “From the rising of the sun,” that is, from the east, “and from the setting,” that is, from the west; “from the north,” that is, from the northern region; “and from the sea,” that is, from the south. Philosophers divide the world into five zones, of which the middle is torrid, two on either side are temperate, and the two extremes are cold. In the torrid zone they place the great Ocean, which, they say, divides the whole world. This sea is here put for the southern quarter, which is also called noon.

Alternatively: when “sea” is used absolutely, it means the great sea which lies between Europe and Africa. This sea lies to the west with respect to the position of the land of the Jewish people; and in this place it will signify not the southern part but vices. And if only three parts of the world are named—east, west, and north—from which parts did he gather them? He says: from the sea, that is, from those who were making God bitter through unbelief and evil works, to faith and good works, by him who came from the south, as it is written: “God shall come from the south” (Hab. 3:3). Christ was born in the south because Bethlehem, in relation to Jerusalem’s location, lies in the south. And he gathered from east and west those who shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.

Therefore now, you servants redeemed by the Lord, praise him; you sheep gathered from the regions, glorify the good shepherd. Or Judea is understood by the south, and the Gentiles by the remaining three quarters [Col. 0666D]. And because this psalm concerns the rejection of the Jews and the gathering of the Gentiles, three regions are named and the fourth is passed over in silence.

Here he begins to speak of the first temptation and mercy: God delivers from unbelief and error and leads into the right way. The true shepherd gathered the sheep who

**VERSE 4.** “Wandered in the wilderness,” that is, in faithlessness and error. As a wilderness is a place where no one comes, so the Gentiles were alone in faithlessness, without God’s mercy; “and in a waterless place,” that is, dry, without the rain of teaching or the dew of grace. They truly wandered, because they did not find “the way to a city,” namely Christ, who leads to the heavenly city; or who is the way of the city, that is, of the Church; or the commandments which lead to [Col. 0667A] the heavenly city Jerusalem, which is our dwelling-place. Socrates and Plato discovered many paths, but because they wished to discover by themselves and through their own powers, they did not discover the way to the city of the Church, the eternal dwelling-place. Yet

**VERSE 5.** they “were hungry and thirsty for it.” For as one who is hungry and thirsty loves food and drink and longs to be restored, so certain philosophers desired and laboured to find the way leading to their homeland. But they did not find it, because they sought to find it not through the Lord’s mercy but through their own powers; and thus “their soul failed within them.” Their reason failed amid their errors, away from the way of truth: they wandered as blind men, did not find the way, and yet thought that they had found it, as Plato did. Or “their soul failed within them” means that the fault lay [Col. 0667B] in themselves, not in God, that they did not find the true way; for if they had asked God, he would have shown it to them. But because they presumed upon their own powers, they fell away from truth.

**VERSE 6.** And, while they were set amid these tribulations—in faithlessness and error—“they cried to the Lord”: not they themselves, but their successors, such as Cornelius and the eunuch of Queen Candace, through alms and prayers, when they were afflicted by the greatness of their misery; “and he delivered them from their necessities.” He delivered them from distress, from the error of the wilderness, by showing them the way of salvation. Or the error itself was their cry, just as a madman does not cry out by voice or intention but by his very evident condition; and he released them from poverty, that is, from incapacity.

In the Hebrew it reads: “He delivered them from their affliction,” or “from their distress.”

**VERSE 7.** “And he led them from error into the right way,” that is, into faith in Jesus Christ and good works; for faith without works is a dead way, namely, not a right one. To what end did he lead them? “That they might go to a city of habitation,” that is, that by this way—namely, through himself—they might go into the heavenly city, where the true dwelling is.

From the passage, “They wandered in the wilderness,” this is drawn from those who wandered forty years in the desert and afterward came to the place of habitation. It signifies the Gentiles who wandered in idolatry and afterward came to the city of God, the Church. Since he delivered them from this unbelief, therefore [Col. 0667D]

**VERSE 8.** “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies,” that is, let these mercies furnish them matter for praising the Lord: in considering these mercies, let them praise the Lord with devotion and a good life; and let them give thanks for “his wonders shown to the children of men,” who are the undeserving children of Adam and Eve. That is to say: let his wonderful mercies furnish them matter and example so that they may give thanks to the Lord,

**VERSE 9.** “because he satisfied the soul formerly empty” with virtues. “And he filled the hungry soul with good things,” that is, with sacred teachings.

Now he sets forth the second temptation and the mercy which frees from the habit of sinning and the difficulty of acting well. For there are some who, after being freed from unbelief, [Col. 0668A] cannot act well because of their habit of sinning, since the tinder of sin and the flesh’s enticement remain in them; and the Lord frees them from these. He delivered them from faithlessness, the habit of sinning, and difficulty in acting well, because they were

**VERSE 10.** “Sitting in darkness,” that is, lingering in sins; “and in the shadow of death,” that is, in more grievous sins. These are called the shadow of death because, just as souls in hell are dead—not in existence, but because they are separated from God—so those who are in mortal sins are dead because they are separated from God through them. And I call them “bound in poverty and iron,” that is, in an iron and insoluble distress from which they could not be released except by the Lord’s mighty hand. Evil habit is like an iron bond: it weakens good will and makes it feeble, so that it cannot resist sins even when it greatly wishes to do so. And this is poverty, because it lacks the strength to resist. And why were they bound?

**VERSE 11.** “Because they embittered the words of God,” that is, they made the Lord’s pleasing and sweet commandments bitter and harsh to themselves, saying, “Who could fulfil everything?” And “the counsel of the Most High,” which he gave through the Spirit of counsel, saying, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have, and give to the poor” (Matt. 19:21), “they provoked,” that is, made void and useless by failing to fulfil it. Or they wished to make void the Most High’s counsel concerning the restoration of the human race, since through evil works they withdrew themselves from salvation.

In the Hebrew it is written: “They blasphemed the counsel of the Most High,” because they regarded the Lord’s commandments as unjust and found them harsh because they did not love them; and therefore they were held by their evil habit in sins. For if anyone loves chastity, he easily avoids lust. So too with the rest.

**VERSE 12.** And when they had laboured to escape by themselves, “their heart was humbled,” that is, afflicted by labours, because they could not bring their purpose to effect; but their soul was overcome in those labours. And when they wished to free themselves by themselves, they became weak, falling from vice into vice. “And there was none to help.”

For because they presumed upon their own powers rather than [Col. 0668D] divine assistance, God’s help was lacking to them—the help that might aid them. Many, when they sin, immediately grieve, confess, do penance, make promises, and labour not to fall again. But because they trust in themselves and presume this of themselves, after one or two months they fall again, because they have become weak. They not only repeat what they had trusted they would no longer do, but commit it more and more, because their soul has been conquered by desire. No other could help them, nor could they stand by themselves. At last, recognizing their miseries and that they could not be freed from them except by divine help, they sought to be freed from them.

**VERSES 13–14.** “They cried to the Lord when they were troubled,” in intention, prayer, and action; and “he delivered them from their necessities,” that is, he drew them out of poverty, because they were incapable of rising. “And he brought them out of darkness,” that is, sins, “and the shadow of death,” that is, such things as lead to death; “and he broke their bonds,” that is, their evil habit. Since they were bound indissolubly in sins, he loosed them, made them love his commandments, and gave them virtues. In this way he brought them out and thus broke their bonds. Therefore:

**VERSES 15–16.** “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men,” as has been said. Therefore let them give thanks to the Lord, “because he shattered bronze gates,” that is, suggestions and sins which are the gates of hell, “and broke iron bars,” that is, the hard habit of sinning which obstructs [Col. 0669B] life. The comparison is with one shut in a prison having bronze gates and iron bars, from which he could in no way escape because he could not break them. And he not only shattered the bronze gates and iron bars in bringing them out, but also

**VERSE 17.** takes them under his protection and defence, removing them from their way of wickedness. And he did this because “they were humbled because of their injustices,” that is, they were afflicted in penitence because they had formerly acted against the Lord.

From the passage, “Sitting in darkness,” this is drawn from the children of Israel in Egypt: some were in prisons, some in chains, some subjected to other affliction resembling death, from which the Lord brought them out. It signifies those who were imprisoned and bound in hell, whom the Lord brought out when he shattered the bronze gates and iron bars of hell. It also signifies those held in the prison of evil habit and the bonds of sins, whom the Lord brought out from there into virtues.

Now he sets forth the third temptation and mercy, for which they rightly ought to praise God. For very many people, after being freed from sins, are afflicted with weariness and sluggishness in prayer and sacred reading; they wish to roam about and hear gossip and tales, and descend as far as the gates of death. God’s mercy delivers them from these things. They are so afflicted by weariness and delight so much in tales and gossip that

**VERSE 18.** “Their soul abhorred every food,” that is, their reason spurned reading and prayer, which are food and refreshment for the soul. The comparison is with sick persons, to whom all food is distasteful. This vice is especially wont to be found among monks and hermits, who, wearied by prolonged labour, fall into tedium in reading or praying and through this often unwittingly fall into vices and slip into crimes. Therefore it is added: “And they drew near even to the gates of death,” that is, they approached in will grave sins which are the gates of eternal death. They approached them in will, but did not enter through action, because:

**VERSE 19.** “They cried to the Lord when they were troubled,” in intention and prayer; he “delivered them from their necessities,” that is, from straits, from weariness [Col. 0670A] of food, and from the gates of death. And how did he deliver them?

**VERSE 20.** “He sent his word,” that is, a visitation, an inward inspiration, “and healed them” from their abhorrence of food and the gates of death; “and he delivered them from their destructions,” that is, from the danger of death. Therefore, because he delivered them:

**VERSE 21.** “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men,” that is, for the mercies performed for the children of men—that is, sinners—let those who have been freed praise the Lord with devotion and work.

**VERSE 22.** “And let them sacrifice a sacrifice of praise,” that is, let them offer thanksgiving; let it be ascribed to God, not to themselves, that they have become such people. This will be a sacrifice [Col. 0670B] of praise, because this will be the sacrifice that praises God. And not only in themselves, but let them also proclaim to others his works, which God has wrought in them, “in exultation,” that is, in gladness, not hypocrisy. Or let them announce his commandments to others with joy.

From the passage, “Their soul abhorred every food,” this is drawn from those to whom all food became abhorrent because of the affliction of harsh slavery. They drew near to the gates of death because some were killed and others scourged. When, in this tribulation, they cried to the Lord, he delivered them from their straits in this manner: “He sent his word,” that is, his messenger through Moses to Pharaoh; he healed them from sorrow and affliction and delivered them from their destructions, that is, from the dangers of Egypt and the Red Sea. For this they confessed the Lord’s mercies and wonders and sacrificed a sacrifice of praise, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord,” etc.

It signifies those who, near the Savior’s coming, abhorred the sayings of the prophets, which are food for souls, when over a long time, deprived of divine help, they saw threats fulfilled against themselves and promises deferred. They drew near to the gates of death because, almost swallowed up by the death of unbelief, they wished to become like the nations ignorant of God and to adopt their rite. In this tribulation they cried to the Lord, like Simeon and Zacharias, and he delivered them from their straits in this way. He sent his incarnate Word, who was in the beginning with God, who was made flesh and dwelt among us; he illuminated the darkness of errors and shattered the chains of the Law and of sins. He broke into the devil’s house, that is, idolatry; he shattered the bronze doors of vices and broke the iron bars of habits, so that the human race might come out. He took them up from the way of wickedness and led them into the way of truth; he healed in virtues those who had been made weak in sins; and he delivered them from their destruction, into which they had plunged themselves, when he himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows. Therefore let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies: because God became man, because the immortal one submitted to death for the life of mortals; and for his wonders to the children of men: because he shattered hell’s bronze gates and iron bars, because he returned victorious to the heights, [Col. 0671A] because he went back to heaven. “And let them sacrifice a sacrifice of praise”: that is, when the old sacrifice has ceased, let them offer the true victim of praise, praising God for their salvation and joyfully proclaiming the works by which he restored humankind.

Now he sets forth the fourth temptation and mercy: after people have been freed from unbelief, evil habit, and weariness of reading and work, they come to prelacy. There they endure many tribulations through their subjects’ negligence or through persecution of themselves; yet, delivered, they are led to the harbour of their desire.

**VERSE 23.** “Those who go down to the sea in ships.” In the Hebrew it reads: “Into the sea,” that is, those who descend from the contemplative life into the sea—that is, into the bitter [Col. 0671B] people, tossed about through vices—set in ships, that is, in the governance and admonition of subjects, “doing work in many waters,” that is, continual labour among many peoples.

**VERSE 24.** “They saw,” that is, understood, “the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep,” that is, in a people of profound wickedness—they saw, understand. When it says, “Those who descend from the contemplative life into the sea,” it shows that no one ought to be chosen for prelacy unless he has been in the contemplative life. Before he describes those works, he introduces the danger in which they occur, from which God’s power delivers them.

**VERSE 25.** “He spoke,” that is, God permitted, “and the spirit of the storm stood,” that is, the devil prevailed; the evil spirit, author of the storm—that is, of the commotion which strikes minds and stirs persecutions and temptations—persisted [Col. 0671C]. “And its waves were lifted up,” that is, the tossings and disturbances grew higher and higher. The Lord permits these tribulations in order that they may know that they cannot stand by their own strength. And amid these storms and fluctuations of their subjects, prelates

**VERSE 26.** “go up to the heavens and go down to the depths.” That is, from excessive grief they become like those caught in peril at sea, who now seem to be lifted up to heaven and now to go down to the depths, as waves raise or lower their ships. Prelates such as bishops are called ships, which carry peoples from the world to heavenly things. “Their soul,” namely that of the prelates, “melted away in evils,” that is, weakened in distress at considering the evils committed by their subjects.

When storms and waves rise, prelates in mind ascend to heaven, that is, to those raised by virtues; and they descend to the depths, that is, from the other side they look upon the filth and depth of vices. From comparing the depths with the heavens, their soul “melted away in evils,” that is, at the sight of evils. And thus, wasting away,

**VERSE 27.** “they were troubled” by sorrow over their subjects and “were moved from reason,” just as a drunkard is moved from reason. As a drunkard lacks the right steadiness of body and mind, so through grief over their subjects they do not retain their former state of praying and reading; and all their wisdom [Col. 0672A] which they had for governing their subjects “is swallowed up” and brought to nothing. It is as though they were saying: “We have warned and corrected them greatly, and yet they refuse to comply. Let them do what they wish; let them be carried wherever the waves drive them.” The comparison is with sailors who utterly lose even their skill in navigation in great danger. The prelates were troubled and moved, but not for long, because:

**VERSE 28.** “They cried to the Lord when they were troubled,” that is, they prayed to God in their tribulation, grieving over the destruction of their people; and “he brought them out of their necessities,” that is, from the anxieties from which they were incapable of emerging by themselves. He called the prelates’ danger “the works of the Lord.” He adds how he brought them out:

**VERSE 29.** “He made its storm,” namely the sea’s, cease, because he caused the floods of persecutions and temptations and their disturbances to cease, “into a breeze,” that is, a gentle, calm wind. The breeze of the Holy Spirit is a gentle and calm wind. Thus the Holy Spirit is called a breeze: he calms hearts from vices and makes them gentle through virtues. And after the breath of the Holy Spirit, “its waves were silent,” that is, the tossings and disturbances of that same sea were stilled, after the correction of the subjects.

**VERSE 30.** The prelates “rejoiced because they were silent,” namely the subjects, silent from contradiction. “And he led them,” the subjects, “to the harbour of their desire,” that is, to the rest and security which the prelates wished and desired. Therefore, from consideration of this benefit:

[Col. 0672C] **VERSE 31.** “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies”: for such great mercies let the prelates praise the Lord in devotion and work, and for “his wonders done to the children of men,” namely to themselves, who are the sons of the apostles because they imitate them, and upon whom he had mercy when he led their people to harbour.

**VERSE 32.** “Let them exalt him in the church of the people,” that is, let prelates praise God in the congregation of a well-ordered subject people. But in “the seat of the elders,” that is, in the well-ordered teaching-office of prelates, let the peoples praise him, both parties giving thanks to God.

From the passage, “Those who go down to the sea in ships,” this is drawn from those who sail the sea in great storms for trade, and afterward tell of the wonders of God which they have seen in the deep. So it happened when [Col. 0672D] the apostles went down in a ship upon the sea with the Lord, because they saw the Lord’s works and his wonders in the deep. For “he spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood,” that is, he commanded the winds, and it ceased, and he calmed the sea. And what was on the sea? While the Lord slept, behold, a great commotion arose in the sea, and its waves were lifted up. The peoples—that is, the apostles—go up with the waves to the heavens and down to the depths, that is, the lowest places; their soul “melted away in evils,” that is, it failed through fear in danger. Then “they were troubled and moved like a drunkard,” and “all their wisdom was swallowed up,” that is, all counsel fled from them. And they cried to the Lord when troubled, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing” (Matt. 8:25). Rising, he commanded the sea and brought them out of their straits. “And he made the storm of that sea into a breeze,” that is, into calmness; “and its waves were silent,” those of the sea, because there was a great calm. And those who were in the ship rejoiced because the sea’s waves were silent, saying: “What sort of man is this, that even the sea and the winds obey him?” (Matt. 8:27). And he led them unharmed to the harbour of their desire, that is, where they wished.

This signifies that the apostles went down into the sea of the world in ships, that is, in churches which bear Christ and are battered by the world’s waves. The apostles, I say, were “doing work in many waters,” that is, many signs among peoples. They saw the Lord’s works among the Gentiles and his wonders in the deep of unbelief, when through their preaching the light of truth shone in profound darkness and they clearly saw the light of the true Trinity amid the densest [Col. 0673B] darkness. “He spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood,” that is, he commanded and worldly temptation ceased; “and its waves were lifted up,” that is, the movements of diabolical temptation which the wicked stir up against the righteous were suspended so that they might not harm. Those waves “go up to the heavens,” that is, they are raised up in pride to injure the saints; and they “go down to the depths,” because they are humbled in confession. “Their soul melted away in evils,” struck by heavenly blows. They were troubled by sins and moved from unbelief to faith, like a drunkard by the drink of the Holy Spirit. And all their worldly wisdom was swallowed up by God’s wisdom, as the dragons of the Egyptians were swallowed up by Moses’ rod. And they cried to the Lord with heart and mouth, in faith and work, while afflicted by vices; [Col. 0673C] “and he brought them out of their necessities,” so that, leaving lust and drunkenness, they might follow God’s wisdom. “And he made its storm into a breeze,” that is, persecution into peace; “and its waves were silent,” that is, the counsels which stirred persecutions ceased. And the converted rejoiced because the waves of the sea—that is, persecutions—were silent; “and he led them to the harbour of their desire,” that is, to peace, and then to eternal rest. “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders to the children of men.” They confessed to all the Lord’s mercies and wonders performed for them. “Let them exalt him in the church of the people, and praise him in the seat of the elders”: that is, in clergy and people, in prelates and subjects, they gave him thanks.

Thus far he has spoken of the temptations whose removal makes God worthy of praise. Now he exhorts us to his praise on account of the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles: namely, because the branches of the olive tree were broken off and the wild olive was grafted onto the olive tree. Through all the foregoing God is to be praised, and also for this: because

**VERSES 33–34.** “He made rivers into a wilderness, and water-springs into thirst; a fruitful land into salt-marsh because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it.” This is drawn from the Pentapolis, where Sodom, Gomorrah, and the other cities were turned into a wilderness and the Dead Sea because of their inhabitants’ sins. The rivers were the scribes, Pharisees, and other teachers of the Jews, [Col. 0674A] from whom teachings flowed to others. The Lord made these rivers into a wilderness because he left them devoid of grace and dried them of all teaching. The water-springs were the prophets, from whom many teachings and writings issued. He made these into thirst, that is, dryness, so that they became arid and dry. For where is a prophet now? Where is a lawgiver? Nowhere.

Alternatively: “He made rivers into a wilderness,” that is, preachers into the Gentile world formerly deserted by grace; “and water-springs into thirst,” that is, he set fountains of water in a thirsty land. The apostles are fountains, and their disciples rivers, such as Titus, Timothy, Dionysius, and others. But he made “a fruitful land into a salt-marsh,” that is, the land of the Jews, once [Col. 0674B] fruitful, into barrenness. This was not unjustly done, but “because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it,” that is, because of the iniquity of the prelates ruling in it, such as the high priests and Pharisees.

A salt-marsh is water retained in pools, from which salt is made; by the drying action of sun and fire it hardens into salt, and that land is called barren. Therefore he made the land of Judea, formerly fruitful, into salt-marsh, that is, into seasoning and correction for our folly. Lot’s wife, changed into a pillar of salt, is our seasoning and correction, so that we may be wise: for if he did not spare the natural branches, much less will he spare proud grafted ones. And this occurred because of the wickedness of those dwelling in it, that is, because of the Jews’ pride.

Rightly is he to be exalted, who placed fountains in the wilderness—that is, apostles in the Church—gave to thirsty souls the word issuing forth in preaching, and filled with eternal fruits the land of the body, which had formerly produced thorns of bitterness; and

**VERSES 35–36.** “He made the wilderness into pools of water,” that is, he provided baptism in the Church. The Gentile world is called a wilderness because it was formerly deserted by prophets and preachers. A pool is called deep and great water, and sacred Scripture is understood. God made the wilderness into pools of water when he filled the Gentiles with knowledge of the Scriptures and established among them teachers of others, such as Hilary, Ambrose, and men like them. And he made the land previously without water—that is, [Col. 0674D] without teaching—into water-springs, that is, into interpreters of the Scriptures, such as Augustine and Gregory, from whom much knowledge flowed. “He made” is said as though “he established,” because wherever any one preached, there he established himself and persevered until death. And there, in those pools and springs, he set “the hungry,” with the bread of life and understanding, that is, he firmly established them in their teaching. Thus they established “a city of habitation,” that is, here they began to establish the heavenly Jerusalem, which is our dwelling-place. Or they established a city of habitation, that is, a Church such that God might deign to dwell in it.

“He made the wilderness into pools of water” is drawn from the water which flowed from the rock in the wilderness. “And he set the hungry there,” and what follows, are drawn from the promised land, [Col. 0675A] all of which are understood of the Church. The teachers established the city,
### Verse 37

“And they sowed fields,” that is, they scattered the word of God among the peoples; “and planted vineyards,” that is, they established churches, intoxicating others with teaching and example. And these fields and vineyards produced “the fruit of their increase,” that is, their natural fruit, namely good works, for the doing of which they were born. Or they produced such fruit as their teachers did, through whose Gospel they were born.

### Verse 38

And God blessed them through the increase of virtues. The apostles indeed planted the churches, and the teachers watered them; but God gave the increase in the growth of virtues. “And they were multiplied exceedingly” in number. He says “exceedingly” on account of those who were to depart from the Church, of whom it is written: “They have been multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX, 6)—understand: beyond the number of the elect. He blessed the fields and vineyards, “and did not diminish their cattle,” that is, the simple and unlearned who nevertheless held the right faith, and who became many.

Or: they were multiplied exceedingly because many became Christians to excess; that is, He did not diminish the foolish and easily deceived, but they were converted to the sect of heretics. For there were more heretics than Catholics. For after they went out from us, those who were not of us,

### Verses 39–40

the Catholics became few; and they themselves, though few, were afflicted—that is, oppressed by the tribulation of evils, namely by the affliction which the wicked themselves inflicted—[Col. 0675C] by heresy and persecution, because they accused them before rulers and took their possessions from them; and they were afflicted by sorrow, that is, by compassion, because they grieved over the destruction of their neighbors.

Whence came that smallness of number? From contention, which came from God’s vengeance. For contention—that is, the heretics themselves began to dispute among themselves concerning their doctrines—was poured out, that is, came abundantly and copiously upon the leaders of the heretics. That contention proceeded from God’s wrath against those who became leaders of the heretics. And thus He caused them to wander in a pathless place; that is, He permitted them to remain in the error of heresy and not to be in the way of faith.

Or: “contempt was poured out upon the princes,” because God despised them—the leaders of the heretics—as He did Arius, whose entrails were poured out. And therefore He made them wander in a pathless place, so that they might believe God to have limbs like a human being, or the Son to be less than the Father; and He did not lead them into the way of truth, in which they would understand God to be incorporeal and the Trinity equal.

### Verse 41

“And He helped the poor man out of want.” That smallness of number benefited the faithful, because the Lord helped the one who knew himself and made him poor and humble through want; that is, through the abstinence of the heretics. For, because of their own small number, He made His poor faithful more diligent in searching the sacred Scripture and sharper in resisting the multitude of heretics, since the saints, seeing their misery, became more cautious and more discerning.

Thus “want” has a double sense here: either because the Catholics were needy when they became few; or because the heretics were destitute of faith and reason. “And He set families like sheep”: that is, He placed those who were in His service like sheep, because He taught them to follow their own shepherd and not a stranger; or He bore Himself toward His sheep with the same affection and care with which a good shepherd bears himself toward his flock.

Heretics wander in a pathless place; but the upright walk in the way. Hence it follows:

### Verse 42

“The upright shall see,” that is, those who held the right faith shall see—understand: the truth—because they will understand much concerning the faith and the Scriptures. For if Augustine had not had so many disputes with heretics, he would not have attained such subtlety in Scripture. “And they shall rejoice” in their condition; and all the iniquity of the heretics, once convicted, [Col. 0676B] “shall stop its mouth,” that is, shall shut its mouth, and the mouth of those speaking iniquity shall be blocked. As a ball is shut up, so their mouth shall be shut.

Alternatively: the Lord helped the poor man out of want, and the heretics shall see, that is, take notice, and shall rejoice, hoping to be delivered if need be. But all iniquity shall stop its mouth, because it has nothing it can say effectively.

These things may also be said of the expulsion of the Jews.

They became few because the works of the Lord were not multiplied among them; and they were afflicted by the tribulation of evils, namely by the siege of the Romans and the sorrow of captivity. Contempt was poured out upon their leaders, because they were despised by the conquerors—who had despised the Lord [Col. 0676C]—and were sold by them like worthless slaves. And He made them wander in a pathless place, that is, in idolatry, and not to be in the way of God.

In the Hebrew it reads: “He shall pour contempt upon princes, and caused them to wander in a wilderness away from the way.” For the leaders of the Jews were despised by the pagans, and they too wandered in the wilderness of Gentile life through idols. “And He helped the poor man out of want,” because He satisfied the Christian people with eternal provisions; “and He set families like sheep,” so that, hearing the voice of the true shepherd, they might follow in faith.

“The upright shall see,” that is, the preachers shall see the conversion of the Gentiles and rejoice in their religion; and “all iniquity shall stop its mouth,” that is, the devil, the Jews, and the heretics, who dared to speak against the faith of Christ, [Col. 0676D] shall be silent. None but the wise will understand all these benefits bestowed upon humankind. And:

### Verse 43

“Who is wise, that he will understand these things?” The wise person will keep these benefits in mind and understand that all these things are the mercies of the Lord: He who led the wanderer into the way and fed the needy; who loosed and freed one struggling against the difficulty of sins and bound in the chains of habit; who revived, by sending the medicine of His word, one who loathed the word of God and was almost dying from a kind of weariness; who brought one endangered amid shipwrecks and stormy perils, after calming the sea, to the harbor of rest; who established him among a humble people, in order to lead him like a sheep to the pastures of paradise. The upright see these things and rejoice; and whoever is wise will keep them, understanding the mercies of the Lord.

# Psalm CVII. On Christ’s obedience

[Col. 0677]

[Col. 0677A] “My heart is ready, O God,” etc. The preceding psalm sang of the mercy of the Lord, which gathered the faithful from the whole world together as sheep into one body and delivered them from various temptations, separating Jews and heretics from them as goats—or rather, as wolves. But this psalm sings of the good shepherd’s voluntary death, by which He redeemed the sheep through death; of His glorious resurrection, by which He restored life to His own; and of His victorious ascension, by which in Himself He raised human nature above the heavens and joined the lost sheep—now found and carried back upon His own shoulders—to the angelic flock.

And because He sent rams through whom He drew the sheep from both peoples into one fold, as though from two sheepfolds, He divided them into the active and contemplative life; and He will yet lead them into the fortified city and establish them in the place of paradise’s pasture. The number itself indicates this. For this psalm is the one hundred and seventh, which is eleven times nine, plus eight. Eleven signifies transgression; nine, the fellowship of angels; eight, eternal blessedness. This number signifies that the human race underwent the exile of this life because of transgression, returned through Christ’s death to fellowship with the angels, and there shall possess eternal blessedness. Its title is: “A Psalm-Song,” or:

### (Verse 1.) A PSALM-SONG, OF DAVID HIMSELF

Song pertains to theory or contemplation; psalm pertains to practice, that is, action. A song, therefore, is exultation; a psalm, work, [Col. 0677C] because through work one comes to exultation. He placed first what is more important, as he does everywhere. This psalm, then, which concerns work and reward, is attributed to David himself—that is, to Christ, the true David.

The subject of the psalm is Christ’s obedience and the reward of that obedience. Its purpose is to urge us, by Christ’s example, toward diligence in good works, so that we may attain the joy of reward. This psalm is taken from the concluding portions of two psalms, the fifty-sixth and the fifty-ninth: namely, “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me,” whose title states that David fled from Saul’s face into the cave; and “O God, thou hast cast us off,” whose title states that David set Mesopotamia of Syria on fire.

This was done to show that the psalms are to be understood not historically but allegorically, since according to the letter both flight and victory could not occur simultaneously in one man; yet according to prophecy both occurred together in Christ, who both fled into the cave of the tomb from Saul—that is, from death—and conquered the devil. Therefore he set another title here, namely “A Psalm-Song,” [Col. 0678A] in order to show that things differing in the literal sense tend toward one allegorical meaning: because through the victory of Christ’s death one comes to eternal joy.

And this is a most beautiful method when some psalm or verse is placed under a different signification from others which are similar in words but unlike in meaning, just as in royal adornment gems of the same name but different colors are set. The words of this psalm, as has been said, are taken from two psalms because the house of the Church is built from two walls, one fold is gathered from two flocks, and one commonwealth is formed from two districts.

This psalm is divided in two because a twofold nature is proclaimed in Christ. One part begins, “My heart is ready,” in which the Passion, resurrection, and ascension are indicated; [Col. 0678B] the other, “God has spoken,” in which the orders of the Church through Christ are enumerated. This one psalm is made from two because from two peoples the one Church, the body of Christ, is gathered. Christ speaks here, recounting to the faithful the obedience of His Passion and the glory He attained through it, exhorting them by His example to work and promising the reward of eternal life.

### Verse 2

“My heart is ready, O God.” O God the Father, my heart—that is, my affection—is ready for obedience. My heart—that is, my will—is ready to undergo the Passion for the salvation of the human race. That is: not compelled, not unwilling, but freely and willingly, I the shepherd will die for my sheep. [Col. 0678C] And I shall do this not sorrowfully but cheerfully. “I will sing and make music in my glory.” Singing indicates joy; the psalm indicates action; as though He said: I shall accomplish the work of my obedience with joy. And this shall be in my glory, that is, from it I shall have glory. What glory? The resurrection. Therefore the voice of the Father follows:

### Verse 3

“Awake, [Vulgate: ‘Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery,’ etc.] psaltery and harp.” The psaltery sounds from above; the harp, from below. By the psaltery is meant Christ’s soul, which comes from the heights; by the harp is understood His flesh, which suffered on earth. It is as though He said: O soul of Christ, which art the psaltery of my Son, return from hell to the body, thy harp; rise from the tomb and praise the Lord, [Col. 0678D] who, for completed obedience, gives thee immortality and impassibility.

Christ’s voice replies to the Father: “I will arise at dawn,” that is, very early. And after I rise:

### Verse 4

“I will give thanks to thee among the peoples,” that is, among the Jews, O Lord Father; “and I will make music to thee among the nations,” [Col. 0679A] that is, among the Gentiles.
