The Jews are called “peoples” because of the two kingdoms, the kingdom of Judah and the kingdom of Israel; the Gentiles are called “nations” because they remained as they were born: they are neither circumcised nor baptized. Among Jews and Gentiles I shall cause thee to be praised; those whom I have purchased for myself by my blood I shall make to confess thee with heart and mouth and to work well for thy praise. And they shall sing this:

### Verse 5

“For great above the heavens is thy mercy, and thy truth unto the clouds.” That is: Christ, through whom thou hast shown great mercy to humankind, is above the heavens—that is, above the angels—though He was made lower than the angels, becoming mortal and passible. And Christ, thy truth, through whom thou hast fulfilled as true all the sayings of the prophets, is mighty unto [Col. 0679B] the clouds, because all power in heaven and on earth has been given to Him.

Or, because thy truth—that is, the divinity of the Word—reached unto the clouds, that is, unto human beings, namely the apostles and other righteous persons. Therefore thy mercy, that is, thy humanity, shall be exalted above the heavens. Or: great above the heavens is thy mercy, by which thou rulest the angels lest they fall, and dost repair the loss caused by their fall through human beings saved by mercy; and thy truth is to be established unto the clouds, that is, the preachers proclaiming thy truth. And so that this may be done:

### Verses 6–7

“Be thou exalted above the heavens, O God.” That is: O God the Word, who didst incline thyself down to earth in order to raise up the fallen, be exalted, ascending above the heavens with the flesh assumed and redeemed humanity, to sit at the Father’s side. Thus thy exalted glory shall appear over all the earth; that is, thou shalt appear glorious over every race of humankind. Be exalted so that thy elect—that is, those foreordained to life—may be delivered from the devil’s power.

For Christ, exalted on the cross, delivered His beloved when He drew all things to Himself. Exalted in heaven, His glory shone over all the earth when He sent the Holy Spirit from heaven, through whom He granted knowledge of every language and rescued His elect, scattered throughout the world, from the devil’s yoke. Or these are the words of the Lord’s human nature: Thou Word united to me, be exalted above the heavens so that thou mayest appear as God; and then thy glory shall be over all the earth, and thy elect may be delivered.

[Col. 0679D] “Save me, the human being, by thy right hand,” that is, by thy power, raising me to the Father’s right hand; and hear me as I intercede for them, so that at judgment the elect may be placed on the right and not the left, and thus be delivered from eternal condemnation. Truly thou shalt do this, because:

### Verse 8

“God has spoken in his holy one,” that is, God the Word has spoken through me, the holy human being, saying: “Where I am, there shall my servant be also” (John XII, 26). And because He who promised thus is true and cannot lie, “I will rejoice,” that is, I shall have perpetual joy in myself and in my own, though in the flesh I was sorrowful in death; “and I will divide Shechem,” that is, I shall separate the obedient from the mass of those to be lost; “and I will measure out the valley of tabernacles,” that is, [Col. 0680A] I shall separate the humble of the churches from the proud.

Shechem, interpreted “humble,” means the obedient, who bear the Lord’s burden. Through disobedience they fell from paradise; through obedience they may return. Valleys are the humble; tabernacles are churches to be raised into the heavenly city. Through pride they fell; through humility they shall return. In this manner I shall divide and measure them, making some martyrs and others confessors, because:

### Verse 9

“Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine.” Gilead means “heap of testimony” and signifies martyrs, Christ’s witnesses; for a martyr is called a witness. It is as though He said: I shall receive the martyrs into my inheritance, who piled up a great heap when they offered themselves in witness to me. Or Gilead means “migration,” and I shall receive those who migrate from vices to virtues, from earthly things to heavenly.

Manasseh means “forgetfulness” and signifies confessors who forget earthly things and seek eternal things; these too I shall receive for myself. Or: the one who, having forgotten his father, devoured his substance with harlots and afterward returned to his father, him too I shall receive. “And Ephraim is the support of my head.” Ephraim means “fruitful” and signifies believers fruitful in good works. These shall be my support—that is, my resting place—I who am their head; that is, I shall rest in them. Or they shall be the crown of my head, surrounding me in glory.

Observe the stages: first they must migrate away from earthliness; then forget all earthly things; next be fruitful in virtues; [Col. 0680C] and then they shall be the Lord’s crown, that is, surround Him. “Judah is my king”: that is, those confessing sins and ruling their conduct shall be mine. For Judah means “one who confesses.” Thus far He has spoken of the Jews; now He speaks of the Gentiles, to specify what He earlier said: “I will give thanks to thee among peoples and nations.” I shall receive not only the circumcised into my inheritance, but also those from the nations, because:

### Verse 10

“Moab is the pot of my hope.” A pot is a bronze cauldron and signifies tribulation. Moab means “law” and signifies the Gentiles, who are uncultivated, without law, idolaters, living contrary to the law—just as Moab was born contrary to the law from Lot’s daughters. Yet they are a pot, that is, boiling vices out of themselves, just as [Col. 0680D] meats are boiled in a pot. They are the pot of my hope; that is, I hope to be refreshed by them, and those are mine who have been boiled in tribulation as in a pot.

Moab also means “from the father,” because he was born from the father; and it signifies the devil, who departed from the Father and never returned to Him. He is God’s pot, in which He boils the flesh—that is, the fleshly works—of his people, so that from them He may make sweet dishes at the banquet of angels. The Lord employs him as an examiner, so that He may test the elect by temptations, cleanse them through adversities, and reconcile them to the King through sufferings. Those boiled in this pot shall be my hope, that is, they shall be in that rest for which my own hope.

“How shall this be?” In this way: “Upon Idumea I will stretch out my shoe”; that is, through apostles from Judaea I shall extend my humanity into the Gentile world that longs after earthly things. [Col. 0681A] Humanity was the footwear of divinity because it was mortal. Idumea means “earthly.” Or the apostles were Christ’s footwear because they strengthened the churches—the feet of Christ—by writings, words, and deeds. He stretched this footwear over Idumea when He sent the apostles to earthly people, through whom He made His incarnation known to the Gentiles.

Thus foreigners became friends to me; that is, idolatrous Gentiles, my enemies, estranged from the kingdom of God, became my friends through faith and works. Therefore I say to them: “I shall no longer call you servants” of sin, “but my friends” and fellow heirs of the kingdom (John XV, 15). In order that I may separate all these from evil:

### Verse 11

“Who shall lead me into the fortified city,” that is, into hell, that I may rescue the elect from punishments? Thou alone, O God. Hell is a fortified city for coming out, but open for going in. No one can come out once he has entered; but one can easily enter. Conversely, the city above the heavens is fortified so that none can enter except with God’s help; but once one has entered, one cannot fall away at all.

God alone led Christ into the fortified city of hell; therefore He alone came forth victorious, having destroyed the city and divided its spoils. Before His coming, indeed, all descended into hell and remained there until the thief opened paradise. Therefore, to rescue Abraham and others from there, who shall lead me even into Idumea, where is the place of punishment and blood? Thou, O God. For Idumea means “bloody,” and it is the place of slaughter, namely hell, where many souls are slain. [Col. 0681C] No one descended victoriously into hell except thou, O God, who said to those bound, “Come forth,” and to those in darkness, “Be revealed,” whom thou didst bring out of the prison-house, sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.

Alternatively: I shall stretch out my shoe. But who shall lead me by preaching into the city—that is, into [Col. 0682A] the Gentile world, fortified by imperial edicts and philosophers’ writings? Or who shall lead me even into Idumea, that is, to those who are earthly and bloody: desirous of earthly things and eager for the blood of the righteous?

### Verse 12

“Art not thou, O God?” That is, no one will dare do this except through thee, O God, who didst cast us human beings out of paradise into this exile and hast now delivered us from miseries through the Son. The head speaks for the members. Through the tribulations sent upon us thou didst cast us off; and because thou wilt not go forth with our armies—that is, thou dost not appear to us through miracles, as thou didst to the fathers, whom thou ledst out of Egypt through the sea with signs and wonders, driving out nations and giving their land to the fathers—on the contrary, thou takest our possessions from us and givest them to the Gentiles; moreover, thou handest us ourselves over to the power of adversaries for various tortures. Therefore:

### Verse 13

“Give us help out of tribulation”: grant that tribulation itself may help us to come to eternal rest. Or grant that we may escape tribulation through thee and attain eternal salvation. And why do you not seek help from rulers? Because human salvation is vain, and cursed is the one who trusts in man. For he soon dies, and his hope perishes.

### Verse 14

“In God we shall do might.” That is, whatever good we do, we shall do not by human help but by God’s help, and attribute it wholly to Him. “And he shall bring to nothing those who afflict us,” that is, He shall destroy all who afflict us and grant us everlasting salvation. This is to say: through preachers strengthened by the Holy Spirit I shall be led into the Gentile world and shall bring back those driven out of paradise. They will suffer tribulation here from the ungodly, but after tribulation they will have eternal salvation. Finally, their enemies are annihilated in punishment, while they themselves are crowned in joy for their virtues.

# Psalm CVIII. On Christ’s humility

[Col. 0681]

[Col. 0681D] “O God, do not keep silence concerning my praise,” etc. The end of the preceding psalm mentioned the tribulation of the righteous; this psalm sets Christ’s Passion before them as a model, lest they fail. The subject of this psalm is Judas and the Jews, persecutors of Christ. For just as Peter in the Gospel bore the figure of the Church, so Judas in this psalm bears the type of the Jews who persecuted Christ and His body, the Church.

There were two apostles named Judas: Judas of James, and Judas Iscariot the traitor. From the holy Judas came the name of the faithful Jews who confess Christ; from Judas the traitor came the name of the faithless Jews who persecute Christ. It should also be known that this psalm contains the curse of the Holy Spirit and of the Church upon the body of the devil, and a judicial sentence striking Judas and extending to the whole body of the wicked. It is not, however, the wish of one uttering a curse, but the prophecy of one proclaiming: for it does not desire that it happen, but foretells what will happen.

Its purpose is to restrain persecutors from persecuting the righteous, because unless they cease, the same punishment which enveloped Judas and the Jews will envelop them. As Christ first suffered in His own person, so He suffers daily in His members; as it is said to Saul: “Saul, Saul, why dost thou persecute me?” (Acts IX, 4). And the same punishment awaits all His persecutors.

The words of the psalm seem to have been drawn from the history in which Ahithophel gave counsel against David, when Absalom and the people had conspired against him; David cursed him, [Col. 0683A] and he hanged himself with a noose. This signifies that Judas betrayed the Lord when the devil and the Jews had conspired against Him; Christ cursed him, saying: “Woe to that man through whom I am betrayed” (Mark XIV, 21); and he hanged himself with a noose and burst asunder in the middle.

This psalm is counted as the one hundred and eighth in order, a number in which fifteen times seven are considered. Five signifies the human race endowed with five senses; ten, the old law because of the Decalogue; seven, the new law because of the sevenfold Spirit. Moreover, ten expresses the reward of life, and seven future rest. This number therefore signifies that all who before Christ’s advent assailed God through the five senses by despising the law, or who afterward, until the end of the world, persecute Him incarnate through the five senses by despising the Gospel, [Col. 0683B] shall not have a reward of future rest with the five wise virgins, but shall depart accursed with the five foolish virgins. Its title is:

### (Verse 1.) UNTO THE END: A PSALM OF DAVID

That is, this hymn is attributed to Christ, the true David, directing us unto the end, that is, to the cessation of persecution. Or, “unto the end” means unto the completion of recompense, which shall be given at the end to each according to his works.

This psalm has three parts. The first division begins, “O God, [do not keep silence concerning] my praise,” in which the Jews, persecutors of Christ, are accused. The second begins, “Set thou over him,” in which Judas, Christ’s betrayer, and the Jews themselves are condemned. The third begins, “But thou, O Lord,” in which are contained Christ’s tribulation according to the form of humanity He assumed, and His prayer for His body. This is the voice of Christ praying to the Father for Himself and His members and rejecting Judas and the whole body of the devil:

### Verse 2

“O God, do not keep silence concerning my praise.” Judas betrayed me; the Jews persecuted and crucified me, thinking utterly to destroy me and erase my name from the earth. But thou, O God the Father, do not keep silence concerning my praise—that is, my praiseworthy fame and glory. Do not permit it to be silenced by failing to raise me and to punish the Jews [Col. 0683D] who silence my praise and regard me as deserving reproach. For as my resurrection is my praise, so is their condemnation. By the resurrection the righteous rejoice; by their condemnation they are delivered.

Therefore do not be silent, because “the mouth of the sinner and the deceitful man is opened against me,” namely Judas, saying: “What are you willing to give me, and I will deliver him to you?” (Matt. XXVI, 15). The sinner opened his mouth against me when he said: “Hail, Rabbi” (ibid., 49–50). He opened it deceitfully when he kissed Him, and thus betrayed Him by deceit: “Whomever I shall kiss, he is the one; seize him” (ibid., 48). In a kiss, peace and friendship are signified. Therefore he is called deceitful because through feigned peace and friendship he carried out murder.

Or he was deceitful when he disclosed to the Jews the treachery [Col. 0684A] which he harbored in his heart. He is called “sinner” by way of eminence because, though he was an apostle, shared in Christ’s teaching and mysteries, saw not only His signs but performed them himself, he despised so many benefits and dignities and sold his Lord and master for a paltry price. This indicates that those who understand the Scriptures are more deserving of condemnation than those who do not understand them. And not Judas alone, but the Jews also.

### Verse 3

“They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue,” saying: “Master, we know that thou art true, and teachest the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not?” (Matt. XXII, 16). Yet they wanted to accuse me; and other similar things by which they wished to ensnare me. “And they surrounded me with words of hatred,” that is, with such words as openly expressed hatred, saying: “Thou, being a man, makest thyself God” (John X, 33)—“Thou art a Samaritan and hast a demon” (John VIII, 48).

They surrounded me with hateful speech when they cried: “If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have delivered him to thee. Crucify him, crucify him” (John XVIII, 30). On the cross they also surrounded me, saying: “If thou art the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matt. XXVII, 40). “And they fought against me without cause,” that is, they scourged me without fault of mine, since I deserved good, not evil—I who healed their sick and raised their dead. Or “without cause,” that is, without effect, because they wished to overcome me and erase my name but could not.

### Verse 4

“In return for my love, they slandered me.” He did not say, “They killed me,” but “They slandered me,” because it was because they slandered Him that they killed Him. They slandered Him by saying: He is a sorcerer; “he casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons” (Luke XI, 15)—“He is a glutton and a drinker of wine, a friend of publicans” (Matt. XI, 19)—“He has a demon and is mad. Why do you listen to him?” (John X, 20).

By this slander they turned away from Him those whose conversion He sought. Therefore he mentions slander, because those who slander Christ and thereby kill souls do more harm than those who, raging against His mortal flesh—especially since it was soon raised again—destroyed it. In place of the love I showed them, or in return for the benefit I required of them, namely that they should love me, they slandered and crucified me. But I prayed for them, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke XXIII, 34). These are the Lord’s weapons; they are also our weapons against enemies: prayer. And they not only attacked me without cause, but also:

### Verse 5

“They set evil against me,” that is, scourges and death, in return for the good I had bestowed upon them in many ways, preaching, healing the sick, and raising the dead. I prayed for them on the cross; but they, on the contrary, said: “Aha, thou who destroyest the temple of God, save thyself” (Matt. XXVII, 40). I was dying for them; but they, on the contrary, called me a deceiver and set guards [Col. 0685A] at my tomb. I rose for them, and they said: “His disciples stole him away by night” (Matt. XXVIII, 13). “And they repaid me hatred for my love.” I loved them unto death; they hated me unto death.

These things have been said of the Jews generally. Certain matters concerning Judas in particular follow, because he who sold the Lord for thirty pieces of silver fell under thirty curses here pronounced. For each denarius he is struck with a curse: a sinner is set over him; the devil stands at his right hand; when judged, he is condemned; his prayer is reckoned as sin; his days are shortened; his bishopric is given to another; his sons become orphans; his wife a widow; his children are driven from their country; they become beggars; they are expelled from their own dwelling; a creditor searches out his substance; strangers seize his labors; he has no helper to protect him nor one who pities to defend his orphans; his offspring perish; his name is quickly erased; he is punished for his fathers’ iniquity; he is penalized for his mother’s sin; his parents are brought before the Lord for condemnation; their memory is erased from the earth; he is surrounded by a curse; blessing is removed far from him; the curse becomes for him clothing upon the body and water in the soul, and oil in the powers of the soul as in the bones; the curse becomes a covering in his actions and a girding of the belt in his purpose; he himself and all his people are confounded before human beings; inwardly before God they are clothed in shame; they are covered with a double confusion, here and hereafter, in body and soul.

Now, as a just judge, He pronounces sentence against Judas and the body of the devil, not as an accuser avenging Himself on the evils of an adversary. An accuser wishes to satisfy his enmities by an enemy’s punishment; a judge wishes, for justice’s sake, to punish the sins of the guilty. For Christ punishes not from delight in another’s misery but from love of justice. O Father, because Judas refused to have me as the master above him whose teaching he should hear:

### Verse 6

“Set thou a sinner over him,” that is, the devil, the inventor of sin, so that they may obey the devil’s persuasion, and he, subject to him, may serve. “And let the devil stand [Col. 0685D] at his right hand,” that is, let him overturn any good works he may have. He always stands at the left hand because he continually inspires evil. Let him stand at the right hand, not to advance good works but to destroy them. Let the devil’s works be his right hand; let him consider evil good. And:

### Verse 7

“When he is judged thus, let him go out condemned from this life,” namely uncorrected and not amended through satisfaction before life’s end. Or, when he is judged in the future judgment, let him leave the judgment condemned. And meanwhile, “let his prayer become sin,” because it is not made through Christ, whom he refused to follow and instead persecuted. For prayer not made through Him is not only unable to erase sin; it itself becomes sin. For everything done outside faith in Christ is sin.

Judas’s prayer was his repentance, [Col. 0686A] when he said: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. XXVII, 4). But this prayer became sin when he hanged himself with a noose, adding murder to murder. For he offended the Lord more in hanging himself than in betraying the Lord. The prayer also of those who seek vengeance on their enemies, or the fulfillment of fleshly pleasures, is turned into sin.

### Verse 8

“Let his days be few,” that is, let him die soon after my betrayal—which indeed happened. For before Christ’s Passion he is said to have been consumed by his own crime. “And let another receive his bishopric,” that is, let another possess the honor of apostleship—which Matthias did, succeeding him in the apostleship. But someone may say: Should a good man succeed in the place of an evil man? The apostleship was not evil because Judas proved evil. Therefore, a good man ought to take a good office.

### Verse 9

“Let his children become orphans.” An orphan is one whose father has died. “And his wife a widow.” A widow is one whose husband has died. *Widow* is said as though *deprived of a husband*, that is, separated or greatly separated from a husband. For *to make a widow* is said to mean “to divide.”

### Verse 10

“Let his children be driven about,” that is, let them be moved from their own place to another, where they are driven about—that is, uncertain and unstable—and beg from others what they may live on, stripped of every support. “Let them be cast out from their dwellings,” that is, let them be expelled from [Col. 0686C] their possessions and habitations.

VERS. 11. Let the moneylender search out all his substance. It is asked how Judas could have had property which a moneylender might search out, since, leaving everything, he followed the Lord with the apostles. It is believed that he left all that he possessed to his wife and children in such a way that he sometimes retained its use, and that he did not follow the Lord sincerely, but in order that he might gain something with him. For, as it is written of him: “He was a thief, and had the moneybags,” that is, purses, “(John 12:6),” contrary to the Lord’s command: “Do not carry a purse, nor a bag, nor have money in your belts” (Luke 10:4); and he secretly took away what was sent by religious people to the Lord and the apostles for necessities, and lent it at interest. [Col. 0686D] But he received certain things on loan at interest from others, which he gave to his wife and children; after his death the moneylender wished to recover these. Therefore he searched out Judas’s substance, to see whether he might repay him with interest. Although the Evangelist did not write this, nevertheless the Prophet, who did not pass it over in silence, is to be believed. And let strangers plunder the fruits of his labor. Let neither his wife nor his children possess what he acquired with labor, but let outsiders seize it—which is what happened. For the Pharisees seized the silver gained through the betrayal of the Lord, and jointly bought a field not for Judas’s children, but for the burial of strangers. Or, let God search out all his substance—his reason and free will, his capacity for doing good—to see how much he gave him in order to bear fruit from it; and, since he finds nothing, let strangers, that is, demons, plunder his labors in this life.

VERS. 12. Let there be no helper for him to protect him, or to deliver him from punishments by prayer; nor let there be anyone to have pity on his fatherless children so as to rescue them.

VERS. 13. Let his offspring be for destruction. Let that which has been generated from him generate no longer. In one generation let his name be blotted out; that is, let it quickly fail, so that it is not even named among human beings.

In the Hebrew it reads: “Let his latter end be destruction; in another generation let his name be blotted out”—that is, in the Christian generation. One generation is carnal, the other spiritual, concerning which it is written: “Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God” [Col. 0687B] (John 1:13).

VERS. 14. Let the iniquity of his fathers return to remembrance before the Lord for punishment, though he had seemed to forget it while he did not punish it. If Judas had remained in the apostolate, like Peter, neither his own past sins nor the iniquity of his fathers would have concerned him. But because he did not heed his adoption into God’s household, but chose the iniquity of the old generation, the iniquity of his fathers was renewed and returned before God. It must be understood that Judas was condemned not for his fathers’ sin but for his own. “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.” Evil parents do not harm good children, just as it did not harm Joshua to have had an evil father; nor do good parents benefit evil children, just as it did not profit Manasseh to have sprung from Hezekiah. [Col. 0687C] And let not the sin of his mother, who conceived him in sins—that is, in concupiscence—be blotted out, but let it be punished.

VERS. 15. Let his parents be continually before the Lord; that is, let them stand in the Lord’s sight not for good but for condemnation, and that forever—that is, let their sin be unforgivable both in this age and in the age to come—and let their memory perish from the land of the living. And why all this?

VERS. 16. Because he did not remember to show mercy. It is asked what harm it did Judas after his death that his wife and children came to beggary, or that the misfortunes written here should befall them. Many people are accustomed to benefit dead friends [Col. 0687D] either by prayers or almsgiving. But Judas’s punishment was increased by this: those who were crushed by poverty and misery would be unable, once dead, to remember him. Or the dead have concern for living friends, just as that rich man was concerned for his five brothers, lest they too should come to torments. And Judas’s punishment is enlarged in this: his household is deprived of necessary goods.

These curses are fulfilled not only upon Judas but also upon the Jews. Because they refused to have Christ as king over them, the Lord will set over them the sinful Antichrist, who is called “the sinner” by antonomasia, because he exalts himself above everything that is worshipped as God. This was expressed when they rejected Christ and asked that Barabbas be released to them. [Col. 0688A] Barabbas was a robber, and his name means “son of the father,” that is, of the devil; Antichrist is the devil’s son. He will be a robber because “he sits in ambush with the rich in secret places,” to kill the innocent Christian people. Before Christ’s passion Barabbas was shut up and bound in prison; afterward he was released by the Jews, because the devil, who had been bound among the ancient people—that is, the patriarchs and prophets—was released to persecute the Jews. Hence it follows: “And let the devil stand at his right hand.” In Greece there is a river called *diabolus*, meaning “flowing downward.” Therefore the apostate angel is called the devil, because he flowed downward when he fell from heavenly grace into the abyss. By the right hand good works are understood; by the left, evil works. It is said that an angel is appointed by God for every human being to urge him toward [Col. 0688B] good; and conversely, a demon is sent by the devil to incite him to evil. He is said to stand at the right who persuades and helps toward good; at the left, he who suggests evil and obstructs good. The devil stood at the right of the Jewish people when he incited them to Christ’s death. It was, as it were, a right hand, because they thought they had done a good work in Christ’s death: they supposed they had rendered service to God when they killed Christ as a destroyer of the Law. Hence it is said: “For they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34)—“For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). When that people is judged, it will go out from judgment condemned to punishment, because, persisting in unbelief, [Col. 0688C] it stores up wrath for itself on the day of wrath. And its prayer becomes sin because it is not made through Christ. For everything done outside faith in Christ is sin. Its days were made few, because after Christ’s passion it was quickly destroyed. “And let another receive his bishopric,” that is, let the people of the Gentiles receive the honor of the priesthood. Its children were made orphans, having lost their kingdom and God the Father. For “whoever does not have the Son does not have the Father either” (1 John 2:23). And its wife, namely the people over whom kings ruled, became a widow when the kingdom was lost. Its children were transferred in a wavering state—that is, uncertain—because they were led captive among all nations. There they beg, living by another’s mercy under the kings of the Gentiles, because they were cast out from their dwellings. For they have now lost both [Col. 0688D] place and nation. Titus the moneylender searched out all its substance, and strangers, namely the Romans, seized its labors. It has no helper, because Christ is not its helper; nor anyone to pity its fatherless children and rescue them from those who seize them. Its offspring was made for destruction—that is, for slaughter; and in the future, for eternal perdition. “In one generation let his name be blotted out.” One generation extends over one hundred years. But the Jewish people was destroyed by the Romans forty-two years after Christ’s passion, while even half of one generation had not elapsed, because “men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days” (Ps. 54:24); rather, they were snatched away in the middle of their days.

Otherwise: there are two generations, carnal and spiritual. [Col. 0689A] In one—that is, the spiritual—its name was blotted out, because it was not reborn of water and the Holy Spirit. Or in the future there will be one generation of those reigning with Christ; in it its name will be blotted out, because it will not be admitted among the elect. The iniquity of its fathers, who worshiped an idol in the wilderness and provoked God in many ways, returns to the Lord’s remembrance, as though consigned to forgetfulness, so that upon this most evil generation may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth. And the sin of its mother, namely Jerusalem, who is in bondage with her children, has not been blotted out: she killed the prophets and stoned those sent to her; moreover, she killed the Lord himself. The Jews have become continually before the Lord, because they stand unceasingly before him as before a judge, accused for punishment. [Col. 0689B] And their memory has perished from the land—namely, from Judaea or from the Church—because, though they were natural branches, they were broken off and wild olive shoots were grafted into the olive tree. And why is this? Because that people did not remember to show mercy: after killing Christ, it refused to repent, so as to redeem its sins by alms, which are works of mercy. And what did it do?

VERS. 17. He pursued the needy and poor man. Judas did so by betraying him; or the Jewish people did so by seizing him: it pursued Christ the man, who for our sake was made poor though rich, and for us made a beggar, having nowhere to lay his head and receiving necessities from others; [Col. 0689C] and it pursued one “stricken in heart,” namely, grieving over its perdition, in order to put him to death—even unto death. Or the Jews persecuted Christ in his members when they drove the apostles from their territories. Judas persecuted the Lord.

VERS. 18. And he loved cursing by practicing iniquity. And it shall come upon him on the day of judgment, when those on the left will be told: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). And he did not desire blessing, turning away from righteousness; and it shall be far from him when those on the right are told: “Come, blessed of my Father” (ibid., 34). Or the Jewish people loved cursing when it said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25); and it came upon it, because the blood of Christ and of all the righteous will be required of that generation. [Col. 0689D] And it did not desire blessing, saying, “You be that man’s disciple”—understand: “We do not wish to be.” And blessing will be far from it. Blessing was made far from it because it passed over to the Gentiles. And Judas, or the Jewish people, put on cursing as a garment. And that curse entered like water into his inward parts, that is, into his soul. It entered like oil into his bones, that is, into the powers of his soul. Note that a garment surrounds the body externally; water enters the interior of the belly; oil penetrates the bones: therefore they are cursed in body, soul, and all their powers. Cursing becomes like oil in their bones when people delight in evil deeds and think themselves strong because they sin with impunity; but in truth it is a curse, because God has foretold torments for such people. [Col. 0690A] Conversely, eternal life is blessing.

VERS. 19. Let it be to him like a garment with which he is covered: that is, let cursing surround him on every side like a cloak, let it cover him as a covering, and let him not see the glory of God. And let that curse be to him like the belt with which he is continually girded, so that, bound, he may be cast into outer darkness. They use cursing in this way, as someone puts on a tunic and is covered with a mantle, when they glory before people in evil action. He is girded with cursing as with a belt when he undertakes not sudden evil but premeditated evil. For everyone girds himself in order to be readier for work; so such a person learns to do evil, in order to be always prepared.

[Col. 0690B] VERS. 20. This is the work of those who speak against me before the Lord—that is, this will be the reward from the Lord for those who speak against me. He used “work” for “reward,” because reward is given for work: the cause for the effect. By the garment, covering, water, oil, and belt, the deeds themselves are denoted, for which cursing and eternal punishments are returned as recompense. Or those who disparage him as existing with the Lord—that is, consubstantial with God—are those who do not believe that he is equal to the Father. Therefore there is not one Judas only, but many. For there are as many as those who disparage him and turn people away from the faith.

Up to this point was the judgment of the Judge upon the body of the devil. There follows the prayer of the Intercessor for his [Col. 0690C] members: “Thus, as I have said, I shall judge the wicked; but I shall save the righteous.”

VERS. 21. And you, Lord Father, and you, Lord Holy Spirit, bring about this salvation with me for your name’s sake, not because of human merits. Or, “bring it about with me,” that is, help me, the man assumed by you, for your name’s sake, that is, for the sake of grace. For with no preceding merits of works, human nature was raised to such a height that the Word made flesh—that is, God and man together—was called the only-begotten Son of God. This was done so that what had perished might be sought by him who had created it. Hence it follows: “Because your mercy is sweet,” that is, the mercy which you wish to exercise toward human beings through me is delightful: deliver me [Col. 0690D] by raising me from death.

VERS. 22. For I am needy and poor—that is, I am mortal and capable of suffering, though I did not sin. And my heart is troubled because I shall die; and this is within me, that is, in my will. And how will this occur?

VERS. 23. As a shadow declines, descending from the mountains, so I was taken away from the disciples, captured by the Jews. As night comes through the decline of a shadow, so death comes through a mortal body. And I was shaken out like a locust. As a shaken locust leaps from place to place, so Christ, shaken out of Judaea by Herod’s persecution, leapt into Egypt; from Egypt into Galilee; from there into Judaea; from Judaea into the wilderness; then, coming to Jerusalem, he was shaken out from it into the field, [Col. 0691A] and was crucified; shaken from the cross, he leapt into the tomb, and thence into heaven. Or he was shaken out like a locust in his members, when the saints, suffering persecution from the impious, fled from city to city.

VERS. 24. My knees were weakened through fasting, when I fasted forty days and forty nights; and my flesh was changed because of oil. The comparison is with one who fasts so much that, with his knees trembling, he cannot stand for prayer, and, eating no fat, his flesh grows pale for want of oil as food. Christ’s knees were the apostles sustaining the Church, Christ’s body. But Christ was the bread of life. Therefore these knees were weakened through fasting when, in the Passion, after Christ, their food, was taken away, the apostles became weak in faith: when, leaving him, all fled, and some denied him. Oil is an image of brightness; oil is, as it were, food for light. I gave the Jews the oil of mercy, the grace of life, the light of knowledge. Because of this oil my flesh was changed, not into joy but into sorrow, because it was afflicted by death and emptied. Or oil signifies the Godhead. Therefore because of this oil, which is an image of paternal brightness, or because of the Holy Spirit abiding in me, who is the oil of spiritual anointing, my flesh was changed in the resurrection into immortality and impassibility. Or my flesh, namely the Church, was changed from idolatry through the oil of chrism, or through the Holy Spirit, the oil of exultation.

[Col. 0691C] VERS. 25. And I, who ought to have been an honor to them, was made a reproach to them through the death of the cross. They were ashamed of me because one such as I had been born from their race. Therefore, making a spectacle of me, they looked upon me hanging on the cross with delight, and moved their heads in mockery of me, because they saw me hanging but did not see me risen. They saw when the knees were weakened; they did not see when the flesh was changed. Having stated the reason, he repeats the prayer.

VERS. 26. Help me, O Lord my God. You who are Lord of all things and God, creator of all, help me as I work the salvation of humankind. Save me through the mercy shown to human beings by me. [Col. 0691D] Make me safe by giving resurrection, immortality, and confession at your right hand.

VERS. 27. And let them know that this is your hand: that is, make my resurrection so manifest that they may know that this operation of my death is yours, and so yours that you, Lord Father, have done it—not they, as they think. For they could do nothing except what your hand decreed to be done. Or make it so manifest through miracles that they may know that this is your hand: that is, let them recognize that I, through whom you work, am your hand—namely, your Son according to the Godhead—and let them know that you, Lord, created that hand according to humanity. That is to say: let them know that I am God and man: man in the Passion, God in the resurrection.

[Col. 0692A] VERS. 28. Those Jews will curse me in synagogues, denying me and my works; but you, Father, will bless in the churches which praise me. Note that he says “but you,” as though saying: “I bless, and you will bless with me by giving them the Holy Spirit.” Let those who rise against me be confounded: those who now persecute me in words and deeds, let them be ashamed when they cannot deny my resurrection. But your servant—that is, I, who served in the world and obeyed you even unto death—will rejoice in the Church or in your glory.

VERS. 29. Let those who speak against me be clothed with shame—those who say in disparagement, “His disciples stole him by night.” Let them be surrounded with shame as though clothed in a tunic, and let them be covered with their confusion as someone is covered in a *diplois*. [Col. 0692B] A *diplois* is a double cloak; hence the Hebrew reads: “Let them be covered with their confusion as with a double mantle”—that is, let them be confounded in body and soul: in soul, when they cannot deny my resurrection; in body, when they are transferred from place to place. Their confusion will be twofold. But I—

VERS. 30. I will greatly confess to the Lord with my mouth; that is, I will praise the Lord strongly in the Church, which is my mouth; and in the midst of many—that is, in the hearts of the faithful—I will praise him. For the heart is in the middle of the human being; and Christ dwells in our hearts through faith, and in the mouth of his body, the Church, praises God. “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” [Col. 0692C] (Rom. 10:10). Or, I will make them confess with love and heart, so that they may praise him in the midst of many—that is, in the fellowship of the faithful—because many will praise him through me. He is said to be in the midst to whom chief honor is due. God is deservedly to be praised:

VERS. 31. Because he stood at the right hand of Judas in order to overthrow and weaken his good works. Thus God stood at the right hand of Christ, who was made poor for us, in order to strengthen his works, so as to save my soul from persecutors; or my life from the Jews persecuting it; or my soul from demons desiring to hold it fast. The Father saved Christ’s soul when he raised him from death and exalted him at his right hand. In judgment also he will stand at Christ’s right hand and save the souls [Col. 0692D] of the elect from persecuting demons, when he gives them eternal joys.

There have been certain heretics, or perhaps there still are today, who deny that Christ had a human soul and think that the Godhead, which is the source of life, gave life to the flesh in place of a soul. Against them, although the Gospel openly cries, “I have power to lay down my soul” (John 10:18), and this book says, “You will not leave my soul in hell” (Acts 2:27), and this passage says, “You will save my soul,” nevertheless we must, guided by reason, consider whether he had a soul. Christ came to redeem the whole human being, who had wholly perished. The whole human being consists of soul and body. For God formed the body from clay and breathed a soul into it. The soul, moreover, is more worthy [Col. 0693A] than the body. If Christ did not have a soul, then he redeemed only the flesh, namely the less worthy part of the human being, and left the more worthy part, namely the soul, in condemnation. But it is certain that he redeemed not only bodies but souls as well. Therefore Christ redeemed the whole human being, soul and body.

There are five psalms which deal more extensively with Christ’s Passion, namely: “My God, my God, look upon me”; “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me”; “Hear, O God, my prayer”; “Save me, O God”; “O God, my praise.” All of them begin first in the person of Christ; second, frame their words as prayer; third, recount the events of the Lord’s Passion; fourth, accord with the words of the Gospel; fifth, conclude their narrative with exultation. This Passion was also accomplished through five wounds; foretold through five books; received by the Church through five virgins. All things agree; all correspond to one another in illuminating symmetry. A virgin gave birth; the Messiah has now come; the spotless Lamb has been slain; the Redeemer rose from the dead; the world heard and believed; the Jew still feigns to grow old without acknowledging what the whole world has recognized.

## PSALM 109. On Christ’s Exaltation

[Col. 0693]

[Col. 0693B] “The Lord said to my Lord,” etc. The preceding psalm concerns Christ’s humility; this one, his exaltation. Its title is:

(VERSE 1.) A PSALM OF DAVID.

That is: this praise is ascribed to the desirable Christ. Since his humility was displayed in the preceding psalm, lest anyone perhaps despair of being able to be saved through one who showed himself so humble and rejected, his exaltation is added in this psalm. And for greater authority, the Father is introduced as speaking to the Son concerning the exaltation which he will possess. The dignity of this psalm also shines forth in the Gospel, where it is said “that David, in the Spirit, called Christ Lord” (Matt. 22:43).

[Col. 0693C] This psalm is placed in the one hundred and ninth position, signifying that through Christ perfect joy will be given to the perfected in fellowship with the nine orders of angels. The subject of the psalm is Christ’s exaltation. Its purpose is to show his exaltation and to invite us to venerate him. Its words are said to be taken from the history in which Abraham’s steward, sent for Rebekah, reported that God had exalted his master with glory and riches and had given him a son as heir; that his master had shattered kings whom he overcame in war when he rescued Lot and the spoil; and that Melchizedek, king and priest, had met the victor with sacrifice. It signifies Christ, sent for the Church, who overcame the devil, divided his spoils, offered himself to the Father as a sacrifice for us, and whom the Father [Col. 0693D] exalted at his right hand and subjected enemies beneath his feet.

This psalm has three divisions. The first is, “The Lord said,” in which Christ’s divinity and humanity are demonstrated. The second is, “With you is the beginning,” in which the divine generation and equality with the Father are declared. The third is, “The Lord has sworn,” in which Christ’s priesthood and royal judgment are proclaimed. This psalm [Col. 0694B] is, as some say, the sun of our faith, a mirror of the heavenly mystery, an armory of the sacred Scriptures, where everything which is narrated in the preaching of both Testaments is stated in summary. It is the voice of the prophet David himself, triumphing after the labor of the Passion, death having been conquered.

“The Lord said to my Lord”: that is, the Lord Father said to my Lord the Son, namely Christ. What did he say? “Sit at my right hand,” that is, rest in my higher possessions. Or, “sit,” that is, reign in equality with me. He said this—that is, he made others understand it. The comparison is with kings, who are accustomed to place at their right hand those of greater dignity or supported by greater power. This signifies that the righteous reign with the Lord. And fittingly this psalm, in which Christ’s kingdom is described, is placed after [Col. 0694C] that psalm in which his death is written, because through the gate of the cross he entered the palace of the kingdom. Reign with me until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet; that is, until I subject all your enemies to you, as a footstool is placed beneath the feet. Of these, some will be friends and some not; yet all will be conquered, and in the future all, evil and good alike, will be subjected to him—some willingly, others unwillingly. “Until I make” your enemies openly the footstool of your feet and subject them to your eternal dominion. He does not say “until” as though, once they are subjected, he would no longer sit, since it is written: “Of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke 1:33). Rather, it is because then it will be manifest that he reigns. For now some doubt whether he reigns or not, just as Jews and Gentiles do not believe [Col. 0694D] that he reigns, because they are not yet subjected beneath his feet. They will see it later, when all things are subjected to him. This was the Father’s voice concerning Christ’s exaltation in heaven. There follows the Prophet’s voice concerning his exaltation on earth.

VERS. 2. The Lord will send forth the rod of your strength from Zion. That is to say: O Lord Son, the Lord Father said, “Sit”—that is, reign over all—and the scepter of your kingdom will begin in Judaea and reach all nations. A rod is a scepter, the emblem of authority. “The Lord will send forth the rod of your strength”—that is, the power of your might—“from Zion,” that is, it will begin from Jerusalem. There the enemies will begin to be placed beneath your feet, from where the dominion of your kingdom will begin—not that kingdom in which the Lord of all things and King of the ages, the Son who created the ages, eternally reigns with the Father, by which he called us into eternity (for this kingdom begins with Christians), but the kingdom which shall have no end. This began from Zion, that is, from Jerusalem, and reached all nations. Since you will be king over Jews and Gentiles, do what befits a king.

“Rule in the midst of your enemies”: that is, reign here amid pagans, Jews, heretics, [Col. 0695B] and false brethren; but in the future you will rule forever, the righteous reigning and the ungodly burning in eternal punishments. And:

VERS. 3. With you the beginning will rule—that is, the Father, from whom you are the beginning and in whose beginning you were the Word. This will be manifest on the day of your power, that is, on the day of the resurrection, by which you will show your power when you rise victorious from death. And this will be in the splendors of the saints, whom, rescued from the darkness of hell, you will make to shine in the light of angels. The splendor of the saints is the Holy Spirit, the light of angels. It is called “splendors” because the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are sent to the faithful after Christ’s triumph in the brilliance of fire, are written of; through them they shone in the world as lamps and afterward will shine in glory as the sun. Or these are the Father’s words: Rule over all, and I am the beginning with you in that nature by which you are day—that is, God—and by which you make the saints shine through virtues in this life. Or: sit at my right hand and rule over your enemies, until, when all have been subjected to you, it becomes evident to all that I am the beginning, one essence with you. And this will be on the day of your power, that is, the day of judgment, which is not a day of weakness but of your power, when you will show your power by condemning your enemies and glorifying your friends: in the splendors of the saints, when the righteous will shine like the sun. Then it will be known how the beginning is with you, because you will be seen with the Father in the Father, as it is written: “On that day you will know [Col. 0695D] that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you” (John 14:20).

And whence does the Son have such unity and such equality with the Father? From this: “From the womb, before Lucifer, I begot you”—that is, from my secret essence I begot you before the first archangel. For before heaven and earth, as certain teachers say, the devil was created, who is called Lucifer because, while he was good, he was more worthy than the other creatures. Before him, who was the first creature, I begot you. It is equivalent to saying: “Before every creature I begot you.” For if before the first, then certainly before what followed. Or he means the star Lucifer, the herald of daylight, through which time is understood. It is as though he said: “Before the times of eternity, I begot you from myself, eternal light from eternal light.” For he through whom times were made was not born in time. Or, simply, Christ was born before Lucifer because, before the rising of daylight, his mother gave him birth, at whose service a star and a choir of angels immediately appeared with immense light. Having indicated his kingdom, he also wishes to note his priesthood. You will be not only king but priest, because:

VERS. 4. The Lord has sworn—that is, he has established by unshakable truth—and he will not repent of having sworn, because he will never at all change what he has promised. For God’s repentance is a change of things; not to repent is to promise inviolably. What did he swear? Namely this: that you are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek—that is, according to the exalted dignity [Col. 0696B] of the priesthood of King Melchizedek. The Jews hand down that Melchizedek was Shem, Noah’s son, king of Salem, later called Jerusalem, and that he lived until Jacob’s time. He met Abraham, it is said, on Mount Tabor with bread and wine, when Abraham returned victorious after kings had been slain and spoil shaken out; and he blessed Abraham, who gave him tithes as to a priest. *Melech* means “king,” *Sedech*, “justice”; from these is formed *Melchisedech*, meaning “king of justice,” or king of Salem, that is, of peace. Christ was priest not according to Aaron’s order, which sacrificed calves and goats, but according to the order of Melchizedek, who offered bread and wine, when he sacrificed himself to the Father as food and drink for the faithful. He was without father on earth and without mother in heaven; he has neither beginning [Col. 0696C] of days nor end; he is king of justice and peace, because for justice he will give the kingdom which is peace and joy. Christ’s priesthood is therefore said to endure forever because Jews think that the priesthood of the Law is still to be restored. Christ, who offered himself as sacrifice in the temple of the Church, now intercedes for us as priest in the temple of heaven; he will yet judge the world as king, when his angelic ministers will gather out of his kingdom all scandals. Hence it follows:

VERS. 5. The Lord at your right hand has shattered kings in the day of his wrath. The prophetic voice turns to the Father, because the Holy Spirit, who speaks here, belongs to the Father and the Son: O Lord Father, the Lord Son, seated [Col. 0696D] at your right hand, has shattered kings also—that is, rulers—on the day of judgment, when he will exercise his wrath. He used the past tense, “has shattered,” in place of the future, “will shatter,” because of its certainty. Then he will shatter kings when:

VERS. 6. He will judge among the nations—that is, he will judge all nations as king, render judgment upon good and evil, fill up from humankind the fallen places of the angels, and shatter—that is, crush—the pride of wicked rich people who were heads upon the earth and were proud in earthly things. Another translation has: “He will shatter many heads in a plentiful land”—that is, he will condemn those who are heads among an earthly people and pride themselves on earthly abundance.

Otherwise: On the day of the Passion, which was the day of the Jews’ wrath, the Lord shattered kings by his patience—namely [Col. 0697A] Herod, Pilate, and the chief priests—when the kings of the earth stood up and rulers assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ. Then he judged among the nations because he executed judgment on demons; he filled the ruins of the Jews—he who was appointed for their fall—and he shattered the heads of many on earth, because he made humble in this life those who had been proud. All this happened because:

VERS. 7. He drank [Vulgate: “will drink”] from the torrent on the way—that is, being on the way, he tasted death. This torrent is the flowing course of human mortality. For just as a torrent is gathered from rain waters, overflows, roars, runs, and by running runs down—that is, finishes its course—so the whole course of mortality runs down, [Col. 0697B] while one generation passes and another comes. People are born, live, and die; as some die, others are born, until the entire torrent has flowed away and the whole human race has passed from this age. Christ drank from this torrent on the way because in this world, as in a passage, he tasted death. Not in his own house but on the way, thirsting for human salvation and hastening to go on to other things, namely [Col. 0698A] to the resurrection, he drank the bitter cup of death. The comparison is with a traveler who drinks muddy water on the road. Thus Christ, journeying to us, drank death for a time. “Therefore”—that is, on account of this drink—“he has exalted” [Vulgate: “will exalt”] the head, namely himself, the head of the Church, at the Father’s right hand. And the Father “exalted him above all and gave him the name which is above every name,” namely God, “that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2:10). And because the head has now been exalted, the body too will be exalted through this drink, where Christ is in the Father’s glory, God blessed above all forever.

Therefore Vespers begins with this psalm, in which Christ’s kingdom and priesthood are sung, because the Church began his kingdom in the evening of the world, and because he himself, the priest, offered himself as sacrifice at the end of the age. Therefore this psalm and the next four are sung at Sunday Vespers, which is assigned to the resurrection, because after the resurrection the Church began to reign in itself, and daily customarily offers him a sacrifice of praise together with the sacrifice of his body.

## PSALM 110. On the Praise of the Righteous

[Col. 0697]

[Col. 0697C] “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, in the council of the righteous,” etc. The preceding psalm sang of Christ’s kingdom and priesthood; this one sings his praise, by which it instructs us to praise God. Its title is:

ALLELUIA.

That is: Praise God; and it signifies the praise of the joy to come, where the Lord is seen by the faithful without interruption and praised without end. Its subject is the praise of God; its purpose is to urge all the faithful, both from the Jews and from the Gentiles, to praise God, who has now given them in reality what He promised to the ancient people in figure. Its words appear to be taken from the fact that God delivered His people from Egypt, fed them with manna in the wilderness, and gave them the land promised to the fathers; and it signifies [Col. 0697D] that through His Son God redeemed the human race from hell, feeds it in the wilderness of the world with the bread of heaven, and will give the land of the living, promised to the saints.

This psalm is the one hundred and tenth, which is eleven times ten. Eleven signifies transgression; ten, the fulfillment of the Law. It indicates that the ancient people, because of transgression of the Law, did not attain the promised inheritance; but the Christian people attained the promise through observance of God’s Law. This psalm is arranged according to the order of the Hebrew alphabet, and perfection is thereby understood. Other psalms too are written in this manner [Col. 0698C]. But in them either certain letters are missing or some are superfluous, some verses are shorter and others longer; this happened more through the zeal of readers than of scribes. Therefore the Seventy Interpreters did not wish to include these letters.

This psalm, however, contains all the letters and signifies those perfect in virtues. It is threefold. The first part is: “I will confess to thee, O Lord,” in which confession of praise in the assembly of the righteous—where there is eternal praise and proclamation without end—is woven with six letters. The second is: “He hath made a memorial,” in which heavenly food and the inheritance of Paradise given to the faithful people are described with ten letters. The third is: “He sent redemption,” in which Christ, sent for the redemption of the faithful, and the New Testament given, are set forth with six letters of the same alphabet [Col. 0698B]. It is the voice of Christ instructing us in the praise of God.

**VERSE 1.** “I will confess to thee, O Lord, with my whole heart,” that is, I shall praise the Lord with perfect affection. “With my whole heart,” that is, in perfect charity, which is understood as devotion and good action, in which love consists. “For he that loveth hath fulfilled the law” (Rom. XIII, 8). That He says not “I confess,” but “I will confess,” shows that one must persevere in confession. I shall confess to Thee in perfection, and this “in the counsel of the righteous,” that is, in the teaching of prophets and apostles, who counsel the praise of God through the perfection of a good life. And I shall praise Thee “in the congregation [Col. 0699A] of the righteous,” that is, in the Church of Catholics, not in the council of heretics, because:

**VERSE 2.** “Great are the works of the Lord,” who made heaven and earth and everything in them from nothing; restored fallen man; distinguished diverse kinds of fish, birds, beasts, and other things by their various species; and governs all these as He wills. These works are “sought out,” that is, carefully made, “in all His wills,” as though he said: He made all things as He willed, and all things do what He wills. For although angels or men may seem, through free choice, to do certain things against God’s will, nevertheless all their deeds are ordered by His will. Or, the works of the Lord are great to the person who understands them and investigates them so that he may proceed “in all His wills,” that is [Col. 0699B], so that he may keep all His commandments. For if someone does not kill, but commits adultery, he is guilty of everything, because by adultery he kills another person’s soul as well. He shows in parts what God’s works are.

**VERSE 3.** Confession, by which a man acknowledges himself to be a sinner, and magnificence—that is, purity of conscience by which he abstains from evils—and the performance of good action, are His work; and His righteousness, that is, His recompense, thereby remains for ever and ever, that is, eternally. Or: confession of sins, through which sinners are justified, and remission of sins, through which God is magnified, are His work, because He Himself works in us both to will and to accomplish according to good will; yet it is also our work through the cooperation of free choice. And this righteousness of His remains for ever and ever: that is [Col. 0699C], to those justified by faith He will give, as the reward for righteous good action, a reward that will remain eternally.

Another translation has: “Glory and beauty are His work,” He who does glorious and beautiful things. By my example, confess to Him in confession and action, and He will reward you, because:

**VERSE 4.** “He hath made a memorial of His wonderful works,” that is, the Lord has made a signification of His signifying wonders; He is merciful in Himself and compassionate toward us—namely:

**VERSE 5.** “He hath given food to them that fear Him,” that is, He gave teaching to the apostles who revered Him. I mean food signified by the food given in the wilderness. This is drawn from the history in which God worked wonders when [Col. 0699D] He delivered the people from Egypt by signs, fed them in the wilderness with birds’ flesh and angels’ bread, and gave them drink from the rock. In these wonders lay a figure of future things, of which the Lord made a memorial, because He bestowed upon the Christian people what those things signified: just as He redeemed that people from Egypt, so He redeemed this people from hell; just as He delivered that people from Pharaoh’s oppression, so He freed this people from the devil’s oppression; just as He led that people through the Red Sea, so He leads this people through baptism; just as He fed that people with heavenly bread, so He feeds this people with the living bread that came down from heaven; just as He gave that people water brought forth from the rock, so He gives this people drink with the blood poured out from His side; just as He brought that people into the land promised to the fathers, so He brings this people into the land of the living promised to the saints.

[Col. 0700A] It should be noted that He placed food before His other wonders. It represented the body of Christ as food for the soul, because among all miracles it is accounted greatest that a human being feeds upon God’s body, and by this food attains the promise. “Merciful” is said from *miser* (“wretched”) and *cor* (“heart”). Since misery cannot befall God, it is asked how He is called merciful. He is called merciful in relation to us when He has compassion upon our miseries and pities the wretched, though He does not suffer an affection of misery. Through those who fear Him, to whom He gave food, He will remember for the age of His new covenant promised to Abraham and signified through the Old Testament; that is, as long as this age endures, He will cause the new law to be preached to Jews and Gentiles. The covenant with Abraham was this: if the people of Israel kept God’s law, He would give them the land [Col. 0700B] promised to them. This bore the figure of the New Testament, in which He promises to Abraham’s seed—that is, to believers—that if it keeps His law, namely love, He will give it the land of the living. He will remember this covenant throughout the age, because He will always give the promised blessings to faithful persons who keep the Law. And through those who fear Him, that is, through the apostles:

**VERSE 6.** “He will declare the power of His works to His people,” that is, through teachers He will expound to His Christian people the significance of the wonderful works that He performed among the Jews. He will declare them for this purpose:

**VERSE 7.** “That He may give them the inheritance of the Gentiles,” that is, that He may join the Gentiles to them, so that the Gentiles may be their inheritance, loved by them as one loves one’s own inheritance. The Jewish nation, which worshipped God, was properly called His people, in distinction from the Gentiles, who worshipped idols. To this people, through Elijah and Enoch, He will declare the significance of His works, in order to give them the inheritance of the Gentiles, that is, Christ, who is their inheritance; through faith in Him they will inherit the kingdom of heaven with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And after receiving instruction, among His people and among the Gentiles there will be works of His hands, namely truth and judgment. Truth means the practice of good works; judgment means contempt for evil deeds, or accusation, in that they accuse themselves of sins; or discernment of good and evil. To such persons the promise will be given, because:

**VERSE 8.** “All His commandments are faithful,” that is, His precepts, when observed, will faithfully fulfill what they promise. [Col. 0700D] “Established for ever and ever,” that is, they have been established—that is, kept to the end. And if they are done in truth, that is, in faith and equity, for eternal rather than temporal things, then His commandments are truly faithful, because He has now fulfilled for the faithful what He once promised to the fathers. For:

**VERSE 9.** “He sent redemption to His people,” that is, He sent Christ, whom He had promised, through whom He redeemed His people from death, just as He delivered the ancient people from tribulation through Moses. And through Him He commanded that His covenant—that is, the Gospel—be kept for ever, in return for which He will give eternal joy. This is drawn from the history in which the Lord sent Moses, redeemed the people from Egypt through the sacrifice of the lamb, and gave them the covenant of the Law on Mount Sinai, [Col. 0701A] promising them an inheritance for keeping it. Therefore, being redeemed, you ought rightly to confess to Him, because His name is holy—namely, “Lord”: beloved, giving security to the good, and terrible to the wicked. For the Lord rewards those who serve well and condemns the negligent. Or, Christ’s name is holy in holy Christians, whom He sanctifies; terrible to pagans, Jews, and heretics, whom He separates from the saints in judgment. And by what is holiness acquired? By wisdom. By what is wisdom acquired? By fear.

**VERSE 10.** “For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” There are two fears: one servile, which turns from evil lest it be condemned; the other filial, which does good lest it be disinherited. This is the beginning of wisdom: not to do evil and to do good. Perfect wisdom, however, [Col. 0701B] consists in charity, which casts out fear, when in unity it will know the Trinity. Therefore, wisdom is to understand the good things of eternal life. And this understanding is good, not for all who understand, but for all who do it—that is, those who do what they understand to be pleasing to God. “For to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin” (Jas. IV, 17). For “knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth” (I Cor. VIII, 1). Whoever has [Col. 0702A] this is praiseworthy, and his praise remains for ever and ever—that is, the practice of good understanding remains eternally. This praise will be the reward, the end, the resting-place, and the everlasting dwelling, because “Blessed are they that dwell in thy house: they shall praise thee for ever and ever” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5).

Note the order of the eleventh decade, which pertains to transgression of God’s Law. In the first psalm is written humanity’s transgression and its restoration through Christ; in the second, the Church’s blessing from the Jews; in the third, the Church’s blessing from the Gentiles for God’s benefit bestowed; in the fourth, God’s benefits bestowed upon both peoples are remembered; in the fifth, humanity’s evils rendered to God in return for good things are narrated; in the sixth, human temptations and God’s mercies are set forth; [Col. 0702B] in the seventh, Christ’s obedience as an example to the faithful and the reward for it are related; in the eighth, Christ’s betrayal by Judas and the affliction of the Church, Christ’s body, by the devil’s body, are expressed; in the ninth, Christ’s exaltation and the Church’s raising through His kingdom and priesthood are indicated; in the tenth, the praise of the righteous for salvation is expressed.

## PSALM CXI. On the generation of rulers

[Col. 0701]

[Col. 0701C] “Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord,” etc. In the preceding decade, which is the eleventh, the transgression of the human race was described. Accordingly Judas is also written of in it: having transgressed the ten commandments of the Law, he fell into the number eleven, when he committed murder against himself and against the Lord. By his fall he also diminished the perfect number twelve of the apostleship; and thus the number of disciples remained at eleven, which is imperfect. But in this following decade, which is the twelfth, the fulfillment of both laws is indicated, because in ten the old Law is expressed through the Decalogue, and in two the new Law through the twofold love, which is perfectly described in the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled.” Therefore it begins with fear, which leads to charity.

This psalm is the one hundred and eleventh, which [Col. 0701D] is twelve times nine, with three added. Twelve signifies apostolic teaching; nine, the society of angels; three, the vision of the Trinity. Thus this number indicates that fallen man, from transgression of God’s commandment, will come through the teaching of the apostles to the fellowship of angels and to the vision of the Trinity itself. This psalm too is written according to the order of the alphabet, because it expresses perfection.

The subject of the psalm is the generation of rulers. Its purpose is to exhort us to fear, which is the guide to love, [Col. 0702C] and love leads to true blessedness. The words are taken from Zerubbabel, who, after returning from captivity, was powerful in Judea, and in whose house were riches and glory. Zerubbabel means “master of Babylon,” that is, of confusion, and signifies the Gentile people, a master of confusion in idolatry, which, returning from the captivity of the devil, is powerful in the land—that is, in the Church—in whose house are the riches of wisdom and knowledge and the glory of virtues. The title is:

**ALLELUIA, THE RETURN [Note: [Col. 0701D] Vulgate: “Of the Return.”] OF HAGGAI AND ZECHARIAH.**

That is: in this psalm there is an admonition to praise God for the return of the faithful from the Babylonian city of this world to the heavenly Jerusalem, from which they had been taken captive and expelled, so that they may build it from themselves as living stones. This title indicates that this [Col. 0702D] book was brought forth through the Holy Spirit, to whom all things future and past are present. For fourteen generations are counted between the time of David and the deportation of the people of Israel into Babylon. Those who returned hoped, according to Jeremiah’s prophecy, for the renewal of the Temple after seventy years. When these years were completed under Darius, the captivity was ended. Then two prophets returned from captivity to Jerusalem with the people and took part in rebuilding the Temple. This signifies all the faithful who return from the captivity of this world to their homeland through good [Col. 0703A] works. Therefore let each person become a living stone fit for the spiritual building; let him understand spiritually the renewal of the Temple from its ancient ruin, which occurred in Adam—namely, the renewal of the new people according to the new and heavenly man—so that, as we have borne the image of the earthly, we may bear also the image of the heavenly. Let each person turn himself from this world’s ruinous stain to the work of building and to the hope of firm joining, like a living stone; and he will understand the title “Alleluia” and the conversion of Haggai and Zechariah. Haggai means “festive”; Zechariah, “memory of the Lord.” They are those who return from the captivity of the devil, into which they had fallen by transgressing God’s commandment, through fear to charity, by which God’s Temple is built. The perfection of this [Col. 0703B] building is that ineffable peace of wisdom whose beginning is the fear of the Lord; in that house there are always festivity and remembrance of the Lord through the sweet Alleluia.

This psalm has three sections. One is: “Blessed is the man,” in which the glory and riches of the God-fearing man are described by six letters of the alphabet; another is: “There hath arisen,” in which Christ, the true light, is shown to have appeared to the upright, and the righteous man to be in everlasting remembrance, by fourteen letters; the third is: “The sinner shall see,” in which the destruction of the wicked is woven with three letters. This psalm is woven through with all the letters of the alphabet, as though with golden rules, because it signifies the perfect, absolved from sins, returned to the homeland of eternal joy. It is the voice of the Holy Spirit exhorting to the fear of God.

[Col. 0703C] **VERSE 1.** “Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord.” The whole Christian people is one man, having one heart and one soul in love. Having returned from the devil’s captivity, he is blessed if he fears the Lord by turning away from evil; through this fear he will come to love, through which he will “delight greatly in His commandments,” that is, have a great desire to fulfill His precepts. This verse is connected with the passage: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX, 10). Note: fear makes a person turn away from evil; love makes him do good. This is the building of the Temple. Such a man is blessed because:

**VERSE 2.** “His seed shall be mighty upon earth,” that is, his teaching and work make him mighty in [Col. 0703D] the land of the living, where “the generation of the righteous,” namely good works, shall be blessed when Christ says: “Come, ye blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV, 34). There shall be:

**VERSE 3.** “Glory and riches in his house,” that is, in the heavenly dwelling, eternal brightness and abundance of every good thing, where they shall be set over all the Lord’s goods. Hence it follows: “And his righteousness remaineth for ever and ever,” that is, the reward of his righteousness will be full joy, which no one shall take from him, but which will remain eternally. This is the festivity in the Lord’s house expressed by the name Haggai.

Otherwise: Blessed is the man who fears God and desires His commandments. “His seed shall be mighty upon earth,” that is, his affection in his own sensual nature will be effective, making it [Col. 0704A] fruitful; and thus, by his example, “the generation of the righteous” shall be blessed, that is, multiplied in good works. In his house, that is, in his heart, there shall be glory, namely the purity of innocence, and riches, namely abundance of wisdom; and righteousness, that is, good action, remains for ever and ever. And who has bestowed this blessedness upon fallen man? Christ, because:

**VERSE 4.** “Light hath arisen in darkness for the upright in heart.” Darkness is sin and ignorance, which covered the human race in the captivity of transgression and lead to outer darkness. Therefore unbelievers are called not dark, but darkness: “Ye were sometimes darkness” (Eph. V, 8). For these the light arose when Christ, the sun of righteousness, shone upon the world, and immediately the angelic choir appeared with light. [Col. 0704B] Or, when the light of truth became known to the Gentiles. And for whom did it arise? For the upright in heart, that is, the righteous. The upright in heart are those who will nothing except what God wills, and to whom all God’s judgments are pleasing; of them it is said: “But now ye are light in the Lord” (ibid.). And what was that light? “Merciful, compassionate, and righteous”: merciful in Himself, compassionate toward us who are wretched, and righteous in the righteous. That is to say: to captives sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death the true light appeared; it drove away the darkness of unbelief and ignorance and illumined them by faith and wisdom. Mercy appeared: it forgave the wretched their sins and made them merciful. Righteousness appeared: it justified the ungodly. Therefore:
