**VERSES 5–6.** “A pleasing man has compassion and lends”:  that is, beloved by God is the man who, following His example, has compassion on the wretched, giving necessities to the poor if he has this world’s goods, or forgiving debts to those who sin against him; and who lends what he possesses to those who do not have it, and, if he has neither gold nor silver, does not deny words of wisdom to one in need. [Col. 0704C] “He shall order his words in judgment,” that is, he prepares himself to render account for these things at the future judgment. Or, he orders his words so as to speak in judgment for the poor oppressed by unjust judges. Or, “he shall order his words in judgment,” that is, in discernment, so that he may know what, how much, and in what manner to say to a ruler, and in what manner to a poor person. Such a man is gracious because he shall not be moved for ever [Col. 0704D] from mercy and lending, or from eternal recompense. For “he that hath mercy on the poor lendeth unto the Lord” (Prov. XIX, 17). But judgment without mercy shall befall him who has not shown mercy. The righteous man shall not be moved from blessedness, because:

**VERSE 7.** “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” [Vulgate: “in eternal remembrance”]; but the wicked are erased from memory. For who remembers Nero, Decius, or other tyrants who once here abounded in riches and vices? Yet who does not remember Peter and Paul, or others such as they, who once here flourished in righteousness and holiness? These shall be in everlasting remembrance both here and in the future; they shall remain eternally in the glory of the saints. Therefore [Col. 0705A] they shall not fear an evil report when they hear: “Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire” (Matt. XXV, 41). The name Zechariah expresses the eternity of this remembrance. Or, the evil report is when persecutors say to Christians: “Sacrifice to the gods; if you do not, you shall perish by a cruel death.” The righteous man shall not fear this report, because his heart is ready to hope in the Lord: that is, his will is prepared for every torment, like Lawrence’s, on account of the hope he has in the Lord.

**VERSE 8.** His heart is established by faith and love; therefore he shall not be moved from the state of uprightness, until he despises his enemies, that is, utterly scorns the power of tyrants, heresies, sins, and vices. Or, he shall despise his enemies when, with them cast down, those who fear and love God receive [Col. 0705B] “what eye hath not seen, nor ear heard” (I Cor. II). Therefore he shall be in everlasting remembrance, because:

**VERSE 9.** “He hath dispersed what he possessed and given it,” not to the rich but to the poor members of Christ. Therefore his righteousness—that is, the reward for this righteousness—remains for ever and ever, which is the age following this present age; and finally his horn, that is, his kingdom for righteousness, shall be exalted in eternal glory. Note that the kingdom of heaven is worth as much as each person possesses. For a poor person can buy it with a cup of cold water just as a rich person can with all his wealth. When the righteous man, here despised by the proud, is exalted in glory, the wicked man shall be taken away for punishment lest he see the glory of God. Every sinner shall see this exaltation.

[Col. 0705C] **VERSE 10.** “The sinner shall see,” when he sees Christ whom he pierced; and then he shall be angry with himself that he did not do such things, saying in anguish of spirit: “These are they whom we once held in derision; we fools thought their life madness. Behold how they are counted among the children of God. What hath pride profited us? Or what hath the boasting of riches contributed to us? All things have passed away as a shadow” (Wis. V, 3 ff.). “He shall gnash his teeth” in punishments, because there “shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. VIII, 12). There is, indeed, a twofold punishment of hell, namely fire and cold, as it is written: “They shall pass from snowy waters to excessive heat” (Job XXIV, 19). He mentioned weeping because of the smoke of the fire, and gnashing of teeth because of the cold. Scripture customarily expresses openly those matters in which there is some uncertainty. No one doubts that there is fire in hell; therefore it did not mention this. But because it was uncertain whether there was cold there, it said on account of the cold: “He shall gnash his teeth”; and amid these punishments he shall waste away, that is, fail. Then sinners’ desire shall wholly perish: the desire of possessing riches, the desire of ruling, and the desire then to have glory with the saints shall perish. When they are cast into outer darkness for eternal punishment, then the righteous shall go into eternal life.

[Col. 0706A] Since all darkness is inward, not outward, it is asked what outer darkness is. It should be understood that the Lord, who is Spirit, spoke to the inner man, that is, to the spirit. Bodily light, shared by us with living creatures, is this sun, or any light proceeding from the moon, stars, or fire; darkness is the absence of light. For the sun, when present, makes day; when absent, night. Spiritual light, however, is God, the sun of righteousness, who is love, as it is written: “God is love” (I John IV, 8). And again: “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (I John I, 5). This light is wisdom, the true light of souls and angels, not of beasts; its vision is understanding. Therefore, just as sea, land, and all things in them appear more pleasing if they are [Col. 0706B] illuminated by light, so all spiritual things are more glorious if illumined by eternal light. Worldly darkness, however, is hatred and ignorance. For one who hates his brother is written to be in darkness. The devil has advanced exceedingly in hatred and persecutes the entire human race in hatred; therefore he himself and the demons are called darkness. Thus humans full of envy, imitators of devils, empty of the light of the Holy Spirit, are darkness, as it is said: “Ye were darkness” (Eph. V, 8); but demons are outer darkness—that is, worse than human beings in hatred and malice. Hence the Lord will say at judgment: “Go into everlasting fire, which was prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41), as though He said: By imitating the devil you are darkness; depart from Me, the light, into that punishment [Col. 0706C] which has been prepared for you and for outer darkness—that is, beings worse than you. Otherwise: the sinful soul is inner darkness; the corruptible body is outer darkness. Therefore the sinful spirit is sent into outer darkness when it is thrust into the fire prepared for bodies.

It should be noted that the first psalm of the first decade and the first psalm of the twelfth decade begin in the same way, “Blessed is the man,” because both proclaim blessedness: the former, blessedness lost; the latter, blessedness promised. The former is consecrated by unity, because the one God in Christ taught the human race the law of love; but the latter is dedicated by the number twelve, because the apostolic order taught the same law throughout the world, which the psalm of this decade, [Col. 0706D] “Blessed are the undefiled” (Ps. CXVIII, 1), fully expounds. In the former it is said: “His delight is in the law of the Lord” (Ps. I, 2); in this one: “He shall delight greatly in His commandments.” In the former: “The Lord knoweth the way of the righteous” (ibid., 6); in this one: “The generation of the righteous shall be blessed.” In the former: “The way of the ungodly shall perish”; in this one: “The desire of sinners shall perish,” because those who meditate on the Lord’s Law day and night are rewarded with eternal blessedness, while the wicked are condemned.

## PSALM CXII. On the humiliation of the saints

[Col. 0705]

[Col. 0705D] “Praise the Lord, ye children,” etc. The preceding psalm [Col. 0706D] concerned those who fear God and relieve the needy; this one [Col. 0707A] concerns the humble and those who despise the world. This psalm occupies the one hundred and twelfth place, because he who imitates the twelve apostles shall receive a hundredfold. Its title is:

**ALLELUIA.**

That is: Praise the Lord. Its subject is the humility of the righteous. Its purpose is to invite us to humility, so that we may attain exaltation. Its words are taken from Hannah’s song, which she sang concerning her son Samuel against her rival, in which it is written: “Raising up the needy from the dust, and lifting up the poor from the dungheap, that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory” (I Kings II, 8); because the Lord raised Samuel from humble stock and placed him, as judge of the people and prophet, with the princes Saul and David. Samuel, whose name means “God,” signifies Christ, whose name is God, whom the Father raised from the earth—that is, from the tomb—and placed in heaven with the princes, that is, with the angels, who are called princes. He raised up the Christian people, poor in spirit, from the dungheap of sins, and set them with the princes of the people, that is, with the apostles. Hannah, whose name means “grace,” bears the type of the Church, which, long barren, bore many spiritual children. Her rival, the synagogue, was weakened in childbearing and therefore cast out, while the mother of spiritual children was chosen for joy.

This psalm has two parts. One is: “Praise the Lord, ye children,” in which Christ’s praise is preached throughout the whole world; the other: “Who is like unto the Lord?” in which His divinity is glorified above the heights of heaven. It should be known that, just as the psalm title “Unto the end” was understood in various ways, so “Alleluia” is placed in titles for very different reasons. At times God is praised because someone escapes danger at sea; at times because he avoids his enemies’ snares; at times because He grants him money, some dignity, learning, or another gift. It is the voice of the apostles to the faithful converted from the Gentiles.

**VERSE 1.** “Praise the Lord, ye children,” who, under the devil’s captivity, had grown old in vices and sins in the old man, but, clothed with the new man in baptism, become children through faith and action. *Puer* (“child”) is said from purity. [Col. 0707D] These are the children who are humble, simple, without malice, pure in chastity and cleanness; such children shall possess the kingdom of God. O you such children, praise the Lord with devotion, mouth, and work. Praise the Lord’s name by obeying the Lord as servants. They praise the Lord’s name—that is, “Lord”—who extol His power and submit themselves to His commandments.

[Col. 0708A] **VERSE 2.** “Blessed be the name of the Lord” by you in faith and affection, from the time when you have recognized His lordship, both now in the present and unto the age—that is, to the end of life—and in the life to come; because not in Judea only, but:

**VERSE 3.** “From the rising of the sun unto its setting, the name of the Lord is praiseworthy”; therefore praise Him from east to west. Or, praise the Lord from childhood to death. And rightly ought you to praise Him, because:

**VERSE 4.** “The Lord is high above all nations”: that is, this Lord is mighty above all nations, and His glory is above the heavens—that is, He is glorious above all angels. For:

**VERSE 5.** “Who is like unto the Lord our God?” That is, who is like Him who is Lord of all and God of the universe, who has beneath Himself all nations and all angels? No one. This is the Lord “who dwelleth on high,” that is, in contemplative persons, and works every good thing in the exalted places, both in angels and in human beings.

**VERSE 6.** “And looketh upon lowly things,” that is, He chooses the humble in the active life. I mean lowly things existing in heaven and on earth, that is, those who live among spiritual and bodily things. For the saints sometimes dwell in heaven by contemplation, and sometimes remain on earth through action. God despises the proud and regards the humble, because He is:

**VERSE 7.** “Raising the needy from the earth,” that is, the Gentile [Col. 0708C] people, needy of another’s aid, freeing them from earthly deeds and turning them to spiritual things; and raising from the dungheap of idolatry or vices the poor in spirit—that is, the humble Christian people—to heavenly things. For what purpose?

**VERSE 8.** “That He may place him with princes, with the princes of His people,” that is, with the apostles at judgment, or with the angels in heaven. For there is an order among angels called principalities. Hence it is written of Michael: “Prince of the heavenly host.” Truly He shall place there those who praise Him:

**VERSE 9.** “Who maketh the barren woman dwell in a house,” that is, He will make that soul which was formerly barren of good works dwell in the heavenly house, as Hannah in her husband’s house; a rejoicing mother of children, [Col. 0708D] that is, fruitful in good works in eternal joy. He made the Gentile people, long barren, dwell in the house of the Church as mother of many spiritual children, namely martyrs, confessors, and other faithful people, rejoicing in the multitude of those born and in the dowry of spiritual gifts and in the future inheritance of joys.

## PSALM CXIII. On renunciations of the world

[Col. 0707]

[Col. 0707D] “When Israel went out of Egypt,” etc. In this decade a certain order of Christian religion is woven together. For in [Col. 0708D] the title of the first psalm the return of captives to Jerusalem is related, and the conversion to faith of the faithful is understood; as catechumens, they are taught in the text of the psalm the fear of God, through which they are admonished to turn from evil and do good. In the second, they are exorcized as children about to be baptized, when, made children in Christ, they are urged to praise God. In the third, baptism is represented when the people are recalled as led through the Red Sea or through the Jordan. This psalm treats of those who renounce idolatry and, already baptized, provoke others still unbelieving to faith by their example. It also treats of those who renounce the world and, already converted, exhort others still worldly to conversion by their example. Its title is:

**ALLELUIA.**

That is: Praise the Lord because He has called you from [Col. 0709B] darkness into His wonderful light. This psalm is the one hundred and thirteenth, which is eleven times ten plus three, and signifies that those belonging to the eleven of transgression return to the ten of the Law in faith in the Trinity.

Its subject is those who renounce the world. Its purpose is that we may renounce the world, vices, and desires, so that we may be blessed with the righteous. The words of the psalm are taken from the history in which the people, leaving Egypt, went to the promised land; it signifies the faithful who leave the world through conversion and hasten toward the homeland of Paradise.

This psalm is divided into five parts, as a human being is distinguished by five senses. The first part [Col. 0709C] is: “When Israel went out,” in which the Church’s departure from worldly to spiritual things is described. The second is: “What aileth thee, O thou sea?” in which Gentiles converted to the faith and faithful persons converted to monastic life are mystically shown. The third is: “The idols of the nations,” in which idols are mocked and their worshippers condemned. The fourth is: “House of Israel,” in which the orders of the righteous are selected. The fifth is: “The Lord hath been mindful of us,” in which blessing is received from the Lord. This psalm is like a pomegranate which, when its rind is removed, tastes sweet; so too, when its historical sense is removed, it distils sweet honey. As many verses, so many graces; as many words, so many fruits of the soul are in it. It is the voice of the Holy Spirit.

VERS. 1–2. “When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob [Col. 0709D] from a barbarous people: Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion.” This is understood literally as follows: after the people of Israel went out of Egypt, it possessed the Temple of sanctification in Judah, and the kingdom in Israel. Judah was the land possessed by the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, in which Jerusalem and the Temple stood; but the land of the ten tribes was called Israel.

This is connected with the preceding psalm in this way: You children, reborn in Christ from wickedness, praise the Lord, at whose departure—that is, at the setting out of the people of Israel from Egypt—Judah became sanctification, that is, holy worship in Judah; and whose dominion the people Israel became at the departure—that is, at the setting out—of the house of Jacob, that is, Jacob’s family, from a barbarous people. A barbarous people is one of another [Col. 0710A] language; such was the Egyptian people in relation to the Hebrew people. And when was this? Then, when:

VERS. 3. The sea saw that Moses was coming with the people—that is, when it understood the will of the Creator—and fled, because it drew back its waves within itself and offered the people a path through its midst. Likewise Jordan saw the people coming and turned backward, because its upper part stood like a wall, and the incoming water rose high like a mountain; while its lower part flowed down into the sea, and the people crossed on dry feet. Then the mountains and hills leapt, said to have leapt because they flowered at the presence of the ark of the Lord. This is understood spiritually as follows:

Egypt is said to mean “darkness” or “affliction,” and signifies the world, full of the darkness of ignorance and the affliction [Col. 0710B] of cares. Israel means “one seeing God,” and signifies the spiritual people, namely the contemplative. The barbarous people are the unbelievers or vices. “Barbarian” is said to derive from *barba* (“beard”) and *urbs* (“city”), because he has never dwelt in a city but always, like a beast, in the field. Jacob means “supplanter” or “wrestler,” and signifies the active people overthrowing vices and wrestling against sins. Judah means “confession” or “praise,” and signifies the Church praising God by confessing him.

Therefore, those go out from Egypt and pass through the Red Sea to their homeland who come from the darkness of unbelief through baptism to the Church. Those go out from the barbarous people who abandon the worshippers of idols, and thus become Judah, that is, confession of God. And this Judah became God’s sanctification, while he is sanctified in such a people, because he is believed holy by those who live [Col. 0710C] holily. Thus this people becomes Jacob, that is, supplanting vices and wrestling against sins; it becomes Judah through confession of sins; it becomes sanctification through remission of sins; and it also becomes Israel, seeing God through understanding of the faith, in which will be God’s dominion, because Christ’s kingdom will be in the house of Jacob forever, “and of his kingdom,” which is Israel, “there will be no end” (Luke 1:33).

Alternatively: those go out from Egypt who abandon worldly cares and leave the age. Those go out from the barbarous people who separate themselves from the blasphemies of the nations, or renounce vices. These are Jews, praising God; they are Israelites, contemplating God in the mind.

Alternatively: “When Israel went out of Egypt,” that is, when [Col. 0710D] spiritual persons go out from carnal persons, and when the house of Jacob goes out from a barbarous people, that is, when those who do good works go out from vices and sins, Judah came to be—that is, confession of sins—his sanctification, namely of Israel, that is, of the spiritual people, who are sanctified through confession; and Israel, that is, spiritual understanding, became his power against demons. The sea saw all this and fled; Jordan turned backward. By the sea is understood the Gentile world; by Jordan, Christianity, because the Lord was baptized in Jordan. Thus the sea—that is, the Gentile world—saw the Israelites leaving Egypt, that is, the apostles seeing God, coming out from the dark nation of the Jews, living in confession and holiness, powerful in signs and wonders; and it fled from unbelief to faith. And Jordan, [Col. 0711A] that is, the baptized people, turned back, following Christ behind him, following his footsteps rather than the world.

Alternatively: Jordan, which is interpreted “their descent,” signifies those who, coming to baptism, saw martyrs suffering many persecutions; turning back, they descended into the sea, that is, into the Gentile world, and denied Christ. That sea is called the Dead Sea, into which Jordan disappears, because those who, apostatizing from faith, relapse into faithlessness die in soul. Afterwards Jordan turned backward, because many, doing penance, were converted to Christ. The part of Jordan which stood higher up and rose aloft signifies those who persevere after baptism in faith and works and rise through virtues toward heaven; that part which flowed into the Dead Sea [Col. 0711B] signifies those who, denying faith and works, descend into the sea—that is, into the death of perdition.

Alternatively: the sea—that is, the worldly people made bitter by the cares of the age—saw Israelites, that is, spiritual persons departing from the world, and fled from the age to the haven of holy conduct. And Jordan—that is, the people descending into vices—saw Jacob going out from the barbarous people, that is, the active people withdrawing from vices, and turned backward to repentance. Seeing this:

VERS. 4. The mountains, that is, the apostles, leapt, because they were like rams, namely leaders of God’s flock. And seeing this, the hills, that is, the teachers, leapt; they were like lambs of sheep, that is, begotten through the Gospel [Col. 0711C] by those very rams. For the apostles, mountains lofty in virtues, rejoiced at the conversion of the Gentiles. Likewise the hills, namely disciples of the apostles such as Dionysius, Timothy, and others of that sort, rejoiced at the conversion of sinners. Here the voice of the unbelievers is introduced.

VERS. 5. “What is the matter with you, O sea, that you fled?” As though they said: O Gentile people, what is the cause that you flee the world? “And you, O Jordan, why did you turn backward?” That is to say: And you, baptized people, tell what cause there is that so many thousands throughout the whole world are converted each day to a better life.

VERS. 6. “Mountains, you leapt like rams”: that is, what is the cause that you preachers rejoice so greatly as leaders of the flock? And for what reason did you, hills, [Col. 0711D] that is, teachers, leap like lambs of sheep—that is, why did you rejoice that you were sons of rams?

The sea replies: I fled because the voice of thunder frightened me, saying: “The world will pass away, and its desire; the wicked will perish from it, and the wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.” Jordan replies: I turned back because a dreadful voice rang out from the clouds: “Repent, for the axe is laid at the root of the tree: every tree which does not bear good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3:2, 10). The mountains and hills reply: We leapt because we convert the nations; for this labor, at the end of the age it will be said to us: “Come, ye blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34), and [Col. 0712A] then we shall enter the joy of the Lord and be set over all his goods. Therefore we leap, because:

VERS. 7. “At the presence of the Lord the earth was moved”: that is, the Gentile world was moved from ignorance—that is, by the face, presence, or knowledge of the Lord—from idolatry; by the face, that is, the knowledge, of God, not of a recent god, but of the God of Jacob, that is, the one worshipped by Jacob.

VERS. 8. This God turned the rock into pools of water, and the crag into fountains of waters. This is drawn from the history in which he brought water forth from the rock. He used “waters” twice because he twice brought water out of the flint. Moreover, the earth was moved when the Lord descended from Sinai. Christ was the rock (1 Cor. 10:4), because his teaching seemed hard to some, who said: “This saying is hard” (John 6:61). This rock was [Col. 0712B] turned into pools when, after the twofold striking of the cross, rising again he opened their understanding and expounded to them all the Scriptures of the prophets. He turned the crag into fountains of waters when he sent the Holy Spirit and gave them knowledge of all languages.

The pools of waters are the Scriptures of the prophets. He turned the rock into pools when he taught that Christ is to be understood in the prophets. The fountains of waters are the writings of the apostles. He turned the crag into fountains when he willed Christ to be known in the teaching of the apostles, who, as fountains, say to God:

VERS. 1. “Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us; but give glory to thy name.” That is: Let it not be ascribed to us that peoples drink from us; but to you, the rock from which we flow. Not to us, but give glory to your name, because the nations are converted to faith. Give glory [Col. 0712C] to your name:

VERS. 2. “For thy mercy and thy truth,” so that all nations may know themselves redeemed through you, God’s mercy, and the prophecies fulfilled through you, the truth; lest the nations at any time say, “Where is their God?” That is: so that those nations which now say, “Where is their God?” may at some time cease to say, “Where is their God?” We see this today: although the nations do not believe, they nevertheless do not dare to ask this, because they see the Church glorious and enlarged. But formerly they used to insult Christians, saying: Show us your God, just as we show you our gods. And they point with a finger to a stone, or wood, or some metal, or the sun, or moon, or stars.

[Col. 0712C] VERS. 3. But our God is in heaven and cannot be shown with a finger.

It is asked: since God is everywhere, how is he said to be in heaven? Is he there in substance but everywhere in power? Or is he at one time in heaven and at another on earth? God’s power is the same as his essence, for his nature is truth, which is wholly present everywhere. The saints are called heaven; in this heaven our God is, because he dwells more familiarly in the saints, although Christ our God is said to be bodily in the material heaven.

Their gods can do nothing; but our God in heaven made all things whatsoever he willed—that is, whatever pleased him, he made through his heavens. What follows is spoken [Col. 0713A] for the correction of the Gentiles, in order to draw them back from idolatry.

VERS. 4. “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands.” He did not say, “The gods of the nations,” but “idols,” because they are lifeless. And although they have idols of stone or bronze, he named those of gold and silver because of their excellence, so that if those more precious things are not to be worshipped, much less are the less valuable. And these are works of human hands, that is, manufactured by human beings. Those idols:

VERS. 5, 6, 7. “They have mouths, and shall not speak; they have eyes, and shall not see. They have ears, and shall not hear; nostrils, and shall not smell. They have hands, and shall not touch; feet, and shall not walk; they shall not cry out through their throat.”

[Col. 0713B] It is as though he said: beasts are better than those idols, for they see, hear, walk, and give voice, insofar as they live; but idols indeed seem to possess limbs, yet do not use them, insofar as they do not live. Note that he said, “through their throat,” because a beast has in its mouth the same kind of voice that it has in its throat. A human being is not so: his voice, confusedly formed in the throat, is shaped in the mouth and becomes articulate speech.

VERS. 8. “May those who make them become like them in the inward man,” so that they neither see nor understand God—those who make them with the intention of worshipping them—and may all who trust in them, that is, all who hope for help from them, become like them, without perception. This is not said as the wish of one cursing, but as the declaration of one preaching. Therefore, since idols are mute and deaf—indeed, devoid of life—they are not to be worshipped. [Col. 0713C] Hope is not to be placed in them but in the Lord, because:

VERS. 9, 10. The house of Israel hoped in the Lord, not in idols; therefore he is their helper and their protector. He was their helper when he delivered them from Egypt; he was their protector when he sheltered them with a cloud on the journey and defended them from enemies. Likewise, the house of Aaron hoped in the Lord, not in idols; and therefore he was their helper for doing good and their protector from evils. The house of Israel was the people of the twelve tribes; the house of Aaron was the tribe of Levi. By the house of Israel are understood subjects; by the house of Aaron, who was high priest, prelates, who hoped not in such gods but in the Lord and were delivered. Or the house of Israel consists of all believers hastening to see God; [Col. 0713D] the house of Aaron—Aaron means “mountain of strength”—consists of priests strong against vices. All of these hope in the Lord, who is their helper and protector. And both these and those:

VERS. 11. “Who fear the Lord have hoped in the Lord,” not in idols. He is their helper in [Col. 0714A] good things and their protector from evils. And when he delivered the children of Israel:

VERS. 12. “The Lord was mindful of us,” because he gave them a shadow, but preserved the truth for us, to whom he sent his Son in the flesh, who delivered us from the yoke of the devil and blessed us with every spiritual blessing. Or he was mindful of us by giving faith and remission of sins, and blessed us by raising us in virtues. He blessed the house of Israel, that is, he multiplied subjects in faith and works. He blessed the house of Aaron, that is, he filled prelates with various charisms.

VERS. 13. He blessed all who fear the Lord, the small with the great, by giving faith and love. This was the voice of the fountains flowing from the rock. There follows the voice of those drinking from them, believing in Christ:

[Col. 0714B] VERS. 14. “May the Lord add unto you.” That is: O preachers, the Lord placed you as precious stones in the foundation of his building, and placed other teachers upon you; may he still add other believers, to be placed upon you. Or may the Lord, who blessed in many ways, add blessings upon you and upon your children, that is, upon your imitators.

VERS. 15. “Blessed are you by the Lord”: that is, you who are set in the Lord’s blessing, he who made heaven and earth—that is, who made you: heaven in the great, earth in the small. There follows the voice of the Holy Spirit.

VERS. 16. “The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord.” The heaven of heaven is the firmament, the heaven of this airy heaven, because these are illuminated by it and the earth is rained upon from the airy heaven. The higher heaven is the apostolic order, which the Father [Col. 0714C] gave to the Lord the Son to adorn, and which he adorned with the sun of wisdom, the moon of eloquence, and the stars of signs or virtues. The lower heaven is the order of teachers—such as Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and Gregory—which is illuminated by the higher heaven, because teachers are enlightened by apostolic teaching. But he gave the earth to the children of men to cultivate. This earth, that is, the Church, is rained upon by the airy heaven—that is, irrigated by the teachers, who are children of men, namely of the apostles living rationally. There follows the voice of the children of men cultivating the earth.

VERS. 17. “The dead in soul shall not praise you, O Lord, nor all who descend into hell,” that is, into the depth of vices. This is said of those who remain in grave sins after [Col. 0714D] baptism. Not they:

VERS. 18. “But we who live in the inward man bless the Lord,” that is, praise the Lord in heart, mouth, and work, from the time when we received his faith, and now in the present age, “unto eternity,” that is, as long as we live, or without end.

## PSALM CXIV. On the Tribulation of the Martyrs

[Col. 0713]

[Col. 0713D] “I have loved, because the Lord will hear,” etc. This psalm occupies the one hundred and fourteenth position [Col. 0714D] and indicates the perfection of both laws. For the number one hundred indicates perfection; ten, the old law [Col. 0715A] because of the Decalogue; four, the new law because of the four Gospels. This number signifies that observers of both laws will receive a perfect reward. Its title is:

ALLELUIA.

That is: Praise the Lord. The subject of the psalm is God’s grace. Its intention is to invite us to love and praise God for the reason that he hears those who call upon him and delivers them from present tribulation and future death. Its words seem drawn from Hezekiah, whom the pains of death surrounded; he called upon the Lord, who inclined his ear to him in sickness and delivered his soul from death, because he pleased him in the land of the living. It signifies fallen humanity, surrounded by the pains of death, which called upon the Lord because of these pains; he inclined the ear of mercy to it in its weakness, because, descending from heaven, he visited it and delivered its soul from eternal death. [Col. 0715B] This psalm is like a cock which compels us to come to the works of the faithful.

It has two parts. One is: “I have loved, because,” in which the faithful person gives thanks because the Lord delivered him from the dangers of death. The other is: “O Lord, deliver my soul,” in which he asks that his soul be delivered from eternal death and placed in the land of the living. It is the voice of the Son, who was dead and lived again, who was lost and found; or of the sheep that had wandered, which the good shepherd found and made his bride.

VERS. 1. “I have loved”: because the Lord has now blessed all, [Col. 0715C] the small together with the great, as he promised Abraham: “In thy seed,” which is Christ, “all nations shall be blessed.” Therefore you all, blessed by the Lord and baptized, love the Lord after my example, for I have loved him. And he deserves to be loved because he first loved us and gave himself for us. To love God is to fulfill his commandments; for whoever loves has fulfilled the law. I, a lost sheep but now made a bride, have loved the bridegroom, the Lord, in heart and work, because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer—that is, whatever I ask of him, he will do. So you too love him, and he will hear your prayer. Therefore I have loved:

VERS. 2. “Because he inclined his ear to me,” that is, his ear, his mercy, to me in my weakness: descending from heaven to one left half-dead by robbers, driving away pain and restoring health. Therefore in my days I will call upon—understand: him. That is, as long as I live I shall pray to him; and this in the days which, by sinning in the first man, I made my own, days in which I am afflicted by misery and distress. For in these days:

VERS. 3. “The pains of death surrounded me,” that is, mortality and passibility, which cause a human being to die, enclosed me; “and the perils of hell found me,” that is, the temptations of mortal sins, which were seeking me, found me and lead to hell. Or the pains of death are evil thoughts; the perils of hell are wicked actions. These, seeking me, found me consenting to them [Col. 0716A] and following them as they drew me to hell. “And I found tribulation and sorrow”: that is, I sought penitence that would afflict me, and found bodily pain for myself, so that I might escape the punishments of hell. Or in those days I sought honors and riches, and found tribulation and sorrow, because they are full of cares and fear.

VERS. 4. “And I called upon the name of the Lord,” that he might deliver me. The name of the Lord is the Lord. I called upon the Lord’s power, saying: “O Lord, deliver my soul,” that is, I pray, Lord, that you may deliver my soul from tribulation and sorrow. Note that he says, “Deliver my soul,” and does not say, “Deliver my body,” because he suffers this tribulation in the inward man. This “O” is not vocative but optative. For in Hebrew [Col. 0716B] there stands *Anna*, meaning “I pray” or “I desire.” Neither Greek nor Latin speech could translate this properly. I called upon him, and:

VERS. 5. The merciful and righteous Lord delivered me. The construction is as follows, for other matters intervene: he who is merciful inclined his ear to me in my weakness—which was the act of one merciful; because he is Lord, he delivered me—which the Lord was able to do; because he is righteous, he heard me calling upon him—which he ought to do. And he is our God, that is, the God of the humble; therefore he has mercy upon such persons. For the Lord is:

VERS. 6. “Preserving the little ones,” that is, the humble, who through conversion become little ones without deceit and without wickedness, of whom it is said: “Of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19). Considering this, I was humbled [Col. 0716C] before him, or afflicted for sins, and he delivered me from tribulation—that is, from the sins for which I suffer distress—by forgiving them in actuality; and from sorrow—that is, mortality and passibility—in hope. Therefore, O my soul, turned away from worldly things:

VERS. 7. “Return to thy rest,” that is, to Christ, who is your true rest, who said: “Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29). Or turn from the labor of this exile through humility to the rest of paradise, where your rest is. Care no longer about earthly things; seek heavenly things, because the Lord has dealt kindly with you: he delivered you from the tribulation of sins and the sorrow of punishments, and restored the lost [Col. 0716D] rest of paradise. And therefore I rightly loved the Lord:

VERS. 8. “Because he delivered my soul from death, and my eyes from tears,” that is, from punishments which force out tears, “and my feet from falling,” that is, my affections from the will to sin, for which the punishments of death are inflicted. Or he delivered my soul from death, that is, from temptation, which is the cause of death; and my eyes from groaning by this, that he will deliver my feet—that is, my affections—from sins which are the cause of groaning. By this I know that:

VERS. 9. “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living,” that is, in eternal glory, where there will be only living persons and from which they will no longer be exiles. He did not say, “I please,” but “I shall please,” because no one, while placed in this mortal flesh, perfectly pleases God [Col. 0717A] in the land of the living. But when this mortal shall have put on immortality, and it no longer delights one to sin, then the righteous shall perfectly please [Col. 0718A] in the land of the living, when they shall shine like the sun and be equal to angels.

## PSALM CXV. On the Confession of the Martyrs

[Col. 0717]

[Col. 0717B] VERS. 10. “I believed; therefore I spoke,” etc. This psalm is placed in the one hundred and fifteenth position, signifying that for the faithful, amid fullness of joys, the denarius of life is repaid for the expenditure of the five senses. This psalm and the preceding one are reckoned as one in Hebrew, but are divided into two by the Seventy Interpreters. Its title is:

ALLELUIA.

That is, Praise the Lord for the land of the living which has been given. Its subject is the confession of martyrs. Its intention is to exhort us to suffer for Christ, so that our death may become precious. The words are said to be drawn from David himself, who fulfilled his vows to the Lord before all the people when he offered the expenses for the Temple in the courts of the Lord’s house, in the midst of Jerusalem. It signifies the people [Col. 0717C] of martyrs, strong in suffering, who fulfilled their vows before kings and princes when they confessed the Lord before all the people and offered themselves as living stones, to be prepared through bodily torments for the building of the Lord’s house.

It has two sections. One is “I believed,” in which the martyrs drink the cup of salvation; the other is “O Lord,” in which they offer a sacrifice of praise and fulfill their vows in Jerusalem. This is Alleluia: the voice of the faithful, the speech of the blessed, the holy melody of those who sing, the definition of hearing, the delight of the soul. It is the voice of martyrs.

I believed that Christ the Lord was born of the Virgin, suffered for our redemption, rose from death, ascended into heaven, and will come [Col. 0717D] for judgment. Therefore I spoke these things: that is, because I believed these things perfectly, I also preached them to others. “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10), as it is written: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father” (Matt. 10:32). Those who love human glory more than God’s, or who fear or are ashamed to confess Christ before people, have no share in the kingdom of Christ and God. But I believed in Christ, confessed him with my mouth before people, and because of this faith and confession I shall please the Lord in the land of the living. Those living in this land of the living have been greatly exalted, but I, still mortal, have been humbled exceedingly—that is, greatly cast down amid transitory things, exceedingly oppressed by evils. Or because [Col. 0718B] I confessed Christ publicly, I was humbled, that is, greatly afflicted, indeed beyond my strength. Or the truth which I confessed cannot be humbled; but I have been exceedingly humbled in labors. Truth desires to be publicly preached, but:

VERS. 11. “I said in the excess of my mind: Every man is a liar,” and therefore may be changed from his purpose. “Excess of mind” is understood in two ways: when the mind is carried away either by fear or by the inspiration of some revelation. Here it is used for fear, which human weakness suffers under the threat of torture or death. I had indeed resolved to confess Christ publicly; but, considering in my mind that people are easily recalled from their purpose through fear of torture, I said in fear: “Every man is a liar,” [Col. 0718C] and therefore, since I am a man, I may lie by failing to fulfill what I proposed—so that through fear, like Peter, I might deny the truth. In Hebrew there is: “Every man is falsehood,” that is, in this life every human being is shadow and image, not truth. Every person is a liar through sinning, truthful by God’s gift. When I trembled in human frailty before the torments proposed, considering God’s benefits, I said:

VERS. 12. “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” For my evils he rendered many goods. What, even one thing, shall I render for all these things? But what one thing shall I render to him? He does not say, “What things shall I render?” And when I found nothing in myself that I could render him for such great goods, I said:

[Col. 0718D] VERS. 13. “I will take the cup of salvation,” that is, I will drink the draught of Jesus; that is, I will die for his cause. Of this cup he himself said: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20:22). Again he says of it: “Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, thy will be done” (ibid., 26:42). He filled this cup when he drank from the torrent in the way. By “I will take,” he means: I will come to martyrdom not unwillingly, but voluntarily. For it does not otherwise profit one to die for the faith, unless it is done willingly. Or, “I will take the cup of salvation,” that is, I will undergo the passion which gives salvation to my soul. The comparison is to one who drinks a bitter potion because of illness and through it gains health. But because I do not presume upon my own strength, since every man is a liar, I will call upon the Lord’s name, that he may himself [Col. 0719A] help me by giving constancy. And through his help:

VERS. 14. “I will render my vows to the Lord before all his people.” That is, what I resolved—to confess him publicly—and what I promised—to receive the cup of suffering—I shall fulfill by his aid in the presence of all the faithful, so that they too may do likewise after my example. But someone will say: It is shameful for anyone to die before people in the manner of thieves or robbers. Against this is added:

VERS. 15. “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.” What concern is it what a person says—what rot is? [Note: [Col. 0719D] Codex Genmicensis: *qui est pulr.* (“which is pulr.”; final word uncertain).] That death is dear to God which someone suffers for his sake, in holiness: “But the death of sinners is worst” (Ps. 33 [Vulgate], [Col. 0719B] 22). The Lord suffered for his servant; therefore the servant ought rightly to suffer for the Lord.

VERS. 16. “O Lord”: that is, I desire, Lord, that this may happen in me. In Hebrew there is, “I pray, Lord”—understand: that I may do as I promised—because I am your servant, obedient to your commands in confession; I am your servant in work, and the son of your handmaid, that is, an imitator of the Catholic Church, which is now a handmaid serving her mistress, who is truth; afterwards she will be free when eternal inheritance receives her. Many are servants of the Lord who are not sons of the handmaid, as are the devil and all evil people. For all serve the Lord. “Because you have broken my bonds,” that is, because you delivered me from sins.

[Col. 0719C] VERS. 17. “To thee I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise”: that is, I shall offer myself in sacrifice to your praise, and call upon the Lord’s name for help. It is said that these three verses—namely “Precious,” “O Lord,” and “You have broken”—have such power that, if they are recited as a third confession at the end of life, through them all sins are forgiven. Sins are the bonds of the soul. Just as, [Col. 0720A] to make a chain, link is joined to link, so crime is joined to crime, producing the bond by which the sinner is bound, as it is written: “Each person is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. 5:22). By these bonds sinners’ hands and feet will be bound at the end, when they are cast into outer darkness. Or: you broke the bonds of mortality and passibility, by which I was bound in the prison of the body, and you wove the crown of victory with fragrant flowers of paradise. Therefore I shall sacrifice to you; and where? In the land of the living. What? A sacrifice of praise: I offer soul and body to your praise. “Blessed are those who dwell in thy house; for ever and ever they shall praise thee.” There:

VERS. 18. “I will render my vows to the Lord in the sight [Col. 0720B] of all his people.” That is, on the day of judgment I shall present to the Lord the works I vowed in words, in the presence of all angels and people—I, I say, to be placed as a precious stone:

VERS. 19. “In the courts,” that is, in the spaciousness of God’s heavenly house, and not in the lowest place, but “in the midst of thee, O Jerusalem,” city of God, namely in the more honorable place where martyrs are to be placed. The earlier verse, “I will render my vows,” concerns fulfilling vows in suffering; the following verse, “I will render my vows,” concerns presenting to the Lord my fulfilled vows for reward. The vows of the faithful are that in baptism we renounce the devil, his works, and his pomps, and endeavor to serve God. Some vow continence, some abstinence, [Col. 0720C] some renounce the world and profess the monastic life. We must fulfill these vows in this life if we desire to sacrifice a sacrifice of praise in Jerusalem. If we do not render them, we shall not be stones in the building of the Lord’s house. Therefore this psalm is sung on martyrs’ feasts, because they drank the cup of suffering.

## PSALM CXVI. On the Praise of God

[Col. 0719]

[Col. 0719D] “Praise the Lord, all nations,” etc. In this psalm all nations are invited to the praise of God, because the house of the Lord in heavenly Jerusalem is built from all nations. Its title is:

ALLELUIA.

That is: Praise the Lord because he chose living stones from every people and set them in the building of his house. This psalm occupies the one hundred and sixteenth position and indicates three orders [Col. 0720D] in the Church. The hundredfold number represents virgins, who bear a hundredfold fruit; ten represents widows laboring in the Decalogue; six represents married persons toiling in the six works of the Gospel. All of them complete the heavenly building.

The subject of the psalm is the praise of God. Its intention is to exhort all faithful persons, both Jews and Gentiles, to a good life, which is God’s praise. Its words are drawn from David, who praised the Lord when he fulfilled his vows [Col. 0721A] to the Lord by offering gifts for making the Lord’s house in Jerusalem. It signifies the people of the faithful, who fulfill to the Lord the vows promised in baptism.

Note: In the psalm “I Will Confess,” the Prophet admonished the faithful by his own example; in “Blessed Is the Man,” by the example of others; in “Praise, Children,” faithful Gentiles only, by the second person; in “When Israel Went Out,” unbelievers through the conversion of others, or those faithful people who lived in a time of peace; in “I Have Loved,” he admonishes those already advanced in faith to perfect love; in “I Believed,” martyrs exhort others to martyrdom by their example. In this psalm the Prophet admonishes all, Jews and Gentiles alike, to God’s praise. From them is built the city of the great King, in which nothing else is done but that the creator is praised [Col. 0721B] by citizens, the king by soldiers. Therefore this psalm is written in two verses, because that structure is completed by two walls, joined by two Testaments, and bound together by the two commands of love. The psalm is divided into four parts, and this building is portrayed by four virtues, four Gospels, and four Evangelists. It is the voice of those rendering vows in Jerusalem:

VERS. 1. “Praise the Lord, all nations,” namely with mouth, heart, and work—you who, abandoning idols, came to him through faith. Matthew portrays this passage, writing that the three Magi offered gifts to the Lord, and by their faith represented all nations. Praise him, all peoples of the Jews converted to our King in faith and love. [Col. 0721C] John portrays this passage, writing that a title was placed upon the cross, on which was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: “King of the Jews.” You nations praise him therefore:

[Col. 0722A] VERS. 2. “For his mercy has been strengthened over us who believe,” through which, having mercy on us, he delivered us from idolatry. This mercy will be firm because each day he forgives sins to those who repent. Luke portrays this passage, writing that Christ received sinners and publicans, or that he poured out the Holy Spirit for the remission of sins. And you Jews praise him therefore, because “the truth of the Lord”—that is, the fulfillment of his promise—remains in us forever. Or his truth remains forever in those promises which he made to the godly, when the chosen stones are built together in heavenly Jerusalem; or in those threats which he made against the ungodly, when they are handed over to unquenchable fire and immortal worms, as Mark writes: “Their fire shall not be quenched, and their worms shall not die” (Mark 9:45).

This psalm is called the atom of the psalms, possessing the dignity of a point, from which a line arises and diverse kinds of figures are formed in most learned variety.

Why does this psalm contain only two verses, whereas the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled” has one hundred and seventy-six verses? This is so that, just as harmony—that is, the beautiful modulation of musical power—makes one perfect melody from diverse sounds and accents, so psalms now short, now middling, now long may be brought together into one concord with the sweetest sweetness. Or, because many have been fashioned in differing ways according to the nature of their subjects, it signifies the future kingdom, where the differing merits of the saints will shine according to the quality of their deeds, although one blessedness and eternal delight are bestowed upon all.

[Col. 0722C]

## PSALM 117. On the rejoicing of the martyrs.

[Col. 0721]

[Col. 0721D] “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good,” etc. This psalm is written in the one hundred and seventeenth place; this number is divided into seventy, forty, and seven. By seventy the whole time of our pilgrimage in this world is indicated, since the fathers of old were captives in Babylon for seventy years. By forty our return to our homeland is shown, since the fathers of old returned from Egypt to the land of promise over forty years. By seven the rest to come is understood, because God rested from the works of the world on the seventh day. This number therefore signifies that through confession of Christ we return from pilgrimage to the rest of paradise. Its title is:

ALLELUIA.

That is: Praise the Lord for this, because from the exile of [Col. 0722D] misery he has led you back into the kingdom of glory. Its subject is those who confess God. Its purpose is to exhort us to a confession of praise, so that we may attain eternal exultation. The words are taken from David himself, who made a tabernacle for the Lord, in which he paid his vows to the Lord, sang praise, and whose right hand exalted him. Yet he signifies the faithful people, who make the Catholic Church a tabernacle for the Lord, in which they pay their vows, sing praise to the Lord, and whose right hand will exalt them in glory.

This psalm is divided into four parts, because the Church is gathered from the four parts of the world to heavenly things. The first is, “Give thanks to the Lord,” in which triumphant martyrs praise God. The second, “It is good to trust in the Lord,” in which they enumerate their calamities and God’s benefits. The third, “Open to [Col. 0723A] me,” in which they enter the gates of Jerusalem and are joined to the cornerstone. The fourth is, “Blessed is he who comes,” in which Christ incarnate is worshipped.

This psalm is, as it were, woven with certain lightning-like colors; at its head it has four verses with one ending, representing the four Gospels. And just as that priestly garment, woven with golden threads and scarlet beauty, shone, having bells on its fringes, so this psalm, arranged in splendid variety, contains the holy proclamations of Christ the true high priest; at its beginning, its end, and in differently placed harmonious verses, it rings out with golden fringes and bells like a cymbal.

In the psalm “I believed,” all martyrs, apostles, and their successors spoke, imitating others by their example [Col. 0723B] unto martyrdom. In the psalm “Praise the Lord,” all nations and peoples are invited to the applause of the martyrs’ triumph. In this psalm the triumphant martyrs themselves joyfully sing a hymn to God in the tabernacles of the righteous, placed in the land of the living; there they recall the evils they suffered and God’s benefits. It is the voice of martyrs encouraging one another to praise God.

**VERSE 1.** “Give thanks to the Lord.” O all you who have entered the land of the living through martyrdom, give thanks to the Lord—that is, praise the Lord—for he is good. For no one is good except God alone, who is essentially goodness itself; all other things are good by participation in this good. Give thanks to him, because [Col. 0723C] his mercy is forever, by which he makes the wicked good—those whom he predestined for the eternal kingdom.

**VERSE 2.** “Let Israel now say”—that is, let all the people from the twelve tribes of Israel who suffered for Christ, now established in joy, say to their companions: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever”; by whose goodness and mercy you conquered the world and entered into the joy of the Lord.

**VERSE 3.** “Let the house of Aaron now say.” That is: let all the people from the tribe of Levi, from which Aaron the priest came, who suffered for Christ, now established in joy, say to their companions: “Give thanks to the Lord, [Col. 0723D] for he is good, for his mercy is forever.” Or: let all who have suffered, from clergy and people alike, or from prelates and subjects, praise the Lord.

**VERSE 4.** “Let those who fear the Lord now say”—that is, not only those from among the Jews, but also all from the Gentiles who fear the Lord and have suffered in his fear—let them now, set in joy, say to all their fellow sharers: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever”; by whose goodness and mercy you escaped the evils of the world and gained eternal gladness. These four verses have one ending. Now they recall God’s benefits, for which they praise him. And throughout this whole book it must be noted that everywhere what is primary is placed first, and then the reason is added. Rightly is the [Col. 0724A] Lord to be praised, who is good, merciful, and the hearer of all, because I, the people of martyrs—

**VERSE 5.** From the great tribulation of my sufferings I called upon the Lord, praying that he would free me from tribulation and pain. And the Lord heard me in a broad place, leading me out from the straits of tribulations into the spaciousness of joys. Or: the Lord heard me when I called upon him in tribulation, in that he enlarged me in love, so that I endured torments for his love and loved my torturers. When they said to me, “Sacrifice to the gods, or you will perish under exquisite punishments,” I said:

**VERSE 6.** “The Lord is my helper” amid punishments; I shall not fear what man may do to me. Man is corruption: he can harm the body that will die, but cannot harm the immortal soul. And when they said to me, “If you do not [Col. 0724B] worship the gods, you will have judges and their soldiers as enemies,” I answered:

**VERSE 7.** “The Lord is my helper” against them, and I shall despise my enemies, whether human beings or demons, because through the Lord I shall conquer them by not yielding to them. And when some carnal friend consoled me while I was afflicted, saying, “Trust, for that powerful man will free you,” I said:

**VERSE 8.** “It is good”—that is, it is better—to trust in the Lord, who delivers from eternal death, than to trust in a powerful man or in any saint; for “the salvation of man is vain” (Ps. 59:13), and “Cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jer. 17:5). And when he said, “Hope, for that ruler will rescue you from your enemies,” I replied:

[Col. 0724C] **VERSE 9.** “It is good”—that is, it is better—to hope in the Lord, who grants eternal life, than to hope in rulers, whose power passes away with this world. The two altered words have made an altogether different sense. Above he said “to trust”; here, “to hope.” There, “in man”; here, “in rulers,” so that there he seems to have spoken of carnal persons, here of spiritual ones. Now they recount the evils they suffered from pagans, Jews, heretics, and false Christians. O people of martyrs, from what tribulation did you call upon the Lord? From a great one, because:

**VERSE 10.** “All nations surrounded me” with persecutions; and in the name of the Lord, because I took vengeance upon them, because they were subjected to me. One takes great vengeance when one’s enemy is made subject to him. The martyrs were greatly avenged when persecutors of the faith were subjugated. Or, then they are avenged when their enemies are cruelly punished, as Nero, Decius, and others suffered a horrible punishment after the martyrs’ death. In saying that all nations surrounded him, he shows that the Church is spread through the whole world and suffers evils everywhere from adversaries. In saying “me,” he shows the unity of the Church, because if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. And not only pagans, but also Jews:

**VERSE 11.** “Surrounding, they surrounded me”—that is, they persistently hemmed me in through persecution—yet they could not prevail; and in the name of the Lord [Col. 0725A] I endured these things. For after they had been flogged, “they went from the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41). And this was so because I took vengeance upon them, as many of them were brought under the faith and were made subject to the Christians whom they had formerly persecuted; or else the unbelievers were dispersed or killed. And not only Jews and pagans, but heretics too:

**VERSE 12.** “They surrounded me with persecutions like bees around a honeycomb,” to take away from me the sweetness which Christ had poured into the soul through the Holy Spirit. A bee is so called because it is born without feet. After bees are enraged, they pursue fiercely and stake their life in the wound. Thus heretics fiercely persecuted the Church and lost their souls through envy. [Col. 0725B] “And they blazed like fire among thorns,” which consumes the thorns and leaves the wheat unharmed. Thus, in their envious persecution, they consumed in me the thorns of sins and left the soul untouched. By bees, moreover, deceitful deceivers are understood. Bees carry honey in their mouth and a sting in their tail. Thus deceivers carry in their mouth the sweetness of flattery, but behind they possess the sting of detraction; and they blaze like fire in the anger of fury. Thus the Jews had honey in their mouth when they said to Christ, the head of the martyrs: “Teacher, we know that you are true” (Matt. 22:16); but they concealed the sting, because they planned to seize him by deceit. They had a sting when they said: “This man is a glutton and a drinker of wine, and has a demon” [Col. 0725C] (Matt. 11:19). They blazed like fire among thorns when, inflamed with anger and fury, they cried: “Crucify, crucify him!” (John 19:6). Thus heretics treated Catholics. And in the name of the Lord they endured these things patiently, because they took vengeance upon them: either they consented when overcome by truth, or, hardened, they perished like Arius. And I suffered these things not only from them, but also from counterfeit Christians.

**VERSE 13.** I was driven by evil counsels so that I might fall from my purpose of holiness, and I was often overthrown by suggestions, because, conquered by torments, I thought of consenting to the persecutors. But the Lord upheld me lest I should fall, because he sustained me in temptation so that I should not fall. I did not fall into evil but stood firm in good, [Col. 0725D] because:

**VERSE 14.** “The Lord is my strength,” who made me strong and steadfast against their assault. Therefore he himself is my praise, because he made me praiseworthy in perseverance in holiness. And he became for me a way leading to salvation, that is, to eternal life. And because he became strength in dangers and praise in the hope of salvation, therefore there rang out:

**VERSE 15.** “The sound of exultation and salvation in the tabernacles of the righteous.” The sound of exultation rang out while they said amid punishments: “I have always desired these things.” The sound of salvation resounded when they said: “These things grant me salvation and refreshment.” This sound rang out in the tabernacles of the righteous—that is, in the bodies of martyrs, who, as valiant soldiers, served in the encampments of the Churches [Col. 0726A] for the crown of heavenly goods. Therefore the voice of Christ’s soldiers made a dancing applause in the tabernacles, because:

**VERSE 16.** “The right hand of the Lord has wrought power”—that is, the power of the Father gave me strength to endure sufferings. “The right hand of the Lord exalted me”—that is, the power of the Son raised me from the humiliation of diverse punishments, giving glory out of subjection. “The right hand of the Lord has wrought power”—that is, the power of the Holy Spirit gave me victory from suffering. By saying three times, “the right hand of the Lord,” he made known the Trinity. Some say: “Do you call a cruel death victory?” In answer he adds:

**VERSE 17.** “I shall not die,” as you suppose, “but live,” with the Lord in eternal life; “and I shall recount the works of the Lord”—that is, I cause them to be recounted by others. For when the faithful celebrate the feast of Stephen, Lawrence, or other martyrs, the martyrs themselves recount the Lord’s works through them, as they set forth in the written accounts of their passion both their own endurance and the Lord’s power. O torturer, your punishment is not, as you suppose, death for me, but fatherly correction, because:

[Col. 0726B] **VERSE 18.** “In chastening, the Lord chastened me”—that is, the merciful Father corrected me from sins by bodily chastisement, and did not hand me over to eternal death, because he trained me as a son for an inheritance. Therefore:

**VERSE 19.** “Open to me the gates of righteousness.” That is: you executioners, permitted for this purpose, rise fiercely against my flesh; inflict multiple punishments, through [Col. 0726C] which I may come to righteousness, through which I may enter into eternal life. And what will it profit you that the gates are open when you are dead? For, having entered them through death, I shall give thanks to the Lord—that is, praise the Lord.

**VERSE 20.** “This is the gate of the Lord,” because the Lord Jesus Christ entered into his glory through the gate of suffering. “The righteous shall enter through it”—that is, through suffering the righteous shall enter their inheritance. For “through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21). The gate of righteousness is the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, because through righteousness one enters the kingdom of heaven. Having entered these gates, I shall give thanks to the Lord, because perpetual confession of praise is in the Lord’s house. The Lord’s gate is Christ, namely the Father’s gate, through whom one enters [Col. 0726D] to the Father, as he himself says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). He is also the door of life, through which the righteous will enter the heavenly Jerusalem; but outside will be dogs and the unclean. I desire to enter there; therefore open the gates to me. But having entered that house:

**VERSE 21.** “I shall give thanks to you”—that is, I shall praise you—because you heard me calling upon you in tribulation; and you became for me a way leading to salvation, that is, eternal life, in which are perpetual salvation and gladness. Through what did you become salvation for me? Through the stone rejected indeed by men, but chosen and honored by God:

**VERSE 22.** “The stone,” I say, “which the builders rejected”—the Jews, who built themselves a temple to the Lord by establishing their own righteousness and rejecting God’s righteousness, erecting the letter and rejecting the spiritual sense. The Jews, building the wall of iniquity begun from Adam, the transgression of the law, found Christ the precious stone. When they saw him as small—that is, humble—they stumbled over him, because they despised him; and therefore they rejected him from their building, when they flogged him and condemned him with robbers. “He became the head of the corner”—that is, the head of the Church, joining both walls, namely uniting in one faith both peoples, from circumcision and uncircumcision. In his passion Christ was a stone of offense and scandal; in his resurrection he became the head of the corner. The comparison is drawn from the builders of the tower of Babel.

[Col. 0727B] **VERSE 23.** “This was done by the Lord,” not by the Jews, so that by this stone the fallen wall of the Lord’s house in heaven might be raised. For the counsel that Christ should die for the restoration of humankind proceeded not from the Jews but from God. “It is marvelous in our eyes” that God willed his only-begotten Son to die for the ungodly. Or: it is wondrous in the eyes of our heart that humankind was given life through a dead man. Or: it is terrible to our contemplation that an impious nation crucified the Lord of glory, who redeemed humankind from the agony of death and restored eternal life.

**VERSE 24.** “This day,” on which this occurred, “is the day which the Lord has made”—that is, sanctified above [Col. 0727C] all others. Although the Lord made every day, he is said, by antonomasia, to have made this day, the day of resurrection, on which greater grace was bestowed than on all other days. Let us exult in faith and rejoice in love on that day—that is, in consideration of the grace bestowed upon us on that day. Or this cornerstone is this day of salvation, namely Christ, whom the Lord Father made when he brought the eternal day into the world, when the Sun of righteousness, rising after the setting of death, shone upon the faithful. Let all who are enlightened in his light exult and rejoice, because with him we rose from death, and in his light we shall see light. This day of salvation—that is, the time of grace—began from the day of Christ’s resurrection and continues until the end of the world. Of this it is said daily: “Today, if you hear his voice”; and on [Col. 0727D] this day those dead in soul rise daily through repentance, while those dying in the flesh daily ascend to heavenly things. This day of resurrection will shine fully upon the saints after the night of this age has passed, the eternal Sun has shone forth, and angelic brightness has dawned, when they themselves will shine like the sun and be equal to angels. This eternal brightness of deity and fellowship of angels is that day which the Lord has made; in it they exult in body and rejoice in soul. The people of martyrs, still laboring in the camp and desiring to come to this glory, cries:

**VERSE 25.** “O Lord, save me.” That is, I pray, Lord, that you save me from sufferings. “O Lord, [Col. 0728A] grant prosperity”: that is, make prosperous the path by which I return to you through many labors, confessing you thus [Note: [Col. 0727D] The manuscript reads *confitentem* (“confessing”).]:

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” That is: because now is the day of salvation, save me on this day—you who came to bless the Gentiles, as was promised to Abraham, for the glory of God’s name. Or, as another translation has it: “Blessed are you who are to come in the name of the Lord”; you, I say, grant prosperity, so that you may come and save us. Christ came in the name of his Father, and they refused to receive him; Antichrist will come in his own name, and they will receive him. The voice of the apostles is added: O Israel, house of Aaron, and you who fear God:

**VERSE 26.** “We have blessed you from the house of the Lord”—that [Col. 0728B] is, we have preached to you the Father’s blessing, namely Christ, sent from the heavenly Jerusalem as a blessing to the Gentiles.

**VERSE 27.** “God is the Lord”—understand: he has blessed us and shone upon us, that is, has openly appeared to us after he rose from the dead. Therefore, following our example, “keep a solemn day amid dense throngs, as far as the horn of the altar.” It was commanded in the Law that on Passover or Pentecost they should observe a solemn day, abstain from servile work, and sacrifice victims. On that solemn day, when the peoples gathered, they filled the Lord’s temple from its doors to the altar. This is what he means by “amid dense throngs.” The house of the Lord is the Catholic Church, in which the altar is Christ, and the horn of this altar is the holy cross. Therefore, in this house, from which we have blessed you, keep a solemn day: that is, abstain from evil works, which make slaves of sin; offer yourselves as a living sacrifice pleasing to God; and do this amid dense throngs—that is, in many virtues—as far as the horn of the altar, that is, as far as imitation of Christ’s suffering on the cross. Or remain amid dense throngs until you come to Christ, who is the horn of the altar—that is, the strength of your mind, in which you ought to offer good works to God. Or “as far as the horn of the altar,” that is, as far as the manifest vision of the Deity, which is the horn—that is, the exaltation—of Christ’s humanity. That humanity is our altar, because in faith in it we offer our works to God. Another translation reads: “Keep a solemn day in frequent assemblies,” [Col. 0728D] that is, in frequent processions which the crowd of people makes dense and renders celebrated by festive devotion, as far as the horn of the altar—that is, as far as the solemn reception of the body and blood of the Lord. Upon this altar the choir of martyrs offers the sacrifice of praise, joyfully singing:

**VERSE 28.** “You are my God, Jesus Christ,” whom I confessed in my passion, and now I shall give thanks to you—that is, praise you—my God, whom I now see in the Father’s glory; “and I shall exalt you”: that is, raised by you from humiliation, I glorify you, who are exalted. “I shall give thanks to you”—that is, I shall praise you without end—because you heard me calling upon you in tribulation, and became for me [Col. 0729A] salvation, so that you might join me to your saints in the heavenly Jerusalem. Therefore all the righteous say:

**VERSE 29.** “Give thanks to the Lord”—that is, praise the Lord with the angels—because he alone is good, because his mercy is forever; through whose goodness and mercy we shall here always be in joy and gladness.

This psalm begins with praise and ends in praise, because here too our life ought to praise God, and in the future rejoice with the saints in a perpetual alleluia. The verse “I shall give thanks to you,” placed above, signifies the martyrs’ confession in suffering; placed a second time, it signifies their praise in reward. “Give thanks,” placed twice, denotes the twofold glory of soul and body.

[Col. 0730A]

It should be noted that first three psalms are entitled by *Alleluia*, because the three orders of the Church rejoice in the vision of the Trinity. Then eight together are inscribed with *Alleluia*, because the faithful enjoy eternal joy in the eight beatitudes. Afterwards two psalms have *Alleluia* in their titles, because they will rejoice forever in soul and body. Finally, seven together possess *Alleluia*, because the saints obtain perpetual rest in the sevenfold Spirit; all these together make twenty-five. Almost all are continued by “Give thanks” or, first, “Praise,” because all exhort to the confession of eternal praise.

## PART TEN.

[Col. 0729]

## PSALM 118. Alleluia.

### ALEPH.

[Col. 0729B]

“Blessed are the undefiled in the way.” This psalm is divided into twenty-two sections, with eight verses counted in each section. Each section likewise has one letter of the Hebrew alphabet as its title. We ask what such titling signifies. We find, however, that it is especially noteworthy that this entire psalm shines on its surface with heavenly pearls; the whole, I say, is woven with names of the Word of God like gleaming gems. For what little verse is there in the whole very extensive treatment of this psalm in which some term does not resound which is rightly predicated of the Word of God, the wisdom of God, the Son of God? For example: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way.” Certainly our way is the Son of God. [Col. 0729C] For he says: “I am the way” (John 14:6). “Who walk in the law of the Lord.” And what is the law of the Lord but the Word of the Lord? “Blessed are those who search his testimonies.” What are testimonies but words? And what are the many words of God but the one Word, the one wisdom of God? The same holds in the rest. For scarcely any little verse is found in which you do not have either truth, commandments, statutes, judgments, sayings, or utterances of the Lord, or something of equivalent force. What, then, does it mean that, though this is such a psalm, its several sections are entitled by individual letters of the alphabet? Did the prophetic spirit of the Word of God wish, after so many psalms, to make us beginners at the alphabet? Certainly, we understand this profitably [Col. 0729D] and confess truly that, however wise we may be, while we are in the body we are like little children learning the alphabet in relation to that wisdom of God; and things go well with us if we attain even its first elements. For, as the Apostle says, “we see through a mirror, in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13:12). Therefore let this psalm of the fourth pericope be the same beginning and end for us.

As has already been said, it is divided into twenty-two sections. This number consists of three heptads, with one added; from the third heptad an octave is made complete. Through this we understand that in the eighth age of the world the fullness of God’s wisdom—signified by the utterances of this psalm already mentioned—will be completed for us; and what the Apostle says will come to pass: “When that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be done away” (1 Cor. 13:10). Therefore let us faithful little children sing the eight verses of each section, [Col. 0730C] until, through his gift, we attain the eight beatitudes of the Gospel. Now let us append the interpretation and understanding of these same letters.

ALEPH: doctrine; BETH: house; GUIMEL: fullness; DALETH: of tablets; HE: this; VAU: and; ZAI [commonly ZAIN]: this; HETH: life; TETH: good; JOD: beginning; CAPH: hand; LAMECH [commonly LAMED]: of the heart; MEM: from these; NUN: eternal; SAMECH: help; AIN: fountain; FE: of the mouth; SADE: of righteousness; COPH: calling; RES: of the head; SIN: of teeth; TAU: signs. Doctrine is called the house of God and is the fullness of the tablets, that is, of the Law written upon tablets. This fullness of the Law is love. This doctrine and this—that is, such—life of human beings is the beginning of hand and heart, that is, of good intention and good action. [Col. 0730D] From these comes eternal help, by which they are helped toward eternal life. And this is the fountain of the mouth [Col. 0731A] of righteousness, that is, the source of the doctrine which Christ preached, through which it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness—namely, love, or the doctrine of God’s house. “This is the great and first commandment” (Matt. 22:38). And this is the calling of the head, that is, Christ, because all are called in this, that they may receive this doctrine. In this doctrine also appear signs of teeth, that is, of apostles and teachers, who are in a sense the Church’s teeth when we explain obscure and difficult commandments to lesser people. Or the signs of teeth are these letters, because they sound in forms made only by the teeth and the plectrum of the tongue, so that all divinely inspired Scripture, written in so many different ways from so few letters, may be read or heard. What is more beautiful, what more delightful, than this alphabet? Behold, it contains the whole [Col. 0731B] doctrine of the spiritual life! Its title is:

ALLELUIA.

Because in these things God is known to be worthy of praise, in which there is instruction for life and forgiveness of sins, by which the faithful become undefiled so that they may be blessed.
