Finally, in the preceding psalm the passion of the Lord was set forth, which washed this world clean, so as to make peoples worthy to praise God with undefiled lips and by their praise instruct others. Hence, in the preceding title, ALLELUIA is followed by:

ALEPH.

It means “doctrine,” so that you may know that the eight verses beginning with this letter in Hebrew are doctrinal not only in the meaning of their words but also in their sequence of verses. For since the first verse is, “Blessed are the undefiled,” and the second, “Blessed are those who search,” who would not readily observe that an undefiled life must come first, so that the doctrine which follows may become acceptable? For if a person’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching too is scorned, because doctrine without life is not complete, since wisdom shall not enter an ill-disposed soul. Yet a good life without doctrine is reckoned as good merit and benefits one’s neighbors by example. But it profits more if to good action is added knowledge of eternal goodness. To know this, one must search in the Scriptures the testimonies of divine truth: first the moral, then the mystical. In the former life is formed; in the latter, faith, so that life may be undefiled and faith unfeigned. The faith of heretics is feigned, because they devised it for themselves, unwilling carefully to search God’s testimonies concerning the truth and sincerity of faith. Therefore they did not receive the true Christ, but invented another for themselves; and therefore, in place of the true Christ, they worshipped an idol. To them he himself says: “Search the Scriptures, for they bear testimony of me” (John 5:39). Blessed, therefore, are those who search the testimonies of truth against impious defenders of falsehood, neither believing wrongly—which is the error of heretics—nor, while believing rightly, living wrongly—which is the error of false Christians. In this very matter they become heretics, if, by believing rightly and living wrongly, they suppose that they can be saved. Therefore the testimonies of truth must be searched, so that one may recognize not only what faith is true and unfeigned, but also what manner of life must be joined to right faith.

[Col. 0732A] In the investigation of this truth the intellects of great men have labored in this psalm: namely Ambrose, Hilary, Augustine, and other expositors of sacred Scripture. This is not because it has obscurity in its words, but because in the plainness of its words it conceals depth of meaning. For, as its first letter ALEPH sounds, it is doctrine instructing all who wish to be blessed in the way by which they may tend toward what they desire. Hence, as has been said before us, this psalm is the instructor of the faithful, a paradise of every fruit desirable to the faithful soul. The more open it appears on the surface, the deeper it is; woven with similar words, mixed with no confusion, but unfolded by novelty of subject matter as the letters change. In it speaks the choir of all the saints from the first [Col. 0732B] righteous person to the last. Therefore, while it is a matter of great difficulty to clarify obscure sayings and, by bringing them to plain sense, to display—as it were from dark water in the clouds of the air—flashes and gleams of lightning, it seems much more laborious to investigate in things plainly spoken and clearly written the height of meanings hidden beneath the plainness of the letter; meanings nonetheless to be found by careful seekers. Hence “the kingdom of heaven” is said to be “like treasure hidden in a field” (Matt. 13:44), not in a forest: namely, in a level field, where it can easily be found by seekers, not among dense woodland thickets, to which Aristotelian or Platonic writings may be compared. Since, therefore, in this most level field—indeed, in a field already diligently ploughed—a great treasure has been found and brought to light by great diggers, let it now, by the favor of God’s grace, be our endeavor not so much to dig deeply here as to gather the dug-up coins [manuscript: *nomismate*] scattered through this field. For the splendid names of Christ shine here like gleaming coins: whether he is called the way in which the blessed walk, or the Word whose remembrance is brought before God the Father where it is sung, “Remember your word to your servant,” or whether his name is invoked among us by any other title—a name in which alone salvation is given. “For,” as the Apostle Peter says, “there is no other name under heaven given among human beings in which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). May he himself deign to help us gather, as we hurry in psalmody through the canonical offices, the precious drachmas of this name, long ago found in this field by the great [Col. 0732D] investigators just mentioned, as it were quickly in passing. But if anyone delights not so much in hurrying through this field with us as he runs, but in remaining awhile and wandering far and wide, as Isaac is read to have gone out into the field to meditate when Rebekah came to him (Gen. 24), let him devote attention to the copious expositions of the aforementioned Fathers. But we, seeking brevity insofar as God helps us, and intending especially to gather the pearls of God’s name, shall run through the text of this psalm not so much by expounding as by singing it. Lest we fail on the way, we desire to pray to him who is the Way himself, that he may join us to those walking and running [Col. 0733A] in him. For although truly most blessed is that runner who can say in this psalm, “I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart,” one should not begin with this running, but first walk, as it were, step by step. Hence, at the beginning of the psalm it is rightly said:

**VERSE 3.** “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.” Do you wish to be blessed? Be undefiled, because the undefiled are blessed; just as, conversely, all who are defiled and stained by crimes are miserable. I know that all human beings by natural desire wish to be blessed, but not all wish to be undefiled; therefore, in their wandering error, they establish blessedness for themselves even in satisfying their own filth, as Epicurus did, or in worldly wisdom, as the Stoic did.

[Col. 0733B] But against Epicurus I say: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.” And against the Stoic: “Blessed are they who search his testimonies; with their whole heart they seek him.” Blessed are the undefiled—not those who have never had stains: “For all have sinned,” and all “lack the glory of God” (Rom. III, 23)—but those who have put away original stains, or even actual ones. Where? In the Way, namely in him who says, “I am the way” (John XIV, 6). Since he alone is the man conceived and born without every stain, he makes undefiled in himself, the Way, not those who stand idle or lie supine, but those who walk in the law of the Lord, diligently applying the steps of their actions to the frequent service which they have learned in the law of the Lord, [Col. 0733C] where they have been instructed concerning love of neighbour.

As they practise this love by walking in it, they become more blessed if, through Martha’s office, they endeavour to ascend to Mary’s repose. Mary’s part is approved as the better by the testimony of him who accepted the service of good action in Martha, yet preferred her sister’s rest. Blessed, therefore, are the active, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed also are the contemplative, who search his testimonies. Both are blessed only if they seek him with their whole heart, desiring no reward of action or contemplation other than him through whose authorship they are what they are.

Unhappy are hypocrites who, while doing good deeds, search for the testimonies of human beings, wishing to be seen by them. Likewise unhappy are those who act wickedly and therefore hate the light, who for this reason search for human witnesses [Col. 0733D] lest their evil works be detected. Hence that saying: “The eye of the adulterer watches for the darkness” (Job XXIV, 15). Therefore, whether doing well or ill, and in this seeking human testimonies—either because they desire praise or because they fear reproof—they are altogether unhappy and wretched.

But blessed are those who walk in the law of the Lord by acting rightly, living soberly, justly, and devoutly, avoiding what is evil; and who, in those matters which they avoid or endeavour to do, search only God’s testimonies, desiring to avoid what displeases him and to do what pleases him. Such was the man who said: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (Acts IX, 6). Likewise another says: “Lord, teach me to do your will” (Ps. CXLII, 9). The foolish virgins, lacking in the vessels of their consciences the true testimony of truth, [Col. 0734A] wish to buy outside themselves a false one from the mouths of people who sell the oil of flattery (Matt. XXV).

Unhappy, then, are those who do not possess God’s testimony. But blessed are those who search his testimonies by diligently investigating what pleases him and what displeases him, so that, approving one and rejecting the other, their mind may always depend on the divine testimony and always submit itself to his judgment: whether walking in the straight way through rational action, or searching his testimonies in contemplation, or alternating their efforts between both, so that they may never be found either idle with respect to good works or busy with evil ones.

**VERSE 3.** For those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways, being far removed from those blessed undefiled persons [Col. 0734B] in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. How much further are they from those blessed persons who search his testimonies! For those who work iniquity belong to neither class: neither active nor contemplative. I do not mean those who have acted and have now ceased to do what is evil, but those who work it—that is, who have the settled purpose of doing what they know to be evil.

Hence, by God’s just judgment, it is sometimes permitted that “he who is filthy may be filthy still, and he who harms may harm still” (Rev. XXII, 11). It is not said that one who was filthy or who caused harm may be filthy or harm still; rather, one who is filthy and presently does harm, stubbornly loving his own iniquity and consequently hating his own soul, may become filthy and harm [Col. 0734C] still further—being left, that is, to his own depraved and malice-hardened will.

Otherwise: Blessed are those who walk in the way, not because they are walking now, but because they will arrive where they are walking. Likewise, blessed are those who search God’s testimonies and seek him with their whole heart, not because they search or seek, but because they will find what they seek. Similar is the statement: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, and those who hunger for righteousness,” not because of this itself, but because of what follows: “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven, and they shall be filled” (Matt. V, 10). Blessedness, therefore, lies not in persecution but in persecution’s reward; nor in hunger, but in the satisfaction to follow. Likewise, “blessed are those who mourn,” not [Col. 0734D] because they mourn, but “because they shall be comforted” (ibid., 5).

So indeed, as has already been said: blessed are those who walk and labour by walking, not because they walk in this way, but because by walking and labouring thus they hasten to enter that rest in which they will henceforth have no labour. “From now on, the Spirit says, let them rest from their labours, for their works follow them” (Rev. XIV, 13).

Likewise, those who search God’s testimonies are blessed not yet in possession but already in hope, because they will find what they seek—provided, however, that they seek God with their whole heart. This is not what those do who search his testimonies in order either to attack them or to hold them merely as knowledge and not in life. Of this sort the worst were heretics, who investigated the testimonies of truth while being [Col. 0735A] enemies of truth. Even today there are clerics like them, learned and highly instructed in the Scriptures of truth, while enemies of truth itself, as is known from their fruits. For those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways—him whom they hate with their whole heart.

Certainly, those are not said to work iniquity or sin who can say with the Apostle: “It is no longer I who do it, but sin which dwells in me” (Rom. VII, 17). For the tinder of sin, which is the weakness of nature, stirs up unlawful desires of carnal concupiscence; this is called the law of the members, and in the members it performs what belongs to it. But the inward person, who delights in God’s law, does not work sin, because he neither consents nor obeys [Col. 0735B] the sin that he feels in his flesh, so as to accomplish what the flesh desires. Indeed, he fights against this sin itself with inexpressible groanings, saying with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” And he adds: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII, 24).

Therefore the statement made here—“For those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways”—does not apply to one who fights in this manner, because his confessing the sin and praying against it pertains to God’s ways. If one perseveres in those ways, sin is not imputed on account of those ways, provided there is no deceit in his spirit—namely, the deceit of one who says that he grieves for the sin which he feels at work in his flesh. The avoidance of this deceit was treated sufficiently in the thirty-third psalm. [Col. 0735C]

Otherwise: In the house of the Lord, whose teaching this psalm is, there are two schools: one of discipline, forming persons to love God and neighbour; the other of knowledge, forming and instructing them to know God and neighbour. The latter had not yet known his neighbour who said: “And who is my neighbour?” (Luke X, 29). When he was finally instructed that the neighbour of the wounded man was the one who showed him mercy, after this instruction in knowledge he received the command of discipline, the Lord saying to him: “Go, and do likewise” (ibid., 37).

Thus, the person to whom it is said, “Go, and do likewise,” is directed into the way of discipline, by which one walks in God’s law. But lest anyone who has once entered this way should be led astray [Col. 0735D] into error, the testimonies of truth must be searched in the school of knowledge. Instructed by them, each person knows how God is to be loved, and how the neighbour is to be loved for God’s sake. Otherwise one will easily go astray, loving for God’s sake what is not God, or loving or hating in one’s neighbour what ought not to be loved or hated.

Therefore, at the beginning of this psalm it is written not only, “Blessed are those who walk in the law of the Lord,” but is added, “Blessed are those who search his testimonies,” so that we may both advance in the school of discipline toward love of God and neighbour, and be enlightened in the school of knowledge and wisdom toward the knowledge of God and neighbour. But lest negligence creep into either school:

[Col. 0736A] **VERSE 4.** You have commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly: you who wish them to be kept exceedingly, that is, very diligently. The word *nimis* (“exceedingly”) may be understood in two ways: either “you commanded exceedingly,” or “I kept exceedingly.” It should be known that here *nimis* does not signify the evil meant in the common proverb, “Everything excessive turns into vice,” but is used in the sense of “very,” as there: “But to me your friends have been exceedingly honoured, O God; their rule has been exceedingly strengthened” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 17).

For the commandments must be kept exceedingly, since not one jot is to be passed over in them; for the things said to the ancients have been greatly heightened by the new commandments. The Lord says: “It was said to the ancients: You shall not kill; but I say to you, everyone who is angry with his brother [Col. 0736B] shall be liable to judgment.” Likewise: “It was said to the ancients: You shall not commit adultery; but I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 21, 27).

So also in the other commandments: by these the old law restrains and prohibits evil actions, whereas the new law restrains even thoughts and affections. This is to command exceedingly—beyond, that is, the powers of human frailty. Therefore, deprived of human strength, I flee to you, who can do all things, saying:

**VERSE 5.** O that my ways may be directed to keep your ordinances! For unless grace bestows what the law commands, sin will revive through the commandment of the law, and what was given [Col. 0736C] for life will become death to me. Therefore, pressed by the yoke of the law, I flee to Christ’s grace, saying: “O that my ways”—that is, the actions of my life, which are of themselves crooked and by no means straight—“may be directed to keep your ordinances”: those commands by which you enjoin what is right and those prohibitions by which you forbid evils. For if I avoid what you forbid and do what you command,

**VERSE 6.** Then I shall not be ashamed, when I look upon all your commandments.

On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says:

> [Note: [Col. 0735D] *Morals*, Book XVIII, ch. 5.] It must be understood that whoever departs from God’s commandments in action is reproved and confounded in heart whenever he hears them, because he remembers what he has not done. For in the very matter in which he sees that he has erred, conscience itself secretly accuses him. Thus the Prophet prays, saying: “Then I shall not be ashamed, [Col. 0736D] while I look upon all your commandments.” For each person is grievously ashamed when, in reading or hearing, he considers God’s commandments which he has despised in his life. Hence John says: “If our heart does not reprove us, we have confidence toward God; and whatever we ask from him, we receive” (I John III, 21–22). It is as though he said: If we do what you command, we obtain what we ask.

> For with God these two necessarily accord very closely: action is supported by prayer, and prayer by action. Thus Jeremiah says: “Let us search our ways and examine them, and let us return to the Lord. Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God in heaven” (Lam. III, 40). [Col. 0737A] To search one’s ways is to examine inwardly one’s thoughts; and the person who strengthens prayer by works lifts up the heart with the hands. Whoever prays but neglects to act lifts up the heart but not the hands. Whoever acts but does not pray lifts up the hands but not the heart. Therefore, according to John’s saying, the heart then gains confidence in prayer when no perversity of life opposes it.

Otherwise: “Then I shall not be ashamed, when I look upon all your commandments.” I shall not be like the one who is a hearer and not a doer, “compared to a man looking at the face of his birth in a mirror” (James I, 23), and immediately forgetting what he was like. Rather, I shall be like the one of whom it is said: “But whoever has looked into the law of perfect freedom and has continued in it, not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, this person shall be blessed in his deed” (ibid., 25).

Made like this wise man through the direction of my ways toward keeping your ordinances, I shall then not be ashamed when I look, as in a mirror, upon all your commandments, lest by sinning against one I become guilty of all. To guard against this, I frequently look upon all your commandments—many by diversity of action, yet one in the root of love—through reading and meditation, so that in them as in a mirror I may recognize whether my ways, that is, my character and actions, are truly directed toward keeping your ordinances. When I find this to be so, I shall not be ungrateful, nor shall I attribute this direction to my own free will, but:

[Col. 0737C] **VERSE 7.** I shall confess to you in uprightness of heart. For to you alone belongs the confession of praise and thanksgiving, not only for the uprightness of heart which your grace first straightened and made right, so that I might be upright in heart, but also because I have learned the judgments of your righteousness. For you too have done this: you have enabled me to learn from them things which I could not understand by myself. Yet I have learned neither from a human being nor through a human being how to do them, but from you, who alone teach a human being this knowledge, by which one knows not only how to understand but also how to do and keep the judgments of your righteousness.

Therefore I constantly say to you: “Teach me to do your will” (Ps. CXLII, 9), because one human being cannot teach another this. Thus, instructed by you through the judgments of your righteousness, in uprightness of heart, so as to be upright in heart, I shall rejoice [Col. 0737D] in those judgments with those to whom elsewhere it is said: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; and glory, all you upright in heart” (Ps. XXXI, 11). But if I have a heart distorted from the uprightness of the judgments of your ordinance, I shall not rejoice in them, because I shall be accused by them. Therefore my most steadfast purpose is that

**VERSE 8.** I shall keep your ordinances. But because without you I can do nothing, do not forsake me utterly—that is, greatly. And if you have forsaken me so that I may appear weak without your help, do not forsake me utterly, that is, greatly, lest I perish. For the world would have been greatly, indeed altogether and utterly, forsaken, had not God, reconciling the world to himself in Christ, brought a powerful remedy against its powerful sickness. Since this remedy heals the world, it has not been utterly forsaken—that is, altogether or greatly. [Col. 0738A]

In the Hebrew it reads: “I shall keep your precepts; do not forsake me exceedingly.” This prayer indeed suits a person trained by temptations, who knows that of himself a human being is and can do nothing. Such a person’s is also that complaint, made too late: “I said in my abundance, I shall never be moved. Lord, by your favour you gave strength to my beauty. You turned your face away from me, and I was troubled” (Ps. XXIX, 7–8). He now anticipates this complaint, saying: “I shall keep your ordinances; do not forsake me utterly,” that is, exceedingly, because you have forsaken me exceedingly by turning your face away from me. Therefore, exceedingly troubled, lest I be troubled exceedingly again when I resolve to keep [Col. 0738B] your ordinances, knowing that I can do nothing without you, I pray: “Do not forsake me utterly,” that is, exceedingly.

**BETH**

**VERSE 9.** By what means does a younger person correct his way? Youth is prone to evil. Thus the younger son squandered his substance by living extravagantly (Luke XV). Yet this age is more suited to conversion than old age, because it is better to forestall youth by correction than afterwards to bewail the sins of youth and ignorance. The latter is a remedy; the former is safety. Here the matter is in danger, because it is exceedingly grave and difficult to cast out evils that have become habitual. There safety is secure, with God’s help favouring us, where from youth a good [Col. 0738C] habit is strengthened in good things.

Therefore, desiring better things, I say to you, my God: “By what means does a younger person correct his way?” Having put forward this deliberation, and as though instructed by your inspiration, I affirm that a younger person corrects his way by keeping your words. For you say: “Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke XI, 28). Therefore, knowing that salvation lies not only in hearing but much more in keeping your words, I purpose to keep your words not merely in memory, against the vice of forgetfulness, but much more in life, against the vice of perverse conduct. For while they teach me, and while I keep them, they preserve me:

**VERSE 10.** With my whole heart I have sought you, proving by happy experience that your sayings and words are spirit [Col. 0738D] and life, and can so awaken and enliven the human heart, though cold or half-dead, to seek you in them with its whole heart. And therefore I pray: Do not drive me away from your commandments, as you drive away the lukewarm person whom you vomit from your mouth; as you drive away the negligent worker, lest he occupy the place of a better person and incur still greater offence; as you drove away the tabernacle at Shiloh because of the undisciplined conduct of Eli, the lukewarm priest (I Sam. IV); and as you also drive away the one to whom you say: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I shall reject you, so that you shall not serve as priest to me” (Hos. IV, 6). Do not, I beseech you, drive me away in this manner, for I have not rejected knowledge. But:

**VERSE 7.** In my heart I have hidden your sayings, as one of your people [Col. 0739A] knowing that you do not reject your people who diligently keep your sayings. Therefore, as a truly precious treasure, I have carefully hidden your sayings in my heart, observing a time for silence and a time for speaking. For I know it is a vice to disclose divine mysteries to the unworthy. This commonly happens either through the speaker’s flattery, so that he may please the one to whom he reveals secrets; or through greed, so that he may gain something; or through boastfulness, so that he may appear to know more; or through the shameful incontinence of the mouth, by which, once uttered, the word flies forth irrevocably.

Therefore, unwilling to cast pearls before swine or to give what is holy to dogs, I have hidden your sayings in my heart, so that I may not sin against you, who say: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. VII, 6). My heart is like an ark; your saying, like a treasure which I have guarded [Col. 0739B] from thieves, knowing that one who carries a treasure openly among thieves desires to be robbed.

Likewise, my heart is like a nest; your sayings were like eggs received by me so that in their time they might be formed into birds that would fly. Therefore, lest they fall from their nest before their time and perish, I kept them in my heart as in a nest, so that I might not sin against you either by sending them out before their time or by keeping them within when they should fly out—not on ravens’ wings but on doves’ wings, which I desired elsewhere, saying: “Who will give me wings like a dove?” (Ps. LIV, 7).

And indeed, by hiding your sayings I kept silent before people who had no ears to hear; yet I did not keep silent in your ears, my God, to whom I continually said and say:

**VERSE 12.** Blessed are you, Lord; teach me your ordinances. In this brief verse sound together both thanksgiving for benefits bestowed and petition for benefits yet to be bestowed. Thus I have said, and constantly say: Blessed are you, Lord, because, as you taught me, I have learned the judgments of your righteousness, which I have hidden in my heart so that I may not sin against you. But lest I have received your money in vain if I always hide it, teach me your ordinances, so that I may know how to put your money on the bankers’ table, and when you come, you may require it with interest, and may not then rebuke me as an evil and slothful servant who hid the entrusted talent in the earth (Matt. XXV).

Thus, constantly praying, heard, and taught what, how, to whom, and when I should speak:

[Col. 0739D] **VERSE 13.** With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth. Some of your judgments I have hidden in my heart, and others I have declared with my lips. For those unsearchable judgments of yours which are a great deep, not comprehensible even to angels, I have believed in my heart to be most just—those by which the world is judged now and at the end. These I have hidden in my heart by believing, reverencing, and fearing them.

But the judgments of your mouth, which are more manifest than the judgments of your heart, I have declared with my lips as I have learned that they are to be declared through your mouth in the Gospel, and “as you spoke through” the mouth of your “holy prophets from of old,” who are also your mouth (Luke I, 70). The Apostles too—one of whom says, “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians” (II Cor. VI, 11)—are your mouth, [Col. 0740A] and the judgments made manifest through them are the judgments of your mouth.

But when the same Apostle cries out: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments!” (Rom. XI, 33), I have reverenced the judgments of your heart, knowing that though most hidden, they are nevertheless most just. With my lips, however, I have declared all the judgments of your mouth, insofar as this has been granted to me by you: an open mouth and a manifest doorway plainly opened, according to my measure, just as your Apostle rejoices in an open mouth and doorway according to his measure: “Our mouth,” he says, “is open to you, O Corinthians” (II Cor. VI, 11). Likewise: “A great and manifest door is opened to me,” he says, “and there are many adversaries” (I Cor. XVI, 9).

As he, by the authority of his apostleship, magnificently declared the judgments of your mouth, [Col. 0740B] so I too, according to my small measure, insofar as I have been able by your gift, have declared all the judgments of your mouth. Yet, as with the Apostle, there have sometimes opposed me many adversaries: namely false witnesses, speaking against the truth and striving to turn me from the way of truth. This they could not do, because I:

**VERSE 14.** Have delighted in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches. For just as a greedy person delights in acquired or attainable earthly wealth, so that it seems easy and pleasant to labour greatly for such things, so I have delighted in the way of your testimonies. This way is Christ, in whom are all the treasures of the depth of God’s riches, wisdom, and knowledge. Consequently this way ought not to be compared with all deceptive [Col. 0740C] riches, but infinitely and incomparably preferred to them. Those riches are compared to thorns that choke the word; in the end they will be assigned to feed the fire in which their lovers shall burn in hell, like that rich man who, tormented in the flame, could not obtain the refreshment of a single drop (Luke XVI).

Therefore, in this place there is an improper comparison between unequal riches. It does not raise up a small matter, but lowers a great one; grammarians call this figure of speech *tapinosis* applied to a great thing. Yet those who love true riches are so pleased by the way of God’s testimonies, which is Christ, that in him they reckon themselves to possess all heavenly and earthly riches: the former for enjoyment, the latter for use, “as having nothing and yet possessing all things, as needy yet [Col. 0740D] making many rich” (II Cor. VI, 10). Therefore they rightly delight in him as in all riches, because in him those who have him who possesses all things have all things. Does not he possess all things who says: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father”? (Matt. XI, 27). Likewise: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII, 18).

These testimonies of Truth himself concerning himself are true. Therefore I have delighted in the way of such testimonies as in all riches, believing—indeed, knowing—that this way in which I walk, the truth through which I walk, and the life toward which I walk, abound in every kind of riches. Therefore I say: “I have delighted in the way of your testimonies as in all riches,” not because I am able either to estimate in my mind or to set forth with my mouth [Col. 0741A] these inestimable riches of your testimonies, but so that I may be enlightened more and more to recognize them.

**VERSE 15.** I shall be occupied with your commandments, and shall consider your ways. This is indeed right. For your testimonies are sometimes obscure; for example: “I am who I am” (Exod. III, 14); or “I am the beginning” (Rev. I, 8); or “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). But your commandments are manifest, such as: “You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. Honour your father,” and so forth (Exod. XX, 12–14).

In this way I reverence your wondrous testimonies even when I do not understand them, knowing that you have words of life even when your “saying” seems “hard,” as in the matter of eating your flesh and drinking your blood (John VI, LX). But I shall be occupied with your entirely intelligible commandments by doing [Col. 0741B] what you command and avoiding what you prohibit. And when the blearedness of my sight has been healed by the eye-salve of such exercise, I shall consider your ways; or, as it reads in the Hebrew: “I shall contemplate your judgments.”

On this passage blessed Gregory says:

> [Note: [Col. 0741D] *Morals*, Book XVII, ch. 9.] What does he suggest by these ways, unless it is that he had despised looking at the paths of human conduct? Thus he says: “I shall be occupied with your commandments and shall consider your ways.” It is as if he openly promises: I now refuse to look at what is mine, because I burn to advance, in the steps of my conduct, along the way of your imitation.
>
> Whoever opposes the present world sets before the eyes of the heart, by continual exercise of love, the ways of his Redeemer, so that the mind may flee prosperity, prepare itself for adversity, desire nothing that caresses it, and fear nothing thought capable of terrifying it; so that it may reckon sorrow as joy, regard the joys of this present life as losses of sorrow, not fear the losses of lowliness, but through them seek the place of abiding glory. Truth showed these ways to the eyes of those who follow him when he said: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John XII, 26).
>
> He recalled to these ways the swollen hearts of the disciples when they were already seeking a place of glory but did not know the road leading there, saying: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matt. XX, 22). They had sought the height of confession at the right and left hands, but did not see how much narrowness of road still remained. Therefore the cup of passion, to be imitated, was immediately set before their eyes, so that if they were striving toward the joys of exaltation, they might first find the way of humility.

[Col. 0741D] Therefore I shall be occupied with your commandments and shall consider your ways. And because forgetfulness easily steals in through the wound of original sin, lest I lose what I have understood once:

**VERSE 16.** I shall meditate on your ordinances, so that I may not forget your words. It is fitting not only that these be seen through understanding but also retained in memory. But especially requiring consideration and meditation are those ordinances which in either the Law or the Gospel say one thing and indicate another. In the Law: “You shall not put on a garment woven of wool and linen” (Deut. XXII, 11). The literal observance of this is no ordinance; but morally, to avoid that duplicity in which simplicity is displayed like wool [Col. 0742A] and cunning concealed like the fineness of linen, is a great ordinance.

Likewise, in the Gospel, where it is said: “But when you fast, wash your face and anoint your head with oil” (Matt. VI, 17). The literal observance of this is little or no ordinance. But inwardly to wash the face of the heart with the water of compunction for past sins, and to anoint the head of the mind—that is, the intention, which is the chief part of the inward person—with the oil of joy, so that fasting or any other exercise of holiness may be performed not from sadness or necessity but in joy and gladness: this is a great ordinance. Prudent meditation is necessary to discern such ordinances, lest they either be understood wrongly or, though rightly understood, be given over to forgetfulness. [Col. 0742B] Therefore I make, as it were, a vow, saying: “I shall meditate on your ordinances; I shall not forget your words.”

Having now completed these eight verses, let us join their two principal letters, *aleph* and *beth*, and from their interpretation say that these verses contain the great teaching of the Church. For *aleph* is interpreted “teaching,” and *beth*, “house”; and thus they are understood to comprise the teaching of the house, that is, of the Church.

There begins another group of eight verses, each verse of which in Hebrew begins with the letter:

**GUIMEL**

This is interpreted “fullness,” or, as Ambrose prefers, “recompense,” because a person instructed through the teaching of the house in this manner [Col. 0742C] and exercised in God’s commandments rightly claims the fullness of recompense, saying:

**VERSE 17.** Reward your servant. In this he ought not to seem arrogant, but steadfast. For it belongs to an innocent and steadfast conscience to seek from him whom it has served the fullness of recompense, and in this to hesitate or doubt in no way. For in the Gospel we are commanded to have faith and not to hesitate concerning things impossible to human beings but possible to God (Luke XI).

Now there are four different recompenses: good rendered for good and evil for evil, which is justice; good rendered for evil, which is grace; and evil rendered for good, which is injustice. God does not know this last recompense, for he repays evil to no one for good. He exercises the other three as he wills. For he rewards good merits—which he himself gives—with good rewards; he repays evil punishments to evil merits, which the evil person has from himself; and he also often rewards evil merits with good rewards, once those evil merits have been acknowledged through repentance. But who gives you this repentance itself except the giver of pardon and lover of human salvation?

Therefore, insofar as I have done good, I, your servant, say to you, good God: “Reward your servant.” But because, half alive as I still am, I feel death in part, by which I am hindered from serving you as much as I ought, I say to you: “Give me life,” repaying your goods for my evils; and when given life, [Col. 0743A] I shall keep your words. But because they cannot be kept through obedience unless first seen through understanding, you who are “the true light, enlightening every person coming into this world” (John I, 9):

**VERSE 18.** Unveil my eyes. Then, when the veil of ignorance together with malice has been removed, I shall consider the wonders from your law. Nothing in the commandments is more wonderful than: “Love your enemies,” which is the same as saying, “Render good for evil.” Likewise, when it is said: “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 33); and: “Go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. XIX, 21); and other sayings of this kind. They are indeed wonderful to say, but possible in action for the believer.

I shall consider this to be so concerning your law, in which I read such wonders. Moses too loved enemies, for whom, lest they perish, he asked that he himself be blotted out from the book of life. Samuel too prayed for enemies, while the shadow of the law still remained. But when truth shone forth, after Christ the true lamb was sacrificed for enemies, countless persons have loved and do love their enemies, praying for those who persecute and slander them; and they who renounce all that they have or can have on earth are sojourners on earth. Admitted into their fellowship either by imitation or by perfect love for another’s perfection, I confidently say:

[Col. 0743C] **VERSE 19.** I am a sojourner on the earth. Hence elsewhere I am accustomed to cry: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged!” (Ps. CXIX, 5). For sojourn is the same as pilgrimage: “I am a stranger, like all my fathers” (Ps. XXXVIII, 13). Their homeland is the heavenly Jerusalem, whose citizens labour in the Babylon of this world; and they would altogether fail unless your commandments, like provisions coming down from above, refreshed them. Thus our fathers wandering in the wilderness were refreshed by the typological bread of angels, and the fathers of the New Testament by the true bread.

Therefore, because I too am a sojourner on earth, journeying toward the homeland of heaven, lest I fail on the way, do not hide your commandments from me. They are hidden from those who savour earthly things and are not sojourners but citizens of Babylon. Thus, though opposing [Col. 0743D] your commandments and even wishing to know them, they nevertheless do not desire to savour them. They seek you day by day and desire to know your ways, as though they were a nation that had practised righteousness and had not abandoned the judgment of its God; but their soul does not desire or wish to savour your ordinances. For either, with the Jews, establishing their own righteousness, they refuse to submit to your righteousness; or, with the Gentiles, they worship their own idols against every righteousness: one sacrificing to Venus whenever he commits fornication, another to Mars whenever he gives way to anger, another to Jupiter whenever he thinks lofty thoughts—as often as he slaughters his soul by the aforesaid or similar crimes.

They also add incense, not of sweetest but of foulest odour, when by a most depraved reputation they corrupt, as it were, the air—especially if, by speaking, they induce others to commit the things they do—according to the saying: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV, 33). Since, however, I am not a citizen among such people but a sojourner and pilgrim, and since I reject the Pharisaic ordinances of the Jews and all the filth of Gentile idolatry:

[Col. 0744A] **VERSE 20.** My soul has longed to desire your ordinances at all times. For by reason I see how useful your ordinances are; but, weighed down by the languor of weakness, I do not desire them as much as I understand that they ought to be desired. Understanding flies ahead, while affection follows slowly—or not at all. I have been granted to know the good which does not yet delight me to do. Therefore my soul has longed for the affection for that good of which it has understanding.

[Col. 0744B] Otherwise: Among all the wonders of your law that I have considered, beyond all the pearls found and considered there, I see one most precious—namely, true love. True love is that by which things worthy of love are loved, just as false love is that by which things not worthy of love are loved. And false love is certainly not to be loved; but true love is to be loved more than all the things loved in it and under it. For it is God himself, according to the saying: “God is love” (1 John 4:8). In this love, although all good things ought to be dear, love itself ought nevertheless to be dearer than all things that are dear. Therefore, desiring to possess love for that very love, love for that very charity, I continually say: “My soul has longed to desire your ordinances.” For I do in some manner [Col. 0744C] desire and long for your ordinances. Yet I strive so to desire and long for the very desire by which I desire, and the very longing by which I long, that henceforth I may not be afflicted by any weariness through which I grow faint in such desire as my soul longs for with a willing spirit, though the flesh is weak. Similar is what the bride says: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon” (Song 1:6). Again: “Have you seen him whom my soul loved?” (Song 3:2). Thus when I say, “My soul longs for” or “loves,” it is both a confession and a complaint of that weakness through which the languishing mortal flesh lusts against the spirit. Yet while it languishes and desires what is contrary to salvation, my soul, breathed upon by your Spirit, [Col. 0744D] has longed to desire your ordinances at every time, both of adversity and of prosperity. And because the flesh is weak, it is for this reason that you

**VERSE 21.** Rebuked our proud parents in paradise, because they yielded to the tempter, who suggested excessive pride and said: “You shall be like gods” (Gen. 3:5). First you rebuked the proud devil; then the human imitator of his pride, saying: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (ibid., 17). To the woman also you said: “I will multiply your conceptions and your pains” (ibid., 16). Hence that woman herself is the cursed earth, bringing forth the thorns and thistles of cursed children, all of whom you cursed in their mother herself by multiplying her conceptions: so that she might conceive not only blessed children, to whom it shall be said, [Col. 0745A] “Come, blessed ones” (Matt. 25:34), but also those cursed ones to whom at the end it shall be said: “Go, accursed ones” (ibid., 41). Even to the children of blessing there clings the stain of this curse, which is not wiped away except through the blessed fruit of your womb. O woman blessed among women, who crushed the head of the cursed serpent because, in opposition to his pride, you, a humble virgin, remained steadfast and abolished the curse of the first woman. For through the blessed fruit of your womb all tribes of the earth shall be blessed, as was promised to Abraham (Gen. 17, 26, 28). Accordingly, those who from every tribe and tongue are blessed in you, O seed of Abraham, are by your grace separated from rebuke and curse already now in their souls, which long [Col. 0745B] for your ordinances at every time (Ps. 71). Yet the weakness of the flesh still clings to them because of your rebuke, by which you rebuked the proud, subduing and buffeting them through mortality and bodily death, so that they might recognize that they are earth or dust and cease to exalt themselves on high. For this reason you also buffet those whom you count among the blessed children, lest either the greatness of revelations or the sufficiency of graces should be able to exalt any of them; while the strength of the mind is perfected in the weakness of the flesh, and, as it were, from the curse of the flesh that brings forth the thorns and thistles of temptations, the blessing of the mind consenting to the law of God—and not loving, indeed hating, the law of the members—is brought to completion. Hence [Col. 0745C] one of such persons says: “For I do not do the good that I wish, but I do the evil that I hate. But if I do the evil that I hate, I consent to the law of God, because it is good” (Rom. 7:16).

Therefore, although children of blessing of this kind are weighed down in the flesh by a certain penalty of the curse, they are not themselves to be judged accursed, because there is no condemnation for those who do not walk according to the flesh and do not permit sin to reign in their mortal body, though they cannot be entirely free from sin while the corruptible body weighs them down, even as the inward person is renewed.

But those who through pride turn aside from your commandments—not deceived through ignorance like Saul the persecutor, nor overcome through frailty like Peter while still [Col. 0745D] young, but drawn away and enticed by the desire to sin, like Judas, the sacrilegious thief and betrayer of the Savior, and remaining in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity, like Simon Magus—these and their like are altogether accursed. For they so detest your commandments, O God, from which they turn aside, that they heap many reproaches upon those who observe them and preach that they must be observed, and judge them contemptible. Against such persons I—the Church, or I as an ecclesiastical person—pray, saying:

**VERSE 22.** Take away from me reproach and contempt, because I have sought out your testimonies. A witness in Latin is called among the Greeks a *martyr*, and testimonies are called *martyria*. These testimonies or martyrdoms were a reproach and object of mockery to the proud, who despised the cross and the whole [Col. 0746A] Christian humility by which alone pride is healed. Certainly the holy martyrs sought testimonies or martyrdoms for the sake of salvation; yet they desired to be delivered from contempt of this sort for the salvation of their persecutors. And in this they were heard, because the suffering of martyrs is now no reproach but an honor in the world. Many from the number of the persecutors have imitated it, seeing that martyrs are honored in this world because it is certain that they are crowned in heaven, as countless miracles attest—miracles by which Christ triumphed after the example of Gideon. For just as Gideon’s battle reached victory when the jars were broken and the lamps flashed forth (Judg. 7), so, when the bodies of martyrs were broken and miracles afterward shone at their tombs, the enemies [Col. 0746B] of Christ were terrified and began to venerate the martyrs, to imitate what they taught by believing and confessing, and at times to endure the very martyrdoms which they had previously inflicted. Thus reproach and contempt were taken away from the martyrs who sought testimonies or martyrdoms.

Then heretics arose, teaching doctrines contrary to sound faith. Against their errors blessed confessors sought out in the authoritative Scriptures testimonies to the truth. They too were often exposed to reproach and contempt when heretics gained strength, as ecclesiastical history bears witness. Therefore each of them rightly prayed at that time, saying: “Take away from me reproach and contempt, because I have sought out your testimonies,” by which I might defend the integrity of the faith—by which I, the Catholic Church, have scarcely been preserved, whether through martyrs or confessors, [Col. 0746C] through carefully sought testimonies. Nor is it surprising that, struggling against such persons, I have been endangered.

**VERSE 23.** For princes sat and spoke against me. If any common person had resisted me, I should certainly have endured it, while some prince defended me. But the conflict was made more grievous for me because princes—holding chief seats or thrones in the world—sat down with delay and deliberation and openly spoke against me the things they had devised in secret: for example, Nero, Decius, Diocletian, and the other pagan rulers defending idols; and after them Constantius, Julian, Valens, and the other rulers who defended heretics. [Col. 0746D] They indeed spoke against me, intending to oppress me; but your servant—for example, the martyr Laurence, the confessor Augustine, or any like them—was exercised in your ordinances, from which the human and diabolical enemy labors to draw him back. Yet they were unable to prevail; indeed, they will provide me assistance for my exercise in your ordinances.

**VERSE 24.** For while they assail me, your testimonies are my meditation, and your ordinances my counsel. Among these, the greatest is to love one’s enemies and to call them back from errors through the testimonies of truth. This frequently happened when tyrants and heretics were converted through the preaching of testimonies and the ordinances of truth, while in times of manifest persecution both the testimonies shone in words [Col. 0747A] and the ordinances in deeds. My bitterness was indeed exceedingly bitter in the time of pagans defending their idols; but it was more bitter in the times of heretics attacking the truth of the faith with a certain appearance of plausibility. But now, behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter, in the time of false brethren and household enemies, who confess God with their voice but deny him by their deeds. For many among them, elevated to rule, have sat down—that is, they have gained lofty seats or thrones by ambition—and such men have spoken against me, most often by attacking the integrity of faith, but more frequently by corrupting the purity of ecclesiastical government. They seek their own gains, not God’s; they are lovers of themselves, covetous, arrogant, insolent, without fidelity, without mercy, disobedient to the rules and precepts of the holy Fathers, lovers of pleasures more than of God [Col. 0747B] (2 Tim. 3:3–4). The Apostle foretold that such people would arise in the last days, when dangerous times were at hand. And behold, such persons have now not only multiplied beyond the number of the good, but even hold the chief seats in the Church, oppressing the good by such cunning “that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error” (Matt. 24:24). Yet the one who is truly elect is exercised in your ordinances among such people and under such people. His is the cry in singing psalms: “For princes sat and spoke against me,” [Col. 0747C] approving entrenched evils rather than unfamiliar goods. But your servant, on the contrary, was exercised in condemning entrenched evils and commending unfamiliar goods, as truth shows in your ordinances, attested by the Law and Prophets, by the Gospel and Apostles, and by the orthodox Fathers.

For your testimonies are my meditation: meditated upon, they soften sorrows and adorn character. And your ordinances are my counsel, among which faith, hope, and love stand preeminent. By these three a person is reconciled and justified to the supreme Trinity, having been corrupted and alienated from God by the three contrary things: faithlessness, despair, and hatred of the good. My counsel is occupied with these against the counsels of the nations, against the thoughts [Col. 0747D] of peoples, against the counsels of princes. I know that “the Lord scatters the counsels of the nations, rejects the thoughts of peoples, and rejects the counsels of princes” (Ps. 32:10). But the counsel of the Lord remains forever. I always intend to direct my counsel according to it, so that it may accord with divine counsel and differ from the counsels of this world. For this I have become a reproach and an object of contempt, especially because, O God, I have sought out your testimonies, by which I have striven to fortify my assertions so that, once established in truth through them, my adversaries could not contradict them. I have become a reproach and contempt to these adversaries because they despise the testimonies of truth—especially those who seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2).

[Col. 0748A] Therefore I continually cry: “Take away from me reproach and contempt,” as you took reproach and contempt away from the holy martyrs and confessors who sought out your testimonies. For they are now in glory, and their memory flourishes even among human beings, while their opponents have been condemned and refuted. For example, the name of Simon Peter flourishes and gives forth a sweet fragrance; the name of Simon Magus smokes and stinks. The martyr Laurence rejoices in heaven, crowned with an unfading crown; the impious Decius suffers in hell, burning in unquenchable fire. Athanasius the confessor, the Catholic defender of the faith, exults; the name of Arius, disturber of that faith, stinks. Thus reproach has been removed from the holy martyrs and confessors who sought out your testimonies.

So, when the uncircumcised Philistine Goliath had been overcome [Col. 0748B] (1 Sam. 17), who had reproached the ranks of the living God—overcome, I say, by the pastoral staff of the holy cross through the blessed martyrs, and also by the sling and stone through the holy confessors, wise slingers—reproach was taken away from the true David, whom that Philistine had despised because he himself was strongly armed with the weapons of tyrants. But our champion advanced prepared to battle against him with pastoral instruments alone, in order to remove reproach and contempt from Israel; and this indeed came to pass.

But what have we gained? We escaped the mouths of lions raging with tyrannical violence and heretical deceit. Nevertheless, we are still “in the midst of lions’ cubs” (Ps. 56:5). Are they not lions’ cubs who, though they neither worship idols [Col. 0748C] nor pervert the faith, nevertheless corrupt good morals through their most wicked conversations, introducing sects of destruction built not upon the rock of truth but upon the sand of falsehood and perverse custom? They have strengthened this custom not by divine authority but by their own, having usurped to themselves power of rule over the Church. For the princes of such people—bishops, abbots, provosts, archdeacons, deans, parish priests in name only—have sat down and occupied lofty seats, and spoke against me whenever I attacked their perverse customs. While they sat against me and proceeded at leisure, I labored as one standing, because, while they occupied ecclesiastical resources, poverty oppressed me, so that I continually [Col. 0748D] said: “But I am needy and poor; O God, help me” (Ps. 69:6).

Accordingly, because of the imminence of excessive poverty—that want of which Job says: “Want shall go before his face,” namely the face of Leviathan or Behemoth (Job 41:13)—I became an object of mockery, reproach, and contempt in the sight of princes speaking against me and sitting for this purpose, that is, acting at leisure. What is this want that goes before the face of Antichrist? Unless I am mistaken, it is the scarcity of virtues and virtuous men. As these become rare in the Church, or fail because of extreme want, the rule of the wicked prevails, in which Antichrist already works the mystery of iniquity.

To what, then, shall we compare the reproach or contempt [Col. 0749A] by which the Church, or any ecclesiastical person, constrained by want, is burdened by evil people abounding in number of persons and abundance of goods, having become “a reproach to the prosperous and a contempt to the proud” (Ps. 123:4)? Certainly to the reproach suffered by blessed Job in his want, whether from his wife or from his burdensome friends, those comforters who mocked his former life and did not sympathize with his misery as they ought (Job 2 and 4); or certainly to the contempt suffered by the holy man Tobias, likewise mocked by his wife and friends, as though blindness and poverty had befallen him because of wickedness (Tob. 2). The most holy king Hezekiah also endured such reproach when Rabshakeh, the messenger of the king of the Assyrians, was sent to him. “And now,” he says, [Col. 0749B] “give yourself to my lord, and I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able to provide riders for them from among your own” (4 Kgs. 18:23). Surely by speaking these and other proud words he reproached the king, then hard pressed, for the small number of men who could be riders of horses, while he himself boasted of the multitude of men and armies fighting against Jerusalem.

But you, God of Israel, took away reproach and contempt from blessed Job by restoring his health and doubling his lost possessions (Job 42:10). From Tobias too you so took away reproach as to restore the light of his eyes and grant him an abundance of things necessary for this present life, together with the most certain expectation and hope of future goods (Tob. 11:15). You also delivered King Hezekiah [Col. 0749C] from reproach and contempt by sending your angel to aid him; in the night the angel struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand men from the army of the king of the Assyrians around Jerusalem, which he was then besieging (4 Kgs. 19:35).

Should not, then, similar consolations be expected and hoped for amid the similar reproaches and contempt by which the Church is now oppressed? Therefore I say: “Take away from me reproach and contempt,” acting toward me in such a way that those who hate me may see and be confounded, because you, Lord, have helped me more than the aforesaid men, heralds of truth. For behold, here is one greater than Job, Hezekiah, or Tobias—namely Christ. Although in this dangerous time there is great [Col. 0749D] scarcity, both in the small number of men who can be riders of horses, that is, rulers of foolish people, and in the lack of resources set apart for the worship of religion, nevertheless the cry of the Church daily saying, “Take away from me reproach and contempt,” must be believed one day to be heard in such a manner that the enemies of the Church will have no occasion to boast against her concerning their multitude of men. For more are with us than with them, as Elisha showed his servant, and as the king of the Assyrians discovered when, after the angel struck down a great part of the men in whom he had boasted, he lost them (4 Kgs. 6); he himself departed in confusion from the siege of Jerusalem, bearing reproach and contempt, according to Isaiah’s prophecy: “The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and mocked you; behind you she has shaken her head” [Col. 0750A] (Isa. 37:22).

Likewise, while enemies of the Church boast that they possess its resources in tithes and other stipends of the religious soldiery, holy Church, desolate like Job or Tobias, should not despair of consolation against such an abomination of desolation, long standing in the holy place according to Daniel’s prophecy (Dan. 9:27). For every church built in God’s honor and enriched by the offerings of the faithful, especially by tithes, is a holy place. And while the resources consecrated to God are used in service of the devil and Antichrist, a great abomination of desolation stands in the holy place. Whoever sees this, according to the Lord’s warning, if he is upon the roof—that is, in the lofty resolve of religious life—must not go down to take anything from the house (Matt. 24:17), that is, he must despise the gains of this [Col. 0750B] world and not descend from on high to what is low in order to acquire such things. Such descent is made by those who seek human favor by flattering the rich and do not, as they ought, rebuke their sins, imitating Elijah or John the Baptist.

Yet the word of the Lord has not failed, promising that before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes, he will send Elijah the prophet, who shall turn the heart of fathers to children and the heart of children to their fathers (Mal. 4). When this has happened—whether Elijah comes in his own person, as many expect and as common report widely declares, or whether heavenly grace’s rain is obtained in the spirit and power of Elijah through lawful sacrifice, after the unlawful sacrifice has first been rejected—we believe and hope that the prayer of the Church saying, “Take away [Col. 0750C] from me reproach and contempt, because I have sought out your testimonies,” will be heard. For princes sat, offering sacrifice unlawfully, and spoke against me. But your servant was exercised in your ordinances. For your testimonies are my meditation, by which I discover that no one can serve God and Mammon. Therefore your ordinances are my counsel, whose sum is that, aided by your grace, I should always strive to serve you alone, desiring that those too may be justified and glorified with me—those through whose reproaches and contempt I became an object of mockery, especially because I sought out your testimonies and was exercised in your ordinances, which, with your grace still favoring me, I do not cease to do. For your testimonies are my meditation, and your ordinances are my counsel.

## DALETH

[Col. 0750D]

**VERSE 25.** My soul has clung to the pavement; give me life according to your word. What is this? A little earlier you said: “My soul has longed to desire your ordinances,” as one wholly devoted to heavenly desires; and now you say: “My soul has clung to the pavement,” as one cast down to low things and estranged from those above. Both are true. I said the former while delighting “in the law of God according to the inward person”; I say the latter while seeing “another law in my members opposing the law of my mind” (Rom. 7:22–23). For however earnestly I exercise myself in spiritual things, I nevertheless feel the inclination of frail and mortal flesh toward these earthly things, which are to be trodden underfoot like a pavement. [Col. 0751A] Standing upon this pavement, people ought to raise their faces to heaven, which is the loftiest roof of this pavement in the vast hall of this world. Its maker and Lord stands above all things, not through local elevation but through a spiritual power, utterly present everywhere and yet most hidden: by this he fills all things without being enclosed, surrounds all things without being excluded, sustains all things without being supported underneath, and surpasses all things without being lifted up. His breadth, height, and depth contain all things, exceed all things, govern all things, and sustain all things. His breadth is love; his length, eternity; his height or loftiness, unconquerable power; his depth, inscrutable wisdom.

I have resolved always to attend to him in my manner of life—that is, in heavenly meditation—fearing him continually because of his unconquerable power and immeasurable wisdom, loving him continually because of his [Col. 0751B] love and the eternity of his love, by which he first loved and loves forever, and hates none of the things he has made. Thus I might be one of those whose voice is: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). But because of the inclination of flesh naturally planted in me, my soul has clung to the pavement. Although my soul continually longs to desire heavenly things, it cannot help desiring earthly things, at least for lawful and permitted use. Frequently exceeding these limits, it clings to the pavement as if held fast by the glue of mortality in an earthly body, already dead because of sin—that is, undoubtedly destined to die. Clinging to it, my soul itself is endangered [Col. 0751C] as though daily about to die by the death of sin; it grows exceedingly faint in a body however polished and smoothed, as if it were paved with white marble in likeness of a floor. To those who cling too much to this pavement, you, O Truth, rebuking the proud, said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear white to people, but within are full of dead men’s bones” (Matt. 23:27).

Therefore, lest my inward parts be like dead men’s bones, give me life according to your word—that is, make me live according to your commandment. For this is your commandment: “That we love one another” (John 15:12). This love is the life of the soul, because “the one who does not love remains in death.” Hence John the apostle and evangelist [Col. 0751D] says: “We know that we have passed from death to life because we love the brethren. The one who does not love remains in death” (1 John 3:14). Therefore, lest I too, while remaining in a mortal body, should remain in death, give me life according to your word, as has been said; or according to Jesus Christ, who is your Word, so that I may live in him and according to him, made from a child of wrath into a child of grace in the promised seed of Abraham. For the word of promise is this: “In your seed all tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 26:4). Again: “Look at heaven and count the stars, if you can. So shall your seed be” (ibid., 15:5). Again: “I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven” (ibid., 26:4). Clearly, the stars of heaven are known not to cling to the earthly pavement [Col. 0752A] but to the lofty firmament of heaven, like a certain ceiling of this vast hall. Therefore, in saying, “Give me life according to your word,” I desire and pray that the word of your promise concerning the brightness and loftiness of the stars may be fulfilled in me, so that, raised up from the pavement, I may shine on high. For as long as children of promise cling to the pavement, they are more rightly compared to dust or sand (Gen. 13:16; 22:17), according to the other promise that Abraham’s seed should be multiplied like the dust of the earth or the sand upon the shore of the sea. This part of the promise belongs to the children of the flesh, who glory in Abraham’s flesh. But I, desiring to be a child of faith rather than of flesh, pray that I may be given life according to your word, in which likeness to the stars is promised.

[Col. 0752B] Finally, after the slaughter of the four kings (Gen. 14) and the deliverance of Lot, Abraham’s kinsman, it was said to him: “Look up to heaven and count the stars, if you can. So shall your seed be” (Gen. 15:5). In this word of promise there was no mention of sand or dust, as in the other promises. Therefore, according to this word of yours, by which likeness to the stars was promised, I desire and pray to be given life: that I, who know myself to be dust clinging to the pavement, may become like the stars clinging to the firmament. Although many promises were spoken to Abraham, nevertheless all tribes of the earth are declared to be blessed not in many seeds but in his one seed (Gen. 28:4)—that is, some from every tribe of the earth, namely the elect predestined to eternal life and to be glorified in the resurrection. [Col. 0752C] For “as star differs from star in brightness, so also will be the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15:41): raised indeed in common from dust, but not glorified in common. “For many of those who sleep in the dust shall awake, some to eternal life and others to reproach, that they may see forever. But those who have understanding shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many unto righteousness, like stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. 12:2–3). Therefore, in that all slept in the dust, they clung as it were to the pavement; but those among them who have understanding and have instructed others in righteousness, raised up from the pavement, shall shine [Col. 0752D] like stars in the firmament—not for a time, like those stars which the dragon’s tail shall drag down to earth (Rev. 12), but through everlasting eternities, shining with the true light, which is God, and living through the true life, which likewise is God. I ask to be joined to their fellowship, saying: “Give me life according to your word,” which you spoke to Abraham our father, promising him one seed to be multiplied like the stars of heaven. For you said: “I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven” (Gen. 26:4).

If, then, by the stars of heaven you intended the angels of light, this word of promise reasonably supports the view of those who assert that as many human beings will be saved and glorified as angels remained in heaven when the apostate angels fell from it. They say that this is also supported [Col. 0753A] by what is written: “He set the boundaries of peoples according to the number of the sons of God” (Deut. 32:8), or “sons of Israel,” since it is also customary for good angels to be called sons of Israel, as the angel speaking to Tobias says that he is one of the sons of Israel (Tob. 5). If, therefore, as stated, by the stars of heaven you intended the good angels, to whom human beings predestined to eternal life are to be made equal in the multiplication of Abraham’s seed, then, praying well and rightly to you, author of this word and promise, I say: “Give life according to your word, that ‘your will may be done, as in heaven, so also on earth’” (Matt. 6:10)—as in the firmament, so also on the pavement—when as many human beings are raised from dust to eternal life as angels possess eternal life. Longing for this, I [Col. 0753B] continually say to you: “Give me life according to your word.”

The beginning of this giving of life, however, consists in confessing my sins:

**VERSE 26.** I declared my ways by the very fact that I confessed and complained that my soul had clung to the pavement, saying: “My soul has clung to the pavement.” This is the same as saying: My soul is sinful. Thus I declared my ways in a declaration brief indeed, yet sufficient before you, the judge who knows all things. I declared to you my ways—that is, my iniquities committed through my perversity—in sincere confession, grieving for the past and gladly wishing to beware in the future. And you heard me by remitting and forgiving these ways of mine. It remains, therefore, that you should teach me yours. Therefore teach me [Col. 0753C] your ordinances, which the one who observes and does them truly knows; just as, conversely, Christ is said not to have “known sin” (2 Cor. 5:21), that is, not to have done it. Therefore teach me your ordinances, since I account mine as nothing, because without you I can do nothing by which I may be justified before you. And so that I may proceed in due order among your ordinances, knowing what must be done first and what afterward:

**VERSE 27.** Instruct me in the way of your ordinances; or, as it is read in Hebrew: “Make me understand the way of your commandments.” Let me not, ignorant of mystical secrets, be led astray, like those who still think that the paschal lamb must be eaten according to the Law; or like certain people who thought that the command in the Gospel to gird the loins [Col. 0753D] (Luke 12:35), carry the cross (Matt. 16:24), and some other things spoken figuratively, must be fulfilled literally. They do not know that even the letter of the New Testament sometimes kills if the Spirit does not give it life. Therefore, lest I be deceived in such matters, I shall be exercised in your wonders. For some of your ordinances are so wonderful that the skilled reader or hearer rightly exclaims concerning them: “Wonderful are your testimonies, O Lord.” I shall be exercised in these wonders of yours through the diligent discipline of meditation, investigating what lies hidden in figures—for example, who is that lamb who took away the sins of the world (John 1:29), and how his flesh ought to be eaten with loins girded and feet shod, not boiled in water but roasted by fire (Exod. 12:11). Again, in the Gospel [Col. 0754A] one is exercised in investigating the truth concerning girded loins, lamps burning and held in the hand, and other such things to be understood mystically: what meaning in commandments of this sort builds up love (Luke 12:35). Since love is the end of the commandment, no commandment of the Lord is judged rightly understood unless its meaning is referred to building up that love which comes from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. But because some wonders of your law are either too obscure to understand or too difficult to perform:

**VERSE 28.** My soul slumbered because of weariness. For to slumber is to grow faint from the pursuit of contemplation or action, as love grows lukewarm through the vice of acedia; but to sleep is, when love has wholly grown cold and failed, to fall into the sleep of idleness, forgetfulness, and dullness. [Col. 0754B] This sleep commonly follows preceding slumber, so that one who, while slumbering, does a little good yet neglects this danger to his salvation, may, when wholly fallen asleep and oppressed by deep sleep, do no good at all. Lest this evil happen to me, strengthen me in your words, especially in those by which you warn us to keep watch: “Watch,” you say, “because you know neither the day nor the hour” (Matt. 25:13). The one who rightly believes and keeps by doing what he believes, watches. The one who keeps the eyes of the mind open to behold the true light, watches. The one who drives away from himself the darkness of torpor and negligence, watches. Strengthen me, therefore, in your words—you who say to your disciples: “Watch and pray, lest you [Col. 0754C] enter into temptation” (Mark 14:38; Matt. 24:42). Again: “Blessed is that servant whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching” (Luke 12:37). Again: “What I say to one, I say to all: Watch” (Mark 13:37). You also rebuke the sleeping disciples because “their eyes were heavy from sorrow” (Matt. 26:43). And to Peter in particular you say: “Simon, are you sleeping? Could you not watch with me one hour?” (Mark 14:37.)

If, then, your disciples, though repeatedly warned to keep watch, had their eyes weighed down with sorrow and could not yet keep watch because they were sad, what wonder is it that my soul dozed from weariness together with sorrow, because, though instructed by your words, it had not yet felt itself strengthened in those same words of yours? For indeed [Col. 0754D] your apostles, although taught by your words through your mouth, could not keep watch, not yet strengthened by the Holy Spirit, who had not yet been given to them because you, the giver of that Spirit, had not yet been glorified. But after you had been glorified by the glory of the resurrection and strengthened them by breathing your Spirit upon them, and, further, after you had been glorified by the glory of the ascension and confirmed them by sending the Paraclete, from then on they were able to keep watch; and to keep watch in those praises and services of yours was sweet to them, not wearisome. For the sorrow that had weighed down their eyes had now passed, when it was the hour and power of darkness, while you, the Sun of righteousness, still lay hidden beneath the cloud of mortality and had not yet sent forth the rays of your powers.

Therefore, just as you then made them glad by the visible glory of resurrection and ascension [Col. 0755A] and strengthened them by giving your Spirit, so too, I ask, strengthen me in your words, by which you teach me to keep watch. For you teach in vain unless you strengthen me in your words, as you strengthened your apostles and made them watchful by your strengthening. For they are the watchmen who guard the city and rouse others to keep watch, saying, for example: “Be sober and keep watch, because your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Pet. 5:8). Likewise: “Be prudent and keep watch in prayers” (1 Pet. 4:7). Likewise: “Keep watch; stand firm in the faith; act manfully and be strengthened. Let all that you do be done in charity” (1 Cor. 16:13). These and similar words, whether yours or those of your servants, are nonetheless yours, because you speak in them [Col. 0755B]; yet they sound in vain in my ears unless you strengthen me in them. Indeed, from knowledge of your words—which I neither keep nor can keep—I am afflicted with weariness because sorrow weighs down my eyes, especially when the hour and power of darkness draws near in tribulations or evil temptations. Therefore, lest I be swallowed up by excessive weariness and sorrow, and, because I have dozed, fall utterly asleep, I ask: strengthen me in your words, by removing evils and granting goods.

By removing evils:

**VERSE 29.** Remove from me the way of iniquity; by granting goods, graciously grant me your law. You gave the law of Moses, which shows sins but by no means heals them; now give your law, the law of faith, which heals the wounds shown and inflamed by the law of works (Exod. 20; Deut. [Col. 0755C] 28). For I did not know that concupiscence was sin unless the law had said: “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17). For through the law comes knowledge of sin; and this knowledge, without grace that saves and helps, is a way of iniquity. For through the commandment—even though holy and just—sin revives unless it is healed by grace, which freely justifies the ungodly and magnifies the godly. “Those whom he justified, he also magnified” (Rom. 8:30).
