He justifies, however, not through the righteousness of works, but through the righteousness of faith in him who justifies the ungodly and makes godly persons out of the ungodly, more by mercy than by justice. For in the law of works, which gravely punishes evil deeds, there is indeed the justice of God, who commands rightly and punishes rightly. But in the law of faith, by which one believes in him who justifies the ungodly, the mercy of God coming to aid triumphs over judgment, when one who ought to have been condemned by justice is saved through mercy.

Therefore remove from me the way of iniquity, which has been worn by those who were under the law and under fear of the law, possessing only the spirit of slavery in fear. And graciously grant me your law—not by giving again the spirit of slavery in fear, but the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15). For I am dead through the weariness in which my soul dozed, like one sleeping in this respect: poised between the law of God and the law of the members, it neither fully kept watch by obeying the law of God, nor, oppressed by deep sleep, voluntarily served the law of the members by following its concupiscences.

[Col. 0756A] Yet while the soul sleeps in that fashion, the mortal body does not sleep but is sick unto death. The Apostle also calls it dead because of sin, which is naturally implanted in its members. Therefore he says: “Because no good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh, but the evil which I hate” (Rom. 7:17). Thus, in dying flesh, in which evil lies close at hand, I who am dead cannot be raised by the staff of the law, which strikes sinners harshly on the way of iniquity but nevertheless does not free them from that way.

Therefore, asking and seeking grace, I say: Remove from me the way of iniquity, and graciously grant me your law. Make it so that, as another Elisha—or rather, you, the true Elisha, whose name means “God’s salvation”—having removed the staff of the law, which, laid upon the dead man, neither removes death nor confers life (4 Kings 4), you yourself, living and Life, may bend over me who am dead, placing your eyes upon [Col. 0756B] my eyes, your mouth upon my mouth, and your hands upon my hands. Thus, enlivened by you through grace, may I see what is true and what must be done; may I teach these things to others with a gracious mouth, believing in my heart unto righteousness and confessing with my mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10:9).

And lest either the faith of my enlightened heart or the confession of my opened mouth, sweetened by your kiss, should be empty, may your hands joined to my hands work through me in such a way, and make me work, grace cooperating, that both from reason enlightened through faith, from grace poured out upon my lips, and from the bright evidence of good works, it may be evident to me and evident to Mother Church that I, her son, who was dead, live—not through the staff of the law, whose letter kills, but through the life-giving Spirit breathed into me while dead from your mouth [Col. 0756C] placed upon mine (2 Cor. 3:6).

When this Spirit, through the three things mentioned above—namely, eyes seeing clearly, a mouth confessing rightly, and hands performing what is right—bears witness to my spirit that I am a son of God, having become a member of the only-begotten Son of God, I shall glory in him and give thanks, saying:

**VERSES 30–31.** I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments. I have clung to your testimonies, O Lord. This I say, and shall always say, in thanksgiving, adding indeed this prayer: Do not put me to shame—with that shame by which those will be confounded who glory in your gifts because they have performed many mighty works in your name and prophesied in your name, to whom you will reply: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; [Col. 0756D] I do not know you” (Luke 13:27). Likewise, the foolish virgins who have no oil in their vessels will suffer great shame when they are separated from the company of the wise virgins (Matt. 25:2). The wicked and slothful servant too will suffer great shame when the talent entrusted to him is taken away and he himself is cast into eternal fire (ibid., 26). Similarly, one who enters the wedding feast and is discovered not to have a wedding garment will be gravely confounded when, separated from the wedding banquet, “with hands and feet bound, he is cast into outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8:12).

In this way, O most merciful God, do not put me to shame. But I shall be most gravely confounded if, when your grace deserts me, I abandon the way of truth which I have chosen [Col. 0757A]; if I someday consign to forgetfulness your judgments, which I have not forgotten; if, torn away from your testimonies to which I have clung, I once more cling to the pavement, as before, when grieving I was compelled to confess and complain, saying: “My soul has clung to the pavement.” I ask: do not put me to shame by abandoning me in your wrath; rather, help me in your mercy so that, running well in the way of truth that I have chosen, always stretching forward toward the goal, I may arrive there and, my race completed, receive the prize of the crown.

For by sweet experience I have learned that the way of perfection is neither narrow nor difficult to run for anyone whose heart has been enlarged in charity. For I too, many times:

**VERSE 32.** I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart. Therefore, since I should not have run [Col. 0757B] along the narrow path unless you had enlarged my heart, I do not attribute to myself or ascribe to my own powers—which are nothing—that I chose the way of truth, that I did not forget your judgments, that I clung to your testimonies, or that I ran the way of your commandments. For it came about by your free gift that I could and did do all these things, when you enlarged my heart, formerly narrow and constricted by fear of the law that punishes sins.

You truly enlarged it when you promised mercy to the merciful, saying: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke 6:37). I heard these two works of mercy—forgiving and giving—and therefore, as if on two feet, I ran the way of your commandments, forgiving quickly and giving as you commanded, while hoping that I too might be forgiven and given to as you promised. But he does not run on this way whom that sorrow makes sluggish in forgiving or giving, which the Apostle forbids when he says: “Not from sorrow or from necessity” (2 Cor. 9:7). Rather, he runs who gives with simplicity and has mercy with cheerfulness, “not from sorrow or necessity” produced by fear, but from the joy of charity; hoping for eternal things in exchange for temporal things, not lukewarmly or slowly, but eagerly and promptly, with good and ready will in that charity which never fails.

In the preceding two groups of eight verses, over which the two Hebrew letters **DALETH** and **GIMEL** are inscribed, a fitting construction of these two letters presents itself. [Col. 0757D] For **DALETH** is interpreted “fullness,” and **GIMEL**, “of tablets.” What then is the fullness of the tablets but love, the fullness of the law? That is, the law first written on tablets of stone, and then on the tablets of believers’ hearts, with the addition of perfection, which could not be preached to the ancients. For the ancients scarcely accepted the saying: “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20:13). Likewise: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (Lev. 19:18). But the new people are commanded not to be angry with a brother and to love not only friends but enemies as well (Matt. 5:43). Such love is the fullness of the law, or of the tablets containing the law.

For the preservation of this law prayer is made in the following group of eight verses, where it says: “Set before me, O Lord, the law, the way of your justifications.” [Col. 0758A] The letter prefixed is that which among the Hebrews is called:

**HE.**

**VERSE 33.** Set before me, O Lord, the law. I ask that the law be set before me, or imposed upon me—not the old law, which is not laid down for the righteous but for the unrighteous and disobedient, because, written on stones, it is burdensome to bear. Indeed, even memory itself, retaining its commandments inscribed without assisting grace, presses and oppresses like a stone. Therefore do not set before me this law that burdens and does not help; rather, set before me the law that is the way of your justifications, which above I also called “the way of your commandments,” in which I ran when you enlarged my heart.

Set before me this law, this way, by writing it with your finger in my heart, so that, having once begun to run in it, I may not fail in my course [Col. 0758B] or ever stray from this way of yours, but may always seek it. You have set before the rivers the law of their course back to their source, to the fountainhead of their origin, and they always seek it by their natural course and motion. Likewise, you have set before the sun, moon, and other stars the law of their return to the same point by a fixed and irrevocable revolution, and they always seek it. Moreover, for the four rational rivers of paradise, to which you commanded that the whole earth be watered by the preaching of the holy Gospel, you set before them the law that is the way of your justifications—not the justifications of the old law.

Those holy Evangelists, knowing that no flesh is justified through the law, in which there was only knowledge of sin (Rom. 3:20), diligently sought the way of your justifications always—that is, throughout every time of their lives. So too those lights of yours, to whom you said: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14), perceived that the law set before them was the way of your justifications, when you said: “I have appointed you that you may go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain; and whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give you” (John 15:16).

For this utterance of your gracious mouth was for them the establishment of the new law, by which, strengthened, they might always seek the way of your justifications by going and bearing spiritual fruit. Thus the lights which we see in heaven bear temporal fruit by their course, producing good weather as the sun traverses all the signs of heaven through which spring, summer, and the other fruitful seasons are regulated, while seeds received into the bosom of the earth grow in their season and ripen through the benefit of the sun, which continually warms the earth with its heat as it proceeds according to the law set before it. So too the spiritual lights, through whose teaching the Church shines like sun and moon, are directed by the law you have set before them in the way of your justifications, which they always seek in order to bear fruit and that their fruit may remain.

Knowing that these things have been, or are to be, fulfilled in others, I pray that the same may be done also in me, saying: Set before me, O Lord, the law, the way of your justifications, and I shall seek it always, advancing from day to day and from strength to strength—always, that is, as long as I live in the flesh; or always, that is, tirelessly, as angels always desire [Col. 0759A] to look into Christ. Although they always have him present with them, they nevertheless always desire him, because they love him whom they possess and always desire to love him. So too, set by you in the way of your justifications in order that I may seek it and bear fruit, although I have it present, I shall nevertheless always seek it by always loving it.

But lest the toil of seeking should be fruitless through failure to find:

**VERSE 34.** Give me understanding, and I shall search out your law. You have set a law for the waters, that they should not pass beyond their bounds (Jer. 5:22). You have set a law for the lights of heaven, that they should not exceed their limits (Ps. 103:9). And they, being without life and sensation, have no understanding and cannot receive the eternal reason by which they are governed. But spiritual rivers and lights have understanding of their course in the way of your justifications, knowing and understanding by what author they are directed—whether by the pillar of fire in the night of adversity (Exod. 13:21) or by the pillar of cloud in the day of prosperity (Num. 14:19). For they understand Christ as the pillar of cloud because of the flesh he assumed, and as the pillar of fire because of his divinity. Keeping him continually before their eyes, they do not stray from the way of your justifications, O God who loves righteousness.

Therefore, lest I stray from the way of your justifications, give me understanding as you gave it to them; and I shall search out your law as they do, and I shall keep it with all my heart, as they do. I shall search out your law so as to reach its inner meaning, upon which “the whole law [Col. 0759C] and the prophets hang” (Matt. 22:10); and I shall keep it with all my heart—that is, I shall love “God with all my heart, with all my soul, and with all my strength” (Mark 12:33), and my neighbor as myself. But because I cannot do this by myself:

**VERSE 35.** Lead me in the path of your commandments. Though this path is narrow to one unwilling and beginning, when you lead me it becomes broad to me when willing, because I have willed it—and I have received this very willing from you, so that I will what I formerly did not will. But lest my will grow lukewarm:

**VERSE 36.** Incline my heart to your testimonies. As a face bent downward looks more carefully where it is stepping than one turned upward, so a heart bowed down by humility looks after itself better than one proud and lifted up in vanity. Therefore, that I may look well after myself in the steps of my conduct, [Col. 0759D] incline my heart to your testimonies, which have been made exceedingly credible by your own witness—you who cannot lie—declaring how you wish to be served: not for a reward, as hirelings serve, but freely, as good sons serve their father. Therefore, because I desire to be a son and not a hireling, I continually pray: Incline my heart—that is, my will—to your testimonies, and not to avarice, whether of praise, human favor, or earthly gain. And lest I should ever be caught by its desire:

**VERSE 37.** Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity—that is, lest they love or desire transient things which quickly fail and vanish away. Consequently, those who serve God for such things become vain. Therefore, lest I become vain, turn away my eyes lest they see vanity, but let them see vanity’s opposite: truth. Let my eyes see and love this truth, which, though invisible, is greatly desirable in the word of truth, promising not empty and transient goods, as the old law does, but true and abiding goods: namely, to see God and the Son of God. One of these is promised to the pure in heart, the other to peacemakers, when Truth says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8); likewise: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (ibid., 9). Despisers of vanity will attain such promises of truth by the way of truth, which is also the way, the truth, and the life. In this way of yours, which is also life, give me life; for since it is the vine and I the branch, I have no life except in that vine, which says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Lest I fail from this life:

[Col. 0760B] **VERSES 38–39.** Establish for your servant your word in your fear; that is, make me serve you as your word teaches, which is established only in one who acts upon it and “serves you in fear and rejoices with trembling” (Ps. 2:11). For holy fear, enduring for ever and ever (Ps. 18:10), is the immovable foundation on which your word is established; and your word itself is the discipline of fear, lest there be zeal not according to knowledge if it is not ruled by the word, or sloth in the knowledge of the word if holy fear is lacking. Those who lack this fear either scarcely receive your word, O God, or receive it negligently, and easily turn aside from it as from fables. Lest this happen to me, O God, I knock continually at your ears with prayers, saying: Establish for your servant your word in your fear.

Yet among all things that I fear with your holy fear, the reproach which I have suspected troubles me most; for suspicion is a most serious fault, since it thinks otherwise than the truth is, whether concerning itself or another. For example, when a person thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself (Gal. 6:3), and thereby deserves truth’s reproach: such suspicion will be reproached to him by the judgment of truth. This will by no means be pleasant to such persons, because they will not be freed from the harsh word by which you will say to each such one: “You wickedly thought that I would be like you” (Ps. 49:21), approving the falsehood of your suspicion. It is not so. Rather, I shall rebuke you and set you before your face, to your reproach, so that you may see [Col. 0760D] it always.

For when truth is laid bare by your judgments, great reproach will be pleasant to those who thought otherwise than the truth proved to be. Your judgments are pleasant to lovers of truth, just as this visible light is pleasant to pure and healthy eyes, whereas it is harsh and wholly unpleasant to diseased and bleary eyes. I ask: cut away this reproach of mine, which I have suspected, by teaching and enabling me not to judge otherwise, either concerning myself or concerning anything at all, than the judgment of truth judges it to be; for your judgments are pleasant, being free from the bitterness of suspicion and very different from the rash judgments of men.

Because human secrets cannot be seen, room is given to rash suspicion. Therefore, when the Lord had commanded his disciples not to perform their righteousness before people with a view to transient reward [Col. 0761A]—for they could suspect others of acting in this way—he immediately added: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged; do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned” (Luke 6:37). By these words the reproach of rash suspicion was cut away from the disciples; and I too ask that it be cut away from me, continually saying: Cut away my reproach, which I have suspected, contrary to your judgments, because your judgments are pleasant, whereas the judgments of suspicion are bitter.

Alternatively: examining myself through your pleasant and true judgments, even when “I am conscious of nothing against myself,” I know that “in this I am not justified” (1 Cor. 4:4). Hence I do not judge even myself righteous, because I have suspected the future reproach of truth. I ask that this reproach be cut away and that I be so justified [Col. 0761B] that no suspicion remains in me of such a reproach as will befall those who consider themselves righteous by their own judgment, when your pleasant judgments pronounce something altogether different concerning them.

Therefore I confess to you, judge of hearts and knower of secrets, not only the fault which I know but even that which I suspect in myself, because your judgments are pleasant to those who judge and accuse themselves: you judge them not to be judged or condemned, because they judge themselves. Those judgments of yours are also pleasant by which we “are judged and corrected, so that we may not be condemned with this world” (1 Cor. 11:32). Hence you scourge every son whom you receive and discipline those whom you love, so that by your pleasant and purgative judgments they may escape the judgment [Col. 0761C] of condemnation. Therefore, by such purgative judgments, like sharp sickles, I ask: cut away my reproach which I have suspected.

For as though by the sickle of true judgment, my reproach is cut away—the reproach which I have suspected concerning others—when others also suspect evils concerning me which they do not know, provided that charity is in me: charity which is not provoked by such suspicions, nor does it envy those who envy it (1 Cor. 13:13); but amid all it bears and endures, it itself never fails. Desiring this charity, therefore:

**VERSE 40.** Behold, I have desired your commandments, which are gathered into the two commandments of charity, on which the whole law and the prophets hang. I have desired these commandments of yours, and behold, I desire openly: I desire to love you with all my heart, all my soul, and all my strength, and [Col. 0761D] my neighbor as myself. Yet because through myself I fail and die away from the vigor of this charity, give me life in your righteousness—yours, I say, not mine, for I have no righteousness or equity from myself, being weighed down and killed by much iniquity.

Therefore I say: Give me life in your righteousness—that is, in Christ, who “has become for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30). He, then, is also your righteousness, because he is God equal to you, God and Father, in justice. He is also my righteousness, given and made for me, because he is man equally with me: God with you, man with me. In this your righteousness—that is, in Christ—give me life, that I may live by the life who is himself, this being required by your righteousness itself: for he, owing nothing to death, died so that I might live. “For as [Col. 0762A] all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:22). This is worthy and just, equitable and saving: that as death came to many through one person’s disobedience, so life comes to many through one person’s obedience. It is rational equity that, as death came through one, so life should come through one. In this your righteousness give me life.

**VAU.**

The following eight verses among the Hebrews begin with this sixth letter, in which prayer is made for the coming of the Savior, who is everlasting mercy. These eight verses are joined to the preceding set of eight in this manner: “In your righteousness give me life.”

**VERSE 41.** And let your mercy come upon me, O Lord, without which I cannot live, because your commandments, which I have desired, cannot be fulfilled without the mercy of helping grace. Therefore I ask that your mercy may come upon me, O Lord, knowing that “your mercy is better than lives” (Ps. 62:4). I do not now ask for that mercy by which you “have mercy upon all,” you “who hate none of the things which you have made” (Wis. 11:24), since this mercy is denied to no creature and never will be denied, and thus need not be invoked by prayers. Rather, I ask for that mercy which is your salvation, that it may come upon me and become my head, as it is written: “Christ is the head of the man” (1 Cor. 11:3); and as the head governs the members, so may my life be governed by him and in him according to your word—that is, according to [Col. 0762C] your free promises, by which you freely promised that Christ would come and that in him all tribes of the earth would be blessed (Ps. 71:17). Let this mercy of yours, this salvation of yours, come upon me, I pray, protecting me mercifully and savingly, as a hen warms her chicks.

**VERSE 42.** And I shall answer those who reproach me with a word: that is, believing with the heart unto righteousness and confessing with the mouth unto salvation, not only among faithful hearers who desire the good word to be poured forth to them, but also among wicked reproachers. I shall not return abuse for abuse or reproach for reproach; rather, I shall answer with a rational word, although it is by no means acceptable to them. For one must not always keep silence against the wicked, provided that they are capable of receiving a word by which, even if they are not convinced so as to yield, they may be constrained to fall silent; nor will they seem superior to themselves when they are rationally persuaded either to believe and yield, or to believe even if they do not yield. But where neither of these is hoped for, speech is given in vain. Therefore, before such people, care must be taken not to cast pearls before swine or give what is holy to dogs (Matt. 7:6). But I shall answer a word to my reproachers because I hoped in your sayings, in which you teach that truth must be confessed before people. For you say: “Whoever confesses me before people, I too shall confess before my Father” (Matt. 10:32).

Alternatively: to those who reproach me with the disgrace of the cross, [Col. 0763A] I shall answer with the Word that “was in the beginning with God” (John 1:2). To those who reproach me because I worship a man, “the carpenter’s son” (Matt. 13:55), I shall answer that I worship the Word of God, the natural Son of God the omnipotent Creator, the one true God alone together with the Father and the Holy Spirit (Luke 4:8), because I have hoped in your sayings, who say: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 6:13).

**VERSE 43.** And I ask this: do not take the word of this truth from my mouth, by permitting the birds of heaven to take the seed of the word from my heart (Luke 8:5). For when it has thus been taken from the heart, it will consequently also be taken from the mouth, as you say: “Why do you recount my justices and take my covenant [Col. 0763B] into your mouth? But you hate discipline,” and so forth (Ps. 49:16–17).

On this passage blessed Gregory says in Book XI of *Job* [ch. 15]:

> When a priest does not do the good things which he speaks, speech itself is also taken from him, lest he dare to say what he does not perform. Hence it is said: “But God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my justices and take my covenant into your mouth?” Thus he now prays, saying: “Do not take the word of truth from my mouth.” For he considers that the omnipotent Lord gives the word of truth to those who do it and takes it away from those who do not. Therefore, what else did the man seek who asked that the word not be taken from his mouth, except the grace of good action? As though he plainly said: [Col. 0763C] “Do not allow me to stray from good work, lest, when I lose the order of living well, I lose the rectitude of speaking.” And often a teacher who dares to teach what he neglects to do, when he has ceased to speak the good things that he disdained to perform, begins to teach his subjects the evil things that he does, so that, by the just judgment of almighty God, the man who refuses to have a good life may no longer possess a tongue for good. Thus, when his mind is inflamed with love of earthly things, he always speaks of earthly things. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. 12:34). “The good man brings forth good things from a good treasure, and the evil man evil things” (ibid., 35). Hence John says: “They are of the world, and therefore they speak of the world” (John 15:3).

Alternatively: Do not take away—that is, do not permit to be taken—from [Col. 0763D] my mouth the word of truth which I answered to those reproaching me, and which I acquired as a precious pearl through difficult trading and bought after selling everything (Matt. 13:46). Do not take this from my mouth by allowing me to fall into the fault of denial; or, if you permit me to deny you, as you permitted Peter, do not permit it utterly—or, as it is read in Hebrew, “exceedingly,” or as another translation has it, “very greatly.”

For the word of truth is taken from the mouth very greatly or exceedingly when it is also taken from the heart; or when one who denies the truth with the mouth doubles the fault by denying it also in deeds; or, worst of all, when one perseveres in fault. But Peter, although he denied with his mouth for a time—when, that is, it was the hour and power of darkness—nevertheless retained Christ, the word of truth, [Col. 0764A] in his heart, like another Hushai, David’s friend, who denied King David with his mouth but loved him in his heart, although he outwardly adhered to David’s adversary Absalom. This was very useful to King David himself, because through that good counsellor the counsel of Ahithophel, who truly hated King David, was rendered foolish (2 Kings 15:11). Likewise, through the apostle Peter, who by his denial had secretly entered into death, Judas’s plan was rendered foolish, because the word of truth which Peter retained in his heart swiftly rose again, as though from the vein of heartfelt love, to the lip of the fountain—that is, to the mouth of Peter, who quickly came to his senses and wept bitterly (Matt. 26:75; Luke 22:62).

May it therefore happen to me as it did to Peter: if ever, which may God avert, I deny you, may I quickly come to my senses after his example and not lose the word of truth utterly—that is, very greatly—while your judgments come to my aid, by which you chastise and rebuke those whom you love. Thus you also rebuked Peter, saying to him: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14:31). You said this to him in plain words when he was endangered in the storm at sea; but in the storm of Jewish tumult you said the same thing in reality, when you looked upon Peter and, by your look, stirred him to bitter weeping, as though saying: “O you of little faith, why did you deny me?”

Thus Peter escaped the judgment of condemnation because he hoped exceedingly in your judgments. For he did not repent despairing of pardon, as Judas did, who said: “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 2:7), and perished in the noose of despair together with his forerunner Ahithophel. But Peter hoped well in your judgments, trusting that he would not be punished or judged unto condemnation, since, by your gift, he judged and punished himself. For, as the Apostle says, “If we judged ourselves, we certainly would not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31). Indeed, the judgments by which we judge ourselves are your judgments, since they are given by you.

In these your judgments I, David—or I, any psalmist—have hoped exceedingly, because your rebukes do not take hope away but increase it. Therefore, in your judgments, by which you rebuked me either inwardly and secretly or outwardly and openly, I have hoped exceedingly, knowing that you can and are wont, beyond what we ask or understand, to show mercy to one who humbly submits to your judgments and corrections, weeps bitterly amid them, [Col. 0764D] and resolves upon future caution—as I too, instructed by your scourges and judgments, resolve, saying:

**VERSE 44.** And I shall keep your law always, for ever and ever; that is, I shall keep charity, which is the fullness of the law and, because it never fails, will remain always, for ever and ever, in the elect among both human beings and angels. What I say, “always,” I explain and make clear by what follows: “for ever and ever,” because charity, the fullness of the law, is kept by the saints both in this age and in the age to come.

**VERSE 45.** And I walked in spaciousness. Thus far are the words of one praying; now come the words of one narrating, as though, having obtained all that he asked, he confesses in praise of God what the Lord [Col. 0765A] has made him. Note the unusual and apparently inconsequent connection. He does not say, according to what precedes, in the future tense: “And I shall keep” and “I shall walk,” or optatively, “may I walk”; rather, so that he may be understood to have been heard, he turns the prayer into thanksgiving, saying: “And I walked in spaciousness.”

As if he said: I am not ungrateful for your grace, by whose gift I walked in the spaciousness of charity enlarged even to loving enemies, or even to that breadth of which “no one has greater”—namely, “that one lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Though I was not perfect in this spaciousness, nevertheless by daily advances I walked with those who, forgetting what lies behind and stretching themselves toward what lies ahead, go from strength to strength. I walked with them. This was evident from the fact that I sought out your commandments, desiring through the breadth of knowledge to be enlarged into the breadth of charity. And having received whatever small knowledge I had of your commandments, which I had diligently sought out, I did not bind that talent in a napkin or bury it in the earth, but preached to others what I understood.

VERS. 46. And I spoke of your testimonies, affirming as good what I understood to be good, and as evil what I understood to be evil—not only among the common people, but even before fearsome kings—and I was not ashamed because of the scandal of the cross. Or, “I was not ashamed,” so as to believe those who reproached me. Thus I, who had previously asked that I might have a word with which to answer those who reproached me, and that the word of truth might not be taken from my mouth, afterwards, having been heard [Col. 0765C] and confirmed in the word of truth, contending for that same word, spoke of your testimonies before kings and was not ashamed. And because in much speaking sin is difficult to avoid, before I spoke, in order that I might speak what was right and speak it rightly,

VERS. 47, 48. I meditated upon your commandments with the contemplative faculty, beholding those things which I loved; and with the active faculty I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which likewise I loved by doing, just as I loved them by contemplating them, knowing that “the end of the commandment is charity” (1 Tim. 1:5). For the attainment of this charity, meditation and action concerning precept or commandment are practised together. This is indicated by the repetition by which I say twice: “which I loved”—namely, meditating upon your commandments, which I loved, and lifting up my hands to your commandments, which I loved. [Col. 0765D] But what is it to lift up one’s hands to the commandments, except to fulfil the commandments by good works for the sake of a heavenly and celestial reward? For he, as it were, lowers his hands to things below who, in doing good, seeks earthly rewards from it—whether favour, human praise, or even temporal gain. But I, whether meditating or acting and lifting up my hands to the commandments which I loved, by your grace inspiring me, shall practise both freely: that is, thinking and acting through the love by which I loved them through the Holy Spirit who was given to me. I shall practise, that is, by frequent meditation and action, so that by my works I may show what I speak and meditate upon in your justifications, that is, in your sayings: sayings by which you also are justified when you fulfil what you promised, so that you are found true; and by which you justify us [Col. 0766A] when you grant us to do what you justly command. For your justifications consist in this: that you make us do what you command—you who promise this very thing, saying through the prophet: “And I will cause you to walk in my commandments and to keep my judgments” (Ezek. 36:27). Likewise in the Gospel: “And whatever you shall ask the Father in my name, this I will do” (John 14:13). Remember this word to your servant, in which you gave me hope.

In this seventh octave is marked the seventh letter, which among the Hebrews is called

ZAIN [manuscript: ZAI].

Here, under the seventh letter, are commended seven highly praiseworthy excellences of a man steadfast in holy purpose. [Col. 0766B] The first is that he remembers the promise according to which a reward is due to one who lives rightly. The second is that, even amid adversities, he consoles himself with hope. The third is that, if he sees the ungodly prospering, he does not for that reason turn aside from the law, but avoids their contagion. The fourth is that he remembers the heavenly judgments, which have brought consolation in every age from Adam onward; otherwise he would turn aside from the law. Evil men fear human judgments, much less divine ones; but good men desire them. The fifth is to grieve over another’s fault, not over one’s own insult; indeed, he even prays for them. The sixth is that the justifications are songs to him. The seventh is that he attends to the praises of God not only by day but also by night, that is, at every time.

VERS. 49. Remember your word to your servant, in which [Col. 0766C] you gave me hope. What is your word, in which you gave me hope, except the word of the promise made to Abraham and to his seed? Surely, when you promised heavenly things to his seed in the multitude of the stars (Gen. 12, 13, 15, 22), you gave hope to me, your servant. And indeed, in yourself wholly unchangeable, you admit nothing of forgetfulness, repentance, or any kind of changeability. Nevertheless, by a moral mode of speech, by which human feeling is moved, you are said to repent when, beyond human expectation, you alter events without altering your counsel; as when you said: “It repents me that I made man upon the earth” (Gen. 6:6). You are also said to forget when you seem slow to fulfil what you promise; but to remember when you do what you promised. Hence that saying: “He has taken up Israel his child, remembering his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham [Col. 0766D] and to his seed for ever” (Luke 1:54–55). Therefore remember your word which you spoke to Abraham your servant, in which you gave hope to me your servant. That servant—indeed, your friend—was made so by believing the word of your promise, in which you gave hope also to me who believe, that I should attain the blessing which you promised to him and his seed, saying: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 28:14). Remember this word of yours—that is, quickly do what you promised, lest you seem to have forgotten your word by which you promised that all nations would be blessed, when you established Abraham himself as the father of many nations. Remember this word for me, your servant, so that the blessing may come upon me, who [Col. 0767A] am your servant: namely, one of those who say, “Behold, as the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so are our eyes upon the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us” (Ps. 122:2). To me, your servant of this kind, you gave hope that in the seed of Abraham, Christ, I should become a partaker in that promised blessing.

VERS. 50. This blessed hope consoled me in my humiliation: that humiliation by which I humbled myself, as Abraham did when he confessed himself to be ashes and dust (Gen. 18:27); or as David did when he confessed himself to be a flea and a dead dog (1 Kings [1 Sam.] 24:15); or as Mary did when she confessed herself to be a handmaid, when she was chosen to be lady of the whole world and queen of heaven (Luke 1:38). In this kind of voluntary [Col. 0767B] humility, which I observed willingly; or in that humility which, burdened by another, I endured patiently; or again in that universal humiliation by which, cast down into the misery of death and mortality, I am compelled to mourn original sin—in every such humiliation, in short—the hope of your word consoled me. By this word you bestowed grace upon the humble, such as Abraham, David, and Mary, whose humility you regarded; and through your Word incarnate from her you promised grace to the humble, he saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3); and again: “Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11). Hence comes my consolation in my humiliation: because your utterance, by which you console the humble, made me alive—gladdening the afflicted, strengthening the weak, healing the sick, raising again one made dead by temptations [Col. 0767C] or tribulations, by that sorrow of the world which works death, wherever your utterance does not console the sorrowful by its life-giving power. But I give you thanks because, amid all my humiliation, lest sorrow that works death should swallow me up, your utterance made me alive. This was most necessary for me when I was among the proud, who

VERS. 51. Acted unjustly exceedingly. The proud—whom even this mortality did not subdue, though it was imposed to humble the human race, God saying to man, “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19)—acted unjustly against the humble; for it was not enough for them to be evil unless they also strove to make the good evil. Of these it was said: “God resists the proud” (Jas. 3; 4:6). For since pride first began with an outrage against God, when both angel and man exalted themselves too highly against God, God rightly resists that vice in particular; he gives grace to the humble, because they together with him detest the pride of reprobate angels and men. Such proud persons acted unjustly against me—whether understood of the Church or of an ecclesiastical person—desiring to make me like themselves by approval or imitation of their wickedness, so that in either or both ways I might be alienated from the fellowship of the saints and humble. In this they laboured exceedingly, that is, intensely. But I did not turn aside from your law: preserving humility among the proud, obedience among the disobedient, gentleness among the harsh, although they mocked me excessively [Col. 0768A] and strove to draw me into conformity with themselves. What, on the contrary, did I do?

VERS. 52. I remembered your judgments from of old, O Lord, and was comforted; or, as it is read in the Hebrew: “I was delighted.” For, searching out the judgments—not those unsearchable judgments which are before or above the ages, but those which are from the age when the world began to be governed in time—I found that your judgments are pleasant and just. By them you order all things justly, and mercifully endure vessels of wrath in order to show the riches of glory in vessels of mercy. You tolerate the proud so that through them you may exercise the patience of the humble; for your judgments have proceeded from the beginning of the age, so that through the malice of Cain the godliness of Abel might be purified and exercised. Recalling these your judgments from the first righteous man to the last, [Col. 0768B] and seeing that your judgments begin from your house, while the righteous are unjustly judged now but will judge justly hereafter, when “they shall judge nations and rule peoples,” I was comforted and delighted (Wis. 3:8).

Some manuscripts have: “I was exhorted,” that is, I received exhortation to be more devout and more ready in reverencing your judgments. By these you now humble your own, that you may exalt them in the future; and conversely, you now permit your enemies to be proud, whom you intend to humble in the future. Yet however great my consolation from remembering your judgments was,

VERS. 53. Faintness seized me because of sinners who forsake your law, because the fault of the proud who forsake your law weighed more heavily upon me [Col. 0768C] than the punishment inflicted on me by them. From this came my faintness, from this my weariness, from this my horror, as it is read in the Hebrew. For the Hebrew text has: “Horror seized me because of the ungodly who have forsaken your law.” That is to say: the piety implanted in me could not but grieve or shudder at the ungodly forsaking your law; and such faintness, such weariness, such horror came upon me because of sinners forsaking your law that I was even weary of living. But in this my soul, O my God, was refreshed: that

VERS. 54. Your justifications were songs to me. In Hebrew it is read: “Your commandments were songs to me.” Hence it is clear that in this place “justifications” means nothing other than commandments, which a person who wishes to be justified ought to practise not only by reading and meditating but also by singing. For “the just lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17; Gal. 3:11), and “faith comes by hearing, but hearing through the word of Christ” (Rom. 10:17). Your commandments, then—or your justifications—were songs to me, David, who, as a shepherd, was accustomed to feed the sheep of your pasture, O God, not only by the gravity of words but also by the sweetness of singing, with musical instruments intermingled. You took me from my father’s house and set me to pasture your people. Your justifications, or your commandments, were likewise songs to me, or to the Church, or to an ecclesiastical person; without knowledge and observance of them a human being is not justified, for “man does not live by bread alone, but by every [Col. 0769A] word which proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. 8:3; Matt. 4:4). Hence the music and the singing choirs at the reception of the returning son who had been lost and was found. Hence those spiritual songs by which the Church, or every faithful soul, is delighted; the Apostle urges us to use them often, saying: “Be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and spiritual songs, singing in your hearts to the Lord” (Eph. 5:18–19). For by such things that Paraclete is invoked, who alone is my sole consolation in the place of my pilgrimage: I, driven from the homeland of paradise, am an exile in the place of my pilgrimage, reckoning the whole world as exile, since I desire only heavenly, not worldly, joys, and continually exercise myself in them. [Col. 0769B] For the daytime is not enough for me for this exercise—whether it is lit by the sunlight made to rule the day, or by the smiling light of prosperity—but moreover,

VERS. 55. By night I remembered your name, O Lord: keeping awake and observing the night watches, after the example of shepherds keeping watch over their flock against wolves and thieves (John 10:12); or after the example of a good householder keeping watch and not allowing a thief to break into his house (Luke 12:39); or after the example of a vigorous soldier maintaining his watch in camp; or guards keeping a city; or a beloved woman seeking her beloved by night—first in her bed, then in the streets of the city (Song 3:5). Often, in imitation of her, I kept vigil literally in bed; or, what was better, in the bed [Col. 0769C] of conscience I rejected the sleep of sin, and then gave myself to the open exercises of nocturnal psalms and morning praises, with both body and mind striving to keep watch in such ways. In this I remembered your name, O Lord, glorying in your name: for example, continually thinking and saying, “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.” Likewise, in the night of adversity, while sinners who forsake your law prevailed against me, among whom the failure of light held me surrounded by the great horror of darkness, I often—indeed, continually—remembered your name, O Lord, invoking you unceasingly with a perfect heart and frequently with my lips, as you yourself commanded, saying: “Call upon me in the day of tribulation; [Col. 0769D] I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Ps. 49:15). The day of tribulation is itself the night of adversity: day to the willing spirit, night to the weak flesh. Or, because this night is illuminated as day, the night of tribulation itself may also be called day: night to those who suffer in tribulation, but day to those who rejoice in hope.

VERS. 56. This night was made for me because I sought out your justifications; or, as it is read in the Hebrew, “kept” them. For I had no other cause of persecution than the seeking and keeping of your law, because on its account I displeased sinners who forsake your law. My dwelling among such people was night to me: they hated and slandered me and inflicted many grievous things upon me. My head was full of night-dew and my locks full of the drops of night [Col. 0770A] because the heavy reproaches and curses of those who hated me chilled my thoughts—my locks, as it were—even though I patiently endured and bore all things, like the drops of winter nights, excessively cold and exceedingly long. Yet because I sought your justifications, remembering your name in such a night, that very night became useful to me for this purpose: that I should devote myself more earnestly to prayers and thanksgivings in adversities of this nocturnal kind than in the prosperities of daytime. For since Judas betrayed by night and Peter denied him, one must devote oneself more earnestly to prayers at the time when dangers are more frequent amid temptations and tribulations in the night, “in which the beasts of the forest pass through, seeking their food from God” (Ps. 103:20), and in which Satan demanded the apostles in order to sift them like wheat (Luke 22:31). This night, therefore, came upon me—understand: usefully—because my remembering your name by night and keeping your law was not done by myself, but was done for me by you; for I sought your justifications, not my own, attributing to you, not to myself, the things which I thought, said, and did rightly.

HETH.

My portion, O Lord. In the eighth letter, whose name is HETH, interpreted “life,” the vision of God is sought through the eight verses beginning with this letter; for to see and know him is to live. To him the faithful Psalmist says:

VERS. 57. My portion, O Lord—or, as it is read in the Hebrew, “My part, O Lord”—understand: you [Col. 0770C] are my portion. For I, like a true Levite, do not wish to possess a share or portion of earthly inheritance, but serve the altar and live from the altar, receiving from it food and clothing and being content with these. I shall remember your word, which says in the law: “You shall not give an inheritance to the sons of Levi” (Num. 18:20); “I will be their inheritance” (Deut. 18:2). A great inheritance, a great portion, a great part falls to him who does not separate himself from the Father, to whom you, Father, say: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31). Great, I say, is the portion of such a son, provided that he does not separate himself from his father by going into a far country. For whoever desires to go away thus says to the Father: “Give me the portion which falls to me” (ibid., v. 12); and, once he has received his portion, he sets aside the law of discipline. But I say: My portion, O Lord; I have said that I will keep your law. Your law forbids earthly inheritance to Levites, whose portion, inheritance, and part you deign to be and to be called, providing for their food from the firstfruits and tithes offered to you. Those Levites who use these well you reward with a heavenly recompense, together with the sons of Aaron, Ithamar and Eleazar; but those who abuse them you condemn with the sons of Eli, priest of Shiloh. Therefore the keeping of your law consists in this: that he whose portion, part, and inheritance you deign to be should himself also be your inheritance, your portion, your part, wholly dedicating himself to your service after the example of the sons of Levi, of whom Moses said to God: “Your perfection and your teaching belong to your holy man, whom you tested in temptation [Col. 0771A] and judged at the waters of contradiction; who said to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to his brothers, ‘I am ignorant of them’; and they did not know their sons. These kept your utterance and preserved your covenant, your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel” (Deut. 33:8 ff.).

You hear that such keeping of the law is set before the Levites: that in God’s cause they should acknowledge no person, but, apart from father and mother—indeed, apart from flesh and blood—should become such that, once they have been taken up into God’s ministry, they no longer yield to flesh and blood, after the example of the sons of Levi. By not yielding to flesh and blood, and by avenging the sin of idolatry, they consecrated their hands in the blood of their brothers.

Such was the Levite of the New Testament who said: [Col. 0771B] “But when it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, immediately I did not yield to flesh and blood” (Gal. 1:15). He finally consecrated his hands in the blood of his brothers when, brandishing “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God,” he “became stronger and stronger and confounded the Jews,” his kinsmen, “affirming that this is the Christ” (Acts 9:22), whom they denied. The other Levites of the New Testament likewise kept God’s law, so that God alone might be their portion and inheritance, for whose sake they had left everything. Hence comes their saying: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:27). And the Giver of the new law himself, who gives a blessing not merely simple but tenfold, repays them tenfold in this [Col. 0771C] life, saying: “Everyone who leaves house, brothers, sisters, children, or lands for my name’s sake shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life” (ibid., v. 29). Thus—yes, thus—the Levites of the new law are rewarded more abundantly than those of the old, because to the latter is assigned the wage of this present life in the number ten, but to the former in the number one hundred. And after this life Abraham’s bosom was open to the former, still held in hell; but after death the kingdom of heaven is open to the latter when they have fought rightly. An eminent Levite burned with desire for this kingdom when he said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). Rightly indeed, because Christ was his portion, for whose sake he had reckoned the gains of the law as dung. Many, imitating him, reckon the gains [Col. 0771D] of this world as dung, so that for them to live is Christ and to die is gain. Each such person can confidently sing, saying: My portion, O Lord; I have said that I will keep your law. You are my portion, O Lord, whom I chose after despising all things, and whom alone I desire to serve. Therefore I have said—that is, firmly resolved—to keep your law, according to what we recalled as said of the Levites: “They kept your utterance,” and so forth. But because this cannot be done except where grace obtains what the law commands, therefore:

VERS. 58. I entreated your face with my whole heart, saying: Have mercy upon me according to your word. The speech of this prayer is directed to your face, namely to your Son, who is your face, upon whom angels desire to look; and I too, a Levite desiring to look upon him, when I perceive myself hindered by the veil of mortal and frail flesh, entreat and have often entreated your face with my whole heart, saying: Have mercy upon me according to your word—namely, [Col. 0772A] “as you spoke through the mouth of your holy prophets who have been from the beginning,” promising “salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us, to show mercy to our fathers and to remember your holy covenant,” according to “the oath” which you swore “to Abraham our father, that you would grant us” fully “that, delivered from the hand of our enemies, we might serve you without fear in holiness and righteousness before” you “all our days” (Luke 1). This brief prayer contains this entire meaning: Have mercy upon me according to your word. I do not ask that mercy be shown me without reason, but according to the utterly just and merciful ordering of your word; for neither mercy without justice nor justice without mercy pleases you, whose “all ways are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). Yet the truth of your word does not permit your mercy or medicine to be bestowed on those who love and foster their own misery and sickness. Therefore:

VERS. 59. I considered my ways, reviewing after confession my crooked paths now past; or I considered beforehand my ways to come, carefully weighing what ought and what ought not to be done. And I turned my feet from my crooked ways to your testimonies, which direct the steps of conduct in the straight way. Strengthened by these testimonies to act justly and to suffer for justice,

VERS. 60. I am ready for both. And therefore I am not troubled by adversities which meet me on account of righteousness, which your testimonies have made certain to me. I could indeed be troubled by the contradictions of the perverse, unless I had been strengthened by your testimonies. But now, because I turned my feet to your testimonies, instructed and prepared by them, I am ready to keep your commandments. I am ready because the spirit is willing, and “I delight in your law” according to the inward man (Rom. 7:22). Yet because I see another law in my members resisting the law [Col. 0772D] of my mind and leading me captive under the law of sin, I am compelled to cry out: “Unhappy man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (ibid., v. 24.) Likewise:

VERS. 61. The cords of sinners have entangled me. Not one cord, but many cords of sinners have entangled me, because I have hindrances both from the weakness of the flesh and from the devil’s temptation, and also from the company of the perverse. Entangled and wrapped in all these, I cannot free myself; indeed, I cannot but perish unless the grace of God through Jesus Christ sets me free. I hope for and seek that grace through this: that although I have been entangled in the cords of sinners, I have not forgotten your law, in which I delighted in mind, and in it. Or, through it [Col. 0773A] I resisted sin, lest it be committed, or repented of it, lest it remain. Do you wish to hear how I resisted it or repented?

VERS. 62. At midnight I arose to confess to you, O Lord, because of the judgments of your justification. At midnight I arose—that is, in most grievous tribulation or temptation. While night was completing its course, I did not so succumb as not to break the middle silence; but at midnight I arose, and, breaking the middle silence, confessed to you, O Lord, because of the judgments of your justice. I did not allow myself to be wholly cast down in the middle of the night by the violence of tribulations or temptations; rather, I rose to make a stronger confession concerning the judgments of your justice, knowing that even this—that the cords of sinners entangle the righteous—comes about, O God, by your righteous judgment, which now begins from [Col. 0773B] your house and your sanctuary. Therefore, taking occasion from the midnight itself, at which Egypt’s firstborn were struck down (Exod. 12:29), and at which the bridegroom will come (Matt. 25:5), I arose either in body and spirit together, or in spirit alone, desiring heavenly things and seeking those things which are above. Thus I arose to confess your name, to which a confession of praise and thanksgiving is due for all that happens to us, since you order all things, whether grace or justice directs them—sometimes by a hidden, but never by anything but a right, judgment. For you are just, O Lord, and your judgment is right. Therefore, although at midnight, because of the thickness and horror of darkness, we cannot see the justice of your judgments, still, in that faith by which we believe what we do not see—namely, that your judgment is always just—a confession of praise must always be offered to you because of the judgments of your justification. No less must a confession of sins be offered to you, sins which we either see or fear to be present in our deeds and conduct. The perfect see their sins; each of them can say: “I know my iniquity” (Ps. 50:5). But the imperfect, always suspecting themselves, fear even when they do not see their sins; each of them continually says: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults.” But I do not, as though perfect, know all my sins or offences: “for who understands offences?” (Ps. 18:13). Rather, as a little one and imperfect, I confess that I

[Col. 0773D] VERS. 63. Am a companion of all who fear you—yet not of those who grow sluggish in idleness, like the wicked and lazy servant who, fearing a harsh master, hides his talent underground or in a napkin (Matt. 25:26), but of those who keep your commandments. Another translation has: “Make me, O God, a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments.” This means the same as if it were said: What I said above—“My portion, O Lord,” and the rest adapted to the perfect Levite—sounds indeed like great perfection. But because I see that the cords of sinners have entangled me, and that I am still in the midnight of ignorance, not knowing whether I am worthy of love or hatred (Eccles. 9:1), terrified by fear I say that I am a companion of all who fear you. Or, not even daring to profess this, [Col. 0774A] I pray: Make me, O God, a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments. For, terrified by your justice, I flee to your mercy, knowing that

VERS. 64. Your mercy, O Lord, fills the earth: you cause your sun to rise upon good and evil, and rain upon just and unjust, offering both temporal and spiritual goods to all in that mercy by which you desire all human beings to be saved and none to perish (Matt. 5). By this mercy of yours, O Lord, the earth is full. But since not all receive it, but only those who seek your justifications, teach me your justifications—you who alone teach humanity knowledge, without whose inward teaching the word of one human being instructing another sounds in vain in the hearer’s ears. Above, when I said that I rose to confess to you because of the judgments of your justifications, I seemed to myself to have understood your judgments of justification to some extent. Yet now, more fully enlightened, I see that my ignorance is so great that I still need to be taught. Therefore I say: Teach me your justifications, which in this life must always be sought by one who fears God, because there will be no fullness of so great a good except in the life to come, where you, God, will be seen face to face, you who now work many things secretly and are seen only through a glass and in an enigma.

Let us join together the four letters already set forth: he, vau, zain, heth. He means “this,” vau “and,” zain “these,” and heth “life,” as was stated above. The sense is: “This and these are life”—that is, these things and whatever things of this kind are perfect, committed to the meditation and memory of the faithful, advance them toward eternal life. Therefore the matters contained under the preceding four letters in four octaves are to be continually pondered.

THETH.

VERS. 65. You have dealt kindly with your servant, O Lord, according to your word. The ninth letter, whose name Theth is interpreted “good,” is rightly placed first where goodness is discussed. When I, David, sing and give thanks, saying, “You have dealt kindly with your servant,” I was a servant, serving out of fear. But you dealt kindly with me by casting out fear through the goodness you inspired, which is nothing other than “perfect charity, which casts out fear” (1 John 4:17). Therefore you dealt kindly with your servant by inspiring charity in my heart, a charity which makes servants into friends, according to the saying: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15:15). Great charity, great goodness, great sweetness, great pleasantness, which makes a servile work, formerly very burdensome, light, sweet, good, and delightful! You did this goodness not merely concerning me or in me—as you often work many good things concerning or in evil persons, even when they are unwilling or unaware, and therefore unworthy of recompense for this goodness—but, so that I your servant might have firm hope of a good recompense, you did the goodness which you effected concerning or in me also with me, raising my free will [Col. 0775A] to the working of your goodness. Thus I might do with you the goodness which you made in me, and you might do with me what I did, so that I could say with the Apostle: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10). It is a devout and great condescension that, in a good work of which you alone are the author, you granted fellowship to me your servant, causing me to perform with you whatever good work I do according to your word. Surely this is what you promise through the Prophet, saying: “And I will cause you to walk in my commandments, and keep my judgments, and perform them.” Therefore, that I might do some good according to your word—according to your commandment, which is that we love one another, without whose observance no virtue is judged good, even if one speaks with the tongues of angels or moves mountains by faith—that I might, I say, do good or goodness, you dealt kindly with me, granting me, your servant, that I might act with you according to your word. My soul continually desired this, saying: “Let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38); and you, hearing me, dealt kindly with your servant according to your word. But lest your goodness, well begun in me, should fail, and instead may advance more and more from good always to better,

VERS. 66. Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge. The order is good. First I ask goodness from you, the good source of goodness; then discipline; lastly knowledge, which, if it were given first while goodness and discipline were omitted, would inflate rather than edify. Our first parents, though they could have tasted in the permitted fruits the sweetness of your goodness while preserving the discipline of obedience, desired the forbidden tree of knowledge more than the tree of life. By that disordered desire for knowledge they deserved to be excluded from the paradise of delight, deprived of goodness and discipline (Gen. 3:1 ff.). Therefore, that I may be restored to the place from which they fell, I ask these three: goodness, discipline, and knowledge. But greater than these is goodness, which is nothing other than charity; I ask first to be taught it, so that, once I have received it, the burden of discipline beneath the yoke of your obedience may become light for me, because you discipline and scourge every son whom you receive (Heb. 12:6). Those who are without discipline, the Apostle declares, are illegitimate and not true sons. Lastly, [Col. 0775D] I ask for that knowledge by which I may know what I lack, because this knowledge does not inflate but humbles, and obtains greater grace; for you resist the proud but give grace to the humble (Jas. 4:10; 1 Pet. 5:5). Long ago philosophers thought that they taught these three in the three parts of philosophy: goodness in ethics, discipline in physics, and knowledge in logic. But they became vain in their thoughts, imagining that one person can give knowledge to another, whereas you alone are he who teaches humanity knowledge. Unless you open the understanding and the sense of the heart, the tongue of a person striving to teach another labours in vain. Therefore you, who alone are able, teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge. Teach goodness by inspiring charity, through which your burden and yoke may become delightful [Col. 0776A] and sweet to me. Teach discipline by moderating tribulation, so that, disciplined amid your scourges, I may not murmur. Finally, teach me knowledge by imparting understanding, so that I may know myself and know you. May I know myself, lest it be said to me: “If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go forth and follow the tracks of the flocks, and pasture your kids” (Song 1:7)—the kids, I say, to be placed on the left, not the lambs on the right. May I know you, lest perhaps, not knowing you, I be unknown by you, as it is written: “But he who does not know shall be unknown” (1 Cor. 14:33). Likewise, to the foolish virgins who do not know you, you say: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). Teach me, therefore, that twofold knowledge, by which I may know myself and know you.

[Col. 0776B] But lest, in ignorance of myself, I exalt myself above myself, or, in ignorance of you, be ignored by you, may knowledge of myself build me up toward compassion and love of my neighbor; and may knowledge of you build me up and ever inflame me toward love of you. Far from me be the hard heart of Pharaoh, who said: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. V, 2). Far from me be the blindness of those “who, since they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God gave over to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting” (Rom. I, 28). Far from me be the hardness of those who said to the Lord God: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways” (Job XXI, 14). Everyone such as these deservedly hears from God that prophetic saying: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I too will reject you, that you may not exercise priesthood for me” (Hos. IV, 6).

[Col. 0776C] Therefore, lest I be rejected by you, teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, because I have believed your commandments. Great is the merit of this faith, to which the knowledge requested ought rightly to be granted as a reward. For what is it to believe the commandments except willingly to assent to them, whether they forbid evils or command goods? Hence, even if no threat of dreadful torments or promise of desirable rewards were added to them, one ought still to believe and freely assent to the commandments, since they come down from the good Father of lights and therefore commend no evil but every good.

Yet because the hired laborer is slow to believe this, and the servant slower still, a dreadful threat is attached to the commandments in order to spur on the lazy servant,

[Col. 0776D] and a sweet promise in order to encourage the hired laborer, so that, while the former fears for himself and the latter desires for himself, both may begin to obey the commandments. But I, as a son, free alike from the servant’s fear and the hired laborer’s covetousness, have freely believed and assented to your commandments themselves, knowing that not only does a due reward follow upon obedience to them, but that there is also great reward in keeping them, since in their observance to serve you is to reign—by that manner of reigning which the rulers of this world, dominating men and serving vices, cannot attain so long as they refuse obedience to your commandments. By doing these, a man shall live in them, especially if, without regard to punishments or rewards, he delights in them, saying with the Son: “My food

[Col. 0777A] is to do the will of my Father” (John IV, 32).

The hired laborer or servant cannot say this unless the servant’s fear has been cast out and the hired laborer’s covetousness excluded, and filial affection has been received. Burning with this affection, I have believed your commandments, not doubting that all your commandments are faithful. “Not so are the ungodly, not so” (Ps. I, 4): our first parents did not believe that the commandment given them in Paradise was faithful, or faithfully given them. Rather, when the devil whispered through the serpent, the woman was deceived, so as to suppose that God, begrudging them knowledge of good and evil, had forbidden her and her husband the tree of knowledge (Gen. III, 1). Thus my parents sinned, and I sinned in them. My mother Eve sinned when deceived; my father Adam sinned, though not deceived, yet assenting to the deceived woman

[Col. 0777B] and not restraining her, as he should have done. In their sins I, David the penitent, was conceived.

**VERSE 67.** Before I was humbled by the penalty of mortality—when God said, “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Exod. III, 19)—I sinned, falling into the death of the soul through disobedience and transgression of the faithful commandment. Had I faithfully observed it, I surely would not have been humbled by mortality, or bodily death. Therefore I have kept your word, instructed and humbled, that is, by your scourges, so that I may beware of sinning lest I again be humbled by the scourges of your wrath. Greatly fearing that wrath, I flee to the bosom of your goodness, saying to you with the continual cry of heart and mouth:

[Col. 0777C] **VERSE 68.** You are good, and in your goodness teach me your ordinances. You are good—not with an accidental or changeable goodness, but with a natural and immutable goodness. And in this your goodness teach me your ordinances, instructing me by an anointing rather than a punishment, by evangelical sweetness rather than legal severity; and make me perform your ordinances, that is, works of righteousness—not Pharisaic righteousness, which does not please you, but righteousness altogether yours and pleasing to you. You also teach this in your goodness when you say: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 20). Again: Beware “lest you perform your righteousness before men in order to be seen by them” (Matt. VI, 1).

[Col. 0777D] Teach me therefore, in your goodness, your ordinances, so that people, seeing them to be yours—that is, understanding that they are from your grace—may glorify not me but you: not me, the unworthy recipient of your righteousness, but you, its most kind and most generous giver. Thus may glory always be yours for my righteousness—or rather, for yours, though given to me. But may humiliation and humility remain to me, with both my enemies and yours cooperating in this very thing, proudly setting themselves against you and me. For I have very often experienced that:

**VERSE 69.** The iniquity of the proud has multiplied against me: that is, open revilings, reproaches, and many insults cast in my face; or secretly fashioned above my back through detractions. But with my whole heart I will search your commandments,

[Col. 0778A] by which you command that enemies be loved for your sake, and friends in you. Therefore I did not return curses for curses or reproaches for reproaches, desiring not to be conquered by evil but to conquer evil by goodness. In contrast:

**VERSE 70.** Their heart has curdled like milk and become hardened, so that it cannot be softened by benefits freely bestowed. Yet in that very hardness they put forward and display a certain likeness of milk, though they do not possess its truth—as does she to whom it is said: “Honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song IV, 11). These, however, are not truly milk but merely appear like milk, for their heart is hard, as Pharaoh’s hardened heart was. But I have meditated upon your law, knowing that “the fullness of the law is love” (Rom. XIII, 10),

[Col. 0778B] especially when not only the loving friend but also the persecuting enemy is loved. And amid all these things:

**VERSE 71.** It is good for me that you have humbled me, while the iniquity of the proud has multiplied against me. From their pride my humility has increased, by your ordering: through those proud persons you humbled me, so that, as adversities exercise my patience, I may learn your ordinances and, through perfection, become meek and humble, as you teach when you say: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29). This is to be righteous by your righteousness, which comes from no other source than from you, who justify the ungodly and give life to the dead: not through the rod of the Mosaic law, but through the law of your mouth.

[Col. 0778C] For when you, the true Elisha, place your life-giving mouth upon the mouth of the dead man, you give him life and justify him through faith held in you, by which the righteous person lives. Therefore:

**VERSE 72.** The law of your mouth is good to me above thousands of gold and silver pieces, because charity loves the law of your mouth more than covetousness loves thousands of gold and silver pieces. Though these are desirable among earthly things, compared with the spiritual riches which the law of your mouth reveals, they are of no value. Such goods do not make their possessor good, as spiritual goods make good those who possess and enjoy them, according to the teaching of the law of your mouth. Since it also teaches the right use of earthly goods, it is more precious than all riches; and all things that are desired cannot be compared with it.

[Col. 0778D] These preceding eight verses begin among the Hebrews with the letter *teth*, interpreted as “good.” In the other languages also, Greek and Latin, they fittingly repeat goodness or the good, when it is said: “You have done good”; “You are good, and in your goodness teach me”; again, “It is good for me that you have humbled me”; “The law of your mouth is good to me.” Through these many proclamations of goodness and good things, that supreme Good is intimated to us: it must be sought with the highest desire and desired above thousands of gold and silver pieces.

## JOD

In this tenth letter, he asks for understanding of the commandments, chief among which are those Ten Commandments,

[Col. 0779A] written by the finger of God and summed up in this brief saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XXII, 37).

**VERSE 73.** Your hands made me and formed me. I give thanks to you, my Creator, because, though you created all other things by a word alone, saying, “Let this or that be,” you made me, a human being, the work of your hands, more excellent than your other works. For although the angel is your noble work, a certain man has nevertheless been predestined and exalted above angelic dignity to the highest throne, where a multitude of angels worships him. I, a member of this man, give you thanks, Lord, because your hands made me from nothing—so far as concerns the soul, created without pre-existing material in the image and likeness of God—and

[Col. 0779B] formed me—so far as concerns the body, fashioned from earthly matter and made alive through the rational soul. And because my rational soul is capable of understanding: Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments. You formed a little vessel; lest it be empty, fill it with understanding of your commandments, as we sing of certain persons: that he established in them the grace of the Holy Spirit and filled their hearts with understanding. Indeed, faith, which comes by hearing, is not received without some little understanding; but faith itself is merit for a fuller understanding, which I ask and desire, saying: Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments. May I learn to do what I have learned to read or understand.

[Col. 0779C] **VERSE 74.** Those who fear you will see me and rejoice. The sinner will see and be angry; he will see and envy. But those who fear you will see me and rejoice. For though I may be burdensome to behold for the envious, I shall nevertheless be pleasing to the kind, who with a good and simple eye consider the understanding granted me by your grace. Their sight—so benevolent in itself—is thanksgiving to you, the giver of grace, and rejoicing with me; to you it is glory, to them joy, because they will see me and rejoice. Not so that man to whom it is said: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matt. XX, 15). Truly evil is the eye that is tormented because God is good; bleary is the eye that is tormented by a bright light delightful to healthy eyes. Therefore the healthy eyes of those who fear you will see me illuminated with clear understanding

[Col. 0779D] and will rejoice, because I have hoped exceedingly in your words, knowing that you can fulfill, beyond all that we ask or understand, the good desire conceived from your words. But when that which is hoped for exceedingly according to your words is delayed or altogether denied, I do not wish to murmur against this, knowing that it happens by your just judgment.

**VERSE 75.** For I have known, Lord, that your judgments are equity, and that in your truth you have humbled me—by withdrawing prosperity, bringing adversities upon me or allowing them to be brought, or denying what I desire.
