In all these things, “All that you have done to us, Lord, you have done in true judgment, because we have sinned against you and have not obeyed your commandments. But give glory to your name and deal with us

[Col. 0780A] according to the multitude of your mercy” (Dan. III, 31).

**VERSE 76.** May your mercy come to console me according to your word: according to the word of promise made to your servant Abraham (Gen. XXII), to whom you promised that his seed would be multiplied like the stars of heaven (Exod. XXXIII). Again, to another of your servants, Moses, you said among other things: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I have mercy” (Rom. IX, 15). Again, you spoke good things to me, your servant David, saying: “I have found David my servant; I have anointed him with my holy oil,” etc. (Ps. LXXXVIII, 21). Again, you say to another of your servants: “I will call ‘not my people,’ and ‘not having obtained mercy,’ ‘having obtained mercy’” (Hos. II, 1).

[Col. 0780B] Therefore you have mercy on whom you will, and harden whom you will; to whom you will you show mercy, and to whom you will you show wrath. But I, David—I, penitent after David’s example—flee from your wrath to you, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, continually saying: May your mercy come to console me according to your word to your servant.

Again:

**VERSE 77.** Let your compassions come to me, and I shall live, made alive by those compassions of yours. I shall live in the present, living soberly, righteously, and devoutly among men; and I shall live also in the future among the good angels, giving thanks to your goodness and singing your mercies forever. I shall now live according to your law, because your law is my meditation, in which is the Spirit of life; for it is a spiritual law, to which I consent in my mind, even when in my flesh I feel a law contrary to your law.

[Col. 0780C] Through this law opposing your law in my members, proud demons and human beings, taking opportunity, attack me. Against them I pray, saying:

**VERSE 78.** Let the proud be put to shame, because unjustly they have committed iniquity against me. Let proud men, who can be converted, be put to shame unto repentance. But demons and their obstinate accomplices, because they cannot be converted from their persistent malice and there is no change in them, “let them be put to shame and clothed, like a double garment, with their confusion” (Ps. CVIII, 29), so that they may be unable to accomplish the evils they have begun against me, because unjustly they have committed iniquity against me. Let them be ashamed

[Col. 0780D] to have begun what they cannot complete. Let them fall into everlasting reproach, so that, even if they themselves are not corrected, others may nevertheless take warning from their example when they see their shame: for unjustly they have committed iniquity against me, maliciously devising evils against me without the judgment of discernment. But I was exercised [Vulgate: “I shall be exercised”] in your commandments, which reveal that charity which “is patient, is kind” (I Cor. XIII, 4): patient, so as to endure evils; kind, so as to repay good for evils. While this charity labors:

**VERSE 79.** Let those who fear you and know your testimonies be turned to me. Among my enemies there are some swollen with pride, others fearful—or rather, God-fearing, fearing you. Therefore, with the proud, hardened in their swelling, excluded from this prayer of mine as belonging to the world, of which you say: “I do not pray for the world” (John XVII, 9),

[Col. 0781A] let those who fear you be turned to me—that is, to my advantage. By the very fear that they have, you separate them from the world, which lies so in the evil one that, for those who sin willingly within it, there remains no sacrifice for sins, because they commit “a sin unto death, concerning which I do not say that anyone should pray,” says John the Evangelist (John V, 16). Therefore, let those who fear you and know the testimonies foretold through the prophets be turned to me, the true David, to me, Christ: for my glory and for their salvation. They know them, I say, even if not yet by action, at least by the devotion of good will, having hearts ready to assent to the true testimonies of truth. But that I, David—I, the penitent praying for others—may deserve to be heard:

[Col. 0781B] **VERSE 80.** Let my heart be spotless in your ordinances, that I may not be put to shame, like those of whom I said: Let the proud be put to shame. “Let them be put to shame, but let me not be put to shame; let them tremble, but let me not tremble” (Jer. XVII, 18), because from a spotless heart, cleansed from every stain through your ordinances, comes great confidence before you, the judge who searches hearts and kidneys. For “if our heart does not reproach us, we have confidence on the day of judgment,” says John the Evangelist (I John III, 21). But if our heart reproaches us, God is greater than our heart and knows all things. Fearing his judgment, I continually say: Let my heart be spotless in your ordinances, that I may not be put to shame.

## CAPH

[Col. 0781C]

That is, “hand,” or “bent.” In this eleventh letter, the pilgrim in this world desires the coming of the Judge, as though weary and bent over by excessive labor and the long postponement of the kingdom. He therefore says:

**VERSE 81.** My soul has failed for your salvation. Failure is commonly understood as evil, and progress as good, unless this understanding is altered by additions, as the Apostle says of evildoers: “They advance from bad to worse” (II Tim. III, 13). Here it is said: “My soul has failed for your salvation”; and: “My eyes have failed for your word.” Concerning this salutary failing, by which the soul of one who psalms well fails into God’s salvation, blessed Pope Gregory says among other things in his *Morals on Job*:

> **[Note: Col. 0781D, Book IV of the *Morals*, ch. 33.]** “My soul has failed in your salvation.” All who are strong in bodily vigor in this world are, as it were, strong and not exhausted. But those who are strengthened in the strength of their Creator: the more they become strong in the desired strength of God, the more they fail from their own strength; and the more vigorously they seek eternal things, the more they grow weary of temporal things with a salutary failing. Thus he says again: “My soul desires and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII, 3). When he said “desires,” he immediately added “and fails,” because desire for the Godhead is very slight if it is not immediately followed by a failing from one’s own self. For one who is inflamed to lay hold of the courts of eternity ought surely to grow weary of love for temporality,

[Col. 0782A] so that he may grow cold toward worldly pursuit in proportion as he rises more ardently in the love of God. If he fully grasps this love, he wholly abandons the world, and so dies utterly to temporal things as he is more deeply animated toward the life above by the breath of eternity. Did not she find herself exhausted of her own strength who said: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song V, 6)? For the mind, when touched by the breathing of hidden speech, is weakened from the state of its own strength and melts through the very desire by which it is absorbed; and from that source it finds itself weary within itself, from which it beholds beyond itself the strength to which it has ascended. Thus the prophet, when he said that he had seen a vision of God, added: “I languished and was sick for many days” (Isa. XXXIII, 24); for when the mind is constrained toward strength, the flesh is wearied of its own strength.

[Col. 0782B] Thus Jacob, who held the angel, immediately limped in one foot, because one who looks upon the heights with true love no longer knows how to walk in this world with twofold desires. He rests upon one foot who is strengthened by the love of God alone; and the other must necessarily wither, because as the strength of the mind increases, the strength of the flesh must undoubtedly grow numb.”

Otherwise: “My soul has failed for your salvation.” As oil or wax melting into flame fails, so my soul has failed for your salvation, being wholly converted into its love, as melting gold is turned into fire. Therefore my soul has failed, wholly converted into spirit, because “he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17). Thus Jacob failed into Israel (Gen. XXXII, 28), Saul into

[Col. 0782C] Paul (Acts XIII, 1); thus all who advance into God fail away from themselves. Therefore this is not a complaint but a thanksgiving when I, David, chanting, say to you, God, Father of mercies: “My soul has failed for your salvation,” or, as some manuscripts read, “in your salvation.” It has failed from itself, advancing beyond itself. The soul has failed when bodily exercise, which is useful for a little, is diminished and the piety of contemplation is increased from day to day—from the day of Martha to the day of Mary, who devoted herself solely to hearing the word.

And I have hoped exceedingly in your word. Martha “was busy with much serving” (Luke X, 40), and to those who serve in this way the kingdom of heaven is promised; to them it will also be said: “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc. (Matt. XXV, 34).

[Col. 0782D] But I have hoped exceedingly in your word, knowing that Mary’s repose, devoted to the word, far surpasses Martha’s activity in serving. Again, even among those serving your least brethren—in whom you are fed, given drink, clothed, received, and visited—the least themselves differ by the greatest distance, since such least ones will be judges, and their servants will be received by them into eternal dwellings. Let those intent upon works of mercy therefore rejoice in hope of reward; but let those who, after the example of the apostles, devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word hope exceedingly and rejoice exceedingly. Considering this, I have hoped exceedingly in your word, to which I have chosen to devote myself in reading, hearing, learning, teaching,

[Col. 0783A] writing, and, more frequently amid these things, praying, setting aside bodily exercise insofar as is fitting, since it is useful for a little. In this pursuit:

**VERSE 82.** My eyes have failed, attentively fixed upon your word. They have failed from the curious beholding of worldly vanities, as I prayed above, saying: “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity.” But after this failing, when they were fixed upon your word, even bodily eyes, as though often anointed with eye-salve of tears, still remain vigorous through your grace. Thus spiritual and bodily eyes alike pant for your word, saying: “When will you console me?” Some also, whose outward sight has failed and grown dim, like another Isaac (Gen. XXVII), see clearly within and foresee the future, saying: “When will you console me?” I too, David—I, the penitent—will not cease to say this until I see what I believe, when clear sight succeeds the obscurity of faith, so that I may see my Lord and Savior not only in spirit but also in my flesh.

[Col. 0783B] Since this will not occur before the future judgment, I shall continually say: “When will you bring judgment upon those who persecute me?” For then you will console me perfectly, wiping every tear from my eyes. But now, because the delay is prolonged so that the deferred thing may come more sweetly, I suffer distress:

**VERSE 83.** For I have become like a wineskin in frost. A wineskin in frost does not feel the frost’s cold, since it is made from a hide wholly removed from sensitive flesh and fashioned into a wineskin through many costly processes: remnants of flesh are scraped away within; hairs are pulled out without; and the hide itself is very frequently pierced with an awl, so that a way may be made for thread to be drawn through with a bristle. Such a wineskin, so made, does not feel the cold in frost; yet, chilled by that very cold, it makes the drink poured into it more pleasant. A warm wineskin—such as Hagar, Sarah’s maidservant, carried while wandering in the wilderness of a hot region—containing lukewarm water that causes vomiting when drunk, is utterly unlike a wineskin placed in frost, containing a cold and therefore pleasant drink.

[Col. 0783C] Certainly I have become such a wineskin by your making: you have withdrawn me from fleshly desires which wage war against the soul; with the iron scraper of many tribulations you have scraped away from me the remnants of fleshly desires, at the same time pulling out the hairs of superfluous thoughts. Then, continually pierced by the awl of servile fear, with the bristle of filial fear going before, you sew me with the thread of your love. And now, with the awl of fear cast out, strengthened by the thread of your love, and cooled by the frost of your grace coming down from above, I contain your ordinances poured into me like sweet drinks, and offer them, as far as I can, to be given to others. Therefore, truly chanting in thanksgiving, I say: “For I have become like a wineskin in frost”—yet not feeling that frost of which Job says: “Those who fear frost,

[Col. 0784A] snow will fall upon them” (Job VI, 16). This means: those who withdraw from righteousness through fear of temporal punishment will be overwhelmed by eternal punishments, when the Judge says: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XXV, 41; XXII, 13). “Weeping” in the smoke of inextinguishably burning fire; “gnashing of teeth” in excessive cold, because, as it is written, “They pass from snowy waters to excessive heat” (Job XXIV, 19). They will fall into those snowy waters because here they feared too greatly the easily trodden frost, and were unwilling to go out barefoot from their beds and their impurities, trembling there with fear where no fear was.

Sandals, however—soles made from hide—are enough for treading upon this frost. Shod with them, the apostles did not in the least fear the frost of temporal affliction; indeed, they did not even feel it, because they too had become wineskins, not old but new, into which new wine was to be poured, so that it was said of them: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts II, 13).

[Col. 0784B] Anyone such as these can confidently say: “When will you console me? For I have become like a wineskin in frost; I have not forgotten your ordinances.”

**VERSE 84.** How many are the days of your servant? Because the days are evil, oppressed by great weariness I continually cry: “How many are the days of your servant?” And because I, the Church, suffer through evil days until judgment—for the faithful will not be absent from the world until judgment—I continually say, longing for judgment: “When

[Col. 0784C] will you bring judgment upon those who persecute me?” Nor is it strange that I am worn down with weariness, for:

**VERSE 85.** The wicked have told me tales, but not according to your law. On this passage blessed Gregory says in his *Morals on Job*:

> **[Note: Col. 0783D, Book VII of the *Morals*, ch. 13.]** “The words of carnal persons, when they intrusively press themselves upon our ears, often create a war of temptation in the heart. Although reason rejects such words and the tongue rebukes them, nevertheless what is judged outwardly with authority is overcome inwardly only with labor. Therefore what the watchful mind repels from the entrance to thought must not even reach the ears. When holy men pant after the desires of eternity, they raise themselves to such a height of life that they consider hearing worldly things to be a burdensome and depressing weight. For they deem exceedingly strange and intolerable whatever does not sound that which they love within.”

[Col. 0784D] Otherwise: “When will you bring judgment upon those who persecute me?” Among them, those do greater harm who not only do evil but also teach it. For “evil conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV, 33), especially in this perilous time, when many “will turn away their hearing from the truth and will turn instead to fables” (II Tim. IV, 4). I do not speak from inexperience, for the wicked have very often told me tales—or, as some manuscripts have it, “they recounted pleasures”—but not according to your law. They told them, but I did not receive their tales, because they were not according to your law. In Hebrew it reads:

[Col. 0785A] “The proud dug pits for me which were not according to your law.” In that law:

**VERSE 86.** All your commandments are truth, contrary to which is the falsehood of their chatter. The wicked have persecuted me: Help me. The wicked were not content merely to weary me with tales, but moreover persecuted me, forcing me to move from place to place or from opinion to opinion, not without danger to both spiritual and bodily salvation. For when faith is assailed by various and strange doctrines, the salvation of the soul is endangered; but when a person is driven from place to place, bodily safety is endangered. Against dangers of this sort, help me, O most powerful, most wise, most kind one, so that I may not be conquered, deceived, or corrupted—what the wicked strive to effect. They even:

[Col. 0785B] **VERSE 87.** Almost consumed me upon earth; but I did not forsake your commandments. “Almost” means that little was lacking for them to achieve what they attempted: namely, to consume me upon earth, so that, like themselves, I might think earthly thoughts and think little or nothing of heavenly things. But I did not forsake your commandments, which command earthly things to be abandoned and despised, and heavenly things to be loved. But lest I fail amid so many dangers:

**VERSE 88.** According to your mercy, give me life, granting me both caution against evils and invincible perseverance in the good undertakings I have begun. I say, “according to your mercy,” because I distrust the quality of my merits, but have great confidence in your mercy. In it, I pray, give me life and preserve me in true life, lest, by loving false life, I lose the true—as some, overcome by the extremity of torments, by loving bodily life lost the life of the heart, which is God. But with you giving life, this is what I hope and seek: that I may live and keep the testimonies of your mouth. In keeping them, many faithful people became martyrs, which means “witnesses”; may I keep their testimonies, or martyrdoms, being kept safe through your mercy.

## LAMECH

The name of the twelfth letter, *lamech*, is interpreted, according to Jerome, as “heart”; according to Ambrose, as “servant.” Both interpretations are fitting, because the eight verses written under this letter contain heavenly mysteries to be kept with the most attentive heart. Chief among them is that broad commandment which is indicated in the final verse: “Forever, Lord, your word remains in heaven. Your truth is from generation to generation; you founded the earth, and it remains.” This cry is the mind stretching from the depths of worldly changes to heaven, where your word remains without change, while an immutable order stands there, established by your immutable word, Lord. On earth, however, your word is despised by people limping in different directions. Weary of these, I lift my eyes to heaven, where your word remains, so that the sight of heavenly things, which serve and obey your word steadfastly and unchangeably, may refresh my spirit wearied by the manifold disorder of earthly things. Therefore I say:

[Col. 0786A] **VERSES 89–90.** Forever, Lord, your word remains in heaven. Heaven turns in a stable and unfailing revolution; hence the Greeks call it *aplanēs*, that is, “without error.” The stars themselves called planets, that is, “wanderers,” keep the courses established for them once for all by your word. The sun, greatest of the planets, in accordance with the order assigned it by your word, now inclines southward and shortens the days, now circles northward and lengthens them. Thus, from generation to generation—that is, always—your truth remains, in which you said: “Let them be for signs and seasons, and let them divide day and night” (Gen. I, 14).

You also founded the earth upon its stability, and it remains, supported by nothing except your word, by which you placed it in the beginning. You so surrounded it with the moist element of the air that it cannot fall into the heaven evenly spread round it on every side. In this heaven the birds of the air fly, as if swimming, and observe their seasons. Hence it is written: “The kite in heaven knew its time; the turtle-dove and the swallow knew the times of their coming” (Jer. VIII, 7).

[Col. 0786B] Thus:

**VERSE 91.** By your ordinance the day endures, because all things serve you, obeying your dispositions unchangeably. But much more fully and perfectly this is so in the heaven of heavens, of which you say: “Heaven is my seat” (Isa. LXVI, 1), namely, the chosen portion of rational creation. In that heaven, I say, your word remains forever, because by your word “the heavens were established, and all their power by the breath of your mouth” (Ps. XXXII, 6).

Again, from generation to generation—that is, in all those who are generated not merely according to the flesh but are also born again according to the spirit—your truth remains. Or: your word remains from generation to generation among the faithful of the Old and New Testaments. Or: your truth remains in the generation in which souls are now regenerated unto faith, like newborn infants, and in the generation in which bodies will be regenerated at the resurrection unto incorruption, into a perfect man. Your truth has no place in the crooked and perverse generation that is generated only according to the flesh and not regenerated according to the spirit.

[Col. 0786C] For not even all who are baptized ought to be called regenerated or reborn. Regeneration is that renewal through which children of wrath become children of grace. Many baptized persons are strangers to this grace: either they approach this sacrament deceitfully, like Simon Magus, or, though they approach with a true heart, turn back and do not return through true repentance—such as those whom the Apostle Peter rebukes by likening them to dogs returning to their vomit (II Pet. II, 22). Although their sins were forgiven in baptism, yet, because they did not preserve the sacrament of baptism, their latter state became worse than their former, when the unclean spirit returned to them with seven other spirits more wicked than itself (Luke XI, 26). This is a perverse generation, and faithless children. Therefore truth does not remain in this generation; it remains “from generation to generation,” that is, in children born again repeatedly,

[Col. 0786D] when regeneration is completed first in the soul and then in the flesh.

For although the souls of the faithfully baptized are now regenerated through baptism, they are still, as it were, growing in the womb of Mother Church and await the completion of their birth through that death by which “blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. XIV, 13). By such a death they come, as it were, from the womb into the light; and that light will be their birthday. Recognizing this, Mother Church rejoices on the birthdays of such children of hers, no longer mindful of the anguish in which she bore them, knowing that they are now born into the spaciousness of heaven, where your word, Lord, remains forever unchangeably.

And because their bodies were buried in peace, awaiting [Col. 0787B] their own regeneration and transformation into unchangeable immortality and impassibility, what is said here fittingly applies to them: “You founded the earth, and it abides.” For the blessed bodies of the blessed will be so spiritual and radiant that, together with their spirit, they will be one day, according to the saying: “And evening came, and morning came: one day.” For the very death of their bodies is, as it were, the saints’ evening; but their morning is the resurrection of those same bodies, having died with Christ, been buried with him, and risen with him. Christ himself also died on the cross toward evening on the sixth day of the Sabbath, and was buried in the evening; but he rose from the dead early in the morning on the first day of the Sabbath (Matt. 28; Mark 16; Luke 24). Thus in that evening and morning too there came to be one day, his flesh and soul together [Col. 0787C] glorified in that glory which he had before the world existed—the glory which he himself asked of the Father, saying: “Father, glorify me in your presence with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:4).

Therefore, when the bodies of the saints are conformed to the body of Christ’s glory by your ordering, God the Father, there abides one day, better in your courts than thousands. Whether it is said in the singular, “The day abides,” as explained above, or in the plural, as some manuscripts read, “The days abide,” in either case the abiding constancy of one light is proclaimed: for everlasting light shall shine upon the saints, glorified in Christ, who is day from day, God from God, light from light. On that day nothing will be cloudy [Col. 0787D] or stormy, because there all things serve you in a most joyful service, celebrating in praise and thanksgiving. There abides the day which the Lord has made, in which all the companies of saints will rejoice, continually singing: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. 117:24). But now, in this mortality, the days are evil, the times dangerous, and the enemies many, of whom I have already spoken above: “They almost consumed me on earth.”

**VERSE 92.** “Then perhaps I should have perished in my humiliation, had not your law been my meditation.” For meditation on your law is a kind of preparation of the armor necessary for battle; without it, whoever enters into battle is easily overthrown. Thus elsewhere it is said of the righteous man: “The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps shall not be tripped up” [Col. 0788A] (Ps. 36:31). Therefore I do not say, “Your law was my meditation before the battle,” but “is,” even after the battle, since my memory continually recalls how many benefits meditation on your law has given me. And therefore:

**VERSE 93.** “I shall never forget your ordinances, for by them you gave me life.” For I was dead, and when the staff of fear was laid upon me there was neither voice nor sensation (4 Kings 4). But when faith in the Incarnation showed me how greatly you loved me—you who gave up your Son in order to redeem a slave—I immediately began to live, as though the true Elisha were warming me by the contact of his body. Thus I was freed from the slavery of sin and death, whose law is that “the soul which sins shall itself die.” I live, then, insofar as [Col. 0788B] I either lack sins or resist them, aided and made alive by your ordinances. Yours, I say, not mine: for just as I could not create myself when I did not exist, so I could not justify myself when I was a sinner; or, to attend to the present literal sense, I could not make myself alive when I was dead. Therefore I shall never forget your ordinances, because by them you gave me life. Therefore:

**VERSE 94.** “I am yours; save me, for I have sought your ordinances.” Once I was my own, fulfilling my own wishes and even pleasures. But now I am yours, breaking my own will and gladly doing yours. I was the slave of as many masters as vices; but now I am yours, set free by you from those masters, to whom I was bound like the common she-ass at the crossroads, until you said to your disciples: “Untie her and bring her to me” (Matt. 21:2). I was also like the colt of an ass (Mark 11:2), upon which no person had sat at the time when I, a youth and a wanderer in a far country, could find no person to instruct, halter, or bridle me. But now, brought to you, tamed by the bridle of your fear, adorned also with the apostolic garments upon which you gladly sit, and in a sense saddled, I am now yours: your ass, your beast of burden, because “I became like a beast before you, and I am always with you” [Col. 0788C] (Ps. 72:23). But lest I cease to be yours, save me—that is, preserve and strengthen me in the salvation begun—for I have sought your ordinances: yours, not mine; yours, by which I may remain yours, not mine, by which I formerly was my own. I have sought your ordinances, and this was very necessary for me, because:

**VERSE 95.** “Sinners waited for me, to destroy me.” By sinners I mean demons and wicked people, who, like robbers lying in ambush, waited to destroy me by drawing me either to do evil or to consent to evildoers. But I escaped their hands and ambushes because I understood that your testimonies were made exceedingly credible through the witnesses themselves, namely the martyrs. By their martyrdoms—that is, their testimonies, confirmed by their deaths—they marked out beforehand and showed the way by which one goes from the Mount of Olives toward Jerusalem: that is, from prevenient mercy to the vision of eternal peace. These are those who spread their garments on the way—that is, gave their bodies, the garments of their souls, over to punishments. Others, namely holy confessors and teachers, taking branches from the olive grove of the Scriptures, likewise made the way of righteousness recognizable by their testimonies. The testimonies of all these, whether martyrs or confessors—testimonies called *martyria* in Greek—must be called not so much theirs as yours, O God. For it was not they who spoke, but your Spirit spoke in and through them. Therefore I understood their testimonies to be yours; and so, delighting in the way of your testimonies, I would not depart from it by yielding to the sinners who waited [Col. 0789B] and desired to destroy me, stripping me and inflicting wounds: stripping me of virtues and wounding me with vices; or stripping me by taking away gifts of grace, and wounding those natural endowments which cannot be removed.

For example, the gift of grace called obedience is taken from a person when that person becomes disobedient. Thus, by angering, we lose gentleness; by pride, humility. So, when the other vices rush upon us and rob us, we are stripped of virtues, which are accidental to human substance and therefore may be absent or present without the destruction of the subject. But reason cannot be taken from a human being without that person ceasing to be rational, because reason or rationality is a natural gift, like memory and free choice. Yet these natural goods are weakened by many wounds [Col. 0789C] when, under the domination and robbery of sins, they are afflicted; so that reason does not fully distinguish truth from falsehood, good from evil, useful from useless, honorable from dishonorable; nor does memory retain what reason has discerned, nor free choice freely preserve it. Thus the whole person lies ruined unless that merciful Samaritan saves him—the one who, moved by compassion, first recognized and loved the person who neither recognized nor loved him. In this love:

**VERSE 96.** “I saw the end of every perfection.” For all who are perfected or are to be perfected are perfected through this love, by which God first loved sinners who did not yet love him. Through [Col. 0789D] it the virtue of people predestined to life is perfected; through it the number of angels is restored and made complete. Therefore, seeing this love, I saw the end of every perfection. For Christ is “the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). This end is infinite, because God himself is immeasurable, and God is love—exceedingly broad in God himself, who has mercy on all and hates none of the things he has made, although he hates what he has not made, namely sins; and exceedingly broad also in people loved by God, who love not only friends but even enemies, although they do not love their enemies’ sins.

On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says [Col. 0790A] [Note: [Col. 0789D] Homily 14 on Ezekiel]: “Nothing is broader than to receive all into the bosom of love and to refuse to endure any constrictions of hatred. Love is broad because, in the expansiveness of love, it is able to contain even enemies. Hence it is commanded: ‘Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you’” (Matt. 5:44). Your commandment, then, is exceedingly broad, because the breadth of love is great. For love is the fullness of the law, upon which the entire law and the prophets hang.

Let us join the four letters already set forth: *Teth* means “good,” *Jod* “beginning,” *Caph* “hand,” and *Lamech* “heart,” as was stated at the beginning of the psalm. The sense is this: in the material contained under these four letters, with eight verses assigned to each letter, one must understand “the beginning of hand and heart,” [Col. 0790B] that is, of action and intention.

## MEM

“How I have loved your law, O Lord.”

According to Jerome, *Mem* means “from themselves”; according to Ambrose, “inner parts” or “bowels.” Let us combine both interpretations by saying, “from the very depths.” That is to say: these eight verses, all beginning with this letter, come from the very depths, because they concern love implanted to the marrow in the inward parts of the one who can truly say:

**VERSE 97.** “How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all the day.” You, O Lord, whose law I have loved, are my witness and know how inwardly I have loved your law from all my inmost being. I have loved exceedingly your law, contained in your exceedingly broad commandment; and that it is exceedingly so appears from this: your law itself is my meditation all day, upon which I meditate day and night—that is, all day. For a whole and complete day is rightly understood when night together with its day, or day together with its night, is included, according to “Evening came, and morning came: one day.” And rightly in this passage, when the complete day with its night is indicated, night is omitted and day alone named, because for the one who always meditates on the law of the Lord, day continually shines, illuminated by that sun who says: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” [Col. 0790C] (John 9:5). He is in the world until the consummation of the age, as he himself promised his disciples: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). From this truthful promise of Truth it is understood that faithful people will not be lacking from the world until the consummation of the age, and Christ, the light of the world, will remain with them. Each of these can faithfully sing: “How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all the day.” All day, because for me there is no night: for one who continually meditates on the light—indeed, in the light—of the law, the day is unbroken. From such continual meditation I receive this fruit:

**VERSE 98.** “You have made me wiser than my enemies”—the Jews, heretics, and all enemies of truth and of myself—by your exceedingly broad commandment, as stated above, and exceedingly long, because it is mine forever. What is longer than eternity? May it be granted to me to comprehend with all the saints the breadth and length and height and depth of this commandment: its breadth is indicated when it is said, “Your commandment is exceedingly broad”; its length, when it is said, “For it is mine forever”; and its height, when it is said, “Above enemies and above all who teach and above elders I have understood.” In this sense the Apostle too, about to speak of love, says: “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12:31). The final verse of this set of eight belongs to the depth of the same commandment, where it says: “From your commandments I understood; therefore I hated every way of iniquity” [Col. 0791B]. For as love, desiring good things, reaches upward, so, considering evil things, it reaches downward: the former by loving greatly, the latter by hating greatly.

To understand these things, you made me wiser than my enemies by your commandment, because your commandment is mine forever: for my love never fails, unlike those who believe for a time and fall away in time of temptation. Among these enemies there were also teachers seated in Moses’ chair and possessing the key of knowledge, and therefore teaching with authority. But I:

**VERSES 99–100.** “Have understood above all such teachers, because your testimonies are my meditation.” This meditation was to me like an anointing, teaching me concerning all things much better and more truly than teachers wise in their own estimation. Although some of them were elders, I nevertheless understood above the elders, because I sought your commandments.

Alternatively: I, David, understood above all who taught me, because I understood Moses and the other teachers of the law who preceded me in instruction in the law; and, moreover, by revelation of the divine Spirit, I understood many things concerning which I sang psalms that speak much more clearly of the kingdom of God than does the letter of the law, with Moses’ face covered by a thick veil. Likewise I, Christ, the true David, understood above all who taught me, standing “in the assembly of gods” [Col. 0791C] (Ps. 81:1), judging and rejecting evil traditions, because such teachers transgressed the commandments of God for the sake of their traditions—for example, by commanding washings of hands while neglecting inward defilements (Matt. 15; Mark 7). I understood above them when I taught that “it is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth: this defiles a person” (Matt. 15:11). Even when I was still a boy of twelve, sitting in the temple among the teachers, listening to and questioning them—I, a mere boy, an adolescent—already then understood above elders (Luke 2:46), who were themselves amazed at my understanding and answers.

**VERSE 101.** “I restrained my feet from every evil way, that I might keep your words.” Because I understood above elders, rejecting their traditions and seeking your commandments, instructed by those same commandments of yours I restrained my feet from every evil way: that is, I diligently checked the impulses [Col. 0792A] of thoughts inclined to rush away from the way of truth which I chose, and with the bridle of your fear held them back from every evil way, that I might keep your words. These words cannot be kept by those who walk in an evil way, who detest and reject your words; but, instructed by them and strengthened by the Spirit of life who is in them:

**VERSE 102.** “I did not turn aside from your judgments.” Those who either refuse to hear your words, or neglect them once heard and understood, call good evil and evil good, sweet bitter and bitter sweet, making light darkness and darkness light. They turn far aside from your judgments—judgments of equity and truth, declaring good to be good and evil to be evil. But I did not turn aside from your judgments, approving only [Col. 0792B] what I believed or understood that you approve, and likewise rejecting what I believed or understood that you reject. For you yourself established the law for me, writing it far better with your finger upon my heart than the old law was written on stone tablets. By that writing the severity of fear cast down the ancients; by this writing the sweetness of your love becomes sweet to the throats of faithful souls. I, David—or I, singing and repenting after David’s example—say this from experience, in wonder and thanksgiving alike:

**VERSE 103.** “How sweet are your words to my throat, O Lord, more than honey to my mouth.” Or, as it is read in other manuscripts, “more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth.” The stern words of the old law, threatening sinners with severe punishments, were exceedingly bitter; but your words, promising forgiveness of sins to penitents, are sweet both to throat and mouth: to the throat of the soul, when they are inwardly chewed over and swallowed in thought; and to the mouth, when they are outwardly preached for the glorification of your name, the edification of believers, or the refutation of unbelievers. Yet the law of Moses had some sweetness of honey, insofar as it promised a land flowing with milk and honey (Exod. 3:13). But your words, promising heavenly and invisible delights, are sweeter to me than such honey, since earthly delights are of little—or rather no—worth in comparison. Therefore I do not say, “sweet as honey,” but that your words are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb [Col. 0792D] to my throat and mouth. This sweetness of your words which promise heavenly delights:

**VERSE 104.** “I understood from your commandments.” It is one thing to understand commandments; it is another, from commandments understood and kept, to attain by the taste of understanding to the inward sweetness of wisdom. This is to understand from commandments, because one does not come to wisdom of hidden things except through obedience to commandments. Hence the saying of the Wise Man: “Have you desired wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will give her to you” (Ecclus. 1:33). But to one who despises commandments it is said: “Do not seek what is too high for you, nor investigate what is too strong for you; but always think on what the Lord has commanded you” (Ecclus. 3:2). He rightly says “always,” so that you may consider the commandments both before receiving wisdom [Col. 0793A] and afterward. For as keeping the commandments introduces one to wisdom’s savor, so negligence and forgetfulness of them blind even the eyes of the wise. This happened to Solomon, who, neglecting God’s commandments and going in to foreign women whom the Lord had forbidden, became foolish though he had formerly been wise.

But I, not departing from observing, meditating upon, and loving your commandments, understood—my understanding being enlarged from the commandments themselves—that inseparable companion of the savor of wisdom is love of righteousness. Therefore I hated every way of iniquity, since love of righteousness inflamed me, and it naturally hates its contrary, namely every way of iniquity. Inflamed by this hatred, I prayed above, saying: “Remove from me the way of iniquity.” This is the same as saying: Make hateful to me not only iniquity but every occasion that leads to iniquity. And, thanks be to God, my prayer was heard, because I hated every way of iniquity. For example, the favor of a flatterer is a way to vain glory; the beauty of a prostitute, a way to impurity; conversation with evil people, a way to malice; desire for another’s property, a way to fraud or robbery. In this manner there are many ways to iniquity, all of which I hated because I loved righteousness [Col. 0793B].

## NUN

This is the fourteenth letter among the Hebrews and has various interpretations. According to Jerome, *nun* means “eternal”; according to Ambrose, it means “only-begotten” or “pastures.” All these converge in one, because this passage concerns the only-begotten Son of God, who is the pasture of believers forever, himself light, himself lamp, of whom it says here:

**VERSE 105.** “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.” Your Word, O God, which was in the beginning and is the light of angels, became also the light of human beings, light shining in darkness. Walking in its light, I say in thanksgiving: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.” For that Word itself is eternal Wisdom, which, illuminating by the flame of its divinity the earthen vessel of the flesh united to it, became a lamp to my feet, directing the steps of my actions by the brilliant examples [Col. 0793D] shown in its life in the flesh. And that same Word, which is a lamp in every rational creature enlightened and kindled by it, is light in itself, like the sun: displaying its light in the body of the moon as in a mirror, illuminating the darkness of night, showing broad roads, and making narrow paths certain by the daylight of its own splendor.

Thus, yes, your word is a lamp in the mouth of prophets, but light in the mouth of apostles proclaiming the Gospel. Hence the Apostle Peter says: “We have the more certain prophetic word, to which you do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Pet. 1:19). But the apostles are told: “You are the light of the world”; by their teaching the Church shines as the moon by the sun [Col. 0794A] (Matt. 5:14). The moon, having no light from itself, is illuminated on that side on which it is lit by the sun’s light. Thus I—the Church, or I, an ecclesiastical person—have no brightness from myself, but from your Word, the Sun of righteousness. Therefore I say in thanksgiving: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.” Delighting in that light and desiring always to enjoy it:

**VERSE 106.** “I have sworn and determined to keep the judgments of your righteousness.” “I have sworn,” that is, I have made a most firm resolve and have determined, holding it fixed in my heart, steadfastly to keep the judgments of your righteousness: judging rightly and discerning between goods to be loved and evils to be rejected, as your bright word shows and admonishes us to reject evil and choose good. While I was intent upon this purpose of uprightness, many adversaries opposed me, through whom:

**VERSE 107.** “I have been utterly humbled,” pressed by adverse temptations and tribulations, so that I was even weary of living and had within myself the sentence of death, that I might not trust in myself but in you. Amid all these various dangers of death I continually cry: “Give me life according to your word,” that I may live according to your word, doing what your word teaches must be done and avoiding what it teaches must be avoided. To know that word is to live; to obey it is to reign—especially when obedience is not forced by fear but arises from voluntary devotion. I promised and promise the voluntary acts of such obedience with my mouth. But lest I be found false, may these:

**VERSE 108.** [Col. 0794C] “Voluntary offerings of my mouth be pleasing to you,” through your grace cooperating and confirming the word of my promise by subsequent deeds and conduct that accord with my vow. Thus, I beseech you, let the voluntary offerings of my mouth become pleasing, so that these three may come together as one: the will of an upright heart, the confession of a truthful mouth, and the completion of a good work. If even one of these is missing, the voluntary offerings of the mouth cannot be pleasing; for the sacrifices of our services are not voluntary offerings of the mouth unless one believes with the heart unto righteousness and confession is made with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10:10). When conduct pleasing to you is added to the heart’s voluntary faith and the mouth’s truthful confession—you to whom all good things are pleasing and all evil things displeasing—the voluntary offerings of the mouth [Col. 0794D] become pleasing. But lest the devil’s deceit or human frailty corrupting me should so deceive me that I suppose displeasing what pleases you, or pleasing what displeases you, instruct me inwardly yourself and teach me your judgments, for “blessed is the person whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach from the judgments of your law” (Ps. 93:12).

In the Hebrew Psalter it is read thus: “I have sworn and shall persevere, that I may keep the judgments of your righteousness. I have been greatly afflicted; O Lord, give me life according to your word. May the voluntary offerings of my mouth please you, O Lord; teach me according to your judgments.” Our manuscripts have:

**VERSE 109.** “My soul is always in my hands,” which may be explained thus: My soul is always in my hands in order that I may offer it to you, always to be given life by you. Therefore I also said elsewhere: “To you I lifted up my soul” (Ps. 24:7). I do not wish to have my soul in my hands as did that younger son who said to his father: “Father, give me the portion which falls to me” (Luke 15:12). Rather, I hold it in my hands in order continually to offer it to you, to be sacrificed as a sacrifice of praise.

Alternatively: “My soul is in my hands,” that is, my intention is in my works, not for an hour but always, so that eternal reward may come to it. But in other manuscripts it is better given thus: “My soul is always in your hands, and I have not forgotten your law.” This means: Let my soul [Col. 0795B] always be kept in your hands, as elsewhere it is said: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment of wickedness shall touch them” (Wis. 3:1). Let my soul, I beseech you, be in your hands, from which no one can snatch it, because “all the ends of the earth are in your hand” (Ps. 94:4), and “there is none who can resist your hand” (Dan. 4:32). And while your hand guards me always, I will always keep your law. I promise this with certainty because I have not forgotten your law so long as my soul has been in your hands.

The Hebrew text agrees with this sense, where it reads: “My soul is always in your hand, and I have not forgotten your law.” I have indeed not forgotten your law; nevertheless, transgressors of the law tried to make me forget it, because:

**VERSE 110.** “Sinners set a snare for me,” so that, because they could not act by their own strength against the hand of your power, they might catch me in the snare of deception. But I, knowing that their snares were not set, nor could have been set, in the way of your commandments but beside the way, as it is said elsewhere: “They set a stumbling-block for me beside the path” [Col. 0795C] (Ps. 139:6), refused to turn aside from the way of your commandments. “And I have not strayed from your commandments,” avoiding snares set beside the way, not in the one way. Against these the keeping of your commandments works like a noble antidote against poison. Knowing this:

**VERSE 111.** “I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance forever.” Formerly I was the heir of Adam the transgressor, myself transgressing the commandments of righteousness; now, made by grace an heir of God and co-heir of Christ, I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance, so that your testimonies may be for me a firm and, as it were, hereditary possession, preserved and to be preserved unto martyrdom forever, after the example of the blessed martyrs. Because of their steadfast witness to truth they are called *martyres* in Greek, “witnesses” in Latin; and their testimonies are called *martyria*. I have acquired them as an inheritance by contending for that truth and faith for which they too contended even unto death. For this is my purpose also: by the help of your grace, to persevere in their conflict even unto death. Otherwise your testimonies and theirs would not be hereditary to me or acquired by inheritance [Col. 0796A]. Yours, because your Spirit spoke in them; theirs, because such testimony was confirmed by their blood and death. Therefore, because it is my purpose, with your grace favoring me, to prefer death rather than depart by denying faith from the testimonies of your martyrs, for which your witnesses and martyrs died, I have acquired their testimonies, or *martyria*, as an inheritance—that is, as a firm possession—not by believing for a time and falling away in time of temptation, but by adhering forever to faith thus testified and readily consenting in my heart to such testimonies, although the flesh is weak, because they are the exultation of my heart even when they are grievous. For “the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41). Therefore, though my weakening flesh refuses excessive labors, yet with a willing spirit:

**VERSE 112.** “I have inclined my heart to perform your ordinances forever, for the sake of recompense.” Far above I said to you: “Incline my heart, O God, to your testimonies.” Now I say: “I have inclined my heart to perform your ordinances,” acknowledging that this humbling and inclining of my heart is both your work and mine: yours through prevenient grace; mine through the freedom of the will consenting to your grace at work. Not that even this consent comes from myself rather than from you; for if I claimed it as my own, having not an inclined but a proud heart, I should deserve to receive wrath rather than grace. For “you resist the proud but give grace to the humble” [Col. 0796C] (Jas. 4:6), and grace for grace: temporal grace in good merits, eternal grace in rewards that abide forever and succeed temporal ministry—the office of Martha, which is someday to be taken away—so that the recompense of Mary’s rest may succeed forever. For the sake of this recompense, which abides forever, I have inclined and humbled my heart to perform your ordinances, ready not only to know but also to do what you command as pertaining to my justification, knowing that “understanding is good to all who do it” (Ps. 110:10), just as, conversely, “to one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” (Jas. 4:17).

[Col. 0796D] The Hebrew text reads: “I have inclined my heart to perform your righteousnesses for the sake of eternal recompense.” There are indeed two recompenses appointed for those who labor well: one on the way and another in the homeland. The one on the way is temporal; whoever seeks this alone and chiefly, and does not seek the eternal, is a hireling. The recompense in the homeland is eternal; one who serves God for that alone can say: “One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:4). Truth commands us to seek this first and principally, saying: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6:33). And lest we should be anxious about provision for the journey, he added: “And all these things shall be added to you” (Luke 12:31). Again: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ For your Father knows that you need all these things” [Col. 0797A] (Matt. 6:31). Therefore, concerning all these things which I need on the way, casting all anxiety upon God, as the Apostle teaches, because he cares for us, I have inclined my heart to perform your ordinances, my God, forever for the sake of recompense. Or, as it reads in Hebrew, “for the sake of eternal recompense,” certain of your providence: when I stretch forward toward the things before me, namely eternal rewards, the temporal necessities will not fail me insofar as their use is expedient for seeking eternal things.

## SAMECH

The name of the fifteenth letter, *samech*, has various interpretations. According to Ambrose, it means “hear” or “support”; but according to Jerome, more skilled in the truth of the Hebrew, it means “help.” All these agree with the set of eight verses placed under this letter, because whoever obediently hears and firmly commits to memory what is said here will thereby have help in the occasions of tribulation in which one is worn down by the wicked, against whom he sings:

**VERSE 113.** “I hated the wicked, and I loved your law.” The wicked are those who oppose your law, O God. Though they were wicked people, I did not hate them inasmuch as they were people, because every person is to be loved by every person insofar as they are human; but insofar as they are wicked, even family members are to be hated with a holy and reasonable hatred, by which not people but human vices are hated. With such hatred I hated the wicked, hating their wickedness, namely their transgression of your holy law. And I did this because I loved your law: in proportion as it is loved and pleasing, its transgression is displeasing. Therefore, because I loved your law, I hated its transgressors; and while “I hated them with perfect hatred, they became enemies to me” [Col. 0797C] (Ps. 138:22).

In Hebrew it reads: “I hated the turbulent, and I loved your law.” Thus the wicked intended here must be understood as those for whom their own wickedness does not suffice for their personal ruin unless, with turbulent importunity, they attack righteousness. Had they attacked me, I should have failed, unless you—
**VERSE 114.** You are my helper and my protector; and I have placed my supreme hope in your word. You are my helper as I labour among turbulent wicked men and contend for your law, which I have loved; and you are my protector after labours and contests, granting me rest in yourself—at times through the taste of contemplation, when you allow me here in part to taste beforehand the best portion, which shall not be taken away; at other times, indeed continually, through hope in the future goods promised me in your word. For, believing your promises, I have placed my supreme hope in your word, knowing that you are able exceedingly beyond what I ask or understand to accomplish all that you have promised to those who follow you—those who, for your sake and for the Gospel, [Col. 0798A] leave everything, and to whom you promise a hundredfold recompense in this life with persecutions, and eternal life in the age to come (Matt. 19:29).

I understand indeed, so far as I can, what it is to receive a hundredfold: either by receiving spiritual things in return for carnal things, which by their incomparable worth will be as a hundred compared with a small number; or certainly in this way, that those blessed in every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ should lack nothing, so that nothing may be wanting to them in any grace as they await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ—when, as needy, they enrich many, and, as having nothing, possess all things (2 Cor. 6:10). Some among them, having become stewards of ecclesiastical resources, receive even in temporal things a hundredfold more than they leave behind; and, when they have faithfully fulfilled the stewardship entrusted to them, they too will possess eternal life. To each such person it will be said: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21).

Yet neither will those be defrauded—rather, they too will be enriched in this pilgrimage by a hundredfold recompense—whom God grants not to preside but to be subject within such a fellowship as that of which it is written: “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul, and no one among them was needy, since distribution was made to each according as anyone had need” (Acts 4:32–35); nor would anyone desire more, being content with what he had received. Therefore, whether in the way stated or in another way your disciples, O Christ, who promise a hundredfold, are to receive a hundredfold in this life, I do not doubt that this promise has been fulfilled in many and will yet be fulfilled in others. For both what I understand I hope and have hoped for, and what I do not understand I have placed my supreme hope in—wholly intent upon your word, which must necessarily be fulfilled, “that you may be justified in your words” (Ps. 50:6), by accomplishing all that you promise to the children of promise. And because I desire to be in their fellowship without evil disturbance:

**VERSE 115.** Depart from me, you wicked ones, and I will search out the commandments of my God. You wicked spirits, I first drive away like flies from the assault upon my mind, [Col. 0798D] as it is intent upon searching God’s commandments; in the Word of God’s power, in whom I have placed my supreme hope, I command you, saying: Depart from me, whom you have grievously tormented with malicious intent, as though you were an evil legion. Depart, I say, and go into the swine granted you by the Word in whom I have placed my supreme hope. In his power I say to you: Depart from me, and do not continue to harm me, whose purpose is to devote myself to the Word in whom I have placed my supreme hope, and to search the commandments of God.

You also, wicked people, companions of wicked spirits, depart from me together with them, rebuked by the Word in whom I have placed my supreme hope, lest you hinder me when I desire diligently to search the commandments of God. For the importunity of your wickedness, although it gives exercise in performing God’s commandments, nevertheless calls one away from searching them—now by persecution, now by disputing, [Col. 0799A] now by asking that the times owed to the Word of God may be spent on earthly business, and that the weaker may be defended by the stronger, or the oppressed rescued. All this disturbance is charged to you, who are wicked, and therefore excluded from the Sabbath of rest. You neither wish yourselves to rest or to give time to searching God’s commandments, nor, so far as lies in you, do you permit leisure to those who desire it—especially when your hour and the power of darkness are at hand, when “night has come, and all the beasts of the forest will pass through it, the young lions roaring to seize and to seek their food from God” (Ps. 103:21).

But now that the sun has risen—that is, now that the brightest truth against you, the sun of righteousness, has been made manifest—depart from me, holy Church; or from me, penitent David; or from me, whoever loves the Word of God [Col. 0799B] and searches his commandments. Depart from me, so that, when you beasts have been placed in your dens, I may go forth; and may every rational person, using reason, go forth to his work and to his labour until evening. Let him go forth, I say, not only to work, but also to meditate in the field with the patriarch Isaac—that is, walking and meditating in the field of the Scriptures, far removed from the crowds of wicked men who desire to disturb this most holy leisure (Gen. 24). You wicked ones, depart from me. But, O God, you:

**VERSE 116.** Receive me according to your word—by fulfilling, that is, your promises. You promise those who go out from their land and from their kindred [Col. 0799C] that they shall be received in the land which you will show them (Gen. 12). What you say to Abraham alone, you say to all Abraham’s children—not children according to the flesh, but according to imitation in good works, as it is said: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham” (John 8:39).

You also promised that the children of Israel, going out from Egypt and separated from a barbarous people, would be received in a land flowing with milk and honey (Exod. 3:17). Likewise, to Zerubbabel, going out from Babylon, you promise: “On that day I will take you, my servant, and make you as a signet before me” (Hag. 2:24). What else is it for me to have withdrawn from the fellowship of wicked men and prepared my mind to search the commandments of my God, than to have gone out with Abraham from my land and my kindred, [Col. 0799D] and with holy Moses, the lawgiver, out of the barbarous people? Or likewise, with Moses himself, to have ascended the mountain, that I may deserve to receive the law of the Lord and, enjoying discourse with God, shine in countenance as he did, whose face shone from the fellowship of God’s speech.

Jesus the high priest also, with Zerubbabel the leader, separated from the wicked captors of God’s people. Though he had previously been clothed in filthy garments, he was at last received into glory when, estranged from the fellowship of the wicked, he heard in the word of the Lord that he was to be crowned with golden crowns and clothed in fine changes of raiment, with a clean turban placed upon his head. In all these cases we have the promiser, and we possess as a pledge your word spoken to Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Zerubbabel: [Col. 0800A] that if we imitate them in withdrawing from the wicked for the leisure of holy contemplation, we may be received by you, and our sacrifice may thus be received by you, as you received their sacrifices.

Indeed, because the sacrifice of praise honours you more than the sacrifice of a slaughtered beast, I, separated from the wicked in order to offer you a sacrifice of praise, a sacrifice of jubilation, confidently ask that I may be received according to your word, saying to you continually: Receive me according to your word, and I shall live, like that son of Abraham who said: “For me, to live is Christ” (Phil. 1:21). Likewise: “Yet now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). For as long as he was in the fellowship of wicked Jews, he could not live. But when it pleased him who separated him [Col. 0800B] from his mother’s womb, the wicked synagogue, that he should know the truth which formerly he had opposed, then he began to live, made alive by that Life which says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

And because I, little penitent David, await by faith and hope a similar life, seeking it after David’s example, you, Lord, receive me according to your word, and do not put me to shame in my expectation. Do not put me to shame, but distinguish me from the wicked by giving me the love which, poured into my heart through the Holy Spirit, makes the expectation of future things firm through the reception of present gifts—through the hope that does not put to shame. A person is put to shame in his expectation when that which he expects does not come to him. Thus the foolish virgins, having no oil in their vessels, were put to shame in their expectation when they were excluded from the long-awaited wedding joy, the bridegroom saying: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12).

Therefore, lest I too be put to shame in my expectation, I ask that the oil of love be given me now. When I have received it sufficiently, because “love hopes all things” (1 Cor. 13:7), hope does not put to shame; nor do you, inspirer of this same hope, put me to shame in my expectation. And so that this expectation may be more and more confirmed by the testimony of a good conscience:

**VERSE 117.** Help me, and I shall be saved, and I shall meditate always upon your ordinances. Although I have already said to you in thanksgiving, “You are my helper and my protector,” I nevertheless still ask to be received and helped, lest I ever lose the gift [Col. 0800D] of your reception and your help. Rather, as it remains with me and I make progress from day to day, may I reach the place where I shall be saved and shall meditate always upon your ordinances.

When I say “always,” I refer to both preceding statements: that I may always remain saved and may always meditate upon your ordinances—ever enjoying everlasting salvation, and ever meditating upon your ordinances, by which those whom you predestined and called, them also you justified and glorified; always giving thanks, both rejoicing in hope in this life and, in the life to come, joined to the fellowship of the blessed, whose meditation upon your ordinances will be everlasting and whose thanksgiving unceasing. Desiring this, I say continually: Help me, and I shall be saved, and I shall meditate always upon your ordinances.

But I propose to meditate upon *your* ordinances rather than mine because those who establish their own righteousness and are not subject to your righteousness are despised by you, like that Pharisee who, glorying in his own righteousness, despised the publican. In despising the publican, you too despised him who despised one not more righteous than himself, indeed, but far humbler—who, standing at a distance and not daring to lift his eyes to heaven, struck his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13). “Woe to you who despise: shall you not yourself also be despised?” says the Spirit of truth in the prophet Isaiah (Isa. 33:17). Therefore, by a just judgment:

**VERSE 118.** You have despised all who depart from your ordinances, because their thought is unjust: attributing their righteousness to their own power rather than to your grace, [Col. 0801B] they refuse to submit to your righteousness; and in disdain they despise others who place confidence in your ordinances rather than their own. They certainly transgress the natural law, by which it is suggested in the heart of every rational person: “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another.” This law is universal. And because where there is no law, neither is there transgression, but where there is transgression of the law, there is violation of the law, I:

**VERSE 119.** Have accounted all sinners of the earth as transgressors: those who did not receive the written law, because they have the natural law, and by not keeping it become transgressors. Infants also, not yet regenerated, because they sinned in Adam, are judged transgressors of the law given in Paradise and not kept, because Adam did not keep the command set before him. [Col. 0801C] In him, as the Apostle says, “all sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23), being freely justified by gratuitous grace, which justifies those who love the testimonies of that grace.

Therefore I loved your testimonies, which bear witness to grace that justifies freely: rejoicing over the lost sheep found, and likewise over the lost drachma found, and preparing sweet feasting for the prodigal son returning to his father (Luke 15:8). I loved testimonies of such graces, through which, released from the burden of a law that weighs down rather than helps—for Moses’ hands were heavy—I now breathe freely. Having cast out servile fear, I continually seek chaste and filial fear, saying:

**VERSE 120.** Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments. That servile fear, by which the rod or staff of the law pressed down the dead, though it in some way bound my flesh, so that through fear of the punishments threatened by the law I did not dare to sin, nevertheless did not pierce it, or crucify it so that, when it had been put to death, there would be no will to sin even were impunity granted. Therefore I ask for a better fear: that, when flesh and fleshly desires—which wage war against my soul—have been pierced, crucified, and put to death, I may have no capacity to sin, even if opportunity or impunity be granted in human tribunals, through my reverent regard for your judgments (1 Pet. 2).

For I have feared your judgments, even when I was conscious of nothing against myself, knowing that I would not thereby be justified even if I were conscious of no crime; [Col. 0802A] because in your judgments not only deeds but also thoughts must be examined. Therefore the Apostle says: “I do not even judge myself; but he who judges me is the Lord” (1 Cor. 4:3). Following his footsteps, I do not think that I have attained. For I have feared, and I fear, your judgments, not knowing whether I shall be found worthy of hatred or of love in your judgment—a judgment which, fearing, I desire; and desiring, I fear.

Let us now join the three preceding letters: *mem*, *nun*, and *samech*, whose names, interpreted into Latin, signify: “From these, eternal help.” Thus understand that from the three octonaries contained under these letters eternal help comes to those who sing faithfully and wisely. Faithfully, with regard to matters not understood and yet believed true; [Col. 0802B] wisely, with regard to matters tasted through understanding—or, better, through experience. Among these most savoury matters is that love of which the first octonary says: “How I have loved your law, O Lord; it is my meditation all the day.” The second says: “I have not forgotten your law,” which is an indication of great love, since what is intimately loved is continually retained in the memory without forgetfulness. But in the third octonary, when it says, “I have hated the wicked and loved your law,” that love is plainly expressed which “does not rejoice in iniquity but rejoices together with truth,” since it both hates the wicked and loves the law that teaches truth (1 Cor. 13:6).

## AIN

This sixteenth letter, whose name *ain* means “spring” or “eye,” [Col. 0802C] rightly suits this octonary, in which the judgment of discernment is treated. This is the spring of just actions, and their good intention is an eye directed toward the salvation of God. Accordingly, the third verse of this octonary says: “My eyes have failed for your salvation, and for the word of your righteousness.” The connection with what precedes is as follows: “I have feared your judgments,” and therefore, anticipating your judgments through confession:

**VERSE 121.** I have done judgment and righteousness, believing your Apostle when he says: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31). Fearing to undergo the judgment of condemnation, I have done judgment and righteousness: judgment, by judging and discerning [Col. 0802D] between good and evil; righteousness, by rejecting evil and choosing good. Fleeing the judgment of condemnation, I have made the judgment of discernment; fearing judgment without mercy, I have made judgment with mercy, assenting to him who says: “Have mercy on your own soul by pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30:24). For he truly pleases God who both distinguishes good and evil by just judgment and, through discriminating righteousness, loves the good and hates evil, as elsewhere it is said: “Hating evil, cleaving to good” (Rom. 12:9).

By thus doing judgment and righteousness, I have stirred up many enmities and slanders against myself, on the part of opposing demons and people together. Fearing them, I pray: Do not hand me over to those who slander me. The devil slandered blessed Job, saying: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” (Job 1:9); and he asked that Job be handed over to him for testing, so that, when he had conquered him in temptation, he might exult in his slander. Job indeed was handed over to the tempter to be tested, but not to the slanderer for slander; for, victorious in all temptations, although he endured false slanders from the devil, friends, and wife, he escaped any true charge. Accordingly, he was not handed over to slanderers.

This occurred as a type of the holy Church of God. Although the Church endures false slanders from demons, pagans, heretics, and even enemies of its own household, such as Job’s wife, for the testing of its patience, it incurs no true ones. For temptation or tribulation produces patience in its children; patience, proof; and proof, hope. That hope did not put them to shame in such a way [Col. 0803B] as to give their enemies a true occasion or basis for slander; rather, the slander deceitfully twisted against the Church was turned back upon their own heads (Rom. 5:4–5). For example, while pagans falsely slander the Church as worshipping a dead man, the Church truly glories in worshipping Christ, the Son of the living God—the living God himself bearing witness to this through the powers and miracles of blessed martyrs who died in his worship.

Likewise, the slander of heretics is turned upon their own heads, by the refutation of the falsehood of those who err and lead others into errors, and by the simultaneous vindication of apostolic teaching, both concerning the purity of faith and the purity of Christian conduct. But as long as false Christians are mingled with true ones, there are no lack of enemies, hidden or open, who are Gog and Magog, [Col. 0803C] always prepared to slander. Therefore I—whether the Church or an ecclesiastical person—pray: Do not hand me over to those who slander me, so that they may ever be able truly to mock and boast of their victory over me. That would be a great slander against me, especially if they so overcame me as to entice or drive me from good to evil. And lest this happen, or be possible in any way:

**VERSE 122.** Receive your servant for good, so that the proud may not slander me by being able to charge me with some evil. I call myself your servant because of the consciousness of humility in which I am always ready, with your help, to serve you, obey your commandments, and humbly make satisfaction for past sins. But I call my slanderers proud, as those who glory either in their own malice, according to: “Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?” (Ps. 51:3), or in false righteousness, like him who said: “I give you thanks, God, because I am not like other people—robbers, unjust persons, adulterers, or even like this publican” (Luke 18:11).

By contrast, he who said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (ibid., v. 13), striking his breast and not daring to lift his eyes to heaven, was already your servant through consciousness of humility and true repentance. You received that same servant for good when you delivered him from the slander of the proud Pharisee, who established his own righteousness and would not submit to yours; indeed, what was worse, he slanderously insulted the penitent publican. [Col. 0804A] Therefore, because I too confess myself your servant by frequently striking my breast, and because I fear the slanderer, the Pharisee—or rather that uncircumcised Philistine, who is accustomed to reproach the armies of the living God for having come prepared to fight against him (1 Sam. 6:12)—you, who resist the proud but give grace to the humble, receive me, your servant, little David humbled by true repentance.

Please receive me for good, while you see the evil Philistine insulting me. Receive me for good, giving me victory over evil: now with sling and stone, striking evil from afar through prayers; now with the two-edged sword, striking it at close range through words. That is, strike down the malice of the proud, who always lay snares and utter slanders, arranging it for my good but for their evil, because, after the example of the proud Philistine, they will be slain by their own sword. Thus they will have no ability to slander me, David—me, your penitent servant, whom you deign to receive for good by giving me a humble and gentle heart, yet not one asleep in sloth, but alert and long watchful. Indeed, in this watchfulness:

**VERSE 123.** My eyes have failed for your salvation, and for the word of your righteousness. They have failed from themselves, advancing beyond themselves toward your salvation: namely, toward your Son, my Saviour, who, willing that all people should be saved and come to knowledge of the truth, issued through his Gospel the word of your righteousness, saying to his disciples, and through them to others: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes and [Col. 0804C] Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20).

The word of this righteousness is manifest throughout the entire text of the holy Gospel. Yet that sermon delivered on the mountain—when he who had formerly opened the mouths of the prophets opened his own mouth to speak—may particularly be called the word of your righteousness, O God, lover and giver of righteousness. There righteousness is taught to be done not before people, after the example of the Pharisees, but before God, after the example of the disciples: not that the disciples themselves may be glorified by people, but that people, seeing the works of this righteousness, may glorify the Father and author of it. Since a human being cannot perform this righteousness, you alone can:

**VERSE 124.** Deal with your servant according to your mercy, [Col. 0804D] and teach me your ordinances. You have already made me your servant by inspiring your fear, the fear of your judgments, so that I might fear your judgments.
