But that perfect love may cast out fear, deal with your servant according to your mercy, not according to my righteousness; and deign to teach me your ordinances, by which you justify the ungodly person who cannot justify himself.

For, just as I could not create myself when I did not exist, that I might become some creature, so, being a sinner born in sins, I cannot justify myself, that I might become some beginning of your new creation. Your Apostle testifies of this: “Neither circumcision is anything nor uncircumcision, but a new creation” (Gal. 6:15). But there is a new creation when the old person has been put off and the new person put on, [Col. 0805A] which cannot happen unless you teach me your ordinances. Therefore I say: Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your ordinances. I say, yours, not mine: yours, by which you justify a human being, and not he himself; by which, now having begun their work in me:

**VERSE 125.** I am your servant, though I was once the servant of sin. But that I may become a friend from being a servant, after the example of those to whom you say: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15:15), give me understanding, that I may know your testimonies. Although I said above, “I have understood more than the aged,” and “I have understood more than all who teach me,” nevertheless I still ask for understanding. Drinking from an inexhaustible spring, I thirst for the increase, completion, and preservation alike of the gift received and begun, that I may know your testimonies—testimonies known by those who can say with the Apostle: “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. 8:16). And again: “For God is my witness how I long for you all in the affections of Christ Jesus” (Phil. 1:8).

Testimonies of this kind are greatly necessary against slanderers. When they make importunate assaults, those inward testimonies of yours are necessary by which a person is persuaded to believe that he is your child—especially one who says: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke 15:19). Such am I, who have sinned, Father, against heaven and before you, and am no longer worthy to be called your son. Nor do I dare to count myself your son unless you give me understanding in this matter, [Col. 0805C] that I may know your testimonies which attest that I am your son: restored after extreme want by the feast of the fatted calf, and adorned at once with the best robe, a ring, and shoes. All these are good and clear testimonies that I, who am not worthy to be called your son, have been received as a son—though the slanderers themselves affirm that I am not worthy, as did that elder son who, angered at his brother’s reception, preferred to slander his received brother rather than feast and rejoice with him.

Against such slanderers, you Father of mercies, give me understanding, that I may know your inward and outward testimonies: inward, in the food of the fatted calf which purifies the conscience; outward, in the best robe, ring, and shoes received, which adorn one’s reputation, and by which feet once muddy become beautiful, as it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace!” (Rom. 10:15). Again: “How beautiful are your steps in shoes, daughter of the prince!” (Song 7:1). There was once a time for such things to be proclaimed through the prophets; but now:

**VERSE 126.** It is time to act, Lord, because the slanderers have destroyed your law by establishing their own traditions contrary to your law. These traditions cannot be resisted by words, however polished, unless you, Lord, confirm and cooperate with the word by subsequent deeds. Therefore now is the acceptable time, the time for mercy, the time for works by which your law, Lord, destroyed by slanderers, may be restored and fulfilled. For you did not come [Col. 0806A] to abolish the law, but to fulfil it (Matt. 5:17).

You said this in the time of speaking. For both through yourself and through your servants, whom you sent to call the invited guests to the wedding, you have altogether sufficiently said what had to be said (Luke 14:8). The cupboards are now full of the spoken and written words of those inviting people to your supper. The sound of the Apostles and your other messengers has gone out into all the earth, not only by utterances but also by writings published everywhere. There is none who hides, or can hide, from the brightness of your word, spoken and written in many ways—so much so that there are now no languages or speeches in the whole world in which the voices of those inviting to the Gospel wedding are not heard.

Yet those who have been called, occupied with other concerns, all make excuses: because they have bought estates, or yokes of oxen, or taken wives; or, as it is elsewhere written: “One went away to his own farm, another to his business” (Matt. 22:5). [Col. 0806B] In this way almost all have destroyed your law, following their own law, implanted in their members and resisting your law. They refuse to consent to your law as did the one who said: “I consent to the law of God, because it is good; but I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin and death” (Rom. 7:23).

Thus, delighting in God’s law according to the inward person and resisting the law of sin as far as he could, he did not destroy your law. Rather, fleeing to your grace, he did not murmur against you but cried out to you: “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Rom. 7:24). He did not, I say, destroy your law when, in such prayer, he fled from the burden of the oppressive law to the bosom of your assisting grace.

But these slanderers, against whom I now complain, have destroyed your law so completely that Gospel writings and sayings avail nothing with them or against them; they contradict them in opposition and slander. It is therefore time to do, rather than to say, something against these destroyers and slanderers, that they may be compelled to say: “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them against us” (Exod. 14:25). At last the Egyptians said this, humbled by deed rather than speech. Since they had despised Moses’ words, they were finally so humbled in the Red Sea by a wonderful and terrifying event [Col. 0806D] that they said: “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them against us.”

So now, against the slanderers and despisers of your law, O God, it is time to do something by which every mouth of slanderers may be stopped and by which those who refuse to come when called by word alone may be compelled to enter the wedding. May they experience the goad of some deed against which it is hard for them to kick, and therefore at least, compelled, come in such numbers that your house may be filled. But though I too may at one time have needed this goad, touched by your scourges, I do not now seek it. Rather, with the bride I long to be drawn after you by the sweetest drawing, “because,” as you know, “I am sick with love” (Song 2:5): with love, or ardent desire, to see you and to cleave to you—not for an hour, [Col. 0807A] but forever; and one cannot reach this except by the way of your commandments.

**VERSES 127–128.** Therefore I have loved your commandments above gold and topaz, because they are desirable to me “above gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. 18:11)—above everything this world has that is beautiful to look upon, such as gold and topaz, a precious stone, or pleasant and sweet, such as honey and honeycomb. Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments, that from what is straight I might become straight. Conversely, I hated every wicked way, because, as the way of your commandments is straight, so the way of error is wicked, crooked, shipwrecking, and dangerous—indeed destructive. Therefore whoever loves the straight way, the way of the righteous, necessarily hates the wicked way. So too I, penitent David, from the time when I began through your grace to be directed toward all your commandments, have not merely avoided but hated every wicked way, delighting to walk in that way which says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

## FE

This seventeenth letter, whose name *fe* means “mouth,” is fittingly placed at the head of these eight verses, the third of which reads: “I opened my mouth and drew in breath, because I desired your commandments.” This statement makes clear that the chief and principal intention of one who sings in this manner concerns desire for the spiritual commandments of God, carnal observances being rejected. These observances were contained in the law of Moses, which bore witness to spiritual grace [Col. 0807C] but did not give it—bore witness, I say, in a most wonderful way, since through many carnal sacrifices the one spiritual sacrifice was signified, by which alone God, angered through the sin of the first human being, was to be propitiated and appeased. Perceiving this, I, David, sing, saying:

**VERSE 129.** Wonderful are your testimonies, O Lord. The greatness and multitude of creatures made by you from nothing bear witness to your omnipotence, by which you could make so many and such great things from nothing. Human reason, considering these things made from nothing—from which neither angel nor human being can make anything—is compelled to marvel. Hence the ancient dictum: “Nothing comes from nothing; nothing can return to nothing.”

Certainly, this impossibility of making something from nothing or reducing something to nothing is rightly assigned to humans and angels. But to you, who have made all things ordered beneath you from nothing, omnipotence is rightly ascribed: just as you made all things from nothing, so you are able to bring all things to completion or restore them *for nothing*, as you say elsewhere: “If my people had listened to me, if Israel had walked in my ways, perhaps I would have humbled their enemies for nothing” (Ps. 80:14). Again, it is most truly said to you: “For nothing you will save them; in wrath you will break the peoples” (Ps. 55:6). It is great omnipotence to have created many and great things from nothing and to have saved for nothing many who, just as they were nothing before you created them, so had done no good, nor could have done any good, before [Col. 0808A] you made them good out of evil. In all these things wonderful testimonies of your power are seen.

Likewise, the beautiful and fitting ordering of things created from nothing bears wonderful witness to your wisdom, which reaches from end to end—from the highest archangel to the smallest worm, from the beginning of time to the consummation of the ages—reaching mightily and disposing all things sweetly. Thus nothing is disordered in your kingdom, which is the kingdom of all ages. For, just as they would not have begun to exist unless you created them, so, once created, they could not continue to exist unless you governed and preserved them.

Moreover, that the governance of all things may work together for good to those called saints according to purpose, and that all things—even those that appear useless—may be useful to them, this is wrought by your goodness. No malice conquers this goodness; rather, it conquers malice, making good use even of evils for the benefit of the good. In all these things the wonderful testimonies of your immense goodness shine forth, just as your power and wisdom likewise are immense. Thus in the quantity, quality, and usefulness of creatures, the power, wisdom, and goodness of the creating Trinity have borne witness wonderfully through wonderful testimonies. For even those things which have become commonplace through use—such as the movement of the stars, the continual courses of waters, and similar things evident to ordinary people—are found wonderful by those who investigate them more subtly.

Therefore my soul searched them out, so that from visible things I might understand invisible things, from mutable things immutable things—namely, [Col. 0808C] eternal power, wisdom, and goodness—and, having understood them, might love them. Yet more wonderful testimonies of yours, O Lord, are found in the Scriptures of truth, where unprecedented miracles are narrated, performed beyond the customary course of nature either through angels, through human beings, or through both working together: such as Moses’ rod changed into a serpent and devouring the rods of the magicians turned into serpents; the sea divided; the rock pouring forth waters; and other great deeds of this kind (Exod. IV and VII). But these were signs of greater things, so that those former things might be called a shadow foreshadowing the body of truth, while the body is the sun of righteousness, at whose rising day would breathe and the shadows would incline.

In all these are your wonderful testimonies, O Lord, [Col. 0808D] of which some show your power, as do the miracles mentioned; some your wisdom, as do your words spoken and written among these things, whether in such matters through Moses or in the legal and prophetic books; and others your goodness, as do the sacrifices instituted for a time for the expiation of sins, until the true and perfect sacrifice should come, which would take away the sins not of the Israelite people alone but of the whole world. Since this could not be accomplished through the blood of goats or calves, it remained to investigate diligently in such sacrifices how they bore witness to the true sacrifice, which, offered for the salvation of the whole world, was a lamb for the innocent, a goat for repentant sinners, a dove for the simple, and a turtledove for the chaste. And, to speak briefly, it was all things to all, that it might gain all, when all sacrifices were fulfilled in itself, the one sacrifice to which these alone bore wonderful testimony—not among fools, who did not weigh such matters, but among believers, who searched them out. Therefore my soul searched them out by reading, and by meditating on what it had read, not for an hour but by day and night. Thus, by searching, I learned that

**VERSE 130.** *The unfolding of your words gives light* to those who search them, first according to the literal or historical sense, then according to the inward meaning, namely the mystical sense, which he has hidden from the wise and prudent but gives to little ones—not to those wise in lofty things, but to those of humble understanding. Therefore incarnate Truth itself says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and [Col. 0809B] earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, because thus it was pleasing before you” (Luke 10:21). Here “the wise and prudent” means the proud. This is clear because they are opposed not to fools but to little ones, that is, the humble, of whom it is said: “Allow the little children to come to me; for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10:14). Likewise: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3). Among these I too am poor in spirit.

**VERSE 131.** *I opened my mouth and drew in the Spirit, because I desired your commandments*: to know them through the understanding given to little ones, and to perform them in actuality—something never attainable unless the Spirit assists the weakness made evident by the commandments of the law, so that, recognizing it, those who were puffed up might be deflated, and, made little ones, might receive the understanding given only to little ones, that is, to the humble. Therefore, to draw in this Spirit, who assists weakness, I opened my mouth through asking, seeking, and knocking, knowing that if we, though evil, know how to give good gifts to our children, much more will our heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

Through this bestowed Spirit charity is poured into the hearts of believers who, through their faith, open the mouth of the mind, which is closed in unbelievers. But I, because I believed, opened my mouth; and, as that very faith cleansed my heart and enlarged the mouth of my heart, I drew in the Spirit, who willingly enters the open mouth of the heart, following the example of him [Col. 0809D] who said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart has been enlarged” (2 Cor. 6:11). For he has a narrow mouth who desires good things only for himself, like a hireling, or fears evils only for himself, like an evil slave. But he has an enlarged mouth toward God the Father who presents himself to him as a son, desiring the Father’s will to be fulfilled not merely in himself or through himself, but in all and through all; for it is not the Father’s will that sinners should perish, but rather that they should be converted and live.

Thus, with my mouth enlarged through the exceedingly broad commandment of brotherly charity, which I desired to keep, I drew in the Spirit, through whom that same charity poured out in my heart might effect in me the perfection which I could not attain through the law, which brought nothing to perfection. But in saying, [Col. 0810A] *Because I desired your commandments*, by which expression the imperfect past tense is indicated, I signify that I am still imperfect. Thus also those who said, “But we had hoped that he would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21), retained scarcely the remnants of an imperfect hope. Therefore, that I may be perfected, you—whose regard signifies mercy, but whose disregard intimates wrath—“do not turn your face away from me” (Ps. 50:11), but

**VERSE 132.** *Look upon me and have mercy on me.* Look upon me with those eyes of which it is said: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears toward their prayers” (Ps. 33:16). This is both to look upon and to have mercy: for those whom a merciful regard justifies, a merciful hearing enriches with virtues. Neither one suffices without the other. Therefore I ask for both, saying: *Look upon me and have mercy on me.*

Look upon me, O Sun of righteousness, driving away the darkness of injustice by your radiant regard; and have mercy on me, miserable as I am, by giving me the riches of virtues—not in any manner whatever, but according to the judgment concerning those who love your name: not as you gave Saul a kingdom afterward to be torn away from him, but according to the never-to-be-dissolved oath by which you swore to Abraham our father that you would give to those who love your name. For, speaking to Abraham our father, you said: “Blessing I will bless you, and I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven and as the sand which is on the shore of the sea” (Gen. 22:17). Those who love your name are rightly compared with the stars of heaven, and are children of Abraham: namely, through faith, faithful and radiant like him. But his children according to the flesh—whether born from him or having acquired the name of his children through an appearance of godliness while denying its power—are found like the sand of the sea, barren and contemptible. Thus those who do not love your name can readily be distinguished from those who do love it by the manifest judgment of discrimination. For the former, being wholly earthly, there is a judgment of condemnation; but for those who love your name there is a judgment of discrimination, which each of them also seeks when he says: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy people” (Ps. 42:1). By this judgment “the Lord will judge his people, and will have mercy on his servants” (Deut. 32:36). He will judge, indeed, by distinguishing [Col. 0810D] his own people from a people not his own, a barbarous people; and, this judgment preceding, he will have mercy on his servants, showing them in themselves mercies to be sung for ever, since they will endure for ever.

Such was not the mercy concerning which it is said reproachfully in Hosea: “Your mercy is like a morning cloud and like the dew that passes away in the morning” (Hos. 6:4). Such was not the mercy of the rich man clothed in purple and feasting splendidly every day (Luke 16:19). For this mercy was given not according to the judgment concerning those who love your name—those whom, because you first loved them with an eternal love before the foundation of the world, it followed that, already anticipated by the blessings of your sweetness and your most sweet love, they too should love your name invoked over them.

[Col. 0811A] For you are named, and are, the Father of lights and the Father of mercies. Therefore to you, Father of lights, I say: *Look upon me*, by enlightening me; and to you, Father of mercies, I say: *Have mercy on me according to the judgment concerning those who love your name*—the name indicating fatherhood. Those who love it are sons, not slaves. Hence, just as “a father has compassion on his children” (Ps. 102:13), so you will have compassion on such persons. Desiring to be admitted to their fellowship, I cry to you from deep darkness, O Father of lights, saying: *Look upon me.* And from many and deep miseries I cry to you, O Father of mercies, saying: *Have mercy on me*—not in whatever way, but according to the judgment concerning those who love your name. To them you give temporal mercies, that through these they may gain eternal ones, making friends for themselves by ministering temporal things to those through whom they may be received into eternal dwellings. Or indeed you withdraw temporal mercies from them when you know that they can be impeded by them from eternal things, so that they may run more freely toward eternal things.

These mercies I desire when I say: *Have mercy on me according to the judgment concerning those who love your name*. For to these lovers of your name all things work together for good, whether their course is ordered through abundance or want, glory or dishonour, good report or ill report: through temporal things, whether dear or grievous, pleasant or harsh, they run toward eternal things, forgetting what lies behind and stretching themselves toward what lies ahead.

Alternatively: *Look upon me*, stripped as Adam was stripped, in whom, just as we all sinned, [Col. 0811C] so we all came into this world stripped in him. The righteous Job also laments this, saying: “Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb” (Job 1:21). But lest I return there naked like those who died naked before the wedding garment of the Incarnation, dyed purple by the blood of the Lord’s passion, look upon me thus stripped, so that you may not be angry with me in my nakedness as you were angry with naked Adam fleeing from your face (Gen. 3:7). Instead, have mercy on me by clothing me—not like that first Adam in a garment of skin subject to decay, in which all his posterity will grow old like a garment, but like the second Adam in the seamless tunic woven from above throughout, and therefore incapable of being torn. Thus, clothed in this tunic of Christ—or rather, having put on Christ himself—I may be found [Col. 0811D] in the company of those to whom your apostle says: “All of you who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27).

Alternatively: *Look upon me*, first stripped of virtues by robbers, then wounded by vices; and have mercy on me by showing mercy within me and caring for me in the inn of the universal Church, lest I again fall among robbers or be harmed by wolves raging about this inn but not daring to enter, because this inn is guarded by the good Gatekeeper, who himself is “the door: if anyone enters through it, he shall be saved and shall find pasture” (John 10:9). Thus I seek mercy according to the judgment concerning those who love your name, so that, entering through the door into contemplation and [Col. 0812A] going out into rational action, I may find pasture in the continual enjoyment of a good disposition toward action and contemplation, with the manifest saving result like most fruitful pastures—enduring now and for eternity for me who love your name, according to the judgment of others who love your name.

Alternatively: *Look upon me*, now no longer worthy to be called your son, having been grievously dishonoured in a far country (Luke 15:13); and have mercy on me, not according to the judgment of the elder brother, indignant at you for showing mercy and at me in my misery, but according to the judgment concerning those who love this name of yours, by which, just as you are called Father, so you show fatherly mercy to those who return to themselves and turn to you. Accordingly, those who love your name gladly take part in the banquet and the dance of those feasting and enjoying music, while the envious brother wastes away outside. Do not judge me, Father of mercies, according to his judgment, [Col. 0812B] but according to the judgment concerning those who love your name.

Alternatively: *Look upon me*, the tax collector standing far off in your temple (Luke 18:11), which is the Church, not daring to lift my eyes to heaven, whose height I am unworthy to behold because of the multitude of my iniquity; and have mercy on me, not according to the judgment of the Pharisee who glories in his own merit and despises others through excessive confidence in his own righteousness, but according to the judgment concerning those who love your name, by which you are called the merciful God, a name by which I also invoke you often, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” [Col. 0812C] (Luke 18:13).

Likewise: *Look upon me*, as you looked upon Peter when he wept—not only because he wept, but also so that he might weep (Matt. 26:75); and have mercy on me, as you had mercy on him—not only by granting pardon, but also by preserving the glory of his apostleship—according to the judgment concerning those who love your name with that love by which Peter himself loved it, he who erased his threefold denial by a threefold confession of love, saying for the third time: “I love you” (John 21:15).

Likewise: *Look upon me*, as you looked upon the sinful woman—not merely penitent, but also so that she might repent and weep; and have mercy on me, not according to the judgment of the Pharisee murmuring against her, or of Judas indignant with her, but according to the judgment concerning those who love your name [Col. 0812D] not with the small love by which one loves less to whom less is forgiven, but with the great love by which one loves much to whom much is forgiven. According to the judgment concerning those who thus love your name, I ask for the mercy of which it was said: “Her many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much.” Likewise: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 7:47–50). But lest after such a regard from you, having been so greatly filled with mercy, I should go back again,

**VERSE 133.** *Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity have dominion over me.* First direct my steps inwardly, in those movements that take place in the mind through thinking and desiring something, so that I may think of nothing except what ought to be thought, lest I be one of those to whom it is said: “Why do you think evil in [Col. 0813A] your hearts?” (Matt. 9:4). Likewise, may I desire nothing except what ought to be desired, either for use or for enjoyment: for use, as temporal things, which should be used, not misused; for enjoyment, as eternal things, which are enjoyed by those who love them, whether to possess them or having possessed them, for their own sake.

For whoever loves eternal things not for their own sake but for something else walks with distorted steps, like Solomon, who sought and loved wisdom not for itself but in order to execute judgment, by which he might be revered and feared among men. He attained this to such an extent that none before him was like him, nor would any arise after him whom subject peoples would fear as his own people feared him; for Scripture says, “They knew that the wisdom of God was in him to execute judgment” (3 Kings [Col. 0813B] 3:28). He rightly received wisdom in the night, who neither desired nor received it for its own sake, as something to endure eternally for him, but for executing judgment, which was a passing good.

Therefore his steps were greatly distorted from that uprightness by which all the upright in heart love temporal goods only for the sake of attaining eternal goods through them; but eternal things themselves, such as charity and wisdom, they love only for their own sake. By loving these and cleaving to them, the soul now has its fruit in sanctification, and its end in eternal life. Thus charity, by which things desired or possessed are held dear, should be ordered so that spiritual things are dearer than bodily things, eternal things than temporal, and heavenly things than earthly, by as much as they are nearer to the highest good, which ought to be most dearly loved. Thus created wisdom is dearer in proportion to uncreated wisdom, and the gift to the giver; yet whoever receives it ought not to turn it toward his own honour, but toward the honour of the giver, nor twist it to the purpose of abounding in pleasures in this life, after Solomon’s example. All who preach the Gospel in order that they may eat are likened to Solomon: this is to walk with crooked steps, when they ought rather to eat in order to preach the Gospel, which would be to stretch forward with upright steps.

Therefore, as stated, I first ask that the steps of my mind be directed; then also the steps of my deeds, so that I may not merely be upright in heart—which suffices for righteousness if opportunity or means for action are lacking—but upright also in conduct, so that as long as I am granted life I may live rightly according to your word, [Col. 0813D] because your word is upright.

*And let no iniquity have dominion over me.* I would indeed be wholly free from every sin or iniquity; but because this does not belong to the present time, in which “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8), all is well with us if our love of righteousness is so great that, though sin is in us, it does not harm us; though it wearies us, it does not reign in our mortal body, so that we obey its desires and present our members as instruments or weapons of iniquity—its instruments by sinning, its weapons by either excusing or defending sin itself. If this is so, my prayer is heard: *Let no iniquity have dominion over me*; and thus my conduct will be righteous even [Col. 0814A] among the unjust, who plot against and slander me. Since I cannot resist their slanders by my own strength, you who can do all things,

**VERSE 134.** *Redeem me from the slanders of men, that I may keep your commandments.* Slanders properly mean false accusations, through which good things are perverted and evil things are maliciously or falsely imputed. Amid these, a grave temptation threatens one who lives well, and he cannot overcome it except through patience. Therefore, by giving me patience, redeem me from the slanders of men; and I, possessing my soul in patience, will keep your commandments, preserved by you, the giver of this patience, through which I may not turn aside from obedience to and observance of your commandments, either amid slanders or because of slanders. That I may persevere in this luminous purpose, you—

**VERSE 135.** *Make your face shine upon your servant*, purifying the mirror of my heart so that the light of your countenance may shine in it, and I may be among those who sing in giving thanks to you: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us; you have given joy in my heart” (Ps. 4:7). Thus, I beseech you, make your face shine upon your servant, for such illumination makes a good servant, for whom a good kingdom has been laid up.

*And teach me your statutes.* Teach me, I pray, not only to know but also to do your statutes. This manner of teaching is possible for you alone, who teach humanity knowledge and teach them to do your will. For everyone who hears and learns from you, Father of lights, comes to Christ; and [Col. 0814C] all these will be taught by God, because such teaching comes neither from a human being nor through a human being, but through revelation that teaches in such a way that the one taught becomes learned. For this is the property of the active verb *to teach*: its passive, *to be taught*, ought to follow from it. But, as has been said, this mode of teaching is possible for God alone, who alone by inward teaching makes people learned; this no human being can do, however earnestly he may labour in outward teaching, just as neither can a farmer who plants and waters give growth.

Therefore you, who alone can do this, teach me your statutes, so that I may be justified freely by your grace, not having my own righteousness in which I may boast, like the Pharisees who despise others, [Col. 0814D] but having your righteousness, by which you are justified in the words by which you promise forgiveness of sins to the penitent. This alone is their justification—the justification of those penitents who have received not even their repentance from themselves but from you. Through this repentance freely granted to me by you,

**VERSE 136.** *Streams of waters flowed down from my eyes, because they did not keep your law.* For I wept bitterly with Peter; I wept with Mary the sinner; I wept with those who weep and sow their seed; I wept not sparingly but abundantly, releasing the reins to tears that flowed forth of themselves, so that I may truly say: *Streams of waters flowed down from my eyes*—or, as it is read in Hebrew: “Rivulets of waters flowed from my eyes”—while my conscience rebuked them inwardly: *because they did not keep your law*, those very eyes of mine defiled by wandering, curious, malicious, and lustful gazing. They were wandering and curious after the example of Dinah, who desired to see the women of a foreign region (Gen. 34:25); malicious after the example of Saul, who looked upon David with eyes not upright, envying his glory (1 Sam. 18:1); lustful after the example of David himself, who saw another man’s wife washing herself on the roof and was captured by unlawful love for her (2 Sam. 11:2).

Therefore he himself, repenting of this very iniquity, as though of death entering through the windows of the eyes, rightly speaks in this psalm, saying: *Streams of waters flowed down from my eyes, because they did not keep your law.* Not so the ungodly, not so; rather, like dust utterly devoid of these waters, they shall be cast from the face of the earth. Fearing this, when I am unable to have tears as I wish, I ask even for tears with the prophet, saying: “Who will give waters to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” (Jer. 9:1). [Col. 0815B] For I believe and hope that the very desire to weep is counted as tears, just as the desire to sin, even when it lacks the intended act, is imputed as sin before you, the judge of hearts, whose judgment, whether hidden or manifest, is always just.

For a judge is not just if, in his judgment, an evil will toward evil for evil counts more than a good will toward good for good. But you are just, O Lord, and your judgment is upright; consequently, as much as a hard and proud heart displeases you even if it lacks the bodily execution of the evil deed desired, so much does a contrite and humble heart please you even if it lacks the execution of a good deed—especially a deed that is not in human power, when or how greatly it occurs, such as the work of weeping. Not even the apostle Peter himself could achieve this fully by himself before the Lord looked upon him.

Therefore, when I say, *Streams of waters flowed down from my eyes*, it is thanksgiving for the grace of weeping once granted me for the washing away of sins. Though that grace is interrupted and I do not always weep before people, nevertheless I obediently hear when it is sung: “Let us weep before the Lord” (Ps. 94:6), because such weeping may also occur secretly without tears through the disposition of a contrite and humble heart, known to God alone, when the manifest effect is denied to the hidden disposition.

## SADE

[Col. 0815D]

**VERSE 137.** *You are just, O Lord, and your judgment is upright.* This eighteenth letter, whose name is *sade*, interpreted as “righteousness,” is rightly placed before this group of eight verses, since the first verse begins with righteousness—“You are just, O Lord”—and, after praises of righteousness have been interwoven, this is inserted among the rest: “Your righteousness is righteousness for ever.” Righteousness is also appropriately commended after the tears and mourning of repentance, because the divine justice that terrified the sinner by threatening eternal penalties consoles the same person when penitent and weeping. Justice declares that one who has judged himself shall not be judged, as the Apostle himself testifies, saying: “If we judged ourselves, we certainly would not be judged” (1 Cor. 21:31 [as printed]).

Therefore let the penitent, after confession of sins, also make confession of praise, praising the judgment and righteousness by which those who mourn are decreed to be comforted and those who now weep to laugh, because God will wipe every tear from their eyes; mercy triumphing over judgment, when eternal joy follows temporal mourning. Conversely, after the brief joy of those who exult in evil things follows mourning that will never end. In this recompense you are just, O Lord, and your judgment is upright.

You are just, namely, by that righteousness which proceeds from your gratuitous mercy, through which you have promised forgiveness of sins to the penitent. Therefore, “that you may be justified [Col. 0816B] in your words” (Ps. 50:6) and found just, you do what you spoke through the mouth of the holy prophets; for example, saying: “I do not will the death of the sinner” (Ezek. 18:32). Likewise: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Isa. 45:22). Likewise: “Though your sins be like scarlet, they shall be whitened as snow” (Isa. 1:18). You have spoken many things of this kind, and therefore you are rightly proclaimed justified and just in your words when you forgive those who bewail their sins. And your judgment is upright when you judge sinners who judge themselves as not to be judged, and those who accuse themselves before you as not to be accused. And because you are just, therefore

**VERSE 138.** *You have commanded your testimonies to be righteousness, and your truth exceedingly.* You have exceedingly commanded your righteousness and truth through fitting and very many witnesses, highly honoured, whose authority has been exceedingly strengthened; and righteousness and truth themselves have, through them, borne your most firm testimonies, attesting that you are just and true, you who require justice and truth from all. Justice: that no one should do to another what he does not wish done to himself, but should do what he rightly wishes done to himself. Truth: that, in keeping this same righteousness, he should neither wish to deceive nor readily be able to be deceived. The former belongs to dove-like simplicity; the latter, to serpentine prudence. You have commanded these to be kept exceedingly, against the excessive assaults of enemies opposed to righteousness and truth. Because of their excessive multitude and importunity,

[Col. 0816D] **VERSE 139.** *My zeal made me waste away*; or, as it is read in Hebrew, *My zeal consumed me*: namely, devouring me inwardly like fire, because I saw many evils done in your house by my enemies—indeed by yours—because these enemies of mine have forgotten your words, unwilling to remember that you said: “My house shall be a house of prayer” (Matt. 21:13), which they have made into a den of robbers against your word—a word which, if they could, they would wholly destroy and extinguish. But they cannot, because

**VERSE 140.** *Your word is exceedingly refined* [or “fiery”]. It will burn up its adversaries, either now with the fire of repentance, by which they may be purified like gold in a furnace, or in the future fire of punishment, when you, the just judge, say: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). The perverse hate this [Col. 0817A] word of yours, but the converted love it: *and your servant loved it.* Who is your servant? I, namely—

**VERSE 141.** *Young and despised*: David, the least among my brothers and despised by them; despised also by the Philistine giant because of my small stature. He was an example of the contemptible whom God chose to confound the strong, and a youth as an example of the younger people whom God chose and who, returning from a far country, deserved through humble repentance to be preferred to the elder brother. And since the sinner who accuses himself justifies you, God who hates sins, I have not forgotten your statutes, as those have who, seeking to establish their own righteousness, are not subject to your righteousness. Yet their righteousness is false, and in boasting of it they despise others; while your righteousness is true, and I praise it in singing this present group of eight verses composed in praise of righteousness.

**VERSE 142.** *Your righteousness is righteousness for ever, and your law is truth.* Human civil or forensic law can be varied according to the time. But your righteousness, containing the natural law that higher things should be subject to lower—namely, the flesh to the rational spirit and the spirit to eternal truth—is eternal and cannot be changed, because your law, by which this righteousness is decreed, is itself unchangeable truth. For this truth and righteousness,

**VERSE 143.** *Tribulation and anguish found me* as I contended for them against hostile people who troubled and distressed me. [Col. 0817C] Elsewhere I said: “I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 114:4). But here I say: *Tribulation and anguish found me, and your commandments are my meditation.* In both places it appears how useful tribulation is: it awakens the sluggish mind either to call upon the Lord’s name or to meditate upon God’s commandments.

There is, however, a certain difference between tribulation carefully sought and found by good people, and tribulation that finds someone wishing to rest. The first tribulation is like “a treasure hidden in a field, which, when a man finds it, he hides; and for joy over it goes and sells all that he has and buys that field” (Matt. 13:44). That field is sacred Scripture: composed indeed in a rustic style, but full of the treasure of its knowledge, concerning which it is written: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Ecclus. 1:18). Hence the Spirit of knowledge, in the third degree of the Beatitudes, makes mourners blessed, just as in the first the Spirit of fear makes the poor in spirit blessed, and in the second the Spirit of piety makes the meek blessed.

Therefore knowledge, which makes people mourn and grieve by first uncovering their wounds formerly concealed, is the efficient cause of that tribulation of which I said: *I found tribulation and sorrow*, and for healing that sorrow I called upon the Lord’s name. This was far more healing for me than that my wounds or sores should have remained hidden through ignorance, hardened or putrefied to the point of insensibility to pain. When the knowledge I found awakened this pain in me, it also moved me to call upon [Col. 0818A] the Lord’s name. Therefore, glorying in the Lord and rejoicing over this precious treasure discovered, I said: *I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord.*

But now, when I say, *Tribulation and anguish found me*, I complain that another kind of tribulation and anguish threatens me, inflicted by those of whom I have already said above: *My enemies have forgotten your words.* From this tribulation I would wish to rest, and to preserve peace even with those who hate peace; but as they assail me and hate me without cause, tribulation and anguish found me—tribulation, because grievous things are inflicted; anguish, because things dear and necessary are at times taken away.

Amid these evils of tribulations and anguishes pressing upon me from every side, preventing me from doing good, and, what grieves me more, hindering me from Mary’s rest, from the bride’s sleep, and tearing me from Rachel’s embrace, I should already have failed unless I were raised up by this remedy: *your commandments are my meditation.* Whether “commandments” is said in the plural or “commandment” in the singular, one must especially understand that commandment of which it was said above: *Your commandment is exceedingly broad.* Upon its two branches—namely, love of God and love of neighbour—hang the whole law and the prophets.

The breadth of this commandment, or of these commandments, enlarged my heart in tribulation, so that even amid pressing anguishes, with the arms of love stretched widely, I might embrace my enemies too: praying for them; returning good for evil; forgiving the repentant; having mercy upon those not yet repentant, after the example of Joseph, the most merciful corrector of his brothers while they were not yet penitent, and their sweetest comforter once they had repented and acknowledged him (Gen. 45). But for those whom I could not correct myself, I prayed that they might be corrected through medicinal chastisements, following the example of Stephen the first martyr, constantly saying: “Lord Jesus Christ, do not lay this sin to their charge” [Col. 0818C] (Acts 7:59). Thus, amid anguish and tribulations, your commandments are my meditation, trusting that my own debts too are forgiven, as I forgive my debtors (Matt. 6:14). Unless I forgave them, it would rightly be said to me: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all the debt because you asked me. Should you not then also have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” (Matt. 18:32). But the same measure will undoubtedly be measured back to me when I generously pardon my fellow servants, because this is equity: that the merciful may obtain mercy (Matt. 5:7). Of this equity I now say:

**VERSE 144.** *Your testimonies are equity for ever; give me understanding, and I shall live.* The equity by which you have mercy on the merciful and forgive the forgiving has your testimonies enduring for ever, as you yourself say in your Gospel: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke 6:37–38). For “if you do not forgive, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:15). These your testimonies have been made exceedingly credible [Col. 0819A] because they shall stand for ever. Heaven and earth will sooner perish or pass away than one jot of these testimonies shall be annulled: they are not given for a time, as was the figurative law concerning ceremonial observances, but are founded for eternity and confirmed by eternal truth.

By your grace, O God, I already hold the faith of this truth, by which we walk and not by sight. But lest I fail on the way, I seek understanding of this matter that I believe without doubt, saying: *Give me understanding, and I shall live.* For this good understanding, if given to me and proved in me by sure experience of works, will confer a sober, righteous, and godly life in the flesh, and eternal life after the death of the flesh. This is what I now desire when I say: *Give me understanding, and I shall live.*

[Col. 0819B] In Hebrew it is read: *Always teach me your righteous testimonies, and I shall live.* This is to say: According to your righteous testimonies, teach me always to live, and I shall live in accordance with this your very teaching, by which all who are predestined to eternal life shall be taught by God.

## COPH
VERS. 145. I cried with my whole heart. This nineteenth letter, coph, has various interpretations. For according to Ambrose it means “conclusion” or “look”; according to Jerome, “calling.” All these suit and agree with one another, because anyone hemmed in by enemies looks about on every side to see by which way he may more easily escape; he also calls for the help of those whom he can [Col. 0819C]. Thus I, David—or I, the penitent, following David’s example and singing psalms—when I was surrounded by straits, cried with my whole heart. For example: I, David, was given a choice of three on account of the sin of pride, when I had caused the people to be numbered: either that I should flee pursuing enemies for three months, that famine should be in the land of Israel for three years, or that pestilence should rage among the people for three days (2 Kings 24:12). And I, as one shut in, said, “I am greatly distressed” (1 Kings 28:15); and, having considered all that was set before me, I cried with my whole heart, calling upon the Lord. For when I saw the angel striking the people, I cried with my whole heart and said: “I am he who sinned; I acted wickedly; but these, who are the sheep, what have they done?” [Col. 0819D] (2 Kings 24:17.)

Likewise, when the parable was put before me concerning the rich man who seized the poor man’s sheep, and I judged him worthy of death, once I had perceived that this sentence of my own mouth had been pronounced against myself (2 Kings 12), hemmed in by my own judgment I cried with my whole heart, saying: “Have mercy upon me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Ps. 50:1). Similarly, when the enemies of God and of myself, Saul’s soldiers, had surrounded me in the manner of a crown, shut in, I looked to the Lord (1 Kings 23:26), and calling upon his help I cried with my whole heart, saying: “O God, save me by your name” (Ps. 53:3).

In this manner, I, the Church, or I, an ecclesiastical person, surrounded by enemies both visible and invisible, confined amid straits pressing upon me from every side, cried with my whole heart. For the most vehement cry of an anxious heart is the very desire for the Deliverer and for deliverance; and it is then more readily heard when it burns in the whole heart, because God, the lover of unity, does not deign to hear a heart divided in prayer. Therefore I cried with my whole heart, saying in the preceding group of eight verses: “Give me understanding, and I shall live,” that is, I shall be righteous; for “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17), and how much more by understanding? For if truth believed by faith justifies, much more does that same truth, rightly understood, save—provided that this understanding is not fruitless. For as there is “good understanding to all who do it” (Ps. 110:10), so there is bad understanding in those who do not do it. For the “servant” who knows [Col. 0820B] his master’s will and does not do it “will be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12:48).

Lest this happen to me, I shall not be content merely to have received faith together with understanding of your testimonies; rather, I shall seek your justifications, so that, as I believe rightly and understand rightly, I may also live rightly. For one who does not believe rightly is counted among the tares; but one who does believe rightly, yet lives wrongly contrary to his faith, is chaff. But one who both believes rightly and also lives rightly according to his faith is an ear full of grain, justified precisely because his faith has its fruit through love—its present fruit in sanctification, and its end, eternal life.

I shall seek these [Col. 0820C] your justifications, O Lord; hear me, O Lord, so that I may obtain them: I shall seek your justifications. By “testimonies,” “commandments,” and “justifications” I understand your words—indeed, your one Word, coeternal with you, from whom proceed many words that are spirit and life. They are called testimonies insofar as they promise future goods; commandments insofar as they prescribe what is right; justifications insofar as they impart good habits. Therefore, since believing promises and assenting to commandments are not sufficient for salvation unless righteous and good habits follow—such as charity, humility, piety, patience, and sobriety—lest, lacking these, I be found unrighteous, I shall seek your justifications. I desire not merely to be instructed through your testimonies and commandments, but also to be justified; I desire by sure experience to prove within myself [Col. 0820D] that your words are spirit and life, and breathe true life into those who love them.

Alternatively: I shall seek your justifications, having no righteousness of my own, which is from the Law and through which there is only knowledge of sin, not correction; for it brings nothing to perfection, weakened as it is through the flesh. Through its command sin revives, whereas your grace alone puts it to death; and that mortification grants eternal life to one justified by faith, because the righteous lives by faith. Since it is not enough to have received only once the beginning of such justifications, I, David, shall always seek them, with my cry multiplied. Therefore, not content to have said, “I cried with my whole heart,” I say again:

VERS. 146, 147. I cried to you: save me; [Col. 0821A] and I add a third time: I anticipated at dawn, and cried. Thus, thus, with my cry multiplied, I call upon the Savior, I who am shut in among enemies, continually saying: “Save me, and I shall keep your commandments.” It is as though I said: Give me life and I shall live; save me and I shall be saved; justify me and I shall be righteous; sanctify me and I shall be holy—while you work in me, through me, and with me, as I keep your commandments.

And because it is not enough to knock at the door of mercy by crying alone, I anticipated this very cry by rising early—or, as some manuscripts have it, “in the early morning,” or “in the untimely night.” The same sense is expressed by different names, which indicate the middle of the night, concerning which it was also said above: “At midnight I rose” (Luke 2:5); at that untimely hour, too, a friend goes to a friend and asks him for three loaves. That part of the night which is unsuitable for activity is called *intempesta*, “untimely,” just as, conversely, what is suitable is called *tempestivum*, “timely.”

At this time—whether it is called dawn because of haste, since we say *maturari* for “to hasten,” or immaturity or the untimely hour because of its inconvenience—I, David, anticipated the lazy workers, the sleeping praisers who will cry too late: “Lord, Lord, open to us,” and to whom it will be answered from within: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). Yet now, although a friend may say to his friend knocking by night, “Do not trouble me” (Luke 11:7), hope of obtaining what is asked is not taken away, provided one perseveres [Col. 0821C] in knocking and crying. At this time I outstripped those slower than myself with the steps of my desires, and cried with the cry of heart and mouth, singing with mind and spirit: “And in your word”—or, “upon your word”—I not only hoped, but hoped beyond hope, beyond what can be understood or said, knowing this: that you are able to do abundantly beyond all that we ask or understand.

Alternatively: in a person’s life, maturity is the age following youth; but I, David, anticipated the years of youth in maturity, that is, showing myself mature even in childhood, surpassing in good maturity even my brothers, older and more senior than I. This was especially so when I confronted Goliath, and then hoped beyond hope in your word, saying to him: “You come to me with sword, spear, and shield; but I come in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have reproached today. And the Lord will deliver you into my hand; I shall strike you and take your head away; and today I shall give the corpses of the Philistine camp to the birds of heaven, that all the earth may know that the Lord is the God of Israel, and that this whole assembly may know that the Lord saves not by sword or spear, for the battle is his” (1 Kings 17:45–47).

Speaking thus, I, then a boy immature in age but mature in understanding, hoped beyond hope not in my own strength but in your word, O God. I placed confidence in your word beyond the confidence of Saul and the others who disbelieved that I, a little one, could fight against that great Philistine. Similarly, I, the Church [Col. 0822A] or an ecclesiastical person, have hoped beyond hope in your word whenever I have ventured to fight against the devil—whether by prayer, disputation, or doing some other good work—not distrusting victory when the contest was for the enlargement of your glory amid human straits, and for its glorification amid the various darknesses of temptations or tribulations in the untimely night, that is, when some great storm was impending.

The Hebrew truth accords with this sense, where it reads: “While it was still dark, I rose and cried, awaiting your Word.” This is fitting language for the holy Church of God, which, before the sun of righteousness had risen, under the night of the Law, rose in faith through the prophets and other faithful persons of that age, awaiting your Word, O God, to be incarnate. But through the apostles, as through most clear-sighted eyes, now seeing that same Word incarnate, it joyfully heard: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke 10:24). Then I, the Church, after the darkness of night, enjoyed the dawn, because then

VERS. 148. My eyes anticipated you at dawn, that I might meditate on your sayings. But I too, an ecclesiastical person, following the example of those same apostles, strove that my eyes might anticipate you at dawn, that I might meditate on your sayings. If a speck of anger or another stain had clouded my eyes so that they could not clearly behold the light of truth, I did not wait for an outside reprover to say: “Cast the beam out of your eye” [Col. 0822C] (Luke 6:42). Rather, before the speck grew into a beam and my eye was wholly darkened by hatred of righteousness, my eyes themselves anticipated you at dawn, forestalling your face in confession. Thus set free and illuminated as though by the dawn of beginning charity, I was unencumbered so as to meditate upon your sayings, being still and seeing “that the Lord is sweet: blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Ps. 33:9).

Yet even with such preceding merits as these, I place more confidence in your mercy, O God, than in my own righteousness, which, if judged strictly with mercy set aside, would be nothing or far too slight to remove wrath and call forth clemency. Therefore I say:

VERS. 149. Hear my voice according to [Col. 0822D] your mercy, O Lord; and according to your judgment give me life. My voice is that of the sinner crying to you from afar and continually saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13). First hear this voice according to your mercy, removing the sins by which I earned wrath and forfeited mercy; then, according to your judgment, once sins have been forgiven—not a judgment to fear, but to sing—give me life by breathing into me the spirit of life, lacking which I am dead, grievously burdened under the law of sin and death.

Yet because I am not altogether dead, but was left half-alive by the robbers, I still possess, in the part in which I live, the voice of confession. I would not have it if I were wholly dead, since “confession perishes from one dead as though he did not exist” (Ecclus. 17:27). I beg you, hear this [Col. 0823A] voice of confession according to your mercy, pouring in oil so that I may be healed; and then, according to your judgment, give me life by pouring in wine, which gladdens the heart and at the same time gives life. For as “the sorrow of the world works death” (2 Cor. 7:10), so spiritual joy works life through wine that gladdens the heart and strengthens it to live according to your judgment, by which you judge that the person who judges himself is not to be judged, as your Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we certainly would not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31). Thus healed by your mercy and given life by your judgment, “I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1).

I shall sing of mercy, because receiving present grace makes my expectation of the future firmer; and therefore “I will sing of your mercies, O Lord, forever” [Col. 0823B] (Ps. 88:2), while, aided by your temporal gifts, I confidently await eternal ones. I shall also sing of judgment, while, judged in time, I gladly await the future judgment: for here I am chastised and far removed from the company of those who are not chastised with other people. Therefore pride has held them fast in their present prosperity; hereafter they will be harshly judged for their wickedness, because they both live wickedly and persecute those who live well. Among them they persecuted me too—me, little David, me, the small one, me, the penitent after David’s example—so that this complaint against them in this psalm is just:

VERS. 150. Those who persecute me have drawn near to wickedness; [Col. 0823C] but they have gone far from your law. My present complaint is not against those persecutors who have zeal for God, though not according to knowledge, and who, moved even by zeal for the Law, think that in opposing me they render you service. Rather, I cry out against those who, hating me without cause, have drawn near to the wickedness of murderous hatred and have gone far from your law, which forbids this hatred and commands love. May their persecution not harm me, but rather profit both them and me unto salvation.

VERS. 151. Be near, O Lord, and all your ways are truth. Be near to me by giving patience. Be near by giving them repentance, so that in me tribulation may work patience, patience proof, and proof hope that does not disappoint; and in them repentance may work both shame [Col. 0823D] and confession, while shame and confession may bring forth glory. Thus all your ways are truth both to them and to me: you judge them in truth, either as not to be judged because they judge themselves, or as to be judged all the more severely because they kick more stubbornly against the goad; and you are likewise gracious to me in truth, when, as I forgive my enemies’ debts from my heart in truth, you also forgive mine, according to what you, Truth, promise in truth, saying: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6:37). Again: “When you stand to pray, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, that your heavenly Father also may forgive you your sins” (Mark 11:25).

VERS. 152. From the beginning I knew from your testimonies that [Col. 0824A] you founded them forever. You have founded forever these your testimonies, together with your other testimonies that promise eternal salvation, O eternal God and Father. For in your Son, coeternal with you, who is the foundation of all your promises and other than whom no other foundation can be laid, you so founded and established all your testimonies that it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for your words, founded in your Word coeternal with you, to be made false. I, David, knew this from the beginning—that is, from the beginning of that declaration of which I said above: “The unfolding of your words gives light and gives understanding to little ones.”

Some read *initio* adverbially, as though it meant “first I knew.” But the Hebrew truth is not so expressed, for it reads: “From the beginning I knew from [Col. 0824B] your testimonies that you have founded them forever.” Therefore from the beginning, or the inception, of the Church being born, of which Abel was a member, I, David, reflecting on your testimonies uttered in many portions and in many ways, knew from those very testimonies that you founded them forever upon the immovable foundation, other than which no one can lay another, which is Christ Jesus.

RES.

VERS. 153. See my humiliation, and deliver me, for I have not forgotten your law. The name of the twentieth letter, *res*, is interpreted “head” or “primacy,” because this group of eight verses principally concerns humility, which is at once the head and beginning of all virtues. It is that poverty of spirit which the fear of the Lord—being the beginning of wisdom—produces before all virtues. Hence the Gospel first says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” [Col. 0824C] (Matt. 5:3); and then, upon the foundation of this poverty, which is none other than humility, the remaining virtues and beatitudes are arranged. If these existed without humility, they would have no head, nor would primacy be due to them, which is promised only to the humble, as Truth says: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 11:11).

It is well said, “who humbles himself”; for some are humbled and held in contempt by others, yet are themselves puffed up in their own estimation, think lofty thoughts, and do not associate with the humble, deeming themselves something when they are nothing, and thus deceive themselves. To these people, proud in their thoughts about themselves, it is not good that they are humbled by others or even by God himself. But to me it is good, and it tastes good, that you have humbled me, O God, through the attacks of evildoers who proudly rise against me. Therefore see, with a gaze of approval, this very humility which you have wrought in me through them; and, appeased by this burnt offering of humility, deliver me from the hand of those who humbled me, because among those troubling and humiliating me I have not forgotten your law. For “the fullness of the law is love” [Col. 0824D] (Rom. 13:10), by which I loved both friends in you and enemies for your sake. I did not forget your law among those troubling me and humbling me by that very tribulation: I loved those who did not love me, not returning curse for curse, but rather blessing them and praying for them. Since, therefore, so humbled I have not forgotten your law, be appeased by the sacrifice of humility and the burnt offering of love; deliver me from my enemies, seeing and approving both my humility and my observance of your law.

VERS. 154. Judge my cause, by which I, the true David, when unjustly judged by the unjust, handed myself over to the one judging me unjustly. Likewise, I, David, while impious Saul judged me impiously, endured his judgment, by which, as though guilty of treason, I was condemned to death and exposed to many dangers. And I, the Church or an ecclesiastical person, unjustly judged by unjust judges, patiently endured unjust judgments, because I awaited you, the just Judge, who will judge justly. Therefore now, lest [Col. 0825B] this expectation of mine be frustrated, judge my cause and redeem me from those judging unjustly. Redeem me, I say, not with gold or silver, but with the precious blood of the Lamb, your Son, who himself is also your Word or utterance.

For and according to this your utterance—that is, your Son—give me life, because he says: “Whoever believes in me shall not die forever, but shall have eternal life” (John 11:26). Again: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, shall live” (John 6:35). Again: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Again: “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John 15:5). A branch has life not in itself but in the vine. In this life of the vine give me life, so that I may be a branch never to be cut off from the vine; rather, may I live according to [Col. 0825C] your utterance, your Word, your Son, who says: “The words that I have spoken are spirit and life” (John 6:64). In this life, in this Spirit, give me life according to your utterance.

Alternatively: Judge my cause, by which I judged myself, believing your Apostle when he says: “If we judged ourselves, we certainly would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are corrected, so that we may not be condemned with this world” (1 Cor. 11:32). Thus I desire to be judged so that I may not be condemned with this world, namely, judged by myself, who judge myself a sinner and continually say: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13). Again: “Against you alone have I sinned, and done evil before you” (Ps. 50:6). Again: “I have sinned beyond the number of the sand of the sea, and my sins have been multiplied” [Col. 0825D] (Ps. 39:6). In these and similar words I judge myself a sinner, sold under sin, and dead; therefore I desire to be redeemed and given life, saying: “Redeem me because of your utterance; give me life, that, dead in myself, I may live in you according to your utterance.”

Alternatively: Judge my cause. Come, righteous Judge, to judge me; but before you examine me, first redeem me, sold as I am, and give life to me who am dead. Give me life, I say, because of your utterance, by which you promised the kingdom of heaven to the humble and poor in spirit. For unless I were conscious, through your grace, of this poverty and humility, I would not have said first: “See my humiliation,” knowing that you resist the proud [Col. 0826A] but give grace and salvation to the humble. But

VERS. 155. Salvation is far from sinners—sinners, I mean, obstinate in their sins. Their obstinacy is evident from this: they have not sought your justifications. But for the humble, who seek your justifications, repent of their unrighteousness, and do not establish their own righteousness,

VERS. 156. Your mercies are many, O Lord; by them judgment will be softened—not for all people, but for those who judge themselves and thus desire your judgment, by which they rightly hope to be given life, recognizing that for your sake they have been put to death and afflicted, as I, penitent David, who now say: “According to your judgment give me life,” made known because of [Col. 0826B] you.

VERS. 157. For many are those who persecute and afflict me. This is the most grievous kind of persecution and tribulation: when many act against one, those many compelling and pressing the one person to turn aside from the testimonies of truth. Nevertheless, I, David—or I, the Church or an ecclesiastical person—although many press me, have not turned aside from your testimonies. I regard as knowledge for myself only, and altogether, that which you approve, and I disapprove what you disapprove, according to the most true testimonies by which in the Scriptures of truth you testify that good is good and evil evil. I have not turned aside from these your testimonies; but many have turned aside from them, and they gave me cause for grief. For

[Col. 0826C] VERS. 158. I saw transgressors, and wasted away, because they did not keep your sayings. I, the Church or an ecclesiastical person, saw heretics transgressing the rule of faith, and I wasted away. For who is scandalized by some error, and I do not burn? Who is weak, even while believing rightly but not living rightly, and I am not weak? Meanwhile, since I could neither correct from their error those who were scandalized and those causing scandal, nor strengthen the weak, I burned so intensely that I wasted away from excessive grief for those who had been scandalized; and, weak for the weak and with the weak, I languished because they did not keep your sayings. Neither did the former keep them by believing in their heart unto righteousness or confessing with their mouth unto salvation, nor the latter by acting according to the right faith which they indeed confess in words but deny in deeds.

[Col. 0826D] VERS. 159. See that I have loved your commandments, O Lord. They transgressed these commandments and grieved me, so that I wasted away, sad almost unto death, as I, the true David, struggling against such people, said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38). And anyone conformed to the likeness of my death, afflicted among such people by my example, may say: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” What I, the Church—or any ecclesiastical person—have experienced in myself beyond measure, I say from the feeling of great sorrow: “I saw transgressors and wasted away, because they did not keep your sayings.”

I saw this with human eyes, as though illuminated through the night by lunar brightness. You too, Sun of righteousness, see this: by your gaze you can drive away the night of imminent sorrow in which I waste away over those who transgress your commandments and also hate me because I loved your commandments. Therefore I desire you to see this, saying: “See that I have loved your commandments,” so that, cheered by your sight, I may breathe again from the sorrow in which I waste away when I see those who do not keep the covenant. For I saw—indeed, I beheld in the vision of the night—transgressors; or, as some manuscripts have it, “those not keeping the covenant,” whether written in the Law or in the Gospel for the preservation of peace between God and human beings. For it is called *pactum*, “covenant,” as though an act of peace.

I saw, then, that this covenant made and contracted for peace was being dissolved; unable to withstand this wickedness, I could not but grieve, could not but waste away, could not but be sad. My soul was, and is, sorrowful unto death—certainly like Israel, who, mourning his son whom he thought dead and devoured by a beast, refused the consolation of this present life and resolved to go down with mourning to the underworld, to which all people of that time descended. But when he learned that his son Joseph, whom he loved, was still alive, “his spirit revived” [Col. 0827B] (Gen. 45:27). As though previously dead and oppressed by heavy sleep, he awoke and said: “If Joseph my son lives, it is enough for me; I will go and see him before I die” (ibid., v. 28).

So too I, because I loved your commandments, O Lord, when I see them not observed and, through transgressions of this kind, the covenant of salvation and peace dissolved, feel myself pressed toward death by the heavy sleep of sorrow, neither willing nor able to receive consolation unless I see the true Joseph living and ruling throughout all the land of Egypt in such a way that no one dares transgress his commandments, which I loved and love—or, if anyone has transgressed, that person is punished in such a way that punishment for the offense restrains the rest from offending. On hearing this, my spirit will revive; and desiring it now, I say: “According to your mercy give me life.” Give me life not by my merits but by your mercy, that my spirit may revive and, awaking as from a heavy sleep, rejoice in the observance of your commandments. For, saddened and wasting away among their transgressors, I was exceedingly pressed as though toward death, those very transgressors judging me worthy of death because I would not consent to their transgressions [Col. 0827C]—which, seeing, I wasted away because I was unable to resist them.

Therefore by them, as though I were dead, “I was counted with those who go down into the pit, and became like a man without help among the dead,” almost dead; and “like the wounded asleep,” cast out in tombs, “whom you remember no more, and who have been driven away from your hand. They placed me in the lowest pit, in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Ps. 87:5 ff.). Therefore, crying as though from the depths, I continually say: “According to your mercy give me life.” Let those who think that I do not live—like another Joseph seemingly devoured by a beast, or like another Jonah swallowed in the belly of the whale and unable to be restored—feel that I still live, so that through me the city in Nineveh may be reproved, namely [Col. 0828A] the world lying in the evil one, concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment, and may be summoned to the most necessary repentance before it is overthrown, according to the truth of the prophets and what was foreordained in your altogether unchangeable words, because

VERS. 160. The beginning of your words is truth, from the time when in the beginning—that is, in your only-begotten Word—you said: “Let there be light, and there was light” (Gen. 1:3). This was the beginning of your words, in which beginning you created heaven and earth, which shall pass away. After they have passed away, the judgments of your righteousness shall remain unchangeably forever, because the sentence pronounced upon good and evil persons at the last judgment shall remain irreversible.

Let us now join together these two elements, *coph* and *res*, which means “the calling of the head,” so that we may endeavor to understand from these two groups of eight verses, marked by these two elements, that Christ is invoked, who is the Head and Beginning. Of him the final verse says: “The beginning of your words is truth.” This Beginning or Head, being truth, as has been said, is near to all who invoke him in truth, as it says in the preceding group of eight: “Be near, O Lord, and all your ways are truth.”

SIN.

VERS. 161. Princes persecuted me without cause, but my heart stood in awe of your words. This twenty-first letter, *sin*, has various interpretations. For, as Jerome holds, the name *sin* itself means “teeth” or “of teeth.” According to Ambrose [Col. 0828C], however, *sin* means “upon a wound.” Both interpretations fit this group of eight verses, because these eight verses concern the persecution of princes, who, in the likeness of teeth, crushed the saints so as to incorporate them into Christ’s body; and divine consolation, by which the sayings of God gladden afflicted elect persons. Of these sayings the righteous person here says: “I shall rejoice over your sayings, as one who finds much spoil.”

This consolation is fitted like a soft plaster over the wound of tribulation when, as the Apostle says, “Tribulation works patience, patience proof, and proof hope which does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:3). Hence those rejoicing in hope will be patient in tribulation, preserving as it were the healing plaster of hope fitted over the wound of tribulation. Whoever is such a person, it belongs to him to glory in persecutions and say: “Princes persecuted me without cause.” The prince of this world persecuted me, the true David, like another Saul rejected by God; but because he has nothing in me, he persecuted me and mine without cause and gratuitously.

Likewise, many princes of this world persecuted me, the one Church, without cause, hating me gratuitously, although, taught by Christ, I was prepared to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, as to God the things that are God’s (Matt. 22:21). Thus instructed by the Apostle, I rendered to all their dues: “tribute to whom tribute is due; tax to whom tax; honor to whom honor” (Rom. 13); and yet these princes, whom I honored in this manner, persecuted [Col. 0829A] me not because of any merit of mine but from gratuitous and self-chosen hatred.

Heretics also, arrogating primacy to themselves, gloried in their own inventions and refused to submit to apostolic authority and Catholic truth. These too, wickedly taking precedence, persecuted me without cause because I would not assent to their lies, which teach doctrines contrary to your words. But your truth carried greater authority for me; therefore I regarded you more than them, and my heart stood in awe of your words. The fear conceived from your words overcame their fear—the fear of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Therefore my heart stood in awe of your words, that fear might drive out fear: the good fear the evil, the holy fear the wicked. I mean that holy fear of which it is written: “The holy fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever” [Col. 0829B] (Ps. 18:10).
