And because this fear is the beginning of wisdom, which by it, as though a thread drawn through an eyelet, makes clear the meaning of your sayings,

VERS. 162. I shall rejoice over your sayings, as one who finds much spoil. Certainly I now have sorrow among those to whom it was said: “Blessed are you who weep now”; nevertheless, because of what follows, “for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21), I shall finally rejoice over your sayings—not merely in any fashion, but as one who finds much spoil; and as Isaiah says: “As victors rejoice over captured prey when they divide the spoils” (Isa. 9:3). For now, while the battle is uncertain and victory unsure, it is not time for me to rejoice with full joy, but to contend vigorously for the law of my God. When the battle is finished and victory gained through pure sayings prevailing over impure sayings, I shall rejoice over your sayings as one who finds much spoil.

For, knowing that I have triumphed through the sword of the Spirit, which is your word, and then recognizing that I have passed through the enemy ranks defended by the weapons of righteousness, I shall rejoice forever over your sayings, which supplied such weapons to me—or rather, which through me, weak as I am, confounded the strong, while truth triumphs mightily against the falsehood of tyrants, heretics, and false Christians who rule wickedly and persecute me without cause. Let hope of this future joy now be held like a plaster over the wound of imminent sorrow, until full joy is attained, where my joy may be full and no one take my joy from me. Then I, the little one whom princes persecuted without cause by speaking against your sayings, shall rejoice over those same victorious sayings, ascribing victory to you and to your sayings, and all the glory of that victory, while the princes persecuting me are partly overthrown and beneficially humbled with Saul, partly condemned with the frenzied king Saul. They persecuted me, little David, especially because

VERS. 163. I hated and abhorred iniquity, but I loved your law. Nor is it strange that such hatred and love should coexist in one breast. For just as the nature of things is such that one who loves righteousness cannot but hate iniquity, as is elsewhere said: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity” [Col. 0830A] (Ps. 44:8), so love of righteousness is proved and made evident by hatred of iniquity. Therefore one is shown to love the good too little if one does not detest and abhor evil.

But I, burning both with hatred of iniquity and with love of the righteousness taught by the Law—obscurely through Moses and clearly through Christ—hated iniquity so that I first abhorred it by separating it from myself, and then reproved it in others according to my ability and measure. And when I perceived that the wicked did not listen to me and despised me, setting aside or interrupting preaching, I turned to entreaties, prayers, thanksgivings, and petitions, and by earnestly urging them—
**VERSE 164.** Seven times a day I have uttered praise to you, because of [Col. 0830B] the judgments of your righteousness. “Seven times a day,” that is, at all times, the seven days being included; or “seven times a day,” that is, enlightened by the light of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit; or “seven times a day,” namely, at the canonical hours, as is customary among religious persons, I have uttered praise to you, O Lord, because of the judgments of your righteousness, by which you scourge every son whom you receive, and by which also you harden whom you will and have mercy on whom you will. Among these judgments of your righteousness—

**VERSE 165.** Great peace have they that love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them. Great peace, though not yet complete, as it will be in the future, where there shall be no end of peace. Peace, I say, good and great, for those who love your law: its abundant love, producing abundant peace, drives from the hearts [Col. 0830C] which it possesses evil disturbances; and there is no stumbling-block for them. Such persons do indeed suffer some weariness, so that at times they are even weary of living, lest they should be confident in themselves; yet there is no stumbling-block for them, because they are not so little as to be capable of being scandalized like those to whom Christ is “a stone of stumbling” (1 Pet. 2:8).

Thus the Jews were scandalized by Christ’s words when he said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Thus certain of his disciples were scandalized when they heard that his flesh was to be eaten and his blood drunk. To them he said: “Does this scandalize you? What then if you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before? It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:61). But because there is great peace for those who love the law of God, and [Col. 0830D] no stumbling-block for them, Peter, a lover of God’s law, although he did not yet understand God’s words, nevertheless suffered no stumbling from them, but said: “You have the words of eternal life, and to whom shall we go from you?” (ibid.).

Thus God is no stumbling-block whatever to those who love your law, whereas a stumbling-block readily arises for those little in faith; for them Christ himself is sometimes a rock of offense and a stone of stumbling. Although, according to Daniel’s vision, he has grown into a great mountain whose greatness has no end, nevertheless in their false estimation he is regarded as though he were a stone of measured size. They do not consider that the man to whom God gave the Spirit without measure has likewise greatness without measure—not through monstrous bulk, but through immeasurable power—as one to whom [Col. 0831A] all power in heaven and on earth has been given. Therefore, although according to his humanity he is less than his immeasurable Father, yet for that same humanity he obtained the brightness and immeasurable splendor of his divinity. While still little, and also made lower than the angels, he asked this of his Father, saying: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was” (John 17:5).

The preaching of this glory bestowed upon the man scandalizes those little in faith. Since words of exhortation spoken or written against these very scandals did not suffice for them or profit them in freeing them from this and other scandals, I, ceasing from instruction—

**VERSE 166.** I awaited your salvation, O Lord, [Col. 0831B] and I loved your commandments. I awaited, I say, using a verb in the past imperfect tense, because my waiting has not yet ceased, by which I await your salvation, O Lord. When it appears in its glory and sends its angels, “all stumbling-blocks shall be gathered out of his kingdom” (Matt. 13:41); and when he himself saves, all his members shall be saved, even the little ones scandalized during the night, while they do not see him, the sun of righteousness—though present everywhere—because “he made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. 17:12), and has not yet clearly appeared.

In this very expectation, by which I await him, I continually say: “You who sit upon the Cherubim, manifest yourself before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh” (792). Again: “Lord God of hosts, turn us, and show us your face, and we shall be saved” (ibid., 3). Again: “Show us your mercy, O Lord, and give us your salvation” (Ps. 84:8). Again: O Rising Sun, splendor of eternal light and Sun of righteousness, come and enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death (Luke 1:79). Again: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1). Again: “Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his trees” (Song 5:1).

I am accustomed to use many spiritual songs of this kind while, awaiting, I await your salvation, O God, which is invoked in these songs. And lest the fruit of my expectation should be delayed through neglect of your commandments, I loved your commandments themselves. Through them—not merely understood, [Col. 0831D] but, what is better, loved and kept—the first and second coming of the Savior, or even his daily coming, is made salutary; he promised this when he said: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). Hoping for and awaiting this coming of the Savior—

**VERSE 167.** My soul kept your testimonies, or martyrdoms, not denying them amid adversities. And because martyrdom does not avail for salvation without love of the commandments, my soul loved them vehemently before it so loved: loved vehemently, so that it itself might vehemently love the commandments of him who loves it vehemently. Did he not vehemently love me, his Church, [Col. 0832A] who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for my redemption? The Son of God himself also loved me vehemently, who gave himself to me and restored me to myself, when I had first been lost in original sins and then in actual sins.

Therefore, in just reciprocity, I too, vehemently loving you who love me vehemently, loved your commandments, sharing in this with the holy confessors who love your commandments. Likewise I loved your testimonies, sharing in this with the blessed martyrs; for a witness is called *martyr* in Greek, and testimonies are *martyria*. Unless I had loved them vehemently, when enemies pressed vehemently from the opposite side that I should deny them, or at least remain silent as though mute and not speak the truth, perhaps they would have swallowed me alive when their rage was vehemently kindled against me. But because “love is strong as death” (Song 8:6), by which I loved your testimonies, my soul kept your testimonies even amid the dangers of death itself and loved them vehemently. Yet I do not attribute it to my own powers that—

**VERSE 168.** I kept your commandments and your testimonies, but to your grace, by which you looked upon me, because all my ways are before your sight. I know this because whenever you turned your face away from me, I was troubled; then I did not walk in the way, but wandered where there was no path, until you again deigned to look upon me and lead me back to the way. Therefore, in thanksgiving I say: I kept your commandments and your testimonies, because all my ways are before your sight.

[Col. 0832C] Alternatively: All my ways—that is, all my actions—are directed before your sight, because, as you enlighten me, I walk by them. Above all, I seek this: that you may graciously look upon me with eyes of mercy while I now walk in the way, so that, having received grace for grace, I may also be found worthy in my homeland to stand before your sight, my wound wholly healed; while the rulers persecuting and wounding me cannot stand before your sight but rather flee from your face, as elsewhere I desired, saying: “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; and let those who hate him flee from before his face. But let the righteous feast and rejoice before God, and delight in gladness” (Ps. 67:2, 4). To this end, then, all my ways are before your sight: that I may be joined with those [Col. 0832D] who shall feast and rejoice before your sight.

## TAU

**VERSES 169–170.** Let my supplication draw near before your sight, O Lord. This is the last letter, whose name, *tau*, directs us to the consummation of which it was said: “I have seen an end of every consummation.” This is suggested by the fact that *tau* is interpreted “he erred,” or “he completed,” or “signs.” It is indeed a great consummation of perfection in this life to acknowledge one’s error and say: “I am an unprofitable servant; what I ought to have done, I have done.” Christ himself urges us to say this: “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done” (Luke 17:10).

If this must [Col. 0833A] be said by those who do all that is commanded them, how much more must it be said by the penitent person who, following David’s example, acknowledges the error by which he departed from the way of uprightness—either by receiving the alien devil for an hour into the lodging of his breast, or, worse, by preparing him a feast through killing the poor man’s sheep; indeed, to speak more expressly, through killing his own soul within himself. For “a mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11); and “the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18:20). When it dies, the hundredth sheep perishes and cannot return by itself, unless the good shepherd carries it back as it confesses its sins and says: “I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost; seek your servant.”

Words of confession and prayer of this kind are signs of inward repentance [Col. 0833B] “whether in the depths of hell or in the heights above.” Proud King Ahaz refused to ask for such signs, though it was said to him: “Ask yourself a sign from the Lord your God, either in the depths of hell or in the heights above”; and he said: “I will not ask” (Isa. 7:11). But I, considering the depth of hell and fearing it, and likewise looking upon the height of heaven and loving it, ask for a sign in the depth of hell, saying: Let my supplication draw near before your sight, O Lord. Likewise I ask for a sign in the heights above, saying: Let my petition enter before your sight.

For although both supplication and petition are prayer, they are distinguished from one another in this way: supplication is customarily made for evils to be removed, while petition is made for goods to be obtained. What evils are more to be fled than those in the depths of hell, or those which draw one into the depths of hell? Likewise, what goods are more to be sought than virtues and deeds by which one goes upward into the heights, or than the rewards themselves laid up on high? Therefore I, David—I, the penitent, singing psalms and striking the harp after David’s example—in the house of the Lord touch the string of fear, saying: Let my supplication draw near before your sight, lest I fall into the depths of hell. And again, touching the string of love, I say: Let my petition enter before your sight, that you may be merciful to me, a sinner, by delivering me from infernal evils. I am far from you, separated by the wall of sins and shut out from the entrance of the sanctuary; yet through love of righteousness I have been made near, [Col. 0833D] and, knocking at the door of the heavenly hall with unutterable groanings, I say: Let my petition enter before your sight, by which I seek the heavenly goods laid up and reserved before your sight for those who draw near to you through fear, and who, through love, now made near, knock at the door of your grace. Therefore I cry from afar: Let my supplication draw near before your sight, O Lord.

But because you, faithful promiser, promised me—a penitent singing a penitential psalm—when you said: “I will give you understanding and instruct you” (Ps. 31:8), give me understanding according to your word, so that you may be justified in your words and found righteous and true. Or: give me understanding according to your word, so that I may think only what your word indicates ought to be thought, lest, following my own judgment, I become vain in thinking something contrary to your word—contrary to your Word, which is eternal wisdom. Desiring in that wisdom alone to think and understand the things above, I say: Give me understanding according to your word.

Having received this understanding, because my petition will be reasonable, entrusted to reasonable understanding, I ask that the petition itself may enter before your sight. Otherwise, if my petition enters without this understanding, it will be said to me: “You do not know what you ask,” as was said to James and John: “You do not know what you ask” (Matt. 20:22), because their petition lacked reasonable understanding and their understanding was alien from God’s word. But I say: Let my petition enter before your sight; and I add: Deliver me according to your word, because I do not ask [Col. 0834B] either to be delivered from evils or to use or enjoy goods except according to the tenor of your word. By it we are first invited to drink the cup of the Lord’s passion, so that afterward we may be made fit to drink new wine in the kingdom of God. For only to those who drank of the fruit of the vine in the time of Christ’s passion was it promised that they would drink new wine in the kingdom.

After my petition has thus entered before your sight, so that I drink of your wine in your kingdom and your most excellent cup intoxicates me (Matt. 14:25), then—

**VERSE 171.** My lips shall utter a hymn, because from the abundance of my heart my mouth shall speak wisdom in your praises and spiritual songs, when you have taught me your ordinances in that manner of teaching which is possible to you alone. For who—whether angel [Col. 0834C] by angel, human being by human being, human being by angel, or angel by human being—can be taught in such a way that, through the teaching of angel or human being, the person taught becomes righteous or justified, unless you, who teach a human being knowledge, also teach righteousness? You do so not merely by opening the understanding so that righteousness may be known, but also by kindling the affection so that righteousness once known may be held fast—either in peace, as in heaven, where no assault presses; or on earth, where there is the malice of a man fighting for righteousness against injustice and unable to triumph unless you teach righteousness in such a manner as, by teaching, to grant and preserve it: to grant it by building, to preserve it by guarding the impregnable city of righteousness. Unless you build it within, [Col. 0834D] those who build it from without by teaching labor in vain; and unless you guard it, those who guard it watch in vain.

Therefore, when you, who alone can teach effectively, have taught me your ordinances, then my lips shall utter a hymn, joyfully pouring forth praises in love for you; and in love for my neighbor—

**VERSE 172.** My tongue shall proclaim your word, so that others also may be taught through me, by the talent entrusted to me and faithfully placed at the bankers’ table. This is silver tested by fire, shining with bright equity, because all your commandments are equity and there is in them no injustice or falsehood, as there is in the teaching of those whose silver has been turned into dross and whose wine has been so mixed with water that it cannot intoxicate as your cup, [Col. 0835A] most excellent and pure with most radiant truth, intoxicates.

That cup, indeed, arouses those outpourings by which my lips shall utter a hymn when you have taught me your ordinances. Refreshed also by a draught of this cup, my tongue shall proclaim your word, not fearing contradiction, because all your commandments are truth and equity, against which no injustice or falsehood can prevail. Yet although the firmness and equity of your commandments cannot be overcome, because very many attack them and threaten adversities against me as I proclaim them—

**VERSE 173.** Let your hand be made to save me, because I have chosen your commandments. Your hand—your Son, your Word—was made over me in order to create me from nothing, giving being to me who was not. But because my creation profited me nothing unless I should also be saved, let your hand be made to save me, that hand by which you created me from nothing. “For your hands, O Lord, made me and formed me; give me understanding that I may learn your commandments”; and thus may your hand which made me itself be made to save me. May that hand which is my creator also become my savior. May that which, in the manifestation of the incarnation, was made among all things—though in its divinity it was before all things—be made to save me, having been that which created me. May that which was creator become savior.

Let this be spoken from the desire of the ancient saints, who awaited and desired the incarnation of the Son of God; the Lord heard their desire, because Christ came to accomplish their salvation.

[Col. 0835C] But I, the Church that follows, or I as an ecclesiastical person, awaiting the second coming of that same Christ, say to you, almighty Father, in whom I believe though I do not see him in whom I believe—for “no one has ever seen God” (1 John 4:12)—I say to you: Let your hand be made to save me. Your hand is your Son, who was certainly made visible in order to redeem me. Let him now be made conspicuous through his works, that he may save me. I know that he ascended into heaven and sits at your right hand, whence he will come to judge the living and the dead. I ask, therefore, that before he examines me in his judgment, he may have mercy upon me; and before he becomes my examiner, he may become my savior.

May he now become physician, to save me lying in great sickness and crying out to him, who, made human, [Col. 0835D] visited me when I was half-dead—not yet crying out, nor even knowing to whom I might cry. Before I chose your commandments, your hand was over me in great patience, preserving me lest I perish in the darkness of ignorance. But now, because I have chosen your commandments, to be loved by me above all that can be loved in this world, and because of this have many adversaries, let your hand be made to save and defend me against enemies wishing to crush or destroy me. And because those oppressors and destroyers are many and visible, while you have made darkness your hiding place and cannot be seen openly—

**VERSE 174.** I have desired your salvation, O Lord, [Col. 0836A] which I know to be visible in the humanity assumed, so that according to its name, which is Emmanuel, God may be with us, namely by displaying among us the power of his divinity. For if he is “God for us” and with us, “who is against us?” (Rom. 8:31). Thus I have desired your salvation, O Lord, that it may show its face to us and we shall be saved when we see that salvation of yours, the sight of which is salvation.

Oh, if it should be granted me to see that salvation in such a way that from heartfelt affection I may say: “Behold the dwelling of God with human beings, and he shall dwell with them” (Rev. 21:3). Again: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). Again: “Behold my God, and I will honor him; the God of my father, and I have chosen him” (Exod. 15:2).

You, Pilate, seeing and mocking him, said: “Behold the man”; again: “Behold your king” (John 19:5). Let your jest be turned into earnest, so that we Christians may say: “Behold the man. Behold our king.” May the man whom you mocked deign to rule us in such a way that you and those like you, who do not believe that that man is King of kings and King of the ages, may in turn be mocked by us as we say in thanksgiving: Behold the man, our King, Savior of all, who is also King of all ages, because all power in heaven and on earth has been given to him (Matt. 21:18), and, as was shown beforehand in Daniel’s vision, “to him were given kingdom and honor, and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him” (Dan. 7:14).

In Hebrew it reads: “Let your hand be [Col. 0836C] my helper, because I have chosen your precepts.” This means: Because I have chosen your precepts to be kept by myself and preached to others, lest I fail from this purpose amid adversities but rather make more and more progress, let your hand—of which no one can snatch anything away—be my helper.

Again, it reads in Hebrew: “I have desired your salvation, O Lord, and your law is my will.” Whether one says “I have desired” or “I have longed for your salvation,” the sense is the same, because whatever is desired is longed for. But what is said in Hebrew, “Your law is my will,” and in our text, “Your law is my meditation,” do not seem altogether identical, because we turn over in meditation many things [Col. 0836D] which we do not have in our will. Yet far be it from me that what is suggested to my heart against and apart from my will should be judged to be my meditation. For in such meditations I do not understand what I do, and therefore it is not I, but the sin dwelling in me, that performs such things. Your law alone is my meditation, because in such meditation my will is present, as the Hebrew truth expresses when it reads: “Your law is my will,” in place of what we have: “Your law is my meditation.”

“My,” I say—not, however, inborn in me from myself, but given from above: the heavens distilling from above subtle meditations like dew, and clouds raining down grosser ones like drops of rain. Watered by these, the dry land of my will may bring forth the Savior whom I desired, [Col. 0837A] whom I longed for while continually singing psalms and saying: I have longed for your salvation, O Lord, and your law is my meditation and my will, which, although now weakened in this body of death, yet at some time, either stripped of this body or reclothed in this same body conformed to Christ’s body—

**VERSE 175.** My soul shall live and praise you, my God, and your judgments shall help me. For now it dies, as it were, as often as it is altered from state to state while meditating on various things; this very changeability is a great image of death to it. But when it is fully and perfectly re-formed to the image and likeness of your immutability, O God, then my soul shall live and praise you. Certainly it shall live and die no more, because its life will not change but will steadily enjoy one and the same most blessed state; and out of this its most stable happiness it shall praise you with unceasing and unchanging praise.

And your judgments shall help me. For your judgments, by which you will distinguish the impious from the pious, saying to the former: “Go, accursed ones,” but to the latter: “Come, blessed ones,” will help me perfectly to praise you for your mercy and truth: mercy shown toward the pious, truth shown toward the impious in your very judgments. These judgments not only help now in the present, but shall also help forever, because “I will sing mercy and judgment” forever. I shall ascribe to your judgments, not to my own powers, the very fact that my soul shall then live and praise you.

But now, while I still make my pilgrimage in a mortal and frail body, it is good to confess past errors [Col. 0837C] and to pray and watch against future ones. Therefore, grieving and repenting of past errors, I say:

**VERSE 176.** I have gone astray like a sheep that has perished. Praying against future errors, I say to you, good shepherd: Seek your servant. Seek me, that I may seek you; seek, I beseech you, until you find me, and at the same time I too may find you. Seek me, a sheep exposed to wolves; indeed, grievously wounded by wolves and so weakened that in no way [Col. 0838A] can I seek you unless you first seek me. For who first loved you, so that he might be loved by you? Or who gave to you, so that you might repay him? But because you first love those who love you, and seek those who seek you, diligently seek me—your servant who wandered grievously, your sheep which perished, your drachma long lost—until you find me in such a way that, gathering your friends and neighbors, the blessed angels, together, you may say: Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep which was lost; I have found the drachma which I had lost.

You sought me when I did not seek you; indeed, when I was wholly ignorant of you. But now I seek you all the more as one who is sought by you. This is evident from the fact that I have not forgotten your commandments. Although I wandered for a time from the keeping of your commandments, I have not forgotten your commandments altogether, as have those who are in the land of forgetfulness, of whom you remember no more; they too have been cast off by your hand because they first cast off the word of God, rejecting the yoke of your commandments and saying to you: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways” (Job 21:14). I desire and long for knowledge of your ways. The certain indication and sign of this is that I have not forgotten your commandments.

Let us now join together these two final letters, *sin* and *tau*, which are fittingly interpreted “signs of the teeth.” For not only these two octonaries enclosed by these two letters, but all divinely inspired Scriptures, when uttered through sounds formed by the plectrum of the tongue around the teeth, fittingly receive this name and are called “signs of the teeth.” These signs are either in the depths of hell or in the heights above, because through them are signified both the glorification of the obedient and the condemnation of the disobedient. The continual consideration of these two things, marked in the signs of the teeth—that is, in the Scriptures—brings forth in the mind of the one considering them both love and fear, enduring for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 119

[Col. 0837]

[Col. 0837D] *To the Lord, when I was afflicted, I cried,* etc. In the preceding psalm the way was described of the good runner, running in the course of this life not uncertainly but in the straightest course toward the most certain prize. Of this course the same runner says: “I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart.” We read of the running of the Lord’s forerunner. We also read of the running of the Lord himself, who “rejoiced as a giant to run his course.” We read also of runners following him upon the straight way, one of whom says: “Therefore I so run, not as uncertainly” (1 Cor. 9:26); and, to urge others also to run, he said: “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all indeed run, but one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it” (ibid., 24).

One may indeed run swiftly in the undefiled way, in the way of truth, in the way of God’s commandments, if one’s steps are directed according to the Lord’s word and God’s word is a lamp to one’s feet, as is written in the preceding psalm. But when one comes to that ladder upon whose steps Jacob saw angels ascending and descending, one must ascend not so much by running as slowly and, as it were, step by step (Gen. 28:12).

And because one must go upward from the valley of tears, rightly here, in the fifth section, there is a return [Col. 0839A] to groaning in the first Song of Ascents. This is the groaning of the perfect: the groaning, indeed, of the dove, the groaning of a soul that longs and loves, and that continually says amid its groanings: “Alas for me, for my sojourn has been prolonged,” etc. Clearly this is the groaning of the perfected person, who from confidence in perfection desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ. But such confidence requires humility of conscience; presumption must be avoided. Therefore, also in the title:

## SONG OF ASCENTS

This title is set down. By it is signified that one ascending to heaven ought to ascend humbly, lest, while wearied by pilgrimage he wishes to fly to heaven, he fall into hell. Since the righteous and God-fearing person is one who ascends in this way, from the confidence of righteousness he has one sound and, as it were, strong foot: confidence, standing at the right hand. But from fear he has humility itself as the other, and weaker, foot—standing, as it were, at the left—because it is anxious concerning evils that either have happened or may happen.

The ascents through these fifteen steps into the temple of the true Solomon are thus arranged: in one Song of Ascents the foot of confidence is put first, and in the next the foot of humility follows. The foot of confidence is strong through good life; the foot of humility stronger through grace. The Apostle walked with these two feet when he said: “I labored more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10). In saying this, when he recalled his labors, as though standing upon the foot of confidence in good merits, [Col. 0839C] he sought things on high; so also elsewhere, after saying, “I have fought the good fight, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith” (2 Tim. 4:7), he sought the heavenly crown from confidence in such merits, saying: “Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will render to me on that day” (ibid., 8).

Yet he rested more firmly on the foot of humility when, attributing both his merits and everything he had to God’s grace, he said: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10). Thus a Song of Ascents is well arranged when in one step a good work is sung, and in another the power of that same work is perfected through true humility, by which the person seeking things above relies strongly not on his own goodness, but on God’s. Let him therefore say on the first step:

[Col. 0839D] **VERSE 1.** To the Lord, when I was afflicted, I cried, and he heard me. Hence comes my confidence: he will not abandon me who suffered affliction for him and was, as it were, threshed like grain on the threshing-floor, because in that very affliction I cried and he heard me. What did I cry? Namely, what follows:

**VERSE 2.** Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue. I remember this occurring at the beginning of my conversion, when I had thought to set out for the heights, despising low and earthly things. Then I was confronted by wicked lips and a deceitful tongue. Wicked lips openly urged wickedness, whether apostasy or some other injustice. A deceitful tongue, under the guise of counsel, tried to turn me away from the first step of the arduous life: now presenting the frailty of weak flesh to a willing spirit, now recalling the difficulty of the ascent to the heights, and frequently insisting that it is better not to vow than not to fulfill vows, since it is certain that many who could have remained standing on level ground have fallen from on high.

In this way the deceitful tongue spoke to me at the first step of that deliberation by which I arranged ascents in my heart. But wicked lips openly opposed me by urging evils and dissuading me from goods. Since I was unwilling to yield to such persuasions, the afflictions of my heart were enlarged. Because I could not of myself have the strength to resist them, I cried to the Lord when I was afflicted, and he heard me so fully that, like a blind man asking for light and crying out ever more loudly amid rebuking crowds, the Savior himself answered me, saying: “What do you want me to do for you?” (Mark 10:51).

**VERSE 3.** What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against the deceitful tongue? And I, as though saying, “Lord, that I may see,” desired the sharp arrows of the mighty one with desolating coals, because in the light of these arrows and the radiance of these coals the way of the saints is directed. Therefore there were given to me—

**VERSE 4.** Sharp arrows of the mighty one with desolating coals, or, as another text has it, devastating coals. These were the words of sacred Scripture, against which none of my adversaries, whether wicked or deceitful, could resist or speak in contradiction. Those words, I say, were sharp arrows of the mighty one, in whose light I went forward, stretching out toward the things before me. The desolating or devastating coals were the bright and illustrious examples of the saints, in which truth shone and charity burned. This charity had made living persons from the dead, righteous from the unjust, good from the evil, strong from the frail, chaste from the incestuous, pious from the impious: like glowing coals from black ones. These may be called devastators or desolators because they lay waste the straw cast upon them, and, burning themselves, set neighboring materials alight until that desolation in which, after wood, hay, and stubble have been consumed, only the foundation remains. The person found on the foundation of faith, below these fifteen steps which I set myself to climb, will scarcely be saved through fire, having despised wicked lips and the deceitful tongue, and also trampled upon evil examples, like dead and extinguished coals, along the way.

In Hebrew it reads: “Sharp arrows of the mighty one with coals of junipers.” This is pleasing for the reason that coals of juniper are said to retain fire longer than coals from wood of another kind. Therefore, by these juniper coals are signified the examples of such saints, whose charity will never fail or be extinguished; if the life of the weak grows cold at any time, it may be rekindled by their brightness. But now, because charity is growing cold and iniquity abounds, many coals are extinguished and black, while few are glowing and shining; consequently my pilgrimage, or sojourn, has become wearisome to me. Therefore I am compelled to cry:

**VERSES 5, 6, 7.** Alas for me, because my sojourn [Col. 0841A] has been prolonged. In this prolongation I longingly desired that shortening of which Truth says: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect they shall be shortened” (Matt. 24:22). For as in Elijah’s days the days of his pilgrimage were shortened by the consolation of the widow of Zarephath while Queen Jezebel persecuted him, so also now, when the synagogue of Satan persecutes someone like holy Elijah—that is, one reproving the vices of that synagogue—the days of his pilgrimage are shortened because many hiding places are found in the holy Church, namely religious monasteries. In them the jar of flour shall not fail nor the cruse of oil diminish, because the gifts of graces abound and in no way fail or diminish: whether in the bread of angels baked with two pieces of wood, which the widow of Zarephath—that is, the holy Church—gathers when she impresses upon that bread the sign of the Lord’s cross; or in the cruse of holy oil, that is, in the pure heart sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

They shall abound until the years of drought, during which Antichrist will reign, have wholly passed; Jezebel has been devoured by dogs; and there is peace in the Church, the sojourn of that Church having been shortened. In that sojourn I, David—I, a little one like David making my pilgrimage—dwelt with the dwellers of Cedar.

Kedar, who was also called Ishmael, was the son of a slave-woman, a persecutor of the son of the free woman, of whom the Apostle says: “But just as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also now. But what does Scripture say? [Col. 0841C] ‘Cast out the slave-woman and her son’” (Gal. 4:29–30). With sons of Kedar such as these I dwelt in the tents of Kedar. But why do I say “in the tents of Kedar” and not of Ishmael, since Kedar himself is called Ishmael? Surely because Kedar is interpreted as “darkness,” [Col. 0842A] while Ishmael means “God hears”; and concerning Ishmael the Lord also said to Abraham: “I have heard you.” For father Abraham had prayed for him, saying to the Lord: “May Ishmael live before you” (Gen. 17:20). Since that prayer was heard, those persecutors are rightly denoted by the name Ishmael, meaning “God hears”: the Church is heard when she prays for her adversaries, following the example of the true son of the free woman, who prayed on the cross for those crucifying him and was heard because of his reverence.

His blood too is still heard, crying from the earth far more effectively than Abel’s blood: for Abel’s called for vengeance, whereas Christ’s asks forgiveness for sinners who act only through pardonable ignorance, as he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke [Col. 0842B] 23:34). For it is not excessively burdensome or wearisome to dwell among persons whom one can, through prayer, summon to better things, so that they may become Ishmael—that is, “God hears.” But “in the tents of Kedar,” meaning “darkness,” denotes wholly unconvertible sons of darkness, for whom the praying Church is not heard. Having dwelt among these for a long time, worn down by prolonged weariness, I said: Alas for me, for my sojourn has been prolonged.

In the Hebrew it reads: “Alas for me, for my pilgrimage has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the tents of Kedar! My soul has journeyed long among those who hate peace.” They hate peace, but I was peaceable and spoke peacefully to them, desiring to make peace between God and them. But they attacked me, gratuitously stirring up [Col. 0842C] conflicts against me, having no cause for war, since I was not merely peaceable, willingly preserving peace, but also a peacemaker, diligently working and praying for the peace of others.

## PSALM 120

[Col. 0841]

[Col. 0841D] **VERSE 1.** “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me,” etc. On the first step, conscious of my good merit because I had been peaceable toward those who hated peace, loving even those who did not love me, I relied, as I thought, upon the sound and strong foot of confidence. But having proved by sure experience that this foot was exceedingly weak, unable with that foot to trample enemies stronger than myself and trampling upon me,

“I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me”: no longer to the foot of confidence, but to the foot relying on grace, in this second Song of Ascents, in which I do not trust in the strength of merits but in the mountains from which help will come to me. These mountains are God’s chosen and beloved ones, elsewhere called the mountains of Bethel and the mountains of spices. Bethel means “house of God,” by which name the holy Church is understood; its foundations in the holy mountains rest upon that most lofty mountain, [Col. 0842D] which has been made the summit of mountains, raised above the hills unto the very highest point. Nor is this surprising. For his going forth is from the highest heaven; and therefore it was fitting that he who grew from a little stone into a great mountain should be raised unto the highest point.

Upon this mountain of mountains, foundation of foundations, holy of holies founded in the heights and exalted to a lofty throne, the other mountains rest in a wonderful manner: the mountains of Bethel, namely the holy apostles. For whereas in earthly buildings foundations placed below support the walls and columns, in this heavenly building the principal foundation is supremely high; to it adhere, as it were, lesser foundations hanging down from above and descending from heaven. Thus John says: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven” (Rev. 21:2). Truly descending, because in it great and lofty mountains [Col. 0843A] stoop down to its smallest stones. Among these I count myself, set upon the next-to-last step toward it; and, still close to the earth, desiring to look upward, I lift, and have often lifted, my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me—help freely given, not obtained by any merits commensurate with it.

Among these mountains that provide help, after the very summit of the mountains, the blessed ever-virgin Mary excels. To her I continually say: “Holy Mother of God, be our helper.” Likewise: “Holy Mary, gracious virgin mother, help us.” Likewise: “Holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, intercede for us with the Lord Jesus Christ.” Likewise: “After childbirth you remained an inviolate virgin; Mother of God, intercede for us.” As I spoke such words, crying as though from the depths to this mountain, help came to me more than once from holy Mary, as from a mountain of myrrh. For she is principally that mountain of myrrh of which the Bridegroom says: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh” (Song 4:6). Since this was said of her in the Song of Songs, it is fitting also to remember her here in the Songs of Ascents, in recalling the mountains from which help will come to me.

Indeed, although the entire white-clad army of martyrs is a mountain of myrrh because of the bitterness of suffering, by which their bodies were, as it were, preserved with myrrh and prepared for incorruption, much more does that blessed virgin and incorrupt mother, whose soul was pierced by the sword of the Lord’s passion and of her own maternal [Col. 0843C] compassion, deserve to be called a mountain of myrrh. Like choice myrrh, she gives sweetness of fragrance by compassionately sharing the sufferings of those who lift their eyes to her and likewise to the other mountains, from which hoped-for help will come, and consolation to the desolate, of whom I am one. Therefore from these mountains I seek and hope for help. Yet this very

**VERSE 2.** “My help is not from the mountains, but from the Lord, who made heaven and earth”: he made the mountains themselves, through whom he gives help, whether in heavenly gifts as maker of heaven, or in earthly gifts as maker of earth. For he, the one maker of all things, made spiritual and bodily creatures, through whom he provides help to those singing this Song of Ascents, in which help is sought and hoped for more from grace than from merits [Col. 0843D]—help sought by eyes raised from low things to the heights, to the mountains, from which help will come, given through them by the Lord who made heaven and earth.

As I sing this Song of Ascents and lift my eyes to the mountains, namely the saints pre-eminent above others—such as seraphim, cherubim, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, virtues, angels, archangels, apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins—from these mountains themselves a voice of exultation and salvation is heard, consoling me and saying:

**VERSE 3.** “May he not give your foot to be moved,” etc. As though one of the mountains were saying: “You lift your eyes to us mountains, and we pray for you to him who is above us, the mountain at the summit of the mountains. What do we pray? Namely this: ‘May he not give [Col. 0844A] your foot to be moved’—that is, may ‘the foot of pride’ not come upon you, and may ‘the hand of the sinner not move’ you (Ps. 35:12); but may you remain firm upon this step of holy humility, by which you trust in God’s mercy more through grace than through merits. May he not give your foot to be moved, nor let him who keeps you slumber—that is, may he not allow you to become drowsy, but make you continually watch toward him, as elsewhere you say: ‘O God, my God, I watch for you from the dawn’ (Ps. 62:2). For if you sleep in relation to him, he too will sleep in relation to you. Lest this happen, we mountains pray for you, that he who keeps you may not sleep in relation to you. For he sleeps in relation to the lazy servant who sleeps, and watches over the good servant who keeps watch: ‘Blessed is that servant whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching’ (Luke 12:37). Therefore, lest he sleep in relation to you, may he make you always watch in spirit, even while you sleep bodily, so that you may say: ‘I sleep, but my heart watches’ (Song 5:2).”

Thus we mountains pray for you, a little stone—for you, a flint or diamond; for you, whether despised and trampled like flint, or honoured and encircled like a precious diamond with the gold of some dignity. And behold, in the midst of our prayers we have been heard, because:

**VERSE 4.** “Behold, he who keeps you will not slumber nor sleep,” Israel: you who are like Jacob, who also became Israel, provided that you do not hunt with Esau, wandering outside and pursuing the fleeting joys of this world, but dwell in the tent of ecclesiastical or monastic discipline with Rebecca, whose name means “patience”; that you love Rachel more than Leah; and that you wrestle in prayer [Col. 0844C] with the angel of great counsel until he blesses you, saying: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name” (Gen. 32:28). From that point you will certainly be assured that he who keeps you, named Israel—that is, “a man seeing God”—will not slumber or sleep in relation to you, because you will see the Lord face to face and your soul will be saved. Therefore do not doubt that help will come to you, because, as we mountains pray to the Lord for you, he himself—

**VERSE 5.** “The Lord keeps you, and the Lord himself is your protection over your right hand,” or, as the Hebrew truth has it, “over the hand of your right hand.” When you contended on the first step against the sons of Kedar, your left hand, armed with the shield of patience, at times protected you by receiving hostile darts amid adversity. But that right hand was far more effective: namely, kindness, by which charity is not merely patient, enduring evils, but also kind, repaying good for evil, praying for slanderers, and driving far away, with the missiles of prayer, the assaults of visible and invisible enemies.

Your right hand also protected you in this way: when it gave alms, your left hand did not know what your right hand was doing; in such work you sought only eternal rewards, having driven far away the desire for human praise and favour. Likewise, your right hand protected you in that it joined you to the sheep set at the right hand, separated from those on the left—the wanton goats—when, without your left hand knowing, that right hand fed Christ hungry in his least ones, gave drink to him thirsty, clothed him naked, received him as a stranger, and visited him sick and in prison. [Col. 0845A] Blessed, therefore, is the right hand that protects from those darts by which the goats to be set at the left will be struck, to whom it will be said: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire; for I was hungry and you did not give me food; I was thirsty and you did not give me drink,” and so on, down to: “As long as you did not do it to one of the least of mine, you did not do it to me” (Matt. 25:41 ff.).

This generous right hand has greatly availed to protect you, whether in bodily benefits, by which bodies are sustained, or spiritual benefits, by which souls are nourished, lest either the former or the latter perish. This right hand of yours, I say, has greatly availed, acquiring for you the merits by which are obtained the delights stored up at God’s right hand, while temporal consolations are in his left. [Col. 0845B] Nevertheless, above this right hand of yours, exercised on the first step, on this second step the grace of God has far greater power to protect you: he will freely protect you above your right hand, or the hand of your right hand—that is, more than your hand, however greatly exercised in holy merits. For when the Lord himself keeps you in peace and protects you in war,

**VERSE 6.** “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night.” The sun is Christ’s divinity; the moon is his humanity, or the whole Church, which is his body. The sun burns heretics who falter in faith in the divinity, such as Arians and Sabellians. The moon also burns those scandalized concerning the veneration of Christ’s humanity, such as Photinus and Mani. One of these strips the man born of the virgin of divinity; the other strips him even of true humanity: the former maintains that Christ is a mere man, not God; the latter says that he is not a true man but a phantom, declaring, among other ravings of his error: “If a virgin gave birth, it was a phantom.”

Likewise, the moon—that is, the holy Church—burns those who, unable to bear the tempered radiance of her holiness, separate themselves from her through schisms and sects of perdition, such as the Luciferians and Novatians. The latter called themselves Cathari, that is, “the pure,” puffed up by an immoderate and excessive, and therefore false, kind of holiness, with the leaven of the Pharisees who despised others. Conversely, the Nicolaitans—ministers of the altar living with concubines—and all the rest who wished to eat and fornicate, namely to consume the stipends due to chaste and continent ministers while committing open adultery and neither having nor wishing to have lawful marriages, corrupted by the leaven of the Sadducees, could not bear in the Church the brightness of continence, like the moon’s brightness, which comes from the sun of righteousness into the body of the Church. [Col. 0845D] Burned by that brightness, they formed sects of perdition: some falsely married, some genuinely living with concubines, some entangled with the prostitutes of many women, yet unwilling to forgo the ecclesiastical offices and benefices forbidden them by the holy Church.

Some too, corrupted by Herod’s leaven, unable to bear the Church’s brightness of patience and gentleness, tyrannize within the Church against the Church, turning the stipends of spiritual warfare into instruments of carnal warfare—or rather of diabolical wickedness. [Col. 0846A] But you, who rely steadfastly on God’s grace, will not be scandalized when burned by the sun’s radiance or the moon’s brightness, because:

**VERSES 7–8.** “The Lord keeps you from every evil,” lest you perish through any scandal. And lest we mountains, to whom you lifted your eyes, have vainly promised this to you and be found, God forbid, to be liars, we turn to the Lord—from whom help will come to you through our mediation—and pray for you, now standing on the second step, saying what follows: “May the Lord keep your soul. May the Lord keep your going in and your going out, from this time forth and for ever.”

Even if the earth of your body is delivered into the hands of the wicked, may your soul always be kept, like Job’s soul; when he was handed over to Satan to be afflicted and tested, the Lord said to the tempter himself: “Nevertheless, spare his soul” (Job 2:6). In the same way, may the Lord keep your soul, so that, even if your body is killed, your soul may not be injured; indeed, purified by bodily affliction, may it shine like a highly polished mirror with the light of sun and moon—by the sun’s light in the day of prosperity, by the moon’s in the night of adversity; or by the sun in the virtue of contemplation, and by the moon in the virtue of action. Thus may night be enlightened as day, and may our Martha be shown to be the sister of our Mary; indeed, may our Leah, fruitful in works, be preferred to barren Rachel, just as Leah herself is preferred to her sister in her appearance and beauty.

Thus, yes, thus, neither sun by day nor moon by night will burn you with its brightness, when neither sister has cause for such jealousy as existed between Leah and Rachel, and as also somewhat burned Martha when she said: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone?” (Luke 10:40). Martha had nearly been distressed by the burning of such jealousy. But at the Lord’s judgment her distress was calmed, so that Martha did not abandon her good portion, and Mary did not lose the best portion which she had chosen. Likewise, when your household is rightly ordered and adorned by active and contemplative persons living peaceably with one another, neither sun by day nor moon by night will burn you; rather, the brightness of both will delight your eyes, whether you enter into the secret place of inward contemplation or go out to work in the fields with him who [Col. 0846D] “went out to sow his seed” (Matt. 13:3). We mountains, to whom you lifted your eyes, wish for you prosperity in both respects: that the Lord, from whom help will come to you, may keep your going in and your going out, from this moment, in which you stand on the second step, unto the world to come, when you have passed through the steps by which we see you supported.

Another interpretation: Going in is the beginning of temptation, into which we pray that we may not enter, instructed by him who said to his disciples, weary in their effort to ascend: “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:38). We mountains also pray this for those who lift their eyes to us, as you do, who sing: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come [Col. 0847A] to me.” But if, by the hidden dispensation of God, it should happen that our prayers cannot prevent you from entering temptation, we strive by every means to obtain this: that the Lord may keep your going in, according to the promise of him who said: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear; but with the temptation he will also make a way out, that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10:13).

But since malicious enemies lie in wait both at the going out and at the going in of temptation, wishing either to wound the head at the beginning or the heel at the end, may the Lord keep your going in and your going out, lest you be conquered when temptations come upon you, or exalted when you have overcome them. And may this protection of the Lord over you remain firm from this present moment, in which now is the acceptable time, unto the world to come, which will be bounded by no end.

[Col. 0847B] Another interpretation: If you are to be appointed to some ministry in the holy Church, may the Lord keep your going in and your going out, so that you may enter through the door and find pasture, according to the saying: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved and will find pasture” (John 10:3). Thus may you too find pasture in going in and going out. Going in, as you pray in your chamber with the door shut, may you find the pasture [Col. 0848A] of prayer’s desire and effect, while your Father, who hears you in secret, gives you ineffable consolations for your unutterable groanings. Going out—whether to a ministry, in serving; or to teach, in doctrine; or to govern, in diligence; or to show mercy, in cheerfulness; or to give, in simplicity—may you find in such departures the very effects of your ministry, so that those who see them may glorify the Father who is in heaven.

May the glorification of his name feed you—not self-praise, not the favour of human approval, not ambition for profit or honour. For those whom such things feed, they kill like poisoned food, unless, having received the antidote of repentance, they either spit it out when it is tasted in the mouth, or vomit it out after it has entered the stomach of the heart. Otherwise, whoever delights in and feeds upon such pastures will die. [Col. 0848B] Therefore may the Lord keep your going in and your going out from these poisonous pastures, from this time forth and for ever. But may you, in going in and going out, find better pastures, by which both you may grow and nourish others unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, whose name be blessed from this time forth and for ever.

## PSALM 121

[Col. 0847]

[Col. 0847C] **VERSE 1.** “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me,” etc. On this third step the voice of confidence returns, because this climber, relying on the foot of merits, rejoices and says:

“I rejoiced in the things said to me by the resounding mountains on the preceding step; among other things, this was included: that the Lord would not give my foot to be moved, nor slumber, he who keeps me. Therefore under his protection, I and those accompanying me will go into the house of the Lord,” where also, through his protection,

**VERSE 2.** “Our feet stood in your courts, O Jerusalem.” As one enters a house through its court, so one enters from faith into sight. Therefore, because our feet—that is, our affections—have not been moved from the firmness [Col. 0847D] of faith, we shall go by walking in faith into the house of the Lord, where the God of gods will be seen face to face in Zion or Jerusalem.

**VERSE 3.** Jerusalem is “built as a city,” whose stones are polished and sawn outside, to be placed permanently in the sacred buildings of that city “whose participation is in the selfsame.” The selfsame is God himself, to whom it is elsewhere said: “But you are the selfsame, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101:28). All citizens of that city will share in that selfsame reality, because there the joy of each will be the joy of all, and the joy of all the joy of each; each will rejoice not only in his own good but also in that of others. This good will always be the selfsame, because it will not change or vary for eternity.

Truly we shall ascend there, because we know that many forerunners have preceded us there, whither Christ, the chief forerunner, entered for us and has drawn and draws to himself all his members, which are the tribes of the Lord. The realization of past things is a certainty of future things, lest we in any way despair of ascending as children to that place—to Jerusalem—where we do not doubt that our fathers have ascended.

**VERSE 4.** “For the tribes ascended there”: not indeed all of them, since not every tribe’s faith is approved, but “the tribes of the Lord,” who have the testimony of Israel, like the man to whom it was said: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no guile” (John 1:47). Such men truly ascended there.

**VERSE 5.** “For there sat,” and will sit, [Col. 0848D] “thrones for judgment, judging the twelve tribes of Israel,” distinguishing believing tribes from unbelieving ones. They are at once judges and judicial thrones of the supreme Judge, according to the saying: “The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom.” Therefore it is truly sung: “There sat thrones in judgment,” for they too will sit—that is, rest in God—and God will sit—that is, rest—in them.

These thrones will judge the house of David, truly “strong of hand” and beloved: Christ, the son of David. His house is the whole Church, mingled with good and evil, but to be distinguished by those judges, who cannot be deceived; for, with God sitting in them, they will judge only justly, assigning to goats and sheep what is due to each. And because the judgment will then be terrible, you who will be judges must now be intercessors; and before you judge strictly,

**VERSE 6.** “Pray for the things that make for the peace of Jerusalem.” For through you, as suitable ambassadors, we send an embassy, “asking for the things of peace” (Luke 14:32), because the king who is to come against us in judgment will come with twenty thousand and demand an account not only of manifest deeds and words but also of hidden thoughts. Against his army of twenty thousand, perhaps we cannot provide even the single force of ten thousand in accounting for outward acts, much less for inward dispositions. Therefore pray for the things that make for the peace of Jerusalem. Ask the very king of the city Jerusalem for peace and forgiveness of sins. And because forgiveness of sins is not enough for complete peace, let an abundance of virtues be added. For whom? “For those who love you”: those who love justice, truth, holiness, piety, charity—all of which you are. For those who love you, I say, there will be abundance; because whoever cannot fulfil all that you command fulfils everything by loving those who fulfil it, loving you yourself in all things with that love which is strong as death. For it kills in us what we were, so that, dead to the world, we may live to God. Therefore, as so great intercessors obtain for us peace—that is, forgiveness of sins—and an abundance of virtues,

**VERSE 7.** “Let peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers.” Let peace come, I say, not through the strength of intercessors, who can do nothing without you, O God, but [Col. 0849C] through your strength; and let an abundance of virtues be in your towers. What, O city Jerusalem, are your towers except ecclesiastical communities and religious monasteries, founded upon the foundation which is Christ, [Col. 0850A] so that lesser buildings may be fortified from them as from lofty towers—for example, the orders of married persons, of those engaged in secular military service, or of those supplying tribute to soldiers?

Unless their teachers and instructors—continent and religious men, shooting as it were the arrows of words from the towers of a higher vocation, so that lesser persons may walk in the light of your arrows and the brightness of your flashing spear—abound in spiritual goods, so that their righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, they will neither enter the kingdom of heaven themselves nor lead others into it. Therefore let this abundance be in your towers, so that they need neither seek oil with the foolish virgins nor, with hypocrites who seek their own interests, desire anything belonging to another; but, having food and clothing from the altar which they serve, may they be content with these.

Yet I spoke peace concerning you, O Jerusalem, not for private advantage, but

**VERSE 8.** “for my brothers,” to be nourished by the common good. I sought forgiveness of sins that provoke God’s fury and wrath, so that, the wall of hostility being removed, there might be peace between us and God. Then:

**VERSE 9.** “For the sake of the house of the Lord our God I sought good things for you,” O Jerusalem, so that, just as the house of the Lord in earthly Jerusalem abounded in gold and silver vessels and other ornaments for the beauty of the whole city, so the vocation of holy religion, richly abounding in good persons and in provisions suited to the house of God, may shine in that beauty [Col. 0850C] of holiness of which it is elsewhere said: “Holiness befits your house, O Lord, unto length of days” (Ps. 92:5).

## PSALM 122

[Col. 0849]

[Col. 0849D] **VERSES 1–2.** “To you I lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens. Behold, as the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters,” etc. In this fourth Song of Ascents, having laid aside confidence in merits, he who strives to ascend places his foot, that he may ascend more effectively, upon the higher step of holy humility, saying:

“To you I lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens. Behold, as the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant upon the hands of her mistress,” even under the severest blows, until either the master or mistress commands that the servant or maidservant being beaten be spared. He greatly humbles himself, for he compares himself not merely with a servant, but even with a beaten maidservant who fixes her eyes upon her mistress’s hands, until she is commanded to be spared, even by a mere gesture.

The ascent from the mountains to the Lord of mountains, from the multitude to the One, should be noted. It is as though he said: “Previously I lifted my eyes to the mountains, from which help would come to me. Now I have lifted my eyes to you who dwell in the heavens.” Those high mountains are called heavens because of their heavenly manner of life. I lift my eyes to you so that, by beholding you, I may despise myself, saying with blessed Job: “I heard you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you; therefore I rebuke myself” (Job 42:6).

Pharaoh had not lifted his eyes to you but had lowered them upon himself, when he said: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. 5:2). So also Nebuchadnezzar: “Who,” he said, “is the God who will deliver you from my hand?” (Dan. 3:15). And that Pharisee who considered himself greater than others, saying, “I am not like other men” (Luke 18:12), kept his eyes fixed upon himself, not lifted upward to you, the inhabitant of the heavens. Conversely, though the publican did not dare lift the eyes of his body toward heaven, he had lifted the eyes of his heart to you, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (ibid., 13). He looked to you and despised himself. You pleased him, and he displeased himself; therefore he lifted his eyes from himself to you who dwell in the heavens.

And I, because I have become burdensome to myself, worn down by the weariness of pilgrimage in this valley [Col. 0851A] of tears, cried from the depths and lifted my eyes upward to you who dwell in the heavens. How?

“Behold, as the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant upon the hands of her mistress,” amid the most grievous blows, until either master or mistress commands that the beaten servant or maidservant be spared: so are our eyes directed to the Lord our God, who is for us both lord and mistress, as he himself compared himself in the Gospel parable both to a man and to a woman, saying: “What man among you, having a hundred sheep?” (Luke 15:4); and: “Or what woman having ten drachmas?” (ibid., 8).

Our eyes are upon this Lord and this mistress until he has mercy on us, seeking us as a lost sheep torn by wolves and distressed among thorns, and as a drachma fouled by much dust. For both in the flesh, which ought to be a clean offering like a sheep, and in the mind, which ought to be a shining drachma stamped in the royal coinage with the likeness of God, we lost in Adam whatever good we possessed. We are beaten by the scourge of a double misery while we are pilgrims, in body and mind alike, away from the Lord God or from Lady Wisdom. Therefore, under the blows, we cry to this Lord, merciful by nature, whose proper work is to have mercy, saying with mouth and heart together:

**VERSES 3–4.** “Have mercy on us, O Lord, have mercy on us.” Have mercy according to the flesh, lifting it upon [Col. 0851C] your shoulders and presenting it to yourself as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to you. Have mercy also according to the inward person, wiping him clean like a drachma [Col. 0852A] fouled by the dust of evil thoughts and the mud of depraved affections. “Have mercy on us, O Lord, have mercy on us,” because now is the time for mercy: we are filled with contempt because our manifest poverty is plain; and our soul is filled with contempt because of its inward defilement, since we have lost the likeness of God and come into the far country of unlikeness. There, while tending swine for a long time, we desired to fill the belly of our memory with the same food on which the swine fed; and we became like swine.

Therefore, now returning to you, most merciful Father, we are a reproach and contempt: we who are humbled, to the proud and envious; we who are poor, to the affluent; we, beggarly and covered with sores with Lazarus, to the rich and prosperous, [Col. 0852B] who feast splendidly every day and do not distribute even crumbs to comfort our contempt. We are greatly filled with that contempt, and our soul also is greatly filled with it. It is misery that we are despised; an accumulation of misery that we are greatly despised; an aggravation of misery that we are filled with misery itself and contempt; and a depth of misery that not only our flesh but also our soul is greatly filled with calamities. Because of these we are a reproach to the affluent and contempt to the proud—although they are not truly affluent but rather more wretched than all other wretches, since they despise others, imagining themselves to be something when they are nothing, and are proud either of bodily riches which they possess or spiritual riches which they think they possess. As we live and labour among such persons, and encounter dangers in many ways, have mercy on us, Father of mercies and God of all consolation.

## PSALM 123

[Col. 0851]

[Col. 0851C] **VERSE 1.** “Unless the Lord had been in us, let Israel now say,” etc. On this fifth step the perfect, conscious of great virtues, sing with voices of great rejoicing: “Unless the Lord had been in us, let Israel now say,” etc. For, as though already possessing triumph, they say in thanksgiving: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of hunters; the snare has been broken, and we have been delivered.” Yet because they do not attribute this deliverance to their own strength, they prudently preface it: “Unless the Lord had been in us, when men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.”

Let Israel, the people of God delivered from Egyptian slavery, say this—partly in reality, partly in hope: in reality, as regards those who now reign in heaven; in hope, as regards those who still journey upon earth. Therefore let all Israel, assured of its deliverance either in reality or in hope, say:

**VERSES 2–3.** “Unless the Lord had been in us, when men—Pharaoh’s taskmasters—rose up against us Israelites, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive,” so that, incorporated into the Egyptians themselves, we would not have cried to the Lord. They would have swallowed us not merely in any fashion, but alive—that is, sinning knowingly. Those who commit crimes in ignorance, through which they pass into the body of the devil, are swallowed while dead; but those who, knowing and perceiving the evil of what they do, commit grave sin under the devil’s impulse, are swallowed alive. Thus, when Egyptian men rose up against us, we would have been swallowed up—perhaps we alive, incorporated into them who were dead—because we would have perished by sinning knowingly, whereas they perhaps sinned in ignorance, as their king Pharaoh said: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. 5:2).

“Perhaps” is an adverb of doubt inserted because the matter could have gone either way: it could have happened or not happened. Yet, since the Lord ruled in us, Pharaoh’s dominion did not prevail. Therefore he who could not keep us by blandishments, whose deceitful tongue, pierced with sharp arrows and burned with desolating coals on the first step, had fallen silent, afterwards turned to anger and rage, raging without reason or even an appearance of reason. With manifest cruelty he persecuted us with his whole army of demons and men serving him, and likewise with carnal desires, which wage war against our soul. And then, as we fled through the Red Sea—that is, through baptism reddened by the blood of the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world—
### Verse 4

Perhaps the water of baptism would have swallowed us up, just as that same water of the Red Sea swallowed up the Egyptians while it conveyed the Israelites safely across. For just as the water of the Flood—by which baptism was likewise prefigured—swallowed up those whom it did not find in the ark, so the water of baptism neither saves nor raises above the mountains except those who remain in the unity of the universal Church, under the rule of the true Noah, or even under Moses—indeed, under the true lawgiver, who gives not the killing letter but blessing; for “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). Since therefore this true Noah, ruler of the Church, this giver of the new law, namely Christ dwelling in our hearts through faith, was within us, therefore by his help—

### Verse 5

—our soul passed through the torrent of fierce persecution and temptation. Those who tormented, or even killed, the body could not kill it, because power had been granted them over the body alone, as to Satan when he sought permission to test Job, and the Lord said to him: “Yet spare his life” (Job 2:6). Therefore, with him protecting us, our soul passed through the torrent—that is, the onrush of violent temptation or persecution. And from the fact that our soul passed through such a torrent, we infer that a storm of still greater persecution or temptation had swollen against us, one intolerable to human strength: perhaps our soul would have passed through intolerable water.

The Latins use *forsitan* (“perhaps”) for the Greek word of questioning, ἆρα, which may more intelligibly be rendered: “Do you suppose that our soul would have passed through intolerable water?” The sense is: the greatness of the danger scarcely permits belief that this could have happened, that we should have passed unharmed through the intolerable assaults of visible and invisible enemies. Yet we did pass through, with the Lord’s help, who did not permit us to be tempted beyond what we were able to bear, but with the temptation also made a way out of it, so that we might endure: by his mercy he mitigated certain dangers, wholly removed others, and changed some enemies—as Saul, whom he made Paul—while he struck down others, such as Saul, who fell by a just judgment on Mount Gilboa because of his stubborn pride. Thus, yes, with our enemies humbled, we escaped not merely unharmed, but even tested through their persecutions as gold through fire. Therefore, giving thanks to the author of our salvation, we say:

### Verse 6

“Blessed be the Lord, who did not give us as prey to their teeth”—to those who snarled at us like ravening wolves, or fierce lions and bears. And when they could not harm us with their teeth after the manner of beasts, they spread before us, like most cunning hunters, snares of deceits, according to the words: “In this way in which I walked, they hid a snare for me” (Psalm 141:4). But—

### Verse 7

—“our soul escaped like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters, because the snare was broken.” For as a sparrow gladly flies away when the snare in which it was held has been torn apart, so our soul, when the body that weighed it down has been mortified either through martyrdom or through the exercises of virtues, gladly flew heavenward, savoring and seeking the things above, not those upon the earth.

We do not say that our snare was broken as though it had been frail or made of tow; rather, in this Song of Ascents we say and sing that the snare was shattered because it was iron, like the two chains by which Peter had been bound. For we too were bound as by two chains: both by sins and by the penalties of sins. Therefore, when sins are forgiven and the penalties of sins are either moderated or entirely removed, the iron snare is shattered and we are set free, so that with Peter we may sing: “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of” the spiritual “Herod” (Acts 12:11).

As we give thanks to the Lord for this victory and escape, we must continually say: “Blessed be the Lord, who did not give us as prey to their teeth”; and we add: “Our soul escaped like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare was broken, and we were set free.” And if, in climbing the remaining steps, there is still work left to do, we trust in the Lord.

### Verse 8

“For our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” Therefore he is able to raise us from earth to heaven after all fifteen steps have been passed; and on the sixth of these we now set the foot of holy humility, saying:

## Psalm 124

[Col. 0853]

### Verse 1

“Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion,” etc. For in singing such things we ascribe to God, not to ourselves, the fact that we have conquered and escaped by his help; and, with that help, victory shall belong to all who trust in him. For:

“Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion, which shall not be moved”—namely Christ, who grew from a small stone into a great mountain; and thus those founded upon him shall themselves not be moved. They shall not be as unstable as the man who, seeing the peace of sinners, almost staggered as his feet slipped, because God’s judgments displeased him—judgments by which God grants peace and riches to sinners while afflicting the righteous. Those who trust in the Lord will not, I say, be moved in that manner; they believe all his judgments to be just and beneficial to the upright in heart, for whom all things work together for good, whether prosperity or adversity. They are neither corrupted by prosperity nor broken by adversity, but stand firm, like Mount Zion, which shall not be moved forever. This mountain dwells—

### Verse 2

—in Jerusalem, according to the Apostle’s saying, “that Christ may dwell through faith in our hearts” (Ephesians 3:17). We are Jerusalem, united by faith with that Jerusalem above which is our mother.
