Behold the ascent from Zion to Jerusalem: from watchtower to vision, from faith to sight; for what we now see in Zion through a mirror and in an enigma, we shall see face to face in the heavenly Jerusalem.

But as long as we are in Zion, living as pilgrims and soldiers in the present Church, yet pressing toward the heavenly Jerusalem reigning in peace—a Jerusalem which the seer sees and, seeing, possesses—we ought not fear the attacks of enemies. Though they are permitted to assault, they will not be able to capture our city Jerusalem, fortified by its natural position, because mountains surround it which enemies cannot cross. The defenses of angels and holy persons, together with the holy angels already reigning with them, are mountains compacted and united into one, surrounding this Zion or Jerusalem. They fortify it so that it cannot be taken. This is because the Lord is around it. The Lord, mountain of mountains and holy one of holy ones, indwelling holy angels and human beings, is himself in the surrounding holy ranks of the heavenly armies around his city: himself wall and outer wall around his people from this time forth and forever—an everlasting helper.

### Verse 3

“For he will not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity.” The rod of sinners is their power, by which God sometimes permits good people to be scourged, so that through patience they may become better—a patience produced by such tribulation itself. Yet he will not leave this rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous, that is, over those who, by the lot of God who calls them, are his inheritance and portion.

In ancient times inheritance was divided by lot; thus too the land of promise was divided by Joshua. Hence, by metonymy, the inheritance itself distributed by lot is called a “lot.” The lot of the righteous, then, is the righteous themselves, because by the lot of grace—which predestines, calls, justifies, and glorifies—they have been chosen into the Lord’s inheritance. Over this lot the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners. While his little children are scourged even to the shedding of tears or blood, he will at the fitting time remove the “rod” and “wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 7:17), and “death shall be no more, neither mourning nor crying,” for the former things “have passed away” (Revelation 21:4)—brief things, so that eternal joys may follow, just as the brief joys of the wicked have passed away so that eternal torments may follow.

### Verse 4

“Do good, O Lord, to the good and to the upright in heart”: good in deed and upright in heart, that is, in will. “How good God is to Israel, to those who are upright in heart” (Psalm 72:1): those who conform their own will to the divine will and approve all that God ordains in his great commonwealth, by judgments sometimes manifest and sometimes hidden, yet always unfailingly just. In these matters the upright in heart do not murmur, but continually praise God’s judgments, saying: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right” (Psalm 118:137); likewise: “Just and true are your ways, O King of the ages” (Revelation 15:3); and again: “All that you have done to us, O Lord, you have done in true judgment” (Daniel 3:31).

Such approval of God’s judgments delivered the three youths from the fiery furnace, Daniel from the lions’ den, holy martyrs from the furnace of torments, and holy confessors from the pit and snares of heretical lions, gnashing their foul teeth against them. With these are joined all who are upright in heart—upright by a right will which does not disagree with the divine will. O Lord, do good to them, that they may never decline or stray from the uprightness of their heart.

### Verse 5

“But the Lord will lead away those who turn aside into bonds with those who work iniquity.” Those who turn aside from the way of uprightness, the Lord will lead into the bondage of crookedness, so that, bound and tied in bundles for burning, blind followers with blind guides may fall into the pit, or bondage, from which they shall be unable to free themselves.

Alternatively: “those who turn aside into bonds,” that is, into earthly prosperity, which binds its lovers to those sinners from whom earthly benefits are hoped for. Just as sinners bind themselves to sinners through homage, an oath, or another form of alliance, so that, whether through fear of loss or hope of gain, they consent to the sins of those people either by silence or by assent. Therefore they will share the punishment with those who commit iniquity, since they consented to their guilt; for, as the Apostle testifies, “not only those who do such things, but also those who approve them, are worthy of death” (Romans 1:32).

“But peace be upon Israel.” Under the name of peace all good rewards are included. Under the name Israel are signified all those who, by serving well for the sake of these rewards—as Jacob faithfully served with Laban—deserve to be enriched with the same rewards; they are fit and strong to wrestle with the Lord until they wrest from him the blessing by which each is told: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name” (Genesis 32:28).

“Peace upon such Israel” must be understood as said both prophetically and prayerfully. By contrast, “the Lord will lead away those who turn aside into bonds with those who work iniquity” is said only prophetically; while what precedes it, “Do good, O Lord, to the good and upright in heart,” is said only prayerfully. For it is appropriate for good people to ask good things for both good and evil persons, but at times to foretell and announce evils to the evil. Thus Paul, when Ananias the high priest ordered him struck in his presence, did not say in wish or prayer, “May God strike you,” but prophetically: “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall” (Acts 23:3). Thus here it is not said, “May the Lord lead away those who turn aside,” but “the Lord will lead away [them] with those who work iniquity”: this is prophecy, not prayer.

## Psalm 125

[Col. 0857]

### Verse 1

“When the Lord turned the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted,” etc. At this seventh step the song of good confidence again sounds from the climbers, now gladdened by their progress:

“When the Lord turned the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted.” And later: “The Lord has done great things with us; we became joyful.”

“When the Lord turned the captivity of Zion”—that is, when the Lord would turn Zion’s captivity—“we became like those who are comforted.” A certain figurative consolation came first to the children of Israel released from Babylonian captivity. When this is carefully considered, we became like those comforted, since the high priest Jesus, the minister of that return, is recorded as stripped of filthy garments, clothed in change of garments, and crowned with golden crowns (Zechariah 3:4). Yet we were not fully comforted by that turning of captivity; rather, we were like those comforted, in likeness of the consolation by which we were fully comforted when Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive.

### Verse 2

Then our mouth was most truly filled with joy, because the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord Jesus, the high priest. He was then truly, not figuratively, stripped of the filthy garments of human mortality; he was clothed with changed garments and crowned with as many golden crowns of victory as the souls captive in hell whom he freed from there and led into the heavenly Jerusalem.

Then, in the apostles who beheld these things, our mouth was filled with joy and our tongue with exultation, when on the day of resurrection Christ breathed into the mouth of their minds, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). And on Pentecost the same Spirit came upon them in tongues of fire, kindling and illuminating them, so that those who had formerly spoken timidly in one language might afterward speak exultantly in diverse tongues of the mighty works of God. Then they said—and until the end of the age they will say among the nations—“The Lord has done great things with them,” namely, with the apostles. And we, in them and through them, said and say:

### Verse 3

“The Lord has done great things with us,” cooperating with us and confirming us by the signs that followed. Yet although, when they returned from the Babylon of this world to the heavenly Jerusalem, the Babylonian confusion of languages was corrected and healed by the Holy Spirit gathering together all languages—then in each individual person, now in the one Church of a single faith, Jerusalem—nevertheless, until the end of the age there are still faithful people journeying in the Babylon of this world. Among them we too labor; possessing the firstfruits of the Spirit, we sing this Song of Ascents for ourselves and pray for our fellow citizens, saying:

### Verses 4–5

“Turn, O Lord, our captivity like a torrent in the south,” so that, as ice and snow frozen by the northern cold do not flow but melt when the south wind blows and, filled with sudden waters, torrents run with great force, so, when the south wind blows—the warm wind, namely the Holy Spirit—our sins may be dissolved. Set free from the confusion of sins as from Babylon, may we run toward our heavenly homeland, now sowing in tears what there we shall change into joy.

Let our seeds be good works, works of mercy, by which the Christian religion must be practiced, and for which joy will be rendered, when the supreme Judge says: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom,” etc. (Matthew 25:34). Then both the blessed poor, in whom Christ was hungry, thirsty, naked, a stranger, sick, and imprisoned, and those blessed merciful persons who provide such people with food, drink, clothing, lodging, and the consolation of visitation, will reap in joy what the former have sown by suffering and the latter by doing according to the Gospel. For both pleased God: the former through tears of suffering, the latter through tears of compassion; above all through tears shed for their own sins or those of others, following the example of Peter, who wept bitterly for his own sin, and Paul, who mourned those who had sinned and stirred others to mourning—especially the Corinthians, to whom he says: “And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned” (1 Corinthians 5:2). Again: “I fear,” he says, “that when I come to you, I may mourn many of those who previously sinned and did not repent” (2 Corinthians 12:20–21).

Those who thus sow in tears while proceeding through these steps—of which we are now at the seventh and are moving toward the eighth—while amid these Songs of Ascents we at times shed tears in mourning for our own evils and those of others, and by those tears hope for the eighth day of resurrection: those who thus weep “shall come, they shall come with exultation, bearing their sheaves”—that is, sheaves of rewards for the seeds of good merits. Then we shall be not like those comforted, but truly and completely comforted; then our mouth shall be filled with joy and our tongue with exultation. Awaiting this and rejoicing in hope, we indeed have joy at this step. But, lest this joy make us insolent, we express it with the wholesome humility now advanced, while at the eighth step we sing:

## Psalm 126

[Col. 0859]

### Verse 1

“Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain,” etc. Its title is “A SONG OF ASCENTS OF SOLOMON.” Rightly and aptly so. For in whom could it better become known that unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain? Solomon built a house for the Lord, and yet he himself could not stand, though among men he possessed singular wisdom.

Therefore, taught thoroughly by this experience that you cannot build a house without the Lord’s help, receive what I say: “It is vain for you to rise before the light.” It is vain, I say, and a foolish purpose, to make yourselves secure before the day of judgment. Rather, “rise after you have sat down”: that is, know yourselves secure only after you have laid aside the misery of mortality and susceptibility to suffering. Therefore you who are laborers in this building, by which the house or city of God is built, following Solomon’s example, know this and commit it to memory:

Unless the Lord himself, through himself, inwardly builds the house of knowledge that puffs up by adding charity which builds up, those who build it labor in vain by speaking and by communicating through their teaching knowledge that puffs up to their hearers. Unless they can say, “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts” [the citation as printed is 1 Corinthians 8:1], those who administer knowledge outwardly by speech labor in vain. For as the killing letter does not profit, indeed harms, without the life-giving Spirit, so knowledge that puffs up does not profit, indeed harms, without charity that builds up.

But perhaps the house, which is smaller, or the city, which is larger, once well founded and firmly built, may stand under human guardianship? Not at all. Unless the Lord himself through himself guards the city, however firmly built, the angel or human being who guards it watches in vain. For this exceeds angelic sublimity, much more human frailty; it belongs only to the Trinity, the Husbandman, that things well planted and watered may receive growth, or things firmly built may suffer no loss. Therefore, you who have labored or labor by uprooting or destroying evils and planting or building goods:

### Verse 2

“It is vain to rise before the light.” Now the light is “the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9). You ought to follow this light, not go before it, since it says: “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John 8:12).

Peter wished to go before this light when he girded himself and walked where he wished, believing himself fit to precede Christ in death. But after Christ had first died and risen from death, and after Peter heard from him, “Follow me” (John 21:19), instructed by his fall he learned to rise and walk not before the light but after the light, which had said to him, “You, follow me.” The sons of Zebedee also wished to rise before the light, seeking the glory of the kingdom before tasting the cup of the Lord’s passion. But they were recalled to the proper order: first to be conformed to the likeness of Christ’s passion and humbled, then to be exalted.

And you whom it delights to rise on high, where Christ sits at the right hand of God: first learn to sit humbly with him on the dung heap, following the example of blessed Job. For the present dwelling in mortal flesh, though it flatters fools, weighs down the wise as though they sat on a dung heap: humbled, namely, by consideration of human frailty, which truly is a dung heap. Sitting in it, every faithful person scrapes away discharge with a potsherd if, through faith in the Lord’s passion and resurrection—by which the soft clay of humanity was, as it were, hardened by fire—he cleanses and wipes away the impurities arising from fragile flesh. After such sitting there will truly be rising, since whoever humbles himself shall be exalted; and whoever humbles himself before the light shall be exalted in the light in which God will reveal hidden things and disclose the counsels of hearts.

Blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 0859D] In St. Paterius, *Exposition of Scripture from the Books of St. Gregory*, Part I, Book XI, chapter 249.] touches upon this passage and says among other things: “In certain places of sacred discourse allegory must be sought, and the words of the letter must be set aside altogether. To mention one instance among many, the Psalmist indicates this when he says: ‘It is vain for you to rise before the light.’ If anyone wishes to take this literally, he contradicts the nocturnal praises of God. For how does the same Prophet say: ‘At midnight I rose to give thanks to you’? If it is vain to rise before the light, why did he rise at midnight to give thanks to the Lord? But that person rises before the light who, before the day of the age to come, seeks to exalt himself in this life, which is like night.” [Note: [Col. 0860D] St. Gregory the Great, *Morals*, Book VIII, chapter 47.]

To rise before the light is to rejoice in the night of the present life before the brightness of eternal recompense appears. One must therefore first sit down in order afterward to rise rightly, because whoever does not now humble himself willingly will by no means be exalted by the glory that follows.

“Rise, therefore, after you have sat down,” you who now, sitting humbly, eat the bread of sorrow. In the valley of weeping, continual tears are your bread day and night, while you savor the saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:4); and again: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21). When, do you suppose, will that consolation and laughter be? “When he gives sleep to his beloved”:

### Verse 3

“Behold, children are the inheritance of the Lord; the fruit of the womb is a reward.” At the coming of death’s sleep, children of this age lose their inheritance and pass it on to successors. But when God gives his beloved death, which shall be rest and sleep for them, then the inheritance of the Lord bestowed upon them will manifestly appear. For they shall be “heirs indeed of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17); and they shall be children so chosen that they are the reward of the fruit of the virgin womb. The fruit of that womb, made poor for our sake, is to be enriched by this reward of children. Therefore Isaiah says: “If he gives his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand” (Isaiah 53:10). And he himself was the grain that died in the earth in order to be multiplied into such children, who are the reward of his death by which they were redeemed.

Alternatively: O holy Church, you now bear in your womb, like Rebecca, two peoples, one of whom shall overcome the other and the greater shall serve the lesser. Your good children, separated from the evil generation of Esau, shall be the reward and fruit of your womb. The rest are not reckoned children or fruit, but thorns and briars, which the soil of female flesh, cursed because of original sin, brings forth. The Lord said to Adam: “Cursed is the earth in your work. When you till the earth, it shall not yield its fruits, but shall bring forth thorns and briars for you” (Genesis 4:12).

By thorns and briars are signified the wicked, who multiply from the female earth under the working of male desire beyond the number of the good, who are born not from the stated curse but from the blessing spoken to the first parents: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28). Such children, begotten from God’s blessing, are rightly called children of God and fruit of the womb of the Church, which bears such children through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit in the washing of regeneration. Such children shall be the reward of the fruit of him who was born from a virgin womb and redeemed them by his death; by that death he acquired them as his inheritance, according to the Father’s saying: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance” (Psalm 2:8).

These are the people of acquisition, to be manifestly separated then from the children of perdition, when God gives his beloved the sleep of rest in Abraham’s bosom and removes the struggle in which Jacob and Esau now clash within the womb of the Church—the beloved and the unloved—according to the Lord’s saying: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Romans 9:13). But while this conflict remains between the beloved and the unloved, weapons of light are necessary, especially arrows, of which elsewhere it is said: “They shall go in the light of your arrows” (Habakkuk 3:11). Of these it is now also said:

### Verse 4

“As arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the children of those who have been shaken out.” An arrow is shot from a bow, and the stronger and more powerful the person who shoots it, the more swiftly and farther it goes and the more surely it strikes. As arrows directed by the hand of a mighty person are sent farther, so the apostles, sent by the Lord than whom nothing is more powerful, reached the ends of the earth. Likewise their children, apostolic men, sent forth and shaken out by the hand of almighty God while cooperating with the same fathers, each reached the places appointed for them: for example, Mark Alexandria, Luke Bithynia, Titus Dalmatia, and the rest the other places assigned to them.

The apostles are called either “shaken out,” as has been said, or “shakers out,” according to: “Into whatever city you enter, if they do not receive you, shake even the dust from your feet as a testimony against them” (Matthew 10:14). By thus shaking dust from their feet, they are rightly reckoned both shaken out and shakers out—just as a garment is called shaken out when dust is shaken from it, and the dust itself is also called shaken out. Thus, however one understands the phrase “children of those who have been shaken out,” no children of those shaken out are intended except the successors of the apostles, who likewise shake off dust and are themselves cleansed and shaken free from dust.

Again, because that which lay hidden within is said to be “shaken out,” as flour is said to be shaken out from a sack—and by that shaking the sack itself too is shaken out—in this sense the prophets are rightly called shaken out. Like sacks, they contained divine mysteries within. But when the Lord opened the disciples’ understanding that they might understand the Scriptures, sacks of this kind were wholly shaken out, and the flour hidden in them appeared outwardly. It was fashioned not into hidden breads, to which the harlot in Solomon invites when she says, “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread more pleasant” (Proverbs 9:17), but into loaves of presentation set upon the table of presentation. From these first the priests are fed, then King David—that is, good kings—to whom it is said: “And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth” (Psalm 2:10).

When priests and secular rulers alike have thus been refreshed and satisfied, even the crowd reclining upon the grass, by trampling carnal desires, shall eat and be satisfied. What remains will be gathered and stored in twelve baskets or seven hampers, because the fragments which the crowd cannot receive will be reserved in disciples of apostolic perfection. Since these things are so:

### Verse 5

“Blessed is the man who has filled his desire from them”—from those preachers who distribute the loaves they have received. But those filled with worldly desires, which fight against the soul, cannot receive the provisions offered or distributed through the apostles and others like them who both shake out and are shaken out, unless they first shake out those desires, so that they too may become shakers out and children of those shaken out. Therefore let whoever wishes to receive the good things he desires cast off and shake out the evils he bears, that he may become blessed from being not blessed. For “blessed is the man who has filled his desire from them.” And he is truly blessed, because “he shall not be ashamed when he speaks with his enemies in the gate”—that is, publicly, not in a corner; in the gate, where entrance and exit are visible, not in the corner where the hypocrite prays. Or in the gate, in Christ, who says: “I am the door” (John 10:9); in that gate speaks the one who, in speaking, seeks not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ.

Alternatively: the departure from this world into another world is a gate, which enemies besiege in order to reproach the soul as it departs at the hour of death, if it has either not shaken out evil through confession and careful repentance, or not filled its desire with good by receiving into affection what it knows through understanding. Then the blessed man who has filled his desire from what the apostles taught and distributed shall not be ashamed when he speaks with his enemies in the gate, because he finds within himself sure answers by which the accusing enemies are put to shame, and not he. As he proceeds toward that same gate, he continually prays: “Let those who persecute me be ashamed, but let not me be ashamed” (Jeremiah 17:18); and again: “Let the proud be ashamed, because they have unjustly wrought iniquity against me; but I shall meditate upon your commandments” (Psalm 118:78).

By fulfilling—and desiring to fulfill—my desire through these commandments, I hope not to be ashamed when I speak with my enemies in the gate: whether before death, when liars assail me and try to draw me back from the gate of righteousness through which I desire to enter; or in death, when demons accuse me and desire to drag me from the gate of paradise to the gates of hell. Those gates indeed shall not prevail against the faith in which, while walking as far as this eighth step, I have always first set the foot of confidence, and thereafter, by the foot of reverent humility, have striven to rise to higher things.

But now, with the order reversed, let the foot of reverent humility be put first and the foot of constancy or confidence follow. For the mode or tenor of the song changes in these Songs of Ascents. Up to this point the psalms alternated in pairs: in the former, strength was sung in a high tone, and in the next, fear answered in a low tone. But henceforth, conversely, in the first of the two fear sings in low tones, and strength answers in high tones, as follows:

## Psalm 127

[Col. 0863]

### Verse 1

“Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways,” etc. The sense is: blessed are all who, in the very fact that they walk in the Lord’s ways, are always fearful and apprehensive. And thereafter: “Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord.”

Fear can be a vice, and fear can be a virtue. The fear by which things not to be feared are feared is a vice and one of the four passions of the mind which even worldly philosophers condemn and discourage. For example, Philosophy says:

> Drive away joys; drive away fear;  
> Banish hope, and let no pain remain.  
> The mind is troubled and held in reins  
> Wherever these hold sway.

—Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, Book I, metre 7.

But the fear by which things that ought to be feared are feared is a virtue: in some it is initial; in others final, filial, and abiding for ever and ever. The vicious fear of which we spoke was left, as it were, outside before ascent of the first step, since no one can sing a Song of Ascents with or in that fear. But initial fear, which is the beginning of wisdom, accompanies the one walking and singing in these Songs of Ascents. Even after the first eight steps have been passed, it is presented as so perfect that perfect blessedness is due to it; and this Song of Ascents begins from that blessedness when it says:

“Blessed are all who fear the Lord,” and who, in evidence of this holy fear of the Lord, walk in his ways. They walk by always stretching forward through certain steps and degrees of virtues, according to the words: “They shall go from strength to strength” (Psalm 83:8). Thus, fearing the Lord, they walk in his ways and commandments; they do not grow sluggish in idleness, because they delight to labor in this walking, in which they have one understanding and press toward one prize. Therefore, though many, they are called one—the one who receives the prize. Rejoicing and applauding this one, I, David, I, the Psalmist, say:

### Verse 2

“You shall eat the labors of your hands”—or, as other manuscripts have it, “of your fruits”—“you are blessed.”

Whoever is weary of labor does not eat labors and cannot say: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:34). But the person to whom not only the fruit or reward of labor in hope, but labor itself in actuality, is pleasing, now eats the labors of his hands and hereafter will eternally eat the fruit of that labor.

In Hebrew it reads: “When you eat the labors of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall be well with you.” This is the same as saying: you are blessed in the present through delight in work and labor, and it shall be well with you in the future through the fruit of labor—especially if you labor and walk in the ways of righteousness and mercy. For to you who labor and perform works of righteousness,
### Verse 3

Your wife—that is, sensuality, subject to reason as a wife to her husband—shall be like a fruitful vine, abundantly producing wine that gladdens the heart of man, within the sides of your house: that is, among those who, trained by the two Testaments or by the two commandments of twin charity, are as it were the sides of your house. [Col. 0865A] The right side is holy contemplation; the left is action pertaining to the necessities of the present life. These are the two sides of your house: either those of thought and memory, which you inhabit without wandering abroad anywhere; or those of the congregation, in which you sing: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1).

Your wife is wisdom, of whom Solomon says: “Love wisdom, and she will embrace you” (Prov. 4:6). Again: “I loved her and sought her from my youth, and I sought to take her as my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty” (Wis. 8:2). This “your wife, like a fruitful vine,” will bear abundant clusters of righteousness.

Where the present text says, “A fruitful vine within the sides of your house,” the Hebrew reads: “In the inner rooms [Col. 0865B] of your house.” By this expression the hidden interior of the house, which does not appear outwardly, may be signified: such as a person’s mind and conscience, known to itself and to God alone. In these inner rooms the wife is like a fruitful vine when zeal for righteousness burns in the conscience itself, inflaming the heart like intoxicating wine.

But lest this righteousness should be cruel and unbearable without mercy, your children, like young olive shoots, shall produce the sweetest oil, to be poured with the wine of righteousness upon wounds, so that the severity of legal wine may be tempered by the oil of evangelical mercy. The young olive trees will bring you this oil; they produce fruits more abundant than old ones, fruits in which there is material for light and for many kinds of medicine. For by [Col. 0865C] the oil of charity and mercy joined to the wine of righteous zeal, the man wounded by robbers is healed.

Understand these children, likened to young olive trees, not as carnally begotten. Otherwise this letter kills, if it generates a carnal sense from the names “wife” and “children”; for under such a sense virgins and continent persons are excluded from this blessing, since they do not happen to have sons or daughters. But the Spirit, or spiritual understanding, gives life. It assigns these children not only to married men or wives, but rather to virgins and continent persons, and even to worthy penitents. They are conceived and brought forth either by sensuality, subject to reason as to a husband, or multiplied within the human spirit by the eternal wisdom of God, joined to it as a bride, according to that blessing spoken to the first parents before sin: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1:28).

Thus spiritual children abound for one who fears the Lord, whether in many persons or in the many charismatic gifts of a single person, when they so occupy every place around the table that there is no place or access open to alien children. And what is this table, if not that from which the body and blood of the Lord are received? Around it there ought first to stand good and suitable ministers, resembling young olive trees: namely, pure and merciful men, desiring not earthly but heavenly gain, and having their hearts set above. For just as the liquid of the olive, when mixed with other liquids, rises upward—so that, if one drop of oil were at the bottom of the sea, it would not rest until it reached the surface—so [Col. 0866A] ought such children, resembling young olive trees, to be around your table, O man who fears God: whether you are understood as Christ himself, whom the Spirit of the fear of the Lord filled, or as a righteous and God-fearing Christian.

In every person who sits and humbly approaches this table, this promise concerning children is fulfilled. For when the Lord’s food has been received, chaste and pure movements of heavenly desire, tending from the depths to the heights, are generated and multiplied in the bridal chamber of that person’s heart; and they cry even from the depths of this world and fly toward heaven.

Moreover, in the universal Church this circuit around the Lord’s table is extended in the likeness of the camps of the Lord. These were so arranged around the sanctuary, which contained within itself the ark [Col. 0866B] holding the manna, that ministers of the Levitical order kept watch nearby around it, while the twelve tribes encamped in a wider circuit around the sanctuary. Likewise, around the sanctuary which now contains the true manna, the Church is arranged: the Lord’s ministers keep watch between porch and altar, set apart from secular persons; and the secular persons themselves, remaining as it were in the surrounding circuit and assisting the ministers of the altar according to their means with arms and alms, represent a Church rightly called “terrible as an army set in array” (Song 6:3), united in holy fear of the Lord and expanded in a broad circuit after the likeness of the camps coming forth “when Israel came out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people” [Col. 0866C] (Ps. 113:1).

In the same way, those who eat the bread of angels in the wilderness of this world now come forth and are separated from a barbarous people through the fear of the Lord. Blessed are all who fear the Lord and, in fear, walk in his ways as though upon two feet: by abstaining from sins, which is the right foot; and by repenting of sins that have occurred, which is the left foot, no less necessary than the right to one who fears the Lord. So great is the power of this holy fear of the Lord, enduring for ever and ever, commended in this ninth Song of Ascents: it brings the lost sheep back upward as far as the folds of the ninety-nine sheep, completing in it and through it the number one hundred, which signifies perfection.

[Col. 0866D] **Verse 4.** “Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord.”

Lest you who read and sing these things should suppose that the foregoing words promise temporal goods, common to good and evil alike, to one who fears the Lord, I tell you: behold, thus shall the man who fears the Lord be blessed, as the following words declare.

**Verse 5.** “May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life.”

Zion and Jerusalem are names of that city which is above, which is our mother. From that Zion, from the Lord who dwells in Zion, may such blessings come to you who fear the Lord himself, that you may be joined to that same Zion and may see the ineffable good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life—that is, eternally.

**Verse 6.** “And may you see your children’s children”: that is, [Col. 0867A] the fruits of your works; or “your children’s children,” that is, those who are successively begotten through your teaching into adoption as sons of God and as your own sons: God’s sons, as of the most high Father, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named; your sons, as those nourished by you with paternal discipline or maternal gentleness.

And, that I may include every good and desirable thing in a brief expression: “May you see peace upon Israel.” May you see Christ, who is true peace, making the two one [Col. 0868A] and dissolving in his flesh the enmity between God and man. May you see him, and rejoice when you have seen him, as the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord; as the angels rejoice, desiring to look into him; and as true Israel rejoices—the man who sees God and says: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved. And I said to myself: You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name” (Gen. 32:30).

## Psalm 128

[Col. 0867]

[Col. 0867B] **Verses 1–2.** “They have often assailed me from my youth,” etc.

In this Song of Ascents, voices are heard not of one fighting timidly, but of one courageously rejoicing as though already a victor, the battle having been completed. “They have often assailed me from my youth,” he says; “let Israel now say: They have often assailed me from my youth, yet they could not prevail against me.”

Certainly it belongs to a victorious conscience to say, “Yet they could not prevail against me”—understand: prevail while standing openly opposed. That Israel, then, for whom in the preceding ascent a blessing was stored up, ending with “peace upon Israel”—that Israel, I say, remembering past conflicts, should speak both in his own voice and that of the whole Church, giving thanks for victory: “The followers of Edom, Israel’s brother, have often assailed me Israel”—that is, earthly and blood-related men. I, Israel, supplanted them in the womb [Col. 0867C] of the Church and, by the counsel of Mother Grace, took beforehand the blessing described in the preceding ascent.

“They have often assailed me from my youth,” so that, while they attacked, patience and endurance might increase either in me Israel or in me, the whole Church. They often assailed me, beginning with the blood of righteous Abel, slain in the field, down to the blood of Zechariah, whom they killed between temple and altar, so that all righteous blood shed openly or secretly might come upon them.

When I say, “I, Israel,” or “I, the Church, have been assailed,” I say it according to their view, not mine; for though they attacked, they did not conquer. “Yet they could not prevail against me”—that is, prevail while standing face to face. Therefore they laid snares behind my back.

[Col. 0867D] **Verse 3.** “Sinners built upon my back,” slandering and making false accusations, as though in secret. I say “upon my back” because many among them were greater than I and higher in this world; exalted above me, the sinners built upon my back. And, doing this after the fashion of a smith lengthening a short piece of iron upon an anvil, they lengthened iniquity for themselves—not in a way that would harm me, but to be imputed to their wickedness, not my endurance—yet not to be prolonged beyond measure, as they suppose.

For:

**Verse 4.** “The righteous Lord will cut down the necks of sinners.”

I do not say their hands, with which they work evil, nor their feet, with which they run to devise evil; [Col. 0868B] but their stiff necks, which in pride they raise high against the Lord. The Lord himself will cut these down, humbling them either for medicinal repentance or certainly for infernal punishment. The one I ask for; the other I prophesy, saying:

**Verse 5.** “May all who hate Zion be confounded and turned backward.”

May they be confounded with a saving confusion, which brings glory, when one is confounded through repentance and piously confesses sins, of which he is ashamed when they are brought into the light, according to the saying: “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11:43). May they also be turned backward, ready to follow the truth to which they were formerly opposed.

But if this prayer which I have poured out for them cannot be heard, because, after receiving knowledge of the truth, they sin deliberately and “there no longer remains a sacrifice [Col. 0868C] for sins” (Heb. 10:26), as the Apostle affirms, then at least may this prophecy quickly be fulfilled, by which I do not ask but pronounce concerning them: “May they be confounded,” so that they fall into everlasting reproach. Let them be confounded, and let me not be confounded; let them tremble, and let me not tremble. Let them also be turned backward, falling backward after the example of those who came to seize Jesus. Of them it is written that, when Jesus said, “I am he,” “they went backward and fell to the ground” (John 18:6). Surely, their faces, struck by the lightning of the Word, went backward; and thus, going away and not seeing where to place their feet, they fell backward.

Thus, thus, when the light of truth has been revealed, may all the enemies of Zion go away and be turned backward; may they fall into a dark land [Col. 0868D] covered by the gloom of death—both those who openly attack Zion and those who, though called friends, secretly hate Zion, namely the holy Church.

Meanwhile, while they live in the flesh, let them be wholly weak: not sturdy as trees, but fragile as

**Verse 6.** “Grass”—not grass of any kind, but grass upon housetops, which withers before it is plucked, since it has no roots fixed in the earth but stands on the summit without inward moisture. So too, let these men who stand at the summit of secular or even spiritual eminence appear dry as they are before they are plucked up by the judgment of death or deposition, [Col. 0869A] lest, while they flourish too greatly, the feet of the weak should again be shaken, as formerly: “My feet were almost moved; my steps had nearly slipped, because I was envious at sinners when I saw the peace of sinners; for there is no regard for their death, and their affliction is steadfast. Therefore pride possessed them” (Ps. 72:2 ff.). They stand high above the roofs, not like those to whom it was said, “What you have heard in rooms, preach upon the housetops” (Matt. 10:27), but like the grass of housetops, near to destruction and withering.

**Verse 7.** “Of which he who reaps shall not fill his hand, nor he who gathers sheaves his bosom.”

For the reapers are angels, who will gather wheat into the Lord’s barns and bind tares into bundles to be burned with fire. [Col. 0869B] They will not gather these men, likened to grass on housetops, either into hand or bosom, because in them [Col. 0870A] they will find no fruit either of action, signified by the hand, or of contemplation, signified by the bosom.

**Verse 8.** Moreover, they did not make as friends for themselves, by the mammon of iniquity, those who passed by as guests and pilgrims, having no abiding city here but seeking the one to come. As these passed by, they did not say to them, “The blessing of the Lord be upon you”; nor did they say, “We have blessed you”—which they certainly said to those living well, adding, “In the name of the Lord.” They did not say, “We have blessed you in our own name,” lest an occasion be given them to trust in a human being; for “cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jer. 17:4). Rather they said: “We have blessed you in the name of the Lord,” because “blessed [Col. 0870B] is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence” (ibid., 7).

## Psalm 129

[Col. 0869]

[Col. 0869B] **Verse 1.** “Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord; Lord, hear my voice,” etc.

In this eleventh ascent, the climber of these steps, although he had seemingly, as one already perfected, reached the tenth step—by which fulfillment of the law is signified because of the Decalogue—[Col. 0869C] nevertheless, seeing that much still lacked for him for the completion of the virtues, after whose completion and after passing through fifteen steps one enters the temple, vigorously humbles himself, saying:

“Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord.” Again: “If you should mark iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who shall endure?” Understand: no human being born of woman, if judged with mercy removed.

This penitential psalm is placed in the eleventh ascent, a number signifying transgression of the Decalogue, just as the same transgression of the law was prefigured by the eleven goat-hair curtains of the tabernacle; it must be covered by penitential endeavors as by curtains of goat hair. For we are plunged in the depths like another Jonah so long as we are held in mortal flesh, always drawing us toward low and deep things, because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15).

From many such depths I cried to you, O Lord, as though from the belly of the whale, where “your waves passed over me, and the sea covered my head, and I said: Perhaps I shall see your holy temple?” (Jonah 2:4–6). Shall I perhaps pass beyond all fifteen steps and come to your holy temple? Thus I cried to you from the depths, O Lord, yet I do not seem to have been heard. Therefore I say:

**Verse 2.** “O Lord, Lord, hear my voice.”

O Lord Creator, who powerfully rules your creature, because it cannot exist except as you will; O Lord Redeemer, who mercifully rule those redeemed by you, because [Col. 0870B] you permit none of those whom you foreknew would be redeemed and saved by you through faith and works—or by faith alone, as little children unable to work—to perish: your creative power ruling over all things, and your redeeming and saving mercy over the elect alone. You, O Lord, hear my voice by the power of your might reigning everywhere; and let the ears of your mercy attend to the voice of my supplication, that I may be delivered from the depths that are my iniquities. Looking upon their turbulent and foaming storms, I am terrified; and, terrified, I cry:

[Col. 0870C] **Verse 3.** “If you should mark iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who shall endure?”

Who shall endure you when you judge sins strictly, when scarcely can a human being endure other people’s sins even by overlooking them, because repentance—necessary even to holy persons—must intervene? If it is worthy, it will also be fruitful. From this it follows:

**Verses 4–5.** “For with you there is propitiation”: namely, Christ, sacrificed upon the cross and thereby made propitiation for our sins. After the humility of death, he himself was crowned with glory and honor before you in highest glory, where he also intercedes for us, to be heard because of his reverence—provided, however, that we remain under his law. Speaking of it, the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2).

While I was still oppressed by the law of Moses, I awaited this law, better than Moses’ law; and because of this your law, I endured you, O Lord. Dead myself and weighed down by your staff, I awaited you, the true Elisha, until you came and adapted yourself, living, indeed Life itself, to me who was dead, and to me who was little; and bestowed life. The prophets foretold that this would be so in the word of the Lord; and in this word of the Lord I endured and awaited the fulfillment of the word, [Col. 0871A] which cannot be falsified concerning the promise of the resurrection, since the Word himself, visibly appearing in the flesh, said of himself: “I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me shall not die for ever” (John 11:25). Again: “And I will raise him up on the last day” (John 15:44 [OCR; presumably 6:44]).

When this word was heard and believed, certain hope was added—indeed, succeeded—to faith. By it my soul hoped in the word of the Lord itself, or indeed in the Lord himself, who now raises souls from the death of sin by justifying faith and hereafter raises also the body through his Spirit dwelling in us, we who are called and are his members. Therefore, made certain by the hope of the twofold resurrection, I call and urge every neighbor signified by the name Israel to the same hope, saying:

[Col. 0871B] **Verse 6.** “From the watch”—or, as some manuscripts have it, “from the morning watch”—“until night, let Israel hope in the Lord.” For he who in the morning, at the morning watch, rose from the tomb despite the soldiers’ morning guard, will likewise, when the day of this temporal existence has ended and night is at hand, when evening has come, summon workers from their tombs and render them their wage. Therefore, from the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord, taking confidence in his own resurrection from the fact that the resurrection of human flesh has already preceded in the Head.

[Col. 0872A] And lest this should come into doubt, as though a sinful human being could not thereby be assured of his own resurrection because a sinless man was born and died and rose: let the person troubled by such temptations consider Christ’s past resurrection and ours, which is to come through him.

**Verse 7.** “For with him is plentiful redemption,” by which he redeemed those sold under sin—he who was without sin.

**Verse 8.** And he not only redeemed by his blood, once shed upon the cross, but also daily, until the end of the age, will redeem those made to drink and be filled by that same blood, provided they drink from it in such a way that it is placed upon both doorposts and likewise upon the lintel of the house. By this sign [Col. 0872B] the houses of Israel are distinguished from the houses of the Egyptians: they are conformed in body and mind alike to Christ’s death. This is to place the blood of the Lamb upon both doorposts. It is placed also upon the lintel of the house when our forehead is guarded by the seal of his blood, so that we may not be ashamed to believe in one who died, whom we confess to have been raised from death. Therefore, just as he once redeemed carnal Israel from the power of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, so he will redeem spiritual Israel from all its iniquities.

## Psalm 130

[Col. 0871]

[Col. 0871C] **Verse 1.** “O Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up.”

In this twelfth ascent, the vigorous climber and singer, conscious of great virtue and great self-restraint, rejoices in thanksgiving, saying:

“O Lord, my heart has not been exalted,” etc. Truly, it belongs to a perfect person to have within the heart such and so great a testimony of humility preserved that he may say: “O Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up, nor have I walked in great things.” But what then? “If I did not think humbly,” etc.

Truly, it is a Song of Ascents to rise through humility, just as it is exceedingly lamentable to fall through pride; for humility’s ascent is a high step, while pride is a deep fall. Considering this, I David, penitent and psalm-singing David, give thanks for the grace of humility granted to me by you, O Lord my God, who resist the proud and give grace to the humble.

O Lord, it is your gift that my heart has not been exalted in secret, nor my eyes lifted up openly. My heart has not been exalted because, taught by God, I have learned to be meek and humble in heart inwardly within myself; nor have my eyes been lifted up outwardly, despising others who seemed less than I and whom I placed beneath myself. Nor have I walked in great things, making myself equal to them while I was small in my own eyes; [Col. 0872C] nor have I walked in wonders above me, because I did not seek miracles beyond myself, beyond my powers, by which I might become conspicuous and admirable among others, like Simon Magus. When he saw two things in the apostles, namely righteousness and power, he despised righteousness and sought power: “Give me this power,” he said, “that whoever I lay hands upon may receive the Holy Spirit” (Acts 8:19).

I did not thus walk in wonders, exalting myself above myself by desiring the power to perform miracles. Rather, I was content with righteousness, whose inseparable companion is humility. It teaches a person not to think high things but to agree with the humble. What I have said concerning my humility is so true that, conscious of this humility, I confidently utter as though a curse binding myself:

[Col. 0872D] **Verse 2.** “If I did not think humbly.”

Distinguishing myself from the gift that was within me, always mindful that I had nothing which I had not received, I knew and felt in my inmost heart that glory for what I received was owed not to me, as though I had any good thing from myself, but to the gratuitous Giver of every good thing. If, I say, I did not think so humbly, but exalted my soul either by arrogating to myself what I did not have; or by regarding what I had as from myself; or by supposing that I indeed received what I had from God but merited it by my own power; or by despising others because they did not have what I had—if by any of these four modes, in which every exaltation is committed, I exalted my soul after the first Song of Ascents, where I was healed from the swelling of pride by sharp arrows and desolating coals—if, I say, afterward I exalted my soul through any kind of wicked exaltation, then may retribution come upon my soul, or within my soul, so that my soul fails and languishes like a weaned child who is still so tender that he is upon his mother.

Finally, such a weaned infant, since he cannot yet take solid food, quickly languishes and comes near death—or dies altogether—unless, weaned before the proper time, he returns to his mother’s breasts. This sense can stand literally.

[Col. 0873B] Yet much greater is the curse by which I bind myself if I consider heretics, who, weaned and torn too soon from their mother’s breasts, failed and refused to rest upon their mother, the Church. They needed to be nourished as though by milk through simple faith: namely, by believing that the bread of angels was made man for us human beings. Thus little children are nourished as though by bread transformed into milk, believing the sacraments of the Lord’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, whence he will come to judge the living and the dead.

Little ones should be nourished with the milk of this faith. Yet those long nourished with milk who, when they can, refuse to advance to solid food—especially if they have been appointed and taught for a long time to do so—the Apostle rebukes in his Epistle to the Hebrews, saying: “For when, because of the time, you ought to be teachers, you again need someone to teach you what are the elementary principles of the words of God; and you have become such as have need of milk, not solid food. For everyone who partakes of milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness, for he is a little child” (Heb. 5:12–13).

And such people are rightly rebuked: though, because of a long time of teaching, they ought to be teachers, as it were adults, they nevertheless refuse to know wisdom and power in the things that are God’s foolishness and weakness. Instead, though still little and as though toothless, needing to be nursed upon their mother, the holy Church, they rush forward to investigate things unsearchable, wishing by reason to comprehend things incomprehensible. [Col. 0873D] They become heretics and therefore need to return to their mother’s breasts, where, like newborn rational infants without guile, they may desire milk, judging themselves to know nothing except Christ Jesus, and him crucified.

Although we confess that he was crucified through our weakness, nevertheless among the perfect we proclaim him to be the power of God and the wisdom of God. Those who have been weaned before their time do not grasp this, because [Col. 0874A] they are neither great in faith so as to believe nor great in understanding so as to comprehend. I shall become like them if I did not think humbly but exalted my soul through pride, which God resists.

Alternatively: I did indeed think humbly, not thinking high things but agreeing with the humble, and I was little in my own eyes. Yet lest, through excessive preservation of humility, the authority of governance should be impaired, I did not wish to humble myself excessively, but exalted my soul by rebuking the unruly and consoling the faint-hearted—being little indeed in malice, but great, against those whom I ought to correct or warn, in authority of mature understanding. This I did by the authority of Christ, who says: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone,” etc., as far as: “Let him be to you [Col. 0874B] as a Gentile and a publican” (Matt. 18:15).

Acting thus, I both thought humbly, because I did not despise sinners in the manner of Pharisees who glory in their own righteousness and scorn others, and nevertheless exalted my soul by correcting the vices of those who err and by not touching what is unclean: that is, by not consenting to the sins of others either through unjust silence or, worse still, through the deceitful tongue of flattery, renounced in the first Song of Ascents. There also I rejected evil silence among evil persons, because when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause.

If all this is not true—unless repentance has intervened or does intervene—I shall become like one weaned, so weak that necessity itself will compel me to return to my mother’s breasts. I rightly said, “unless repentance has intervened,” because in every curse contained in Scripture repentance must be understood. For example, “Cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jer. 17:4): understand, unless he repents. Again, “Cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments” (Ps. 118:21): understand, unless they repent.

Perhaps someone, hearing of the perfection of humility already described in me, David the king, and pressed by the consciousness of his own weakness, does not trust that he will ascend to this twelfth step, where the perfect song of perfect humility resounds. Against this I say:

[Col. 0874C] **Verse 3.** “Let Israel hope in the Lord from this time forth and for ever.”

Let him hope in the Lord, I say, not trust in his own powers—whoever, as Israel sleeping at Bethel, that is, resting in the Catholic Church, contemplates this ladder of fifteen steps. For the Lord leans upon that ladder, and Israel ought to hope in him, that he will assist by his power those striving to ascend. But let him hope not merely for an hour, but from this present moment even unto the age to come, where there will be no hope but the reality itself.

## Psalm 131

[Col. 0873]

[Col. 0873D] **Verses 1–5.** “Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness,” etc.

In this thirteenth Song of Ascents [Col. 0874D] it is shown to us how greatly, and why, David humbled himself when he said: “Remember, [Col. 0875A] O Lord, David and all his meekness,” and the rest, as far as: “Until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.”

That is, because he knew that Christ the Lord would be born from his seed, he desired also to know the place of his birth. For this reason he sat meek and humble; for this reason, keeping watch, he did not give sleep to his eyes nor slumber to his eyelids. For this reason, allowing no rest to his temples, he prayed continually; and his prayer was heard, as that of one meek and humble in heart. Therefore, as though suddenly astonished, he exclaims:

**Verse 6.** “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah”: namely, the Lord’s birth, whose place I sought. For this Ephrathah is Bethlehem. But thereafter it is found in the fields of the forest—that is, in the breadth of the universal Church drawn from the Gentiles, after the narrow confines of Judea have been left behind.

The Hebrew truth reads: “Behold, we heard of him in Ephrathah.” The sense is this: I, David, knowing beforehand that the Son of God would become man and would be born from my line, but still ignorant of the place in which he would be born, kept careful watch and labored in earnest prayer that the place of his birth might be revealed to me. And behold: we heard that he would be born in Ephrathah, namely Bethlehem. I prayed alone, but I did not hear alone, for while I was keeping watch and praying, it was heard not by me alone but by other prophets also—indeed by all the faithful whose ears of faith stood open—that the Son of God chose Ephrathah, otherwise called Bethlehem, for his birth.

There we first heard him, [Col. 0875C] namely the Lord, or it, namely the ark of his sanctification. For “God is known in Judah, and his dwelling is in Zion” (Ps. 75:2). But afterward we found him, the Lord, or it, the ark, in the fields of the forest: namely, in the breadth of the Gentiles. They are like forest fields, resembling land newly cleared and cultivated after forests have been uprooted; for, once the thickets of errors have been cut down and rooted out, they have now received God’s seed when he who sows his seed went forth.

For this sower was, as it were, inside when he preached within the narrow confines of Judea in the Hebrew language alone; but afterward he went out into the fields of the forest through his apostles, teaching the Gentiles in every language, so that there are no “languages or speeches whose voices are not heard.” For “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:4). We believers heard these words in the fields of the forest, and therefore, instructed by such hearing, we go forth to battle.

**Verse 7.** “We shall enter into his tabernacle,” first to serve as soldiers in his camps; and afterward, when the military service has been completed and the desired victory over visible and invisible enemies obtained, we shall not ascribe glory to ourselves as though the triumph had been achieved by our own power. Rather, giving thanks to him, we shall “worship at the place where his feet stood.”

In the first Adam God’s feet did not stand when he walked in Paradise, finding no place to stand in one who had been moved in temptation by the foot of pride and the hand of the sinner. But in the second [Col. 0876A] Adam, who was born in Ephrathah, his feet stood, because the foot of pride never came to him; nor could the hand of the sinner—tempting him in the wilderness and afterwards attacking him through the Jews—move him from his steadfastness.

Therefore in him the feet of the Lord stood firm: namely, the Word of God united to flesh, and his Spirit resting upon him. Since the Father is not said to have been sent, but the Son and Holy Spirit are said to have been sent by the Father—who, because he is from no one, could not be sent by anyone, but himself sent his Word to be incarnate, and afterward, through that Word incarnate and suffering, gave the Paraclete to the faithful—the two Persons whom the Father sent forth, namely the Word and the Holy Spirit, can rightly be understood as his feet. They were never moved in the man assumed into God. [Col. 0876B] Therefore in him, as in the most steadfast place, the Father, Word, and Spirit are to be worshipped.

Indeed, the human being himself is to be worshipped in God in such a way that, in the worship itself, he is in no way separated from God, because he is God—not as the many gods and many lords who are not to be worshipped, being adoptive gods and lords, but as the most high God. Though he was born in Ephrathah, he himself, the Most High, founded it; and consequently he is to be worshipped with the Most High Father in one indivisible worship, as the holy Fathers defined at the Synod of Ephesus, saying at the end of the council:

“If anyone dares to say that the assumed man must be co-worshipped with God the Word, and co-glorified and called God as one other alongside another—for the addition of one syllable, namely *co-*, compels this understanding—and does not rather worship Emmanuel with one reverence and render him one glorification, according as the Word became flesh, let him be anathema.”

It is therefore clear, according to the tenor of the aforesaid council, that God is to be worshipped not only in the man assumed into God; rather, the man himself, as God, is to be worshipped with the one and undivided worship with which no creature other than Christ is to be worshipped.

Therefore we shall rightly worship at the place where his feet stood, because that place of God—namely, the man assumed into God—is so holy that he is rightly worshipped by all the saints and reverently honoured with every cult due to the Godhead; for, as the Apostle affirms, he is not among all things but “God blessed above all” (Rom. [Col. 0876D] 9:5), and is endowed and glorified with the name which is above every name. We shall therefore worship in him, being incorporated into him through the sacrament of baptism and of the altar, and made his members. For outside his unity he cannot be worshipped by anyone placed outside his body—which is the Church—in any schism or heresy. For this reason he is to be worshipped not elsewhere but in his place, that is, in his body; and continual prayer is to be made for that body of his, partly already translated into its rest and partly still to be translated. That translation having begun, we pray continually that it may be wholly completed, saying:

**VERSE 8.** “Arise, O Lord, into thy rest, thou and the ark of thy sanctification.” Noah’s ark, long tossed by the waves in the flood, at last, when the flood had ceased, rested [Col. 0877A] upon the mountains of Armenia. Likewise the ark made through Moses was long moved from place to place in the movable tabernacle; and, after the tabernacle at Shiloh had been overthrown, it is even recorded to have been carried about among foreigners. Yet finally, after the handmade temple had been built at Jerusalem, the ark itself was brought there and rested.

All these things happened as figures, and did not provide everlasting rest, because you, Jesus Christ, greater than Noah, greater than Moses, and greater than Solomon, had not yet arisen into your rest—indeed, had not yet been born in Ephrathah. Therefore I, David, burning with a great desire for that rest to which no disturbance of unrest would succeed—as a great disturbance came to pass when Jerusalem was devastated and the Temple burned, and the ark of God was hidden by Jeremiah in a secret place, there to remain concealed for seventy [Col. 0877B] years—longed for your coming, which I had heard would begin in Ephrathah and spread into the fields of the forest.

But because your birth would have profited us nothing unless your death and resurrection had profited us by redeeming us, I also longed for your resurrection, continually saying: “Arise, O Lord, into thy rest, thou and the ark of thy sanctification.” That is, the holy Church, already partly gathered in Abraham’s bosom, rested there in part; but there was not full rest in the infernal regions, outside Paradise, which had been closed by the first man’s sin but was to be opened by your death and resurrection. Thus there was an unceasing cry in the hearts of the ancient fathers, who, in continual longing, cried aloud and said: “Arise, O Lord, into thy rest, thou and [Col. 0877C] the ark of thy sanctification.”

Arise from the dead, and enter into God’s rest: you, the true Noah, wearied by the flood of the Passion, but after your resurrection never again to be wearied, because death shall no longer have dominion over you. Arise and enter into God’s rest, because he saw you righteous before him among all nations. You slept amid turmoil; therefore arise, never again to be troubled. You slept; and while sleeping upon the cross, you were mocked by your son, the Jewish people, as though by impious Ham—as though, being naked, you lacked the adornment of divinity inherent in you. Yet although dying and dead, you did not cease to be God, because there “thy strength is hidden,” not destroyed (Hab. 3:4). Therefore arise, and show your strength to your enemies and friends alike, so that your enemies, made as dead men, may cease [Col. 0877D] to insult you, while your friends rejoice at seeing you as Lord, seeing your dominion by which you rule in the midst of your enemies.

Arise to curse the posterity of the son who mocked you as Father, and to bless the children who honour you and celebrate the memorial of your death beneath the veil of venerable sacraments, as you yourself said: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19).

Thus arise into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification, lest the stormy flood further assail either you or your ark, namely the holy Church; its waters entered even unto your soul, and unto the souls of all who faithfully sing and say: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even unto my soul” (Ps. [Col. 0878A] 68:2), and the rest to the end of the psalm. Your ark has been greatly shaken by these waters of temptations and tribulations; and now, amid all things, it seeks rest, continually saying to you: “Arise, O Lord, into thy rest, thou and the ark of thy sanctification.”

For although you arose once and entered into your rest with many saints delivered from hell, yet you still sleep, as it were, in relation to your Church or to any faithful soul, when you permit it to be shaken by excessive storms of temptation. To calm storms of this kind, O Lord, arise often; command the winds and the sea, that there may be a great calm in which you and your ark may rest—that is, the holy Church or any faithful soul.

Once you were roused as the Lord sleeping, as a mighty man made drowsy by [Col. 0878B] wine, and struck your enemies upon their backs, because they had placed the ark of your sanctification in the temple of Dagon. You did not cease to work your wonders around that ark of yours until it was brought into your rest, being set in his holy temple, where lawful priests might minister, holy men altogether distinct from the priests of Dagon.

Now therefore arise as one mighty, and strike your enemies, the worshippers of Dagon or Mammon, delivering from them the ark of sanctification, namely your body, which they treat unworthily. Do not cease to work your wonders against them until, when they have been humbled to everlasting reproach, lawful priests may freely minister in the churches built and consecrated to you, especially [Col. 0878C] in episcopal churches constructed for this purpose: that the ark of your sanctification may rest in them, with an abundance of worthy ministers to whom the consecration of the Lord’s blood may be entrusted. For such ministers we too now pray continually, saying:

**VERSE 9.** “Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness, and let thy saints rejoice.” Let Dagon’s priests, who do not rightly handle your ark by turning the sacrament of your body to their own gain, be clothed with penitential confusion—which is what we pray for—or indeed with punitive confusion, which we grant by assenting to divine justice. But let your priests, who minister to you, seeking your glory rather than their own, serving you rather than Mammon, be clothed with righteousness: namely, that righteousness which is from faith and justifies the ungodly, so that the righteous person may live by faith.

And [Col. 0878D] because dead faith does not give life, let the faith of your priests so live, so flourish, so thrive in the root of charity, that it may never fail, as prayer was made for Peter that his faith might not fail. Since it did not fail, he remained in the priesthood even after the sin of his threefold denial, which he wiped away with tears and a threefold confession. Hence he was clothed with righteousness, and rejoices among the saints—indeed, even before the holy apostles who had not denied him at all.

Thus, thus, O Lord who wast born in Ephrathah: let thy priests, especially the successors of Peter, prince of the apostles, in the apostolic see, be clothed with righteousness; and let thy saints, established under such rulers, rejoice with that rejoicing of which it is said: “Let the righteous rejoice before God, and delight in gladness” (Ps. 67:4). Again: “Rejoice [Col. 0879A] in the Lord, O righteous; praise befits the upright” (Ps. 32:1). Again: “Let the daughters of Zion rejoice in their King” (Ps. 149:2). Again: “The praises of God [shall be] in their throat, or in their mouths” (ibid., 6). Again: “Let Mount Zion be glad, and let the daughters of Judah rejoice” (Ps. 47:12). Thus let thy saints rejoice now and for ever. And lest their rejoicing ever be disturbed, but may be perpetuated eternally:

**VERSE 10.** “For David thy servant’s sake, turn not away the face of thy Christ, O God the Father.” Turn not away the face of thy Christ from the nations believing in thee, as thou didst turn it away from the unbelieving Jews. Or, because Israel limps, believing in part and not believing in part: the face of thy Christ, which thou hast turned away from unbelieving Israel, do not at least turn away from the remnant of Israel, among whom the Apostle Paul [Col. 0879B] counts himself, because last of all the face of thy Christ was seen by him as by one untimely born.

For those who, as soon as they heard his voice, left all things and followed him when he called—for example, Peter and Andrew and their like—are more rightly called firstfruits than remnant. There is also a remnant of Israel like them, of whom it was said to Elijah: “I have left for myself seven thousand men in Israel who have not bowed the knee before Baal” (Rom. 11:4). Thus, in this time also, as the Apostle affirms, a remnant of Israel is saved. For though children of the flesh, who are not counted as seed, may be lacking—for “not all who are of Israel are Israelites” (Rom. 9:6), as the Apostle says—yet the word of promise is not made void, [Col. 0879C] because children of faith are received in place of children of flesh, and branches of the wild olive are grafted into the olive tree. Thus the word of promise, confirmed by oath, is fulfilled, so that through two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God, who promises and swears, to lie, we who believe in him who promises and swears may have the strongest consolation—for we ought without doubt to believe him.

**VERSE 11.** “For he swore truth to David, and he will not disappoint him.” He swore, and he will not repent of it (Ps. 109:4), because he will not change the counsel of his oath, even though he changes his work. His oath, therefore, shall stand firm: he who swore said first to Abraham, “By myself have I sworn, because thou hast done this thing and hast not spared thine only-begotten son for my sake: blessing I will bless thee, and I will multiply thy seed; and in thy seed [Col. 0879D] all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:16).

In this promise made to Abraham, the Saviour of the world was promised, to be a true man, because he was to be born of a human being according to the flesh—indeed, also according to the faith by which Abraham believed God’s promise that a son would be born to him, contrary to nature, from his barren and aged wife. For this faith, by which he believed what was above or contrary to nature, was reckoned to him for righteousness. “He believed God, and this was reckoned to him for righteousness” (Rom. 4:3).

Moreover, the word of promise confirmed by God’s oath was enlarged in David. He who was promised to Abraham as a man to come is promised to King David as a king to come and to succeed him upon the throne of his kingdom, when it is said to him: “Of the fruit of thy womb will I set upon thy throne.” I do not say: Of the [Col. 0880A] fruit of thy loins, but of the fruit of thy womb, because in his conception a man will not act; rather, as I, God the Father, act, a virgin’s womb shall be made fruitful, so that what is born of the virgin shall be called and shall be the Son of God and the Son of Man: of God as Father and of a human being as mother. Since she, O David, will be born from your stock, her womb shall be reckoned as your womb. Therefore I, God the Father, say to you, David, father of one and the same Son: “Of the fruit of thy womb will I set upon thy throne.”

Upon the royal throne, so that he may reign—not as you reign, whose kingdom shall end, but as the eternal King, “of whose kingdom there shall be no end,” because “he shall reign in the house of Jacob for ever” (Luke 1:32); in that house you, David, retain a temporal kingdom. Yet he alone shall not reign: your other children also, regenerated through the only-begotten Son of Sarah, the free mother who is above, and consequently counted among your children as children not of flesh but of your faith, shall sit upon [Col. 0880B] your throne. That is, they shall reign in the eternal kingdom prefigured by your temporal kingdom. They shall sit, I say, and reign—your children—

**VERSE 12.** “If, however, thy children themselves keep my covenant,” written in the blood of my only-begotten Son, which your children themselves shall receive in baptism, renouncing the devil and all his works. To this covenant shall be added my other testimonies: not those fabricated in Pharisaic traditions, but those which I myself shall teach them, giving the Spirit of truth who shall lead your children into all truth. If they keep these, they shall sit upon your throne [Col. 0880C] and reign: first, those to whom it shall be said, “Ye shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28); and again: “Ye are they who have continued with me in my temptations; and I appoint unto you, as my Father appointed unto me, a kingdom, that ye may sit at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22:28).

Those to whom this is said by the King of kings shall be the first to reign after him. Their children, succeeding them unto ages of ages and keeping my covenant and my testimonies, which I shall teach them, shall in their own degree or measure be kings or lesser kings, sitting upon your throne as has been said. Kings and lesser kings, destined to reign with the King of kings, are distinguished in this: some possess great [Col. 0880D] faith, like the kings who, seeking the King of the Jews, offered mystical gifts—gold as to a great King, frankincense as to the true God, myrrh for his burial, in which his flesh, embalmed with myrrh and aloes, was not to see the corruption of decay. This great faith made great kings.

But the royal official to whom it was said, “Unless ye see wonders and signs, ye will not believe” (John 4:48), bore the image of those who, because of little faith, shall reign beneath great kings such as the apostles were, just as angels reign beneath archangels. This will not arise from their preceding merit but from a gratuitous gift:

**VERSES 13–14.** “For by grace alone the Lord chose Zion; he chose her as a dwelling for himself”—that is, the holy [Col. 0881A] Church—thus saying and establishing most firmly: “This is my rest for ever and ever; here will I dwell, because I have chosen her.” He chose her first in the apostles, to whom my Son himself said: “Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, that ye should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15:16); and finally in their fruit, which shall remain until the end of the age. Therefore it was said: “Behold, I am with you unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). By this saying it is signified that until the consummation of the age there shall remain in the world such persons in whom, and with whom, God remains, governing and consoling his Church betrothed to his Son. To her God the Father still promises, saying:

**VERSE 15.** “Blessing, I will bless her widow.” [Col. 0881B] The Church herself, or any faithful person, is a bride through love and a widow through sorrow.
