For while the bridegroom is present and shows her his face, she loves him and rejoices, nor can she grieve or mourn while the bridegroom is with her, visibly manifest through signs and benefits of his presence, sustaining her with his left hand and embracing her with his right—while he raises her up through bodily aids and adorns her with spiritual gifts.

But when the bridegroom is taken from her, and neither consoler nor helper appears to her amid tribulations and various temptations, then she does not rejoice as a bride over her bridegroom whom she does not see. Rather, “as a widow, weeping she shall weep in the night, and her tears are upon her cheeks, because there is none to console her” (Lam. 1:2); indeed, she does not wish to be consoled, like that Rachel of whom it is written: [Col. 0881C] “and she would not be comforted” (Matt. 2:18). Hence she says within herself: “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. 76:3), because nothing in this world can make her glad while her beloved is absent—or rather, while he is present but hides his face from her. Since she mourns him as though dead, she is rightly called a desolate widow, that is, one deprived, as it were, of marital consolation.

But to this widow the bridegroom’s Father promises his consolation, saying: “Blessing, I will bless her widow,” as Anna the widow, intent upon fasts and prayers. I, God the Father, shall turn those prayers into blessings by showing her my Son, presented in the Temple in virgin arms, so that she may rejoice with aged Simeon as he says: “Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, [Col. 0881D] according to thy word in peace, because mine eyes have seen thy salvation, which thou hast prepared before the face of all peoples” (Luke 2:29–30).

In this manifestation of my salvation I shall satisfy the poor of that same salvation with bread. Because they hunger and thirst for righteousness, they shall be satisfied with five barley loaves or seven wheaten loaves, feasting upon the understanding of the old or the new law with my salvation, my Son. But that these loaves may rightly be distributed to those who feast with my Son, I, the Father—

**VERSE 16.** “Will clothe her priests with salvation,” so that, baptized into Christ and clothed with Christ himself, they may be honourable and worthy ministers for distributing the loaves with which I shall satisfy the poor—the humble who hunger, [Col. 0882A] not the rich abounding in their pride, who disdain my loaves and therefore shall be sent away empty, according to that saying: “He hath filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he hath sent empty away” (Luke 1:53). And the saints of that same Son of mine shall rejoice with rejoicing—that is, they shall rejoice exceedingly—as elsewhere it is said: “The saints shall rejoice in glory; they shall be glad in their resting places” (Ps. 149:5). Nor is it surprising that they shall rejoice in Zion, which I chose as my dwelling, as was said above: “Here will I dwell, because I have chosen her.” Therefore with good cause the saints shall rejoice there with rejoicing, because:

**VERSE 17.** “There will I bring forth the horn of David,” the strong and desired Son of mine. His horn and strength are his very divinity, higher than the weakness of his flesh, just as a horn, though it is in the flesh, is higher than flesh. Yet [Col. 0882B] his flesh itself, baked hard by the fire of the Passion like a potsherd, possesses no less strength than the power of divinity itself, because the divinity of the Word is the strength of the flesh united to it.

Thus, as the boy David, anointed from a visible horn with visible oil, was strengthened by God so that he could break the mouths of lions and shatter the limbs of bears, so the Son of Man was strengthened, anointed with the oil of divinity and fortified with the horn of divine power. Hence Zechariah says: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he hath visited and wrought redemption for his people, and hath raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant” (Luke 1:66).

His enemies did not see this strength in weak flesh, where his very strength is hidden. To refute and confound them, I, God the Father, prepared a lamp for my Christ, anointed with the Spirit of strength. For John the Baptist, whom I sent before him to prepare his way and a perfect people for him, “was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35): burning with love, as the bridegroom’s friend; shining in word, as the bridegroom’s herald, testifying that he had come from heaven and was above all, and that the Spirit had not been given to him in measure. As a sign of this, John saw the dove upon him; and on seeing it he was assured concerning him that this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit. By such testimony concerning my Christ:

**VERSE 18.** “I will clothe his enemies with confusion,” so that, confounded [Col. 0882D] by their falsehood in resisting the truth, they may not dare deny that Christ is the Son of God—he to whom the Father spoke from heaven, with John hearing, and said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

Thus the enemies of Christ, my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased, shall be clothed with confusion; but upon him my sanctification shall flourish. The sanctification of divinity by which he himself is holy and sanctifies others so perfectly that it not only thrives in the root of the heart but also flowers in the branches of works; or, to speak more expressly, my sanctification shall *effloresce*, that is, shall visibly flower, with the unfading flower of holiness. Such a flower could not bloom in a human being who was not God, because human “glory [is] like a flower of hay, which today is and tomorrow is cast into the oven” [Col. 0883A] (Isa. 4:6 [apparently an erroneous reference]). But through assumption of flesh the Word of the Lord became the flower of the field and remains for ever [Col. 0884A] ever flowering; and his flowers shall bear fruits that remain now and for ever.

## PSALM 132

[Col. 0883]

[Col. 0883A] **VERSES 1–2.** “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity,” etc. In this fourteenth step there is a good and pleasant glorying in strength, good and pleasant, that is, like the ointment upon the head which runs down upon Aaron’s beard. For although God’s servants remember all the meekness of David, and are themselves meek and humble in themselves, nevertheless they know themselves in God to be Aaron’s beard—that is, strong and manly men who have received from Christ their head the anointing of the Holy Spirit. Being anointed with it, they delight in frequently singing this Song of Ascents:

“Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.” This verse, known throughout the world as the trumpet of the Holy Spirit, has gathered together those who were divided, given birth to monasteries, and made many to be one heart and one soul. Having tasted the sweetness of this unity, they say: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.”

“Behold” is the voice of one pointing, because that good which brethren dwelling in unity taste is seen more fully in its manifestation than [Col. 0883C] the tongue can explain. Something may be good but not pleasant, as martyrdom is. Again, something may be pleasant but not good, as drunkenness with wine, in which is debauchery; it is not good. But for brethren to dwell in unity, I do not say merely that it is good and pleasant, but *how* good and *how* pleasant—that is, so good and pleasant that words cannot explain how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell in unity, with different offices rightly ordered among different persons as among the various members of one body.

For just as in one body all members, though they do not have the same function, nevertheless labour together toward one end in the one body—the eye by seeing, the ear by hearing, the tongue by speaking, and the other [Col. 0883D] members by performing what belongs to them, each not for itself alone but for the whole body—so the eye sees for the whole body, the ear hears for the whole, and likewise the other members are useful not only to themselves but to the whole body.

How good and how pleasant this is cannot be explained; but it can be shown somewhat by its opposite, if we consider how evil and bitter it is for brethren to be at discord, especially where both parties in the conflict tend toward evil. Thus Romulus and Remus, founders of the city of Rome, both evil men tending toward evil, extended dominion against one another until one killed the other and would not suffer him to rule with him. Why should I mention the brotherly battle-lines and rival kingdoms fought for with profane hatreds among peoples ignorant of God? The first two brothers, both knowing God and both offering gifts to God, experienced in themselves and showed to their descendants how evil and bitter is the poison of discord: one, hating the other out of envy, killed him. The blood of the slain brother also cried [Col. 0884A] to God against his brother, not asking pardon but vengeance, because the ointment had not yet been poured out upon the head. Anointed with it now, the members pray for enemies to be converted and saved, following the example of the head himself praying on the cross for his enemies: “Father,” he says, “forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).

By this saying we are taught especially to pray for those enemies whom ignorance renders in some degree excusable, since they do not know how to weigh the magnitude of the sin they commit—above all those who sow discord among brethren. God’s soul especially abhors this evil, as Solomon says: “There are six things which God hates, and a seventh his soul detests: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands shedding innocent [Col. 0884C] blood, a heart devising wicked thoughts, feet swift to run to evil, a false witness, and one who sows discord among brethren” (Prov. 6:16 ff.).

Such a sower of discord, if he is in a community of brethren dwelling in unity, is in it like a restless beast in a yoke: it does not draw the cart, but disturbs the beasts drawing it and causes the cart to be wrecked, unless it is either tamed or entirely left behind, according to what is written: “One shall be taken, and the other left” (Matt. 24:40). That is, the lover and preserver of brotherly concord shall be taken; the sower of discord shall be left, who, though he may appear to dwell in unity bodily, nevertheless always seeks quarrels in his heart.

But with evildoers of this kind far removed from this fourteenth step, let us, placed on that same step, sing: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell in unity.” For since this step is the next to last, it may fittingly be applied to these next-to-last times of the Church, when that final step is believed already near—the step in which the elect, exalted through God’s judgment, shall sing: “Behold, now bless the Lord, all ye servants of the Lord.” But now, on this penultimate step before judgment, let this Song of Ascents be sung by us as we dwell together in unity.

How? As in the beginning of the Church’s birth, when the ointment of the Holy Spirit, poured upon the head, flowed down thence first upon the beard adjoining the head and then upon the hem of the garment. I mean the upper hem nearest the head, through which the head is normally put in. Thus [Col. 0885A] at last the Paraclete descended from Christ into the apostles, who are rightly likened to the beard of Aaron’s head, since they acted manfully and adhered to the head of Aaron himself, namely Christ, whose head is God: “for the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3). Through them it descended, as it were, upon the hem of the garment: the primitive Church, of which it is written, “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

The same ointment descended not as rain upon the fleece, or as dew gathered entirely into one upon the fleece of flesh assumed from the Virgin while the rest of the earth remained dry, as happened in Gideon’s sign. Rather, after the fleece had been pressed by the winepress of the cross, it descended thus:

[Col. 0885B] **VERSE 3.** “As dew on Hermon, which is a pasture mountain, as [upon] Mount Zion.” For the dew of the Holy Spirit, which first descended upon Mount Zion, sanctifying the Church gathered from Judaea, signified by Mount Zion, afterwards became dew upon Hermon, which lies outside Judaea. Hermon signifies the Gentile nations, not only as foreigners alien to the Jews by geographical location, but also by its name: Hermon is interpreted “anathema,” because the Gentile world, through idolatry and other enormous sins, had been as though anathematized and separated from God.

But when the dew which first descended upon Mount Zion, filling the apostles, descends upon Hermon—that is, upon the fullness of the Gentiles—unto the hem of the garment, which is the universal Church, then, just as the upper hem of that garment near [Col. 0885C] the head and beard was anointed, so its furthest hem is anointed. Thus the end of the Church is made like its beginning through multiplied monastic communities formed by the apostolic rule. In them it shall be good and pleasant for brethren to dwell in unity, as it was pleasant for the apostles and their disciples to dwell together in the beginning.

This, assuredly, is fittingly desired whenever it is sung in God’s Church, especially at the end of this canticle: “Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. As it was in the beginning,” namely at the birth of the Church, “is now and ever shall be, world without end”—even to the hem of the garment, by which the same garment is to be completed and by which it was begun at the beginning. Thus its two hems, the first and the last, agree with one another, as we read that Aaron the high priest’s garment was fittingly adorned both at its end and at its beginning (Exod. 28).

For at the top, around the hem adjoining the head, it had the breastplate and likewise the ephod, joined with golden chains and interwoven with gold. At the bottom, near the feet, at the end of the blue tunic, golden bells and pomegranates adorned the same garment on its lower hem. By this the Holy Spirit signified that in the last times, as also in the first, God’s Church would not lack suitable ornaments, such as may fittingly be understood in the golden bells and pomegranates placed on the outermost hem of the pontifical garment.

Indeed, at the beginning of the Church’s birth, the apostles and other teachers, speaking the mighty works of God and persevering in prayers and praises of God, were like golden bells sounding sweetly. Were not their hearers, men and women alike, who with the Blessed Mary kept their words, like chosen seeds—like pomegranates? Hence the primitive Church is told in the Song of Songs: “Like a piece of pomegranate are thy cheeks, apart from that which is hidden within” (Song 4:3). Do you think that the same does not fittingly apply to chaste and modest persons set among holy teachers, as among bells, as it were at the lower part near the feet of the tunic, now in the final times of the Church? The Church is to be completed by the common life in the same manner as it was begun by it.

[Col. 0886B] “For there the Lord commanded the blessing and life for ever.” There—that is, in the common life of brethren dwelling in unity—the Lord commanded blessing, because such people bless the Lord, and their blessing is acceptable to God. He blesses those who bless them, and through them diffuses his blessing among the multitude of a lower order. To those blessed by it he shall say at the last judgment: “Come, ye blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom,” etc. (Matt. 25:34).

This blessing is obtained there, where the brethren who are least, dwelling in unity, are devoutly served by those below them, namely the rich of this world, through the six works of mercy. For there especially the Lord commanded blessing to be sought and obtained, saying: [Col. 0886C] “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity, that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings” (Luke 16:9). For they shall receive their benefactors into everlasting dwellings when, because of benefits bestowed upon them, Christ himself says: “I was hungry, and ye gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and ye gave me to drink,” etc., down to: “As long as ye did it to one of these my least ones, ye did it to me” (Matt. 25:35).

These least brethren of Christ gladly dwell in unity, either in heart and body together, like that multitude which, under the apostles and with the apostles, was “of one heart and one soul; nor did any one call anything that he possessed his own, but they had all things in common” (Acts 2:45); or in heart alone, as the Apostle [Col. 0886D] Paul, though separated from that multitude for the Gospel of God, was in no way separated in spirit from that holy multitude of Christ’s poor. He collected many alms for them, which he either brought himself to Jerusalem or was accustomed to send through faithful messengers, among whom blessed Luke was pre-eminent. Among the Gentiles he taught this: “He who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly; but he who sows in blessing shall also reap of blessing; for there the Lord commanded blessing and life for ever” (2 Cor. 9:6). For such poor of Christ, dwelling in unity bodily and in heart, or in heart alone, continually bless and praise the Lord and also lay up blessings for their benefactors, and life for ever—[Col. 0887A] that is, life remaining eternally after the passing age, and lasting into the age that never passes away.

Behold: through the twice-seven Songs of Ascents, seven times from this side—that is, from fear—and seven times from that side—that is, from strength—the enemy who lay in wait for the climber upon each step has been conquered. But what, finally, do these alternations mean—first strength and fear, then fear and strength? Surely this: that the man of God ought not to be ignorant, as Ecclesiastes says, that “all things have their season, and all things under heaven pass through their allotted intervals: a time to weep and a time to laugh; a time to mourn and a time to dance; a time to keep silence and a time to speak” (Eccl. 3:1 ff.).

According to these vicissitudes of times, there is a time to act manfully and a time to rest. For when the invisible enemy suggests to God’s servant that he has too great a contempt for himself, then it is time to act bravely and steadfastly and to remember [Col. 0888A] God’s benefits, received from him who does not forsake those who hope in him. In remembering them there is abundant cause for laughter, dancing, and speaking confidently. But when, conversely, that wily deceiver suggests exaltation on account of virtues, as to a soldier who has earned his reward, then it is time to weep, mourn, and keep silence—that is, to rest humbly and consider that he is dust and ashes, who, like a little dog, has scarcely received a few small crumbs of mercy from the Lord’s abundant table. He is far inferior to the beloved sons; and lifting humbled eyes to them as to high mountains, he may say: “I have lifted up mine eyes unto the mountains, from whence help shall come to me.”

Thus, through the twice-seven Songs of Ascents, with the adversary now defeated through the virtue of reverent humility and now through the steadfastness of righteous confidence and strength, there follows the fifteenth Song of Ascents, in which the victorious servant of the Lord, united to the other servants of his Lord, speaks thus:

## PSALM 133

[Col. 0887]

[Col. 0887C] **VERSE 1.** “Behold, now bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord,” etc. As though he said: You who stand, who do not lie fallen in idleness, but stand in great steadfastness, having conquered the adversary—now, without delay, for as long as “now” is said—bless the Lord, ascribing to him, not to yourselves, the fact that, having ascended so many steps, you now stand in the house of the Lord, contemplating the inward adornments of that house. This house is the body of the Lord, whether that which he assumed from the Virgin, or the whole Church incorporated into his flesh.

For this house has many interior ornaments able to delight the eager beholder: namely, the lampstand of seven lamps, the altar of incense, the table of the bread of offering, and many other things made of the purest gold, with diverse engravings and raised carvings. [Col. 0887D] It is not now the time to discuss each of these separately, since elsewhere the holy Fathers have expounded them in eloquent discourse, interpreting the ark of sanctification, discussed above, as nothing other than the sacrament of the Lord’s incarnation; the mercy-seat, as the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion; the lampstand, as the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection or ascension; and its seven lamps, as the Paraclete Spirit of sevenfold grace, by whom that house is inwardly illumined in the splendours of the saints standing in that house.

To these we now say: You who stand in the house of the Lord, bless the Lord, glorifying his grace, through which and in which you now stand in the house, free for contemplation of his vision, according to what was said elsewhere: “Be still and see, for the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 45:11).

Now, in the courts of that same house, labour outwardly [Col. 0888C] to relieve the needs of neighbours or to repel adversities, which are likened to nights, as prosperity is to day. But because these nights of adversity are sometimes exceedingly dark and unbearable and unconquerable by human powers, owing to the dark storms of tempests, you who stand in the courts of the house of our God, desiring that your charity may also be extended to those outside,

**VERSE 2.** “Lift up your hands toward the Holy of Holies,” into which you have not yet entered, but into which you know that the high priest has entered. Into these holy places lift up your hands, after the example of Moses, so that you may conquer the nightly bands of Amalek more by prayer than by fighting. Amalek means “licking people.” By this name are signified those dogs which licked the blood [Col. 0888D] of Naboth in the field of Jezreel. Jezreel means and signifies Christ, the seed of God eternally begotten and the seed of Abraham made in time, whose blood the Jews licked when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25).

All those are joined to them who, by drinking that same blood unworthily, become guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. When such persons are multiplied in the courts of the house of our God and transgress with impunity, darkness and night come, as it were, over the whole earth while Christ dies. In these nights, you who stand in the house of the Lord and in the courts of the house of our God, lift up your hands toward the holy places, praying, sacrificing, and doing good works—not for gain from some earthly advantage, but for the fruit of the heavenly reward which is among the Holy of Holies, into which Christ our forerunner entered. Toward him our hands must be lifted up on high, lest in praying, sacrificing, [Col. 0889A] or working you seek anything earthly, like those to whom Scripture reproaches that they turned “sacrifices” “into the deep” (Hos. 5:2).

On the contrary, with your hearts fixed on high, on the Holy of Holies, on the things above, direct and lift up your hands also thither—that is, your works and sacrifices—and bless the Lord, not only in days when prosperity smiles upon you, but also in nights when you are wearied by the terror of the night or by the thing that walks in darkness, or know that others are wearied by them. You ought to have compassion on such people, following the example of him who said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” Thus to you, O climber of the steps already set forth, blessing the Lord—or blessing “to the Lord,” that is, for the Lord’s honour—there shall be returned the reciprocal reward of blessing in this concluding statement:

[Col. 0889B] **VERSE 3.** “May the Lord bless you from Zion,” from which the law of the New Testament went forth, when, having become man, he fulfilled the law; and he who, before proceeding as man from Zion, remained God with God the Father, made heaven and earth. Hence his blessing is effective not only in earthly things, such as Esau desired when he said: “Have you only one blessing, Father?” (Gen. 27:38), but also in heavenly things, with such a blessing as Jacob received, when his father said to him: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which God has blessed,” etc. (Gen. 19:27).

Such a blessing, embracing heavenly and earthly benefits, though it is desired by many, including those like Esau who hunt for earthly profit, nevertheless comes to one alone; for many indeed run, but “one receives the prize” (1 Cor. 9:24). Therefore, although it was said above in the plural, “Bless the Lord,” the final conclusion uses the singular number, when it is said to one—or rather, to the unity of many—“May the Lord bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth.”

The next two psalms, entitled *Alleluia*, which means “Praise the Lord” and is an angelic song, provide those standing in the house of the Lord with matter for always praising the Lord himself, because he is good, because his mercy is everlasting.

Now it was as though, having passed over the fifteen steps, one should rejoice in the house of the Lord. But because the children of Kedar, [Col. 0889D] among whom I once lived bodily, even now grievously harass me though I am far away, I think it not unfitting briefly to recall how my prolonged dwelling among them gave me cause for mourning, and how they have burdened—and still burden—me even in my absence.

For in my youth I was called a canon of the Church of Augsburg, when Emperor Henry V was undertaking great measures against Pope Callixtus in the conflict in which that emperor was compelled to surrender to the said pope the investitures of ecclesiastical dignities. By long refusing, he had been excommunicated by Callixtus himself and by his two predecessors, Paschal and Gelasius, together with his supporters and assistants in this affair. One of these was the bishop of the Church of Augsburg. Since at that time I refused to communicate in the sacraments with him, and since I was then master of the schools, and episcopal offices in the Church of Augsburg could not have been arranged without my assistance, I was compelled, as a rebel against the bishop, to flee the city from the face of the children of Kedar persecuting me. I turned aside to the monastery of Rettinbog, and there lay hidden for some time, until that disturbance, in which the Lord was not, ceased, and the whisper of a gentle breeze came, in which the Lord was. It made the two one, concord being restored between priesthood and empire through three legates of the Apostolic See: Lambert, then bishop of Ostia, afterwards Pope Honorius; Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, afterwards Pope Innocent; [Col. 0890A] and Saxo, cardinal-priest.

While these three, I say, were then carrying out their embassy, the excommunication of the emperor and of the princes excommunicated with him was removed, and, with the hostility between priesthood and kingdom in some degree mitigated, peace was established between Lord Emperor Henry and Pope Callixtus. Thus, after a great storm, great tranquillity followed; truly, when winds and sea had raged, peace was made for the empire of the supreme pontiff and emperor and for those obedient to him. Thus, through the grace of God, the Church was united, which from the time of Gregory VII had appeared divided over the dispute concerning investiture.

I was recalled to Augsburg by the aforesaid Hermann, bishop of Augsburg of blessed memory, and was taken by him and with him to Rome to the council held under the presidency of Pope Callixtus. At that council the concord of kingdom and priesthood was also discussed in the presence of imperial legates, as seemed fitting to the wise men assembled there.

From that time, while I lived in the city of Augsburg, I had some measure of peace with the inhabitants of Kedar—even with those who hate peace—because, while I said nothing against them, they maintained a sort of friendship with me. But when I spoke to them of the religious character of clerical life, they attacked me without cause—not with open persecution, but with secret harassment. Their dissimilarity of conduct burdened me, desiring as I did to live piously among the impious, justly among the unjust, religiously among the irreligious. Such were then my fellow canons, [Col. 0890D] with the exception of a few who resembled righteous Lot, though not in every respect. For they did not go out and ascend with him to the heights of the mountain, but, as though remaining in little Zoar, mourned the great ruin of the great city—rather the destruction of morals than of walls.

As regards the walls, the church was great; but ecclesiastical discipline in it was none or slight. A fairly respectable cloister adjoined the church, but it was wholly devoid of cloistered religious life: the brethren neither slept in the dormitory nor ate in the refectory, except on the rarest feasts—especially those on which, in representing Herod, Christ’s persecutor and slaughterer of infants, a contribution was gathered for holding a feast [Col. 0891A] in the refectory, which was empty at almost all other times—or for staging other games or quasi-theatrical spectacles.

Here I am compelled to recall my own folly, grieving and repenting in bitterness of soul that on more than one occasion I not only attended such madness but also presided over it, being master of the schools and teacher of youths. I not only loosened the rein for them in these vanities but even added the spur, through my affection for folly, by which I was then infected and in which I had advanced beyond many of my contemporaries.

But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me, from the Church of Augsburg, to a higher and stricter purpose of common life, I did not yield to flesh and blood. For, leaving three brothers—kinsmen and countrymen—in the world, I entered the regular life with two whom I had taken with me. A third brother, having returned from the schools of France, followed me and left the other two in the world: namely, Ruodiger and Frederick. The canons of Augsburg received both of them into their fellowship, somewhat moved by affection for me, but more strongly attracted by Hermann of happy memory, then bishop of the Church of Augsburg.

After his death Bishop Walther succeeded him: slow in governing the Church, since he was an old and aged man, but very useful in increasing its outward possessions. He not only gathered together what had been dispersed, but also bestowed his own hereditary goods, which were many, under a most binding, almost testamentary, deed, so that any successor who should either grant them in fief or alienate them in another way [Col. 0891C] would stand cursed under anathema, and would render account to God and the Church. The authority of the Apostolic See was added to confirm this anathema. For Octavian, then legate of the Apostolic See, with the cooperation of three bishops—Walther of Augsburg, Otto of Freising, and Emehard, bishop of [lacuna]—excommunicated, after the candles had been extinguished, those bishops who should succeed and alienate from the bishop’s table goods bestowed upon the Church of Augsburg by the aforesaid Bishop Walther or recovered by him.

All the prelates of the Church of Augsburg were present and took part in this sentence: abbots, provosts, archdeacons, and many from other bishoprics, one of whom was I.

[Col. 0891D] But when Bishop Chuonrad succeeded the aforesaid Bishop Walther, he dissipated all the episcopal goods, partly by granting them in fief, partly by mortgaging them, so that, as is apparent even today, the bishop’s table, once wealthy, is now almost completely deprived of episcopal revenues. This desolation was reported to Pope Adrian, with the testimony of my letters, by the canons of Augsburg, and especially by my aforesaid full brother Ruodiger. By that pope’s judgment, my brother and the other canons, who were pursuing a just cause, were sentenced to penalties, while the plundering bishop was dismissed with honour.

Returning to his own affairs, he became so inflamed against me and my full brothers that he proved fiercer than every beast toward them, and, in them, harassed me as he wished and was able. Yet his harassment was moderated by Lords Cardinal Henry, priest of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, and Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. Through the mediation and cooperation of Duke Welf, they reconciled us in a peace which I thought most secure, but which I later found to be most deceitful.

For after the lord cardinals departed—they had made one of my brothers, Ruodiger, dean there, and had urgently commended him to the lord bishop, the bishop giving his hand as a pledge of grace and peace to be kept toward him forever—the bishop, forgetting the faith pledged by his hand, harassed him more cruelly when an opportunity arose from the office of deanery.

[Col. 0892B] For he urged my brother, then dean, to act manfully in cutting off inveterate vices and establishing disciplines then unfamiliar, because they had ceased to sleep in the dormitory, and very many of them, occupied in frivolous vanities, absenting themselves from choir and chapter, had dissolved into worldly desires. When the dean, aided for a time by the bishop, tried to restrain them, the bishop himself, seeing that the brethren were fiercely enraged against the dean, joined them against the dean. He compelled the dean to relinquish the deanery, though the brethren neither alleged nor could allege any cause except their own will. They declared and judged that their will alone sufficed to change the deanery, which no one ought to hold against their wishes.

Burdened by this judgment, my brother, because of the impending schism did not know which of the two named popes was the true successor of Peter, appealed to a general council, which was hoped would soon be held to settle the question of that schism. When they heard of this appeal, the brethren rejoiced, as though an opportunity against the dean had been offered them, because in the appeal he had not specifically named, as they called him, their victorious pope, whom the bishop had accepted and the papal court had approved.

[Col. 0892C] Therefore bishop and brethren cried out that an insult had been done to Caesar and to their Pope Victor. Yet, without injury to either, this appeal could have been accepted, especially since the dean was ready in every court, even before Caesar, to give the reason for his appeal: that, unjustly burdened, he had rightly appealed to the general council which was expected to take place, and which the lord emperor himself was striving—and still strives—to assemble for his own right, not by compelling ecclesiastical persons to submit to his judgment, but by kindly inviting them to a council, or to so great a consultation that the great danger of schism arising from the existence of two Roman pontiffs might be removed. It is evident that there cannot be more than one at one and the same time, so that unity may always endure in the one universal Church, one pope dying and one succeeding.

But while the question of this duality had not yet been fully examined, and while two Roman pontiffs were said to exist, it was not unfitting for persons under burden to appeal to a general [Col. 0893A] council, by which the evil of such schism ought to be cut away, since it can scarcely, if at all, be cut away by local and particular councils.

Therefore, although the appeal to a general council had then been made not improperly, the Augsburg brethren with their bishop most improperly held, not so much a local council as a cabal, in which they said: “What shall we do, since this dean of ours brings in many burdens? If we let him remain thus, we shall all be oppressed. Therefore it is expedient for us that this one man should be cast out, and that we should not all be oppressed, or incur the wrath of Caesar and of Pope Victor.”

Having heard such counsel, they devised to expel him under a pretended fear of Caesar and Victor, though neither knew what was being done. Thus, when he was called toward evening to their chapter, with their bishop present and presiding, like another Caiaphas, he was judged as though excommunicated by Victor and proscribed by Caesar. Therefore, stripped and despoiled of all his possessions except only the equipment for riding, he was cast out of the city as the sun was already setting.

There remained in that city another brother, his and mine, named Frederick, half alive and beginning to die, for he had long been ill and lay at death’s door. By casting him out of his house—indeed, even from his sickbed—and taking away the necessities of nourishment, they expelled by these torments the remaining breath by which he still breathed. For, first expelled from his fine house into the kitchen, from the kitchen [Col. 0893C] into the weaving-room, and from the weaving-room cast into the mill-house, possessing neither dwelling nor food except what was begged, he was compelled to go down by the course of the river. He could not be taken by any kind of vehicle, but hastened by boat as far as me, then as far as our full brother, the provost of Neuburg, for medical treatment.

But the sick man, afflicted by so many vexations and by deprivation of provisions, could not be restored by any care of physicians, because the illness, aggravated and inflamed by the lord bishop of Augsburg and his supporters, had become too strong. He persecuted the poor and needy man, striving to kill one contrite in heart, with a Herodian zeal; he hated me and my brothers and, like another Decius, burned us as though on an iron grating.

At last executioners, pressing on, supplied coals beneath the iron grating, while the fleshly counsellors of the fleshly bishop suggested the worst counsels of his hardened wickedness, to torture me in my brothers—especially in the brother who was already beginning to die, whom they did not allow to die in his own house or in his own little bed, but expelled stripped and naked.

[Col. 0893D] It may be that, to make excuses for sins, they will say that he could not have lived even in his own house because of the violence of his illness. Oh, if there were now granted to me, either in the Apostolic See or on the throne of David’s kingdom, another David, either prophesying, as befits a pope, or ruling, as befits [Col. 0894A] an emperor, I should have no doubt that he would most severely punish this homicide, which is in no way excusable on the ground that the man whom they killed, whose death they hastened, could not live after the dreadful collapse caused by his illness—a fact known to all Augsburg and not unknown to the lord cardinals who stayed in his house.

For that Amalekite who killed King Saul could not excuse himself before King David by saying of Saul: “For I knew that he could not live after his fall” (2 Sam. 1:10). Saul, grievously wounded by his own sword, was leaning upon his spear, and indeed could not live after his fall. Yet that Amalekite, who had hastened Saul’s death by adding a wound to wounds, was convicted by David of blood-guilt and judged a murderer for the homicide he had committed.

But my brother, thus killed, died a blessed death. For, sensing that the end of his mortal life was near, he fled to the author of immortality, renounced the world, took up the Lord’s yoke, and professed the regular life in the monastery of Saint Mary of Neuburg. Nevertheless the cry of his blood and death, if God wills, will be heard both here in the Church that is on pilgrimage in the long sojourn of which we spoke above in the first Song of Ascents, and in the Church reigning above, whence help shall come to me as I rely on the second step, insofar as he deigns to help me, to whom I say: “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

[Col. 0894C] Moreover, the spoils taken from my aforesaid brothers, if it pleases God, when prosperity through God’s inspiration smiles upon either apostolic or imperial government, shall be claimed, by the favour of God’s mercy, either by me or by some successor of mine in the monastery of Reichersberg. There the surviving brother, the aforesaid dean, still lives; the goods taken from those two brothers and offered to the Church of Reichersberg now belong to him alone. That Church, in which the surviving brother lives, who offered himself and his possessions to that Church, will demand judgment, either here or at the last assize, when “the just shall stand with great constancy against those who afflicted them and who took away their labours” (Wis. 5:1).

So the Augsburg men took away [Col. 0894D] the labours of my brothers, reckoned in benefices, books, garments, buildings, and other movable and immovable goods, exceeding the value of two hundred marks. By their labours I mean not only their own property but also ecclesiastical benefices which, though alienated by others, they recovered with great labour and in part redeemed with their own money. These are now possessed by their enemies, to whom, because of the deadly vexations inflicted upon our Frederick, it may rightly and truly be said: “You have killed, and moreover taken possession” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 20:19).

They differ little or not at all from those who said: “Come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance” (Matt. 21:38). And would that the price of his blood had gone toward the burial of strangers—that is, toward the rest and consolation of religious persons dwelling above in heaven and journeying here on earth. That would indeed be a great consolation to us brothers still surviving. But now, with the sole exception of the hospice which the poor possess, those who, together with their bishop, tortured him with deadly vexations have enriched themselves by the price of his blood and death. Their principal men are Provost Sigfrid, parish priest Hermann, his brother Oudalric, and Archdeacon Tiemo.

What reputation—or rather infamy—marks them will be clearly known if the Roman pontiff proves himself such that one may confidently say to him: “Son of man, dig through the wall” (Ezek. 8:8). For, when that wall, muddy within and not whitewashed without, is broken through, greater abominations will appear than those now committed in the expulsion of two brothers guilty of no notable fault. We desire and pray that they may repent of this fully.

[Col. 0895B] And indeed, now that one brother has died and, as has been explained, has been killed, while the other is bound under the Rule of blessed Augustine among us, there is no one to reclaim either the deanery or the canonical prebends. Nevertheless, those who wrongfully took them committed sacrilege, as Pope and martyr Callixtus judges. In his decrees he says:

> The prebends of deaneries and the other goods of the Church are the alms of the faithful, the prices of sins, the redemptions of souls, the patrimonies of the poor. They ought to be received freely and given freely; the poor of Christ ought to be fed from them; they ought to be retained and distributed according to law. Whoever takes them from one obedient to the laws is to be regarded as sacrilegious and like Judas the betrayer. But whoever leaves them to one disobedient is to be judged guilty with respect to his office.

No legitimate successor of this Roman pontiff and eminent martyr Callixtus, whoever he is or will be, will disagree with this ruling. Such was Pope Eugenius of holy memory, most gracious toward me, as is known; this is still evident from his letters most graciously directed to my lowliness. Likewise, letters addressed to me by other Roman pontiffs—Innocent, Celestine, and Lucius—sufficiently show with how much graciousness of apostolic favour I was regarded in the time of those who knew me and whom I knew.

[Col. 0896A] But while Pope Adrian, who did not know me, presided, I was delivered into the hands of enemies. For our letters, containing true testimony against the lord of Augsburg, came into the hands of that same man of Augsburg, who hated me and my brothers. I do not know who the betrayer was in the curia; but I know that this had never happened to me before, though I had written many things to Roman pontiffs who loved and protected me against my adversaries. I had many such adversaries, contending for the law of God, especially in the times of the schisms of Burdin and Peter Leo. From their supporters I suffered many adversities; but, aided by God’s grace and protected by the authority of the Apostolic See, I triumphed with and in the holy Church. I still hope for triumph over the impending schism, although those who trouble me now have multiplied, saying to my soul: “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Ps. 3:3).

Among these, those trouble me more gravely who deny that the man assumed into God has been so exalted that he rules in the commonwealth of his Father as powerfully as his Father himself, equally omnipotent in both natures, divine and human. For the glory of both natures is one and undivided, and the name of dominion is one: innate to the Word, but given to the man whom God exalted and to whom he gave the name that is above every name. Concerning that name, by the favouring grace of him whose glory we proclaim, we have proposed to speak in the following psalm, insofar as he himself deigns through me, unworthy as I am, to glorify his name.

**PSALM CXXXIV**

[Col. 0895]

[Col. 0895D] **VERSE 1.** “Praise the name of the Lord,” etc. This psalm bears in its title *Alleluia*, which means “Praise the Lord,” and signifies not just any praise but that which has no end, by which the blessed who dwell in your house, O Lord, shall praise you for ever and ever: first, the angels established there from the beginning of their creation, after the fall of him who did not stand in the truth; second, blessed human beings standing there after passing the fifteen steps. I, David, now address them, saying:

“Praise the name of the Lord,” which is above every name, given not to me, David according to the flesh, but to my Son, to whom the Most High Lord said: “Sit at my right hand,” and, “Rule in the midst of your enemies” (Ps. 109:1–2). Likewise elsewhere: “Be lord [Col. 0896D] of your brothers” (Gen. 27:29).

Thus, having received the highest dominion and sitting at the right hand of the highest Father, the true Joseph now rules over the whole land of Egypt, while every knee bends to him, even those of Egyptians and infernal beings—how much more, then, those of the heavenly angels and earthly beings, namely human beings, both wicked and good.

This true Joseph was indeed sold as a slave; indeed, he was sold to be killed for thirty pieces of silver, just as that figurative Joseph is read to have been sold as a slave for twenty pieces of silver. Nor is it surprising that this one was sold for a greater price than that one, because the number three in thirty suits this one, and the number two in twenty suits the other. For the person of this one consists of three united essences: a rational soul, human flesh, [Col. 0897A] and divinity; whereas that person consisted of only two, namely, a rational soul and human flesh. Thus this one is more than Joseph, and rules more than Joseph did in the kingdom of God the Father than the other did in Pharaoh’s kingdom.

For Pharaoh had said to him: “Only by the royal throne shall I precede you” (Gen. 41:40); but to this one the Father said: “Sit at my right hand.” This is the same as if he had said: Reign with me and rule with me. Therefore, because, as the Apostle says, “he has now sat down at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heights” (Heb. 8:1), those who set limits to his boundless dominion deserve pity. They behave as though the form of a servant, once greatly humbled but now exceedingly exalted, had not laid aside the servile yoke and received the highest dominion, in no point whatever to be distinguished from the dominion of the Father, Word, and Holy Spirit, after that service had been completed, of which he himself said on the cross, when he had received the vinegar: “It is finished” (John 19:30).

[Col. 0897B] Therefore, although the essence of the servant-form remains in him, it has nevertheless been so exalted, deified, and glorified that it is far removed from the servile obedience under which, while still mortal, he said: “But that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father gave me commandment, so I do” (John 14:31).

That commandment, then, having been fulfilled and consummated in the death of the cross, from now on he must be acknowledged in the glory of God the Father as one Lord with him, the Most High, one in both the exalting and the exalted nature. To him also we sing: “For you alone are holy; you alone are Lord; you alone are the Most High, Jesus Christ, with the Holy Spirit, in the glory of God the Father.”

Therefore, with this praise—“Praise the name of the Lord, which is above every name”—because the man to whom this name has been given now rules and shall rule for ever, with undivided dominion together with his Father and the Holy Spirit; together, I say, with his Father, who acknowledged him as his Son, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). And the addition, “Hear him,” is rightly understood as though he had said to all creatures: Obey him.

Accordingly, the sea and winds obeyed him, and, what is greater, even the evil spirits, whom he commanded, obeyed him. And now he commands the winds and the sea, and they obey him. He commands the north wind to arise and, having arisen, to give place to the south wind as it comes, that it may blow through his garden and its spices may flow forth. He commands the sea to be still and not shake his little ship beyond measure—namely, the holy Church entrusted to the fisherman Peter. He commands as Lord, though he had been roused by the prayers of servants. Therefore praise the Lord, you servants, and by unceasing prayers rouse him lest he sleep, especially you devout and good servants,

[Col. 0897D] **VERSE 2.** “Who stand,” and do not lie down, “in the house of the Lord.” You stand, I say, in the house of the Lord, devoted inwardly to contemplation, and likewise stand in the courts of the house of our God, working outwardly what is good for all, but especially for those of the household of faith, who themselves gladly stand in the house or in the courts of the house together with us. To all these I, David, say—David who in the Spirit calls him Lord, though I do not fail to know him to be my Son—I say,

**VERSE 3.** “Praise the Lord.” I add the reason for praising him, saying: “For the Lord is good.” If all things praised are praised chiefly because they are good, and evil things are chiefly blamed because they are evil, then one little phrase fully states the perfect reason for praise when it says, “For he is good”—especially since this Lord is good not by an accidental gift but by essential goodness. Although his name is terrible to the wicked, it is sweet to the humble, to whom I now say: “Sing praises to his name, for it is sweet” to those tasting his sweetness, as is said elsewhere: “Taste and see, for the Lord is sweet” [Col. 0898B] (Ps. 33:9).

And because perhaps many among you, still like little children, do not grasp the inward taste of that flavour and need milk rather than solid food, hear his manifest works, by which you may be stirred to praise the good and hidden maker of good and manifest works. Thus long ago, when he said to Moses, “I am who I am,” knowing that this name was beyond comprehension, he added: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob.” Because this name was given with reference to temporal human beings, lest it appear temporal, he added: “This is my name for ever” (Exod. 3:14–15)—not because those men are eternal, but because he himself, who has prepared his mercy for them from eternity unto eternity, makes them eternal.

[Col. 0898C] **VERSE 4.** “For the Lord chose Jacob for himself from eternity,” as he himself says: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1:2–3), with no preceding or meriting desert. Therefore the goodness of the Lord is greatly to be praised, because the Lord chose Jacob for himself; and he chose the same man, named Israel after his struggle with the angel, as a possession for himself, to cultivate, sow, possess, and preserve as a field. I, David, proclaim this not from uncertain opinion:

**VERSE 5.** “For I have known that the Lord is great, and our God above all gods.” Those unable to know this should believe me who know it, because I, caught up to heavenly places and instructed there, have known that the Lord is great, as is apparent in his magnificent works, because

[Col. 0898D] **VERSES 6–7.** “Whatever he willed, he did in heaven and on earth and in all the depths. Bringing clouds from the end of the earth”: either literally, raising mist from marshes and gathering it into clouds; or in a mystical sense, choosing the weak and despised things of the world in order to confound the strong. Leaving aside the strong, he makes those weak things like clouds to rain doctrine and to flash with miracles, turning the flashes themselves into rain when he bends terrible threats toward mercy. For the preachers themselves are rightly called clouds because of the flesh, and winds because of the spirit.

And because clouds are seen while winds are not seen, though they are felt, the origin of clouds is appropriately said to be from the end of the earth, on account of human bodies; but concerning winds [Col. 0899A] it is said: “He brings forth winds from his treasuries,” because the origin of souls created from nothing is unknown.

We have already said above: “Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good; sing praises to his name, for it is sweet.” To establish this sweetness and goodness, we have added the gracious works of the Lord. But what follows:

### VERSE 8

He who struck the firstborn of Egypt, etc., down to: “O Lord, your name is for ever,” plainly indicates that the Lord’s name is not only sweet but also terrible. For both literally he struck the firstborn of Egypt, from man to beast, and now he strikes the principal vices among both the learned and the unlearned, sparing neither the former because of their subtlety nor the latter because of their simplicity.

[Col. 0899B] ### VERSE 9

He sent [Vulgate: *And he sent*] signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt: against Pharaoh, that is, the devil, and against all his servants, evil human beings and angels.

### VERSE 10

He struck many nations, by putting to death in the elect innumerable troops of vices; and he killed mighty kings, namely malignant and unclean spirits who usurp lordship for themselves, that is:

### VERSES 11–12

Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan. And he gave their land as an inheritance to Israel, his people. Pharaoh means “dispersion.” Sihon means “temptation of the eyes” or “useless offspring.” Og is interpreted “closure.” By these royal names is understood the prince of this world, who, scattering [Col. 0899C] those whom he can, reigns in Egypt—that is, amid darkness and the children of darkness. Through temptations, especially those of the eyes, he makes them useless offspring; for the shameless eye is the messenger of the shameless person, and the malicious eye of the malicious heart. He reigns in the kingdom of the Amorites—that is, “those who embitter”—and in the kingdom of the land of Bashan, interpreted “confusion,” whose king is called Og, that is, “closure,” because those whom the devil confounds through vices he also shuts off from the ways of life.

But when these kings, together with the evil angels and human beings who agree with them, have been driven out, their land—from which evil angels were cast out and evil human beings were removed in Adam—will pass into the possession of the children of Israel, as it is written: “And he gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people.” Do not doubt that these things, once done historically, are still being enacted, for it follows:

### VERSES 13–14

“O Lord, your name is for ever; O Lord, your memorial throughout generation and generation. For the Lord will judge his people, and he will be entreated for his servants.” Or, as it is read in Hebrew: [Col. 0900A] “And he will be gracious to his servants.” The Lord will judge his people by distinguishing true Israelites from Egyptians and Canaanites; after condemning the latter, he will be entreated for his servants and will be gracious to them, as to his worshippers and true adorers, who worship the Father in Spirit and truth.

### VERSES 15–17

But the idols of the nations are to be despised, since they are cast from material gold and silver, or even from the gold of worldly wisdom and the silver of worldly and deceptive eloquence. All these are works of human hands, of no use whatever; for although they have mouths, they will not speak; although they have eyes, they will not see; although they have ears, they will not hear; nor indeed is there spirit in their mouths. For both handmade idols and sophistical fabrications [Col. 0900B] are empty of the vision of truth and full of the spirit of falsehood, and therefore must be despised and reckoned as nothing.

### VERSE 18

“Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them,” so that they too may be despised and reckoned as nothing in the house of Israel by all ecclesiastical ranks. In these ranks, the house of Aaron is understood to be the rulers; the house of Levi, their ministers; and those who fear the Lord, the people subject to them in the fear of God. From all these the house of Israel consists—to which I say:

### VERSES 19–20

House of Israel, bless the Lord with a universal blessing: that is, so that the house of Aaron in its rulers, the house of Levi in its ministers, and the house [Col. 0900C] of all who fear the Lord may bless the Lord, saying:

### VERSE 21

“Blessed is the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem.” Blessed is the Lord, long awaited by prophets watching from earthly Zion, and at last manifested bodily there; spiritually he has dwelt and always dwells in Jerusalem, where we shall see him in eternal peace, not only in his glorified body but also in spirit. For God, who is also man, is man with us; and with the Father he is the eternal Spirit, to be seen by the pure in heart in the vision of eternal peace.

Glory to the Father, who gives his name—by which the Lord is named—to the assumed humanity. Glory to the Son, who rules supremely in each of his natures, divine and human. Glory [Col. 0900D] to the Holy Spirit, who is the goodness and sweetness consubstantial with the Father and the Son, by which the Lord is proclaimed good and his name sweet in this psalm composed concerning the praises of God and of his name.

## PSALM 135

[Col. 0899]

[Col. 0899D] ### VERSE 1

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good,” etc. Again this psalm bears the title **ALLELUIA**, and rightly so, since it is wholly an exhortation to praise the goodness and mercy of God: wholly filled with sweet-sounding praises, running from beginning [Col. 0900D] to end with ringing thanksgivings. Its various verse openings converge upon [Col. 0901A] one conclusion: the praise of mercy. For whatever is said is referred to mercy, without which nothing subsists; mercy is the chief cause of God’s acts of compassion over all his works.

The great power of this psalm is shown in Chronicles, where we read: “When they began to praise God and to say” (2 Chron. 5:13–14), “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is for ever,” “the glory of God filled the house of God.” This shows that God’s presence is at hand if this psalm is sung purely, for in it both the original and final cause of all God’s works is commended. The original cause is God’s goodness, for which he made all things; the final cause is his mercy, to be sung for ever, especially by those who, having been lost, [Col. 0901B] were sought out and rescued from misery solely by the compassion of God’s mercy. Near the end of the psalm they say: “For he remembered us in our low estate, and redeemed us from our enemies.” This verse shows that the psalm belongs more particularly to Christians than to Jews, because he delivered the latter from Egypt without payment, whereas he redeemed us Christians by his precious blood. Therefore you who have been redeemed must not be ungrateful for God’s grace.

### VERSES 2–3

“Give thanks to the God of gods. Give thanks to the Lord of lords,” since “there are many gods and many lords” (1 Cor. 8:5), above all of whom he excels. He also judges the gods, to whom the word of God came; he is certainly greater than they, because the Father himself [Col. 0901C] sanctified him and sent him into the world. It should indeed be noted that this psalm and the preceding one chiefly concern Christ, who bodily came from Zion, as was stated in the preceding psalm, and who by his death redeemed us from our enemies, as will follow in the present one. You who have been redeemed, give thanks to him: he is not merely created according to the flesh, but is also Creator according to his divinity, from whose omnipotence comes this:

### VERSE 4

“He alone does great wonders.” When “alone” is said, neither his Father nor the Holy Spirit is excluded, because these three are one and work inseparably. With every verse one must understand: “Give thanks to the Lord,” which appears more clearly in Greek. It is as though it said: “Give thanks to the Lord who does wonders, who makes the heavens in understanding,” and so forth. Do you wish to know, beloved hearers, at least in part, what those wonders are which he has done or does?

### VERSE 5

“He made the heavens in understanding”: either rational heavens, declaring God’s glory in sound understanding, or bodily heavens preordained in his understanding.

### VERSE 6

He also established the earth upon the waters, so that it has no other support than the waters of this dense and moist air, through which birds swim by the rowing of their wings. These waters, surrounding the globe of the earth, in some manner support it; and this is wonderful in our eyes. Yet far more wonderful, and at the same time beyond measure venerable, is this: the Church was founded [Col. 0902A] upon the waters of baptism flowing from Christ’s side, and was strengthened by those very waters, lest it be like dust devoid of water and therefore dry, unable to withstand the wind that casts itself forth from the face of the earth.

### VERSES 7–9

“He made the great lights: the sun to rule the day, the moon and stars to rule the night.” Taken literally, this also produces great admiration in those who behold this sun shining alone throughout the day and obscuring the moon and stars by the brilliance of its radiance. Likewise, the moon and stars shining by night offer a great marvel to their observers, especially to those who calculate their courses and returns, risings and settings.

But a consideration of the sun—Christ, risen from a star; the moon—the Church illuminated by him; and the stars—the various virtues or orders within her—provides even greater matter for thanksgiving and praise. For if we consider the solar body, what among inanimate things is more like Christ’s body? As in that body is the source of all ethereal fire, from which it is scattered throughout the whole world, so “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” in Christ’s body (Col. 2:9), and from it he illuminates the whole Church through the diverse gifts descending from above, from the Father of lights. If this sun, though still concealed beneath the cloud of mortality, so enlightened the twelve apostles like the twelve hours that he could truly say to them: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14), how much more does he now, when the cloud of mortality has been removed and he remains in the glory of the Father’s brightness, illuminate all things?

The light [Col. 0902C] of this sun indeed shines even in darkness, although the darkness does not comprehend it, just as blind eyes do not take in the sun’s light, though it is most brilliant and present to them in daylight itself. Moreover, the same light causes suffering to diseased eyes which delights sound and clear eyes. Something similar occurs when the glorification of Christ’s body, proclaimed through the Scriptures, delights believers as they hear that every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. But unbelievers, who have either no faith or only very little, and therefore are blind or weak-sighted, take no delight in this brightness of Christ’s solar body. Nor is this enough for them: adding to the measure of their faithlessness, they deny that Christ’s body is to be worshipped, and accuse us who worship it of serving the creature rather than the Creator and therefore of being idolaters—as though we separated the Lord’s body from the Lord and worshipped it separately.

To return to the metaphor: it is as though, by worshipping that solar body separately, we stripped it of the brightness of its divinity. This would be impious, and Catholic faith does not allow it. That faith rightly holds that the Word made flesh is so united to his flesh that the flesh of the Word may not be separated from the Word; for such flesh would profit nothing, whether to those who eat it or those who worship it.

Therefore we venerate the Lord’s body as the sun of righteousness, full of the warmth and radiance of divinity. As blessed Augustine says, no one eats it spiritually unless he first worships it: not beneath God, but in God; not as a footstool, but, as Jerome says, as a throne; not as a sun in the west, without form or beauty, but as the sun which “ascends above the west” (Ps. 67:5). It ascends, I say, to the East—that is, to the height of its inherent divinity. For his divinity is rightly called “rising” (*oriens*), not “risen” (*orta*), because his generation from the Father has no end.

But of the man born into God and of the Virgin, this is rightly understood which is said elsewhere: “The sun has risen” (Ps. 103:22); and: “Light has risen for the righteous” (Ps. 96:11); and what the wicked will say at judgment: “The sun of righteousness has not risen for us” (Wis. 5:6); and: “Truth has sprung from the earth” (Ps. 84:12). This truth, indeed, always rising from the Father and eternally being born in his birth from the Father, admits neither before nor after, because he remains always “today,” according to the saying: “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). Accordingly, he is rightly called not “risen” from the Father but “rising.” Yet the same truth, risen from the earth—that is, born from the Virgin—has a before and after in this birth, since he was at one time to rise and now has risen. Therefore it is rightly sung that, in the assumed humanity, he ascended from the virgin earth to the East—that is, to the height and brightness of the divinity that assumed him.

Thus the whole Christ is to be believed true light, in both natures, enlightening every person coming into this world. Nothing in this light, in this sun of righteousness, is to be judged dark; for even his body, [Col. 0903C] although it rose from the earth, is now most radiant in heaven, and in its own light is not less bright than the brightness of his divinity. Egyptians—that is, dark human beings and angels—do not see this; nor do Amorites, “those who embitter,” or the people of the king of Bashan, “the confounded.” Let them fear the plagues here recalled literally as past, but which in mystery are still to be expected, when like guilt requires them. For:

### VERSES 10–12

“He struck Egypt with their firstborn; he struck great kings; and killed mighty kings,” namely Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, whose names were interpreted in the preceding psalm. He likewise now, and until the end of the age, strikes and will strike those like them: some, that they may repent, like Saul; others, that they may perish, like Judas, that utterly wicked trader.

Likewise, just as he then led Israel out from the midst of the Egyptians, Pharaoh having been drowned in the sea through which he led his people and brought them across the wilderness, to whom he also gave the promised inheritance: so now he leads out, and will not cease to lead out until the end of the age, through the sea of baptism that suffocates the devil, the true Israelites in whom there is no guile. From among the wicked he says to them: “Go out from their midst, and touch no unclean thing” (2 Cor. 6:17). That is: do not touch uncleanness by consenting to it, or another’s wickedness by cowardly silence; but come out by openly rebuking manifest sins and secretly rebuking hidden ones.

Thus, as they go out, God leads them [Col. 0904A] by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm—that is, in his Word, in his Son, of whom it is said: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1). He will also divide the Red Sea for these people into divisions: when evil and bitter peoples disagree among themselves and are divided against one another—as appeared among heretics teaching contrary doctrines—the people of the Lord pass through their midst. For example, when Arius and Sabellius were divided against one another, the Church passed between them, holding the evangelical saying: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30): “one” against Arius, “are” against Sabellius.

Likewise, when Nestorius divided Christ into two persons because of his two natures, while Eutyches, because of the unity of the person, attempted to assert a unity also of nature, the holy Church maintained the middle way, passing through those opposed to each other and affirming the unity of the person consisting of two natures and existing in two natures. All this was done by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, so that we also, though little ones, may trust that we shall be delivered by the same arm, by its mighty hand, according to its mercy.

### VERSES 23–24

“For he remembered us in our low estate”: whether we were humble inwardly through the strength of the mind, or humbled outwardly through adversities. “And he redeemed us” at the price of his own blood from our enemies, because of his mercy; “for his mercy is for ever.”

### VERSE 25

He gives the food of his flesh to all flesh—that is, to everyone who has a heart of flesh and not of stone. He gave shadowy manna only to the Jews; but, as has been said, he gives true manna to all flesh, according to his own words: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52). Therefore throughout the whole world he gives food to all flesh, excluding the hard and stony-hearted, who said: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (John 6:61), and: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:53). While they and those like them dispute—hard, stony, and unbelieving—you who have hearts of flesh, who with Peter receive the words of eternal life:

### VERSES 26–27

“Give thanks to the God of heaven, for he has mercy for ever upon all,” giving food to all flesh [Col. 0904D] not only sacramentally and spiritually, as has been said, but also universally, feeding every flesh from the greatest living creatures down to the least. Hence: “Consider the birds of heaven: they neither sow nor reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matt. 6:26). Those whom the Father feeds, the Son also feeds, because whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise. Therefore he feeds all flesh, he who together with the Father made all flesh.

But you who hunger for the heavenly things above, give thanks to the God of heaven, setting your hearts on high and striving thither, where you may eat the bread of angels as the holy angels eat it: not in a sacrament or beneath a veil, but seeing face to face and tasting it with ineffable relish. For he is good; [Col. 0905A] for his mercy is for ever; for he is Lord of lords; for he will bring good servants into his joy and make them reign always for ever beneath him and with him. For his mercy is for ever.

[Col. 0906A] Glory to the Father of mercies. Glory to the Son who obtains eternal mercy. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is eternal mercy itself, by which people are delivered from misery. So be it, so be it. Amen, amen.

## PSALM 136

[Col. 0905]

[Col. 0905A] “By the rivers of Babylon,” etc. The title reads:

**A PSALM OF DAVID CONCERNING JEREMIAH.**

[Col. 0905B] From this psalm the sixth *periocha* is now woven in a briefer course. For it returns to the weeping of those who love, to the sighs of those who long, “concerning Jeremiah,” that is, according to Jeremiah’s meaning. Just as Jeremiah historically wrote of the captivity of the children of Israel effected by Nebuchadnezzar, yet understood that something else was signified there, so these speakers, although they utter the words historically, indicate that something else must nevertheless be understood beneath the same words.

“By the rivers of Babylon,” they say, “there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion.” “As long as we are in the body,” says the Apostle, “we are away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:6). And truly so: we are captives in the captivity of sin brought about by Adam. All of us who are children of Zion groan and weep over this captivity, sitting by the rivers: [Col. 0905C] seeing many immersed in the flowing vices of this present age, and fearing that we ourselves may fall in and be immersed.

These things, and the rest of the psalm, are the tears of those who love God, the sighs of those who long to see the God of gods in Zion and say:

### VERSE 1

“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept.” We did not stand erect in pride, as though we thought we could accomplish anything by our own strength; nor did we lie down through sloth, as though despairing of God’s aid. But we sat in humility, knowing that it is vain to rise before the dawn of prevenient grace, which awakens human efforts, assists them lest they be fruitless, and preserves them in good perseverance lest they fail before the end.

We awaited this grace not by lying down and sleeping, but by sitting and weeping. And for us, citizens of Jerusalem held captive in Babylon, there was great cause for weeping: we saw many of our fellow citizens immersed in the rivers of Babylon. Because the muddy banks of those rivers are slippery, we also feared for ourselves lest we slip and, dragged away and enticed by the desires of the flesh or of the eyes, be immersed in the same rivers—rivers that draw us into the depths of pleasure and curiosity. By contrast, the river of pride, with stormy and foaming waves, lifts on high those whom it makes glory in their own strength; for example, saying: “I am not like the rest of men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers” (Luke 18:11). We feared these Babylonian rivers and therefore wept as we remembered Zion, [Col. 0906A] from which we were exiled in Adam, in whom all sinned. In him we too were cast out from Zion, that is, from paradise; under the king of Babylon, the devil, we are distressed in this pool [Col. 0906B] of Babylon with Daniel. Our distress is greater because in its midst we find neither attentive, receptive, nor teachable hearers.

Among those who remain in Babylon, some are near its exits, resolving to flee from it and return to Zion. But others are so fixed in its midst that they may be compared to fruitless trees which nonetheless have leaves vainly green: to the willows that grow green there because they are watered by the rivers flowing in the midst of Babylon.

### VERSES 2–3

Upon willows such as these we hang our instruments, unwilling to give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine. For those who are willows are also dogs barking against truth—indeed, deceitful foxes—because there they questioned us, those who carried us captive, desiring to catch us in our speech by seeking words of songs from us. Do they not seem to you like foxes, those who said: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matt. 22:17)

Likewise, the mockers of God’s word are little foxes to be caught, lest they destroy the flowering vineyards, since they ask us for words of songs only in order to mock us. Those who carried us captive through crafty and deceitful questions sought words of songs from us in order to deride and criticize us. And those who led us away from useful matters which we had intended to discuss concerning moral conduct, craftily and with excessive cleverness, pretending to wish to hear loftier matters, said: “Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion.” That is, as though they said: “Speak of the heavenly and hidden matters transacted in the heavenly Zion, where God orders all things that he foreknew would come to pass. Sing us a hymn concerning this foreknowledge of his and the other heavenly mysteries of this kind, for we gladly debate songs of Zion of this sort.”

To them we sometimes answer:

### VERSE 4

“How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” The conventicles of heretics and Platonists, and of Aristotelian sophists philosophizing according to the elements of the world rather than according to Jesus Christ, must be regarded as a foreign land. When questioners, critics, and flatterers in such a land ask a Catholic man to speak of heavenly things, he suffers great anxiety and uncertainty whether he should speak or be silent, since in both silence and speech he fears danger.

In such anxiety, I, a citizen of Jerusalem, have no consolation except your remembrance, O heavenly Jerusalem. Finally, in friendship with the Babylonians my soul refused consolation; and therefore I remembered God, the king of Jerusalem, and was delighted, because through Jeremiah he promised the release of the captivity of Jerusalem’s citizens. Therefore, if I do not remember you, O Jerusalem, or:

### VERSES 5–6

If, forgetting you, I do anything merely to please the Babylonians, let my right hand be given over to forgetfulness. And if I should wish to say anything to please the citizens of Babylon, in saying which I do not remember you, let my tongue cleave to my jaws. For I would rather do and say nothing than say or do things which do not concern you, O Jerusalem.

And so I speak these imprecations, not as the wish of one desiring them, but in the office of a prophet: “Let my tongue cleave to my jaws if I do not remember you, and let my right hand forget me,” so that I may say or do nothing rather than fail to do or say well.
