Let these imprecations, I say, come upon me if I do not set Jerusalem before me at the beginning of my joy: namely, so that, even if some small joy in worldly prosperity steals upon me, Jerusalem may nevertheless not be at the beginning of my joy, and I may chiefly rejoice in this: that in everything I say or do, I keep the memory of her within me at the beginning of my joy, in my chief joy, according to the Gospel: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” [Col. 0907C] (Luke 10:20).

Let this be said concerning Babylonians who are altogether alien, manifest enemies, and destroyers of Jerusalem. But because the Edomites, kinsmen according to the flesh of the children of Israel—for Esau, who was called Edom, was Israel’s brother—were an obstacle to those rebuilding Jerusalem, or favored the Babylonians in its destruction, and therefore signified false brothers, falsely friendly but truly hostile, the complaint of me, David king of the city of Jerusalem, or of any citizen of Jerusalem, is greater against Edom. Its wickedness is found in false brothers, against whom I pray, saying:

### VERSE 7

“Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day,” or “for the day,” “of Jerusalem”: by doing something against them which may be *for the day*, that is, for the consolation of Jerusalem. Thus we read in Chronicles that it happened in the days of King Jehoshaphat. When the children of Edom from Mount Seir had assembled with the other eastern peoples to ravage Jerusalem, and were about to engage at dawn while night still remained, the children of Edom themselves, disagreeing with the children of Ammon and Moab, killed one another and prepared a joyful day for the children of Israel, citizens of Jerusalem (2 Chron. 20).

For when the said enemies had assembled against Judah and Jerusalem, all Judah came together in Jerusalem and in the Lord’s temple to beseech his face. As they stood before the Lord with their wives, little children, and offspring, crying out to the Lord, Jahaziel son of Zechariah, son of Berechiah, a Levite, in the midst [Col. 0908A] of the multitude, received the Spirit of the Lord upon himself and cried out, saying: “O Judah and Jerusalem, do not fear. Tomorrow go out, and the Lord will be with you. Stand firm, and you shall see the help of God upon you” (2 Chron. 20:17).

As he foretold, so it happened: by mutual wounds the dead enemies of Jerusalem made a joyful day for King Jehoshaphat and the other citizens of Jerusalem. Gathering the spoils of the slain, they became very wealthy and rejoiced not only over Jerusalem’s slain enemies but also over the spoils collected in the valley of Jehoshaphat, which means “valley of judgment” and from that time was called the valley of blessing. Then, O Lord of rulers, you remembered the children of Edom for the day and consolation of Jerusalem.

So now likewise remember the children of Edom for the day and consolation of Jerusalem, so that domestic enemies who disagree may chew up their own tongues, as is read in Revelation (Rev. 16:10–11), and may fall through mutual wounds, leaving peace to God’s holy Church once they have been utterly humbled. For now, puffed up and exalted, they exhort one another, saying: “Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation.” That is: destroy the city of Jerusalem so completely that it may be empty and bereft of its citizens and riches, with not one stone left upon another, even down to the foundation. For no one can lay another foundation in it besides the one already laid. Therefore, with the foundation alone remaining, you its enemies take away all that has been built upon it, so that the foundation of faith, dead without works, may avail them nothing.

Or rather, lay it bare even to the foundation, so that you leave not even the foundation of faith. This occurs when, through multiplied questions in the doctrine of faith, error is so widespread that even the elect, if possible, are led astray—especially when the children of Edom, who was Jacob’s brother, grievously harass the children of Jacob, also called Israel. To Israel the Lord says: “Israel, if you will listen to me, there shall be no new god in you, neither shall you worship a strange god” (Ps. 80:9–10). Therefore, when a new god is pressed upon the children of Israel by the children of Edom through importunate and undisciplined questions, let Israel beware of receiving a new god; and let it cry to the ancient God, saying: “Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem.”

[Col. 0908D] ### VERSE 8

“Wretched daughter of Babylon: blessed is he who repays you with the recompense which you repaid to us.” “Babylon, mother of fornications,” is spoken of in Revelation (Rev. 17:5); by it is understood the desirable beauty of this world, with which her shameless lovers commit fornication, loving the creature more than the Creator. This is the woman ugly within but beautiful without; whoever looks upon her to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

This Babylon also has a daughter very like herself: namely, the image of her appearance formed in memory. When the image of some outwardly desired thing is reflected inwardly in the mind, whoever embraces it begets from it thoughts: first little ones, [Col. 0909A] then larger ones, nursed by the mind’s assent. Blessed is the person who holds and dashes these against the rock, for the rock is Christ. Through his invocation those are delivered from mother Babylon and from her daughter who prefer love of him to love of this world.

Thus you, wretched daughter of Babylon, are recognized when you have lost your children. Those who love you are wretched, as are those who nurse and nourish by the heart’s assent the children born from you until they commit wicked deeds. These deeds are no longer to be regarded as little Babylonians, especially when a long and evil habit has joined itself to them; such a habit cannot be overcome without great difficulty.

But while they are still little, they can most easily be held and dashed against the rock. For unlawful thoughts entering the heart do not harm a soul that loves Christ when they do not please it and are not received, but are driven away like flies by good thoughts. These are not daughters of Babylon but daughters of Zion, or of Jerusalem, received from above and conceived in the womb of the mind. When they grow to a completed work, they invade and lay waste the citizens of Babylon like citizens of Jerusalem, repaying them a just recompense: devastation for devastation, dashing for dashing, emptying for emptying, captivity for captivity, suspension for suspension.

For just as they compelled us not to cast away or break our instruments, but to hang them up for a time, so they too, when captured among us and brought beneath Christ’s yoke, will be compelled not to lose the members which were instruments of wickedness, but to suspend them from wickedness by restraining them under Christian discipline.

Mindful of the words of this psalm, holy Pope Gregory says in his exposition of Job [Note: [Col. 0909D] Book XXXIII of the *Morals*, chapter 5]:

> “Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments.” What is signified by the barrenness of willows but the life of sinners? For if this were not so, the Psalmist would never have said, speaking in the voice of preachers against Babylon: “Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments.” Willows are described as standing in the midst of Babylon, because all who are unfruitful and alienated from love of the heavenly homeland take root with all the inward parts of their heart in this confusion of the world. Therefore holy preachers do not play their instruments upon these willows, but hang them up; for when they see unfruitful and reprobate minds, [Col. 0909D] they do not exert the force of their preaching, but instead are silent in mourning.

Likewise, the same author in the same work [Note: [Col. 0910D] Book XXV, chapter 10]:

> “Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation.” Whoever despises preserving works worthy of faith loses even the faith which he seemed to possess. Concerning such persons the Prophet aptly recalls, under Jerusalem, the words of her destroying enemies, who say: “Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation.” For Paul says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” [Col. 0910A] (1 Cor. 3:11). Therefore Jerusalem’s enemies lay it bare even to the foundation when perverse spirits, after first destroying the edifice of good work, drain from the hearts of the faithful even the solidity of religion. For as a building is constructed upon a foundation, so works are constructed upon faith. Thus to lay it bare even to the foundation is, after overthrowing the work of good living, to dissipate even the strength of faith.

Blessed therefore, O daughter of Babylon—that is, worldly desire—is the person who repays you with the recompense which you repaid to us.

VERS. 9. Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock. Blessed, I say, with true blessedness, is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock. This indeed is what we do when we pray: “We beseech you, [Col. 0910B] almighty God, do not permit us to be shaken by any disturbances, whom you have established upon the rock of the apostolic confession.” For since you, Babylon, mother of fornications, and you, daughter of Babylon, by seductively working through your fantasies strive to take away from us our foundation, which is the solid rock, we in rendering you a just requital strive to take away your foundation, which is sand.

You attempt in vain either to assault the walls of Jerusalem with open and lofty engines of war, or secretly to undermine them through the hidden contrivances of your schemes. And we, citizens of Jerusalem, render you the return of just recompense: either by battering against your walls with the written and spoken words of open preaching, with battering-rams and other lofty engines set in a circle; or by the hidden digging-tools of prayers [Col. 0910C] undermining the foundations of your walls or towers. These therefore admit being undermined because they are nothing other than sand. But the foundations of our walls and towers, set upon the holy mountains, are supported by the most lofty rock, which you will never be able to undermine; and by that rock you will be destroyed, when your little ones have been dashed against that very rock. For the Church, firmly built upon this firm rock, humbles and condemns you together with your prince, and commends in prayer every one of her faithful members to her almighty Prince—he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock.

For every person is little, or least, who does not hear the word of God, or, if he hears it, does not do or keep it. “But whoever shall do and teach it, he shall be called great [Col. 0910D] in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19); and such a one is fit to fight against your great citizens with sling and sword and to strike them down, as I David did when I killed the Philistine, and to dash your little ones against the rock.

Glory to the Father-Lord, to whom it is said: “Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom.” Glory to the Son, that Rock against whom the little ones of Babylon are dashed. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is that blessedness by which blessed is he who shall seize and dash his Babylonian little ones against the Rock.

## PSALM CXXXVII

[Col. 0911]

[Col. 0911A] “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart,” etc. After the weeping expressed in the preceding psalm, as though in the winepress of afflictions, now tears of sorrow are changed, as it were, into wine of gladness, and confessions and praises resound. For I too, a citizen of Jerusalem, although captive in Babylon, nevertheless placing Jerusalem herself first among my joys, will confess to you, O Lord, in my heart. And, urging and exhorting others to the same, I say: “Let all the kings of the earth confess to you, O Lord”—not only for benefits bestowed individually upon each, but also for all those conferred upon the human race, or yet to be conferred when Babylon has been destroyed. Although we do not yet possess these things in actuality, nevertheless, possessing them in hope, we ought to offer continual praises and confessions to you, Christ the true David, according to the title of this psalm:

VERS. 1. OF DAVID HIMSELF.

Therefore, to you yourself, true David, King of the city of Jerusalem, I will confess—to you, I, whatever kind of citizen I may be of that same Jerusalem—with my whole heart, so that all my heart may burn with the flame of your love, and the small spark by which I now begin to burn, while placed in and held captive in Babylon, as if in the growing fetter of the body, may increase into an abundant fire. May it make all my heart like a glowing furnace, preparing the whole burnt offering of praise. This now begins when we citizens, wandering in the body, sigh for the fellowship of angels, in whose presence I will sing psalms to you, my God.

Singing thus, this citizen of Jerusalem first praises the benefits specially given to him, saying: “Because you have heard [Col. 0911C] the words of my mouth.” Second, he asks that the number of those who confess may be increased, saying: “Let all the kings of the earth confess to you.” At the end he asks that his confession or prayer, though he is a sinner, may not be despised, when he says: “Do not despise the works of your hands.”

Since therefore I, a citizen of Jerusalem, cried out to you, my God, and you heard the words of my mouth—which became certain to me because, seated beside the rivers of Babylon, I had weeping rather than laughter—I will confess to you also with my whole heart, since you gave me this weeping, through which you also heard the words of my mouth. Therefore, in thanksgiving and continual confession, both of my fault and of your praise, I will sing psalms to you sometimes in the sight of human beings, but constantly in the sight of angels, to whom my inner things speak even while my lips are closed.

Even thus [Col. 0911D] I will sing psalms to you in the sight of angels: either by working with my hands and singing on the ten-stringed psaltery through gladly observing the ten commandments of the Law, or by rejoicing in heart or voice, so that I desire nothing other than that which the holy angels desire—namely, your face, “into which angels desire always to look” (1 Pet. 1:12). Since I do not yet see him as I desire to see him with the angels, I am at least refreshed by his praises in the psalms; and in praising I set before myself the angels, with whom I expect to be joined, as now in praise, so afterwards together in exultation and glory.

Their multitude—consisting of those already exulting before God and in God, and at the same time increased and still to be increased from human beings already blessed and still to be made blessed—is itself both the holy temple in angels and human beings already blessed, wholly foreign and estranged from Babylonian confusion; and the temple still to be sanctified in human beings wandering here and sighing for the heavenly homeland, of whom I am one, not yet holy. And therefore, that I may become holy:

VERS. 2. I worship toward your holy temple, continually desiring that your name, invoked over me, may be sanctified [Col. 0912B] upon me; and I will confess to that same name of yours for your mercy, by which you justify the ungodly, and for your truth, by which you reward those justified, “that you may be justified in your words” (Ps. 50:6), by which you promised pardon to penitent sinners and glory to those justified.

The firstfruits of that glory you, Holy Father, displayed in our head, Jesus Christ, because you magnified above every name your holy name—humbled for our sake in this Babylon, but now glorified above every name in the heavenly Jerusalem. What greater mercy is there than that the Most High mercifully humbled himself in order to exalt the wretched? What greater or more just truth than that the human nature in which he humbled himself should now reign above all things?

For this mercy and this truth [Col. 0912C] I will confess to your name, believing with the heart unto righteousness and confessing with the mouth unto salvation, that Jesus Christ is in your glory, O eternal Father, having been given the name which is above every name: so that the human being assumed into God may truly be called God most high and immortal—not among the many adopted gods to whom the word of God came, and to whom it is said: “I said: You are gods; yet you shall die like human beings” (Ps. 81:6–7)—but just as his Father is immortal God, with an immortality not angelic but divine, eternal, supreme, and beyond all angels. Thus the human being assumed into God now reigns in the most exalted glory of the Trinity, as himself one in the Trinity, the second Person.

Thus every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth rightly bends before the exalted human being, and every tongue truthfully confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. Therefore, among all tongues confessing this, I too will confess to your name for your mercy and truth, in which you magnified your holy name above every name. Through him, the propitiator:

VERS. 3. On whatever day I call upon you, hear me. Sin is night; virtue is day. Therefore I do not ask to be heard in the night, which is called *nox* (“night”) from harming (*nocendo*), because it also harms the eyes: hence, if anyone walks at night, he stumbles. But I ask to be heard in the day, which aids and delights the eyes and drives away the darkness of night.

For virtue, driving away the darkness of vices and illuminating the powers of the rational soul—namely memory, understanding, intellect, and will—which, like clouds having no light in themselves, are darkened by nocturnal shadows when disturbed by vices, is necessary for those walking on the way. Beside this way many snares are laid, which cannot be avoided by human powers unless divine virtue illumines them, so that these natural powers of the soul may be like bright clouds shining with heavenly virtue. Therefore I say to you, my God: “On whatever day,” that is, in whatever virtue I call upon you to obtain, [Col. 0913B] hear me. For if you hear me, I know that you will not only give the virtue requested, but will also multiply the virtue given in my soul, so that my soul may be good ground, in which the seed of the virtue given bears much fruit, to be expanded and multiplied in such a way that, when that fruit is considered, very many may be justified by my example, and glory may thereby come not to me but to you, the author of virtues; so that:

VERS. 4. Let all the kings of the earth confess to you, O Lord: namely, that they are kings of the earth, that they govern their flesh well, that they are not enslaved to vices but serve you alone, the King of kings, to whom to serve is to reign. When they attribute all this not to themselves but to you, and seek not their own glory from it but yours, their confession will be acceptable in the sight of angels. Applauding these kings as they seek your glory, I continually say: “Let all the kings of the earth confess to you, O Lord.” Why? Surely because they have heard all the words of your mouth, announced partly through me, David, and partly through others—not only in Judea but among every nation—to all the kings of the earth walking in the ways. In those ways it is just, fitting, and salutary that they should praise not themselves but God:

VERS. 5. And sing in those ways of the Lord, because great is the glory of the Lord—not the glory of kings, unless perhaps of those who glory in the supreme King rather than themselves and humble themselves beneath him. That indeed is good and useful.

[Col. 0913D] VERS. 6. Because the Lord is exalted, and he regards the lowly; and he knows the proud from afar. It is very wonderful that the Most High regards lowly things from near at hand and knows lofty things from afar. This is clearly so because “he gives grace to the humble, but resists the proud” (Jas. 4:6). Although he does not love them, they are nevertheless not hidden from him, to whom every heart lies open, every will speaks, and from whom no secret is concealed. He both mercifully looks upon the humble heart and knows the proud from afar, because “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous,” the humble, “and his ears are toward their prayers. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. 33:16–17), especially when, in the height of their own hearts, they afflict the humble.

For their hearts are high because they are permitted to afflict the just; but because they are afflicted by the proud and high, the humble just are humbled more and more. Yet amid these things, I David, poor and humble, trust that my faith will not fail, because:

VERS. 7. If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will give me life—you who owed nothing to death but died for me; you who, by dying, destroyed our death and, by rising, restored life. In the midst of tribulation you will give me life by granting that I may love not only those who love me, but also those who hate me, praying for them with that love in which every blessed person lives: loving friends in God and enemies for God’s sake. Conversely, “he who does not love remains in death” (1 John 3:14), because true love is the life of the soul, just as the soul itself is the life of the body.

And therefore, as a body deprived of the soul is left dead, so a soul deprived of love for its neighbor is left dead. For this reason, guarding against falling into death, I do not wish to avenge myself, in accordance with that saying: “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath” (Rom. 12:19). Nevertheless, you who say, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. 32:35), have stretched out your hand over the wrath of my enemies, being more angry at my enemies than they were at me.

For since either King Saul, puffed up, or my son Absalom, led astray by Ahithophel’s wicked counsel and lifted up by his own pride, persecuted me, humble David, in their wrath, you stretched out your hand over their wrath, punishing them with a greater penalty than they could have inflicted upon me. For although they thought to deprive me [Col. 0914C] of the glory of an earthly kingdom, you deprived them of the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

Likewise, I Christ, the true David, to whom this psalm is entitled, prayed for the salvation of those who crucified me and did not know what they were doing. But over my enemies, the evil tenants, who, recognizing me as the heir and Lord of the vineyard entrusted to them, cast me outside the vineyard and killed me, you stretched out your hand. Just Father, whom the world did not know, but I knew you as the just Judge: you stretched out your hand over the wrath of my enemies when you destroyed the evil tenants miserably and leased your vineyard to other husbandmen. And your right hand saved me—whom they cast outside the vineyard and killed—by raising me from death and placing me, lifted above all the heavens, upon the throne of glory at your right hand as judge of the living and the dead, so that I might be King of kings who trust in you and on that account praise you, because they have obediently and intelligently heard all the words of your mouth, and sing in the ways of the Lord because great is the glory of the Lord. To each of these kings belongs what follows:

VERS. 8. The Lord will repay for me what I cannot repay, since I observe that apostolic saying: “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. For it is written: Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Rom. 12:19). Thus the Lord will repay for me, because when he judges, my enemies—the enemies of the Church—either die, are converted, or are otherwise humbled so that they cannot injure me, even if, by the Lord’s permission, they can weary me.

Alternatively: The Lord will repay for me, because the Lord Christ himself is that first fish caught by the hook of death, the first to rise from the depth of the sea, the firstborn from the dead, in whose mouth we find two didrachmas—that is, four drachmas, namely the four Gospels—by which we are freed from the harassment of this age and no longer remain debtors. For in him all our sins are paid, through him who owed nothing for himself, in whom the prince of this world found no sin for which to kill him.

There is indeed great consolation for me, or for any poor person of Christ, that he himself will repay my enemies for me. Yet in his repayment I remind him rather of mercy than of justice, saying to him: [Col. 0916A] “Lord, your mercy is for ever; do not despise the works of your hands.” Turn your face away from my sins, which are my works; but do not despise the works of your hands, which you made in me and in other human beings, hating none of the things you made. Rather, look upon them in that mercy which has no end, because your mercy is for ever: here giving good merits, by which you may render rewards enduring unto age upon age, because they will be eternal.

Glory to the Father, who magnified his holy name above every name. Glory to the Son, sanctified above every name, whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is mercy abiding for ever. Amen, amen.

## PSALM CXXXVIII

[Col. 0915]

[Col. 0915B] “O Lord, you have tested me and known me,” etc. The title of this psalm:

VERS. 1. UNTO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID.

It directs us to Christ, truly strong-handed, truly desirable, who in this psalm speaks now in his own person, now in the person of the Church, which is his body. For the leader of confessions and praises, saying to the Father concerning himself, “Lord, you have tested me and known me,” aims, by setting forth his perfect righteousness according to his humanity and his sublimity according to his divinity, to instruct the faithful in faith and in the righteousness of faith. Thus, believing him to be true God and true man, and led by his example, they may not shrink from being afflicted and trampled underfoot, hoping that, as they are companions of his sufferings, so [Col. 0915C] they will also be companions of his consolations. Therefore he says in thanksgiving:

“O Lord, you have tested me.” Lord Father, whom I acknowledge as Lord in the form of a servant, and whom I serve by bearing human weaknesses, you tested me in my passion. For since it is written, “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. 27:6), you tested me through the fire of passion. In it the earthenware of my flesh was not shattered by cracking apart, as happens with those who fail amid adversities that break them, since they are earthen and reprobate vessels.

But I remained so strong in the fire of passion, in which “my strength dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21:16), that it became clear that this very earthenware [Col. 0915D] of my flesh had been changed into gold, from which the golden candlestick was made, shining brightly with seven lamps. The place where this gold was to be melted was the Virgin’s womb. Entirely aglow with the fire of divinity, it could in no way have endured unless your power, most high Father, had overshadowed the Virgin herself.

But for this gold, melted in this manner, there was prepared a furnace of temptations when the devil tempted me in the desert, [Col. 0916B] where you, Lord, tested and knew me. Although I had been tested and known by you from eternity, you made known to angels and human beings this very thing: that I was a golden vessel which no temptation could break. Moreover, this testing was intensified when the gold of my flesh was beaten with many hammers of tribulation, by which it might be fashioned into a golden candlestick visible to the whole world.

And amid these tribulations you again tested me and knew me, for you made known to angels and human beings concerning me that I was stronger than that strong one who afflicted me through himself and his members, and who could neither overcome me nor press me so far that I, the true Job, should utter any foolish thing against you, Father. Through that most wicked smith, you tested me by many beatings and pressures. Amid these pressures:

[Col. 0916C] VERS. 2. You knew my sitting, by which I, innocent and patient Job, sitting on the dung-heap, was humbled for the human race lying in the dung-heap of sins and miseries in the depths. This sitting of mine you, Father, knew and approved. You knew it because you loved it, just as conversely you are said not to know those whom you do not love.

And because you loved me, to whom you also said, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7), and elsewhere said of me, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17)—because, I say, you so loved me, you surely knew and approved my sitting. Sitting on the dung-heap, I used the potsherd of my flesh, hardened by the fire of passion, to scrape the discharge from my members. They were so full of the ulcers of sins that they had to be scraped and cleansed, so that they might first be conformed to me sitting and humbled through humility itself, and then be conformed to me rising. For if they die with me, they shall also rise with me; if they have been planted together in the likeness of my passion, they shall also share my resurrection.

Such persons sit when they are patient in tribulation; they rise when they rejoice in hope. They sit by patiently and humbly bearing temporal misery; they rise by setting their minds on and desiring things above. They sit by confessing their sins; they rise justified by grace. To those thus sitting and rising, you, Father:

VERS. 3. Understood my thoughts and the thoughts of those who are mine from afar—that is, from eternity. For you are neither locally far off nor locally near, since you are everywhere and every place is in you. But temporality and eternity are far apart from one another, not by local distance but by a difference of mode: in the one there are beginning and end, in the other neither; the one moves in its mutability, the other stands in its immutability. You are therefore said to understand from afar [Col. 0917B] human and changeable thoughts, which you see in your unchangeable eternity.

You also see from afar those going away from you into the far country, where they feed swine. There indeed you understood my thoughts—that is, those of my members—because, when the prodigal son there thinks within himself, “I will go to my father” (Luke 15:18), you meet him as he returns while he is still far away. Kissing him, you give him the certain sign of your grace: after the confession of the mouth, the justification of the heart. For you not only forgive sins to one who confesses, but also give garments of various graces: the first robe, ring, and shoes. By these it is shown that you have searched out my path and my line—or my direction—that is, the path and direction of those who are mine.

A path belongs to silent thoughts, ways to human actions, direction to just judgments, and a line to a boundary or inheritance, because the ancients customarily marked off the boundaries of fields and inheritances with a line. All these things, both mine and those of my members, you have searched out.

VERS. 4. And you foresaw all my ways and those of my members, while also understanding this: that there is no speech upon my tongue.

Speech is then upon the tongue alone, and not in the heart or in deed, when confession of sin does not arise from the root of a penitent and contrite heart. Such was Saul, when rebuked by Samuel for his sin, who said: “I have sinned; but now honor me before the elders,” [Col. 0917D] etc. (1 Sam. 15:30). By saying this, he showed that he grieved not for the sin committed but for the loss of honor.

Likewise Judas, saying, “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27:4), showed that he grieved less for the sin he committed than for his plan having been frustrated. So too his forerunner Ahithophel, seeing that his plan had been frustrated, hanged himself in grief. Judas, certainly, imitating him in guilt and punishment, took his own life by the noose, because the speech by which he had said, “I have sinned,” was only on his tongue and not in his heart.

This interpretation is supported by another translation, which reads: “There is no deceit on my tongue.” The tongue of those who speak in this way is not my tongue, because they are not my members. But upon my tongue, or that of those who are mine, [Col. 0918A] there is no speech without reality. For when any one of them says, “I have sinned”—as I David, when grieved that I had sinned concerning Uriah, said “I have sinned!” at the rebuke of the prophet Nathan (2 Sam. 12:13)—there was no mere speech or deceit upon my tongue.

Likewise, when I Peter said, “I love you” (John 21:15), a second and a third time, there was no mere speech upon my tongue. Likewise, when I, the prodigal son, said, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you” (Luke 15:18), there was no speech without reality upon my tongue. You yourself are witness of this, and you do not need another’s testimony, because:

VERS. 5. Behold, O Lord, you have known all my latter things and ancient things.

My latter things, when I fed swine; my ancient things, when I asked for my share of the property. Ancient things, when we fell; latter things, when we came to this mortality, which is the latter and final punishment for those returning to you, Father. In these latter things you formed me for labor, saying: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3:19); and you placed upon me your avenging hand, which might beneficially weigh down the proud in order to raise the humble. Thus, with your hand made heavy upon me because of me—that is, because of my sin—

VERS. 6. Your knowledge became wonderful, marvellous, and incomprehensible, because it is not easy for me to contemplate you, whom I proudly abandoned when I fled from your face, ashamed in paradise at my nakedness. Thus, on my account—namely, because my fault required it—your knowledge, once visible and lovable to me, became hidden [Col. 0918C] and marvellous, since you hid your face from me and I became troubled. Hence I am unable of myself to apprehend or comprehend knowledge of you.

For I consider this in myself: it is no wonder that knowledge of you has become difficult and marvellous to me, because I cannot even know myself, and knowledge of my own essence is strengthened beyond the powers of my intellect. Much more is knowledge of you strengthened beyond the powers of human understanding, and I shall not be able to attain it.

Alternatively: I, Christ, the first and the last—first by divinity, last by humanity; or first, before whom there is none, and last, after whom there is none; or first in resurrection, because firstborn of the dead, and last and most despised in the passion, because I was reckoned among the wicked and condemned to the most shameful death—I confess to you, Father, and praise your providence and care concerning me, because you knew all things, my latter things and ancient things: latter in humanity, ancient in eternal divinity.

You also formed me as a human being, so that I might be most beautiful above the children of humankind: I, the son of a human mother and likewise Son of God the Father, to whom it is rightly said: “Proceed prosperously, attend to your beauty and loveliness, and reign” (Ps. 44:5). Likewise in Isaiah: “Who is this who comes from Edom, in dyed garments from Bozrah? This one, beautiful in his robe, striding in the abundance of his strength” (Isa. 63:1).

You indeed, my Father, eternal Father, first formed the human being [Col. 0919A] from the mud of the earth, and afterwards breathed into him “the breath of life,” by which “he became a living soul” (Gen. 2:7). But you formed me, the second Adam, from the blessed earth, to which it was said, “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:28), not merely into a living soul, so that I might live a mortal life, but also into a life-giving spirit. By this spirit, death being swallowed up through my death, I might not only live eternal life but also give life to others united to me. Thus you formed me into a life-giving spirit.

But before I gave this Spirit, or made my faithful people alive by it—for this Spirit was not given as long as I had not been glorified, nor did living, life-giving water flow from me, the rock, before I was struck by the rod of the cross, upon which, pierced by a lance, I sent forth the water flowing from the right side [Col. 0919B] of the temple of my body—before this, I say, when I was not yet crowned with glory and honor, you placed upon me your hand. Under it, as it chastened and scourged me, I was beaten while paying what I had not taken: I, free from sin, chastened for the sins of others.

Then your knowledge, formerly contemptible because the world, blinded by original and actual sins, did not know you, became marvellous when I gave the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, and when that same Spirit, sent into their understanding, filled the hearts of those who received the same Spirit first on the day of the resurrection and then on the day of Pentecost. From that time your knowledge was strengthened: formerly as if weak, it afterward prevailed and grew strong against the wisdom of this world, because through me it was strengthened against and above all the philosophers, tyrants, magicians, and diviners of this world.

“And I shall not be able to attain it.” This is said not in the voice of the omnipotent head, but in the voice of the members, to whom it is said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). In them Christ himself, though omnipotent in himself, is still made weak, imprisoned, hungry, thirsty, naked, and needy. In their voice he says: “Your knowledge has become marvellous through me,” because through my fault—indeed, through the fault of those who are mine—it has been so hidden that they can admire it rather than investigate it. It has so prevailed that every one of my members can truly say: “It has been strengthened, and I shall not be able to attain it,” because it is incomprehensible even to the blessed angels.

Although this can fittingly be said of the members, I, the assumed human being, can also say in my own person concerning the wisdom united to me: “It has been strengthened, and I shall not be able to hold it.” I shall not be able from myself, but I shall be able from you, Father, because I am not from myself but from you. Hence elsewhere I say: “I can do nothing of myself” (John 5:19).

Yet because the incarnate wisdom of God, like the angel sent to Jacob, permitted itself to be held, I, David wrestling like another Jacob, shall indeed not be able to seize it—I am not strong enough to seize it of myself—but strengthened by you, God, I shall hold you and say to you: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Gen. 32:26). Nor shall I flee from you, but to you: from you angry to you appeased.

VERS. 7–8. For where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from [Col. 0920A] your face? Neither from east nor west, nor from deserted mountains, is there a place of escape open; neither above nor below. For if I ascend into heaven, you are there. If I exalt myself too highly, I find you checking me. If I am lifted into heaven through false righteousness, you are there, rejecting false righteousness by true, painted righteousness by sincere. If, by sinning and condemning my sins, yet making light of them though they are great, I descend into the abyss and, refusing to confess them, say, “Who sees me?” you are present to punish. Yet I find where I may flee from your wrath.

VERS. 9. If I take up my wings at dawn, or, as other codices have it, “in direction,” and dwell at the furthest parts of the sea. If, repenting, at dawn—in the very beginning of good conduct—or “in direction,” so that I am neither raised by presumption nor plunged into despair, I take up the wings of twofold love which I lost by sinning; and if I dwell not in the midst of the sea, where danger is great, but at the furthest parts of the sea, where the shore of eternal stability is near, there I can have a safe refuge from the storms of the sea. I can come there and rest there, not by my own strength but by your hand, my God, rowing for me.

VERS. 10. For, when my prayer to you—“Draw me after you”—has been heard, your hand will lead me there; and, lest I depart, your right hand will hold me, because “delights are at your right hand unto the end” (Ps. 15:11). Held by these delights at your right hand, I shall make light of all the good things that are at your left hand. For “length [Col. 0920C] of days is in your right hand” (Prov. 3:16), a length which is infinite eternity, infinitely surpassing all temporal goods that are at your left hand.

Alternatively: I, Christ, the true David, to whom this psalm is entitled, weary from the journey, sat beside the well as a weak human being—indeed, truly weak in passibility and mortality—yet pressing down beneath me the well of fleshly desire and worldly wisdom. Whoever drinks from its water will thirst again, because such water does not quench thirst but increases it.

But if I take up my wings, the wings of divinity—my wings, accordingly, because they are so attached to me, a human being divinely conceived and born, that on account of them I am rightly likened to a flying eagle—if therefore I take up my wings and dwell in the furthest parts of the sea, upon the shore of everlasting rest, then it will be clear to the faithful that you knew my sitting, in which I, the true Jonah, was in the depth of the sea, and my resurrection, in which the sea-monster vomited me out onto the dry shore. For your hand will lead me there, and, that I may remain there, your right hand will hold me: namely, your power and wisdom united to me as a human being.

VERS. 11–12. And I said: “Perhaps darkness will trample me.” This was said ironically, in mockery of those who thought that darkness would trample him. But seriously and truthfully he adds: “And night is my illumination in my delights,” because just as [Col. 0921A] at night the firstborn of Egypt were struck, Pharaoh the king was troubled, and the people of Israel were saved and delivered, so it will be in the night of my resurrection. It will be illuminated like day, now that the sun of righteousness has risen and the darkness of sins has been driven away through me, the true light enlightening every human being coming into this world.

Alternatively: I, David, sinner and penitent, fearing the long road set before me all the way to the ends of the sea, and especially those perils of the sea amid the darkness of night, when the wind is contrary, said: “Perhaps darkness will trample me down.” So many evils of this world overflow that I am compelled constantly to say: “Perhaps darkness will trample me down.” The flesh, desiring against the spirit through the law of the members resisting the law of God, brings such great [Col. 0921B] darkness upon the mind, which consents to God’s law, that I am compelled constantly to say: “Perhaps darkness will trample me down.” Likewise, the multitude of evildoers, who are darkness, swells so greatly against me, the one and only Church, or against me, one faithful person, that I am forced to cry out: “Perhaps darkness will trample me down.” He who does not confess his sins makes darkness yet darker; but if he confesses them, God gives light.

The night of our night—that is, of miserable and dark human life—is the adversity of the world; its day is prosperity. But if God dwells in the soul, promising another light and teaching it neither to rejoice in prosperity nor to be broken by adversity, a person begins to use these things indifferently. Thus, the night of this world is to him like its day, and at every time [Col. 0921C] he blesses God as Job did. And if this is so, darkness will not trample down one whom light does not exalt. Night, which had been terror, has become an illuminated delight. Whence comes this indifference to you? Because the inner Possessor holds not only the heart—that is, the thoughts—but also the reins—that is, the delights—so that the light of night does not delight, but the light of his wisdom.

When the heart flies back to God, God enlightening it and possessing the reins, how great is the exultation and abundance of one who says: “Night is illumination amid my delights!” The apostle James invited us to these delights when he said: “Count it all joy, brethren, when you fall into various trials, knowing that tribulation produces patience, etc.” (Jas. 1:2–3). The apostle enjoyed these delights both in night and in day, when he said: “We glory in the hope of the glory of the children [Col. 0921D] of God”—this was delighting in the day. And he added: “Not only so, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience; patience, tested character; and tested character, hope; and hope does not put to shame, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” (Rom. 5:2 ff.).

Thus night is illuminated by the lamp by whose light the drachma is found, in which the image of God shines forth the more brightly the more thoroughly it has been cleansed and polished by various trials and tribulations. Such a night, I say, so illuminated, has many delights, because you, true Wisdom shining in the vessel of assumed flesh, illuminate darkness while by the night-time scourges you train the children of light. Once they have been trained, night shall be illuminated as day, because for those who love you with filial love, whether scourging or consoling, [Col. 0922A] all things, both adverse and prosperous, “work together for good”—but only for “those who are called saints according to the purpose” (Rom. 8:28). Among their number I, David, I the penitent, trust that I shall be joined.

**VERSE 13.** For you have possessed my reins by giving me a purpose of continence, so that, although I feel concupiscence in my reins, it nevertheless does not reign in my mortal body so as to fulfill the unlawful desires customary to me in Babylon. Born and long resident there, I did not regard the light and darkness of night indifferently, since I was still associated with the children of night and darkness—until you received me from the womb of my mother, or of the Synagogue, as you did him who said: “But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb [Col. 0922B] and called me through his grace, I did not immediately yield to flesh and blood” (Gal. 1:15–16). Or certainly from Babylon, in which, born and reared, I was long an exile from the city of Jerusalem. From the womb of this mother you received me, drawing me back from worldly and vain conduct into Zion—you, Jesus, great priest and rebuilder of the city of Jerusalem, which is our mother. In her,

**VERSE 14.** I shall confess to you, because you have been magnified terribly: you who, born a little child from a mother, have been raised and magnified up to the session of the most high Father, terribly and wonderfully at once. Terribly with regard to the Jews, whom you left blinded; wonderfully [Col. 0922C] with regard to the nations, among whom your wondrous works shone forth, and who believed in you when those works were disclosed through the apostles. In this matter your wonderful knowledge has been strengthened, and I shall not be able to grasp it; but in astonishment I cry: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, etc.” (Rom. 11:33). I cannot, I say, by myself; but I can to some extent through you. Therefore I venerate your wonderful works, and my soul knows exceedingly—now in part, but afterward as it is itself known.

We citizens of Jerusalem, delivered from captivity and still awaiting, are not yet secure, because precisely in that in which we marvel at you, you are terrible; and therefore we rejoice with trembling, lest through pride we lose what we received through humility. My soul knows this exceedingly, that is, very greatly: for formerly your knowledge was wonderful to me from myself, and I could not attain it; but now I can, because you illuminate night, possess the reins of your servant, whom you drew from his mother’s womb and, having drawn him out, received. Hence I know that:

**VERSE 15.** My bone is not hidden from you, which you made in secret, once concealed in the hidden place of flesh, that it might sustain the weakness of the flesh. Therefore you said to one of your bones: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). This was as though you had said: You who are strong—called *osseus* (“bony”) from *os* (“bone”), as Peter is named by me from the rock—strengthen your brothers, still weak and burdened with the frailty of flesh, by which you too are in part burdened, you who will deny me three times. [Col. 0923A] But afterward, strengthened, you will confess for the third time that you love me. Therefore I entrust to you for feeding the sheep still frail and weighed down by bodily weakness, and for establishing through you, Peter, upon me the Rock.

When you spoke these things, my bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret; it was also foreknown when the first man, in the figure of the second man, said: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2:23). By these words the Holy Spirit signified that in the Church there would be strong and weak persons, as bones and flesh, perfect and imperfect. Concerning these imperfect persons, I, Christ, I, the second Adam, I, the bridegroom of the Church which has bones and flesh from me—holding firm and weak, perfect and imperfect members in the unity of its body [Col. 0923B]—cry to you, Father, and say:

**VERSE 16.** Your eyes saw my imperfection, when you predestined for me, your Son the bridegroom, a bride having within herself flesh and bones, perfect and imperfect persons. Then your eyes saw my imperfection with the merciful gaze of compassion; and in your book—which book I am—there shall be written, indeed they are already written, all of them, and no one among them shall perish, because my substance is preserved in the lower parts of the earth, that is, among the weak. And no one among them shall perish; or, no one among them shall be the author of salvation, lest anyone say: “I belong to Paul; I belong to Cephas”; but let each say: “I belong to Christ” (1 Cor. 1:12). For only through me, Christ, the Sun of righteousness, shall days be formed. I formed the twelve apostles [Col. 0923C] like twelve hours; and none among or from them perished except the son of perdition, the son of night, who also went out into the night, leaving room for another, so that another might receive his episcopal office, worthily to be numbered among the ministers of light and children of day. Such ministers of salvation, indeed, shall be despised in their own eyes and contemptible to the world, like the refuse and offscouring of this world.

**VERSE 17.** But to me, Christ—or to me, a Christian and believer sound in wisdom—your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured; their authority has been exceedingly strengthened.

On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says in Homily 28 [Note: [Col. 0923D] *Homilies on the Gospels*.]: A friend is called, as it were, a guardian of the soul. Therefore, because the Psalmist foresaw God’s elect, separated from love of this [Col. 0923D] world, preserving God’s will in heavenly commandments, he marvelled at God’s friends, saying: “But to me your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured.” And as though we immediately sought to have the reason for so great an honour made known to us by him, he at once added: “Their authority has been exceedingly strengthened.” Behold: the elect subdue the flesh, strengthen the spirit, command demons, shine with virtues, despise present things, preach the eternal homeland by word and conduct, love it even by dying, and reach it through torments. They may be killed, but they cannot be bent. Has their authority, then, been exceedingly strengthened? But perhaps so great persons are few? He added:

[Col. 0924A] **VERSE 18.** I shall count them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand. [Note: [Col. 0924D] The same, ibid.] We see the whole world filled with martyrs. By now we ourselves, whom we see, are almost not as numerous as the witnesses of the truth whom we possess. Thus they are countable to God, but multiplied beyond the sand to us, who cannot comprehend how many they are. But whoever has reached this dignity of being called a friend of God should look upon himself within himself; and he should attribute none of the gifts he has received to his own merits, lest he break out into enmity.

While these witnesses and friends of mine bear witness, it is known to believers that I, Christ, rose from the dead and am still alive with you in the life by which you, Father, live—though my enemies thought this life had been taken from me by death’s setting and by the sealed tomb. But I, [Col. 0924B] though buried in body and though my soul descended to the lower parts of the earth to despoil hell, am nevertheless with you upon the high throne. There too I am with you in such a way that, as you, Father, are hidden, so I too am still hidden from unbelievers who lack the eyes of faith. Yet it shall come to pass that all flesh shall see me, salvation, seated in a manifest judgment that is as yet hidden. Therefore I am still with you, Father, in concealment, as you are concealed. I am now with you in the hidden judgment in which:

**VERSES 19–20.** If you kill sinners, you, Father, I also shall kill them by separating them from my living body, saying to them: “Men of blood, depart from me,” because you say in thought—which is worse than if you said it [Col. 0924C] with the mouth—you say, I say, concerning my friends, though you are enemies: “Let them take their cities in vanity” [Vulgate: “your cities”]. This is what you, enemies of mine and of my people, say: you judge cities and ecclesiastical congregations to be vain, whereas you yourselves are vain, and all that you do is vain—especially in the schism by which you depart from me. But I too depart from you, not so much in body as in mind: I do not hate you, but your iniquity. From this conviction I say to you, my God:

**VERSE 21.** Shall I not hate those who hate you, O Lord?

Alternatively: If you, God, kill sinners, saying to them, “Men of blood, depart from me,” then, cut off and killed, they shall take their cities in vanity, forming sects allied not in the truth of the Christian name but in the vanity of Antichrist. As though those who are cut off [Col. 0924D] should ask and say: “Why do you call us men of blood, who have killed no one, seeing that we are unarmed clergy?” The answer is: You are rightly called men of blood because you speak in thought, which is worse than if you spoke with the mouth. What do you say? Namely, such things as cause you to be judged murderers, as is written concerning you and your like: “For they themselves, being murderers, have stored up evils; foolish and malicious men have hated wisdom and become guilty in their thoughts.” Therefore, while you waste away in murderous hatred, I, the Church, rightly say to you: “Men of blood, depart from me,” because you speak in thought such things as prove you to be men of blood and deceitful.

Suppose, then, that [Col. 0925A] such murderers take their cities in vanity, creating vain and evil sects of perdition, fortified in the manner of a city by the sayings of teachers or even holy Fathers twisted to suit their will, so that they appear to have many defenses in their cities and cannot be overcome by arguments—especially when secular power protects them, as many powerful persons protected the Arians. Suppose, I say, that they thus take their cities in vanity: shall I, David, a man of the Church, therefore cease to oppose such people, even though I cannot overcome them? Should not good hatred be returned for evil to those who hate you, O Lord, so that not persons but their errors are hated? Knowing this, I hated those who hate you, O Lord. Since I could neither [Col. 0925B] overcome nor even disturb them, I burned with zeal for your house, and:

**VERSE 22.** With perfect hatred I hated those enemies of yours, to such a degree that they also became my enemies; for while I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause and became enemies to me.

On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0925C] *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, ch. 32.]: To hate God’s enemies perfectly is both to love what they have been made, and to rebuke what they do; to restrain the conduct of the wicked, and to benefit their lives. It must indeed be considered how great a fault it is, when one ceases from rebuke and keeps peace with the worst people, if so great a prophet offered this to God as a sacrifice: that for the Lord’s sake he stirred up against himself the enmities of the wicked.

[Col. 0925C] But because in disputes and contentions of this sort, in which the wicked contend, as it were, against the good and the good against the wicked, stains easily creep in, whether in speech or thought, you, O God:

**VERSE 23.** Test me—you to whom every heart lies open, every will speaks, and from whom no secret is concealed. To you I continually say: “Test me, God; make me approved, God.” At the beginning of this psalm I said to you: “Lord, you have tested me”; and now at the psalm’s end I say: “Test me.” You tested me in me, Christ, in me the head, in whom the ruler of this [Col. 0926A] world found nothing blameworthy. But because my ministers, however much they may be tested, do not lack stains while they wander in the body—for which reason the fishermen themselves must wash their nets in the troubled sea after drawing them for the catching of fish—at the end of their fishing let all say, let each say, let me too, the Psalmist, say: “Test me, God, and know my heart,” making me know my heart. I, Peter the fisherman, did not yet know it when I presumed above my fellow disciples, and from that presumption fell into the fault of threefold denial.

But afterward you questioned me, saying to me for the third time: “Do you love me?” And when I answered, “I love you,” you knew my paths: both those in which, girded by you, I had walked where I wished, and those to which you directed me, saying: “Feed [Col. 0926B] my lambs” (John 21:15 ff.). Therefore, after Peter’s example, I, David, I who sing in this psalm, say to you, my God: “Test me, God, and know my heart; question me and know my past and future paths,” wiping away the former stains contracted on those paths, because unless you wash my feet, I shall have no part with you. Then, lest I henceforth soil my feet, lead me into the eternal way, in which there is no stain. But first:

**VERSE 24.** See—making me too see—whether there is a way of iniquity in me, so that when this iniquity has been abolished, I may henceforth walk among those of whom it is said: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118:1). But since my strength does not suffice for this, O God, remove the way of iniquity from me (ibid., 29), if you see it in me—to you I continually say: “See whether there is a way of iniquity in me, and lead me in the eternal way,” by which, with you drawing and leading me, I may attain the homeland of eternal brightness—you who are the way, the truth, and the life.

Glory to the Lord Father, to whom the Son says at the beginning of the psalm: “Lord, you have tested me and known me.” Glory to the Son himself who says this. Glory to the Holy Spirit, filling the whole world, concerning whom this psalm says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit?”

## PSALM CXXXIX

[Col. 0925]

[Col. 0925D] “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man,” etc. Title:

**VERSE 1. A PSALM OF DAVID, UNTO THE END.**

This is clear. This psalm is the beginning of the final division, in which all the righteous and perfect alike pray and confess with one voice, as though from one body: “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man; deliver me from the unjust man.” In saying this and the rest, they pray to the Lord that he may preserve in them perfection of faith, and [Col. 0926D] may deliver them from perversity and faithlessness—indeed, from the attack of malignant spirits, who, lying in wait around the end of this life, sharpen their tongues to accuse and convict. For because this is the last division [thus the manuscript], we rightly look from here to our own end, when the ruler of the world comes and seeks in each of us something that is his own. Therefore everyone anxious about that day and watchful for that approaching hour says: “Keep me from the hand of the sinner.” And afterward: [Col. 0927A] “Lord, Lord, the strength of my salvation, you have overshadowed my head in the day of battle.” And immediately: “Do not hand me over, O Lord, from my desire to the sinner,” etc.

The body of Christ, placed among the wicked and not yet possessing good except in hope, where there shall be full exultation, groans and prays in this psalm, by which it invites us to pray. First it sets forth which enemies and which evils have risen up; secondly, what help it has against evils, at: “I said to the Lord: You are my God”; thirdly, what the enemies’ evils are, at: “The head of their circuit”; and it concludes the psalm in blessedness at: “And the righteous shall dwell with your countenance.” Therefore it cries and says among the wicked: “O Lord, deliver me,” and repeats:

**VERSE 2.** Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil [Col. 0927B] or malignant man—that is, from the prince himself, who is figuratively called a man. Hence in the Gospel: “An enemy man has done this.” Observe that when he said “from the malignant,” he added, as though explaining it, “from the unjust,” wishing to signify that all unjust persons are malignant. There are indeed many unjust persons who do not appear malignant, yet they are like those who are not cruel and do not oppress others, but are nevertheless lustful and given to pleasures. Even if they do not appear to injure others, they injure themselves and are therefore unjust. Yet, if one considers the matter deeply, they are malignant because they harm by example and cause us afterward to struggle to overcome what they have caused.

For oppression proceeds from pleasure itself. Once someone living luxuriously has spent what he possessed, he plunders. Thus [Col. 0927C] soft thorns at the root send forth from the root what will prick. But just as, if the root is burned, the thorn does not grow, so if excess is corrected, plunder will not be nourished. I said in the singular: “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man, from the unjust man,” namely from the devil, who is figuratively called man and “man” (*vir*) because he is strong. Yet because this man, this *vir*, has many associates, I pass from the singular number to the plural, saying:

**VERSE 3.** Those who have devised iniquities in their heart, all day long prepared battles. All day long, not wearied by the length of the delay, they devised iniquities in their heart, sometimes putting on a show of good things with their lips, but intending evil in their heart. For when the wickedness long hidden suddenly [Col. 0927D] breaks forth, all day long they prepared battles to be waged against the good in three ways: by heart, tongue, and hand. For in heart they devised iniquity—or, as another text has it, “wicked deeds”—and from that very wickedness they all day long, that is continually, prepared battles, either by heresies attacking the truth and purity of faith, or by schisms tearing apart the unity of ecclesiastical peace. And in order that they might do this more effectively:

**VERSE 4.** They sharpened their tongues, so that they might possess polished words, honed by a certain whetstone of practice. They did this like serpents—indeed, in imitation of that serpent which was the devil’s instrument for deceiving the first woman, speaking sophistically, promising one thing and intending another: [Col. 0928A] namely, promising good things, such as knowledge of good and evil in likeness to God, but intending the evils which followed from such presumption, the chief of which was the death of the soul. The Lord had foretold this, saying: “On whatever day you eat from the tree of knowledge, you shall die the death” (Gen. 2:17).

The tongue of this serpent was sharp, and by its example the tongues of heretics are sharp for deceiving or wounding first the female sex—that is, ordinary and simple people—and then the strong. They speak smoothly indeed, but beneath their lips is the venom of asps. In the serpent there are craft and a harmful deceit. Thus the serpent has no feet, lest its approach be heard; it is gentle indeed, but not straight, because it moves in winding paths. So the perverse [Col. 0928B] creep craftily to do harm under a gentle touch, bearing hidden venom. For although their lips sound smooth, the venom of asps is beneath their lips, because in sweet and tinkling words they offer falsehood, calling good evil and evil good, putting darkness for light and light for darkness, bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter. Against the prince of such persons, the devil, I pray, saying:

**VERSE 5.** Keep me, O Lord, from the hand of the sinner, who is strong—hence called “the ruler of this world” (John 12:31; 14:30). And against his members I pray, saying: Deliver me from unjust men, who have devised to trip up my steps while they prepare pits of lies beside the way of truth, [Col. 0928C] and:

**VERSE 6.** They hid a snare for me, because the proud, driven by the spur of pride, do not wish to be conquered but always to conquer, even though they speak falsely and hide a snare of falsehood under the appearance of truth. When I say “the proud,” I briefly set forth under this name the whole body of the devil, which will raise itself most of all against God in Antichrist, who “exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped, so that he sits in God’s temple, showing himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. 2:4). And because every proud person is envious, like the devil, who envied humanity what he himself, once lost, had lost, they are not content with their own perdition but strive also to destroy me by drawing me into the fellowship of their perdition.

Therefore they stretched out cords for a snare. [Col. 0928D] Those who add sins to sins—as I, David, added murder to adultery—twist and stretch out for themselves a cord by which they are dragged with hands and feet bound, unless they break that cord through repentance, as I broke it when I repented. But my enemies and God’s enemies stretch out their cords, unwilling to shorten their sins through true repentance; extending and drawing those cords out far too long, they prepared a snare for me, so that, seeing their prosperity in sin, I might not recoil but imitate their iniquity. Beside the path they set a stumbling-block for me: not in the way, but beside it, placing obstacles because they tried to overthrow me not by truth but by a certain likeness of truth. Praying against them:

[Col. 0929A] **VERSE 7.** I said to the Lord: “You are my God; hear the voice of my supplication.” Voice properly belongs to living beings when uttered with the awareness of a living being through the passages of the throat. The collision of stones, the ringing of cymbals, and things of that kind make sound, but not voice. They resemble those who pray without the understanding of faith and love. Hence the Apostle says: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels but do not have love, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. 13:1). Therefore the voice belongs to one who prays and pours out petitions in faith and love. Thus, conscious of faith and love, I say: “Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication,” by which I cry to you, saying:

**VERSE 8.** Lord, Lord, whose servant I am [Col. 0929B] both a natural servant by creation and a purchased servant by redemption, the strength of my salvation, because I have no salvation except from you, who grant perseverance; without it I cannot be saved. “For whoever perseveres” in good “to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22). But that I may persevere in a good purpose, I ask it from you, who overshadowed my head in the day of battle.

The inward enemy is carnal lust. While that enemy attacked me, you overshadowed my head, defending the head of the inward person, which is the rational mind, so that, not yielding at all to the heat and movement of carnal lust, it might delight in the law of God, which says: “You shall not covet” (Rom. 7:7). Thus cooled, I should not walk after the lusts [Col. 0929C] of the flesh, but should hold to that counsel which says: “Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh” (Gal. 5:16).

But the outward enemy is the hostile man sowing tares, when he mixes evils among good things, either personally or through his servants, evil angels and evil human beings. While that enemy attacked me and provoked me to be scorched by the heat of pride and despise those below me, to waste away in the heat of envy and envy those above me, to be inflamed with the heat of anger and repay evil for evil, abuse for abuse, curse for curse, openly or secretly, and at the same time burn with the heat of avarice and covet what belongs to another—you were present with me in the day of battle, overshadowing my head: that is, cooling my mind by your grace and extinguishing the flames [Col. 0929D] of evil desires, as I, calling on you in the day of battle, have constantly said:

> Extinguish the flames of conflicts,  
> Take away harmful heat,  
> Grant bodily health,  
> And true peace of heart.

If, while I sang this hymn, you were present to me, lending a gracious ear and overshadowing my head in the day of battle. But because the battle is not yet ended, and because in it the domestic enemy is most to be feared and guarded against—namely the disordered desire of one’s own will, which, if the devil finds it in me, he can kill me with it as with a sword—I pray:

**VERSE 9.** Do not hand over my desire to the sinner, lest I become like those of whom it is said: “God handed [Col. 0930A] them over to the desires of their hearts, to do what is unfitting” (Rom. 1:24).

Another translation has: “Do not hand me over from my desire to the sinner.” This means: Henceforth may your shade, by which you have frequently overshadowed me in the day of battle, avail me, so that I may not suffer the heat from myself, from my evil desire, through which room is made for the devil. Without this, however fiercely the enemy rages with his entire army gathered from evil men and angels, he does no harm. Against them I need your help, since they have considered with cunning and long deliberation how to destroy me. But you, helper in due seasons, do not abandon me, lest perhaps they be exalted and boast in their strength against me—indeed, against you. [Col. 0930B] For my victory over them shall be not my glory but yours. Deign to magnify that glory in me, little David, in me, however insignificant an imitator of David, lest the uncircumcised Philistine, the devil with his fellow soldiers, boast, as Goliath boasted when he said to the children of Israel: “Why have you come prepared for battle?” (1 Sam. 17:8). On seeing him, the children of Israel fled and did not dare resist. But at last, felled by sling and stone and slain by his own sword, he gave great occasion to your people, O God, for glorying in you, and to the enemies for confusion and humiliation.

As it happened then, so let it now happen, with justice triumphing over the unjust, lest perhaps they be exalted. For as the good angels rejoice over one sinner repenting, so [Col. 0930C] the devil who deceives, evil angels, and malignant persons together rejoice when one person is seduced. Therefore, because such persons have devised against me, grant help against their counsel; do not abandon me, lest perhaps they be exalted. As I prayed, desiring this for my enemies, so it shall happen to them, so that they have no occasion to glory in their strength, because:

**VERSE 10.** The head of their circuit: the labour of their lips shall cover them. “The ungodly walk about in a circuit” (Ps. 11:9), because they seek shifting and temporal things, in which they do not find the end of their desires. For whoever drinks from the water of temporal desire shall thirst again; and by his thirst is drawn into a circuit in which he finds no end to his journey. It is otherwise with one who [Col. 0930D] seeks eternal things and walks and runs straight ahead: he will at last finish his course, like him who said: “I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth a crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (2 Tim. 4:7–8). Thus all who hunger and thirst for righteousness shall find an end to their thirst, for they shall be filled. Not so the ungodly: they shall not be filled, because, walking in a circuit, they do not find the end of their course; and the things for which they thirst here, they shall thirst for also in hell, like the rich man who asked for a drop of water and did not receive it.

But what is the head of their circuit but diabolical pride? From it this circuit took its beginning, with him going before who says: “I have gone around the earth and walked through it” (Job 1:7). This head of their circuit, namely pride, is also the labour of their lips because, [Col. 0931A] when each proud person is ashamed to be convicted by the truth of his lie, he labours in turn at lying, because one who lies labours.

On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0931D] *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, ch. 2.]: Nothing is safer for preservation than purity, nothing easier to say than truth. For when one is compelled to uphold one’s falsehood, the heart is wearied by hard labour. Hence it is written: “The labour of their lips shall cover them.” What now fills then covers, because the thing which now expands a person’s mind by flattering restlessness later weighs it down by harsh recompense. Hence Jeremiah says: “They taught their tongues to speak falsehood; they laboured in order to act wickedly” (Jer. 9:5). As if it were plainly said: Those who could have been friends of truth without labour labour in order to sin; and because they refuse to [Col. 0931B] live simply, they exert labour in order to die.

Alternatively: “The labour of their lips shall cover them,” because one who feigns what he says labours, whereas truth is spoken easily. Thus the labour of the lips is called falsehood, and it shall cover its author and fabricator; for the very thing by which he is protected and defended for a time will also overcome and crush him when his falsehood is disclosed and the liar is refuted by his own assertion. But that the liars themselves, especially heretics and schismatics, may be more forcibly crushed:

**VERSE 11.** Coals shall fall upon them; you shall cast them into fire; they shall not stand amid miseries. Coals of fire—or saints burning and shining in the fire—are defenders of truth. Brought forward as authorities against liars, they shall fall [Col. 0931C] upon them, crush them, and burn them in the fire by which they enlighten willing hearers and torment ill-disposed ones. Hence they say: “We are the good odour of Christ: to some an odour of life unto life, to others an odour of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:15–16). Through these coals you shall cast down those who resist truth, and once cast down they shall be impatient. Therefore they shall not stand firm amid the miseries of the present life, in which the good are tested and shall possess their souls; but the ungodly shall fail and shall not advance. Yet among them there are some who are deceived, some deceivers, and some simple persons, as though speechless, for whom there is some hope of conversion.

**VERSE 12.** But the talkative man shall not be guided on the earth: one whose will and desire is to speak, who does not attend to what he says provided only that he flatters itching ears or persuades others of what he urges, whether true or false. Speaking against this vice of talkativeness, the apostle James says: “Let every person be swift to hear but slow to speak” (Jas. 1:19). For it would be more perfect if all listened to the bridegroom, as John says: “The bridegroom’s friend stands and hears, and rejoices because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29). Would that all were so perfect as to need no teacher, as in the kingdom of heaven, where all shall be taught by God.

But because this blessedness does not belong to this life, it is sometimes necessary to speak for the sake of the unlearned, with the intention that they may become learned and [Col. 0932A] no longer need human teaching. For one who always wishes to teach always wishes his hearers to remain unlearned; such a teacher is convicted of envy, always desiring to be found wiser than the rest. This teacher should be exhorted not, being envious himself, to teach his envy to others. Therefore let joy consist in inwardly hearing the bridegroom, even while the voice of teaching sounds outwardly, so that the will may always be to hear the bridegroom, but speaking to others may arise from necessity. One who speaks thus, even if speaking much, will not be a talkative man who shall never be guided on earth—that is, in the present Church—because no human being can tame his tongue.

But because what is impossible for human beings is possible for God, and what is impossible on earth is possible in heaven, such persons are not to be despaired of; rather, the nets of prayer must be spread wide to catch them, since they cannot be caught by the nets of preaching. Meanwhile let the faithful servant enter into the joy of his Lord, so that inwardly he may hear what he speaks outwardly; and let our joy be inward, where the Bridegroom is heard. For one who delights in going out and in being heard rather than hearing is puffed up; and, because what he loves is outside, he will be cast into the outer darkness. Therefore let joy belong to inward things, and in outward things let there be necessity, not choice. Otherwise, one is unjust who neglects inward good and desires to embrace outward things, which are vain, since they vanish amid the embrace. Evils shall seize this wicked man in destruction.

All flee evils, both good and bad; yet evils seize all alike, both good and bad, because no one is free from the miseries of this age. Everyone born of woman, living for a short time and filled with many miseries, comes forth like a flower, is crushed, flees like a shadow, and never remains in the same condition. Yet in this there is a great difference between the righteous and the unrighteous: evils seize the unrighteous man in destruction, sending him from present misery into eternal misery unto destruction; but the righteous, seized by temporal misery, are chastened and purified through it and escape destruction.
