As for the wicked and unrighteous, although their destruction is now hidden while each of them exults in most evil things, in the future it will be manifest what difference there is between the righteous and the unrighteous. For I—

[Col. 0932D] VERSE 13. I have known that the Lord will execute judgment for the needy in this world, discerning their cause—those afflicted by the ungodly—from an unholy nation; and will execute vengeance for the poor who lie with Lazarus before the doors of the rich, and for all who are needy, distressed, and afflicted, of whom the world is not worthy that they should rule it. For the places of dignity are occupied, at the world’s bidding, by the worst and most worthless people, who do not assist the poor and needy from the resources belonging to the poor, but afflict them and sometimes compel them to the iniquity which they ought to forbid.

VERSE 14. Yet the righteous, although thus distressed and sent into the furnace of poverty by the Babylonian king—that is, by the devil or Antichrist—will not cease to sing the hymn of the three youths and the other songs of praise, by which they will confess to your name, praising your name and your righteous judgment even now in their distress; and much more abundantly and perfectly when, having entered the tabernacle not made by hands, those upright ones shall dwell with your countenance. With it, and in it, it shall be well with those for whom it was ill in their own countenance, in whose sweat they ate their bread.

[Col. 0933A] From that time onward, those good persons, perfectly delivered from the wicked and avenged upon their enemies, will not give glory to themselves, but will confess to your name, ascribing to your grace rather than their own strength both that they were not seized by evils unto destruction and that they attain the sight of your countenance, with which they shall also dwell forever.

Glory to the Father, the Lord delivering me from the evil man. Glory to the Son, the countenance of the Most High, with whom the upright shall dwell. Glory to the Holy Spirit, by whose kindling those coals glow which shall fall upon the wicked.

## PSALM 140

[Col. 0933]

[Col. 0933B] “Lord, I have cried to you,” etc. Title:

VERSE 1. A PSALM OF DAVID.

This is clear. The title fits this psalm well, in which David speaks—Christ himself, one for all who belong to him. Here David also speaks as a penitent, troubled and anxious concerning God’s judgment, especially at the departure from this present life. For who does not need to cry out in the hour of death? “Set, O Lord,” he says, “a guard upon my mouth, and a door of enclosure around my lips.” Whoever justifies himself, whoever trusts that he will appear righteous before God in his own right, has neither that guard nor that door. But he had them who said: “If he should wish to contend with me, I could not answer him one thing out of a thousand.” And afterwards: “If I should wish to justify myself, my mouth would condemn me.” Likewise: “Even if I had anything righteous, I would not answer, but would entreat my Judge” (Job 9:3, 20, 15). For this is what is said here: “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head”—that is, lest, in that emergency, my lamp having gone out and being without oil, I should go in vain to buy it. Therefore, while I live, let the righteous correct me; but let the flatterer not deceive me.

One man is head and body: it belongs properly to the head to speak for the members, just as our tongue assumes the role of all the members and serves as speech for all of them. Charity makes us one with Christ, whether the head speaks or the members. Christ speaks; but in his voice let each person recognize his own. At times he says what belongs to himself alone, yet he does not separate himself from our words. Therefore let Christ speak in his own person:

VERSE 1. Lord, I have cried to you for a long time, ever since Abel’s blood cried from the earth. My cry in the blood of that witness and of my other witnesses slain for righteousness has not ceased. Therefore I, Christ, say to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth: I have cried to you not only from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zachariah, whom the fratricidal followers of Cain killed between the temple and the altar, but I shall also cry until the end of the age through the mouths of all the saints crying beneath God’s altar, and of all who are troubled and yet to be troubled for righteousness until the end of the age. For there must be no ceasing from crying while tribulation remains until the end of the age.

For the sake of this cry of mine and of my people, I, the Son, say to you, Father: “Attend to my voice,” swiftly and effectively hearing me when I cry to you, with my blood and the blood of my people crying to you from the now-holy earth—that is, the Church. By believing in and reverencing the blood of my passion, she opens her mouth in confession of her sins and praise of your name; she has received and receives my blood, which cries more certainly and more effectively than Abel’s blood. For Abel’s blood, crying out, obtained a destructive vengeance against one fratricide; but my blood, shed on the cross or on the Mount of Olives while I prayed, obtained for many of my enemies forgiveness freely offered without vengeance, and for many others vengeance that was not destructive but corrective. Whoever patiently endured this vengeance and confessed that he suffered justly—as the thief said to the thief, “We indeed receive what our deeds deserve” (Luke 23:41)—obtained, through the correction of a very brief and very light punishment, pardon and eternal life.

So also, even now and until the end of the age, the momentary and light tribulation will, for those confessing their sins and promising better things of themselves, work beyond measure an eternal weight of glory, while I, the Son, intercede and you, Father, attend to my voice as I cry to you—my blood crying to you upon the altar and the blood of my people beneath the altar.

[Col. 0934D] For my blood cries upon the altar, or before the golden altar, when the memorial of my passion is celebrated in a faith precious beyond gold: in it my vocal and crying blood is drunk through the mouths of those who worthily drink that same blood, while they either pray for what ought to be prayed for or preach what ought to be preached. Thus, yes, thus, while I intercede above as upon the altar and my people cry below as beneath the altar on earth:

VERSE 2. Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight, so that prayer may be to you incense burning with the fire of charity, from which the smoke of spices may rise in the sweetest fragrance. But because the intention and voice of one praying are then heard when aided by the hand of good action: Let the lifting up of my hands be an evening sacrifice—that is, as acceptable as the evening sacrifice in the Law was more acceptable, because it was a figure of that true sacrifice which I, made obedient, offered to you, God the Father, upon the altar of the cross.

On this passage blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0935D] *Morals*, Book XX, chapter 2]: “Because our Redeemer suffered the force of persecutors near the end of the world, he gave himself for us as an evening sacrifice.”

Otherwise: Our evening is the end of life; if at it we worthily offer the sacrifice of repentance, we are purified, so that no one who repents at the end may despair.

Otherwise: Those who, by doing good works or offering sacrifice, seek earthly things rather than heavenly—as those who do not eat in order to evangelize, but evangelize in order to eat—do not lift up their hands or hearts, though they hear in vain what is said: “Lift up your hearts.” “We have them unto the Lord.” To them the prophet says: “Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to heaven” (Lam. 3:41).

Although this is necessary in all our works, it is especially fitting where the memorial is celebrated of that evening sacrifice which obtained for us the morning light in the hope of the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who by dying destroyed our death and by rising restored life. We faithful people, faithfully believing this and purely loving him who died and rose again for us, offer an evening sacrifice when we venerate him who died for us.

[Col. 0935C] But the morning sacrifice is ascribed to us when we magnify, believe, and preach him, now risen and exalted to heaven at the right hand of God the Father, as worthy to receive power, divinity, wisdom, honor, and glory, so that every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

What follows now does not suit the Head, but any one of his members who faithfully sings and says:

VERSE 3. Set, O Lord, a guard upon my mouth, and a door of enclosure around my lips, so that neither an evil thought may have savor in the mouth of my heart, nor anything foolish may burst forth through my lips against God. A “door of enclosure” properly means a door around which cautious gatekeepers stand on every side, lest anyone enter or leave who has no right to do so; it is opened at the appropriate time and closed at the appropriate time. So our mouth should be opened for confession of sin and closed against such excuse-making, especially that which is commonly made through words of malice. This is the chief vice of proud persons who wickedly excuse themselves and refuse to yield to truth when it rebukes them. Thus Samuel said to Saul: “To resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse to submit is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 15:23). Against this chief vice the door of the mouth must be shut, lest it open into words of malice.

On this passage blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0936D] *Morals*, Book VII, chapter 17]: “The tongue must be carefully restrained by the balance of great moderation, not bound so that it cannot be loosed, lest, if relaxed, it run into vice, or, if restricted, grow sluggish even for what is useful. The Psalmist, rightly considering this, embraced it in a brief petition, saying: ‘Set, O Lord, a guard upon my mouth, and a door of enclosure around my lips.’ For a door is opened and closed. He therefore who asked that not an obstacle but a door be placed upon his mouth plainly taught that the tongue should both retain discipline and be relaxed when necessity requires, so that a discriminating voice may open the mouth at the fitting time and silence may again close it at the fitting time. Thus one sage says: ‘The wise man will be silent until the proper time,’ so that, when he judges it opportune, setting aside the rule of silence, he may by speaking offer fitting things for useful service. Thus Solomon says: ‘A time for silence and a time for speaking.’ The times must be weighed with discerning alternation, lest the tongue, when it ought to be restrained, scatter itself uselessly in words, or, when it can speak usefully, sluggishly restrain itself.”

[Col. 0936B] Yet this discernment of speaking and silence, according to what is expedient, is not in human power, since no human being can tame the tongue. Therefore I, David, ask you, Lord, who can do all things, to set a guard upon my mouth and a door of enclosure around my lips, and:

VERSE 4. Do not incline my heart to words of malice, to make excuses for excuses in sins. When one of the members prays here, I, David—I, Christ—pray this, I who hunger and thirst also in them, on account of whom, my least ones, I shall say at the judgment: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25:35). Thus I now pray for them and in them, saying to you: Father, do not incline my heart—that is, the heart of my people—to words of malice, so that through accident, necessity, or some other means they may excuse their guilt with people who work iniquity. The first of these were Adam and Eve, wickedly excusing their own faults and striving to transfer blame from themselves to the serpent—indeed, even to the serpent’s Creator.

[Col. 0936D] Many of their descendants still follow them: people, that is, who work iniquity and transfer it either to the frailty of the flesh, as to a woman seduced by the serpent, the devil, or to the devil himself, the ancient serpent. I, David, will not consent to such people, and I will not share in their chosen company. By “their chosen ones,” not God’s chosen ones, I mean those for whom it does not suffice falsely to excuse themselves, but who also despise others, inflated with false righteousness and alien from the true. I will not share with them, or, as another manuscript has it, “I will not be bound together with them.” Persons are said to be bound together when two are fastened at once, so that one may hinder the other from free escape. Therefore I will not share or be bound together with them, desiring, like them, to be soothed by false praise and regarded as excused from my sins. On behalf of these persons:

VERSE 5. The righteous one shall correct me—either God, or any good brother, or certainly my mind correcting my flesh as a husband corrects his wife. He shall correct me, I say, not in fury or anger, but in mercy: first between myself and him alone, then with witnesses brought in. If I do not hear them, he will openly rebuke my sins, telling the Church. I desire and pray that this be done: that I be corrected and rebuked by a righteous person burning with zeal for righteousness, yet not without mercy, but with that mercy which the corrector would justly desire shown to himself if he needed correction as I do.

“But let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head.” What is meant by the designation “head” but the mind, which rules the body? Therefore the oil of the sinner fattens the head when the favor of a flatterer soothes the mind, says blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 0937D] Homily 12 on the Gospels]. I, David, do not want this oil. But neither will those flatterers, sellers of this oil, want it if at some time they recover their senses through righteous rebukes. This will surely be fulfilled in many, since many such people will still be converted in the future; and my prayer—the prayer by which I, David, I, Christ, taught that one should seek not earthly gain or human praise, but the coming of God’s kingdom, forgiveness of sins, not to be led into temptation, and deliverance from evil—this prayer, I say, of myself and my people, or also that by which I intercede above for my own, shall be pleasing to them. It shall please them to ask for the things I taught should be asked, and which I asked on the Mount of Olives when praying for them—not for the world, nor that they should be taken out of the world before their time, but that they should be preserved from evil; and that the love with which you, Father, loved me might be in them, and I in them.

But those to whom it does not please that worshippers should be ordered by my prayer through me—because in their own judgment and their own arrogance they are powerful and learned judges of conduct—are not ready to judge for the correction of those faults, but sluggish in prayer: such are their judges, such their teachers.

VERSE 6. They were swallowed up, either because the sea swallowed them with Pharaoh’s army, or because the earth swallowed them with Dathan and Abiram in righteous judgment. For they were joined to the rock through a likeness to the truth, which is the rock, being near it; but they were not founded upon me, the rock—neither the philosophers nor the malignant heretics who overthrow many by elaborate and polished words. Yet some who have been converted from among them will hear my words rather than theirs, because my words have been able to prevail and, as more powerful than theirs, have overcome them. Thus my words, compared and set alongside their words, have swallowed them up and reduced them to nothing, just as Moses’ rod swallowed the rods of the magicians: it could prevail against them, but they could do nothing against it.

[Col. 0937D] So too their judges—that is, evil teachers of the wicked—speaking separately in their own little gatherings or disorderly schools, seemed to be something and to say something. But, joined to the rock, they were swallowed up; for when compared with Christ, who is the Rock, they were swallowed up and annihilated by the teaching of the Church founded upon the rock. She opened her mouth, as was revealed to John, and swallowed the foul river which the dragon, the devil, sent from his mouth (Rev. 12:16), inspiring heretics to teach falsehood against the truth, which is the solid rock. The words of this truth have been able to prevail and have prevailed over the words of heretics through the weak and contemptible things of this world, which this world despised as dung. Yet from what it despised the world received richness, so that from it the harvest of the Church might spring up more fruitfully. For “the death of the saints is precious in the sight of the Lord” (Ps. 115:15), though for a time it appeared contemptible in the sight of the world, shut up in tombs along with their closed bodies, as though no good could come from it upon the earth. But:

VERSE 7. As the richness of earth, broken up upon the ground—or breaking forth—enriches the earth, so by the death of the saints the holy Church has been enriched and made fruitful for many harvests.

[Col. 0938B] In the Hebrew it reads: “For even yet my prayer is against their wickedness; their judges have been lifted up beside the rock, and they shall hear my words, for they are beautiful. As when a farmer splits the earth, our bones have been scattered at the mouth of hell.”

Otherwise: Rich uncultivated soil produces thorns, thistles, nettles, and other useless plants. So human nature in Adam was rich and idle. Placed in paradise to work and guard it, he would not work; and, through the abundance of free will, neglecting the commandment, he presumed to taste the fruit of the forbidden tree. Therefore the cursed ground—that is, human nature itself—spontaneously produces vices both in the roots of thoughts and in the bushes of sinful actions.

[Col. 0938C] But as a farmer ploughs up the ground lest it luxuriate further, so he scattered our bones—that is, our inward parts, where we ought to have been bony and firm—because he made us weak and fragile, cast down beside hell and subject to that curse in which it was said to Adam: “Cursed is the earth in your work,” etc., as far as “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3:17–18).

This accords with the meaning of what, as was said, is read in the Hebrew: “As when a farmer splits the earth, our bones have been scattered at the mouth of hell.” Whether one says “beside hell,” as our manuscript has it, or “at the mouth of hell,” as the Hebrew truth has it, the sense is the same in the heart of believers who lament that, just as the richness of earth, when it bursts forth upon the ground, spreads pestilence widely among human beings, so the pride of the wicked wounds the bodies of martyrs with the infection of its malice. The martyrs are the bones and support of faith. And this happens “beside hell” or “at the mouth of hell”: beside hell, yet not in hell; at the mouth of hell, yet not in the belly of hell. For although they die the common death, and thus are reckoned to be beside hell or at hell’s mouth, they shall nevertheless be in eternal life, according to: “Whoever believes in me shall not die forever” (John 11:26).

[Col. 0939A] Those are in hell who, remaining in the depths of vices, despise their own danger, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “When the sinner comes into the depths, he will despise” (Prov. 18:3). They would be far from hell if, joined to the immortal angels in blessedness, they could no longer sin. But now they are beside hell or at the mouth of hell because they have the power to sin and not to sin: free indeed from any necessity compelling evil or preventing good, but not free from weakness. Yet this weakness of the flesh will not harm a spirit ready for good:

VERSE 8. For to you, Lord, Lord, are my eyes. To you, not to the threats of adversaries, are my eyes—the eyes of the mind, the eyes of faith—always, as I, David, said elsewhere: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. 24:15); and the bodily eyes too are often raised to heaven. And, that what I have said rather obscurely—“To you, Lord, Lord, are my eyes”—may be clearer, I say more plainly: “In you I have hoped; do not take away my soul.” Rather, preserve it against those who, though they kill the body, cannot kill the soul. Concerning them I pray: “Do not take away”—that is, do not permit my soul to be taken away—even if you permit my outward goods to be taken away as you did blessed Job’s. But as you said to Satan about him, “Nevertheless, preserve his life” (Job 2:6), so do not take it away; indeed, thus guard my soul, you, Lord, Lord.

I call you “Lord” twice because there is a twofold reason for which I owe you service: you created me from nothing when I did not exist, and mercifully restored me when I was lost. Therefore you, Lord, Lord, in whom I hope:

[Col. 0939C] VERSE 9. Guard me from the snare of deceitful cunning which they have set for me, and from the stumbling-blocks of violent malice, not merely of those who think, but also of those who work, iniquity. So long as this iniquity is tangled up like the idle nets of fishermen or hunters, it is not excessively dangerous; but when it is stretched out in length and breadth—in breadth, through expanded luxury; in length, through hardened obstinacy—

VERSE 10. Sinners shall fall into its net. Those who stood before being tested shall fall in temptation, as my own disciples did, to whom I said: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41). When they fell and fled, abandoning me, I, Christ, was alone in my passion until I passed from this world to the Father. Then, after the earth was melted—that is, after the frailty of human weakness was displayed in the chief members of my body—I, risen from death, shall strengthen its pillars, because confidence is conceived in the faith of the resurrection, so that they may not fear the death of their bodies, whose resurrection shall be hoped for from my resurrection.

[Col. 0940B] Meanwhile I am alone and, as it were, solitary upon a roof until I pass over; and when I have passed over, I shall be multiplied. For I, the grain of wheat put to death by the passion by which I shall fall into the earth and be buried in it, when I rise again shall bear much fruit, strengthening my disciples and sending them into all the world to gather abundant fruit.

Glory to the Father, to whom the Son cries. Glory to the Son, who cries to the Father. Glory to the Holy Spirit, the eternal fire, by which prayer, inflamed, is directed like incense in the sight of the Lord.

## PSALM 141

[Col. 0939]

[Col. 0939C] “With my voice I cried to the Lord.” The title of this psalm is:

(VERSE 1.) AN UNDERSTANDING OF DAVID, WHEN HE WAS IN THE CAVE: A PRAYER (1 Sam. 24).

The history teaches how David was in the cave; nevertheless, the title draws us away from the history, since it reads, “An understanding of David,” warning that the sense of the one singing should be raised from history to spiritual understanding. Thus David in the cave is Christ in the flesh or in the tomb, or Christ himself with his members in the world, where he prays to be saved from Saul, that is, from the devil, the ruler. Hence this is the fifth psalm entitled “Prayer,” in whose first part the whole Christ, praying, briefly recounts his evils; in the second part, their end, at “I cried.” Therefore, teaching by his intention what we should do while we remain in the flesh, he says in the cave:

VERSE 2. I cried to the Lord with my inward voice, and he repeats, “With my voice.” But since blasphemers also cry out, he explains how he cried: “I made supplication.” Therefore, with my voice—not a blasphemous voice but one of prayer and supplication—I often cried to the Lord, distressed by the weariness of this life, with a twofold cry, of mouth and heart. By this cry of outward and inward voice I longed to depart and be with Christ. What did I cry? What did I entreat? What prayer do I pour out before him? “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess to your name.” Out of prison, I say, out of the jail of this captivity, where I cannot see my God because of the guilt of the first parent, who, cast out of the light of paradise, begot all of us here as though in prison.

[Col. 0940D] This relates to the psalm’s title, “An understanding of David, when he was in the cave.” Principally, as stated, it concerns Christ while he was still in the cave, namely in mortal and passible flesh, with Saul—that is, death—pursuing him; secondarily, it concerns every faithful person desiring to be led out of this miserable life as from a prison. He desires this through fear, and fears it through desire. I, David—I who sing with David—both desire and fear, fearing I desire and desiring I fear. Therefore, unable to contain the inward heat of a heart that fears and desires—a heat hidden from human beings but known to God—

[Col. 0941A] VERSE 3. I pour out my prayer before him. I pour it out as a pure spring flowing from the secret place of the heart. I pour it out abundantly because, in my anxiety, I sigh and my groaning is like flooding waters. I pour it out before him, where he himself sees, he who will reward in secret, according to the saying: “Having shut the door, pray to your Father, and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you” (Matt. 6:6). In this hope, praying in tribulation, I cry to him and declare before him my tribulation, which is:

VERSE 4. When my spirit fails—that is, while my spirit fails. This failure is from myself, my fault requiring that my spirit fail within me, so that, utterly deprived of my own powers, I fail unless your good Spirit renews me, who does not fail when my spirit fails. My spirit fails so that I may not presume upon my own strength and thereby fail more completely, because “he who thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself” (Gal. 6:3). Conversely, one humbled by the failure of his own spirit, who understands that no good belongs to him from himself, is guided by your unfailing good Spirit either in the way of your commandments or on the narrow paths of your counsels.

Of the way of commandments it is said: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17)—such as: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property,” and the other such commands proposed and imposed upon all who wish to enter life. But of the paths it is said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21). Likewise, “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7:25), says the Apostle, urging the narrow path but not closing the broad way. For he said: “If a virgin marries, she has not sinned” (1 Cor. 7:28), namely before a vow of chastity; for if she marries after the vow, she will sin, because, making void her first faith, she will incur condemnation, from which she will not escape without worthy repentance.

[Col. 0941C] But I have resolved to walk in your counsels as through narrow paths. Yet as enemies disturb me on every side, I am so troubled that through the excess of distress my spirit already fails, and I think that I can neither stand nor walk upon the paths or the way of righteousness. But you see, and you have known my paths, in which, with your help, I still stand so long as I am supported by your Spirit while my own spirit fails, because by my own strength I cannot escape the snares set for me. For in this way in which I walked they hid a snare for me. They placed snares in the way according to their own judgment; but in truth their snares are placed outside the way, outside Christ, outside you, who say: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Snares are not only heresies and schisms separating persons from the Church of God, but also wicked customs within the Church, by which habitual evil is approved more than unfamiliar good.

With these snares distressing me and enemies, both domestic and foreign, raging on every side:

VERSE 5. I looked to the right and saw, and there was no one who recognized me. I looked to the right, gazing upon eternal things, and I saw what the wicked, who are to be placed on the left, do not see. I would be consoled by the hope of eternal goods amid the tribulation of impending distress in these evil days, in which iniquity abounds and the charity of many grows cold. Yet there was no one who recognized me, because those known to me withdrew from me, David the Christian, while they favored Antichrist. Or they withdrew from me, David the true Christ, when not even the apostles stood at the right, but all abandoned me and fled, terrified by fear of death.

They fled indeed, but I did not flee, because escape perished from me. While still a child, fleeing into Egypt, I hid myself; and at times, fleeing, I hid from enemies who wished to throw me down a precipice or stone me, because my hour had not yet come, nor was death at the hands of those wishing to stone or throw me down a death appointed for me. But after my hour came and the death of the cross was set before me, as appointed beforehand by my Father, I did not wish to flee, because then escape perished from me, when it was not fitting for me to flee.

[Col. 0942B] Otherwise: Escape perishes in two ways. It perishes for one shut in, who cannot flee because he is besieged on every side, as Peter was in prison, with four squads of soldiers guarding the prison. It also perishes for a strong man’s flight: one who, though able to flee, does not wish to do so, taking care not to imitate the hired servant who sees the wolf coming and flees, or the cowardly soldier who throws down his weapons and flees from battle, not daring to resist the enemy face-to-face.

In both ways escape has perished from me, David—from me who am little: because, strong in spirit, I do not wish to flee; and, weak in flesh and at the same time surrounded on all sides by enemies, I cannot flee. Though I long, by a victorious death, to depart and be with Christ, there is no one who seeks my soul in order to take it from me; my enemies wish instead that it be chastened in afflicted flesh, as in the cave of a dark prison, rather than that it leave the prison. Or, there is no one who seeks my soul in order to imitate or console it. Amid these distresses:

VERSE 6. I cried to you, O Lord. I, Christ, cried upon the cross, saying: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). I, Peter, cried while bound in prison by Herod. I, the Church—or I, an ecclesiastical person—cried in every distress exceeding my strength. I cried to you, Lord, who rule in heaven and on earth. Crying, I said: “You are my hope in this land of the dying,” in which hope, not yet possession, consoles me as I hope for invisible goods that I do not see; “but you will be my portion in the land of the living,” in which possession will succeed faith’s hope and hope itself.

Therefore here, Father, you are my hope—that is, the hope of my members—because they do not see you, in whom they hope. “For what a man sees, why does he hope for it?” (Rom. 8:24). But I, in my own person, always see you, because you and I, Father, are one. Yet I call you my hope because I transform into myself my members who hope in you, and, singing to you in their voice, I say: “You are my hope,” as though your face had not yet been seen by me, although you are always in me and I in you.

[Col. 0943A] I also say in the voice of my members that you are my portion in the land of the living, although in the land of the living you are not merely my portion but my entirety. I distribute this entirety as I will, as I said to one of my own: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), which is the land of the living. In that land, whoever is with me, I shall give and reveal myself to him, so that I myself may be the portion of the living in the land of the living. It is promised to those of whom it is said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4). Likewise: “But the meek shall inherit the earth” (Ps. 36:11).

Because I, David—I, the imitator of David who sings and repents—am a pilgrim and exile far from that land, and because at the beginning of the psalm I cried, “I made supplication,” fearing that my supplication might come into forgetfulness, I cry again and say:

**Verse 7.** Attend to my supplication, O Lord, to whom I cried out in entreaty. Attend, I beseech you, to me, David, greatly distressed, because I have been exceedingly humbled: for inwardly I humble myself before you, not daring even to lift my eyes to heaven, but striking my breast and saying: “Be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13), who have sinned beyond the number of the sands of the sea; my sins have been multiplied, and I am not worthy to behold the height of heaven because of the multitude of my iniquity. Since, therefore, I thus humble myself inwardly, and am also outwardly humbled and oppressed by persecutors, it is necessary that you, who know all things and never forget anything, should attend—that is, show that you attend to my supplication—because I have been exceedingly humbled: I, needy and poor among the rich; I, weak among the strong; I, despised among renowned persecutors and oppressors.

Considering and weighing this—or rather, since you are attentive, showing yourself to attend—deliver me from those who persecute me, because they have become strong against me: their number has increased, iniquity abounds, and the charity of many has grown cold; nor is there anyone able to resist their strength and multitude, unless you, strong and mighty in battle, deign to gird your sword upon your thigh against them, O most mighty one. If you will, you can deliver both bodies and souls, as you delivered me, David your servant, from the evil sword of visible and invisible enemies. But whatever may happen to my body—whether, if you will, it be crucified like Peter’s body, or, if you will, delivered like the body of John resting in peace—deign to preserve my soul, for which I pray, saying:

**Verse 8.** Bring my soul out of confinement, or out of prison, that it may confess—or, for confessing—your name: so that, truly knowing myself delivered from Herodian malice and from every expectation of the wicked, I may be able to confess and say: “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel and delivered me from the hand of Herod and from every expectation” (Acts 12:11) of evils—of those desiring evil against me. And let the expectation of the righteous be wholly and solely concerning me, because the righteous await me until you repay me.

And the righteous await me, the true David, placed in the cave of the tomb—namely, the apostles—until, risen and summoned from the cave of the tomb, I appear to them having received the recompense of my Passion; for the glory of the Resurrection shall be recompense for the shameful Passion. The righteous await this concerning me, Christ the true David, while I am held in the cave of the tomb, the stone sealed over me and guards set there. The righteous detained in the infernal prison also await this concerning me; into that prison my soul will descend, for which I pray, saying: “Bring my soul out of confinement.” Dying upon the cross, I also commend it into your hands, Father.

Amid all these things, while in the cave—of the tomb according to the body, or of hell according to the soul—I pray: “The righteous, men and angels, await me, until you repay me,” thus humbled, giving me the name that is above every name, so that at my name, which is Jesus, every knee may bend, of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings; and every tongue may confess that I, Jesus, shall be in the glory of the Father’s majesty.

Likewise, this is fittingly understood of me, whatever sort of psalmist I may be, after the example of David repenting and wisely singing psalms, when I sing here: “Bring my soul out of confinement or prison.” In saying this, I, David, do not here desire the common death by which the souls of evil and good alike are brought out of the prison of the flesh; rather, I desire the death precious in the sight of the Lord. By it my soul, even now while remaining in the flesh, may nevertheless remain free from the vices of the flesh, always to confess your name; and, when the obedience of remaining in the prison of the flesh has been fulfilled—as long as you will, as long as it is expedient or necessary for me or for others in any way pertaining to me—then my soul may also be brought out of the confinement or prison of the body through the sleep in which the flesh itself sleeps and rests together. For while it decays, it weighs down the soul, since the earthly dwelling presses down the mind full of many thoughts.

There is also another manner of being brought out from this prison, this cave, this confinement, which I desire when I say: “Bring my soul out of confinement or prison.” Namely, let my soul remain in the body until the hour when it is called from this life, not as in a dark prison-cell, but as in a military tent bright on every side. Thus he who said of himself and those like him: “Though remaining in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh” (2 Cor. 10:3); and, “Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation, configured to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:20–21).

This soldier of God’s camps says these things: although he was in the body, the body itself was not for him a dark prison from which he could not raise the gaze of his mind to heaven. Rather, it was a military tent with a view on every side: not only toward the west, to the Lord’s Passion and death upon the cross, but also toward the east, to the Lord’s Resurrection. Likewise, when he said, “He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph. 4:10), looking upward and downward from his bright tent, when he saw the one filling all things, he saw all things in him, insofar as was fitting for one still a soldier, not yet reigning or keeping full sabbath-rest.

So I beseech you, Lord Jesus: you who have now been brought out from the cave of the tomb and reign in the heavenly palace, bring me out of the prison of the flesh, so that, after Paul’s example, my citizenship may be in heaven, and my soul may always be free to confess your name. You are in heaven, where the righteous await me, now wholly delivered from the prison of the flesh, until you repay me as you repaid them: for faith preserved, for the good contest, for the course completed, with the crown of righteousness. Those who are now crowned await others to be crowned, as they received the divine answer that they must wait a little longer until the number of their brothers is completed.

In the Church still on pilgrimage the righteous also await me, until you repay me with provision for the journey, by which, fittingly assisted, I may reach eternity. Let it happen to me as the righteous and good themselves await: for they desire and expect that good be repaid to me for evil, with that expectation of which it is said: “The expectation of the righteous is joy” (Prov. 10:28). Thus let those who desire my righteousness exult and rejoice, and always say: “Let the Lord be magnified, who desire the peace of his servant” (Ps. 34:27)—that is, peace in serving you, Lord, whom to serve is to reign.

Otherwise, following Augustine’s exposition of this psalm: he asks to be brought out of confinement who suffers distress in the corruption of the flesh, which is penal, as though under the custody of a prison. He is distressed by confinement in corruption, which is the punishment of the body. After these distresses, in the house of God all life will be confession—that is, praise of God. Now the prison hinders confession.

This prison or cave may be called the world, where all things are vain, from which the soul asks to be delivered because it suffers much there. Or the body is called a prison; but it is no great matter to leave the body, since the wicked also do so, and everyone does so sooner or later; nor is it charity if a righteous person is excessively hasty for this. Or rather, the body is a prison not because God made it good, but because of its corruption resulting from sin, from which one wishes to be brought out so that it may become incorruptible. Merits make a prison: a dwelling is a prison to one enclosed, a house to one keeping guard. Freedom makes a house; slavery, a prison. Thus it is not the flesh, which God made, but its corruption and temptation, that are prison.

## Psalm 142

[Col. 0945]

[Col. 0945C] “Lord, hear,” etc. Title:

**(Verse 1.) A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN HIS SON WAS PERSECUTING HIM.**

The history is well known. As Absalom persecuted David (2 Kings [Samuel] 17), so Judas persecuted Christ; false brethren persecute his body, the Church; and unlawful motions of the flesh persecute each individual. Against this persecution Christ in his totality prays here.

This is the seventh of the penitential psalms. First, in its opening, it seeks favor. [Something is missing.] Secondly, it recounts its evils and what it has done against them, at the words: “Hear me speedily, O Lord; my spirit has failed.” The fourth part is a joyful conclusion, as in the other penitential psalms, lest anyone despair of pardon, at the words: “Your good Spirit will lead me into a straight land.” In order to teach the penitent to pray, he says:

“Lord, hear my prayer; with your ears receive my supplication in your truth; hear me in your righteousness. And do not enter into judgment with your servant, because no living person shall be justified in your sight.” For if the matter concerns merits alone, no one shall be justified. Therefore he likewise says: “For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will make me live”—namely, so that everything may be of grace. Again: “Cause me to hear your mercy,” because “I have hoped in you”: mercy, I say, which triumphs over judgment, saying in the morning—that is, on the day of judgment—“Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34).

[Col. 0946C] Accordingly this psalm fittingly has the title: “A Psalm of David, when his son was persecuting him.” For apart from Christ alone there has not been, is not, and will not be any David so strong of hand that he has not begotten a son whom he suffers as an enemy; that is, no one who has not contracted sin by which he is oppressed, should God enter into judgment with a human being.

Therefore I say, I David, I repenting like David: Lord, hear my prayer. Lord, Father and ruler of my life, while my son—my sin—is persecuting me, hear me as I pray, so that I may not fall before my adversaries, lest my enemy Ahithophel rejoice over me: the evil counselor, man or devil, who incites against me, toward my ruin, my son—that is, some deed of mine beautiful in human eyes, as Absalom was beautiful—so that through it I may be slain by the sword of pride, exalting myself excessively because of such a deed.

If I do this, I shall be driven from the kingdom, as though by my own son, beautiful, deceitful, and exceedingly treacherous. Thus King Nebuchadnezzar was driven from the kingdom. Through his own work, as through his son, he was driven from his kingdom when he became proud, glorying in his work and saying: “Is not this Babylon, which I have built in the strength of my power?” (Dan. 4:27). For while the speech of the king glorying in his work was still in his mouth, a voice fell from heaven announcing that he was to be driven from among human beings and numbered with the beasts.

So Saul likewise, excessively elated by the victory achieved over Amalek, was overthrown through what seemed to him a precious work—as by a beautiful son—to such a degree that he despised the prophet rebuking him and, tearing his mantle, deserved that the kingdom be torn from him. Thus many have been wounded, even slaughtered, by the sword of pride through a glorious work, as though by a beautiful son. Hence it is written in Job concerning the person for whom God has care: “He also rebukes through pain upon the bed, and will cause all his bones to waste away, that he may deliver a man from the things he has done, so that he may not pass into the sword” (Job 33:17–19).

I do not fear this sword of pride in some foul deed, the recollection of which humbles rather than exalts. I fear it more in a precious and beautiful work, likened to Absalom, whose hair was precious and whose face was beautiful. Against this sword I now pray, saying: Lord, you alone are the author of every good, precious, and beautiful work, and glory for it is due to you. Hear my prayer, giving me true humility and charity that is not puffed up, whatever greatness of beauty in virtues or works may arise from it; for it “does not rejoice over iniquity” (1 Cor. 13:6), that is, the iniquity of flatterers and of those who soothe human ears with false praise, “but rejoices with the truth,” attributing glory to God alone for every good work.

Therefore I, David repenting in this last penitential psalm, flee the beautiful son Absalom: I fear, that is, even that manner of life of mine which appears honorable, as I fear the folly by which I ordered the children of Israel to be numbered. Because of this I deserved anger so great that pestilence raged among the people by the angelic sword.

I repent, I say, no longer merely of a foul deed, which in another penitential psalm I bewailed, saying: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Ps. 50:1). For then I repented of having gone in to Uriah’s wife, an ugly work far unlike Absalom—that is, unlike some honorable and beautiful work now persecuting me and suggesting that pride should arise from it, as if something good had been done in my works by my own virtue or piety. Yet in those works nothing is mine except sin and evil mingled among God’s good gifts. Therefore boasting has no place in any of my works, since there is in all of them something requiring much repentance.

Yet when I am compelled, among detractors who twist all my actions, to recount—like holy Job or the apostle Paul—my words or deeds that seem lovely with a certain fair abundance of hair, I fear Absalom’s deceit, lest perhaps my own deed overwhelm me. Thus we read that Samson was overwhelmed by a valiant deed when he shook the two columns: when they fell, and the house supported by those columns collapsed, he himself was overwhelmed (Judg. 16:30). So also in the book of Maccabees we read of that exceedingly brave soldier Eleazar, who killed an elephant, that he himself died, crushed beneath the falling elephant (1 Macc. 6:47). Thus many who act valiantly are overwhelmed by the very weight of virtue when they seek glory from it not for the author of virtue, but for themselves.

Those driven from the kingdom by their own work, as by their own son, need great repentance, through which such an Absalom may be killed, so that he may not persecute his father but, himself dead, may leave the throne of the kingdom to his father. This undoubtedly happens when this final penitential psalm is sung from the heart, in which charity that does not puff up is sought against every vain self-exaltation. This charity, indeed, is that Spirit of whom God is told near the end of the psalm: “Your good Spirit will lead me into a straight land.”

May the Holy Spirit therefore be present to me as I sing and expound this psalm; led by him into the straight land, may I escape the sword and deceit of Absalom, which is manifold. For as Absalom persecuted his father David, so Judas persecuted Christ; false brethren persecute his body; and so do unlawful impulses and wicked activity—especially that which is veiled under an appearance of honorableness or goodness, and can therefore deceive or exalt, so that one who thinks himself something, though he is nothing, deceives himself.

This too must be observed: Absalom was beautiful in appearance and utterly shameful in deed—so shameful that he did not refrain from his father’s concubines. By defiling them in the sight of the sun, openly before the multitude, he foreshadowed those enemies of the true David who “rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2:14). Fleeing this manifold Absalom from before his face, I sing and say:

[Col. 0948C] “Lord, hear my prayer,” by which, fearing my evils, I ask for your goods. I even fear all my good works as not sincere; praying, I ask and desire your true and sincere goods. This desire itself is prayer; supplication is added when, knocking at the doors of divine mercy through the sacraments of the Passion or Resurrection and other such things, I say: “With your ears receive my supplication.”

Your ears are mercy and power; the one who said, “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me” (Matt. 8:2), knew these two ears. For he immediately experienced both mercy in your will and power in your act, and obtained what he sought, because without delay he was cleansed: he was heard, that is, through the two ears of mercy and power.

By these ears, I pray, Lord, receive my supplication in your truth, so that you may be found true: you who have promised pardon to penitents, mercy to the merciful, and who are accustomed to have mercy upon those praying for their persecutors. Behold, I David have mercy upon Absalom who persecutes me, for whose salvation I would wish to die if I could; therefore I say: “My son Absalom, who will grant that I may die for you, my son Absalom?” (2 Kings [Samuel] 18:13). Behold, I, the true David, pray upon the cross for those persecuting me, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Behold, I, a Christian, pray for those persecuting me and wish them pardon. Therefore it is just that the pardon which I ask should also be given to me, when I say: “Hear me in your righteousness,” “that you may be justified in your words” (Ps. 1:6 [citation as printed]), in which you will be found just and true when you do what you promise.

You promise pardon to those who grant pardon, saying: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke 6:37–38). What you promise I claim in your righteousness, not in mine, so that you may be justified and found true in your words. Yours is the righteousness that is through faith, by which your words are believed. Thus faith itself was reckoned as righteousness to Abraham when he believed your words. Your righteousness—your righteousness of faith—is that very righteousness in which I ask to be heard, saying: “Hear me in your righteousness,” which is not through the law showing wounds, but through the grace of faith healing them. But the righteousness of deeds, however rightly performed, does not raise up but weighs down if they are judged and examined strictly according to the law; hence the hands of Moses giving the law were heavy.

And therefore I ask that:

**Verse 2.** “Do not enter into judgment with your servant,” not even concerning those acts in which I seem to serve you or to have served you. I do not wish you to contend mightily with me in strict judgment as with your adversary, for one who establishes his own righteousness, as if he had done something by his own strength, cannot truly be called your servant. Being proud, he does not flee his enemy Absalom but nourishes him, while he attributes righteousness to himself.

But I, who am not worthy to be called your son, desire to be called and to be your servant, who say: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, because no living person shall be justified in your sight.” Therefore the Wise Man rightly said: “Do not praise a man in his lifetime” (Ecclus. 11:2), as though he said: Praise him after death or after life; glorify him after the victory has been completed. For as long as a person lives in mortal flesh, dangers and wars do not fail—external wars, indeed, but internal ones as well. “Without, conflicts; within, fears” (2 Cor. 7:5), says the Apostle, because he was not yet secure about himself while still living.

For his own Absalom persecuted even him when, through the greatness of revelations, he was pressed toward self-exaltation. Lest this should happen to him, he was struck with blows by an angel of Satan; delivered, as it were, from his own Absalom, he attributed no good to his own strength but ascribed all the good he possessed to God’s grace, saying: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10).

What I think concerning myself, therefore, I declare universally concerning every living person: namely, that no living person shall be justified in your sight, O God, even if he appears righteous to himself or to other human beings. For not even the stars of heaven are clean in your sight when compared with you, although some of them are clean or cleansed through participation in your purity. Therefore it is no wonder that I, frail David, tremble before your judgment, O just God. If you should wish to contend judicially with me, I could not stand against you, being weak, wearied, and weakened by many persecutions and temptations.

**Verse 3.** “For the enemy has persecuted my soul”: an open enemy such as Herod, or a hidden enemy such as Judas—of whom it was said: “Those who sought the child’s soul are dead” (Matt. 2:20). Such an enemy “has humbled my life to the ground.” I, the true David, say this because he strove to destroy my life by a most shameful death; and afterward “he placed me in darkness,” namely, in the tomb. I was not dead to the world, since I had no cause of death in myself by which I could be called dead to the world; nevertheless, I underwent burial as one dead to the world. And before I yielded up my spirit upon the cross:

**Verse 4.** “My spirit was distressed within me,” when my soul was sorrowful even unto death. As death drew near, my heart was troubled within me, when I began to be weary and afraid of my son, my disciple, who like another Absalom persecuted me, the father, the true David—while I willingly endured these things, the just one for the unjust.

Let each person who sympathizes and is planted together with me say this concerning himself, truthfully recognizing that he justly endures what I, the just one, willed to endure for the unjust. Let him say concerning himself that the enemy—the devil, or anyone like Herod, the open enemy; or Judas or Absalom, the domestic enemy; or even my own outward person—has persecuted my soul, so as to take away from my soul its soul, its life: God, who is charity, who is the life of my soul, just as the soul itself is the life of my flesh.

Although he could not utterly kill it by extinguishing charity in it or inspiring hatred in it—which is the death of the soul—he nevertheless humbled my life to the ground. By either taking away earthly goods or bringing earthly evils, he made me disturbed and caused me to be humbled and bowed down from that height of charity, from which I had resolved always to keep my heart above, in true and sincere charity: patient in enduring others’ evils, kind in bestowing its own goods.

With the single, serene, and luminous eye of this charity, which illumines the whole body, I wished to look upon friends and enemies alike, loving the former in God and the latter for God’s sake. But the persecuting enemy, clouding this eye, placed me in darkness—not wholly in darkness, however, for “he who hates his brother is in darkness” (1 John 2:11). Yet one who neither hates perfectly nor loves perfectly is in obscurity. He is not altogether dead to the world, wholly lacking spiritual life, but is indeed like one dead to the world, as though in ecstasy.

[Col. 0950D] Such was I, David, when Absalom persecuted me and nearly all Israel had joined him. Such also was I, a sinner like David, for every sinner and penitent whom various enemies have persecuted and driven toward hatred of a brother. Recognizing this now, I am greatly grieved, and “my spirit was distressed over me.” When I say “over me,” it is the same as saying “concerning me,” because the disturbance of all anxiety comes to me from myself. Or my spirit, stretched upward above me and thence beholding the deep miseries of this world, was distressed within me; or my spirit itself was over me.

From such anxiety there comes to me some fruit of repentance, by which “my heart was troubled within me.” “Within me” means against me: my heart was troubled because it was severely angry with myself. For what is a penitent person but one angry with himself, according to the saying: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5)? That is: “Be angry,” grieving over past sins, “and do not sin,” guarding against future ones. In such anger my heart was troubled in my conscience, or within me—that is, against me. But lest excessive sorrow swallow up my troubled heart:

**Verse 5.** “I remembered the days of old,” recalling that you did good to the ancients: though sinners, they did not love their sins, but rather accused them, saying even amid your scourges: “We suffer these things deservedly, because we have sinned” (Gen. 42:21). And, hoping for your grace through your scourges, “I meditated on all your works,” attributing all your good works to your goodness. For “you spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 148:5), all things at the beginning of the world; nor are any good things still done except when you speak or will them to be done.

Among them, those which are especially eminent are called works of your hands, concerning which it is fittingly sung: “A praiseworthy people, whom the Lord of hosts blessed, saying: ‘The work of my hands are you, my inheritance, Israel’” (Isa. 19:25). I meditated upon these works of your hands, considering how our fathers were saved in the Red Sea and in other dangers, when Moses stretched out his hands in prayer. While they were stretched out, Israel prevailed; when they were lowered, Amalek prevailed. And likewise I:

**Verse 6.** “Stretched out my hands to you,” whether while sacrificing, praying, or performing what is good, seeking in all these things nothing except to please you alone, who dwell on high and especially accept that evening sacrifice which innocent David, Christ, offered for me, David repenting: sacrificed for the whole world, with hands stretched out upon the cross.

Indeed, I speak to one who knows all things; yet if you ask me, “What do you want? What do you ask? Why do you stretch out your hands?” I say to you: “My soul is to you like land without water.” Or, as it is read in Hebrew: “My soul is like thirsty land toward you.” Land without water either becomes excessively hard or is crushed and scattered into dust, when it resists no wind. So my soul, wholly dry without dew and rain coming from above, and by itself fit for no fruit, thirsting toward you—indeed, thirsting for you—continually cries: “Drop down dew, heavens, from above; and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness spring up together” (Isa. 45:8).

Thus, as I cry to you:

**Verse 7.** “Hear me speedily, O Lord,” so that your Spirit may complete, fill, and refresh me, “because my spirit has failed.” It has failed so that I am now poor in spirit, having within me no spirit that puffs up my spirit: no spirit of pride and boasting, which especially lies in wait when Absalom—that is, some work outwardly beautiful and inwardly foul—persecutes. This spirit of mine has failed.

And therefore you, who turned your face away from me while my spirit was proud, in order to show me myself—namely, that I can do no good without you—do not turn your face away from me now that I am humbled. For if you turn it away, I shall be like those descending into the pit: that infernal depth where sin is not attended to but despised, and confession perishes. “For in hell who will confess to you?” (Ps. 6:6). Indeed, “when the sinner comes into the depths, he despises” (Prov. 18:3); and the wicked person shall be silent in darkness. Therefore, lest I descend into this darkness:

**Verse 8.** “Cause me to hear your mercy in the morning.” When the night of this world has ended, in the universal Resurrection, when the light of eternity is revealed, cause me in that morning to hear your mercy spoken to those to whom it is said: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34). Or likewise, in that morning when, after the night of sins, the light of righteousness begins to shine, cause me to hear your mercy.

Or “morning” means when, after the night of the present life is ended, the soul leaving the body begins to see what it did not see before—whether good things, evil things, or both, according to the character of its life now passed. In that morning, I beseech you, cause me to hear your mercy, so that you may receive my soul gently and mildly, and lead it from morning to noon, where you feed and rest at noon: feeding there in full light the ninety-nine sheep, the hundredth sheep having been restored after its loss and added to them.

As I ask such great things, I do not put forward the merits of works, which, if strictly judged—if, may your mercy deign to prevent it, you enter into judgment with me—are of no value for earning the future glory promised to the faithful. But I put forward this alone: “Because I have sinned against you,” to whom I said: “You are my hope in the land of the living” (Ps. 141:6). This has already been explained in the preceding psalm and need not be explained again.

But because believing in the heart and hoping for the goods promised from heaven are insufficient for salvation unless one also presses forward by the steps of works toward the promised prize—toward which I cannot run or which I cannot attain by myself, since I do not know the way and may easily be led away by paths so close to the true way that, if possible, even the elect are led into error—make known to me the way in which I should walk. May I avoid every error that your elect must beware, and that I, guarded by your grace, must despise and leap over. “For I have lifted up my soul to you”: having my heart above, I have raised my soul to you, seeking the things above, not those upon the earth.

Thus far, as if speaking and praying against one Judas or Absalom, I have used the singular number: “The enemy has persecuted my soul; he has placed me in darkness.” But because there are many like Judas, whom Satan fills and in whom Satan himself, raging, seeks to sift the elect like wheat; and many like Absalom and Ahithophel, persecuting the true David in his members, sifting him in his least members, and treading him as in a winepress, he passes from the singular to the plural, saying:

**Verse 9.** “Deliver me from my enemies, O Lord,” for I do not flee from you as Adam fled and hid himself; rather, through the repentance sung—or wept—in the seven penitential psalms, I flee from you when angry to you when merciful. This psalm is the last of the penitential psalms. In it I ask to be made perfect and to be so delivered from self-will, which persecutes like Judas or Absalom, that, freely subject to your will alone, I may avoid what you do not will and do what you will.

But because no human being can give this to a human being, nor an angel to an angel, nor an angel to a human being, I flee to you alone, who can do all things; and in prayer I unceasingly say to you:

**Verses 10–11.** “Teach me to do your will.” I do not now say, “Teach me to know your will,” which can be accomplished through a human being or an angel by human or angelic speech. But I say now: “Teach me to do your will.” This manner of teaching exceeds angelic and human ability and is possible to you alone, to whom I say: “Teach me to do your will, because you are my God.”

Of this manner of teaching it is said in the Gospel: “They shall all be taught by God” (John 6:45). Again: “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me” (ibid.). Therefore, “Blessed is the one whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach out of your law” (Ps. 93:10), so that he may do your will, not his own. Desiring to be so instructed, I continually say to you: “Teach me to do your will, because you are my God.” You alone can do this, since you have already taught many in this way—not by making sounds in their ears with voices, but by putting your good Spirit into their hearts.

So, I pray, do this also for me: grant me your good Spirit, and he will teach me all truth and announce to me the things to come, as the Gospel promise has it; and he will lead me into a straight land, whom my own evil spirit had led astray into a crooked land.

I ask these things not as one claiming my own merit, but for your name’s sake, O Lord, so that you may thereby be praised and recognized as the renowned and glorious physician and Savior: when you not only heal the sick person but also make me, dead though I am, alive. This surpasses all physicians’ arts, concerning which elsewhere it is said: “Will physicians raise [the dead], and will they confess to you?” (Ps. 87:11). Understand: certainly not; for to you alone it is possible to give life after death—so that the one made alive may die no more, but may live in righteousness and not die through iniquity; may live not in his own righteousness but in yours.

This I, David—I, Christ, prophesying in my own person and that of my members—pray; and praying, I prophesy, certain that what I say will occur: “Your good Spirit will lead me into a straight land; for your name’s sake, O Lord, you will make me live in your righteousness.” For it is your equity, just Father, that as death came through one, so life should come through one; and as all die in Adam, so in me, the new Adam, all who cleave to me are made alive.

And so, by the blessed sleep of precious death, you will bring my soul out of tribulation. Let every David now say, every penitent together with David:

**Verse 12.** “And in your mercy,” not by my own merit, “you will destroy all my enemies,” so that they cannot harm my soul, whether it is fighting in the body or leaving the body after its warfare has been completed. Here you will destroy my enemies—that is, you will destroy them in different ways: some by casting them down, like Saul, whom you destroyed and found as Paul; others by casting them away, like Judas, in place of whom, once destroyed, you appointed Matthias.

But at the future judgment you will destroy in one manner all who afflict me, especially hating me because I am your servant. For you will say to all: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). Then all who trouble me will perish together. You, righteous Judge, will do this because I am your servant: namely, one of those least ones concerning whom you will say on that day: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” (ibid., 40).

Glory to the Father, who hears his Son, the true David, in this psalm. Glory to the Son, praying here for his members. Glory to the Holy Spirit, good and leading every David, every truly penitent person, into a straight land. Amen.

## Psalm 143

[Col. 0953]

[Col. 0953D] Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle. From here to the end come continuous blessings, confessions, and most fervent songs of praise, which faith suggests, hope conceives, and charity pours forth, as David begins with a blessing and says: “Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle,” etc. For these are the words of one who is rightly conscious that he has with him and fighting on his behalf Christ, the man who is his friend, and who says in contemplation of that hour when he is to contend with the prince of this world, who will without doubt come against him: “You who delivered David your servant, [Col. 0954D] rescue me from the evil sword.” And that I may be able in that hour to escape that sword, meanwhile, he says: “Deliver me from the hand of alien sons,” that is, heretics or all the ungodly, “whose mouth has spoken vanity,” etc. Hence the title rightly has:

**(VERSE 1.) A PSALM OF DAVID AGAINST GOLIATH.**

For he who, while living, conquered Goliath—that is, the devil—in his members, confidently blesses the Lord God in this psalm, trusting that when he dies he will be delivered from the devil’s evil sword. This triumphal psalm deals first with the victory by which David individually conquered Goliath, and spiritually David himself together with the other saints conquered the devil. [Col. 0955A] This entire victory is said to arise from the fact that Christ came from David’s seed to conquer the pride of the world. Therefore David—Christ, head and body—prays for his coming.

The Jewish people were adorned with weapons: circumcision, sacrifices, and other visible sacraments. But because the Law cannot give life, Christ, head and body, laid aside the sacraments of the Law as oppressive rather than helpful in the time of grace. He took five stones, that is, the Law itself, those five books, from the stream: in that people the stones lay unused and useless. But in order that the Law might be useful, David received grace, without which the Law cannot be fulfilled, because the fullness of the Law is charity, which is from the Holy Spirit. This is to put the stones into the shepherd’s bag in which he was accustomed to milk sheep. Thus armed, he advances against [Col. 0955B] the proud man.

He casts one stone, because unity conquers. He struck him in the forehead: he killed him in the place where he did not bear Christ’s sign. When Goliath had fallen, he cut off his head with his own sword, because, when Goliath’s great ones believe, those by whom he slaughtered souls speak against him; and thus the head is cut off by its own sword. David killed Goliath; Christ killed the devil—that is, humility killed pride. For God becomes humble, so that the proud, who scorned to follow humble saints, may at least be willing to imitate him.

Therefore let David speak of his figurative and mystical victory—the victory of the whole Christ, whose members are all Christians. Let him say, I repeat: “Blessed be the Lord my God.” Glory, honor, and blessing to my God, who teaches my hands, directing my works toward warfare [Col. 0955C] against the spiritual Goliath: namely, the devil and his satellites, the princes of darkness, rulers of this world set in evil, wrestling against me not only through “spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places,” suggesting those vices by which the spirit is corrupted, such as envy, pride, and others of this kind, but also through fleshly desires by which the flesh lusts against the spirit. Thus, as these oppose one another, I may not lack the battle of which I now say: “Blessed be the Lord,” whose servant I am; “my God,” whose creature I am; or God of all generally by creation, but specially mine by love, because he first loved me, David, a boy, humble and less than my other brothers, and gave me grace to love him in return.

Thus he is God of all, [Col. 0955D] yet my God, as he says: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob,” because of their particular faith in him. Thus “my God,” the God of David, the God of every faithful person who is rightly called David, is rightly said and is blessed by such persons, each of whom says: “Blessed be my Lord, who teaches my hands for battle to be carried out at close quarters with the sword, and my fingers for war,” so that stones may be directed by the sling, arrows by the bow and crossbows, to strike Goliath and his members from afar.

For as we strike enemies nearby with the sword, and at a distance with the sling or bow, so by preaching we reach those present and by prayer those absent. In such warfare we must have discernment, by which we distinguish vices from persons. This discernment is signified in the fingers taught for war, lest either vices be spared because of persons, [Col. 0956A] or persons be consigned to destruction because of their vices, provided, however, that they are willing to abandon those vices. In this warfare blessed is the Lord my God,

**VERSE 2.** “My mercy,” so that I may go forth to war not cruelly, with the intention of oppressing anyone, but mercifully, with the intention of freeing the oppressed, as the people of Israel were freed when Goliath, who had reproached the armies of the living God, was killed. He was struck in the forehead by one stone; so may all enemies of God and of the Church be struck down, overcome by one faith, one hope, one charity, one indivisible unity of one body—especially those who seek to cut down the Church by introducing sects of perdition or by persecuting the armies of the living God. They reproach these armies as though they were little David, [Col. 0956B] when their small number and poverty are despised by the proud, Goliath-like men.

But I, David, one though little among those armies, armed with one faith as with one stone, go forth to battle against such a proud prince, trusting in the Lord, who is my mercy—more in the intention to show mercy than to injure before battle begins—and my refuge, should it happen, while adversaries harass me, that I must flee from city to city. Thus I, the figurative David, fleeing from Saul’s face, fled to foreigners, fearing the Ziphites and my other fellow-tribesmen.

I also, the true David, fleeing Herod into Egypt, found refuge there prepared. In the apostles [Col. 0956C] also, and in my other members driven from city to city, you were my protector and refuge, preparing suitable places for them, such as monasteries and regular communities. You, therefore, are my defender, lest I be captured by enemies; my deliverer, lest I be reduced by them to slavery; my protector, lest I be struck by them. And I hoped in him not only that my enemies might be driven back by his aid, but also that those of my own household might be subjected to me.

For you, my God, who teach my hands for battle against enemies, likewise establish peace for me among friends, household members, and subjects: you who subject my people beneath me, when Goliath, Saul, Ahithophel, Absalom, and all my enemies are slain—those who stir up the people Israel against me as king, against me as little David, against me as Christ, or against any [Col. 0956D] Christian.

On this passage blessed Pope Gregory says in his exposition of Job: “Peoples are subdued to holy minds when, before the presence of their strict severity, many thoughts leap down from them, so that they do not sweep them away over the precipice of fantasies, but, subjected to reason, rest humbly in the heart.”

**VERSE 3.** “Lord, what is man, that you have made yourself known to him? Or the son of man, that you esteem him?” As I call to mind your benefits, O God, bestowed on me, David, or on any human being, I say, as if carried away in wonder: “Lord, what is man?” Certainly, of himself, nothing good; yet he is something because you have made yourself known to him. The old man is Adam; the son of man is the new Adam. The former would be nothing, with all his posterity, if you had not made yourself known [Col. 0957A] to him through angels, prophets, and your signs and wonders. But the son of man is something great and worthy, because you esteem him, utterly unlike the old man of whom he is the son. For that old

**VERSE 4.** man, though created like truth, became like vanity by sinning; and his days pass like a shadow, though they would have been stable had he not sinned. But this son of man is to be called not so much like truth as Truth itself, who says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). This son of man is indeed “truth sprung from the earth” (Psalm 84:12), never subjected nor ever to be subjected to any vanity. In his divinity he is eternally exalted above all heavens, and in his humanity he is temporally exalted, so that he cannot be comprehended by human understanding unless he humbles himself to our lowliness. Therefore I cry out:

**VERSE 5.** “Lord, bend down your heavens and descend.” On this passage blessed Gregory says in his exposition of Job: “What is signified by the name of the heavens except the order of preachers? Unless holy preachers descended, as by a certain bending, from that immensity of inward contemplation which they grasp to our weakness through most humble preaching, they would never beget children in the faith. For they could not benefit us if they persisted in the uprightness of their own height. If holy men wished to preach what they grasp when they are intoxicated in heavenly contemplation, [Col. 0957C] rather than tempering their knowledge to sobriety by a certain moderation, who, with the still narrow bosom of understanding, could receive those streams of the heavenly fountain? Thus it is rightly said: ‘Lord, bend down your heavens and descend.’ For when the heavens are bent down, the Lord descends, because when holy teachers draw themselves down in their preaching, they pour the knowledge of the Divinity into our hearts. God would by no means descend to us if his preachers remained inflexible in the strictness of contemplation. Therefore the heavens are bent down so that the Lord may descend, because surely, if they did not condescend to our weakness, they would never raise us to their height.”

Therefore I, weak David—I, whatever member [Col. 0957D] of the true David I may be—ask help from heaven for myself, saying: “Lord, bend down your heavens and descend.” Temper the great and lofty to the little, so that the little may be raised upward through the great when they have bent down. But those who are not little by humility, but high by arrogance: touch them with the hand of your grace that pierces, moving them to repentance, and they will smoke with smoke that calls forth tears, so that by bitter weeping they may escape punishments and find grace.

But if some are too hard, do not leave even them secure in their hardness with an evil security; rather,

**VERSE 6.** flash lightning: by terrifying them with terrible and bright miracles, you will scatter them—namely, those strongly gathered together in one conspiracy—away from one another by the flash of your brightness or thunderbolt, [Col. 0958A] so that, violently terrified, they may flee and kill one another with mutual wounds, as happened on the day of Midian, when the Midianite army, terrified by the flashing lamps, fled before Gideon, leader of Israel. And behold, one greater than Gideon is here. For the true David, greater than Gideon, is the leader of this battle, in which war is waged against Goliath—that is, the devil—or Antichrist, or any eminent minister and army of his. You, my God, who teach my hands for battle, will terrify and scatter them.

And lest this be delayed too long: “Send forth your arrows,” namely men like arrows, such as he who said: “The Lord made my mouth like a sharp sword, and made me like a chosen arrow; he hid me in his quiver” (Isaiah 49:2). Such men, O my God, you have in your quiver, that is, in your hidden purpose: now send them against your Goliath-like enemies, the proud, and you will throw them into confusion.
