The Hebrew truth has: “Flash with lightning and scatter them; send your arrow and kill them.” I rightly desire that those who live wickedly should be killed, just as Saul was killed and died, and Paul began to live.

Alternatively: “Send forth your arrows,” namely sharp judgments discharged from the bow of Holy Scripture in such a way that what is said elsewhere may be fulfilled: “He bent his bow and made it ready; and in it he prepared instruments of death; he made his arrows for the burning ones” (Psalm 7:13–14). [Col. 0958C] But if, even after arrows, thunderbolts, and flashes of lightning have been displayed through human agents, they refuse to be corrected in their terror: you, Christ, Son of the living and most high Father,

**VERSE 7.** “Send forth your hand from on high,” in the voice of the archangel and at the last trumpet; for that archangel in whose voice the dead will rise is your hand. Or again, the angels who are reapers, who will gather out of your kingdom all stumbling-blocks, are your hand, which I ask you to send forth and no longer keep within. Send forth that hand from on high, and through it rescue me, little David, from the hand of alien sons.

Alternatively: O most high Father, send forth your hand [Col. 0958D] from on high, that is, your Son from your throne, to be humbled in the fullness of time, made of a woman, made under the Law. I, the figurative David, pray this while prophesying, and prophesy it while praying. Or, “send forth your hand from on high,” namely your Son himself, your Wisdom from the throne of your majesty, that he may be with me and labor with me, so that I may know what is acceptable before you at all times. Or from this high throne send forth your hand to be manifested at the final judgment; and through it rescue me, captive, and free me, reduced to slavery. Free me, I say, “from many waters,” which are waters of contradiction. Many waters are many peoples contradicting the truth. Desiring to be freed from them, I say: “Free me from many waters, and from the hand of alien sons,” such as those to whom it is said: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44).

**VERSE 8.** “Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” Hence they are vain not only in their vain words, but even their right hand—that is, those of their works which seemed good, and in which eternal things alone, which are true, seemed to be sought; even their good right hand—is a right hand of iniquity. For that right hand does not work in such a way that its left hand does not know what it does. Hence it is rightly said: “Their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” Their mouth indeed speaks vanity; but I, by contrast, speak truth. And when truth is not heard by men who “will turn away their hearing from the truth and will be turned unto fables,” taking more pleasure in the spirit of many waters than in the teaching [Col. 0959B] of truth, I turn away from such men and turn to you, my God.

**VERSE 9.** “I will sing to you a new song,” praising and reverencing the works and sacraments of the New Testament; “and on the ten-stringed psaltery I will sing psalms to you,” by observing in action the Decalogue of the ten commandments from the Old Testament, to the honor of your name.

**VERSE 10.** “Who gives salvation to kings”: now that the mountains are smoking, so that the mountains themselves—the kings themselves—having attained salvation, may sing a new song, singing psalms upon the ten-stringed psaltery through observance of charity. Whoever lacks this charity may carry a psaltery, but cannot sing psalms or sing a new song. “You who redeemed David your servant” through the ineffable price of redemption—Father, who, in order to redeem him as a servant, gave up your Son—“rescue me from the great [Col. 0959C] sword”; from the evil sword, I say, for there is also a good sword, of which it is said: “I came not to bring peace, but a sword” (Matthew 10:34). This sword, therefore, by which God speaks truth, is good. But the sword by which vain men speak vanity is evil.

On this passage blessed Gregory says (*Morals*, Book 34, chapter 8): “What is expressed here by the evil sword except the anger or persuasion of the evil enemy? For the sword of holy preaching is good, by which we are struck so that we may die to sin. Therefore the sword of diabolical persuasion is evil, when someone is struck wickedly so as to be extinguished from the path of uprightness. [Col. 0959D] This danger will prevail especially in the last times. For that sword of the ancient enemy is a man condemned at that time and taken into the service of his ministry. He sharpens him by the malice of deceit and pierces the hearts of the weak.”

As Saint Gregory says this concerning the final Goliath, who is called Antichrist, we, now in the approach of the dangerous time, must sing psalms against this evil sword, which is now sharpened against truth while falsehood, whether heretical or schismatic, is asserted by subtle persuasion. So that no believer may be killed as if by an evil sword, let each little one say, together with the little David, to our great helper God: “You who redeemed David your servant, from the evil sword

[Col. 0960A] **VERSE 11.** rescue me.” You, great David, who are Redeemer in yourself and redeemed in your body, which is the Church, rescue me, little David, whatever member of your body I may be, from the evil sword of the persuasion of those speaking vanity. “And deliver me from the hand,” and from the power, “of alien sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity,” as has been explained above and is now repeated again, so that by this very repetition these alien ones, alien sons, may be shown more detestable. From their sword and hand I, little David, desire to be delivered, armed with sling and stone of prayer and fortified with the staff of the holy cross.

When I behold in that cross the five wounds of the Lord’s body, and carry them in the case of memory as in a shepherd’s bag, I do not advance unarmed against [Col. 0960B] Goliath. For he is brought down by one stone when, through the sacrament of water and blood flowing from the one wound in Christ’s right side, that proud man is struck in the forehead. Had he borne the sign of the Lord’s cross there, he would not be struck but saved through this one sacrament of Christ’s blood, as through a most clear stone. By it the forehead of Goliath—who is head and king of all the proud—is struck; the foreheads of the humble are marked; and by this holy seal they are distinguished from the alien sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity.

**VERSE 12.** “Whose sons are like young plantations”: because they have been begotten by perverse teaching, they have not flourished in the ancient rites of the Fathers; but, sprouting with new errors, they grow green like young plantations in their youth, [Col. 0960C] which they refuse to put away because they always wish to play the fool, alien to that old age of which it is said: “Venerable old age is an immaculate life” (Wisdom 4:8–9). This was said of their sons, as of the stronger among them. But concerning the weaker I say this: “their daughters are adorned, decked around like the likeness of a temple.” They are adorned, not beautiful by nature, but made up by men. These are their perverse sects, decorated round about externally with vain customs, not inwardly, unlike that daughter whose “whole glory” is “within,” though she is also outwardly “clothed round with variety” (Psalm 44:14–15): beautiful inwardly and outwardly, and rightly called the temple of God.

But these daughters, these sects—made up [Col. 0960D] and ornamented outwardly, ugly and foul within—do not escape the satirical mockery of the pagan who says of such people:

> Ugly within, beautiful in their fair skin.

Accordingly, however greatly those sects of perdition may adorn themselves outwardly—those which, like young plantations, lack the ancient foundation of paternal traditions—they do not deserve to be called a temple like those to whom it is said: “You are the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6:16), and: “The Holy Spirit dwells in you” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

Nevertheless, they are so ornamented as to have the appearance of a temple, though not its reality; for they are not the Church, which is the congregation of the righteous, but the synagogue of Satan, which is the congregation of the wicked. [Col. 0961A] Nevertheless, they glory in earthly riches, because:

**VERSES 13–15.** “Their storehouses are full, pouring out from this into that. Their sheep are fertile, abundant in their goings forth. Their oxen are fat, male or female. There is no breach in the wall, no passage through it, nor crying in their streets.” Without lack of possessions, they live a quiet life in secure peace, which they themselves deem blessed. For they “called blessed the people to whom these things belong.” But I, David, thinking quite otherwise, say that they are wretched; and blessed is the people whose Lord is its God, even if that people is poor like Lazarus the beggar. “Blessed is the nation whose Lord is its God, the people whom he chose for his inheritance” (Psalm 32:12).

Blessed is the people whose Lord is its God, so that the Lord of all may be its God, as he deigned to be called “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6). Though they may have abounded in flocks of sheep and herds of fat oxen, male or female, and though it could have been said of them, “their oxen are fat, male or female,” nevertheless God deigned to be called their God because they did not speak this vanity: they did not say or think that the people possessing these things was blessed. Rather, they called blessed the people whose Lord was its God, just as he was their God, as he himself declares: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”

Not so the ungodly, not so. They do not have the Lord as God, whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame, and whose god is Mammon, [Col. 0961C] because they serve it by greedily pursuing earthly gain rather than serving God by pursuing spiritual gain, as did the one who said: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). For he desired to gain nothing but Christ, whether by living as was necessary for Christ’s members, or by dying in order to be with Christ [Col. 0962A] and see Christ, whom to see is supreme blessedness.

Alternatively: “Their storehouses are full” means hearts stuffed with diverse things, from which they exhale the worst belchings, foul-smelling “from this into that,” because, defeated in one matter, they flee unsteadily into another, having no root of truth. “Their sheep,” literally, because he wishes to show that they cling to transitory things; “their cattle are fertile,” while they themselves are barren, or while their disciples beget others. “In their goings forth,” not in their comings in, because everything that goes out from them quickly perishes. Oxen are fat, not thin from labor but fat from idleness, like those who abound in riches while themselves fasting from truth. Or the oxen are teachers who abound in earthly goods.

A wall made merely of stones is found in gardens or vineyards; yet even it does not collapse for them, so prosperous are they, [Col. 0962B] and no passage or tumultuous cry interrupts their rest. Or the wall is the art of philosophers, which cannot be destroyed so that the righteous may pass through, nor is there the cry that belongs to the narrow way. He does not blame them for abounding in these things, but because they regard them as the right hand—that is, as blessedness—and this is the vanity they have spoken. Abraham and Jacob also abounded in these things. Such prosperity is happiness, but a left-hand happiness: temporal and mortal. To despise it and conquer it through desire for a better and eternal happiness is the best victory.

With this victory he has, as it were, brought to an end all worldly matters. For after this he will say nothing about persecutors of the Church, the miseries of the age, repentance, the anxieties of the godly, or the pride of Antichrist. But the seven psalms that remain are full of divine proclamations: with the clouds of sinners driven away, minds clear in heavenly joy come to the praises of God; and, as though all things by which human ignorance had to be instructed were now completed, one must henceforth devote oneself to God’s proclamations alone. Thus the following psalm is entitled specifically as praise.

## PSALM 144

[Col. 0961]

[Col. 0961D] “I will exalt you, my God the King, and bless your name,” etc., etc. This psalm briefly contains what is widely set forth in the divine Scriptures. Where are not works, power, and the rest read? The following psalms belong to the praises of this psalm; together with it they are seven, in accordance with: “Seven times a day I have spoken praise to you,” and with the seven spirits and seven trumpets. In these God sufficiently taught how he wishes to be praised, so that no one may err. God fills the saints with his Spirit so that they may praise him; and, lest we err in praising, he established in Scripture the way of praise. If a man praises himself, it is arrogance; if God praises himself, it is mercy, because by praising himself he makes himself lovable, and by loving him we become better.

As there are seven penitential psalms, so also there are seven psalms of praise, and seven spirits, in accordance with that mystery by which God commanded Moses to set in the tabernacle “seven lamps” [Col. 0962D] shining with perpetual light (Exodus 25:37). The title, namely:

**VERSE 1. A PRAISE BY DAVID HIMSELF,** directs us to the true David, to whom this praise is sung from the mouth of one who loves him. It begins with blessings, runs through blessings, and ends in everlasting blessings; whoever does not begin them here will be mute in the future. Therefore I, David—I, little and least like David—I, a member of the supreme King, the true David—

“I will exalt you, my God, my King,” making known to others that you, Christ, having now triumphed over the prince of death, proud Goliath—whom you struck down by your death, putting him to death—are now exalted and crowned as King with the height of your Father’s divinity, the glory of your resurrection, and the honor of your ascension. And I say, invoking you yourself within me: “My God, my King,” desiring both that you rule me by royal [Col. 0963A] power so that I may not sin, and, if I have sinned, that by divine clemency you may blot out my sins: “my God” in the one respect, “my King” in the other. My God, by freeing me from sins; my King, by ruling me so that I may not thereafter sin destructively—ruling me so that I grieve for past sins and guard against future ones.

Or you are my God because you created me; my King because you govern me in yourself, the way, truth, and life, lest I stray into deadly byways and falsehoods. Therefore, established in you, the way, truth, and life, I will exalt you by proclaiming you the Most High’s most high Son, and I will bless your name, by which you are called God and King, since the name above every name has been given to you. I will bless this your name, praising it “for an age,” namely now, and “for age upon age,” here and eternally. Repeating the same sense, I say:

[Col. 0963B] **VERSE 2.** “Every day,” as long as days vary with joyful and sorrowful events, I will bless you without interruption, giving you thanks both in prosperity and adversity: in adversity, because you correct and purify me; in prosperity, because you console me. You alternate these two things around me, lest excessive adversity break me or excessive prosperity exalt me. Therefore every day, joyful and sad, I will bless you, giving thanks in all things. “I will praise your name for an age,” while I remain in this age, “and for age upon age,” when I come to the age that follows this present age: eternally. Thus praising continually, I will say:

**VERSE 3.** “Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy,” that is, very praiseworthy. When I say “exceedingly,” I signify by this one little word that it cannot be fully comprehended how great he is who is immense—not extended locally in mass into length, breadth, height, and depth, but great in length, which is infinite eternity; in breadth, which is immeasurable charity; in height, which is his unconquerable power; and in depth, which is unsearchable and eternal wisdom. There is no end to his greatness because it neither began nor ends. Therefore there will be no end to his praise, because:

**VERSE 4.** “Generation and generation shall praise.” “A wicked and provoking generation, a generation that did not direct its heart, a perverse generation” (Psalm 77:8), generated only according to the flesh and not regenerated according to the spirit, whether it has received the sacrament of regeneration or not: nevertheless, because it lives like the Gentiles and retains the image of carnal generation and of the old man, it is designated by the simple name “generation.” But the renewed and twice-begotten generation—born once according to the flesh and born a second time by putting on Christ through the laver of regeneration—is rightly called “generation and generation,” the name being repeated because of the two generations, one in the flesh and the other in the spirit; or one through the laver of regeneration and the other through the renewal of that transformation of which the Apostle says: “The dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:52).

That generation and generation shall praise; and for it to love is certainly to praise, because for it to praise through ages of ages is nothing other than always and without failing [Col. 0964A] to love, and always to see you, the sun of righteousness, whose vision face to face has nothing more delightful or better. Therefore the generation of the upright shall praise. When it truly sees you face to face, it will praise your face because it will love eternally. But now, while your face is hidden from it, it has as material for praise these nine marks of your grace: your works, your power, magnificence, holiness, wonders, the strength of fearful judgments, greatness, remembrance, and righteousness.

From these, as from commonplaces and principal propositions, every praise of God is drawn, just as in the art of argument a multiplicity of arguments is drawn from a few topics. Therefore the generation of the upright shall praise your works, not as philosophers did, who praised your works [Col. 0964B] but did not glorify or praise you through them. Rather, this generation of the upright will praise your works so that they praise you, the maker, in them. They will look upon your works as upon a mirror in which they recognize you, the praiseworthy worker. For they do not praise the works except in order to proclaim your power.

But some eloquent persons praise and love the creature, forgetting the Creator. The holy praisers indeed praise works, but praise still more the worker, whom they love in his works and proclaim to be loved. For if any artisan is to be praised in his artistic work more than the work itself, which he made from pre-existing material, though he did not make the material, how much more should the power of him who made all things from nothing be praised? Rightly, therefore, the praisers of God’s works will also proclaim his power, because what you, my God and King, work, you work by your own power, needing the work of no one, having in yourself the power by which you can do all that you will. Therefore those who praise your works will also rightly proclaim your power.

[Col. 0964C] **VERSE 5.** “They shall speak of the magnificence of the glory of your holiness,” because you, though great, make great persons from little ones; you, though glorious, make glorious persons; you, though holy, make saints from the despised things of this world—which are your wonderful works. And fathers will recount these wonders of yours to sons in generation and generation, through the succession of those begetting, begotten, or yet to be begotten.

**VERSE 6.** “And they shall speak of the power of your fearful deeds,” so that those whom gentle exhortation concerning the sweetness of your promises does not invite may at least be frightened by the power of the terrible judgments with which you threaten. And lest anyone think that he can escape your terrible judgments, they will recount your greatness, testifying that “there is no place for flight, neither from the east nor from the west nor from the desert mountains, because you, O God, are judge,” and are present everywhere. But lest anyone be excessively terrified by the threats of your fearful deeds:

**VERSE 7.** “They shall utter the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness,” with which they are inwardly filled, because what they have drunk through meditation, reading, and prayer they will utter in speech, testifying that, when you are angry, you will remember mercy in wrath—not in scant measure but in an abundance of sweetness. You, sweet and gentle, do not forget those who forget you; indeed, by benefits or by scourges you bring remembrance of yourself to them so that they may not come into the land of forgetfulness, where are “the wounded sleeping in the tombs, whom you remember no more,” because they are “cast off from your hand” (Psalm 87:6), deprived of mercy while your justice punishes them.

And those who escape punishments will exult when they consider this justice of yours; or they will exult in your righteousness, not their own, because they attribute their righteousness not to their own virtue but to your mercy, confessing that:

**VERSE 8.** “The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient and very merciful.”

He is compassionate in manifest effect; merciful in manifest effect; merciful in hidden disposition. Compassionate and merciful toward those to whom he has already given pardon; patient toward those to whom he has not yet given it but waits in order to give it—in which waiting he is kind—and very merciful toward those to be saved. And lest anyone be excluded from the multitude of his mercies, he is kind and

**VERSE 9.** “The Lord is sweet to all,” good and evil alike: “he makes his sun rise upon the good and evil, and sends rain upon the just and unjust” (Matthew 5:45), calling them to himself by benefits even when they flee from him to his adversary, the devil. Yet, although they flee, he distinguishes in them his works, which he made, from their works, which they do, and will render suitable recompense to each. For although, justice requiring it, he punishes their works, nevertheless his mercies are over all his works, because he hates none of the things he made, but has mercy on all, although he punishes the evils that he did not make.

Or, though God’s works are great, displaying the power by which he made many great visible and invisible things from nothing, surpassing all these works is that mercy by which he restored what was lost. It was a great work to create one hundred sheep from nothing and set them in high places; but it was far greater to carry back one of them when it was lost upon his own shoulders. The former was a work of wonderfully immense power; the latter a work of ineffably immense mercy. Therefore, although in you, O God, power is not one thing and mercy another, yet, when the works of each are considered, mercy exalts judgment concerning itself: human beings and angels judge the work of mercy, by which what was lost was restored, to be greater than the work of power, by which things were created from nothing, because the latter was done without labor and the former with labor. There one word was spoken, through which all things were made; here many things were said and done, through which what was lost is restored. Both these and those works of yours, O my God and King, are great matter for praising you. Therefore it is right that no one boast in his own works, but
VERSE 10. Let all your works confess you, O Lord, by prompting rational minds, through consideration of themselves, to confess your praise—especially in the saints; and may your saints also bless you. This indeed they will do. For:

VERSE 11. They shall speak of the glory of your kingdom, glorifying and magnifying your kingdom, by which you mightily govern what you have mightily created [Col. 0966A], so that you leave nothing unordered among the things created by you. Your wisdom and power reach mightily from end to end and dispose all things sweetly, from the highest to the lowest depth of things—from the archangel to the little worm, from heaven’s highest palace to the lowest depth of the infernal prison. Your saints shall speak of this glory of your kingdom and shall proclaim your power, by which you can do all things and need no one’s assistance in your rule, although you sometimes make human beings and angels participants in your governance, accomplishing through them what you will. They shall proclaim your power, not so that they themselves may become known to people and please them, but:

VERSE 12. That they may make known to the children of men your power and the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom. Compared with this kingdom, an earthly kingdom—such as that of the Babylonians, the Romans, and others shown to Daniel under beastly forms [Col. 0966B]—has no glory. Or, if it seems to possess some glory, it has no magnificent glory, because every temporal glory passes like the flower of grass. But the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom will endure, because:

VERSE 13. Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages, and your dominion is in every generation and generation: whether that which now endures or that which will hereafter succeed it, through infinite ages. All these things said concerning your power, O God my King, pertain chiefly to the might of your terrible deeds, which your praisers shall declare, and they shall also recount your greatness, in order to rouse the sluggish through fear. But in order to kindle the devout and dedicated [Col. 0966C] toward love, they attach to these the following matters, which concern the abundance of sweetness that they shall pour forth. For what is sweeter, what more delightful, than that the Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in his works? Faithful in promising good things, holy in fulfilling the same promises; so that faithfulness may be recognized in all his words that promise, and holiness in all his works that bestow what was promised, if anyone considers the abundance of sweetness in them. Yet among all his works, these are especially sweet and delightful:

VERSE 14. The Lord himself lifts up all who fall, by humbling themselves; for as “everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled,” so “everyone who [Col. 0966D] humbles himself” shall be “exalted” by him and lifted up (Luke 14:11). One falls through voluntary humility, and, though falling, is not dashed down and broken: thus blessed Job is read to have fallen upon the ground when he heard of the death of his children; yet in falling he was not broken into the sin of impatience (Job 1:18 ff.). There is also one who, although elect, is nevertheless allowed to fall through humiliation, in order to heal or guard against pride. Thus Peter, lifted somewhat by presumption above his fellow disciples, was allowed to fall and was somewhat dashed down by the fault of denial; yet he was not crushed, because, although falling, he remained righteous. And it is written of the righteous: “Though he falls seven times in a day, he rises again” (Prov. 24:16). “When the righteous man falls, he shall not be crushed, because [Col. 0967A] the Lord supports him with his hand” (Ps. 36:24). Peter therefore was dashed down in his fall when he denied—not through impiety, but through frailty—denying with his mouth him whom he loved in his heart. For the charity by which he loved Christ had not utterly failed, and Christ had not become hateful or wearisome to him. Thus many frail persons are dashed down like Peter; many impious persons are utterly crushed like Judas. But the Lord rejects those who are crushed, as stubborn in their wickedness; he raises up all who have been dashed down, namely by giving them repentance together with pardon. What is more delightful than this abundance of your sweetness, O God my King? But so that this sweetness may be felt seasoned with the salt of justice—concerning which it was proposed above, “they shall exult in your justice”—let what follows be considered:

[Col. 0967B] VERSE 15. The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord, and you give them their food at the fitting time; and the rest to the end of the psalm. For it belongs to your justice, O God, that just as you reject those who do not hope in you, so you graciously regard those who hope in you—and this you do. For, excluding from the multitude of “all” the unbelievers, who are nothing and tend toward nothingness, the eyes of all who truly exist—who by fearing and loving you tend toward true being—hope in you, O Lord; and you give them bodily and spiritual food at the fitting time, as is expedient for the salvation of those who hunger, not according to their desire when they desire something else, or desire otherwise than they should. Food is not always to be given, but at the fitting time. For many petitioners are beneficially delayed. The Apostle asks for the angel of Satan to be removed [Col. 0967C] and does not receive it, but this is for his perfection. The devil asks to test Job and receives permission, but to his own condemnation. Christ himself had come to die; yet, taking the weak upon himself, he says: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”; and although he did not receive what he seemed to ask, he says: “Not what I will, but what you will” (Matt. 26:39), blessing God his Father at every time.

Here it should be noted that those to whom food is promised are indicated to have been hungry. Of them Truth says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6); and of them it is also said here: “You give them their food at the fitting time.” Food, therefore, here means righteousness [Col. 0967D], and those who “hunger and thirst” for it “shall be filled”—not in accordance with their hasty and perhaps disorderly desire, but at the fitting time. At that time:

VERSE 16. You, O God, open your hand, the power of your goodness, and fill every living creature with blessing. I say every living creature, not every beast: for *beasts* are called untamed animals, such as wolves, lions, and bears; while *animals* are called tamed animals, such as oxen, sheep, and cattle of the field. Therefore the gentle and tamed animals are filled with blessing, and to them it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34); while beasts are filled with curse, and to them it will be said: “Depart, accursed, into eternal fire” (ibid. 25:41). What should those who praise God’s works say concerning these matters [Col. 0968A]? This, namely:

VERSE 17. The Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works. Among the nine proclamations indicated above, the last was justice. Here it is signified and magnified by its explicit name, when I, David, say: “The Lord is just in all his ways.” These ways are his dispositions, judgments, and wills, which never depart from supreme justice, whether he strikes or heals, according to the saying: “I will strike, and I will heal” (Deut. 32:39). The Lord is therefore just in all his ways; nor are they blameworthy because “his judgments are incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable” (Rom. 11:33). They are not unjust because his judgments and counsels, in all of which he is just, are hidden; and he is also holy [Col. 0968B] in all his works. “Ways” belong to disposition, “works” to effect. These two are distinguished among us, but with him to will is to do. When he wills, he opens his hand, granting blessings at the fitting time; and when he wills, he closes it, delaying rather than taking away blessings which are to be given—not according to human and importunate desire, but at the fitting time. This belongs to the beauty of justice: that only the one who asks receives, the one who seeks finds, and it is opened only to the one who knocks; and that in asking, seeking, and knocking, one invokes God himself within oneself as in a fittingly adorned house—not that he may lodge there as a traveler, but that he may possess the house itself as Lord. Those who tasted the sweetness of his word invoked him in this manner when they said: [Col. 0968C] “Stay with us, Lord” (Luke 24:29), as though they said: Rule over us within us. When they called and invoked him as Lord, he was near them, although their eyes were held so that they did not recognize him. Thus also now and until the end of the age, although he may sometimes not appear present:

VERSE 18. The Lord himself, Lord of all, is near to all who call upon him. Although he is everywhere through the essence of his majesty, he becomes more present through his mercy to all who call upon him in truth. I say “in truth,” because everyone who prays calls upon what he desires to obtain. If that is something other than God himself, the Lord himself, he does not call upon the Lord in truth [Col. 0968D], because he does not desire the Lord to rule over him when in prayer he seeks not him but something else. Therefore it would be contrary to justice if the Lord gave himself to one asking for something else; just as, conversely, it is just that:

VERSE 19. He will fulfill the will of those who fear him, hear their supplication, and save them; because those who fear him advance through the fear of God to love of him. The Lord guards those who love him as the pupil of the eye, because they are both dark through humility and bright through the oil of charity, like the black and shining pupil of the eye, which needs great protection. Such persons:

VERSE 20. The Lord guards, and he will destroy all sinners; that is, he destroys different people in different ways: some as he destroyed Saul, whom in converting he found to be Paul; [Col. 0969A] others as he destroyed Judas, so that he went into his own place. Or he will destroy all sinners who persevere in sins. And all this is the work of God’s justice. For it is equitable both to guard those who love him and to destroy sinners. Having now explained all the things proposed above, the last of which was justice, a brief conclusion follows near the end of the psalm, plainly commending it and comprehending what cannot be expounded, in this way:

VERSE 21. My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord. As though it were said: since all the things mentioned—namely works, power, magnificence, holiness, wonders, might, terrible deeds, greatness, remembrance, and justice—show him to be praiseworthy, from whom they are and in whom they are: my mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord [Col. 0969B], to whom I say: “Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth [Col. 0970A] shall proclaim your praise” (Ps. 50:17). And may all flesh bless his holy name. “All flesh,” that is, every human being who has a heart of flesh, not of stone; a feeling heart, not an unfeeling one. Having considered the wonders of God, let such a person bless his holy name for ever and ever: that is, now and always, and unto ages of ages.

Glory to the Father, the Lord faithful in all his words. Glory to the Son, who is the Father’s hand, which, when opened, fills every living creature with blessing. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is the blessing proceeding from Father and Son, by which the living creatures were filled, of whom it was said: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit.” Glory to the one and triune God, “who fulfills the will of those who fear him and guards all who love him” (Acts 2:4). [Col. 0970B] Amen.

## PSALM 145

[Col. 0969]

[Col. 0969B] “Praise the Lord, O my soul.” Title:

VERSE 1. ALLELUIA.

It indicates with what affection and what labor he directs praise. He addresses his soul and says: “Praise the Lord, O my soul.” And it replies: “I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing praise to my God as long as I exist.” From what source shall I praise, from what source shall I sing? From power, from [Col. 0969C] mercy: from power, because he made heaven and earth, sea and all things in them; from mercy, because he frees those in fetters, enlightens the blind, and so forth.

One may ask here: who gives counsel to whom when it is said, “Praise the Lord, O my soul”? Does the flesh advise its soul, or does the soul advise itself? It is said that the flesh does not, for counsel is always sought from the better. Just as gold, though not pure, is nevertheless by nature better than the purest lead, so too a human being, though utterly wicked, is nonetheless better in kind than a most valuable horse. Thus the rational soul, even if sinful, is by nature better than its body. For the soul is a spiritual thing, near to the highest Spirit; it moves, governs, and gives sensation to the body. [Col. 0969D] Therefore the flesh, even if tamed and at peace, cannot give counsel to the soul, which is superior.

Here it should be observed that the Apostle names three things in a human being, saying: “May the God of peace sanctify you wholly, so that your spirit, soul, and body may be preserved entire and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thess. 5:23). Of these three, the spirit, higher than the other two—the soul, namely, and the body—is to be understood as giving counsel to the soul, saying:

VERSE 2. “Praise the Lord, O my soul.” Why do you wander among outward and lower things? Call yourself back to inward and higher things, setting your mind on what is above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God. The soul replies: “I will praise the Lord in my life.” As long as I am in the corruptible body that weighs down me, the soul [Col. 0970B], as long as the earthly dwelling presses down my mind, occupied with many thoughts, I cannot praise perfectly even though I wish to do so. For my changeable thought is drawn in different directions, and, as it were, dies as often as it changes from state to state, or from movement to movement. Therefore, I—the soul, midway between spirit and body—am in a life that is half death. I do not yet enjoy my life, which is nothing other than the divine essence, the life of blessed spirits. I, the soul, am a stranger from that life as long as I am in a mortal body. But when I shall be in my life, when the highest Life gives life to me, the life between the two, then in my life I shall praise the Lord perfectly and fully.

Meanwhile, as I am able, I shall sing praise by doing good works, as long as I exist; because until the end of this present life I, the soul, shall obey the spirit obedient to its superior. I shall also be obedient and subject to every human creature for God’s sake: whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good, because I shall support to the best of my ability those who devote themselves to such a just rule. Likewise, and still more, [Col. 0970D] I shall be obedient to the Roman pontiff as supreme, and to other rulers sent by him—indeed, by God—as was that man of whom it is said: “There was a man sent from God” (John 1:6). By obeying and supporting such persons sent by God, I shall sing praise to my God as long as I exist.

Or: here, in death, I shall sing praise; but in my life, which will endure eternally, I shall praise as long as I exist. As long as I am there, so long shall I praise—namely, eternally. I shall encourage others also to the holy purpose of similarly praising and singing, to whom I say:

VERSE 3. Do not put your trust in princes. You who wish to praise and sing to God, first free yourselves from worldly cares. For unless you turn away from evil, you cannot do good; and only those who despise and reject earthly things will reach heavenly things. Now a great nourishment of worldly cares is to trust in a human being rather than in the Lord. For one also trusts in a human being who trusts in oneself, since one too is human. Therefore, whoever, trusting in oneself and one’s own strength, thinks oneself to be something when one is nothing, deceives oneself. For this reason, do not trust in human beings, nor in those who rule others; much less in those lower persons, namely in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation.

Alternatively: “Do not put your trust in princes,” namely in demons, who are “the rulers of this world, the rulers of darkness, spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). Those trust in such persons who seek answers or help from them: pagans, diviners, magicians, and other confederates, who say in Isaiah: [Col. 0971B] “We have made a covenant with death and have made an agreement with hell” (Isa. 28:15). Do not trust in princes of this sort, because they deceive in answering and are not faithful in helping.

Or: do not trust in princes, such as Pharaoh, prince of Egypt, who, when the supreme Prince was angry, could help neither himself nor his army. Or do not trust in princes, however holy, as those did who said, “I belong to Paul; I belong to Cephas”; but trust in the one Prince, as those who said, “But I belong to Christ” (1 Cor. 1:12). Do not trust in other princes, in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. Yet he is not a son of men, but the Son of Man, in whom salvation is found. Any other prince, a son of men, cannot save [Col. 0971C] either himself or others, because suddenly, when he does not wish it:

VERSE 4. His spirit shall depart, and when his spirit departs, his body shall return to its earth, from which it took its beginning. On that day of death all the thoughts of those who stretch themselves out toward various gains and ambitions shall perish; these designs fail them when they die. You therefore say to me, O my soul—or you, whoever hears me dissuading trust in princes—“In whom, then, should one hope?” I, the Spirit, answer: one ought to hope in the God of Jacob, because:

VERSE 5. Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob. Truly blessed, because he will make Jacob into Israel, saying to one who struggles after Jacob’s example: “You shall no longer be called [Col. 0971D] Jacob,” that is, *wrestler*, “but your name shall be Israel” (Gen. 32:28), *the man who sees God*. Your struggle shall be turned into rest when the sorrow in which you struggle, so long as you do not see God face to face, is changed into joy. And your soul—which you now address, saying, “Praise the Lord, O my soul”—shall be saved. Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob: a helper in respect of present assistance; his hope in respect of future, endless joy to be possessed in the Lord his God. Though God is not now seen face to face by Jacob as he struggles in prayers and tears—for this vision is reserved for Israel—yet even now, as this Jacob labors and wrestles through the whole night, the angel of great counsel will reveal himself to him, as though in a mirror, by the visible works of his power and [Col. 0972A] his mercy. For his great power appears in him:

VERSE 6. Who made heaven and earth, the sea and all things in them. I mean all things visible and invisible, greatest and least, so that we may know that he who made all things cares for all things. And because he cares for all things, since he is the Lord and Creator of all, do not doubt, O my soul, that he also cares for you. Do not doubt, O Jacob, his omnipotence, who made all these things from nothing: heaven and earth, the sea, and all things in them. That he cares for all these things is evident from this, that:

VERSE 7. He keeps truth forever, detesting every lie, because he is true in his promises and requires truth from the human being in the good things promised. He kept truth for Jacob, or Israel, to whom he said: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.” He also demanded truth from him concerning the things he had vowed, when Jacob said: “If the Lord my God shall be with me in this way in which I walk,” and so on, up to: “I will offer you tithes and peace-offerings” (Gen. 28:20 ff.). The God of Jacob keeps such truth in his own sayings and promises and in those of his people. And if anyone injures the truthful who are faithful toward him, as Jacob’s uncle Laban did in defrauding him, God himself executes judgment for those who suffer injustice and bear it patiently, as Jacob did. God rendered judgment for him in this: that amid the deceit of those who cheated him he stood by him, made him honorable, preserved him from enemies, and protected him from deceivers.

He likewise gives food to the hungry [Col. 0972C], not only in giving food to all flesh, but also in hearing all who are pilgrims in this world and, with Jacob, ask for bread to eat and clothing to cover themselves. They are content, that is, with daily bread, which is sought daily in the Lord’s Prayer, and with clothing to cover the nakedness contracted from Adam. This food and this clothing are the righteousness for which those who hunger and thirst are blessed, because they shall be filled.

God, thus manifested through works of power and justice, is no less manifested through works of evident mercy. The Lord himself releases those fettered by the chain of iniquity or mortality, so that they may now be righteous and hereafter immortal. This is one work of mercy. Five others follow, so that he may rightly demand six works of mercy from us, since he bestows six works of mercy upon us. The first is that he releases the fettered, so that they may walk in the way. Then, so that the way itself may be clearly seen and one may not stray into a byway, he:

VERSE 8. The Lord enlightens the blind. If they have been dashed down by the enemy, the same Lord raises up those who have been dashed down. Or if they have voluntarily humbled themselves and have been broken and cast down through humility, they are exalted through the Lord himself, who raises up the fallen. The Lord also loves those who are now righteous—upright after being cast down. And so that they do not lose the righteousness freely bestowed upon them by grace, he:

VERSE 9. The Lord guards strangers, who do not have here an abiding city but seek the one to come [Col. 0973A], and who accordingly need help like widows and orphans. All are orphans in this pilgrimage, grieving at the absence of their Father. Though he is everywhere, he is sought as though absent, and with sorrow, by his desolate children, as long as they do not see him face to face. Likewise, all faithful souls betrothed to God are widows, yet are desolate because they have not yet entered the wedding feast; and they fear that the doors may be shut against them so long as they do not know whether their oil will be sufficient. Such orphans and widows he himself will receive, and he will bring them into the wedding feast. But he will destroy the ways of sinners: the broad and winding ways he will destroy, because those who neglected to do the six works to be recalled at the divine judgment will be strangers to these six works of God’s mercy. To them it will also be said: “Depart, accursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). When this has taken place [Col. 0974A], what remains for us to expect? Surely the most peaceful kingdom, because then the kingdom of sin and death will have been destroyed.

VERSE 10. The Lord shall reign for ever. Which Lord? Your God, O Zion, because you are his kingdom in which he shall reign, not Babylon, which he shall condemn. He shall reign, I say, with no end to his reign; but through generation and generation—that is, eternally, without end.

Glory to the Father, the Lord who made heaven and earth, the sea and all things in them; glory to the Son, the Lord who releases the fettered; glory to the Holy Spirit, who enlightens the blind, raises up those who have been dashed down, and loves the righteous; glory to the one Trinity and triune Unity, who works all these things inseparably. Amen.

## PSALM 146

[Col. 0973]

[Col. 0973B] “Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good.”

The title, ALLELUIA (VERSE 1), urges praise. In the preceding psalm he exhorted his own soul, saying: “Praise the Lord, O my soul.” But not content with praise from himself alone, in this following psalm he exhorts others also to praise, saying:

“Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good.” And truly a psalm is good; or, as Jerome prefers, “for the psalm is good,” that is, a psalm is a good thing. Truly, I say, the psalm is good, because these three cooperate in it: strings, sound, and movement of the fingers. By the strings we understand the drying-up of the flesh; by the sound, the virtues of hearts; and by the movement of the fingers, good action performed with sound discernment. When these are present, praise of our God is truly pleasing and fitting [Col. 0973C]. He immediately adds the reasons why we should praise, saying:

VERSE 2. The Lord, building Jerusalem, will gather together the dispersions of Israel. The Hebrew text has: “Praise the Lord, for he is good; how fitting is a song to our God; praise is beautiful.” This means: Praise the Lord, first because he is good—indeed, because he is goodness itself. For he is not good through an accidental gift, as a good angel or a good human being is good, but through essential goodness, so that for him being is not one thing and being good another; rather, for him, to be is to be good. Therefore praise the Lord because he is good; and for this reason, when one praises, a song to God is fitting and praise is beautiful.

But if someone cannot contemplate the hidden essence of his goodness, let that person contemplate [Col. 0973D] the manifest evidence of his works, from which to draw matter for praise. For the Lord who builds Jerusalem is truly worthy of praise. Jerusalem is the city of angelic citizens who continually contemplate God, and the human being also was created as its citizen. But he “went down from [Col. 0974B] Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers” (Luke 10:30). Thus that city was diminished in part, and it could not be restored by angelic or human power until that Samaritan came who, though human, is also the almighty Lord. In building Jerusalem he shows himself both praiseworthy and lovable: through the power by which he gathered the dispersions of Israel, drawing near to the half-dead human being; through the abundance of sweetness by which:

VERSE 3. He heals the broken in heart, pouring the oil of grace into those whose “spirit is afflicted, and whose heart is contrite and humbled” (Ps. 50:19). Lest this oil poured into wounds perish or run out, he binds up their wounds. The bindings are temporal sacraments, by which we have consolation for the present; they will then be removed when perfect health comes. Moral precepts also are salutary bindings, by which the wounds of penitents—who grieve over their wounds—are bound up. Such persons still have something alive in them, by which they are able to feel, as half-dead rather than wholly dead. For those alien to the sorrow of repentance are entirely dead; they cannot be healed and do not receive bindings unless first raised from the dead by him:

VERSE 4. Who numbers the multitude of the stars—for example, the seven stars of the seven churches—and, seeing that one has fallen from its first charity, says to it: “Repent” (Acts 8:22). He therefore numbers the multitude of stars, that is, those who instruct many unto righteousness and consequently “shall shine like stars for everlasting ages” (Dan. 12:3). Even the stars in the literal sense can be numbered by him. This, however, is not surprising in one who knew all things before they came to be, and whose memory is never succeeded by forgetfulness. Thus this is an argument drawn [Col. 0975A] from memory, of which it was said: “They shall pour forth the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness” (Ps. 114:7). He numbers the stars, therefore, and calls them all by name, because the names of the elect are written in his memory.

What more need be said? As he is praiseworthy for ineffable knowledge, so also he is praiseworthy for ineffable magnificence. For those who speak of the magnificence of the glory of his holiness truly say:

VERSE 5. Great is the Lord, and great is his power, and there is no number to his wisdom. For although God made all things in measure, number, and weight, no one can measure, number, or weigh the measure, number, and weight themselves in which God disposed all things, because these are incomprehensible. Therefore let no one stretch oneself toward comprehending the incomprehensible. These things may be apprehended by faith as they are, but not comprehended by intellect. Hence the bride says: “My beloved, I will lay hold of you” (Song 8:2); she does not say, “I will comprehend you.” For those lay hold of him who become his participants in that city of which it is elsewhere said: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in the same” (Ps. 121:3). Thus the citizens of Jerusalem shall be participants in him who is *the Same*, yet they shall not grasp him wholly.

But since *the Same* has no parts, who can explain how many persons may participate in one who is so one that there is in him no diversity either of parts or of forms, since he is the simplest Form itself? All composite things are from him, while he remains in his own simplicity [Col. 0975C]. I do not think this can be comprehended, though it can now be apprehended by faith and hereafter by clear vision—just as we now believe that the visible sun is beneath the earth at night, while by day we see it above the earth; yet even when we see its radiance, or the sun itself, or other things through its participation, we do not take in all its brightness.

Therefore, as long as we cannot see the wisdom of God, which has no number, let us not criticize his dispositions as though something could have been done, or could be done, better than he has disposed and disposes it. For, in his ordering, created things were made as they had to be made, and the Scriptures were spoken as they had to be spoken. Let not the sick person correct the medicines that the physician prepares: in creation, adversities correct and prosperities console; in Scripture, obscure things exercise and clear things feed. Whom do they exercise and whom do they feed? The gentle, devout, meek persons, who do not speak against or rashly criticize what they do not understand, but meekly receive the implanted word that can save their souls—whether obscure or clear, whether it strikes their vices or commends their virtues. It must always be received meekly, because:

VERSE 6. The Lord receives the meek. He receives such persons meekly, who receive his word meekly and contradict him in nothing. But he humbles [Col. 0976A] sinners and opponents down to the earth; indeed, he permits them, in heavenly words, to understand nothing but earth—like Jews and Manichaeans, who in the words of the Law promising grain, wine, oil, milk, and honey understand earthly things alone, and in the names of earthly goods do not perceive heavenly and spiritual things to be promised. Such persons are therefore humbled down to earth, while they understand nothing but earth.

Since it is great, and belongs to divine gift alone, to advance to an understanding and savoring of the spiritual things hidden within God’s sanctuary, let us not burst into that sanctuary, which is closed to the proud and unmeek. Rather, meekly and humbly knocking at the friend’s door, let us do what follows:

VERSE 7. Sing before the Lord in confession. “Sing before,” or, as another manuscript has it, “Begin for the Lord in confession”: first confessing sins by which your heart has been darkened, so that it does not see the true light in the Scriptures; then also by confession of praise glorifying the justice that orders all things rightly. In this manner one comes to the understanding of heavenly things, when the eye of the heart is cleansed so as to see God, as it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). But lest your confession be empty and lest the pleasing and fitting praise be uttered by the mouth alone: sing praise to our God on the harp. Thus after confession good works follow, both in spiritual exercise—such as laboring in the word of God by learning, teaching, writing, reading, and sowing in whatever way, and guarding what is sown from birds and other disasters; this is the pleasing psaltery—and in bodily exercise, such as work of the hands, Martha’s service, or the chastening of the flesh through abstinence; this is the harp, of which it is said: “A pleasing psaltery with the harp” (Ps. 80:3). Therefore sing praise to our God on the harp, to whom I say:

VERSE 8. Who covers heaven with clouds and prepares rain for the earth. He covers the heavenly meaning in the Scriptures with mysteries and figures, so as to incite people to ask, seek, and knock at the friend’s door. But for believers who faithfully ask and say, “Drop down dew from above, O heavens, and let the clouds rain down the Just One” (Isa. 45:8), he who covered heaven with clouds—whether literally [Col. 0976D] or mystically—he who veils Scripture in figures and mysteries, prepares rain from those very clouds through the diligence of teachers and interpreters. As they clarify the obscurities of Scripture, human hearts are watered, so that they may bear fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold. Nor is it surprising if through this rain he makes fields and valleys—the meek and humble—fruitful, when he also produces grass and herbage upon the mountains for the service of human beings: that is, when he makes those exalted in the world fruitful in almsgiving toward spiritual persons who serve God.

On this passage blessed Gregory says in *Job* [Note: [Col. 0975D] Book 29 of the *Morals*, chapter 26]:

> What is meant here by “herbage,” except the support [Col. 0977A] of preachers, when it is said: “Who produces grass upon the mountains, and herbage for the service of human beings”? For grass is produced upon the mountains, and herbage for the service of human beings, when the exalted persons of this world, called to communion of faith, provide temporal sustenance to holy preachers who serve spiritually on the journey of this life.

VERSE 9. Who gives their food to the beasts, and to the young ravens that call upon him [Note: [Col. 0977D] St Gregory the Great, Book 30 of the *Morals*, chapter 9]. Beasts receive food when minds formerly brutish are satisfied with the nourishment of Holy Scripture. Food is given to the young ravens—that is, to the children of the Gentiles—when their desire is refreshed by our manner of life. This raven was food while the Church sought him; but now he receives food because he himself seeks others for conversion. His young [Col. 0977B], that is, the preachers born from him, do not presume upon themselves but upon the strength of their Redeemer. Hence it is rightly said: “And to the young ravens that call upon him.” For they know that they can do nothing by their own power; and although with devout desires they hunger for the gain of souls, they nevertheless pray that this may be accomplished by him who works all things. For by true faith they understand that “neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3:7).

Physicists say that young ravens are not fed by ravens before they become black, but are said to be fed by dew coming down from heaven; and, by the benefit of their age, they do not know their fathers’ food—that is, the stench of corpses. Such are the innocent children of pagans. And truly our fathers were [Col. 0977C] ravens, whether in paganism, clinging to the foul carnal desires and seeking nourishment from them; or in Judaism, clinging to carnal observances, likewise foul and, in comparison with spiritual sacrifices, likened to dung. But we, their children, like young ravens, despise such things; and, desiring to be fed by the grace of the Holy Spirit as by dew from heaven, we continually call upon that same Spirit. We also prepare a dwelling for him within ourselves through humility and gentleness, knowing, as was said above, that the Lord looks upon the gentle but detests the proud and unyielding, because:

**VERSE 10.** He will not take pleasure in the strength of the horse, nor will he delight in the legs of a man. By the horse, whose high neck signifies pride, are denoted the insolent and exalted, who are hateful to God. By the legs [Col. 0978A] of a man is denoted the slippery gait of the insolent person, who is designated by the name “man,” because, although *vir* (“man”) is derived from *virtus* (“strength” or “valor”), those who consider themselves men and strong, trusting in themselves, do not call upon God—as we, the frail and fearful young ravens, call upon God, knowing that the Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him and in those who hope in his mercy.

Instead of what we have, “in the legs of a man,” another translation has, “in the tents of a man.” These differ greatly from that tabernacle of which it is said: “Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he shall dwell with them” (Rev. 21:3). For the tents of the man Antichrist are conventicles: he, being an unjust and talkative man, “shall not be directed on the earth.” From whose [Col. 0978B] tents I—David, I penitent like David, I little one like David, desiring to be far away—“have chosen to be an outcast in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 83:11). Despised and cast out by such persons, I desire to remain in the tents of the righteous, who fear God and hope in God, because:

**VERSE 11.** The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, and in those who hope in his mercy. Hope is fittingly joined to fear, like the upper millstone to the lower; for neither is useful without the other. Therefore the Lord takes pleasure in those who fear and hope. Judas, repenting, feared, but did not hope in mercy; therefore he went away and hanged himself with a noose. Thus, whoever [Col. 0978C] fears God as a just avenger should, strengthened by hope in God’s mercy, flee to him as a merciful forgiver. Let him flee from him to him—from him when angry to him when appeased. Although he is angry because of sin, yet he is appeased toward those who fear him and hope in him through the sacrifice offered to him upon the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor, power, and victory unto all ages and through all ages of ages.

Glory to the Father, who is the great Lord. Glory to the Son, who is his great power and wisdom, of whom there is no number. Glory to the Holy Spirit, who is his mercy, with which this psalm concludes when it says: “The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him and in those who hope in his mercy.”

## PSALM 147

[Col. 0977]

[Col. 0977D] **Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion.** From that congregation of Israel, from the salvation of those contrite ones, from the calling or numbering of those stars, of which the preceding psalm treated, one city is made: the heavenly Jerusalem. Accordingly [Col. 0978D] David invites it in this psalm to praise, saying, “Praise, O Jerusalem.” The title is:

**ALLELUIA, OR A PSALM OF HAGGAI AND ZECHARIAH.**

Although these two prophets were troubled in captivity and exile, they nevertheless prophesied, rejoicing in hope and patient in tribulation, the restoration of Jerusalem. As Jeremiah had foretold, this took place after seventy years, as a figure of the heavenly Jerusalem, which is to be completed after the course of this present time, which is conducted through seven days. Saint David foresaw this; and although he was still a captive exile detained among the citizens of Babylon, he lifted his heart on high and applauded that city which is above, the free Jerusalem, our mother. Let us also applaud her, continually saying:

**VERSE 12.** Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem. O Jerusalem, now seeing peace; O Zion, now contemplating that for which you had hoped. Praise the Lord, who has mightily built you. Praise your God, who has led you to the vision of his divine brightness. Praise him securely [Col. 0979B], your labors and distresses having passed away, all your enemies having been shut out, who will no longer be able to break into or creep into you.

**VERSE 13.** For he has now strengthened the bars of your gates, which he ordained before the ages. The foolish virgins having been excluded, the door is shut; and “God has wiped away every tear from the eyes” of those who are within, “and death shall be no more, neither mourning nor crying, for the former things have passed away” (Rev. 21:4). No friend goes out; no stranger enters. Therefore praise securely, O heavenly city built from living stones: no one will trouble you any longer. No member of the household goes out; no enemy enters. No one leaves, for whom you may grieve; no one enters, whom you may fear. Thus the delights of the blessings with which your Creator [Col. 0979C] has blessed his children resting in you and feeling no external evils may be disturbed by no scandal—as we still experience them, because while we remain in the body we are exiles from you. Yet, raising our hearts upward, we live in you in mind and spirit, like that citizen of yours who said: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Those who say this truly and sincerely have already been saved in hope, though not yet in the reality enjoyed by your children who are within you; for whatever is within enjoys the vision of peace. Outside are Gehenna and Babylon, hostile to your citizens. From its assaults he has made you secure.

**VERSE 14.** He has made your borders peace. And lest, in the peace which you possess from evils, there be any want or deficiency [Col. 0979D] of good things: he satisfies you with the fatness of wheat—he who became a grain of wheat for your sake—lest you should fail amid labors. You are to be refreshed and satisfied in peace, not in any ordinary manner, but with the fatness of wheat: so that those who are now nourished in pilgrimage, as it were, by the crust of the living bread, veiled under visible sacraments, when introduced into the vision of peace may be satisfied with the fatness and richness of that same bread. Longing for this satisfaction, I, David, say: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. 62:6). Blessed, then, are those who now hunger and thirst for the living bread which came down from heaven, for they shall be satisfied when filled with the fatness of this bread. This satisfaction shall belong to those keeping sabbath-rest in their homeland. But here, for pilgrims, who will be their comforter and shepherd, lest they fail on the way? For if they are sent away [Col. 0980A] fasting, without the refreshment of provision for the journey, they will fail on the way. Some of them have come from far away—so very far that some are compared with excessively cold snow, especially in those days in which, because iniquity abounds, the love of many will grow cold. Others are likened to mist, because the darkness of sin obstructs the eyes of the mind. And some, excessively hardened in the evil purpose of their minds, though brilliant in natural intellectual subtlety, are compared to crystal. For sinners such as these—cold, misty, hard—to be gathered into the city of Jerusalem and converted from their wickedness, what craftsman, what worker, will be fit? Certainly he:

**VERSE 15.** Who sends forth his word to the earth, of whom elsewhere it is said: “He sent his word and healed [Col. 0980B] them” (Ps. 106:20). This utterance, this Word made flesh, sent to the earth—that is, to the Church—like manna, indeed truly manna, the bread of angels, refreshes in the desert of this pilgrimage those hastening to that land of promise. There they shall be satisfied with the fatness of wheat, no longer needing the outward crust of the visible sacraments of the living bread, by which they are refreshed now and shall be satisfied in the future. This will come when all the wondrous works for whose completion this utterance, this incarnate Word, this speech proceeding from the Father’s mouth, was sent into the earth, have been accomplished: so that “his going forth was from the highest heaven, and his circuit unto its height.” In order that this course may swiftly be completed, so that we too may meet “unto a perfect man, unto the measure [Col. 0980C] of the age of the fullness of Christ,” this speech runs swiftly. We too must run in its fragrance, not so much with the steps of our feet as with the advances of virtues stretching forward, forgetting what is behind. He runs as a giant, whose course nothing can hinder. Let the bride also run after him; if she feels herself hindered by snowy cold or misty darkness, let her continually say to the swiftly preceding bridegroom in prayers and unutterable groanings: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3). As we thus pray, that our flight may not take place in winter or in mist, may he hear us.

**VERSE 16.** He gives snow like wool; he scatters mist like [Col. 0980D] ashes. He does so literally: snow falls softly and, as it were, in small tufts like wool; and mist, spread broadly like ashes, fills plains and valleys and covers mountains. These are great works of God, possible to none but himself. Yet by these things others are signified, far greater and more wonderful. For he gives snow like wool when from cold and utterly wicked people he makes material for weaving that garment signified when, at Christ’s transfiguration on the mountain, “his garments were white as snow” (Matt. 17:2). In those garments the Church was prefigured, which, when Christ appears in his glory, shall then also appear with him in glory. Thus he gives snow like wool who, by making the impious devout, increases the holy [Col. 0981A] Church—his seamless tunic, woven from above throughout by faith working through love. This faith is, indeed, that strong woman, whose industry is shown in this: “she sought wool and flax and worked with the counsel of her hands” (Prov. 31:13), while her husband, God, grants counsel and help for the whole work. He also scatters mist like ashes when he makes truly humble and penitent those darkened by the gloom of sin. Such persons are signified by ashes, as holy Job says: “I repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:6). Abraham also, speaking with God and conscious of his great humility, said: “I will speak with my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18:27). God makes such persons out of mist when he makes the proud humble, [Col. 0981B] because pride blinds the eyes of the mind, whereas the eye-salve of humility and repentance enlightens them. Thus, in the Apocalypse (3:18), one blinded by pride is advised to anoint his eyes with the eye-salve of repentance, which, as has been said, is denoted by ashes. God not only causes these ashes to exist but also scatters them so that they may benefit others, when he sets truly humble and penitent persons before many as examples for the conversion of others by such an example. Thus the penitent thief, weeping Peter, mourning Mary, and others humbly repenting, widely displayed for the knowledge of many, invite many to repentance to be undertaken in ashes—that is, in humility. Hence, when universal and Lenten penance is imposed, at the imposition of ashes it is said: [Col. 0981C] “Remember, man, that you are dust, and unto dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19). The name dust or ashes expresses humble repentance, through which, while it is not yet completed, veils hang in the Church, obstructing the sight of the eyes, until repentance having been performed through Christ’s passion, the veil of the temple being torn, our own veils also are taken away—even in the Church made by hands, signifying another Church not made by hands, built of living stones, whose altar and priest is Christ:

> Whose builder is the author of light,  
> Whose gate is the sign of the cross,  
> Whose walls are living stone,  
> Whose guardian is the festal King.

**VERSE 17.** He casts his crystal like morsels; [Col. 0981D] or, as some manuscripts have it: “He casts his crystal like pieces of bread.” But who could assert literally that morsels or pieces of bread are made of crystal, when the nature of things forbids it? Therefore the literal meaning cannot stand here as it can in the preceding, ordinary and seemingly natural miracles. For snow falling from above is literally scattered like wool, and mist likewise is scattered by the great miracle of the Creator; and the same thing takes place much more magnificently in the mystical sense, as has partly been shown. But for bread to be made from crystal is altogether unprecedented literally. Mystically, however, this is certainly accomplished by him who softens his crystal—or, as grammarians prefer, *suam* [feminine]—[Col. 0982A] when he makes hearts hardened by the cold of wickedness soft and savory like pieces of bread through the warmth of his love. For all believers are one body, one bread, while individual persons are pieces or morsels of bread. Crystal is a kind of stone resembling white, transparent glass; it is said to be snow hardened into ice through many years of prolonged cold, so that it cannot be dissolved. As long as snowy water, changed into ice, assumes the hardness of stone and becomes *crystallum* or *crystallus*—for both forms are used—no human ingenuity can cause it to dissolve back into the water from which it derives. But there is no doubt whatever that God can do this. Likewise, some who are naturally gentle become so hardened through wickedness that they become obstinate and so persistent in evil that no human effort can [Col. 0982B] turn them from evil to good. But what is impossible with human beings is possible with God, who casts his crystal like morsels or pieces of bread by tempering the winter cold. Unless he tempers it, who can endure before his cold? I mean his cold not as something he causes, but as something he permits because human sins demand it: when the north wind blows, many waters—that is, many peoples—harden, frozen in wickedness, yet not to be despaired of (Rev. 17:15), because, when the Lord wills:

**VERSE 18.** He will send forth his word and melt them—those frozen by the north wind, whether into snow easily dissolved, or ice difficultly dissolved, or crystal, dissolvable by no human ingenuity [Col. 0982C] but by God alone. He sends forth his utterance, commanding the north wind to arise and depart, and the south wind to come. When it blows, he will melt them: namely, the ice, snow, mist, and crystal. For his Spirit has blown—the south wind, that is, a warm wind coming from the region of the sun—which the Father will send in the name of the Son, the eternal Sun; and waters shall flow, so that others may drink from that by which previously no one could be refreshed.

On this passage blessed Gregory says in Job [Note: [Col. 0981D] *Morals*, Book XXVII, ch. 29]: “By flowing waters the Lord signifies a people running toward him. For waters run from frost, because many who were harsh persecutors become great preachers. Frost melts into water when the numbness of inner cold is changed into the irrigation of preaching. Was not Paul frost, when, having received letters and going to Damascus [Col. 0982D], he sought to restrain the seeds of the word scattered in the hearts of the faithful, as though cast upon God’s earth, lest they should rise to the perfection of works? But this frost returned to water, because those whom he had first endeavored to oppress through persecution he afterwards flooded with the stream of holy exhortation, so that a more abundant harvest of the elect might arise insofar as God’s rain watered it even from the mouth of the persecutor.”

As Saint Gregory says these things, we, thinking consonantly, say that Paul was crystal: hard and bright, skilled in the law; but God dissolved this. Yet unless he dissolves it, who can endure or stand before his cold? His cold is when he abandons, does not call, and does not illumine. And who will dissolve it? No one. [Col. 0983A] “Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24). I grow cold; no one dissolves me except the grace of God, who sends forth his word. When the Word comes, let neither snowy cold, nor the darkness of mist, nor the hardness of crystal despair. They are beneficially melted and pour forth streams of spiritual benefit for others, not by their own strength but by his gift.

**VERSE 19.** He declares his word to Jacob even through such ministers; and he who, appearing in the flesh in person, declared his word, of which he himself said: “And the word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me” (John 14:24). Therefore he declares his word to Jacob, the younger people, while the elder brother Esau is occupied outside—that is, the Jewish people and every carnal person, devoted to hunting after temporal things. To this simple Jacob, resting in tents with Rebecca—that is, with patience—he declares his righteousnesses and judgments: namely, that by a just judgment Esau, that is, every carnal hunter of temporal things, whether Jew or Gentile, is rejected, and simple Jacob is blessed.

**VERSE 20.** He has not dealt thus with every nation, as he has with Israel, born from whatever source according to the flesh yet loved eternally, as it is said in the person of God himself: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1:2–3). By the name Jacob, who is also Israel, are signified all the elect, loved by God before they were born. Before they existed, and before they had done anything good or evil, God did them good by predestining them to salvation [Col. 0983C]. He has not dealt thus with every nation, nor has he made his judgments known to them—namely, why he chose this one rather than that one, when neither the one nor the other had merited or demerited prevenient grace. as the Apostle shows in the two twins, Esau and Jacob; and he, marveling at these judgments declared to him though not fully made manifest, cries: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33).

Glory to the Father, who sends forth his Word. Glory to the Son, the Word himself. Glory to the Holy Spirit, by whose blowing the waters flow. Amen.

As we indicated above, the final seven psalms are woven into the praise of God. We have already set forth four of them [Col. 0983D], to which three still remain to be joined; these are customarily recited under one *Gloria*, to show the glory of the supreme Trinity. In the four preceding psalms, moreover, a most fitting order appears. In the first [Col. 0984A] are the precepts of the divine proclamation; in the second, the perversity of the world which must be fled; in the third, the gathering of the Church; in the fourth, the Spirit speaking in these psalms commands the praises of those gathered into one city.
