To the choir of that city, assembled from the regions of the world, he adds that they should rejoice with a threefold exultation, so that the grace of the Trinity may shine forth in this work, as the uninterrupted jubilation of the following three psalms indicates. For, after all the psalms on diverse subjects have been set forth, at last, as though choirs had been appointed for praise and the multitude had sounded forth, universal praise begins with all creatures jubilantly raising their voices; and an unceasing harmony, without interruption or interval, extends its cry through the three remaining psalms.

[Col. 0984B] First, the Holy Spirit, who is charity, says in the title, “Alleluia.” Then, as though explaining the title, he says: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights.” The choir of heavenly beings praises; all angels praise; all powers praise; all heavenly things, visible and invisible, praise. Why? “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5). Then the earth and all earthly things praise, because he visited the earth which he created and caused his praise to be not only above heaven but also upon earth. Therefore the subject of praise in this psalm is that he created all things and redeemed the human race. In the following psalm likewise the Holy Spirit says, “Alleluia. Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise [Col. 0984C] in the Church of the saints.” Why? Because, he says, “the Lord takes pleasure in his people”; because the saints shall exult in glory; because the exultations of God are in their throats; because two-edged swords are in their hands to execute vengeance among the nations, that they may execute upon them the written judgment. Thus the subject of song or praise in this psalm is that he will judge the world and glorify his saints in judgment. In the final psalm likewise the Spirit of charity says, “Alleluia: Praise the Lord in his saints; praise him in the firmament of his power.” “Praise,” he says, and adds or inserts no reason why they should praise. Thus he concludes at the end: “Let every spirit praise the Lord.” Therefore the subject of praise in this psalm is the ineffable blessedness of the future age—or such blessedness as cannot [Col. 0984D] be spoken or valued, which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which has not entered into the heart of man.

## PSALM 148

[Col. 0983]

[Col. 0983D] **Praise the Lord from the heavens.**

Some manuscripts have in the title: **A PSALM OF HAGGAI AND ZECHARIAH. ALLELUIA.** (VERSE 1) Since this title was explained in the preceding psalm, it does not require repeated [Col. 0984D] explanation. Yet this admonition should be added: remembering the citizens of the heavenly city while among the citizens of Babylon, who continually praise God, let us despise Babylon, raise our hearts above, and join ourselves to the angels who praise God, rejoicing and assenting in intention to their praises. Thus their praises will be reckoned to us as merit deserving an eternal reward. Conversely, those who consent to the devil, his angels, and others who do evil will perish together with those who act, unless they repent. We know, however, that you heavenly angels continually praise the Lord even without anyone’s admonition. But that we, weak and burdened by our earthly habitation and held captive in Babylon, may become participants in your jubilation, by which “glory to God in the highest” is sung, we, applauding you as you praise, say: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights.”

**VERSE 2.** Praise him, all his angels, who announce outwardly the counsels or judgments you hear within. Praise him, all his powers, through whom miracles are customarily done; or because all those heavenly spirits may generally be called powers. Of these, thousands upon thousands minister to God, sent forth outwardly and therefore called angels—that is, messengers; and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stand before him in supreme rest, enjoying him. All you heavenly powers, however distinguished in your orders and ministries, praise the Lord. For his praise not only heavenly but earthly things are invited; not only things perceptible by the senses but also things lacking sensation. Although they have no voice of praise in themselves, when considered they produce praise in the hearts of those considering them, namely human beings. Thus, in their own manner, they praise their Creator, whom they show to be praiseworthy by the beauty of their arrangement, as they kindle those who behold them to praise their Creator and Ordainer. In this way all created things cooperate in the praise of their Creator, although only rational creatures can possess the understanding and affection of praise. Just as, in the musical instrument called a psaltery, the strings alone sound, while the wooden material to which the strings are attached cooperates toward the same end, so in the whole universe only good human beings and angels praise the Creator with affection, while the other creatures cooperate toward this same end and, through the contemplation of themselves, show the Creator to be praiseworthy: first, through his power, by which he created all things from nothing; then through his wisdom, by which, ordering all things and reaching from end to end, from archangel to little worm, and from the primal cause to the final, he leaves nothing in his kingdom unordered, whether good or evil. Finally, he is shown praiseworthy by that goodness through which he makes all things cooperate for good for those who are called saints according to his purpose.

This power, wisdom, and goodness is the eternal Trinity in unity and unity in Trinity, invisible and hidden in itself, but visible in creatures powerfully, wisely, and beneficially ordered, as through a mirror and in an enigma. For example: in this visible sun, essentially rather than accidentally bright and warm, God the eternal Father is recognized; he has the Son consubstantial with himself, as brightness—indeed, truly coeternal brightness—and the eternal warmth of the Spirit proceeding from both. In praise of this Trinity, the Church sings hymns, like the moon placed beneath the sun, and individual believers, like stars, in this manner:

> Splendor of the Father’s glory,  
> Bringing forth light from light,  
> Light of light and source of light,  
> Day illuminating days,  
> True Sun, enter in,  
> Shining with perpetual radiance,  
> And pour the beam of the Holy Spirit  
> Into our minds.

To such praises, by the contemplation of your fullness, arouse us who are slow to praise: praise the Lord, all heavenly bodies.

**VERSE 3.** Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and the light of the firmament—whether of clouds shining white by day, or of all things, from whatever source and in whatever way, that shine.

**VERSE 4.** Let the heavens of heavens praise him, for there are many heavens: this air near the earth is called heaven, in which the birds of heaven swim and fly; and there are other, higher heavens, the circles of the distinct planets, whose highest are rightly called the heavens of heavens. And the waters which are above the heavens,

**VERSE 5.** let them praise the name of the Lord, through whose dominion the upper waters are separated from the lower by means of the firmament, as it was said and written: “Let there be a firmament in the midst [Col. 0986C] of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters” (Gen. 1:6). Let all these praise the Lord by showing the Lord himself to be praiseworthy, because he spoke and they were made: when he spoke through his Word, all things were formed in their natural forms. He commanded, and they were created in their matter—not in matter coeternal with God, as some philosophers thought, but from nothing, receiving from absolute non-being a material existence underlying natural and accidental forms. Though created things themselves vary as these forms change, nevertheless:

**VERSE 6.** He established them. For although heaven and earth shall pass away so that there may be a new heaven and a new earth, their nature remains even when their form has passed away, because he who created them from nothing has also [Col. 0986D] established them for age and for age of age, lest they ever perish utterly and be reduced to nothing. Some shall remain improved and renewed in the new heaven and new earth, as in a royal palace; some shall be separated from God’s court and cast down into prison, and there so ordered that even such an ordering owes praise to the Creator and Ordainer. He has set a command upon the creature he created, and it shall not pass away. This is especially apparent in the revolutions of the firmament, the sun, moon, and other stars, for he set them a command that they should be for signs, months, seasons, and years; and none of these will depart from its appointed course. For even if the sun stood still at Joshua’s command (Josh. 10:13), and returned ten lines at Isaiah’s prayer (Isa. 38:8), this itself was ordained to be a sign of future things: namely, of the greater Jesus, the teacher, to whom not only the sun but all created things would be obedient; and of the greater Isaiah, who would have power not only to prolong mortal life but also to give eternal life. As it is said, “Behold, more than Solomon or Jonah is here” (Matt. 12:41–42), so we may truly say: “More than Joshua or Isaiah is here.” Having enumerated heavenly things, whose motion is most ordered, he now mentions earthly things, such as:

**VERSES 7–8.** Dragons and deeps, etc. The deeps are the depths of waters, especially all seas. Though enclosed by shores, they nevertheless seem in many places to lack a bottom; this is denoted by the term “deep.” Cloudy air also belongs to the deep: there are clouds, winds, storms, rains, lightning flashes, thunder, hail, snow, and whatever God wills to be made over the earth from moist and murky air. He has called it all by the name of earth because it is exceedingly changeable. Yet all these things, though changeable and disturbed, have their own place and order, fulfill in their own way the beauty of the universe, and thus praise God. Therefore he exhorts it—that is, us by the consideration of them—to praise. “Which do his word”: for some supposed that God governs the higher things but neglects these lower things, which are governed by chance. Yet God acts also in these, and in these least things he is praised and Alleluia is sung. Since fire is joined with hail, it is clear that fire here means that which is discharged from hail-bearing and lightning-bearing clouds. Likewise, since ice is joined with stormy winds, and this spirit is understood as the wind moving storms, ice is rightly understood as hailstones, which are nothing other than snow or water frozen in the air by the cold spirit or wind of storms. All these do his word, so that nothing happens through them by accidental motion, but all act at the command of God’s Word, ordered from heaven. Having partly described those things which move in the air, such as dragons, which move in the waters and are said to come out of caves into the air—than which no larger flying bodies exist above the earth, and therefore praise from the earth began with them—let us come to mountains and hills and all other earthly things, [Col. 0987D] and say with the Psalmist:

**VERSE 9.** Mountains and all hills; fruit-bearing trees, such as apple, pear, and fig; and non-fruit-bearing trees, such as fir and cypress, and all cedars. Although they do not bear fruit, cedar, cypress, and fir timbers are useful in buildings and stir up praise of God; for example, when the Bride said to her immortal Bridegroom: “The beams of our houses are cedar, our ceilings are cypress” (Song 1:16): let them praise the name of the Lord.

**VERSE 10.** Untamed beasts, such as bears, wolves, lions, and tigers; and all cattle, such as oxen, sheep, and other domesticated animals; serpents creeping upon the earth without feet; all creeping things which do not walk with feet but press forward by bristles or scales; and winged birds: let them praise the name of the Lord. After the heavenly bodies—the luminaries of sun, moon, and stars—and wholly earthly bodies, such as beasts, cattle, and serpents, let us come to human beings, surpassing all these; for humanity was not created for these things, but all these things were created for humanity. Therefore, in and above all these things, human beings ought to praise the name of the Lord. To this I, David, invite them, saying:

**VERSES 11–12.** Kings of the earth and all peoples, rulers and all judges of the earth, young men and virgins of every sex and age, old men with the younger: let them praise the name of the Lord, who is worthy of praise, deriving the ground of praise from his magnificence and power.

**VERSE 13.** For his name alone is exalted. The apostate angel wished to be like the Most High in heaven; and, entering the man of sin, the son of perdition, and exalting himself above everything called God or worshiped, he wished to be considered higher than the Most High. [Col. 0988C] But when the angel in heaven and Antichrist upon earth are confuted, his name alone is exalted—he who alone is holy, alone is Lord, alone is Most High: Jesus Christ with the Holy Spirit in the glory of God the Father. Since every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings bows to him, and every tongue confesses, it is truly said:

**VERSE 14.** His praise is above heaven and earth, because “the heavens and earth are full of his glory” (Isa. 6:3). And he shall exalt the horn of his people, because all “the horns of sinners” shall be broken, and “the horns of the righteous shall be exalted” (Ps. 74:11). A hymn—that is, praise of God with song—shall be forever among all his saints, the children of Israel. And that it may be understood more clearly whom I call saints and children of Israel, I say plainly: the people drawing near to him, as Jacob, who is also Israel, drew near to him, wrestling with him in prayers and tears until, at the rising of dawn, he received the blessing (Gen. 32:26 ff.).

## PSALM 149

[Col. 0987]

[Col. 0987D] **Sing to the Lord, etc.**

The title, “Alleluia” (VERSE 1), is clear. Just as the preceding psalm, divided into two parts, invited heavenly things in its first part to praise God and likewise admonished earthly things to praise God in its second part, so this following psalm also is divided into two parts. Its subject is the praise of God who exalts his people.

In the first part it treats of the kindness God bestows [Col. 0989A] on his own, making them Israel. In the second, it treats of their joy and the power which they will exercise over the impious in executing vengeance upon their wickedness. It should be noted that, while in the preceding psalm the great ground for praise was the power that created all heavenly and earthly things, the greater ground for praise in this psalm is the mercy that exalts the meek unto salvation and strengthens those same persons to execute vengeance among the nations, as it is written: “They shall judge nations and rule over peoples” (Wis. 3:8). Considering this power and this mercy, O all you faithful,
Sing to the Lord a new song, instructed by the New Testament, so that you may walk in newness of life and praise your Redeemer with a new song concerning the mystery of redemption: with a new manner of living, the old leaven purged away, the image of the old man laid aside, and conformity to the new man put on. Thus praise God—not anywhere whatsoever; not in a schism or manifest heresy; not in gatherings of perverse doctrines or destructive customs—but in the Church of the saints. For praise is acceptable only in the Church of the saints, not in the synagogue of Satan, not in the assembly of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, who rise up against the true Aaron, against the true and holy priesthood, which exists only in the Church of the saints, whether they are now pilgrims or reigning in heaven, offering in either place the sacrifice of praise, the sacrifice of rejoicing. Joined to the assembly of such saints:

**VERSE 2.** Let Israel, in whom there is no deceit, rejoice: let him rejoice, I say, not in himself but in him who made him Israel when he had formerly been Jacob. Let him rejoice not in his own strength, but in the goodness of him who granted victory to him as he struggled against vices, saying to him: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name, because if you were strong against God,” from whom you wrested a blessing by prayers and tears, “how much more shall you prevail against men” (Gen. 32:28), to execute vengeance upon the nations and rebukes among the peoples?

Let Israel rejoice—the man who sees God face to face, by which vision his soul was saved. Let him rejoice in him who made him such that, transferred to the heavenly Jerusalem, either in hope or even in reality, from the present and pilgrim Zion, he may see God, like those who can say: “But our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). And let the daughters of Zion—that is, weaker persons, scarcely contemplating through a mirror and in an enigma—their king clothed in the robe of flesh and adorned with the diadem with which his mother crowned him, exult in their king, continually singing to him: “The Lord has reigned; he has put on majesty” (Ps. 92:1). Likewise: “The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult” (Ps. 96:1). Likewise: “I will exalt thee, O God my King” (Ps. 144:1). Likewise: “Thou art the King of glory, O Christ; thou art the everlasting Son of the Father,” and the other songs glorifying this King.

And because the praise of God does not sound well amid the division of discordant minds, which the hoarseness of discord disturbs, and because the God of peace does not rest in contention and rivalry:

**VERSE 3.** Let them praise his name in the choir of those who sound together and dwell together in unity, who speak and think the same thing in that charity which “is patient, is kind, is not puffed up, is not jealous, is not provoked, thinks no evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together with the truth” (1 Cor. 13:4–6).

Likewise, because God cannot be served in revelries and drunkenness, in beds and indecencies, let the daughters of Zion praise him on the timbrel, drying out, mortifying, and crucifying their flesh; for a timbrel is dried skin stretched over wood. On such a timbrel our King played when, stretched out on the wood of the cross, he prayed for those crucifying him. So the holy martyrs played the timbrel, who, struggling in tribulation, prayed for their opponents and slanderers. So all those play the timbrel who, abstaining from vices and pleasures of the flesh, while they chastise themselves outwardly, exult inwardly, anointed with the oil of gladness; nor do they, sad like hypocrites, disfigure their faces. Rather, they join to their timbrel the pleasant psaltery, which, because it sounds from above, signifies heavenly joy.

In the future there will be great exultation concerning timbrel and psaltery: not the action itself of playing the timbrel or psaltery, but thanksgiving for past actions. Therefore let them sing to him with timbrel and psaltery who wish wisely to sing to that King who loves purity of flesh and the chaste joy of the mind—as it were a timbrel with a psaltery, as a lamp burning outwardly with oil hidden in the vessel of conscience. Let Israel rejoice; let the daughters of Zion exult; let them sing a new song. Why? For what reason?

**VERSE 4.** Because the Lord is well pleased in his people. In the creation of things God saw all that he had made, and they were very good; nothing displeased him among the things which he, being good, had made wholly good. But afterward, when sins arose, God repented that he had made man, because he was not well pleased in sinful man, who deformed God’s work in himself.

But after the sinless man was born of a virgin, God the Father was so well pleased in him that he said to him: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17); and he graciously remembered in the good pleasure of his people all those who cleave to him through faith and love. This is what they pray to him, saying: “Remember us, O Lord, in the good pleasure of thy people; visit us with thy salvation” (Ps. 105:4).

Let God therefore be praised with timbrel and psaltery, because he is well pleased in his people, and he will exalt the meek unto salvation. The world, which lies in evil, despises the meek and does not willingly exalt them to any spiritual or secular dignity, fearing that it may be constrained by them to good; but it exalts the wicked to their own ruin and that of others. Yet the Lord, ruler over affairs, will himself, as he wills, exalt the meek unto the salvation of themselves and others.

This shall take place universally on the day of judgment, when, as the Lord rebukes on behalf of “the meek of the earth,” “the righteous shall stand in great steadfastness against those who afflicted them” (Wis. 5:1). But even now, in particular, as the Lord rebukes on behalf of “the meek of the earth,” “the meek themselves shall be exalted” (Isa. 11:4), when either through a dignity bestowed upon them or through goodness conspicuous in them they are so preferred to the wicked that the blessing is fulfilled for them by which God, blessing Noah’s sons, said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth; and let your fear and dread be upon the beasts of the earth” (Gen. 9:1–2). Therefore, when the meek are exalted for the salvation of the people and untamed, savage beasts tremble, even in this pilgrimage there is a foretaste of the glory of which it is now said:

**VERSE 5.** The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their resting places. For even now, when the Church of God has peace through meek rulers, the saints exult in glory, while he makes each one of them like the saints in glory and tames monsters by their words. Once these are tamed, they shall rejoice in the resting places of their consciences and religious tabernacles, saying: “How beloved are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts!” (Ps. 83:2).

But far more in the future, when all the meek have been exalted to the kingdom of God and all the unmeek have been humbled and imprisoned, the saints shall exult in eternal glory, which never fails them, and shall rejoice in their resting places—that is, in eternal tabernacles. Glory is the frequent praise of good actions; the righteous rejoice in this in the resting places of their consciences, assigning all glory to God, the author of good and praiseworthy works, who gives sinners repentance, penitents innocence, and the innocent glory. Foolish virgins rejoice in people’s fables; the wise refer their joy to him who gave them that in which they may rejoice or glory.

Therefore, when they exult in the praises of good works, their exultation is not outward, but:

**VERSE 6.** The exaltations of God—not human but divine—are in their throats, where God sees and not man; and two-edged swords are in their hands: that is, judgment according to the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments shall be in their power,

**VERSE 7.** To execute vengeance upon the nations: vengeance long desired, from the blood of righteous Abel crying out and demanding it to the blood of the last righteous person to be slain by Cain’s successors, whether in act or in malicious disposition, since whoever hates his brother is a murderer. The saints therefore shall have two-edged swords, sharpened as it were on the double whetstone of both Testaments, ready to cast bodies and souls into Gehenna, for condemning evil human beings and angels, to execute vengeance upon the nations and rebukes among the peoples: now in part, and universally when they sit upon judicial seats at the final examination. Then vengeance and rebuke among the peoples shall truly take place.

**VERSE 8.** To bind their kings with fetters, and their nobles with iron manacles. For then the kings of the earth, who are now free to do what they wish, shall be bound with fetters, and their nobles with iron manacles, according to the saying: “Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the furnace of fire” (Matt. 22:13). By iron manacles is denoted the hardness, inescapability, and heavy weight of the bonds by which the wicked, bound, shall be dragged into prison, into outer darkness. The saints therefore shall be armed against the wicked with two-edged swords, fetters, and iron manacles.

**VERSE 9.** That they may execute upon them the written judgment, of which the Apostle says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3). But lest anyone suppose that the apostles alone shall judge with the Lord, let him observe what follows: *This glory is for all his saints.* That is to say: not only Christ and his twelve apostles will share the glory of judicial power, but this glory belongs to all his saints: imitators of the apostolic manner of life, not in miracles, which are granted to few, but in holy morals, which are set before all, the Apostle saying: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4:16).

By this saying we are not urged to work miracles after the example of Christ and the apostles, but to imitate the good morals of the apostles. For the glory of miracles was given to few—namely, that they might raise the dead, give sight to the blind, and cleanse lepers in Christ’s name. Yet even some wicked persons work many mighty deeds in his name, though they shall be told at judgment: “I never knew you” (Matt. 7:23). But this glory belongs to all his saints who love and pursue perfect holiness: according to their purpose of holiness, they shall sit in judgment to execute vengeance upon the nations and rebukes among the peoples, that they may execute upon them the written judgment, because it is written: “The righteous shall shine, and shall run to and fro like sparks among reeds; they shall judge nations and rule peoples, and their Lord shall reign forever” (Wis. 3:7–8).

## PSALM 150

[Col. 0991]

[Col. 0991D] “Praise the Lord in his saints,” etc.

**VERSE 1. ALLELUIA.** The title is clear, and rightly suits this final psalm, which is wholly concerned with the praise of God. All psalmody will be consummated in that praise, when what is said at the end comes to pass: *Let every spirit praise the Lord.* Therefore, when the judgment treated in the preceding psalm has been completed—a judgment in which “all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6)—the elect alone shall be so changed that they may more properly be called spirit than flesh, when the body “which is sown animal shall rise spiritual” (1 Cor. 15:44), and “which is sown in weakness shall rise in power” (ibid., v. 43). The substance of flesh nevertheless remains in them, however spiritual that flesh itself becomes, then made uniform with the spirit cleaving to its supreme Spirit.

Therefore, when flesh and blood, which do not possess the kingdom of God, have been excluded and cast down into hell, when “the wicked shall be silent in darkness” (1 Sam. 2:9), only the spiritual, admitted to the wedding feast, shall praise the Lord. Of them it is said at the end of the psalm and at the end of the whole Psalter: *Let every spirit praise the Lord.* And because that praise will come when toil has ended and the denarius for which they labored in the vineyard has been received, the saints are also urged to praise by a tenfold exhortation, since “Praise” is said ten times; and finally all praise is brought to a close when it is said: *Let every spirit praise the Lord.*

The preceding psalms are variously divided either by a *diapsalma* or for other reasons investigated by the Fathers. But this final psalm is indivisible—that is, incapable of being divided—because it is not divided into praises and reasons for praise, as are the preceding six, in which praises and their reasons are separately contained. These reasons are plainly expressed in the first and carefully investigated in the following four, where generation after generation is introduced as praising God’s works, power, magnificence, strength in terrible deeds, and God’s other wonders, which are various reasons for praise.

But in this psalm, although “Praise” is repeated ten times, the reason for praise is left unspoken, because it is ineffable. As we have touched on above, neither ear has heard it, nor eye seen it, nor has it entered into the human heart. For ineffable are the things which God has prepared for those who love him.

This psalm is connected to the end of the preceding one in this way: *This glory is for all his saints, that they may execute the written judgment.* Therefore, you who desire to be joined to the saints:

Praise the Lord in his saints. Praise him who sanctified them by cleansing them from sins and earthly desires. Praise him in the firmament of his strength, because those whom he cleansed from evil by sanctifying them, he strengthened in good.

**VERSE 2.** Praise him in his powers, or, as another translation has it, in his dominions. God’s dominion in the saints consists in their reigning forever. Praise him according to the multitude of his greatness; and because it has no end, your praise also has no end.

On this passage blessed Gregory says in his *Morals on Job*:

> [Note: Col. 0993D, Book IX of the *Morals*, chapter 12.] We fulfill the deeds of divine strength more truly when we recognize that we cannot fulfill them. We speak more eloquently when, stupefied by them, we fall silent. In recounting God’s works, our inadequacy, however fully it exerts its tongue, may fittingly praise in silence what it cannot adequately comprehend. Hence the Psalmist now well says: “Praise him in his powers; praise him according to the multitude of his greatness.” For that person praises God according to the multitude of his greatness who sees himself fail in completing his praise.

**VERSE 3.** Praise him with the sound of the trumpet. Since we read of seven trumpets, which the seven angels sounded in the Apocalypse (ch. 8:6 and following), the last trumpet is rightly understood here. When it sounds, as the Apostle affirms, “the dead shall rise incorruptible,” that is, whole, “and we,” he says, “shall be changed” (1 Cor. 15:52). Therefore, you who are changed at the sound of this trumpet, praise the Lord with the sound of the trumpet. For of the rest, who shall not be changed, it is written that “all the tribes of the earth shall mourn.”

Praise him on the psaltery sounding from above, and on the harp sounding from below: praise him from heavenly and earthly things, as him who made heaven and earth.

**VERSES 4–5.** Praise him with timbrel and choir. On this passage blessed Gregory says in his *Homilies on Ezekiel*:

> [Note: Col. 0993D, Homily 8.] How great is the power of concord is shown when, without it, the other virtues are demonstrated not to be virtues. Abstinence is indeed a great virtue; but if someone so abstains from food that he judges others in their eating and even condemns among believers the very foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving, what has the virtue of his abstinence become but a snare of fault? Thus the Psalmist, showing that there is no abstinence without concord, says: “Praise him with timbrel and choir.” On the timbrel, then, dry skin resounds; in the choir voices sing in harmony. What, therefore, is signified by the timbrel but abstinence, and what by the choir but the concord of charity? Therefore, the person who so maintains abstinence that he abandons concord indeed praises with the timbrel, but does not praise in the choir.

> [Note: Col. 0994D, the same author, *Pastoral Care*, part III, chapter 22.] Often some who receive certain gifts in a special way lose, through pride, the gift of concord, which is greater; for example, someone may subdue his flesh more than others by restraining gluttony, yet despise to be in concord with those whom he surpasses by abstinence. But whoever separates abstinence from concord should consider what the Psalmist admonishes. For he says: “Praise him with timbrel and choir.” On the timbrel dry and struck skin resounds; in the choir voices harmonize. Thus, whoever afflicts his body but abandons concord does indeed praise God with the timbrel, but does not praise in the choir.

“Praise him with strings and organ. Praise him with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with cymbals of jubilation.” All these, compared figuratively with human actions, are said there to sound forth God’s praises. By them the city of God—the unity of all saints—is admonished to sing with mouth and mind. To this all psalmody is brought, and it is consummated in wedding sweetness.

For although the sound of the last trumpet will thunder terribly at judgment, after judgment sweet harmony and symphony will resound in timbrel and choir, in psaltery and harp, in strings and organ, in well-sounding cymbals—or, as other manuscripts have it, *well-ringing* cymbals. [Col. 0995A] That all these musical instruments, suitable to a wedding celebration, may be understood spiritually rather than carnally, this whole symphony is fittingly concluded when it says:

**VERSE 6.** Let every spirit praise the Lord. For after judgment the timbrel will cease, by which the chastisement of the flesh is signified. It will not be necessary when the saints’ flesh is wholly spiritual, according to the Apostle’s saying: “An animal body is sown; a spiritual body shall rise” (1 Cor. 15:44). There too the well-sounding or well-ringing cymbals will cease, since no one there will need mutual admonitions for fraternal consolation or edification. Yet the Lord shall be praised with cymbals of jubilation, when the labors of works necessary in this life have been removed and their fruit and merit remain. Delighting the city of God by that fruit, let every spirit praise the Lord.

Glory to the Father, who spoke and things were made; who commanded and all things were created. Glory to the Son, who was humbled for this purpose, that he might exalt the meek unto salvation. Glory to the Holy Spirit, by whose power every spirit shall praise the Lord. Glory to the supreme Trinity and undivided Unity, in whose praise three sets of fifty psalms have been woven into one Psalter.

In the first set of fifty, holy David commended faith; in the second, hope; and in the third, charity—when he ended the first fifty with a penitential psalm, the second with a judicial psalm, and the third with a psalm of jubilation in cymbals of jubilation.

[Col. 0995C] Nor is it without significance that the first fiftieth concerns repentance, the second mercy and judgment, and the third the praise of God in his saints. For this is how we proceed to eternal life. First we condemn sins, God calling to repentance those whom he predestined for himself in secret. Then through mercy we live well, so that we may not fear judgment, as God justifies those whom he called through mercy and fear of judgment, where those who work iniquity are scattered from the city of the Lord.

To this pertains what the Lord says: “Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected” (Luke 13:32 [printed 38]); this he also showed in his passion, sleep, and awakening. On the cross he triumphed over the devil; in the tomb he rested; in the resurrection he exulted. Repentance torments, righteousness gives peace, eternal life glorifies.

That there are one hundred and fifty psalms indicates a great mystery, which will become clear if one considers the significance of the number fifteen. For what fifteen is in the order of units, one hundred and fifty is in the order of tens, fifteen hundred in the order of hundreds, and fifteen thousand in the order of thousands. Fifteen signifies the concord of the two Testaments. In the Old Testament the Sabbath was observed, which is the seventh day; in the New, the Lord’s Day, which is the eighth and also the first.

According to this mystery, the number fifty of the Psalms consists of seven weeks of weeks, with one added as if the eighth itself, to complete the fiftieth. When so many days had been completed after the resurrection, the Holy Spirit came upon those assembled in Christ; this Spirit is commended by the number seven. Fifty is divided into forty and ten. Thus on the fortieth day after the resurrection he ascended, and after ten days sent the Spirit. By forty is shown the temporal dwelling of this world. The number four predominates in forty. Both the world and the year have four parts, with ten added as the reward rendered for the law fulfilled, by which eternity itself is signified. But when fifty is multiplied by the Trinity, it makes one hundred and fifty.

Jerome speaks of five books. It is also said: “In the book of Psalms” (Luke 20:42). And rightly are many called one book, just as many churches are one Church, many heavens one heaven—whence the waters above the firmament, that is, heaven, and the waters above the heavens. “In the book of Psalms” may also mean in one of those five books. The twelve prophets too are called one book; likewise all comic writings are called one book, because they agree in a wonderful unity.

This is “the book of the wars of the Lord” (Num. 21:14), which Moses mentions—not because any book about the wars of the Lord had been written before him, since he himself was the first writer, but because all Scripture divinely inspired, whether administered through himself or through others, is the book of the wars of the Lord, or the book of the righteous.

It is especially fitting, however, that the book of Psalms be called the book of the wars of the Lord, because in it, through the mouths of those who wisely sing psalms, the true David—truly mighty of hand—fights and accomplishes wonderful wars against the invisible Goliath, the devil, and the visible Antichrist. Singing against him, he says: “Blessed be my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war” (Ps. 143:1). When this war has been completed by the killing of Antichrist, as is written in the book of the wars of the Lord, there shall be eternal praise for Christ the victor in the mouths of those singing psalms and saying: “I will exalt thee, O God my King,” etc., down to “let every spirit praise the Lord” (Ps. 144:1).

In the book of Numbers one reads: “Arnon is the boundary of Moab, dividing the Moabites and Amorites. Hence it is said in the book of the wars of the Lord: As he did at the Red Sea, so shall he do at the streams of Arnon” (Num. 21:13–14). In the book of Kings also one reads: “David lamented with such a lament over Saul and Jonathan, and commanded that they should teach the sons of Judah the bow, as it is written in the book of the righteous” (2 Sam. 1:17–18).

Although the book of the righteous may be understood as some book which can nowhere be found today, more firmly the same book is here understood as that of which Numbers writes: “Hence it is said in the book of the wars of the Lord: As he did at the Red Sea, so shall he do at the streams of Arnon,” etc. And what is the book of the wars of the Lord except all divinely inspired Holy Scripture, from which without doubt we are taught to wage the Lord’s wars? For nothing of this kind had been written before Moses, who said it.

Therefore, David’s command that they should teach the sons of Judah the bow, as written in the book of the righteous, is to be understood thus: because the sons of Israel had fought badly through their own fault, and had been routed and overthrown by archers after Saul was slain, at least the sons of Judah, their fellow tribesmen, should learn to fight evil archers with bow and arrows, as all the righteous did. All their victories were wonderfully accomplished, with God cooperating, through their sword and bow, by which “the bow of the mighty was overcome, and the weak were girded with strength” (1 Sam. 2:4), as the Holy Scriptures testify. Though divided into many books, they were written by one Spirit, and therefore are rightly regarded as one book, according to the saying: “And I saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seals” (Rev. 5:1).

Since, then, all Holy Scripture is the book of the wars of the Lord and the book of the righteous, by which we are taught to fight against flesh and blood, also against the rulers of the world, the rulers of darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places, the book of Psalms may rightly be called in a special sense, among the other writings, the book of the wars of the Lord and the book of the righteous. In it the true David fought in his own person, saying: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). Likewise: “Into thy hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46).

And now he sings psalms among the nations, according to the saying: “I will confess thee among the peoples, O Lord, and sing psalms to thee among the nations” (Ps. 56:10). Hence that custom has been most beneficially adopted in the Church: at ecclesiastical assemblies the Psalms are recited daily, whereas other writings, such as Genesis and others of that kind, are usually recited once a year. “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also” (1 Cor. 14:15), says the Apostle. And to urge others to this, he says: “Do not be drunk with wine, wherein is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing psalms in your hearts to the Lord” (Eph. 5:18–19). This is to fight with a flashing sword and a most powerful bow.

For example, when we say to God: “Draw forth thy sword, and shut the way against those who persecute me” (Ps. 34:3), we fight as it were with a sword. Likewise, when we say: “Send forth thy arrows, and thou shalt trouble them” (Ps. 143:6), we fight with a bow. Those who are like Saul, lacking this bow, even if they are considered stronger than lions and swifter than eagles, will easily fall on Mount Gilboa, wounded in their pride by the archers, the demon tempters, if they do not return arrows for arrows and repel the demons striking them either with sword or bow, as they are taught in the book of the righteous and the book of the wars of the Lord. Their evil temptations are most effectively resisted when one sings psalms with spirit and mind, so that the psalm is continually on the lips and a pleasing and beautiful praise of our God is constantly in the heart. So be it, so be it. Amen, amen.

## EXPOSITION OF THE SONG OF ISAIAH  
*(Isaiah 12)*

[Col. 0997]

[Col. 0997C] “I will confess to thee, O Lord, because thou wast angry with me,” etc. This prophecy precedes this song of Isaiah:

> “And the Lord shall lay waste the tongue of the Egyptian sea, and shall lift up his hand over the river in the strength of his Spirit, and strike it into seven streams, so that they may pass through it shod; and there shall be a way for the remnant of my people, which shall be left from the Assyrians, as there was for Israel on the day when he came up out of the land of Egypt” (Isa. 11:15–16).

“And thou shalt say in that day: I will confess to thee, O Lord, because thou wast angry with me” (Isa. 12:1).

Therefore, if the prophecy preceding this song is carefully considered and understood not only historically but also spiritually, it discloses the subject and meaning of this entire song. For what is the tongue of the Egyptian sea except the eloquence of this world, metaphorically signified by Egypt and its sea? The Lord struck this tongue when he made the wisdom of this world foolish. Hence the Apostle says: “Where is the wise man? Where is the disputer of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (1 Cor. 1:20).

For it was foolish to abandon the Creator and worship the creature; this is what the wise men of this world taught, who, as the Apostle says, became vain in their thoughts. Their wisdom and eloquence have been so struck down that great folly is recognized not only in those who worship idols as the true God, but also in those who, in the service of the true God, seek not God himself but things created by him.

What, moreover, is the river of Egypt except the kingdom of this world? God struck it with his own hand in the strength of his Spirit, and divided it as it were into seven streams—first historically and then mystically. For literally, the once most powerful kingdom of Egypt was divided, by God’s ordering, into seven princes through the power of the Romans after Cleopatra’s death. Libya had one king, Pentapolis another, the Thebaid another, Alexandria another, Egypt another; and the other cities of that kingdom, namely Heliopolis and Taphnis, had their own rulers.

In the same strength of his hand he also divided into tetrarchies the Jewish kingdom, which had been made wholly Egyptian: under Herod the deadly tyrant, as under another Pharaoh, it had been bloodied by the slaughter of males, and now the Davidic kingdom and its sceptre had been removed. Thus, when the kingdom of this world, like a great river, was divided into many streams, a way was prepared for those entering Egypt, just as at Israel’s departure from Egypt the sea, divided into divisions, provided a way for the sons of Israel going out.

Therefore, just as Moses said in thanksgiving: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honoured; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea” (Exod. 15:1), so Isaiah now foretells in thanksgiving a song to be sung near the end of the world. For just as the river Nile of Egypt, before it was divided by Alexander, was impassable, and although the Romans enlarged its streams it was nearly so dried up, winding through the lowest sandy valleys, that it could be crossed dryshod; so the kingdom of this world, while it flourished in the monarchy of its integrity—so that one man was emperor of the whole world, as Augustus was, in whose time Christ was born—offered no dry way either to those leaving Egypt by renouncing this world or to those entering Egypt to conquer this world.

The great flood of martyrs’ blood proves this. Those who either fled Egypt or conquered Egypt sailed through it in the ship of the cross; unable either to withstand universal persecutions or to withdraw from them, they triumphed through their death. But now, through the grace of God, the monarchy of this world has been wholly destroyed: kingdoms have been weakened within themselves and so divided against one another that there is a dry and sufficiently passable way for all who are shod in the preparation of the gospel of peace. For if they suffer persecution in one kingdom, they will flee into another; if in one city, they will flee into another.

To dry out or level the way further, kings and princes of this world now seek not the blood of saints but their goods, while a Christian is compelled either to consent to evil by silence or speech, or to abandon temporal goods. These dangerous times now threaten, when prelates of God’s holy Church are compelled either to lose the dignities they have received, or, in order to retain them, to consent with schismatics cut off from the Church of God.

In such straits of compulsion, those well shod will easily pass through by esteeming temporal goods lightly and seeking eternal things; and when these have been sought, all things necessary for the journey and for life shall be added. For the widow of Zarephath receives and feeds those persecuted by Jezebel’s wickedness. Ravens also minister to such persons when they flee into the wilderness, lest they waste away through hunger; for those who hunger and thirst for righteousness find it among the humble—sinners black in their own estimation, yet faithful.

This is the day which the Lord makes, not permitting those like Elijah or Isaiah to be tempted beyond what they are able, but with the temptation also making an outcome, that they may endure and, after flight, having recovered the Spirit of strength, act bravely. And in that day you, O Church, or you, an ecclesiastical person, shall say:

**VERSE 1.** I will confess to thee, O Lord, because thou wast angry with me; thy wrath has turned away, and thou hast comforted me. I will confess to thee concerning the justice by which thou wast angry with me, and concerning the mercy by which thy wrath turned away and thou hast comforted me. I will confess with a confession of praise, because I who deserved wrath from thy fury have now obtained mercy.

And this is my consolation: that my Savior, who had hidden his face and who had fallen asleep in the ship in which I sail, now, awakened by the prayers of the disciples, appears openly; plainly showing that he himself is my saving God, who saves for nothing the person whom divine power created from nothing, according to the saying in the psalm: “For nothing thou shalt save them” (Ps. 55:8)—that is, thou shalt save, through no merit of their own power, those whom thou foreknowest to be thine.

[Col. 1000B] **VERSE 2.** Behold, God is my Savior: if he is for us, who is against us? If he himself justifies, who is there to condemn? Therefore I shall act confidently in him—in him, I say, not trusting in myself. I shall hold firm and shall not fear what man may do to me, because the Lord is my strength in battle and my praise in triumph. Strengthened by him I have fought and shall fight; in his faith also I have triumphed and shall triumph. For “this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith” (1 John 5:4), by which I believe without doubt that the Maker himself was made.

For the Son of God himself, who was God before the ages, was himself made in time, born from a virgin mother for my salvation. “For he himself shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21). Therefore, you apostles and all other faithful, despising the turbulent rivers of Egypt,
### Verse 3

“You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour”: because, having despised worldly wisdom and desire—for whoever drinks such waters will thirst again—you shall draw better waters, changed into wine, from the fountains of the Saviour, whom I, Isaiah, call “Saviour,” so that there may be no doubt that he is the one whom Gabriel also calls Jesus, that is, “Saviour,” because “he shall save his people from their sins.”

### Verse 4

“And you shall say in that day,” in that manifestation of truth: “Confess your sins to the Lord” first, so that your house may be cleansed; and then, for him to dwell in it, call upon his name, that very name which is “Lord,” so that he himself may rule in you—indeed, also throughout the whole land of Egypt—like another Joseph: distributing grain to the peoples, drawing to himself his brothers, the remnant of Israel, and forgiving those who sold him.

But lest anyone perish through ignorance by failing to recognize this true Joseph, ruling over the whole land of Egypt—indeed, over heaven and earth, all authority having been given to him—you apostles, and all others divinely instructed by God, make known among the peoples his works of discovery: namely, the good works by which he is found; or his incarnation, by which he found the lost sheep and drachma, becoming little for humankind’s salvation, reckoned among the wicked, and subjected to many insults.

[Col. 1001A] Amid all these things, although by emptying himself he appeared small, yet remember, you faithful, that his name is exalted: the name given him above every name excels, since he, man assumed into God, is not God among all things but God above all things, blessed for ever, King of kings and Lord of lords. Believing this,

### Verse 5

Sing to the Lord, serving him willingly and giving thanks; for he has acted magnificently, conquering and destroying death by his death and restoring life to his own by his resurrection. Announce this not only in Judaea, but throughout the whole earth, so that your sound may go forth into all the earth and your words to the ends of the world. Once such proclamation has been spread abroad:

[Col. 1002A]

### Verse 6

Exult and give praise, O dwelling-place of Zion. Exult in heart; praise with your mouth, you dwelling-place of God, O Zion—that is, the holy Church—for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel. Great, certainly, not by physical extension, but in wisdom, strength, and goodness, “reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly.” Therefore he is not confined within some sectarian corner, but is in your midst, O dwelling-place of Zion, as he himself promised: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, I am in their midst” (Matt. XVIII, 20). Likewise: “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 2).

[Col. 1001]

## Exposition of the Song of Hezekiah, Isaiah XXXVIII

[Col. 1001B] “I said: In the middle of my days.” In Isaiah the following introduction is given: “The writing of Hezekiah, king of Judah, when he had been sick and had recovered from his illness.” This brief preface indicates the subject of this song. For when God had granted Hezekiah victory without effort, and he had not rendered him fitting thanks, compelled by illness he paid the praises which he had neglected in prosperity. After recovering, he declares what he had thought in distress: “I said,” etc.

Hezekiah walked before the Lord in truth and with a perfect heart, and did what was right according to all that David his father had done. But lest his heart be lifted up after incredible triumphs—when one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp had been slain by the angel, and Sennacherib himself had returned to Nineveh and been killed—he was visited [Col. 1001C] by illness and heard that he was to die, so that, turning to the Lord, he might bend his sentence: not because God changed his purpose, but because he summoned humankind to knowledge of himself.

Or, as the Hebrews relate, he fell ill because after his victory he did not sing praises to the Lord. He prayed, not setting a number of years, but leaving to God’s judgment what he might wish to give; and he wept because of the Lord’s promise to David, which he saw would perish in his death. For he did not yet have sons, and thus despaired that Christ would be born from his seed. Salvation, promised to him, is confirmed by a sign: the shadow moved back ten lines on the sundial, as the sun returned through the steps by which it had descended.

After recovering he wrote: “I said.” This is not a prayer, since it is in the past tense, [Col. 1001D] but an act of thanksgiving, in which a pattern and example is given to all who have been delivered from some illness: that they too should give thanks to God their deliverer, especially if, delivered from the punishment of some mortal sin, they have been healed—as King Hezekiah himself was. For ingratitude is a grave fault, such as was found in Hezekiah. As has been said, the Hebrews relate that King Hezekiah fell ill because, [Col. 1002B] after an unheard-of victory, he did not sing praise to the Lord, as Moses did when Pharaoh was drowned, Deborah when Sisera was killed, and Hannah when Samuel was born. Thus he was reminded of his frailty.

Again, after the healing of his body and the greatness of the sign shown by the sun’s backward movement, another occasion for pride was presented—one which, as a prudent worshipper of God, he should have avoided. He should not have displayed to foreigners the riches which he possessed by God’s gift. When, for this sin, punishment to fall upon his descendants after his own days was foretold to him, he should have confessed his sin with David and removed God’s wrath from his descendants, following the example of Moses, who, pitying the people committed to him, said to God: “Either forgive them this sin, or blot me out of your book which you have written [Col. 1002C] (Exod. XXXII, 31).”

But because he did not do this, and instead said, “Only let there be peace in my days” (Isa. XXXIX, 8), the Prophet did not answer him as he spoke, but turned away from him and toward the people, saying in the word of the Lord: “Comfort, comfort my people, says the Lord your God” (Isa. XL, 1). As though saying: Your king has no pity upon you; “be comforted” in Christ, because when human assistance fails the glory of the Lord shall be revealed and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.

These things were written for our correction: that we may not expose the treasures of God’s house to foreigners, cast pearls before swine, or give what is holy to dogs, and thereby provoke God’s wrath against us. If that wrath is stirred against us, [Col. 1002D] let us not say, “Only let there be peace in our days”; but, asking God for grace both for ourselves and for our descendants, let us say with the Psalmist: “Let there be peace”—that is, forgiveness of sins—“in your strength, and abundance” of strength and of every good thing “in your towers” (Ps. CXXI, 7). I say this not merely for my own deliverance in my days, but “for my brethren and my neighbours” (ibid., 8), to be saved [Col. 1003A] for eternity.

Therefore, avoiding evils, let us take an example from the good qualities of Hezekiah, resuming through the reminder of adversity the praises of God which we neglected in prosperity. For he himself resumes in sickness, followed by recovery, the praises and thanksgivings neglected in prosperity, saying:

### Verse 10

“I said: In the middle of my days I shall go to the gates of hell.” Rightly shall I give thanks, healed from so great an illness, in which, through excessive despair of life and salvation, I said: Alas for me, unhappy and wretched that I am, who have not completed my days like Abraham, who died full of days in a good old age, his son having already been born, in whom lay the promise of blessing! But I, being of David’s stock, from whose seed the Messiah is hoped to be born and [Col. 1003B] to sit upon the throne of his kingdom, have not yet begotten a son to reign after me, from whom Christ may be hoped to come; and behold, I die in the middle of my days, like those of whom it is said: “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days” (Ps. LIV, 24), because they do not fulfil works of virtue or correct their offences, but in the midst of their course of errors are led to Tartarus.

Thus I too shall go in the middle of my days to the gates of hell, where the house is appointed for every living person, until he comes who will deliver his elect from there. Since he was hoped to be born from my stock, I sought the remainder of my years, which failed me; fearing that they would be denied me, and almost despairing, I said:

### Verse 11

“I shall not see the Lord God in [Col. 1003C] the land of the living.” I shall not see Christ, the Lord God, whose day Abraham saw and rejoiced in, because he most faithfully believed that Christ would be born from his son Isaac, whose name is interpreted “joy.” But I, Hezekiah, dying without a son, shall go to the gates of hell. Therefore I shall no longer behold man and the inhabitant of rest.

Some manuscripts have, “My generation has ceased,” which Jerome too once translated, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, and later corrected. Hence he says: “Formerly we joined this to the following verse because of the ambiguity of the word.” “Generation has ceased,” that is, it has died. Earlier I, Hezekiah, said: “I shall not see the Lord God”; now I say: “I shall not behold man,” because the same Christ is both God and [Col. 1003D] man. Many prophets and kings desire to see this God made man; but I, Hezekiah, because my sins demand it, shall no longer behold man—the man, I mean, who gives and inhabits rest—because, behold, I die without a son, and from the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham,

### Verse 12

“My generation is taken away and folded up like the tent of shepherds,” who fold up their tent lest it remain stretched out. Thus, lest it be stretched out further, my life has been folded up and cut off like a web from the loom, long before the fabric of my own life was completed; for while I was still weaving its beginning, he cut me off. Therefore I said: “From morning until evening you will make an end of me.”

Thus Job also, amid extreme distress, awaited night during the day and looked for daylight during the night, thinking [Col. 1004A] that a change of seasons might change his affliction—as anxious people still do.

### Verse 13

“Like a lion, so he crushed all my bones,” because through the excessive violence of illness all my strength was crushed.

Otherwise: morning was the first age of the world, while evening was the coming of the Redeemer of the world. Therefore, cut off in this way, he feared that he would come to an end and would not belong to the generation of the Saviour, who was to come in the evening of this world. Struck by this fear, I, Hezekiah, said to you, my God: “From morning until evening you will make an end of me.”

### Verse 14

Therefore, as a swallow’s chick cries to its mother to receive food, so I shall cry; and, wearied by crying aloud, I shall meditate like a mourning dove. And while amid tears and groans I waited for help from heaven with my eyes raised on high, [Col. 1004B] my eyes grew weak as they looked upward. Therefore I said: “Lord, I suffer violence; what I suffer is beyond my strength,” or even beyond my deserving—though conscious of my merit, praying and weeping, I said: “I beseech you, Lord, remember, I pray, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your eyes” (IV Kings XX, 3).

Since, then, I have done good and suffer evil, “Lord, I suffer violence;” answer for me. You heard me as I prayed, and answered for me. For your word came to Isaiah, saying: “Go, and say to Hezekiah: Thus says the Lord God of David your father: I have heard your prayer and seen [Col. 1004C] your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your days, and I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of the Assyrians, and I will protect it” (Isa. XXXVIII, 5). Thus, God, you answered for me, and did as you said, adding fifteen years to my days. And now, behold, healed:

### Verse 15

“What shall I say? ‘What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?’” (Ps. CXV, 12). What shall I say—I, clay, to the potter? Or what will the potter himself answer me, the clay? What will he answer me, since he made me? Certainly nothing remains except patiently to endure, and to entreat the Maker himself to preserve what he has made, he who made what he willed.

Otherwise: What shall I say, or what will he answer me, when I myself have done such deeds as rightly deserve [Col. 1004D] the affliction I suffer, which is not to be relieved except by bitter repentance? Therefore I shall recount to you, my God, all my years in the bitterness of my soul, weeping bitterly even for the beloved days of my youth, but much more for the years of my whole lifetime. Unless fifteen years had been added by your grace, O God, all my years would have passed in vain.

For this reason I shall recount to you all my years in the bitterness of my soul, recognizing that in the years now past I had deserved that the bitterness of the coming illness should befall me. Yet, “because power is made perfect in weakness” (II Cor. XII, 9), and life is thus lived better when the life of mortals is chastened, lest it become insolent through excessive prosperity, I not only thank you, Lord [Col. 1005A] God, for past correction, you who rebuked me, but also consent and agree with you as you continue to scourge me, you who scourge every son whom you receive. For:

### Verse 16

“If life is thus lived,” if the mortal human life is thus delivered from death by paternal scourges, and in such scourges the life of my spirit is strengthened, you will rebuke me by striking and give me life by healing, you who say, “I will strike, and I will heal” (Deut. XXXII, 39). Asking this, and desiring your blows and healings, I rejoice that I have been heard amid my prayers. For among your blows belongs this:

### Verse 17

“Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter,” while the pain of repentance still torments me over the past and fear over the future. But among your healings and consolations belongs what follows:

[Col. 1005B] “But you have delivered my soul,” so that it should not perish or descend in the middle of my days to the gates of hell, but should be saved by living fifteen more years and ascending fifteen steps into the temple—seven and eight, which make fifteen—namely, by observing the Sabbath of legal rest and the eighth day of the Lord’s resurrection. And lest past sins hinder this, you cast all my sins behind your back, consigning them to oblivion, according to the words: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Ps. XXIV, 7). Likewise: “Remember not our former iniquities; let your mercies quickly come before us” (Ps. LXXVIII, 8).

For I shall not descend into hell [Col. 1005C] because of my sins, nor go in the middle of my days to the gates of hell, since I am a confessor of truth both in accusing my own sins and in praising your mercies, by which you blot them out. This would certainly not happen if my life were tending toward and descending into hell.

### Verse 18

“For hell shall not confess you, nor shall death praise you,” because those condemned to everlasting damnation, who constitute hell, inhabited by the devil, neither perform worthy repentance nor render praises to God. The devil himself also, who is death most hostile to the Life which is Christ, will not praise you; for, a deserter from the light, in his darkness he will blaspheme you, the true light. Those who descend utterly damned into the pit will not await your truth—that is, [Col. 1005D] that deliverer who is eternal Truth, who also says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6).

### Verse 19

“The living, the living”—that is, one living perfectly and rightly—“shall confess you,” as I too today, delivered from the Assyrians and healed of illness, shall confess you, praising your mercy and truth: because in your mercy you delivered the one whom in the justice of your truth you scourged.

Therefore, that your praise may be prolonged through every succession of generations and continued from fathers to sons, “the father shall make your truth known to the sons.” A good father like David, or a good prelate like Peter, shall make your truth known to his sons and subjects—that is, Christ, whom Peter confessed as Son of God and concerning whom he instructed his sons and subjects in the same confession. David made him known to his descendants by singing psalms, and I, Hezekiah, being one of these and an imitator of a good father, make your truth known through this present song, at whose conclusion I say:

### Verse 20

“Lord, save me.” You saved me from the Assyrians and from bodily illness. Since this does not suffice for the blessedness of eternal salvation, save me also from the invisible Assyrians—that is, the demons—and from every infirmity of mind and body. Save also all who, following my example, believe in you; and thus, delivered and healed by your aid, we shall always praise you after your example, because “we shall sing our psalms all the days of our life in the house of the Lord.”

It is one thing to make music on the psaltery, another to sing psalms. One makes psalmody who [Col. 1006B] performs what is good; one sings psalms who does so devoutly and cheerfully, not from sadness or necessity. This we shall do all the days of our life, knowing that “he who perseveres” in good “unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. XXIV, 13), praising his deliverer in the house of the Lord, which is the Catholic Church, outside which no praise and no sacrifice is pleasing to God. Hence elsewhere it is said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; they shall praise you for ages of ages” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5). Likewise: “His praise is in the Church of the saints” (Ps. CXLIX, 1).

Above, in the person of a righteous man scourged—as King Hezekiah was, and before him holy Job—it was said among other things: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me.” It is as if the righteous man says: Since I have done good and suffer evil, Lord, I suffer violence. But it ought to be familiar and constant not only to righteous men, but also to sinners, men and women alike, that when they suffer violence from someone violent, they should cry to the Lord, each saying: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me.”

The first Abel, suffering violence from his brother, could have said this. Though he did not say it with his mouth, his blood cried out, and the Lord answered for him, reproving and condemning the fratricide as was fitting. Thus holy Job first suffered violence from Satan, who asked to test him, falsely accusing him before God without cause. But God himself too, allowing him to be afflicted by the tempter, did violence to him, although he was upright, righteous, and God-fearing [Col. 1006D] in his sight. Further, he suffered violence from his friends, burdensome comforters who pressed him by their arguments toward distrust. Above all, he suffered violence from his wife, who urged him to blaspheme God. And arrogant Elihu, winding together accusations against him, hemmed him in so closely that he had to say, with mouth or heart: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me.”

For the Lord, hearing his cry, answered for him by condemning that arrogant man, calling his friends to repentance, and consoling Job himself. Yet all these things happened to him in figure.

They were fulfilled more magnificently in Christ, who, suffering violence, cried on the cross: “My God, my God, [Col. 1007A] look upon me,” etc. (Ps. XXIV, 16). Therefore, hearing the cry of his blood, God answered for him, making it evident in words and deeds that he suffered violence unjustly, though he would judge justly. For the Paraclete, speaking through the apostles, glorified him whom Satan, in Pilate and the Pharisaic assembly, had condemned.

Thus every righteous person unjustly suffering violence cries out in the voice of that very suffering: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me.” At such a cry the Lord, roused “like a mighty man overcome with wine,” struck the enemies who did violence and freed friends patiently enduring violence, as though answering for them according to his promise: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 20).

[Col. 1007B] This has been said concerning the righteous. But now let us see how it is fitting for sinners to say: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me.” Did not the younger son, received back by his father through repentance, when his sins were rehearsed by the elder son before his father and the whole household, have need to say to his father: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me”? Perceiving this cry of his heart, the father answered for him, saying: “It was fitting for you, son, to rejoice, because your brother was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.”

Thus God the Father answered the Jewish people, who envied the people of the Gentiles returning from a far country. He received that people; and at its reception he instituted great music and renowned dances, with which the whole household—that is, the universal Church—celebrates at the feast of the fattened calf, while the elder brother, namely the Jewish people, is tormented by his envy.

[Col. 1007C] Likewise, whenever any weak person, likened to Mary the sinner but now repentant, anoints Christ’s feet and head, reverently honouring in writings and words Christ’s humanity and divinity, that person is often disparaged and murmured against by people resembling Pharisees or Judas, because she is a sinner and because the ointment might have been distributed to the poor. Amid such things this weak person suffers violence and must say: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me.”

So too, when a soul devoted to the word of God delights in sitting sweetly at the Lord’s feet with Mary the sinner, cleansed from her sins and desiring to be filled with God’s word, it sometimes happens that an active person, busied like Martha with much service and troubled over many matters, breaks out into complaints against one resting in this way. It is fitting for the person hearing these complaints to say, in heart or mouth: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me.” The Lord hears such a prayer and, if not in words, certainly by clear realities answers for that person, saying: “She has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken from her.”

Grant me, Lord, now with Mary, repentant and devoted to your word, to sit at your feet—that is, to trace the footprints of your feet by which you run swiftly—so that this best part may not be taken from me. To those who wish to take it from me, answer for me, whether they are [Col. 1008A] Pharisees murmuring, disciples complaining about the waste of ointment, or active persons wishing to involve me with them in their occupations. Among them all, while I suffer violence, answer for me.

But most of all when that elder brother accuses me—the devil, that is—who is called brother because he was created by God the Father, by whom I too, a rational human being, was created; and elder because, while man was created on the sixth day, he was created on the first, when God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. Before his fall—when he fell like lightning from heaven and became prince of darkness—he was Lucifer.

This elder brother, the accuser of the brethren, especially accuses that younger one who, after the Jewish people was rejected, returned to the Father from the Gentile people: undoubtedly myself, a sinner, although clothed with the first robe and adorned with the ring of faith. He accuses me both by himself and through his own agents, and reproaches me with sins already forgiven, doing violence to me, as it is written: “Those who sought my life did violence.” Therefore, whenever now or at the hour of death I suffer such violence, may you, Lord, Father of mercies, deign so to answer for me as to say: “My son was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.”

And because that elder one is unworthy in himself to take part in the chorus and music of your household rejoicing at the younger brother’s return, turn back certain people growing old through envy, who cling to that ancient elder brother—especially among the remnant of the children of Israel. Invite them [Col. 1008C] away from the food of the goat which they desire, toward the food of the fattened calf, answering that people for me, a Gentile returned to you through repentance: “It was fitting for you, son, to rejoice, because your brother was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke XV, 32). Thus, suffering violence, I desire that answer to be made for me.

For I, guilty as I am, have nothing to say, since I have done no good by my own powers and have done many evils, which either that elder brother or the Pharisee reproaches me with. What then shall I say to those reproaching me with my sins, when I myself have done what they reproach me with? For some manuscripts read, “when I myself have done.” But because the more reliable manuscripts read, “when he himself has made,” it must be read thus, so that this wording may stand, as was explained above.

[Col. 1008D] For what shall I, the thing fashioned, say to my maker, since he himself has made me? Whatever I am, whatever good I can do, he made it; I fell away from him when I went into a far country, and he made me return. Since he himself made me, and himself made all my merits, if any are good, what shall I say to him? I have nothing with which to defend myself against those who reproach me and do violence to me, or who, by his permission, do violence to me in persecution.

Therefore, turning to him, I continually say: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me” with such answers as none of my adversaries can resist, whether demons accusing me or human beings assailing me. Thus defended from them, may I with holy Hezekiah sing psalms all the days of my life; and may those who sympathize with me in my suffering sing with me, so that in us all may be fulfilled what is said: “The living, the living shall confess you, as I also do today.” And so that from now on this confession of sins and praises may be perpetuated for ever through the succession of all ages: “May the father make known, and shall make known, your truth to his sons,” so that every son instructed by his father may say, following his father’s example: “Lord, save me, and we shall sing our psalms all the days of our life in the house [Col. 1010A] of the Lord.”

At such psalmody may the army of the Assyrians—that is, of wicked angels and human beings—flee in terror; and may there be added to us all and to our own that long duration of good living signified by the fifteen years added to Hezekiah, so that, having passed through fifteen steps, we may sing our psalms all the days of our life in the house of the Lord. Amen, amen.

[Col. 1009]

## Exposition of the Song of Hannah, I Kings, Chapter II

[Col. 1009B] “My heart has exulted in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my God,” etc. The one singing these words is a prophetess, and she is the same woman made fruitful by grace, which her very name signifies: for Hannah is interpreted “grace.” Taught inwardly by this same grace, she prophesies or proclaims not so much her own individual present state as the future common blessings of the whole holy Church.

Accordingly, let us understand the same thing in Hannah as in Sarah, the same in Peninnah as in Hagar—although the latter was a slave woman and the former free—and the same in Elkanah as in Abraham. For the historical event is in part similar and their names are related in meaning. Abraham, that is, “father of many nations,” was first called Abram, interpreted “exalted father”; and Elkanah, interpreted “possession of God,” is written to have been from Ramathaim, that is, “the heights.” Hagar means “turned”; Peninnah means “turning.” But Sarah means “princess,” Hannah “grace”; and in both is to be understood the sovereignty of grace, because they bore children not according to the flesh or the condition of their flesh, as Hagar and Peninnah did, but according to grace, after having previously been barren.

Thus Peninnah and Hannah are the two covenants: one of the flesh, bringing forth into slavery; the other of faith, bringing forth into freedom. Elkanah, that is, “possession of God,” is the people of God themselves, to whom it was said: “He possessed you and made and created you” (Deut. XXXII, 6). In Abraham—indeed, in Abraham’s seed, which is Christ—they received the covenant of faith, the covenant of freedom; but on Mount Sinai, after four hundred [Col. 1009D] and thirty years, the covenant of flesh, the covenant of slavery.

But the covenant of flesh, like Peninnah or Hagar, first bore many children, while the covenant of faith, like Hannah or Sarah, long mourned barrenness. For the children of the flesh first multiplied in that people, glorying in Abraham’s flesh, while his faith scarcely produced any offspring in a very few. Finally, all those who came out of Egypt, from twenty years old and above, except Joshua and Caleb son of Jephunneh, showed that they had arisen from Abraham’s flesh only, not also from his faith.
