At last, faith or grace, formerly barren, bore many children through the Gospel; and the boasting of the flesh, which had many children, was weakened—indeed, excluded. Knowing that this had been prefigured within herself by the prophetic Spirit, she exults and gives praise in the person of the Church, saying:

### Verse 1

“My heart exulted in the Lord, and my horn was exalted in my God.” Where the flesh alone is fruitful, the heart has no ground for exultation; for there is no exultation of heart except in the Lord. Accordingly, when she says, “My heart exulted in the Lord,” she indicates that she sings that exultation of the universal Church which another prophet foretold: “Because of fear of you, O Lord, we conceived and brought forth Spirit; we have not wrought salvation [Variant/Code: ‘we have wrought your salvation,’ etc.] upon the earth” (Isa. XXVI, 18).

There it is not the flesh but the heart that exults, although the heart’s prior exultation also raises the flesh into partnership with its exultation, according to David’s words: “My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God” (Ps. LXXXIII, 3). That exultation is strong, and its joy is not vain but most powerful. She therefore adds: “And my horn was exalted in my God.” The Prophet says in the singular: “My horn shall be exalted like that of the unicorn” (Ps. XCI, 11); and likewise in the plural: “The horns of the righteous shall be exalted” (Ps. LXXIV, 11). The meaning is not different: the one horn of the Church is the one Christ, while its many horns are the many gifts of the Holy Spirit. Thus that true Lamb is written to have not only seven eyes [Col. 1010D] but also “seven horns” (Apoc. V, 6).

“My horn,” she says, “has been exalted in my God”—in my God, I say, and not in myself, which would be empty confidence and deceitful strength.

Hence there is inward exultation of heart and outward confidence against my enemies. For this is what follows: “My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies, because I have rejoiced in your salvation.” Let my formerly talkative enemies, children of flesh and not of faith, be humbled and speak from the earth. For, by a reversal, authority to speak has been granted to me, so that I no longer whisper in corners or speak with a half-opened mouth, but speak with an enlarged mouth over my enemies, who reproached me with barrenness, so as to be heard throughout the whole world. “Because I have rejoiced in your salvation.” God’s salvation is Christ.

Does one woman, then, exult only in Samuel, rather than the one holy mother, the universal Church, singing her true exultation in Christ? In these first two verses of the song the sense is not different, but the words differ and are set in reverse order. For “My heart exulted in the Lord” is the same as “I have rejoiced in your salvation”; and “my horn was exalted in my God” is the same as “my mouth has been enlarged over my enemies.” Now let us hear what worthy matter she brings forth through her enlarged mouth.

[Col. 1011B]

### Verse 2

“There is none holy as the Lord; for there is none other besides you, and there is none strong as our God.” He rightly enlarges his mouth who proclaims not himself but the Lord; he rightly exalts his horn who commends not his own righteousness but God’s. “There is none holy as the Lord.” She had said too little. Therefore she added: “For there is none other besides you,” and thereby said the same as if she had said: Apart from him, no one is clean from defilement. And, she says, “There is none strong as our God.”

Certainly others are strong falsely, of whom the Prophet says in the psalm: “The strong attacked me” (Ps. LVIII, 4). He is truly strong and the true strength of the humble. “There is none holy as the Lord,” she says; “there is none strong as our God.” It is as though the children of Hannah said to the children of Peninnah, the children of grace to the children of the synagogue, the children of promise to the children of flesh: Why do you boast, saying, “We are Abrahamites by nature, we are Israelites by nature, and not sinners from the Gentiles”?

“The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men to see whether there was one who understood or sought God. All have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII, 2–3). The law says this. And certainly, whatever the law says, “we know,” says the Apostle, “that it speaks to those who are under the law” (Rom. III, 19). Therefore no one is holy; there is none other besides you—none other, I say, who can sanctify apart from you, O Christ, Holy of holies. Even those saints, before you came, confessed in their own words: “All our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruating woman” (Isa. LXIV, 10).

And why do you glory in mighty Moses and Aaron, in the strength of your law and priesthood? “There is none strong as our God,” as our Christ. Neither Moses nor Aaron, neither your law nor your priesthood, conquered the spiritual Pharaoh or destroyed him who held the power of death—that is, the devil. But he conquered him; he broke hell; he rose again after overcoming death. Therefore there is none strong like this our God, like this our Saviour.

### Verse 3

“Do not multiply lofty speech in boasting.” You boast greatly, lift yourselves high, and speak many lofty things through empty glory; for example, saying: “Abraham is our father; the covenant is ours; legislation is ours; worship is ours; the promises are ours; glory is ours; the adoption as sons is ours. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are our fathers.” Do not speak thus; do not thus multiply the lofty speech of a boastful mouth; do not boast thus.

Let the old things depart from your mouth, because the Lord is the God of knowledges, and thoughts are prepared for him. These lofty things which you have hitherto multiplied in speech are antiquated; they have now grown old, and must be cast away when the new things come upon them. For this is what God, the Lord of knowledges, says in Jeremiah—he who once gave you the knowledge of the letter and now gives us the knowledge of the Spirit as he wills:

> “Behold, days are coming, and I will make a new covenant with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant which I made with your fathers on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt—the covenant which they made void, though I ruled over them, says the Lord. But this shall be the covenant which I will make with the house of Israel: after those days I will put my law in their inward parts and write it upon their heart,” etc. (Jer. 31:31, 33). [Col. 1012B]

“And prudent thoughts are prepared for him”—this is understood. For, conversely, he will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding. Thoughts are prepared as an offering for God, the Lord of knowledges. If you wish to deserve or obtain the gift of knowledge, not many offerings of rams and bulls, but holy thoughts are preparations for that matter. Hence the Psalmist also says: “Your ear heard the preparations of their heart” (Ps. 10:17). Again: “The thought of man shall confess to you, and the remnant of thought shall keep a feast for you” (Ps. 75:11). “The remnant of thought,” he says. If the firstfruits of thought have been hostile, at least let its remnant, through repentance or confession, keep a feast for you. Therefore I also said: Let the old things depart from your mouth; let the lofty things depart; let your boasting cease. For what follows?

**VERSE 4.** “The bow of the mighty has been overcome, and the weak have been girded with strength.” This has not happened only once. When the strength or power of the Egyptians was overcome and the Israelites were strengthened, then indeed the bow of the mighty was overcome and the weak were girded with strength. So too now. For the bow—that is, the pride and strength of Peninnah, by which she boasted in her children—has been overcome; and I, who had been made weak through barrenness, have been girded with the strength of children. For this is what follows: “Until the barren woman bore many children, and she who had many children became weak.” The intervening words, “Those formerly full hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry were filled,” are not sung according to the present historical narrative. Yet this and other such things have happened and happen, so that whenever the wicked man is proud, you may sing that royal proverb: “Let not him who is girded boast equally with him who is ungirded.” [Col. 1012D]

In the Hebrew and in the translation of the Septuagint, not “many” but “seven” is read. The Jews understand this passage thus: when Samuel was born, Peninnah’s firstborn son died; and thereafter, as each of Hannah’s sons was born, one of Peninnah’s sons died, in the order of their birth. But it must be asked how this can stand, since Peninnah had seven children whereas Hannah had no more than five. In resolving this question, the Hebrews count Samuel’s two sons among Hannah’s children. [Col. 1013A]

According to the anagogical sense, the bow of the mighty is the confidence of the Jews—those who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie. I mean those Jews who presume upon their own strength and wish to establish their own righteousness, and therefore refuse to submit to the righteousness of God: their bow of strength has been overcome. “They bent their tongue like a bow of falsehood, and not of truth,” says the Prophet (Ps. 10:3). Such a bow of the mighty has been overcome, for by shooting against the truth they achieved nothing, as it is written elsewhere: “The arrows of little children became their wounds” (Ps. 63:8). But the weak—those, namely, who ascribe nothing to their own powers, who boast not in their own works but in faith in Jesus Christ—have been girded with strength: with that strength, I say, by which they can do violence to the kingdom of heaven and seize it forcibly. [Col. 1013B]

**VERSE 5.** “Those formerly full,” he says, “hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry were filled.” We Gentiles were formerly hungry, while the Jews were full—that is, satisfied. And it is plain that now the Gentiles have been satisfied by the word of God through the Gospel of his Son Jesus Christ, while the Jews are hungry, following the letter alone, the chaff, and lacking the life-giving Spirit. But have these hired themselves out for bread? Do they not prefer to hunger rather than eat the living bread with us? For the parable of the evangelical father says this: when he had received his hungry son, who had gone into a far country and there squandered all his substance in prodigal living—when, I say, he had received him on his return and was celebrating a great feast, his elder brother, being indignant, “would not go in” (Luke 15:28). Thus for the present those who were formerly full are hungry, while the formerly hungry are satisfied, in accordance with the prophetic threat: “Behold, my servants shall eat, and you shall hunger” (Isa. 65:13). But it will come to pass that they will not disdain to hire themselves out for bread. For when the fullness of the hungry Gentiles has entered in, the remnant from among them will be converted to the food of life. [Col. 1013C–D]

Not slightly has the bow of the mighty been overcome, and the weak girded with strength; nor is it a small matter that those who were formerly full now hunger, while the hungry are filled. But what then? “Until the barren woman bore many children, and she who had many children became weak.” So great was the change of the right hand of the Most High in the breaking of the mighty and the girding of the weak that she who was barren bore many, while in turn she who, having many children, had been proud, became weak. Thus was fulfilled the prophecy which another prophet sings in these words:

> “Praise, O barren woman, who do not bear; sing praise and neigh for joy, you who did not bear, says the Lord; for the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who had a husband, says the Lord. Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare. Make your cords long, and strengthen your stakes. For you shall break forth to the right and to the left; and your seed shall inherit the nations and inhabit desolate cities” (Isa. 54:1 ff.). [Col. 1014A]

And the rest. The matters sung hitherto concern all the Lord’s ways, namely mercy and judgment. Therefore, in praise of those same great realities—mercy and judgment—she continues more resonantly and more fully, with exultant heart and opened mouth, saying:

**VERSES 6–7.** “The Lord kills and makes alive; he brings down to hell and brings back. The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and lifts up.” That the Lord kills belongs to judgment; that he makes alive belongs to mercy. Likewise, that he brings down to hell belongs to judgment; that he brings back, to mercy. In the same way, making poor belongs to judgment, making rich to mercy; humbling to judgment, lifting up to mercy. Thus by these antitheses—that is, opposites—all the Lord’s ways are displayed for those who seek his covenant and his testimonies. But toward what persons is judgment, or truth, exercised; and for whom is mercy laid up? For whom but the proud does he kill, bring down to hell, humble, and make poor? Conversely, whom but the humble does he make alive, bring back from hell, lift up, and make rich? Therefore it follows:

**VERSE 8.** “Raising the needy from the dust, and lifting the poor from the dungheap, that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory.” For what is “the needy poor man” but the person whom the Lord blesses in his Gospel—the poor in spirit, that is, the humble? He raises from dust and lifts from the dungheap the one whom, wisely knowing what dust and ashes are and blushing at the dung of his sins, he justifies and adorns with the gifts of his grace, so that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory—with those, namely, whom he foreknew and predestined before the ages, called, justified, and glorified. This has occurred not rarely nor only in a few persons. Yet more abundantly and chiefly we rejoice and continually sing that it was accomplished in him who is certainly known truly to have said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29). [Col. 1014C–D]

Of him also is that saying: “And he persecuted the poor and needy man, and the one pierced in heart, to put him to death” (Ps. 108:17). For the Lord God the Father truly put him to death and brought him down to hell by the command of his love; he made him poor and humbled him. And by the power and omnipotence of his divinity he again made the same one alive, brought him back from hell, enriched and exalted him. He raised him from the dust of our mortality; he lifted him from the dungheap, so that his flesh should not see the dung of corruption. And behold, he sits with princes—indeed, above all princes—at the Father’s right hand, and holds the throne of glory. That this is the right understanding is proved by the conclusion of the canticle. For it concludes thus: “And he shall give dominion to his king, and shall exalt the horn of his Christ.”

“For the hinges of the earth are the Lord’s, and he has set the world upon them.” In the Hebrew it is thus: “For the afflicted of the earth are the Lord’s.” By “the afflicted of the earth,” the Hebrews understand the poor in spirit and the humble in heart, upon whom, they say, the Lord has set the world because they maintain that the earth stands by their merits. The proposition, then, by which he said, “Raising the needy from the dust,” etc., is splendid; but the reason confirming it is more splendid, when he now says: “For the hinges—that is, the afflicted—of the earth are the Lord’s, and he has set the world upon them.” The evangelical truth agrees with this, placing the poor in spirit at the foundation of blessedness when, about to enumerate the eight beatitudes, it begins: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3). [Col. 1015A]

**VERSE 9.** “He shall keep the feet of his saints.” Those needy and poor persons—those, I say, who are the hinges or afflicted ones of the earth—are the Lord’s saints, whose feet he shall keep. It is understood that he will not keep the feet of the proud. Fearing their fall and irrecoverable ruin, the Prophet says: “Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the sinner move me” (Ps. 35:12). And he immediately adds: “There the workers of iniquity fell; they were cast out and could not stand” (ibid., 13). Therefore, “the feet of his saints,” he says: the feet, I say, of the saints—that is, of the humble—he will preserve, so that they may reach the throne of glory and, indeed, may bear with steadfast merits the world set upon them. Thus far he has expressed what kind of people the Lord makes alive, brings back from hell, enriches, and exalts; now he declares what kind he kills and brings down to hell, makes poor, and humbles. For it follows:

“And the wicked shall be silent in darkness, because man shall not be strengthened by his own power.” The wicked, he says—that is, the proud, who now in this their day lift up their horn on high and speak iniquity against God—shall be silent in darkness. While the humble hold the throne of glory and praise the Lord God who possesses them, the wicked shall rest in the darkness of hell; indeed, they shall howl, gnash their teeth, and weep, for “there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8:12). [Col. 1015C]

“For man shall not be strengthened by his own power.” How much strength will man then possess, when shortly afterward his neck has been reduced to mud? Then the wicked man shall confess that no one is strengthened either by a horse or by his own legs, as another prophet also says: “He shall not take pleasure in the strength of a horse, nor shall he delight in the legs of a man” (Ps. 146:10 [printed 19]). Again: “A horse is deceitful for salvation; and in the abundance of its strength it shall not save” (Ps. 32:17). Moreover, to speak in a more spiritual sense, “man shall not be strengthened by his own power” means that no one shall be justified before God by works of the law, in which Peninnah’s children, namely the Jews, boast. Nor shall anyone at all, Jew or Greek, be saved or justified in judgment if he is judged without mercy, or only according to his own merits. [Col. 1015D]

**VERSE 10.** “His adversaries shall fear the Lord, and he shall thunder over them in the heavens.” This has at times visibly happened, when the Lord thundered in the heavens over his adversaries, as in the book of Joshua:

> “And when they fled from the face of Israel and were in the descent of Beth-horon, the Lord sent great stones from heaven upon them as far as Zecha, and they died; far more died from the stones of hail than those whom the children of Israel struck with the sword” (Josh. 10:11). [Col. 1016A]

But since then this has happened more magnificently: the Lord thunders in the heavens over his adversaries from the time when he himself, who as needy and poor was put to death and brought down to hell, was again made alive, brought back from hell, and exalted to sit with the Father as prince and hold the throne of glory. Since then he has thundered over his adversaries with the great and dreadful thunder of the Gospel, and he does not cease to thunder until the end of the age, as the Apostle says: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness and injustice of those men who hold the truth of God in injustice” (Rom. 1:18), and the rest. Hence too is what the Prophet foretold: “And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice—hail and coals of fire; and he sent forth his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied lightnings and troubled them,” etc. (Ps. 17:14–15). The final movement of the thunderer shall strike the terrified adversaries with a great and irrevocable thunderbolt. For he shall say to those on the left: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 24:41 [cf. 25:41]). [Col. 1016B]

“[The] Lord shall judge the ends of the earth, and shall give dominion to his king, and shall exalt the horn of his Christ.” [Col. 1016C] It is as though she said: This distinction between the proud and the humble, which I have foretold, does not yet appear. For not every needy and poor person yet holds the throne of glory; not every wicked person has fallen silent in darkness; nor do all his adversaries fear the Lord in the present life. On the contrary, the wicked now live in such security and exalt themselves so greatly over the humble that the humble person, still weak, is almost shaken. For he is the one—or the Prophet speaks in his person—who says in the Psalm: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps were almost poured out, because I envied the wicked when I saw the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72:2), and the rest. Therefore the distinction does not yet appear; but do not be troubled. For the Lord shall judge the ends of the earth.

For the present he overlooks the beginnings, because he does not immediately judge or punish the pride of the earth where it begins; but he will certainly judge its ends. For the merciful Creator both endures human evils through his patience and sometimes remits them through the conversion of some, so that they may return even late and at least blush because they have been so long awaited. But the proud earth, which despises the riches of his goodness and, ignorant of God’s patience waiting for it, stores up wrath for itself according to its hardness and unrepentant heart, he will at last judge at the end, on the day of wrath and revelation of his righteous judgment, in which he will render to each person according to his works. [Col. 1016D]

“And he shall give,” he says, “dominion to his king”—to his king, that is, Christ; for there follows: “And he shall exalt the horn of his Christ.” The end of the canticle agrees with its beginning. For at the beginning it says, “My horn has been exalted in my God”; but here at the end it says, “He shall exalt the horn of his Christ.” He shall give dominion to this King and exalt his horn, so that all things may be subject beneath his feet. The Apostle says: “The future, he says, of which we speak. For, he says, we do not yet see all things subject to him” (1 Cor. 15:27). He shall give, according to his humanity, to him who possesses all things according to his divinity. [Col. 1017A–1018A] He shall give, I say, to one who has merited it by obedience in his Passion, as he himself, now rewarded after conquering death, says: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18). The Apostle, speaking with distinguished eloquence of his exalted horn, says: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:9–11).

[Col. 1017]

## EXPOSITION OF THE FIRST CANTICLE OF MOSES, EXODUS CHAPTER 15

[Col. 1017B] “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified,” etc. “When Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, the Lord removed it by a strong and scorching wind blowing, and turned it into dry land; and the water was divided, and the children of Israel entered through the midst of the dry sea,” etc. (Exod. 14:21 ff.). The deed displaying the Lord’s glorious magnificence is clear: the water was divided and the children of Israel entered through the midst of the dry sea; and the Lord destroyed Pharaoh’s army, overturned the chariot wheels, and they were carried into the depths. Thus the Egyptians knew that the Lord himself is God, so that they said: “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them against us” (ibid., 25). But as they fled, the Lord enveloped them amid the waves, looking upon their camp in the morning watch—that is, the fourth watch. For four watches of the night were counted, three hours being assigned to each watch.

But in the mystical sense, the morning watch is the Lord’s resurrection itself. For in the morning an angel sat at the Lord’s tomb; and after the deep night of sorrow, he announced to the women—and through them to the grieving apostles—the day of great joy. Hence the Psalm says: “From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord” (Ps. 129:6). By “the morning watch” he meant the watch of soldiers terrified in the morning, as an example to all the ungodly; for the women were made joyful as an example to all the godly. What is Israel to hope in the Lord from that morning watch? Namely, that what was then made known as accomplished in him shall take place in Israel: he rose from the dead, “for with the Lord is mercy, and with him is abundant redemption; and he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities” (ibid., 7). It is understood: just as he redeemed those children of Israel from all the Egyptian men. Therefore the morning watch in which the children of Israel crossed while the Egyptians remained behind is, mystically, for us the joy of the Lord’s resurrection: in it, putting off the old man, we were reborn, while the devil, whom we renounced together with all his pomps, remained behind. [Col. 1017C–1018B] For the Apostle says:

> “Because we were baptized in Christ Jesus, we were baptized into his death; we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life. For if we have been made planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall likewise be in that of his resurrection” (Rom. 6:3–5).

Therefore we ought no longer to be silent about the most celebrated mystery of this glorious deed, since we possess the following canticle of Moses; for here is the wisdom which opened the mouth of the mute and made the tongues of infants eloquent, so that together we may praise your victorious hand, Lord our God. For that this canticle ought not to fail from the mouth of any of us who have received this grace is intimated by the passage from Revelation:

> “And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire, and those who had conquered the beast and his image and the number of his name, standing upon the sea of glass, holding harps of God and singing the canticle of Moses, the servant of God, and the canticle of the Lamb, saying: Great and marvelous are your works, Lord God Almighty,” etc. (Rev. 15:2–3). [Col. 1018C]

Behold, we stand upon the sea of glass—that is, we strive to preserve the innocence which we received through baptism; a sea, I say, of glass, on account of the pure confession of sins to be forsaken which we made there. Yet it is mingled with fire—that is, made alive by the Holy Spirit, by whom those sins themselves have been consumed. He is also mystically signified here by the scorching wind, since it says: “When Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, the Lord removed it, while a strong and scorching wind blew throughout the whole night.” Therefore, holding the harps of God—that is, the mortification of the flesh which God commanded—let us sing this canticle of Moses, the servant of God, and of the Lamb, rejoicing in both respects: in the deed performed through the hand of Moses, and in the mystery of the spotless and undefiled Lamb, Christ, which Moses prophetically understood in that same deed. [Col. 1018D]

[Col. 1019A] **VERSE 1.** “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he cast into the sea.” The first voice of the precentor is an exhortation urging all who are in the Shunammite—“the choirs of the camps”—to raise their harmony in accordance with the greatness of the feast, with the magnitude and character of the divine works. “Let us sing,” he says, “to the Lord.” Let us sing with the spirit; let us sing also with the mind. For the Apostle says: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15). To sing or chant with the spirit means to retain the deed in memory and have it alone as the subject matter of the song; to sing with the mind means to perceive inwardly the mystery in the outward event. Let us therefore sing to the Lord. Why? “For he has been gloriously magnified.” In what respect? “Horse and rider he cast into the sea.” It is truly glorious magnificence, even if you consider only the outward deed. But if you perceive the inward mystery also, there is a more glorious abundance of magnificence there. For the horse here is the world; the rider is the devil.

When did he cast down that rider and such a horse of his? Namely when he said: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John 12:31). And let us hear him immediately afterward explain in action what he had said: he took the horns of the cross in his hands, and there his strength was hidden, so that death, daring to creep upon him, went forth conquered before his face, and the devil went forth before his feet. Then he cast him down, and since then he does not cease to cast him into the sea: for us, indeed, a sea of glass mingled with the fire of the Holy Spirit; but for him, a pitchy sea, fiery and sulphurous. For that sea through which the children of Israel passed both sent these out and swallowed those; but our sea, in which we are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, does not admit the horse and his rider at all. Rather, as we pass through this sea of glass, he is cast into the depths of hell. [Col. 1019B–C]

It is exceedingly glorious that the Lord has done this. Long ago he brought down and cast into this darkened air that rider who said: “I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I shall exalt my throne” (Isa. 14:13). But now he casts into the depth of the pit, into the abyss of burning hell, the one seated upon the horse—that is, upon the unbridled folly of proud people deceived by themselves. “Yet,” says the Prophet, “you shall be brought down to hell, into the depth of the pit; those who see you shall bend toward you and look upon you,” etc. (ibid., 15). Behold, we see it, and we shall yet see it on the day of judgment; for then he shall be cast down before the sight of all. Therefore let us sing to the Lord, says this learned and melodious precentor. [Col. 1019D]

**VERSE 2.** “The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become salvation for me.” Having received the exhortation, the whole choir—one body composed of many members—enters upon its song with this beginning: “The Lord is my strength and my praise.” What follows? “And he has become salvation for me.” Then has your strength become salvation for you? Certainly—my strength. For the strength of my head is my strength; indeed, if my head is strong, it is my strength. And who does not know that the magnificent Lord himself is my head, since the Word became flesh and I, the one Church summoned to this song, am his one body? Therefore it is permitted both to the whole body together and to each member individually, without injury to the grace of the head, to glory and say: “My strength has become salvation for me, and this is my praise.” For the praise of the head does not dishonor the whole body. [Col. 1020A]

Otherwise, unless I had a most strong head, I would, as until now—since I drank from the Lord’s hand the cup of his wrath and drank it to the dregs because of Adam’s transgression—as until now, I say, there was none of all the children whom I bore to raise me up; so also I would sleep for ever like that beast caught in a snare and full of the Lord’s indignation. [Col. 1020A–B]

“This is my God, and I will glorify him; the God of my father, and I will exalt him.” This one, I say—once despised, the last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness, who by dying cast down such a horse and such a rider—is my God. He is both man and my God. I shall glorify him; I shall not be ashamed of him. But the adversaries of the people who ascended and became angry say to me—namely, the synagogue of the Jews and the assemblies of heretics, whom pains have seized: “If this one is your God, then he is a new God, a foreign God within you, and you act against the Scripture which says: ‘Israel, if you hear me, there shall not be in you a new god, nor shall you worship a foreign god’” (Ps. 80:10). To this I shall say, and shall sing confidently: “This is my God, and I will glorify him, the God of my father Abraham, and I will exalt him.” “Your father Abraham rejoiced,” he says, “that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56). Again: “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am” (ibid., 58). Therefore there is no new god in me, nor do I worship a foreign god, but the God of my father, the ancient God. For although he is Son, although begotten or born, yet he is not younger than his Father, the Ancient of Days, by one point or atom. I shall glorify him; I shall exalt him; and I shall say:

**VERSES 3–5.** “The Lord is like a warrior; Almighty is his name. Pharaoh’s chariots and his army he cast into the sea. His chosen princes were submerged in the Red Sea. The depths covered them; they went down into the deep like a stone.” Read parenthetically: “Almighty is his name,” so that in the midst of the sentence the adversary may be rebuked, to whom it seemed excessive that he should be called “Lord.” “Like a warrior,” he says—that is, he did these things after the manner of a warrior. For just as a warrior adapts and arms himself according to the kind or quality of his enemy, so this one had to order battle in new and wonderful ways according to the nature of his enemy. His enemy, however, was not flesh and blood, but a certain principality and aerial power, ruler of this world and of this darkness, spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places. [Col. 1020D–1021A]

Therefore the All-Powerful One did not gird himself with a material sword upon his thigh; he did not put on a visible breastplate or an iron-woven helmet. But against such a principality and power he put on the beauty of humility and obedience in opposition to pride; against spiritual wickedness he put on and girded himself with the strength of love. Thus, like a warrior, he cast into the sea Pharaoh’s aerial chariots, in which he imagined that he rode above the height of the clouds so as to be like the Most High; and he cast in also his army, both the vices and the demons whom he had appointed over the temples and shrines of the Gentiles. For by dying he received power in heaven and on earth and drew all things to himself. Since then his chosen princes have been submerged in the Red Sea. For his wave-like tribulation, of which he says in the Psalm, “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even unto my soul” (Ps. 68:2), overflowed their heads from the moment when, pierced in the side by the lance, he poured forth blood and water. Thus the depths covered them, their memory perished, and they went down into the deep like a stone, weighed down by their own iniquity. For they have no claim at all over any of those whose God this is, who glorify him, and who confess that this one is the God of their father. Hence the praises; hence the thanksgivings. [Col. 1021A–B]

**VERSES 6–7.** “Your right hand, O Lord, has been magnified in strength; your right hand, O Lord, struck the enemy. And in the multitude of your glory you cast down my adversaries.” Let this voice be especially that of our martyrs. For through them the Lord’s right hand, which stretched out heaven and founded the earth, was glorified by miracles: it overthrew the temples of demons and destroyed idols. Thus it struck the enemy—not by iron but by the blood of martyrs—and in the multitude of his glory, for the praise and honor of his glorious grace, O holy Church, it cast down your adversaries. Therefore let these victors, these combatants of faith, these defenders of truth, say: “You sent forth your wrath, which devoured them like stubble.” [Col. 1021C]

**VERSE 8.** “And by the breath of your fury the waters were gathered together; the flowing wave stood still; the depths were gathered together in the midst of the sea.”

You sent forth your wrath—that is, your zeal—O Lord God. For you were zealous for the nations that did not know you, which, led astray into error, went to dumb images as they were led; and your wrath or zeal devoured the frenzied gods as fire devours stubble. Where now is adulterous Jupiter? Where is Venus the harlot? Where are the monstrosities of the other gods? Where are the horses of those who neighed under them against your martyrs—that is, the savage kings and governors who shed the martyrs’ blood for their sake? Your wrath devoured them like stubble. And “by the breath of your fury”—that is, by the threat of the future judgment—the waters were gathered together. [Col. 1021D]

According to the letter, “by the breath of your fury the waters were gathered together” means that the Lord removed them while a strong and scorching wind blew all night; and they stood as a wall on the right and on the left. This circumstance, of course, brought aid to those fleeing and fury upon those pursuing. But according to the mystery begun above, the waters are peoples. Hence: “Blessed are you who sow upon all waters” (Isa. 32:20). Again: “The Lord thundered over many waters” (Ps. 28:3). These waters could perceive or hear the breath of the Lord’s fury—that is, the threat of the coming judgment—because they are rational, and in fear of him they were gathered together. Where were they gathered? “In the midst of the sea.” For only at last, after a threefold repetition through the trope called periphrasis, that is, circumlocution, which is customarily used for the adornment of a subject, did he specify it: “The waters were gathered; the flowing wave stood still; the depths were gathered in the midst of the sea.” [Col. 1022A]

For by the name “waters,” as has already been said, he signifies the people; by the expression “flowing wave” or “depths,” he signifies the shifting and deep misery of peoples, as is said elsewhere of this persecutor: “He shall swallow up a river and not marvel” (Job 40:18). But this river, or flowing wave, stood still. It stood when the waters—that is, many peoples—were gathered together, so that through faith they might be united to the standing and eternal God. Scripture also says elsewhere: “The heart of man is perverse and inscrutable; who shall know it?” (Jer. 17:9). Therefore the depths too were gathered in the midst of the sea when perverse human beings flowed from the hidden darknesses and the depths of vices to the one universal baptism of Christ. “Middle” is rightly said of what is common, public, or universal—what we call catholic. [Col. 1022B]

It is beneficial to the gathering of the waters that they be gathered to the middle. For what is partial is not authentic. That belongs to heretics, who seek corners, in which stolen waters are sweeter.

**VERSE 9.** “The enemy said: I shall pursue and overtake; I shall divide the spoils; my soul shall be filled.” This was said by the enemy, that is, the devil, who is called “the enemy” antonomastically—that is, as if by his proper name. What wonder if he said this, being confident that the Jordan flows into his mouth? He who said falsely, “I shall ascend into heaven” (Isa. 14:13), desiring to be like the Most High, had his hope frustrated. What wonder, I say, if, now excluded from the hearts of those reborn in Christ, he speaks and talks thus—he who, cast down from heaven with his angels, still opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped? “I shall pursue,” he says, “and overtake.” Let him pursue as much as he is permitted. For of those who have entered the sea he shall seize no one except some pretender or hypocrite, in whom he has confidence enough to say: “I shall divide the spoils, and my soul shall be filled.”

He says: “I will draw my sword; my hand shall kill them.” To draw the sword is to stir up open persecution, just as, conversely, to bend the bow is to wish to deceive secretly. Expressing both modes of persecution, the Psalmist says: “Sinners have drawn the sword; they have bent their bow.” [Col. 1023A] “Therefore,” he says, “I will draw my sword”: that is, having been excluded from their hearts, I shall employ the manifest tyranny of cruel kings, emperors, and pagans; and, since I cannot reach the soul, my hand—my power, by divine permission—shall kill them bodily. But, the Lord says to blessed Job, “He who made him will apply his sword” (Job 40:14); that is, he will be permitted to rage or kill, not as much as he wishes, but as much as is useful. Therefore let the victorious people of God, hastening toward the inheritance promised by God, not fear. For this enemy, while he persecutes and kills, advances their purpose all the more, so that they, as pilgrims, may reach their homeland more quickly. Thus he is proved foolish, because while he attempts to act for himself against God or against God’s people, he acts rather against himself [Col. 1023B] and helps God’s purpose to be fulfilled. Thus it is said of him to blessed Job: “Will you put a ring in his nostrils?” (ibid., 21). By this saying his extreme folly is indicated. And shortly afterward: “Will he make a covenant with you, and will you take him as an everlasting servant?” (ibid., 23)—with the implied sense: so that he may cooperate with me, whom he opposes by his own will, as though he had sworn obedience and were striving to show himself a most faithful servant. It follows:

**VERSE 10.** “Your spirit blew, and the sea covered them; they sank like lead in mighty waters.”

The catholic faith firmly maintains this: for us who have entered the sea of Christ, the Spirit of the Lord breathes upon us—[Col. 1023C] the Spirit of grace and remission—who, according to the Prophet, removes all our iniquities and casts all our sins into the depths of the sea. Here lies the Devil’s downfall. For what our Head first accomplished in himself at the time of his death—“blotting out,” as the Apostle says, “the handwritten record of the decree which stood against us and was contrary to us; and he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross; and, stripping principalities and powers, he openly displayed them with confidence, triumphing over them” (Col. 2:14–15)—what, I say, the Head then accomplished in himself, he accomplishes here, that is, in baptism, in his members, where there is the likeness of that same death, to which we are planted together, as the same Apostle says. Rightly, therefore, and truly you may say and sing, whoever you are who have come up from this sea reborn in Christ: “The sea covered them; they sank like lead in mighty waters,” fulfilling the truth of the prophecy which says: “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, great dragon, who lie in the midst of your rivers and say, ‘The river is mine, and I made myself.’ I will put a bridle in your jaws and will fasten the fish of your rivers to your scales; I will draw you out from the midst of your rivers, and all your fish shall cling to your scales; and I will cast you out into the wilderness, you and all the fish of your river” (Ezek. 29:3–5). [Col. 1023D] Notice that above he compared them to a stone, on account of the weight of sin; here he compares them to lead, on account of the punishment or recompense of sin, according to the prophet Zechariah, in whom a talent of lead is placed upon the mouth of Wickedness. Again, praises; again, thanksgivings.

**VERSE 11.** “Who is like you among the mighty, O Lord? Who is like you, magnificent in holiness, terrible and praiseworthy, working wonders?”

This is opposed to what Pharaoh said: “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14). It was not enough to proclaim in him strength by saying, “Who is like you among the mighty, O Lord?” unless holiness too were proclaimed by adding, “Who is like you, magnificent in holiness?” For strength and holiness differ here in the same way as judgment and mercy elsewhere. Strength is that of judgment against proud persecutors; holiness, that of mercy toward devout fugitives. In accordance with these two, he adds the terms of praise: “Terrible and praiseworthy.” Terrible, [Col. 1024A] namely, through the strength of judgment; praiseworthy through the holiness of mercy. In respect of both, he adds, “working wonders.” What wonders?

**VERSE 12.** “You stretched out your hand, and the earth devoured them.”

This is the wonder of strength whereby you, Lord, are terrible. “The earth devoured them”: the earth, I say, which according to blessed Job is “a dark land, covered with the gloom of death, a land of misery and darkness, where there is the shadow of death and no order, but everlasting horror dwells” (Job 10:21).

**VERSE 13.** “In your mercy you were a guide to your people whom you redeemed; and in your strength you bore him to your holy dwelling-place.”

This is the wonder of your holiness or mercy. In this respect, O Lord, you are praiseworthy: terrible and praiseworthy, you have wrought such diverse wonders. “And you bore him,” he says, “in your strength,” and so forth. He uses the past tense for the future, saying “you bore” in place of “you will bear,” knowing with complete certainty that he would complete what he had begun, or because no one could frustrate his purpose. But what is God’s holy dwelling-place? Is it the land of sinners, the land of the Canaanites? There was indeed a holy dwelling-place there: the holy city Jerusalem, or the Temple and the Holy of Holies. But these were holy not for their own sake, but because they were representations of heavenly holy things. Therefore he called God’s holy dwelling-place not so much that earthly place as the land of the living, of which it was a shadow—the place to which he foresaw that all the people of the saints would be borne through the glorious magnificence of God their leader [Col. 1024D] in the strength of God, which is none other than the Son of God.

**VERSES 14–15.** “The peoples rose up and were angry,” etc. How could he know, so as to speak as if of the past about what lay in the future: “Then the princes of Edom were troubled; trembling seized the mighty men of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan were frozen with fear”? For concerning his words, “Pangs seized the inhabitants of Philistia,” perhaps this answer may be given: the land of Philistia was nearby, and before they entered the sea they had to beware of attempting to pass through it, as has already been said above, because their pain—that is, their envy—had already become known when Israel departed from Egypt. But when they said to Edom, “We beg you, let us pass through your land,” Edom had not yet replied, “You shall not pass through me; otherwise I shall meet you armed”; nor had the king of Moab said, “This people will destroy all who dwell within our borders, just as an ox is accustomed to crop grass down to its roots” (Exod. 20:17–22). [Col. 1025A] Whence, then, except from the prophetic Spirit, had he learned to sing these things?

Moreover, spiritually, Edom—that is, “earthly” or “bloodstained”—and Moab, which means “from the father,” namely the Devil; Canaan also, which means “commotion”; and Philistia, meaning “those who fall through drink”: by both their names and their deeds they signified and prefigured all those who, after Christ the victor had been crowned, while the heavens proclaimed his glory and the sound of his Apostles went forth into all the earth, undertook, as it were, the defense of the Devil’s defeated cause and, inflamed by his spirit, rose up and became angry against all who believe in Christ.

**VERSE 16.** “Let dread and fear fall upon them through the greatness of your arm.” Dread concerns future things; fear, present things. He justly calls this down upon those who are tormented by God’s glory—namely, all enemies of the faith or of the Lord’s name, visible and invisible alike. “Let them become immovable,” he says, “like a stone,” so that they may be unable to harm those who are moving and running well toward God, until your people, O Lord, pass over—understood of the people who have here no abiding city, but seek the one to come—until this your people, whom you have acquired, pass over. The repetition of the passing-over people is indeed, in the literal sense, an ornament of speech or song; but in the mystery it is more fitting, if you wish, to understand after the former people of the Hebrews also the subsequent people of the Gentiles, whom Christ the leader acquired, having bought them with his own blood, the Father saying: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Ps. 2:8). [Col. 1025C]

**VERSE 17.** “You will bring them in and plant them upon the mountain of your inheritance, in your most firm dwelling-place, which you have made, O Lord.”

This is spoken according to the image of a vineyard, which the Psalmist also applies to the Lord in song: “You transplanted a vine out of Egypt; you drove out nations and planted it,” etc. (Ps. 79:9). “Upon the mountain,” he says, “of your inheritance.” That land which God gave to that people is indeed mountainous; but incomparably higher is the land which may rightly be called the mountain of the Lord’s inheritance, especially since he immediately adds: “Your most firm dwelling-place, which you have made, O Lord; your sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands established.” Therefore the mountain in which it is a great thing for God’s people to be planted—the mountain rightly called the Lord’s most firm dwelling-place, made by him, the Lord’s sanctuary, established by his own hands—is that Lebanon of which the prophet says that the apostate planting was cast out, in these words: “Behold Assyria, like a cedar in Lebanon, beautiful in its branches and thick in foliage, lofty in stature, and its top was raised among dense boughs.” And shortly afterward: “No tree in God’s paradise was like it in beauty; for I made it beautiful,” etc. “To whom are you like, O glorious and lofty one among the trees of delight? Behold, you have been brought down with the trees of delight to the lowest land; you shall sleep among the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword. This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, says the Lord” (Ezek. 31:3 ff.). [Col. 1026A] Upon this mountain he first planted the thief—which is wonderful—by saying: “Amen, I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

**VERSE 18.** “The Lord shall reign for ever and beyond.”

This is the most brilliant and resonant ending of a most beautiful song. For what follows—

**VERSE 19.** “For Pharaoh entered,” and the rest—returns to the beginning and concludes the whole as though in a brief epilogue. “The Lord shall reign for ever.” Everyone who knows the Lord is certain of this: the Lord shall reign for ever. But who can grasp what is meant by “for ever”? The meaning of this expression is too vast. Our sight cannot measure its length and breadth or height. Hearing this expression, perhaps we lift up our heads; but we do not see the whole extent of eternity. Therefore he added “and beyond,” as though to say: As far into the distance as you are able to see, the Lord shall reign—and beyond what you can see; beyond what the very expression “for ever” conveys to your mind or understanding. As though you were to ask, “How do you know that the Lord shall reign?” he gives this reason: [Col. 1026B] “For Pharaoh entered,” etc. Does it follow, then, that unless he had entered the sea, and unless the Lord had brought the waters back over him, the Lord would not reign? Certainly he would reign everywhere by power; but he would not reign by that possession of human beings concerning which the Prophet sighs: “Lords have possessed us apart from you.” Unless, I say, that spiritual Pharaoh had been overthrown, the Lord would not reign over us; that is, the ruler of this world would not have been cast out, Christ the Son of God would not possess us, and the Savior of the world would not reign in us.

**VERSE 20.** “Then Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and dances,” while she led them in song, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord,” etc.

The order of the narrative is beautiful: first Moses with the men, then Miriam with the women, sings one and the same song. Understanding this order spiritually, let us at least, as women among women, because we are weak souls, sing with the same faith. For we acknowledge that the Apostles and apostolic men—who came up armed from Egypt and are strong for battle—are men; and in comparison with them we are as women, and are entirely unable to stand in the same choir or sound in the same tone. It should be noted that Scripture here calls Miriam a prophetess, because, as has been foretold and partly expounded, the words of this song contain prophecy of future things, though they seem to speak only of things present [Col. 1027A] or past. She is rightly said to have taken a timbrel, because this musical instrument is skin stretched over wood and signifies the mortification of the flesh, without which no soul can show itself a worthy singer. “And all the women,” he says, “went out after her.” The word *woman* (*mulier*) is derived from softness (*mollities*). Yet a faithful soul must emerge a little from its own softness, so that it may imitate men and sing worthily to God. For one must depart from Egypt and cross the sea, in order that you, fleeing the invisible Pharaoh, may sing the first song. Yet you are still far from the Song of Songs, just as one who enters the holy place needs much in order to enter the Holy of Holies. [Col. 1028A]

[Col. 1027]

## EXPOSITION OF THE SONG OF HABAKKUK, CHAPTER III

[Col. 1027B] **VERSES 1–2.** “O Lord, I have heard your report and was afraid. O Lord, revive your work in the midst of the years. In the midst of the years you shall make it known; when you are angry, you shall remember mercy.”

What report of the Lord, and what kind of report, did this man hear and fear? Surely that which he himself afterward declares: “God,” he says, “will come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran; horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden,” etc. Truly, to hear such a report and to fear or tremble is the mark of a faithful and wise mind. For how great a thing it is that God and Lord of all, coming into this world—the supreme Majesty, feared and adored by all the powers of heaven—should, having assumed flesh, hang with his hands fastened to the arms of the cross; and that the fault of rebellious servants should have been the reason why so great a Lord suffered this and was treated so shamefully! Whoever among those servants hears this report—that is, perceives or understands it (for to hear the report means to perceive with the ear of the heart that which the bodily ear has heard)—whoever, I say, among those servants has heard and considered this, how could he fail to fear, how could he fail to tremble? Suppose he said in astonishment: “Alas! What will become of us wicked servants, for whose crime so great and such a Lord had to be treated so shamefully?”

I know someone—God is my witness—who in a vision, lifting his eyes upward, thought that he beheld the height of the supreme and unbounded greatness, and in a wondrous [Col. 1027D] and ineffable manner felt the power of that divine might. As though in the midst of that very height, magnitude, and immensity, he saw standing the exceedingly exalted and ineffably most high Son of Man, who was crucified for us. And while the sight of him oppressed him with a weight great indeed, yet sweeter than words can tell, the thought I mentioned came to his mind: “Alas! What will become of us wicked servants, for whose crime so great and such a Lord had to be treated so shamefully?” Immediately another thought, as though sent down from above by the Son of Man himself, responded most sweetly to this thought: “Nor would I now be so great a Lord unless, for the sake of servants, I had been treated so shamefully; and that which was the cause of my passion is also the cause of my glory and honor.” [Col. 1028B]

Whatever the nature of these things may be, I would rightly say this: this work is so great and so incomprehensible that whoever has been worthy to hear its report should rightly fear and pray for his ignorances. For no one ought to be ignorant of this matter; yet there is no one who does not have *ignorance*—that is, failure to consider it—because no one can consider or estimate it fully. Yet fear of this kind is not servile or penal fear, but the holy fear which endures for ever and ever, which charity does not cast out but brings within: the fear in which angels praise the majesty of the eternal God, dominions adore it, and powers tremble. This is sufficiently clear from the matter itself. For where he said, “I have heard your report and was afraid,” it is not desirable to understand, “lest that which I heard would happen should come to pass,” since he immediately says: “O Lord, revive your work in the midst of the years.” He desired and prayed that the very thing which he feared on hearing that it would occur might happen more quickly. Therefore this is good fear, holy fear, of which the Psalmist elsewhere says: “I shall worship toward your holy temple in your fear” (Ps. 137:2).

“O Lord,” he says, “revive your work in the midst of the years.” In a wonderful manner this man is not fearful but reverently fearful, both praying and prophesying. For what is “in the midst of the years”? What are these years, in whose midst he prays that what he fears, having heard it foretold, may occur? We gladly understand these years as the years of human life, which the Psalmist, having calculated them, declares: “The days of our years are seventy years” (Ps. 89:10). Some stronger and more durable persons have indeed exceeded this number; but “if they are eighty years in the strong, their abundance is labor and sorrow” (ibid.). Therefore the years of human life are seventy. Now it was to come about that in the midst of this number of years the Lord would revive his work: his work that had been put to death—his work, namely the human race. Heaven, earth, sea, and all things in them are indeed the Lord’s works. But man is a special work of the Lord, a work of the Lord’s hands. For of the rest, “God spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 32:9). But in order to make man, he took clay, fashioned it, and made a work of his hands. Hence Isaiah says: “And now, O Lord, you are our Father; we are clay, and you are the potter, and all of us are the works of your hands” (Isa. 64:8). [Col. 1029A] And holy Job says: “Your hands made me and fashioned me wholly round about” (Job 10:18). Therefore, although the Lord made the other things, man is nevertheless a particular work of the Lord’s hands, which the Devil through the serpent put to death by the death of the soul, followed, by God’s just sentence, by the death of the body. This work, so put to death, was to be revived in the midst of the seventy years, the years of human life. And so it came to pass. For when the Lord himself had become man, a little short of the middle of seventy years—being thirty-three years old—by dying and rising again he revived his work, the human race: by dying he destroyed the death of our souls; by rising again he restored the life of our bodies. Thus, in a wonderful manner, he feared who in that very fear prophetically prayed that what he feared might happen more quickly, and by praying prophesied what was to be done more quickly.

Again he says: “In the midst of the years you shall make it known.” What will you make known in the other middle of the years? For we have said that in the midst of the years of human life you revived your work, that is, you raised up your Temple, the Temple of your body not made by hands, which Jewish impiety had destroyed; and with it you restored the life of the human race. What will you make known in the other half [Col. 1029C] of the years, except this very fact—that you have truly revived the work already mentioned? For when seventy years have been completed since you built that work of yours, that Temple of yours, from the body of your virgin mother, then what you accomplished will be made known by the coming of the Romans and their fulfillment of your truth in the destruction of the Temple made by hands—the Temple concerning which you endured slander from those who said: “This man said, ‘I can destroy the Temple of God and rebuild it after three days’” (Matt. 26:61). Again: “Ha! You who destroy the Temple of God and rebuild it in three days!” (Matt. 27:40). For not one stone shall remain upon another which will not be destroyed. Wonderful and fearsome is the swiftness of your work, O Lord, because in the middle of our years—the seventy years which are the years of our life—you will revive it, as has already been said; and in the other middle of those same years, with the Apostles preaching, you will so make known what you have done that the rivalry of the Jewish Temple, the Temple made by hands, cannot conceal or obscure the glory of that work of yours, because it will have been destroyed. Great wrath, great affliction, will then come upon this people. But what then?

“When you are angry, you shall remember mercy.” We shall not be like Sodom, nor become like Gomorrah; rather, a remnant from among us shall be saved. Isaiah also says: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we would have been like Sodom and would have resembled Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:9). The meaning is: Unless the Lord had ordained that a remnant should be saved from among us and that all Israel should be saved when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, our entire nation would have been consumed without a remnant, just as all the Sodomites were consumed by fire and sulfur, except Lot, who was not one of them. [Col. 1030A]

That which among the Seventy Interpreters is read thus, “You shall be known in the midst of two living creatures,” should not be passed over, especially because it is customary in the assembly or congregation of the Church. Blessed Jerome says that the simple interpretation and common opinion understands it of the Savior: that he was recognized crucified between two thieves. Others, however, give a better explanation: they say that in the first Church, which was gathered from circumcision and uncircumcision, the Savior was understood and believed, with the two peoples surrounding him on either side. Some understand the two living creatures as the two Testaments, New and Old, which are truly living and life-giving, breathe, and in whose midst the Lord is known. It follows:

**VERSE 3.** “God will come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran.”

Up to this point he had continually cried out in wonder. Now he begins to speak more fully of the matter itself, at whose magnitude, overwhelmed, he had prefaced an exclamation: “God,” he says, “will come, and the Holy One will come.” From where will he come? From the south and from Mount Paran. We gladly understand, in these words of the prophet, what we know or believe, and therefore speak, concerning Christ the Son of God: that he came forth from God and came into this world having become man through the operation of the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit, as in many places in Scripture, so also here, is rightly understood through the south, a warm wind opposite the cold north, by which the evil spirit opposed to the Holy Spirit is customarily signified. But the person of God the Father himself is signified by Mount Paran—or, according to the Seventy Interpreters, by the shadowy and thick mountain—because his judgments are incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable, and because the height of the riches of his wisdom and knowledge is immeasurable. This, as we said above, is indicated by the title itself: “The prayer of Habakkuk the prophet for ignorances.” [Col. 1030C]

Moreover, God and the Holy One is Christ himself, the Son of God: truly God and holy man, not conceived in iniquities, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found. “He,” therefore, says the prophet, “will come from the south”; that is, the Holy Spirit will bring it about that he comes. For because of his great love God the Father will send him; and what is the love of the Father who sends and of the Son who is sent, other than the Holy Spirit? Therefore he will come from the Holy Spirit; that is, as we have already said, the Holy Spirit will effect his coming, and it will be the operation of the Holy Spirit that an incorrupt virgin conceives him and bears true God and true man.

According to these three persons of the one true and supreme Godhead, the prophetic song is divided by three divisions. The sign of these divisions is the word which in Hebrew is *selah* and which Greek translators rendered *diapsalma*. It should be known that this word occurs only in the Psalter and in the present passage. Blessed Jerome says: “I think it is a mark of some musical sound, or at least an indication of the enduring force of the things previously spoken.” Wherever *selah*—that is, *diapsalma* or “always”—is added, we should know that what is said pertains not only to the present time but also to eternity, or to the things which have preceded. [Col. 1031A]

The first division begins at this verse: “His glory covered the heavens”; the second: “You will cleave the rivers of the earth”; the third: “You cursed his scepters.” The first division concerns God the Son of God, of whom he had said: “God will come from the south”; for, he says, “horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden,” etc.

In the second division it is clear that he speaks to another person. For he says: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ.” That person is rightly understood as the Holy Spirit, whom we understand to be signified by the south, and who gave visible signs of his presence as he went forth with his Christ for the salvation of his people, as will be explained more fully in its proper place.

In the third division there is another person to whom he speaks: “You cursed his scepters”; afterward he says, “But I will rejoice in the Lord, and exult in God my Jesus.” We gladly understand the person to whom, while speaking, he makes this confession concerning his Lord Jesus to be the Father. Let us now follow the sequence itself.

“His glory covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise.” He speaks these and the following words as one full of fear and inwardly overwhelmed by that report which he prefaced: “O Lord,” he said, “I have heard your report and was afraid.” He had said: “God will come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran,” or from the shadowy and thick mountain. Now, as though you were to ask what kind of God or how great a God, and how holy this Holy One is: “His glory,” he says, “covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise.” When he says, “His glory covered the heavens,” what else does he wish to indicate than that he is as shadowy and thick as the mountain itself—that is, the Father himself—from whom this same God came? Indeed, he testifies that he is exceedingly shadowy and thick, exceedingly incomprehensible, when he says, “His glory covered the heavens”; which is the same as saying: [Col. 1031D] His divinity is incomprehensible even to the heavens, that is, to all angelic spirits. So great, so glorious is this God. If you ask how holy he is: “The earth,” he says, “is full of his praise.” Distinguish well between God’s glory and God’s praise. He is glorious because he is God; he is praiseworthy because he is holy. And just as, as has been said, the glory of his divinity covered the heavens, so the earth is full of the praise of his holiness, the praise of his holy humanity. Neither can the heavens, that is, the angels, fully behold the glory of his divine brightness, nor can people on earth praise worthily enough the holiness and humility of his humanity. The great and exalted God has no end; God made man, holy and good, exceeds estimation. Why then if his glory covered the heavens? How will he be known, if he is shadowy and thick? He says:

**VERSE 4.** “His brightness shall be like light.”

As though he said: He is not so shadowy and thick that he cannot be seen, nor so incomprehensible that he cannot be known. For he will shine, and his brightness will be like light; that is, it will adequately enlighten creation. He indeed dwells in inaccessible light, but he knows how to emit a brightness that can be endured. Creation cannot approach or penetrate the depth of light itself, but light itself can advance toward creation in a brightness adapted to it. His glory shone even upon the heavens which it covered, and it shone upon the earth, where, having become man, he lay hidden among human beings. His brightness is the effect of his wondrous works. He did wonders in heaven and on earth; and as often as he wrought a wonder, so often he sent forth brightness. This brightness of his is like light, and will be like light, because it sufficiently enlightens and will enlighten his angelic and human creation for knowing himself. [Col. 1032B]

What, finally, is more shadowy or thick than what follows: “Horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden”? By “horns” he means the standards and trophies of the cross, upon whose arms his hands had been fastened. For “though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:7). Therefore on the cross his strength was hidden for a little while, when he said to the Father: “My soul is sorrowful unto death”; “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:38–39); and upon the cross itself: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). What could be more shadowy, more thick? For, as the Apostle says, “We preach Jesus Christ crucified: a stumbling-block to Jews, and folly to Gentiles” (1 Cor. 1:23).

But how, or for what purpose, was his strength hidden there? Surely as a hook is hidden in flesh in order that a fish may be caught, so the iron barb of divinity lay hidden, as it were, veiled by humanity, in order that the Devil might be caught. For this is what the Lord says to blessed Job concerning Behemoth or Leviathan: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook?” (Job 40:20). The implied answer is: I can. Therefore, when he says, “Horns are in his hands,” he does not wish us to attend merely to the fact that his hands were fastened to the horns, or arms, of the gibbet. Otherwise he would have said more properly, “His hands are on the horns,” just as we do not usually say, “the cross is in Christ,” but “Christ is fixed upon the cross.” Rather, he wishes us to consider that because of the fastening whereby he was fastened to the cross or lifted up on the cross, all power and all dominion—which are customarily figured by a horn—were given into his hands, or hand, as he himself foretold: “If I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32); and as he afterward said: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18). [Col. 1033A] The prophet himself immediately announces what would result from the fact that his strength was hidden there. For he says:

**VERSE 5.** “Death shall go before his face, and the Devil shall go forth before his feet.”

What is this except as though he said: By that hook Leviathan shall be caught? For as a fish caught on a hook comes out of river or sea before the feet of the one catching and drawing the hook, so, he says, the Devil shall go forth before his feet: that is, he shall come into his power, and the ruler of this world shall be cast out. He says two things: “Death shall go before his face, and the Devil shall go forth before his feet.” These are the things we believe and confess, and in believing hope: before his presence death flees, for he rose again and gave us the glory of resurrection; and he caused the Devil, author of sin and death, to go forth at the preaching of his Gospel, and to be trampled underfoot before his feet—that is, before his preachers. It follows:

**VERSE 7.** “He stood and measured the earth; he looked and dissolved the nations; the everlasting mountains were crushed; the hills of the world were bowed down by his eternal ways.”

He who died on the cross, where his strength was hidden, rose from the dead and stood, surely with strength no longer hidden or needing to be hidden, but henceforth manifest—understood as standing at the right hand of God’s power—to overthrow the remnants of sin and wage war against the enemies of his Gospel. For Stephen the first martyr says: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power” (Acts 7:55). And Isaiah had long before declared: “The Lord stands to judge, and he stands to judge the peoples” (Isa. 3:13). Therefore the Lord stood, strong and mighty, mighty in battle, having the conquered Devil beneath his feet.

“And he measured the earth.” How did he measure it, except as judge of the living and the dead? Surely what was written beforehand concerning David—that “he struck the Philistines and struck Moab, and measured them with a cord, making them lie upon the ground. He measured two cords: one for killing and one for keeping alive” (2 Sam. 8:2)—must reverently be understood of this mighty-handed one: that he measured the earth and measured two cords, one cord of mercy and one cord of judgment—the cord of mercy for giving life, the cord of judgment for killing. Thus, in measuring the earth, he looked upon the nations, had mercy upon the nations, and measured over the nations the cord of mercy for giving life. But he measured over the Jews the cord of judgment for killing, so that, blinded, they might fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations. [Col. 1033D]

The saying “He dissolved the nations,” and the following words, “The everlasting mountains were crushed, and the hills of the world bowed down,” beautifully suggest what we say about his look of mercy by which he looked upon the nations. For what does “he dissolved” mean except that they were softened unto repentance? Conversely, the ungodly person is said to harden his heart. And what does it mean that “the everlasting mountains were crushed and the hills of the world bowed down,” except that the greater rulers of the world—understood by the mountains—and the lesser, signified by the hills, were grieved unto repentance? “The earth was shaken and trembled,” says the Psalmist, “and the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because he was angry with them” (Ps. 76:19). Good is the crushing that comes from his eternal ways. For this is the contrite and humbled heart which God does not despise. All this was, or is, the measuring of one cord: the cord of mercy for giving life. But what immediately follows:

### Verse 7

“For iniquity I saw the tents of Ethiopia; the skins of the land of Midian shall be troubled”: this is the measuring of the other line, the line of judgment unto death. For the discourse here concerns that Ethiopian who will not change his skin, and that Midian which always and obstinately [Col. 1034B] declines judgment, in accordance with the very meaning of the name Midian. For Midian is interpreted “declining judgment,” and signifies those who do not believe that judgment is to come.

Therefore he who looked upon and dissolved the nations with a look of mercy, himself looked upon them for iniquity—that is, he judged as iniquity every unbeliever, every soul of a man who is unbelieving and works evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek. Indeed, the tent of Ethiopia is every soul of a Jew doing evil, rather than the tent of Lebanon—that is, the Temple itself, in whose brightness or religious observance he used to glory and say: “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord it is.”

Yet it may truly be said that, from the time when darkness came about noon at the crucifixion of the Savior, and that presage [Col. 1034C] was fulfilled in Israel, their eyes were darkened, and both the Temple itself and all the sacred things of the Jews became tents of Ethiopia. For as Ethiopians have been darkened by the heat of the bright sun close at hand, so the Jews, in a wondrous way, through their envy at the Savior’s presence, were made dark, and their eyes were darkened through hatred of the light. Therefore, “for iniquity I saw the tents of Ethiopia”: that is, he judged and condemned as true and consummate iniquity all the festivals formerly fit for his own dwelling, or the ceremonies of the Jewish religion.

Then, he says, “the skins of the land of Midian shall be troubled.” Both this prophet and the other prophet, namely Isaiah, who, having said, “For thou hast overcome the yoke of his burden, and the rod of [Col. 1034D] his shoulder, and the sceptre of his oppressor,” immediately added, “as in the day of Midian” (Isa. 9:4), direct us to that place in the history where Gideon, leader of Israel, wondrously troubled the camp of Midian.

All Midian, Amalek, and the peoples of the east had assembled together. Gideon sought a sign in the fleece, wishing to know whether the Lord would save his people by his hand, as he had spoken. He divided into three companies the three hundred men whom he had retained with himself out of all Israel, and gave them trumpets in their hands, empty jars, and lamps within the jars. When, following their leader’s command and example, they sounded in three places around the camp, and shattered the jars, they held the lamps in their left hands and the sounding [Col. 1035A] trumpets in their right, and cried: “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon!” Thus the entire camp was thrown into confusion; and as they fled, they slew one another.

According to the likeness of that event, he says, “the skins of the land of Midian shall be troubled”: that is, all the sacred rites or secrets of the Gentiles who decline judgment, who do not believe judgment will come. The holy Fathers have discussed more fully elsewhere how Gideon prefigured Christ according to the interpretation of his name—for Gideon is interpreted “surrounding the womb”; how his three hundred men signified Christ’s martyrs, striving and dying for faith in the Holy Trinity; and how the breaking of the jars signified the deaths of fragile bodies, while the flash of the lamps signified the grace of miracles which shone forth after the slaughter of the martyrs, by which all the frenzied rites of the Gentiles were overcome and confounded. Since these matters are found in their proper places, we do not write them out here, avoiding weariness for the reader.

Therefore, he says, “the skins of the land of Midian shall be troubled”: that is, the vanities and false madnesses of those who, contrary to the preaching of the Gospel, will not believe judgment is to come, shall be overcome and destroyed through the marvelous and unheard-of battles of martyrs, who give their bodies over to torments and conquer by dying.

It follows:

### Verse 8

“Art thou angry with the rivers, O Lord? Or is thy fury against the rivers, or thy indignation against the sea?”
