Other prophets too could sometimes ask, and did ask, questions of this kind—except that this prophet asks with greater amazement. [Col. 1035C] For example, when Daniel saw in a vision that the four winds of heaven were warring upon the great sea, that four great beasts, differing from one another, arose from the sea, and then that thrones were set up, the Ancient of Days sat down, and that great beast was slain by his judgment, while the power of the other beasts was taken away, Daniel himself might have wondered and asked in the same way: “Art thou angry with lions, O Lord? Or is thy fury against leopards and bears, and thy indignation against the winds and the sea? Is there such concern for thee in these things that thou shouldst sit in judgment because of them?” And since reason itself would answer, “No,” it followed that through those images certain other and greater matters were signified. Wishing to know these, he said: “I approached [Col. 1035D] one of those who stood by, and sought from him the truth concerning all these things” (Dan. 7:16).

In the same way Zechariah asks about many things and says: “What are these, my Lord?” But this man, more greatly astonished and stirred by deeper wonder—for he saw and heard with a prophetic ear or eye things from which he might fear, as he had stated earlier: “O Lord, I have heard thy report and was afraid”—asks and says: “Art thou angry with the rivers, O Lord? Or is thy fury against the rivers, or thy indignation against the sea?” And without doubt the answer was: “No.” For inanimate elements have deserved no wrath; and, as Daniel and Zechariah were told when they asked, so this man too was told what the things he saw were or signified.

Yet no such mystery was expounded to anyone in such a way that he was permitted [Col. 1036A] to write it plainly for understanding; rather, he was commanded: “But thou, shut up the words and seal the book until the appointed time” (Dan. 12:4). What this prophet saw when he said, “Art thou angry with the rivers, O Lord?” and what follows, is expressed a little more openly when he says: “The waters saw thee, and the mountains were in pain; the torrent of waters passed by; the deep gave forth its voice,” and so forth.

Therefore, just as in the sayings of the Law, “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain,” when we hear the Apostle say, “Is God concerned for oxen?” (1 Cor. 9:9), we know to answer: “No; rather, the spiritual Law says this concerning preachers.” So also in these prophetic visions, while he says, “Art thou angry with the rivers, O Lord?” both the seer or prophet himself, and we who desire to possess the seer’s understanding, should know how to answer: “No.” Under the names of mountains and hills, horses and chariots, rivers and waters, shining arrows and flashing spear, and other things—about which God is no more concerned than about oxen—we should understand those realities about which God is undoubtedly concerned.

Let those rivers be understood by us as those whose voices have been heard, or could have been heard: those waters, that sea, and those rivers of which it is written in the Psalm: “The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voice. The rivers have lifted up their waves because of the voices of many waters. Wonderful are the swellings of the sea; wonderful is the Lord on high” (Ps. 92:3–4). For the rivers that lifted up their voice are the sacred dogmas of the catholic faith, the Lord saying: “He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:38).

But the other, contrary rivers, which have lifted up their waves because of the voices of many waters, are those in which the great dragon glories, as the Lord speaks through Ezekiel: “Behold, I am against thee, Pharaoh king of Egypt, great dragon, who liest in the midst of thy rivers, and sayest: The river is mine” (Ezek. 29:3). For they are restless and violent peoples who have raised their waves—the waves of persecutions and seditions—because of the voices of many waters, that is, because of the voices of Christ’s disciples possessing an abundance of heavenly graces.

That sea is the whole world—the world of the ungodly and unbelieving—whose swellings, as of a sea, were wonderful. Yet wonderful on high is the Lord, the Lord who restrained those swellings. Whatever the terms may be, both here and in what follows, we must understand those realities against which it does not conflict with reason that God, supremely wise and supremely just, should be angry or indignant.

It follows: “Thou shalt ascend upon thy horses, and thy chariots are salvation.”

### Verse 9

“Rousing, thou shalt rouse thy bow: the oaths which thou hast spoken to the tribes.”

Since he asked once, “Art thou angry with the rivers, O Lord?” and by asking opened for us the way of both question and answer, let us ask concerning these things also: “Didst thou, or wilt thou, O Lord, ascend upon four-footed horses and ride in chariots like kings and consuls? Wilt thou bend a bow and become an archer, piercing men’s shoulders, striking between lung and stomach, or causing an arrow to pass through their fleshy hearts?”

And you will answer: “No.” For indeed thou shalt ascend thy horses—but thy horses are human beings who willingly submit to the bridle of thy obedience. Thou shalt indeed ascend thy chariots—but thy chariots are the four Gospels, or the four mysteries of thy Gospel, running through the whole world: namely, thy incarnation, thy passion, thy resurrection, and thy ascension. These are undoubtedly our salvation, and without faith in them there is no salvation for us.

With these thy horses and chariots, “rousing, thou shalt rouse thy bow”: that is, preaching, thou shalt preach thy coming judgment, that thou wilt come to judge the living and the dead, just as those witnesses of thy resurrection and ascension saw thee going into heaven. For preaching that judgment is in a sense like someone drawing his bow; for as a bow strikes from afar, so the day of judgment comes from afar, so that before it strikes, it cannot be foreseen.

“Thou shalt rouse the oaths which thou hast spoken to the tribes.” What are those oaths? Thou didst speak oaths to two men, namely Abraham and David, saying to Abraham: “By myself have I sworn, because thou hast done this thing” (Gen. 22:16). And, as Scripture says concerning David: “The Lord swore truth to David” (Ps. 131:11).

Nevertheless, all thy sayings may be called oaths because of their firm and indissoluble truth. For thou art the angel of whom it is written in the Apocalypse: “And the angel whom I saw standing upon the sea lifted up his hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives for ever and ever, who created heaven and earth and the things which are in them, that there shall be time no longer,” and so forth (Rev. 10:5). Whatever thou hast spoken is as true and as firm as if thou hadst sworn by thyself or by the blessed Trinity, living for ever. For heaven and earth shall pass away, but thy words shall not pass away. Ascending upon thy horses and chariots, and rousing thy bow, thou shalt fulfill all that thou hast spoken as oaths, whose end will be to give the tribes a land truly flowing with milk and honey.

### Forever

It has already been said above that from the verse, “God shall come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran,” or “from the shadowy and thick mountain”—by which we understand the holy Trinity—this canticle is divided into three divisions; and the sign of each division is “forever,” for which the Greek has *diapsalma* and the Hebrew *selah*. Wherever it is inserted, we should understand that either what follows or what precedes does not pertain only to the present time.

Therefore, it is clear that what has already been said pertains to the person of God and of the Holy One who was to come from the south and from the shadowy and thick mountain—that is, from the Holy Spirit and God the Father. Now, with “forever” inserted, what follows is spoken to the person of the Holy Spirit. This is especially clear from the verse: “Thou hast gone forth for the salvation of thy people, for salvation with thy Christ.” He therefore says: “Thou shalt cleave the rivers of the earth.”

### Verse 10

“The waters saw thee, and the mountains were in pain; the torrent of waters passed by.”

The preceding question—“Art thou angry with the rivers, O Lord? Or is thy fury against the rivers, or thy indignation against the sea?”—forbids us to understand rivers, waters, or torrents of waters here in the ordinary sense. Therefore, “thou shalt cleave the rivers of the earth” means: Thou, good South Wind; thou, Spirit of wisdom, shalt cleave all the sages and all the eloquence of worldly philosophy; thou shalt cause the river—that is, evangelical teaching—to run unbroken, with signs following it.

Why wilt thou cleave those rivers? Certainly so that, broken and weakened by their divisions, they may have little or no power, and people wearing shoes may pass through them. [Col. 1038B] For this is what Isaiah says: “And the Lord shall lay waste the tongue of the Egyptian sea, and shall raise his hand over the river in the strength of his Spirit, and shall strike it into seven streams, so that men may pass through it wearing shoes” (Isa. 11:15).

For the tongue of the Egyptian sea is the eloquence of the sages of the world, which the Holy Spirit made foolish. Once it had been split and divided against itself, all those whose feet were shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace could pass through it more easily.

When this had been done, “the waters saw thee, and the mountains were in pain”: that is, the peoples recognized thee, and some rulers grieved with the sorrow of repentance, others with the sorrow of envy. Many peoples indeed will swell, just as waters sometimes swell; but their swelling shall come to an end. This is what he now says: “The torrent of waters passed by.”

It follows:

### Verses 10–11

“The deep gave forth its voice; the height lifted up its hands. The sun and moon stood in their dwelling-place; they shall go in the light of thy arrows, in the brightness of thy flashing spear.”

When the torrent of waters—that is, the whole force of those who slew thy people—had passed away, the deep, that is, hell, praised thee. Then also the things above, that is, the angels, clapped their hands in applause and, by a kind of gesture and dance of uplifted hands, displayed the victor. Thy sun and moon, and all the brightness which had formerly shone upon thy people but had afterward been covered over by the burden of evils and the horror of darkness, received their light and recovered their former radiance.

Thy arrows and flashing spear—that is, thy blows and thy instruction—gave light to thy people. Finally, in the light of thy arrows and in the brightness of thy spear, which rebuked them in order that it might correct them, thy people walked, fearing thee, loving thee, and holding thee in great wonder.

Immediately it follows:

### Verses 12–13

“In wrath thou shalt tread down the earth; in fury thou shalt strike the nations with amazement. Thou hast gone forth for the salvation of thy people, for salvation with thy Christ. Thou hast struck the head from the house of the ungodly; thou hast laid bare the foundation even to the neck.”

The mind, wishing to proceed and hasten onward, is drawn back again to the preceding statements. For the prophet seems to himself to have said less than he wishes. He has, indeed, said nothing at all about the tenses of the verbs, as though they were varied in these prophetic utterances by chance and without any reason.

The prophet had said in the future tense, “Thou shalt cleave the rivers of the earth,” and suddenly began to speak in the past tense: “The waters saw thee, and the mountains were in pain; the torrent of waters passed by.” Then, immediately, the future tense appears again: “They shall go in the light of thy arrows”; “in wrath thou shalt tread down the earth”; “in fury thou shalt strike the nations with amazement.” Immediately afterward he returns once more to the past tense: “Thou hast gone forth,” he says, “for the salvation of thy people, for salvation with thy Christ,” and so forth.

Does the Holy Spirit customarily vary the tenses of his words in the prophets by chance and without regard to any reason? Certainly not. The reason, although not wholly clear to us, is nevertheless sweet and delightful to perceive in some measure.

To attentive consideration it occurs that prophetic discourse more often declares in the past tense those things which were to come or be done at some definite time; whereas it announces in the future tense those things which would not cease to be done every day until the end of the age. For it would not fail that the Lord should have his preachers in the world and that he should preach the coming judgment until the end of the age; therefore he expressed this in future tenses: “Thou shalt ascend upon thy horses; rousing, thou shalt rouse thy bow.”

But that the power of his divinity should be hidden in the weakness of his passion was to occur at a certain and brief time; therefore he said in the past tense: “There his strength was hidden.” The same distinction appears more clearly where, speaking of his passion, he says in the past tense: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21:17), which had to happen once. But in the future tense he says: “I shall declare thy name to my brethren; in the midst of the Church I shall praise thee” (ibid., v. 23), which is done and shall be done until the consummation of the age.

Accordingly, it is pleasing to resume from the words, “Thou shalt cleave the rivers of the earth.”

Yet first it is somewhat relevant to the present matter to consider that going forth of which he says: “Thou hast gone forth for the salvation of thy people, for salvation with thy Christ.” “Thou hast gone forth,” he says—that is, thou, invisible God, hast given human beings visible signs of thy presence or coming. Thus thou hast gone forth with thy Christ.

Therefore the one to whom these words are spoken is a person other than Christ himself. Nor should the person of the Father be understood here, since no authority of Scripture relates that person as appearing to human beings in such a way as to furnish visible signs of his presence. The Son of God, invisible God, became visible man; and, when he thus went forth, the Holy Spirit went forth with him for the salvation of his people, giving a visible sign of his coming. For he descended upon his own Christ in bodily form like a dove, and appeared upon the disciples of his Christ as fire and sat upon each of them.

Thus he went forth for the salvation of his people with his Christ—that is, in order to save the people with Christ our Savior. In his first going forth he was seen at the waters of Jordan, where his Christ was being baptized. Fittingly, then, from the image of waters begins the work of the same Savior, in praise of him who went forth for the salvation of his people: “Thou shalt cleave the rivers of the earth; the waters saw thee,” and so forth.

The word “thou shalt cleave” is broader and signifies more than if he had said “thou shalt send forth” or “thou shalt open.” For by this one word he signifies both the desolation of evil rivers and the outpouring of good rivers. Concerning the evil or contrary rivers, the example cited above says: “The Lord shall lay waste the tongue of the Egyptian sea, and shall raise his hand over the river in the strength of his Spirit, and shall strike it into seven streams, so that men may pass through it wearing shoes” (Isa. 11:15). Concerning the good, it is said elsewhere: “Waters have been cleft in the desert, and torrents in the wilderness; the dry land has become a pool, and the thirsty land fountains of waters” (Isa. 35:6).

The evil rivers are rivers of the earth; the good rivers, however, do not belong to that earth, but, having been cleft, are given to the earth through dividing grace. Both began to take place at the Jordan waters, through that going forth in which the Holy Spirit, in the form of a dove, went forth to the Jordan waters with his Christ for the salvation of his people. From that point Jesus Christ began publicly to preach, and to cast out demons by the finger of God.

Having thus gone forth, “the waters saw thee,” he says, “and the mountains were in pain”: that is, the peoples recognized thee and the rulers were envious. For the crowds marveled, but the Pharisees said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons” (Matt. 12:24). The waters, I say, saw thee and the mountains were in pain, because the crowds came out to meet thy Christ with branches of palms, devoutly crying *Hosanna*, while the chief priests, envying him, plotted his death: “You see that we achieve nothing; behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12:19).

Of any such person it is said in the Psalm: “He conceived pain and brought forth iniquity” (Job 15:35). Both the waters and the mountains saw thee—that is, that thou wast with thy Christ and that he performed many signs, not by Beelzebub but by thee. Yet the waters saw and praised thee, whereas the mountains saw and envied.

Then “the torrent of waters passed by.” What was that torrent of waters except the deep and seditious malice of the Jews? For as we understand the crowds which saw and praised under the name of waters, and the chief priests and Pharisees under the name of mountains, so we rightly understand under the name of the torrent of waters the council which they convened and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. This is why thy same Christ long before said through the Psalmist in prayer: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even unto my soul” (Ps. 68:2).

That torrent of waters passed by—understand: over thy Christ. It passed by, I say: it came indeed, but it did not remain long upon him. It entered even unto his soul—that is, until he died. But what immediately followed? “The deep,” he says, “gave forth its voice; the height lifted up its hands; the sun and moon stood in their dwelling-place.”

[Col. 1041A] Immediately after the passing torrent of waters, the deep gave forth its voice, because as soon as he said, “It is finished” (John 19:30), and gave up the spirit, hell immediately trembled; and the people of saints who were in that deep gave forth their tearful voice, which we understand by faith as well as if we had been present there. That voice was of this kind: “Thou hast come, O Desired One, whom we awaited in darkness, that thou mightest bring forth tonight those bound from their prisons.”

After such a voice from the deep, the height also lifted up its hands: he rose from the dead. Seeing this, all the height of heaven, full of joyful wonder, applauded and exulted in dancing. Without delay, then, “the sun and moon stood in their dwelling-place.” For thy sun—that is, Christ—ascended into heaven and stood or sat at the right hand of God’s power; and his Church, lifted from hell, also stood at the right hand, as the Psalm foretold: “The queen stood at thy right hand” (Ps. 44:10).

From that point it began to happen, does happen, and shall happen until the consummation of the age, what immediately follows in altered tenses—that is, with the transition from the past tense to words in the future tense.

“They shall go in the light of thy arrows, in the brightness of thy flashing spear. In wrath thou shalt tread down the earth; in fury thou shalt strike the nations with amazement.”

For the apostles were enlightened and began by preaching to send forth words of truth. Those words are arrows—thy shining arrows, showing by their light the path of life and piercing by their sharpness the hearts of peoples unto repentance. Thus it says in the Psalm: “Thy arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath thee, in the heart of the king’s enemies” (ibid., v. 6).

The meaning is: The words of thy preaching are sharp, reaching to the soul and killing not human beings but human vices. Peoples pierced by them shall fall beneath thee in the heart of the king’s enemies—that is, in their own heart, since they had formerly been enemies of King God or of God’s kingdom—and, having been brought under thy rule, shall adore thee.

Nor will there be words of preaching alone; terrible signs will follow as well. Therefore, having said, “In the light of thy arrows,” he rightly added, “In the brightness of thy flashing spear.” The flashing spear is the power of performing signs. “In this brightness and in that light of the arrows they shall go,” he says—understand: both preachers and hearers of the Gospel.

And so it was done, is done, and shall be done until the end of the age. The light of the arrows and the brightness of the flashing spear advanced so far that the Christian faith obtained primacy over the world and exercised over the nations, in the strength of good zeal, the severity of religious discipline. Therefore he says to the Lord, the Holy Spirit, concerning arrows of this kind and such a spear: “In wrath thou shalt tread down the earth; in fury thou shalt strike the nations with amazement.” For where discipline is exercised over the conduct of people who savor earthly wisdom, there the earth is trodden down in wrath; and where those who live as Gentiles are punished according to the measure of their sin—for example, when they are handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh—there the nations are struck with amazement by righteous fury.

At last we must consider more carefully what he said in this manner: “Thou hast gone forth for the salvation of thy people, for salvation with thy Christ.” This repetition is not to be considered empty: “for the salvation of thy people, for salvation with thy Christ.” For the Spirit is one and the salvation of his people is one; but in the Gospel of Christ two goings forth of the same Spirit are read, and the work of that salvation is twofold.

The first going forth was in the form of a dove at the Jordan waters; the second was in the upper room upon the apostles, in fire and divided tongues. This has already been said above. Concerning the twofold work of salvation, we should likewise know that the first work is forgiveness of sins, and the second distribution of graces.

The first and most necessary work, forgiveness of sins, began to be accomplished from the passion of his Christ. For he, rising from the dead and standing in the midst of the disciples, breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). And we must understand: for the forgiveness of sins. For it follows: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (ibid., v. 23).

The second work of salvation, the distribution of graces, was indeed partially effected in some before Christ’s passion: some had the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge, faith and prophecy, the working of miracles, and discernment of spirits. But after his passion, on the day of Pentecost, it was performed more abundantly, with kinds of tongues additionally given, so that from then on that same salvation might become known to all nations.

This work is performed individually in each believer: first, when the person is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit; then, when confirmed through the laying on of hands and anointing with chrism. Thus, having gone forth for salvation, “thou hast struck,” he says, “the head from the house of the ungodly; thou hast laid bare the foundation even to the neck.”

### Forever

The ungodly one is the devil, and his house is the world, or everything in the world: namely, the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life. What then do we understand as the head of this house except either the devil himself, prince of this world, or original sin, which was the head and beginning of his kingdom or house? Thou hast struck this head with the blow of the stone in Christ’s passion. Thus it is rightly said that thou hast gone forth for the salvation of thy people.

Then thou hast laid bare the foundation of his house even to the neck: that is, whatever errors and vices existed in the world, thou hast left none unexamined—whether what lay hidden, as the foundation of a house lies hidden, or what stood open, as the neck of a body stands open. For by those fiery tongues, which thou didst show outwardly, those who were inwardly fervent and strong, made wise and eloquent, did not cease until they exposed how great was the folly of this world’s wisdom and how great were the sacrileges of the things called sacred in the temples of the Gentiles.

This is the third “forever,” whose meaning has already been stated once and twice. It follows:

### Verse 14

“Thou hast cursed his sceptres, the head of his warriors who come like a whirlwind to scatter me. Their exultation is like that of one who devours the poor in secret.”

Since this canticle is divided into three divisions, the sign of which division is “forever,” or *diapsalma*, now inserted for the third time; and since in the preceding portions the two persons of the Son and the Holy Spirit are clearly distinguished, it is pleasing to refer this third part of the canticle to the proper person of the Father, so that it may be a canticle or praise of the whole Trinity.

“Thou hast cursed his sceptres,” he says, and so forth. It is as though he said: It was not only on this occasion, nor for the first time on this occasion, that the ungodly one was struck, when Christ suffered; rather, he had long before been condemned, and his condemnation is threefold.

First, thou hast cursed his sceptres. Second, thou hast cursed the head of his warriors. Third, thou hast cursed all his warriors who come like a whirlwind to scatter me. Thou didst curse his sceptres when in heaven thou didst condemn his pride in wishing to hold the sceptres of heaven and divine rule, and to make himself the Most High. For he said in his heart: “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14). Thou didst curse those sceptres of his—that is, because of that presumption thou didst condemn him beyond recovery.

But thou didst curse the head of his warriors when thou saidst to the serpent by which he deceived humankind—which was the beginning of his war against the human race, and on which account the serpent himself is rightly called the head of his warriors—“Because thou hast done this, thou shalt be cursed above every animal and beast of the earth,” and so forth (Gen. 3:4). In the serpent he himself was cursed, and from it he received the designation by which he is called the ancient serpent.

Thou dost curse, even now, all his warriors who come like a whirlwind to scatter me and all like me who fear thee. The first of them was Pharaoh, king of Egypt; the last will be Antichrist. For that Pharaoh, the first after the word of promise, wished, like a whirlwind, to scatter me—that is, to take away from me the effect of the oath thou didst swear to Abraham in the promise of the blessed seed, that is, Christ. For, so that no seed might come, he ordered all male children to be killed. But who does not know what befell him and the rest?

### Verse 15

“Thou hast made a way in the sea for thy horses, in the mud of many waters.”

When he, pursuing them, dared to enter after them, he was drowned with his army in the sea; there thou didst cast him down, and he perished with his chariots and horsemen. They were the first of all those who openly persecuted thy name by persecution; all the rest, as they are or have been like them, have acquired and continue to acquire a similar condemnation.

Such warriors are justly cursed, because they exult in the very fact that they have opportunity to kill and persecute, which is to make themselves like the devil or Antichrist. This is what he says: “Their exultation is like that of one who devours the poor in secret.” For who is that one who devours the poor in secret except he who, while lying in wait to seize the poor, and seizing him as far as he can, says in his heart: “God will not require it”?

And indeed it was a great and glorious thing that the sea covered that fleshly Pharaoh, his chariots, and his army, while thou didst make a way in the same sea for thy horses—that is, thy people. But far greater and more glorious is the fact that the same water, through Christ’s sacrament, conveys those who believe in him to the eternal kingdom, covering all sins, which are the camps of the spiritual Egyptians; and that in the sea of this age, where there was the mud of many waters—that is, the excessively carnal and turbid way of life of the Gentiles—thou didst make a way for those thy horses, of whom I spoke above: “Thou shalt ascend upon thy horses, and thy chariots are salvation.”

### Verse 16

“I heard, and my belly was troubled; at the voice my lips trembled.”

This verse has the same meaning and renews the same amazement which he stated at the beginning: “O Lord,” he said, “I heard thy report and was afraid.” He has explained what he heard and feared; and now, as though returning through that part of well-ordered discourse which rhetoricians call the conclusion, he returns to the original proposition: “I heard,” he says, “and my belly was troubled; at the voice my lips trembled.”

This disturbance or trembling is desirable because it is beneficial and brings great advantage from the divine regard. For he says: “But to whom shall I look, except to the poor little one, to the contrite in spirit, and to the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

With his belly therefore troubled, and with his lips trembling at the voice which he had heard within, he desires that the same disturbance and trembling may be increased in him; and in so desiring he says: “Let rottenness enter into my bones, and let it bubble up beneath me, that I may rest in the day of tribulation, and may go up to our girded people.” I rejoice, [Col. 1044C] he says, that I have now been able to say: “My belly was troubled”—which he does not deserve to say who has no tenderness of belly, but rather hardness of heart like the hardness of a stone, whose heart God has not softened, such as Pharaoh king of Egypt is famously shown to have had in the holy Scriptures. I rejoice, I say, that, considering your works, Lord, I trembled through the Spirit of humility; but I desire that you increase in me humility of heart, so that, speaking to you, my Lord, I may recognize more and more that I am dust and ashes, and soon to become rottenness and a worm. Let that rottenness—that is, the remembrance of that decay by which I shall afterward rot—bubble up in my bones and beneath me: that is, let it humble everything within me that is of strength or good work, and let it grow more and more at the root of the heart, in the depth of conscience [Col. 1044D]. For thus it shall come about that I may rest in the day of tribulation. Knowing this, your Christ, where he said, “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart,” immediately added: “And you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI, 29). And what is that day of tribulation? We need not look far. For this present time in which we are, in which we live, is a day of tribulation. Whether you call it “day” in the singular or “days” in the plural, it is a day of tribulation; the days are evil, because they are full of adversities, full of sins. “Blessed is the man,” says the Psalmist, “whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach him out of your law, that you may give him relief from evil days” (Ps. XCIII, 13). Directing his purpose toward this relief, your Christ, in the passage mentioned, begins thus [Col. 1045A]: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28). For what else is “and I will refresh you” than “and I will give you relief from evil days”? And showing in what way: “Take,” he says, “my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart.” And finally he added: “And you shall find rest for your souls” (ibid., 29). Therefore, to admit rottenness into one’s bones and to have it bubbling up beneath oneself, on account of the awareness of the decay which you, a human being, will soon become—to be meek and humble of heart—this is already to rest, not only in the age to come but also in the present world.

But what is meant by this, that after saying, “That I may rest in the day of tribulation,” he added: “And may go up [Col. 1045B] to our girded people”? What else but that to be meek and humble of heart is truly to be girded and to go up to the girded people—the people from whom the kingdom of heaven suffers violence and is seized violently? By what other girding than the spirit of humility do you suppose Moses was girded, so that he held fast the God of all flesh, mightiest of spirits, saying, “Let me go” (Gen. IV, 54), and bent him to his own will? It must unquestionably be known that without this girding there is nowhere any strength of righteousness. However many works a person may possess, without this safeguard of righteousness he is nothing; nor is that people his girded people which, with loins girded, ate the flesh of the lamb and went up through the sea, as he had just said here: “You made a way in the sea for your horses.” Vainly [Col. 1045C] does the Synagogue trust in works, because it is impossible for those to be justified who, wishing to establish their own righteousness, are not subject to God’s righteousness. This is what he immediately says most aptly through a metaphor:

**VERSE 17.** For the fig tree shall not blossom, and there shall be no shoot on the vines. The work of the olive shall deceive, and the fields shall yield no food. The flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls.

Under this number of six he rejects all the works of the law, which permits work on six days. And he rejects them for this reason: the Jewish worker under the law does not aim to keep the Lord’s Sabbath; he lacks the faith and humility which Christ commended when he said: “You shall find rest for your souls” [Col. 1046A]. In this passage the fig tree, the vine, and likewise the olive are the Synagogue; the fields that bring forth no food are Jewish ceremonies. The flock and the herd are the lesser and greater Jews, or the people and the priests. All their works are rejected, since they lack the faith and humility of Christ, when he says: “For the fig tree shall not blossom,” etc. It is as though he said: Therefore I so earnestly desire the grace of humility, because in the works of the law there is no fountain of righteousness, no shoot of righteousness, no work of righteousness, no living nourishment whatsoever for the soul. The flock is cut off from the fold and the herd driven from the stalls in this respect: the Jew does not believe, does not wish to submit to the righteousness of God [Col. 1046B], and does not hear the voice of the Lord, or of the good shepherd. Hence he says: “But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep” (John X, 26). Likewise: “Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John VIII, 47).

**VERSES 18–19.** But I will rejoice in the Lord, and exult in God Jesus my own. The Lord God is my strength.

What he says is this: Therefore Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not attain to the law of righteousness, because it did not pursue it by faith but as though by works. But I shall believe, not as though by works, but by faith, in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. For in saying, “I will rejoice in the Lord,” he confesses the Father; in saying, “I will exult in God Jesus my own,” he confesses the Son; in saying, “The Lord God is my strength,” he confesses the Holy Spirit. “And he shall make my feet like those of hinds, and [Col. 1046C] shall lead me, victorious, upon my high places, singing in psalms.” For as the feet of hinds are swift for leaping thickets and seeking heights, so by this faith I shall be swift to attain the law of righteousness and not stumble at the stone of stumbling. And this righteousness of faith shall lead me upon my high places, that is, above the righteousness of works. God, one and victorious—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—shall lead me, I say, singing in psalms the victory of my course, attributing it not to my works but to his grace, and thereby giving eternal thanks.

[Col. 1045]

# EXPOSITION OF THE SECOND SONG OF MOSES, DEUTERONOMY, CHAPTER XXXII

[Col. 1045D] “Hear, O heavens, what I speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth,” etc. By metonymy the address is directed to the inanimate heavens and inanimate earth; and from things which have neither ears nor any faculty of perception, the rational and wise human being seems to demand attentive hearing—as if he said: Since I am a mortal man, yet know that these people, or their descendants, after my death will act wickedly and will quickly turn aside from the way which I prescribed for them: at least you heavens, who will survive, and you earth, which shall stand forever, come to hear; stand as witnesses, so that when they have acted wickedly and turned aside from the way of the Lord [Col. 1046D], you heavens, according to the curses stated above, may be bronze overhead, and you earth which they tread may be iron.

But according to the truth of the inward senses, those heavens are summoned to hear of which the same Spirit says in the Prophet: “The heavens,” he says, “declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. XVIII, 1); and that earth of which elsewhere it says: “The Lord,” he says, “will give goodness, and our land shall give its fruit” (Ps. LXXXIV, 13). Those heavens and that earth, I say, are summoned here to hear, concerning whom it also says in another prophet: “Drop down, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior” (Isa. XLV, 8) [Col. 1047A]; namely, so that they may not doubt that the speaking heavens—that is, the prophets and all preachers—will leave behind this foolish nation, in order that their sound may go forth into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world; and, according to the testimony of the present song, will invite the nations to praise God or the people of God. Thus the earth once desolate and trackless—that is, the Church—may not doubt that it shall receive the saving rain from the heights of heaven, that is, from the mouth of the apostles, by the same hearing of faith through which the beginning of this earth received it—namely, the blessed Virgin—and gave its fruit by bearing Christ, God and man.

[Col. 1047B] **VERSE 1.** Therefore hear, O heavens—that is, apostles; let the earth hear—that is, the Church to be gathered from all nations. How shall you heavens hear, and how shall the words of my mouth reach the hearing of this earth?

**VERSE 2.** Let my doctrine thicken into rain; let my utterance flow like dew, like a shower upon the earth and like drops upon the grass.

How does rain thicken? How does dew flow? It is known that, as waters below exhale a fine mist, moisture condenses in the clouds; and from the clouds, rain, having condensed, flows down to the earth. Dew, however, condensing without clouds through the coldness of night, falls from heaven to earth in the clear morning. Thus these heavens, which declared the glory of God, learned that same glory partly through the study [Col. 1047C] of sacred reading, partly through God’s revelation alone. What they learned by reading and poured back to us by speaking, they gave back as gracious clouds give rain to the grass: moisture received from below and condensed into rain. What they received through God’s revelation alone, they gathered as nocturnal dew by meditation and contemplation, and distilled it by preaching and also by writing upon the flourishing grass of our faith or hope. In both ways the perfect heaven, or the firmament made firm, ought to be a firmament—that is, an apostle or capable preacher—who does not speak from his own heart or from himself, but testifies to what he has heard and proclaims and speaks what he has learned in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, in you, O heavens who hear, let my doctrine thicken into rain [Col. 1047D], and through you let my utterance flow like dew: that is, both from the present reading of the law and from the revelation of the Holy Spirit, let the counsel of God become known to you all, and then through your mouths let my utterance flow over every herb, over all the grasses flourishing throughout the whole world.

**VERSE 3.** “For I shall invoke,” he says, “the name of the Lord.” Therefore, O heavens, show good will toward your speaker; offer a kindly ear to your singer, who asks this from the very subject at hand, because it is indeed a great thing to invoke the name of the Lord. With you I shall invoke the name of the Lord—of the Lord, I say, God, whose glory you are to declare, whose works you are to proclaim. Therefore hear me, O heavens; therefore let the earth hear the words of my mouth. Give magnificence to our God.

[Col. 1048A] **VERSE 4.** The works of God are perfect, and all his ways are judgments.

This is what I first wish you heavens to hear; these are the words of my mouth which I desire you earth to hear. When the Lord our God commands you, O heavens, not to rain upon this vineyard the rain for which he looked, expecting it to produce grapes but it produced wild grapes, expecting it to produce judgment but behold iniquity, and righteousness but behold a cry; when, I say, he commands you not to rain upon it but rather upon the desert and trackless land, do not murmur, do not resist from zeal for the nation of your flesh. Give magnificence to our God; follow and account as magnificent that which has pleased our God. For although the cause or reason may be hidden from human beings, nevertheless the works of God are perfect—perfect, I say, and beyond reproach—and all his ways are judgments [Col. 1048B]: judgments true and just, justified in themselves. For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. This way by which he migrated to the nations is mercy; this way by which he withdrew from Israel is truth. Therefore give this magnificence to our God: believe that the works of God are perfect; confess that these ways, indeed all his ways, are judgments. For what then? Because he made a covenant with Abraham, because he said, “And I will establish my covenant between me and you, and between your seed after you in their generations, as an everlasting covenant” (Gen. XVII, 7)—but has now withdrawn from this seed of his—are his works therefore not perfect, his ways therefore not judgments? Indeed, God is faithful and without any iniquity, just and upright: faithful, I say, in all his words; without any iniquity in all his judgments; just in all his ways; upright in all his works. Why then, or on what account, has he forgotten the covenant which he made with Abraham? If he is faithful, without any iniquity, just and upright, how has he disregarded the oath which he swore to the fathers? Here is the answer: they themselves—

**VERSE 5.** Sinned against him, and are not his children in their filthiness.

They sinned—that is, they themselves made the covenant void; supply: enemies, and no longer his children. They made void, I say, the covenant of him who, foreknowing this, said to me above: “Behold, you shall sleep with your fathers, and this people, rising up, shall commit fornication after foreign gods in the land into which it shall enter to dwell. There it shall forsake me and make void the covenant which I made with it” (Deut. XXXI, 16) [Col. 1048D]. They sinned in filthiness; in filthiness they made the covenant void—not only in the filthiness of the calf made by Aaron or of Baal-peor, filthinesses which had indeed long since been committed, but also in the filthiness of Baal and Astaroth and the other demons; and finally they sinned in the filthiness of Barabbas the robber, whom they asked should be released to them. They sinned, I say. For it is certain that they shall sin. Therefore, when they have thus sinned, are no longer his children in their filthiness, and for this reason the faithful God has cast them away, say that God is nevertheless faithful and without any iniquity, just and upright, although he has rejected those [Col. 1049A] with whom he made the covenant in their fathers. For they sinned against him and made that covenant void: these people are now not his children in their filthiness. Therefore, O heavens and earth, whoever hear these words of my mouth, rebuke—not God himself, who is faithful and without any iniquity, but those who sinned and are not his children—with all your utterances, all your words which are to be heard throughout the earth and to the ends of the world; and say: “A crooked and perverse generation.”

**VERSE 6.** Do you thus repay the Lord, O foolish and senseless people?

A crooked generation, I say, which is the same as if you were to say with the evangelical denunciation: “An evil and adulterous generation” (Matt. XII, 39). Therefore it is a crooked generation: though born from good parents, it is badly begotten, because it arose not from faith but from the flesh of the fathers alone. Therefore, I say, it is crooked and perverse, because it has not imitated the faith of the fathers and is far unlike the fathers in character. Do you thus repay the Lord? Do you thus, I say—that is, evil for good—repay the Lord, O foolish and senseless people? For you are foolish, knowing evil and not avoiding it; senseless, whoever you are from this people, because you do not know the good which you were able to know. You are foolish while, in reading the prophets, you contentiously distort the meaning of the prophets; senseless because you have not even read, because you were unwilling to understand in order to act rightly. Therefore, O foolish and senseless people, do you thus repay the Lord? Is he not your Father, who possessed you, made you, and created you? How great a thing it is that he himself is your Father, as he said to Pharaoh: “Israel is my firstborn son”! How great a thing it is that he possessed you, made you, created you! He possessed you as Lord, made you as a potter, created you as God. He made, I say, each person individually; he created in the common mass; he possessed you in grace. That he made and created you is common to you with the other nations; but that he possessed you is a singular benefit. As regards the proper force of the words or the distinction of meanings, “possessed” signifies great power, “made” greater power, and “created” the greatest; conversely, “created” was a great grace, “made” a greater grace, and “possessed” the greatest grace. Do you thus repay the Lord your Father, your possessor, your maker, your creator, for so many benefits?

[Col. 1049D] **VERSE 7.** Remember the days of old; consider each generation.

Namely, so that you may know that he whom you betrayed, whom you denied before Pilate, is your Father, who possessed, made, and created you; so that you may know this, remember the days of old, consider each generation. For in ancient days all things were made through him, and through every generation his mysteries were prefigured by words and deeds. But perhaps the remembrance of ancient days and consideration of each generation do not yet satisfy you. What then do you do? “Ask your father, and he shall tell you; your elders, and they shall speak to you.” Your father is God himself; your elders are the law and the prophets. Ask therefore your Father by praying; ask your elders by reading. Ask your Father God, I say [Col. 1050A], with earnest prayers whether this counsel or work, whose sound has gone out into all the earth, is from him; and he will tell you. For if he graciously heard Cornelius, a gentile, praying and giving alms for this very purpose, and wonderfully showed him through his angel what he ought to do, how much more, if you ask and desire to understand in order to do rightly, will he tell you through some revelation. Therefore, as has been said, ask God your Father by prayer; consult your elders, the prophets, by reading. He will tell you, and they will say to you, that this man whom you betrayed, whom you denied, whom you fed with gall and gave vinegar to drink, whom you fastened with nails, whose side you pierced with a spear, is your Father, who possessed you. But how did he possess you, or how did he begin to possess you? Plainly, they will tell you this also.

**VERSE 8.** When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel.

You know that when the sons of Adam journeyed from the east and, finding a plain in the land of Shinar, began to make a tower whose summit might reach to heaven, so that they might make a name for themselves, the Most High confused their language there, so that no one might hear the speech of his neighbor; and thus he divided them from that place over all lands. Then indeed the Most High divided the nations, namely into differing languages, and separated the sons of Adam—that is, imitators of Adam’s pride—over all lands. He did not destroy them, as he had formerly done, by a flood, but [Col. 1050C] set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel: that is, he decreed that the human race should endure until the number of the elect is completed, all of whom according to faith are sons of Israel.

**VERSE 9.** But the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the line of his inheritance—supply, in that division of the nations, in that separation of the sons of Adam. For when the languages had been confused, the original language remained in the house and family of Eber; hence through Abraham, who himself was called a Hebrew from Eber, this Hebrew people came forth as the Lord’s portion alone; this people of Jacob alone, I say, the line of the Lord’s inheritance, among whom alone God was known, among whom alone his name was great. Hence Balaam says: “The people shall dwell alone and shall not be counted among the nations” [Col. 1050D] (Num. XXIII, 9). But the Lord’s portion, or the line of his inheritance, does not mean that those who are of his flesh alone or all belong to the Lord; rather, that those alone or all are the Lord’s who are of his faith. In this way he possessed them, and thus he began to possess them.

**VERSE 10.** He found him in a desert land, in a place of horror and vast solitude.

He found him in a desert land: that is, he made himself known to him in the wilderness for forty years; indeed, he first made himself known in a place of horror, that is, in the dreadful bondage of Egypt, by striking the Egyptians with ten plagues; and afterward in a place of vast solitude, by raining manna and bringing water out of the rock for forty years, as has already been said. He led him round about, taught him, and guarded him like the pupil [Col. 1051A] of his eye. He led them round about, I say; for he did not lead them by the road of the land of the Philistines, which is near, but led them round by the road of the wilderness that lies beside the Red Sea. And in thus leading them round he guarded them like the pupil of his eye, taking thought lest perhaps the people might repent if they saw wars rising against them and return to Egypt. For their spirit, inclined to vice, was more tender than the pupil of an eye, so that when slightly offended it often wished to return to Egypt. Therefore he led them round and taught them not only by many experiences of good and evil, but also by the written teaching of this law.

**VERSE 11.** As an eagle stirring her young to fly, and hovering over them, spread her wings, took them up, and carried them upon her shoulders.

Thus he led them round, thus he taught them, thus he guarded them, as an eagle does her young—according, that is, to her natural disposition toward her young, not with severity devoid of affection nor with affection devoid of severe discipline. For she is said always to test those whom she has begotten, lest the deformity of a degenerate offspring tarnish the certain royal eminence of her race among all birds. It is therefore asserted that she exposes her young to the rays of the sun and suspends her little ones by her talon in mid-air. But if one, with the sun’s light reflected, keeps an undaunted sharpness of vision and retains unimpaired strength of gaze, that one is judged to have demonstrated the genuineness of its nature by the constancy of its clear sight. But if, dazzled by the sun’s rays, it turns aside its eyes, it is rejected as degenerate and unworthy of so great a parent; nor is it considered worthy of rearing when it was unworthy of being received [Col. 1051C]. Thus, by leading and teaching them, he tested and proved them as an eagle tests her young. For those who murmured, tested him, and lusted in the wilderness he struck down; but those who believed and obeyed he took up, as it were, upon the wings of grace and carried upon his shoulders.

**VERSE 12.** The Lord alone was his guide, and no foreign god was with him.

**Reproof of them.** “What have you to do,” he says, “O foolish and senseless people, with the multitude of foreign gods? Did foreign gods bring you out of Egypt, the house of bondage, or assist the Lord your God as he brought you out?” Not so. Rather, “The Lord alone was his guide,” he says, “and no foreign god was with him”: not that horned golden calf, not utterly foul Baal-peor, not Baal, nor any foreign god whatsoever [Col. 1051D].

**VERSE 13.** He set him upon a high land, that he might eat the fruits of the fields.

Him whom he found in a desert land, in a place of horror and vast solitude, he set upon a high land—that is, a mountainous land—that he might eat the fruits of the fields; that he might inhabit cities which he had not built, drink wine from vineyards which he had not planted, and possess the territories of nations and the labors of peoples. This high land, as has already elsewhere been said, is not like the land of Egypt, where, after seed is cast, waters are led for irrigation in the manner of gardens; but it is mountainous and level country, awaiting rains from heaven [Col. 1052A], which the Lord God continually visits and upon which his eyes rest from the beginning of the year until its end. Therefore he set him upon a high land, that he might eat the fruits of the fields; that he might suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone. That he might suck honey from the rock—that is, accustomed to the love of the Creator, he might finally receive the sweetness of heavenly teaching from the rock struck by the rod of the cross and passion: namely, from Christ preaching in his earthly presence with honeyed mouth; and oil from the hardest stone—that is, the Holy Spirit from the same Christ, made incorruptibly firm through the power of the resurrection.

**VERSE 14.** Butter from the herd and milk from the sheep, with the fat of lambs and rams, sons of Bashan; and goats with the marrow of wheat; and that they might drink the purest blood of the grape.

All these things in temporal and material reality that people obtained, whom the Lord their God had found in a desert land, in a place of horror and vast solitude, so that, nourished and trained by these bodily goods, they might in due time willingly receive spiritual butter, spiritual milk, and spiritual fat from the spiritual herd, from spiritual sheep and lambs, or rams, sons of Bashan—that is, of the fat ones: namely, from the deeds to be imitated or the sayings to be followed of the fathers or patriarchs, from the Scriptures of prophets and apostles, truly rich; in accordance with what each such person most truly says: “You have anointed my head with oil, and the purest blood of the grape” (Ps. XXII, 5), that he might drink—that is, the most holy blood of Christ, the Son of God [Col. 1052C]. Therefore he was set temporally upon that high [land], and obtained these temporal goods, so that he might advance to desire spiritual and eternal goods. But what followed?

**VERSE 15.** The beloved grew fat and kicked; grown fat, grown sleek, grown broad.

Beloved, yet ungrateful to the one loving him; beloved, I say, yet, abusing love itself proudly and fiercely, he grew fat in thought, grew fat in deed, grew sleek in obstinacy, and grew broad in arrogance. Such a beloved kicked: that is, he cast aside with his heel the commands of his benefactor. But this fatness is swelling, not fullness. For one who knows true fullness, true richness, however abundant he may be in butter, sheep’s milk, or the fat of lambs and rams, until he lays hold of God himself says: “But I am needy and poor; O God, help me” (Ps. LXIX, 6). But the person whose god is his belly, after filling it from the things stated above, when grown fat, sleek, and broad, appears to himself sufficient in false estimation and falsely judges that he lacks nothing. What then did this beloved one, so fattened, do? He forsook God his maker and withdrew from God his savior. God—that is, maker—is the same as the saving God, or savior. Yet “maker” has one significance, “savior” another. God is maker because he himself made man; God is savior because, having become man, he came himself to save human beings. Thus he grew fat, so as to care for neither grace. For even before he came, he forsook God [Col. 1053A] his maker; and after he came, he withdrew from God his savior. How did he forsake him? How did he withdraw from him?

**VERSE 16.** They provoked him by foreign gods, and stirred him to wrath by their abominations.

He continues with the same point: both that they provoked him by foreign gods and that they stirred him to wrath by their abominations. Yet these are different and arise from different sources. For the gods are foreign, whereas the abominations are their own—the abominations for the sake of committing which without restraint they worshiped foreign gods. For example, the calf which they made and Baal-peor, into whose rites they were initiated, were foreign gods. But that after eating and drinking they rose up to play, and that amidst sacrifices they committed fornication with the Midianites—these were their own abominations. Thus they provoked the gentle one by foreign gods and stirred him to wrath by their abominations. Likewise, in repeatedly lapsing into idolatry before he came into this world, they provoked him by foreign gods; and in blaspheming him when present, saying, “He has a demon and is mad, and by Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (John X, 20), they surely stirred him to wrath by their abominations. But by what sort of gods did they provoke him?

**VERSE 17.** They sacrificed to demons and not to God; to gods whom they did not know. New and recent ones came, whom their fathers had not worshiped.

The gods whom they worshiped are not gods, but rather demons called gods: new gods, because they had not formerly known them; recent gods, because their fathers had not worshiped them [Col. 1053C]. Now therefore, O heavens and earth, return to the opening of the reproof and say to the crooked and perverse generation: “Do you thus repay the Lord, O foolish and senseless people?”

**VERSE 18.** The God who begot you—that is, who granted to your parents, long barren, the ability and accomplishment of begetting you. For apart from his only Son, whom he begot from the womb before the morning star and whom he sent into this world through a virgin’s womb, that Father begot no one from his own substance. Therefore, he who begot you—that is, he who at last granted conception to Sarah, long barren, and, when Isaac prayed, granted to barren Rebecca her beloved Jacob, so that she might conceive and bear, from whom or through whom the stream of your descent flowed—him, your begetter, you forsook with detestable ingratitude. And you forgot the Lord your creator—supply: whom you had first known through the present teaching of the law and through the examples of those same fathers, who stored up for you the inherited knowledge of him [Col. 1053D]. Thus your sin is greater than if he had never been known to you.

**VERSE 19.** The Lord saw, and was stirred to wrath, because his sons and daughters provoked him.

He whom nothing escapes saw this with eyes that never sleep, with which he sees all things. He saw this sin of yours written with an iron pen upon an adamantine point, crying out through his prophets by the Holy Spirit, so that your sin might not be blotted out from before his face [Col. 1054A]. And he was stirred to wrath—namely by a movement of his mind. For God is neither moved nor troubled; but the truth of judgment persecutes impiety in such a way that he is felt no longer as a gracious Father but as a strict judge. And this is because his sons and daughters provoked him, which in every respect is less tolerable than if strangers, male or female, had provoked him. They provoked him, namely, in that they sinned not through ignorance or through a weakness born of need, but knowingly and deliberately; indeed, they were ingenious in devising sin and seeking out evil.

**VERSE 20.** And he said: “I will hide my face from them, and I will consider their latter end.”

“He said,” that is, he fixed a sentence—for him, to say is to do—so that heaven and earth would more easily pass away than his word. For God is not like a man that he should lie, nor like a son of man that he should change. Therefore he said—that is, he rendered this judgment: “I will hide my face from them,” that is, I will blind them so that they cannot find the way of truth. I will blind their hearts, make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them; and I shall say to them: “Hear indeed, but do not understand; see the vision, but do not know” (Isa. VI, 9). Thus, hidden from them, I shall consider their latter end: that is, I shall await the end and completion of their sin, silently observing their astonishing audacity [Col. 1054C]. For they are a perverse generation and unfaithful children. The preceding grounds of that condemnation in which I said, “I will hide my face from them,” are that they are a perverse generation, that they are unfaithful children; and the Holy Spirit likewise testifies through the prophet that they are princes of Sodom and a people of Gomorrah. Otherwise what was said above would not stand: “God is faithful and without any iniquity.” Therefore the judgment is just in this: I have given them the shield of my heart, my labor; although, like a bridegroom coming forth from my chamber, I have set my tent in the sun, nevertheless they cannot see me. Indeed, it is a scandal to them when my tent of flesh is pointed out to them and they are told: “Behold, this is our God.” But hear further, O heavens, the just order of judgment, the equitable reciprocity of the judge.

**VERSE 21.** They provoked me by that which was not God, and stirred me to anger by their vanities; and I will provoke them by that which is not a people, and by a foolish nation I will stir them to anger.

They first provoked me, not by some slight offense or human transgression, but by that which was not God—that is, by treating me as though I were not God. They first stirred me to anger by their vanities: that is, they preferred their vanities, their vain gods, to me; and finally, when they were given the choice, they did not hesitate to prefer Barabbas, the author of sedition, to me. I shall therefore repay them in kind, provoking them by that which is not a people: that is, by treating them as though they were not a people [Col. 1055A], so that they may be without king, without prince, without priest, without ephod and without teraphim; so that they may altogether not be a people, but even now be scattered among peoples and nations, and in the future be reduced to nothing with those who are not, and assigned with those who are in hell. And thus I shall stir them to anger by a foolish nation. I shall stir them to anger, I say—that is, “I will provoke them to jealousy by a non-nation; by an unwise nation I will send them into wrath” (Rom. X, 19)—so that they may see reigning in their place a nation once foolish but afterward wise, which they may envy and by whose rivalry they may be tormented.

### Verse 22

“A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn unto the deepest parts of hell.” I shall provoke them, I say, and irritate them; and the beginning of this provocation and irritation is that a fire has been kindled [Col. 1055B] in my wrath; its completion, that it shall burn unto the deepest parts of hell. For the fire now kindled is the fire of the Romans, by which the holy city became a deserted Zion, Jerusalem was made desolate, the house of their sanctification was laid waste, their glory was turned into the burning of fire, all their desirable things were reduced to ruins, they fell by the edge of the sword, and were led captive among all nations. That fire of punishment has already been kindled; but the fire of vengeance shall burn unto the deepest parts of hell. For from this temporal vengeance they proceed to everlasting torments.

Do you then ask whether God judges twice for the same thing, or whether a double tribulation shall arise? Certainly not, if in the present vengeance or tribulation you acknowledge your guilt [Col. 1055C] and put an end to sins. But because the impious will of the foolish and senseless people persists even amid punishment, he now brings upon them a day of affliction, and hereafter the fire that has been kindled shall burn unto the deepest parts of hell. This another prophet also imprecates: “Crush them with a double destruction, O Lord my God” (Jer. XVII, 18). Otherwise, there is but one blow, which begins here and is completed there, so that for those who remain uncorrected there may be one scourge: it begins temporally but is consummated in eternal punishments, so that the chastisement of present scourges may be the beginning of ensuing torments for those who altogether refuse correction.

Therefore the prophetic rule is in no way harmed or distorted, when it was said, “A double tribulation shall not arise,” or, [Col. 1055D] according to the Septuagint, “God shall not take vengeance twice for the same thing”; and here, “A fire has been kindled in my wrath,” and in the future, that is, “It shall burn unto the deepest parts of hell.”

“And it shall devour the earth with its increase, and burn the foundations of the mountains.” It shall not, as has often happened, devour only the earth’s produce, so that there is famine in the land because of the people’s sins; it shall devour the earth itself—namely, that land concerning which, while speaking deceitfully in anger, they devised plots, so that they said: “If we let him go on like this, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come and take away both our place and nation” (Jer. XI, 48). The land itself, I say, with its increase, it shall devour—that is, it shall take it away so that it is no longer their land and they lack it no less than if it had been consumed by hostile fire.

And it shall burn the foundations of the mountains: that is, it shall take away the confidence of the proud—[Col. 1056A] namely, the beautiful Temple and the renowned city. Supported by their settled condition, they think themselves to stand firmly in the hereditary God of their fathers, and they, as mountains, despise all other peoples as very low valleys. The elemental fire shall burn the Temple, I say, and the city founded upon mountains.

Moreover, the earth—that is, their flesh; the sinful earth, I say, that is, the people who are proud though they are earth and ashes—the fire shall devour with its increase, that is, with its lusts and evil works. And the foundations of the mountains—that is, the souls themselves which animate their bodies—the fire shall burn: both that already kindled, as has been said, and that which in the future burns unto the deepest parts of hell.

### Verse 23

“I will heap evils upon them, and I will expend my arrows upon them.” And the Lord says this, certainly, provoked [Col. 1056B] to wrath. He says it, I say, not only secretly and inwardly, with the prophets hearing, but also publicly, with the apostles hearing, while the Jews blaspheme—and with all nations throughout the world to hear through the Gospel. For when he had said, “Behold, I send unto you prophets, and wise men, and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city,” he immediately added: “That upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zachariah son of Barachiah, whom you slew between the Temple and the altar . . . Amen I say unto you, all these things shall come upon this generation” (Matt. XXIII, 34 [Col. 1056C] and following).

This utterance concerning the heaping up of evils was made with the apostles hearing, although he had already said this, with Moses hearing, before man came into being: “Therefore I will heap evils upon them”—that is, I will bring upon them all the righteous blood which has been shed upon the earth. And this justly, because by killing me and shedding my blood they will fill up the measure of their fathers: wicked and impious fathers who killed the righteous and shed the blood of the prophets.

“And I will expend my arrows upon them,” because, when so many evils have been heaped together, a few arrows, or a portion of my arrows, would not suffice to expiate them. Therefore I will expend—that is, I will use up all my arrows upon them: the arrows of the curse which, a little earlier, I stored in the quiver of a certain ordinance in these words: “But if you will not hear [Col. 1056D] the voice of the Lord your God, to keep and do all his commandments and ordinances which I command you this day, all these curses shall come upon you and overtake you. Cursed are you in the city; cursed in the field; cursed is your storehouse and your remainder; cursed is the fruit of your womb,” and so forth (Deut. XXVIII, 15–18).

I will expend them, I say—that is, I will use all these arrows upon them—which I have never otherwise done, although many times I have cast some portion of my arrows against them. For example, when Benhadad king of Syria, with his whole army, was besieging Samaria, there was a great famine in Samaria, and it was besieged for so long that an ass’s head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and a fourth part of a *cab* or [Col. 1057A] vessel of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver. One woman said to another: “Give your son, that we may eat him today, and tomorrow we will eat my son.” When these things occurred, I did indeed cast my arrows, but I did not expend them all. For amid these events Elisha said: “Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Tomorrow at this time a measure of fine flour shall be sold for one stater, and two measures of barley for one stater, in the gate of Samaria” (IV Kings VII, 1). And it happened accordingly. But it will not be so when I hide my face in them. But what then?

### Verses 24–25

“They shall be consumed by famine, and birds shall devour them with most bitter bite. I will send upon them the teeth of beasts, with the fury of those dragging upon the earth and of serpents. Outside the sword shall lay them waste, and within terror: the young man together with the virgin, the nursing child with the aged man” [Col. 1057B].

This, indeed, shall be the expending of my arrows upon them. They shall be consumed by famine: namely, gathered in Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover, as though compelled by some deadly power. Josephus says that there were three hundred thousand men, thirty times ten thousand. This time of vengeance was justly chosen, so that those who on the days of Passover had violated their Lord Christ, their Savior, with bloody hands and sacrilegious cries might, on those very days, be shut up as though in a single prison, and might receive the destruction of the deathly punishment which they deserved.

Whoever desires to know more fully by what ruinous famine they were consumed should read the fifth book of the histories of the aforesaid Josephus, from which he will learn their entire mournful tragedy [Col. 1057C]. Among its especially dreadful episodes was this: a certain woman named Mary, daughter of Eleazar, noble by birth and wealth, driven almost to madness or insanity by the extremity of famine, slaughtered her little son, whom she had at her breast, roasted him after placing him upon a fire, consumed one half, and kept the other half covered. Immediately, robbers rushed in, attracted by the odor of the cooked flesh—for they searched houses belonging to those starving and made mad by hunger. When this evil deed was discovered by the robbers, it at once filled the whole city with a dreadful report, as she produced what she had covered and said, “I have saved the best portion for you.”

“They shall be consumed,” he says, “by famine”—understand: and they shall not be buried; but [Col. 1057D] birds shall devour them with most bitter bite. For neither the multitude of the dead nor the weakness of the living allowed them to bury the bodies of their neighbors. At first, because the stench was intolerable, they ordered the dead to be buried at public expense. But when the multitude of the dying began to exceed every expenditure, they threw the corpses from the wall in such numbers that the trenches were filled with dead bodies and their native earth was soaked with the corruption of human flesh. Therefore birds shall devour them, namely, the unburied, with most bitter bite, because this spectacle shall be a most bitter bitterness to those who remain alive and see it.

Nor shall birds alone devour them: “I will send upon them the teeth of beasts dragging them furiously over the earth, and the teeth of serpents.”

[Col. 1058A] Alternatively: “I will send upon them the teeth of beasts, with the fury of those dragging upon the earth and of serpents.” The teeth of beasts—that is, the cruelty or weapons of the Romans—I will send upon them, with the fury of those who, without mercy, drag the survivors into captivity throughout every land; and the teeth of serpents—that is, the cruelty of evil spirits who drag them, through bodily tortures and deaths, unto the deepest parts of hell.

For that Romans, strong and fierce, are rightly understood by beasts is shown for testimony or example by this passage: when the Psalmist, lamenting the same calamity, had said, “Why hast thou broken down her hedge, so that all who pass by the way plunder her?” he immediately added, “The boar out of the forest has laid her waste, and the solitary wild beast has fed upon her” (Ps. LXXIX, 13–14), signifying by the boar and the solitary wild beast the Roman emperors Titus and Vespasian.

Therefore the teeth of beasts dragging over the earth are the weapons of the Romans who kill and drag people into captivity. For the aforesaid historian, calculating the entire number of those destroyed either by famine or by the sword, recorded eleven hundred thousand. He states that the remaining brigands, assassins, and robbers perished after the city’s destruction through mutual wounds. He says that the most choice young men, commended by bodily beauty and stature, were reserved for triumph; that the rest, above seventeen years old, were bound and assigned to labor in the Egyptian mines [Col. 1058C], or dispersed through other provinces—some to be used in gladiatorial games, others to be given to wild beasts. Those found between their seventh and tenth year were ordered to be sold into slavery throughout the provinces. Their number rose to ninety thousand.

This indeed was to be dragged over the earth by the teeth of beasts, and then for souls to be led to hell: this was to be dragged by the teeth of serpents. Hence it is significantly not said, “the teeth of beasts and serpents, dragging furiously over the earth”; but, concerning serpents, understand: teeth dragging furiously into hell.

Finally, in one short verse he comprehended the totality of all evils: “Outside the sword shall lay them waste, and within terror: the young man together with the virgin, the nursing child with the aged man.” For outside is the sword—that is, every external calamity of bodies; within is terror—that is, a terrible conscience, because they knew that the blood of Christ, as they had imprecated upon themselves, was falling back upon them and their children.

### Verse 26

“And I said: Where are they? I will cause their memory to cease from among men.” These and these things he said—the things already set forth. Then at last I said—I, to whom these future calamities, indeed all things past and future, are present: “Where are they?” That is, because sinners have failed from the earth, and the wicked, so that they are no more.

Woe to those of whom God does not know where they are, when he himself is the place of all who are and are not evil. Thus Job says: “As a cloud is consumed [Col. 1059A] and passes away, so he who descends to hell shall not rise, nor return any more to his house, nor shall his place know him any more” (Job VII, 9).

“I will cause their memory to cease from among men,” as if he said: It is not enough that I, once their place, shall know them no longer; in addition, I shall cause their memory to cease among men, so that neither before God nor among human beings may any memory of them remain for good.

### Verse 27

“But because of the wrath of their enemies I delayed, lest perhaps their foes should become proud and say: Our exalted hand, and not the Lord, has done all these things.”

Thus, as has been said, I shall expend all my arrows upon them, so that not even one curse remains. I could have done this, and they deserved that their memory should so cease from among men [Col. 1059B] that no remnant of them remained. But perhaps their enemies would become proud and say, “The Lord has not done all these things; our exalted hand has done all these things.” Therefore I delayed and did not utterly blot out all memory of them. Indeed, I also said, “Though their number be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Rom. IX, 27).

By this means their enemies do not become proud and do not say, “Our exalted hand, and not the Lord, has done all these things,” because the survivors from them, dispersed among all nations, carry books with them and the curses of the Law. Their enemies, reading these curses and recounting their causes, may know and say that the Lord has done all these things.

Moreover, their remnant is also of benefit in this respect: whatever persons among their enemies have been converted to the faith of their fathers, when they read that, once the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel will then be saved, may not become proud because blindness has happened to Israel while they themselves have been enlightened. The Apostle also checks this pride when he says: “If some of the branches have been broken off, and you, though a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became a partaker of the root and fatness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, you do not bear the root, but the root bears you,” etc. (Rom. XI, 17–18).

Such restraint of pride is plainly a concern worthy of God.
