Therefore he fittingly says, in taking precautions: “Because of the wrath of their enemies I delayed, lest perhaps their foes should become proud and say: Our exalted hand, and not the Lord [Col. 1059D], has done all these things.” Therefore it is said in the Psalm: “God showed me concerning my enemies; do not slay them, lest at any time my people forget; scatter them in thy strength” (Ps. LVIII, 12).

Now, after this dispersion, the following words of the canticle immediately indicate what the disposition of the apostles and of the wise Christian people ought to be toward the scattered remnants of the foolish and senseless people.

### Verses 28–29

“For they are a nation without counsel and without prudence. Would that they were wise, and understood, and foresaw their latter end!”

What else does the Apostle desire when, groaning, he says: “I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in my spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart; for I wished that I myself might be anathema from Christ for my brethren,” etc. (Rom. IX, 2–3)? What, I say, does he desire, what does he say, except: “Would that they were wise, and understood, and foresaw their latter end”?

Would that they were wise, namely, concerning what evils were foretold to come upon them from the Law written above, and for what causes; that they might understand that the realities and effects of present evils correspond well to past declarations; that they might foresee—understand: the evils of hell which will follow their present sufferings, since not even present distress can give understanding to their hearing.

This we desire; this we wish for them, all of us who know in right and humble faith that they are the natural branches, whereas we were naturally a wild olive, and, after those who stood naturally were broken off, we were grafted in contrary to nature. Yet until the fullness [Col. 1060B] of the Gentiles enters in, this nation is without counsel and without prudence: that is, it will not be wise, nor understand, nor foresee its latter end. Nevertheless, though wasting our words and gaining none or very few of them, we say: “Would that they were wise, and understood, and foresaw their latter end!”

### Verses 30–31

“How did one pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight?” Or rather, let us recall the very words of the curse by which this was foretold: how did the Lord hand over this nation to fall before its enemies? How did it go out against them by one way and flee by seven? Was it not because their God sold them and the Lord shut them up?

“For our God is not as their god, and our enemies are judges.” What then? Is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob their God, as they suppose? Certainly not. For they themselves are among those—and especially among them—whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shameful parts. Whatever gods they worshiped, they undoubtedly worshiped them for the sake of this greatest of their gods: that is, for the sake of their belly and their genitals, in order that they might sit down to eat and drink, and then rise up to play a shameful, dishonorable game.

Therefore their god is their belly, which gives them cause to worship many gods. And this their god sold them—this god, I say, dispersed them for the price of fornications and lusts. For in order that they might sate their god, their belly, and then pour out in lusts those things which are beneath the belly, they handed themselves over; they lost their lives; they lost their souls. Thus through the prophet they are openly called princes of Sodom and a people of Gomorrah.

The Lord shut them up when sold in this manner: first, he shut them up in blindness and madness of mind, so that they might grope at noon as a blind man customarily gropes in darkness, and, although their life hung before their eyes, they would not believe in that life itself. Then he shut them up with a hostile army, where one pursued a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight. Did they not therefore suffer these things because, as has been said, their god sold them and the avenging Lord shut them up?

“For our God is not as their god”: that is, their god is not such as our God is. We profess this so freely that we do not evade the hearing of the whole world, nor fear the judgment of any people who use reason. Our enemies themselves are judges—for example, Platonists or Pythagoreans, or whatever pagan philosophers. Although they are still our enemies and have not yet received the faith of Christ, let them be judges. Behold: let our God and his cross be set forth here before all, and their god be set there with the attendants of their belly, their Baal-peor—that is, Priapus:

> And a red stake, stretched forth from his obscene groin.

Let our enemies be judges in these matters; let our enemies judge which is more beautiful and honorable: to worship the piety of Christ crucified, or the erection and obscenity of Priapus? Tell us now, judges—our enemies indeed, but possessing knowledge for judgment—which appears more beautiful to you: to worship the cross, or adulteries? The cross, I say, unjustly fastened upon a righteous man, or fornications and debaucheries?

What our enemies would answer—indeed, what they have answered, what judgment they have rendered—the whole world has now heard. Having condemned debaucheries, they submitted devout necks to the cross; having condemned the lusts of the belly and of what is under the belly, they proclaimed the glory of Christ. But these people are not yet wise, do not yet understand. Why?

### Verses 32–33

“Their wine is of the vine of Sodom, and of the suburbs of Gomorrah.” Their eyes have therefore been darkened so that they do not see; they have therefore been blinded, so that they are not wise, do not understand, and do not foresee their latter end: because their wine is of the vine of Sodom and of the suburbs of Gomorrah—that is, because they live in the manner of Sodom.

“Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is exceedingly bitter. Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps.” By the vine understand the roots of wicked thoughts; by the grape and cluster, the wickedness of works; by the wine, the evil conversations and perverse doctrine of blasphemers. Assuredly, whoever shares in their malignant deeds shall be tortured with everlasting bitterness. Therefore he said: “Their grape is a grape of gall and their cluster is exceedingly bitter.” And whoever receives their fables or whisperings shall be made drunk with the everlasting intoxication of death. Therefore he said: “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps.”

### Verse 34

“Are not these things stored up with me and sealed in my treasures?” Namely, because no repentance has erased these things, because the baptism of Christ—by which alone sins are remitted—has not swallowed them up: therefore they remain stored with me and sealed in my treasures, to be repaid according to the weight and measure of wrath which they have stored up for themselves.

### Verse 35

“Vengeance is mine, and I will repay them in due time, when their foot shall slip.” Vengeance is mine, I say; judgment is mine; and I will repay them, namely, each according to his works, in due time, on the day of wrath: so that their foot may slip, that they may fall into everlasting reproach, be brought down into the pit of destruction, [Col. 1062A] and be cast down unto the deepest parts of hell.

You say: “This will happen in distant times.” But I say: “The day of destruction is near, and the times hasten to come.” It is near, even if a thousand years intervene. For “a thousand years in thy sight are as yesterday, which has passed” (Ps. LXXXIX, 4). But grant that a span of a thousand years—or indeed ten thousand or a hundred thousand years—is hoped to precede that day: is not the day of destruction nevertheless especially near to each individual sinner?

For our years, as the Psalmist says, shall be reckoned like a spider; the days of our years—understand: are contained—within seventy years. But if in the strong—that is, among those who are of more robust and healthy nature—there are eighty years, for some are stronger and healthier by nature than others; if, I say, among the strong there are eighty years, whatever time extends beyond those eighty years is no longer life, but rather labor and sorrow. Therefore even in this way the day of destruction is near, and the times hasten to come. For fleeting years slip away, and one day drives another onward.

Thus far the discourse has been directed against the nation without counsel and without prudence, concerning that part of them which has been blinded. Now the consoling discourse is directed to those remnants which are to be saved.

### Verse 36

“The Lord shall judge his people, and shall have mercy on his servants.” These are the two most manifest offices of the Lord’s throne: mercy and judgment, upon which the entire ground or subject of divine praise depends, as the Psalmist also says: “I will sing to thee, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. C, 1).

For there is nothing in the words and works of the faithful and just Lord which is not either mercy, judgment, or the concurrence of both, as the same Psalmist says above: “Mercy and truth have met each other” (Ps. LXXXIV, 11). Therefore the Lord shall judge his people—understand: according to the matters stated thus far, because he saw them provoking him and stirring him to wrath with their abominations. He saw, I say, and was stirred to wrath.

But he shall have mercy on his servants: that is, on the remnants whom he shall behold as being otherwise disposed.

“He shall see that their hand is weakened, and that those who were shut up have failed, and that the remnant is consumed.” He shall see, I say, that that hand is weakened and recognizes its own weakness—the hand which hitherto seemed to itself healthy and strong, so that, made mad by the force of its weakness like a frenzied person, it struck the true physician. Thus the Psalm says: “The mighty rushed upon me” (Ps. LVIII, 4).

For being weak and lacking the power of true righteousness, they gloried in works of the Law, by which no one shall be justified before God; and they stood against the Lord and against his Christ, saying: “Let us break their bonds asunder, and cast away their yoke from us” (Ps. II, 3). He shall see that such a hand, such strength, is weakened, humbled, and longing for the justification which is from faith and not from works of the Law.

And he shall see [Col. 1063A] that those who were shut up have also failed: those, I say, whom, as stated above, the Lord shut up. That is, they shall no longer have any confidence in themselves. And the remnant is consumed: the remnant, I say, those remaining from Israel, in that they recognize themselves as nothing; confessing that they have been reduced to nothing, they ask the aid of a restorer and deliverer, and shall say:

### Verses 37–39

“Where are their gods, in whom they had confidence? Of whose sacrifices they ate the fat and drank the wine of drink-offerings? Let them arise and help you, and protect you in your necessity. See that I alone am, and that there is no other God besides me.”

They are so weakened, so failed and consumed, that they say—or rather, they themselves no longer speak, because they have failed and been consumed: the Lord speaks in them; the Spirit of the Lord speaks in them: “Where are their gods, in whom they had confidence?” Understand: those whom they thought strong, who had not failed or been consumed, that is, changed by repentance. Where, I say, are their gods? Understand: they are nowhere; they are nowhere present, because they are not gods but demons.

Therefore, you remnants of Israel, see that I alone am: I, I say, alone am, as I said when speaking from the midst of the bush, “I am who am” (Exod. III, 14). I said this then and say it now, to distinguish myself from all things that are not truly or simply “are,” since they are mutable; and especially to distinguish and separate myself from all gods which are not, even though they are called gods. For though there are “many gods and many lords” so called, they are not gods or lords.

But I exist and live immutably; my Son also exists and lives immutably. For though he died through the weakness of the flesh, he lives through the power of God—that is, because he is the power of God. See this, and see that there is no other God besides me. For the Father is one person and the Son another person, yet the Father is not one God and the Son another God.

“I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal; and there is none who can deliver out of my hand.” See this also; know it to be proved by present effects. For I once killed the Gentile people—that is, I condemned it while devoted to idolatry and worshiping foreign gods besides me—and now I have made that same people alive through the Holy Spirit. Likewise, I struck my people, the Jewish people, who provoked and irritated me, with blindness; and behold, I myself healed remnants from it.

“And there is none who can deliver out of my hand”—understand: one who has fallen into my dreadful hands through the empire of pride. There is none, I say, who can deliver from my hand, as the prophet also says: “Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, should be in their midst, as I live, says the Lord, they shall deliver their own souls by their righteousness, but they shall not deliver sons or daughters” (Ezek. XIV, 14, 20). For who could even touch that hand?

### Verse 40

“I will lift up my hand to heaven, and say: [Col. 1064A] I live for ever.” Who, then, can deliver from my hand—from the hand most high, lifted so high into heaven that no one can touch it? My hand, which made all things, stretched out heaven, and founded earth and seas—even in its weakness, while clothed in flesh and seeming as though bound, it then struck the proud one, and, with that hand acting as midwife, the twisting serpent was brought forth. How much more, after I raised it into heaven and said, “I live for ever”? This is hence apparent, because my very hand, which for a time seemed dead, lives for ever, as he testifies who said: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall have no more dominion over him” (Rom. VI, 9). How much more, I say, from that point is there no one who can deliver from this hand of mine?

### Verse 41

“If I sharpen my sword like lightning and my hand takes hold of judgment, I will render vengeance to my enemies and repay those who hate me.” What is my hand, which takes hold of judgment, except the Son who said: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22)? And what is his sword except the division of good and evil persons, who, divided to the right and to the left, shall be separated beyond reconciliation?

Lightning indeed shines only briefly, but strikes irreparably. Therefore, if I sharpen my sword like lightning—that is, if I make, as will unquestionably and secretly happen, divisions between the evil and good, to the right and the left, briefly indeed but openly before all—and thus my hand takes hold of judgment, as I have already said, there shall be no one to deliver. But I will render vengeance to my enemies: namely, the unquenchable fire of Gehenna; and there I will repay a fitting recompense to those who hate me.

### Verse 42

“I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh.” My arrows are all the sentences of judgment, designated there by the number six: “For I was hungry, and you gave me nothing to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me nothing to drink; I was a stranger, and you did not receive me; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick, and you did not visit me; in prison, and you did not come to me” (Matt. XXV, 42–43).

These arrows of mine I will make drunk with blood, so that [Col. 1064D] all are expended in the effective execution of vengeance. “And my sword shall devour flesh,” not because it will annihilate the substance of flesh, but because it shall eternally punish lovers of carnal things, followers of the vices of the flesh, gluttons, gourmands, worthless fellows—both evil spirits and unclean human beings. Because their wickedness is common to both, their punishment is likewise equal, according to the words: “Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41).

For this is what follows: “From the blood of the slain, and from the captivity of the stripped head of the enemies.” I will make my arrows drunk with the blood of the slain—that is, with the condemnation of impious human beings—and from the captivity of the head of the enemies, namely, the devil, who is the head and prince of the enemies: the head, I say, stripped bare, that is, revealed. For he shall be revealed to all and cast down before the sight of all.

### Verse 43

“Praise, O nations, his people, for he will avenge the blood of his servants. And he will render vengeance upon their enemies, and will be merciful to the land of his people.”

Praise his people, O nations; rejoice, O nations, with his people; call blessed, O nations, the people whose Lord is their God, because the patience of his people or servants shall not perish. For he will avenge the blood of his servants and render vengeance upon their enemies, saying: “Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire”; and he will be merciful to the land of his people, saying: “Come, you blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

Thus today we nations praise. For this is our faith; this is our confession.

## [Letter to Eberhard]

[Col. 1065]

## Notice concerning the following letter

Gerhoh’s letter to Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, on how, according to St Hilary, the Father is greater when about to glorify the Son, but the Son, once glorified, is not lesser; although in the Athanasian Creed the Son is called equal to the Father according to divinity and lesser than the Father according to humanity. It rightly ought to be placed before his book *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*, since it supplied him with the occasion for writing that work when opponents were murmuring against it.

A copy of the letter was conveyed to us through the kindness of the distinguished Reverend Doctor Eugenius, prefect of the library at Klosterneuburg. In that library we discovered it inscribed, in a hand nearly contemporary with it, on the front board of a certain ancient codex.

Gerhoh, moreover, resolves the question proposed in section 1. He says that blessed Athanasius, who affirms the Son to be lesser than the Father, assigns that lesser status to human nature when he says, “lesser than the Father according to humanity”; whereas St Hilary, who denies that lesser status, magnifies the glory of the man glorified in God when he says: “The Son, now glorified, is not lesser.” Therefore these Catholic authorities are by no means opposed or contradictory to one another, but require readers and interpreters who distinguish completely between human nature, small by condition, and its divine glory, utterly ineffable and immeasurable, etc. All these matters he treats much more extensively and elegantly in the book printed below, *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*.

[Col. 1065]

## Letter of the Venerable Gerhoh, Provost of Reichersberg, to Eberhard, Bishop of Bamberg

How, according to St Hilary, the Father is greater when about to glorify the Son, but the Son, once glorified, is not lesser; although in the Athanasian Creed the Son is called equal to the Father according to divinity and lesser than the Father according to humanity.

(D. B. Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, part II, p. 315, from a manuscript codex of the distinguished canonry of Klosterneuburg, of the Order of Canons Regular of St Augustine in Austria, through the diligence and kindness of the most worthy, reverend, and distinguished Dr Eugenius Purcklbauer, canon and librarian of the same place.)

[Col. 1065B]

To E., venerable bishop of the Church of Bamberg, brother G. offers devoted service with continual prayers.

I. As the Apostle warns, I gladly take care to avoid foolish and undisciplined questions; and therefore I am unwilling to discuss tangled matters with undisciplined or foolish disputants. But since you showed yourselves very unlike such persons, when you conferred with me wisely and in a disciplined manner, I am pleased still to confer with you face to face or in writing concerning that little work of ours which you have seen. In it, as you say, you were troubled because Saint Hilary is introduced there as saying: “The Father who is about to glorify the Son is greater; but the Son, once glorified, is not lesser” [Col. 1066B]; whereas in the faith of Athanasius we sing concerning the Son, now glorified: “equal to the Father according to divinity; lesser than the Father according to humanity.” For it seems to you that we maintain Hilary to be contrary to, or contradictory of, Athanasius—which is not so.

For in contrary or contradictory propositions affirmation and negation cannot both be true at once, since in them the same thing is affirmed and denied of the same thing. But here it is not so, because, although the same thing is affirmed and denied, it is not affirmed and denied of the same thing. For blessed Athanasius, who affirms that the Son is lesser than the Father, assigns that lesser status to human nature, saying: “lesser than the Father according to humanity.” But Saint Hilary, who denies this lesser status, magnifies the glory of the man glorified into God [Col. 1067A], saying: “The Son, now glorified, is not lesser.”

Therefore these Catholic Fathers are in no way contrary or contradictory to one another; rather, they require readers and interpreters to distinguish between human nature, lowly by condition, and its divine glory, utterly ineffable and immeasurable. He considered the nature: “A little child is born to us.” He also proclaimed the immeasurable glory of this little child, adding: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace. He shall sit upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom, to establish it, even unto eternity” (Isa. 9:6 ff.).

“Upon the throne,” he says, “of David,” because Christ is plainly likened to his father David [Col. 1067B], who, though remaining small in bodily stature, grew in royal glory; small in size, he became great in power, so that he could defeat Goliath, far larger than himself in bodily stature but inferior in strength. This power did not come to David from human nature, but from the holy anointing which advanced his nature—not so that he might be greater in essence, for essence, as even secular philosophers affirm, does not admit of more and less in the category of substance. This belongs only to forms, whose denominative terms admit comparison, as “white,” “whiter,” “whitest.”

Therefore David, anointed king or prophet, did not grow in human essence, which is one and undifferentiated by nature in all human beings, although many differences of persons attach to it. And, not to seek examples far away: when you [Col. 1067C] were recently anointed bishop, you indeed increased in dignity and power, but not in essence. Saint Basil affirms, however, that the anointing by which Christ’s humanity was anointed above its fellows is eternal divinity. For in the book *On the Dispensation of God*, among other things, he says:

> We teach that Christ is of one composite nature, and that he is not one thing from one thing and another from another, as our human being is from soul and body, or as a body is from the four elements; rather, he is the same from both. For from divinity and humanity he anointed himself: anointing as God, but anointed as man. We confess that he is and is called the same perfect God and perfect man, existing from two natures and in two natures. And we say that “Christ” is the name of a person, significant not in one way but of two natures [Col. 1067D]. For he himself is this and that; and the anointing of humanity is divinity.

II. Since Saint Basil says this, we, thinking in agreement with him, believe and confess that the man anointed by divinity, while human nature remains in its own essence, advanced in power without measure, because he was anointed without measure. His father David, indeed, was anointed according to measure, to reign for a short time over the narrow kingdom of Judaea. Before him Aaron too had been anointed, to be high priest over one people only, the Hebrews. But this one was anointed into the eternal kingdom of all ages: King of kings, king of angels and men, whose kingdom and dominion endure without end [Col. 1068A] unto ages of ages. To him too it is said: “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4).

It is therefore not unsuitable that, with Athanasius, we proclaim the man, little in his humanity and lesser than the Father, but sharing the Father’s seat upon the throne of the kingdom and the throne of grace in royal and priestly power and glory, to be lesser than the Father according to humanity; and, with Hilary, equal to the Father according to royal or priestly dignity. For although humanity is neither diminished in its essence or nature by misery nor increased by blessedness, a human being nevertheless increases or decreases in glory according as each human person is made blessed or miserable.

Hence Saint Athanasius carefully added, when he said that the Son [Col. 1068B] was lesser than the Father, “according to humanity,” thereby signifying nature by the term “humanity,” not person. For the person of that new man, although he has in himself a human nature lesser than the Father and than his own divinity, nevertheless granted that same nature equality with the Father’s glory. He granted it, I say, and received it: he granted it in divinity and received it in humanity.

For humanity in Christ received the glory of divinity, which it otherwise did not possess—namely, while it was still undifferentiated in the mass of the human race. But once it was distinguished into a person, it always fully possessed wisdom, omnipotence, and every divine power, because that man was never a man who was not God: he was conceived and born divinely, not humanly. Thus, in the very conception he was formed by the form of divinity [Col. 1068C], made “fairer in form than the children of men,” and already perfected in the fullness of grace and truth. Therefore, since even then he was in the form of God, he did not deem equality with God a thing to be seized.

But unless that grain of wheat, falling into the earth, had died, it would have remained alone in the form of God; nor could other grains have been conformed to it or re-formed through it. Therefore, in order to bear much fruit in many grains, he emptied himself, concealing the form of God and taking the form of a servant, in which “he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:8–9) [Col. 1068D].

He possessed that glory, received at conception, before the humiliation of the Passion, but for himself alone. And so, as was said, unless the grain of wheat had fallen and died, it would have remained alone. But for us human beings and for our salvation, Christ had thus to suffer and so enter into his glory, in order to prepare the way for us—or rather, to present himself to us as the way.

III. Hence, when he prayed, saying, “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had before the world was” (John 17:1), and when the Father’s voice sounded from heaven, “I have glorified [Col. 1069A] and I shall glorify again,” he said: “This voice came not for my sake, but for yours” (John 12:28). For he was not to be glorified for his own sake by the glory of the resurrection, since he had not died for his own sake but for ours. For in dying, he died for our sin, not his own; but in living, he lives to God.

He lives, I say, to God, because he lives as God—not like the first human being, made into a living soul, but into a life-giving Spirit. Hence not divinity alone, but his flesh also is life-giving, giving life by the same power by which divinity itself gives life. For since the wisdom of God “reaches mightily from end to end, and disposes all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1), how can it be believed not to reach mightily so as to bestow the power of living and giving life upon its own flesh? [Col. 1069B]

Otherwise flesh would profit nothing unless there were a spirit to give life. And if that spirit gives life to the lower members in Christ’s body so that they live, then, if it is able to give life to Christ’s flesh, it gives life to it in such a way that it not only lives itself, but is equally able, like the spirit, to give life. For if, as Ambrose testifies in his commentary on Luke, the flesh of the elect, sown in weakness, when it rises in power must be believed to be of equal power with its spirit, how much more is the flesh of God—which, though dead through our weakness, lives in his power—rightly and devoutly believed to possess one undifferentiated glory and power with its divinity in Christ? We confess Christ as subject to the Father, not in his own person, as you say, but in his members, as Ambrose affirms [Col. 1069C]. Whoever wishes will find authorities consonant with our assertion collected in the following anthology.

IV. Hilary, in the third book *On the Holy Trinity*, on the words, “Glorify me, Father, with yourself”:

> But what is this which he now awaits as glorification with the Father? Surely that which he had with the Father before the world existed. He had, and has, the fullness of divinity; for he is the Son of God, and had begun to be the Son of man. For the Word had become flesh. He had not lost what he was, but had begun to be what he was not. He had not ceased to possess what was his own, but had received what was ours. He demands the advancement of the glory which he had received, from that glory from which he had not departed. Therefore, because the Son is the Word, and the Word [Col. 1069D] became flesh, and the Word is God, and was in the beginning with God, and was the Word before the foundation of the world, the Son, now made flesh, prayed that flesh might begin to be to the Father what the Word was: that what belonged to time might receive the glory of his timeless splendor; that the corruption of flesh, formed into the power of God and the incorruption of the Spirit, might be swallowed up.

V. The same author, in the ninth book, on this: “Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in him” (John 13:31):

> “If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and God will immediately glorify him.” I consider the first meaning of the Lord’s saying unambiguous when he says: “Now the Son of Man is glorified” [Col. 1070A]. For all glory was acquired, not for the Word, but for the flesh—that is, not for the nature of God, but for the dispensation of the man who was born. But I ask what is signified by the following words: “And God is glorified in him.” For I hear that God is glorified in him, but what this means, heretic, I do not know according to your understanding. God is glorified in him—in the Son of Man, certainly.

> And I ask whether the Son of Man is the same as the Son of God. And since the Son of Man is not one thing and the Son of God another—for the Word became flesh—and since he who is the Son of God is himself also Son of Man, I ask: who is the God glorified in this Son of Man, who is also Son of God? And because God is glorified in the Son of Man, who is also Son of God, let us see what the third clause adds: “If God is glorified [Col. 1070B] in him, God also glorified him in himself.” What mystery of the sacrament, I ask, is this? God, glorified in the glorified Son of Man, glorifies the glorified God in himself. In the Son of Man is the glory of God, and the glory of God is the glory of the Son of Man. God glorifies in himself; the man is certainly not glorified through himself. Nor, again, is God glorified in a man who receives glory, yet is not himself other than God.

> But when, the Son of Man having been glorified, God—glorifying God—glorifies in himself, I find the glory of nature, the glory of the one who glorifies, assumed into the glory of nature. For God does not glorify himself, but glorifies in himself the God glorified in the man. And what he glorifies in himself, although he does not glorify himself, he nevertheless assumes, into the glory of his own nature [Col. 1070C], the glory of the one glorified. And since God glorifies and is glorified in the man, he glorifies in himself the one whom he demonstrates to be God present in himself, when he glorifies him in himself.

VI. The same author, in the same work:

> “The Father who is about to glorify the Son is greater; the Son, glorified in the Father, is not lesser. Or how is he lesser who is in the glory of God the Father? Or is the Father not greater? Certainly the Father is greater insofar as he is Father; but the Son, insofar as he is Son, is not lesser. The Son’s birth makes the Father greater; but the nature of that birth does not permit the Son to be lesser. The Father is greater when asked to restore glory to the assumed man; the Son is not lesser when he resumes glory with the Father.”

[Col. 1070D]

VII. Likewise Pope Leo the Great, in a sermon on the Passion of the Lord:

> “Thus God united man to himself, so that nothing human is lacking to him who assumed, and nothing divine to him who was assumed.”

VIII. Likewise Pope and martyr Caius:

> “Since the one Lord Jesus Christ is of true divinity and true humanity, there is in him who is utterly one, one and the same person. Yet we understand the exaltation by which, as the Teacher of the Gentiles says, God exalted him and bestowed on him the name that excels every name, to pertain to that form which was to be enriched by so great an increase of glorification. For in the form of God the Son was equal to the Father, and there was no distinction in essence nor diversity in majesty between begetter and only-begotten. Nor had anything been diminished in the Word through the mystery of the incarnation [Col. 1071A] which might be restored to him by the Father’s gift. But the form of a servant, through which impassible divinity fulfilled the sacrament of great godliness, is human lowliness, raised into the glory of divine power.”

IX. Likewise Pope Leo, in a sermon to the people:

> “The marks of the nails and lance were preserved to heal the wounds of believers’ hearts, so that it might be held with faith not doubtful but most steadfast knowledge that the nature which had lain in the tomb would sit upon the throne of God the Father.”

X. The same author, in a sermon on the Lord’s Ascension:

> “Great and ineffable was the cause of rejoicing, when, before the sight of the holy multitude, the nature of the human race ascended above the dignity of all heavenly creatures [Col. 1071B], about to pass beyond the orders of angels and to be raised above the heights of archangels, and thereafter to have no limit of advancement in any exaltations, so that, received into the eternal Father’s fellowship of sitting, it might be joined in the throne’s glory to him whose nature it was united with in the Son.”

XI. Cyril, bishop, at the Council of Ephesus against Nestorius:

> “If anyone does not confess that Christ’s flesh is life-giving as the flesh of the very Word of God the Father, but as if it belonged to some other person besides him—one joined indeed according to dignity, or as though he had only a divine indwelling—and does not rather confess it life-giving, as I said, because it became the proper flesh of the Word of God, to whom it is possible to give life to all things: let him be anathema.”

[Col. 1071C]

XII. Likewise the same author, in the same place:

> “If anyone dares to say that the assumed man ought to be co-adored with God the Word, and co-glorified and co-called God, as though one other were added to another—for the addition of the one syllable *co-* compels this understanding—and does not rather venerate Emmanuel with one act of reverence and render one glorification, according as the Word became flesh: let him be anathema.”

XIII. Ambrose, in the fifth book of *On the Trinity*, addressed to Emperor Gratian:

> “Let us review the apostolic passage: ‘Last of all, death, the enemy, shall be destroyed. For he has subjected all things beneath his feet. But when all things have been subjected to him, then he himself also shall be subjected to him who subjected all things to him’ (1 Cor. 15:26). We see [Col. 1071D], therefore, that Scripture speaks not of him as subjected, but as yet to be subjected. For just as, if the flesh lusts against the spirit in me and the spirit against the flesh, I do not appear to be subjected; so, because the whole Church is the one body of Christ, as long as the human race is divided, we divide Christ. Therefore Christ is not yet subjected, because his members are not yet subjected. But when we shall be not many members but one spirit, then he himself also shall be subjected, so that through his subjection God may be all in all.”

XIV. Likewise, a little later:

> “Just as the Apostle said that in him, through that flesh which is the pledge of our salvation, we sit in heavenly places, though we do not sit there; so he is said to be subjected in us through his assumption of our nature. Again it is written: ‘When we were dead in sins, he made us alive together in Christ, by whose grace you have been saved, and raised us together and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus’ (Eph. 2:5). I acknowledge what is written, but not as though God permitted human beings to sit at his right hand; rather, that they sit in Christ, because he is the foundation of all and the head of the Church, in whom the common nature according to the flesh earned the prerogative of the heavenly seat. For in Christ, who is God, the flesh is honored; and in the flesh the nature of the human race, shared by all human beings [Col. 1072B], is honored.

> Therefore, just as we sit in him through the communion of bodily nature, so he, through assuming our flesh, became a curse for us—although a curse certainly cannot fall upon the blessed Son of God. So also, I say, through the obedience of all, he will be subjected in us: when the Gentile has believed; when the Jew has recognized him whom he crucified; when the Manichaean has adored him whom he did not believe had come in the flesh; when the Arian has confessed him omnipotent whom he denied; and finally when, in all, the wisdom of God, righteousness, peace, charity, and resurrection are present.

> Therefore through his works and through the various kinds of virtues Christ will be subject to the Father in us; when vices have been cast aside and sin has been struck down, one spirit of all peoples shall begin, in one mind, to cleave to God in all [Col. 1072C]. Then God shall be all and in all. Let us therefore briefly gather the conclusion of the whole resolution. Unity of power excludes the notion of an injurious subjection. The laying aside of power and the victory over death sought by the conqueror do not diminish power. Obedience effects subjection; Christ assumed obedience; obedience unto the cross; the cross unto salvation. Therefore where there is the work, there also is the author of the work.

> When, therefore, all things have been subjected to Christ through Christ’s obedience, so that at his name every knee may bow—for now, because not all believe, not all appear subject—then, when all have believed and have done God’s will, Christ will be all things and in all things [Col. 1072D]. When Christ is all things and in all things, God will be all things and in all things, because the Father always remains in the Son. This is the interpretation of devout subjection.”

XV. Likewise elsewhere:

> “But if you ask how he is subject in us, he himself has shown it, saying: ‘I was in prison, and you came to me; I was sick, and you came to me. For what you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me’ (Matt. 25:36). He is sick in the one in whom he is subject.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM LXIV

[Col. 1073]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK

(D. B. Pezius, *Anecdota*, vol. I, preface, p. LXIX.)

The following little book, in a contemporary quarto manuscript at Petershausen, bears this title: “On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man.” It is addressed to Blessed Hartmann, bishop of Brixen, to whose judgment Gerhoh entrusted several of his compositions. In it he acts especially against those who interpreted his more difficult statements, in various little works, concerning the adoration of the man in Christ as though he had affirmed that “the humanity by which man is man, and which itself is not man, is most highly glorified in the glory of God,” whereas Gerhoh meant “the humanity which is man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh.”

Accordingly, from various Fathers, in this work—certainly subtle and learned, if Gerhoh wrote any such work—he teaches that Christ the man is to be adored not only with *dulia* but also with *latria*, since “Christ, who is God by divinity and man by humanity, cannot truly be understood as man except together with the Word which became flesh,” etc. Into chapter 12 is inserted a letter of Bruno, bishop of Strasbourg, in which he extols Gerhoh’s teaching with remarkable praises. Various opponents in the dioceses of Salzburg, Passau, and Bamberg were troubling Gerhoh, especially that Folmar whose errors he refutes in chapter 13 and following.

[Col. 1073]

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM LXIV, OR BOOK ON THE CORRUPTED STATE OF THE CHURCH

(We restore this little work of venerable Gerhoh, previously published separately, to the Commentary on the Psalter published above.)

[Col. 1073]

## LITTLE WORK OF VENERABLE GERHOH, PROVOST OF REICHERSPERG, ON THE GLORY AND HONOR OF THE SON OF MAN

(Edited by D. B. Pezius, *Anecdota*, vol. I, col. 163; again published by Galland, *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, vol. XIV, col. 595, which edition we follow.)

## GERHOH’S LETTER TO HARTMANN, BISHOP OF BRIXEN

[Col. 1073A]

To Lord Hartmann, bishop of the venerable Church of Brixen, Brother G. of Reichersperg offers devoted prayers together with faithful service.

As I promised in your presence, I have examined all my principal writings with the greatest care. But, thanks be to God, I found nothing in them which, rightly understood [Col. 1074A], is contrary to the faith. Certainly, I have endeavored in the appended little work to clarify matters which might be understood ambiguously, lest through their obscurity or ambiguity they trouble anyone and offend sober readers.

But if drunken readers, intoxicated beyond measure with scholastic rather than theological wine, are offended by my writings [Col. 1075A], they must be forgiven—unless perhaps they are so obstinate that they refuse to yield to the certain and plain testimonies of the holy Fathers, with which we have shown in the appended little work that our writings agree. Accordingly, we have composed it in rustic speech, so that even simple readers may readily find here a treasure hidden in the field of rustic style: easy to find, not for those who always err in heart and have an evil eye, but for humble and kindly readers, who have the dovelike and simple eye that makes the whole body bright.

Knowing that your eye is such, after the lord archbishop—to whom I first offered this, since it was composed with reference to his person—I offer this present little work to you also [Col. 1075B], for you to read, show to your faithful people, and return to me through the bearer of this letter. I believe, moreover, that you possess not only the eyes of a silvered dove [Col. 1076A], with which, winged, you may fly in such a way as not to be caught in spiders’ webs: though subtly woven, they are yet so frail that they can hold only flies or gnats.

Such indeed are the arguments of scholastic subtlety, by which too much is derogated from the man assumed into God, while he is denied to be equally Most High with God his Father. Yet God who assumes and man who is assumed are not two Most Highs but one Most High—eternally glorious in the assumed nature, and in that assumption exalted with supreme glory and supreme power unto the highest point.

I do not doubt, dearest Father, that this is your faith. But lest you be moved by those who teach another faith, I send you in this present little work many authorities consonant with our faith. I ask you to deign to consider them [Col. 1076B], and briefly to inform me what they appear to you to signify.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 1075]

I. To you, venerable Father Eberhard, metropolitan of the Church of Salzburg [Col. 1075C], I recall that when I first began to write certain things on the Psalms, I chose you as reader and corrector of my writings, together with Otto, bishop of Freising of blessed memory, a prudent and powerfully learned man. I was ready to correct anything found in my writings by which the mind of those reading simply or maliciously might rightly be offended. And behold, I am still ready to do the same, according to the ordinance of the Law, in which the Lord speaks through Moses, saying:

> “When you offer a sacrifice baked in an oven from fine flour—namely, unleavened loaves mixed with oil, or unleavened cakes anointed with oil—and if your offering is from the pan, of fine flour mixed with oil and without leaven, you shall divide it [Col. 1075D] piece by piece and pour oil upon it. But if the sacrifice is from the griddle, it too shall be sprinkled with fine flour and oil” (Lev. 2:4–7).

II. For one who bakes the fine flour of God’s word in an oven—that is, expounds Holy Scripture in the Holy Spirit—making loaves without the leaven of all heretical perversity or vain glory, mixed, as has been said, with the oil of charity: for such a one, persecution is ever present. For either he is disparaged by those within, false brethren, or more openly attacked by those without, impious and godless people.

Therefore he says: “If your offering is from the pan, of fine flour mixed with oil and without leaven.” That is, if you have within you conflicts of words from false brethren because of your devotion to Holy Scripture—which you have handled with the oil of charity and without the leaven of falsehood—“you shall divide it piece by piece”: that is, you shall examine every saying most diligently, lest perhaps anything may justly be reproved. And “you shall pour oil upon it”: upon the fine flour already mixed with oil, and again divided piece by piece, you shall pour oil—that is, upon Holy Scripture elucidated through charity and reconsidered again individually [reading perhaps *retractatae*, “reconsidered”] against opponents, you shall add the oil of that same charity, not with the zeal of bitterness but with a more ardent zeal to gain them.

III. The word *sartago*, “pan,” is derived from the noise of its sound. For oil sounds and sputters while it fries in it. It therefore signifies the inward fire of divine zeal—that is, the inwardly resounding and clamorous envy of false brethren. The griddle, on the other hand, signifies the open malice of those outside, who also burned holy people stretched out bodily over fires beneath them while they offered to God the fine flour of truth [Col. 1076D]. There too oil is sprinkled. For when the body is roasted, charity overflows and boils up more fervently.

Therefore he says: “But if the sacrifice is from the griddle, it too shall be sprinkled with fine flour and oil.” Note that if the offering is from the pan, it is commanded to be divided piece by piece and then have oil poured upon it. But if it is from the griddle, it is commanded not to be divided piece by piece, but only to be sprinkled with oil. For against false brethren who, under the Christian name, lie in wait against truth, there is need for most careful division and the fine discrimination of subtle analysis. For, lurking maliciously beneath the same names which we use for the faith, they too strive against the faith. Hence our Lord says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7:15).

But against those who hate Christ’s name, the conflict is not so doubtful or subtle. There, as though on an open field, even the simplicity of unlearned faithful people can recognize the enemy [Col. 1077A]. For just as our Lord himself, when he was being assailed, as though in a noisy pan, by the seditious clamour of questions posed by the Jewish chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees, defended the cause of his righteousness through subtle recollection of the Scriptures; but when he stood before Pilate, he said nothing to him from the Scriptures. So too his chosen disciples, whenever they are disturbed by perverse questions from persons professing knowledge of the Scriptures, ought to answer watchfully from the Scriptures and divide their words, as it were, piece by piece. But whenever they are troubled by persons who do not receive the Scriptures or have not heard them, they should not pour out discourse about such matters.

IV. The same command of the holy Law continues: “Having offered it to the Lord, you shall hand it over into the priest’s hands; he shall pour oil over it and put incense upon it” (Lev. 2:1) [Col. 1077B]. Oil signifies charity; incense, the fragrance of a good reputation. Therefore the divine discourse commands that the priest who receives from the offerer’s hand fine flour thus examined piece by piece should endeavor to season it with the liquid of radiant charity and commend it with good testimony among those who are outside.

This was done by the high priest who pleased God in his days, Pope Eugenius. How graciously he received the fine flour received from my hand, with what clear eye of charity he regarded it, and what fragrance it had in his presence, is sufficiently shown by his letter, which reads as follows:

V. “Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son G., provost of Reichersperg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“We have graciously received the writings of your devotion, and from examining them have clearly recognized the fervor of your religious commitment. Your heart grew warm within you, and in your meditation fire will blaze forth; your speech too is greatly inflamed. Therefore, since we have learned that you burn with the zeal of charity against the most wicked novelties and also against the disturbances arising against the Church of God, we rejoice with paternal affection and commend your devotion in the Lord.

“But because it is good to begin, yet far better to bring to completion, we exhort your belovedness in the Lord [Col. 1077D] to persevere firmly in your good purpose. For we love your person with paternal charity as a learned and religious man, and wish, insofar as we can before God, to honor and support you.

“Given at Sutri, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June.”

VI. After Eugenius, however, no similar pontiff was found in the Roman Church who so graciously smiled upon my writings, poured oil upon them, and put incense upon them. For those who succeeded him did not know me as he did. Nevertheless, I sent my writings, like fine flour most carefully ground, to Pope Anastasius; but he gave no reply, and I do not judge why. Likewise, when Pope Adrian was at Benevento, treating there concerning concord between himself [Col. 1078A] and the Sicilian tyrant, a little book composed for him was presented to him, in which I assembled to a great extent the novelties of this age; and I asked him for a response, by which he might either approve or disapprove what I thought and think. I was ready to agree with him in every respect, because I never wish to dissent from the holy Roman Church in the doctrine of faith.

From Pope Calixtus of blessed memory to the aforesaid Pope Eugenius, its pontiffs knew me and held me in their favor, pleasing and dear through their favor, in such a way that their charity was to me like the liquid of oil duly poured upon my sayings and writings, while their favor was like fragrant incense. It gave forth its fragrance to me when I frequently wrote something to them, and more often to the lord cardinals. Thus very recently, at the request of Lord Henry, cardinal priest of Saints Nereus and Achilleus [Col. 1078B], I composed a little work on faith, expounding the words: “Who shall find a strong woman?” (Prov. 31:10).

VII. Although I wrote various things to the Roman pontiffs Anastasius and Adrian, I could extract no answer to my questions from them. I suppose for no other reason than that they were occupied and troubled by very many matters. Recently, however, I received the writing of Pope Alexander, promising that he wishes to hold me in favor as his predecessors did. I therefore thank him for writing to me, although I have as yet written nothing to him, hindered by the great chaos which lies between us and him. Thus those who wish to pass from here to him, or from him to us, are opposed by the great impediment [Col. 1078C] of that discord which, because sins require it, has arisen between priesthood and empire; for the life of rulers is ordered according to the merits of their subjects.

Therefore, while in our sacrifice of the pan its sound and clamour are heard, and no free way from us to the Roman pontiff lies open, you, archbishop of the Church of Salzburg, have been chosen for me in his stead out of thousands. At your urging I write these things also, so that the fine flour offered to you by me and examined piece by piece may, wherever it appears acceptable, be seasoned with the oil of your charity and defended against rivals by the incense of your fragrant testimony.

## CHAPTER ONE

How the statement in Gerhoh’s writings is to be understood: “Christ was born in heaven without a mother; on earth [Col. 1078D] without a father.” He sets forth the doctrine of the new Nestorians, who, under the leadership of their master Giselbert, divide Christ into two sons, man and God: one begotten of the Virgin, the other of God the Father. Accordingly, they say that the man, the natural Son of Man, was adopted by God as a son and is not in the Father’s glory, etc.

I. There are, however, two principal stumbling-blocks, as it is said, in my writings: namely, that “I say that the man is in the glory of God the Father,” and that “I say that this same man is the Father’s natural and only-begotten Son,” because I maintain that his conception in the Virgin was not accomplished without God the Father, who sent his mercy and his truth into the Virgin’s womb. Hence, in her, mercy and truth met one another; and truth sprang up from the earth—the truth which, eternally rising in heaven from on high, in that birth has no mother, but God alone as Father. But in the birth by which he arose from the earth of virginal flesh, no carnal father performed anything; yet that spiritual Father did act, who sent his Word to be incarnate in the Virgin’s womb. The Virgin, made pregnant by this Word, brought forth God for us: the Son of God, and at the same time her own natural son.

By this statement simple readers may be offended when they read concerning Christ that he “was born in heaven without a mother, on earth without a father.” They do not notice that, although in his heavenly and eternal generation he was wholly without a mother, yet, when he arose on earth and from the earth, he was not entirely without every father. Joseph, Mary’s husband, was his adoptive father; and God, who made the Virgin fruitful through his Word by the Holy Spirit, is his natural Father. [Col. 1079B] Therefore, when one reads, “On earth without a father,” one must understand: without a carnal father begetting carnally. For without such a father the Virgin Mother conceived him, God alone working in her, so that what was born from her might be called the Son of God.

II. Yet, in order that the same one might be shown not to have been entirely without a father or fathers on earth also—fathers from whom Christ himself was according to the flesh—he was called “the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matt. 1:1). Nor did he refuse to be called the son of David when it was said to him: “Have mercy on me, son of David” (Matt. 15:22); and likewise, “Hosanna to the son of David” (Matt. 21:9). For he recognized himself as David’s son, not only according to the flesh but also according to the promise.

For just as a man to be born from Abraham’s seed was promised to Abraham, so too a king, to be raised up from the fruit of David’s womb upon his throne, was promised to King David; God saying to him: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your seat” (Ps. 131:11). Therefore the title of the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham, is not false, since he was specially promised to those two fathers; and from them he was begotten both according to the flesh and according to the promise. Because they believed God who promised, that faith itself was reckoned to them for righteousness; and by the merit of that faith they are rightly called Christ’s fathers.

In Matthew’s genealogy three kings are found cut out, who did not have faith in him who was to come; indeed, they also persecuted the holy prophets [Col. 1079D] who spoke of him. Rightly, therefore, as has been said, they were cut out and lopped off like dry branches, where it says: “Joram begot Ozias” (Matt. 1:8), three kings being omitted—Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah. It profited them nothing that Christ descended from their flesh, because they did not believe his heralds, whom they even persecuted. Accordingly, they ought not to be named Christ’s fathers as Abraham and David are, whose son Christ is according to the faith of the promise.

III. In these foregoing stumbling-blocks, then, care seems necessary lest Christ’s little ones be scandalized. Since they are of small and meagre faith, they may easily be offended when that which is contained in the catholic faith in a veiled manner is, in some measure, disclosed and distinguished [Col. 1080A] under compulsion from those bulls which are allowed to frolic and rage among the cows of the peoples, in order to exclude those who have been tested in silver (Ps. 67:31).

For timid human hearts would not presume to search out the secrets of faith unless the gravest necessity compelled them: new heresies springing up, or, what is worse, old ones, formerly condemned, springing up anew. Thus in our days “Nestorius grows green again, dividing Christ into two sons, man and God: one begotten of the Virgin, the other begotten of God the Father. Consequently, the Nestorians of this time say that the man, the natural Son of Man, has been adopted by God as Son, and that he is not in the Father’s glory, nor does he possess the name which is above every name.”

Lest we appear ourselves to have invented this perverse teaching and falsely [Col. 1080B] imputed it to others, since we have heard several men assert this upon the authority of Master Gislebert, let us set down his own words. For, glossing the Apostle and expounding, “Wherefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name,” he says among other things (Phil. 2:9):

> “To some it seems that this name was given to the man—which is fitting on no account. For to be a son is God’s gift; to be God is this name, which is above every name not by appellation alone but by nature, and which he receives not after the Passion but rather, when he is begotten, from the Father, from whom he has all things. Therefore this was not given to the man, unless one says that it was given by adoption. But every knee is not bent to an adoptive God, nor is he in the glory of God the Father; for this belongs to one born from God. Yet the Apostle says: for this reason God gave him the name which is above every name. He says this because he received it when he was born, in order that it might be manifested after the cross: that which he received from the Father while he was begotten.”

## Chapter II

He teaches that the statement in his letter to Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg—“Humanity has been most highly glorified in the glory of God”—must be understood not of the humanity by which a man is a man, and which is not itself a man, but of the humanity which is a man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh; and that it is less correctly said that “the man in Christ was deified.”

I. Since I perceived that many were infected with the leaven [Col. 1080D] of this teaching—men whose writings I read and whose words I frequently heard—I endeavoured, against them, to erect in my writings, according to my small measure, such a tower as is described in the Song of Songs, where it is said to the Bride: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus” (Song 7:4). For just as foul and fragrant smells are distinguished by the nose, so through the spirit of discernment true things are distinguished from false in the doctrine of faith.

This is especially necessary where citizens of Damascus, fighting against citizens of Jerusalem, confuse and diminish the ancient boundaries of faith. They deny that to the man assumed into God there was given the name which is above every name; and they take away from him the glory in which, crowned, he sits at God’s right hand—equal to him according to divinity, but less according to [Col. 1081A] humanity. Because I appeared to deny this in a letter sent to the lord of Bamberg, this letter itself seems to require some explanation here.

In it, when I affirmed that “humanity has been most highly glorified in the glory of God,” a sober reader ought to have understood not the humanity by which a man is a man, which is not itself a man—as Boethius maintains in his book *On the Trinity*—but the humanity which is a man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh. For the term “humanity” is customarily understood in both senses. An example need not be sought far away: it may be observed in the Athanasian Creed itself. For when, speaking of Christ, it says, “less than the Father according to humanity,” it correctly means the humanity “by which he is a man,” not the humanity “which is a man.”

Concerning that humanity [Col. 1081B] it was sufficiently shown in the aforesaid letter that it neither diminishes through misery nor increases through glory. For Judas in hell is no less a man than Peter in heaven; nor is Peter in heaven more of a man than Judas in hell. The man of sin, the son of perdition, is neither more nor less a man than the Son of Man in heaven. Therefore, in this sense, Christ is rightly said to be less than the Father according to humanity—although that unique humanity, by which not only is man man but God is man, far surpasses every dignity of angels and holy human beings, who are merely human.

Indeed, on account of the excellence and reverence due to its dignity, set apart from the whole multitude of humans who are merely human, if we consider pure and bare humanity in all human beings, we undoubtedly find it so invariable in all that it in some fashion imitates eternity, in whose image it was made. Yet one person is found more miserable, and another more blessed, than another; among the miserable Antichrist is most miserable, while among the blessed he is accounted most blessed of whom it is written: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly” (Ps. 1:1), etc.

II. Truly above all blessed people, that blessed man—or human being—must be proclaimed who, stained neither by original nor actual blemish, was made for us a high priest, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens—not through the nature [Col. 1081D] of humanity or through grace alone. Yet no less a man is he to whom it is said: “Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?” (Ps. 51:3). For it follows: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper” (ibid., 9). And in the Gospel it was said of Christ: “Behold the man!” (John 19:5); and in the Psalm it is again said concerning Antichrist: “Behold the man.”

But the latter was cast away by God like Saul; the former, however, was assumed into God and anointed better than David. Thus the man subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh, assumed into God, and the God who assumes him are not two, but one: “Hence Athanasius: one altogether, not by conversion of divinity into flesh, but by the assumption of humanity into God.” Here “not the humanity by which man [Col. 1082A] is” is rightly understood, for it was not so assumed into God that it itself is God, although it is in the God-man; rather, it is the humanity “which is a man,” subsisting from rational soul and human flesh, which was assumed into God in order to be God, while nevertheless remaining man and remaining so for eternity: “equal to the Father according to divinity and less than the Father according to humanity.”

He is less, I say, not according to the omnipotence of divinity, divinely innate to himself as God and given to himself as man in time, as he himself testifies when he says: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18). Therefore he is not less after receiving by grace what he did not possess in nature—in nature, I say, before it was assumed. For after it was assumed, that human nature itself, namely rational soul and flesh, was never without omnipotence. At the conception, when it was formed into a person and began to have the name of a perfect human being, it at the same time received the name of perfect God, so as to be “perfect God and perfect man.”

Although he was born a little child and given to us in a cradle, nevertheless, already magnified by the Father’s gift without measure, he was made equal in omnipotence to the Giver. Hence Hilary says in the book *On the Trinity*:

> “If, therefore, the Father is greater by the authority of the Giver, is the Son less by the confession of the gift? The Giver, then, is greater; but he to whom oneness of being is given is no longer less. If this is not given to Jesus—that he is to be confessed in the glory of God the Father—he is less than the Father. But if it is given to him to be in that glory in which the Father is, he has both, in the authority of the Giver, that the Father is greater, and in the confession of what is given, that they are one. Likewise: The Father is greater when he is asked to restore glory to the assumed man; the Son is not less when he resumes glory with the Father. Likewise: The Father who is about to glorify the Son is greater; the Son glorified in the Father is not less.”

III. From these considerations it is apparent that all power in heaven and on earth was given to the man. In that power—indeed, rather, omnipotence—there is no inequality, since God who assumes and man assumed into him are called omnipotent; for God and man are not two omnipotent beings, but one omnipotent being. And although God exalted the man in himself, the exalter and the exalted are not two Most Highs, but one [Col. 1082D] Most High; the divine nature deifying the human, so that God and man are not two gods, but one God.

In this God-man, although the deified nature and the divine nature which deifies may be understood, nevertheless the God-man, who is a human and at the same time divine person, ought not to be called “deified,” lest a bad understanding arise from this expression—namely, that Christ was a man before he received deity. On account of this understanding John of Damascus forbids the phrase “a deified man,” though he confesses him to be God.

Therefore, lest anyone be offended in the *Exposition of the First Psalm*, where I wrote “concerning the deified man,” let him either understand by “man” nature rather than person, or carefully note the correction which I immediately placed there. For, after speaking of the deified man, I at once added: “rather, made God and born into God.” I also affirmed him to be “Most High,” as the true God, Son of God. This also supports us: Gregory Nazianzen, in a certain letter of his incorporated into the Council of Ephesus, expressly affirms “God made man and man deified.” This deification is nothing other than the advancement of man to the highest things, so that he may be Most High—a title which belongs to God alone. Accordingly, the man who is God, having been given the name above every name, is rightly called Most High.

## Chapter III

He shows, by the authority of Hilary, Ambrose, the Synod of Sirmium, and Jerome, that the man in Christ may rightly be called “Most High,” and that Paul does not oppose this teaching (1 Cor. 15:25–26).

I. But the opponent says: How is the man Most High when, even after all things have been subjected to him, he himself will be subject to him who subjected all things to him? For the Apostle testifies to this, saying: “But when all things shall be subjected to him, then he himself shall be subject to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:26).

This passage has been treated sufficiently fully by Saint Hilary in Book XI, by Saint Ambrose in the book *On the Faith* addressed to Emperor Gratian, and by Saint Jerome in the letter he wrote to the presbyter Amandus. It need not be expounded otherwise than they expounded it. Let whoever wishes read them, and he will find that the subjection now under discussion is glorious rather than dishonourable, especially since, as Pope Leo says, “weakness has passed into strength, dishonour into glory.”

For Saint Hilary, near the end of Book XI of *On the Trinity*, indicates that this subjection of the man to God, which is to come and to endure, is nothing other than the yielding of one nature into another: not in order that it should cease to be, but in order that it should be better, just as the human body will better be subject to its spirit in eternal life. Such subjection is the advancement of an inferior nature into the glory of a superior nature, when the flesh will no longer resist its spirit, but, perfectly subject to it, will enjoy in it and with it supreme blessedness.

II. But lest anyone suppose that the voluntary subjection by which the glorified man is subjected to God should be reckoned as a diminution of glory, let him consider that, at the Synod held at Sirmium by orthodox Fathers against Photinus, Sabellius, and Arius, subjection was proclaimed even of the divinity of the Only-begotten itself, by which the Son is read to be subject to the Father. Yet from that subjection he is not to be understood as less in his divinity or in the glory of divinity. For in that synod it is read:

> “If anyone understands ‘Lord and Lord,’ ‘Father and Son,’ so as to call the Lord from the Lord two gods, let him be anathema. For we do not so make the Son equal or compare him to the Father as not to understand him to be subject. For he did not descend into Sodom without the Father’s will; [Col. 1084A] nor does he rain from himself, but from the Lord—that is, by the authority of the Father; nor does he sit at the right hand by himself, but hears the Father saying: ‘Sit at my right hand.’”

III. Explaining this synodal statement in his book *On the Synods*, blessed Hilary says:

> “Both what precedes and what follows entirely remove whatever suspicion these statements may seem to contain: lest a diversity of unlike and distant beings be proclaimed in ‘Lord and Lord,’ and lest the Son not be compared because it would be impious to call them two gods. Since it is anathema to deny that Christ is God, it cannot on that account appear profane to name two gods, lest Christ too be proclaimed God; for, by the proper character of natural essence, God is one because the only-begotten Son of God, born from the unbegotten God the Father, who is the one God, has from no source other than God the being which is God. Nor could the essence of him who was begotten be different from that of him who begot. For ‘indifferent’ is one designation of essence and nature. And especially in this respect the Son is neither compared nor made equal to the Father: he is subject in the service of obedience; the Lord rains from the Lord; he sits at God’s right hand after it has been said to him, “Sit at my right hand”; he is sent, he receives, and in all things obeys the will of him who sent him. But subjection in piety is not diminution of essence, nor does the office of religion make the nature inferior. For, while the unbegotten Father is God and the only-begotten Son of God is God, both the Son’s subjection is taught and his dignity, since he is subjected to that very one to whom none but the Son may be subjected. Though he is of God the Father, he is nevertheless of him by nature, possessing a name not alien but belonging to the one whose Son he is; and he is subject to the Father both in service and in name—yet in such a way that the subjection of the name testifies to the property of a natural and undiffering essence.”

IV. According to these synodal statements, presented and expounded by Saint Hilary, it is quite clear that, as he himself says, “subjection in piety is not diminution of essence, nor does the office of religion make the nature inferior.” Here both the Son’s subjection is taught and his dignity, since he who is subject to the Father is called Son, not servant. Yet he is remembered as subject to the Father when the Lord rains from the Lord, when he is sent, and when in all things he obeys the will of him who sent him.

None of these things detracts from the dignity in which he, though sent, is equal to the Father who sends him. Therefore, since in the divine nature subjection does not entail indignity—where divinity itself is neither diminished nor advanced, because it is immutable in itself and cannot be reduced, increased, or magnified—so likewise in human nature, which by submitting itself to God in all things has been glorified and magnified without measure, so that dishonour has passed into glory and weakness into strength, subjection does not produce indignity or a lessening of glory. For, as we have already recalled above, according to Hilary, disputing this matter in Book XI, this subjection is nothing other than “the advancement of the inferior nature into the glory of the superior nature,” in that person who, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is wholly to be worshipped by angels and blessed human beings with an undifferentiated worship, as will be shown in what follows, God granting it. For the present, these things said according to Hilary’s understanding concerning that subjection, which he treats fully in Book XI, are sufficient.

V. Blessed Ambrose, however, in his book addressed to Emperor Gratian, assigns this subjection to Christ’s members: when they have been subjected, then he too will be found subject to God the Father, by the same truth by which he now hungers, thirsts, and is weak in those same members of his. Of them he will say: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40). For he says among other things:

> “Let us rehearse the apostolic passage. ‘Last of all,’ he says, ‘death, the enemy, shall be destroyed. For he has subjected all things under his feet. But when he says, “All things are subjected to him,” doubtless this excludes him who subjected all things to him. But when all things have been subjected to him, then he himself also shall be subject to him who subjected all things to him’ (1 Cor. 15:27). We see, therefore, that Scripture records not that he is yet subject, but that he is to be subjected. For just as, if the flesh in me lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, I do not appear to be subject, so, because the whole Church is the one body of Christ, as long as the human race is divided, we divide Christ. Christ, therefore, is not yet subject, whose members are not yet subject. But when we shall be not many members but one spirit, then he too will be subject, so that through his subjection God may be all in all.”

Likewise, shortly afterward:

> “Just as the Apostle said that in him, through that flesh which is the pledge of our salvation, we sit in the heavenly places—although we do not yet sit—so he too is said to be subject in us through his assumption of our nature.”

Likewise:

> “It is written: ‘When we were dead in sins, he made us alive together in Christ—by whose grace you have been saved—and raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus’ (Eph. 2:6). I acknowledge what is written, but not in such a way that God permits human beings to sit at his right hand; rather, that they sit in Christ, because he is the foundation of all and the head of the Church, in whom the common nature according to the flesh merited the prerogative of the heavenly seat. For in Christ, God is flesh; but in the flesh the nature of the human race is honoured, participating in the honour of all human beings. Therefore, just as we sit in him through the communion of bodily nature, so too he who, by taking our flesh, was made a curse for us—although a curse certainly cannot fall upon the blessed Son of God—so too, I say, will he be subject in us through the obedience of all: when the Gentile believes; when the Jew acknowledges the one whom he crucified; when the Manichaean worships him whom he did not believe had come in flesh; when the Arian confesses as omnipotent him whom he denied; when finally, in all, there shall be God’s wisdom, righteousness, peace, charity, and resurrection. Through his works, therefore, and the various kinds of virtues, Christ will be subject to the Father in us, when vices have been cast off and sin has ceased its assault, and one spirit of all peoples begins in one mind to cleave to God in all. Then God will be all and in all.

> “Let us therefore briefly gather the conclusion of the whole explanation. Unity of power excludes the notion of an injurious subjection. The abolition of powers and the victory won over death by the triumphant one certainly do not diminish power. Obedience produces subjection; Christ assumed obedience; obedience reached to the cross, the cross to salvation. Therefore, when all things have been subjected to Christ through Christ’s obedience, so that at his name every knee may bend, then he himself will be all in all. For now, because not all believe, not all appear to be subject. When, therefore, all have believed and have done God’s will, Christ will be all and in all. When Christ is all and in all, God will be all and in all, because the Father always remains in the Son. This is the interpretation of pious subjection.”

Likewise:

> “But if you ask how he is subject in us, he himself showed it when he said: ‘I was in prison, and you came to me; I was sick, and you visited me. What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me’ (Matt. 25:36, 40): he is weak in that in which he is subject.”

Thus far Ambrose.
