VI. Jerome proceeds midway between these two. For he both praises Hilary and repeats Ambrose’s understanding in his own words, writing thus to the presbyter Amandus:

> “The question arose from the Apostle’s epistle, where, arguing about the resurrection, he came to that place where it is written: ‘For he must reign until he has put all his enemies beneath his feet. For he has subjected all things beneath his feet. Last of all, death, the enemy, shall be destroyed. But when he says that all things are subjected to him, it is beyond doubt that this excludes him who subjected all things to him’ (1 Cor. 15:27). But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself is subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all. And I wonder that you wished to ask this of me, since Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, completed his eleventh book against the Arians with this question and its solution. Yet let us say at least a few things.

> “The whole scandal here is this: Why is the Son said to be subject to the Father? What is more shameful or lower: to be subject to the Father—which is often an act of piety, and of which it is written in the Psalm, ‘Shall not my soul be subject to God?’ (Ps. 61:2)—or to be crucified and made the curse of the cross? For ‘cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree’ (Deut. 21:23). He, then, who was made a curse for us in order to free us from the curse—do you wonder if he is subject for us in order to make us subject to the Father, saying in the Gospel: ‘No one goes to the Father except through me’ (John 14:6); and, ‘When I have been lifted up, I shall draw all things to myself’ (John 12:32)?

> “Christ is subject to the Father in those who are faithful, because all believers—indeed, the whole human race—are reckoned members of his body. But in those who are unbelieving, Jews, Gentiles, and heretics, he is called unsubdued, because a part of his members is not subjected by faith. At the end of the world, however, when all the members see Christ in those who are subject—that is, see their own body—they themselves will be subjected to Christ, that is, to their own body, so that Christ’s whole body may be subjected to Christ and the Father, that God may be all in all.

> “He does not say, ‘that the Father may be all in all,’ but ‘that God may be all in all’; this is the proper name of the Trinity and may be referred to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit alike, so that humanity may be subject to divinity. By ‘humanity’ in this place we mean not gentleness and kindness, which the Greeks call *philanthrōpia* [love of humankind], but the whole human race. Further, when he says, ‘that God may be all in all’ (1 Cor. 15:28), it must be understood in this sense: our Lord and Saviour is not now all things in all people, but in each he is a part—for example, wisdom in Solomon, goodness in David, patience in Job, knowledge of future things in Daniel, faith in Peter, zeal in Phinehas and Paul, virginity in John, and other things in others. But when the end of all things has come, he will then be all things in all, so that each of the saints may possess all virtues and Christ may be whole in all.”

## Chapter IV

Saint Augustine does not contradict the teaching stated, nor does it bring dishonour upon Christ. The distinction is further established between humanity which is a man and which belongs to a man, and humanity by which a man is a man.

I. Blessed Augustine appears, however, to be opposed to these three orthodox Fathers, saying thus in the first book *On the Holy Trinity*:

> “We shall contemplate God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit when Christ Jesus, the man, mediator between God and human beings, has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, so that he may no longer intercede for us as our mediator and priest, the Son of God and man. But he himself, insofar as he is priest, having assumed for our sake the form of a servant, may be subject to him who subjected all things to him and to whom he subjected all things: so that, insofar as he is God, he may have us subject with him; insofar as he is priest, he may be subject to him with us.”

II. By these words of Augustine the ineffable [Col. 1087D] sacrament of piety is indicated to us who believe and hope it: that this great priest, in the days of his mortality, offered upon the cross a sacrifice of propitiation, obedient and subject to the Father; but in the days of eternity he will offer for us and with us a perpetual whole offering of praise and thanksgiving. In this very act he will be subject to the Father with us: we shall give thanks to God in him and through him, our mediator, while he leads this thanksgiving as chief singer.

His human nature received all this by grace which he himself possessed in his divinity by nature. This subjection, therefore, will be glorious, full of the mystery of piety and glory. By it the man is glorified in God after he has passed to the Father, there to give thanks for human nature glorified in himself and his members, and to be fully glorified at the end [Col. 1088A] of the world, when all his members have been subjected to God.

Even before this paschal passage, while he was still made lower than the angels through passibility and mortality, the subjection by which he—still mortal—was read to be subject to mortal parents, because it was a great sacrament of piety, did not darken his dignity. Rather, that dignity was more greatly made glorious through his inestimable condescension. Thus, yes, thus: in the pallor of gold, when the dignity of divinity and the splendour of majesty disappeared in him, as though his dignity had been emptied out, then the brightness of his condescension appeared more greatly.

III. What shall I say of that diadem with which his mother, the Synagogue, crowned him by placing upon him a crown of thorns? Did not the precious stones of the diadem of Aaron’s head then shine, when he was sacrificing himself to God the Father and God’s work was completed and brought to its end? Thus the high priest himself said: “I have completed the work which you gave me to do” (John 17:4); and on the cross he said: “It is completed” (John 19:30).

The work was then perfected and completed: the work of piety, love, compassion, and such great fellow-suffering that the servant of Isaiah suffered himself to be sacrificed in order to free the wicked servant and the enemy, the son of the handmaid, whom he made his co-heir by such a death. Who, then, can worthily weigh how precious were the stones that shone in that thorny diadem, where inestimable love, immeasurable piety, and infinite mercy shone forth? Stretched from eternity unto eternity, that mercy redeemed through death—indeed through the death of the cross—into eternal life those whom he recognized as predestined in himself by his eternal Father, sold for nothing because they had been defrauded by the promises of the most deceitful enemy, who promised likeness to God in order to draw them into conformity with himself.

Without doubt, the sun’s brightness could not endure the radiance of these and other precious stones, then shining in the diadem of Aaron’s head; therefore it was darkened from the sixth hour until the ninth. Let the earth, then, rejoice, irradiated by so great a splendour of precious stones. Let mother Church also rejoice, delighted in the brightnesses of the holy stones. By their radiance the bleary eyes of demons and human beings who detract from Christ’s glory are tormented, and are certainly convicted of not loving him. For if they loved him, they would surely rejoice that, going so gloriously to the Father, he was crowned for his thorny crown as with a golden plate, inscribed with God’s name: having been given the name which is above every name, so that at his name every knee of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings may bend, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:11)—true man by true humanity, and true God by true divinity; equal to the Father according to divinity, less than the Father according to humanity.

By “according to humanity” I mean the humanity “by which he is a man,” not the humanity “which is a man.” For although “the humanity by which he is a man” did not increase—for it is not capable of increase—the man who is man by it nevertheless increased, so that Daniel’s vision was fulfilled in him: Daniel saw the stone cut from the mountain without hands grow into a great mountain, so that it filled the whole world (Dan. 2:35).

Likewise the youthful David, after he had been anointed king, increased—not in stature, but in virtue and strength—so that he broke the mouths of lions, tore apart the limbs of bears, and slew with his own sword the Philistine feared by all. Just as he was increased not in the nature of humanity by which he was a man, and which was not itself a man, but in royal glory, eventually becoming king of the Jews: so Christ, David’s Son, anointed above his fellows, while the nature of true humanity remained in him, according to which he is proclaimed a little child, became the great king. Having already obtained triumph over lions and bears and other infernal beasts, and over the devil himself, prince of demons, the uncircumcised Philistine, he is king of the Jews—that is, of all who confess that he is in the glory of God the Father.

IV. I say that the man is in the glory of God, because that man is God, and there never was a man who was not God; for from the moment he began to be a perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh, he was also perfect God, existing eternally in himself. Man subsists from many things which are not man; but God exists in himself from eternity. “For,” as Boethius says, “man is not wholly man himself: for what he is, he owes to other things which are not man, for example his parts or forms, of which man consists, though none of them is man. But God,” says the same author, “is God himself. For he is nothing other than what he is, and by this very fact God.” And the seventh rule in Boethius suits him alone: “Everything simple has its own being and that which it is as one.” But what is said in the eighth rule—“For every composite thing, its being is one thing, and the thing itself another”—may be applied to man, whose being-by-which-he-is is other than himself; because the humanity by which he is man is not itself man. Thus also corporeity, by which something is a body, is not itself a body; and many other things are found in man in this manner which belong to man but are not themselves man, for example memory, mind, understanding, and will. But nothing is found in God which is not God, because God’s will is God, and his divinity itself is God. It is not so in man, whose will is not man, nor is his humanity man; for such things in man are not man, but are man’s. Hence Augustine says in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity*: “We find also in man a trinity: namely, mind, the knowledge by which it knows itself, and the love by which it loves itself. Certainly these three are in man, so that they are not themselves man. For man is, as the ancients defined him, a rational, mortal animal. Therefore those things are eminent in man; they are not themselves man. And one person, that is, an individual man, has those three in his mind. Even if we define man thus, saying: Man is a rational substance consisting of body and soul, there is no doubt that man has a soul which is not body, and has a body which is not soul. And therefore those three things are not man, but belong to man, or are in man.”

[Col. 1090A] As Saint Augustine says these things, our assertion agrees with his, by which we distinguish the humanity by which man is man—which belongs to man and is not itself man—from the humanity which is man, although in the treatises of the saints the name “humanity” is found used in both senses. For where the assumption of humanity into God is preached, by “humanity” is meant the man thus assumed into God, so that he is God. But where that same man is preached as equal to the Father according to divinity and less than the Father according to humanity, by “humanity” is properly understood the human nature by which man is man, which belongs to man and is not itself man.

## Chapter V

[Col. 1090B]

Christ, who is God by divinity and man by humanity, cannot truly be understood as man except together with the Word that was made flesh.

I. Photinus thought that this nature alone was in Christ, saying that he was man and not God. But Eutyches thought it consumed, teaching that Christ subsists from two natures, not in two natures. Apollinaris, however, mutilated that same human nature in Christ by depriving it of a rational soul, teaching that divinity itself was in Christ in place of a soul. Refuted in this error by Christ’s own words, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38), [Col. 1090C] he conceded that Christ had a soul to animate the body, but denied that it possessed human rationality, on the ground that it did not need it because it had divinity in place of reason. Nestorius, on the other hand, while confessing an entire humanity in Christ, separated it from divinity in such a way that he made one person of God and another of man. He forbade the Son of God to be called the son of man, and did not concede that God could be begotten from a human being. Hence he forbade Christ’s mother to be called *Theotokos*, that is, Mother of God.

II. Amid these monsters of diverse heresies, the holy Catholic Church held and holds the middle path of truth, turning neither to the right nor to the left. It distinguishes in Christ the nature of divinity from the nature [Col. 1090D] of humanity, in that divinity is not humanity and humanity is not divinity. Yet it believes that the one and same Son of God and of man is man through true and entire humanity, and God through all the fullness of divinity: indeed less than the Father according to the humanity by which he is man, but equal to the Father according to the divinity by which he is God. Divinity can in some manner be understood without humanity, or humanity without divinity: as when we say that the former lacks a beginning and the latter has a beginning. But Christ himself, who is God by divinity and man by humanity, cannot truly be understood as man except together with the Word that was made flesh; for God the Word is the head of this new man. “For God is the head of Christ,” says the Apostle (1 Cor. 11:3). [Col. 1091A] But Christ is the name of the man who, as Peter says, was anointed with the Holy Spirit and power above his companions (Acts 10:38). Whoever understands him without his head imagines him, as it were, as a trunk through a feigned faith, and does not believe in him with unfeigned faith.

For if someone understood any man possessing a head without his own head—whether the bodily head, which stands above the other members, or the spiritual head, namely the mind which is pre-eminent in the soul—he would have a false understanding, or indeed a feigned faith, if he believed true what he understood, or rather imagined he understood. So too, whoever believes Christ to be man but separates him from his head, which is God, is not guided by feigned faith but deceived by feigned faith, fashioning for himself something other than the true Christ, something which is not Christ. For just as a man deprived of his head is no longer a man but a trunk, so Christ deprived of his head is no longer Christ in the faith of one who believes him to be what he is not. Certainly Christ thus understood—or rather, thus imagined—as a man without his head, is truly less in glory than his Father God; for such a Christ is not God, and therefore God’s glory is not his, because God is not his head. But God is the head of the Christ proclaimed to us through the apostles; and therefore, in the faith of believers, he is to be made equal to his Father God in divine glory. Nevertheless, it must not be denied, but rather confessed, that he who is equal to the Father in his divinity is less than him according to humanity.

III. Hence comes that long conflict between the house [Col. 1091C] of David and the house of Saul: the house of David, namely the holy Church, refuses to receive any Christ except him anointed from the horn of divine strength. But the house of Saul, namely the crooked and perverse generation, seeks another Christ, anointed from a lentil-shaped earthen vessel, by which feigned faith is symbolized. This may be understood of him of whom Christ says: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you have not received me; another will come in his own name, and you will receive him” (John 5:43). But the true Christ, anointed from the horn of salvation, is he of whom we sing: “He has raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant” (Luke 1:69).

IV. Am I the first, or the only one, to think that God is the head of Christ? Does not Augustine also hold the apostolic understanding which I maintain? For in the sixth book *On the Trinity*, among other things, he says: “What the Father is together with the Son is the head of that which the Son alone is; for together with the Son the Father is God, but the Son alone is Christ, especially because the Word made flesh now speaks. According to this lowliness, the Father is also greater, as he says: ‘For the Father is greater than I’ (John 14:28). Thus, that very being-God which he shares with the Father is the head of the man who is mediator, which he himself alone is. For if we rightly call the mind the ruling principle of man, that is, as it were the head of human substance, since man together with the mind is man, why should not the Word together with the Father, which is simultaneously God, much more fittingly and much more truly be the head of Christ, although Christ as man cannot be understood except together with the Word that was made flesh?”

[Col. 1092A] Behold: in these words of Augustine one may clearly distinguish between the lowliness of that humanity according to which the Father is greater than Christ—which is neither man nor God, because it can be understood, as it were, bare and without the head of divinity—and that lowliness which is man, whose head is God, and which therefore cannot be understood without its head by a true understanding, or believed with true rather than feigned faith. That by the term “humanity” is sometimes meant the very form by which man is man, which is not itself man, no sober philosopher is ignorant of who considers the forms of things through mathematical contemplation: although not abstracted, they are to be contemplated abstractly, as Boethius teaches. But that the term “humanity” is again sometimes used to signify soul and flesh, which joined together are man, Jerome openly teaches in his exposition of the Catholic faith, saying: “Thus we confess one person of the Son in Christ, while saying that there are two perfect and complete substances, namely divinity and humanity, the latter consisting of soul and body.” Here he plainly shows that soul and body are meant by the name humanity—the two which the Son of God is indicated to have assumed wherever he is said to have taken man, humanity, or human nature.

## Chapter VI

The author would prefer, following the example of Saint Hilary, that the definite term “man,” rather than the ambiguous term “humanity,” had been used in those places in his writings where he says, “glorifying humanity into God.” He further establishes from the Fathers that Christ the man is to be worshiped not with *dulia* alone but also with *latria*.

I. Here the simplicity of those who reason thus about mysteries hidden and lofty beyond all reason seems deserving of censure: Christ’s soul was fully and perfectly wise, yet it was not made equal to the very wisdom which it possessed. For it is one thing to be wise by wisdom, and another to be wisdom; the former, which is lesser, belongs to the assumed man, while the latter, which is greater, belongs to the Word assuming the man and governing the assumed man.

II. In speaking thus either of Christ’s soul or of Christ himself as possessing wisdom, they do not attend to the manner in which he possesses it. For he does not possess wisdom as Paul or any other saint illumined by wisdom does, to whom that very wisdom is accidental and can be separated from him in thought. Rather, just as any man has a head in his body or a mind in his soul, so the man assumed into the Son of God, who is eternal wisdom, has God’s very wisdom in himself—not merely in some fashion, but as his head, indeed as the head of his true subsistence. Therefore, just as it is absurd to call a man less than his own head or his own mind, so it is absurd to call the Son of man less than his own head, that is, his ruling principle, which is eternal wisdom.

III. Since, therefore, there is a great difference between humanity by which man is man and humanity which is man, wherever I have said or written that humanity is to be glorified [Col. 1093A] into God, I meant nothing other than the man subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh, and having God’s Word as his head. Of him the bride also says: “His head is the finest gold” (Song 5:11). Because he was given the name above every name, I rightly proclaimed him equal to God the Father according to the truth of that same name, according to the eternal splendor of his head, not according to the humanity by which he is man, according to which he always is and will be less than the Father, himself, and the Holy Spirit. Therefore, wherever in my writings man is signified by the term “humanity,” since the little ones may be scandalized by this—and we ought to have concern for their scandal—or even the perverse, hostile, slanderous, and envious, whose scandals are to be despised, because Christ said of such persons, “Let them alone; they are blind guides of the blind” (Matt. 15:14), I would now prefer that the unambiguous term “man” had been used rather than the ambiguous term “humanity.”

IV. Thus blessed Hilary, in the ninth book *On the Holy Trinity*, set before us a pattern of speech, saying: “For this was acquired for man: that he should be God.” He says “for man,” not “for humanity.” “For to man,” as Augustine affirms, “was given the name above every name.” He says “to man,” not “to humanity,” because it was given to man to be called and to be God Most High. That name cannot be predicated of the form of a servant, which is humanity, though this form itself is sometimes signified by the name “man”: as when man is called the form of a servant, by which the form of God is greater—the form understood as divinity itself, by which man is beautiful and fair above the sons of men, and in which form he did not regard equality with God the Father as plunder. Hence Hilary says in the ninth book: “But the assumed [man] could in no way remain in the unity of God unless, through the unity of God, he should pass naturally into the unity of God; so that, since the Word was God by nature, the Word made flesh might in turn exist in the nature of God. Thus the man Jesus Christ would remain in the glory of God the Father, if flesh were united to the glory of the Word; and then the Word made flesh would return, even according to man, into the unity of the Father’s nature, when the assumed flesh had attained the glory of the Word.” Thus far Hilary.

V. It should be noted that this Catholic teacher says “according to man,” not “according to humanity,” when he speaks of the glory given to Christ according to man. He says “according to man,” not “according to humanity,” because Christ has many things according to man which he does not have according to humanity, by which he is man. For that man is God, but his humanity is not God. The man who is man by humanity and God by divinity is properly called both God and man, so that reciprocally God may rightly be predicated of man and man of God, and one may say “man is God” and “God is man.” But humanity by which he is man is neither man nor God; nor is divinity humanity itself, [Col. 1094A] nor humanity divinity. Therefore, wherever I see this to be necessary, I promise that I shall clarify what I stated ambiguously, although I stated it with sound understanding and it can be understood with sound understanding, once the distinction has been made between humanity by which man is man and humanity which is man.

VI. “Humanity” is also found used to indicate divine kindness, as in: “The goodness and humanity of God our Savior appeared” (Titus 3:4). The words which follow show that this was said of the Father: “Not by works of righteousness which we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior” (ibid., v. 5). This humanity, which the Greeks call *philanthrōpia*, is wholly common to the three persons in the Trinity and equal in all of them. Who would deny it to the man assumed into God, through whose passion the work of supreme mercy was accomplished, and who is called and is the good shepherd—not by an accidental gift, but by essential goodness, as blessed Gregory says? For mercy or goodness was not accidental to that supreme shepherd who was slain for his sheep, as it is to other good shepherds; for goodness was not given to him by measure, since no one is good except God alone. Therefore God the supreme good is man together with his Father and the Holy Spirit. And certainly God-man knows all things and can do all that he wills. Plainly, God-man is to be worshiped—not, as certain utterly foolish people rave, with only the worship called *dulia*, but with the worship called *latria*, to be offered to God alone, the supreme God. Hence one reads in the Synod of Ephesus, over which the great Cyril of Alexandria presided with two hundred bishops: “If anyone dares to say that the assumed man ought to be co-worshiped with God the Word, and co-glorified, and called God, as though one were added to the other—for the addition of one syllable, namely *co-*, compels this meaning—and does not rather worship Emmanuel with one reverence and render him one glorification, according as the Word was made flesh, let him be anathema.”

VII. Likewise Augustine, from the Lord’s saying, “Let not your heart be troubled” (John 14:1), says: “Heretics say that the Son is not God by nature [Col. 1094D] but a creature. They must be answered that, if the Son is not God by nature but a creature, he is not to be worshiped at all, nor adored as God; for the Apostle says, ‘They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator’ (Rom. 1:25). But they will reply to this and say: Why then do you worship his flesh, which you do not deny to be a creature, together with divinity, and serve it no less than divinity? Answer them thus: I worship the Lord’s flesh—indeed, the perfect humanity in Christ—because it has been received by divinity and united to deity, so that I confess not one person and another, but one and the same God and man, to be the Son of God.” And shortly afterward: “Whoever disdains to worship humanity not alone or bare, but united to divinity—namely the one Son, true God and true man—shall die eternally.”

VIII. Likewise Jerome, on Jeremiah: “If,” he says, “death has been swallowed up in victory, why should not the lowliness of flesh, which was assumed for human salvation, have passed into the majesty of divinity, so that both make one, and we worship not the creature but the Creator, who is blessed for ever?” Likewise Ambrose, in the first book *On the Trinity*: “Let us prove,” he says, “that the Son of God is not a creature. For we have heard in the Gospel that the Lord commanded his disciples: ‘Preach the Gospel to every creature’ (Mark 16:15). He who says ‘every creature’ excepts none. Where, then, are those who call Christ a creature? For if he were a creature, he would command the Gospel to be preached to himself, and he would be subject to futility, because, according to the Apostle’s witness, every creature is subject to futility (Rom. 8:20). Therefore Christ is not a creature, but the Creator, who entrusts to his disciples the office of teaching the creature.”

IX. These statements of Ambrose and Jerome should not appear to have been introduced as if they urged belief that the created element in Christ was consumed by conception or glorification so as no longer to exist. For the animated body in Christ remains created, just as the uncreated Word remains uncreated. Rather, they show that what is created must not be doubted to have been exalted in the glory of the uncreated Word and therefore is to be worshiped in the glory of the Creator, and not reckoned among creatures subject to futility. For, as the Apostle says, “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16). That is, we do not now know him among all created things, but as God above all, blessed for ever.

## Chapter VII

By the example of the three Magi and the authority of Leo and Augustine, the author confirms that the man in Christ is to be worshiped with the worship of *latria*.

I. What then shall we say about those who worshiped Christ while he was still mortal? Foremost among them were the three Magi, who worshiped him while he was still wrapped in swaddling clothes and offered him gifts. Did they, in worshiping a mortal, become idolaters by serving the creature rather than the Creator? This might in some manner be thought if the Creator had not become creature, and if the creature had not been united to the Creator. But now, because God appeared clothed in man as in royal purple and adorned as with a priestly robe, they rightly and lawfully worshiped him and offered him gold, frankincense, and myrrh: gold as to a great king, frankincense as to the true God, and myrrh for his burial. Therefore they worshiped also in him that nature to which burial was to be given. Although they saw him in the swaddling clothes in which his mother had wrapped him, from whom he had also drawn the garments of flesh and bodily members, the sight of the worshipers was not delayed by those garments from recognizing God in the man—or rather, man as God. For the fragrance of these garments, like the fragrance of incense, was sweet in the hearts [Col. 1096A] of those burning with faith. They believed that the man born into God, not adopted or reborn like the other saints, was true God: not ceasing to be man because of the divinity innate to him, nor ceasing to be God because of the humanity assumed in himself. He was therefore rightly to be worshiped on account of the fragrance of the garments with which his mother had clothed him.

Long before, the patriarch Isaac, perceiving this fragrance with his prophetic nostril, said to his son Jacob, who bore the type of Christ: “Be lord of your brothers, and let the sons of your mother bow down before you and let the tribes worship you” (Gen. 27:29). What wonder, then, that the Magi perceived as present and worthy of worship the fragrance in the true Jacob who would supplant the prince of this world, when the patriarch, perceiving it so long beforehand, declared that it was to be worshiped by the tribes, of whom these Magi were the firstfruits, who perceived this fragrance at close range? I think that even then they beheld with the eyes of faith written upon his garment and thigh, “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19:16). To him, as King of kings, they offered gold; and they worshiped him as Lord of lords, although they saw him wrapped in swaddling clothes. For his garment and thigh may suitably be understood as his flesh, by which the Word was clothed, and which was adorned by the omnipotence of that Word above all kings, as though containing inscribed within itself: “King of kings and Lord of lords.” This was hidden from plotting Herod but disclosed to the worshiping Magi.

II. Hence, as Pope Leo says in his sermon on the Epiphany: “What they believe in their hearts they declare by gifts. They offer incense to God, myrrh to man, and gold to the king, knowing that human and divine nature are to be worshiped in unity. For what was proper to the substances was not divided in power.” Likewise Pope Leo, on the Nativity of the Lord: “Let the monstrous opinions of heretics withdraw far away and fall back into their own darkness, along with the sacrileges of mad falsehoods. We, however, have been taught by the exulting multitude of heavenly beings, and the shepherds instructed by angels, that, once the proofs of both natures are known, we should worship both the Word in Christ the man and Christ the man in the Word. For, as the Apostle says, ‘He who is joined to God is one spirit’ (1 Cor. 6:17); how much more is the Word made flesh one Christ, where nothing belongs to one nature which does not belong to both? For although one remains from eternity, the other began in time, yet they came together in unity and can have neither separation nor end. The exalting and the exalted, the glorifying and the glorified, so adhere to one another that, whether in omnipotence or in humiliation, the divine things in Christ are not without the human, nor the human without the divine.”

How rightly this Roman pontiff has offered and distinguished these things: discerning distinct natures in Christ but assigning one glory to each nature! The impious do not do so; they tear Christ apart in such a way as to assert that *latria* is owed to the Word but *dulia* to the man. They try to support this as though by Augustine’s authority, producing, I think, an excerpt from his exposition of the Psalm, “Worship his footstool” (Ps. 98:5). Peter, the modern glossator [Note: [Col. 1097D] Peter Lombard], inserted this under Augustine’s name into his glosses, where he assigned *dulia* to the man and *latria* to the Word, though blessed Augustine held nothing of the kind. In treating of the aforesaid footstool to be worshiped, Augustine makes absolutely no mention of *dulia*. The said Peter is believed afterward to have discovered this, since in the third book of his *Sentences*, where he sets out the opinions of some who think that *latria* should be rendered to God and *dulia* to the man in Christ, he makes no mention of Augustine. But in that same book, where he recalls Augustine’s opinion concerning worshiping the Lord’s footstool, there is absolutely no mention of *dulia*, as these liars assert is to be given to the assumed man.

[Col. 1097B] III. For that eminent doctor did not regard the man united to the Word as though he were a garment attached externally. This is clear from his statement in the first book *On the Holy Trinity*: “The man was assumed, in whose form the person of God the Word might be manifested—not so that he might have the Word of God as other wise men do, but beyond his fellows; not indeed because he had the Word more abundantly than others, so as to be wiser in a superior way, but because he was the Word itself. For the Word in flesh is one thing, and the Word made flesh another; that is, the Word in a man is one thing, and the Word as man another. For ‘flesh’ is used for ‘man’ where it says, ‘The Word was made flesh’ (John 1:14).” Again, in the fourth book, explaining, “Send forth, Lord, wisdom from the throne of your greatness” (Wis. 9:10), he says: “It is sent in one way to be in a man; it was sent in another way to be itself man. For it passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets; it also fills angels and works through them everything fitting for such ministers. But when the fullness of time came, it was sent not to fill angels, nor to be an angel—except insofar as it announced the Father’s counsel, which was also its own—nor to be with men or in men, as it had previously been in the patriarchs and prophets, but that the Word itself might become flesh.”

IV. The impious Nestorius did not teach in this way. He said: “Because of the one who is clothed, I honor the garment; because of the hidden one, I worship the visible one. That which was fashioned in the womb, created of the Spirit, and buried in the tomb, is not God in itself. For then we would plainly be worshipers of man and worshipers of the dead. But God, in the assumed man, has the assumed [reality] from the one assuming, so that it is united to the assuming God.” Again: “We preserve,” he says, “the unconfused nature; we confess the conjunction; in man we worship God; we honor the divine conjunction—the man is to be co-worshiped with almighty God.” Thus that blasphemer taught that the assumed man was not to be worshiped in himself, but co-worshiped with the assuming God. Because of this pestilential doctrine, read out at the Synod of Ephesus, he was proscribed and condemned. The orthodox Fathers especially detested in his doctrine that, by dividing the assumed man excessively from the assuming God, he denied him the worship of divinity as God. For he asserted not that the man was God, but that he was God’s garment and temple, receiving the name of God only through adoption and conjunction; and he said that the Son of God, who was made for us human beings, ought not to be called God. He even dared, as is recorded in the acts of the council, to say in disputation against the most reverend bishops: “I do not call a two-month-old or three-month-old God.” This pestilential doctrine is wholly contrary to the foregoing assertion of blessed Augustine: “The Word in flesh is one thing; the Word made flesh another; that is, the Word in a man is one thing, and the Word as man another,” and so forth, as above, down to “that the Word itself might become flesh.” Does not this outstanding teacher thus worship God clothed in tender limbs, so that, in his faith, the garments assumed from his mother have the fragrance of incense and are therefore to be venerated with every worship belonging to supreme divinity?

## Chapter VIII

The worship of the cross redounds to Christ, who is Son of God according to man, not according to the humanity by which he is man; nor is he an adoptive Son of God, but the natural Son. The author teaches that a distinction must be made between a naturally natural generation and the wonderfully natural generation by which the God-man Son was begotten.

[Col. 1098C] I. This faith also burned in that blessed woman who said: “If I touch the fringe of his garment, I shall be healed” (Matt. 9:20). And so it happened: she touched the fringe and was healed, and immediately heard, “Your faith has made you well” (ibid., v. 22). She touched Jesus, whom the crowd pressed about; she perceived that the grace of healing had come into her from the Savior, and he perceived that power had gone out from himself: “I,” he says, “perceived power going out from me” (ibid.). “From me,” he says, “not from the fringe”; nor did he say, “Someone touched the fringe,” but “Someone touched me” (ibid.). Thus it may plainly be observed that veneration rendered to his flesh and to the things which he did or suffered in the flesh redounds to God himself, from whom power goes forth and proceeds into all who touch him faithfully, and not into those who merely press him in the crowd.

II. Hence, when we worship the traces of his feet, we believe that we worship him himself. We also worship the cross, venerating in it the Crucified One. As blessed Andrew says, because it was consecrated in Christ’s body and adorned with his members as with pearls, it is rightly set forth in the Church to be worshiped by wise and simple alike. Such worship does not make idolaters, because it is directed to him who hung upon it. To him is due not *dulia*, as to the other saints, who are many, but *latria*, as to the true God, the unique, not adoptive Son of God the Father in both natures. Hence Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*: “What did human nature in Christ deserve, that it should be singularly assumed into the unity of the person of the only Son of God? What good will, what pursuit of a good purpose, what good works preceded, by which this man might deserve to become one person with God? Was he a man beforehand, and was this singular benefit granted him so that he might singularly merit God? Assuredly, from the moment he began to be man, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God, and that the only Son; and therefore the Word of God, which, having assumed him, was made flesh, is certainly God. Thus, just as any man is one person, namely rational soul and flesh, so Christ is one person, Word and man.” Again: “Accordingly, as we confess, our Lord Jesus, God from God, but man born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, is in both substances—divine and human—the only Son of God the almighty Father, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds.”

III. Since, therefore, as has been shown, Christ in both natures is the Father’s only Son, let those blasphemers be silent who assert that the Son of man is not the Son of God according to man. I do not say “according to humanity,” lest anyone suppose that I assert humanity to be equal to divinity—a claim which I have by no means made. But on several occasions, treating of the God-man under the name “humanity,” I asserted that he was glorified in the glory given to him and made equal to God, so that he is in the glory of God the Father: less indeed than the Father according to humanity, but equal to him according to the divinity innate to him. This came to him not after conception but in conception through the Holy Spirit, so that that man is immeasurable God—not according to the humanity by which he is man, which is not itself man, but according to the man to whom the glory of divinity was given. Thus understand that this man is the Son of God the Father, whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world.

IV. For if Scripture cannot be broken, in which Truth that does not lie calls gods and sons of the Most High those to whom the Word of God, or speech of God, came, how much more rightly is the man who was made the Word of God called God and the natural Son of God, since he himself is the Word of God—not adoptive, like those to whom the Word of God came? For he adopted them as sons when they had previously been by nature children of wrath. They were freed, and are freed, from that wrath not by generation but by regeneration. But this man, sanctified by the Father in his mother’s womb far more than Jeremiah or John, whom we read were sanctified in their mothers’ wombs, received by being born that he should be the Son of God—by being born, I say, in his mother’s womb, with the Holy Spirit working through divine love. Hence, even before he came forth from the closed womb of his mother like a bridegroom, the angel is recorded to have said to Joseph: “Do not fear to take Mary your wife; for that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit,” etc. (Matt. 2:20). Likewise the angel says to Mary: “That which shall be born from you, holy, shall be called the Son of God.” But he had first given the reason, saying: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

[Col. 1100A] Therefore that man, whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world through the working of the Holy Spirit—that is, divine love—in the conception of his flesh, may without blasphemy be proclaimed God, the natural and proper Son of God, even according to his being man; just as he is likewise proclaimed Son of man even according to his being God.

V. Because Nestorius dared to deny this, forbidding Mary to be called *Theotocos*, that is, “God-bearer” or “Mother of God,” as though she had borne only a human being and not God, he was rightly condemned and judged a heretic. Likewise Photinus, because he taught that Christ was only the son of man and not of God, and consequently was not God himself, but merely pre-eminent among the saints, in whom indeed the whole fullness of divinity dwelt beyond that in other saints, while he himself nevertheless was not God. Saint Jerome thus summarizes his doctrine in his commentary on Jeremiah. He too was condemned with all his followers, who deny that the man born of the Virgin is God, God’s proper Son, not an adopted son.

But some Photinian adversary objects, stripping the man who is God of his divinity, maintaining that the man is only a son in name, and cannot be called God or the Son of God, except perhaps, as they say, by adoption or union. For, they say, if the man is God’s natural Son insofar as he is man, then the man is consubstantial with God his Father, just as every individual in natural generation is consubstantial with his father—for example, Isaac is consubstantial with Abraham. But Christ, according to his humanity, is not consubstantial with God the Father; therefore neither is he his natural Son.

A further absurdity follows. For if one son has parents of such unlike kinds—namely, God as his natural father and a human being as his natural mother—he resembles a mule, whose parents are of different natures and which is con-natural to neither parent. He is also like a bastard human being, born of a father nobler than his mother. They say that these absurdities must be avoided by confessing that the Word was begotten of God alone and the man born of the Virgin alone, but united to the Word in such a way that he has a share in that name by adoption or union rather than by generation—the name by which the Word of God is called the Son of God. For, they say, it is impossible for either spirit to be born from flesh or flesh from spirit. They add also: it is evident that nothing capable of sensation can be born from what is insensible.

VI. A certain man, more importunate than the others, tried to prove to me from such assertions that, if the man were the Son of God, then, since what is born of spirit is spirit, the man born of God, who is spirit, would not have flesh and bones. Those who say and think such things do not distinguish between generation naturally natural and generation miraculously natural.

For example, Ishmael’s generation from Abraham, because it was according to the flesh, was naturally natural: nature readily admits that a young woman may conceive by a man, even an old one. Isaac’s generation, however, was indeed natural, because Isaac himself was conceived and born from bloods, from the will of the flesh, and from the will of a man; but it occurred beyond nature, not naturally but miraculously, when a barren old woman, whose monthly courses had ceased, conceived by an old man now sexually spent.

Therefore the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “By faith even Sarah herself, though barren, received power for the conception of seed, even beyond the time of age, because she judged him faithful who had promised” (Heb. 11:11). “Therefore there sprang from one man—and him as good as dead—descendants as numerous as the stars of heaven, and as the innumerable sand upon the seashore.” Again the Apostle elsewhere says: “It is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But he who was of the slave woman was born according to the flesh; whereas he who was of the free woman was born through promise” (Gal. 4:18).

But the word of promise to Abraham was this: “In your seed all tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 28:14). Again: “Behold, Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac” (Gen. 17:9). Abraham believed God’s promise, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. Hence all Abraham’s descendants who share this faith and are its heirs are rightly called children of promise rather than children of the flesh. For, as the same Apostle says, “Not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor, because they are Abraham’s seed, are all children; but, ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called.’” That is: “It is not the children of the flesh who are God’s children, but the children of the promise are reckoned as seed.” For the word of promise is this: “At this time I shall come, and Sarah shall have a son” (Rom. 9:9). “And just as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so it is now also” (Gal. 4:29).

VII. In these words of the Apostle there plainly appears a distinction between children of the flesh and children of promise, who are also called—and are—children of God, although it has not yet appeared what they are and what they shall be. Their head is Christ, God and man, promised to the ancient fathers and given as a son. They too say: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6).

Born to us, I say, is God from God and man from man, the Son of God and likewise the son of man. In whose birth, although it is natural that man is begotten from man and God from God, this nevertheless lies beyond nature through admirable and ineffable grace: that the man is the Son of God and God is the son of man; that a woman is the mother of God; and that God Most High is truly proclaimed the begetter of a human being—to whom he also says: “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7), and to whom Peter said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16).

## CHAPTER IX

Just as God is the Son of God from eternity, so Christ, through the unity of the sacrament, existed before his mother; and therefore, for the same reason Nestorius permitted her to be called *Christotocos*, he could and should have permitted her to be called *Theotocos*.

I. At this point Nestorius, the heresiarch, took offense when the Son of God was also called the son of man, and he refused to accept that the Virgin was the mother of God. In confirmation of his error he introduced two false arguments, as is found in his writings.

One argument was that no one can give birth to someone older than herself; but God is older than the Virgin. Therefore he forbade her to be called *Theotocos*, or Mother of God, while readily allowing her to be called *Christotocos*, that is, mother of Christ, because Christ was not before her, as he supposed. He did not know that, through the ineffable mystery of unity, Christ the Son of God existed before Mary.

He is also read to have been tempted in the wilderness by the murmuring people, as the Apostle says: “Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him” (1 Cor. 10:9). From the blood of righteous Abel to his own blood, he suffered much in his members before he was born. He also, before he knew how to call an adoptive father and his own mother by name, as Isaiah says (Isa. 8:4), took away the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria, avenging and defending the people from whom he was to be born. Hence his name was rightly called “Hasten to take the spoil; hurry to plunder” [*Maher-shalal-hash-baz*] (ibid.), because this child was in great haste in thus waging war, before he knew how to call father or mother according to that nature in which he was to become a child and have a mother and an adoptive father. Therefore this child existed before his mother, who bore him though he was older than she. Since Nestorius did not think this possible, he forbade her to be called the mother of God.

[Col. 1102C] II. Speaking against this error, blessed Jerome says among other things in his sermon on the Assumption of Saint Mary: “He who spoke indicates that he already existed in eternity through the mystery of his incarnation.”

The Apostle Jude, wishing to make this clearer, says: “Jesus, saving the people out of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe” (Jude 5). And Paul elsewhere: “Let us not tempt Christ, as some tempted him.” This is not because Jesus or Christ had already been born of the Virgin Mary, but because in that one Son of God the unity of person, then hidden in mystery, is already set forth.

The same is evident elsewhere: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1:4), because indeed everything God did from the beginning Christ did wholly through the unity of the sacrament. Thus Jesus was already in the Son who led the people out, and Christ in him who was tempted; and there is no doubt that he was always in God through the unity of the sacrament. Otherwise, unless you believe thus, either Christ will not be God at all, or, contrary to the prophet, God will appear to be recent.

III. But lest we be shaken by such calumnies, we must search the Scriptures, in which the unity of person in Christ is set forth—a unity which does not make time an obstacle to his always being called one. Thus blessed Peter, speaking of the fathers, says: “We believe that through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved in the same manner as they.” For the Lord alone led them, and no foreign god was with him.

Therefore God is not recent among us either, because he is one and the same: he was their leader and, through the passion of his flesh, our redeemer. He is one in his flesh, one in the sacrament, and one in the Spirit; and he admits no understanding whatever that there is one son of man and another Son of God. He is neither limited by time nor divided by suffering. Rather, the whole God passed into Christ and Christ into God, so that whatever belongs to the Son of God is called Christ’s, and whatever Christ suffered in the flesh may rightly be said to have been suffered by God.

Otherwise, if you attend to rational calculation and human perceptions, divinity and the human condition could by no means have been able to agree with one another in this fashion. Yet they came together in Christ, and Emmanuel is one from both. Therefore it seems to me that those who imagined either two sons, or at least a Christ other than the Son of God, could neither love nor perceive the height of so great a mystery.

IV. Therefore neither do we worship or adore the man separately—which would be impious—but him who, in himself, was always the one true Son of God. Accordingly, we worship and adore no one other than the same and very Son of God, who was compelled to nothing in himself because he assumed manhood, and who was neither diminished nor changed because “the Word was made flesh.” Therefore the one and same Son is always worshipped with God the Father: not new, not recent in time, not alien in nature or kind.

If it seems new to you that he assumed humanity for your sake, know that this was always with him and in his counsel, that it should be so done. And now, when the fullness of time came, that was accomplished which was always in Christ.

[Col. 1103C] From what has been said it is clear that, just as God is the Son of God through eternity, so Christ, through the unity of the sacrament, was before his mother. Therefore, for the same reason Nestorius permitted her to be called *Christotocos*, he could have permitted her to be called *Theotocos*. But because he granted one and denied the other, when human reason supported him in neither case—for both Christ and God were before his mother—she who bore both God and Christ truly bore God. For God was in Christ; indeed, Christ himself, whom the Virgin bore, was God. Consequently, just as she is truly called and is the mother of Christ, so truly she is called and is the mother or begetter of God, of her Son who was older than she. This is wonderful to the eyes of reason and worthy of reverence to the eyes of faith.

V. Similarly, Nestorius’s reasoning, by which he denied that the Virgin could truly be called the mother of God’s Son not coessential with herself—because the Son did not have the essence of divinity from his mother, just as he did not have the essence of humanity from his Father, to whom he is not coessential as man, just as God is not coessential with his mother—is overcome and nullified by the reasoning of faith. By this faith, the man is believed to be God’s Son with the heart unto righteousness and proclaimed with the mouth unto salvation.

Although this Son of God is said to have been made from the seed of David according to the flesh, or made from woman according to the flesh—so that, as Ambrose explains, “made” is attributed not to divinity but to flesh—yet, so that his birth may be known to be attributable rather to God’s operation than to that of flesh, the same Apostle who calls him made according to the flesh declares him born according to the Spirit.

For, speaking of Isaac, son of a barren woman and son of promise, as a type of Christ—whom the naturally barren Virgin bore while her virginity remained—he calls Isaac born according to the Spirit, so that you may understand Christ, whom Isaac prefigured, as born according to the Spirit: born, I say, not made according to the Spirit. Christ was made from David’s seed according to the flesh, but was not born from that same seed of David according to the flesh; rather, he was born according to the Spirit, when the Virgin, believing God, conceived in faith God the Father’s Word to be made human within her. This was far more wondrous than the conception of a barren woman, likewise believing in faith God’s promise, by an old man now sexually spent and, as the Apostle says, having a body “as good as dead” (Rom. 4:19).

Yet because both occurred by God’s miracle, both the typical Isaac and the true Isaac were born not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit, so that the former may as properly be called Abraham’s son as the latter is called God’s Son. God “did not spare his own proper Son, but delivered him up for us all,” just as Abraham did not spare his own proper son but, at the Lord’s command, prepared to offer him as a sacrifice.

VI. Since therefore all the elect, called by the Apostle children of God, are children of promise, as having been promised by the God of Abraham, the true Isaac must above all be called the Son of God: the Son whom God himself generates naturally in divinity by an ineffable and wonderful generation, and whom, through the power of that same generation, he so formed as man in the most excellent daughter of Abraham—purified and ineffably ennobled through the Holy Spirit—that, when she conceived through the operation of God alone, being wondrously and naturally barren as a virgin without a man, he who was conceived as man might be the one only Son with the eternal Word of God who gave the promise.

Therefore, when one reads in the Fathers’ treatises, “Christ in heaven without a mother, on earth without a father,” this must be understood as meaning without a human father. Blessed Augustine adds this qualification in his sermon on the Nativity of John the Baptist, saying: “The Lord himself made for himself a servant in a barren womb, from an old father and a servant-woman mother; and that same Lord made flesh for himself in the Virgin’s womb without a human father—he who made the first man without father and mother.” When he says “without a human father,” he sufficiently indicates that the only-begotten Son of his bride was not conceived without God the Father.

## CHAPTER X

In his exposition of Psalm 17:5, he warns that what he said concerning the chamber, kisses, and marriage of bridegroom and bride must be understood spiritually, not carnally; nor did he intend, in expounding the sixth verse of the same psalm, anything other than what Augustine and Hilary taught concerning the man assumed into God through grace.

I. But, as I perceived, this offended certain carnal-minded persons: in my writings, where this only-begotten Son is mentioned as “a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber,” I said that *tanquam* (“as,” “like”) is here an adverb signifying truth rather than resemblance. Thus: “I saw a Lamb *as though slain*,” that is, truly slain (Rev. 5:6). Again: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John 1:9), meaning, the glory of one truly only-begotten.

Likewise, I say, when he is called “as a bridegroom,” he must be understood as truly a bridegroom; hence, “He who has the bride is the bridegroom.” He also has children, concerning whom it is said: “Can the children of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Matt. 9:15). He has also a bride: namely, the holy Church and every faithful soul, just as his Father had as bride the ancient Synagogue, and in it every faithful soul or person.

Now the blessed Virgin Mary was the most chosen portion of that ancient Synagogue, so loved by God the Father that he kindled her above all others with his love and made her fruitful by his Word. This Word, uttered within her and conceived first in mind and then in womb, came forth from her like a bridegroom from his chamber, intending to love the new Church and, in it, every faithful person, as a bride adorned for her husband.

Among all brides, however, the blessed Virgin Mary was and remains adorned above all: as the consummation of the Synagogue, being the most chosen daughter of the patriarchs; and, after her Son, as the new beginning of the holy Church, being the mother of the apostles, to one of whom it was said: “Behold your mother” (John 19:25).

II. What was said to one could have been said to all the holy apostles, the fathers of the new Church. And because Christ prayed for those who would believe through their word, that all might be one, what was said to the one who loved Christ—and among the others was loved more—applies to all the faithful who love Christ with their whole heart.

That blessed mother gave birth to all of them while standing beside the cross, when, knowing that her only Son was suffering in order to free and save them, she was tormented as she laboured to give birth, as the sword of compassion pierced through her soul. Therefore we do not vainly cry to her not only, “Hail, star of the sea, kindly Mother of God,” but also, as is added, “Show yourself to be a mother”—namely because of a twofold motherhood: one by which she bore her only Son without pain; the other by which she bore many children, to herself and to that same only Son, with great pain and grief—her own grief, that of her beloved, and that of his disciples.

Of this grief the bridegroom’s saying may fittingly be understood: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38). Again, to that new bride—the primitive Church of the apostolic order, of which blessed Mary was the chief portion—the same Bridegroom then said, among other things, because the wine that gladdens hearts was lacking: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow, because her hour has come,” and so forth, “your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 16:20). This is almost the same as if he had said: “Your water shall be turned into wine.” For the hour was already approaching when, through his passion and resurrection, human nature—mortal and corruptible like water—was to be changed into the wine of blessed immortality. Having tasted it, the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.

III. Among them, that woman who, together with them, had been more deeply saddened and had suffered more keenly while giving birth, because the sword of sorrow had pierced her soul, not surprisingly rejoiced more abundantly as well when she saw the Lord, her most beloved Son and Bridegroom, and when the guests at these marriage-feasts were already rejoicing because of the wine of immortality first tasted in Christ.

With this wine all who rise again and are changed will also be made drunk on that day of the universal marriage-feast, “in which we shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed.” Those who are changed will likewise be made drunk from the torrent of delight—not, as certain heretics dream, with delights that are carnal, enduring for a thousand years and then ceasing, but with spiritual delights that remain in them eternally. Of these it is said in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who comes up, abounding in delights and leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8:5).

Christ himself was already contemplating these nuptial delights when he said to his mother, who desired wine: “My hour has not yet come” (John 3:4). But when that hour was now at hand, he said: “Woman, behold your son” (John 19:26); and to the disciple: “Behold your mother” (ibid. 25). This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. For it is handed down that this disciple was the bridegroom at the marriage where, when the wine failed, water was changed into wine. That was then the beginning of signs; its completion will be when, in the spiritual marriage-feast, those who suffer with Christ—like his beloved mother and beloved disciple standing beside the cross—will rejoice by rising with him: first in hope, then in reality.

And since it is written regarding the carnal union of carnal persons, “Pleasure is vain”—though the goods of marriage excuse it so that it is pardonable [*venialis*; the OCR reads *venalis*]—yet outside marriage, if voluntarily admitted and deliberately sought, it is criminal. But in that spiritual union of Christ and the Church, of the Word and the soul, delights are true and new; the pleasure is true and not vain. The man who, deceived by its empty shadow, is summoned to the spiritual marriage-feast and says, “I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come” (Luke 14:20), will be condemned. For such people, when they hear bridegroom, bridal chamber, and kiss named, know how to think only of carnal things, because they themselves are carnal.

IV. But because “to the pure all things are pure,” spiritual persons too are pure and desire to be made still purer; in carnal things they understand only spiritual realities. Thus, in the bridegroom they understand God as the lover of the rational creature; in the bride, the rational creature itself, chosen among angels and human beings; in the love by which God loves that bride, the Holy Spirit; and in the seed by which he makes her fruitful, they reverently understand the very Word of God, through whom, just as all things that have been made were made, so all fruitful things are made fruitful.

For since God spoke once, saying, “Let the earth bring forth” (Gen. 1:11), by the power of this word the earth still brings forth green grass and fruit-bearing trees. It brings forth, I say, sometimes when cultivated, and sometimes—more wondrously—when not cultivated. Hence that virginal earth gave its fruit, though no man had cultivated it. “I do not know a man” (Luke 1:4), she said to the angel who announced to her that the Word was to be incarnate in her womb, so as to come forth from it like a bridegroom from his chamber.

V. When I dealt with this chamber in Psalm 17, I indeed used carnal terms, naming the chamber and kiss and other things fitting for a bridal chamber. But I understood, and proposed for the reader to understand, nothing in them except spiritual delights, in which there is not a likeness but the reality of eternal pleasure. From its torrent the true lovers of truth shall drink: they conceive the Word of God by believing in their hearts unto righteousness, and give birth by confessing with their mouths unto salvation.

Above all of these stands that most blessed bride, in whom the same Word of God was conceived and made flesh. Nor should readers of my writings be offended because I called her God’s bride and declared her made fruitful by God’s Word. I did not say this in a sermon to the people, who perhaps could not receive such language, but in an exposition of the psalm suited to spiritual persons, should any of them deign to read our writings.

VI. In the same psalm, where I expounded, “His going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his course reaches to its summit,” I said among other things: “The highest glory which he always possessed in divinity he also obtained in fullest measure for his humanity.” Lest this statement perhaps offend anyone, let him read and understand the statements of the holy Fathers asserting the same thing; and at the same time let him observe that by “humanity” is meant the assumed man, to whom was given the name above every name, so that he may truly be called what he is—namely, God, the only Son of God.

Thus Augustine says in *On the Predestination of the Saints*: “What did this man deserve, that he should be the only-begotten Son of God, assumed into unity of person by the Word coeternal with the Father? What good preceded, that he might attain this ineffable excellence? The man himself, from the moment he began to exist, was made and assumed by God the Word.” Again, the same author says: “Any man becomes a Christian by grace, just as that man was made Christ by grace from the beginning.” Again, in Book XIII of *On the Trinity*: “The grace of God is commended to us because not even he himself attained, by any preceding merits, to becoming, in so great a unity with the true God, one person with him, the Son of God; rather, from the moment he began to be man, from that moment he is also God. Hence it was said: ‘The Word was made flesh.’”

VII. Likewise Hilary, in Book X: “In preaching this timeless and initial generation of the Only-Begotten, surpassing every capacity of human understanding, we have also taught the mystery of God born as man from the Virgin’s childbirth. We have shown that, according to the dispensation of the flesh, when he emptied himself from the form of God and took the form of a servant, the weakness of the human condition did not weaken God’s nature; rather, with the power of divinity preserved in the man, God gained power unto man. For when God was born as man, he was not born so as to cease to remain God, but so that, God remaining, the man might be born into God. For Emmanuel is his name, meaning ‘God with us,’ so that this is not a falling-away of God toward man, but an advance of man into God. Or when he asks to be glorified, this indeed benefits not the nature of God, but the assumption of humility. For he asks for that glory which he had with God before the foundation of the world.”

Again, after some intervening words: “Emptying himself from the form of God and taking the form of a servant, and the Son of God being born also Son of man, without failing in his own power, God the Word brought to completion a living man. For how will the Son of God be the son of man, unless, being born or remaining in the form of God, he took the form of a servant? If the powerful God the Word were not able from himself both to assume flesh within the Virgin and to give a soul to flesh, Christ Jesus would not have been born perfect in our soul and body as man, nor would he have assumed a body such that the body conceived from the Virgin became the form of a servant. For the Virgin bore only what she bore from the Holy Spirit. Although she contributed from herself to the birth of the flesh as much as women ordinarily contribute from themselves to the beginnings assumed for bodies to be born, nevertheless Jesus Christ did not grow together according to the nature of human conception. Rather, the entire cause of his birth, brought in through the Spirit, retained in his human birth what belongs to a mother, while retaining in the origin of that birth what belongs to God.”

VIII. Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*: “Those who are born of the Holy Spirit no one would call children of water; but they are certainly called children of God the Father and of Mother Church. Thus the Son of God the Father obtained birth from the Holy Spirit, not as the son of the Holy Spirit.” And shortly afterward: “Certainly, the manner in which Christ was born from Mary as son, and from the Holy Spirit not as son, shows us God’s grace: by it, at the very beginning of his nature, when he began to exist, a man was joined to the Word of God—without any preceding merits—in so great a unity of person that the Son of God was the same as the son of man, and the son of man the same as the Son of God. Thus, in the assumption of human nature, grace itself in a certain manner became natural to that man, by which he could admit no sin. This grace is represented through the Holy Spirit because he is so properly God as also to be God’s gift. Therefore, in saying that Christ’s birth is from the Holy Spirit, what else is shown but that very grace by which the man was joined and united in a wonderful and ineffable way with the Word of God, and filled bodily with divine grace?”

IX. Observe, prudent reader, that Augustine maintains that the grace by which the assumed man was Christ from the beginning was in a certain manner natural to that man. He rightly says “in a certain manner,” that is, in a wonderful manner. For it occurred not naturally but miraculously that, when the Virgin conceived and believed the word of promise, the true Isaac was born from her—not according to the flesh, as are all sons of the slave woman, the sons of Eve, but according to the Spirit.

And we, who were by nature children of wrath, have been reborn through the same Spirit, so that we may be called and may be children of God. But he became the Son of God not by being reborn, but by being born. Therefore such sonship is natural to that man: namely, that he is thus truly called by birth the Son of God, not adopted, as those are who, having first been children of perdition, curse, wrath, and Gehenna, are afterward called and justified as sons of adoption—not through the nature of generation, but through the grace of regeneration. As Peter says, we have been reborn “not from corruptible seed, but incorruptible, through the word of the living God.”

## CHAPTER XI

What likeness there is between the grace by which God begets his Only-Begotten and that by which he regenerates children of wrath into the adoption of his children. Christ is God’s natural Son in each nature: naturally in his divine nature, but wonderfully in his human nature. What Psalm 98:5 means: “Worship his footstool.”

I. There is a certain likeness between the grace by which God begets his Only-Begotten and that by which he regenerates children of wrath into adoption as his children. For just as “of his own will he begot us by the word of truth, that we might be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures,” so he also voluntarily begot the new man, who was created according to God, that he might be his Son and Word; for “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

And just as, in the sacrament of regeneration, the word comes to the element and the sacrament is made—the sacrament itself becoming in some manner a visible word—so in the sacrament of the generation and conception of Jesus Christ, son of David, the Word came to the element of human flesh, and the great sacrament was made: “which was manifested in flesh, justified in spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:16).

It was truly manifested in flesh, because the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. Remove the word from water: what is water but water? Remove the Word from human flesh: what is flesh but flesh? And such flesh certainly profits nothing. But the Spirit was united to flesh and gave it life, because the Word is spirit, just as the Father and Holy Spirit are spirit. The Word made flesh—that is, made man—proclaimed and believed, is the salvation of believers, those who hope, and those who love. For this is the great sacrament of godliness: to believe the Word incarnate, to believe the man to be the Son of God and therefore natural, because by being born he received that he might be the only Son, just as every Christian receives by being reborn that he may be an adopted son.

II. Just as regeneration does not take away flesh and bones from those reborn in baptism—and, even in the regeneration of bodies unto incorruption, flesh and bones will remain in their nature in the risen saints, though in another glory—so the generation of the new man, who was created according to God, did not take flesh and bones away from him. Therefore he is a foolish reasoner who thinks it follows that, if the man is God’s natural Son, he has neither flesh nor bones.

For if the son of the free woman, whom the Apostle affirms to have been born according to the Spirit, had flesh and bones no less than the son of the slave woman, who was born according to the flesh, how can the Son of the Virgin, truly a free mother, who was born according to the Spirit and conceived from the Holy Spirit, be denied to have flesh and bones? Or why should he be denied to be the natural and only Son of God through such a generation, whose author is God the Father himself? He sent his Word incarnate into the Virgin’s womb, through the working of the Holy Spirit, who is the love of God the Father, so that what was born from her should be called holy, the Son of God.

For if he were God’s Son by adoption, he would not be the only Son, since there are many such sons. Again, people are sometimes called sons by imitation, as in: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (John 8). If the man born of the Virgin were God’s Son in no other way, he would not be the only Son, for there are many sons in that manner too. One of them says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4).

III. Since therefore Christ himself is the only Son in each nature, as has been shown above through the authorities already cited, it remains that, just as he is the only Son in each nature, so he is the natural Son of God in each nature: naturally in divinity, because it is natural for all begetters to beget offspring of their own kind, con-natural and consubstantial with themselves; but wonderfully in humanity, because in that nature he is not consubstantial or con-natural with God the Father.

Likewise, since the Virgin bore God and therefore deserved to be called *Theotocos*, that is, Mother of God, God himself, the Virgin’s Son, is not in his divinity consubstantial with his mother, just as he is not consubstantial with his Father in his humanity. Yet he is the same Son of God and son of man, the proper son of each parent: namely, natural Son not by adoption but by generation. This nevertheless is by miracle, not by nature. For nature does not allow that what is begotten should differ in substance or nature from its begetter.

That a mule is born from an ass and a mare, or a leopard from a lion and a panther, is an abuse of nature; yet here consubstantiality of genus is maintained, not identity of nature—if indeed one wishes to understand “nature” as Boethius defines it, teaching that the specified difference of each thing is its nature, as humanity is the nature of a human being, leoninity that of a lion, and bovinity that of an ox. But far be it from us to fit that generation to these natural examples, concerning which it is written: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 13:20).

“For who,” as blessed Gregory says, “is sufficient to investigate how the Word is embodied? How the supreme and life-giving Spirit is animated within the Virgin’s womb? How he who exists is conceived and born?” Truly, this is the unloosenable strap of his sandals: wondrous nature, wondrously clothed, so assumed what it was not that it did not cease to remain what it was.

IV. And what wonder is it if the divine nature, which is wholly immutable, remains what it was in Christ, when even human nature, which is naturally mutable, has now through grace been made immortal and remains immutable in Christ?
