It has indeed been assumed into the glory of divinity, but, as regards its own essence, it has not been assumed through glory itself—according to which [Col. 1111A] the Son himself is also subject to God, who subjects all things to him—so that this subjection belongs to the created nature in the Son of God, not to the glory, power, wisdom, and goodness bestowed upon it without measure through ineffable and immeasurable grace. Photinus did not measure this grace rightly: although confessing Christ to be man, he denied omnipotence to that man. Hence blessed Ambrose, explaining the passage in Luke: “Behold, a leper coming worshipped him, saying, ‘Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.’ And Jesus, stretching out his hand, touched him, saying, ‘I will: be cleansed’” (Luke 5:13), says among other things:

> “He commands because of Arius; he touches because of Manichaeus; he says, ‘I will,’ because of Photinus.”

For Arius asserted that the Son was unequal to the Father; [Col. 1111B] to refute him, Christ commands without first being addressed by any prayer, saying: “Be cleansed.” But because Manichaeus asserted that Christ’s body was phantom-like, such that it could neither be touched nor touch, he rightly touches, because of Manichaeus. And because of Photinus he says, “I will,” in order to show that, though man, he is nevertheless co-omnipotent with his Father, of whom it is written: “Whatever he willed, he did” (Ps. 113:3).

V. Surely praiseworthy is the faith of this leper, who, falling down, worshipped the man whom he did not doubt to be omnipotent. “Lord,” he says, “if you will, you can cleanse me.” He worshipped not with the worship called *dulia*, such as Scripture records as lawfully rendered even to angels before Christ’s advent. Nathan the prophet also lawfully worshipped [Col. 1111C] King David, though he knew that he was a sinner and had even severely rebuked him for his sin. It was not, I say, with such worship that this leper worshipped the one whom he confessed to be omnipotent, but with that supreme worship with which the Creator alone is to be worshipped. And rightly so: for this man, though thus created, is so united to the Creator that he is the one Son of God and consequently is to be worshipped as God. Hence we read: “Worship his footstool, for it is holy.”

VI. Blessed Augustine, as some maintain, interprets the Lord’s footstool as the assumed man; and he says that it too is to be worshipped, because he whose footstool it is is holy. But blessed Jerome, not ignorant of the Hebrew truth, does not say [Col. 1111D] “for it is holy,” but “for it is made,” namely the footstool itself. Yet he forbids this to be understood of the assumed man, interpreting the Lord’s footstool either as the places where his feet stood or as the blessed souls in whom his footprints are perceived. He teaches rather that the assumed man should be called a throne than a footstool, speaking thus:

> “What is this footstool of Jesus’ feet, ‘for it is holy’? We read in this place: ‘Heaven is my throne, but earth is the footstool of my feet’; and now it is said: ‘Worship his footstool.’ If earth is the footstool of Jesus’ feet, and it is said, ‘Worship his footstool,’ then earth is to be worshipped. How can this be, when we read in the Apostle that, apart from the Creator, we ought not to worship a creature? In the Scriptures [Col. 1112A] ‘to worship’ is used in two ways. There is worship as directed toward God, and there is worship of God. Properly speaking, worship is directed toward God. But when it is used of a human being—for example, Sarah worshipped Abraham, and Elijah worshipped the utterly impious King Ahab—it is not said that Elijah worshipped Ahab as God; rather, this worship signifies a greeting. Let us therefore now consider what is meant by the words, ‘Worship his footstool.’ In what sense are we said to worship the footstool of God’s feet? Do we worship it as God, or greet it as a human being? We read in the Lamentations of Jeremiah, and also in another prophet, how, he says, the Lord sanctified the footstool of his feet; and there his footstool is called Jerusalem or the Temple. Therefore, according to the historical sense, [Col. 1112B] we read also elsewhere: ‘Worship his footstool’; but feet do not stand except upon a footstool. Thus the saying, ‘And worship where his feet stood,’ is also said concerning the footstool. Therefore according to the letter we can say, for example, where he was born, where he was crucified, where he rose again. We say this for beginners. But the footstool of Jesus’ feet is the soul of the believer. Blessed is the person in whose breast Jesus’ feet are daily set. Would that Jesus’ feet might be set in my breast also! Would that his footprints might always cling in my heart! Would that I too might say with the bride: ‘I will hold him and not let him go’ (Song 3:4). The Bridegroom is quickly offended; he always loves cleanliness; wherever he sees filth, he quickly departs. ‘Worship [Col. 1112C] his footstool, for it is holy.’ Not every footstool of his feet, but whatever is holy—namely, all who persevere in holiness. For example: worship his footstool, Peter and Paul and the other apostles; that is, honor them, because it is holy. Worship those who persevere in holiness. But do not worship those who were footstools and are not holy. For example, Judas the betrayer was his footstool; but because he is not holy, do not worship him.”

VII. “I read in a certain man’s book,” he says, “*assumptio* [perhaps *assumptionem*, ‘the assumption’] of the human body—that is, the man whom he deigned to assume from Mary—I call that very man the footstool of his feet. Although the man was indeed assumed, and in comparison [Col. 1112D] with God every creature is the footstool of his feet, nevertheless this very footstool is united with God and is of his *essens* [being/person]. See what a thing I dare to say. I worship the footstool which once was as I now worship the throne. For although we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him according to the flesh. Perhaps he had a footstool before his death, before his resurrection, when he ate, when he drank, when he underwent our conditions. After he rose, he ascended victoriously to heaven. I do not understand one thing as seated and another as a footstool; rather, in Christ the whole is a throne. You ask and say: why or how? How it is, I do not know; yet I believe that it is. Do you wonder that I do not know the mysteries of divinity, when I do not know myself? You ask me how [Col. 1113A] divinity and incarnation are one, when I do not know how I live? To have understood God is to have believed; to know God is to honor him. It is enough for me to know what is written. It is enough for me to know what I believe. Beyond this I neither will nor desire. For if I should wish to know more, I begin to lose even what I believe. We are called believers, not reasoners. Finally, the Lord says: ‘Do you believe that I can do this?’ And it is said to the woman: ‘Your faith has saved you’—not reason, not inquiry, not why or how it happened, but because she believed.”

Thus far Jerome.

## CHAPTER XII

An exposition from Augustine of the same Davidic verse. In worshipping Christ, neither the man is to be separated from God nor God from the man. Letter of Bruno, bishop of Strasbourg, commending Gerhoh’s treatise to [Col. 1113B] Pope Adrian.

I. Augustine, moreover, says on the same psalm:

> “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship his footstool,” etc. (Ps. 98:5). What are we to worship? His footstool. A footstool is called a *suppedaneum*. What the Greeks call *hypopodion*, the Latins have called *scabellum*, and others have called *suppedaneum*. But see, brothers, what he commands us to worship. Elsewhere in Scripture it is said: ‘Heaven is my seat, but earth is the footstool of my feet’ (Acts 7:49). Does he therefore command us to worship the earth because elsewhere he says that it is God’s footstool? And how shall we worship earth, when Scripture openly says, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone’ [Col. 1113C] (Matt. 4:10), while here it says, ‘Worship his footstool’? Yet, explaining to me what his footstool is, it says: ‘But earth is the footstool of my feet.’ I have become uncertain: I fear to worship the earth, lest he who made heaven and earth condemn me. Again, I fear not to worship the footstool of my Lord’s feet, because the psalm says: ‘Worship his footstool’ (Ps. 98:5). I ask what his footstool is, and Scripture tells me: ‘But earth is the footstool of my feet.’ In my perplexity I turn to Christ, because I seek him here; and I find how earth may be worshipped without impiety, how his footstool may be worshipped without impiety. For he took earth from earth, because flesh is from earth, and he took flesh from the flesh of the Virgin Mary. And because [Col. 1113D] he walked here in that very flesh, and gave us that very flesh to eat, while no one eats it unto salvation unless he has first worshipped it, a way has been found by which such a footstool of the Lord’s feet may be worshipped; and not only do we not sin in worshipping it, but we sin in not worshipping it. But does flesh give life? The Lord himself says, when speaking of this same commendation of earth: ‘It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing’ (Mark 6:64).”

II. Having set forth these remarks concerning the footstool which is Christ’s flesh and is truly to be worshipped, Augustine adds concerning the other footstool, this earth which we tread, as follows:

> “Therefore, when you bend and prostrate yourself toward any earth, you do not regard it as earth, but him whose [Col. 1114A] footstool is what you worship; for you worship on account of him.”

In these words of Augustine it is clear that worship of the footstool is not to be understood properly when you bend and prostrate yourself upon any earth—for example, upon the pavement of the consecrated house of the Lord. When you kiss that ground, you do not worship it with the worship with which God alone is to be worshipped; yet you honor it on account of him whose footstool it is understood to be, especially in holy places where his bodily feet stood—for example, on the Mount of Olives, or in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, or at Bethany. These holy places, certainly, some caress with bodily kisses and many with spiritual ones: worshipping there not the places themselves but Christ, while venerating the traces of his feet. But where the object contemplated is not earth beneath heaven, but [Col. 1114B] that which, above the heavens, in the one person of the Trinity, is exalted over all created things, far be it that in its worship it should be distinguished from the divinity united to it, or divinity from it! For Augustine neither thought nor taught this; and the Council of Ephesus forbids this very thing under anathema.

III. To this is added, and it agrees sufficiently with our meaning, what is read in Jerome’s words quoted above: “This very footstool is united with God and is of his *essens*.” In these words, following the idiom of Greek speech, he used *essens* for the person of Christ, existing from two or in two natures, namely divine and human, inseparably united in himself. From this it is clear that God-man and man-God, the one Jesus Christ, third person in the Trinity, subsisting from two and in [Col. 1114C] two natures, is to be worshipped with one worship, as the Council of Ephesus defined above, condemning by anathema those who distinguish worship of the man from worship of God. Without doubt, those incur this anathema who say that *dulia* is to be offered to the assumed man, but the highest *latria* to God. Of this number is that blasphemer who inserted into his writings against us corrupted words of Augustine, affirming, as though on Augustine’s authority, that anyone who worshipped with the worship called *latria* the man assumed by the Word—worship which is due to the Creator alone—must be considered an idolater.

IV. But with the aforesaid leper we worship Christ, not half but whole: namely, the God who assumes [Col. 1114D] and the man who is assumed. For, as blessed Augustine says in the book *On the Trinity*, “Such was that assumption as to make man God and God man.” Again, he says: “Both are God because of the one receiving; both are man because of the one received.” Thus one leprous man rightly worshipped the man-God then; and now that great leper—the unclean world, needing to be cleansed or already cleansed of the leprosy of idolatry—rightly worships the omnipotent and most high man, the Son of God almighty and most high. In him, God exalted and man exalted are not two Most Highs, but one Most High, to be worshipped inseparably and indivisibly: not man on account of God, but man in God and God in man. Hence John of Damascus:

> “Christ is one, [Col. 1115A] perfect God and perfect man, whom we worship with the Father and the Holy Spirit with one worship. We do not say that his flesh is not to be worshipped; for it is worshipped in the one person of the Word. We do not worship a creature, since we do not worship it as bare flesh, but as united to divinity.”

V. Ambrose says thus in the book *On the Trinity*:

> “Therefore we say that he was made man, and this must be referred to his manhood. Thus elsewhere we have: ‘Who was made to him from the seed of David according to the flesh’ (Rom. 1:3). According to the flesh, certainly, David’s descendant was made from seed. Yet ‘being made’ is not always referred to creation. For it is written: ‘Lord, you have become a refuge to us’ (Ps. 89:1).”

And a little later:

> “Therefore, if ‘being made’ is frequently [Col. 1115B] referred to something other than making, we understand that here the text written concerning the Lord’s incarnation, ‘The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works,’ signifies that, for the redemption of the Father’s works, the Lord Jesus was created from a virgin.”

Again, in the same work:

> “Paul forbids me,” he says, “to serve a creature, and instructs me that Christ is to be served. Therefore Christ is not a creature. Paul says: ‘A servant of the Lord Jesus Christ’ (Rom. 1:1). He is a good servant who recognizes his Lord; the very creatures forbid us to serve them. How, then, would Paul himself serve Christ if he considered Christ a creature? See therefore how he affirms that Christ was made and created in one respect, yet denies that he is [Col. 1115C] a creature.”

Likewise, in the same book, he attests that Christ is not an adoptive but a natural Son, saying:

> “We are called sons by adoption; he is Son by the truth of nature. How, then, is he from nothing who made all things from nothing? Thus we ought, according to the testimonies of Scripture, to shape the traces of faith, so that to right belief we may join the purity of sincere confession; and in Christ may believe in our hearts and confess with our mouths not only the uncreated divine nature, higher than heaven and the powers of heaven, most high, and no longer to be reckoned among creatures, but also to be worshipped above all creatures with the same worship with which God the Father is worshipped.”

For in the holy Council of Ephesus we read that it is forbidden under anathema for anyone to say that Christ’s humanity is to be co-worshipped with the Word of God [Col. 1115D]. The holy Fathers in that council proclaim it to be worshipped with a single worship, in which man is not distinguished from the Word. Rather, Emmanuel, one from two and in two natures, God blessed above all things, is to be worshipped. Again, in the book *Ecclesiastical Definitions*, attributed by some to Augustine and by others to Isidore, it is read that the Son is *homoousios* with the Father in divinity, and the Holy Spirit *homoousios* with the Father and Son; that the one Son is *homoousios* with God and man, remaining God in his man, desirable to be seen in the glory of God the Father by angels. As the Father and the Holy Spirit are worshipped by angels and every creature, so too he is worshipped: not man on account of God, nor Christ together with God, as Nestorius blasphemes, but man in God and God in man.

I. Concerning this worship and other questions now briefly touched upon [Col. 1116A], we have said so much in our treatise addressed to Pope Adrian that it seems unnecessary to repeat it, since what is found there can satisfy the kindly reader. Reading that treatise satisfied also the lord Bruno, of blessed memory, formerly bishop of Strasbourg, a prudent man, vigorously learned. To our writings, read and understood, he also kindly replied by a letter, whose text is as follows.

VII. “To Lord G., provost, a religious and learned man: B., a sinner, may you eat of the hidden manna. Amid the grievous pressures and manifold tumults of a falling world, which sweeps its lovers along with it, I have read your writings as far as I could. I have observed your zeal, your studies, your struggle, and your learning; and [Col. 1116B] I judged that what the queen of the south said of King Solomon ought to be declared concerning you truly and confidently. Namely, that the report which speaks of your merits is less than the treasure of wisdom disclosed to one who approaches more closely and digs more deeply. John the Baptist knew and pointed out the Lamb of God in one respect, and in another respect did not know what he was to recognize through the dove descending and remaining upon him. Something of that kind has happened to me concerning you: I knew you, but neither as such nor in your fullness. Therefore, though I have sampled your writings hurriedly and only upon the surface, I long with great and ardent desire for the favor of receiving your writings and likewise your most sweet presence, [Col. 1116C] so that matters which are hidden or seem to raise questions may be opened, as it were by certain keys, through mutual conference and friendly conversation. May almighty God preserve for many years your well-being, and that of all who live with you in Christ, mindful of us.”

VIII. I have inserted this letter for this reason: that it may thereby be known that in the church of Bamberg, where we are now assailed with disputes, we once had a place of rest in the lodging of a lord and friend then most faithful, whose memory is a blessing to me. By contrast, the memory of that other man is a curse to many, who recently spewed out in the same church writings full of lies and blasphemies against us. Yet that noble church rejected them, just as the bishop of Passau also despised the same writings when sent to him. Likewise, when he sent his blasphemies to the church of Salzburg, to the lord archbishop, that malicious man and his writings—fit to be erased, since they contain many lies against us and even pervert the rule of faith—were reduced to nothing in the archbishop’s presence. By this rule we are taught that the man-God is to be worshipped with the worship of highest veneration, together with and in his divinity; in that divinity the Apostle proclaims that man, not among all things, but above all things, to be God blessed for ever.

## CHAPTER XIII

Christ is truly present and to be worshipped in the sacrament of the Eucharist; the author pronounces anathema upon those who deny that the Lord’s body can be [Col. 1117A] simultaneously in two places, such as Folmar after Berengar, whose blasphemies Gerhoh gravely challenges.

I. But to return to the leper mentioned above, the worshipper of Christ and confessor of his omnipotence: such a worshipper should rightly here be set forth as an example for believers who believe that, as Christ was then worshipped in his body, so now he is to be worshipped as present in that same body, able to cleanse one who worships and eats him. Let the world, defiled by the leprosy of sin, therefore believe that Christ Jesus, while remaining bodily in heaven, is nonetheless bodily present in his temple, which is the Church, and nourishes it with his body and blood—not merely sacramentally, as a certain Berengar maintained, [Col. 1117B] and as the aforesaid blasphemer, the follower of that same Berengar, still maintains; but in the reality of the thing itself, so that Christ’s true body, taken from the Virgin, is presented, sacrificed, and eaten upon the altar, and consequently is beneficially worshipped. For, as is read in Augustine’s words set out above, “no one eats Christ’s flesh unto salvation unless he has first worshipped it.” Those who worship it in the sacrament of the altar believe it to be present there and to give life to those who eat it, according to the saying: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). Again: “As the living Father begot me, and I live because of the Father, so he who eats me shall himself live because of me” (ibid., 58). Christ, however, is not eaten except where he is believed to be present. He is now continually presented in his temple, which is the Church, just as he was formerly presented in the Temple, according to the saying: “And immediately the ruler whom you seek, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire, will come to his temple” (Mal. 3:1). The righteous and God-fearing also receive him into their arms, clasping him to themselves with the arms of good works, when they do not receive in vain so great a grace, namely the holy Eucharist, in which they believe the very fountain of grace to be bodily present.

II. Because the aforementioned Berengar denied this, he was compelled in a public council to condemn and abjure this pestilential doctrine of his, and silence was imposed upon him. But now in his place has arisen that blasphemer, aptly called Folmar—as though *follis amarus*, “a bitter bellows”—affirming in speech and writing that the Lord’s body, since it ascended, has never been beneath heaven. When, among other objections, we urged against him that many saints had seen Christ bodily after he ascended into heaven, just as he was bodily seen by Peter when he said to him: “I come again to Rome to be crucified” (Acts 28:14), he said that all this was fabulous and unsupported by canonical Scriptures—perhaps not knowing that what Luke relates in the Acts of the Apostles, namely that the Lord Jesus Christ after his ascension was seen and heard by the apostle Paul, ought to be counted among canonical Scriptures. Hence Paul himself says: “Have I not seen our Lord Jesus Christ?” [Col. 1118A] And Ananias says to him: “The Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road, has sent me to you, that you may see and be filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 9:7). But our greatest authority rests in the faith of the universal Church and in the writings of the orthodox Fathers—Ambrose, Hilary, Augustine, and Gregory. Since their sayings are very well known, we do not think it necessary to insert them.

III. This, however, must be carefully observed: although the condition of human nature is found to be distinguished in many ways by the holy Fathers—namely, as it is understood before sin, after sin, and after restoration—the assumed man possessed something from all these distinct conditions. He was without sin, which belonged to the condition of creation [Col. 1118B]; he bore the penalties of sin in likeness to a sinner; and he could not sin, in likeness to the saints confirmed after the resurrection. Yet beyond all such conditions he possessed that by which he could blot out with his blood the sins of those who believe in him—a thing surpassing every condition of the whole human nature lost in Adam. For neither Abel’s blood nor the blood of all the righteous slain before him for righteousness’ sake could take away sin. Again, blessed Gregory distinguishes flesh in three ways: according to sin, as in: “My spirit shall not remain in human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3); according to corruption, as in: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor shall corruption possess incorruption” [Col. 1118C] (1 Cor. 15:50); and according to nature, as in: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6)—using the name “flesh” to signify the whole human being. This is quite commendable against those who disputed against the resurrection of the flesh, the foremost of whom was the patriarch of Constantinople, refuted by blessed Gregory himself when he was then legate in the imperial city.

IV. Yet beyond all these distinctions of flesh is that flesh which, free from sin and corruption—that is, decay—though naturally flesh was and is nevertheless above every nature of human flesh, so that it not only itself lives eternally but also grants eternal life to those who partake of it, having life abiding in itself and abiding of itself [Col. 1118D]. Hence that which the Church receives as most holy upon the altar must not be called the body of a man, as the heretic Nestorius wished, but the body of the Lord. Because the aforementioned Nestorius denied this, he was condemned along with his doctrine in the Council of Ephesus. In refutation of that same pestilential doctrine, the orthodox Fathers said and left in writing:

> “We approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, having become partakers of the body and precious blood of Christ, the Redeemer of us all: not receiving common flesh—far be it!—nor the flesh of a man sanctified and united to the Word by a unity of dignity, or as one possessing a divine indwelling; but truly life-giving flesh, made proper to the Word [Col. 1119A] himself. For since he exists naturally as life, being God, and since he has made the flesh properly his own by uniting it to himself, he professed it to be life-giving. Therefore, although he says to us, ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood’ (John 6:54), we must nevertheless not suppose it to be the flesh of a human being, one of us. For how could the flesh of a human being be life-giving according to its own nature? Rather, it has truly become the proper flesh of him who for our sakes was both made and called Son of Man.”

Again:

> “If anyone denies that Christ’s flesh is life-giving, as being that of the very Word of God, but regards it as the flesh of some other person besides him, joined indeed according to dignity, or as one possessing only a divine indwelling; and does not rather [Col. 1119B] confess it to be life-giving, as we have said, because it has become the proper flesh of the Word of God, to whom it is possible to give life to all things: let him be anathema.”

V. Therefore let those be anathema and alien from the holy Church who suppose the Lord’s living and life-giving body to be so enclosed in some single place of heaven and, in a manner—horrible to say—imprisoned, that it cannot at one and the same moment be wholly in many places, as it wills and as human salvation requires, for which reason that body was assumed into God. Blessed Jerome, writing against Vigilantius—indeed, Dormitantius, “the Sleeper”—mocks their intelligence, or rather stupidity, and says among other things:

> “Read the Gospel: ‘God of Abraham, [Col. 1119C] God of Isaac, God of Jacob; he is not God of the dead but of the living.’ If, then, they live, how are they shut up in an honorable prison? For you say that the souls of the slain apostles and martyrs sit either in Abraham’s bosom, or in a place of refreshment, or beneath God’s altar, and cannot be present at their own tombs or wherever they wish. They are evidently of senatorial rank, so that they may be confined not among murderers in the foulest prison, but in free and honorable custody, in the Isles of the Blessed and the Elysian Fields. You lay down laws for God; you put chains on the apostles, so that they are held in custody until the day of judgment and are not with their Lord, of whom it is written: ‘They follow the Lamb wherever he goes’ (Rev. 14:4). If the Lamb is everywhere, then those who are acknowledged to be with him must also be believed to be everywhere. And while [Col. 1119D] the devil and demons, who roam throughout the whole world, are everywhere present with exceeding swiftness, will martyrs, after shedding their blood, be shut up under an altar and unable to depart from there? In your little book you say that while we live we can pray for one another, but after we have died no one’s prayer for another is to be heard—especially since martyrs, while still in the body, can pray for others when they must still be concerned for themselves. How much more can they do so after crowns, victories, and triumphs? One man, Moses, obtains pardon from God for six hundred thousand armed men; Stephen, the imitator of his God and first martyr in Christ, prays for pardon for sinners. After they have begun to be with Christ, will they have less power? The apostle Paul [Col. 1120A] says that two hundred and seventy-six souls in a ship were granted to him; and after he begins to be released so as to be with Christ, will he then close his lips and be unable to utter prayer for those throughout the world who have believed his Gospel? And will Vigilantius, a living dog, be better than that dead lion? You would rightly urge this from Ecclesiastes if I confessed Paul to be dead in spirit.”

VI. This is Jerome against the Vigilantius—indeed, Dormitantius—of his own time. But we disdain to write against the Folmar, the Dormitantius, of this age. Yet, with the Lord’s favor, we shall write concerning him unless he ceases to chatter malicious words against us—indeed, against Christ, whom he denies to be bodily present in the sacrament of the altar. So far as lies in him, he destroys the faith [Col. 1120B] and hope of the whole Church, which believes that Christ, ascending into heaven and mindful of his promise, will not leave us orphans, but comes to us again, not only in spirit but also in his flesh. Hence Hilary, in the eighth book *On the Trinity*:

> “If the Word truly became flesh, and the man who was born assumed our now inseparable fleshly nature; if he has mingled the nature of his flesh with the nature of eternity in the sacrament of the flesh to be communicated to us; and if we truly receive as food the flesh of the Word in the Lord’s Supper, how is he not to be thought to remain naturally in us? For we are all one because the Father is in Christ and Christ is in us. Whoever, then, denies that the Father is naturally in [Col. 1120C] Christ must first deny either that he himself is in Christ or that Christ is in him; for the Father in Christ and Christ in us make us one in them. Therefore, if Christ truly assumed the flesh of our body, and that Christ is truly man, and we truly receive under the mystery the flesh of his body, then through this we shall be one, because the Father is in him and he is in us. How, then, can a unity of will alone be asserted, when the natural property given through the sacrament is the sacrament of perfect unity? We must not speak of God’s things by human or worldly understanding, nor by a forced and imprudent exposition of heavenly sayings must perversity be wrested into an alien and impious interpretation. For if we have not learned from him what we say concerning the natural reality of Christ in us [Col. 1120D], we speak foolishly and impiously. He himself says: ‘My flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him’ (John 6:56). No room has been left for doubt concerning the reality of flesh and blood. For now, both by the Lord’s own declaration and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood; and when received and drunk, these make us be in Christ and Christ be in us. Christ is therefore in us through flesh. But that we are in him through the sacrament of the flesh and blood communicated to us, he testifies when he says: ‘But you will see me; because I live, you also shall live. Because I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you’ (John 14:19). If he had wished only unity of will to be understood, why did he set forth [Col. 1121A] a certain order and progression for the consummation of unity? Unless it was so that, as he was in the Father through the nature of divinity, we in turn might be believed to be in him through his bodily birth, and he again in us through the sacrament; and thus perfect unity through the mediator might be taught: while he remained in the Father, we remaining in him, he might remain in us; and so we might advance to unity, because we too should naturally be in him in whom that which exists naturally according to birth exists, he himself naturally remaining in us. But he himself testifies how natural his humanity is in us: ‘He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him’ (John 6:55). For no one will be in him unless he is in the one in whom Christ himself is [Col. 1121B], having in himself only the assumed flesh of the one who has taken his own flesh.”

## CHAPTER XIV

Further concerning the vices and heresy of Folmar, who utterly denies that Christ is present in the Mass on the basis of a misinterpreted and corrupted passage of Augustine.

I. I rejoiced in the things said by holy Hilary against the bitter bellows, not yet born—indeed not yet cast forth from the womb of Mother Church, or even from the womb of a religious community—though he falsely bears the name of a regular canon. For he lives contrary to the Rule, which says: “In your walking, standing, and all your movements, let nothing be done that may offend the sight of anyone; but let everything befit your holiness.” We ourselves have seen how unseemly his tonsure is; and from others we have heard enough concerning his vain and wandering conduct. Therefore we not undeservedly say that he has been estranged from his mother’s womb. Unless he ceases to utter the perverse things he utters, he is truly one of those of whom we sing: “They went astray from the womb; they spoke falsehood,” and the rest down to, “Fire fell upon them and they did not see the sun” (Ps. 57:4). But those saw it who could say: “We have seen his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Peter saw that same sun, still clothed in the cloud of mortality, when, asked concerning the Son of Man, he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). And now, with the veil of mortality removed, Folmar the bat, unable to see this radiant sun of righteousness, dares to contend against eagles who gaze with the clear sight of faith upon this sun, shining not only in heaven but also on earth and imprinting the radiance of his brightness upon pure and clean hearts as upon well-polished mirrors. Thus one of them is recorded to have said: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). But did Christ speak in Paul alone, or dwell in him alone?

II. Hear Pope Leo in his sermon to the people: “There is no doubt, dearly beloved, that human nature has been assumed by the Son of God into so great a union that not only in that man who is the firstborn of all creation, but also in all [Col. 1122A] his saints, Christ is one and the same; and, as the head cannot be divided from the members, so the members cannot be divided from the head. For although it belongs not to this life but to eternal life that God may be all in all, nevertheless even now he is the undivided inhabitant of his temple, which is the Church, according to what he himself promised, saying: ‘Behold, I am with you all the days of life, until the consummation of the age’ (Matt. 28:20). To this the Apostle adds: ‘He is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that he may hold the primacy in all things, because it pleased [God] that all fullness should dwell in him, and that through him all things should be reconciled in him’ (Eph. 3:19). Again: ‘Therefore, dearly beloved, embracing the one pledge of Christian hope, let us not be torn away from the [Col. 1122B] compact unity of Christ’s body, in whom, as the Apostle says, all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, and you are filled in him’ (Col. 2:9). For, since the substance of God is incorporeal, how does it dwell bodily in Christ, unless the flesh of our race has become the flesh of the Godhead, so that in him we may be filled with God?”

III. The aforementioned Folmar, however, is said to rely upon Augustine’s words in writing to Dardanus, where Augustine instructs him how he should think of Christ according to the reality of his body remaining in a particular place in heaven. But I am astonished that Folmar does not attend to what is there stated beforehand and demonstrated by careful argument: that the same Christ is in his temple, which is the Church, which is his body. For that blessed man nowhere [Col. 1122C] said or wrote that the Lord’s body is shut up in heaven, when in very many places he affirms that it is present in the Mass. Thus, in his sermon on the Lord’s body, he says among other things:

“Recall the name and consider the truth. For it is called *missa* [Mass], because the heavenly messenger comes to consecrate the life-giving body, in accordance with the priest’s words: ‘Almighty God, command these things to be borne by the hands of your holy angel to your sublime altar,’ and so forth. Therefore, unless the angel comes, it cannot rightly be called a Mass. For if a heretic should dare to usurp this mystery, does God send an angel from heaven to consecrate his offering? Especially since by the prophet he threatens such persons, saying: [Col. 1122D] ‘I will curse your blessings’ (Mal. 2:2). But if he declares that he will curse their blessings, what then will become of the sacrifice? Shall we therefore say that one can be blessed by him whom we know will be cursed by God together with his blessing? For if God curses and a simoniac blesses, which of them will prevail? Can the blessing of one who is cursed reduce to nothing the utterly true words of God who threatens?”

Again, Augustine, *On the Words of the Gospel*: “When Christ is eaten, life is eaten. But who would dare eat his Lord? Yet, inviting us to eat, he says: ‘He who eats me lives because of me’ (Matt. 6:58). Christ is not killed in order to be eaten; rather, though dead, he gives life. When eaten, he refreshes; he is not diminished. [Col. 1123A] Eaten, he lives; slain, he rose. Nor, when we eat, do we make parts of him—yet this is so in the sacrament.

“Again: The faithful know how they eat Christ’s flesh: each receives his own part; hence the graces themselves are called ‘parts.’ He is eaten in parts and remains whole and entire. He is eaten in parts in the sacrament and remains whole and entire in heaven; he remains whole and entire in your heart. Therefore these are called sacraments, because one thing is seen in them and another is understood.

“Again, *On the Words of the Gospel*: What is it to eat Christ? It is not merely to receive his body in the sacrament—for many receive it unworthily—but to remain in him and to have him remaining in oneself. For he eats spiritually who remains in the unity of Christ [Col. 1123B] and of the Church, which the sacrament signifies. But one who is at discord with Christ neither eats Christ’s flesh nor drinks his blood, even if daily he receives, unto judgment, the sacrament of so great a reality.”

IV. From these passages it follows that Christ’s body is made present only in the Church, where the Mass is celebrated by Catholic priests according to the ecclesiastical rite.

> [Note: [Col. 1123D] As we have elsewhere warned with regard to this author, these statements must be received with a grain of salt. What is properly said concerning fruit and benefit seems to be transferred by Gerhoh rather boldly [Col. 1124D] to the reality itself. Yet allowance must be made for the zeal of a man living in times sufficiently calamitous.]

Among their fellowship are not counted simoniacs, persons interdicted under excommunication, namely Nicolaitan priests and the remaining ministers of the altar who are openly incestuous. For *incestus* means fornication committed not only with a blood-relative but also with a consecrated person. The excessive number of such incestuous persons and simoniacs makes these times dangerous, [Col. 1123C] in which uncleanness and Simony reign, like unclean Jezebel, according to her name, which is interpreted “dung-heap” or “flow of blood,” and her daughter Athaliah tyrannizing in Judah. For just as she, except for one little child secretly removed, killed all the royal seed so that she alone might reign in Judah, so now Simony destroys legitimate government so that it alone may reign in the Church, while persons who have sought and obtained divine offices simoniacally and ambitiously, though interdicted and anathematized, celebrate them. God does not regard their sacrifices, since Moses said to God of such persons: “Do not regard their sacrifices” (Num. 16:15). Therefore, just as the unlawful sacrificers then perished, so their like will now perish unless they repent. Let Folmar, [Col. 1123D] condemned and anathematized by the Synod of Ephesus, beware lest he celebrate Mass. In it, like another Berengar, condemned with the followers of his teaching, he denies that the Lord’s body is true, asserting that it exists only in heaven and nowhere else until the Day of Judgment, when the age shall end.

V. I think that this deceiver has himself been deceived by Augustine’s words in his commentary on John: “The Lord is above, yet the Lord who is truth is also here with us. For the body in which he rose can be in one place; but his truth is everywhere.” Corrupt manuscripts read, “must be in one place.” By the word *must* (*oportet*) some introduce a kind of necessity, as though it must—that is, it is necessary—to understand that the Lord’s body is only in some one secret place in heaven and cannot, at one and the same instant, be wholly present in many places. Against this, holding to the true, uncorrupted [f. letter] reading, we maintain with Augustine that Christ’s body can be in one place in heaven; yet his truth, that is, his divinity, is everywhere. His truth also—that is, his true body—is on every altar wherever Mass is celebrated within the Catholic Church. Hence Augustine himself, in Prosper’s book of *Sentences*: “This is what we say, what we strive by every means to establish: the sacrifice of the Church is constituted of two things, consists of two things—the visible [Col. 1124B] species of the elements, and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body. Therefore there is sacrament and reality of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body.” Again, in a sermon on the words of the Gospel: “As true flesh was created by the Spirit without sexual intercourse, so by the same Spirit, from the substance of bread and wine, the same body and blood of Christ are made.”

VI. By these and similar sayings of blessed Augustine, his well-disposed and attentive readers may be instructed, lest, attending more than is right to his words addressed to Dardanus alone, they suppose that he denies that Christ is bodily in the Church, which he feeds with his body and blood. That body, as corrupt manuscripts have it, [Col. 1124C] “must be in one place,” as though it could not be elsewhere; but, as the more correct manuscripts in our possession have it, “can be in one place,” while nevertheless, insofar as the salvation of the predestined requires, it is lacking to them nowhere. Thus he is also read to have come to the funerals of certain saints; yet one must not believe that he abandoned heaven even while he was seen bodily beneath heaven. Thus blessed Gregory relates that he came at the death of his aunt, Saint Tharsilla. But Folmar calls such things fabulous, contending that he has neither been seen nor will be seen beneath heaven before the Day of Judgment, when he shall appear even to those who pierced him; meanwhile, as Folmar says, he must be in one place.

VII. He has been deceived by the word *must*, where [Col. 1124D] we have *can*. For indeed, he who ascended where he was before can be in one place in such a way that he is by no means confined by the local circumscription of one place, so that his body cannot be bodily present—or rather, inwardly present—to those who eat it, as he himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:55). But whoever, on account of the word *must* just mentioned, introduces necessity, as though Christ’s body, or Christ bodily, must necessarily be confined in one place, relies foolishly on a fragile little branch—namely, a word inserted by falsifiers. When [Col. 1125A] that branch is broken, he will fall into the abyss of perdition, entangled in the heresy of Berengar, deacon of Angers, which was condemned and anathematized by Pope Nicholas together with all followers of that perverse teaching, who deny that the true body of Christ is truly handled, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful upon the altar in the priests’ hands. The said Folmar is shown in his utterances and writings, which he has vomited out against us—or rather, has breathed out like a bitter bellows full of bitterness—to be a follower of this pestilential teaching. Perhaps the wretch thinks himself free to snarl or chatter against us whatever he pleases, because the Apostolic See is now disturbed and Peter’s little ship is shaken.

## CHAPTER XV

Folmar ought to be excluded from correcting and judging the author’s writings; the author declares that he will never be moved from the judgment of the holy Fathers, who affirm that Christ has been exalted to the very seat of the most high God the Father.

I. Forgive, reader, one who speaks sharply and, as it were, rubs with much salt the putrefaction of a foul-smelling error. Do not suppose that I have forgotten what I promised at the beginning of this little work: that I would pour oil over the sacrifice of my writings. For since oil is the true charity of truth, this charity itself is never without that zeal of which it is said: “Love is strong as death; zeal is hard as hell” (Song 8:6). By this stern zeal of charity the heretic must indeed be pursued; and, like a fox destroying the vineyard—that is, the [Col. 1125C] Church of Würzburg—he must be dragged, God willing, from his pit into the light, where he lies hidden weaving deceits at the place called Trufenstain, when the holy Roman Church, as we hope, has peace. For we trust that Christ, who now seems to sleep, will soon rise and command the winds and the ship, so that there may be a great calm.

Then, if the Lord wills and I live, with his help I shall present this little book itself to the Roman pontiff, either personally or through a reliable messenger. Meanwhile, with my rivals—who spread the report that I utterly failed in the conflict at Bamberg—set aside, you know that report to be false, since you were present at that conflict; and after that conflict you asked me to retract certain stumbling-blocks after the example of blessed Augustine, advising rather than commanding. The same was also urged at the counsel of the lord of Bamberg and others who were then, as I thought, friends, though, as I later discovered, not altogether friendly. For through one of them that little book worthy of rejection was written against me, which I have never seen or read, and sent to Lord Peter of Vienna to increase the tearing down of my reputation. I ought not to neglect this reputation, because, as Augustine says, “He who neglects his reputation is cruel.” Therefore whoever the sender of this little book may be, he is not to be admitted as a judge of our writings, but guarded against as a detractor. With rivals of this kind excluded not from reading but from correcting my writings, I shall be content with your judgment, venerable Father Heberard, archpresul of the Church of Salzburg [Juvavum]. [Col. 1126A] If anything in this treatise of mine reasonably displeases you, I shall be prepared, by God’s favoring grace, to amend it for the better. Likewise, in my other little works, whatever I know or shall learn displeases you, I shall not hesitate either to correct, to clarify by a reasonable interpretation, or indeed to remove altogether—while preserving in all things my faith, in which I have learned through orthodox teachers that Christ has been exalted to the seat of the most high God the Father, according to the sayings of the holy Fathers appended below.

II. Pope and martyr Gaius: “Since the Lord Jesus Christ is one, and in him who is one there is one wholly identical person of true deity and true humanity; and since the solidity of this union cannot be separated by any division, we understand that the exaltation by which God, as the Teacher [Col. 1126B] of the Gentiles says, exalted him and gave him the name above every name, belongs to that form which was to be enriched by the proof of so great a glorification. For in the form of God the Son was equal to the Father, and between the Begetter and the Only-begotten there was no distinction of essence, no diversity of majesty; nor had anything been diminished from the Word through the mystery of the incarnation which would have to be restored to him by the Father’s gift. But the form of a servant, by which the impassible Godhead fulfilled the sacrament of great piety, is human humility, raised into the glory of divine mercy; from the very conception of the Virgin, deity and humanity being joined in so great a unity that divine acts were not performed without the man, nor human acts without God. [Col. 1126C] Therefore, just as the Lord of majesty is said to be exalted.”

III. This same statement of Pope Gaius is found in the creed of Pope Leo addressed to Saint Flavian against Eutyches and Nestorius, which blessed Pope Gregory wonderfully praises in his letters, saying: “Whoever adds to or subtracts from the faith of holy Pope Leo, or does not wholly embrace it down to a single atom, is not merely not to be called a bishop, but must be punished with everlasting anathema.” Leo himself says in his exposition of this faith: “Neither was the Word changed into flesh nor the flesh into the Word; but each remains in the one, and one is in each: neither divided by diversity nor confused by mixture; neither one from the Father and another from the mother, but the same one differently [Col. 1126D] from the Father before every beginning and differently from the mother at the end of the ages, so that the man Christ Jesus might be mediator between God and human beings, in whom the fullness of deity might dwell bodily. For it is the advancement of the assumed, not of the one assuming, that God exalted him and gave him the name above every name. Nor does it matter from which substance Christ is named, since, while the unity of his person remains inseparable, the same one is wholly Son of Man because of the flesh and wholly Son of God because of the deity one with the Father. There is no falsehood in this unity, while both the humility of humanity and the height of deity are mutually present. For as God is not changed by compassion, so the human being is not consumed by dignity. Each form acts in communion with the other what is proper to it: [Col. 1127A] namely, the Word performs what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carries out what belongs to the flesh. Although in the Lord Jesus Christ there is one person of God and man, nevertheless that from which the glory common to both arises is different.”

IV. Again, Pope Leo says in a sermon to the people: “The eternal Son of God, remaining in the form of a servant, unchangeably and timelessly possessing no other being than the Father, received the form of a servant without loss to his majesty, so that he might advance us in what is his, not fail in what is ours. Hence so great a communion of unity has been made between the two natures remaining in their properties that whatever is divine there is not separated from the human being, and whatever is human is not divided from the Godhead.” Again: “Let the poisonous falsehoods of diabolical inspirations be far from our hearts, dearly beloved. Knowing that the Son’s eternal deity increased by no addition with the Father, wisely consider that the nature to which it was said in Adam, ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall go’ (Gen. 3:19), is the same nature to which it is said in Christ, ‘Sit at my right hand’ (Ps. 109:1). According to that nature by which Christ is equal to the Father, the Only-begotten was never inferior to the sublimity of his Begetter. Nor is the right hand of God the Father temporal, of which Exodus says: ‘Your right hand, O Lord, has been glorified in strength.’ And in Isaiah: ‘Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?’” Again, Pope Leo, in a sermon on the Lord’s Passion: “The Only-begotten of the most high Father entered into such fellowship with human lowliness that, having assumed the substance of our flesh and soul, [Col. 1127C] the one and same Son remained, increasing what was ours, not what was his own. For weakness was to be advanced, not power, so that when the creature was united to its Creator, nothing divine might be lacking to that which was assumed, and nothing human to the one assuming.”

V. In the same author’s sermon on the Holy Spirit: “When the blessed Apostle John says, ‘For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified’ (John 13:31), the Lord’s ascension was the reason for giving the Spirit. He must necessarily deny that the Spirit was given who denies that a true human being in Christ has been advanced to the seat at the Father’s right hand. But we, dearly beloved, let the most sacred feast of this day, which adopts us through the generation of the Holy Spirit to the blessed eternity of both soul and body, be celebrated with rational worship. [Col. 1127D] Let us confess with the blessed Apostle Paul that the Lord Jesus, ascending on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings, so that the Gospel of God may be preached through every expression of human speech, and every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father.”

Again: “For the healing of the wounds of faithful hearts, the marks of the nails and spear were preserved, so that it might be held with faith not uncertain but most steadfast knowledge that the nature which had lain in the tomb would sit upon the throne at the right hand of God the Father.” And a little later: “Then, he says, a more instructed faith began to approach the Son equal to the Father with the step of the mind, and it began no longer to need the bodily touching of Christ’s substance, which is less than the Father, because, while the nature of the glorified [Col. 1128A] body remained, the faith of believers was called to that place where the Only-begotten, equal to the Begetter, was touched not with a fleshly hand but with spiritual understanding.”

Again: “Great and ineffable was the cause of rejoicing when, in the sight of the holy multitude, the nature of the human race ascended above the dignity of all heavenly creatures, about to pass beyond the orders of angels and be raised above the heights of archangels, and to have no limit to its advancement through any heights, unless, received into the fellowship of the eternal Father, it should be joined in the throne to the glory whose nature it was united with in the Son. Therefore, since Christ’s ascension is our advancement, and the hope of the body is called where the glory of the head has gone before, let us, dearly beloved, exult with worthy joys and rejoice with devout thanksgiving. For today [Col. 1128B] we have not only been confirmed as possessors of paradise, but in Christ we have also penetrated the heights of heaven, having obtained through Christ’s ineffable grace things greater than those we lost through the devil’s envy. For those whom the venomous enemy cast down from the happiness of their first dwelling, the Son of God, incorporating them into himself, has placed at the Father’s right hand.”

VI. Hilary, in Book IX of *On the Trinity*: “This is the true faith of human blessedness: to preach God and confess flesh; neither that God should be ignorant that he is also man, nor that the flesh should be unaware that he is the Word. Since God, remaining God, is born a human being contrary to the nature of our perception, it is no longer contrary to the nature of our hope that the human being who has been born should remain God; since the higher nature, born into the lower, affords the lower nature confidence that it can be born into the higher.” And he adds: “Therefore this will be the confession in the glory of God the Father: that what was born in humanity no longer remains in the weakness of our body, but in God’s glory. Every tongue will confess this, and earthly knees will bend with the heavenly.”

Again, Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*: “Whoever is faithful believes that in him true human nature was so exalted by the assumption of God the Word that the one who assumed and that which he assumed became one person in the Trinity, that assumption ineffably bringing about the reality of one person in God and man.” Again, on Psalm 68: “My eyes have failed in hoping for my God. Far be it from us to take this of the person of the head! Far be it that [Col. 1128D] his eyes should have failed in hoping for his God, in whom God was all the more reconciling the world to himself, and because the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, so that not only was God in him, but he himself was God!”

## CHAPTER XVI

The author’s teaching concerning the divine glory of the Son of Man is confirmed by testimonies of both ancient and recent doctors.

I. Ambrose, expounding the passage where the angel says of the Virgin’s son to be born, “He shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke 1:32): “He shall not be great because he was not great before the Virgin gave birth; rather, because the power which the Son of God has by nature was, in time, to be received by the man, so that God and man might be one person.”

[Col. 1129A] II. Bishop Maximus, *On the Nativity of the Lord*: “The Word was made flesh not so that God might be emptied into a human being, but so that the human being might be glorified into God.” Again: “How can a human being comprehend God—the made comprehend the unmade, the mortal the eternal? If you strive to investigate how God passed into a human being, or a human being into God, first investigate, if you can, how the world was made from nothing.” Again: “By an incomprehensible decree and plan, divine offspring proceeds from a mortal woman. Nor is it at all surprising that there was a divine birth where there was no human conception. Therefore God, who was with God, came forth from God; and the flesh of God, which was not in God, proceeded from the woman.”

III. Augustine, *On the Creed*: “When the Father is said [Col. 1129B] to sit, this must not be imagined as sitting with bent knees, lest we fall into that sacrilege in which the Apostle condemns those who changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of corruptible humanity. For it is wicked for a Christian to place such an image in a temple; still more wicked is it to do so in the heart, where the true temple of God is, if it has been cleansed from earthly desire and error. Therefore, when God is said to sit, this signifies not a position of limbs but judicial power, which that majesty never lacks, always giving worthy things to the worthy. His right hand is supreme blessedness, just as his left hand is the misery in which the goats are placed.”

Again, in Book XX, chapter 13, of *The City of God*: “A certain divine power has received the name of a book. For in it, in a certain manner, whatever is remembered through its action is read. As the Apostle says: ‘For we shall all stand before the judgment-seat of the Lord, so that each may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or evil’ (Rom. 14:10), calling the Lord’s judgment-seat the exalted height of his majesty, which will appear to all everywhere in all things. When it is revealed, the wicked will see him whom they pierced, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over themselves.”

IV. Ambrose, expounding: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1): “The Lord, about to fulfill the commandments, concludes the faith and mercy of his covenant with an end. The faith is that we should believe Christ to be God and our Lord, and to sit at God’s right hand—not that he who is everywhere [Col. 1129D] sits bodily. Indeed, he himself is in the Father, because God’s substance is one, power is one, majesty is one. Therefore he himself is in the Father, and the Father in him, because God is in the Word and the Word is in God. He sits in the Father at the Father’s right hand because he shares the Father’s status and is second to none. He is sent by the Father because he descended from the Father’s heaven to fulfill the Father’s will. Remove from this the questions of unbelief, and religion is complete. He is not preferred because he sits at the right hand, nor is he dishonored because he is sent; no rank of dignity is sought where there is fullness of deity.”

V. Bede, expounding “That which the Father gave me is greater than all,” says in a homily: “What the Father gave, greater than all, to the mediator of God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, is this: that he should be [Col. 1130A] his only-begotten Son, in no respect unlike the Begetter in nature, inferior in power, or later in time. This equality the Lord himself had in his divinity with the Father before the world existed; in his humanity he received it from the time of the incarnation.”

VI. Jerome, to Paula and Eustochium, in the sermon *On the Assumption of Saint Mary*: “I beseech you, daughters, do not receive in vain so great and such grace as is in Christ Jesus, in whom God and man are so united in one and the same person that in the divine Scriptures one may often read of the man as coeternal with God because of the union of subsistence, and then of God as suffering compassion with the man; although the human being is not unoriginate, nor is God passible. Yet God is so united [Col. 1130B] to his body that human thought can allow no distance between God and man, lest—God forbid!—one Son of God and another son of man be believed. Especially because Scripture joins and incorporates God and man, so that no one can distinguish the man from God in time, nor God from the man in the Passion.”

VII. Augustine, in the book *Questions on the New Testament*: “Christ, the Son of God, is from eternity according to the Spirit of holiness; but according to the flesh he was born, from David’s seed, Son of God, so that in neither respect may he be considered a Son of God made, but born.” And after some passages: “Therefore the Savior was also born Son of God according to the flesh. For that which is holy, born of the holy, could not be born other than from God.”

[Col. 1130C] Again, in the Epistle to the Romans: “Christ is rightly said not to be predestined according to that in which he is the Word of God, God with God. For why should he be predestined, since he already existed, eternal without end? But that which did not yet exist before time was predestined to come to be in time. Therefore, according to that in which he is man, he was predestined not only to be our head without merits, neither drawing sin by origin nor committing it by will, and to be glorified from mortal nature into immortality, but also to be Son of God in power. From the moment he began to be human, he began to be the unique Son of God. This advancement of human nature, so lofty and supreme, was predestined, so that it had no higher place to which it could be raised. Hence it is also said to have been made according to the Spirit of sanctification. For the only-begotten Son of God was conceived and born not through the desire of flesh but solely by God’s gift.”

VIII. Ambrose: “I have turned and returned to the divine Scripture, and nowhere have I found the Son of God to be adoptive. But as Christ, insofar as he is God, has by nature that he is the natural Son and is God, so insofar as he is man, he has by grace that he is the same natural Son of God.”

IX. These testimonies of the saints have been made exceedingly credible, testifying that holiness befits the house of God not made with hands for length of days. But that they may be believed more firmly, let the testimony of God the Father crying from heaven be added: “This is [Col. 1131A] my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 12:18). Saint Ambrose, expounding in Luke this testimony of the Father commending the Son from heaven, and referring in that same testimony the title “Son” to Christ’s wholly and altogether divine generation, says: “What more evident sign of divine generation is there than that, when he is about to speak of Christ’s generation, he first brings forward the Father himself speaking: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’? When he says, ‘in whom I am well pleased,’ he praises in the Son not what is alien but what is his own.”

Again, in the same work: “He who is the author of faith ought also, Scripture asserts, to be the author of divine generation. Hence Luke judged that Christ’s origin should be referred to God, because God is the true begetter of Christ, either Father according to true generation [Col. 1131B] or author of the mystical gift according to regeneration in the washing. Therefore he did not begin to describe his generation from the first, but after explaining his baptism, wishing through baptism to show God as the author of all things, he also asserted that Christ came from God in the order of succession; weaving the whole together in order to show that, both according to nature and according to grace, he is according to the flesh the Son of God.”

X. With Saint Ambrose saying these things, confirmed by the Father’s own testimony and the good tidings of the faithful Evangelist, a threefold cord is woven by which our party is confirmed and the adversary bound: Christ is shown to be the Son of God also according to the flesh, when his own fleshly and temporal [Col. 1131C] descent is continued upward as far as God. Therefore this man is “fairer in form than the children of men,” having surpassed the nature of all human beings so greatly that the testimony of the Father thundering from heaven properly belongs to his whole person: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” These testimonies of the Fathers concerning the immeasurable glory of the man assumed into God, and his divine magnificence raised above the heavens, could suffice. But since every scribe instructed for the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old, let us add testimonies newly published in our own times to those of the ancients.

XI. Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, expounding John [Col. 1131D] on the testimony of the Father crying from heaven, “This is my beloved Son,” etc., says: “Certainly he did not say this in the beginning, when he created the universe, when he stretched out the structure of heaven or set a boundary to the sea, and, as a marvelous craftsman, arranged all visible and invisible things, distinguishing each in its own place or order. Indeed, all the good things he had made pleased him, because they were very good; yet in none of them did he ever indicate that he himself was well pleased in himself. But in this one he is well pleased in himself and says, ‘I was well pleased,’ which is far different from saying, ‘You pleased me.’ Let us therefore consider what has been done in Christ, and we shall see that the Father rightly was well pleased in him because of the greatness and character of the work. For although God [Col. 1132A] made all things from nothing, he had made nothing altogether like or equal to himself, even though he made the human being in his image and likeness. For it could not be that a creature should be formed like or equal to the uncreated God.

XII. “Therefore the Creator’s good pleasure was not satisfied merely because all the things he had made were very good. For among them all he saw nothing like or equal to himself; rather, as has been said, nothing altogether such as he is could be created. Accordingly, the frail multitude of creatures, being made from nothing, had partly fallen and was altogether unable to restore itself by its own powers. Then that same gentle and benevolent charity of the Father, which had previously appeared in the form of a dove, suggested that he should unite to his creation that very Power, that very Word [Col. 1132B] through whom he had made all things, since he had created nothing equal to himself, and thus bring forth one thing lacking nothing in the order of nature: it would be a creature, though unlike in condition yet equal to the Creator through its assumption and glorification in God. When this was done, omnipotent goodness rejoices, and the dovelike love, ignorant of all envy, applauds itself because by its aid the human creature has been made equal to itself. It judges worthy of praise the fact that it has so aided that needy nature from the riches of its own nature that henceforth it is fit to govern the Father’s whole kingdom, administer the entire commonwealth of heaven and earth, and reign equally with him upon his throne.”

XIII. “He so highly commends this work of his, and judges it so pleasing to himself, [Col. 1132C] that whoever does not find it pleasing, whoever does not behold it with praise and thanksgiving—him he drives away, as ungrateful and truly proud and envious, from his salvation and from the kingdom of this same Christ his Son. Since this kingdom indeed has no end, because it is boundless, its king himself is rightly proclaimed boundless. Conversely, a petty king is so called whose kingdom is cramped, even if he himself should happen to be extended in gigantic stature. But Christ—that is, the man anointed above his fellows as king of the kingdom of all ages—although he appeared a little child in the cradle, now, upon the throne of the Father’s majesty, feeds even the angels by the greatness of his brightness and [Col. 1132D] gives joy to the entire court of the Father. While still mortal, he invited his disciples to this joy, saying: ‘If you loved me, you would surely rejoice because I go to the Father, because the Father is greater than I’ (John 14:28). For since he has never been less than the Father in divinity, it is clearer than light that, when the Son of God said this, he was speaking concerning the nature of man, as though he said: ‘So long as I am mortal man, the Father is greater; but after I pass from this world to the Father—when, namely, my humanity has been exalted to the height of the Father’s glory, from which I have never departed in my divinity—then you shall see me, your Lord and Savior, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death. Therefore, if you loved me, you would surely rejoice that I pass from the exile of the world and enter into the glory of my kingdom, to sit eternally at the right hand of the [Col. 1133A] Father. For up to this point, from the time I put on flesh, he is greater than I; and I, according to the mortality of that flesh, am made a little lower not only than the Father but even than the immortal angels. But after I shall have been exalted to sit with the Father, then what is written shall be fulfilled: “The Lord said unto my Lord,” etc.’ (Ps. 109:1). Likewise: ‘Thou hast crowned him with glory and honor, O Lord; and hast set him over the works of thy hands’ (Ps. 8:6).

XIV. “What great cause of rejoicing there is for those who love Jesus Christ! Great indeed and ineffable. Hence those who refuse to rejoice with the faithful rejoicing over the exaltation of man, already accomplished, up to the Father, are plainly not found to love Christ: [Col. 1133B] they contend that the Son of Man, who is also the Son of God, is still less than the Father in his humanity, however glorified. If they refer this inferiority to the natural condition of humanity, not to its supernatural exaltation, they are rightly tolerated, since in this sense they oppose neither us nor the Catholic faith. But if they judge that the man already glorified into God does not have the same glory, omnipotence, all-wisdom, all-power, and all-majesty as the most high Father, there is no doubt to fear that they will be driven from his kingdom as envious disparagers, destined to share fellowship with him who first envied the height of this Most High, saying in his heart: ‘I will be like the Most High’ (Isa. 11:14).”

[Col. 1133C] XV. Again Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: “The Word was made flesh; and, according to the prophet, ‘All flesh is grass’ (Isa. 40:6). But this grass was by no means dried up, nor did its flower fall away, because the Spirit of the Lord rested upon it. For this reason, indeed, an end once came upon all flesh: because the Spirit of life had departed. Thus he says: ‘My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh’ (Gen. 6:3). By the name ‘flesh’ here we understand vice to be signified, not nature. Therefore because of vice all flesh is grass, and all glory is as the flower of grass. ‘The grass has dried up,’ he says, ‘and the flower has fallen’ (Isa. 40:7); but not that flower which sprang from the rod and root of Jesse, since upon him [Col. 1133D] rested the Spirit of the Lord. Nor that grass which the Word became, because what follows in the prophet is: ‘But the word of the Lord remains forever’ (1 Pet. 1:25). For if the Word is grass, and the Word remains forever, then the grass too must necessarily remain forever. Otherwise how does it bestow eternal life if it itself does not remain forever? For he says: ‘If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever’ (John 6:52). And he makes clear what bread he means when he adds: ‘And the bread which I will give is my flesh for the life of the world’ (ibid.). How then can that by which one lives eternally not itself be eternal? But now recall with me the voice of the Son speaking to the Father concerning himself: ‘Thou wilt not give thy Holy One to see corruption’ (Ps. 15:10). Without doubt he speaks of the body [Col. 1134A] that lay lifeless in the tomb. For the angel also calls this body holy, when he spoke to the Virgin and announced, saying: ‘And that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God’ (Luke 1:35). How, then, could that holy grass see corruption, which arose from the ever-green pasture of an incorrupt womb and is able, by delighting them perpetually and without satiating them, to fix upon itself even the eager gaze of angels? Let the grass indeed lose its greenness, if Mary has lost her virginity. Thus the food of man changed itself into fodder for beasts, man having been changed into a beast. Alas for the sad and tearful change: that man, a dweller in paradise, lord of the earth, citizen of heaven, member of the household of the Lord of hosts, brother of blessed spirits, co-heir of the heavenly powers, should by a sudden transformation find himself [Col. 1134B] lying in a stable because of weakness, in need of hay because of his beast-like likeness, and tied to a manger because of untamed ferocity. As it is written: ‘With bit and bridle bind fast their jaws, those who do not draw near unto thee’ (Ps. 31:9). Recognize, O ox, your possessor; and you, ass, the manger of your lord, so that God’s prophets may be found faithful, who foretold these wonders. Know, O beast, him whom you did not know when you were man; adore in the stable him from whom you fled in paradise; honor the manger whose rule you despised; eat grass as bread, you who spurned the bread of angels.”

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 1134C] While teaching the equality of glory which human nature possesses indivisibly with divine nature in Christ, he by no means confounds the natures with Eutyches. Concerning certain Nestorians at the synod of Friesach.

I. Let these sayings of the ancient and modern Fathers concerning the equality of glory, which human nature possesses indivisibly with divine nature in Christ, suffice. But lest, in proclaiming equality of glory between the divinity which gives it and the humanity which receives it, we seem to confound the natures themselves with Eutyches, let us add a few points distinguishing the nature of the Word and that of flesh.

II. For, as blessed Ambrose says, although we believe that flesh was assumed by the Word, we must nevertheless distinguish the nature of the Word and of flesh. And it is said to us: “If you offer rightly but divide not rightly, you have sinned.” Therefore, although in Christ’s person we venerate such a union [Col. 1134D] of man with God and of God with man that man has communion in divine acts and God in human acts—because, as the authority of Pope Caius and of other saints affirms, human things were not done without God, nor divine things without man—yet the proper character of those acts must be so distinguished that we render to God what belongs to God and to man what belongs to man, in one and the same person performing divine and human acts. Hence, although we read that the Lord of glory was crucified, we properly assign the punishment of the cross to the man, for it cannot fall upon the impassible Lord of glory—whom, nevertheless, as I have said, we read to have been crucified. And although the man says, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18), we properly assign this vision to God, [Col. 1135A] since it took place before man’s creation. By making these distinctions appropriately, we oppose the error of Eutyches, who proclaims only one nature, one will, and one operation in Christ.

III. But behold: while the Scylla of the Eutychian error is avoided, one easily runs into the Charybdis of the two-formed monster of the Nestorian pestilence. Nestorius, opposed to the falsehood of Eutyches but not in harmony with Catholic truth, distinguished Christ excessively and forbade the Blessed Mary to be called *Theotokos* (“God-bearer”). By a deadly error he taught that the assumed man was not to be adored as God, but was to be co-adored in God, for God, with God, as sanctified by the indwelling of divinity. Against him the Council of Ephesus assembled and taught that the man personally united to the Word of God is truly and properly God, and supremely worthy of adoration and every worship proper to divinity: not sanctified by the indwelling of divinity and adopted into divinity, but, as I have said, properly and truly honored by the name of God. Therefore, near the end of the council, one reads: “If anyone dares to teach that the assumed man ought to be co-adored with God the Word, co-glorified, and co-called God, as though one were added to the other”—for the addition of one syllable, namely *co-*, compels this interpretation—“and does not rather venerate Emmanuel with one reverence and render him one glorification, according as the Word was made flesh, let him be anathema.”

IV. Master Hugh, *On the Sacraments*: “Many questions are asked concerning Christ’s soul. One of them is [Col. 1135C] whether it had knowledge equal to divinity. I argued this question at greater length in another small work entitled *On the Soul of Christ*.
