Here it suffices to recall that, just as that soul had the full and perfect wisdom of God united to it, so it was fully and perfectly wise from that wisdom and through that wisdom; yet it was not equal in nature to wisdom itself. For it is one thing to be wise by wisdom and another to be wisdom. From the moment divinity was joined to humanity, humanity received from divinity by grace everything that divinity possessed by nature: so that, according to that ineffable union, everything belonging to humanity was God’s in his humanity, and [Col. 1135D] everything belonging to divinity was man’s in his divinity.”

V. In these words of Master Hugh, the nature of humanity and of divinity is cautiously distinguished, while the wisdom of both natures is undivided. For by saying that “it is one thing to be wise by wisdom and another to be wisdom,” he fittingly shows that Christ’s soul was not equal in nature to eternal wisdom; but he subsequently demonstrates how equal to it in power it was from the very conception of the Virgin conceiving God-and-man, when he adds: “Thus we believe that the humanity of the Word, in its rational soul, received from its first conception, by the ineffable union of divinity, full and perfect wisdom, power, strength, and goodness; [Col. 1136A] and we confess that it remained unchangeably both inseparable in the union of divinity and in that fullness of power which arose from the union.” For God-man did not will to dwell among men in order that, as though advancing in wisdom or power through intervals of time, he might acquire merit for himself and become better than himself; but so that, by the dispensation of human salvation, he might fulfill according to his ineffable ordering that wisdom and goodness which he always possessed full and perfect in his divinity and received full and perfect in his humanity at once and together. Therefore, what the Evangelist says—that Jesus advanced in age, wisdom, and grace—must not be understood as though he became better than himself, but because he increasingly disclosed to men, as the order of times required, the wisdom and grace which he possessed but which lay hidden [Col. 1136B]. Thus he advanced among men insofar as men advanced in knowledge of him; but before God he advanced in that, by showing himself full of the wisdom and grace of God, he continually stirred them more and more to praise God the Father, from whom he testified that he had this.

VI. [Col. 1136C] Having set forth the testimonies of the Fathers, and holding views consonant with them, we do not count Christ among creatures. Rather, we proclaim him God blessed above all creatures and consequently worthy of adoration, made equal to God his Father in all power, set above all adoptive gods and sons, and made so much better than they as he inherited a more excellent name than theirs.

VII. [Col. 1136C] A certain man, wise in his own estimation and great in his own eyes, at the chapter held at Friesach pronounced curses against those who dissented from the faith which he had there recited. Another too, speaking in agreement with him, delivered an oration more scholastically than ecclesiastically. At the time these received a sufficient response from two of our brethren who were present there: approving some things and disapproving others which he said, since they knew how to reject evil and choose good. For his confession that Jesus Christ exists from two natures and in two natures, equal to God the Father according to divinity and less than the Father according to humanity, can be approved [Col. 1136D], as soundly stated and consonant with the Catholic faith. But his denial to the assumed man of omnipotence and the other higher goods of divinity—in which, made equal to God his Father, he now sits and rests and reigns jointly at the right hand of God the Father—wholly agrees with the heresies of Paul of Samosata, Nestorius, and likewise Photinus, condemned and anathematized at the Council of Ephesus, together with all followers of Paul, Nestorius, and Photinus. That such persons had long ago been cursed through the prophet Jeremiah is shown by the illustrious Jerome in his exposition of: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” (Isa. 9:20 ). “If,” he says, “every man who trusts in man is cursed, while Paul of Samosata and Photinus, although they preach the Savior as holy and exalted in every virtue, nevertheless confess him to be a man, then those who place their hope in man will be cursed.” Behold: in the words set down in Jeremiah and expounded by Jerome, our accursed cursers are plainly shown to be cursed, since they curse us because we think differently from Paul and Photinus. By following them the impious Nestorius too deserved to be condemned and anathematized at the Council of Ephesus with the followers of his doctrine—such as many now emerge, like little foxes destroying the vineyard of the Lord of hosts.

VIII. Lest perhaps the curse be directed also at us, as trusting and placing hope in a man, the son of man, Jerome himself defends us and adds this: “But if it should be objected to us [Col. 1137B] that we too believe in him who says: ‘But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth which I heard from God. Abraham did not do this; you do the works of your father’ (John 7:20), we shall answer with the Apostle: ‘Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer’ (2 Cor. 5:16). Finally, the same Apostle writes at the beginning of his Epistle to the Galatians: ‘Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead, and all the brethren who are with me’ (Gal. 1:1). For if death has been swallowed up in victory, why should not the lowliness of flesh, assumed for human salvation, have passed into the majesty of divinity, so that the two might make one, and [Col. 1137C] we might not adore a creature but the Creator, who is blessed forever?”

IX. Since holy Jerome says this, we who adore with the adoration due to God alone that man who is God blessed forever—not among all things, but above all things—are sufficiently cleared of idolatry, as being the Son of the Most High announced by the angel. For when the power of the Most High overshadowed the Virgin, it was not a man’s love but the love of God the Father, namely the Holy Spirit, that worked in her conception, so that what should be born from her would be called the Son of the Most High. “Son,” he says, “of the Most High,” namely of the eternal Father, who, having spoken once, indeed begot him once; but in his one begetting made these two things heard: first, that power belongs to God; second, that mercy belongs to thee, O Lord. Thus you may know that in the one and same Son of God and man the power by which he was created from nothing and the mercy by which he was restored from ruin through that same Son of God and man, the Father’s and Mother’s one only-begotten Son, are to be venerated without dissimilarity.

X. For the Holy Spirit did not work in the Virgin’s womb in such a way as to be there himself in place of seed, as certain false speakers whisper that I think. Rather, while the eternal wisdom of God built itself a house from human flesh, his power and Spirit worked with it in such a manner that this house, raised by seven most high pillars to its own height, was not inferior to the most high Father in its exaltation; although in its created condition, as a creature less than the Creator, it then was and now [Col. 1138A] is inferior, and can never be made equal to him with respect to its created condition. Yet by its ineffable elevation it has been made equal in omnipotence, knowledge, and every glory of the most high divinity, possessing that glory as fully in the human nature which received it in time as in the divine nature which possessed it eternally. For in both natures there is one only Son of God the Father. For the Holy Spirit did not so effect his conception in the Virgin that what would be born from her was the son either of the Holy Spirit or of the eternal Word, but the Son of the most high Father, who uttered his Word into the heart and womb of the Virgin to be incarnate through the working of the Holy Spirit. This operation was indeed also that of the Father and the Word, because the supreme Trinity worked inseparably. For whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does; and whatever the Father or the Son does, the Spirit of both likewise does.

XI. Therefore it is the work of the whole Trinity that the man conceived in the Virgin is Son of the Most High—the Father’s only Son, only-begotten and first-born—exalted infinitely above all blessed angels and men, with that nature now sitting upon the high throne which had lain in the tomb, as great Leo says. For in the nature in which the Son of God was made, he was made so much better than all angels as he inherited a more excellent name than they. For to which of the angels did God say, “Thou art my Son”? Or of which men is it fitting for God to say, “Thou art my Father,” except of this only only-begotten Son, made and begotten by God the Father: [Col. 1138C] made, indeed, not into a living soul as Adam was, but into a life-giving spirit; begotten, moreover, not as an adoptive son but as a proper Son, according to the text: “God did not spare his own Son” (Rom. 8:32). Begotten, I say, and only-begotten, to whom alone it is fitting to say to God: “Thou art my Father.” This is sufficiently clear in the text of the holy Gospel, because wherever he says “my Father” with the possessive pronoun, making himself equal to God, he speaks such things as show him not unequal to God the Father. For example: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5:17). Likewise: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 22:28). “And I appoint unto you a kingdom, as my Father appointed unto me” (Luke 22:29).

[Col. 1138D] XII. Because of sayings of this kind, by which, calling himself the Son of God, he indicated that he was equal to his Father, though he was like us subject to suffering, he was accused by the chief priests and Jews, who said: “We have a law, and according to our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:7). Likewise: “We do not stone thee for a good work, but for blasphemy, and because thou, being a man, makest thyself God” (John 10:32). Likewise the Evangelist says: “Therefore the Jews persecuted him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God.” But elsewhere, where he accommodated himself to his members, he says “Father” without the possessive pronoun, not adding “my.” For example: “That the world may know that I love the Father; and as the Father gave me commandment, so I do” (John 10: [Col. 1139A] 18). Likewise: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (John 10:18). Thus, naming the Father without a possessive expression, he did not make himself equal to the Father; but by observing the Father’s command, he humbled himself as a servant obedient to him in the form of a servant, becoming obedient unto death. And I rightly say “unto death.” For after death God exalted him and gave him the name above every name, that at his name every knee should bend, of beings in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father: God in God’s glory; the only-begotten Son in the Father’s glory, distinguished by ineffable glorification from adoptive gods and sons.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 1139B] He argues against scholastic theologians favoring Paul of Samosata, Nestorius, and Photinus, who maintain that neither the worship of *latria* nor love above all things as God is to be given to the assumed man.

I. Therefore the Photinians and Nestorians of this age vainly detract from the divinity of the man divinely conceived and born, not from bloods, nor from the will of flesh, nor from the will of a man, but from God into true God. They do not confess the man to be God, but a dwelling-place of God, in which the Word of God is, rather than he himself being the Word of God. They do not observe that “the Word in flesh” differs from “the Word made flesh,” and “the Word in man” from “the Word man.” For the Word was in a man—for example, in Isaiah—but Isaiah himself was not the Word of God [Col. 1139C] or the only-begotten Son of God, as this man is. He alone among men can say to almighty God, “Thou art my Father”; and, “I will make him my first-born, above the kings of the earth” (Ps. 88:28).

II. There is, therefore, a great distinction between that singular fatherhood which belongs to the first-born and only-begotten Son alone, and that common fatherhood by which we invoke him, saying, “Our Father who art in heaven.” By the former is signified the glory of the only-begotten Son from the Father, full of grace and truth; by the latter is commended the grace of adoption, by which sons of wrath become sons of God. Although they are to be called great in the kingdom of heaven, according to the text: “Whoever shall do and teach shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 1139D] (Matt. 5:19), none of them shall be equal to the only-begotten Son. For the Spirit was given to them by measure, but to the only-begotten Son not by measure. Made also into a life-giving Spirit, he infinitely surpasses every man made into a living soul. For the first man’s being made into a living soul signifies extreme poverty, because man made in this way could neither live by himself nor confer life upon anyone else. But the second Adam’s being made into a life-giving spirit signifies immeasurable riches, by which the man born into God and enriched in God could and can not only live by himself but also give life to others. Hence, just as his eternal divinity gives eternal life in heaven to angels who worthily partake of it, so also his flesh gives eternal life on earth to those who worthily partake of it. [Col. 1140A] After the universal resurrection, as the human spirit will be conformed to God, the life-giving Spirit, so the bodies of the saints will be conformed to Christ’s body of glory—according to likeness, certainly, not equality. For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord, or who among the sons of men shall be like God? Only that man, who is truly proclaimed not a son of men but the Son of Man, because although he has a human mother, he has no human father. Since he calls himself the Son of God and glories in having God as Father, he rightly claims for himself this privilege: that in the kingdom of his Father he reign with power equal to that of his Father, having written upon his garment [Col. 1140B] and his thigh, “King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Tim. 6:15).

III. If anyone thinks it contrary to this assertion that blessed Augustine affirms in his book *On the Trinity* that a creature, even glorified and healed of all weakness, can never be made equal to the Creator, let him consider that Augustine there treats of the creature wounded in Adam and restored through Christ, not of the creature united to the Creator and never wounded by either original or actual sin. And this creature, as we have already shown by the words of Ambrose and Jerome, should no longer be called a creature, because, exalted above all creatures, it has sat down at God’s right hand, obtained the omnipotence of the omnipotent Creator, and been girded with the power of the most high divinity, according to the text: “The Lord has reigned; he is clothed with majesty; the Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself” (Ps. 17:1). Though in this girding the created remained created, as John of Damascus says, nevertheless, as was shown above on Jerome’s authority, in the Son of God the lowliness of flesh so passed into the majesty of divinity that the two made one; and we adore not a creature but the Creator, who is God blessed above all things.

IV. Against Photinus and Paul of Samosata, the illustrious Jerome reasoned as follows. Both taught that the man Christ was not to be adored because they did not believe him to be God blessed above all things, but held him to be set above all the other saints while remaining among all things. Yet they did not hold him to be honored with the glory of the Creator and thus, as they wished, not at all to be adored, lest anyone placing hope in a man and worshipping a creature should incur the curse as an idolater. But God-man himself teaches that the man is to be believed in, when he says: “You believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14:1). “For,” says blessed Augustine, “it follows that if you believe in God, you ought also to believe in me.” This would not follow if Christ were not God. Against them, as I mentioned above, Jerome, already cited, arguing in his exposition of Jeremiah, says among other things: “If every man who trusts in man is cursed, while Paul of Samosata,” etc., as appears above.

[Col. 1141A] V. No one among the scholastics and scholars has accepted this testimony of his, namely holy Jerome. In their doctrine they imitate Paul of Samosata, Photinus, Nestorius, and also Bonosus, heresiarchs; in their disputations and writings they revive in our days these heretics long buried, maintaining that Christ, according to his humanity, is not to be adored with the adoration called *latria*, by which the Creator alone is to be adored. They concede, however, the adoration called in Greek *dulia*, which may be offered not only to holy men but even to wicked men. Thus we read that Joseph’s brothers adored him, whom they thought wicked; and Nathan the prophet adored King David, whom he knew to be a sinner. Such [Col. 1141B] adoration they allow to be offered to the assumed man, though somewhat more excellently than to other men. Likewise, as is read in the masterly *Sentences* collected by Peter Lombard, they do not allow him, according to his humanity, to be loved with the love by which God is loved, in accordance with the greatest and first commandment; but with that by which one loves one’s neighbor, because he is that neighbor who showed mercy to the wounded man left half-dead, by whom the human race, healed through Christ as mediator, is signified. On account of this singular benefit, they allow him to be loved somewhat more than other neighbors; but not as God, whom we are commanded to love with all the heart, all the soul, and [Col. 1141C] all the strength, with that special love which they deny is to be offered to the assumed man. In this they favor the heretics named above, who exclude the assumed man from the worship of supreme divinity.

They likewise assert that his soul received divine knowledge, but not divine omnipotence, lest, if the human soul or the man himself be called omnipotent, he should consequently be understood to be God—which they consider unsuitable, since God alone is omnipotent. They deny that this omnipotence was given to the assumed man, except, as they say, “in the person,” as though the Word were the person not as man but in man. Yet according to the Catholic faith God and man are one undivided and individual person: God with the Father, man with the mother. They say many things of this kind, in which they agree with the heretics mentioned above. Likewise, they interpret the Apostle’s words, “Found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:7), in a superficial fashion: as an external garment, comparing human nature in the Son of God to clothing. They do not observe that God is so clothed with man that the man himself is also read to be clothed with God, or with divinity. For what is that strength with which that man is clothed, and the power with which he is sung to be girded, if not the eternal divinity with which humanity is adorned in the Son of God and man?

VI. Lest I seem the first or only person to think this, I am pleased to recall what holy Ambrose says on Luke: “What,” he asks, “does it mean that Joseph and Nicodemus bury Christ—one righteous and steadfast, the other in whom there was no deceit? The righteous man [Col. 1142A] covers Christ’s body with a linen cloth; the innocent man anoints it with ointment. Therefore you too clothe the Lord’s body with his glory, so that you may yourself be righteous. Even if you believe him dead, nevertheless cover him with the fullness of his divinity. Anoint him with myrrh and aloes, that you may be the good fragrance of Christ.” In the same work, explaining the words, “Who shall find a strong woman?” he says: “Let us see what she does for her husband, what her work and service are, and why Christ trusts in her. A good wife clothes her husband. Let our faith clothe Jesus with his body; let it clothe his flesh with the glory of his divinity, just as that woman made two garments for her husband, that she might honor him both in the present and in the future age.”

VII. [Col. 1142B] But these new disputants pay no attention to this, and proclaim God found in the appearance of a man as though man were not also found in the appearance of God, now sitting in heaven at the right hand of God the most high Father, and hereafter to be found by the elect, judging upon the throne of his majesty. Then every eye shall see him, including those who pierced him by wounding him with nails and spear upon the cross; and now they are not ashamed, in disorderly scholastic disputations, to pierce him by questioning him. Then they too shall be removed, lest they see his glory, which will then be shown to the elect and hidden from those who do not now love it—especially from those who argue against it. For their assertion that the assumed man is to be called Son of God or God, not by generation or adoption but by union, agrees too closely with Nestorius. Because of man’s conjunction [Col. 1142C] with God, he said that man was to be co-named with God and co-adored. It is right, indeed, that they remove adoption from the only-begotten Son. But when they deny generation to him, though in his divinity he is the only-begotten and in his humanity the first-born among many brethren, they agree far too much with the heretics already named, who proclaimed that the assumed man was adopted, not begotten, into the Son of God. And indeed the holy interpreters of Scripture very often treat of the unity of the person in the Trinity, who is God and man. In these two names are understood not two persons but two things. These two things are united into one person, who is Christ, the giant of double substance, without duplication of person and without confusion of substances; so that in [Col. 1142D] him both the unity of person and the union of natures are to be venerated. Concerning this personal unity and the unconfused union of natures, we have argued, so far as God granted us power, in a small work addressed to Pope Adrian, against the disputants already noted, who wish to be called masters and dialecticians, imitating ancient heretics condemned long ago and deceived by the form of human appearance.

VIII. Speaking of this appearance, Augustine says: “By the term ‘appearance’ the Apostle sufficiently indicated how he said, ‘made in the likeness of men.’ For he was made not by transformation into man but in appearance, when he put on man; and, by uniting and in some manner conforming him to himself, he made him a sharer in immortality and eternity.” In the fourth book of *On the Trinity* [Col. 1143A] he says: “If it is asked how the incarnation itself was accomplished, I say that the Word himself was made flesh, or was made man. Yet he was not converted or changed into that which he was made, but was clothed with flesh, so as to appear suitably to fleshly persons.” Here the new scholastics, or the scholarly disciples of them, as though snatching a word from Augustine’s mouth, say: “See how Augustine says that man is put on by God!”—as though he plainly testified that man is God’s garment. Augustine elsewhere also calls him purple, as it were royal clothing, to be honored not outside the king’s person by royal honor, but in the king’s person. Therefore one of my friends wrote to me thus: “Although human nature has been exalted above every creature in Christ, it nevertheless remains a creature. [Col. 1143B] It is adored in Christ without impiety, just as purple is adored in a king, or the purple-clad king himself. Similarly humanity is adored—that is, God made man is adored with *latria*.” But he had first said of human nature in Christ that it is not to be adored with *latria* as God, but with a higher kind of *dulia*. These and similar things are said more scholastically than ecclesiastically by the new disputants, who deny to the man assumed into God the worship of divinity, except insofar as it concerns a garment. They do not deny that this garment is to be adored with *latria* because of the one clothed, or in the one clothed; yet in such a way that *latria* is offered not to the garment but to the one clothed. For, as they say, *latria* is not owed to God’s garment, which is man, but *dulia*.

## CHAPTER XIX

The Virgin’s Son is truly God, although not from himself, yet through himself; and therefore man is not to be co-adored with God, as Nestorius wished, but is to be adored entirely with one simple adoration.

I. Speaking of these matters, Peter Lombard says in the third book of his *Sentences*: “Some hold that Christ’s flesh or soul is not to be adored with that adoration which is *latria*, but with that which is *dulia*. They say that this has two kinds or modes. There is one kind of *dulia* which may be offered to any creature; and there is another which is to be offered to Christ’s humanity alone, not to any other creature. For Christ’s humanity is to be venerated and loved above every creature, though not so far that the worship due to the Divinity [Col. 1143D] should be offered to it. This worship consists in love, in the offering of sacrifice, and in reverence. In Latin it is called *pietas*, but in Greek *theosebeia* [reverence or worship of God].”

II. In saying this, Master Peter—the distinguished compiler of many and diverse ecclesiastical and scholastic opinions, both ancient and modern—indicates not that this is his own opinion, but that it is the opinion of others who retain something of Nestorius’s dregs. His perverse doctrine was indeed condemned; nevertheless, its dregs have not been drained away. The sinners of the earth drink from them, maintaining that the earth is not to be adored in the Son of God except as a footstool, imagining that in this sense blessed Augustine agrees with them. For, as we recalled above, where he asserted that Christ’s flesh is to be adored, he afterwards added:

“Therefore, when you bow and prostrate yourself even toward any earth, you do not look upon it as earth, but upon that Holy One whose footstool it is, and whom you adore. For his sake you adore. Here one must not understand the adoration by which God alone is to be adored, when, bowing and prostrating yourself toward any earth, you adore—that is, honor—the earth itself by bending your knees upon it and kissing it. For you do all this because of him whose footstool this earth is. But when you adore the earth—that is, Christ’s flesh—lest your thought remain upon earth or flesh, and lest you not be made alive by the Spirit, the same Augustine says: ‘It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing.’”

[Col. 1144B] III. Thus, in his careful treatment of the adoration of God’s footstool, he speaks differently of the earth above, in heaven, which is worthily adored in God, whose own flesh it is; and differently of the earth below, to be trodden underfoot not only by the feet of God—that is, those chosen for life—but also by the impious and by beasts. He gives no support to the Nestorians, who teach that Christ’s flesh—or rather Christ, flesh, or man—is not God, but the garment or footstool of the Divinity, and is therefore to be worshipped not with the *latria* due to God alone, but with *dulia* alone, as has been shown above.

Cyril the bishop, the chief assailant of this error, answered those who revive Nestorius’s ancient error. Presiding in the place of Pope Celestine over the Synod of Ephesus against Nestorius, he inserted among other things the following:

“We refuse to say concerning Christ: ‘Because of the garment worn, I venerate; because of the invisible, I adore that which is seen.’ It is full of dread to say this also and that: ‘The assumed one is called God together with the one assuming.’ For whoever says these things cuts Christ in two, and separately establishes a man and likewise a God. For he plainly denies the union, according to which one is not, as one distinct from another, co-adored, nor even called God together with another; but one Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son, is understood, to be adored with one adoration together with his flesh.”

Likewise, chapter 5 of the same council reads: “If anyone dares to say that Christ is a God-bearing man, rather than truly God, as one Son by nature, insofar as the Word became flesh and likewise shared in blood and flesh with us, let him be anathema.”

Likewise, chapter 7: “If anyone says that Jesus, as a man, received operation from God the Word, and that the glory of the Only-begotten was added to him as to another existing apart from him, let him be anathema.”

Likewise, chapter 8: “If anyone dares to say that the assumed man ought to be co-adored with God the Word, co-glorified, and called God together with him, as though one were added to another—for the addition of the syllable *co-* compels this meaning—and does not rather honor Emmanuel with one adoration and render him one glorification, according as the Word became flesh, let him be anathema.”

Likewise, chapter 9: “If anyone says that the Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Spirit as though using through him a foreign power, and received from him the ability to act against [Col. 1145A] unclean spirits and to perform divine miracles in a man, rather than saying that the Spirit is his own, through whom he also wrought the signs of divinity, let him be anathema.”

Likewise, chapter 11: “If anyone does not confess that Christ’s flesh is life-giving—or, as some manuscripts have it, life-making—and is the own flesh of the Word from God the Father, as though the Word were another besides him joined to him, let him be anathema.”

IV. If these chapters are examined with clear sight, do they not show rather a man clothed with God than a God clothed with a man? Especially since they forbid the man to be called God-bearing, or as though possessing God’s indwelling—a teaching of the heretics Photinus, Paul, and Nestorius. These denied that the man was God, but proclaimed that the man born of the Virgin was God’s garment, dwelling-place, or instrument of the Divinity. The Synod of Ephesus plainly refuted them and their followers in the aforesaid chapters and in many letters read and approved there.

It is not now necessary to discuss each of those matters separately. Here it suffices especially to reject the statement which, as we have noted above, Nestorius made and even left in writing: “Because of the garment worn, I worship; because of the hidden one, I adore the visible one. God is inseparable from the visible; therefore I do not divide the honor of the undivided. I divide the natures, but unite the adoration.”

V. These words might somehow appear tolerable; but what follows reveals their heretical sense, when he says: “That which was formed in the womb is not God in itself; that which was created by the Spirit is not God in itself; that which was buried in the tomb is not God in itself. For then we should plainly be worshippers of a man and worshippers of a dead person. But because God is in the assumed one, the assumed one, from the one assuming, is called God together with the one assuming, as joined to him.”

In saying this, he separates the assumed man from adoration, denying that he is God in himself, though he maintains that he is to be called God together with the one assuming him. But we believe in our hearts unto righteousness and confess with our mouths unto salvation that the Virgin’s Son is truly God, though not from himself, yet in his own right. Not from himself, because in neither his humanity nor his divinity does he possess anything except from the Father, from whom he has not only that he is God, the Son of God, but also that he is the Son of man. Yet what he has from the Father he has in each nature in his own right.

[Col. 1145D] The man himself possesses the divinity which he received; the same God possesses the humanity which he assumed. Thus the man is God by true divinity, and God is man by true humanity; yet in the one and same person divinity is not humanity, nor humanity divinity. That person is to be adored not in part but wholly, as one person in the Trinity. In him man is not co-adored with God, as the heresiarch Nestorius wished, but is altogether adored with one simple adoration: for he is true, not false God; the unique, natural—not adopted—Son of God. Although in him what is created remains created, insofar as the same Son was found in outward condition as a man, it is nevertheless so united to the uncreated Word that it is not to be distinguished from him in adoration or in any veneration of divine worship, [Col. 1146A] nor loved less than the Creator—as those dream who write that in Christ the man is to be loved less than God.

VI. May my soul not enter into the counsel of those who, like the brothers of the true Joseph, ungrateful and envious of his glory in which he is to be adored, strip him of his seamless tunic woven from above. This may fittingly be understood as the very glory of divinity which his Father gave him, who loved him above all his other sons. Yet, whether they wish it or not, he, living with eternal life, rules over the whole land of Egypt—indeed, over heaven and earth. He is clothed far better than the first man, who, having lost the adornment of innocence together with obedience, fled from God ashamed of his nakedness.

But this one, beautiful in the beauty of divinity, is adorned in God with that garment upon which is written: “King of kings and Lord of lords.” When those who love him behold the name “King of kings and Lord of lords,” surpassing every name, inscribed upon his garment as it were in golden—indeed divine—letters, they rejoice that the garment itself is so clothed because of the radiance of the divine inscription. They know that the inscription of this name or title is not to be corrupted or erased from that garment, however much those who introduce *dulia* into his adoration may err.

Nevertheless, whether they will or not, every knee shall finally bend to him; and he shall be adored by the brothers who sold him and acknowledged worthy of adoration. This will occur when the man himself is seen “clothed with light as with a garment,” according to Isaiah: “The light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun [Col. 1146C] shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, on the day when the Lord binds up the wound of his people and heals the blow of their injury” (Isa. 30:26).

What is the moon that will then shine like the sun, without the changing increase and decrease by which it is now varied in this age, if not the Church, which will then be like her sun, her God? “We know,” John says, “that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 2:28). But how great will the sun’s light be? “Like the light of seven days,” he says. That is to say: as great was the brightness of the Word when all things were made during six days and his work was completed through him on the seventh day, so great will be his brightness in his flesh—that is, in the assumed man—then with [Col. 1146D] his Father.

For he himself prayed for this, saying: “And now, Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was made.” Explaining these words of his prayer for the glorification of his flesh, Hilary says in the third book *On the Trinity*:

“But what is this which he now awaits, in the Father, of glorification? Surely that which he had with him before the world existed. He had the fullness of divinity, and he has it, for he is the Son of God. But he who was the Son of God had begun also to be the son of man. For the Word had become flesh: he had not lost what he was, but had begun to be what he was not. He had not ceased to possess what was his, but had received what was ours. He asks that what he received should advance into that glory from which he did not depart. Therefore, because the Son is the Word, and the Word [Col. 1147A] became flesh, and the Word is God, and was in the beginning with God, and the Word was the Son before the foundation of the world, he now, having become flesh, prayed that the flesh might begin to be to the Father what the Word was; that what was temporal might receive the glory of his timeless brightness; that the corruption of flesh, transformed into God’s power and the Spirit’s incorruption, might be swallowed up.”

VII. Here it should be noted that Hilary teaches not that flesh, but that the corruption of flesh, is to be swallowed up. This too will be swallowed up in the saints glorified by resurrection, while the nature of flesh remains in the glory of that resurrection whose voice is: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). How much more, then, will the brightness of resurrection shine in his own flesh, since he himself is resurrection and life?

Whoever believes in him [Col. 1147B] shall not die forever, because he shall remain in resurrection and life, and resurrection and life shall remain in him, according to his promise: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me and I in him.” Likewise: “He who abides in me and I in him bears much fruit” (John 6:55). How much more expressly—indeed, more impressively—does the man assumed into God abide in God and God in him, not as one distinct being in another, because the same one is God who is man, although he is not God from that source from which he is man.

For he is God by divinity and man by humanity. In him the essential differences of the distinct natures remain: one is uncreated and the other created. Yet those natures are united, so that each performs what is its own in communion with the other: God remaining in the form of a human being, in which he is the firstborn from the dead; and man remaining in the form of God, in which he was begotten before the morning star, the firstborn of every creature.

## Chapter XX

In the conception and generation of the Son of Man, true faith holds that what was born in the Virgin through conception and from the Virgin through generation is wholly the Son of the Most High and wholly the son of the Virgin. Thus God is rightly called Son of Man, and man Son of God.

I. Since some affirm that the man is to be called the Son of God by union rather than by generation, let us now consider the modes of union by which one thing is united to another. It will then become plainly evident that those err who distinguish the union by which man is united to God from the generation of man into God, saying that the man was made Son of God rather by [Col. 1147D] union than by generation.

This might perhaps be said correctly if generation itself were not the natural and native union by which one son consists from different essences united through birth. For example, one who is born from bloods, from the will of the flesh, and from the will of a man, does not have the whole essence of his body either from his father or from his mother; and he has his spirit from neither, but from him whom the Apostle calls “the Father of spirits,” saying: “We had fathers of our flesh and revered them; shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live?” (Heb. 12:9).

Therefore, although the different essences of different bloods are united with a rational spirit, there is not in one son a divided sonship, such that the man born of a woman is partly son of his father and partly son of his mother. Rather, he is wholly son of the father and wholly son of the mother. He would also be wholly Son of the Father of all rational spirits if the rational spirit, given from the essence of God the Father rather than created from nothing, were united to the human body. The Manichaeans thought this, and were consequently condemned and anathematized because they taught that the rational soul is consubstantial with God. But because, in the creation of the soul united to the body, the power which acts is known to be God’s alone, without human agency, God himself is rightly called by the Apostle Father of spirits, not of bodies.

II. But in the conception and generation of that man whose essence demonstrably consists not only of a human body received from the Virgin and a human soul [Col. 1148B] created from nothing, but also of the Word of God, consubstantial with God the Father, true faith holds that what was born in the Virgin through conception and from the Virgin through generation is wholly Son of the Most High and wholly son of the Virgin. Thus God is rightly called Son of Man, and man Son of God. For by a native union, from three ingredients—the Word of God, a rational soul, and flesh—fermented into one, one bridegroom, a giant of twofold substance, came forth from his bridal chamber.

In this union, let no human being separate the three ingredients which God has joined, so as, following Nestorius’s example, to cut the one Son of God and man into two sons. He is united by a native—or, as Boethius calls it, natural—union from diverse essences, namely divine and human. Although this was done above nature, it was not done contrary to nature, because it is natural to man, created in God’s image and likeness, to be able to receive the wisdom of God through whom and for whom he was created, just as good ground receives good seed.

What soil was ever better than the Virgin Mary? Though never tilled by the plough of male activity, she was so fertile that, when the angel announced it, the seed of God—that is, the Word of God—fell into her and grew united to human substance, so that the man born in her is called and is the Son of the Most High: Son, I say, not adopted, as the heretics Photinus and Bonosus taught, but the proper, only-begotten Son, unique to his Father and mother.

In this native union, *electrum* was made one, fused by the fire of the Holy Spirit from the silver of human substance [Col. 1148D] and at the same time from the gold of divine substance. In it, when the brilliance of the gold was for a time emptied and, as it were, grew pale—in the very pallor of the gold through the death of the cross and other humiliations—the brightness of the silver that had grown pale was brought to completion, to such a degree that the prayer was fulfilled: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1). Likewise: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was” (ibid., v. 5).

III. Nor is it surprising that the silver of such human substance should be united to the gold of divinity and glorified, or made radiant, together with it. For it is written: “Silver has the source of its veins, and there is a place for gold where it is refined” (Job 28:1). The origin of this silver was eternally preordained so that, in the refining-place of the virginal womb, it might be fashioned by native union into one *electrum* together with the eternal gold of divinity.

After this had been accomplished from the Virgin, no condition can be added or assigned to the Son of God and man by which, considered separately, abstractly, and mathematically, he could truly be called or be either Son of God or son of man. He did indeed display distinct appearances in himself, showing himself now as a gardener, now as a traveler, and even as a lamb with seven horns and seven eyes to those who loved him. But such appearances were not produced by the native union, for they came to the Son after he had already been born.

IV. If it is pleasing to demonstrate by some analogies, what we have said concerning divine and supernatural matters is apparent in human and natural ones. Suppose, then, that a man has an only son, only-begotten, proper, natural. If something is united to this son born from the man, it may be united in such a way as to be converted into his substance, as bread which changes and is changed: being converted into flesh, it makes a lean person fat. Or it may be like a ring, which neither changes nor is changed from his being a ring-wearing son; or like wisdom, which makes a foolish son wise, changing him but not itself; or like a garment, which clothes a naked son without changing him, but is itself changed, because when it is folded outside the body and then fitted to the body, it is stretched out in a certain way so that it is rightly called the person’s outward condition. From this condition he may, for example, [Col. 1149C] be called purple-clad, armored, or something similar.

But does either the bread which the son eats or the ring which he takes on become the son of the father who begot that son? Certainly not. Likewise, does the wisdom which makes the son wise from foolish, or the purple garment which presents him clothed instead of naked, receive—or could it receive—the name of son or daughter from the son? By no means. Yet the purple garment, when put upon the limbs, receives a form which it did not have when removed; and in the person of the king it is to be shown an honor which is not shown to it when removed.

V. Blessed Augustine applies an analogy from this matter to the mystery of the Incarnation in his book *Eighty-Three Questions*:

“We speak of an outward condition in many ways: either an inward condition of mind, such as the apprehension of disciplines strengthened by practice; or a bodily condition, as when we say that one person is stronger than another; or a condition of things externally fitted to the limbs, as when you call someone clothed, shod, and the like. In all these kinds it is evident that a condition is spoken of in a thing which happens or is added to someone in such a way that he may also not have it. This name is derived from the verb *to have*. Therefore, a condition is spoken of in a thing which happens or is added to us so as to be possessed.

“Yet there is this difference: some of the things which happen or are added so as to make a condition are not changed, but themselves change their recipient, remaining whole and unmoved in themselves. Thus wisdom, when added to a person, is not itself changed but changes the person, making him [Col. 1150A] wise from foolish. But some happen or are added in such a way that they change and are changed, as food: losing its own form, it is converted into the body, while we, refreshed by food, are changed from thinness and weakness into strength and health. A third kind occurs when things that happen or are added neither change that to which they happen nor are changed by it, as a ring placed on a finger; this kind is found very rarely. The fourth kind occurs when things that happen are changed, not from their own nature, but by receiving another appearance and form, as a garment which, when cast aside and laid down, does not have the form which it assumes when worn; when worn, it does not have the form it has when removed. This kind suits the present comparison.

“For the Son of God emptied himself, not changing his own form, but taking the form of a servant; nor was he converted or transformed into man, losing his unchangeable stability, but was made in the likeness of men. He who assumed took up a true man, and was found in outward condition as a man—not for himself, but for those to whom he appeared in man. But when he says ‘as a man,’ he expresses the reality. By the term ‘outward condition,’ therefore, the Apostle sufficiently indicated how he said: ‘He was made in the likeness of men’ (Phil. 2:7). For he was made not through transformation into a man, but through an outward condition, when he clothed himself with the man whom, uniting to himself, he in some way made a partner in immortality and eternity. Therefore one should not understand the Word as changed through the assumption of man, any more than limbs are changed by the garment put on them, [Col. 1150C] although that assumption ineffably joined the assumed one to the one assuming.”

VI. By these words Augustine appears openly to suggest that God is said to have become man according to an outward condition. Seeking also to express the manner of the Incarnation itself, he says to questioners in the fourth book *On the Trinity*:

“If one asks how the Incarnation itself was accomplished: I say that the very Word of God became flesh, or became man, yet was not converted or changed into that which he became; rather, he was clothed with flesh, so that he might appear suitably to fleshly persons. Thus he was made, so that there should be there not only the Word of God and the flesh of a human being, but also the rational soul of a human being; and this whole is called God because of God, and man because of man. If this is difficult to understand, let the mind be cleansed by faith through abstaining from sins and doing good works; for these things are difficult.”

VII. The same writer, in *On Faith to Peter*, says: “The Son of God, although he is eternal and true God, became for us true and complete man. He is true in that he has a true human nature; and truly complete in that he assumed human flesh and a rational soul.” Likewise: “The emptying of the supreme God was nothing other than the assumption of the form of a servant, that is, of human nature. Therefore both substances, divine and human, are in Christ.” Likewise, in the book *Against Maximinus*: “Though invisible in himself, he appeared visible in the man whom he deigned to assume from a woman.” Likewise, in the same work: “We believe that Christ the Lord assumed a true man, [Col. 1151A] that the invisible appeared visibly to human beings in him, lived among human beings in him, suffered human things from human beings in him, and taught human beings in him.”

VIII. Hilary, in the book *On the Trinity*, says: “How is the Son of God born from Mary except because the Word became flesh? That is, because the Son of God, when he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant. Yet we confess one and the same person, not through God’s diminution but through the assumption of man: both in the form of God by divine nature and in the form of a servant, through the conception of the Holy Spirit, found in outward condition as a man. Yet that condition was not that of a man, but ‘as of a man’; nor was that flesh sinful flesh, but was in the likeness of sinful flesh.”

[Col. 1151B] IX. On cautiously weighing these statements of Augustine and Hilary together, we find that the Son of God was found in the outward condition of a man, although that condition, as Hilary says, was not that of a man but “as of a man.” The Apostle teaches that the Son of God humbled himself by taking the form of a servant and was found in outward condition “as a man”; that is, by having man in himself. He was found as a man because he clothed himself with man, whom, by uniting and in some way conforming him to himself, he made a partner in immortality and eternity, as Augustine says.

But could such union, conformity, and association have conferred—or have been able to confer—upon the assumed man his being the natural, proper, and unique Son of God, without participation in that generation of which it is said: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). For God the Father begot one Son, connatural and coeternal with himself, like the sun’s radiance from his glory, because, having spoken once, he brought forth a good Word from his heart. Yet in this one utterance the Psalmist heard these two things: namely, that power belongs to God and mercy as well. God’s power, in which the same Word once uttered deigned to be called Son of God; mercy, in which the same Word likewise deigned to be called and to be Son of Man.

X. Let us now weigh, in the same balance of truth, the dignity of power and the dignity of mercy in the one and same Son of God, lest we judge either less or greater, earlier or later, than the other. We shall surely find that blessed Hilary rightly thought in the ninth book *On the Trinity*, where he says:

“It is a matter of the same danger to deny that Christ Jesus or the Spirit is God, or to deny Christ’s bodily flesh. He himself is established as mediator in himself for the salvation of the Church; and, in the sacrament of the mediator between God and human beings, the one person being both, since he is himself the same reality from the natures united into one, a reality of each nature, yet in such a way that he lacks neither in either, lest perhaps God should cease to be God by being born, and man in turn should not remain God. This, therefore, is the true faith of human blessedness: to preach God and man, to confess Word and flesh, neither to let God fail to know that he is man nor flesh fail to know that it is the Word. But when God, while remaining God, is born man contrary to the nature of our understanding, then it is no longer contrary to the nature of our hope that the man who was born should remain God, since the higher nature, born into the lower, gives assurance of faith that the lower may be born into the higher nature.” [Col. 1152A]

XI. The same writer, in the tenth book, says: “That he who was in the form of God took the form of a servant is stated by comparison of opposites, so that as true as it is that he remains in the form of God, so true it is that he took the form of a servant. For, in order that the property of nature may be understood, we are led by the meaning of the word common to both expressions. For he is in the form of a servant who is also in the form of God. And though the one pertains to nature and the other to the dispensation, nevertheless what he is in both possesses the property of the same truth, so that he is as truly in the form of God as he is truly in the form of a servant. But just as taking the form of a servant is nothing other than being born man, so being in the form of God is nothing other than being God. Yet we confess one and the same person, not through God’s diminution but through the assumption of man: both in the form of God by divine nature and in the form of a servant, through the conception of the Holy Spirit, found in the outward condition of man.”

## Chapter XXI

The same point is established more fully, and it is shown that the Word was in no way changed in himself through union with human nature, and that the man was born as the unique Son of God the Father—something which assumption alone, or that outward condition, could not confer.

I. When these things have been carefully weighed, it appears that the man is called Son of God, and God Son of Man, not so much from a union considered in some outward condition [Col. 1152C] as from birth. As Hilary affirms: “God, remaining God, deigned to be born man; and the man who was born remains God, so that the higher nature, born into the lower, gives assurance that the lower can be born into the higher nature. For taking the form of a servant is nothing other than being born man, and being in the form of God is nothing other than being God.”

Therefore, just as God begotten from God is his Son by birth, so no less by birth the same God became Son of Man, being born from a human being divinely rather than merely humanly: for the Virgin conceived him not through a man, but through God working by his Spirit. Hence Augustine says in *On Faith to Peter*: “Eternal and divine nature could not be conceived and born temporally from human nature, unless, by the assumption of reality, ineffable divinity accepted in itself a true temporal conception and birth. Thus eternal God was truly, according to time, both conceived and born from a virgin.”

II. Since this is so, conception and birth rather than outward condition gave the man his being Son of God, and God his being Son of Man. Yet in that native union, by which God was born into man and man into God, there is much resemblance to the outward conditions previously described. For in the fact that a ring-wearing son is not changed into the ring by wearing it, nor the ring into him, may be signified the permanence of the assuming and assumed natures: both divine and human natures remaining in Christ.

Boethius also suggested this in writing against Eutyches, introducing the analogy of a crown composed of gold and gems. In the union of gold and gems their natures remain. So also in a gemmed ring, although there is a certain union of distinct natures, there is found neither confusion nor mixture of those natures; but neither is there such division that gold without a gem or a gem without gold can be called a gemmed ring. Thus God, the renewer of nature, became man, remaining what he was and assuming what he was not, suffering neither mixture nor division. The heretic Eutyches taught mixture or confusion; Nestorius, however, asserted division. Both were rejected by the holy Church through that faith by which Christ is believed to exist from two and [Col. 1153B] in two natures, perfect God and perfect man, altogether one—not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person.

III. Again, in the inward condition—such as the condition of a mind possessing wisdom, where wisdom is grasped by the intellect and strengthened through practice—there is found a great likeness in the man who is God. His human intellect, formed by the apprehension of eternal wisdom and strengthened by its exercise, knows no less in any respect than the eternal wisdom itself by which it is formed and strengthened. For every wise person knows to the extent of the wisdom that he possesses: little if he has little, much if he has much, according to the inward condition of his wisdom. Yet this wisdom itself is not changed into him, but changes him, making him wise from foolish.

Thus the eternal wisdom of God, united to man and given to him as an everlasting condition, was not changed in him, since it is unchangeable and incapable of any change. Nor is it in any way capable of accidents, through which alone changes occur in things subject to forms. Rather, it is the eternal form itself, lacking matter; remaining unchangeable, it changes man, according to the saying of the wise man: “Remaining steadfast, you make all things move” (Wis. 7:23).

Most blessedly it makes those heavens move of which it is said: “The heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; and all shall grow old as a garment, and like a cloak you shall change them and they shall be changed. But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101:27). By the name of heavens are signified the saints—both human beings and angels—who are God’s clothing, because God’s wisdom is adorned with them as with its garment.

That seamless tunic, woven from above throughout, also consists of them: namely, the holy Church, anointed with that ointment which descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, and descended to the hem of his garment. Therefore, if we turn from considering the inward condition of the mind to the outward condition, according to which we call one person stronger than another in body, or better clothed, shod, or armed, eternal wisdom—which united to itself not only a human spirit but also a human body—changed the man united to itself infinitely more blessedly than blessed angels and human beings. Thus the three ingredients—Word, flesh, and soul—are one bread [Col. 1154A] which came down from heaven. The Word, which is and was, remains unchangeably; but the human soul and flesh are so changed that, although their essence remains and the essential difference by which creature differs from Creator remains, divine power, wisdom, strength, and glory nevertheless belong to them in the one person of the Trinity, who is God and man, Son of God and Son of Man, possessing both by birth rather than by outward condition.

IV. For those who, by having God within themselves through this indwelling, were called gods or sons of God—as Moses was called the god of Pharaoh, and those to whom the word of God came were called gods and sons of the Most High—were not sons of God or gods by nature. For they had not received by birth that which they were called; rather, after they had already been born and formed, [Col. 1154B] a small share was granted them of that holiness by which the Father sanctified and sent into the world him who is known to be the Holy of holies. Of him the angel also says to Mary: “That holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). He did not say, “He who shall be born of thee, being holy, shall be called the Son of God,” lest you suppose that what is called the Son of God belongs to the person of the Word alone. Rather, he says: “That holy thing which shall be born of thee”—namely, the body animated by a rational soul and united to the Word of God—shall be called the Son of God, not as possessing God within itself, as Photinus, Paul of Samosata, and Nestorius, arch-heretics, taught, but as truly being the true God and the only Son of God.

Hence Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, says: “Whoever is faithful believes that in him true human nature [Col. 1154C] was so exalted by God the Word assuming it that he who assumed and that which he assumed were one person in the Trinity, that assumption ineffably bringing about the reality of one person in God and man.” The same writer says in the *Enchiridion*: “Christ Jesus is God from God, but man born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary; in both substances, namely divine and human, he is the only Son of God the almighty Father.” The same writer, in his book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, says: “What merit had that man, in order that, assumed into unity of person by the Word coeternal with the Father, he might be the only-begotten Son of God? What good of his preceded, that he might attain this ineffable excellence? By God the Word’s making and assuming, that man [Col. 1154D] began, from the moment he began to exist, to be the only Son of God.””

V. In saying these things, holy Augustine emphatically expresses the birth of the man into God the Son of God, which alone made the assumed man the only Son of God—so that, as he himself says, he is the only Son in both substances, namely divine and human. This could not have been conferred on him by assumption alone, assimilated to an outward garment—not by a false interpretation but truly, yet not in a manner contrary to the man’s divine birth. For the man is so assumed into God that he is also born into God; and he is so created by God that he is also born into God: speaking from one [nature], “I ascend to my Father,” and adding from the other, “and to my God” (John 20:17).

[Col. 1155A] VI. For the Father became the God of the man, supernaturally effecting his conception and birth through his Spirit; and he was also his God by creating him among the other creatures. Therefore the created man was assumed by the uncreated Word as, so to speak, a garment, in which he who was God was found as man; but he was born as the only Son of God the Father—something that assumption alone, or that garment, could not confer upon him. For those whom God assumed but did not beget—for example Moses and Aaron, whom he assumed in order to lead his people out of figurative Egypt—could not have done this unless God had assumed them for that ministry. Although they are called sons of God among those to whom the speech or Word of God came, none of them became the [Col. 1155B] Word of God, except only this only-begotten one of the Virgin: not merely assumed for ministry, but also born as Son.

Hence he not only ministered as a servant, saying, “But I am among you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27); but also, as Son and Lord, commanded the winds and the sea, when Pharaoh, prince of darkness, was drowned in his own blood. He could not have done this unless he were the omnipotent Son of the omnipotent Father: he who, hanging and dying on the cross, was found to be man; and, despoiling hell and rising from the tomb, was found to be God. For God was found in the form of a servant by suffering as a human being, and man was found in the form of God by performing divine works—works which no other [Col. 1155C] performed, because by a mere nod he did whatsoever he willed.

Thus he made wine from water, without even saying, “Let wine be made from water,” because creation perceived the silent command of its Lord. So too, by a silent nod, he drew the sinful woman to himself. For, as blessed Pope Gregory says: “He himself drew her inwardly who mercifully received her outwardly.” This woman bore the type of the Church gathered from the Gentiles. The Father draws her to the Son; and the Son draws her to himself and, through himself, together with himself to the Father, according to the saying: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him.” Likewise: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 6:44).

The Father did not draw the heretic Nestorius to the Son, nor did the Son draw him to himself, since he did not believe the assumed man to be the Son of God, but God’s [Col. 1155D] garment. “I venerate,” he says, “because of the garment that has been put on.” As though the man born into God were not God the Son of God, to be worshipped for his own sake equally with his Father. But he who separates the man from God the Son of God, like a garment from the one clothed in it, no more believes the assumed man to be the Son of God than he believes that any garment worn by any son is the son of that father. Therefore the Father did not draw him to the man whose Father he did not believe to be the Most High, deceived by the mere comparison with a garment. Even now many of Nestorius’s followers are deceived by this: they are not drawn to the faith by which it is believed that the man is not only so assumed as to be God’s garment, but also so born of the Virgin as to be [Col. 1156A] God’s Son, to be venerated and adored not for another’s sake but for his own, as the true God, the Son of God.

VII. Therefore the Fathers assembled at the Council of Ephesus, as we have also mentioned above, said and left in writing:

> “We refuse to say concerning Christ: ‘Because of the garment that has been put on I venerate; because of the invisible I adore that which is seen.’ It is full of terror to say this and that: ‘The assumed one is jointly called God with the one who assumes him.’ For whoever says these things cuts Christ in two and separately establishes the man as one part and God likewise. For he plainly denies the union according to which one is not, as though one other beside another, jointly adored, nor indeed jointly called God; but Christ is understood as one, to be honored with one adoration together with his flesh.”

Likewise, as we have set out above [Col. 1156B] and do not hesitate now to repeat, chapter 5 of the same council reads:

> “If anyone dares to call Christ a God-bearing man, rather than God in truth, as one Son by nature, since the Word became flesh and likewise shared with us in blood and flesh, let him be anathema.”

VIII. The Father drew these venerable Fathers to the Son, because they believed that the man was not merely assumed by God like a garment, but also born into God the Son of God. Likewise the Father drew Father Augustine to the Son. For when he had said that God was clothed with man, he added: “Uniting him to himself and in some fashion conforming him, he might make him a partner in immortality [Col. 1156C] and eternity.”

The same Augustine, commenting on the Lord’s saying, “Let not your heart be troubled,” says: “I adore the Lord’s flesh—or rather, the perfect humanity in Christ—because it has been assumed by divinity and united to deity, so that I confess not one person and another, but one and the same, God and man, to be the Son of God.” And shortly afterward: “Whoever disdains to adore humanity, not alone or bare, but united to divinity—that is, one Son, true God and true man—shall die eternally.”

IX. Observe in these sayings of Augustine that, when he had taught that the humanity united to divinity is to be adored, lest anyone understand anything other than the Son of God in the humanity united to divinity, he then explained what he himself [Col. 1156D] meant, adding: “Whoever disdains to adore one Son, true God and true man, shall die eternally.” Therefore the Father drew him to the Son because he believed and confessed the man to be the Son of God, although his human garment is rightly compared to purple, not lying outside the person of the king, but to be adored in the person of the king.

Since he is King of kings, he also has written upon his garment and upon his thigh, “King of kings and Lord of lords,” lest anyone suppose with Nestorius that, because the man himself is God’s garment, he is not also truly to be adored as King of kings and Lord of lords—not for God’s sake as one person for another’s sake, but in God the Word of God, to whom the man is so united [Col. 1157A] that he is God, the proper and only Son of God.

## CHAPTER XXII

**In Christ’s person, man is God and God is man: because God is man by the humanity which he assumed, and man is God by the divinity which he received.**

I. When the question is asked concerning his person, who he himself is, it is rightly answered: God and man. But if it is asked whether, in Christ’s person, man is God and God is man, it is rightly answered that both are true. For God is man by the humanity which he assumed, and man is God by the divinity which he received.

Likewise, when it is said, “Man is God” and “God is man,” if it is asked what is the subject and what is the predicate, it may fittingly be said that the person is the subject and the nature is predicated. [Col. 1157B] For the man who is one person in the Trinity with the Word has the nature of divinity naturally implanted in him by the natural power of birth, received through the Holy Spirit by the power of the Most High overshadowing him. And the Son of God, God, who is one person with the assumed man, so united to himself by native union the nature of humanity in being born from man that the Son of God himself is rightly also called Son of man. Therefore, with this person as subject, each of his natures—divine and human—is most rightly predicated of him.

For God is from God by the nature of his essence, and the same one is man by the grace and also the nature of birth from man; for it belongs to the nature of those born to be connatural with those who beget them. Thus man born from God is connatural with God the Father in divinity; and [Col. 1157C] God born from man is connatural with the Virgin Mother in humanity. Therefore, whether the person is put forward under the name of God or under the name of man, either nature is rightly predicated of that person: God is said to be God and man, and man to be man and God—although man is not God by that by which he is man, nor is God man by that by which he is God. For man is God by his divinity and man by his humanity; and God is man by his humanity and God by his divinity.

II. The sayings of the Fathers that follow agree with what we have said. Hilary, in Book X, says:

> “We have also taught the mystery of God born as man from the Virgin’s childbirth, showing that, according to the dispensation [Col. 1157D] of the assumed flesh, when he emptied himself from the form of God and received the form of a servant possessing weakness, the nature of God as human was not weakened; rather, while the power of divinity remained safe in man, God acquired power toward man. For when God was born as man, he was not born in such a way as not to remain God, but so that, while God remained, man might be born into God. For Emmanuel is his name, which means ‘God with us’: so that it is not God’s falling away toward man, but man’s advancement toward God. Or when he asks to be glorified, this surely benefits not the nature of God but the assumption of humanity. For he asks for that glory which he had with [Col. 1158A] God before the foundation of the world.”

The same writer, in the same work:

> “They also reproach us because we say that Christ was born as man, not as a man of our body and soul; although we proclaim that the Word became flesh, that Christ emptied himself from the form of God and assumed the form of a servant, and that, according to the condition of conformity and likeness of humanity, a perfect man was born, so that the true Son of God might be born the son of man. He was neither not born as man from God, nor, because he was born as man from God, did he cease to be God. But as he assumed for himself from the Virgin a body from himself, so he assumed for himself from himself those things which are surely never furnished from the origins of human begetters. For if the Virgin did not have conception of flesh except from God, much more necessarily can the soul of the body have come from no source other than God. And since that very [Col. 1158B] Son of man is also the Son of God—because the whole Son of man is the whole Son of God—how ridiculous it is that, apart from the Son of God who became the Word made flesh, we should proclaim some other person, I know not whom, as though a prophet animated by the Word of God, when the Lord Jesus Christ is both Son of man and Son of God!”

III. From the creed of the Council of Ephesus of two hundred bishops:

> “We adore one Son and Lord, Jesus Christ, not setting man and God in parts and dividing them, as though joined to one another by a union of dignity and authority. For this is a novelty of language and nothing else.”

IV. Augustine, in the book *Questions on the New Testament*, says: “Christ, the Son of God, is from eternity; but according to the Spirit of holiness, according to the flesh from the seed of David, [Col. 1158C] he was born Son of God, so that in both respects he is held to be not made Son of God, but born.”

And after some further remarks: “Therefore the Savior was born, and according to the flesh was the Son of God. For what is born holy from the Holy could not fail to be born from God.”

Florus, from the Decade:

> “Exalt the Lord our God. How greatly ought he to be exalted? ‘And adore,’ he says, ‘the footstool of his feet.’ The footstool of Christ’s feet is to be understood as that holy flesh, assumed from the virginal womb not by the will of a man but by the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High, in which he walked here. For he gave it to us to eat. Yet no one eats that flesh unless he has first adored it. For the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Nor must that which is joined [Col. 1158D] by unity be divided from adoration, because God and man, Word and flesh, are one Christ.”

V. From the sermons of the Abbot of Clairvaux on the Gospel, *The Angel Gabriel Was Sent*:

> “Therefore, ‘that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God’ [Luke 1:35], means this: because you will conceive not from man but from the Holy Spirit. Yet you will conceive the power of the Most High, that is, the Son of God; and therefore that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.”

The same writer:

> “Not only he who, coming from the bosom of the Father into your womb, overshadowed you, but also that which from his substance shall be joined to you, shall for this reason be called the Son of God. Likewise, he who was begotten from the Father before the ages [Col. 1159A] will in some manner be accounted your Son. Thus too, that which is born from him will be yours, and that which is born from you will be his; yet they will not be two sons, but one. And although one thing is indeed from you and another from him, yet neither will henceforth belong severally to each, but one Son will belong to both. Therefore that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.

> “Consider, I beg you, how reverently he said: ‘That holy thing which shall be born of thee.’ Why did he say simply ‘holy,’ without an addition? I believe because he had no proper and worthy name for that excellent, magnificent, venerable reality which from the most pure flesh of the Virgin, together with its own soul, was to be united to the Father’s only Son. Had he said ‘holy flesh,’ or ‘holy man,’ or ‘holy infant,’ or used any such expression, he would have seemed to himself to have said [Col. 1159B] too little. Therefore he used the indefinite term ‘holy,’ because whatever that was which the Virgin bore was without doubt holy, and uniquely holy, both through the sanctification of the Spirit and through the assumption of the Word.”

[Note: At Col. 1157D, read *quoque amodo*—“also henceforth.”]

VI. When these sayings of the Fathers are carefully weighed, it is clear that they understood—or believed beyond understanding—that the man is God and the Son of God, the Holy of holies. Since the Father sanctified and sent him into the world, we do not blaspheme when we proclaim him God, the only, natural, and proper Son of God; for birth, not adoption, bestowed upon him the status of being the only Son of God in both natures.

As was shown above by the sayings of Augustine and [Col. 1159C] other Fathers, they teach that the man who is the Holy of holies is to be adored with one reverent adoration—or, to speak more expressly, the Holy One or Holiness of all holy ones. As Augustine says: “He was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.” To this also belongs the saying in the Law: “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Luke 11:23). As Ambrose affirms in his commentary on Luke, this is properly said of the Virgin’s firstborn alone, because he alone opened the womb and is called the Holy of holies, whose holiness is not accidental. It is said improperly of every firstborn, since we read that many firstborn were not holy. Yet because of the one firstborn who is truly and substantially holy, the Law said, “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord,” although [Col. 1160A] this applies only to that firstborn whom the Virgin conceived of the Holy Spirit.

VII. Likewise, the saying in the Epistle of John, “Everyone who is born of God does not sin; but the generation of God preserves him” (1 John 5:18), properly applies to this man alone, who alone among human beings lacked both original and actual sin. Because he was born from God, God’s generation preserved him free from sin, wholly and in every respect pure and holy. Generation conferred this on him, just as regeneration confers a share in his holiness on adoptive sons through the remission of sins.

Yet no one of them, however sanctified, is called the Holy of holies, because none is holy by the essential good of holiness, however greatly sanctified by an accidental [Col. 1160B] gift—as John the Baptist or Jeremiah. Although they are read to have been sanctified in their mothers’ wombs, they nevertheless did not lack the stain of original sin contracted at conception.
