But this one alone, conceived of the Holy Spirit, is called holy not accidentally but essentially—or, expressing the meaning more forcefully, “that holy thing”: one for whom to be is to be holy. Therefore the angel announcing his conception did not say, “He who shall be born of thee, holy,” but: “That holy thing which shall be born of thee.” It is as though he said: that which will be holy not accidentally but essentially, sufficient to sanctify all who believe in him.

VIII. I am reluctant to answer the evasions of those who, whenever human things are predicated of God or divine things of man, introduce various tropes [Col. 1160C] and figures of speech in order to empty the meaning of truth. For example, they say: “God suffered and died on the cross”—not in truth, but by reason of association; as though the man hanging on the cross were not himself God in his own person, but merely had God within himself. We believe him to be God in his own person, although not from himself. Therefore, when that man suffered, God himself suffered—yet not according to his impassible divinity, but according to his then passible humanity.

Again, they say that when man is called omnipotent, this is a trope of accidentality, because the predicate is not assigned according to its cause. For he is not omnipotent by that by which he is man. So also among human beings one may say that “the colored person understands.” In this manner, by their falsely understood tropes, they estrange man from God.

# BOOK AGAINST TWO HERESIES

[Col. 1159]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING SHORT WORK

(D. B. Pez, preface to vol. I, pt. II, *Anecdota*, p. LXX.)

This book, which Gerhoh dedicated to the venerable Godfrey, Abbot of Admont, a foremost ornament of the twelfth century, is his helmeted prologue to the *Exposition of the Psalms*. This exposition was prepared for print in a very large volume by the Reverend Father Felix Wirtenberger, of the Order of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary, a man most experienced in these studies and one who would one day, if the governors of that most sacred order favored him as he deserved, become incomparable.

Since this work was not so closely and necessarily connected with the *Exposition of the Psalms*, which the distinguished Father Felix yielded to us for publication, it seemed that it ought to be brought to light at the earliest opportunity. Gerhoh himself teaches in the preface, in these words, what the two heresies are against which he sharpens his pen in this short work:

> “In the present short work my discourse is chiefly directed against two heresies, partly ancient and partly new. The one, together with Nestorius, detracts from the man divinely conceived, assigning him a glory less than the glory of God the Father, because his human nature, according to its condition, is less than the nature of the Father—although he is equal to the Father in glory; for, as every tongue now confesses, the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. The other does not take from Christ, but attributes too much to Antichrist, when it asserts that priests synodically deprived of divine office or Christian communion can, in offices they have presumptuously undertaken, while the Church protests, consecrate the body of Christ.”

This is Gerhoh’s own statement. Against the former heresy he has sought, by almost the same arguments with which in the preceding book he defended the glory and honor of the Son of man, to strike a fatal blow. The latter heresy, which he attacks in all his writings without exception, he addresses by the authority of councils, Roman pontiffs, holy Fathers, and especially Hugh of Reading, later Archbishop of Rouen.

You have the latter’s entire letter concerning the nonexistence of sacraments administered by excommunicated and deposed priests in chapter 3. Gerhoh rejoices that he received it from the archives of the Roman curia. Toward the end Gerhoh’s argument develops to the point where he says that what a schismatic deprived of priestly office consecrates is not Christ’s body as regards the essence, reality, and efficacy of the sacrament, though it may be called Christ’s body in appearance and sacramentally. If you wish to understand this completely, read the final chapter of this work.

If you find there anything expressed too harshly or not sufficiently consistent with the received mode of speech in our schools, do not, if you are wise, blame us for it. Our sole purpose is to publish what the ancient theologians thought, not to teach what should now be thought or how they ought to have spoken. Moreover, we owe the use of the contemporary manuscript from which this present little book was copied with singular care by the Reverend Father Felix to the most reverend and most kindly disposed toward us Lord Herculanus, Provost of Reichersberg.

[Col. 1161]

# BOOK AGAINST TWO HERESIES BY THE VENERABLE GERHOH, PROVOST OF REICHERSBERG

(Extracted from a manuscript codex of the illustrious canonry of Reichersberg by the very reverend and distinguished Father Felix Wirtenberger, theologian of the Order of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary and prior of the monastery of Schönbichl in Austria; edited by D. B. Pez, *Anecdota*, vol. I, part II, p. 281.)

## GERHOH’S LETTER TO GODFREY, ABBOT OF ADMONT, OFFERING HIM HIS BOOK AGAINST TWO HERESIES

[Col. 1161A]

Brother G. [Gerhoh], to G. [Godfrey I], venerable abbot of the monastery of Admont: devoted service, with constant prayers.

Frequent experience has taught me that, if he walks among robbers, a traveler, however unburdened, is not safe from the arrow that flies by day. Such robbers are accustomed first to shoot at the traveler, before troubling to examine his bags. Yet there is another kind of robber who does not strike with an arrow, but with a sword—before they have seen whether the traveler is laden—though they would not injure him if they saw him unburdened. Hence the pagan poet says:

> “The unburdened traveler will sing before the robber.”  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* X.22

Since, therefore, my path lies not only among assassins—of whom it is said, “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Psalm 56:5)—but also among malignant archers, I must heed what is written about such people: “For behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot at the upright in heart in darkness” (Psalm 10:2).

For such robbers, ready to wound even the upright in heart, are fearful. Their poisoned arrows are fearful and are to be avoided by all the upright in heart, against whom they especially lie in wait—but in vain. For the upright in heart, whom truth will surround with its unconquerable shield, shall not fear “the terror by night, the arrow that flies by day, the pestilence that walks in darkness, the assault, and the demon at noon” (Psalm 90:6).

Wishing to surround his disciples with such a shield, Truth said: “If you remain in my word, you shall truly be free, and the truth shall make you free” (John 8:36). Therefore, that I may proceed safely and freely in the exposition of the Psalms, and may not fear a harsh word directed against me—since some troublesome persons are accustomed to call schismatic or heretic anyone whom they perceive to be less in agreement with their own opinion—if perhaps some matters unfamiliar to modern readers are introduced, surrounded here and there by the true judgments of the orthodox ancient Fathers and encircled with the shield of truth:

Yet because, for one living among enemies, a shield is insufficient unless his very head is also protected by a helmet, I have judged that this present preface, addressed to your fatherly wisdom, should be placed before my treatise divided into sections. Thus its head and beginning may be protected—or helmeted—against archers striking from afar and assassins striking at close range, ready even in darkness to wound the upright in heart (Psalm 10:3).

You, therefore, whose uprightness of heart I do not doubt, since you do not walk in darkness, have no need at all to be fortified by this little work of mine. Yet for the sake of others who walk in darkness, I dedicate it to you: where it pleases, let it be approved; where it reasonably displeases, let it be corrected, or cautiously returned to me so that it may be corrected.

The letter ends.

## THE PREFACE BEGINS

In the present short work my discourse is chiefly directed against two heresies, partly ancient and partly new. [Col. 1163A] The one, together with Nestorius, detracts from the man divinely conceived, assigning him a glory less than the glory of God the Father, because his human nature, according to its condition, is less than the nature of the Father—although he is equal to the Father in glory. For, as every tongue now confesses: “The Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11).

The other does not take from Christ, but attributes too much to Antichrist, when it asserts that priests synodically deprived of divine office or Christian communion can, in offices they have presumptuously undertaken while the Church protests, consecrate the body of Christ.

## CHAPTER ONE

**The glory, power, and wisdom of the Son of man are not less than the glory, power, and wisdom of God the Father.**
Those imbued with these heresies were offended when they read my writings [Col. 1163B], and regarded this as a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense: that I introduced blessed Hilary in the ninth book of *On the Trinity* as saying: “The Father, who is about to glorify the Son, is greater. The Son glorified in the Father is not less. The Father is greater when He is asked to restore glory to the assumed man. The Son is not less when He resumes glory with the Father.” For these words of Hilary were received as though contrary to Athanasius’s words concerning the Son: “Equal to the Father according to divinity, less than the Father according to humanity.” But, as we have shown more clearly in the letter to Lord Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, Hilary is not contrary to Athanasius: Athanasius declares the Son less than the Father according to humanity; Hilary [Col. 1163C], however, speaking not of the nature of humanity in Christ but of the immeasurable glory of that humanity itself, declares that the glorified Son is not less than the Father. For the immeasurable glory which Christ always possessed in His divinity, He likewise received fully in His humanity.

This is also attested by the modern doctor Master Hugh, who, as you too reminded me, while maintaining that Christ’s soul is not equal to divinity according to nature, nevertheless does not deny that it is equal according to glory. For he says in the book *On the Sacraments*: “Just as Christ’s soul had the full and perfect wisdom of God united to it by nature, so through and from that wisdom it was fully and perfectly wise; yet it was not equal in nature to Wisdom itself, because it is far different to be wise through wisdom from being Wisdom. For from the moment that divinity was united to humanity, humanity received from divinity by grace everything which divinity possessed by nature; so that, according to that ineffable union, everything belonging to humanity by nature belonged to God in His humanity, and everything belonging to divinity belonged to man in His divinity.”

In these words of Master Hugh, the natures of humanity and divinity are carefully distinguished, while the wisdom of both natures is undivided. For in saying, “It is far different to be wise through wisdom from being Wisdom,” he suitably shows that Christ’s soul was not equal in nature to eternal Wisdom. Yet he subsequently shows that it was equal to Wisdom in power from the very conception of the Virgin conceiving the God-man, when he adds:

“Thus, then, we believe that from its first conception the humanity of the Word, in its rational soul, received through the ineffable union with divinity full and perfect wisdom, power, strength, and goodness; and we confess that it remained unchangeably in that fullness of power by virtue of the union, just as it remained inseparably in the union of divinity itself. For God-man did not will to live among men in order that, as though progressing through intervals of time in wisdom or power, He might hope to earn merit for Himself and become better than Himself; but in order that, by the dispensation of human salvation, He might fulfill according to His ineffable ordering that wisdom and goodness which He always possessed fully and perfectly in His divinity, and which He received fully and perfectly in His humanity once and all at once.

“Therefore the Evangelist’s statement that Jesus advanced in wisdom, age, and grace is not to be understood as though He became better than Himself; rather, He increasingly revealed to men, as the order of the times required, the grace and wisdom which He possessed but which lay hidden. Thus He advanced among men when men themselves advanced in knowledge of Him. But He advanced before God insofar as, while showing Himself full of the wisdom and grace of God, He increasingly urged them to praise God the Father, from whom He testified that He possessed this.”

And indeed I accept this testimony of Master Hugh concerning the Lord Jesus. But as Jesus Himself says, “I have testimony greater than John” (John 5:36), so He too may say: “I have testimony greater than Hugh.” For the Apostle proclaims Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God,” which is glory infinitely greater than being powerful through power and wise through wisdom. Since the wisdom of God reaches mightily from end to end, existing everywhere and in all things universally through essence, and in good angels and men specifically through the presence of His grace, nevertheless no creature can be proclaimed in such a way as to be called Wisdom except the God-man. He who is truly called God, the Son of God, is equally truly called the wisdom of God and the power of God.

Therefore, although to be fully, perfectly, and unchangeably wise—which Master Hugh attributes to Christ’s soul—is “every good gift and every perfect gift” descending “from above, from the Father of lights” (James 1:17), and although we believe that certain of the elect share in this gift, yet I prefer to proclaim with the Apostle Christ as the power of God and wisdom of God, rather than to call a soul or man wise through wisdom. Eternal Wisdom does not inform Him accidentally, as it did King Solomon or another holy wise man, but wholly essentially or substantially, so that He is thereby “fairer in form than the children of men” (Psalm 44[45]:3).

For since divinity is in Christ in every manner in which it can be present, no creature receives this entire mode of divine presence; rather, from His fullness it receives some mode, according to the measure of the distribution of gifts which exist without measure in Christ. Divinity is present in things in three ways. First, whole and undivided, it is present in every creature through the omnipresent entirety of its substance, which fills every essence, according to the saying, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24).

> [Note: Col. 1165D. In the Vulgate edition it reads: “Do I not fill heaven and earth?”]

But it is not present in every creature through justifying and beatifying grace, but only in rational creatures, which alone it justifies and saves among the elect. Yet in no created thing—Christ excepted—is it present as the form of its definition. For, when defining what any creature is, we do not say, “It is God,” even though it has divinity abiding within it. Thus, when asked what a human being is, we do not answer [Col. 1165B], “God,” but “a body”; and we say this on account of corporeity, which is the substantial form of the subject.

But in Christ—or, if we prefer to say it, in that man who is Christ—divinity is present whole, not merely through the presence of substance, as in the entire fabric of the world, nor merely through indwelling grace, which is the mode of presence found only in rational creatures. Beyond these two modes of presence, namely through substance and grace, it is present in a third way: through the form of definition. Since He is God-man, the form of humanity and the form of divinity are wholly substantial to Him. Thus, when asked what the Son of God is, we answer that He is God because of the form of God [Col. 1165C], and man because of the form of man. Again, when asked what that same Son of the Virgin is, we answer that He is man because of the form of man, and God because of the form of God.

For as, when asked of the Father or the Holy Spirit, we answer that He is God, so, when asked of Christ, we say that He is God. In Him the fullness of divinity exists in the three ways mentioned: through substance, through grace, and through the form of definition. Therefore, as the Evangelist says, “From His fullness we have all received” (John 1:16).

> [Note: Col. 1166D. The Vulgate edition reads: “From His fullness,” etc.]

To us, who have been freely given grace, participation in deity is given in the first two modes, but not fullness. Thus we have received not the fullness, but from His fullness. No saint receives wisdom or power in such a manner that he himself is called wisdom or power, as is that man who, “being in the form of God,” does not consider it robbery to be equal to God in wisdom and power; for He Himself is the very power of God and wisdom of God.

For He alone, singularly, “like a solitary sparrow” (Psalm 101[102]:8), was chosen “out of thousands” (Song of Songs 5:10) for this: that, remaining in the form of God, He should consider Himself equal to God—not by robbery, like the devil puffed up in heaven or man deceived by him, but through fullness of grace and truth. Contemplating Him in that fullness, the holy Evangelist says: “We saw His glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The fullness of grace consisted in this: that humanity, without any merit of its own [Col. 1166A], was freely assumed into the form of God. The fullness of truth and righteousness consisted in this: that after the merit of obedience necessary not for Himself but for His own, in which He emptied the form of God for the sake of servants, being for a time made lower than the angels, His very servile nature was exalted to the confession of the Father’s loftiness. There it has not been emptied so as not to exist, but so glorified that every tongue rightly confesses that even the human nature of the Son of God is in the supreme glory, power, and might—or rather omnipotence—of Divinity, because “all power in heaven and on earth has been given to Him” (Matthew 28:18).

## Chapter II. The same point is further confirmed from Rupert of Deutz, Leo the Great, and the Council of Ephesus.

[Col. 1166B] Therefore I do not judge it absurd that, in the writings of Rupert, abbot of Deutz—which we too discussed together face to face—I find this man, fairer than the children of men, made equal to God most high, not according to human nature, which without any contradiction is, according to its condition, less than divinity, but according to the power, wisdom, and glory bestowed upon human nature in that man at His conception, birth, and glorification. This power, wisdom, and glory are certainly not less than the power, wisdom, and glory of God the Father, but are altogether the very same and not less in the God-man, the Son of God and man, than in God the Father, the begetter of God-man. Hence He is said not to be degenerate but generated, or begotten [Col. 1166C]: begotten and only-begotten in divinity, but first-born in humanity, while in both natures there remains complete equality of power without any degeneracy.

Therefore He says: “Today I have begotten You” (Psalm 2:7). “I have begotten,” He says, not only the Only-begotten in divinity but also the First-born in humanity, equally noble in both natures because of the timeless, perfect divine generation and the deifying generation made in time. For God eternally begot God; and the Virgin conceived God made man, not by a man, but because God the Father impregnated her. She received His seed—that is, the Word—through His love, which is the Holy Spirit; and this Word, made flesh, she bore, by a generation more divine than human, because she was impregnated by God and not by man. Therefore the man born of her is called the Son of God as properly as He is called the Son of man—not by adoption, but by generation.

Accordingly, those who assert that the man whom the Apostle says was “predestined Son of God in power” (Romans 1:4) is, in power, less noble or weaker than the Father who begets Him seem to me not to understand the power of generation at all. For though He “was crucified from our weakness,” in which He truly bore our infirmities (Isaiah 53:4), yet that man possesses invincible power, equal to that of His Father: equally omnipotent and equally great, not according to humanity but according to power. For He was not only, as Paul says, predestined Son of God in power [Col. 1167A], but, as Peter affirms, “God anointed Him with power” (Acts 10:38).

> [Note: Col. 1167D. “God anointed Him with the Holy Spirit and with power.”]

He was not anointed by measure as His father David was, but so fully that the anointed man is no less strong than the God who anoints Him. Finally, as Saint Basil says in the book *On the Dispensation of God*: “The man is anointed, God anoints, and the anointing of humanity is divinity.”

If, therefore, King David, though remaining small by nature or stature, nevertheless grew in power and dignity through Samuel’s anointing, what wonder if that little one who “was born to us,” the Son “given to us” (Isaiah 9:6), while remaining little according to human nature, is nevertheless believed through being anointed with divinity to possess divine greatness? Hence He overcomes Goliath and, Himself stronger, defeats the strong armed man, because the strength or greatness of humanity is divinity. Thus the man, at His very conception, was anointed like David in his father’s house. Even when He appeared a little man, through the anointing which is Divinity He was a great king and also a great priest. The three Magi reverently testified to this, venerating Him as king with gold and as priest with incense while He still lay a little child in the cradle.

At that time, indeed, the magnificence of the wailing infant was glorified in gold, to show royal power. But now those who detract from the greatness of Him who has been exalted to heaven recognize neither the king in gold nor the great priest in incense. We, however, believe that in human nature He ascended where He had previously been in divinity, He who “in the beginning was with God” (John 1:2). Then the Word Himself was with God; now the man Himself is with God. Then the Word was God; now the man is God. Then all things were made through the Word Himself; now all things are restored through the man Himself. Then nothing was made without the Word Himself; now nothing is sanctified without the priest Himself.

Therefore it rightly seemed good not only to my littleness but also to your prudence to reject the teaching of those who affirm that these false priests, cut off from the body of this priest, can sanctify anything outside Him. In refuting their sacrifice, as you know, in my first defense no one stood with me; all deserted me. But afterwards, when, on the advice of the venerable man Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, I had been summoned to Pope Innocent of blessed memory [Col. 1167D] and had remained long with him, he stood very firmly by me. Relying upon the testimonies of ancient and modern Fathers alike—whom it would take too long to list—he neither listened against me to the abbot himself or to others who seemed to be pillars, nor in any way assented to the opinions of the Frankish masters who taught doctrines contrary to me and to Lord Hugh of Reading. We shall place below, at the beginning of our work, his letter consonant with our assertion, so that whoever deigns to read our writings may, before entering upon the reading, be fortified both by this letter of ours addressed to you, my lord and friend, and by his letter addressed to his friend [Col. 1168A], lest he take offense at our words in which my soul magnifies my Lord, to whom the Lord said: “Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 109[110]:1).

From on high He seems to me to cry, “Do not touch me” (John 20:17), to every weak faith in which He has not yet ascended to His Father, but is still sought as though shut in the tomb, because He is thought, being confined by local circumscription, unable to show His entire presence everywhere as He wills. If He could not do this, the whole Church throughout the world would not have Him wholly present in the sacrifice of the altar. When He presents Himself there in His indivisible body, He is never absent from the Father’s assembly on high. For, as Leo the Great affirms in a sermon to the people: “He who sits at the Father’s right hand is Himself the indweller of the whole body, and He who confirms below for endurance is the same who invites above to glory.”

Again, shortly afterward: “It is not enough for us to know the Son of God in the Father’s nature alone, unless we recognize that He has not departed from what is His own in ours. For that emptying which He devoted to the restoration of humanity was an arrangement of mercy, not a deprivation of power. Since, by the eternal counsel of God, no other name under heaven had been given to men in which they must be saved, the invisible made His substance visible, the timeless temporal, and the impassible passible—not so that strength might fail in weakness, but so that weakness might pass into incorruptible strength.

“For this reason the feast called Pascha by us is called *Phase* by the Hebrews, that is, ‘Passage,’ as the Evangelist testifies when he says: ‘Before the feast day of Passover, Jesus, knowing that His hour had come that He should pass from this world to the Father’ (John 13:1). But of what nature was that passage to be, if not ours, since both the Father was inseparably in the Son and the Son in the Father? Yet because flesh and Word are one person, the one assumed is not divided from the One who assumes; and the honor of the one advanced is called an increase for the One advancing him. Thus says the Apostle, as we have already recalled: ‘Therefore God exalted Him and gave Him a name which is above every name’ (Philippians 2:9).

> [Note: Col. 1167D. The Vulgate reads: “Therefore God also … and bestowed on Him the name,” etc.]

“Here the exaltation of the assumed man is commended, so that He in whose sufferings Deity remains indivisible may be coeternal in the glory of Deity. The Lord Himself prepared for His faithful this blessed passage into participation in the ineffable gift when, close upon His imminent Passion, He prayed not only for the apostles and disciples but also for the whole Church, saying: ‘I pray not for these only, but also for those who shall believe in me through their word, that all may be one, as You, Father, are in me and I in You, that they too may be one in us’ (John 17:20).”

> [Note: Col. 1168D. The Vulgate has: “But also for those … through their word in me,” etc.]

Again Leo the Great, in a sermon to the people on the coming of the Holy Spirit: “As the blessed apostle John says: ‘For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.’ The Lord’s Ascension was the ground for giving the Spirit. Whoever denies that the true man in Christ was advanced to the session at the Father’s right hand necessarily denies that the Spirit was given. But we, beloved, adopted through the generation of the Holy Spirit to the blessed eternity of both soul and body, should celebrate the most sacred feast of this day with rational devotion, confessing with the blessed apostle Paul that the Lord Jesus, ‘ascending on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to men’ (Ephesians 4:8), so that the Gospel of God may be preached through every utterance of the human voice, and every tongue may confess that ‘the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father’ (Philippians 2:11).”

Again in the same sermon: “The marks of the nails and the lance were preserved to heal the wounds of faithful hearts, so that it might be held, not by doubtful faith but by most steadfast knowledge, that the nature which had lain in the tomb was to sit upon the throne of God the Father.” And shortly afterward: “Then, he says, a more instructed faith began, with the step of the mind, to approach the Son as equal to the Father; and it began no longer to need bodily touching of the substance in Christ which is less than the Father, because, while the nature of the glorified body remained, the faith of believers was summoned to that place where the Only-begotten, equal to His Begetter, was touched not by a carnal hand but by spiritual understanding.”

Again: “Great and ineffable was the cause for rejoicing when, in the sight of the holy multitude, the nature of the human race ascended above the dignity of all heavenly creatures [Col. 1169C], to pass beyond the angelic orders and be raised above the heights of archangels. It would have no limit to its advancement through any exalted ranks unless, received into the session of the eternal Father, it were joined on the throne as partner in the glory of that nature with which it was united in the Son.”

Ambrose, *On Luke*: “‘The Lord said to my Lord’ (Psalm 109[110]:1). The Lord, about to fulfill the commandments, concludes the faith and mercy of His covenant with this end: faith in Him, that we should believe Christ to be our Lord God and to sit at God’s right hand—not that He sits bodily, He who is everywhere. For He is in the Father because He is in the substance of God, because there is one power, one majesty. Thus He is in the Father, and the Father in Him. He sits at the Father’s right hand in the Father, because He shares with the Father and is second to none. He was sent by the Father because He descended from the Father’s heaven to fulfill His will. Put away from this all questions of faithlessness: it is religion, and complete religion. He is neither preferred because He sits at God’s right hand nor dishonored because He is sent. Degrees of dignity are not sought where there is fullness of divinity.”

The same, *On Luke*: “What is meant by Joseph and Nicodemus burying Christ—one righteous, and the other one in whom there was no deceit? The righteous man covers Christ’s body with linen, and the innocent anoints it with ointment. You too, then, clothe the Lord’s body in its glory, so that you yourself may be righteous; and if you believe it dead, yet cover it with the fullness of His divinity. Anoint it with myrrh and aloes, so that you may be the good fragrance of Christ.”

Again, in the same work, explaining, “Who shall find a valiant woman?” (Proverbs 31:10): “Let us see what she does for her husband, what her work is, what service she performs, and why Christ trusts in her. A good wife clothes her husband. Let our faith clothe Jesus with His body; let it clothe His flesh with the glory of His divinity. So too she made two garments for her husband, that she might honor him both in the present age and in the age to come.”

Again: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is at the right hand of God the Father” (Colossians 3:1). “And lest we should suppose it a duty of the eyes rather than of the mind, he added: ‘Set your minds on things above, not on things upon the earth’ (ibid., 2). Therefore, if we wish to find You, Christ, we must not follow You upon the earth, nor in the earth, nor according to the flesh.”

Again, Saint Augustine in a sermon on the Creed: “When the Father is said to sit, we must not imagine bent knees, lest we fall into that sacrilege in which the Apostle condemns those who ‘changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of corruptible man.’ For it is unlawful for a Christian to place such an image in a temple. It is far more wicked to place it in the heart, where the true temple of God is, if that heart has been cleansed from earthly desire and error. Therefore God is said to sit, not because of a position of limbs, but to signify judicial power, which that majesty never lacks, always giving to the worthy what is worthy. His right hand is supreme blessedness, just as the left is misery, in which the goats will be set.”

[Col. 1170C] The same, in Book XX, chapter 13, of *The City of God*: “A certain divine power must be understood by which it comes about that each person’s works, whether good or evil, are all recalled to memory and seen with marvellous swiftness by the mind’s gaze, so that knowledge may excuse or accuse conscience, and thus all and each may be judged. This divine power has received the name of a book; for in it, in a certain manner, whatever is recalled by its agency is read, as the Apostle says: ‘For we shall all stand before the tribunal of the Lord, so that each may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or evil’ (2 Corinthians 5:10).

> [Note: Col. 1169. The Vulgate reads: “For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, that each may receive the things proper to the body, according as he has done,” etc.]

“In calling it the tribunal of the Lord, he means the exalted height of His majesty, which will appear to all everywhere and in all things. When it is revealed, the wicked will see Him whom they pierced, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn themselves.”

Many things could be gathered in this fashion concerning the height of the Most High in the city of the Lord, “where the man was born, and the Most High Himself founded her” (Psalm 86[87]:5). Therefore we glorify and adore the highest man, the Son of the Most High, in the height of the highest royal glory in which His Father is. We believe His flesh to be life-giving for men, just as His divinity is life for angels; and we proclaim the God-man’s substance as twofold indeed, but His glory one and not twofold, and in worship we do not distinguish the man from God.

For thus the Synod of Ephesus commands among other things: “If anyone does not confess that the flesh of Christ is life-giving, as being the flesh of the Word of God the Father Himself, but regards it as the flesh of some other person besides Him, joined indeed to Him according to dignity, or as though He had merely inhabited it; and does not instead confess it to be life-giving, as I have said, because it became the Word’s own flesh, to whom it is possible to give life to all things: let him be anathema.”

Again in the same council: “If anyone dares to say that the assumed man ought to be co-worshipped with God the Word, co-glorified, and called God as another added to another—for the addition of one syllable, namely *co-*, compels this meaning—and does not rather venerate Emmanuel with one act of reverence and render one glorification, because the Word became flesh: let him be anathema.”

Avoiding, therefore, the anathema of the Council of Ephesus, we agree with the teaching of John of Damascus in not separating God from man. Those who assign humanity to the man alone and divinity to God alone make Christ as though half man and half God, whereas He is wholly man and wholly God. Thus John of Damascus says in the book *On the Dispensation of God*: “We confess Him to be one Son of God, and after His humanity still one, the same Son of Man: one Christ, one Lord, the only-begotten Son and Word of God. Thus we venerate the two generations of our Lord Jesus Christ: one from the Father before the ages, beyond cause, reason, time, and nature; and one in the last times, for us, according to us, and beyond us, not from seed but from the Spirit and the all-holy Theotokos, beyond the law.

“For we do not preach Him as God bare of our humanity, nor, in calling Him man, bare of divinity; nor do we preach one and another, but one and the same, at once God and man: perfect God and perfect man, wholly God and wholly man; the same wholly God with His flesh, and wholly man with the divinity of His Deity. By saying ‘perfect God and perfect man,’ we show the completeness, not the deficiency, of the natures. But by saying ‘wholly God and wholly man,’ we show the singularity, not the division, of the person.”

Let these testimonies suffice for the wise, lest the writings of Lord Rupert or our own appear less wise in proclaiming the Son of the Virgin, the man conceived by divinity, as the Most High: less indeed than the Father according to humanity, but not less according to the power given to Him, because “all power in heaven and on earth has been given to Him” (Matthew 28:18). Let the Nestorians of our time, who detract from the greatness of the man of whom it is written, “Great is the Lord, and great is His power, and there is no number to His wisdom” (Psalm 146[147]:5), therefore be silent. “There is no end of His greatness” (Psalm 144[145]:3).

For just as it is truly written of Him that “a little child was born to us” (Isaiah 9:6), so it is no less truly added that “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (ibid.). He was always great in divinity [Col. 1172A], and “He shall be great” (Luke 1:32), says the angel speaking of His conception according to man. The angel does not assign one greatness to man and another to God, because that man is God, and “shall be called the Son of the Most High” (ibid.).

We have answered one heresy. Let Hugh’s letter answer the other, because it is pleasant to use defenses already prepared, so that our assertion and his may, like two very sharp horns, fortify the brow of our treatise against the two heresies noted above, resembling the two horns mentioned in the Apocalypse, where the beast is described as having “two horns like a lamb” (Revelation 13:11). For the beast, understood as Antichrist, greatly boasts that in one heresy Christ is excessively disparaged, when the man—God, the Son of God—conceived and born as man is asserted to possess glory, power, and strength less than that of His Father [Col. 1172B]. In the other, however, Antichrist himself is magnified, when priests cut off from Christ and incorporated into Antichrist himself are ascribed as much efficacy in the sacraments as Catholic priests. The following letter, which we received from the archives of the Roman curia, will make clear to the well-disposed reader with what great, and how wolfish, falsehood this is done beneath a lamb-like appearance of plausibility.

## Chapter III. Letter of Hugh of Reading, demonstrating that the sacraments of excommunicated and deposed priests are null.

To his most illustrious lord, Abbot W., HUGH, unworthy servant of the brethren of Reading: may you think soundly and teach rightly [Col. 1172C].

> “I have heard that you wished to retain for yourself our little book, which, by your own wish and not by our permission, has been widely circulated and, as you yourself testify, gratefully received—except that they do not rightly accept what is there said concerning a deposed or excommunicated priest. Therefore, one whom Christ, through the Church, has deprived of office by deposition or excommunication, if he presumes to minister at the sacred altar, now that he is no longer a minister, does nothing. For God so ordained that these things should be done that none may be performed except through a minister.
>
> “In this judgment it seems rightly said, both by our people and by all Catholics hitherto, that one who acts in the sacrament of the altar while not being a minister does nothing. We read that it has been handed down by the Fathers, and we hold it firm: the Spirit of graces does not follow the person, whether worthy or wicked, but the order of transmission. Thus, although someone may be of good merit, he nevertheless cannot consecrate unless he has been ordained, so that, as a minister, he may perform the office; but it belongs to God to grant the effect of consecration or blessing.
>
> “Therefore, since what had there been set down with the Church as witness was not rashly to be criticized, the question which the doubter should rather have asked was whether one whom the Church has once appointed as a minister to perform a sacrament can later, when fault deserves it, depose or excommunicate in such a way that he cannot act in the sacraments as he formerly could. The answer was that living and all-powerful is the word of the Lord, who said to the keys of the Church [Col. 1173A], which he sanctified: ‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven’ (Matt. 16:19).
>
> “On this basis the Apostolic See and Catholic teachers throughout the world, as the writings of the ancients testify, customarily proclaim that priests as well as all ministers in clerical orders retain, at the time of their deposition or excommunication, the grace once received, but lack the office. They add also that, if those who are not ministers presume to consecrate in the sacraments or sacramental offices, they certainly do nothing. Blessed Pope Innocent, with the assent of the Apostolic See, wrote that a certain Nezelon, ordained by heretics, could give nothing to the man upon whom he laid hands, because he himself had nothing to give. If, indeed, this man had been ordained by ministers who, though unworthy, had not been [Col. 1173B] deposed or excommunicated, then, however unworthy he himself might be, if he were a minister he would certainly confer by virtue of his office upon the one on whom he rightly laid hands.
>
> “Give us a minister, however unworthy; give us a minister: we acknowledge that he possesses office. It is one thing to speak of the sacrament, another to speak of the office. The priestly office is forbidden to many, but the sacrament is not taken away from them. Hence, when it pleases the Church at some time to restore them, it absolves and reconciles those restored; it does not reordain them. Again, it is one thing to speak of a bad office-holder who ministers improperly but who nevertheless ministers so long as he remains a minister, however evil he may be. It is another to depose the man himself from office, lest he perform ministry.
>
> “Do we not know that some sacraments are necessary, while others pertain to office? Baptism is necessary for all; but every priestly or clerical dignity is entrusted to certain persons for an office. The work of baptizing is forbidden to no one, for no baptized person is suspended from Christian practice; indeed, even if he has strayed, he is recalled in many ways. But priestly or clerical office is often curtailed for fault, and some are more frequently deposed from it. By the former all live in Christ; by the latter some serve at the Church’s command. The former builds the Church’s house; the latter administers the house once built. This administration is not undertaken by just anyone; it is ministered by an office-holder appointed by the Church.
>
> “But if he is deposed from office through the Church, the sacrament once conferred upon him remains. [Col. 1173D] Therefore, as you read in our little work, it remains for judgment, not for office. So also, for every Christian who is excommunicated, the sacrament of baptism remains not as a remedy but for judgment; it remains not for salvation but for condemnation. Therefore we say that when he comes to his senses he is reconciled through the Church, not rebaptized. For if he lost the sacrament by sinning, then when he returned penitently to the Church he would undoubtedly have to be rebaptized. Divine sacraments cannot be taken away through a human being from one who possesses them. The sacraments therefore remain; but, when fault requires it, the offices of the sacraments are often taken away.
>
> “It must also be understood that there is a great difference between a Christian’s being cast out of the Church by excommunication and a minister’s being removed from office. The former constantly burdens; the latter often relieves. The former condemns; the latter corrects. If a minister acts unworthily, it is beneficial that he be deposed; but it is deadly for a Christian to be separated from the Church. For while he is severed from the Church, he is certainly judged an unbeliever—indeed, worse than an unbeliever. The Lord says: ‘He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me’ (Luke 10:16). To dissent from the Church, therefore, is to fall away from Christ. But to fall away from Christ is not to possess faith. And one who lacks faith has no good work.”
>
> Hear the Apostle: “Everything,” he says, “which is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23). Therefore, although a Christian possesses the sacrament of baptism, while he strays from faith he does no good. Not everyone who possesses a sacrament, then, also possesses the office of that sacrament. Hence we are astonished that certain people say of an excommunicated or deposed priest that, because he retains the sacrament once received in his ordination, he has efficacy in consecrating whenever he presumes to do so.
>
> Therefore whoever undertakes to instruct others concerning the sacraments of ministers must, in teaching, distinguish the sacrament of ordination from the office of the ordained person. Let him say that the sacrament once received remains in its recipient, but that the Church’s censure often removes the recipient’s office. Let him also say that the Church’s authority is as real when it deposes a minister from office as when it rightly appoints him to office. And let him teach that the man who does not consent to the Church is a schismatic, concerning whom authority says: “What the schismatic consecrates is not the body of Christ” [Col. 1174C].
>
> And elsewhere: “Outside the Catholic Church there is no place of true sacrifice. Hence the Lord also commands concerning the lamb through Moses: ‘You shall eat it in one house, and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside’ (Exod. 12:46).” [Note: [Col. 1173D] The Vulgate reads: “It shall be eaten in one house,” etc.] “And no uncircumcised person shall eat of it.” [Note: [Col. 1174D] The Vulgate at the same place, verse 48, reads: “But if anyone has not been circumcised, he shall not eat of it.”] “It is therefore received in unity, not in schism; it is not obtained outside the Catholic Church, nor from a foreigner.
>
> “Therefore do not believe empty talkers; do not yield to the proud. Believe the humble and obedient, who receive the sacraments of Mother Church with reverence—not by disputation, but by humbly reverencing the authority of their institutor. For from him Mother Church, who powerfully looses and binds, receives efficacy in the sacraments: she sometimes entrusts it to one ordained and denies it to another by a valid authority [Col. 1174D], not by frivolous verbosity.
>
> “But let your prudence know that, if the acts of consecration performed by schismatics or by the deposed were efficacious, every see would now have countless bishops, and Rome how many popes! In horrible confusion they would both loose those bound by others and improperly bind those loosed. Thus—yes, thus—if you consider it carefully, valid acts would be annulled and invalid acts preferred. Thus nothing among ecclesiastical acts would be certain; everything would be frivolous; and, to speak the truth, there would be no Church at all.
>
> “But enough on these matters. We have written these things back to you briefly, we who hold the acts of Mother Church to be not frivolous but valid, and who have preferred to follow the authorities of the holy Fathers rather than our own opinions.” [Col. 1175A]

*Here ends the letter of Hugh.*

When carefully considered, this makes manifest that those preach a lie who attribute to deposed priests an efficacy in the sacraments equal to that of Catholic priests. Likewise those teach a lie to be received as truth who deny that the man conceived by the Holy Spirit is the Most High. Whoever, therefore, receives the teaching of these people—whether by imagining Antichrist equal to the Most High in the sacraments or by setting Christ beneath the Most High in the glory of power—is not a disciple of truth but a companion in another’s error. He makes that error his own if, having been reproved, he does not come to his senses. Therefore truth does not set him free, but falsehood ensnares him—a falsehood which, Blessed Augustine declares, is the worst of all lies.

For, in discussing eight kinds of lies, that blessed man especially execrates the lie in which error in the doctrine of faith is obstinately defended as truth. This is characteristic of heretics. As we proceed in the light of the arrows—that is, the sayings of the Fathers—we frequently strike them in our work and scatter their darkness, because we desire to rejoice not merely for an hour in their light, but forever in the light of truth. And, with God’s help—he in whose hand are both ourselves and our words—we intend to call kindly hearers and readers to that same joy in our commentaries on the Psalms.

For one who rejoices in a lie rejoices only for an hour, because however much falsehood may be painted over with plausibility, it does not endure long [Col. 1175C]. But truth remains forever. Therefore those who love it and rejoice in it will rejoice forever, and no one shall take their joy from them. We say not only that falsehood passes quickly; it is established also that every form of this world passes quickly. Even the visible form of the Lord’s body, in which he was seen by the world, has now passed away. Hence the world no longer sees him; “but you see me” (John 14:19), Truth said to his disciples, because they are neither delighted nor fed by a form that is passing away, but by Truth itself, which remains forever.

While he was still among his own in a passing form, Truth itself said: “If you loved me, you would rejoice [Col. 1175D] because I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). But when he had already laid aside his passing form and the form of a servant had now been emptied, the Lord himself reigned, clothed in splendor and girded with strength. He did not say, “The Father is greater than I,” but: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18).

If, therefore, we loved him, we would surely rejoice in this truth, which will never pass away and never at all be changed: because Christ, having gone forth from the highest heaven and returned to the highest, now dies no more. He is equal in immortality to him “who alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6:16). [Note: [Col. 1175D] The Vulgate reads: “inhabits.”] For as God alone possesses immortality—that is, unchangeability—so he gave immortality to the human being assumed into himself: not such as angels possess, but such as God himself possesses, to whom it is truly said: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101:28).

## CHAPTER IV. It is proved from Saint Hilary that the human being was glorified not beneath God but in God—glorified in such a way as to be God in God. It is also explained in what sense the Son is subject to God the Father.

Therefore the human being was glorified not beneath God but in God—glorified in such a way as to be God in God. Hence Hilary, in Book IX of *On the Holy Trinity*, expounding the Gospel text, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him” (John 7:39 [sic]), says:

> “If God has been glorified in him, God has also glorified him in himself. I consider the first meaning of the Lord’s saying to be unambiguous when he says: ‘Now the Son of Man has been honored.’ For all glory accrued not to the Word but to the flesh—yet not to the nature of God, but to the dispensation of the human being who was born.
>
> “But I ask what this that follows signifies: ‘And God has been honored in him.’ I hear that God has been honored in him, but what this means according to your understanding, heretic, I do not know. God has been honored in him—in the Son, certainly, of Man. And I ask whether the Son of Man is the same as the Son of God. And since the Son of Man is not one thing and the Son of God another—for ‘the Word became flesh’ (John 1:14), and he who is Son of God is himself also Son of Man—I inquire: who has been glorified as God in this Son of Man, who is also Son of God, and why has God been glorified in the Son of Man, who is also Son of God?
>
> “Let us see what is meant by what is added third: ‘If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself.’ What mystery of the sacrament is this, I ask: God glorifies in himself God who has been glorified in the Son of Man. In the Son of Man is the glory of God, and the glory of God is the glory of the Son of Man. God glorifies in himself; certainly the human being is not glorified through himself. Nor again is God, who is glorified in the human being, anything other than God, although he receives glory.
>
> “But when the Son of Man has been glorified, and God, glorifying God, glorifies in himself, I find the glory of nature assumed into the glory of the nature that glorifies [Col. 1176D]. For God does not glorify himself; rather, he is glorified in the human being, while glorifying God in himself. Although he does not glorify himself, he nevertheless assumes into the glory of his nature the glory of the one glorified. And since God, glorifying God because he has been glorified in the human being, glorifies in himself the one whom he glorified, he demonstrates that God is present in himself when he glorifies him in himself.”

Likewise, in Book III:

> “But now, what is that glorification expected with the Father? Surely it is that which he had with him before the world existed. He had, and has, the fullness of divinity, for he is the Son of God. But he who was the Son of God had begun to be also the Son of Man. For the Word had become flesh. He had not lost what he was, but had begun to be what he was not; he had not ceased to possess what was his own, but had received what was ours. What he had received demands for him the advancement of that splendor. Thus he did not cease to be, so that what belonged to time might attain the glory of his timeless splendor.”

As Saint Hilary says these things, we, holding thoughts consonant with his, affirm that the human being is God glorified in God, not beneath God—the one whom God glorified in himself. First, by making him God in his conception; then by showing him to be God equal to himself in powers; also by subjecting all things to him except himself, and establishing him over all things, subject to none. but [he will be] most high in the Most High himself, sitting at his right hand beside him and reigning with him eternally in the same glory, power, and might [Col. 1177B].

Therefore we understand the Apostle’s statement that he “will be subject to him who subjected all things to him” (1 Cor. 15:27) in the sense explained by Saint Ambrose. In Book V of *On the Holy Trinity*, addressed to Emperor Gratian, he says among other things:

> “Let us review the apostolic passage: ‘Last of all,’ he says, ‘death, the enemy, shall be destroyed, for he has subjected all things beneath his feet’ (ibid.). But when he says, ‘All things have been subjected to him,’ it is unquestionably excepting him who subjected all things to him. ‘But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also will be subject to him who subjected all things to him’ (1 Cor. 15:26–27). [Note: [Col. 1177D] The Vulgate reads: ‘But the last enemy,’ etc.; ‘who subjected all things to him’; ‘but when,’ etc.; ‘who subjected all things to himself.’]
>
> “Let us see, therefore, that Scripture speaks not of God as subjected but as yet to be subjected. For just as, if the flesh lusts against the spirit in me and the spirit against the flesh, I do not seem to be subject, so, because the whole Church is one body of Christ, so long as the human race dissents, we divide Christ. Therefore Christ is not yet subject, because his members are not yet subject. But when we are not many members but one spirit, then he too will be subject, so that through his subjection God may be all in all.”

Likewise, shortly afterward:

> “Just as the Apostle said that in him, through that flesh which is the pledge of our salvation, we sit in the heavenly places—although we are not sitting—so he too is said to be subject in us through the assumption of our nature.”

Likewise:

> “It is written that, when we were dead in sins, he made us alive together in Christ—by whose grace you have been saved—and raised us together and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus (Eph. 2:5). [Note: [Col. 1178D] The Vulgate text reads: ‘And when we were dead in sins,’ etc.; ‘by whose grace you have been saved’; ‘and raised us together, and made us sit together in heavenly places,’ etc.]
>
> “I recognize the Scripture: not that God permits human beings to sit at his right hand, but that they sit in Christ, because he is the foundation of all and the head of the Church, in whom our common nature according to the flesh has earned the prerogative of the heavenly seat. For in Christ God, flesh is honored; and in the flesh the nature of the human race, shared by all human beings, is honored.
>
> “Therefore, just as we sit in him through sharing his bodily nature, so also he who, through assumption of our flesh, was made a curse for us—although a curse, of course, cannot fall upon the blessed Son of God—so too, I say, he will be subject in us through the obedience of all. When the Gentile has believed; when the Jew has recognized the one whom he crucified; when the Manichaean has worshiped the one whom he did not believe had come in the flesh; when the Arian has confessed as almighty the one whom he denied; when, finally, in all people there are the wisdom of God, righteousness, peace, love, and resurrection—then through his works and the diverse kinds of virtues Christ will be subject to the Father in us. When vices have been renounced and sin is at rest, one spirit, in one understanding, of all peoples will begin to cleave to God in all. Then God will be all and in all.
>
> “Let us therefore briefly gather the conclusion of the whole exposition. The unity of power excludes the notion of an injurious subjection. The abolition of powers and the victory won over death do not diminish the power of the conqueror. Obedience brings about subjection; Christ assumed obedience; obedience extended to the cross; the cross to salvation. Therefore, where there is the work, there is the author of the work. When, then, all things have been subjected to Christ through Christ’s obedience, so that at his name every knee may bend (Phil. 2:10)—now, because not all believe, not all appear to be subject. But when all have believed and done God’s will, Christ will be all and in all (Col. 3:11). When Christ is all and in all, God will be all and in all, because the Father always remains in the Son [Col. 1178C]. This is the interpretation of devout subjection.”

Likewise elsewhere:

> “But if you ask how he is subject in us, he himself showed it, saying: ‘I was in prison, and you came to me’ (Matt. 25:36). ‘I was sick, and you came to me.’ For ‘what you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me’ (ibid., 40). He is sick in the person in whom he is subject.”

Having carefully considered what has been said by Hilary and Ambrose, and likewise by Leo the Great, no one ought to doubt that the human being is God most high, as the Son of the Most High. The power of the Most High overshadowed his mother when she conceived this very human being, of whom it is written: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86:5).

He is in the Father’s bosom; he sits at the Father’s right hand; he also indwells the whole of his body and his temple, which is the Church. In it the crowd presses upon him, faith touches and anoints him, now pouring costly genuine nard upon his feet, now upon his head: at one time revering him in his members, at another in himself, without doubting that he is present to itself. For just as life, which gives life to a body, is present to the body that it vivifies, so Christ, its life, is present wherever faith is not dead but living. Hence the Apostle says that Christ dwells through faith in the inner person [Col. 1178D].

## CHAPTER V. What are the reality, the outward form, and the effect of the sacrament; and who receives any or all of these?

[Col. 1179A]

Where, then, living faith exists, ecclesiastical sacraments live through the presence of him who is the life of faith and of the faithful, unto the salvation of those who communicate and minister. As he himself says: “He who eats me lives because of me” (John 4:58 [sic]), “just as I live because of the Father” (ibid.). Likewise: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26). “He who eats me lives because of me.” Likewise: “I wish,” he says, “that where I am, there also my minister may be” (John 12:26). [Note: [Col. 1179D] The Vulgate reads: “And my minister shall be.”]

Yet not every person who ministers will be with him, nor does every person who eats him live because of him. It must therefore be understood that he spoke in this great promise of honor and life concerning those who minister and eat—not those who merely possess and receive the outward form of godliness sacramentally while denying its power, but those who taste the reality, or power, hidden in the Spirit, according to the saying: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Ps. 33:9).

In the treatises of teachers, whether ancient or modern, the *res*—the reality—of the sacrament is variously discussed. Some say that the *res* of the Lord’s body and blood is its true substance; others, its saving efficacy; still others, the savingly effective imitation of the Lord’s passion. Blessed Augustine appears to hold the latter view where, in *The City of God*, he affirms that the ungodly who communicate only sacramentally receive the Lord’s body [Col. 1179C], but by no means its reality.

Likewise, where the Apostle says: “For the sake of this thing I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person; that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, rooted in love, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth” (Eph. 3:14–17)—by the name “thing” he signifies conformity to the likeness of the passion of Christ crucified. For only those can comprehend the breadth, length, height, and depth of the cross who, as is said there, are rooted and grounded in love, conformed to Christ crucified, and receive the reality for whose sake the Apostle bent his knees.

But in order that we may truly recognize what the reality of the sacrament is, let us review the passage taken from the Gospels: “On the day before he suffered, he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat of this, all of you; for this is my body, which shall be given for you for the forgiveness of sins.’” [Note: [Col. 1179D] From the Canon of the Mass.]

Four things, distinct from one another, are observed in these words: the outward form, the substance, the reality—which may also be called power—and the effect of the sacrament. The outward form is what the demonstrative pronoun indicates to bodily eyes: by it he shows the form of bread when he says, “This is”—and adds—“my true body.” The pronoun referring to his body expresses the substance of his body, whose shadow preceded it in the legal sacrifices and yielded to the body now substantially present. By adding also, “which shall be given for you,” he denotes his death, which is acknowledged to be the reality, or power, of the sacrament. Many possess the outward form of godliness but deny it; and only that person partakes of it who mortifies his flesh with its vices and desires, being conformed to the likeness of his death—the death of him who said: “Father, not what I will, but what you will, be done” (Matt. 26:39).

Therefore the one who, for God’s sake, denies himself before approaching the Lord’s table receives there, unto salvation, the reality or power [Col. 1180B] of Christ’s body. Its efficacy is denoted when it is said, “for the forgiveness of sins.” Hence Blessed Gregory says in Book IV of the *Dialogues*: “Then a true offering for us will be made to God when we have made ourselves an offering.”

For sinners and unworthy recipients within the Church, it is indeed the true flesh and true blood of Christ, but in sacramental outward form and in the true substance of flesh—which “profits nothing”—not in reality or in the efficacy of that reality. The Apostle, however, calls the faithful to participation in the reality rather than the outward form, saying: “As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. 11:26). The person truly and fittingly proclaims the Lord’s death who, conformed to the likeness of his death, denies himself to himself and carries his cross daily, so that on it he may mortify his members which are upon the earth and crucify his flesh with its vices and desires.

Such a person without doubt receives, together with the reality of the sacrament, its effect also, which cannot be separated from the reality. For the person who receives forgiveness of sins in this sacrament obtains its effect, while he himself passes into Christ’s body and becomes a member of Christ’s body, receiving the holy, rational, acceptable offering in such a way that he too becomes a holy, rational, acceptable offering. For the reality of the sacrament, understood more in power than in substance, and denoted by commemoration of the Lord’s passion, is inseparably accompanied by its effect. For “if we have been made conformed to the likeness of Christ’s death, we shall also be conformed to his resurrection” (Rom. 6:5). [Note: [Col. 1179D] The Vulgate reads “his” in place of “Christ’s.”] Likewise: “If we die together, we shall also live together” (2 Tim. 2:11). [Note: [Col. 1180D] The Vulgate reads: “If we have died together, we shall also live together.” At verse 12 it reads: “If we endure,” etc.] “If we suffer together, we shall also reign together.”

Nor are any who eat a portion of broiled fish deprived of the honeycomb, because their sorrow shall be turned into joy (John 16:20): those, namely, who proclaim the Lord’s death in the mortification of their own will and flesh when they celebrate this sacrament. They proclaim the Lord’s death who show themselves, in character and deeds, crucified for Christ. These, indeed, receive in the sacrament of the altar the four things already mentioned [Col. 1181A]: the outward form, the substance, the reality or power, and the effect.

But all who, living for themselves, deny the reality also lack the effect, which is forgiveness of sins, even if outside the Church they receive the outward form alone, and within the Church receive also the substance of Christ’s body. For Blessed Augustine, writing to Boniface, grants concerning the outward form that heretics receive it outside the Church, although they do not possess its reality:

> “Let heretics not seek the Holy Spirit except in the body of Christ, of which they possess the sacrament outside, but do not hold within the reality itself of which it is the sacrament. And therefore they eat and drink judgment upon themselves.”

The same author, in a sermon to the people:

> “Let your charity observe that many who are not of us receive the sacraments with us: they receive baptism; with us they receive what the faithful know that they receive—blessing, Eucharist, and whatever belongs to the holy sacraments. They receive with us communion at the very altar, and they are not of us.” [Col. 1181B]

Likewise:

> “If you do not wish to be corrected, but love and embrace your sins, you are opposed to Christ. Whether inside or outside, you are Antichrist; whether inside or outside, you are chaff.”

The same, in Book III against the Donatists:

> “Heretics possess sacraments and Scriptures for outward appearance, not for salvation.”

The same, in the exposition on the Epistle of John:

> “Even an evil person can receive the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood; but an evil person cannot possess charity.”

Likewise elsewhere: “Outside the Church there is no place of true sacrifice,” not because heretics lack the true sacrament, which is accomplished in the outward form alone, provided that it is celebrated according to the Church’s rite by ordained persons, whether they possess or lack office; but because they lack the true sacrifice, which consists in the other three things. It is received when, in the Church, the substance, the reality, and the effect of Christ’s body are jointly given or received—not because these three are always present together. For flesh according to substance “profits nothing” (John 6:63) to communicants or ministers within the Church, unless the Spirit gives life through the reality and effect to the person who worthily ministers or communicates.

For, as Saint Augustine says, in the altar offering there is a sacrament, which worthy and unworthy alike receive, because they alike eat the body of Christ sacramentally; and there is also the reality of the sacrament, which only the worthy can receive. Yet we do not receive the sayings of this orthodox teacher in the manner in which some have understood them. They thought that he had said that what any unworthy person receives is not Christ’s body or blood, and that, according to the meaning of so great a teacher, what we visibly receive from the Lord’s table is not Christ’s body or blood but only a figure or sign of body and blood. He did not say this; indeed, he did not think this. For he was not accustomed to oppose Christ.

But Christ speaks, both in his own person, saying, “This is my body” (Matt. 26:26) [Col. 1182A], “This is my blood” (ibid., 28), and through his Apostle—of whom we have proof that Christ speaks in him—when he says: “Therefore whoever eats the bread or drinks the Lord’s cup unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person test himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For the one who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:27–29).

He did not say: “One who eats and drinks unworthily eats ordinary or common bread and drinks wine such as it was before, when consecration had not yet been celebrated.” Rather, he says that the person “shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” and “eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.” Therefore let us seek an understanding not from anyone’s contentious disputation but from apostolic truth: in what sense has the aforementioned Doctor distinguished sacrament from the reality of the sacrament?

Christ called the reality of the sacrament the mystery, or power, of his passion, as we have already said. Holding this visible sacrament in his hands, when he said, “This is my body,” he added, “which shall be given” (Luke 22:19). [Note: [Col. 1181D] The Vulgate reads: “which is also given.”] When he said, “This is my blood,” he added, “which shall be poured out” (Matt. 26:28).

But the person who approaches unworthily does not share in Christ’s sufferings. He does not touch with the mouth of his mind what he receives with the mouth of his body. He does not put the lamb’s blood upon both doorposts of his house, but upon one only: he receives the sacrament with his mouth, but does not receive its reality with his mind. And this is precisely why he is unworthy. Therefore this visible sacrament which he receives with his mouth is indeed Christ’s body and blood [Col. 1182C]; for his unworthiness cannot nullify the dignity of so great a consecration. Yet he does not attain the reality of the sacrament, because in mind, in faith working through love, and in the devout intention of imitation, he does not look to Christ’s passion.

For this reason he does not attain the effect of that sacrament: namely, that this body was given and this blood shed for him—that is, for his forgiveness—so that he may have eternal life and be raised on the last day (John 6:39), in the resurrection of life (John 5:29). Rather, he receives what is contrary to that effect: he becomes guilty of the Lord’s body and blood and eats and drinks judgment upon himself. Thus the Apostle says: “Let a person test himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup” (as above), because a sacrament of such dignity must not be given to unworthy and untested persons.

Many who do not test themselves have received outside the Church, in the visible sacrament, the outward form of Christ’s body. They have obtained neither the substance, nor the reality, nor the effect. Therefore they have eaten judgment upon themselves, because they deserved to be judged and condemned by that through which they separated the outward form of the sacrament from its substance and reality. Hence they could not possess the effect of the reality.

Among those who do not test themselves, many today receive within the Church both outward form and substance, whether from good or evil ministers. But because, denying its power [Col. 1183A], they refuse to receive the reality, since they are unwilling to die together with Christ, they will not possess the effect, which is forgiveness of sins, if they remain such persons. Instead, they eat judgment upon themselves: they are worthy of judgment and condemnation through and because of the fact that they have separated the outward form and substance of so great a sacrament from its reality and effect, by a most wicked sacrilege removing the sacred from the sacred and dividing what God has joined together.

For he himself, as was said above, joined those four things: the outward form, the substance, the reality, and the effect of the sacrament—the outward form in the showing of the visible figure; the substance in naming his own body; the reality or power in the commemoration of his passion; and the effect in the forgiveness of sins.

## CHAPTER VI. What a schismatic and a person deprived of priestly office consecrates is not Christ’s body with respect to the substance, reality, and efficacy of the sacrament, although with respect to outward form and sacrament it may be called Christ’s body.

[Col. 1183B]

But the heretic or schismatic, and the deposed priest, since he is not a minister of the Church, when he presumes to minister, possesses indeed the sacrament but not the office of the sacrament. He has the visible appearance of Christ’s body, but its essence, reality, and effect are far from him; for, as Pope Pelagius says: “He does not consecrate, but desecrates,” and by a sacrilegious division he separates the appearance from its essence and reality. Hence he becomes guilty of the body and blood of Christ, altogether like those who, by killing Christ, separated life from the Living One. [Col. 1183C] For just as Christ’s dead flesh did not benefit those among whom, and through whose crime, he lay dead in the heart of the earth, so the lifeless appearance does not benefit these persons. Indeed, it greatly harms not only those who minister in this manner, but also those who knowingly communicate with them after the Church’s prohibition; whoever does not heed it shall be as a heathen and a publican.

Accordingly, Saint Gregory, in the two-hundred-and-fortieth chapter of the second part of his Register, strikes with perpetual excommunication a condemned priest who usurps his former office, scarcely even granting him viaticum at the end of life. Accordingly, the holy Fathers, in the fourth chapter of the Council of Antioch, utterly denied to any condemned person who should undertake anything of the ministry of the sacraments every hope of restoration or opportunity for satisfaction; and they condemned, along with him in their communion, all who communicated with him while he remained condemned.

But when those who possess the office minister within the Church, whether worthily or unworthily, the sacrament is valid; and it is a saving sacrifice only for those who receive the reality together with its effect—whether they eat Christ’s body by visibly communicating according to its essence, or refrain from visible and sacramental eating, content with participation or communion in the reality and effect alone—provided that they do not despise visible and sacramental eating, or omit it through negligence at its proper time, attending to what Christ says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink [Col. 1184A] his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). This is understood as said both of visible and invisible eating, so that neither may be neglected.

Moreover, if an unordained person presumes to offer sacrifice, because he departs from the ecclesiastical rite, he must not even be said to possess the appearance of a sacrament; for it belongs to the form of the sacrament that none but one consecrated should consecrate. Hence Augustine, in Book II against the Donatists: “The sacraments which schismatics or heretics possess and administer in no other way than does the true Church, when they come to us, we do not correct but approve.” From the converse it may certainly be inferred that things performed, whether within or outside the Church, by unordained persons contrary to the Church’s rite, are not to be approved as sacraments, since they act otherwise than [Col. 1184B] the true Church, which judges to be called sacraments only those things performed by ordained persons, acting no otherwise than she herself acts.

If these matters that have been stated are weighed and considered carefully, it is easy to determine those authorities which, when speaking of sacraments, seem discordant: some teach the sameness of sacraments both within and outside the Church, while others teach a difference. Those which teach sameness, asserting that the sacraments, wherever they are found, are themselves the same, refer to the visible appearance, which in baptism, ordination, and the celebration of Masses is alike, within and without, and indifferent to good and evil ministers. But those which teach the difference of sacraments refer to the reality and its efficacy, which is not obtained outside the Church and is not possessed within it by evil persons, [Col. 1184C] although the essence of Christ’s body is nevertheless found alike among bad as among good ministers by whom Mass is celebrated without the Church’s objection. Those who celebrate while lacking office, if they have never been ordained, must not even be said to possess the appearance of a sacrament. This appearance cannot be denied to persons who have been ordained and deprived of office, on account of the sacrament of office, which cannot be removed even from those from whom office is removed.

Therefore, when an authority says, “That which a schismatic performs is not Christ’s body,” it must be understood with respect to the essence, reality, and efficacy; nevertheless, with respect to its appearance and sacramental character, it can be called Christ’s body.
