Those who, being such persons, celebrate, [Col. 1184D] or knowingly communicate with such persons in offices that have been prohibited, annulled by ecclesiastical judgment, and already condemned, eat judgment unto themselves. But where Mass is celebrated within the Church by evil ministers who have not been prohibited, because they possess the appearance and essence of Christ’s body, their wickedness harms in no way those who communicate simply and receive the reality. The saving effect can never be absent from them, even though the minister through whom the visible administration takes place be evil; for invisible grace descends from above, from the Father of lights (James 1:17), through the mediator of God and men, Jesus Christ, to whom, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory and honor through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1185]

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM LXIV, OR THE BOOK ON THE CORRUPTED STATE OF THE CHURCH, ADDRESSED TO POPE EUGENIUS III

We restore this exposition, first published separately in Baluze’s *Miscellanies*, to Gerhoh’s very extensive commentary on the Psalter, following Dom Pez. See above, col. 9.

[BOOK ON GOD’S BUILDING.]

[Col. 1185]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK

(D. B. Pez, Preface to vol. II of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, p. XXVI.)

In the preliminary observations to the second part of the first volume, in which we published Gerhoh’s book *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man* and the little book *On the Two Heresies*, etc., we promised that we would also bring to public notice several other outstanding literary monuments of this great man. We now begin to discharge that pledge, bringing to light two notable works of the same author: the first is entitled *On God’s Building*, the other, *Letter, or Dialogue, on the Difference between the Regular and the Secular Cleric*.

In publishing both, we saw that in each certain matters are reproved more sharply and vehemently than the more delicate ears and eyes of our times can endure. Yet, when we considered the most honorable judgments of Roman pontiffs and most holy bishops concerning Gerhoh’s writings; the very high reputation for learning and holiness by which this distinguished author flourished in his own age, renowned among the most learned men; and finally the common esteem which he has deserved among the most learned men of our own time, it seemed that we could not suppress the writings of so great a light of the Church, leaving them to be devoured by moths and bookworms, without impiety and serious guilt.

Moreover, such ancient monuments are not published—as we writers in Germany cannot sufficiently emphasize—with the intention of offering the doctrine or ecclesiastical discipline of our own age for derision by unbridled people. They are published so that learned men may ascertain what opinion ancient writers held on certain questions not yet settled and defined by any common and public authority; what arguments the parties employed; by what stages and steps matters reached a definite condition; and what causes existed for either tightening or somewhat relaxing the rigor of ecclesiastical discipline. How necessary all this knowledge is for a complete understanding of ecclesiastical affairs is known by those of sound learning. Neither severity of expression, nor more forceful declamations against the vices of the clergy, nor weakness of argument—for such blemishes regularly attach themselves to ancient writings—can deter such men from publishing ancient monuments.

How greatly does Chrysostom rise up against the corrupt morals of nobles! What deserving of reproach does Jerome conceal among priests? And, to name Gerhoh’s particular friend, who recounts more openly, attacks more sharply, or rebukes more severely the vices of monks—indeed, of bishops and popes—than Saint Bernard? Yet no one has hitherto departed so far from sound reason as to resent that the works of such great ornaments of the Church were ever published for the public.

What reason, then, is there why the works of Gerhoh alone, marked by these blemishes of human intellect but otherwise most useful and elegant, should be condemned to everlasting night? What does Gerhoh offer that one cannot find in many other ancient doctors whose writings are available in print? Does he frequently conduct and conclude his case by means of forged papal decretals? The same weapons and arms were used by countless other writers for almost seven centuries; nor are there lacking in our own age persons unaware of that fraud and imposture of Pseudo-Isidore, who attributed those decretal letters to the earliest Roman pontiffs. Does he press too strongly for the common life of clerics and pursue and condemn their private property beyond measure? The same thing is found in other authors contemporary with Gerhoh. Thus innumerable most holy bishops thought in that age, through whose efforts the institution of common life was introduced even into greater and cathedral churches. Has he bitterly attacked the lavish tables of ecclesiastical prelates, the luxury of their clothing, the pomp and society of soldiers? You will read nothing more frequently in other authors who wished declining ecclesiastical discipline to be measured against and restored to the ancient apostolic institution.

Finally, we beseech and entreat those to whom Gerhoh’s writings are so hateful and bitter: let them at least make some allowance for the ardent spirit of this most devout man, for his immense zeal to enlarge divine worship, for the freedom of the age in which he flourished—a freedom employed even by most holy men—and finally for the judgment of the Roman pontiffs concerning Gerhoh’s writings, from which no private person has dissented unless proud, arrogant, or malicious.

Lest, however, we should seem falsely to invoke the authority of the Roman See on behalf of Gerhoh’s writings, it is fitting to insert here in full the letter of Eugenius IV, by which he praised and approved Gerhoh’s *Exposition of Psalm LXIV*, or book *On the Corrupted State of the Church*—God of goodness, how sharply, passionately, and harshly it was written! Gerhoh frequently inserts it into his works and uses it as a shield by which he protects and defends himself and his writings against the attack of adversaries. The letter is as follows:

> Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son G., provost of Reichersperg: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> We have graciously received the writings of your devotion, and from examining them have clearly recognized the fervor of your religious devotion, [Col. 1187] etc.

It appears at the end of the *Exposition of Psalm LXIV*, above, col. 116. This is the letter of Eugenius IV which doubtless furnished the exceedingly learned and modest Étienne Baluze with an incentive to publish Gerhoh’s entire book *On the Corrupted State of the Church*, however bitter and vehement, at Paris in 1700, in octavo, in Book V of the *Miscellanies*.

But, having prefaced these remarks on Gerhoh’s works—remarks which those well acquainted with our times know have been made not merely without idleness, but even necessarily—let us now proceed to review Gerhoh’s writings included in this volume. The first is the excellent and very extensive book *On God’s Building*, in which he shows with great elegance and subtlety what befits, and what does not befit, each condition in the Church. He began to write it at the request and command of Chuno, bishop of Regensburg, as Gerhoh himself testifies at the beginning of the prologue.

When he had inserted into his work some passages which, once read to certain persons little suited to the rigor and rule of ecclesiastical discipline, displeased them, he was compelled to return the work to the anvil and fortify all its parts with the weightiest authorities of holy Fathers and councils, so that Gerhoh could not be rejected without rejecting the Fathers and councils, sacred to all. Gerhoh himself explains the matter in the letter to a certain priest prefixed to the work. The very learned Father Carolus Meichelbeck, archivist of the monastery of Benediktbeuern, believes this man to have been none other than Arno, Gerhoh’s brother and successor in the provostship of Reichersperg; see the *Chronicle of Reichersperg* under the year 1180 and Hund, *Metropolis Salisburgensis*, vol. III, p. 245.

Some years ago, while, through the favor of the most reverend and illustrious Provost Francis Claudius Kroll, a most humane prelate, we were examining the manuscript codices of the canonry of St Florian in Upper Austria, there came into our hands a quarto parchment codex about four hundred years old. It contained a certain apologetic treatise by Arno, a regular canon, who perhaps is not different from Arno, provost of Reichersperg and Gerhoh’s brother. You will learn its character from its opening:

> “I, Brother Arno, a humble servant of the canonical order, composed the following little work, which is called *The Shield of Canons*, on the occasion of a certain dispute: namely, with certain monks occupying our places and drawing our professed brethren to themselves, as though under the pretext of a more perfect religious life, etc.”

We would gladly have published the whole notable little work here, if we had been able to obtain a copy. But after the death of the most reverend Claudius, the letters which we sent more than once for that purpose to the aforementioned canonry were without result. But let this be said in passing and on the occasion of Arno, to whom Gerhoh seems to have entrusted his book *On God’s Building*, the first offspring, as it were, of his intellect.

[Col. 1187]

## THE BOOK OF THE VENERABLE GERHOH, PROVOST OF REICHERSPERG, ON GOD’S BUILDING, OR ON ZEAL FOR AND CARE OF ECCLESIASTICAL DISCIPLINE

(From a manuscript codex of the illustrious Benedictine monastery of Benediktbeuern in Bavaria, extracted by the venerable Dom Leopold Wydemann, Carthusian of Gaming; edited by the Rev. Fr. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum* II.ii.224.)

### HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE TO A CERTAIN PRIEST

[Note: [Col. 1187] Perhaps Arno, Gerhoh’s brother and successor in the provostship of Reichersperg. See Hund, *Metropolis*, vol. III, p. 245.]

[Col. 1187A] We read that the distinguished patriarch Isaac dug four wells in the land of his sojourning. The first he called *Accusation*; the second, *Enmities*, because he suffered accusation and enmity when the shepherds of Gerar quarreled over the water of these wells. He dug a third well, to which he gave the name *Breadth*, [Col. 1188A] because there was no contention over it. He called the fourth *Abundance*, because he suffered no quarrel through it either.

In Christ, dearest brother, you compel me to recall the accusations and enmities which I once endured, when the shepherds of Gerar quarreled with me because I presumed to dig anew wells which the Philistines of the land [Col. 1189A] had filled in, striving to reach living water and disdaining muddy water—that is, the depraved conduct of clerics, excessively altered from the purity of the apostolic spring from which the clerical order derives its origin.

When, therefore, by writing as if digging, I began to seek out this vein of waters, the shepherds of Gerar—the friends of the Philistines, that is, of the fallen—quarreled bitterly against my insignificance. They were indignant when I dug the first well: that is, when I presented this book, which you now ask me to read, to my lord Chuno, of blessed memory, angel of the Church of Regensburg, so that, if it pleased him, he might have living water in it for himself and offer it to others to drink. I recount with joyful recollection that this did indeed occur, because he so clearly displayed in popular sermons the Building which I had drawn for him in this book [Col. 1189B] that those who built otherwise, and rejected the cornerstone which this Building necessarily has both in its foundation and at its summit, were compelled to be ashamed.

Although they reject it, it has nevertheless become the head of the corner, as, through God’s grace, the manner of apostolic governance flourishes anew in many churches. This rests not upon the authority of any human founder, but upon that of Christ himself, who in himself and his disciples displayed the pattern of the clerical order and vocation, formerly prefigured in Aaron and his sons, deprived of earthly inheritance and consecrated to the Lord’s portion.

In accordance with this model, clerical life is flourishing anew in many churches [Col. 1189C] in regular communities of brothers dwelling together, neither calling nor possessing anything their own. Clerics who live otherwise and oppose Christ’s lawful ordinance seem to me comparable to the shepherds of Gerar. For as those men brought accusation against the patriarch Isaac when he renewed the ancestral wells filled in by the Philistines, so these men have raised against me accusations and enmities almost without number for a similar reason.

Therefore, if you deem it worthy to drink from the well which they have made bitter to me by their accusations and enmities—while my stomach was made bitter concerning the truth which was sweet in my mouth—beware of all bitter persons and those who make bitter. And if anything from [Col. 1189D] the water of this well pleases you, offer it to drink only to the sweet and gentle, one of whom the bishop of Freising is believed to be. You ought carefully to suggest this to him in private: if he deigns to drink from our well, let him follow the counsel of Wisdom, which says: “Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel, because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, lest perhaps they drink and forget judgments, and alter the cause of the children of the poor” (Prov. 31:4–5).

Do not proud and secular clerics lord it like kings? Do they not, intoxicated with many writings, often forget judgments and alter the cause of the children of the poor—namely, of him who, though he was rich, became poor for our sakes, that through his poverty we might be rich (2 Cor. 8:9)? They ought to become rich not by greedily pursuing private gain in ecclesiastical ministries, but by devout longing eagerly to desire [Col. 1190A] only the things above. But while they seek earthly profit in ecclesiastical offices, as their love for heavenly desires grows cold, they truly forget judgments and alter the cause of the children of the poor: transferring the Lord’s grace—that is, alms—to luxury, while wholly neglecting the poor of the poor Christ.

Lest that bishop, beloved of God, should thus enter their fellowship and become like the high priest of that year in which Christ was crucified, you must forestall and fortify him early and swiftly. Perhaps this may fittingly be done by reading this little book. If you and he, together with other friends of truth, receive it favorably, then, despising the judgment of the faithless, I shall rejoice in the Lord that I have been happily enlarged among devout minds; [Col. 1190B] and, God’s grace assisting, I shall change the name of this well, so that what was formerly called *Accusation* or *Enmities* may henceforth be called *Breadth*. This was the name of the third well mentioned above, which the patriarch Isaac dug and over which there was no contention.

Therefore let all contention likewise be far from us; and for those who have hitherto contended against us, let our sole response be prayer to God, that in them as in us he may change what displeases his majesty and strengthen what is pleasing to him, so that at last we may drink together from the fourth well, called *Abundance*: as having nothing and yet possessing all things; as needy, yet enriching many. For the well of divine generosity, which may be called abundance, does not fail. [Col. 1190C] God’s goodness and mercy accompany and follow the elect, whom he has preceded with abundant aids and gifts of grace, so that any of the elect may deservedly sing amid such abundance: “The Lord governs me, and I shall lack nothing,” down to: “And thy mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days” (Ps. 22:1, 8–9).

I think that for those who sing this song truly, the desirable well of breadth and abundance lies open—indeed, an inexhaustible fountain. Seeking to attain it, we have labored by writing various little works, as though digging. Of these little works, this book was the first, written at the command and request of Chuno, bishop of Regensburg, beloved of God. After his death we kept it with us and permitted only a few to read it. Yet because you, dearest brother in the Lord, to whose charity I owe everything that, with God’s help, I can do, ask to read and perhaps copy this little book; and because it may happen that, once sent forth, the word will be irrevocable, I ask you also to take care to add the authorities which I placed in the margin, so that our Building may be fortified by them as though by strong beams or walls, in accordance with the command of the Law in Deuteronomy: “When you build a new house, you shall make a wall around the roof, lest blood be shed in your house and you become guilty should someone slip and fall headlong” (Deut. 22:8). Likewise the Law says in Exodus: “If [Col. 1191A] anyone opens a cistern or digs one and does not cover it, and an ox or donkey falls into it, the owner of the cistern shall pay the price of the animals. But what is dead shall be his” (Exod. 21:33–34).

Therefore add the authorities of the holy Fathers in the margin, or even insert them into our composition, so that they may be a defense for our Building and a covering for our cistern, lest, if someone falls headlong through an occasion given by us, we suffer loss. Something like this almost happened to us before, when word went out among the bearded brothers of the cloisters that we had excluded them from the Building discussed here, although they paid no attention to the fact that they were included among penitents equally with monks—unless perhaps they live so dissolutely that they do not keep the laws of penance.

[Col. 1191B] Certain learned cloistered persons were also offended, both monks and regular canons, because they seemed, through the published writings of the Fathers on dividing tithes and offerings into four portions, to be charged with transgression, since tithes and offerings are not divided into quarters in cloisters where people live in common.

Mindful of these and similar past offenses, and wishing to guard against future ones, we are making our composition more carefully revised, cutting out some things and adding others. The authorities of the Fathers, from which nothing could be added or removed, we have partly inserted suitably into the text of our discourse and partly placed in the margin. [Col. 1192A] Having carefully examined them, we believe that we shall be free from blame and excusable before God, even if some of those for whom Christ himself is a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense (1 Pet. 2:8) should be offended and scandalized by our words. For since he himself says to his disciples, “If they have kept my word, they will keep yours also; if they have persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John 15:20), we ought not to be surprised if, on account of the truth which produces hatred in them, his enemies become hostile to us, and therefore take offense and are scandalized by truthful statements.

[Col. 1192B] We have endured many reproaches, curses, and vexations from persons of this kind. That perfect repentance and most generous pardon may be granted them by God, we beseech his mercy, his omnipotence, and his almighty mercy through the truly peace-making sacrifice which, though unworthy, we offer not only for friends but also for enemies whenever, through his favoring grace, we celebrate the mystery of the altar.

### HERE BEGINS THE LITTLE WORK *ON GOD’S BUILDING*, BY A CERTAIN UNLEARNED AND SINFUL MAN, ADDRESSED TO CHUNO, BISHOP OF REGENSBURG

[Col. 1191]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1191C]

At your request and command, venerable bishop Chuno of the holy Church of Regensburg, I confess that I have been encouraged to this undertaking: since you urge me and demand a great work from my smallness, I do not hesitate to endeavor to render what you ask. Yet I know that no such thing is stored up in me, from which I might satisfy you, a most refined searcher of the holy Scriptures, and prepare suitable delicacies—since I too waste away in my soul through the danger of famine, and, possessing a little oil in the flask of conscience and a small quantity of flour in the handful of action, stand near to death—unless the true Elijah comes. Making much from my little, while asking to be fed, he himself feeds me all the more; and may he never withdraw from my heart the presence of his incarnation [Col. 1191D] until the time of famine has suitably passed, heaven is opened, and my want is restored by a marvelous abundance, in accordance with the Prophet’s words: “I shall be satisfied when thy glory appears” (Ps. 16:15).

Meanwhile, if through the stealthy approach of sin the son—that is, my mind—should be overtaken by sudden death, the presence of that Elijah, remaining in the lodging-place of my memory, [Col. 1192C] can continually recall him from death and present him living to Mother Church; so that the mother herself may rejoice in this, and the truth of the word that raises him may be magnified in my life.

Therefore, since Elijah is interpreted “God the Lord,” I trust indeed that the Lord God speaks openly to me through you. For after you perceived me gathering two pieces of wood for a cross—that is, holding hope in faith in the Lord’s Passion—you immediately commanded me to construct from those two pieces of wood, as it were, a certain building, or rather to show one already constructed. According to the Apostle, God is its architect and builder; and therefore it cannot be moved or shaken by any blast of winds or rush of rivers.

[Col. 1192D] Therefore let this little work receive, as you yourself have decreed, the title *On God’s Building*; and let readers know, both from the Prologue and from the title, that this book is sent to your fatherhood. But let my name be wholly unknown. For if any good has been set forth here through me, then praise, grace, and [Col. 1193A] thanksgiving for it are due “not to us, not to us, but to the name of the Lord” (Ps. 113:9). And whoever may rightly take pleasure in anything that, at your urging, I shall say by God’s grace will also owe thanks to you, the one who has urged and exercised my smallness.

## CHAPTER I. Who is the author and architect of this Building? What is its material, and what are its instruments? What is that by which its parts are joined and endure? This Building is not overthrown or destroyed by the storms of the wicked, but is made firmer and raised higher.

In completing every building, three things are necessary: the craftsman who works; the material from which he works; and the tools or aids by which he works. Therefore, if we inquire who is the architect and builder of this Building of which we are to speak, the Apostle declares that it is God. [Col. 1193B] The material is the chosen portion of rational creation, from which, as God builds, the city that will never fall is constructed. The rejected portion of rational creation, together with every irrational or insensible creature, are certain aids employed by this architect. Although he needs no one’s assistance in making anything, the Psalmist declares that he has nevertheless made all these things in wisdom (Ps. 103:24).

Thus anyone who says that even the least worm is superfluous in the whole fabric of this world contradicts the wisdom of its Maker, which has made and makes nothing superfluous, nothing unbecoming. For from creation itself, which, considered in itself, is judged ugly by foolish minds, the structure of the universe as a whole is fittingly adorned. But the blind mind, which does not consider the whole, often either despises or mocks a part, because it does not see what is suited to what.

For example, if someone considered a nose or an eye, which are parts of the human body, apart from the whole, he could discern little beauty in them. Yet although these parts, separated from their whole, present to the eyes or minds of observers ugliness rather than beauty, they nevertheless adorn the universe in the integrity of their whole in such a way that the nose cannot be denied beauty, nor the eye both beauty and usefulness. It is not they so much as their critic who must be judged blameworthy. Thus, whoever censures anything in creatures as superfluous shows himself blind and blameworthy. For one free from blindness, [Col. 1193D] seeing the whole, would censure nothing in God’s works but would say with the Psalmist: “The Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works” (Ps. 144:13).

This is that great fabric of the whole world, a kind of universal workshop, in which, through God’s wonderful working, a certain Building is being made. When it is finished, the hammer will be broken, and the workshop itself, in the condition which it now seems to have, will be utterly destroyed. But the City of God, which consists in chosen rational creation, will be destroyed neither now nor then: it is now being built with irrevocable progress, and then it shall stand without failing.

But since the future and abiding stability of this city is established, let us speak of its temporal condition; and, God showing us the way, let us see how it has been built from the beginning of the world in that part [Col. 1194A] of itself which is still imperfect.

Let us therefore set before the eyes of our mind and faith that most mighty craftsman, whose Son is undoubtedly Christ, who is called in the Gospel “the carpenter’s son” (Matt. 13:55). We likewise do not doubt that the Father is a craftsman, for the Apostle, speaking of him, also describes the house whose builder he declares him to be: “This one,” he says, “has been judged worthy of greater glory than Moses, inasmuch as the one who built the house has greater honor than the house. For every house is built by someone; but God is the one who created all things. And Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of those things that were to be spoken; but Christ as a Son in his own house, whose house we are, if we hold firm unto the end the confidence and glory of hope” (Heb. 3:3–6).

This house, as the Apostle here defines it, began to be built when God created heaven and earth; when he created angelic and human creation; when he took a rib from the first man and built it into a woman (Gen. 2:22). The man, indeed, is said to have been formed; but the woman, because she signifies the Church, is said not to have been formed but to have been built. Thus, when you hear that she was built by the Lord, think of the woman and understand the Building; and strive by God’s grace to be what you understand. For striving is necessary until we are made perfect, lest, struck by the hammer of temptation, we be broken away from the confidence and [Col. 1194C] glory of our hope. Unless we hold this confidence firm to the end, the Apostle does not admit us into his description of God’s house. For when he had said, “Whose house we are,” he immediately added, “if we hold firm the confidence and glory of hope unto the end.”

The first woman failed and fell away from this confidence and hope when the hammer of temptation struck her. Had she believed God’s predictions, she could never have been seduced into hoping, at the devil’s suggestion, for life and likeness to God from that which God had threatened with death. Thus, giving faith rather to the devil’s words than to God’s, she did not consider God faithful in all his words. Hence she shifted her fault onto the serpent, whom she knew had been made by God and placed in paradise, as though her fall had occurred not without the Creator’s fault, since he had placed in paradise that serpent which suggested sin, and had placed man there also, giving him a command not to sin.

[Col. 1194D] But let us faithfully sing and say: “The Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works” (Ps. 144:13). For he promises nothing in which the trust of the saints is deceived; he does and has done nothing in which their holiness is hindered. Rather, in him every structure that is built grows and does not diminish; nor can any planting be uprooted except that which he has not planted.

But who is planted by God and in God, except the one [Col. 1195A] who is so rooted and founded in charity that he cannot in any way be turned away from this faith: that God’s words are most faithful, that is, health-giving and true? They are health-giving indeed only to believers, but true both to unbelievers and to believers. For even the first parents, though these words were not health-giving to them because of their unbelief, nevertheless proved by experience how true the things God had foretold were, and how false were those promised by the devil.

Believing false promises, they fell away from faith in the truth, because they had not held charity, which never fails, so firmly that in it they believed all things and hoped all things. For those who believe most firmly every good and evil thing which God foretells, and do not doubt at all—these are the persons who do not fall away in the time of temptation but persevere in faith. And if they sin, hoping every good thing from the good God, they do not hide their shame against him as did the first parents; rather, they reveal their fault to the Lord and hope in him, and he will act and bring forth their righteousness as light and their judgment as noon.

Thus the Lord appeared to faithful Abraham in the very heat of the day, namely at noon; but to the unbelieving first-created man, walking in the breeze after noon. To the former the Lord stands; to the latter he walks. For Abraham, believing most firmly and not doubting at all concerning the Lord’s words and promises, received the charity by which he might be built up, never fall away, but stand most firmly. The latter sought the knowledge promised by the devil; by seeking it he was not built up to stand, but puffed up and exalted so as to fall.

What then shall we say? Has God’s purpose been made void? Has the rib which he built been reduced to nothing, so that the building begun from it cannot be completed? Far be it! This builder is not such a one as cannot bring to completion what he has begun to build. For Jerusalem is still being built by him as a city, “whose participation is in the same” (Ps. 121:3). Let us consider what this participation is, or what is meant by “in the same.” If man had emerged victorious in the first temptation, neither he himself nor any of his offspring would have been liable to perdition or death; and there would have been no participation in the whole human race. For [Col. 1195D] the blessing of the Creator, who said, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. 9:7), would have been fulfilled in such a way that none but the elect would be born. From them that same building which God purposed would be completed; and thus no division or partition would take place; nor, as we now see, would one person think this and another that, but [Col. 1196A] all would think the same thing. Now “the same” is God, according to the saying: “But thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail” (Ps. 101:28).

Therefore, if man had perfectly and perseveringly tasted God—the true food of the rational soul—and had wholly rejected the poison of the serpent’s persuasion, the human race would, under God’s blessing alone, have increased and multiplied up to the predestined number of the elect, and without the sweat of his face would have fed upon his supersubstantial bread. But because sin crept in at the devil’s urging, while the good God rightly orders both the evil of man and evil man, such a curse followed that it was said to the woman: “I will multiply thy sorrows and thy conceptions; in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children” (Gen. 3:16); and to the man: “In the sweat of [Col. 1196B] thy face thou shalt eat thy bread” (ibid., 19). Hence, by this just and irrevocable sentence of curse, many are born besides the elect; and because they refuse to think the same thing, they are divided not only from the elect, but also among themselves and against one another by irreconcilable discord. But the elect, because, even though with labor and the sweat of their faces, they strive to eat the bread of charity, think the same thing among themselves and live peacefully in the present life; and when the sleep of death comes upon them, they shall sleep and rest “in peace in the same” (Ps. 4:9).

Thus the city “in the same” is built only from the sons of blessing; but from the sons of the curse there results a certain division which benefits the elect and assists them toward that same end. For although their perversity does not consent to be built into the golden couch of the true Solomon, [Col. 1196C] yet by his wondrous wisdom he makes them the footstool of his feet (Ps. 109:1); and thus through them the structure of the heavenly building is not so much hindered as expedited, rising all the more high because the number of evil persons, like floodwaters, increases and multiplies over the earth. While they overflow and rage with foaming, stormy violence, the ark built by the true Noah is not submerged but is raised even to heaven. For the ark of the heavenly building, which is constructed on earth, is in no way lifted to higher things without the waters of the flood. Therefore, when we see these things happen, we ought not to grieve, but lift up our heads, because our redemption draws near—provided [Col. 1196D] that we suffer with him, so that we may also reign with him; provided that we are not a partition or division against another and against the very building of the holy city, but its participation in the same.

> [Note: [Col. 1195D] Pope Leo to Anastasius of Thessalonica: “To this end we direct all our effort and care: that nothing which pertains to the unity of concord or to the preservation of discipline may be violated by dissension or neglected through indolence.” A little later: “I exhort and admonish you that what has been piously ordained and salutarily arranged be disturbed by no contention. Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another (1 Cor. 10:24); and, as the Apostle says: ‘Let every one of you please his neighbor unto good for edification’ (Rom. 15:2). For the firm bond of our unity cannot stand unless the bond of charity binds us into inseparable solidity. For, ‘as we have many members in one body, but all the members have not the same function, so we, being many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another’ (Rom. 12:4); the joining together of the whole body produces one health and one beauty. This union of the whole body indeed requires unanimity, but especially demands concord among priests.”]

For there are many who, together with the soldiers, the crucifiers of God, divide the Lord’s garments among themselves; and therefore, [Col. 1197A] themselves divided into parts from Christ, they perish, because they become not his participation in the same, but his partition against himself. But there is one who shall possess the seamless tunic not by dividing it but by casting lots: a tunic never capable of any division and wholly free from partition. Therefore he is not a partition, but its participation in the same. For those who obtain it by lot speak and think the same thing; nor are they a mutilation (*concisio*), but circumcision in him, in whom the Apostle declares us not mutilated but circumcised: “With a circumcision not made by hands, in the putting off of the body of the flesh” (Col. 2:11).

Thus it is one thing to be cut off from Christ and another to be circumcised in him. For although the tunic of Samuel—that is, of Christ the true priest—cannot be torn, since it is known to be seamless and woven from above, nevertheless kings hold and tear its cloak, its outer covering, together with proud King Saul; and therefore they themselves become a mutilation. For when Christ, who was prefigured in Samuel, departs from such men, the kingdom too is torn from them; and they, with all who cling to them and consent with them in the swelling of pride, shall be torn apart and slain, as though on Mount Gilboa; and they will often visibly be delivered into the hand of the sword, but invisibly they shall be the portion of foxes—that is, of evil spirits.

> [Note: [Col. 1197C] John Chrysostom, in his sermon on the Conversion of St. Paul, says the following concerning Valens, persecutor of the Churches: “The emperor’s own uncle, because by a profane touch he had rashly violated vessels consecrated to God, perished eaten by worms. The superintendent also of the imperial treasury, because of another injury which he had inflicted upon the Church, [Col. 1197D] was suddenly burst asunder in the middle.”]

For what is the tunic with which the Lord’s body is clothed, except the power of the Holy Spirit, by which the Church is invisibly adorned? “But you,” says the Lord, “remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high [Col. 1197C]” (Luke 24:49). It is “from on high” because the tunic is woven from above; nor is it sewn by human workmanship in such a way that it can be divided by the soldiers, the crucifiers of Christ, or held and torn by kings who transgress divine laws and imitate proud Saul. For the power of charity, poured out through the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the elect—by which the bride of Christ is adorned as with a nuptial garment—cannot be seen by carnal persons, and consequently cannot be held [Col. 1198A] or torn by them. Indeed, they themselves could in no way be torn or divided if they saw it with the eye of the heart and held it with the hand of action.

> [Note: [Col. 1197D] John Chrysostom, in his sermon on the Conversion of the Apostle St. Paul, mentioning the emperor Valens, who lost the success of victory, recalls the cause of his misfortune in these words: “Even now the springs of our country, which formerly surpassed the rivers themselves by their flooding course, suddenly recoiled and disappeared into themselves. They had never suffered this before, except after those places of sacrifice had been defiled with victims. Why should I now mention the famine which prevailed throughout the world under that impious king? His death in the land of the Persians? And, before his death, the derangement of his mind? The army left amid the barbarians and, as it were, enclosed in a certain net? Its return from those places, unforeseen and miraculous? For after that impious king was miserably slain and another, pious ruler—namely Gratian—succeeded him in the empire, all adversities were immediately removed; and the army, which had been entangled as though in the midst [Col. 1198C] of nets and believed it would never find any escape, was then, by God’s command, delivered from its enemies and returned in complete safety. And who could fail to be drawn toward piety by these things?”]

## Chapter II. By ecclesiastical resources the spiritual building, like the ark of the Lord, is adorned with gold and skins and fortified. Secular rulers and wicked clerics do not plunder these resources without great harm to themselves.

What, then, are the garments which either soldiers may divide among themselves or Saul may tear, except ecclesiastical resources? Tithes, indeed, and the other offerings of the faithful, like an outer garment, adorn and fortify the Church, just as skins adorned and fortified Solomon’s holy ark of the covenant. For the Church, which is truly called the ark of the covenant, the ark of sanctification, [Col. 1198B] is protected by outward resources as by skins and certain veils, so that, covered around on every side within, it shines with the splendor of spiritual gold. Neither the sun can discolor it nor any rain of persecution ever darken it. For just as, through many storms of persecution once sent upon God’s people because of sin, no king or tyrant was permitted to strip that ark, covered round about with gold, of its gold, so it is neither lawful nor possible for any king, tyrant, or soldier in any way to touch or scatter the spiritual treasures of the Church, by which she is covered and adorned on every side. Yet just as that ark is read to have been captured and carried about through a foreign land, so the Church herself is in a manner [Col. 1198C] carried about and, as it were, held captive among the princes of the Philistines, when evil rulers compel her to this: that spiritual matters be dealt with in the palace at the will of themselves and their soldiers.

> [Note: [Col. 1198D]
>
> From the Council of Aquileia, chapter 3: “Let tithes given by the faithful people be brought into baptismal churches; and let the priests themselves who are ordained over those congregations take every care for the cause of Christianity among the people entrusted to them. And let the people offer their tithes to their own priests; and let the priests divide them into four portions, as the ancient rule of the holy Fathers provides: one for themselves, one for the clergy, one for the poor, and one for the furnishing, lights, or incense of the churches. And we decree that the aforesaid priests shall have, beside their church or cell, an appointed place where the fourth portion, which we said should be given to the poor, may be brought.”
>
> From the Council of Antioch, chapter 24: “The possessions of the Church ought to be preserved for the Church with all diligence, good conscience, and faith in God, who sees and judges all things. They are also to be distributed by the judgment and authority of the bishop [Col. 1199B] to whom the people and the souls gathered within the Church have been entrusted.”
>
> From the same council, chapter 25: “Let the bishop have authority over ecclesiastical goods to distribute them among all who are in need, with the highest reverence and fear of God. Let him himself also share in what he needs, if indeed he is in need, for the necessary uses both of himself and of the brethren whom he receives, so that in no circumstance they may be defrauded, according to the holy Apostle’s saying: ‘Having food and covering, let us be content with these.’ But if he is not content with these, and instead turns the goods of the Church to his own domestic uses, and administers its revenues or the fruits of its lands not with the knowledge of the priests and deacons but entrusts their control to his household servants, relatives, or brothers, so that through such persons the other churches are secretly harmed, let him pay the penalties imposed by the provincial synod.”
>
> Although there are many chapters concerning the four portions of tithes, some of which you will find set down later in this work, reader, we wish you carefully to note this: no community maintaining the common life is compelled by these chapters to divide tithes or offerings into four portions. For this law of quartering was not instituted by the apostles, but was established after the destruction and violation of the common life, on account of transgressing clerics and bishops. It is to be observed by those transgressors of the common life until the common life is restored—a life to which every offering of the faithful has been committed, to be ordered through faithful ministers in the hand of the Mediator. That this ought to be so is demonstrated by the writings of Pope St. Gregory to Augustine, archbishop of the English, which you will find later.]

Whenever, then, it happens that the ark of the Lord is placed in a palace as in the temple of Dagon, the ark is not thereby harmed; rather, their tyrannical power—which, although it stands against God and is feared by some more than [Col. 1199A] God, ought more properly to be called the idol Dagon—is driven to its fall, and, with its hands cut off—that is, with every success of victory divinely taken away—it is utterly destroyed. But the power of Christ and of the Church shall always stand; the ark of sanctification shall at last be restored by the Philistine rulers, never without honor but with honor. For the Roman kingdom, in which this crime was most especially committed, is now plagued by mice—that is, by utterly insignificant people. Nor will these mice cease to persecute the kingdom and its rulers until the ark is sent away with honor and gifts to its own people, where a temple is built for it by Solomon the peaceful king, a temple in which authority to minister is granted not to kings but only to priests. But if any king presumes to intrude upon priestly [Col. 1199B] functions, he shall bear leprosy upon his forehead with presumptuous King Uzziah (2 Chron. 26:19).

> [Note: [Col. 1199D] Hilary, bishop of the Catholic Church and president of the synod of the city of Rome, said: “Let no one dare, without peril to his rank, rashly to violate either divine constitutions or decrees of the Apostolic See.”]

But since in our own time we see mice reigning, let us not doubt that the time is also approaching when the ark of God shall be established in a temple built for it from heaven, in freedom. There it shall have priests and ministers only from the Levitical stock, to whom the law denies an inheritance in the land for this purpose: that the Lord may be their portion. His participation is only in the same, because he himself truly is the same. Those participate in him especially and [Col. 1200A] abundantly who dwell in the same, who taste how good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell as one—that is, in the same.

> [Note: [Col. 1199D] Jerome to Nepotian: “We should understand that what Aaron and his sons were, the bishop and presbyter are. ‘Feed,’ says Peter, ‘the flock of the Lord which is among you, exercising oversight not by compulsion but willingly according to God; not for shameful gain, but freely; neither as lording it over the clergy, but becoming an example to the flock’ (1 Pet. 5:2).” Likewise: “Let the cleric who serves Christ’s Church first interpret his own title, and, setting before himself the definition of the name, strive to be what he is called. For if *cleros* is Greek and in Latin is called *sors*, ‘lot,’ clerics are so called either because they are the Lord’s lot or because the Lord himself is the lot—that is, the portion—of clerics. And because either he himself is the Lord’s portion or has the Lord as his portion, he ought to conduct himself so that he may possess the Lord and be possessed by the Lord. If he possesses anything else besides the Lord, the Lord will not be his portion. For example, if he has gold, silver, estates, or various household goods, the Lord does not deign to become his portion along with these portions. But if I am the Lord’s portion, I receive no portion among the other tribes; rather, like a Levite and priest, I live on tithes, and, having food and clothing, I shall be content with these; naked, I shall follow the naked cross.”]

But proprietary and acephalous clerics, who dwell not as one but separately through their private properties and inheritances, testify that they are not of the Levitical tribe. Nor do they proceed straight ahead like the cows that drew the ark (1 Sam. 6:12); rather, straying beyond the rules of the Fathers: “They have all turned aside; together they have become unprofitable; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:3). This one is Christ with all his own who dwell as one; through them the ark is built, to be completed by one cubit; through them the city of those dwelling as one is built, whose participation [Col. 1200B] is in the same. Through them Beth-shemesh—that is, “to the house of the sun”—the ark is drawn most directly, because they turn aside neither to the right nor to the left.

Therefore, leaving the palaces of kings, as though temples of the Philistines, wholly behind them, the Catholic clergy hasten with the ark of the covenant toward the house of the sun, where, beholding Christ, the Sun of righteousness, they obey divine laws rather than kings. There the rules of the apostles are to be observed in such a way

> [Note: [Col. 1200C]
>
> Leo the Great to all bishops established throughout Sicily: “We enjoin upon your charity that henceforth you depart in no respect from apostolic institutions, because after this no one can go unpunished if he thinks the apostolic rules may be neglected in any matter.”
>
> Peter, at the ordination of Clement: “You must live irreproachably and strive with the utmost diligence to cast off every occupation of life: do not stand surety, do not become an advocate in lawsuits, and do not be found entangled in any occupation of worldly business whatever. Today Christ does not wish to ordain you as judge or investigator of secular affairs, so that, with men’s present cares cast aside, you may be freer to devote yourself to the word of God and to distinguish good from evil according to the rule of truth. Let the laity perform for one another those tasks which we have explained above to be less fitting for you, saying the same thing; and let no one occupy you away from those pursuits through which salvation is given to all. For just as it is a crime of impiety to undertake the concerns of secular business while neglecting the word of God, so it is a sin for each of the laity unless they faithfully render one another assistance even in matters pertaining to the use of the common life. Let all labor together to make you free from care and available for those duties to which you owe yourself. But if the laity do not understand this of themselves, they must be instructed through the deacons, so that they may leave to you alone the cares of the Church, because you must be sufficient, as is fitting, to administer them and to serve the word of truth more abundantly and diligently. For if you are occupied with worldly cares, you will deceive both yourself and those who hear you. You will not be able fully to explain to each person the things which pertain to salvation; and so it comes about that you will be punished as one who has not taught what pertains to salvation, while your disciples sin through ignorance. Therefore devote yourself solely to this: to teach them the word of God suitably and without interruption, through which they can attain salvation. Let them receive your words with such reverence, knowing that you are the envoy and herald of truth, and being certain that ‘whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall also [Col. 1202C] be loosed there’ (Matt. 16:19). For you will bind what ought to be bound and loose what is expedient to loose.”]

that laws of kings and customs of pseudo-clerics, opposed to Christ, may [Col. 1201A] be utterly annihilated. We maintain that all these things are to be accomplished thus not by dreams or empty conjectures; rather, we know through this and from this, and do not doubt at all, that they must inevitably happen thus: just as they were once prefigured and prophesied, so we see them begun in our own times, though not yet completed.

Has not Emperor H. been struck for so long in his posterior parts—that is, in temporal goods? Has he not been so long harassed by mice, namely people of small importance and almost no rank, that he deliberated with his princes how he might release the Church, the true ark of sanctification, from its captivity? They indeed gave counsel, but not counsel altogether complete. For they advised [Col. 1201B] that he should send back golden hemorrhoids with the ark—that is, that he should wholly relinquish the golden rings by which he had been accustomed to invest bishops and abbots. But they did not add to this counsel that the ark should altogether leave his territories, drawn by cows, and, entrusted only to priests and Levites, leave behind among the Philistines the animal and fleshly mice; and that, retaining the golden ones with itself, it should make peace by its departure, while the plague inflicted upon kingdoms and kings because of the ark should be mitigated when that ark was restored to its own people. This would have been perfect counsel, undoubtedly well suited to mitigating the plague of discord. But the ark is still held within the borders and boundaries of the Philistines, while bishops, abbots, and abbesses, after an election has been made, are compelled to go to the palace in order that [Col. 1201C] they may receive from the king certain regalia, I know not what, for which they may render the king either homage or an oath of fealty. Therefore let rulers now employ sounder counsel: let them leave bishops, abbots, and abbesses complete freedom, and no longer presume to compel the holy Church of God in spiritual dignities.

## Chapter III. Clerics who shrink from the common and apostolic life are to be excluded from God’s Building and punished; nor are those to be heard who defend private property by the constitution of Louis the Pious.

[Col. 1202A]

Who does not see how great is the difference between golden mice, which harm no one, and fleshly mice, which gnaw at everything they can? Certainly as great, and much greater, a difference is found if the sons of light and the sons of this age are examined spiritually. The former, precious in the golden adornment of wisdom, harm no one; the latter, through the prudence of the flesh, which is hostile to God, are always ready to harm and gnaw. Yet while they seem to harm the Church, they benefit it. For they free her not only from the powers of tyrants and unjust exactions of kings, but also send forth from their own number golden mice—that is, good [Col. 1202B] converts—who, placed upon some good and regular cloister as upon a new cart, may be drawn with the ark of the covenant to the house of the true Sun.

They are drawn by cows that give lowing from inward and maternal affection and yet do not look back; for good rulers of the Church preach the word of God from the abundance of the heart and proceed straight forward in such a way that, although they grieve for clerics subject to them who are shut up in private houses, like calves tied behind them, yet they themselves, with all whom they can bring with them, submit to the yoke of the apostolic rule and, bound to that yoke by the observances of the cenobitic life as by certain reins, never turn aside. For they love not the crooked turnings of a perverse and novel custom, but the way of ancient authority and truth, [Col. 1202C] chanting with the Prophet: “I have chosen the way of truth” (Ps. 118:30). “The way of truth,” he says, not of custom, because Christ did not say, “I am custom,” but “I am truth” (John 14:6). But there is no truth or authority that can defend proprietary clerics against Christ and the apostles, if bishops should choose to assail their perverse custom. We have also the prophets; we have Christ and the apostles and apostolic men [Col. 1203A] on our side against them. If, then, they are for us, who is against us?

> [Note: [Col. 1202C] “Clement the bishop, to the beloved brethren, fellow disciples dwelling at Jerusalem with our most dear brother James, fellow bishop [Col. 1202D]: The common life, brethren, is necessary for all, and especially for those who desire to serve irreproachably and wish to imitate the life of the apostles and their disciples. For the common use of all things that are in this world ought to have belonged to all people; but through iniquity one person says that this is his own and another that that is his, and thus division has arisen among mortals.” And a little later: “Retaining the practice of this custom, the apostles and their disciples, together with us and you, led a common life. But Ananias, a stern man, and Sapphira his wife were both carried out dead from the presence of the apostles because of their sin and the lie which they committed. Therefore we command you to guard against these things and order you to obey the teachings and examples of the apostles. For those who set aside their commands become not only guilty but also exiles. These matters must be guarded against not only by us, but preached to all.”]

God is he “who makes those of one manner dwell in a house.” But King Louis, in a certain booklet of his, releases clerics from the house of one manner and permits them houses, properties, and diverse manners of life. Thus they attempt to fortify themselves by this booklet, though they are called canons and yet do not wish to lack private property. What, then, shall we call this booklet except a sort of bond by which those clerics are tied like calves in their houses, so that they may not go forth with the ark of the covenant? Far from our building—far from it—be this booklet, because it does not agree with that foundation upon which the cornerstone is laid. Connecting the different walls, he makes both one; and upon him, as living stones, are built [Col. 1203B] brethren dwelling as one; upon him also is built the city whose participation is in the same. Therefore let that booklet be placed by us under anathema; indeed, since it has already been placed under anathema, let it be removed from our building, because in it a gospel is preached contrary to him who said: “If anyone preach to you a gospel other than that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1:9). For whereas our building tends toward the same, that booklet does not gather clerics with Christ into the same, but scatters them in different directions. Yet it is not so much the author as the booklet itself that we condemn, because its author Louis is surnamed “the Pious” on account of his excessive piety; and therefore we do not despair of his salvation, though only as through fire. For he had to suffer loss because of his [Col. 1203C] building, since it was constructed not of gold, silver, and precious stones, but of wood, hay, and stubble. If, therefore, the builder deserved to be saved on account of his piety, he had to be purified through fire.

For, that he might be convicted out of his own mouth as a servant not pious but wicked, he set forth as a foundation a collection of the most firmly grounded authorities of the Fathers, strongly approving the apostolic and common life of clerics. In that foundation the building is prefigured as wholly round; and, like a circle equally distant from its center, it is so brought back into the same that in it may be seen the city whose participation is in the same. But once such a foundation has been laid, the structure which Louis afterwards builds upon it, not rightly rounded about the indivisible point of unity, is found to be so angular that it in no way looks toward the center of unity; rather, through private houses as through various angles, it spreads out in such a way that it is not at all supported by the foundation already laid.

Therefore, to overthrow that perverse construction there is no need to bring in external engines: the foundation itself need only be moved somewhat, and without doubt whatever is not rightly fitted to the foundation will fall. For if bishops invoke against those proprietary clerics the authorities contained in that work, and by pontifical authority compel the clerics themselves to observe them, they must either prove that their rule is not opposed to the rule of Christ or abandon it and receive the rule of the apostles, [Col. 1204B] with which, as all see, the authorities of the orthodox Fathers agree.

> [Note: [Col. 1203D] Pope Urban II, writing among other things in a certain decretal letter to regular canons, says: “It is fitting for us, who, although unworthy, sit in Peter’s place, to correct what is perverse, confirm what is right, and throughout the whole Church let the judgment of its Judge proceed as our judgment, and let our eyes see equity. Therefore we give thanks to almighty God, whose mercy is better than lives, because you are those who renew the praiseworthy life of the holy Fathers and, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, revive the apostolic institutions of discipline which arose in the beginnings of the holy Church but, as the Church increased, have now almost been destroyed.
>
> “For from the beginnings of the holy Church, two ways of life were established for her children: one by which the weakness of the infirm is sustained; the other by which the blessed strength of the stronger is perfected. One remains in little Zoar; the other ascends to the heights of the mountain. One redeems daily sins by tears and almsgiving; the other gains eternal merits by daily earnest endeavor. Those who hold the lower life use earthly goods; those who follow the higher despise and abandon the good land. This latter life, which turns away from earthly things, is divided almost into two portions of one and the same purpose: namely, that of canons and that of monks. The second of these, through divine mercy, has become widespread and now shines brightly throughout the whole world. But the first, as the fervor of the faithful has grown cold, has now almost entirely fallen away. This life the martyr and pontiff Urban instituted. Augustine ordered it by his rules. Gregory commanded that it be established by Augustine, archbishop of the English. Therefore it is not to be judged a work of lesser merit to revive this life of the primitive Church as the Spirit of the Lord inspires and advances it, than to preserve the flourishing monastic religion through the perseverance of that same Spirit.”]

But if they refuse, and presume to defend their own sect, they shall bear anathema, because they preach things contrary to the apostles. They are therefore to be excommunicated; or, if this cannot be done because of their multitude and the entrenched custom of evils, they are to be removed alike from ecclesiastical ministry and maintenance, so that no milk of prebendal sustenance may be supplied by bishops, upon whom the yoke of the Lord has been laid, to those calves shut up at home. If bishops turn aside to this, to offer milk to calves tied behind them, they do not rightly carry the ark of the Lord to the house of the sun. For they stray far from truth and from the authority of the holy Fathers if they confer upon such men the stipends due only to those who serve God, though it is clear that they do not serve God, since the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2:4).

Furthermore, the holy martyr and pope Urban declares that all the resources of the Church are in the bishop’s hand, so that every bishop may strive from them to establish the common life among the clergy through the mother churches, and, once established, to sustain it. He also says that anathema maranatha rests upon anyone who presumes to violate this institution. The other orthodox Fathers agree with him, removing proprietary clerics from the Church’s maintenance. Although blessed Gregory permitted ecclesiastical [Col. 1205A] stipends to be given to English clerics retaining private property, because that people had then only recently been planted in the faith, he nevertheless indicated in his decree that such clerics were neither to be admitted to holy orders nor maintained within communities of clerics living in common. He decreed that, outside the communities and outside holy orders, they should be maintained according to the necessity of that time, so that it was not even lawful for the bishop to live separately from those clerics who both exercised holy orders and, united in cloistered fellowship, were maintained by the bishop through an administrator.

> [Note: [Col. 1205D]
>
> Gregory, that most humble teacher, describes among other things as follows how a bishop ought to live with his clerics, in response to Augustine’s inquiry: “Because your brotherhood has been trained in the rules of a monastery, you ought not to live separately from your clerics. In the Church which has recently been brought to the faith, you ought to establish that manner of life which existed at the beginning of the newborn Church, in which none of them said that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them. But if there are clerics appointed outside holy orders who cannot remain continent, they ought to take wives and receive their stipends externally. For we know it written of the same Fathers whom we mentioned: ‘It was distributed to each according as anyone had need.’ Provision and care must also be made for their stipends. And they are to be kept under ecclesiastical rule, so that they may live in good morals, be diligent in chanting psalms, and, with God’s help, preserve heart, tongue, and body from all unlawful things.” After a few intervening words: “But concerning those who live the common life, what need is there for us to speak of making portions, showing hospitality, or fulfilling works of mercy, except that everything which remains over must be expended upon pious and religious causes, as it is written: ‘Nevertheless, give what remains as alms, and all things shall be clean to you’?” (Luke 11:41.)
>
> From the Book of Ivo: “Although it had been established by ancient rules that no one who belonged to the clergy should have association with unrelated women, but only with women who excluded every suspicion, blessed Pope Gregory moderated this rigor for English clerics in such a way that, if any were appointed outside holy orders and could not remain continent, they should take wives and receive their stipends outside. He understood that it was a lighter fall if those who fell were received into the bond of marriage than if they were swallowed up by wandering concubinage, the abyss of unbounded lust. But dispensations admitted after salutary deliberation ought themselves to cease when the necessity ceases.”]

The most blessed Gregory himself, a most holy promoter of the common life, lived with his clergy in such a way that the writer of his life attests that the apostolic and primitive life of the Church was revived by him and under him. From this one may infer how greatly he cared for the common life: having learned it, as a monk, with monks, when he was raised to the pontificate he not only maintained it with his clergy, but also commanded that it be observed in the remote regions of England. He followed the proper order of teaching, since, as is written of the Lord: “He began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1). For he would have taught in vain unless he had first done himself what he taught. Knowing, therefore, that it greatly avails for the spread of this holy institution if a bishop first lives regularly in his own episcopal household and then establishes regular life in the churches subject to him, he so instructed bishops in his decrees that they should not have soldiers as attendants, after the fashion of kings, “in whose houses are those clothed in soft garments”; but should be content with chamberlains chosen solely from the religious communities of clerics or monks, with whom they should live in such a way as to give no one occasion to murmur against them.

## Chapter IV. How greatly Saint Augustine promoted the common and apostolic life of clerics, and how he abhorred among them the vice of private property.

Blessed Augustine also dealt with proprietary clerics with such firmness that, if any of his own withdrew from the common life—even though, because of the many defenders of such persons, whom he laments were not lacking, he could not strip him of clerical status—nevertheless, where Augustine was bishop, such an apostate was not permitted to remain a cleric. For this holy Father declares that not even a thousand councils could induce him to allow such persons to hold clerical office within his jurisdiction. What would this blessed man say if he lived in our time and mere custom, or even the above-mentioned ordinance of Louis, were set before him so that he might depart from Christ’s law? Would he yield to wicked customs, who testifies that he would not yield against Christ and the apostles even to a thousand councils? Far be it! He did not build so upon sand that he feared his structure would collapse, although in his own day Africa had many bishops whose lives were opposed to his. Among them, not to speak of apostolic life, scarcely even the Catholic faith remained.

For at that time the heresy of the Donatists reigned in Africa; the poison of Arian perfidy had also crept in. So great too was the multitude of Circumcellions that they harassed Catholic churches in extraordinary ways and did not fear to mutilate or kill God’s ministers. Yet this blessed man, though distressed by so many evils and compelled to keep watch against all these plagues and to fight almost alone, nevertheless, confident as a lion and fearing no encounter with anyone, did not abandon the course once undertaken, so that at the end he might say with the Apostle: “I have finished the course; I have kept the faith” (2 Tim. 4:7).

In this great athlete of God, therefore, the bishops of our age are given a model: they should do as he did, since a similar or greater evil presses upon them. He so elucidated the rule of holy communal life, briefly set down in the Acts of the Apostles, that no one could lead his clerics astray in any direction, although in Africa there was a great number of brethren walking disorderly and not according to the tradition which they had received from the apostles. In accordance with the Apostle’s command, declaring in the Lord’s name that “we withdraw ourselves from every brother walking disorderly” (2 Thess. 3:6), he was accustomed so to withdraw himself with his own from all such persons that he might in some sense say with Moses: “Whoever is for the Lord, join himself to me” (Exod. 32:26). For, just as the Gospel proves that one cannot be Christ’s disciple without renouncing all things, so no one could be Augustine’s cleric who refused to renounce all things.

> **[Note: Col. 1207A]**  
> The following assertion, confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See through Pope Paschal II, proves that the order of clerics holds the place of the Levites and the apostles, and ought to imitate their lives, renouncing both private possessions and their own wills:
>
> No sound-minded person doubts that the order of clerics in the Church holds the place of the Levitical tribe, preserves the rights of apostolic dignity, and performs its offices. Hence it is certain that they ought to imitate the rules and lives of the Levites and apostles, whose place they are known to occupy, whose dignity they possess, and whose offices they perform. Whatever law is prescribed for the Levites, and whatever rule is given by the Lord to the apostles, is unquestionably imposed likewise upon Catholic clerics who supply their place until the end of the world [Col. 1207B]. Indeed, what is forbidden to the Levites while they still walk in the shadow—how can it be permitted to us who now abide in the truth, when we read that many things were permitted to them which are unquestionably forbidden to us?
>
> Thus the Lord says to Aaron, his sons, and the other Levites: “You shall possess nothing in the land of the children of Israel, nor shall you have a share among them. For I am your portion and inheritance among the children of Israel” (Num. 18:20). And shortly afterward follows: “But to the sons of Levi I have given all the tithes of Israel as a possession, in return for the ministry by which they serve me in the tabernacle of the covenant” (ibid., 21). And, concerning the same men, a little later: “They shall possess nothing else, being content with the offering of tithes, which I have set apart for their use and necessities” (ibid., 23).
>
> These things are indeed in the Old Testament. But in the New Testament, let us hear what he said to everyone wishing to adhere to the perfection of discipleship: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21). And elsewhere: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). And in another place, when he sent the apostles out to preach, he forbade them, saying: “Do not possess gold or silver” (Matt. 10:9). Peter plainly shows that he fulfilled this, saying: “Silver and gold I do not have” (Acts 3:6). The same Peter testifies that the other apostles did likewise, when he asks the Lord for himself and his fellow disciples: “Lord, behold, we have left all things and followed you. What, then, shall we have?” (Matt. 19:27). To him—and in him to all who do the same—the Lord answered: “Amen I say to you, that you who have left all things and followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left house, or father, or mother, or brothers, or sisters, or life for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life” (ibid., 28).
>
> “These commands were given to Levites and apostles; one rule and the same law are prescribed to both. Possession is taken away from both; earthly property is forbidden to both. Who, then, are bound by this rule and law if not clerics, who hold the place of the Lord’s Levites and Christ’s disciples, fulfill their ministry, perform their functions, and hold their ranks? For the observance and perpetual fulfillment of this command God established that the price of sins, the vows and offerings of the faithful, first-fruits, and tithes of goods should be given to their churches, so that those devoted to divine worship and stripped of private possessions might have fixed and perpetual stipends, from which they might live, serve the Church, supply the needs of the poor, more diligently fulfill every ministry of their order, and never withdraw themselves from these duties for the sake of any thing or necessity, nor devote themselves to secular affairs.
>
> “From this it is plainly shown that clerics serving Christ are forbidden both to hold earthly property and to receive the possessions of the Church: to have patrimony in the world and to receive a share of church goods. To confirm this judgment the Apostle’s saying is apt: ‘No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, that he may please him to whom he has pledged himself’ (2 Tim. 2:4). And Solomon’s: ‘Woe to the sinner who walks in two ways!’ (Ecclus. 2:14). Therefore, whoever wishes to follow Christ’s discipleship must renounce secular affairs; and he who, once made sacred, has begun to live from sacred things is thereafter permitted to use sacred things for his livelihood.
>
> “But lest we seem to be alone in holding this view concerning the life and rule of Catholic clerics, let other witnesses agree with us: men most religious and most fully learned, namely Jerome, Augustine, and Prosper. Let us hear what they said or understood on this matter.
>
> “Jerome, writing to Nepotian on *The Life and Conduct of Clerics*, says among other things: ‘The cleric who serves the Church of Christ,’ etc. See chapter 2, letter f. See. And a little later in the same letter he writes to him: ‘How can those be clerics who are stewards and managers of the houses and estates of foreigners, when they are commanded to despise their own possessions?’ Thus far Jerome.
>
> “Augustine, however, writes as follows in chapter nineteen of the book *On the Words of the Lord*: ‘Tax collectors also came to John to be baptized by him and said to him: “Teacher, what shall we do?” But he said to them: “Demand nothing more than what has been appointed for you”’ (Luke 3:12). And a little later: ‘The soldiers also asked him: “And what shall we do?” John said to them: “Do violence to no one; make no false accusation; but be content with your wages”’ (ibid., 14). From this every person who serves as a soldier ought now to recognize himself. For Scripture does not speak only of those soldiers who are held in armed military service; whoever wears the belt of his office is enrolled as a soldier of his rank. Therefore this saying may be applied, for example, to soldiers, protectors, other governors, and whoever receives public stipends: if he seeks more, he is condemned by John’s sentence as an extortioner and oppressor.
>
> “And shortly afterward he adds: ‘For the Catholic cleric also is bound by this saying. If he is not content with the stipend which, by the Lord’s command, he receives from the altar, but engages in trade, sells intercessions, and eagerly accepts gifts from widows, he appears more a merchant than a cleric.’ So that his deeds might speak more strongly than his tongue, he established a monastery of clerics in the bishop’s own house, where no one was permitted to own anything privately, as he himself testifies: ‘I wished to have in this house of the bishop a monastery of clerics. Behold how we live: let no one in our community be allowed to have anything of his own. Perhaps some do have something? No one is permitted to do so. If any do, they do what is not permitted.’ Thus Augustine.
>
> “But now let us hear what blessed Prosper thought on the matter: ‘Therefore,’ he says, ‘let him whom the ambition of possessing delights possess God, who created all things, with an unencumbered mind; and in him he will have whatever he desires to possess in holiness. But since no one possesses God unless he is possessed by him, let him first become God’s possession; and God will become his possessor and portion.’ And shortly afterward he adds: ‘What more does he seek whose Creator becomes all things to him? Or what suffices for him to whom God himself does not suffice?’ And a little later in the same chapter: ‘Who,’ he says, ‘to whom God is appointed as a possession, seeks anything else? Or who, because of love for him, does not despise all things thought great? Therefore, whoever wishes to possess God must renounce the world, that God may be his blessed possession. Nor does one renounce the world if the ambition of earthly possession delights him. So long as he does not leave his own things, he serves the world whose goods he retains; and certainly he cannot serve the world and God at once. As though for this reason God wished his worshippers to renounce all things through which the world is loved: so that, once the desire for the world has been excluded, divine charity may grow or be perfected in them. And therefore he established that tithes and first-fruits, the firstborn of crops, sacrifices for sins, and vows which God commanded to be offered to himself should be distributed to priests and ministers, so that, as a most devout people supplied their necessities, they might serve their Creator and Shepherd with unencumbered minds.’ Thus far Prosper.
>
> “That you must also renounce your own wills, dearest brethren, the Lord plainly shows in the Gospel, saying: ‘If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and follow me. Whoever wishes to save his life shall lose it; and whoever loses it here shall save it’ (Matt. 16:24). And elsewhere: ‘I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me’ (John 6:38). And elsewhere Holy Scripture teaches us: ‘Son, turn away from your own desires’ (Ecclus. 18:30). For, as is said elsewhere: ‘Pleasure has punishment, and necessity brings forth a crown.’ And elsewhere it is commanded: ‘Do not go after your desires’ (ibid.).
