Let those who follow them hear what is said of them through the Prophet: ‘They became corrupt and abominable in their desires’ (Ps. 13:1). Therefore the same Prophet, taking up the voice of prelates, writes: ‘He has subjected peoples to us and nations beneath our feet’ (Ps. 46:4). Warned by these examples, brethren, let us not refuse to be subject to others for God’s sake; but let us carry out Christ’s will instead of our own wills, according to another’s judgment—yet one that is spiritual and discerning.”

[Col. 1208A] Since, therefore, he had joined to himself only those who belonged to the Lord, he triumphed in so great a multitude of opponents like another Moses, so that after the apostles he possesses this glory as a kind of [Col. 1209A] triumphal crown: those who pursue apostolic life among the clergy make special profession of his rule. They also glory in him as their leader and prince after the apostles, because they use his rule, which points out the one royal road in such a way that whoever keeps it cannot depart from the paths of the apostles.

For as there is one Catholic faith, concisely gathered in the Apostles’ Creed, so there is one rule briefly set forth for the holy rulers and ministers of the Church in the Acts of those same apostles. Although the apostolic faith was later expounded more fully both in the Nicene Synod and by Saint Athanasius, someone who recites “I believe in God,” or “I believe in one,” or “Whoever wishes,” is not said to have recited one faith and then another, because there is only one faith. Likewise, although the rule of the apostles’ common life was more fully expounded by Blessed Augustine, there is no rule for clerics besides the one marked out briefly by the apostles in the phrase “one soul and one heart,” and afterward elucidated in eloquent discourse by Blessed Augustine and the other holy Fathers. Therefore, just as there is only one faith among all Catholics, so there ought to be only one rule among God’s ministers: namely, the apostolic rule.

Recognizing this, the holy Father Augustine, just as he fortified the Catholic faith against heretics by many arguments, so by singular discernment he elucidated the apostolic rule against the multitude of disorderly clerics. He delivered this rule to his own—or rather, confirmed the rule handed down by the apostles. He allowed neither any multitude of wicked persons, however numerous, nor any perverse custom, however long established, to turn himself or his followers away from it. For, just as he wished one apostolic faith to be observed among the people, so he wished one apostolic Rule to be observed among the clergy.

> **[Note: Col. 1210D]**  
> Augustine, *Confessions*, book 8: “From a perverse will arises lust; and while lust is served, habit is formed; and while habit is not resisted, necessity is formed. It should be noted that such necessity has no power to excuse; rather, concerning it and because of it, one must cry out with the Psalmist: ‘Deliver me, Lord, from my necessities’ (Ps. 24:17).”
>
> Gregory VII, to Guimannus, bishop of Aversa: “If perhaps you appeal to custom, it must be observed that the Lord says: ‘I am the truth’ (John [Col. 1211C] 14:6). He did not say, ‘I am custom,’ but ‘the truth.’ And certainly, to use the judgment of blessed Cyprian, every custom, however ancient or widespread, must altogether be subordinated to truth; and a practice contrary to truth must be abolished.”

## Chapter V. How unworthy it is that ecclesiastical goods should be granted by bishops themselves to soldiers, and how bishops thereby become contemptible among laypeople because they depart so far from Saint Ambrose’s example, etc.

[Col. 1210A]

Behold, we have seen that this prudent architect chose such a foundation and raised such a structure upon it, whose whole fellowship was “in the same thing,” because he would have neither people in faith nor clergy in Rule differ from the holy apostles. Secure in this building, therefore, he did not fear to be overcome in any way by heretics or pseudo-clerics. In this city of strength he used Christ not only as a wall but also as an outer rampart.

If in our time any bishop left behind a cohort of soldiers—the sort which Judas alone among the apostles is recorded to have led, when, as the Gospel relates, “he was leader of those who seized Jesus”—if, I say, he left the cohort behind [Col. 1210B] and trusted with Blessed Augustine in this city of our strength, Zion, then, as Augustine prevailed against heretics and proprietary clerics, so he would prevail against heretics, namely Simoniacs and Nicolaitans, and likewise against proprietary clerics. For God would not abandon his own portion if the bishop abandoned the cohort that accompanies him with swords and clubs wherever he goes, so that he is recognized as more like Judas leading a cohort than Peter carrying only a staff. God does not seek in a bishop the likeness of Judas, but the likeness of Jacob, whom he loved. Let the likeness of Jacob, then, be expressed in the bishop: so that, as Jacob did, he may rather flee willingly and, if necessary, suffer exile than feed armed soldiers from the stipends of the poor and, while possessing a kingdom not of this world, take to himself attendants whom Christ did not wish to have on earth. If Christ’s kingdom had been of this world, his attendants would certainly have fought to prevent his being handed over to the Jews. But because his kingdom was not of this world, he did not have soldier-attendants in this world; rather, he suffered them to divide his garments and crucify his body.

He endures such persons even to this day, while ecclesiastical resources are distributed through soldiers and the Church, which is his body, is afflicted not only by bodily poverty among widows, orphans, pilgrims, and other poor persons [Col. 1211A], but is also crucified with wondrous torment in the minds of the perfect who have zeal for God. It is crucified not so much by soldiers who strip him bodily and fasten him with the nails of affliction as by pontiffs who, through the Church’s resources, hand him over into the soldiers’ hands.

> **[Note: Col. 1211C]**  
> Jerome, to Nepotian: “The bishop’s glory is to provide for the resources of the poor; the priest’s disgrace is to pursue his own riches. Likewise: it is shameful for the lictors of consuls and soldiers to stand guard before the doors of a priest of Christ, who was crucified and poor and ate another’s food. If you object that you do this in order to petition for the wretched and those subject to you, a worldly judge will show more respect to a self-restrained cleric than to a rich one, and will venerate your holiness more than your wealth. Or if he is such a man as listens to clerics only among drinking bowls, I shall gladly do without his favor and shall ask Christ on behalf of the judge, for he is more able and quicker to help.”
>
> **[Note: Col. 1211D]**  
> Jerome: “To steal anything from a friend is theft; to defraud the Church is sacrilege. To receive something for distribution to the poor, and then, though very many are hungry, to wish to keep it safe or to be timid about spending it—or, what is an act of most manifest wickedness, to take something from it—surpasses the cruelty of all robbers.”

For soldiers would have no power against the Church unless it had been given them from above. Therefore bishops, who have handed over the Church—and Christ in the Church—have the greater sin. For although the soldiers’ fault is not small but great and full of sacrilege, the wickedness of the pontiffs is greater, because they dissipate the Church’s revenues under the pretext of securing peace, as though they said with the Pharisees and Jewish high priests: “Lest the Romans come and take away our place and nation” (John [Col. 1211B] 11:48).

Certainly, “there they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. 52:6). They fear to suffer evil with Christ and the apostles, but do not fear to do evil with the Pharisees. Yet doing evil is always evil; suffering evil is so far from evil that every holy martyr or pontiff would choose to suffer a thousand evils rather than commit one. Thus, when Saint Ambrose was compelled by the emperor to hand over a church, the holy pontiff chose, at no small risk to himself and his people, to offend the king rather than the law. He affirmed that it was lawful neither for himself to give the goods of the poor to anyone except the poor, nor for the emperor to receive them.

> **[Note: Col. 1211D]**  
> Ambrose: “I am approached by counts and tribunes, that through me the basilicas might promptly be handed over, saying that the emperor had lawfully commanded that everything under his power ought to be surrendered. I replied that, if he asked from me what was mine—that is, my estate, my silver, or any such property of mine—I would not oppose him, although all that is mine belongs to the poor. But what belongs to God is not subject to imperial power.” And shortly afterward: “It is neither lawful for me to hand it over nor expedient for you, Emperor, to receive it. No right may violate the house of a private person; do you suppose that God’s house is to be taken away?”

Therefore, because there he trembled with fear where fear did exist—since he refused to associate himself with the Pharisees who handed Christ over as though to avert Roman offense—and because he had read: “Honor the king,” so that he gave due heed to what came before, “Fear God” (1 Pet. 2:17), he preserved God’s favor and softened the emperor’s fierceness with a free and priestly answer. Thus, by fearing God and honoring the king without compromising that fear, he preserved his place and nation. To preserve them against the emperor’s displeasure, he refused to distribute even the smallest part of the poor’s resources. But the Jews both lost Christ by betraying him and were exterminated by the Romans from the place for whose sake they had handed him over to the Romans.

So too the dignity and power of modern pontiffs are chiefly destroyed and trampled underfoot by those to whom ecclesiastical resources are known to have been distributed. These same persons, from whom they receive several denarii in every way corresponding to the thirty pieces of silver for which Christ was sold—received, as they say, for an ecclesiastical benefit, but in truth for an evil deed—hold them in such contempt that, either openly in reproach or in secret whispering, they say to them: “What is that to us? See to it yourself” (Matt. [Col. 1212B] 27:4).

“What is it to us,” say the soldiers, “if bishops sell to us at a cheap price the Church purchased with Christ’s blood, and afterward cast away the very price of blood by expending it uselessly?” Would that even this price were spent on the burial and rest of pilgrims, and that at least in his last moments some bishop would say: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (ibid.). Then he would obtain pardon too, if, not despairing with Judas but hoping with David the prophet, he confessed that he had sinned. Yet I would prefer that, while still sound in health, he should weep most bitterly over his sin with Peter and flee from soldiers betraying Christ—if not clothed, then at least, with Christ’s beloved disciple, naked after leaving behind his linen cloth [Col. 1212C]. For it would be better and undoubtedly more salutary to flee naked from such men than to remain clothed and laden with many riches among them.

> **[Note: Col. 1212D]**  
> Augustine, *On John*: “Behold Judas is a thief—and do not despise this: he is a sacrilegious thief, not merely a thief of money-boxes, but a thief of the Lord’s money-boxes, of sacred ones. If crimes are distinguished in court between ordinary theft and peculation—for peculation is theft from the commonwealth—and theft of private property is not judged as theft of public property, how much more severely should a sacrilegious thief be judged? It is not theft from just anywhere; it is theft from the Church. Whoever steals anything from the Church is compared with Judas the traitor.”
>
> Innocent, pope, to the bishops of Apulia: “Many decrees of the elders contrary to ecclesiastical canons are usurped; these could indeed easily be cut away if bishops were not found to be their authors. While they strive to show favor either to friends or to dependents, they violate religion and corrupt the orders.”

Nevertheless, since the Lord Most High, terrible, the great King over all the earth, has subjected peoples to bishops and nations beneath their feet, he himself is in all things their protector and helper, so that the princes of the world may not dare excessively to persecute those who withdraw from them, terrified by fear of him—just as Laban, long ago pursuing Jacob as he fled from him and carried all his possessions with him to the land of his fathers, was terrified. God has so fully chosen in bishops his inheritance, the likeness of Jacob whom he loved, that, if in every respect the likeness of Jacob whom he loved is expressed in them, none of them will lack God’s most certain aid. This is proved by the examples of those in whom the image of Jacob has thus far been expressed: Jacob, that is, the vigorous wrestler and Israel, the man who sees God. It would take too long here to introduce Martins, Augustines, and the other holy Fathers, who did not grow rich through ecclesiastical resources but “conquered kingdoms through faith” [Col. 1213B]. They did not fill the mouths of lions—that is, of most powerful kings—from the stipends of the poor, but shut them by the word.

Yet it is pleasing to set before the eyes and impress upon the ears of each and every bishop what Blessed Ambrose was to the emperor himself. Ambrose utterly forbade him the Church’s resources and rebuked him so freely for his sin that he denied him entrance into the Church until public penance reconciled him. Before that very emperor, I say, whom he did not spare for the truth’s sake, Ambrose possessed such authority and affection that it is plainly evident that his awe restrained the emperor, who beheld in the holy pontiff the likeness of Jacob whom God loved. For just as Jacob is recorded, in fleeing from Laban, not to have consulted him in the least concerning his daughters and other things belonging to him, so Ambrose did not consider it necessary to consult the emperor concerning the care of souls and the ordering of Church resources. He went so far as to impose public penance upon him for killings committed without judicial procedure at the emperor’s own command; and if the emperor asked for anything from the Church’s resources, he unhesitatingly denied it, affirming that everything possessed both by himself and by the Church belonged to the poor.

> **[Note: Col. 1213C]**  
> Ambrose: “It is alleged that the emperor may do all things, that all things are his. I answer: Do not burden yourself, Emperor, by imagining that you have any imperial right over divine things. Do not exalt yourself; rather, if you wish to reign longer, be subject to God. For it is written: ‘Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s’ (Matt. 22:21). Palaces belong to the emperor; churches to the priest. You have been entrusted with authority over public affairs, not over sacred things.”
>
> The same, when compelled to surrender the vessels of the Church, said: “If anything were demanded of me—an estate, a house, gold, or silver—whatever belonged to my own right, I would willingly offer. But I can neither take away nor hand over anything belonging to God’s temple, for I received it to guard, not to surrender. Moreover, I also take thought for the emperor’s salvation, since it would be expedient neither for me to hand it over nor for him to receive it. Let him heed the voice of a free priest: if he wishes to be well advised, let him withdraw from injury to Christ.”
>
> Ambrose, in a sermon to the people: “You remember that today it was read how Naboth, a holy man and owner of his vineyard, being pressed by a royal request to give up his vineyard, replied: ‘Far be it from me that I should hand over the inheritance of my fathers!’ (3 Kings 21:3). What great evil it was that the king was grieved because another’s right was justly denied to him by refusal; yet, deceived by a woman’s counsel, Naboth defended his vines even with his own blood.” And a little later: “If he did not hand over his vineyard, shall we hand over Christ’s Church [Col. 1214C]? What answer, then, was given boldly? I said to the assembly: ‘Far be it from me that I should hand over Christ’s inheritance!’ If he did not hand over the inheritance of his fathers, shall I hand over Christ’s inheritance? And I added this: ‘Far be it from me that I should hand over the inheritance of the fathers: that is, the inheritance of Dionysius, who died in exile for the cause of the faith; the inheritance of Eustorius the confessor; the inheritance of Morolus and all the faithful bishops before them.’ I gave the answer appropriate to a priest; let the emperor do what is appropriate to an emperor. He may take my life before my faith.”

Who, then, gave modern bishops the permission which Ambrose did not possess? They have handed over to soldiers not only estates offered to God in sacrifice, but even tithes themselves, sanctified for divine worship by the authority of both Old and New Testament, as though that which Blessed Ambrose denied to be lawful had begun to be lawful. He considered it wicked not to distribute the goods of the poor to the poor; modern bishops regard it as not wicked but necessary that they should acknowledge the soldiers’ claimed right in Church goods under the law of benefices. They neglect Christ’s justice precisely because the soldiers’ justice has become too deeply established, whereas Christ’s justice seems unusual in our age [Col. 1214B]. Thus royal and ecclesiastical matters have been so confused that a bishop now seems to despoil the kingdom if he wishes to deny ecclesiastical resources to soldiers.

This is the confusion by which the hands of those building in God’s holy Church are hindered, just as, after the Babylonian exile, the efforts of those rebuilding the Temple were delayed because of this: as these men mingled ecclesiastical affairs with royal affairs, so those men, although Israelites, contrary to the divine prohibition took foreign wives, mingled among the nations, and learned their works.

Are not bishops mingled with secular princes [Col. 1214C], and have they thus learned their works, so that some of them know how to storm camps, march against enemies, and arrange other matters more suited to a military commander than to a pontiff?

> **[Note: Col. 1214D]**  
> Augustine, to Valerius: “Nothing in this life, and especially at this time, is more difficult, laborious, or dangerous than the office of bishop, presbyter, or deacon; but before God nothing is more blessed if one serves in it as our Emperor commands.”

What, then, is a bishop who wishes to be what he is called to be to do, except wholly to despise the multitude and custom of the perverse and follow Christ alone, so that he may appear like a certain holy Tobias?

> **[Note: Col. 1214D]**  
> Jerome, to Heliodorus: “It is not easy to stand in Paul’s place, to hold the rank of Peter, who now reign with Christ, lest perhaps an angel come who tears the veil of your temple and removes your lampstand from its place. If you are about to build a tower, calculate the cost of the work to come. Salt that has become tasteless is good for nothing except to be cast out and trampled by swine” (Matt. 5:13). “If a monk falls, the priest will pray for him; but who will pray for the fall of a priest?”
>
> The same: “Woe to the man who, binding the talent received in a cloth while others make profit, preserved only what he had received! (Matt. 25:25). Immediately he will be struck by the Lord’s answer: ‘Wicked servant! Why did you not give my money, that I might have demanded it with interest?’ (ibid., 26)—that is, you should have deposited at the altar what you could not carry. For while you, an idle merchant, hold the coin, you occupy the place of another who could have doubled the money. Not all are bishops. You look to Peter, but consider Judas too. Do you welcome Stephen? Then look also at Nicolaus, whom the Lord condemned by his judgment in the Apocalypse (2:15). Let each person prove himself, and so approach.”

## Chapter VI. The former defenders of churches were those who inflicted the greatest injury upon them; hence their feigned homage. The Church’s goods belong not to the king but to the poor; bishops also are condemned for being too yielding in defending the Church’s rights.

Concerning Tobit, indeed, we read thus: when all went to the golden calves which the king of Israel had made, he alone, avoiding their company, came to Jerusalem to worship the Lord God of Israel (Tobit 1:5). Thus this man, while all go to the palace to deal with worldly affairs, should alone learn, in the vision of peace, to offer to God the sacrifices and oblations due to Him. But perhaps the king will persecute him with his soldiery, and, casting Christ’s law behind his back as though it were [Col. 1215B] something unfamiliar, will press his own “justice” upon him, having the soldiers as supporters in this matter—those who, together with Pilate’s soldiers, sold a lie in order to receive the Church’s maintenance. For they have performed homage to the bishops, in order to be defenders of the Church, though they are altogether worse than foreign enemies, because they divide the Church’s goods among themselves, and whatever seems to remain from their benefices they wish to consume by feasting lavishly with bishops, so that scarcely anything can remain for the soldiers’ expenses, from which the poor and widows may be supported, guests and pilgrims received, and the other duties of episcopal generosity performed.

What, then, is that homage except a kind of [Col. 1215C] lie? For although they call themselves the bishops’ men, they claim for themselves such power to lord it over them that, giving nothing except a lie, they drain the whole treasury of the Church; so that they prove in every respect worse than those soldiers who, after receiving payment from the chief priests, fabricated such a lie: namely, that they made it liable to dissolution and refutation by saying that Christ had been stolen while they slept (Matt. 28:13).

For who does not see that the testimony of one who testifies to something said to have occurred while he was asleep is fragile and false? Their lie, then, has been annulled, because there is no doubt that Christ rose again. The chief priests perished, from whom this lie is known to have been purchased with the Temple’s money. Yet scarcely anyone dares assail with the sword of truth the homage [Col. 1215D] and lie which bishops purchase from the Church’s resources, unless he is resolved not to fear so greatly those who kill the body as he ought to fear [Col. 1216A] the judgment of Him who, after killing the body, has power to cast the soul into the hell of fire (Luke 12:5).

But someone will say: did not the righteous Judge Himself command that what belongs to Caesar be rendered to Caesar (Matt. 22:21)? Did He not confirm this very point by example, when He paid the didrachma? What bishop, then, making himself greater than Christ or even Peter, would dare deny to the higher powers, contrary to the teaching of the Apostle Paul, the tribute which they paid? We answer that in this very matter we desire all bishops to be conformed to Christ and Peter: so that, just as He received from elsewhere the price to be given to Caesar, not from Judas’s purse, which was the common property of the poor, so bishops too [Col. 1216B] should supply it to soldiers and the king from elsewhere, if they could—not from the Church’s resources, which ought to be held in common solely for the poor and for those serving God. They should heed what the holy Fathers say: that it is sacrilege not to distribute the property of the poor to the poor. But if the emperor or another prince should demand the Church’s resources, the bishop should fittingly reply, with blessed Ambrose, as quoted above: “It is neither lawful for me to surrender them nor expedient for you, Emperor, to receive them.”

But if, for royal “justice,” as they call it, the emperor should determine to extort something from the poor’s possessions from a bishop, it would be better to burn with blessed Lawrence, from whom not even fire could extort the Church’s property, [Col. 1216C] than to value Florentine or Courtly justice so highly as though it could excuse us against divine justice. For no custom, however ancient, nor ordinance, however confirmed by kings, can or ought to stand if it is found to conflict with prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic institutions.

Yet an objection is still raised: that [MS: “which”] things are known to have been granted to them by their predecessors, especially if antiquity has accrued to the grant, so that there is in it a kind of hereditary succession through many generations. We reply that the predecessor bishops who did this, unless they were afterward purified through the fire of repentance for the sacrilege committed, undoubtedly perished; and they left their successors [Col. 1216D] an inheritance of destruction, unless the latter strive to correct what is known to have been presumptuously undertaken by them against God’s laws.

> [Note: Col. 1215D]
>
> From the synod of Pope Hilary, chapter 4: “[Col. 1216D] Whatever any bishop has unlawfully committed, or has found committed by his predecessors, he shall condemn, if he wishes to avoid danger to himself. For he will find in himself whatever he does not cut away in another.”
>
> Gelasius, to Cresconius, John, and Messala, bishops, among other things: “As it is fitting for a successor to preserve the ordinances of predecessors when they are lawful and just, so he ought also to correct what has been wrongly done.”
>
> Pope Adrian, to Engelramnus: “Constitutions contrary to the holy decrees of the Roman pontiffs are of no force.”
>
> Gregory, in the *Register*: “It has been expressly enacted by imperial constitution that things done contrary to the laws are not only invalid but must also be held as though never done.” [Col. 1217D]
>
> Pope Innocent, to bishops established throughout Macedonia: “It ought not to have seemed burdensome to your most devout minds that anyone’s judgment should be reconsidered, because truth, more often tested, shines more brightly in the light; and ruin, recalled to judgment, is condemned more severely and without repentance.”
>
> From the Roman laws: “Those writings granted in accordance with the request of each petitioner shall prevail and be put into effect when they agree with the reason of right and law. But those which may perhaps be obtained by fraud or false petitions shall bring no remedy to the petitioners.” [Col. 1218A]

For if they lay hands upon things which, under Court laws, are to be confirmed in the power [Col. 1217A] of soldiers, though by God’s law they must be wrested from their hands, then, just as the Jews living today, because, in error, they succeed their fathers, the slayers of Christ, are not exempt from their fathers’ condemnation, so bishops succeeding wicked bishops cannot escape the condemnation of their predecessors unless they strive to reform what was wickedly ordered into a just order.

## CHAPTER VII. God’s building cannot stand unless bishops cast off the yoke of this age—that is, the pomp of retainers, military services, the neglect of evangelical life, and the like.

No one should find it strange that we linger so long in distinguishing ecclesiastical from royal matters, [Col. 1217B] because we judge this to be of great importance for the structure of the building which we have undertaken to discuss. For just as, long ago, under Zerubbabel the leader and Joshua the high priest, the rebuilding of the Temple was delayed because the law of God—which forbade the sons of Israel to marry foreign wives—was so profaned and neglected that Joshua himself is recorded to have taken a foreign wife (and thus blessed Jerome says that for this reason he appeared to the prophet Zechariah in filthy garments [Zech. 3:3]), so in our own time the building of God’s holy Church has been hindered because, contrary to the command of divine law that permits no one serving God to be entangled in secular affairs, secular affairs have been so thoroughly mixed with ecclesiastical ones that even the priest whom the law forbids to go out from [Col. 1217C] holy things appears outside clothed in filthy garments—that is, entangled and enmeshed in worldly business. Therefore Satan, both in himself and through his members, greatly opposes him; and concerning the Church’s material possessions, as concerning the body of Moses, he often contends with him through the tongues of soldiers. The archangel of Christ, sent to assist the Church, does not dare rebuke this Satan, because he sees bishops clothed in filthy garments justly subjected to the harassment of soldiers.

This agrees with the account that the good angel who attended Daniel’s prayers and desired them, offered as they were by a man of desires, to be swiftly heard, nevertheless endured a delay of twenty-one days through opposing angels [Col. 1217D] because the prince of Persia—that is, the evil angel—had, as it were, a just case against him. For although Daniel’s prayers were pure, they ought nevertheless to have been heard more slowly because those for whom he prayed had incurred so much guilt that, by the just vengeance for sin, they deserved to be subject to evil rulers. Yet because [Col. 1218A] the man of desires, who had denied himself desirable foods, prayed for them, the good angel at last prevailed.

> [Note: Col. 1218D] Jerome to Augustine: “So great is the dignity of souls that each one has, from the moment of its birth, an angel appointed for its protection.”

Bringing Daniel joyful consolation concerning the shortened period of captivity, he carefully explained the delay also: namely, that evil rulers had opposed his prayers. None of these will be able or dare to oppose before God the good angels laboring for salvation unless, because human sins require it, he has received from God a just permission.

Therefore Satan, who has a just power to oppose bishops so long as priestly grace is dishonoured in them by a filthy garment, cannot be restrained by the good angel unless the bishop, with Daniel, sets his heart to understand and afflicts himself [Col. 1218B] before the Lord; unless he casts away the filthy garment and, clothed in linen and having at his loins the writer’s inkhorn, inscribes the letter *tau*—that is, the mystical figure of the cross—upon the foreheads of God’s servants. Then the sword of another Satan will not be able to oppose him; but, whether it wishes or not, the opposing party will be compelled in every way to serve him, injuring and killing only those who do not have the figure of the cross so impressed upon their foreheads that, grieving and mourning over the things done in their midst, through the excessive torment of zeal for good they may, as it were through the sign of the cross, escape vengeance.

Therefore, just as the princes themselves who tear the Church apart will be given into the hands of the sword in this present age and will become portions for foxes in the age to come, so all who consent to them [Col. 1218C] will be devastated by the sword without and terror within. Yet neither the sword without nor terror within would devastate them to their injury if, naked and following the naked cross, they were marked with the letter *tau*. But because they love earthly things, which may be given or taken away by the rulers of the world, they must be devastated by terror within and by the sword without whenever they see that earthly peace is not maintained through worldly rulers. This devastation will therefore begin at the sanctuary, because clerics who are proprietors, unworthily lying upon the Church’s sanctuaries, will be the first to be destroyed, when the wealth they possess is taken and consumed by soldiers, with no one defending it. Then they will either perish, scattered from one another, or—what is more to be desired by all good people [Col. 1218D] and hoped for from the very fountain of goodness—they will be saved through conversion.

Indeed, if a bishop, scorning once and for all the multitude, however numerous, and the custom, however deeply rooted, shines forth in linen and apostolic dress and bears the writer’s inkhorn at his loins—that is, girding himself with the holy authority of the Scriptures—[Col. 1219A] and proceeds so that he marks with the figure of *tau* the foreheads of those whom he can, takes to himself those who profess the apostolic life and bear the cross of Christ, and provides the care of souls only with them, the rest will without doubt be devastated by the swords of the six men—that is, worldly rulers. They are comprehended under the number six because, in this present world created in six days, they are permitted through six ages not without reason to bear the sword. But in the present time this sword serves a bishop clothed in linen and in the white garments of purity and innocence in such a way that, even where it is believed to oppose him, it harms them not at all, and sometimes, blunted by divine terror, it comes to rest, according to the words: “He did not permit anyone to harm them, and for their sake He rebuked kings” (Ps. 104:14).

[Col. 1219B] Far, therefore, be from the bishop the allure of secular pomp, which, like a filthy garment, disfigures episcopal insignia. For what need has he of costly clothing or a troop of soldiers? Is Christ to be seized and crucified again, so that a bishop may lead a cohort for this purpose, conformed rather to Judas the betrayer than to Peter the shepherd? For just as, according to Paul’s judgment, whoever sins against a brother for whom Christ died sins against Christ Himself, who died for him, so likewise a bishop who gives over the poor’s goods to soldiers undoubtedly afflicts with hunger and kills Christ’s poor; and thus, sinning against the brethren, he sins against Christ, who was once delivered over in His own person to soldiers to save such people, and who is now again delivered by bishops to soldiers in [Col. 1219C] His members, to be afflicted and killed. For the bishop who surrenders the poor’s maintenance surrenders their souls and lives, and is so much worse than Judas the betrayer as he more greedily gathers from such betrayal the price of blood and keeps for his own uses what Judas did not wish to possess, but grieved to have received until his death.

Therefore, as has been said, the bishop is conformed to Judas the betrayer, not Peter the shepherd, when he leads a troop of soldiers whom he feeds from the poor’s maintenance. But would that he were conformed to Peter and might come out from the midst of the soldiers, among whom he is held bound with two chains, so as to cast off both and say with the Psalmist: “Let us burst their bonds and cast away their yoke from us” (Ps. 2:3).

[Col. 1219D] What, then, are these two chains by which a bishop is bound under the rulers of this world’s darkness, enduring also a dark prison? Certainly one chain

> [Note: Col. 1219D] Jerome to the presbyter Paulinus: “Flee crowds of people, official duties, greetings, and banquets, as though they were chains of pleasure. Let your food be simple and taken in the evening: consider vegetables, legumes, and occasionally little fish the greatest delicacies. He who desires Christ and feeds on that bread does not much ask from what costly foods he produces excrement. Whatever is not perceived after it has passed the throat should be the same to you as bread or vegetables. Let sacred reading always be in [Col. 1220D] your hand; keep frequent vigils, and often sleep with an empty stomach. Love whisperings, petty fame, and flattering admirers as enemies. Distribute relief from your provisions with your own hand to the poor and brethren. Faith is rare among human beings. Think of Judas’s purse. Do not seek humility of dress for the sake of a swelling mind. Avoid the company of secular persons, and especially of penitents.”

is homage, by which he is bound to soldiers; the other is that fear by which he suspects that, if deserted by soldiers, he will be injured and badly treated. But both these chains, with the angel of great counsel assisting, [Col. 1220A] will be broken: for, when homage is disregarded and fear cast aside, even the iron gate will open of its own accord for his departure, provided only that he rises swiftly at the angel’s command and, strengthened in the Lord and in the power of His might, puts no confidence in military force but in the strength of Him before whom every knee bends. Under Him even earthly power is bent so far that it honours and fears more a bishop who, with Christ, does not wish to have soldiers as attendants and uses only the pastoral staff than one who leads a thousand soldiers in his retinue.

## CHAPTER VIII. How ecclesiastical resources are to be divided and administered by bishops; whether maintenance is to be paid to a prince from Church estates and tithes, and related matters.

[Col. 1220B] Whence, then, comes such power in that staff of uprightness, except because the Lord has reigned and girded Himself with strength? (Ps. 17:33.) Let the bishop, then, be girded with this strength, and all Egypt will fear him when he uses only the staff, with Moses. By this staff the king of Egypt too, with his army, will be struck if he rashly pursues a bishop departing from him. For if a bishop, withdrawing from the court with his own people, preserves in this also the likeness of Jacob, whom the Lord loved, by allowing him to search all that is his, as is recorded of Laban, who is marked as acting wickedly in searching Jacob’s possessions (Gen. 31:33 ff.); if, I say, the bishop allows the same to the king and other princes, what of their own can they find in the Church for which they ought to press into forced service a bishop withdrawing from them? “The estates,” they say, “which kings have offered to churches.” To this we answer that, as the golden idols carried from Laban’s house by Rachel could not be found when Laban searched, because they lay hidden beneath Rachel’s garment, so now, among the many estates of churches, which the Church has received partly from kings and partly from other God-fearing persons, it does not appear that she has any estates belonging to royal authority for which she ought either to fill the royal treasury or provide soldiers with campaign pay. Unless, perhaps, bishops judge it right to render some assistance to those who fight for the Church, not against the Church—yet not from the holy offering of tithes or from any other possession of the poor, [Col. 1220D] which the bishop ought to give to no one as his own property, but, as the canons command, administer as something entrusted to him.

For one portion is due to the clerics; another, to the building and repair of churches; a third, to widows and others who have no consolation in this world; a fourth, to the bishop—not that he may [Col. 1221A] feast from it with soldiers, but that, as a generous steward, he may expend what can remain for himself and his household servants upon pilgrims and guests, so that his door stands open to every traveller. For if he does not receive all, according to the Fathers’ judgment, he is inhuman. Therefore the fourth portion which the bishop receives from tithes and other offerings is owed chiefly to pilgrims and guests. Soldiers and princes are not counted among these guests, unless perhaps they travel outside their own land. Then, if they too need consolation, the bishop ought to show them charity insofar as his means and the needs of his household permit, because a fourth part of the tithe of his entire diocese is entrusted to him for this purpose: that he may be found beneficent and generous toward all who need consolation.

[Col. 1221B] If, therefore, the bishop conducts himself in this way in administering the Church’s resources, what estates would the emperor dare or be able to take from him—estates covered by such charity, with which the Church, prefigured in Rachel, is clothed as with a wedding garment, and by which the multitude of sins that kings and princes themselves fashion like certain idols is entirely covered? For charity, which adorns the other virtues and reigns among the few spiritual people by enfolding them like a garment, itself covers the multitude of sins among the crowd of secular people—provided that these secular persons, searching everything for their own gain, do not disturb the Church, but allow her, like Rachel, to sit in quiet repose and to remain at rest, extending the garment of charity with which she is adorned even to cover the sins [Col. 1221C] and idols of her persecutors.

Therefore it benefits kings more than the Church that she deigns to possess estates offered by them, provided that they do not so persecute her when she withdraws with her lawful husband that they speak anything harsh to the Catholic bishop, the beloved spouse of that Church, just as Laban spoke nothing harsh to Jacob. To prevent him from presuming this, God had frightened and warned him on the way, saying: “Take heed that you speak nothing harsh to him” (Gen. 31:24). Behold how truly God loved the likeness of Jacob, whom He guarded with such care that He would not allow His beloved Jacob to be injured even by a harsh word, but compelled Jacob’s persecutor, by the hidden power of His fear, to enter into a covenant with him [Col. 1221D].

## CHAPTER IX. The goodwill and generosity of rulers toward the Church were greatest in the early centuries, but not in later times. Episcopal elections must be canonical—that is, free.

[Col. 1222A]

Who, then, can doubt that this very thing will occur in the holy Church if the bishop, expressing Jacob’s likeness in himself, is willing to imitate the figurative Jacob in this: that, just as Jacob, without consulting his father-in-law, alone in solitude with his two wives alone, formed such a plan as to depart from the house of Laban their father because he saw that Laban’s face had changed toward him, so this religious bishop, not waiting for the counsel of princes or of the multitude, alone in the solitude of his heart, employing the wisdom of contemplation and action, should firmly determine upon such a plan: withdrawing himself wholly with his own people from the court full of cares, he should make for the ancient seats [Col. 1222B] of the Fathers by the royal road and in an irrevocable course, because it is evident that the countenances of kings and princes toward bishops have greatly changed.

For if we review what the most Christian emperors Constantine,

> [Note: Col. 1221D] Constantine began the episcopal assembly at the Council of Nicaea in this manner: “The Lord has appointed you priests and has given you authority to judge even us; and indeed we are rightly judged by you. But you cannot be judged by human beings. You have been given to us by God as gods; and it is not fitting for a human being to judge gods. Hear the case among yourselves and make peace. For if I saw a priest of God sinning, I would cover him with my cloak.”

Constans, Valentinian, Theodosius, Arcadius, Honorius, Charles,

> [Note: Col. 1221D] The glorious emperors Charles and Louis, in the first book of their capitularies, decreed, not ignorant of the sacred canons: “That, in God’s name, holy Church may enjoy her honour more freely, we give our assent to the ecclesiastical order: namely, that bishops be chosen from their own diocese by the election of clergy and people according to the statutes of the canons, with all respect of persons and acceptance of gifts removed, on account of merit of life and the gift of wisdom, so that they may benefit those subject to them by word and example.” [Col. 1222D]

Louis, and those like them in empire and religion, were toward the Church—men who enriched with most ample gifts churches built either by themselves or by others, and did not wish to claim for themselves any lordship or jurisdiction over the clergy or the Church’s possessions; indeed, some of them prohibited by law anyone from claiming it. If, I say, we review these and compare them with the Ottos, Henrys, and others like them, we truly find that the face of royal dignity has greatly changed, [Col. 1222C] not only against the bishop, the lawful spouse of Rachel and Leah, but against the Lord Himself and His Christ, pressing His holy and free bride into forced service and reducing her to slavery.

Those earlier rulers enriched the churches; these plundered them. They carefully observed holy councils, in which the power of princes is excluded from the promotion of bishops, never intruding themselves into such matters, and indeed forbidding lesser princes to do so unless they were invited by the Church to assist in good works. Thus, after the election had been made, the imperial support came at the request of the Church of Milan

> [Note: Col. 1222D]
>
> From the Tripartite History: “Justinian, speaking to the people of Milan, said: ‘You know, being instructed by the divine words, what sort of man a bishop ought to be. And because it is fitting that he govern those subject to him not only by word but also by conduct, and display himself as an imitator of every virtue, having good conduct as the witness of his teaching, therefore appoint such a man to the episcopal seat, one to whom we also, who govern [Col. 1223D] the empire, may sincerely submit our heads, and whose admonitions, when we have sinned as human beings, we may receive as necessary remedies from a healing physician.’ When the emperor had said this, the synod asked that he himself should decide, since he was wise and pious. But he replied: ‘Such an election rests with you. For you, being empowered by divine grace and shining with that splendour, will be able to choose better.’
>
> “Likewise he said to Ambrose after his election: ‘Do not fear, for God, who chose you, will always help you; and I will always be your helper and defender, as befits my office.’”

so that they might obtain blessed Ambrose. Though elected bishop, he resisted so strongly [Col. 1222D] that the emperor’s help seemed necessary in the matter, since he was then not far from Milan—not in order that he might invest the man elected, but that he might incline the reluctant man by the weight of imperial authority [Col. 1223A] to acquiesce in the election made by God.

Likewise, after a canonical election of himself had been made, Saint Gregory resisted so strongly that he sent letters to the emperor Maurice asking him never to give assent to the Roman people concerning Gregory’s election—not because the emperor had power to annul the election, but because Gregory was planning flight and withdrawal. Therefore, under an emperor ruling then over both East and West, Gregory, wishing to make his flight and hiding-place safer, devised by his letters to induce and secure the emperor’s opposition, lest by withdrawing from the election he should offend one from whose vast empire he could not entirely depart [Col. 1223B]. The man of God, thinking this over, considered that he had found a useful plan. But “There is no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. 21:30). For those letters did not reach the emperor; nor could they have impeded the election if they had arrived. For among all those ancient and Catholic emperors none is found who attempted to annul or reconsider an election by clergy and people, or to claim for himself any authority in it, although at that time it was an established custom, when a bishop of the city of Rome had been elected, to send written notice of it to the emperor, so that, by his assent adding to the people’s favour, the election itself might be held more firmly established. Yet this was not always observed, but only [Col. 1223C] when utility seemed to require it, as in the election of this blessed man then being made, when, as we said of blessed Ambrose, the emperor’s aid and assent appeared necessary.

Blessed Pelagius, Gregory’s immediate predecessor, however, was ordained immediately after his election without consulting the emperor, because then there was no benefit or necessity for his election to be made known to the emperor, since no lay authority has any power in the election and promotion of pontiffs, as the sacred authority of the canons testifies. It prohibits not only bishops but even presbyters who obtain churches through lay power from being consecrated and ordained, so strongly that it judges the ordainers of such persons not only to be deprived of office but also [Col. 1223D] to stand under anathema.

> [Note: Col. 1224D] From the Council of Antioch, chapter 128: “If any presbyter or deacon obtains the Lord’s church through secular rank, let him be deposed from the clergy; and let both he and his ordainer be cut off in every way from communion and be under anathema, like Simon Magus by Peter.”

Hence the Eighth Synod forbids, under anathema, elections to be made through lay power; and that synod was held at the request and in the presence of the great emperor Basil. Yet neither Basil himself [Col. 1224A] nor the other Catholic emperors complained that this was done in contempt of them, because no deference was paid to their authority in the election of pontiffs. Rather, they are recorded to have embraced the institutions of the holy Fathers, and some of them confirmed those institutions with their own subscriptions after the subscriptions of the five patriarchs. For at that time laypersons in the Church had no authority to decree anything,

> [Note: Col. 1224D] From the synod of Pope Symmachus with 218 bishops: “It was not deemed fitting that laypersons should have any authority to enact anything in the Church; they have the necessity of following, not the authority of commanding.”

no authority to command, but the necessity of following and the humility of obedience.

When all this is considered, do we not in some measure perceive that the most gracious countenance of kings and other princes toward the likeness of Jacob, that is, the holy priesthood which God loved, once shone forth? But now, because sins demand it, not only [Col. 1224B] has the countenance of clemency in kings changed, but scarcely any bishop can be found in whom the likeness of Jacob, which God loves, appears in such a way that he strives to approach that ancient Jacob in special likeness: namely, crossing the Jordan—that is, the flowing world—by the staff of the cross or pastoral rule; feeding flocks of poor people rather than companies of soldiers; loving Rachel more than Leah, yet embracing both; departing with all his own from the house of Laban—that is, from the rulers of the world; conquering his brother Esau, who meets him armed, not by arms but by patience; and specially carrying out the other things which Jacob performed figuratively. If a bishop observed all these things as his office requires, he would truly order such a space between flock and flock [Col. 1224C] that there would not be, “as the people, so the priest” (Isa. 24:2); nor would a man be a priest or guardian of a flock merely by his own will—a man who, in his own house, gathers prey as though in a den of wolves rather than interceding for sins, together with priests and God’s ministers, between the porch and the altar within the cloistered enclosures.

## CHAPTER X. What goods, and on what grounds, may a ruler lawfully give to the Church? Ecclesiastical offices are to be administered by ecclesiastics, secular matters by secular persons.

Let these remarks concern estates, few of which the Church has received from kings in such a way that they come from the resources of the kingdom itself. For just as we do not doubt that any believer may make an offering to churches, whether from his inheritance or from another lawfully acquired possession, so no one doubts that kings may do the same; nor does anyone think such offerings should be refused by the Church.

[Col. 1225A] But from the resources of the kingdom, which are public property, the king ought not to make a private gift. Such property ought either to be kept whole for kings who will succeed in future or to be given with the counsel of the princes jointly consulted.

From private property, however, a private gift may be made both by kings and by other princes. Thus Emperor Constantine, if he gave anything to churches from the public resources of his kingdom, did so only after consulting the consuls and the other great men of the realm, and had charters concerning such grants drawn up with their approval, lest his transfer be called into question by posterity. But concerning things belonging privately to himself, he was so generous toward God’s Church that anyone wishing to read the book written at Rome concerning his donations will find him as [Col. 1225B] cheerful a giver in private matters as he was a faithful and prudent administrator in public ones. For he gave generously from his own property, while administering royal resources with the greatest discretion—not, as some accuse him, confusing and mingling ecclesiastical and royal matters, but honouring the Church from royal resources themselves.

For he neither planned that the pontiff should administer royal concerns nor rashly usurped anything for himself from ecclesiastical government. Hence at the Council of Nicaea, seated last after all the bishops, he presumed to judge nothing concerning priests’ causes; but humbling himself reverently in every way beneath the bishops’ dignity, he considered himself bound by their judgment.

This confusion, therefore, and the destructive abuse of certain succeeding emperors did not proceed from Constantine: namely, that kings and princes, of their own accord intruding into the promotion of bishops, abbots, and abbesses, should administer ecclesiastical affairs—matters which Constantine is not recorded to have administered. Again, who gave a bishop authority to gather soldiers for campaign and perform the other duties of a commander—authority which neither blessed Sylvester nor any other bishop had from Constantine or under Constantine? The origin of this confusion, then, did not begin with Constantine and Sylvester, because the former performed the king’s office and the latter the pontiff’s office so simply and sincerely that one did not refuse, fighting for peace, to command an army and take part in camps and wars; while the other, caring only for God’s ministers and Christ’s poor, not only diligently amassed spiritual gains for souls, but also most carefully provided for their need from the Church’s material resources [Col. 1225D].

Accordingly, blessed Pope Sylvester, wishing to leave his example to posterity and seeing that the common life among the clergy had then failed—a life which had no law concerning tithes, nor has any, except that held by the apostles, who distributed all that was offered according to each person’s need and left what remained to the poor—seeing all this, I say, Pope Sylvester, the first of all Roman pontiffs after the failure of the common life in which no one called anything his own, opposed the disease of greed that seeks its own advantage by such a decree, through which he might wrest the poor’s portion from the rapacious hands of bishops [Col. 1226A] and clerics seeking their own interests.

Accordingly, presiding over the assembly of bishops, with the agreement of all who were present, he established by a general decree that tithes and the other offerings should be divided into four portions. He assigned none of them to the pay of soldiers, because his concern was not military service but the Church; and he preferred to be surrounded by a crowd of poor people rather than by a troop of soldiers. Nor did he desire to be called the Lord of soldiers by their rendering him homage, but both to be called and to be the servant of Christ’s poor. For, knowing it to be written that “every high priest, taken from among men, is appointed for men in matters pertaining to God” (Heb. 5:1), he laid aside entirely matters belonging to the world and concerned himself only with [Col. 1226B] matters belonging to God. Dukedoms, counties, tolls, and coinage belong to the world. Tithes, first-fruits, and the other offerings belong to God. The former were anciently administered by the princes of the world, the latter by pontiffs, with this proviso and distinction: that neither should the pontiff preside over matters belonging to the world nor the prince over matters belonging to God; but each, content with his own right, should not exceed the limit divinely ordained.

The Apostle says that, after the death of the testator, no one makes further dispositions concerning a man’s testament (Heb. 9:16); and does anyone suppose that the testament confirmed by Christ’s blood may so easily be annulled and trampled underfoot that, contrary to the Gospel—which is Christ’s own New Testament—the sword forbidden to Peter should be restored anew to bishops’ hands? And that Matthew, called away from the toll-office, should be compelled to resume in a bishop the very office to which Matthew is nowhere said to have returned?

In saying this, I do not intend to persuade that a bishop should reject tolls and other things which undoubtedly belong to the king in such a way as to give offence to those who say that, if such things once given to churches are taken away from them on any pretext, sacrilege is committed, since the Church cannot lose a thing once received and made over to it by long possession. I do not answer them at present; but I simply affirm this: just as laymen can assert no rightful possession of tithes under any pretext of justice [Col. 1226D] or false colouring, because a tithe is beyond doubt an ecclesiastical possession, so those royal and military administrations cannot be governed by bishops without a definite apostasy from their order. For if Matthew had returned to the toll-office, he would have deserved to be reckoned not among the apostles but among apostates.

## CHAPTER XI. Saint Martin is proposed to bishops as an example: not a lover and associate of soldiers and nobles, but of the poor and monks.

Who indeed can blame—or rather, who is not compelled to praise—a bishop if he forbids laymen, under anathema, to possess tithes, and makes himself so wholly removed from public offices concerned with military affairs [Col. 1227A] that, with the ancient Martin, he strives rather to gather and care for the poor than, with the modern man of Mainz, soldiers? We know what Martin attained with his poor; we do not yet know what the man of Mainz will attain with his soldiers. Martin, poor and modest, enters heaven rich; the man of Mainz, neither poor nor modest, still walks upon the earth. Not all bishops can do what the man of Mainz can do; and, by God’s grace, they could do, if they wished, what Martin could do. Few can arrange with the man of Mainz such costly banquets as many princes and soldiers can and wish to attend. But all, by God’s grace, if they wish, can arrange with Martin the daily meals of themselves and their disciples with [Col. 1227B] such frugality that soldiers will prefer to stay away rather than attend their tables, while praising their virtue of thrift.

But what benefit is it to the man of Mainz that the people sit before him to eat and drink, and then rise up to play? Martin, however, greatly benefited in himself and his disciples from frugality joined with discernment; in strangers, from hospitality without complaint; in widows and all poor persons, from an affection of compassionate love and, according to his means, from the practical effect of generosity. The man of Mainz customarily comes to court with a troop of soldiers; Martin—the patron in whom the metropolitan church of Mainz glories—did not customarily act thus. But whenever necessity pressed him to make a journey to the king or elsewhere, he was content with the company of his poor and his disciples alone. [Col. 1227C] Neither he nor his companions rode on foaming horses; rather, they used cheap beasts only as needed for the journey—if, indeed, the distance to be travelled was so great that a mount was necessary because of bodily weakness.

> [Note: [Col. 1227D] Sulpicius, in the *Life of Saint Martin*: “After assuming the episcopate, what and how great a man Martin showed himself is not within our power to set forth. For he persevered most steadfastly as he had been before. The same humility was in his heart; the same plainness in his dress. Thus, full of authority and grace, he fulfilled the dignity of a bishop, yet did not abandon the purpose and virtue of a monk.”
>
> And shortly afterwards: “There were eighty disciples, trained after the example of their blessed Master. No one there possessed anything as his own; all things were brought into common. No buying or selling of anything was permitted, as is customary among most monks. No craft was practised there except copying manuscripts; and the younger members were assigned to this work, while the elders devoted themselves to prayer. Rarely did anyone leave his cell, except when they assembled at the place of prayer. All took food together after the hour of fasting. No one knew wine unless illness compelled it. Most wore garments of camel’s hair; softer clothing there was counted a fault. This must seem all the more remarkable because many among them were nobles, who, though brought up very differently, had constrained themselves to this humility and patience. We afterwards saw many of them become bishops. For what city or Church did not desire to have priests from Martin’s monastery?”]

Thus all bishops could more readily conform themselves to Martin, patron of the people of Mainz, than to the lord of Mainz himself, if, aided by grace, they wished to strive according to their ability. And what shall I say of Martin? Surely in Christ Jesus all could do what Peter could do—indeed, what Christ himself could do. Few in this age can possess sufficient silver and gold and furnish soldiers with sufficient maintenance. But who cannot, with Peter, have neither gold nor silver? Who [Col. 1227D] cannot, with Christ, do without soldier-servants, whom he himself chose not to have in this world? Certainly every bishop can—indeed, is obliged—to possess neither silver nor gold [Col. 1228A] if, amid so many perishing through hunger, thirst, and nakedness, he wishes to possess charity alone. Still more easily can he do without soldiers if he wishes to exercise the military service appointed for him by God. For soldiers voluntarily flee such a service; nor are they at all necessary for bishops to carry it out vigorously with religious brethren. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, to be waged with a material sword; but spiritual warfare must be continually undertaken against principalities and rulers of the world. In this warfare no soldier entangles himself in worldly affairs; no one gladly occupies himself in administering royal affairs. Rather, setting aside entirely dukedoms, counties, tolls, and other public functions, he fights not as one beating the air, and runs [Col. 1228B] not as one running uncertainly; and he follows the leadership not of modern men but of the ancients.

Since these matters stand thus, it is evident that the resources of churches are divided three ways: namely, into offerings of tithes, possessions of land, and royal and public functions. And concerning tithes there is no dispute that laymen possess them sacrilegiously. The preceding argument has shown that lands once offered for the use of the poor are defended by the Church under the protection of charity, so that no persecutor can justly take them away. But the Church is not greatly concerned to defend public functions; Rachel does not care to spread out her garment to conceal them, because spiritual men prefer to lack such things rather than become entangled, by occasion of them, in worldly affairs [Col. 1228C].

## CHAPTER XII. On the households, servants, and ministerials of churches, whose former condition was very different from the present. It is shameful that a bishop can scarcely appear anywhere except surrounded by soldiers.

Here I think something should be added concerning the households of churches, which we see treated far otherwise than the venerable limit prescribed by ancestral tradition. For the primitive Church was not accustomed to possess servants; rather, all who were converted, from whatever condition, living together as brothers, endeavoured to do this: that, just as the rulers of the Gentiles exercise lordship [Col. 1228D] over those whom they possess, so they themselves should not exercise lordship over anyone; but, serving one another through charity, should follow in the footsteps of him who came not to be served [Col. 1229A] but to serve. Yet although the apostolic Church had no slaves, the Apostle nevertheless teaches slaves to obey their carnal masters. Nor, when he had said, “Slaves, obey your masters,” did he add “carnal” idly (Eph. 6:5); rather, he wished to distinguish such masters from those who were perfect and wholly spiritual. For all converted persons made free those servants whom they had possessed before conversion itself. Nor was it yet customary to give servants to the Church, because the Church, exposed to many persecutions and as though prepared for battle, could not even possess lands; and therefore lands were not offered, but the price of lands was laid at the apostles’ feet. Yet, as Pope and martyr Urban testifies, lands subsequently began to be offered to churches for greater advantage, [Col. 1229B] so that, through the annual yield of these lands and the prudent provision of bishops, there might be more certain resources for common life. For cultivating the lands, tenant-farmers were offered together with the estates themselves. But ministerials who ranked above the condition of tenant-farmers were granted freedom by masters who converted themselves completely, as is read in the passions of Saint Sebastian and other martyrs concerning many persons. Such masters considered themselves not converted unless they first granted freedom to all their servants.

> [Note: [Col. 1229C] From the Passion of Sebastian the Martyr: “When Chromatius was asked whether he believed, he said, ‘I believe.’ Asked again whether he renounced all idols, he replied, ‘I renounce them.’ The priest then asked whether he renounced all sins. But he said: ‘You ought first to have asked this before I entered these halls of the heavenly King. Must I now put on again the garment of an unbaptized man, so that I may first forgive all against whom I am angry? Shall I return the written obligations to all my debtors? If I have violently taken anything from anyone, shall I command that it be restored in full? I have two concubines after my wife’s death: shall I endow them and give them to husbands? Shall I loosen the bonds of every servile, freeborn, private, and public obligation of my actions; and only then promise that I will renounce every diabolical sin and worldly pleasure?’ Polycarp the presbyter said to him: ‘The heavenly water will wash over you more blessedly when you have completed with all haste those things which you say you will do by your own decision.’”
>
> And shortly afterwards: “Chromatius received the newness of sacred baptism together with one thousand and forty souls from his household, of both sexes. He first released them all from the bond of servitude by granting manumission, and endowed them with excellent gifts, saying: ‘It is not fitting that those who are beginning to have God as Father should be slaves of a human being.’”]

For, while persecution reigned, the Church could scarcely protect either lands or tenant-farmers; and therefore the saints preferred that their servants be granted freedom rather than given to churches.

But after persecution had ceased and peace and liberty for the churches had been confirmed by Constantine, the most Christian emperor, [Col. 1229C] the holy Church of God was so greatly exalted that, with the fullest liberty, it possessed not only servants and tenant-farmers but also protected its freedmen, by the strength of great authority, against [Col. 1230A] every unjust violence of the world.

> [Note: [Col. 1229D]
>
> From the Decrees of Pope Miltiades, chapter 3: “Finally, kings, governors, and magistrates not only bestowed adjacent properties, but themselves also gave their own possessions throughout all the kingdoms of the earth, from which those who possessed nothing in the world might be maintained; churches might be built and restored; and they granted, without necessity, provisions for the servants who duly serve God and his Church.”
>
> From the sayings of the same: “Among them, the most religious man Constantine, having first openly embraced the faith of truth, gave permission throughout the whole world for those living under his rule not merely to become Christians, but also decreed that churches should be built and estates granted. Finally, this same aforesaid prince established immense gifts and the construction of the first church at the seat of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to such an extent that he left the imperial seat, over which Roman princes also presided, and granted it for the benefit of blessed Peter and his successors.”
>
> [Col. 1230D] Council of Agde, chapter 28: “Let the Church, if necessary, protect freed persons lawfully made free by their masters; but if anyone should wish or presume to deprive them of a hearing, or to strip them of their possessions, let him be excluded from the Church.”
>
> Council of Toledo, chapter 73: “Freed persons, however they have been manumitted and who are commended to the Church’s protection, are, as the rules of the ancient Fathers have established, to be protected by priestly defence from the insolence of any person, whether in their state of freedom or in the danger in which they are known to be.”
>
> *Life of Blessed Gregory*, book III, chapter 46: “Gregory nevertheless defended the liberty of every person against judicial insolence with frequent protests.”
>
> From the Council of Orange, chapter 6: “If anyone attempts to reduce into slavery, subjection, or tenant status persons manumitted by the Church or commended to the Church by testament, he shall be restrained by ecclesiastical discipline.”]

It consequently happened that, when great princes were converted, their ministerial servants preferred to be entrusted to the Church’s protection rather than be granted freedom altogether. From that time the Church began to have ministerials whom it protected—not persons by whom it was protected, as some ignorant of history imagine. They think these men were given to the Church so that bishops might feed them from the resources of the poor and keep as many of them as they could constantly with them. For they do not think a bishop can take luncheon or supper honourably if a multitude of soldiers happens to be absent and only brethren devoted to frugality and Christ’s poor are present. They dream this because they do not know what was done or why it was done [Col. 1230B]. Soldiers did not come under the Church’s right and power in order to become its plunderers, as we see happening daily. For while bishops serve them out of the Church’s goods, nothing is reserved for widows and orphans.

What shall we say to this? Certainly, if pure and undefiled religion before God the Father is this—“to visit widows and orphans in their affliction” (Jas. 1:27)—then it is clearly irreligion and impurity to feed soldiers from their resources. Therefore whoever does this, even if he now appears honourable and religious to men, will stand dishonoured and stained at the final judgment. There, I think, Augustine will stand more safely—or rather, as I more strongly believe, he will sit in judgment over many bishops and condemn them by comparison with himself [Col. 1230C], so much the nearer to the apostles as he followed the apostles’ rule with his clerics. That poor and modest Martin will also sit there. Then he certainly will not regret having once been badly treated by soldiers; [Col. 1231A] yet he is never recorded to have been surrounded by them after admitting them into his service. For when this poor man, with his fellow poor, was once travelling in his usual way—not imperially but episcopally—he was beaten and badly treated by soldiers whom he met on the road. He had no retainers fighting for him; nor could such severe blows compel him afterwards to travel with troops of soldiers.

Certainly, we do not condemn it if a bishop, where he has reason to suspect evil persons, sometimes receives armed escorts from a prince—for Paul the Apostle is recorded to have done this—not so that he himself may harm his enemies, but so that he may not be harmed by them. They had bound themselves by oath not to take food until they had killed Paul. But the tribune, not Paul, provided wages for those escorts [Col. 1231B], because only the poor and those living in common were supported from the collections of the churches (Acts 23:12). Yet I think that, if soldiers were to be fed from the collections, they could more rightly be supplied to no one than to Paul’s escorts: for through his exertions the goods of the poor had been collected through many churches, as his own letters testify. Thus, if it can be done without burdening the poor and the churches, and a bishop receives armed escorts from one of the princes along a route he considers dangerous, he should not immediately be called a leader of soldiers. For to lead soldiers—which no apostle but Judas is recorded to have done—is one thing; to be escorted by soldiers, as Paul the Apostle was, is another.

[Col. 1231C] But it will be far more glorious for a bishop if, placing his confidence not in man but in the Lord, he says with blessed Martin: “Protected by the sign of the cross, not by shield or helmet, I shall safely penetrate the ranks of the enemy.” For the Apostle affirms: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God for the overthrowing of strongholds, destroying counsels and every lofty thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of Christ” (2 Cor. 10:4–5).

## CHAPTER XIII. Let bishops conduct themselves after the example of Saint Lawrence the Martyr: not as masters of ecclesiastical goods, devoted to feeding soldiers, but as their stewards, benevolent toward the poor.

With such weapons Peter conquered Rome, and the humble fisherman gained victory over the city victorious over the world [Col. 1231D]. After the apostles this armour also existed among holy bishops, especially among those whose purpose and care concerned the poor more than feeding soldiers. By it Pope Leo triumphed over King Attila when, as the history of the Lombards relates, the tyrant dared neither to afflict the pontiff with a harsh word nor to refuse him the requested peace. For, as Attila himself afterwards disclosed to his companions, at the pontiff’s approach he was so moved by a certain terrifying vision that there should be no doubt that angelic ministry was present with the holy pontiff; and that the proud king was more powerfully frightened than any proud prince now would be frightened [Col. 1232A] if a bishop approached him with soldier-servants. For these soldiers, called servants, desire bishops to serve them so thoroughly that they are feared more than they fear, because they imagine themselves to be bishops’ defenders, believing that the bishop will be utterly ruined if his servants withdraw from him. Hence they also judge the Church’s resources to be expended upon them as though by right, unaware that they are owed to Christ’s poor to such a degree that whoever despoils the poor—and indeed Christ in the poor—in order to endow soldiers commits sacrilege.

Understanding this, the distinguished martyr Lawrence chose to suffer the soldiers’ torture on the gridiron rather than give them the Church’s resources.

But someone says: The Church’s resources were not given to Lawrence, but entrusted to him by Blessed Sixtus; therefore he was not permitted to give them away at his own discretion, but had to preserve a trustee’s fidelity toward his master. We entirely agree, because the Church’s property was entrusted to Lawrence. But is not the Church’s property likewise entrusted to a bishop or priest when he is ordained pastor for the purpose of being a faithful and prudent steward toward the poor, not a lavish donor toward soldiers? Therefore, just as with Lawrence, the Church’s resources are not given to a bishop as his own property but entrusted to him as another’s.

This is that “other’s property” of which the Lord says: “If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?” (Luke 16:12). For he speaks to those to whom he had earlier said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for [Col. 1232C] theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 6:3). To those, therefore, for whom the kingdom was their own, he threatens that the kingdom itself will be taken away if they have not faithfully administered what belongs to another. For whether in God’s word or in ecclesiastical maintenance, a bishop possesses nothing except what belongs to another. If he faithfully administers it to those to whom it is owed, he will possess the kingdom of God as his own in return for that other’s property. But if he is not faithful in what belongs to another, no one will give him the kingdom which might have been his own.

Lawrence was faithful in this other’s property because “he scattered abroad and gave to the poor”—to the poor, I say, not to soldiers—although he was tortured in many astonishing ways: not, as the other martyrs were, in order that he might deny the faith, but in order that he might give the goods of the poor to soldiers. Yet [Col. 1232D] the holy martyr understood through the Holy Spirit that to deny Christ’s faith and to prove unfaithful in what Christ had entrusted were equivalent in sin. For everyone who becomes unfaithful in what Christ has entrusted is proved to have denied the faith of Christ.

There is therefore no difference between the cause of suffering in this martyr and in the other martyrs who died for Christ’s faith, except that he was pressed toward shipwreck of faith all the more perilously because he was tempted concerning that faith more secretly. For he was not merely told, “Deny the faith,” but also, “Hand over the treasure.” If he had betrayed the Church’s treasures to soldiers, then, having become unfaithful in what belonged to another, he would altogether have lost the treasure of faith which was his own. Therefore he chose, by enduring the soldiers’ tortures, to remain Christ’s servant rather than conciliate soldier-servants from the Church’s treasure [Col. 1233A]. He would not, though it might have seemed possible to do so without loss of faith, appease his raging torturers with a little money while not verbally denying the faith.

O perilous temptation! O deceitful tongue of the serpent!
