How many stewards of churches in this age you make suffer shipwreck concerning Christ’s faith: they are not compelled by tortures verbally to deny the faith, but are persuaded by gifts and soldiers’ false promises not to keep faith in what Christ has entrusted, as if it were a lesser matter not to keep faith with Christ than to deny Christ’s faith! O how much more tolerable, between two evils, it would be to deny Christ with fearful Peter in words than to betray him with impious Judas under a kiss of peace [Col. 1233B]! For bishops who hand over the Church’s goods to soldiers put forward a kind of kiss of peace: they receive soldiers into homage under a kiss of peace, and maintain those received under the pretext of peace, as though they could have no peace unless their servants and princes surrounded them. But by God’s just judgment it comes about that they suffer worse things from no one than from those very persons to whom they distribute the Church’s goods—to whom, more plainly speaking, they hand over Christ himself in his members to be crucified. For when Christ’s poor person is afflicted by hunger and nakedness on account of soldiers, Christ is tortured in the poor person and in some sense crucified.

Understanding this, Blessed Lawrence preferred [Col. 1233C] to be tortured by soldiers rather than assist those soldiers in torturing Christ’s poor. Thus he triumphed in Christ’s faith all the more gloriously because he was tempted to lose that faith more secretly and dangerously. He could, under a plausible appearance of prudence, have given away the treasures to mitigate the rage of princes and have sought for himself and the other faithful a kind of peace in this way—as many now do who distribute ecclesiastical goods to servants and princes, ostensibly to purchase peace for themselves and their own. But the blessed martyr sought peace in no such fashion, either for himself or for the other confessors, because he saw that poison lay hidden beneath the appearance of honey. Therefore, because he could have transgressed under the appearance of securing peace but did not transgress, because he could have done evil but did not, the whole Church triumphs more joyfully in [Col. 1233D] his praise, exults more gladly, and celebrates his feast more universally than it does, after the apostles, that of any martyr who openly struggled and conquered solely for the faith. It is fitting that, inasmuch as the cause of faith in this martyr’s struggle was more hidden and his victory rarer, his feast should be more illustrious throughout the whole world: as a testimony to those who do not follow the martyr, and as an aid to those who faithfully follow his example, distributing ecclesiastical resources only to those to whom the sacred canons command them to be distributed.

## CHAPTER XIV. The ancient sacred canons grant no portion of ecclesiastical goods to soldier-ministerials or wealthy clerics.

[Col. 1234A]

There, I think, no portion of the Church’s goods is assigned to the pay of soldiers; yet bishops furnish them with a larger share of goods offered to God than they furnish to widows and other needy persons, who either have no consolation in this world with Lazarus or, with Peter, refuse to have it. To these two kinds of poor persons the entire ecclesiastical estate is owed, except the fourth part which is allotted to the fabric and maintenance of churches.

Since, therefore, Church maintenance is owed only to those who, with Lazarus, have nothing, or who, with Peter, have chosen to have nothing, in which class of these poor are we to place servants, soldiers, and clerics who possess property of their own? They do not belong with Lazarus, because they have their consolation. They differ greatly from Peter, because they cling tenaciously to what they possess and greedily seek what they do not possess. Moreover, whenever soldiers or those half-clerics give something from their own resources, they spend it not so generously and cheerfully upon afflicted poor persons as upon those very afflictors of the poor. Nor is this surprising, since they themselves are the poor’s afflictors and, so far as lies in them, crucifiers of Christ himself.

If the whole series of canons is reviewed, no share of Church goods is assigned to servants, soldiers, or wealthy clerics. Nowhere in the decretal letters of Roman pontiffs, nowhere in the sayings of the holy Fathers, is this approved: that either a soldier [Col. 1234C] who is a servant or a cleric wealthy from his own property should be supported by the Church’s maintenance. Nor should anyone be moved by the fact that Blessed Gregory permitted a bishop to give a portion of maintenance to English clerics who possessed their own property (see ch. 3, l.). He expressly indicated that they were neither to be supported within the congregation nor admitted to sacred orders. This, too, we could and ought to tolerate, if proprietary clerics were willing to serve in the holy Church of God outside sacred orders, within or below the rank of acolytes, and did not presume to claim the care of souls or sacred orders before renouncing property and submitting their necks to the yoke of the apostolic rule. Then they would be ordained in proper order, provided that diligent examination showed them not to be bigamists, husbands of widows or repudiated women, or stained by any offence which the canons hold to exclude men from sacred orders [Col. 1234D].

If, then, they approached orders in this way, it could sufficiently be tolerated that, remaining outside the congregation and outside sacred orders, they should receive outside the stipends owed to their functions, although those who share in the Church’s goods cannot possess their own goods without sin. For, as Prosper testifies, only those who receive nothing from the Church possess their own goods without sin. Those, however, who wish to possess Church maintenance together with their own goods do indeed commit a blameworthy act; but, under the permission of Saint Gregory, this is in some manner tolerable [Col. 1235A] if, receiving their maintenance outside, they neither disturb the peace of brethren living in common nor presume the administration of sacred order.

> [Note: [Col. 1233] From the *Life of Saint Gregory*, book II, chapter 11: “Gregory, a most prudent ruler, having removed secular persons from his household, chose as his closest counsellors and associates the most prudent clerics: among them Peter the deacon, Paterius likewise a notary, John the defender; and among monks he chose the holiest as his intimate companions. With them Gregory” (chapter 12) “spent day and night, leaving aside neither monastic perfection in the palace nor pontifical discipline in the Church. Most devout monks were everywhere seen attached to the pontiff together with the most learned clerics; and common life prevailed among the several professions, so that the Church of Rome under Gregory was such as Luke records it to have been under the apostles, and Philo under Mark the Evangelist at Alexandria” (chapter 14). “For profound pontifical deliberations, wise men rather than powerful men were summoned; humble philosophy, inwardly investigating by rational and skilful arguments what ought preferably or most especially to be followed in each matter, while wealthy idleness—hateful to the wise—remained despised” (chapter 15). “No layman administered any ministry of the palace or any ecclesiastical patrimony; rather, ecclesiastical men likewise undertook all duties of ecclesiastical jurisdiction, laymen being assigned solely to military service with arms or to the continual care of lands.”]

We therefore find that, in a certain measure, clerics possessing property of their own may be supported by the Church; but nowhere do we find soldier-servants so commended in the Fathers’ writings that they ought to be endowed from Church goods. For holy pontiffs, successors of the apostles and predecessors of modern men, did not have soldier-servants as attendants, but tried chamberlains chosen from clerics and monks. Nor did they set laymen over the Church’s resources, but chose stewards or vice-domini from the clergy. Thus they entrusted only clerics with the administration of the goods of the poor, because they did not wish to transgress the bounds of the Fathers [Col. 1235B], who permit even highly religious laymen nothing in the administration of Church offerings. But now, contrary to the Fathers’ custom, we see lay vice-domini, superintendents over the goods of the poor, and bishops’ servants; and at their banquets we grieve that the noise of a crowd of soldiers and shield-bearers resounds more than anything from the Fathers’ writings. Discussions of the Fathers and soldiers’ chatter cannot occupy the same space; and perhaps the soldier-servants would be offended if the reader’s voice sounded a little too loudly at table.

Avoiding this evil with the greatest discernment, Blessed Augustine took care to admit to his frugal table such guests as could contribute reading and holy discussion [Col. 1235C]. He did not want idle chatter at his table and utterly abhorred detraction from absent persons. So that this might be known to all who came to his table, and no one might loosen his tongue in his presence to slander absentees, he caused these verses to be inscribed on his table:

> Whoever delights in gnawing the life of the absent with evil speech  
> should know himself unworthy of this table.

And because he either saw in his own time—or the Spirit speaking through him foresaw in ours—the brief little readings which at meals are begun and ended in a single breath [Col. 1236A], he gave his followers a rule, indicating that the word of edification should begin with bodily refreshment and end with the same steadfastness.

> [Note: [Col. 1236C]
>
> Augustine, in the *Rule for Clerics*: “Subdue your flesh by fasts and abstinence, so far as health permits.” And shortly afterwards: “When you come to table, listen without tumult or dispute, from the time you sit down until you rise, to what is customarily read to you. Let not your throats alone take food, but let your ears also hunger for the word of God.”
>
> [Col. 1236D] Gregory writes to Natalis, bishop of Salona: “From many persons coming from your city, dearest brother, I have learned that, having abandoned pastoral care, you are occupied only with banquets. I would not believe this report unless the evidence of your deeds confirmed it,” etc.
>
> Likewise, to the same man, when he excused himself in writing: “Your Holiness rightly praises in your letters banquets held with the purpose of exercising charity. Yet it must be understood that they genuinely proceed from charity only when no absent person’s life is attacked in them, no one is reproved in mockery, and not empty tales of worldly affairs but words of sacred reading are heard; when no more is given to the belly than necessity requires, but only its weakness is restored, so that it may serve in the practice of virtue. If you do these things in your banquets, I acknowledge that you are teachers of abstinent persons.”]

Would that reading were pleasing to soldiers and shield-bearers, or that bishops could somehow be persuaded to withdraw with Jesus from the crowd and, rejecting the detestable abuse of modern times, to observe the holy laws and customs of the Fathers.

Then certainly they would not attach soldiers to themselves as retainers at the cost of their souls’ salvation; but would administer those persons’ ministerial freedom with ecclesiastical firmness, so that the property of the poor should by no means be divided among them. But now not only are estates handed over to soldiers; but, what is more detestable, the tenants of the Church themselves are oppressed under soldiers with a heavier servitude than if they were those soldiers’ own slaves. Their oppression, therefore, will all recoil upon the heads of those men. For what business is it of theirs to furnish the servants of the Church to soldiers, from whom the ministers of the Churches ought to receive either their due service or, in place of service, a rent that does not burden them excessively? For this alone is known to be the purpose for which they were offered to the Churches: that they might be oppressed less under the dominion of the Church than under that of a man—not that soldiers might be granted benefices from them.

Indeed, the prelates of Churches may establish certain mutual supports from among their household dependants; that is, among the servants of the Church, they may cause one to assist another when an imposed office cannot suitably be administered by one person without help. Thus peasants are subject to a steward, not as a benefice, but as a necessary assistance for his administration. Thus the *vicedominus* [chief household administrator] has stewards subject to him, as persons very necessary for assisting his ministry. Thus also servants of Churches may be assigned to others occupied in ecclesiastical duties for this very purpose, [Col. 1237A] that those who are subject to persons set over them may strive faithfully to assist them. Yet if those who have been placed over some such office lose that office, the servants lent to them for assistance owe them no service.

## CHAPTER XV. The households and estates of Churches are not to be entrusted or granted to soldiers and other secular officials, but to upright clerics.

Moreover, in order that ecclesiastical offices might be administered more fittingly, and that the servants of Churches might not be oppressed beyond measure, the holy Fathers rightly decreed—as is found in the acts of councils—that no lay person should be placed over such offices as entail the subordination of stewards and estates.

> [Note: [Col. 1237B]  
> From the *Life of St. Gregory*, Book II, chapter 15: “No layman administered any service of the palace or ecclesiastical patrimony; rather, men of the Church themselves undertook all offices belonging to ecclesiastical jurisdiction, while laymen were assigned exclusively to military service with arms [Col. 1237C] or to the continual care of fields.”
>
> Likewise Gregory, writing among other matters to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, says: “It has been reported to us that, having entrusted the care of your patrimony to certain laymen, they were afterwards detected in plundering the peasants and thereby in oppressing them. If this is so, it is fitting that the matter be strictly investigated by us, and that the case between them and the peasants of your Church be examined more carefully; and that, should any fraud be found in them, they be compelled to make restitution, with the penalty prescribed by law. But henceforth your brotherhood must take care that the property of any Church not be entrusted to secular men who live outside your rule, but to clerics tested in your own service; so that, if any wickedness should be found in them, you may be able, as with subjects, to correct what has unlawfully been done. Their office, indeed, which is appropriate to their manner of life among you, ought rather to bind them than excuse them.”
>
> Likewise, *Life of St. Gregory*, Book II, chapter 54: “He used to direct that each several office belonging to ecclesiastical jurisdiction be entrusted separately to individual persons, maintaining that, just as we have many members in one body, yet all members do not have the same function, so in the body of the Church, according to the true saying of Paul, in one and the same Spirit this office should be conferred on one person and that entrusted to another. Nor should the offices of two matters be committed at one time to a single person, however experienced; for if the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? For just as the diversity of members, through their different functions, both preserves the strength of the body and displays its beauty, so also the diversity of persons distributed among different offices manifests both the strength and the venerable antiquity of the holy Church of God. And just as it is unbecoming for one member in the human body to perform another’s function, so it is surely harmful and at the same time most shameful if the individual ministries of affairs are not distributed among an equal number of persons. Hence he frequently imposed the reins of restraint upon certain ambitious persons—as may be found in his letters, which I have omitted for brevity’s sake. Thus, among other instructions, he commands the subdeacon Anthemius concerning Bishop Paschasius, who by himself remained both chief household administrator and *vicedominus*: ‘We wish our brother Paschasius to appoint for himself both a *vicedominus* and a chief household administrator, so that he may be capable and prepared for arriving guests or for cases that arise. But if you observe him to be negligent, or slow to carry out what we have said, his whole clergy must be summoned, so that by common counsel they may choose persons fit to be appointed to the matters we have mentioned.’”]

[Col. 1237B] This practice descends from the Acts of the Apostles, where it is clear that the provision of tables was entrusted to deacons alone. It is also proved by the fact that the sacred canons direct that the *oeconomus*, whom we call the *vicedominus*, be chosen from the clergy; they impose upon him the whole administration, for carrying out which he has no need of soldiers, because he will receive the revenues of estates better from stewards than from soldiers placed in command.

> [Note: [Col. 1238C] From the *Life of St. Gregory*, chapter 53: “For the preservation of sacred religion and the vigorous administration of the goods of the poor, Gregory called industrious men of his Church to be directors of its patrimonies throughout the various provinces: among them the deacon Cyprian, the notary Pantaleon, the subdeacon Anthemius, and the priest Candidus. This most prudent Father Gregory judged that these arrangements ought to be observed perpetually not only in the Roman Church but also throughout the various Churches.”]

Otherwise, if, contrary to the judgments of the Fathers, a soldier is placed over ecclesiastical resources, the household of the Church [Col. 1238A] will be oppressed beyond measure by military violence and compelled to serve the soldiers’ private uses, though one once offered to the Church ought to remain only in the Church’s service.

No servant of a Church ought, nor can, be consigned by a bishop to that service unless he wishes to be devoted to the observance of religion, whether among clerics or among monks. For then, as blessed Gregory says, lest bishops be found to deny something to Him whose are all things, a bishop may, for the sake of pursuing religious life, free someone of taxable or tenant status from the due payment or service owed to the Church.

This freedom, as I have said, with the permission and counsel of St. Gregory, ought not to be denied by bishops, [Col. 1238B] abbots, and other prelates of Churches to all servants of the Church; but neither ought it to be granted to all. The same blessed man clearly indicates in one of his decretal enactments the discernment by which this should be done.

> [Note: [Col. 1238D] “St. Gregory the pope, seated before the most sacred body of the blessed apostle Peter with all the bishops and priests of the Roman Church, while the deacons and all the clergy stood by, said: ‘We know that many from the household of the Church hasten to the service of almighty God, so that, freed from human servitude, they may live in monasteries in the divine service. If we release them indiscriminately, we provide everyone with an opportunity to flee the dominion of ecclesiastical jurisdiction. But if we carelessly retain those hastening to the service of almighty God, we are found to deny something to Him who gave all things. Therefore it is necessary that whoever wishes to turn from the bond of ecclesiastical service to the service of God should first be tested while remaining in lay dress; and, if his character and conduct bear witness to his good desire, he should be permitted without any hindrance to enter a monastery for almighty God, and depart free from human service, since he desires to undertake a stricter servitude in divine obedience.’”]

Therefore, just as nothing is taken from God in this matter, but what has been offered is offered to Him more abundantly and more purely when a servant of the Church is freed from owed service in order to be subjected to the stricter observance of religion, so in truth the holy Church of God is despoiled by bishops [Col. 1239A] and other prelates when they grant servants of Churches to soldiers, to be afflicted and constrained by those soldiers far more harshly than any soldier’s own hereditary slave.

## CHAPTER XVI. Every effort must be made to reclaim the possessions of Churches from secular hands. Therefore bishops should set Abraham before themselves as an example, and clerics his armed household servants.

O holy Church of God, one simple dove: what advantage is it to your servants given to you that you do not tear them with your own claws, unless you stretch out your wings to protect them and to snatch them from the talons of kites? For soldiers, like certain kites and vultures, tear and devour your own. And bishops, who have placed them beneath those talons, think that they have done something lawful. But because you are called a dove, which does not cease to groan among your own for your own, heed the groans of the poor who are oppressed by soldiers; deliver both them and the bishops who betray them; rouse your bridegroom, the heavenly King, for the liberation of your people, so that with his two-edged sword he may distinguish ecclesiastical things from royal and secular things, lest, through their intermixture and confusion, the building of his house be hindered—a building known to have long been delayed by this confusion.

Let clerics be under bishops like the armed household servants of Abraham, father of all believers, in former times (Gen. XIV, 14), upon whom this sole military duty is imposed: that ecclesiastical property and household may be rescued from the hands of kings [Col. 1239C] and soldiers, who have long held the Church captive while she dwells with Lot in the plain and remains among Nicolaitan clerics as though among the Sodomites themselves. But now, at last, let armed household servants—not men taken from royal courts, or rather forced in by kings themselves, but faithful members of Abraham’s household, found among good canons or monks and appointed by God for this warfare when they were canonically ordained as rulers of Churches—let such household servants, I say, manfully pursue the kings and soldiers who hold the Church captive and slay them with the sword of the Holy Spirit. Thus, rescuing also those Sodomite clerics—that is, the Nicolaitans—who are in distress, together with all the furnishings of the Church, they may attain such a victory that nothing may be withheld from the offerings and tithes of Churches which is not faithfully offered to the true Melchizedek through the bishop, as through Abraham, the steward.

> [Note: [Col. 1239D] From the First Book of Ezra, chapter VII: “For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, to do it, and to teach precept and judgment in Israel.” Likewise: “I, King Artaxerxes, have established and decreed that everything pertaining to the worship of the God of heaven be diligently supplied in the house of the God of heaven, lest perhaps he be angry against the kingdom of the king and his sons. We also make known to you that you have no authority to impose tax, tribute, or provisions upon any of the priests and Levites, [Col. 1240D] singers, gatekeepers, Nethinim, and ministers of this house of God. But you, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God which is in your hand, appoint judges to judge all the people who are beyond the river, namely those who know the law of your God; and freely teach the ignorant as well.”]

For if, according to the judgment of blessed Jerome, the best steward is one who reserves nothing for himself out of all things, Abraham most plainly prefigured such a steward when, after liberating all by his own and his followers’ effort, [Col. 1240A] he made it his concern to shake his hands clean, so that, as sacred history relates, he allowed not even a thread of a covering nor a sandal-strap (Gen. XIV, 23) from these things to come to his own use.

Let the bishop, therefore, imitate him, reserving nothing for himself from all things. Nor should he himself take away the shares of the clerics labouring with him, nor leave them in secular hands. For Abraham also most clearly foreshadowed this when he neither left with strangers the shares of the men who had laboured with him in war nor applied them to his own use, but, before Melchizedek the priest and king, judged that they should be given to those whose valour in battle had been tested. But those who remained at home and were not armed for battle [Col. 1240B] received nothing from all these things and took no part in those sacred and mystical offerings in which bread and wine were offered. For no one, unless armed and enrolled in Christ’s army, either deserves to receive a stipend from the Church or lawfully performs priestly and Levitical ministry. This belongs only to those who have renounced the world, to whom bread of the Lord’s body and the cup of Christ’s life-giving blood are offered by the King and Priest himself. Let such persons, then, by every means be assigned to this purpose, so that those may be nourished by the sacred provisions of Churches who do not wish to remain in their own homes, but, with faithful Abraham—that is, a valiant bishop—wish to fight armed against the enemies.

Truly true is the apostolic saying that the word [Col. 1240C] of God is living and effective, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit (Heb. IV, 12). For this sword, by distinguishing secular from spiritual things—as though dividing soul from spirit—now establishes, in the portrait it gives, such a bishop with his clerics that I seem to see in him faithful Abraham with his armed household servants. A faithful bishop attended by such men will easily triumph over the realm of the four passions, or the fourfold world. Attended by them, and spiritually tasting the sacrifice of bread and wine according to the order of Melchizedek, he will minister all the tithes to him. And, that he may be found wholly faithful and like faithful Abraham, let him shake his hands free from gifts offered to him, refusing everything even to a thread of a covering.

[Col. 1240D] For what is indicated by the fact that faithful Abraham, even after his labours had been completed, neither asked for a gift nor consented to receive one freely and spontaneously offered, considering lest any Sodomite or Gomorrite might say, “I have made Abraham rich” (Gen. XIV, 23)? What, I say, is thereby indicated except that, in order to avoid simony and preserve the honour of a bishop’s reputation, his hands should be shaken completely free [Col. 1241A] from every gift? For the prophet, calling blessed the man who shakes his hands free from a gift, did not without reason preface it with “from every” (Isa. XXXIII, 15), since a great distinction may be observed among gifts themselves.

## CHAPTER XVII. Let bishops, who are in the house and building of God both certain pillars and pictures, keep their hands from gifts of every kind.

For in every administration of a spiritual benefit, three kinds of gifts commonly tempt the mind of the administrator; and they may be distinguished from one another in this way. One is a due gift; another an undue gift; another a gift contrary to duty. A due gift is one offered lawfully. An undue gift [Col. 1241B] is one offered freely. A gift contrary to duty is one offered as a purchase. The people offer tithes and the other stipends of those who serve God as a legal obligation, because the Law says, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading grain” (I Cor. IX, 9), which the Apostle affirms should be understood of preachers. Paul shook his hands free even from such a due and lawful gift when, preaching to the Corinthians, he refused to exercise the authority due to him. Something not owed by law is also often offered gratuitously and freely, voluntarily supplied to one neither asking nor needing it. Thus Naaman the Syrian freely and generously offered the prophet Elisha a voluntary gift; and the holy prophet, although the offering was praiseworthy, more praiseworthily refused it, because he preferred [Col. 1241C] to shake his hands free even from gifts actually offered than to give, through himself, an occasion for a bad example (IV Kings V, 15 ff.).

But when someone has a case to be examined in court, whether unjust or just, whatever he offers to judges and managers of cases he offers as a purchase, because he intends to buy the judge—whether for a just cause, which is an evil nevertheless tolerable, or in order to prosecute an unjust cause according to his own will, which is an intolerable evil. For now it is tolerated, in some fashion, that a judge or advocate should be bought for a just cause; but since transactions must not be conducted in the house of the Lord, I believe that, when the Lord comes, neither buyer nor seller will be able to defend himself from his scourge even by means of a just cause, because in his house they were not afraid [Col. 1241D] to trade while pursuing what was just unjustly. For it pleases God far more that we should sometimes allow justice to be oppressed together with our own suffering than that we should commit injustice as though to liberate justice. Certainly it is better and more salutary that we ourselves should be unjustly oppressed with Christ by the unjust than that we should be found, against Christ, to be traders in his house.

Let someone, then, have a cause however just; let him come, if he wishes, to Rome itself, the examiner of causes. Yet if he prosecutes his cause by gifts, he will be received not by Simon the Great but by Simon Magus; nor will he be his companion in blessing, but in curse. For Peter is still crucified in Rome, because every good son of that Church and true disciple of Peter, canonically promoted in the house of Peter either to the episcopate or to the cardinalate—and by God’s grace their number here is not small—such a man, I say, is grievously afflicted; and in him Peter himself is crucified by Simon Magus and his disciples whenever he sees not even a just cause handled without gifts, though all ought to support it freely.

Therefore whoever offers a gift as a purchase for any spiritual grace [Col. 1242B] will not find Peter receiving it, but shaking his hands so forcefully free from this gift as to say: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed for a price” (Acts VIII, 20). Let the bishop, therefore, refuse with Elisha a gift freely offered, so that he may enjoy a more honourable reputation even among outsiders. Let him also sometimes set aside with Paul a gift legally owed to him, so that he may gain more people. But let him strongly shake his hands free with Peter from a gift offered as a purchase, so that, even if he receives a gift in a just cause, he may remain far removed from the lot of those concerning whom it is written: “Their right hand is full of gifts” (Ps. XXV, 10).

There is also a person who carries a gift in both left hand and right, because, whether the cause be unjust or just, he does not refuse the gift offered him. But the one who loves and demands a gift only in a just cause has his right hand full of gifts. For just as it is highly blameworthy to carry a gift in both left hand and right, so it is highly praiseworthy to raise both hands in holy prayers shaken and emptied of gifts, so that we may say with the Psalmist: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells. Do not destroy my soul with the wicked, nor my life with men of blood, in whose hands are iniquities; their right hand is full of gifts” (ibid., 8, 10).

> [Note: [Col. 1241D] *Life of St. Gregory*, Book III, chapter 24: “Gregory rejected with all the effort of his mind, as a kind of pestilential burden, the customs of payments or gifts (*xenia*) received from his bishops.” Likewise chapter 27: [Col. 1242D] “It is no wonder that this most generous pontiff accepted no customary payments and no gifts from his suffragans, since he himself supplied them most cheerfully with whatever necessities they seemed to require.”]

Since this virtue of despising gifts belongs to [Col. 1242D] the beauty of the house of God, which the Psalmist confesses that he loved, let this beauty be so fitted to our own building as well, that the bishop, the wise architect of this building, constructing upon the sole rock of truth and not upon the mist of custom, keeps every kind of gift and every form of commerce far away, lest, through neglecting the beauty of God’s house, he lay an ugly colouring over its solid walls. At one time the pillars support this building; at another the pictures provide its fitting adornment. If a pillar is moved, [Col. 1243A] the whole structure threatens ruin. If a picture is erased, the eye of those looking upon it is greatly offended.

> [Note: [Col. 1243D] Pope Alexander: “A church which is known to have been consecrated by a bargain over a price—or, more truly stated, execrated [Col. 1244D]—must in no way be regarded as a church.”]

Peter, therefore, resting upon the most solid rock and striving to support God’s building, could not be moved or bent by a gift offered to him, because he himself was also a most firm and upright pillar; and he established this justice in the holy Church of God as a pillar, so that whatever is offered for purchase should be wholly despised by all his successors. But Elisha and Paul adorned the same house like most beautiful pictures when the former refused a freely offered gift, and the latter set aside for such glory the gift legally due to him—a glory of which he himself confesses that it would be better for him to die than for anyone to make it void (I Cor. IX, 15).

[Col. 1243B] For what is this glory except a kind of shining picture which the bleary eye of those men could not bear—men who plainly did not eat in order to preach the Gospel, but preached the Gospel in order to eat? But Paul, because he loved not only the stability but also the beauty of God’s house, set before sound eyes, rather than bleary ones, such a picture: that whoever wishes to adorn the house of God should learn to shake his hands free from every gift—not only from the gift offered for purchase, which devises ruin, but also from the gift received when freely offered, which dishonours the beauty of the building.

## CHAPTER XVIII. A bishop acts wisely and beneficially if he avoids things that are permitted but not beneficial, and therefore sometimes abstains even from gifts otherwise not unlawful.

[Col. 1243C]

But someone may say: Do not the sacred canons, which most severely forbid anything to be demanded from founders at the consecration of Churches, nevertheless permit that, if something happens to be freely offered to a bishop, it should not be refused? Would not the justice of tithes be utterly neglected if the people were not compelled by priests to pay them? Why then are Elisha and Paul offered for imitation, when the sacred canons do not prohibit acceptance of a freely offered gift, and even direct that people unwilling to give tithes be constrained by ban?

[Col. 1243D] Someone may object these and similar points, attempting to call into doubt what we have set forth. But whoever he is should consider that we seek to demonstrate the construction of such a building that it may not merely stand solid through stability, but may display through its very adornment an appearance so precious and delightful that even passers-by are invited to enter and, with an inward taste, sample what is set before those feasting in the house that is outwardly adorned with paintings so golden and mosaic-like.

For since the prophet calls blessed the man who shakes his hands free from every gift (Isa. XXXIII, 14), those whom I have proposed for imitation were such shakers-off of gifts, [Col. 1244A] shaking their hands utterly free from every gift, so that whoever imitates them may deservedly be called sons of those who shake off gifts. Of such persons the Psalm says: “Like arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of those who shake off” (Ps. CXXVI, 4). See how the prophetic testimonies agree with one another: there it is said, “Blessed is the man who shakes his hands free from every gift”; here, after mentioning those who shake off gifts, it immediately follows: “Blessed is the man who has filled his desire from them” (ibid., 5). Unhappy is the person who fulfils his desire contrary to them by receiving gifts; blessed is the person who fulfils his desire from them by shaking his hands free from every gift. The former fulfils his desire against those who shake off gifts; the latter fulfils his desire from them, because he borrows [Col. 1244B] examples of integrity from them. The former, as from a crooked bow, does not aim straight; the latter, like an arrow in the hand of a mighty man, is shot straight, reaching strongly from end to end throughout his whole diocese and ordering all things sweetly. For nothing will be stronger than his word because of its authority, and nothing sweeter because of its charity.

All worldly power will yield to this word, strong in sweetness and sweet in strength, when such integrity shines in the bishop himself that, with the apostle Paul, he does not permit his glory to be made void, even sometimes foregoing the stipend due to his ministry in order to speed the course of God’s word, if it cannot otherwise be expedited except by disregarding even the gain of a due stipend. And, with the prophet Elisha, he does not accept a gift offered after he has bestowed [Col. 1244C] some spiritual benefit, if he sees—wherever he sees—that the course of God’s word is delayed through accepting such gifts. This delay occurs only slightly where the secular giver resembles Naaman the Syrian, who readily understands the chaste intention of one who refuses the offered gifts. But sometimes even the person who offers does not clearly discern the motive of the one who receives, just as Naaman the Syrian did not discern Gehazi’s motive but indiscriminately offered even more than was requested. Yet in such a transaction it is the conscience of the recipient, not that of the giver, which is injured.

Nevertheless, since Gehazi had placed a stumbling block before a Gentile, whereby the avarice of Elisha, God’s servant, could be noted and, through evil suspicion, even the conscience of the giver [Col. 1244D] could be scandalized, it was altogether just that Gehazi should receive the leprosy which had departed from Naaman. He had supplied the occasion of scandal, so that he alone might bear the infamy, since he had neglected his own reputation and, what was worse, his master’s. Had the master overlooked this matter, he too would have neglected his own reputation and would have been cruel. By this example a bishop is warned that, if any of his people has become a Gehazi, he should exclude him from the fellowship of the brethren as a leper.

“All things are permitted, but not all things are beneficial.” A bishop may lawfully receive a gift freely offered after the consecration of Churches; but I think that the course of preaching is hindered rather than expedited by this. Whatever is not beneficial, if the bishop refuses it, his word runs swiftly.

There was once such integrity among men that any good bishop could receive spontaneously offered gifts. There was such beauty in Sodom that righteous Lot could have lodging there. But now, with the world’s evening drawing on and the ruin of all Sodom approaching, it is not enough for a just man to leave it, unless, also passing through the surrounding plain—as through a kind of neighbourhood of sins—he strives in swift course to make for the higher places of the mountain and says with Paul: “All things are permitted to me, but not all things are beneficial” (I Cor. VI, 12).

A bishop may lawfully receive a freely offered gift at consecrations of Churches; [Col. 1245B] but because the days are evil, he will act better and render the course of preaching more unimpeded if, by accepting nothing, he redeems the time, so that his swiftly running word may suffer no obstacle from the tongues of detractors who, as it were, gnaw at his life. For however much he may employ strong and lofty fortifications, if he remains in the plain of a more lax life and, like Lot’s wife, is changed as it were into a pillar of salt (Gen. XIX, 26), because he becomes savoury to detractors’ tongues, he is defended by no wall against their licking tongues—unless, abandoning the fortifications, he hastens, as I have said, to the higher places of the mountain and turns aside in his conduct even from permitted things, unless indeed they are permitted in such a way that they are also beneficial.

But if, enticed by gain, he wishes to proceed along the way which God [Col. 1245C] forbids, he cannot have an unimpeded and swift course, even if he drives the she-ass with spurs—that is, when he constrains the Church subject to him by commands (Num. XXII, 23 ff.). For because the sword of the word is now often seen even by simple people, the life of a pontiff will be rebuked by the people subject to him, as though by the she-ass. But his word runs unimpeded if he shakes his hands free even from permitted gifts when they are not beneficial. Then he will not be ashamed when he speaks with his enemies in the gate (Ps. CXXVI, 5), because the entrance and gate for detraction will be closed even to his enemies, so that, like the blinded Sodomites, they may circle the house of the just man and find no door of detraction against him.

## CHAPTER XIX. At times gifts are lawfully accepted by bishops—namely, when they are distributed to the poor under the witness of their Church; this was done by Peter, Paul, and Martin.

[Col. 1245D]

It should certainly be noted that hands are shaken free from lawful gifts in two ways, whether they are offered freely or legally. Sometimes they are wholly despised and refused, as I recalled above that Paul and Elisha did. But sometimes, when evil days do not hinder, they are indeed accepted without damage to the recipient’s integrity, but are so distributed under the witness of Christ and the Church that the hands of prelates are shaken free even from received offerings.

Thus Peter did not receive the offerings of believers into his hands, but entrusted them—placed at his feet, as things to be trampled underfoot in the pursuit of contemplation—to blessed Stephen and the other deacons, to be distributed carefully according to each person’s need, under the knowledge of the entire holy multitude. By this deed he openly instructs us that it greatly benefits preachers [Col. 1246B] to have even lawful offerings distributed under the witness of the Church in such a way that no subject may suspect the presiding person of private advantage in these matters.

If he acts thus, if he thus shakes his hands free even from lawful gifts, he may lawfully and without reproach demand by ban tithes and other lawful offerings from persons who unjustly withhold them. For, made a son of those who shake off gifts, like an arrow in the hand of a mighty man, he powerfully wounds adversaries until he utterly wrests the stipends of the poor from the hands of soldiers and princes.

Therefore the outstanding teacher, maintaining that the Churches of the Gentiles were debtors to the poor and to the apostles in material things, freely demanded from the Gentiles those material things as a due tribute; because, doing everything with witnesses, he could not be reproached with seeking his own advantage. In all things he had as companion in his journey and administration the brother whose praise was in the Gospel, providing what is good not only before God but also before human beings. And Paul was therefore one of the good shakers-off of gifts, because he shook his hands free even from offerings he had received.

Martin also was such a shaker-off of gifts, who wisely expended the lawful offerings of believers not on soldiers or horses but on the poor and clergy. And if anything happened to be freely offered to him after miraculous benefits had been bestowed, he either wholly—

> [Note: [Col. 1245D]  
> From the *Life of St. Martin*: “At the time when he was first made bishop, he had occasion to go to the imperial court. Valentinian then held the highest power. When he learned that Martin was seeking things which he was unwilling to grant, he ordered him to be kept from the palace doors. For the emperor’s harsh and proud mind had been influenced by his Arian wife, who had entirely turned him away from the holy man, so that he would not render him due reverence. Therefore, after Martin had once and again attempted to approach the proud prince, he had recourse to his customary defences: he wrapped himself in haircloth, sprinkled himself with ashes, abstained from food [Col. 1246D] and drink, and persevered day and night in prayer. But on the seventh day an angel stood by him, commanding him to go confidently to the palace: though closed, the royal doors would open of their own accord, and the emperor’s proud spirit would be softened. Strengthened, then, by the address of this present angel and trusting in his aid, he sought the palace. The thresholds stood open; no one opposed him; finally he came even to the king, with no one preventing him. When the king saw him coming from a distance, he ground his teeth, asking why he had been admitted; nor did he deign to rise for the man standing before him, until fire covered the royal seat [Col. 1247D] and a flame struck the emperor on that part of his body upon which he was seated. Thus the proud man is shaken from his throne and unwillingly rises for Martin; and, embracing at length the man whom he had previously resolved to despise, he confessed, now corrected, that he had experienced divine power. Without waiting for Martin’s requests, he granted everything before being asked. He frequently invited him to conversation and a meal; finally, as he departed, he offered him many gifts, all of which the blessed man rejected, as always the guardian of his poverty.”]

Likewise: “Licontius, a faithful man among the vicars, when his household was afflicted by a deadly plague and, in an unprecedented calamity, sick bodies were falling throughout the whole house, implored Martin’s aid by letter. At that time the blessed man sent word beforehand that the matter would be difficult to obtain; for in spirit he perceived that that house [Col. 1248D] was being scourged by divine power. Nevertheless, he did not cease, continuing for seven whole days and as many nights in prayer and fasting, until he obtained that which he had undertaken to pray for. Immediately Licontius, having experienced the divine benefits, threw himself before him, reporting and at the same time giving thanks that his house had been delivered from every danger. He also offered a hundred pounds of silver, which the blessed man neither refused nor accepted. But before that weight reached the threshold of the monastery, he immediately assigned it for the ransom of captives. And when the brethren suggested to him that some of it should be reserved for the expenses of the monastery, since food was scant for all and many lacked clothing, he said: ‘Let the Church feed and clothe us, provided that we do not appear to have sought anything for our own use.’”

like Elisha, [Col. 1246D] he refused it, or he caused it to be distributed among the needy under the witness and knowledge of all, so that the whole was bestowed upon poor outsiders; lest, if either he himself or anyone of his community obtained anything from such gifts for domestic uses, however necessary, the holy man himself should be censured by the malicious, either for having sold a spiritual benefit in [Col. 1247A] a miracle, or for not having shaken his hands free from every gift.

He is therefore rightly called a jewel of priests, because, like a most noble jewel, he is set by the hand of the supreme craftsman among the holy apostles, as though among the twelve gates of Jerusalem, so that by the splendor of so precious a stone any priest may be invited away from modern customs to ancient and apostolic traditions.

## Chapter XX. Concerning revenues restored to clerics living in common and without private property, whom he recognizes as Peter’s genuine sons, one day to be led by him into the heavenly Jerusalem.

Among these twelve gates Cephas is said to be the principal one. No acephalous person enters through it, because an acephalous person cannot be received by Cephas, being [Col. 1247B] contrary to him both in possessions and in name. For Cephas renounced everything; the acephalous person does not do this. He left the rule of common life to his successors in the clergy; the acephalous person does not keep it. Therefore the acephalous person will not enter by this gate over which Cephas is set; nor can he in any way be fitted into that building, “whose fellowship is wholly united in itself.”

Let those, then, who glory in the rule of Louis enter, if they can, through another gate, because, being without a head, they do not find Cephas’s gate open. Through this gate Augustine entered with his clerics; Martin with his; Pope Gregory with his; Augustine, bishop of the English, with his; and many others following the apostolic rule and inviting, [Col. 1247C] so far as they could, others to keep it. Peter, therefore, will bring in his own. It is doubtful whither Louis will lead his property-owning followers; for he cannot take from Peter’s hands the keys entrusted to Peter alone, until he brings in the acephalous.

Therefore, despising Louis, who leads by a byway while introducing evil customs, let us follow him who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). For those who abandon truth, which is Christ, for the sake of custom arrive not by the way at life, but by a byway at death.

To this is added the fact that Jesus, standing by the sea, saw not three or more boats, but only two: one in which were John and James, and the other in which was Simon Peter (Luke 5:2–3). Those who strive to cross the waves of this age with dry feet ought either, in the [Col. 1248A] monastic order with John, to devote themselves to prayer, meditation, and contemplation; or, with Peter and under Peter, to serve in the active life and minister to Christ’s poor. No one does this sincerely and devoutly unless he wishes either to be a shepherd with Peter or a sheep under Peter. To pursue private property in Christ’s warfare is not to be with Peter, but against Peter. He is not a shepherd with Peter who does not keep the apostolic rule, just as he is not a sheep under Peter who does not keep the Catholic and apostolic faith.

Those, therefore, who receive holy orders become bound to keep the apostolic rule, just as all who are baptized become bound to preserve the apostolic faith. Behold: just as all who are baptized become debtors to every observance belonging [Col. 1248B] to the Catholic and apostolic faith, so everyone legitimately advanced to holy orders becomes bound to that observance belonging to the apostolic rule—especially if he is joined to the congregation of some church, which, though under a false designation, is nevertheless called canonical. For there, when he is received, he promises obedience to be carried out according to God’s commands and those of the saints. By this obedience, therefore, he is bound to strive to observe apostolic traditions, if he wishes to be crowned with the apostles rather than condemned with apostates.

## Chapter XXI. Church pastors should be appointed from clerics who have first vigorously trained themselves in cloistered and common life.

[Col. 1248C] Since there are some who maintain that they have promised certain customs to their prelates—customs which we find contrary to apostolic and patristic traditions—they do well if they correct their vow. But if, defending more wickedly what they wickedly vowed, they preach another gospel besides that which we have received, the Apostle consigns them to anathema.

But if someone outside holy orders and outside a congregation uses his own resources, or even, if he wishes, enters into marriage, this is in some manner tolerated by blessed Gregory, as was said above; because he plainly has neither holy orders, to which the discipline of apostolic observance is owed, nor has he entered a canonical congregation, in which, as blessed Augustine affirms, no one may possess private property. If any do possess it, [Col. 1249A] they do what is not permitted. Hence it is necessary that, if any such persons occupy canonical churches, they themselves either obey apostolic and canonical commands by having no private property—which may not be possessed in cloisters—or be deprived of the cloisters themselves, which, if they are to be inhabited, ought to be possessed only by those living in common.

For in God’s holy Church a fellowship of those living in common is gathered, so that from them pastors of the Church may be legitimately set apart; just as Paul and Barnabas are read to have been set apart, at the Spirit’s command, for preaching to the Gentiles (Acts 13:2). They would not have been set apart by the Spirit for this work unless they had first been joined by the same Spirit to the apostolic fellowship and common life. Thus, first joined together and then set apart, they left a model for posterity, [Col. 1249B] so that pastors of peoples should be appointed not from courtiers or acephalous persons, but from the fellowship of those who, gathered into one under the apostles’ rule, are first tested in the battle line as soldiers, so that afterwards, if necessity requires, they may be appointed lawful leaders.

> [Note: [Col. 1249D] Augustine, *On the Power of Binding and Loosing*: “They alone possess the power of binding or loosing, [Col. 1250D] as did the apostles, who, placed in this flesh, hold at once their examples and teaching.”]

Thus they will serve in the churches they receive, together with their own men, and order the army entrusted to them in the manner they learned in the cloisters in which they had been joined by the Holy Spirit to common life.

Peter, chief of shepherds, proves that pastors are to be chosen only from those gathered with the apostles. Discussing the election of one apostle to take the place of Judas the traitor, [Col. 1249C] he addresses the others thus: “It is necessary,” he says, “to take from those who have been gathered with us one for the place of this ministry” (Acts 1:21, 25). “It is necessary,” he says, “from those gathered with us”—as if to say: it is not necessary from others. This was a true and sincere election, worthy of the apostolic college: there Joseph, the rich man of Arimathea, is not preferred to the others because of his wealth; indeed, by this very statement he is excluded from Peter’s election, because, though he was a good disciple and had proved himself at Christ’s burial, he had not yet, having abandoned private property, been gathered with the apostles to live in common.

At that time there were many good disciples, proved when Christ revealed himself to them. Among them were the more than five hundred brethren who, as [Col. 1249D] Paul testifies, saw Christ after the resurrection just as the apostles did (1 Cor. 15:6). Thus someone from their number might seem worthy of the apostolate, because those who saw Christ after the resurrection are not recorded as having hesitated, whereas some of the apostles are recorded as having doubted. Yet what does Peter say? “It is necessary,” he says, “from those who have been gathered with us,” and so forth. Therefore, however good a Christian any possessor of private property may be found to be, pastoral care is rightly entrusted only to those who have been gathered with the apostles—provided they have been approved by the Spirit who sets apart. We believe that this Spirit [Col. 1250A] works invisibly in canonical election and in the people’s petition.

If, then, peoples deprived of a pastor are presented with such a choice—that they should request, not a courtly cleric, not an acephalous person, not one ordained without assignment and therefore, according to the Synod of Chalcedon, forbidden from every ministry, but some good canon; or, if a canon cannot be found, at least a good monk—then, while the clergy elect and the people petition, Jerusalem the city is rebuilt, as though Jesus the great priest were teaching among the clergy and the people were returning home after the disgrace of an entrenched abuse, as after a long Babylonian captivity. Its whole fellowship is united in itself.

For the bishop, or another canonically appointed prelate from him and under him, [Col. 1250B] will establish common life in the greater and baptismal churches, in which no one will call anything his own, but the whole fellowship will be united in itself. For brothers will dwell together in one through a good and pleasant manner of life, which is that same unity.

## Chapter XXII. Clerics, and especially their prelates, should not be deterred from introducing common life by the objections of the powerful. No one should be received into a religious fellowship without examination and testing by the Spirit.

Here it is relevant that, in the rebuilding of Jerusalem, certain principal gates were called by mystical names, by which things now to be done in the Church were prefigured through prophetic figures. For all [Col. 1250C] that historically happened to those rebuilders of earthly Jerusalem was a kind of prophetic sign of what we now see.

Tobiah and Goshem, and the other chiefs of the Gentiles, said to them: “What is this thing that you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?” (2 Esdras 2:19). The same words will be spoken by many when rebuilders of spiritual Jerusalem, setting aside the king’s command and despising the whole world as though it were a Babylon, are occupied solely with spiritual pursuits or are devoted to cloistered disciplines.

For if a prince or soldier comes to such men and offers the kiss of Judas, compared with the more exalted kiss, in order to obtain the Church’s property through homage, as through a lie; and the bishops, guarding against this as sacrilege and fearing to tear the mantle of the true Samuel, refuse them and forbid benefits possessed for so many years, they will immediately hear: “What is this thing that you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?” For you destroy the kingdom by denying us benefices.

What, then, should bishops answer to this, except what was then answered by the priest Nehemiah? “And I returned them an answer,” he says, “and said to them: ‘The God of heaven himself helps us, and we are his servants. Let us arise and build; but you have neither part nor right nor memorial in Jerusalem’” [Col. 1251A] (2 Esdras 2:20). If the bishop uses these words with the priest Nehemiah humbly and steadfastly, the victory of the word accomplishes this in the hearts of his adversaries: they are struck dumb by these words, though nevertheless afflicted with great sorrow, just as those men were saddened. Of them Scripture says beforehand, before they came to the priest Nehemiah: “And Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard, and they were exceedingly grieved that someone had come seeking the prosperity of the children of Israel” (2 Esdras 2:10).

Let the bishop, therefore, and every spiritual prelate seek, with the priest Nehemiah and with the God of heaven as helper, the prosperity of the children of Israel. Let him not fear any earthly prince in God’s cause, saying with the Psalmist: “God is my helper; I will not fear what man may do to me” (Ps. 117:6). Then, whether the children of this age will it or not, the structure of an enduring building will arise.

In it, before all the gates, the Sheep Gate is built. Of it Scripture reads: “And Eliashib the high priest arose, and his brethren the priests, and built the Sheep Gate. They sanctified it, and set up its doors, and built it as far as the tower of one hundred cubits” [Col. 1251B] (2 Esdras 3:1). What is this Sheep Gate but common life? In it, under one shepherd, that little flock is gathered into one fold, to whom the kingdom is promised by Christ (Luke 12:32).

Doors are set in this gate when not just anyone, anywhere, and in any fashion is received into it; rather, he is admitted after being examined through the door [Col. 1251C] of most diligent testing. This precaution is certainly required: even should he offer all his possessions, he himself is not to be received into the fellowship of common life without careful examination.

For many offer their goods in such a way that they wish to enter without objection or examination. Yet Peter must first slaughter them and then eat them (Acts 10:13), lest, if they are heedlessly admitted through the doors, because they pass living and un-slaughtered into the belly of common life, they begin to tear it more grievously in its womb than, standing outside, they might seem to attack it. Thus Peter wished to slaughter Ananias by his examination and then to eat him. But Ananias, approaching deceitfully like unfit food, experienced indeed the tooth [Col. 1251D] of stern rebuke beneath Peter’s jaw as Peter searched out his hidden matters; yet he was not admitted to the vital parts (Acts 5:3 ff.). His goods, nevertheless, because they had been offered to God, are not said to have been rejected. Nor was it said to Ananias, as it was to Simon, that his money should be with him unto perdition (Acts 8:20).

For it is one thing deceitfully to lie to the Holy Spirit—which all do who approach falsely under the appearance of religion. It is another thing to wish to purchase the Holy Spirit himself—which all do who offer their goods in such a way that they themselves may be received in exchange for the goods they have offered, with the diligence of examination omitted. These persons do not wish the quality of their lives to be closely examined [Col. 1252A] after their offering has been received, being certain and wholly secure of admission because of their gifts. They wish, therefore, to be eaten, but do not wish first to be slaughtered. They wish to enter through the Sheep Gate, but do not heed that doors have been set in it, whose keys Peter received from the Lord: so that neither one found to have lied to the Holy Spirit may be admitted even though his gifts have been received, nor one who schemes to purchase that same Holy Spirit may be admitted in any degree. Rather, both he and his money should remain in perdition, because he approaches by a most wicked sort of bargaining, saying with Simon: “Give, and I will give” (Acts 8:19).

He clearly intends thereby that he should not be rejected in examination but, because perhaps of an abundant [Col. 1252B] offering, be joined to the congregation without any objection. When such a person is discovered, he must be reproved as being in the gall of bitterness, so that he may either be corrected by repentance and, once corrected, received; or, if he remains in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity, hear with Simon: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts 8:20). Otherwise, if those who approach are received indiscriminately, without long probation and careful examination, the doors of the Sheep Gate are not well guarded.

This gate is built as far as the tower of one hundred cubits, because many in common life offer a hundredfold fruit; and all who follow it perfectly will receive that hundredfold which the Lord promised to Peter and Peter’s like, and which a cleric possessing private property [Col. 1252C] cannot attain. For only to those who leave their possessions and follow the Lord is it promised that they shall receive a hundredfold here and possess eternal life in the future (Matt. 19:29).

The custody of the flock is rightly entrusted to such persons, because they stand lawfully in the Sheep Gate. But the conventicles of acephalous persons, full not of canons but of pseudo-canons, are certain gates of hell.

> [Note: [Col. 1251D] Augustine, *Book IV against the Donatists*: “I take the gates of hell to be vices and sins, or certainly the teachings of heretics [Col. 1252D], by which deceived men are led to Tartarus.”]

They will not prevail against this Sheep Gate, founded by the Lord upon the rock, entrusted to Peter, and established so firmly that all the gates of hell will not prevail against it (Matt. 16:18). For he defends this Sheep Gate as his own fold—the one to whom every knee shall bend; and therefore the crowd of pseudo-canons seems in vain to resist him for a time.

## Chapter XXIII. Concerning vicars and those who possess canonries in several places at once.

In vain is resistance offered to them by vicars and thieves; neither of these can retain the churches they occupy, if the bishop, most skilled in uprooting and planting, chooses to exercise due severity against them, allowing neither churches to be occupied by vicars nor anyone to be endowed with one. For no priest is to be tolerated in a church unless the doorkeeper has admitted him; and he admits no one except one who approaches lawfully [Col. 1253A]. But one does not approach lawfully if he receives a church when a layman gives it to him. For a layman, by giving, does not appoint a shepherd, but introduces by his gift a thief or robber. He is rightly called a thief and robber who obtains a church while a layman gives it and the doorkeeper is unaware. A shepherd, however, is created not by any donation of laypeople but by canonical election.

> [Note: [Col. 1253C]
>
> From the Seventh Ecumenical Synod, held by the five patriarchs with three hundred Fathers under Pope Adrian I, chapter 3: “Every election of a bishop, priest, or deacon made by secular rulers shall remain void, according to the rule which says: ‘If any bishop, using secular powers, obtains a church through them, let him be deposed and separated, together with all who communicate with him.’”
>
> From the Eighth Ecumenical Synod likewise, held by the five patriarchs with two hundred and forty Fathers under Pope Nicholas I: “In agreement with earlier councils, this holy and universal synod has determined, established, and lawfully promulgated that promotions and consecrations of bishops shall be effected by the election and decree of bishops, and that none of the lay princes or powerful persons may insert himself into the election or promotion of a patriarch, metropolitan, or any other person, lest disorderly and unsuitable confusion or contention arise from this. Especially since it is fitting that none of the powerful laity should have any authority in such matters, but should rather remain silent and attend to himself until the election of the future pontiff is regularly brought to its conclusion by the college of the Church.
>
> “But if any layperson is invited by the Church to join in deliberation and cooperation, he may, if he wishes, respectfully comply with those inviting him [Col. 1254C]. For in this way the Church regularly advances a worthy shepherd for its salvation. But whoever, among secular princes or powerful persons, or any layperson of another rank, attempts to act against the common, harmonious, and canonical election [Col. 1254D] of ecclesiastical order, let him be anathema until he obeys and assents to that which the Church has shown itself to desire concerning the election and ordination of its own prelate.”]

This applies whether he is found in the very church needing a shepherd, or is sought from another church which nourishes, in one fold of common life, such rams that the sheep may be made fruitful through them if they are elected. The sheep do not follow a stranger, because he is not a ram but a wolf and a plunderer.

For the canons sufficiently permit that, when in a church there is either no clerical congregation or none such as contains a suitable pastor, one may be sought from another church [Col. 1253B]. Yet this must be so: once regularly elected, he is no longer to share in the possessions of the church from which he is transferred to another, just as a monk should not share in the possessions of his monastery after he is proposed for governing a church either as bishop or priest. No one can properly administer different offices at the same time; no one ought to bind himself to the titles of two churches. For it appears monstrous that someone should be bishop in one church and canon in another, receiving there a portion of the stipend where he pays no due service.

But for someone remaining in one church to appoint a vicar in another in his place is wholly contrary to divine ordinances, especially if the care of the sheep is entrusted to the one called vicar [Col. 1253C].

> [Note: [Col. 1254D]
>
> Synod of Chalcedon, chapter 10: “It is not permitted for a cleric to be enrolled at the same time in the churches of two cities, both that in which he was originally ordained and that to which he fled, as though to one of greater importance, through desire for empty glory. Those who do this must be recalled to their own church, in which they were first ordained, and minister there only. But if anyone has already been transferred from one church to another, let him share in no respect in the goods of the former church, or of the martyr-shrines subject to it, or of the hospices. Those who dare, after the definition of this great and universal synod, to perpetrate anything of what has been forbidden, the holy synod decrees must be removed from their own rank.”
>
> Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna: “If any abbot or monk from whatever monastery comes to the clerical office or holy order, let him, as we have said, retain no further authority there [Col. 1255D], lest monasteries be compelled, under the cover of this occasion, to endure the burdens which we prohibit.”]

For what is this vicar but an open hireling? If he is a hireling whose sheep are not his own, it is evident that all vicars are hirelings. Whether a vicar serves in an urban or rural church, the sheep are no concern of his, because no judicial sentence can rightly be pronounced by him over the sheep of the church in which he is a vicar. In the spiritual office which he performs for payment, [Col. 1254A] he sells the Holy Spirit. In the Mass, however, Christ is sold together with the Holy Spirit; and when he is sold, his Father is gravely offended—not only against the hirelings themselves, but also against bishops who consent to such commerce and do not, as duty of their office requires, cast such merchants out of the temple.

For by silence they consent, when, like dumb dogs unable to bark, seeing these things they despise them as trivial—though they are greater precisely because they are more customary. When a crime is committed with a certain shame, there is a dangerous muttering against God in a kind of whisper. But when criminal fault is committed publicly and without shame by many, there is then an openly destructive outcry against God, as the Sodomites cried out against God when they proclaimed their sin.

[Col. 1254B] Then truly good angels—that is, holy bishops—ought no longer to delay general vengeance, but, once the certainty of the outcry has been established, pronounce a general sentence of anathema, excepting and rescuing from it only those who, according to their counsel, wish to depart from the multitude of evildoers and be saved either in little Zoar through the active life or on the mountain through the contemplative life. But if the bishop is not moved by the multiplied outcry of iniquity, he will not be, like a good angel, a rescuer of the few good people; rather, he himself will likewise be counted among the multitude of evildoers.

## Chapter XXIV. Punishment for crimes formerly condemned in common by the holy Fathers must not be postponed, even though the multitude of criminals be great, etc.

[Col. 1254C]

But someone says: With whom will the bishop take counsel against the sin of the multitude? For scarcely anyone ventures to pronounce anathema when sin is so strengthened by both multitude and custom that in a great city not fifty, not ten, but scarcely one person turning away from evil is found. To this the answer is that, even if only one [Col. 1255A] counsellor adheres to the bishop, who, though he does not know how to give counsel, nevertheless knows how to acquiesce with faithful Abraham in a wholesome and just judgment, the bishop, content with that one person’s counsel, ought not to delay punishment—especially if it is certain that the crime committed by the multitude has been condemned and marked with anathema in some authoritative council or decree of the Roman pontiffs.

> [Note: [Col. 1255D] In the Book of Wisdom: “Do not take counsel with fools; for they cannot love anything except what pleases them” (Sirach 8:20). Likewise: “Let many be at peace with you, but let one counsellor out of a thousand be yours” (Sirach 6:6). Likewise: “Before every work let a truthful word go before you, [Col. 1256D] and before every act, firm counsel” (Sirach 37:20).]

Drunkards and other criminals of this sort, though, as Paul testifies, they shall not inherit the kingdom of God, are nevertheless tolerated in the holy Church because of their multitude. Nor is anyone put under excommunication for such things unless he lacks an accompanying multitude. Yet the shepherd’s care ought not to sleep over the custom and multitude [Col. 1255B] of such persons; he must say and do everything by which reigning sin can be so opposed that the attack upon iniquity is not the dissolution of unity, nor, conversely, the preservation of unity the fostering of iniquity.

But when such a fault is committed as is known to have been condemned by the judgment of the Fathers, it is not in the pontiff’s power to postpone the sentence of punishment, lest he too, by silence and consent, incur the danger of anathema. For just as, if the Arian heresy were to spring up in some bishopric, no one would think it should be tolerated, as already once condemned, because of custom or the multitude of some people, so also in the other crimes condemned and excommunicated by the judgment of the Fathers no one ought to hesitate. Rather, whenever they are discovered in someone, if after [Col. 1255C] the first and second admonition they are not corrected, they must be reported to the bishop, so that their condemnation is not then first pronounced upon rebels, but is confirmed and published by the bishop as having long ago been pronounced; lest any incur the ancient anathema who, after such publication, knowingly share in a condemned and excommunicated crime.

Therefore, since an open hireling is openly a simoniac, condemned by Peter, the first Roman pontiff, and cut off by the sentences of many later Fathers, a bishop ought more to fear being condemned with such persons by tolerating them in his parish than accept anyone’s counsel that they should be tolerated because of the crowd of the multitude or a custom [Col. 1255D] long established.

This must be observed not only concerning hirelings, but also concerning Nicolaitans and those invested through a lay hand, since it is most certainly established that such persons are not to be admitted by a faithful bishop who is the doorkeeper, when, having received a church as a gift through some other person, they offer or send themselves to him in order to receive from him the care of souls, although they have already received the church from some other person.

For it is certain that neither emperor, nor any layman, nor provost, nor abbot, nor abbess, nor finally any person at all has the right or permission to give a church which, redeemed by Christ’s blood and ennobled by great liberty, is known to have been entrusted—not given—to the bishop alone. Thus, according to the manner in which he himself approached the mother church, he should entrust the care of souls to those approaching in the same and no other manner. He must especially guard against allowing anyone to be bound to two churches at one and the same time, since he himself cannot divide himself between governing two bishoprics [Col. 1256B].

This order, moreover, is easily observed where one to be placed over a church is elected only from regular canons or religious monks. This election proceeds ecclesiastically if, on the death of a priest, once his death is known, the bishop sends some prudent and religious person to summon the more prudent clerics of the deanery in which the church has been left vacant, so that an orderly election may be made with their counsel. The bishop’s representative, moreover, ought to address the people, that they may take care concerning the election of a shepherd, so that they make their petition for such a person as the clergy can consent to have set over them and whom the bishop’s careful examination cannot reject.

For since one and the same beauty of the Church ought to appear in the ordering both of the head and of the members [Col. 1256C], just as, according to Leo the Great, no reason permits one to be counted among bishops whom neither clergy elected, nor people requested, nor his metropolitan ordained, so no reason permits one to be counted among parish priests whom neither clergy elected, nor people requested, nor his own bishop invested with care of souls.

Therefore the gift of any particular person accomplishes nothing in appointing either priest or bishop, because the Church is not to be given away as a female slave, but legitimately joined to her lawful husband as a bride.

> [Note: [Col. 1256D]
>
> From an epistle of Pope Clement: “It belongs to you, O priests, who exercise the Lord’s embassy, to teach the peoples; and it belongs to them to obey you, as they do God.”
>
> From an epistle of Pope Alexander: “Let no count, no judge, and absolutely no one, whether established in clerical office or secular rank, hinder or presume to disturb the embassy of bishops.”]

Whether those who give churches or those who receive churches from givers, because they transgress paternal laws, if, having been corrected, they do not repent, [Col. 1256D] they will be held under that penalty of disgrace and condemnation by which voluntary violators of paternal laws are struck.

But unless the bishop pursues such wickedness with the sword of the word—excluding some, correcting some within, and for a while tolerating some [Col. 1257A] even with discerning protest, until he finds a time to make a whip of cords and cast out those who must be cast out—unless, I say, he acts thus, he himself will certainly be excluded by divine judgment from the Sheep Gate, because he has no care for the flock. If the lawful shepherd himself had that care, he would permit only lawful shepherds to preside under him; nor would any counsel lead him to tolerate vicars, these thieves and robbers, of his own accord.
