Nor would he allow Christ’s bride to be made an adulteress. For, as blessed Ambrose testifies, a church not legitimately joined to a lawful husband is called an adulteress.

Far be it, then, that there should be delay in excluding such adulterers, whom no reason allows to be regarded as lawful husbands! Let those who are not good guardians of the flock be excluded from the Sheep Gate. By such exclusion they themselves are sometimes drawn more effectively, and are pulled out of the depths of death, as from the bottom of the sea, by the true guardian watching over the Sheep Gate [Col. 1257B]. For the gatekeeper of this gate is a most prudent fisherman. At Christ’s command, he knows how to let down his nets for a catch; he knows how to draw them, filled with great fish, onto the land.

## Chapter XXV. Clerics submerged in the mire of vices must be reformed to the apostolic life; Gerhoh rejoices that this has already been done at Rome, Salzburg, and elsewhere.

The Fish Gate is therefore rightly placed beside the Sheep Gate, of which it is written: “The sons of Asnaa built the Fish Gate. They roofed it and [Col. 1257C] set up its doors, bolts, and bars” (2 Esdras 3:3). Who are these fish but clerics still lurking in their slippery custom, as though in the mire of a pool, and wandering in a fluid manner of life? A great part of them, willing or unwilling, will be drawn out while Peter fishes and placed in the gate of common life, which, as has already been said, is called not only the Sheep Gate but also the Fish Gate. For just as it gathers sheep who do not yet know how to swim, so it turns those who have been gathered into certain rational fish, who know not only how to walk by touching the ground through action, but also, possessing as it were a natural use of swimming after the manner of fish, are raised from the earth’s bottom through contemplation.

Thus, in the rebuilding of Jerusalem, the Fish Gate is rightly joined to the Sheep Gate, because common life—of active and contemplative persons, as though of sheep and fish—is fitted together in the building of heavenly Jerusalem by the craftsman’s hand in such a way that Christ its builder is rightly called in the Gospel the son of a craftsman. For he now manifestly fulfils a certain work of craftsmanship which he once promised to his Church; as is apparent in many churches in our own time.

For that powerful and true craftsman, the craftsman’s son, speaking through the prophet Isaiah to the Church, his bride and his city, says: “I will turn my hand upon you, and will smelt away your dross to purity, and remove all your tin, and restore your judges as they were formerly, and your counsellors as in ancient times. After this you shall be called the city of the righteous, the faithful city” (Isa. 1:25–26).

[Col. 1258A] Has not that craftsman already begun to fulfill this prophecy in the Church of Salzburg? There he has removed the pseudo-canons, as it were a pond; and he has begun so to refine the regular canons planted there, by the fire suited to his craftsman’s furnace, that we do not doubt that he will refine it utterly from every dross, and that thereafter it will have no judges or counsellors except those whose entrance, manner of life, and departure shall be such as they were of old among bishops judging and clerics counselling.

This craftsman is working at Rome in the Lateran patriarchal palace, where, through his grace, canonical life is already flourishing anew, and will cast off all dross all the sooner because the furnace of tribulation, as though it were set in the midst of Babylon, will be continually kindled for it by certain palace officials—not disciples of Peter, [Col. 1258B] but servants of King Nebuchadnezzar. Yet in that furnace the apostolic lord himself, like an angel, will comfort the afflicted; so that, while they have him relieving their distresses in the midst of tribulation, they may seem to feel, in the midst of the furnace, as it were a wind of dew blowing.

But one of those who kindle that furnace will be burned in such a way that either, converted with Saul, he will defend the Church, or, perversely and irrevocably corrupted with Saul, he will go down into hell. The children of Christ—that is, the true canons—will not be touched by the fire at all; it will neither grieve them nor bring them any trouble. Rather, it will confer such benefit that, their bonds of sin consumed by this fire, they will walk freely [Col. 1258C] and, as though with one mouth, bless God in the midst of the furnace.

For some years ago that Church was exposed to clerics who did not sing as though with one mouth, but as though from a mouth divided and greatly discordant: both because of the unharmonious arrangements of their voices, varied by certain theatrical tunes, and because of undisciplined habits and a great divergence that divided them against one another. But now, thanks be to God, psalmody and singing are performed in that Church as though with one mouth, both in the measured and harmonious modulation of the voice and in the holy ordering of morals according to cloister discipline. And if anything still needs to be added there, he who began will himself bring it to completion.

Let, therefore, the church of Saint Fridianus at Lucca rejoice. Like a watered garden, it enriches the Roman tables with its [Col. 1258D] fruits, while from it however small a number of canons is sent into the Roman Church, like a little grain of mustard to be ground in a mortar, so that through this the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ may be spread far and wide, when the order of common life flourishes anew in the very head of the world.

What rabble of acephali will henceforth dare to appeal to the Roman Church, if a Catholic bishop, rejecting those among them whom he cannot convert, begins to restore common and apostolic life? If professors of apostolic life and defenders of apostate life come before the Apostolic See—which now fosters apostolic life in its own chief church—which party, do you suppose, will triumph in that See, except the one whose cause Simon Peter freely aids and favours? And who will be confounded and shattered by a grievous fall except the one who, in that city, dares to extend his flight with Simon Magus against Simon the Great? For there Peter himself presides in the apostolic lord; and Peter’s order is loved by the greater number of the cardinals, who foster it there in the state of antiquity, already begun in part, and to be most swiftly extended thence, as from the head, throughout the whole body of the Church.

These pseudo-canons themselves make themselves highly vulnerable to attack, since, for fear of losing their private property, they fear worldly princes to such an extent that they become disobedient to their bishops when those bishops command what is just, lest through worldly persons they lose the goods they love. They are also frequently entangled in such crimes that, when detected, [Col. 1259B] they are easily deprived by bishops of ecclesiastical maintenance. Therefore, if a bishop wishes to triumph, let him arm himself not with carnal but with spiritual weapons, and let him undertake to attack the pseudo-canons by fighting with the sword of the word, ready to punish every disobedience, until, by uprooting, destroying, planting, and building, he arrives at victory.

For this will be the victory of the word, powerful in itself and conquering in itself; but the crown of victory belongs to the one who rightly utters the word. He rightly utters the word, rightly draws the two-edged sword, who cuts off criminal or disobedient clerics with the sickle of anathema in such a way as to leave them like useless branches cast [Col. 1259C] out and dried up, to burn in that fire which came upon the companions of Korah; which also burned in Caiaphas’s courtyard, where Peter warmed himself for a time. But when the Lord looked upon his heart, Peter departed from that fire and wept most bitterly; and weeping, he was received back.

Thus these men too are then received back when by weeping or by other certain signs of repentance they testify this concerning themselves: that they are more ready with Peter, in the upper room of common life, to await through fasting and prayer the fire coming from heaven, than in Caiaphas’s house to seek for themselves, from the fire of covetousness, a remedy against the cold of sorrow.

[Col. 1260A] For this is not so much a remedy as a foment of greater sorrow; because the wretched soul, from the source by which it is temporarily made cheerful—food, drink, clothing, money—is made yet more miserably to waste away, when the man who does not wish to leave the smoky courtyard of the world cannot hear even a maidservant’s voice without trembling.

We must therefore pray for such people, that the Lord may look upon them. To him alone it is possible to gather again branches that are broken and dried up, so that, grafted in through the grace of reconciliation, they may grow warm in the unity and wholeness of the true vine, which is Christ. Thus either they may henceforth lawfully exercise his warfare with Peter, or at least they may no longer disturb in any way those who, through God’s grace, wish and are able to exercise it.

Although it is especially desirable that, grafted in again, they should [Col. 1260B] taste how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity, nevertheless, if—even if unwilling or unable to do this—they promise to live canonically in such a manner that, as branches drawing life from the pith of the vine, they do not impede others, they may in some manner be received in the Church and tolerated, as it were, in the bark of the mother tree.

For if, content with fellowship among Christians and with the salvation of their souls, they wish to live without sacred orders and outside congregations—as we find that blessed Gregory permitted infirm clerics to do—they do something not to be praised, but still in some way to be tolerated. But this can in no way be tolerated: that persons established outside the rule should exercise sacred orders.

[Col. 1260C] Who would judge such persons fit to be received into sacred orders, except one who appears to disregard or be ignorant of the decrees of councils and the acts of pontiffs? For, to say nothing of the other Fathers—who command that those to be advanced to sacred orders be carefully examined, so that not only their past life may be investigated, but also their future conduct in a holy resolution may be recognized as established—Pope Leo of the city of Rome alone wrote to Januarius, patriarch of Aquileia:

> “Having read the letter of your brotherhood, we have recognized the vigour of your faith, which we had known of old. We congratulate you that, for the guarding of Christ’s flock, you vigilantly discharge pastoral care, lest wolves, who have entered under the appearance of sheep, tear apart the simple by their bestial savagery, and not only themselves make no progress through correction, but also corrupt those things which are sound.
>
> “Lest the viper should accomplish this by deceit, we have thought it necessary to admonish your charity, informing you that it concerns the peril of the soul if any person among those who have fallen away from us into the sect of heretics and schismatics, and who has in any manner defiled himself with the contagion of heretical communion, is received upon repenting into Catholic communion without a profession of lawful satisfaction.
>
> “It is most salutary and most full of the benefit of spiritual medicine that whether priests, deacons, subdeacons, or clerics of any order, who wish to be considered corrected and desire to return again to the Catholic faith which they had long ago lost, should first confess without ambiguity that they condemn their errors and the authors of those errors themselves; so that, their perverse opinions having been destroyed, no occasion of hope may remain, lest any member of such persons be violated by association, when their own profession begins to oppose them in every respect.
>
> “Concerning them we also command that the following ordinance of the canons be kept: they are to regard it as a great benefit if, all hope of promotion having been removed from them, they remain with permanent stability in the order in which they are found—provided that they have not been polluted by repeated baptism. He incurs no light guilt before the Lord who judges that such persons are to be advanced to sacred orders. If promotion is granted, after great examination, to those without accusation, much more must it not be permitted to those under suspicion.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Moreover, let not your charity doubt that you will be more vehemently admonished if—something we do not suppose—those matters which we decree for the safeguarding of the canons and the integrity of faith are neglected. For the faults of lower ranks are to be imputed to no persons more than to slothful and negligent rulers, who often foster a great pestilence while they neglect to apply the necessary remedy.”

[Note: [Col. 1259C–1260D] Pope Leo of the city of Rome to Januarius, patriarch of Aquileia; quoted above.]

Leo the Great and Gregory the First suffice for removing those who reject even suspect persons. But what are Leo the Great [Col. 1261A] and Gregory the First except the two vicars of Peter?

[Note: [Col. 1261C–1261D] Gregory says in his Synodal Letter concerning the four councils:

> “I reject all persons whom the venerable councils reject. Those whom they venerate, I embrace. For whoever presumes, against what has been established by universal consent, either to loose those whom they bind or to bind those whom they loose, destroys not the councils but himself. Whoever therefore thinks otherwise, let him be anathema.”

Bishops by whom acephali and absolutely ordained persons are not rejected—that is, persons not regularly attached to any church, to whom the Council of Chalcedon forbids every ministry—incur that Gregorian anathema.]

But whoever does not think with Peter does not gather with Peter. Whoever does not gather with Peter certainly does not gather with the Rock itself, which is Christ; and whoever does not gather with him scatters, and whoever is not with him is against him. Whoever is against Christ is Antichrist. And now there are many Antichrists who receive the mark of the beast and the number of its name not only on the hand but also on the forehead: not only acting contrary to Christ, but even defending themselves against the Church with shameless brow. Thus, dissenting from the Roman Church, they undoubtedly become heretics, because it is established that whoever dissents from the Roman Church is a heretic.

By the Roman Church I mean that Church whose head is [Col. 1261B] Christ, whose members are Peter and Paul and every spiritual son of that Church, established not only in that city but also throughout the whole world upon the rock which gave Peter his name. Every spiritual person, I say, belongs to the Roman Church, which judges all and is itself judged by no one. For, as Paul declares, “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2:15).

## CHAPTER XXVI. Bishops should beware of exercising lordship over the clergy; rather, they should labour to show themselves kindly toward their clerics and generous toward the poor. The bishops’ table should be the same as the table of clerics, poor persons, and so forth.

Let inquiry therefore be made not only of Peter, but also of every [Col. 1261C] Catholic teacher, what he thinks concerning the life of clerics, so that everyone who does not wish to dissent from the Roman Church may assent to their spiritual judgment. Speak, Peter: what do you think? “I exhort the elders,” he says, “as a fellow elder: feed the flock which is among you” (1 Pet. 5:1–2). Observe that he does not say, “Follow the king with soldiers”; rather, he says, “Feed the flock which is among you,” and so forth. Defining the life of a shepherd by these words, he concludes his teaching thus: “Not exercising lordship over the clergy, but made an example to the flock” (1 Pet. 5:3).

Blessed Gregory in some manner glossed this teaching [Col. 1262A] when he forbade Augustine, bishop of the English, to live apart from his clerics, lest a bishop who was separated from the clergy should seem to exercise lordship over the clergy.

But now many exercise lordship over the clergy. Separated from their clerics, whatever their quality, they retain for themselves the greater part of the Church’s lands, leaving the smaller part to the clerics and none to the poor. Thus, exercising lordship over the clergy, they are not an example to the flock by governing the clergy and feeding the flock; rather, they are a great scandal to both clergy and flock, feeding soldiers and the king. To do this is dangerous; but to defend it is undoubtedly pernicious. Scripture does not say, “Woe to those who do evil”—although that is dangerous—but rather: “Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil, who make light darkness and darkness light” [Col. 1262B] (Isa. 5:20). Therefore there is danger for those who do evil; but eternal woe for those who defend it with obstinate zeal.

For as Saint Gregory expounds the lamentations, the dirge, and the woe over Ezekiel, we may observe this distinction among lamentations: that we may assign to sinners who repent the lamentation of temporal affliction, but to defenders of sin the woe of everlasting condemnation; and, lamenting with Jeremiah, say: “How the gold has grown dim; the finest colour has changed; the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lam. 4:1). For the finest colour of the purest gold was present when a bishop could say with Christ to his disciples: “But I am in the midst of you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27).

For when common life is absent, the sacred canons decreed that a fourth part of tithes and offerings should be bestowed upon bishops, not for soldiers but for pilgrims and guests to be received by them. Yet Blessed Gelasius prohibited them from dividing Church lands, because they ought rather each year to distribute both the revenues of the lands and the tithes into four portions: so that the bishop’s share, under the witness of [Col. 1263A] the Church, may be spent in relieving the poor and in the duty of hospitality. Thus the bishop, not exercising lordship over the clergy but made an example to the flock, may appear as a second Job, saying with him:

> “If I denied the poor what they desired, or made the eyes of the widow wait; if I ate my morsel alone and the orphan did not eat from it—for compassion grew up with me from my childhood and came forth with me from my mother’s womb; if I despised one passing by because he had no clothing, or a poor person without covering; if his sides have not blessed me because he was warmed from the fleece of my sheep; if I raised my hand against an orphan when I saw that I had the advantage in the gate—may my shoulder fall from its joint and my arm be broken with its bones. For I have always feared God as though waves swelling over me, and I could not bear his weight. The stranger did not remain outside; my door stood open to the traveller” (Job 31:17–24).

[Note: [Col. 1261D–1262D] Pope Gelasius, ch. 27:

> “It is fitting that four portions be made, both from income and from the offerings of the faithful, insofar as the resources of each church permit, as has long ago been reasonably decreed. One is to belong to the bishop, another to the clerics, a third to the poor, and a fourth to the fabric [maintenance] of the church. Just as it concerns the priest to pay in full to the Church’s ministers the stated amount, so the clergy should know that they are not insolently to demand anything beyond the sum assigned to them. Those things assigned to ecclesiastical buildings must truly be extended to that work, as the visible restoration of the holy places will show; for it is impious, when sacred buildings have been left destitute, for a bishop to divert to his own profit the expenditures allotted to them. Likewise, although he may seem likely to show in his accounts that he has administered the portion assigned to the poor, it must nevertheless, as it is written, ‘Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven,’ be publicly attested and not concealed from the praises of good repute.”

Chapter 28:

> “Therefore, lest any cleric should suppose himself immune from this offence: if, in those matters which we have set forth as salutary duties, he sees bishop, priest, or deacon transgressing and does not promptly take care to bring it to our attention, presenting appropriate proofs, so that punishment of the transgressor may deter others from wrongdoing—then he too shall by every means be a violator of his order and honour if he judges that these matters ought to be suppressed from the hearing of any cleric or of the whole Church.”]

Can a bishop truly speak these words if soldiers and tyrants enter for his dinner while the pilgrim remains outside? If his door is shut to the traveller but opened to the soldier and the emperor? Martin could say these things: he never made his meal common with a king, but frequently with a poor person. Both king and queen also received as a great favour the fact that, compelled by entreaties, he once deigned to attend their dinner.

[Note: [Col. 1263D–1264D] From the Life of Saint Gregory, ch. 22:

> “Gregory maintained such hospitality even in the patriarchal palace that, besides those whom he mercifully supported by ecclesiastical alms, both throughout various regions and at Rome itself, while they fled the swords of Lombard treachery, he invited every day to his own table whatever pilgrims there were.”

Likewise, ch. 27:

> “In his time the Lord’s steward distributed grain, wine, cheese, vegetables, bacon, edible animals, fish, and oil with the utmost discrimination. Spices and other more delicate commodities he honourably offered to eminent persons, so that the Church was thought to be nothing other than a sort of common storehouse.”

Likewise, from book three, ch. 48:

> “Gregory restrained the greed or crimes of all judges, as though by a curb and bridle, with the very strong authority of his pontificate. And if he could not gently correct some from their perversity, he publicly exposed them by the rebukes of his decrees.”]

Gregory could say these things, for he scattered all the Church’s resources and gave them to the poor, not [Col. 1263C] to soldiers or princes. Yet he was accustomed to win the devotion and affection of such persons without harm, offering precious spices or other rare little gifts of foreign products to eminent men. This was done without loss to the poor—indeed, with much gain for them—because, whenever he offered balsam or another such precious product to eminent persons, he moved them to love himself and the Church; and through their devotion the resources of the poor remained safe and undiminished.

So far as could be done without harm to the poor, he showed himself in this manner even toward great persons, so that he himself might be loved by all and the Church might be regarded as a common storehouse. Far be it, however, that he should be thought to have feared princes or soldiers so much as to be accustomed somehow to conciliate them at the cost of harm or offence to the poor. Rather, we read this concerning him in his Life: that he restrained the greed or crimes of all judges as though by a curb and bridle, with the very strong authority of his pontificate.

[Col. 1264A] Thus he was a fellow elder of the elder Peter, not exercising lordship over the clergy but made an example to the flock; and every saying found concerning Job could most truly be applied to him. He could preserve all these things without hindrance to common life, which he both maintained with his clerics while pope and commanded Augustine, bishop of the English, to maintain. For if common life could not be observed by a bishop with his clerics while administering pontifical care, Pope Gregory would have given Augustine two contradictory commands. Yet he commanded him to preserve common life, not allowing a bishop to live apart from his clerics; and in a certain decree concerning Church revenues he assigned to that same bishop a fourth share from them, indicating in that decree that it was to be made for hospitality [Col. 1264B] and reception of guests.

Hence the same blessed man, rebuking Bishop Marianus for avarice, declared that he bore the empty title of bishop because, devoting himself only to prayer and reading, he produced no fruit from his hand; whereas a bishop ought to have a generous hand, assist those suffering need, and count another’s poverty as his own. For, he says, “if he does not have it thus, he holds the empty title of bishop.” The holy man was stirred to this stern rebuke by zeal for God because he had learned that certain beggars had passed through the church of that same Marianus and had received nothing from him.

O blessed pontiff, who wished all men to be such as he himself was! His hand was truly a common treasury for all in need, because he took care to receive not for himself but for others. He would indeed have received nothing from anyone had he not done so for the needy. Therefore it was not improper that offerings were then laid at his feet, as at Peter’s feet, because they were distributed from there not to the rich but to the poor. No one, then, ought to have been dissuaded from offering at the feet of such a pope what he could, because the offering was given not so much to him as transmitted through him into the bosoms of the poor. For he himself, poor, ministered to the poor; and in the palace, as in a monastery, he maintained apostolic life in a wondrous and difficult manner, not exercising lordship over the clergy [Col. 1264D] but made an example to the flock.

It is therefore not impossible for a bishop both to administer the care of a bishopric and to observe common life with his clerics. For in the plainness of clothing, frugality of food, ordering of fasts, and indeed every [Col. 1265A] quality of his habits and actions, a bishop may preserve regular measures in such a way that, when he cannot himself attend the assembly of his clerics, no cleric or monk, however religious, will be unwilling to be at his side, since at the bishop’s house no one is compelled to relax regular strictness.

Thus blessed Augustine, who allowed meat to be served at his table for the sick and for guests, nevertheless provided a simple and regular diet of vegetables and legumes for those who were healthy and living with him. He took care, that is, to observe toward strangers and the infirm the duty of hospitality and condescension in such a way that he did not in any degree relax regular strictness for those who lived with him and were healthy.

Who, then, however great a lover of cloister discipline he might be, [Col. 1265B] would not gladly be with such a bishop, in whose company one heard not empty tales of secular affairs but the words of sacred reading? In whose company the body was not served beyond what it needed, but only its weakness was restored, that it might possess the strength necessary for its function?

If bishops act thus, they will be not merely companions but also regular masters of those who live in community. Nor will they live apart from their clerics, since, when they cannot attend their assemblies themselves, they will gather the better members from the cloisters to themselves and treat them regularly, not carnally. Therefore there was no contradiction in what blessed Gregory wrote to blessed Augustine, since regular and communal life can be preserved even [Col. 1265C] in the episcopate, so that, according to Peter’s teaching, the bishop is not one exercising lordship over the clergy but one made an example to the flock.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Whether bishops may devote themselves to secular affairs, the courts of princes, military pursuits, and so forth; and what the apostles and holy doctors of the Church thought on this matter.

It is clear what Peter thought concerning the life of bishops; after Christ, he is to be heard before all others in the Roman See. Let us also hear what Paul says, he who must be counted with Peter among the chief members of that Church which judges all and is itself judged by no one.

Speak, Paul: what do you think concerning a pontiff? Ought a [Col. 1265D] pontiff to administer royal functions? Hear what he says: “Every pontiff, taken from among men, is appointed on behalf of men in those things which pertain to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins” (Heb. 5:1). If, therefore, a pontiff is appointed only in those things which pertain to God, what has he to do with things that pertain to royal office? If he is set over this task, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, why is he occupied in assembling soldiers and arranging campaigns with the king? Is doing this an offering of sacrifice for sins, when, leading an army, he cannot spend even one night in any town without countless sins of soldiers and squires?

If God is appeased by such a sacrifice, then truly the lord of Mainz ought to be preferred to blessed Martin in the kingdom of heaven. But it is better that we pray Martin to pray for the man of Mainz than believe that he is to be preferred to Martin in this way. For if we believe or think this, we do not agree with the Roman Church instructing us through Paul. For Paul himself openly affirms, not only concerning a pontiff but concerning every person professing Christ’s warfare, that no one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs (2 Tim. 2:4). Behold, we have two witnesses, pre-eminent among all the judges of the Roman Church. [Col. 1266B] Their testimony may suffice us, because every matter stands upon the testimony of two or three witnesses.

Nevertheless, if anyone thinks that their words ought to be interpreted in such a way as not to commend common and apostolic life to the clergy in these matters, let him consider the later Fathers. They did not seek allegory in these words but applied them to that rule of life which the Lord gave to his disciples and, through his disciples, to all ministers of his word, saying: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

Pope and martyr Urban understood these words in such a way that, by decretal [Col. 1266C] enactment, he ordained that all congregations of clerics throughout mother churches should be established so that apostolic and common life might remain in them perpetually in times to come. It is therefore pointless for anyone to think that advice must be sought from the Apostolic See, as though this were a new matter, concerning whether common and apostolic life ought to be restored. We have ready to hand the decrees of Pope and martyr Urban, who promulgates a terrible anathema against violators of his constitutions.

[Note: [Col. 1265D–1266D] Pope and martyr Urban:

> “It is fitting, beloved, that all Christians imitate him whose name they have received. We know that you are not ignorant that common life has hitherto flourished among good Christians and still flourishes through God’s grace, and especially among those chosen for God’s portion, that is, the clerics. As is written in the Acts of the Apostles (4:32): ‘The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul.’”]

These decrees are found, without the labour of travel and without great expense, in almost every church archive; and yet bishops delay in arming themselves with them, seeking and waiting to be strengthened for this work by new decrees or charters of privileges. Yet God himself, who makes those of one manner dwell in a house, established it in himself, founded it through the apostles, [Col. 1266D] and confirmed it by the teachings and examples of many orthodox Fathers.

If we must consult the Apostolic See concerning matters that are certain and evident, why do we not consult it whether we ought to believe in God the almighty Father? But if it is thought superfluous, in a matter so plainly established by the faith of the apostles, to await the counsel of the apostolic lords, why, in other equally certain and evident institutions of apostles and apostolic persons, is one made to wait until a new charter or privilege is brought from the Roman See?

[Col. 1267A] Blessed Pope Honorius—and blessed the saying of his mouth!—I heard him give such an answer to the lord archbishop of Salzburg, who through his legate was consulting the Apostolic See about certain matters already settled:

> “There are,” he said, “writings long ago promulgated concerning these matters in the possession of the lord archbishop himself. He need not inquire concerning them or wait for some new document from us. Let him use the ancient writings; for, having zeal for God, he will have our help in all matters in which the ancient traditions of the Fathers favour him.”

I afterward preserved these words, or words not greatly unlike them but adequately expressing this sense, as though I had received them from a divine oracle. For we see many persons so lukewarm and timid in matters certain and even often decided by the judgment of the Fathers that they need to be reminded by these words, so that in clear cases they may act confidently without awaiting any counsel, certain that Peter and Peter’s vicar will help them when their building is supported by the rock of truth, not the sand of corrupt custom, and is everywhere strengthened by the ancient statutes of the Fathers as by firm and incorruptible columns.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The life of clerics is not inferior to the life of monks. What clothing a monk made pope or bishop should use.

For if one carefully considers what the ancient Fathers thought and left written concerning the life of clerics, although the holy strictness of monks is great, we nevertheless read that they equated in every respect the holiness and strictness of clerical life with it, so that we find clerical life preferred even with great earnestness by Blessed Ambrose and John Chrysostom.

[Note: [Col. 1267C–1268D] Ambrose, in his Register, on the distinction between clerics and monks:

> “Who can doubt that these two things were more excellent in the earlier devotion of Christians: the offices of clerics and the institutions of monks? The former are trained in courtesy and moral discipline; the latter in abstinence and patience. The former are as it were in a theatre; the latter in secret. The former is seen; the latter is hidden. Therefore the good athlete says: ‘We have become a spectacle to this world’ [cf. 1 Cor. 4:9]—indeed worthy to be watched by angels while he wrestled to attain the prize, while he contended to establish in the world the life of angels and refute in heaven the wickedness of angels. For he wrestled with spiritual wickednesses. Rightly did the world behold him, so that the world might imitate him.
>
> “This life is in the stadium, that in the cave. This is against the confusion of the world, that against the desire of the flesh. This subdues bodily pleasures; that flees them. This is more gracious; that safer. This governs itself; that restrains itself. Yet each denies itself so as to become Christ’s. For to the perfect it was said: ‘Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me’ (Matt. 16:24). Therefore he follows Christ who can say: ‘I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me’ (Gal. 2:20).
>
> “Paul denied himself when, knowing that bonds and tribulations awaited him in Jerusalem, he voluntarily offered himself to dangers, saying: ‘I do not hold my life dearer than myself, provided I may complete my course and the ministry of the word which I received from the Lord Jesus’ (Acts 20:24). At last, though many stood around him weeping and entreating him, he did not turn back his mind. Thus ready faith is a stern judge of itself.
>
> “This life therefore fights; that withdraws itself. This conquers enticements; that flees them. For this, the world is triumphed over; for that, it is exiled. To this, the world is crucified—or it to the world; to that, the world is unknown. This has more temptations and therefore a greater victory; that falls less often and is more easily guarded.”]

[Note: [Col. 1268D] John Chrysostom, in his dialogue addressed to Saint Basil:

> “The soul of a priest ought to be brighter than the rays of the sun themselves, so that he may never be abandoned by the Holy Spirit, but may be able to say: ‘I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me.’
>
> And shortly afterward:
>
> “A priest indeed needs a far greater brightness of life than monks do. Although he needs it more intensely, he is nevertheless subject to more necessities than the monk, which can make him largely unclean unless, by continual care and utmost exertion, he always shows himself impenetrable. Great indeed is the struggle of monks, and great the hardship of their labour. But if anyone compares the toils of their resolution with a priesthood well administered, he will find them to differ as much as a private person differs from a king.”]

For since the monk ought to conquer the world by flight, but the cleric by battle, Blessed Ambrose so defines the life of each that, in [Col. 1268A] his judgment, neither monk may insult cleric nor cleric monk by claiming that one ought to be found superior or inferior to the other in the strength of holiness, if both cleric and monk wish to rely perfectly upon his teaching. Thus he describes them as equal in holiness, though different in battle.

For this reason holy monks of old consented with difficulty to be advanced to clerical order, and with still greater difficulty to clerical warfare. Many exercise clerical order within the enclosure of monasteries who would not easily consent to labour in clerical warfare through the office of government and preaching. But whether willing or unwilling, holy and well-regulated monks must without exception be drawn and compelled to this; just as all acephalous and irregular clerics must be rejected.

For in our time this is necessary because of the scarcity of regular clergy, whereas formerly, when all episcopal, baptismal, and other provostial churches fostered the common life of clerics, it rarely occurred. For no shortage of regular clerics compelled it, except when someone shone among the monks with such great virtues that he seemed deservedly worthy not only to be distinguished with clerical rank, but also to be appointed leader and prince in the very warfare of the clergy.

Thus appointed, he governed the holy order of clerics, himself becoming not merely one of the clerics but also their master; so that he always proved by life and action [Col. 1268C] that he had not lost the holiness of a monk, but had gained clerical dignity. Hence a monk advanced among the clergy, when about to perform some clerical office, does not put off the monastic garment, but puts the clerical one over it. For if he is elected pope, once enthroned he will thereafter never appear publicly without clerical dress, because the necessity at once rests upon him of laboring with Peter, prince of the clerics, whose place he holds. Nor can he enjoy, with Benedict [Col. 1269A], leader of monks, the beloved silence—though he does not abandon Benedict’s holiness and purpose.

But a bishop chosen from among monks and advanced among clerics, to whom it is sometimes granted to enjoy Rachel’s embraces with Benedict and at other times, by Peter’s office, to pursue fruitfulness from Leah, may during the days and seasons of his repose wear the holy monastic habit without clerical dress. But when he is required to attend the choir of clerics in some episcopal ministry, he should suitably use clerical vesture. That is, episcopal insignia are to be added when appropriate to the common clerical garments, sometimes worn without a mitre: when he solemnly performs the offices in church or examines clerics’ cases [Col. 1269B] in a public assembly. In this assembly, which they call a chapter, just as he himself ought not to appear without clerical dress, so he ought to permit none of the clerics to join that holy assembly unless he wears clerical clothing—namely, a full-length tunic. We ought to love this all the more because it is commended to us by the authority of both the Old and the New Testament.

## CHAPTER XXIX. What the alb and the full-length tunic of clerics signify mystically, by what figures they were prefigured in each Testament, what their tonsure is like, etc.

In the garments of Aaron, the first high priest, twisted fine linen shines conspicuously; his sons gleam in God’s ministry with linen garments; their descendants [Col. 1269C] use a linen ephod. Since, therefore, priests shine with the whiteness of linen from the drawers up to the tiara, together with their other adornments, what does this signify except the inviolable authority of our order, radiant chastity, and the purity of an honorable life? What does the tunic of Samuel, who appoints kings, signify but our linen, full-length tunic? If we keep it with a pure heart, according to the etymology of its name, we shall stand before the supreme King as a royal and priestly race.

Let that man come to mind who in Ezekiel is said to be clothed in linen and to have a writer’s ink-horn at his loins (Ezek. 9:2). Such power is ascribed to him that, beginning at the sanctuary, he preserves through the figure of the letter *tau* those whom [Col. 1269D] he judges worthy; but those whom he judges unworthy he does not hesitate to expose to the swords of six men without the mark of that letter. The sublimity of this power is truly attributed to those who, joining bodily chastity to purity of heart through discernment, are most powerfully girded with the sword of God’s word upon the thigh; who guard the bed of the true Solomon; and who, with a pure eye, unceasingly contemplate the King himself in his beauty.

Let us now come to the New Testament—to the Son of God and man himself, who, as is certain, consecrated in himself every grade of clerical order and handed down to his disciples, and through the disciples to us, the rule of common life which we live. He himself, I say, the true high priest and priest, sanctified our habit in himself when, [Col. 1270A] transfigured upon the mountain, he appeared in a white garment. In his Passion he was clothed in purple and white: as in the purple he sanctified martyrdom, so in the white garment he sanctified priesthood.

Angels likewise are read to have appeared in white garments both at his resurrection and at his ascension, so that all clerical persons may bear witness to the Lord’s resurrection and ascension by their very habit, whenever they are seen wearing only the white, full-length tunic. The white garment in a cleric also signifies the Lord’s Passion, which the black habit of monks represents: both because through much chastisement one is brought to whiteness, and because the very shape of its sleeves displays an image of the Lord’s cross.

[Col. 1270B] Yet the effeminate garment of the acephali does not represent this most beloved image of the holy cross. Its sleeves do not end at the hands, from which they take their name, but at the feet, or even on the ground together with the robe itself. Thus through the same garment they display in themselves more the form of vanity than of religion, more of wantonness than of the cross or Crucified One. And by the deformed habit of their religion, though it be costly and splendid, they disfigure their order just as much as if, as many of them do, they cast it off altogether. For, as Isidore testifies: “Just as a woman without a veil disfigures her head, so a cleric walking without his habit disfigures his order.”

[Col. 1270C] But let us adorn the clerical order not only in bodily dress but also by the tonsure and shaving of the head, though with Elisha we bear from children a hundred years old the reproach of being bald for Christ. For we are shaven and, as it were, made bald according to the pattern of him whom we adore as crucified for us on the place of Calvary. Therefore let the sign of the cross and the baldness of the Crucified One suitably appear in our habit; and at the hour of temptation let the cross itself be faithfully impressed upon our breasts and foreheads, so that the devil, seeing the sign of his condemnation both in our movement and in our bodily habit, may be crushed by the power of Christ crucified for us.

This custom was once most celebrated and most beloved by Christ’s faithful, who with the Apostle gloried [Col. 1270D] in nothing but Christ’s cross. Hence certain holy martyrs were discovered by persecutors through this: they were accustomed always, and at nearly every hour, to fortify their foreheads with this most renowned sign. Nor could they be turned aside from this holy and salutary practice even by fear of death. I think—or rather, I do not wish to doubt—that God’s holy martyrs, glorying in Christ’s cross, experienced some great benefit in this practice. They did not wish to omit it even when they saw nearly the whole world raging to hunt them down. For they knew that if they were ashamed before men of Christ and even of his outward insignia, he too would be ashamed of them before his angels.

Thus, if the holy martyr Narcissus had been ashamed of the outward insignia of his [Col. 1271A] religion, Affra—then a pagan but later to become a holy martyr—would not have discovered that he was a bishop of the Christians; and both she and the entire city of Augusta would then have remained in paganism. But because the holy bishop, even while avoiding persecution, was not ashamed of the cross, frequently impressing it upon his forehead, the persecutors recognized him as a Christian. Recognized, he was sought; sought, he was hidden beneath linen by Affra; and, lest he be found through more diligent searching, he was transferred from the mother to the daughter. In all this Affra imitated the ancient prostitute Rahab in such a way that it is not vainly believed that, just as Rahab deserved to be numbered among God’s people by receiving, concealing, and sending out by another way Joshua’s envoy (Josh. 6:17), so Affra deserved to be joined to the heavenly city by receiving, concealing, and sending by another way to her mother the envoys of the true Jesus.

This whole benefit would have been lost had Narcissus been ashamed of the cross. But because he was not ashamed of the cross and the other outward signs of holiness, Affra was converted through him together with all her kin and household. Affra, I say, was converted into a most noble plant of future fruit, and into the choicest grain, seed of a future harvest. Falling to the ground through the sprinkling [Col. 1271B] of blood, it died for this purpose: to bear much fruit, transmitting examples of great virtue to posterity. For the holy and precious martyr, brought before the persecutor’s tribunals and questioned concerning her property, proved herself truly a fellow-disciple of the apostles and, after them, a follower of Christ. Before the judge she gloried in the Lord that she had already distributed all her possessions to the poor; and, clinging more closely to Christ himself, she rejoiced in the priceless treasure of the one precious pearl.

## CHAPTER XXX. The customs of the primitive Church must be expressed by clerics and monks in life and virtues. Bishops should exclude from sacred orders those unwilling to do so.

For it was the custom of ancient times that whoever was perfectly converted made all his goods common to the needy: either remaining in his own house, himself poor, and ministering from it to the poor, as Tabitha did, who remained in [Col. 1271D] her house full of good works and alms; or leaving house and goods together, all at once, and contributing them to the common fund, as many men and women did under the apostles in the primitive Church. Therefore, excepting those bound by the marriage bond who used this world as though not using it, bought as though not possessing, rejoiced as though not rejoicing—occupying, that is, the place of the imperfect, and escaping the sulphurous punishments of the Sodomites in little Zoar—excepting these, I say, and counting among them the women who followed the Lord from afar, only those clung more closely to Christ with the disciples and were judged worthy above others of the name of disciples, male or female, who, bound by the laws of continence, left all their possessions together for the Lord.

[Col. 1272A] These were divided into three classes. Some, having distributed all their own possessions, sought their livelihood from the labor of their hands, burdening no one, as Aquila and Priscilla did; the Apostle joined himself to them while they sought a livelihood by their handiwork. Others, contributing their possessions into one fund, gave themselves over to another’s direction, not to be treated delicately but to be rightly disciplined, as many men and women are recorded to have done under Peter. Others again remained in their own homes and, keeping the law of chastity under someone’s direction, poor persons ministered to poor persons: as the widow Tabitha did under Peter; as the martyr Valerian and Caecilia did under Saint Urban; and as Chromatius, father of the martyr Tiburtius, did under Pope Gaius. They retained their goods in their houses for this purpose, themselves living more sparingly [Col. 1272B] than certain others whom they supported as needy.

Among these three classes I do not venture to judge who among the perfect were more perfect. Yet I say that those were safer who, leaving everything once for all, either lived by the labor of their hands, as those fellow-workers of Paul did—whom many most perfect Fathers of Egypt later imitated—or, living from the offerings of the faithful, devoted themselves wholly to God’s word, both teaching and learning it, as the leaders and disciples did after the Lord’s ascension when, through the Holy Spirit, they were gathered together at Jerusalem.

The clergy ought to imitate these, serving not the world but the altar, just as, according to the Apostle’s testimony, the Lord himself [Col. 1272C] ordained. Neither a bishop nor a king nor anyone whatsoever may, has ever been allowed to, or ever will be allowed to establish anything contrary to his ordinance in God’s holy Church. For Pope Felix testifies that at the final judgment God will require from the rulers such a Church as was ordered by Christ and the apostles, not such as it is now corrupted by soldiers and acephali. Hence, as the same Pope Felix testifies, whoever among bishops does not strive to restore Christ the Bridegroom’s bride in the condition in which we read that she was ordered and adorned by the apostles, her first bridal attendants, is now recognized as alien to the holy and apostolic Church and will then manifestly be excluded from it.

For in writing to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, not yet separated from the Church, he says among other things: “Listen to the voice of the Lord warning: ‘Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters’ (Luke 11:23). And consider carefully that not resisting what is opposed to Christ is nothing other than openly professing oneself his enemy.” And shortly afterward: “I warn, exhort, and urge you to correct what has been omitted, and by subsequent efforts to cause better things to be thought of you. For to neglect, when you can, to cast down the perverse is nothing other than to foster them; nor are those free from the stain of secret partnership who fail to oppose an evident crime.” And after a few intervening words: “For,” he says, “it is certain that on the day of judgment such a Church as we received from the Fathers will be demanded from us. Let him know even in this life that he does not belong to it who not only attempts to inflict what is harmful upon [Col. 1273A] its fullness, but also neglects to provide what is fitting for it.”

If these words are true, then at the day of judgment it is not an acephalic but an apostolic Church that will be required from bishops’ hands. Nor will the righteousness of soldiers—which they devise for themselves against God’s righteousness, that they may possess the goods of the poor—be able either to save them when the world burns, or to excuse bishops before God the Judge for yielding to multitude or custom and neglecting divine justice in favor of the ingrained custom of the acephali or the unjust justice of soldiers. For although they could not wholly uproot evil men, they could nevertheless disturb them by protest; they could excommunicate the leaders of error; they could exclude acephali from their fellowship and counsels; they could attack the same men continually and courageously, even if they could not quickly defeat them. They could constantly set before monks the examples of Paul, Aquila, Priscilla, and the Egyptian Fathers, that they might walk in their footsteps, devoting attention to work; placing Benedict’s Rule, which greatly commends manual labor, before modern customs, and vigilantly walking by it in the path of uprightness. Bishops could rebuke those monks who presume through their privileges to emancipate themselves from the obedience of the bishops themselves, charging them with transgression of the Rule, which in the third degree of humility teaches that a monk must submit to his superior with every obedience. But a bishop is superior to a monk established in his diocese. Therefore, if they wished, [Col. 1273C] bishops could either recall such monks to obedience and observance or exclude them, as transgressors of the Rule, from fellowship with themselves and with those obedient to them.

Bishops could also set before clerics the holy apostles and their disciples, apostolic men, serving the altar of a private household, living from the altar and not luxuriating from private property. They could compel all who are dedicated, or are to be dedicated, to sacred orders to conform to their rule; or exclude from sacred orders those who wish to live outside the rule, as rebels and disobedient to the rule. For ancient councils indicate that all clerics ought to obey and submit to this apostolic rule, frequently calling clerics subject to the rule [Col. 1274A] by the general and customary name then in use. This rule is without doubt understood to be the apostolic rule, according to which clerical life was once ordered throughout all the Churches.

Relying therefore upon the authority of holy councils, bishops could bind all clerics to submission to the Apostolic Rule; or, if they were unwilling to submit to the rule, deprive them of sacred orders.

For the holy Synod of Nicaea, chapter 17, decreed that clerics so constituted under a rule should live in such a way that this rule can only be understood as apostolic—provided one notices that, together with every pursuit of avarice and shameful gain, even private property itself is so completely cut off from clerics there according to the rule [Col. 1274B] of the apostles that, if a cleric conducts business in any manner whatever, he is to be deposed from the clergy and deemed alien to the rule.

The Synod of Chalcedon strongly supports this holy and great council in the same sense. In chapter 3 it testifies that the bishop together with his entire clergy must be subject to the apostolic rule, so as to forbid to both them and monks every concern for estates and prohibit their involvement in secular business in any degree—unless the laws impose an inescapable care, namely upon the lord bishop, who by law is bound through pastoral care to concern for many; or unless the bishop himself commands a cleric or monk to take charge of ecclesiastical property [Col. 1274C]. “Ecclesiastical property,” they say, not private property, because a cleric is not allowed to have private property—unless he is a reader or a psalmist. Unless they are bound by a vow, it is lawful for these not only to retain their own property but also to contract marriages and beget children. But, as Pope Leo affirms:

> [Col. 1273D] Pope Leo to Rusticus of Narbonne, chapter 6: “The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and presbyters. When they were laymen or readers, they could lawfully take wives and beget children. But when they attained the aforesaid ranks, what was lawful became unlawful for them. Therefore, in order that a carnal marriage may become a spiritual marriage, they must leave their wives and have them as though they had them, so that the status of their marriages may remain intact while marital intercourse ceases.”
>
> Extract from chapter 13 of the Council of Nicaea: “Because many persons constituted under a rule pursue avarice and shameful gains, the holy and great Synod rightly decreed that if anyone, after this definition, is found conducting business in any manner for the sake of shameful profit, he is to be deposed from the clergy and deemed alien to the rule.”
>
> Synod of Chalcedon, chapter 3: “Equating clerics and monks perfectly in the renunciation of secular business, it says as follows: It has come [Col. 1274D] to the holy Synod that certain persons seem to have been enrolled among the clergy in order to become, for shameful gain, lessees of others’ estates and to undertake secular business under their care, making light indeed of God’s service while running about the houses of secular persons and, through avarice, taking upon themselves concerns for estates. Therefore this holy and great Council decreed that henceforth no one—not bishop, cleric, or monk—shall lease estates or involve himself in secular business, except perhaps in the unavoidable care of orphans if the laws impose it; or if the bishop of the city commands him to take charge of ecclesiastical property, or of orphans, widows, and persons who lack all provision and especially need the Church’s help, where the cause demands it for fear of the Lord. But if anyone hereafter attempts to transgress these enactments, he shall be subject to ecclesiastical censures.”

When they are promoted to the grades of sacred orders, even if they make a vow, what was lawful begins to be unlawful for them, because ministers of the sacred altar must be subject to the apostolic rule and must not involve themselves in secular business, since this is wholly contrary to apostolic rules. But if, whether after profession of the rule or reception of sacred order, he conducts secular business in any manner whatever [Col. 1275A], he must, according to chapter 17 of the Nicene Synod, be deposed from the clergy and excluded from the rule.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Why Saint Gregory the Great permitted private property to clerics who stood outside sacred orders.

I believe that Saint Gregory relied upon these authorities when he wrote to Augustine of the English. He judged only those worthy of the bishop’s fellowship who, living communally under the apostles’ rule, exercised sacred orders; and he forbade the bishop to live separately from them. None living outside the rule were admitted among them. For the blessed man judged that these chief holy councils, like the most sacred Gospels, [Col. 1275B] were to be observed.

These matters are therefore highly necessary for our present argument, because, in Saint Gregory’s judgment, even if they seem to be stones, violators of the four principal councils do not belong to the building of the Church’s structure. Nor would the same blessed man have permitted private property to clerics established outside sacred orders had he not found it permitted in the Synod of Chalcedon. There, in chapter 14, readers and psalmists are permitted even to take wives; but this concession was not universal. For the Fathers of that council say: “Since in certain provinces readers and psalmists have been permitted to take wives,” etc. What is granted [Col. 1275C] in certain provinces must not be presumed in all provinces. Thus Saint Gregory extended this dispensation from that concession not to clerics of every province, but only to clerics of the English, because he saw that it was not contrary to the four sacred councils. But he refused to admit to sacred orders those clerics who enjoyed this dispensation and lived outside the rule, because he saw this to be contrary to the same councils, upon whose violators he pronounced an anathema in his synodical letter.

Bishops do not adequately guard against this anathema when they admit to sacred orders persons whom they know to be living outside the rule and devoted to secular business. They also frequently ordain acephali, wanderers, neither bound by a rule nor established in a place, contrary to the Fathers assembled at the Council of Chalcedon [Col. 1275D]. These Fathers judge such an imposition of hands invalid and declare that persons thus ordained ought to minister nowhere. Hence not only do bishops gravely sin by presuming, contrary to the canons confirmed under anathema by Saint Gregory and equated with the four Gospels; but also those [Col. 1276A] who knowingly hear the masses of persons ordained in this unrestricted manner, or believe that those whom the six hundred and thirty Fathers affirm can minister nowhere are able to minister anywhere. Whoever affirms that what they say cannot be done can in fact be done is presumptuous and contradicts the Holy Spirit, who spoke through their mouth.

> [Col. 1275D] Decrees of Gregory VII and Pope Urban concerning priests’ sons: “We decree that sons of presbyters are to be removed from the ministries of the sacred altar unless they have been proven to live religiously either in monasteries or in houses of regular canons.”
>
> From the Council of Toledo, chapter 20: “Under the old law Levites were commanded to serve in the tabernacle from their twenty-fifth year; the holy Fathers followed this authority in the canons. Forgetful of the command of both divine law and councils, we make infants and boys Levites before the lawful age and [Col. 1276D] before they have experience of life. Therefore, lest this be done further by us, we are admonished by the judgments of divine law and the canons: deacons are to be ordained at twenty-five years of age, so that, according to the apostolic command, they may first be proved and then minister, having no crime.”
>
> From the Council of Laodicea: “No metropolitan may presume to ordain a bishop or presbyter before thirty years of age, or before he has attained the age of a mature man, lest through youth they be restrained in some manner, as has sometimes happened.”

A great necessity therefore rests upon Catholic bishops not to permit persons so ordained to minister within their territories, lest they be found to bind themselves under anathema by opposing the principal councils. Even if this is now treated as nothing because of the vast multitude of acephali and the ingrained custom of abuses, it will nevertheless be examined at the final judgment before those who were the most vigilant observers [Col. 1276B] of these councils. One of them was Saint Augustine, who permitted no one to minister in sacred orders within his jurisdiction if he knew him to have departed from the holy purpose of the apostolic rule. Nor could the multitude of property-holders move him from this firmness. In a sermon to the people he complains of these defenders of transgressors, who had withdrawn from observance of the Rule in order to escape the strictness of that blessed Father, and yet were willing to exercise clerical office outside under the protection of the multitude.

Against them, as we noted above, that blessed man bound himself so strictly that where he was bishop, none of them was to be a cleric. Otherwise, he could not pursue them, because their defenders were property-holders; and, dwelling outside his boundaries, they murmured against him and called his life excessively austere. But because he knew that he must present to Christ such a Church as is known to have been founded by Christ, planted by the apostles, and watered with martyrs’ blood, he disregarded the custom and multitude of the wicked and followed only apostolic examples, from which he did not permit himself to be torn away.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Saint Augustine composed different rules, by which clerics and monks, virgins and widows alike, should regulate their conduct, etc.

For above, among the perfect children of the apostolic and [Col. 1276D] primitive Church, we distinguished three orders: we observed that some, with Peter and the apostles, devoted themselves to the word; others, with Paul, lived by manual labor; and others, with Tabitha the disciple, ministered in their homes to the poor, as Onesiphorus did, whose deeds the Apostle Paul commends. This wise architect so reformed all [Col. 1277A] these orders of perfection in the Church entrusted to him that he also composed special treatises for each order. In order to have in his Church clerics such as he knew had been established by the apostles—namely, men conformed to the Church’s teachers, devoted to doctrine rather than private property—he composed a short book elucidating the rules of the saints, which begins: “Before all things, most beloved brothers, let God be loved.” We have indicated the beginning of this little book because we know that it has been mutilated in many cloisters. In them the first chapters of the book are cut off because certain lesser brothers are offended partly by their obscurity and partly by their severity. Hence, at some persons’ request, we too have been compelled [Col. 1277B] to explain its more obscure passages, entrusting to God the task of making its difficult matters easy through grace poured out. For if he is in all things and through all things our illumination and salvation, through him our blindness will overcome every obscurity by seeing clearly; through him also our aided weakness will overcome every difficulty by acting courageously. His commandments, heavy as they seem to the unwilling, are not at all burdensome to those who will purely and sincerely. Let good will therefore be present, and there will be no difficulty for clerics in keeping the Rule of Saint Augustine and becoming truly fellow-disciples of Peter and the other apostles. Thus there may appear in them and under them such beauty of the Church as once existed in the apostles and under the apostles [Col. 1277C], once the custom of vanities has been destroyed—a custom now reigning among and under the acephali, who, because they are irregular, cannot govern the people subject to them.

But if monks keep the book composed by the same Father on the work of monks, conformed to the Apostle Paul they will duly fulfill their purpose; and the life not only of clerics but also of monks will be wholly apostolic: clerics serving the altar with Peter and living from the altar; monks, with Paul, diligently giving attention from time to time to work.

For under Saint Augustine the life of both, namely clerics and monks, was ordered according to the pattern handed down by the holy apostles in such a way that no one converted from the world was received into monasteries [Col. 1277D] unless he came to be suitably joined and incorporated into one or the other profession: either with clerics devoted to learning or teaching the word, or with regular monks occupied in the pursuit of labor, so that he might consider the paths of his household and not eat the bread of idleness.

If there is a true widow who wishes to remain in her own house, let her read the little book on widowhood composed by the same blessed Father Augustine—or, if she does not know letters, have it read to her—in order to learn how apostolic perfection is to be pursued with Tabitha, Peter’s disciple. She will truly be numbered among Christ’s disciples if she perseveres in understanding and doing the precepts of that book.

But women who are said to live [Col. 1278A] under a virginal profession, whether they live canonically according to Saint Augustine’s Rule or are nuns by professing the Rule of Saint Father Benedict, can never be restored more effectively to the ancient pattern of apostolic discipline, after the lamentable ruins of many abuses, than if they intelligently read, willingly reread, and obediently observe Saint Augustine’s book *On Virginity* and another, concisely composed, *On Worshipping God*. There humility is instilled in virgins, by which virginal integrity is nourished and, when nourished, preserved—integrity of virginity itself. There a discerning strictness and a strict discernment are commended, by which a woman’s body is so treated vigorously that it cannot indulge itself womanishly. For the body is like a beast of burden of the soul: it must be refreshed with sufficient food lest it fail on the way, and chastened with such restraint that it does not sometime throw into the mud its mistress riding upon it and make her, by some stain, less acceptable to the Bridegroom of virgins—she who ought to appear without spot and wrinkle.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the vices and excesses of religious women to be corrected by bishops.

For this purpose God has placed Catholic bishops over his Church as bridal attendants: that, among all those entrusted to them, they may with greater care examine those souls whom they know to be betrothed under a virginal profession to the Virgin of virgins, the Bridegroom and virginal Son. This Bridegroom, indeed, since he will be greatly offended unless his bridal attendants present to him such brides [Col. 1278C] as have neither spot nor wrinkle, will be offended if a bishop sleeps while correcting the abuses of contemporary depravity that now reign in women’s conventicles—not dwelling under apostolic teaching, but lying under apostate ruin.

These are women who, casting away modesty, the teacher of decency, think lawful whatever pleases them; and count as wholly pleasing whatever the apostles and holy Fathers have forbidden. Thus their irreligious rule works among them by forbidding, so that what has been forbidden becomes more desirable to them. They practice their desires as though lawful, while the guardianship of their bridal attendants sleeps over this. If those guardians wished to keep watch, they could surely moderate such madness to some extent, if only, against the widespread abuse of the multitude, they were willing to arm themselves with the aforesaid books of Augustine and other ancient authorities, and to be priestly inflamed against Midianite women with zeal for uprightness, like Phinehas son of the priest. For Phinehas stood up and made atonement; he did not wait for judicial procedure in an open crime.

What then is this delay of bishops amid such great and manifest apostasy of women, as though what they do were done in secret? It is shameful to say what they do in secret; yet they do so much openly that, if the bishop, in accordance with the prophet’s teaching, dug through the wall (Ezek. 8:8), a door would soon appear to him through which he might gain access for destroying what is done within [Col. 1279A]. For the wall is, as it were, dug through when outward indiscipline is touched by the rake of the word, as by an instrument for digging. To one digging there then appears a door to the inner things when the minister of the word, through God’s revelation, finds an entry for overcoming what had previously been hidden. Therefore let the bishop dig through the wall:

> [Col. 1279D] From the Council of Rouen, chapter 3: “Let a bishop frequently enter the monasteries of monks and religious women; and, sitting in their assembly with grave and religious persons, let him diligently examine their life and conduct, and strive to correct whatever he finds blameworthy. Let him also diligently investigate the chastity of religious women; and if any woman is found who, neglecting her profession of chastity, shamelessly associates with a cleric or layman, let her be sternly restrained by scourging and confined in private custody, where she may worthily repent of what she has wickedly committed. By the authority of the holy Fathers it is also decreed that no layman or cleric shall have access to their cloisters and private dwellings; nor even presbyters, except only for Mass. When Mass is completed, they are to return to their own churches.”

Let him do so by forbidding religious women costly clothing, which is not given from the sisters’ common wardrobe, but is received and retained by each woman from whatever source, through unlawful and wicked presumption—not to mention garments that they receive from lovers and those that friends privately bestow.

Accordingly, no one is permitted to make anything for herself; rather, all their work must be done in common, with greater zeal and more fervent eagerness than if they were doing it for themselves—things which they ought not to do. [Col. 1279B] The holy Fathers forbid this as though it were a crime. Indeed, on account of private work itself, lest it perhaps be done secretly, they order that beds be inspected frequently and carefully, wishing this evil not to be gently handled but cut off at the root [Note: [Col. 1280D] Rule of our holy Father Benedict, ch. 33.]: so that every person in the community, content with the food supplied from the common storeroom and the clothing brought forth from the common wardrobe, may do nothing except for the common good; because she ought to live only from the common stock and ought to possess nothing except from the common stock. For even if something is bestowed upon someone, it must not be received secretly, but presented publicly, so that, having been put into the common store, it may be supplied at the discretion of the superior to the person [Col. 1279C] who needs it.

Unless, perhaps, the garment is so precious that, if it is given to one person, it somehow makes her differ from the common fellowship; and, contrary to the Apostle’s teaching, the Church is held in contempt, while shame and embarrassment are caused in the community to those who do not possess such things. Hence blessed Augustine, truly an apostolic man, was so concerned to preserve community even in clothing that in his own community the master and bishop himself wore the same kind of garment as the priest, deacon, and subdeacon wore. For, as he himself testifies in a sermon to the people, if a somewhat more precious garment was offered which could not be common property, it was sold so that its price might be put to common use.

Therefore, by the example and instruction of so great a teacher [Col. 1279D] we are taught that a garment which by its costliness introduces inequality, and by that inequality exceeds the common standard of the community, should not be assigned to one person; rather, it should be sold and its price applied to common use. If this vice of singularity is not to be tolerated in common life even in the case of a bishop, how much less is it to be borne in one little woman, [Col. 1280A] that she should wear a precious garment through which she appears singular among the members of the community, when she ought not to keep a singular life but a common life? This abuse reigns widely among communities of women, through which common and apostolic life has altogether failed; while singular and apostate life reigns.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Religious persons who do not live religiously are to be expelled from monasteries and excommunicated.

What then will the bishop say at the final examination, when he must present them to the heavenly Bridegroom as trained and ordered in common and apostolic life, not corrupted in singular and apostate life? [Col. 1280B] When he undertook pastoral care over them, he then betrothed them to one husband, to present a chaste virgin to God. Therefore, mindful and solicitous concerning his own espousal, let him be jealous over such women with God’s jealousy, so that he may present to God in them such a bride as we find described in the aforesaid little books of Augustine, the letters of Jerome, and the words of the Apostle himself: namely, that they may be holy in body and spirit (1 Cor. 7:34).

But how will one be diligent concerning greater things who is negligent in correcting lesser things which nonetheless plainly serve greater evils? For what does private work serve, if not the great crime of apostasy? What do adornment, singularity, costliness, and superfluity in dress serve, if not the most ruinous pride and luxury? [Col. 1280C] Truly, whoever despises small things falls into great ones, because the bishop who neglects to attack the outward instruments of irreligion and cut them off with the sickle of anathema will be compelled on the day of judgment to render an account of the greatest sins to which these things lend service.

If he cut away the outward things we know, and things like them, as branches luxuriating uselessly, knowing that the time of pruning has come (Song 2:12), he would surely guard faithfully the vineyard committed to him, usefully wielding the sickle of the word. He holds it in his hand for this purpose alone: that, if he expects fruit from the hidden root of the vine, he may strive to cut away evil abuses appearing in outward dress and bearing, like useless branches clinging to the bark, when they first begin to sprout. For unless such things are cut off, [Col. 1280D] the vine cannot produce abundant fruit.

Indeed, in every community their male and female governors ought diligently to watch for this purpose, because they are commanded to stand at the Sheep Gate and the Fish Gate and to keep continual watch: that they may correct what they can, and report to the bishop what they cannot. Thus whoever in such matters was not corrected after a first and second admonition duly administered [Col. 1281A] should be cast from the midst of the flock like a diseased sheep; and if the fault were greater [Note: [Col. 1281D] Pope Siricius, in his decrees, ch. 6, says among other things concerning such persons: “We command that these shameless and detestable persons be removed from the company of monasteries and the assemblies of churches, so that, shut up in their own houses of confinement, bewailing so great a crime in continual lamentation, they may be purified by the cleansing fire of repentance, and thus pardon may assist them, at least at death, through the grace of communion, solely in view of mercy.”], being pierced by the bishop with the sword of anathema, he might provide an example to the rest, lest anyone should presume to become disobedient even in similar matters after they had been forbidden by the bishop, or even by lesser persons presiding under him in the community—even if the things forbidden seemed not unlawful, but altogether lawful and good.

For the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was not evil, but good; and before the prohibition it was lawful, nor would touching it have harmed anyone at all. But after the prohibition, those who tasted its fruit and, when reproved, did not acknowledge their fault, were shut out and condemned by the sentence of death; and they showed beforehand in themselves this judgment: [Col. 1281B] namely, what the holy Fathers later ordained should be observed in the Church, and especially in communities.
