That is, if something lawful is presumed upon after it has been forbidden, and the presumption, once rebuked, is not acknowledged, the one who forbade it should be ready to punish every disobedience by casting out the presumptuous person—not on account of the thing itself, which is lawful and good (though perhaps it furnished the cause or material for disobedience, as that tree forbidden to the first parents did), but on account of disobedience, which is never good, never lawful, and never to be passed over without punishment, especially when it is defended after reproof and doubled by that very defense.

## CHAPTER XXXV. What sword should bishops rightly use?

[Col. 1281C] If, therefore, the prohibition of bishops and other Fathers carries such weight that, while they forbid it, not even their holiest and most innocent subject may presume to receive the Lord’s body—which no one doubts is holy and good—or, if he presumes, escapes judgment; what are we to judge this power of forbidding to be, except a certain sword by which unlawful things must be cut off? If it is sharp enough sometimes to cut away things that are lawful and good, with what sharpness, do you think, will it cut off unlawful things? Provided, however, that this two-edged sword proceeding from Christ’s mouth is not stored by the bishop in the sheath of silence, and that he does not take up the material sword for which Peter was rebuked.

[Col. 1282A] For of the former it is written: “Woe to him who keeps his sword back from blood” (Jer. 48:10); but of the latter the Lord says that everyone who takes the sword shall perish by the sword (Matt. 26:52). The ancient shepherds of the Churches, guarding the gate of the flock with Peter, did not consider this sword, forbidden by the Lord to his disciples, necessary for themselves, so as to seek servants whom the Lord did not have and feed soldiers from the property of poor people who were hungry. Rather, they kept themselves so far from this terribly forbidden sword, and wished their successors also to keep far from it, that the sacred canons testify that bishops are shedders of, and guilty of, human blood if, though under legal procedure, they presume to participate in a secular judgment of blood.

[Col. 1282B] Formerly, when a case was tried judicially and secularly before a ruler, no Catholic bishop involved himself in a case punishable by death or mutilation of limbs—unless perhaps, after a judgment had been rightly given, it was in order to rescue a helpless person from the hand of one stronger than he, as blessed Nicholas is recorded to have done. By contrast, certain modern bishops investigate worldly cases with kings and princes and arrange military expeditions [Note: [Col. 1281D]

From the *Life of St. Gregory*, book 36: “Gregory did not permit any bishop to leave his diocese even for a short time without utterly unavoidable necessity; and he most vehemently forbade them to occupy themselves in worldly cases. Hence he writes to the defender of Rome, saying: ‘It has been reported to us that our most reverend brother Basil, bishop, occupies himself in lawsuits as though he were one of the laity, and needlessly attends the law courts. Since this both makes him contemptible [Col. 1282D] and destroys priestly reverence, as soon as your experience has received this command, compel him by strict enforcement to return, so that he may not be permitted to remain there for five days under any pretext while you are present. For if you allow him in any way to remain there longer, you will begin to be guilty before us along with him.’

Likewise, to Anthimus the subdeacon: “Primennius has come to our notice,” etc., as appears in ch. 37 of the *Life of St. Gregory*.]

—where the blood of not one man but many is shed, and where the helpless are not rescued from the hand of one stronger than they. Rather, peasants and the poor are miserably afflicted, when soldiers do not follow the counsel John gives to soldiers who wish to be saved: that they should extort from no one and make no false accusation, [Col. 1282C] but be content with their wages.

Why, then, do we wonder that they hold back God’s sword from blood, when through soldiers they conduct the business of robbery and through princes the judgment of blood? Certain bishops who participate in handling and examining cases use the most wretched cloak of excuse. Yet at the end, when the judicial sentence itself is delivered, they withdraw for the moment of a single hour, so that they may appear thereby to observe the decrees of the canons forbidding bishops to take part in a judgment of blood. They also often try to avert the sentence of vengeance which they themselves previously endeavored to dictate.

Thus the devil also [Note: [Col. 1282D] Augustine, in his sermon on John: “See the kind of murder, brothers. The devil is called a murderer; he did not come to a man armed with a sword or girded with iron, but sowed an evil word and killed him. Therefore do not think that you are not a murderer when you persuade your brother to evil. If, by persuading your brother to evil, you kill him—and that you may know that you kill him—hear the Psalmist: ‘The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword’ (Ps. 56:5).”] took part in the judgment of blood in Christ’s passion, but withdrawing near the end and foreseeing his own [Col. 1283A] condemnation, he even worked through Pilate’s wife for Christ’s release. Yet not merely homicide but, so to speak, deicide is rightly imputed to him in full, since that judgment of blood is recognized as having been begun and to a great extent conducted through his agency.

Likewise, the Jews, saying, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death” (John 18:31), tried thereby to appear excusable, because they did not themselves crucify him, but Roman soldiers did; yet whatever those soldiers did is most rightly imputed to the Jews, whose will the soldiers thereby served. Therefore, just as then, so now, the sin of a prince judging wrongly, and of a soldier and shield-bearer proclaiming it, falls wholly back upon the bishops who devise worldly counsels, from which they themselves ought to be exempt even when these are conducted according to law. [Col. 1283B]

## CHAPTER XXXVI. By what means a bishop should bring nuns living irreligiously back to fruitfulness and regular observance.

Thus, yes, thus the sword forbidden to Peter is wielded by bishops; but the sword of the word, which they ought always to have ready and never to hold back from blood, lies hidden in the sheath of silence. They do not restrain by it even princes raging against the Church; nor do they dare to strike with it weak women who have professed the apostolic life and, in apostasy, have turned aside with the devil. I do not mean binding them in matters lawful, in which not everything permitted is beneficial; but in exceedingly unlawful excesses [Col. 1283C] which are not only not beneficial, but greatly impede all holiness.

For, to say nothing of the private property of nuns—or rather, demon-nuns—which, in pursuing and retaining it, they commit the most manifest crime of apostasy, what good does superfluity and costliness of clothing do their holiness? Or private work, and every disordering of regular ordinances, while no such community of demon-nuns proceeds according to rule, as the Rule commands? They put on clothing which they do not receive from the common wardrobe. They eat food which they have not received from the common storeroom. They give their old clothing, as though it were their own property, to whomever they wish. They send the leftovers of food, as though their own, [Col. 1283D] to whomever they wish. They do private work in which they serve not the common benefit, but, as they wish, whom they wish, and for as long as they wish, in order either to gain friends thereby or to pursue private profits by working privately.

A bishop, the faithful friend of the Bridegroom, could first forbid these disorders and others equal to or certainly greater than them; then, if those under prohibition did not obey, [Col. 1284A] he could cut off the disobedient with the sickle of anathema, delivering such persons to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved—provided that any of them, healthfully pierced with compunction, came fully to her senses [Note: [Col. 1283D] From the decrees of Pope Vigilius: “It must be known that those who falsify or deny ecclesiastical or synodal judgments canonically made, once convicted by reason, are to be punished by a sentence of excommunication; that is, they are to fast seven Lents on bread, salt, and water, [Col. 1284D] because in truth despisers of synodal decrees have been anathematized by all councils. Therefore it is fitting that despisers and deniers of sacred Scripture should fast as many Lents as excommunicated persons are ordered to observe in their absolution on account of the sevenfold negligence concerning the legally appointed periods of truce,” etc.].

But if all who turn back should say, “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (John 6:60), ought the bishop to abandon this hard and true saying because of those who are hardened? Certainly, this saying is not hard except to the hard. But to those who do not have a heart hardened with Pharaoh, these sayings are softer than oil, and they are themselves darts (Ps. 54:22). For they anoint, like oil, those who faithfully obey; but they prick, like darts, those who do not obey. Thus the sayings are oil and darts because of the great difference among their hearers, [Col. 1284B] healing some and wounding others.

Wounded and struck by these darts from the watchmen of the city, the Bride, grievously languishing, would seek the Beloved—provided, however, that the cloak of false religion or evil defense were first stripped from her by those same guardians of the walls, so that the naked wound might appear. This wound lay hidden for a long time, veiled as though by a cloak through the protection of the multitude and the fault of inveterate custom.

This cloak is stripped from nuns if the disorder just described is forbidden by the bishop under anathema; if he commands throughout all their communities that they be fed from one storeroom, clothed from one wardrobe, and that no woman have any power over leftovers of food. Rather, the female steward of the poor should gather all such leftovers, not to put them out again on another day of the month, but to give them on that same day to Lazarus perhaps lying before the gate. [Col. 1284C] Those receiving new garments from the wardrobe should also surrender their old ones; these too, like the leftovers of food, insofar as they can remain beyond the needs of the household, are to be given to Lazarus.

Doing no private work, they ought to work for the common good in such a way as to prove that they have renounced private property so completely that they do not even have hands of their own with which they may presume to do anything—except what, how much, and how they are commanded by those persons who are set over them according to the Rule. Thus they deny themselves to themselves if they do not do with even their own members what they wish; if they do not proceed even in good works as they wish. Rather, in all things and through all things they should strive to obey the Rule, praying at a fixed time, reading at a fixed time, and distributing in due order all that they do over the hours, so that they may be found together in prayer, together in reading, together in work, together in refreshment, together in nighttime rest, together in the performance of night watches—[Col. 1284D] unless perhaps some are, because of unavoidable necessity, regularly exempted for a time from this ordered battle-line, to return to order if the necessity should cease.

If the bishop commands all these things and forbids every disorder, he will quickly see some obedient and proceeding according to rule, while others are disobedient and go forth outside after the tracks of the flocks.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Above all, a bishop must take care to introduce into his episcopal church regular canons who profess the common life.

But the whole holy and regular order, among clergy as among nuns, will proceed regularly [Col. 1285B] if the bishop first becomes a true Jacob; if he himself, being circumcised, has circumcised sons—that is, if he himself, being regular, has regular clergy; if he receives into his own right his only daughter, namely, the Church entrusted to him, which, like Jacob’s daughter Dinah, has been defiled by irregular clergy as by an uncircumcised man. Once received, he must never return her to those defilers and uncircumcised persons, unless they are circumcised and joined to the twelve apostles, as to twelve patriarchs, by the sign of spiritual circumcision in the observance of regular life.

For thus they will either be Israelites, receiving not only the regular habit but true circumcision of the heart; or they will be Shechemites, outwardly feigning religion so that they may obtain [Col. 1285C] the desired revenues of churches, as Shechem, prince of the land, sought by outward circumcision to obtain Dinah’s desired embraces (Gen. 34:19 ff.).

Therefore, just as Israelites are called from Israel, so Shechemites are called from Shechem. For among many who profess religion, some are made like Israel not only outwardly through the regular habit but much more inwardly through true circumcision of heart. Each of these will hear from the Lord: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no guile” (John 1:47). But others are made like Shechem, prince not of heaven but of earth, who circumcised himself not from love of God but for pleasure of the flesh. Yet if Shechem had not consented even thus to be circumcised, [Col. 1285D] he would not have obtained the daughter of the truly circumcised Israelite for God’s sake; nor would Israel, truly circumcised, have entered into a covenant with one falsely circumcised, a covenant which was to be broken on the third day.

For on the third day Simeon and Levi killed that same Shechem with all the males circumcised for pleasure; nor did they suffer any danger for this from the tribesmen of those killed. For the terror of God, seizing everyone round about, did not allow them to pursue the people beloved of God and faithfully circumcised.

Now all these things happened to them figuratively. No uncircumcised person, no one who is not distinguished by the form of religion, ought to obtain any church. Or if an uncircumcised and irregular person, obtaining it irregularly, has corrupted it, he ought without doubt to relinquish [Col. 1286A] it until either he becomes a faithfully circumcised Israelite, able, struggling, to defend the daughter of wrestling Jacob and, once defended, make her fruitful; or certainly, if he is circumcised not faithfully but faithlessly in order to enjoy the pleasure of ecclesiastical honor through an outward image of holiness, he should be tolerated by true Israelites for two days and killed on the third day.

For as long as a professor and exhibitor of holiness sins only in thought or in an act of concealed uncleanness, he is, as it were, tolerated for two days and the covenant which he has with true Israelites is not broken, because no one is deposed from rule on account of intended or secretly committed uncleanness. But if the third day dawns—if the previously hidden uncleanness plainly appears—then Simeon and Levi, namely every Catholic of priestly and Levitical [Col. 1286B] order, ought to gird himself with the sword, so that vengeance for fornication may be taken in such a way that the sinner of three days does not become one of four days, stinking and putrid.

But if it happens that he becomes one of four days and his stench spreads, he must no longer sit in the chair of pestilence and contaminate the Church. Rather, humbled in some penitential place of confinement, as though lying in a tomb, he should await Jesus, the raiser of such dead persons—he who is able even to call the dead from the tomb and, as a testimony to his power, restore them anew to the lost duties of sacred order.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. A fallen cleric is not to be admitted to the functions of office and order unless he has completed penance according to ancient discipline.

[Col. 1286C]

Hence it is that, in the rebuilding of the city of Jerusalem, the children of Israel, having built the Sheep Gate and the Fish Gate, next rebuilt the Old Gate (2 Esdras 3:6). Whoever can stand and persevere at the Sheep Gate and the Fish Gate does not seek entrance through the Old Gate. But whoever has fallen from there through sin, having undoubtedly been cast out by divine judgment or by human judgment divinely authorized, cannot enter except through the Old Gate—that is, through the ancient law of penitential observance.

For those who, in imposing penances, set aside the laws and determinations of the Fathers and follow the crooked paths of customs do not introduce sinners into the city of peace, because [Col. 1286D] they do not lead them through the entrance of the Old Gate. Rather, they themselves wander in error together with those whom, fallen into criminal sin, they restore without the ancient order of penance and satisfaction either to ecclesiastical communion or, more dangerously, to the exercise of some sacred order.

For we have, as it were, the Old Gate: the holy and ancient constitution of the holy Fathers, through which criminal sinners ought to be introduced into Jerusalem. To this Old Gate, as though at its side in the rebuilding of that city, is added a tower called in the book of Ezra the Tower of the Furnaces (2 Esdras 3:11). The Holy Spirit would by no means have ordered this in an earthly building unless it were full of the sacrament of heavenly realities.

[Col. 1287A] What, then, is this tower but bodily chastisement? It is a tower providing, as it were, safe and certain refuge if anyone flees to it after sin in hope of pardon. This tower is placed by the Old Gate because bodily chastisement must be observed according to the ancient tradition of penitence, not according to the perverse abuse of modern people. For if the penitent is not fortified by this tower of bodily chastisement, deceived by a certain false security, when he says, “Peace and security,” sudden destruction will come upon him, as pain upon a woman with child, and he shall not escape.

Bodily chastisement is therefore rightly called the Tower of the Furnaces, because the ancient constitution concerning penitence [Col. 1287B] has certain furnaces for purging sinners and cautiously and diligently baking them into the house of bread. In these furnaces God himself is as a steadfast fire refining silver, and he will purge the sons of Levi (Mal. 3:2): that is, also those who have fallen from Levitical or even priestly order, whom we understand through the sons of Levi.

In such a furnace blessed Remigius baked a certain bishop, his suffragan. Having confined him in a penitential place of detention for seven years, he finally restored him, once purified and well and carefully baked, to the office of sacred order at the admonition of an angel. This penitent did not seek or aspire to restoration to the pontifical office; but, with the prodigal son, saying, [Col. 1287C] “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before thee; I am no longer worthy to be called thy son” (Luke 15:18–19), he obtained this by his humility: that the heavenly Father should say through an angel to his servant, namely holy Remigius, “Quickly bring forth the first robe” (ibid.), the priestly robe, “and put it on him,” giving a ring on his hand and shoes, that is, sandals, on his feet.

[Col. 1288A] Whoever wishes to know more fully by what great miracle all these things were done should read diligently the acts of Saint Remigius. Let this one point suffice us: the bishop was not brought out of confinement before seven years of penance had been completed, nor was he restored to the office of lost dignity at his own request, but by angelic admonition. In this respect the bishops of our own time provide badly for themselves, restoring priests or deacons exposed in a fall of the flesh far too quickly and far too easily to their lost ranks.

Therefore such persons, restored otherwise than they ought to be and set over the Lord’s table, like raw loaves not well baked, make the bridegroom and bride celebrating the wedding feast nauseated. For there is no precious or beautiful praise in the mouth of a sinner (Sirach 15:9); nor does the bread taste [Col. 1288B] good which that fire has not carefully baked in the furnace of penitence—the fire of which it is written, “Our God is a consuming fire.”

O holy Fathers, O judges chosen for the heavenly court: what is the benefit of your having established a number of years and a mode of chastisement in which penitents are to be baked, as in a certain furnace, if the abuse of modern people is to prevail over your ordinances? A murderer, or another criminal person of this kind, ought to be lawfully chastised for seven years under the testimony of an approved elder—that is, a priest of tested religious character—who, after the years of penance were complete, should present him to the bishop, testifying and truthfully affirming that he had lawfully completed the penance imposed upon him, [Col. 1288C] relaxing the fast on no day unless, by the elder’s counsel, an appointed bestowal of alms made compensation for that fast.

Assisted by such testimony, the penitent could be reconciled to the Church and become a participant in sacred communion, certain that, if he thereafter returned to his vomit, he would never find the grace of communion before his last day, never before the peril and crisis of death [Note: [Col. 1287C]

John Chrysostom, *On Repentance*: “O repentance, which, through God’s mercy, forgives sins and opens paradise; which heals the contrite, cheers every sorrowful person, recalls life from destruction, restores standing, renews honor, renews confidence, and pours forth more abundant grace. You loose all things bound; you open all things shut; you soften all adverse things; you heal all contrary things; you make clear all confused things; you give life to all desperate things. Repentance rejects avarice, abhors luxury, puts fury to flight, [Col. 1287D] strengthens love, tramples pride, restrains the tongue, orders morals, hates malice, excludes envy. Perfect repentance compels the sinner willingly to endure all things. If a violent man demands what he possesses, repentance does not forbid it; if someone takes his garment, it does not resist; to one striking his cheek, it offers the other also; when pressed into service, it adds more of its own accord; when chastised, it gives thanks; when provoked, it is silent; when exasperated, it speaks gently to a superior; as a suppliant, it submits to an inferior. In its heart is contrition, in its mouth confession, and in its work complete humility. This is perfect and fruitful repentance.”

Gregory, *On False Penances*: “Therefore we admonish all who desire to escape the punishments of eternal damnation and to attain the glory of true blessedness, that they should guard themselves against false penances. For just as false baptism does not wash away original sin, so after baptism false repentance does not blot out a sin committed. Therefore it is very necessary [Col. 1288C] that anyone who knows that he has committed some crime should entrust his soul to prudent and religious men, so that through true repentance he may obtain certain pardon for his sins.

“For this is true repentance: after committing some graver crime, such as premeditated and voluntary homicide, or perjury committed for desire of honor or money, or other things similar to these, each person should so turn himself that, abandoning every iniquity, he thereafter remains in the fruits of good works. For thus the Lord says through the prophet: ‘If the wicked man turns from his wickedness and keeps all my commandments, he shall live and shall not die’ (Ezek. 18:20–21). In these words it is plainly made clear that those who plunder the property of others and, when able, refuse to restore or make restitution for it; or those who bear arms against justice; or those who retain hatred in their heart; or those entangled in occupations or offices which cannot be carried on without fraud, falsity, envy, or deceiving their brethren—such persons are not to be believed to have turned to God or to be performing true repentance for the crimes they have committed.

“Therefore, above all things, we exhort and admonish you not to run for the receiving of penances to those in whom there is neither religious life nor knowledge of counsel, and who lead human souls more to destruction than to salvation—according to the testimony of Truth, which says: ‘If the blind lead the blind, both fall into a pit’ [Col. 1289C] (Matt. 15:14)—but to those who, instructed in religious life and the teaching of the Scriptures, are able to show you the way of truth and salvation.”]

.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Why those who formerly fell again into sin after once performing public penance were no longer admitted to ecclesiastical reconciliation.

[Col. 1289A]

Certainly, the holy Fathers wisely and beneficially provided that if anyone, after once performing public penance, should again fall into a criminal offense, he should no longer be received to reconciling penance; but, wholly cut off from communion at the altar, should remain delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved.

According to the testimony of blessed Augustine, this was not done from despair of pardon, but from disciplinary rigor, lest the ecclesiastical remedy become cheap and thereby less useful. For although second penance and [Col. 1289B] full reconciliation are denied to such persons according to the decrees of the canons, blessed Augustine nevertheless beneficially advises those who have fallen again to this course: that by not only restraining themselves from unlawful things but also restricting themselves in lawful things, generously giving away what is theirs, weeping more abundantly, and perseveringly performing the other fruits worthy of repentance, they should trust in God’s mercy, although before the day of death they can scarcely obtain entrance into a church and can never obtain sacred communion. Thus the censure of the canons may retain its force, in which the holy authority of the Fathers affirms that a second penance is to be granted to no one.

Blessed Ambrose teaches that this should be observed in this way: just as there is one baptism in the Church, which, once given, is not to be repeated, so there should be one place of repentance, which is not thereafter to be granted freely to those who have fallen again—although none even of such persons should be frightened into despair. For although they have no hope [Col. 1290A] of reconciliation in this life, they can nevertheless be saved, aided by communion as viaticum at the end, if, not despairing of themselves, they do not add worse things to worse, but, while excluded from hope of reconciliation, seek the hope of salvation firmly, constantly, and perseveringly.

Truly, the holy Fathers, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, foresaw that the remedy would become cheap if this rigor ceased. For we see this happen in our times, because the lawful order is not maintained toward penitents. Any priest, anywhere, relaxes a fast for any penitent without compensatory almsgiving, something which formerly only that man, or those men, were accustomed to do who were to present the penitents themselves to bishops on the day of their reconciliation, [Col. 1290B] giving suitable testimony concerning the completion of their penance.

Let bishops, then, at last awake, preserving the laws of repentance handed down by the ancient Fathers. Let them prohibit priests, and, under threat of suspension, deposition, or indeed anathema, forbid them from indiscriminately granting penitents useless and dangerous permissions to eat; and from imposing *carrina* upon someone who, after once performing penance for a condemnable crime, sins criminally again, thereby granting them a second place of penance which the saints forbid. For such people have only this left: to despise the world and, without hope of ecclesiastical reconciliation, seek hope of eternal salvation.

But clergy do not know how rightly to deal with lay penitents because [Col. 1290C] they themselves are not rightly dealt with when they are publicly exposed as truly detected in some criminal sin [Note: [Col. 1289C]

Decree of Pope Nicholas the Younger: “Let no one hear the Mass of a priest whom he certainly knows to have a concubine beyond doubt, or a woman surreptitiously introduced into his household. Accordingly, this holy synod itself placed this provision under excommunication, saying: ‘Whoever among priests, deacons, or subdeacons, after the decree concerning clerical chastity issued by our predecessor Pope Leo of blessed memory, has openly taken a concubine, or has not dismissed one whom he has taken, we command and altogether forbid, by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, that he sing Mass, or read the Gospel or [Col. 1289D] Epistle at Mass; nor may he remain in the sanctuary for the divine offices in accordance with the aforesaid constitution, nor receive a share from the Church, until, God granting it, judgment concerning such a person proceeds from us.’”

Nicholas to Charles, archbishop, and his suffragans: “If priests fall into the snare of fornication, and the act of the crime is evident or proved, they cannot retain the honor of the priesthood according to the authority of canonical institution.”

Leo II to the bishops and king of the Dalmatians: “If henceforth any bishop, priest, or deacon takes a woman or retains one whom he has taken, let him fall from his own rank until he comes to make satisfaction. Let him not remain in the choir of those chanting psalms, nor have any portion of ecclesiastical property.”

Pope Martin to Amandus: “Whoever, after his ordination, has once fallen into sin shall thereafter already be deposed and shall be able to attain no rank of the priesthood.”

[Col. 1290C] From the Council of Agde, chapter 4: “If any priest, negligent of his life, has by depraved examples allowed evil to be suspected of him, and the people, bound by the bishop under oath or by a ban of Christian discipline, have disclosed his ill repute, yet reliable accusers of his crime are lacking: first let him be admonished privately by the bishop; then before two or three witnesses. If he does not amend, let the bishop admonish him by public rebuke in an assembly of priests. But if he does not correct himself even thus, let him be suspended from office until worthy satisfaction has been made, lest the body of the faithful suffer scandal on his account. But if there are no lawful accusers able to prove his crimes by manifest indications, and he denies them, then, if able, let him clear himself of the charge together with seven companions of the same order. A deacon, however, if accused of the same [Col. 1290D] crime, shall clear himself together with three.”

Pope Stephen V to Leo, bishop of Sciana: “In a matter manifest and known to many, witnesses need not be sought. Thus St Ambrose says in his Epistle to the Corinthians, explaining the Apostle’s judgment concerning fornication: ‘It is not the judge’s role, I say, to condemn without an accuser; for the Lord did not cast out Judas, though he was a thief, because he was not accused. But when this deed became known, he judged that the man must be expelled from the fellowship of the brethren. For all knew his crime and did not rebuke him. Publicly, indeed, he had his stepmother in the place of a wife. In this matter neither were witnesses needed, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion.’ And a little later: ‘Absent in body but present in authority through the Spirit, who is absent nowhere, I have already judged, as though present, that the man who committed this deed be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.’”

.

[Col. 1291A] For laypersons, on account of the salutary strictness involved, Pope Leo and the other saints prescribe a narrow mode of repentance: namely, that after performing penance they do not enter into marriages—unless, perhaps, in order to guard against a fall arising from frailty, this is permitted to younger persons, not according to rule but according to indulgence. Leo the Great, as I have said, allowing this only to penitents in youth, says: “In this we establish not a rule, but judge what is more tolerable.” And, as though he were asked, after this pardonable concession for young persons to whom he permits marriage, what the rule of lawful penance is, he immediately added: “For according to true understanding nothing is more fitting for one who has [Col. 1291B] performed penance than persevering chastity of mind and body.”

[Note: [Col. 1291D]

Augustine: “Nothing is more fitting for one who has performed penance than persevering chastity of mind and body. Let him always bear shame upon his brow in remembrance of his offense. Without true confession and penance no one shall be saved. Whoever accuses and confesses his sins makes a covenant with God.”

John Chrysostom: “Penance is refreshment for the [Col. 1292D] soul, a furnace for sins, the mother of the languishing, the helper of the weak. Every sin receives the healing of its wound through penance. Nothing is worse than to acknowledge one’s fault and not mourn it. Only in this life is freedom for penance open; after death there is no opportunity for amendment.”]

But this must be understood of the penitent who has performed penance while still free from a wife. For if he is bound, after performing penance he may render the marital debt to his wife; yet from the penitent’s side it must never be demanded. But if it is demanded of him, he must render it, so far as possible, not from desire but from marital obedience, with fear and care. If, however, one of the two dies and the penitent survives, he ought not to contract a new marriage, but, according to the rule confirmed by Leo, persevere in chastity of mind and body. Penitents must also obey the same Leo, who establishes the rule of penance, [Col. 1291C] so that, if they happen to have a lawsuit, they never await a civil or court judgment, but only an ecclesiastical judgment; in order that, by the counsel of ecclesiastical judges or from love of their own perfection, they may either renounce it, or pursue it through those judges without injury to their neighbor.

## CHAPTER XL. On the form and distinction of ecclesiastical and secular judgment; for what sins an offender is to be struck with anathema, etc.

This difference is recognized between ecclesiastical and secular judges: in ecclesiastical judgment the spiritual judge gains nothing earthly from either the guilty or the innocent person, but, favoring justice, generally incurs the resentment of one and obtains the favor of the other. The secular judge, however, standing as mediator between guilty and innocent persons, generally gains something under secular laws from the guilty party, when that guilty person is to be punished not by execution or mutilation of limbs but by confiscation of possessions. If he gains anything beyond the judgment from the innocent party in order to favor justice, he sins dangerously, because he sells justice, which he ought to favor freely. [Col. 1292A] But if he receives something from the guilty party in order to treat that party’s case more leniently, this is certain destruction both for giver and receiver; for this is not like selling justice while it lives, but trafficking for gain in justice altogether strangled.

But if the seller of living justice is to be punished with eternal death for favoring it in return for a reward—though justice alone ought to have been the reward of those who favor it—how must the person be punished who, so far as lies in him, kills that same justice by favoring, against it, an unjust cause which he ought in no way to have favored, not even to save his own life?

Therefore let both the sale and the killing and strangling of justice be far from the judges of the Church, who ought to [Col. 1292B] handle all cases of clerics, monks, nuns, widows, orphans, those who have performed penance, and all who have devoted themselves to ecclesiastical functions. But they ought not to handle cases of soldiers and other laypeople, except those concerning the salvation of the soul and the justice of the Church. For in disputes over money, whether to recover or retain it by secular justice, and in other such matters belonging to secular affairs, the bishop ought not to involve himself, but should leave such matters to the earthly judge. Yet when he makes a peaceful and just settlement between persons at discord and in such disputes, so that neither must pay an earthly judge, the bishop does what belongs to [Col. 1292C] his office, to which the Gospel of peace has been entrusted.

But such a settlement may lawfully be made by the bishop when the case has not yet been brought before a secular judge. For just as an earthly judge ought not, nor can, take up a case undertaken by one who presides spiritually, so a bishop ought not wrong one who does not bear the sword without cause. Yet, just as the bishop ought not hinder a judge acting judicially, so, if a person becomes an oppressor of the innocent by disregarding judicial order, it is lawful for the bishop, rescuing the poor and needy from the hand of the stronger, to bind that strong person and exclude him from the Church until he repents and promises better conduct [Col. 1292D] concerning himself. For they have authority “to bind kings with fetters, and their nobles with chains of iron” (Ps. 149:8).

This authority proceeds victoriously if they “execute upon them the written judgment” (Ps. 149:9). They ought not to compel persons outside the judicial order laid down in writing by the holy Fathers. For according to what is prescribed, by lawful admonition, summons, and waiting for a period of grace, the bow is, as it were, drawn, so that the arrow [Col. 1293A] of excommunication, accurately aimed at the rebel, may be sent with greater force. Nevertheless, if something is known to be forbidden under anathema, as soon as anyone commits it, let him know that he is immediately excommunicated.

Thus blessed Gregory calls excommunicated those bishops who, knowing that the consecration of Maximus of Salona had been forbidden under excommunication, nevertheless knowingly consecrated him. He says: “We can by no means call that act a consecration, because it was performed by excommunicated persons.” See: he already identifies them as excommunicated in the commission of that sin which had been forbidden under excommunication. Therefore they were already excommunicated, without any period of grace and without prior summons, because they knew that the consecration which they performed had earlier been forbidden [Col. 1293B] under excommunication.

It must, however, be noted that although many sins shut the kingdom of heaven against those who commit them, not every grave sin is forbidden, or ought to be forbidden, under anathema before it is committed. For if drunkenness, fornication, and lying were forbidden under anathema before their commission, the number of excommunicated persons would extend without limit. This prohibition with the addition of an anathema is ordinarily made when a newly arising schism is being resisted; for if the offense is committed before the prohibition has been heard, delay must necessarily be granted through judicial procedure. For a person must be summoned and awaited through lawful periods of grace, [Col. 1293C] whatever crime he has committed, unless either he becomes openly disobedient by stubbornly opposing sound admonition, or knowingly commits something prohibited under anathema. It is therefore most necessary that matters specially forbidden under anathema be carefully noted; once noted, they should be publicly proclaimed by the bishop and priests before the others, because what is proclaimed is more readily avoided. Or, if some do not avoid them, they themselves must be guarded against because of the anathema, and are regarded as publicly declared so by episcopal sentence until they submit to penance.

For the regular performance of that penance, as we said above, this also belongs: that a person [Col. 1294A] doing penance for a condemnable crime must refrain not only from marriage and involvement in secular litigation, but also from commerce and military service.

[Note: [Col. 1293C]

Pope Gregory VII, in a synod held at Rome, chapter 6, says: “He calls those false penances which are not imposed according to the authority of the holy Fathers in proportion to the character of the crimes. Therefore, whoever is a soldier, merchant, or devoted to an office that cannot be exercised without sin, and comes to penance ensnared by graver faults—that is, one who unjustly retains another’s property or bears hatred in his heart—must recognize that he cannot perform true penance, through which he may attain eternal life, unless the soldier lays down his arms and thereafter bears them only by the counsel of religious bishops and for the defense of justice; unless the merchant abandons trade; and unless the official leaves his office. Let each restore the goods which he unjustly took, and put away hatred from his heart.”

Ambrose, in the book *On Penance*: “Some seek penance for this reason: that they may wish communion to be restored to them at once. Such persons desire not so much to free themselves as to bind the priest. For they do not so much strip off their own conscience as wish the priest to put it on, though he has been commanded: ‘Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine’ (Matt. 7:6). This means: do not readily grant the fellowship of communion to unclean spirits.” The same work continues: “They suppose this to be penance if they abstain from the heavenly sacraments. These are stricter judges of themselves, who prescribe punishment for themselves if they decline the remedy—though punishment ought to destroy them—because they are deprived of heavenly grace.”

Ambrose, book III of *On Penance*: “I have found more easily those who preserved innocence than those who performed penance suitably. Does anyone consider that to be penance where there is ambition to acquire rank, lavish consumption of wine, or use of sexual intercourse itself? One must renounce the world; one must indulge even sleep less than nature requires; it must be interrupted by groans, broken by sighs, set apart for prayer. One must live so as to die to this life; one must deny oneself to oneself in this practice and be wholly changed.”]

Accordingly, Leo the Great writes to Rusticus of Narbonne, who consulted the Apostolic See concerning the rule of penance: “It is one thing,” he says, “to demand just debts; another to scorn one’s own possessions out of love of perfection. But one seeking pardon for unlawful acts ought also to abstain from lawful things, as the Apostle says: ‘All things are lawful, but not all things are beneficial’ (1 Cor. 10:22). Therefore, if penitents have a case which perhaps they should not neglect, it is more expedient to seek ecclesiastical rather than civil judgment.” The same Leo also proves that no penitent should engage in the profits of trade, saying: “The nature of the gain either excuses or accuses the merchant, for there is an honorable profit and a shameful one. Nevertheless, it is more useful for a penitent to suffer losses than to be bound by the dangers of trade, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in transactions between buyer and seller.” Again, proving that one should not return to secular military service after penance, he says: “It is altogether contrary to ecclesiastical rules to return to secular military service after performing penance, since the Apostle says: ‘No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs’ (2 Tim. 2:4). Therefore he is not free from the snares of the devil who wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service.”

## CHAPTER XLI. How those who refuse to perform canonical penance for crimes committed are to be punished; and what is the office of converts in communities of clerics and monks?

[Col. 1294C]

If, therefore, according to the decretal judgments of this great pontiff, the rule of penance requires that a penitent be free from secular litigation, the exercise of commerce, and secular military service; and if, as we have proved above, he does not contract marriage but remains continent, since he is known to have accepted the yoke of penance upon himself, then surely a penitent who transgresses this rule ought to be punished in some way.

Asked about the punishment of such transgressors, Pope Siricius of blessed memory writes to Hunerius, [Col. 1295A] bishop of Tarragona, as follows in chapter 5: “Concerning those who, after performing penance, return like dogs and swine to their former vomit and wallowing, and again seek the military belt, theatrical pleasures, new marriages, and intercourse with concubines once renounced—their sons born after absolution having revealed their professed incontinence—because they now have no refuge in penance, we have judged that this must be decreed: they are to be joined to the faithful in prayer alone within the church; though unworthy, they may be present at the celebration of the sacred mysteries; but they shall be separated from the banquet of the Lord’s table. Thus, at least corrected by this strictness, they may themselves punish their errors within themselves and provide an example [Col. 1295B] to others, so that they may be withdrawn from shameful desires. Yet, because they fell through carnal frailty, when they begin their journey to the Lord, we wish aid to be given them by the grace of communion, as viaticum. We judge that the same rule is to be observed concerning women who, after penance, have bound themselves by such defilements.”

It should be noted from these words how strict a mode of humiliation has been attached to the rules of penance, which require the penitent to withdraw so completely from a new marriage, the military belt, and every slippery pleasure that such persons are almost distinguished from secular people as monks are. Hence the ancient custom prevailed that, because no one is admitted to clerical orders after publicly performing penance, both cleric and layperson who performed the stricter [Col. 1295C] penance should be joined to a community of monks. They were not to be treated as we now see laypersons guilty of many crimes treated in monasteries: either living dissolutely within them and not eating bread by the sweat of their faces; or being carelessly sent out so that they may live on estates as stewards, deceived by the empty name of “converts,” and live among secular people almost secularly. Such people either ought never to have gone out, or, leaving the cloister in obedience, like Peter leaving the little boat, and walking over the world as over a fluid sea, ought to return most swiftly to the boat (Matt. 14:29), lest the swelling storm of temptation overwhelm the vessel itself in their case. Indeed, even a strong wind ready to raise [Col. 1295D] a storm will easily expose them to peril unless they are raised up by the Lord’s right hand and, before the full storm overtakes them, brought back to the boat.

But there are some such converts who profess the apostolic life—would that they also imitated the apostles! Those devoted with Peter to the study of the heavenly word are rightly judged to be in the apostolic life by imitating the Apostle, just as secular clerics [Col. 1296A] gathered together for common life are. Again, those who work with their hands at what is good, in order to have something to give to one suffering need, living together content only with necessities, likewise lead the true apostolic life by imitating the Apostle Paul—as the ancient monks did under energetic leaders, namely the great Fathers of Egypt, not living idly. Thus the Apostle Peter, like a reliable standard-bearer, leads in the apostolic life those whose minds keep watch over God’s word, whether teaching or learning it. Likewise the Apostle Paul, an outstanding standard-bearer in the apostolic life, marshals and leads the ranks of those who sometimes perform manual labor in imitation of him. Therefore one professes the apostolic life happily and without deception who follows Peter with Augustine or Paul with Benedict; or at least, to remove every excuse, strives with all one’s strength through God’s grace to follow and imitate them. Whether such a person is governed in the apostolic life by one leader or the other, or follows now the one in the study of the word, now the other in the exercise of work, he truly lives the apostolic life; indeed, through the apostolic life he is led to eternal life, if, forgetting what lies behind, he always stretches himself toward what lies ahead.

Certainly, if business must be conducted outside, the examples of the apostles must be observed when brothers are sent out. For through them this discipline is set before us: a brother must never be sent far away alone, nor, when sent, allowed to remain absent long. Hence, when the apostles heard that Samaria had received the word [Col. 1296C] of God, they sent to them not Peter alone or John alone, but Peter and John (Acts 8:14). Hence the Apostle Paul, on his journeying, took pride in such a companion, “whose praise was in the Gospel” (2 Cor. 8:18). Hence he writes in an Epistle to a disciple whom he had sent, telling him to hasten to come quickly to him (2 Tim. 4:8), because it is fitting for a disciple sent by a master to return quickly to that master.

[Note: [Col. 1295D]

Gregory to the bishop of Ravenna: “No one can both serve ecclesiastical duties and remain properly within monastic rule, so that he maintains the strictness of the monastery while being compelled to remain daily in ecclesiastical ministry.” Likewise, to Maximinian, bishop of Syracuse: “Those who have resolved to remain in the place of abbot must by no means be permitted [Col. 1296D] to undertake the service of the clergy. For it is quite incongruous that, when because of its magnitude one cannot diligently fulfill either of these offices, he should be judged competent for both. Thus the ecclesiastical order obstructs the monastic manner of life, and the monastic rule obstructs ecclesiastical usefulness.”]

Therefore those who, having become professors of the apostolic life, imitate the apostles both outside and within—whether they use clerical, monastic, or penitential habit and dress—their life is called, and is, apostolic, because they are governed by apostolic rule. Penitents as well as innocent persons may properly be associated with persons living thus [Col. 1296D] and trained commendably in the study of books, the practice of works, or indeed both—provided that the greatest care is taken that no penitent be admitted to sacred orders. Under the rigor of the canons, not even one who is known simply to have served as a soldier after baptism is admitted to them.

Thus Pope Innocent writes to Felix, bishop of Nocera: “The classes of persons who cannot attain the clergy have been specified: namely, if a believer has served as a soldier, if a believer has pleaded cases—that is, acted as an advocate—or if a believer has held public office.” And shortly afterwards: “But laypeople who were baptized while having wives and have thereafter so ordered themselves that their reputation does not in any way waver; who, from the time of baptism, have attached themselves either to clerics or to monasteries; who have known neither concubine nor mistress; and who have kept watch in every good work—such persons are not prohibited from being admitted to the rank of the clergy.” In this passage, this point must be noted: it is one thing to be attached to clerics, another to be admitted to the rank of the clergy. For he first speaks of laypersons attached to clerics, and afterwards says that, if no fault prevents it, they are to be admitted to the clerical rank.

[Col. 1297B] But what is it to be attached to clerics except to be devoted to learning and practicing the Scriptures in the fellowship of clerics? In the primitive Church, as the Acts of the Apostles testify, many were daily attached to Peter, persevering with one accord in the Temple. So these persons ought to persevere in the cloister: either teaching God’s word, like Christ; or learning it, like Mary sitting at his feet; or else providing necessities for such learners and teachers and attending to continual service after Martha’s example.

When this kind of ministry is well managed by industrious lay brothers who have converted, the devotion of learners and teachers is reckoned to them as an increase of good merit; and the continual ministry of these brothers is aided by the devotion of those learners and teachers. These are the fruits of worthy penance which converted laypeople can render while remaining in the community of regular clerics.

## CHAPTER XLII. More on the same subject, and how those who leave neither secular dress nor their own household ought to perform penance

As for monks, there is no question that a penitent is properly joined to their community, because their dress is recognized as properly that of penitents—provided, however, that it is not disfigured by loose and effeminate garments. Therefore, a penitent associated either with clerics or monks should not doubt that he is being slaughtered and eaten by Peter, and wholly incorporated into the apostolic [Col. 1297D] life itself, if he keeps apostolic rule either with Augustine or with Benedict. Otherwise there is reason to fear that the way of life of one who is neither properly united with clerics nor monks, nor endeavors to experience after professing the apostolic life the penitential strictness which he ought to have observed outside, is more apostate than apostolic—especially since they first assume penitential garb when, according to the rules of the Fathers, they lay aside the military belt, put on religious dress distinctly different from secular clothing, and openly distinguish themselves from secular people.

For this was formerly done by all who performed penance rightly, though they did not all abandon their own homes. Changing their secular dress and observing the rule of penance, they strove to imitate, if not the apostles, then [Col. 1298A] the apostles’ disciples. For one who lives in his own home as Onesiphorus, Paul’s disciple, lived—concerned no longer with the world but only with Christ’s poor; who does in his own household what Tabitha, Peter’s disciple, did, being concerned only for widows and the poor; who orders his household as we believe the household of Stephanas was ordered (which the Apostle Paul took care to exhibit to all as an example for imitation of the saints, saying, “You know the household of Stephanas” [1 Cor. 16:15], and which he honored with his greeting); who so orders his household and himself in his household that he spends himself and what is his solely in the service of the poor (as we do not doubt that those did of whom the Apostle bears witness that they “devoted themselves” [Col. 1298B] “to the service of the saints”)—such a person, imitating these men and women, followers of the apostles though not their companions, disciples of the apostles though not apostles themselves, walks a surer way while remaining in his own household than if he abandoned that household and, taking the name of convert, decided neither to follow perfectly the apostles’ male and female disciples nor to strive according to his ability to do so.

If such a person were reduced to poverty in the service of the poor, then he would truly embrace the apostolic life—especially if, then seeking his livelihood by his hands, though still strong himself, he served those weaker persons unable to work, as we read that Paul did. Seeking food by his hands not only for himself but also for those who were with [Col. 1298C] him, he ministered to them. If he were reduced not only to poverty but also to bodily weakness in such ministry, then the Church’s prelate ought to gather him into the parish—that is, the house of the poor—and provide generously for him with the other poor from the fourth portion of tithes.

If, however, she is a widow impoverished in such service and bears testimony that, while able, she received the poor and washed their feet (1 Tim. 5:10), and has carefully observed the other things by which the Apostle describes a good widow, then, even if she seeks nothing from the Church, it is nevertheless just and altogether commanded by the Apostle that the prelate of the Church gather her in, in whose parish she is known to have lived commendably—especially if she has already passed forty years of age and has no children able to provide well for her. Otherwise the Church may either be discredited for gathering young women or burdened with feeding those whom their children can and ought to support, if they do not wish to deny the faith and be worse than unbelievers: “Whoever does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8).

We have seen the lofty examples of the apostles, imitable by few; we have considered the disciples, male and female, of those same apostles, so imitable by all that not only unmarried persons remaining in their own homes can imitate them, but also married persons who have perhaps advanced so far that, although the bonds of marriage remain between them, they nevertheless resolve by equal vow to make themselves eunuchs from works of the flesh for the kingdom of heaven.

If these live rightly by visiting orphans and widows in their affliction and keeping themselves unspotted from this world, though they do not run with the apostles, who ran very swiftly and unencumbered, leaving all things together and at once, they nevertheless walk with the apostles’ disciples under the guard of pure and certain religion. For the Apostle James, consoling and strengthening his disciples, included in his Epistle a rule of compact brevity which fits such people well. He says: “Religion pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unspotted from this world” (Jas. 1:27). This rule [Col. 1299B] suits the apostles’ disciples and persons like them as the rule of common life suits the apostles and persons like them.

Do you wish to hear the rule of the apostles? “They had one heart and one soul in God, and none of them said that anything which he possessed was his own,” etc. (Acts 4:32). If you can undertake this rule, under it either devote yourself to the word of doctrine with Peter, or, by giving attention to work, become like the Apostle Paul, and by following now the one, now the other—indeed Christ in both—avoid the deviations of those who, living either inquisitively or idly, follow neither of these apostles. To all who wish to observe the apostolic life, these two offer, like two eyes, a double light [Col. 1299C] and sure guidance. But if, by leaving all things, you cannot follow naked the naked Christ, hear the rule of disciples under the apostles, ordered through the apostles so as to occupy a middle place: lower than the apostles, higher than married persons, devoting themselves and all that they possess to the service of the saints.

Such was Tabitha, full of good works and almsgiving. Though she was not joined to the widows living in common under Peter, she was nevertheless Peter’s disciple, diligently taught by him, so that in her own household she somehow preserved the common life, making all her resources common to the needy. She made tunics and garments which, after her death, the weeping widows showed to Peter when he came; and by their tears they obtained this, that Peter said: “Tabitha, arise” (Acts 9:40). Giving her his hand, he raised her up and presented her alive to the saints and widows. Could Peter not at least after her resurrection have drawn his disciple into the common life, if he had thought this more expedient for her salvation and the benefit of the poor? But he presented her, restored to life, to the saints and widows, as a prudent and faithful servant of holy poor persons and holy widows.

For the poor who possess nothing for God’s sake are themselves the saints. Those who minister to such persons, as Tabitha did, are ministers of the saints. These will sit with the apostles in judgment; these will hear, “Come, blessed ones” (Matt. 24:35); these are those whom the Apostle designates when he says: “Greet all the saints” (Phil. [Col. 1300A] 4:21). He commends their ministry, praising in his Epistle those men and women who had devoted themselves to the service of the saints. In brief, he embraces the office and order of both when he greets in his Epistle everyone who works and cooperates with the truth. For the person who perfectly imitates the apostles performs, not merely along with others but outstandingly above others, what truth commands and counsels. But the person who ministers to such people for that very purpose is one who cooperates with the truth.

Likewise, one who, lying in poverty with Lazarus before the gate, is oppressed by it, yet does not plan thefts or covet the abundance of the rich, but desires to be satisfied, not to indulge in luxury, from their surplus—as from crumbs falling from a table, that is, from what exceeds the measure of necessity as though beyond a table—does not complain or unjustly seek what belongs to another: such a person truly works in patience. But one who comforts such a person according to his ability cooperates with one who works. Therefore, even if poor Peter is sometimes lacking, poor Lazarus is seldom or never lacking.

To these two poor persons belong the surplus goods of all the rich, goods which are without doubt necessities of the poor. Therefore one who devotes himself to their service ought to give none of his possessions to anyone except what is necessary for the needy. If a guest comes to him, let him receive the guest as fitting; yet let him spend little of the food of the poor on the meals of jesters, preserving the agreement which Paul and Barnabas ratified by giving and receiving right hands with [Col. 1300C] the other apostles—namely, that they should remember only the poor (Gal. 2:10). Therefore, from the property of the saints administered through Paul’s hand, not idle chatterers but the poor were fed. For Peter, James, and John gave right hands to Paul and Barnabas, receiving from them, as it were, a covenant of fellowship: only that they should remember the poor. The Apostle himself was diligent in doing this, administering the collections of the churches solely to the poor.

Martin likewise carefully observed this, administering tithes and other stipends of the poor solely to the poor. Other Catholic men also kept this agreement, providing from the property of the poor solely for the benefit of the poor. Not so the impious, not so: their people sit down to eat and drink, and afterwards rise to play, either at tables or at other utterly vain games invented by the devil. Cyprian, martyr and bishop, testifies that the game of tables was invented in honor of a certain idol.

## CHAPTER XLIII. How tax officials, judges, soldiers, and others unwilling to renounce their own possessions may follow the apostolic rule.

If, however, there are some who desire to be saved in the lowest rank, not willing or able, by leaving everything, to be saints with the saints, or to dispose all that they possess, together with the perfect disciples of the saints, for the service of the poor and saints [Col. 1301A]—being not yet fed with solid bread, but simply given the milk of faith to drink—let these also have recourse to apostolic teaching. In it, married persons find such a rule, such a discipline of now abstaining and now returning to the same act, that, if they follow their rule perfectly, they may not at all be separated from the lot of those who are saved, but may be, with blessed Job, upright, simple, and God-fearing.

If there are judges and agents in secular lawsuits, who in the Gospel are called tax collectors, let them follow the teaching of John, doing nothing beyond what has been appointed for them. For one who, in administering public offices, observes the order established by law and judicial authority will not follow wandering errors: since he has Joseph in Egypt, Daniel in Babylon, and Constantine ruling in the [Col. 1301B] Church as guides and forerunners of his path. By rightly following them he is led, on a surer course, to Him who does not reject the mighty, since He Himself is mighty, than is the man who professes the apostolic life yet follows the leadership of no apostle.

Let the soldier set before himself such a rule—rather, let him know that it has been set before him in the Gospel: that he extort from no one, bring no false accusation, and be content with his pay (Luke 3:14); that he not take up the iron sword, lest he perish by the flaming sword. For it is one thing to take up the sword and another to bear the sword. He who rightly exercises the sword is God’s minister and bears the sword, imposed upon him by God’s ordering, as a burden and not without cause. But he who acts outside order is the minister, not of God, but of his own greed, because he takes up the sword to oppress the poor [Col. 1301C], avenge his own wrongs, and heap up profits of unrighteous mammon. Unless he is saved through lawful repentance, he will without doubt perish by the flaming sword set before Paradise.

Maurice bore the sword with his legion; yet he would not take up that sword, because contrary to the order of divine justice he would not move it even in defense of his own blood. For the sword is often rightly wielded by a soldier defending his country or the Church at the decree or command of rulers and lawfully enforcing public law. But no one ever rightly wields the sword in defending himself, Scripture saying: “Not defending yourselves, beloved” (Rom. 12:10). David, defending not himself but God’s people, killed the Philistine who was fighting; in his own defense he would not kill Saul while he slept. Thus, in bearing the sword he pleased God, though afterward, by taking up the sword against Uriah, he offended God so greatly that, unless he had extinguished the flaming sword with tears of repentance, he would have perished by the sword because he had taken up the sword.

Soldiers, therefore, have a sure guidance both in King David, who served well as a soldier under the evil Saul, and in the holy Theban legion, which preserved godliness under an impious emperor. Such guidance is lacking to the convert who, following neither Peter among clerics nor Paul among monks, boasts under the empty name [Col. 1302A] that he is a convert—being so unaware of his own perversity that his profession of the apostolic life becomes evidence for his condemnation—unless he employs, in this ordered battle-line of camps, a fixed rule of service, a fixed sign, a fixed leader, and a fixed standard; lest, with the acephali, those without a head, he be driven away from the crown, Christ crowning only those who contend lawfully.

Certainly, it would not be altogether blameworthy if a layman, pierced with compunction for his sins, contributed all that he possessed to those living commonly under a rule, but, being unable or unwilling to bear regular strictness in himself, associated himself with them in such a manner that, testing himself and exercising according to his strength, he submitted himself to the prelates of the Church, observing and professing the common life in an approved manner [lacuna]; provided nevertheless that he never promised the apostolic [Col. 1302B] life unless he were ready to keep all regular statutes in every respect and wished to become either a cleric or a monk. For either profession is governed by fixed guidance, under which one who contends lawfully is crowned. Therefore let a person test himself, and so approach the contest of apostolic profession, lest, rashly professing the apostolic life, he incur the crime of apostasy by failing lawfully to keep what he professes.

But lest anyone, walking by a crooked path outside the rule suited to his profession, fall from the crown—which no one receives unless he contends regularly and lawfully in the duty of his own profession—the holy orders of clerics, monks, virgins, and widows [Col. 1302C], distinct in their uniformity and uniform in their distinction, ought to keep the rule set before them by the Lord and the apostles. Closely following them comes the body of those who have not yet wholly left their homes, but nevertheless order themselves and all that they possess for the service of holy persons, the poor, and pilgrims. After these, the remaining married persons, the rich, judges, and soldiers will not lack a rule if they wish to remain in Christ’s teaching. We have briefly touched upon their rules above; we leave it to the teachers of the Church diligently, fully, and frequently to impress them upon people, so that no one who is recognized as an enlisted soldier in this battle-line of camps may be allowed to proceed irregularly and disorderly.

For he who in baptism renounced the devil and all his pomps and promptings, even if [Col. 1302D] he never becomes a cleric or monk, is nonetheless shown to have renounced the world, because the whole world, placed in the evil one, is the pomp of that evil one; and all Christians have renounced his pomp. Therefore, those who use this world should be as though they did not use it: so that whether rich or poor, noble or slave, merchants or farmers, and indeed all who are marked by Christian profession, may reject those things hostile to that name and follow those suited to it. For every order, and indeed every profession, in the Catholic faith and apostolic teaching has a rule suited to its own character, under which, by contending lawfully, it may attain the crown.

> **Note: [Col. 1301D] Athanasius:** “Whoever wishes to be saved must, before all things, hold the Catholic faith. [Col. 1302D] Unless each person keeps it whole and inviolate, without doubt he will perish eternally.”

[Col. 1303A] Yet because people often depart from the rule of innocence, a rule of repentance has been established, as though a gate in the holy city: so that through it those who would not remain within through innocence may in some sense enter by force. They did not walk lawfully because, either ignorant of their own rule or disregarding it though frequently impressed upon them by their teachers, they thought that only clerics or monks had renounced the world. Therefore let them at last, even now, learn the Catholic faith. Let the soldier learn; let the farmer learn; let every Christian learn the faith briefly handed down by the apostles; let each learn from the holy apostles the rule of life appropriate to his profession and condition.

Formerly, when adults were baptized, they were by no means admitted to baptism, except at the point of death, unless they had first been carefully catechized—that is, instructed—in the Lord’s Prayer and the apostolic faith. Hence those still lacking baptism but instructed in the Catholic faith were called catechumens. But lest anyone insufficiently instructed in the apostolic faith or the Lord’s Prayer secretly intrude himself for baptism and, not yet knowing the faith by heart, unworthily receive the sacraments of faith, an examination was held for each individual. In it the priest carefully inquired what each person believed in his heart unto righteousness and confessed with his mouth unto salvation. Therefore, according to ancient rules, those to be baptized at Easter were diligently trained throughout Lent in learning the faith and the Lord’s Prayer until the day of examination. [Col. 1303C] At that examination, if someone was found to have grasped this word made brief upon earth less cautiously, less learnedly, or not sufficiently by heart, his baptism was postponed until Pentecost, so that he might then receive the sacrament of faith when, having acquired knowledge of the faith and the Lord’s Prayer, he did not fail to know what and how he ought to believe, and what and how he ought to ask. But if anyone was baptized because of danger of death before obtaining full knowledge of this abbreviated word, then, if he escaped death, he was bound after baptism by the command of the canons to learn after baptism what he ought to have learned before baptism, lest, ignorant of his faith, he bear the sacrament of faith in vain. Whoever in those days refused to obey the statutes of the Fathers, after a first and second warning and regular public notice of his disobedience, was regarded by every Catholic as a heathen and a tax collector [Col. 1303D].

Could not, and should not, all Christians, after the weakness of infancy, be compelled and admonished to learn and understand the apostolic faith and the Lord’s Prayer, and to recall and keep the renunciation of the world once made in baptism and repeated often after baptism? If this were done, if ecclesiastical discipline flourished, then each person would lawfully serve in the battle-line of some ecclesiastical or secular, yet Christian, order according to the covenant and rule of his faith; or, departing from the lawful course, he would bow his head beneath the lawful rules of repentance [Col. 1304A]; or, if unwilling to do this, he would remain an exile from the Church until, becoming obedient, he was made worthy of consolation and reconciliation.

## CHAPTER XLIV. How great humility is required in penitents, especially clerics.

Thus, having been brought in through the law of ancient repentance, as through the old gate, and refined like gold in the tower of furnaces, he should beware of going out again; he should beware of again corrupting the purity of life with the tin and dross of iniquity. Yet this is so only if, brought in through the old gate, he proceeds as far as the valley gate, rightly joined and connected with the tower of furnaces, because penitential chastisement has no value without continual humility of heart [Col. 1304B] and body.

For what is the valley gate in the city of Jerusalem, built under the direction of Jesus the high priest (2 Esdras 2:15), except true humility, fashioned by Jesus Christ, truly the great priest and king, with wondrous craftsmanship? In its loftier and more worthy part He placed Himself as a noble pearl—He who emptied Himself and, humbled, obeyed the Father unto death.

Not penitents alone, but also the innocent must enter through this gate, conformed to Christ’s humility, if they do not wish to be excluded from His glory. For thus, thus Christ had to suffer and so enter into His glory (Luke 24:26), so that He might set before us [Col. 1304C] His humility as a kind of doorway through which we might enter into His glory. Why should either the innocent or the penitent seek another entrance besides that which the doorkeeper freely opens to those wishing to enter? He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant; and you, though a penitent, exalt yourself, eagerly seeking to take the form of a soldier—or, what is worse, the form of a priest—contrary to prohibition? He humbled Himself, obedient to the Father unto death; and are you burdened by remaining humbled—that is, deprived of office or rank—until death?

For we see that, before even a year of penitence is complete, one man presumptuously lays claim to the priesthood through ambition, another resumes the soldier’s belt through presumption; though each should, after repentance, remain humbled without office, not merely until [Col. 1304D] a year has elapsed but until death, unless some great compensating need compelled one to serve again in sacred offices and the other in military camps. Thus he would not take upon himself the form of a ruler, because he did not seek it as acceptable or pleasing to himself; but he would retain until death the form of a servant, the form of one degraded, the form of one dishonored, even though by obedience to the Church commanding him he outwardly bore the form of a lord, the form of a prelate, the form of one honored. Thus we read that some—not only presbyters but bishops as well—were restored after repentance, repentance having been performed not publicly but in the penitential prison-cells of cloisters. They did not rashly seek this restoration [Col. 1305A], but yielded to the command of their superiors.

> **Note: [Col. 1305D] Gregory, to Peter the subdeacon and legate:** “Concerning fallen priests or anyone from the clergy, we wish you to observe that you do not involve yourself in their affairs with any contamination; but seek out very poor regular monasteries, which know how to live according to God, and thrust the fallen into those monasteries for repentance.”
>
> **Pope Leo, to Rusticus of Narbonne, chapter 16:** “It is foreign to ecclesiastical custom that those who have been consecrated in priestly honor or the rank of the diaconate should receive, by laying on of hands, a remedy of repentance for some crime. This without doubt descends from apostolic tradition, according to what is written: ‘If a priest sins, who shall pray for him?’ (1 Kings 2:25.) Therefore, for such fallen persons, a private withdrawal must be sought in order to obtain the mercy of God, where their satisfaction, if it is worthy, may also be fruitful.” [Col. 1306D]

But for those who have at some time performed public repentance in the sight of the Church, or who, because of their fall, have been removed from the clergy and sent under the hand and yoke of an abbot, the sacred canons take away every restoration to rank. This is not through despair of pardon, but through the rigor of discipline, so that the medicine of repentance may be more useful insofar as it is humbler, and humbler insofar as return to lost orders is more difficult.

The holy Fathers have made this return difficult in some places and utterly impossible in others. For after publicly performed repentance for a condemnable crime, no one ought to exercise the ministry of sacred orders in the clerical state, although he may take part in the choir of those who chant [Col. 1305B]. But those who are not so rebellious that they cannot be treated more leniently because of their humility, and who are confined not publicly before the people but in some penitential prison-cell within clerical cloisters, and are not admitted to the choir of chanters during their days of repentance, may—if they remain in their humility—be recalled not only to the choir but even to their lost orders, provided that they are found perfectly established in the virtue of humility.

For the very virtue of humility may be understood in God’s building through the valley gate, beside which was the dung gate (2 Esdras 3:13); and in the neighboring place the fountain gate is said to have been joined to it (2 Esdras 2:14).
