For when the humbled sinner judges himself unclean in his own eyes, as though a dung heap, he himself becomes before God a fountain gate [Col. 1305C], while in him there comes to be a spring of water leaping up unto eternal life. Outwardly he will present himself in such a way that the righteous are refreshed by his example as by a fountain, while the weak, prone to sin, and stained with crooked desire are cleansed by considering him.

For if the laws of repentance were observed as required, many would thereby be restrained from crimes and saved. First, each person after baptism ought to live under the laws of innocence. Second, if he departed from these, he ought to be bound under the laws and rules of repentance. Third, if he would not submit even to these, he ought to be deprived of ecclesiastical fellowship. Fourth, if some consideration for preserving peace [Col. 1305D] and preventing slaughter among the multitude hindered this, it ought to be borne not silently but with judicious protest. Fifth, if the multitude were not corrected by this protest of the priests, a judicial sentence ought to be pronounced against the leaders of error and authors of crimes, so that the multitude might be spared while error was nevertheless opposed.

[Col. 1306A] Yet great discernment must be exercised in such a sentence. For when an error has either no defenders or no defenders capable of producing schism, measures of separation ought more swiftly to oppose the disease lest it spread like cancer. But when it has defenders such that, if they are separated from the Church, there is no doubt that schism will arise, then indeed, as blessed Augustine says, measures of separation are both fruitless and pernicious and sacrilegious, because they become impious and proud and disturb weak good people more than they correct resolute evil people.

## CHAPTER XLV. What distinction must be observed in correcting the faults of clerics, especially where there is a great multitude of offenders. How, by whom, and from what source ecclesiastical alms must be dispensed.

[Col. 1306B]

What then? Must the bishop therefore keep silent? Must he therefore cease from crying out, he to whom it was said, “Cry aloud; do not cease” (Isa. 58:1)? Far from it! For when complete separation cannot be effected lest the multitude be ruined, there are, according to the laws of the Fathers, many other kinds of restraint which, like medicinal draughts, do not provoke vomiting and wholly expel what is diseased, but heal inwardly with a certain pain of the bowels. In this manner clerics may be salutarily and medicinally tormented inwardly: if—since they ought not to be excommunicated because of their number, yet ought not to be tolerated because of their irregular manner of life and manifest disgrace—they are suspended from office while preserving lay [Col. 1306C] communion; and the people subject to them are forbidden by public interdict from hearing and obeying them. This is especially so if such are clerics as the ancient Fathers condemn or deprive of office: as at the Synod of Chalcedon they deprive of office all those ordained absolutely; as many saints condemn Simoniacs and Nicolaitans. And as for vicars or hired substitutes, and all who occupy a church which they obtained not by election but by lay appointment—because, as blessed Ambrose declares, they are not lawful husbands but adulterers—which bishop would not keep them from the marriage chamber of the Church if, with the Apostle, he were jealous over those entrusted to him with God’s jealousy?

All these could be recalled from their errors by a first and second [Col. 1306D] admonition, and invited through every baptismal church to regular and apostolic life, so that the people, instructed in the apostolic faith, might be governed throughout the whole bishopric by apostolic life, everywhere avoiding the apostate sect. For persons of this sort do not serve Christ the Lord, but their own belly; and by sweet speeches they deceive others.

[Col. 1307A] Those, therefore, who were either ordained absolutely or acephali and would not submit to sound admonition, even if it seemed difficult and less useful to excommunicate so many and such persons, could be healed by some restraint, as by a salutary draught, if only bishops, through God’s cooperating grace, applied themselves diligently to this.

Then, in every baptismal church, the fountain gate would be built, because, according to the resources of the tithes, homes for the poor would be established, especially for widows to be supported from the fourth portion of the tithe. These homes were formerly called *xenodochia*, that is, hostels for strangers; deacons and archdeacons were appointed over their administration and were to render account yearly to the bishops for their stewardship. Hence blessed Gregory in his decrees signifies that preaching properly belongs to presbyters, while the distribution of alms belongs to deacons, according to the pattern known to have been observed in the Acts of the Apostles: there Peter, with the other apostles, devoted himself to word and prayer; Stephen, with the other deacons, ministered in caring for widows and the poor [Col. 1307B].

Hence the sacred canons command that every baptismal church must never be so destitute of clerics as not to have at least a presbyter and a deacon, namely for the twofold office of preaching and distribution. For just as public preaching is not permitted to those below the priesthood, so the distribution of ecclesiastical resources is never rightly permitted to those below the diaconate. Therefore deacons or presbyters alone ought to have charge of widows, who are to be supported freely by the Church under the rule of common life from the fourth part of the tithes. Any surplus which may remain after provision for widows chosen, according to Paul’s teaching, solely for poverty and good testimony, should be faithfully bestowed, under the testimony of Christ and the Church, upon orphans and others enduring need and asking the Church, as their mother, for help. Thus every poor person may find at his own mother’s house a fountain gate, where he may repair his lack from pure alms when the dung gate does not enrich him [Col. 1307C].

This is the difference between almsgivers who still retain their own possessions and in great part serve the world, and those stewards of ecclesiastical property, whom the bishop appoints in each baptismal church as having nothing of their own and seeking nothing for themselves: as the water of a fountain is clean in comparison with dung, so the alms of the Church—which receives freely and gives freely—should be clean in comparison with the alms which secular persons give from the profits of unrighteous mammon [Col. 1307D].

[Col. 1308A] Therefore the holy and chosen leaders of Israel who returned from Babylon were not content to rebuild the dung gate, but added to it the fountain gate. For alms from unrighteous mammon, like a certain richness of dung, cure the barrenness of the rich by aiding the dryness of the poor; and they represent the dung gate in the spiritual Jerusalem. Through it the rich man and tax collector, with Zacchaeus the rich man and tax collector, passes like a camel through the eye of a needle into the holy city of the saints—provided that he gives his own possessions in such a way as to restore what belongs to others.

What belongs to others is not to be given, but restored. If it cannot be restored fourfold, it must at least be restored in full. For so long as anyone knowingly usurps another’s property, even what he appears to possess justly, whether from his own labor [Col. 1308B] or by inheritance from his parents, is another’s property to him. For it is written: “If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you what is your own?” (Luke 16:12).

Therefore the robber and withholder of other people’s goods possesses nothing justly; for even if he is called noble, he does not possess even himself, being the slave of as many masters as he has vices. If he served one Lord, keeping His commands before all else, he would be free even if called a slave. But now, sharing in the manifold lordship of the servants of evil spirits, he is altogether unclean. For in the Law everything unclean is called common, because whatever does not serve one lord, having been subjected to the dominations of many evil spirits [Col. 1308C], is alienated from the author of purity and tormented by many masters. Thus “unclean” and “common” are rightly said under the same meaning.

But because the heavenly voice commanded Peter not to call common or unclean those whom God, by calling them to His service and freeing them from the common dominion of many, purifies and cleanses (Acts 10:28), the dung gate is not to be despised. There the poor become friends to the rich through unrighteous mammon, so that they may receive them into eternal dwellings—provided that the rich, while giving their own possessions, do not retain what belongs to others. For possessions lawfully acquired are themselves called unrighteous mammon, because they are scarcely possessed without the contagion of iniquity. But other people’s goods are not called unrighteous mammon [Col. 1308D], but sheer wickedness of iniquity. Therefore, when sacred Scripture gives, as it were, the reason why the alms of the impious do not please God, it says that they do not please God because they are offered from wickedness, especially when the giver remains still in approval or defense of that very wickedness.

> **Note: [Col. 1307D] Gregory, to Syagrius of Autun:** “Therefore the enemy’s cunning must altogether be feared and avoided, lest those whom he cannot overthrow by open temptation he may more cruelly slaughter with a hidden weapon. For that is not to be reckoned almsgiving when what is received from unlawful sources is distributed to the poor, because the person who receives wrongly with the intention of distributing, as it were, rightly is burdened [Col. 1308D] rather than helped. The almsgiving of our Redeemer which pleases Him is that which is not accumulated from unlawful means and iniquity, but expended from permitted and well-acquired goods. Hence it is also certain that even if monasteries, hostels, or anything else are constructed, this does not profit toward reward, since the one who has received the administration of money from him destroys by evil ordering more than he can [Col. 1309D] build. Therefore, lest under the pretext of almsgiving we endeavor to receive anything with sin, sacred Scripture openly forbids us, saying: ‘The sacrifices of the impious are abominable, which are offered from wickedness’ (Prov. 21:27). For whatever is offered from wickedness in sacrifice to God does not appease the wrath of almighty God, but provokes it.”
>
> In these words of blessed Gregory, let monks [Col. 1310D] and other religious canons carefully note that they dwell dangerously in the cloisters of masters of this kind, or are fed by the alms of persons whom they know to be sacrilegious possessors of ecclesiastical property and obstinate defenders of this practice.
>
> **From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 33:** “One ought not to receive *eulogiae* from heretics, for they are curses rather than blessings.”

For if such offerings were made from unrighteous mammon—that is, from possessions lawfully held—they would not on that account be rejected because they were offered by an impious person nevertheless seeking godliness; rather, they would draw the giver himself toward godliness. Thus the impious and Gentile centurion was drawn to Christianity by his alms. Therefore, in the figure of that man and of like persons who offer from unrighteous mammon, Peter was told: “Kill and eat”; and again: “What God has cleansed, do not call common” (Acts 10:13–14). For the alms of such persons are not to be rejected by the saints, nor is their soul to be called unclean or common; rather, it is to be brought by Peter—that is, by any saint established in Christ—into the body of the Church. This is accomplished when their almsgiving is proclaimed accepted in heaven and their mind, baptized by sound teaching as by a kind of baptismal water, puts on Christ [Col. 1309B]. Thus, although the person who gives alms in this way, together with the centurion Cornelius, is somewhat occupied with worldly affairs, he is nevertheless truly called a Christian by Christ. For he enters the heavenly Jerusalem through the dung gate, making friends for himself from unrighteous mammon.

But those who retain what belongs to others and offer from wickedness, provoking God and harming their neighbor, run through the gates of hell unto death. They do not find the dung gate through which they may enter the holy city unless they first strive, by restoring another’s property as they are able, to be reconciled with their brother; and then make themselves and their possessions an acceptable offering to their Lord and God [Col. 1309C], no longer to be called common or unclean. For they will not be pressed beneath the heavy and unpleasant yoke of many masters; rather, bearing the light burden and easy yoke of one Lord, they will be holy and clean. Nor are they, because of past deeds, to be abhorred by Peter—that is, by any Catholic—for no one ought to call common or unclean what God has cleansed. Indeed, even while they still sin deliberately, prayer should be made for their cleansing. For God is able to offer Peter creeping things and beasts enclosed in the sheet-vessel for killing and eating, and, purged of their uncleanness, to lift them into heaven: persons who offer not from the acquisition of wickedness but from unrighteous mammon, so that when they fail they may be received into eternal dwellings, having been brought in through the dung gate [Col. 1309D]—that is, cleansed by restoring what belongs to others, giving generously from their own possessions, and fully incorporated into the fellowship of the holy ones.

## CHAPTER XLVI. The fourth part of tithes is to be distributed to widows and the poor, not to soldiers; for assuredly their intercession will not have as much effect before the divine tribunal as that of widows and the poor.

[Col. 1310A] Therefore let the gate of hell, the gate of death, which is built by unjust offerers from the acquisition of wickedness, be far from our holy building. But let the dung gate (2 Esdras 3:13) be established among secular almsgivers, by the example of Zacchaeus and the often-mentioned centurion. Further, let the fountain gate be rebuilt through the regular cloisters of canons, in which no division into fourths is to be made; instead, following the apostles’ example, all things are to be distributed according to each person’s need, and what remains is to be given to the poor in accordance with the Gospel’s command. But where the common life is not maintained, let at least the synodal statutes of the Fathers be maintained, so that, just as in every baptismal church the baptismal font [Col. 1310B] cleanses believers through invisible grace, as by clean water, so the fourth portion of tithes, providing continual and pure refreshment in the manner of a fountain, may console the needy through a kind of visible grace—more graciously, indeed, to be bestowed upon widows and other needy persons.

This almsgiving is the purest fountain water because it is offered not from unrighteous mammon but from the grace of equity. For this almsgiving a widow who has good testimony, who is truly a widow and desolate, is to be sought out of one’s own accord and chosen according to Paul’s teaching; this almsgiving is to be sold to no one, but bestowed upon the despoiled, widows, and needy persons.

[Col. 1310C] The ancient Fathers, intimate friends of the Father of orphans and Judge of widows, and therefore greatly concerned for widows and orphans, did not enrich soldiers from the portion of the poor as certain modern bishops do. Thus, departing this life, they found tranquility and rest with that same Father, whose children they had not defrauded in this portion. But these men have peace neither here among soldiers possessing the goods of the Church nor will they find favor with the Father of orphans and Judge of widows through a military hand. For they are now afflicted by soldiers; but at the final judgment all alike will be disturbed because of the desolation of widows and orphans—those who, by giving, granting, or receiving the portion of the poor, are proved their despoilers [Col. 1310D]. They will be disturbed, I say; but let us ask by whom they will be disturbed. Assuredly, by His face. Whose face? The face of the Father of orphans and Judge of widows (Ps. 67:6). Then neither will the soldier be able to defend the bishop with his sword, nor the bishop excuse the soldier, when that Judge of widows asks why the former granted [Col. 1311A], or the latter received, the goods of the poor and widows.

Gregory, Martin, Ambrose, and Augustine will not fear that judgment of the Father of orphans and Judge of widows, because they will have the favor of the poor and widows. Nor will they be found to have defrauded anyone of the poor’s portion, which they did not diminish for soldiers; indeed, they strove to increase it even from goods that could have remained beyond their own narrow necessities, so that they themselves endured voluntary poverty because of another’s necessary poverty. Therefore they will not be disturbed by the face of the Father of orphans and Judge of widows, but with Him they will execute judgment against their oppressors.

> **Note: [Col. 1311D] Life of St. Gregory, book 2, chapter 55:** “How Gregory, through the managers of ecclesiastical estates, carried the eyes of his pastoral concern throughout the breadth of the whole world, like a certain most luminous Argus, I have perhaps not without reason thought fit to mention briefly. For he says in a letter to Anthemus the subdeacon: ‘When you were departing, we commanded you, and afterward I remember that in written instructions sent out I enjoined you to care for the poor and, if you learned that any there were in need, to inform us by returning letters; and you have scarcely taken care to do this even for a few persons [Col. 1312D].’”

Then, in so great an assembly of angels and saints, documentary tablets concerning Christ’s inheritance, drawn up by the Fathers [Col. 1311B], will be produced, and all who administer ecclesiastical property disorderly will be convicted by them. For if, when one favored by a testator brings complaint before a judge, no one who has made a contrary additional disposition escapes judgment under a human will, how will they escape judgment in the presence of the assembly of saints whose decretal statutes they have violated? For, neglecting what has been written concerning Christ’s inheritance, they have either introduced new usurpations or failed to correct usurpations already introduced.

For we see few persons who foster the common life in baptismal churches from church revenues, or who annually make four portions from them and distribute these according to the statutes of the canons. The bishop possesses some estates; the soldier possesses others; the cleric has little; the widow and Lazarus receive nothing. Nowhere is the fountain gate found, where the hungry and thirsty Lazarus is refreshed, because the poorhouses (*ptochia*) of the poor—in which the fourth portion of ecclesiastical revenues ought to be brought in every church—are found not even at the episcopal see itself [Col. 1311C]. The dung gate has been entirely destroyed, because the almsgiving of those who unlawfully divert there the goods of the poor to another purpose is not called dung, by which the field of their life may be made fruitful; rather, whatever is offered is offered from wickedness, so long as the poor’s portion is not restored by them to its proper uses, and so long as this very iniquity is loved, defended, and approved by them.

[Col. 1311D] For Holy Church—having few clerics for whom, in the common life, all things are held in common, but supporting many clerics scarcely worthy of a fourth part of the tithes—still awaits the grace of God to raise up for her clerics of the Levitical stock for whom all things may be common. Meanwhile she does not wish to be content [Col. 1312A] with the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees; and therefore, from what she receives freely, she sets apart not a tenth but a fourth part for the poor. For the number of those who, with Peter, are willing to possess nothing is still small; while the number of those who, with Lazarus, lie needy before the doors of the rich is great. Therefore it should not seem excessive if a fourth part of all Church revenues is contributed to the *ptochia*, the bishop, from his own fourth share, providing through whomsoever he chooses *xenodochia*, that is, hostels for strangers. In former times *ptochia* was the name given to those houses established in each Church, to which the poor’s share was brought.

Concerning this, the Council of Aquileia reads as follows: “We decree that presbyters shall have beside their Church, [Col. 1312B] or within their dwelling, an appointed place to which the fourth part, which we have said is to be given to the poor, shall be brought.” This house, as has been noted, was formerly called a *ptochium*, and in it there was a shelter for destitute widows living in common. Whatever could remain over was faithfully distributed through deacons and their assistants to orphans and other needy persons—whether those seeking consolation there, or those awaiting it at home because they were sick or ashamed to beg.

[Note: [Col. 1312D] *Life of St Gregory*, book II, chapter 27: “Every day, through the streets and crossroads of all the districts, he sent fixed allowances to the sick and to persons disabled in any bodily member, by appointed couriers. But to those of greater modesty, before he himself took food, he took care that a dish from his own table, with the apostolic blessing, should be sent door to door; so that the benevolence of this most merciful provider excepted absolutely no one whom knowledge of the almighty Creator had drawn to the faith.”]

O blessed are those who built such gates of fountains; and wretched are those who destroyed them! For in those houses which, in the construction of the Church, we have identified as the gates of fountains, every baptismal Church had [Col. 1312C] an open fountain offering pure refreshment—a single fountain from which no stranger shared. For in the *ptochia* of each Church were gathered widows who had earned their rest and had been chosen in that Church under testimony. Whatever was left beyond their need was added to the relief of the other poor children of that Church, so that the poor might find with their mother in Christ, rich in children, not only spiritual but also bodily consolations.

For the households of the faith had *ptochia* built for them, in which the fourth share ought to have been administered according to the prescribed rule: so that its steward, having from the Church and within his Church a reputation for good administration, might be a sweet savour and, like Stephen, be crowned as a minister to widows and the poor; or else, if disgraced by theft or any shameful act, might be branded with the disgrace of Judas the thief and Nicholas the fornicator, [Col. 1312D] and rejected from the ministry. Therefore the testimony of the Church is necessary concerning such administration, since that share must be bestowed upon poor sons and daughters in full public accountability.

[Col. 1313A] Hence Pope Gelasius says in his decrees: “Even though a man may appear likely to show that he has administered by divine principles that portion assigned to the poor, nevertheless, as it is written, ‘that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven,’ it must also be publicly attested and not passed over in silence without the proclamations of a good reputation.” The same pope, to Justin the archdeacon and Faustus, says: “Let four portions be made from offerings and the income of estates: one is to be taken by the bishop for himself; another he is to distribute among the clerics according to his judgment and choice; the third he is to cause to be disbursed to the poor with full accountability.” Did not this wise architect build the gate of the fountain? Of this it is read in the book of Ezra: “And Shallum built the gate of the fountain. He [Col. 1313B] built it, and roofed it, and set up its doors, its bolts, and its bars” (2 Esdras 3:12–13).

## CHAPTER XLVII. It is shown by the authority of councils that a fourth part of the tithes must be bestowed upon the poor.

Who are these bars, if not the strongest authorities, by which this gate is so fortified that whoever superimposes something else upon the testament written concerning this gate destroys himself, not it? The Fathers once wished, at a certain Council of Toledo, to impose another arrangement upon the testament concerning tithes, decreeing that they should be made not into four but into three portions, two for the clerics and the third assigned to bishops. But since, by failing to take due care for the cause of the poor, they seemed to destroy the gate of the fountain so fortified by [Col. 1313C] bolts and bars, it was proved that not the gate but its destroyers could be destroyed: for that chapter was annulled and condemned by later and more authoritative councils.

For the Fathers at the Council of Agrippina, unwilling to tolerate the Toledo chapter, speak thus: “The tithe given by the faithful is to be called God’s due, and must therefore be rendered in full; a third part of it, according to the canon of Toledo, ought to belong to the bishops. We, however, do not wish to exercise this power, but wish to have only a fourth part of it each year, according to the usage of the Roman pontiffs and the observance of the holy Roman Church. If any contentious person be found in this matter, whether cleric or [Col. 1313D] layman, he shall be deprived of communion and judged by synodal censure.”

See how that which was improperly superimposed upon the ancient testament of tithes was annulled and condemned. Roman authorities, indeed, like iron and unbreakable bars, fortify this testament concerning the gate of fountains. By commanding that the fourth share be administered in full accountability, they do not permit tithes to be divided into three thirds, but prescribe, according to the decrees of the canons, that four fourths be made both from the income of ecclesiastical estates and from the tithes themselves.

One of these shares, that which belongs to the bishop in a baptismal Church, may be set apart from the remaining portions and transferred wherever the bishop decides, because, [Col. 1314A] as blessed Gregory testifies in writing to Augustine, bishop of the English, “the bishop is bound from this portion to provide for the reception of pilgrims and guests.” Therefore, if he wishes to devote it more diligently to carrying out the office of hospitality, let him leave it to the discretion of his successor whether it should be done in this way or in a more advantageous one. For if he wishes his grant or endowment to remain perpetual, thereby prejudicing his successor and dissolving the testament made concerning tithes, then—even should he endeavour to fortify his grant by some new privilege—the grant or endowment made against the canons cannot endure after his death if his immediate, second, or any later successor wishes to alter it.

[Col. 1314B] For no one can establish another testament concerning tithes besides that which has been established. It is fortified and confirmed by such bolts and bars that neither the new privileges of monks nor the unjust justice of modern men can overthrow it through knights improperly enfeoffed with tithes and Church estates. And because monks and knights think that a grant or endowment once made to them by bishops from tithes has passed into a law to be observed forever and violated by no successor, let us see what not only the laws of the Church but also secular laws judge concerning this matter. For this conflict is carried on not only against certain ecclesiastical persons, but also against secular persons seeking to dissolve the legal testament concerning tithes. Let us see, I say, [Col. 1314C] whether that can stand which appears to be confirmed against the canons by a new privilege, or supported by the unjust justice of knights.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. It is contrary to the sacred canons for bishops permanently to alienate the tithes of Churches.

From the synod of Pope Hilary, chapter 4: “Whatever any bishop has unlawfully done, or has found to have been done by his predecessors, he must condemn if he wishes to avoid danger to himself. For whatever he fails to cut away in another, he will find in himself.”

Gelasius, to Bishops Cresconius, John, and Messala, among other things: “Just as it befits a successor to preserve his predecessors’ enactments when they are lawful and just, so also [Col. 1314D] he ought to correct what has been badly done.” Pelagius, to Armentarius, master of soldiers, among other things: “Once the rights of Churches have been made firm by the authority even of intervening documents, the pontiff must by no means be permitted to have freedom to depart from them, even if he wishes.”

Adrian, to Engelram: “Constitutions contrary to the holy decrees of the Roman bishops shall have no force.”

Gregory, in the *Register*: “It has been expressly enacted by imperial constitution that acts done contrary to laws are not only void but must also be regarded as not having been done.”

From the Roman laws: “Only that may derive substance from a sacred rescript which is supported by [Col. 1315A] the aid of the laws.” Likewise: “A general command is to be preferred to a special favour.” And again: “Rescripts contrary to law have no force, however they may have been obtained. For judges ought rather to follow what public laws prescribe.” And below: “Personal rescripts that accord with the law shall remain valid according to ancient custom, and the disposition of the case of which our rescript speaks shall be judged within the bounds of the sentence rendered. But any special provision that brings injury upon laws and right is to be abolished and uprooted.” Likewise: “Those writings granted at the request of an individual petitioner shall prevail and be carried into effect when they accord with the principle of law and the laws; but those perhaps obtained by fraud or false petitions shall provide petitioners with no remedy.”

[Col. 1315B] Likewise, at a council held in Rome under Pope Symmachus, when a certain perverse constitution had been read aloud in the presence of all, Lawrence, bishop of the Church of Milan, said: “This document could bind no pontiff, especially since neither has a pope subscribed to it nor is the assent of any metropolitan, according to the canons, found recorded.” Peter, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, said: “It is manifest that the document published in our assembly has no force, because it does not accord with the canons.” Eulalius, bishop of the Church of Syracuse, said: “The document read in the assembly of priests is invalid by the clearest proofs: [Col. 1315C] first, because it appears to have been made contrary to the rules of the Fathers; secondly, because it is shown to have been confirmed by the subscription of no bishop of the Apostolic See.” The same bishop said: “The holy Fathers decreed that whatever priests of any province, after holding a council within their own boundaries, establish without the authority of their metropolitan is void. Therefore there is no doubt that what is known to have been presumptuously undertaken lacks force and cannot in any way be reckoned among ecclesiastical enactments.” The holy synod said: “It seems certain to us that this very document has no force, and that it should properly be weakened and reduced to nothing by the prudent judgment of your Blessedness, lest it remain as a precedent for any lay persons, however religious or powerful, in any city and in any manner [Col. 1315D] to decree anything concerning ecclesiastical property, the care of which is plainly shown to have been entrusted by God without qualification to priests alone.” Pope Symmachus said: “It is necessary that we extend our concern not only to the present but also to future ages. Therefore, if any document has been drawn up contrary to divine law, it shall be resisted with every power, even though from the beginning it had no … [lacuna]. And any ecclesiastical persons whatsoever may raise a voice of objection and be supported by ecclesiastical authority.”

From these authorities it is clear that neither divine laws favour monks who possess permanently by right the bishop’s share, nor secular laws favour knights who wish to hold tithes and Church estates by benefice-right and leave them to their descendants. For, by the plain authority of canons and secular laws, void is whatever anyone confirms by a new document against the canons defending divine and ancient justice, or presumptuously claims without a document through the unjust justice of modern customs. [Col. 1316A]

Therefore, if a bishop wishes to give or assign something from his own portion, his gift or assignment shall stand during his lifetime, whether for his salvation or condemnation, according to the character of the gift or assignment. Yet if before death he recognizes its danger, he too, relying upon divine laws, may undo his own act, guarding against danger both to himself and to the recipient. For long ago [Col. 1316B] Pope Symmachus published throughout the world the peril attending the giver and the wrongful recipient. He says: “Whoever, forgetful of God and unmindful of this decree, attempts permanently to alienate anything belonging by right to titles or to the Church: let the donor, alienator, and seller be punished by loss of his office.” See what penalty is prescribed for the giver and alienator, unless, as the same pope determines in what follows, the practice be observed in making grants which, in consideration of souls, seems fitting to the purpose of religion. We have heard the penalty of the incautious giver; let us hear with what penalty the same pope commands that the incautious petitioner or recipient be struck. “Whoever,” he says, “shall ask for or receive it, or whoever among presbyters, deacons, or defenders subscribes to the giver, [Col. 1316C] shall be struck with anathema, by which an angry God smites souls.”

But so that, in prescribing vengeance upon giver and recipient, he might nevertheless show a way out of and escape from that vengeance, he says: “Let the punishment which we have set forth be upon the alienator, recipient, and subscriber, unless perhaps the alienator provides for himself by taking it back, and the person who received it by swift restitution. But if anyone, through too little concern for his soul, should perhaps neglect the remedy offered, beyond the forms of punishment set down above: if any document has been drawn up contrary to divine law, it shall be resisted with every power, even though from the beginning it had no … [lacuna]. But any ecclesiastical persons whatsoever may raise a voice of objection and be supported by ecclesiastical authority, [Col. 1316D] so that they may reclaim what is another’s together with its fruits. Nor may one protect himself by any obstacle before the tribunal of Christ if he scatters, contrary to divine law and without any consideration of mercy, resources left by religious souls for the substance of the poor.”

## CHAPTER XLIX. Gerhoh exhorts bishops to correct and retract wrong acts, after the example of Peter rebuked by Paul.

With such great authorities set plainly before us, what bishop would not gladly use the remedy offered to him by reclaiming what he has wrongly given or assigned? For what man may not happen to sin with Peter through fear or ignorance? And if this should happen, what remains for those who have fallen with Peter except to rise with Peter? For Peter, [Col. 1317A] walking wrongly through ignorance with respect to the truth of the Gospel, as soon as he recognized his error after being rebuked by his fellow disciple, gladly yielded to the truth under the correction made to his face. He provided a great and illustrious example for imitation, so that no one, however exalted, should be ashamed to alter his opinion if it is revealed to him, even by one beneath him, that he is proceeding contrary to the truth of the Gospel or the canons.

For the Apostle Paul, though surpassing all the apostles in labour, nevertheless calls himself an untimely birth because he persecuted the Church and was called last of all (1 Corinthians 15:8–9). Yet the prince of the apostles did not so refuse his correction according to the truth of the Gospel that, preferring his own reprover to himself in wisdom, he [Col. 1317B] praised that very epistle in which he saw his own dissimulation rebuked.

And so I, speaking only of Saul, not yet Paul, and drawing a comparison from the great persecutor, not the great preacher, call myself an untimely birth and the least of all Christians. For I too, according to my measure—indeed, beyond my measure—have persecuted the Church of God, not only by squandering my paternal substance upon myself and long feeding swine, but also, which I greatly dread, and would that I dreaded enough, by supporting for my pride and profit a certain evil tree of anathema cut down by the sickle. Even if it bore good fruits, evil recompense would still await me because of my utterly wicked intention, [Col. 1317C] unless that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world is able both to convert the person of whom I speak and to heal me, who confess my fault before him to all who will read these things. I withhold both his name and mine, revealing only a confession of iniquity, so that pardon may be sought for sins and that I may avoid shipwreck through both pride and envy. For while he of whom I speak, though still bearing evil fruit, is tolerated by the master of the household among the bishops, my own person should fittingly and truthfully be judged the reproach of men and the outcast of the people. The disclosure of my name would not lack the colouring of pride, especially since in this little work I wish the person and name of the writer to remain unknown, [Col. 1317D] while the person and name of him who commands me [Col. 1318A] to write should be known. Since he is bishop of Regensburg, sufficiently religious by God’s grace and full of charity, he must not be drawn by us into envy or hatred so that anyone should be angered against him in any degree because, in a structure built by his command, a certain pseudo-bishop is censured by name. For this building, though made by an ugly painter, is nevertheless to be presented as beautiful to the supremely beautiful One; and therefore it must not be disfigured by the openly stated name of any detestable person, but suitably adorned with delightful pictures through examples of memorable Fathers.

Therefore, to return to the subject: although the Apostle was as an untimely birth, while I am truly an untimely birth and the vilest of all, nevertheless, as God reveals it to me and with his help, I shall bring forward [Col. 1318B] that in which I see the bishop not to have walked rightly according to the truth of the Gospel or the canons. Thus he will be considered of so much greater virtue as he does not disdain to listen in such matters to one lesser than himself, and he will imitate Peter by retracting and dissolving his own judgment, even if he knows that he confirmed it with an oath to the peril of his soul. For if Peter had not changed his denial made with an oath, Peter himself would not have remained Peter, having been utterly cut off from the rock of truth.

Therefore, that the rock of truth may prevail over custom, and that wicked abuse, which is the gate of hell, may not prevail against this rock, let the bishop endeavour to retract these gifts or assignments wrongly made by his predecessors or even by himself. For we possess [Col. 1318C] examples of great men

[Note: [Col. 1317D]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1110, a synod was held in the Lateran Church under the presidency of Pope Paschal II, in the third indiction, on the Nones of March. There the same Paschal, condemning and retracting his own decision, is recorded to have spoken as follows; and the text is preserved at Rome: “Hear, most beloved brothers: I confess to God the almighty Father and to you that I repent that that privilege—or rather, that *pravilege* [evil privilege]—extorted from us in the tents, was ever given to anyone. We consented contrary to the decrees of our predecessors; and in this synod, as in the former one, we excommunicate it and all those who wish to treat it as a privilege. To God and to you we promise, so long as this wretched soul dwells in an unworthy body, that we shall never consent to anything contrary to the decrees of our Fathers, if it please his majesty. Therefore I ask you to pray for me, a wretched sinner, that he may deign to forgive me [Col. 1318D] this crime and all my sins.” Immediately Lord Bishop Bruno said: “Let us praise God and give him thanks, because our lord and head repents of having promulgated that heresy.” Then John, indignantly protesting, asked: “Do you say that we promulgated heresy? No one ought ever again to listen to you.” Bruno said: “I wish to prove that it is heresy.” The bishop of Vulturia said: “What is heresy can be done with such an intention; but he acted unwillingly and under compulsion. It must not be called heresy. If he had acted voluntarily, it could be proved to be heresy.”

In these things it should be noted that an enactment made by bishops against the canons then becomes heresy if it is either perpetrated knowingly or, after the truth has been recognized, is not condemned by the person who established or confirmed it, lest, if he does not condemn it, he himself be condemned.]

who retracted their enactments, judging themselves so that they would not be judged by the Lord. Thus Pope Boniface II is recorded to have decreed that the deacon Vigilius should succeed him in the pontificate. Since this appeared to the Roman clergy to oppose the canons, it was, in the presence of the clergy, thrown into the fire by Boniface himself before the confession of blessed Peter the Apostle.

Blessed Augustine too composed the book of *Retractions* to correct matters he had earlier written incautiously; and he urges every wise person to do the same in these words. For he says in the prologue of that book: “No one, unless shameless, will dare to rebuke me [Col. 1318D] because I rebuke my own errors. But if he says that I ought not to have [Col. 1319A] said things which later displeased even me, he speaks truly and acts with me. For he is a rebuker of those matters of which I too am a rebuker. But however anyone may take what I do, I must nevertheless heed even in this matter the apostolic saying: ‘If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord.’”

## CHAPTER L. The teaching that Church property must not be alienated is confirmed by the authority of Saint Leo the Great.

But in order that it may plainly appear which donations, assignments, and alienations of Church property, however made, should be ratified and which should be rejected, let us hear the rule concerning gift, exchange, and sale prescribed generally by Pope Leo the Great to all [Col. 1319B] bishops, though sent by him particularly to bishops established throughout Sicily.

“LEO, bishop, to all bishops established throughout Sicily. The occasion of special complaints demands from us the care of general providence, so that we may by a perpetual constitution cut away from every episcopal usurpation what has been wickedly done and unjustly presumed in two Churches of our province. For the clerics of Tauromenium lamented the impoverishment of their Church, because its bishop had dissipated all its estates by selling, giving, and alienating them in diverse ways. Likewise the clerics of Palermo, for whom a bishop has recently been ordained, brought a similar complaint before the holy synod [Col. 1319C] over which we presided, concerning the usurpations of their former bishop. Therefore, although we have already ordained how provision is to be made for the welfare of both Churches, nevertheless, lest this destructive example of most wicked plundering become hereafter imitable by anyone, we wish this form of our command to be perpetual among your Belovednesses. Without delay, we decree that no bishop dare to give, exchange, or sell anything from the property of his Church, unless he does something of this kind in such a way as to secure something better, and chooses, after deliberation and with the consent of the whole clergy, what cannot be doubted to benefit the Church. For presbyters, deacons, and clerics of any order whatsoever who enter into an agreement to the detriment of the Church should know [Col. 1319D] that they will be deprived both of office and communion. For it is full of justice, dearest brothers, that the Church’s welfare be kept unharmed by the zeal not only of bishops but also of the whole clergy, and that the gifts remain inviolate of those who have contributed their own property to Churches for the salvation of their souls.”

See: we have heard the mighty roar of Leo the Great, terrifyingly execrating and branding with fitting names the destructive example of most wicked plundering. Let knights call, as they please, a “benefice” that by which, in return for their deceptive homage and a small price—sometimes no price at all—they receive a great estate of the Church. Certainly, the Holy Spirit, speaking through his instrument, as we have [Col. 1320A] read, calls that benefice, given and received against the prescribed rule, an example of most wicked plundering. O that every word of this decretal letter might be carefully observed, and intelligently and obediently put into practice by bishops and clerics! O that, as it decrees, clerics of every order who take part in agreements damaging the Church might be deprived of office and communion! O that those displeased by the Church’s losses might imitate the clerics lamenting the impoverishment of their Church, of whom we have read there! Certainly, if these things were done, whatever has been wickedly done and unjustly presumed against this holy constitution would either, through God’s triumph, come to an end, or would not bring bishops and clerics everlasting condemnation. For they would either be punished here, or, by fighting against the plunderers of the Church through their protest, would be rendered safe before God and praiseworthy before the Church. If they persevered in continual protest, perhaps moving the plunderers little, perhaps greatly, then testimony would soon be given even by those on the opposing side—both to bishops concerning repentance for wicked usurpation and to clerics concerning innocence. [Col. 1320B]

Victory must not be despaired of when a potsherd struggles with a rock; nor should we doubt at all that the Lord is present with those contending for his inheritance. Thus either common life may be restored throughout the mother Churches according to apostolic institutions, or, if this cannot be done, at least synodal commands may be observed: namely, that not only the fourth portion for clerics, [Col. 1320C] the fourth for Church buildings, and the fourth for the poor be restored to their ancient and due uses, but also that the bishop’s own fourth, claimed back from monks and especially from knights, be spent by him as ordained for him—unless perhaps, according to the canons and with clergy approving and subscribing, a fiftieth part of some ecclesiastical possession is demonstrably granted to monks.

For the holy Fathers permit a bishop to make this assistance from the resources of Church property in order to support and console some monastery: that a fiftieth part of the income from certain estates or of the tithes of villages be assigned to monks. A grant of this fiftieth part, made solemnly and lawfully with the clergy’s approval, remains irrevocable, because it is permitted by the ordinances of the Fathers. But if no solemn and canonical grant has been made even of this fiftieth part, then a bishop who finds no living or written testimony concerning it may restore their rights to the mother Churches, lest those who possess by a kind of invasion a share taken from Church property be rendered hateful to God—the share the share of the stranger asking support from the bishop, the share of the cleric serving God, the share of the poor person who finds no consolation in his Church, and the share of the Church buildings needing restoration. [Col. 1320D]

## CHAPTER LI. Reply to the objections of monks who claim for themselves a fourth part of the tithes while refusing to undertake the care of souls. The same applies to certain canons.

[Col. 1321A] Here the monks object: “If,” they say, “the bishop’s fourth share, collected from the whole bishopric, were spent on receiving pilgrims and guests, rather than on gifts and banquets for knights, squires, minstrels, and actors; if that holy bishop, commended by blessed Gregory in his *Dialogues* because he did not allow a minstrel to enter his meal—not a minstrel uttering slander, nor one exciting itching ears by empty tales, but one playing simply and innocently with a monkey and a drum—indeed, because the minstrel at the door introduced a playful sound while the bishop was intent on divine matters, he announced that the man would die very soon; if bishops [Col. 1321B] content with religious chamberlains,

[Note: [Col. 1321D] Pope Gregory, seated before the most sacred body of blessed Peter the Apostle with bishops and all the presbyters of the Roman Church, while deacons and all the clergy stood by, said: “Truly, in our time the evil of indiscretion has grown strong: laymen, boys, and secular persons attend the pontiffs of this See in the private services of their chambers. And since the life of a shepherd should always be an example to disciples, the clerics often do not know what the private life of their pontiff is like, though, as has been said, secular boys know it. For this reason, by the present decree I establish that certain persons chosen from the clerics or even from the monks shall attend to the service of the pontifical chamber, so that he who holds the place of governance may have such witnesses as see his private conduct and, through constant observation, draw an example for their improvement.”]

with troops of knights and military attendants removed from them, lived in such a way that, according to the counsel of blessed Jerome, the poor and pilgrims, and Christ as their guest with them, knew their table; if bishops provided *xenodochia*, that is, hospitable houses, from what might remain beyond their own domestic and strict necessity—if,” they say, “bishops thus administered their fourth share rightly, we monks would perilously contend to retain it, because we ought to be content with worldly offerings and food procured by the work of our hands. But now, to say nothing for the present about the other portions, why is the bishop’s fourth demanded back from us, so that from it either a knight may be fed, or a horse fattened, or a minstrel [Col. 1321C] and public slanderer of the absent and flatterer of those present rewarded, or a castle rather than a hostel built?”

The monks say further: “If clerics in every mother Church, provost’s church, and baptismal Church lived canonically and apostolically rather than apostatically, the fourth portion of tithes would rightly be provided for them. But for those who proceed crookedly, that same fourth belongs more fittingly to none than to us monks who lead the apostolic life. For the monk who has entered the clerical order does not regard as robbery what the clergy ought to receive, and is therefore a cleric—especially since he is prepared to surrender the clergy’s share if he sees the clergy walking in a clerical manner.”

[Col. 1321D] Here we are compelled to recall an ancient history, whose tenor enables us to give an appropriate answer to monks who say these things. We read in the book of Ruth that a certain Elimelech, because of the severity of famine, left Bethlehem as a sojourner with his two sons and his wife Naomi, and came into the land of Moab. After he died, Naomi returned with her daughter-in-law Ruth because she had heard that there was food in the country [Col. 1322A] from which she had departed because of famine. It is enough to have recalled this familiar story, which whoever wishes may find fully in the book of Ruth. There he will find also, among other things, that a certain kinsman of the deceased Elimelech, when he wished to possess Elimelech’s field by right of kinship, was obliged also to take Ruth the Moabite as wife, in order to raise up offspring for his deceased kinsman and thus obtain the field by lawful right. But because he did not wish to raise up offspring for his deceased kinsman, he yielded the possession of the field to another, namely Boaz, the gracious raiser up of his brother’s seed. For this Boaz, taking Ruth, the wife of his deceased kinsman, begot Obed by Ruth, the father of Jesse, father of King David, who was the illustrious glory of his ancestral stock.

[Col. 1322B] Similarly, we confess that the true Elimelech, whose name means “My God is king” (Ruth 1), driven by the famine of the word of God, has in some manner left his city Bethlehem and, as though dead—indeed, truly slain not only by Jews but also by false Christians—needs one to raise up his seed, that is, the divine word, lest he lack a lawful succession of offspring. Therefore, if monks who are truly kinsmen of the Saviour wish to possess the tithes of any Church in such a way that, through priestly governance, they raise up from it, as it were from Ruth—whose name means “seeing” or “failing”—a lawful government, prefigured by David the lawful king, this may well be approved. For thus, through the industry of monks, the order of canons may be restored to life; indeed, the monks themselves will truly be clerics [Col. 1322C] and canons, as successors of the blessed monks Gregory and Martin, who, without impairing the virtue of monastic life, became clerics by feeding sheep and canons by observing canons—the one in the papacy, the other in an archbishopric. Hence it is clear that what was done in great Churches can also be done in small ones: namely, that they may be governed by monks using their tithes. For neither monks nor cloistered canons use the tithes of congregations without peril unless they have their care.

For apostolic authority confirms that the one who feeds the flock should eat of the flock’s milk, and the one who plants a vineyard should share in its fruit; and since clerical provision and clerical service are joined, [Col. 1322D] like body and soul, whoever divides these from one another—though the Church’s life subsists through their union—kills the Church, and exposes himself to the anathema which Pope and martyr Urban pronounced in his decrees, where he confirmed the common life of clerics in all mother churches. Therefore, even if a religious bishop is rarely found; even if no canonically living cleric rightly employs tithes; even if no church is restored from them; even if no poor person is fed from them: nevertheless, whoever introduces a new disorder contrary to the ordering of tithes, confirmed by divine and patristic authority through the Gospels, many councils, and the decrees of the Fathers—an innovation, as we have said, forbidden under anathema—none the less incurs anathema.

For whatever is demonstrably forbidden under anathema, if knowingly committed, or if, having been committed in ignorance, is not immediately abandoned once recognized, undoubtedly brings anathema upon those who presume it and persist in their presumption. Even though the ecclesiastical assembly now tolerates them in its fellowship, it undoubtedly awaits their removal from its midst at the last judgment, when the [Col. 1323B] Son of Man will send his angels to gather out of his kingdom all scandals (Matt. 13:41). Then there will be the anathema *Maranatha*, which the Church now awaits because of the multitude of tares.

Let us now consider the words of Pope and martyr Urban, who promulgates that terrible anathema against knights, monks, and all those who disarrange the ordained system of tithes:

> “The property of the Church,” he says, “is to be faithfully administered, not as though it were private property, but as common property offered to God, with the greatest fear, and only for the aforesaid uses; lest those who withdraw it from the purposes to which it was assigned incur the guilt of sacrilege, and—what is worse—become anathema *Maranatha*. And though they may not, bodily, fall dead as Ananias and Sapphira did, [Col. 1323C] yet let the soul, which is superior to the body, fall dead and alienated from the fellowship of the faithful, and slip down into the depths of the abyss.”

If, then, according to these words, those who withdraw Church property from the purposes to which it was assigned incur sacrilege and anathema *Maranatha*, what will defend, at the last judgment, monks who retain tithes not their own? I do not now mean tithes from the fruits which they have produced by their own hands and at their own expense; for tithes are not to be demanded from monks for such fruits, unless they were lay and military monks requiring the ministry of the clergy. Some Roman pontiffs approve this arrangement, placing monastic enclosures in such liberty that monks may freely devote themselves to God, although their tenants must nevertheless pay all tithes to the churches [Col. 1323D] in which they baptize their children. We therefore do not now censure monks or canons who retain their own tithes with the permission of Roman pontiffs; rather, we speak of their carrying tithes away from another parish—perhaps one so distant that it is plainly evident that transferring the goods of that church elsewhere is nothing other than their ruinous removal from the place to which they were assigned. In that place, that special clerical service is neglected and destroyed, from which the pay of that service is withdrawn. The aforesaid pope calls such removal of offerings sacrilege and condemns it under anathema.

Treating this unjust seizure of tithes, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, in one of his letters [Col. 1324A] indeed stresses the danger of such injustice, whereby a monk who does not serve in the clerical ministry usurps its stipend. Yet he does not approve the abandonment by monks subject to abbots of their own abbots because of such a transgression. They may obtain pardon for this before God if they condemn this evil as contrary to justice and, if unable to remove it, endure it while making a discerning protest.

This also seems to accord with the divine law given through Moses, which allows a carcass to be carried under necessity (Lev. 11:25), provided that the person carrying it is considered clean only after washing his garments with water. Likewise, a monk who, from the necessity of preserving stability, carries a deadly sin committed not by himself but by others is judged clean by us, [Col. 1324B] if he grieves over this necessity and washes himself with tears of repentance, and by frequent tears or groans testifies that he carries the carcass from necessity, not by choice—so that through that necessity he may deserve pardon according to God’s law.

For the law does not permit a carcass even to be touched or carried except under necessity. Hence I do not see how those brethren, especially superiors of monastic or canonical congregations, can be excused when they are constrained to perpetrate such disorder not so much by necessity as inflamed by their own greed. Even if they wished, they could entirely remove from their midst this carcass, by whose contagion the sick flock is defiled; so that in no way could that complaint of the Lord be directed against them, in which, through the prophet, he pronounces woe upon shepherds feeding themselves: “You were eating the milk and clothing yourselves with the wool; and my sheep became plunder” (Ezek. 34:3 ff.). By guarding against this reproach, let them also guard against the anathema contained in the decretal writings of Pope and martyr Urban against those who alienate tithes.

This anathema is accordingly avoided by ensuring that, in the baptismal church to which tithes ought to be brought and distributed according to the canons, clerics are supported together and according to rule from one quarter; widows, poor persons, and the sick are gathered and sustained from another quarter; and the worship of the mother Church flourishes through the third quarter, which is to restore [Col. 1324D] and adorn it. Whatever is done with the quarter belonging to the bishop—whether, by his command, it is spent in the baptismal church upon the duty of hospitality, or brought to the mother and episcopal church, to be spent upon his episcopal maintenance or, at his direction, conveyed to his hospice, which ought always to be open in the city for strangers and travelers needing relief, so that, whether the bishop is absent or present, no one may pass by uncomforted insofar as resources permit—whatever is done from the bishop’s quarter (concerning which, as blessed Gregory testifies in writing to Martinian, bishop of Ravenna: whether the bishop is absent or present, the duty of hospitality and reception must be maintained at the episcopal see; and therefore, unless something remains over there, it ought not to be spent outside the city), nevertheless those three quarters—for clerics, the poor, and the church—must never be transferred from parish to parish, leaving despoiled the baptismal see to which they were originally assigned.

## Chapter LII. Further matters on the same subject, including an explanation of Gregory VII’s decree concerning the tithes of monks and regular canons.

Yet when that see itself is reasonably transferred from one place to another, this necessitates bringing the tithes to it. Those tithes ought to be distributed by clerics living according to order and by the people who pay tithes, in such a way that they retain one portion for themselves, expend one upon buildings, [Col. 1325B] and spend one upon the poor, especially those in need from and within that church, under such testimony that, in their orderly college, the gate of the flock and of the fish—discussed above—may be seen built into the hospice of the poor; that the Fountain Gate may be found continually open to refresh the needy; and that, throughout the whole people, formed by imitation of the goodness of mother Church, the Dung Gate may be constructed through generous almsgiving. Thus may the building of which we speak be fittingly adorned with these four gates.

The Church, moreover, should receive from its portion sufficient splendor in books, vestments, and other furnishings that the lampstand placed in the midst may furnish not only usefulness through spiritual illumination, but also [Col. 1325C] adornment and outward beauty to the surrounding parish.

This beauty and usefulness are wholly destroyed whenever a baptismal church is despoiled of the three portions which, according to the canons, ought to be administered there—whether by monks through false justice or by knights through open injustice. The aforesaid pope makes both parties, who withdraw Church property from the purposes to which it was assigned, guilty of sacrilege in many words consonant with his own, and strikes them with anathema—though now disregarded by them—namely *Maranatha*, that is, the anathema to be manifested at the Lord’s coming. For he intended the order described above to endure so firmly through mother and baptismal churches that he threatened condemnation not merely against monks or knights, but even against bishops themselves and every kind of person in all future [Col. 1325D] ages, should anyone strive to overthrow his apostolic and decretal enactments. In these enactments, after strongly commending the preservation of common life among the clergy in all churches, he confirms what we have said in these words:

> “By the increases and endowments mentioned, the churches over which bishops preside have grown, with the Lord’s help, to such an extent; and the greater part of them has so abounded in possessions that no one choosing the common life is needy among them, but receives all necessities from the bishops and their ministers. Therefore, if anyone in present or future times should attempt to tear this away, let him be struck by the condemnation already stated.”

What use is it that the tithes belonging to mother and baptismal churches have been confirmed by such ancient decrees and subsequently by many councils, if the novel and unjust justice of monks or knights is to be preferred to the ordinances of the Fathers? Indeed, in order to seem to claim parish tithes by authority, and to give some appearance of cover to their impious plundering of the needy, the monks fortify themselves with the authority of a certain chapter issued by Gregory VII, whose text is as follows:

> “By apostolic sanction we establish that no abbot shall retain tithes, first-fruits, or other things which, according to the statutes of the canons, belong to bishops, without the authority of the Roman pontiff or the consent of the bishop in whose diocese he dwells.”

In a remarkable way, shrewd monks are deceived by the text of this chapter. For although the same chapter carefully indicates how, by dispensation, they may lawfully possess their own tithes—that is, tithes from the labor of their own people—which they ought not to retain by their own usurpation, through the permission of the Roman pontiff or their own bishop, since they do not require the service of the clerical ministry; they seize on the occasion of this chapter to claim other people’s tithes. Yet Gregory VII grants only this: that, with the Roman pontiff’s permission in his own particular parish, or another bishop’s permission in his own, monks may retain their own tithes and first-fruits; not that they may invade those of others.

The recent constitution of Pope Innocent, issued at the Council of Pisa, confirms the same point: monks, like regular canons, are not to be required [Col. 1326C] to pay tithes from fruits acquired by the labor of their own hands or at their own expense. Similarly, other edicts of Roman pontiffs confirm this liberty for monks within monastic enclosures: no tithes are to be required of them from domestic produce. Yet no authority confirms, or can confirm, their right to possess in perpetuity tithes which the most authoritative testimonies of the Fathers prove must be brought to baptismal churches.

For the ancient rules are known to establish carefully that the tenants of monks must pay tithes where they lawfully baptize their children. If monks cannot retain even those tithes which their tenants owe to the baptismal church, with what presumption do they maintain that they may utterly overthrow the foundation of canonical [Col. 1326D] institution and introduce such novel laws? By these laws, they collect tithes which by ancient right must be brought to baptismal churches and there either used for the common life or divided into quarters according to the canons—collecting them half, whole, or in some other wrongly divided fashion—and, by despoiling either bishop, clergy, church, widow, or poor person, do not fear to incur the terrible anathema so often pronounced against voluntary and knowing violators of the canons.

A certain holy Father is highly commended by blessed Gregory in his *Dialogues* because he refused the offering of a person who was known to have withdrawn his own offering from God. But these men take away God’s offering and do great wrong to the poor who, like Lazarus, are in need in every parish, [Col. 1327A] by destroying in baptismal churches the Fountain Gates which ought always to stand open, from one quarter of the tithes, for the refreshment of the poor.

How much more rightly they would act if, duly imitating the Father mentioned above, they also avoided the offerings of laymen who, retaining tithes contrary to divine and human law, vainly offer their offerings to religious persons so long as they withdraw their offering from God. For while they destroy the holy religion of which it is written, “Religion pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from this world” (Jas. 1:27)—while, I say, they destroy such religion and thereby incur anathema *Maranatha*—monks and all religious persons should take care [Col. 1327B] not to be harmed by this anathema when, through them, despoilers of the poor are strengthened in their iniquity. If they avoided such persons’ offerings until they had first acknowledged their offering to God, I think that Saint Gregory would praise them too—not now speaking in his *Dialogues*, but reigning with Christ in heaven.

Yet in writing to Augustine, archbishop of the English, Gregory clearly indicates that this ecclesiastical law of dividing possessions into quarters was established only because of transgressors against the apostolic life, namely secular clerics. No law has been laid down for those living the common life, except that all surplus should be given to the poor and needy. Therefore, after blessed Gregory had reminded the aforesaid Augustine, archbishop of the English, of the law established because of transgressors, lest it be thought that the same law established for transgressors was given to those living in common, he says:

> “But for those living the common life, what need shall there be for us to speak of making portions, whether for offering hospitality or fulfilling mercy, except that everything remaining over must be distributed to pious and religious causes, as it is written: ‘Nevertheless, give what remains as alms, and behold, all things are clean for you’?” (Luke 11:41)

Behold, thanks be to God, blessed Gregory plainly indicates that the division into quarters of which we speak does not apply to observers of the common life. Yet he declares it so necessary for other clerics living outside the common life that he does not hesitate to call it usurpation if any bishop [Col. 1327D] or cleric living outside the common life should, in his own time, dispose otherwise than established of tithes and other ecclesiastical revenues. For he intended not only annual tithes and the ancient payments from lands to be distributed by ecclesiastical ministers under the bishop’s judgment; he also ordered this same rule to be observed concerning new acquisitions of churches, so that the bishop should have no other authority over them than to distribute both new and old acquisitions in quarters according to the canons.

Thus he writes to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse, among other things:

> “We have learned that the canonical arrangement of quarters is by no means applied to newly acquired revenues of the Church; rather, local bishops distribute only a quarter of the old revenues, while retaining for their own uses what has now been acquired. Therefore let your Fraternity hasten vigorously to correct this evil and newly introduced custom, so that quarters may be distributed according to the canonical arrangement both from former revenues and from those which have newly accrued or shall accrue. For it is improper that one and the same property of the Church should be assessed, as it were, by a double standard: that of usurpation and that of the canons.”

Having heard, O monks, how blessed Gregory, execrating new usurpations and commending the sacred canons, commands that the evil custom which he finds contrary to the sacred canons be vigorously corrected, what remains?

If the authority of so great a pontiff does not permit bishops to distribute even new acquisitions otherwise than is established by the venerable ordinance of the canons, why do bishops presume to hand them over in this way? Or why do monks receive them from those who transfer them, asserting that this is a lawful transfer which blessed Gregory, as has been read, calls “usurpation, and an evil and newly introduced custom”? If Gregory VII had given monks a decision as plain in favor of receiving parish tithes as is the plain and full authority of Gregory I prohibiting such usurpation, I think the stronger and older authority ought rightly to be preferred, if Gregory the lesser opposed Gregory the greater. But far be it from us to suppose that the last Gregory disagrees with the first concerning the ordering of tithes, since, like the first, the last also commands that the enactments of the canons be observed by monks in this matter, and scarcely permits them to retain even their own tithes with the bishops’ permission. This permission of Gregory VII does not greatly conflict with Gregory I, who greatly supports monastic liberty and repose in his decrees, provided, however, that—as is read in the Council of Chalcedon—the monks remain subject to the bishops; otherwise, the decrees of that same council deprive them of communion.

If, therefore, monks become rebellious when the bishop requires justice in respect of tithes, they are to be excommunicated because of that rebellion according to the decree of the Council of Chalcedon; and they expose themselves to that anathema by which blessed Gregory, in his synodal letter, punishes violators of the four principal councils. For if, in his judgment, whoever does not hold fast the solidity of those four councils lies outside the building, even though he may seem to be a stone, monks—whom the Council of Chalcedon restrains under excommunication to obedience to the bishop—must beware of presuming in any degree to resist a bishop who commands what is holy and wishes to administer tithes according to the canons. For Gregory VII, in whom they deceitfully trust, neither wishes nor can free from the anathema of blessed [Col. 1329A] Gregory those who engage in such rebellions. Indeed, he is himself more gravely offended because his chapter, given not against but according to the canons, is distorted by them through a perverse interpretation.

## Chapter LIII. He strengthens the foregoing teaching with further arguments, especially by the authority of Saint Gregory the Great, whose example urges bishops to care for the poor and travelers.

Let these few answers suffice for monks and knights, neither of whom can claim tithes for themselves by any justice if they wish to avoid the anathema promulgated against voluntary violators of the canons. Whoever of their number is concerned for his soul will not find it burdensome to restore ecclesiastical resources even when the bishop does not demand them. Nor can the consent or silence of a bishop still subject to death make them secure, against whom cry out the Fathers enrolled in heaven—especially since the bishop is not permitted to dispose even of his own particular portion otherwise than the paternal rule of tradition prescribes.

Hence blessed Gregory, writing to Augustine, bishop of the English, says:

> “It is the custom of the Apostolic See to give instructions to bishops at their ordination. From the revenues of the Church, or from those things which come to the altar through the offerings of the faithful, four portions should be made: one for the bishop and his household, for hospitality and reception; another for the clergy; a third for the poor; and a fourth for repairing churches.”

Behold, we have heard that the bishop’s fourth share of tithes is not assigned in order to enrich and comfort monks or knights, but so that he may receive such persons in the episcopal see. This duty is owed by the justice of the canons in such a manner that a bishop is to be seriously accused if a needy traveler passes through his church without receiving, insofar as possible, the relief owed by the pontiff.

Hence blessed Gregory also, as we mentioned above, writing to Secundinus, servant of God, says among other things:

> “Stir up our brother Marinian, the bishop, with such words as you can, for I suspect that he has fallen asleep. For some people came to me, among them certain elderly beggars. I questioned them about what they had received from various persons, and they reported in detail what had been given, when, and by whom on their journey. [Col. 1329D] When I carefully asked them about the aforesaid brother—what he had given them—they replied that they had asked him, but received nothing from him, not even bread for the journey, though it had always been customary for that church to give this to all. For they said that he replied: ‘I have nothing that I can give you.’ And I wonder whether one who has garments, silver, and storehouses has nothing which he ought to give to the poor. Tell him, therefore, that with his place he must change his mind. Let him not think reading and prayer alone sufficient for himself, so that he may seek to sit apart and produce no fruit from his hand; rather, let him have a generous hand, assist those suffering need, and regard another’s poverty as his own. For if he does not act thus, he bears the empty name of bishop.”

In these words it must be carefully considered that the bishop, who is indicated to have been devoted to reading and prayer, seemed deserving of rebuke by the holy pontiff solely because no relief had been provided for travelers requiring and seeking relief from the bishop, although it is established that one quarter of the tithes from the whole parish of the bishopric was assigned for relieving them. If that bishop had been a religious man who had not feared to give the possessions of the poor to the rich, or to build military camps from them, blessed Gregory, so diligent a patron of the poor, would not have passed this over in his rebuke. As was said above, he sharply reproved Bishop Paschasius because, neglecting the poor, he presumed to build a ship from Church property; in his letter he even reproached him with the number of solidi which he had heard that Paschasius spent in building that ship.

> **[Note: Col. 1329D] Gregory to Anthemius, subdeacon of Campania:** “It has come to us that our brother and fellow bishop Paschasius is so slothful and negligent in all things that in nothing is he recognized as a bishop. Thus neither his church nor the monasteries, his spiritual children, or those oppressed under him experience from him any earnestness of affection; nor does he provide any assistance of defense to those who petition him in matters where this is just. And, what is still more grievous to say, he will by no means consent to accept the counsels of prudent men or of those advising rightly; [Col. 1330D] but, setting aside matters which belong to a shepherd’s care, he occupies himself wholly and uselessly with building a ship.
