Consequently, it is reported that he has already lost four hundred solidi, or more.” And after some intervening material: “But if, which we do not believe, after our exhortation he should still attempt to remain negligent in his accustomed manner, he must by all means be sent to us, so that, being here, he may learn what and how a priest ought to do in the fear of God.”

The holy man so greatly desired the possessions of the Church to be distributed not according to new usurpations but according to the ancient [Col. 1330C] canons that no one could, in his view, be excused from receiving those in need on account of bodily illness. He wished the provision drawn from the bishop’s portion always to be ready in the episcopal church, even in the bishop’s absence. Thus he addresses Marinian, bishop of Ravenna, who could not remain in the city because of bodily illness:

> “Certain people of Ravenna came to me, and I found myself struck by the deepest sorrow because they reported that your Fraternity was ill with vomiting of blood. On this account we carefully and individually consulted the physicians here whom we know to be learned in their profession; and we sent your Holiness in writing what each thought and prescribed. [Col. 1330D] Yet above all they prescribe rest and quiet, and I very much doubt whether your Fraternity can have these in its own church. Therefore it seems to me that, after arranging the church there—appointing someone able to perform the solemnities of Mass, someone to administer the care of the bishopric and provide hospitality and reception, [Col. 1331A] and someone to preside over the safeguarding of the monasteries—your Fraternity ought to come to me before the summer season, so that I may personally care for your illness as far as I am able and preserve your rest.”

What would this holy man say if in our time he saw bishops remaining in their military camps, neglecting the reception of the needy which ought to be provided in the city, and distributing to soldiers that which was owed to the needy? I think neither such lordship in bishops nor such homage in soldiers would please him, through which he would see the poor despoiled. I think neither would the importunity of monks please him, by whom the authority of the canons is so despised that they say it is lawful for a bishop to do what the holy Fathers declare [Col. 1331B] unlawful for him.

> **[Note: Col. 1331D] From a Roman council:** “Whoever among soldiers, or of whatever rank or profession, has received or shall receive ecclesiastical estates from any king or secular prince, or from unwilling bishops, abbots, or any rulers of churches; or has invaded them; or has held them even with the corrupt or vicious consent of those same rulers—unless he restores those estates to the churches, let him be subject to excommunication.”
>
> In these words it should be noted that alienation of ecclesiastical property is condemned under excommunication even when it is confirmed or tolerated by the corrupt consent of prelates.

For they say that at least the bishop may give his own portion to monks or anyone else whom he chooses, although by canonical rules he must use it to provide hospitality and reception in the episcopal church and, where he permits, in other places. By framing new laws, they devise plans which they cannot establish. We, however, show that the matters already stated have long been established so firmly that whoever opposes us in them is found opposed not to us but to the saints reigning in heaven. Yet we hope for better things, and things nearer to salvation, from monks concerned for the salvation of their souls. For, by the Lord’s gift, it may come about that many of those who have sinned in ignorance against the property of the poor [Col. 1331C] and still sin will assent to the truth once disclosed; and that the monks themselves will more forcefully restrain the knights who were accustomed to be encouraged and given cover by their example to retain tithes. This will happen when monks relinquishing tithes make manifest to knights that a grant or payment made by a bishop contrary to the canons brings death and anathema *Maranatha* not only upon the giver but also upon the receiver, as is clearly shown by the authorities set forth above.

Indeed, since churches not regularly ordered bear the appearance of orphans in need of guardians and administrators, it could in some sense be tolerated if monks undertook to govern and protect such churches altogether, as minor heirs, [Col. 1331D] until a fixed time set by the bishop—provided that the monks wished to be faithful rather than treacherous guardians. For a guardian is marked by treachery if he does not strive to nurture the minor heir entrusted to him so that the heir may become fit to govern his inheritance himself. Likewise, monks are marked by treachery if they administer a church in such a way [Col. 1332A] that, although it has resources to support even a small congregation according to rule, yet because they obstruct it and draw its resources to themselves, it never becomes free and fit for regular ordering, the monks wishing perpetually to possess its hereditary estate. Even this might in some sense be endured if the monks who receive the milk and wool of the sheep of any church fed the sheep themselves. But it is wholly intolerable and excessively detestable that monks should wish to gather wool and milk from the sheep while refusing to have care of the sheep—or, what is still worse, to entrust them to some hired hand or wolf. Since monks have long done this dangerously, would that they might, in compensation for past excesses, still preserve their own order and favor the ordering of the sacred canons!

Then, if the monks lawfully contended and defended the Church’s justice, the Fountain Gates would be rebuilt in every mother or baptismal church for the refreshment of the needy who ought to be fed there. Then, if they labored together with the clerics wherever the bishop invited them, such a building would arise that it would be evident to rest upon the rock of truth, not the sand of evil customs, because it could be shaken by no assault even if all the rivers of temptations should beat against it. We hope in the Lord that what we desire can come about; and when it has been accomplished, the building of which we speak will stand firm.

[Col. 1332C] For there will be clerics, not headless ones, but men made regular, the chief overseers in this building, keeping their watches and guard-duties, so that it may be sung of them: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have set watchmen; all day and all night they shall not be silent, praising the name of the Lord” (Isa. 62:6). Thus, while the clerics keep watch and praise the Lord’s name, holy monks, entering the wine-cellar, will be intoxicated by the abundance of God’s house; for this building, of which by God’s bounty we have spoken, is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven.

In this house is gathered the household to which the measure of wheat is to be dispensed in due season through the bishop. Against this household the world fights through its rulers. [Col. 1332D] Yet although gigantic stature is visible in our adversary, he will nevertheless undoubtedly be overthrown by the bishop, as by a humble and small David—provided that the bishop himself chooses not Saul’s royal arms, customary to those who trust in themselves, but David the shepherd’s arms and pastoral instruments, with which he is to go forth to fight against the pride of the world.

## Chapter LIV. Gerhoh’s epilogue and concluding address to Chuno, bishop of Regensburg.

[Col. 1333A]

And now, venerable Bishop Chuno, to whom, by God’s gift, we offer this little work composed for you, let me address you especially at the end. Were you not a shepherd of sheep, that is, a vigorous ruler of monks? Were you not elected bishop and, as it were, appointed to battle for the salvation of many? Did you not put on Saul’s garments and arms when, according to the custom of your predecessors—not the ancient ones, but the recent and immediate ones—you received knights and princes into homage, as though you would fight against and triumph over the world through such men? [Col. 1333B] These arms are not suited to you, small and trusting in God alone; you feel, and will feel, yourself burdened and impeded by them, unless you lay them aside, strip them off, and take up only the pastoral instruments which you were accustomed to carry before, when you walked in pastoral fashion attended by no prince and no knight.

Yet a considerable difference must be observed between your former monastic and your present episcopal condition. Then it was enough to gather into the shepherd’s bag such foods from curdled milk as you judged should feed the innocent and simple and nourish them toward mature strength. But now, because you are going forth to fight against the world’s pride, you must also gather the clearest stones from the water of Scripture [Col. 1333C] so that anyone who is not strengthened by the milky teaching drawn from the most holy treasury of your breast, but—what is worse—exalts himself against your humility, may be struck by a judicially pronounced sentence, as by a well-balanced sling-stone of anathema, cast down utterly to the ground, and handed over to be slain by his own sword and deprived of that head whose members crucified Christ and crucify him to this day in their own members. Then, as you return from battle and ascribe every victory to the word of truth, not to yourself, the crowds meeting you and supporting your efforts with pious favor will sing to you: “Saul struck a thousand, and David ten thousand among his thousands” (1 Sam. 18:7). For although your predecessor, in some sense comparable to Saul, was greatly feared because he towered above all the people from the shoulder upward through the multitude of his princely kinsmen, [Col. 1333D] you, born of the tribe of Judah and ennobled by confession of the truth, will be more formidable to the rulers of the world than if, going forth to fight rulers, you should put your trust in rulers—in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation.

Of you, however, thus fighting, like a man desirable and strong of hand, there shall be born a peaceful Solomon; because after some fighting you shall be rewarded with peace upon peace, so that, with you cooperating in the Lord, you may glory in the Temple built—that Temple whose construction began when God built the rib of the first man. From its entrance, since because of my sins I am far repelled, I beg to be helped by your prayers and by those of all who will read this work, lest it be imputed to me as sin that I, though defiled, have displayed in part the fair building of God to the world. Much more might still be shown concerning it, if so great a splendor could be endured by the bleary eyes of my heart. But I think it is not expedient for us to proceed further, since the holy Fathers have treated this building in many ways: they expressly teach what is the tower of David built with battlements; what the tower of Lebanon is, which looks toward Damascus; what are the other towers of Jerusalem, built with gems; and finally what are all the things figuratively mentioned either in the Temple or in the Tabernacle.

[Col. 1334A] Therefore, since the holy Fathers have dealt abundantly with all these matters, I beg you, Father, and all who will read this little work, to obtain pardon for me: for although commanded and compelled by your prayers, I have presumed to raise my foul eyes toward so great a beauty, and to show it to others far wiser and better than myself, though I myself am not worthy even to behold it from afar. Nor could I in any way have been admitted to look upon it, except as an unworthy and base servant is sometimes admitted into the sight of his masters—not to handle the masters’ table, but to supply something behind the backs of worthy servants approaching the table.

[Col. 1334B] Yet, when his service is completed, he is again assigned to carry dung or to perform some other useful duty outside; nor has he a place at the feast—he who, because of his foulness, is scarcely looked upon even for an hour by the banqueters in the lowliest service.

But if the worthy and comely servant, whom the unworthy and uncomely one assists, removes his back from burdens, lest his hands serve in the basket—that is, the vessel for dung—and, being occupied with more honorable tasks, may in some measure cast off the foulness contracted from dung and assume beauty, it may come about that he holds at least the last place among the great number of those at the feast. Previously his foulness excluded him, scarcely allowing him to enter behind the serving attendant as far as the threshold, or a little beyond it.

[Col. 1334C] Therefore you, Father, since you are God’s comely minister and have been pleased to have in me, miserable as I am, an assistant who is neither worthy nor comely: act by praying, act by working—worthy for the unworthy, sanctified for the defiled—lest I be wholly excluded from that building, from that number of banqueters within the building (which, while assisting you, I saw in some measure, as far as the blearness of my sight allowed); and lest I be left, as my foulness and wickedness demand, in the work of dung, in the toil of mud and brick. Rather, let me be admitted and allowed at least in the last place to await the last day, trusting that I shall be saved, not in my own righteousness, but in the infinite mercy of the highest Father through Jesus Christ his Son, our Lord,

[Col. 1334D] to whom, together with the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1335A] “The book having been written through, let there be praise to Christ for the ages. In the year of the Lord 1460, on the vigil of Saint Damasus, Pope.”

Amen.

## Treatise of the Venerable Gerhoh, Provost of Reichersberg, against the Simoniacs

(D. Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, p. 1457, from a manuscript of the monastery of Dunes.)

[Col. 1335]

## Preliminary Notice

The following treatise against the Simoniacs was supplied to us by an ancient manuscript of excellent quality from the Cistercian monastery of Dunes near Bruges, communicated to us with his customary kindness by the most reverend Lord Luke, its abbot. The first leaf of this treatise, bearing the author’s name, had, by some mischance, been torn away. This defect, however, was supplied by the index of the little works contained in the manuscript, prefixed to it and written in the principal scribe’s own hand. It is as follows:

“In this volume are contained these books:

I. The Rule of the Templars, published by the authority of many Fathers, especially of the lord abbot.

II. A book of the lord B. addressed to them, concerning the praise of the new knighthood.

III. An apologetic book.

IV. The letter of Lord William, abbot, to the brothers of Mont-Dieu.

V. The letter of Brother Geroch to Lord B., abbot, concerning the Simoniacs.

VI. The letter of a certain hermit to Rainard, abbot of Morimond.

VII. The book of Peter of Cluny to Lord B., abbot, concerning the objections and replies of both orders.”

Geroch, or Gerhous, or Gerhohus, was a regular canon of the Order of Saint Augustine, provost of Reichersberg in the diocese of Salzburg: a man of no ordinary learning and of no lesser piety, dear to the rulers of the age and of the Church—that is, to bishops and supreme pontiffs—who more than once assailed by speech and writing the corrupt morals of his age. Among the various monuments of his genius, of which you have a long catalogue in the *Chronicle of Reichersberg*, few have hitherto been published: namely, the *Syntagma on the State of the Church under the Emperors Henry IV and V and Pope Gregory VII, and Certain Subsequent Pontiffs*, published at Ingolstadt in 1611 by Gretser; the *Chronicle of the Monastery of Reichersberg*, published at Munich in the same year; and the exposition on Psalm 64, or *Book on the Corrupt State of the Church*, addressed to Pope Eugenius III, which Stephen Baluzius made public in volume V of his *Miscellanea*.

Those, therefore, who bring to light from obscurity the hitherto hidden works of so great a man ought to be thought to confer a very welcome service on learned men; and we hope that those who publish the following treatise against the Simoniacs—certainly not inferior to Gerhoh’s other little works—will deserve well of us. Although in it the author attacks all Simoniacs whatsoever, he especially pursues hired clerics, who, bound by no title, perform sacred ministry solely for money; and on their occasion he discusses at greater length the validity of sacraments administered by heretics. Moreover, although the heading prefixed to the manuscript gives it only the title of a letter, its length nevertheless seems to require the designation of a treatise or book.

The abbot B. to whom it is addressed is none other than Saint Bernard, the great abbot of Clairvaux. Gerhoh may have seen him while he was at Rome or preaching in Germany; and near the end of his treatise or letter he addresses him thus:

“To you, holy man, abbot of Clairvaux—to you, I say, illustrious in name and life—since once I had begun to speak, I was compelled to exceed the bounds of brevity. And I have set forth to you, as to a spiritual father, my opinion, which offends secular clerics and especially hired ones, so that, where you approve what I think, you may show yourself my defender and helper; but where you judge anything among these things to require disapproval, you may show yourself my corrector.”

[Col. 1335]

## Letter of Brother Geroch to Abbot Bernard, concerning Simony

[Col. 1335B]

1. [lacuna] Pharaoh and all Egypt—that is, this whole world lying in wickedness—because it is not yet apparent that, although the sacraments and signs are altogether alike, the invisible finger of God does not cooperate everywhere. Many maintain that this finger is present in all sacraments, whether celebrated outside or within. You, however, thank God, do not attempt to establish this; rather, between the diverse and opposing parties of the world you are accustomed to present yourselves as a middle course, so that by neither affirming nor denying you support the view just mentioned. Perhaps this is because, like Elijah avoiding Jezebel’s snares, you wish to hide concerning this question in the cave of silence, having secured for yourselves and your followers a certain safety which you could not possess if, just as you rebuke the world concerning sin and righteousness, you also wished to rebuke it concerning judgment—namely, by maintaining that the prince of this world has already been judged not only in himself, but also in some of his members.

[Col. 1336B] Whether this is so, or seems to you to be so, we rejoice indeed in your security; we rejoice that all men are your friends, even the enemies themselves of the Christian religion—provided it is evident that you are enemies and adversaries to their wickedness, however much you may think yourselves loved by them. Yet those men cheer us greatly in every respect who, with Elijah, are accustomed not only to hide themselves but also, with him, to make themselves known in this way: that they may destroy the sacrifices of false prophets and slay those same spirits with the sword.

[Col. 1337A] But what shall I say of those who never hide themselves with Elijah, but always remain in cities with Isaiah, Zechariah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets, who had none or few disciples? Yet their resistance to wicked men face to face makes them glorious before God for this alone: that, having endured mockings and scourges, and moreover bonds and prisons, they were stoned, sawn apart, tested, and died by slaughter of the sword.

[Col. 1337B]

2. My soul, thirsting to imitate such men, is nowhere refreshed more sweetly than when it beholds the leaders of the Apostolic See. For through them Simon Magus has been crushed; through them bands of companions are driven from ministry at the sacred altar—namely, those who commit fornication with Nicolaus, Ebion, and Paul of Samosata, or who trade in the house of God with Simon Magus himself and Judas, the worst of merchants. For, to say nothing now of the others in whom the prince of this world has already been judged, who would think that the impious Simon, with his followers so often condemned, ought again to be summoned to judgment as though still awaiting judgment, when in him

[Col. 1337C] the prince of this world has already been judged so decisively that Saint Gregory, writing to Bishop Victor concerning those who tolerate him, says:

> “Whoever does not burn vehemently, from consideration of his office, to correct this crime—namely, the heresy of Simony or of neophytes—should not doubt that he has a share with him from whom this accursed offense first took its origin.”

Certainly we wish this to be noted: we do not say that the prince of this world is condemned in doubtful cases or in the cases of unknown persons, since such persons and their cases await the divine judgment of the final examination. We say that the prince of this world is condemned only in those cases or persons concerning whom we find a clear judgment from the Apostolic See. For this See, employing cautious distinctions, does not destroy the righteous with the wicked. Hence no persons are judged with Nicolaus and Simon Magus, or named Nicolaitan or Simoniac heretics, by its bishops, except those hardened in the sect of their error, plainly disobedient to the synodal definitions of the holy Fathers and to their decretal statutes, and who, with the obstinacy of apostates, resist them deliberately and willingly.

[Col. 1337D] Long ago the sentence of anathema was pronounced against such persons, and their offices were wholly forbidden, although they are permitted to have communion with them in the Church in eating, greeting, and other such matters. For if they were forbidden even in such matters, we would have had to leave this world, which is full of Nicolaitans and Simoniacs. Who doubts that hired clerics and those who hire them are Simoniacs and heretical traders? Who doubts that ministers of the altar who commit fornication, usurp offices forbidden to them, and obstinately defend such presumption against the teaching of the Apostolic See, are heretics, as being at variance with and rebellious against the Roman Church?

[Col. 1338A] But because it is exceedingly difficult to determine which such incestuous and presumptuous persons are obstinate defenders of the presumption and disobedience which they commit in forbidden offices, and therefore are to be called heretics and publicly avoided—especially when their own bishops teach that they are to be avoided—and which are not to be publicly avoided but cautiously shunned: particularly because they either do not defend or teach that what they do ought to be done, or because their own bishops still tolerate them although they have been forbidden by the Roman See, perhaps it is more correct to reckon such men among perverse and forbidden Catholics than among excluded heretics.

Yet at a synod held in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1059, under the presidency of Pope Nicholas II, that pope is found, with the consent of the whole council, to have called them Nicolaitans and to have termed their perversity heresy. Therefore, although by the authority of this Roman pontiff and the council held under him we may proscribe the aforesaid incestuous and presumptuous persons among other heretics, nevertheless, because, as I have said, they can scarcely be examined, we are content that they be called perverse and forbidden Catholics, so that no one obedient to the Roman See may hear their offices, which that See has terrifyingly forbidden to be heard.

[Col. 1338B] “For,” as Gregory VII says, “whoever, while professing himself a Christian, despises obedience to the Apostolic See incurs the sin of divination.” Those who have bishops obedient in all things to the Apostolic See can easily observe this obedience, namely by avoiding—and teaching others to avoid—those whose offices that See forbids to be heard. But where bishops, like the angel of Thyatira, do not wish to expel from their territories the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, but allow her to offer forbidden sacrifices, to commit fornication likewise, and to seduce God’s servants, there true Catholics must either endure persecution from this Jezebel, or flee as Elijah fled the ancient Jezebel, or conceal under this Jezebel both their caution and their obedience to the Roman See, as once the seven thousand men who did not bend the knee before Baal concealed their caution while Jezebel reigned.

[Col. 1338C]

3. What has been said concerning incestuous clerics is enough. But if anyone has made himself so conspicuous and notorious in the leprosy of Simony that he may be recognized as being in the gall of bitterness and the bond of impiety, I do not doubt that he must be guarded against as a heretic and an enemy of the Church. For in Simon Magus himself he has been proscribed and condemned by blessed Peter and by many of Peter’s successors; because, as Pope Gelasius testifies, whenever the authors and teachers of any perversity were consigned to anathema, all their accomplices and followers were likewise anathematized and cut off by the sword of the Spirit, and condemned beforehand before they were born—just as Canaan, son of Ham, was cursed before he was born, Noah saying: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be the servant of servants to his brothers” (Gen. 9:25).

Why was Canaan, Ham’s son, still unborn, cursed in the impious mocker of his father, Ham, unless because in every condemned heresiarch all his posterity must be understood to be cursed? Read, if you have leisure, Pope Gelasius’s letter to Euphemius, and you will find that the authors of every perversity once condemned, as well as their successors and those who communicate with the successors, are equally to be avoided. For Saint Pope Gelasius himself says, among other things, in that letter:

> “If anyone rightly minded concerning the Catholic faith communicates with heretics or their successors, it is not lawful to name him among Catholic altars.”

[Col. 1339A] To the Eastern bishops, likewise:

> “All accomplices, followers, and communicants of a perversity once condemned are judged alike.”

Likewise, to all the bishops of Dardania:

> “Our Fathers judged that, once the author of any error had been condemned together with the error, it was sufficient that whoever at any time should be found a participant in that error should be condemned by the principal sentence against it, whenever he could plainly be recognized either by his profession or by his communion.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The form of Catholic faith and communion set forth by the Nicene Council excludes without reconsideration all Arians, and whoever has fallen into this pestilence either by consent or by communion.”

The same writer continues:

> “The error which has once been condemned with its author carries, in every participant in the effect of perverse communion, both condemnation and punishment.”

[Col. 1339B]

4. Does not the Spirit of Truth, speaking through this Roman pontiff, rebuke the world concerning judgment, clearly showing that the prince of this world has already been judged not merely in the authors of condemned heresies themselves but also in all their followers, successors, and communicants? Roman diligence foresaw well this judgment already passed upon the prince of this world, teaching that hired clerics must be tolerated in no churches, as persons first condemned in the impious Balaam as hirelings, and marked under Balaam’s detestable name in the Apocalypse of the Apostle John, in the Epistle of the Apostle Peter,

[Col. 1339C] and in that of Jude; indeed, also anathematized many times in Simon Magus.

We rightly call such hired persons and those who hire them, or public sellers and buyers of prebends or churches, Simoniac heretics, even if they do not defend the commerce once condemned—indeed, severed many times—as Simon Magus did not defend it. For although he was in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity, he nevertheless said to the apostles: “Pray to the Lord for me, that none of the things you have said may come upon me” (Acts 8:24).

Therefore, although those accused of Simony, who are not plainly stained either with the leprosy of a Simoniac act or of a Simoniac bargain, are to be summoned to judgment, so that those who still have a voice of denial may have room for defense; nevertheless, hired clerics and those who hire them are such manifest traders in the house of God that not only a Simoniac act but also a Simoniac bargain is so evident in them that it ought certainly to be clear that they were long ago condemned with Simon and in Simon Magus, and that they have no share whatever in Christ’s priesthood. For Simon Peter says to Simon Magus:

[Col. 1339D] “You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God” (Acts 8:21). Like case is subject to like judgment. For when Peter condemned that Magus, did he not state the very ground which no one can deny exists now among hirelings and those who hire them? “For your heart,” he says, “is not right before God.” Thus now also, if the hired clerics ask why they have been proscribed by Peter’s vicar, let them think it said to them what was said to Simon Magus: “For your heart is not right before God.” In what is it not right? Namely, because you thought that God’s gift could be possessed with money.

[Col. 1340A]

5. It pleases me, bringing nearer the lamp of Scripture, to consider why Simoniacs were condemned more sharply than all heretics, while the light itself which enlightens every human being shows the way. For although all heresiarchs are recorded as condemned because they stubbornly defended their perversity, a curse was pronounced against Simon Magus alone even while he was asking pardon—not because he had possessed God’s gift with money, but because he thought this could be done. So beyond price is this gift that whoever thinks it can be possessed or obtained for a price is judged a heretic and a son of condemnation and perdition, like that son of perdition to whom Peter said: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts 8:20).

The other son of perdition, the seller of Christ, was not condemned in this way or with such severity, that the price of Christ’s blood should perish together with him. For though that worst trader himself perished, a great use was made of the price of the blood, when, according to the authority of prophetic Scripture, the potter’s field was bought with it as a burial-place for foreigners. But to Simon it is said: “May your money be with you unto perdition,” so that we may thereby clearly recognize that Simon’s crime is greater than Judas’s crime.

[Col. 1340B] For Judas sold a certain Christ whom, as mortal, he did not understand to be God himself, coeternal with God the Father. We readily infer this from the fact that on the very night when Christ was betrayed, we read that the disciples were rebuked thus: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me?” (John 14:9). If this could be said to good disciples, how much more to him whom greed—which blinds even the eyes of the wise—blinded so that he did not recognize Christ as God?

For compensation, as it seemed to him, for the ointment lost—which he had said could have been sold for three hundred denarii—greed urging him, he was content by selling Christ to gain a tenth of this price, that is, thirty denarii; for thirty denarii are a tithe of three hundred denarii. How blind a seller, to sell for so paltry a price him of whom it is written in the Song of Songs: “His head is finest gold, and his hands are rounded gold, full of hyacinths” (Song 5:14), things far more precious than thirty pieces of silver; indeed, him who is that Wisdom of whom it is said: “She is more precious than all riches, and all things desired cannot be compared to her” (Prov. 3:15).

[Col. 1340C] Yet, just as it is said of the rulers of this world that, had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8), so it can be said of this man that, if he had perceived the golden head, golden hands, and all the other desirable things in Christ, veiled by the mortality of flesh, he would never have sold the Lord of glory so cheaply.

Nevertheless, Judas, that worst merchant, is not excused by what we say. Even if he could know nothing else about Christ than that he was an innocent man and a doer of good works, by selling such a man to death for thirty denarii he deservedly and justly inherited from the Psalmist the thirty curses foretold against him. The first is: “Set a sinner over him” (Ps. 108:6); the last: “Let them be covered with their confusion as with a double garment” (ibid., 29).

[Col. 1340D] Yet both Judas and all heretics who sinned against the person of the Son are judged to have sinned more tolerably than those who sinned against the person of the Holy Spirit. For example, Arius sinned more tolerably in his blasphemy by saying that the Son was a creature than the impious Macedonius did by saying that the Holy Spirit was a creature. For Arius could initially have been led to call Christ a creature by Christ’s own words concerning himself according to his humanity, words misunderstood by Arius; for example, when Christ says, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:8). But when, stubbornly attacking the judgment of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, unanimous concerning the consubstantiality of Father and Son in one Spirit, and confirmed by the unquestionable authority of the Holy Spirit, he judged himself unworthy of eternal life, Arius sinned not only against the Son but also against the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1341A] For the unquestionable authority of the Holy Spirit is the unanimous judgment of orthodox Fathers speaking the same thing and thinking the same thing on a given proposition. Whoever despises it and so acts in a discordant spirit that he never returns from dispersion to the gathering which the Holy Spirit works, according to the testimony of blessed Augustine speaks a word against the Holy Spirit, which shall be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come.

Thus, yes, Arius or any other heresiarch, or even some defender of an inveterate schism, by loving his own opinion too greatly or envying those who speak better, becomes obstinate and stubborn; and, after the beginnings of his errors—at which perhaps he did not sin against the Holy Spirit—when those errors have gained strength, he falls into blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which shall be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come.

But Simon Magus, or any Simoniac whatsoever, is convicted of blaspheming the Holy Spirit in the very beginning of Simoniac commerce, by which God’s gift is thought to be possessed with money. For that the Holy Spirit is called and is the gift of God is so evident that it needs no proof. Thus Christ said to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that speaks with you, perhaps you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John 4:10).

[Col. 1341B] We find this expounded by great teachers so that we understand the gift of God of which Christ speaks as nothing other than the Holy Spirit. Since this is so, whoever thinks God’s gift can be possessed with money reduces the Holy Spirit—who, equally with the Father and the Son, is Creator of all things—to a price created by the Holy Spirit, the Creator.

Therefore, when he either compares or subjects the Creator to a cheap creature, he sins far more grievously than Arius. Arius indeed maintained that the Son of God was a creature, but nevertheless a most excellent creature, to which he did not allow even angelic dignity to be equal. But the Simoniac, believing and thinking that the gift of God—that is, the Holy Spirit—can be bought from a human being with money as though it were that human’s own property, subjects the Holy Spirit, who is the gift of God—indeed, who is God—to man. For everything possessed by a human being as his own property is cheaper and inferior to the human being. The Simoniac equates grace beyond price with a price and compares a thing incomparable when we consider all created things, with none of which the Creator Spirit can be valued or compared, any more than can the Father or the Son, whose one Spirit this is, equally free with the Father and the Son.

[Col. 1341C] Indeed, although the Son, taking the form of a servant, was a servant for thirty years and was made a little lower even than the angels who ministered to him, the Holy Spirit possesses such freedom that he makes free even the servants whom he fills. Hence the Apostle says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17). And again: “But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law” (Gal. 5:18).

For the yoke of the law which produces wrath, and the yoke of sin which weighs heavily, are removed only by this Spirit when he comes, according to Isaiah’s saying: “The yoke shall rot away because of the oil” (Isa. 10:27). Does not a human being therefore commit a great and abominable sacrilege when he sells or buys this Spirit—the one wholly free Spirit, the maker of all angelic or human freedom or liberation—as though he were his own slave?

[Col. 1341D] Indeed, since he cannot do this, he thinks that he can buy or sell him who comes to human beings through no purchase, but, rather, as one who is free, breathes only where he wills and distributes his gifts to each person as he wills (1 Cor. 12)—not according to the price for which he is bought, not according to the demand of ambition, but, as I have said, according as he wills.

The impious Macedonius sinned against this Holy Spirit by asserting that he was the servant of Father and Son, though superior to all angels; but the Simoniac sins far more, thinking that this most free Spirit can be sold by him as though he were his own slave. But the one who attempts to buy him both loses his price and does not gain the thing valued; rather, the seller’s whole leprosy, in a wondrous manner, though it does not leave the seller, migrates to the buyer, so that both buyer and seller perish among the members of him who exalts himself above everything called God.

[Col. 1342A] For the Simoniac seller and buyer exalts himself above the Holy Spirit, who is called and is, with Father and Son, one supreme God. Since in this exalted rank the Holy Spirit is subjected to a cheap creature, as has been shown, his divinity is denied to that same Holy Spirit. This is proved to be a most fitting crime and blasphemy against the Holy Spirit; and this crime is more wicked than Macedonius’s crime and that of those who blasphemed the Holy Spirit with him, saying that he was the servant of Father and Son.

Lest we seem to prophesy out of our own heart, it is fitting to append the testimony of no few Fathers, whose authority and number alike can move a faithful and non-contentious hearer and persuade him of what we say.

[Col. 1342B]

6. The Seventh Ecumenical Synod, held by the five patriarchs with three hundred and fifty Fathers, said among other things in the letter which it sent to Pope Adrian:

> “The divine Apostle Peter, whose see your Holiness has obtained, deposes as Simon Magus those who have imposed hands, or impose hands, for money. For the impious heresy of Macedonius and those around him who oppose the Holy Spirit is more tolerable. In their madness they confess that the Holy Spirit is a creature and servant of God the Father and the Son; these men make that same Holy Spirit their own servant. For every master, if he wishes, sells what he has, whether a slave or anything else which he possesses. Likewise, one who buys, wishing to be master of what he has bought, acquires it by the price of money. Thus those who perform this wicked deed degrade the Holy Spirit, sinning equally with those who blasphemed by saying that Christ cast out demons through Beelzebub. And beyond doubt the grace of the Holy Spirit—that is, the holiness of priesthood—is not in them. For Peter says to Simon: ‘You have neither part nor lot in this matter’ (Acts 8:21). Moreover, the twentieth and twenty-eighth Apostolic Canons, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Third and Fourth Books of Kings declare wholly alien from the priesthood anyone who at any time has given or received money, whether before the laying on of hands or after the imposition. For to receive is to receive whenever one receives.”

[Col. 1342C] Likewise, from the final letter of the same synod:

> “Whoever consecrates anyone for money, or has been consecrated for money, is alien from the priesthood, as we, children of all the Churches instructed from canonical disciplines, know.”

Whom would not the harmonious authority of so many Fathers sitting in one synod move, when they proclaim the very thing which even our smallness proclaims? If anyone thinks that it is easy to contradict this authority, it remains for him to destroy the authorities of so many Fathers agreeing with us and affirming with us that the Simoniac surpasses the heretic Macedonius in his heresy.

[Col. 1342D]

7. But because many concede concerning the imposition of hands that, if it is conferred for money, both giver and receiver become heretics, while they do not concede the same concerning other ecclesiastical things, let them hear the following from Pope Paschal’s letter addressed to the Milanese:

> “If anyone objects that it is not consecrations but the things themselves which arise from consecration that are sold, he seems indeed to say something, but understands absolutely nothing.”

For a bishop or abbot of the bodily Church, or anything of that kind, avails in no respect without bodily and outward things, just as the soul does not live temporally without the body. Whoever sells one of two things without which the other cannot be possessed does not leave either unsold.

[Col. 1343A] Yet the sacred canon of Chalcedon utterly destroys this objection, when it forbids a steward, defender of a Church, or anyone subject to a rule to be ordained for money, so completely that it cuts down even the intermediaries of so great a crime with the sword of anathema.

What more need be said? If Simoniacs and neophytes, anathematized and excommunicated, are separated from the Church as true heretics, who does not see that the masses and prayers of such priests provoke God to wrath against the people whom we thought were being reconciled to him by such persons? For it is written: “The place of the true sacrifice is not outside the Church.” And again: “After a first and second admonition, avoid a heretical person” (Titus 3:10).

Therefore, because we do not avoid such bishops, abbots, or other clerics if we hear their masses or pray with them, we undergo excommunication with them.

[Col. 1343B] To believe them to be priests at all is wholly erroneous, since Peter says to Simon: “May your money be with you unto perdition, because you thought that God’s gift could be possessed with money” (Acts 8:20). In saying “because you thought,” he condemns Simon not for what he did, but for what he believed himself able to do; and to think is less than to believe. Therefore, in what follows—“You have neither part nor lot in this matter” (ibid., 21)—it is plainly shown that nothing of sacred ordination is received in this promotion.

[Col. 1343C]

8. After these and other most powerful authorities, some still dare to defend hired clerics against the charge of heresy, saying that what has been said about Simoniacs does not apply to them, because the hiring arrangements of which we speak do not seem to be named expressly in the authorities just cited. Let these hear what is said by the council of Pope Clement:

> “It was ordered long ago, and we also forbid forever under anathema, concerning the foolish heresy of Simony, which has grown, concerning which the holy synod decreed: that no one sell either the consecration of churches, an archpresbyterate, the commendations of altars, the transfer of churches, abbeys, or provostships; and whoever hires out, sells, or buys [these] shall be anathema. Amen. And all responded three times: ‘Let it be done, let it be done.’”

[Col. 1343D] Let hired clerics hear this, lest they think it a novelty that we say hiring arrangements no less than purchases or sales of ecclesiastical things belong to the anathematized commerce of Simony.

[Col. 1345B] 9. Likewise, there are those who try to defend hired clerics and other such traders against the Simoniacal heresy on the ground that they sin from greed for profit rather than from a zeal to deceive; as though their perverse greed diminished, rather than increased, the evil they do—although it is precisely through that greed that they are most culpable. For Gehazi could not thereby remove from himself the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian because he had sinned more from greed for garments and silver than from a desire to deceive someone. Pope Urban II plainly counters such persons, saying:

> “Whoever grants or obtains ecclesiastical things not for the purpose for which they were instituted, but for personal gain, by the gift of speech, of undue service, or of money, is a Simoniac. For Simon’s principal intention was money alone, and avarice—that is, idolatry, as the Apostle says: ‘And avarice, which is the service of idols’ [Eph. 5:15].”

10. Some make a foolish objection to this authority of the Roman pontiff. They say: “If the granting or obtaining of ecclesiastical things through the gift of speech, undue service, or the gift of money is Simony, then the whole earth is now full of Simoniacs; for ecclesiastical goods are sometimes granted to estate-managers, other tenants, and lay soldiers, with the transaction of speech, service, and gifts intervening.” Those who say this do not sufficiently distinguish sacrilege from Simony. For since an ecclesiastical benefice and office are joined as body and soul, whoever acquires one of them in such a way that the other does not accrue without it, certainly sins against the Holy Spirit, without whom no ecclesiastical office can rightly be administered.

Ecclesiastical offices are those bearing such names as bishopric, priesthood, diaconate, provostship, abbacy, clerical office, and whatever others are of this kind, which cannot rightly be administered without the gift of the Holy Spirit. To discuss a single example, let us suppose that someone obtains episcopal resources by a gift, and possesses estates and other goods owed to episcopal administration in such a way that he neither wishes to be nor wishes to be called a bishop—something known to have been done by certain associates of tyrants. [Col. 1345D] Shall we judge such a person to be a Simoniac, because he in no way thinks, or wishes others to think, that he possesses God’s gift? On the contrary, if we give things their appropriate names, we call such a person not a Simoniac but a sacrilegious man. For, by taking what is sacred from what is sacred, he makes ecclesiastical things, so far as lies in him, secular, and causes them not to be ecclesiastical.

This sacrilege must be imputed to laypeople who possess things owed to ecclesiastical administrations through secular service unfitting for such things. Lay possessors of tithes are marked by this sacrilege, as are bishops who voluntarily grant them those tithes, in accordance with the statement of blessed Pope and martyr Urban:

> “The possessions of each parish were and are, even until now, and always will be in the future, under the authority of bishops, who hold the place of the apostles. From these possessions bishops and their faithful stewards must, as well as they can, furnish all necessities to those wishing to live the common life, so that no one among them may be found needy. For these things are called the offerings of the faithful because they are offered to the Lord. Therefore they ought not to be diverted to uses other than ecclesiastical ones and the uses of the aforesaid Christian brethren or persons in need, because they are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and have been entrusted to the Lord for accomplishing the aforesaid work.

> “But if anyone—God forbid!—acts otherwise, let him beware lest he incur the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira and become guilty of sacrilege, as were those who withheld the proceeds of the aforesaid goods. Of them it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘But a man named Ananias,’ etc., down to, ‘great fear came upon all who heard these things’ [Acts 5:1]. [Col. 1346C] These matters, brothers, must be most carefully avoided and feared, because the possessions of the Church must be faithfully administered, not as private property, but as common goods offered to the Lord, and with the utmost fear, for no uses other than those aforesaid. Otherwise those who withdraw them from the purposes for which they were entrusted incur the guilt of sacrilege; and, worse still, they become anathema, falling—not in body, as Ananias and Sapphira did, who fell dead—but in soul, which is more important than the body: their soul dies, is estranged from the fellowship of the faithful, and falls into the depths of the abyss.”

Let this quotation from Urban I suffice for our emphasis upon the crime of sacrilege committed by bishops in alienating ecclesiastical goods. In unlawfully granting tithes to laypeople, they do not commit Simony, since they impose upon them no spiritual administration along with those tithes; rather, they commit manifest sacrilege, as we believe has been sufficiently shown above, because, so far as lies in them, they make an ecclesiastical thing non-ecclesiastical.

But Urban II spoke of persons of this kind:

> “Those who give or possess ecclesiastical things as ecclesiastical things—that is, joined to a spiritual office or ministry as body to soul—when they possess them or grant them to others together with spiritual ministry, under Simon’s intention, namely avarice or greed for profit, are truly proved to be Simoniacs. For they suppose that the gift of God contained in holy ministry can be possessed by money, and they insult the Holy Spirit, whom they suppose can thus be obtained.”

For, as the authority of Pope Paschal quoted above shows, whoever sells one of two things jointly connected does not leave the other unsold. Whoever secretly commits this crime is liable to judgment, namely divine judgment. But whoever, as though saying “Raca,” gives in himself a manifest and unquestionable sign of this crime is liable not only to divine judgment but also to a human council, since he is known to be subject to the decrees issued against Simoniacs in any council of the holy Fathers. But if, when rightly rebuked by anyone, he calls his rebuker “Fool,” he shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna [Matt. 5:22]; and he is altogether like those who, when Christ rebuked them, said: “You have a demon” [John 7:20].

[Col. 1347B] 11. Therefore, leaving for divine judgment those who are liable to judgment because their crime is hidden, let us deal with those who are liable to a council because their Simony is open: manifest sellers and buyers of churches, prebends, and other ecclesiastical things as ecclesiastical things. We are compelled to number among them hired clerics and those who hire them, since they too commit not hidden but open Simony: the hired clerics sell, and those who hire them buy, a Mass or an administration to be performed in the Holy Spirit.

We first strike them as persons liable to a council—or rather, show them already struck—in the Council of Chalcedon. There, concerning such wandering clerics, ordained to no fixed title, every council has decreed and defined that they can minister nowhere, to the injury of the ordaining bishop. Leo the Great, in agreement with this holy and great council, says: “A consecration which is neither founded in a place nor fortified by authority must be considered void.”

Holy Pope Gregory, approving this council together with the other principal councils, says in his synodical letter:

> “I confess that I receive and venerate four councils just as I do the four books of the holy Gospel: namely, Nicaea, in which the perverse doctrine of Arius is destroyed; Constantinople, in which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius is refuted; the first Council of Ephesus, in which Nestorius’s impiety is judged; and Chalcedon, in which the depravity of Eutyches and Dioscorus is condemned. I embrace them with all devotion and preserve them with most complete approval, because upon them, as upon a square foundation, the structure of the holy faith rises. Whoever does not hold their solidity—even if he seems to be a stone—lies outside the building, whatever his life and conduct may be. I reject all persons whom the aforesaid venerable councils reject, and I embrace those whom they venerate; for, since they have been established by universal consent, whoever presumes either to loose those whom they bind or to bind those whom they loose destroys himself, not them. Whoever therefore thinks otherwise, let him be anathema.”

And so, holding views consonant with holy Gregory, we reject wandering clerics, ordained to no fixed title, roaming everywhere and carrying about their office for sale, as rejected in the Council of Chalcedon, lest we either incur the anathema pronounced by holy Gregory or, by his judgment, lie outside the building.

[Col. 1348A] 12. Some object that, when these wandering clerics were ordained, they were assigned certain titles, though they themselves were not regularly bound to those titles. They were named to those titles when ordained, but they were neither prelates of those titles or churches nor canonically or monastically attached to their prelates; they were merely titularly assigned. We judge their consecration to be like that of a bishop consecrated to some episcopal see to which he had not been elected and in which he was never received. That bishop being ignored and rejected, the see would be governed by another, regularly elected and consecrated; nor would any place of episcopal rule, either there or elsewhere, be granted to him.

Yet if such persons were regularly attached somewhere, so as to become canons or monks, some charitable assistance could be provided for them as persons founded in a definite place. But now, because they are nowhere regularly or lawfully established, they wander here and there, carrying their offices for sale, offices which they celebrate nowhere except under a Simoniacal agreement. Other chapters must therefore be cited against them, demonstrating that their offices are wholly void and invalid, both because they were ordained without a title and because they are manifest Simoniacs.

The Council of Piacenza, held under the presidency of Pope Urban, says:

> “In agreement with the decrees of the holy canons, we decree that an ordination performed without a title is to be regarded as invalid.”

In the same synod it was said against Simoniacs:

> “We likewise confirm, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and apostolic authority, the decrees established by the holy Fathers concerning Simoniacs. Whatever has been acquired in holy orders or ecclesiastical things by money given or promised, by service, or by speech, we judge to be invalid and never to possess any force. Yet if some persons were ordained by Simoniacs without Simony, and can prove that when they were ordained they did not know them to be Simoniacs, and if those men were then regarded as Catholics, we mercifully tolerate their ordinations in the Church, provided that a commendable life recommends them. But those who knowingly suffered themselves to be consecrated—indeed, execrated—by Simoniacs, we decree their ordination to be altogether invalid.”

We could collect many decrees consonant with these; but we believe these suffice for the intelligent reader to prove our position: namely, that all offices of manifest Simoniacs are, in the foregoing chapters, utterly rejected and condemned as invalid, just as we likewise maintain that the offices of Donatists and of other condemned and excluded persons are altogether invalid, although they possess the same sacraments as we do.

[Col. 1348D] 13. Here I know that many disagree, saying that where the sacraments are complete, nothing in Masses or other offices can be called invalid. Let us then inquire into the meaning of the word *invalid* (*irritum*) and of the other word *complete* (*integrum*), since these two words seem to some to signify, as it were, contrary things that cannot both be predicated of one and the same subject. Thus white and black, sweet and bitter, and other names of contrary things do not simultaneously apply to one and the same subject.

But concerning one and the same subject—namely, one and the same sacrament belonging to an excommunicated person or a condemned heretic—we predicate both: that it is complete and yet invalid. For Augustine, when disputing about Hagar and Ishmael, affirms that the same sacrament is found in heretic and Catholic, equally complete, provided it has been celebrated in both places according to the ecclesiastical rite, with the word added to the element—just as Isaac and Ishmael, both born of Abraham’s seed, possessed an equal nobility of birth with respect to their father’s seed.

[Col. 1349B] 14. Let us therefore see whether a sacrament complete in both cases is also valid in both cases. To see this, let us set forth a kind of definition of each term, “valid” (*ratum*) and “complete” (*integrum*). We call a whole complete when it lacks none of its principal constituent parts. For example, when a house lacks neither roof, walls, nor foundations, it is called a complete house; but if any of these is lacking, it will not be called a complete house—indeed, it will not be called a house at all.

We call valid that which we signify as firm and full of power and efficacy; and invalid that which we show to be empty of efficacy and lacking power. Likewise, we appropriately call valid that which signifies that it can never lose the power it contains. Thus, for example, a proposition or statement containing or signifying an immutable truth—when it affirms that something is which cannot fail to be, or conversely—may be called a valid statement and, properly, an utterance of reason. For *ratio* [reason, statement] is said to derive from *ratum* [settled, valid], although a false statement is also called a statement; yet it does not produce a settled—that is, firm or true—understanding, and therefore, just as it is false, it can rightly be called invalid, because it lacks a settled and true understanding: the reality is otherwise than it signifies it to be.

Let this be an example of what we mean. If someone proposes, “God is true” [John 3:33], this proposition is so true and so valid that everyone who has received His testimony may subscribe and seal that God is true. For what truthful people say, they intend to be true; what they not only say but also write, they signify more strongly and durably to be true; and what they say and write and seal with some inviolable seal, they intend to remain true under that seal. Hence John, speaking of Christ, says: “He who receives His testimony has set his seal that God is true” [ibid.].

In what respect is He true, except because, as He spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and his seed for ever, so He has done, does, and will do for ever? In what respect is He true, except because, sending His Son to be incarnate, He visited and accomplished the redemption of His people [Col. 1350A] and raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David His servant—not in another manner, not at another time, not from another tribe, not in another town, but through a Virgin in the fullness of time, from the tribe of Judah, in Bethlehem, David’s town, as He spoke through the mouth of His holy prophets from ancient times? Therefore, having received Christ’s testimony, we rightly write in our hearts what we believe and seal what has been written: namely, that God is true.

For this proposition is not only complete but also valid. It is complete because no principal constituent part is lacking in the statement. For just as the principal constituent parts of a house are roof, walls, and foundation—and if even one is absent, the house will be incomplete, indeed not a house at all—so the principal constituent parts of a statement or proposition are noun and verb; if either is absent, the proposition or statement lacks completeness. In speaking of the kind of statement that dialecticians call declarative, we take “noun” and “verb” broadly, including pronouns under noun and participles under verb, so that in so great a matter we may drive away the troublesome flies of sophisms with this very slight qualification, as with a little fan.

Therefore, a statement lacking noun and verb will not be complete; indeed, it ought not to be called a statement, since it lacks a principal and principally constituting part of speech. But the statement “God is true” is altogether complete, because it lacks no principally constituent part, although it lacks secondary parts of speech—conjunction, preposition, and the rest—the absence or removal of which does not diminish the completeness of the statement, that is, does not destroy its character as a statement, just as the removal of pegs or tiles does not destroy a house. Forgive me, reader, for lingering so long over such trifles, since the points we have noted avail us in demonstrating the completeness of every sacrament.

[Col. 1350C] 15. Let us say again: “God is true” is a complete statement—complete, I say, because it lacks no principally constituent part. But if it were only complete and not also valid, it ought by no means, according to the counsel of John the Baptist, to be sealed; rather, despite being complete, it ought to be rejected. Yet this statement is so true and valid that it is more possible for heaven and earth to be reduced to nothing than for this statement to become invalid; for what it signifies is so true, so unchangeably existent, that it can never fail to be.

Let another person propose: “The devil is true.” This statement likewise is complete, being composed of noun and verb; but it is by no means valid, because it has often been proved false, although the devil sometimes speaks truths or things that seem true, in order to persuade people of things that are altogether false. Therefore we confidently say that the proposition “The devil is true” is altogether invalid and false, empty and devoid of truth, supported by the testimony of Truth concerning the devil Himself: that he is a liar and the father of it [lying], and that he did not stand in the truth [John 8:44].

[Col. 1351A] 16. Therefore, to return to the matter under discussion: every sacrament is like a certain complete whole, for it has constituent parts when the word is added to the element and a sacrament comes into being. For example, when someone is baptized, these words—“I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit”—are added to the element of visible water, and there comes into being a sacrament of invisible grace, perfected from audible speech and visible water as its principal constituent parts.

For the other prayers which precede or follow the words already mentioned, and other things customarily or ordinarily employed there besides the element of water—such as oil or chrism commonly mixed with baptism, and other such things—are not principal or constituent parts of the sacrament of baptism. Rather, as I have said, these words alone, “I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” when rightly joined to the element of water, constitute a complete sacrament, equally perfected whether celebrated in the Church or outside the Church.

These words to be applied to visible water were not handed down to the Church by an apostle or prophet, but were woven from above by the weaver, God’s own Wisdom; just as the words poured over the elements of bread and wine which effect Christ’s body and blood are entirely woven from above. For both traditions—the performance of baptism and the consecration of His body and blood—take their origin from Christ alone, through words first uttered by Christ’s own mouth: either when He instituted baptism, saying, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” [Matt. 28:19]; or when He made His body and blood from bread and wine and commanded His disciples to do the same, saying, “Do this in remembrance of me” [Luke 22:19].

Whatever is added in the celebration of baptism or Mass to this tradition, to this word completed and made concise by Christ, neither destroys the completeness of the sacraments if omitted nor perfects it if added, any more than the additional parts of speech, removed or added, destroy or perfect a statement consisting of noun and verb.

[Col. 1351C] 17. We are now compelled to use the comparison of such trifles as well. In former times the solemnities of Mass were not celebrated with such a great outward display of adornment, nor was all this grace of religious service completed and polished by any one individual. For the sacred pontiffs, brilliant lights of the Roman see, shone forth at different times; and so, by the brightness of their labors, they gradually perfected the beauty of this saving office.

And just as David and Solomon especially enlarged more splendidly the order of the ancient sacrifice handed down by the Lord through Moses—by the ministry of priests and Levites, a numerous company of singers, the festive movement of divine psalms, the splendid glory of temple and altar, and a multitude of sacred vessels—so the holy Roman Church, receiving through the first apostles the wondrous rite of the new sacrifice handed down by the Lord, embraced it with religious faith, preserved it with faithful care, and adorned it with diligent provision. From her treasury she brought forth new memorials of piety, and fashioned for the holy sacrifice a kind of diadem of religious office, as it were from gold and precious stones: one Roman pontiff instituted an antiphon to be sung at the entrance, another *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”—another *Gloria in excelsis Deo*—“Glory to God in the highest”—and another something else to be sung or said in the Mass.

This was not to enlarge the one sacrament, but to adorn the most divine worship of that sacrament and to venerate the unique sacrifice handed down by Christ to the apostles and, through the apostles, to us. It is not holier on that account than it was before, when it was consecrated with the Lord’s words alone and the Lord’s Prayer alone. But it was most fitting that faith, still unformed at that time and, as one learned no less than faithful man says, “clouded by rustic cultivation, bare of shoulder, unshorn in hair, with arms exposed,” should, where it could be adorned, be gilded especially in this part as in its head, and fittingly adorned as though with golden chains variegated with silver.

[Col. 1352B] 18. Therefore, although, as I have said, the completeness of the sacrament instituted by Christ is not diminished if such things are omitted, nevertheless anyone rashly stripping away what the holy Fathers added to the Lord’s words would be comparable to the soldiers tearing and dividing Christ’s garments.

But those words of the Lord, woven from above throughout—where Christ Himself is introduced speaking and saying: “Take and eat of this, all of you, for this is my body. Take and drink of this, all of you, for this is the chalice of my blood,” etc., down to “Do this in remembrance of me” [Luke 22:19]—those words, I say, poured over the bread and wine, which, when added to the element of bread and wine mixed with water, make the sacrament, represent the likeness of that seamless garment woven from above, which even Christ’s crucifiers were not permitted to tear.

This is the word which makes complete and concise the entire completeness found in the sacrament of bread and wine, if it is applied to the same element to which Christ applied it, according to the ecclesiastical rite which we know was handed down by Christ Himself. But if a baptizer or celebrant abandons Christ’s tradition, so that in perfecting the sacraments he uses species of elements other than those Christ instituted, or omits and despises Christ’s own words, he does not effect the completeness of the sacrament. Indeed, what he does no more bears the name of sacrament than a thing can bear the name of a house when it is known to lack roof, walls, or foundations.

Yet a house could exist if it lacked painted walls, tile-nails, or other such things. A statement could likewise exist if all the parts of speech except noun and verb happened to be lacking; but if noun and verb were removed, there would be nothing from which a statement could be constituted. So, in celebrating the office of baptism or Mass, certain things known to have been added by the holy Fathers are sometimes omitted. Thus, when we baptize an infant in danger and recite only the words of the one triune name, or when we sometimes omit *Gloria in excelsis* (“Glory in the highest”) and *Credo in unum* (“I believe in one”), we nevertheless effect the completeness of the sacrament.

But if, while baptizing, we disdain to name even one person of the three persons; or, while celebrating sacrifice and reciting everything added by the holy Fathers, we do not introduce Christ speaking at His supper, what we do cannot be called a sacrament. Hence the holy Fathers prohibit the rebaptism, even in heresy, of persons baptized by heretics in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, recognizing in them Christ’s character, that is, the completeness of the sacrament. But persons baptized by those heretics who did not baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit they judged not so much to require rebaptism as baptism from the beginning, because no sacrament of baptism is reckoned to exist where the invocation of the triune name has not been made over the element of visible water according to the divinely handed-down rite.

[Col. 1353B] 19. The Donatists and many other heretics, however, celebrated the divine sacraments according to the ecclesiastical rite. Therefore blessed Augustine vigorously contends, in certain writings, against those who rebaptized persons baptized by them and against those who reordained persons ordained by them. He defends, I say, the completeness, not the usefulness, of such sacraments, maintaining that they can indeed be present outside the Church but cannot be beneficial there; and he shows this in many passages.

Nevertheless, many who read his writings carelessly, seeing that he recognizes the completeness and form of the sacraments both outside and inside, think that the efficacy of the same sacraments operates equally inside and outside the Church. That blessed Father never held this view, for although he proves heretical sacraments to be complete in every respect, he nevertheless proves them to be dead and deprived of every power of the Holy Spirit. Nor are these contrary: something may be complete and dead. We have often seen a human body complete and yet dead. It often happens that a severed branch remains whole yet has no life-giving sap. A severed hand may retain the form of a limb but not exercise the use of a limb.

Therefore Augustine is not inconsistent when he maintains that the sacraments of heretics are complete and are never to be repeated, while nevertheless proving them to be dead. For in his sermon on blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, he says:

> “The visible form of a branch can exist even apart from the vine, but it cannot possess the invisible life of the root except in the vine. Accordingly, the bodily sacraments which those separated from the unity of Christ’s body bear and celebrate can display the form of godliness. But the invisible and spiritual power of godliness cannot be in them, just as sensation does not remain with a human limb when it is amputated.”

Does not blessed Augustine, in saying this, prove the sacraments of heretics to be dead? Yet Roman authority teaches that, as regards their outward form, these sacraments are not to be repeated when their recipients return to the Church, but are to be confirmed solely by the invocation of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands.

Hence Pope Leo, writing to Nicetas, Patriarch of Aquileia, says:

> “Those who received baptism from heretics, having not previously been baptized, are to be confirmed solely by the invocation of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. They received only the form of baptism without the power of sanctification. We proclaim that this rule must be observed by all Churches: the washing once begun must on no account be violated, as the Apostle says, ‘One God, one faith, one baptism’ [Eph. 4:5]. Its washing must not be rashly repeated; but, as we have said, sanctification alone must be invoked from the Holy Spirit, so that what no one receives from heretics, he may obtain from Catholic priests.”

[Col. 1354B] Let heretics now go and glory in the completeness of their sacraments, provided it remains established for us that those same sacraments are altogether dead, altogether extinguished. Hence the same Pope Leo, speaking to Emperor Leo about the excommunicated Alexandrians, who nevertheless celebrated sacraments according to the ecclesiastical rite, says:

> “It is clear whom Your Piety ought to assist and whom it ought to oppose, lest the Alexandrian Church, which has always been a house of prayer, now become a den of robbers. For it is plain that, through most cruel and monstrous madness, all the heavenly light of the sacraments has there been extinguished. The offering of sacrifice has been interrupted; the sanctification of chrism has failed; and by parricidal hands all mysteries have withdrawn themselves.”

[Col. 1354C] 20. Behold, we have proved the sacraments of heretics to be dead and extinguished. Let us now be permitted to affirm that they are likewise invalid unless they have been confirmed through the Church. Let us now be permitted to agree with the Council of Piacenza (canon 2), which affirms that whatever has been acquired in holy orders or ecclesiastical things by money given or promised, by service, or by speech, is altogether invalid and possesses no force. This synodal judgment also strikes those who sought again offices lost through some crime, and reacquired them by money given or promised, undue service, or speech.

21. Four points have now been demonstrated concerning sacraments celebrated outside the Church, though according to the ecclesiastical rite: namely, that they are complete as regards the parts principally constitutive of them [Col. 1354D]; that they are dead, according to Augustine’s testimony; that they are extinguished, according to the testimony of Pope Leo; and that they are void, according to the testimony of the Council of Piacenza. Now it is desirable to distinguish between the sacraments themselves, which can be dead, extinguished, or void, and the power of the sacraments themselves, which can never be dead, extinguished, or void, but wherever it is, is living, luminous, and valid. There is no small distinction to be considered here; it will readily appear if the effect of the sacraments itself is first distinguished.

For the effect of the sacraments is not uniform, since “effect of the sacraments” is said passively—namely, that by which we designate the sacraments themselves as being brought about. It is also said actively—namely, that which the sacraments bring about. And [Col. 1355A] the former effect consists in their being celebrated whole according to the ecclesiastical rite. For if anyone performs either the Mass or other divine offices according to a rite other than that which the Church holds to have been divinely handed down, no sacrament is effected there. Thus acted those heretics who did not baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and therefore what they did was not regarded as the sacrament of baptism. Those who repented of such things within the Catholic Church were baptized afresh as though they had never been baptized. But those baptized outside according to the ecclesiastical rite, when they came to the Church, were confirmed by the laying on of hands, as persons having in themselves that effect of the sacrament by which the sacrament could be effected even outside the Church.

But that active effect which the sacraments perform and bring about [Col. 1355B] exists only in the Catholic Church. The former effect is discerned by eyes and ears, since the sacrament itself—that is, the sign of a sacred thing—is completed from audible words and visible elements. But the active effect of the sacraments, which the sacraments bring about, is seen only by the eyes of faith. Therefore, since a manifold understanding arises if the effect of the sacraments is named without qualification, I ask pardon for being compelled by necessity to speak of the passive and active effect of the sacraments, in a manner hitherto unused. For the Apostle says that not every novelty of terms, but only profane novelties, must be avoided. Yet a novelty of expression which sets forth no new truth of things is not profane. It has been permissible, and always [Col. 1355C] will be permissible, to state the truth of a thing in terms fitted in some manner to it which introduce no error—as the holy Fathers did in the Council of Nicaea. Under pressure of necessity, they caused the new term *homoousion* (“of one substance”) to be recited in the Creed, though by this term they expressed no new reality. Thus we too, pressed by necessity, are compelled to distinguish by terms as well the effects of sacraments which are greatly distinct in fact, so that it may appear more clearly of which effect of the sacraments we say that heretics are deprived.

For just as the Apostles, when they saw a certain man casting out demons in the Lord’s name but not following them, forbade him, and were therefore reproved by Christ because, in the matter in which he was with them, they forbade the man whom they ought rather to have invited to follow him in whose name he performed signs [Col. 1355D] of power; so we too could be rebuked if we reproved heretics in the matter in which they act with us and sometimes cast out demons—namely, when they baptize infants, or others who, through excusable ignorance, do not recognize the errors in which those heretics are themselves involved; or even those who, pressed by the crisis of death and unable to obtain Catholic baptizers, receive through heretics what they would prefer to receive through Catholics. In the case of those so baptized, since they do not in their hearts deny the power of godliness, it ought not to be believed in vain that the sacrament of godliness itself is present in them.
