With this consideration, the aforesaid Council of Piacenza (can. 3) judges that persons ordained by simoniacal heretics, but not ordained simoniacally, are to be tolerated mercifully, provided that they can prove that, when ordained, they did not know their ordainers to be simoniacs; that the ordainers themselves were then held to be Catholics; and that a praiseworthy life commends those ordained. And if, for the causes already stated, we in some fashion tolerate those ordained by such persons, much more may the Catholic Church acknowledge as her own children those who, through ignorance or necessity, were baptized by such persons and in no respect agree with their error—provided that, once they recognize the error of such baptizers, they are willing to detest heresy and pursue Catholic truth and peace.

22. Therefore, simoniacs and other heretics performing signs in the Lord’s name—namely, sacraments, which are signs of sacred things—we do not forbid from doing them as they do them, since they do them with us; but we forbid them to do them where they do them, because in making signs outside the Church they do not gather with us. And [Col. 1356B] because no benefit from signs of this kind comes to them or to those who agree with their perversity and, with them, lie under anathema, we earnestly warn them not to glory in signs, as Pharaoh’s magicians gloried. For the finger of God operates nowhere except in the Church of God; nor does it work anything through them even in those whom they baptize or ordain, unless it is shown that the person’s mind is not separated from the Catholic Church and is excused either by infantile or other invincible ignorance, or even by the crisis of death. This excuse, however, is not found in every other sacrament as it is in baptism.

Hence Saint John of Alexandria says among other things:

> “Baptism may be received from any heretic or criminal, provided it can be administered in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But penance is to be received from no one except a Catholic.”

And shortly afterward:

> “If no Catholic priest, whether good or criminal, is present, it is better to remain without visible communion and to be communicated invisibly by the Lord than to receive communion from a heretic and be separated from Christ. ‘What agreement has Christ with Belial?’ says the Apostle; ‘what share has the faithful with the unbeliever?’ (II Cor. VI, 15). Every heretic is an unbeliever; but a simoniac is a heretic; therefore he is an unbeliever. Although Catholics cannot visibly and bodily possess Christ’s holy communion because of threatening heretics, nevertheless, while they remain joined to Christ in mind and deed, they possess Christ’s holy communion invisibly—as did very many saints, who, removed into the desert, were seen by no one either while living or dying. We believe them to be so much the more closely joined to God as they were separated from human beings.”

Likewise, testimony from the same author:

> “Never, at any time, participate in the communion—indeed, the defilement—of heretics, even if throughout your whole life, through some pressure or necessity, you find no communion of the Catholic Church and remain without communion. For if, while lawfully possessing a bodily wife, we remain for a long time in a distant region without that woman, we are forbidden by God and the laws to leave her and join ourselves to another; and if we do so, we are punished. How then do you suppose that we, joined to God through right faith and the Catholic Church, as the Apostle says, ‘I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a virgin to Christ’ (II Cor. XI, 2), if we adulterate the orthodox Church and holy faith by communion with heretics, shall not share in the future torment which awaits heretics? For communion is so called because it makes common and binds the communicant to those with whom he communicates. Therefore, I beg you, O children, do not attach yourselves to oratories of this kind.”

We infer that this last statement about oratories refers to those dedicated by heretics from the fact that we find the same John saying elsewhere concerning Catholic churches: “Though Catholic churches have been invaded by heretics, let no one fear to enter them for prayer; for though executioners have wounded Christ’s members [Col. 1357B] and divided his garments, they nevertheless remained most holy in themselves.”

23. Let us now return to what was left aside, and distinguish still more fully the effects of the sacraments distinguished above. That effect of the sacraments which we called passive is always uniform, and both outside and inside the Church is of one institution or constitution as regards its principally constitutive parts. In secondary and accessory parts, however, the manner is sometimes varied and manifold, according to the usage of the individual churches. But in the principal constitution of the sacraments the manner is always one and uniform in all churches, Greek and Latin.

For in offering leavened [Col. 1357C] bread, the Greeks do not omit Christ’s principal institution, which they would omit if they offered something other than bread—for example, cheese or something of that kind which Christ did not offer. Thus, though they would act more reasonably if, in offering unleavened bread, they conformed with the holy Roman Church, the Church nevertheless long tolerated their leavened sacrifice—not negligently, but after much and repeated effort to bring the Greeks into agreement with the Roman Church. Hence [Note: [Col. 1357D] Read Leo IX.] Leo VIII, pope of that name, the 148th from blessed Peter, wrote an outstanding letter against Michael, Patriarch of Constantinople, defending the Roman custom as sounder and more consonant with Christ’s institution. Yet the Greeks persist in their custom, [Col. 1357D] without differing from us in the principal constitution of the sacraments.

Likewise, among the Latins themselves, although some differ in that, while nearly the whole Church follows the Gregorian order, they still observe the Ambrosian institution, all churches agree so fully in the principal constitution of the sacraments that not even any heretic dares alter it. If anyone changes it—by offering something else, baptizing in another liquid, or reciting something other, in offering or baptizing, than the ecclesiastical tradition contains—what he does is in no way reckoned a sacrament. Therefore sacraments are inviolable, because wherever they are, they are the same; and once conferred, they can never be abolished. For when those ordained or baptized are excommunicated, they are by no means deprived of the sacraments which they received according to the ecclesiastical rite; rather, the sacraments of ordination or baptism remain in them, though dead, though extinguished, though void—that is, effective for no power or salvation.

Such persons, therefore, in baptizing confer only the outward form of godliness which they possess; but the power of that godliness, which they do not possess, they cannot confer, especially not on those who agree with their errors, dissent from the Church, or knowingly receive their forbidden sacraments. Accordingly, when persons baptized by such people return to the Catholic Church, [Col. 1358B] the washing of the flesh is not repeated for them; but, so that what is lacking may be completed, they are joined to their Catholic mother, in order that through her reconciliation they may deserve to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit is given in her alone, because God is not in a division of minds, but in unity and peace, which is the bond of perfection.

Though begotten in a less lawful marriage-bed, these persons are nevertheless regarded as children. For from every tribe of the children of Israel there were numbered children known to God, where “the servants of our God” are sealed on their foreheads: namely, both from the tribes of Gad and Asher, who were born from that woman, and from the tribes of Judah and Joseph, who were born from lawful marriages. Yet if they were taken from this light before reconciliation with their lawful mother, they would be cast out with Ishmael from their father’s house and inheritance and would by no means be counted among the heirs of God’s kingdom. For the free mother says: “Cast out the bondwoman and her son; for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. XXI, 10).

Explaining this, blessed Augustine says:

> “The Church says: ‘Cast out heresies and their children; for heretics shall not be heirs with Catholics.’ But why shall they not be heirs? Are they not born from Abraham’s seed? And how do they possess baptism? Baptism would make Abraham’s seed an heir, unless pride excluded it from the inheritance. You are born by the same word, by the same sacrament; but you do not attain the same inheritance of eternal life unless you return to the Catholic Church.”

When these statements of blessed Augustine and his other writings [Col. 1358D] are carefully examined, it is easy to observe what effect of the sacraments he maintains to be complete among human beings: clearly, none other than what we may call passive. By this name we denote not the effect which sacraments effect, but that by which sacraments themselves are effected, so that they are sacraments—that is, signs of sacred things. Thus baptismal water is a sign of the Holy Spirit; holy oil in the ordination of a bishop is a sign of the Holy Spirit; and sacrificed bread and wine are signs of unity, in that just as that one bread is made from many grains and that wine has flowed together from many grapes, so the Church is one from many human beings through the unity of faith.

We say that the one Church is signified by that bread, not in its being offered and consecrated, but in its being made, as stated, from many grains. For in being consecrated, it does not signify even the individual body of the Lord; rather, it is the Lord’s body, the Word of God having been poured into it through faith in the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension. For the Lord does not signify this but says, “This is my body” (Matt. XXVI, 12). Therefore that bread is one thing and signifies another. For it is the Lord’s body, but it signifies the one Church, which, though it too is the Lord’s body, is nevertheless different: the Lord’s body which redeems is one thing; the redeemed body is another. The Lord’s body which is also the Lord himself is one thing, of which Mary says: “They have taken away my Lord [Col. 1359B], and I do not know where they have laid him” (John XX, 13); the Lord’s body which cannot be called Lord or God, though it is the Lord’s body, is another.

The Lord’s body by which we are redeemed is the individual body itself, of which Christ said: “This is my body, which shall be given for you and for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. XXVI, 28). But the Lord’s body which is the Church is not one individual body, nor is it the redeeming body; rather, it is one body through one faith, redeemed by Christ’s body: the one Church in many individuals or persons. In signifying this Church, the bread of sacrifice is and is called a sacrament, that is, a sign of a sacred thing. For the unity of the Church is a sacred thing, which that bread signifies by being made [Col. 1359C] from many grains and becoming one thing.

Although the same thing may be signified in any bread made from many grains, the holy Church nevertheless venerates this signification as a sign, as it were, of a sacred thing and as a sacrament—indeed, as a true sacrament—more fittingly in that bread which is prepared for the most holy altar and over which Christ’s word is recited according to the Church’s rite. Since both heretics and Catholics who sacrifice according to the ecclesiastical rite recite this in one and the same manner, both alike represent the sacrament, that is, the sign of a sacred thing. For what the bread offered by a Catholic priest signifies, the bread offered by a heretical or simoniacal priest according to the Church’s rite also signifies.

And in a remarkable way that bread signifies unity even where the unity of the Church itself is known not to exist. For the unity of the Church cannot possibly be both inside and outside: unity undivided exists in the one Church. But the sign, or sacrament, of unity can exist even outside unity; unity itself, however, as I have said, cannot exist outside itself, nor can anyone divide indivisible unity. Therefore, when the sign of unity is apart from the unity which it was instituted to signify, the sacrament itself indeed has its own effect—the effect above called passive—but it does not have the effect which we may call active. For the sacrament itself is effected or made when, with the word added to the element, the sign of a sacred [Col. 1360A] thing is completed. But because the sacred thing is absent there, the sacrament itself does not produce its effects.

For as a body accomplishes nothing without a soul, so the sacrament of unity accomplishes none of its effects without unity. As the soul cooperates with the body in order that it may do anything, so unity itself cooperates with the sacrament of unity in order that it may do anything. And as a body is living when it has within itself a life-giving spirit and, when that is withdrawn, is dead, so the sacrament of unity lives if it itself exists in unity and unity in it; but when separated from unity, it is utterly dead and powerless to produce those effects which it ought to produce.

25. When unity cooperates, the sacraments accomplish something, because they work in creatures the Creator’s threefold work [Col. 1360B]: sanctification, transformation, and salvation. Sanctification is worked even in inanimate things, as in chrism or in a man-made temple, which are sanctified as signs of sacred things through other words. Transformation is worked in bread and wine, which, when sacrificed, are transformed into something else. Salvation is worked because faithful persons who worthily participate in the sacraments and persevere in unity are saved through them.

But one and the same Spirit works all these things—sanctification, transformation, and salvation—in the sacraments and with the sacraments, concerning those creatures which are sanctified, transformed, and saved, through our Lord Jesus Christ. The Catholic celebrants of the sacraments adhere to him as branches to a vine. For as long as, through unity of faith, they agree with the teacher of truth, preserving the bond of unity and all sharing the same mind, they remain in Christ; and each, living from his Spirit, possesses the grace of inward greenness. Whatever sacrament they celebrate in Christ’s Church lives for the salvation of those who communicate in it. For Christ speaks in them, and whatever is done by them is rightly believed to be done by him and confirmed by his Spirit, even if they are found blameworthy in their conduct, provided that they remain in the fabric of unity and adhere to the one vine which is Christ.

But where, dissenting and dividing themselves from the Church’s unity through heresies and schisms, they cut themselves off from Christ, every word and sacrament of theirs is dead [Col. 1360D]; whatever they seem to do is void, and whatever they are thought to sanctify is defiled.

25. Let them then go and be eager to bear fruit: plantations of death and shoots assigned to eternal fires; simoniacal employers and hirelings, and the other traders, driven by the Lord’s scourge from God’s house; all heretics and schismatics cut off from unity and therefore wholly fruitless. For whatever is done among them, whatever purportedly sacred thing or sacrament is celebrated, lacks the word of life and the Spirit of truth as truly as a branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine, or as truly as a hand severed from the body cannot live or act.

Therefore, since in all deeds and words in which we receive Christ’s testimony this must be noted [Col. 1361A] and marked—that God is true—this testimony of his, uttered by God and by the most truthful witness, must be carefully observed and sealed with the inviolable seal of faith, where he says: “Remain in me, and I in you”; and adds: “As the branch cannot bear fruit from itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me” (John XV, 4). This true testimony of the truthful God and most faithful witness must be carefully marked, not only against heretics and schismatics, but also against all presumptuous persons, and always carried in the remembering heart.

Who does not know the unity of the vine and its branches? As long as branches remain in the vine, they ascend through its innermost veins, drink the native moisture of its root, live and flower, and their flowers bring forth fruit. But if a branch is cut from the vine, it can no longer share in its good sap; it neither lives nor has any other use except to be cast into the fire and burn. Therefore, O heretics and schismatics who cut yourselves off from the body of the Church and are cut off by the hoes of your own inventions, do not think that you can bear the fruit of life.

Likewise, you presumptuous persons and excessive defenders of free will, who suppose that you do not need the aid and mercy of God’s grace, as though by willing and running at your own speed you could lay hold of the fruit of everlasting life: know that you will be taken up by the dreadful hand of the husbandman and cast into the fire [Col. 1361C], unless you confess that every beauty and all loveliness of fruits proceed not from yourselves but from the vine’s inmost root. For our faithful and truthful witness says: “He who remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit; because without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5).

Absolutely nothing, because sin—which alone we can do without him—is nothing. Sin is not any substance, but the corruption of a substance. Likewise, a lie is to be regarded as nothing. For a lie signifies that what is not, is; or that what is, is not. Therefore, when we hear someone lying, we are accustomed to say, “You are saying nothing”; which is the same as saying, “What you say is not.” Things do not exist as your words signify them; and thus a lie is rightly called nothing, because it has nowhere to subsist when existence is removed from or denied to the thing signified.

Thus, after Christ was born—of whose future birth circumcision had been a sign—the Apostle declares, “Circumcision is nothing” (I Cor. VII, 19), that is, it is a false sign. What was signified by that sign as future is now past, Christ having been born from Abraham’s seed. Circumcision itself had been set as the true sign of his future birth in that part of the body through which seed is transmitted, so that there might be no doubt that he was to be born from Abraham’s seed, he who was promised to Abraham for the blessing of all nations. Once he was born, whoever is circumcised does nothing, because, as the Apostle testifies: “Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God” [Col. 1362A] (I Cor. VIII, 19).

In a similar way, one who celebrates outside the Church sacraments given to the Church does nothing, because there he applies the sign of a sacred thing where the sacred thing cannot exist. There he presents a sign of sanctification where nothing is sanctified; and therefore that sign or sacrament is nothing. Therefore Truth truly says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5). For this testimony of Truth is so true that, before him, the sacrament itself—that is, the sign itself of a sacred thing—of which cut-off branches display the outward form, is nothing; it is an appearance lacking every fruit, every power, and every verdure and sap of the true vine, and is therefore altogether like the circumcision of Jews who blaspheme Christ. For as Jews blaspheme Christ and yet bear the sign indicating his birth, so heretics—and especially, as shown above, simoniacs—blaspheme the Holy Spirit and yet celebrate signs signifying the operation and power of the Holy Spirit.

26. We wish the reader to remember that, as we determined above, we are speaking only of heretics who are manifest, indubitable, and condemned synodically. We assert to be simoniacs liable before a council only those who have been condemned in holy councils, whose being in the gall of bitterness and the bond of impiety is established by their manifest simony, and whose office is consequently prohibited by the Roman See. Where simoniacs or other heretics remain concealed, so that Catholics regard them as Catholics [Col. 1362C], we do not judge them liable before a council, as one who says “Raca” to his brother shall be liable before a council. Rather, we judge them liable to judgment, as we say that one angry with his brother is liable to judgment: judgment, that is, not human but divine, to which belong all things done in secret.

What reality there may be concerning the sacraments of secret heretics, we think must be left to the judgment of him whose great mercy is commended if, even through those not yet openly excluded, he works something of power and salvation. But if the Holy Spirit, who in the sacraments flees the openly heretical undisciplined man, also flees one who feigns discipline—that is, a hidden heretic, a wolf clothed in sheep’s skin—who will dare say to him, “Why do you act so?” Yet we believe that Christ’s faithful, who do not know these hidden heretics and participate in their sacraments in Christ’s faith, are not defrauded of Christ’s gift and the working of the Holy Spirit, who breathes where he wills and likewise breathes through whom he wills, even through persons like Caiaphas, Christ’s slayer. Though they are rightly to be condemned, they nevertheless have, after Caiaphas’s example, authority even to judge Christ himself in his members, whereas, as I have said, they ought rather to be judged and condemned by Christ’s members.

Therefore, as long as Christ endures such persons in his members, a Caiaphas-like high priest presides, as it were, in the house of God. His companionship is no more welcome to the true followers of Christ and the Apostles than Caiaphas’s companionship was welcome to the Apostles themselves. Yet they unwillingly tolerate the whitewashed wall until God strikes [Col. 1363A] it. But those who prop up that wall differ greatly from the Apostle Paul, who, standing before such a high priest and being struck at his command, said: “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall” (Acts XXIII, 2).

But let us leave this whitewashed wall, clad as it were in a certain mortar of righteousness, to be struck by God; and let us at least withdraw secretly, insofar as we can, from it as it is now about to fall, lest, if we strive to prop it up like supporting timbers, we be crushed when it begins to fall. The timbers supporting this wall are clerics powerful in learning, lay enemies of religious life, and all their friends of the same sort—such as that friend of the high priest who, striking Christ, said: “Do you answer the high priest thus?” (John XVIII, 22).

The Lord’s arm could indeed have struck back at the striker [Col. 1363B], and could at once have overthrown not only him but also the whitewashed wall supported by so rigid a timber—that is, the one falsely called a high priest. But he accepted the injury, preserved patience, and sought no mercy for himself from so unjust a high priest. So let us too, aided by him, preserve patience and seek no mercy, favour, or generosity from unjust high priests, if we prefer to be saved with Christ rather than condemned among the flatterers of impious high priests.

These Caiaphas-like high priests, sitting in Moses’ seat, share another resemblance with that Caiaphas: as he held Christ captive and put him to death, not only by his own tongue but also by the Roman [Col. 1363C] hand, so these men hand Christ over as if captive in the sacraments to persons to whom he himself does not wish to be handed over, so that they may become guilty of the Lord’s body and blood. This occurs not only when they themselves eat and drink judgment upon themselves, but also when they give the very body of the Lord to be eaten, spat upon, and crucified by those whom they ought to expel from the Church until they have performed worthy penance. For, as the Apostle testifies, guilt concerning the Lord’s body and blood is incurred when his body and blood are eaten unworthily.

But those manifest heretics—branches cut off, dry, and altogether dead, and useless ministers of dead sacraments—ought not even to suppose that they possess Christ, or his life-giving body, even in the manner in which Caiaphas had him in his own custody, although they do possess the sacrament of the Lord’s body, as was shown above [Col. 1363D].

27. Nor should they again flatter themselves on the ground that, if Christ is not present in their sacraments, then by partaking of them they do not become guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. For it is clear that they are bound by an equal, or even graver, guilt. Christ’s killers, while persisting in their guilt, were heavily charged with his very murder; but the division of Christ himself would have been charged more heavily, if they had divided him as butchers do, torn him limb from limb, and broken his bones. Yet this was not fitting to be done, because the Son of Man, going to the Father according to what had been determined concerning him, permitted no suffering or injury to be inflicted upon himself or his body except what was written concerning him [Col. 1364A]. Hence, when all that had been written about his Passion was fulfilled, the executioners could do nothing further to him. But had they not been divinely restrained, they would gladly have broken his bones and legs, and perhaps torn and divided him as we read that many of his servants were torn apart and dismembered.

But Holy Scripture, which foretold Christ’s killing, nowhere foretold—indeed, in every way prohibited—the breaking of his legs. For the Lord said through Moses concerning the paschal Lamb, a type of Christ: “It shall be eaten in one house” (Exod. 12:46); which is the same as if he had said: That one Lamb shall not be divided among several houses, but shall be eaten in one house. “And you shall not break a bone of it” (John [Col. 1364B] 19:36). Therefore, in the Apostle’s judgment, the fault of evil persons who receive the body and blood of the Lord unworthily in the Church is to be reckoned as a kind of killing of Christ, since he declares that the person who eats and drinks unworthily is guilty of the Lord’s body and blood. This fault is indeed great, yet it does not conflict with the Scriptures.

But a heretic or schismatic is blamed less for killing Christ than for dividing Christ, because, contrary to every authority of Holy Scripture, he attempts to divide Christ, supposing that he can be eaten in different and multiple houses, although the law says: “It shall be eaten in one house.” Therefore, although Christ is never divided, those who contentious­ly [Col. 1364C] affirm that the paschal Lamb is eaten both outside and within the Church become guilty of this division in their thoughts. Indeed, the heretic or schismatic is worse, more detestable, and more accursed than the Jews and soldiers who killed Christ, because these attempt to do what the others could not do. Yet they do so in vain, because Holy Scripture does not allow Christ to be divided, or divided both outside and within the one house of the Church, as the appended testimonies of the Fathers prove with the greatest clarity.

Cyprian, in his letter to Cornelius: “Does anyone suppose that great and weighty matters happen either without God’s knowledge or without his permission, and that priests—that is, God’s stewards—are ordained otherwise than by his judgment? This is not to have faith that we live; this is not to give honor to God. But those who are made outside the Church, who act contrary to the order and tradition of the Gospel, are not ordained by his judgment. Thus the Lord himself sets forth and says in the Twelve Prophets: ‘They set up a king for themselves, and not through me.’ And again: ‘Their sacrifices are like the bread of mourning; all who eat them shall be defiled’ (Hos. 9:4). And through Isaiah the Holy Spirit cries out and says: ‘Woe to you, rebellious children, says the Lord: you have taken counsel, but not through me, and have made an agreement not through my Spirit, adding sin upon sin’ (Isa. 30:1).”

The same author, to Magnus the presbyter: “The Church is one, and it cannot be both inside and outside. For if it was with Novatian, it was not with Cornelius; but if it was with Cornelius, Novatian is not in the Church [Col. 1365A] and cannot be counted a bishop.”

Jerome, on the Twelve Prophets: “God hates the sacrifices of heretics and has cast them away; and whenever they are gathered under the Lord’s name, he will abhor their stench and close his nostrils. To hate, cast away, and not smell are expressions spoken in human likeness, so that we may understand God’s disposition in our own terms.” Speaking of the paschal Lamb, he says among other things: “Let us not suppose that this Lamb can be eaten everywhere. We are commanded to eat it in one house, that is, not to suppose that the Lamb is sacrificed outside the Church.” From this it is plain that Jews, heretics, and all assemblies of perverse doctrines, because they do not eat in the Church, eat not the flesh of the Lamb but that of the dragon, “which was given [Col. 1365B] as food to the peoples of Ethiopia.” But we eat “the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”

Augustine, to Boniface: “Let heretics not seek the Holy Spirit except in Christ’s body; they have the sacrament of it outside, but do not hold within the reality of which it is the sacrament.”

The same author: “The man who bought Joseph was a eunuch. Thus one who purchases the grace of the Holy Spirit has no living seed in his dried-up genitals. Likewise, the sacrificial fire which had lived under water during the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity was extinguished when Jason sold the priesthood to Antiochus. This signifies that the fire of the Holy Spirit does not shine in the sacraments of Simoniacs.”

Origen, in his exposition on Leviticus: “Such a man is sought as can eat the holy flesh, not in any place whatever [Col. 1365C], but in the holy place, within the court of the tabernacle. Let those who split Churches hear this: those who introduce strange and corrupt doctrines and suppose that they can eat the holy flesh outside God’s temple and outside the Lord’s court. Their sacrifices, performed contrary to the law of the commandment, are profane. They are commanded to be eaten in the holy place, within the courts of the tabernacle of testimony—courts surrounded by the wall of faith, supported by the pillars of hope, and enlarged by the expanse of charity. Where these are absent, the flesh is not holy and can neither be possessed nor eaten.”

28. If, however, authorities promulgated from the Apostolic See and consonant with our assertions are required, the authorities previously cited [Col. 1365D] from the writings of Leo the Great and Pope Paschal may suffice. One of them declares that, in the Church of Alexandria, because of the excommunicated, the offering of sacrifice was interrupted, the consecration of chrism failed, and all the light of heavenly sacraments was extinguished. The other, in a letter addressed to the Milanese, approves that saying of blessed Augustine: “There is no place of true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church.” Since we have set forth above the words of these two Roman pontiffs, it would be superfluous to repeat them here; yet we have thought it fitting to recall them.

Nevertheless, if anyone seeks more authorities from the Apostolic See, let him hear what follows. Pope Pelagius [Col. 1366A] says to Victor and Pancratius, among other things: “If we are guided by truth, what a schismatic makes is not Christ’s body; for no one can devise a divided Christ without the Apostle’s condemnation. As has often been said, the Church, which is Christ’s body, is known to be one and cannot be divided into two or more. For as soon as anyone departs from it, the Church ceases to be. There is one temple of Jerusalem; whoever has divided himself must necessarily sacrifice to idols.”

The same author, to John the Patrician: “Do not continually defile a Catholic mind through any communion with schismatics. Christ’s body—the Church—is known to be one. One divided from unity cannot consecrate the truth of Christ’s body. For, if we examine the very name of consecration with rational and living understanding, to consecrate is to make sacred together. But he who is divided from the bosom of the Church and separated from the apostolic sees rather desecrates than consecrates. Therefore do not, as though there were no difference between schismatics and the Church, wish indiscriminately to join in the sacrifices of both.” [Col. 1366B]

Gregory, in the *Register*: “We can in no way call a consecration that which is celebrated by excommunicated persons.”

The same author, in Book 35 of the *Moralia*: “It should be carefully noted that Job’s friends are commanded to offer the sacrifice of their conversion to the Lord not by themselves, but through Job. For he says: ‘But Job my servant shall pray for you; I will accept his face, so that your folly may not be imputed to you’ (Job 42:8). As though he said openly to heretics: I do not receive your sacrifices; I do not hear the words of your petitions, except through the intercession of him whose confession concerning me I recognize as truthful.”

And shortly afterwards: “Seek your salvation through the Catholic Church, which I love; for through her I wish to remit what you have sinned against me in her, so that she may obtain your safety, since she suffered from your sickness. For she alone is the one through whom the Lord willingly receives sacrifice; she alone intercedes confidently for those who err.” Therefore the Lord commands concerning the offering of the Lamb, saying: “It shall be eaten in one house, and none of its flesh shall be carried outside” (Exod. 12:46). “The Lamb is eaten in one house because the true victim is offered in the one Catholic Church. The divine law forbids its flesh to be carried outside because it forbids what is holy to be given to dogs.” [Col. 1366D]

29. These sayings of the Fathers are so open and manifest that they need no elucidation. For they demonstrate most plainly that the sacrament [Note: [Col. 1365D] A word appears to be missing here, perhaps *sacrament*.] and sacrifice of Simoniac and other heretical priests are void; indeed, they prove that these persons have no true sacrifice, although they possess a true and complete sacrament when they perform the rite according to ecclesiastical usage.

For *sacrifice* and *sacrament* are two terms, and their meanings differ widely. The life-giving body of Christ is properly called a sacrifice; it is not properly called a sacrament except with respect to the form presented to the senses [Col. 1367A]. This form may fittingly be called a sacrament, as the sign of the one body which is the Church, compacted into one from many persons as from many grains, and made one body as one loaf. The actual existence of Christ’s body does not signify this union to us, since it is too far removed from our senses; rather, it is the visible and perceptible appearance and form itself that does so.

Since a sacrament is a visible sign of invisible grace, I do not dare call Christ’s hidden body, secret and concealed from our sight, a sacrament; for it does not signify a sacred reality but is itself a sacred reality—unless perhaps it is called a sacrament by its effect, because it makes its worthy recipient holy, just as an ornament is so called because it adorns. I am compelled to wonder at the opinion of certain masters who assert that the visible and tangible body of Christ is signified by Christ’s flesh and blood, both invisible and intelligible; for invisible things are ordinarily signified by visible things, rather than visible things by invisible.

Therefore, heretics, schismatics, and all those cut off by the Gospel sickle may indeed possess with us an identity of sacrifice, for whom that Lamb is the one sacrifice; yet the most evident truth of the authorities cited above proves that he is eaten only in one house. [Col. 1367B]

30. Even if certain other authorities seem somewhere to oppose these, affirming that the same things exist both within and outside the Church, in the manner of the four rivers of paradise, which are both within and outside [Col. 1367C] paradise, we are not troubled by the diversity of such authorities. For we do not deny that the completeness of sacraments can exist outside the Church; but we deny the reality of sacrifice, in accordance with the assertion of the authorities cited above. Properly examined, those other authorities do not conflict with them, since they affirm that outside the Church there can be not a holy sacrifice, but a complete sacrament; not the Lord’s body, but the sacrament of the Lord’s body.

31. In determining these diverse, not contrary, authorities, one must carefully note that there is a great difference between sacrament and sacrament. Some sacraments are performed only with respect to a rational creature, such as the sacrament [Col. 1367D] of ordination and baptism. Others are performed with respect to inanimate things, such as the sacred signs produced when divine words are applied to elements in the consecration of chrism, an altar, or bread and wine.

Those sacraments performed with respect to a rational creature, when celebrated outside the Church and thus void, empty, extinguished, and dead, become valid, luminous, and living when the Church’s confirmation is added to the sacraments celebrated outside after the rational creature—that is, the penitent person—has entered the Church. But sacraments performed with respect to inanimate things can in no way be confirmed, because those creatures cannot repent.

Thus we sometimes read that sacraments of persons administered outside were confirmed by Catholics through intervening repentance [Col. 1368A], or excused because of ignorance. Pope Anastasius, for example, excused the sacraments of ordination and baptism celebrated by the condemned Acacius. Some read his words carelessly and suppose that he holds an opinion contrary to the authorities previously cited. But it will be clear to one who reads correctly, if he is willing to attend to the difference between sacraments: namely, between those which can in some manner and at some time be excused through the venial or invincible ignorance of persons receiving the sacraments and seeking in them only God’s grace; and those sacraments which, performed outside in relation to inanimate things, are never read of as confirmed or excused inside, but are everywhere and in every way rejected.

Hence Pope Alexander says: “A church which has become known to have been consecrated by a bargain for a price—or, to speak more truly, execrated—must by no means be regarded as a church.” What is said of a church may fittingly be said of all inanimate things: that is, neither wine nor bread nor oil, when execrated rather than consecrated by any heretic, ought to be called or considered holy. Thus we have set out, however imperfectly, what we think concerning sacraments, without prejudice to those who are better and speak better. We are prepared to yield to them when a reason or authority is shown to us which we ought not resist and for which we ought to change our statements. [Col. 1368B]

32. I would also like to say something concerning the wicked pest, Simony. Among all the little foxes that destroy vineyards, no fox is more wicked or more cunning than Simony. For, as someone says:

> By what knot can I hold Proteus, who changes his form?

So we may say: By what knot may we hold this most cunning little fox, Simony—manifold in appearance, thousand-formed in habit, and almost always unlike not merely other little foxes but even herself? So much so that, while she destroys Christ’s vineyards, she is sometimes seen in the dress of the very vinedresser. Whenever she begins to be recognized in any one of her skins, she immediately puts on another; and she sometimes pretends to plant the very vineyards she devastates.

This little fox has often been caught by Christ’s discerning hunters and stripped of her skin; but now she has found a skin in which she can scarcely be recognized [Col. 1368D], because in it she does not employ fox-like cunning and does not at all appear as a beast, but as a domestic sheep. When prelates of monasteries demand gifts from those whom they admit to their fellowship, they conceal that very simoniacal avarice under the name of an offering. This is surely highly improper: an offering is one thing, an exaction another; one thing is voluntarily offered, another is taken and extorted even from the unwilling.

Blessed Benedict did not command this to be done in his Rule (ch. 59); indeed, he forbade it. He teaches that poor persons who offer their children should simply make a petition. From wealthy parents, however, he does not permit anything to be demanded; but if they voluntarily offer anything, he allows it to be received. What is received in this manner may be called an offering, not an exaction.

Christ also, when urging perfect conversion upon a certain rich man, did not say, “Go, sell what you have and bring it to me”; rather, he said, “Give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Luke 18:22). The Apostle Peter likewise, while governing the common life at Jerusalem, demanded none of anyone’s possessions, although he received what was laid at his feet as a voluntary offering. He did not require Ananias and Sapphira to dedicate their goods to Christ; rather, he consecrated to Christ goods already dedicated, and inflicted due punishment upon those who defrauded them. This example requires great severity toward those who defraud tithes or other offerings already assigned to the use of the common life. Thus bishops and other ministers of the altar should not be blamed either when they demand their rightful stipends or when they severely punish those who defraud such things. [Col. 1369A]

But what is it, when God’s ministers demand things not owed to them, except the most blatant Simony, clothed in a new cloak so that it cannot be recognized, while Simon Magus seeks to appear Simon Peter? Bishops say that extensive service and expenses are owed to them when they consecrate churches. We do not deny that they are owed service and even very extensive expenses; nevertheless, these must not be demanded from church founders, nor accepted from them at all unless they offer them voluntarily—not through exaction, but through devotion.

For bishops possess tithes, estates, and villages, just as the Levites of old possessed tithes and cities with their surrounding lands, so that the ministry of the altar might be carried out chastely. Yet it is astonishing to say it: bishops feed themselves from episcopal resources for courts, secular affairs, and the business of this world [Col. 1369C], and demand other sustenance in the very performance of episcopal ministries. To consecrate churches, ordain clerics, and sign Christians with chrism belongs to the episcopal office; tithes, firstfruits, and other ecclesiastical resources ought to support the bishop in this office and therefore may rightly be required for the use of the bishop and the clerics cooperating with him. If anything beyond this is demanded in the administration of spiritual offices, the leprosy of Gehazi is incurred, and in such administration one serves not God but Mammon.

Hence the entirely just judgment of Pope Honorius deserves praise: he deposed Otto, called bishop of Halberstadt, and publicly declared him a Simoniac in his letters, because, at the consecration [Col. 1369D] of a certain church, he was convicted of demanding money under the pretext of service.

33. Therefore, all you to whom the Bridegroom says, “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song 2:15), catch this fox, most ancient in time but ever new in her novel renewal of frauds. Separate yourselves from oratories that are less consecrated than execrated by an open bargain for a price or by the exaction of undue service. For if you regard such churches as consecrated, you will be disobedient to the Roman See. As we noted above, Pope Alexander II teaches that churches consecrated through a bargain [Col. 1370A] for a price are less consecrated than execrated and must in no way be regarded as churches.

The same pope, while holding a synod in the Church of Constantinople of more than one hundred bishops, struck the little fox of which we speak with three blows.

[Note: [Col. 1369D] Three councils were held at Rome under Pope Alexander II: one in 1063 and two in 1065. These three canons, absent from the printed editions, seem to belong to the first council, which was assembled chiefly against the Simoniacs [Col. 1370D].]

For among the other chapters of that council we read: “Churches and altars are neither to be sold nor bought; and those who henceforth sell or buy them shall be subject to anathema. Likewise, churches consecrated for a price or by Simoniacs are to be consecrated again. Likewise, let presbyters knowingly ordained by Simoniacs from the time of Pope Nicholas until now and hereafter know that they are deposed.”

Wounded by such blows, this little fox might seem completely slain, if she were not perhaps that beast of which the Apocalypse says: “which had the wound of the sword and lived” (Rev. 13:14). The Arian pest or any other heresy is then extinguished by the sword’s wound when it has been condemned and anathematized by synodal judgment. But Simony, although struck more than once by the sword of anathema, still lives, because its death-wound appears to have been healed by the fact that even certain religious persons receive the sacraments of manifest Simoniacs, although Roman pontiffs, as though with Peter’s own mouth, have forbidden them many times. [Col. 1370B]

Simony plainly still lives—not in reality, indeed, but in the estimation of those who believe the sacraments of Simoniacs alive, because they see Simon Magus no longer walking on earth but flying near the heavens. We too grant that Simon Magus still lives in his accomplices; nevertheless, he is already dead and dies daily. Indeed, he is regarded by the elect who belong to Christ and flee his contact as a stinking corpse. Thus the law forbade anyone to touch a dead body; if anyone touched one, the law judged him unclean. It should be noted that the law absolutely prohibits touching or eating a corpse. Yet it permits carrying a corpse when necessity presses, saying: “And if it should be necessary for him to carry any of these dead things, he shall wash his clothes and be unclean until sunset” (Lev. 2:22).

For this reason, we grant that a corpse may be carried when necessity presses, but never grant that it may be touched or [Col. 1370D] eaten. For example, when we deal with a Simoniac whom some may contend to be alive but whom we do not doubt to be dead, we never allow such a dead man to be touched, because his sin must not be assented to. Still less do we allow such a dead man to be eaten, because his deed must not be imitated. Yet we admit that, under necessity, this corpse is sometimes to be carried until a pit is dug for the sinner, into which, once cast, he will no longer be carried.

Then a fitting pit will be ready for the stinking dead man when God, either acting directly or through lawful judges, casts him out of the Church [Col. 1371A] into the grave of either infernal punishment or, what is much more to be desired, penitential punishment. But where there is no power to execute false judgments, corpses must be carried—yet not without tearful compunction, by which we must wash our garments, that is, so shape and cleanse our outward conduct that we may not appear to tolerate, willingly rather than from necessity, sinners especially anathematized in councils.

We also wash our garments if we pour out tears and prayers for them, lest perhaps, as the Apostle says, God give them a reprobate mind; rather, may they recover themselves from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive at his will. Thus King David bore Saul, divinely deposed from the kingdom but still powerful through human support. The king, alive in God, bore a king dead to God; yet he did not, as it were, touch him, because he did not approve Saul’s deed. Rather, lest he be compelled to touch him, he fled from Saul, hid in the woods, and finally went into exile. [Col. 1371B]

David also washed his garments when he did not rejoice in his enemy’s ruin, but mourned with great lamentation over Saul and his son Jonathan. The Apostle Paul likewise bore the high priest Ananias, but did not at all approve his high priesthood; he foretold Ananias’s destruction, saying, “God will strike you, whitewashed wall” (Acts 23:2). Paul also washed his garments, having great sorrow for his brethren. Therefore, taught by the examples of King David and the Apostle Paul, let us bear the dead where necessity requires, while nevertheless avoiding their touch as far as we can. [Col. 1371C]

34. I have become foolish by treating matters above me. But because I have been compelled to say what I have said, I believe and hope that my imperfection can be perfected by that incarnate Wisdom of God, by whose adversaries I was compelled to become foolish—not only, as I have said, by handling matters above me, but also by writing to a most wise man while I am most foolish. For I do not fail to know to whom I speak. But following the example of Abraham, who said, “I speak to the Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18:27), I too, though obscure in family, manner of life, and even name, speak to you, holy abbot of Clairvaux; to you, I say, illustrious in name and life. Once I had begun [Col. 1371D] to speak, I was compelled to exceed the brevity I had intended.

I have laid before you, as before a spiritual father, my view which offends secular clerics, especially stipendiary ones, so that where you approve what I think, you may show yourself my defender and helper; but where you judge anything of it deserving disapproval, you may show yourself my corrector. I adjure and entreat you by him from whom you have the power to do what I ask.

For if those tokens are visible in our sayings and writings by which Tamar, lest she be burned, is read to have been defended—namely, the ring, staff, and bracelet, through which faith, hope, and charity are understood—I beg you not to believe that my soul has committed fornication with the father of lies. Rather, confess that it is pregnant by the seed of Judah, that is, Christ, [Col. 1372A] so that, following Tamar’s example, it may give birth as it were to a son called Perez, that is, “division.” For God is witness: through no pursuit of personal glory, but solely through zeal for truth, I either separate myself from the sacraments of heretics or demonstrate in speech and writing that there is a great division and distinction between their sacraments and those of Catholics—without prejudice, as I have said, to better persons.

35. Long ago, compelled by necessity, I came at Pope Innocent’s summons to the Lord Pope Innocent. When he examined me and asked by what faith I live, in what hope I rejoice, and by what love toward God and the holy Church I am moved, through Christ’s gift, he treated me graciously, as though he had heard from my mouth, “I have conceived by the man to whom these things belong.” By his letters he commended my lowliness to my lord the Archbishop of Salzburg for protection. I wished him, above all others, to be given and become my defender because he too, no less than I—indeed, far more, by the majesty of his authority, he the eminent archbishop than I the insignificant cleric—strives to establish this: that the prince of this world, not only in himself but also in his members separated from the Church, has now been so judged that he ought wholly to be despised, even though through empty sacraments he may be found transformed into an angel of light. [Col. 1372B]

Accordingly, stirred by zeal for justice, he does not permit either stipendiary clerics or manifestly incestuous persons to minister at the altar in his diocese. For though his diocese is broad and extensive, stretching over a journey of ten days or more, you could not find within so great a territory even one stipendiary cleric or one openly incestuous cleric. He has also expelled irregular canons from his monasteries as true Canaanites unworthy of the Holy Land, and introduced regular canons in their place as true Israelites.

Although we approve this action when we compare irregulars to Canaanites and regulars to Israelites, we do not ignore that some among the irregular will be saved and some among the regular damned—just as certain people lived commendably in Babylon and certain people perished in Jerusalem. But because it is not safe to sit by Babylon’s rivers, nor is there secure standing upon the shores of those same rivers, which are very muddy, the good conduct of people living well there does not commend Babylon itself, just as the dwelling of wicked persons does not condemn Jerusalem so as to prevent one from saying of one of these two cities, “Go out from there,” and of the other, “There the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, to give thanks to the name of the Lord” (Ps. 121:4). [Col. 1372D]

Therefore we rightly rejoice wherever we see an irregular congregation, as though Babylon, destroyed, and Jerusalem built from its better stones, as it were, for the restoration of the common life. We rejoice, I say, and pray that our joy may be full through Christ our Lord. Amen.

# [EPISTOLARY BOOK TO INNOCENT II]

[Col. 1373]

# NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING TREATISE

(D. P. Pez, preface to vol. II of the *Anecdota*, p. XXVIII.)

Gerhoh’s work, entirely exceptional and resplendent with zeal for divine honor, is here published by us not without considerable apprehension. Thus, if any old monument requires a prudent and moderate reader, this one certainly does. In it Gerhoh discusses the difference between secular and regular canons in such a way that he repeatedly inveighs with the utmost severity against the former’s opinions and morals, and judges that irregular canons cannot be saved unless they convert. These are Gerhoh’s own words at column 479, where he also adds that they were judged true by Gualther, Archbishop of Ravenna, a prelate of holy and venerable life, when Gerhoh was at Regensburg on the lord pope’s legation.

Indeed, in his letter or prologue to Innocent II, he openly writes that Pope Honorius II held the same view in the presence of Norbert, Archbishop of Magdeburg. “Now,” says Gerhoh at col. 441, “I have done what the law commands, going to the place which the Lord God chose for his name to be invoked there—namely, the Roman See—on the embassy of my lord Conrad, Bishop of Salzburg. And I approached the priest who was in those days, Pope Honorius of blessed memory, and discussed with him the teaching which I preach among clerics still secular, lest perhaps I might run or had run in vain. The occasion for this teaching was that, through speech and writing, I urged my uterine brothers to leave the assembly of such persons, distinguishing between the good seed of apostolic life, which Christ willed and ordained to bear fruit among the clergy, and the tares of secular clerics sown over it by the enemy. Though these statements of mine were troublesome to some, they were acceptable to the man of holy memory, Pope Honorius.”

We do not impress these things upon readers in order that they should make the same judgment concerning the present condition of secular canons—a condition later approved by supreme pontiffs and synods of bishops and protected by most holy canons—but solely in order to reconcile readers somewhat more to Gerhoh, who had as admirers of his teaching, however severe, men of such authority and holiness. Besides, from this Dialogue of Gerhoh we learn so many outstanding and singular things that it cannot be suppressed without serious detriment to the commonwealth of letters. Let us select some examples.

At column 453 Gerhoh says that some perversely and falsely attribute to St. Udalric the claim that he wrote to Pope Nicholas in defense of the marriages of presbyters and other ministers of God, lest continence become an occasion of fornication. He says this is shown to be utterly false because, in Udalric’s time, no one named Nicholas presided over the Apostolic See. “Men like this holy man,” Gerhoh continues, “living holy lives themselves and not defending the disorderly life of others, but rather, as far as they can, destroying it at least by apostolic examples, may be called flourishing, since they have the flourishing desire to be released from those living disorderly lives and to be with Christ in apostolic and holy conduct.” We read that St. Udalric had this desire: after resigning his bishopric, he wished to live the apostolic life among monks, because at that time he could scarcely find it among the clergy.

So writes Gerhoh, a most weighty authority for the period when that fine little letter on clerical marriages, under the name of the most holy bishop of Augsburg, was especially circulated by concubinary clerics. Meanwhile Johann Gottfried Olearius, in volume II of the *Bibliotheca of Ecclesiastical Writers*, writes as follows:

“Udalric, bishop of Augsburg, otherwise Count of Dillingen, flourished around the year of the Lord 930, according to Grynaeus’s account in the preface to the *Orthodoxography of the Ancient Fathers*. There is extant in the same work, volume I of the Latin Fathers, folio 481, and in Calixtus, *Treatise on the Marriage of Clerics*, appendix, folio 1, his letter *On the Marriage of Priests*, written to Nicholas I, Roman Pontiff. In it he contends that marriage is equally permitted to everyone, and thus also to priests, and cannot be forbidden them either by law or on any pretext. See an epitome of that letter in Schopff, *Academy of Jesus Christ*, Class 9, folio 143. Compare Heilbrunner, *The Uncatholic Papacy*, folio 656; Calixtus, *On the Marriage of Clerics*, p. 502; and Lydius, notes on Clemangis, folio 25.”

Bellarmin and his other accomplices do not mention it, perhaps because it does not serve their purpose.

But Bellarmine and the other Catholic librarians did not fail to mention Udalric’s letter—whose existence even in the codex of Udalric of Bamberg we publicly indicated in their very presence—for that reason; rather, because they held it most certain that it was fabricated and foisted by concubinary clerics upon a most chaste bishop. Nor would Olearius himself, an erudite man, have judged otherwise, had he weighed the letter’s title together with Gerhoh, whose authority in all other respects will be greater for every learned person than that of all the modern writers whom Olearius heaps up and brings forward on his side.

In column 491 and the following one, Gerhoh writes much concerning Manegold, dean of Raitenbuch, and his book published for Gregory VII among the public. “Read,” he says, “the book composed by Manegold, formerly dean of our cloister, against the assailants of Gregory VII, and you will find proved in it by most forceful authorities what we too strive to prove: namely, that clerics who commit fornication and, in addition, usurp forbidden offices are Nicolaitans and heretics, not only along with Nicolas, but also with Ebion and Paul of Samosata.” By arguments of this kind he defended Gregory VII, who was attacked on this account by the clerics of our land because he prohibited ministers of the altar living in fornication not only from office but even from entrance into the Church.

And when an opponent reproached Gerhoh with Manegold’s importunity and death, and with the common opinion that Manegold’s book, although composed in defense of Gregory VII, had nevertheless not been approved by Gregory himself, Gerhoh replies that he does not himself hold that book as an authority, although he knows that it pleased even Catholic bishops, who, driven out because of the schism of Wibert, were then frequenting the cloister of Raitenbuch. “But to this,” says Gerhoh, “I reply to you, who believe me to be at variance with the regular community of my brethren: my more reputable brethren are admirers of that Manegold, formerly dean there, and hold his writings as though they were responses of a heavenly oracle. By them some were strengthened toward Catholic unity during the Wibertine schism, and by them secular disputants against the Church were at that time somewhat refuted. Hence, from that time onward, in the cloister of Raitenbuch that dean is heard by the more prudent brethren as though he still lived: though dead, he still speaks; and in his writings he still detests the sacrifices of fornicators,” etc. In the same place Gerhoh praises a letter by a certain Anonymous author of Raitenbuch, and a certain Chunrad of the Wood, likewise a canon of Raitenbuch, whom he writes had already grown old in the judgment of truth.

Moreover, as regards Manegold’s book, in our Bavarian Journey, inserted in the preface to the first volume, we conjectured that it was no different from Manegold’s tract against Wolfhelm of Cologne, published by the most learned Muratori in volume IV of the *Ambrosian Anecdota*. But the words reported from Gerhoh’s *Dialogue* alone [Col. 1375] prove the contrary. For since it is clear from them that Manegold, dean of Raitenbuch, wrote while Gregory VII was still alive, and since it is no less certain from the last chapter of Manegold’s tract in Muratori that it could not have been published until Gregory had already passed to heaven, how can the two works be identical?

Accordingly, not only must these two books be carefully distinguished from one another, but also Manegald and Manegold themselves. For if one and the same Manegold had been author of both works, in the work which he published against Wolfhelm after 1080—and in which he promised a certain writing for Gregory VII against the calumnies of Weneric—he would certainly not have concealed that, while Gregory was still alive, he had composed another work to defend that same pope’s dignity. Let it therefore remain firm and certain that Manegold, dean of Raitenbuch, was different, though contemporary, from Muratori’s Manegald, just as the former’s book for Gregory VII was distinct from the latter’s tract against Wolfhelm and against Weneric’s letter.

Finally, Muratori’s Manegald appears to us altogether identical with the Manegold praised by the Anonymous of Melk, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 105, in these words:

> Manegold the priest, the master of masters of modern times, was a vigorous defender of truth, from which neither the promises nor the threats of the schismatic king could bend him. Indeed, in that conflict which arose between Gregory VII and Henry IV, he labored to defend justice even unto imprisonment. There survives a certain exhortatory letter written to him by Ivo, bishop of Chartres. He divided the text of the prophet Isaiah by page divisions; upon Matthew he wrote continuous glosses. He also wrote upon the Psalter a most excellent work, more precious than topaz and refined gold.

Thus the Anonymous of Melk, a writer near to those times.

But let us return to Gerhoh’s *Dialogue*. In column 497 the provost of Reichersberg writes that Conrad I, archbishop of Salzburg, with the Lord’s help, made almost all the communities of his diocese regular; and he laments that among the suffragan sees subject to him, one of which was the Church of Regensburg, “the son of the slave woman” still reigns, and, what is worse, persecutes “the son of the free woman.” Finally, there is a notable and elegant passage in column 493 and following, where, as elsewhere, he attacks the more lax teachings of the schoolmen:

> I know well that certain masters occupy themselves in the schools with bending the Scriptures to their own meaning rather than directing themselves to the rectitude of Scripture. Since they say that all terrible things were said for terror, they strangely endeavor to empty terror of its force, asserting that those very terrors contain nothing of serious truth—imitating, of course, the serpent, who in paradise vainly attempted to invalidate God’s terrible words. They bluster this with round mouths and puffed cheeks, in order to display their knowledge that puffs up and defend the dissolute life in themselves and their like. But those who speak of the magnificence of God’s holiness and recount his wonders will likewise speak of the power of his terrors; nor will they pour forth the remembrance of the abundance of his sweetness to any except those in whose righteousness they can rejoice, and who do not hear the power of his terrors with deaf ears.

Gerhoh then relates what happened to him when he gave an account of his condition and manner of life before a certain hermit. Since that passage contains the history of this great man’s conversion, it deserves to be read by everyone. We should indeed exceed every limit of a preface if we wished to extract all the noteworthy matters from this *Dialogue*, which we brought forth from a contemporary parchment codex of the illustrious monastery of Rott on the Inn.

[Col. 1375]

# THE VENERABLE GERHOH, PROVOST OF REICHERSBERG: EPISTOLARY BOOK, OR DIALOGUE ADDRESSED TO POPE INNOCENT II

Concerning the difference between secular and regular clerics.

(D. B. Pez, *Anecdota*, vol. II, part II, p. 437, from a manuscript of the monastery of Rott in Bavaria.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1375A] To INNOCENT, by the favor of divine mercy nourishing pontiff of the holy Roman see, G. [Note: Gerhoh, as he calls himself in the epilogue of the little work.], an unworthy brother called priest: to fight with Peter, to triumph with Peter.

That I, the most unworthy and lowest of all the Church’s children, presume to address in writing the vicar of Peter, prince of the apostles, must not be imputed to the boldness of rashness. For I do this partly because necessity compels me, partly because the authority of God himself encourages me to it—God of whom Moses says in the Spirit: “Hear, O Israel, the things which I command you today. When you enter the land which the Lord your God is about to give you to possess, [Col. 1376A] and you have taken possession of it and dwell in it, you shall take the firstfruits of all your produce and put them in a basket; and you shall go to the place which the Lord your God has chosen for his name to be invoked there. You shall approach the priest who is in those days and say to him: ‘Today I declare before the Lord your God, who heard us and looked upon our humility, toil, and distress, and brought us out of Egypt with a strong hand and outstretched arm, amid great terror, signs, and wonders; and brought us into this place and gave us a land flowing with milk and honey. Therefore I now offer the firstfruits of the produce of the land which [Col. 1377A] the Lord your God gave me.’ And you shall leave them before the Lord your God; and, having worshipped the Lord your God, you shall feast upon all the good things which the Lord your God has given you” (Deut. 26:11).

Why these words? Assuredly because I too—alas!—was in Egypt, while among secular clerics I was vain beyond vainness. Unless the Lord had terrified me by great terror, signs, and wonders, Egypt itself would have pleased me so much that I should never have wished to join those fleeing from it; so pompous was I in secular attire. But in, as I recall, the sixteenth or seventeenth year of my age, struck by a blow and unbearable pain, I directed my mind to the resolution of chastity; and, cured of the infirmity then present, I immediately devoted myself wholly to scholastic exercises.

When freed from the pursuit of studies and established in the resolve of chastity alone, I, miserable man who had lost virginity, was almost—indeed, truly, I strove to be—a follower of Julian the Apostate. For I disdained to adorn the clerical state I had received with the tonsure and other religious marks of clothing, decently; I was accustomed so to fashion—rather, disfigure—myself that the fortieth canon of the Third Council of Toledo could have singled me out in particular. It reads as follows:

> “All clerics or readers, as Levites and priests, having their heads shaved entirely above, shall leave below only the crown formed by a circle; not as readers appear hitherto to do in the regions of Gaul, who, with long hair like laymen, have a small circle only at the crown of the head. For this custom has hitherto been that of heretics in Spain. Therefore, in order to remove scandal, this mark of disgrace must be taken away, and there must be one tonsure or dress, as is the practice throughout Spain. Whoever does not observe this shall be guilty against the Catholic faith.”

[Col. 1377C] Therefore I too was then guilty against the Catholic faith under the present canon, because I shared in the poison of heretics, namely the Julianists, at least in lay, or quasi-lay, dress.

But now, rescued by God’s grace from these vanities, and having for several years followed as best I could the rule of the apostles according to the teaching of Saint Augustine, “I declare today before the Lord your God,” who heard me, looked upon my humility, toil, and distress, and brought me out of Egypt with a strong hand and outstretched arm. I have already done what the Law commanded: I went to the place which the Lord chose for his name to be invoked there—namely, the Roman see—on an embassy for my lord Conrad, bishop of Salzburg; and I approached the priest who was in those days, Pope Honorius of blessed memory. I conferred with him concerning the message which I preach among clerics still secular, lest perhaps I should run, or have run, in vain.

The occasion of this message was that I urged my brothers by the same mother, in speech and writing, to depart from the company of such men, distinguishing between the good seed of apostolic life, which Christ wished and ordained to bear fruit in the clergy, and the tares of secular clerics sown over it by the enemy. Though such things said by me were troublesome to some, they were welcome to Pope Honorius, a man of holy memory. When, in the presence of Nortpert, archbishop of the Church of Magdeburg, I asked why these tares, now fully ripe, were not utterly uprooted, he said that such flocks of apostates—abusive speakers, liars, and drunkards—were to be counted among those whom the Apostle declares shall not inherit the kingdom of God; yet the multitude prevents their excommunication, lest, when such persons are cut off, the weak who are good be disturbed more than the bold who are evil are corrected.

[Col. 1378A] At that time those words satisfied me. But I regret that I did not then tell him what I now tell you, his lawful successor: granted that they cannot be excommunicated, at least let it be preached concerning them, as concerning abusive speakers and drunkards, that they cannot possess the kingdom of God if they persist in such sacrilege as Pope and martyr Urban condemns in his decrees. He teaches that ecclesiastical property is to be bestowed by the bishop and his ministers upon those living in common and apostolically, and on others possessing nothing; he declares sacrilegious those who transfer it to other uses. This secular clerics do, wickedly defrauding those who ought to hold it in common. For the aforesaid martyr, under anathema, forbids anyone to withdraw ecclesiastical goods from the common and apostolic life, as Ananias and Sapphira did and therefore fell dead at Peter’s rebuke. It is fitting, Father, that you follow Peter’s footsteps by rebuking them and threatening eternal death against those who knowingly and rashly oppose the ordinance of the aforesaid pope and martyr, which establishes common life throughout all mother churches.

[Col. 1378C] Nor do I think it sufficient for obedience to the command mentioned above that I approached the priest who was in those days while offering him nothing from the produce, or firstfruits of the produce, which divine authority commands to be placed in a basket and thus offered. Therefore, what I recognize that I did too little then, I shall now, with the Lord’s help, attempt to supply. In this little book, as in a basket, I offer you, the lawful priest, judgments or firstfruits from all my works, for which I suffer persecution from secular clerics.

For after I began, following the example of the patriarch Isaac, to cleanse wells filled with earth by the Philistines and to call them again by the same names which his father had called them—that is, after I began to define the regular and spiritual clerical life, setting aside the heap of earthly matter that is separate from that life’s purity and blocks the vein of living water for true Israelites—the shepherds of Gerar quarreled with me, wishing to drive me from the land, because I dared reject the name “secular clerics” and presumed to compare them to the sons of the slave woman.

That you may most easily discern, Father, whom you ought to assign to the sons of the free woman and whom to those of the slave woman, I have chosen to arrange what follows so that we may present two disputants, one secular and the other regular, playing with one another as though the free mother were present—whose eye we acknowledge in you—in such a way that the maternal compassion within you may be compelled to awaken paternal severity, lest you any longer allow to dwell together in [Col. 1379A] one house as co-heirs those whom maternal nobility or ignobility makes very unlike.

For one was begotten by the promise of Christ, who says in the Gospel: “Everyone who has left house, fields, etc., for my name and for the Gospel, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. [Col. 1380A] 19:29). The other, born according to the flesh, is alien to promises of this kind. And because such a one willingly quarrels, in this debate let the secular cleric, who seeks his own interests, speak first, so that the regular cleric may be compelled to answer him justly.

# THE DIALOGUE BEGINS

Between a secular cleric and a regular cleric, concerning the difference between them.

[Col. 1379]

[Col. 1379B] **SECULAR CLERIC.** You who are called regular canons, because like monks you ought to be dead to the world, have no voice in the Church, whose government must be entrusted to us, as ancient custom has hitherto maintained. You violently oppose this custom by introducing the novelty of regular life and preaching that it must be observed by all congregations of clerics, without evidence from any certain and indubitable authority.

**REGULAR CLERIC.** Would that we who are called, and desire to be, regular were dead to the whole world and joined to the most perfect monks in those gardens of delights of which the Bridegroom speaks in the Song of Songs: “You who dwell in the gardens, make me hear your voice” (Song 8:13). For the Bridegroom desires the voice of that Christian, whether monk or [Col. 1379C] canon, who dwells with his whole affection in the gardens of Scripture. I say, he desires that person’s voice, whether in preaching, prayer, or praise; and he consoles him amid your objections, you who deny that such persons have a voice in the Church. But he says, “Make me hear your voice”; and he gave the reason first, saying: “The friends listen” (*ibid.*). As though he said: Do not care what enemies object, for they love neither me nor you nor themselves, since “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul.”

Yet even encouraged by these exhortations, we do not usurp for ourselves the office of preaching, so as to mount uninvited a pulpit in a church not entrusted to us and from there lift up our voice like a trumpet. But when questioned—or sometimes when unasked, prompted by salutary commands—we speak [read: “we speak”] the truth at least into the ear, at least in private rooms, which we still hope may be preached upon the housetops.

But you do wrong in accusing us of novelty. For if you consider what was sown in Christ and what afterward was oversown, while men slept—that is, while the rulers and guardians of the Churches slept—by the hostile man, you will find that Christ entrusted the Church’s governance to Peter, a renouncer of property, indeed of himself; he was unwilling earlier to entrust Peter with that rule until, after confessing his love for Christ three times, he was found to love nothing outside the Church. But though the guardians of the field were still watchful, the enemy sought to sow tares over it, when he raised up Simon Magus, the chief trader, Nicolas, the fornicator in the clergy, [Col. 1380B] and Ananias, the first lover of unlawful private possession. Their seed, through sins demanding it, has so flourished in God’s field that wheat scarcely appears, and scarcely anyone takes care not to eat of the darnel.

Therefore our institution is that of the ancients. If you think that we teach without authority that apostolic life must be observed throughout all mother churches, read in full the decrees of Pope and martyr Urban, who under a terrible anathema forbids ecclesiastical goods to you and those like you, and judges it sacrilege wherever the property of Churches is diverted to the use of persons not living apostolically.

**SECULAR CLERIC.** Then, by your opinion, Saint Gregory sinned, since from ecclesiastical property he ordered stipends to be given to certain clerics who were unwilling either to abstain from wives or renounce private possessions.

[Col. 1380C] **REGULAR CLERIC.** One thing is what Saint Gregory commanded Augustine, bishop of the English, to observe: namely, that he should establish the manner of life that existed among our fathers at the beginning of the newborn Church, among whom none said that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them. Another thing is what the same Father permitted the newly converted English clerics, not according to the law but contrary to the law, because of hardness of heart, just as Moses permitted a bill of divorce to the Jews. But at the beginning of the newborn Church it was not so: that anyone should minister who did not live chastely, or should live from any source other than the altar.

Therefore the most holy Father granted this indulgence only to clerics outside holy orders—and never to ministers of the sacred altar—that they might live separately with wives and receive their stipends externally. But for the rest, who stand outside the vow and outside the holy orders of priesthood, diaconate, and subdiaconate, Gregory’s authority may allow some separate share of ecclesiastical property, provided at least that they obey ecclesiastical rules to this extent: that, as that most holy man defines, they live in good conduct, diligently sing psalms, and, by God’s help, preserve heart, tongue, and body from everything unlawful.
