**SECULAR CLERIC.** Either defend Saint Gregory from the sacrilege which you claim is condemned by Pope and martyr Urban, [Col. 1381A] or you must accept the absurdity that one Roman saint condemns another, a man likewise of recognized holiness.

**REGULAR CLERIC.** I have already told you, and you heard. Do you wish to hear again? Just as Moses is excused from transgression of the law for permitting, to hard-hearted Jews, what was contrary to God’s law, so Saint Gregory is excused for permitting what the martyr and Pope Urban had forbidden—indeed, what the most mighty Spirit of God had forbidden in Urban himself, by whom that blessed man was moved even to the shedding of blood. To this is added that, with the same consideration, he could grant this to newly converted English clerics as he permitted marriage in the fifth or fourth degree of consanguinity to newly converted English people: not by laying down a law, but by providing milk to those still weak.

Therefore, it is a pardonable, not a legal, arrangement: clerics outside vows and holy orders may live not from the altar but from their own resources; and to those so living something may be supplied from the stipend due solely to those engaged in apostolic warfare. Yet this new concession is supported by the ancient example of King David: when he pursued the raiders who had burned Ziklag, certain men, weary from the journey, remained with the baggage and could not go on to the battle itself; nevertheless, by David’s judgment, an equal portion of the spoils fell both to those who remained weary and to those who reached the battle. What do you think would have happened if all had wished to remain with the baggage?

**SECULAR CLERIC.** I think they would have received nothing from the spoils.

[Col. 1381C] **REGULAR CLERIC.** You speak truly. Therefore you must agree that those communities in which no one serves lawfully commit sacrilege if they presume to take anything, contrary to Urban’s prohibition, from the stipend not due to them at all. But where apostolic life is observed in a community at least by those who hold holy orders, there Saint Gregory, like another David, may without sacrilege ensure that a stipend is not denied to married clerics sitting, as it were, with the baggage: paid to the soldiers as a right, but to these men as an indulgence.

For whoever are such that they serve those living apostolically at least in the farthest line—indeed behind the line—while holding lesser offices and helping them as though guarding baggage, may receive their stipends externally by the same justice by which, as we read, the weary men mentioned above, though occupied with the baggage, received spoils. But those communities which, wholly irregular, say to the apostolic order, “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways,” should know beyond doubt that heaven shall reveal their iniquity, the earth shall rise against them, and their sin and sacrilege shall be made manifest on the day of the Lord’s wrath, because they hold down justice in iniquity by occupying seats which regular clergy ought to hold.

Hence at the synod held in the Lateran Church in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1110, presided over by Pope Paschal of blessed memory, among other enactments the following chapter was promulgated and confirmed by the whole council:

> [Col. 1382A] “There are, moreover, those who, whether by violence or favor, do not permit churches to be ordered regularly; we decree that these too are to be judged sacrilegious.”

**SECULAR CLERIC.** You strike me too harshly and stretch yourself beyond your proper measure. For if, according to that chapter of Pope Paschal, those are sacrilegious who do not permit churches to be ordered regularly, but—as you think—hold God’s justice down in injustice while preventing the justice of regular life from advancing, then the Church is full of sacrilegious persons, and the Fathers themselves are greatly to blame for having permitted such things hitherto.

**REGULAR CLERIC.** Which Fathers, I ask? And what did they permit?

**SECULAR CLERIC.** In the time of King Louis bishops and clerics assembled; and, with the same king acting as mediator, they collected rules in which they also inserted this provision: that [Col. 1382B] canons might be permitted to live in private houses of their own.

**REGULAR CLERIC.** This is what the Lord laments through the Prophet: “My people have done two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves cisterns which cannot hold water” (Jer. 1:23). For it was not enough for them to take the apostolic rules away from the clergy unless they further presumed to fabricate evil rules, comparable to defective cisterns. But you wander far from the truth in thinking that Pope and martyr Urban, the lawful successor of Peter, prince of the apostles, should be opposed by the authority of Louis or of those bishops who joined him in assenting to error.

For their rule contains no distinction between ministers of the sacred altar and the other clerics, to whom Gregory’s indulgence granted to English clerics could apply with discrimination. But this royal edict, indiscriminately pronounced concerning all clerics, may be compared with the edict by which King Antiochus wrote to his whole kingdom that all the people should be one. But we, with Mattathias, ought to obey the law rather than the king.

**SECULAR CLERIC.** There are still authoritative councils in which private property is permitted to us, and ecclesiastical goods are not forbidden; indeed, they may be possessed by priests together with private property. We read in the Council of Carthage, ch. 22:

> “Likewise, it has been decided that bishops, presbyters, deacons, or any clerics who are ordained possessing nothing, and during their episcopate acquire fields or any estates in their own name, are to be held guilty of the crime of invading the Lord’s property, unless, when admonished, they transfer those things to the Church. But if anything comes to them personally, whether by the succession of relatives, let them do with it as they please.”

[Col. 1382D] **REGULAR CLERIC.** You have produced a corrupted and badly truncated chapter, perhaps as you found it in certain excerpts. Read through the complete Council of Carthage, and you will find it there decided as follows:

> “But if anything comes to them personally by someone’s generosity or by the succession of relatives, let them do with it what accords with their profession. If they deviate backward from their profession, let them be judged unworthy reprobates of ecclesiastical honor.”

Now, since this chapter concerns those who are ordained possessing nothing, and are indeed persons possessing nothing—persons whom either birth or choice has made poor—it is more properly understood to concern those whom choice or holy profession has made poor than those whom necessity or birth has placed among those possessing nothing, while they have no profession at all of possessing nothing. For it commands that they do nothing concerning property coming to them contrary to their profession; this can scarcely be applied to persons having no profession of holiness.

The praiseworthy profession of a presbyter is summarized by the prudent man Prosper in these words:

> [Col. 1383A] “A priest entrusted with the care of stewardship receives from the people, not merely without greed but with the commendation of devotion, things to be distributed; and he faithfully distributes what he has received. He has either left all that was his or joined it to the Church’s goods, and has placed himself among the number of the poor out of love for poverty, so that from the same source from which he supplies the poor, he himself lives as a voluntary poor man.”

Therefore, to a priest of this kind, since he is in a good profession, the aforementioned chapter rightly commands that he not deviate backward from his profession. But how that same command can at all be applied to a cleric wholly irregular does not appear to me, since he has no profession from which he may be warned not to deviate. But let it be granted that in that chapter and in certain others ministers of the altar are permitted to have private property. Yet neither in those nor in any other authoritative chapters is the sacrilegious presumption excused by which, contrary to the prohibition of Pope and martyr Urban, common life is hindered throughout the mother churches. To it the resources of ecclesiastical property are principally due, so that they may be distributed by it to lovers of poverty, to persons like Lazarus, to guests, or—if we make a very great concession—to infirm clerics living tolerably outside holy orders and rendering service to the Church according to their measure, at least in psalmody.

**SECULAR CLERIC.** Do we not seem excused by the fact that the Fathers judged us tolerable? In certain councils they established a law concerning the private estate of a deceased presbyter, namely how it ought to be divided between the bishop, the heirs, and the Church itself.

[Col. 1383D] **REGULAR CLERIC.** Those Fathers whom you mention acted prudently, moderating an illness which they could not utterly remove. This was also perceived by those who ordered the private property of a bishop to be kept distinct from Church property. For it happened that, when bishops or presbyters died, the Church was harassed by heirs—and, more shamefully still, by the carnal masters of presbyters—when disputes arose about their private property. Those who made laws concerning private estates intended to prevent this evil: namely, to establish how they were to be kept distinct from ecclesiastical goods and how they were to be divided at the deaths of presbyters.

Set before your eyes a presbyter whose holy profession is that described above in Prosper’s words. Does he need this arrangement or remedy to restrain heirs from the malady of sacrilege or acquisitiveness?

[Col. 1384A] **SECULAR CLERIC.** I know that the things I defend do not suit the perfect. But my aim is this: that we ministers of the altar may not be condemned because we have private possessions, which those men also had for whom the aforementioned laws were established, so that they might know under what safeguards they ought to hold their own property together with Church property.

**REGULAR CLERIC.** My principal purpose is to speak about Church property, which has been offered for a certain holy profession and assigned by the Fathers; whoever diverts property from it commits sacrilege. But inherited possessions or possessions acquired from elsewhere, which have never been offered for holy uses, may be held as private property without sacrilege. Yet presbyters and deacons who possess them are owed nothing from the Church’s sacred property. They possess their own goods without sin, Prosper testifying, if they leave to the steward, for distribution to those possessing nothing, those things which come to them from the Church.

This, however, is said concerning those not bound by a vow of common life. Although for presbyters and deacons, even those outside a vow, the indulgence which Prosper’s authority grants to the weak—of retaining their own goods without Church property—scarcely or not at all befits them. For those who serve the altar must altogether be such, as Saint Hilary, Saint Ambrose, and Blessed Jerome testify—whose sayings, being known to many, I omit for brevity’s sake—that their portion may be in the land of the living and that they possess nothing of their own in this land of the dying. Rather, they must be free from the yoke of secular powers.

[Col. 1384C] As Blessed Augustine testifies, no one among them can be such who has occasion to say, “my servant, my estate, my property,” because private possessions are held by human law, which is subject to the powers of this world; but by divine law, “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness.” Nor can anyone say by this law, “my land, my servant.” Hence one who refuses to be freed from possession of private property is not free from the snares of the world; and such a man is rightly excluded, under apostolic rigor, from the ministry of the holy altar, as still secular and entangled in worldly snares.

Lest I seem to prophesy from my own heart, let Pope and martyr Antherus speak on this point in his decretal:

> “Those who possess God as their inheritance ought to serve God without any impediment of the world, so that they may say: ‘The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.’”

From these considerations it is plain that private property is unlawful for ministers of the sacred altar, although the aforesaid Council of Carthage appears to indulge it. And indeed it is so. For the Fathers allowed private possessions because of hardness of heart—possessions which they could not wholly take from those hard-hearted men—and they even established laws by which those men might possess them, not wholly lawfully, but with less trouble to others and less damage.

**SECULAR CLERIC.** I am glad that my property is permitted to me in some fashion, for I relinquish it unwillingly.

**REGULAR CLERIC.** Let your own possessions be permitted you. But since you do not live outside a community or outside holy orders, like those to whom Blessed Gregory in England permitted not only stipends to be provided externally but also marriages, who has permitted you, or could permit you, to receive ecclesiastical stipends—strictly forbidden to you—when you neither serve in apostolic warfare nor minister to those who do so?

[Col. 1385A] **SECULAR CLERIC.** Where, I ask, are ecclesiastical goods forbidden to me? Where do they appear assigned solely to those living apostolically?

REGUL. Read, as I said, the decrees of Pope Urban, martyr, who among other things says: “The very possessions of the individual parishes were, and are still, and must always be in future times, under the authority of the bishops, who hold the place of the apostles. From them bishops and their faithful stewards [Col. 1385B] ought to provide all necessities, as best they can, for all who are willing to live the common life, so that no one among them may be found needy. For these possessions are called the offerings of the faithful, because they are offered to the Lord. Therefore they ought not to be diverted to uses other than ecclesiastical uses and those of the aforesaid brethren or of the needy, because they are vows of the faithful, the price of sins, and have been entrusted to the Lord for accomplishing the aforesaid work. But if anyone—God forbid!—acts otherwise, let him beware lest he receive the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira and become guilty of sacrilege, like those who defrauded the proceeds of the aforesaid possessions.” And shortly afterward: “These things, brothers,” he says, “are greatly to be feared and guarded against, because the property of the Church [Col. 1385C] must be faithfully administered with utmost fear, not as private property but as common property offered to the Lord, and for no uses other than those aforesaid; lest those who remove it from the purposes for which it was entrusted incur the guilt of sacrilege and—what is worse—become anathema maranatha. Though they may not fall dead in body as Ananias and Sapphira did, yet in soul—which is superior to the body—they may fall dead and estranged from the fellowship of the faithful, and plunge into the abyss of the deep pit.” After inserting a few words, he concludes the ruling: “Therefore, if anyone should arise in present or future times and strive to tear this away, let him be struck by the condemnation already stated.”

SAECUL. What you say is harsh.

REGUL. It is harsh only to the hard.

[Col. 1385D] SAECUL. True. Yet it would be good if we who are so hard were drawn by gentler means—which Pope Urban himself seems to have considered when he says: “If anyone should arise in present or future times and strive to tear this away, let him be struck by the condemnation already stated.” For before us there were those who strove to tear this away, namely, the nurseries of apostolic life. We admit that they were condemned, while we ourselves are mercifully exempted from condemnation, since we do not strive to tear this away. For, those having already been uprooted before us, another planting now seems to flourish, in which there are many worthy persons who, if apostolic life now existed in their churches, would not strive to uproot it. I believe that the curse promulgated through Pope Urban does not touch these persons, because they are not themselves destroyers of apostolic life or the first alienators of ecclesiastical [Col. 1386A] property. Indeed, our churches, established in this manner long after Pope Urban, are believed to have been so founded by their founders that they never assigned their property to those living apostolically. Moreover, St. Udalric, bishop of Augsburg, an eminent man in Christ, is not recorded as having required his canons to relinquish private possessions and live apostolically. In some of his sayings it is also found that he was very indulgent toward the frailty of clerics; nevertheless, he is regarded as a saint in the Church, though removed from apostolic life.

REGUL. No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid. For in the above-mentioned decree of Urban you find that bishops hold the place of the apostles; and it follows that they are indebted to imitate [Col. 1386B] their manner of life. Otherwise they will hear: “Friends, how did you enter here, into the place of those whose example you have not imitated?” Whether they themselves were destroyers of apostolic life, or came to the episcopate and held the apostles’ place after that life had already been uprooted and another custom introduced, Christ alone was to be followed and retained as the foundation.

For when He says, “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John XII, 26)—that is, let whoever among bishops, priests, and deacons serves Him at the holy altar imitate Him—if he likewise imitates Him in renouncing his own possessions and himself, in freedom from private property and in common life, he is like a man building a house who digs deep and lays the foundation upon rock. But those who presume to appear either [Col. 1386C] in the place of the apostles, as bishops; or in the place of the seventy-two disciples, as priests; or in the place of the seven deacons, as the other ministers of the altar, while refusing to live the life which those lived who simply and without bitterness received Christ’s command, “Whoever serves me, let him follow me”—such persons, in all their offices and ministries, are like a man building upon sand, because they have no rule of life founded in Christ.

Therefore you spoke most improperly in saying that another planting now flourishes in which apostolic life is not lived. Those who plant something other than what Christ planted, or follow what others planted, should more rightly be said to stink than to flourish. Among these are the persons [Col. 1386D] whom you call worthy, perhaps because they are generous toward the poor and preserve chastity. They are so much the more rejected by God insofar as they sustain, like pillars, the walls of Babylon which are eventually to fall. If they gave alms in order that God might change their wicked, foundationless manner of life, grant them as the foundation of their life the rule of apostolic conduct like a rock, and prevent them from defending a clerical life contrary to apostolic institutions, it might happen either that they themselves would change and the walls of Babylon which they uphold would fall; or, if they died in this desire, they would not lose through the onset of death the fruit of the way of life that their will desired.

For we read of certain bishops who observed apostolic perfection in themselves, so far as they could, but could not establish common life among the clergy entrusted to them according to the arrangement of Blessed Gregory addressed to Augustine, bishop of the English. Yet they are considered saints, because they are not recorded either to have lived a life contrary to that of the apostles, so far as lay in them, [Col. 1387A] or to have defended it in others; rather, they are believed to have aspired with all affection to establish it among their clergy. Some, however, perversely and falsely charge St. Udalric with having written to Pope Nicholas in defense of the marriages of priests and other ministers of God, lest continence become an occasion for fornication. This is proved utterly false by the fact that in his time no one named Nicholas presided over the apostolic see.

Those like this holy man, living holily in themselves and not maintaining the disordered life of others, but rather destroying it as far as possible, at least by apostolic examples, may be called flourishing: they have a flourishing desire to be released from those living disorderly and to be with Christ in apostolic and holy conduct. We read that St. Udalric desired this: having resigned his episcopate, he wished to live apostolic life among monks, because at that time he could scarcely find it among the clergy. But the marriage bond already contracted—of which the Apostle says, “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release” (1 Cor. VII, 27)—compelled him to remain with his wife, however bleary-eyed she might be. But those whom you say now flourish among the disorderly desire to cling to the very disorderly themselves—not like [Col. 1387C] St. Udalric, or St. Wolfgang, or any saint to whom Leah was laid beside him by night; and, to go farther back, not like Jacob, who, while possessing Leah, was more deeply moved by love for Rachel. Rather, they are like Reuben who, though firstborn and noble, nevertheless defiled his birthright and nobility because, himself free, he joined himself to a slave-woman and defiled his father’s bed.

SAECUL. I do not know where this digression of yours is tending. I defended those who live well in the company of the wicked, while you try to show them defiled by I know not what association with a slave-woman.

REGUL. It is indeed so. For apostolic life is that free woman, to whom Christ was joined when He assumed the form of a servant. This woman, beautiful in contemplatives and those at leisure, bore bleary-eyed children to God among the active; for she is the one who converted the whole world. But when she failed among the clergy, among whom she had been more fruitful than among monks, a slave-woman’s life entered in. In it, although many good children were born through those who baptized and preached lawfully and were enrolled for the inheritance, she herself is nevertheless rejected as a slave-woman. Everyone who willingly clings to her and is defiled by her companionship is rejected—especially in such a Church as is likened to the bed of God the Father, indeed is called God’s bed or couch, as is an episcopal or baptismal church, in which a generation of those who seek God rather than themselves ought to be begotten and nourished.

For this is what Jacob punished most severely in his son Reuben: that he slept with Bilhah on [Col. 1388A] his father’s bed. For among other things the holy patriarch said: “Reuben, you are the beginning of my sorrow; you have been poured out like water; do not increase, because you ascended your father’s bed and defiled his couch” (Gen. XLIX, 3–4). Observe: he censures not so much the shameful act as the fact that it occurred in a place where it was least fitting for it to occur. Therefore you also, who as it were sleep with a slave-woman, having neither share nor lot with the free woman, seek churches—or rather synagogues—in which neither baptism nor preaching ought to take place, lest that curse of God come upon you which condemns those like your Reuben. For all these things, as the Apostle testifies, happened figuratively and were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. X, 11). Seek leaders other than bishops. For since these, as Pope Urban affirms, hold the place of the apostles and ought to imitate their examples, they cannot agree with you unless they wish to apostatize together with you.

SAECUL. How do you separate us from the mother churches, when you said above that Blessed Gregory granted this: that such persons should be tolerated in the churches of the English—certainly baptismal churches, indeed episcopal churches—and maintained from the Church’s property?

REGUL. When you considered this, ought you not also to have noticed that in the same Church he permitted no one to minister at the altar, baptize, or preach except one living the apostolic and common life? Thus no servile man might lie in God the Father’s bed, and a corrupt life corrupt God’s ministers, if the apostolic rule did not [Col. 1388C] keep them outside. Therefore, as I said, seek for yourselves other churches, built apart from God; seek other ecclesiastical revenues. For that decretal ruling of the aforesaid Pope Urban and martyr, strengthened by the writer’s blood as by the death of a testator, forbade under threat of anathema not only the possessions then held by the mother churches, but also whatever they would thereafter possess and will possess in future times—the offerings of the faithful.

If some of you find consolation in being continent and giving alms, examine whether you are continent and give alms for this reason: that, being ministers of the altar and sustained from the goods of the Church, [Col. 1388D] you may be freed from the dissolute life in which you are and strengthened in apostolic life, to which alone the ministry of the altar and ecclesiastical maintenance are due. For those who are married outwardly, free from both the ministry of the altar and the vow of common life, receive support from it as free persons from those living apostolically, provided that according to the teaching of St. Gregory they are recognized as serving God under such persons; just as servants of churches receive it. If they received it from persons other than those living apostolically and served those living dissolutely, they could not safely receive their daily maintenance as owed to that service—if indeed they could in any way avoid it and did not wish to oppose evildoers and withdraw their own service from them.

But you, all the lesser with the greater, ministers of the altar with the juniors—to say nothing of the things done in secret which it is shameful even to mention—are so united in defending that life of yours that I am compelled to fear for you lest the divine description spoken to blessed Job be applied to you: the scales of Leviathan are like cast shields, pressing one another so closely that not even a breath can pass between them. Thus, if you who appear holier in that life of false and real death fast, give alms, and chant psalms for the purpose not of being freed from that life but of being saved within it, you strive to corrupt the Judge, that He may spare not the human being but the human being’s fault. This is wholly impossible; yet He has cause to condemn you even for this, because, though in vain, you wished to corrupt Him.

[Col. 1389B] SAECUL. You have touched us harshly in assigning us, as it were, to the scales on Leviathan’s body.

REGUL. Truly, to say nothing of you, whose conscience I do not behold, I would be greatly relieved to cast the hardest and sharpest weapons in speech and writing against that Leviathan, except that, as the Lord testifies concerning blessed Job, the stones of the sling have become straw to him.

SAECUL. What stones? And whose sling?

REGUL. Have I not already shown that your way of life is forbidden under anathema in the mother churches? What, then, is the *anathema maranatha* hurled by the martyr Urban in the aforesaid ruling, except a hard stone in the sling by which, when the Lord comes, the height now exalting itself against the knowledge of Christ will finally be cast down? But many now mock this sling with the Philistine Goliath: they dare rashly to commit not only the acts forbidden under anathema in Urban’s aforesaid ruling, but also other acts so prohibited. To them may be applied what is said in the Apocalypse concerning the beast that has the wound of a sword and lived (Rev. XIII, 14). For one who despises an anathema invoked against himself has the wound of the sword and lives by his own judgment, because he despises it as though it were nothing. In the case of such persons we must fear lest they belong to the body of that beast whose mortal wound is said to have been healed, when it is said to be healed not truly but falsely.

SAECUL. I agreed with you, according to the tenor of Urban’s ruling, concerning the first destroyers of that life: that they were endangered under anathema. But do you wish to stigmatize all of us who follow them?

REGUL. If the first Urban seems to have said too little, Urban II, in his Decretals, says: “Whoever bestows or obtains ecclesiastical goods not for the purpose for which they were instituted but for private gain, whether by the gift of speech, of undue service, or of money, is a simoniac. For Simon’s chief intention was mere greed for money—that is, idolatry, as the Apostle says: ‘greed, which is the service of idols.’” Thus the old and new Urban agree: the former affirms that ecclesiastical property was instituted for common life; the latter shows that anyone who diverts it to private gain is a simoniac and idolater, whether by the gift of speech—which consists [Col. 1390A] in rashly presuming to assume offices—or by the gift of undue service, which occurs in carrying out a ministry that ought to be rendered by persons of a higher profession; or by money, which is the plainly visible form of simony to all.

SAECUL. It is remarkable that you try to establish that persons who alienate ecclesiastical property from the purposes for which it was instituted by the aforesaid kinds of gifts fall into the contagion of idolatry or simony. Yet we were not the first alienators, which perhaps renders us exempt from this ruling.

REGUL. Let Pope Lucius, martyr, answer you—not I. In chapter 7, among other thunderous words concerning robbers, defrauders, alienators of ecclesiastical property, and those consenting to them, he says: “Whoever takes away, defrauds, or plunders the money of Christ and of the Church shall be accounted a murderer in the sight of the just Judge. Thus Judas also, who defrauded the money which, by the Savior’s command, was distributed for the uses of the Church—that is, to the poor whom the Church ought to feed, since bishops hold the Savior’s place—became not merely a thief but a thief and sacrilegious person. The decrees of prophets, apostles, their successors, and all the Catholic Fathers forbid these acts and judge such presumptions to be sacrileges. Following their examples, by apostolic authority we drive from the thresholds of holy mother Church, anathematize, condemn, and judge sacrilegious all such presumptuous persons, robbers of the Church, and alienators of her resources. And likewise [Col. 1390C] all those consenting to them: for not only those who act are judged guilty, but also those who consent to those acting. The same punishment encompasses both agents and those consenting.”

See, brother: you congratulated yourself that you had not been the first to alienate Church property from the use of apostolic life, to which the martyr and Pope Urban declares it assigned. Yet you have not heard how his fellow bishop and fellow soldier, Pope and martyr Lucius, shows that those consenting with the actors are involved in the same judgment.

SAECUL. Although we possess Church property alienated from apostolic life, we do not alienate it from the Church, because we serve, after a fashion, that same Church whose property it is which we possess. Therefore, I hope, we shall escape the anathema pronounced by Pope Lucius against the aforesaid robbers, defrauders, and alienators.

REGUL. Judas also served after a fashion; yet Lucius in the chapter cited judged him a sacrilegious thief, because he diverted to other uses money which by the Savior’s command was to be distributed to the poor. So you too, though you serve the Church after a fashion, incur the same ruling because you consume while possessing what is owed to those who lack it.

SAECUL. How many among us are so needy that what they receive from the Church they serve does not suffice for them at all! Do they also lie under the aforementioned anathema?

REGUL. If they do not obtain such support by an undue service rendered, as you have above seen distinguished, they may live from the property of churches—not because they are clerics living in that manner, but because they are poor.

SAECUL. Never before now have I heard it asserted that those doing something forbidden under anathema immediately lie under anathema. I believe they have deserved anathema; but unless bishops have named them through judicial procedure, I do not think they are wounded by the sword of anathema.

REGUL. This is what I complained of above: that the stones of the sling have become straw, because the word believed more penetrating than any two-edged sword is thought to be weakened by the silence of modern bishops, while those now in Christ’s presence cry out.

SAECUL. You must show certain authority on [Col. 1391B] this matter, if you wish me to assent.

REGUL. Recall the ancient history: after Jericho was destroyed under Joshua’s leadership, Achan son of Carmi presumed to take from what was under anathema. Yet Joshua was not compelled to repeat the sentence of anathema; rather, he was to exact the anathema already incurred. For the Lord said to him: “Israel has sinned and transgressed my covenant; Israel will not be able to stand before its enemies, but will flee from them, because it is defiled by the anathema. I will no longer be with you unless you destroy him who is guilty of this crime” (Josh. VII, 11–12). See: the person who appropriated what was forbidden under anathema is declared by divine authority not to require a new anathema after the deed, but to have been anathematized in the very act; and at Joshua’s command he is stoned by all the people.

SAECUL. Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a man who brings forth from his treasure things new and old. You have brought forth old things; produce, if you have it, something from the Fathers of the New Testament concerning this ruling.

REGUL. Let it be done. Gregory I, in his letter to the patrician Theotista, says among other things: “If there are any who say that a person compelled by necessity is not bound by the bond of anathema if he presumes to act against things forbidden under anathema, they themselves bear witness against themselves that they are not Christians. For they think by empty efforts to dissolve the bonds of the Church; and therefore they do not consider the holy Church’s absolution, which it grants to the faithful, to be real, if they do not judge its bonds to be effective. There is no need to argue at length against them, because they are utterly to be despised and anathematized; and from the very source by which they think to deceive the truth, they are truly bound in their sins. Therefore, if any under the Christian name dare either to preach this or silently hold it within themselves, beyond doubt I, all Catholic bishops, and the whole Church anathematize them, because they think and speak things contrary to truth.”

SAECUL. According to these words, you appear to deprive modern bishops of judicial power, if those whom the ancient Fathers anathematize are already judged and anathematized.

[Col. 1392A] REGUL. As the Apostle testifies, the deeds of some people are manifest beforehand, going before to judgment; those of others follow afterward. Therefore those deeds which nonetheless require a manifest judgment ought to be judged by bishops, because they precede judgment—that is, because they have not yet been judged but still await judgment. But things that are both manifest and follow a judgment already regularly rendered and proclaimed are reckoned among those already judged, whether modern bishops condemn them or overlook them.

SAECUL. Give an example of what you mean.

REGUL. I shall. In Paradise Eve corrupted her husband by evil persuasion, and the husband sinned by eating the forbidden tree. Of these two faults, one preceded judgment and the other followed it. For eating the forbidden tree had been condemned beforehand, when the Lord said: “On whatever day you eat, you shall die” (Gen. III, 5). But the woman’s seduction through evil persuasion was judged and punished not before the deed but after it: namely, by the multiplication of her pains and conceptions, and by her hearing, “In pain you shall bear children” (ibid., 16).

Thus the fault of forbidden eating, prohibited under a grave anathema—that is, under a grave death of the soul—was punished in the very act. For both their souls were dead in sin as soon as they presumed to take the fruit of the tree forbidden under threat of death. Nor did God, the just Judge, take care to repeat this condemnation concerning the death of their souls. Rather, He struck with a judicial sentence the other faults: the fault of the seducer and the fault of the one obeying the seducer more than God’s voice. He assigned pains to the woman in place of glory and thorns to the man in place of pleasant fruit.

But that same serpent who then said, “You shall not die at all” (ibid., 4), when God had said, “You shall die,” is plainly the same ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan. He now strives to deceive the whole world by persuading carnal people to despise the condemnation already pronounced concerning certain crimes. Their acts do not precede but follow judgment; yet they are secure unless a new judgment is made and what is acknowledged to have been condemned and anathematized is condemned anew, or assigned some milder sentence and milder penalty.

[Col. 1392D] SAECUL. I do not understand what you now say concerning the form of a milder punishment, unless you append an example to make it clear.

REGUL. I shall do as you ask, though I do not know whether you ask these things faithfully or faithlessly. For similar matters have previously been asked me with much ill will, so that I might be trapped in speech and unjustly condemned by persons justly condemned. Still, I shall say what I have said before.

Pope Alexander II, holding at Constantinople a synod of more than one hundred bishops, said among other things: “We command by injunction that no one hear the Mass of a priest whom he certainly knows to have a concubine or a woman introduced into his household; for the holy synod has long ago deprived such a priest or deacon of office.” Armed with this authority, when a certain canon, questioned about this matter, said that clerics manifestly living incontinently were not still to be deprived of office but had already been deprived, the defenders of such people—perhaps they themselves were such, that is, incontinent—gnashed their teeth at him, saying that he was to be counted among heretics because he removed the bishops’ authority.

But after he perceived that they would not tolerate that milder mode of condemnation, by which office is forbidden, he added the greater one, by which Gregory VII, truly filled with the sevenfold Spirit, also forbade them entry into church, saying: “If any priests, deacons, or subdeacons lie in the crime of fornication, we forbid them, on the part of Almighty God and by the authority of St. Peter, entry into church until they repent and amend. But if any prefer to persevere in their sin, let none of you presume to receive their office, because their blessing is turned into a curse and their prayer into sin, as the Lord testifies through the prophet: ‘I will curse your blessings’ (Mal. II, 2). Whoever refuses to obey this most salutary command incurs the sin of idolatry, as Samuel testifies and Blessed Gregory teaches: ‘To disobey is the sin of divination, and to refuse assent is the crime of idolatry.’ Therefore whoever, while claiming to be Christian, despises obedience to the apostolic see incurs the sin of paganism.”

SAECUL. What are you driving at by all this?

REGUL. Clearly, what I have said resolves your question [Col. 1393C] about the lesser form of condemnation, which I could not show without comparing it with the greater. For fornicating ministers of the altar, if after committing fornication they do not presume to exercise their offices, will be under the lesser condemnation, namely deprivation of offices only. But if they presume to act contrary to the prohibition of the apostolic see, both they and those who knowingly hear their forbidden—indeed excommunicated—offices incur the sin of paganism.

SAECUL. And this is an unheard-of novelty: you say that their offices are excommunicated. Where, I ask, was this excommunication made, or at least where were they forbidden under excommunication?

REGUL. Ask Pope Alexander and Pope Nicholas, whose ruling is nearly identical and has this tenor: “Let no one hear the Mass of a priest whom he certainly knows to have a concubine or a woman introduced into his household.” Hence the holy synod also established this from the outset under excommunication, saying: “Whoever among priests, deacons, or subdeacons, after the ordinance of most holy Pope Leo of blessed memory concerning clerical chastity, and so forth.” See: these two Roman pontiffs testify that it was established under excommunication that incontinent persons should not celebrate the office forbidden to them. Ask them about this excommunication; for me, what Pope Gregory said above is enough, where he shows their offices to render one pagan.

SAECUL. What do you say to those decrees of Pope Nicholas given in answer to Bulgarian inquiries, which contain among other things: “It is not for you, who are laypeople, either to judge priests or investigate anything concerning their lives; whatever the matter may be must be reserved for the judgment of bishops.” And shortly afterward: “Receive Christ’s mysteries fearlessly from every priest, for all things are purified in faith.” Pope Nicholas said this, as the answers themselves show, to persons asking not only about fornicating priests but also adulterous ones, indicating that their offices ought to be heard until a just sentence is pronounced against them by their bishops.

REGUL. I know, brother, that these chapters are found, but I do not see Catholics obeying them.

SAECUL. Catholics do not obey them now, but formerly they did.

REGUL. Certainly, brother, neither now nor formerly were fornicators and adulterers acceptable to persons of sound mind; and they were reprehensible even then, when they had not yet been removed by Gregory VII. Hence it is permissible to suppose that, if this command concerning hearing the office of fornicators was issued by the later Nicholas, it was a milder initial measure, dealing with them in order that they might correct themselves. Once they proved incorrigible, he himself corrected his position when in a synod he forbade them their offices. Therefore, according to the rules of the canons, the more authoritative ruling must be followed; or else one must hold that in that synod the bishops’ judgment itself was made, after which their forbidden office is no longer to be heard. But if that command was issued by the earlier Nicholas, it was rightly corrected by successors because it conflicted with stronger enactments. Therefore, obeying many authorities rather than one and, among others, hearing Gregory VII as though a trumpet, I care no more for their Masses than if they were sung by a pagan.

SAECUL. Beware lest you injure the sacraments, which do not lose their force even when celebrated by a heretic. But these persons have not yet been condemned as heretics, although in fact they are close to the heresiarch Nicholas.

REGUL. One thing remains to be proved: namely, that the sacraments of heretics celebrated outside the Church, although whole as regards sacramental form—as an amputated hand is sometimes whole—are nevertheless as devoid of the power of the Holy Spirit as an amputated hand is devoid of human sensation and spirit. It must also be shown that the name of heresy has sometimes been branded upon both Nicolaitans and simoniacs who, hardened in adherence to their erroneous sect, knowingly disobey the synodal definitions of the holy Fathers and their decretal enactments, and with the zeal and will of apostate obstinacy resist them.

I make this qualification carefully, lest anyone think that I ascribe heresy to one who fell in such a way that both before the fall and afterward he maintained a purpose of continence. Thus Peter, both before and after the fall of his denial, maintained the purpose never to deny Christ; therefore we say that Peter fell, and we do not close to those who have fallen the easy way of recovering salvation. But Judas, who sought an opportunity to betray Jesus, is not called one who fell, because he did not have the purpose in his mind of avoiding sin; rather, as I said, he sought an opportunity to do it. Therefore Peter’s restoration does not suit those who before and after fornication are outside the purpose of living holily and chastely. Indeed, like Judas they seek an opportunity to practice their iniquity. For this purpose they love private dwellings and abhor cloisters, because private houses offer opportunity for their desired wickedness.

Concerning such persons, Bruno, bishop of Segni, did not hesitate to say among other things in the synod of Pope Paschal of blessed memory: “Let us clergy and monks, holding to the norm of the primitive Church, follow Christ, the apostles, and the holy Fathers, and condemn all simoniacs with them by perpetual anathema. Let us imitate Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, and excommunicate the impious Nicholas with all his followers, lest at the coming of the Judge we be accused of having consented to their error through silence.” See how this Catholic bishop harshly marked Nicholas and his followers—that is, clerics seeking or loving opportunity for fornication—and declared that both these and simoniacs must be condemned. No one in so great a synod rejected his ruling as excessively severe.

SAECUL. Although this good man treated Nicholas’s followers with the same ruling as the followers of Simon Magus, he nevertheless did not call them heretical Nicolaitans. Therefore, if you wish to satisfy me, you must introduce someone of greater authority [Col. 1395C] who, speaking of these people, names them openly Nicolaitans or heretics. Otherwise you will be blamed for having first imposed this upon them most unjustly, since they neither teach nor defend, with Nicholas, that marriage ought to be common to clerics or to themselves.

REGUL. I shall do as you ask, since you press far too insistently. Hear, then, what Pope Nicholas says: “Pope Nicholas, to all Christ’s faithful. In the year 1059 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the first of our pontificate, the twelfth indiction, in the city of Rome, in the church of the Savior called Constantinian [*Constantiana*, so written], with holy Fathers—namely, one hundred and thirteen bishops, besides abbots, clerics, and laypeople—we canonically celebrated, God favoring us, a holy synod concerning the state of holy Church for the common [Col. 1395D] benefit. Among other things, concerning the heresy of the Nicolaitans—that is, married priests, deacons, and all persons established in the clergy—the whole council established and confirmed this: ‘Whoever is a priest, deacon, subdeacon,’ etc.” Let it suffice to have quoted from Pope Nicholas only this much, in which, as you have heard, the heresy of the Nicolaitans is ascribed to the same persons as to whom we ascribe it.

SAECUL. He speaks only of married priests where he uses that name, saying: “Concerning the heresy of the Nicolaitans, that is, concerning married priests.” Therefore clerical concubinage does not seem to be addressed there.

REGUL. You compel me to set down the whole chapter, which [Col. 1396A], in my concern for brevity, I had wished to omit. “Whoever,” he says, “priest, deacon, or subdeacon, after the decree concerning clerical chastity issued by my predecessor of blessed memory, the most holy Pope Leo, has openly taken a concubine, or has not dismissed one already taken, by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul we command and absolutely forbid him to celebrate Mass, proclaim the Gospel, read the Epistle at Mass, remain in the sanctuary for the divine offices with those who have obeyed the aforesaid decree, or receive any share from the Church, until, God being the author, a sentence concerning such persons proceeds from us.” And, so that you may recognize that Pope Nicholas cut off not merely the crime of incontinence, whose [Col. 1396B] entry he was also attempting to block, hear what follows, which enjoins the apostolic life: “And by commanding,” he says, “we decree that those of the aforesaid orders who, obedient to the statutes of our same predecessor concerning the clergy, have observed these things, should live together, eat together, and sleep together near the churches to which they were ordained, as is fitting for religious clerics.”

SAECUL. Might they not live, eat, and sleep together, while still retaining their own houses and their own money, without violating this command?

REGUL. Had the pope intended that, he would not have added the command to live, eat, and sleep together “as is fitting for religious clerics.” For it is foreign to the religious life to serve two masters in such a way [Col. 1396C] that a cleric is maintained in the cloister while money, or a little sum of money from the mammon of iniquity, is kept at home. But we must return to the name Nicolaitans, which the ruling of the Roman pontiff shows to belong to ministers of the altar who love wives no less than to those who love concubines.

SAECUL. What if they have neither concubines nor wives, yet do not practice continence? Do they also in this way belong to the lot of Nicholas the fornicator, who is said to have loved his wife and to have taught that wives, like other things, ought to be held in common by those living apostolically?

REGUL. Observe carefully whom I excepted above, where I distinguished some as fallen with Peter and others as lost with Judas, according to their respective disposition and intention. [Col. 1396D] Consider also this: those who sin with Peter against their own intention, through an incidental and unlooked-for occasion, atone for their faults with bitter tears and associate themselves with that life in which they know that Peter, after repenting, was saved. They abandon the sect of those who do not live apostolically, in which they will not be able, by sure proofs, to show that any continent person has been saved. That fallen clerics ought to make atonement in regular monasteries and not afterward return to their former possessions is attested by the words of St. Gregory, who among other instructions commanded Peter the subdeacon as follows:

> “Concerning fallen priests, or anyone whatsoever of the clergy, we wish you to observe this: do not involve yourself in their property by any contamination; rather, seek out very poor regular monasteries which know how to live according to God, and hand over the fallen men to those monasteries; and let the property of those fallen men benefit the place in which they are handed over to perform penance.”

Therefore, for those who repent in such a way that, in accordance with Blessed Gregory’s command, they consent to hand over themselves and their possessions to monasteries of persons living apostolically, a great entrance to mercy stands open with Peter in repentance. But all who, apart from these exceptions, presume to minister—whether married, maintaining concubines, or defiled by the wandering habit of fornication—come to the lot of Nicholas. As I showed above, Gregory VII also deprived them of entrance into the Church until they make worthy penance, such as you have above from St. Gregory. Nor do we deal with others than those whom St. Gregory excludes, whose worthy penance Gregory I—of the same name, as I said—defines in writing to Peter the subdeacon. [Col. 1397B]

SAECUL. What you say might stand, if you could show even one sound-minded man of our own time who attributes the heresy of the Nicolaitans—which Pope Nicholas plainly assigns to married men and to keepers of concubines—to those whose life is such that no one who knows them is allowed to doubt their promiscuous lust, though they have neither wife nor concubine. They have neither because both the people specifically identify such women and Pope Nicholas specifically names them where he, almost alone and perhaps improperly, declares the Nicolaitan heresy to concern such persons.

REGUL. I show you one sound-minded man of our own time, who affirmed in writing what I also affirm: a Catholic man who agrees exceedingly well with Pope Nicholas—indeed, in defining that heresy, he supplies what seems to have been left untouched by others concerning the wandering defilers of wandering women.

SAECUL. Who is he?

REGUL. Rupert, abbot of Deutz [the manuscript reads *Tutiensis*], a man of holy memory and very distinguished among interpreters of Holy Scripture. At the request of the venerable Chuono, then abbot of Siegburg and now bishop of Regensburg, he expounded the Apocalypse. When he came to the passage in which the angel rebukes the Church of Pergamum because it has among it persons holding the teaching of the Nicolaitans, he says among other things:

> “They come forth adorned like the daughter of Midian, playing and walking with studied step in order to deceive Israel. This assuredly happens whenever men tender and soft, overflowing with vices and possessing no manly strength for constancy of life, after receiving honours, though obscure in their morals, desire to appear notable in the Church under Christ’s name. Do not men thus advanced hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans? For Clement relates that Nicholas, rebuked on account of jealousy concerning his most beautiful wife, answered that anyone who wished might take her as wife; and for this reason he taught unbelievers that the apostles permitted indiscriminate and common intercourse with women for all. Is not this teaching akin to the conduct of those who, unable to have lawful marriage because ecclesiastical laws forbid it, so that they may be holy and purified because they bear the vessels of the Lord, nevertheless remain incontinent—indeed, rush into something worse—changing their unions whenever they wish? Having no lawful bed, do they, while wandering thus, trust that they have broken no bond of marriage? He therefore says: ‘But I have a few things against you, because you have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam’ (Rev. 2:14). Immediately he adds: ‘So you also have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.’ Therefore he calls the fornications which Nicholas is reported to have introduced against ecclesiastical purity ‘the teaching of Balaam,’ and confirms that this is the scandal of the Church of God: to eat and to fornicate (ibid.).”

Does not Rupert’s statement—or rather, the definition given by the Holy Spirit in the Apocalypse that the teaching of the Nicolaitans is to eat and to fornicate—most rightly establish that what has also been confirmed by Roman pontiffs must be observed: namely, that men who consume ecclesiastical stipends, repeatedly forbidden to them and due only to the continent, while they themselves are lovers of pleasure rather than of God, must be avoided as persons rebellious against truth, lying in that teaching of the Nicolaitans—that is, in that scandal which the Spirit speaking to the Churches defines as consisting in eating and fornicating? For if they either ceased to fornicate and repented rightly, or did not consume ecclesiastical stipends, they would not be in that Nicolaitan teaching, which is: to eat and to fornicate. [Col. 1398B]

SAECUL. Truly, if they defended this very eating and fornicating, regarded it as just, urged that it ought to be practiced, and did it obstinately, they would without doubt be heretics. But now, because they do not defend that scandal as just, the Nicolaitan heresy is not properly attributed to them. For according to the definition of heresy by the Fathers, it is not a wicked deed but a wicked opinion obstinately defended that makes a heretic; and this can be confirmed by many testimonies of the Fathers.

REGUL. This is indeed held concerning all heresies except two: that of the Nicolaitans and that of the Simoniacs. For the Spirit speaking to the Churches in the Apocalypse reproved the Nicolaitans solely for eating and fornicating. But Peter, in condemning Simon, reproved his evil intention and judgment, saying: “May your money perish with you” (Acts 8:20), “because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money.” Here it is not the defence of an error that is censured, but the prior thought and will to sin itself, which the same Blessed Peter called “the gall of bitterness,” saying: “I see you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity” (ibid., v. 23). Similarly, where the eating and fornicating of those who were in the teaching of the fornicator Nicholas is rebuked, the defence of the deed is passed over in silence, and the matter concerns the wicked deed alone. And rightly so, assuredly: whether, as some maintain, they ate things sacrificed to idols and fornicated, or whether, while fornicating, they consumed things consecrated to God and intended for the use of the continent—things which Nicholas, himself a fornicator, also consumed, and of which he had been steward as one of the seven deacons—they are to be bound with him in one bundle for burning, unless regular aid is given them through the remedy of penance. [Col. 1399A]

SAECUL. If, as you maintain, the innumerable Nicolaitans and Simoniacs are all heretics, why were they not wholly and absolutely excommunicated by the ancient pontiffs of the Roman see, like the Arians and Sabellians?

REGUL. The sheer multitude of such persons alone compelled the postponement of that universal winnowing. But although, because the ruin of the multitude had to be avoided, they have long been tolerated and have not been forbidden social intercourse or greeting, the sacraments of the Simoniacs are nevertheless read to have been repudiated even by the ancient Fathers. As for those lying in fornication and, moreover, presuming to exercise ecclesiastical offices and enjoy benefices: Pope Nicholas, the first among Roman pontiffs, is found to have called such men, who eat and fornicate contrary to the prohibition, Nicolaitans. From that time their offices are publicly proclaimed to be avoided, like those of other heretics and like idolatry. Thus, although they themselves have not yet been excommunicated—that is, though social intercourse and greeting with them have not been forbidden—their offices have nevertheless been completely excommunicated and prohibited. This is not a simple prohibition, but one imposed under excommunication, as Pope Alexander testifies.

Therefore, where the offices and sacraments of Simoniacs and Nicolaitans are prohibited and excommunicated, and such persons are manifestly known, they are undoubtedly to be avoided, as the very severe decrees of Pope Nicholas and Gregory VII teach, lest we likewise be entangled by the excommunication inherent in the prohibited and excommunicated office. For, as Pope Alexander testifies, it was prohibited under excommunication; and, as Gregory VII testifies, it is likened to the sin of divination and idolatry. This lawful pontiff is truly believed to have been inflamed by that Spirit in which Moses, speaking against Dathan and Abiram, said to the children of Israel: “Depart from the tents of these wicked men, and touch nothing that belongs to them, lest you be swept away in their sins” (Num. 16:26). Did not this Gregory VII, speaking in the same Spirit, say—as we showed above—that those knowingly refusing obedience to the most salutary commands of the apostolic see, which plainly forbade the offices of incontinent men, incur the sin of paganism? [Col. 1399D]

SAECUL. This Gregory VII seems to us excessively harsh and hasty, in saying that they incur the sin of paganism, whereas we scarcely grant that they have deserved even to be rebuked according to the Gospel: first before one witness, then before two, then before the Church; so that, if they hear even this, they may be Christians, and only if they refuse to hear it may they then first be as heathen and tax collectors.

REGUL. This order of rebuke must be followed in concealed cases not yet judicially condemned. But where something is known to be forbidden under so terrible a prohibition that anyone knowingly presuming it has against him a judicial or decretal pronouncement, or a synodal decree, declaring that whoever does this or that is to be anathema or reckoned as a heathen and tax collector, then the person doing it and despising the known sentence thereby separates himself from the Church in the very act, so that he does not have the Holy Spirit, who is in the Church. This is according to what is written: “Animal men, separating themselves, not having the Spirit” (Jude 19).

Hence Gregory I, whose follower this seventh Gregory was, dealing with the ordainers of Maximus of Salona against a similar prohibition, asserted that they had not merely deserved but had already incurred excommunication. He wrote to Maximus in these terms:

> “An unheard-of crime is reported: after our prohibition—which was imposed under our excommunication and that of those who then ordained you—you are said to have been brought forth into public by military force, after priests and deacons had been beaten. For this reason, we cannot by any means call a consecration that which has been celebrated by excommunicated persons.”

And if you suppose that this seventh Gregory departed even in this respect from the footsteps of Gregory I, because he forbade fornicators the ministry of the altar, read and you will find that Gregory I forbade it them more strictly. This man deals with those lying in fornication; Gregory I decreed that even someone who had fallen after receiving sacred orders should lose his order. For in writing to Januarius of Cagliari, he says among other things:

> “Anyone who, after receiving sacred order, has fallen into the sin of the flesh is so to lose sacred order that he may no longer approach the ministry of the altar.” [Col. 1400C]

SAECUL. I understood this to mean that such a man, by reason of his merit, ought to be deposed and deserved to lose office—not that, being already deposed, he must lose it.

REGUL. You judge, according to your own understanding of the pontiffs’ words, that those whom they judge already deposed according to their understanding ought to be deposed. For Pope Martin, a vessel of the same Spirit as Gregory I and Gregory VII, says in his Decretals: “Whoever, after his ordination, has once fallen by a lapse shall thereafter already be deposed and shall be able to attain no rank of priesthood.” Likewise Pope Alexander II writes to Dominic, patriarch of Grado:

> “Let the impious be ashamed and plainly understand that, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, we exclude from the dignity of those same orders those established in the three ranks—presbyterate, diaconate, and subdiaconate—who have not put away their little women and have not lived chastely. We speak of manifest cases; but God is the knower and judge of secret ones.”

Do not those who, after these judgments, presume to exercise offices forbidden to them, trusting in the indolence of modern bishops, whose judgments they await and yet evade in a cause already judged—do not such persons, I ask, resisting the judgments of the Fathers, trampling the commands of the Roman see, fornicating with Nicholas, Ebion, and Paul of Samosata while still ministering at the altar, rightly count as their participants and accomplices? For the holy Church rejected Ebion, a heresiarch, with his followers, because in Christian times he introduced Jewish incontinence. Paul of Samosata, as ecclesiastical history relates, while he himself clung to shameful service from women so as to become less conspicuous, granted the same whirlpool of pleasure to his clerics; and among the other poisonous emissions of his vomit, he did not fear to assert that the enticements of intercourse with women were lawful for them. Therefore, because he became the author of such foulness, the Church deservedly condemned him with his followers. And those are proved to be his followers who are found persistent in his shamefulness. [Col. 1401A]

SAECUL. You have said enough—more than enough, in my view—about these wicked Catholics. Whether they are heretics or not should be reserved for the judgment of the Roman pontiff. Now fulfill your promise concerning the nullification of heretics’ sacraments.

REGUL. I desire to hear Pope Innocent’s judgment on this matter, and I am prepared to obey it. But before we discuss heretics’ sacraments, let us distinguish those sacraments themselves—or rather, let us show that they have already been distinguished before us. Pope Nicholas, zealously opposing those ordained simoniacally by Simoniacs, says very severely and very justly in his Decretals: “We decree that no mercy is to be shown to Simoniacs in preserving their rank.” Likewise: “Henceforth, if anyone permits himself to be consecrated by one whom he does not doubt to be a Simoniac, both consecrator and consecrated shall undergo an equal sentence of condemnation; both shall be deposed, perform penance, and remain deprived of their own rank.”

The same Nicholas, proceeding more leniently elsewhere, distinguishes three classes: some ordained simoniacally by Simoniacs; some ordained simoniacally by non-Simoniacs; and others ordained non-simoniacally by Simoniacs. He declares that the last class must be tolerated out of necessity. Why, unless a pure and simple conscience supports them, because they approached a Simoniac ordainer with a Catholic mind? In view of such a consideration Pope Leo, after declaring that those whom neither clergy elected, nor people requested, nor their own metropolitan ordained were by no means to be counted among bishops, added:

> “But if any clerics have been ordained by these pseudo-bishops in churches belonging to their proper bishops, and if their ordination was performed with the consent and judgment of those presiding, it may be held valid.”

Acacius also, though wholly excommunicated by Pope Felix and condemned even after death by Pope Gelasius, and though under great anathema and complete excommunication, had ordained certain persons. Pope Anastasius affirms that in these the sacraments themselves retained their efficacy. Writing to Emperor Anastasius, he says:

> “According to the custom of the Catholic Church, may your Serenity’s most sacred heart recognize that no share of injury arising from the name of Acacius touches any of those whom Acacius baptized, or whom he ordained as priests or levites according to the canons, lest perhaps the grace of the sacrament, bestowed even through an unjust man, appear weak.” [Col. 1402A]

SAECUL. You promised to make heretics’ sacraments void, yet these statements prove them to be firm and valid.

REGUL. I did not propose to void them, but to show empty those sacraments which were given and received by any anathematized heretics outside the unity of the Church. But since the dove eats nothing living, my simplicity in Christ aims to distinguish carefully, and to exempt from the nullification of sacraments, those whom Roman pontiffs also took care to exempt: namely, those ordained by heretics yet with a Catholic intention. These are the persons whom Pope Nicholas calls ordained “by Simoniacs, but not simoniacally.” His phrase “not simoniacally” means the same as “Catholically,” or “with Catholic intention.” These also are those whom Leo the Great receives with the integrity of their orders, though ordained by pseudo-bishops, because they were ordained under the judgment and consent of the presiding authorities to a definite title.

For as long as the presiding authorities and ecclesiastical judges—whether archpriests, priests, archdeacons, other cardinals, or cathedral prelates of any church—agree and judge that their bishop should be obeyed and regard him as Catholic, so long may anyone seeking ordination approach him with a Catholic mind, led by the consent and judgment of those presiding. His ordination too will be valid, provided that, being consecrated Catholicly, though not by a Catholic bishop, he adheres, so far as lies within him, to the title for which he is ordained; for it may happen that he is justly compelled to leave that place. Otherwise, Leo the Great says, the consecration is to be considered vain, since it is neither founded upon a place nor fortified by authority.

Was there not in this Roman pontiff the eye of the dove that eats nothing living—the eye of one unwilling to nullify anything done Catholicly? Although, in accordance with the meaning of his name, he was about to speak most powerfully like a lion and declare pseudo-bishops’ consecrations void, he first distinguished between dead and living, lest the lion’s teeth—that is, harsh definitions extending to the sacraments of pseudo-bishops—touch both alike. But because these pseudo-bishops, though pseudo-bishops, might perhaps not be heretics, we shall say later what this Leo roars against every kind of heretic, after we have distinguished, in the manner of the dove, every living thing from their dead sacraments. [Col. 1402D]

SAECUL. Proceed as you wish, provided that there is at last some end to your words. They are burdensome to me, and many judge them heretical unless they are supported by the strongest authority, showing how sacraments can be void when, according to St. Augustine’s teaching, they are everywhere whole and everywhere inviolable.

REGUL. I believe you can be satisfied. But first I shall carry out what I proposed. For should the righteous be destroyed with the wicked? Should those whom diversity of mind and intention has distinguished be swept together in one bundle for burning? By no means. To use the words of Pope Anastasius writing about Acacius: “That soul alone which sins shall by just judgment be liable in its own person, and pride always brings ruin upon itself, not upon others.” Hence he says: “When, though condemned, he claimed for himself the name of priest, the swelling of pride was fixed upon his own head, because the people who thirsted for God’s gift in the mysteries were not excluded.”

See with what dove-like compassion he distinguished Catholic hearts thirsting for God’s gift from the impiety of a wicked—indeed, heretical—baptizer or ordainer. Whoever notes that Pope Anastasius defends in the foregoing words those baptized and ordained by Acacius should also note the reason he gives for defending them. For, as we showed above from his words, he does not defend without qualification those ordained by Acacius, but those whom Acacius ordained according to the canons. We must understand those to have been ordained according to the canons who, while he baptized and ordained them, had a Catholic mind through the judgment and consent of the presiding authorities, as was defined above in Leo the Great’s words—“thirsting,” as Anastasius observes, “for God’s gift in the mysteries of God.”

Since this is so, we may say that, just as Pope Nicholas distinguishes that not all ordained by Simoniacs are ordained simoniacally, so not all sacraments celebrated by persons cut off are performed in separation. In a marvelous way, what excommunicated persons do outwardly is accomplished inwardly when the mind of the person seeking the blessing is Catholic and has not yet been fully instructed concerning the ordainer’s condemnation and separation. Therefore, Pope Anastasius affirms that the evil minister did no harm to such baptized and ordained persons by administering good things; and thus no laying-on of hands is recorded as having been done to any whom Acacius baptized or ordained when they were reconciled—indeed, they were never proved to have been outside.

But where what is performed in the sacraments is entirely outside, outside the life of the true vine, all is dry and all is dead, because neither the giver nor the receiver of the blessing bears a Catholic heart grafted into the true vine. Therefore neither can draw the life-giving Spirit into himself. Hence those baptized, so to speak, heretically by heretics are said not to possess the gift of the Holy Spirit unless they receive it in the Catholic Church: either through renouncing error; or, as Westerners observe, through laying-on of hands; or, as Easterners wish, through anointing with chrism; or certainly, as Blessed Gregory permitted in writing to the bishops of Ireland, through an open renunciation of error and a profession of faith. Therefore, whoever is alien in mind from the Church of God and nevertheless receives from a likewise alien heretic the sacrament of baptism or ordination—that is, the visible sign of invisible grace—does not possess the grace of which it is the sign. [Col. 1404A]

SAECUL. Explain to me first concerning baptism alone how you wish the gift of grace to be distinguished from the sacrament, while grace itself is distinguished as the reality of the sacrament; once this is settled, it will become apparent what should accordingly be held concerning the other sacraments.

REGUL. Triple immersion, performed in water with triple invocation, is a sign of Christ’s three-day burial; but the grace of that sign, or the reality of this sacrament, is what the Apostle describes when he says: “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27); for “you were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:4). This grace—by which Christ is put on and a new person is made from the old—is not given by a heretic who agrees with condemned error. But its sign, which is called and is a sacrament, is inviolable both outwardly and inwardly, and, so to speak, cannot be repeated. Yet the Holy Spirit is possessed only inwardly, through whom a person is made new from old and truly buried with Christ. [Col. 1404B]

SAECUL. What you say does not altogether displease me, for thus both the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament are given even through Simoniacs and other heretics to infants who are strangers to every error and consent to no schism—a point which I know some deny.

REGUL. We do not condemn with heretics anyone except, as I have defined, those who are alien from Catholicism together with them and mentally consent to their error. Therefore, if anyone denies the kingdom of Christ and the efficacy of the sacrament to infants baptized anywhere according to ecclesiastical rite, he disagrees with me—or rather, to say nothing of insignificant me, with Pope Anastasius, who affirms that the gift of baptism given even through such persons reaches its recipient uninjured.

SAECUL. Certainly, where Pope Anastasius says this, he does not specify that he is speaking of infants alone.

REGUL. Yet he certainly specifies that he speaks only of those who love Christ, where he says that the people thirsting for God’s gifts in the mysteries were not excluded from participation through the condemned priest. Allow me, therefore, to associate infants with those loving Christ, concerning whom I hear Christ say: “Allow the little children to come to me” (Matt. 19:14).

SAECUL. Although you call me secular, allow me now to say that I know a certain spiritual and Catholic man, a person greatly revered in the Church, raised this objection against you: What if the infant’s parents, approaching a heretic, think with the heretic against God? [Col. 1404D]

REGUL. We know that the parents’ good faith is beneficial. But we do not know whether their unbelief harms infants lawfully baptized unto eternal damnation, since the Church’s faith benefits the infants. By that faith it is believed that the gifts of the Holy Spirit accompany baptism celebrated anywhere according to ecclesiastical rite, except where a heretical wickedness occupying the heart excludes him—a wickedness not present in infants, since they cannot distinguish between right and left. Yet if they reach lawful age, they lose the grace received in baptism unless, abandoning and detesting heresy, they love the Catholic Church.

But for adults baptized outside, the statement of Blessed Augustine writing to Orosius applies: “Although the baptism of heretics—namely, those baptizing in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and that of the Church are one, nevertheless, because they are baptized outside the Church, they receive baptism not unto salvation but unto destruction, possessing indeed the form of the sacrament but denying its efficacy.” Let this be said of those who have the ability to deny or not deny the efficacy of the sacrament. For infants, who lack that ability, the same blessed man says elsewhere, writing to Boniface:

> “Do not be troubled because some persons offer little children to receive baptism, not in the faith that they may be regenerated by spiritual grace unto eternal life, but because they think that by this remedy the children may retain or recover bodily health. They are not, however, for that reason not regenerated there, because they are not offered by these persons with that intention.”

Elsewhere he says: “Although the faith consisting in the will of believers is not yet present in a little child, nevertheless the sacrament of that faith itself makes the child a believer.” Armed with these authorities, we faithful persons affirm baptism for infants, even under unbelieving parents, by whatever baptizers baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

But those who deny the efficacy of the sacrament without a Catholic mind should know that they possess an empty sacrament. To them may be applied what Leo the Great writes to Nicetas of Aquileia:

> “Those who received baptism from heretics, having not previously been baptized, are to be confirmed only by the invocation of the Holy Spirit through laying-on of hands, because they received only the form of baptism without the efficacy of sanctification.”

You now have what you asked concerning the sacrament of baptism. Let us proceed to the other sacraments of heretics, which must be annulled and nullified in such a way that, after the manner of the dove that eats nothing living, we condemn no person of Catholic mind. [Col. 1405C]

SAECUL. There is no need to linger over the sacrament of ordination, because from what has already been said I understand whom you count condemned with condemned ordainers and whom you wish to regard as excused from this: namely, those who approach with a Catholic mind one whose heresy they either wholly do not know or do not fully understand, as is believed of those who received sacred orders from Acacius.
