Speak now only concerning those sacraments of heretics in which there is no admixture of any Catholic mind, such as the making [read: consecration] of bread, wine, and chrism. I see whom you defend from the sword of condemnation through a Catholic mind, as though through the letter *tau*. It remains now, since you make yourself so bold as to spare none of us, that you begin at the sanctuary and try, if you can, to defend the statement you are accused of making: namely, that sacraments impressed by heretics upon insensible things—in which there neither is nor can be a Catholic mind—have no power either to change any such creature for the better or to sanctify it in any manner, since it is certain that neither in the sanctifier nor in the thing sanctified is there Catholic intention.

Unless you have several authoritative witnesses supporting and agreeing with you in this opinion, we shall accuse and condemn you as a heretic, as we proposed, in the presence of the bishop of Salzburg and your lord, the bishop of Regensburg. In the hearing of several of our bishops and many clerics, who consider you a heretic, it has been objected that one is a heretic who supports a heretic. Therefore, for the defense not only of yourself but also of your lord, prove what you are reported to have said. For, to use the words of one of our spokesmen, you denied the efficacy of sacraments administered by wicked priests only in inanimate things—bread and wine—used for the venerable sacrament of the altar, which we believe can be consecrated by any priest whatsoever, however wicked he may be. Answer also the statement you are reported to have made: that mute and secret confession does not avail fallen priests for the restoration of their violated order without the word of a pontiff, whereas we believe of every priest that, when he looses a sinner on earth, that same sinner is loosed in heaven.

REGUL. I shall not begin with the sanctuary; rather, with the Lord’s help, I shall show from the outset that my lord the bishop should be left unmentioned in this matter. For his faith and manner of life, beloved and venerable in the eyes of all, have no need to be defended or excused by my words. Let him therefore remain safe, though I am engaged in danger. Let my entire body be exposed to dangers on this condition: that my head be not harmed. Let me have with me that prudence of the serpent which teaches one to preserve the health of the head. [Col. 1406C] Therefore I do not now wish to call as a witness my lord bishop, father, and ordaining prelate; I have other Catholics wholly in agreement with me.

For last year, when G., archbishop of Ravenna, a man of holy and venerable life, was at Regensburg on the lord pope’s embassy, I was vigorously challenged before him concerning this statement and others. In the presence also of my lord bishop I was examined by him concerning everything, and was at last confirmed by him in the opinion that I had stated. The principal charge then laid against me was that I said irregular canons could not be saved unless they were converted, and that the body of Christ could not be made outside the Church. This the lord of Ravenna himself testified to be true. No one [Col. 1406D] accustomed to hearing me has said that I asserted this concerning wicked priests—of whom, within the Church, I am one, through my own fault exceedingly wicked, unworthy that Christ should enter beneath my roof. Yet I most certainly believe that the Lord’s body is made both by me and by all who bear the priestly name in the Church.

But when heretics have repeatedly been anathematized and all who have been cut off from the true vine are concerned, although I grant them a sacrament in respect of the forms of visible signs—the tracing of the cross and the words instituted for this purpose, by which a work of power is effected—nevertheless, because they deny that very power, so long as they sacrifice outside the Church, we deny that there is present among them, sacrificing there where, as blessed Augustine testifies, there is no place for a true sacrifice (even if there is a place), the power of the true sacrament, invisibly working through the visible sacraments [Col. 1407A] so that bread becomes the flesh of the lamb, according to the law that it is to be eaten in one house.

May God forgive the man who falsely affirms that I have said or written of wicked priests within the Church what I say concerning those under anathema. Moreover, what I myself say is affirmed with me by great and authoritative witnesses, neither few in number nor slight in authority, whose sayings I gladly append.

First, Christ himself says: “As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me” (John 15:4). Likewise, he says: “Without me you can do nothing” (ibid.). Thus speaks that Lion from the tribe of Judah. But Leo the Great also, attendant upon Christ himself, writing to the Emperor Leo concerning Alexandria, says: “It is manifest [Col. 1407B] that through the most cruel and monstrous madness there the light of all heavenly sacraments has been extinguished. The offering of sacrifice has been interrupted; the sanctification of chrism has failed; and all the mysteries have withdrawn themselves from parricidal hands.”

Pope Pelagius, to John the patrician: “Do not continually defile a Catholic mind by any communion with schismatics. It is established that the body of Christ is one, and that the Church is one. One divided from unity cannot consecrate the truth of Christ’s body. One divided from the Church’s bosom and separated from the apostolic sees rather desecrates than consecrates. Therefore do not, as though there were no difference between schismatics and the Church, wish indiscriminately to join in the sacrifices of both. [Col. 1407C] For what a schismatic makes is not Christ’s body, if we are guided by truth.”

Let us add a third bishop of the Roman see, so that every word may stand in the mouth of two or three. Pope Gregory, in Book XXXV of the *Moralia*, says among other things: “It must especially be noted that Job’s friends are commanded to offer the sacrifice of their conversion to the Lord not by themselves but through Job. For he says: ‘But Job my servant shall pray for you; I will accept his face, so that your folly may not be imputed to you’ (Job 42:8). As though he openly said to heretics: ‘I will not receive your sacrifices; I will not hear the words of your petitions, except through the intercession of him whose words of profession concerning me I acknowledge to be true.’”

And shortly afterward: “Seek your salvation through the Catholic Church, which I love; for through her I wish to forgive you [Col. 1407D] what you have sinned against me in her, so that she may obtain your safety—the Church which suffered from your sickness. For she alone is the one through whom the Lord willingly receives sacrifice; she alone faithfully intercedes for those who err. Hence the Lord also commands concerning the victim of the lamb: ‘It shall be eaten in one house, and none of its flesh shall be carried outside.’ The lamb is eaten in one house because the true victim of the Redeemer is sacrificed in the one Catholic Church. The divine law forbids its flesh to be carried outside because it forbids what is holy to be given to dogs.”

Likewise Augustine, to Boniface: “Heretics should not seek the Holy Spirit except in Christ’s body. Outside it they possess the sacrament, but do not inwardly hold the reality of which it is the sacrament; and therefore they eat and drink judgment upon themselves.” The same author [Col. 1408A] elsewhere: “Outside the Church there is no place for a true sacrifice.” Elsewhere again: “Just as the eunuch who purchased Joseph had no living seed through his dried genitals, so he who purchases the grace of the Holy Spirit has no living seed. Likewise, the fire which for seventy years of Babylonian captivity lived under water was extinguished when Jason sold the priesthood to Antiochus. This truly signifies that the fire of the Holy Spirit does not shine in simoniacal sacraments.”

Likewise Jerome, in his sermon *On the Paschal Lamb*: “Let us not suppose that this lamb can be eaten everywhere. We are commanded to eat it in one house—that is, not to suppose that the lamb is sacrificed outside the Church. From this it is manifest that Jews, heretics, and all assemblies of perverse doctrines, because they do not eat in the Church, eat not the flesh of the lamb [Col. 1408B] but that of the dragon, which was given as food to the peoples of Ethiopia. But we eat the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”

Likewise Origen, on Leviticus: “Such a man is sought as can eat the holy flesh, not in any place whatever, but in the holy place within the court of the tabernacle. Let those hear this who rend the Church and, introducing alien and perverse teachings, suppose that they can eat sacred flesh outside God’s temple and outside the Lord’s court. Their sacrifices are profane, since they are performed contrary to the commandments of the law. The things which are commanded to be eaten in the holy place, within the courts of the tabernacle of testimony, are enclosed by the wall of faith and hung with the doves of hope. Where these are absent, [Col. 1408C] holy flesh can neither be possessed nor eaten.”

Go now to those interpreters of yours who read God’s Scripture not ecclesiastically but scholastically. Ask them to determine all the foregoing for you in such a way that the table of the shewbread may be found outside God’s temple, though it is placed only within, opposite the lampstand with its seven lights. Argue and dispute as much as you please. Outside God’s paradise there is no fruit of the tree of life; it is surely denied to those whom that flaming sword of most keen anathema separates from the garden of delights, the Church. You despise this anathema, presuming to do what is prohibited under anathema as though it were permitted; and therefore you are anathematized, you who voluntarily violate the canons, since Leo IV declares: “All voluntary violators of the canons have been anathematized in all authentic [Col. 1408D] councils.”

Glory now in the sacramental signs of mysteries performed at the altar: in the tracing of the cross, the elevation of the chalice, the extension of the hands, and the representation of the other signs sacramentally expressing either Christ’s death or resurrection. But beware lest so many signs, lacking their realities, be those lying signs prophesied concerning the ministers of Antichrist. For the sacraments of heretics are so similar to those of Catholics—indeed, so truly the very same as to outward form—that, if possible, even the elect would be led into error. Yet they are strengthened by this: Catholic priests and ministers, together with Moses and Aaron, have the finger of God at work; and finally even those ministers like Pharaoh’s magicians will acknowledge it—the heretics, that is, and all who have been cut off from the Church. [Col. 1409A]

SAECUL. Which of us do you assign to Pharaoh’s ministry, when we are all under the title of the Christian name?

REGUL. Are not the accomplices and supporters of that recently condemned—indeed, long ago pre-condemned—Peter Leo, invader of the Roman Church, plainly ministers of Pharaoh?

SAECUL. What has he to do with us?

REGUL. That impious man pertains more to you and to those like you than to me and those like me. For if you go through all the houses of regular canons, I believe that you will find not even one among them who agrees with Peter Leo. But among secular clerics some, [Col. 1409B] especially the incontinent and the hired or employing clerics, condemned with Nicholas the fornicator and Simon Magus, partly secretly and partly openly desire him to prevail against Pope Innocent. We who are called regulars unanimously confess with one voice that Innocent is Peter’s legitimate successor. Before his papacy we knew him as a friend of chastity and religious life, just as we knew that other man as an enemy of God and the Church.

As for your assertion that I spoke of the secret and mutual confession of fornicating priests, by which they seem to cure their own falls, know that this arose because I once cited, before opponents, the canon of the Council of Lleida, which reads as follows: “Those who serve God’s altar, if they suddenly fall into the lamentable frailty of the flesh and, the Lord looking upon them, worthily repent, so that, having mortified the body, they offer God the sacrifice of a contrite heart: it shall remain in the bishop’s power either not to suspend for long those who are truly afflicted, or to separate the negligent from the body of the Church for a more extended time. Yet they shall receive again the places of their offices in such a way that they cannot thereafter be promoted to higher offices. But if, like dogs returning to vomit, they relapse a second time, they shall not only lack the dignity of office but shall not receive holy communion except at death.” [Col. 1409C]

By the authority of this canon, I ask: who gave priests this power, which we do not even find granted to bishops? The bishops at the Council of Lleida permit mercy to be shown to those who have suddenly fallen into the frailty of the flesh and who, the Lord looking upon them, worthily repent. But these excessively merciful—or perhaps mad—priests of our time make their fellow priests sing Masses though they have fallen not after the manner of men but, like pigs, have long been immersed in a mire of mud, have not been refined by any worthy repentance, and have not received permission from the bishop, which is to be granted only to those who repent worthily and avoid returning to their vomit. [Col. 1409D] Whence, I ask, do priests have this authority, which authority does not grant even to bishops: namely, to permit offices to men not worthily repentant, repeatedly returning to their faults, and fornicating in confidence that an impure fellow-priest can absolve one who is impure through water?

Certainly, if such a penitent and such a confessor were punished with worthy penance, both would be deprived of their offices, because one deserves to lose a privilege who abuses the power granted him. Oh, how much more rightly it would be done if canonical penance were imposed upon those who had fallen—yet in such a manner that a hidden fall would not be disclosed! Once this penance had been accepted, office could consequently be permitted; it should never be permitted to one who does not repent canonically. [Col. 1410A]

SAECUL. What do you call canonical penance?

REGUL. That which is imposed according to the authorities of the Fathers. This is distinguished in two ways among both clerics and laypeople. One penitent retains something of himself for himself; another, offering once and together in holocaust to God all that he is, all that he has, and all that he can do, imitates that prodigal son—or rather the son, penitent after prodigality—who returned with such a disposition that he would no longer wander from his father’s house, but would minister and serve there and do everything his father commanded him, not daring in any way to desire to be called a son, much less aspiring to be clothed with the first robe. [Col. 1410B]

This manner of penance is observed by those who come to regular cloisters and, renouncing themselves wholly, strive under obedience toward the purity of holiness. Once their intention has been declared in this way, the father of the monastery may deal more gently with them, and may determine that such a penitent, clothed also with the first robe, may exercise priestly office; and that, if he had been a layman, he may eat the fattened calf as a layman, or, if a priest, may sacrifice it as a priest.

But one and the same form does not suit clerics who repent with such penance. The man whose secret fornication in the world, or any other offence destructive of priestly honor, has not been made public may choose as physician and father a vigorous superior, whether of monks or of regular canons. Wholly subject to this father, one not detected in crime may, unless I am mistaken, exercise his office when it seems fitting to his father and confessor. For although we read that only bishops are everywhere assigned the power to restore the stole to priests who repent worthily, nevertheless, when a priest has not publicly lost his stole but secretly incurred the penalty, if he resumes it at the command of the father and confessor under whom he has arranged to serve until death, I do not think [Col. 1410C] this should be censured. Yet it would be more prudent also to consult the bishop concerning such a penitent, because of the aforesaid canon of the Council of Lleida, which declares without distinction that, at the bishop’s discretion, penitent priests who are truly afflicted are either not to be suspended long or the negligent are to be separated from the Church’s body for a longer period. [Col. 1410D]

SAECUL. If matters were conducted as you say, a hidden crime would easily be revealed, since each brother would wonder privately at a priest’s prolonged suspension.

REGUL. In properly religious cloisters it is not customary for one newly converted, however chaste he may be, to minister so quickly that a prolonged suspension identifies him as unchaste. There even the holiest and most chaste are so humbled, voluntarily chastised by vigils, fasts, and other good exercises, that they cannot at all be distinguished from those who chastise themselves for hidden crimes.

These things have been said concerning hidden crimes to be consumed among monks or regular canons—as though a goat, foul while alive, were consumed in the sanctuary, having nevertheless been killed and roasted within the holy places. This goat, indeed, is incorporated into Aaron and his sons when such a profession is made by such a man: that he shall live in common life, in which Aaron and his sons properly serve. The law does not permit them an inheritance among the allotments of the other tribes, because the Lord is their portion; and they are commanded in the law to possess nothing except the Lord. [Col. 1411A]

But a different form must be observed with regard to those whose fornications and other crimes are known to the people, especially such crimes as forbid those committing them from the mysteries of the altar. Those who wish to repent are much better advised to seek monasteries of monks than those of regular canons, because of the strictness of the rule, which excludes every public stain from the exercise of holy orders. For, if associated with clerics, such persons must be treated according to the canons and must never be restored to office without the bishop’s authority. This is fitting, since they did not lose office without the authority of bishops, who in many councils forbade the divine office to fornicators and traders—that is, manifest accomplices of Nicholas and Simon—and turned God’s people away from hearing the forbidden offices. [Col. 1411B]

Therefore, one such person wishing to repent among regular canons must be compelled to observe the canons and to heed Clement and the other Roman pontiffs, who scarcely permit psalmody with the brothers and lesser offices, unless perhaps, after the time of canonical chastisement has been completed, he is supported by the testimony of the brethren and reconciled by the bishop. This is permitted by Pope Calixtus and blessed Gregory only to those performing worthy penance and thereafter living well. Behold whom among penitents I judge must not be restored to the offices they have lost without the bishop’s authority. [Col. 1411C]

SAECUL. After how long does it seem to you that a penitent may be reconciled for public acts?

REGUL. To speak now of public fornication alone: although the holy Fathers distinguish periods in various ways, some fixing seven years and others a somewhat shorter term for penance, because Miriam, Aaron’s sister, was commanded to remain outside the camp for seven days on account of her fault, nevertheless I approve what we have learned above was determined by the Fathers: that it should remain in the bishop’s power either not to suspend for long those truly afflicted or to separate the negligent from the Church’s body for a more extended time.

But I cannot approve the practice by which certain spiritual monks, without consulting bishops, make manifest fornicators who come to monastic life sing Masses, for I do not know by what authority they act. Yet I judge this highly detestable: that secular clerics fornicate deliberately; and much more do I detest that those who thus fornicate minister either without penance or under feigned or false penance. [Col. 1411D–1412A]

SAECUL. What do you call false penance?

REGUL. First hear what true penance is, so that you may infer from it what false penance is. Blessed Ambrose, in the third book *On Penance*, says: “I have found more easily those who preserved innocence than those who performed penance fittingly.” And, as though you asked the manner of fitting penance, he continues: “One must renounce the world; one must indulge sleep less than nature requires; sleep must be interrupted by sighs and set apart for prayers; one must live in such a way as to die to this vital use; a man must deny himself to himself and be wholly changed.”

You hear, brother, that in true penance one must renounce the world; the penitent must deny himself and be wholly changed. Can anyone perform this penance in a splendid and secular dress? [Col. 1412B]

SAECUL. To say nothing now of clerics, do we not see many penitent laymen in not merely secular but even military dress?

REGUL. Let Leo the Great answer you on this point; among other things he says: “It is altogether contrary to ecclesiastical rules to return to secular military service after performing penance, since the Apostle says: ‘No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs’ (2 Tim. 2:4). Therefore he who wishes to entangle himself in secular military service is not free from the snares of the devil.”

The Nicene Synod also says in chapter 12: “Whoever, called by grace, first showed zeal by laying aside the military belt, but afterwards relapsed to his own vomit—so that some even gave money and sought military service through favors—shall remain in affliction for ten years after the three-year period during which they shall be among the hearers.” [Col. 1412C]

SAECUL. I see few who repent in this way, apart from bearded brethren wholly subject to the vigorous rulers of cloisters. Therefore I venture to infer that such a form of penance, in which secular life is not permitted, applies to them alone.

REGUL. Let the Second Council of Toledo answer you, whose tenth chapter reads: “Whoever, healthy or sick, asks penance from a bishop or priest: above all, bishop and priest shall observe this, that if the person is a man, healthy or sick, they first tonsure him or make him change his dress for ashes and haircloth, and thus impose penance—that is, *carrina*. But if she is a woman, she shall not receive penance unless she has first been veiled or changed her dress. For when penance is often carelessly granted to laypeople, they relapse after accepting penance into deeds once again to be lamented.” Likewise, the Third Council of Toledo, chapter 16: “If anyone, forgetful of the penance he has received and professed, relapses into secular things, he shall by no means be able to communicate unless he is restored to the profession that he unlawfully abandoned.” [Col. 1412D]

SAECUL. I agree, in whatever sense, concerning public penitents, because splendid and secular dress does not suit them well. But those clerics whose penance [Col. 1413A] we are discussing do not repent together with public penitents; perhaps therefore secular dress does not impede their salvation, provided only that the heart is contrite and humbled. David too, after penance, wore not merely secular but royal dress; and Ahab, king of Israel, humbled himself for a time in sackcloth and afterward wore soft garments.

REGUL. The Apostle says: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15). Although certain prophets preached penance, nevertheless from the days of John the Baptist—who first preached the baptism of penance and displayed penitential dress in himself—the kingdom of God began to suffer violence; and the violent, not the lukewarm, seized it and seize it, producing fruits of penance not unworthy but so worthy that, after the example of Hannah, their countenances are no more changed in different directions. Rather, they preserve to the end the same dress and same appearance in which penance was undertaken. [Col. 1413B]

For the cross of penance is not, after Simon’s example, to be borne either under compulsion or only to be laid down before death; it is, after Christ’s example, to be borne willingly until death. Thus, after penance has been received, the penitent must always have despised dress and a continuous rigor, most prudently intensified, of chastising himself until death; it must never be relaxed except so far as the holy Fathers moderate it. Though after the initial severity of penance they allow a milder rule in clothing and food, they never permit secular dress. Indeed, on account of such dress they exclude penitents from the body of the Lord until death, as we have shown partly above and partly leave for the diligent reader to seek out. [Col. 1413C]

For everyone who seeks finds. To say nothing now of a cleric or layperson performing public penance, no one who bewails a mortal sin by secret satisfaction communicates without danger in Christ’s body and blood so long as secular dress conforms him to this world. Therefore blessed Augustine, in the book *On Ecclesiastical Definitions*, says: “I urge him who is burdened by mortal sins committed after baptism first to make satisfaction through public penance, and then, reconciled at the judgment of the priest, to be joined to communion, if he wishes to receive the Eucharist not for his judgment or condemnation. Nor do we deny that mortal crimes may be absolved by secret satisfaction; but first secular dress must be changed, and through correction of life, the professed pursuit of religion, and continual—indeed perpetual—mourning, he must, by God’s mercy, obtain pardon. [Col. 1413D] This is so only on the condition that he does the opposite of the acts of which he repents, and receives the Eucharist every Sunday, suppliant and humble, until death.”

The same author in the same work: “True penance is not to admit the deeds one must repent, and to bewail those already committed.” Likewise: “The satisfaction of penance is to cut off the causes of sins and not allow entrance to their promptings.”

Here you have the rules of penance which penitent laypeople and clerics alike must observe if they wish to be secure concerning their salvation. Laypeople who, contrary to the prescribed rules, take up arms after performing penance may perhaps escape condemnation if they resemble David, who bore arms after penance, in the cause—that is, if they fight only for justice. Yet even this cannot excuse them from departing from penitential life if they do it on their own presumption, without the permission or command of any ecclesiastical ruler. [Col. 1414A]

But those transgressors of penance who possess tithes forbidden to laypeople; who seize others’ goods and, though able, refuse to restore or make amends for them; who bear arms against justice; who retain hatred in their hearts; or who are entangled in such trades or offices as cannot be exercised without fraud, falsehood, envy, or deception of their brethren—such persons are not to be believed either to have turned to God or to perform true penance for the crimes they have committed. [Col. 1414B]

SAECUL. As I hear it, you are exceedingly harsh toward soldiers and merchants who, after the penance which we call *carrina*, return to military service and trade.

REGUL. If I seem harsh to you, hear what Gregory VII judges concerning such people in his *Decretals*: “We call false those penances which are not imposed according to the authority of the holy Fathers in proportion to the character of the crimes. Therefore, whenever a soldier, merchant, or person devoted to an office that cannot be exercised without sin, entangled in graver offences, comes to penance—that is, one who unjustly retains another’s goods or bears hatred in his heart—let him recognize that he cannot perform true penance by which he may attain eternal life unless the soldier lays down his arms and does not thereafter bear them except on the counsel of religious persons and for the defense of justice; unless the merchant abandons trade and the officeholder leaves his office; unless each restores the goods he has unjustly taken and dismisses hatred from his heart. [Col. 1414C] Yet, lest meanwhile he despair, we exhort him to do whatever good he can, so that almighty God may enlighten his heart toward penance.”

SAECUL. These words altogether show more what true or false penance is for laypeople than what true penance is for clerics, concerning whom, however, the discussion was specifically proposed.

REGUL. Can the words of blessed Augustine above not satisfy you? He grants pardon not even to those making satisfaction for secret mortal sins unless they first change their secular dress and profess the pursuit of religious life. Yet these clerics, whose false penance I complain of, enter God’s house even after open crimes, having professed no pursuit of religion and undertaken no purpose of holiness. They are so secularly dressed that, if you see a cleric, you would suppose him to be a layman, although the sacred canons command all clerics not to wear lay clothing—that is, a mantle or other garments without a cowl—but always to go about in religious and decent dress. [Col. 1414D]

Furthermore, blessed Gregory, as we noted above, writing to the subdeacon Peter about penance owed by clerics, so completely excludes the world that he commands their possessions either to be given to a monastery or left for their relatives’ use. This makes manifest that a cleric falsely repents unless he renounces the possessions he had—something which would have been proper even before his fall, so that one serving the altar might live only from the altar. [Col. 1415A]

SAECUL. I neither wish nor am able to oppose so many authorities; nevertheless, it pleases both me and my accomplices to defame you, because you disparage our reputation and our life, which, although secular, has nevertheless hitherto been held in honor. But your own reputation has been sufficiently stained everywhere by things spread concerning you, whether through truth or through occasion.

REGUL. Whoever spreads and speaks a lie about me speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and the father of lies. But those who speak truth about me do not trouble me, because I gladly confess the truth about myself. [Col. 1415B]

SAECUL. Since you say that you are ready to confess the truth, tell me, I beg you, whether it is true what many affirm that you have said concerning a pregnant woman and her husband who has intercourse with her at that time.

REGUL. It is not fitting that I answer these things which iniquity has invented about me. It is enough for me to defend the things I know that I have said. As for the shameful and filthy claims which shameless people fabricate about me—saying that I preached this and that, things too gross even to say or write—I briefly excuse myself by saying: “These things I neither said nor say.” I am accustomed to speak thus when asked whether I said such and such things that are plainly to be rejected, not only as false but also because of their extreme indecency. [Col. 1415C]

SAECUL. It may be that those who hate you lie about you, saying that you said what you did not say. But we gladly lend an ear to everyone who speaks ill of you, so that somehow we may root you out and crush you from the land of the living. For you are burdensome to us even to look upon, especially because you alone seem to assail us. This is what troubles us somewhat: in the very cloister in which you were raised, none of your brethren agrees with you.

REGUL. Read the book composed against the detractors of Gregory VII by Manegold, formerly dean of our cloister, and in it you will find proved by the strongest authorities what we too endeavor to prove: namely, that clerics who fornicate and, in addition, usurp forbidden offices are Nicolaitans and heretics condemned not only with Nicholas but also with Ebion and Paul of Samosata. By such arguments he defended Gregory VII, who was attacked for this reason by the clerics of our land: because he forbade fornicating ministers of the altar not only their office but also entrance into church. [Col. 1415D]

SAECUL. Manegold too was an importunate man, and he is now dead. Therefore we wish his book to be buried with him. We believe that even the brethren of your cloister despise it, [Col. 1416A] since, although the book was composed in Gregory VII’s defense, it is not believed to have been approved by Gregory himself.

REGUL. Nor do I hold that book as an authority, though I know it pleased even Catholic bishops who, expelled because of the schism of Wibert, frequently visited the cloister of Raitenbuch at that time. But I answer your belief that I dissent from the regular community of my brethren as follows: my more reliable brethren praise that Manegold, formerly dean there; they possess his writings as though they were responses of a heavenly oracle. By them some men were strengthened in Catholic unity during the Wibertine schism, and secular disputants against the Church were then somewhat refuted.

Therefore from that time onward, in the cloister of Raitenbuch, that dean has been heard by the wiser brethren as though he still lived; though dead, he still speaks, and in his writings still condemns the sacrifices of fornicators. Thus recently one of the brethren of that cloister wrote to me: “Here it must be noted that those priests who serve the altar for silver and gold are not merely worshippers of golden calves but mad adorers of Baal. For while you strive to prove them worthy of apostolic office without apostolic life, and they resist the truth with certain outcries, they in some sense add Baalim to their golden calves, feigning themselves to be the kind of persons whom the Lord accepts, when in fact they are the kind whom he rejects. [Col. 1416B] You should know that through their fault the continual sacrifice is now trodden underfoot, while by remaining in the holy place they produce such an abomination of desolation that they turn to luxury the Church’s offerings, which not even holy widows married twice are permitted to consume as food. Thus the rich men of this world eat what they ought not to eat except as chaste despisers of this world.”

The words of this fervent brother have been inserted among my own words so that no one may suppose I alone among my brethren obey the Apostle’s command that we withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition received from the apostles. And our brother Conrad of Silva has now grown old in this judgment of truth, by which we are commanded to beware of false prophets. Although they sing Masses in sacred vestments belonging to holiness and innocence, inwardly they bear a wolfish heart, greedy for their own profit and plunder rather than God’s glory, as is recognized from their fruits. [Col. 1416C]

Therefore it should not be seriously charged against me if, agreeing with my brethren who place faith in Christ’s words, I refuse to gather figs from thorns or to harvest grapes from a bramble after some condemned and anathematized wickedness has revealed itself to me through evil fruits. Let those who wish gather the fruits of thorns and brambles; I believe Christ’s words affirming that neither figs are gathered from thorns nor grapes harvested from a bramble.

For the grape and cluster of Cyprus, which is in the vineyards of Engaddi and is pressed in the winepresses by the press of the cross, [Col. 1417A] of which the Psalmist speaks, is not found outside the Church or outside the vineyards of Engaddi, which are the many churches in the one faith of Christ. Therefore the cluster of Cyprus is found only in Christ’s vineyard, in the one Church of God.

**SECULAR CLERIC.** You seem to me to understand the words of God and the words of the saints without the discernment of dispensation. Many things have been said by them to inspire fear; some things are permitted, some advised, some commanded. All of these appear to you as necessarily to be observed. And though you pretend willingly to hear all the words of God and the saints, you nevertheless refuse to obey those sayings of theirs which deal with dispensation, in which charity bears all things and endures all things. But your impatient and undiscerning mind bears nothing, endures nothing [Col. 1417B]; if it could, it would wish to root out the tares before the harvest, although the Lord says: “Let both grow together until the harvest” (Matt. 13:30). You also separate the useless branches far too soon from God’s vineyard, although one enclosure contains them together with the grapes. In all this your great lack of discernment is apparent, as is the fact that the virtue of dispensation is wholly unknown to you—a virtue much impressed upon students by the diligence of teachers in the schools.

**REGULAR.** I know well enough that certain teachers in the schools busy themselves with bending the Scriptures to their own understanding, rather than directing themselves by the rectitude of Scripture. Since they say that all terrible sayings were spoken merely to inspire terror, they strangely attempt, by repeatedly insisting upon terror, to empty terror of its force, affirming that those very terrible sayings contain no serious truth. They do this in the manner of the serpent, who in Paradise vainly sought to annul God’s fearful words. They bluster this out with rounded mouths and puffed cheeks, in order to display their knowledge, which puffs up, and to defend their own dissolute life and that of those like themselves. But those who speak of the magnificence of God’s holiness and recount his wonders also declare the power of his fearful deeds; nor will they utter abroad the remembrance of the abundance of his sweetness except concerning those in whose righteousness they can rejoice, and those who do not hear the power of such terrors with deaf ears.

I have experienced this in myself. Formerly, according to the teaching of your masters, while praising dispensation, I greatly offended a certain religious hermit. [Col. 1417D] He was the first to thunder into me the power of God’s fearful judgments, and vehemently warned me not to cloak “words of wickedness devised to make excuses for sins” under the respectable name of dispensation. At that time I was a most eager investigator of what religious men thought of the life of secular clerics, of whom I then was one: namely, whether there was in it any certain hope of salvation, especially for chaste clerics such as I had then resolved to become. Yet, still seeking and loving what was my own, I could understand very little concerning true honourableness and true chastity. For I had not considered for long that a man so divided—now thinking of the things that are the Lord’s, now of those of this world; now how he may please God, now how he may please this age—differs little [Col. 1418A] from a married man; indeed, he is inferior to the latter if the married man, having a wife, lives as though he had none, being concerned how, even in having a wife, he may please God alone.

Yet, whatever I was then, I wished gladly to be saved, even should death find me a minister of the altar wearing secular dress. But that aforesaid hermit, whom I approached as a crafty investigator, set before me matters so terrible—indeed, the power of terrors so terribly—that I myself came to hate him for it. But afterwards, having digested what I had heard from him, when I perceived that the holy Fathers agreed with him, I was like one found by the watchmen of the walls: I lost the contrived cloak of defence and dispensation by which the enormity of many transgressions is covered. Then, struck and wounded by the watchmen of the walls [Col. 1418B] and, as I have said, stripped of that cloak, I was not ashamed before many people to confess and bewail the wretched excesses of my former life. Therefore, as I hope, I obtained mercy—perhaps for this purpose: that I might be wholly opposed to the manner of life in which I had nearly perished, and might be set as an example to those wishing to turn away from it.

“For this is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptance: that Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first and greatest”—I who once also persecuted the Church of God, defending evils as if by dispensation. And therefore perhaps by God’s just judgment I suffer many who persecute me as if by dispensation, thinking that they render service [Col. 1418C] to God if they either kill me or in some other way remove me from the good memory of mankind, placing me “in dark places and in the shadow of death,” and saying to my soul: “There is no salvation for him in his God.” May this not be imputed to them, nor be set down to them as sin. Yet let them know that I am not so blind as not to see that some things are commanded, others advised, others permitted, all of which are fitting in their proper place and time. I also assent to charity, which bears all things and endures all things. But again I assent to that same charity when it does not bear, but cuts down, certain scandals, lest useless trees occupy even the ground—trees that bear neither fruits worthy of a good life nor fruits of penitence worthy in view of an evil life.

As I believe that the Apostle Paul endured certain things through charity, so I know that in that same charity it happened that he yielded to certain persons not even for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with him. [Col. 1418D] By this act he taught sufficiently that one must not yield to falsehood against truth, not even for an hour. Yet those shoots of wickedness which have not yet been cut off by the apostolic sickle and are not found prohibited from their offices—such as lustful clerics, gamblers, hunters, men devoted to buffoonery rather than thanksgiving—if they are endured through charity, so long as they are thought to be within the enclosure of God’s vineyard and free of simony and other condemned and anathematized perversities, do not impede the salvation of the good who endure them. Indeed, the good are purified by carrying within them evil men, whether unknown or not yet condemned, so long as [Col. 1419A] God tells the prelates to let both grow and they, obedient to this saying, allow both to grow. For both are still tender, and both the evil tares and the good shoots have a capacity for growth.

But when, according to what is read in the Apocalypse, it is said to the angel holding a sharp sickle—that is, to the pontiff of the Apostolic See, who has authority to excommunicate those rebellious against God—when, I say, such an angel is told: “Send forth your sharp sickle and gather the clusters of the vineyard of the earth, for its grapes are ripe” (Rev. 14:18), we believe that Gregory VII obeyed this command. From that time we believe that what follows in the Apocalypse took place: “The angel sent forth his sickle and gathered the vineyard of the earth and cast it into the great winepress of God’s wrath; and the winepress was trodden outside the city” (ibid., 20). For the Nicolaitans and Simoniacs were like certain clusters of the vineyard of the earth, not of Christ’s vineyard. Before Leo IX they had almost occupied Christ’s vineyard itself, as though it were lawful to possess women and churches together, and to obtain churches and ecclesiastical stipends by money and services. But from the time when the pontiffs of the Apostolic See moved the sharp sickle at God’s command, it is apparent that these clusters of the vineyard of the earth did not belong to Christ’s vineyard even then, when they were endured by their predecessors—perhaps because they were not yet ripe.

But now, since the vineyard of the earth is wholly ripe, and a great part of it has been gathered by pontiffs of the Apostolic See and thrown outside the city of God and heaped up in the city of the devil, [Col. 1419C] we rightly hear now the voice in the Apocalypse saying: “Come out from her, my people, lest you share in her sins and receive of her plagues; for her sins have reached unto heaven. Repay her as she herself repaid you; as much as she enlarged herself and lived in luxury, give her so much torment and mourning. For she says in her heart: ‘I sit as a queen, and am not a widow, and shall not see mourning’” (Rev. 18:4–7).

Yet in saying this I do not wish to persuade anyone that we ought bodily to flee all evil men without exception, but that we should wholly strive to avoid those who are prohibited in prohibited matters: by not hearing the masses of certain persons, and yet still saying “hail” to them; but to others, not even saying “hail.” We must hold most firmly that the tongues of the Roman pontiffs have been made the keys of heaven. Therefore, whatever masses are sung in opposition to them are outside heaven—indeed, outside the Church; and those who rashly hear them incur by their disobedience the sin of paganism, as Gregory VII affirms.

**SECULAR CLERIC.** Thus far I have endured you speaking or writing. Now I reject you as profane and as a heretic, because you do not agree with the sayings of the masters who govern schools throughout all France. Therefore we too have agreed not to hear your masses, and to repay you in kind for execrating our offices, since you are the offscouring of all men—not to say, of all priests. But nearly all of us excel in lineage, nobility, and wealth. Therefore, disdaining to hear your [Col. 1420A] words any longer, we shall make you a reproach before the whole world.

**REGULAR.** Behold, O Roman Church, free mother: hear how your son is mocked—indeed, insulted—in your house, which has been entrusted to you to govern. If there are maternal bowels within you, come to the aid of your little son against that man who in no way ought to be tolerated as yours.

> [Note: [Col. 1419D] A verse is lacking in the manuscript.] [lacuna] where he does not persecute the son of the free woman; for it may happen that by brotherly concord he too may receive something of the paternal inheritance.

But because he persecutes me, your son, such as I am, write to the Father and my archbishop, Conrad of Salzburg, that he may cast out the slave woman and her son—something which, by God’s grace, he himself has done in part. With the Lord’s cooperation he has made nearly all the communities of his diocese regular. [Col. 1420B] But among the suffragan sees subject to him, one of which is the Church of Regensburg, the son of the slave woman still reigns; and, what is worse, he persecutes the son of the free woman—if indeed you deign to recognize me as your son, who serve you with filial affection, often wishing that you might have such rulers as Gregory the First, not to mention Peter the Apostle. One of these, Peter, planted in you the apostolic life; the other, Gregory, restored that same life in you in such a way that at Rome, in Babylon itself, the life of clerics and monks was such as Blessed Peter is believed to have planted, and such as was observed under Mark, his disciple, at Alexandria.

We know and grieve that you are shaken in the head, so that you cannot order Rome, which frequently rises in tumult against the knowledge of Christ. [Col. 1420C] Therefore, if you cannot fight at close quarters with the sword, fight at least with the drawn bow. Those Gregorian letters were sharp arrows of a mighty man, which he voluntarily pressed upon archbishops and bishops; he touched upon everything blameworthy in them and established the apostolic life even in the far-distant Church of the English. In his time, indeed, no one needed to extort apostolic letters or obtain them with difficulty. They were voluntarily offered and sent to bishops who had not asked for them. Afterwards, however, it often happened that even under devout and generous popes there was complaint about chancellors and notaries who were too sparing and slow in writing and issuing letters—though Peter’s vicar, who was certainly devout in himself, did not know or did not consider this. [Col. 1420D] We too have already experienced you as devout; therefore we judge that we should speak briefly concerning a just cause known also to you.

Therefore, O Pope Innocent, while Antichrist is already striving for kingship—not to say reigning—take counsel with the holier and more prudent men whom you know to be elders, and help us. Besides the lord cardinals whom you have as faithful attendants of God’s bride, I hear that you have with you the lord of Tarragona and the abbot of Clairvaux, illustrious men. Having called these to counsel, arise and measure the temple and those who worship in it. But cast out the court which is outside the temple, and do not measure it, because it has been given to the Gentiles. Distinguish by decretal writings [Col. 1421A] who are those false teachers, “having eyes full of adultery and of unceasing sin,” whom the Apostle Peter marks in his epistle, teaching that such men must be avoided. He also shows that their sacraments are dry, by calling them “springs without water”; extinguished, by calling them “clouds driven by whirlwinds,” for whom “the blackness of darkness is reserved.”

Blessed Gregory, once writing to John of Constantinople, says:

> “The Apostle cries: ‘Little children, it is the last hour’ (1 John 2:18). In accordance with what Truth says, pestilence and sword rage throughout the world, nation rises against nation, the earth is shaken together with its inhabitants; the earth fails, all things are dissolved. All that was foretold is taking place; the king of pride is near, and—what it is dreadful even to say—an army of priests is being prepared for him, because those who had been set in place to provide the leadership of humility serve under the banner of prideful exaltation.”

What do you think that blessed man would say if he lived in our time and saw the army of priests, which he said was being prepared for the kingdom of pride, already prepared? I think he would no longer say that the king of pride is near, but that he is already present. Perhaps he would now say, and weep, that by the same king of pride the two witnesses, Elijah and Enoch—that is, teachers fervent with Elijah and gentle with Enoch—have been extinguished. For we see teachers of both kinds suffocated by the world: so that few walk with God after the example of Enoch, and few burn with such zeal for God’s house as he burned [Col. 1421C] who first invalidated the sacrifices of the false priests and then slaughtered the priests themselves.

Yet though teachers are killed, the divine word cannot be killed. For the divine word cries through the Apostle Jude, who is also called Thaddaeus:

> “Woe to them, because they have gone in the way of Cain, and have poured themselves out in the error of Balaam for reward, and have perished in the rebellion of Korah. These are stains at their feasts, feasting without fear, feeding themselves; waterless clouds carried about by winds; autumnal trees, fruitless, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars.”

And shortly afterwards:

> “But you, beloved, remember the words foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, who told you that in the last [Col. 1421D] time mockers will come, walking in ungodliness according to their own desires. These are those who separate themselves, sensual persons, not having the Spirit” (Jude 11–19).

Supported by this apostolic teaching, we judge it sound to withdraw ourselves from every brother walking disorderly, especially from those who separate themselves from Christ’s body by doing what is forbidden under anathema. For it is not enough for them to walk disorderly unless they also persecute those who desire to walk orderly. Therefore we wretches, who are called regulars, are oppressed by seculars, especially by those whose leaders are the unclean Nicholas and Simon Magus. By these two, as by two smoking firebrands’ tails, the lights of the Churches are weighed down. Since they sit, as it were, in the citadel [Col. 1422A] because they preside over cathedral Churches [thus the manuscript], not even bishops of good will can cleanse God’s house with Mattathias, or at least plant the apostolic life in baptismal churches—a life which ought to govern every church, including episcopal and mother churches. Added to this is that certain bishops are found far too lukewarm for this task of uprooting, destroying, scattering, dissipating, building, and planting, according to the prophet.

Therefore, O Pope Innocent, take hold of weapons and shield, and rise up to aid the few good men. At least send to the bishops of the German land one edict like that Gregorian judgment in which he writes to Bishop Victor:

> “Whoever, from consideration of his office, does not burn vehemently to correct this crime—namely simony and the heresy of neophytes—let him not doubt that he shares the lot of him from whom this peculiar abomination first took its origin.”

You too should tell all bishops that if anyone, by reason of the authority entrusted to him, does not burn vehemently to plant the apostolic life in which Christ reigns, and uproot the irregular life in which Antichrist reigns, he should not doubt that he shares the condemnation which the rigor of the apostolic saying pronounces upon those who commit such acts.

As for me, think of me whatever you wish: I am and always shall be faithful to you. And lest anyone persuade you that the name of profane heretic is truthfully applied to me by men who are lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God, know, [Col. 1422C] my father—you whom I acknowledge as the lawful successor of Peter the Apostle—that I am always prepared to give satisfaction to everyone who asks an account of the hope that is within me. I affirm nothing obstinately, since I am and always have been most ready to change that very thing which I say if it appears to any Catholic to disagree with the truth and he can show this reasonably.

Catholics love me of their own accord—not only clerics and monks, but also archbishops and bishops, especially the lord of Salzburg and the lord of Ravenna. When the character of my life and teaching became known to them, one of them, namely the man of Salzburg, particularly commended fortitude to me among the four virtues; the other, namely the man of Ravenna, impressed upon me more strongly the sweetness of temperance. But both advised me that, since I had given sufficient testimony to the truth according to my measure, I should thereafter remain quiet. Yet men whom I once offended by speaking the truth oppose my quiet with insatiable hatred.

For I do not deny that I once went to cut down forest trees when, at the Apostle’s urging, I rebuked the unfruitful works of darkness. In this undertaking it could have happened that iron slipping from its handle—that is, an excess in rebukes—might wound or offend a neighbour, though I did not lie in wait for his life. But I have always loved, and since I began to understand still love, the one city of refuge—that is, the indivisible unity of the Church—so greatly that I hope to escape death, protected in my smallness by the great and supreme pontiff, of whom I believe you, Pope Innocent, to be a member and vicar.

Therefore, Father, I need your consolation [Col. 1423A] against the enemies of all religious life. I shall obtain it if you write to the archbishop of Salzburg that he should bring assistance to the bishop of Regensburg, who desires to impose the regular life upon the communities of clerics entrusted to him, or at least to intermingle regulars among them. In his diocese I sit like a solitary sparrow upon a roof, so surrounded by a numerous host of enemies that, when you recently came to the city of Liège, I did not dare to come to behold your desirable presence, Father.

I ask, Father, that in writing to the lord bishop of Salzburg you may deign to keep in kindly remembrance me, the unworthy priest named Gerhoh, so that he may protect me from the attacks of enemies. Your name too is hateful to them because you rebuked them at Clairvaux concerning the colour of their garments and made their life and dress conspicuous. For we who are called regulars, if anyone does not obey your word, mark and rebuke him as a brother by letter; but they persecute the one who rebukes them. It is therefore yours, Father, to console those whom you recognize to be endangered among the enemies of God, and that you may obtain perfect consolation by the extermination of the enemy of God and of yourself, concerning whose character I would now have something to say.

But I have done this by writing to the venerable man John, bishop of Ostia, whom I sought to persuade that Peter, together with those agreeing with him, belongs to the body of the son of perdition—unless he himself is that beast whose deadly wound is said in the Apocalypse to have been healed. For he despises the most powerful anathema as if he had no wound of death; and as if his wound of death had been healed precisely because a multitude of wicked men has joined him. Therefore, whether he is a member or the head of the great Antichrist spread throughout the world, the Lord will destroy him by the brightness of his coming.

But you, Pope Innocent, will be like the mouth of the Lord if you separate the precious from the vile; if you distinguish the wolves from God’s precious sheepfold; if you divide the flocks of companions from the tents of shepherds, according as you yourself discern the difference between that planting which the Father did not plant, which will at last be uprooted, and that which God the Father planted in Christ, which shall never be uprooted.

For it is known and clear to you, once a distinction has been made between clerics living apostolically and non-apostolically, in which portion Aaron the priest stands with his sons in continual watches of the holy tabernacle. On the opposite side Balaam the diviner resists him and curses him—indeed, unwillingly blesses him—a prophet hired together with all the hirelings. On this side stands Samuel in the linen tunic which his mother gave him: that is, the apostolic life, fruitful after long barrenness. On the other side the sons of Eli behave wantonly: they sleep with women, do not know the priests’ duties, and seize with a three-pronged fork—by gift, by tongue, by service of hand—the stipend appointed for holy uses.

On this side legitimate priests bear the ark of the Lord, having, that is, the body of Christ, in which, as in the most holy ark, the salvation of the world is laid up. [Col. 1424A] On that side are priests of the high places, who fill the hands of their ordainers or of the donors of churches and thereby ascend the high places. Their fur-trimmed and splendid garments more plainly reveal that they govern churches through hired and purchased offices—which is the most manifest simony. They lack that holy ark because their sacraments are empty.

On one side Elijah stands; and, as he sweetly invokes God, his sacrifice is consumed by heavenly fire. In opposition to him, on the other side, is the choir of priests of Baal who sell and buy, and the flock of priests who hire and are hired, singing in the highest voice, so that they too make fire descend from heaven when they presume to invoke the Holy Spirit. Yet he does not descend upon the sacrifices of those who invoke him falsely [Col. 1424B] and simoniacally, though they cry in a loud voice; so that Elijah mocks them, saying: “Cry with a louder voice; for your god—whether money or Beelphegor—perhaps is speaking, or is in an inn, or is on a journey, or perhaps is sleeping and must be awakened” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 18:27).

On one side stands Christ, the true vine, with the branches clinging to him. Through them, in the sacrament of the altar, that cluster of Cyprus grows—the cluster which is not outside, but only within the vineyard of Engaddi. On the other side—that is, in the sides of the north, among cold men, on the mountain of the Testament, that is, among lofty and learned men—he claims for himself a seat who, by the identity of sacraments however empty, boasts himself to be the Most High. It is as though he said through the mouths of his own men: “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14), because there is as great a power in the masses and sacramental signs of excommunicated persons as in the masses of Catholics.

If this is so, as they wish, where is that which the Apostle foretells Antichrist will perform through lying signs? And what are void and empty sacraments but lying signs, not only lacking the effect of salvation but also denying that power by which the invisible creature is changed or sanctified? For, as the Apostle affirms, the coming of Antichrist shall be according to the working of Satan, not according to the working of Christ. It shall also be in every power and in signs and wonders (2 Thess. 2:9). And lest you should suppose this power true, these signs true, these wonders true, he adds: [Col. 1424D] “With lying signs and with every deception of iniquity for those who perish, because they did not receive the love of truth that they might be saved. Therefore God sends them the working of error, that they may believe a lie, that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity” (ibid., 10–11).

O spectacle worthy of the wonder of the whole world, if on this side Moses and Aaron with effective signs are considered, and on that side Jannes and Mambres with lying signs. On this side Aaron, chosen by God; on that side Balaam, brought in by an impious king. For those have not yet failed who are thrust in by violence and royal power. On this side stand Peter, Paul, and Stephen, together with the choir of those who strive to live apostolically and to serve God chastely; on that side Simon Magus, unclean Nicholas, and faithless Ananias, who was fraudulent with goods designated for the use of the poor and was anathematized together with his accomplices who share in his iniquity.

And, to conclude briefly: upon Mount Zion—that is, upon the apostolic life begun from Mount Zion—stands the Lamb, and with him the one hundred and forty-four thousand who were purchased from the earth. But upon the sand lies that beast of which John says: “And I saw a beast rising from the sea” (Rev. 13:1). With it is the flock of those [Col. 1426A] who build upon sand, having no rock in their foundation, because they are proved to be neither rightly married with Job, nor chaste with Daniel, nor just rulers with Noah. Therefore, unless they are willing to bring forth fruits worthy of repentance, they cannot enter life. Yet many of them would undoubtedly repent if they heard from Peter’s vicar those words: “Save yourselves from this crooked generation” (Acts 2:40).

[LIVES OF BERENGER AND WIRNTO.]

[Col. 1425]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING WORK

(D. B. Pezius, preface to vol. I of *Anecdota*, p. LXXXV.)

Very few of those received into the choirs of the blessed have obtained the fortune of finding so learned and celebrated a writer of their lives as did the blessed Berenger and Wirnto, illustrious abbots of the Benedictine monastery of Formbach on the Inn. This writer is the great Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, of the Order of Regular Canons of St Augustine. His work, however, long remained hidden and would doubtless still today lie concealed, wrapped in ancient parchments, had not the industry and kindness of the most reverend and learned Father Clarus Fasmann, prior of Formbach, brought a copy of it into our hands.

This copy was prepared according to the authority of a parchment codex preserved in the archives of Formbach, which, when we saw it, appeared to us to be more than four hundred years old. We saw another handwritten copy of the same work in a paper codex in the library of St Peter’s at Salzburg, but it is only three hundred years old. Moreover, what Gerhoh here recounts is so much the more worthy of belief because his testimony is in many respects more uncorrupted. In the prologue he indicates that he will write and treat of signs which, in his own time, by the Lord’s bounty, he had seen with his own eyes as though in his own household, and had as it were touched and handled with his own hands.

As for the cult of these two blessed men, we wrote to the celebrated Father Clarus about it, and on 10 December 1720 he replied in these words:

> “Thirteen years ago, while a burial crypt was being built, nearly the entire pavement of our whole church was excavated, in the hope that perhaps some trace of the tomb of the blessed Berenger and Wirnto might be found. But we laboured in vain, although we dug up the ground to a considerable depth. The two blessed abbots are honoured by neither public nor any other cult. Yet in our necrology we read the following:
>
> ‘On 6 March, the holy death of the most blessed Wirnto, second abbot of this place, worker of rare miracles, in the year 1127, the nineteenth of his rule, buried before the altar of the Holy Cross.’
>
> Again, concerning Blessed Theoderic, the same necrology reads:
>
> ‘On the third day before the Kalends of July, the pious death of Theoderic, third abbot of our community, returning from Jerusalem; on the day of his burial God, manifesting his innocence, made it illustrious by three miraculous signs.’
>
> And finally:
>
> ‘On the fourth day before the Kalends of November, Berenger, holy first abbot of our community, in the year 1108. He presided for fourteen years.’”

These are the words of Father Clarus, most knowledgeable in the affairs of his own house.

[Col. 1425]

## THE LIVES OF THE BLESSED ABBOTS OF FORMBACH, BERENGER AND WIRNTO, OF THE ORDER OF ST BENEDICT, BY GERHOH, PROVOST OF REICHERSBERG

(A certain Benedictine of Formbach extracted this from a manuscript codex of his illustrious monastery; D. B. Pezius published it in *Anecdota* I, III, 397.)

Here begins the prologue of Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, to the lives of the blessed abbots Berenger and Wirnto.

[Col. 1425A] Divine mercy, which everywhere bestows its benefits upon all persons according to the riches of its goodness, when the time came to show mercy looked down from heaven [Col. 1426A] to hear the groaning of those in fetters and to loose the bonds of the afflicted. For our land, which once, struck by the hail of sins, brought forth no fruit [Col. 1427A] for the salvation of those who languished—while other lands shone far and wide with miracles—has now, watered by the drops of grace, received the Lord’s goodness, and our land has yielded its fruit. The signs which we marvel at as performed in other lands we now, by the Lord’s bounty, see with our own eyes as though in our own homes, and as it were touch and handle with our hands.

This, Lord Jesus, is the condescension of your mercy; this is the customary visitation of your compassion. Overlooking our sins, you have commanded us to behold grace and glory in the manifestation of signs. For in this you have shown that you hate nothing that you have made, you who make your sun rise upon the good and the evil and rain upon the just and the unjust. Therefore, since it is good to conceal the secret of a king and glorious to proclaim the righteous acts of God, [Col. 1427B] for the edification of the faithful who love God and his saints—not fearing or heeding those who disdain not only to read the deeds of saints [Col. 1428A] but even to hear them, and who habitually hate and despise them, loving the inventions of Maro, the writings of Cicero, and the trifles of Naso more than the signs of Nicholas, the virtues of Aegidius, and of Christ’s other friends—we commend to memory an evident example of God’s mercy in the glorification of saints. God deigned to reveal them for this reason: that in their bodies he might declare what their blessed spirits merit in his presence.

And because the day of the Lamb’s wrath is near, he wishes to anticipate his own with praises; he wishes to visit and console those who desired him with their whole heart, lest their merits remain hidden and lest these others be able to offer any spark of excuse. Let him who wishes read; let him who does not wish reject it, because, as the poet says: “No poems please.” And our other poet, the truthful one, says: “Not all have faith” (2 Thess. 3:2), and “not all obey the Gospel” (2 Thess. 1:8).

Here begins something concerning the life and virtues of the holy abbot Wirnto.

[Col. 1427]

## CHAPTER I. Wirnto’s birth; his holy childhood and youth; his entrance into the monastery of Formbach under Berenger, its first abbot; and Berenger’s holy death.

[Col. 1427B]

Therefore, as faithful antiquity relates—a source to which I do not think it unfitting to give unquestioning belief—Wirnto was born in the western regions, of a noble stock, a blessed stock, and a holy root. Given by his parents to scholastic disciplines, he chose the way of truth and sought knowledge of the truth. But he considered no knowledge profitable except the mystery of the cross. For he did not, as this age commonly does, embrace the world’s wantonness; rather, he wholly and altogether devoted himself to God. He loved the solemn exercises of prayer, vigils, and fasting, and judged the service of God to be the highest freedom.

But when he came to the fork of Pythagoras’s letter, leaving the left-hand branch with all the vanity of the world, he embraced the right with all eagerness—indeed, with complete perfection. He followed Christ, who is the Way and the Truth, so that he might deserve to be crowned among those at the right hand. Therefore, leaving relatives and acquaintances so that he might devote himself more freely to God, he departed from his homeland and, by God’s ordering—without whom nothing was made and nothing ever shall be, and who knows all things even before they occur—entered Noricum. There he devoted all that he possessed, and himself, to God through prayer and psalmody night and day.

There is in Bavaria, beside the banks of the River Inn, a place called Formbach, consecrated in honour of the Mother of God. It was then governed by a man of great holiness, remarkable abstinence, and remarkable foresight, beloved by God and men, named Berenger. What he taught in words he showed by example: he was a comforter of widows and orphans and a refreshment to the poor. Since we are hastening on to other matters, let it suffice to have touched briefly on these things.

But when it pleased the King of kings to give his soldier the reward of life for his day’s labour, his flesh—now no longer flesh, but thin, pale skin worn by scourges—was seized by fever. In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1108, in the fourteenth year of his rule, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, at God’s command his holy soul was released from the flesh, entered the palace of heaven, and was received by rejoicing angels into their fellowship. His body was committed to burial in the basilica of Blessed Mary.

That this blessed soul now reigns with Christ is attested by the benefits of miracles which occur at his tomb, not yearly [Col. 1428C] but daily. He was the first abbot predestined by God for the Church of Formbach. And if a better fortune follows a mournful beginning, how much more does a pleasant beginning await a blessed outcome in every respect. Blessed Church, blessed household, whose foundation is Christ, which this man inaugurated—Christ who is Alpha and Omega. Blessed, I say, was the beginning, but better is the end, through the gift of him who is the author of all good things.

## CHAPTER II. Wirnto succeeds Berenger in the government of the abbey; his virtues, reputation, and favour with princes; his singular mercy and generosity toward the poor and needy.

The Church of Formbach, therefore, bereft of its shepherd, turns with its whole heart to the Shepherd and Bishop of our souls [Col. 1428D], and humbly prays that He may grant it a suitable pastor. And because the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and His ears unto their prayers, they were not defrauded of their desire, but He heard them in abundance. Why should I delay further? By God’s command, then, Wirnto is unanimously chosen; having been chosen, he is consecrated; having been consecrated, he is proclaimed worthy of the office by all.

Having undertaken pastoral care, he now strives to break with his former observances. Once his honours had increased, he began to increase his labours; he began more austerely to subdue the flesh, to prolong his vigils, to love the frequency of prayers ever more frequently and earnestly; to enlarge the place entrusted to him in possessions and benefactions; abundantly to refresh the flock committed to him with temporal and eternal nourishment [Col. 1429A]; and to commend good things to them more by his examples than by his words. No human speech, I think—indeed, I do not think it, but truly know it—is able to express the generosity of his almsgiving and the constancy of his virtues. Yet a man knows only so much as he receives from God.

And it would be altogether unworthy if the deeds and miracles of one through whom so many have been healed, and are daily healed, should remain hidden; especially when we see committed to memory the vain glory of weddings, the various outcomes of wars, and the praises of victories—things which bring us no other benefit than that they occupy the time of those who read them and pleasantly tickle their ears.

God gave Wirnto such favour in the sight of princes that, because of the merits of his holiness [Col. 1429B], they revered him as a father, as a righteous man, and as a saint—as indeed he was. They strove to touch his garments as though they were relics of holiness, thinking themselves fortunate if they might anywhere deserve his company. They also offered many gifts, all of which he distributed among the poor; nor could he distribute as much as they eagerly endeavoured to offer. And deservedly so, because he whom God had suffused with grace was loved by all, and “all things work together for good to those who love God.”

Whenever money ran short and the cheerful giver’s hand ceased from distributing, he would summon his steward and say: “Go out into the streets and lanes of the city, and gather the poor and feeble, the blind and lame; for tomorrow salvation will be ours; tomorrow we shall enjoy such abundance that we may comfort those who [Col. 1429C] are in every distress.” When morning came, the prophecy of the blessed man was fulfilled: envoys of individual princes rushed in crowds to him and heaped up innumerable gifts.

He himself then went forth, as he often did; his servant, burdened with heaps of coins, followed panting, so that you would have thought him another Geta. A little seat was placed for him to sit upon; a crowd of poor people flew upon him from every side; and that treasure was distributed to Christ’s treasure, through which the treasure of the heavenly kingdom is attained.

I am about to tell a very small matter—and yet I shall tell it. If he encountered a woman with child, though she did not yet show an evident sign of pregnancy, he gave her two coins, saying: “One is due to you; the other to him whom you carry in your womb.” What more need be said? She departed, smiling just a little, joyful at having been enriched by the double gift [Col. 1429D].

## CHAPTER III. Water repeatedly changed into wine by Wirnto’s miracle.

Trustworthy witnesses—whose testimony it would be madness to impugn—state that he once came, at the invitation of a certain knight, to that knight’s lodging. The knight rejoiced to receive him as a guest, as though he had received Elijah or one of the prophets. He hurried eagerly to meet him, received his horse, led Wirnto into the lodging, arranged a seat with his own hands, prepared a festive banquet, summoned relatives and acquaintances, and, as cheerfully as though Peter or one of the apostles were his guest at table, sat down to feast.

About the middle of the meal, a servant offered the knight a bowl; and another man served the saint water drawn from a spring, as he himself had humbly and secretly requested before the meal [Col. 1430A]. One of the guests, wishing to share in his blessing, asked that a cup of water be given to him. The servant, hesitating not at all and suspecting nothing untoward, offered the cup to the man who requested it, supposedly for a blessing, unaware of what had happened.

He received it and drank: for the water had been divinely changed into the sweetest wine. But ignorant of what had occurred, he made this mocking remark, as is the habit of laymen, “the hammers of the learned”: “Oh, what a blessed man! Oh, what a holy man, who knows how to drink nothing but the finest wine! I too could readily equal this holiness, if I were commanded to labour amid such delights.”

The servant who had drawn the water was troubled; and, fully aware of the matter, he maintained that he had offered water, not wine; if it had now become something else, he did not know it. But when they recognized that God had performed this miracle through him, they rejoiced, were glad, and all shared in the blessing of the new wine. The knight who had mocked the saint was abashed and blushed; he asked forgiveness and received pardon; thereafter he was a supporter of his holiness, not a detractor.

O wonderful event, and, after Him who was the author of this miracle at Cana of Galilee, quite unprecedented! But the blessed man, in order to avoid human fame, earnestly asked that they tell no one of it. I do not know whether he obtained this request. His servants who still survive, however, affirm that the same thing frequently occurred when he sat at table in familiar company; but we omit even well-known matters, lest we become burdensome to anyone.

## CHAPTER IV. The corpse of a boy formerly guilty of an offence against his mother, struck with rods by her at Wirnto’s command, and thereby—though it had previously been unable to do so—reduced to ashes.

[Col. 1430C]

At another time, as those whose testimony must be believed assert—and whose names we would have included, had this not wearied readers—the blessed man was on a journey and was making for a church situated beside the road. A certain woman, lamenting and tearfully accompanying the small funeral procession of her son, met him. For she had buried the boy’s brother nearly three or four years before, and had asked the grave-diggers to place brother beside brother, so that one grave might cherish those whom she uniquely loved.

They came, then, to complete the funeral rites [Col. 1430D], and the blessed man, out of human kindness, approached in order that he too might render service at the funeral.
