When the grave was opened, the body buried three years earlier was found so fresh and uncorrupted as though it had been buried the previous day. At this sight the mother fell backward with all who were present; she beat her breast with her palms, tore out her hair with pitiful wailing, and by her weeping stirred those standing around into tears.

For it was a misery to behold. Her heart was indeed moved over her son; and she was all the more distressed because it was not readily apparent what cause had intervened to make the body remain uncorrupted for so long. Then young men gathered around the tomb; the body was handled and tossed this way and that, yet, as before, it appeared incorrupt.

The mother, recovering her breath, with her hair dishevelled, hurried up and, like another Mary, watered the saint’s feet [Col. 1431A] with tears, beseeching him with prayers of this sort: “If you have, O holy man, any confidence in Christ; if, as I hear, you have any hope laid up in heaven, come to the aid of one who groans; pity a widow and a desolate woman; have mercy on my misery and unhappiness. Deign to entreat with prayers Him who refuses you nothing, that He may reveal to you what offence this boy has committed, for which he did not deserve to remain within the law of those buried, although he seemed to me wholly conspicuous for goodness, as befitted a simple and upright child.”

He fled the woman’s embraces; he fled worldly favour, crying out that he was unworthy of such an embassy. Rather, he said, she should go to the shrines of saints who by their prayers and merits might obtain for her the assistance she sought; she should leave him alone [Col. 1431B] and not mock one who, being set among earthly things, served earthly things.

Nevertheless, overcome by the people’s plea and especially by the woman’s anguish, he took her aside and carefully asked whether she had ever inflicted any insulting injury upon her son, or her son upon her. “How,” she said, “could I harm the light of my eyes, the staff of my old age, the consolation, hope, and salvation of body and soul?”

But he said: “Recall carefully; for no one is free from sin, not even an infant of one hour.”

“I am conscious of nothing,” she replied, “except that once, while playing and joking with me, the boy struck my head in childish simplicity with the stick he carried in his hand. In striking me he wounded me, and a little blood flowed.”

“Was the boy punished for that?” asked the saint [Col. 1431C].

“By no means,” she said.

“Go, then,” he said, “take rods, and in the Lord’s name correct your son with blows; for, as I perceive, what you have said is an obstacle to him.”

The saint prayed; the mother, though unwilling, multiplied blows upon her son. After the blows, the body dissolved into ashes and vanished, united to mother earth. Let no believer be ignorant that this was accomplished not by chance but by the prayers of the saint: he gave counsel as to what should be done, then the power of release, and finally applied the effectiveness of his whole prayer.

## CHAPTER V. The soul of a certain man almost snatched from the jaws of demons through Wirnto’s action.

A knight, brought to his last extremity, sent to Wirnto an honourable and distinguished messenger [Col. 1431D], humbly begging that he might restore his wavering soul by his coming. For he believed himself fortunate if he might deserve the favour of his visitation.

There was another man in another province, tormented by an evil spirit. Amid his other ravings and pratings, uttering now truths and now falsehoods, he told those present that his master, with all the attendants of iniquity, was gathering to gain the knight’s soul, and that he himself must be present.

Wirnto, therefore, who would spend not only temporal goods but even himself, if necessity so required, for his neighbour’s salvation, hurried his journey when he heard the message. Immediately at his arrival every wicked power vanished like smoke. He snatched that soul, refreshed by the grace of prayer, confession, and the Eucharist, as though from the midst of the abyss [Col. 1432A], and joined it to the Lord; he entrusted the material of its flesh to the earth.

But after the struggle the demon wickedly revisited the house which he had temporarily left. Asked about the profit of the undertaking, he said: “We came with fruitless labour; we received nothing but disgrace. A certain most wicked heretic, Wirnto, violently snatched our own possession from us.” For what is this? “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11:12).

## CHAPTER VI. A few little fish multiplied through the merits of the blessed man. Why the author refrained from recounting more miracles performed by Wirnto while alive.

[Col. 1432B]

On one occasion, while the blessed man was travelling beyond the Enns on Church business, a venerable widow invited him, like another Elisha, and asked him to dine. He consented to her request, entered, reclined at table, and rested. But she, unaware that he did not live on meat and fat but sustained his humble life only with vegetables, prepared such a meal as she could afford, set the tables, and bade the guests sit down.

A little before the hour of the meal, Wirnto summoned the widow privately: “What dishes, mother, have you prepared,” he said, “for your son? Is everything ready? Must we then sit down?”

“My lord,” she answered, “I have no more delicate foods, no more pleasant dishes. Far from me are all novelty, variety, and multitude of courses. But what I have, that I give you: namely rustic bread with garlic and whatever else is available to me.”

But he said: “You ought not to trouble yourself much on my account. For I know how to abound, and I know how to suffer want. Give what you have prepared to my companions. But for me—what I tell you in your ear, lest the others hear it or speak ill of us—prepare a little vegetables and a cup of water.”

She seized her cloak, covered her shoulders, and, with uncombed hair, hurried out. She rushed this way and that at the swiftest pace, in case something might present itself suitable for the nourishment of the man of God. For in this hope she had placed her confidence. And because hope does not put to shame, she met a boy carrying three little fish. Had he carried one fewer and had five loaves, you might not inaptly have thought him the one whom Andrew pointed out to the Lord in the Gospel [Col. 1432D], though the Lord did not fail to know him, He who knew all things, both last and first.

But He who then caused the boy with fish and loaves to be present for Himself now likewise provided the widow with a carrier of so many fish, so that His servant might be fed and so that His providence—which provides, holds, and governs all things—might not fail in its own ordering. She therefore bought the little fish, heaven-sent to her, for a small coin, quickly returned home, cooked them, placed them cooked upon a dish, covered them with garlic, and set them before Wirnto.

By God’s command the fish were so increased in their hands and, so to speak, grew, that he himself had abundance and generously supplied all the guests from them. Of this matter I shall introduce not one witness, but the whole region beyond the Enns [Col. 1433A], who still remember the deed, reverently believe it, and publicly confess it. The abbot of Formbach holds the parish in which that widow lived; it is governed, provided for, and administered by him, or by another deputy whom he may appoint.

There are many more and much greater benefits of his miracles, by which the Lord deigned to glorify him while he yet lived. But some, lest I lie, forgetfulness has stolen from us; others, although well known to us and worthy of the pen, we have omitted because of their length and because of the envy of people who, with beast-like manners, rage at the happiness of others, and because of the cunning of detractors. Otherwise they might say that we had not [Col. 1433B] proved or seen the things of which we speak, nor heard them in such a manner as to deserve belief, but had rather dreamed them up for the sake of flattery.

But let none of the wise be disturbed if the hostility of unbelievers opposes the glory of believers, since rivals likewise assailed the King of Glory Himself with reproachful insults. [Col. 1434A] Does it seem rare or new to you that there are lilies among thorns, wheat among tares, grapes among wild vines? Thus the chaste live among those devoted to lust, the poor among the rich, the elect among the reprobate and heretics, and those suffering persecution among persecutors. Therefore the elect will be so much the more glorious as they have been more frequent in persecutions. How, indeed, could they be called steadfast in faith if no adversity shook them?

“How,” someone asks, “can a rose be distinguished without even the thorn injuring it; wheat, without the tares corrupting it; a grape, without the wild vine tainting it?” “He will separate them,” He says, “as a shepherd separates sheep from goats” (Matthew 25:32). And: “The Son of Man will send His angels, and they shall gather out of His kingdom all scandals” (Matthew 13:41); and He will say to the reapers: “Pull up the tares [Col. 1434B] and gather them into bundles to be burned; but gather the wheat into my barn” (ibid., 30).

Let us leave aside these superfluous matters, lest we weary anyone, and turn to the miracles which the Lord performed through him after his death.

*The Life of Blessed Wirnto ends.*

*Concerning his death begins.*

[Col. 1433]

## CHAPTER VII. Wirnto’s final words to his own people; his illness, death, and burial in the place where Perngerus had been committed to the earth.

After that master of the household, lord of all things [Col. 1433C], wished to give his labourer—Wirnto, namely, who had faithfully laboured in His vineyard from morning, that is, from his earliest age, until evening, that is, until the completion of his life, and had borne the burden and heat of the day—the denarius of life, the blessed man was seized by a fever and laid low in a bed that offered him poor comfort, while his whole spirit was raised to God.

Then indeed there was grief and mourning; all lamented with one voice: “To whom, Father, do you abandon us? To whom do you leave us desolate?”

Moved by their tears and their mournful voices, he tried to calm their complaint in this way: “Do not grieve, brothers; do not so afflict yourselves over the absence of a little dust. Rather, knock by prayers upon Him who fashioned human birth, that He may revive the soul which He created. For God [Col. 1433D], not for my sake but for His own, has now for many days, as it seems to me—I do not know whether it seems so to you—mercifully governed, protected, and preserved us and our place. He has supplied the necessities of life, as seemed very good to Him and to us. Let us render Him such thanks as we can.

“For I shall go, not many days hence, when it pleases the Lord. But provide another for yourselves, whom you may establish in my stead, through whom you may please God; for you will not have me long.”

But the brothers, confused and distressed by the sadness of grief, said: “To whom, Father, shall we flee? To whom shall we go? Give counsel; bring help. We believe that the Lord, since He has had mercy through you [Col. 1434B], will still have mercy upon us.”

“If,” he said, “you obey me, you will not go astray. And what I can say with a safe conscience is this: not I, but the Lord will show you whom you should choose, whom you should appoint as your Father, through whom you may be fully governed in matters relating to God and to people [Col. 1434C]. Theodoric, whom you appointed as my chaplain, I know to be a man of virtue, desiring God with his whole heart. If it pleases you, let him be appointed in my place.

“Yet I say this in persuasion, not in command: if you receive any of those whom I excluded from this place because of the enormity of their deeds, you will immediately be cut off from unity; you will immediately be destroyed.”

Behold, the spirit of Elijah rested upon this blessed man: what he foretold in hope came to pass in fact. O blessed man, ineffable in virtues, wondrous in signs, not unfittingly to be compared with the prophets!

Then Wirnto said: “Come, brothers, if I have found favour in your sight, consent to my prayers; do not disappoint me in my hopes, so that I may receive from you at least this final gift of reconciliation [Col. 1434D].”

“Ask,” they said, “Lord, for we are ready to go with you into prison and into death.”

He said: “Join my bones in burial with the bones of Perngerus, my righteous and holy predecessor, so that those whom God assigned to one place, enriched with one name of adoption—that is, that of abbot—and united by the bond of charity, may, when He comes to be glorified in His saints, find their united bodies in a single tomb.”

They assented, granted his request, and promised to fulfil his vow. Why did he ask to be joined to him? Was it that he might be made blessed by him? I do not deny this; but perhaps rather because that place was destined to be made illustrious by signs, and this honour would be attributed to his companion rather than to himself, just as Benedict attributed to Maurus the rescue of Placid.

Wirnto, therefore, having commended himself and all his flock to the Lord, was released from the prison of the flesh. At once the scent of balsam spread through the whole dwelling, so that you would have believed some angelic visitation to have been present. Thus, with angels accompanying him and even singing a hymn, that holy soul entered the heavenly palace. This was in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1127, in the nineteenth year of his ordination, on the sixth day before the Ides of March.

The brothers, judging it unworthy that so great a Father should be separated from the fellowship of the greater church, resolved to go and, should necessity demand it, to disinter Perngerus and join him to Wirnto. After deliberation, they reverently buried Wirnto in the middle of the monastery before the altar of the Holy Cross, where he now rests in the Lord [Col. 1435A].

Not much time elapsed when some frightening apparition, I do not know what, appeared near the church of the Mother of God, where blessed Perngerus lay. Those who came there did not dare remain long, but were shaken and driven back by terror and wondered at it. Therefore, meeting together, they perceived that the terror occurred because the bodies of the saints had been separated. After taking counsel, they disinterred him, brought him into the monastery, and honourably joined him to saint Wirnto, as Wirnto himself had requested, so that those whose merit before the Lord was equal might not have their bodies divided even by the wrong of separate burial [Col. 1435B].

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the appointment, persecution, and death of Theodoric, appointed abbot on Wirnto’s advice.

[Col. 1435C]

After the grief and mourning following the departure of blessed Wirnto had somewhat subsided, the brothers met unanimously, took counsel, unanimously elected Theodoric, and, in accordance with the command of their pious Father, set him over themselves as Father. Having obtained authority, he strove, through prayers and vigils and every kind of virtue, to persevere as he had learned from a good master.

He transgressed his master’s command concerning the reception of the excluded brothers. Seeking to become all things to all people, he delighted and rejoiced to accommodate himself to the ways of all. And while he wished to become excessively humane [Col. 1436A], while he wished to cherish his own men with charity and mercy as a father cherishes his children, while he wished to gather the scattered and preserve those gathered, he received enemies among the brothers, wolves among the sheep, destroyers rather than protectors, lovers of discord. Nor is it surprising, since the serpent often lies hidden in the grass.

Having entered the monastery, they stirred up the people and disturbed the flock. Conspiracies arose; detractions arose; letters were written; property was dissipated. Some accusations were sent through them to the bishop of Passau, others through others to the margrave of Neuburg; shortages, losses, and other things of that kind were brought forward.

When an opportune day came, the bishop and margrave assembled with clergy and people. The abbot was surrounded, assailed, and slandered; and because he preferred to be subject rather than to rule, because he was willing to be driven out, he was easily driven out and easily deposed. He left his place and people and sought where he might serve the Lord in holiness and righteousness, so that he might be delivered without fear from the hands of his enemies [Col. 1436B].

But the sounder party, seeing the Father’s disgrace and sympathizing with him, likewise left the place; strangers entered in. The princes, seeing that violence had been inflicted upon God’s servant through envy, were moved by an unjust compassion and sent a delegation after him and on his behalf, asking, commanding, and ordering him to return to his own people. But unwilling to submit to lay service or any unjust allegiance or power, he could not be recalled. With God’s help, not long afterwards he set out for Jerusalem, to worship in the place where the Lord’s feet had stood. On his return journey, weakened by illness, he fell asleep in the Lord on the third day before the Kalends of July [Col. 1436C]; and, it is said, three signs shone forth on the day of his burial.

But what God has done through him from that day to these times, or is doing, is beyond our ability to know. Many also say that none of his adversaries departed this world with an equal end or without vengeance. The margrave—whose name, lest his supporters be angry with me, I suppress—died in Emperor Frederick’s expedition against Milan; nor did the standing or prosperity of this place thereafter flourish as it had before.

# Concerning the signs and miracles which the Lord manifested through the merits of the blessed man

[Col. 1435]

## CHAPTER IX. At the tomb of Saint Wirnto sight restored to blind persons, the use of her hands restored to a certain woman; demons driven from the bodies of the possessed, etc.

[Col. 1435D]

On the day after blessed Wirnto’s burial, a certain poor blind widow, whom he had supported with alms during his lifetime for the honour of God, clung to his tomb, keeping vigils and devoting herself to prayer. Night and day, amid sighs of tears, she uttered this complaint: “Why, O Lord,” she said, “why have You done this to me? You have taken away the light of my eyes; You have made me a naked widow, a poor woman deprived of every resource. Yet because You are merciful and compassionate in thousands, You bestowed all these things upon me in Wirnto [Col. 1436D], and in him You have taken all these things from me. Oh! Oh, why have You done this?”

Having said this, wearied by grief, pain, and labour, she fell asleep; and upon waking she was suddenly enlightened through the merits of the saint and returned joyfully to her own home.

There was another woman, deprived of livelihood and possessions, blind from birth. It was revealed to her in a vision that if she visited the tomb of the blessed man and offered some offering, however small, with prayer, she would regain sight through the merits of the saints. When she awoke from sleep, she ran, went, and hurried, carrying with her whatever she could lay hands upon.

While she was on the way, not far from the place and upon a hill, the Lord granted her sight; she rejoiced so greatly at having recovered it that, seeing the entire lay of the place from a distance, she described everything to her companions. Nevertheless [Col. 1437A], she completed the journey she had begun, offered prayer with her offering, and departed joyfully.

A certain woman’s hand was so withered that it denied her its service; it hung down in such a way that you would have thought it cut off. Her friends urged her to seek the help of the saints for restoration of her hand, in case health might be given back to her. But she, as though already despairing, ignored their advice and neglected to seek the saints’ help.

Her friends therefore compelled her and, almost against her will, accompanied her all the way to Formbach. They placed her hand upon the blessed man’s tomb and poured out prayers to God with her and for her; then they returned home. But on the journey she declared that she felt things like ants moving around her arm; and the longer this continued, the more the sensation increased [Col. 1437B], until the pain began to creep away like running ants. What more need be said? Before she entered her house, the hand was so completely restored to health that no woman could be found her equal in any work within female capacity, whereas previously she had not even been able to move it.

On a neighbouring estate of the monastery there was a man who had served the brothers and had been blind for two years. Remaining steadfast in perfect faith, he visited the saint’s tomb and devoted himself for some time to prayer. As he returned home, he withdrew his hand from his guide and went on alone along a straight path. “Go,” he said to his guide, “to your guide: through you the Lord has done great things for me, because He is mighty and His name is holy. For through the merits of blessed Wirnto no one will be able to see more clearly than I [Col. 1437C].”

Certain trustworthy witnesses, venerable even for their grey hair, whose faith seems to me not to be despised, assert that on one day they saw three persons cleansed of an evil spirit: two at the monument of the blessed man, one of whom was cleansed of as many spirits as Mary Magdalene; the third was healed in the church of Saint Martin. These same persons also affirmed under oath that nearly forty and more miraculous benefits were accomplished there in their own time. But they said these had been given over to oblivion through the passage of time and especially through human negligence, because, although great, they occurred rarely.

But because a lamp should not be hidden under a bushel, but placed upon a lampstand so that it may give light to all who are in the house, we have taken care to set forth for posterity those things set before our eyes which we saw, with those whom mercy aided and the peoples of many regions as witnesses, so that God may be praised in His saints.

## CHAPTER X. A demon, more obstinate than the others, driven from the body of a possessed woman through the merits of Saint Wirnto.

In the time of Lord Abbot Henry, who was sixth after blessed Perngerus, the first overseer of the place of Formbach, and who governed, enlarged, and protected the place and its people wisely, honourably, and vigorously, a certain woman came, escorted to Passau. She had visited almost all the shrines of saints—namely those of Peter and Paul at Rome, of James in Galicia, of Aegidius, of Leonard, and then those saints who are magnificently venerated because the grace of God has been manifested through them in the Church of Salzburg [Col. 1438A]. For she was afflicted by three evil spirits, as later became clear.

Finally, by God’s ordering, accompanied by a great crowd, she was brought to Formbach. Since night was approaching, lodging was assigned to her; she was enclosed under watch through the night and given such refreshment as humanity could provide. At daybreak the dean of the monastery, being asked, went out and ordered her to be led to the church. As she walked far ahead and he followed, he slowly raised his hand amid the crowd and, murmuring something good within himself, made the sign of the cross behind her.

She turned back, raged, burned with fury, threatened, and commanded him not to do so again. She was then led into the church, placed at the tomb, and surrounded by the crowd. Devout prayers and petitions were poured out to the Lord for her [Col. 1438B]. Meanwhile the evil spirit disturbed the woman, grievously constrained her, and cruelly tortured her, while all the people begged the brothers to offer prayers for her, in case God might show mercy to those who asked.

The Father of the monastery, moved by mercy, pitied the afflicted woman from the depths of his heart and assembled the community. “Brothers,” he said, “if I judge rightly, agree with me; if wrongly, correct me. We have, like many others, the patronage of saints; by God’s gift, we possess bodies which the Lord glorified by miracles even while they lived in this life. And, as it seems to me—I do not know whether I proceed rightly—if the clouds of our sins did not hinder us, they would shine forth in miracles even now [Col. 1438C], while they reign with the Lord.

“If, then, it seems right in our eyes, for the glorification of the saints, the redemption of sins, and especially the salvation of the persons now present, let us undertake a three-day fast, that we may obtain mercy and find grace in time of need.”

This proposal pleased everyone. They most gladly promised their assent, saying that God should be prayed to for people’s salvation, according to the saying: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfil the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). And again: “Ask and you shall receive” (John 16:24); everyone who asks receives. He who asks nothing, I do not know what he receives; nor does the kingdom of God come to those who sleep.

But because, as someone said, nothing is blessed in every respect, two brothers wished to break the unity of that agreement [Col. 1438D]. They said that what pleased the Lord had been done; if it pleased Him, it could be done otherwise; therefore there was no need to fast, because He Himself deliberates without you what He determines concerning a matter.

The lord abbot, seeing them obstinate in their purpose, left them to their own judgment, permitting them to do what they wished lest they scandalize others; for an incurable wound must be cut away with the sword lest the healthy part be infected. The institution mentioned above was therefore devoutly undertaken by the rest. Prayers, entreaties, petitions, vigils, and almsgiving were more frequent than usual; and, as the Ninevites cried to the Lord with strength, He heard them in abundance.

Thus armed with spiritual weapons, they approached the woman whom the ancient enemy tormented. That wicked spirit was bound and constrained through the power of Christ’s servant [Col. 1439A] and through the merits and names of saints, and was commanded to leave God’s creature. “You labour in vain,” it said, “and vainly expend your pratings; my hour has not yet come.” It professed now that it would drive away Virgil, now Vitalis, now Pilgrim.

Because it was a liar from the beginning and its father was such, they did not believe it as it sought evasions. Instead, they persisted in prayer, rebuked it more strongly, and adjured it at least, as the third spirit, to indicate to them where it was to be expelled. Considering it unworthy to cast words further to the winds, they implored, entreated, and continually besought with heart and voice Him to whom every heart lies open and every desire speaks, for the person’s salvation.

That night was spent sleeplessly; everyone’s whole attention was directed to God [Col. 1439B]. About midnight, amid sighs of tears and the solemnities of prayer, the voices of laypeople, as is the custom of those keeping vigil in church by night, resounded loudly in praise of God and His saints. By God’s mercy, and through the intercession of blessed Andrew, as we believe, the woman lost one of the unclean spirits, though those standing around did not know it. For they had often previously seen her displaying the same gestures and the same frenzies, and therefore they could not readily be persuaded that this expulsion had occurred.

Then, with the people following, she was led to the greater altar of the Mother of God. There, as shortly before, she was exorcized, adjured, and commanded to leave God’s creature. But one of the two demons that remained wickedly behind, crying and wailing in a wondrous and pitiable manner, said [Col. 1439C]:

“Oh, crime! Oh, Christian treachery! Oh, the deceit of Christians—or rather, of heretics—by whose cunning I have lost one of my companions. Why then do you stand there? What are you waiting for, most wretched race? Why do you not exalt Andrew with voices and prayers? Why do you not heap thanks upon him for the expulsion of my little brother? Oh, fear! Oh, punishment, which makes me eloquent even in my guilt!”

Then, turning to the fugitive spirit, it said: “Why, you of little faith, why did you doubt? Did you reverence Andrew more than your master? Go, go; flee, flee. You will be solemnly received and will obtain a reward worthy of your labour.”

All who were present therefore gave praise to the Lord for the grace bestowed upon themselves and upon the woman; and still [Col. 1439D] placing great confidence in His mercy, they lifted hands and minds to heaven and importuned the Mother of Mercy with voices and prayers, humbly begging her to remember their common sex. Then, as some suggested that perhaps God had determined to honor another place by the expulsion of another demon, and as all waited in this hope, she was led to the church of the Mother of God outside the monastery. Everyone persevered in prayer, and, through the merits of the Mother of Mercy, the person was cleansed of a second demon, and praise was rendered to the Creator of all.

Although two spirits of wickedness had been driven out, a third still remained. He boasted that he was the prince of the others and, as though exercising free power, arrogantly maintained that he would remain there a perpetual guest. He declared that the other two fugitive spirits [Col. 1440A] were cowardly, fickle, unstable, with the heart of a hare; indeed, he proclaimed them lowborn and poor. This one uttered marvels in a marvelous fashion: now he hurled whirlwinds of mockery and detraction; now he rolled forth thunderclaps of terror; now he provoked people to laughter and guffaws. Thus, if it had not been evident that one person was being consumed by laughter and another by grief, such spectacles would have pleased fools and simpletons.

It happened that a certain garment, which need not be named, had been secretly removed; acquaintances mixed with strangers were brought in and ordered to stand around the possessed woman, wishing to discover whether they might believe anything certain from her words—whether the wicked robber truly lodged there—although they had already hoped that the woman was wholly healed, and especially wished [Col. 1440B] to be made certain regarding the loss of the garment. The demon, however, addressed each person by name, disclosed each person’s deeds, good and bad alike, finally pointed out the guilty thief, and indicated where the stolen article lay concealed.

The father of the monastery resolved to undertake a three-day fast without food for the man’s salvation. But on the second day, when guests arrived, he broke the fast for the sake of humanity and charity, though unwillingly. When he approached the woman among the others, she raved, snarled, spat, and called him unclean, an empty vessel, full of malice and perfidy.

But the brethren, trusting in the Lord and directing their hopes and minds toward Him, gave themselves to stricter observance. They increased prayers, vigils, and fasts beyond their customary measure; [Col. 1440C] through the assistance of litanies they implored the patronage of the saints for the sufferer’s healing. Such zeal of devotion burned among them that even boys of tender age—to say nothing of old men and younger men—submitted themselves voluntarily to penance, gave themselves up to be scourged, and suddenly strove after some degree of perfection, as far as their age allowed.

All the priests came forward, armed beforehand with spiritual weapons; by invoking the divine name they bound, adjured, and constrained the demon to leave the vessel which he wickedly possessed, or at least to declare where or when he would leave it. For they no longer wished to labor further, because they could not. [Col. 1440D] After long struggles and the long and miserable torments by which he tortured God’s creature, the demon said: “This night your Wirnto will come with Margaret”—for her feast fell that very night—“then I am tortured, then I am cast out; for I know that I shall be received festively by my master. Alas, alas! What shall I do? Whither shall I flee? Looking to right and left, I do not see where I may flee. While I seek to seize prey, I become prey; I am tortured while I torture.”

But the brethren, knowing that hope does not disappoint, were not deprived of their desire. As they celebrated vigils, at about midnight, through God’s mercy the person was cleansed at the tomb of the blessed man. Lest she seem ungrateful for God’s benefits, she devoted herself to her deliverer and to the saints resting there, with the abbot and brethren consenting. She resolved to spend the remainder of her life there in the service of the saints and brethren; and even today [Col. 1441A] she may be seen there in the habit which she herself chose in her affliction. For we need not offer any further testimony in this matter: she is of age; let her speak for herself.

## Chapter XI. A boy suffering from a most grievous disease, in which worms were bred in his brain, is delivered after Wirnto’s aid is implored.

Moreover, a certain woman came to the tomb of the blessed man, encouraged by the many healing miracles accomplished there. She brought a boy—whose age has escaped my memory—who had for a long time been held and tormented by a new, miserable, and unheard-of kind of illness. His brain, as I suppose, corrupted by superfluous humors according to the physicians, had produced swarms of worms in the very sheath of the brain; nourished and strengthened there to their evil purpose, they afflicted, distressed, and tortured the wretched boy miserably. At times they even flowed out in streams from both ears and seemed to equal a spindle in thickness, though not in length. [Col. 1441B]

It is dreadful even to recall such a spectacle in one’s mind; I do not say to write, narrate, or behold it. But who could endure that suffering? Who could bear such things? He indeed, because it was fitting that this should happen, endured and bore it until He who is glorious in His saints glorified His saint in him by the efficacy of His power. For what else? The sick boy had little food and scant sleep; by night and day pain and groaning were heard.

Then, after many sighs, he was brought to the tomb with great confidence of devotion. Through the prayers of his parents his pain was commended to the Lord, [Col. 1441C] and they humbly implored Him, through the merits of the saints, to have pity on the miserable sufferer. A sleepless night passed; the day likewise was consumed in such labors, yet no benefit of healing was perceived. Thus disappointed and almost despairing, they went home in grief.

Thereupon that Father, who knows how to give good gifts to those who ask Him, aided the wretched boy through the interceding merits of the blessed man, granting health together with healing. Now the dead worms flowed from his ears; pain and groaning ceased, and the boy was restored to soundness. After some time, lest they seem ungrateful for the good done to them, they returned to the monastery, related the event to all, gave thanks to God and His saint, and thus re-entered their home with joy and gladness.

## Chapter XII. Another boy, hideously contracted in his limbs, is healed after his mother makes a vow at the tomb of Saint Wirnto.

[Col. 1441D]

Since we have begun with children, let us join to the preceding miracle another worthy of narration. Across the Inn, in the neighborhood of the monastery, there lived a housewife who had a weak and lame boy whose feet were twisted backward, seeming almost to cover even the parts that serve nature’s necessities. The little fellow was pitiable to behold: one no longer saw a man, but a miserable likeness of one; and, as the poet says:

> “He was like a fig-tree trunk, useless wood,”

so that even his acquaintances disdained to look at him.

One night, therefore, when his mother had given herself to sleep, [Col. 1442A] she was warned in a dream that if she and the boy sought Wirnto’s tomb with due reverence, that afflicted child would be restored to his former health. When she awoke, made much happier by the vision, she silently debated many matters with herself. For a long time she wavered in mind, wondering, deliberating, and hesitating about what the vision foretold might mean for her.

At last, recovering confidence and heartened by hope, she took up the boy, intending to go to the monastery and visit the blessed man’s tomb. She made for the Inn, promising the boatman his fare, provided that he would not delay in ferrying her across. But the boatman said: “Do you not see the force of the waters? Do you not hear the roar of waves crashing against each other? Save yourself and the poor life of your son, lest you lose both yourself and him by voluntarily entering danger; and allow me to live, so long as it pleases the Lord, lest for a small fare I seem to purchase death for myself and for you. [Col. 1442B] Return then to your dwelling until the floodwaters subside, and then you will cross without loss either to me or to yourself.”

That year there had been such frequent heavy rains and so continual a flooding of the waters that in many places it had even destroyed houses situated near the banks and laid waste vineyards and crops. Sad and groaning, fearful that her vow would be rendered void and her hope frustrated, she returned home with the boy. She answered nothing to those who questioned her, but gave herself to weeping and groaning.

Yet the woman, strong in God and trusting in her Lord, instilling a manly spirit into feminine frailty, and knowing also that nothing is impossible to God, quickly rose and, taking [Col. 1442C] the boy, placed him upon a table as though it were an altar. She offered the sacrifice of a contrite spirit; she offered an oblation with her child; she offered the devotion of sincere prayer. Then, wholly poured out toward God, she said:

> “You, Lord, who possess holy knowledge, who know all things, both last and ancient, plainly know that, had it been within my power, I would have sought the tomb of Your servant, even at my own loss. But You, who are everywhere, who are never absent, who chiefly make known Your omnipotence by sparing and showing mercy, remember what our substance is; remember that we are dust. Remember that, whatever we may be—blind or lame, healthy or sick—we are nevertheless Your creatures. Through the merits of blessed Wirnto, whom the evidence of his miracles proves to reign with You and to be able to obtain all things from You, have mercy on Your creature and free him from this affliction of illness, lest he be a reproach among men, though for him You gave the price of Your blood.
>
> “For Your mercy and power are not greater in churches or temples and less in fields or forests; rather, You are wholly everywhere, everywhere powerful, and You show mercy where You will, to whom You will, when You will, and how You will. Therefore, if Your joy is our strength, if You hate nothing that You have made, have mercy upon my tears, groans, and pains; comfort the sorrow of my heart; let the suffering of my child move You.”

She finished speaking, and more swiftly than speech, the cracking of bones was heard; the boy was raised up and restored to health. When this occurred, the people gathered; the mother dissolved into tears for joy; praises were sung to God and blessed Wirnto. [Col. 1443A] Not much time afterward, the mother took the boy—an evident spectacle of God’s mercy—to the blessed man’s tomb. She made and fulfilled vows, rendered to God and His saints such thanks as she could and knew how to offer, and then recounted the mighty works of God.

Then all rejoiced together in [Col. 1444A] God; great devotion burned in both mother and son; and He was glorified by all—the giver of every good thing, who alone performs wonders—to whom be honor and glory through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1443] Here ends the Life and Miracles of Blessed Wirnto.

Appendix added by the most reverend and illustrious Dom P. Clarus, prior of Formbach.

## Chapter XIII. Appendix to the Life and Miracles of Saint Wirnto, containing ancient verses concerning the blessed Pernger, Wirnto, and Theoderic, the first abbots of Formbach.

[Col. 1443B]

In a certain ancient volume concerning the series and succession of the abbots of Varnbach, I also found another brief eulogy of blessed Pernger, as likewise of blessed Wirnto and Theoderic. I inserted it in my chronicle and thought it proper to transfer it here from there.

### Berenger

In the year 1094 from the Virgin’s childbirth, he happily began to occupy the helm of this monastery as its first ruler, and lived miraculously.

> Behold the first three fathers, and marvel at them together,  
> Whom one same zeal kept all watchful.  
> Benedict was their rule; their life was without fault,  
> Their conduct innocent, their chastity without stain.

### Wirnto II, Abbot

[Col. 1444A]

Unchanged from the first, he held an equally blessed course.

> One piety, one virtue, one mind belonged to all;  
> One love of fair renown, and one faith.  
>
> [Col. 1444B] Such wholly were those whom the golden age produced,  
> In the time when every splendor of things flourished.

He presided for nineteen years and died in the year of the Lord 1127, on the sixth day before the Ides of March [10 March]. He is buried in the greater church, with this inscription engraved upon a marble stone:

> Happy and gracious Wirnto, that second father—  
> Behold, he lives with God, whom Formbach buried here.

### Theoderic III, Abbot

Encouraged by the example of both, he showed himself the same. He died at Jerusalem, renowned for three miracles on the day of his burial. Concerning him are these verses:

> And although their bodies now lie hidden, enclosed in dark tombs,  
> Until they reclaim their rights and their proper place,  
> Yet the hour will come when they shall rise alive from their graves,  
> And soon shall be like a shining star.

[Col. 1443]

## A Syntagma of the Venerable Gerhoh, Provost of Reichersberg, concerning Emperors Henry IV and V, Gregory VII, and certain subsequent Roman pontiffs.

(Printed in the works of Jacob Grets­er, S.J., vol. VI, p. 235.)

### Letter

Jacobus Grets­er of the Society of Jesus, to the noble, illustrious, and most learned lord Christoph Gewold, Doctor of Both Laws, intimate councillor of the most serene Maximilian, Duke of Bavaria.

When I came to Munich in the autumn of last year, you offered me, most illustrious sir, wholly unexpectedly and beyond all expectation—though not beyond my wish—Gerhoh, or Geroch, once provost of Reichersberg in Bavaria. I had known him by name from the testimony of Aventinus and was most eager to know him more closely and, as the saying goes, “by sight.” I had given a sufficiently clear indication of this desire in the prefatory remarks or prolegomena to Paul of Bernried, Gerhoh’s companion in defending Gregory VII, the supreme pontiff.

You yourself, an eyewitness, can testify with what joy and delight of mind I embraced the book, whose acquisition I had already despaired of. For nothing is usually dearer or more pleasant to me than literary treasures, especially those in which the cause of God and of the Catholic Church is treated against heretics and schismatics. Though I universally honor and venerate all Roman pontiffs as Christ’s vicars and Saint Peter’s successors, yet for some reason my mind is especially borne—indeed swept—toward Gregory VII among the pontiffs of former memory: a man outstanding alike in holiness and greatness of spirit, accustomed neither to grow slack, much less insolent, in prosperity, nor to be broken by the storms of adverse fortune.

This moved me diligently to devote myself to vindicating that great bishop from the accusations of recent and ancient sectarians, seeking out and producing new and old resources by which the assault of opponents upon this supreme shepherd and ruler of the Christian religion might be repelled. Witnesses to this undertaking of mine, such as it is, are Paul of Bernried, the *Apology*, and the priest Bernard, or Bernald, of Constance, included therein.

Yet although, from reading Aventinus, I had supposed that Gerhoh or Geroch had set down in writing a formal life and account of the deeds of Gregory VII, or had composed an *Apology* properly speaking for Gregory himself against his attackers, when I saw the author himself I learned that the matter stood otherwise. In that volume Geroch had principally undertaken an investigation of Antichrist. Led by a peculiar opinion, not to be approved, he holds that Antichrist is not one individual man who will arise at the end of the world, but all the enemies and persecutors of the orthodox Church, whether pagans, heretics, or schismatics.

And because Henry IV had grievously afflicted the Church, as had also his son Henry V, by creating several antipopes—such as Cadalus, Guibert, and Burdinus—Gerhoh discusses them and their wicked attempts and deeds, because he wished to show that those who had undertaken such impious and criminal attacks upon Peter’s see and the orthodox faith had more than sufficiently fulfilled the scriptural prophecies concerning Antichrist’s ferocity and tyranny.

But setting aside this paradox—although Gerhoh himself openly affirms in his dedicatory letter to Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, that he presents it in the manner not of one defining but of one investigating—let us take what he supplies to us in historical style, as he himself says, concerning Henry IV and V, Gregory VII, and certain other subsequent pontiffs.

I offer you, noble and illustrious lord doctor, these transcribed and excerpted passages from Gerhoh’s work: first, that I may discharge my obligation; secondly, that this common benefit bestowed upon Gregory VII and his defenders may return and, as it were, flow back to you as its fountain and source. For you brought forth from hiding Gerhoh—whom I had sought everywhere, even at Reichersberg, vainly, though with the greatest diligence—and delivered him into my hands.

I should therefore be not merely ungrateful but wholly shameless if I were to attach any title to Gerhoh’s pages other than this: **CHRISTOPH GEWOLD DISCOVERED [THIS].** Thirdly, by this public testimony, as it were, I wished to make known to all that amid the weightiest affairs of the Bavarian commonwealth, by which you are daily occupied, you are a man who by no means withdraws his care and thought from libraries and from the ancient monuments lying hidden in them, but devotes wholly diligent labor to examining them. You need no herald in me to proclaim to all lovers of antiquity the praise you deserve, since I am far too ineloquent; nor can anyone prove more clearly than you yourself that what I have said accords with the truth, when you cause the Chronicle of Reichersberg, discovered through your care, to come forth and benefit many.

Meanwhile receive this fragment from your Gerhoh [lacuna]. But now I shall make my words brief, and I ask again and again that you may be pleased to receive favorably this modest token, whatever it may be, of my respect for you, considering not so much how great it is as from how great a heart it proceeds.

Ingolstadt, 12 December, in the year of the Redeemer 1610.

## Gerhoh’s Syntagma concerning the state of the Church under Emperors Henry IV and V, Gregory VII, and certain subsequent pontiffs

[Col. 1445]

### Introduction to the following Syntagma

[Col. 1445]

In Book I of *On the Investigation of Antichrist*, Gerhoh compares the Church of God with the man-made Israelite temple built by Solomon, and compares its attackers and destroyers with the enemies of the Church. As that temple suffered various disasters at the hands of unbelievers, so too, he teaches, the Christian Church has been repeatedly attacked and harassed by pagans, heretics, and schismatics. This is why I have wished to weave into this *Syntagma* also these chapters concerning Solomon’s temple.

## Chapter I. Of the man-made temple: how often it was destroyed and restored after its first construction

[Col. 1445A]

There now comes to mind what happened long ago concerning the building of the temple at Jerusalem. The ill-omened Herod, bloodstained by the slaughter of infants, murderer of his own wife and sons, and utterly a man of blood, ordered the temple itself—originally built by Solomon to a height of 120 cubits—to be razed to the ground. After it had been destroyed by the Chaldeans, the children of the captivity, under the leaders Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, at the prophets’ exhortation, had rebuilt it to a height of sixty cubits (2 Esdras 2:3). [Col. 1446A] Herod, of whom we speak, lamenting that the temple first constructed through Solomon lacked half of its former height, ordered it razed to the ground; and within one year and five months he restored it to the height arranged under Solomon.

Perhaps he imagined that he was rendering service to God; or rather, what is truer, he was serving his own vain glory, foolishly setting himself above the devoted efforts of the holy fathers and prophets in the speed of the work and the expenditure of money.

[Col. 1447A] Add also that King Antiochus of Greece did not fear to profane this same temple, rebuilt, as stated, by the children of the exile (1 Maccabees 2:3, 5). But when the Maccabees resisted him and fought for the ancestral laws, the undertaking prospered in their hands through the Lord’s cooperation. When city and temple had been recovered, the temple was consecrated anew and adorned with golden crowns (2 Maccabees 10).

After all this, the ill-omened Herod, as stated above, laid hands upon it. Razing the same temple to the ground, he rebuilt it to double height with stones so polished and immense that, as was also mentioned above, the astonished disciples [Col. 1447B] said to the Lord: “Teacher, look what stones and what buildings!” (Mark 13:1). To them the Lord gave the answer known to all: “Amen, I say to you, not one stone shall be left upon another that shall not be thrown down” (ibid., v. 2).

## Chapter II. Of the spiritual meaning of the temple’s dimensions

But to what end are these matters related? Surely because it is worth knowing that what was typologically prefigured in the construction of that man-made temple is now enacted in truth in the Church, which is the true temple of God, and has continued to be enacted down to our own time.

For the true Solomon—that is, our peaceful Lord Jesus Christ, who is our peace (Ephesians 2:14)—and His Spirit [Col. 1447C] built the holy Church, the true and living temple of the living God, out of living stones. He also provided it with dimensions corresponding to that man-made temple, which had preceded this truth as a shadow.

## Chapter III. The length of the temple

The length of that man-made temple, including the oracle, was sixty cubits. For the oracle measured twenty cubits in length, breadth, and height alike—that is, it had the form of a cube—and thereby signified the perfection of holy and spiritual persons in the Church. Prosperity does not exalt them, nor adversity cast them down; but they are always of even mind, rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, [Col. 1447D] and sharing in the needs of the saints (Romans 12:13).

For in these three things you have, as it were—indeed, truly—spiritual dimensions of saints and perfect persons: their rejoicing in hope is height; their patience in tribulation is length; their sharing in the needs of saints is breadth. For to extend oneself spiritually toward one’s neighbor in charity is to be enlarged. The length of the house before the doors of the oracle was forty cubits; by this number are signified the sufferings of this life, in which the Church must be worn down for Christ through persecutions and sufferings of her own.

By this same mystery Moses and Elijah alike abstained from all food for forty days, for their own sins and the sins of the people. The Lord Himself likewise fasted forty days and, for our iniquities, was as though struck by forty legal lashes. [Col. 1448A] Since the world subsists through four elements and runs through four seasons, and since we have violated the law of the Decalogue by preferring love of the world to love of the Creator, we are justly struck four times ten; that is, we stretch forth the endurance of our long-suffering through every trial of the present life. The Apostle affirms: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

This mystery also accords with the fact that the whole length of the temple extended to sixty cubits. Since man was created on the sixth day and set above the whole visible creation, and since he himself preferred himself to the love of the Creator and through excessive self-love corrupted in himself the Decalogue of the natural law, [Col. 1448B] the length of his patience should likewise rightly be six times ten, so that he may be prepared to endure for Christ and His law whatever trials the creation made in six days can bring upon man.

But the Lord’s mercy divided the trials rising against the Church, as is said to Job: “The heat is divided over the earth” (Job 38:24), so that although it must undergo every kind of trial and no season passes free from trials, nevertheless all trials rarely, or never, rise against it together—unless perhaps in the final persecution of Antichrist. Yet the Lord shortened even those days; for unless they had been shortened, no flesh would be saved [Col. 1448C] (Matthew 24:22).

For God is faithful, and He will not allow His Church, nor any member of the Church predestined to glory, to be tested beyond what it can bear; but with the trial He will provide the means of escape, that it may be able to endure (1 Corinthians 10:13). Hence the patience of the saints will not perish forever (Psalm 9:19). This patience, as we have said—endured for God’s laws even unto death—is the sixty, or six-times-ten, length of the temple not made by hands, which is the Church.

## Chapter IV. The breadth of the temple

The breadth of this temple, which we understand to be the Church, extends after the pattern of the man-made temple to twenty cubits. This is twice ten, [Col. 1448D] a number signifying the breadth of charity extended toward one’s neighbor, which cannot exist between fewer than two persons. It must also be tenfold, so that it does not transgress the Decalogue of the law; otherwise, one who does and loves iniquity would hate his own soul and therefore could not love his neighbor as himself, since he would not love even himself.

But one who loves himself rightly loves first and before all things his own principle, which is God. And one who loves God keeps the commandments of Him whom he loves. Thus charity, formed by love of God and of oneself, safely extends toward one’s neighbor and now rightly obeys the command: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:30). In that one saying, indeed, the whole commandment is fulfilled.

[Col. 1449A] Let charity therefore be tenfold, so that a person may first love himself according to God and His commandments. Let this ten be doubled, so that it may extend itself to the neighbor. When, first, you do not do to your neighbor what you do not lawfully wish done to yourself—which is the beginning of charity—and then do for your neighbor what you lawfully wish done for yourself—which belongs to perfection—you have fulfilled the twenty-cubit breadth of the holy temple in which God dwells. For this holy breadth befits God’s temple in the length of days: in it the number two extends toward one’s neighbor and does not exceed the Decalogue of the law.

## Chapter V. The height of the temple

The temple’s height, according to the book of Kings, [Col. 1449B] extended to thirty cubits (3 Kings 6:2), but according to Chronicles is said to have been 120 cubits (2 Chronicles 23:4). Yet lest these sacred testimonies seem to contradict one another, it is rightly understood that the thirty cubits reached to the lower storey, while the 120 cubits extended to the very top of the temple roof.

For the house contained three upper chambers—lowest, middle, and highest—by which we recognize that the three orders of the Church are prefigured: the married, the continent, and the teachers. These were also prefigured by the three men Noah, Daniel, and Job in Ezekiel’s prophecy (Ezekiel 14:20). Whether in the height of thirty or of 120 cubits, the sublimity of our hope according to faith is indicated. For as we now believe in God the Father Almighty, in His only-begotten Son, and in the Holy Spirit of both, so we hope to be made blessed by the vision of that same Holy Trinity. [Col. 1449C] The Apostle John commends this height of our hope to us, saying: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that, when He appears, we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2).

The height of 120 cubits, extending to the topmost pinnacle of the temple, seems to me fittingly to correspond to the complete number of the elect, upon whom, at the beginning of the Church’s birth—the true temple of God—the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out. For, as Luke says, “there was a gathering of people together, about 120” (Acts 1:15).

[Col. 1449D] Why this number pleased God, whether in the height of the man-made temple to be sanctified for the Lord or in the number of the elect to be consecrated by the coming of the Holy Spirit, I think should be investigated. For I do not believe that what is marked in the event is devoid of great mystery. Indeed, the man-made temple of which we speak was, not without God’s direction, though through the ill-omened Herod, as we said, restored to the same height of 120 cubits before the Lord was presented in it by His parents with an offering; and this was that temple’s greatest sanctification and glory. Hence it was foretold by the prophet: “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than the former” (Haggai 2:10).

[Col. 1450A] Likewise, the complete number of the elect was not consecrated by the Holy Spirit to God as a temple before it attained this number predetermined by God. Let us therefore, according to our modest ability, investigate the mystery of this sacred number pleasing to God.

All students of sacred Scripture know that the number fifteen is commendable because of its two parts, seven and eight. For Solomon says: “Give portions to seven and also to eight” (Ecclesiastes 11:2). We give seven portions when, according to the law of the old commandment, we keep a spiritual sabbath by resting from vices. We give eight portions when, according to the principle of the new law, we exercise ourselves through the eight grades of virtues and tend toward the eightfold reward of blessedness. [Col. 1450B] For this reason the eighth day was consecrated by the Lord’s resurrection. Eight is the first cube number, signifying for us the enduring stability and solidity of eternal blessedness in soul and body alike. Seven likewise enjoins upon us not only the rest of the spiritual sabbath, but also promises participation in the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, through which we are made fruitful in virtues.

We therefore join these two parts of fifteen, namely seven and eight, together in the devout effort of our way of life. We sing to God acceptably a song, as it were, of fifteen steps, when, resting from vices and enriched by the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit, we rise with Christ through the exercises of the eight virtues and attain the eightfold summit of the beatitudes. [Col. 1450C]

“But,” you may say, “what do these matters have to do with the number 120, whose mystery is being sought?” Much in every way. For if, beginning with one and counting by that number which mathematicians call cumulative, you proceed to fifteen, you complete 120 in the total. This number, when set out on a plane, also presents the form of a triangle, whose three outer lines, brought together, are of equal length, each containing fifteen units.

And what is more beautiful than the mystery of this number? In it the figure of a triangle forms the faith of the Holy Trinity; and fifteen, occurring three times at the outer limits of the triangular figure, instructs conduct through its two parts, namely seven and eight, and in addition promises the faithful blessedness through an unchangeable state.

[Col. 1450D] For this reason, as I judge, this number of years—120—was granted for repentance also to the original world which perished by water, when the Lord said to Noah: “The days of man shall be 120 years” (Genesis 6:3). Thus the evangelical man, taught by God through the Spirit, might know that repentance is pleasing to God and sufficient to appease Him when it is performed in faith in the Holy Trinity and accompanied by rest from vices and devotion to virtues.

For one who repents in this way through seven and eight, as though satisfying God through 120 years, [Col. 1451A] not only rests from vices and escapes the punishment of eternal and final vengeance, but also attains the summit of virtues and the eightfold state of eternal blessedness, as the Lord says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” and so forth (Matthew 5:3).

## Chapter VI. Recapitulation of the dimensions and the spiritual ornament of the temple

These dimensions, therefore—this length of faithful patience and faith that endure all things for the Lord; this breadth of charity expanding itself toward one’s neighbor in God and for God; this height of heavenly conduct and hope raising itself to God—make the holy Church, His pleasing temple to God: possessing sixty spiritual cubits in length, twenty in breadth, and thirty or even 120 in height.

[Col. 1451B] The gold of this temple is knowledge, worship, and love of the divinity. Its silver is eloquence in divine matters. Its precious stones are the pearls of virtues. Its incense is the fragrance of good repute. Its most radiant frankincense is purity of conscience and the incense of prayers. Its altar of incense is Christ Jesus, receiving the petitions and prayers of the saints. The altar also of burnt offerings, sacrifices, and victims is the same Christ, who does not reject the repentance of converts or the vows of the faithful. Each stone of this temple is one of the faithful; its storeys, prepared for fastening with gold, are the piety of hearts and devotion of minds.

[Col. 1451C] We have neither leisure nor purpose to survey individually the spiritual structures or ornaments of this temple. It is enough that we have introduced these points, so that we may know that God, its builder, has a greater care for this temple than for any man-made temple, however ornate or spacious. For all other temples of God made by hands have been made and are made for the sake of this one. But this house was built for the price of its very self by the labor of the Lord Jesus Christ’s own preaching—indeed, by the expenditure of His death—and was consecrated by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven.

[Col. 1451D] Therefore, as this house surpasses every temple made by hands, so its profanation is more abominable and more detestable to God and men, and ought to be so. And there can be no doubt that Antichrist claims for himself whatever is most detestable among things and most opposed to Christ.

## Chapter VII. Application to the Church of those things which occurred in that temple
Accordingly, how greatly the enemy raged against this holy temple of God, which is the Church—and, moreover, against that temple at Jerusalem made as its type—I shall, with God’s help, attempt to sketch; likewise, how greatly that same enemy, by the Lord’s permission, raged there, as a figure of the sufferings and struggles of the Church. I shall compare truth and shadow with one another, so that a sound judge of things may know what kind of abomination of desolation is to be sought, and in which temple. [Col. 1452A] For that temple, built by the kings David and Solomon at divine prompting, was burned with fire and razed to the ground by the king of Babylon. The Church likewise, built and dedicated by the true David, our Lord Jesus Christ, and by His Spirit as by the true Solomon, was, so far as lay in him, destroyed and burned by the Babylonian king—that is, the emperor of the city of Rome, which Peter figuratively calls Babylon (1 Pet. 5:13)—namely Nero, and every successor to his power and impiety, raging against her by persecutions, proscriptions, and tortures of every kind. Indeed, he made the whole world a Babylonian furnace, in which, as was also mentioned above, worshippers of the Holy Trinity laboured in holy contest like the three youths. [Col. 1452B] In that storm innumerable thousands of saints, unwilling to pass from the worship of the one God to the worship of the creature, gained glorious martyrdom.

But the Lord was present with His saints in that same trial: either strengthening them in their suffering, or tempering their sufferings so that they could be endured. He drove the flame of fire from the furnace; moreover, refreshing them by the consolations of His Spirit, He made the middle of the furnace for them like a wind blowing with dew. Thus, after the furnace of sufferings, they repeatedly testified by miracles that they lived: demons fled from possessed persons to their tombs, and those held by any infirmity received comfort.

## CHAPTER VIII. On heretics who hindered the rebuilding.

[Col. 1452C]

Then Cyrus, king of the Persians, released the captivity of the Jews and permitted the temple and the city of Jerusalem to be rebuilt (1 Esdras 1:6); and likewise Darius and Artaxerxes, kings of the Persians and Medes, granted the same permission. Yet the work was long delayed, since powerful men dwelling nearby hindered them, restraining them by force and power. At times those same neighbours even promised deceitfully to build together with them. But they were not admitted, since they were men of an alien faith and proved enemies in many respects. Zerubbabel, leader of the sons of Judah, and Nehemiah the priest, however, persevered in the work until they brought that same house of God [Col. 1452D] to completion (3 Esdras 4:6). This time of building was extended over forty-six years, because the aforesaid adversaries had long opposed the work. Hence the Jews said reproachfully to the Lord: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?” (John 2:20).

These periods seem to me to correspond to the times of heresies, when the imperial power had inclined toward the faith, evil laws had been removed, and good laws had been enacted for the Church. For then diverse heresies sprang up against the Church through Arius, Sabellius, Photinus, and very many others. By hindering her building, they became enemies all the more harmful [Col. 1453A] because, as neighbours, they agreed with us in many things. Indeed, drawing the minds of kings into the doctrine of their perversity, they stirred them up against the Church. Thus Constantius, son of Constantine, inflicted many evils on the saints of God. The Arian kings of the Goths likewise inflicted many severe persecutions upon the saints of God, especially upon priests throughout Africa. All these matters are found set out in their proper places, and we too shall mention them as occasion requires.

But the holy confessors and teachers of God—Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and other illustrious men—setting themselves like a wall before the Catholic faith, resisted falsehood until, the heresies having been condemned, their judgment came unto victory.

## CHAPTER IX. On the deeds of Antiochus Epiphanes, and how they typologically correspond to the condition of the Church.

[Col. 1453B]

Thirdly, this same handmade house of God was defiled under Antiochus Epiphanes by the introduction into it of a little statue [an image, icon] of Jupiter. [Note: [Col. 1453D] On these matters consult the books of Maccabees, especially the Second.] Such an abomination of desolation stood in the holy place for three years, while the city of Jerusalem lay devastated for six years. At that time, as the book of Maccabees relates, the temple’s chambers were demolished and brushwood grew in its courts. Shameless women also voluntarily intruded into the sacred buildings, bringing in things forbidden by law; and the temple was filled with revelry. For Antiochus then commanded—and exacted by tortures—[Col. 1453C] that the Jews should abandon their ancestral laws and pass over to the rite of the Gentiles, so that the whole people might be one people.

Judas Maccabaeus and his brothers resisted this impiety; and the Lord protecting them, the undertaking prospered in their hands. Though few in number, they triumphed over great kings and a multitude of enemies, and at length recovered the city and the temple. At that time the priesthood also became a commodity for sale at the king’s court. Jason, having supplanted his own brother Onias, a most excellent man, through payments and promised sums of money, held him in captivity; Jason himself was supplanted by Menelaus, who outbid him by three hundred talents of silver.

But because Menelaus neglected to pay the money he had promised, [Col. 1453D] he too was driven from the priesthood, and his brother Lysimachus succeeded him. Again seeking the priesthood, Menelaus gave Andronicus certain golden vessels that he had stolen from the temple. When Onias reproved him for this, Menelaus advised Andronicus to murder Onias; and so it was done. Menelaus remained in power through fraud together with violence. This was the third tribulation of that handmade temple. It seems to me to resemble that evil which, likewise in the third place after the events [Col. 1454A] already described, began to be carried on in the Church and against the Church of God through the devil’s contrivance.

## CHAPTER X. How the condition of the Church in the time of Henry IV corresponds to the times and deeds of Antiochus.

[Note: [Col. 1453D] On this, see my little commentary on the generosity of emperors, kings, and princes toward the apostolic see. On this privilege of investitures, see what I wrote in the *Apology against Baronius*, chapter 1, and in the *Basilicon Doron*, chapter 5. Gerhoh names Adrian II and Leo III. Others name Adrian I and Leo VIII, the pseudo-pope. From this the vanity of the invention is apparent.]

For after the Church had gained victory and peace through holy and illustrious men, the heresies having been overcome, and while meanwhile the same Church had been increased and enriched with royal wealth and honours by kings and princes, the obstinacy of ambitious men began to ravage her as though by civil war. Kings, indeed, from the time of Charlemagne claimed for themselves, by concession of certain Roman pontiffs—namely Leo III and Adrian II—the right of investiture in ecclesiastical dignities. They very often raised in the Church [Col. 1454B] of God to the height of episcopal sees not those whom the Church wished, but those whom they wished; and they cast down whom they wished.

Some of these kings, however, at the beginning of this disaster behaved in these matters more modestly and with greater restraint, deferring to ecclesiastical elections in granting honours, and bestowing dignities not for favour or the price of money, but rather according to excellence of character and learning.

But when kings arose who knew not Joseph, the Church, which had been mistress, became a slave. And just as, when the tribe of Dan began to seek a possession for itself, there was no longer a king in Israel and everyone did what seemed good to himself, [Col. 1454C] there had already begun to be an idol in the Church of God, or in Micah’s house, and a hired priest: so, in ordaining bishops, neither election by the clergy, nor the consent of the honourable, nor petition of the people was sought; no deference was given to holiness of life or to more distinguished learning (Judges 17–18). Rather, whoever wished filled his own hand and became a priest—not now of the Lord, but of Mammon and of the prince of this world, who says: “All these things will I give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9).

For what else was it but the worship of the devil, prince of this world lying in wickedness, to serve as retainers of princes in whom the spirit of pride and avarice dwelt, so that whoever served them more familiarly might sooner attain the summit of some ecclesiastical dignity? [Col. 1454D] When men thus ascended by another way, for what else were they advanced except to become heretics? For these very ordainers of such men—called bishops—being unquestioned Simoniacs, long ago condemned in their author by the great Simon Peter and by his other lawful successors, were able to confer upon those whom they ordained nothing besides the condemnation which they possessed. Those ordained by them carried away, through the laying on of their hands, a head wounded by them.

[Col. 1455A] What danger or evil should we not suppose the holy Church, bride of Christ, suffered under such groomsmen and companions of the Bridegroom? Men everywhere rushed upon her—those, as has been said, who entered by another way; men either rich and already trained in every vice, or descended from noble families and devoted to every vice of the flesh. Anyone who approached to admonish or rebuke them would depart as though torn and lacerated by thorns and briars. Such men freely assaulted the chastity of the Lord’s bride, none forbidding them—not in order to raise up seed for a deceased brother, but to satisfy the blind desires of their own frenzy.

Who would spring forth to rebuke men of this sort, whom imperial authority protected, as did resources of wealth, the power of friends or relatives, the service and multitude of retainers, [Col. 1455B] and a host of men like themselves? Thus, from the head—that is, the emperor, not sound in health—and from pontiffs stained with the contagion of this leprosy, the plague spread through nearly the entire body of the clergy. For when a bishop had purchased a bishopric for several hundred marks, what dignity subject to him would he not sell to recoup his loss? Abbots, provosts, archpriests, archdeacons, and priests were thus appointed by him; and what would they themselves not hold for sale among ecclesiastical offices and administrations, down to the place and office of burial, in order either to amass wealth or at least refill emptied purses?

[Col. 1455C] Yet I have said too little in saying that ecclesiastical honours were bestowed by lay hands upon young men for favour, money, or the rendering of service. Rather, for an increase of impiety and misery, those more readily obtained such honours who were most notorious in their crimes—especially while Henry IV held the empire. He himself surpassed all kings or emperors before his time; indeed, as may be believed, all human beings in wickedness. For, according to what was said to John in his Apocalypse by the permission of divine judgment: “Let him who harms, harm still; and let him who is filthy, become filthy still” (Rev. 22:11).

When I recall with an averted mind this man’s filthiness, which public hearing recoils from, [Col. 1455D] I judge that the phrase “become filthy still”—that is, beyond measure or more abundantly—was finally fulfilled in this man. I do not think one could be found his equal in filthiness, much less his superior. If you recall to me adulterous Jupiter, foul and criminal Nero, Maximinus, likewise cruel and vicious, I would still give this man the palm in wickedness. He could equal them, or even surpass them, in crimes; and to increase his guilt, he committed the same crimes under the title of Christianity. For, says the Prophet in the person of the Lord, “If my enemy had cursed me”—for example, a Jew or pagan—“I should surely have endured it. But you, Christian, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance” (Ps. 54:13–14)—understand, by bringing evils upon me—you are not to be endured.

A herd of shameless persons, clergy and laymen of more distinguished lineage, was gathered in his household. There was likewise joined to him such a multitude of young women and matrons as no royal residence or royal progress could have sustained without complaint. Yet most of them were seized from their own husbands and led unwillingly and captive to a wicked purpose. By their mingling, besides the daily filthiness sacrificed to the devil morning, evening, and noon, when he wished to sacrifice more solemnly to Beelphegor as his god, he caused them to assemble together in his own chambers. He himself stood among them amid the unholy rites, arranging, it is said, by whatever art he could, for the lights to be extinguished, [Col. 1456B] so that brother might unite with sister, or any persons of close blood-relationship who could not recognize one another in the darkness.

Although it is customary, and almost natural, for all men to conceal their own wives lest they consort with other men, he, on the contrary, prostituted in that public assembly of shameless people, in theatrical fashion, his own wife—who was joined to him, shall I say fittingly or unfittingly, in beauty, nobility, and honourable character—whenever this pleased him at the prompting or indication of demons. Thus it once happened that she, foreknowing the time and place of this abuse, invoked the aid of the bishop of the city where the affair was being conducted, a man zealous for God. By force of arms, after the example [Col. 1456C] of Phinehas the priest, she was rescued from the midst of the shameless people; there, it is said, she was found bound and prepared for the wicked act.

## CHAPTER XI. Greatest abominations.

Since we are speaking of the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, we shall not be abominable if we speak further of abominations greater than these. It was the most holy night of the Lord’s Nativity, on which, as is known, the whole Church of Christ customarily celebrates solemn vigils, with the solemn offices of Mass also interposed. On this night he chose, undoubtedly at the prompting of demons, to celebrate solemn vigils for the devil, wholly opposed to Christian vigils; in them he inserted a sacrifice entirely contrary to Christian sacrifice [Col. 1456D] in place of the Mass.

There was present a herd of shameless people, clergy and laity gathered together, inserting prostitutes, as the report goes, among the individual psalms and lessons. But when they came to the place of the Mass and sacrifice, everything was performed upside down, perversely, and contrary to holiness. Thus, instead of the kiss, the profane priest and sacrilegious ministers touched the altar with the posterior part of their bodies exposed.
