I refrain from saying what foul offerings were presented there, lest the reader detest the speaker together with the sacrifice. Yet everything is reported to have been defiled with human semen. I myself saw that episcopal chapel in the city of Regensburg, deservedly profaned for such a sacrifice.

And what should I think of this chief of all the wicked [Col. 1457A] except that Beelphegor was consummated through him—the deity to whom, as we read, the sons of Israel were once initiated in the wilderness with the daughters of Midian (Num. 25:6; Ps. 105:28)? Though all these things, and even more than these, were carried on as secretly as possible, they were nevertheless exposed by the matrons who had been unwillingly and captive employed in the unholy rites, and finally by his own wife’s public complaints.

For after the death of one wife, from whom, as is reported, he had honourably begotten children in the earlier part of his reign, while he himself was still comparatively respectable—whom the Lord mercifully removed, grieving and sorrowing, from before this iniquity—he married another, Gisela, daughter of the king of the Ruthenians, who knew nothing of this mystery of iniquity. When she first experienced the cult of impiety in others, and the same thing in herself through shameless men admitted to her, she kept silence for some time out of womanly modesty. But when the magnitude of the crimes overcame even a matron’s patience, she first disclosed the matter to bishops and priests faithful to Christ and sought an opportunity for flight and secret separation.

Meanwhile a royal expedition to Lombardy, in the regions south of the Alps, was imminent; the emperor requested the queen’s attendance as well. For more private reasons, however, alleging illness—such as it was—she declined the exertion of the journey. When the bishops urged her, as the king wished, to set out, she is reported to have said among other things [Col. 1457C] that she was wasting away in justified sorrow and rightly refusing the journey, since she had been prostituted by her own husband in such a manner that she could not know by whom she had conceived a child.

Nevertheless she departed, and on the journey itself, with the aid of certain God-fearing persons, made her escape. As best she could she concealed herself; then, sending letters to the bishops of Germany, she publicly declared in complaint the causes of her flight and separation. Thus the mystery of iniquity, formerly said to be in darkness, began to be spoken of in light and openly—so far, however, as public hearing could bear it. The queen, finding no security in hiding within the kingdom of her own husband, whom she had left, first fled to the Hungarian kingdom, where she had certain relatives. When the emperor sent envoys to bring her back from there, [Col. 1457D] she returned to Ruthenia, her native kingdom, where she passed the rest of her life in holy widowhood.

The king himself persevered in the wickedness of his obscenity and impiety, selling bishoprics and granting ecclesiastical honours to all manner of vile persons, sometimes as payment for his own vile acts. So, while sporting in the beds among prostitutes and among the very companions, male and female, of his obscenities, he is said to have extended the investiture of a bishopric to someone by a ring in a shameful gesture too shameful to describe. A certain man then mocked and ridiculed the affair, or one like it, in learned verse as follows:

[Col. 1458A]

> A seducer of abbesses and queens,  
> He took a bishopric for adultery.  
> If Rome, head of the world, does not avenge this—  
> She who was the world’s head—let her be a tail and fear.

[Note: [Col. 1457] Aventinus recites these verses in Book V of the *Annals of Bavaria*.]

## CHAPTER XII. The city of Gibeah and the violated wife of the Israelite: an application to the condition of that time.

At that time the condition and aspect of the Church were most miserable, so that it is not easy to find a passage of Scripture to which it may suitably be compared (Judges 19). Yet the wife of the Israelite comes to mind: in the time of the Judges she was abused all night unto death by the men of the city of Gibeah. Her husband, finding her dead in the morning at the threshold of the house with her hands outstretched, carried her home upon an ass and cut her into twelve [Col. 1458B] pieces (Judges 20:6). Sending the portions to the twelve tribes of Israel, he moved them all to pity and zeal for vengeance.

For this cause, all assembled as one, they fought fiercely once and twice, with heavy slaughter of their own men, against the men of the city of Gibeah for justice, according to the Lord’s command. Finally, at the third engagement, victory was gained: all the men of the city of Gibeah, together with their brethren of the tribe of Benjamin, were destroyed, and their cities overthrown, women and little children alike being slain, so that scarcely any survivors could be found to restore the tribe.

Who is this woman, leaving her father and joined to an Israelite, except the holy Church, which has forsaken the devil or the world as father and has been united in marriage to Christ? [Col. 1458C] She returns to her Father as often as, deserting her husband, the Church, when love for Christ grows cold within her, joins herself in the fellowship of unfaithfulness or wicked conduct to this world or to its prince, the devil. But Christ her husband calls her back as often as, through the mouths of pastors and teachers and through the infusion of His Spirit, He rekindles in her the warmth of His love, gently saying something such as this: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house; and the king shall desire your beauty” (Ps. 44:12).

But while the Church passes through this life among proud and pestilent people, she is corrupted by the perverse teaching or wicked conduct of those same proud and pestilent people, as by men of the city of Gibeah, which is interpreted “lofty.” [Col. 1458D] Although the Church has often suffered this from wicked and depraved persons, never, as it seems to me, was she subjected to a fouler corruption than now, when a troop of Simoniacs, with reins loosed, burst in to satisfy their desires upon her chastity.

Finally, as it is written of the Gospel boats that they were filled so that they were almost sinking (Luke 5:7)—not that they sank, but that they were endangered even to the point of sinking—so we may say of the Church that, while her corruptors now abuse her throughout the whole night, that is, the hour of darkness, she has become dead—that is, near to death. Indeed, in many churches the life-giving warmth of the sacraments, by which they could have life, has been wholly extinguished; just as the fire of the Lord’s altar, preserved through so many years of the Babylonian captivity, is said to have been extinguished when Jason and Menelaus purchased the priesthood.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Gregory VII and his excellent zeal.

I do not think it should be passed over in silence what Christ, the husband of this woman, did through His vicar, Peter’s successor Gregory VII, then bishop of the city of Rome; or what zeal He showed for the death of His adulterated wife. For it is fitting that the mournful tragedy of that time and the Church’s struggle against the obstinacy of wicked men should be made known to posterity. The aforesaid Pope Gregory [Col. 1459B] VII, endowed with the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, after many forceful warnings sent to the aforesaid emperor and his counsellors by messengers and letters, commanded them to correct the monstrous excesses of his personal life. Above all, he commanded that he should wholly abstain from conferring upon anyone the ecclesiastical honours that he sold, since this did not belong to his office: kings are not to administer ecclesiastical dignities, but only lay ones. Men should come to the episcopal rank through merits of life and election by the clergy preceding, and through the laying on of episcopal hands. Pope Nicholas, Gregory’s predecessor, had likewise vigorously begun to reclaim churches, ecclesiastical offices, and their appointments for priests and ecclesiastical persons.

[Note: [Col. 1459D] Missing in the manuscript.]

[Col. 1459C] Therefore, after many exceedingly forceful admonitions and grave rebukes, and after applying the remedies of gentle instruction and exhortation, when he had accomplished nothing by all these means, he finally used the knife of cutting-off, delivering such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord (1 Cor. 5:5). Thus, when the Lord said, “I came not to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34), he too sent the sword, like another Maccabaeus: if he could not correct the wicked, he would at least disturb them, lest by sparing the sword of God’s word he might seem, through silence, to have consented, and wickedness might proceed unchecked.

How far from rash or hasty—indeed, how restrained—Pope Gregory VII was in pronouncing against him the sentence of excommunication is testified by his own apologetic letter addressed to bishops, princes, and other faithful persons established in the German kingdom. We have thought it not superfluous to insert that letter in this little work of ours.

“After the letter Gerhoh adds and continues the following.” Thus Gregory used his office both moderately and steadfastly against the perversity of Henry IV, as the apologetic letter quoted above teaches. But as it is written of Pharaoh, “His heart was hardened” (Exod. 4:21; 8:19), and another Scripture says of Leviathan, “His heart is hardened like a stone, and is compacted like a smith’s anvil; the archer shall not put him to flight; sling-stones are turned for him into stubble” (Job 41:15), so this strong man, broken in order that he might be corrected by the Lord, regarded as nothing the sword of God’s word and the wound by which he was struck. Not only was he not grieved unto repentance; cut off from the unity of the body, he attempted outside it, as it were, to construct another Church.

## CHAPTER XIV. Wigbert is set over Gregory.

Accordingly, by setting up against Gregory a certain Wigbert as another pope and naming him Clement, he must be judged to have erected an idol rather than ordained a pope. For whoever wishes to be second after the One is no longer second, but nothing. Therefore, when this image—not a pope—had been raised in the city of Brixen, [Col. 1460B] where the man who should no longer be called king but tyrant had celebrated Christmas, he made for Rome. Having driven out Gregory, the supreme pontiff, he placed this thing of his—not a pope but an image—on the seat of blessed Peter.

[Note: [Col. 1459D] These same words occur almost verbatim in the Reichersberg Chronicle, recently published by D. Gewold, under the year 1080.]

Gregory, however, went into exile in the kingdom of France; from there he sent letters strengthening the faithful of the Church whom he knew against iniquity, warning them not, by communicating with the schism, to defile the unity and holiness of Catholic peace. Henry, no longer king but tyrant, drove bishops and other faithful persons who would not join his party from their own sees, and set over them others—not bishops, but schismatics and heretics. Hardly a bishopric in his kingdom was found in which the division of this duality [Col. 1460C] did not exist. Hence came killings; hence mutilations of limbs among laity and clergy and the gouging out of eyes; hence public conflicts of citizens against citizens, some fighting for lawful pastors and others against pastors.

From that time, many faithful and prudent persons believed that what John had prophesied in the Apocalypse was fulfilled, or had begun to be fulfilled: “When the thousand years are completed, Satan shall be loosed from his prison, and shall go out and deceive many nations which are upon the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog,” and so forth (Rev. 20:7).

For until that time, through the Angel of Great Counsel, the same Satan, as is said there in the preceding verses, had been bound with a great chain in the abyss—that is, in the hearts of the wicked and in the depth of his own malice. It had been shut and sealed over him for a thousand years, so that he should deceive the nations no more until the thousand years were completed. For after this, as the same Scripture says, “he must be loosed for a short time” (ibid.). But at the time when the devil, through the aforesaid and still-to-be-discussed King Henry, began to exercise tyranny as though loosed—indeed, truly loosed—a thousand years had passed since the Lord’s Passion, when, as has been said, the devil was sent to prison and it was sealed over him. From that point began that duality of the papacy and discord between priesthood and kingdom, which certainly contributed greatly [Col. 1461A] to Satan’s release.

For as long as the priesthood stood strong, shining and burning through the good of unity and the worship of religion, and as long as the kingdom cooperated with the priesthood, it too flourished in goodness, being a terror not to good works but to evil. By the presence of these two lights Satan and his ministers, wicked men, were kept shut up in their dens like beasts before the presence of God. But when these two lights too were troubled against one another and grew lukewarm in the worship of religion; when, as it were, pope stood against pope, each attempting to loose what the other had bound, and conversely; when through the evil of simony and the depravity of incontinence the priesthood became like smoking flax—indeed, when in many cases it itself was a terror not to evil work but to good, while any bishop wishing to correct his clergy did not dare because of fear of the Roman court, as they call it, since they would find support there even for injustice through money—then [Col. 1461B] Satan was loosed. For night came, in which all the beasts of the forest passed through, the young lions roaring to seize prey and seek their food from God (Ps. 103:21): that is, they painted their cause with a certain appearance of piety, so that what they acted wickedly and bestially they might seem to do with God as author—namely, that they might “seek their food from God,” and so forth.

These seem to me to be the principal causes by which Satan was released: ecclesiastical and secular princes began to be a terror not to evil works [Col. 1461C] but to good; ecclesiastical honours began to be bestowed on the wicked and treated as saleable; and there arose that long-lasting and implacable dissension between priesthood and kingdom, through which the priesthood, together with the Church, was divided—although the Church cannot be other than one, nor the priesthood other than one.

But may the Lord, according to His promise, cause Satan’s release to endure only for a short time: “He must,” He says, “be loosed for a short time” (Rev. 20:3). “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the elect’s sake,” He says, “those days shall be shortened” (cf. Matt. 24:22; cited here as Job 17:1). Let it be enough that for almost seventy years the Church of Christ has laboured in the darkness of that time in which Satan was loosed, and in which all the beasts of the forest pass through, the young lions roaring [Col. 1461D] to seize prey and seek their food from God. Let the sun now arise, as it is written immediately afterward: “Let these beasts gather together and be placed in their dens; and let man go forth to his work and to his labour until evening,” and let him say: “How magnified are Your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom,” and so forth (Ps. 91:6). Now let us return to the point from which we digressed, and record what remains of Henry’s tyranny.

## CHAPTER XV. The deposition of Henry IV from the empire, and the appointment and death of Rudolf and Hermann.

Seeing Henry, under the name of king, exercising tyranny against the Church of Christ and that evil increasing daily, the faithful, following Pope Gregory’s counsel, assembled together wishing to oppose Henry’s tyranny. They first made this most firm agreement: that Rudolf should never claim for himself any power in appointing ecclesiastical dignities. When he learned this, Henry, now no longer king but tyrant, equipped his forces and prepared for war against King Rudolf. King Rudolf met him with a strong hand, relying especially on Saxon assistance. Battle was joined near the river Unstrut, at the place called Hohenmölsen [Welfesholz]. There, after great slaughter on both sides, it happened—by what judgment God knows—that the man who had undertaken war for the Church of Christ and justice fell in battle.

After Rudolf was killed, not long afterward the faithful of the Church elected another of the princes, named Hermann, as king. He too, having possessed the kingdom for not even the span of one whole year, was treacherously killed by Henry’s supporters. Thus the likeness of the contest concerning the violated woman, which we presented above, was not lacking in the Church’s struggle (Judges 20:5). For just as the adversaries of justice were victorious twice there, so too in this contest, with two kings killed in defence of justice, the adversaries gained victory twice.

If a likeness to the woman cut into pieces is also sought in the present case, it will be this: the lawful husband Christ, or His vicar—for example Gregory VII—cut the woman into pieces out of good zeal, that is, showed forth the Church as torn and lacerated by schismatics, in order to stir the minds of the faithful to vengeance for so great a crime through the display of the cutting. In this manner of speaking, “to cut the woman apart” may mean “to show that she has been cut apart.” For the Lord also, speaking to Abraham, says: “Now I have known”—that is, “I have made known”—“that you fear the Lord” (Gen. 22:12). This kind of expression, which puts the efficient cause for the effect, or conversely, is commonly called metonymy by grammarians.

## CHAPTER XVI. Pope Victor succeeds Gregory; Urban succeeds Victor.

Meanwhile, while these events were taking place concerning Kings Rudolph and Hermann, Gregory VII died in exile, and Victor was appointed in his place; Urban in turn succeeded Victor, while Wigbert—whom they had called Clement—still occupied the see of Peter in the city of Rome [Col. 1462D]. This Urban showed himself the lawful successor of Gregory VII, not only in rank but also in virtue—indeed, of Peter himself. In his time the Franks, stirred by his exhortation, wrested from the pagans, by mighty strength and with the assistance of a visible ministry of angels, the city of Jerusalem, namely the place of the Lord’s tomb, as the little book giving the connected account of this teaches.

In that city also, through the clergy who migrated there, the pattern of common life which is known to have first begun there through the apostles flourished anew. They judged, very rightly, that no other rule of life ought to be introduced into that city than one corresponding to the foundations of its first apostolic institution. This planting of the lawful shoot, revived in that holy city, now spread its branches widely from there, as the soil of good hearts readily and gladly received what had first been planted by the very right hand of the Lord in the little field of His own colony [Col. 1463A]. Persecution too cooperated in this good work. For when the better clergy were expelled from cities because they withheld communion from the excommunicated prince and from his supporters and communicants, they lived together in woods and in fields near the towns. There certain faithful and powerful persons, to whom God had given this inspiration, protected them; and they began to observe that rule of life which they had recognized as especially pleasing to Christ, for whose sake they were also enduring persecution.

Thus, among both clergy and monks, the life of apostolic institution—which first revived in deserts and wooded places—gradually returned even to ancient monasteries and those near towns, their evil inhabitants having been expelled or changed for the better. As it is written: “The lovely places of the wilderness shall grow rich, and the hills shall gird themselves with exultation” (Ps. 64:13). Another Scripture also says: “And he will let out his vineyard to other husbandmen” (Matt. 21:41) [Col. 1463B].

At the same time the ancient canons concerning the continence of the ministers of the holy altar began to be renewed, with new commands added, against those living otherwise than continently. The people, when they knew this without doubt, were also forbidden to hear the masses of simoniacs and of those who held office for hire. These three Roman pontiffs—Nicholas, Gregory, and this Urban of whom we speak—successively affirmed and commanded the same things, as though with one voice, so that every word might stand “in the mouth of two or three witnesses” [Col. 1463C].

Urban himself, moreover, was deceitfully brought into the hands of his adversaries and was held captive for some time in one of the towers of Rome.

## CHAPTER XVII. Robert frees the pope.

But divine mercy delivered him from there through the hand of Robert, surnamed Guiscard, while a large district of the City was blazing in fire and the tower meanwhile was stormed. The people, hurrying to the fires, were occupied there. Thus, with the Lord cooperating, he was freed and returned to France. There he confidently performed the duties of the apostolic office: he renewed the sentence of excommunication against Henry [Col. 1463D], and by letters and embassies encouraged the faithful to stand and act for the Church.

He recalled to peace the French themselves, who were disputing among themselves over lands and earthly matters. He urged them and, speaking among them with Urban’s voice, pleaded that if leisure displeased them and their own land seemed too narrow, they should make for the lands of the East and there strive to recover the holy city and rescue the Lord’s tomb from the hands of the gentiles. There either, by the Lord’s gift, they might triumph gloriously, or it would be more glorious to die for Christ; and happy would be those who either conquered for Christ or died for Christ. His word attained its victory [Col. 1464A], the Lord cooperating and committing the word to its effect “with signs following” (Mark 16:20), aided by angelic powers which, as stated above, visibly manifested their presence.

But in the City Guibert, whom they called Clement, laboured vigorously on behalf alike of the leadership of his sect and of Henry’s tyranny. He presented himself as the true abomination of desolation of which we are now speaking: standing in the holy place—that is, occupying the seat of blessed Peter as an abominable counterfeit pope. On this subject someone, in the form of a dialogue, played scholastically with the words of both men in alternating verses as follows:

> [Note: [Col. 1463D] Cited from Aventinus, book V.]

> You are called Urban, though you have been cast out of the City:  
> Either change your name, or return to the City.

Likewise:

> You bear the name Clement, but you cannot be merciful,  
> Since no power of binding and loosing has been given to you.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Henry is raised as king against his father.

Meanwhile, very many princes and other men of courage feared the sentence of excommunication, sympathized with the Church and acted for it; and, at the urging of Pope Urban, they resolved to raise Henry, son of Henry, as king. They hoped that through the son, lawfully reigning, they might resist the father’s tyranny; and this was done.

When the son had been raised as king and was making for the city of Regensburg [Col. 1464C], his father met him with a multitude of armed men, aided by the duke of Bohemia and the margrave of Upper Pannonia. But the clash of battle was prevented by the river called Regen. While a delay intervened, the aforesaid princes, having received certain pledges from the father’s side, went over to the son. From then on Henry the father was driven back, struck down, and diminished, until, wholly deprived of the princes’ aid, he at last presented prayers and supplications to his son that he might be granted security in a private life. It came about that at a celebrated assembly he resigned the imperial crown and asked to be absolved from the excommunication by which he was bound, and restored to ecclesiastical communion.

But he did not obtain what he requested. The Catholics feared and took precautions lest, once absolved, he might perhaps devise something hostile to the Church or the empire [Col. 1464D]. Thus he was kept without communion in a certain castle, having become so abominable that even grooms and very small boys would not touch the remains of his food, as though to preserve the Church’s communion, but threw them to dogs in his sight.

This is testified by a letter which he sent to the princes from the very confinement in which he was held. Among other lamentations he complains that “on the holy night of the Lord’s Nativity, while all Christians hastened to churches and partook of the sacred mysteries, Christ, who was born for the salvation of all, was denied to him alone” [Col. 1465A]—indeed by God’s just judgment. For he who had expelled many bishops and priests from their own sees was himself justly deprived of the kingdom; he who had unjustly cast others into chains was bound and committed to custody; and he who had defiled the most holy mysteries on the sacred night of the Lord’s Nativity was most justly considered unworthy of and excluded from those same mysteries. What his repentance was, the Lord sees. He ended his life outside the communion of the Church.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Henry V and his tyranny.

The son, then, once established in the kingdom, at first acted modestly, showed himself gracious, and preserved the rights of ecclesiastical liberty [Col. 1465B]. But the piety which had been feigned for the sake of obtaining the kingdom and empire, like the appearance of gold laid over a base surface, began to reveal what it was within when it had been slightly worn away by the exercise of rule.

What sort of man he showed himself in secular causes is of no concern to us to say. But we judge it not irrelevant briefly to indicate what he was shown to be in the affairs of the Church, if perhaps we may find in his deeds also the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, concerning which our inquiry is being made.

## CHAPTER XX. Wicbert is cast out.

Meanwhile, while the events already described were taking place between the two Henrys, father and son, Wicbert, called Clement, was overthrown and cast out with the agreement of Henry the younger. Pope Urban returned to Rome [Col. 1465C]; and when he too died, Paschal II succeeded him, likewise an excellent champion of God’s law, ancestral traditions, and ecclesiastical liberty.

But King Henry, following the precipitous path of his father, regarded it as a very great loss to his kingdom and empire if he allowed the investitures of bishoprics to remain free, as he had promised at his elevation. Like another Haman, he counted all the glory of his kingdom as nothing unless Mordecai—that is, the priestly order caring for the Church, the royal bride—should bend the knee before him for the gaining of ecclesiastical honours.

## CHAPTER XXI. Henry V usurps priestly powers.

[Col. 1465D]

Accordingly, when bishops died, he too began either to forestall lawful elections for appointing others or to disregard elections already made; he conferred bishoprics according to his personal favour, in return for money, or for service rendered. When Pope Paschal addressed fatherly admonitions to him, calling him back to the right way—that, content with the justice proper to his kingdom, he should not usurp pontifical functions, should show honour to the Church of God, his mother, and should not rashly violate her liberty, which she ought to possess in electing priests—he returned fine words, words which might seem reasonable, if only toil and pain had not lain hidden beneath his tongue [Col. 1466A].

For he said and wrote that he was ready to grant liberty of episcopal election, to resign investitures, and even to remit tithes to the churches, provided that the apostolic lord wished to restore to the empire throughout his kingdom all regalian rights: namely duchies, marches, counties, lordships with their benefices, mints, tolls, and fortifications.

In making this promise, he knew that especially the bishops of Germany, France, and Saxony—who possessed many royal riches and honours through ancient grants of kings and emperors—would not consent. Yet through promises bearing a certain appearance of piety he sought to obtain the imperial crown, to be placed upon him through the blessing of the Roman pontiff. The apostolic lord too, accepting these promises, wrote back to him concerning what he had requested: namely, the placing of the imperial crown and the restitution of all regalian rights, provided that the king fulfilled his promises concerning the liberty of the Church [Col. 1466B].

These dealings between the king and the Roman pontiff were conducted with few witnesses; the bishops—with the sole exception of the emperor’s chancellor—and the other princes of Church and empire were wholly unaware of the promises made on either side. Therefore, once such promises had been given and accepted on both sides, the king proceeded to Rome with a great company of bishops and other princes. On arriving, he entered the city after oaths had been sworn and faith pledged that peace would be fully preserved for the Roman pontiff and the City.

## CHAPTER XXII. Pope Paschal is taken captive by King Henry.

[Col. 1466C]

They had now reached the middle of the church of St Peter, where they were to discuss the respective rights to be maintained and the terms of concord between priesthood and kingdom. Seats were placed on either side, and, surrounded by a dense circle of armed men, they met.

Letters sent from the emperor’s side to the Roman pontiff were brought forward. The pope’s chancellor asked the emperor and his chancellor whether they acknowledged them as their own letters and as sent by them.

> [Note: [Col. 1465D] Read Baronius, vol. XII, years 1100 and 1101.]

When they had answered that they did, those letters were read publicly, containing the lord king’s promises to the lord pope [Col. 1466D]. Likewise, letters sent by the lord pope were brought forward from the lord king’s side; they were questioned and answered concerning them, and the letters were publicly recited in turn, containing the lord pope’s promises to the lord king.

When the unheard-of promises struck the ears of the bishops, they realized that, in order that the imperial crown might be placed on the king’s head, they and their churches were to be stripped of their ancient possessions. As though with one voice they objected, saying that they were unwilling to buy an imperial crown for the king at so great a loss to their churches. Armed men standing around them pressed them with threats and terrors, as though they would immediately be killed unless they consented [Col. 1467A]. But Conrad, archbishop of Salzburg, offered his head to be cut off rather than give consent to what was demanded. And after a confused outcry had risen on both sides for some time, the king rose in anger and agitation and began to depart. The lord pope too, by order of the soldiers, was forced to go with the king and after the king.

Then robbery raged; Roman citizens who wished to free their shepherd were slaughtered. The lord cardinals and the other clergy found within the enclosure of St Peter’s church were dragged away as captives. All the doors of the church had been barred, so that no one could escape freely. Seeing what was being done, the bishops groaned, denounced the deed, and cried out that it was sacrilege [Col. 1467B].

After a great and unspeakable slaughter had been inflicted upon the citizens, the king departed, and Lord Pope Paschal went with him—compelled by another and led where he did not wish to go. It was a sight of misery. Cardinals and other clergy were led out bound with ropes and dragged by horsemen; they followed as they could through the streets, scarcely emerging from deep, clinging mud. Since the foot soldiers could not keep pace with the horsemen, the latter pricked their backs and sides with transverse spears to force them to run, so that some expired in the hands of those dragging them. Those who survived were held through the night, shut either in sacks or bound with chains or other restraints lest they escape, until money was perhaps extorted from them—money which they themselves or their friends might possess [Col. 1467C].

Nor is this surprising in the case of the living, since, when the citizens had been defeated, they had even sold many corpses, for a money-price, to ransom captives. The pope was led away and held in custody. Bishops and others who feared God nevertheless continued to honour him. The king held him captive with the intention of extorting from him, by the cord of captivity, the imperial blessing; and thus, together with the blessing, either obtaining investitures of bishoprics or drawing all regalian rights back to the empire. “I will not let you go,” he says—Jacob the patriarch—“unless you bless me in this manner” (Gen. 32:26).

But he was very unlike the one who first spoke those words. For Jacob obtained a blessing from the angel by humility, tears, and prayers, as is written of him: “In his strength he strove with the angel; he prevailed over the angel, he wept and entreated him” [Col. 1467D]. But this man, by captivity, threats, terrors, and many sacrileges, extorted the blessing—or should I call it the curse?—of the imperial crown as he desired.

Jacob, the patriarch, when blessed by the angel, limped on one foot because the sinew of his thigh had withered. Thus he was greater in spiritual things, in which he had grown through the blessing, and lesser in temporal things; for it is characteristic of one who limps to walk stronger with one foot and weaker with the other. But this man, once he had received the imperial blessing, claimed equal authority for himself in spiritual and temporal matters [Col. 1468A]. For, elections being despised, the man was accounted more worthy than all others of the honour of a bishopric who was more familiar to him, or who offered him more service or money.

And in the very tents he had obtained the privilege, such as he wished, for drawing all regalian rights back to the empire, from the pope whom—while the age wondered and was indignant—he carried with him as his captive.

> [Note: [Col. 1467D] Read Baronius, vol. XII, years 1111 and 1112.]

For this reason nearly all the bishops of France assembled a council in order to excommunicate Pope Paschal himself as an enemy and destroyer of the Church unless he himself, who had granted it, condemned that privilege [Col. 1468B]. And this was done. For Paschal, presiding at a council and supported by a multitude of bishops together with the lord cardinals, condemned the very privilege—or rather, the “perversion-privilege” (*pravilegium*)—which had been extorted from him under captivity, thereby bringing a curse in place of blessing, since all kings were abusing that privilege to dishonour or lay open the Church.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Gelasius succeeds Paschal; Burdinus is imposed upon him by the king.

Not long afterwards Pope Paschal entered the way of all flesh, and Gelasius succeeded to the pontificate, likewise an excellent champion of God’s law and ecclesiastical liberty [Col. 1468C]. On the fortieth day after his ordination, Emperor Henry entered the City and thrust over him a certain beast named Burdinus, Pope Gelasius having been driven from Rome.

> [Note: [Col. 1468D] In the year of Christ 1118. Read Baronius for this year.]

Once more one could see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, and the son of perdition sitting in the temple of God, which is the Church, and exalting himself “above all that is called God or that is worshipped” (2 Thess. 2:3): Pope Gelasius being in exile, while Burdinus occupied the seat of blessed Peter—indeed, the seat of Christ. Of him and those like him I might rightly say that he has exalted himself above all that is called God or worshipped. For they strive to set themselves above not only Christ’s true priests, of whom the Lord says, “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 86:6), but also above Christ, besides whom there is no other God, when they despise and reject Him, the true bridegroom of the Church, and with adulterous boldness invade His place [Col. 1468D].

## CHAPTER XXIV. Conflict between kingdom and priesthood.

Burdinus, occupying the seat of blessed Peter, laboured earnestly to fulfill the mystery of iniquity. Gelasius, however, in exile, invited King Henry to correction as a father invites a son: that he should leave to the Church her liberty in the elections of bishops and hasten to remove the statue which he had set up in the holy place against God. Conversely [Col. 1469A], the emperor resisted, saying that he either wished to draw all regalian rights back to the empire or to retain the ancient custom in appointing bishops. If the Church desired the power freely to elect bishops, it should restore to the empire what belonged to it; and only then should it enjoy free election.

The bishops, rich from regalian rights, argued in opposition: elections of bishops, according to the rules of the canons, ought to be wholly free. It was not just, however, that churches should lose royal riches or honours freely conferred upon them by the generosity of kings. Indeed, they said, it was too little that, because God’s holy martyrs had suffered not merely torments but also insults from pagan kings, they should now be elevated by kings with glory and honour in recompense for the insult endured [Col. 1469B].

They said that a type of this matter—both of glory and of insult—had preceded in Joseph. From the prison of the king of Egypt, which he had suffered unjustly, Joseph was elevated second in Pharaoh’s chariot and additionally adorned with the royal ring. This, they said, was what the bridegroom says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots” (Song 1:8). Nor, they say, does the Church cease for that reason to be Christ’s friend and beloved because she has been compared to Christ’s cavalry, typologically exalted in Joseph, among Pharaoh’s chariots; just as Joseph did not cease to be a patriarch beloved by God and men because he sat in Pharaoh’s chariot. Pharaoh’s chariot, they say, did not crush or extinguish him but exalted him.

Thus too, they say, Pope Sylvester of Rome did not cease to be a pontiff beloved by God and men because Constantine Augustus placed him upon a royal horse and saddle and further adorned him with certain royal insignia [Col. 1469C].

> [Note: [Col. 1469D] See the edict of Constantine the Great.]

To crown his honour, Constantine himself held the bridle and performed for him the office of groom through the city. Hence, even to this day, the memory of both—the devout prince Constantine and the blessed Roman pontiff Sylvester—is held in blessing and ought always to be so in times to come.

They add also and say that the same view should be held of the Church as of Christ Jesus. For just as in Christ Jesus distinct periods are found, of suffering and of glory: the period of suffering being past, when, after receiving vinegar, He said, “It is finished” (John 19:30); and the period of glory beginning among men when, having risen from the dead, He was appointed by God judge of the living and the dead (Acts 10:42) [Col. 1469D]. Hence He Himself, risen from the dead, says: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18). And the Psalmist, embracing both in one verse, says of Him: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour, and appointed him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things under his feet” (Ps. 8:6).

So also in the Church are found distinct periods of suffering and glory. Her period of suffering, that is, of persecution, lasted while the blood of martyrs was shed by the cruel decrees of pagan emperors, up to the times of the devout prince Constantine [Col. 1470A]. Then the Church was glorious only before God, not before men. From that time, however, increased also by glory, honour, and royal riches, she began to be glorious not only before God but also before men. Kings and the highest powers of kingdoms bowed to her, and magnificently honoured the confessions of the saints, in recompense for their former disgrace, by buildings and grants of estates. Among these certain royal honours were conferred upon her, so that it is fitting that Christ her bridegroom should say of her, as we have stated: that His beloved has been compared to cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.

They say that a type of this matter had also preceded in the three youths and their fourth companion Daniel (Dan. 3) [Col. 1470B]. For after overcoming the Babylonian furnace, the three youths were afterward held in high renown by the king and exercised magisterial office in the province of Babylon. Daniel too, after interpreting royal dreams, and after reading and interpreting the writing inscribed on the wall of the royal hall opposite the lampstand, deserved to be crowned with a golden collar and ranked third in Belshazzar’s kingdom, just as he had been renowned in Nebuchadnezzar’s kingdom (Dan. 5). Thus it is manifest that in those three youths the labour of martyrs and their subsequent glory, and in Daniel the vigilance of holy confessors and teachers, their skill in loosing those who are bound, and likewise their subsequent glory both temporal and eternal, shone forth typologically [Col. 1470C].

A clear type of these three things—martyrdom, confession or skill in resolving hidden matters, and the glory to follow both before God and before men—also shone forth in Joseph alone. For as a type of martyrdom he innocently endured prison; as a type of confession or teaching he interpreted the king’s dreams; as a type of glory to follow, he too was glorious and was accounted second in Pharaoh’s kingdom after the king.

Therefore, they say, since such images shone forth beforehand in the Old Testament, it should not seem unseemly but rather worthy and just that the holy Church, for consolation after her past labours and disgraces, should be assisted not only with necessary resources [Col. 1470D], but also adorned with royal honours, riches, and insignia of honour. Although perhaps not all these things were said at that time by bishops and others of the clergy in defense of ecclesiastical eminence, they could nevertheless have been said on the authority of Holy Scripture.

But those who took the king’s side said that tithes and free offerings—that is, offerings subject to no royal or imperial service—ought to be sufficient for ecclesiastics. Lands which emperors had granted to churches on the condition that bishops holding them owe service to kings ought either to be restored to the empire or their episcopal holders ought to render to kings the customary homages and services [Col. 1471A]. This was especially required, they said, by the Lord’s command: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21).

And since the apostle Paul, in whom Christ spoke, says: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has proved himself” (2 Tim. 2:4), it is sufficiently evident, they say, that priests who bind themselves to kings by homages cannot adequately please God, given the rank of their office. Therefore, that they may please Him to whom they have proved themselves, let them leave military service and the rest for which homages are owed to kings free to the realm. Let them themselves devote themselves to prayer and keep watch over feeding Christ’s sheep, for which they were appointed. For the Lord says to Peter: “Feed my lambs; feed my lambs”; and the third time, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:15) [Col. 1471B].

Peter himself, duly concerned for the ministry of his office, says: “It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables” (Acts 6:2). Likewise, in his ordination of Clement, he says: “Christ does not wish to ordain you to become a judge of secular causes or a hearer of forensic disputes,” etc. If, they say, it is not right for a priest of the Lord, leaving the word of God, to serve tables or become a judge in secular disputes, how much less right is it, after leaving the word of God, to lead troops, attend royal camps, carry earthworks for overthrowing cities, and construct the means by which killings are frequently committed? Even if such acts are sometimes justly undertaken by the side of kings in command, it is not lawful for God’s priest to participate in them, lest holy eyes be violated—unless perhaps necessity should for a time demand his presence, in order to exhort citizens to defend their country against foreigners; or unless it should be necessary for the Lord’s priest to go to royal camps to conduct divine matters and offer salutary counsel [Col. 1471C].

Therefore, they say, since the most divine authority of the Gospel commands these things, reason agrees, and necessity requires them, let what belongs to Caesar be left to Caesar, lest bishops entangled in such matters be unable to render to God what belongs to God. For, they say, devotion to God and service in the world are very contrary. Or if bishops, retaining regalian rights, strive to serve both God and the empire and suppose themselves equal to both tasks [Col. 1471D], emperors ought, they say, to have the first place also in ordaining and appointing bishops. For it is not fitting for the empire that anyone be raised to be a prince of the realm except by the emperor himself, with the counsel of the other princes.

It would take a long time to recount these and similar things which in that dispute were said, or could have been said, on either side to establish or weaken the other party’s case; or to recount what the mediating envoys carried back and forth. For while Pope Gelasius held a council at Reims and Emperor Henry remained at Verdun, the affair was conducted through messenger-mediators. For the present matter, it is enough to know this: at that time the emperor hardened his heart so as not to leave free elections to the churches [Col. 1472A], while the bishops hardened their resolve so as not to surrender regalian rights to the empire.

Rather, they said that things once consecrated to the Lord could not be alienated from the dominion of the saints (Lev. 27:20). The divine law also says that if anyone wishes to exchange what has been consecrated to the Lord, both things belong to the Lord: both what is exchanged and that for which it is exchanged. They admitted that for these regalian rights they owed customary obligations to the empire, and declared themselves ready to serve the king in defense of his crown, insofar as this could be done consistently with the integrity and observance of their office. Thus they would render to Caesar what was Caesar’s and to God what was God’s.

But whether being bound to kings by homages and oaths is an entanglement in secular affairs—the thing rebuked in priests by Paul’s words—the lord priests and bishops themselves must see; it is above us to judge their conduct [Col. 1472B]. They may also sometimes redeem with money the time for prayer and reading, so as, though entangled, to be almost free. But whether even such an entanglement, and the rendering or redemption of such service, lightens or burdens the Church of God more, the Lord sees; and may He at last provide His holy Church with fitting liberty.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the excommunication of Henry V.

Meanwhile the aforesaid Emperor Henry, unwilling to surrender the Church of God’s elections and investitures, hardening his heart ever more against salutary admonitions, and defending and supporting the beast—that is, Burdinus—intruded into the seat of blessed Peter, was separated from the Church of God as a schismatic and rebel against the Lord by Gelasius, Roman pontiff, with the concurrence of many bishops assembled in the city of Reims [Col. 1472C]. Thus they parted ways.

Henry, becoming fiercer like a wounded beast, exacted vengeance as upon rebels against the empire when the clergy did not receive him as he departed and entered certain cities of his kingdom with their customary favour and praises; some had withdrawn themselves from receiving him. He ordered their houses to be overthrown.

Not long afterward Gelasius died, and Callistus succeeded him [Col. 1472D]. In his time the Church was at last granted freedom to elect its bishops, and the investiture by ring and staff—that is, the pastoral rod used in the consecration of bishops—was recognized as belonging to her. For the emperor, seeing the Church’s heavy hand upon himself and fearing that, if his iniquity were exposed through the rational heavens, that is, the bishops and saints of God, even the earth—that is, earthly princes—might rise against him, and that he himself might thus be deprived of the kingdom as had happened to his father, assembled a court at the place called Lobwise. There the envoys of the Roman see were present. He surrendered to the Church, as stated above, free elections and investitures, so that a person elected or consecrated should receive regalian rights from the hand of emperor or king by the sceptre [Col. 1473A], after doing homage and swearing fealty to him.

Thus Burdinus was removed from the midst and sent into the monastery called Cavea; the emperor too was absolved from the bond of anathema; and peace was restored to the Church of God.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the abomination of desolation.

We must now recall why we have pursued, in the manner of historical writing, these matters concerning Henry IV and V. For our inquiry concerns the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, and likewise the son of perdition sitting, or to sit, in the temple of God. Yet I judge that the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place is nothing other than the son of perdition himself sitting in the temple of God.

The arrangement of our preceding discourse proceeded as follows: the man-made temple of God, which was built at Jerusalem as a type of the Church, and the events that occurred concerning it, have been set before us as a mirror or as though a divining cup. We compare with them the things that have occurred concerning the Church of God down to our own time, perhaps so that from their mutual comparison it may become known to us from what time the abomination of desolation began mystically to stand in the temple of God, which is the Church [Col. 1473B].

Certainly it is quite customary to compare typologically Solomon’s work in building the temple with the works of Christ, who built His Church through preaching, miracles, and finally the expenditure of His own Passion. For the Lord Jesus died; He rose for our justification; He ascended for our consummation; and He sent the Holy Spirit for our sanctification and strengthening—we who ought to be, and are, His holy temple [Col. 1473C].

But the king of Babylon—the devil, prince of confusion—did not permit this holy temple of God, which is the Church, to remain at peace. He stirred up against it the Roman emperors, or the rulers of the other Babylon, through whom he attempted both to overthrow that same holy temple and to undermine the faith. For Rome, as we have also taught above, is figuratively designated by Peter under the name Babylon because of similarity of manners: “The Church gathered in Babylon greets you” (1 Pet. 5:13). He wrote this epistle while residing at Rome in the time of Caesar Claudius, with Mark his disciple dwelling there with him.

How greatly the enemy acted maliciously, through the rulers of both Babylons, in overthrowing this holy temple of God—which is the Church—and likewise the temple made by hands, as we have also recalled above, requires no demonstration from us. The books of Kings contain the overthrow of the material temple. And the struggles of the Church, the acts of the martyrs, attest deeds full of the most savage cruelty, which are daily brought before our ears in reading. Concerning each house alike—namely, that made by hands and this one which is the Church of God—there is rightly understood that lament which the voices of the Church utter in psalmody:

> “O God, the nations have entered into thy inheritance;  
> they have defiled thy holy temple;  
> they have made Jerusalem a watch-house for orchards;  
> they have given the corpses of thy servants as food to the birds of heaven,  
> the flesh of thy saints to the beasts of the earth;  
> they have poured out their blood like water round about it,  
> and there was none to bury them,” etc.  
> (Ps. 78 [79]:1–3)

## Chapter XXVII. Comparison of the Christian faith, under pagan kings, with the furnace of Babylon

Thus the times of persecution inflicted upon the Church by Roman rulers correspond most fittingly to the times when the temple was overthrown by Babylonian rulers. There they were compelled by tortures to worship a golden statue. Here they were compelled, by innumerable kinds of torments, to worship the silver and golden images of the nations. There a single furnace was prepared for those who despised the royal command; here the whole world, inflamed for the slaughter of the saints, was as one furnace for the martyrs. There three youths under one king; here worshippers of the Trinity—many thousands of martyrs, that is—despised the unjust commands of kings.

There, through the three youths and their companion Daniel, the beastlike heart of King Nebuchadnezzar put on so much humanity that he confessed the true God and his Son, saying: “Truly your God is the God of gods and the Lord of kings, revealing mysteries, because you were able to disclose this mystery” (Dan. 2:47). Again: “Behold, I see four men unbound, and there is no injury in them; and the appearance of the fourth is like a Son of God” (Dan. 3:92).

And in what follows he says: “Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who sent his angel and delivered his servants who believed in him; and they changed the king’s word and gave up their bodies, so as not to serve or worship any god except their own God. Therefore this decree is issued by me: that every people, tribe, and tongue which speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall perish, and his house shall be laid waste” (Dan. 3:95–96).

Scripture then continues:

> “Then King Nebuchadnezzar promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon. King Nebuchadnezzar to all peoples, nations, and tongues who dwell throughout the earth: may peace be multiplied to you. The Most High God has performed signs and wonders for me. Therefore it pleased me to proclaim his signs, because they are great, and his wonders, because they are mighty; and his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his power is from generation to generation.”  
> (ibid., 97–100)

Thus, as we have said, the three youths with their companion Daniel brought the beastlike heart of the king, transformed into a human one, to knowledge and confession of the one and only true God. Similarly, the perseverance of the holy martyrs—like three youths confessing the holy Trinity with one voice—brought it about that that terrible beast of Daniel’s vision, having iron teeth, devouring, crushing, and trampling the remainder under its feet, namely the beastlike and terrible Roman empire, put on a human mind and, acknowledging the Lord of majesty, subjected itself to him in true humility.

## Chapter XXVIII. The cessation of persecution by Roman rulers and Babylonian kings; and a comparison of better decrees enacted on both sides

The decree that anyone speaking blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego should perish and have his house laid waste was a type indicating that, through the Roman emperors already mentioned, better decrees than the former ones were to be enacted for the Church of God.

But a clearer type of this matter shone forth in the later kingdoms and kings: namely, Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, kings of the Persians and Medes, who released the captivity, restored the vessels of the Lord’s house, permitted the house itself to be rebuilt, and supplied expenses for its construction. This was a type of that splendid event later accomplished in the Roman empire through the pious ruler Constantine. For when that ruler, already mentioned, came to the faith, the evil laws instituted through him were abolished and better laws established for the peace and advancement of the Catholic Church, as it is written:

> “Lift up your gates, O rulers,  
> and be lifted up, eternal gates,  
> and the King of glory shall enter.”  
> (Ps. 23 [24]:7)

The gates of rulers which were to be removed were their evil laws, at times set forth against the Church even on bronze tablets. The eternal gates were the good laws enacted for the Church; and they were lifted up when, as has been said, the pious ruler Constantine and other emperors after him established excellent laws for the Church of God.

Indeed, this ruler devoted himself so fully to the peace, advancement, and exaltation of God’s Church that, as is written of the king of Nineveh—that, upon hearing the preaching of God’s word through the prophet Jonah, he rose from his throne and put on sackcloth (Jon. 3:5)—so this ruler Constantine, whose memory is blessed, repenting of his former ignorance, granted the place of his throne, namely the city of Rome, to the prince of the apostles and to his successors, the Roman pontiffs. Within the Lateran palace, which was higher than all palaces, he caused a church to be consecrated in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior. He established for himself the seat of empire in the eastern regions, on the excellent soil of the land, consecrating Byzantium. For he judged it inequitable that the primacy of the priesthood in Peter’s vicar and the imperial seat should be enclosed within the bounds of one city. Thus the truth of later events corresponds to the ancient type: the pious grants made to God’s churches by the ruler Constantine fittingly answer to the grants concerning the rebuilding of the temple made by Cyrus, Artaxerxes, and Darius.

## Chapter XXIX. The hindrance to the rebuilding of the temple compared with the machinations of heretics

Certainly, when captivity had been released by Cyrus, the holy vessels brought back from Babylon to Jerusalem, and the foundations of the temple laid, the work was obstructed by rulers beyond the River in the regions of Samaria. Their names were these: Rehum, Beel-Theeman, and Shimshai the scribe, and their other counselors. They sent a letter of accusation against the Jews first to King Artaxerxes and afterward to Darius (1 Esdras 4:17).

That this work was impeded by these persons until the second year of Darius, king of the Persians and Medes, the devil himself had earlier attempted to construct, through men who had moved away from the east—that is, from knowledge and love of the one true God—as a type of heretics against the house of God and as a type of future heresies. So too he severed the ten tribes from God’s house by means of golden calves, not only envying that material house of God but also aiming at the future schism of heretics against the Church.

The scheme of those persons, already mentioned, who impeded the work, achieved this: at their instigation King Artaxerxes ordered that the same work should not be allowed to proceed until they should perhaps learn some other command of the king concerning it. Counting the period of this hindrance together with the period during which it was built, the Jews said: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it in three days?” (John 2:20). Yet the Lord, to whom they said this in their attempt to construct an accusation, had spoken not of that temple made by hands but of the temple of his body: “Destroy this temple,” he said, “and in three days I will raise it up” (ibid., 19).

Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arab also strongly resisted those rebuilding the same house of the Lord. They brought against them Ammonites, Arabs, and Ashdodites, preventing them by force and power (2 Esdras 4). At times, moreover, feigning peace, they offered deceitful assistance in building with them. But they were not admitted, being deceitful men and strangers to the faith.

What is more rightly understood by their open hostility and fraudulent association than the heretics’ sometimes manifest cruelty and sometimes deceitful agreement against the Church? “They were with me in many things,” he says.

“But the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has greatly increased his treachery against me” (Ps. 40 [41]:10).

Who does not know the circumcellions of the Manichaeans [Donatists]? Roaming about the cells, they plotted deceit against God’s saints, and, using cruel hands while pretending zeal for God’s zeal, inflicted countless killings. Who is ignorant of the obstinacy of the Arians—now pretending, through a gloss of words, that they hold the same faith as we do; now openly spewing blasphemies against Christ; and, moreover, inciting against the Church kings infected with the doctrine of their perversity? Through these kings, by open violence, they closed the churches of Catholics, drove their bishops into exile, and installed bishops of their own sect in the cities—or rather fashioned certain idols of bishops.

All these things proved not merely a very great hindrance but also a loss to the house of God, which is the Church, in its rebuilding. For first, as stated above, that same house was built through Christ, the true Solomon; then it was destroyed through persecuting kings and princes, as though Babylonians; afterward it was rebuilt, by the kings’ concession, through the children of the migration. Those men just mentioned opposed the builders, as types of heretics.

Nor would it be unfitting to assign to them the type of heretics. For, dwelling in the regions of Samaria, they possessed the books and law of God (4 Kings 17:28), from which they searched out resemblances for their idols. While offering sacrifices to the Lord, they also sacrificed to their images. What could be more like their conduct than that of heretical assemblies? For although they received with us the books of both Old and New Testament, and were with us in profession of one God, nevertheless they did not abandon the monstrous falsehoods of their heresies. Neither the purpose of this little work nor its brevity permits a catalogue of those heresies, much less an argument against each one. But it is enough to know that, considering all that occurred concerning the temple’s construction or condition, the wickedness of the men hindering the rebuilding-work especially bore the type of heretics. They too were the greatest hindrance to the rebuilding of God’s Church after the tyranny of persecutors, as after Babylonian captivity.

## Chapter XXX. On Haman, enemy of the Jews, and how he bears the type of heretics

This too contributes somewhat to the figure of heretics: in the same kingdom of the Medes, through Haman, enemy of the Jews, the devil plotted against that people, deceiving King Ahasuerus so that Mordecai might be fastened to a cross and the whole Jewish people killed in a single day. [Note: Read the Book of Esther.]

But through the intervention of Queen Esther, his deceit and sorrow were turned back upon his own head, and his iniquity descended upon his own crown. For he himself was hanged on the gallows which he had prepared for Mordecai, and likewise his ten sons were fastened to gallows. Moreover, all who had prepared themselves for the slaughter of the Jews were, in reversal, slain by the Jews.

Further, Mordecai, explaining his dream, says: “The two dragons are I and Haman” (Esth. 10:7). This signifies not only the cunning of heretics but also the prudence of the holy Fathers. For, both in an evil and in a good sense, a serpent or dragon is sometimes understood in Scripture (Exod. 7:9). Hence Moses’ rod, changed into a dragon, devoured the dragons of the magicians: clearly a type of heresies to be annihilated by the prudence of the righteous.

Therefore, just as through Moses’ hand the dragon devoured dragons, and as in Mordecai’s dream a dragon was defeated by a dragon, so in the conflict between heretical cunning and holy prudence, Wisdom, once aroused, conquered malice: “reaching mightily from end to end, and ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1).

This was likewise prefigured by a marvelous vision in the Apocalypse of John. For there the dragon, whom we understand as the devil, emitted from his mouth—which mouth was, namely, the madman Arius [Luther, Zwingli, Calvin, Beza]—water like a river, that is, heretical doctrine, in order to make the woman, namely the Church, which through her faith had borne the male child Christ, be carried away by the river. But the earth—that is, the Church assembled in the Council of Nicaea—opened its mouth and swallowed the river, namely by condemning Arius’s pestilential doctrine.

So too Haman, as a kind of forerunner of Arius [Luther, Calvin], brought forth from his heart and mouth a most evil plan against that same people, from whom that male who was expected to rule the nations would come, so that, once the people had been destroyed, Christ’s coming might be hindered. Yet then too the earth, as it were, opened its mouth when Queen Esther acted first by prayers to God and then by interceding with the king, so that Haman’s most evil plan rebounded upon his own head and that unique people—or tree—from which the fruit of salvation was awaited remained safe.

There swords were prepared for the bodily slaughter of the Jews; here Jewish tongues, namely sharp swords, were drawn to kill souls. And just as we read that certain kings, corrupted by the counsel of heretics, raged against the Church, so on the other hand we read that, when wisdom conquered malice, heretics were condemned by royal judgment. As we have said, this was suitably prefigured alike in Haman’s malice and condemnation, and in the prudence of Queen Esther and Mordecai’s solicitude.

## Chapter XXXI. On the dimensions of the temple

Meanwhile, as I considered the dimensions of the temple established by Kings Cyrus and Darius when they released the captivity, the number sixty cubits in height and breadth seemed suspicious to me. For Cyrus’s grant itself is recorded among other things as follows: “Let them lay the foundations, sixty cubits in height and sixty cubits in breadth” (1 Esdras 6:3).

For since the temple, so far as can be estimated, was made after the likeness of the former one, and with the oracle was also sixty cubits in length, the number six times ten recurs everywhere in its dimensions. This perhaps seems to me not undeservedly suspicious, as I said, because of its resemblance to that Babylonian golden statue set up by King Nebuchadnezzar, which itself was sixty cubits in height and six cubits in breadth (Dan. 3:1).

In the Apocalypse of John we likewise find the number of the beast—who is certainly understood as Antichrist—six hundred and sixty-six (Apoc. 13:1), concerning which number of the beast there will be discussion later. Meanwhile, it should be known that six is the number of the creature alone and not of the Creator. For God created the world in six days; on the seventh, as though wearied after the labor of six days, he rested from all his work.

But what is this seventh day of God’s rest understood to be except his wisdom, which is nothing other than himself? Since God is spirit, it is clear that he does not seek rest for himself in a sensible creature such as inanimate earth; nor can irrational living creatures offer God rest in themselves. Only the rational creature was created fit for the Lord’s rest, such as angel and human being.

But when the foot of pride came upon the angel, the hand of the sinner also moved the human being in pride; and, expelled, they could not stand. The Godhead did not find rest for itself in them, for it rests only upon the spirit that is humble, quiet, and trembling at God’s words.

Nor, while the good angels had not yet been so perfectly established in humility that they lacked nothing, could they bear the entire weight of the Godhead pouring itself upon them without danger of pride or of their fall. How much less could any human being do so, apart from the only Son of God, who, existing as God from eternity, was also predestined as man. Apart from him, I say, no one could be found who, together with the highest virtues, immediately and at once attained the summit of humility, so that the Lord would have no labor to undertake in his words and deeds.

Therefore the Son alone, in whom the Father was well pleased in every respect and who never caused the Father any labor in himself or from himself—he alone, I say, is he in whom the Father found full rest. Hence he is most rightly understood as that seventh day on which God the Father rested from all his work.

Therefore, as we began to say, just as six is the number of the creature, so seven is the number of the Creator. Consequently that golden statue rightly did not exceed six in its height and breadth, because the devil set it up in order to serve the creature rather than the Creator.

## Gerhoh’s Preface to the Book *On the Investigation of Antichrist*

*(Works of Jacob Gretser, vol. VI, p. 243.)*

When I first wrote this book, *The Investigation of Antichrist*, and the recent schism arising from the contest for the papacy between Alexander and Octavian—whom they call Victor—was already raging, each side appropriating to its own advantage whatever seemed useful, and disparaging the other either through truth or through occasion. And while both sides fortified themselves with the support of a multitude of great and by no means contemptible priests, and moreover with the favor of the king and princes, I confess that, while this mist of contention covered the whole earth and obscured the face of the Church with a foul darkness, neither the purity of the ecclesiastical election made in Alexander nor the obstinate presumption of Octavian’s party was sufficiently clear to me.

Accordingly, proceeding with hesitant step amid those divisions and, as it were, holding the judgment of a preacher in suspense, I was not quick to incline to either side. With the ignorant I was ignorant; with the doubting I doubted. I became like one who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth, as though not knowing how to reject evil and choose good.

But now, after the mists of lies fabricated against Alexander’s canonical election have begun to thin—those very persons also denying, and preparing solemnly to deny, the things they were said sacrilegiously to have conspired against the empire, and being unwilling to render an account of these matters to any mortal, as though owing their innocence to heaven alone—and after the apostolic sees have joined in consent to Alexander’s election: namely, the Jerusalemite see, in which the apostle James sat; likewise the Antiochene, in which blessed Peter first sat, both of which churches also received apostolic letters; and the holy Roman Church, where the greater and more powerful number of cardinals, only three excepted, consented to the election of that same Alexander—which assembly of lord cardinals we understand to be the Roman Church—these points having been established, there is now no room further for doubt that he must be regarded as lawful pope whom both canonical election and consecration by those pontiffs advanced to the seat of blessed Peter, whose possession of that right according to the custom of the ancient Roman Church is proved by established practice.

We say this because we wish the ambiguities of our own doubt to be excused. For the conclusion of a speaker is to be heard; one must not cling to a preacher’s questions.

## Appendix to Gerhoh

### Seven Letters on the Venerable Sacrament of the Eucharist

Six of these refute the madness of Folmar, provost of Trieffenstein, or of the Dripping Rock; the first letter sets forth and explains the proposition.—Now published for the first time, from manuscript C of the monastery of Raittenhaslach.

*(Works of Gretser, vol. XII, part II, p. 100.)*

### To the Reader

There lived around the time of Alexander III, Roman pontiff, a certain Folmar, provost of the Dripping Rock, or Trieffenstein, in Franconia below Würzburg. Whether from ignorance, malice, or both, he attempted to disseminate various errors, partly through letters and partly through treatises and books, and to introduce them elsewhere, especially into Bavaria. Among these was that most pernicious and thrice-execrable error concerning the venerable sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, which he himself sets forth in explicit words in the first letter to Saint Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg.

The remaining letters strongly labor to destroy and overthrow that error utterly. I do not doubt that the second was written by command of Saint Eberhard the archbishop. The third is by Gerhoh, or Geroch, provost of Reichersberg in Bavaria, who also argues sharply against the Nestorianisms of the same Folmar in the second book *On the Investigation of Antichrist*. Gerhoh’s own brother, dean of Reichersberg, does the same in a separate and lengthy volume against Folmar. If God wills, we shall someday publish both works, since we have already arranged for both to be copied from ancient manuscripts. In one of these, from the monastery of Rottenhasl in Lower Bavaria, we found these letters, which we have ordered to be published together with writers against the Waldensian sect.

### I. Folmar’s Impious Letter

To his lord Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg, Folmar, by God’s grace whatever he may be, wishes continual joy and freedom from every adversity.

I have carefully set forth in writing my faith concerning the truth of the Lord’s body and blood to Lord A., abbot of York, and also to other learned and religious men. I found them in no respect whatever opposed or differing from me. For the wise of this world, since they do not at all taste the sweetness of this mystery, do not understand its purity; and therefore we believe that this sacrament has been revealed by the Spirit of the Lord to those humble in spirit.

Therefore, in the most holy mystery, just as I do not doubt that I drink the most unmixed spiritual blood of the grape under the taste and appearance of wine—yet alone and pure, without flesh—so I believe that I eat the flesh of Christ alone and pure, without bones, without bodily limbs, indeed without the fullness of a human body, under the taste and appearance of bread. And I confess that I eat not the Son of Man but the flesh of the Son of Man.

But where Christ’s flesh is, Christ himself consequently is there: not in part, but wholly—wholly separately in the flesh, wholly separately in the blood, wholly together in both. Nevertheless, he is separately in either one; he is not more wholly or complete in both conjoined. This, I judge, must be referred not to the completeness of the human body, as some dispute, but to the indivisible unity of Christ’s person. For in this sacrament it is necessary both to make the offering properly and to distinguish rightly, and to distinguish the nature of the Word from the nature of the body. For wherever Christ is, he is whole, although the whole is not there; just as, at one and the same time, he was wholly in the tomb and wholly in hell, but the whole was not there, because something of the three substances that make one person in Christ was lacking.

### II. Refutation of the Preceding Letter

To Folmar, learned man and provost of the Dripping Rock, R., a humble brother of the Church of Salzburg, wishes that those who do not know may think soberly and teach sound doctrine.

I believe that the streams of your overflowing and uncontained fountain, dripping down to us from your Rock, are meant to water our dryness, since we live in mountainous regions. Keep it for yourself instead; let it have nothing in common with us or with Christians. Among the other ways in which your keen wisdom endeavors to instruct our ignorance, concerning the body and blood of Christ you preach, as a new evangelist without author or example, a new faith—indeed a detestable unbelief.

For you say: “I believe that under the appearance of the grape I drink the most unmixed blood alone and pure.” And since all this could soundly have been understood, so that “pure” referred only to holiness, and to a separate reception of one and the same sacrament rather than a division of the substances of flesh and blood, the wisdom of your flesh determined the matter by adding, “without flesh.” The error still lies hidden [lacuna] and has not yet wholly betrayed itself. Hear what follows: “Thus,” you say, “I believe that I eat Christ’s flesh without bones.”

What does this impious sect introduce here except that whoever, with the narrow throat of faith, fears choking on bones in the flesh should likewise flee from raw flesh in the blood—or even from flesh in the blood? Would you also wish to eat a roasted and cooked portion of Christ’s flesh, because you abhor rawness and the grossness of limbs? Do not be afraid. It is food for the soul, not for the body. It is indeed broken bodily and perceptibly in the sacrament; it is ground by the teeth of believers, while the integrity of the incorruptible flesh remains, so that truth is in no respect absent from the sacrament and sound faith need not fear an abomination in the throat.

O faith’s excessively delicate palate! Through the habit of fleshly custom, it finds the soft flesh of Christ pleasing, as it were, but not the bones. Forgive the expression: the unworthiness of the question compels it. You also assert that you eat Christ whole. And lest this too be referred to fullness of substances, you determine that “whole” is to be referred not to integrity of limbs but to unity of person, on account of a part. And you added: “I believe that I eat the flesh of the Son of Man, not the Son of Man.” I ask: where now is what you afterward seemed, for authority’s sake, to concede—namely, that Christ whole is eaten in the sacrament, but in part? Why do you not grant even that to the Son of Man? Is eating Christ one thing and eating the Son of Man another? Are Christ and the Son of Man not one and the same? Where does your self-contradictory and diffuse eloquence lead—or rather, whither does it mislead, or has it been misled?

Although all this may be rejected with the same ease with which it is proved, since it has not even on its surface a semblance of truth, nevertheless let us question for a moment this very novel sharpness of intellect.
