Tell us: do you drink Christ’s blood without flesh, as you say here, with the substance of flesh separated? For thus your distinction has taught us to understand you. Tell us, I say: do you drink a part of the blood or the whole? If a part, tell us from which limb it is drawn—from the head or from the foot? You force me to say this. Madness is sometimes repelled more lightly by madness than by reason. I believe you will return to the position that you drink Christ’s whole blood. If, according to your tradition, you drink it whole with flesh separated, what kind of flesh, I ask, remains meanwhile for Christ—dry, or rather dead, without blood? Surely no one but a madman would say this.

Therefore Christ’s blood is received by believers not as abstracted from flesh, but blood with flesh and flesh with blood; indeed Christ whole, with the integrity of both substances. And although these are received separately, they are not received as separated: separately because of the divine signification of the mystery, not separated because of the indissoluble bond of deified immortality.

What then is the consequence which you introduce as though the preceding point were established? “Thus I believe that I eat Christ’s flesh without bones.” What does “thus” mean except this: if drinking blood with flesh seems abominable, then eating flesh with bones must also be impossible? O mad fear! O fleshly and execrable thought! You fear bones in the throat, though they are united to the Word of God—bones which entered to the disciples while the doors were closed. Tell me, I ask: when you eat—or rather, in your view, gnaw—flesh without bones, what kind of bones meanwhile remain? Are they bare, or are they immediately clothed with other flesh? These things are profane. This is to gnaw flesh with a heretical tooth rather than to eat Christ in the sacrament with a Christian mind.

Let such blind presumption and such vain question therefore cease. For just as it is an idle curiosity to ask whether, since God is everywhere, he is also in a shoe, and similar things, so none, either ancient or modern, has thought it necessary to ask in such a form of words: “Is the flesh received in the sacrament with Christ’s bones?” Since so great a majesty of things has everywhere been expressed with fitting dignity of language, in the manner in which it ought to have been said, no one will doubt further unless he is a heretic.

The Church, therefore, eats the flesh of the Son of Man—not a part of the flesh, but the whole body which was born of the Virgin and suffered on the cross:

> Not dry, without blood; but living with blood.

Indeed, [Note: Because Christ’s flesh gives life.] life-giving flesh. The Church eats flesh, I say; it does not gnaw it after the bones have been bitten away, as you teach. It eats indeed, not by consuming that flesh, but by passing salutarily into it. It eats Christ’s flesh whole and entire, without diminution and without division; indeed, in the flesh it eats Christ whole—the Son of God whole and the Son of Man whole—in an ineffable and inconceivable manner, but in the manner known to him himself.

And I refer “whole” not to a part merely as a part, as you make subtle distinctions, but to the fullness of the substances of flesh and blood. Augustine says: “I say that that body is offered likewise upon the altar which was born of the Virgin, which hung upon the cross, which rose again, which ascended into heaven.” Did the Virgin, I ask, bear that body without bones and sinews? Did it hang upon the cross without bones and sinews?

Thus it is eaten, as has been said, and yet it lives, whole though eaten, because it rose again though slain. It is whole, not in place of a part but as a whole, visible in heaven in human form; likewise whole according to the body, invisible in the sacrament upon the altar, everywhere at one and the same time. It is wonderful if you attend to yourself; you cease to wonder if you consider the Lord.

So too the Christian soul drinks the blood of its Lord. It does not suck or draw from the flesh either the whole blood or part of it, as your invention—though indirectly—suggests. Rather, without diminution and without division, it receives in mind and body the fullness of both in each kind—that is, sacramentally and spiritually—in the one same ineffable sacrament. Against dreams of this kind, which even old women can ridicule, although arguments and authorities are abundantly available even to the little-trained, we have for the moment denounced them rather in mockery than argument, lest by silence we appear to have assented to absurdities.

### III. Gerhoh to A., Abbot of York

“Recently there came,” etc. It appears among Gerhoh’s letters, in the preceding volume, col. 476.

### IV. Letter of A., Abbot of Ebora, to Gerhoh, Provost of Reichersberg

To the venerable lord, the provost of Reichersberg, Brother A., called abbot of Ebora [Ebrach today], offers the service of devoted prayer.

Know that when the provost of Trieph [the Dripping Rock] formerly wrote that he had set forth his faith to us, it was only as follows, as we wrote below or appended. Once, in our presence, bringing forth a little book, he said: “This is my faith,” and read from it in our hearing, while we paid no attention and suspected nothing of the kind concerning it.

But after we had received your writings, which you had published against him in Catholic fashion, we acted at the command of the bishop of Bamberg to bring him with us before the bishop at Bamberg. There, in the presence of a considerable number of religious and learned men, as the bishop proceeded against him, he humbly professed that henceforth he neither held nor would write anything of that kind.

For our part, we assent to what your writings contain, and judge it Catholic. Henceforth we desire and pray to divine mercy that it may enlighten the eyes of your heart unto every knowledge of truth and love of virtue.

### V. Folmar’s Recantation

Folmar, by God’s grace what he is of the Dripping Rock, to all prelates established in Bavaria and Austria: continual joy and freedom from every adversity.

“Whoever does not offend in word is a perfect man,” as Scripture bears witness (Jas. 2). My humility is far removed and wandering in exile from this perfection, for it offends not only in words but often even in writings. This is all the more dangerous because an error which is written is corrected more laboriously and recalled with greater difficulty. For if even a spoken word does not know how to return once sent, how much more so a written word. If a word once uttered remains irrevocable, how, I ask, can a written word be recalled? Let confession therefore heal what cannot be corrected by retraction.

I wrote to my former lord Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, concerning the body of the Lord—something I ought not at all to have done—asserting that it was indeed true upon the altar, but not whole, that is, not in the fullness and distinction of all its members. I seemed to myself to have argued this with many arguments, reasons, and even authorities, which perhaps I had not yet understood. If anyone rejects this, so do I; if it displeases anyone, it displeases me too. If anyone erases it and spits upon it, he does so with me.

For I confess that the body of Christ upon the altar is not only true, but also full, perfect, and entire; and there, in the truth and integrity of human substance, though under another appearance, he who visibly reigns at the Father’s right hand is received wonderfully and invisibly. How the whole is present in a part, entire in each individual portion; how it is broken in form yet not divided in essence; how, when consecrated repeatedly, it does not admit even the number of angels; and many matters of this sort—these are beyond every understanding not only of human beings but, as I think, of angels. They have no cause except the absolutely first cause: namely, the will or power of the Creator.

This perhaps has been more fully expressed in the little book which I wrote to Gerhoh, *On the Flesh and Soul of the Word*, but without prejudice to a better opinion. For in questions and articles of faith, there is no shame in being taught even by an enemy, where no one ought to follow natural principles or defend his own opinion as though it arose from reason. For the majesty of faith surpasses the use of nature, the limits of reason, and physical or logical capacities; therefore, where faith is at issue, arguments have no force.

Perhaps this is why, contrary to the ordinary use of nature, we are commanded to eat the lamb’s head with its entrails and feet, but not to break its bones. For we receive in the most holy mystery whatever is divine or human in Christ, but we do not presume in the least to investigate the profundity of this act. For I have learned by experience that whoever scrutinizes majesty contrary to the law is overwhelmed by glory.

## Judgment concerning Folmar’s aforesaid recantation

These things were said by Folmar, acknowledging his error—not in every respect, but in part. For very many of his errors still remain embedded in his writings or have already been made public in his undisciplined words. Since he has not yet acknowledged these, let us pray, both for him and for his supporters, that the truth may be so revealed that, as its light shines back upon their consciences, they may be compelled either to acquiesce in sound doctrine or to fall utterly silent.

## VI. R. of Rohr to Gerhoh

To the most reverend father, Lord GERHOH, venerable provost of the Church of Reichersberg: R., the least of the brothers of Rohr, his pupil—may you be able most gloriously to overcome all adversities.

This year, after the Nativity of the Lord, the messenger of the provost of Triefenstein, passing through our house, showed me letters which he was carrying to the provost of Salzburg. They contained a certain stubbornness of his aforesaid sender concerning the heresy with which he had defiled himself. He also showed me the little book which that same erring man was sending to you, which he called, I do not know how aptly, *On the Flesh and Soul of the Word of God*.

In the letter that arrogant and foolish man had set down your name most unworthily and crudely; but in the little book, with open effrontery and mockery, he repeatedly accused your person of erroneous understanding and absurd doctrine. I, not unaware of what I owe you, could not but grieve at your treatment. And since he was attacking your reputation without cause—not incidentally, but from long habit—I could not and would not conceal my grief by silence, as I had done before, lest you say to me: “He who is not with me is against me” (Luke 11).

Therefore, being utterly certain that the Spirit of truth will everywhere guard your heart and mouth, while the spirit of falsehood claims no small share in the tongue and lips of your adversary, I wrote to him—not so much trusting in talent as provoked by zeal—perhaps rebuking his arrogance too unreservedly, but certainly giving him what he deserved. For since he neglected the Apostle’s precept, “honour to whom honour is due” (Romans 13), in regard to one greater and older than himself, he too should receive no honour from one younger and lesser than himself. Yet since many have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, lest the same should perhaps happen to me, I send you the very letter of invective, so that, if you judge that I have sinned, you may call me to repentance; but if not, you may reassure me by your letter.

## VII. Brother R. to Folmar

[Col. 1487C]

To Lord FOLMAR, provost of Stillantis Petra: brother R., as a little one of God, wishes that he may love peace and truth.

Because we ought to defer to elders, and a young man is scarcely permitted by the wise to speak even in his own cause (Ecclesiasticus 32), in past years, though I often heard and read your curses and many, serious insults against Lord Gerhoh, our father, venerable in age and life, and though they disturbed my heart greatly, I nevertheless resolved to overlook them. In reverence duly owed to elders, I wished to be like one who does not hear and has no reproof in his mouth (Psalm 37), so that I might say with the Prophet: “With those who hate peace, I was peaceable” (Psalm 119).

For I hoped—since you are not altogether unlearned, having indeed something of that knowledge which puffs up, though nothing of the charity which builds up—I hoped, I say, that at length the oft-repeated threat would together frighten and correct you: “Those who do evil shall be cut off” (Psalm 36); and that “abusers shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6); together with many other things from the sacred books which are known to urge adversaries toward conversion.

But now, since it pleases you to imitate those “whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness,” who “have not known the way of peace,” and before whose eyes “there is no fear of God” (Psalm 13), and since the habit of cursing has now almost become your nature, I do not think that I now exceed the bounds of discipline if, no longer able to bear the injury done to our father, I—a boy—rebuke an old man, I—a little one—one great in his own eyes, zealously reproving an envious man. For the younger Daniel condemned the old judges, liars and shameless men, who, unable to violate holy Susanna, therefore sought falsely to condemn the innocent woman (Daniel 13).

Would that the same spirit were given to the heart of the whole people, so that, similarly armed and animated now with zeal for godliness, they might rise with stones of fitting rebuke and just reproach against all who are arrogant, envious, and “speak wickedness on high” (Psalm 72), so that on both sides the mouth of the sinner and deceiver may be stopped, as then the mouth of those speaking iniquity was stopped (Psalm 62), and he may learn not to blaspheme.

No less fittingly than upon those who do like things would like things befall you, so that you might follow in punishment those whom you imitate in guilt. As are the fathers, so is the son. They, deceived by a spirit of fornication, thought and spoke wickedness against the mother in Israel; but you, puffed up by a spirit of pride, intend to defile her who dwells in the house—not yet barren (Psalm 112), as you are, but a mother rejoicing in children.

For in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, he begot us—not, as you chatter, say with polluted mouth, and keep writing with sacrilegious hand, feeding us poison of error instead of the milk of sound doctrine—but plainly fortifying the faith of godliness by understanding of the truth. He possesses that manner of teaching which the Apostle hands down: he nourishes the simpler with the milk of easier doctrine, and abundantly sets before the more perfect the more solid food of the judgments and sacraments of God.

Therefore he does not yield to you when you urge him not to read Hilary, as though he does not understand him. He reads and expounds him; and, himself enlightened by the Spirit of truth, he sheds light on the obscure sayings in him and powerfully destroys every poison of error. If you cannot grasp the subtlety of his words and the depth of his understanding in those matters in which you shamelessly charge him with unsound faith, and consequently impose another meaning upon them, as all who adulterate the word of God do, we are not surprised; for it is nothing new. For in this way the ancient heretics also dealt with our fathers, adapting their statements to their own meaning and understanding one thing in place of another.

But persuade yourselves as you please. We do not believe you. He, as a good man, brings forth good things from his good treasure; but an evil man has sown tares over it. You are wholly striving to encrust a pure vessel. We cannot set your conjectures above what we have heard and seen. We have heard words of life and the law of discipline from his mouth. We have seen him doing wonders in his life: an expert physician of hearts, not bodies. We have proved that he is good, since an evil tree could not bear such good fruit. We know him by his fruits.

Therefore let your malicious speech against the man cease—the man whom the Lord of hosts has adorned with virtues—especially since whatever you say, you say not from love of God’s word but from envy, the devil’s vice. By this you too are goaded against him, perhaps because you have not been found like him, keeping the law of the Most High (Ecclesiasticus 44); but certainly because of excessive arrogance of heart, so that you may gain glory for yourselves rather than for God. Accordingly we say to you: “May your glory be with you in perdition.” For you lose for yourselves the glory which you do not acquire for God, to whom alone belong honour and glory.

Yet your self-glorification is not small. It is something great boldly to challenge great men; and one who is not ashamed to disparage the good deserves a great name—not, indeed, that of teacher, but of detractor. But I say this because you no longer have the right to judge others’ faith, since you were unwilling to keep your own unblemished; for one against whom the same charge is made cannot be an accuser.

Therefore be silent; and while others are silent—those who do not have a seared conscience—lay your hand upon your mouth, lest you again set it against heaven and your latter state become worse than the former.

For I still fear for you:

> The newly scented jar will long retain  
> The fragrance with which it was once imbued.  
> —Horace, *Epistle* I, book II, v. 69

If true faith cleanses hearts, then there is no true faith where sincere charity, the inhabitant of a pure heart, is absent. For charity is kind and not envious; it does not nourish hatreds but produces concord—everything contrary to you. See, therefore, whether you have perfectly corrected your faith. Unless you correct what still needs correction, fear, having experienced, that just judgment of God: “He who digs a pit falls into it” (Proverbs 26).

Read these things and say: “As I have done, so the Lord has repaid me” (Judges 1).

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1175: BROTHER ARNO, PROVOST OF REICHERSBERG

[Col. 1489]

## Historical Notice

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. I, p. 137)

Arno, dean and prior of the Abbey of Reichersberg in Bavaria, died in the year 1175. His *Shield of the Regular Canons* was published by the distinguished Raymond Duellius in book I of the *Miscellanea*, Augsburg, 1723, quarto, pp. 3–55. The same Arno, with his brother Gerhoh, whom he succeeded in the prelature in 1169, wrote a lengthy work *On the Eucharist*, directed against Folmar, provost of Triefenstein, or Stillantis Petra, in Franconia below Würzburg.

But the prologue and fragment of the work against Folmar, published by Stevartius in his *Sylloge veterum scriptorum*, p. 243 (in Basnage’s new edition of Canisius’s *Antiquae Lectiones*, vol. III, part II, p. 200), and in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, vol. XXIII, p. 240, are not by Beatus or Heterius, who wrote against Felix and Elipandus many centuries before Folmar, but by Adam, dean of Reichersberg. Adam dedicated his vast volume against Folmar to P., dean of Würzburg, and mentions Folmar’s letter to the “archbishop of Tavanum” [read *Juvavum*, that is, understand Salzburg; but this is a different letter from Folmar’s extant letter to him], in which Folmar inflicted insults upon Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg.

Finally, Stevartius noted that, besides Adam’s work, the Bavarian libraries contain Gerhoh’s book *On the Investigation of Antichrist*, in which he undertook to refute Folmar; likewise in his book *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*, addressed to Hermann, Bishop of Brixen, published by Bernard Pez in vol. I, part II, p. 163 of the *Anecdota*, Augsburg, 1721, folio.

## Brother Arno’s *Shield of the Canons*

(Raymond Duellius, *Miscellanea*, book of Sentences I, Augsburg and Graz, 1723, p. 3.)

[Col. 1489]

## Preliminary Observation

Brother Arno’s *Shield of the Canons*, that is, of the Regular Canons. The eleventh century from Christ’s birth had passed in the world when the *palingenesia* (renewal) of our whole order began to take place. For at that time in Italy Saint Abbot Romuald taught many canons and clerics, who lived in a secular manner after the fashion of laypeople, to obey provosts and live together in a community.

[Note: [Col. 1491] Peter Damian, *Life of St Romuald*, ch. 35.]

The Council of Ænsham urged English canons to a chaste and communal life.

[Note: [Col. 1491] Council of Ænsham, ch. 1.]

The canonical life was introduced into the Church of Girona.

[Note: [Col. 1491] Charters of Girona, in Baluze, *Marca Hispanica*, col. 1066.]

The Congregation of Saint-Ruf arose.

[Note: [Col. 1491] See the inquiry concerning the Order of Canons, p. 337.]

And, what must by no means be passed over, Alexander II himself, in the first Roman synod of 1063, at Peter Damian’s urging, commanded the canons “that, as befits religious clerics, they should eat and sleep together and hold in common whatever belongs to them in the church.”

[Note: [Col. 1491] Binius, vol. III of the Councils, part II.]

To confirm these words by example, he established in the Lateran basilica canons living according to rule. Very many men of holier life took to heart the example of the supreme vicars on earth, labouring everywhere to restore the canonical discipline that had by then fallen into decay. Among their number were Rajambald, Archbishop of Arles, who in 1064 “led the canons of the metropolitan basilica to embrace a stricter life and the Order of Saint Augustine”;

[Note: [Col. 1491] Sainte-Marthe, *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, p. 48.]

Lietbert, Bishop of Cambrai, who about 1066 established in the church of Saint Aubert and another church on Mount Saint Eligius clerics “living in common, and set over them an abbot of their own profession”;

[Note: [Col. 1491] Book I of the Belgian Diplomas, chs. 36 and 43.]

Ivo, Bishop of Chartres, under whom about 1078 the canonical order, first instituted by the Apostles and enlarged with rules by Saint Augustine, began to flourish again;

[Note: [Col. 1491] Thus Urban II in a diploma given in 1093 to the canons of Saint Ivo. See further Sigebert’s chronicle, A.D. 1078.]

Saint Altmann, Bishop of Passau, who about 1074 established the college of Regular Canons at Göttweig in Austria and that of Saint Nicholas at Passau. He also reformed with remarkable severity certain canonries—namely, those of Saint Hippolytus and Saint Florian—in 1080; after banishing the brothels of concubines and expelling clerics who had departed from the rule, he restored them to their former order.

[Note: [Col. 1492] Hund, on Altmann.]

What followed was this. The order of canons saw itself enlarged by very many followers throughout almost the whole world; and this aroused the envy of certain malicious and degenerate monks—among whom, alongside good men, not merely monastic cells but every age and place alike have always nourished some. In order to impede so great an increase, they devised one thing after another: with countless tricks to turn candidates for the regular life away from their resolve, to entice those already professed to themselves with a thousand allurements, and, in short, to plot everything conducive to the extirpation of the Regular Canons.

Their design would surely have succeeded, had not the supreme pontiffs and councils interposed their authority, turning the thunderbolt of anathema against the contrivers of such things and issuing a decree that Regular Canons should not dare to transfer to monks.

[Note: [Col. 1492] See note 1 to Arno.]

Yet even then no remedy was so applied to this evil as to prevent it from reviving in the following century. The malice of the aforesaid persons advanced so far that they did not shrink from occupying our colleges with unheard-of audacity—men unworthy to live alongside the innumerable most devout men then among the monks.

In order somewhat to restrain such great assaults by enemies, our Arno, a most vigorous defender (*hyperaspistēs*, “champion”) of the canonical order, composed this little work and entitled it *The Shield of the Canons*. A copy of this writing exists in the library of Saint Florian.

[Note: [Col. 1492] Pez, introductory dissertation in vol. II of the *Thesaurus Novus*, p. 28.]

Yet it never came into our hands. We transcribed this copy from a manuscript in the Imperial Library, of the late twelfth century, or at any rate not much later than the thirteenth, which was generously brought to us by the most illustrious Lord Gentilotto of Engelsbrunn, imperial librarian and councillor.

Who, moreover, this Arno was, we cannot determine authoritatively (*authentikōs*), for there is no basis upon which anything certain may be established. Bernard Pez, well known to the learned world—to whom I acknowledge that I owe a great part of my studies—discusses Arno as follows:

> “While some years ago, with the favour of the most reverend and illustrious Lord Provost Francis Claudius Kröll, a most humane superior, we were examining the manuscript codices of the Canonry of Florian in Upper Austria, there came into our hands a parchment codex in quarto, about four hundred years old, containing a certain apologetic treatise by Arno, a Regular Canon. Perhaps this Arno is not different from Arno, provost of Reichersberg, brother of Gerhoh.”

[Note: [Col. 1492] See Hund, *Metropolis*, part III.]

A certain slip of paper supports this conjecture. The very reverend Lord Lucas Faber, dean of the Canonry of Gars, found it among the manuscripts of his predecessor, Johann Chrysostom Hager, most learned in our affairs, and in his kindness toward us communicated it. It reads as follows:

> “Arno, a Bavarian Regular Canon and dean of Reichersberg, brother of Master Gerhoh and his successor in the prelature, was not inferior to his own brother in learning and virtue. He sent his canons to a Roman council. He died in 1175, on the Kalends of February.
>
> He wrote a lengthy volume against Folmar, provost of Triefenstein, concerning the latter’s errors against the most holy Eucharist. A manuscript is preserved in the monastery of Raitenhaslach.”

[Note: [Col. 1492] On this writing see the Cologne edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, vol. XIII, p. 344; likewise Miraeus, *Auctarium*, no. 406.]

When we carefully consider this man’s date, standing, learning, and likewise this other apologetic writing, it seems as certain as can be that the provost Arno is the same as our Arno: a Regular Canon, learned, devout, and well at home in sacred letters, who wrote about the middle of the twelfth century.

[Note: [Col. 1492] See note 15.]

No one who reads the present little work will deny this. We leave these matters to each person’s free judgment and proceed to that distinguished commendation which the most illustrious Lord Gentilotto—a man, if anyone, *polymathēs* (“very learned”)—has attached to Arno’s apology in the work which he intends shortly to publish:

> “It is,” he says, “a little work not unworthy of being brought to light some day, especially because it explains fully the manner of life, customs, and rites by which the institute and discipline of the Regular Canons were maintained about the middle of the twelfth century.”

There remains one point that we wish the reader to observe: namely, that Arno’s present *Shield* should be read in comparison with the condition and customs of those times. Whoever does otherwise exposes himself to innumerable prejudgments. A word to the wise is enough.

[Col. 1493]

# The Shield of the Canons

## Prologue

[Col. 1493A] I, Brother Arno, a lowly servant of the canonical order, composed the following little work, called *The Shield of the Canons*, on account of a certain dispute. Certain monks were occupying our places and enticing our professed brothers to join them, under the pretext of a more exalted religious life.

[Note: [Cols. 1493D–1494D] That this occurred both then and in preceding centuries is clearly indicated by the synodal decrees and those of the supreme pontiffs found in *Causa* 19, question 3.]

Nor should it prejudice the title and purpose of this little book that I have inserted in it, briefly, an account of our customs, which are our daily garments and certain instruments of our sanctification. For I have used these customs themselves—like our daily garments and the instruments of our work—as a shield and weapons in defence of our practice, as we know is often done with material things when necessity compels.

For when robbers perhaps come upon travellers or people engaged in some work, or when civil war unexpectedly breaks out, garments are seized for shields and work tools for weapons. With these, even armed enemies are sometimes courageously driven back, justice lending its aid. Once these are put to flight, the garments and instruments are again resumed for their former use; nor will they thereafter be any less serviceable for decency or usefulness because they were employed for other purposes.

Thus we read that the children of Israel sometimes fought with hoes, mattocks, and tridents, and that one of the Judges, named Shamgar, killed six hundred men with a ploughshare (Judges 3). But here we do not intend to kill our adversaries, but only to repel the weapons of slanderers, so that, once they are pacified, we may be allowed to live together with them and dwell as harmonious households in the great house of the heavenly Father—not to be puffed up against one another or to glory without measure.

Compelled by this same necessity, I have interwoven visions and revelations of the Lord made to certain brothers of our own time, and not without apostolic precedent. For the Apostle Paul first did so when constrained by the same necessity. Peter also, compelled by the importunity of the Jews, explained the revelation concerning the vessel like a sheet which had been made to him. Thus no one will rightly blame us if we have employed, in our defence, visions made to our acquaintances and fellow-dwellers.

Therefore let all brothers of the canonical household who wish use this little work of our humility without distinction: either as a shield in war or as a necessary garment of daily customs in peace. I think they will find in it nothing that does not contribute to the propriety of the regular form of life, the restraint of slanderers’ malice, or indeed the ordering and preservation of charity. Thus may those whom diversity of professions or customs separates be united by one charity in God and under God.

For although people advance by a variety of different paths, customs, or professions, they nevertheless advance not in different directions but toward one goal and under one ruler. Nothing is taken away from salvation or propriety; rather, provision is made for the diversity of dispositions. Indeed, the beauty of that queen is brought to perfection, of whom it is written: “The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, clothed round about with variety” (Psalm 44).

Let the zeal of piety and religion, then, burn fervently in all orders and in every individual person. Let the gold of divine and fraternal charity shine forth in every profession; and so, in the diverse customs of different orders, may the beauty of the aforesaid queen be completed—though all her glory is within, even while she is commendably clothed with the variety of which we speak.

Therefore our glory too must be within in the Lord, from a pure conscience, because we are members of that queen. Nevertheless, meanwhile we are compelled to glory outwardly in bodily observances by those who are religious beyond measure. Yet we do not fail to know “that bodily exercise is profitable for a little, but godliness is profitable for all things, having promise not only of the life which now is, but also of that which is to come” (1 Timothy 4).

Let us therefore also glory outwardly for the time being, provided that all our glory is within and in the Lord, and that this very glorying comes not from our vanity but from the importunity of those who disparage us.

*The prologue ends.*

## The Little Work Called *The Shield of the Canons* Begins

[Col. 1493]

Source/review notes: The draft supplies the numeral “I” for Urban, although the source prints only “Urban.”

[Col. 1493D] Lords and brothers of the canonical order, fathers and sons, have mercy, have mercy on yourselves and on us! Have mercy [Col. 1494D] on the canonical order, at least you who are its friends! For the hand of the Lord has touched it—an order which, in the first beginnings of the Church, was great among all the sons and daughters of the East, made strong by the sevenfold Spirit and beautiful through faith in the Holy Trinity. It possessed sheep and oxen, asses and camels, in the thousands of converts from Jews and Gentiles; in the breaking of the Lord’s bread it held daily banquets of holy feasting with rejoicing. Then Satan demanded it, that he might sift it like wheat, beginning with the persecution which occurred under Stephen. [Note: [Col. 1495D] In the year 257 after Christ’s birth, under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus.]

So too in our own time, through the sluggish negligence of certain masters and the vigilant treachery of false brothers, power over it was given by the Lord to Satan. It lost all its substance and its children, so that in very many places where it once flourished it has almost been reduced to nothing and has perished; and thus, like salt that has lost its savour, [Col. 1495B] our canonical order may be cast out and trodden underfoot by men—an order established not by men nor through man, but by God. It flourished in figure in Aaron’s priesthood and the Levitical ministry; in Christ, his apostles, and disciples; and in those first believers “who were of one heart and one soul in God” (Acts 4), it brought forth the fruit of sweetness and salvation. In the holy Roman pontiffs from blessed Peter the Apostle down to Pope and martyr Urban, the sixteenth after Peter, [Note: [Col. 1495D] Urban I is reckoned seventeenth from St Peter by the chronologists of our time. I suspect that our author followed those who confused Cletus with Anacletus. Urban’s letter, cited by our author, is found in Binius, *Councils*, vol. I; it expressly maintains that common life and a vow of poverty flourished among the clergy at that time.] throughout almost all the clergy of those times—as Pope Urban himself testifies—and later in the holy confessors and pontiffs Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine, it brought forth to the world the shoot of righteousness’ planting.

For a time after those ages it had been dead, but it came to life; it had perished, but it was found; and behold, through its harmony and choirs, the house of the Church is now gladdened. Therefore certain of our monastic brothers ought to have rejoiced, rather than to have mocked the same order as it was dying in some of its members or to have seized the inheritance of one half-dead. For if its enemy, namely the company of headless clerics, had cursed it—the canonical order—it would indeed have borne this; and if the one who hated it, seeking his own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, had spoken great things against it, perhaps it would have hidden itself from him. But now the sons of its mother fight against it; and the man of one mind with it, its leader and acquaintance, who together with it took sweet food of the divine word and walked in the house of God [Col. 1495D] in concord—the man of its peace, in whom it trusted—has enlarged his treachery against it. Thus it may now, with the Apostle, glory in the Lord not only in dangers from the Gentiles, but also in dangers from its own people and in dangers among false brothers.

But let the name of false brotherhood be charged only against those who, lacking bowels of compassion, not only do not restore to their brother his wandering ox or ass, but even seek to steal it away; who not only do not aid a brother wounded by robbers and left half-dead, but inflict wound [Col. 1496A] upon wound; who do to others what they would not have done to themselves, while they try to draw away the sons and disciples of others from the masters under whom they could be saved, and to attract them to themselves—as though Christ were found among them alone, as though the kingdom of God had proceeded from them or had come to them alone. So that we almost hear it said, as was said once in times of heresy: “Behold, here is Christ,” or “Behold, there” (Matt. 24).

But we will not go, nor will we follow; for our Lord Jesus Christ is not so poor that he has servants only among monks living by the labour of their hands, nor so harsh that he delights in the deadly cold of those deprived of fur garments, or desires his servants to be burdened to the point of collapse by a multitude of woollen tunics, or commands them to be consumed [Col. 1496B] by multiplied vermin—things which all amount, in actual practice, to not sparing the body. But “in the house of God are many dwellings” (John 14). And: “The Lord knows those who are his; and let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity” (2 Tim. 2). And: “Pure and undefiled religion before the Lord is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from this world” (Jas. 1).

In these, certainly, and in other practices of true religion and exercises of devotion, insofar as they are with us—whether they go before us, accompany us, follow after having preceded, or are followed by us—lords and monastic brothers, whatever colour of garments they wear, are truly our household members and brothers. And all of us among them who have understanding acknowledge them as our brothers and members of our household. As cherubim and seraphim in heaven, so on earth they celebrate in shared rejoicing with us, singing harmoniously and in unison, “Holy, Holy, Holy,” to the Lord of Hosts. Nor do we begrudge them, under the name of Seraphim, their flight with six wings, provided that they too permit the canonical order, under the name of Cherubim, to share their rejoicing. Otherwise—to say nothing of Cherubim and Seraphim—they cannot even be counted among the ranks of angels. For the kingdom of heaven belongs not to the proud, who glory in their superlative holiness to the disparagement of another and sing, in this manner, “Holy, Holier, Holiest,” but “to little ones and the humble” (Matt. 18); and whoever wishes [Col. 1496D] to become greater in it must become least of all and servant of all.

Now, since one must glory, though it is not expedient, let the canonical order also glory—yet not in itself, but in the Lord. Let it say: “In whatever anyone dares—I speak as a fool—I also dare. They are followers of Christian poverty: so am I. They are emulators of apostolic perfection: so am I. They profess and observe common and cenobitic life: so do I. They are ministers of Christ: so am I. I speak as one less wise: [Col. 1497A] I more—in many labours, more abundantly in prisons, beyond measure in stripes, frequently in deaths. By Jews and Gentiles alike I have often been handled with scorpions, leaded thongs, and whips; a thousand times I have been beaten in my members with rods; often stoned; more frequently shipwrecked; often delivered to flames; often immersed in water; often exposed to beasts; a hundred times raised upon the rack; a hundred times stretched upon the *catasta*; often I have endured iron combs; more than once roasted on the gridiron; a thousand times subjected to the sword. Often in journeys: dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from fire, dangers from Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers; in labour and hardship, [Col. 1497B] in many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness. Besides those things which are outward, my daily pressure: concern for all the Churches.”

In all these labours, dangers, anxieties, and sufferings, how I have toiled in priests and Levites, and in other confessors and martyrs of Christ belonging to my profession, in times of persecution, is known to the Church of Christ; its libraries are seen filled with my sufferings and trophies for Christ, while not even the monastic name yet existed in the time of persecution. For when true solitude was sought through flight by Christian confessors, necessity having been turned into choice, only then did the monastic order arise and grow strong, so that it rightly recognized itself as the son of the priesthood and of the confessor.

Why, then, should a son, however vigorous and noble, exalt himself above his parent’s virtue, dignity, and nobility? Or how, when we all call upon the one Lord as Father and are all brothers, are we to be two orders—namely, I, the canonical order, and the monastic order—as two true uterine brothers, sons of Jacob, of whom the same father Jacob said to his ten sons: “You know,” he says, “that my wife bore me two sons. One went out, and you said, ‘A beast has devoured him,’ and he has not appeared until now. If you take this Benjamin and anything happens to him on the way, you will bring down my grey hairs with sorrow to the underworld” (Gen. 44).

Let us, then, I say, be these two orders like the two patriarch Jacob’s sons, uterine brothers, both sprung from one noble mother Rachel, both zealous for beholding truth and pursuing devotion. Let the canonical order, as has been said, be Joseph the elder, shining with the gifts of priestly dignity and ecclesiastical governance; and let the younger monastic order be Benjamin, who was called by his mother “son of sorrow,” but by his father “son of the right hand.” For his mother, the Church, bore him in the sorrow of her passion, as was said above, and of death, when in confessors she brought forth from flight from suffering and death a love of solitude, necessity having become choice. But by the Father he was reckoned a son of the right hand, as a beloved heir of eternal goods.

But I, Joseph the elder of these sons, that is, the canonical order, was sold by my brothers into Egypt [Col. 1498A] in the time of persecution and endured prisons, when the iron of manifold suffering pierced my soul and my flesh together, until, when my word reached the testimony appointed by the Lord, the world was brought under the yoke of faith. In the time of Pope Sylvester and Emperor Constantine, when peace was restored to the Churches of the Lord through that pious emperor, I was wondrously exalted in the aforesaid pope, in the priests of that age, and in the clergy, and among men. I was not only brought out of prison as another Joseph; I moreover rode in Pharaoh’s chariot and was made lord of Egypt, prince of the world, and governor of kingdoms.

Indeed, this was fulfilled almost historically and literally in Pope Sylvester himself, when the emperor, as he sat upon the imperial horse in the city of Rome, performed for him the office of groom through the middle of the city. And in the time of heresies, who was weak without my being weak? Who was scandalized without my burning? For again a most wicked beast devoured me, Joseph, the firstborn of the true Jacob and Rachel. At that time, in my Hilary and Athanasius and the other bishops, priests, and ministers of that age, I was driven into exile and cast innocent into the pit. But when the impious King Constantius died in that departure, and Julian the Apostate—the true Antichrist—was removed from the midst, he who was slain without human hand and by the breath of the mouth of the Lord Jesus, kings again sent and princes of peoples released [Col. 1498C] and dismissed me.

At that time, through my archimandrites Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine, and the other teachers of my school, so great an abundance of spiritual grain was stored in the granaries of Egypt—in the libraries of the Church gathered from the Gentiles—that it is sufficient even now to replenish us in the famine and scarcity of this age. Yet, as someone says:

> Nothing is blessed in every respect.  
> (*Horace, Odes*)

For, as has been said, after peace was restored to God’s Churches, secular pomp and the vanity and concupiscence of this world again devoured me, the canonical order, Rachel’s firstborn. Thus the heavenly Father might justly say mournfully over me: “A most wicked beast has devoured my son Joseph.” [Col. 1498D] Meanwhile, as charity grew cold and iniquity abounded, Benjamin also—that is, the monastic order—departed from the father into the Egypt of this world as an exile, and the sorrow of Father Jacob increased.

But behold: in our time, by God’s providence, the canonical order is flowering again; and news is brought to my father, the true Jacob, that his son Joseph lives. As though awakened from a heavy sleep, he says: “If my son Joseph still lives, it is enough for me: I will go and see him before I die” (Gen. 45). That is to say: If I see my son, the canonical order, living once more in my posterity, I shall not die.

But now also, revived and flourishing again, it is not a small matter to recount how much I, the canonical order, have suffered from impious kings at this end of the ages for the defence of ecclesiastical liberty. For in the time of the Henrician schism, in my Herlembald of Milan, who was the foremost among my sons called Patarines, [Note: [Col. 1499D] That is, defenders of clerical celibacy. See Pagi, *Critica*, vol. IV.] I incurred a cruel death. In the Roman pontiffs Gregory VII and Urban I endured persecutions; in Pope Paschal and his clergy, in Manegold of Lautenbach, and in very many others, I was captured and imprisoned. In my Eppo of Salzburg [Note: [Col. 1499D] Tengnagel wrote here in the manuscript: “It is clear from this that the author was from Salzburg.” But, as the learned Gentilotti aptly observed in his usual manner, a little earlier he also called Herlembald of Milan his own. I add that Arno speaks here not in his own name but in that of the canonical order.] I was deprived of my eyes; in Azelin of Padua and many others I was scourged with rods to the horror of onlookers. For in the time of Mattathias Maccabee, any one of mine who fled the pollution of excommunication, by which the princes of that age were held, could scarcely appear in public without immediately being proclaimed [Col. 1499B] by all as an abominable monster.

Yet this same little flock of mine did not even so lose confidence in the truth that was to reign, but, confessing the truth before kings and princes, was not ashamed of Christ’s words; therefore the heavenly Father will not be ashamed of it. In that storm, however, my brother, the monastic order, looking after its own quiet, either kept itself within the enclosure of its silence or, what was worse, even consented to iniquity, while I, the canonical order, fought in my sons privately and publicly unto death. For who then was scandalized without my burning? Who was weak without my weakness? If I must glory, though it is not expedient, I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord.

I know certain pupils [Col. 1499C] of my institution still living in the flesh, who wear not woollen but linen tunics and shirts; who take care that their dress is not conspicuous, seeking to please by conduct rather than clothing. I know, I say, such persons who, amid their devotion to fasts, reading, and prayers, and the other exercises of spiritual discipline, have more frequently and for longer breathed in through their nostrils paradisal fragrances; who, at times transported beyond bodily sense, have heard with a most divine hearing the sounds of heavenly hymnody full of honeyed sweetness; who, amid songs of God’s love and praise, have sometimes inwardly received in their souls the kisses of the word of God; whose belly, at the sensible touch of the Bridegroom stirring them to spiritual work, has often trembled; whose spiritual eyes [Col. 1499D] have many times been shown by the Bridegroom’s friends little golden ornaments inlaid with silver—visible forms, that is, corresponding to the spiritual gift granted to their minds through the ministry of angels.

I know a man of this kind, a disciple of my school, Theophilus, still living in the flesh, who fourteen years ago, having entered into an agony and for a long time become pale and sung hymns amid paradisal scents, was seized with an unusual trembling of flesh and spirit exulting in the Lord, so strong and yet so sweet that, because of its strength, his soul could scarcely remain within the sheath of flesh, and because of its sweetness, almost dissolved, it dwelt in paradise. Thus such a person may not vainly glory in the Lord, as one so abundantly forestalled by blessings of sweetness and crowned at the gate of paradise.

And I know a man of this sort who, after the public and private vigils, prayers, and morning praises, wished, in bitterness of soul, to give his limbs to rest as he sat in a place within the precincts of the cloister remote from the brothers’ assembly. While his heart kept watch, he was divinely lulled to sleep and received from the Lord no slight experience of that miracle shown to the disciples sitting in the upper room on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection. For he suddenly heard a sound from heaven like that of a violent spirit [Col. 1500B] which began gently, grew greater, approached the house in which he sat, and poured itself in through a window adjoining his head. In that rush of spirit, a certain fiery substance—not burning but shining, like a talent of gold in a blazing furnace—struck with great force against that window, which was glazed. Once it had entered, it immediately dissolved like a thin mist and filled the whole house where he sat. The atoms of this mist, full of sweetness and blessing, poured themselves with a certain force through every pore into the body and soul of the seated man, until the rush of such a stream gladdened the city of his soul, abundantly filled. Then he returned to himself and went away, wondering in holy fullness and praising the Lord, who thus consoles the humble. His grace, which even to this day stirs him toward holy pursuits, has not been fruitless, as he himself is accustomed to confess in his confidences in Christ. He walks to this day in the strength of that food amid the temptations of this life, and, as he hopes, will walk in it to the end of a good consummation. “For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow caused by turning” (Jas. 1).

There is also another member of my institution’s household who, while expounding the word of God in church, was continuously seen by persons of unquestionable faith as though a tongue of flame issued from his mouth, while he himself experienced nothing but the good grace of God in speaking. At another time, an invisible finger of a hand was seen continually marking his mouth with the sign of the cross while he expounded the divine word. On another occasion, while in an agony and praying for a long time, he experienced, with no small astonishment and wonder, the power and grace of sparks running to and fro among themselves and especially filling his face. Again, on a birthday feast of blessed Ambrose, while he was celebrating the solemnities of the Mass, blessed Ambrose himself was seen standing beside him as he offered sacrifice and consecrating the offerings with him. [Col. 1501A] At another time, as he stood at the altar intending to celebrate Mass, when the Canon and the action of the heavenly mysteries had been reached, a kind of fire was seen rising around him. Gradually increasing, it finally enveloped the whole priest, so that nothing but fire could be seen in him. And, wonderful to say, the wall standing between did not prevent the sight of a certain faithful person, to whom it was granted to see this: by a double miracle, in what was seen and in the one seeing it, the divine fire was visible through the obstacle of the wall just as if nothing stood in between.

At another time, something secret concerning this same priest was revealed to a person of good faith and love, and it may perhaps not be unworthy of being known. This priest was among the tents of Kedar, surrounded by the darkness of some foreign iniquity, as it seemed. Regarding it, silence was not safe so far as the Lord was concerned; yet to expose it would not have been possible without the danger of persecution. As he spoke about this matter among his own people, he said with a certain intense heat of heart that both things were praiseworthy: when no cause exists, or when the cause for which one must fight is entirely hidden, to enjoy peace in Christ; and, when the cause demands it, to suffer persecution for Christ, in accordance with the saying of the wise man, distinguishing “a time of war and a time of peace” (Eccles. 3). But he said that the intermediate lukewarmness, in which neither peace nor persecution is glorious, must be wholly rejected by an ecclesiastical man, lest he himself deserve to be rejected by the Lord, who says to the angel of the church of Laodicea: “Would that you were either cold or hot; but because you are neither cold nor hot, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth.”

While, I say, the aforesaid priest spoke such things and encouraged himself by these and similar words to endure persecution, the aforementioned person, a lover of Christ and of him in Christ, knowing well and devoutly considering that Christ both is and speaks in his elect, looked upon the speaker’s face amid his words. Then this desire came upon her: in her heart she wished and said to him, “Would that I might be able to recognize some invisible manifestation of Christ dwelling and speaking in you!” And while she silently revolved this thought in her mind, suddenly the speaker’s face, like the face of Moses long ago, made radiant by communion with the Lord’s speech and clothed in a certain divine splendour of the Lord’s countenance, was transformed—beyond perhaps what can be said or believed—into the radiant and glorious face of Christ himself. Thus the aforesaid person saw this and was greatly delighted; nor was she disappointed in her devout desire to see Christ in his priest. Yet amid this the priest himself experienced nothing other than a divine fervour of good zeal within himself, greater than usual—just as while offering sacrifice he perceived nothing outside himself other than the good grace of God present within him.

And these are your gifts, Christ; this is the abundance of your bestowals upon us, O God the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who thus console the humble and are accustomed to offer pure draughts to sincere minds. Thus your mother, O Lemuel—that is, “man in whom God is,” O Lord Jesus Christ—asked you, saying: “Do not, O Lemuel, do not give wine to kings, because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, lest they drink and forget judgments and alter the cause of the sons of the poor. Give,” she says, “strong drink and wine to those who are bitter in soul; let them drink and forget their poverty, and remember their sorrows no more” (Prov. 31). It is not necessary now to speak of these words one by one.

And: “I give you thanks, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent” (Matt. 11)—that is, from the aforesaid kings, who possess this world’s consolation, neither seek this consolation nor can therefore receive it—“but have revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, for so it was pleasing before you” (ibid.). Even amid visions of this kind, outwardly appearing and declaring the presence of the Holy Spirit, you work inwardly and invisibly in holy souls, while, in accordance with the form of the visions, you pour into them spiritual gifts: for example, the word of wisdom and knowledge, steadfastness of courage, or another such gift. In these your humble ones have consolation; and while they exercise themselves in them, they forget their poverty and remember their sorrow no more. Through them, when speaking or writing, whoever else hears the voice of the Holy Spirit does not know whence it comes or whither it goes.

But I spare myself glorying in such things, for it is not expedient, lest perhaps it be said of me: “Behold, the dreamer comes; come, let us kill him” (Gen. 37). Yet even when I am silent in this way and serve the Lord in humility, certain evil husbandmen say of me: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. 21). For in episcopal sees the black or grey monastic order, clothed in breeches or stripped of them, is not feared so greatly; nor is a clergy clothed in woollen tunics, an invention of recent date, feared so much that it ought to sit in those sees as the lawful heir. But among my household members, clothed in wool and furs for necessity and in linen for the dignity and mystery of their order, the byssine brightness of Aaron’s vestments and the white *collobium* of the Apostle James are greatly feared; hence it is said of it: “This is the heir,” and so forth.

Nor ought my sheep, that is, the souls of my household, to shrink from the habit of their innocence because they have seen very many wolves clothed in it. For God is able to make lambs out of wolves, or, once wolves have been expelled, to bring in lambs. Perhaps the devil hates this also in that order: that, in likeness of the Apostles’ primitive institution, it is established so moderately and commonly for all that not only companies of men, but also of women, live together within their proper bounds, separated by fitting enclosure; little boys and girls, old people with the young, praise the Lord’s name in it. As was foretold through Isaiah in a figure: “how the lion would dwell with the ox, the calf with the bear, and the wolf with the lamb, and their young would rest together.” Thus our true Jacob regulates the progress of his journey according to what he sees his flocks and little ones can endure; for if he forced them to labour more in walking, all the flocks would die in one day.

And while Moses, in my household men—true Israelites—sings to the Lord gloriously magnified, Mary together with the women, leading the choirs of common life, celebrates the same song with musical melody, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified” (Exod. 15). Thus one may see near the Lord’s cross the disciple on this side, in the male sex, and the mother on that side, in the female sex, entrusted to the disciple, standing by. Let princes see and be angry; let pain seize the inhabitants of Philistia; let trembling seize Moab; let the inhabitants of Canaan grow rigid; let dread and fear fall upon them in the greatness of your arm, O God, while true Israel, with you as leader, proceeds to the land of promise, terrible as an ordered army.

And perhaps the devil, enemy of all good things, hates this in my household as well: that, zealous to avoid the twofold leaven according to the Lord’s command, they abstain on the one hand from the pomp and enticements of worldly excess, as from Herod’s leaven; and on the other hand they guard against the superstition of novelty, as against the leaven of the Pharisees. They regard the ancient practice of the Church as authoritative—in dress, in the manner of abstinence, fasts, and divine offices—and do not readily depart from it either to the right or to the left. Thus, observant of the rule of Father Augustine, they appear careful, both in the fineness and austerity, and in the cost and usefulness, of their clothing, “that their habit may not be conspicuous.”

For behold: in the tonsures and shaving of their heads, my household members of whom I speak, made participants in the royal and priestly anointing of Christ their Head, their supreme King and true Priest—whom the Lord God anointed king, priest, prophet, and lord above his fellows—desire also to be conformed to him in a visible form. Not as was once the custom of heretics, who shaved a small circle at the crown of the head—a misuse still persisting among some even today—but, in accordance with the Fathers’ definition, they shave the whole surface of the head, leaving only a circular crown of hair below. Thus the shaved or flat portion of the head bears the form of the priestly tiara, while the circle of hair displays the badge of the royal crown. And this prevents any of them, burdened with locks like Absalom and thereby conspicuous under the weight of sins, from walking not crowned and mitred but as if wearing a cap, as in the manner of Jews who still have a veil over their heart.

Now in the shaved part of the head, as has been said, there is rightly a sign in us of priestly holiness: just as nothing intervenes between the summit of our head and heaven, so at the time of prayer no obstructing concern may cover our mind, stripped of earthly cares, and prevent it from cleaving immediately to God. Yet because in these matters, though we do not wage war according to the flesh, we nevertheless walk in the flesh, in which, as our heavenly Father knows, we need every earthly support, it is fitting in the perfect man that these same earthly supports be suitably subordinated to the dignity of the mind, according to the saying: “His left hand is under my head” (Song 2). That is, they must neither weigh down the spirit nor darken the mind, but crown it through the ordering of wise disposition. Thus, by wise contemplation on the one hand and prudent arrangement of things to be done on the other, we are adorned not in vain with the insignia of the priestly kingdom.

But since this perfection and the preservation of perfection are not the work of a single day—for the hairs of our affections are not plucked out by the roots but shaved by the razor of holiness once undertaken, and from the remnants of misery inborn in us and dwelling with us grow again upon the purity of our mind, until, by making provision for the flesh or procuring temporal things, we exceed the bounds of necessity and multiply superfluous cares that burden the senses, according to what is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses a mind burdened with many thoughts” (Wis. 9)—therefore that frequent renewal by daily penitence and mutual confession is necessary to us, in which our youth is renewed like the eagle’s. Seeking this, the Psalmist says: “I was occupied, and I swept my spirit” (Ps. 76).

For the outward signification of this renewal, in accordance with what was said to us—“Cleanse what is within, and what is without will be clean”—we are accustomed to admit frequent renewals of the heads of our bodies by washing, razor, and scissors, so that even in this respect the hands of the priestly or clerical order, as of the Bridegroom of the Church, may be like turned work of gold, full of hyacinths, through the mystical heavenly meanings.

In order that the shaven part of the head and the remaining ring of hair may each retain its proper proportion, so that nothing be taken from or added to either part in excess or deficiency, certain prudent men have judged the following rule of shaving suitable for every clerical head [Col. 1504D]: namely, that the third part of a line passing round the head should extend across the head from one edge of the crown to the other. This rule of measurement also suits the length of the shaving on well-rounded and spherical heads; but on elongated heads nothing should be added, lest the ring of hair surrounding the head appear to be of equal breadth. This precaution concerning measurement seemed necessary to note because of certain persons who are either excessive, lax, or irreligious.

Once this pattern of the heavenly coinage has been properly begun in us, it belongs to the diligence of the Father of the monastery to ensure that it is not spoiled by the negligence of barber or shaver: at each time of shaving he should inspect the heads, or entrust them to another careful inspector to be examined and any faults of shaving corrected [Col. 1505A]. He shall see to it that the entire upper part of the head is shaved according to the measurement already stated, that the lower edge of the crown reaches only the top of the ear, and that the whole ear remains uncovered.

We read that this form of tonsure and shaving, after its legal authority among the Nazarites and its evangelical authority among the apostles, was introduced also by the Third Council of Toledo. Its forty-fifth chapter [Note: [Col. 1505] Here an error has apparently crept in through the copyist’s fault, for the words now cited occur not in the Third Council of Toledo but in the Fourth, chapter 40, or, as others have it, 41.] reads as follows:

> “All clerics and readers, like Levites and priests, having had the whole upper part of the head shorn, shall leave below only the circular crown. They shall not do as readers have hitherto appeared to do in the regions of Gaul, who, wearing long hair like laymen, shave only a small circle on the crown of the head. For this custom has hitherto been that of heretics in Spain. Therefore [Col. 1505B], in order to remove scandal from the Church, this mark of disgrace must be taken away, and there must be one tonsure and habit, as is the usage of all Spain. Whoever does not observe this shall be guilty against the Catholic faith.”

Likewise, retaining the ancient usage of the Church in the white linen, ankle-length, apostolic garment which we call the *surplice*, and displaying upon it the pattern of the Lord’s cross, they admit no novelty. In the whiteness of the linen garment they signify innocence of life and purity of flesh achieved by much self-discipline; in its breadth, generosity of charity; in its length down to the ankle, perseverance in good work to the end. They also show themselves blessed peacemakers, since Roman nobles too in ancient times wore the ankle-length toga in peace [Col. 1505C].

The tongue of this tunic is always loose and serviceable, showing that we should always be ready to give an answer to anyone who asks us for a reason; able to exhort in sound teaching, refute opponents, and be useful in speech for edification, teaching and instructing at every time of speaking. More fittingly, however, the tongue of the undershirt or shirt is always closed and fastened upward, signifying the perpetual guard or closure of our heart and mouth against idle and evil speech. We ought sometimes, on account of silence, to refrain even from edifying conversation, so that we may be able truly to say to the Lord with the Prophet: “My secret is for myself, my secret is for myself.” Again: “I became mute and kept silence even from good things” (Isa. XXIV). And: “I set a guard upon my mouth when sinners rose up against me” (Ps. XXXVIII [39]) [Col. 1505D]. For one seldom repents of having kept silence; often one is harmed by having spoken. “Death also and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII); and: “He who does not stumble in speech is a perfect man” (Jas. III).

No human being has been able to tame the tongue; but what is impossible among human beings is undoubtedly possible with the Lord. Therefore the tongue of our heart and mouth is fastened upward, so that, as it is closed against earthly and human speech, it may thereby be joined to the mysteries of divine utterances and to solitary converse with the Lord. For “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV) [Col. 1506A]. Thus the tongue was created as a servant not only of human speech but also of divine utterance and conversation; nor should one complain of excessive silence among human beings when he is granted to mingle in conversation with the Lord and angels through prayer.

This too may fittingly be understood as signified in the tongue of the skin tunic: because we sometimes close it, for practical use, to warm the body and ward off cold, but at other times leave it loose when a better mildness of air has come with the south wind. The mystery here may be that the Lord must be blessed by us at every time—that is, in adversity as well as prosperity—and that, according to the Psalmist’s saying, “His praise” should “always be in” our “mouth.” Or we should pray in secret for the driving away of diabolical temptations and the invocation of the grace of the Holy Spirit; or, with the tongue loosened, celebrate his praises in the common assemblies of the Church with voices raised high. Thus, entering and departing from the sanctuary, we may not be found without sound, and may find pasture everywhere; and whether the north wind rises or the south wind blows upon the garden of our hearts, may its spices always flow forth [Col. 1506B].

Also belonging to our habit is the woollen garment called a *cappa*, which Augustine, the steward of my household, calls a *birrum*. Enclosing and wrapping the body on every side in a black, almost funeral covering, it signifies in us the humility of mortification and renunciation of the world. For as one clothed in a cappa is in some sense withdrawn from the world and enclosed almost as in a tomb [Col. 1506C], so that he cannot easily look back, free his hands for fighting or striking back, or stretch them out for worldly embraces—for this shortened garment, worn in front, cannot cover both hands—so my household members should remember that they ought to live as dead to the world and removed from all worldly pomp, works, and enticements.

Our use of this garment is almost daily, but especially in Lent and times of penance, so that we may know that we ought to be not only righteous but also penitents for daily sins. Moreover, if you count the two wings of this garment, covering us on either side, together with the four parts of the ankle-length tunic—that is, front and back [Col. 1506D], and the two sleeves—what is lacking from the flight of the six-winged Seraphim in the sacred symbolism of our own holy habit?

In fasts and abstinences, likewise, seeking to retain the Church’s ancient practice, they discipline themselves now by fasts of two or three days, now by daily fasts. From fasting observance they except Easter and the other feasts of the Lord, as equally celebrated with Sunday, and also the feasts of apostles and martyrs; by a double refreshment of food they share in the joy of those saints’ birthdays and, meanwhile, in their mystery according to the flesh, whose sufferings and righteousness they appear to have mourned with through the preceding vigils and fasts. Thus they may not seem vainly to profess in the Apostles’ Creed the communion of saints [Col. 1507A], while neither mourning with their sufferings nor rejoicing with their joy.

Knowing also that it is good not to eat flesh, they abstain from it in the common refectories; yet they do not deny its use, at suitable times and places, to the sick until their strength is restored, nor to children and the weak, nor to guests. In poorer monasteries, where fish and milk are less plentiful, they have not prohibited the use of fat as seasoning for vegetables and legumes on intervening days. They judge that means and capacity must be weighed not only in individual persons but in communities also.

Yet they do not condemn other monks who abstain entirely from these things, deny such consolation to their sick and children, and hold guests to the rule of regular abstinence—although they criticize them for some lack of discretion, because they exceed the limits established by the Fathers. For anyone of our age wishing to be holier, better, wiser, and more discerning than Augustine and Benedict will be reckoned to superstition rather than religion, since it is enough for the disciple to be like his master, lest he be marked by that apostolic rebuke: “Do not touch; do not handle; etc.” (Col. II) [Col. 1507B].

But neither do those who eat flesh and permit its use once or twice a week at the table of regular brethren dare, when rebuked by the apostolic sentence, to despise it—especially if they live in regions where the larger number of brethren of the same order, living more strictly, do not require otherwise. For, since in every profession the better are to be imitated, just as I consider it superstition for a monastery to presume something which neither regular precepts prescribe nor examples of elders encourage, so I consider it disgraceful for others to remain beneath the custom of the good persons among whom they live, especially if no reasonable cause exists compelling this to be done [Col. 1507C].

Knowing that silence at night hours and at times allotted to the divine office or reading is a worship of piety, my household members strive for silence in the morning for two hours of daylight—hours which some, indeed almost all religious persons, have transferred to reading and spiritual exercise—also on weekdays and continuously in Lent, and in secluded places, namely the oratory, dormitory, and refectory. They restrain the tongue even from good speech, unless the superior has occasion to arrange something; and he too shall arrange it, as far as possible, in fewer words and with less noise, or indicate it by a gesture or sound.

Likewise, from the morning, after the office of Saint Mary has been said about the beginning of the third hour, and after chapter has been concluded, my household members sit at work in silence until the principal Third Hour, unless necessity requires someone to speak. This principal Third Hour, on account of the work-time to be celebrated, especially in summer, should begin later, so that it may suitably continue with Sext, when the Masses have been completed [Col. 1508A]. During this work-time I endeavor to regulate my household’s speech so that that same worship of piety, silence, is not excluded, while each person speaks quietly with his fellow worker concerning what necessity requires—as Martha, according to the Gospel narrative, called her sister Mary silently, saying: “The Master is here” (John XXI). Here brevity of words and moderation of voice did not exclude the grace of silence.

But if anyone considers that more must be said, he shall take the person with whom he needs to speak outside the assembly of workers, with an elder as witness—unless the superior judges that something should be said to all in common. If it is a fast-day, after Sext has been said, those to whom it is permitted must devote themselves to reading until None [Col. 1508B], unless perhaps during summer days something seems to need to be taken from this time because of the midday rest and to spare the eyes.

But on private days, when the fast is relaxed, after Sext has been said and the brothers have eaten, together with the table-servants, and after the sign has been given for it and the midday rest has been taken on summer days, after None too has been said they are to work, whether in the garden or wherever necessity requires. The same is to be done if the brothers have eaten after None. In this work, indeed, we believe that the following accords both with propriety and with the purpose of exercise: they should converse about necessary and useful matters not in the common vernacular but in the learned language, all taking care together that excessive or idle speech does not begin to spread [Col. 1508C], nor a word of buffoonery be heard.

If anyone, after being warned, does not immediately cease from such speech, he shall be subject to regular discipline. To prevent excessive talk, in which sin will not be lacking, they have carefully adopted this pious custom: no one is to speak of what necessity requires except with the prior or the person in charge of the work. But if something concerning the divine office must be discussed, they shall do it briefly while seated in chapter, or after chapter if the head of the order approves, or else after None, once *benedicite* has been said, while standing. If outdoor work is lacking, even after None, they shall sit at their indoor work with discipline until Vespers.

That the course of our daily regimen may proceed properly and in order, they give no little diligent attention to observing the signs for the Hours and having them rung at their proper times [Col. 1508D]. Thus they rise for the night watches at midnight; in winter, Prime is rung at the first dawning of day, but in summer immediately after sunrise. In winter the principal Third Hour is held near the end of the third hour; in summer, as has also been said above, it is delayed long enough for Mass and the following Sext to continue suitably together. But lest the third hour pass without prayer, the office of Saint Mary for the Third Hour is to be taken at its beginning, and then they are to go to chapter.

No day is to pass without at least two hours being left for reading. During the summer these may be kept in the morning; from the Ides of September until Easter, either in the morning or from Sext until None [Col. 1509A]. I judge either arrangement indifferent, except that one of them more nearly approaches the regular constitution. I especially approve that reading should not be omitted daily at its proper time, lest, if it is omitted, the day’s regimen be as though blind. For reading, after prayers and praises of the Lord, is a kind of eye of this same regimen; if it is absent or dark, the whole body of the regimen will be dark.

If, however, the superior should sometimes, because the matter requires it, order work for the whole day, whether for the whole community, for some specifically, or in turns now for these and now for those, then, as I think, the merit of obedience repays in them the fruit of reading—especially if the work is done without noise and in accordance with the discipline of silence. For these persons too, especially during summer days, fasting may be relaxed, and the psalmody of the canonical Hours performed not melodically but in recitation [Col. 1509B]. Night silence and weekdays entirely devoted to silence and spiritual exercise can restore the mind to rest and compensate for what has been spent less on reading.

Even on these free days, anyone who happens to be overcome by sleep in reading or prayer should be assigned some such work as will shake off his sluggishness without disturbing the rest of others. On free days, None should be rung when that hour itself begins; on other days, when the eighth hour has passed beyond the middle, so that sleep may be shortened in summer and the meal on fast-days advanced for those of weaker age or sex. From the Ides of September, however, None is not to be rung before the beginning of the hour itself [Col. 1509C].

During summer, Vespers should be rung at the beginning of the eleventh hour; in winter, when daylight begins to fail as those at work are seated. After Vespers, where the community must proceed or sit, two or three lanterns, according to the size of the community, should be carried. In psalmody, I also prefer that it be moderate: neither too hurried nor too prolonged, but with articulation and melody; and that it be uttered neither in a voice too low nor too loud. The head of the order may sometimes, omitting the silence of the middle division because of the gathering of the people or another reasonable cause, sing more briefly; or, when the people are absent, extend it somewhat for solemnity’s sake [Col. 1509D].
