For this too seems to be intended by the precept of the Law, when the Lord said to Moses: “If a longer and broken trumpet-signal is sounded, they shall move camp” (Num. V). And shortly afterwards: “But when the people must be assembled,” he says, “there shall be a simple sounding of the trumpets, and they shall not sound them in broken notes.”

I neither require a multiplication of familiar psalms nor forbid speaking in tongues in such matters. Above all, I approve this: those who chant psalms and pray should take care that what is uttered by the mouth is considered by the mind; and that the exercise of work and reading, or the turtle-dove sacrifice of private prayer, is not excluded by the solemn communal celebration of prayer and psalmody, since “these things ought to be done, and those not left undone” [Col. 1510A].

Since sluggishness and sleep are apt to steal upon those chanting psalms, especially in the night hours—and this, if it becomes habitual, is exceedingly deadly and destructive to the soul—the more diligent communities of those keeping vigil commonly appoint in choir a single watchman. Standing in the middle of the choir, sometimes sitting and, when necessary, walking about, he hands a book to anyone whom he sees sleeping or drowsy. If the man does not bow to it, thereby showing that he is awake, the watchman places the book before him to awaken him. Then he goes back to his place, and the person caught takes his turn until he too places the little book, on the same condition, before another sleeping person.

Not only, as has been said, are watchmen used in the choir during vigils, but guardians are also appointed for all cloistral discipline [Col. 1510B]. They are called *circatores* or inspectors, because especially during the time of silence they walk around and inspect the interior of the cloister. If they find anyone absent from the seats assigned to them and lingering away, or inattentive as they should not be even in their proper places, or two or three persons joined somewhere in disorderly conversation, they shall report them in chapter in the morning.

Likewise, any brother who discovers an offense committed by another shall report it there, after, however, a brief silence following the saying of *benedicite*, so that each person may have opportunity to accuse himself where appropriate, according to what is written: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. XVIII). Anyone reported shall immediately rise and stand in the middle [Col. 1510C]; when the charge has been heard, he shall humble himself by prostrating his whole body. Ordered to rise, he shall humbly speak words of confession; or, if he has grounds on which he can truthfully excuse himself and the cause is important, he shall do so after requesting permission. Tumultuous noise is to be wholly excluded from chapter. To exclude it, brothers shall not exchange words with or among themselves, but whatever must be said shall be addressed directly to the person presiding over chapter.

Nor should common matters be handled there, or complaints made about food, drink, or clothing. Only chapter matters, and matters pertaining to the observance, protection, or dignity of the order and religious life, should be discussed. Once these have been discussed, if it pleases the head of the order, it will not be unfitting to speak also of other matters which the occasion requires [Col. 1510D].

But if a brother reported in chapter does not immediately humble himself by speaking words of confession, and instead utters words of defense to make excuses for sins, he shall not thereby gain impunity. Nor should there be long argument with such a person. If the case is evident and he disputes the fault, the matter shall be investigated; the elders, or even the community, should be consulted about it. If they judge him guilty, then, as one convicted, he shall be punished more severely. If it seems good to the superior, he shall also be reduced to penance and shall not depart from it until he has paid everything, even to the last farthing of confession. For it is written: “By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Matt. XII) [Col. 1511A].

But if his confession is true and from the heart, it will benefit both himself and others. If it is feigned, his condemnation will thereby be less, since he does not corrupt others by the example of perverse self-defense. Let him confess even if, darkened by a certain blindness of heart, he does not yet fully recognize his own fault. Let him confess this, I say, knowing without doubt that the judgment of others concerning his case is truer than his own judgment. I think it may happen that, through the merit of such confession—which, if not from knowledge, is nevertheless from faith—the Lord looking upon him, he too may be enlightened and acknowledge his fault; acknowledging it, he may groan; and, as he groans, the divine mercy, made propitious, may forgive.

But if anyone, hardened to the end against the judgment of his own conscience, persists in refusing to confess, while not refusing to undergo punishment, such a person seems not to be cast out as pestilential or dead, but tolerated as sick, lame, or blind. Of such persons Augustine, steward of our household, says: “I would rather have lame persons than mourn the dead” [Col. 1511B]. But concerning those who refuse to undergo punishment, as pestilential and dead persons, he himself prescribes in the Rule:

> “A convicted person ought to undergo corrective punishment; if he refuses to bear it, let him be cast out from your fellowship. For this too is done not cruelly but mercifully, lest by pestilential contagion he destroy many.”

This casting out or separation first takes place within: namely, from the table, the choir, or conversation [Col. 1511C]. If they cannot be healed by these means, only then shall such a person be cut off as a dead member and driven and cast out from the entire body of the community—yet with such moderation as is appropriate, which Pope Gelasius prescribes in these words:

> “If anyone, after making profession according to the Rule of blessed Augustine, disturbs brothers desiring to serve God in canonical order, and, devoting himself to quarrels and continual contentions, persistently troubles the community in disobedience to God and the Rule, such a person, if he wishes, with the counsel of his superior and brothers, to go to some place where he may be saved under a superior according to the customs of his order, shall be given permission to depart. But if, led by a spirit of obstinacy, he prefers—not for the salvation of his soul but in order to return to the mire of a more spacious way, and, like the raven that went out from the ark, to gorge and feed himself on flesh and blood rather than, with the dove, delight in being refreshed by virtues—then, without permission or blessing, he shall be dismissed, according to the Prophet, to the desires of his heart. For if the unbeliever departs, let him depart; for, according to blessed Augustine, this is done not cruelly but mercifully, lest by pestilential contagion he destroy many. Yet if, when outside, he disturbs the brothers or the house, and after a second or third admonition does not come to his senses, let him be excommunicated by the superior and brothers.” [Note: [Col. 1511] See concerning expulsion, chapter *Cum in Ecclesiis*, “On Majority and Obedience.”]

Younger persons, indeed, should not lightly be subjected even to lesser excommunications, much less, I would say, to greater ones. For through frivolity of mind they sometimes take more pleasure in separations than are corrected by them. Rather, when they begin to rebel, after verbal rebukes, rods, fasts, and silence have been applied, they must be constrained by confinement and seclusion rather than allowed their own pleasure, until it is tested by certain and prolonged experience whether they may perhaps be willing to amend their way for the better, as it is written: “By what means does a young man correct his way?” (Ps. CXVIII) [Col. 1512A].

Boys who offend are corrected with rods and ferules according to the greater or lesser seriousness of their offenses. But it is better that, through the safeguard of the rod, they be restrained as much as possible from offenses. Therefore the supervision of an elder or tutor must never be absent from them, through which necessary care can also fittingly be provided for tender childhood [Col. 1512B]. When adolescents are transferred from the boys’ school and from under the rod into the company of elders and chapter discipline, they shall not be left to their own will, idleness, or wandering. Rather, they too, singly or in pairs or threes, shall remain under elders’ supervision; under their oversight they shall read and work in their assigned places, nor shall they be allowed to linger away from their places without a definite and reasonable cause.

It shall be common to all, both elders and younger members stationed in the cloister square, not to go beyond the cloister enclosure without the permission of the superior, dean, or prior and without a definite reasonable cause [Col. 1512C]. The only exceptions are officials: the cellarer and chamberlain, their assistants, and those assigned obediences outside the same enclosure. Nor shall the father or superior of the monastery make a practice of spending the night outside his cell without having made known to the dean or prior the reason for his departure. If he intends to remain away longer, he shall communicate the reasons for his departure to the elders, or, if appropriate, to the entire community.

Thus also in important matters that must be done or arranged, he shall not employ his own judgment, but shall consult now the elders, now the entire community, so that what pleases all, or the greater part, may be carried out with the scandal of murmuring removed. His table shall be with guests, especially those of spiritual—that is, canonical, clerical, or monastic—professions [Col. 1512D]. Such visitors, especially those arriving from more distant regions, shall be received with devout cheerfulness, according to the degree of respect due to them, sometimes by the whole community and sometimes by several brothers going to meet them with psalmody, as persons in whom we receive Christ dwelling. Thus they shall be brought within the cloister enclosure to lodgings prepared for them.

At their table, too, reading shall not be lacking, to remove the uselessness of excessive talk and to provide greater opportunity for spiritual conferences. But the rest who arrive from secular or military occupations [Col. 1513A] shall have their lodging outside; they likewise shall be treated with kindly cheerfulness, because they sometimes earn respect for themselves through terrors, acquire it through benefits, or demand it by the mere claim of necessity.

The care of the poor—whether newcomers or those whom we always have among us—must certainly not be undertaken sluggishly or negligently. It shall be entrusted to one God-fearing brother, who, in lodgings arranged separately for men and separately for women, shall provide for each person, according to the means available, from the tithes of the monastery’s provisions or from the brothers’ leftovers. He shall also take care to wash their feet, provide and clean their bedding, and meet their other needs [Col. 1513B], with diligence all the greater because these things are done or neglected for the poor solely in view of divine recompense, as it is written: “Do not invite the rich, but the poor, who have nothing with which to repay you; but you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous” (Luke 14). For some, by receiving angels as guests, have thereby found favour.  

Amid these pursuits and works of ours, from morning until before the meal we arrange indoors such tasks as can be carried out in quiet and silence; nor do we devote that time to outside work unless a greater necessity demands it, knowing what the Apostle said to his disciple Timothy: “Train yourself in godliness; for bodily exercise is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for all things [Col. 1513C], having promise not only of the life that now is, but also of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4). Nor are we ignorant that Pope Sylvester established holidays for clerics for the same reason. Yet neither do we disdain agricultural and servile work in its proper season, knowing that the Apostle laboured with his own hands and commanded, saying: “If anyone does not work or labour, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3). Therefore, lest idleness have any place among us, we exhort the elderly, the weak, and those unable to work, to sing psalms in silence. Young and stronger persons able to work, if any withdraw themselves from work or distract others, we call back to work by the discipline especially of silence and fasting. We also forbid adolescents to join one another in work or converse together unless elders are present as witnesses [Col. 1513D]. Hence at least one of the elders must also be assigned to outside work, lest the young be without the supervising presence of elders working alongside them.

Certainly, my household customarily moderates its fasts and abstinences according to the most judicious rule of the Fathers, as Augustine, the steward of my household, has spoken very briefly concerning them: namely, fasting from the Ides of September until Easter, and excepting no day from the observance of the regular fast save Sunday feasts, Sundays, and those feasts of the saints on which it has been established that the people should have holidays. From the octave of Pentecost until the Ides of September they fast on Wednesdays and Fridays, unless there is outside work [Col. 1514A] for which the fast ought to be relaxed.

The measure of food and drink is likewise laid down scrupulously, because some need to take more and others less. Bread and beer are provided abundantly for each; two cooked dishes seem sufficient, while a third—on account of a greater feast’s solemnity, if there is one—called a *pitantia*, is set before each pair. On other days too a third dish is admitted, but of fruit, raw herbs, or newly growing vegetables. Something special shall also be set before the head of the order, if it can be had, so that he may have something to share and send to whomever seems fitting. From the institution of these same Fathers they have likewise been accustomed to borrow profitably the methods of excommunicating the disobedient and the midday rest during summer days, together with other useful institutions.

[Col. 1514B] And this is almost the daily occupation of myself and my people: fasting, abstinence, prayer, reading, and moreover work, solicitude for all, and the administration of many churches. In these, while my household go about labouring—preaching the word of God, visiting the sick, burying the dead, catechizing and baptizing—I deem my ministry no less acceptable to God than monastic quiet or the agricultural labour of monks. Nor do I think that the fragrance of prayers ought to be preferred by God to this scent of my garments, since he himself says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “And the scent of your garments is like the scent of incense” (Song 4). This, indeed, is our defence against those who malign us.

But let those know themselves excluded from this defence of mine who, under the profession of common life in the clergy, claim some private property for themselves; who, restless and talkative, pursue wandering idleness; especially if, when rebuked for these things, they despise amendment. Likewise excluded are the establishments called monasteries in which such things are freely permitted, and in which capital sins pass without a fitting penalty, while those matters said to require greater penance likewise pass almost unpunished, since any punishment that exists is neither great enough nor such as to correct. Such persons, therefore, unless they take care to amend, shall justly exclude themselves from this defence of my sons [Col. 1514C].

In compensation for these excluded persons, I receive under the protection of my defence priests and clerics who live commendably, even outside monastic enclosures, in the administration of churches. Prosper, bishop and follower of Augustine, the steward of my household, first received such persons under the patronage of our defence, saying:

> “A priest entrusted with the care of administration receives from the people, without greed and even with the praise of piety, things to be administered, and faithfully administers what he receives—he who has either abandoned all his own possessions or joined them to the property of the Church, and has placed himself among the poor out of love for poverty, so that from that from which he supplies the poor he himself also lives as a voluntary poor man. Clerics likewise, whom either choice or birth has made poor, receive the necessities of life, whether living in their own houses or in a community, with perfection of virtue; because it is not the desire of possessing that leads them to receive these things, but the necessity of life compels them.” [Col. 1514D]

This is Prosper. When he says “in their own houses,” it must be understood not of houses which they possess by hereditary or proprietary right, but through ecclesiastical responsibility or benefice. Thus it is written of the disciple whom Jesus loved that he received the Lord’s Mother “into his own” (John 19); yet he possessed nothing by proprietary right, but possessed his own share, and that of those to be provided for by him, from the distribution of common goods, through the disposition and use of sharing. Prosper also made a good and careful distinction when he said, “whether in their own houses or in a community,” so that you may understand that no one can both have a private house and, besides, remain in a community.

The clerics whom he says receive the necessities of life “with perfection of virtue” while living in their own houses [Col. 1515A], I judge to be the legitimate priests of God among the people. Possessing ecclesiastical houses indeed, but as their own and by their own right, they are suitably supported by the share of tithes and offerings that falls to them, living, of course, such a life as is adorned with perfection of virtue. But I understand that he cannot mean clerics constituted outside sacred orders, whom the holy canons permit to take wives and to receive their stipends separately. For they are entangled in worldly snares and therefore remain below the summit of perfection, the Lord saying, and prescribing the rule of perfection: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19).

[Col. 1515B] Those are still strangers to this rule of perfection who can say: “my house, my field, my male servant, my female servant.” Concerning each such person Augustine, the steward of my household, says that, as long as they can say these things, they are not free from the snares of the devil.

Among those same communities which, contrary to the name and rule of their profession, live privately and separately in their own houses, I do not deny that there are some who, though not commendable in every respect, nevertheless live tolerably according to human judgment. Yet the judgment of truth does not admit them under the shield of my defence, because, still possessing private property, they have not yet attained perfection of virtue. They may nevertheless be saved among the perfect, if they love those whom they know or think to be perfect, according to what is written: “Your eyes saw my imperfection, and all shall be written in your book” (Ps. 138 [139]) [Col. 1515D].

They may be saved, I say, if, while outwardly appearing before human beings to lead a life free from crimes and vices, and devoting themselves to ministry or to leisure for the word, they do not lend assistance by sharing or participating in others’ forbidden offices, nor become implicated in a common cause with those with whom they have one communion. Of such persons, as Prosper likewise seems to say, the Apostle speaks: “Those who labour in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary, and those who serve at the altar share with the altar” [Col. 1516A] (1 Cor. 9). Unless he had wished this to be understood of those who despise their own possessions, he would never have added immediately: “So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel.”

“They live by the Gospel,” he says, who wish to have nothing as their own, who neither have nor desire to have, possessing not their own things but common things. Thus, in accordance with the reasonable statement of Prosper, consonant with apostolic teaching, it is not improper that priests and clerics who live commendably even outside monasteries should be received under the protection of my defence.

I have wished, as it were, to sketch this as a shield of our defence: to weave from the omen of our customs and manner of life [Col. 1516B] a theme in which the common life among clergy speaks for itself and glories in the Lord. I have become foolish, but I was compelled by those who glory beyond measure in their supposedly singular holiness, striving to make even one proselyte from the canonical order into the monastic order. Having made him, they should fear lest perhaps they have made him a son of Gehenna, liable to condemnation because he has made void his first faith. Such a man is also shown to be disobedient to the Holy Roman Church through Pope Urban, who commands and says:

> [Note: [Col. 1515D] C. *Mandamus*, 19, q. 3.] “We command, and in commanding universally forbid, that no canon professed according to rule become a monk, unless—God forbid—he has fallen publicly. If anyone, presuming to act against our decree, attempts to do so [Col. 1516C], we command that he return to the canonical order, that thereafter he wear the cowl as a memorial of his presumption, and that he remain last in choir.”

There is, indeed, among some persons a dispute or doubt about this word: does the command prescribe that he should *wear* (*deferre*) or *lay aside* (*deserere*) the cowl? We do not dispute about the word; yet we know beyond doubt that Pope Urban himself, the issuer of the command, and after him other Roman pontiffs, stripped such presumptuous persons of the cowl.

Pope Innocent II agrees with this in the letter he wrote in defence of the canonical order, in these words:

> [Note: [Col. 1515D] It is also found in Book V of Baluze’s *Miscellanea*. This is Conrad I, who established Regular Canons at Salzburg under the Rule [Col. 1516D] of St Augustine; he died in 1147. *History of Salzburg*.]
>
> “Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Conrad, Archbishop of Salzburg: greeting and apostolic blessing. Holy Scripture teaches us much concerning the dignity and excellence of the life of canons; and much might be said, because the life of canons is apostolic life. For the apostles, having despised all things, lived this life with the Lord; and after his ascension they lived this life with the multitude of believers, whose soul and heart were one, and left it to posterity to be maintained by their example.
>
> “The martyr and pontiff Urban took care to recall this in his decrees for the instruction of the faithful, saying: ‘We know that you are not ignorant that common life has hitherto flourished among good Christians, and still flourishes by the grace of God, especially among those chosen for the Lord’s portion—that is, clerics—as is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul”’ [Col. 1517A; Note: [Col. 1517D] C. *Scimus*, 12, q. 1.].
>
> “Saint Jerome set in order through his letters this life, which had been ordered by the rules of blessed Augustine. Therefore, fortified by the authorities of these and others, we judge it to be of no lesser merit, with the Spirit of the Lord inspiring and sustaining, to observe the canonical life than to preserve the monastic religious life through perseverance in the same Spirit. Hence we remember that it was established by the decrees of our predecessors that no one of canonical profession, after he has placed a man over his head in God’s stead, should dare, through any impulse of levity or under the pretext of a stricter religious life [Col. 1517B], to depart from the cloister without permission of prelate and community.
>
> “Following in their footsteps, we forbid by apostolic authority the attempt which certain brothers in the cloister of Perengerscadem [Note: [Col. 1517D] That is, Berchtesgaden, situated not far from Salzburg, whose provost is an elector of Cologne. [Col. 1518D] Baluze reads *Berthersgadmensi*.] have wished to make through vain presumption to change their order. We command them to render to God what they have vowed and, with the Lord’s help, strive faithfully to observe the Rule of blessed Augustine which they have professed. If perhaps you find them lax and less fervent in its observance, we exhort your brotherhood, according to the wisdom given you by God, strictly to admonish them—as concerns you—to preserve their profession and order and obey the commands of the Rule. Given at the Lateran, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April.”

[Col. 1517C] Similarly, the Council of Autun [Note: [Col. 1518D] C. *nullus*, 19, q. 3.], likewise supported by the authority of the Roman See, restrains the presumption of abbots and monks in such matters, saying:

> “Let no abbot or monk presume to recall regular canons from the purpose of canonical profession, or to receive them by drawing them into the monastic habit so that they become monks, so long as they can find a church of their own order in which, living regularly and canonically, they may serve God and save their souls. If anyone should attempt this in rash daring, let him be bound by the bond of anathema.”

These pronouncements of the Fathers, issued with the weight of authority and reason, could have sufficed both to repress the presumption of monks and to restrain the insolence of our own people, lest they be carried about by every wind of doctrine [Col. 1517D], had not the love of their own excellence driven the former more fiercely, and the foolish desire to try novelty driven the latter. In this they are at once found transgressors of the Lord’s command, who ordered his disciples not to go from house to house, but commanded: “Into whatever house you enter, remain there” (Luke 9).

Perhaps among human beings a holiness clothed in rags, stripped of breeches and fur garments, and sweating at rustic labour is more prized, because it excepts neither the Lord’s days nor the feast-days of the apostles from the severity of fasting. But to me, and to everyone of sound mind, it is a very small matter that we should be judged by human beings or by a human day; nor do we judge ourselves. Rather, we glory in the Lord, and our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience—that, striving according to the most divine command of the Lord Jesus to beware of the leaven of Herod and the Pharisees, we avoid wickedness on one side and superstition on the other. For us, instead of the willow (*saliunca*), shall the fir-tree rise, and instead of the nettle shall the myrtle grow: while divine contemplation and heavenly manner of life, in place of worldly covetousness setting down roots in the stream of transient things, are changed, as fir for willow; and novice fervour is changed into moderate abstinence, that is, nettle into myrtle—so that our flight may be neither in the winter of excessive rigour nor on the Sabbath of worldly or Jewish [Col. 1518A] laxity.

Here indeed I see a third leaven, that of the Sadducees, greatly lying in wait for us and therefore greatly to be avoided; it occupies a middle place between those two leavens. For the Sadducees, neither so secularly impious as Herod nor so superstitiously holy as the Pharisees, situated in a kind of intermediate sluggishness, passed this present life with as much pleasure as they could, because, believing neither in angel nor resurrection, they hoped in the Lord in this life only.

But we have been instructed otherwise by the Lord our God. We rejoice that we have been called to the liberty of the glory of the children of God and to the hope of eternal life, so that we need be subject to none of these three leavens: Herod’s, the Pharisees’, or the Sadducees’. We have been called to liberty, I say—only let us not give liberty as an occasion for the flesh, but through the flesh serve one another. For neither clothing nor the lack of a fur garment or breeches is anything, but the keeping of God’s commandments. Nor is the kingdom of God food, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit [Col. 1518B].

Yet meanwhile I rejoice that, through the excess of some toward the right, the excess of others too far toward the left is reproved and judged; and meanwhile we too learn how tenaciously we ought to hold divine commands when we recognize others to be so observant even of human regulations. But one thing grieves me: that such indiscretion is imputed to our Fathers Augustine and Benedict, when they are asserted to have been the authors and teachers of such great austerity.

For Father Augustine never forbade linen clothing among clergy. Indeed, he recognized the use of hair-shirts and the garb of penitents as alien to the clerical profession, unless perhaps someone should choose inwardly and secretly, as in Lent, to humble his flesh with such clothing; yet this should not be done without the counsel of a spiritual father, otherwise it will be reckoned more as superstition than as religion. Nor did Benedict, a most discerning man, take fur clothing away from his monastic disciples. He himself used a sheepskin garment, and, though in his Rule he spoke according to the climate of his own region [Col. 1518C], he nevertheless allowed monks a hairy tunic for winter. What else, surely, is the fur tunic we customarily use than a hairy tunic? For it is plainly hairy, and it cannot be denied to be a tunic, since it is written in Genesis (Gen. 3) that the Lord gave Adam and his wife tunics of skins. But let each person abound in his own understanding; and would that all things might be done for edification and not for the destruction of some. And if some think otherwise, God will reveal this also to them.

But I say these things not to disparage those brothers of whom we speak. In almost every respect they seem to me of admirable and praiseworthy humility, holiness, and patience; among them I revere and embrace some distinguished men as heavenly [Col. 1519B] lights. Thus, in our own order, Hugh [Note: [Col. 1519D] A priest and abbot of Saint Victor at Paris, of the Order of Regular Canons of St Augustine, Saxon by birth. Thus Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; Meibomius, vol. III of *German Affairs*.], magnificently enlightened in our age by the gift of knowledge, shone forth like the morning star. And as, in the Cluniac order, Abbot Rupert of Deutz [Note: [Col. 1520D] On him let the reader consult the Anonymous of Melk placed at the end of the Benedictine-Maurist Library.]—the illustrious interpreter of nearly the whole Old and New Testament—adorns that golden order like a topaz, so in the Cistercian order Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, endowed with the gift of humility and wisdom, is a great light of the heavenly court and an outstanding ornament of that order. Likewise Archbishop Norbert, pre-eminent in the gift of magnificent learning, undoubtedly shone forth as a splendid light in the Church of God.

But those among them whom I know to be wiser and revere do not think otherwise about these matters than we do [Col. 1519C]. For Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, disapproves of deserters from our order to his own; and Father Norbert, himself the introducer of woollen tunics among clergy, later became the corrector of his own institution. While young, he girded himself and walked where he wished; and thus, through novice fervour and youthful strength of spirit, he was led into that affectation. But when he had grown old and had become archbishop, yielding both to the authority of the Church and to ancient custom, he himself accepted linen tunics, as one girded by another; and he commanded his disciples who were present with him to wear them. He wished to accomplish this same thing throughout all the clergy of his institution, but death overtook him, and a practice adopted by many could not suddenly be removed [Col. 1519D]. But enough on these matters.

Meanwhile, a certain trace of this saying seems to shine for me in what the Lord foretold in the Apocalypse of John: “And I will give,” he says, “to my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth” (Rev. 11). For since martyrs and confessors are rightly understood in the two witnesses, these two orders too, of clerics and monks, may not inappropriately be understood through them. In our own time, through wisdom divinely given, their mouth has been opened for prophesying and preaching the mystery of God [Col. 1520A], and this for one thousand two hundred and sixty days—that is, in that tempest of Antichrist when iniquity abounds, since that superfluous number signifies the abundance of iniquity, which is not now to be discussed point by point.

They prophesy also clothed in sackcloth, that is, in every humiliation of penitence, which both clerics and monks exhibit outwardly in humble and lowly dress, clothed in grey and black, woollen and linen. In their clothing they seek not brilliance, price, or softness, but what may suffice necessity with propriety; taking common care, that “their attire may not be conspicuous.”

But perhaps someone may think that the canonical order, in its linen and white clothing, is somewhat inferior to the monastic order in the rank of propriety [Col. 1520B]. This is not surprising, for there is some difference between the two orders in profession and witness. The monastic order, mortifying itself to the world in mournful dress, declares to us the death of Christ and how we ought to die with him to vices and desires. The clerical order, in white dress, shines forth with the angel as witness to Christ’s resurrection, showing, of course, how we ought to rise with Christ and walk in newness of life.

Perhaps the ignorant also object to us, because of the softness of wool in sheepskins, as though we appeared conspicuous according to the Lord’s saying concerning John the Baptist’s dress: “What went you out into the wilderness to see? A man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” [Col. 1520C] (Matt. 11). But they do not properly observe that in this saying the Lord condemned not every softness of clothing, but especially that softness accompanied by costly material, such as garments made of the skins of foreign mice and woven of silk, and things of that kind, in which costliness joined with softness exceeds the simplicity and humility of Christian poverty. Luke the Evangelist makes this plainer, saying: “Behold, those who are in costly clothing and luxury are in kings’ houses” (Luke 7).

Therefore, while Matthew the Evangelist names soft garments, but Luke, as said, costly clothing, it is clear what softness in clothing the Lord condemns. Thus the innocence which they strive to attack through the Gospel may be defended through the Gospel both in us and in monks who use fur garments, but not costly ones [Col. 1520D]. In sacred vestments, however, we admit costliness without blame, and those themselves customarily admit it who think soundly concerning the monastic order: namely, so that by such ornaments, which have a mystical rationale, we may fittingly cover the nakedness of him who, in our name, was mocked on the cross. Moreover, by the splendour of such garments we prefigure the glory of the future resurrection that shall be revealed in us, proceeding on the highest solemnities clad in copes of rich cloth [Col. 1521A].

These two orders, then, ought to run together in the Church as twin witnesses of twin grace, so that neither exalts itself above the other, but each outdoes the other in honour, although one may run ahead of the other in certain respects. Their course is beautifully prefigured in the Gospel by the running of the two disciples, Peter and John (John 20). We know where it is read that two ran together, and that the other disciple ran faster than Peter and came first to the tomb; yet he did not enter, but, seeing the linen cloths, stood outside. Then Peter came following him, entered the tomb, and saw the linen cloths, and so on. Then that disciple also entered who had come first to the tomb [Col. 1521B].

Truly, an event worthy of wonder and reverence! Two disciples of Christ run together: one loving more than the rest, the other loved more; one called from a wedding, the other from working upon the sea; one sweetly reclining on Christ’s breast, the other walking with Christ upon the waves of the sea; one a beholder of heavenly marvels, the other made a spectacle to the world; one more accustomed to quiet and contemplation, the other readier for the ministry of the word. They ran together: one more lively in youthful body and mind, the other steadier through the gravity of age. They ran together, and because one outran the other, he did not therefore put himself before him; rather, he yielded to the elder the priority in recognizing the mysteries. For although he came first to the tomb, he did not enter, but, seeing the linen cloths, stood outside; whereas Peter, following him and coming to the tomb, entered first [Col. 1521C].

In every perfect person intention and action also run together: one more beautiful and lovable, the other more patient and fruitful; one free for seeing the Word, the other devoted to ministry. They run together; for because intention runs ahead of the ministry of the word, it should not therefore be judged more worthy. Often in the ministry of the word mysteries are revealed which, before that ministry, while contemplation alone existed, lay hidden in secret. This is Peter’s entering the tomb; hence the saying: “The unfolding of your words gives light and gives understanding to the little ones” (Ps. 118 [119]).

Nor should we judge concerning intention and the ministry of the word as we do concerning Mary’s part and Martha’s part, the former having been preferred by the Lord: as though intention devoted to mystery were the worthier. Otherwise Peter, theoretically recognizing in the linen-sheet vessel the ministry of saving the Gentiles, would be judged worthier than Peter himself preaching the word of life to Cornelius—which would be a great absurdity, especially because Peter did nothing in the ministry of action except what the preceding contemplative vision taught him. I do not know whether that vision was merely the sign of such action or also its efficient cause. Thus also the repose of Mary listening would seem worthier than Christ’s office of preaching [Col. 1521D].

But there is a very great difference between Martha’s ministry and Christ’s: Christ refreshes the soul, which shall live eternally, by the word of life; Martha sustains with earthly bread the flesh that will die. For Martha, ministering, is anxious and troubled about many things; Christ, ministering by the word, is occupied in one thing and about the one thing that alone is necessary. Of this ministry he himself says: “I am in the midst of you as one who ministers” (Luke 22). Of the dignity of this great ministry Peter says: “It is not fitting that we should leave the word of God and serve tables” (Acts 6). And Luke says of this in the Acts of the Apostles: “While the apostles were ministering and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas” (Acts 13).

Likewise, at the beginning of his Gospel Luke himself says: “As those who from the beginning themselves saw and were ministers of the word have handed it down to us” (Luke 1), joining vision to the ministry of the word as John to Peter [Col. 1522A]. Yet vision precedes ministry by the order of time, and John ran more swiftly than Peter. And, so that you may doubt less that intention and vision—which are prior in order—are signified in John, while the following ministry of the word is signified in Peter: after the Lord’s resurrection, when the seventy disciples were fishing together, Jesus appeared to them and stood on the shore. The disciple whom Jesus loved, recognizing the Lord first, said, “It is the Lord.” Therefore Simon Peter, when he heard that it was the Lord, girded himself with his tunic and cast himself into the sea; but the other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net of fish (John 21).

Behold, the disciple whom Jesus loved recognizes him first; yet he does not cast himself into the sea. Peter, who recognized later, more steadfast in mind, casts himself into the sea. Thus you may know that in John is signified the endeavour of recognition and the gift of contemplation, which is prior in order; while in Peter, as has already been said, is expressed the ministry of the word, in which the waves of the world must often be borne and trodden underfoot, and in which they often also undergo the bitterness of death, so that through martyrdom they may come to Jesus [Col. 1522B]. The other disciples come in the vessel of cloistered quiet, drawing the net of fish—through the endeavour of prayer and the intention of pious desire—as though by a certain rope.

Yet they run together; they strain and hasten to enter. Peter and John in the sea, intention and action, vision and the ministry of the word, run together—but differently around and toward the one thing, the one thing necessary, which shall not be taken from us. For as eternal vision shall be eternal, so too shall be the ministry of the word that enlightens us, the Lord promising us that, girding himself, he will make us recline and, passing by, will minister to us (Luke 12) [Col. 1522D].

Accordingly, let these two orders also run together in the Church—the monastic and the canonical—as John and Peter: both beloved by God and loving God; the one fleeing the world, the other overcoming it; the one, with John, keeping watch upon Jesus’ breast, the other, with Peter, walking upon the sea of the world; the one more accustomed to contemplation, the other more devoted to ministry; the one, with John, a beholder of wonders, the other, with Peter, made a spectacle to the world; the one more patient in bodily discipline, the other better suited to moral instruction. Let them run together, yet neither prefer himself to the other, even though in certain respects one seems to run ahead of the other.

For although the monastic order runs ahead of our order in the humility of endurance and in bodily discipline, it is not therefore first also in the dispensation of God’s mysteries, as John was before Peter in these matters; rather, it yields precedence to the clerical order, to which it was said in Peter: “Feed my sheep” (John 21). This order, too, first with Peter draws the Church’s dragnet; and it has authority to signal to and summon its companions from the other boat—that is, from the monastic order—whom it recognizes as fit for this work, that they may come and help him as fellow-workers in Christ’s Gospel.

Indeed, although these two orders differ somewhat from one another in the purpose of their profession and in the variety of their habit, they are not opposed to one another. Rather, like the two cherubim, they look upon each other in brotherly familiarity, with their faces turned toward the mercy-seat. Hence they often usefully converge in a single person: when clerics who possess property, leaving all things behind, turn toward monastic and cenobitic perfection; or when men of proven learning and manner of life within monasteries are admitted to ministry at the altar, or called to govern churches. Such were Gregory I and Gregory VII, Roman pontiffs, illustrious lights of the Church; and the Church now glories in the holiness of her Roman bishop Eugenius.

> [Note: Col. 1523. From this the author’s date is inferred. Eugenius III became pope in 1145 and remained so until 1153.]

And many other pontiffs and priests from the same order are found to have presided very profitably over the Church in diverse places and times. They shone both through the power of miracles and—what is no less than this—through the prerogative of learning. Thus in the Lord Jesus both were equally commended in the Gospel: the power of miracles and the grace of teaching. It is written that two men walking together on the road spoke “of Jesus of Nazareth, who was a prophet mighty in deed and word” (Luke 24). Likewise in the Acts of the Apostles: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1).

Luke himself makes this clearer in his Gospel, writing the words of the Lord Jesus to John’s two disciples: “Go, report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise” (Luke 7). Then, equating the grace of evangelizing with the power of miracles—and this is no less—he added: “the poor receive the Gospel.” Therefore let those who wish marvel at the power of miracles in Martin and Benedict; I shall no less marvel at and venerate, as the Lord testifies it is no less, the grace of doctrine and learning, joined to holiness of life, in Ambrose, Hilary, and Augustine. Through this grace many poor persons have received the Gospel; and many who were until now blind have been enlightened, lepers cleansed, and dead raised. These miracles, certainly, are the more spiritual and therefore are judged by right-thinking persons, without doubt, to be the greater.

God distributes his gifts: one shines through miracles; another excels through gifts of wisdom and knowledge, or through the cultivation of teaching. And in all these matters the two disciples, Peter and John, the canonical and monastic orders, run together when they laudably meet in one person: when clerics, for whom it is lawful, become monks, and proven monks become clerics; when the grace of evangelizing among clerics is no less lofty than miraculous power among monks; when Christ’s and the apostles’ ministry of the word is no less worthy than Mary’s silence as she heard and obeyed; when those who draw the fish-net over the sea’s waves with Peter walk over them with no less courage and hasten to Christ than those who recline sweetly upon Jesus’ breast with John, or come to Christ seated in the boat.

The victory over tyrants, and the contempt for tortures and deaths, displayed among clerical ministers of the word with Peter and Paul, are no less lofty than the monastic withdrawal into the wilderness with John exiled on the island of Patmos, and the frequent, manifold revelation of heavenly visions. In all these matters, I say, and in very many others which it would now take too long to enumerate, these two orders have thus far run together laudably in the Church, and will not cease to run together until the end of the age. Both are beloved by God, and both love God. Which ought to be preferred to the other is placed not in human judgment but in God’s alone—except that he is believed to be greater in the kingdom of heaven who is found to have lived more holily, humbly, and commendably, whether from their order or from ours. There many widows and married women will be placed above many bishops and monks who are now held great in human estimation, each receiving his own reward according to his labor.

Moreover, even in our own cenobitic houses these two orders—namely, canons and monks, John and Peter—run together. Among us men enlightened from a lay manner of life, leaving all things to take Christ’s yoke, are converted. They neither wish nor are able to be promoted to clerical rank, yet they live commendably in every monastic perfection: working with their own hands and crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires in penitential clothing. They are also accustomed, after the manner of monks, in certain cloisters to gird themselves for work with the garment called a scapular; so that, in the respect in which some appear to glory, they may be thought scarcely to lack, in this likeness, the flight of the six-winged cherubim.

In all these things these two of whom we speak run together, proceeding with united steps, as we likewise read of Peter and John. They went with joined steps, not with one running ahead of the other, but walking together. Hence it is written: “Peter and John went up to the temple at the ninth hour of prayer” (Acts 3). There, by their word, walking was restored to the lame man, who immediately, with his ankles and soles strengthened, leapt up and walked; and he entered with them “into the temple, walking and leaping and praising God.”

And indeed, wherever priestly authority, understood in Peter, and monastic holiness, signified through John, are joined either in one congregation or in one person, such joint walking will without doubt advance to the praise and glory of God and bring salvation to many imitators. For when, in a priest, the holiness of his own life and of the brethren dwelling with him adorns the word of teaching like a golden setting adorning a precious pearl, such men can surely say rightly and effectively to every lame person on the path of moral life: “Look at us,” being a pattern made for an enfeebled flock. Likewise: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4). And: “Raise the slack hands and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet” (Heb. 12), so that God may be praised for the correction of many and joy may come to the Church.

This is the fruit of John’s and Peter’s walking together, arising from holiness of life joined with priestly authority: when an ecclesiastical man, full of strength and grace, authority and holiness, on the one hand reproves offenders by the censure of his teaching, and on the other most gently intercedes for the sins of those who stray. He is plainly like Moses: on the one hand most powerfully brandishing the sword against sinners, on the other most gently interceding with the Lord for offenders.

And these were the two beaten trumpets: namely, the authority to rebuke and teach, joined with the strong and persistent fervor of prayer. Their use ought to belong to the jubilee, that is, this time of remission. If the priests of our time, lawfully circling the city of Jericho, sounded them in harmony, its walls could not stand long in defense of sin. But now, because in many cases Peter seems to go up to the temple without John, and John without Peter, and they do not look upon the lame man together or address him together—while one is gentle without zeal for justice and another stern without the affection of compassion and the intervention of prayers, their witness in word and intention discordant—neither will the fortifications of impiety fall nor will the lame man leap up. “One building and another destroying achieve nothing but toil” (Ecclus. 34).

Therefore in all these things the two beloved disciples, the two apostolic orders—both established according to the rules of the holy Fathers after the pattern of the primitive Church, of which it is written: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul in God,” etc.—both shoots chosen from the true vine, which is Christ, and two channels of saving waters from the one fountain of paradise, run together for God’s glory and the healing of the nations. They produce flowers and fruits; by teaching and acting they relieve the thirst and hunger of Christ and of the holy angels. While they bear witness in prayer and pray while bearing witness, after the likeness of Moses praying on the mountain and Joshua fighting, they will complete victory over Amalek, Christ helping and protecting them.

One glories in the Lord and says: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts” (Song 1). The other no less rejoices and glories in the Lord, saying: “My beloved is to me a cluster of henna in the vineyards of En-gedi.” They run together, walk in union and fellowship, and do not frivolously prefer themselves to one another with youthful levity.

There are also cases in which John laudably runs ahead of Peter by reason of order. For example, John the Baptist dwelt in the wilderness, until the time of his manifestation to the people, among wild beasts, angels ministering to him, eating nothing in those days. Before he came forth in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, he entered the synagogue according to custom on the Sabbaths; when the book of Isaiah the prophet was handed to him, he stood up to read. Thus in fitting order, after the silence of monastic quiet, he began clerical ministry by teaching in the synagogues and performing the reader’s office.

Likewise in Peter himself, when the Lord examines his love three times and then entrusts to him the feeding of his sheep and lambs; and when he says to the apostles, “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24), there is no doubt that in us he first requires the foundations of monastic humility and holiness of life with perseverance in love for him, and then grants ascent to ecclesiastical office. We endeavor to imitate this, as the Apostle commands: “Let them first be tested, and then let them minister” (1 Tim. 3), by inviting to ecclesiastical orders only those whom life and knowledge commend. In all these respects that other disciple is to be understood as running before Peter more swiftly, and the monastic order as taking precedence over the clerical order by reason of order, though not by privilege of dignity.

Yet there are again cases in which Peter goes before John with more confident constancy: when, speaking for the disciples, he confesses Jesus Christ to be the Son of God; when he brandishes the sword against the servant of the high priest; when he himself enters the tomb first; when, drawing the fish-net, he surpasses those sailing on the water. In all these instances the primacy of the apostle Peter and the dignity of the clerical order may fittingly be understood.

We willingly grant them, indeed, that in running to the tomb, in seeking the silence of quiet, and in the vow to mortify the flesh, they themselves are first. Yet let them not despise us or judge us to be of lesser account because of the labor of fishing and the activity of ecclesiastical ministry. For it is no less praiseworthy to live for Christ on behalf of brotherly love and salvation than for a man, through humility, to judge himself unworthy of so great a ministry—provided that for both alike the world is crucified, and they to the world.

Hence among two men equally perfect this difference may be found without fault: one, called to ecclesiastical office, more readily rests in the will of God with due modesty and fear; another, fearing for his own quiet, more persistently resists, without changing, lest the salvation of others be lost. Yet the latter must be free from the vice of lack of devotion and must not persist in resistance to the end; otherwise that will not be true humility which disobedience accompanies.

This can readily be seen in two outstanding prophets. One, namely Isaiah, after his lips had been cleansed by a coal taken from the altar, said more confidently to the Lord, who sought whom he should send: “Here am I; send me” (Isa. 6), freely exposing his soul to a most laborious obedience. But another, namely Moses, when the Lord sent him to Pharaoh, most humbly declined the office of the mission, saying: “Lord, send whom you will send” (Exod. 4). In these very words he was also calling for the Lord’s advent into this world through the incarnation: he who, as the Angel of Great Counsel, was to announce the fulfillment of perfect deliverance and accomplish it by his death, that is, by the immolation of the true Lamb. Moses desired, namely, that the shadow might be passed over and the truth revealed.

John the Baptist also, though himself most humble, declined the sublime office of baptizing Jesus, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” (Matt. 3). Likewise: “I am not worthy,” he says, “to loosen the strap of his sandal” (John 1). But the apostle Paul, more confident, as soon as he had been baptized, remained for several days with the disciples living at Damascus and immediately preached Jesus in the synagogues. He also rejoices in this ministry of his and says: “I give thanks to him because he considered me faithful, appointing me to ministry” (1 Tim. 1).

In these men, as was said, equally perfect, the humility of the one does not prejudice the confidence of the other, nor conversely. So too among the heavenly living creatures, it is evident that the face of the calf does not prejudice the face of the lion, nor the face of the man the face of the eagle, nor conversely; but in every face the one and same Lord Jesus is to be understood and venerated.

Likewise in ecclesiastical images, when the Lord Jesus is depicted now in the form of a lamb and now in the likeness of a right hand, there is indeed some outward difference in the depiction, but inwardly the one and same Lord is worshipped. Thus certainly in the woolen habit of our monastic brethren, and in their humble and laborious endurance, there is an outward likeness of the lamb; while in our ministry and operation of the heavenly sacraments there is the figure of the right hand. Yet in both places the one Lord Jesus is without doubt present, equally to be venerated in us and in them—provided only that the appearance of piety which we display outwardly is supported inwardly by virtue and truth, lest the image remain upon emptiness.

It is therefore utterly vain for anyone, however exceptionally he may seem to be a monk or a canon, to glory in the outward habit of his profession or in an appearance of piety, since all the glory of the king’s daughter is from within. Yet she is also clothed outwardly in this variety, in which both the adornment of the royal chamber and the distinction of diverse professions are maintained, not without spiritual significance.

Far therefore be from these two orders that foul dispute of the two harlots, one of whom said to the other before King Solomon: “Your son is dead, and my son lives, and your son is dead”; while the other said conversely: “It is not so; my son lives and your son is dead” (3 Kings 3). Such contention before the heavenly King does not become us. For one and the same Christ Jesus, our Lord, brother, and son, suffices for us all, as he himself deigned to confess: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that one is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12).

Let us possess him in common and not envy one another. He suffices for all. Although at some time he may have died either in us or in them, now, rising among both of us, as we hope, he dies no more and death has no further dominion over him. The Lord Jesus stands living not in a part or in a corner, but in the midst of his disciples, equally to be seen, touched, and possessed by all.

This, fathers and lords, I have sent from my humility to your holiness, both as a shield of defense against troublesome persons and as a reminder of caution: that, as you have begun to do, you may take care through annual assemblies for the reform of the common life among clergy. This is not so that new decrees may constantly be issued for sparing the body less, but so that those things in which religious vigor consists—silence, work, reading, obedience rendered to superiors, renunciation of possessions, diligence in prayers at their appointed time, and holiness of life—may not be dissolved by idleness, talkativeness, wandering, contempt, and other plagues of this kind, which enter through the bilge of negligence.

Unless careful diligence continually drains out these intrusions, the entire health of the common life will be endangered and will become liable to contempt not only from God and angels but also from men. As it is written: “He who despises small things shall fall little by little” (Ecclus. 19); and as the Lord said through the man of God to Eli: “Whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me shall be dishonored” (1 Sam. 2). But now, through the favor of divine mercy and your diligent efforts, the canonical order shall flourish like a palm tree and shall multiply like a cedar of Lebanon in the house of the Lord.

[Col. 1529]

## Fragment from the Book against Folmar, published by Peter Stewart of Liège

### Peter Stewart, etc., to the Reader

Around the time of Alexander III, supreme pontiff, there lived in Franconia a certain Folmar, provost of the Dripping Rock, or of Trieffenstein. Besides the other errors with which he was infected, he also fell into the error of Elipand or Nestorius concerning Christ’s person and adoption. When he attempted to disseminate it in Bavaria, two not unlearned Bavarian monks confronted him: one, Gerohus or Gerochus, provost of the monastery of Reichersberg; the other, the dean of the same monastery. The latter composed a substantial volume against Folmar; the former, in the work entitled *On the Investigation of Antichrist*, did not omit to refute Folmar as well.

Both works survive in Bavarian libraries, and both would deserve publication, were it not that these writers, seeking to withdraw as far as possible from one extreme—Elipandism or Nestorianism—came nearer to the other extreme, namely Eutychianism, or the modern Lutheran doctrine of ubiquity. For they teach that the divine perfections were really transferred into that which was assumed, that is, into the assumed human nature, so that the assumed thing, because of this communication of divine perfections, is truly and in every respect equal to God or to divinity. These are the native ravings of the Ubiquitarians.

But, dear reader, in order to give you some taste of the *Apologetic* which the dean of Reichersberg wrote against Folmar, here is the author’s preface and the beginning of the book.

## Jacob Basnage’s Observation on This Fragment and Its Author

*(Canisius, Lectures on Antiquity, III, II, 197.)*

The learned man erred in his literary history when he attributed this Fragment to Etherius and Beatus. “There is,” he says, “a Fragment of a certain book written by Etherius and Beatus against Folmar in Stewart’s Supplement, p. 243.” The cause of the error was that Stewart joined that Fragment to the books of Etherius. Yet the learned man should have observed that Folmar, though he shared some opinions with Elipand, lived only more than four hundred years later. Folmar flourished in the twelfth century under Pope Alexander III; therefore that book should not have been attributed to Etherius but to the dean of Reichersberg, as Steuart notes.

I am also surprised that the learned man doubts whether Folmar lived in the twelfth century under Alexander III. For he had disputes with two Eberhards, one bishop of Bamberg and the other bishop of Salzburg. The latter supported Alexander III, while the former supported Frederick Barbarossa against Alexander.

## Here Begins the Prologue of the Following Work

[Col. 1529A] Since different persons hold differing views concerning Christ’s birth according to the flesh and also concerning the glory in which he is now glorified with the Father; since some of them tear to pieces our sayings or opinions on these matters, and furthermore impute certain falsehoods to us—the necessity of the following work has been laid upon me. I had thought that it could for the moment be concluded in the brevity of a letter. But while I asserted our own position, countered the words and objections of hostile slanderers, and repelled the accusations falsely brought against us, the work grew lengthy. We wish it, with the letter set aside, to be called an *Apologetic*, because in it we show that what has truly been said by us is free from the blemish of perversity, and we also repel what has falsely been imputed to us.

[Col. 1529B] I received this assault by slanderers as though, through them and amid the diverse opinions of diverse persons concerning the Lord, I heard him himself say to us: “But who do you say that I am?” (Matt. 16:15). To his supremely divine generation according to the flesh, and likewise to the glory acquired through the merit of his passion for the man in the presence of paternal majesty, I have borne witness with such devotion and caution that I hope I have not departed from Peter’s testimony—“You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., 16)—nor from the other evangelical and apostolic testimonies borne to the divinity and glory of the assumed man.

Although the book itself is directed to one person living in a distant region, let all who take care to read our work not captiously but devoutly suppose it addressed to themselves. For their admonition I shall be ready to correct whatever they can show in our writings to be contrary to reason, discordant with Holy Scripture, or opposed to the assertions of the holy Fathers.

If they discover that one or two of the Fathers have remained short of saying what we say, I beg them not to be too hasty in judging us and our statements. For what one or two perhaps said less fully in one place, if they seek, they will find supplied by other men of no lesser authority, or by those same Fathers elsewhere. Accordingly, in this same work we have gathered, in suitable places, a heap of testimonies from the holy Fathers which support us, so that adversaries who pursue us as far as that may not presume to go further.

Nor have we omitted those passages which are thought contrary to us; by defining them, we have endeavored, so far as we could, to make them agree with the sense of Holy Canonical Scripture. For where the Fathers speak things agreeing with the very letters of Holy Canonical Scripture, what is needed is not interpretation but greater faith, even if what is said exceeds the capacity of human understanding. Nor should anyone, having read a single little page of this work, if he finds in it something contrary to what he has perhaps heard in the schools or what his own opinion dictates to him, rush into contradiction or abuse of us; nor should he detest the book like teeth made sore by unfamiliar food. Rather, let him compare what he has read with what precedes and follows, and, as I hope, all will be sound.

> [Note: Col. 1531D. This heading was added in the manuscript by a different and later hand.]

### The Opinion of Adam, Dean, concerning Heresies

To Master P\*., venerable dean of the Church of Würzburg, Brother A., likewise so called, by divine mercy dean of the monastery of Reichersberg: whatever a sinner’s prayer may avail.

Knowing that the person of your integrity is not unaware what great and grave injuries your neighbor Folmar, called of the Dripping Rock, inflicted upon our master, the provost of Reichersberg [Gerhoh], in the letter which he sent to our lord the archbishop of Tavaves [uncertain reading], I do not suppose I shall be judged rash by you if I attempt to set myself up as a shield for him whose brother I am according to the flesh and whose son I am in the Lord.

But, to confess the truth, that accursed and accursable letter—since it is full of curses, sprinkled with lies, and infused with the gall of bitterness—being, in accordance with its author’s name, sent from a bitter bellows and of bitterness, had not yet been seen by our master when I began to write this to you.

> [Note: Col. 1532D. This letter of Folmar is not extant.]

For among the other good results of this controversy, it is right that when the letter might reach the person against whom it was written, he should also receive at the same time what had been said against it by his own supporters; and that one whom perhaps the human bitterness of injuries had saddened might be consoled by the repelling of injuries and the exposure of lies.

Yet not even this ought to sadden us, as though something new had happened to us. For it is nothing new that wicked men envy the virtuous and seek for themselves, through detraction against notable men in the Church, a name, though they are of no name or merit. They consider themselves unfortunate and born without purpose unless, having found an occasion, they spread their own name among the people, so as to deceive men both living and dying—if they cannot leave behind among them a memory through an opinion of false virtue, then at least a memory for evil, when they cannot do so for good.

This purpose has made many persons assassins, robbers, pirates, and leaders and captains of other crimes: they sought rather to be celebrated among men through evil deeds, and even through lies, than to have lived a happy life in silence.

Hence our bitter bellows does not rest: he writes and rewrites, circulating letters to be read, full of unrestrained rebuke. He secretly defames princes in writings, though flattering them to their faces, and gladly accepts their small gifts in the manner of Gehazi. Moreover, he pollutes the very air by perversity of doctrine; he disparages the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, saying—as we have heard with our own ears—that in so far as he is man, he is no more the Son of God than one of us. He also denies that, glorified by the glory of resurrection and the honor of ascension, he entered, or could have entered, into the glory of equality with the Father.

But he besmirches us, who resist him in this pestilential doctrine, with lies. He endeavors by nocturnal fraud—yet with open boldness before princes and laymen—to foist upon us his own dead son, while claiming our living one for himself. But under the judgment of King Solomon he will not succeed. In his letters he accuses and convicts archbishops and bishops of ignorance or negligence, appointing himself a guide not only of the blind but also of those who see, as though he himself knew better from afar what should be done among them than they knew close at hand concerning their own affairs.

He strives at this vigorously and rashly, not in order to make them hostile to iniquity, but rather hostile to our innocence. Let them endure his folly as long as they wish, since they themselves are wise; but our [Gerhoh] surpasses sweet patience. Against him Folmar sharpens his serpentine tongue, vomits poison, opens his viperous mouth—not wishing to extinguish our temporal life, indeed, but that by which we live to God, by which we are true Christians, and which we desire both to be and to be called.

But let him act and strive as much as he wishes, and as much as, with God’s permission, he is stirred by his rider, the devil. For with God protecting us, while breath remains in us, we shall not fall into that abyss of denial against God into which he seeks to hurl us: so as to utter blasphemy against the Lord Jesus with him, and deny that the man assumed into God is God, is the proper Son of God the Father, and is that which he was assumed into, and that into which he was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

He compares our master [Gerhoh], who resists this perverse doctrine to its face, to a dragon hissing in secret, as though our master had until now spoken in secret rather than openly the things he says about the true divinity of the man assumed into God; as though, speaking and writing against the new Paulianists, Nestorians, and Photinians, he had not filled even the ears of the Roman Church with this teaching.

There is no shame in proclaiming the Gospel concerning the glory of Christ and of the man assumed into God, just as the apostle Paul was not ashamed of the Gospel of the blessed God—without doubt, of our Lord Jesus Christ—as he says: “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel of Christ” (Rom. 1:16). “His name is oil poured out” (Song 1:3); and long ago it was publicly preached, and openly great is that mystery of godliness: “which was manifested in flesh, justified in spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, believed in throughout the world, taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:16). Indeed, every tongue now confesses that the Lord Christ Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:11).

Therefore whoever deprives the man assumed by the Word of the confession that he is in the Father’s glory is altogether tongueless and utterly unfit to be heard in Christ’s Church. For he must be understood as numbered among all tongues which confess him now to be in the Father’s glory. He says that we hiss after the manner of dragons; but rather the hissing of the one eager to speak thus is that of the ancient serpent. When that serpent, desiring the place of the Son of God in heaven—that is, likeness to the Most High—and persuading man of the same, fell from the course of his purpose, he now proceeds by another path, twisting and slippery. Envying the Son his preeminence of glory, he strives to bring him down from the Father’s seat to the common level of men, so that in the faith of men the Son of God in human nature may be believed to be no more than one of the great angels or men, though possessing some small measure of glory greater than that of holy men and angels, but not attaining to the immeasurable glory of divinity.

## Here Begins the Book

[Col. 1533]

[Col. 1533B] The craftiness of this detestable ancient serpent is exceedingly astonishing: just as formerly he found an instrument suited to his wickedness, so now he has selected for himself Folmar, a bitter bellows, through whom he may persuade men that Christ Jesus ought not to be believed in as God; that that man assumed into God is not the natural and proper Son of God the Father; and that, having completed obedience unto death, he did not pass into the fullness of the Father’s glory. Consequently, not *latria*—the worship owed to God alone—but rather *dulia*, is to be rendered to him.

Behold, then: this man is worse even than Nestorius. For Nestorius taught that the man should be co-worshipped with the Word, as he says: “I distinguish the natures; I unite the worship.” Likewise: “Therefore we maintain the unconfused conjunction of the natures. We confess God in the man; we venerate the man, to be co-worshipped with almighty God because of the divine conjunction.” But this man judges that he is not even to be co-worshipped. Therefore he is more worthy of condemnation than Nestorius to the extent that he excludes the flesh of the Word farther from the worship of the Word.

Likewise, Nestorius forbade the Blessed Mary to be called Mother of God, teaching that she had borne not God but only a man joined to God. This man proceeds even further in his most evil error, since he also dares to deny that God the Father is the Father of the man assumed by the Word. He offers as argument the philosophical dictum that nothing capable of sensation is born from what is insensible.

For if this argument is admitted from natural philosophy into theology, the faith is emptied by which the Church has hitherto confessed without doubt that the Virgin’s son is also the Son of God. Since he is wholly God and wholly man, he must be confessed as wholly the son of each parent. Yet not even in natural matters does the argument that nothing sensible is born from the insensible seem wholly sound; conversely, we see that from the life of a grain, which is not perceived by the senses, arise plant and ear, and other grains within the ear.

Set some grains of wheat in the sun or dry them in an oven. Of these, some—namely those dried in the sun—will still be fit for seed, while others will not, because their living vigor has been extinguished. Yet the senses perceive in neither the one nor the other either that vigor or its extinction. But if “insensible” is said of that which does not perceive by sense, and if it is said that nothing sensing is born from it, the claim is proved false by very many arguments. For we see worms and very many living creatures born from the earth; just as a certain species of caterpillar is also produced from horse dung.

Yet, just as in the faith that we have in God we are not led by arguments drawn from nature, so, when those arguments fail, they cannot weaken faith. “Remove arguments,” says a certain wise man, “where faith is sought.” And the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, [Col. 1534C] the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1). And blessed Pope Gregory says: “Faith has no merit when human reason supplies proof for it.” Therefore, in matters to be believed concerning God, the more reason fails, the more we are taught that the merit of faith is perfected. Nor indeed was our father Abraham weakened in faith because he saw his own body as dead and Sarah’s womb as dead; if we are truly his children, we ought to imitate his examples.

We also see in nature certain adulterations of nature, concerning which there is also that commandment of the Law: that a Jew should not cause his beasts to mate with animals of another kind. From such mating, namely, the animals born do not fully retain the form of either parent, but are something two-formed, monstrous, and mixed in kind, as the poet says. A certain man has even dared rashly to accuse us on such grounds: because we wish to make Christ, born of God and the Virgin Mary, a two-formed kind. But far be it from us ever to conceive, either in speech or in thought, that horrible saying: that we should compare God’s supernatural works with nature’s adulterations, or suppose our Lord Jesus Christ to be something two-formed, [Col. 1535A] neither fully God nor fully man! For God’s supernatural works neither corrupt nor exclude the natural qualities of human nature, made in his image; rather, by their union they wonderfully raise those qualities above themselves into the divine, while they themselves remain in their own nature and retain human powers. For that which is supernatural has power in every way over all natural things, while preserving in all things the due right of its own sublimity and excellence, and never wholly lowering itself to what is unworthy. Thus God is said in Holy Scripture to see and hear after our manner, although after our manner he has neither ear nor eye.

Therefore David neither wished nor ought to have said, “He who planted the ear, does he not himself have an ear? And [Col. 1535B] he who formed the eye, does he not himself have an eye?” Rather: “He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not see?” (Ps. 93:9). Therefore, as he hears and sees, so too, in the manner of his divinity, he touches whatever he judges worthy of his touch. In the manner, I say, of his own sublimity, God sees, hears, touches, and acts, using and needing no bodily member or instrument. How could he need an ear, eye, or hand for hearing, seeing, touching, or acting, he who is wholly ear, eye, and hand to himself? God sees, hears, and touches not in the manner of our capacity for suffering, but by the power of his own impassibility and eternity.
