He sees and hears all things, not because his sight acts upon an object placed before it, or because his hearing receives sounds striking it and flying toward it, [Col. 1535C] but because none of our movements, thoughts, or—still less—words escapes him; nor can anything he has made or willed conceal from him his regard and knowledge. “For all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. 4:13). He sees all persons and all things done either in heaven or on earth, but with a different regard, as is apparent from their effects: some, namely, through grace; others through wrath. Hence it is written: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears toward their prayers. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. 33:16–17).

Likewise God acts without either using or needing his own hand to act; for to will is, for him, to have done. God also loves and is jealous, not passibly in the manner of our weakness, [Col. 1535D] but impassibly by the privilege of his own power. Just as he is wholly eye, so he is wholly love. He also touches souls worthy of his touch—those, that is, whom he himself has made worthy through his touch. For him to have touched them is to give a perceptible sign of his presence and entrance into holy souls; indeed, in a wondrous and ineffable way, whenever he wills, to affect them with a marvelous sweetness wholly unknown to this age—now in intellect, now in affection, and sometimes even in sensation. For he himself is wholly sweet, true, and supreme sweetness. He also rouses some souls to emulation and zeal against vices and the vicious by a certain fiery breath of his Spirit. He acts thus, so that [Col. 1536A] while awake or asleep they sometimes recognize within themselves certain signs of a divine visitation—experiences especially familiar and known only to the saints whom God knows—when he wishes to stir them to some spiritual work. Of such souls, loving God and beloved by God, this utterance in the Song of Love speaks of their experience of the divine touch: “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my inward parts trembled at his touch” (Song 5:4).

Concerning the fruit of spiritual activity that follows such a touch, she immediately adds: “I arose to open to my beloved.” For souls that have been roused and made fruitful cannot refuse their ministry to God; rather, they rise and, with the bolt of their mouth unfastened, by expounding the Word of God introduce him into the hearts of hearers or readers. Such fecundity of souls arises from love.

Others, however, conceive also through fear; their voice is: “Lord, from fear of you we conceived and gave birth; we brought forth the spirit of salvation upon the earth.” Yet in all things the Godhead does nothing unworthy of itself with human beings or angels when it dwells in them and acts in them and through them for their own salvation or that of others. Indeed, this condescension greatly becomes God: that he should be concerned for our salvation and for the enlargement of his praise through us. For we are that Zion of which it is written: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, and to you shall vows be rendered in Jerusalem” (Ps. 64:1). Nor is it unnatural for God to dwell [Col. 1536C] with human beings, whom he made to contemplate his image, just as our eye alone, before all the members of the body, was created for the light of the sun. Hence he has deigned to call the whole Church, and likewise every individual soul beloved by him and loving him, his bride; nor does he disdain to be called bridegroom by her. Indeed, between this bride and himself he has caused an epithalamium—that is, a wedding song—to be sung and written through his Spirit. Thus the whole of Solomon’s third book is composed. Concerning the experience of this love the Apostle Paul likewise did not hesitate to say: “The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4:7). Again: “Now I know in part; then I shall know as I also am known” (1 Cor. 13:12). [Col. 1536D] Again: “The body is not for fornication, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body” (1 Cor. 6:13). And: “He who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her; but he who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit” (ibid., 10:17).

We say this in order to show that love between God and a rational creature is neither unfamiliar nor unnatural. For scarcely anything is more natural to God, the maker of all things, than to love his creation—especially that creature which he made in his own image and likeness, and created to know and love him. Likewise it is very natural for a rational creature, in return, to love its maker. For if rational spirits do not see or love God their maker, this comes rather from a defect of their nature than from their nature itself. Therefore all angelic spirits and human beings who have come to years of discretion can, by the nature of their own condition, know and love God; yet they make no progress even in that for which they are naturally fitted unless aided by God. The fact that not all are aided does not arise from any defect of divine power or goodness, [Col. 1538A] but from their own fault, because they do not seek his help—although we cannot even seek him beneficially without him—so that all our good may be attributed rather to his grace than to our merits, and glory may belong to him alone, whose is also the grace, etc.

## In the Year of the Lord 1169: Rilindis, or Regilindis, and Herradis, Abbesses of Hohenburg

[Col. 1537]

## Notice and Fragments

P. Ziegelbauer, *Literary History of the Order of St. Benedict*, Augsburg and Würzburg, 1754, folio, 4 vols., vol. III, p. 508.

### [Notice I]

[Col. 1537B] The monastery of the Holy Cross at Pergenium or Bergen [Note: [Col. 1537] Brusch, *Monumenta Germaniae Chronologica*, pp. 97 and 154.]—a very extensive monastery of Benedictine nuns, situated in the diocese of Eichstätt and the prefecture of Hersbruck, half a mile from Neuburg on the Danube and two miles from Eichstätt—is recorded as having been founded in the year of the Lord 976, under the reign of Otto II and his consort Lady Theophanu, by the most illustrious princess and lady, Lady Willitrude, the most virtuous wife of Berthold, the last duke of the Bavarians. On account of her remarkable virtue and integrity of life, she deserved to bear the surname “the Pious.”

Lady Rilindis was elected abbess of this convent several five-year periods after 1095, the year in which the basilica of the Bergen monastery is recorded as having been reconsecrated. She is said to have ruled piously and holily, but the length of her rule has not been recorded in the annals. Rilindis was a heroine most richly endowed with virtues and learning, exceptionally learned in Latin, and so renowned for chastity and uprightness that Emperor Frederick Barbarossa sent her from this Bergen monastery to reform and restore to a better life the monastery of St. Odilia at Altitona, or Hohenburg, in Alsace, whose nuns were living wantonly amid luxury and wealth. There, after being appointed abbess and expelling the dissolute women, she gathered thirty-three veiled virgins within a few years, [Col. 1538B] and instructed them so well in Latin learning and Christian piety that they were an object of admiration throughout the surrounding region. Some poems by this Abbess Rilindis and reformer of Altitona survive; I judged that they should be inserted here from Caspar Brusch.

A most learned hexameter tetrastich by Lady Rilindis to the sisters of Hohenburg, in the person of Christ:

> You whom this mournful prison confines, breaks, burdens, draws, and burns—  
> This labor, exile, sorrow, heat—  
> Seek, hope for, know, hold fast, and call upon me:  
> Light, rest, homeland, healing, and shade.

A five-line poem by the same Rilindis, ingeniously playing on monosyllables, addressed to the community of sisters at Altitona:

> O pious flock, for whom the heavenly law is no dregs of deceit.  
> May he who is Mount Zion itself, the bridge to the homeland, and the fountain of good,  
> Who is the way and light, be your guide; may the gracious cross protect you.  
> May he who is gentle dew, steadfast gift, and virginal flower  
> Rule you, ever and everywhere, while having compassion on me.

### [Notice II]

“This distinguished and most learned abbess—how long she presided over the monastery of Hohenburg, when she departed human affairs, or from what family she was born—I do not discover,” says Brusch. “Certainly, she deserved to be called the second founder of this place.”

Brusch seems to have been ignorant not only of these facts, but of many others concerning this highly praised [Col. 1539A] abbess. The Rilindis whom he calls by that name is none other than Regilindis, or Regilla, of whom the Chronicle of Admont [Note: [Col. 1539D] It is extant in vol. II of *Writers of Austrian Matters*, p. 188.] records the following under the year 1156: “The monastery of Bargen, that is, Bergen near Neuburg on the Danube, is established by the Admonters under Lady Abbess Regilla.”

For a better understanding of this, it should be carefully known that Wolvold, the most devout abbot of Admont, around the year 1115 founded a convent of our order near his own monastery. In it, from its very beginnings, flourished studies not only of virtue but also of learning. From this convent, Abbot Godfrey of Admont, from 1138 until 1165, was accustomed to send forth most prudent teachers of religious life. Through their labor and study he strove to restore other holy convents—when he discovered that they had departed from the observance of the ancient discipline—to the right way. For this praiseworthy purpose he sent Rilindis, or Regilindis, or Regilla, to the monastery of Bergen. When she had restored there the ornaments of ancestral discipline and the safeguards of a holier life, Emperor Frederick I ordered her to go to the monastery of Hohenburg in Alsace, there with equal industry and prudence to tighten the rather slack string of regular discipline. This she accomplished nobly, and restored the convent to the standard of its former rigor. She passed to the Bridegroom on 4 April 1169, as the distinguished Johann Dietrich von Falckenstein attests in his *Nordgau Antiquities*, [Col. 1540A] part II, chapter 4, §2, p. 320, where he corrects Brusch’s chronological error.

This same Rilindis was excellently versed in both polite and sacred learning. [Note: [Col. 1540D] See Bernard Pez, *Introductory Dissertation* in vol. IV of *Anecdota*, p. 11, no. 2.] During the time she spent in the convent at Admont, she used to hang entirely upon the words of Irimbert, a most learned monk and later abbot of Admont, while he expounded the Holy Scriptures, and to commit his sayings to writing in Latin. An enduring memorial of this survives in Irimbert’s commentary on Judges, chapter 19. Nor should this notable passage of Irimbert be omitted, in which he speaks as follows of the sacred studies of the virgins of Admont:

> “A few years ago, because I had expounded to the sisters of Admont the story of the concubine who was cut into twelve parts, and also the history of Ruth, two of them devoted the diligence of their study to preserving the memory of my interpretation. Therefore I have judged it fitting to attach to this little work a brief explanation of those histories, as arranged by the sisters themselves.”

Now, the sisters or nuns whom Irimbert praises for their devotion to learning were Rilindis, or Regilindis, and Irmingardis. The former took down in writing from Irimbert’s lips the exposition of the history of the concubine in Judges, chapter 19; the latter, the explanation of the book of Ruth. This is shown by a parchment folio manuscript of Admont, elegantly written by those same virgins and surviving to the present day.

### [Notice III]

[Col. 1539C] When Rilindis was called from this mortal life, Lady Herradis, born of the noble family of Landsberg, a professed nun of the monastery of Altitona and inferior to Rilindis neither in virtue nor learning, was appointed and installed in her place by the same advocate of this monastery, Lord Frederick Barbarossa, then Roman emperor, with the unanimous consent of all the sisters and nuns. Desiring to enlarge divine worship, she founded in the year of the Lord 1181 the monastery of Truttenhausen, situated at the foot of the mountain, and endowed it most generously from her own property.

At Altitona there was still, a few years ago, a book of sacred sayings of moderate size, written in her own hand on very clean parchment and collected by her from various monuments of both the Bible and the ancient doctors. She dedicated it to the sisters with the following prefatory letter:

Herradis, by the grace of God abbess, though unworthy, of the Church of Hohenburg, to the virgins of sweetest Christ faithfully laboring in that same Church as in the vineyard of the Lord: grace and glory which the Lord will give.

I inform your holiness that, like a little bee, by God’s inspiration I have gathered together flowers from diverse writings of sacred philosophy. For the praise and honor of Christ and the Church, and because of my love for you, I have joined them together, as it were, into one honey-sweet comb. Therefore you ought diligently to seek food in this very book and refresh your weary soul with its honeyed drops, so that, always occupied with the bridegroom’s delights and filled with spiritual pleasures, you may pass securely through transitory things and possess eternal things in happy joy. And may you, by your fruitful prayers, draw me—walking perilously through the various paths amid the waves of the sea and withdrawn from earthly affections—upward with you into the love of your beloved. Amen.

The most learned woman poet of her age also added the following dithyrambs.

[Col. 1539]

> Of Hohenburg,  
> White as the lily,  
> Loving the Son of God.
>
> Herrad, most devoted,  
> Your most faithful  
> Mother and little servant,  
> Sings songs to you.

[Col. 1540]

> And daily desires  
> That in joyful victory  
> You may overcome transitory things.

[Col. 1541]

> I pray you, despise the world;  
> Heap up virtues,  
> Little troop of the true bridegroom.
>
> Persist in the struggle  
> To crush dreadful enemies;

>

>
> Delights befit you;  
> Riches are due to you;

>

>

> And beautify your face,

>
> Christ hates stains  
> And despises old wrinkles;  
> He desires beautiful young virgins  
> And drives away ugly women.
>
> With faith like that of the turtledove,  
> Love this bridegroom in return,  
> So that your beauty  
> May become enduring brightness.
>

>

> Amid the rivers of the world;

> After dangers.
>

> Despising the world’s prosperity;  
> Be now a companion of the cross,  
> Later a sharer in the kingdom.
>
> Sail across this sea,  
> Pregnant with holiness,

>

> Holding fierce wars,

[Col. 1542]

> Counting all the arrows  
> Of the tempter as little,

>
> The shining Star of the Sea,  
> The Virgin, the unique Mother,  
> Will join you to her Son  
> In an everlasting covenant.
>

> To draw me with you  
> To the sweetest bridegroom,  
> The virginal Son.
>
> That I may be found  
> A sharer in your victory,  
> In your great glory,

>
