> My joy;  
> Live without sin;  
> Always love Christ.
>
> If this book is useful  
> And pleasing to you,  
> Do not cease to turn it over  
> Within your heart.
>
> Lest, in ostrich-like fashion [perhaps *struthinio*],  
> Forgetfulness steal it away,  
> And lest you abandon the way  
> Before you arrive.

[Col. 1541A] A tetrastich by the same Herradis to the same sisters:

> O snowy flowers, giving forth the fragrances of virtue,  
> Ever resting in divine contemplation:  
> Despising earthly dust, run toward heaven,  
> That you may be able to behold the bridegroom now hidden.

A distich by the same to Christ:

> Be, O Christ, the gracious reward of our labors,  
> Numbering us among the lot of your chosen ones.

### [Notice IV]

[Col. 1542A] Mabillon mentions Herradis in his *Benedictine Annals* in these words: “Herradis, abbess of Mount St. Odilia, wrote in Latin the *Garden of Delights*—for this is the name they give her book—and dedicated it to the virgins of Mount St. Odilia.” See Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 58, etc.

## About the Year of the Lord 1169: John the Deacon

[Col. 1541]

## Notice

(Fabricius, *Library of Medieval and Later Latin*, vol. IV, p. 70.)

John the Deacon, a Roman and canon of the Basilica of the Savior in the Lateran patriarchate, wrote around 1169, for Pope Alexander III, a book *On the Roman Lateran Church*. He says that, at the command of Prior John and the brethren of that church, he renewed it from the archive, concerning the Holy of Holies. Mabillon published it in the appendix to the booklets on the Roman Order, vol. II of the *Italian Museum*, pp. 560–576. This John may be called “the Younger,” to distinguish him from another of the same name, a famous writer who flourished during the pontificate of John VIII. There was also another John the Deacon, but a Neapolitan, who wrote at the beginning of the ninth century a book *On the Deeds of the Bishops of His City*.

[Col. 1543]

## The Book of John the Deacon on the Lateran Church

(Mabillon, *Italian Museum*, vol. II, p. 560.)

### Here Begins the Prologue to the Book on the Holy of Holies

[Col. 1543A] To the most blessed lord and most reverend father Alexander, by divine grace supreme pontiff of the Catholic Church and apostolic see: John, an unworthy deacon and canon of the Basilica of the Savior in the Lateran patriarchate, presents the book *On the Holy of Holies*, renewed from the archive.

Since, according to the proclamation of the wise man, “the glory of kings is to conceal a matter, and the glory of God to search out a word” (Prov. 25), it is so much the more commendable for those who profess each estate to render careful and devoted service for the pleasure and honor of both, as a reward worthy of their service is hoped for from the fullness of the grace of both and is undoubtedly believed to be at hand, etc. Therefore, considering this point, I have taken care, by the authority and command of Your Holiness and also at the command and wish of the venerable Prior John and the brethren of the same Church, to renew for preservation by posterity and benefit to their devotion the little book *On the Holy of Holies*, containing an account [Col. 1543B] and kept in the archive of this most sacred basilica from our predecessors’ time down to our own. It had been almost effaced by the age of its antiquity; yet, since this was pleasing and welcome to Your Blessedness, it was most necessary that so celebrated an account of sacred things—carefully preserved and handed down to us by our predecessors—not fail among our descendants through oblivion caused by our negligence, to the honor of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

Certainly, because we shall without doubt render an account before the tribunal of the living God—into whose hands it is dreadful to fall—not only for falsehoods but even for idle words, I desire Your Paternity, reverenced by God and human beings for the fullness and sincerity of its merits, and all who enjoy the record of this little book, to know that I have by no means inserted any novel inventions presumptuously or from superstition. Rather, while simply preserving the ancient sequence in writing, if I add anything else, it is without doubt what I myself have seen with my own eyes during the space of five decades while living in canonical profession in this most sacred basilica, or what I have learned by truthful report from our predecessors: namely, matters concerning the translation of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria; the discovery of Saints Rufina and Secunda and of Saints Cyprian and Justina; and also those matters drawn from the histories and authorities of the saints to repel the doubtful opinion held by some concerning the concealment of the tabernacle and the ark and the things contained in it, or of the altar of incense. So that these matters may become plainly clear, I have taken care to state more explicitly in what follows the names of the historians and books, their times, and the names and volumes of the doctors, etc.

## Book on the Lateran Church

[Col. 1543]

[Col. 1543C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity begins the writing concerning the supreme sanctuary of the holy Roman Church of God, that is, the Lateran Church, compiled from archives and ancient acts of the Roman pontiffs. This church, namely, by the privilege and prerogative of the patriarchal and imperial apostolic see, through the gift of the grace of God the Savior Jesus Christ, holds dominion and primacy over all churches throughout the whole world; by divine ordinance it also possesses the glorious name of the apostolic eminence and the Roman Empire.

[Col. 1544C] Since the whole world ought to render the service of due submission to this mother Church, many petitioners from diverse regions gather here. Because they do not know how great and how precious a sanctuary of God is hidden in this aforesaid church, we wish this to be made known through these written notices, at least when they gather here to pray to God’s Son, Jesus Christ, our Lord, Savior of the saints, for the peace of the holy Church, for the forgiveness of all sins, for the gaining of the glory of the eternal vision of God, and for fellowship with [Col. 1545A] the eternal citizens and holy souls.

Therefore, after the blessed and saving Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, his glorious resurrection from the dead, and his wonderful ascension into heaven, and after they had received the consolation of the most glorious coming of the Holy Spirit, the apostles directed their way toward the portion assigned to their preaching. By the disposition of the ineffable mercy of God, the outstanding senators of the heavenly kingdom, Peter and Paul—that is, the head of the whole world—entered this city of Rome. There, in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, they faithfully placed the foundation of the Catholic faith upon the Rock, that is, Christ. For the growth of this building they fought until death; for its love they poured out their glorious blood; and finally, undergoing the temporal death of cross and sword, they came as crowned victors to the court of the heavenly King. These are the holy men by whose teaching the Church shines. The ancient enemy assaulted and shook it first through Nero, then through successive rulers, for three hundred years and more, but was altogether unable to overthrow it.

For when it pleased him who permitted his faithful ones to be tested by the fire of suffering, Constantine Augustus, son of Constantius and Helena, assumed imperial authority and for a time practiced the tyranny of earlier princes against the servants of Jesus Christ. But the boundless mercy of God, compassionate toward the sorrow and anguish of his chosen people crying to him, did not delay to impose an end upon the calamity and misery of so great a persecution. Why say more? As is read in the *Life of St. Sylvester*, the aforesaid Emperor Constantine was struck by God with elephantine leprosy. The pontiffs of the Capitol gave him this counsel: that he should descend naked into a pool full of the blood of slaughtered infants, and thus, cleansed from leprosy, recover his former health, etc.

He then granted a privilege to the pontiff of the Roman Church: that throughout the whole Roman world priests should have him as head and prince, just as all judges had customarily had the king. In that privilege, among other things, the following is read:

> “Together with all our satraps, our entire senate, the nobles also, and all the people subject to the glory of Rome, we have judged it expedient that, just as blessed Peter appears to be established on earth as vicar of the Son of God, so the pontiffs of that prince of the apostles may obtain, by virtue of their primacy, a power greater than the clemency of our earthly imperial serenity appears to possess, etc.”

As is read in the *Acts of Blessed Sylvester*, which blessed Pope Gelasius recalls as being read by Catholics in a council of seventy bishops, the aforesaid Emperor Constantine on the second day of his procession promulgated a law concluding in these words:

> “Let it be known to all that we have become worshippers of Christ, so that within our palace we may construct a temple for this name, etc.”

Afterward, when that church had been built and completed, blessed Sylvester solemnly consecrated it publicly—something not done previously—[Col. 1546A] on the fifth Ides of November, that is, 9 November. It remains to this day a most celebrated feast in the City, on which the first church was publicly consecrated and the image of the Savior set in the walls first appeared visible to all the Roman people. It is entitled the Dedication of the Basilica of the Savior. Hence every church in the City and throughout the world specially named after the Savior observes and venerates the memorial of its celebration on the aforesaid day. Apostolic authority decreed that the solemnity of this dedication should be celebrated for eight days, because on the tenth day after the feast of this dedication the basilicas of Saints Peter and Paul were afterward dedicated.

Hence the Roman pontiff of this Savior Jesus Christ, who is gracious and abundant in mercy to all who return to him, relying soundly upon the certain mercy of almighty God, ordained at the dedication of this most sacred basilica—called by the name of Mercy—that a great remission of sins should be granted to all who came to the joy of this festival, provided that they were known to have confessed worthily to God and the Church through penance, or confessed with true and God-pleasing contrition of heart up to the eighth day. This remission, established by apostolic providence, is distinguished in three parts: remission of sins for one thousand years remains for Romans and those living nearby; for Tuscans and Lombards, two thousand years; and for those known to cross the seas, three thousand years. The same institution of remission is shown to have been made in this first and most sacred basilica on Maundy Thursday, when sacred chrism is consecrated by the apostolic lord, and when obstinate heretics who exalt themselves against this holy Catholic and apostolic Church are, by the apostolic sentence, handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh under the curse of public excommunication, so that, when at last they repent through God’s mercy and escape the devil’s snares, their spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### I. On the Mystical Names of This Most Sacred Basilica

This Church, I say, is distinguished by the holy Fathers, as is found in their writings, by many mystical names. It is principally called a basilica because, since it is dedicated to the Savior Jesus Christ, King of kings, it is shown to be entrusted to him who on earth is supreme king and priest. It is also called the Golden Basilica, or the Constantinian Basilica, because, it is said, Constantine had it entirely adorned with golden mosaic. It is also called the Temple of Mercy because, as may still be seen today, although it had many entrances, it was closed neither by day nor by night except with hangings, so that, as though another asylum, it might always stand open to all offenders, so that they might no longer be punished by secular laws. It is also called the Apostolic Church, instructed solely in the teachings of the Apostles; the Apostolic See, because no one except the pope presumes to sit there; the First See, because Antioch is second and Alexandria third; and the See of Peter, because Peter himself sits there through his vicar. It is called the Roman Church from the city of Rome; and from its place, the Lateran Church, Lateran Basilica, Lateran episcopal residence, and Lateran patriarchate. This is called the universal Church because its bishop possesses authority to judge all others, while no one has authority to judge him. For this reason it is called the head of the Churches, mother of the Churches, and teacher of the Churches, because all receive nourishment and instruction from it. It provides for all and watches over all; and for its faith, that it may never fail but may confirm its brethren, the Savior himself prays. By these and other names this hall of God is nobly adorned and honored in the sacred writings.

### II. That Helena the Mother Carried to Her Son Everything Found in the Temple after Its Destruction

[Col. 1547B]

The most blessed Helena, mother of Constantine, after receiving the sacrament of holy baptism, enriched this most sacred basilica, revered by the whole world, with the incomparable treasure of a sanctuary. At the request of her son Augustus, she brought it from the regions of Jerusalem: things which had been stored away by the ancients before the Lord’s incarnation, and which remained there after the destruction carried out by the Roman rulers Titus and Vespasian. Thus almighty God deigned to open the bowels of his mercy to this Roman Church when the aforesaid queen transferred into the dwelling-place of this most sacred basilica—priestly and royal—the sanctuary which, by God’s will, she had brought with her from the holy city of Jerusalem to her son. Since this sanctuary is not yet designated by its own name, although I am unworthy to pronounce its name, I will nevertheless not delay reverently to name it in honor of its praise.

Likewise, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1260, Pope Alexander IV, on the feast of the Dedication of this most sacred Church, ratified and confirmed every indulgence granted at any time by any supreme pontiffs; and especially those which blessed Sylvester abundantly established and bestowed at the just entreaties of humble and most Christian Constantine. Out of special mercy and grace he extended them until the feast-day of the dedication of the Apostles Peter and Paul.

### III. On the Ark and the Holy of Holies Which Are in the Basilica of the Savior

In this most sacred Lateran Basilica dedicated to Jesus Christ, God the Savior—which is the head of the world, patriarchal and imperial, and the seat of the apostolic pontifical chair—there is, at the principal altar of the same church, the ark of the Lord’s covenant. Or, as they say, the ark is below, and above it an altar has been constructed to the measure of the ark’s length, breadth, and height, beneath a beautiful ciborium supported by four columns of red porphyry. In it, they assert, there is much sanctuary treasure, [Col. 1548A] but they do not know what it is; for they do not know its name.

In the upper altar, which is wooden and covered with silver, and beneath it below, there is the following sanctuary: the seven lampstands which were in the first tabernacle. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “The first tabernacle was made, in which were the lampstands, and the table, and the setting forth of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place; and the golden censer, and the golden urn containing manna, which belonged to the second tabernacle, which is called the Holy of Holies. And there the rod of Aaron, which had put forth leaves, and the tablets of the covenant” (Heb. 9); and the rod of Moses, with which he struck the rock twice and waters flowed forth. There are also relics there from the Lord’s swaddling-clothes; from the five barley loaves and the two fishes. [Col. 1548B] Also, the Lord’s table; the linen cloth with which he wiped the feet of his disciples; the seamless tunic which the Virgin Mary made for her son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and which, at his death, was allotted by lot among the soldiers and not divided. So long as the Saviour preserves it there, no heresy or division of faith will long endure in it. The purple garment of the same Saviour and Redeemer; two vials of blood and water from the Lord’s side; the Circumcision of the Lord; the cloth which was upon his head, one of the five linen cloths in which the most holy body of our same Lord was wrapped.

There is there material from the place of Christ’s Ascension into heaven; from the blood of Saint John the Baptist; from the dust and ashes of the burned body of that same Forerunner of Christ; his hair-shirt [Col. 1548C] of camel hair; a full vial of manna from the burial-place of Saint John the Evangelist; and the tunic of that same apostle and evangelist, upon which, when it was laid beneath the bodies of three young men, they arose. For they had died from poison which they had drunk.

### IV. The explanation concerning those who object regarding the concealment of the tabernacle, ark, or altar of incense

But very many people, investigating the profound mysteries of sacred books and histories with too little judgment, and understanding neither what they say nor whereof they affirm (1 Tim. 1), because the second book of Maccabees records the concealment of the tabernacle and ark, and also of the altar of incense, suppose, in a superfluous opinion, that the tabernacle itself, [Col. 1548D] and the ark or altar, have remained concealed until now and lie hidden until the time of the future judgment, and so forth.

### V. That, in the time of Titus and Vespasian, the things which had been in the Temple were brought to Rome

At what time, by whom, and where the vessels and furnishings of the Temple, or all its gifts, were brought to Rome and deposited, the aforesaid teacher Jerome—whose special quality it was always to seek out new matters and elucidate hidden ones—attests in his exposition of the prophet Joel. He says that Titus and Vespasian, Roman rulers, after the Lord’s Ascension, when Jerusalem and the Temple had been destroyed, carried away with them, as a victory-monument for the Roman people, all those chief and beautiful things which the Jews had possessed in the Temple—or rather, commanded that they [Col. 1549A] be carried away by the Jews themselves. Having built at Rome the Temple of Peace, they wondrously placed them there in its shrine, as Greek and Roman history relates. Nor should there be any doubt about that which so great a man taught, since he wished it to be confirmed by Greek and Roman history.

The same thing is still plainly perceived today in the triumphal arch called that of the Seven Lamps, which is shown to have been constructed in memory of the aforesaid rulers and of the entire Roman people, beside the church of Saint Mary the New. On it are visibly and marvelously sculpted the lampstands which were in the first tabernacle, and the ark with its garments, which was within the veil in the second.

Pope Leo, that most eloquent teacher, likewise seems to establish this by still clearer proofs in his sermons on the Lord’s Passion. When, speaking against the unbelief of the Jews, he protested concerning the veil torn in the Temple at the very time of Christ’s Passion, he declared that all the elements of the world had more clearly convicted the blindness of the Jews. In the sermon beginning, “Although Jewish impiety laboured in many ways,” he wrote: “But if neither the things of heaven nor those beneath can suffice to convict you, and if rocks and tombs were more able to perceive the cross of Christ than your hearts, then at least heed knowingly what was done in the Temple. The veil, by whose interposition the Holy of Holies was shut off, was torn from top to bottom; and that sacred and mystical secret place, into which the high priest alone had been commanded [Col. 1549C] to enter, was laid open,” and so forth.

Beneath this most sacred altar, of which we are presently speaking, is an image wholly of gold, dedicated to the Lord Jesus Christ; and images of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Saint John the Baptist, the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, and Saint John the Evangelist, made in electrum, gold, and silver; likewise images of the other apostles wholly in silver. Constantine the emperor, servant of God, who took care to have these images made in honour of Jesus Christ the Saviour and his disciples, devised their concealment in a certain women’s apartment in such a manner that no craftsman may gain access by any device whatsoever.

### VI. That it is festively rung every day at Matins, Mass, and Vespers

[Col. 1549D] In this church, because it bears the figure of the heavenly Church, the bells are rung festively day and night at Matins, Mass, and Vespers. This is why at Masses there is not sung in it, “Lamb of God, who takest away the sins of the world, grant us peace,” because there Christ himself will be the supreme peace of the just, where that peace is perfect and complete in the elect and needs neither petition nor increase.

### VII. On the Lord’s Prayer, which is repeatedly used in every office

Preserving the apostolic institution, this church uses no prayer in the offices except the Lord’s Prayer, since the other prayers were added later. It is fitting and proper that the first and highest of all other churches should frequently use the first and highest [Col. 1550A] of all other prayers; and that the church consecrated in the Saviour’s name should always hold preeminent, above all others, the Saviour’s prayer which he taught his disciples to pray. There are, moreover, certain other collects appointed for Matins or Vespers, which may be said in this church only by the Apostolic Lord or by his seven suffragan bishops, and by no others whatsoever.

### VIII. On the seven weekly bishops and the other officials of the same church

Thus, at this so solemn and most holy altar, where, as we have said, the garment allotted by lot, but not divided, is kept, together with much other incomparable sanctuary which we forgo naming here in full, no one dares approach to offer sacrifice except [Col. 1550B] the Apostolic Lord and the seven cardinal bishops of that church who serve in weekly rotation. They celebrate Mass in this most holy basilica in their respective weeks, and divide equally with the canons of the same church, who assist them in the ministry of the altar and in the offices, every offering received in that Mass from the beginning to the end of the office, whether it be in gold, silver, or any other offerings, including those at ordinations and consecrations—except the offering of bread and wine, which belongs only to the canons.

The seven names which ought to be set down here are these: the Bishop of Ostia, who above all others must consecrate and bless the Apostolic Lord; secondly, the Bishop of Saint Rufina; [Col. 1550C] thirdly, the Bishop of Porto; fourthly, the Bishop of Albano; fifthly, the Bishop of Tusculum; sixthly, the Bishop of Sabina; seventhly, the Bishop of Palestrina.

On certain Sundays and feast days, and on the chief solemnities of the saints, the celebrant is sometimes a royal and imperial bishop, indeed a patriarch; and the Apostolic Lord himself must celebrate Mass at the aforesaid most sacred altar of the Saviour in this Lateran basilica. When the lord pope, vicar of Saint Peter, celebrates, his aforesaid vicars and suffragans must also assist him: namely, the seven bishops together with twenty-eight cardinals, presiding in an equal number of churches within the walls of the city of Rome. They possess authority to render judgment [Col. 1550D] over all bishops throughout the Roman Empire in all councils or synods at which they have been present as legates or in person.

The archdeacon must also be present there with the six palatine deacons, who must read the Gospel in the palace and in the Lateran basilica; and the other twelve regional deacons, who are accustomed to read the Gospel at the appointed station churches of Rome. These eighteen deacons have an equal number of churches within the city walls. Yet all are canons of the patriarchal Lateran basilica. There must also be present seven palatine subdeacons and the school of singers, namely seven other subdeacons called regional subdeacons. These must read the lessons and epistles at the appointed Roman stations. The other seven, namely [Col. 1551A] the school of singers, must sing the office when the lord pope celebrates Mass in the Lateran basilica and elsewhere. The other seven palatine subdeacons must read the epistle in the palace at the Apostolic Lord’s Mass and in the same patriarchal Lateran basilica, and likewise at the Masses of the Apostolic Lord. Acolytes, chaplains, readers, exorcists, and doorkeepers are also present there, each striving to fulfil his own office as established there by the holy Fathers.

In this aforesaid Lateran basilica there are altars of certain saints, whose names are as follows. In the choir of the canons is the altar of Saint Mary Magdalene, in which her body without its head was deposited by the hands of Pope Honorius III, who consecrated that altar.

Behind, beneath the apse, is the altar of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria, in which their precious bodies had formerly been deposited. But when it had been desecrated by schismatics, they were taken up again from there and transferred to the church of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, and Saint Pancras Martyr, which lies on the right-hand side of the basilica. They were deposited in that church’s altar, consecrated by the hands of Pope Innocent II, who placed in it precious relics of the saints: namely, Saints Pancras, James the Apostle, Matthew the Apostle, Thaddaeus the Apostle, Timothy the disciple of Paul, Stephen the first martyr, the Holy Innocents; relics of the Lord’s linen cloth and of his tomb; of the unburned bush; and of Blasius, Nicomedes, Vitalis, Gervasius and Protasius, Nazarius and Celsus, Saint Felix, and the Forty Martyrs.

On the same side are the tombs of the Apostolic Lords, among them Pope Lucius II, of holy memory. He lived for a long time in the canonical life in this church, and from here was raised to become a cardinal priest in the church of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. That church he restored from its foundations out of ruins, with splendid and admirable workmanship, and, before becoming pope, enriched with many processions after reforming it according to the pattern of religious life under the Rule of Blessed Augustine. He also loved this church in every way, mindful of his elevation and of his former way of life, and honoured it with great benefactions. For on the eighth [Col. 1551D] day after his consecration he offered upon the altar a Gospel-book covered in gold plates and most beautifully adorned with enamel and many precious stones. Not long afterward he gave a most excellent *sarantasmum* for ornamenting the altar.

> [Note: [Col. 1551] Below, *tarantasmum*, as a covering for the altar. A little farther down, *sarantasmum*. This seems to be the authentic reading.]

He also gave two large silver-gilt vials, splendidly sculpted, for use in the sacrifice, weighing four pounds. He also drew up a privilege in which he gave this basilica the church of Saint John before the Latin Gate, with all that belonged to it, and likewise the hospice beside the gate.

Nearby lie Pope Leo V and, beside his tomb, Pope Agapetus II. Straight ahead, on the right, [Col. 1552A] lies Pope Paschal II, who with salutary forethought and diligence renewed the canonical order in this church. Beside him lies Pope Callixtus II, who restored peace with Emperor Henry. Next to him rests Pope Honorius II, and then, beside the latter, Pope Celestine II. In the portico are many tombs of bishops of this church. In the same portico lies Gerbert, Archbishop of Rheims, who, having become pope, was called Sylvester. His tomb often visibly gives forth drops of water, even in the clearest weather and although it is not in a damp place—a matter quite astonishing to men.

There is also an altar of the Forty Martyrs near this altar. In the nave of the church Pope Innocent II lies in [Col. 1552B] a porphyry sarcophagus which had been Emperor Hadrian’s tomb. He renewed the roof of this basilica at his own expense with new beams, which the glorious and powerful King Roger of Sicily had sent to that church at his request. That roof had fallen in his time and was restored in his time. He also ordered the tower before the church, which seemed close to collapse, to be renewed. During his lifetime he offered very many gifts to the church for the ornament of the altar: namely, an excellent gold-woven *cyclas*, from which were afterwards made a cloth for adorning the altar and a chasuble for celebrating Mass; a *tarantasmum* to cover the altar; a silver censer weighing two pounds; and one hundred pounds of Luccan coinage for purchasing [Col. 1552C] properties to support the canons. With these funds Lord Bernard, prior of this basilica, who afterwards became cardinal of Saint Clement and then Bishop of Porto, prudently and beneficially bought estates not far from the city, near the aqueducts beside the church of Saint Helena.

Likewise, on the same side near the doors of the church rests a pope named Sergius, formerly called Peter. Beside him lies Pope Alexander II, who had been Bishop of Lucca. He drew up an excellent privilege for the aforesaid basilica and renewed in it the common life of the regular canons. In that privilege he gave the canons half of all offerings made at the principal altar, the houses around the basilica, and many [Col. 1552D] other landed estates situated in various cities and places, as the testimonies of that privilege, worthy of remembrance, relate to us. Between the two doors lies another pope who has no epitaph. And again, on this side near the church doors:

> There rest the limbs of John, supreme pontiff.

He renewed the same basilica. And again, between the two church doors on this side:

> Here is seen the tomb said to be  
> Of John, the supreme prelate, so called.

This was Pope John XVII. Before the doors of the church rests a certain prelate named Peter. Above the church doors, on the inside, was written:

> [Col. 1553A] This devout Pope Sergius the Third, that devout pope,  
> Began it from its lowest foundations, fashioning the hall which you behold.

In the courtyard of the same basilica there is a beautiful oratory, with an altar of Saint Thomas the Apostle. In this oratory, made by the Pope John who renewed the church, the pontiff puts on his priestly and pontifical vestments when he is to celebrate Mass at the stations of this basilica. Emerging from this oratory in procession, he enters the basilica and proceeds to the most holy altar of the Lord, which alone possesses primacy over all altars. Pope Celestine III lies near Saint Mary of Repose. Pope Alexander III lies before the church pulpit, or beside the way by which one goes to the curia. Pope Clement III lies before the choir of canons.

[Col. 1553B] On the left side of the basilica is the altar of Blessed Mary of Repose. Nearby lies Pope Anastasius IV, who was Bishop of Sabina, in a porphyry mausoleum splendidly carved, in which Helena, mother of Emperor Constantine, had formerly lain. This mausoleum the pope had caused to be brought from the church which that emperor had built outside the City in honour of his mother. While still bishop, he loved this church above all others, uniquely and devoutly; and, after being raised to the apostolic office, he honoured it with many benefactions. He formally made two privileges for the canons of the aforesaid basilica, in which he confirmed what they then possessed and added very much from his own generosity and favour: the church of Saint Gregory in Marcio with the palace in which it is situated and all its appurtenances; and land with a mill outside the gate at the head, where there had once been a place, which he gave to this church.

He also offered very many gifts for the adornment of the most holy altar of the Lord, while still bishop and subsequently when raised to the most holy Apostolic See. On the eighth day after his consecration he offered one *cyclas* to the altar of the Lord; on the fifteenth day thereafter, one excellent white chasuble, bordered with precious gold embroidery, for celebrating Mass. After an interval of some time, he offered for the altar’s ornament two excellent cast-metal lampstands and one splendid and excellent *sarantasmum*, [Col. 1553D] and three pounds of silver to support the brethren. On the anniversary of the dedication of this most holy basilica, he also gave a rather large and remarkable chalice, admirable both for the greatness of its weight and for the variety of its marvellous workmanship. It is wonderfully wrought all over by carving, adorned with various histories and verses, and weighs twenty-eight pounds.

> “In the name of the Lord, amen. In the year of the Incarnation 1297, on the . . . day of February, the altar of the chapter was consecrated in honour of God and Blessed Mary Magdalene, by command of Lord Pope Boniface VIII, through Lord Gerard of Parma, Bishop of Sabina. In this altar he deposited the body of Blessed Mary [Col. 1554A] Magdalene herself, without the head, the arm of Blessed Zachariah, and relics of many other saints.

“Some judges are palatine, whom we call *ordinarii*; others are consular, distributed among the judicial districts; others are petty judges appointed by the consuls. In the Roman Empire, and in the Roman Church even to this day, there are seven palatine judges, called *ordinarii*, who arrange the emperor’s accession and elect the pope with the Roman clergy. Their names are these: first, the *primicerius*; second, he who is called the *secundicerius*, both taking their names from those offices. Standing at the emperor’s right and left, they seem in some sense to reign with him, and without them the emperor cannot establish anything great. But in the Roman Church, in all processions, they lead [Col. 1554B] the pope by the hand, precedence being yielded by bishops and all other magnates; and on greater feast days they read the eighth lesson above all bishops.

“The third is the *arcarius*, who presides over the revenues. The fourth is the *sacellarius*, who distributes pay to soldiers; at Rome, on the Saturday of the scrutinies, gives alms; and grants benefices to Roman bishops, clergy, and *ordinarii*. The fifth is the *protoscrinarius*, who presides over the *scrinarii*, whom we call notaries. The sixth is the chief defender, who presides over the defenders, whom we call advocates. The seventh is the *adminiculator*, who intercedes for orphans and widows, the afflicted and captives. They do not judge criminal cases or pronounce a deadly sentence against anyone; and at Rome they are clerics, never to be promoted to any other orders. But the others, called consuls, govern judicial districts, punish accused persons under the laws, and pronounce sentence upon offenders according to the nature of the crime.”

### IX. On the oratories by the fonts, and their sanctuaries and gifts

Behind the basilica of the Saviour are four oratories. One has two apses. Beneath one is the altar of the holy virgins Rufina and Secunda, under which their precious bodies are deposited. They were discovered by Pope Anastasius IV, of happy memory, before he was raised to apostolic dignity. After their discovery, he had an altar built in their honour and consecrated it with his own hands, all of us standing by, and with the canons of the basilica of the Saviour and very many others present, [Col. 1554D] both from the City and from outside it.

Under the other apse is the altar of Saint Andrew the Apostle and Saint Lucy the Virgin. Pope Anastasius aforesaid also consecrated this and placed in it relics of both—namely Andrew the Apostle and Lucy the Virgin. On the feast of Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr, and Saint Justina the Virgin, he placed and deposited their bodies, set in a marble coffin, beneath the same altar. He had discovered them in the altar of the aforesaid virgins Rufina and Secunda, when he had ordered us to search and dig for the bodies of those virgins.

Another oratory adjoins the aforesaid one. It has only one altar beneath its apse, under which are deposited the precious bodies of saints whose names are these: Saint Venantius, Saint [Col. 1555A] Domnio, Saint Anastasius, Saint Maurus, Saint Asterius, Saint Septimius, Saint Jelius, Saint Antiochianus, Saint Paulinianus, and Saint Gaianus.

The third oratory is beyond it, where the fonts stand between two altars: one of Saint John the Baptist and the other of Saint John the Evangelist. The fonts are round, set among porphyry columns in the middle of a beautiful round church, where Emperor Constantine’s chamber had stood. Pope Hilary [variant: Hilarus] constructed the oratories themselves, namely those of Saint John the Baptist and Blessed John the Evangelist, arranged opposite one another on either side; he adorned them all with silver and precious stones. He gave a silver confession-shrine of Saint John the Baptist weighing one hundred pounds, a golden cross, and in both [Col. 1555B] oratories bronze doors overlaid with silver. Before the confession-shrine, a silver crown weighing twenty pounds; a lampstand (*farum cantarum*; reading uncertain) weighing twenty-five pounds; likewise, within Saint John’s, beside the holy font, a golden lamp with ten lamp-lights, weighing five pounds; a silver tower with dolphins, weighing sixty pounds; and a golden dove weighing two pounds. Nearby he also made the monastery of Saint Stephen in the Lateran baptistery, and in the same place he made two libraries. He placed all these things in the Constantinian basilica of Saint Mary.

### X. On the oratory of the Holy Cross and its ornaments

The fourth oratory is that of the Holy Cross, in which there is much sanctuary of that Holy Cross. There, at an angel’s dictation, Blessed Pope Gregory wrote an antiphonary [Col. 1555C] and many other works. This oratory is exceedingly beautiful, made in the form of a cross and decorated with mosaic; it was established by the aforesaid Pope Hilary, who offered very many gifts there likewise: a confession-shrine in which he placed the wood of the Cross, together with a golden cross and gems, weighing twenty pounds; silver doors in the confession-shrine weighing fifty pounds; above the confession-shrine, a golden arch weighing four pounds, supported by onyx columns, on which stands a golden lamb weighing two pounds; a golden crown before the confession-shrine; a lampstand with dolphins weighing five pounds; and four golden lamps weighing two pounds.

He also made a nymphaeum and triple portico before the oratory of the Holy Cross, where there are *exatopentalaic* columns [uncertain reading], [Col. 1555D] two fluted basins with perforated, radiating porphyry columns pouring out water, and in the middle a porphyry pool with a handled basin in its centre pouring out water. It is enclosed around the middle, on right and left, by bronze railings, columns with pediments and epistyles, and is everywhere adorned with mosaic and with Aquitanian, Tripolitan, and porphyry columns.

Again, very near this oratory is another oratory of Saint Pope Gregory, where even to this day the bed on which that saint used to rest may be seen remaining beside the altar.

> [Note: [Col. 1555D] Anastasius mentions another bed of Gregory at the end of the Life of Stephen VI, when he praises the oratory of Blessed George, where Gregory’s bed is kept, beside the church [Col. 1556D] of the Prince of the Apostles. But there “bed” means a tomb.]

### XI. On the church of Saint Lawrence in the palace

[Col. 1556A] In the sacred palace is an oratory of Saint Lawrence, in which three most holy altars are reckoned. At the first, in a cypress chest made by Pope Leo III, are three caskets. In one is a cross of the purest gold, adorned with gems and precious stones—namely jacinths, emeralds, and green stones. In the middle of the cross is the navel of our Lord Jesus Christ; above it is anointed with balsam, and this anointing is renewed every year, when the lord pope with the cardinals makes the procession on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross from the church of Saint Lawrence itself to the basilica of the Saviour, called the Constantinian. In another casket, silver and gilded and bearing figured scenes, is an enamelled cross; and within that casket is the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Col. 1556B] In the third casket, which is silver, are the sandals—that is, the footwear—of our Lord Jesus Christ.

There is also another gilded casket containing wood from that Holy Cross which Heraclius, after defeating Chosroes, brought with him from Persia together with the body of Saint Anastasius Martyr. It is in the marble altar of Saint Lawrence there. There are also the arm of Saint Caesarius Martyr; two bones of Saint John the Baptist; one bone of Saint Jerome; the shoulder-blade of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite; a bone from the leg of Pope Saint Stephen; relics of Saint Damasus and of Saints Primus and Felicianus; the head of Saint Praxedes; relics of Saint Anastasia with many others; and relics of the virgin saints Agape, Chionia, Irene, Pistis (Faith), and Elpis (Hope); of Nereus and Achilleus; and of Prisca and Aquila. [Col. 1556C] There are also relics from the knee of Saint Tiburtius, son of Chromatius. In this same cypress chest are one bread of the Lord’s Supper, thirteen lentils from that same Supper, material from the reed and from the sponge with vinegar placed at the Lord’s mouth, and wood from the sycamore tree which Zacchaeus climbed.

Upon this altar is an image of the Saviour marvellously painted on a panel, designed by Luke the Evangelist but completed by the power of the Lord through angelic service. Beneath its feet, in a band of precious stones, are deposited the pledges of this sanctuary, whose names are these: the stone on which Holy Mary sat; a stone from the holy Jordan where the Lord sat while he was baptized; a stone from holy [Col. 1556D] Bethlehem; a stone from the Mount of Olives where the Lord prayed to the Father; the holy stone on which the angel sat at the tomb; material from the holy column where the Lord was bound and scourged; material from the Lord’s tomb where he rested dead in body; material from the lance by which the Lord’s side was pierced; wood from the Lord’s Cross; material from the place called the Lithostrotos; material from the place of Calvary; the holy stone where the Lord was laid; a stone from Mount Sion; the stone on which the Lord was transfigured on the mountain; wood from the Lord’s holy manger in which he, born as a child, was placed; a stone from Mount Sinai, where the Law was given; and a stone from the tomb of Holy Mary.

[Col. 1557A] In another altar of the same oratory are the heads of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, and the heads of the holy virgins Agnes and Euphemia.

In the third are coals sprinkled with the blood of Saint Lawrence and with the fat of his body. There are also in the same oratory relics of the Forty Martyrs and of many others.

### XV. On the church of Saint Mary Major and its sanctuary

The church of Saint Mary Major, which the younger Pope Sixtus built and Pope Paschal restored, has as many columns in its layout as there are days in a year’s cycle.

> [Note: [Col. 1557D] That is, Sixtus III, as the Book of the Pontiffs attests. But before him Liberius had built that basilica near the market of Livia or Livy, according to the same book; whence it was first called the Basilica of Livia.]

The dedication of this church is celebrated on the Nones of August. This venerable church of Saint Mary furthermore has [Col. 1557B] seven cardinal priests, who in the order of their respective weekly turns must celebrate Masses at their holy altar. In the altar of this venerable church are deposited relics from the hair of Saint Mary, Mother of the Lord; from the milk of the same Virgin; from the veil of her head; and from the cloth of her garment. The Lord’s cradle, in which he lay as a child, is there. There are relics from the Lord’s manger there.

> [Note: [Col. 1558D] According to Anastasius, Sergius II richly adorned the chamber of the manger of our Lord Jesus Christ with silver-gilt panels.]

There are relics of the Apostle Matthias, who was added among the Apostles in Judas’s place and is called “Little of God.” Some say that he rests beneath this altar of Blessed Mary Major; others say that he is deposited in the altar. Some believe that he rests in the ground under a huge marble stone, which lies before the altar-window. For this window is [Col. 1557C] beneath the altar in the same manner as the ark beneath the altar of Saint Peter. In Saint Peter’s church very many assert that the body of the aforesaid Saint Matthias the Apostle is in the wall above the great arch, which extends continuously through the middle of the church from one wall to the other. In the apse of Saint Mary is the pontifical chair in the middle beneath the five windows in the apse. This apse is exceedingly beautiful, made in mosaic. Many people see there fishes among flowers and beasts with birds, between the choir and the altar.

### XIII. On bishops and cardinals arranged by patriarchates

The seven cardinal bishops of the first see, who must daily celebrate in their weekly turns in place of the Apostolic Lord at the most holy altar of the Lord in the basilica of the Saviour, are these: the Bishop of Ostia, the Bishop of Porto, the Bishop of Saint Rufina, the Bishop of Sabina, the Bishop of Tusculum, and the Bishop of Palestrina.

The cardinals of Saint Mary Major are these: Saints Apostles; Saint Cyriacus at the Baths; Saint Eusebius; Saint Pudentiana; Saint Vitalis; Saints Marcellinus and Peter; Saint Clement.

The cardinals of Saint Peter are these: Saint Mary in Trastevere; Saint Chrysogonus; Saint Cecilia; [Col. 1558A] Saint Anastasia; Saint Lawrence in Damaso; Saint Mark; Saints Martin and Sylvester.

The cardinals of Saint Paul are these: Saint Sabina; Saint Prisca; Saint Balbina; Saints Nereus and Achilleus; Saint Sixtus; Saint Marcellus; Saint Susanna.

The cardinals of Saint Lawrence are these: Saint Praxedes; Saint Peter in Chains; Saint Lawrence in Lucina; Holy Cross in Jerusalem; Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill; Saints John and Paul; the Four Crowned Saints.

There are eighteen deaconries: Saint Mary in Dominica, where the archdeacon is; Saint Lucy in Circo, beside the Seven Seats; Saint Mary the New; Saints Cosmas and Damian; Saint Adrian; Saints Sergius [Col. 1558B] and Bacchus; Saint Theodore; Saint George; Saint Mary in the Greek School; Saint Mary in Portico; Saint Nicholas in Carcere; Saint Angel; Saint Eustace; Saint Mary in Aquiro; Saint Mary in Via Lata; Saint Agatha at the Marble Horse; Saint Lucy at the head of the Subura; Saint Quiricus.

The abbeys are these: Saint Caesarius in the Palace; Saint Gregory on the Clivus Scauri, where there is the head of the arm of Saint Andrew the Apostle; Saint Mary on the Aventine, where there is material from the body of Saint Sabinus, bishop; Saint Alexius, where his body and that of Saint Boniface Martyr are; Saints Prisca and Aquila, where their bodies are in part; Saint Sabas of the New Cell, where there is the head of Saint Tiburtius Martyr; Saint Pancras on the Via Aurelia; Saint Cosmas and Damian in the Golden Street, within the City of the Ravennates in Trastevere; likewise Saint Sylvester between the two gardens, built by Pope Dionysius, who also rests there; Saint Mary in the Capitol, where is the altar of the Son of God; Saint Basil beside the palace of Emperor Trajan; Saint Agatha Virgin, which is on the Suburan hill; Saint Lawrence in Panisperna, where he was laid upon the gridiron; Saint Thomas near the Claudian aqueduct; Saint Blaise between the Tiber and the bridge of Saint Peter; Holy Trinity of the Scots; Saint Valentine near the bridge; Saint Mary in the Golden Castle; Saint Mary in Pallara, where Saint Sebastian was shot with arrows; Saint Mary in the monastery beside Saint Peter in Chains.

### XIV. On the fall and restoration of this basilica: at what time it was effected by Pope Sergius III, and on the gifts and ornaments which he offered in it, as is written in the epitaphs on the walls here and there beside the bronze columns

[Col. 1558D]

In the year in which the most devout Emperor Constantine Augustus was baptized by the most blessed Sylvester, pontiff of the holy apostolic see, and cleansed of leprosy through the washing of sacred baptism, he built this basilica in honor of Christ Jesus our Lord and Savior and in commemoration of Saint John the Baptist. From that time it remained standing for some years, until the time of Stephen VI of pious memory, although the separation of its walls and the bending of its roofs already foretold its collapse. In his time it fell, and lay ruined, scattered, and broken down until the time when the lord Sergius, a priest, was recalled from exile, elected, and consecrated as the third bishop of the Romans. During those times in which usurpers held the apostolic see, they carried away from this basilica all its treasures, all ornaments of gold and silver, and every utensil that had been offered here from the beginning; nor were divine offices celebrated in it, but it lay desolate, like baths overgrown with brushwood and thorns. Therefore, after his ordination, Pope Sergius III grieved greatly over the desolation of this most noble church. For there was no human hope or consolation for its restoration. When all alike despaired of raising it again and human help was lacking, he turned to the aid of divine mercy, in which he had always trusted. Beginning with the old foundations, he brought this work to completion and adorned it with ornaments of gold and silver, as is read below—and with more besides, since, while he lived, the aforesaid most holy Pope Sergius III added further gifts there.

> “After the aforesaid Lord Pope Sergius III, through many struggles and labors and from your gifts, O Savior of the world, had rebuilt from its foundations this basilica, which lay in ruins, in honor of your name and in commemoration of you, Saint John the Baptist, he zealously undertook, with a devout mind, to replace and offer to you other ornaments, since all ornaments of gold, silver, and bronze had been taken from it by usurpers. Although he was beset by many disturbances, he nevertheless did not cease to serve your majesty. He made and offered to your omnipotence this most beautiful image, which he adorned with five pounds of gold; a ciborium of marvelous beauty, of purest silver and gold with gems, whose completion required two hundred and fifty pounds in number and weight; a golden cross with a crucified figure; two silver crosses, one having its entire crucified figure in gold and a golden lamb with gems; a golden crown with two crosses, and two others of mixed metals; a golden clasp with gems; two gilded silver pouches with five gems; silver crowns with their ten dolphins; thirty-nine silver baskets; twenty-five silver bowls; four silver crosses, from which bowls hang, and one small silver cross likewise; three silver chalices, one of them gilded; a silver paten; three silver censers; three silver images, one of them having a right hand of gold and a clasp on its breast with gems; six silver arches; a silver beam; six silver little columns; twelve silver apples; two vestments woven with gold; one covering with gold, and another plain one; fifty-two silk veils. All these things he devoutly prepared for you; and, so long as his spirit governs his limbs, the lord Pope Sergius III will not cease to prepare and offer things to you.”

If anyone, perhaps sorrowfully, wonders why these ornaments, and the other things noted above as having been offered by Emperor Constantine, are now no longer visible, let him read and examine the Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs; he will find when and how they were unjustly taken from here by usurpers.

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1167: HUGH OF POITIERS**

[Col. 1559]

## NOTICE

(FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, III, 297)

Hugh of Poitiers, monk and notary of William, abbot of Vézelay, in the district of Avallon in the kingdom of Burgundy, began, by command of Abbot Pons, in 1156, to write the *History of the Abbey of Vézelay* from 846 to 1147, prefacing it with a brief history of the Counts of Nevers; he completed it in four books in 1167. It was first published by D’Achery in volume III of the *Spicilegium*, p. 446 (new edition, vol. III, pp. 498–560). The first book abounds throughout in letters and privileges of popes Nicholas I, John VIII, and their successors down to Adrian IV.

[Note: [Col. 1559] Order of Saint Benedict until 1537, when the monks, having obtained bulls from Paul III, laid aside the cowl and adopted the customs and dress of secular canons, as D’Achery notes on William of Newburgh, p. 658.]

[Col. 1561]

## DOM LUKE D’ACHERY’S PREFACE TO HIS EDITION OF THE HISTORY OF THE MONASTERY OF VÉZELAY

(*Spicilegium*, folio edition, vol. II, p. 498.)

Four years have now elapsed during which my mind recoiled from publishing the *History of the Monastery of Vézelay*, disfigured by very wide gaps. For there was hope that the complete work might someday be recovered from ruins or from the recesses of monasteries, where perhaps it still struggles amid dust, decay, and moths. Yet repeatedly importuned by the exhortations and persuaded by the arguments of friends, lest they should suffer refusal from me, I finally yielded to their wishes—for they are men outstanding among the learned alike in scholarship and piety. I did not wish the history, though gaping with lacunae, yet ennobled by ancient documents and composed with learning and elegance, to remain any longer wrapped in darkness; indeed, since it would be useful to learning, I willingly brought it forth into the light.

The author Hugh of Poitiers chose to set forth his history in four parts. In the first part he placed charters of the founders, letters of the city of Rome, royal diplomas, and other documents of that sort, as the foundations of the matters which he was about to bring forward. In the second he portrays the bishop of Autun, by fair means and foul, violating the liberties of the Church of Vézelay and attempting to usurp rights belonging to the Roman pontiff alone. In the third and fourth he reveals the lamentable tragedies committed by the Counts of Nevers, who, through incursions and plundering, both personally and through their agents, repeatedly ravaged the monastery of Vézelay and all its territory in order to annex it to their own dominion. In barbarian fashion they expelled the monks and openly, by force, withdrew the townspeople from the laws and subjection of their lord, the abbot. Nevertheless, the author does not omit to describe the victories won by the abbot and monks—though not without immense labor and loss of property—against both the bishop and the men of Nevers, with the inspiration of the divine Spirit, the aid of Roman pontiffs, and, above all, the favor of King Louis VII. He also inserts the more notable events of his own age, which greatly illuminate civil and ecclesiastical history.

[Col. 1561]

# HISTORY OF THE MONASTERY OF VÉZELAY  
By Hugh of Poitiers, notary of William, Abbot of Vézelay, who began to write it at the command of Abbot Pons in 1156 and completed it under William himself in 1167.

## BOOK ONE: PRIVILEGES AND CHARTERS OF THE ABBEY OF VÉZELAY

[Col. 1561A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, begins the instrument or testament of Count Gerard, founder of the monasteries of Pultarias and Vézelay, together with the following privileges of apostolic and royal authority confirming and strengthening this testament forever.

### Testament of Count Gerard

To all Christ’s faithful who await the blessed life with piety, love, and fervent desire, and who everywhere remain in the unity of Christianity under obedience to God’s commandments: to those now present and to those who are to come, who are to live in the bond and union of charity and succeed one another in the Church of the saints until the consummation of the world.

I, Gerard, raised by the gift of divine mercy to the honor of count at the glorious royal court, acting from the common resolve and desire of my dearest and most loving wife Bertha, since it has pleased us alike and with one mind, by the Lord’s inspiration, to establish from our possessions and titles of property a perpetual memorial to the Lord our God, where his praise might be continually offered. And since, through the pious gifts of our lords and superiors, who have most generously enlarged us in honors and dignities—namely, our most merciful lord and emperor Louis, the glorious lady and queen Judith, and their son, equally our lord and superior, King Charles—we have received very many possessions, it seemed most just to us that, moved by love for them, we should found this place also, where solemn and unceasing supplication should be made in prayers for their gracious gifts, and continuous intercession before God for their salvation.

For we are not unmindful of their goodwill toward us: that is, of our lord and superior Louis Augustus, Lady and Queen Judith, and their son Charles, likewise our lord and superior, who still reigns. We also render due honor to our fathers and mothers—Leuthard and Grimildis, and our most beloved Hugh and Bava—and to their beloved sons and daughters, whether already asleep in the Lord or still living, who are joined to us by blood, marriage, and kinship; namely, the most illustrious counts Leufred and Adalard. For them intercession and continual prayer are to be made, forgiveness for their sins obtained, and their enduring remembrance preserved in the place which, with Christ’s aid, we found, throughout succeeding ages. Thus also the perpetual memory of those relatives to whom we succeeded in these possessions by hereditary right, of all others, of all our friends, and generally of all the faithful, may endure; and there may be offered there through all ages a common prayer for all.

### The Foundation of the Monastery of Pultarias for Monks

[Col. 1563C]

Therefore I, Gerard, together with my most beloved wife, have in pious and faithful devotion established and built a monastery and dwelling-place for God’s servants in a suitable and fitting location. From the gift and offering of our wealth and possessions, we have supplied there, with pious and diligent foresight according to the means God has granted us, whatever is necessary for the support of those serving God and for the observance of religion. With the most ready mind we have offered the very things received from his hand, returning thanks for his benefits.

The place of our devotion has therefore been founded and established in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and in veneration of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, beside the river Seine which flows past it, in the territory facing the estate which from ancient times they call Pultarias, in the district of Laticensis, in the kingdom of Burgundy. There may the venerable house of prayer be frequented by the vows and supplications of the faithful, and the heavenly manner of life of those living under the strict rule and institution of Saint Benedict be sought and pursued with every desire and inward fervor.

There we have granted these estates: Pultarias itself, where the monastery is situated nearby; whatever we possess there by inheritance; whatever our lord King Charles granted us there by authority of his charter; whatever has accrued to our property there by another lawful arrangement, with all its appurtenances and everything anywhere pertaining to it. In the district of Sens, Sexta with everything belonging to it and all its appurtenances; likewise the estate of Mannisca with everything belonging to it and its appurtenances. Veron also, and the hamlet in the aforesaid district, with all things belonging to them and their appurtenances. Likewise in the same district, in the estate called Piscatoria, situated on the river Yonne, all and entire whatever we acquired from Ildinus, the lord’s vassal, and whatever pertains to that fishing-place, but only in all matters in which our lordship appears or is known to exist there; and whatever belongs to our right in the district of Troyes.

### The Foundation of the Monastery of Vézelay for Nuns

[Col. 1564B]

In like fashion we founded another monastery with the same zeal and devotion, so that there might be a dwelling-place for God’s handmaids, living under strict rule and the institution of Saint Benedict, in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the place or territory called Vézelay, in the district of Avallon, in the kingdom of Burgundy. There we granted these estates: Vézelay itself, in which the sacred and venerable monastery of Vézelay is situated. We exchanged it with the lady and glorious Queen Judith, who negotiated and obtained it from our lord and superior Louis, emperor of most pious memory. Whatever that most merciful emperor bestowed and granted us, with the confirmation of his charter, as belonging to that estate, and whatever anywhere pertains to the same estate, we assigned to the aforesaid monastery. Finally, the estate of Dorniciacum, the estate of Cisternas, Fontanas, and Molnitum; and whatever we acquired in the named districts of Avallon or Tonnerre, with all appurtenances of the aforesaid estates, wherever and in whatever district they may be.

Therefore all and entire whatever we have acquired or have been able to acquire in the above-named estates or territories, we have united to these most sacred places and monasteries and permanently bound to the common life and benefit of those who serve God there. We have reserved only the usufruct for ourselves while we remain in this bodily life, retaining also the care and defense of the aforesaid monasteries.

Accordingly, whatever has been bestowed on the aforesaid monastery of men by our religious offering, whatever by God’s inspiration shall be added or given there in property, services, or any kinds of goods, or shall at any time be offered by any faithful persons, is to remain inviolate through the perpetual force of this present testament, free from all external services and exactions of services, for the stipends and necessary expenses only of those serving the Lord there. Except that, for a blessing, two pounds of silver shall be offered each year at Rome to the most reverend see of the blessed apostles, to which we have subjected these places, for the blessed pontiff of the City; and such daily benefits as voluntary charity and the duty of humanity teach should be performed. Yet the monks, free from these imposts, shall live in peace under regular observance, solemnly offering the services of prayer to God for our most glorious lords and superiors Louis Augustus and his son Charles; for our ladies Judith and Hermengarde of most eminent memory; and also for Hermentrude, venerable wife of our lord Charles; likewise for their fathers, mothers, sons, and daughters of most illustrious memory, whether living or already asleep in the Lord; for us, our sons and daughters, living or dead; for all our friends; and for the whole multitude of the faithful.

### Both Monasteries Are Subjected to the Roman Pontiff

[Col. 1565B]

This monastery and the other named above, with all things bestowed upon them, we have subjected to the most blessed apostles at Rome. By this testamentary document, we have entrusted them forever to the holy pontiffs of that city, who in succeeding years shall hold the apostolic see, to govern, order, and administer—not, however, so that anyone should have license to grant or alienate them by a benefice. Thus, by their diligent care and watchful provision, religion marked by piety and integrity may ever increase there, in accordance with our devotion, to God’s glory, and a more abundant fruit may be produced before God.

We especially will it to be firmly established that whenever an abbot or abbess of the aforesaid monasteries, dedicated by our religious devotion to the holy apostles, departs this life by God’s appointment, the communities that God wills to exist in those venerable places shall have the granted authority, after consultation and with the counsel of holy men, to appoint from their own company and community, with the Lord’s assistance, another man or woman of good life and good repute, chosen as abbot or abbess, subject to the approval in this matter of the pontiff then holding the apostolic see. The amount of property must always be considered in admitting brothers or sisters, lest those communities, burdened by an excessive number—God forbid—perhaps fall into ruin.

We also earnestly admonish and solemnly forbid that anyone be permitted forever to alter the vow of our piety or, by an inverted order, to disrupt it. If anyone—though we do not believe this will happen—should presume to do so, let him be condemned by the charter of our lord and superior, the pious King Charles; and, God our Lord rendering him the due recompense of his deed according to the sentence of the holy pontiff of the City, let him, as a sacrilegious person and plunderer of sacred things, be excluded from the assembly of God’s people and incur eternal punishment unless he repents.

And we entreat all you most holy fathers and bishops, through our Redeemer, always to deign to be in every respect supporters and helpers of this work of our devotion. Finally, this must be urged upon our pious and beloved servants living in the said monasteries, founded by us with such pious zeal: let them show pious and watchful care for devotion and religion, and in all things conduct themselves as God’s ministers, giving no one any occasion to reproach the most religious and sacred order of their ministry. Let the pontiff of the apostolic see be their ruler, constant comforter, and guardian, so that, united to the body and members of the Church by most faithful charity and most religious obedience, they may deserve also to be joined in union to the head of the whole body, which is Christ.

This testament, drawn up by us in full piety and devotion, we have decreed should be strengthened by the subscriptions of our own hand and of illustrious men, so that it may possess unassailable force for all time.

S. of Count Gerard. S. of his wife Bertha, who offered this gift to God for the remedy of his soul, confirmed it by making this testament, and ordered it to be confirmed.
