### Letter of Count Gerard to Pope Nicholas Concerning Apostolic Jurisdiction and Protection

To the most blessed lord and apostolic ruler of the most sacred see, and our special father, NICHOLAS: GERARD, raised by the mercy of almighty God to the honor of count at the royal court, together with his most beloved wife BERTA.

Gerard desires that the monasteries founded by him be subject to the jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff alone. We desire it to be publicly known to your blessedness, to the clergy, and to all the people of the holy City, that, out of most devoted faith in our Lord Jesus Christ and a most ready offering from our resources—for the Lord has granted us an ample possession of goods—for love of him and the eternal salvation of our souls, it has pleased us alike, with one mind and common purpose, by the Lord’s inspiration, that, excepting those things reserved for the descendants of our family and offspring, we should make God himself and his blessed apostles Peter and Paul heirs of the rest of our possessions, and appoint them our perpetual intercessors before him.

And because, with the help of him who is the giver of every good will and inspirer of every holy vow, this has been added to our devotion—that we should build monasteries and dwelling-places for God’s servants from these same resources of ours, in a suitable and fitting place; should provide there, with pious and diligent foresight according to the means granted by God, whatever is necessary for the support of those serving God and for religious observance; and should establish a lasting defense and guardianship for their order and religion, so that the fruit of our devotion might remain forever—we have resolved to subject them and commit them to the most sacred and reverend City and place where the eternal memory of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul is celebrated, under the authority of the most holy pontiff of that City. Thus that blessed pontiff may order their administration and condition with ecclesiastical piety and firmness; yet so that he may never grant them to anyone as a benefice, except to those to whom we ourselves, providing for them in this testamentary gift, have indicated that they are to be granted, as this document below will also indicate.

Therefore, fulfilling our most ready devotion and our most complete desire in Christ, and lawfully making the Church of God heir to our possessions by testamentary right of donation, we have established and founded the venerable and sacred place of our offering in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in veneration of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. It is to be a dwelling-place for God’s servants, living under a regular order and the profession of Saint Benedict, beside the flowing river Seine, in the territory facing the estate called from ancient times Pultarias, in the district of Laticensis, in the kingdom of Burgundy, and in the parish of the city of Langres. There the venerable house of prayer may be frequented by the vows and supplications of the faithful, and the heavenly life may be sought and desired with every longing and inward ardor.

To it we have lawfully transferred and conveyed, by testamentary right of donation, with God’s help and in full accomplishment of our devotion, our possessions and the resources of our properties which have come to us by the most generous inheritance of our parents, by most affectionate gifts, by the charter which our most gracious lord and superior King Charles deigned to grant us, or by worthy purchase. Namely: Pultarias, the territory or estate in the district of Latincourt where the monastery stands nearby; whatever the pious king has granted there by his charter and has come to us from parental inheritance; whatever has accrued to our possessions there by another lawful arrangement, with all its appurtenances and whatever anywhere belongs to it. In the district of Sens, Sexta with everything belonging to it and all its appurtenances; likewise the estate of Magnisca with everything belonging to it and all its appurtenances.

[Note: [Col. 1567] *Magniscam.* Above it is given as *Manniscam*. Other places are also named there; perhaps someone more learned will see why they are not enumerated at this point.]

Therefore, as stated above, we have joined all and entire whatever we have acquired or have been able to acquire in the above-named estates to the most sacred place and monastery and to the servants of God who will serve there; we have permanently bound it to serve their common life and benefit, reserving only usufruct for ourselves while we remain in bodily life, while undertaking rather the guardianship and defense of the place.

Likewise, we have enriched and endowed, from our possessions and by common resolve, another equally venerable and sacred place in honor of the same God and our Lord Jesus Christ and in veneration of his Mother, the Blessed Virgin Mary. It is in the place or territory called Vézelay, in the district of Avallon and kingdom of Burgundy. There we have granted these estates: Vézelay itself, where the sacred and venerable monastery of Vézelay is situated, which we exchanged with Louis, emperor of most pious memory. Whatever that most merciful emperor, in confirming his charter, granted us in exchange as belonging to the same estate, and whatever pertains to that estate, we assigned to the aforesaid monastery; finally, the estate of Dorniciacum, the estate of Cisternas, the estate of Fontanas, and Molnitum, together with whatever we acquired in the named districts of Avallon or Tonnerre, with all the appurtenances of the aforesaid estates, wherever and in whatever district they may be.

Whatever, therefore, we have granted to the aforesaid places, monasteries, or churches; whatever has been bestowed there by our offering; whatever has been added by us, under God’s inspiration, in property, services, or goods of whatever kind; or whatever shall ever be offered by any faithful persons—we have decreed shall endure by the perpetual force of our authority and the written testament, free from all external services and exactions, solely for the stipends and necessary expenses of those serving the Lord there, while the usufruct is reserved to us only during our lifetime. Except that, as a blessing, two pounds of silver shall be offered each year from each monastery to the most reverend see to which we have subjected those monasteries, for the blessed pontiff of the City; and such daily benefits as voluntary charity and the duty of humility teach should be performed.

No rash person, nor any person whatever, may ever presume to seek anything else from this, diminish the sacred gift through invasion, or unlawfully claim it by transferring it to personal use as private property. Rather, let what has proceeded from us in regard for God remain unshaken, in fear of the dreadful judgment.

Therefore, these venerable dwellings of God’s servants, together with those who serve or will serve God there, we commend, subject, and permanently entrust, with all the devotion of our heart before God, to you, most blessed pontiff, and to your successors, out of reverence for the blessed apostles, whose place and office you hold in Christ’s Church. We ask that, through the zealous exercise of your apostolic office, you may deign to govern, protect, and defend them in all things with paternal and ecclesiastical piety and most merciful administration; that they may not, contrary to our vow, be transferred by grant as benefices to anyone other than those designated in the testamentary document. Under the attestation of divine majesty and the fearful consideration of the future judgment, when each of us will without doubt render an account before Christ’s tribunal for his deeds, we cast ourselves down with every effort of humility at your most holy feet, that we may deserve to obtain your command that this be kept with immovable firmness and canonical, paternal authority.

Thus the servants of God in the aforesaid monasteries constructed by us, and the community of nuns ever dependent on your blessing, may lawfully administer, according to our devotion and desire, the possessions we have offered to the Lord in full devotion by a lawfully completed testament. Protected and defended by you, they may live under their own rule in regular observance, owing nothing to anyone except charity and subject in service to no one except the Prince of the Apostles and his vicar. But after our departure—for while life remains we desire them to remain under our care with your blessing—may peace and tranquility, present and future, be provided by God’s mercy both for them and for all whom divine grace has gathered or will gather there.

And whenever an abbot or abbess departs this life from the community which God wills to exist in these venerable places, the communities shall have granted authority, after consultation and with the counsel of holy men, to appoint from their own society and community, with the Lord’s assistance, another man or woman of good life and good repute, chosen as abbot or abbess, subject to the approval of the blessed pontiff who at that time holds the apostolic see. That person, according to the regular order of Saint Benedict, shall freely supervise both within and without all matters belonging by right to the monasteries and, by grace infused from the Lord, diligently fulfill them.

But because we greatly fear that, as iniquity has abounded, the charity of many has grown cold and avarice has spread everywhere, if after our death any person, or the bishop of the diocese itself—to whom neither any right of ordination nor lordship over the place is granted—or any powerful person, or anyone else, should attempt through evil counsel and greedy impulse to disturb the congregation of God’s servants or handmaids, to confound the regular order, to replace an abbot or abbess regularly chosen by the community with another man or woman, or to presume to exercise unlawful lordships over the monasteries or over the goods of the monasteries which we have there permanently granted, we entreat your most reverend fatherhood through God not to delay in giving assistance by whatever means your blessedness can. Under the attestation of divine majesty and fearful contemplation of the future judgment, may your holiness commend this provision to your pious successors to be observed with immovable firmness and paternal authority. Let your authority suspend from ecclesiastical communion the person who has dared to violate so sacred a gift to God, as a plunderer and seeker of sacred things; let apostolic severity or censure immediately condemn him; and let him never, inflamed by his most perverse avarice, be able by legal contest to alter anything of the aforesaid pious will and religious devotion which, for God’s sake, we have most trustfully commended to you before the Lord and his holy apostles. Rather, having at once experienced the most worthy canonical and apostolic judgment, with the apostles themselves repaying him for his wickedness, let him also be struck and condemned with a fine of three hundred pounds of gold, as is included in the testament.

Moreover, most holy shepherd, wholly bowed down and submissive in spirit, we entreat you and your successors, through Christ the Lord, through his Virgin Mother, through the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and through all who glorify the whole Church of God by their blood, that you may always, with pious and fervent zeal, give support in a special fatherly manner to the inhabitants of the monasteries entrusted to your fatherhood and reverence. Never permit the things which we have committed to your protection in good hope either to be granted as benefices or alienated. Rather, deign piously to preserve our vow intact and to leave and command your successors to preserve it likewise. Strengthen with pious blessings the brothers and sisters whom we place under your protection; defend them against attackers; and diligently endeavor to render them secure for fruitful leisure and peace, receiving the reward from him who crowns his saints with eternal recompense, Jesus Christ our Lord.

This letter of our will, or testamentary offering, drawn up by us in full piety and devotion, we have decreed should be strengthened by the subscriptions of our own hand and of illustrious men, so that it may possess unassailable force for all time; and we have also sent it to be kept for perpetual remembrance in the archives of the most blessed apostles.

S. of Count Gerard. S. of his wife Bertha, who offered this gift to God for the remedy of his soul, confirmed it by making a testament, and ordered it to be confirmed.

S. of their daughter Eve, who, by hearing and approving, consented to her parents’ will and to the offering made to God, and by consenting confirmed it.

To his beloved daughter in Christ, the Countess of Nevers, Brother BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and prayers.

### Letter of the Abbot of Fleury to Pontius

He writes what ought to be done to defend the rights of Vézelay.

To Lord PONTIUS, Abbot of Vézelay, Brother M., Abbot of Fleury: the peace proclaimed to people of good will.

Having read your letter and considered its tenor more carefully, I write back to your affection what seems to me the more prudent course. If your peace were offered to you for sale—a peace which would free you from the bondage of so great an affliction, humble your adversaries, and gladden your allies—it would seem very dear to purchase, provided that your Church retained unimpaired the uprightness of its condition and the privileges of its liberty.

But to regard your brother with such suspicion that, when the count entrusts himself wholly to him, you decline his arbitration, seems very harsh. Therefore, after weighing the case on both sides, we judge and say that you should await the legates whom you sent to the lord pope. When they arrive, show the lord abbot the pope’s answer and the privileges of your Church; and then, at last, faithfully commit your affair to his judgment. For we do not believe that he will judge contrary or opposed either to your privileges or to the commands of the lord pope.

[Col. 1576A] ### Letter of King Louis to the Same

He promises clemency and protection.

LOUIS, by the grace of God King of the Franks and Duke of Aquitaine, to the venerable PONTIUS, Abbot of Vézelay: greeting and our favor.

Excessive harshness does not befit a king, and pardon ought not to be withheld from one who pleads in truth. We understand from your request that our faithful Archambald of Bourbon and his wife, our maternal aunt, have interceded with us for you. Heeding them, for the honor of God, the holiness of your Church, and our own honor, we wholly remit whatever offense we hold against you, wipe away every cloud of resentment, and henceforth graciously receive you into favor and the things belonging to you into royal protection.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1575]

[Col. 1575D] ### Why the Author Undertook to Write This History

The grace of divine goodness, providing in many and varied ways for human weakness, has bestowed upon humanity, among the equally innumerable remedies of its benefits, the aids of letters: so that the diligence of those present might be stirred, the affection of those absent awakened, and the posterity of the future instructed. And because forgetfulness, the enemy of all prudence, so often obliterated the memory of things most useful, the custom arose in ancient times of committing the records of the Fathers to the knowledge of posterity through the characters of writing, as though through visible sounds.

[Col. 1576D] We too, following this custom according to our small measure, have endeavored to set down concisely, for the benefit of many, the pressures which our Church has endured in many ways through long courses of time on account of its liberty innate to it. In pursuing brevity in this work, we wholly avoid the arrogance of overstatement. For if, as the subject itself demands, we were to apply ourselves to the full treatment of events, the enormity of the danger might somehow seem to detract from credibility, while an unbelieving hearer would attribute to talkative boasting what might in some degree serve historical completeness.

Thus, looking to both considerations, [Col. 1577A] we proceed along the middle path: the knowledge of events remains whole, and no trace whatsoever of falsehood is disclosed. Certainly, although we do not fail to know that we are less fit and less adequate for these things, we are nevertheless prompted by love of the Church; we are also invited—indeed, if I may say so, urgently compelled—by the obedience owed to our most reverend father, the venerable Abbot Pontius. Though in time he appears the latest of his predecessors, in defending the liberty of his Church he is deservedly shown to be the first of all the ancients. For even if they contributed more, whether by acquisition or by construction, he certainly labored more than them all when, against those plundering it and seeking to uproot it, he courageously kept it safe, whole, and uninjured. For it is less to possess what you guard than to guard what you possess. But now, having begun our undertaking, enough on these matters.

### What Were the Privileges of the Church of Vézelay; Humbert, Bishop of Autun, First Attempts to Disturb Them

Therefore, since the Church of Vézelay, nobly born, had been yet more nobly reared, it bore before all the Churches of the West the preeminence of freeborn liberty. For at the very beginning of its foundation, being dedicated to most blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, it was nobly assigned by its most noble founders to that Apostolic See alone and uniquely, and endowed with the gift of perpetual liberty by Nicholas, then supreme and apostolic pontiff.

His successors, adhering down to these times to the footsteps of his piety, confirmed it in its privileges by apostolic authority and Roman dignity, and decreed that, as the proper right and freehold of blessed Peter, it should be wholly exempt from all subjection to any other person or Church.

[Col. 1577C] Accordingly, through the clemency of Roman privileges and apostolic liberty, they granted it leave to receive ecclesiastical offices—such as the sacred ordinations of its monks or clerics; the consecration of churches or altars; the grace of chrism or holy oil; and whatever else is of this kind—wherever it wished and from any Catholic bishop of any province. Proclaimed with such great praises of so freeborn a liberty, it presented an envious spectacle to its sister Churches.

[Col. 1577D] Hence, after several hundred years, a certain Humbert, presiding over the Church of Autun, attempted to mar the beauty of that liberty with the blemish of defiling servitude. At that time the venerable Pontius held the governance of the Church of Vézelay; he was the uterine brother of Peter, Abbot of Cluny, and Jordan, Abbot of La Chaise-Dieu. Noble by birth, therefore, and having received a most noble Church, he invited Elias, Bishop of Orléans, according to the custom of its liberty, and humbly asked him to confer sacred orders there. After examining the privileges of Roman authority, Elias most willingly acceded to his devotion and advanced several monks and some clerics to sacred orders in the basilica of the Church of Vézelay.

When this had been done, the Bishop of Autun was angered and prohibited the clerics from exercising the orders they had received. Innocent, the apostolic pontiff of the Roman See at that time, of good memory, reproved this insane audacity [Col. 1578A] and restored the clerics suspended by the Bishop of Autun to their orders; he further warned the bishop not again to presume to violate the rights of the Roman Church.

Then the Bishop of Autun, having tasted apostolic displeasure, repented of what he had begun, but was ashamed to disavow his undertaking. Nor did he cease to harass the abbot until, frustrated by his very own efforts, he finally renounced the dispute which he had proposed, into the hands of the Abbot of Cluny and other honorable persons. Through the hand of the aforesaid venerable Abbot Pontius, he restored between the two Churches the former condition of peace.

### Henry, His Successor and Brother of the Duke of Burgundy, Makes a Similar Attempt

Though he was most distinguished by birth and most worthy in uprightness of character and piety, the Church of Lyons, being deprived of its bishop, sought him as its archbishop. When he had been taken away, Henry, brother of the Duke of Burgundy, assumed the bishopric of Autun. Without delay, the instigators of the old discord approached him and, striving to revive the dormant calumny concerning the liberty of Vézelay, pressed it upon his eager ears.

He, however, trusting in the power of his lineage and wealth, in both of which he was equally strong, and attempting, as a man of exceptional power, to do something unprecedented, sought to claim the Church of Vézelay as his own right, reduce it to his diocese, subject it to his parish like the other churches, and make it obey his synods. But, God protecting it and blessed Mary Magdalene, beloved of God, acting as patroness, he could not take the club from Hercules’ hand. Clearly, so far as lay within him, he left nothing unattempted by which he might usurp for himself what belonged to Peter alone. For blind greed flatters itself that everything is easy which it already hopes to obtain by the very act of desiring it.

[Col. 1578C] Thus he summoned the aforesaid venerable Abbot Pontius, who had undertaken the Church’s cause as his responsibility, first concerning synodal procedure, then concerning clerical or priestly examination, and finally concerning the administration of ecclesiastical sacraments; and he demanded from him the justice due by law. But Pontius answered that he was the Church’s guardian, not a litigant—indeed, he was the vicar of apostolic fatherhood insofar as the right of the Church of Vézelay was concerned—and that he would have no case with him on this matter without the knowledge of the lord pope.

[Col. 1578D] Repulsed in this way, the bishop wished to extort by force what he had been unable to steal by litigious persecution. He therefore began to harass the Church, oppress its people, plunder its possessions, and try every means within his power to harm it. Believing his own power insufficient to accomplish his planned attacks, he incited his brother the duke and his other brothers to hatred of the Church; through them he brought and drove what was, as it were, the power of all Burgundy to the ruin and overthrow of the Church. The abbot, however, having gained steadfastness, despised, broke, frustrated, and reduced to nothing all the bishop’s assaults, as empty and futile things.

[Col. 1579A] ### The Dispute over the Immunities of Vézelay Before the Supreme Pontiff; the Bishop of Autun Loses His Case

At this time the most holy Eugenius presided over the universal Church. When he heard of the madness by which the Bishop of Autun strove to corrupt the chastity of his special daughter—the Church of Vézelay, I mean—he often admonished him, often rebuked him, and warned him that, unless he came to his senses, his episcopal rank was in danger.

At last, frustrated in his own expectation and losing confidence in the vanity of his power, the Bishop of Autun went to the Roman curia. Inventing falsehoods and constructing things like the truth, he brought a complaint against the abbot, asserting that what he claimed from the Church of Vézelay had been possessed by the Church of his see, without the challenge of any dispute, by prescription of long time down to the present.

[Col. 1579B] The most clement Pope Eugenius, taking every care to safeguard the dignity of apostolic authority while preserving the integrity of truth, fixed a day for both parties and specified it to the abbot. By his letters of favor, he ordered the abbot to appear before him on the appointed day, either personally or through adequately qualified representatives, with the evidences of his Church, to answer the charges brought.

Accordingly, each party, bringing with it an adequate and, as it seemed to each, lawful company of witnesses, appeared before the universal curia, each believing that, under so great a tribunal, it would obtain the end of its case.

Meanwhile Abbot Pontius, deservedly called a steadfast defender of justice, approached the supreme pontiff and complained that he ought by no means to undergo an action or a judgment in a matter which he held through the apostolic hand and perpetual possession, and of whose perpetual liberty he had been made heir by the testament of the same apostolic authority through numerous ancient Roman privileges.

[Col. 1579C] The kindly Apostolic replied that he ought to seek the test of judgment all the more fairly and freely because he was more conscious of his own justice, knowing beyond doubt that his cause would always be stronger insofar as, weighed in the balance of judgment, it would thereafter be released from every knot of dispute. Even if, perchance—though he did not hope this possible—it should in some way be burdened by an inconsiderate adverse judgment, then at last he need not doubt that, by the authority of his privileges, he could resist the violent determinations of any such judgment.

Moved by this reasoning, the abbot consented to accept the action, and now each party pursued its case. In the course of the proceedings it was determined that the Bishop of Autun could establish nothing in dispute by proprietary right, by possession through investiture, by prescription of long time as he claimed, or even by usufructuary or legatory title; rather, he could establish only a use granted or permitted, according to the custom of the liberty of Vézelay, to any bishops, even of any province.

[Col. 1579D] By contrast, the Abbot of Vézelay claimed neither prescription of long time nor legatory title, nor any other use acquired from another; rather, he maintained that the Church of Vézelay had always possessed the aforesaid liberty by proprietary right and ancient investiture of perpetual possession. He sufficiently argued that this liberty had not been granted to it by a merely emancipating act, but was innate and connate with it, had grown with it, and had continued in it incontrovertibly to the present times.

Since each fortified his allegations with witnesses, it was decreed by judgment of the assembly that the witnesses produced should confirm their testimony by the sacrament of an oath. The form of this oath was that each should disclose what truth he knew concerning the cause of the two parties and wholly suppress falsehood. Bound by this oath, the abbot produced his witnesses. The manner of their testimony was as follows.

[Col. 1580B] ### The Abbot’s Witnesses Report What They Knew of the Rights

Gerard, Prior of Alborn, said:

> “Before I became a monk, I attended the council which Pope Paschal held at Guastalla, and I saw him bless Renaud, Abbot of Vézelay, there. Afterwards I became a monk at Vézelay. The same abbot sent me to Auxerre with Peter Aribaldi, a cleric, and several other monks—Gilbert, Achard, and Aimon—and there I received four orders, up to the subdiaconate. Peter Aribaldi was ordained there also, but I do not remember what order he received.
>
> “At another time I was ordained subdeacon by the same Bishop Humbald. Later, when the Bishop of Angers was on his way to Rome, he prepared chrism and holy oil at Vézelay in the greater church; and I firmly believe that the chaplains of the same town received that holy chrism and oil. On another occasion the same Bishop of Angers ordained me deacon at Vézelay, as well as other monks and certain clerics of the same town; but I do not remember the names of the clerics.
>
> [Col. 1580C] “The same abbot sent me and the monk John to Hugh, Bishop of Nevers, who consecrated us priests. When I was at Saint James in Esconio, an obedience of Vézelay, I saw William Barzelim, messenger of Abbot Renaud, going to Auxerre for chrism. On his return, when he rested somewhat during the night, he entrusted the chrism to me; later, having taken it back from me, he brought it to Vézelay.
>
> “At another time I saw Amicus of Ulme sent by the same Abbot Renaud to the same Bishop Hugh for chrism and returning with chrism. In the time of that same Abbot Renaud, a certain parishioner of his, Stephen Aicaphit, went to Jerusalem. While he remained there for seven years, his wife married another man. Afterwards the said Stephen returned and claimed his wife. Since she was denied him, he brought an action against her before Abbot Renaud; when the case had been heard, she was restored to her husband by the judgment and authority of Abbot Renaud. With Peter, chaplain of Upper Saint Peter’s, present, the adulterer and adulteress received penance from the abbot.”

Hugh, Prior of Moret, under oath, said:

> “Matthew, Bishop of Albano, ordained me subdeacon and many other monks at Vézelay, in the chapel of Saint Lawrence, in the time of Abbot Alberic, while Pope Innocent was at Auxerre. I saw, in the time of the same abbot, that Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, consecrated the altar of Saint Giles in the greater church. I also saw the marriage of Arduin and Cecilia, concerning which there was a dispute, confirmed by the authority and judgment of Alberic, Abbot of Vézelay, with Walter, Bishop of Chalon, present and assisting. The father and his young son were from the parish of Autun, namely from Glun.
>
> [Col. 1581A] “Garnier, subprior of Vézelay, brought me to Auxerre, where I was ordained priest by Bishop Hugh, who had been Abbot of Saint-Germain, together with several monks of our monastery. Afterwards, when I was chamberlain, at the summons of Abbot Alberic, he had fourteen monks ordained at Auxerre by Hugh of Auxerre, who had been Abbot of Pontigny.
>
> [Col. 1581B] “Stephen, Bishop of Autun, consecrated the altar of Saint Andeolus situated in the monks’ choir. I heard Bishop Stephen of Autun tell the Count of Nevers that, at the summons of Peter, Abbot of Cluny, and of the monks of Vézelay, he had come to bless Abbot Pontius; this took place in the abbot’s chamber. I often saw Guifred, Bishop of Chartres, and Hugh of Auxerre, formerly Abbot of Saint-Germain, celebrating Mass in the Church of Saint Mary Magdalene on her feast day, with Stephen of Autun present and offering no objection.”

Anselm, monk of Vézelay, under oath, said:

> “I saw Abbot Pontius entrust the Church of Lower Saint Peter to a priest named Bernard, in both spiritual and temporal matters, and this in chapter. The same abbot entrusted the Church of Upper Saint Peter, for spiritual and temporal matters, to the priest Guy in the presence of the chapter. Likewise, the same abbot entrusted the Church of Saint Stephen to the priest Andrew in chapter. All these things occurred after the agreement made at Molinos.
>
> [Col. 1581C] “Matthew, Bishop of Albano, ordained me deacon and three other monks in the chapel of Saint Lawrence. Hugh, Bishop of Auxerre, formerly Abbot of Saint-Germain, ordained me priest and many others at Pontigny. I saw Henry, Bishop of Autun, received in procession at Vézelay, and many others.”

Hugh of Silviniac, monk and priest, under oath, said:

> “Elias, Bishop of Orléans, ordained me priest in the greater church of Vézelay, along with many other monks, Guy, who is now chaplain, and Renaud Reialta; I saw this myself. In the same year as my ordination, I saw Durand, the messenger of Abbot Pontius, go to Frotmund, Bishop of Nevers, for chrism and oil, and return with chrism and oil.
>
> “Since, by the custom of the monastery of Vézelay, no cleric of the town ought to go to synod without the abbot’s permission, I saw, at the time of a synod, Abbot Pontius summon Sadon and Peter Aumbald, the senior chaplains, and order them not to go to the synod. [Col. 1582A] They obeyed. When the priests asked, near the feast of All Saints, for permission to go to synod, the abbot did not grant it, and they did not go.
>
> “I saw Arnulf of Ferrières, by the abbot’s command, go to Auxerre for chrism and oil and return with chrism and oil. This was after the agreement, and it has now been six years. After the agreement, I saw the altar of Saint Michael in the greater church blessed by Hugh, Bishop of Rouen; and after the agreement I saw Hugh of Auxerre carry out ordinations at Vézelay.
>
> “I saw three marital cases brought before Abbot Pontius: those of Obert Saltarelli and Elizabeth; Aimeric the wax-chandler and the daughter of Blaucart the tailor; and Brother Drogo and the daughter of Peter the merchant. They were decided by the abbot’s authority. [Col. 1582B] In the case of Obert and Elizabeth, the advocate was Ermannus, now archdeacon and archpriest of Avallon. Concerning the grant of the three churches, he states precisely what Anselm, monk of Vézelay, states.”

Hugh of Scola, monk and priest of Vézelay, said:

> “In the time of Abbot Alberic, Hugh, Prior of Moret, took me with several others to Auxerre and had us ordained there by Hugh, formerly Abbot of Pontigny: me as subdeacon and the others in different orders. In the time of Abbot Pontius, Elias, Bishop of Orléans, ordained me deacon and several others in different orders—Guy, now the senior chaplain, and Renaud Raiaza, as priests—and this was in the greater church.
>
> [Col. 1582C] “In the time of Pontius, I saw Humbert of Lyons, then Bishop of Autun, summoned by the same abbot to Vézelay, ordain several in the pilgrims’ church: some as priests, some as deacons, and others in different orders. I saw Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, consecrate the altar of Saint Michael in the greater church, after peace had been restored; and I saw Hugh of Auxerre ordain two men named Guifred as subdeacons.
>
> “Concerning the grant of the three churches, he says exactly what Anselm and Hugh say. I saw Humbert, now Archbishop of Lyons, and Henry, now Bishop of Autun, lodging in the borough of Vézelay and at times in the greater church, and at times being supplied in the borough at their own expense.”

[Col. 1582D] Ursus, under oath, said the same as Hugh of Silviniac concerning chrism and oil, and likewise concerning the synod. Concerning the marital disputes and their decisions, he says the same as Hugh, except that he made no mention of the archpriest of Avallon.

Benedict, the abbot’s cook, under oath, said the same as Hugh, Prior of Moret, concerning the marital case of Arduin and Cecilia; and concerning the marriage of Obert and Elizabeth, the marriage of Aimeric the wax-chandler and the daughter of Blanchard the tailor, and the marriage of Brother Drogo and the daughter of Peter the merchant, he says the same as Hugh of Silviniac, monk and priest.

Alegreth, under oath, said the same concerning the marital case of Obert Saltarelli and Elizabeth, and of Aimeric the wax-chandler and the daughter of Blanchard the tailor, as Hugh of [Col. 1583A] Silviniac and Benedict the cook had said. He also said that a certain woman went to Jerusalem; while she remained there, her husband took another wife. Afterwards the woman returned and claimed her husband. When the case had been heard in the presence of Pontius himself, she was restored to her husband by the judgment and authority of the abbot; but he does not remember their names.

The witnesses of the bishop of Autun are produced. When these had withdrawn, the bishop of Autun produced his witnesses. The first of them, the sworn abbot of St. Margaret’s, said that he had seen on several occasions the priests of Vézelay at the synod of the bishop of Autun; whether continuously or regularly, he did not know. He had seen Sado, Peter, and Bernard—and this in Stephen’s time, Sado and Peter; in Humbert’s time, Bernard. Whether they came by obligation or voluntarily he did not know; whether together, he did not remember. Nevertheless, [Col. 1583B] “I often heard the monks say that they did not go to the synod as a matter of obligation. I heard complaint when the priests of Vézelay did not come, but no punishment or satisfaction. I know that priests suspended by the bishop of Autun were restored by the lord pope, and I saw his letters. At the restoration of peace, I heard the abbot promise that henceforth he would be a faithful friend to the bishop of Autun, and would behave toward him as his predecessors had behaved toward the bishop’s predecessors. I saw that the abbot offered this bishop the privilege of Eugenius; and then the abbot of Cluny said to the bishop of Autun: ‘When there is need, go to Vézelay and act as bishop in the presence of Pontius, abbot of that monastery.’”

John, prior of St. Symphorian, being sworn, said: [Col. 1583C] “I saw Humbert, bishop of Autun, celebrate Mass at Vézelay and preach a sermon, on a certain solemn occasion; and at the time of the synod I saw Sado and Peter at Autun, and believe that they came to the synod.” Concerning the restoration of peace, he said that he had heard from someone that the bishop was to go to Vézelay and perform his office there, after the restoration of peace.

Eberard, archpriest, being sworn, said: “I saw Stephen, bishop of Autun, celebrate high Masses on Easter Day and on the feast of Mary Magdalene, at least twice. On the day of St. Mary Magdalene, when the bishop of Autun celebrated Mass, the bishop of Chartres was there and himself preached to the people, while the bishop of Autun gave the blessing. The same Stephen dedicated [Col. 1583D] the Church of the Pilgrims while Pope Innocent was at Vézelay; at what time this was, I do not know. The same man dedicated the altar of the monks’ choir and the altar of the chapel of St. Stephen; I saw him bless Alberic of Auxerre, and I saw Pontius blessed by the same man; and I saw the ordinations of monks and clerics performed by the same Stephen in the Church of the Pilgrims, once.

“I saw Bellinus, Angilbert, Sado, and Bernard, chaplains of the Lower Church; Peter Grael, Blain, Sado, and Guy, of the Upper Church, come regularly to the synod, except in two years: the present year and the year when there was a dispute between Humbert, bishop of Autun, and Abbot Pontius, over ordinations [Col. 1584A] performed there by the bishop of Orléans; and this for thirty years. The same is true of chrism and oil. Concerning the peace, I say the same as the abbot, except that he did not say the words, ‘Go to Vézelay.’ But later I saw the bishop perform ordinations there once; and I saw two clerics, Bonnamicus and Peter, wishing to be ordained, carry letters from the bishop of Autun to the bishop of Auxerre. I saw two chaplains—namely, those of St. Stephen and St. James of Esconia—come to the synod of Autun, once at least.

“I, the same Eberard the archpriest, saw two offences of clerics punished, namely those of Blandinus the sub-chaplain and Mainard of Esconia; and I saw Angelbert, chaplain of Lower St. Peter’s, receive the cure of souls from Lambert, priest of Avallon; and Bernard receive it from Humbert of Autun. I heard him say—for he wanted the abbot not to know—that Peter, Andrew, Sado’s chaplain, and Walter of Esconia [Col. 1584B] brought me their parishioners to receive penance for crimes; and this often and by the ancient custom of the land. For forty years I saw parishioners from the town of Vézelay, one from each house, come to the church of Avallon, where each pays the Church a coin, or a coin’s worth of wax. I saw Sado and Peter receive the cure of souls from Stephen, bishop of Autun. I saw Rainald, archbishop of Lyons, perform ordinations there, both of monks and of clerics. I saw that the abbot of Vézelay sent his monks to whichever bishop he wished for ordination. I saw the founder’s charter, which I read before Pope Innocent, [Col. 1584C] and which stated that the monastery was free from every monetary exaction except one pound of silver offered annually to the Church of St. Peter. When it had been read, the lord pope said to the bishop: ‘Go; do what is yours.’ And I saw that for forty years past the Church of St. Peter paid five shillings annually to the Church of Autun as a provision.”

Arnulf, being sworn, said: “I saw Bishop Stephen bless a certain altar in the Church of St. Stephen. Yet I do not know which altar it was, since there are several there. The same man blessed the altar of the choir in the Church of St. Mary. The same man blessed the Church of the Pilgrims, and Pope Innocent was there, as I believe. In that same church he performed ordinations of monks [Col. 1584D] and clerics of that town and of others from his diocese. And when I was serving in the place of the archpriest, I saw Bishop Aganon going to Vézelay to perform ordinations, and saw clerics returning who said that they had been ordained. I heard that on the following day after the ordinations he dedicated the Church of Esconia.

“The same Stephen celebrated high Masses at Vézelay on the Resurrection of the Lord and on the feast of St. Mary Magdalene; the bishop of Chartres preached, and the bishop of Autun gave the blessing. This happened several times in my sight. For thirty-five consecutive years I saw the priests of Vézelay come to the synod of Autun. Some of their names are these: Blandinus, Sado, Peter Grandella, Peter Armenbald, and Guy. I saw [Col. 1585A] Bishop Narigald received by the monks of Vézelay in procession. I saw Stephen bless Alberic at Auxerre, but I do not remember in which church.”

Walter, archpriest, being sworn, said that Bishop Stephen blessed Abbot Pontius and blessed the altar of the choir. Concerning the agreement, he said the same as the others; and afterwards he performed ordinations in the Church of St. Peter, and Stephen confirmed everyone there. He saw the priests of Vézelay come many times to the synod of Autun, including Guy and Bernard, who are now living; and for ten years he received five shillings as a provision, and each household paid one coin for the crosses. He saw this once and heard it many times. He also heard that the abbot of Vézelay sent monks to whatever bishop he wished for ordination.

[Col. 1585B] Walter the priest, being sworn, said that for thirty years past he had seen the clerics of Vézelay seek chrism from the archpriest of Avallon, except in the present year and the year of the dispute. Who the messengers were he did not know. He saw the Church of the Pilgrims blessed by Bishop Stephen while Pope Innocent was staying in the town; at what time this was, he did not know, and the abbot was there, though he did not know his name. The same bishop consecrated the altar of the choir of the greater church; which consecration came first, he did not know. He saw Landric, Peter, and Angibert come to the synod of Autun for thirty years. He saw Angilbert receive the cure of souls from the archpriest of Avallon. For [Col. 1585C] thirty years he saw Peter Gradella, Sado, Blandinus, and their successors come to the synod. He saw the Church of Lower St. Peter pay the episcopal officers’ provision for thirty years. He saw Blain, chaplain of Sado, punished by the archpriest of Avallon for his offences; likewise Mainard and Walter of Walteria. And he heard that the abbot of Vézelay sent monks wherever he wished to be ordained.

John Gentilis, being sworn, said that for thirty years he had seen the clerics of the Church of St. Peter, both Upper and Lower, come to the synod, though not regularly. He saw Angilbert of the Lower Church receive the cure of souls from Lambert, archpriest of Avallon. He heard Peter, Arebald, and [Col. 1585D] Sado say that they had received the cure of souls from Bishop Stephen, but did not see it. He saw the chaplains of Vézelay receive chrism from the archpriest of Avallon and at Montreuil for thirty years, though not continuously; and he saw Peter Gradella request an archpriest from Bishop Stephen at the synod, and the latter granted the present one. Concerning Blaiv’s offence, he says the same as the others. He saw the cross-money paid, and saw the chaplains of Vézelay bring their parishioners to receive penance from the archpriest of Avallon. Concerning the dedication of the Church of the Pilgrims he says the same; concerning the bishop’s celebration of Masses, likewise the same as the others.

Bonusamicus says the same in every respect as Gentilis, except for the present year and the year of the dispute.

[Col. 1586A] Geoffrey, being sworn, said that he often saw Sado and Peter come to the synod in the time of Stephen, and Bernard and Guy in the time of the present Humbert; and he saw a cleric of Vézelay request from the bishop permission to be ordained.

Constantine, being sworn, said that he often went to the synod with the clerics of Vézelay, and that a cleric of Vézelay was ordained by letters from the bishop of Autun.

Geoffrey, bishop of Nevers, before the holy Gospels placed before him, said: “I saw that Stephen, bishop of Autun, whether summoned or sometimes unsummoned, was received at Vézelay as bishop; sometimes he was entertained by the monks, sometimes at his own expense. On the feast of Blessed Mary Magdalene he often celebrated [Col. 1586B] solemn Masses with certain other bishops present. Once, while the bishop of Autun was celebrating the solemnities, the bishop of Chartres preached. I saw the same Stephen bless Abbot Alberic at Auxerre; the same Stephen consecrated the Church of the Pilgrims while Pope Innocent was at Vézelay. At another time the same Stephen blessed the altar in the monks’ choir; at another time he blessed the altar in the Church of St. Stephen. I was present when peace was restored between Autun and Vézelay through the mediation of Cluny, where in conclusion the bishop of Autun was told: ‘Go to Vézelay and perform your ministry.’ But whether the abbot said this or someone else on his behalf, I do not recall.

“On another occasion Abbot Pontius, coming from Rome with Humbert of Autun, was afterwards received at Autun with a procession by that bishop and his clerics, although the bishop had preceded him. [Col. 1586C] Then, coming into the chapter-house of Autun, the abbot promised friendship and affection to the bishop of Autun according to the custom of his predecessors.”

Humbert of Lyons, before the holy Gospels placed before him, said: “When I was bishop of Autun, I went unsummoned to Vézelay and celebrated the solemnities of Mass in the greater church at Easter, believing that I was exercising my episcopal right; I preached to the people and gave the blessing, with another bishop present.” Concerning the agreement, he says precisely the same as the bishop of Nevers, except that he affirms that the abbot said to him: “Go and do at Vézelay what your predecessors [Col. 1586D] were accustomed to do.” Afterwards, when summoned, I celebrated ordinations at Vézelay, both of monks and of clerics of the town, and of certain clerics of my diocese. On another occasion, while celebrating ordinations at Autun, I examined and promoted clerics of Vézelay with my other clerics according to custom. Throughout the time I was bishop, the clerics of Vézelay came to my synod annually, or sent an excuse. The archpriest of Avallon brought to me at Vézelay a man of Bourges who had dismissed his wife because of sterility; I ordered him to compel the man of Bourges, as justice dictated, to take back his wife.

Having thus completed their testimonies, the witnesses of Autun withdrew. Their depositions, if carefully weighed, are shown to investigate the case of Autun rather than [Col. 1587A] support it. For the celebration of Masses, the consecration of altars, the conferral of orders, the granting of blessings, the request for holy oil or chrism, and other matters of that kind were allowed, by the liberal permission and at the discretion of Vézelay’s liberty, to a neighboring and fellow-provincial bishop just as to a stranger. What therefore is shared by him with others does not accrue to him as a peculiar right.

Moreover, by testifying that those suspended by the bishop of Autun were restored to their orders through apostolic liberty, they make the case for Vézelay and utterly destroy their own—that is, Autun’s. Their assertions that Vézelay’s clerics frequented the synod of Autun, requested from the bishop of Autun permission for ordination, received from him the cure of souls, paid the provision, and brought their parishioners to the archpriests [Col. 1587B] for penance, reveal, if it is permitted to say so, both the fraudulence of the priests and the rashness of the bishop of Autun. They admit that these acts were carried out, indeed, without Vézelay’s knowledge; and thus a grave charge is brought against the plaintiff, which rests upon clandestine encroachments.

Accordingly, after the witnesses of both sides had testified as stated above, the supreme pope decreed that the controversy in so great a lawsuit should be settled by judgment. Since the supreme fear is evidence of a guilty conscience, it sometimes happens that a mind, reduced by extreme dangers, is compelled to consider what in peace it had formerly in some measure disdained to foresee. Thus, with the case placed at a critical point, the bishop of Autun, conscious of his own rashness, was troubled. [Col. 1587C] Since he knew well that Roman equity was fixed solely upon the rule of legal justice, he began to waver and could not conceal himself; nonetheless, he asked for the judgment to be postponed, saying that he still had most effective witnesses to support his case, but that they were weakened by sickness and age and could not undertake the labor of so great a journey. Yet, if a hearing were provided for him within Gaul at a suitable place and day, he promised without doubt to produce them; and after their testimony, at a date appointed in his presence, he would unquestionably submit himself from that time to the apostolic sentence—unless meanwhile the desired peace should intervene.

Then the man of Vézelay, judging the adjournment unnecessary and seeing that the bishop of Autun hoped rather in indulgence of time than in the strength of his case, [Col. 1587D] urgently demanded an oath or a judgment of law. Yet apostolic clemency prevailed, and at last the judgment was postponed. A day was fixed for the renewed sentence, and bishops were designated within Gaul as deputies to assist his witnesses: namely, Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, and Peter, abbot of Tournus, and Stephen, abbot of Réigny. By letters he ordered them to undertake, at a fitting day and place, the aforesaid case between Autun and Vézelay; to hear, under the prescribed form of oath, the witnesses whom the bishop of Autun should lawfully produce; and to send their written testimonies, sealed with the protection of their seals, through the same persons to him on the appointed day of judgment. The text of this letter is contained above in the series of letters [Col. 1588A] which he issued to various persons for the protection of Vézelay’s liberty.

Indeed, Pope Eugenius, of incomparable memory, in pious concern for future contingencies, ordered the testimonies of both parties to be written down on three schedules. One he gave to the bishop, another to the abbot, and the third he deposited in his archives, so that, if this same controversy should perhaps again be agitated in the presence either of himself or of his successor, the recorded testimonies, like living voices, might refute every novelty, and neither a judgment nor the altered succession of the litigants might be deceived by substituted witnesses. These matters having been transacted, each returned home.

But the bishop of Autun, having obtained the desired delay, sought to conceal the matter at issue and to gain time, [Col. 1588B] and took no concern whatever for the matters which he had promised the supreme pontiff as grounds for the postponement. Since the abbot bore with difficulty these delays, which he perceived to create an obstruction to his case rather than an end to the lawsuit, he approached the bishop of Langres, who happened one day to have arrived at Vézelay, and asked him concerning the pope’s mandate. He replied that the man who had brought the action ought rather to make this request, since one often renounces a lawsuit by keeping silent; but the bishop of Autun had not yet said anything to him about this affair.

Meanwhile, Eugenius, apostolic bishop of the holy see, of holy memory, entered upon the way of all flesh. Anastasius, vicar of the Holy Roman Church, succeeded him. When he learned this, the man of Vézelay, fearing that the old enemy might forestall the face [Col. 1588C] of the new prelate, wrote to him at once, explaining how greatly the Church of Vézelay had always been esteemed, even to that day, in the eyes of all the apostolic bishops who had preceded him. He further begged that, after the example of his fathers, the Roman pontiffs, he would defend the Church of Vézelay, as the proper right and freehold of St. Peter, from the assaults of its attackers, and especially at that time from the bishop of Autun’s rash presumption. He described how the case both of the bishop and of Vézelay had been argued in the presence of his predecessor Eugenius of pious memory, but had remained unresolved because the bishop requested a deferred day of legal judgment. Finally, he prayed that Anastasius’s piety might renew in his presence the date for sentence which had lapsed through the judge’s death, and summon the bishop of Autun.

At last the abbot makes peace with the bishop of Autun. Therefore the holy apostolic lord, accepting the prayers of the special patron of the church, ordered the renewal of the case of both parties and prescribed the fifteenth day after Easter for each, unless by mutual consent peace between the churches should meanwhile be restored, so that what his predecessor had left unresolved might, through God’s action, be brought by him to a good conclusion.

Then the stiff neck, twisting itself about as if struck by unexpected darts, despairing now of its cause, approached the duke; and now he negotiated with his brother for his own peace, though formerly he had negotiated with him for another’s oppression. Fearing that, while he coveted another’s possessions, he might be compelled to lose his own, he renounced the contest and considered restoring peace. He who until then had endeavored to usurp another’s rights by himself [Col. 1589A] now hastened to secure his own interests through others’ mediation. So that brotherly malice might not be suspected, the duke himself and the bishop appealed to men of religious life and honorable reputation—namely, the abbot of Cîteaux and several others of that order. They approached Pontius, abbot of Vézelay, offered with supplication the duke’s prayers, and, on behalf of the bishop, proposed and sought peace. Nor did they deserve to be refused, since among noble spirits the strictness of rectitude is always accompanied by the gentleness of meekness. Therefore the abbot yielded humbly to one who had not yielded to arrogant pride; and, through their mediation, peace was restored between the two churches by the duke’s hand, every controversy was reconciled, they gave each other kisses of friendship, [Col. 1589B] and entered into a covenant of perpetual peace. In order that this settlement of peace might remain inviolate even among their successors, he made a charter in his own hand and confirmed it with the protection of his seal, as the following document proves.

> “Let it be known to those present and to posterity that I, Henry, by the grace of God bishop of Autun, with the counsel of religious persons and certain brothers of our church, have wished the controversy and complaint long debated between Autun and Vézelay to be ended by a friendly settlement on these terms: that both I and Pontius, abbot of the aforesaid church, may remain and continue in good peace and concord, with the right during my lifetime and the privileges of both [Col. 1589C] churches preserved.
>
> “I decree, moreover, that the aforesaid agreement or settlement shall remain valid during my lifetime, in such a way that after my death neither church shall suffer any prejudice from it. Witnesses from both sides are: William, abbot of Fontenay; Hugh, abbot of Bussière; Peter, abbot of Mont-Saint-Jean; Otbert, abbot of St. Margaret’s; Master Otbert; Signinus of Ligniac; Gislebert, prior of Oisey; Girard Buca; Hugh of Moncellis; and many others.”

These things concerning the liberty of the Church of Vézelay we have briefly set forth, according to the measure of our small ability, with as much truth as we could, entrusting fuller—but perhaps not truer—treatment to greater leisure. In truth, we believe that we have done enough for the sons and lovers of this church; by brevity, moreover, we have taken care to accommodate the scoffers of such matters. For some are accustomed [Note: [Col. 1589C] “Are accustomed.” Thus restored; the printed text had “Always.”] to be angered at those who write useful things, whether captivated by envy of deeds or ignorant of what is brought forward. Yet just as the leisure of a wise person judges nothing idle, but regards another’s leisure as his own duty, [Col. 1590B] so conversely it is the chief business of a fool to ascribe to idleness whatever prudent study has labored to produce. Weighing this at its proper value, we adopted brevity and drove our pen swiftly.

Though the Church has brought us forth younger in age than the times, this does not diminish our devotion toward her, if with wholly sincere affection we devote whatever power we have to her advancement. Nor do we doubt that she herself will supply strength—she who supplied both will and grace—provided we are permitted to live without reproach. But because certain persons, mercenaries in place but not sons by nature, seeking their own advantage and not the interests of the office they have received, pursue private gain in a common cause, or under the pretext of a common cause, we have kept our mind so clear from this kind of corruption [Col. 1590C] that, with the sole and simple regard for the common good, we have labored for the common good unto the common good. Indeed, we have placed our hope in him alone and toward him alone, who decrees that no good shall remain unrewarded from age to age and unto eternity.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 1589]

[Col. 1589D]

> Pontius, the most renowned virtue among the abbots of the realm,  
> ruled the flock of Vézelay by lot.  
> And while he prepared for himself the instruments of good morals,  
> while he provided for the Church entrusted to him,  
> a mob more turbulent than all others stirred up envy—  
> a seditious band of servants against its lord;  
> a people armed with fraud, a duke both leader and path for treachery,  
> skilled in breaking doors and plundering homes;  
> daring thereafter to launch an assault upon sacred buildings  
> and to lay sacrilegious hands upon the lord, to his death.  
> What evils, what disasters would unjust frenzy have brought about,  
> had the prudent abbot not brought swift help?  
> If, reader, you seek to know the causes of these events,  
> the page of this book will disclose the way.  
> Our Hugh, a man Pictavian by lineage,  
> [Col. 1590D] chose freely to set this before you in mind and hand.  
> Read through it: you will learn how well, how wisely,  
> and how brilliantly the work proceeds in its proper order.  
> Be silent, envious tongue, to whom virtue is an enemy,  
> whose constant desire is to harm the good.

At the command of Abbot Pontius the author undertook this work. A most famous proverb of a certain Greek is said to have been found on Apollo’s tripod: “Know yourself, and see yourself.” Nothing in human nature is clearer, more precious, or indeed more excellent than these two things. For through them man is set above all passible beings by a singular prerogative, and by a connected unity is joined also to impassible beings. To know oneself is to know and understand the condition of one’s own dignity; to see oneself is [Col. 1591A] to cultivate that dignity by the purity of faith and the worship of piety.

Since what we intend belongs to the first of the aforesaid kinds, namely knowledge, we have dealt, as briefly as we could, in the preceding book with the dignity of Vézelay. There, while we strove to commend matters rather than display words, we sailed as though ploughing the surface of a calm sea, knowing that the devout reader would infer from the surface of the words the weight of the subject. But since certain men, trusting in audacity rather than relying on virtue, attempted with dog-like mouth to tear, or with beastly foot to rend, the garments of the aforesaid liberty or dignity—that is, the possessions of the Church—it pleased our most serene and valiant father, the venerable Abbot Pontius, to commit to writing for future ages [Col. 1591B] how and in what manner, by divine providence, the efforts of the rival came to nothing and the Church shone more brightly through its very calamities.

We do not devote ourselves to this task as idle men exercising some peculiar talent, whose desire would be to attend to our own rather than another’s instruction. Rather, we are moved by the integrity of our contemporaries, the benefit of those who come after, and the dignity of Mother Church. We are also moved by the irresistible command of the aforesaid father, who fought for this same liberty and dignity even unto blood. Although the assailant did not achieve his criminal purpose, nothing was lacking in him by which he might almost wholly devote himself to the Church’s immunity and neglect his own safety for hers.

Burning with chaste love for this Church, his bride, he zealously arranged her rights for several years [Col. 1591C] and administered them most vigorously. Yet, through Fortune’s envy, he perceived her violated by the stain of a corrupt union. Then, stirred by zeal and standing in opposition for the house of Israel, he offered himself as a barrier to adulterous gazes and, through many dangers to his life, made the pure liberty of his bride more conspicuous and manifest. With God helping our weakness and the authority of that father strengthening our littleness, we shall take care to make this known in what follows, according to our custom of brevity, so that those now living may have something in which to delight and those to come may know what to emulate.

Since it belongs to the devout to seek the common rather than private advantage, we too have labored to provide for the advancement of those to come [Col. 1591D] and to extend the garment of charity down to the heel. Let the devout reader, therefore, read this devout work devoutly; let the whisperer and detractor stand far away. Whoever dislikes our writings will be judged either an illegitimate son, if indeed he is worthy of the name of son, or a household servant—let us not say an enemy of the Church. For if the ancients deemed fit to consign to memory old wives’ tales or monstrous prodigies merely to display elegant talent, and if these are sometimes read even in our times not without profit, we believe it will be much more welcome and fruitful for future generations to know both the truth of events and the honorable nature of their result. We by no means present such matters as though disdaining the scrutiny of brotherly charity; rather, let what may perhaps have overflowed through excess be removed, and likewise let what escaped our knowledge or the brevity of our pen be supplied. In both respects we appeal to simple goodwill, by which we have neither been ashamed of our poverty nor neglected the labor of so great a burden.

### On the immunity and nobility of the Church of Vézelay

[Col. 1592A] Origin of Vézelay’s liberty. Since the Church of Vézelay possessed liberty through the founder’s gift and the prerogative of Roman authority, and was especially eminent through the oracle of God’s blessed beloved and handmaid Mary Magdalene, who is said to lie buried there and is proclaimed and adored throughout the world, many people flocked to it from many regions. By their own abundance and by the affluence of goods they made that town illustrious and renowned. Its estates too, being very extensive and contiguous, made the place itself so pleasant in situation and so [Col. 1592B] rich that it shone conspicuously to the ends of the earth and stood out gloriously throughout the world.

The body of this place was joined and bound with such great and special affection to the Church, the head of its proprietary right, that in any part of itself it shrank from admitting anyone’s share in lordship or partnership, as something profane and an incitement to insolence. Standing through apostolic grace in the freehold of its testator, it bowed its neck under no bond of servitude to anyone except the apostolic pontiff. Whoever directs the chaste eyes of ingenuous simplicity toward knowledge of this complete liberty should reread the founder’s testament after reading it through, as well as [Col. 1592C] the privileges of the Roman pontiffs of primitive and ancient authority—namely, the venerable Nicholas; both Johns; Benedict and another Benedict; Leo; Sergius; Stephen; Marinus; and Urban of holy memory, who, raised from the monastery of Cluny to the administration of the apostolate, willed that the privileges and decrees of his predecessors concerning the liberty of the aforesaid monastery of Vézelay should not merely remain inviolate, valid, and unshaken, but also confirmed them with the protection of his own authority.

Having diligently examined all these documents, one will certainly find nothing contrary or inconsistent, nor prove them in any respect fictitious or fraudulent. For it is surely impious and sacrilegious to suppose that apostolic [Col. 1592D] men decreed things contrary to one another, or contradicted themselves by what may be alleged on the opposite side. Count Gerard of blessed memory, with his devout wife Bertha, out of fear of God and for the salvation of himself and his people, founded a monastery above the River Cure, on his own wholly free freehold, and established there a community of women servants of God. By a testamentary charter he entrusted that monastery, with all the goods bestowed upon it, to the most blessed princes of the apostles and to their successors through the ages in the Roman see, to be possessed and defended forever; he removed and entirely excluded every person’s authority, held by way of benefice, to grant or exchange it.

But because that monastery [Col. 1593A] had almost been destroyed by repeated Saracen raids, lest hostile envy prevail against devout purposes, the same count rebuilt it on the adjacent hill or fortress of Vézelay. The female sex having been exchanged for males, Eudo became the first abbot of servants of God.

### Summary of the apostolic privileges

The Roman see, gratefully and kindly receiving the piety of such devotion in this count, chose to enroll that monastery among the proper right and freehold of St. Peter and to protect it, enlarged by the grace and gift of apostolic authority. For in granting privileges of this kind by decree of their apostolic authority, the Roman pontiffs conceded and confirmed them, and decreed that no emperor, king, bishop, or person endowed with any [Col. 1593B] dignity whatsoever might, under the pretext of any cause or occasion, diminish, take away, apply to his own uses, or grant to others—even for supposedly pious causes used as an excuse for his avarice—anything that had been bestowed upon the monastery by that count or anyone else from their own right. Rather, such property was to be possessed inviolate and without disturbance by those living religiously in that place.

This was on the condition that none of the Roman pontiffs, anywhere or at any time, should allow any portion of those same possessions to be bestowed as a benefice, exchanged, granted subject to rent, or retained for the future. The Roman see was only to receive from the monastery [Col. 1593C] annually the rent of one pound of silver specified in the testamentary act of transfer, and was diligently to provide, in the solicitude of pastoral care, the support of pious fatherhood against every attacker.

The apostolic see further decreed that, an abbot having been elected without any deceptive contrivance by the common consent of the brothers or the counsel of the sounder part of that monastery, and approved by the Roman prelate, no bishop, king, or faithful person, ecclesiastical or secular, should dare, personally or through a subordinate agent, to receive or claim any right in respect of his installation, or of the ordination of monks, clerics, or priests; the granting of chrism; the consecration of a church; or any benefit of spiritual or temporal service.

[Col. 1593D] Once the apostolic privileges had thus been arranged, the majesty of the kings of the Franks also graciously provided for that monastery. Favoring the prayers of the illustrious Count Gerard, it ordered an edict to be issued to the monastery declaring that whatever the decree of the apostolic see had deliberately established by sanction should remain unshaken forever, without any scruple of contradiction. It commanded that no secular person, including royal agents, should impose lodging by authority upon the aforesaid monastery, the aforementioned fortress, or the villages belonging to that place; nor should any such person exact provisions, *freda* [judicial fines], *cespitaticum* [a ground-rent or turf-dues], *pontaticum* [bridge-toll], or any impost to be rendered by it.

Whoever presumed to violate this decree of immunity was to be compelled to pay a fine of six hundred shillings: one half [Col. 1594A] to the royal fisc and one half to the Church against which he had brought suit. In order that this command of their authority might possess fuller force of validity, they confirmed it with their own hand and authenticated it by the impression of their seal.

## Many Envy Vézelay’s Freedom. Count William of Nevers Attempts to Usurp the Rights of the Monastery of Vézelay.

Under the full integrity of such great liberty and immunity, the new plantation put forth shoots from new turf and, in the green fruitfulness of its branches, drew very many provinces to itself. But since, among the other vices which human nature contracted in the transgression of the first parent, the stain of envy has infected the human race more grievously, many persons corrupted by this plague, both among the neighboring ecclesiastical and secular powers, attempted to strip the aforesaid monastery of the robe of liberty [Col. 1594B] and deprive it of the glory of its nobility. They spoke wickedness from heart to heart, devised iniquity together, and, passing into the desire of their hearts, carried away the disgrace of their own confusion.

For although at different times, either jointly or in succession, they endeavored to harass, disturb, and trouble the peace of the sacred monastery, and did not fear to afflict in many ways and by many means the eminent Fathers of that monastery, men of great authority, yet that wicked and viperous generation poured out all the venom of its malice and the whole power of its perversity upon Pons, the most distinguished and prudent abbot of our age. In pouring it out, they wasted away and failed; they were disembowelled and brought to nothing.

For the pious solicitude [Col. 1594C] of the abbots of Vézelay, because of the frequent attacks of wicked men, often bestowed voluntary service with most generous indulgence upon the counts of the city of Nevers, so that they might more devotedly bring aid to the Church against all opponents—a Church which was subject to them by no right, yet diligently bestowed free benefits upon them. But a degenerate spirit always abuses benefits and sometimes becomes more insolent through gratuitous services; nor is service counted as a favor when it is granted to an ungrateful person.

Thus it happened that William, who later became a monk at the Charterhouse, while he held the office of count of the city of Nevers, insolently abusing stipends and other benefits of the Church, sought by tyrannical force to exact from it certain customary dues hostile not only to peace but even to liberty [Col. 1594D]. The venerable abbot Pons, scorning his insolence, reasonably denied what was unjustly demanded and prudently preserved what was forcibly exacted.

Grieved at having been thus repulsed, the count of Nevers blazed into such anger that he diverted the royal highways away from Vézelay and forbade public traffic to the village. Then, since the man of Vézelay could not bend the count from his purpose either by a benefit or by earnest entreaty, he reported to the holy mother, the apostolic see of the Roman Church, the oppression of his monastery and explained with what tyranny the count was persecuting the right or allod of blessed Peter.

The supreme pontiff, writing repeatedly to that count, admonished him to desist from persecuting his special daughter, the Church of Vézelay [Col. 1595A]. He commanded him also to provide, out of reverence for blessed Peter, for its peace and liberty by showing it favor, lest, if he presumed to usurp apostolic rights, he should be judged an enemy and violator of the universal Church. If he believed that any right in that monastery belonged to him, he was not to distrust apostolic favor, provided that he did not trouble the Church’s peace; otherwise, if he persisted to the contrary, he should not suppose that he would escape bearing the weight of the apostolic staff.

The same prelate also warned the man of Vézelay by apostolic authority not to yield to anyone in any respect concerning the monastery’s right, nor presume to overstep the boundaries established by the Fathers; rather, he was to trust in the help of God and blessed Peter and fight manfully for the Church, lest, by allowing the Church’s integrity to be stained, he should prove a traitor to that integrity [Col. 1595B].

## Arbitrators of the Dispute Between the Abbot of Vézelay and the Count of Nevers. The Man of Nevers States His Claim; the Man of Vézelay Replies and Refutes Him.

The controversy between Vézelay and Nevers having thus long continued, they finally came to this: by mutual agreement, abbot and count submitted themselves to the judgment and concord—or decision—of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, Hugh of Tilly, and those whom they themselves might wish to call to this settlement, so that they would observe without dispute whatever those persons should decide unanimously on this matter.

Accordingly, on the solemn feast day of Easter, when nearly all Gaul had gathered at Vézelay in greater numbers than usual because of the multitude of pilgrims [Col. 1595C], and also out of reverence for the most pious and religious King Louis the Younger, who there took upon his own shoulders the banner of the Lord’s cross as he was about to journey to Jerusalem, the count likewise came with the persons already mentioned. On the appointed day, namely Wednesday within the octave of Easter, they assembled at Bussières, the Church’s grange. The count began his complaint as follows:

“The Church of Vézelay,” he said, “is under my advocacy. I wish that, whenever I command the abbot, he shall render justice to me and my men according to the judgment of my court; he ought not refuse. And if anyone wishes to say against him that he has denied him justice, he ought to defend himself according to the ruling that I give.”

To this the abbot replied that he ought by no means to do so, because he did not hold the abbey of Vézelay from the aforesaid count [Col. 1595D]. Since he was a monk, priest, and abbot, he was unwilling to submit himself to lay judgment; nor ought he or his monks receive sentence through persons of this kind.

The count again claimed that the people of Vézelay belonging to the Church were subject to his jurisdiction; and that whenever he pleased, he might command the abbot to bring them to his court for the compulsory acceptance of judgment. If, perhaps, some complaint arose between those people and the abbot, the same count said that they ought to reach agreement only through his hand, and only in the abbot’s court.

The abbot replied that the Church of Vézelay had not been founded by him or by his ancestors, that its people were not of his fief, and that neither abbot nor Church held them from him [Col. 1596A]. It was therefore unworthy that they should be subject to the judgment of one through whose benefice they did not hold anything.

Concerning the reconciliation of the burgesses, he said that nothing could be more unjust than the proposal which he had heard, or more contrary to truth and every justice, since peace is common to all, and the blessed feet of those who proclaim peace are declared in the divine Scriptures and by the holy Fathers; nor had this or any similar custom existed in the Church from ancient times.

Again the count said that, when his men from Clamecy came to the fair or market at Vézelay, they laid down their merchandise in its streets and claimed exemption from the customary dues paid by other persons; he therefore complained that the abbot’s toll collectors exacted these dues from them by force.

The abbot replied [Col. 1596B] that from ancient times the Church had held the streets for its own use and that no one possessed any exempt right there. Since all persons arriving at the fair or market of Vézelay gladly paid toll according to the different kinds of merchandise, he wished these men likewise to render the customary dues, since they did not say by what justice they ought to retain exemption.

Then Hugh of Tilly testified that the count had no right in this complaint, because in the time of lord Renaud, abbot of Vézelay and later archbishop of Lyons, the count himself had raised a complaint concerning this matter. Having received money from that abbot through the hand of Hugh of Tilly, he had wholly abandoned the claim and faithfully promised never thereafter to pursue it [Col. 1596C].

Again the count claimed the road running from Escouains as far as Blannay, that from Précy, and other roads established from the crosses and boundary markers as far as Vézelay. The abbot answered that the road from Vergigny—which the count claimed from Escouains to Blannay—had belonged to Hervé of Donzy and Savaric of Vergigny, lords of the castle of Censois. They gave and sold that road, and the whole land of Vergigny with all its appurtenances—namely running waters and everything else which they possessed hereditarily as an allod—to abbot Artald of blessed memory and to the Church of Vézelay. Before many witnesses, they offered it upon the altar of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul to God, blessed Mary Magdalene, and those apostles, with all its appurtenances [Col. 1596D].

For forty years and more, the Church of Vézelay had until then possessed that whole land peacefully and entirely, without any claim, by hereditary right. It hanged there thieves captured on the public road, administered justice upon other evildoers, and peacefully held without violence whatever was found there.

The land of Précy, moreover, had been an allod of the duke of Burgundy. Certain knights held it from him and gave and sold it to blessed Mary Magdalene.
