From that time until the present, therefore, both the Church and abbot of Vézelay had held and possessed in peace, without any interruption, that entire land and the public road within and outside the town, together with its public roads and paths.

The abbot had and named many witnesses regarding this and the other matters mentioned above: namely Martin [Col. 1597A] and his brothers of Précy, and many others living in the town. They said that they had seized six thieves carrying counterfeit coin on the road and delivered them to the provost at Vézelay for justice to be done. Moreover, they had rendered to Renaud, monk of Précy, who was then dwelling there, a cow found on the public road without an owner, as the right of the Church required. The aforesaid men were ready to prove all this without delay.

Regarding the other roads—namely those from Fontenay, Crai, Mont Tirohet, and the rest running as far as Vézelay—the abbot replied that his predecessors had held their jurisdiction over them long and extensively without challenge. Those roads also passed along the Church’s route. Concerning all of them he had many witnesses: Guinimer, once dean [Col. 1597B]; Gerard, dean; Hugh, provost; Renaud Dautran; Renaud of Saint Christopher; William of Pont and his brother Jonah; Arnulf of Ferrières; Robert of Monterohillone; Guy Forester; Duran of the village of Lohet; Duran of Chastenay; Constance, provost of Fontenay; Stephen, provost of Blannay; Aimon the Moneyer; Bonamicus of the castle of Censois; Geoffrey Bertin; Blanchard of Sarcitorium; Stephen Beurand; Odo of “fair likeness”; and many others.

All these matters had been confirmed by the supreme pontiff to be held forever; and, under anathema, it had been forbidden that anyone should trouble the Church or abbot concerning them [Col. 1597C]. Such were the count’s complaints, and such their rebuttals by the abbot.

## The Abbot’s Charges and the Count’s Replies.

After this the abbot complained of the aforesaid count because, along the public road from Auxerre to Vézelay, he diverted all pedlars and merchants and did not permit them to go to Vézelay. The count replied that he had formerly done so and that no abbot had challenged him about it.

The abbot countered that the road leading to Vézelay was as much a royal, public, ancient road as that to Nevers, and safer; it was unjust to turn travellers back from the road which seemed easier and better to them, especially since more gathered there for prayer than for commerce.

Again the abbot complained of the count’s toll collectors [Col. 1597D], who continually plundered his people travelling through Auxerre, saying that the abbot ought, on three feasts—Easter, Pentecost, and the feast of blessed Mary Magdalene—to provide for them with all their companions, and to give each a pound-weight of wax in payment for the toll on Auxerre wine which he customarily bought. The count replied that these servants of his possessed this custom in the Church, established by abbot Renaud. The abbot said that he did not know of this custom; even if it were true, it had not been made with the counsel of the chapter and therefore neither could nor ought to be valid or binding.

## The Count’s Sons Set Out for Jerusalem with the King. The Count Himself Assumes the Monastic Habit at the Charterhouse and Is Afterwards Devoured by a Dog.

After the most pious King Louis the Younger had taken the sign of the Lord’s cross in order to set out for Jerusalem, many people, stirred by the report and example of this deed, undertook the pilgrimage overseas. Among them, too, the two sons of the count of Nevers, William and Renaud, joined the royal company and undertook the same journey.

Their father himself likewise, changing his former life through desire for another, received the religious habit and the end of his life at the Charterhouse [Col. 1598A]. But because he had unjustly harassed and afflicted the glorious sepulchre, most holy in devotion, of Mary Magdalene, the venerable beloved and servant of God, he received the punishment for his crime by being devoured by a dog, and left the vengeance for his injustice to his heirs.

For Renaud shamefully suffered the misery of captivity and was unhappily delivered into the slavery of a barbarian people, so that the father who had tried to corrupt the liberty of the Church of Vézelay might experience in his son the disgrace of servitude. William, however, heir to his father’s county and crime, suffered shipwreck while returning from Jerusalem and was in peril of his life.

When the facts had been laid out and, now at the point of death, he was urged by all those standing around to relinquish, for the common salvation of himself and his family, the things which his father had claimed for himself in the monastery of Vézelay by usurpation contrary to right and justice, he at last yielded, though only under pressure of danger. Under sworn attestation he vowed that henceforth he would claim no provisions … [Col. 1598C] at Easter and the solemnities of the feast of the Translation of blessed Mary Magdalene in the monastery.

Without delay, by God’s wondrous power and through the aid of blessed Mary Magdalene herself, God’s beloved, he was miraculously rescued from the narrow straits of the precipitous rock against which his ship had run, and, after crossing the stormy sea, was restored to a quiet shore.

## The Count of Nevers, Rescued from Shipwreck, Fulfils His Vow Before the Chapter of Vézelay.

Meanwhile the eminent abbot Pons was administering the land and household of the aforesaid count of Nevers and defending them against attacks on every side, both because he hoped that the count would thereafter look after his monastery, and because this William was related to him by kinship. When William returned shipwrecked from Jerusalem, the abbot received him; going out to meet him [Col. 1598D], he honorably and adequately relieved the want that pressed heavily upon him.

At last he delivered to him, safe and sound, his household together with the whole immunity of his possessions; and not long afterwards he also reconciled his enemies to him with satisfaction. Then he summoned him, at Vézelay and before the brethren, and admonished him to pay to God the vow which he had made. William obeyed outwardly, though he was turning deceit over in his mind.

Entering the chapter of the brethren, he set before them his shipwreck, confessed that he had been delivered through the intervention of blessed Mary Magdalene, fulfilled the vow made in thanksgiving, and, with the consent of his wife and his son William, in the presence of countless witnesses, remitted, granted, and confirmed the stipends and provisions usurped by his father.

When many wars arose against him [Col. 1599A], abbot Pons stood by and assisted him in all things, hoping that he might soften spirits fierce and prone, indeed headlong, in usurping another’s right. Although he burned with all his heart to attack the Church, he was nevertheless restrained by the excessive benefits of his kinsman, whom he feared to assail with any prejudicial act.

Hence, because vice was innate to him by nature, he meditated with his whole mind how he might somehow find an occasion to bring an accusation against the Church or abbot. But men of iniquity, whose heart was a furnace of impiety, grieved that they had lost the great profits of their greed, which they had enjoyed in the banquets frequently provided for the count at Vézelay. They therefore ensnared the prince’s mind, already inclined to every evil, and suggested that he should make good the loss which he had voluntarily incurred by renewing, or entering into, another dispute [Col. 1599B].

## Hugh of Saint Peter, Author of the Persecution Carried Out Against the Monks of Vézelay.

There was at Vézelay a certain newcomer named Hugh of Saint Peter, ignoble in birth and character. Nature had brought him forth poor, but a hand trained in mechanical craft had made him wealthy. Sharp-witted as he was and practised in every sort of wickedness, he sometimes enticed the count with gifts and sometimes encouraged him with deceitful hopes, so that he might extort from the Church the right of administering justice or deciding and examining the cases of the people of Vézelay.

For this utterly wicked man hoped to rule the whole town [Col. 1599C] if, through the favor of the tyrant, he were granted the choice of judicial jurisdiction. He therefore associated with himself in this malicious scheme certain persons like himself in depravity, through clandestine gatherings, so that under a pretence of liberty they might devise treachery and under the appearance of piety contrive frauds. For abundance of possessions always produces insolence in degenerate minds. And when one person has greater power through wealth than another has by nature, he even sets himself above hereditary royal power; forgetting himself, he straightway exalts himself, walking proudly in his hidden condition while boasting of private possessions.

Now a monk of the monastery of Vézelay, while making a circuit of the Church’s possessions, happened to come into a certain wood which belonged by right to the Church. Finding a man cutting down prohibited woodland, he wished to take his axe [Col. 1599D] from him as a pledge. But the man turned upon the monk, struck him severely, overpowered him, and threw him from the horse upon which he was riding.

The monk, dishonored by the injury received, returned home and disclosed the insult inflicted on him to the servants of the monastery. Unable to bear such an outrage, they came by night to the man’s house and, having gouged out his eyes, brought upon him the night of perpetual blindness. When the count learned of the deed, he concealed his joy as though he had found an opportunity to make an accusation, threatened destruction upon those who had done it, and, gradually bringing forth the wickedness long conceived in his heart, resolved to renew the dispute which his father had left dormant.

## The Count Plunders the Possessions of the Monastery of Vézelay.

When, therefore, the solemn feast of Mary Magdalene, the most blessed beloved of God, arrived, the count sat, according to custom, in the monastery’s lodging. He ordered his servants to stand before the doors so that, if the abbot came perhaps to visit him, they should prevent him from entering. Carrying out their master’s orders [Col. 1600A], they shut the doors as a barrier against the abbot when he arrived and answered that the count was inside in his chamber.

Repulsed, the abbot bore this insult too with patience; suspecting the wickedness of the ungrateful man, he maintained a free spirit on both sides. When the count was at Cluny, the abbot went in to him and asked the reason for his displayed anger, on the pretext of the complaint concerning the blinded man. The abbot replied that the injured man was not his man. But the count said that the man’s little son was his man—that is, designated as such from his mother’s womb.

The abbot smiled as though at a jest and asked whether the count would deign to receive from him the right of justice. When the count refused, the abbot repeatedly asked whether he would at least return to concord through the hand of his friends and household, and those of the abbot. When he likewise rejected this, the abbot again asked whether it necessarily lay upon him to guard himself and his possessions against the count.

When the count answered that it was indeed necessary for him to do so, the abbot, having renounced faith with him, departed. The count sent his retainers into a certain possession of the monastery and plundered it, carrying off animals and much spoil [Col. 1600B].

The abbot accordingly begged that what had been taken from him be restored. At last the count poured out the venom hitherto concealed: he demanded that, whenever summoned by him, the abbot should administer the justice of the law in his court concerning any matters whatever.

The abbot replied that what was demanded was wholly contrary and opposed both to divine laws and to the customs of the Church, and also to apostolic decrees. “It is shameful and dishonorable for me,” he said, “that the liberty of the monastery—which flourished for many ages under different Fathers and even at present remains in force—should perish, reduced to servitude through the kinship which I have with you. What you attempt is hostile not only to kinship but even to nature: you, a man, seek to subject divine rights to yourself—rights which you, as my kinsman and relative, ought to preserve for me safe and unimpaired and to enlarge.

“How inhuman it is to repay benefits with such a return is plain to see: while I offer you honor and generosity, you seek to impose everlasting disgrace upon me [Col. 1600C]. Yet henceforth I promise you service acceptable to you; but in this demand know that I shall by no means yield to you.”

## He Uses Every Effort to Win the Count’s Favor, but in Vain.

On hearing this, the tyrant was greatly inflamed. Threatening much and inflicting graver injuries, he devoted himself wholly to the destruction of the Church. The abbot appealed against him, through messengers, for Roman aid.

Meanwhile, through mediating friends, he pleaded with the count for peace; he entreated that the count’s malice toward one undeserving it should cease; he proposed reconciliation while preserving the right of the privileges and the dignity of the Church. Accordingly, there were many conferences in many places among numerous and very great nobles, and various opinions were debated [Col. 1601A]. Yet nowhere did peace advance toward friendship, because the firebrand of discord ran everywhere.

When the tyrant learned that the abbot had sent envoys to Rome, he immediately launched an expedition through the estates and possessions of the monastery of Vézelay. Wherever the Church held any right in the districts of Nevers or Auxerre, he invaded, plundered, carried off, and despoiled everything. He also compelled the provosts and administrators of the monastery’s individual properties, by oaths promising loyalty, to obey the monks in no affair and to render no account of anything to the abbot or his representatives.

By crafty cunning he was indeed striving to forestall the abbot’s envoys, in case he might somehow wring from the abbot, even against his will, some word of concession [Col. 1601B]. But the abbot wisely took counsel in the dangerous circumstances: he promised the count appropriate satisfaction concerning what was due, recovered what had been lost, and bestowed many gifts and presents upon him as he set out to the shrine of blessed James. But what abundance of benefits can satisfy the devouring appetite of greed? A corrupted spirit, indeed, knows nothing except either to pervert what is right or to draw evil inferences from what is right.

At last the count returned from Spain and, by command, appointed a day for the abbot to submit in his presence to the judgment of the prince’s court in whatever matters he might be accused. But one to whom Peter’s staff had been entrusted could not be wholly devoid of Peter’s constancy and greatness of spirit [Col. 1601C].

Accordingly, while the abbot disregarded him, the tyrant at once issued a public edict declaring that no one should enter Vézelay for trade, travel, or religious observance, nor should anyone from Vézelay go out to public fairs or public traffic. Whoever presumed to violate the established edict was to lie open to plunder by anyone who encountered him.

With the townspeople thus besieged, some began inwardly to whisper in secret murmuring that the abbot was both author and cause of all their evils: he burdened them with new and unjust laws and stirred up against them, to their destruction, the fury of the tyrant within whose boundaries they were shut. They proclaimed that they would at last be happy and blessed if, throwing off the Church’s yoke, they placed themselves under the count’s discretion [Col. 1601D]. Then, they said, they would fear neither the most distant enemies nor internal tax collectors, whom they would drive away from themselves like insignificant flies. If necessary, they could contend with the abbot in court on equal terms, since the many, relying on one stronger, would free themselves from the dominion of the few and weak.

The count was not unaware that they were whispering such things among themselves, for the profane Hugh conveyed their impious counsels to him. Embracing the stratagem proposed to him, he reasoned that, if he came to Vézelay and cautiously sounded out the townspeople with a word about abandoning the abbot, there was no doubt that the greater and more numerous part, favoring him, would immediately offer him their hand in surrender. Having made an agreement by which he would everywhere grant them his protection and help, he came to Vézelay. When he unexpectedly lodged in the monastery’s guest-house [Col. 1602A], he secretly summoned the townspeople to himself, urged them to desertion, and asked them to act with him against the abbot, saying that they could nowhere remain while he was angry, whereas, if he were peaceful, they need not fear even their own lord.

## The Count Urges the Burgesses of Vézelay to Withdraw Themselves from the Abbot’s Lordship.

“You see,” he said, “that, although I am the lawful advocate and protector of this Church, the abbot alone strives to obstruct the common safety of you all. In seizing what belongs to another, he claims from me the right of administering justice—justice which he himself would disdain to administer when claimants sought it, with me acting as judge or advocate. Who could tolerate such arrogance—rather, such iniquity—that, while claiming his own, a man keeps another’s property without judicial examination?

“What case can I make against those who despoil your goods, when their own right is tyrannically withheld [Col. 1602B]? Indeed, it is of greater value to be able to do something than to be continually asking for it. What, how great, or how extensive our power may be, nothing demonstrates more plainly than experience. Yet the monks’ prayers, even when they do not deserve rejection, are often weakened by their ineffectiveness.

“Therefore, the direction of your wishes concerns you. If you favor us and share in our power, you will no longer care for the monks’ futile prayers or the abbot’s worthless assistance. You will have safe and free entrance and return wherever you wish to go, enjoying perpetual security both for yourselves and for your goods.”

## The Brethren of Vézelay Entreat the Count to Desist from His Undertaking.

Speaking thus and bursting into sobs, he shed tears of impiety, drawn from the well of filthy greed. The abbot, foreseeing the temptation of this deceitful suggestion, summoned the assembly of the brethren and urged them to go and, prostrate together upon the ground, entreat the count to have pity on them and spare the Church.

The sons, obedient to their father’s warnings, fell together at the tyrant’s feet, leaving their tables, and earnestly begged him, for love of God and reverence for His beloved, not to harm them—or rather the Church—and not to pervert their men or those of the Church by seducing them [Col. 1602C].

But he, with a serpent’s body rather than a dove’s mind, answered them in turn with lowered countenance that he asked nothing else of them except this: since they claimed what was properly theirs, they too should administer another’s right through his hand.

“And I am greatly astonished,” he said, “to what equity such great insolence can be attributed: you compel others while I am advocate and judge; but when others compel you, you disdain to administer what is just with me likewise as advocate and judge. Nor, indeed, do I seek, as you say, either to seduce your men or draw them away from you. Rather, those whom, according to my custom and right, I everywhere protect and defend against everyone, I decree to be either cleared or justified by the lawful and public judgment of my court. For whoever claims what is his own,” he said, “must likewise submit to another’s right.”

The brethren replied that, according to the custom long maintained by their Fathers and the apostolic statutes, they refused no one what was just. At once the whole house was filled with confused shouting [Col. 1602D].

Again, because the solemn feast of blessed Mary Magdalene was at hand, the brethren begged the count to grant them at least a truce of a few days so that they could celebrate the feast days amid the public gathering. He answered that they were neither enclosed by siege from him nor condemned to captivity, and therefore asked why they sought such a thing.

“Because,” they said, “by threats you have forbidden any outsider to approach us and any one of us to go outside for provisions, we declare that we innocent men are besieged in a miserable condition.”

At length, overcome by the prayers of so many brethren, he granted an eight-day truce and immediately departed, his business of treachery unfinished. The brethren, though not with their customary attendance, nevertheless celebrated the feast days with no lesser solemnity.

When they were completed, the abbot summoned the bishop of Auxerre and went to the count [Col. 1603A]. He informed him of the apostolic commands by which he was ordered to go to Italy in order to settle the accusation brought by the bishop of Autun. Then he asked that, just as the abbot had faithfully preserved the count’s rights as if they were his own while the count was on pilgrimage and had defended them unharmed from attackers, so the count should protect his kinsman’s monastery with its appurtenances, receive it under his faith, and guard it faithfully until the abbot returned from Rome.

He further promised to persuade the lord pope to permit the man of Vézelay to submit to the hearing of the man of Nevers; if he should obtain this, he promised to lay down the entire controversy completely. To ensure that this truce remained valid and unshaken, the abbot offered him sixty pounds in current coin.

## Having Granted a Truce, the Count; the Abbot Sets Out for Rome, Where He Triumphs Over the Bishop of Autun. The Pontiff Urges Him to Be Strong Against the Count.

The tyrant, bent by prayers, enticed by promises, and moved by gifts, granted the requested truce and promised henceforth to be a faithful friend, if the abbot carried out what he had promised. Since nothing finds lying easier than a double mind, he promised much and performed little. Yet because charity believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things, the noble simplicity of the abbot trusted his pledged word.

At last he departed for Rome and, entering the universal court, so completely triumphed before the supreme pontiff over the accusation of the bishop of Autun that not even a hair of his head was cast down in any direction, while he reduced the bishop of Autun so thoroughly that, avoiding the hearing of the judicial case, the bishop shamefully asked for a postponement [Col. 1603C].

After this the abbot entered before the apostolic lord and set forth the grievance by which the count of Nevers was harassing him and the monastery of Vézelay, which until then had been blessed Peter’s own possession and wholly free under the Roman Church. “Since he,” he said, “is bent neither by the prayers of the powerful nor by the entreaties of friends, softened neither by services nor turned back by gifts, nor restrained by ecclesiastical censure, let apostolic wisdom decide what must be done: whether apostolic liberty ought to yield to tyrannical arrogance, or not. Perhaps the greedy rage of the enemy, once sated, will provide the Church with the safeguard of peace and perpetual protection [Col. 1604A].”

The apostolic lord replied:

“By no means. Rather, if the priest of Vézelay should be subjected to a secular or plebeian tribunal, not only will the monastery be deprived of peace, but the whole ecclesiastical order will also be entangled in the knot of utter disgrace.

“We shall therefore rebuke him with a warning and persuade him, as we have already done once, to desist from this insolence. We shall declare that, if he thinks any right in your monastery belongs to him, he should recover what is his under judges appointed by us, and leave what is another’s. If he should perhaps despise our clemency, behold the halter, behold the bridle, behold Peter’s sword, by which the ear of obstinacy may be cut off.

“Finally, we wish your diligence to be fortified by apostolic authority, so that you yield nothing whatever to anyone from the possessions of your monastery—that is, from the right of blessed Peter [Col. 1604B]—and do not, through any faint-heartedness, betray the Church’s innate liberty, increased by apostolic favor. Although you are far away, we shall hold you in no less favor as one watchful for apostolic right, with the care and authority fitting for a son.”

He scorns the apostolic letters and incites the leading men of Burgundy against the monks. Thus instructed by these admonitions, the abbot, having taken leave of the court, returned joyfully to the monastery. When he had delivered the apostolic warnings to the count, the latter scorned, rejected, and cast them aside, replying that he owed nothing to one from whom he likewise possessed nothing. He then asked whether, as promised, the abbot had obtained from the pope a hearing and enforcement of judgment before his own court. “I have kept the word of my mouth,” said the abbot, “but I have been forbidden to comply with your request.” Thereupon the count, enraged and filled with gall, [Col. 1604C] again forbade the people of Vézelay freedom of going out and coming in; and, fearing to make war upon the monks in his own person, he incited the magnates of the province—namely Gibbald of Saint-Vérain, Iterius of Brioude, Geoffrey of Arcy, and their accomplices—to attack the men of Vézelay wherever they might encounter them, seize and appropriate their goods, spare not the monastery, plunder its possessions, manufacture a charge against the abbot, and replenish their own poverty from the Church’s storehouse. These men therefore, as though loosed like dogs, invaded the monastery’s estates, beat the monks, shamefully abused them after stripping off their clothes, and, plundering all its household goods, robbed the Church of slaves, beasts of burden, and livestock. No religious status was respected by them; [Col. 1604D] clerics were everywhere beaten, priests dragged off dishonourably, travellers stripped of their possessions, pilgrims taken captive, and noble women prostituted. Therefore the patience of the Church of Vézelay is remarkable to consider, and still more remarkable the courage and greatness of spirit of the prudent abbot Pons. On one side stood the count of Nevers, on the other the bishop of Autun; on one side tyrants, on the other lords of the land: with one assault, one spirit, one intervention, they ran about here and there like savage beasts, harassing the abbot, afflicting the Church, and tearing apart its rights to such a degree that whatever came into hostile hands wholly passed to the occupier. Yet nobility of spirit, adorned by the innate distinction of noble birth, bore indignities the more equitably [Col. 1605A] as it perceived more wickedly that evils were being inflicted upon it.

### The abbot presents the king with the privileges of Vézelay and implores his protection

Accordingly, considering that evils were multiplying on every side, the abbot came to the king, seeking his help against the count. Summoned by the king, the count replied thus: “By the grant and favour of your pious father and of your own serenity, I have hitherto held and possessed, from my fathers and grandfathers, by right of marriage, without objection from anyone, the advocacy and protection of the monastery of Vézelay, together with the revenues belonging to it. By what reasoning a right inherited by me from my fathers for so long a time is now contested against me, I wholly do not know.”

The abbot replied: “The Church of Vézelay, [Col. 1605B] nobly founded by the illustrious Count Gerard and still more nobly dedicated by him to the name of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, was assigned to their right, entrusted to their governance, and committed to their protection. Moreover, through the intervention of that same pious Count Gerard, it deserved to be endowed by the most excellent kings of the Franks with the prerogative of such a privilege that, all claims being remitted which royal right had anciently held there, no authority or person whatsoever should have power to exact any right or custom on any pretext or occasion of piety or benefaction, but that it should remain free from every condition of servitude and from exaction of payment. That this is so is demonstrated by the privilege of your pious great-grandfather Louis, which we have at hand, if your serenity deigns to hear it.”

After the privilege had been read, [Col. 1605C] the king asked the abbot whether, if he submitted himself to royal examination, he would abide by the judgment pronounced concerning this claim. The abbot, perceiving that the court hostile to him favoured the opposing side, feared to submit himself to an uncertain judgment, lest the Church should suffer prejudice—she who, under Peter alone as judge, was still breathing a little. Finally, he begged the royal highness to command the tyrant to desist from harassing the monastery of Vézelay, and to accept judicial process at the hands of the legate of the Apostolic See, or of those to whom the lord pope had entrusted the matter. Since the count rejected all this with mockery, the abbot took leave of the king and returned to his monastery.

When he heard that John, cardinal priest of the Roman Church, to whom the pope had entrusted the controversy between Vézelay and Nevers, was returning from England after completing his legation, he sent to meet him, begging him to come as swiftly as possible, because the Church of Vézelay, deprived of every assistance, now threatened to become almost a wilderness. Upon receiving the message, John hastened his steps and ordered both parties, namely the abbot and the count, to meet him at Auxerre. But when this John heard that Cardinal Jordan had been appointed legate to the French, he wrote to him that he should come quickly to Vézelay, and that they should jointly celebrate there the approaching feast of St Mary Magdalene. When both were present at Auxerre, the abbot and the count standing before him, the legate gently and courteously exhorted the count to make peace [Col. 1606A] with the abbot, laying aside the dispute, lest, by persecuting the vicar of Christ and of Peter, he be proved an enemy of God and thereby show himself like Saul, persecutor of the Church. “Indeed,” he said, “if you prove a despiser of us, you will not even be found worthy to imitate Saul; for Saul, when he experienced rebuke, immediately followed the Master.” But the count, contemptuously ignoring these pious admonitions, had again forbidden public passage or access from Vézelay. The cardinal therefore asked him for a truce, so that the solemnities of St Mary Magdalene might be celebrated with festal worship and public attendance as was customary. When this was with difficulty obtained only until the octave, Cardinal John and Abbot Pons came to Vézelay; and Cardinal Jordan, legate to the Gauls, arriving also, spent the holy days with them.

### The count attempts to turn the subjects of Vézelay from submission

Meanwhile the count, having returned from the king, went down and took his seat in the open place where the king, about to go on pilgrimage, had taken up the trophy of Christ’s cross. Having assembled the greater part of the men of Vézelay, and pouring forth impure tears—feigned compassion wrung from eyes of greed—he spoke to them thus:

“O most illustrious men, renowned for abundant prudence, most vigorous in courage, and enriched with wealth acquired by your own valour: I deeply lament the most wretched condition of your estate. Though outwardly possessors of many things, in reality you have become masters of none; indeed, you do not even enjoy in any degree your own inborn freedom. [Col. 1606C] For I see excellent estates, most beautiful vineyards, abundant streams, most fertile pastures, productive fields, dense woods, fruit-bearing thickets, conspicuous dwellings—all these surrounding you by their very position—yet no power is granted you to enjoy them. Seeing this, I pity you with no ordinary feeling.

“I am greatly astonished where your once highly celebrated courage has gone, or to what degree of cowardice it has fallen: you killed the most prudent and very generous Abbot Artald over only two station-houses; yet this foreigner from Auvergne—savage in his very presence, cruel in his absence, arrogant in speech, vulgar in manners, exacting not only your goods but even your very lives—you endure with such stupidity [Col. 1606D] that you may now rightly be compared to brute animals. Finally, to increase and complete your ruin, your lord abbot is attempting to snatch and take from me the right of lawful advocacy by which I am bound to protect you and answer on your behalf, so that, when you are abandoned, he may more freely impose extortionate customs upon you. Therefore, dearest friends, I urge your prudence and greatness of spirit to provide for the pressing necessity and turn away from that man who exercises such tyranny over you. Know that while I am favourable to you, no loss will befall you; whereas, conversely, so long as you keep faith with the adversary, there will be no welfare for you. But if, swearing a mutual league with one another, [Col. 1607A] you are also willing to keep faith with me, you shall everywhere enjoy my protection. I shall endeavour to make you free from every evil exaction of bad customs, and shall defend you from the threatening onset of evils.”

Having said this, he fell silent, repeatedly interrupting his speech as though simulating grief by deception. The men answered: “We have sworn faith to our lord by oath; and although he treats us unjustly, we judge it wrong nevertheless to betray faith. Having taken counsel and become more fully informed, we shall meet in the nearby place appointed, on the fixed day and in your presence, and answer you on these matters.”

They came and reported the count’s words to the abbot, asking what counsel he offered [Col. 1607B] concerning them. He answered: “By no means, my faithful men, can your prudence fail to see that he is hostile to me for this reason alone: that, deceiving you by fraud, he may subject you more completely to his servitude, after taking away the lordship that is full of freedom. I, however, having toiled until now in contending for your freedom—if you should wish to repay me with so impious a return for such great ingratitude that you do not fear to become traitors to me and to your mother Church—I shall bear alone, though groaning and ashamed, both the injury to the Church and your destruction: that is, you and your children paying forever the penalty of treason. But if, yielding to sound counsels, you stand wisely for yourselves, keep without doubt the sworn faith owed to me and to the Church which nourished and reared you with her milk, [Col. 1607C] and steadfastly act with me against all persecutors for your freedom and salvation, and indeed for your glory and honour, I shall most willingly devote myself for you, not doubting that prosperity will follow favourable events and that after many storms of tribulations and calamities we shall at last be granted the serenity of peace.”

They replied: “We wholly believe and hope that matters are as you assert. Yet it seems more expedient to us to renounce the dispute, yield to the adversary, and make peace with him. But if the matter appears otherwise to you, we are and shall certainly remain yours. Do not doubt that we, as your faithful men, shall sincerely stand by you everywhere and in all things.”

The abbot answered: “There is in truth no dispute at all on my side, but only an answer or defence against one who brings a dispute. Moreover, to yield to the adversary in the present case is the most senseless cowardice and a written bond of perpetual disgrace. I have often sought peace by prayer, payment, and service; more often offered it; most often demanded it; but from the son of discord I could not obtain peace. Therefore, if, as you have said, you stand for the common welfare, I also pledge my labour for your salvation and freedom; and together with you, trusting in courage and justice, I shall undergo every misfortune and blind chance.”

### Conspiracy of the young men against the abbot

Having said this, he dismissed them. And behold, wicked men rushed in, pouring out poison long concealed in the hiding-places of their savage consciences. [Col. 1608A] Having gathered to themselves a great multitude of criminal young men, they made a mutual compact of criminal conspiracy against their lord of most equitable governance and native piety. Betraying the faith they had hitherto feigned, cutting themselves off from their mother Church, and assembling at the appointed day and place, they allied themselves with the tyrant, renouncing their lawful lord. By the tyrant’s accursed hand they made a mutual agreement and conspired against their head, that they might cast from their necks the yoke of the Church’s freedom and attach themselves to the count. He swore to them that he would never, in any place or matter, fail them in counsel and aid against anyone. He also appointed them leaders or judges, whom they decided to call consuls. [Col. 1608B] This deed did not escape the notice of the aforesaid lord abbot, nor of the cardinals who, as has been said, had been invited to the feast.

### The cardinals try to deter them from their undertaking

The older men, who appeared to be the heads of the people, entered before the cardinals. Trusting in the authority of their treachery, they demanded remission of certain customs which they called innovations and tyranny. The cardinals replied: “Since we owe the care of our solicitude to you as much as to sons of the Roman Church, we shall willingly urge upon the abbot whatever appears suited to your peace and advantage and to honour and integrity. We know that he is of such gentleness that, obeying our admonitions without resistance, he will mercifully [Col. 1608C] grant whatever the rule of equity shall dictate. Nevertheless, since he is now placed in danger of death for your common freedom and safety, you must render him in every respect the faithfulness of aid and work with him for your own sakes, because the matter plainly concerns the danger of you all. But if anything—which we least believe—has been committed by any of you in conspiracy against your lord the abbot, this must first be renounced, purged, and amended. Then afterward whatever just complaint may arise shall be settled, with the Church’s right preserved.”

The abbot likewise spoke to them: “You see,” he said, “how grievously I am oppressed and harassed by the count, to whom you also have given your hand for your own destruction, mutually conspiring against me. It is therefore unjust that, having allied yourselves with shameless violence, you seem to demand remission rather than request it—as though you possessed it not as a remission but as something extorted or exacted. Yet if you utterly abandon what you have wickedly agreed, you shall deserve not merely remission but also forgiveness, as befits our gentleness.” But they cried out that they would not do so, but would rather bring rebellion upon the Church.

### The cardinals, having vainly discussed the controversy, are repulsed by the count and depart

The cardinals therefore begged the count to lay aside the discord and moderate the anger of his mind. But he pretended not to hear them. When they persisted long in their entreaties, he swore [Col. 1609A] that he would admit no agreement whatever until he recovered all that he claimed to be his right. Then the abbot complained before the cardinals of his wrongdoers, namely Geoffrey of Arcy and the others whom the count was inciting to destroy the Church. The count replied that those men belonged neither to his household nor to his military following, and that they brought their charge against the abbot by their own choice, not at his instigation. The cardinals of the Roman Church therefore decreed to strike the devastators of the Church with the sword of anathema. The count opposed them, saying that they were his men, whom he had ready to execute justice, if the abbot would answer him and them regarding the matters raised against him. A day was appointed at Jaligny to decide the matters which the count was bringing forward as a claim. On the ninth day from Vézelay, [Col. 1609B] the cardinals departed with great fear, conducting the abbot in their midst because of the conspiracy of the faithless men who had vowed his death.

When they came to Jaligny, the cardinals ordered the count to state his case. In stating it, he demanded that the abbot submit, both concerning himself and concerning the men of Vézelay, to justice when summoned by him to court. The cardinals and the other prudent men present did not think that such things ought to be required from the abbot; justice was offered to the count according to the tenor of the apostolic command. But he, being unjust, rejected justice, and, being iniquitous, rejected judgment. Apostolic letters were read in his presence, declaring a sentence of excommunication against him unless he repented. On hearing them, he was enraged [Col. 1609C] and for a long time denied the cardinals safe passage through his land. At last the distinguished persons present barely obtained permission for their safe-conduct. But he would give the abbot assurances of safety only as far as Vézelay. The abbot had no intention of going there, since his faithless men had conspired against him. The bishop of Nevers took him up and, by command of the cardinals on the pope’s behalf, led him from the church at Jaligny and conducted him as far as the port of Saint-Mayeul. After crossing it, the abbot turned aside to Montet and stayed there for several days.

### The burgesses of Vézelay adhere to the count

The treacherous men of Vézelay, adding sacrilege to perjury, adhered to the count. [Col. 1609D] Forgetting their Maker, who had enriched them when poor and needy and filled with every good those who had been destitute and wandering—forgetting God, I say, and turning away from Him—they worshipped gods whom they had not known. They bowed their necks to the count and to the other tyrants of the province, surrendering themselves and their possessions to them. By committing fornication in the pride of their eyes, so far as lay in them they defiled the holy seed, adulterating the chastity of the incorrupt Church.

The tyrant himself, besides all the evils which he had inflicted upon the monastery by taking whatever he found outside the town and by bringing in many other acts full of violation of immunity and cruelty, added this further: that he should receive, against all justice and against apostolic privileges, those deserters of God and the Church; that he himself should induce them to this by various [Col. 1610A] promises and flatteries, provoke them by threats and terrors, and further promise never to make peace with the abbot without them, never to consent to an agreement with the abbot.

### The townspeople of Vézelay plunder everything belonging to the monastery, harass the monks, and destroy buildings

Trusting in his aid and bound by their conspiracy, these mice burst forth from their holes; torrents of Belial, they rose against the Church their mother. Like an abyss they encircled her, and like a sea the townspeople, or those called burgesses—once at least nominally her own children, now made strangers, and more grievous because more inward—covered her head. When they learned that the abbot had secretly withdrawn from them, they immediately violated the most sacred [Col. 1610B] church, occupied its towers, stationed guards in them, and placed food and arms there. Heaping worse upon grave injuries, they shamefully mistreated the servants of God, the monks, and their lords. Deprived of all possessions and all human assistance, the monks were shut away within the monastery walls, so that no one was permitted to go out without an external escort. Moreover, they invaded the dependent settlements, usurped the monastery’s rights and revenues due to it, demolished many houses of the Church, plundered estates, mills, and all household goods, spared neither movable nor immovable property in their raging assault, and razed the walls and enclosures of the monastery to the ground. By day and night they held malignant counsels in their secret gatherings, devising tricks, frauds, and ambushes, [Col. 1610C] unanimously conspiring and daily threatening grave evils and worse things still.

Meanwhile the ever-watchful Abbot Pons went to Cluny, where the cardinals and legates of the Apostolic See had gathered with many religious and honourable persons. Having made known to them how great were the evils which the profane men of Vézelay had inflicted upon his monastery, he asked them to request of the abbot of Cluny, namely his brother, that he might grant him a single cell in which he could lodge safely and seek peace. Sympathizing with his affliction, they begged the Cluniac to show mercy and compassion to his brother by blood, who was placed in the greatest distress, and mercifully to grant him, for a time until the tribulation had been stilled, the monastery of Souvigny [Col. 1610D] as relief for his exile. The latter assented to their request and promised that he would do so shortly, once a suitable place had been identified.

After this Abbot Pons urged his brother and the leading men of Cluny to arrange for the cardinals to pronounce a sentence of anathema upon his sacrilegious and faithless traitors at Vézelay and their supporters. Since they declined and evaded doing this, the cardinals considered it expedient to act as the abbot had begged.

### A sentence of excommunication and interdict is pronounced against them

The sentence having therefore been issued, they cut off those evildoers, violators of holy things, and traitors to their lord from the body of Christ, which is the Catholic Church, with the sword of anathema. The abbot asked them [Col. 1611A] to reveal his cause fully to the lord pope, as they had seen it with their own eyes and touched it with their own hands. Having entrusted to them his messenger, who was to report the universal pontiff’s sentence concerning the count, he returned to Montet with the document of excommunication against the traitors of Vézelay. After he sent it to Vézelay and ordered the sentence of the Romans to be proclaimed, the priests assembled together in a certain upper chapel of St Peter and, before all the people, announced the sentence. They publicly anathematized those designated by name; they placed all the rest, with the entire town, under complete interdict from divine offices and ecclesiastical sacraments, allowing only the baptism of infants and the confession of the dying.

Some sacrilegious persons, enraged, attacked the priest [Col. 1611B] who had pronounced the sentence. The first was Odo of La Palud, who, throwing off his cloak, sought stones to throw at him; then David Longbeard and his son Robert, who, loosening his cloak, drew out his *patinos* [an uncertain term, perhaps weapons or implements] to strike the priest. Had some persons not intervened, he would have been cut into a thousand pieces; fleeing to the altar, he barely escaped the hands of the impious. On the following day, when the church doors had been removed and its entrance blocked with thorns, Hugh and Peter, both surnamed “of St Peter,” instigators of every wickedness, took away the thorns and restored the doors. From the church of St Stephen, they took a chalice, a book, and priestly vestments from a cleric whom they had abused because he resisted their sacrilege. Afterwards, entering the monastery enclosure with a great tumult [Col. 1611C] of rage, they shamefully assailed Prior Hildin, with certain brothers standing by, in abusive insults over the excommunication, and with great arrogance demanded a truce. When he would not yield to them, they unanimously answered: “Because you have undeservedly excommunicated us, we shall make you appear excommunicated. Therefore we shall no longer pay you tithes, rent, or other customary revenues.”

They went to the count and complained about the sentence. He said to them: “I can do nothing else; they will do the same to me if they wish.” They said: “Where shall we grind or bake our bread? For the monks refuse to grind with us.” He told them: [Col. 1611D] “Go, light an oven with your own wood and bake. If anyone resists, burn him alive; and if the miller resists, likewise grind him alive in the mill.”

### Regarding the sentence of excommunication as nothing, they subject the monks to insults

Encouraged by these and similar replies, they returned to intensify their evils. Thus it came about that they inflicted whatever damage, injury, and adversity they wished upon the monastery; drove the Church’s boys from their homes; beat them; and with great boasting vowed that they would afflict the monks so severely that the latter would seek absolution at their feet. Renouncing altogether the authority of the abbot and the Church, they regarded the sentence pronounced against them as nothing, and did not in the least restrain themselves from entering the holy church, heaping up their sins, neither fearing God nor reverencing His sanctuaries. [Col. 1612A] The prior complained of all these things and many similar matters in the count’s presence. The count, promising what was wicked and perverse, replied that they had done well and said, heightening the provocation: “Would that all the monks would depart and the monastery be utterly destroyed! Why did he excommunicate them?” Then, plucking a hair from the garment with which he was clothed, he added: “If the whole hill of Vézelay were cast down into the abyss, I would not give this hair. I entrust you with guarding the Church’s treasure and its offerings. Take care firmly that he receives or obtains nothing. For his sake I want the burgesses to scatter everything, destroy everything—especially those who are of the abbot’s confederacy.” It happened, moreover, that they buried a certain person who had died under anathema, without a priest, ringing the bells themselves; and they drove the priest himself from his house.

While the abbot was staying at Montet, word was brought to the abbot of Cluny that the abbot of Vézelay, intending to send to Rome, would seek the monastery of Souvigny from the supreme pontiff. He took this badly and, delaying, evaded fulfilment of his promise. Yet, reflecting that perhaps the pope would pronounce an anathema against the count and his land, and that consequently the many monasteries under the care of Cluny within the count’s territory might be endangered, he sent the count the following advice through his confidential agents: [Col. 1612C] “All of us who bear the name of Christianity are wholly unable to evade apostolic censure. You will therefore do well if, committing yourself in faith to good hope, you make peace with the abbot of Vézelay through our hand. It shall be our part to provide for affairs on both sides in such a manner that you also gain benefit from that peace.”

Having received these messages, the count agreed. He sent to the abbot of Vézelay Bernard, an elderly priest, prior of St Stephen, whose death he thirsted for as something more precious than every spice. Coming, Bernard praised the constancy and greatness of spirit still vigorous in him; but he declared that, if obstinacy were disguised as courage, the abbot would inflict no small loss upon his monastery. He accordingly urged him to be so magnanimous in adversity as to provide for honour in prosperity; said that the fortune of war was uncertain, whereas nothing could be safer, quieter, or more certain than peace—even though it might be judged an extreme measure; and testified that the count favoured the peace offered to him through the hand of Cluny, if he would deign to accept it. Nor, he said, ought one born of the same blood to appear suspect:

> Though kinship opposes, the identity of the enemy remains;  
> Defeated by its own judgment, it will remain forgetful of itself.

### They meet at Luzy, where they discuss peace

The abbot believed the adviser, and did not expect that prejudice could be stealthily introduced where the entire case plainly stood with justice on his side. Therefore the abbots of Cluny and Vézelay and the bishop of Nevers met together at the town of Luzy in the district of Autun. Present at this conference were Stephen, abbot of St Michael of the Cluse, and [lacuna] abbot [Col. 1613A] of Moissac, as well as other weighty persons from Cluny. Meeting there, after many unjust and undue demands made by the count, those who had assembled in the capacity of advocates, favouring the adverse rather than the just side under a pretence of piety, composed a certain form of peace: suspect as regards liberty, subject to servitude, and given over to instability. They then urged Abbot Pons to accept what brotherly love and collegial arrangement had provided for his peace, buying time and yielding to pressing necessity; they said that it ought to suffice him if the other obtained what he desired in diminished measure. To this he wisely and repeatedly appealed both to reverence for God and to the injury done to honour, and repeatedly begged that impiety should not enjoy the services of ministers of piety.

Finally, the count declared that if the abbot accepted the settlement of such great friends, he himself would break up and wholly abolish the commune, or sacrilegious confederacy, of his men; he would establish the abbot safe and unharmed in his monastery, with the abbot’s right of lordship wholly preserved. But as many arguments were exchanged on both sides, and the abbot persisted in his case, the result fell away into confusion. At length, after consultation, they fixed Nevers as the end of the conference and the place where peace should be concluded. The tyrant sent for the leading men of the treasonous conspiracy and ordered them to be present at the future agreement. The abbot likewise instructed the prior and certain other brothers of his monastery to meet him, having first consulted the whole community generally whether they decreed that the proposed peace settlement between themselves and the count [Col. 1613C] through the hand already described should be ratified. With equal and unanimous judgment they wrote back to their most watchful lord and father that whatever paternal providence should decree or establish would remain ratified, firm, and unshaken by the decision of the brothers, with the rights of their privileges and the freedom of the Church preserved.

### The Cluniacs pursue the same matter

When the meeting at Nevers took place, the count sent Abbot Pons certain gifts and various cups, displaying a feigned peace. Seeing this, the sacrilegious traitors were confounded and feared that they had been abandoned by their tyrant. The count then went in to the abbot of Cluny and was more fully admonished by him to restore friendship with his kinsman. The count repeatedly protested and swore that he loved no one more dearly; that he would ask nothing of him which would not serve both his advantage and his honour. Saying this on his knees, and even folding his hands within those of the abbot of Cluny, he wiped away splendid tears, which the deceitful man shed in abundance.

While the Cluniacs secretly discussed some peace settlement, they excluded all the abbot’s companions from their deliberation. The men of Vézelay consequently became suspicious, and, guarding against suffering prejudice under the appearance of peace and a disgraceful condition, some of them entered before the abbot of Cluny. In the name of God and apostolic authority, and on behalf of the chapter of Vézelay, they gave notice and objected that nothing should be contrived by a peace settlement contrary to the rights of dignity and privileges of [Col. 1614A] their monastery. For this reason the abbot of Cluny, angered, ordered preparations for departure. Summoning his brother, he rebuked him: “What are you doing? Why do you disgrace me so shamelessly? Do I seem to you a boy or a madman? I labour everywhere for your peace and tranquillity; I watch without hesitation over your welfare and success. But you in return destroy what I build, scatter what I construct, disperse what I gather, and, while I publicly proclaim matters for the sake of your peace, secretly oppose me by maligning me. Therefore, since our labour seems useless to you, carry your own burden alone.”

Astonished at this, the abbot of Vézelay asked who had presumed to do such things. The Cluniacs told him: “William who is called of [lacuna].”

> [Note: [Col. 1613] “Is called of.” Here twenty-eight leaves have unfortunately been cut out of the manuscript codex.]

The queen, mother of the king, sister of the wife of Archimbald of Bourbon. [lacuna]

And also the daughter of the same [lacuna] who was afterwards married to the count of Saint-Gilles. [lacuna]

But Macharius, abbot of the monastery of Fleury, casks, jars. [lacuna] My lord, while I was administering in truce and peace the rights of the church committed to your reverence, it happened that I undertook a lawsuit against a certain serf of the church concerning a possession of that church, which I adjudged should be settled by trial of combat. [Col. 1614C] Therefore, as soon as the time for the contest arrived, these men who are present turned to sedition and attacked me with my brothers and boys. Having put us to flight while we were caught unawares and unsuspecting, they violated the monastery enclosure, scattered its ornaments, plundered utensils of various kinds, broke open the casks, poured out the wine, made spoil of all goods, trampled and defiled the sanctuaries, inflicted slaughter upon our monks and servants, and sought my death. Had they found me, they would surely have cut me into a thousand pieces. Then they besieged us, untrained for fighting; broke down houses, overthrew mills, seized everything of ours that they had at hand, and, in contempt of royal majesty, satisfied themselves with our punishments. [Col. 1614D] At last, finding an opportunity, and again at the pope’s command, as may presently be seen, I fled to you as my singular protection. Therefore, standing before the judgment of your equity, I demand from the hands of these men my blood and that of my people, and my death; I seek from them recompense for the losses of my house, while preserving in every respect your right and that of the Apostolic See, whose injury I can neither wholly remit nor ought to remit.” Having said this, he fell silent.

But the tyrant, that is, the Count of Nevers, rising to pursue the case of the faithless men, said: “Since it is evident that the town of Vézelay is filled with a mixed populace of many thousands, and that the people are not [Col. 1615A] of one character or condition—being for the most part newcomers from many different places, pursuing diverse interests and following custom according to inclination rather than law—it is not right to impute to the elected native citizens, men approved in every law and uprightness, whatever wrongdoing the errant mob is shown to have committed through excess. Otherwise the law of justice is not justice, if the righteous and the wicked are bound by an equal charge.

“Moreover, since everywhere the common people are more numerous and therefore in some measure stronger than the senate, what can be demanded from a very few respectable men, concerned only with their own household affairs, when the authority of a prince cannot restrain popular disturbances? Therefore, if it pleases Your Majesty, let the abbot name the authors of the crime, so that, once the innocent have been absolved, the censure of justice [Col. 1615B] may be pronounced against the guilty.”

To this the tyrant received the reply: “Since by natural and legal right it belongs to citizens to guard and defend their lord and prince, to preserve him immune from every danger, and not to shrink even from voluntary death for his safety, those who, when he was placed in such extremity of necessity, deprived him of both their comfort and their aid must now be called and judged not innocent, but traitors and deserters of their lord. And therefore from their leaders must be exacted whatever the mob committed wickedly at their instigation, with their assistance, and through the help they gave.”

Then all alike who had not departed Vézelay with the abbot, or had not joined the brethren besieged in the monastery, or had not brought assistance, [Col. 1615C] were adjudged guilty of treason, disloyalty, sacrilege, perjury, and homicide.

This having been done, the first article of the king’s judgment was put forward: that the abbot should establish by testimony the losses suffered by himself or by the Church, and that those condemned on a capital charge should restore in full whatever was lawfully proved. The abbot objected to this article as follows:

“Since it is publicly known that these men, because of the monstrous obstinacy of their conduct, have been excommunicated and anathematized by three apostolic authorities, it seems improper to me to make a lord depend upon slaves, faith upon faithless men, an oath upon perjurers, testimony upon profane persons, and law upon sacrilegious men.”

The Bishop of Langres replied to him—for he was always and everywhere opposed to the cause of Vézelay, and, through Humbert of Talay, Archdeacon of Nevers, acting by means of the count, had undertaken the advocacy of the cause of the traitorous burghers [Col. 1615D]: “Even if,” he said, “a sentence has merely been pronounced, we do not legally regard men as excommunicated until they have been formally named, summoned, and publicly proclaimed by the Church; and we do not know that this has been done in their case.”

To this the abbot said: “The lord of Sens, the lord of Paris, and also the lord of Troyes are present, who, by command of the apostolic pontiff, publicly proclaimed these sacrilegious traitors by name.”

When the bishops testified that this was so, the abbot was persuaded to make the proof, since it was clear that it would in no respect prejudice his right. But because the officials and ministers of the Church through whom the proof [Col. 1616A] had to be made were not fully present, it was deferred until the following Saturday, when both those present and those absent were to assemble at Moret.

### They meet again at Moret. Sentence is pronounced against the Count of Nevers and the faithless townsmen of Vézelay.

It was the day called Tuesday, that is, the third feria. When those who had been summoned had assembled, all went out with the king and his magnates into the planted wood above Moret. There, when the abbot stated the total of his proof, he said that it amounted to one hundred and sixty thousand solidi, apart from the damage to woods and waters, apart from the injury of treason, apart from the blood of those killed, and apart from the sacrilege committed against the holy and inviolable church that had been invaded and violated.

On hearing this, those conscious of their crime [Col. 1616B] were dismayed in spirit and immediately turned to flight. They did not remain to allow the proof to be made, but, without the king’s knowledge, returned to their accomplices and partners in crime. The abbot, however, by the king’s command, made his proof in the presence of the count and of the auxiliaries named above.

When the king learned that the faithless men were absent and had rashly withdrawn from the royal court without permission, he said: “Happily the abbot has established his justice, while the traitors have established their faithlessness. Therefore, since they have fallen away from justice, let a sentence appropriate to their guilt be pronounced.”

Then the Archbishop of Reims spoke: “We have dictated one article,” he said, “and were prepared to pronounce others, had they waited and allowed themselves to be found worthy of judgment. But now, since, being devoid of reason, they have fallen away from every right of justice, we determine by the king’s judgment [Col. 1616C] that the Count of Nevers, who is here present under his oath of fealty to the king, shall seize those profane traitors by force and bring them to the king for punishment wherever he is commanded. Moreover, he shall hand over all their movable and immovable property in full to the abbot as restitution for the damage inflicted.”

The count was asked whether he accepted the sentence dictated from the king’s mouth. “I accept it,” he said.

But the Bishop of Langres sought to refute the judgment. The Archbishop of Reims said to him: “If the judgment elaborated upon seems unjust to you, I summon you before the Roman court, so that there, before the supreme pontiff and universal judge, you may raise whatever objection you have.”

“I by no means accept this appeal,” said the Bishop of Langres, “nor do I challenge the king’s judgment; rather, whatever seems good to his equity, I approve as is fitting.”

[Col. 1616D] The king again asked the count whether he accepted the judgment pronounced concerning the surrender of those condemned. He replied: “If my lord king commands it, I accept; but I ask that they be granted the truce which, trusting in the king’s mercy, I gave them.”

The king replied: “I plainly command it, and by royal authority, in accordance with the fealty by which you are sworn to me, I order you to carry out what has been determined and omit nothing of the sentence. As to the truce, that shall rest with you; for I grant none either to you or to them: what has been decided must be carried out on the following Sunday.”

Although the count had reluctantly assented to the sentence, he resisted it by every means and attempted to prevent it from taking effect. [Col. 1617A] After a council had been held there for two days, the assembly was dissolved. The abbot, having taken leave of the king and his magnates and friends, came near Vézelay and remained at Givry until the appointed Sunday.

But the tyrant, grieving over the impious men whom he had incited to conspiracy, whom he had provoked to crime, to whom he was bound by oath, whose resources he had drained because they trusted him, and by whose assistance he hoped to secure for himself dominion over the monastery of Vézelay; grieving also that he had been so powerfully and publicly defeated, put to shame, and refuted by the abbot, and that the abbot had triumphed according to his desire both over him and over his followers and accomplices in madness—was sorely troubled in spirit and considered how he might provide for the condemned or help the desperate.

But [Col. 1617B] because a confused mind is incapable of reason, his plan became foolish; and, by God’s ordering, while providing for the condemned populace he unwillingly and unknowingly devised what benefited the Church. He accomplished for the oppressed all that he strove to effect by deceit: while he set a snare, he himself raised up his companion; he was caught on the goad, wickedly sated with what he desired.

Accordingly, having sent his retainers, he ordered a herald to proclaim in the count’s name to all the townsmen and villagers that, taking up all their movable goods, they should all flee wherever they could to strongholds where they hoped he would not come, since, by the king’s judgment, he would seize on the following Monday everyone whom he found within Vézelay and, though unwilling, would drag them to Paris for punishment by the king.

And God sent His terror upon those people, [Col. 1617C] and all who belonged to the opposing party fled, from the least to the greatest, abandoning houses, wives, children, possessions, and merchandise. Thus, of so many thousands, absolutely no one appeared early in the morning; and, as though invaded and plundered by enemies, the town remained empty and deserted.

The crafty and shrewd count, thinking that the abbot would not dare enter his monastery while he himself was absent, feigned illness. Then the abbot, scorning his folly, came in triumph to Vézelay on that very Sunday evening and took possession of his monastery. Great rejoicing occurred in the church, because the adversary had been confounded and the enemy crushed.

The tyrant [Col. 1617D] then sent his retainers to Vézelay, ostensibly to oblige the king by carrying out his command, so that they might seize the profane men whom he had ordered to depart from the place. When the retainers entered, they told the abbot that their lord the count had long awaited a messenger from him, so that, when he came, he might be honorably introduced into his own monastery; and that they greatly wondered that he had entered there so unexpectedly without fearing a hostile uprising. They said that their lord had sent them in order that they might inflict, at the abbot’s command, the punishment determined against the adversaries.

The abbot replied: “When I heard that your lord was ill, I did not wish to burden him; but I entrusted myself to God and to blessed Mary Magdalene, whose cause I pursue with all my vows, and I have received, through God’s granting, what my rival strove [Col. 1618A] to snatch away. Besides, you yourselves know by whom you were sent. If he has commanded you to do anything, it is for you to decide whether you will do it or not; as for me, I shall patiently await the outcome of the matter.”

They answered that they had been sent to seize the men of that town, but that upon entering they had found no one except women and their small children. He said to them: “Is this how you four men have come to seize so many thousands?” Then one of his men said: “Look—if you have come to capture faithless traitors, you will find nearly eighty men hiding and committing robbery in the neighboring wood.” But they said: “We have another journey to complete; our road does not now lead that way.” Thus evading the matter, they departed; for the disciple’s cunning proves the master’s deceit.

Some of the brethren then came out [Col. 1618B] with armed youths and broke down the signboard of the impious Simon and the entrance-front of his house. He had built that house unlawfully in contempt of the protesting brethren and had thus far retained it against the will of the Church, relying upon the faction’s conspiracy. Proceeding thence, they destroyed the wine presses which the impious Hugh Bread-breaker (*Hugo Fricans-panem*) and the utterly wicked Hugh of Saint Peter had fraudulently erected in the cellars of their houses.

The impious men were scattered through the tyrant’s towns and lands; he ordered his retainers and provosts to conceal them, excuse them, and show them every kindness, provided only that they instructed them to avoid his presence. The remainder wandered and were scattered in every direction; [Col. 1618C] many of them became exposed to plunder, robbery, and captivity. Poor and homeless, they occupied the adjoining forest, built huts there, and from there committed robberies, plundering travelers and pilgrims. By day they avoided encounters with those seeking them and withdrew to companions in strongly fortified places. By night, dwelling in the aforesaid forest, they sent hidden scouts into the town in pilgrims’ clothing, to bring them necessities and report the plans they had learned. The fugitives gathered at Corbigny and planned to make an incursion and recover by force the homes which, in their fear, they had voluntarily abandoned.

### The abbot orders an army assembled to oppose the faithless townsmen.

Then the abbot assembled an outside army, [Col. 1618D] a very strong force, with men skilled in bow and crossbow. Keeping the knights within the castle, he divided the rest among his young men and stationed them in the strongholds of the wicked men, so that the impious might be overcome by the very places through which they had tried to attack the monastery’s defenses. He ordered them all, in turns by day and night, to patrol and range around the town and its estates.

Any of the fugitives who were captured were punished either by the misery of imprisonment or by extensive mutilation. The church obtained the justice due to it by right and was not compelled to resort to the tyrant’s court to secure vengeance for justice. Abbot Pons avenged the church upon its worst adversary, Hugh of Saint Peter, and ordered all his substance to be plundered, all his goods confiscated, and [Col. 1619A] all his buildings—houses, mills, and water-reservoirs, which he had erected with great arrogance and by which he had exalted himself to heaven—to be demolished. Thus all his property was destroyed, so that he might become a byword and a proverb for all generations to come.

The censure of most just retribution also fell upon the ministers of the sedition: Aimon of Saint Christopher, who was called “the Madman”; Peter, who has already been named of Saint Peter; Aimon of Phalèse; Robert of Four; Renald Daudet; Walter the Northman; Robert of Champ-Petreux; Durand Gulos; Alard Claud; and Peter Galimard. Their houses were razed to the ground and burned, and the goods which they had wickedly abused were plundered.

In the case of the others—namely Eustace, Simon, Durand, [Col. 1619B] Alburn, David, Hugh Bread-breaker, Felix, and their other accomplices—the abbot’s mercy moderated his sentence: only their wines were poured out by the church’s faithful men. Shields and arms of various kinds were also found among the spoils of the plundered houses. Many were put in chains until the king should pronounce judgment upon them. The pride of the impious was humbled, and the insolent common people of Vézelay learned that they had been subdued.

The tyrant saw that justice had prevailed and impiety had been confounded. He had no means by which to aid those whom he had deceived; he was ashamed to face them and could not bear their sight, because his own cowardice accused him and his conscience tormented him. Nevertheless, he prevented the impious men from surrendering themselves voluntarily [Col. 1619C] and making satisfaction at the abbot’s discretion, promising them peace according to their desire. Since he was ashamed to intercede for them, lest he seem to assist them contrary to his oath, he devised a plan of provocation against God. Blasphemous toward the worship of piety, he took staff and wallet, as though about to seek the oracles of St Denis, whose feast was approaching, and set out for the king.

When asked the reason for his arrival, he falsely represented himself as a pilgrim of the blessed martyr Denis. Having secured an audience with the king, he fell at his feet and most earnestly begged him to spare those exiles and also spare the monastery of Vézelay, which, if the town were abandoned, would plainly be left desolate. He promised upon oath and solemn adjuration [Col. 1619D] that he would bring those men before the king and that they would make satisfaction to the abbot and the church at the discretion of the royal mercy, and would establish a covenant of perpetual peace.

### The count fraudulently makes many representations to the king, which the abbot counters.

Moved by these prayers, the king appointed him a day at Auxerre, namely the third day after the feast of All Saints. He informed the abbot of the count’s petitions and promises, and requested that in the meantime he spare their houses until the day fixed for reconciliation. On hearing this, the abbot immediately informed the abbot of Fleury and his other friends of the king’s command and the count’s appointment, and asked them to be present with him at the forthcoming conference.

But the other magnates, with whom the king [Col. 1620A] had appointed a conference concerning the cause of Vézelay, informed the king that they would by no means attend where they knew the Count of Nevers would be present. When the tyrant learned this, he wished shamelessly to make use of this further wickedness. He again hastened to the king, asking that the day and place of the conference appointed concerning Vézelay be brought forward, alleging pursuit by his enemies, from whom he had to defend himself. For he hoped that, if he found the abbot stripped of counsel and alone through the absence of his friends, he could easily bend him by persuasive deceits.

But a mind long tested by his frauds could not be deceived through carelessness. Yet the king believed him and wrote to the abbot that he should attend the appointed conference on the feast of All Saints itself at Saint-Julien-du-Sault, there to make peace [Col. 1620B] and receive peace, if suitable terms were offered.

After taking counsel, the abbot answered that he could not come so hastily, since he had summoned his friends for the day first designated and would both make and accept peace by their counsel, if suitable terms were offered; especially since it was not fitting for him to undergo alone a conference concerning so great and weighty a cause. Upon hearing this, the king declared the abbot’s answer just and ordered that matters proceed as had first been settled.

### On the appointed day the king, abbot, and others assemble at Auxerre. The townsmen of Vézelay are condemned anew.

On the appointed Thursday after the feast of All Saints, the king and abbot assembled at Auxerre with their magnates and friends; the count also came with [Col. 1620C] the townsmen of Vézelay. On the next day, called Friday, the king sat and asked the burghers what they preferred to do. They answered that they would do everything according to the good pleasure of his mercy.

It was therefore decreed by the king’s judgment that they should utterly renounce, in whatever manner it had been made, the conspiracy and mutual confederacy which they had formed; that they should either seize, wherever found, those who had killed the church’s servants, if they could, or denounce them by whatever public cry and information they could provide; that they should swear upon sacred things the fealty, life, and bodily safety of the abbot and his people, and of the church and its people; that they should pay forty thousand solidi for the damage inflicted; that they should demolish the fortifications and outer defenses of their houses by the term fixed, namely by the feast of St Andrew; and that they should swear to perform all this honestly and fully.

Then, with their necks broken, subdued, and made humble, they promised to do so, and swore that they would honor and preserve the abbot as their lord. Those present immediately took the oaths prescribed: namely Guibert of Lotaringia, Hugh Bread-breaker, Durand Alburn, and nearly more than forty others. The abbot returned to Vézelay with his men, who had now been made faithful out of faithless traitors. They entered with him rejoicing in great gladness and celebration, and lived in peace like wild beasts made tame.
