Those who had been scattered abroad, rejoicing when they heard the terms of peace, returned and daily gathered in groups [Col. 1621A] to take the oath and make submission. From among them the abbot appointed collectors to exact the imposed payment from each individual, under this arrangement: after each person’s possessions had been appraised upon the obligation of an oath, and the assessments brought into a total, a tenth part of a pound was paid—that is, two solidi out of twenty. No one among them resisted or opened his mouth in contradiction, for the horn of their pride had been taken away, the rod of their strength had been broken, the liberty of the Church had been restored through the hand of the distinguished Abbot Pons, and all those who prostituted her chastity were confounded.

Yet they deliberately neglected to destroy the outer defenses of their houses, because this command was a scandal to them and like [Col. 1621B] a thorn piercing their eyes.

### The abbot punishes one who refuses to submit to his decrees.

After the Kalends of the Lord’s Nativity had passed, the abbot summoned them and warned them to fulfill, according to the peace agreement, what they had not yet done: the demolition of their houses’ fortifications. He fixed a deadline for them to carry out his orders. When they again delayed, he warned them with threats, predicting that, if they neglected any longer to obey his commands in deed, they would experience his wrath.

Frequent letters of entreaty were sent to the abbot by the princes of the region, especially on Simon’s behalf, asking him not to contain his mercy in wrath against Simon, but rather to show compassion and spare Simon’s house, which had indeed been the cause and beginning of the evils. [Col. 1621C] Therefore the impious Simon himself, greatly relying upon the favor and familiarity of the princes, despised the abbot’s admonition to cast down what he had wickedly built. He added insult to contempt, building battlements and the fortification of a tower he had begun.

When the abbot saw that the mark of their obstinacy and the glory of their pride remained in their houses, he summoned a rural multitude from the monastery’s estates. On the Saturday after the Purification of the Lord (*Hypapante Domini*), he sent them and certain brethren to the house of the impious Simon. They utterly cast down his outer defenses, battlements, and tower, while Simon himself sat by the fire in the same house with his wife and children. Seeing this, the others were greatly afraid; groaning and blushing with shame, they gave [Col. 1621D] hostages as security for demolishing their fortifications within the appointed time.

### At last, in 1155, the church of Vézelay obtains its liberty; at the abbot’s request, ordinations are conferred.

[Col. 1622A] In the year 1155 of the Incarnation of God, in the second year of the apostolic pontificate of Nicholas, who was called Adrian, while the pious Louis the Younger reigned and governed as king of the Franks, rest was granted to the Church of Vézelay through the hand of the illustrious and most renowned Abbot Pons, outstanding in birth, character, and rank. The church obtained its most complete and unrestricted liberty, both in private affairs and in matters before public courts.

For in private matters, while the rival was still alive, Alan, the pious bishop of Auxerre, was invited by the aforesaid abbot. He celebrated solemn ordinations at Vézelay in the oratory of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, on the Saturday of the March fasts, with [Col. 1622B] Odo of Bonne-Casa, cardinal subdeacon, present in the monastery. Having inspected the authority of Roman privileges, he ordained three acolytes, one subdeacon, and four deacons; moreover, he advanced six brethren to the grade of priesthood, with Stephen, Abbot of Reigny, present and cooperating.

In the following year, that is, the year of peace and victory, two bishops—the Bishops of Le Mans and Évreux—came from Rome with the Abbot of St Alban and celebrated holy Easter at Vézelay. At the request of the venerable Pons, after completing the office of the holy vigil, they solemnly conferred holy orders. The Bishop of Évreux ordained doorkeepers, exorcists, readers, and acolytes in the oratory of Mary the *Theotokos*, Mother of God. The Bishop of Le Mans made seven subdeacons [Col. 1622C] and one deacon, and consecrated five priests. In all these matters the adversary was silenced, pierced through the throat by envy and cast down by the authority of justice. On that same Saturday Abbot Pons received holy chrism from the archpriest of Auxerre.

Moreover, in public legal matters, the church first obtained, through the king’s hand and by apostolic authority, the free right of justice against faithless traitors and rebellious servants—not by legal right or custom, but through necessity. Thereafter, through the hand of Abbot Pons, it authoritatively judged both his causes and those of his people in its own court; and the judgment of no lay or clerical person ever, anywhere, intervened in its judicial right. Every calumnious claim was annulled, [Col. 1622D] because confusion and disgrace took possession of the calumniators; and the enemy failed, because the righteous man prevailed.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1621]

[Col. 1621D] As fathers lay up treasures for their children through the increase of estates and money, so the foresight of predecessors stores up knowledge for their successors through the writing of books and the commemoration of deeds. For through writings the past is in some manner joined to the future, since the written letter represents what antiquity had carried away.

Having therefore described in the preceding little books the dignity, origin, and liberty of the Church [Col. 1623A] of Vézelay, together with the labors it endured steadfastly and tirelessly for the justice of its liberty, we now turn our pen to what remains—not to supply omissions, indeed, but to continue the narrative, since these things have been experienced by sight and hearing. We describe for the pious sons to imitate the virtue of pious Fathers, so that they may not neglect to maintain what the vigorous prudence of their Fathers acquired only through grievous labors.

Once all the adversaries of the liberty of the Church of Vézelay had been defeated, Abbot Pons, of venerable and ever-memorable memory, attained the summit of undiminished dignity. As though the right had been renewed, he wholly abolished every error introduced by servile spite; and, peace having been obtained, he thereafter ruled his monastery peacefully for five years with the rod of equity.

[Col. 1623B] ### In 1159 a schism arises in the Church.

In the year 1159 of the incarnate Word, a foul dissension arose in the Roman Church—alas! After the death of Pope Adrian, Roland, chancellor of the sacred chancery, was elected by general counsel and universal agreement. While he modestly hesitated to assume so great a burden, Octavian, one of the apostolic cardinals and a man of higher nobility among the senators of the City, fraudulently seized the apostolic insignia for himself and—wickedness beyond measure!—usurped the apostolic office. Respecting neither divine nor human law, he had only three supporters of his schism from the entire apostolic consistory: Ismar, Bishop of Tusculum; [Col. 1623C] Guy of Cremona; and John of Saint Martina. Ismar and John, both schismatics, met death while still in schism.

When the other cardinals learned of the schismatic usurpation, they immediately departed from the City with their own elect, called Alexander, who had been consecrated by Humbald, Bishop of Ostia. A grave schism arose in the western Church: the German emperor favored Octavian, who was called Victor, while the Sicilian king favored the Catholic Alexander.

Alexander sent his legates into Gaul and the British Isles, to Louis, king of the Franks, to Henry, king of England, and to the whole Church of both kingdoms: William of Pavia, Henry of Pisa, and Otto of [Col. 1623D] the Tullian Prison. As they passed through Italy, they were not received by the monastery of Cluny; but the first, and indeed foremost, among all persons in Gaul to receive them was Pons, Abbot of Vézelay, of worthy memory. He commended the Catholic and orthodox election of Alexander to all princes of both orders.

### The Cluniacs refuse to adhere to Pope Alexander. They are excommunicated.

After Alexander had been received by both kingdoms, the legates wrote to the Cluniacs concerning the reception of Alexander. At that time Hugh, prudent in morals but simple in intellect, presided over the church of Cluny. He summoned a chapter, as was customary in such matters, and consulted his brethren concerning the reception of Alexander.

But they detested the preeminence of Father Hugh. Since they could not [Col. 1624A] sink the tooth of envy into the person of the innocent man, they employed a crafty plan: with a solemn warning they forbade him to receive either the Catholic or the schismatic, lest, if—as often happens in such cases—they favored the defeated party, they might incur the victor’s hatred. Lest he suspect danger in a counsel that was deceitful rather than salutary, they promised unanimously to share his view and to undergo with him whatever adversity might thereafter occur.

Since the apostolic legates feared to approach Cluny and pronounce a sentence against the schismatics, they sent Henry, then Bishop of Beauvais and afterward Archbishop of Reims. Because he was a kinsman of King Louis, [Col. 1624B] he seemed able both to come more safely into those regions and to wield the sword of the apostle Peter entrusted to him by Alexander through the aforesaid legates.

When he arrived and met at Luzey, and was preparing to impose a sentence of anathema upon the Cluniacs, he deferred it at the request of Dalmatius and other princes of that land. He wrote to the Cluniacs, exhorting them to come to their senses and receive Alexander, as other monasteries of France had done; otherwise, by the apostolic authority entrusted to him, he would no longer delay pronouncing the sentence of excommunication upon them and all their supporters.

On the day appointed at Melun, neither the Abbot of Cluny himself, held back by the treachery of his own men, nor his representatives were present. But the abbot’s enemies stood on the other side: namely Theobald, prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, who at some later time held the position of prior after the abbot in the monastery of Cluny, [Col. 1624C] and many others who seemed to be the heads of their church. Accusing their own abbot as sons who had murdered their father, and removing the blame of schism from themselves, they declared that they and the monasteries entrusted to them committed themselves to the submission and protection of the Catholic Alexander. With their support, Henry publicly excommunicated Hugh, Abbot of Cluny, and all his subjects and supporters.

### When Pons, Abbot of Vézelay, dies, William, Abbot of Saint-Martin at Pontoise, is substituted in his place.

Our Pons, rightly to be named an abbot of holy memory, had been summoned to this conference, with some favoring it, so that, after Hugh’s expulsion, he might be set over the monastery [Col. 1624D] of Cluny. Yet blessed and glorious Mary Magdalene, lover of God, to whom he had always rendered devoted service, would not allow him to be torn from her candlestick, from which he had shone most brightly. She retained him for herself even in body: him whom, nurtured from childhood and granted to her by Michael, prince of the angels, she had wholly claimed and consecrated anew as her own.

Nor did she allow the enemy of the liberty of her sepulchre to exult over him even for an hour, lest he should become contrary to himself—he who had fought for his homeland might in some fashion conquer his homeland—or lest malice should overthrow virtue by means of virtue, and cowardice cast down excellence through excellence.

Seized by an unexpected illness, in the twenty-fourth year of his appointment he entered the way of all flesh. [Col. 1625A] Amid the grievous mourning of his people, he was buried before the tomb of the woman who served Christ’s tomb; and, as it is lawful to believe, he was taken away lest the glory of human excellence should alter his understanding.

Immediately upon his removal, the brethren of the monastery of Vézelay elected with one voice and common consent as their Father a man noble by birth, distinguished in virtue, instructed from youth in sacred disciplines—both in Vézelay itself, where he had been received, and in the monastery of Cluny—namely William, Abbot of Saint-Martin of Pontoise. He had governed that monastery for fifteen years and had enlarged it with many possessions and buildings.

### To prevent the election from taking effect, the Count of Nevers places an obstacle. The count’s consent is not required for the election of an abbot.

[Col. 1625B] At this time William, Count of Nevers, son of William of Chartres, son of Renald of Hubenc, son of William, son of Renald, son of Landric—who first received the lordship of Nevers from the Count of Burgundy—was suffering from a grave illness. This count, after the many injuries which he had inflicted upon the Church of Vézelay, as partly related in the preceding volume, was beginning to taste the cup of divine vengeance.

When his son William heard that the people of Vézelay had elected an abbot, believing in his inherited insolence that everything depended upon his own nod, he came to Vézelay in great anger and fury. He forbade the brethren to carry out an election made in his father’s absence and without his consultation, and stationed guards lest anyone [Col. 1625C] from Vézelay should pass to the elect.

But how perverse and irrational this action was is shown by the records of the Roman pontiffs and the privileges of the kings of France. The following written instrument of his grandfather, who with similar arrogance challenged the election of Abbot Renald—afterward Archbishop of Lyons—also makes this clear:

> “I, the Count of Nevers, relinquish to God, to the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and to blessed Mary Magdalene, a certain evil custom which I was enforcing in the Church of Vézelay: namely, that henceforth no consent of mine, or of my heirs or successors, shall be required concerning the election of the abbot of that place. Rather, the aforesaid church shall have whomever has been elected, so that none of us may challenge anything or demand anything from the Church [Col. 1625D] because our consent has not been obtained. I also promise that I shall henceforth make no claim concerning either the entry or the departure of abbots.”

The cardinal legate confirms the election. The abbot takes possession.

The people of Vézelay, therefore, setting aside the unjust challenge of the young count, sent Renald of Merlot to summon their elected abbot. When he arrived, he would neither enter the monastery nor accept the brothers’ solemn procession, lest he seem to have entered by a lesser door; for such a transfer from monastery to monastery, or from church to church, without consulting the Roman pontiff, is in no way judged valid. Therefore the people of Vézelay wrote through Geoffrey Hospitaler [Col. 1626A] to Otto, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, informing him of the manner of the election and of the person elected. After reading the apostolic privileges, he approved the election as sound, confirmed that it was to stand by apostolic authority, and entrusted to the elected man, on behalf of the lord pope, the care of the church of Vézelay, through the hand of Peter of Pisa, dean of Saint Anianus of Orléans.

And Abbot William entered Vézelay, received with the favour of the entire people and the brothers’ solemn procession. With him were Macharius, abbot of Fleury; Theobald, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; and Stephen, abbot of Reigny. Not many days later he sent to Pope Alexander the aforementioned Geoffrey and his clerk John the Italian, with letters from his chapter [Col. 1626B] describing the proceedings of his election, together with letters from the king of the Franks, the king of England, and the aforementioned abbots, commending the person elected and the manner of the election.

Alexander reaches Genoa. He ratifies the abbot’s election and renews the privileges. The Cluniacs usurp the government of the monastery of Vézelay.

Meanwhile Pope Alexander, avoiding the snares of the schismatic Octavian, came by sea to the city of Genoa. When this was heard, the envoys of Vézelay went there. Honourably received by Alexander, they remained with him in the palace for several days. Alexander, seated with the whole body of cardinals, while a great multitude from many regions stood by, [Col. 1626C] heard the representatives of the monastery of Vézelay, received the letters they brought, ratified the appointment of Abbot William, and granted to him and all the brothers of that monastery a privilege in which, following the precedents of the ancient Roman pontiffs, he decreed that, upon the death of their abbot, the brothers of the monastery of Vézelay should have free election in appointing a successor; and that no person, under pretext of any cause or religious claim, should presume to appropriate to himself, or in any manner demand, any assent concerning that election.

This liberty, which the church of Vézelay had peacefully and without challenge possessed for almost three hundred years from the very beginning of its foundation, and under which it had indiscriminately set over itself as fathers men both from its own community and from the brothers [Col. 1626D] of other monasteries, the Cluniacs, who arose much later, endeavoured by stealth to claim for themselves. First they arrogated assent, and then indeed the right of election, falsely alleging that Paschal had entrusted to them the care of the order of the church of Vézelay. On this very account that church suffered a grave scandal under Pope Innocent II, while asserting its native liberty: when, through the violence of that same Innocent and the count of Nevers, a certain Alberic was imposed by the Cluniacs, almost all the brothers of the often-mentioned monastery were put in chains and scattered shamefully here and there through Provence, Italy, Germany, Lotharingia, France, and Aquitaine, while foreigners entered upon the freest soil, who, as though [Col. 1627A] gathered from every quarter under Sennacherib, made for themselves one name of Samaritan superstition.

Since therefore, in the time of temptation, Cluny’s pride had swelled, and the monastery, which until then had been a particularly special member of the Roman Church, had strayed from Roman unity, it rightly pleased the apostolic judgment that the church of Vézelay, the daughter sprung from the womb of blessed Peter, should not once more be subject to the calumny of schismatics. This was especially so since Pope Alexander himself, being Catholic, no less than Paschal and all his other apostolic predecessors, by God’s gift possessed the keys of blessed Peter, by which, according to the merit of faith, that which had at some time been claimed as done or bound under pretext of religion was to be remitted or loosed.

Finally, because of the insolence of the Cluniacs, not only in [Col. 1627B] this matter but throughout the whole body, the liberty of the church of Vézelay was endangered. For when the aforementioned newcomers abused great abundance, and allowed the native inhabitants of neighbouring places to plunder the Church’s goods, attending rather to indolence and sloth than to the liberty due to it, they induced the count of Nevers and, under the appearance of familiarity, supplied him with material for an unprecedented tyranny and an unheard-of custom. In their time there arose the exaction of undue justice, frequent requisitions for maintenance, burdensome pretexts, and the submission to evil customs. Through all these things the same Church has in our time been almost reduced to nothing. For, creeping gradually, the pestilential poison both of Cluniac servitude [Col. 1627C] and of the count’s tyranny infected, from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, all the elders of that age, down to Pontius of blessed memory—whom the noble and fertile land of Auvergne, producer of distinguished men, brought forth—and to the William of Merlot now under discussion, whom the vigorous offspring of Charlemagne’s line at Roche-Merlot produced. These, indeed, true sons, grieved over the fate of their true mother, and resisted for her justice even unto blood.

Accordingly, Pope Alexander, leaving the city of Genoa, landed in the harbour of Maguelonne. The aforementioned William, abbot of Vézelay, met him. Just as his predecessor Pontius had received the first fruits of the apostolic legation, not without the envy of his own men and of certain magnates, so this man [Col. 1627D] was the first of all the priests of Gaul to receive the supreme pontiff as he came ashore from the seacoast. He found favour in Alexander’s sight, and Alexander exalted him before the assembly of the entire Roman Church. Again reviewing Count Gerard’s testament, and comparing the documents of ancient privileges with modern ones, Pope Alexander, in the consistory at Montpellier, confirmed, according to the copy subscribed below, the immunity of the liberty of the church of Vézelay and its freedom to elect or appoint an abbot, by the common counsel, will, and judgment of all the bishops, priests, deacons, subdeacons, and cardinals.

Pope Alexander confirms the privileges of the church of Vézelay and exempts it from the authority of the Cluniacs.

[Col. 1628A] “ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons William, abbot of the monastery of Vézelay, and his brothers, present and future, who profess the monastic life: in perpetuity.

“The most holy Roman Church, which renders to each according to the quality of his merits, is accustomed to treat with more gracious favour those whom it finds faithful, and to adorn with the prerogative of honour those whom it perceives to be more fervent in its service. Our predecessor Pope Paschal of good memory, as we have learned from the privilege of our predecessor Pope Calixtus of blessed memory, is known to have entrusted the monastery of Vézelay—which properly and especially belongs to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter—to the church of Cluny, considering the fervour of religion [Col. 1628B] then maintained there, because religious observance had at that time largely perished in the monastery of Vézelay. And the aforesaid Pope Calixtus confirmed the same by the privilege of his authority: namely, that when the abbot then appointed there should die, another was to be installed there by the common consent of the brothers, or of the sounder part of their counsel, with the advice of the abbots of Cluny.

“But we, considering more carefully the constancy of your devotion and the firmness of faith which, in this stormy time, both you and Pontius, abbot of Vézelay of good memory, have shown toward the Roman Church; and considering also how manifestly the church of Cluny has erred in this time [Col. 1628C] of disturbance, and how, falling from its former religious observance and integrity, it has made itself alien to the unity of the Church; while your aforesaid monastery has remained most steadfast in devotion and faith toward the Church, and religious observance has there been fully restored through God’s grace: so that each church may seem to receive the fruit due to its merits, we have judged, by the common counsel of our brothers, that the commission which our predecessor Pope Paschal made should be revoked. We decree that the said monastery ought in no respect whatever to be subject to the church of Cluny, nor be bound to answer to anyone except the Roman Church alone; and that your election shall in every respect be free, so that neither the counsel nor the consent of the abbots of Cluny may in any way be required. Indeed, we will that the man be given and placed over you as abbot [Col. 1628D] whom the brothers, by common consent or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, and whom the Roman pontiff shall either judge ought to be ordained or, upon the representation of the monks of that place, consent to have been ordained.

“And in order that this our enactment may be observed inviolate for all future time, we confirm it by apostolic authority and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing that no person whatsoever may be permitted to infringe this page of our constitution or in any way oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But to those who observe these provisions, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.”

The abbot, received kindly by the pope, returns home. His enemies defame him.

After Abbot William had remained many days with the apostolic lord Alexander, enriched by his favour and blessing, he departed for home with the support of the entire Roman Church. Returning, he was received with great glory by his brothers and by all his people, with a solemn procession [Col. 1629B] amid the decoration of the streets and the smoke of incense. When prayer had been made, as was customary, he offered two precious silk cloths and two excellent tapestries. Then all the opponents of the liberty of the church of Vézelay were confounded; and men of ready tongues rose up—men whose habit it is to envy the prosperity of the good—and began to slander Abbot William before the young count, for his father had died. They alleged that William had squandered all the Church’s goods and given an immense sum of money to the Romans, declaring it wicked that so noble a church should be ruined, and that this wickedness rightly rebounded upon the count’s own head, since, although he was the Church’s guardian and defender, he did not resist so great a despoiling.

[Col. 1629C] There was a young man named William, son of Peter of Montreuil, among the attendants of Abbot Pontius. Though younger in years, he was sharper in intellect. Clever in judgment and pleasing in service, he obtained such favour with Pontius that he surpassed all the courtiers in power and almost claimed the second place in rule. Whomever he excluded was excluded; whomever he admitted was admitted; whom he justified was justified; and whom he condemned was condemned. Justice and injustice, gift and merit, and even favour itself—than which nothing is more brilliant in every fortune—were reckoned as nothing without William’s favour. Those whom age and wisdom had formerly made intimate with Pontius became outsiders.

And although, with a childish mind, he presumed greater things than men greater than himself, [Col. 1629D] he even began to slander the brothers, accusing his own lords while himself a servant in condition and character. Having excluded everyone else, he alone abused, in his lord’s name alone, the favour bestowed upon him. Right and wrong were of one price to him, since he was wholly intent upon extending his own bounds out of the poverty of the poor. Abusing his lord’s confidence, he repaid thirty for a hundred and received a hundred for a denarius. He increased enormously in many possessions and countless sums of money, and the affairs of all men were in his mouth. Content to abuse the favour of one man only, he stirred up against himself the hatred of all, both within and without.

For he was proud, arrogant, and impure: he despised, accused, and dishonoured all honourable and most approved men. By crafty flatteries he had so deceived the simple mind [Col. 1630A] of the pious father that Pontius granted him everything which in any way pleased him. Thus puffed up, and in a marvellous manner lifted above himself, the young man for four years grew insolent rather than strong; then, in a single moment of one night, the wretch suddenly fell and burst, becoming as though he had never existed—and would that he never had existed! For when Abbot Pontius of happy memory breathed out the last breath of life, that treacherous servant—who ought to have died from grief—set aside the funeral rites, immediately took the keys, plundered the cupboards, and secretly carried off whatever he could seize. Having repeatedly committed such sacrilegious theft, he was discovered and arrested by the brothers.

When questioned concerning the abbot’s treasures and concerning the golden candlestick [Col. 1630B] which the Empress Matilda, mother of Henry king of England, had once given to the monastery of Vézelay, he denied everything. But after his house was searched and, finally, the key which he had denied possessing was obtained from his household, there were found the candlestick he had denied, the abbot’s seal, and likewise the chapter’s seal, which had been hidden from the brothers for two years already. In the morning he gave the brothers sureties for five hundred pounds, to be held for the execution of justice in the hand of the future abbot, who on that same day of the venerable Pontius’s burial was unanimously elected, in the year of the divine Incarnation 1161, on Friday, the fourteenth day of October.

Meanwhile the profane William of Montreuil went [Col. 1630C] to the young count, who was celebrating his father’s funeral; the latter had ended his human life on the eighth day after the death of the pious Pontius. After constructing many falsehoods, William promised the new count eighty pounds and seventeen silver cups if he would give him aid against the people of Vézelay, and also two marks of silver every year to the count as a payment for protection. The count, for his part, promised him the aid he had sought against all men.

When the elected Abbot William had therefore been solemnly received, all together cried out against William of Montreuil, who, relying upon the count’s aid, refused to submit to the execution of justice. Therefore, by Abbot William’s command, he was seized and consigned to prison. Then, employing his usual craftiness, since he lacked the help [Col. 1630D] on which he had hoped, he began to entreat the abbots who had happened to assemble for the new abbot’s entry—namely, the abbot of Fleury and the abbot of Paris. Under pretext of a confession, which priests may not reveal, he offered to disclose, insofar as he knew them, the treasures that were being sought. He declared that he would abide by their decision concerning the charges laid against him, if the new abbot agreed. The abbot, yielding to their prayers and counsel, said that he too would do the same. Immediately, at the twilight of that night, holy relics were brought into the abbot’s grove. The impious William was brought from prison and swore upon the sacred things that he would do whatever the aforementioned abbots determined on the following morning and that meanwhile he would flee nowhere.

But what faith is there in a traitor? For there is no trace of truth where there is no foundation of faith. As the common saying has it, one should not trust an enemy proved such by experience; likewise no faith should be placed in a traitor when he swears. The profane man swears with his mouth to justice, but from his heart he speaks in his heart wickedness; falling into the depth of evils, he despises justice and follows the purpose of impiety. Thus this criminal William, scorning his oath and setting faith aside, shamelessly fled that very night as a perjurer. When Abbot William heard this and established the outcome of the matter, he immediately sent his servants to the house of the fugitive traitor and caused grain, wine, vessels, cloths, and all the household furnishings to be carried away. He exacted from the sureties the promised sum of five hundred pounds. The sacrilegious man secretly fled [Col. 1631B] to the count, who received him and, after a few days, brought him back to Vézelay.

When the count was challenged by the abbot as to why he had received his faithless fugitive and brought him back to Vézelay contrary to the custom of the town—for by law he was permitted neither to receive a protected man of the monastery nor to grant safe-conduct into the town to any enemy of it—a day was fixed at Reigny to settle these and other matters. When they met there, the abbot first complained that the count was receiving his protected men contrary to the Church’s custom. He asked that the count without delay restore to him his fugitive William of Montreuil, who was the Church’s chief servant and had been convicted of wrongdoing and perjury.

Then the count consulted his leading men concerning the complaint laid before him regarding the law of custom. They all unanimously declared that the count had no protected man among the men of the church of Vézelay, neither against the Church nor in any other way. At once the count dismissed the shifty William and ordered him to return to his lawful lord and obey his command in all things. Seeing that he had achieved nothing, William submitted himself at the abbot’s command, willing or unwilling. Having sold his house along with some of his possessions, he released his sureties.

The monks of Vézelay offer prayers to God for the sick count of Nevers; nevertheless, he proves ungrateful.

After this it happened that the count fell sick unto death. Abbot William, greatly compassionating him, served him freely as best he could, although the count hated him; and the church of Vézelay made daily prayer to God for him. Yet when he recovered while it prayed, he ungratefully forgot all the benefits shown him by the Church and by the abbot. Giving willing ears to slanderers, he considered what occasions he might find for harassing the abbot or the monastery. He wrote to the abbot demanding that he repay him the money which the profane man named William of Montreuil owed him by agreement. He instructed the messenger carrying his letter that, if the abbot delayed or evaded payment, he was immediately to plunder the abbot’s land.

Thus, on a Sunday, the messenger brought the abbot the count’s letter [Col. 1632A] concerning the aforesaid business. The messenger was called Geoffrey of Melun. The abbot immediately replied that he owed the count no money whatsoever, but that, if the impious William owed anything to the count, he should unquestionably demand it from him. Geoffrey replied that it was none of his concern except to carry out his lord’s command. “Will you then,” said the abbot, “plunder our goods on this Sunday?” “No,” said Geoffrey, “but tomorrow I shall not be able to disregard my lord’s command. Nevertheless, if you please to send to my lord, I shall gladly go with the messenger and plead your cause.” When he had been entertained by the abbot there, that is, at Campmollé, and had accepted that a certain monk, the abbot’s messenger, would go to the count, [Col. 1632B] he left the monk on the road, came to Château-Censoir, chose the strongest young men, and, as that Sunday was already drawing toward evening, immediately plundered all the abbot’s flocks of sheep at Campmollé, where he had eaten with the abbot that day.

There was no delay: divine vengeance followed him. Before seven days had passed, he was seized by madness and threw himself from the window of his house into the river Yonne below. Drawn out half alive, he began to tear his own limbs, and so, raging mad, he died unworthy of life. When all the brothers and the entire people of Vézelay cried out against the most criminal William, because on his account they suffered both the hostility of so great a lord and the plundering of their goods, the abbot ordered that William satisfy the count concerning the agreement or else restore the losses inflicted upon the Church. Failing in both, he was cast into chains and consigned to prison.

Bound in iron and enveloped in darkness, he could not disregard the income from his money because of the stench of prison; indeed, he thought it sweeter to undergo every misery than freely to diminish his money. For he had lent it at interest in many places, and willingly endured the filth of prison, the privation of food, and, what was more grievous, the injury to his honour. At length, compelled by the prolonged pressure of imprisonment, he again made peace after selling possessions. Thereafter he was like a wolf among sheep, ensnaring his neighbours, accusing the poor, and slandering the rich. Yet the count, satisfied neither with this man’s miseries nor with his own wrongs, caused the herds, livestock, and people of the monastery of Vézelay to be plundered. For, as the common proverb says, “For one wishing to do harm, opportunity alone suffices.” Resting on no ground of any just complaint, he sought an occasion by which he might subject the Church to his lordship and strip it of its inborn liberty.

Louis, king of the Franks, supports Pope Alexander’s party, but is rebuffed by him.

In these days the Western Church suffered from a grave schism. Count Henry of Troyes, however, favoured the emperor’s party. King Louis of France sent his envoys to meet Pope Alexander, the Catholic: Theobald, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and his clerk Carducus. When Alexander received their embassy less favourably than they wished, they returned to Vézelay. Abbot Theobald fell into a bed of illness and died on the ninth day before the Kalends of August [24 July]; he was buried within the entrance of the basilica of Blessed Mary Magdalene, of which he had been a monk.

When King Louis learned that his envoys had been rebuffed, he angrily regretted having received Alexander while scorning Victor. Through Manasses, bishop of Orléans, he wrote these words to Count Henry of Troyes, who at that time was hurrying to the German emperor. Henry, rejoicing at the opportunity found, advised the emperor to hold a conference with the king, gathering the leading men and ecclesiastics of both realms. He swore that, after hearing an examination of the elections of the two claimants to the apostolic see, the king would, according to the judgment [Col. 1633B] of the persons of both kingdoms, abide by Henry’s counsel. A conference was proclaimed at the village of Lovigennes, on this side of the river Saône, within the borders of the kingdom of France. It was decreed that Alexander the Catholic and Victor the schismatic should attend the conference and discuss their respective elections in the sight of the whole Church.

The pontiff, by sounder counsel, sends envoys to the king to soothe his mind.

When Alexander learned this, he sent envoys to King Louis—Bernard, bishop of Porto, and his deacon Hyacinth—to soften the king’s anger and enter into familiar discussion with him. Alexander and Louis accordingly met at Silviniacum, a village belonging to the monks of Cluny. King Louis [Col. 1633C] asked Alexander to come to the appointed conference; or, if he perhaps shrank from the emperor’s presence, at least to go as far as the regions near the castle of Vergy, which was impregnable. When Alexander would not agree, the king said: “I will conduct you and your entire company safely there and bring you back safe, as I would my own body.” Yet Alexander did not agree even then, fearing the emperor’s tricks. The king replied: “It is remarkable that one conscious of his own justice should evade the testimony of his innocence or the hearing of his case.” The king then went to the conference proclaimed with the emperor, not yet knowing the terms which Count Henry had made with the emperor on his behalf.

[Col. 1633D] The king meets at a conference with Count Henry of Troyes, who, favouring the emperor, opposed Alexander.

When the king had arrived at the castle of Dijon, Count Henry met him and for the first time disclosed the agreements he had made with the emperor:

“Providing for the reverence due to your majesty and the advantage of your kingdom, my lord king, I have arranged a conference upon the river Saône. There, my lord king, you and Emperor Frederick, meeting with the pontiffs, abbots, and leading men of both kingdoms, in the presence of your pope and the emperor’s pope, will choose from each side the most approved men, ecclesiastical and lay, who will judge the election of the two claimants to the apostolic see. If the election of Roland shall be judged sounder, Octavian’s election shall be annulled and the emperor shall fall at Roland’s feet. But if Victor’s election prevails, Roland shall be declared null; and you, my lord king, shall come to Octavian’s feet. If Octavian should be absent, the emperor, abandoning him, will obey your Alexander; but conversely, if Alexander should be absent, the same consequence shall follow, and the king shall support Victor. But if your majesty will neither agree to the aforesaid terms nor assent to the judgment of the judges, I have sworn an oath that I shall go over to his side and, surrendering to the emperor whatever I hold as a fief from the king’s fisc, shall thereafter hold it from him.”

Astonished, King Louis replied: “I wonder whence you have the confidence to make such agreements with the emperor without my knowledge and without consulting me.”

Henry replied: [Col. 1634B] “You yourself, king, gave me this confidence through Manasses, bishop of Orléans.”

When questioned concerning this statement, the bishop, fearing the king, began to dissemble, concealing the schemes by which he had induced Henry to do this. Then Henry produced the king’s letter, stating that the king’s envoys had been rebuffed by Alexander. Indignant because of this, the king directed Henry to proceed freely to Emperor Frederick and undertake a conference concerning the hearing of the two claims, being certain that the king would in all respects abide by Henry’s counsel.

Another conference on the imperial frontier. The king’s envoys.

Emperor Frederick had built for himself a palace of remarkable size at a place called Dolah, [Col. 1634C] on the frontier of his empire. The French learned that Victor the schismatic was not with the emperor and rejoiced at his absence. When the Teutons, or Germans, learned this, they hurried off and brought him back with the greatest haste that same day. The emperor took him and, in the middle of the night, led him to the middle of the bridge; then, as though he had fulfilled the terms of the agreement, he withdrew.

King Louis, as though setting out to hunt, passed through a wood to the place of the conference. He sent Joscius, archbishop of Tours; Maurice, bishop of Paris; and also William, abbot of Vézelay, with other leading men of his kingdom, to the emperor’s envoys assembled there and awaiting the king’s word. Among them was also Count Henry, who, because of kinship by marriage, wholly supported the party of Victor the schismatic. The king’s envoys therefore requested from him a suitable truce, because the terms of this conference had been unknown to the king until the day before yesterday; especially because the emperor had compelled Count Henry to swear that he would not in any way reveal the aforesaid arrangements to the king before the day of the appointed conference. It would be improper, moreover, to decide so great a matter so rashly.

When Frederick’s spokesmen refused the requested truce, the king returned to Dijon. The cardinals whom Pope Alexander had sent there, hoping the conference had been dissolved, returned to Vézelay. The king stationed guards on the borders of his kingdom. On the following very early morning Count Henry came to the king in the palace of the duke of Burgundy [Col. 1635A] and argued that the king was by no means released from the terms. Therefore Henry would necessarily leave the king and put himself into the emperor’s hands, so that henceforth he would receive from the emperor, as a grant from him, the whole land which he had previously held as a fief from the king, and render homage to him.

Nevertheless, he said that, out of favour for the king, he had obtained from the emperor a truce of three weeks, on condition that the king should promise the emperor, after giving hostages, that on the appointed day he would come, bring Alexander, hear there the case of both parties, and submit to the judgment of worthy men of the empire and kingdom; or else surrender himself bound to the emperor at Chrysopolis, the noble city of the Byzantines. The king consented; his spirit failed, and he was wearied in mind. He agreed that he would do so, giving hostages: [lacuna] the duke of Burgundy [lacuna] the count of Flanders, and William, count of Nevers.

But every ecclesiastical order, hearing what the king had done, grieved deeply; and all cried in their hearts to the Lord that he might have mercy upon his holy Church and free the king from the deceit of those who had ensnared him.

The emperor’s deceptions are exposed; the king withdraws from him.

The king went, therefore, to the aforementioned village of Lovigennes, where the emperor was to meet him. But the emperor deceived Henry and sent his chief supporter of the schism, Rainald, his chancellor of the church of Cologne. When the terms which Count Henry had proposed to the king as coming from the emperor’s own mouth were repeated before him, divine power suddenly came to the aid of [Col. 1635C] its Church and to the pious simplicity of the royal majesty. For Rainald, supporter of profane error, replied that the emperor had said nothing of the kind: namely, that he would allow anyone a share in judging the Roman Church, which was properly subject to its own jurisdiction.

Filled with joy, the king asked Count Henry whether the agreements stood in the form which Henry had laid before him. The king said: “Behold: the emperor who, according to your word, ought to have been present, is absent; behold also: his envoys, in your presence and with you as witness, alter the form of the agreement.”

“It is true,” said Count Henry.

And the king said: “Am I not therefore released from every agreement?”

“Released,” said Henry.

The king then said to all his leading men, bishops, and abbots present there: “You have all heard and seen how I have freely performed everything that lay upon me. Say whether I seem free from these terms.”

They all said: “You have fulfilled your word.”

The king immediately turned back the swift horse he was riding and at once departed. The Teutons, greatly confused, pursued him and begged him to return to the emperor, who was prepared to fulfil all that Henry had proposed. But the king, making little of what was said, recoiled from the trap he had escaped, saying: “I have done what was mine to do.” Thus, the assembly being dissolved, the king returned to his kingdom.

Pope Alexander is received by the king at Paris. He consecrates the church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. He holds a council [Col. 1636A] at Tours.

Pope Alexander the Catholic, fearing King Louis’s anger, went to Bourges, the metropolitan city of Aquitaine, and then to the monastery of Déols, near Châteauroux, where he spent the winter. In the following Lent he came to King Louis in the city of Paris. Received honourably by him according to the custom of the Roman Church, Alexander himself carried the golden rose on the Sunday on which “Laetare, Jerusalem” is sung. After the Easter solemnities had been completed, he consecrated the basilica of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, ruled by Hugh of Monceaux, a monk of the church of Vézelay.

William, abbot of Vézelay, again came there and asked Pope Alexander to confirm more fully, for the third time, the liberty and possessions of his church and the immunity of the banns of his monastery prescribed by his predecessors. [Col. 1636B] Alexander gave his gracious assent and granted him a third privilege. From there he went to the metropolitan city of Tours and held there a council of one hundred and five bishops from the provinces of Lyons, Narbonne, Vienne, Bourges, Sens, Reims, Rouen, Tours, Bordeaux, Auch, the Alps, the Apennines, and the Maritime Alps; also of Canterbury and York, and of Scotland and Ireland; together with abbots and persons of diverse religious professions, arriving gladly from every direction. For several bishops of the Germans also secretly wrote to [Col. 1636C] Pope Alexander, humbly offering him obedience and every reverence appropriate to the place and time. No small part of Italy was present, partly by letter and partly in person. Sardinia and Sicily, together with all Calabria, the entire Eastern Church, and Spain also humbly submitted the devoted head of obedience to Pope Alexander the Catholic.

Various cases were argued in that council; especially that of the Parisian clerics against the monks of Saint-Germain. Present at the aforesaid council were Stephen, abbot of Cluny, and William, abbot of Vézelay. The Cluniacs considered bringing forward a suit for renunciation against the Vézelay monks; but, conscious of their own injustice and of Roman rectitude, they all fell silent [Col. 1636D], nor thereafter dared even to murmur on the matter, although very many controversies of this sort were proposed and settled on both sides in the same council. Such was the case of the Parisian clerics and the monks of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which, having been more fully debated, imposed perpetual silence upon the unjust claims of the clerics. Alexander therefore, when the synodal council had been dissolved, returned to the city of Bourges, the capital of Aquitaine. As autumn thereafter advanced, he went to the city of Sens, and remained there for eighteen months. But when Octavian, author of the schism, who had been called Victor, had unhappily been removed from this life, Guy of Cremona was substituted by the schismatics in his place; he had been the first among those responsible for Alexander’s election to apostatize.

[Col. 1637A] The count of Nevers does not cease persecuting the men of Vézelay. Meanwhile the count of Nevers grievously harassed the Church of Vézelay, and through agents—men who conceal falsehood beneath a sheep’s color—persisted in defaming the character of Abbot William and his brethren. Eager only for the submission of Vézelay, he was afflicted with the sickness of envy against the abbot, who resisted his wicked undertakings as steadfastly as he did shrewdly. His greatness of spirit was especially evident in this: he resisted the count alike when he accused and when he plundered. Therefore, when the deceit of envy, wasting away within itself, accomplished absolutely nothing and was deprived of every legal ground, he finally set justice aside, despised honor, scorned reverence for religion, and armed the madness of his rage with tyrannical recklessness.

And when, by evasion [Col. 1637B], he labored to act unjustly and could find no lawful pretext for oppressing the Church, he demanded back from the Church, against all right and justice, the procurations which his father, driven by peril at sea, had remitted, and which he himself, with his mother’s consent in the chapter of Vézelay, had confirmed. When the abbot refused what was unjustly demanded, the count sent him a formal defiance. Through the intervention of friends from both sides, they held a conference above the pond of Noverria, to see whether they might settle the dispute which had arisen.

When the count pressed his claim concerning the aforesaid exaction, the abbot replied that what the father had relinquished and he himself had granted was neither to be demanded back by him nor restored by the abbot, particularly since the count had found the Church invested with this remission of a share and with his own grant. Then suddenly [Col. 1637C], stirred by anger, the tyrant came raging and snarling to Vézelay—it was the vigil of the Nativity of Christ’s Forerunner—and, after entering the monastery, when the brethren had, upon hearing of his approach, barred their cloister-gates, he burst in and, taking an axe, was the first to break down the kitchen door. Seeing this, his retainers at once occupied the Church’s buildings, broke down the other doors, struck down monks as they drove them away, and that night, against the brethren’s will, supplied their lord from the monastery’s resources while lodging in the monastery.

The brethren, however, removed the crosses and reliquaries, stripped the altars, and ceased to celebrate the divine office in all their churches.

The pope warns the count to cease harassing the men of Vézelay. [Col. 1637D] That night the abbot lodged at Campummollem; the following night at Gibriacum. From there he sent to the king, while he himself set out for the Roman pontiff, who, having returned from the Council of Tours, was staying at the monastery of Dol. But because the king was then conducting an expedition against the Auvergnats, he did not wish to provoke the count; nevertheless, he warned him to postpone the suit until he himself returned from the expedition.

Alexander likewise, reflecting upon the schism by which the Church was weakened, and fearing that, should he proceed somewhat harshly against secular princes, he might afflict the Church with a more serious scandal, merely admonished the count in a simple letter to desist from the burdens imposed upon the Church of Vézelay, which was a daughter of Saint Peter and an allod of the Roman Church. But the heart of this Pharaoh-like count [Col. 1638A] was hardened, and in place of a sweet spring he assumed the hardness of stone. Thus, scorning both papal and royal admonitions, he came to Vézelay on the very holy feast of blessed Mary Magdalene, with a great and numerous army of cavalry, infantry, and mixed rabble, as though he were about to besiege a hostile people.

When he entered, the brethren immediately ceased the divine offices; separately, with lowered voices, in the chapel of the Mother of God, the cloister doors shut, they rendered to God the vows due to Him, judging it unworthy to lay open holy things to a sacrilegious man. The abbot withdrew to Saint Peter’s. The count entered the monastery in his customary manner, but with an unusual retinue, took lodging there, and, since the brethren denied him the procuration, provided it for himself at his own expense.

[Col. 1638B] The abbot and the count make peace, subject to certain conditions. The count asks pardon for the injuries inflicted. That night the abbot went up to the tomb of blessed Mary Magdalene, and there rendered to God the solemn observances due for the feast as circumstances allowed. At daybreak he descended to Esconium and offered the sacred Host to God. His kinsman Renald of Merlot followed him, together with Durannus Alburg, and asked him to rest there for a little while. For Renald had sent men to Gibriacum to prepare the refreshment he needed.

Renald then went up and spoke concerning a peace settlement with the count. The abbot having therefore been recalled, the following agreement was reached: the count was publicly to make satisfaction at the altar for violating the monastery; he was to pay twenty pounds for the usurped procuration; he was again to grant and confirm in writing [Col. 1638C] the remission made by his father concerning occasional procurations; and he was to make his brother Renald, likewise his brother Guy, and his sister grant all these things, giving a pledge of faith and hostages on behalf of Ignarus, viscount of Joviniacum, Stephen of Petrapertuis, and Hugh of Tornella, so that, when they had reached lawful age, they should again grant the aforesaid remission.

In return for the favor of this written confirmation and for preserving peace forever, it was settled that the abbot should give the count seven hundred pounds and pay two hundred and fifty-three pounds for the procuration of that day, on the condition that the count entirely relinquish the procuration for the following feast [Col. 1638D] and thereafter demand no more than one hundred pounds for another procuration. When these matters had thus been arranged and agreed on both sides, at the sixth hour of the day, as the bells were ringing, the brethren celebrated the solemnities of the holy feast. The count approached the altar, made satisfaction for the injury inflicted on the monastery, and, as agreed, paid twenty pounds in execution of what was right. On the following day, entering the brethren’s chapter-house while the abbot presided, he granted before them all the aforesaid remission of occasional procurations made by his father, confirmed it in writing, and strengthened it with the protection of his seal.

He again initiates litigation and persecution. After this William, count of Nevers, fell gravely ill, so that he was despaired of. But when he fulfilled vows of humility [Col. 1639A] to God, he at last recovered, and sought the intercession of the saints in the oratory of the Blessed and undefiled Virgin Mary at Anicinum, city of the Vellavians. Returning thence physically to his homeland, but in mind to the hatred of Abbot William of Vézelay which had been instilled in him, he ordered the latter to render him justice concerning a salt-payment which had not been supplied to him, to appear before him, and to submit to the judgment of his court at Nevers.

The abbot replied: “I had hoped that I had made peace with the count concerning all disputes of the past. Nevertheless, since I seem inexperienced and not yet fully instructed in the customs of this monastery, I shall speak with the elders of this town and with the other wise men, and, in accordance with the counsel granted us from heaven, I shall reply through the count’s own messengers.”

But Abo of Mont-Gualguerii—for he was carrying the message entrusted to him—said to the abbot: “If you are willing to accept from me the day of hearing designated for you by the count, well and good; but if not, the count will act as he does when justice is denied him by you.” Thus Abo departed and reported to the count matters worse than his words. The abbot, however, took counsel and sent messengers to reply to these words. As they went, they met the count’s retainers, who were going ahead of their lord as he came to Vézelay in great fury. The tyrant immediately burst into the monastery, seized its workshops, and at once sent heralds throughout the whole town of Vézelay, Esconium, and Saint Peter’s, commanding all the monastery’s men to assemble together and appear before him on the morrow. But they all unanimously [Col. 1639C] despised his command.

Then, carried away by fury, contrary to the custom of the town, he had his herald proclaim that anyone who did not come before him would undoubtedly be seized wherever found, and that man’s house would be confiscated. Hearing this, all were stunned, and many came to him out of fear. Standing before them, he said: “Because the abbot has denied me justice, I have invested myself with my right. Therefore I wish you, having renounced the abbot under oath, to give me fealty, and henceforth to pay no customary dues to the abbot or monks.”

The burgesses replied: “We have sworn fealty to the abbot and the Church. It therefore seems unjust and most shameful that we should perjure ourselves without cause, so far as lies with us. We therefore ask [Col. 1639D] you to grant us a truce, so that we may speak with our lord and confer with him concerning these words.” “Your lord,” he said, “is at hand, and you will soon be able to speak with him.” “Then permit us,” they said, “to go to him.” He replied: “Choose two or three among yourselves to carry your message to the abbot and bring his reply back to you.”

Thereupon Simon of Silviniacum and Durannus Alburg, who were especially favorable to the count’s impiety, rose and came with a few others before the abbot. Word was made known to the abbot that the count had detained his men lest they come to him. Immediately he summoned John Caprarius and a few elders of the Church and promptly sent them to his burgesses in the lodging-place with these words: “To you who owe fealty to the abbot and the Church, [Col. 1640A] the abbot commands and enjoins, by that very fealty which you have sworn and owe to him, that you depart from this tyrant and come to him as swiftly as possible.” They came at once.

As they discussed the count’s claim extensively on both sides, the burgesses asked the abbot to provide for himself and for them in so great an emergency, and to gain time by accepting the count’s appointed day on this condition: that on that day he would do for the count only what he was bound to do. The abbot yielded to his people’s counsel and sent word to the count:

“Since you have unexpectedly and tyrannically invaded my house, although what you demand is entirely unjust, I nevertheless accept your day, assigned at Auxerre, as one suffering violence, and I shall do there only so much as I prove myself bound to do.”

The count, immediately frustrated in his purpose—for he had intended by this condition to subject Vézelay to his own lordship—departed in a fresh outburst of madness. When the day arrived, the abbot sent the leading men of his Church to the count at Decize: Gilo, then prior, Geoffrey Angligena the senior, and Gislebert the almoner. The count told them to follow him to Nevers, where he would hear them. When they had done so, they renounced, on the abbot’s behalf, the appointed day and requested that he assign another in a nearer place. When he refused either to accept or to grant the renunciation or alteration of the day, they added: “The lord abbot of Vézelay replies to you through us that he is under no legal obligation to obey your command; and if you again wish to harass him by violence, he appeals you to the hearing [Col. 1640C] of the Apostolic See, to which the lordship of the monastery of Vézelay properly belongs, and to the hearing of the lord king, under whose protection and guardianship the same monastery stands. He appoints you a day before Pope Alexander on the octave of Easter, meanwhile committing himself and his possessions into the hands of the pope and the king.”

After they had said this and, owing to his excessive anger, had failed to obtain leave to depart, they went a little way off and returned to their lodging at the monastery of Saint Stephen, adjoining the city, pretending that they would return to the count’s court on the following day. But by night they mounted their horses and returned to Vézelay. The abbot, avoiding the rage of the frenzied count, went [Col. 1640D] into France.

The abbot then went to Pope Alexander, informing him how and how unjustly he and the Church of Vézelay were being oppressed by the count. From there he went to the king and complained in his hearing of the unjust harassment inflicted upon him by the count. Moved both by compassion for the complainant and by Pope Alexander’s admonition, the king summoned the count to a conference in the city of Sens. They met there on both sides, and after exchanging many mutual complaints, when no prospect of peace appeared, the king’s request finally induced the count to postpone the day for the justice sought, under the king’s summons.

King Louis held the feast of Epiphany at Vézelay, and the abbot received and served him diligently. When the king had departed, [Col. 1641A] the count, prompted by envy, summoned the abbot to a day at Auxerre. The abbot accepted the day only to the extent that it lawfully concerned him and sent envoys to the pope for advice as to what he should do. Having received the pope’s counsel, and having prudently committed it to secrecy, they returned.

A monk carries about relics of the saints to seek assistance. A certain brother of Vézelay, named Renald, went forth from the monastery adjoining Moret, carrying relics of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, Saint Blaise, and other saints, in order to collect abundant alms from the faithful for building the basilica of that monastery. As he traveled through various places and, by heavenly grace aiding him through many miracles of the saints, had made the district of Amiens renowned, he came with those relics to the castle [Col. 1641B] called Arborea. Having stayed there a few days, while many miracles were performed there through the merits of the saints and crowds of people came together from every side, he eventually proposed to depart.

But when they took up the litter, as was customary, they could not move it even a little way from the church. They tried one turn after another, setting now some men in place of others, now stronger men in place of the strong; the lord of the place, named Alelmus, together with another nobleman, lifted the litter, yet could not even bring it to the threshold of the basilica. They therefore replaced the litter upon the altar and devoted themselves to prayer.

Then one of the brethren who had come with Renald, named Peter, began in foolish rashness to strike the litter with rods, as if forcing the saints out by lashes. Without delay vengeance fell upon him: immediately stricken with paralysis, he died a few days later. The nobleman Alelmus, therefore, perceiving that these things were divinely wrought, gave thanks to God, the author of all good things, for the heavenly favor granted him. On the boundary of that castle, on his own allod, he gave a site where an oratory might be built, in which the relics of the saints might be placed and honored by the brethren with religious service to the glory of God.

He also ordained that the place should remain under the governance and administration of the Church of Vézelay, because the sacred pledges of the saints had been brought there from that Church by brethren of the same place. When Abbot William himself [Col. 1641D] came there at their invitation, he brought with him other relics and many precious ornaments, which he left there in honor of the saints and in response to the devotion of the faithful of those regions. The place was called Arborea from the name of the neighboring castle. Thus amid the waves of persecution, the success of good works always gains an increase of strength; and the more the Church is afflicted, the more it is enriched.

The count of Nevers rages against the monks of Vézelay. Count William was held by grave hatred against Abbot William, and because he was less able to accomplish what he wished, he vented his rage in plundering the monastery’s asses, livestock, and dependents. There was a thoroughly evil man, Hugh surnamed Lethardus, a serf of the monastery by hereditary status. His mother was indeed a blood-relative of Simon, son of Odo, provost of Vézelay and a serf of the Church; this Simon had betrayed and struck his lord, namely Artald, abbot of the monastery of Vézelay. The count made this Hugh his provost at the castle of Censurium; above all the count’s retainers, he persecuted the Church. It is impossible to recount how many and how great were the ways in which he harassed it night and day, and, while acting unjustly, pressed the Church in the name of law. Yet while demanding law, he rendered no justice; rather, whatever he violently extorted against all right and justice counted for him as his right.

When the abbot again complained to Pope Alexander of the unjust and multiple oppressions inflicted upon himself and his people by the count’s retainers, [Col. 1642B] Alexander wrote to the count and his mother in the following terms:

Alexander the pope writes to him that he should refrain from harassment. “ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman WILLIAM, count of Nevers, and to IDA, his mother: greeting and apostolic blessing. Since the monastery of Vézelay …” See Alexander III, *Patrologia*, vol. CC.

The count scorns the pope’s letter. Peter, subdeacon of the Roman Church, after celebrating the solemnities of the Lord’s Nativity at Vézelay, came to the count and his mother and delivered the apostolic letters to them. After delivering the apostolic letters, he also offered them his own exhortation, as a most highly educated man; but they stopped their ears [Col. 1642C] and, on the contrary, began to disparage the abbot and his brethren with insults and many different falsehoods, and to defame their good name. When he negotiated peace with the enemies of peace, he found no trace of peace, unless the abbot, contrary to the custom and dignity of the Church, submitted to the judgment of the count’s court.

Having taken common counsel, all the brethren resolved together to undergo exile, even unto death, rather than submit to so great a tyranny. The abbot therefore, putting aside every pretense of truces, accepted the day appointed at the beginning of Lent and sent to the pope for aid. The pope sent him Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of the Roman Church, Peter de Bona, his subdeacon, and John, his marshal.

[Col. 1642D] Peace is negotiated. At that time the brethren of Pontigny were appearing before the Apostolic court, having been summoned by the Cluniacs because they had either dismissed their former abbot William to the men of Vézelay without the Cluniacs’ consultation, or had substituted another for him. But the Cluniacs abandoned their case and did not even presume to appear on the appointed day. Consequently, the brethren of the monastery of Pontigny, absolved by the Roman pontiff, returned freely to their own house. Their abbot Lecelinus was then staying at Vézelay and awaiting there the outcome of the affair.

For the Cluniacs, in their excessive arrogance, thought it beneath them to summon him into court, but cited only his brethren as though they were headless; they complained only about the monks, not the abbot, as though there were no abbot. Accordingly, Pope Alexander subsequently sought a hearing of the brethren, not of the abbot. But because neither Satan nor an evil encounter was present, he confirmed, with the approval of all the cardinals, the proven liberty of the monastery of Pontigny.

William, abbot of Vézelay, Lecelinus, abbot of Pontigny, and the abbot of the monastery of Saint-Jean-des-Prés met at Auxerre, with many other brethren and friends of the monastery of Vézelay. The papal legates also met them there. The count, in deference to their presence, now willingly wished to alter the day which until then he had not allowed to be postponed even when requested. On this matter the abbot consulted prudent men. Hyacinth answered him: “Until now you have suffered a tertian fever; do you now wish to undergo a quartan? Rather, break off all evasions and act without delay concerning the right of your liberty.”

The abbot put his words into the mouth of the abbot of Saint-Jean-des-Prés; but neither he nor anyone else dared speak for fear of the count. Seeing this, the sons of the liberty of the Church of Vézelay, armed with faith, cast off every fear altogether and judged it unworthy for their own dignity to be defended by another’s speech. Gilo, then prior of the monastery of Vézelay, rose and said to the count: “Until now the lord of Vézelay has heard your allegations. Some of them indeed readily yield to agreement; the rest he will consider himself. For you vainly suppose that he is bound to submit to your judgment, since he has never been under any legal obligation to you.”

At this the count [Col. 1643C] was seized by excessive rage. He was ashamed at words spoken contrary to his expectation. The abbot and his party left the count. Hyacinth, however, tried to soften the prince’s fierce temper and pressed for peace; but, rebuffed, he asked that at least some truce be granted to the Church. The count consented and granted a truce, though a false one, until the octave of Easter.

The bishop of Sion performs episcopal functions at Vézelay. Therefore, as the holy solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection approached, the bishop of Sion came to Vézelay, sent from the side of the lord pope to visit and strengthen the brethren. There he consecrated the most holy chrism and the holy oil on the sacred day of the Supper, and on Holy Saturday of Easter he celebrated ecclesiastical [Col. 1643D] ordinations. He ordained as priests Henry, Peter, and Humbert, monks of the Church; he also made Gerald, a cleric of the same town, a priest. He ordained three monks as deacons, namely Ansellus, William, and Geoffrey; as subdeacons, William and the boy Guy. Moreover, he made Laurence of Moret an acolyte.

Saint Thomas, exiled in Gaul, entrusts himself to the king’s protection. Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, was living in exile at Pontigny, fleeing King Henry. He had once been most intimate with that king and, distinguished by polished energy, had been his chancellor; no one had seemed more influential with the king of England. But when he undertook the care of ecclesiastical rule [Col. 1644A], he took care in every respect to put God before man. Hence, when the king, after the manner of Uzziah, usurped ecclesiastical rights, Thomas steadfastly resisted him as another Jonah.

For this reason the king grew angry and, exchanging immeasurable favor for implacable hatred, resolved to seize him and confiscate his goods. But the resourcefulness of the innocent man forestalled the wicked designs: he secretly crossed the sea with a small retinue, came to Louis, king of the Franks, and committed himself and his people into his hands. Louis received him most kindly and liberally provided him with the aid he needed. Yet Thomas judged that he ought to approach Pope Alexander and abide wholly by his counsel. When he came to Alexander and set forth the cause of his arrival, Alexander sympathized with him [Col. 1644B] and entrusted him to Guichard, abbot of the monastery of Pontigny, who was later consecrated by Alexander himself as archbishop of Lyons.

King Louis sent to Henry, king of the English, concerning these and other matters, and the kings appointed a mutual conference. When Alexander intended to attend it, he came to Paris. When King Henry learned this, hostile to Alexander because of his resentment of Thomas of Canterbury, he renounced the conference appointed with King Louis. Alexander had now again received envoys of the Romans asking him to return and come back to the see of Saint Peter. Therefore, bidding farewell to King Louis, he came to the city of Bourges.

[Col. 1644C] Hugh Lethardus plunders the possessions of Vézelay at the countess of Nevers’s instigation. The utterly impious Hugh Lethardus, a wicked serf by birth and character, persistently engaged in seizing and plundering the people and property of Vézelay. And that old Herodias, daughter of Jezebel from the seed of Amalek—namely Ida, mother of William, count of Nevers—continually poured the poison of hatred from her pestilential mouth into her son’s breast. She was the rival of honor and enemy of every good thing; siding, as it were, with the party of her son, she fiercely urged on her retainers to persecute the monastery of Vézelay. Hence came killings, plunder, captivity, various tortures, and different kinds of death: all flowed from the cave of female wickedness. Nor was an easy way of escape open to any inhabitant of Vézelay.

The brethren had prepared a lime-kiln of remarkable size for constructing their dormitory, and, after kindling a fire, were drawing timber from their adjacent wood with wagons. Therefore, this hydra, inflamed by the plague of envy, sent out the retainers of her madness during the very solemnities of the Holy Spirit to carry off the horses of the teams that were drawing the timber. Thus, when the fire failed, the work of the kiln, valued at one hundred pounds, was lost. This viper’s son had ordered Abbot William’s route to be watched, so that, without his knowledge, he might be dishonored by base serfs.

The abbot complains before the pope on many grounds. Thus afflicted from every side by so many evils, Abbot William pursued Pope Alexander. Having found him in the aforesaid city, he laid before him, as best he could, [Col. 1645A] all the evils which he suffered from the count and his mother. He told him that his cause was the cause of the lord pope and of the whole Roman Church, to whose jurisdiction his monastery properly belonged; and that therefore the Apostolic See ought to undertake the cause of Vézelay as its own, especially since the monastery was endangered by this one alleged offense alone: that it freely professed itself Roman, and acknowledged itself subject to no one except the Roman pontiff alone.

He added that, if the pope neglected swiftly to assist the endangered monastery, he would, as though repudiated, hand it over to an adulterer, and would no longer be bound by the right of tribute; especially since, in the pope’s own presence, both recent and ancient enactments of Roman pontiffs, and the safeguards of privileges [Col. 1645B], were being violated with impunity; the shepherd stood by while wolfish rage ran wild; and liberty, which could be destroyed by the silence of a single word of justice, had little security.

Finally, he said that he had not so often appealed to the apostolic ear against the count out of cowardice or arrogance. Indeed, he had repeatedly purchased the count’s favor with both entreaties and money; yet the count, ungratefully repaying him with such dreadful calamity, had reduced him, almost exhausted, to nearly complete poverty. Nor had the count been satisfied with ransoming men or despoiling the monastery’s possessions: for two years now he had taken away even the brethren’s daily sustenance.

Although this act grievously afflicted the monastery, it lamented yet more deeply the injury to its innate liberty. The count strove entirely to annul that liberty under cover of a certain usurped protection, fraudulently obtained through the negligence of some of his predecessors [Col. 1645C]. For the generosity once charitably bestowed upon him was now no longer sought as freely given generosity in devotion; rather, it was tyrannically demanded as a service due. Those who had formerly been content with an offering and few in number now, a great army, greedily sought plunder, so that the procuration for one lodging cost two hundred and fifty pounds or more.

The abbot continued to press such matters with such words, saying that the daughter of Saint Peter—that is, the Church of Vézelay—would be exposed to every evil, so that now from the sole of the foot to the crown there was no soundness in her: “For,” he said, “she is given over to plunder and trampling by every passer-by; and the more junior she was before, the more abject she is now found to be. Those who formerly envied her liberty now lift their heads against her in insult and deride the Sabbaths of Roman dignity, reproaching the subjection of the Church of Vézelay.”
