Now Autun incites and urges Cluny against Vézelay, and Cluny, in turn, Autun. “It is time,” they say, “that, when the head of the Roman fortress has been broken, its eyes too be gouged out, and that we subject to ourselves the runaway handmaid who boasts that she is Saint Peter’s daughter.” Now Autun represents Moab, now Cluny Idumea, reckoning that in attacking Vézelay they attack another Jerusalem, and saying: “It is a foolish, poor, and proud people. I, Autun, shall crush its pride; you shall mock its folly, and its poverty shall supply our luxuries. Let us therefore invite Assur with prayers, incite him with persuasions, hire him with gifts, so that he may crush its arrogance with an iron rod and a strong hand. And since there is no helper or defender to deliver her, let us divide her between us, and let each take his own portion. You, Cluny, shall hold the fortress of the chapter-house; I, Autun, shall claim the altar for myself. Assur—that is, the count—will plunder the town.”

“And who, holy lord Father,” he said, “will withstand these things? Would that there were a migration! Would that perhaps we might be divided! Would that times and seasons might be appointed for us! Perhaps then the Lord would raise up for us an ambidextrous Ehud, in whose hand would be Israel’s salvation. But now we are slaughtered in our dwellings, subjected to servitude in our own house; redemption of the time becomes for us perpetual subjugation. To this accumulation of so many evils, of all misery and extreme disgrace, is added this further aggravation: that we are slaughtered before the eyes of our father; that we are torn from the embrace of our shepherd; that we are prejudged while our lawful protector is present; and that, to crown the entire accusation, we are condemned by the silence of the universal judge.

“Certainly, if the action proceeded openly, if reason intervened, if right and justice, or judicial procedure, had any place, the loss would be lighter, and the punishment, though prejudicially imposed, would rejoice in its gain, even if it seemed less deserved in the judgment of conscience. But now our case is bandied about in the mouths of the crowd, and our judgment is being publicly proclaimed by the hand of our enemies [Col. 1646C].”

Pope Alexander answers the abbot and attempts to deter the count from harassment. Having heard these things, Alexander and the whole Roman Church sympathized. He wrote to the count that he should make restitution for the damage inflicted upon the monastery of Vézelay and again refrain from harassing it; but if he thought that he possessed any right against the abbot, he should appear before him at Clermont on the octave of Pentecost, first making satisfaction there to the abbot and then receiving from him the justice due.

But the count wholly scorned the apostolic command and, moreover, laying snares for the abbot, so hemmed him in that even his horses could not go out to water. The abbot therefore sent his clerk John to Alexander. [Col. 1646D] The count too, while concealing his contempt, sent Theobald, dean of Nevers, Humbert, archdeacon, and Bernard, prior of Saint Stephen. The apostolic pontiff received them kindly and asked whether they had come as duly authorized representatives for the count. But since they advanced excuses rather than compliance with justice, he dismissed them and wrote through them to the count, ordering that within eight days after receiving his letter he should restore to the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Vézelay what had been taken; release and set free the imprisoned burgesses and their hostages; and permit them free entry and exit upon the public road which they were known to have possessed from times long past.

He was then to appear before the pope so that he might reconcile [Col. 1647A] him with the aforesaid abbot and brethren. If it seemed burdensome to him to appear before the Apostolic See, he was to come with the abbot before the archbishops of Sens and Bourges, who should restore peace and concord between them. Moreover, he wrote to the archbishops of Bourges and Sens with the text of the aforesaid command to the count, ordering that, if the count complied with it, they should make a suitable settlement between the abbot and count. But if not, he commanded the archbishop of Sens alone to proceed according to the tenor of other letters, the contents of which are as follows:

He writes concerning this matter to the archbishop of Sens. “ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, archbishop of Sens: greeting and apostolic [Col. 1647B] blessing. To the knowledge of your brotherhood …” See Alexander III, *Patrologia*, vol. CC.

Of the same purport. “ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren HENRY, bishop of Autun; WALTER, bishop of Langres; ALAN, bishop of Auxerre; and BERNARD, bishop of Nevers: greeting and apostolic blessing. To the knowledge of your brotherhood …” See ibid.

He asks the king to restrain the count. “ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing. To the knowledge of your royal serenity …” See above.

He informs the abbot and monks of Vézelay of the aforesaid letters written by him. “ALEXANDER, bishop, [Col. 1647C] servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, abbot, and the brethren of Vézelay: greeting and apostolic blessing. Having received your letters …” See ibid.

The Archbishop of Sens, appointed arbiter by the pope, conducts the case between Vézelay and the count. Accordingly Hugh, Archbishop of Sens, in obedience to the apostolic mandate, set the count and his mother a day by which they were to restore what had been taken from the Church of Vézelay and appear before himself and the Archbishop of Bourges, in order to reach an agreement with the Church of Vézelay. But they asked the Archbishop of Sens to appoint a day for themselves and the abbot alone, saying that they would willingly settle the matter with the abbot according to his counsel. The Archbishop of Sens and the abbot, with his brethren and friends, accordingly met at Saint-Julien-de-Saulce. The count and his mother, however, sent their envoys, not to make a settlement, but to appeal to the Apostolic See.

The prudent foresight of Abbot William had anticipated this: a little earlier, with great speed, he had sent his messenger, begging that every possibility of appeal be removed from those who sought evasion rather than judgment. Having obtained what he requested, the messenger hastened back; and on the fourth day after the appeal, entering the city of Sens, he found the abbot and gave him the desired letters of the lord pope. The abbot immediately went in to the archbishop and delivered the apostolic mandate, which contained the following: unless the count and his mother, within the prescribed term of twenty days which the pope had lately fixed in the foregoing letters, restored what had been taken from the Church, made satisfaction for the injuries inflicted, and thereafter ceased their oppressions of the Church, the archbishop was, all appeal being set aside, to pronounce sentence, according to the tenor of the other letters, against their persons and their lands.

On hearing this, the Archbishop of Sens was greatly astonished, wondering at the swift removal of the appeal. For he was angered that the judgment of the Apostolic See had been delegated to him, since he feared the violent temper of the Count of Nevers. The count himself, heavily burdened with debt, heard that great wealth lay in a certain town of Auvergne called Montferrand. Suddenly and unexpectedly he attacked a peaceful people who suspected nothing, plundered all the spoils of the aforesaid town, and detained with him, as hostage for the stipulated money, the lord of the town itself. While he raged there with mad tyranny, a messenger of Hugh, Archbishop of Sens, came to him and offered him, on behalf of his lord the Archbishop of Sens, letters containing the following:

### Unless the count restores what he took from Vézelay, the archbishop threatens sentence of excommunication

“HUGH, by the grace of God Archbishop of Sens, to his dearest William, noble Count of Nevers, greeting and affection.

“We have received letters from the lord pope on behalf of the Church of Vézelay, which you have in every way burdened, as the monks complain. We immediately sent to you my brother William, that he might carefully admonish you to have all things taken and all damages restored, and the injuries redressed; and a day was fixed for you. Yet within that period, as the monks have complained, you caused twenty-four oxen to be seized. On the appointed day you sent before us your representatives, who seemed insufficient, since they had brought no letters from you establishing that you would abide by whatever they did in this affair. Nor, therefore, could they act fully in the matter.

“The abbot, indeed, sought full restitution of what had been taken, as the lord pope commanded; or else, within the term of twenty days, as is contained in the same letters of the lord pope, that full justice should be rendered against you and your land. On the other hand, your representatives said that they would give security to the abbot; but the abbot wished to have nothing but full restitution. Meanwhile, among these and other matters, your men appealed to the lord pope, and we therefore ceased to proceed further in the affair.

“Afterwards letters came to us from the lord pope, enjoining us, all excuse and appeal ceasing, that if you do not cause the damages and all things taken to be restored, we should thereafter pronounce sentence of excommunication against you and your land. If, therefore, you do not do so within ten days after seeing these letters, we shall, by the authority and command of the lord pope, though sorrowful and unwilling, pronounce sentence of excommunication against you and your land.”

### The count is bound by excommunication

The Archbishop of Sens sent similar writings to Ida, the count’s mother. The prescribed days were completed on the third day before the feast of St Mary Magdalene, and the count and his mother incurred the apostolic sentence. Nevertheless, the count presumed to come to Vézelay on the feast, in order to exact the customary procuration—not to render due honor to the handmaid of God. But, in their abbot’s absence, the brethren did not dare provide hospitality for one excommunicated by the lord pope; indeed, they ceased to celebrate the divine offices while he was present. Greatly perplexed by this, he wished to use force against the monastery and the burgesses, but was recalled by Milo and his other barons.

### Certain degenerate monks take the count’s side

And Satan added to his assaults upon the monastery of Vézelay, entering the hearts of certain false monks. Since outward calamity seemed insufficient to destroy the monastery’s dignity, an internal war was to enslave even its very freedom. For one Peter, an Auvergnat by birth, reared in the monastery from youth, concealed a viper’s cunning beneath an ass’s simplicity—or rather beneath the pretence of hypocrisy. And because virtue worn as a cloak is accustomed to deceive the simple more effectively, he was promoted through the successive grades of the order to the priorship of the monastery, and was finally placed, through the industry and aid of Abbot Pons of worthy memory, over the monastery of Tournus.

Having unworthily obtained this dignity, though unworthy of it, he immediately loosened the reins of vice and reduced the goods of the house almost to nothing. He was further disgraced by his companionship with a certain young man named Theobald, whom he had clothed in the sacred habit. Often warned by the brethren of his monastery and often rebuked by his own bishop, Geoffrey of Langres, he neglected correction no less than admonition, and was at last compelled by the aforesaid bishop to renounce the companionship of that brother. Having added the infamy of perjury to the squandering of the house, he was removed by canonical judgment from the care and government of the monastery of Tournus.

When he had been deposed, the venerable Abbot Pons, exercising his innate compassion, received him and treated him with much, though undeserved, honor. When Pons had been joined in peace to his fathers, that madman Peter began, by soliciting the brethren of the monastery of Vézelay, to turn them aside from their sacred liberty and to obstruct, by every means he could, the election of this William of whom we are speaking. But the counsel of Ahithophel was made foolish, and all Satan’s machinations were scattered. Yet Peter infected foolish hearts with many words and stirred up inward hatreds.

Geoffrey of Latigniac became his companion in folly, powerful in speech and effective in persuasion, but still more effective in cunning. Joined to the aforesaid Theobald—a man of such character and influence—he secretly solicited now one man, now another, by furtive conversations and nocturnal whisperings: questioning, provoking, inciting, and urging them to the scandals of detraction and hatred. Thus the two, coming together, brought forth from the seed of Canaan a son of dissension, material for scandal, fuel for enmity, an incentive to discord: the bastard Bartholomew, born of a prostitute by an adulterer.

To these four wheels of Pharaoh’s chariot, joined like four horses, were added four others whose names are suppressed, because they could achieve nothing beyond increasing the number, and because at the time of examination they repented of their purpose and recognized their folly. Through all these men murmuring gradually spread and in some measure infected the discipline of the sacred order. Soon, having bound to themselves all whom they could entice, they wrote with one consent to Peter, who had been expelled from Tournus and who, a few days earlier, had gone with the abbot’s favor and blessing to visit the obediences subject to him in Auvergne. They humbly begged him quickly to aid the desolate house of Vézelay, declaring that all the brethren were of one mind in obeying his counsel in this emergency.

On learning this, Peter arrived suddenly and unexpectedly. He delighted those bent on evil, while filling the others with great astonishment at his sudden and unforeseen arrival. The plotters of the abominable sedition came secretly to him, poured into his ears the gall of their conspiring treachery, and begged, adjured, and devoted themselves to him, that he would take up their accursed cause against the abbot—indeed, against the Church. They promised never to fail him until death and to bring over to him the greater part of the entire convent.

He secretly approached the count, who, as stated above, had come for the feast, and disclosed to him the wishes of the rebels. The count, exulting with incredible joy, promised on his faith to furnish Peter and his accomplices with the most steadfast assistance in all things: horses, expenses, and, should need arise, secure strongholds in every part of his land. He gave him four knights of his nobility as hostages. They pledged under oath that the count would keep his promises both to Peter himself and to all whom he could induce to join him in the count’s allegiance against the abbot.

Peter and Theobald, moreover, swore fealty to the count against the abbot, promising to subject the greater part of the Church’s convent to the count’s allegiance; and they themselves would go to Pope Alexander to proceed against that same Abbot William. This conspiracy was made on the very sacred feast of St Mary Magdalene, beloved of God, in the upper chapel at St Lawrence’s, through the hands of Stephen of Pontoise, Stephen of Pierre-Perthuis, Milo, and Hugh of Argenteuil. Thus did the impious and adulterous men profane the holy day, while the brethren and sons of freedom grieved and mourned that they could not render their patroness the celebration due to her with proper dignity. There were also present Henry, Cardinal of Pisa, the Archbishop-elect of Mainz, and the Bishop-elect of Chartres. In appearance they seemed to be acting for peace, but moved by the spirit of the flesh, they favored more and more the party of the count and his mother.

### The count tries to entice the monks against the abbot

The count, made bolder by the suggestions of the traitors, asked permission to enter the chapter of the brethren. When this had been granted, he complained of the abbot, by whom, he said, he was being disinherited and subjected to many injuries. Though he endured all these things undeservedly, he declared that he especially lamented the desolation of a Church once wealthy in possessions, adorned with honorable persons, renowned for the strictness of religious discipline and the charity of its hospitality. Once surpassing, after Cluny, all the churches of Gaul in these and many other benefits, it was now so marked by lack of resources, the burden of debts, scarcity of persons, disrepute of morals, and inhumanity in hospitality that it had become the talk not only of all churches, but even of the meanest people of the populace. All this, he asserted, had plainly arisen from the pride and laxity of the abbot, with the assent of those brethren who favored him.

“Where,” he said, “are those honorable and weighty persons of former times—the cellarer, guest-master, sacristan, almoner, and chamberlain—by whose prudence and even power this house once flourished? There is now none among you who can help another or answer anyone seeking counsel; only the empty name of dignity remains. Therefore the laxity of you all is openly evident, since like favor like, and you endure what is, as it were, an unprovoked injury.

“Until now I have endured my own injuries; until now I have suffered the loss of this Church. Since this Church is mine and, whether your abbot wishes it or not, stands under my protection, I shall no longer endure such disgrace and such oppression. Yet I wish you to have been warned, so that you may persuade the abbot to spare this Church henceforth, to desist from its destruction, and to restore to me what is mine by right. I demand nothing new; I reclaim the ancient rights of my fathers. How could I burden with new or unjust exactions that Church which I must protect from the assaults of all men? Finally, I advise you to take counsel for yourselves; otherwise, I shall exact from all of you an account of your assent to so great a perversity.”

### The prior answers the count

After hearing this, Prior Gilo rose to reply. He called the elders of the Church, including that other Judas whose treachery was still concealed, and withdrew with the brethren and burgesses into the oratory of Blessed Mary, Mother of God. After taking counsel, Gilo answered:

“As you yourself, lord count, have professed, so we too recognize and desire you to be our guardian and patron, and the guardian and patron of this Church. We receive gratefully and gladly your compassion for the desolation of our house. And, with this disposition, we earnestly beg your highness that, in matters belonging to your own person and in those belonging to other princes, you should take thought and provide for this Church, which is under your protection.

“Although inwardly it flourishes in fraternal peace and concord, and in sufficient food and clothing, outwardly it suffers from the diminution of its goods and from the oppression of certain enemies. We do not yet know it to be oppressed by debt, which, as we know, does not exceed seven hundred pounds. The strictness of the chapter, the discipline of the cloister, and the ordering of its persons seem to us to flourish no less than usual. If any mark of lying infamy harms the Church, it has been produced not by the assertion of truth but by the envy of rivals.

“As for the character of our abbot, we both desire and believe it to be good and honorable. If, with hatred as judge, anything otherwise is thought of him by anyone, it is proved false in the balance of reason. Therefore we rejoice to think the same and to feel the same with him, as members ought with their head; and we hope that no fault lies in so common and lawful a harmony of head and members.

“Nevertheless, if through some personal offence or through another’s accusation he has perhaps incurred anything hateful in your sight, this grieves us, and we greatly regret it, although until now we have not learned what he has incurred or why. When he comes, we shall humbly admonish him, as monks their abbot and subjects their lord, to strive to earn the favor of your dignity. But we beseech your discretion to spare the Church which, as you say, is under your protection, and not to attempt to destroy it through hatred of one man. So far as lies in it, it is subject to its abbot, but it has always been devoted to you.”

The traitor Peter had secretly instructed the count through Simon of Silviniac to speak more mildly to the brethren, especially regarding anything that might seem to concern their disgrace, lest, while pursuing the abbot, he should appear to alienate the offended brethren.

### The count replies

The count answered: “I do not disapprove of your conduct, but I grieve at your great poverty, which you endure because the abbot has squandered the goods of this Church. Therefore, as I have said, either you yourselves will provide for yourselves and this Church, or I shall endure no further loss of this sort. For, although I have not yet been publicly declared by canonical process, at your abbot’s command you ceased from the divine offices merely because of my presence, and, for some reason unknown to me, did not render me the procuration due to me, as the whole world knows.

“Though you say that the Church’s debt does not exceed seven hundred pounds, I know that between the two seas you owe more than a thousand pounds. And what you complain of as oppression by external enemies redounds upon the head of your abbot, whose arrogance is known to be so great that he will not pursue what is just either for me or for anyone else. Yet I do not bring you into the lawsuit; I merely advise you to reflect and provide for yourselves. If you do so, you will have me as a faithful helper in all things; if not, it will concern you. I shall provide for myself.”

He said these things in order to encourage the traitors and incite the others to agree with them. Leaving the chapter, he spoke with Peter the traitor. Together they devised a plan by which Peter himself would go to Pope Alexander to accuse the abbot, and by which he would send with him the Abbot of Bonirad, who under a sheep’s appearance would bite the innocent man more fiercely with a wolf’s tooth. And, so that the deceit of their mutual consultation might remain concealed, the count promised Peter that he would have repaid to him the money owed by the Church of Tournus for the surrender of a certain obedience.

The day of the meeting appointed for the count and the abbot by the Archbishop of Sens was approaching; but neither count nor abbot attended. There appeared, however, on the abbot’s side Prior Gilo and this same Peter, still a concealed traitor. As each side argued in the archbishop’s presence at Bazolles, and Prior Gilo, with the count standing by, recounted the injuries which the count had inflicted upon the Church, Peter, belching forth the force of his boiling deceit, began boldly to accuse Gilo as though he had spoken too harshly and irreverently against the count. At this Gilo, Geoffrey, then guest-master, and the other brethren who had gathered there for the abbot blushed deeply.

The count gave hostages with respect to the portion of the damages which was to be restored. Concerning the remaining complaints, he requested another day, with the consent of the Archbishop of Sens, preparing a snare for the innocent into which they themselves fell. For the archbishop sent a petition of excuse to Pope Alexander, asking that another judge be delegated to pronounce sentence upon the count, lest the savagery of the young prince rage against both himself and his people, and the injury done to one involve two in the same punishment.

Conversely, the count was preparing to send the aforesaid Peter and other chief men of his party to Pope Alexander against William, Abbot of Vézelay. Their hope was that, while the archbishop excused himself and the count accused the abbot, the pope would delegate judges to hear the case between the count and the abbot. But events took a contrary turn, and the design of folly was frustrated.

### The prior reports to the abbot what he has done with the count

The business therefore remaining unfinished, they withdrew from one another. Gilo came to the abbot at Saint-Julien-de-Saulce and reported to him what they had done three days earlier at Vézelay and on that very day, and how shamelessly Peter, his intimate friend, had confounded them in the presence of the count and the archbishop. The abbot was no little astonished, but in his abundant kindness he gave no credence whatever to the report. Rather, holding Peter free from all suspicion, he instructed him, after receiving the money from the men of Tournus, to go to his house at Saulce. Peter was to await him there, for the abbot intended shortly to go to Pope Alexander; or, on seeing the abbot’s messenger, Peter was to meet him at Le Puy, ready to set out with him.

The abbot had sent beforehand to the papal court his clerk John. When he received letters from him stating that Alexander would embark at sea on the Kalends of August [1 August], he abandoned the proposed journey and came through the duke’s territory to Vézelay on the second day after the Octave of Blessed Mary Magdalene. All who belonged to Peter’s faction were astonished at the abbot’s sudden and unexpected arrival; they had not expected him to return once more invested with the dignity of abbot, as they had already predicted—or rather raved—to their companions.

### The abbot at last recognizes his traitors

At length the abbot, having been informed of his traitors, summoned Vincent the dean and told him how he had learned the same things from another informant. He also summoned Prior Gilo and recounted everything he had heard. It would have seemed incredible to Gilo, had not the wickedness of Peter’s words returned to his memory. Geoffrey the superior was afterwards summoned and was astonished at what was said. Nor was such amazement at so great a novelty surprising. For the Church of Vézelay had flourished for three hundred years and more in such discipline of peace and honor that until that time no stain of disgrace and no rumor of scandal had defiled it.

The abbot exhorted all in common to devote themselves to peace, quiet, silence, and charity; and he begged them to apply themselves more earnestly to prayer and to raise their hands to heaven against Amalek. Then, after the customary solemn procession, he offered sacrifice to God. Those who had renounced the sedition wrote to Peter and Theobald, telling them to abandon what they had begun, since they kicked against the goad in vain. Their design seemed to have been scattered at its very beginning, and, if they themselves were detected, they would have renounced the wickedness they had committed.

They also wrote to Alexander, supreme pontiff, and to all the cardinals of the Apostolic See, explaining how they had been deceived by a certain man hardened in evil days. They begged that, when he came to the feet of the Apostolic See against his abbot and his mother Church, he should not be received; and they implored that darkness might not obscure light and error blunt truth.

But the vessels of iniquity, sons of Belial—namely Geoffrey of Latigniac and William Pidet—remaining in the gall of wickedness and devising foolish deceits, asked the abbot to permit them to go after Peter and Theobald, so that they might either bring them back or convict them in the Roman court of the wickedness of treachery. Yet the dovelike simplicity of the prudent sometimes guards against the serpent’s cunning; for evil once experienced scarcely remains free of suspicion.

### Author of this history

After dinner, then, setting out secretly, Abbot William came by night to Avallon, a castle of the Duke of Burgundy. Rising from there, on the seventh day he entered Montpellier. In his company were Geoffrey Angligena, subprior; Vincent, dean; Franco, his chaplain; and Hugh of Poitiers, his notary and the author of this work.

Hugh of Varennes had followed the traitors Peter and Theobald. He found them in the castle called Gannat, together with the Abbot of Bonirad, who had already established himself there at that hour. Hugh therefore produced letters from Abbot William and the whole chapter of Vézelay and delivered them to Peter. Looking at Peter with a grim expression, Theobald said:

“What is this, most foolish of fools, that you have done? Who is that abbot in whose name you have received this formal letter (*formata*)? We do not regard as abbot one who stands opposed to the count’s allegiance.”

Saying this, he snatched the still unbroken formal letter from Peter’s hand and threw it upon the ground to be trampled. Hugh answered Peter and Theobald:

“This injury harms not only the abbot but also the entire convent of the monastery of Vézelay. Therefore, on behalf of Abbot William and of the whole chapter, I tell you to return to Vézelay within four days to answer the charges made against you. Otherwise the abbot and the entire convent will pronounce upon your persons a sentence of excommunication by apostolic authority; and I announce that sentence to you on their behalf.”

He departed and met the abbot at Le Puy, city of the Vellavi, where he reported the traitors’ rebellion. The traitors had arrived before the abbot; but, having been recognized by John the abbot’s clerk, they could obtain no entrance to the court.

### The abbot is honorably received by the Roman pontiff; the traitors are repulsed

Entering to Pope Alexander, the abbot was received by him and by the whole court with great honor and full favor. When the traitors tried to approach the court, they were shamefully driven away even by the doorkeepers, branded with the mark of treachery. The Abbot of Bonirad entered as though he were to transact matters belonging to his own order. But when he began to plead the count’s cause and to prosecute, as if they were innocent envoys of the Church of Vézelay, the case of the traitors against the abbot—representing him as a squanderer of goods and overthrower of religious order—he was immediately repulsed by Pope Alexander, with Humbert, Cardinal Bishop of Ostia, resisting him to his face.

Finally Henry, Cardinal of Pisa, and the Archbishop-elect of Mainz supported, as far as they could, the party of the count and traitors. By many entreaties they so wearied the pope that they barely compelled him to write to the excommunicated count. When the abbot learned this from the notaries, he entered and, kneeling, said to him:

“What is this, lord, that you have done? We have not yet obtained full justice, and already you have revoked that little portion of justice which you had done for us.”

“How?” said the pope.

“By writing,” he replied, “contrary to apostolic custom, to the man whom you yourself have excommunicated.”

“Then,” said the pope, “has the sentence already been promulgated?”

“It has,” he replied.

And the pope said: “Show me your rescript.” He gave it to him. Alexander immediately sent to the treasury of the notaries and ordered that the surreptitiously obtained document be retained. When he learned that the Archbishop-elect of Mainz had already received it, he was greatly angered and ordered that it be demanded back from him at once.

Once it had been returned, the Archbishop-elect of Mainz entered to the pope and requested that the apostolic letter be given back to him. The pope began to rebuke him for having improperly procured the document. When the archbishop-elect bore the rejection of his request with indignation, he burst into tears. The pope, moved by this, said:

“See, take it as you wish; but you shall obtain no benefit for your kinsman from it. For we have made new writings against those surreptitiously obtained letters.”

Peter and Theobald the traitors, seeing that they were accomplishing nothing, withdrew. As they went away, they met William Pidet and Elias, empty indeed of letters but full of folly. These men returned to their vomit and resumed the infidelity they had renounced. By night they secretly left the cloister, climbed the monastery wall, and lowered themselves by ropes. But when a rope broke, Elias fell and injured his arm.

### Judges delegated by the supreme pontiff

After fleeing all that night and coming to the count, they complained that the abbot had subjected them to most grievous torments solely because of his hatred for them. The count gave them horses and expenses and sent them after Peter and Theobald. When they met one another, they all returned together to the court. Watching for Pope Alexander’s departure, since they could obtain absolutely no access to him, they finally encountered him as he was leaving the oratory. William Pidet prostrated himself before him and complained that, after appealing to the Apostolic See, he had been beaten and imprisoned by Abbot William.

“Are you, then,” said the pope, “also one of those excommunicated traitors to your Church?”

As all those standing by cried out, the traitors were expelled from Alexander’s presence and from the consistory. The abbot, however, paid no heed to any of this, nor did he even deem them worthy of a word in the court. He wished that the delegation for executing the apostolic sentence against the tyrant and his mother should be transferred from the Archbishop of Sens and delegated to someone else. This was also greatly desired by the Archbishop of Sens himself, who had already requested it in writing.

But because the larger and principal part of the count’s land lay within his diocese, the pope refused to transfer the delegation of the sentence. Instead, that the Archbishop of Sens might proceed more securely and forcefully to execute the sentence, he gave him as colleague Stephen, Bishop of Meaux. He wrote to both of them that they should summon the Count of Nevers and his mother and urge them to make an amicable settlement with the Church of Vézelay; or else, setting aside every surreptitious document and removing every appeal, they should pronounce the delegated sentence against the contemners and announce that it was to be observed by the bishops of Autun, Langres, Auxerre, and Nevers, according to what he himself had commanded them in the same writing.

### The delegates meet at Joigny and subject the count and his mother to excommunication

It happened, therefore, on the Monday following the Assumption of the undefiled Virgin and Mother of God Mary, that the most holy and universal pontiff, Pope Alexander the Catholic, ascended the altar to offer to God the sacred and life-giving victim for the soul of Ivo, dean of the Church of Chartres. While the sacrifice was being completed, those traitors were disputing with Geoffrey Angligena. Geoffrey himself went up to Humbert, Bishop of Ostia, and told him what great irreverence the traitors were showing to the lord pope.

Turning, the Bishop of Ostia saw the detestable traitors and said to Alexander: “Why, lord, do you permit those profane traitors of Vézelay to attend the sacred offices in your presence?”

“Where are they?” he asked.

“They are here,” came the reply.

And he said: “Throw them out at once.”

When they pretended not to depart, the bishops of Ostia and Segni immediately summoned officials and expelled them from the church. Seeing this, the Archbishop-elect of Mainz, who happened then to be speaking there with the Abbot of Vézelay, went out after them in great indignation. The Abbot of Bonirad also, at whose side the traitors always clung, seeing himself frustrated in his purpose, was deeply ashamed and withdrew. The traitors followed him and carried back to their lord the count the confusion and disgrace they had deserved.

Abbot William did not leave until he had accompanied Pope Alexander himself as far as the sea. Returning safely, enriched by the apostolic blessing, he entered Vézelay on the last day of August. A few days afterwards he came to Paris, where he handed the apostolic writings to Hugh, Archbishop of Sens, and Stephen, Bishop of Meaux. They immediately appointed a day for both the abbot and the count at Joigny.

When they had assembled there, the abbot produced documentary proofs of the privileges of Roman pontiffs and kings of France, as well as Pope Alexander’s letters delegating to the aforesaid prelates the execution of either a settlement or a sentence. As many arguments were presented on both sides, the day ended with the controversy unresolved. When the bishops learned that the count was the reason why no peace settlement was made, they pronounced against the count and his mother the sentence of excommunication delegated to them by Pope Alexander.

### They again examine the dispute at the Elm of Bazolles, but in vain; the abbot approaches the king

On the following day, at the request of the bishops themselves, the parties again met at the Elm of Bazolles. After the damages inflicted upon the Church had been enumerated, some attempted to arrange a settlement on these terms: the abbot was to remit all his damages, the count was thereafter to keep peace with the abbot and Church, and all other controversies were to be laid to rest.

The abbot replied: “What security will the count give for keeping the peace?”

They said to him: “He shall be bound by his word alone. If you can compel the count to this, he will give his hand in pledge into the hands of the bishops.”

“And if,” said the abbot, “he violates the pledged faith of the peace, who will render me justice?”

They answered: “You will see.”

The abbot therefore did not consent to remit such great losses; rather, he insisted that the burdens of procurations be entirely remitted by the count. For by the authority of the founder and of the privileges, no one may exact procuration from the Church except voluntarily and out of charity. The count replied that he would rather be disinherited than abandon the custom received from his fathers. Indeed, unless the abbot paid him three hundred pounds that very day for the procuration recently denied him, he would accept no peace settlement.

Abbot William said: “I have by no means brought my money-bag to this market in the manner of a money-changer. Yet now the superstition of the count’s tyranny or rapacity is plainly exposed: he demands three hundred pounds for one day’s procuration. What peace can stand beneath so great a scourge?”

Thus, since the count rejected the settlement of peace, they departed. That night Prior Gilo came to Pontigny with the Bishop of Meaux, who celebrated the feast of All Saints at Vézelay. Geoffrey the subprior, with Renald the almoner and the other companions, came, not without fear, to Auxerre; rising in the night, they entered Vézelay early in the morning.

The abbot spent that night at Saint-Julien-de-Saulce with the Archbishop of Sens and the Abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. From there he met the king at Moret, earnestly begging him, out of his innate compassion and reverence for the apostolic mandate, to assist the Church of Vézelay in so great and grave a necessity. He received this reply: that the king would never fail Blessed Mary Magdalene or her servants, but would contend for the monastery of Vézelay as for the crown of his kingdom. The abbot, however, ought to endure a little longer, to avoid the madness of the raging tyrant, and to see whether perhaps he would extend his hand even to sacrilege, so that, once this had been brought to completion before the testimony of the whole world, they might be punished.

### The Archbishop of Sens declares the count and his mother excommunicated

The abbot therefore accepted the king’s advice and sent his notary Hugh with instructions to the archbishop of Sens publicly to declare the count and his mother excommunicated, in accordance with the apostolic mandate. Accordingly, while the archbishop stood at the sacred altars, after the apostolic reading had been completed and the solemn jubilation was being performed, with the people standing by and the deacon waiting, he addressed the people, explaining with what grievous burdens the count of Nevers and his mother were persecuting the most renowned throughout the world tomb of the blessed Mary Magdalene, lover of God.

“For these burdens,” he said, “by command of the lord pope, we pronounce the sentence of excommunication upon both of them; and unless they come to their senses before the approaching feast of St Martin, we place their whole land under an interdict from every divine office, except the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying.”

The same archbishop Hugh wrote this sentence to Alan, bishop of Auxerre; Bernard, bishop of Nevers; Henry, bishop of Autun; and Walter, bishop of Langres, as follows.

### His letter to the bishops concerning this matter

“HUGH, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Sens, to his venerable brothers and friends HENRY, bishop of Autun; WALTER, bishop of Langres; ALAN, bishop of Auxerre; and BERNARD, bishop of Nevers, bishops by the same grace: greeting and love in the Lord.

“We inform your discretion that the lord pope, repeatedly and by frequent letters from Clermont, Le Puy, and Montpellier, has written to us—both exhorting and commanding by apostolic authority—concerning the unjust burdens and wicked oppressions which the count of Nevers and his mother are known to inflict upon the monastery of Vézelay and the people belonging to it. Finally, as you may see from the tenor of his letters, which we send you on his behalf, he commanded us that [Col. 1659A] we should summon both persons—that is, the count and his mother—without delay; and that we should exhort them with all diligence to restore without delay to the abbot of the aforesaid monastery everything taken away, to make satisfaction for the damages and injuries inflicted, and thereafter to desist from harassing and unjustly burdening them.

“But if, within twenty days, they should scorn to obey our admonition, we were to pronounce the sentence of excommunication upon them and utterly interdict throughout their land all divine offices, except the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying. By his authority we were also to command you to observe that sentence inviolably, all appeal and occasion for delay being set aside.

“We therefore, carrying out the Lord’s command, since our admonition achieved nothing, pronounced the sentence of excommunication upon both persons; but we deliberately delayed until now in notifying you of it. For we persisted in desiring to establish peace between the abbot and the count and, as far as we could, laboured to do so, both we and our venerable brother, the bishop of Meaux, to whom the lord pope had specifically entrusted this very matter. But because we were repeatedly frustrated in our purpose, finally meeting at Joigny and negotiating for peace for two days, and being unable to obtain even a trace of peace, we confirmed the sentence long ago pronounced by us at the command of the lord pope. We now declare and command you, by the authority of the lord pope and our own, to uphold and firmly observe it: henceforth regard them as excommunicated, and from the approaching feast of St Martin immediately and without delay publicly declare them excommunicated in all your parishes; and prohibit all divine offices throughout all their land, except the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying. Above all, this must be proclaimed and enjoined, under peril to their orders, upon those priests who are specifically called chaplains of the count and of his mother the countess, so that they may beware of transgressing the apostolic command and ours.”

### The tomb of blessed Mary Magdalene catches fire; relics are found in an image of the Blessed Virgin

Such was the archbishop’s letter. The bishops, however, endeavoured less firmly to observe the sentence laid upon them.

Meanwhile Abbot William, making the circuit of his monasteries situated in the district of Beauvais, entered the territory of Noyon and came to the monastery of Villers-in-the-Wood. It was Saturday in the first week of Advent. That same night one of his boys, named Giroldus, came to him and reported the sorrowful condition of the Church of Vézelay.

At the same time, in that church, there occurred an event which was both a presage of future calamity and a consolation. In the crypt above the tomb of blessed Mary Magdalene, lover of God, a fire accidentally broke out so great that it burned even the huge beams—which the French call *trabes*—in the upper part. Yet the wooden image of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, placed upon the floor of that crypt, suffered no burning at all, but was merely blackened. Moreover, the silk amulet hanging at the neck of the image of the boy Jesus neither acquired the smell of smoke nor changed colour in the least, whether greatly or slightly.

It therefore became plain that the image itself had not been smoke-blackened even a little, except so that, on the occasion of its repair, an inestimable treasure hidden within it might be disclosed by divine providence. For when the aforesaid image had been sent to a restorer, he said that it seemed to him to have a very concealed little door between its shoulders. When Gilo the prior heard this, he ordered it taken to the sacristy; and, calling with him Geoffrey the subprior, Gervase the sacristan, Gerard the constable, Maurice the subchanter, and Lambert himself, the restorer of the image, he took a knife and himself scraped away the colours. When the wood had been uncovered, they could discover no indication of any joint. At last he took a small iron hammer and attempted by hearing to perceive what all were unable to discover with their eyes. Hearing, as it were, the sound of a hollow object, and encouraged by joyful hope, he piously and boldly opened that little door with his own hands.

There he found hair of that inviolate Virgin, who has appeared to have neither a first equal nor a successor; a piece of the tunic of the same Mary, Mother of God; and one bone of blessed John the Baptist. He also found, in one wrapping, bones of the blessed apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew; one inch of the thumb of blessed James, brother of the Lord; two wrappings containing bones of the apostle blessed Bartholomew; as it were one arm-bone of the Holy Innocents; relics of St Clement; one mass of the hair of St Radegund, queen; garments of the three boys Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego; and part of the purple garment in which the Lord Jesus Christ was clothed in his Passion.

For every item listed above they found individual little written labels identifying the respective relics. Since all these labels were so old that they could scarcely be read, three others were found that were illegible; but of whom or of what they were, God alone knows. Those which they could read they had copied, and they bound the old writings together with the new ones as testimony. When they had carefully inspected everything, they restored it to its former place and placed the image itself, with the aforesaid pledges of the saints, upon the high altar. Then, all clothed in copes and with all the greater bells rung, they praised the Creator of all things, who had deigned to grant so many and such splendid pledges for their protection and the safeguarding of the place.

Then, as crowds of pilgrims and neighbours flocked together, there was the greatest joy and exultation, both in the church and throughout the whole town and nearby places, as people hurried from fields and villages on every side to celebrate the rejoicing. At last Gilo, scarcely able to restrain the cries of all, commanded silence with his hand and briefly explained the cause of their praise and joy. All wept for joy; and afterward, when they strove to restore the image to the crypt of the tomb of the lover of God, such a crowd of people wishing to kiss or even touch it gathered that they could scarcely restore it to its former place in the sight of all. Their reason for not permitting the image to be touched was that they might not be accused of greed.

Thus the divinely erupting fire was a presage of the impending tribulation; but the discovery of the sacred pledges taught that this same tribulation would have the best outcome. The men of Vézelay wrote these words to their abbot William as consolation in his undertaken journey.

### A.D. 1165: the count of Nevers begins a new persecution against Vézelay

In the year of the Word Incarnate 1165, on the twenty-sixth day of the eleventh month, Thursday before Advent, Count William of Nevers and his mother Ida entered the town of Vézelay with a multitude of armed men, as though to overthrow it utterly. The count lodged in the monastery’s guesthouse adjoining the alms-house at the entrance to the cloister. His mother, the instigator of all evils, took up residence in the house of Simon of Silviniac; and great fear came upon all the inhabitants of the town.

Word of this thundered to Prior Gilo and all the brethren then sitting in chapter. Gilo took all the keys of the monastery and forbade anyone to leave the cloister. The count remained quiet that day. But on the following day, seeing that none of the brethren came out, he mockingly asked whether the monks were solemnizing a ridiculous *parasceve*, or whether perhaps, with their customary pride, they disdained his presence.

He said this in mockery; but in truth the brethren were celebrating the *parasceve* of the imminent restoration of their freedom. For just as the dignity of the human condition was restored through the *parasceve* of the Lord’s Passion, so, through the *parasceve* of the brethren’s common exile, tyrannical usurpation having been expelled, the integrity of their ancient freedom was restored.

The count sent word to the brethren that he wished to enter their chapter house and speak with them. They replied that they could not have communion with an excommunicated person; but that, if he pursued matters of peace, they would speak with him through their prior. Gilo therefore came before the count with a few companions. Looking at him with a grim eye, the count rebuked him harshly on many points; finally he insisted that Peter and Theobald, those detestable traitors, together with their accomplices, should be received into the monastery.

Gilo replied that he neither could nor ought to receive persons excommunicated by the lord pope. But the count said: “These are not excommunicated. Rather, because they did not choose, like sensible men, to share in your stupidity, you expelled innocent men from among yourselves.”

Gilo answered: “We came in peace and for peace, but you assail us with unjust injuries. Therefore let this be certain to you: we shall not seek your presence again for such a gift.”

Having said this, Gilo returned to the cloister. The count then sent a herald and commanded, under threat, that all the burgesses assemble before him. Some of them, having often experienced his wickedness, secretly withdrew to hiding places within the monastery. For he had stationed guards to watch the gates, so that no burgess might enter the monastery.

### The prior urges the brethren to be of good courage

Those who presumed upon favours received from the tyrant, whether through personal service or secretly given allegiance, appeared before him. He immediately ordered them to renounce the loyalty which they had pledged to the abbot and the Church. They replied that they would take counsel upon this matter.

“Have your counsel ready,” he said.

He caused the doors of the guesthouse and the gates of the monastery to be locked. He sent his chancellor Stephen, Stephen of Pierre-Foraminis, and Furnerius of Droia, and commanded Prior Gilo to send him the keys of the monastery.

Gilo replied: “Then is the count the abbot, or the key-bearer, of this monastery?”

“They say that the count so commands.”

Gilo answered: “I shall speak with my brethren about this.”

Entering the chapter house, where all the brethren were seated, he exhorted them as follows:

“Behold, brethren, behold: the day is here which was long foreseen by our venerable abbot and by ourselves, and frequently foretold to you—the day on which there is no longer a matter for discussion, but rather for decision, concerning your freedom and that of your Church, and concerning the common danger to yourselves and your people. This day is the boundary between slavery and freedom, rest and labour, cowardice and courage, honour and disgrace. Whichever you choose will stand established by an inviolable bond.

“Until now you have endured the plundering of your goods; until now you have received with patient ears the threats and reproaches of the impious, as though they were the raging of winds. Set upon the stage of this fortune, all eyes are fixed upon you. Now the very body of your affair is in the arena, and there is no delay in whether you conquer or are conquered. It is not enough for this tyrant to tear away your clothes, pluck out your hair, and pinch your skin; now he even tries to knock out your molars. He demands your keys, that he may boast that he has shut up your freedom in the fetters of slavery.”

At this word all immediately rose and with one voice forbade him, on behalf of the Apostolic See and on behalf of their abbot, to give the keys of the monastery to the count. They urged that, leaving only a few guards behind, all should together undergo exile for the sake of freedom.

Gilo replied: “It seems unwise to me to abandon the house while the revenues of the house remain.”

### The count’s retainers enter and plunder the monastery by force

While this was happening, Furnerius of Droia turned aside, took with him the count’s retainers, and came from outside to the lower gate of the abbot’s house. Having driven out the gatekeeper who guarded the door, he took the keys, which happened to hang in the doorway of the great gate, and seized the house both above and below. He left wicked men in it, to hold it in the count’s place, as though the count possessed such lordship in the monastery that he could drive out the abbot’s men and introduce his own at will.

Then the count burst forth and entered the cloister, while Isnard, viscount of Joigny, cried: “Hurry, proud monks, and be subject to my lord the count!”

When the count hastened to enter the brethren’s chapter house, some who met him forced him to retreat. The brethren immediately left the chapter house and entered the church, to await the outcome; not to celebrate divine offices there, since the church was vacant of them because of the count’s presence. As they sat there, looking up, they saw the tyrant’s retainers above their heads: they had already broken open the door and invaded the tower of St Michael.

Overtaken by the sudden arrival of their enemies, the brethren could not resist this unforeseen wickedness. Indeed, the wiser among them thought it better to yield than resist, lest the tyrant’s provoked fury overthrow both monastery and town utterly.

After this the brethren entered the refectory. Mixing their bread with tears and their drink with weeping, they tasted scarcely a little food and quickly departed to answer the burgesses concerning the renunciation demanded by the count. They said to them:

“If you are of sound mind, you will prefer honourable poverty to the faithlessness of riches. For it is better to live honourably in fidelity than abundantly in the disgrace of faithlessness. Consider for yourselves which course is wiser. We labour for your sake; we are persecuted for your cause. What value is our rough woollen cloth, or this black hood which you see? Your wealth is sought; your own head is specifically attacked, if, in serpent-like fashion, we expose you, our members, to the blow. Behold us: like a mutilated head, we might enjoy whatever peace we could. But far be this from us! Far be it that we should purchase a disgraceful peace by your surrender. For we do not glory in your tribulations for our sake; rather, we glory in our tribulations for yours. Now it is both pleasing and necessary to test what fidelity, what covenant, what love has hitherto existed among us; and whoever is ours shall now suffer no argument to tear him from us.”

Encouraged by such words, those who proved faithful remained with the brethren within the monastery. When he heard this, the count stationed armed retainers in each person’s house, ordering them to be content only with sustenance from the contributions of those besieged.

He gave the house and revenues of Esconium to the excommunicated traitors and false monks, namely Peter and his accomplices. All the other revenues of the monastery he entrusted to Hugh Letard, provost of the castle of Censory, who was a servant of the Church and of the family of Simon, son of Odo, provost of Vézelay. This Simon had killed his lord, Abbot Artaldus. Hugh then handed everything over to Maurice of St Andrew, of the same condition and family.

Word of this came to Gilo. When evening came, he sent servants to collect the oven-dues; but the count’s retainers, attacking them with Maurice’s wife, took away their bread and sent them back beaten. The count also ordered the release of prisoners held in the provost’s house.

Then, according to monastic custom, the board having been struck, Gilo entered chapter with his brethren and said:

“Now we are compelled by necessity to do what we had reasonably delayed. Our houses and those of our people are occupied by enemies; the revenues necessary to us are taken away; and, what is worse than death, scoundrels with prostitutes trample with unclean feet the most sacred tomb of the lover of God. Nothing now holds us back, since both sustenance and honourable life are denied us. Let grief give way to reason, and let indiscriminate despair be far from us. For what has happened is neither new nor unforeseen. It is almost two years since we pondered this same matter in our minds, having before our eyes this violence of the tyrant and the coming exile, and telling you all these things. You yourselves often cried out in agreement with us and begged that what had been premeditated might be carried into effect. And behold: the night of tribulation and of time presses upon us, and deeds, not words, are needed.”

There was great lamentation and weeping among the brethren, servants, and burgesses who had taken refuge within the monastery.

### The monks, cruelly harassed, flee

Prior Gilo accordingly arranged who should remain and who should go, and which servants should attend those who went. After they had been given drink, they kept watch throughout the night. They took down the images, crosses, and all the vessels containing relics of saints. During this removal, as they more carefully inspected the icon of the great cross which hangs over the altar in the middle of the basilica, they found some of the milk of the inviolate Virgin and Mother of God Mary.

In the commotion of persons going and returning, Prior Gilo secretly left by night. He went on foot down to the lower quarter of St Peter; immediately mounting a horse, he came to an estate called Pont-Arbert. While he rested there briefly, Geoffrey the subprior and Geoffrey the hospitaller arrived from Gibray. Having dismissed the hospitaller, the prior and subprior made their way to Joigny by long circuitous routes through Burgundy, avoiding the count’s territory.

At dawn, when the count saw that the brethren who were about to depart were packing their baggage, he withdrew to the house of Simon Silviniac. The brethren, having made all preparations, entered the chapter house. After receiving the blessing, they tearfully exchanged farewells. They then entered the great basilica, where almost all the people had gathered, with little children and women. Before the tomb of their blessed patroness they prostrated themselves and entrusted their cause to her protection.

Then there arose an immense roaring of weeping and lamentation, of people tearing out their own hair, so that the cry of wailing reached heaven. It was an intolerable horror to see what could scarcely be looked upon for grief: a mingled cry and indiscriminate weeping of people striking their breasts and heads on the very pavement. Indeed the elements themselves seemed in some manner to sympathize with so great a calamity: the air was darkened, the sunlight obscured, flowing water frozen, and the earth continually covered with a rain of snow; all displayed a sorrowful countenance.

At last, accompanied by the weeping and wailing of the whole people, the brethren departed from the church, nearly sixty in number.

The count had already left the town, though his mother remained. The traitor William Pideth, mounting his horse, came dancing after the brethren and said that the countess commanded them to halt and await her. But they pretended not to see the hated man, crossed Esconium, and, accompanied by the people, arrived at the cross of Montjoie. There, pausing for a while and looking upon the basilica of Mary Magdalene, the lover of God, revered throughout the world, they fell upon their faces and sang as best they could: “O consolation of the sinner!”

No one can describe the weeping and grief of those departing and those accompanying them—men and women rolling their heads in the snow in their anguish—when this very iron pen nearly sweats all over with tears. To speak truthfully, this mourning surpasses the mourning of a funeral; for the mourning of a funeral is relieved by the succession of an heir. But the desolation of the heir is the abolition of the inheritance: a desolation unheard of in our world and in our age! A Catholic prince expels innocent monks from their monastery; and the very people related to him cruelly lay waste the place which almost the whole world bearing the Christian name venerates. If a cause is sought, freedom is charged as the crime; if reasoning is examined, prejudice is twisted into accusation.

### The count’s mother pretends sympathy and tries to persuade the monks to return

While tears and groans were poured out alike by the brethren and by all the people, Ida, the viperous mother of the tyrant, followed them as they slowly departed. She approached more closely and dismounted from her horse, asking with feigned humility that the brethren might hear her.

But they, mindful of the Apostle: “Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good” (Rom. 12:21), rose from the ground and stood still.

Then she displayed counterfeit tears and reproached them for their unreasonable and groundless departure. Her son, she said, loved them and the Church of Vézelay most affectionately; he was hostile only to the abbot, by whom he was unjustly disinherited, although her son demanded from him nothing except what was his own by right. They ought, she said, to remember the Gospel saying: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21).

She then begged them to return, promising that she would entreat her son to have pity on them and restore to the monastery the revenues he had usurped. Or, if she could not bend her son to this, she herself would supply their daily subsistence until the abbot came to an agreement with her son.

The brethren replied that neither place nor time allowed a dispute concerning her son’s right, since it was openly evident that he had claimed for himself right and wrong alike. It seemed unwise to return on an uncertain hope; and they thought it intolerable to accept another’s alms without consulting their abbot. They judged it unworthy that they, pensioners of Mary Magdalene, handmaiden of Christ Jesus, should become stipendiaries of the despoiler of the tomb of that same most blessed patroness.

Having said this, they turned their backs upon the woman and spent that night at Brécy.

On the following day, as they hurried to Auxerre, Arduin, the venerable abbot of St Germanus, met them and begged them to lodge at St Germanus. Once this was granted, he returned to prepare their lodging. The brethren entered the city two by two, with covered heads, commending their calamity in Davidic melody. There was a gathering of all the people of the city—men, children, and women—who wept and cried:

“Alas, sorrow! Who has ever seen such things? Who would believe such things could happen? What madness or insanity has wrought such things? O glorious and blessed lady Mary Magdalene, why do you endure such things? What confidence can we sinners hope to place in you, when you allow your servants to suffer such things? May all perish and be confounded by whose counsel such things are done.”

The tyrant himself also arrived mounted on horseback. Looking at each one, he mocked them, saying: “Thus and thus should such men earn their bread.”

But the brethren, taking no notice of any of this, passed on with downcast faces. They were honourably received at the monastery of St Germanus and rested there that night. On the next day, turning aside to Joigny, to the house of Hugh, formerly provost, they were honourably provided for by Aimeric of Le Puy and his brother Stephen.

Hurrying thence to the city of Sens, they sent forward stewards. Simon, surnamed the Child, happened to meet them while going for a walk; when he learned the cause of the great hardship endured by so many and such men, he was deeply grieved. Descending from his horse, he humbly begged them, for charity’s sake, to lodge in his house. Having scarcely obtained this, he received them and provided for them most honourably.

In the morning he led them to a hired boat—for they had travelled thus far on foot—and himself put down much hay for them. They spent that day rowing; and only as night was falling did they land at a little village called Miriacus. Since no lodging suitable for so many persons could be found there—they were nearly eighty souls—they entered a peasant’s barn, filled with cattle dung. Although they had fasted all day, nothing at all could be found nearby except a little common bread and two strings of garlic, which they ate raw as best they could with bread and water.

A remarkable thing to tell: afflicted by so many hardships, they endured everything cheerfully. Embracing exile for freedom’s sake as though it were their homeland, they passed the squalor of the journey with singing and mutual rejoicing. At first light they returned to their boat and arrived at Chona. There they first found Prior Gilo and his companion Geoffrey. From there they came on foot to Moret on the second day of December, and remained there for the following day and the day after that.

They sent Renaud, prior of Arborea, to Hugh, the venerable abbot of Paris, reporting their arrival and the reason for their coming to the king. When Hugh heard this, he was deeply grieved; filled with tears, he hurried to King Louis and showed him with what criminal sacrilege the count of Nevers had seized the renowned monastery of Vézelay, and with what labour almost all the brethren of that monastery had fled to the feet of royal majesty.

Immediately the king, moved alike by anger and grief, ordered the count to abandon what he had unjustly seized; within eight days to restore to the brethren the church, towers, houses, town, all revenues, and possessions in the condition in which they had stood eight days before the monks’ departure; to restore also what had been diminished; and to make satisfaction to the king for so grave an injury inflicted upon the whole kingdom.

The count replied to the king’s envoys: “I have dealt with the monastery of Vézelay as with my own, and I owe the king nothing for this act.”

“On the contrary,” they said, “you owe satisfaction for an offence committed in the king’s fief.”

But he angrily forbade them ever again to appear before him.

They replied: “We are the king’s servants, and we must report your answer to the lord king.”

The count immediately sent John of Orléans to the king to excuse him for the tyranny committed, as though he had acted for the public welfare of his land: the abbot and monks of Vézelay, he alleged, had brought in his enemy, the duke of Burgundy, and, unless they had been forestalled, would have handed over to him the towers of the monastery.

### At last the monks arrive in Paris and tearfully disclose the cause of their grief to the king; he receives them mercifully

Meanwhile, on the night before the dawn of the second Sunday of the Lord’s Advent, the brethren rose and entered their boat. They came to a possession of the monastery of blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris. Entering the house of a certain man, they were excellently supplied by an envoy of the abbot of that monastery, named Renaud, who arrived there.

Rising from there and entrusting themselves to their watery conveyance, they came to Paris. The whole city was stirred: everyone, from the least to the greatest, flocked together and wept. Entering the mother church, they prayed and sat there for a short while, while all the people nevertheless remained standing and thronged around them.

When King Louis heard of the arrival of the men of Vézelay, he turned back, leaving the business concerning the settlement of the monastery of St Denis to which he had been going. The brethren came therefore to the royal palace. As the king went to meet them and stood upon the steps of the palace, all fell with immense weeping at his feet. In return, the king himself, weeping and moved with compassion, fell down; and he rose with them as they rose.

Gilo, who was the leader of the company, then said:

“You know, my lord king, the reason for our coming; but grief and the crowd of people hinder us from setting forth fully before you at present the manner of our case. Therefore, at a place and time appointed by you, some of us will come to you and explain more carefully what evils the count has inflicted on us. Meanwhile we shall return to our lodging, imploring your favour and mercy for us all.”

And all fell upon their faces.

The king replied:

“Before you arrived, as soon as the shameful report came to my ears, I sent my messengers to the count. What he will answer or do, I do not yet know. But know this for certain: even if the count had as much land as the king of England possesses, besides his own proper territory, I would in no way allow so great an injury to go unpunished. For I am a pilgrim of my lady, blessed Mary Magdalene; and as far as I am able, I can never fail her servants. Therefore I also ask you to deign to remain in my house, and I will provide everything necessary for you.”

They humbly gave thanks, replying that his assistance in so great a necessity was sufficient for them. Seeing at the king’s side their host Simon, surnamed the Child, they thanked him in the king’s presence for the service he had rendered them. The king likewise showed him great favour.

As the men of Vézelay departed and the people followed them, all the brethren of the monastery of St German-des-Prés came out to meet them as far as the old palace and received them with weeping and heavy groaning. Entering, as custom required, two by two, and after offering solemn prayer, they came into the abbot’s house, where tables were laid for them.

### The abbot hastens to Paris to see the brethren

When William, abbot of Vézelay, heard at Villers-in-the-Wood of the misfortunes of his house and of the arrival of his brethren, he groaned; and all who were with him were cast down in spirit, especially because they were so far away. They rose on that very night, on which the brethren also set out from Moret, and rode all day fasting, afflicted by cold and snow, through the various turns of an unfamiliar journey. At last, weary and sorrowful, they came to Merlot in the second watch of the night.

On the following day they arrived in Paris and found their brethren still sitting at table. When the latter wished to rise, the abbot ordered them to remain seated. The abbot, putting on firmness, restrained himself from weeping and manfully repressed his inward grief. His companions, however, were seized by such anguish of sorrow that they could scarcely distinguish one another or answer the greetings of the exiled brethren.

In a wonderful manner, the exiled brethren—exhausted by the misery of travel and hunger—consoled their brethren, who had escaped their share in such great hardships. They exhorted them to place confidence in God’s mercy and in the king’s promised aid.

### He Pleads His Cause Before the King

When morning came, and divine aid had been invoked, Abbot William and Abbot Hugh entered the royal palace [Col. 1668D], accompanied by Gilo and Geoffrey, Frank and Robert, Peter and Vincent, Hugh and Theobald, a kinsman of the king, together with a few witnesses summoned concerning the events. The king was seated with his brothers, Henry the archbishop of Rheims, Count Robert, Peter of Courtenay, and other great men of the palace. Gilo rose and set forth at length the manner of the tyrannical invasion and the expulsion of his brethren from their order.

John of Orléans replied on the other side that the abbot had taken away the count’s right which he held in the town of Vézelay from the royal fisc, and had denied the count justice regarding the injuries inflicted.

“If,” said the king, “he possesses by my fief the right which he claims for himself, then he ought first to have made complaint to me concerning an injury to my fief, before expelling the monks [Col. 1669A] from their monastery.”

John said: “My lord the count did not expel the monks; rather, they went out of their own accord, in contempt of my lord.”

Robert, surnamed the Fat, one of the brethren of Vézelay, answered: “The person who takes from my hand my morsel sufficiently shuts my mouth.”

“That is so,” said the king.

“Therefore,” said Robert, “after the count invaded our monastery, stationed his retainers there, and placed all our revenues, having taken them from us, in their hands, what dwelling-place then remained for us there?”

“None,” said the whole court.

And the king said: “I have sent my messengers to the count; and if indeed he acts rightly—would that he may! But if not, my power shall not fail the Church.”

Giving thanks, the abbot returned with his companions to his lodging [Col. 1669B]. The abbot and his brother stayed for three days at Saint-Germain; then they returned to Moret and remained there for thirty days. Hugh, archbishop of Sens, wrote to William, abbot of the monastery of Vézelay, as follows.

### He Directs the Abbot to Come to Sens to Settle Peace with the Countess

“HUGH, by the grace of God archbishop of Sens, to his dearest William, venerable abbot of Vézelay: greeting and affection.

“Concerning the business of the Church of Vézelay and of yourselves, we have sent to the countess of Nevers. Since she greatly desires peace, she has given us security for one hundred pounds in pledges of gold and silver; and if the claim [Col. 1669C] should exceed this amount, she will give me security for it through good hostages and sureties. We therefore command and advise you to come to Sens next Thursday; and according to what you lawfully prove to have been done, you shall receive restitution.

“But if you do not come on the appointed day, the countess will regard herself as injured; and if she should wish this statement to be brought before the highest hearing, we shall not be able to deny testimony to her according to what she offers. Farewell.”

### He Goes to Sens and Disputes Concerning the Right and the Injuries Inflicted upon Vézelay

“The abbot replied to this letter that the date set seemed unsuitable, because, being so far from his monastery and having the enmity of the countess herself and of her son, he could by no means attend. Nevertheless, if the countess herself would furnish safe-conduct, both going and returning [Col. 1669D], to the men who were to prove lawfully the injuries inflicted, he would gladly attend on a day suitably assigned to him.”

And so it was done. Both parties assembled. When the abbot demanded restitution for the injuries inflicted and wished to prove them lawfully, the countess denied the greater part; some matters, however, she cast back upon her son, saying that she ought not to be held responsible for her son’s wrongdoing. He answered that the wrongdoers were the countess’s own men and the provosts of that territory; therefore he justly required from her what he lawfully proved had been taken by her people, to the value of two hundred marks.

Those who were on the countess’s side were astonished—above all the archbishop himself and his clerics—and begged the abbot to state the limit of the losses proved, lest he exasperate the countess by so weighty a demand [Col. 1670A].

The abbot answered: “Though undeserving, I have experienced her utmost exasperation; in what respect can she now be exasperated further? Yet, in order to recover her favour—if this could truly be done, as would undoubtedly be evident—I would freely remit half of what I can prove, without prejudice to the execution, in the remaining matters, of the mandate of the lord pope.”

“Of what mandate?” they asked.

He replied: “That she make satisfaction for the injuries inflicted and furnish security for the preservation of peace.”

It was the Saturday before the Nativity of the Lord. On that day William, bishop-elect of Chartres and brother of Count Henry, who had also come there for the sake of his brother’s interests, was ordained deacon. Wearied by fasting, he departed in great indignation against the abbot; and the matter was postponed [Col. 1670B] until the next day.

Although much labour was expended on both sides toward a settlement, they departed without result. The countess would neither restore the injuries inflicted nor furnish security for keeping the peace, saying that she could not do what was demanded without the consent of her son. Accordingly, the action itself was deferred until the third day of the Circumcision.

### Counts Theobald and Henry Offer Themselves as Arbitrators for the Count of Nevers

The king’s envoys, having returned from the count, reported that they had obtained nothing from him concerning the king’s command, but had been abundantly rewarded with injuries and threats. The king at once summoned his clerks, ordered an army to be assembled from every side, and commanded [Col. 1670C] all men under arms to meet him on the twentieth day after Christmas.

Count Theobald and Count Henry, having scarcely obtained leave from the king, met Count William. Having reproved him for the wrong he had committed, and obtained from him a pledge that he would abide by the king’s decision, they led him to the city of Sens, where the king had assembled at the beginning of January on other business.

The abbot of Vézelay had also happened to come there, in the presence of the archbishop of Sens and the bishop of Meaux, for the purpose of reaching a settlement with the countess.
