But since she declined either to restore what had been taken or to furnish security for keeping the peace, their labour proved useless.

The following night Count Theobald sent to the abbot, asking him not to leave on the next day until he had spoken with him concerning his own business [Col. 1670D]. When the abbot went to the king’s court the following day, Count Henry and Count Theobald met him and attempted to negotiate a peace settlement.

The abbot replied: “I am in the hands of the lord pope and of the lord king; without their direction I do absolutely nothing.”

They then entered before the king and petitioned him concerning the same matter. The abbot was summoned before the king and was pressed by some persons, not so much concerning his own peace as concerning the tyrant’s peace. The abbot recognized their stratagems: by every means they were endeavouring to turn the king’s favour away from him. He therefore deliberately placed the entire outcome of his affair in the king’s decision, removing from himself alike the blame and the favour for the whole business.

The king asked the count’s spokesmen—for he did not speak with the count or wish to see his face while the question was being debated—whether the count would bring this affair to a conclusion according to his promise. When they answered no, the king became intensely angry and said:

“What then? The abbot, who has suffered injury and is in no respect subject to me, places himself wholly at my disposal; while the count, who inflicted the injury and is bound to me both by his personal homage and by reason of his complaint, refuses to obey my counsel and that of my court? Henceforth let the abbot beware lest he be deceived, for I shall never fail him” [Col. 1671A].

### The Count of Nevers Is Brought Before the King and Promises to Repair the Losses He Inflicted

After many verbal disputes, the count was at length summoned before the king. By placing his hand in the king’s hand, he pledged that he would restore to the abbot and his men the Church, revenues, houses, and every possession of the monastery, in the condition in which they had stood eight days before the brethren’s departure; without prejudice to those claims which they had previously held against one another, and without prejudice to the sentence of excommunication and interdict by which he was bound [Col. 1671B].

He further promised to restore everything that, from the third day before the brethren’s departure, appeared in any manner to have been diminished or lost from the Church’s property, and thereafter to preserve peace with the Church and its possessions, the abbot and monks, and their men. The following right was reserved: if a dispute should arise between the count and the abbot or the Church, the burgesses of Vézelay would have a truce for fifteen days after a declaration of defiance, during which they could remove themselves and their property to safe places, while the Church remained at peace with all its own possessions.

For restoring the recent damages according to the proof furnished by the Church’s men, the count gave as hostages Anselm of Traînel, his brother Garnier . . . . . the count, and Isgnard, viscount of Joigny. These four, each for a fourth part, gave their pledge into the hand of Count Theobald: if the count, after forty days allowed for lawful proof, should refuse to restore the proven damages, they were to remain under guard at Sens, after fifteen days’ summons by the abbot, until they or the count had made satisfaction to the abbot and the Church [Col. 1671C].

### The King Restores the Abbot and the Monks of Vézelay All at Once

When these matters had been settled, the king, at the abbot’s request, hastened to appoint the feast of Epiphany at Vézelay, and joyfully restored the abbot to his place. The sons of Belial were expelled from the monastery and from the houses of the burgesses, and great joy and gladness came upon all. The wicked traitorous pseudo-monks likewise left the house at Écône, carrying off and dispersing every good which they could lay hands upon, and took flight.

Thus, after forty-five days had elapsed, the brethren returned from exile in rejoicing and immense gladness. One of the excommunicated men, named William Pideth, possessed by a diabolical spirit, began to attack the monastery and make raids. After he had done this for a long time, a great crowd of country people from both the town of Vézelay and the town of Campimol pursued him; finally the wretch was struck down and died [Col. 1672A].

Accordingly, in the presence of the king’s knights and the count’s retainers, the abbot calculated the total losses inflicted upon the Church by the count’s men from the brethren’s departure until the present; the sum was two hundred and forty pounds.

### The Count Attempts to Soften the Abbot’s Mind

After this, men sent by the count demanded from the abbot the expenses of the procuration for the feast of Blessed Mary Magdalene and certain other absurdities. The abbot answered: “When the count, having made peace with me, has been received into communion with the Church, I shall then answer him concerning the question raised.”

The archbishop of Lyons and the archbishop of Canterbury met at Crisenon [Col. 1672B], attempting, if perhaps they could, to arrange a settlement between the abbot and the count and countess. But their labour was in vain. Since the burden of all the oppressions lay in the excessive procurations, neither the abbot nor the Church wished to accept any settlement which would plainly introduce not true peace but a pretended peace, unless the count either relinquished all procurations entirely or limited them by a fixed specification of expenses.

### The Abbot Complains to the King Concerning the Count

As Lent again approached, William of Moret and his brother Reynald came to their uncle William, abbot of Vézelay, attempting to incline his mind toward a peace settlement. The abbot on one side and the count on the other met at Escolnias [Col. 1672C]; but there too they laboured in vain.

The abbot then hastened to the king and found him at Sens. He informed him how the count had broken the agreed truce of forty days. For it had been said in the settlement at Sens that, after proof of his losses, the abbot and Church should have from the count an eleven-day truce concerning every claim which the count might have against the abbot. Thereafter, if the count should not wish to endure matters any longer, the abbot was again to have fifteen days’ truce from the day of a declaration of defiance.

But eight days into the forty-day truce, the count declared defiance against the abbot in such a way that he would allow only eight days of truce; those eight days were to be completed together with the preceding forty days [Col. 1672D]. When the king heard this, he took it badly. He told the abbot to return with him to Auxerre, rebuked the count, and ordered him to restore the violated truce. The count was deeply grieved, almost to tears; nevertheless, compelled to obey, he granted a truce of fifteen days from that point. These days were completed during Palm Week.

### The Count of Troyes and Others Negotiate a Peace, but Unsuccessfully

Finally Henry, count of Troyes, Theobald, count of Blois, and Anselm of Traînel met William, count of Nevers, and William, abbot of Vézelay, and laboured long and earnestly to settle peace between the count of Nevers and the abbey of Vézelay. These two counts were related to the count of Nevers by close kinship [Col. 1673A].

In brief: concerning all his claims, the abbot said that he would abide by their counsel and decision, except concerning the two procurations by which the count was utterly destroying the Church. The aforesaid illustrious men therefore ruled that the abbot should pay the count sixty pounds for each procuration, provided that, for a feast which the count did not honour with his presence, the abbot or Church should pay him nothing whatever.

Further, in order that this settlement might be acceptable to the count and be ratified as a permanent law, it was ruled that the abbot should give the count seven hundred pounds. The abbot, however, offered only fifty pounds for each procuration and five hundred pounds for the settlement.

They then came before the count of Nevers [Col. 1673B]. Urged on by his clerk Stephen and by Stephen of Pierre-Perthuis, he entirely rejected the settlement unless the abbot gave him eighty pounds for each procuration and one thousand pounds for the settlement. The demand seemed harsh in the abbot’s eyes; Count Henry both urged and opposed him, lest he give anything beyond what had been offered. Thus, when evening came and the business remained unresolved, they departed from one another.

At the abbot’s request, the king wrote to Count Henry, giving thanks and entreating him to make every effort for the settlement described above. Count Henry assigned the abbot the Monday of Palm Week at Troyes. He also sent to the count of Nevers, begging him as a kinsman to deign to come to Troyes for the sake of a settlement between himself and the abbot [Col. 1673C].

But the count sent word back that Henry himself ought rather to come to Auxerre, if he had any business. Henry, horrified at such arrogance, wrote these very words to the king and to the abbot.

The abbot then returned to the king and found him at Orléans on the holy day of the Lord’s Supper. Bishop Manasses invited him to celebrate with him the solemn rites for making the sacred chrism. When this had been done, he sent some of the same chrism to Vézelay by the hand of Vincent, the dean. When the abbot informed the king of Count William’s reply to Count Henry, the king was greatly astonished and sent to him, ordering him to appear before him at Moret on the Wednesday after Easter.

### Conference Before the King

Meanwhile, the count was to refrain from harassing [Col. 1673D] the monastery of Vézelay and grant the men of Vézelay safe-conduct to come to the aforesaid conference. The abbot celebrated holy Easter at the monastery of Villars.

On the fourth day, the king, the count, and the abbot met in the wood above Moret, each with his own following. The king asked the count to accept the settlement according to Count Henry’s counsel.

The count replied: “What I hold in the monastery of Vézelay, my fathers received in fief from your fathers. To litigate or negotiate concerning that fief seems to me more violent than peaceful, more so than concerning my entire inheritance.”

The king replied: “If it is so, that my fathers granted that fief to your fathers, then beyond doubt it was granted for protection, not destruction [Col. 1674A]. Yet you, as seems to us, strive with all your strength for the destruction of the monastery.”

The count answered: “Saving the king’s word, I do not destroy it.”

The king said: “So far as your actions show, destruction itself is at hand. But let us set these matters aside and discuss a settlement, if the abbot is willing.”

The abbot replied: “The count says that the monastery of Vézelay was given to his fathers by your fathers. Yet we have before us the privileges of your fathers, by which the liberty of this very monastery is confirmed and every possession and custom of all secular powers is wholly excluded. Nevertheless, I commit both these privileges, apostolic and royal alike, and the monastery of Vézelay itself into your hands: settle and dispose of the matter according to the judgment [Col. 1674B] of your justice.”

### The Count Refuses to Abide by the King’s Judgment

The king therefore asked the count whether he would abide by the settlement proposed by Count Henry at Auxerre.

The count replied: “I made absolutely no statement concerning a settlement with Count Henry.”

The king said: “Indeed, I had heard it as I said. But in this matter, consider what you will do for my sake.”

The count replied: “For your sake I shall do what I can; but I shall never negotiate concerning my right.”

The king said in anger: “The abbot, who is bound to me by no right, submits himself concerning his own right and places himself wholly under my judgment; and you, who are bound to me by the right of personal homage, regard me, your lord, with suspicion and refuse to abide by my counsel? Until now, yielding to your youth, I have endured your injustices; until now I have incurred a great sin by tolerating the overthrow of the shrine of blessed Mary Magdalene. Henceforth I shall not fail the monastery in justice, if the abbot makes complaint against you and seeks justice. Meanwhile, by royal authority I forbid you henceforth to presume to harass the monastery of Vézelay, or the men and possessions pertaining to it, knowing that whatever fresh evil you do to that monastery redounds to the injury of the crown of the realm. But if you have anything against the abbot, behold: I present him to you for justice” [Col. 1674C].

The abbot then approached the king and requested justice against the count. The king replied: “Since he came when summoned by me for a settlement, royal clemency does not permit that he be drawn into litigation at present. Wait, therefore, until he departs; afterward I shall appoint for you and for him a day and place for proceedings.”

They met again the next day in the house of the brethren of Vézelay, situated above the river Loing at Moret [Col. 1674D].

### The King Again Holds a Council at Moret

Present with William, abbot of Vézelay, were Hugh, abbot of Saint-Germain; Stephen, abbot of Saint-Remi of Sens; Stephen, abbot of Châtelet-Melun; . . . . abbot of Château-Landon; Mainerius, a jurist; and Osmund, canon of Paris.

Some persons made various attempts to turn the king’s mind away from the abbot or from the Church of Vézelay. But all Satan’s attempts were frustrated [Col. 1675A], and the snares of covert greed were broken. For the abbot in no respect departed from the king’s will and judgment, whereas the count refused altogether to abide by the king’s decision. The count complained that the abbot was holding one of his men captive.

Asked whom he meant, he replied: “Andrew of La Palude.”

The abbot said: “Andrew of La Palude, who belongs to you in no respect whatever, is mine from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, as a proper serf of the monastery of Vézelay.”

The count said: “Andrew does not acknowledge this condition of servitude except under compulsion.”

The abbot replied: “Behold, I also submit this matter to the judgment of the royal court.”

The king’s magnates and counsellors said: “The custom of the royal court is this: if anyone is challenged by another concerning servile status, he is to be brought freely into the middle by his possessor [Col. 1675B]. If he recognizes only his possessor as his lord, the claimant, after the suit has been settled, shall have no right in him. But if he says that he is the claimant’s serf, he shall go naked into the claimant’s possession; while the possessor shall seize all his goods, movable and immovable alike, leaving only his naked body.”

The abbot replied: “I approve this judgment and custom, and shall gladly observe it.”

Then the embarrassed count wished to transfer the disgrace of his case onto the abbot. He brought forward a charge concerning that traitor William, who had perished by a deserved death, saying that the monk who had been in his protection had been killed at the abbot’s command. The whole court cried out against so foolish and wicked [Col. 1675C] an accusation by the count.

The abbot said: “Although the charge made is wholly false, I shall nevertheless make no answer to you concerning it.”

When the king learned about that pseudo-monk, he burst into loud laughter and said to the count: “Are your monks, then, of this sort?” When he heard the manner and cause of the ruined man’s death, he again said mockingly and reproachfully: “O the count’s just and fitting complaint! O accusation worthy to be pursued by so noble a prince! What does he demand concerning this? The traitorous monk has paid his body to the earth and his soul to the devil.”

### Meanwhile Hugh Letard Ravages the Territory of Vézelay

While these matters were occurring at Moret, Hugh Letard, taking with him the count’s retainers, entered the lands of the monastery of Vézelay and made an exceedingly great raid there, carrying off cattle, sheep, and diverse household goods. He even drew unfinished hides belonging to the householders out of the mire and sold them, obtaining from all this two hundred pounds or more [Col. 1675D].

Ascending, he caused a proclamation to be made in the market: if anyone of any condition thereafter brought anything for sale within the town of Vézelay or anywhere in its whole district, they would incur the loss of their property and bodily injury or captivity.

When Easter week had passed, he stationed the most wicked men—robbers made especially fierce by their very poverty—at every approach, so that no man or woman, child or old person, dared go down to draw water or grind wheat. Consequently matrons and virgins, trusting in the respect due their sex, sometimes went down and were dishonoured and violated by the vilest men, and were afflicted with many outrages [Col. 1676A].

Driven by such necessity, the brethren themselves went down to draw water and gather vegetables. They too were subjected to outrages and despoiled; nor did the attackers feel shame either at the poor value of their garments or at the unserviceable character of their patched, ragged clothing.

Stephen of Béliac had received from the brethren five hundred shillings, together with no small quantity of pepper and wax. He set out for the abbot, who at that time was staying at the monastery of Villars and avoiding the count’s ambushes. Since Stephen suspected the count’s retainers, he took his brother, a knight, and travelled by byways, coming to Poseium [Poiseux?], trusting in the safe-conduct of William, provost of Droues, who had married Stephen’s sister. Yet treachery sometimes abuses the claim of blood relationship.

When the knight had departed from his brother, William, provost of Droues, immediately sent William of Lensech, who pursued Stephen as he went away and took from him the money, horses, and everything he was carrying [Col. 1676B].

Stephen returned and went to Ida, the count’s mother. On the king’s behalf he requested that what had been taken be restored, since everything belonged to the house of the monastery of Villars, which was under the king’s lordship and protection. But she scorned the king’s name; while pretending that the monastery of Vézelay, which was under her and her son’s protection, was being plundered by her son’s adversary, she was scarcely overcome by the entreaties of Stephen’s friends and ordered the horses and part of the wax restored.

This report reached the ears of the people of Vézelay. They were dismayed in spirit, grieving more for their ancestral impoverishment than for their own distress. A rumour arose that the count had ordered the elders and leading men of the people of Vézelay to be seized and their goods plundered or confiscated. Terrified, they withdrew within the monastery’s enclosure [Col. 1676C].

### The Abbot Goes to Beauvais to Complain to the King About the Raids Made by the Count’s Retainers

Geoffrey the Englishman, who then held first place in the abbey of Vézelay after Gilo, wrote together with his brethren to the abbot, informing him with what affliction and devastation [Col. 1676D] the town of Vézelay was being besieged by the count’s retainers.

The abbot then came to Beauvais, where the king had happened to assemble with a multitude of his bishops and magnates. When the king learned the evils which William, count of Nevers, had inflicted upon the monastery of Vézelay, he appointed the Sunday before Pentecost at Orléans as the day for the count to plead with the abbot before him. But first the count was to satisfy the king concerning his contempt and violation of the king’s command, in persecuting the aforesaid monastery after the king’s prohibition.

Having received the date, the count became greatly indignant and departed with many threats. The abbot then approached the duke of Burgundy and begged him to deign to bring aid to those under siege. The duke immediately wrote to Gunthard, provost of Avallon, ordering him without hesitation to convey every kind of merchandise from his territory to Vézelay and, if necessary, defend it by arms [Col. 1677A].

But the provost, a boy in age and character, was ensnared by the count through the craft of Anseric of Montréal, who was no less hostile than the count to the abbot and monastery. He falsely repudiated everything he had promised, prohibited merchandise, and ordered the seizure of every man of Vézelay found in his territory.

King Louis summoned his clerks and wrote to all the governors and princes of his realm, ordering them to assemble cavalry and infantry and meet him at Sens on the Sunday before the feast of blessed Mary Magdalene.

The count, fearing the judgment of the royal court, excused himself from the day assigned to him. The king immediately appointed the first Sunday after Pentecost at Paris [Col. 1677B]. When the count again excused himself from this day, he gave him the third Sunday after Pentecost at Laon. On excusing himself for the third time, the count sent William of Dompierre, begging the king to deign at least once to enter into a conference at which, after hearing the allegations on both sides, he himself would in every respect abide by the king’s judgment. This proposal seemed good in the king’s eyes: rest was welcome to him, whereas war had always been hateful.

### Genealogy of the Capetian Kings: Louis VII Goes to Jerusalem

This is King Louis, son of Louis, surnamed the Fat; son of Philip; son of Henry; son of Robert; son of Hugh Capet, who was the first king after the extinction of Charles’s line, which had ruled for almost two hundred years. From Hugh’s first year to the first year of this Louis—who ruled with his father for five years—there were nearly one hundred and forty years [Col. 1677C].

This is King Louis whose father Louis had extended his kingdom in every direction and joined to him in marriage the daughter of William, duke of the Aquitanians and count of Poitou. Through her he acquired all Aquitaine, Gascony, the Basque country, and Navarre, as far as the Pyrenees and as far as Charles’s Cross.

This is King Louis who, in the fifteenth year of his reign, while Eugenius occupied the Roman see, went to Jerusalem with a great army marked by the banner of the life-giving Cross, to wage war against the people hostile to the faith. But, by God’s inscrutable judgment, after losing the greater part of his men, he returned without triumph. Following bad counsel, he dismissed his wife together with the aforesaid land—which had formerly been a kingdom in its own right—and afterward married the daughter of the emperor of the Spaniards. When she died, he married for the third time the sister of Count Henry, by whom he first received a son named Philip, in the thirty-third year of his reign, Pope Alexander having returned from Gaul [Col. 1677D].

### The King, the Count, and the Abbot Meet at Moret

The king, count, and abbot met at Moret. After the disputes had been presented on both sides, the king wished each party to abide by the decision of Henry, archbishop of Rheims, and Henry, count of Troyes. The count gave his faith into the hand of Peter, the king’s brother, that he would do so [Col. 1678A]; the abbot promised the same only upon his word of truth.

When they asked for the day of the decision—for the arbitrators were not present—the king replied that he would appoint them a suitable day around the feast of Saint Denis. Meanwhile the abbot was to return to his monastery, and he and his men were to enjoy the peace and security they desired until the dispute had been settled by the aforesaid arbitrators. The count confirmed by an oath of faith that he would preserve this peace.

Thus, each returning to his own affairs, Abbot William went to Troyes to Count Henry and thence to Clairvaux, where he hoped to find Henry, the king’s brother and archbishop. Not finding him, he returned and celebrated the feast of blessed Mary Magdalene in the monastery [Col. 1678B].

King Louis, however, led an army against William, count of Chalon, because of the very wicked slaughter which his son William had carried out against the Cluniacs. After occupying the castle of Lordon, which belonged by right to the abbey of Cluny, the older men and young men of the town of Cluny went out. The count’s trained force of knights immediately attacked them, who were unwary like an ignorant populace, forced them to flee, and destroyed almost all of them utterly.

The king therefore marched with an army, seized the count’s castles and fortifications, the city of Chalon itself, and all his land as far as the River Saône. He handed it over, after devastation, into the control of Hugh, duke of Burgundy [Col. 1678C], and William, count of Nevers, until that young man, who had been the cause of the evils, came to Vézelay before the king with his mother and made satisfaction to the king as best he could.

Since the whole weight of that affair occupied the count of Nevers, the king postponed until the approaching feast of Saint Martin the decision of the dispute between that count and the abbot.

In the year 1166 of the Incarnation of the Word of the Lord; in the 286th year from the reception of the sacred body of blessed Mary Magdalene, lover of God; in the eleventh year from the destruction of the accursed commune of the burgesses; on the tenth day of November, William, abbot of Vézelay, and William, count of Nevers, met before the king at Paris [Col. 1678D], and the count proposed—

> **[Note: Col. 1677D. Six leaves cut out are missing here.]**

[lacuna]

### Guy, the Count’s Brother, Still a Boy

[lacuna]

His sister, still unmarried, and his younger brother.

[lacuna]

Milo of Nuceria.

[lacuna]

### The Count’s Oath to Keep Peace with the People of Vézelay

Accordingly, concealing the malice of his mother’s words, the count rose and bent his knees before the holy Gospel, the life-giving cross of Christ, and the sacred relics. When the abbot wished to dictate to him the form of the oath, he said: “Wait, and allow me to utter myself what I feel in my heart and hold in faith. But if I say anything too little or too much, you may correct it.” [Col. 1679A] And he said:

“As it has been recited from the present charter, and as I understand it in good faith—and as all of you standing here understand it—so I shall keep and observe it, and shall make my people observe it. So may God and these holy things help me.”

And all cried: “Enough, enough. It has been well and clearly said.”

Calling Guy, his brother, he ordered him to swear in the same manner. And he did so, saying: “As my lord the count, my brother, has sworn in good faith, so I too shall keep and observe it in good faith. So may God and these holy things help me.”

Then John, provost of Auxerre, Columbus, provost of Tonnerre, Milo, provost of Mailly, Hugh Letard, provost of Châtel-Censoir, and others from the surrounding district [Col. 1679B] swore as had been determined in the charter.

But Ida, the count’s mother, seeking to evade the matter, entered the oratory of the inviolate Virgin Mary, adjoining the chapter-house. She summoned Milo with her and many others whom she hoped would comply with her folly. As they discussed in various ways how the countess might avoid the oath, and no honorable way out appeared, they summoned the count. In his presence his mother begged him not to compel her to swear. The count replied: “If you wish me to incur perjury, do not swear.” She said: “Willing or unwilling, I grant, by a lawful undertaking, whatever you have sworn according to your will.” The count said to her: “If this will suffice for the abbot, it will suffice for me as well.” But she said: “Ask him, my son, [Col. 1679C] to give you this oath.”

The count returned to the abbot and said: “It is shameful for a woman to swear, especially for my mother, who is noble both in birth and in power, and is also a widow. Spare her, I beg you, and do not compel her to swear. Instead, accept her agreement by a lawful undertaking; and I shall be bound on her behalf that she will observe it thus.”

The abbot replied: “Do not—do not undo the foundation of peace. For I know that your mother was the beginning and cause of all your hostilities; and it is certainly established that she promises much but brings little into effect. Nevertheless, out of love for you, if she pledges by a lawful undertaking that she will observe the terms of the settlement, as you have said, I shall allow any lawful knight, with her standing before the holy things, to swear in her stead.”

And so it was done. Baldwin, who was named on her behalf, swore. [Col. 1679D] There was great joy and exultation among all the people that day. Great concord and friendship arose between the abbot and the count; nor was there any difference between them, so that one did not think the very same thing as the other.

Those who had been the makers and instigators of all the hostilities came to the abbot’s feet and humbly begged him to reconcile them to the count, whom they had offended. King Louis came to Vézelay, and the abbot and his brethren gave him thanks for the peace obtained. The son of the count of Chalon also met him, and, through the abbot’s action, made peace with the king.

Stephen, abbot of Cluny, also came to this conference. Because he hated the person of William, abbot of Vézelay, he disdained to enter the town of Vézelay. [Col. 1680A] He stopped at an estate called Nine Fountains and sent word to the king that he should meet him wherever he might be. The king appointed him a place for the next day at Lower Saint Peter’s, an estate of the monastery of Vézelay.

When William, abbot of Vézelay, learned this, he sent to him Rainald the almoner and Gaudric, prior of Champ-Mou. Stephen scarcely admitted them to his presence; having heard them, he dismissed them without returning William’s greeting, saying that he would confer with his brethren regarding what they had proposed.

With Stephen, abbot of Cluny, were Bernard, prior of Saint Stephen at Nevers; Hugh of Silviniac; Thomas; Amblard; and many others. All unanimously asked and urged him to grant the request of the abbot of Vézelay. [Col. 1680B] For the abbot of Vézelay requested that the abbot of Cluny should come to Vézelay; that he himself should meet him with the duke of Burgundy, the count of Nevers, and the entire knightly retinue of the magnates then assembled there; that, with the streets adorned and fragrant with abundant incense, he should receive him in solemn procession to the sound of all the bells; that he should hold chapter as he pleased, sit at the refectory bell if he wished, or remain as many days as he pleased in the abbot’s chamber.

Therefore the abbot of Cluny, yielding to the advice of his men, sent Hugh and Amblard to tell the abbot of Vézelay that he accepted his request. Immediately the abbot ordered the church and all the streets to be adorned. Through a public crier he ordered all the people [Col. 1680C] to decorate suitably the doors and entrances of their houses and to proceed honorably with him to meet the abbot of Cluny.

But Theobald, prior of Cluny, who afterward became abbot of the monastery of Molesme, arrived and condemned the counsel of his brethren. Coming with Pons, then prior of the monastery of Paray, he tested the intention of Abbot William, asking with what honor he intended to receive the abbot of Cluny.

The abbot replied: “Taking with me the counts, magnates, and knights whose multitude you see present, I shall meet the lord abbot of Cluny and offer him a solemn procession. When he has entered here, he may hold chapter and use the refectory as he pleases, or remain in this very chamber [Col. 1680D] of mine as long as he wishes; and I shall show him every honor in grain, wine, meat, and fish.”

As Theobald murmured, Pons replied: “All these things which you propose are indeed good, but they are less than sufficient for the person of the abbot of Cluny.”

“What further, then,” he said, “do you think ought to be done?”

Pons replied: “You know very well what befits him, especially in this monastery, which owes him a more ample reverence in addition to ordinary hospitality.”

“I know well,” he said, “what befits him, and therefore I shall show him every honor due to him. But if perhaps you intend something further, I want this to be certainly understood among you: once this seat has been entrusted to me, I shall not yield it to him.”

They said to him: “Then do not trouble yourself, for the lord abbot will by no means come here [Col. 1681A] to receive your service.”

The abbot himself said to them: “He shall see to that. I have done what was mine to do.”

### The Abbot of Cluny’s Conduct Condemned by the King and Magnates

The king and his magnates heard this report, and it displeased them greatly. They said: “What great arrogance in this man, who scorns so great an honor offered to him and demands that the lord king and all of us should go out to meet him!”

While they were saying these things, and Abbot William was before the king, word was brought to him that Stephen, abbot of Cluny, had already descended to the outer steps of the great basilica and was standing before the altar of the apostles Peter and Paul. William went down to him and led him into the upper house before the king. There Stephen remained fasting throughout the entire day to no purpose; then, as nightfall approached, he returned to the aforesaid estate. [Col. 1681B]

That day Abbot William was greatly honored in the sight of the king, the count of Nevers, and all the magnates. He obtained the favor of the count of Nevers and advanced more and more each day in the count’s affection, so that the count entrusted himself to him in all matters and confided his secrets to him.

### William of Nevers Sets Out for Jerusalem

After these events, William, count of Nevers—son of William of Auxerre, son of William of Carthus, son of Rainald of Mailly, son of William of Nevers, son of Rainald, who was the son of Landric, the first count of Nevers of this line—received at La Charité the sign [Col. 1681C] of the life-giving cross for the sake of a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, from Hugh, archbishop of Sens.

### The Toll-Collectors, or Poplicans, Brought to Trial: Principal Articles of Their Heresy

At that time certain heretics, called Toll-Collectors or Poplicans, were discovered at Vézelay [Note: [Col. 1681] “Telonarii,” as Baluze advised it should be written; the printed text had “Deonarii.”]. When brought to examination, they tried, by evasions and circumlocutions, to conceal the utterly foul sect of their heresy.

The abbot therefore ordered them to be confined separately until they could be convicted by bishops and honorable persons who were arriving. They were held for nearly sixty days or more, and were frequently brought forward. They were questioned concerning the Catholic faith, now by threats and now by persuasion. At length, after much labor had been spent in vain, through the intervention of the archbishops [Col. 1681D] of Lyons and Narbonne, the bishop of Nevers, abbots, and many other highly learned men, [Col. 1682A] they were convicted of confessing with their mouths only the divine essence, while utterly nullifying every sacrament of the Catholic Church: namely, the baptism of infants, the Eucharist, the making of the sign of the life-giving cross, sprinkling with exorcised water, the buildings of churches, the remedies provided by tithes and offerings, the marriage union of married persons, the institutions of monks, and all offices of clerics and priests.

As the solemnity of Easter approached, two of them, having heard that they were soon to be destroyed by the judgment of fire, pretended to believe what the Catholic Church believes, and to be willing, for the peace of the Church, to satisfy the ordeal of water.

Accordingly, during the procession of the Easter solemnity, they were brought into the midst of an enormous crowd occupying the entire cloister. Present were Guichard, archbishop of Lyons; Bernard, bishop of Nevers; Master Walter, bishop of Laon; and William, abbot of Vézelay. [Col. 1682B] Being questioned article by article concerning the faith, they declared that they believed as the Catholic Church believes. Questioned concerning the execrable sacrament of their error, they said that they knew nothing except the previously stated unbelief concerning the Church’s sacraments. Asked whether they would prove by the ordeal of water that they believed as they professed and knew nothing further of the secret of their error, they answered that they would do so voluntarily, without any judicial compulsion.

Then the entire Church cried out with one voice: “Thanks be to God.” The abbot replied and said to all present: [Col. 1682C] “What then, brethren, do you think should be done with those who still persevere in their obstinacy?” All replied: “Let them be burned, let them be burned.”

On the following day the two who seemed to have recanted were brought to the judgment of the water ordeal. One of them was, in the judgment of all, declared safe by the water. Nevertheless, some afterward gave an uncertain verdict concerning him. The other, however, was submerged in the water and was condemned by the voice of nearly everyone. Therefore he was committed to prison, because differing opinions were expressed by some, even by priests. At his own request he was again brought to the judgment of water; and, submerged a second time, he was not admitted by the water even slightly. Finally, having been condemned twice, he was sentenced to fire by all. But the abbot, deferring to his presence, ordered him to be publicly beaten and expelled. [Col. 1682D] The remaining seven were handed over to the fire and burned in the valley of Esconii, in the year 1167.

# In the Year of the Lord 1155–1169: Isaac, Cistercian Abbot of l’Étoile; Alcher and Peter of Roye, Monks of Clairvaux

[Col. 1683]

## Notice

*(Literary History of France, by Benedictine Religious, XII, 678)*

### I

Isaac was born in England, where he embraced religious life in a monastery of the Cistercian Order [Note: [Col. 1683] *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. II, col. 1352.]. After he had been sufficiently tested in that house, he was sent by his superiors to found another on an island whose situation and name are unknown [Note: [Col. 1683] *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, vol. VI, p. 20, col. 2.]. From there he went to France in 1147 and became abbot of l’Étoile, in the diocese of Poitiers.

History provides no details of his administration. Yet the learning and piety evident in his writings give grounds for supposing that it was very wise. The year of his death is uncertain. He was still living in 1155, and Valise, his successor, first appears in the domestic records only in 1169.

Isaac holds one of the foremost places among the writers of his order, less because of the number than because of the merit of the works he left. Dom Bertrand Tissier collected almost all of them in the sixth volume of his *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*. They are:

1. Sermons, fifty-four in number. The first six concern All Saints’ Day; the following thirty-one treat the Sunday Gospels from Epiphany to Easter; then come two sermons on the Resurrection, one on the Ascension, three on Pentecost, three on the feast of Saint John the Baptist, two on that of Saints Peter and Paul, three on the Assumption, and one on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin.

In the first sermon for the third Sunday after Epiphany, explaining the Savior’s words, “I will; be healed. Go, show yourselves to the priest,” the author says:

> “The Church can remit nothing without Jesus Christ, and Jesus Christ wills to remit nothing without the Church. The Church can remit nothing except to the penitent—that is, to one whom Jesus Christ has touched; and Jesus Christ wills to remit nothing to one who has despised his Church. As almighty, he can do everything by himself: baptize, consecrate the Eucharist, ordain, absolve, and similar things. But the humble and faithful bridegroom wills to do nothing without his bride. Therefore let no human being separate what God has joined. I say that this sacrament is great in Christ and in the Church. Do not therefore cut the head off from the body, so that Christ may be nowhere whole. For Christ is nowhere wholly present without the Church, just as the Church is nowhere wholly present without Christ; for Christ in his integrity consists of head and body. This is the one man who remits sins: first he touches inwardly, in order to produce repentance of heart; then he sends the person to the priest for oral confession, and the priest himself sends the person back to God for the offering of satisfaction. These three things produce perfect healing: contrition, confession by mouth, and satisfaction in works. Before these, no one may call himself truly healed.”

In another sermon Isaac thus depicts the situation of the monastery that he was then governing:

> “It is in order wholly to withdraw you from the world, my brothers, that by a well-considered design we have brought you into this remote, barren, unpleasant solitude, where you can be humble and cannot be rich; into this solitude, I say, situated far out in the sea and having almost no intercourse with the rest of the earth. Thus, deprived of every secular consolation and almost every human aid, you may wholly forget the world—you for whom, except for this small island, farthest from the mainland, there is now no world anywhere.”

This text certainly does not designate the abbey of l’Étoile, which is not on an island; it can apply only to the first monastery of which Isaac was abbot.

The beginning of the seventh of the nine sermons on the Gospel for Sexagesima indicates the circumstance in which it was preached:

> “Now, brothers,” says the author, “we see fulfilled in us that sentence pronounced against man after his sin: ‘You shall eat your bread by the sweat of your brow’ [lacuna]. Behold, crushed by labor and scorched by the heat of noon, we are dripping with sweat, while clearing uncultivated ground, so that we may not sow among thorns. Excessively wearied by the care of earthly seed, let us take a little rest in the shade of this leafy oak which you see nearby. There, not without a certain inward sweat, let us sift, grind, knead, bake, and eat the seed of the divine word, lest we collapse from excessive fasting.” [Col. 1685]

Most of the other sermons were preached on similar occasions. It is apparent that they were not prepared at all in advance, but arose immediately from questions put to the author. Thus, in the second sermon on the Gospel for the second Sunday of Quinquagesima, Isaac, taking as his text the disciples’ words to the Savior, “Send this woman away, because she cries after us,” begins:

> “Come, brothers, enough manual labor. Let us take a moment of rest and use it to answer, as divine goodness may inspire us, the question which this good brother put to us at the end of yesterday’s sermon. He is astonished that, although the Lord deigned to give this woman no answer, his disciples nevertheless, moved by compassion, dared to intercede for her—as if they were more compassionate and merciful than their Master, who is himself the fountain of all mercy. But first, my brother, how do you know that pity rather than annoyance led the disciples to act in this way, when you hear them saying: ‘Send her away, because she cries after us’? But let us grant it: let us attribute to them sentiments nobler and more in keeping with charity. Tell me: who among us would not wish all people to be saved and none condemned? Certainly God, whose goodness we do not equal, would do this, if he judged it fitting, as easily as he wished [lacuna]. But, brothers, there is no comparison between Creator and creature. There is no proportion between our piety and God’s. He often wills his own people devoutly to desire what he himself does not will to do, out of a motive of greater piety.”

The whole remainder of this sermon, as well as the following one, treats predestination, which the author explains according to the principles of sound antiquity. The editor, poorly enlightened in this matter, overturns in a note the teaching of these two sermons.

In the first sermon for the third Sunday in Lent, Isaac says:

> “Scripture, brothers, does not permit us to be ignorant that each of us has his own particular demon, exceedingly inquisitive about all that concerns us, following us everywhere, carefully observing all our conduct; and no one, still less a monk, is allowed to fail to recognize him. For my part, I think I know mine well. Nothing is more present to me, because nothing is more harmful to me; nothing is more familiar to me, because nothing attends me more constantly.”

At the opening of the first sermon on the Assumption, the author speaks as follows:

> “One does not readily find what can be said with certainty concerning today’s feast, namely, the Assumption of Mary. Confined as we are within the limits established by our fathers, which we are not permitted to overstep, we dare determine nothing except that today Mary was carried away—whether with her body or without her body, I do not know; God knows. She was carried away, I say, not for a time, nor only as far as the third heaven—if indeed there are actually several heavens—but into the eternal dwelling of supreme blessedness and to the highest heaven.”

We shall not pursue the account of these sermons further, despite the extreme satisfaction we derived from reading them. We invite readers desirous of instruction and edification to read them, and we dare promise that they will find there profound theology, pure and accurate morals, great knowledge of the human heart, and a clear, lively, moving style nourished by well-chosen expressions from Holy Scripture.

2. A very extensive letter concerning the nature of the soul. Alcher, a monk of Clairvaux, to whom it is addressed, had asked the author to put in writing the result of a discussion held with him on this subject. Isaac does this in the work, which is concerned not with what the soul was before sin according to Scripture, what it is now under sin, or what it must be after sin, but with its essence, its faculties, how it is united with the body, and in what manner it departs from it. Our author answers all these questions as a sound metaphysician, in a way that removed Alcher’s doubts and enabled him to compose, as will be seen below, a fairly good work on the same subject.

Isaac says at the close of his letter:

> “This, brother, is what obedience has induced me to write to you amid the countless afflictions under which we are oppressed. For this year the Lord has sent upon this province two great scourges, pestilence and famine, such that none like them are believed to have occurred in past ages. They did not take us unawares. We had seen and observed their precursor signs last year, persuaded as we are that all events have their causes from which they arise, their preparations for the manner in which they are to occur, their signs for the time when they are to arrive, and their final usefulness in the reason why they occur. For Wisdom does nothing except wisely, and the supreme Good does nothing except what is good, in a good manner and for a good end.”

3. Another letter, shorter than the preceding, to John of Bellême, bishop of Poitiers, concerning the Office of the Mass. It is a mystical commentary on the words of the canon of the Mass, containing excellent material. The author closes it with these words:

> “While I delighted in writing these things to you, both because of the subject and because of the person to whom I had the honor of speaking, behold: your man Hugh of Chavigny interrupts me and prevents me from exceeding the bounds of a letter. For he suddenly attacked our people, struck several of our lay brothers with his own hand, put our servants to flight, uttered many insolent words against us, and made many threats against our house. Moreover, he carried off eight oxen from us, which, I think, he has already sold; and his hand is still raised for greater excesses. From the rooftops he cries that he will avenge himself upon all Englishmen in my person. Would to God that I were not of that nation, or that, in the place of my exile, I had never seen an Englishman!”

As has been stated elsewhere, when Dom d’Achery first published this work in the third volume of the *Spicilegium*, he attributed it to Isaac, bishop of Langres. But later, in the general index to the collection, he corrected this attribution in accordance with the authority of two manuscripts in the king’s library (nos. 1252–1258), which assign the letter to the abbot of l’Étoile, and because in the time of Isaac, bishop of Langres, there was no bishop of Poitiers named John.

4. A commentary, not yet published, on the Song of Songs. It is preserved in manuscript in the king’s library (no. 1252), but without an author’s name. It follows Isaac’s letter on the soul and sufficiently resembles his manner of writing.

[Col. 1687] We shall not pause to refute Oudin [Note: [Col. 1687] *Script.* vol. II, p. 1485.], who credits Isaac with the three books *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, which have been discussed under Alcher [Note: [Col. 1687] *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXX.]. It is incontestable that this work belongs to the latter; the evidence may be seen in his article.

Isaac is one of the thirty-one authors whom Ottomarus Luscinius compiled for the composition of his great work, *Allegories and Tropologies of the Old and New Testaments*.

### II

[Col. 1687]

Alcher, of whom we have just spoken, cultivated letters with piety in the abbey of Clairvaux under the government of Saint Bernard and his successors Fastred and Geoffrey. He was well versed not only in sacred learning but also in the human sciences.

Isaac, in the letter he wrote to him on the nature of the soul, having observed that the head is the seat of that substance, speaks to him as follows:

> “For the head, as you know better than I—you who excel in physics, that is, medicine in the language of the time—is an assemblage of six bones, supported by the seven columns of the neck. If you judge it fitting to write to me concerning the structure of the human body, perhaps I shall give you a reply in which I shall show how the soul willingly receives this instrument of its activity and pleasure; how it afterward carefully preserves it; how it always leaves it reluctantly; how it eagerly desires to take it up again after leaving it against its will; and finally how it will rejoice when it has taken it up again, never to lose it.”

As has been said, Alcher doubted these three points because he could not comprehend the truly incomprehensible mystery of the union of body and soul. Yet, far from confusing the two substances composing human nature, he composed a treatise in which he sought to demonstrate their distinction. This work is the second of the four books *On the Soul*, printed among the works of Hugh of Saint-Victor; it is also the work called *On Spirit and Soul*, found in the appendix to the sixth volume of Saint Augustine.

It has previously been shown that attributing it to either of these writers is absurd, since Boethius, later than Saint Augustine, and Isaac, more recent than Hugh, are cited in it. Dom Tissier, who likewise inserted it in the sixth volume of his *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, has no better basis for assigning it to Isaac himself, since he has no authority for that attribution. Erasmus, speaking of this book, says that its author displays much reading but does not understand the art of connecting a discourse, so that his learning resembles sand without lime.

André Rivet’s criticism is somewhat less severe [Note: [Col. 1687] *Critica Sacra*, book IV, ch. 12, p. 422.]:

> “Although this book is unquestionably foreign to Saint Augustine, it nevertheless deserves to be read, and many things are found in it suited to satisfy readers’ curiosity.”

It is divided into thirty-three chapters in the edition of the works of Hugh of Saint-Victor, and into forty-four in the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*. But the new editors of Saint Augustine, who assign it to our author as we do, divided it into sixty-six chapters. In this edition, much more accurate and fuller than the preceding ones, care has been taken—no small labor—to indicate in marginal notes the authors from whom Alcher borrowed his expressions.

To state our view of this book: we regard it as a fairly good compendium of the best things the ancients said concerning the nature of the soul, its difference from the body, the immortality of its being, and the nobility of its destiny.

The treatise *On Loving God* (*De diligendo Deo*), divided into eighteen chapters and placed in the new edition of Saint Augustine after the preceding work, appears to us, because of their agreement, to be by the same author. In the judgment of Erasmus and the theologians of Louvain, luminous and affective piety is the dominant characteristic of this work. Its style, however, is very different from that of Saint Augustine. Saint Anselm, Hugh of Saint-Victor, and Saint Bernard, cited in it as recent writers, show that its author lived in the twelfth century.

Vincent of Beauvais, in book twenty-three of his *Mirror of Nature*, reports a passage drawn from this book under the name of Peter Comestor. But it is known how little reliance can be placed on his criticism. What is certain is that the author was a cloistered man, since he thanks God for having withdrawn him from the world.

The latest editors of Saint Augustine are inclined to place among Alcher’s works both this composition and all the other works they collected in the appendix to the sixth volume of that Father: namely, the *Soliloquy of the Soul with God*, the book of *Meditations*, the short work *On Contrition of Heart*, the *Manual*, formed partly from the meditations of Saint Anselm and partly from the fourth book *On the Soul*, printed, as stated, among the works of Hugh of Saint-Victor. The foundation on which they rely is the great resemblance these books bear to each other and to *On Spirit and Soul*.

But there is a difficulty concerning the *Soliloquy*: in its thirty-second chapter one finds, with only a few words changed, the whole first chapter of the Fourth Lateran Council, held not in 1198, as our editors say, but in 1215 under Pope Innocent III. Did the council copy this passage, or is the council its original source?

### III

Peter of Roye, in Latin *de Roia*, was educated among the clergy of Noyon. He obtained a canonry there, and by his abilities earned the confidence and esteem of the bishop, who made him one of his household. The comfort and favor he enjoyed made him forget his duties. He fell into dissipation and led a life little in accord with the canons.

In the midst of his wanderings, he nonetheless reflected from time to time on the vanity of the world, the brevity of life, and the uncertainty of the final hour. These thoughts bore fruit at the time appointed by divine mercy. At last he felt so keenly the desire to do penance that he went to Clairvaux to embrace monastic life.

He himself tells us these circumstances in a fairly long letter written during his novitiate to C., provost of the church of Noyon. This friend and others attached to Peter had greatly feared that he would be unable to endure so austere a way of life. He reassures them on this point, declaring that he had never experienced a joy purer or more constant than that which he enjoyed in this holy solitude. He announces that he is approaching the time of his vows, which he must pronounce on the Sunday after the Ascension.

There follows a picture of the observance kept at Clairvaux:

> “Among these poor and fervent solitaries, in whose midst I have the happiness to live, there are some who have been bishops, others consular men, others distinguished either by offices or by talents. You knew Geoffrey of Péronne, Rainald of Thérouanne, G. of Saint-Omer, and Walter of Lille. But how different they are here from what they were in the world!”

To this description he adds that of his former life, such as has just been given in summary.

Whether one regards this letter for its sentiments or for its style and learning, it may be called one of the finest of its age. Saint Bernard himself would not have disowned it. Dom Tissier first communicated it to the public in his *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis* (vol. III, pp. 271–276), from a manuscript of the abbey of Aumône. It reappeared in the new edition of Saint Bernard and is the forty-fourth among his letters.

## Sermons

[Col. 1689]

### Concerning the Author of the Following Works

*(Dom Bertrand Tissier, Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium, Bonfontaine, 1664, folio, vol. VI, p. 1.)*

Receive these few remarks concerning the authority of the following works. Lord Isaac, or, as he is called in some places, Blessed Isaac, was English by birth and a monk by profession. He was the third abbot of the monastery of l’Étoile in the diocese of Poitiers, distinguished for wisdom and learning, as is evident from his book *On the Soul* and his many sermons. He was a contemporary of Saint Bernard, as is sufficiently clear from the end of the second sermon on the Assumption.

Moreover, in several sermons he indicates that his monastery was established on an island. It consequently follows either that the monastery of l’Étoile was formerly situated on an island, or that he had earlier presided over some other monastery. For the letter written to John, bishop of Poitiers, declares that he was at some time abbot of l’Étoile.

Nor can that island mean England. For he lived not in England but in France; and he says that he was an exile on that island and remote from all people. Would he have been an exile in England? No one is exiled in his own country, nor would he have been remote from people in England.

[Col. 1689]

**SERMONS OF THE BLESSED FATHER ISAAC, ABBOT OF STELLA, OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER.**

**SERMON I. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS.**

[Col. 1689A]

“Jesus, seeing the crowds, went up the mountain” (Matt. 5). Would that it might sometime be granted to us also, brothers, to see the crowds and, leaving them, to order ascents in our heart! It is difficult to see a crowd while in a crowd; yet in a crowd one must be disturbed; and one who is disturbed can never see clearly, distinguish, or judge with the eyes. Therefore the crowd must be left, so that the crowd itself may be seen and judged. For whoever sees it well despises it utterly, gladly flees it, and freely leaves it.

He who has never seen light has never recognized darkness. Thus, after the Almighty had said that light should shine out of darkness, then He divided light from darkness; then He distinguished them, then judged them, then called the light day and the darkness night. “And He saw,” Scripture says (Gen. 1), as though He had not seen before. So indeed, one has not seen the crowd who has not at all raised himself above the crowd.

He has not felt the agitation of the crowd or heard its tumult who has not tasted the silence of solitude. My Lord Jesus—and perhaps He alone—could, while in a crowd, see the crowd without being disturbed by it. Yet when He saw it, He left it and withdrew to a mountain where the crowd could not follow Him. Alas, brothers, how many today resolve to flee crowds, yet settle precisely where crowds are likewise found and are pressed even more tightly by them, so that the latter turmoil of the crowd becomes worse than the former!

Therefore, brother, flee far away and do not return to the crowd; remain in solitude, follow Jesus, climb the mountain, and say to the crowd: “Where I am going, you cannot come.” Although, beloved, the historical narrative may concern some earthly mountain and some outward crowd, I nevertheless attend to the mystery—especially to that mystery which most instructs conduct and builds upon a foundation.

And although a material crowd can scarcely, or never, exist without tumult, still more strongly suspect to me is a certain inward crowd, and it is more effective in troubling precisely because it is inward. On account of this crowd, brother, go out on high and follow Jesus. He descended into you so that after Him and through Him you might ascend above yourself, even to Him within you. O great mystery! Having left the crowds, He went up the mountain. The disciples follow—at once all and yet alone.

Were they all physically stronger than every person in the crowd? Or rather, as I think, more fervent in spirit, so that they walked wherever their impulse led? But why is it that, after leaving nearly all the disciples—so ready, devout, strong, and ardent—He again ascends another mountain with a few, a mountain which Scripture calls high? (Matt. 17.) Indeed, brothers, what are we to think of the fact that sometimes, leaving even these and others—indeed, absolutely all people—He alone went up a mountain to pray? (Matt. 14.)

What do these mountains signify? On the first He ascends to teach; on the second, to show His glory; on the third, to pray to the Father. Is this perhaps the mountain of the house of the Lord, prepared on the summit of the mountains? (Isa. 2.) Thus perhaps He comes “leaping upon the mountains and bounding over the hills” (Song 2). First, leaping over all the crowds, He springs up the mountain with the disciples; second, leaping over the disciples themselves as lesser in comparison with the three; third, where no one can follow Him, He leaps beyond the whole creation—alone to the Alone, equal to the Equal, Son to Father.

On the first mountain the Son alone is heard; on the second the Son is seen and the Father heard; on the third no one has seen or heard the Father except the Son, nor the Son except the Father. Or are these perhaps the ineffable things which it is not permitted for a human being to utter? What if the three mountains may be understood as the three heavens? In the first, the spiritual life of human beings is formed; in the second, the angelic life is shown; in the third, the divine life lies hidden.

In the first is signified present righteousness; in the second is shown future glory; in the third, as in the heaven of heaven—whither He ascended beyond the west, whose name is the Lord, toward the East—the glorious Trinity, known to itself alone, dwells in inaccessible light, together with the human being assumed into God. There, in that peace which surpasses every understanding (Phil. 4), that Man nevertheless prays to the Father for us, as the blessed Apostle says: He stands before the face of the Father (Heb. 9) and intercedes for us (Rom. 8).

See how great is the hidden place in which He prays who taught us to pray to the Father in secret. Therefore, brother, make within yourself a hidden place into which you may flee from yourself, if you wish to pray to the Father in secret. Let us now hear, then, concerning the first hidden place, the first secret chamber, the first room, the first heaven or mountain, what the Lord God says there: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5).

The crowd has been left behind. He weaves no discourse about weakness, vice, or the malice of the day. His entire discourse concerns the virtue of life, the blessedness of glory, and the kingdom of heaven. “Blessed,” He says, “are the poor in spirit.” Wisdom always acts and speaks wisely. Wishing to draw the maidens after Him, He opened before them seven caskets of perfumes, so that, delighted by the fragrance, they might run after Him, as it is written: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song 1).

“And when He had sat down, He opened His mouth.” May it be granted me to sit with Jesus, and upon the mountain; to sit at His feet and receive from His teaching. In the crowd He stands and walks; He acts, grows weary, and is pressed upon, so that it is as though neither He nor His disciples is permitted to eat the bread of life and understanding or drink the water of wisdom—which is drunk in repose, and those who lessen their activity draw it forth. For the well is deep.

“He opened His mouth”: the mouth from which the Bride asks for a kiss (Song 1); the mouth of precious treasure, in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge were hidden; the mouth through which day pours forth the word to day. Many have sought wisdom, many blessedness; but because they did not hear this holy mouth or see the day, they fell into the palpable darkness of errors. Thus night declared to night a knowledge falsely so called.

Therefore, opening His mouth to the heart of Jerusalem, speaking to her in the wilderness, or upon the mountain, He said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.” Blessedness itself speaks of blessedness; having become poor, He speaks of poverty; the King, of a kingdom; the Meek One, of meekness; the Paraclete, of consolation; the true Bread, of fullness; Mercy itself, of mercy; Purity of heart, of pure hearts; and the true Son, Son by nature, of peacemaking and sonship. The true Word of the Father speaks what He is; divine Wisdom teaches what He is, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.”

With complete wisdom He places first, and first proposes to all, that which everyone seeks, desires, and longs for, but from which nearly everyone wanders astray. For who does not wish to be blessed? Why does every human being quarrel, fight, trade, serve, harass, and suffer harassment? Is it not in order somehow to seize from somewhere that which seems good to him and by which he thinks himself in some measure blessed? For each person believes himself happier insofar as he accomplishes what he prefers.

Thus all people unanimously desire blessedness, though they think differently about it. Some have judged it to lie in bodily pleasure and temporal delight, others in virtue of mind, others again in the knowledge of truth. Therefore the Teacher of all, who through charity is debtor both to the wise and to the foolish, first corrects those who have wandered, then directs those travelling, and third admits those knocking at the door, as He says: “Knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Luke 11).

For those astray the Prophet cries: “Lead me, Lord, in Your way” (Ps. 85). For travellers he cries: “And I shall enter into Your truth” (ibid.). For those knocking he cries: “May my heart rejoice, that it may fear Your name” (ibid.). For those astray he cries: “Lead me in Your righteousness” (Ps. 5). For travellers: “Direct my way in Your sight” (ibid.). For those knocking: “Let all who hope in You rejoice; they shall exult forever,” etc. (ibid.).

Therefore the Way, the Truth, and the Life, correcting, directing, and admitting, begins thus: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.” The false wisdom and true folly of this world, not understanding either what it says or the things about which it makes assertions, pronounces its judgment: it calls blessed the sons of strangers, whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity and whose mouth speaks vanity, because of storehouses full and pouring out from one thing into another, fruitful sheep, fat oxen, and the rest that belongs to the uncertainty of riches, to a peace which is no peace, and to foolish joy.

Against this, the Wisdom of God, the proper Son, the Father’s right hand, the mouth speaking truth, declares the poor blessed and destined to be kings of an eternal kingdom. It is as though He said: “You are mistaken and need correction. You seek blessedness, but it is not where you seek it. You run, but outside the way. This is the way; by this one goes to blessedness. Voluntary poverty for My sake is the way itself; the kingdom of heaven in Me is blessedness itself. You run much, but badly: the faster you run, the farther you are from the way.”

Poverty is the way, not blessedness. One travels by the way in order to arrive. Let us not be afraid, brothers. Let us hear the poor Christ commending poverty to the poor. One must trust the experienced. He was born poor, lived poor, and died poor. He indeed willed to die, but did not will to become rich. Let us therefore trust Truth concerning the way to life. If it is rough, it is short, while blessedness is eternal. If it is narrow, it leads to life, brings one out into spaciousness, and will set our feet in a broad place. Yet it is steep, since the ascent is upward and stretches toward heaven. Therefore it is worthwhile for us to be unencumbered and not burdened as we walk.

What do we want? Do we seek blessedness? Truth shows us the true blessedness. Do we seek riches? The King grants kingdoms and makes kings. The most wretched plague of curiosity has ensnared humanity: it is readily agreed what is sufficient, yet people toil after superfluities. Five yokes of oxen excuse them from the heavenly wedding feast (Luke 14), whereas from poverty comes abundance, from lack sufficiency, from lowliness preeminence, from worthlessness dignity, and from labor rest.

Elisha slaughtered his oxen for this reason, that he might follow Elijah more unencumbered (3 Kings 19); and we should follow Christ in the same pattern. Brothers, we must pause here today, so that on the second day we may begin the second sermon concerning the second virtue, aided by the discourse of the Father Himself, through whom and for whom we speak, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

**SERMON II. ON THE SAME FEAST, II.**

[Col. 1693D]

“Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5). The evil of curiosity is followed by the vice of pride. That wisdom which is not from above but earthly, animal, devilish, full of jealousy and contention, buys an estate so that it may rule others and never lack an occasion for litigation, counting dominion as blessedness.

Therefore, brothers, the disciples who leave behind this wisdom—truly devilish and the devil’s own firstborn offspring, which sought to set its throne above the other stars—turbulent and troubling together with the crowd, are worthy to hear: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” He does not say that particular tract of land, or another, or any portion whatever, but “the earth.”

Who has ever obtained more than a part of the earth by his labor, ingenuity, money, or fighting? Even this few have been able to do, while many have not. But who has been able to possess it? Why labor long to acquire what one must quickly lose? Heaven belongs to the poor, earth to the meek: what remains for the contentious? Or what more do those who wish to become rich desire? If heaven and earth do not suffice for them, what will become of them?

“Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? How long will you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4). The vanity of earthly domination lies about dignity and blessedness. Why do you remain with a portion? Why do you desire little? Why do you aspire to what is slight? The whole is promised, and the way is shown: one travels by poverty and hastens by meekness. The blessedness of heaven is owed to the poor; the blessedness of earth to the meek. What, I ask, remains for wretched contenders except infernal misery?

What will you do, rich people? What will you do, powerful people? Counsel is needed. Here is money; here is meekness. A robber approaches. If you defend the money, you lose meekness; if you hold to meekness, you incur the loss of money. I fear for both sides, lest the robber take the money and the devil at the same time take away patience. O my dearest brothers, would that this money had never existed—a possession which in these evil days cannot be possessed together with meekness, which cannot be carried on the road by Jesus’ disciples!

Perhaps for this reason the wisdom from above (Jas. 3), which is first pure and then peaceable, taught that neither purse nor money should be carried on the road; that one should contend with no one in court; leave still more to one who takes; not demand back what has been taken; and retain meekness, which is the way to blessedness.

Paul, praising certain people, says: “You gladly bear with fools, since you yourselves are wise. If anyone devours you,” etc. (2 Cor. 11 [the printed citation reads II Cor. II]). O Lord Jesus, who today believes our report, and to whom has this Your way been revealed in his life? O way exceedingly narrow, by which how few walk! This Your way was in this great sea, and Your footsteps today are not known. That which Your Apostle calls wisdom is now reckoned the height of foolishness, sloth, and inertia.

Alas, brothers, how are these things read everywhere and, I endure to say, everywhere neglected! The Carthusians nevertheless hear these things to some degree with ears that hear: they willingly have little so that they may not contend much. They possess few things so as not to provoke the world against themselves. The Grandmontines do even more: they possess nothing. For the Grandmontine, a traveller of heaven, will sing empty-handed before the robber of the world, and happily—except that, as they are reported, many of them greet people on the road. Let them see to it. What is it to us to judge another’s servant?

I say nothing of others whose hands are the hands of Esau, but whose voice is Jacob’s voice; whose hand is against all, and the hands of all against them. But the meek will possess the land of the living in eternity with as much ease as happiness, while we, bold and strenuous for God, fight in time for the land of the dying against God’s command or counsel.

“The meek shall inherit the earth, and shall dwell upon it for age upon age” (Ps. 36): that is, they shall possess the face of God, which alone always remains unmoved, however all other things may turn, as the earth remains while the other elements turn. “A generation comes and a generation passes away, but the earth stands.” What follows:

“Blessed are those who mourn.” These things, brothers, might have sufficed to correct those in error, had not devilish malice spread more widely and the cancerous evil crept more deeply, nearer the marrow. Cerberus still lies hidden and shakes its third head: namely, prudence of the flesh, which is hostile to God, savors only itself, has glory in shame, and has the wind as its dwelling; whoever dwells in it cannot please God.

“What are heaven and earth to me?” it says. “What are riches, gathered to the harm of their owners? What are powers, always fearful and to be feared? All these things are outside me; I am concerned with myself. ‘Soul, you have many goods: feast and drink’” (Luke 12). “What more has a human being from all his labor under the sun?” (Ecclus. 1). “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (1 Cor. 15:32).

Fool, you store up treasure and do not know for whom. A rich man has coins but does not have life. Live while you live. Why ruin yourself before the time? You suffer from lethargy; you have forgotten yourself. Begin to know yourself, love yourself, possess yourself, be gracious toward yourself, and you will be blessed.

This, brothers, is that final error, worse than the earlier ones: that pool of misery, that mire of dregs, that joy whose end mourning will seize—and perhaps too late, when consolation will no longer be possible. Therefore that sublime Wisdom, which was pleased through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe in Him, mercifully calls those who have so miserably erred back to the way, saying:

“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” It is as though He said: “The way to joy is mourning; to consolation, desolation; to finding one’s soul, losing it; to possessing it, rejecting it; to loving it, hating it; to saving it, despising it. If you wish to know yourself and possess yourself, enter into yourself, and do not seek yourself outside yourself. You are one thing; what is yours is another; what is around you, another. The world is around you; your body is yours; you, inwardly, are made in the image and likeness of God.”

Return, therefore, transgressor, to your heart. Outwardly you are a beast, in the image of the world; hence man is called a lesser world. Inwardly you are a human being in the image of God, and therefore can be deified. Thus, when a human being returns into himself, like that younger prodigal son, where does he find himself except in a far country, in a land of unlikeness, in a foreign land, where he should sit and weep while remembering his father and homeland?

If he feeds swine and is hungry, does he not find in himself cause for mourning? If many hired servants in his father’s house abound in bread while he, a son, an exile, and a pauper, vainly seeks husks for his belly, does he not readily find tears for his eyes? (Luke 15.)

“O Adam, where are you?” Perhaps you are still beneath the shade, so that you do not see yourself; you have sewn together the leaves of folly to cover your shameful parts, seeing the things outside around you and the things that are yours—for such eyes have been opened to you. Look inward; see yourself. There are things there of which you should be more ashamed, things which should make you ashamed even of outward things.

Return inward, transgressor, to your soul. See it and mourn it: subject to vanity and iniquity, and, lest it be able to rise, to captivity. Go out to the flesh: see it and mourn it, subject to corruption and mortality, and, lest it be able to rise, to weakness.

And, beloved, not to make this too long: no one who enters into himself, knows himself, penetrates the abyss of his own misery, ignorance, difficulty, and passions, or measures his own conscience—no one, I say, is more readily moved to tears, stirred to mourning, and prompted to lamentation by the funeral of any near relation, where people easily mourn, than by his own funeral, especially since he is his own nearest relation because most inward. Why does he pity another who does not pity himself?

It is clear, then, brothers, that we are outside ourselves, turned backward rather than forward, and finally either forgetful of ourselves or utterly ignorant of ourselves whenever we laugh, jest, delight in idle pastimes, feed on stories, indulge in words that provoke laughter, gorge ourselves with feasting and drunkenness, and dissolve into the other softnesses of the body.

Therefore sober Wisdom has always taken care to invite people rather to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting: that is, to call back into himself the person who was outside himself, saying, “Blessed are those who mourn.” And elsewhere: “Woe to you who laugh now” (Luke 6). He who exhorts us to weep wept; we do not read that He laughed.

The sisters’ tears merited their brother’s resurrection. The sisters’ tears made the Resurrector weep (John 11), so that you too may raise yourself by weeping. Come then, brothers: a serious matter is at stake; what we have undertaken is manly. When Elijah entered the wilderness, he dismissed the boy (3 Kings 19). Let us take nothing childish with us, let nothing childish follow us, and above all let us never return to anything childish.

“The body,” says the Apostle, “is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of righteousness” (Rom. 8).
