Therefore let that which lives in us weep and pray, so that what lies dead and stinks may sometime rise again. “Unhappy man that I am,” says one mourning his own dead, “who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7.) But consolation follows: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ.”

O how great was the concern of the holy fathers and prophets of old, to whom nearly all things happened in a figure, to act and suffer, mourn their dead, and observe solemn days of mourning, often extending them to seven days because of the week of time! And we, for whom they wept, laugh with wanton spleen; we die—or have long since died and stink. We neglect and are neglected. There is no one who mourns his own pain before going where no one returns; no one who moves the gracious Jesus to tears.

O sisters, what are you doing? What are you doing, active soul—why do you not labor and weep? What are you doing, contemplative soul—why do you not pray and weep? Why is there not mourning everywhere, desolation everywhere, both at home within and in the street outside, until Jesus groans and, troubling Himself, says not so much to the dead man as to death: “Come forth,” so that this mortal thing may be swallowed up by life?

Finally, brothers, let us at last be corrected by the teaching of heavenly Wisdom. Whether busy or at leisure, let us be miserable and mourn. Let us weep before the Lord, who is gracious to forgive, turning to Him in fasting, weeping, and lamentation over ourselves, so that at last, according to the multitude of sorrows in our hearts, His consolations may gladden our souls. For blessed are those who mourn, not because they mourn, but because they shall be comforted. Mourning is the way; consolation is blessedness.

See how He who judges peoples in equity has corrected the world. For it is fitting that the gracious and wise God should correct the perverse, direct the corrected, and receive those who have been directed. Three and three: one set against another. Three things call from God to the world; three call back from the world to God.

“All that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, or worldly ambition” (1 John 2). The first takes a wife; the second tests oxen; the third buys an estate (Luke 14). Luxury, avarice, pride; carnal and worldly desires; and spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.

Therefore, having left the crowd and ascended the mountain, the disciples—as though leaping from lower things to higher, from outward things to inward, from bodily things to spiritual—hear: “Blessed are the poor, the meek, the contrite; for theirs are the kingdom of heaven, the earth, and themselves”: sufficiency, power, delight, kingdom, authority, peace—and all these inwardly, where the simple and gentle one remains at home, while the rough, shaggy man hunts in the field and is deprived of the prerogative of the firstborn (Gen. 25). That prerogative the Firstborn transferred to us in many brethren—He who reigns with the Father as the Only-begotten through all ages of ages. Amen.

**SERMON III. ON THE SAME FEAST, III.**

[Col. 1697C]

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. 5). Brothers, the book of Wisdom is written within and without. He speaks, as it were, outwardly when He corrects the perverse; inwardly when He directs the converted. Let us therefore hear to what end and in what manner He directs those who place blessedness neither in the body nor in bodily things, but in virtue of mind.

For virtue is the settled disposition of a well-ordered mind. The mind’s affections must therefore be composed, trained, and ordered through reason applied to what they ought to do and how they ought to do it, so that they may advance into virtues. They are the things that impose the name upon the outward act; they either fail into vices or advance into virtues.

When they are trained prudently, temperately, courageously, and justly, they rise into the virtues of prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice, which are called, as it were, the hinges or roots of all virtues. Since justice seems among these to hold a kind of cone or summit—the highest peak—it possesses, in an emphatic sense, the name of virtue itself. Blessed, therefore, are those who, choosing the shorter course, hunger and thirst for justice.

Just as some have thought that, from the rays of all the stars shining upward, a conspicuously bright circle is formed in the cone of the firmament, which they call the Milky Way (*Galaxia*), so likewise in the spiritual firmament justice is thought to stand forth from the radiance of all virtues. Accordingly, they call it a certain equality and measure in things—indeed, a definite limit beyond or short of which what is right cannot stand. For justice is that which makes all things equal, rendering to each what is his own.

The law of nature contains it; Scripture commands it; the Gospel completes it: not merely that we should not do to another what we do not wish to suffer from another, but that we should do to another whatever we wish to be done to ourselves. Therefore the person seeking blessedness should not be called away from this, but called back to it and directed by it, lest he remain with natural justice, like the philosopher, or establish the justice of the Law, like the Jew; but should submit himself to the righteousness of faith, like a Christian, and, as a humble accuser of himself, follow toward the prize of the heavenly calling in Christ Jesus.

For here, whatever justice is or can be, is partial; there is what is perfect. In the partial is the way; in the perfect is the fullness of blessedness. Therefore follow from part to part, as from virtue to virtue, until you grasp that for which you were grasped. Take care that justice never escape from hand, mouth, or heart; for one who holds fast to justice shall possess it full, perfect, and at rest—not now holding it with the labor of exercise, but being preserved by it with as much ease as happiness.

Therefore, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice.”

“The same Teacher says: ‘Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness’” (Matt. 6). See, O human being, what you ought to seek; see what your God asks of you: that you seek it from Him. For the nations inquire what they shall eat, drink, or wear. Your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. Cast all your care upon Him; keep the labor for yourself. He cares for you, if you do not lack care for justice.

Care for justice; seek it above all things and seek all things for its sake. Seek even the kingdom of God for its sake, not justice for the kingdom’s sake, lest you again begin to be a hireling and, understanding commerce, fail to enter into the powers of the Lord as one who is not mindful of His righteousness alone. The other things are additions, as though lacking substance and therefore unworthy of being sought. “The other things,” He says, “shall be added to you” (ibid.).

How many today, and with what effort, seek what should not be sought, while seeking less what should be sought, so that if someone, trusting the word of the Word and secure concerning such matters, devotes himself more earnestly to justice, he is laughed at and held in contempt! But what are we to make of the fact that He does not say “seek” justice but “hunger” for justice, except that we understand justice to be for the soul what food and drink are for the body?

Justice is provision for the journey, according to its partial state; it is the banquet in the homeland, where it is perfect; it is milk for little ones and food for mature people. Hence the Prophet’s imprecation: “As one weaned from his mother, so will You repay against my soul” (Ps. 130). Therefore blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, because they shall be filled.

Then there will be full blessedness, when there is full satiety; then I shall be fully filled with that of which I now enjoy a part in part. Now it is for healing; then for delight. Now it is for training, which at present seems to have some difficulty and sorrow; then for glory, when, by means of it, it has brought forth for those trained through it the most peaceful fruit of righteousness (Heb. 12). Thus here there appears, as it were, a flower of justice or of every virtue; there the fullness of the fruit is gathered.

Thus indeed, from beginning through progress to the perfection of justice, those must be directed who seek blessedness in virtue. Its beginning consists in doing no injury to anyone; its progress, in patiently bearing injury inflicted; its perfection, in doing good to all, if one can, or, if not, in willing to do so. Hence follows:

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” It is not safe, even for the righteous, to contend with the supremely righteous; for he cannot answer Him one thing out of a thousand (Job 9). It is foolish to meet with ten thousand the one who comes against one with twenty thousand (Luke 14). Therefore, while He is still far away, it is worthwhile to send an embassy of peace, saying: “Do not enter into judgment with Your servant, Lord” (Ps. 142)—even with Your servant who is righteous by Your testimony, whom You found according to Your heart, whom You anointed with Your holy oil—“for no living person shall be justified in Your sight” (ibid.).

What is that embassy of peace? Mercy. For mercy alone shall obtain mercy. It is the golden crown upon the righteous person’s head, marked with the sign of holiness. It is that through which the righteous person shall be saved, where he will scarcely be saved; for righteousness without mercy is cruel and shall not be saved. It is that which will not fear an evil report or a harsh word when a thousand fall at God’s side and ten thousand at His right, without mercy, though righteous.

Indeed, gladness and joy shall be given to his hearing when it is said: “Come, blessed of My Father; receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25). Why? “I was hungry, and you gave Me food” (ibid.), etc. It is as though He said: “Because you have shown mercy, you shall obtain mercy.” Therefore, blessed are the merciful, because they shall obtain mercy.

I perceive here the groans of some among you and discern your sighs. “Speak in your hearts; be contrite upon your beds” (Ps. 4). You say: “Woe to us! Mercy alone shall obtain mercy; it has been said, proved, and is true. What are we to do? According to what we do, so shall it be done to us.

“What, then, can we do for the hungry, thirsty, naked, homeless, sick, and imprisoned, when we have left all things, have nothing, and are sternly forbidden every work of private possession? Where, then, is that mercy which alone shall be praised, saved, and received?”

This is the sorrow renewed within you; your heart has grown warm—we know it. This fire has blazed up in your meditation. But you have become silent and humbled; and because of the gravity of silence and the good of quietness, which is the worship of justice, you are silent even concerning good things. Let us therefore speak—we to whom stewardship in speech has been entrusted, not our own speech but the Lord’s—and make known the conclusion of this matter, so that you may know what you lack.

David sings to the Lord of “mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100), but judgment comes after mercy; otherwise there is cause for weeping. For judgment without mercy is for the one who has not shown mercy. Mercy has two forms: giving and forgiving. Therefore it is said: “Give, and it shall be given to you; forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6). This is proportionate. Hence: “Forgive us, as we forgive” (Matt. 6); and: “With what measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. 7).

More than this: each form has a threefold division. In each there is mercy that is great, greater, and greatest; beginning, mature, and strong; measure answering measure. Whoever has stood in no degree of mercy shall stand in no place of forgiveness.

The first degree of mercy gives from what is one’s own. Thus the Savior exhorts: “Give alms, and all things are clean for you” (Luke 11). The second gives all one’s possessions, so that one may say: “Behold, we have left all things; and what shall there be for us?” (Matt. 10). The third gives oneself, so that one may be able to say: “Not only will I spend, but I will also be spent for your souls” (1 Cor. 12). No one has greater love than this. It repays the Lord as far as it can, receiving the cup from the Savior’s hand and, trusting in the Lord, calling upon His name.

Likewise, you have the same in the other form: debts are remitted, debts are forgiven, and one who owes his whole self is at times set free. Nor are these things done only outwardly and in bodily affairs. Injury too is forgiven; counsel is given; prayer is offered; a good example is shown; discipline is imposed; and there are countless other acts in both forms—sometimes indeed against the recipient’s will, often for his benefit, since benefits are often bestowed on the unwilling.

Where, I ask, is what you feared? If you have left all things, you shall judge even those who shall obtain mercy. If each day, beyond every possession you have left, you expend yourselves, preserving for yourselves neither control nor freedom of body or will, saying, “Abba, Father, not what I will, but what You will,” you shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel by comparison and authority.

Therefore blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Rightly, as the summit of this mountain, mercy is placed as the sum of the whole discipline of the active life; for there is nowhere farther for your feet to go. But if it pleases you to renew your strength so that you may fly into contemplation, take wings like eagles. Or, if that is too much for you, say: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly and be at rest?” (Ps. 54:7.)

For what more can a human being, among human beings in this mortal life—or life-giving death—do either for himself or for another than this: through voluntary contempt for the mammon of iniquity, to be moderate and steadfast in himself; through meekness, calm and serene toward others; through compunction, watchful and devout; through justice, wholly smooth and rounded in outward matters and within himself; through mercy, beneficent to many and well-disposed to all?

By love of poverty, let him reject the laughing world; by meekness, despise the angry; by the gift of compunction, withdraw into himself; by pursuing justice, submit himself to God; and by mercy, bind his neighbor to himself. Let him be content with little through love of poverty; hostile to no one through the balance of moderation; attentive to himself through the ardor of compunction; acceptable to God through the rigor of justice; and, through the sweetness of mercy, become all things to all people.

**SERMON IV. ON THE SAME FEAST, IV.**
“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). It is natural for everyone to wish to see what they love. Therefore, after the rest, this fittingly follows: “Blessed are the pure in heart,” etc. For only the pure in heart shall see God, and God will be seen only by a pure heart. But what, I ask, brothers, have we done so much, for so long, and with such effort, if we have not yet cleansed the heart? If we have cleansed it for virtue, it must be cleansed for truth; if we have cleansed it for loving, it must be cleansed for seeing. We have indeed healed the lame man, but the blind man must be enlightened. For Adam’s children suffer two penalties: ignorance and difficulty; one closes the eyes of reason, the other binds, as it were, the feet of the soul—its affection. Lamenting these common afflictions, the Prophet says: “My strength has forsaken me, and the light of my eyes is not with me” (Ps. XXXVII). Strength is formed in affection—or rather, affection itself is formed in strength. Truth is shown to reason, but reason is enlightened by truth itself in order to see it.

Thus, when the Lord cleanses the eyes of the mind for seeing truth, he enlightens, as it were, a blind man. Hence the discourse which follows concerning purity of heart is framed not in order that the heart may be cleansed of vices, which are classed under the name of perverse love or disordered affection, but of phantasms—those things absorbed through bodily senses and stirred within the imagination. Like little interposed clouds, they hide from us the brightness of the sun [Col. 1701C]; or, being entirely removed from that source of light, more familiar to us through the solar body itself, they shut it off from us, or at least blunt our keenness of vision.

For just as, if someone had the power of flying through this visible heaven, he would have to leave behind the earth and the waters said to be higher than the earth, and also those lighter substances which are suspended by wondrous art and become clouds; so surely one who raises the mind’s gaze to behold what is purely incorporeal must transcend not only every body and likeness of body, but also the whole shifting course of thoughts. Why are you surprised? When, by wakefulness of mind and purity of heart, you have passed beyond all the clouds we have mentioned—when every thought has fallen silent, or rather has been left behind [Col. 1701D]—there will at last appear a bright cloud, a radiant cloud: no longer turbid, no longer dense; no longer a cloud of ignorance, but of wisdom.

For there is darkness in light, and much more in great light: so that the light itself, when it enters into its own incomprehensibility, its own inaccessibility in which it dwells, and finally its own peace which surpasses all understanding, may be withdrawn from our eyes. Thereafter you may learn anything concerning it by revelation rather than contemplation, as the holy apostles did from the men who stood beside them in white garments (Acts I).

And just as this visible world rises upward in a fivefold distinction—earth, water, air, ether or firmament, and that highest heaven itself, called the empyrean—so there are five advances toward wisdom for the soul travelling in the world of its body: sense, imagination, reason, intellect, and intelligence. By sense it perceives bodies; by imagination, likenesses of bodies; by reason, the dimensions of bodies and the like—the first kind of incorporeal thing, indeed, which nevertheless requires body for its subsistence and therefore place and time. By intellect it rises above everything that is body or a created spirit belonging to body, which does not require body in order to subsist and therefore does not require place, but cannot exist without time, since its nature is mutable. By intelligence it immediately beholds, as far as is possible and permitted to a created nature, above which the Creator alone stands, that which alone is supremely and purely incorporeal: that which requires neither body in order to be, nor place in order to be somewhere, nor time in order to be sometime [Col. 1702B].

Therefore the heart must be cleansed, and one must withdraw far from all earth and water, in order to emerge into the serenity of reason. To discern the first incorporeal reality, it must rise into the solidity of intellect; to behold the second kind of incorporeality, it must ascend into the fiery brightness of intelligence, as onto Mount Tabor, “very high,” in order to see the third and invisible incorporeal reality. Thus it may behold with its eyes Jesus transfigured and glorified: his garments, because of the glory of the flesh, such as no fuller on earth can make (Mark IX); but his face, because of the simple form of incomprehensibility, incorporeality, and invisibility, in which he remains equal to the Father, it cannot endure. Rather, reason, intellect, and intelligence fall upon their faces; Peter, James, and John hear the Father but do not see him; and, descending, they tell no one what they have seen or heard [Col. 1702C].

For many wondrous, sweet, delightful things, full of light, beloved brothers, spiritual men see, taste, and feel in their prayer and contemplation, swiftly and as though in an ecstasy of mind—men who have their senses trained by practice. Once restored to themselves, they can in no way express these things, indeed can scarcely remember them. Behold from what things, to what degree, and for what end the heart must be cleansed, so that it may behold that which subsists without any body, is beautiful without quality, great without bulk, everywhere without place, and always without time. Otherwise it cannot see God at all. And therefore: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God”—here through a mirror and in an enigma; there, as he is.

This is that beautiful one, clear-sighted in her eyes, whom that fugitive and exile chose and desired for himself; for whom he served seven years, scorched by heat and frost; and the whole period seemed brief and light to him because of the hope in which he rejoiced (Gen. XXIX). She is the one whose name, because of simplicity, is interpreted “sheep” or “the beginning of sight.” May it be granted to me, brothers, I beg you, to investigate in every thing, from the condition in which it is perceived, its property and differences, nature and form, cause and bare essence, until I see its efficient, formal, and final principle: that is, whence it is and how; whence it comes and why.

For all things possess in themselves nature, form, and use; number, measure, and weight. But whence these things come, and what is their principle, I ask, and do not easily find. For this reason I gladly serve and endure everything. But according to the custom of the homeland, bleary-eyed and laborious Leah is placed before me, though I did not seek her. “It is not our custom,” says Laban, “that the younger should marry first or be given to a husband” (Gen. XXIX). She is the soul’s affection, or concupiscibility, of which we have already spoken at such length: it must first be led, composed, and ordered by rational perception, and always left at home, so that in the heat of the day the man himself may safely go out to meet the three angels, like Abraham, leaving Sarah at home (Gen. XVIII).

For, to speak more plainly, no one can be fully and perfectly spiritual, nor gird himself fittingly for the leisure of contemplation, nor safely leave the tent, unless he has first left it emptied of vices—that is, of every perverse and disordered love—adorned and ordered by good habits, endowed and fortified with virtues. Otherwise, if the adulterous and unclean spirit should return, lying in wait for the lawful marriage-bed, and find the house swept and adorned but empty of virtues, it may burst in or creep in, occupy the house, fortify itself with seven other attendants more wicked than itself, corrupt affection itself, the mistress of the house, and make the last state of this spiritual person worse than the first: for he began in the Spirit and is consummated—or rather consumed—in the flesh [Col. 1703B].

Therefore, to put it briefly, affection must be trained discreetly, soberly, courageously, and justly, so that there may be in it the settled disposition of a well-ordered mind, which is called virtue, and so that it may be formed and ordered in charity, as we read: “He ordered charity in me” (Cant. II). He who desires to be spiritual must first be so in affection rather than reason, and in conduct rather than meditation. Let him stand on his feet in order to rise into flight; and because he cannot always fly, let him return to his feet lest he fall headlong. That is, let not affection fall—the affection which manages the house, all its furnishings, and the care of the entire household.

It is anxious and troubled about all things; it assigns a name and office to every work and movement of the members. If it is good and ordered, what it produces is good and ordered; but if it is evil, evil; if perverse, perverse; if corrupt, corrupt. Therefore, as action is subject to will, so let will or affection be subject to reason; and reason to wisdom and the Word of God. Thus the man may be wise and, with unveiled face, behold God as though he were God’s own image; and he may have no veil over his head, since he is immediately subject to God alone.

But let the woman be prudent and not contentious, covering her head, subject to the man whose image she is, so that there may be peace in her house; that she may deserve to be blessed and multiplied exceedingly, and that even her cattle may not diminish. Let there be sons and daughters, the fruits of spiritual meditations; a household exceedingly rich in virtues; fruitful sheep, of sweet and simple manners; beasts of burden and oxen, of bodily exercises. Let the whole house be ordered, enriched, and made fruitful by the wise and prudent; and finally let it be kept, as it is written: “That he might work it and keep it” (Gen. III). Thus let all that they possess be in peace [Col. 1704A].

And once they have “made peace their borders”: that is, between the man and his Lord—reason, mind, and God; between the woman and her man—that is, the affection of the soul and the rational mind; and finally between that masculine woman and the one owing obedience to her rule—then they may consequently hear: “Blessed are the peacemakers,” etc. But, brothers, await from another beginning what the Lord of hosts may deign to reveal concerning this final and highest virtue. Meanwhile, today let us rest in Christ. Amen.

## SERMON V. ON THE SAME FEAST, V

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. V [Col. 1704B]). What more does a servant seek than to become a son? Indeed, my brothers, who would even dare faintly to imagine this unless the very goodness of God both allowed and promised it? We were ungodly, and therefore enemies, making no provision for salvation and hoping for nothing. Yet he came freely and anticipated us when we did not expect him—Christ, who truly loved us first and died for the ungodly.

This is what the Apostle says in astonishment: Why did Christ die for the ungodly, when no one is willing to die for a righteous man? (Rom. V). For perhaps someone may dare to die for a good man—that is, for a friend and one advantageous to himself (ibid.)—as is told of Pylades and Orestes. But we were enemies, as follows: “If, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more now,” etc. (ibid.). What is “much more”? Truly, that through the Son himself we may receive sonship. Observe the steps; distinguish the advances.

We were enemies, slaves of sin, free from righteousness. The Son set us free, and we were truly made free from sin and the devil, and made servants of righteousness. This is the first step. Desiring it, someone cries: “O Lord, deliver my soul” (Ps. CXIV); and, having obtained it, rejoices: “O Lord, because you have delivered me, I am your servant, and the son—not yet, I say, your son—but of your handmaid. You have broken my bonds” (Ps. CXV), by which the devil had bound me like a four-footed beast, so that I was free neither to go out nor to work, as it is written: “Man goes forth to his work and to his labour” (Ps. CIII).

Now I move my foot; now I stretch out my withered hand. Changed from perversion, I have become from an enemy a servant, so that I may do good to you—wholly useless though I am, since you do not need my good things, yet useful to myself, since I work out my salvation with fear and trembling. “When you have done all things well,” he says, “say: We are unprofitable servants,” etc. (Luke XVII). Behold: one who does evil, or does good badly, is counted an enemy; one who does everything well is not yet called a friend, but a servant [Col. 1704D].

Thus doing good, performing the works of virtue, righteousness, and mercy, belongs to a servant; but a friend shares in secrets and knows counsels. Therefore, at the second step, those once made servants from enemies hear: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends,” etc. (John XV). What do we still await? That at the third step, from friends, we may become brothers of Christ, children of God, and therefore finally his heirs—for if children, then heirs. “Blessed,” he says, “are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.”

To the pure in heart, through contemplation, all things which the Son heard from the Father have been made known; and they too shall be called children because of peacemaking. What is this peace, or peacemaking, most beloved brothers—this peace so worthy of love, so worthy of desire, so dear, I ask you through the charity of Christ—which is set above every degree of virtue, placed above every merit, has occupied the citadel of all things, and bestows the loftiest and greatest of all beatitudes?

Let us ask human beings; let us ask the holy angels who attend upon us and our affairs. Above all, since we need this wisdom in every way, let us ask him who gives abundantly and does not reproach. Let us seek by praying, meditating, and reading, never failing. For if we seek while seeking, we shall surely find, because of the truth itself which we seek, which says: “Seek, and you shall find” (Luke XI). This is the treasure hidden in a field; this is the most precious pearl, to be sought most diligently, bought most dearly, possessed most eagerly. This is the mountain of mountains, upon which the Son alone is naturally with the Father. But lest he should be the sole heir, he deigned to adopt brothers.

Therefore we must seek with the greatest care whatever it is through which we may become brothers of Christ and children of God: heirs indeed of God, but coheirs with Christ. And behold, one of the seraphim cries out, in whom is the fullness of love—and perhaps the very thing for which we seek: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John I). Did he say, “As many as saw him”? The pure in heart see, but the peacemakers receive. Here perhaps—indeed, truly here—is the field in which the treasure is hidden. “As many as received him,” he says (John I). “I came in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me” (John V).

What, then, is it to receive the Word of God? It is wretched not to see God’s Word; most wretched to see it and not receive it. How and where is this Word to be received? There are two parts of household stewardship: working and keeping. Hence it was said of the first man: “That he might work it and keep it” (Gen. III). The first belongs to the man, the second to the woman. It belongs to him to go outside to his labour—for man is born for labour—and to carry home what he has acquired. It belongs to her to remain at home, wait for her husband, and depend upon his return; to prepare for use what he has brought, so that when he comes they may feast and drink together and delight in gladness [Col. 1705D].

Many labour greatly and make little progress: in the sweat of their face they gather riches and put them into a bag with holes; they fall to the ground and are lost.

These matters must be stated more plainly. Have you understood everything? You know well enough, and have already heard above, who that man is of whom we intend to speak; who the woman is; what his labour is; and what the banquet and the remaining matters mentioned are. For many, through keenness of intellect, earnest application of mind, liveliness of understanding, and familiarity with the very subject, investigate deep things and penetrate lofty ones, so that what may be known of God is manifest in them, as also his eternal power and divinity, leaving them without excuse. But because they do not seek wisdom itself for its own sake, they become vain in their thoughts; they delight in empty glory among men, in reputation, or even in gain. Though they have seen, they do not receive it in the affection and love of the heart which comes from the Father. Instead, in the desire of their souls they draw in wind; pursuing vanity, they become vain. What they have acquired above, they hurl down below; prodigally and adulterously they squander every portion of their precious substance.

Consequently, they have no peace at all with their lawful marriage-bed, and so they are unworthy to hear: “Blessed are the peacemakers,” etc. These are those who, lifted high, admire themselves; looking down, they suffer vertigo, and, having nothing to which they may cling, fall headlong. For by a lofty judgment a spirit of dizziness is mingled with them and makes them err, as a drunken and vomiting man errs. For they vomit outwardly that by which they ought to live inwardly. Their foolish heart is darkened, and while boasting of their wisdom they appear foolish, loving darkness, by which they may be further darkened, more than the light by which they had been enlightened [Col. 1706B].

Thus, brothers, that holy mind truly devoted to God, which had entered into the sanctuary of God and understood their latter end, having served, like holy Jacob, at the beginning, and having understood in the last things, considered what was laid up for it in heaven. Rebuking itself because it had desired anything on earth, it says, when its flesh—and the heart with which it had desired—is now spent: “God [is] the meditation of my heart, and my portion” (Ps. LXXII): the one whom I await, toward whom I stretch, in whom I delight, where I set my end, for whom I labour, so that I may carry God himself home to ordered affection, that she may dine with me and I with her.

He is my meditation; he is my delight. I seek him above myself for his own sake. By him, from him, I feed inwardly. He is the field in which I labour; he is the fruit for which I labour. He is my cause; he is my effect; he is my beginning; he is my end without end, forever. “And God,” he says, “is my portion forever” (ibid.). For those who withdraw themselves from you, so as not to hear you, or, if they hear, not to see; or, if they see, not to receive; but who hear, seek, see, and preach you not for your own sake, while committing adultery with other things apart from you, shall perish. For in your hidden judgment you have already destroyed all who commit adultery apart from you. Therefore, he says, “It is good for me always to cling to God,” so that through him I may ascend to him and, when I have ascended, may not fall away from him. And because we do not yet rest by sight but walk by hope, he says, “to place my hope in the Lord God.”

Behold, my brothers, in what field, with what hands, and in what hope you ought to labour—you who have entered not only the solitude of place but also of spirit, or even of God, where he left the ninety-nine sheep. Behold where you ought to bring the fruits you have received, and where and with whom you are to feast and drink: the bread of life and understanding, and the water of saving wisdom. For the labouring farmer must receive a share from the firstfruits of his crop. “For who plants a vineyard and does not drink its wine?” (I Cor. IX, 7).

Keeping this always in view and in all things, take the greatest care, beloved, that in this secret marriage of yours the man neither grow sluggish in idleness, nor labour for another, nor acquire anything except for his lawful wife; and that the wife, without consulting her husband, does not dispose even a small thing among those subject to her. If you strive to preserve order, preserve it first inwardly in your own dwelling. Let every bodily exercise, which profits little, be subject to devout affection; every affection and will to reason; and the rational mind to the Word of God, so that it may never depart from his teaching, but may judge, moderate, and order all things below according to what it has heard and seen there.

Let it learn there what it is to teach, saying: “My teaching is not mine, but his to whom I am subject.” Let it always cling to him with untiring love; let it delight to look toward him, saying: “It is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII). For “he who clings to God is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17). If he who clings to the flesh in that emasculating and enervating pleasure, in which the spirit itself is almost wholly made flesh, becomes one flesh—so that those who cling carnally are no longer two, but one flesh—then surely he who, with a masculine heart and manly mind, not with a lesser love but with a chaster and purer love, pours his whole self into God, retaining and reserving nothing of himself for himself, and clings to him after putting off himself, becomes one spirit with him.

Is that plague more powerful to harm, to enslave, to swallow up, and to transform than this virtue is to help, to free, to unite, and to change? The almighty Word says—he whose power is present when he wills, indeed whose power and will are identical—“Father, I will that, as I and you are one, so they also may be one with us” (John XVII). O pious will! A will of God worthy of God; a will full of grace and charity; a will full of truth, because it belongs to Truth: “As I and you are one, so they also may be one with us.”

Behold to what the servant is raised, to what the enemy is reconciled: from enemy to servant, from servant to friend, from friend to son, from son to heir, from heir to one—indeed, one even with the inheritance itself. Thus, just as he cannot be deprived of himself, so neither can he be deprived of the inheritance which is God himself. Therefore he says: “God is my portion forever.” Behold: “that they may be one with us” [Col. 1707D].

O one One! O One, unite us into one! O One altogether necessary! The One for whose sake all the sweet things of this world must be abandoned, bitter things endured, shameful things avoided, and honourable things embraced. The One toward whom people run in many ways, in whom they stand, rest, and delight in unity. Oh, if boldness were granted to words! If it were permitted to compare the shameful with the beautiful, the dishonourable with the chaste, the highest spirit with the lowest flesh! Never is this holy, spiritual, divine union shown better, more closely, or more expressively amid these shadows than by a likeness drawn from its contrary. For nothing is more unlike truth, and nothing more like it by comparison.

For just as, at the moment of carnal intercourse, the entire spirit passes into flesh, emasculated, powerless over itself, forgetful of itself, with every care and anxiety put to sleep, so that meanwhile the greedy person thinks nothing of money, the ambitious person of honour, the vainglorious person of glory, nor rejoices, grieves, desires, or fears outside that one and only pleasure by which he is absorbed; so surely—indeed, far more—the whole spirit, soberly drunk and vigorously enervated, will be all-powerful in God and rejoice in all things when, through the fullest truth, virtue, and charity, it clings to him who will be all things in all his own.

It will behold him for his own sake; it will love him for his own sake, so that it delights to see nothing else in all things but him whom it loves, and to see nothing else but him whom it sees. By vision it will be enlightened for loving; by love it will be inflamed for vision. Thus, while it is always aided from one by the other, it will follow the circuit of infinite blessedness, upon which none but the godly shall ever walk: worthy to see and know because it loves; longing to love because it knows. For he cannot be seen and not loved; nor ought he to be withheld from one who loves. “And I,” he says, “will show myself to him” (John XIV).

These, beloved, are those wings of the blessed seraphim by which they always fly toward the One seated upon the throne (Isa. VI), upon whom all the angels desire to gaze (I Pet. I): always gazing because of desire, always desiring because of their gaze. Therefore, brothers, to bring at last this lengthy discourse to a close, I set down this as the sum of all religion and the aim especially of spiritual exercise. For just as cherubim and seraphim are known as the highest orders in the heaven of the celestial angels, so in our heaven—that is, in the soul of the righteous, in which wisdom sits—knowledge and love, like cherubim and seraphim, hold chief authority. There too the same orders and ranks ought and can exist as virtues, like their own angels, lest our heaven be without angels; and every troop of virtues ought to be subject and serve them. If it has not escaped you that you once heard this from us, you may remember it.

Therefore, I beseech you, my brothers, let your labour strive, your solitude grow austere, and your attention keep watch—whether in bodily exercise or spiritual study—for no other purpose than this: that, after vices have been expelled, habits ordered, and virtues put on, you may, living soberly, justly, and devoutly in this age as good active persons, cleanse your hearts for contemplation and kindle them for loving in the blessed hope of the divine vision. In it, full peacemaking will bestow the noble sonship of God. May he who lives and reigns as God through endless ages of ages deign to grant it to us through the Son in the Holy Spirit. Amen.

## SERMON VI. ON THE SAME FEAST, VI

“Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up onto the mountain.” Today, beloved, we see the heavenly physician opening the alabaster jars of ointment which he brought with him from the bosom of the Father, in order to cure the wounds of him who, going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers. This man who goes down is the common Adam; because he went down willingly and foolishly, he justly fell among robbers. For Adam could have remained, if he had wished, in the peace in which he was created—rich in all things and secure from every assault.

Thus he did not fall under compulsion; but because he chose to go down, and because he went down, he fell into violent hands, so that he might suffer what he did not wish—he who would have suffered nothing had he wished to remain. These robbers are malicious spirits, and also the manifold passions of our body and spirit; wounded among them, he himself laments thus: “How many great and evil tribulations you have shown me!” (Ps. LXX). He suffers these unwillingly; yet he deservedly fell among robbers, and through them into pains, because, as has been said, he went down willingly.

For he would never have been permitted by the merciful Lord to fall into such cruel hands unless, because of an inward and inborn vice, he had first forsaken, within himself, the one to whom he ought to have kept his strength. While he forsook, therefore, he went down; and because he went down, he was forsaken by him who remained. Forsaken, then, he fell into the hands of the one to whom he was given over—that is, the devil—who spared him in nothing, but stripped him, wounded him, and left him half alive. He left him wholly dead, half alive; for if half alive, certainly half dead. For human life is mortal in such a way that there is also a living death; but the devil’s death is wholly mortal, possessing nothing through which it may be restored to life, just as an angel’s life is wholly living, possessing nothing through which it may incline toward death [Col. 1709C].

Thus man is left half alive: alive, yet of himself inevitably tending toward death; dead, yet still capable of being repaired by medicine. “Having inflicted wounds,” he says (Luke X). But let us see which wounds—although we examine them better by experiencing them than by discussing them. Apart from bodily infirmities and wounds, which have multiplied beyond number, the wounds by which the human race was corrupted in the first parent are seven in kind, many in species, and infinite in number. For there are seven general and original corruptions from which every perverse generation and viperous offspring of vices or sins is born. They are roots of bitterness springing up, kindlings of sin, dens of demons, cradles of death.

The first in descent, in number and vice, in order and malice, is pride. Pride is love of one’s own excellence. By robbery, as far as lies in it, it makes itself equal to the Most High; and because it disdains to give another the glory of its works, envy, its firstborn offspring, is born from it. For every arrogant person must be envious. Envy is hatred of another’s happiness.

Anger follows envy—that is, a disturbance of the mind. For you cannot be serene toward one whom you envy. If anger has lodged more deeply in the mind, it gives birth to sadness; and sadness, swallowing up the disturbed person too immoderately, plunges him into the abyss of despair. There avarice, that is, love of the world, receives him as one deprived of a better hope, gently and smoothly consoles him, and then hands him over to gluttony, saying: “Soul, you have many goods stored up for many years; feast and drink” (Luke XII). Gluttony swallows him and ejects him through lust, so that from a most precious human being he becomes most vile dung. Thus is fulfilled in him what is said: “Those who were nourished in saffron have embraced dung”; and again: “They have rotted like beasts in their dung” (Lam. IV).

Behold how the man who did not understand his honour is compared not merely to irrational beasts but to unclean ones, and made like them. Pride stripped him of God; envy, of his neighbour; anger, of himself. Sadness cast him to the ground; avarice bound him; gluttony devoured him; lust turned him to dung. These are the powers which wage war against the soul and lie in wait for the wretched one: the robbers who beset the way of one descending, into whose hands falls the person who descends—flesh, world, and devil. From the flesh come want and excess, lust and gluttony; from the world, avarice and sadness; from the devil, anger, envy, and pride. These are carnal and worldly desires and spiritual wickednesses in heavenly places.

Through pride the angel fell; through envy he cast down man; through Cain anger first committed fratricide (Gen. III and IV); sadness first drove that fratricide into despair; through the despairing man himself avarice first founded the earthly city. Gluttony and lust did so because:

> Without Ceres and Bacchus [Liber], Venus grows cold.  
> *(Terence, Eunuchus, act IV, scene V, verse 5.)*

They disturbed the order of distinction between the sons of God and the daughters of men, compelled God himself to repent that he had made man, brought in the flood, and destroyed man. For one who is such is erased from humanity and changed into a beast—except that the beast is so by nature, whereas he becomes so by vice.

These are the wounds of the common Adam, natural or original corruptions, because they are born with us in our origin and rise with us together with our nature. Our father the Amorite and our mother the Hittite have forsaken us. One born in this condition is seed of Canaan, not Judah. One born in this condition is not washed with water, salted with salt, wrapped in swaddling-clothes, nor is his navel cut. For there is no one to show him any mercy, though such persons need it. Behold the sort of parents we have had on earth—earthly parents from the earth: parents of guilt or punishment before they are parents of nature; parents of death before life; sowing what they possess, giving what they find, begetting what they are. Everywhere, such as the father is, such is the son.

And just as they reap from diverse sources, so they sow diverse things: nature from God, guilt from the devil. Hence we too must derive our stock from both, so that we are children of God and children of the devil: good from the Good, well made; evil from evil, badly corrupted. From the one source we have nature, through which we are something; from the other we draw guilt, by which we have been made nothing. And this is the whole work of the devil: our being made nothing. The Son of God came to dissolve it, and to free and save something that is ours. For he came to repair what is his, destroy what is alien, bind back to himself what is his—whence *religio*, “religion,” is so called—loose what is alien, and finally separate what is his from what is alien, and what is alien from what is his, as the precious from the vile. “If you separate the precious from the vile,” says the Prophet, “you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. XV). Christ, therefore, is the mouth of his Father.

Let us therefore hear how he came equipped and prepared for this task. “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse,” says Isaiah—for it could not come from the branch—“and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. II). Now I begin to hope; for the flower is understood as the hope of fruit. “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him.” O what a good fruit! Rightly is the spirit of wisdom and understanding, and so forth, conceived at Nazareth and born at Bethlehem. O soul fruitful in virtues, full of graces! Seven for seven, and seven against seven: seven graces in Christ, seven concupiscences in Adam; seven wounds, seven medicines; everywhere one against one.

In Adam, on one side nature, on the other guilt—yet nature and guilt together. For just as, if wine and water should spring together from one fountain, though through separate veins, neither could be drawn except as wine mixed with water and water mixed with wine; so, O children of Adam, our wine is mixed with water, so that natural guilt and culpable nature arise together. You are not first good from the Good through nature, and afterwards evil from evil through guilt; but, as human is begotten from human, so sinner is begotten from sinner. No good nature in us exists without evil guilt, nor can evil guilt exist except in a good nature.

Therefore, brothers, consider three things in us—or attend to yourselves in these three: carnal concupiscence, animal perception, and rational mind. These are, in the paradise of each one, the man, the woman, and the serpent. Concupiscence stirs; animality takes delight; the rational will consents; and sin is completed, and the sinner is cast out of himself. This, brothers, still takes place today, from a human being within a human being, when he sins. For a person is tempted by one of those seven concupiscences; animal perception is delighted, and sin is conceived; rational will consents, and sin is brought to birth. But when sin has been consummated—that is, born through the full consent of the will—it kills both parents and thus produces death. For on whatever day they eat the forbidden thing, they shall die by death.

“Each one,” says the Apostle (Jas. I), “is tempted, drawn away and enticed by his own concupiscence; and concupiscence, when it has conceived”—that is, through delight—“brings forth sin. But sin, when it has been consummated through consent, brings forth death” to the one consenting and the one taking delight, namely, to the man and woman. This is that crooked and perverse generation, wholly sprouting upward from the root of bitterness, wholly from viperous and poisonous seed, and continually flowing forth. Without it no child of Adam is conceived, born, lives, or dies. Hence he is conceived in filth, born in pain, lives in labour, and does not die without danger. Therefore medicine was necessary; one who was ill had need of a physician.

Let the Samaritan therefore come; let him bring the wine of compunction and the oil of consolation: the wine of repentance, [Col. 1712A] the oil of pardon. Let the physician enter to the sick man—indeed, let him enter into the sick man. Let him assume wholly what belongs to nature, cast out wholly what belongs to fault, endure wholly whatever punishment is expedient, and impart wholly what belongs to grace; so that nature, at last aided by grace, may conquer concupiscence, which by itself it could not conquer. “Woe to him that is alone; for if he fall, there is none to lift him up” (Eccles. 4:10).

When, therefore, the Lord entered into man, man necessarily put on God. “As many of you as have been baptized have put on Christ”; as many as have put on Christ have put off Adam, so that concupiscence may now assail from without while grace assists within; and grace may, through this regeneration, be natural, just as fault is original through generation. Within, let the image of God shine with the newness of truth; without, let the old likeness of sinful flesh still lie foul. Thus, on this side is concupiscence, on that side grace; while nature now stands between them. Concupiscence pricks, tempts, and suggests: if nature takes delight, it conceives; if it consents, it gives birth; if it gives birth, it dies. For the viper’s offspring is not born unless its parent is ruptured. Grace too suggests and exhorts nature, puts forward counsel, and offers help: if nature takes delight, it conceives; if it consents, it gives birth to virtue. Virtue, once acquired, gives birth to blessedness, so that it ought now to hear: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” etc. (Matt. 5:3). Poverty of spirit is virtue; the kingdom of heaven is blessedness: this is the offspring, that the parent.

Grace, by which nature conceives through delight and gives birth through consent to this virtue, is the spirit [Col. 1712C] of fear. “Through thy fear,” he says, “we have conceived and brought forth a spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26:18). And the beginning of ascent to wisdom is the fear of the Lord.

There are, therefore, seven general charisms—graces, or gifts of the Spirit—now made original through Christ: many in species, infinite in number. Each of them, through the consent which it first creates, begets and forms in the soul its own virtues; and these virtues merit their distinct blessednesses. Thus everywhere and in all things the gift, called grace because it is freely given, is from God; virtue and merit come from the gift; the reward, which is blessedness, corresponds to merit; and God himself is in the reward. From God, therefore, comes every gift; from God’s gift, every merit; for merit, the reward—and God himself: so that all things may be from him, through him, and [Col. 1712D] in him.

Grace is that which goes before, that we may will; which assists, lest we will in vain; which receives us, because we have not willed in vain. There are therefore seven graces against seven corruptions; from these come seven virtues and seven blessednesses, against seven sins and their seven punishments. They are all general, and each is opposed to its corresponding counterpart. In the Lord’s Prayer there are likewise seven petitions, each requesting one of the graces. For he who asks receives, and he who receives conquers. Thus, while life is lived on earth in this seven-day cycle, Christian warfare has its equipment in seven sets of seven.

How, however, some are born from others and contraries are opposed to contraries, we leave, brethren, for your meditation to compare. For there is nothing, either here or in the future, good, evil, miserable, or blessed, that is not born from one side or the other and contained under this general classification. Yet, in assigning and distinguishing sins, we suffer from a poverty of names, since they arise from vices; and we confuse very many things, though they are different realities, under the same terms—and still more so in distinguishing punishments. But blessed be God, who has made us richer in the better part through Jesus Christ our Lord.

## SERMON VII. ON THE FIRST SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF EPIPHANY

“When Jesus had become twelve years old,” etc. (John 2) [the citation is printed thus].

What the Lord Jesus did in his childhood before the time of baptism, canonical reading teaches us little about; and, if I remember correctly, it teaches us only this. Therefore it is the more to be wondered at what this means, and to be asked why this alone is recorded. For it is madness to suppose that through so great—indeed, through the whole—course of his life he did nothing and lived idly.

Yet whatever he did, and however he did it, I judge that the present reading teaches us: namely, that he acted wisely and kindly. For wisdom is most clearly denoted by the number ten, and charity by the number two. It is superfluous to prove what is plain. Hence the holy apostles also—lamps of the world, shining with the radiance of wisdom and burning with the ardour of charity—are adequately represented under this number. Thus this passage signifies that on this occasion he acted so, and on other occasions did all things likewise. For what the sacred Gospels disclose concerning his infancy contains rather what was done to him or concerning him than what he himself did.

“According to the custom,” [Col. 1713C] etc. It belongs to duty, if you do not wish to give or suffer scandal, to follow the customs of those among whom you live, especially when they are not to be condemned; otherwise, either change the people among whom you live or follow their customs. It is also a matter of discipline for a child to follow and obey parents. But his remaining behind after his parents is a sure sacrament and a sweet mystery.

They go one day’s journey without Jesus, but with that man of whom no infant upon earth is without defilement. Jesus, however, holy and separated from sinners, holy as from holiness itself, was conceived not sanctified but holy. He did not make the journey of that day. When his parents therefore went down, Jesus remained alone. “All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none that doeth good,” save this one alone. He never turned aside, and therefore did not go down with the others. He was always useful; he alone did good.

But whence did his parents go down, and where did they leave him? Surely from Jerusalem—from that very place whence that foolish and wretched man went down who fell among thieves. O Adam, would that you had remained in your peace and vision, where creative grace had placed you; and that we, all your children, were not now sitting blind and begging beside the road near Jericho!

We have followed, brethren, our father through natural necessity; we follow him daily by culpable will. No one stands. No one remains. No one remains in that which he received or in which he was created, except Jesus alone. We go down, slip, and fall headlong; and unless we had returned to him alone who remained, our soul would almost [Col. 1714A] already have dwelt in hell.

But if, troubled and terrified because we walk in this world without God, we say that our foot has gone astray, and retrace our steps with corrected gait toward Jesus, his mercy will undoubtedly help us to find him—at least after three days: departure through fault, return through repentance, and searching through diligence. The Temple, or Jerusalem, is rational nature, established and created so that it might see God, who is true peace, and become a temple in which he might dwell. We ascended to this at our first movement, coming from non-being into being, from nothing into something. From it we return through fault, declining from being to non-being, from something to nothing. For if sin is nothing, it certainly does not exist; and consequently he who inclines himself toward [Col. 1714B] sin returns toward nothing and non-being.

Man too, taken from the earth by nature and raised above it by creative grace, returns to it through fault. Hence it is said to him: “Thou art earth, and unto earth thou shalt go” (Gen. 3). From there he returns through repentance—but fruitful repentance, if he finds Jesus. Jesus alone, however, remained in that which he was made; therefore he did not descend from the Temple, except that above he advanced in wisdom and age (Luke 2), while below he wholly did not fail. His holy and healing flesh never incurred imbalance through intemperance, nor descended into corruption through defilement. Conceived of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin, it was born holy and virgin, lived holy and virgin, and endured death holy and virgin.

Blessed also was that soul united to flesh which did not cleave to flesh. It could love flesh by the law of natural affection—as Adam laments, “My soul cleaveth to the pavement” (Ps. 118 [119])—but it could not be glued to flesh by the sticky substance of concupiscence. Created good by the Good One, and joined to good flesh, likewise created good by the Good One, it preserved in each its good condition so that, though they came from non-being into being, since they are creatures, they never looked back but advanced greatly toward what lies ahead.

“For who shall boast that he hath a chaste heart?” Who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord Jesus, or be like God among the sons of God? John the Baptist was a cloud, and Jeremiah too was a cloud. Both were born holy, but both were sanctified: “Before,” he says, “thou camest forth from the womb, I sanctified thee” (Jer. 1:5). Both were born holy; but were they holy when conceived? Where then, and from what, were they sanctified? And if sanctified, they were surely at some time defiled. Where, and from what, was this? But who is so competent for these questions?

The Good One creates good flesh and infuses a good soul; yet I find each evil, each corrupt, such that each needs sanctification and neither is good before being evil, sound before being corrupt—lest corruption be proved not original but actual.

Neither, therefore, remains even for an instant in the condition in which it is called into being; but through the vice of origin it returns to non-being as it begins to be. Thus, wonderfully and miserably, it begins not to be before it begins to be; returns before it comes; descends before it ascends. Nor does the soul miserably begin to give life before it gives death, so that flesh may mortify that by which it is enlivened, and the soul enliven that by which it is mortified.

Here meet those mournful marriages: the seven husbands and the seven-times murderous daughter of Raguel, whom Tobias, son of Tobit, could take without danger because he had as companion—indeed, as guide—an angel stronger than the demon (Tob. 8). Tobit and Tobias, father and son, old and new, blind and seeing: Adam and Adam, first and second, father and son, old and new, blind and seeing, man and son of man. But speech concerning “man” or “son of man” is sometimes made according to the flesh, sometimes according to the soul, and sometimes according to both.

Here, therefore, Tobias signifies the soul of the Son of Man; Sarah signifies human flesh generally; and the angel, Tobias’s guide and companion, signifies the Lord, the Word of God. To the soul that he once assumed, he wisely supplied guidance, faithfully companionship, strongly assistance, and prudently counsel. The seven husbands, married rather to death than to the woman, signify all souls except Christ’s soul: souls united to death before they were united to flesh; united to death on account of flesh, and separated from flesh on account of death. The suffocating demon signifies that natural and original concupiscence which is not cast out of Raguel’s house and Sarah’s chamber unless one stronger comes upon it.

When, therefore, the stronger power of the Word comes upon it, the strong one is cast out, put to flight, and bound; his vessels—that is, the natural faculties which were held captive—are plundered. Captivity is led captive; the bridal chamber is cleansed; the house is freed; [Col. 1715C] Sarah is taken without danger; the father marvels, recognizes the mystery, thanks the angel, prepares a feast, and invites the neighbours. These things are full of mysteries and overflow with sacraments.

While the angel celebrates Tobias’s marriage, he departs, so that Tobias may appear as a true man, being born, crying, and nursing—not speaking—as a bridegroom. But after a time he returns not empty-handed and not without the written bond for the precious deposit, so that in some respects he who is man may be revealed as God. Therefore, on that day of departure and forgetfulness, the child Jesus is sought in vain among relatives and acquaintances. He is left in the Temple and remains in Jerusalem; he is found in the Temple by one who returns and seeks.

O blessed soul that never forgets or leaves the child Jesus! More blessed is the soul that always meditates upon the great Jesus; most blessed, the soul that can always contemplate the immeasurable Jesus. Scripture says: “The son of Abraham”—whose name is interpreted “laughter”—“grew until he became very great” (Gen. 26). Let the Son of God, brother, who is already formed in you, grow in you until he becomes immeasurable to you, and becomes from you for you laughter, exultation, and full joy, which no one shall take from you.

But if you have at some time forgotten him or carelessly left him, begin from the memory of him, that you may come to his presence. Memory drives away forgetfulness, brings repentance; repentance brings conversion; conversion corrects departure, so that you may return as far as you had departed, as the Seer cries: “Return, as deeply as you had withdrawn” (Isa. 31). Yet you return in vain from your evil way [Col. 1716A] on which you walked without Jesus, unless you seek him in conversion. For diligence in seeking merits the joy of finding. “If you seek,” Isaiah says, “seek” (Isa. 21)—that is, diligently—and you shall find. “And they found him in the Temple,” etc.

But here we must be silent, so that we may rise to the small remainder of our day’s labour. Perhaps Jesus too will be found there. For Isaac—that is, laughter—was also found outside by Sarah. May he grant you to find him both without and within, he who lives and reigns as God for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. ON THE SAME FEAST, II

Come then, brethren: now that we are somewhat weary, let us take breath, and, refreshed for rising again to our labour, taste a little of yesterday’s repast which we reserved.

“And they found him,” he says, “in the Temple among the teachers and wise men, asking questions; and they marvelled at his prudence and answers” (Luke 2). It belongs to propriety that one younger in age should listen and ask questions; it is not contrary to propriety that a younger person, when questioned, should answer. But let us return to the course of the first exposition. And in these matters, as blessed Jerome says, note Christ as a man from the womb—indeed, as Jeremiah says, in the womb: “The Lord shall make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man in the womb” (Jer. 31)—Mary, Christ.

For a manly mind—wise, strong, and great—was in an infant, weak, and little body. In other human bodies, moreover, the qualities and quantities of bodies do not determine those of souls, so that misshapen bodies contain misshapen souls and beautiful bodies beautiful souls, or large bodies large souls and short bodies short souls. Such things are far from the nature of the soul, which bears the divine image. In quality, it is neither white nor black nor of any other colour; in quantity, neither long nor broad; nor is it locally here or there. In itself and according to movement, it has no upward or downward, forward or backward, rightward or leftward direction in which it is carried. Such quantities, qualities, dimensions, and movements belong to corporeal natures. But the rational soul is pure spirit, having above itself only the divine nature, which itself is spirit; the soul bears its image, but does not equal its essence.

The soul nevertheless is of a certain quality and quantity, and moves: in another manner it is white or black, long, broad, and high; it has something upward and downward, before and behind, to the right and to the left. But all these things are according to its own mode, and it does not follow the body in them. Wisdom makes it beautiful and bright; ignorance ugly and dark; a good conscience white, light, and cheerful; an evil conscience dusky, heavy, and sad. Faith makes it long, charity broad, hope high; fear contracted, avarice narrow, faint-heartedness small. Here virtue acts, elsewhere vice: it has before it what it seeks; behind it what it does not remember; above it what it does not comprehend; beneath it what it despises; to the right what delights it; to the left what troubles it.

In all these respects, therefore, the child Jesus has a manly mind: prudent, temperate, courageous, and just; trained by the companion and teacher, divinity; everywhere knowing how to reject evil and choose good, on account of food of milk and butter. Let us therefore also marvel at his wisdom and answers. For he alone, an infant of that age, so relished the virtues and could so answer vices.

“Son, why hast thou done thus to us?” Rather, mother, why have you done this to your son? Let it be that Joseph, who did not beget him, could forget; how could you forget the son of your womb? “Can a woman,” says the prophet, “forget her infant, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb?” (Isa. 49:15). If another woman could do so, surely you ought not. What? During that whole dark and gloomy day, did you not pray to God, think of God, or remember God? Who could believe this? Surely he himself is the one.

But perhaps you prayed to the Father, forgetful of the Son. Yet who can do this, when the Son is named in the name of Father? Moreover, he who does not have the Son does not have the Father either. Or perhaps, conscious of the sacrament, you speak mysteriously? “Son, why hast thou done thus to us?” I would judge that this ought to be read admiringly rather than interrogatively or reproachfully. For wonder contains inquiry, and inquiry merits knowledge. She wonders at what she does not, nevertheless, fail to know; by her wonder she invites you to investigate, saying with gravity and amazement: “O Son, what have you done thus for our instruction and education—that is, by remaining here while we departed?”

Or if you read it interrogatively, nothing is lost from the sense. But someone says: It is unfitting to charge the mother of Jesus with forgetfulness; for she did not forget her son, but thought him to be in the company of others and for that reason did not see him. Let it be so, lest we seem contentious. Yet diligence found him whom carelessness had not known. Thus you too are warned in every way to seek diligently, grieving deeply for what you lost through carelessness.

“I and thy father sought thee sorrowing.” To this Jesus says: “Did you not know that I must be in the things that are my Father’s?” Behold where the Son is to be sought: certainly in the things that are the Father’s. Behold where the Son does not wish it to be unknown that he is. Hence to one seeking him among the dead it was said: “Do not touch me: I have not yet ascended to the Father in your heart” (John 20)—you do not yet seek me in the things that are my Father’s; you do not yet know that I must be in the things of him whose whole being is his own, as though I were not he himself but his—yet not something other than he.

Yet apart from this unity of nature and natural unity of Father and Son, from which neither Father nor Son withdrew, the Son did not depart from the Father even in his abasement, because he always remained in the Father’s obedience and will. Hence, rebuking some, he says: “You are of your father the devil, and you do the desires of your father” (John 8:44). It is as if he said: You remain and exist in the things that belong to your father.

There are, therefore, three fathers of Adam’s children: God, man, and the devil. God is father by reason of nature; man by reason of species; the devil by reason of wickedness. Thus they must exist in what belongs to man by necessity; in what belongs to God by good will; and in what belongs to the devil by malignity. If you love, preserve, and direct to the purpose for which it was made the nature in which you were created good by the Good One, well and for good, then you remain in the things of God your Father, do not depart from Jerusalem, and make even the wicked spirits—your tempters—marvel at the prudence and answers by which you answer a thousand temptations of flesh, world, and devil, which question you sharply and very cunningly as they tempt you.

But if you do not understand the honour of your created nature, which was made “beautiful among women,” and go after the tracks of the flocks, beginning to become like senseless beasts; if, further, you infect by wickedness conceived from the wicked one the very good which is in you, so that you are swollen with pride, consumed by envy, turbulent with anger, cast down by sadness, anxious with avarice, greedy in gluttony, and unclean in lust—then you are manifestly shown to be in the things of your father the devil.

But in the things that belong to man our father, because we have an animal body and therefore the necessity of existing—or rather, of passing away—let us seek food and clothing only. Let no temptation beyond what is human seize us, so as to prevent our being content with these. For those who desire to become rich are drawn by diabolical temptation; they fall into his snares and into one temptation after another, and into many further temptations, so that they rightly deserve to hear from the Son of God: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44). And the universally true rule applies to them: Like father, like son—devil from devil. “Have I not chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:70). God from God: “I have said, Ye are gods.” Man from man.

Let man therefore leave diabolical things, lest he ever be in them; through human things, without which he cannot exist, let him pass to divine things, in which alone he will fare well. Let him flee the devil with all that belongs to him; return to man and be content with what belongs to man; ascend to God and be enriched in what belongs to God. Yet all the devil’s children are blind, for their own wickedness has blinded them, so that, though rich, they think themselves poor. They do not see that what is sufficient for the nature of the animal body is at hand; nor do they hear the divine voice promising that those who fear God will lack nothing. For they are deaf as well, and therefore always labour for superfluities.

But you, most beloved, attend to the teacher granted to you from heaven. He assumed man not only to heal him, but also to instruct him; he stripped him of the devil and clothed him with God. Follow the manner of his life: he was born poor, lived poor, and died poor. For in this is confidence: if we are in this world as he was, and if he who says that he abides in him walks as he walked.

By the spirit of fear he was so humble that, though he was God, he was subject to human beings: “And he was subject to them” (Luke 2:51). By the spirit of piety he was so gentle that he was not disturbed by injuries done to himself. He especially commended these two virtues in himself when he said: “Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). By the spirit of knowledge he was so compassionate and humane that, seeing the hostile city, he wept over it; and he who could not be troubled by enemies when meekly enduring them, troubled himself more affectionately over a friend, groaned in spirit, and wept. By the spirit [Col. 1719A] of fortitude he so loved justice that for its sake, even unto death, he spared no one by silence, as he repeatedly says: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees,” etc. (Matt. 23). By the spirit of counsel he was so merciful that he did not spare even himself, but gave his life—a charity than which there is none greater—as a ransom for many. By the spirit of understanding he was so pure in heart that his holy soul, united to God, saw God more excellently than every creature. By the spirit of wisdom he was so peace-making that he reconciled all to God in himself; and, though by nature the only-begotten Son, by this union of adhesion he became firstborn among many brethren.

Here, therefore—here, my brethren—let Christ alone be your teacher. Let him also be the book written for you within and without. Read this book concerning him; learn him from himself; from this exemplar transcribe him as an example, inwardly into your hearts and outwardly into your bodies. Offer your manner of life to others to be read, according to the way in which he lived. Therefore it is said: “Glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20). May he himself deign to grant this to us all. Amen.

## SERMON IX. ON THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EPIPHANY

“A wedding took place at Cana of Galilee,” etc. (Luke 2) [the citation is printed thus].

As I consider these weddings, brethren, I confess that the inward mystery delights me more than the outward miracle, great though it is. The latter builds faith; the former builds upon it. The latter is a sign for unbelievers; the former a sacrament for believers. Yet both are useful, both great, both divine.

The Book of Wisdom is written within and without, so that those who enter and go out may find pasture. Without is history; within, tropology. The first Book of Wisdom is written wholly within: in it those are blessed to whom it is given to see and read the place where the Father wrote all things at once and eternally, from which all things have, as it were, been copied that can be read in the second book, namely the rational mind. Thus the first book is the Word of God himself, Wisdom itself; the second is the created mind, itself wholly written within. There are all things at once; here is the likeness of all things—indeed, in this latter is the image of the former.

As every bodily form lies hidden in every body, and one who knows how to uncover it easily finds it, so every form of wisdom is contained in the rational mind, made in the image of total wisdom; it would not need to learn from without unless it were dark within. The holy angels, who have not grown old so that their eyes should grow dim, are content with these two books. By contemplation of themselves and of God, as though by evening and morning, they complete their day.

There follows a third book: corporeal and visible creation, likewise written within and without, so that through the things made, understood, one may behold the things which Wisdom made. It is an obscure book, so that eyes dimmed by excessive brightness may not be dazzled, as though they needed a lamp in order to see the sun. Yet because that ancient sinner laments that he is blind within—“his iniquities have taken hold of him, so that he could not see”—with the eyes of understanding he could not see God within, nor with the eye of intellect his own [Col. 1720A] mind; and because the eye of reason was disturbed by the fury of concupiscence, so that as he could see nothing within, he could discern little without: Wisdom in mercy, that is, by the finger of God, wrote a fourth book for the ear.

Therefore it was said by the Seeing One to the blind man: “Who is blind but my servant Israel?” (Isa. 42:19)—you who can see only in order to desire: at least hear outwardly from another what you ought to have seen inwardly: “The Lord thy God is one God” (Exod. 20). Moreover, because the blind man became deaf even to this trumpet, so that, despising the one true God, he committed fornication after many false demons; blind and deaf, following like an ox to sacrifice; and because, as Wisdom herself reproaches, “Moses gave you the law, and none of you keeps the law” (John 7:19): a fifth book was written for him, capable of being handled, and Wisdom itself became touchable, so that Wisdom might be justified in all things by her children and might prevail when judged.

“For the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.” “That which we have heard,” says the Apostle, “and have seen, and our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life,” etc. (1 John 1).
