What more ought he to have done which he did not do? My brethren, that true Word made flesh, the Lord Jesus himself, Christ our one teacher, becomes a book even for us. He assumed man precisely in order to teach how man ought to be borne. The holy Word itself, which the blessed eyes of the apostles saw in the flesh and handled with their hands, is today with us: visible in the letter, touchable in the sacrament. But though he departed in the flesh, the letter remained.

For the fulfilment of what the Seer foretold—“Thine eyes shall see thy teacher, and I will cause thy teacher no longer to fly away from thee” (Isa. 30:20)—he kindly granted us a sixth book, namely the holy Gospel, so that the text of the holy Gospel might be as the present visible body of the Word.

Let us therefore see what, in this reading of the sixth book, the Word of God has spoken outwardly to us through this outward work of miracles. For the work of the Word is itself a word. Let us see him in his work as though in his body; for the work itself is a kind of veil.

There are, then, as presently occurs to me, three kinds of weddings. The first is outward, the second inward, the third higher; the first external, the second interior, the third inmost; the first between human beings, the second in human beings, the third above human beings; the first between flesh and flesh, the second between flesh and spirit, the third between spirit and God.

The first makes one out of different things: “They shall not now be two,” he says, “but one flesh” (Matt. 19:6). The second makes one more fully out of contraries: for the rational soul and flesh are contrary natures, but one person. The third makes one most fully out of incomparable things: “He that is joined to God is one spirit.” In the first, flesh cleaving to flesh becomes one flesh. In the second, flesh cleaving to spirit, or spirit to flesh, becomes neither one flesh nor one spirit but one human being. In the third, spirit cleaving to God becomes one with him, and what [Col. 1721A] he is.

Hence the Son speaks thus to the Father concerning his brethren: “I will, Father, that, as I and thou are one, so these also may be one with us” (John 17). O One before all things, One above all things, One after all things, One from whom are all things, One for whom are all things! Very much one, where two in one flesh are now no longer two but one flesh; more one, where two in one human being are now no longer two but one person; most one, where the spirit cleaving to God is now no longer two but one.

The first unity generates being; the second specifies being; the third perpetuates and glorifies being itself. In the first, man is initiated; in the second, formed; in the third, perfected. In the first he comes to be; in the second he subsists; toward the third he naturally tends, for the sake of which he comes to be first and subsists second. Man is made by human beings for God.

But so that he might at some time arrive by grace where he always tends by nature, certain mystical weddings were made between the second and third marriages—far removed from the first—namely, those of the Word and flesh, of Christ and the Church. God was far from the soul, but without God it could not fare well or lawfully be fruitful. “Our sins,” says the prophet, “have withheld good”—that is, God—from us, and have divided between us and God, as between a woman and a husband (Jer. 5). Hence the adulterer and oppressor entered in, by whom she conceived pain and brought forth iniquity.

Therefore one was found—not by us, but by God for us—to lay his hand upon both, joining both in himself, excluding the third, narrowing the bed so that the adulterer falls off, and shortening the covering so that it cannot cover two. Thus he took away the middle wall of sin through which the adulterer had crept in, and made both one: reconciling in himself the woman to her husband, humanity to God; and removing the ancient enmities from the midst, he fastened them to the cross.

This is, most beloved, the sacrament of the Mediator, who, in order to intercede fittingly, subsists from both [natures]; so that he might reconcile sufficiently—that is, wholly—the whole to the whole, he brought all that belongs to God and assumed all that belongs to man, and, in order to fulfil [his office] faithfully, mingled in nothing of a third. For there is nothing but God and man—yet this is the whole. Therefore through him alone the woman who, dismissed by her husband, committed fornication with many lovers, has access and, above the law, permission through grace to return to her husband. As it was formerly foretold through the prophet: “But you,” he says, “have committed fornication with many lovers; and yet return to me, says the Lord” (Jer. III).

These are the marriages which we called mystical: to be joined after the second and third, now to be placed between the second and third; so that the first may be of flesh and flesh, the second of spirit and flesh, the third of the Word and man, the fourth of God and mind. The first are historical, the second moral, the third allegorical, the fourth anagogical. Through the first Jesus neither came nor made a passage, since neither was he begotten through them nor did he beget through them; but he came when invited to them, consecrating them by his presence and defending them by miraculous power against the detractors of marriage. Above all, in those in which he was, and for which he had come, he mystically signified [something]: for in the second and third he was already present—in flesh and soul and Word, three substances, two natures, one person, God and man. He had come for the sake of the fourth, which he already possessed in himself more excellently than all human beings. For no [soul] obeyed God more humbly than that holy soul, submitted itself more fully, or clung to him more firmly.

Man, divided in his duality and without God; God, threefold in his Trinity and without man: because there, where there was nothing but duality, there was no one to calm the duel; because there was only Trinity, there was no one to disturb the peace. There a fourth is not admitted into the Trinity, lest peace be disturbed; here a third is not found in our duality, that the duel may be calmed. There no one is dismissed from the Trinity, lest a duel be begun through duality; here, unless a third intervenes, the duel will not end. It was necessary, my brothers, as you see, that a great counsel be devised, so that heaven might not lose the glory of its peace and the wretched [human race] might at last find peace.

Accordingly, the angel of great counsel and mighty help was sent, yet not dismissed: the third of the three in the Trinity, the Son. At his saving birth the heavenly things were not disturbed, but earthly things were summoned to peace; a multitude of thousands of angels sings a hymn, saying, “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth” (Luke II). O great and wondrous counsel: that the eternal Trinity in God should not be diminished, and that a new Trinity should arise in man, through which one may ascend from natural and inward conflict to untried and undisturbable peace! O great and truly divine counsel, which so ordered all things that God, coming into man, made a Trinity necessary, while man, passing into God, did not make a quaternity superfluous!

This is so, undoubtedly, as we have said, because the one person, the Son of God and son of man, subsists in three substances and two natures: in the eternal divine Trinity—Father, Son, Holy Spirit—one God; in the new Trinity of man—flesh, soul, Word—one man. There are three persons and one substance; here, three substances and one person. There is natural unity and personal diversity. There all three persons are coeternal and coequal; here all three substances are different and unequal. There, finally, is nothing greater or lesser; here, by ascending and descending in stages, one thing is greater or lesser than another. Thus you too may ascend by degrees, always from the lesser to the greater: from flesh to Spirit, from spirit to God; from the second marriages, to which you came through the first, through the mediating third—and they are a ladder—to ascend to the fourth; from Adam, who is carnally begotten through concupiscence, to Christ, who spiritually regenerates through grace; and through him to the Father, who happily makes the regenerated person his heir as a son; from oldness through newness to eternity; from vanity through truth to virtue; from wandering through the way to life.

You must remember, most beloved, that in zeal for this migration these marriages are made, to which you have been invited with Jesus, if you are his disciples. “Jesus,” it says, “and his disciples were invited to the marriage” (John II). But while we have held the day with discourse, the hour has nearly passed, so that we cannot now discharge without difficulty the task of manual labour. Therefore we must hasten, so that, after late labour, we may taste the little that remains of the discourse as a morsel of fish with barley bread, through the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ, God’s Word. Amen.

## SERMON X. ON THE SAME FEAST, II

“Jesus and his disciples were invited to the marriage” (John II). Since, as we have said, these marriages were made in zeal for migration, it was also necessary for us to say what you heard above: namely, from where, by what route, and whither we must migrate, so that we may return to the place from which we fell, and lean where we fell, in order to rise from there.

We must migrate as if upon two feet: understanding and affection. By one, from letter to spirit; by the other, from vice to virtue. Indeed, brother, you must continue migrating: always passing from understanding to understanding and from virtue to virtue, until by perfect knowledge you behold him whom your soul loves; and, as it were with certain arms of full love, embrace him whom you behold; and, rejoicing and marveling because of knowledge, say, “Such is my beloved” (Song V); and because of love add, “And he is my friend”; and: “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine; he shall dwell between my breasts” (Song VI).

This is the way of migration, which you must traverse neither tepidly, nor timidly, nor slowly, but with an enlarged heart, with zeal and fervour, and with inexpressible sweetness; and wherever the impulse of the Spirit bears you, may you always be carried away. Consider with what zeal the Son of God migrated beneath himself, since above himself he could not [go]: as far as you, since beneath you he ought not [go]; and all for you, that he might arrive at these marriages.

Therefore, brothers, have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, seeking and understanding from where, why, and how far he emptied himself from the form of God into the likeness of sinful flesh. But why? Certainly not from fear of loss or desire for gain, but solely and only through love for us: that we, step answering step, may not depart and migrate from the pit of sin through fear of punishment, like slaves, nor through desire for a kingdom, like hired servants, but solely through love of God, like sons. He could neither descend nor ought to descend into that pit; and let us meet him in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that there mercy and truth may meet one another, justice and peace may kiss.

Let us migrate from the pit of sin to the form of God, through the likeness of sinful flesh; to the Lord from sin through repentance—everywhere being filled in understanding and virtue—until full knowledge, that is, wisdom, and full love, that is, charity; as it were to the highest angelic Cherubim and Seraphim, just as he emptied himself down to folly and weakness. For it pleased him through the folly of preaching and the weakness of suffering to save believers, as if making those who drink at the marriage feast drunk. For that very folly or weakness is perhaps the water which he nevertheless turns into wine—that is, into wisdom and virtue—when “what is foolish in God is found wiser than men, and what is weak [in God] is recognized as stronger” (I Cor. I).

“The best wine,” he says—and truly so. In comparison with and praise of it, the first is rebuked: that is, the wisdom of this age, which the wisdom of God made foolish—the wisdom, namely, of philosophers, which failed in itself. “Truths have been diminished from among the children of men”; hence each has spoken vain things to his neighbour, master to disciple. “Those joined to the rock,” that is, Christ—the philosophers of the nations—“have been set free.” “Where is the wise man? Where the scribe? Where the inquirer of this age?” “The wise have been caught in their own craftiness”; “they were troubled and shaken like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up,” and the wine they had drunk failed.

It is also good and useful for you, brother, that your own wine should fail you and that you should not follow your own judgment. Let Jesus first cause your vessels to be filled with water, which afterwards he may turn for you into wine. Hear the teacher of the nations; hear one of the servants who know whence the good wine comes and how it is made. “If anyone among you seems to be wise”—that is, to have wine—“let him be well emptied, that he may be most fully filled”: let him “become foolish, that he may be wise” (I Cor. III). Let arrogance be emptied, because “he who thinks that he knows does not yet know how he ought to know” (I Cor. VIII). Indeed, “woe to those who are wise in their own eyes.” For “professing themselves wise, they became foolish.” Let him be filled with water—that is, let him recognize his own foolishness and weakness—and thus let what he is appear to him, so that what he is not yet may more quickly come to be. Let him receive water, that he may drink wine; let him fail from himself—that is, from his own judgment and will—that through the virtue of obedience he may advance in wisdom and charity.

In this sense, brothers, we understand the saying: “You will take away their spirit, and they shall fail, and return to their dust” (Ps. CIII): so that what there is dust is here water; what there is their own spirit is here the former wine; what there is the Spirit of God is here Christ’s wine. “Send forth your Spirit,” he says (ibid.), as though, “Offer your wine,” and they “shall be created into a new man”: as though they shall be made drunk. And the mother of Jesus was there: certainly she who suggested [the matter] to her Son and, by suggesting it, interceded. She obtained the miracle and did not fail to understand the mystery. For when the Son answered, “What is [there] between me and you, woman?” it was as though he said: “Powers concern me and my Father; weaknesses concern me and my mother.” Understanding all this, she forewarns the servants to obey in everything that Jesus may say.

Many wise persons of this age, treating at length of the soul and God—of its creation by him, its purification through him, and its blessedness in him—have failed in their searching inquiry. They had presumed to be attendants of the bridegroom without Jesus, as though they did not invite Jesus to the marriage; therefore they wandered far from truth. The Apostle says: “[That] Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Eph. III). But whence is this Jesus for us—that is, this faith—and who is his mother, who bore it for us? What merits preceded it? Let us return to the Apostle; let us hear the disciple who was most deeply present at the mystical marriage: “By grace you have been saved through faith” (Eph. II).

Therefore this is the mother who gives birth to Jesus within our hearts: grace, which precedes the unworthy; the depth that is unseen, from which is born and rises every length, breadth, and height that is seen. Justice, as it were, answers her: “What is [there] between me and you, woman?”—that is, pious, affectionate, and full of charity [though you are]. Yet justice obeys mercy. The Apostle briefly embraces the whole matter, saying: “Not from works of justice which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus III).

Grace, therefore, the mother through whom faith is created, was there: faith, which is the first of the virtues and is stirred to action by love, lest the righteous person be idle and the disciples not believe in him. But who are these disciples who follow Jesus, if not the other virtues, which follow faith and obey faith, without which they have no worth? They can have appearance, but without faith they cannot possess truth. For without faith it is impossible for them to please God; indeed, everything that is not from faith is sin.

But what are the six hard and cold water-jars meant to signify? Perhaps such were human works. For the number six signifies activity, just as seven signifies rest from work and eight resurrection after every work. Thus the worship of the nations, by which they honoured demons, and the Jewish traditions, by which they purified themselves, were made foolish by faith, as if filled with water: useless and tasteless vanity was discovered in the former, while useful and savoury truth was found in the latter. For this is the proper order of teaching: first to repel the perverse from folly, then to instruct the converted in wisdom. Hear this whole matter in the Apostle: “Circumcision is nothing” (I Cor. VII), as though he said, “It is water”; “and uncircumcision is nothing” (ibid.).

With these two statements, embracing all the worship of the nations and the carnal rites of the Jews, and filling them with water—that is, with uselessness and folly—he finally changed [the water] into wine, saying: “But the keeping of God’s commandments.” Under this figure Jesus abolishes the carnal Sabbath, and the disciples eat with unwashed hands (Matt. XV), drawing all things to spiritual understanding and turning water into wine. Hence, when Peter asks what the parable means, he hears: “Are you also without understanding?” (ibid.).

The water-jars hold two or three measures, since the Gentiles, interpreting their sacred rites, discern a physical and a Gentile meaning; while we, in the Jewish writings, investigate beyond history a moral meaning, also an allegorical one, and sometimes an anagogical one. That wise Solomon, compressing the prolixity of all things and discourses as it were into the narrowest wine-cask, says in agreement with Paul: “Fear God and keep his commandments; for this is the whole man” (Eccl. XII).

For this fear itself is perhaps water. One who abandons self-confidence, readily recognizing his own folly and weakness, begins to fear and advances toward wisdom; for “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” Wisdom, however, perfects charity, which casts fear out and turns water into wine. Fear is understood as twofold, or threefold, when we fear that, on account of fault, we may fall from glory into punishment. Repentance from dead works may likewise rightly be understood as water—for six signifies works—just as the kingdom of God is wine. Hence the beginning of Jesus’ preaching, like the beginning of his signs, was: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. IV). Repentance itself is also marked as twofold or threefold: contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and, if it is permitted, satisfaction by work.

The servants who fill the sinner either with self-knowledge, fear of God, or sorrow for evil are understood as angels, apostles, and preachers. Being conscious of the sacrament, where and when Jesus commands, they draw [the water] and carry it to whom he commands. “When the steward of the feast tasted,” etc. Let those who sit first and drink last be ashamed. It ought to be offered to them so that they may taste and test it first. But drunk with the former wine, they still sleep off their intoxication: chosen as teachers of spiritual things, they have become traders in secular things. Going almost into the interior of the desert, they do not lead the sheep but drive them; wicked to themselves, indulgent to others; caring for their own bodies and for others’ souls; worthy of the saying: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII).

Thus, my brothers, concerning a community which deals with secular matters and tends what belongs to others, it seems to me, when it compels subjects into order, as if I had seen a handsome-bodied man walking head downward. Would that we might at times restrain our mouth from judging another’s servant—a mouth which perhaps it would altogether have been expedient to keep shut. We understand this ruler of the banquet as the free choice of the human person, to whom faith is first offered and to whom alone, with God, belongs judgment concerning contempt or obedience. It presides over the whole soul, which is threefold on account of its rational, irascible, and concupiscible faculties.

## SERMON XI. ON THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY, I

[Col. 1726D]

“When Jesus had come down from the mountain,” etc. (Matt. VIII). Heaven is a mountain; earth a valley. God is a mountain; man a valley. The form of God is a mountain, and the form of a servant a valley. Therefore, when God in the form of God came down from heaven to earth, he emptied himself into the form of a servant and was found in appearance as a man. The crowds which awaited him could no longer follow him: without him, they could not go where he himself went. Yet where does he lead them? First, indeed, to heal the leper—perhaps they themselves were [lepers] and did not know it.

The first misfortune of a sick person is not to possess health; the second, not to know the sickness; the third, not to seek medicine; the fourth, to neglect it when offered. Therefore the wise physician and gracious God leads [the crowd] where he teaches them, where a man is encountered who sees his weakness and therefore seeks health, confesses power, and entreats will; so that from what the crowd sees outside, it may be instructed, and the blind person, weaker than the sick person who sees, may follow him.

The Apostle says that promises were made to Abraham and his seed; therefore Christ was also a minister of circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises of the fathers; while the nations glorify God for mercy (Rom. XV). Therefore I understand in the crowd which waits and follows, and in the leper who comes to meet him and is cleansed, these two peoples: namely, circumcision, which, awaiting the bodily presence, saw first; and uncircumcision, which, coming afterwards, deserved first to receive the benefit and grace, easily believing the preaching of the apostles, truly confessing its leprosy, and humbly entreating the physician. For he had not yet healed anyone from the crowd that followed.

But what is this crowd that follows? Just as the Pharisees watched him in order to rebuke him, questioned him not to learn but to catch him in speech, and sought him not to save but to destroy him, so circumcision followed—not to attain him, but to persecute him; not to apprehend him, but to catch him out. For those from among it who, uncovering their sins, adoring majesty, and asking goodness, came to meet him, are mystically counted with this leper.

Just as formerly circumcision was preferred to the nations, to provoke them to zeal for the worship of one God, so afterwards the Gentile people was preferred in order to provoke the Jews to faith in the divine Trinity. This can be seen even today: the last become first and the first last; teachers become disciples and disciples teachers; those who did not see see, and those who saw have become blind.

Israel did not attain what it sought; indeed, it persecuted [it]. The election attained it. Foreigners daily devour its regions before its face, and newcomers consume the wilderness of the letter, transformed into the fertility of spiritual understanding. The kingdom of God has been taken from them and given to a nation producing its fruit. Before those who are badly healthy, the one who is well sick is healed; and, acknowledging his sin, he speaks first in order that he may be justified. For the righteous person is first of all his own accuser: that is, at the beginning of his justification he accuses himself; by accusing himself, he begins to be righteous. The first part of a sinner’s righteousness is accusation of fault; the second, correction; the third, observance. “And I shall be blameless with him, and shall keep myself from my iniquity” (Ps. XVII).

Therefore the leper who comes says first: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me” (Matt. VIII). He confesses two things: his own uncleanness and the Lord’s power; he entreats the third, namely beneficence. Praising, he invokes the Lord; therefore he is sent away healthy from leprosy. Praising power, he invokes grace, which cannot possibly be absent from the first two confessions—of fault and of praise. For everyone who thus invokes the name of the Lord shall be saved and shall hear: “I will; be cleansed.” Hence the blessed prophet says: “Praising, I shall invoke the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies” (Ps. XVII).

Touched by Jesus, he is cleansed; but lest he call himself clean, he is forbidden by his cleanser until he has shown himself to the priest and offered the legal gift. What do these things mean, brothers? Can one cleansed by Christ keep silent about Christ’s praises? Having praised power before experiencing it, will he keep silent about grace after experiencing it? One cleansed by Christ perhaps needs a priest who is unclean; or else he commands idle things—far be it!—or he speaks mysteries.

Two things belong to God alone: the honour of confession and the power of remission. We must offer him confession; from him we must await remission. For to God alone belongs the forgiving of sins, and therefore confession must be made to him. Yet when the Almighty betrothed the weak woman to himself, the Exalted [one] the humble [one], he made the handmaid a queen: her who had formerly been under his feet he took to his side. For she came forth from his side, from which he gave her to himself as a pledge. And just as all that belongs to the Father belongs to the Son, and what belongs to the Son to the Father, since they are naturally one, so the bridegroom gave all his own things to the bride, and the bridegroom shared with himself all things belonging to the bride; whom he made one also with himself and the Father. “I will,” says the Son, interceding with the Father for the bride, “that, as I and you are one, so they too may be one with us” (Ps. VI).

Therefore the bridegroom, one with the Father and one with the bride, removed from the bride what he found alien: fastening it to the cross, where he bore her sins upon the wood and removed them through the wood. What was natural and proper [to her], he assumed and put on; what was proper and divine to himself, he bestowed. For he removed what was diabolical, assumed what was human, and bestowed what was divine, so that all the bride’s things might be the bridegroom’s. Therefore [the bridegroom] says: “Who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth: Have mercy upon me, Lord, for I am weak,” etc. (Matt. VIII), so that he who has her weakness may also have her lamentation, and all the bride’s things may be the bridegroom’s.

Hence come the honour of confession and the power of remission; therefore it must be said, “Go, show yourself to the priest” (Luke V). For these things are no less Christ’s alone if they belong to the Church; yet they are not the whole Christ’s if they do not belong to the Church. Likewise they are no less God’s alone if they belong to Christ, yet they are not, so to speak, the whole God’s if they do not belong to Christ. Therefore no sinner who has groaned inwardly, where Christ alone—but not the whole Christ—forgives, should call himself healed, if he has despised showing himself to the priest, to whom the dispensation of remission has been entrusted and to whom, on that account, the honour of confession is due. For if he does not speak, the leprosy returns; and he is rightly called more unclean when he despises the cleanser, who cleansed under this condition: that the leper should by no means call himself clean unless he showed himself to the priest and offered a gift.

For just as forgiven [debts] return to one who does not forgive, so pardoned sins avail nothing to one who scorns to confess outwardly what he has confessed inwardly. As one who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him, so one who despises the bride dishonours the bridegroom who received her; and one who despises the bridegroom—that is, the Son—certainly despises the Father and offends the Holy Spirit, without whom neither Father, Son, nor Church forgives sins.

Almighty mercy has its own rules, according to which it gives and forgives. “Give,” he says, “and it shall be given to you” (Luke VI); otherwise even what you have been given shall be taken from you. Likewise: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (ibid.); otherwise what has been forgiven you will be exacted from you in wrath, to the last farthing. In accordance with these rules, too, the following is rightly understood: “Behold, you have been made whole; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John V); and: “Neither do I condemn you; sin no more” (John VIII). Likewise the text presently in hand: “I will; be cleansed. Go, show yourself to the priest,” etc. (Luke V), so that what is often said may always be understood even where it is not said.

Therefore the Church can forgive nothing without Christ, and Christ wills to forgive nothing without the Church. The Church can forgive no one except the penitent—that is, one whom Christ has touched; Christ does not will forgiveness to remain with one who despises the Church. Christ Almighty can do everything by himself: baptize, consecrate the Eucharist, ordain, forgive sins, and the like. Yet the humble and faithful bridegroom wills nothing without the bride. “What God has joined, let no man separate.” “I speak of this great sacrament in Christ and in the Church.” Do not utterly break off the turtledove’s head; do not sever the head from the body. For Christ did not will to be beheaded, but to be extended, stretched out, and suspended on the cross, so that he might join the lowest, highest, and middle things.

Therefore do not withdraw the head from the body, so that nowhere may the whole Christ be: for the whole Christ is nowhere without the Church, just as the whole Church is nowhere without Christ. For the complete and whole Christ is head and body; therefore he says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the Son of Man, who is in heaven” (John III). This is the one man who forgives sins: he first touches inwardly, to work contrition of heart; afterwards he sends [the person] outwardly to the priest, for confession of mouth; and the priest [sends him] to God, to offer the gift of satisfaction. For these three make complete cleansing: contrition of heart, confession of mouth, satisfaction by work; before these, no one may call himself cleansed.

But I see, brothers, that I have not satisfied your expectation, for you drink more eagerly the moral sense by which you may be built upon the foundation in which you are placed. Therefore, insofar as our ability permits, we shall comply with your custom—though, I confess, against our own custom, since mysteries delight us more everywhere. Yet because the kingdom of God is not in speech, let us rise to the labour which remains and must today be completed wholly. For we ought not to be free for discourse so that we may not labour; rather, we ought sometimes to moderate labour so that we may be free for the word of God.

Since man is not flesh alone or spirit alone, and is not yet wholly spiritual in the life-giving Spirit, he cannot live wholly either by bread alone, for which we labour, or by the word alone, to which we give attention, while he still lives partly as a beast and partly as an angel—until every animal likeness has been consumed and he becomes equal to God’s angels, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

## SERMON XII. ON THE SAME THIRD SUNDAY

“When Jesus had come down from the mountain,” etc. (Matt. VIII). You must remember, brothers, from this passage the one where the Lord Jesus, seeing the crowds, went up the mountain, so that, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, you may always ascend in the Spirit, as the blessed Apostle urges: “If you live by the Spirit, walk also by the Spirit” (Gal. V). For order requires it, reason demands it, and we are almost never silent about it: whoever wishes to be truly spiritual must first be so in life, conduct, and virtues, in order that he may at some time be so in meditation, understanding, and teaching; he must first be so in affection rather than reason. Therefore he says: “If you live by the Spirit, walk also by the Spirit.”

The eager, ready disciples, fervent in spirit, follow [him] up the mountain; a heavy crowd waits for him as he comes down. My Lord Jesus, the Saviour of all, becomes all things to all in such a way that he is found everywhere humbler than the humble and higher than the exalted: so bending himself down that he frees the soul caught in adultery and accused by demons, writing with his finger upon the earth—he who was formed by God’s finger, earth from earth, for earth (John VIII); and so raising himself that he ascends even above the Cherubim and flies twice upon the wings of the winds, surpassing, that is, all the virtues of the righteous and contemplations of angels. “For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Who shall be like God among the sons of God?”

I understand him himself, then—the valley into which he descends, the plain through which he walks with the crowd, and the mountain to which he ascends, now with all his disciples, now with a few, now alone to pray to the Father. For he remains wholly what God is and wholly what man is: he cannot ascend above himself lest he exceed God, nor ought he to descend below himself lest he become a beast.

Thus he himself is the holy and lofty ladder which the sleeping pilgrim saw—for perhaps the inhabitant and the watchful person would not see it—raised from earth to God or extended from God to earth. When he wills, he ascends through himself into himself, where now few, now more, now no human being can follow him. But when he wills, he restrains himself for the common crowd, in order to speak what it can receive. At times he eats with tax collectors and sinners, so that he may be called a glutton and a drinker of wine (Matt. XI). At times he also touches the sick in order to heal them, rather than merely saying, “I will; be cleansed.”

Blessed, dearest brothers, is the soul able to follow the Lord Jesus in all things, running after the fragrance of his ointments wherever he goes: ascending upward in the repose of contemplation, being still and seeing that he is God; descending downward in the office of charity, following him into the subjection of service, love of poverty, endurance of hunger and thirst, weariness, work, weeping, prayer, compassion, and finally suffering—him who came to obey unto death, to minister rather than be ministered to, and to give to many not gold or silver but counsel and help, and his life for many.

O blessed soul of Paul, who, following Jesus in all things, could say: “Whether we are beside ourselves, [it is] for God; whether we are sober-minded, [it is] for you” (I Cor. V). Though to be with Christ was far better—for it is good to be there—he did not refuse to remain in the prison of the flesh for the charity of the brethren.

Therefore let this be your pattern of life, brothers; this is the true discipline of holy conduct: by thought and desire to dwell with Christ in that eternal homeland; in this wretched pilgrimage to refuse no office of charity for Christ; in following the Lord Christ upward to the Father, to be made thin, simple, and one in the repose of meditation; in following Christ downward to one’s brother, to be stretched out in action, divided in many ways, and become all things to all. Let nothing be despised for which Christ is the cause, and nothing be dear which is not for Christ. Let [the soul] thirst for one thing and give itself to one thing, where Christ is one; let [the body] wish to serve all, where Christ is manifold.

Hear how rightly one divided [these matters] who rightly offered himself wholly: “My soul thirsted for you. How manifoldly [longed] my flesh for you” (Ps. LXII). The soul, he says, [longs] uniformly; the flesh, manifoldly. The soul uniformly for the One; the flesh manifoldly for the One—that is, many things for the sake of one. The soul upward, the flesh downward, so that the whole human being may follow the whole Christ and wholly serve the whole. For the whole Christ is God and man; the whole human being is rational soul and flesh.

Let the soul in contemplation of truth visit its likeness above itself; let the flesh in the office of charity visit its likeness near itself; and neither will sin in itself. “Visiting your likeness,” Scripture says, “you shall not sin” (Job V). If therefore the flesh sees even its own likeness beneath it in weakness, let it not shrink from it or flee its service, nor recoil from a touch of compassion. For the soul will never deserve to see its likeness above itself more fully through truth than when the flesh bends itself down through charity to its likeness beneath itself.

Therefore divine wisdom, both medicine and teaching, chose rather to cure the leper by touch than by word alone, though it could have done so by word, that you may confer a benefit not by the easier means but by the more effective; that you may fulfil the work of compassion, shrink from nothing, and always attend to him for whose sake you act. For he is always beautiful, always clean, always honourable, always worthy—in every person, place, and work.

“I will; be cleansed.” What shall we say, brothers, about those who can do more good than they are willing to do, when daily we hear your complaints, groans, and sighs that you cannot, as much as you wish, either upward or downward, toward father or brother, toward the one or toward the many? “If you will,” he says, “you can cleanse me.” Truly, most beloved, the Almighty can do all things: ability is subject to him whenever he wills; but willing and being able are not always together. For he can do many things that he does not will, although he can do nothing unwillingly. Therefore no one confessing leprosy doubts his power; but because he does not will all that he can do, while he can do everything that he wills, [the leper] entreats his will and worships his power.

Thus in God will and power are distinct. Yet, as he teaches the leper—because he both can and wills to heal him—saying, “I will; be cleansed,” [he teaches] us never to be sluggish in the good which we can do. Rather, as the Apostle says, “While we have time, let us do good to all, not failing; for in due season we shall reap” (Gal. VI). For there is a time for sowing and a time for reaping. Therefore, brother, do the good that you can, while you can, for whomever you can. For night will come when neither for yourself nor another will you be able [to act], even if you wish it.

If here, while it is day for us, it is very wretched not to be able when you wish though you could [formerly act], it is wicked not to will when you can. Therefore ability is deservedly taken from one who does not will, so that at some point he may neither be able nor will, or may wish in vain when he cannot; and it is given to another, so that ability may be present when he wills. God will in us perfect full ability in response to good will—he who now has worked willing in accordance with his own will; he who first gives by grace alone what afterwards he justly rewards.

Therefore, though he could easily [heal] by word alone, divine wisdom and power taught affection when he healed by touch, acting and teaching, driving away leprosy and ignorance: Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. ON THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY, I
As Jesus went up into the boat, his disciples followed him (Matt. 8). Now, brothers, we read of the Lord Jesus both going up and going down; and, considering his whole person, we wonder where he can go up, since he is God Most High, or where he can go down, since he is the lowliest of men. Above God there is no place to which he can go; beneath man he ought not to go: the one is impossible, the other unworthy. But if it is understood materially, only and wholly in terms of goods, it is astonishing where this man goes, or whence he returns, who is always everywhere, and from whom nothing is ever absent. Wherever, then, he goes, he is already there; and whence he returns, he is by no means lacking. But these things belong to majesty and the divine nature; let us seek what belongs to humanity and grace.

The boat, then, signifies the Church, which still sails by human hands upon this great and broad sea of the world. But why did he go up into it rather than go down into it? For he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. [Col. 1732D] III); in that form, or through it, he entered the Church, and went down into her, or upon her, as a head upon a body. Yet there are two things by which the administration and office of every congregation and household—even a private house—is ordered: namely, subjection and precedence. No one, however, is fit to preside who has not learned to be subject; nor to command who has not obeyed.

Therefore that sublime Majesty, whose nature it is to be before all things and whose proper right is to command all, from whom comes every order and all authority, bowed himself down in order to assume human nature, perform an office, and pay a debt not owed by him—paying what he had not taken. Thus he conformed in everything to order, so that among the miraculous works which he performed, nothing is more wonderful as a miracle, nothing clearer as instruction, than his own holy manner of life, by which, a man among men, he lived. Hence, to the Baptist, who trembled with reverence and cried, “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?”, he answered, “Allow it now” (Matt. 3)—that is, “Wait still; do not disturb the order.” “For thus,” that is, by following order and beginning with humility, “it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness.”

For in the stages mentioned above, all the righteousness of office is maintained, exercised, and fulfilled: that is, in subjection and precedence. A man takes the lead according to order and obeys in subjection; nor does he ever approach a position of precedence by his own presumption, but through another’s orderly call. For the blessed Apostle says: “No one takes the honour for himself, but is called by God, as Aaron was” [Col. 1733B] (Heb. 5). Thus also the Lord Jesus, first subject in the rank of office, came with the people and among the people to baptism. He did not choose to ascend to the second rank, that of presiding office, by assuming it himself, but was elected and appointed by God—as the blessed Apostle writing to the Hebrews affirms—when the Father bore witness to him, advanced him, and said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3), at the time and in the office of subjection.

“Listen to him henceforth,” who has learned obedience. He who has hitherto kept silence should now speak. For it befits one who knows how to be silent to speak. Let him be heard as Teacher who has heard what he is to teach. He is worthy to preside who did not disdain to be subject. Let him at last hear, “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14), who for thirty years reclined in the lowest place. [Col. 1733C] This has been said because Jesus was said to have gone up into the boat. It follows:

His disciples followed him. Which disciple has not followed this example of the Master? Who took honour for himself? Who made himself an apostle, who an evangelist? Who preached unless sent? “He gave some to be apostles, others evangelists,” and so forth (Eph. 4). Hence they hear, “You do not know what you are asking” (Matt. 20). Brothers, disciples still follow today, reclining below until they are called higher. For those who thrust themselves forward and take honour for themselves are not his disciples and do not follow him. Nor are they sent by him; rather, they come before him, anticipating their calling under the impulse of ambition, and for this reason he called them thieves and robbers.

What, I ask, can be more foolishly requested, presumed, or desired by a man than that one should be placed over all, one alone over many? What else did the foolish angel say when he said in his heart, “I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and above the stars of heaven—that is, the angels my equals—I will place my throne”? (Isa. 14). Therefore the mind that seeks this either is proud or is mad. For if it judges itself wiser and worthier than others in its own eyes, it is proud and has blinded itself concerning itself. For how will he not be blind who carries himself as gross and swollen in his own sight? Pride always blinds the mind, just as a spot blinds the eye where it arises. Hence no proud person believes himself proud, nor can he know himself, since he is altogether unable to see himself. [Col. 1734A] But if, while considering himself less fit, he nevertheless seeks such a position, does he not plainly go mad? It follows:

And there arose a great disturbance in the sea. The contrary wind is the north wind, the burning wind, from which every evil is revealed. Rebuking it, she who had foreseen its fury says: “Arise, north wind; come, south wind; and breathe upon my garden, that its spices may flow” (Song 4). The contrary wind, then, is the devil and Satan, who stirs up the depths of the sea—that is, he rouses the children of this age and, by repeated assaults of disturbances, threatens the Church with shipwreck. In his strength he even shakes the mountains, because of the tribulations which have overtaken them exceedingly.

But where, I ask, is that strength which they followed into the boat, concerning which they confidently said: “We shall not fear though the earth be shaken and the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea”? (Ps. 45). Behold, their waters have already thundered and been troubled—that is, the waters of the mountains in the sea. Certainly the mountains of the Church, the mountains of the little boat, have been disturbed by the strength and rage of the storm. Why are they disturbed? Why do they fear? Surely because their strength and security are asleep. How could fear fail to reign where strength sleeps?

Let the wind, therefore, remain awake while Christ sleeps. Let the sea’s rage remain awake while Christ’s faith sleeps. Let fear, finally, remain awake while Christ’s strength sleeps, so that at last those who are fearful and of little, sleeping faith may flee to him in whom they ought to have kept their strength, lest they fear; and may say: “God is our refuge and strength, a helper in tribulations that have found us exceedingly” [Col. 1734C] (ibid.). Save us while awake—you by whose sleeping we perish. The disciples’ first duty would have been not to let the Master fall asleep; their second, at least to awaken him when asleep. The former is strength; the latter, refuge. The former belongs to zeal; the latter to fear. Zeal keeps him awake; necessity awakens him asleep. Yet happy is the necessity which drives one to strength! For the first virtue is courage, that no one may fear; the second is to seek counsel and help, that he may not perish.

Therefore, brothers, whenever persecution rages against us, let us flee to Christ after the example of the holy Apostles. Let us awaken Christ’s faith in ourselves, and the remembrance of his passion, as of sleep; for perhaps this sleep not inappropriately signifies that passion also. Since in ourselves we are weak and fearful, or wickedly bold, in him we find the example of patience; from him we receive the strength to endure; we learn the pattern of steadfastness. Without him we can do nothing, while in him we shall be able to do all things, as the blessed Apostle says: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4).

His eyelids test us. He closes his eyes; the sea rages; all things are fierce and hard. Lest we be broken, he opens his eyes: all things are quiet, and the voyage is prosperous. Lest we be exalted, all things are secure and peace is on every side. Lest we grow slothful, let us hope for prosperity in adversity, and fear adversity in prosperity. For all things change and have their alternations. It is therefore the mark of the wise man to fear less in adversity and more in prosperity, but in neither to become slothful or sleep, lest in the one he despair or in the other vanish away. Therefore, brothers, placed between fear and hope, let us keep watch over the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ within us. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. ON THE SAME FEAST, II

And when he had fallen asleep, there arose a great disturbance (Matt. 8). What, most beloved, did the Lord accomplish while sleeping in body, except that he might awaken disciples who were, as it were, sleeping in heart? For power worked while he slept, bringing winds out of its treasuries; and the Word, wholly silent and asleep, spoke, teaching them their danger if they allowed their Master to be silent, sluggish, and asleep.

Wisdom, indeed, is learned in repose, but not in idleness. Nothing is more occupied than that repose, nothing more laborious than that leisure, in which wisdom is learned, the Word of God is questioned and heard. Martha laboured; Mary was at leisure (Luke 10), but she was not languishing. Lazarus, however, languished, passing from sickness into death, and from death into stench (John 11). O how many today, outwardly at rest from useful work but inwardly idle and slothful, careless of necessities and intent upon tales and thoughts devoid of understanding, have lost Martha’s concern and not found Mary’s devotion! Thus even in Bethany—that is, the house of obedience—they have fallen into the languor of idleness.

O wretches, weak while power is present, foolish while [Col. 1735C] wisdom is present, blind in the light, mute before the Word, wasting away with hunger while the bread of life and understanding is set before them—such as those of whom it is written: “Their soul abhorred every kind of food, and they drew near to the gates of death” (Ps. 106). And just as there the Lord says that the sick man came unto death so that he might be raised from it, so here he himself wished to sleep among Apostles who were, as it were, sick—or who signified such persons—so that at least those in danger might awaken him. Therefore he slept outwardly, though such men had already, as it were, fallen asleep inwardly. What they were inwardly he showed them outwardly. But because gentle and subtle instruction could not be received by them, they are warned more harshly through outward things. Therefore the sea rises wonderfully, so that the Lord may appear wonderful on high. Sleeping amid the storm, he instructs those wrongly secure; when awakened, by calm he teaches those rightly troubled.

Believe me, brothers: both are words of that holy Word—the storm and the calm, his sleeping and his waking. For by the word of the storm, while sleeping, he condemns sloth, which is followed by the fluctuation of thoughts, like a certain inward and intolerable tempest. Awakened and watchful, he commends the watchfulness of the mind and the fervour of the spirit by the utterance of calm.

Therefore, my brothers, we must keep watch with the utmost care, and all the more attentively because we have chosen a more remote wilderness, lest the Word of God should ever sleep in the little boat of our inward person, for whom the outward person is like a sea—the Word which never sleeps or slumbers in itself. An idle Christ cannot keep watch for us. In short: he always wishes either to be asked for something, or questioned; or, when he himself speaks, to be heard. For if, brother, you begin to sleep while he speaks, immediately he too sleeps for you. But woe to you if he sleeps for you! The wind is awake, the sea is awake, the storm is awake, the waves of thoughts and the surge of a thousand temptations are awake for you, if he alone sleeps for you.

Therefore, praying with the Prophet, say to him: “Enlighten my eyes, O Lord, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. 12). Indeed, unless you first begin to sleep for him, he will always remain wholly wakeful for you. Peter could not keep watch one hour with Christ, and so he was able to deny Christ three times. For he had slept when the Lord said to him: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26)—as though into a tempest of the soul.

Where are those who doze over their books in cloisters, snore during readings in oratories, or sleep at the living voice of sermons in chapter meetings? In all these things the Word of God speaks and is neglected. The Lord, the Teacher, speaks, and the human disciple sleeps. There are three things: reading, meditation, and prayer. By reading—or by a sermon, which itself is a kind of reading—God speaks to you. Therefore he says: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8). By meditation you question him; by prayer you ask him. Therefore he says: “Ask, and you shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Luke 11). Prayer asks; meditation knocks.

Those who through spiritual practice have their senses trained by habit know what I mean. For the natural man does not perceive such things, even if his life is spiritual. For there is, as I always repeat to you and wish you to remember, one who is natural in perception but spiritual in life; another whose life is natural but whose perception is spiritual; a third natural both in life and perception; and a fourth spiritual in both. In these three, then—reading, meditation, and prayer—lies the whole exercise, at least, of spiritual perception, and a certain converse of the mind in heavenly things, where, like Moses on the mountain, it may speak, hear, and converse with God as with its neighbour, though by perception alone. There is also a distinct drawing near to the Lord by one’s manner of life. Hence: “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (Jas. 4). Some, therefore, as we have said, are near in perception and far in life; others near in life and far in perception; others far in both; others near in both. Thus one near in perception, nearer in life, becomes nearest in both.

[Col. 1736D] Let us therefore keep watch, brothers, especially against the plague of sloth, which untimely security is accustomed to produce. Thus those more perfect, as though their vices had already been subdued, recline securely in a good conscience when there is no one to frighten them; while those less perfect find all things readily available through bodily connections, because others provide everything for them. Hence, most beloved, the holy Fathers—whose arduous and narrow footsteps we, burdened and broadened men, not to say fattened or made sleek, have dared to attempt—placed poverty as the cornerstone, as it were, of the two walls of the spiritual building. They divided it in two and extended it to either side: namely, poverty of perception and of spirit, so that whoever sees himself slight in both may remain watchful and diligent on both sides, and may be idle in neither.

For this reason, most beloved, we have led you into this remote, dry, and desolate wilderness—shrewdly, indeed—where you can be humble but cannot be rich. Into this wilderness, I say, lying as though far out at sea and having almost nothing in common with the world, so that, deprived of every worldly and nearly every human consolation, you may be wholly silent from the world; for beyond this small island, now the furthest of all lands, there is nowhere any world for you. O Lord, withdrawing, I fled; and fleeing, I withdrew, so that I wholly do not know where further I may flee or withdraw—you know. Long ago, desiring flight and thirsting for solitude, I finally reached this wilderness, so vast and remote that some who had, as it were, conspired for this expedition failed me, and very few followed. To them even the very horror of solitude is a horror—a feeling which, I confess, is sometimes not absent from me as well.

Moreover, solitude has increased upon solitude, silence upon silence. For so that we may be more eloquent and more accustomed in converse with you alone, we are compelled to be silent even from one another. Yet it is also greatly to our advantage, beloved, to consider with thanksgiving and praise the mercy of God, upon which we have hoped, shown toward us. In his condescension he has so moderated this exile of ours that we are free to pray, meditate, and read, but obliged to labour, so that there may be something for us to give to the needy body, which is still natural. For we ought to eat our bread by the sweat of our own brow, rather than by that of hired labourers or oxen.

Therefore, brothers, my fellow captives and fellow fugitives, as the Prophet says: “You who remember the Lord, do not be silent, and give him no silence” (Isa. 62). Keep watch for him, lest he sleep for you. But I will always cry to you, O Lord; but you, my God, do not be silent to me, do not at any time keep silence from me, lest I become like those in peril at sea. Open when struck by meditation; answer when questioned; hear when entreated. You will surely do this most graciously and abundantly—unless, while speaking, you turn away from our hearing. When heard, you hear; when heeded, you answer. But he who turns away his ear [Col. 1737D] from hearing your law—his prayer shall be an abomination.

Speak therefore, Lord, for your servant hears; and answer the one who speaks. While both sail, let neither sleep. For if you sleep for me, your servant, the sea does not sleep: the memory of the world does not sleep. The waves and surges of thoughts do not sleep if you sleep. If I sleep for you, the flesh does not sleep for me. Therefore, Lord, at last my refuge—you who could first have been my strength, so that I should not flee—awaken, stirred by my sobs, the groans of my heart, and my very necessity, which never keeps silence. Arise; command the winds and the sea; save me from faintness of spirit and storm, that great calm may come outwardly and inwardly, and that men and angels, to whom we have become a spectacle, may see and say in wonder: “What sort of man is this, that even the sea and winds obey him?” [Col. 1738A] Without doubt, brothers, this will happen to us if we obey him who lives and reigns as God for ages.

## SERMON XV. ON THE SAME FEAST, III

As Jesus went up into the boat, etc. (Matt. 8). O human inquisitiveness and the bold presumption of fragile creatures! What first came into the minds of wretched mortals, that, as though cramped by the narrow limits of their own lands, they should make their way across the seas, entrusting their souls to frail wood? Behold, the sea lies before your eyes; the little boat, as you see, brothers, is tossed by waves. What, I ask, separates those wretched sailors between life and death except wood—as we have said—frail, and itself thin [Col. 1738B] as well?

But let us sit a little while and consider this more deeply. As is our custom, let us draw outward sights into inward instruction. We are already weary, and some of the hour remains. Believe me, brothers: if we compare this sea with this world, those whom you see at sea do not seem to me to be in greater danger than all people in the world, or in the flesh. Indeed, our flesh itself may not unfittingly be called a sea. Between them, at least, there lies something—though thin, frail, and untrustworthy—between the breathable, life-giving air and the thick, deadly brine. But between us and our flesh nothing whatever intervenes, nor does anything divide flesh from the world.

Hence, from the moment we come into this corruptible flesh, we have surely come into death. We are not conceived in it before we are received into its gulf; not brought into life before we are plunged into death; not men before sinners; not born before shipwrecked. From the moment we came into the world, we were immediately unclean from the world. But while we are in the flesh, we cannot please God; while we are of the world, we cannot belong to Christ’s kingdom.

The blessed Prophet perceived this shipwreck. Therefore he cries forcefully: “Save me, O God, for waters have entered even unto my soul. I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (Ps. 68). But you ask: “Then have all souls been submerged and endangered in the flesh, and have all who come into the world suffered shipwreck?” Certainly. For we have this most aptly signified in that great and famous universal Flood, [Col. 1738D] where the abyss covered the earth as a garment, where waters stood above all the mountains so that dry land appeared nowhere at all (Gen. 7). That there a few souls were preserved alive by wood, as you see here in the boat, is a type of the life-giving wood, or the vivifying cross of Christ. By the protection and defence of that cross alone, a few elect are saved; though many are called, more who are not called perish utterly.

Therefore only the single, solid wood of faith divides life from death for us. I readily understand the boat into which the Saviour went up to be the cross itself, where he separated death from us—or us from death—and withdrew, separated, and freed us from the world, the flesh, and the devil. “He went up,” it says: not unwillingly, not dragged, but willingly. He went up; he voluntarily offered sacrifice to the Father—both sacrifice and priest, himself offered because he willed it. He laid down his soul when, how, and for however long he willed, he who ran with joy toward the contest set before him.

Where are the murmurers and complainers, the fearful, lukewarm, slow persons, those who must be dragged and driven toward the cross and passion of the Order and penance to which they have sworn themselves and bound themselves? “His disciples followed him,” it says (Matt. 8). For disciples ought to follow their master, servants their lord, children their father. “All who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.” Even if an external persecutor is absent, the disciples of Jesus must crucify their outward person with its vices and desires; and their inward person also must be fastened to the crossbeam of Jesus’ obedience, so that the humble disciple may say in every respect to his spiritual father: “Abba, Father, not what I will, but what you will.”

And if weak flesh is burdened, the soul troubled, and sadness begins to be afraid and weary, still let the spirit always be willing. It alone has its judgment with God, that it may restrain the lower things and make them obey itself while it obeys its superior. I should not without reason call this discipline of your profession and hidden wilderness a cross, where, as solitude separates you from others, so the discipline of obedience separates you from yourselves. You may do nothing that you please; you possess no property in substance or body, no freedom in work or rest. What is this, I ask, except to be fastened for Christ by certain nails of obedience to the rigour of another’s command, to be crucified with Christ?

Now what Christ’s sleep in the boat signifies follows readily from what has been said. To sleep in the ship, indeed, is to die upon the cross, according to the saying: “I slept and was overcome by sleep” (Ps. 3). For who, with such ease or power, falls asleep while awake when he wills, or wakes while asleep when he wills, as the Lord, who laid down his soul when he willed and took it up again when he willed? But while he sleeps, the sea rises, broken loose by winds, and the troubled disciples fear shipwreck. So when he dies, the Jews, driven by demons, exult and insult, while the disciples nearly despair, overcome by fear. These matters are most familiar in the Gospel; we believed them to require notice rather than extended treatment.

For Christ’s awakening, like resurrection from the dead, produced first in the hearts of the Apostles and then in the whole Church—now that the world had been subdued and its prince bound—such tranquillity that whoever does not wonder joyfully at it remains, in his painful astonishment, himself a wondrous and pitiable thing.

Let us therefore consider, brothers, how great he is, and how safe it is to sail for him and with him, to suffer with him and die with him, that we may complete in ourselves, namely in his members, what is lacking of his sufferings. For all members must suffer together wherever the head suffers; the whole Christ must suffer and be perfected by suffering, and thus enter into his glory. Therefore whoever does not suffer with him shall not reign with him at all.

The winds and sea obey him; unless he permits it—as though he slept—no inward or outward, higher or lower temptation can do anything; and when he rebukes it, it is powerless. For as the sacred Psalm contains: “He spoke, and the storm-wind stood; and its waves were lifted up. They rise up to the heavens and go down to the depths,” etc.; and, “He made its storm into a breeze, and its waves were silent” [Col. 1740A] (Ps. 106). For he is faithful and will not permit his own to be tempted beyond what they can bear; but with the temptation he provides an outcome, so that if temptation grows, the strength of patience may grow, and thereby the crown may grow—a crown attained by perseverance alone.

Therefore, brothers, whenever any temptation seizes you—whether of illness, poverty, harsher discipline, more prolonged residence, weariness even with such remote solitude and profound silence, or of whatever kind, for they are altogether innumerable—let us awaken Christ asleep for us by reading, meditation, and prayer. Let us fix our eyes upon the example of his cross and passion for us, as, suddenly bitten by a serpent, we look up at the serpent hanging above (Num. 21). For, as the blessed Apostle Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2).

From this, beloved, we shall receive not only an example to follow, but an antidote lest we die; not only encouragement to endurance, but grace for perseverance; not only a pattern for battle, but strength for victory. Here the prudent and simple dove nests in the clefts of the rock, in the crevices of the wall. [Col. 1740C] Here the turtledove finds herself a nest in which to place her young: your altars, O Lord of hosts. From them there rises so sweet an odour of myrrh and incense, as it is written: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50).

Knowing this, a certain person says, knowing where he or she goes and by what way: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of incense” (Song 4). For the soul, wearied within itself and troubled concerning itself, began to remember the Lord Jesus—that is, its saving countenance—not from the summit of heaven, where he ascended to the glory which he had with the Father before the world existed, but from the land of Jordan, that is, “ascent,” and from little Mount Hermon, where deep calls to deep: that is, our mortification calls upon the death of Christ the Lord; suffering calls upon his passion; and patience likewise calls upon his patience, as its example and aid. Paul also placed on this mountain of myrrh those whom he addresses thus: “You have been mortified, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3).

Therefore, mindful of our Saviour, and especially of his passion and patience, in which he displayed his greatest love toward us and set before us a pattern, let us be tireless and stand immovable against every kind of trial, companions in his sufferings for his sake, that we may also be companions in glory. May he himself grant this to us—without whom we can do nothing and in whom we can do all things—who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit for endless ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. FIRST SERMON FOR SEPTUAGESIMA SUNDAY

[Col. 1741A]

“The kingdom of heaven is like a householder,” etc. (Matt. 20). Truly, beloved, although God’s wisdom is most simple, it is manifold in form; though uniformly one, it is found to be multiply manifold. “Many shall pass through,” says the Prophet, “and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12). It is this wisdom, indeed, which is rightly called “a fountain of gardens and a well of living waters” (Song 4): a fountain because of its inexhaustible abundance; a well because of its incomprehensible depth; and a well of living waters, that is, of senses ever bubbling forth.

Therefore the same parable, or even a passage of Scripture which seems plain, is rightly explained and discussed differently and in different ways by different persons. Yet it is not utterly exhausted by any of them, as though one who spoke before had said everything that could be said from it, leaving nothing for a later interpreter to discover. For whatever can in any way be wisely and truly said of a thing is all, in every mode, simultaneously and always present from eternity in eternal wisdom and truth.

Accordingly, when the Spirit speaks through someone—the Spirit who searches the deep things of God not by investigation but by containing them, of whom it is said, “He who contains all things has knowledge of speech” (Wis. 1)—he simultaneously perceives, understands, and intends all things which can in some measure be truly and usefully said by means of that utterance. The person through whom he speaks may sometimes be empty of that understanding; sometimes content with one sense; sometimes illumined by several senses at once; but never filled with all of them. Hence it is often possible that persons differing or holding diverse views upon the same Scripture may be in full harmony, or agreement, with the Holy Spirit, provided it is established that they do not differ from the faith of truth, the edification of charity, and the overthrow of covetousness, toward which every intention of Holy Scripture is directed.

For one and the same person also thinks differently and in various ways about the same thing at different times, yet not by a different spirit, provided that in both cases, as stated, he agrees with truth and charity. Truth must not be asserted against charity, nor charity maintained against truth. We have touched briefly upon these matters as a kind of preface, lest, when you learn that we venture upon something differently from what you have heard elsewhere or read in others, anyone suspect that we either wholly fail to know the older interpretations, or despise those we know, or vainly delight in novelties of our own. Rather, the attentive hearer must everywhere consider the rationale of what is said in light of the occasion for saying it.

For we have undertaken not so much to expound the readings of the holy Gospel as, taking occasion from them, to say something for the edification of our brothers and ourselves, according to the fear, place, and persons involved—you who do not allow me to remain silent among you. Yet the Apostle exhorts us not to receive any grace of God in vain (2 Cor. 6); indeed David exhorts us not to receive even the soul itself in vain, saying: “He who has not received his soul in vain” (Ps. 23), that is, rational understanding. In the Gospel, too, every talent is required back doubled (Matt. [Col. 1742A] 25). The son of promise likewise cultivated his father’s wells and dug new ones for himself.

Therefore, while preserving with due reverence the interpretation that faithfully and appropriately makes this universal vineyard the Church—in which Christ is the vine, Christians the branches, the Father both cultivator and householder, the day the whole duration or life of man, the hours the ages of the world or of the individual human being, and the marketplace the world’s own covetous and curious commerce—I understand my own soul, and not only that but also my body, and both together—that is, my whole self—to be a vineyard which I must not neglect. It must be dug and cultivated, lest it be trampled by alien shoots and foreign roots; pruned, lest it be overgrown by its own native offshoots and become wild; cleansed, that it may bear more fruit; hedged about on every side, lest it lie open to plunder by those who pass along the way, especially to the boar from the forest and the solitary wild beast, lest they destroy it. In short, it must be cultivated with the utmost care lest the noble offspring of the chosen vine degenerate and turn into a foreign vine, which neither gladdens God nor human beings, or perhaps grieves both; and guarded with the utmost watchfulness lest what has been laboured over so greatly and awaited so long be worn away by the stealthy encroachment of those who devour the poor in secret, or suddenly perish through unexpected devastation.

Hence to the first man, concerning paradise as though it were his own vineyard, it was said: “That he might work it and keep it” (Gen. 3). Yet just as time itself is interspersed with light and darkness—that is, day and night—so also the temporal life of humankind is sometimes in darkness even under the midday sun, and sometimes in light at midnight. And just as God did not say that light shone from day, but from darkness, so the child of this age is born in darkness, who is called a child of night and darkness; and the one whom the Apostle calls a child of light and day is born only from darkness: “You are all,” he says, “children of light and of day, not of night nor of darkness” [Col. 1742D] (1 Thess. 5). Again: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

The child of light is called light, and the child of darkness darkness; for everywhere the child is such as the father is. Therefore unbelief is night and faith day; sin night and virtue day. Ignorance is darkness and wisdom light; hatred darkness and charity light. The devil is darkness and God light; Adam darkness and Christ light. Finally, an evil conscience and delight in sin are night and deep darkness; a good conscience and love of virtue are serene light. Carnal perception or life is darkness; spiritual perception and life are day.

Thus, in the matters of which we have spoken, there is a night in which, as the Savior says, no one can work (John 9). For whoever acts wickedly does not so much act at night as suffer; for every evil action is a certain suffering of a good nature. For he who misuses the good which he naturally is or possesses, while corrupting himself is himself corrupted; and while he produces corruption, he suffers it. The sufferings of night, therefore, [Col. 1743A] and of darkness, are not actions; actions belong only to day and light. Hence the sufferings of Christ’s holy martyrs are more commonly called deeds and victories, their deaths birthdays. For nothing is more laborious than that work which produces incorruptibility and impassibility. Nothing is more laborious than the steadfastness of a strong mind, which at one and the same stroke treads underfoot flesh, world, and devil, whether raging or flattering.

It is therefore clear how subtle and ever true is that assertion of Truth: that no one can work in the night, but only in the day. “I must work,” he says, “while it is day; night is coming, when no one will be able to work” (ibid.). Yet this is fittingly understood of that night after which no one will be able to work, but will forever and eternally only suffer. For among those below there is always only night and suffering; among those above, in eternal day, there is eternal and sole action of praise and thanksgiving. Hence the blessed Prophet sings: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord: for ages upon ages they shall praise you” (Ps. 83 [84]). The first night, therefore, is that from which day may shine forth and work may follow, although it cannot be done within it. But the second night is perpetual darkness: within it no one can work because it is darkness; after it no one can work because it is perpetual. For there is neither work, nor reasoning, nor counsel among the dead: whither the children of this light and of that darkness hasten.

Therefore, beloved, while we have time—that is, day—not the day of man, as the prophet says, “I have not desired the day of man; you know it” (Jer. [Col. 1743C] 17), a day which he here, and blessed Job also, as you know, devoted to many curses—let us do good to all, beginning nevertheless with ourselves. For one who is evil to himself—to whom is he good? “Have mercy,” he says, “upon your own soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30). One who neglects his own vineyard—how shall he cultivate another’s?

We could not work in the night. Behold, light freely came into the world and went before the world. We were born in night, reared in night; but [he came] from spittle above and mud below: from spittle on the head, from mud beneath the foot. The eyes of the man born blind were opened when they had been anointed. A universal night went before, in which all sinned; but when the sun truly began to shine, it departed and the darkness vanished, so that those who previously could not work now have no excuse at all if they refuse to work in the day. “For if,” says Day itself, “I had not come [Col. 1743D] and spoken to them”—that is, had not shone upon them—“they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15).

Whoever does not use grace once received is idle in the day and is rightly reproved for idleness. “You have appointed darkness,” says the Prophet, “and night came to be, in which no one can work; in it all the beasts of the forest shall pass through”—against which the vineyard must be fenced and guarded—“the young lions roaring, that they may seize [their prey]” (Ps. 103 [104]). Because of them man could not go out to his work. But behold, the sun has arisen and, shining upon the earth, makes day, so that the man who has ceased to be a beast may go out to his work in the morning—that is, anticipated by prevenient grace—and may sweat at his labor until evening. For at whatever hour he begins to work, the work is required until evening; nor is the wage paid before evening. For perseverance in good work comes last and receives first.

Thus, since the hour has passed, let us speak briefly. Turning away from God—whether the turning of rational understanding from truth, or of life from charity—is night, in which no one is able to work. But turning toward God through inquiry and imitation is day, in which man goes out to his work: that is, to know and love God, and to delight in his knowledge and love. For this purpose man was made in the image and likeness of God, and by these things he is restored and re-formed to the same: through understanding, to the image; through life, to the likeness. Yet, though made in image and likeness, he is restored to likeness and image, being re-formed through conformity of life unto participation in the divine nature [Col. 1744B].

To know the true God is eternal life; but to love him with the whole heart is the eternal way. Charity, therefore, is the way; truth, life. Charity is likeness; truth, image.
