Charity is merit; truth, reward. By charity one goes; in truth one stands. Hence Lucifer, who “rose in the morning” (Isa. 14) but did not endure until evening, “did not stand in the truth” (John 8), because he strayed from charity. But because charity never fails, when charity has reached truth it does not come to an end; rather, through the truth of charity and in the charity of truth, life is lived as happily as it is everlastingly.

Therefore, beloved, when a man goes out from the night of sin and [Col. 1744C] fleshly conduct to this his work, by the first illumination of grace, as though in the first morning of his conversion to God, his conscience meets him. He sees how he lived while he lived wickedly; in light he discerns what he was in darkness. Thus, when this conscience is first sent into the vineyard, accusing itself, carefully recalling everything and bringing all things back to memory, it undoubtedly bends itself down humbly and digs deeply. Cutting away the roots of every injustice, it begins, indeed, to cultivate itself unto righteousness. “For the righteous man is first the accuser of himself” (Prov. 18).

Yet, just as one turning to God gravely accuses himself concerning the past, so it is necessary that he judge all things with precision and examine them strictly according to the quality, quantity, and cause of the act. Thus reason, offered afterward and making subtle judgment, follows the conscience that accuses and labors in the vineyard of this very accusation; grief and contrition of heart torture that conscience. Therefore, in a certain inner tribunal of ours, let conscience accuse, reason judge, and grief torture, so that while we accuse, judge, and condemn ourselves, we may be absolved by the Lord and not condemned with this world.

Confession of the mouth follows contrition of heart, and finally amendment of conduct follows confession. Though it works last, it is rewarded first. Without it, confession of the mouth is airy breath; contrition of heart is vapor; reason’s judgment tends to condemnation; and conscience’s accusation becomes evidence. For he is a mocker and not penitent who weeps for sins committed and commits sins that should be wept for. Therefore [Col. 1745A], with amendment of conduct all these things profit and receive the reward of labor; without it, they harm and become testimony for just condemnation.

There is still something that might be said differently, and perhaps more deeply, concerning these hours and the vine-growers. But, overtaken by the hour, we have rather touched upon what you have heard than treated it in extended discourse. We have preferred to reserve it for another beginning, to be spoken to your brotherhood, if through your prayers Divine Wisdom itself may deign to grant it: Christ the Lord, the Word of the Father, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

## SERMON XVII. ON THE SAME FEAST, II

Concerning this day, beloved, which in the Gospel parable is divided into morning, the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours, and evening, for labor and labor’s reward (Matt. 20), we do not alter today what we said yesterday: namely, that conversion to God in understanding and affection is to be understood as day, just as turning away is night, in which no one can work.

For human beings have understanding and appetite, according to which they are called animate creatures; and by these they are not separated from beasts by any superiority. Yet if reason is set over them, to rule both, they are indeed at once animate beings in understanding and affection, and human beings in rational mind and penal mortality, necessarily destined after sin and because of sin to die—though before sin and without sin they could have not died. Thus those in whom understanding or affection does not yet follow reason, but resists it, and—as, shamefully, occurs in some—abuses reason itself against itself: these, however shrewd, cunning, perceptive, charming, or gentle, are not yet human beings. Or if, for the sake of speech, they are called human because of reason, then, since they walk head downward, they are shown to be not so much human beings as monsters derived from human beings. “He gave,” says the poet, “man an upraised countenance” (OVID, *Metamorphoses*, I.84).

In such persons, beloved, reason sometimes resists, but is nevertheless overcome and dragged captive—the one thing which is reason. “Woe to the one alone, for if he falls, there is none to lift him up.” At other times it follows willingly, feeble, broken, and emasculated; it yields and freely gives itself over to every defilement. The former, then, are evil; the latter, most evil. Both are children of night and darkness; but some love their night, others desire day; some have nothing human in them, others little; some are unbound, others bound. Both are in darkness and walk in darkness; they have become the nocturnal prey of the beasts of the forest—that is, fleshly passions and worldly desires—and of the young lions—that is, spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places—as it is written: “You have appointed darkness, and night came to be; in it all the beasts of the forest shall pass through, the young lions,” and so forth (Ps. 103 [104]).

When, therefore, a man turns his attention to himself, whether to his own understanding, will, or even reason, although he has progressed so far as to put off the beast and put on the human being, he neither escapes night nor enters day. “My soul was troubled within me,” says the Seer; “therefore it began to remember God as day” (Ps. 39 [40]). For God is wholly light, and in him alone there is no darkness whatsoever. For holy angels, although they find morning in him, encounter evening in themselves; and from their evening and God’s morning one day, or the first day, is completed. Thus God alone finds day in himself; and when, by prevenient grace, he begins to shine upon the rational mind, he makes morning for it and divides between darkness and light.

The dawn-before-daybreak of the spiritual day, then, is grace, which goes before reason and turns it from itself toward God. It brings it out of the darkness of ignorance—or, as has been said, of impotence or even malice—into the day of wisdom, virtue, and righteousness: that is, into Christ the Lord. Yet I do not think that only one day of Christ should be named; for he himself speaks of several, saying: “Your father Abraham rejoiced that he might see my days; and he saw and was glad” (John 8). There is a day of fear, a day of love, a day of joy, a day of labor, a day of rest, a day of exultation. “Let us exult,” says the Prophet, “and rejoice in the day which the Lord has made” (Ps. 117 [118]). There is the day of the cross, the day of the tomb, the day of resurrection. “He will revive us after two days,” he says; “on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. 6). There is the sixth day, on which every work is completed; the Sabbath, on which one rests from every work; and the Lord’s Day, on which one rises to new joy and to “a solemn day amid dense throngs, unto the horn of the altar”: that is, to the glory of the Passion, the fruit of labor, the exaltation [Col. 1746C] of the cross.

O blessed soul, which, though still weighed down by earthly dwelling, could be in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day and hear behind itself a voice (Rev. 1)—a voice which I wish that I might hear before me, even if only from afar! But meanwhile, beloved, let us restrain this impetus of the Spirit and measure ourselves by ourselves. Let us return to the day of fear, the day of weariness and dread, so that we may begin to be weary and afraid with Christ; and, on the day of his labor and sweat, labor and sweat with him, suffer with him also, and be crucified with him. For the Lord Jesus truly endured all things for us on the day of his struggle, and mystically set before us what we must endure in conformity with him.

Therefore, as one goes out from darkness and the shadow of death—that is, from turning away from God and turning perversely toward the world or oneself—in order to turn toward God, as though from the back of the head to the forepart of the head, there first meets him the remembrance of past evils, fear of future ones, weariness at what has been done, and dread of what must be suffered. For he begins to recall that he lived wickedly and to fear lest he die more wickedly; and conscience, accusing itself, is found to be the first laborer in the vineyard. This is the first grace of the penitent and the hour of conversion.

Memory, moreover, presents to the heart—that is, to affection—what it recalls; for affection is thought to have its seat in the heart, as understanding has its seat in the head. Rational understanding is recognized as existing in three faculties: natural capacity, reason, and memory. These are believed to flourish and exercise their proper functions in distinct and ordered chambers of the animal head: the forepart of the head, the crown of the head, and the back of the head. Thus, for understanding returning from behind to before, as the Apostle says, “forgetting the things behind and stretching himself toward those before” (Phil. 3), the remembrance of past things first meets it, as has been said; and it begins to see the things in which it was while it was evil.

Affection, or feeling, is also understood as twofold. For the heart is affected in two ways toward all that those three faculties offer it: by love or by hatred. From these, owing to time, whose changeableness the mutable heart follows and by which it varies temporally, arise the four named and familiar affections—the foundation and common material, and, so to speak, the elements of all virtues or vices. Consoling his foster-child, Philosophy sang thus concerning them:

> [Col. 1747B]  
> Drive away joys,  
> Drive away fear,  
> Put hope to flight,  
> Let no pain be present.  
> The mind is clouded  
> And bound with reins  
> Wherever these hold sway.  
> (*BOETHIUS, On the Consolation of Philosophy*, I, poem 7, vv. 25–31.)

Thus, according to present, past, and future, joy and hope arise from love; fear and grief from hatred. Love and hatred themselves, moreover, flow from the concupiscible and irascible faculties, so that, just as the head is three-chambered, the heart may be found two-chambered; and the whole soul, brought to natural completion in understanding and affection, may be concupiscible, rational, and irascible.

Hence, for the transgressor returning to his heart, the irascible faculty first meets him—the faculty which was last when he was departing—and it is the third part in the whole soul. Thus not inappropriately at the third hour the second grace is sent into the vineyard: so that whatever conscience rationally accuses through memory, compunction or inward grief may torment through the irascible faculty according to its quality and quantity. Thus everything that formerly tasted sweet in life through pleasure may be bitter in memory through compunction, as it is written: “I shall review for you all my years in the bitterness of my soul” (Isa. 38). Thus recollection works first, bitterness afterward: recollection in the morning, bitterness at the third hour. It is miserable and foolish to forget sins; more miserable to remember them without repentance of heart; most miserable to take delight in them through revisiting them.

At the sixth hour, because work pertains to the number six, good affection itself works. For affection gives a work its name, and the quality of intention is recognized from the fruit of the work. “You may discern,” says the poet, “the inward disposition from the outward.” Thus, when the heart’s affection is changed, the exercise of the body is necessarily changed. For the movement of the heart uses the movement of its body as a master uses a slave subject to him. Therefore bodily motion is of itself external to judgment, just as it is external to free choice. For judgment concerning obedience or disobedience, virtue or vice, rightly belongs only to the movement of the heart, to which alone God has granted freedom of choice. Therefore, just as the man turned away from God, delighting in evil, gave the members of his body to serve that which he himself served—namely, impurity and iniquity unto iniquity—so, turned toward God, he gives these same members to serve righteousness unto sanctification.

At the sixth hour, therefore, bodily exercise is sent into the vineyard as the third grace, so that, as grief cultivates the inward person, labor may cultivate the outward: chastening through abstinence, wearying through work, attenuating through vigils. For when man comes forth from the darkness of the womb into the light of the world, he is indeed born for labor, but begins with pain. In a similar manner, one who comes forth from the darkness of carnality into the light of spirituality begins with pain and rises toward labor, as it is written: “Man is born for labor” (Job 5). Yet the words that follow—“and the bird for flight”—accord excellently with the thread we have woven.

For by the name of bird the reason of the mind itself is rightly understood: it surpasses beasts, as creatures that walk on feet, and is of a nature akin to angels. Hence at the ninth hour the fourth grace is sent into the vineyard, when reason rises above the active life, which is lived through the exercise of the lower soul, on the wings of reading, meditation, and prayer to seek God, and is directed to love him. Therefore, as reason is sent into the vineyard at the ninth hour, so delight is sent at the eleventh. For what remains after the active life except the contemplative, which is perfected by the vision and delight of God? But because in this wretched pilgrimage, where all things are partial and nothing perfect is found, neither is brought to completion: the former is not shown to have reached ten, nor the latter twelve [Col. 1748C].

Delight therefore comes later, labors less, but receives first. “In the way of your commandments,” he says, “I have delighted as in all riches” (Ps. 118 [119]).

Whatever sweetness, delight, and pleasantness we feel in our exercises and wearisome labors, we undoubtedly taste as though from the reward of labor. For before we begin to delight in and love the discipline of the Lord, everything is scarcely endured, scarcely borne, under the burden of the day and heat; in pain and compulsory service, under fear and murmuring, weariness and sloth afflict us. But when at the eleventh hour charity, the fifth grace, is joined to discipline, and good affection to labors—an affection which makes one delight and rejoice in everything—then every burden becomes light and every yoke pleasant. There begins a certain setting of fear and labor, weariness and sadness; but a rising of love and sweetness, fervor and cheerfulness: the evening of the first day and morning of the second. That is, a certain delight, enlargement of heart, and inward exultation and gladness of mind, which undoubtedly no one knows except one who receives it: the beginning of perfection, which ends the beginning; the beginning of fullness, which empties what is partial; finally, the beginning of perfect charity, which casts out fear, removes labor, and wipes away sorrow.

Thus, when memory has long labored, when the irascible faculty and bodily exercise have borne the burden and heat of the day, and rationality also has finally sweated, the concupiscible faculty comes last, yet seizes first. It ends labor and begins the reward; by laboring less than all the others, it lessens their labor; by receiving first, it causes them to receive; and, while itself rests, it draws everything into rest. Therefore the spirit delighting in God speaks thus to its soul, which it had formerly felt wearied, fearful, sad, anxious, troubled, and laboring in its exercise: “Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you, because he has delivered my soul from death”—that is, from sin—“my eyes from the pit”—that is, from the sorrow of past sin—“my feet from slipping” (Ps. 114 [116])—that is, from fear of the future.

Whoever, therefore, delights in everything he does and suffers is troubled by nothing at all, labors at nothing, and is burdened by nothing. Thus under the light yoke and pleasant burden he truly finds for his soul, as the reward of work, rest, as the Savior promises: “And you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11). And so, in holy conduct, with heart enlarged by the inexpressible sweetness of good habit, he joyfully and praisefully runs the way of God’s commandments on the second day—that is, the day of charity, which casts out fear. On the first day, namely the day of fear, he had been oppressed by the burden and heat of cultivating the vineyard; he found the narrow way, entered through the narrow gate, and within dug up hard and intractable soil.

But when we have come to that great abundance of God’s sweetness, which he has hidden for those who fear him but revealed to those who love him, nothing that is established as being for Christ will be hard, harsh, or burdensome for us. But because we shall feel sweetness and delight everywhere, this alone shall be our complaint: that all we do is too little. We shall gladly and fervently gird ourselves for more exacting exercises of devotion, that everywhere we may taste beforehand a greater pleasantness of delights. Even the remembrance of sins will no longer serve for compunction of fear, but will kindle thanksgiving.

Such persons are saddened in their exercise on the day of weariness and labor, the sixth day of work, the day of Passion and cross, while they are still living and are crucified with Christ. But on the day of peace and rest, the day of tranquility and silence, the day of burial and Sabbath, as though dead to sins and the world, they are buried and rest with Christ within themselves. Thus on the third day, the day of exultation and salvation, the day [Col. 1749D] of solemnity and joy, the day of resurrection and glory, finally the Lord’s Day, the eighth day and first of the new light, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so they too, raised with him, may walk in newness of life, living in the Spirit and walking in the Spirit. Amen.

## SERMON XVIII. ON SEXAGESIMA

“A sower went out,” etc. (Luke 8). Amid the abundant lack of the quiet and lovable poverty of ours, we are rich, as you see, in the poverty of books, and especially of commentaries. For as someone rejoicing said commendably, “I gave up the Gospel for the sake of the Gospel,” so we left books for the sake of books. Taught by holy books the virtue of holy solitude, the fruit of quiet, and the grace of poverty, we went out not only, as once before, from house and fleshly kindred, but even, as though forgetting many holy brethren and the house of our spiritual father. Renouncing both the rest of abundance and the numerous variety of manuscripts, and making loss of almost the whole world and the human race, a few of us, naked and shipwrecked, escaped to this remote island enclosed by the Ocean, embracing the naked cross of the naked Christ.

Therefore, because you do not allow us to be silent and demand the frequent exercise of our living voice instead of reading, in the other readings of the holy Gospel we do not follow explanations common everywhere. Rather, we expound more freely what we judge suitable to the time, place, business, and persons. For an exposition is not discordant with the meaning of the supreme Scribe—that is, the finger of God—when it excludes the riddles of Scripture in order to destroy in its hearers the kingdom of desire and build up that of charity. But in this reading we are banished from such unfettered freedom, since the one who sets forth the text also expounds it.

The seed, therefore, is the Word of God; the sower is the Son of Man, but he himself is the Word of God. Thus the seed and the sower are the same: hence he sows himself. He alone is able worthily to sow—that is, to preach—himself. “We do not preach ourselves,” says the outstanding preacher, “but Jesus” (2 Cor. 4). I fear that today there may be one who preaches himself, who wishes by speaking of Jesus to make a name for himself; who seeks his own glory or gain by speaking of another; who, casting himself outside himself, sows into the wind, so that he remains empty within and does not gather himself without; who puts truth before others but brings vanity in himself; who offers an antidote but drinks poison himself; who argues all the better about humility as he grows worse in pride; who preaches poverty while craving wealth, contempt of the world while coveting it, mercy while being miserly, submission while being ambitious.

The holy Word of the Father speaks what it is and does what it teaches; of it it is written: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1). And thereby this sower sows himself by the example of life and the word of teaching, saying: “Learn from me what you see in me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). But from where did he go out in order to sow? He went out from where he did not depart; he came to where he did not arrive. The Word went out from the bosom of the Father and came into the womb of the Virgin; thence, going out in flesh, he came into the world as the sower into a field: the Son of Man.

Those who sow customarily draw seed from hidden granaries, fill certain baskets which they carry for sowing, and thus go out into the field to sow. Therefore this seed and sower, going out from the hidden and unsearchable granary of divinity, where fullness dwells, was sent by the Virgin’s giving birth into the basket of flesh. From it he sows himself from himself: seed, sower, and basket alike. “But while he sowed,” etc. (Luke 8).

This wise farmer knows the differing character of his land, yet he sows the earth indiscriminately and, as if ignorant, industriously makes a loss of costly seed. What does this mean? Does he sow differently? For there are several sowings of the word: one inward, another outward; one to the ears of flesh, another to the ears of the heart; finally, one outward to the ears by the word of teaching, another to the eyes [Col. 1751A] by the example of life, another inwardly to the heart by the inspiration of grace.

In these three things, then, Christ possessed the perfection of heavenly teaching. For he who teaches hearts has his chair in heaven. The scribes and Pharisees, disciples of Moses, speak but do not act: sowing in ears, not in eyes. But the righteousness of Christ’s disciples abounds beyond theirs: for they speak and act, sowing in ears and eyes. Christ, the one teacher, sows outwardly by life and voice; inwardly he assists by the gift of grace. Thus he does not sow indiscriminately in the field, although he scatters the seed of the word outwardly among all. “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice,” etc. (John 3). You hear the voice outwardly without distinction; but by what cause, reason, grace, discrimination, and hidden counsel of God it comes, and why the voice universally uttered outwardly goes inwardly in a particular way to this person or that, you do not know.

There is, then, a fourfold distinction among hearers of the word. Some have hearts trampled down and hardened. They hear preaching outwardly with the ear, but do not receive it in the heart; for them words fall beside the way, not on the way of faith or obedience. “For faith is not of all” (2 Thess. 3), nor do all obey the Gospel (Rom. 10). For the demon flits between ear and heart and draws out through one ear what enters through the other, lest it descend to the heart. When the preacher rises to speak outwardly, the devil rises to speak against him inwardly: either suggesting that what is said is false, or perverting it, or attacking the one by whom it is said, or burdening the hearer with sleep or other thoughts.

Others have ease of obedience but lack the strength of steadfastness. Like the children of Ephraim bending the bow, they turn back on the day of battle: quickly pierced with compunction, more quickly dried up; temporary and shallow, having no deep root of charity. In peace they believe; in temptation they withdraw. While nothing inwardly pricks them, they are chaste; while nothing outwardly rages, brave; if no one troubles them, gentle; if all things prosper, devout. To them applies: “He will praise you when you have done him good” (Ps. 48 [49]). Truly children of Adam: like father, like children. He stood only so long as he had no occasion to fall; he stood until, lightly struck, he collapsed. As the first are excessively hard, so these are excessively soft; the former obstinate, the latter faint-hearted; the former do not receive the word, these do not retain it.

The third retain it, yet not for fruit to themselves but as testimony against themselves: they are ground, barren and uncultivated under the old curse, bringing forth thorns and thistles. Against them the prophet cries: “Break up your fallow ground, and do not sow upon thorns” (Jer. 4). Malice hardens the first; poverty of heart dissolves the second; avarice constricts the third; anxiety lays them waste, cares oppress them, riches choke them, pleasures emasculate them, gluttony and drunkenness weigh them down. Thus, in the hand of a drunkard, thorns grown up instead of grain prick and tear it.

Who today, when this very Word of God adduces it, Truth itself expounds it, and divine Wisdom interprets it—the Wisdom which knows the nature and power of all things—regards riches as thorns? Who refuses to embrace them as thorns? Believe God’s Word: riches are thorns. Whoever embraces them, like a bundle of thorns, is pricked more sharply the more tightly he binds them to himself. Yet fools, thinking delights lie beneath brambles, are torn by true and inward wounds while they are deceived by false and brief pleasures.

When we frighten people away from these thorns as food for hell, they all cry out that riches truly are thorns, yet do not abandon them. They praise and call us happy, as though we had already escaped; they accuse themselves and curse the world which they love; they serve it and speak against it; they carry hay and murmur. They are not possessors of the world but possessed by it—indeed, thrown down and crushed beneath it. Like that fire-vomiting giant beneath the mass of mountains, they cannot rise. Where the love of this world reigns, the charity of the Father has not, to use a rustic expression, a deep crumb; yet this alone receives the seed of the Son unto fruit.

Let us give thanks to the Father, the farmer, who through the Holy Spirit has made us fit for the seed of the Son, pouring the fire of charity into our hearts. With the thorns burned away, our cultivated soil bears fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or even a hundredfold in patience. For obedience receives the seed of the word; patience makes it fruitful; perseverance harvests it. And as the Apostle says of athletes: “All run, but one receives the prize” (1 Cor. 19 [9]); so it may be said of virtues. All run toward the kingdom of God, but one receives the prize. Contempt of the world runs, poverty, almsgiving, abstinence, obedience, patience: perseverance alone is crowned. “For he who perseveres unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10); and the Lord judges the ends of the earth. For middles, like beginnings, undergo no examination; and it is not beginning but completing that is counted as virtue. Thus patience commends obedience, and perseverance crowns it.

## SERMON XIX. ON THE SAME FEAST, II

“A sower went out to sow his seed” (Luke 8). The Son of Man indeed went out from the Virgin’s womb and sowed himself—that is, the Word of God—in human ears by voice, in eyes by example, and in hearts by grace. But while he sows, four kinds of hearers are found. The first hear, but are not permitted by the Evil One, to whom they have enslaved themselves, to believe so that they may act well. Enslaved to him as servants, they have been, as it were, conquered and sold by him so that they may act wickedly. The second hear and receive with joy—that is, easily—but with the same lightness with which they are touched, reject it in the heat of temptation and make it abortive. To such applies Jeremiah’s saying: “Faith has perished and has been removed from their mouth” (Jer. 7). The third confess with their mouths but choke [the word] by their deeds. The fourth believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation.

But on closer consideration it is clear that this sower neither first went out from here, nor first sowed here, nor first found these differences in the field now. “I went out from the Father and came into the world” (John 16), certainly—but through the womb. Hence he did not first go out from a human being, nor did he first sow among human beings. For God did not first speak to human beings, but even to angels. “God has spoken once,” he says, “and does not repeat it a second time” (Job 33). We ask—and the question is worthy to be asked: a question of reverence, not curiosity; of devotion, not presumption—to whom God spoke once something which he cannot repeat, nor speak anything else before it: he who can do all things.

Therefore, my brothers, a certain mind devoted to God and impatient with love sought her Beloved in bed; she sought outside the bed, in the city; she sought through the lanes; she sought through the streets; and altogether she could not find him, until she had passed beyond the watchmen—that is, the angels, who never sleep. But when she had passed beyond the whole height of angelic nature, then at last she found him; having found him, she held him and did not let him go. O blessed soul, [Col. 1753B] which sought so earnestly, found so happily, held so firmly, and kept so wisely! What are we doing, brothers? Should not these few things, though not small things, suffice for every spiritual exercise: she sought, she found; she held, and did not let go? What else must be done, or remains to be done besides?

That clear-sighted, God-seeing eagle sought what we seek—the first and one Word—and, having traversed all that came from non-being into being, found in the beginning that which did not begin to be: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). But how can that be in the beginning which cannot exist without a beginning? For everything that is a word cannot possibly exist without any beginning. Everything which is a word must be someone's word; and it is evident that, in order to be a word, it proceeds from its speaker. Therefore the Word proceeded from him whose Word it is. But how, when, of what sort, and from whom did the first word proceed? For who spoke first, how, and to whom?

But, that we may investigate these matters more fully, we must begin a little higher up, from ordinary and customary speech. Before all things, therefore, in order that any things whatsoever may in any way be, it is altogether necessary that they simply be. For that which in no way is is altogether nothing; and that which is not is utterly in no way and is nothing. Thus pure essence is encountered first in every composition and last in every resolution. Before it, indeed, nothing is found which underlies forms; nor after it anything, once forms have been abstracted from it in thought. [Col. 1753C]

For the intellect divides what actuality does not divide; and from that to whose condition something may be added, so that it may be that thing, something may also be withdrawn, so that it may not be that thing. Moreover, form itself, which can be added to matter and withdrawn from it—if it is not, it too is nothing. Therefore whatever is, receives the form of being and subsists, so that it may be this or that thing—that is, so that it may be held within some species. For everything that is, is because it is numerically one, so that it can subsequently be distinguished by measure and situated by weight. No one denies that all things whatsoever are bounded by number, measure, and weight, except one who is ignorant of all things.

Thus, in investigating any thing, the first question is, since it is, what it is; then, what sort of thing it is; third, for what purpose it is—that is, concerning its nature, form, and use. Hence those devoted to such studies discovered—not, indeed, that they themselves made them—that there are three natural disciplines, [Col. 1754A] in which the whole study of wisdom is sufficiently occupied: namely physics, logic, and ethics—that is, natural, rational, and moral philosophy. Let us therefore first follow natural philosophy and ask what every thing that is found to exist can be. Everything that exists, then, either exists through itself or needs another in order to be able to exist.

Therefore, as we seek God, than whom nothing is worthier, let us gladly follow whatever appears better and worthier, until we attain, at least by reason, to that which is most worthy and than which nothing can be better; may we hold it by affection and preserve it by diligence.

Having therefore set aside that which does not subsist through itself but inheres in another in order to be able to exist—whence it is rightly called an adjunct or accident [Col. 1754B]—let us consider the thing existing through itself. Yet for this we need the second discipline which we mentioned, in order to discern in what manner any thing may subsist through itself.

A thing is said to subsist by nature or in actuality, by reason or in reality. For example, for a human being to subsist in reason, or by nature, nothing beyond “rational mortal animal” is required. For this is the whole being of a human being, and nothing further is added for a human being to subsist as human. But whether he is wise or not; of this or that size; father or son; white or black; sitting or not sitting; here or elsewhere; acting or being acted upon at a given time; armed or unarmed—none of this is required for being human. Yet no one exists, it is clear, without some such determinations; that is, no one subsists in reality and actuality without them.

Thus a human being subsists through himself insofar as he is human, and every individual human being subsists through himself insofar as he is some human being. Hence both are called substance: both “human being,” which subsists in reason, and “some human being,” which subsists in actuality. But that which is known to subsist in actuality is called substance properly, principally, and most especially; whence it is termed first substance. That which subsists only by reason and intellect has received the name of second substance. Every substance, that is, every thing existing through itself, is therefore either first or second. [Col. 1754C]

But they differ: first substance subsists through itself and in itself; second substance through itself, but not in itself. For second substance is found to exist only in first substance. Second substance therefore subsists only by reason, or nature, or abstracting intellect; first substance by reason and reality together, by nature and actuality, by intellect and determinate condition. Hence that substance is called truer and better which subsists as numerically one both in reason and in reality, than that which is understood only in reason and intellect, as though common, indeterminate, and suspended. For a human being is nowhere found to exist who is not some particular human being. Yet neither does any particular human being, this one or that one, exist unless he is altogether human.

Therefore, just as second substance does not subsist except in first substance, so first substance does not subsist except from second substance. For second substance takes precedence in reason, in order that first substance may be able to be; but first substance subsists in actuality, lest second substance be nowhere and thereby nothing. For there is no human being if there is not altogether a human being; but neither is there a human being anywhere if there is no individual human being. The same holds likewise concerning substance itself. For if substance itself [Col. 1754D] is not, neither this nor that substance will be. Yet although it is itself, it cannot exist except in this or that substance.

Substance, therefore, lies before all things existing through themselves—that is, before substances—as their rational and causal nature and, as it were, matter: so that they may not only be, which belongs to essence, but may be what they are, namely substances. Yet this substance, being such—that is, common to all and general—nowhere subsists. Although it has nothing before itself as material from which it may be, it nevertheless contains beneath itself those without which, and except in which, it can nowhere subsist.

Thus we may conclude generally that every substance is first or second; every second substance indeed exists through itself, but none in itself; every first substance exists through itself, but none from itself. Both are therefore imperfect and needy: the former lacks existence in itself, the latter existence from itself; the former needs something before it from which it may be, the latter something after it in which and from which it may be. But behold, beloved brethren—I confess that I do not know by what impatience my mind leaps beforehand—from the imperfection of these, which are the only and entire substances, there begins to shine through, as it were, a certain supersubstance, if it may be called so: one which subsists through itself, in itself, and from itself, altogether in reason and reality, nature and actuality, intellect and determinate condition. Nothing is before it, in order that it may be something; nothing beneath it, lest it be nothing; nothing above it, from which it may derive; nothing below it, except that in which it cannot subsist; nothing before it for nature, nothing after it for determinate condition, nothing outside it for form.

If this is true, and the mind is not mocked by an empty phantasm, then that is far better than every substance. Therefore I must in no way worship substance, whether first or second, when something better—even if perhaps it does not exist—can at least be conceived. Accident, as we have said, is subsequent to every substance; and therefore, since it cannot exist except in substance, without substance it must be nothing. Thus, if substance is not, accident is not. But if accident, which comprises the nine predicaments, is not, there will be no second substance at all, by which lower substances are specified from higher ones and by which second substances descend into first substances. Therefore, if there is no form, no first substance will subsist in actuality. If no first substance subsists, there will be no second substance at all, which has no subsistence except in the first. [Col. 1755A] Therefore no substance is proved to exist if no accident exists; yet accident is nothing without substance, nor is substance anywhere without accident.

For second substance, as it is understood by abstraction, is nowhere in itself and is nothing in actuality; rather, it is conceived confusedly in the mind and held suspended in the intellect until, as forms arrive, it is clothed as it were and established in some first thing and actuality. Yet that first thing will be nothing at all if form is absent; nor will form exist unless substance itself exists.

Thus each, that is, subject and accident, or substance and form, considered by itself without the other, is manifestly found to be nothing and empty; so that from two nothings—matter considered by itself and form considered by itself—a third being can consist only as nothing, namely every composite. As the prophet plainly says, speaking generally of humanity: “All nations, he says, are before him as though they were not”—namely before him who truly is, through himself and in himself, not in another before him or above him—“and they are reckoned as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. 40), as though made from nothing and emptiness. Therefore, “he who thinks himself something, when he is nothing, deceives himself.”

Let us therefore cease seeking something, since we are nothing; cease seeking that which truly is, since we truly are not at all. For the distinction from all things was made when it was said, “I am who am” (Exod. 3), so that everything which is not that may say: “I am who am not,” or, “I am not who am.” Come then, brothers: what progress have we made? Seeking something, we found nothing. Seeking God, [Col. 1756B] we lost ourselves. For when through a very narrow crevice something of not-nothing began to glimmer, it then shone upon us with great light how much we are nothing from nothing. Lord, truly in your light we shall see your light—and our darkness.

But here, beloved, we must pause today, since we are wearied by labour and speaking. For while we are pilgrims away from that house where there is “the sound of exultation and confession, of one feasting,” we eat both kinds of bread in the sweat of our face. May he bring us there, for whose sake we are exiles, here on this island and in this wilderness, from almost the whole inhabited world.

## SERMON XX. ON THE SAME FEAST, III

[Col. 1756C] Yesterday, beloved, while seeking God, as you know, we found him as we lost ourselves. Fittingly indeed: as those who fell below and outside ourselves, let us return inwardly through ourselves to him. Reflected by the divine light of the countenance streaming through a narrow and confined lattice, we fell upon our faces—that is, from our estimate of ourselves as above what we are, into recognition of what we are.

Finally, investigating what God is, we found what he is not. Going about through lanes and streets—that is, through all rational substances and real states—we did not find him in them: him whose nature is not something, nor a thing of nature; him who is not otherwise conceived by mental abstraction than he subsists in reality. Therefore none of all things is anything; or rather, all things are nothing, [Col. 1756D] he alone neither being nothing nor existing from nothing.

He must therefore be sought, as you see, above all things which, from nothing, are nothing: he who is neither any one of all things nor altogether nothing. But where shall we go, Lord our God, outside the universe? With what wings shall we fly above every corporeal and incorporeal substance—we human beings burdened with flesh and weighed down by sins—to seek you, for whom nothing outside you can be sufficient or pleasant to us? Lord, behold, we have left all things for you; and if we have found favour before you, show us yourself, desirable and lovable as you are. Our soul refuses every consolation; we delight only in remembrance of you and in such exercise. And behold, our spirit has failed because it has not yet seen you. If you are neither corporeal nor incorporeal substance, what are you?

Let us see, then, whether perhaps you are incorporeal substance, like the watchmen whom she nevertheless passed beyond—the woman who diligently sought and happily found. Substance, therefore, which is conceived in the mind as the most general genus, is first and sufficiently divided into corporeal and incorporeal substance. Every substance must be of one kind or the other; and what is neither is not substance. But the proper property of substance, and that which is coextensive with it, is receptivity of contraries. Hence this receptivity of contraries is called the rule of coextensives in respect of substance itself. Thus this substance and that, just as each is substance, are likewise receptive of contraries. From this it follows that it is mutable not only through things divided and unlike, but even through contraries. Hence, according to another discipline, substance has been called the foundation of the elements and of all changes, mutable in every respect, underlying all things, and never remaining constant to itself. [Col. 1757A]

But we were seeking not a changeable foundation of accidents, but the unchangeable Father of lights, “with whom there is no change nor shadow of turning.” Clearly he cannot properly be called even incorporeal substance; and it would be impious to declare him receptive of contraries. For it is plainly better to be unchangeable than changeable. And, as is clear from what precedes, what is unchangeable must be confessed to be neither substance nor in substance, but above every substance, and accordingly to be called supersubstance.

For substance itself altogether admits no division whereby one substance is called mutable and another immutable, since receptivity of contraries is proper to it and cannot at all be said of the immutable. Nor is a higher genus divided into lower things in this way: mutable substance does not fall below substance itself, but is altogether the same thing; and substance, in the same generality, contains all substances and underlies forms. Therefore that which is called immutable substance is in no way subordinated to substance, but is set above it in dignity, opposed to it by contrariety of nature, and set beneath it in efficient causation. As mutable substance lies beneath all things, so this immutable reality stands above all things. The former is mutable in and through all things; the latter is unchangeable outside and above all things. [Col. 1757B]

The former is understood only as abstracted in the conception of the mind and exists in things of its own nature; the latter truly exists in itself, comprehensible by no mind, having no higher nature in which it may be conceived, nor lower natural thing in which it may be established. For what is one is simple and stable; and this cannot be found at all among all things. Hence it is above all things: as one, above matter; as simple, above what is material; as immovable, above every creature. For as every creature comes from non-being into being through movement, so it is variable through being and can tend toward non-being. But you, Lord my God, are the same: you are simple, and your years shall not fail; you are immutable; and from these things you are understood to be eternal.

Come then, brothers: since we are weary from flying, let us return to our feet, descending to what remains of the day’s labour, alternating the human being for work and the bird for flight. In both we are taught and aided by him who displayed both in himself, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages. Amen. [Col. 1758A]

## SERMON XXI. ON THE SAME FEAST, IV

Seeking, beloved, our Lord—of whom it is written, “Seek his face always” (Ps. 105)—for whose sake we must seek him while he may be found, we almost gladly lost the whole human race and ourselves. The day before yesterday we went about through lanes and streets; yesterday we passed a little beyond the watchmen of the city (Song 3). Thus, above all matter and form, and above the incorporeal substance of simple nature, we found, by opposition to matter itself, the one, simple, and immovable reality. If nothing is better than this, and nothing can be better, it is surely our God.

Let us then seek today no longer among all things, but now above all things, examining what we have found: whether it is best not merely among all things that are, but, as we said, among all things that can be. First, what is immutable can neither improve nor deteriorate in any respect. Therefore it cannot become, from what it is, either greater, or lesser, or other, or otherwise; and whatever it already is must always be that. Second, because it is simple, what it has, that it is. For it is impossible for what is truly simple, whether in nature, form, or property, to have anything other than what it itself is. Third, since it is one, it cannot have something before itself from which it might be. For one must necessarily be before all things. It is impossible for there to be many if there is not one; indeed it is equally impossible for there to be several except from one.

Therefore the one is before all things; all things are from the one; and the principle of all things is altogether one. The one is before all things, the simple after all things, and the immutable above all things. From unity comes the plurality of all things; from simplicity, the diversity of the universe; from immutability, all mutability. From the one comes everything numerically multiple; from the simple, everything numerically composite; from the immovable, everything moved in whatever manner. For just as every movement arises from the immovable, so every composite arises from the simple.

And what, I ask, my brothers—whose eager hearts I perceive—can be better than that which now shines clear to investigation through the unveiling grace: namely, something before all things, from which are all things; after which nothing is, and above which nothing is; the principle by which all things are brought into being; the end which contains all things lest they fall back into non-being; eternity moving and governing all things in being; creator, ruler, and sustainer of the universe; the immutable principle for which Jacob, beloved of God, served seven years—for this is what Rachel is interpreted and signifies; the principle in which that blessed theologian, fishing, caught what we seek, the holy Word of God; [Col. 1759A] the principle which is all that it is and cannot be otherwise or something else.

Are you this, Lord my God, whom I sought among all things and found above all things: neither something among all things nor altogether nothing; neither the intermediate between all things and nothing, where Plato placed matter, but that from which matter itself flowed by a wondrous operation?

You have shown us two things, Lord, to us your servants: that you are, and what you are not. And we burn for the third, namely to know what you are. Truly, “he who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccl. 1). For we are shaken with a greater burning to know what you are, because neither that you are nor what you are not can remain hidden or deceive us. O that we did not know what you are not, and were deceived by some pleasing phantasm in your place; or rather, that we knew what you are and truly and sweetly embraced you.

But show us yourself, Lord—you whom, as you know, we desire today only, and love only for your sake; we who have fled with our mind from the whole world and almost with our body from the whole world, that unencumbered we might seek you. But since I am not yet able to satisfy my thirst by seeing you, let me at least vomit out the indignation of my spirit against the fool who blasphemed you. For you, O fool, said in your heart, yourself outside your heart: “There is no God” (Ps. 13). Yet you could not even have said this if he whom you deny did not exist, without whom nothing could exist.

Therefore, if you exist who said this, without doubt he of whom you spoke also exists. For whatever is must either be a principle or be from a principle. Hence, if you are from a principle, there necessarily is a principle from which you are; but if you yourself are a principle, then you are what you deny to exist. Again, whatever is is either simple or composite—that is, it must be from the simple. Thus either you do not exist, or you are one of these. Likewise, whatever is is either immovable or derives its capacity for motion, however it moves, from the immovable; for every motion arises from the immovable. Therefore, if anything is, it is either one, simple, and immovable, or it must be from these.

But if there is altogether nothing of all things, God himself nevertheless is: from him can come whatever it is possible to be. For with him are present not only the things that are, but whatever things can be: he “calls those things which are not as though they were.” Moreover, O senseless and foolish one, who by denying affirm what you deny: [Col. 1759B] if what you affirmed is true, you have truly lied to your own destruction. For if this is true, something is true; and if God never existed, this was always true. But if this was always true, something true existed from eternity. Thus truth existed from eternity, because this was true. Therefore, before all things at least this one thing existed, when it was true that nothing yet existed. But if it was composite, it was surely mutable; and if mutable, temporal. Thus time too existed from eternity—which could be said more foolishly?

Nevertheless, this must follow from the fool’s proposition if that one thing, whose eternal existence cannot be denied, is composite. But if it is simple, it is also immutable. This very thing which we rejoiced to have found above, he affirms while denying it; while destroying it, he establishes it. Believe me, brothers—or rather believe the certain and necessary connections: no one can deny that God exists without the consequence that he himself exists. This follows not from the force of propositions or the inference of words, but from the nature of the thing itself. For if anything exists, then he also exists. And if nothing exists, as was the case before that which is something came to be, he nevertheless exists, from whom can come into being all that does not yet exist. For nothing can make itself, since nothing can be prior and posterior to itself.

Therefore nothing is more certainly true to me than that he whom the fool said does not exist, without whom nothing can exist and from whom all things have being, is alone, one, simple, and immutable: the source of number, measure, and weight, within which all things that are subsist, each in its own manner—numerically one because of number from the One; held within some species because of measure from the Simple; ordered because of weight from the Immovable. For each thing that is, is because it is numerically one; it has a measure in its composition, lest it exceed the species of its genus; and by motion it is borne toward some likeness of its weight, so that it may have peace. [Col. 1760B]

Come then, brothers: because we have passed beyond, found, and become Idithun—that is, “the one who leaps across”—passing beyond the many to him, that is, from the many to the one. This, therefore, is he whom we sought. Let us hold him and not let him go; let us question him urgently and importunately about himself. He permits himself to suffer force; he wishes to be overcome; and unless overcome, he does not bless at all. And though he wishes altogether to be held, he asks to be released: “Let me go,” he says, “for the dawn has come” (Gen. 32).

Let us therefore hold him, brothers, in understanding; hold him in affection; hold him in conscience; hold him in life; hold him for his own sake, delighting in him and conforming ourselves to him. Thus, gathered from many into one, let us be united to the One; and, simplified in the simple, let us stand immovable, as far as we can, with the Immovable, sleeping in the selfsame and resting in peace. They do not know this peace who, multiplied by the fruit of grain, wine, and oil—not by God but by themselves—are distracted among many things, intent, stretched out, and troubled.

For as one who wishes to force a thick, many-stranded thread through the narrow eye of a fine needle twists and makes it single with all the strength of his fingertips, so one who fixes his mind upon this pursuit of wisdom deceives himself and labours in vain unless he withdraws his heart from every anxiety, curiosity, ambition, and carnal will; disciplines it by twisting it tight; and sharpens it with the utmost vigilance of study. For, as the Word of God says, “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (Matt. 19). What is that kingdom but to behold God and delight in him? How can those do this whose thoughts, pleasures, and consolations are elsewhere, away from him? “Woe to you rich,” he says, “who have your consolation here” (Luke 6). But the kingdom of heaven is said to belong to the poor in spirit—that is, in will (Matt. 6). [Col. 1761A]

Yet, my brothers, just as a desired and long-sought food is prepared for the sick: they know it is good and excellently prepared, but when they ought to taste it, strength fails them, appetite is blunted, flavour grows dull, because the palate has no taste—so too for us, still infirm because of sin, the leisure once desired, the rest long sought, the solitude of place, the desolation of the world, meditation, prayer, reading, and the very Word of God have too little flavour. When we have been healed, we shall perceive that alone as savoury; all labour will be removed; there will be no weariness, but full, easy, and joyful refreshment.

Therefore let us not shun or abhor the life-giving food of our soul. Holy custom itself will make it profitable, savoury, and sweet, so that it alone may delight us if it alone is received; through the grace and love of God assisting our weakness in all things, through Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen. [Col. 1761B]

## SERMON XXII. ON THE SAME FEAST, V

Because, my brothers, weakened by a lack of books, you ask of us a living voice in place of reading, necessity compels us to say something. Often, therefore, when we attempt to inquire what it is that we seek, we repeatedly fall back; for “investigators of majesty are overwhelmed by glory.” We seek things too high for us, but if we seek piously, we do well.

From what preceded, then, we have that all things are nothing; yet that God is neither something, nor a middle term between something and nothing, but above all things—not understood by abstraction, but truly and properly God; that all things are from him and nothing can be anything except through him; and that he himself always is, even if there are no things, since all things can come into being from him. It remains only to inquire what he is, who has already graciously shown himself to be one, simple, and immovable.

Everything truly simple must be what it has. We must therefore ask what it has, if perhaps through this we may learn what it is. And, not to wander through many things, I ask whether it has reason and affection. If it does not have them, it does not seem best; if it has them, it is supreme. For reason and affection exist in some subject and cannot exist without a subject. Therefore, if that which has them is itself these things, it cannot exist without a subject; and substance is now below it. What shall we say, brothers? It either has them or does not have them, and everything that it has, it is. Otherwise it consists of different things and is neither one, nor simple, nor immutable.

But if it is reason and affection, or virtue or wisdom—which it indeed is if it has them—where is that which we achieved through so much labour above: namely, that it is none of the things that are, but above all things, and all things are from it? If that is true, these are from it as other things are. Therefore, if it has these, how is it supreme? If it does not have them, how is it best? Woe to us: we have failed in searching our searchings. I thought I held the whole; I lost the whole. Would that I had not known letters! Truly there is darkness in light, and much more in much light. The Lord indeed is light, and in him there is no darkness; but from his inaccessible light darkness arises in us. For there are two things that produce darkness: scarcity and excess of light. “Turn away your eyes from me,” says the very source of light, “for they have made me fly away” (Song 9). O Lord, since you have thus far lit my lamp, enlighten, I beg you, even these my darknesses. [Col. 1762A]

If we say, brothers, what we often read and undoubtedly believe—namely, that God is his own wisdom, his own reason, his own power, his own justice—it is easy to say but difficult to understand. What is God, if he is justice? Or what is justice, if it is God? Either he will be beneath substance, or justice above quality. The former is unworthy; the latter impossible.

Perhaps, however, just as he himself is unity—not number or quantity, but the source and origin of number; and just as simplicity is not quality or species, but the principle and origin of species or measure; and immobility likewise is not motion or the weight carried by motion, but the principle of motion and weight—so surely he is not wisdom, nor a species of quality, nor a genus of learning, but the source and origin of wisdom, and likewise of justice, virtue, and such things. Thus he should be called neither wisdom nor any such thing, just as he is called neither number, measure, nor weight, but the principle, source, and efficient cause of all creatures above all things.

Yet he is called number without number, measure without measure, and weight without weight; so he may be called wisdom without quality, justice and virtue without affection or habit of mind. But we judge it better to call him super-wisdom, super-justice, and likewise in other respects, as he is called supersubstance—not in order to say what he is, but lest we be altogether silent, or lest, since he is nothing among all things, he be posited by removing all things. Of him negations are truer. For we deny all things of him more properly than we affirm that he is something among all things. [Col. 1762B]

According to the propriety of his divine theology, therefore, he neither has nor is substance, just as he neither has nor is wisdom. Yet according to the poverty and narrowness of our rational theology, he is called this and that. According to symbolic and, in some fashion, sensory theology, he is also called heaven and earth, sun, fire, lion, ox, bird, wood, stone, and gold; and all things are applied to him all the more freely by likeness either of nature, office, or use, because none of all things applies to him by propriety. Therefore, just as “heaven” and the like are said metaphorically, so “substance,” “wisdom,” and similar terms are said by the trope opposite to what is called hyperbole. Hyperbole exceeds truth and goes beyond what may be believed; this trope does not attain truth or approach propriety. For we say what we can when we wish to speak of the ineffable, of whom nothing can properly be said. We must either be silent or use borrowed words.

You see, brothers, how great are the straits we suffer and how we languish from poverty of words, desiring to say something properly of the unspeakable and to teach concerning the incomprehensible. This is entirely so that you may not merely believe others, but may yourselves understand that what God is cannot be understood or comprehended. Nor is this, beloved, due to our weakness, dullness, or bluntness, but to his own power and subtlety. Hence those holy, sublime, winged seraphim, whose wings signify the flight of contemplation, were seen to veil his face and feet, so that their ignorance might not veil from them his beginning and end, but rather the super-wisdom of incomprehensible God. [Col. 1763A]

For just as, seeing nothing, we see invisible darkness, and hearing nothing, we hear inaudible silence, so surely, by not seeing and not enduring the superabundant and intolerable light, we see the invisible—not as blind persons, but as those overcome by light. Truly, Lord, I have laboured to seek you; and my spirit has failed, not away from you but in you. My soul longs and fails in your courts; my spirit fails while beholding him whom it longs for; my soul fails and melts while delighting in him whom it sees. Yet, enlivened by delight, ever fresh and eager to behold, and aided by beholding to delight, I am borne into you as though upon two middle wings—in you, into whom angels desire to look.

Therefore, although I am dust and ashes, since I have once begun, I shall still ask you one further question concerning yourself: since you are the source and origin of the things mentioned, how are you this? We think this must be asked, brothers, because we know well that these terms can be understood in different ways. The source is the principle and origin of a river; yet the source is of the same nature and the same water as that which flows from it. Likewise, the root is the principle of a tree, and the genus is the principle of every species. The seed is also the principle of a shoot; a seedbed, of seed; the elements, of the seedbed; and of the elements, the primal “forest,” or *hyle*—that is, primordial matter. [Col. 1763B]

In all these and similar cases, when we examine a natural principle—where nature produces, as it were, a body from a head, like from like, or effects from natural causes—we observe that every craftsman is the principle of his work. Yet one craftsman precedes and surpasses nature itself; another merely imitates it. The latter always begins with something from something and does not exceed nature’s image in any work. For example, he can make or fashion from gold only something golden, from stone something stony, from wood something wooden, because he is merely an imitator of nature.

But in the work of any maker, since three things are always necessarily found—matter, form, and cause, that is, from what, in what manner, and why it is made—when we add the one by whom it is made, namely the craftsman, four distinct principles necessarily occur: material, formal, final, and efficient. But whoever can make something from nothing; turn what has been made into nothing; transform something into a different species; increase without addition; or diminish without subtraction, is manifestly a craftsman before and above nature, indeed the author of nature; and he is necessarily of a nature unlike everything that he makes.

Therefore, since “principle,” “source,” or “origin” can be spoken in as many ways as presently occur, who can doubt that the mode which is worthier, loftier, and more excellent than the others [Col. 1764A] belongs to the highest and most excellent God of all?

Unity, therefore, is not a number but the principle of number; neither final, nor formal, nor material, nor natural according to the seminal causes of things, or the proportion of like things, or the unity of a body; but wholly efficient—the source from which it is, and without which it cannot at all exist—of another nature and dissimilar essence. Unity is one, whereas every number is many; it is simple, whereas number is composite; immutable, whereas number is divisible. It truly exists in itself, yet gives to others an existence unlike its own. For the number two, though it is a number and has from unity the being that it is, is not itself identical with unity; yet in the number two nothing truly exists except unity. For what is two, [Col. 1764B] except twice one, or unity? Yet unity is not in two as a part is in a whole, but as its efficient principle, without which it cannot be. And where is two if unity is not? When, however, unity is somewhere called a part of two, or the simple a part of the composite, or time a part of eternity, the rationale of the expression must be considered in view of the reason for speaking. Otherwise, if unity is one part of two, what will the other be? If it is another unity, there will then be two unities; but if there are two, there are none at all. For unity, existing before all things, is the principle of all things; but for there to be two principles of all things is impossible. For if they are equal, neither will be the principle of the other, and consequently neither of all things, nor before all things, nor truly and properly one. Therefore unity is only one, and is one by its very unity.

[Col. 1764C] Thus, as we have said, two is truly twice one, not two ones or two unities; and every number is as many times one as it contains units—unless someone is too ill-equipped to rise from the things counted and the attendant quantity by which they are counted to this unity of number of which we speak. Therefore, in numbers nothing truly exists, and nothing ought truly to be called the existence of number, except unity. Unity is neither a number nor a part of number nor of the same nature as number; yet it produces number, exists before number, without it number does not exist, and in it number truly exists, because it has unity existing within itself. The same applies to simple and composite, and likewise to immovable and movable. For no reasoning permits there to be two simples or two immovables: one containing all things after all things from nothing, the other ruling and moving all things above all things toward some end.

There are, then, three: one, simple, immutable; and these three are at once one, likewise simple and equally immutable. These three alone—or rather, that which alone and one truly exists in all things—does not subsist: if it should withdraw itself, there is then nothing that either stands with or inheres in all things. Since all things exist vainly and emptily in themselves, as the Wise Man says, “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. 1); in him they exist living and eternal—indeed, they are eternity and life—as the blessed apostle says: “What was made in him was life” (John 1). Thus all things are in him, but there they are what he is. He is here and in all things, the essence of all things: not, indeed, the changeable essence according to which they are vanity, [Col. 1765A] being not essence but an image, as it were a trace, of essence; but that essence in which all things are truth and life, together, once, and always. He is, that is, the fountain and efficient principle of being, wisdom, justice, and the like: possessing these and being these, not as they are in things, but as that from which they are and without which the things that are in things cannot exist. They offer some trace of him to the inquirer, so that through beautiful and good created things the mind may behold the most beautiful and best one, from whom they were made, who lives and reigns as God. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII. ON THE SAME FEAST, VI

True, brothers, is the promise of Truth: “Knock,” he says, “and it shall be opened to you” (Luke 11). We have knocked, [Col. 1765B] and, as you see, a great and manifest door has been opened: through it it has clearly appeared that the one whom we call God exists before all things, can exist without all things, and is he without whom nothing is and from whom all is. We have seen how all things are from him, and in what way he is in all things—things which are more truly and more primarily in him than in themselves; in him all things are from eternity which were made in time, as a certain philosopher says of him:

> … He himself, the supremely beautiful,
> 
> Bearing the beautiful world in his mind …  
> > (Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, metrical poem 9, vv. 9–10.)

And another says: “He made the things that shall be” (Isa. 41). And: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18). Now therefore, beloved, [Col. 1765C] emboldened by the goodness of God, let us not give him silence—him for whose sake we are silent toward the world and toward one another. Let us cry out to him; nor may he himself be silent, nor be silent toward us, lest we become like those descending from the lofty and exalted throne, where we saw the Lord, into the pit of ignorance and forgetfulness—like that foolish man who, having considered in a mirror the face of his birth, forgot what sort of person he was (James 1).

For here God shows or reveals nothing of himself so that the sight may suffice or delight us, but so as to kindle us to seek; nothing so as to satisfy us here, but so as to stir us to thirst. “I shall be satisfied,” he says, “when your glory appears” (Ps. 16). But meanwhile: “My soul has thirsted for God, the living fountain” (Ps. 41). Whoever is satisfied with what he has already seen thereby loses even that very thing, because he no longer seeks further. Let us therefore inquire into his holy [Col. 1765D] mind, in which he bears the world before the world, in which he made the things that were to be, in which he created all things together.

But if he has a mind, how is this not himself, he who is all that is his? For the philosopher was pleased to say even of human beings: “Each person’s mind is that very person.” And the saying about the human mind is certainly established: “God made man in his image and likeness” (Gen. 1), provided that man has a mind, without which he could possess neither wisdom nor justice. Two things indeed present themselves: to be oneself, and to have something; oneself and something belonging to oneself, which nevertheless is from oneself and is what oneself is. And behold, by some wondrous manner of reasoning, truly one is found to be truly two: that which is, and that which is his; that which is from no one, and that which is from him. Yet these two are one, because what he has, that he is. [Col. 1766A] And the one itself is two, because nothing can be from itself, have itself, or properly and fittingly be said to belong to itself.

Therefore, in this blessed and ineffable unity which we have found, a wondrous duality is proved to exist without departing from unity: something from someone else, one from another; two indeed, yet one; one, yet two; a principle and that which is from the principle—and this principle itself is the same one who is before all things; mind, in which all things are. Yet there are not two principles, because what he has, that he is: Father and offspring; one being from no one, the other unable to exist except from someone. For what is from no one, and from which something always is, what could more fittingly, by a borrowed term, be called the father of that which is from it? And that which is from it may not incongruously be called [Col. 1766B] its offspring as well, unless some other consideration precludes it.

Since, therefore, there exists one simple and immovable reality which is nevertheless plainly two, since it is and has what is its own—yet is only one with that which it has, and has in itself and with itself only what it has from itself—whatever in that incomprehensible truth is found to be from no one we call Father. Whatever is from him alone, who is from no one and is called Father because something exists from him as his offspring, we call Son: other in property, because he is of him, in him, and with him; the same in unity of essence with him, because he who is all that is his is all that he has. And what is his, from him, [Col. 1766C] can in no way be other than he himself, who is altogether simple and indivisible.

For the simple is not divided so that one may become two; nor is one doubled; nor has one begun to have what it did not formerly have; nor does the immutable cease to be what it has always been. For he is always, before all things, one and from no one; and always, in that same one, something is from someone: so that he may always be Father, and his Son, who is from him alone, may be everlasting. But he who is from no one is never from someone, nor he who is from someone from no one, lest the father ever be his own son or the son his own father. He who is from no one and he who is from him are always one and the same in him: simple, eternal; so that Father and offspring are one nature, the same essence, and likewise in all other respects. Thus eternity is Father, and from eternity the Son is eternity; the Father is principle, [Col. 1766D] and from principle the Son is principle; and so with power, wisdom, and the like. In accordance with our rational theology, as we have said, these are many; but in the supreme and divine reality they are ineffably one. Thus, although he possesses all these, the one possesses one only, in whom all things are together, once, and always one—things which, when reckoned in themselves, are vainly many and are found truly to be nothing.

Descending also to symbolic theology, we follow the same path of truth, so that when he is called Word, image, radiance, imprint, figure, brightness, arm, hand, right hand, something of someone may everywhere be understood; and in all these, one of one, of the same essence, though with distinct properties.

Accordingly, let us investigate the point from which [Col. 1767A] we began: why he is called Word. The rational mind has three operations, with respect to present, past, and future, arising from its three natural powers: reason, memory, and intellective ingenuity. Ingenuity seeks the unknown; reason judges what has been found; memory stores what has been judged and offers it again for judgment. Ingenuity therefore brings what it discovers to reason; memory brings back what it has concealed; but reason is occupied with them as present, and, as it were, in the mouth of the heart always either chews what the teeth of ingenuity have seized or ruminates what the stomach of memory presents. For what we have apprehended and now call knowledge is either in the mouth of the heart, so that from it we speak with ourselves as though in the present—that is, think; or, if it may be [Col. 1767B] said more properly, meditate, that is, inwardly behold what is present and discuss it first within ourselves. This very thing which we now speak is, of course, first the word of the heart before it is the word of the mouth. Or it is hidden from us also in the belly of memory. For not everything that we know always occurs to us, nor does everything a knower knows always remain before that person’s gaze. Yet, in time and by parts, it is drawn from memory as from a repository, and in the mouth of the heart a present word is formed which makes a sound outwardly in the mouth of flesh.

Therefore, as is clear from what has been said, because for God nothing is future and nothing past, but everything that is, or can in any way be, however variously it is or can be varied, is present all together, [Col. 1767C] once, and always in the instant of his beholding; because thought brings nothing back from memory—or rather, neither thought nor memory has any place there, whence nothing goes and to which nothing returns; because effort contributes nothing from ingenuity—or rather, neither has any place there where nothing was lacking—it is fittingly said that all things are for him as super-present and immovably eternal in the Word and in the reason of his mind, which considers all things with itself, speaks to itself, together, once, and always.

For he speaks not only what is, was, or will be, but also everything that can be: in whatever way and from whatever source, how, for what end, and why what is exists, and why what is not does not exist. Nor does he speak by parts—as though this first and that afterward—for with him there is no change; rather, he knows all in one simple, eternal, fixed [Col. 1767D] act of vision, together—or, if it can be said, beyond together. Nor does he discover this more than once, as something finite; for what is equal to the infinite must necessarily be infinite. Nor can he speak of something else after this, or abandon this for another, because it is clear that here he ineffably utters whatever is or is possible in any manner. Hence there can be no other word, no differently uttered word, nor even the same word uttered a second time, where nothing old passes away, nothing new arises, and all remains eternal; where there is no change, not even the shadow of alternation. And just as all is together, so it is once; and because he never fails to see all things above himself and all things in himself, it is also always.
