For he was not first without sight and afterward saw himself; nor, being unwise, did he discover the wisdom by which he might be wise; nor, being idle, begin to consider what he should do; nor did the immutable afterward change what [Col. 1768A] he had once thought and inwardly said to himself; nor did the infinite bring to an end what, just as it could not begin, so neither could it end. His inward counsel does not begin and pass away, but is born and remains wholly for eternity; and the thoughts of his heart are perfect, but not bounded, neither begun nor past, throughout generation and generation. For there nothing is begun, nothing finished; all is infinite, yet not imperfect; nothing is past, nothing future, but all is present—yet not even this properly.

For if we say, “God speaks” or “God thinks,” the Word or thought does not yet seem complete, as though he had not yet spoken or thought everything. And if we say, “He spoke,” it seems to have passed away, as though he were now silent; but if we say, “He will speak,” it seems future, as though he had not yet begun. [Col. 1768B] Hence it is clear that when we are compelled to speak of the ineffable supernature or Word of God, though we are not permitted to be silent, just as no name can be conceived that expresses the thing of which it is spoken, so no word can properly signify that which is rightly said of it.

But behold: following the Word himself, made “a lamp to our feet,” and holding fast wherever he goes, wherever he passes, and wherever he turns himself, nor wherever he passes and wherever he turns himself—nor letting him go wherever he penetrates and enters—at last he has brought us into the house of his father and into the chamber of her who bore him (Song 3): that is, into the unbegotten paternal essence, wisdom, and power. For the Father begot the Son from his essence. We too have brought in the Word, because it is written [Col. 1768C] there: “Into the house of our mother.” For while we sought the origin of this holy seed, that is, the Word of God, we surely found our own origin—not from elsewhere, but otherwise from the same source. For while all things are from the one by temporal creation and with a beginning, he alone is from the same one by natural and eternal generation, without beginning.

Therefore, with the lamp shining, as we have said, and making light for our feet, we have in part found what we proposed to seek, and have spoken of it only in part. Perhaps even only a part of us has understood only in part what we have spoken: namely, from where the Word arises, how, when, and what it is—that is, who spoke first, what he spoke, to whom, how, and when. Yet in all this [Col. 1768D] the Word has not yet been sown outwardly; rather, that which can be outwardly sown has been found. Let us therefore seek another beginning: where, why, how, and when it was sown; asking the sower of the holy and secret Word to deign to sow in us understanding of these matters. Amen.

## SERMON XXIV. ON THE SAME FEAST, VII

> [Note: [Col. 1767] This sermon was delivered in a field while work was being done.]

Now, beloved, we may see in ourselves how the whole human being eats bread in the sweat of his face. For truly the sword, passing through the flesh, has reached even to the soul. Behold, as we cut down the fallow ground for ourselves lest we sow among thorns (Jer. 4), we are dripping with sweat under the burning noonday sun. Therefore, exhausted by our earthly seed, let us rest awhile beneath the covering of the spreading holm-oak which you see nearby. [Col. 1769A] There let us, with a certain inward sweat, thresh, grind, knead, bake, and eat the seed of the divine Word, lest we fail from hunger.

Our first bread for today will be to investigate why he who went out went out to sow his seed. For within there could be no fear of loss such that increase would be sought without. And just as the one cannot be diminished, so the infinite cannot be multiplied, the simple cannot decrease, the immense cannot be increased, nor the immovable be moved. You see, then, that another question must be added: namely, when can he go out who cannot be moved?

Brothers, before this sensible world came to be, there was absolutely nothing less than there is now; indeed, there was infinitely more than exists in this realm of sense. For everything which appears in the copy must [Col. 1769B] necessarily have proceeded from the archetype; but it is not yet true that everything which is in the archetype has come into the copy. For there exist more beautifully and truly not only the things that have been made, but whatever things can be made, where they are not changeable and vain but truth and life. For this sensible state is the final end of things, just as that supreme archetype is their source, of which it is written: “Reaching mightily from end to end, and sweetly ordering all things” (Wis. 7).

This holm-oak beneath whose benefit we are refreshed was more beautifully and wonderfully whole in its small acorn than it now exists in so great a trunk; and, completing its circuit, it is again consummated in the acorn. For from the acorn, as from a point, the line of root, trunk, branch, leaf, and flower is traced round, and returns likewise to the acorn. The acorn itself, [Col. 1769C] the small seed of so great a tree, exists more beautifully and wonderfully whole in the seed-bed of mother earth. And it exists also in the elements, and in matter itself; while matter itself, with all the rest of the universe, exists in every respect more excellently and truly in the divine mind. Thus the holm-oak exists actually in the trunk, seminally in the acorn, originally in the earth, causally in the elements, potentially in matter, and potentially in God; in the other instances changeably and mortally, in God immortally.

Since, therefore, all things are in God not only by the power through which they come to be, but also by foreknowledge—indeed by present wisdom—what did that great theologian of the Gentiles mean when he said that God was lifted up with immense joy [Col. 1769D] after he had completed the world? Did he see something new without that he had not foreseen within? Did he see in the copy something beautiful that was not more beautiful in the archetype, in the work than in the art? Therefore, if he had reason to rejoice, there was a higher occasion for rejoicing within. Yet I would not believe that so great a philosopher—Plato, that is—had said this childishly, especially when our theologian Moses has uttered something similar: “God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1). As though he had not seen them more radiant within or approved them as better.

Or perhaps, at the completion of the work, each theologian subtly indicated the final cause of the work in its end: the former joy, the latter goodness. How great, we may suppose, is the joy, delight, and gladness that he possesses within, in such and [Col. 1770A] from such majesty of power and light of power, where he beholds in himself and above all things every beauty, every reason, every order, every cause, every effect! Why, then, did he desire outward things, certainly incomparably less beautiful? Perhaps because of that very ineffable and incomprehensible joy and delight.

But behold, within this incomprehensible, one, simple immobility, something third begins to shine through, which can be neither from no one nor from one only. For if within he rejoices and delights in this his light and with it, it is evident that this joy and delight proceed from both: namely, from him who rejoices and from him in whom and with whom he rejoices. Both are plainly principles of the joy which is from the one concerning the other. But [Col. 1770B] since it has been established above that he who rejoices is one with him concerning whom he rejoices and in whom he delights, and that whatever the one has, that one himself is, he is surely one with his joy. For nothing alien can enter into him, nothing new begin, nothing old perish; all remains eternal. Yet a Trinity has now been found.

Moreover, he loves him concerning whom he rejoices and in whom he delights. Hence love is from both and in both, yet is itself the same as both. Therefore, since in this adorable unity whatever is found to be from no one we call Father, and whatever is from the one alone we call Son, it remains that whatever is found in him to be from the two is called of both. Yet it is not called Son, lest confusion arise; rather, it is called the Holy Spirit, so that the property may be distinguished, the sweetness, love, peace, and delight of both may be understood, and the whole may firmly be held to be one, lest we depart from unity because of the Trinity.

Thus [Col. 1770C] the true Light, exulting and rejoicing in its own light, what need had it of our darkness, to see outwardly what was obscure when inwardly it possessed it so bright? For if it was light, it was surely shining. What else is it to shine than to generate light from oneself? But what light does light generate from itself while it shines, except that which it itself is—the light that shines? Do “light” and “shining” signify two lights? Yet they do not signify the same thing without distinction. “Light” signifies the essence of light alone; “shining” declares light to be light from light. Yet it does not signify another light from another, [Col. 1770D] but the same light otherwise: so that the property is different, not the truth of the light.

What indeed is shining except giving forth light? And certainly no other light than that very light which shines from light. Yet, although light is light, it does not give forth light unless it shines; and if it is not light, it cannot shine at all. Therefore shining is from light, and from both is the giving forth of light. When, then, this alone is said—namely, giving forth light—it is understood and, as it were, jointly signified that there is shining and that there is light. But when shining is said, it is likewise understood that there is light from which it may shine, and that by shining it illuminates and gives forth light. And when light alone is said, it is also understood that by shining—that is, by generating light from itself—it gives forth light and illumines.

These senses, however, [Col. 1771A] are jointly signified and all are contained in each of the terms, and each in all, not so much by the propriety of the words or the differences which they themselves express, as by the undifferentiated—that is, one—nature of the thing signified, namely light. One nature of light is designated by three properties through those three terms. Come then, brothers: because Rachel could not bear, she put forward her maidservant (Gen. 30). Since we were unable properly to say what that inaccessible light truly is, we have used an imaginary contemplation and said by likeness what is similar in a profoundly dissimilar way.

Since, then, light exists and generates from itself light by which that light itself may be seen, and from its own nature makes itself visible, so that through itself and by its natural gift it is itself seen: is not this especially what makes light—and most especially that light—lovable, namely, that it is itself capable of being given, received, and enjoyed? What is every powerful, strong, wise, just, good thing to me if it is not communicable, if it cannot be shared? Therefore what above all makes [Col. 1771B] light lovable is that through its radiance it makes itself visible and enjoyable, even if there is no one to see it or use it. Yet this is the nature of light, and, so far as it lies in itself, it always gives generously. Therefore there is naturally in it and from it a certain gift, namely that which shines; and it has shining from the fact that it is light. Thus all its use is in its gift; and from that very gift comes the reason why it is held dear and loved.

Let love, therefore, be from use; use from gift; gift from the appearance or natural image—that is, from native radiance or brightness; and gift and image from the [Col. 1771C] eternity of light, that is, from the very being or essence of light. In that inaccessible light which, so far as we can, we portray through this bodily light, this essence is wholly from no one and is the source of radiance and illumination. Therefore, my God, my illumination, this is what I most love in you: that by which I am able to love you, know you, and participate in you—your natural gift, namely that you are by nature able to be given, received, and enjoyed.

Whenever I ask anything of you, I attend to this: your Holy Spirit, natural goodness, and gratuitous generosity—not something accidental or temporal, stirred up by any affection or work of mine, but eternal and immutable, by which you are always such. But because in you, [Col. 1771D] my God, who are the holy Trinity, the true Light, this gift of light is not from itself, everything is from him for us, to whom it has been given to enjoy him in some measure; but it is from the appearance and radiance, as though the offspring of the paternal light, and through it from the paternal light itself. For because light shines, it is the gift of light, and use comes from the gift.

With one worship and undifferentiated love, in you we love the Holy Spirit, in whom also the Son, through whom also the Father, from whom comes “every good gift and every perfect gift” (James 1). For the Father gives the Spirit in the name of the Son—that is, through the Son; the Son gives the Spirit from the Father; the Spirit gives himself from the Father and the Son. For nothing is given, when nothing is owed, except freely—that is, as a gift. Nor is a debt remitted, nor is good rendered to one who has deserved ill, except by a great, greater, [Col. 1772A] greatest gift. Therefore all is given or remitted in the Holy Spirit. Yet he himself, with all his use, is through the Son, through whom all things are given or forgiven in the Spirit by the Father, in a manner as the principal and fountain-like goodness, from whom [lacuna].

Therefore, brothers, giving thanks to the Trinity, God, for this light and illumination of his, let us henceforth ask the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit to reveal to us why he willed to go outward, though nothing was lacking to him within and nothing could accrue to him without; and why he willed to sow what could neither fail while kept within nor be multiplied when sown without. But, tired today, let us pause here. Tomorrow we shall speak of another beginning, as the giver and eternal gift, the Holy Spirit, deigns to give it: to him be honor and dominion for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXV. ON THE SAME FEAST, VIII

[Col. 1772B]

As we investigate, beloved, the final cause of the universe, the first point that occurs is that the Omnipotent, constrained neither by necessity, nor he who possesses all things by desire, nor wisdom by curiosity, nor truth by vanity, could not have made anything except by free will and a gift, as it were, of his own liberality. Nor did he newly conceive in his mind what he would finally complete in work, but possessed it from eternity in mind and will.

For since his nature is such that it can in some measure be received and participated in, and since he exults in himself and from himself in continual, stable, ineffable joy, it belonged not only to natural goodness but also to the nature of that joy itself to will to have a participant in so great and delightful a good. [Col. 1772C] This is not, as it often is in us, the fault of curiosity or boasting: an inability not to communicate inward joy to another, and the greater it is, the less able to conceal it. Rather, it belongs to the grace of liberality, the nature of goodness, and the freely given and natural good of gladness, to will to pour or infuse itself into many and freely gather them into participation in itself. For liberality can never be miserly, goodness envious, love idle, nor gladness desirous of being hidden or solitary.

Thus, when he willed—though he never began to will it—the undivided Trinity made indivisibly from nothing a rational mind capable of himself, capable of sharing his delight, joy, peace, and gladness: that is, a mind made in his image. [Col. 1772D] For there was nothing but nothing from which, as was said, he might first make something by free liberality, not by a necessity of his nature, as some have said, as though he could not remain inactive, but by natural goodness simply because he willed it. Yet blessed is the nature that compels beneficence: for what a person is compelled to do by natural goodness, what does that person do except freely and willingly?

Natural goodness, therefore, and the inward delight of the mind were the cause of the work: by “work” I mean the rational spirit, and likewise all bodily nature. For the whole of bodily nature serves the rational spirit for its instruction and in some way speaks its own principle; nothing is without a voice. The rational spirit was therefore made so that it might rejoice and delight with God in God and in all things in him alone. It was made rational, so that [Col. 1773A] it might seek God himself in itself and in all things; concupiscible, so that it might love and desire him alone; irascible, so that it might reject everything opposed to this contemplation and delight—as it is written, so that it may know, namely through rationality, to reject evil through the irascible faculty and choose good through the desiring faculty (Isa. 7).

The sole and supreme good of the created rational spirit, then, and the natural end of rational and moral effort or exercise—the purpose for which it was made—is to contemplate and delight in God. The way to this dwelling is seeking and imitating, inquiring and desiring: desiring by inquiring and inquiring by desiring. Its sole sin and evil is turning away from this conversion toward God, this inquiry [Col. 1773B] and desire, so that, having conceived this, it seeks and loves something else.

Come, brothers, why do we run through so many things and anxiously seek what we find with difficulty? What is sufficient is brief; what is perfect is near. It is joy, love, delight, sweetness, vision, light, brightness: that which God requires of us, that for which God made us. It is true order and religion to do that for which we were made. Let us contemplate that than which nothing is more beautiful; let us delight in that than which nothing is sweeter; let us be angered at everything that hinders these. Let us refer to this every exercise of ours, whether labor or rest, speech or silence.

For whatever is not referred to this, and is not done by us for that for which we were made by God—so that [Col. 1773C] the cause and intention of his work and ours may be the same—is neither virtue nor deserving of reward. For there and from there, and that itself, will be the reward of our deeds: where, from where, and what the gift was by which we came to be. This is our beginning and end: the final beginning and principal end; a perfect beginning because of the end, an infinite end because of the unceasing beginning. For wherever it begins, it always ends; wherever it ends, it always begins: it can neither lack progress nor incur decline.

In every habit, every place, every person, pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: this alone must be pursued, and for its sake one must keep oneself undefiled from this world (James 1). But since it is difficult in practice to live in the world and not be defiled by it, one must also flee [Col. 1773D] the world for this reason. Yet from this so sweet and lovable leisure of contemplation, in which every power of reason ought to be exercised and every effort of affection fixed, only a rational love and care for one’s neighbor justifiably—or even praiseworthily—delays us. The apostle is thought to have inserted into the course of the preceding sentence: “to visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (ibid.).

Therefore, if our discipline is true, let it always labor toward contemplation and delight—that is, love—either in free leisure devoted to God alone or in ordered service to one’s neighbor. For only the concern undertaken through ordered love of neighbor can, at times and even usefully, turn the mind away from the constancy and vigilance of this contemplation. And when we devote ourselves to the labor of bodily exercise so that we may [Col. 1774A] have something to give to one suffering need—namely, to the body itself, which is still animal—we judge this not wholly alien to love of neighbor. For what is closer to a soul than its own body, which it ought not only to love but cannot hate? Therefore, because the soul is still living and has not yet become life-giving spirit, it cannot suffice to give life from itself alone; it must reasonably provide for itself external assistance toward that which inwardly it is less able fully to accomplish by itself. For the spirit is debtor to the flesh in order to give it life, not in order to live according to it.

Every care or delight, therefore, that is not in God alone—except, as has been said, love of neighbor for God’s sake—is superfluous and adulterous, alien to the reason why we are human beings, turned away from God’s purpose toward us [Col. 1774B] and from our duty toward him.

See, then, brothers, how much fervor of spirit and untiring effort is needed if, setting aside thoughts that lack understanding—such thoughts from which the Holy Spirit of discipline withdraws, “fleeing deception” (Wis. 1)—we are to attend to that deifying light which illumines toward truth and inflames toward love. So that you may do this more freely and unrestrictedly, you have assigned the concerns of the animal body to another. If labor is forbidden you, anxiety is removed; care is forbidden. For anxiety necessarily troubles, as it is written: “You are anxious and troubled about many things” (Luke 10); care weighs down. Hence the Lord says: “Let not your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and the cares of this world” (Luke 21).

Anxiety [Col. 1774C] wrongly lifts up; care more grievously presses down; sloth most grievously dissolves. For a mind slothful in leisure loses the fruit of action and does not find the light of contemplation. A mind weighed down by cares cannot rise on high; a troubled mind cannot be serene. For a heart that is not tranquil cannot at all be serene; and if it is not serene, neither can it be transparent. But the heart of one who contemplates must be transparent, like a mirror or utterly clear and still water, so that in it and through it, as in a mirror and through a mirror, the mind may see its image made in the image of God.

Therefore the heart of one desiring to behold God must be cleansed not only of harmful and superfluous cares, but even of necessary cares; and it must be stirred by reading, meditation, [Col. 1774D] and prayer. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). May he himself deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON XXVI. ON THE SAME FEAST, IX
By a natural gift from God, the rational mind is made capable of sharing in His joy. As it alone and first receives His image, so it can receive knowledge and love. For through reason and will—that is, through the faculty of understanding and loving—it has been made capable of Divinity, as through certain vessels and instruments of its natural condition. Just as the first gift of grace creates these so that they may exist, so the second fills them, lest they be empty or wrongly full. They are wrongly full when suffused either with erroneous understanding or with perverse love. [Col. 1775A] But they can rightly be filled by God alone, from whom and for whom they were created, though they cannot contain Him wholly. “God,” says the Apostle, “is greater than our heart, and knows all things” (1 John 3). After God there is nothing prior to the rational spirit when created, nor anything greater. Therefore, though it can be filled with something else, it can never be wholly filled thereby. Accordingly, the spirit which desires something other than God alone thirsts the more the more it drinks; and while it seeks sufficiency outside God in desire for money, praise, power, and the like, it cannot be satisfied, for God Himself is greater than everything it absorbs.

Thus, as a vessel into which the Wisdom and Power of God pours itself, in order to suffuse it with His knowledge and love, so it is also a field in which that same Wisdom and Power sows itself, so that from such [Col. 1775B] seed may arise the light of knowledge and the fervour of love. Therefore by the first grace, that which was not yet a field is created fit to receive and multiply seed: namely, the natural faculty, as we have said, of understanding and loving, from which free choice consists in the rational mind. But by the second grace the seed of the Word is now scattered into the field of free choice. For first a lamp capable of burning is constructed; afterwards fire is applied, by which it may be kindled.

This seed of the Word, then, is sown in the field both inwardly and outwardly, in accordance with the nature of the field. Outwardly, every external creature speaks to the rational mind concerning the Creator and gives a lesson; inwardly, its own inmost rational nature does so. And over both, [Col. 1775C] grace divinely inspired sometimes speaks more deeply. Yet just as the bodily eye, although it naturally has the capacity for sight, and the ear for hearing, never by itself and from itself attains the act of seeing and hearing unless aided by external light and sound, so the rational spirit, though by the first gift of creative grace it is fitted to behold the divine light, can in no way attain the act of that vision unless illuminated by a ray of higher light. For just as the eye does not see the sun except in the sun’s light, so the mind can see the true and divine sun and light only in its light. “In thy light,” says the Prophet, “we shall see light” (Ps. 35 [36]).

Therefore, just as from the sun proceeds that by which the sun itself can be seen, and without which it cannot be seen—yet what proceeds from it does not leave the sun but reveals it—so the Word, remaining in God, which proceeds from Him, irradiates the mind, so that it may first behold the very flashing of light, without which it would see nothing, and may also behold Him from whom it flashes, neither leaving Him nor itself left by Him. [Col. 1775D] For just as the bodily eye first sees the light shining from the sun, sees other things in it, and, following the ray upward, sees the sun itself from which the ray proceeds and gleams—the ray which illumines the eye as by its own gift and natural benefit—so from that inaccessible light proceeds a splendour which the mind first sees, without which it would see nothing, and which draws it upward to disclose whence it proceeds and reveal the source of its origin. Yet it would not do this unless it proceeded from there.

It proceeds from there, therefore, in order to illumine; and it illumines [Col. 1776A] because it proceeds, so that its natural benefit is one thing and its natural principle another. Both, however, are from the one fountain of light: from which it shines in order to illumine, and from which it illumines because it shines. Yet it is not first light, then shining, and thirdly illumining; rather, at once, because it is light, since it is light, by shining it always illumines, as far as lies in itself—though something is not immediately illumined.

For just as an eye capable of seeing, if created in this sun’s light, would immediately be illumined by the present sun’s ray without any change in itself, and might immediately be darkened by chance without any defect or alteration in the sun, or even altogether blinded, so that creation, illumination, and darkening would be nearly indistinguishable in time: so the mind, which was not, having been created from light in Light that was always and everywhere, is immediately suffused by its presence; nothing new arises in that Light, and, without any shadowing of it, the mind in a light-fleeing spirit is immediately darkened. [Col. 1776B] Thus a face turned toward the sun is illumined, and, though the sun remains unmoved, is darkened when turned away.

Therefore the sower of light and Word—the Light itself and the Word—going forth, first freely sowed seed from the bosom of the Father, that is, by the gift of the Holy Spirit, in the field of angelic nature, when He shone upon it inwardly through natural reason and instructed it as though by a command of nature. But while He sowed, some seed fell beside the way. For the way by which the Creator’s benefit comes to the creature is His love and affection alone, freely given; and likewise the way by which the service of the rational creature ascends to the Creator is its love and affection alone, owed as a duty.

When, therefore, as has been said, He had first sown in the angels, some turned from themselves to God with thanksgiving, sent down the root of humility, and bore upward the fruit of obedience, as it is written: “That which shall be saved of Judah shall send forth root downward and bear fruit upward” (Isa. 37:31). Others, turning to themselves, “became vain in their thoughts, and, professing themselves wise, became fools.” Their foolish heart was darkened, as though turned away from the light. [Col. 1776C] For they did not glorify as was fitting Him by whom they were illumined, or Him by whom they were sown as a field; rather, exalting themselves, they generated from themselves proud, vain, and lofty thoughts—robbers of light, because robbers of humility—trampling the minds that generated them and snatching the blessed seed from the heart, lest they bear the fruit of love from the root of humility in obedience. Such are those who “did not stand in the truth even for an hour.” For them, as we have said, creation, illumination, and blinding were almost indistinguishable in time. Their own wickedness blinded those whom creative grace had illumined.

The wise Sower did not fail to know that the seed had perished in these; yet, eager for harvest, He did not cease sowing. But while He sowed, other seed fell upon the rock (Luke 8). This rocky ground is human nature in Adam, which, having experienced itself in David and now knowing itself, says to the Lord: “My soul is like waterless ground before thee” (Ps. 142 [143]). In a second sowing the Word of God sowed this ground, when He illumined it not only inwardly by the gift of the rational soul, “which enlightens every man coming into this world,” but outwardly as well by the command of discipline, saying: “Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil thou shalt not eat” (Gen. 2). [Col. 1777A] Therefore He first sowed in heaven, secondly in paradise.

Here the ground received the Word with joy and stood for an hour; but when the heat of temptation boiled up through the deceived woman, it assented wrongly to her evil counsel, she who had first given counsel most wickedly. Obeying the woman’s voice more than God’s, it had already inwardly dried up, at the root of humility, from the moisture of love; and so it swiftly withered from the greenness of external obedience. God the Sower added a third sowing through Moses in the wilderness; but while He sowed, other seed fell among thorns. For the Jews, always attending only to temporal and earthly things in the observances of the commandments and the rewards for observing them, while they long only for carnal things, choke in the Law every fruit of spiritual understanding. [Col. 1777B]

Nevertheless, because, as it is said, “relentless labour conquers all things” (Virgil, *Georgics*, book IV, verse 145), this Sower, the Son of God made Son of Man, still further added to His sowing: first by Himself and then through the Apostles, He sowed His seed—Himself—in the world. There the remnant of Israel and the fullness of the Gentiles, like good ground, received the Word with the sword and bore fruit in endurance of heat and cold.

Therefore it was first sown in heaven, secondly in paradise, thirdly in the wilderness, fourthly throughout the whole world: “Go,” He says, “into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16). First among angels, secondly among the first human beings, thirdly among the Jews, fourthly among the Gentiles. First by the command of nature, secondly by the command of discipline, thirdly by the command of the letter, fourthly by the Gospel of grace. First the Word in reason, secondly in voice, thirdly in writing, fourthly in flesh. “The Word,” he says, “was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). [Col. 1777C] First wholly inwardly to reason; secondly outwardly to the ears; thirdly also to the eyes; fourthly also to the hands. “That which we have heard,” he says, “and seen, and our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1).

Thus throughout the whole time of the world this division of the field and this difference among hearers has been found—indeed, even when the Word Himself, present in flesh, spoke Himself through Himself. And today, when we or others scatter the seed of that same Word in common, some hearers are found rejecting it, others casting it aside, others choking it, and others bearing fruit in patience—something which the angel could do by steadfastness and the first human being by obedience alone. The first, then, do not conceive; the second bring forth an abortion; the third crush the living fetus; the fourth nurture it with motherly devotion and care. May Christ our Lord grant us this through His inward sowing of Himself. Amen.

## SERMON XXVII. ON QUINQUAGESIMA SUNDAY, I

“Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered up,” etc. (Luke 18). Brothers, may the God of our salvation grant us a prosperous journey. For behold, [Col. 1778A] we too are going up to Jerusalem. This is why we came down to this island, the farthest of all lands—after, as the prophet says, there is no other, small and hidden in the great sea (Isa. 18)—that we might go up to Jerusalem. Yet not to that Jerusalem which is earthly and is in bondage with her children, but to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is free above, the mother of us all, where no one is a slave, but all are kings. For that entire city reigns eternally as queen with her children as kings, and with her bridegroom the King, the King’s Son.

For just as birds, in order to raise themselves on wings into the air, press themselves more deeply into the ground than their whole bodies rest upon; and as humans and beasts alike possess the same art of nature—or nature of art, or rather natural art—so that, desiring to leap upward, they bend low toward the ground as though crouching with their whole [Col. 1778B] bodies: so we too, aspiring to heaven, have withdrawn from the common world. Longing for fullness, we have cast away riches; desiring honours, we have been thrown aside as the refuse of this world. We who appeared to be something in the world, and were perhaps also accounted something among the assembly of brethren, have, in order that we may truly be something, behold, been reduced to nothing.

For what estimation of us remains in the world now—not to say even memory? Given over to oblivion by the world, as dead men from its heart, may we, at least, not utterly forget it; and may it die in our hearts, removed from our hearts, so that, as regards place no less than mind, each of us may say: “The world is dead to me, and I to the world.” May we, abandoning the things behind us not only with our hands but forgetting them also with our hearts, stretch with all our thought and eagerness toward what lies before us; like battering rams drawn back, may we be driven more forcefully toward what is before us.

Certainly, what we seek to ascend is steep, and what we attempt to penetrate is narrow. Therefore may He grant that we be unencumbered and slender. [Col. 1778C] For it is difficult to climb upward burdened and to enter through narrow spaces swollen. That riches should not puff a person up, cares not burden him, and excesses not weigh him down, may be a divine miracle; for human weakness it is impossible, but with God all things are possible. Therefore the text continues:

“And the Son of Man will be delivered to the Gentiles to be mocked and crucified.” Our old man, the son of the old man, has at some time been crucified with the new Son of Man, as the blessed Apostle says: “Our old man was crucified together with him” (Rom. 6). Therefore, beloved, it is still necessary that in each of us, while the sixth day, the Sabbath’s eve, is still in progress, he be crucified.

For though I am personally one human being, body and soul, I nevertheless find in myself two persons and the sons of the two: old and new, earthly and heavenly, a son of man and a Son of God; a human being, son of man by carnal generation, where “that which is born of flesh is flesh”; and God, Son of God by spiritual generation, where “that which is born of the Spirit is spirit,” or God from God, in accordance with His granting human beings power to become children of God. [Col. 1778D] For regenerated from the Holy Spirit and from the virgin mother, which is the Church, what else are we but born in a wondrous, new, and divine manner—marvellously, from old persons made new, from sinners righteous, from carnal persons spiritual, from humans gods—being such as are born “not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God”?

For just as the eternal God, made a new human being, appeared as Son of Man, not from nothing nor from something alien, but from the old human being—yet not from a human being, but from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary—without any sin: so the old son of the old man is reborn as a Son of God, not from nothing nor from something alien, but from the old human being, himself; and not from a human being, but from the same Spirit and the virgin mother, the Church, for the remission of all sins. Yet this [Col. 1779A] new reality lies hidden within us, just as it lay hidden in Him; outwardly, however, the earthly image of the earthly person is manifest in us, the old image of the old person, in the reality of sinful flesh—just as it was manifest in Him, but in the likeness of sinful flesh.

For the conception and birth which He accepted for us, from us, and in us, He bestowed also upon us, so that, conceived and born likewise, we may likewise live, die, and rise again. “He who says that he abides in Him ought himself also to walk as He walked.” Therefore He went up to Jerusalem so that the Son of Man, who appeared outwardly, might be handed over, scourged, crucified, and on the third day raised by the Son of God, who lay hidden within—yet with the human being, Son of Man, and God, Son of God, personally one: the former by nature, the latter by grace; the former first, the latter later.

Thus, though I too, as has been said, am personally one human being and by nature a son of man, whose image is outwardly manifest, but by God’s grace a Son of God, God in the inward image and likeness, I did not without reason say above that I am one and double, and that within me, one human being, are contained two sons of two persons. [Col. 1779C] So Abraham had two sons in one house, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman (Gal. 4): the former first, the latter later. For what is animal always comes first, then what is spiritual.

And just as there, according to the Apostle (ibid.), the elder persecuted the younger—though Sarah saw the slave woman’s son playing with her own son, not persecuting him (Gen. 21)—so it is in me today. The greater persecutes the lesser: that is, the earlier the later, the outer the inner, the animal the spiritual, Ishmael Isaac, the slave woman’s son the free woman’s son, the son of man the Son of God; but he persecutes through play, coaxing, and caressing, enticing him to shameful, unlawful, unfitting, and unbecoming uses. For thus the flesh fights against and desires against the spirit: not by expelling it from itself but by drawing it to itself; not by casting it out but by enticing it. “Each one,” says the Apostle James, “is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (Jas. 1). These are those deceitful kisses of the enemy, far worse than a friend’s quarrels or blows.

Therefore the son of man in me hates and persecutes the Son of God—that is, the flesh persecutes the spirit—with deadly blandishments and allurements, according to the saying: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. 10). [Col. 1779D] But the Son of God, who am I, new in the old, loves the son of man with whom He contends. He strikes him to correct him; scourges him to discipline him; hands him over to free him. For if the Son of God sets him free, the son of man will be truly free; and if He scourges him, He receives him; if He rebukes him, He loves him. At last He delivers him over to suffering and death, but in order that on the third day He may raise him from passibility and mortality.

In all these things He pursues him without mercy, even to death—by scourges and nails, lance and thorns, blows and spitting, reproaches and insults—yet all are not death-dealing but life-giving, not from hatred but from love, compassion, and wise purpose, until He kills him utterly and the saying of Sarah is fulfilled: “Cast out the slave woman and her son” (Gen. 21; Gal. 4), so that the son of the free woman, of promise and grace, may reign alone in the Father’s house as Son of God, and that God may be all in all in complete peace.

Therefore, beloved, as we ascend to behold this peace within ourselves—for this is what Jerusalem signifies—the son of man must be handed over: that is, our outward human being must be handed over by the inward one, and not without some seduction, to alien Gentiles, that is, to the disciplines and strict observances of the Rule: abstinence and vigils, ashes and haircloth, labours and silence, poverty, lowliness, and an altogether alien authority. [Col. 1780B] By these he is to be scourged and crucified, until he is utterly killed to his own judgement and will and to the habit of his old life; so that, dead to sin, he may live to righteousness within us with the Son of God—that is, so that we ourselves, entirely dead to sin through repentance and raised to a new life, may live to righteousness.

Therefore, beloved, let us be cruel and hard toward ourselves in outward matters, lest we offend the cruel and hard Judge in inward and outward things. “If we accuse ourselves,” he says (1 Cor. 11), truly judge ourselves strictly, and condemn ourselves severely, we shall not fear another accuser, offend no other judge, and endure no other torturer. Why do we seek comforts or rest? We are on the cross; we were in the world. We are in hell, but in the hell of mercy, not wrath; we shall be in heaven. We sinned in the world; here we are punished, there we shall rest: there in delights, here in punishments; there in glory, here in filth; here in purification, there in repose. What do we seek? A pleasant hell? Why then did we abandon the pleasant and delightful world?

Let our abbot be father of souls and torturer of bodies. [Col. 1780D] He is father, nourisher, pedagogue, and guardian of the Son of God within us, while He is still a little child, destined to be heir and to remain in the house forever. But let him be scourger, betrayer, seducer, despoiler, and finally crucifier and burier of the son of man. If he himself is negligent toward us, we are our own abbots: murderers of the son of man, but nourishers of the Son of God, so that He may grow and become very great, as is said of Isaac, and as the Apostle says: “Until Christ be formed in us, and we attain unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Gal. 4; cf. Eph. 4:13), who lives, etc.

## SERMON XXVIII. ON THE SAME FEAST, II

As the Lord Jesus foretold His passion to His disciples, and, as follows, His resurrection secretly, [Col. 1781A] “they did not understand the saying.” Perhaps He spoke to them secretly under this mystery because what He says is secret from them. “The saying,” he says, “was hidden from them, and they understood none of these things” (Luke 18). I too understand nothing of what I spoke at such length yesterday concerning the crucifixion of the son of man in myself. I do not know what all my striving and continual labour mean, what end they will have, what they signify, or by what name they are to be called before Him who has no need of our good things. For often what is high among human beings is abominable before God.

We do not doubt that our merits signify rewards, and that all we do are like certain prophetic and predictive voices of what will come upon us—rewards or punishments. “For each shall be repaid according to his works” (Rev. 22:12). And: “We must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, that each may receive according to what he has done in the body” (2 Cor. 5:10). Yet when I see tax collectors and prostitutes entering the kingdom of God, prophets and virgins excluded, workers of wondrous signs likewise excluded, and those who bore the burden and heat of the day receiving nothing more than those who worked one hour, and that later, I confess that I do not understand what I do in all I do; and even when I have done all good things and endured evils, I do not know whether I am worthy of love or of hatred (Eccl. 9:1). [Col. 1781B]

O saying most secret, exceedingly hidden: it can neither be kept silent nor known. Works are words; all things cry out, and nothing is without a voice. Yet we have not heard what the end of the discourse will be. Therefore we do not understand what all things mean or what they signify. The judgement of the discourse depends upon its ending. Every speech is held in suspense until its end; the end is acclaimed, answered, and judged. Before the end all things are hanging and settled nowhere. Before the end, ill-spoken words can be corrected, omissions supplied, superfluities cut away, and well-spoken words corrupted. The end concludes, settles, and perfects all things, so that before the end it is rashly determined what anything is.

Thus all uncertainties are reserved for the future. But wherever the tree falls, whether to the right or to the left, whether to the south or to the north, there it will be; there is its place before the Lord, for whom nothing is past and nothing future (Eccl. 11:3). Everything we live is a point or a moment; everything we do, however diverse and variable, is one work, whose end the Lord awaits and judges. “The Lord,” it says, “shall judge the ends of the earth” (1 Sam. 2:10). Beginnings and middle stages are movable, shifting in place, and therefore free from judgement; the end settles all things, and in it all things are settled. “He who perseveres unto the end shall be saved.”

For the righteousness of many, laboriously cultivated long and greatly, will be forgotten because of a different ending. Since such persons did not complete, they did nothing; or rather, what they completed and did not bring to an end, that alone they did; all the rest, because they abandoned it, is counted as begun but not done, and deserved to be abandoned. [Col. 1782A] Thus everything born of God does not sin (1 John 3), because it does not sin through to the end. Thus the Spirit of the Lord, from David’s anointing onward, did not depart from him (1 Sam. 16), because He returned—because He held to the end. The Lord likewise prayed for Peter that his faith might not fail; and, speaking to him in accordance with this meaning, said: “And thou, once thou hast turned again, strengthen thy brethren” (Luke 22). You see that the Apostle’s faith, which so failed that at a servant-girl’s voice he denied three times knowing Him whom he had followed for three years, is said not to have failed at all, because, having at some point turned back to Him, it did not fail utterly away from Him.

Because of all these and similar considerations, I said that I do not understand what I myself do or suffer within myself; rather, all that belongs to me is wholly hidden from me. Therefore, good Jesus, Thou must be entreated to make before us some certain and unquestionable sign, by which Thou mayest make us certain concerning what is doubtful: just as before Thy disciples, whose minds were still blind, Thou gavest bodily sight to a blind man, so that through the wonder which they saw in the present, they might believe without doubt concerning the future things they heard.

“And it came to pass, when Jesus drew near to Jericho, that a certain blind man sat by the way,” etc. [Col. 1782B] Jericho, they say, is interpreted “moon.” Therefore, when the seeing one drew near to the moon, the blind man drew near to the sun: the former to darkness, for the moon also has some darkness; the latter to the sun, who is wholly light and in whom there is no darkness; the former to decline, the latter to increase; the former to changeability, the latter to stability; and, if it may be so said, the former to folly, the latter to wisdom. For “the foolish man changes like the moon, but the wise man remains like the sun” (Sir. 27:11).

And, to settle the matter briefly: to the degree that God the Son of God was emptied in the Lord Jesus in order to become human, to that same degree was the human being, son of man, exalted in order to become God. For when the time appointed before all ages for this holy and saving Incarnation drew near, the Divinity, standing and seeing, commanded the holy angels to bring to Him humanity, blind and sitting in darkness; and He illumined it from Himself, lest, blind and inert in mind, it should beg outside the way because of poverty, but rather, luminous and strong, rejoicing bodily upon the way itself from the fullness of illuminating light, should praise and glorify God—at last restored to that for which it had formerly been made.

But since we believe that the Saviour’s works were done for us for redemption and written for us for instruction—done for healing, written for teaching—for “whatever things were written were written for our instruction” (Rom. 15:4), following the line of the preceding exposition, one may find every one of us at once seeing and blind, walking and lying down, as the foregoing sermon showed that we are compounded and double. [Col. 1782D] For our mother Cethean, when she went into the counsel of the ungodly—that is, into her own desire and the serpent’s hiss—cast our father Amorite outside the way. For he obeyed the woman's voice more than God, and thus lost the way, namely obedience itself, by which alone one truly proceeds to life.

We therefore, portions of the substance of each, have from then on both lived badly with our mother and lain still worse with our father: badly seeing and proceeding on the way; worse, lying and begging outside the way. Yet when the seeing one approaches Jericho, the blind one breathes again toward the light. In short: when our inner human being, through disobedience to the higher God and obedience to the lower woman, is blinded with respect to understanding, the outer is illumined with respect to desire. But when the outer is weakened in desire and draws near to its decline, the inner grows strong in understanding and is led toward its advance.

The inner person is, in a manner, male and the image of God; the outer person female and the image of the male. Before sin it is not said that the eyes of both were opened (Gen. 3), but the man alone saw what he should call all things, as one spiritual, judging all things. [Col. 1783A] The outer person, however, is animal even before sin and has neither the inner person’s vision of the Creator nor discernment of creatures: the inner beholds the Creator with the eye of understanding and examines the creature with the eye of reason. The former eye, extinguished by the beam of disobedience, and the latter disturbed by the speck of obedience, lies outside the way, raging, blind, and begging, and thus laments: “Mine iniquities have overtaken me, and I was not able to see” (Ps. 39 [40]). And elsewhere: “Mine eye is troubled because of wrath” (Ps. 6:7). And as though you asked why he lay down and did not at least walk while blind, he says: “My heart is troubled; my strength has forsaken me, and the light of mine eyes, even that is not with me” (Ps. 37 [38]).

But what does it mean that after sin the eyes of both are said to have been opened, except that the inner person is drawn out with the outer through ambition, curiosity, and pleasure? Made carnal with the flesh and animal with the animal, he is blind toward God, sharp-sighted toward the world, dull toward knowledge, keen toward desire. The man who has lost his own eyes uses only the woman’s eyes. Shame! The woman has become the man’s head, the female the husband’s guide. Thus “the wise man’s eyes are in his head” (Eccl. 2:14); thus the foolish man’s eyes are in his wife’s head (Prov. 17 [uncertain citation]), and through her at the ends of the earth.

For our outer human being is only a son of man: he is from the earth and speaks of the earth; earthly, he handles and meditates earthly things; he delights in earthly things, seeing and knowing those things in which and from which he has his origin. [Col. 1783C] But what the inner person could once behold of the Creator with his eyes, approach with his feet, and grasp with his hand, he now, blind and feeble, sitting, begs for: namely, knowledge of truth from the creature. Through the things made he seeks their Maker; through the cry, as it were, and teacher of his own study, he seeks outwardly from a master what he bears inscribed inwardly by God. Nor can he approach the light of truth until he withdraws from the darkness of vanity; nor can he advance toward the former unless the latter approaches its decline.

For the moon, which is what Jericho means, is fittingly set for the decline of the inner human being’s desire. Therefore, when and insofar as the outer human being declines from his own desire, by which he desires against the spirit, then and to that degree the inner advances in his desire against the flesh; and when the flesh draws near to the darkness of its own light, the spirit draws near to the illumination of its darkness. Yet this cannot happen unless One intervenes who leads the former away and brings the latter near, as the Psalmist cries in prayer to the Father: “Send forth thy light and thy truth: they have led me and brought me unto thy holy mountain and unto thy tabernacles” (Ps. 42 [43]). May Christ, the Light and Truth, who lives and reigns as God, lead us there. Amen.

## SERMON XXIX. ON THE SAME FEAST, III

God the Son of God, beloved, Light and Truth, Jesus Christ, sent forth by the Father, intervened between the flesh and spirit, rebellious and desiring against one another; and, dissolving the old enmities, He at last restored peace in Himself. [Col. 1784B] He did this not with the ease with which the Almighty could have done it, but with the love and patience befitting the most gracious One, and with the degree of instruction required by our dullness. For, as we have often said already, God took humanity upon Himself not only to redeem humankind but also to instruct it.

Therefore, in taking the whole human being—that is, flesh from Adam’s flesh, because of which He often calls Himself Son of Man, and a rational spirit—He sanctified both simultaneously and at once; yet by His manner of bearing them, throughout almost all the ages, He taught how they ought to be borne. Accordingly, while the Son of God Himself—that is, the Father’s Word—acts and leads, the Son of Man—that is, the flesh, or our outer human being—draws near to the decline of its desires; while He Himself leads the spirit, it draws near to the desired light.

Did He not Himself, in His own person, powerfully weary, weaken, and dry up the Son of Man—that is, the flesh taken from humankind—by fasts and the barrenness of the wilderness, hunger and thirst, labour and weariness, vigils and disciplines? Later He cruelly gave it over to bonds and scourges, spitting and blows, thorns and nails, and the hands of the ungodly, as it is written: “The earth is given into the hand of the wicked” (Job 9:24). [Col. 1784C] Thus, in order that the Son of Man may ascend to Jerusalem while the Son of God leads him, Jericho draws near to its decline, and, at His command to bring him, the blind man hastens back to light (Luke 18). For in order that the flesh may advance toward peace with its spirit, it must, by God’s grace, decline from its carnality; and in order that the rational spirit may return to the light of understanding, it must, as carnality declines, approach the Word of God without sluggishness, being led by the same grace, as it is written: “Draw near unto him, and be illumined” (Ps. 33 [34]:6).

Both, beloved, are as impossible for us as they are easy for the Son of God to accomplish. For what are we but darkness and vanity? But He is Light and Truth. Unless, then, the Son of God is in us and works in us, we neither decline from evil nor advance toward good, neither fall from vanity nor rise to truth. Yet just as in Him the Son of God by nature assumed flesh and soul, by grace rendering the former blind to concupiscence and illumining the latter unto wisdom—being naturally one with the Father, yet made, through the duality He assumed from us, in a manner three in substances, two in natures, while remaining one in person—so, brother, [Col. 1785A] though you are one in person and two in nature, through reception of grace you too are made in your own manner three, according to what is said: “He gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

Thus, as that Son of Man is the Son of God, so you, Son of God, are a son of man. Therefore, just as in him the Son of God bore and governed, led forth and brought back the son of man, so in us may our Son of God bear, govern, lead, and bring back our son of man: in part toward the dying away, in part toward the advancement—toward the dying away of carnal and earthly things, toward the advancement of spiritual and heavenly things. And just as he, as though making his love for us known, frequently calls himself that which he became by grace for us, namely the Son of Man, so too let us, with thanksgiving always mindful of what we have been made by him—namely, sons of God, a new [Col. 1785B] creation in Christ Jesus, according as he willingly begot us by the word of truth—reverently call ourselves sons of God, disdaining to be or to be called what we were carnally born, namely sons of men. Rebuking such people through the Prophet, the Holy Spirit says: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Ps. IV). And elsewhere he reproaches through the prophet: “You are your mother’s daughter, and you are the sister of your sisters” (Ezek. XVI).

I confess that I am now here an alien and a pilgrim throughout this whole world, as one who is by no means native to it; not the son of man, but the Son of God lying hidden in the form and likeness of a man. Henceforth, though they may say, affirm, and swear that I am theirs, I am neither the son of my father and mother [Col. 1785C] nor brother of my brothers. Even should they produce witnesses and display beforehand the very marks in skin and flesh, conscious as I am of whence I come, I persistently deny it, plainly disavow it, maintaining that I am not whom they suppose; they are deceived by the likeness. And stretching out my hands toward you, I say: these are my brothers. Together we are all fatherless children and orphans; we have no father on earth, for our Father is heavenly, and our mother is the Virgin. There we are natives; here we are aliens and pilgrims, as were all our fathers. We are by no means earthly, of the earth, but heavenly, of heaven, though clothed in an earthly sackcloth, and therefore judged earthly, until we can say to our Father: “You have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness” (Ps. XXIX).

[Col. 1785D] I see what I am; I discern the wrappings in which I am enveloped. Why? Unless it is because, before me, the blind man has been illumined; before me has been wrought the sign of present grace, confirming faith in future glory. For it is written: “The Lord will give grace and glory” (Ps. LXXXIII). The one sign is grace; the other is merit. To him to whom he has given this grace, he will without doubt give glory. Whom he has illumined unto faith, he will raise unto sight. Through what I see, I believe what I do not yet understand. As I consider what I was and what I have become, I hope for what he promises that I shall become.

Therefore, considering not human merits but God’s gifts, I infer the promises from what I have received, greater things from great things, and more wonderful things from wonderful things; as the blessed Psalmist says, consoling himself: “Return, my soul, to your rest, [Col. 1786A] because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you” (Ps. CXIV). And elsewhere: “I shall cry to God Most High, to God who has dealt bountifully with me” (Ps. LVI). I establish for myself no certain sign of righteousness in my fasts, human traditions, Pharisaic dress, any righteousness of works, or works of righteousness which I do; but in the righteousness of faith, which freely goes before and illumines those whom it saves. For many sinners deeper than I are freely taken up by grace; and men more highly righteous are justly cast away by righteousness. The righteousness of works is always vain, and a work of righteousness is often deceptive; but the righteousness which is from faith in Christ Jesus has deceived no one. I set it as a seal upon my heart, and as a seal upon my arm; I understand it as the sign wrought with me for good, so that those who hate me may see and [Col. 1786B] be put to shame.

Therefore he who is my illumination is also my salvation. I shall follow him to himself, praising and glorifying God in him. Though a thousand kinds of temptations or disturbances cry out that I should be silent, I shall cry aloud boldly; and, crying, I shall overcome the outcry of those who cry against me, until I fix my gaze upon Jesus passing by and make him who is passing stop. For, to continue the line of the preceding discourse: as diverse things from diverse sources accompanied the Lord Jesus, Son of God and likewise Son of Man, along the way of his pilgrimage—some from flesh, others from spirit; some from the Word; some from humanity, others from divinity; some from weakness, others from power—so surely these too may readily be discerned in us, and it is impossible not to feel them. We experience this more certainly in the book of experience [Col. 1786C] than we learn it from the preacher’s voice.

Yet, brethren, it is worth the effort, with rational discernment and watchfulness of the senses, to judge whence arise within us all the things that arise in us; what are the sources and roots of our thoughts and affections, desires and wills, suggestions and delights. Thus, just as works of power and miraculous signs accompanied him, as though testifying that Jesus was the one making the passage, and stirring many to believe in him—of which it is written, “Your testimonies have become exceedingly trustworthy” (Ps. XCII), while he himself says, “The works which I do bear witness concerning me” (John V)—so, on the other hand, sufferings of weakness cried out in order to deter people from faith in him, lest they believe to be God one whom they saw suffer human things. Summing up both in brief, he answered those sent by John: “Report to John what you have heard and seen: the blind see, the lame walk,” and so forth (Matt. XI). And then: “Blessed is he who shall not be scandalized in me” (ibid.). For scourges and spittle, cross and tomb, caused scandal.

[Col. 1786D] So also in myself, beloved, I bear along with me, throughout every path of my life, some things that attest salvation, some that draw me back, some that acclaim, some that cry against me; nor do I go anywhere without these companions. I am visited at dawn, and suddenly tested; I am lifted up, and immediately abandoned; I am raised, and immediately cast down, like one walking through mountains who finds no level path. At times, joyful and praising, flooded with excessive light and affected by wonderful sweetness, [Col. 1787A] I exult in an inexpressible hope of unexpected salvation: everything cries assent, everything bears good testimony, so that no place remains for doubt, as though I had already laid hold of it. At times, trembling and weeping, wrapped in darkness and full of bitterness, I waste away in such a turmoil of weariness and acedia that everything cries against better hope and compels me to be silent. Woe to the miserable man who can neither persist with God according to his desire nor stand fast in himself according to his resolution! I confess that I am never constant in myself: continually I am ground between hope and fear; I carry within me roots and seedbeds of both. Each sprouts upward and stretches its branches through my inward parts. From God’s grace in me I have cause always to hope; from myself I have, indeed, cause continually to fear. Now I hold all that I hope for; [Col. 1787B] now I lose everything that I had held, and again after darkness I hope for light. I ascend even to the heavens and descend even to the abysses; my soul wastes away amid such alternations. “I am troubled and shaken like a drunken man, and all my wisdom is swallowed up” (Ps. CVI).

Nevertheless, as the sacred Psalm goes on to say, and as this blind man in the Gospel teaches, only one thing remains for me: to overcome importunity and to cry all the more to the Lord Jesus when I am afflicted, until he brings me out of these necessities, makes this storm a gentle breeze, and silences its waves which he has brought upon me; and, rejoicing because they are still, leads me into the harbor of my will and desire (ibid.). Today, hiding in the farthest corner of the earth and surrounded by the sea, I desire—he himself being witness—him alone: with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the one true and good God and Lord of the universe. To him be honor and glory, praise and power, splendor and dominion, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXX. ON THE FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT I

“Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness,” etc. (Matt. IV).

My Lord Christ Jesus does everything either led, sent, called, or commanded; of himself, however, nothing. Sent, he comes into the world; led, he goes into the wilderness; called, he rises from the dead, as it is written: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. CVII). But he hastens to the Passion freely and willingly, as the prophet foretold: “He was offered, because he willed it” (Isa. LIII), [Col. 1787D] yet in this very matter made obedient to the Father unto death. For, as teacher and example of obedience, apart from it—which alone is truly the way to life—he willed neither to do nor to suffer anything.

Therefore he was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, or, as another says, “he was driven by the Spirit into the wilderness” (Luke IV). “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.” But he, as Son in a more special and worthy manner, is also led or driven into the wilderness in a manner more distinctive and excellent than the rest. “Filled,” it says, “with the Holy Spirit, he returned from the Jordan” (Luke III), and was immediately driven by that same Spirit into the wilderness. To others the Spirit is given by measure, and according to the same measure they are led in all things; but he received fullness, in whom it pleased the fullness of divinity [Col. 1788A] to dwell bodily. Therefore he is led more powerfully and fully to fulfil all the Father’s commands.

“He returned from the Jordan and was driven into the wilderness.” Before this, I do not recall having heard the word “return” applied to the Lord Jesus. Jordan, they say, is interpreted as “their descent.” Therefore he comes from the Jordan and returns thence who descended into the world; and, returning from here, he again leaves the world and goes to the Father. Accordingly, whoever desires to ascend and return from the place from which he did not descend but fell, let him come to the Jordan; let him come to descent; let him come to humility, which alone is the place of ascent. For everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted. “Arise,” says the Psalmist, “after you have sat down” (Ps. CXXVI). [Col. 1788B] There he will find the Holy Spirit, who rests upon the humble, the gentle, and the one trembling at the words of the Lord; who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble: grace by which they may despise the world, flee the age, conquer the devil, avoid crowds where corrupt speech corrupts good morals; seek the wilderness and secluded places, where they may be free for God; where, like a swallow’s chick, they may cry to him, and like a dove meditate upon him; where, answering them, he himself will speak to their heart, according to the prophet who says: “I will lead her into solitude, and there I will speak to her heart” (Hos. II).

Thus our Lord Jesus Christ, gentle and humble in heart, after descending to such a degree of humility and gentleness that he submitted himself for baptism to the hands of one lower than himself, immediately deserved to ascend to the rank of preeminence, as the Father’s voice testified: “This is my beloved Son, in whom [Col. 1788C] I have been well pleased because of humility and obedience; therefore I rightly advance him and set him above the rest; henceforth hear him.” The Holy Spirit too visibly descends upon the humble and gentle, as upon his own proper and familiar temple. Filled with him, Christ returns from the Jordan and is led into the wilderness.

Therefore, beginning from the Jordan to return by the way from which he had come forth, first assuming the dignity of preeminence and the authority of preaching, he goes alone into the wilderness. There, he who was to preach to others first tests in himself, fulfilling what he was to teach others; he first conquers flesh, world, and devil, against whom he would exhort his own to fight. [Col. 1788D] For it is foolish, untried, and unseasoned in Christian warfare to thrust others into battles in which one has neither gone ahead nor dares to follow; to exhort to conflict one who has not stood in battle-line, or has first fled; to aspire to teach what one has not first done—indeed, what one has not yet begun to do; to assume the rank of teacher and not know the office; finally, to bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them upon others’ shoulders, when one is unwilling to touch them with a finger.

But Jesus Christ, our teacher and leader, teaches what he does, as Scripture says: “What he began to do and to teach” (Acts I). He preaches what he is: “Learn from me,” he says, “for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI). He brings his army to the field where he himself first conquered. “Take courage,” he says, “I have conquered the world” (John XVI). For in this first encounter, fighting alone with the solitary foe in the wilderness, he secretly overcame the common yet individual enemy of the human race; by overcoming, he weakened him and made him weaker, easily conquerable, and enfeebled for his own people. In the second encounter, in the public arena of this world, before angels and men looking on, he humbled, threw down, and wounded him, as it is written: “You humbled the proud one as though wounded” (Ps. LXXXVIII). Having thrown him down, he bound him, took away his weapons, and plundered his vessels. For binding the strong man with one stronger, he entered the world through his own, and hell through himself; he plundered his vessels and rightfully transferred them to his own service (Luke XI).

[Col. 1789B] Here he wisely repelled the foe while he flattered him, feigned kindly concern for his reputation, supported his standing, and pitied his poverty; later he patiently endured him when raging and courageously conquered him. Here, therefore, is wisdom of the saints; there, patience and power. For Christ, the power of God and wisdom of God, came to teach and bestow both; in both he was tempted, and in both was found proved. Thus the deceitful one first attacks wisdom, transforming himself into an angel of light and a spirit of counsel.

“Tell these stones to become loaves,” he says, “lest you waste away from hunger in the wilderness while fasting; and you who have trampled abundance and luxury by power, at least now, though late, come to the aid of extreme necessity with bread alone.” But because, at the first bite, where he had believed he would find the tenderness of flesh, the serpent broke his tooth on the solidity of bone, he withdrew his sting from the heel of the foot and raised himself to higher things, which he thinks softer but finds harder. Thus, taking him up, [Col. 1789C] he set him on high, but in order that he might cast him headlong into the deep. As if he said: “You are indeed exalted and lofty, for by the power of abstinence you have trampled the flesh’s desire. You please God and are near to him, because you have transcended the flesh. You ought no longer to be unknown and lowly. Therefore make yourself manifest to men. Let them see you flying, you whom the crushed weight of flesh has made light; you who, conquering that you were born of flesh and are flesh, are now, born of Spirit, spirit; and, born of God, are the Son of God. Cast yourself down, then, so that angels may serve you, since you have acquired by merit of virtue what they possess by the gift of grace. Therefore they ought to serve you and carry you in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone.”

[Col. 1789D] This is that basilisk, king of serpents, which kills by its glance alone, which infects merely by sight what the asp does not kill with its breath. Therefore, after the temptation of the lust of the flesh—that is, of the asp—the king of serpents brings forth the temptation of the lust of the eyes. Yet our athlete and champion, just as he later bravely trampled the lion’s rage, now wisely avoids the serpent’s poison, walking over asp and basilisk with the steps of sobriety and humility. He also tramples the great dragon of worldly ambition and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world, when, by love of poverty, he scorns all the kingdoms of the world and their glory offered to him. See what sort of adversary, in what way, conquers what sort of foe. Wisdom conquers cunning; abstinence, gluttony; humility, empty glory; poverty, worldly ambition.

[Col. 1790A] When the prince of this world came to Wisdom—abstemious, humble, poor—he found in him nothing of his own, nothing not his own that he could seize. Having shot all the arrows of his cunning, he withdrew for a time, that is, until the hour of the Passion, when the lion attacks the Lamb; but cruelty is conquered by gentleness. Power is tempted by savagery, just as wisdom here was tempted by cunning. Yet by the strength of patience he conquers the lion, whom by the foresight of providence he conquered as a dragon. For patience is the greatest of all virtues. In it lies possession of souls, even when bodies are lost into the hands of persecutors; in it Truth testifies that good soil bears every fruit. Of it the Apostle says: “You have need of patience, so that, doing the will of God, you may [Col. 1790B] receive the promise” (Heb. X). It is that which, as the blessed James says, has a perfect work.

It is therefore divided twofold, namely into temperance and fortitude, and makes the mind it possesses sober and strong in prosperity and adversity alike: both against the enticing impulses of flesh and the wellsprings of inward vices, and against the outward luxuries and cruelties of the world. May Christ Jesus grant us this, that we may suffer with him and for him—he who suffered in it for us—and who, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXI. ON THE SAME FEAST II

[Col. 1790C] “Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil” (Matt. IV).

This Lent of our Lord and Savior, prefigured by the forty-day fasts of Moses and Elijah, and likewise by the fathers’ pilgrimage of the same number of years in the wilderness, should by no means be thought empty and barren of mystery and saving sacrament. Yet, brethren, it is difficult and exceeds the understanding of our littleness to distinguish the progress of rational abstinence by so many stages, and, for one ascending from Egypt to the land of promise—that is, from this world to the Father—to assign so many resting-places of virtues in the wilderness of his own spirit, while this ascender once inhabited flesh: resting-places through which he may withdraw from flesh in order to draw near to God, as it is written: “He has set ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place which he has appointed” (Ps. LXXXIII).

[Col. 1790D] Yet because in the number forty the four is multiplied tenfold, or the ten fourfold, this is presently intimated to us by these numbers: so long as we are temporal here, weighed down in the body which corrupts and burdens the soul, and are pilgrims away from the Lord’s table and delightful refreshment, we should chastise our bodies and subject them to the service of God’s law; nor should we lose through negligence, or misuse in pride, the time of truce granted for amendment. Rather, let us make use of the time and exercise the body in keeping and obeying God’s commandments, while meditating with the heart upon his law day and night. But where that law itself opposes our desires, let us come to terms with it while we are still on the way, lest after the [Col. 1791A] way it hand us over as rebels to the Judge, and the Judge to the torturer (Matt. V). Therefore let us torment ourselves, beloved, under the law, lest we be tormented by the law. Let us abstain from what opposes the law, and fast, lest we experience the law as hostile—especially when it judges, though we now oppose it while it gives counsel.

For this is the fast that the Lord has chosen: abstaining from every evil, not only outwardly from the deed but inwardly from a perverse will. Outwardly another is injured; inwardly one injures oneself. For no one harms another before harming himself. Through another’s garment you pierce your own body. The mother, greed, harms you more than her daughter, robbery or theft, which is born from her, harms another. Envy brings you more evil than your slander takes good from the one whom you disparage through envy. [Col. 1791B] For the perfect fast, and the one God has chosen, is not for a person to afflict his soul for a day, bend his head like a hoop, greedily demand all his debts, and fast for litigation and strife; it is to abstain from every evil and apply oneself to every good; not to do another the evil one would not wish done to oneself, and to do the good one wishes for oneself: thus, as it were, to multiply the coin of the law fourfold by the Gospel, and multiply the fourfold Gospel tenfold by the law.

For the perfection of the Gospel formerly lay hidden in the law, just as now the law’s imperfection is disclosed in the Gospel. The law prescribes a fast of deed; the Gospel, a fast from evil will. The law punishes the act.
