[Col. 1791C] Hence our preacher in the Gospel says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill.’ But I say to you: do not be angry,” and the rest in this manner (Matt. V). It continues: “And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights.” For he did not fast openly and in the light, and eat secretly in darkness; but as he was in public, so he was in private; as in outward appearance, so in heart. It continues:

“Afterward he was hungry.” God fasted as long as he willed, and man was hungry when he willed; and then the tempter came to him. Why not before? Because he did not dare, or it was not fitting. He craftily feared the strong man; he opportunely attacked the weak. For every human temptation has a threefold origin: sometimes wholly inward and from ourselves; sometimes wholly inward and from another; sometimes inward and outward, from ourselves and from another. [Col. 1791D] Not every temptation is from the devil, nor is sin committed only by his suggestion. We are tempted when drawn away and enticed by our own desires, while the devil suggests nothing, or perhaps is unaware. Desire, however, is twofold: one by which flesh desires against spirit; another by which spirit desires against God. Both are evil. Moreover, there is a desire by which spirit desires against flesh, in order to restrain it from vices and subject it to reason; and another which desires toward God, in order to grasp him and enjoy him. Hence it is written: “My soul desires and faints for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII). Both of these are good.

[Col. 1792A] Therefore, evil desire sometimes arises without the devil; but once it has arisen, he gladly assists it to grow. Every good desire, however, is forestalled by God’s grace at its arising, aided toward progress, and brought to perfection in its completion. Thus, although good desire can be wholly enacted inwardly, it cannot be wholly from ourselves. A temptation wholly inward and from ourselves, therefore, arises either from the necessity of the animate body, from the itching weakness of corruption, from the recurrence of a bad habit, or from the insolence of grace and virtue. When the crafty tempter and malicious ambusher detects by any sign the tinder of a spark, he gathers straw from every side with utmost haste and diligence—desires which he finds suitable—in order, if he prevails, to strike flame from the spark and burn the house of our breast [Col. 1792B] with what is ours and his, as it is written: “They burned your sanctuary with fire upon the ground” (Ps. LXXIII).

[Col. 1792B] But the Lord Jesus, confirmed in God against sin from the womb, as it is written, “In you I have been established from the womb” (Ps. LXX), was nevertheless animate in flesh, like man before sin; weak, however, as Son of Man, because of the father’s sin. He could suffer only that passion, when he willed and in whatever degree he willed, which proceeds from the necessity or weakness of the animate body. For since there are three states of human mutability—before sin, near sin, and after sin—the true teacher and physician willed to display something of each in himself: that the teacher might remind us what we were and what we are, and the physician might show what we shall be.

[Col. 1792C] Thus, as animate in the first state, he could desire food and drink; as weak in the second, he could undergo sorrow, weariness, fear, and death; as confirmed in the third, he could admit no stimulation from his own nature even in thought, nor any evil suggestion from another. Thus all that temptation on the pinnacle and mountain was external and from another; the first appears to have had something from his own nature, where the serpent lay in ambush, as it were, for his heel. Yet since that suggestion neither created nor increased nor could in any way stir natural and therefore blameless hunger, all of it, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1791D] Gregory, Homily 16 on the Gospels.], was an external, diabolical temptation, although an inward human temptation had preceded it.

[Col. 1792D] Therefore, when after long and astonishing fasts the tempter perceived his hunger by some external sign, after long suspense and astonishment he finally found his opportunity and presumed to approach him. See, then, beloved, how greatly it behooves us to be sober and watchful, as the blessed chief of the apostles warns (1 Pet. V), against our adversary the devil, who with such diligence goes about, with such vigilance investigates our entire manner of life, our mode of living, necessities, weaknesses of body and character, sudden and varied contingencies, and the very constitutions of our nature, to see whether anywhere he may find an entrance from us into us, and material and an occasion for temptation.

[Col. 1793A] Why are we, brethren, less concerned to seek opportunities for salvation in one another, so that where we see the need greater, we may more greatly assist one another and bear one another’s fraternal burdens? For the blessed Apostle, urging this, says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. VI). And elsewhere: “Supporting one another,” he says, “in charity” (Eph. IV). This indeed is the law of Christ: when I see in my brother something incurable, either from necessity or from weakness of body or character, why do I not bear it patiently and willingly console him, as it is written: “Their children shall be carried upon shoulders and comforted upon knees” (Isa. LXVI)? Is it because I lack that charity which bears all things, which is patient so as to bear and kind so as to love? This is surely the law of Christ, who truly bore our infirmities in his Passion and carried our sorrows in compassion, loving those whom he bore and bearing those whom he loved.

[Col. 1793B] But whoever assails a brother in necessity, whoever lies in wait for his weakness of whatever kind, undoubtedly subjects himself to the devil’s law and fulfils it. Therefore let us be compassionate toward one another, lovers of the brotherhood, bearers of infirmities, pursuers of vices—especially we few who, because of the discipline of a more arduous purpose, have escaped to this hidden solitude and island remote from the common world. For every discipline that pursues more sincerely the love of God and, for his sake, love of neighbor, whatever observances or habit it may practice, is more acceptable to God. [Col. 1793C] For charity itself is that for whose sake everything ought to be done or not done, changed or not changed. It is both the principle why and the end toward which all things ought to be directed. Nothing is done culpably that is truly done for and according to it. May he deign to grant this to us—the one without whom we cannot please God, and without which we cannot at all—he who lives and reigns as God through immortal ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXII. ON THE SAME FEAST III

“Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness,” etc. (Matt. IV).

While we were in the flesh, brethren—where no one can please God—we savored what belonged to flesh and delighted in carnal things, speaking and treating of carnal things; and so, wholly—that is, in thought, delight, [Col. 1793D] speech, and action—we inhabited flesh, having deserted spirit and rational mind. But when, anticipated by the leadership of a stronger Spirit, we penetrated our inward parts and entered our own spirit, once neglected and deserted by God, angels, and ourselves, imposing restraint upon ourselves and prescribing fasting to carnal desires and longings, we immediately incurred the envy of the evil dwelling in us—that is, in our flesh. For you know with the Apostle that “good does not dwell in us,” that is, “in our flesh” (Rom. VII). We roused Leviathan against ourselves; from him we suffered the snares of one newly made a hermit. Hoping to be solitary and secure in quiet, we encountered a crafty tempter and malicious ambusher (Job III). Thus we were compelled to keep frequently in mind that saying of the Wise Man: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II).

[Col. 1794A] And the tempter came and said to him: “Tell these stones to become loaves.” What offense would there be in making bread from stone or in an hungry person’s eating? But it is dangerous to trust an enemy even when he speaks truth or recommends useful things. For this reason he sets forward truths, that he may introduce falsehoods; he urges advantages, that he may draw one into disadvantages; he puts on the guise of a counsellor, that he may creep in more secretly; he transforms himself into an angel of light, that he may deceive more easily. Further, spiritual men who have departed from the kindred of flesh and blood, forgotten their people and the house of flesh, and entered the wilderness of spirit do not immediately yield to every necessity of flesh and blood. For such men, it is not enough to cut away every superfluity unless they also circumcise necessity itself. And what they dare not wholly deny to the animate and weak body, they nevertheless grant at last, late and sparingly, not without pride and complaint. [Col. 1794B] Whoever refreshes himself the moment he is hungry knows nothing whatever of fasting, whose power and merit only begin with hunger. For not eating is not fasting: just as eating after satiety is superfluous, so eating before hunger is idle; with hunger it is permissible; after hunger it is strenuous, and more strenuous the longer it is deferred. The same is true of sleep and the other necessities of the animate and weak body. Against these a certain spiritual man—a hermit in cities, a poor man on a royal throne—cries to the Lord: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. XXIV).

[Col. 1794C] There is another, holier and loftier fast, which those who have entered the solitude of their own spirit must not only observe carefully and diligently, but must prolong through the continuous forty days and nights—that is, through the whole period of this life—in prosperity as well as adversity, in preeminence as well as subjection, in contemplation as well as action. That is: they must abstain from every unclean consolation and delight of this world, in which are curiosity, pleasure, and pride of life; but inwardly, where the malignant spirit cannot see, they should be refreshed by spiritual meditation, lest they utterly fail through fasting, and by the delight that is in God alone and by the pleasure of good action undertaken for his sake.

[Col. 1794D] For it is impossible in this mere shadow of death, or image of life, before one arrives at life altogether dark and covered with death’s gloom, where no order exists but everlasting horror dwells, for the soul to be sustained by no consolation and held by no delight—even though the soul itself does not hold that delight. For as individual bodies are borne by their own weights, so spirits are situated by their own delights. In the body of the universe, God’s creation, in which individual things are as members of a certain body, the rational spirit alone, as the eye of the whole body, can perceive the Creator’s light, share in its delight, and enjoy it; and in that light it can judge all the members as obscure, and dark in comparison with it.

[Col. 1795A] For just as the light of the sensible world is fire, and the light of the human body is the eye, so the rational spirit is, as we have said, the luminous part—namely the eye—of that greatest body, the most beautiful and orderly universe. Yet just as the eye, though created as a suitable instrument for seeing, a lesser lamp somehow made in image and likeness of the greater, worldly light, is nevertheless unable to see through itself, as from itself, unless it is first met and flooded by that whose image it bears; so the rational spirit, the greatest created light, would not see beyond the other members of its body unless it had been made in the image of its higher, uncreated, and supreme light. Nor can it see what it wills, either from itself or through itself, unless its higher reality, [Col. 1795B] whose image it bears, is present to it and illumines it according to its measure; in whose light it can see light. “In your light,” he says, “we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV).

The remaining members of the universe, therefore, participate in the Creator according to the capacity appropriate to their differing natures—without any participation in whom they could not exist at all. Some participate only in being and form; others in some sort of life; others in sensation; others in imagination. But the rational spirit alone, by a prerogative of nature chosen above all others, can participate in God himself, through reason and affection, for the knowledge of him and delight in him, in him; and it has been created by him through these two faculties to enjoy him. Alone it is capable of receiving divinity and, by natural bounty, communicable, endowable, and enjoyable. [Col. 1795C]

For the supreme light is always shining and therefore, so far as lies in itself, illuminating. At last, when it willed, it created in its own image that which could be illuminated by it: namely, the rational spirit alone. Its sole business ought to be that for which it is known to have been created; its desire, that which is known to be God’s purpose concerning it; its sole food and refreshment, delight in God himself and, through him, in all things. From every pleasure of the flesh, curiosity of the senses, and worldly ambition it must always abstain for his sake. These are the heads of the dragon, crushed by the Lord Jesus in this wilderness and given as food to those peoples who refuse to fast with Christ: namely, the black peoples, who, like the Ethiopian, do not know how to change their skin. “You crushed the heads of the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians” (Ps. 73).

Moreover, just as God made two great lights for this world, that great living creature, and two globes of eyes for the lesser world, that little living creature, so indeed he joined together the eye of the greatest body, the universe: instituting the angel and the human mind, of one nature indeed, but of differing condition and lot. Those angels, ever radiant in the splendor of truth and joyous in the sweetness of delight, have never been touched by hunger for an alien pleasure; no tempter has approached them. There the ninety-nine sheep graze in their wilderness and lie down amid ever-green grass, in rich pastures upon the mountains of Israel, and there is none to terrify them. [Col. 1796A]

But we, wretched wanderers and fugitives, who have strayed like that lost sheep which the good shepherd came to seek, and, once found, laid upon his sacred shoulders in order to carry it back to the flock of angels, so that there might be one shepherd and one fold: through our own weakness we fail inwardly into evil hunger, and by alien suggestion are outwardly invited to a worse refreshment. Forgetting to eat our own bread, we hunger for another’s.

Therefore, when he who always envies and always lays snares sees us slothful and lukewarm, he takes this as a sign of inward failure; he approaches and shows us how we may be refreshed. What he could not introduce, he hastens to foster and increase as something innate. He does not dare approach one who is strong, steadfast, and fervent; rather, he watches from afar. To one who is slothful and inwardly occupied with fables—that is, with thoughts lacking understanding, from which the Holy Spirit withdraws—the evil one draws near. He does not rush in or break through, but approaches gently and, as it were, modestly, lest he frighten him, under the appearance of a counsellor. Thus he says: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.” Yet this was said not because the Son of God was such, but because that hunger of his could symbolize such things. O malice deserving to be stoned! You advise the Son of God to be refreshed with a stone. Though human beings are evil, they know how to give good gifts to their children; and would the heavenly Father give a stone to his Son asking for bread? Or a scorpion to one asking for a fish, or a serpent instead of an egg?

He invites the spirit, numbed to the desire and contemplation of heavenly things, away from the bread of angels to the cold, dry, hard stone—that is, to love and delight in earthly things—so that, if it has lost that consolation, it may be received by this one and deceived by the devil, having first been proved to have failed within itself. For, as we said above, the soul cannot subsist without some consolation. Consolation is its refreshment and bread. But if it comes from the world and flesh, it is certainly from a stone. The tempter therefore invites to this the mind which he sees languishing away from delight in God. Hence in the ordering of vices avarice follows sloth, because this world flatters one who falls from heaven. The truly spiritual mind of blessed David, detesting its consolation, says: “My soul refused to be comforted by the world and by all that is in the world”—that is, by the desire of the flesh, [Col. 1796D] the desire of the eyes, and worldly ambition. What then? Can you exist without the consolation of delight? By no means. “But I remembered God and was delighted; and, because idleness is the enemy of the soul, I was exercised by meditating upon him; and my spirit failed—not away from him into the world or into myself, but away from myself and the whole world into him alone” (Ps. 76).

Thus my Lord Jesus too, in the wilderness, neither idle nor intent upon vain things, meditating day and night upon the law of the Lord, met every temptation with the holy Scriptures. Although this evil one is called a craftsman of a thousand devices because of the countless kinds of temptations which he devises, yet I confidently say that every one of his inventions can readily and fittingly be refuted from holy Scripture. Far be it that malice should overcome wisdom, or that it should be able to devise a poison for which wisdom contains no antidote! [Col. 1797A]

Therefore, beloved, following the example of the Lord and Savior, let us continually meditate upon his law, following him into the wilderness—not only that of place, but of spirit, and at times even of God himself, surpassing our own spirit with the angels. Let us meditate upon it whether it is written outwardly in the letter, inwardly in our nature, in the figure of this world, or in the very wisdom of God, which is the eternal law and may be called the law of laws. Here we shall be fed with the bread of life and understanding, and drink the saving water of wisdom, so that inwardly refreshed and filled with delight, we may despise outside ourselves the devil’s stony bread. Let us also disdain the world’s exaltation, which ruin follows—for “the heart is exalted before ruin”—and which casts one downward. Let us, standing and upright above, with him who makes the promise, blow away from the desire and thought of our hearts every abundance and glory of this age which is promised to one who falls, saying: “Begone, Satan.” For every impulse that invites us to fall is Satan—that is, an adversary to us: “If, falling down,” he says, “you worship me.”

Let us rather stand, beloved, with our feet in the courts of Jerusalem; and without doubt we shall go rejoicing into the house of the Lord, into that very unity where all participation shall be in the One who will be all in all. May he deign to bring us all there: Jesus Christ, without whom no one can attain it, who by his temptation strengthened us to stand when by his victory he weakened the tempter; to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be [Col. 1797C] honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIII. ON THE FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT

“Jesus departed and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon” (Matt. 15).

Beloved, insofar as the Lord Jesus is the eternal Word of the Father, neither passing nor finite, there is in him an eternal going forth from the Father, an eternal abiding in the Father, and an eternal return to the Father. For he returns to that from which he arises, and there he remains. Just as he does not cease when, born from it, he proceeds, so neither does he arrive when, returning to it, he is brought back, as it were, to where he always remains and has remained. Yet we do not think any human being capable of comprehending this incomprehensible going forth of ineffable generation. Holy angels have a happier and thus easier capacity for it, provided that they have gone forth from their own boundaries—that is, surpassed themselves.

But why do we attempt things too high for us, things of which we are wholly ignorant? Perhaps with immature desire, like fledglings feathering in the nest, we move wings still unequal to flight: they can indeed be shaken, but cannot raise the body’s weight. Besides this eternal going forth of nature, then, there is a temporal going forth of grace: when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1); when he went forth from the Father and came into the world; when, although he was in the form of God, going out, as it were, beyond the borders of his homeland, he emptied himself. Thus he could be found in the form of a servant and in the likeness of sinful flesh, as though in the region of Tyre and Sidon—but by those who, having gone beyond their own borders, meet him in that same region. [Col. 1798A]

The Son of God came free, that he might liberate, into the form of a servant and the likeness of sinful flesh, but not into slavery itself or the reality of sinful flesh. He came to sinners, but did not enter into sin; he came to the infirm, but did not come to the cause of infirmity; he came to punishment, but did not reach guilt. In short, the Savior came: from the first state, free from sin; in the second, infirm because of sin; in the third, strong against sin. Therefore, if anyone is enslaved under sin, infirm because of sin, weak against sin, and desires to be saved by him, let him go out from his sin in repentance, meet him in faith, and cry after him in prayer. For he is always moving onward who has not stood in the way of sinners. Let the captive come to him who is free and can therefore set free; the infirm to him who knows how to sympathize from what he suffered in infirmity; the weak to him who, by the word of his power, accomplishing purification from sins, can save forever.

Let the Canaanite woman, therefore, go forth from her inward borders and meet, in the outward parts of her region, the physician who has voluntarily come forth mercifully from his own borders and graciously meets the sick person in foreign parts; for while she remained in her own place she could not at all have been visited by him. For he, as blessed God, just, and strong, was above, where it was not permitted for unhappy humanity to ascend. Nor was it safe for the unjust to appear before the just; nor could one send another into the dwelling-place of strength, where none was not sick. The compassionate one therefore did what compassion required: he came to sinners, but he neither ought nor could come to sins. He came to the greedy, but not to greed; to the covetous, but not to covetousness; to the lustful, but not to lust; in short, he mercifully came to the vicious, but miserably did not come to their vices.

Let us then go out, let each one of us go out from the place of his iniquity. Let us go out from the midst of Babylon and meet our Savior God at its borders, as the prophet exhorts: “Be ready, Israel, to meet the Lord, for he comes” (Amos 4). Let us go out from the pit of sin into the likeness of sinful flesh. Let us go out from the will to sin into repentance for sin; for there we shall find Christ. For he underwent repentance for sin which he did not commit at all. There he will save those who repent, he who hates sinners and has mercy on the repentant.

But you say: “If we go out from sin, what need have we of a physician? Or who can by himself go out from sin?” Truly, the greatest sin is love of sin; the greatest iniquity is the will to sin. Therefore do not will to sin, even if you cannot yet avoid sinning. Hate sin, and you have gone out from sin. You have hated sin, and you have met Christ where he is: he does not wish sin to be committed, but hates sin; and, because he makes common cause with the one who hates it, he for the present forgives guilt, until he wholly removes sin even from action.

But you also say that it is too much for you and impossible for a human being without God’s grace to hate sin and desire righteousness—to be unwilling to sin and willing to repent. Let them therefore confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men. For he who freely withdrew openly into the regions of Tyre and Sidon, where the woman could meet him, secretly drew the woman by grace out of her inward parts so that she might meet him—the woman whom the Son openly received outside. This woman, then, signifies the Church, predestined from eternity, called and justified in time, and to be glorified after time. She continually prays for her daughter, that is, for each of the elect. Yet she is neither easily nor immediately heard, nor is she finally dismissed empty from being heard. All things have their time, and await the order, time, and measure in which they are to occur. But, as I see, you prefer a moral exposition, and have long been awaiting what this woman, or her daughter, is to signify morally. [Col. 1799B]

The woman, then, signifies any soul anticipated by God, so that it hates sin and desires righteousness, but lacks the ability to do so with the same ease with which it desires it. The will to do good lies near at hand, but it does not find the power to accomplish it; it does not do the good it desires, but the evil it hates, that it does. Therefore it prays for its daughter—that is, for natural freedom, which is oppressed by difficulty. And while the will is, as it were, sound in that it loves what is good and just, the capacity is nevertheless held captive under sin so that it cannot do this. Hence, instructed as though by the Apostle, it cries: “Wretched woman that I am, who will deliver this daughter of mine from this body of death—that is, from the oppression of this demon?” For this is the demon of which the Apostle says: “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. 7). For evil lies near at hand when I will to do good: namely, a harsh and dreadful demon, by which this woman’s daughter is grievously afflicted. But because nothing can save her except God’s grace, and that through Jesus Christ, she cries persistently: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me” (Matt. 15).

For David is interpreted “strong in hand.” Strong aid is required if so strong a demon is to be cast out. Beloved, I foresee that my own case is being dealt with here, nor can I easily find another matter of greater concern to me. For, freely anticipated by the grace of God, I withdrew with a contrite heart into this hidden and arid wilderness—not only away from sins and every occasion of sinning, but, as may be seen, from almost all human society and the common world as well. I did so in order to punish past pleasures and vain, frivolous curiosities by the aridities, fastings, and desolations now within me; and thereafter, with the material and occasion for like things removed, more easily and freely, forgetting what lies behind, to stretch myself toward what is before. Yet this daughter of mine is so grievously tormented by this demon, and my capacity to fulfill the good which I rightly will, desire, and have purposed—the good for which I fled and withdrew far from human beings—is pressed by such difficulty that even the mother, who seemed sound, cannot be quiet or secure. Nor can she attend to that which belongs to sound desire, that is, to the contemplation [Col. 1800A] of tranquil wisdom; rather, all the mother’s concern and fear is directed toward her daughter, lest she waste away under such great evils, the mother herself fail together with her, and both be lost.

O Lord Jesus, “who can endure before your cold?” Why does an idle incursion weary a person who desires only serious and eternal goods? Why does an unclean memory of the world ever draw back the mind which love of heaven has once drawn out of the world? Why is it not permitted freely to follow you as one wishes, to one who seeks nothing but you? O Lord, save me from faintness of spirit and tempest—that is, from the demons proper to the wilderness. For I fear that, through faintness, the will may relapse unless the capacity is delivered from the tempest of difficulty. O Lord, strong in hand, almighty Jesus, you who have freed my reason from the demon of ignorance and rescued my will from the plague of concupiscence: free my capacity from this difficulty, so that, with your holy angels, to whom the power belongs when they will, we who are devoted in will may be powerful in strength, “doing your word, to hear the voice of your words.”

Yet because I have labored crying out until my throat has become hoarse, and he himself did not answer me a word, you pious and holy brothers, his disciples worthy to be heard, speak a word for me to the Word. For I cry out even after you and through you to him, from whom alone help can come, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit before the ages, now and always. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIV. ON THE SAME FEAST, II

[Col. 1800C]

And the disciples say: “Send her away, for she cries after us” (Matt. 15).

Come, brothers, we are tired from manual labor; but let us rest a little while I answer, as the Lord deigns to grant, this brother’s question about the conclusion of yesterday’s sermon. For he wonders what it means that, while the Lord did not answer the woman, the disciples, moved by compassion, asked on her behalf—as though they were more pious and merciful than their Lord, who is the fountain of compassion, when it should suffice the disciple to be like his master. But how do you know, brother, whether they acted from compassion or overcome by annoyance, whose words are known to be: “Send her away, for she cries after us”? Still, let us hope better things of them, things nearer to compassion.

Yet who among us does not wish every person to be saved and none at all condemned in hell? God, however, than whom we are certainly not better, could do this as readily as he wills, if he willed. Again, when we see a poor person freezing in winter or wasting away from hunger in summer, we abound indeed in feelings of compassion; but, having no means to relieve that person’s want, we at least groan deeply. But God, who is rich in all things—if he is compassionate, how does he neglect them, and why does he not help when he can do so easily? There is no comparison of creature with Creator, no equivalence between our compassion or will and the divine. For he often makes his own people piously will what he himself, more piously, does not will. He often permits those who are not his own impiously to will what he piously wills; he also often makes his own people piously will what he piously wills, and those not his own impiously not will what he piously does not will. But, to discuss the disciples’ petition more fully, we must begin, as they say, a little higher up.

Blessed is the election which has obtained what Israel pursued and did not obtain. As you know, there is said to be one body whose head is Christ, God’s elect one; hence all those under this most holy head are called the members of this body. The body is one, as the head is one, though the members are many. All this is by analogy with the human body, which has its head above and its stature upright. Animals, called beasts, bend face-down toward the belly: their head, feet, and belly naturally incline downward and tend in one direction. But God gave humanity an upturned face. Hence one poet says:

> He gave humankind a face held high, and commanded it  
> To look upon heaven and lift its erect gaze to the stars.  
> (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, I.85–86)

Hence human beings are called by natural philosophers an inverted tree: they have the head above, as it were a root, and send downward their leaves—that is, their limbs—and branches, as it were the joints of their limbs. The head is one, from which the multiplicity of members has sensation and movement. The rounded summit of the head is also one, from which are paired the eyes, ears, nostrils, lips, breasts, arms, sides, buttocks, thighs, knees, shins, and feet. Where a human being touches the earth, namely by foot and hand, he becomes fivefold: multiple below, one above; fivefold toward the earth, where earthly; one toward heaven, where heavenly. [Col. 1801C] But “one thing is necessary”; concern and disturbance concern many things.

In a similar arrangement, in this mystical body under the one head, Christ, and the one root—for he too is both the one man who cries “from the ends of the earth” and the one tree which yields its fruit in its season—there are many members. Some are higher and nearer the head than others; others are lower and farther from the head, and thus more numerous and more dependent on the earth. Yet just as from the life of the root alone greenness, strength, and life proceed into the whole body of the tree, so from the holy Spirit of Christ and our God alone the whole body of the Church lives, senses, and moves. And just as the life of a root belongs only to its own tree, and to that whole tree, so the Spirit of Christ, insofar as this mystery is concerned, reaches only to his own body, and to that entire body, so that it all may live and move from him, and only in him.

Likewise, though there is one soul in the human body, wholly everywhere by essence, it nevertheless operates differently by power and activity. Similarly, in the Church there is one Spirit in all, yet differing in activity, office, and grace. As the members in a human body neither placed themselves there nor chose their number, position, or office, so in Christ’s body no one placed himself there, chose his position or office, or determined his number. Therefore, just as in the human body the members have differing actions but nevertheless need one another by a most fitting necessity and help one another with a most dutiful love, so also in Christ’s body, although each is necessary to the others and, as none is superfluous, so none suffices by itself, “the one who has much” does not have too much, and “the one who has little” does not have too little; rather, all share themselves with one another in love.

Likewise, in the human body the lower members, duller and harder, bear the higher members, which are more tender and more vital, though they receive life and power from them. So in Christ’s body, the sensory and active are to support the spiritual contemplatives in bodily necessities, from whom they receive things far better—that is, spiritual things. Thus the blessed Apostle says: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. 9). Neither can the eye walk on the ground nor the foot give light to the body; yet both are necessary to the body, although both functions cannot belong to one member. [Col. 1802B]

Therefore God, who can do all things, though he could suffice for all through himself and accomplish whatever he wishes, nevertheless wills, for the office of brotherly love, that within his body there should be a place for need and an occasion for humility, so that a brother helping his brother may be like a strong and fortified city. Thus the lower members help the higher and are helped by them; the equal members do likewise; indeed all help one another in every way. He who predestined that temporal need should not be lacking to all his own here, and that blessedness should be present in the future, each differently and in its own way, also predestined the distinction and manner, and what he would give to each. He who can himself sustain all here and perfect all there predestined how much, how, when, where, and through whom particular things should come to particular persons.

For he did not make the world and hand its governance over to another. Nor does anything happen in it by chance. He who made it governs it: without whose will neither does a leaf fall from a tree nor a sparrow fall to the ground. Therefore he who predestined life in heaven for his own also predestined for them a way in the world; he who predestined there the reward predestined here the merit; he who will give glory there gives grace here. For one does not promise and another perform. Rather, what he predestined to occur, he himself brings about; and he who predestined the rank there also predestined the means by which that rank is attained.

Yet, as some rave, it does not follow that, if God has predestined life for someone, he will attain it whatever his life or deeds here may be. Rather, he who predestined life for that person also predestined that he should live in such a way as to attain it: namely, through such or such righteousness of his own, though not from himself; or through another’s faith or prayer; or as God himself knows how to distribute to each. He himself does what he predestined; and what he prepared—where, at once and together, he established all things—he grants when he wills, in the manner in which he prepared it.

But you say: “If God has predestined for each of his own not only salvation but also, as he predestined it, the way of attaining it, then one predestined, and made by God, to live in that way cannot live otherwise than he does, just as one predestined to salvation cannot perish.” Truly, one who is predestined can perish. He can be saved in this sense, and he can perish in this sense. For even one who will not perish can perish; and one who will not live otherwise can live otherwise. God did not predestine such a person to be unable to perish, since, possessing free choice, he can turn either way; nor did he predestine him to be unable to live otherwise than he does. Rather, he predestined simply that he should live thus and not perish. For “not to perish” and “not to be able to perish” are very different. He predestined the former, not the latter, though he has granted both. For the power to perish belongs to our nature; not to perish belongs to his mercy; but to perish will belong to our fault and his justice. Therefore one who is predestined can perish through the mutability of nature, but will not perish because of the predestination of grace. Heavenly generation preserves him; if he could not perish at all, he would have no need of preservation. [Col. 1803B]

Thus it has been predestined that one who can perish should not perish, and assuredly he will not perish, though he can perish, because he has been predestined. For this is impossible: that this person should be predestined and perish. If he is predestined, he must not perish, lest predestination fail—not because he cannot perish, since predestination certainly does not contain that. Therefore he who predestined the daughter’s deliverance also, for its sake, predestined the mother’s prayer and its obtaining through the apostles. Hence, in order that what was to occur might occur—and what was not otherwise to occur, though it could have occurred otherwise—the mother’s concern is not found superfluous, nor the Lord’s seeming disregard, nor the disciples’ compassionate prayer. Rather, since all appear necessary as the means by which that which was to happen thus was brought about—[Note: [Col. 1803D] Something seems to be missing.]—this did not bring about some new word in God’s disposition, but fulfilled the eternal counsel.

He who could either deny or bestow otherwise preferred to do it thus, so that in one act he might confer benefits on several: the gift of health upon the daughter, the debt of compassion upon the mother, and the office of love upon the disciples. He who did not answer the woman a word outwardly was inwardly working, both in the woman and in the apostles—the very Word of the Father. And he who, by just and hidden reason, had handed the daughter over to Satan for the affliction of the flesh, as it were taking occasion from this, according to the saying that all things work together for good to those who are good, created for the mother and disciples the merit of virtue. For “whoever does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5). This concerns mother and daughter. Concerning the disciples and the mother: “Whoever sees someone in need and closes his heart against him does not have the Father’s love in him” (1 John 3). Therefore, while merit is acquired for these persons and the daughter is at last restored to health, the devil alone is mocked by the Lord, as it is written: “This dragon, which you formed for him to play with” (Ps. 103). For if he had foreknown that this would result, he certainly would not have wished to torment the girl—unless his malice, as it blinded him, also hardened him. [Col. 1804A]

The compassion of our God is therefore clear: it virtually extracts merits from us, while outwardly preparing an occasion for action and inwardly creating the affection. For while he performs within us, together with us, what he commands outwardly, as it is said, “Not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15), what does he do but create merits in us, for which he himself may render rewards? In what he does without us, he finds nothing for which to reward us, even though what he does is done for us. Although merit does not intervene there, the benefit is nevertheless evident. But what we do without him always deserves punishment, since it can only be evil. Certainly no action can be done without him; yet it is plain that nothing but good is done through him. Just as he often does through someone a good that does not benefit that person at all, so too someone sometimes does through him something which is not merit reaching to a reward.

Therefore only those things acquire merit reaching to the reward of eternity which God perseveringly does with us, and by which he makes us act with him. The foundation, as it were, of all these is faith, which he certainly does not create in us without us. For no one believes unwillingly. Almighty and gracious God gently compels us inwardly and, without violence, draws the willing where he wills, dividing within us and between us, so that we gladly will what we do not will and powerfully do not will what we do will. Let us therefore, beloved, gladly give the whole to God, since nothing is ours, as blessed Cyprian says (*On the Lord’s Prayer*). For he, as the prophet testifies, has worked all our works for us (Isa. 26), just as “he made us, and not we ourselves.”

Yet he does not work us or our works as a human craftsman works: once he has finished some piece of work, he ceases working and, while the work remains, turns his attention elsewhere. Rather, he works as the soul works life in the body, or equality health, or the sun daylight, or external light sight in the eye. For these do not work in such a manner that, while their work remains, they depart, or that their works remain when they depart. Rather, when they have effected something, they do so always; and when they do not effect it and withdraw themselves, nothing whatever remains of what they effected. So too God continually and unceasingly works in all things which he has made to exist, lest they cease to be, according to the Truth itself, through whom all things are made, who says: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5). For just as everything that is has being from the essence, so, once the essence is withdrawn, whatever exists by that essence cannot exist at all. But if the essence itself cannot exist without itself, how shall anything that is from it exist without it? Therefore all things need it always to be, in order that they may be; but he alone is sufficient to himself, who is all that belongs to him and does not need another besides himself. [Col. 1804D]

By his eternal and unchangeable essence—that is, by him who is, ever working—whatever exists exists only in such degree, at such time, and for as long as he works this. [Note: [Col. 1804D] “God is he who is” (Exod. 3).] By his eternal wisdom—that is, by him who is, by which he is wise, ever working—whoever are wise are wise only in such degree, at such time, for such duration, and in such manner as he works this. By his eternal goodness and love—that is, by him who is, by which he is good, ever working—those who love the good are good only in such degree, at such time, for such duration, and in such manner as he works this. The same holds for strength and for everything whatever that has any being at all, because just as “without him nothing was made” (John 1), so without him what has been made remains nothing, or cannot make any progress whatever beyond what it has received from him. For who has anything that he has not received from him? Who can do anything without him?

But things made by him with mutable nature can fail through themselves, though he permits it; and, just as he does all things willingly, so he permits nothing unwillingly; just as he does nothing without reason, so he permits nothing without cause. His judgments are often hidden, always just. Therefore, while creating essence, illuminating wisdom, inflaming love, and strengthening power are at work, essence, wisdom, love, and strength are created in us, so that we may be, know, will, and be able. [Col. 1805B]

All these things, then, through our love—formed within us from the love by which God loves us, and turned toward him—make us here, for the present, good and devout. But when that love has fully turned toward us and has perfectly drawn us to itself, it will certainly make us blessed, where, for the eternal merit which he himself will work eternally, he will pay the eternal reward which he himself is. For he will always deserve to be loved fully and perfectly, who always loves in this manner. Meanwhile, however, whoever loves more is loved more, because he loves more those who love more. For he first loves us so that we may love; and as he apportions to each the measure of faith, so too the measure of love, wisdom, and strength, having with himself, according to which he apportions, the *gomor* (measure).

Yet of the things mentioned above—being, wisdom, love, and strength—love alone appears to acquire reward here; the others, though never without love, which never fails, are thought rather to belong to the reward. For to exist forever, to know perfectly, to be fully able, and to delight in these by the sweetness of love—what is this but the reward of the blessed life? Clearly, the merit of that reward is to live well. But no one lives well except by love, by which God is loved. Nor can that love be possessed by us except when and insofar as it is created and formed in us by the love with which God first loves us.

Therefore let us pray to God the Father himself through the Son in the Holy Spirit, with the whole, inmost, and unfailing affections of our hearts, ourselves anticipated by him for this very purpose. Let us attribute everything to him, that by his love he may create and, by pouring it out, may create in us that love which loves God the Trinity above all things, and the neighbor for God’s sake. In these consists all merit [Col. 1806A] which reaches to the reward of eternity. May he grant it. Amen.

## SERMON XXXV. ON THE SAME FEAST, III
It was fitting, dearest brethren, that by today’s exertion we should make up the loss caused by yesterday’s labour. For yesterday’s sermon, as you know, being rather long, almost stole from us an hour of work. Someone says, “He detained the day with his sermon”; but while we were detained by the sermon, the day slipped away. Therefore, since scarcely anything of the hour now remains, and we have paid the full due of labour, let us say scarcely anything.

“I was sent only to the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel,” says the Lord (Matt. 15). It may be said briefly, since the hour too is brief: he was sent to those to whom he had been promised. “The promises,” he says, “were made to Abraham and to his seed” [Col. 1806B] (Gal. 3). A promise made in time is fulfilled in its proper time; and salvation is from the Jews and for the Jews, as it is written: “For salvation is from the Jews” (John 4). For Christ, born in the flesh from them, was sent at the end of time to those to whom he had been promised from the beginning of time, having been predestined before all times. Predestined for Jews and Gentiles, he was nevertheless born in the flesh, immediately and directly, from Jews alone; according to his carnal birth he was manifested to those to whom he had been promised through a temporal utterance.

Yet, if it pleases us to lift our minds higher and contemplate the mystery of the words, the grace of the Word—whose words these are—will by no means fail us. For it is written: “When the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels also were lifted up with them, following them” (Ezek. 1). [Col. 1806C] For words uttered through the Holy Spirit will readily follow into a spiritual sense.

Israel, then, since it is interpreted “the man seeing God,” is rightly understood as the rational mind. The house of Israel, therefore, is rightly understood to contain those minds whose number, by divine predestination, is certainly foreknown from eternity as destined to see God himself. Thus, while the ninety-nine sheep of this house were roaming widely on the mountain of the vision and love of their own shepherd—that is, of the Word of God—and lying without fear in the rich pastures of ever-green grasses, the merciful shepherd descended from the Father when the time for showing mercy came. He was mercifully sent in time; but in the word of eternal predestination, where God spoke all things together and once for all from eternity, he was promised from eternity to seek the one sheep that had perished. He was sent to that one in time; promised to it from eternity; born for it; given to it; predestined for it from eternity.

This is the one sheep from Jews and Gentiles, among Jews and Gentiles: one mystically, many personally; many naturally according to the flesh, one spiritually according to grace. Finally, the sheep is one and many. Therefore, he who came to seek the one that had perished was sent to “the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel.” Not to goats, but to sheep: certainly to them alone, and to all of them. For just as the apostate angels, like goats, once departed from the sheep—that is, from the holy angels—yet were not of them; so also many departed from these sheep that had strayed, yet were not of them. They are indeed of the same nature as sheep by creation, and alike in corruption because of disobedience; but grace is distinctive to those who are predestined. “The gifts and calling of God,” says the Apostle, [Col. 1807A] “are without repentance” (Rom. 11).

Therefore his sheep—that is, the angels and human beings of the house of Israel—remain, so far as the shepherd’s predestination and knowledge are concerned, whole in number and unchangeable in the mark of election. They have this foundation: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2), and they have a faithful and strong protection; for the heavenly generation preserves them. No outsider, however, can join himself to them in this lot. Others, meanwhile, either are not added to them at the pastures of the sacraments, or at least are multiplied beyond their number. But what this shepherd knows as his own, no one can snatch from his hand. Power cannot compel him; [Col. 1807B] wisdom cannot be deceived; love cannot cast away. Hence he speaks confidently: “Of all that the Father has given me, I shall lose none of it” (John 6). Again: “Of those whom you gave me, I have lost none” (John 18).

Nevertheless, by a deep and inscrutable judgment, he permits his own to be mingled here for a time with those who are not his and to go astray, though elsewhere, on the mountains, he preserved them from mingling with strangers. Therefore, promised by eternal predestination in order to separate and gather these sheep, and sent in a new incarnation, he says: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15). Thus he was sent as truth to those deceived, the way to those wandering, life to the dead, wisdom to the foolish, medicine to the sick, redemption to captives, refreshment to the hungry; and in all these respects [Col. 1807C] he was sent to the sheep that had perished of the house of Israel, lest they should perish.

Finally, he was sent as a soul into a dead body, so that, warmed by his coming, its limbs might come alive and there might be new life in old limbs, spiritual life in fleshly limbs, heavenly life in earthly limbs: namely, by the first resurrection. Hence it is said: “Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear shall live” (John 5). Thus it is also said of the sheep: “They shall hear my voice, and they shall not follow a stranger” (John 10).

Or perhaps it may be said more properly that he was sent as a head placed from above upon a body that was mutilated and without a head, so that it might receive sensation and movement from it; so that this body, as it were from the heart—which is created first of all in the body—might possess some share of vital spirit, though without the benefit of the head it could neither be illuminated [Col. 1807D] for perception nor moved [Col. 1808A] towards strength in any way. For, as those curious about such matters maintain, vital spirit arises in an animal’s heart and life is diffused from there through the whole body; but sensation comes from the front part of the head, and movement from the rear. Thus, as in a man left half alive—who himself is the sheep that had perished—there remained, from the condition of his first creation, a vital spirit, namely rational will or natural freedom, which could be illuminated for perception by Christ, the wisdom and power of God, and moved towards strength.

Therefore Christ was sent first to give perception for faith by his own preaching, and afterwards to move towards strength by sending his Spirit. “Remain,” he says, “in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke [Col. 1808B] 24). For from him come to rational nature, or natural reason, perception and movement towards good action, truth and power. Meanwhile faith, hope, and love—without which it could become foolish and weak, be deceived by fantasies, and delight in false madness—come from him; for without him it could do nothing but nothing, he who, sent to the sheep, said to them: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). Without him natural freedom was alone and could only fall; to it is said: “Woe to one who is alone; for when he falls, there is none to lift him up” (Eccl. 4).

Therefore the merciful shepherd was sent, to bind up what had been broken and strengthen what was weak. But what was broken and weak was the human free will, which once, straining above itself, fell beneath itself; unable to bear itself, it oppressed and shattered itself in itself and by itself. Broken by itself and thereby weakened within itself, it could not rise through itself. At last, strengthened and made firm through faith and love for Christ himself, and thus made pregnant—because it is not yet altogether fat and strong, until it is placed with the ninety-nine in rich pastures—he carries it in his arms. “He shall lift the lambs in his bosom,” he says; “he himself shall carry those that are with young” (Isa. 40).

Thus he was sent for these reasons and for many others that may be expressed in many ways, to the sheep that had perished, according to their manner of life and the desert of their error, of the house of Israel. At last, the grace prepared from eternity was manifested, formerly prefigured in many ways by events and words, lest those should perish whom election does not allow to perish and whom natural [Col. 1808D] freedom is unable to save.

> **[Note: [Col. 1807D]** The opinion taught here by Isaac, concerning election and reprobation before foreseen works, was formerly, and still is, held by many. Yet certain indubitable points must be adduced which place the work of our salvation in our own power. First, God wills all to be saved (1 Tim. 2), and wills no one—that is, not even one person—to perish (2 Pet. 3), by his antecedent will, that is, so far as lies in him. Therefore, by that antecedent will he has excluded no one from salvation, whether positively or negatively.  
>
> Likewise, Christ died for all, even for those who perish (2 Cor. 5; 2 Pet. 2; Rom. 14), as the apostles teach and the pontiffs define against Jansenius. For what purpose would he have suffered for persons whom God did not will to be saved? What benefit would his suffering have brought them? But if they exclude themselves from salvation, let them impute it to themselves, not to God.  
>
> Again, God invites human beings to salvation, which he says lies within their power: “Before man are life and death, good and evil; what pleases him shall be given him” (Ecclus. 15). Again: “Come to me, all” (Matt. 11). “If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19). A person unable to attain heaven would be mocked by these words. Yet salvation is impossible for one who has not been comprehended in that antecedent election. For how could one not called force his way into the assembly of the blessed, or one not invited come to the wedding of the Lamb, or alter the order established by God?  
>
> Hear St Augustine (*Eighty-Three Questions*): “To the supper which the Lord declares in the Gospel to have been prepared, not all who were called wished to come . . . those who did not wish to come must attribute it to themselves, because their coming when called lay in their free will.” Therefore they were not excluded from the heavenly banquet by a prior decree of God. Elsewhere (*Sermon on the Creed*) he represents Christ the Judge speaking thus to the reprobate: “For you this side was opened, and you refused to enter.” St Prosper (*Response to the Chapters of the Gauls*, ch. 3) says that the reprobate were not predestined because they were foreknown to be evil through voluntary transgression. The same author (*Seven Sentences*, near the end) says: “Because he foresaw that they would do this evil by voluntary falling away, he therefore did not include them in the lot of predestination.” I pass over countless other points. The arguments advanced to the contrary are answered in the treatise *On Predestination*.]

But while he answered these things to his disciples privately and familiarly, as though secret matters, [Col. 1809A] the woman came hastening up and worshipped him. Let us also worship him and pray that he may deign to enlighten us for what follows: the living and true God, with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVI. ON THE SAME FEAST, IV

“It is not good to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs” (Matt. 15).

As we discussed in yesterday’s sermon, “the gifts and calling of God are without repentance”; whence, in respect of the unchangeable truth of his predestination, those who are once children are never not children, and those who are once not children are never children. But with regard to works of righteousness, or the righteousness of works, non-children become children, and children become non-children, in turn. Yet who are truly children and who are not children is known in the presence of the true Father, “with whom there is no change nor shadow of turning” [Col. 1809B] (Jas. 1); with him are both the number and the rationale. For he knows what, in his only-begotten Son, his unchangeable Word, perfect once for all, he said by eternally begetting him, and by saying begot: there he established all things together and once for all.

Nothing whatever of these things can fail to come about, just as he himself could not be deceived; for he did not so much foresee future things which he would make as establish beforehand future things which he would see made. For he did not make whatever he made because it would be, or because it ought to be made; rather, it would be and ought to be made because he was to make it. Thus there would be no future things except those which he willed, and they would be future because he willed them. Just as he never began to will what he wills, [Col. 1809C] so neither can he end it by not willing, alter what he willed by willing what he does not will, or add to his first will, through a newly adopted plan, something that he had not previously willed. For his counsel remains for ever, and the thoughts of his heart from generation to generation.

The Almighty can do all things; but truth cannot deny itself; nor could wisdom overlook something that it would later need to recall; nor could love act perversely in a way it would subsequently correct. Thus, just as what is seen to have been made did not become necessary because it ought to be made, but ought to be made because he established it beforehand; so likewise, what is called good does not make him act and love it so much because it is good, as it is good because he himself acts and loves it. For whatever is made and good among created things must receive both being made and goodness from him as from its efficient principle. Hence the Son, who perfectly knows the Father, rejoicing in spirit and acknowledging to him his work, says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” [Col. 1809D] (Matt. 11). As though assigning the cause of this operation, he added: “Yes, Father, because thus it was pleasing before you” (ibid.).

[Col. 1810A] Let us believe, my brethren, let us believe, I beseech you, servants, the Son speaking to us of his Father. For the Father shows the Son all that he does, and does absolutely nothing without him; indeed, he does all things through him, since the Son, maker together with the maker-Father, makes from the Father all the same things, and in the same manner. “Yes, Father,” he says, “because thus it was pleasing before you.” This is, principally, the entire rationale of all things made; this is the primary and principal cause of events. After this, under this first and greatest cause, many different causes of diverse effects may arise. But one who seeks another cause of this cause of causes goes, as the saying has it, beyond God by reasoning.

Therefore, whatever is pleasing before the Father is good, and only good, and this alone is good among created things; and it is good because it is pleasing, not pleasing to him afterwards because it was first good in itself, from itself, or through itself. But whatever is not pleasing is not good, and only not good, and this alone is not good; and it is not good because it is not pleasing. Therefore all that alone is good, and wholly good, which is well pleasing to him; and it is good because it is well pleasing to him.

Since, therefore, beloved, we altogether do not know in what way he who has no need of our goods accepts the goods we think we perform, we doubt, with such trembling and expectation, whether in all things we are worthy of love or hatred. If nevertheless we can somehow know that these things are good because they are pleasing to him, how do we know for whom they are useful, for whom profitable, for whom they ought to be good—whether for us or perhaps for others? [Col. 1810C] For by a high and hidden judgment the foolish person serves the wise; the foolish person changes like the moon; and one who has advanced through long growth suddenly fails through decline. But the wise person remains like the sun, and one who perseveres shall undoubtedly be saved; and he has laboured not only for others but also for himself. What he has done is not merely good because it is pleasing, nor good only for outsiders; it is good for himself because in it he pleased God.

For sometimes, in the sight of the heavenly Judge, what someone does is pleasing, yet the person who does it is not thereby pleasing; nor is what is simply good always universally good. For not everything good is good for everyone. Therefore the woman was not told, “It is not good for dogs to take away the children’s bread and for it to be given to them”; but simply: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs.” For it would be as good for the dogs, if this were done, as it would be evil for the children. Similarly, not every evil thing is evil for everyone; but that is simply evil which is not pleasing to God, just as that is simply good which is well pleasing.

Therefore it is not good—that is, it is not pleasing to God—to take the grace of the predestined and the heavenly bread, [Col. 1811A] namely that bread which cannot be shared with outsiders but is, for the predestined, like a source proper to them, and give it not to the non-predestined and those reprobated from eternity, but to those who are evil in time. Yet they are not evil because reprobated, nor indeed were they first reprobated because they were later evil; nevertheless, they are justly reprobated when they are evil in will or action. Yet, if it were possible, this would be as good for these as it would be evil for those.

Hence it is clear that not every good is good for everyone; that something is evil for someone, but through that person’s own perversity; that not every evil is evil for everyone; and that something is indeed good for someone, but through divine goodness. Nor is everything good for someone simply good, just as everything evil for someone is not at once evil. Good things are good for the good, as evil things are evil for the evil. [Col. 1811B] Good things are evil for the evil, just as evil things are good for the good. Yet evils are never good, nor goods evil. Perhaps good things are also evil for the good, just as evil things are good for the evil.

But that is always simply good which is pleasing to God and good from him who is through himself, in himself, and not through another outside himself, always the supreme good itself, as it is written: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10). That which is not pleasing to him is simply not good; his good pleasure is not good from some other good, but is goodness itself. Hence whatever does not accord with him departs from the good and thereby becomes evil.

Come then, brethren: amid such multiplicity of things and diversity of changes, in which this multiplicity itself is not allowed to remain fixed—for even good and evil things are by no means always recognized uniformly as evil or good for all—consider how and to what extent we must always be uncertain, fearful, watchful, and anxious, lest those things which we desire as good should be evil for us; or what is good today be evil tomorrow; or what we guard against and flee as evil be good for us; or what is evil today be good tomorrow. [Col. 1811C]

Consider also that we do not know, as we ought, not only what to do but also what to pray for or desire (Rom. 8). Yet let us always ask the Spirit, who searches the depths of God not by inquiry but by penetration and knows every will and good pleasure of the Father, according as he intercedes for the saints, to help our weakness: [Col. 1811D] so that we may will not what we will because we will it, but only and always what the Father wills because the Father wills it; waiting rather to learn from him what he wills and loving that, than determining what we ourselves wish and desiring it. Taught by his Word, let us say to him: “Your will be done in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 6); and: “Not what I will, but what you will” (Matt. 26).

To this blessed Father Augustine, speaking devoutly in his *Confessions*, says: “Your best servant is one who does not seek to hear from you what he wants, but rather seeks to will what he has heard from you.” But you ask: Why do we pray for what he wills, when it will occur even if we do not pray? Or why would you pray for what he does not will, when it will in no way occur for you, I do not say though you pray, but though you burst your hearts in prayer? Yet if the sermon of the day before yesterday has not slipped from your minds, this small question could not disturb you now. For he wills many things which he nevertheless does not will to give except through prayer. But nothing that he does not will to happen can be obtained in any manner whatsoever. Nor, however, do we always pray foolishly or impiously for what he does not will, nor always devoutly or wisely for what he wills. But you should remember that we have spoken copiously above about these matters.

Nevertheless, because we often do not know his will, we should always pray for what we see to accord more closely with piety; not, however, absolutely, but according to the pattern given us by Wisdom himself, who said to the Father: “If it is possible,” or, “If you will, let this cup pass from me” (ibid.); and likewise, saying everywhere: “Abba, Father, not what I will, but what you will” [Col. 1812A] (Mark 14). For if one knows that God wills something, how can it be pious to wish that he should afterwards will the contrary? Indeed, how can it not be sacrilegious to desire to make God, altogether immutable, change his will in order to fulfil our will? I do not at all desire such a God, whose truthfulness to his word my feeling can alter for my own sake, but one whose effect my own empty word may alter; not one who begins, because of me, to will what until now he did not will, but one who causes me, for his own sake, to will what he has always willed.

My teacher and Lord Jesus Christ, true God, true priest, true sacrifice, who made himself a victim and offering to himself, to the Father, and to the Holy Spirit for us, prayed to the Father only for what the Father willed and for those for whom the Father himself willed, saying: “Holy Father, preserve those whom you gave me from the world” [Col. 1812B] (John 17). These, beloved, are those for whom he still intercedes, standing before the Father’s face and possessing an everlasting priesthood, he whom death does not prevent from remaining and who offers an everlasting sacrifice. For he has not changed either voice or will, so as to pray here for some and intercede there for others.

To him, as the high priest, the choir of the saints there responds concerning this prayer as “Amen,” filling, as it were, the place of the unlearned; they feel and will nothing contrary to him or different from him. For there neither ignorance obscures them nor emotion confuses them. In his holy light, the saints truly see what they ought to will; and in his strength they powerfully accomplish what they see they ought to do. [Col. 1812D] In accordance with them, beloved, as far as our littleness permits, let us love everything God does, will what he wills because he wills it, retain nothing from our heart for ourselves, and answer in all things, “Amen,” and “Thanks be to God,” to God, the maker and ruler of all: to whom be honour and power in all things and above all things, for ever and beyond. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVII. ON THE SAME FEAST, V

“It is not good to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs” (Matt. 15).

Today, beloved, with God’s help, we have done well. For some of the hour still remains, and behold, we have already fully paid the day’s allotted labour. Therefore it is worth while now to set ourselves to what we completed less fully in yesterday’s sermon. As we briefly touched upon it, in sacred discourse persons are called children in one way according to the truth of predestination, and in another according to the quality of life. Likewise, divine judgment over the children of men is one thing according to the purpose of its own counsel, and another according to the desert of human action.

For according to the work of righteousness, or the righteousness of the work, an evil person becomes good, and a good person evil; a dog becomes a child, and a child a dog. The Hebrews, because of the giving of the law and the covenant, the promises of God made to them, the common sacraments also, and obedience to the commandments, were formerly called children; conversely, all Gentiles without these things were dogs. But when children among them, alien to predestination, lied to God and reverted to old age, and departed from the paths [Col. 1813A] of their fathers—who were children by purpose—then, just as the kingdom of God was taken away from them and transferred to the Gentiles, so too was the name. Hence the Psalm follows: “O God, who gives me vengeance and subdues peoples beneath me; therefore I will confess you among the nations, O Lord” (Ps. 17).

Thus, just as those who were formerly dogs are now children, so those who had been children were afterwards called dogs. “Many dogs have surrounded me,” he says, and so forth (Ps. 21). Nor only dogs, but serpents also, as it is written: “They sharpened their tongues like serpents” (Ps. 139). Indeed, to crown their disgrace, though once called children of God, they hear from the true, natural, and only Son of God—who assuredly knows the Father uniquely and knows all his brethren by name—“You are from your father the devil” (John 8).

Yet because there is a time for every matter under the sun, and from that point, as it were, where all things are together, the line of the universe is drawn out in the lawful course of order, so that things do not flow simultaneously and confusedly, but each in its own order, it is not good even for that which is to be done to be done except when and as it ought to be done. Thus Moses says concerning the Amorites, who were to be expelled as their offences demanded, though those offences had not yet reached their due fullness: “The sins of the Amorites are not yet complete” [Col. 1813B] (Gen. 15). Therefore they could not yet be expelled so that the children of Israel might be brought in. Nor, however, ought the Hebrews to have waited in Egypt once the Egyptians’ sins were already ripe for punishment. Hence they wandered forty years in the wilderness.

Similar to this is what the Apostle says of certain persons: “That they may always fill up their sins” (1 Thess. 2); and: “Let him who is filthy become still more filthy” (Rev. 22); and conversely: “Let him who is righteous become still more righteous” (ibid.).

Therefore nothing happens rashly, by chance, in confusion, without reason, or without a cause, in all the variety of things, so far as the governance of the heavenly ruler extends. Bread was indeed to be taken away from a perverse generation and unbelieving children, and given to the dogs that would go about the city; but it was not yet good, because it was not yet to be done. The murderers of the prophets had not yet killed the Lord of the prophets; the limbs, dead before their head, had not yet severed themselves from their head, so that life and perception might utterly flee from them; the Spirit departing from them had not yet filled the centurion, [Col. 1814A] so that he might openly cry out: “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Matt. 27). Thus the time had not yet come for them to hear: “It was necessary that the kingdom of God should first be preached to you; but since you have judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). Before that were threats; after this, their fulfilment. Therefore it was not good beforehand because it was good afterwards in its own time—namely, to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs.

Perhaps the woman, inwardly enlightened by the Spirit, knew that through Christ, to whom she spoke, the sonship of the Jews would be transferred to the Gentiles. Therefore, impatient through the devotion of faith and desire for the thing itself, she presses him and reveals the mystery before its time, saying: “Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.” [Col. 1814B] Hence she hears: “O woman, great is your faith”—faith which, leavened by desire and outgrowing her narrow breast, cannot contain itself within the barriers of its secret.

Hence Isaiah, overcoming a womanly breast with manly restraint, cries: “My secret is mine, my secret is mine” (Isa. 24). And certainly, according to the truth of the narrative, she lawfully uses the parable when she says: “For even the little dogs eat from the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.” For while Christ broke the bread of the Scriptures for the children by teaching and working healings, even before his passion certain crumbs of his benefits flowed down to the dogs. And, not to seek a distant example, they came to this very Canaanite woman, whose words we turn over upon our tongues, and to her daughter. To her he says: “Let it be done as you asked,” because great, namely, is the faith with which you asked.

For one who can believe all things can obtain all things: “All things are possible to one who believes” (Mark 10). Therefore we often do not obtain what we ask because we hesitate in asking. Nothing is too great for sufficiently great faith. Compared to a mustard seed, it even moves mountains. Faith, however, in the matter now before us, is called great in four ways: by knowledge, confidence, devotion, or constancy.

The first is great in its enlightened countenance of mind and has power to give a reason to every person asking concerning the hope that is in us, and to destroy every height exalting itself against the knowledge of Christ. This shone most excellently in the blessed Apostle Paul, [Col. 1814D] concerning which he also says: “If I have all knowledge and know all mysteries,” and so forth (1 Cor. 13).

The second is great and powerful not merely in speech and knowledge but also in power, by which signs and wonders are readily performed. Of this the same Apostle likewise says: “If I have all faith, so that I move mountains” (ibid.). Again, elsewhere: “To another is given faith in the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12). And James says: “Let him ask, doubting nothing in faith” (Jas. 1).

The third is great and powerful for compunction and tears, for contempt of this whole world, and for longing for the face of God. According to this faith, the Prophet sighs: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God? My tears were my bread by day and night” (Ps. 41). And elsewhere: “My heart said to you: My face has sought you; your face, Lord, I will seek” (Ps. 26). [Col. 1815A] This is the faith which, in the silence of monks, speaks to the Lord in a sweet whisper, mouth to mouth, as a man to his neighbour. Hence their mouth is holy and their lips clean, because of the word of the Lord in which they are frequent. Desiring this purity, they withdrew from the midst of peoples with unclean lips, fled every pleasure of this world, and remain clean in solitude.

The fourth is great and powerful in firmly and steadfastly overcoming the world both when it rages and when it flatters. Of this blessed John says: “This is the victory which conquers the world: our faith” (1 John 5). The first conquers the world by reasoning; the second by doing wonders; the third by fleeing; the fourth by fighting it down.
