Yet by which kind this woman’s faith was called great, he himself knows, who formed inwardly what he praised outwardly. We, however, believe because he himself spoke, who can neither be deceived nor deceive.

But if it pleases us to carry the discourse back upwards to higher things, so that by the children we understand the holy angels and the spirits of the just—admitted to the table of the Word of God, feasting in a voice of exultation and confession before God’s presence and delighting in joy, now drunk with the abundance of his house—while we still stand watch, begging and waiting, before its doors: I shall briefly relate, in ordinary language, what I am sometimes accustomed to picture to myself from this higher contemplation, when it has been let down to imaginative devotion.

Let us suppose, then, that my Lord Jesus Christ is like a householder feasting in his house behind closed doors with his friends and servants, rejoicing in abundance and security, as it is said: “Do not trouble me; behold, I and my children are with me in bed” [Col. 1815C] (Luke 11).

But we, who still wander away from the Lord, like a poor, lowly, weak, hungry crowd commonly waiting outside the doors of wealthy diners, stand watch everywhere. We call out the Lord and Lady by name, and address any of the diners whom we know; we recall the cold and hunger that we endure in order to move them to pity; nor do we conceal the particular afflictions which we suffer differently—blindness, lameness, withering, contraction, paralysis, leprosy, or a thousand others. We also urge one another to cry out more strongly. Often overcome by impatience, we accuse those inside of deafness; while they indulge themselves more freely, we charge that they are unconcerned about others; we blame them for not caring about, or not knowing, the needy condition of the poor, calling them inexperienced or unmindful.

Why say more? Those who have peace within endure with great patience the impatience of those who suffer, until the lawful time and hour arrives for leftovers to be distributed or for some persons to be admitted to full refreshment. This is what certain wealthy people are accustomed to do every day—unless perhaps the householder, wearied by the excessive insolence of some shameless person, sends something especially to him, not because he is his friend—as it is written: “He will rise and give him as many as he needs” [Col. 1816A] (Luke 11).

Nor will I keep silent about this: while poor persons wait and keep watch outside as beggars, some often withdraw from the entrance in order to sit more comfortably, more honourably, or more warmly. Indeed, sometimes they contend bitterly and violently over worthless bedding, scraps, straw, or the like, to put under their bare feet; and they impiously strike one another with their fists, so that the outcry rises to the ears of the householder and those reclining with him, arouses their anger, and brings either shame or perhaps contempt upon the beggars.

What else, I ask, are the contention, rivalry, and provocation of religious persons today—especially monks—over lands, woods, pastures, and livestock, when neither lands suffice for people nor people for lands, nor pastures for cattle nor cattle for pastures? “Surely these things are in my ears,” says the Lord of hosts. For who does not know that because of these things the name and reputation of religion have become cheap in human eyes?

Moreover, it must be feared that, when the Lord comes, to distribute something for the present to some, but to admit others once for all, these men may be far away at their quarrels and lawsuits, or, more dangerously, may be present after their quarrels and lawsuits, appearing for vengeance rather than refreshment. For their claim that in such matters they are acting for God’s cause, and that, for God’s love, contrary to every counsel of God, they harass a brother over a straw, is as frivolous as it is alien to their profession of perfection. [Col. 1816C] They litigate for themselves and pursue their own causes, though they do not know it. For what belongs to all belongs to God. Will not a brother, and his Church, be God’s if you leave it to him—he being religious as you are—just as it would be if you extorted from him the thing over which you contend with him? Is it of such importance before God to take from one Church or monastery what you give to another, that such a cause of yours ought to be called God’s cause? Why is not also the cause God’s which the other man defends, lest God lose on this side what He gains on that, since God possesses both, whose is the world and its fullness, and since He cannot gain here without losing there? Is it not evident that men litigate for themselves, in order either to preserve or acquire straw for their own feet? Where did God command litigation and contention? Or where did He counsel, teach, or permit it?

“But,” they say, “He permitted it.” Certainly the good God permitted adultery, murder, and other evils; but an evil person commits them wickedly. But let us return to what was said above: each person shall bear his own burden and give account to God for himself. Therefore, just as, when the master of the household has distributed or admitted people according to his own judgment—he who owed no one anything and gave freely to whom he wished—the one who receives less murmurs more: so too among us, when anyone humbly considers himself to have received less grace than his brother, he murmurs, as though devoutly against the master of the household, like those Gospel laborers (Matt. 20); he emulates, without envy, greater and better gifts, zealously with a good zeal for his brother’s conduct, whether in humility, obedience, charity, or prayer. But those who at the last receive absolutely nothing will go away blaspheming, in the fashion of those who today are called *trutanni* [vagabonds], and are most readily recognized by this habit; and thus, guilty of an eternal offense, they will suffer just punishments for eternity.

If, however, someone more subtle, and more impudent and anxious than the rest—for such a man conquers everything—can make his way in through the lattice or some little crevice, he will be fit to taste beforehand the crumbs that fall beneath his masters’ table, and also to lick and lap up certain things, so that his soul may be filled with them as with fatness and richness. Yet although such a person is among us rightly considered rare, perhaps unique, in greatness and dignity, there he is compared not with a human being, not even with a dog or puppy, but with a little dog. For he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.

Hence David, not only a servant of that household but also the bridegroom’s attendant of its bridal chamber, calls himself with fear not merely a dog but also a flea (1 Sam. 24 and 26). Yet such a person is compared to a little dog not merely because of his importunity or humility, but also because of his irrationality, faint-heartedness, and changeability. For whoever has been able to enter into true wisdom, dignity, and greatness recognizes himself as brute, mute, irrational, lowly, and small—however wise or powerful he may be among mortals. He truly knows how weak our strengths are, who has been able to climb above himself into divine things; yet, still bearing an insipid palate from earthly folly, he cannot fully taste [Col. 1817C] the sweetness that is there, any more than, because of the bleary weakness of his eyes, he can gaze upon the brightness there. And whatever he has heard or perceived, once returned to himself he is utterly unable to utter. For such things are ineffable, things which it is not permitted for a human being to speak. Once restored to himself, he is still human, though, while caught up to such things, he is for the moment more than human.

Hence that great father of faith and model of obedience, Abraham, after the vision of heavenly things, calls himself ash and dust (Gen. 18). Hence Moses, after the vision of the bush, acknowledges himself inarticulate and slow of speech (Exod. 3). Daniel too is sick and languishes for a long time (Dan. 10). Ezekiel falls upon his face and needs someone to raise him so that he may stand upon his feet (Ezek. 2). John the apostle and evangelist is afraid; and that great theologian falls as though dead [Col. 1817D] at the feet of Jesus, whom he loves exceedingly (Rev. 1). Peter, James, and that same John, at the voice from the cloud, rush to the ground, and, like men drunk or out of their minds, do not know what they are saying (Matt. 17).

Therefore we, who are still far from this subtlety and importunity, this most wise irrationality, this most powerful weakness, and this lofty fall, should await the common alms with peace, patience, and a shared manner of life, crying to the Lord and His saints that they may at some time admit us, and meanwhile not dismiss us fasting from the grace of the Lord Jesus.

## SERMON XXXVIII. FOR THE THIRD SUNDAY IN LENT I

Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute [Col. 1818A] (Luke 11).

It was easy, beloved, for the Lord Jesus Christ to cast out a demon, since without His permission and allowance it could not enter anyone. For there is nothing in all the multiplicity of nature which the Father does not both create through Him and govern through Him. Therefore, when, why, and how He wished, He permitted it to enter; and when and how He wished, He cast it out. He who was then present bodily, casting out the demon, both before and afterward—and still today, wherever it happens—casts out demons by divine power, through whom He wishes, whether angels or human beings, whether good or evil, and in whatever way He wishes: by prayer, adjuration, incantation, herbs and stones, or various other means.

For all authority in heaven and on earth is His: according to His divinity He always possessed it from the Father; according to His humanity He received it at a particular time. “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me,” He says (Matt. 28). To ensure that this should everywhere and always be truly believed, He once taught it openly in a certain occurrence. He had given His disciples power over all demons, yet someone brought them his demon-possessed son, whom they could not heal while Jesus was absent. How then did they have power over all demons if they lacked power over this one? Or, if they had it, why did they not cast it out? This, plainly, was what, as we said, His bodily absence and the disciples’ inability signified: that without the presence of His divine power and the grace of His cooperation, no demon could anywhere be cast out. Accordingly, when they asked why they could not cast it out, He answered: “Because of your unbelief” (Matt. 17). For they either did not yet know this, or did not believe it as they ought.

This is also why elsewhere He recalls to themselves disciples who were, as it were, arrogating something to themselves: “Do not rejoice in this, that spirits are subject to you,” and so forth; “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). We have said these things beforehand lest anyone dare arrogate anything to himself or foolishly boast in what he has received. For God is He who works all things in all persons: mercifully casting out evils and bringing in goods, and justly sometimes taking away goods and bringing in evils. Jesus, therefore, was—and to this day is—casting out a demon.

Let each of you, beloved, continually ask the gracious Jesus for himself, that He may utterly cast his demon out from him, or at least restrain it for the time being. For although all demons are hostile to us and rejoice at our harm, whether they have caused it or learned that it has occurred, and though they often bring many works upon many people as though wandering and incidental, in order to deceive: nevertheless, Scripture does not conceal that each person has his familiar demon, especially inquisitive concerning him, observing him everywhere and in everything—a demon whom a monk ought by no means to ignore. I think that I know and recognize mine very well. Nothing is better known to me, because nothing is more harmful to me. Nothing is more familiar, because nothing is more frequent. I do not fail to know what temptation, and of what kind, presses me more often and more severely. I also know in what part I am more easily troubled [Col. 1819A]. Therefore I ought to cry out to the One who sees my weakness and knows my enemy: “Lord Jesus, who alone are mighty, rescue the needy from the hand of those stronger than he, the destitute and poor from those who despoil him” (Ps. 34). Rescue the poor and needy; deliver him from the hand of the sinner. Rescue me from the hand of the sinner and from the hand of the lawless and unjust man.

For, beloved, when I sing these and similar words, I certainly direct the psalm secretly against him. “And it,” he says, “was mute.” Mine is exceedingly talkative to me: it spins out very long and utterly false tales about the glory, beauty, and delights of this world; it whispers a thousand suspicions about this person and that; it promises marvels and threatens marvels; it tells me a thousand lies—that I can do many things I cannot do, and cannot do many things I can; it says that remarkable good and evil things are said about me; now it discourses with me about my learning, now my religious life, now my morals, now my lineage, now grace, now eloquence, now refinement. Why say more? It often so tears away and occupies my ears that I have no leisure either to read or to hear another reading. Thus, while speaking to me, it makes me wholly mute, dull, and deaf.

Perhaps, then, the evil spirit is called mute, though it never ceases to speak evils, because it makes those whom it attacks mute in the praise of God and in the proper offices of their rational tongue: “If anyone speaks,” says the apostle Peter, “let it be as the utterances of God” (1 Pet. 4). This, therefore, I recognize as the office of a rational tongue. For to speak vain or lying words, words of contention or destruction, words of detraction or boasting, of greed and lust, or any kind of buffoonery irrelevant to the matter—in all these, though the tongue cries out and chatters outwardly in human ears, or inwardly in familiar conversation with its demon, it is mute before God. As it is written: “Because I kept silent, my bones grew old, while I cried out all day long” (Ps. 31).

The tongue therefore speaks God’s utterances in three ways: when it praises God, accuses itself before Him, and builds up its neighbor. But one who is silent concerning these is mute, however loudly he cries. O Lord Jesus, cast out my demon and open my lips to humble confession of my sins, so that my mouth may worthily proclaim [Col. 1819D] Your praise; otherwise praise will not be fitting in the mouth of a sinner. “You have put on confession and beauty,” it says (Ps. 103). For confession adorns, and beauty praises. But if I, a sinner—that is, one concealing sins—presumptuously praise, God immediately says to me: “Why do you, that is, such a person, recount my righteous deeds, you who keep silent about your injustices and take my covenant in your mouth” (Ps. 50 [Latin Ps. 51]), though that mouth has not been cleansed by confession?

“Confession with the mouth is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). Confession, therefore, cleanses the mouth, and contrition the heart. “But you hate discipline and cast my words behind you” (Ps. 49 [Latin Ps. 50]). In God’s utterances confession of sins comes first; without it, neither the praise which ought to follow is becoming, nor the building-up of one’s neighbor appropriate. For one who desires to praise God in due order first gives Him thanks for opening his mouth to praise Him. Confession opens the mouth, as obstinacy closes it. And one who wishes to instruct his neighbor—does he not first instruct him in repentance and confession? Thus Wisdom and the herald of Wisdom began their preaching, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of God is drawing near.” “And all the people,” it says, “went out to John and were baptized by him, confessing their sins” (Matt. 3). The counsel of the apostle Peter likewise is found to have been: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized” (Acts 2). James’s command is: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. 5).

This, then, is the order of God’s utterances. But if, concealing your sins as though they were gold, you allow them by festering to produce wounds in you, and, transgressing the order of God’s utterances, burst forth into His praises, you hear, as was said: “Why do you recount my righteous deeds and take my pure covenant in your impure mouth?” (Ps. 50 [Latin Ps. 51]). But if you turn to teaching your neighbor, the Apostle rebukes you: “You who teach others, do you not teach yourself? You who preach that one must confess, do not confess? You who preach that one must not steal, steal confession?” (Rom. 2). Therefore, brother, either be silent concerning all good things, as Jesus commanded the demons to be silent concerning His praise and preaching; or confess all evil things, so that you may worthily be admitted to praise and preaching. “Your mouth abounded in malice”; let it abound in righteousness.

But the beginning [Col. 1820C] of a sinner’s righteousness is confession of sin, as it is written: “The righteous man is first his own accuser” (Prov. 18): second, a praiser of God; third, a teacher of his neighbor. Therefore confession is the first part of righteousness. “And your tongue devised deceit” (Ps. 49 [Latin Ps. 50]). Let it therefore confess these things without deceit, if it wishes to emerge from sin, as it is written: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin, and in whose spirit there is no deceit” (Ps. 31 [Latin Ps. 32]). If you impute it to yourself, God does not impute it to you. If you accuse and uncover it, He forgives and covers it. “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31 [Latin Ps. 32]).

“You sat speaking against your brother” (Ps. 49 [Latin Ps. 50]). Sit before your Father; confess against yourself. “Against the son of your mother,” the Church, “you laid a stumbling-block” [Col. 1820D] (ibid.). Set a stumbling-block—shame and judgment—against the son of your carnal mother, that is, against yourself, because you have done these things to your brother. Otherwise, He who now keeps silence and listens, waiting for you first to speak and be justified, and to come before His face in confession, will rebuke you at the end and say: “You wickedly imagined that I would be like you” (ibid.); you were silent, and I was silent. But shall I always be silent? By no means shall I be like you, whether you are silent or speak. For if you are silent, I shall not be silent; if you speak, I shall not speak; if you cover, I shall uncover; if you uncover, I shall cover; if you accuse, I shall excuse; if you excuse, I shall accuse. Therefore I shall not be like you, because if you acquit, I shall condemn; if you condemn, I shall acquit.

This, beloved, is the benefit of humility in confession: that it has the Judge as its defender and the avenger as its pardoner. Knowing this, crafty deceit, once it has crept into the mind’s consent through the pleasure of sin, immediately tries to shut the door of the mouth upon itself; and, lest it may at some point be drawn out through confession, it binds the tongue with the bond of desire, fear, and shame. These are the three things which hinder confession. But You, Lord Jesus, who open and no one shuts, who appeared for this purpose, to destroy the works of the devil, cast out from me, Your servant, every pleasure of sin, that with a contrite heart I may repent. By a better desire, a stronger fear, and a wiser shame, loosen for me the bond of my tongue, so that, once mute, I may speak in confession, and the crowds may marvel—not only crowds of human beings, but also of angels and even of demons. [Col. 1821B] “For we have become a spectacle to this world, to angels and to human beings,” both good and evil (1 Cor. 4).

Make them marvel, then, at the speech of Your servant, not only of his mouth but of his deed; for deeds too are words. Let it speak of the humility of Your servant, Your sublimity, and the benefit of the neighbor—by mouth, heart, and deed. Let him not be ashamed to confess to one person in the ear, lest he be confounded before many face to face. Let him not fear, as though ruined, to lose what cannot but be lost, lest he lose what can be kept forever. Let him not shrink, as though worthless, from falling away from a hope which often deceives, lest he truly fall away from the reality which always refreshes. Nor are those whom You, wise and good Lord, have set over us so foolish or evil that they either do not know or neglect to have compassion on our infirmities. But while we are oppressed by the foolish and mute one, we naturally suppose foolishly and wrongly concerning prudent and good persons. Therefore cast out from us this most wicked and mute spirit, You, Lord, who are the Word of the Father, so that through the word of power and truth we may receive the word of praise and confession: You who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, live and reign as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIX. FOR THE SAME FEAST II

“He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons” (Luke 11).

As you see, dearest friends, the evil of the day presses us so that we cannot extend the sermon as usual. “Sufficient for the day,” says the Savior, “is its own evil” [Col. 1821D] (Matt. 6). But in these perilous times, the day’s own evil is not sufficient for the day; for the days are evil. Therefore, beloved, the wicked have this characteristic habit: filled with envy, they conceal another’s praise as long as they can; when overcome by evidence and unable to do so, they either diminish it or distort it. Thus, while the crowd rejoices in devotion and marvels at Christ’s works, the scribes and Pharisees always either conceal what they know to be true, diminish what is great, or distort what is good.

In one place, while concealing the matter, they say to the worker of many and marvelous signs: “What sign do you perform, that we may believe you?” (John 6). But here, what they cannot shamelessly deny, they maliciously disparage, seeking a sign from heaven as though this one were earthly and insignificant; and they distort it, saying: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.” This, beloved, is that blasphemy against the Spirit which, once it takes possession of someone, binds him with the chain of eternal guilt. Not because everything is denied to one who repents, if he produces fruits worthy of repentance, but because, oppressed by the weight of such malignity, he can by no means recover breath for the repentance worthy of the pardon he ought to receive.

For by God’s deep and just judgment, anyone who clearly understands God’s grace and the Holy Spirit’s operation in his brother, and, though unable to deny it, is spurred by envy and does not shrink from distorting and calumniating it, shamelessly ascribing to an evil spirit what he truly knows to be the Holy Spirit—such a person is abandoned by that very Spirit of grace whom he insults, so that, his own malice darkening and blinding him, he never wishes to repent in order to obtain pardon. For what is more grievous than that someone, through envy of a brother whom he is commanded to love as himself, should presume to blaspheme the goodness of God, which he ought to love above himself, and insult Majesty while desiring to detract from a human being?

Therefore, my brothers, let us guard our hearts with every vigilance from this plague of malice: hatred of another’s happiness. If we love that happiness, by loving it we make it our own. This is that viperish mother which bore death into the world. “Through the devil’s envy death entered into the world” (Wis. 2). He was indeed the first proud being and likewise the first envious one; as he generated arrogance from himself, so together with it and from it he generated envy. For he was not arrogant first and envious afterward, but wholly both at once, because the arrogant person is envious, and no arrogant person is without envy. Therefore an envious person must be arrogant: the one follows from the other, the one necessitates the other, and both are true.

But arrogance is the desire for one’s own glory, envy the hatred of another’s. There is also another arrogance, which may be called animal and earthly: namely, the desire for temporal things. It bears a daughter of its own kind, namely carnal or worldly envy; for like mother, like daughter. But the parent and offspring previously mentioned are spiritual wickednesses in heavenly places.

Therefore, beloved, whoever desires to be entirely free of envy must strip himself of all arrogance. For in the entire generation of vices there is nothing so wicked and perverse as the twofold arrogance and envy, nothing so opposed to the charity of God and neighbor. Accordingly, as charity is the summit of virtues, so these are the abyss of vices. Nevertheless, as it is written, “wisdom always conquers malice” (Wis. 7). But charity conquers by suffering—for charity is patient and bears all things—while wisdom conquers by reasoning, for it too is the Word. Since the Lord Jesus is substantially both, that is, charity and wisdom, He patiently hears the calumny and wisely refutes it, according to the prophecy once uttered of Him: “He shall save the children of the poor and humble the slanderer” (Ps. 71 [Latin Ps. 72]). For He saved the poor man oppressed by a demon, and most sharply refuted the calumniating Pharisee, saying: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste.”

It is as though He said: I came for this purpose, to destroy the devil’s kingdom among human beings and to build God’s kingdom in human beings. But if I brought it about that Satan should cast Satan out of human beings, I have beyond doubt accomplished my purpose. For the adversary is divided against himself, and desolation will follow division. Therefore his kingdom, divided against itself, must necessarily be laid waste; and once laid waste, it will be scattered and fall. For just as the smallest things grow by harmony and counsel, so the greatest are worn away by discord and desolation.

Therefore He says, coming into the world: among demons themselves, between flesh and spirit, between demons and human beings, and among human beings themselves, between the children of darkness and the children of light, “I came not to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10). Paul likewise wisely divided from themselves the Pharisees and Sadducees, who had been perniciously united against him, so that he might escape through their division when their concord could easily have destroyed him. Therefore the chief point of victory is to sever the concerted unity of conspirators against oneself and, with the greatest prudence, introduce discord among enemies.

Further, He proves that their malice lied by saying:

“If I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons”—that is, the apostles from among the Jews—“cast them out?” If I have a prince, whom do they have, who likewise cast out demons? For just as many demons can be in one human being, so one demon cannot be in many. Therefore they themselves shall be your truthful judges, since they now know concerning themselves that you are lying accusers. Thus, if Satan casts out Satan, his kingdom cannot stand; rather, it must yield to God’s kingdom, which I proclaim. But if I cast out demons not by Beelzebub but by the finger of God, then surely God’s kingdom has come upon you.

Before me the devil’s kingdom, divided against itself, cannot stand, just as the demons themselves cannot stand before me and mine. Therefore, whether, as you lie, I cast out demons, or, as is true, I do so, Satan is certainly defeated; and those who belong to his kingdom, who together with him scatter against me from unity and truth, shall be conquered. But those who are with me and gather with me into unity and charity shall conquer. For the devil’s kingdom is greed, which shall be destroyed; but God’s kingdom is charity, which never fails.

If, then, I am so strong that I even rule the prince of demons, so that at my command he rages against his own people and destroys his own kingdom and household, who are you, who presume to resist? He further proves that He has conquered him and has power over him by the saying, “When a strong man armed,” and so forth. It is as though He said: If that prince, formerly strong over human beings born in sin because of sin’s weakness, possessed his own people in peace and tranquil subjection, but I—conceived, born, and living without any sin, and therefore stronger than demon and human being—came upon him, bound the oppressor, subjected him to my dominion, and freed the oppressed; and if I have not merely plundered him but, as you say, have even caused him at my command to cast out demons, why do you endeavor to resist, more obstinate than demons? [Col. 1824A]

You see, beloved, the wise caught in their own craftiness, malice plainly conquered by wisdom, and perversity, wherever it turns, enclosed by the proofs of truth. But let us beseech the gracious Jesus with humble supplication that He may deign to cast out from us every kind of demon; to free the tongue from every hindrance to confession; the will and affections from every desire of this world; reason from every ignorance; and freedom from every difficulty. Thus may we be willing, know, and be able always to be with Him here and to gather with Him, until at last we are gathered by Him to Himself and to our Fathers. Following their Rules and Institutions, we shall surely be acknowledged as their children and gathered to God, the common Father of all, who then shall be known from least to greatest, His Only-begotten revealing Him to all: He who with Him and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XL. ON EASTER DAY

“If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Col. 3).

Truly, beloved, as blessed Gregory says, God’s loving-kindness has overcome our hardness; indeed, it has surpassed every human kindness. Great, certainly, is the bond of kindness and human covenant between husband and wife. “Therefore a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and they shall be no longer two but one flesh.” Yet God’s wondrous clemency toward us plainly surpasses this bond, as wonderfully as mercifully.

For this reason Scripture says: “If a woman puts away her husband and, departing, takes another, shall she return to him again? Shall not such a woman be defiled and polluted?” She shall not return, because she has committed fornication and been polluted—even if perhaps only once. “But you,” Scripture continues, speaking to the soul under the figure of Judaea, “have committed fornication with many lovers; yet return to me, says the Lord” [Col. 1824C] (Jer. 3). The Gospel too permits spouses to be separated only because of fornication. But God’s loving-kindness, after a thousand fornications of body and soul, sorrowfully calls back those who have turned away; gently embraces them when they return, as though calling after them from behind; and sweetly kisses them with the kiss of His holy mouth. Those who remain, He brings into the wine-cellar, where they may be intoxicated by the abundance of His house. Once intoxicated and, through the wine’s strength, removed from the senses of the flesh, He brings them into the bedchamber, where, placing His left hand beneath her head, He embraces her with His right; there, though the flesh sleeps, the heart keeps watch, and she may say: “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine; he shall abide between my breasts” (Song 1).

There is also, secondly, the bond of human kindness between parent and child. Yet this too is surpassed by God’s kindness toward the rational soul, a kindness pure, gratuitous, and prevenient, as Scripture testifies: “Can a woman forget the infant of her womb, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb?” (Isa. 49). Such conduct would surely be so cruel, inhuman, and bestial as to exceed even the hardness of the Furies, as it is written: “Even jackals have uncovered the breast and nursed their young.” “Even if she can forget, yet I will not forget you,” says the Lord [Col. 1825A] (Lam. 4).

We, alas, wretches that we are, either easily forget Him or proudly despise Him. But He, by that loving-kindness which He Himself is, mercifully remembers those who forget Him, diligently attends to those who despise Him, and cares for those who do not ask. For just as, when as yet no one existed, no one asked or could deserve to be created, so, when all were wicked under sin, no one could deserve or ought to have been heard in asking to be redeemed. Who ever either asked or dared imagine that God would give up His Son lest an evil and wicked servant should perish?

Finally, the third—and strongest—bond of human love is that between body and soul; for no one can in any way fail to love himself. Hence this self-love in human beings seemed to divine Scripture to require regulation rather than commandment.

Therefore this surpassing and superabundant divine mercy broke even this bond in itself, as strongly as mercifully, lest anything be lacking to that supreme charity than which no one has greater, “that one lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). “Father,” He says, “if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. 26). What, I ask, could God do more to empty Himself than become human; or a human being than die; or God the Lord than become a servant; or a servant than die shamefully? “Let us condemn him,” it says, “to a shameful death” (Wis. 2). The innocent one was counted among the wicked; the godly one was delivered into the hands of the ungodly. Yet He freely gave His life over to death and was counted with criminals. Thus the godly one suffered ungodly things from ungodly people, doing godly things.

What kindness could be so wondrous except divine kindness—or perhaps all the more wondrous because it is more divine? He alone does wonders; assuredly He alone is wondrous above all. Why say more? I confess that I do not know whether it ought to be called more or less wondrous than divine. For what is remarkable if God is most merciful? Yet how can that which is so merciful toward enemies and ungodly persons not be called most gentle? The Apostle, likewise marveling at this whole matter, says: “While we were still wicked, why did he die for the ungodly?” [Col. 1825D] (Rom. 5).

Yet boundless mercy ought to give wondrous proofs of mercy. Christ’s death and resurrection, performed for our death and resurrection, as it is written, “He was delivered up for our offenses and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4), cannot be merely single; but our death, being twofold, needs a twofold resurrection. The first death, then, is the soul’s death, when, because of the evil of disobedience, it is abandoned by God, its life. This death is swallowed up by life through resurrection, when, commanded by faith, it lives. For although the body remains dead because of sin, the spirit nevertheless lives because of justification, when through obedience it submits itself to God, as it is written: “Shall not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation” [Col. 1826A] (Ps. 61 [Latin Ps. 62]). For just as, when it departs from God, it departs from life and falls into the first death, so when it approaches God, it approaches life and finds the first resurrection.

“Blessed,” says the apostle John, “are those who have a share in the first resurrection; the second death shall not harm them” (Rev. 2). That is, the death of the body will not harm them, because it will not cast them into the third death, which is the eternal death of both soul and body. Rather, it will assist them by freeing them and leading them out of the body’s prison, until they return to that which was sown as an animal body and shall rise as a spiritual body, conformed to the body of Christ’s glory. This is the second resurrection, regenerating the whole human being together unto life.

But that beloved and blessed soul of the Savior, which came to pay what it had not taken, though weak because of another’s sin, was nevertheless strengthened against its own, as it is written: “In you I was strengthened from the womb” (Ps. 70 [Latin Ps. 71]). As it could not fall into the death of sin, so neither could it rise from sin into the life of righteousness. For once united to the Word of Life, it adhered inseparably, both by personal union and by love of righteousness, rejoicing above all things and saying: “It is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. 72 [Latin Ps. 73]); and, “He who clings to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6).

In Christ, therefore, who subsists as man from a rational soul and human flesh, and as Christ from God and man, there are, as it were, two bonds [Col. 1826C] and two distinct relations. For the bond of divinity and humanity, joining Christ’s essence insofar as He is Mediator of God and human beings, is utterly indissoluble; it admits neither death nor resurrection. For humanity, once assumed by divinity, has never suffered divorce nor received a bill of repudiation. Rather, the sacrament of this blessed union remains great and eternal—the sacrament also of venerable nuptials and an undefiled marriage-bed—having this authority and safeguard: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19).

But the bond of flesh and soul, joining humanity alone, did not indeed deserve dissolution by any penalty for its own sin. Nevertheless, so that He, released from the bonds of sins which had entangled us, might free us, and, bound again to God from whom we had been loosed, might bind us again, He encountered death and found resurrection by the wondrous ordering of the mystery. He had from divine mercy and patience this promise: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will rebuild it” [Col. 1826D] (John 2). You destroy; I shall rebuild. I, who built yours, shall rebuild mine. You, who deserved the dissolution of your own temple, destroy mine. Destroy it not by the merit of my iniquity nor by the command of your power, but by the disposition of my will. “For no one takes my life from me; but I lay it down when I will, and when I will I take it up again” (John 10).

For He was able to raise Himself, He who lived while dead only in the flesh. Thus Christ could and willed to die and rise again only according to this bond, in which, as was said, humanity adhered inseparably to divinity by a personal union, and the soul never for an instant departed from delight in and love for the Word through any alien love. Therefore He lived though dead, who died while living: at one and the same time living and dead. Humanity lived by union with divinity; the rational soul lived by charity with God’s Word. The flesh alone died through the separation of the soul; and by its restoration alone it rose again.

If, therefore, most beloved, you have meanwhile risen in the soul alone with Christ rising in the flesh alone, seek the things that are above, with the intention and desire of the soul, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God, also in the body (Col. 3:1). For many seek the things above down below: such are those who seek dignity and grace, sufficiency and pleasure, in earthly things. These are they who have set their eyes to turn toward the earth, seeking the highest things in the lowest. Others seek the things below up above: that is, vain glory in virtue, boasting in wisdom, curiosity in truth; finally, in spiritual pursuit and religious habit, some temporal gain—whether of praise, dignity, money, or unrestrained freedom. Others seek the things below below: earthly things in earthly things, namely, and carnal things in carnal things. All these altogether “think upon the things that are on the earth,” and not upon those above. But others seek the things above above: that is, true things among true things, spiritual things among spiritual things, heavenly things among heavenly things, and divine things among divine things; being mindful of the things of God and walking in newness of life, conformed to the likeness of Christ’s death while they are dead to sin, flesh, and the world; conformed to Christ’s resurrection while, estranged from the life of former corruption and sensuality, they live in the flesh in a manner above the flesh; seated also with him in heavenly places, while their rest and their manner of life are in heaven; and reigning with him, while they compel all that belongs to them to serve spiritual progress. Moreover, those who seek a heavenly reward in earthly actions undoubtedly seek the highest things in the lowest laudably, just as those blameworthily seek the lowest things in the highest who seek what is earthly in spiritual things. Less blameworthily indeed do those act who seek the lowest things in the lowest; but most laudably of all are those who seek the highest things in the highest. This, most beloved, is our profession and purpose. May he deign to fulfil it in us, whose resurrection we celebrate and imitate insofar as we can: Christ the Lord, without whom we can do nothing and in whom we can do all things; who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLI. ON THE SAME FEAST, II

“The Lord said to me: You are my Son; this day I have begotten you” (Ps. 2). You ask, dearest brethren, why blessed Paul, when speaking of the resurrection, employed the testimony of this verse, since it seems more fitting for a birth than for a resurrection. But we do not hesitate to call the resurrection itself a birth, especially because we know that the Saviour calls it regeneration. For if the first resurrection, which is that of the soul, is called regeneration, why should the second, which is that of the body, not also be called regeneration? Therefore, although Christ’s resurrection can be only one, it nevertheless signifies the first of our resurrections, which are two, as the same Apostle testifies when he says: “As Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6). It initiates the second, whence Christ is called “the first fruits of those who sleep.” Thus there are, in a manner, three births of human beings and two resurrections.

For we are born as human beings from human beings, through human beings, carnally—flesh from flesh. No instance comes to mind in which this birth is called a resurrection. We are reborn from God as gods, spiritually through the Spirit, where “that which is born of the Spirit is spirit”; and this is the first resurrection and the second birth. But we shall be regenerated from corruptible beings into incorruptible, from dead beings into immortal, from the dust of the earth into a heavenly condition. This is the third birth and the second resurrection. Christ did not know the first birth; he underwent the second from the Virgin; the third, from the tomb. For as we are reborn from the font, so Christ was born from the Virgin; and as Christ was regenerated from the tomb, so shall we be reborn in the future. This is the state for which man was made; nor will man be complete before that for which he was begun is perfected in him. Then he will properly be said to have been generated when he has been fully generated; then made, when completed. Meanwhile, he who is generated and made in the first two births is only fully generated and made in the third. Hence Christ is fittingly and subtly said to have been begotten on the day of his resurrection, as though on the day of his perfection and consummation he had been fully begotten. Thus he himself says: “Today and tomorrow I perform cures, and on the third day I am brought to completion” (Luke 13).

Therefore, just as God prepared for the first man, before he was born, that by which he might be sustained, so for the second man, before he was reborn, he fashioned beforehand that by which he might be fed. Hence, before his one resurrection—which is the figure of our first resurrection and the example of the second—on the day of the chalice, he transformed bread and wine into the sacrament of his body and blood. For just as he created the new man from the old man, so too, from the old food of the old man, he transformed a new food for the new man. “Behold,” he says, “I make all things new” (Rev. 21). A new creature, a new food; a new life, a new birth; a new death, a new resurrection.

For just as the first man, made into a living soul, needs nourishment lest he fall away from life, but may through it be sustained, grow, and be strengthened in it—not so as to receive another life through nourishment, but lest he perish from that very life through want, since the soul alone can give life but cannot by itself retain it—so also the new creature in Christ, before it is perfected in the second resurrection into a life-giving spirit, needs nourishment after the first regeneration, by which it may live, grow, and be strengthened in the life in which it was regenerated; not so as to receive another life after baptismal grace, but lest through want it lose the life it has received. For by diverse sacraments we are regenerated and nourished into the same life; yet we are not perfected in it until we are born for the third time into the life-giving Spirit, into whom Christ was born—or made—from the tomb, as the Apostle says: “The second man was made into a life-giving spirit” (1 Cor. 15).

For then the whole flesh will live immediately and sufficiently from the soul alone; the whole soul immediately and perfectly from God alone, when neither will the flesh need food nor the soul sacraments. Then all who are children of God will truly, securely, and fully hear: “You are my Son, because this day I have begotten you,” because I have fully begotten you. In the beginning I began you, where it is said: “God made man in his image and likeness” (Gen. 1). In the middle I restored you, whence it is said: “In the midst of the years make it live” (Hab. 3). In the third I consummated you, whence it is said here: “This day I have begotten you.” This day I have begotten you such as you are in the third state, for which I created you in the first and made you live in the second. First I created you as a living soul; second, I refashioned you into a life-giving Spirit; third, I consummated you into a life-giving Spirit, who gives life to the flesh without food and himself lives from my presence without sacrament.

This is the grace; this is the fruit of the second resurrection, in which no one will have a share unless he has been a participant in the first. Yet no one can be a participant in the resurrection unless he has been a participant in death; nor can one be a participant in death unless he has been a participant in the Passion. Therefore, if we suffer with him and die with him, we shall rise with him and reign with him. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLII. SERMON ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

“No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven” (John 3). These, my brethren, are those heavenly things difficult to believe, more difficult to understand, and most difficult to explain. “If,” says the heavenly Teacher, “I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” The heavenly one speaks subtly of heavenly things; the earthly one is slow to believe earthly things; and he who can be a teacher of carnal persons is not equal to heavenly instruction. But for us, most beloved, whose manner of life has long been in heaven, heavenly things ought not to be unknown. For it is exceedingly shameful to be ignorant of the place in which you dwell, and foolish to dwell where you are ignorant.

Therefore, by the familiar abasement of the expression “Son of Man,” he designates himself. For the Son of God alone descended from heaven, by his own will as well as power; whence the devil, cast out, fell, while the good angel obedient to a superior power withdraws for a time. But how did the Son of Man descend from there, where no human being has ever been? Is not the Son of Man a man? Although not every man is a son of man, every son of man is nevertheless a man. How then did the Son of Man descend from where he was neither born nor had yet ascended? Or perhaps was the Son of Man born in heaven as the Son of God was on earth—bodily Son of Man everywhere as the unlocalized Son of God is somewhere; temporal and eternal, as the eternal is temporal?

But let it stand: those things that are wonderful are wonderful for this reason, that one and the same person is before himself and after himself, earlier and later than himself; likewise lesser and greater, made by himself, maker of himself, servant and Lord. One and the same is God and man: one person, two natures; or rather, in two natures, three substances. According to his humanity, God ascended; according to his divinity, man descended. The Son of Man, who according to the Son of God is at once in heaven and on earth—indeed everywhere and truly nowhere—God-man: all this is required by the wondrous logic of personal union. And the heavenly one, comparing heavenly things with heavenly persons, as spiritual things with spiritual persons, or even divine things with divine persons, judges all these things.

Yet what use is the descent of the Son of God to us if the ascension of that same Son of Man is unique? Or where will he place us, who, setting all things aside, follow him more closely? We flee hell and despise the world: where are we to go if we do not ascend to heaven? Yet “no one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven.”

Accordingly, either we descended from there, remain there still, and are that Son of Man there; or we shall by no means ascend there and cannot be where we wish to be. And thus surely we have become more miserable than all human beings. Yet, most beloved, to those who attend to the force of the words and the freedom of the Spirit in divine speech, it readily appears that “Son of Man,” “Son of God,” “Word of the Father,” “Christ,” or any similar expression by which he who speaks these heavenly things is designated, does not have a simple meaning or occur with one uniform reference.

For Christ is sometimes said to be that simple nature itself which neither began nor ends, which cannot be changed or moved; which is from the Father alone, with the Father, and in the Father; which is neither the one who is the Father nor other than the Father, but always is. Thus he himself says to the Jews: “The beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8). And elsewhere: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). For the Son of God and man are one in such a way that they are one person, not one thing, just as he and the Father are one thing, not one person. Here are two natures and one person; there, two persons and one nature. Likewise: “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8), and six hundred other statements, which cannot be true except in this sense and belong to the property of the higher nature, though they are stated without distinction about him who, as we have said, is both higher and lower than himself.

Conversely, he is sometimes designated by these same expressions in ways that cannot truthfully be said of the person except with reference to the lower nature: for example, his being made a little lower than the angels, his temporal birth, and the like. Some things are also said of the soul alone, some of the flesh alone; some of both together—that is, of humanity alone; while others are said of Christ’s whole person together, that is, of divinity together with humanity, as when the Apostle calls him “the mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus.” For a mediator cannot stand between two parties unless he is from both.

But in all this, what benefit is there for wretched human beings if the divinity of that man descended from heaven in such a way that the humanity of that God ascends only with it? Hence we are compelled to draw from the foregoing yet another understanding, in which by the designation of Christ or Son of Man not only Christ whole, or in a part or parts, is understood, as set forth above. For when he long ago rebuked his persecutor from heaven, he said: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9); and he will one day say: “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matt. 25). And by what reasoning are these said, except by reason of the unity of bridegroom and bride, or head and body?

Just as the head and body of one man are that one man himself, so that Son of the Virgin and his chosen members are one man and one son of man. Scripture says that Christ whole and entire is head and body; indeed, all the members together are one body, which with its head is one son of man; and this one son of man with the Son of God is one Son of God; and he himself with God is one God. Therefore the whole body with its head is Son of Man and Son of God and God. Hence also that saying: “I will, Father, that as I and you are one, these also may be one with us” (John 17).

Therefore, according to this familiar sense of Scripture, the body is not without the head, nor the head without the body; nor are head and body—the whole Christ—without God. For the head of the woman is the man; the head of the man, Christ; the head of Christ, God. Thus Christ is the head of the woman through the man; God is the head of the man through Christ. Therefore God is head of woman, man, and Christ. Thus all things also are one God with God; but the Son of God is with God naturally, the Son of Man personally with that Son, and that Son’s body sacramentally with him.

Therefore the Son of Man alone descended from heaven by reason of his divinity, but not wholly by reason of his humanity; and he alone and wholly ascends by reason of the unity of head and body. No one, therefore, ascends except that one who alone and wholly is he who descended alone, yet not wholly. If, whenever a poor person is fed, Christ is fed, how is it that when a poor person ascends, Christ does not ascend? “What God has joined, let no man separate” (Matt. 19). This mystery is small in man and woman, but great in Christ and the Church.

Thus, if my foot could speak as my tongue can, it would say what my tongue says, namely, “I am Isaac.” So the faithful and rational members of Christ can truly call themselves what he himself is: even Son of God and God. Yet what he is by nature, they are by fellowship; what he is by fullness, they are by participation. Finally, what he is as Son of God by generation, his members are not merely by constitution, as Moses was “a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7), nor merely by title, as there are “many gods and many lords” (1 Cor. 8), but by adoption, as it is written: “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, Abba, Father” (Rom. 8). In accordance with this Spirit he gave them power to become children of God, so that, being taught especially by him who is firstborn among many brethren, they may say: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6). And elsewhere: “I ascend to my Father and your Father,” and so forth (John 20). For though he is the common Father and God of all by creation, he is ours in a special manner through gracious adoption, as he is the Father of the Only-Begotten through unique generation.

Therefore Christ’s generation—his birth, inasmuch as from the beginning he is Son of God, and at the end Son of Man, and in the mystery head and body are one Christ—must be understood in a threefold manner. The first is from the Father without a mother; the second from a mother without a father; the third, according to substance, neither from father nor mother, but according to sacrament, from God the Father through the Holy Spirit and from the virgin mother Church. For by the same Spirit through whom the Son of Man, our head, was born from the Virgin’s womb, we, his body, are reborn from the font of baptism as children of God. And as he was without all sin, so we are reborn for the remission of all sins. For just as he bore all the sins of the whole body upon the wood in the body of flesh, so by the grace of regeneration he granted to the spiritual body that no sin should be imputed to it, as it is written: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. 31).

This blessed man is undoubtedly Christ, who, insofar as God is the head of Christ, forgives sins; to whom, insofar as he is one man as head of the body, nothing is forgiven; but insofar as the body of the head consists of many persons, nothing is imputed. He is righteous in himself and himself justifies himself. He alone is saviour, he alone saved; he alone ascends, he alone descends; he who gives gifts with the Father, gifts which he himself receives in human beings. “You have received gifts in men,” he says (Ps. 67): he who bore upon the wood in his body what he removed from his body through water. Again saving through wood and water, he is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world which he bore; priest and sacrifice and God, who, offering himself to himself, reconciled himself through himself to himself, as to the Father and the Holy Spirit.

The first birth is eternal, in which God is born from God: as is the Father, so is the Son. The second is temporal and brief, in which man is born from man: as is the mother, so is the son. The third is temporal and long, in which “that which is born of the Spirit is spirit,” just as that which is born of God is God, and that which is born of flesh is flesh. Therefore this birth—or life, death, resurrection, or ascension—of Christ has been begun, but not yet completed. It begins with the first righteous person and is consummated with the last; throughout the whole intervening period it is enacted, as someone elegantly said: “Under Noah, under David, under Christ, there were sacred things.” Hence also the Apostle: “All were baptized under Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink” (1 Cor. 10).

These, then, are those earthly yet spiritual things which the earthly person does not believe because he thinks carnally; but they are spiritually examined. Hence it is foolishness to him that a man can be born when he is old. This very birth is elegantly set forth in those ancient writings of which that teacher was master—the one who did not believe new things. For, as those curious about such matters affirm, there are naturally three differing modes in which living beings are born: either with the feet proceeding first and the arms joined to the sides; or with the head proceeding first and the arms similarly arranged; or certainly with the arms crossed over the head which itself goes before.

But holy Jacob, so that through his singular birth the author of nature might signify something above nature, came forth with his arm extended before his head, grasping in his hand the sole of the firstborn’s foot. What, then, does Jacob signify here except Christ—not uniquely according to his own person, but according to that in which Christ whole and entire is head and body? What is the arm arising before the head except the earlier people of the elect, anticipated by the Saviour’s grace before his temporal birth; embracing the age first through the five ages of the world, as through the fingers of a hand; or binding the carnal people also through the five books of the Law? The remaining body, however—the fullness of the Gentiles together with the few believers from Israel—is joined together through both sides; while the head is born in the middle. Yet when it has been born, the arm that had come forth before is assigned, with the remaining members, to its proper place beneath it, so that he may be recognized as head of the whole Church, to whom “all power in heaven and on earth” has been given (Matt. 28), and to whom every knee also bends, he who has “the name above every name” (Phil. 2). “For there is no other name under heaven given among men, by which we must be saved” (Acts 4). As Abraham, so all the earlier saints rejoiced to see his day; “they saw it and were glad” (John 8). May it be granted to us also, most beloved, to behold him in the kingdom of his glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

## SERMON XLIII. ON THE DAY OF PENTECOST, I

The Holy Spirit, most beloved, is given today from heaven; the same Spirit was once given by the same giver to the same persons on earth. Therefore it seems necessary to ask why he did this, he from whom nothing could be done without a rational cause. Yet he who received at once and all together the fullness of that Holy Spirit by whom he was conceived distributed it to whom, when, and in what measure he willed. Hence the Apostle says: “To each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4). He, therefore, who—so to speak—measured it, erred neither in person, nor in time, nor in quantity; nor did he make anyone equal to himself in the fullness either of power, strength, or glory. “Who,” it says, “among the clouds shall be equalled to the Lord? Or who among the sons of God shall be like God in equality?” (Ps. 87). Who that is adopted will be equal to one who is natural? Who among many, to the only one? Who among those who come later, to the firstborn? Who among those reborn by grace, to one born from substance? Who among those rescued from deepest darkness, to one born in inaccessible light?

For he was not, like others, called from darkness to light by being born; but, born light from light, he freely came by his birth from light into darkness. As it is written: “The light shone in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1). For those who comprehended it were illuminated and did not remain darkness. “For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord”; and “darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters” (Gen. 1). Yet he was not submerged in the waters or drowned; but held the waters apart from the waters, cherished them, and made them fruitful.

Likewise darkness—the ignorance of good things—lay over the hearts of all human beings; and they were oppressed by the torpor arising from the difficulty of things to be done, tossed by the shifting flow of wandering desire, until through Christ they were enlightened by the Spirit to knowledge, as he says: “He will lead you into all truth” (John 16); and until they were inflamed and made fruitful unto virtue. Hence: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24); and until they were loosed and melted away like “living waters springing up into eternal life,” as it is written: “He shall send forth his word and melt them; his Spirit shall blow and the waters shall flow” (Ps. 147).

Thus the same Spirit was given from the higher heaven for strength, who had previously been given in lower places and would at some time be given from the highest places unto the highest. He was given for power on earth, where principalities and powers still reign; today he is given for strength from heaven, because there remains struggle not against flesh and blood, but “against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6). Finally, after the resurrection of bodies, when the Son has handed over the kingdom to God the Father, when every principality and power is abolished and “God is all in all” (1 Cor. 15), he will be given for glory and peace, delight and joy and security, as it is written: “You shall take away their spirit, and they shall fail, and return to their dust. You shall send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth. May the glory of the Lord be for ever; the Lord shall rejoice in his works” (Ps. 103).

This is the gift of the principal Spirit for confirmation after every weakness. Seeking it, the Prophet says: “Confirm me with a principal Spirit” (Ps. 50), he who had already received the Holy Spirit for justification and the right Spirit for conversion. For by the right Spirit we are directed toward God; by the Holy Spirit we cleave to him; by the principal Spirit we do not depart from him. By the right Spirit we are corrected from evil; by the Holy Spirit we are strengthened for good; by the principal Spirit we are confirmed in it. By the right Spirit we turn away from evil; by the Holy Spirit we do good; by the principal Spirit we dwell for ever and ever.

Therefore it is given on earth for power, from heaven for strength, and from the Father’s presence for confirmation. Of power it is said because he breathed upon them, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20). And elsewhere: “He gave them power over all demons and to heal diseases” (Luke 9). Thus power lies in three things: casting out demons, healing diseases, and forgiving sins; and fourthly also in conferring graces. Although all these are great and works of divine power, as it is written: “The works that I do, you shall do also, and greater works than these shall you do” (John 14), they are nevertheless in a certain manner external, work externally, and can be common to sons and those who are not sons, to pretenders and to true persons. For Judas too is believed to have done such things with the other apostles; and at the judgment many will say: “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name and perform signs in your name?” Yet they will hear the harsh word: “Depart from me; I do not know you” (Matt. 7).

But blessed be God, who has given such power to human beings. Yet strength was needed, so that one powerful in relation to others might be strong in himself. What benefit, however great the power, to cast a demon out of another through the grace of exorcism, while through pride, envy, anger, sadness or acedia, greed, gluttony, or lust one has within oneself a demon dwelling—or is filled with many demons through many vices? What profit is it to be able to forgive others’ sins and yet oneself not be able to resist sin or escape from sin?

“Is any one of you sick?” says the Apostle. “Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and they shall pray over the sick person” (Jas. 5), although perhaps they themselves are more sick or more deserving of sickness; and he shall be relieved of his illness—especially of that which sin has caused, as the Apostle says of those who communicate unworthily: “For this reason many among you are weak, and many sleep” (1 Cor. 11). “And if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven him” (Jas. 5)—and most often by those who walk burdened with sins and cannot obtain forgiveness for themselves. A slave of sin forgives sin: as glorious in power as he is shameful in weakness. “Physician,” he says, “heal yourself” (Luke 4). “You who preach that one must not steal, why do you steal? You who teach others, teach yourself.”

But for one who is powerful to be able to do this, and for one powerful in others to be strong in himself, he needs help from heaven and to be clothed over with power from on high, though he has received power in one respect. As it is written: “The Lord is strong and mighty; the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23). Gloriously mighty for commanding demons, but beneficially strong for resisting vices. Peter performed miracles by power, but through weakness feebly denied him at a maidservant’s voice. The Jews, marvelling at this power in the Saviour, say: “Tell us, by what authority do you do these things?” (Matt. 21). Simon Magus, seeing this power in the apostles, deserved to hear: “May your money perish with you” (Acts 8). For he did not desire strength by which he might be strong against wickedness in his heart, but power by which he might appear glorious in action.

Some today, if we may speak without offending many, contrary to the Apostle’s counsel when he says, “Desire the better charisms” (1 Cor. 12)—plainly preferring gifts of strength to power—rather desire the lesser more and the greater less. Either glorying beyond measure in power received and perversely desiring what has not been received, they are greedy for power and unconcerned for virtue, seeking rather to be exalted than humble, to preside rather than benefit, to be able rather than to be. To this power belong the acts performed by priests, bishops, or prelates: blessings, consecrations, ordinations, exorcisms, and the laying on of hands; offices of superiority, preaching, baptisms, absolutions, excommunications, and above all the greatest power, the consecration of the Eucharist.

In all these things, therefore, we think three matters must be considered with the greatest care: for what end persons approach them, what manner of persons they are, and why they approach; lest what is divine be thought human; lest proud, greedy, and impure persons presume to undertake what belongs to the humble and holy; or, to put it briefly, lest those needing correction contemplate that which belongs to correct persons, or contemplate something earthly or carnal in spiritual and heavenly things. So far we have spoken of power, concerning whose abusers it is said: “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments, and a stronger punishment threatens the stronger” (Wis. 6). And elsewhere: “He has put down the powerful from their seat and exalted the humble” (Luke 1).

But no one abuses the strength given for guarding the soul. Strength wholly consists in the truth of charity and in the charity of truth: illuminating for knowledge so far as it comes from truth, and inflaming for love so far as it comes from charity. For as knowledge without charity puffs up, so charity without knowledge goes astray. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “When they do these things to you, they will suppose that they offer service to God” (John 16). Likewise charity, grieving for similar persons, says in the Apostle: “I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10). Knowledge, therefore, without charity puffs up; charity with knowledge builds up.

But when the disciples were clothed today with consummate strength from on high, there was given to them from heaven, in the charity and ardour of fire, the Spirit, leading them by brightness into all truth and setting them aflame by ardour into all charity. Their strength, then, which had dried like a potsherd from soft clay, shone forth like a lamp to our feet. Hence those who shortly before, silent and fearful during his Passion, all either abandoned or denied the Lord, now speak eloquently and fervently: “We cannot but speak the things that we have heard and seen. Judge yourselves,” they say, “whether it is more fitting to obey God or men” (Acts 5). O you who, a little before, feared human beings as human beings: whence comes to you such sudden courage that now you no longer fear human beings above human beings? You who, a little before, on my account were confined in a narrow and dark house of the Jews, how are you now speaking openly in the Temple with such confidence? Truly, as it is written: “Those who trust in the Lord shall renew their strength” (Isa. 40).

This, then, dearest brethren, this is the change of the right hand of the Most High. For “the Spirit of the Lord has adorned the heavens today, and by his hand in travail the crooked serpent has been brought forth” (Job 26). The crooked serpent inflicted upon our first parents and parricides—who killed us before they begot us—the seeds of all crookedness. Thus the crooked serpent has been brought forth with his crookednesses, because the prince of this world has been cast out; and now, when he comes to the disciples, he has nothing in them. For the Spirit has filled the whole world; and he who has knowledge of speech fashions tongues for every kind of utterance (Wis. 1). Hence the Spirit, who came in fire for the reason stated above, both filled the whole house and assumed the form of tongues.

Now, therefore, there is a judgment of the world, as there once was of heaven. For just as then, when Leviathan had been cast down and the crooked serpent defeated, heaven was cleansed, and the Spirit of the Lord—that is, the charity of God—filled and adorned the heavens, that is, the angels confirmed in charity; so now, when the world has been judged and the devil with his crookednesses cast out, the heavens that declare the glory of God are cleansed; and, with the charity of God poured into their hearts through the Holy Spirit, they are filled, adorned, and confirmed, so that fear is cast out and they speak the word of God with confidence.

For the serpent’s crookednesses and windings are to fear what should not be feared and not to fear what should be feared. Infected with this poison, Peter withered away into a threefold denial. Likewise, they are to love what should not be loved and not to love what should be loved. Judas also sinned in this respect, betraying the blood of the righteous one unjustly. These, therefore, are the origins and springs of all crookednesses and vices, of evils; when charity dries them up, it fills everything, possesses everything, and, embracing all things, leads into all knowledge of truth.

For the Spirit of the Lord today has filled the whole world; which whole world, after the world laid in wickedness was rejected, existed seminally only in those whom the Spirit filled today. Of them it is written: “For he has established the world, which shall not be moved” (Ps. 92). For one is established by power from on high through the coming of the Paraclete, so that he may not be moved by fear or love into willing to sin; and he will yet be confirmed by the presence of the Father’s countenance so that no occasion of sinning will be possible. But now charity fills all things, strength contains all things, and truth illumines all things through knowledge. Then, however, the one God will be all in all: the unfailing fountain of charity, strength, and truth.

Virtue, then, which charity kindles and truth enlightens, is prudent, sober, patient, and just. By prudence it avoids rashness, presumptuous innovations, fraudulent counsels, falsely named knowledge, the wiles of Satan, and the snares of the wicked. And, to put it briefly, it treads down the dragon and swiftly crushes beneath its feet Satan when he transforms himself into an angel of light. By sobriety [Col. 1838A] it restrains desire and cools the heat of inward springs; it walks upon the asp and basilisk, while through abstinence it escapes the inciters of pleasure and, through love of poverty, outwits the ministers of avarice. By patience, moreover, it comes about that it fears no one any longer; it is delivered from fear of enemies who kill the body and afterwards have nothing further that they can do; having endured mockeries and scourging, bonds also and prisons, stonings, sawing asunder, and deaths cruelly devised of every kind, it bravely overcomes them, treading down the lion and triumphing in magnanimity over every fury of diabolical invention—both, that is, the spirit of faint-heartedness and that of tempest (Heb. XI). By justice it preserves fairness toward all, accepts no person, does good to those whom it can [Col. 1838B], wishes well to all, pays what is due to the wise and unwise, loves all as itself, and takes especial care of its own household. And having conquered demons by the other virtues, by justice it is meanwhile made like the angels, until by the third gift of the Holy Spirit it may be made equal to them.

Behold, beloved, what kind of persons, and how strong, the Spirit today has made by the second gift from on high: those whom he made mighty by the first gift below, and whom by the third he will make glorious in the highest. Come then, beloved: we have discussed, perhaps with the more scrupulous care because we possess it less, the power and strength which the Lord has given. But concerning glory, when we are glorious, discussion will be as easy as possession is blessed. May the Holy Spirit deign to grant this to us—he who with the Father and [Col. 1838C] the Son lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLIV. ON THE SAME FEAST, II

“Eat, my friends; drink and be inebriated, dearly beloved” (Song of Songs V).

According to custom, the vintage is celebrated after the harvest; and the ordered succession of the seasons is known to serve heavenly mysteries. The face of creation too is illumined, so that the face of the Creator may be contemplated. For from the creation of the world, the invisible things of God are perceived through the things that have been made (Rom. I). This visible world therefore serves its lord—that is, humankind—for sustenance; it serves also for instruction. A good servant feeds, instructs, supports, and teaches, provided that he does not have a bad master. The teaching of God is outwardly in creation; the image of God inwardly in the soul; and between these two great luminaries—the greater and the lesser luminary, which rule day and night—the fool, as though without light, gropes with his hand, blind all day and night. [Col. 1838D] Foolish and wretched is he whose eyes are at the ends of the earth, so that he sees nothing but darkness; he compels the whole world to serve his belly and his back, because he does not know why the world was made. He thinks that God made so great a world for so small a belly. O most wicked fire of the belly, which consumes so much and again says: “Bring, bring” (Prov. XXX)! Alas, the belly has driven some to such slavery that they worship it as though it were God, and at its command despise him who is the true God.

Such persons, beloved, while they sit down to eat [Col. 1839A] and drink and afterwards rise up to play, are mourned by the Apostle, who says: “Many walk, of whom I often told you, but now tell you even weeping, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ; whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame” (Phil. III). When such persons hear in the divine Scriptures what we have just proposed—“Eat, friends; drink and be inebriated, dearly beloved”—and things like it, they can taste nothing beyond familiar flavors and customary relishes. For practice makes the master, and habit is a second nature. When such people are reproved by us and by others, they say: “Why did the Lord make these things except for us to use them?” Is, then, every use of all things in the mouth? Truly, then, “all human labor is in his mouth.”

But we, beloved, whose spirit is [Col. 1839B] God, ought, as we perceive intelligible things in created things, so also to perceive spiritual things in carnal words. Especially today, when the Spirit has been sent from heaven to help us search out spiritual things, we should not despair. At the preceding Paschal solemnity, therefore, we harvested our bread from heaven. For it was gathered and threshed when, having been seized and scourged, it was ground by many questions and examinations among Jews and Gentiles, and finally baked by the fire of the Passion and the oven of the cross: the bread which came down from heaven and gives life to the world (John VI).
