Eat this, friends: that which enemies prepared. For, as it is written elsewhere, “The fool shall serve the wise” (Prov. XI). “Others have labored; enter into their labors.” Eat, therefore [Col. 1839C], friends, and eat for this reason: that you may be friends. For whoever refuses to eat can by no means be a friend.

The angel eats as a citizen and member of the household, with a full mouth; in a voice of exultation and praise he is satisfied with the fatness of wheat. Let the pilgrim and poor human being, according to his measure, eat flour with bran, lest, not at least refreshed by such provision, he fail on the journey he has begun. “If,” he says, “I dismiss them utterly fasting, they will fail on the way; for they have come from afar” (Mark VIII), and have endured for three days because of faith in the Trinity. For Jesus does not entrust himself to unbelievers.

Today, therefore, after such a harvest, a corresponding vintage is celebrated. For fifty days after holy Easter, that Paraclete Spirit—in whom is the sabbath-rest of the saints, from every evil work, in every good work, and beyond every work, in tranquility and peace—flowed abundantly from the fullness of the true vine, whose husbandman is the Father, into the hearts of the disciples. [Col. 1839D] He filled the storehouses of their minds, most thoroughly purified and bound up by the Son of God, with strong and shining wine. For the Spirit of the Lord, sent from Father and Son, filled the world; claiming the whole person for himself by his power, he encompassed memory, understanding, and will; and, in the manner of the strongest wine, wholly estranging that person from himself, he taught him the knowledge of speech which he possessed, so that, soberly sober, he was moved, directed, and spoke not by his own understanding and spirit, but all things were done by the heat, fragrance, and power of the wine. Rightly, therefore, the Jews judged those whom the Spirit had filled [Col. 1840A] to be drunk with new wine (Acts II). For they were inebriated, but by the abundance of God’s house. The Son is indeed the house of the Father, and the Father the house of the Son. “Do you not know,” he says, “that the Father is in me and I in the Father?” (John XIV). The abundance and fullness of both is the Holy Spirit; and the torrent of their delights, from which these men had drunk and been inebriated, is in the Father and Son the unfailing fountain of abundance, for the disciples a torrent of delights, and from them a torrent overflowing into the glory of the nations.

The Spirit, who by proper nature is neither wine nor water, is called both by likeness: wine, because he inebriates through the fervor of charity; water, because he refreshes from the heat of desire. Desiring this water, the Prophet says: “Relax me, that I may be refreshed, before I depart” (Ps. XXXIX). He invited people to it who stood and cried: “If anyone thirsts, [Col. 1840B] let him come to me and drink, and rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John VII). “This,” says the Evangelist, “he spoke concerning the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.” Behold: they do not drink this wine, or this water, except those who believe in him, just as none eat that bread except those who endure him for three days. Let us endure and eat; let us believe and drink; let us eat, that we may become friends; let us drink, that, made dearly beloved by charity, we may be inebriated.

For charity is mixed like wine, especially where wisdom sets her table, mixes the wine, and calls little ones to the banquet. Humility alone is invited to wisdom’s banquet, where truth is bread and charity wine. Charity too is poured out like water where it is granted for washing. This order is fitting: one who is about to approach the table should first wash his hands. “Wash yourselves,” he says; “be clean” (Isa. I). And elsewhere: “If the Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion, in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning” (Isa. IV). Desiring this, the Prophet prays: “Wash me yet more, O Lord, from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (Ps. L). And elsewhere: “I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will encompass your altar, O Lord” (Ps. XXV). [Col. 1840C]

The altar of the Lord is the table from which we eat and drink the flesh of Christ, which is truly food, and his blood, which is truly drink. Baptism washes; the altar feeds. But without charity, which is the fruit, neither profits. Charity, therefore, accomplishes everything; without it, whatever is done has no value. Charity, then, is the water that washes and the wine that inebriates. It washes from vices; it inebriates with virtues. It washes those defiled by love of this world; it inebriates those cleansed with love of God. It washes those dirtied by self-love; it inebriates those purified with love of their neighbor. Charity, moreover, is Spirit, because the Spirit is charity. Thus truth feeds, charity gives drink, and power strengthens. Truth is the Son, charity the Spirit, the Father power. Through truth and charity, which have been sent to us for our sake, we shall attain power when we attain the Father.

The Father will bestow complete satisfaction in every respect, as it is written: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. XVII). That wondrous satisfaction from the countenance of the Father will confer perfect strength and remove every suffering of hunger and thirst, [Col. 1841A] as it is written: “They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more” (Rev. VII). That eternal banquet will give every delight without weariness, and will desire without suffering. Then there we shall eat and drink, as the Son—who does not deceive—here promises: with him at his own table in the kingdom of his Father, at that sublime altar, in the presence of the divine majesty; radiant with truth, fervent with charity, strong in power.

Meanwhile, by participation in this lower altar, let us taste with Christ what he himself tasted for us. Sitting at the table of the rich man, who became poor for us, let us prepare like things, so that by his poverty we may be enriched and may enjoy with him the riches of him whose poverty we have not refused. Here, eating and drinking the wheat of the elect and the wine that makes virgins flourish, let us invite him himself to us, so that, as it is written, he may enter in to us and dine with us. But because we are lukewarm and either readily forget such a guest or neglect to invite him, behold, he stands at the door and knocks; and if anyone opens to him, he enters and dines with that person. Let us open to him, beloved, and willingly and devoutly refresh his abundance from our poverty, so that one day we may be filled with the good things of his house, through him who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen. [Col. 1841B]

## SERMON XLV. ON THE SAME FEAST, III

“The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. V).

It was too little, beloved, that the Son of God should be given to us, as it is written: “A little child is born to us; a son is given to us” (Isa. IX), unless the Holy Spirit too were given to us. And will the Father himself someday be given to us, so that we, who are nothing, may receive the whole; and we, who have lost the whole of humanity, may be endowed with the whole divinity? Who has heard such things? We were blind; in darkness a light was born to illuminate us. And this is Christ’s birth for us, from us, in us: what he received for us, he also bestowed upon us. This too is Christ’s baptism for us, as though another birth by which we might be born in him who was born in us. And as he is in us, so we too are in him: he, by the Holy Spirit, the Son of Man from the Virgin Mary; we, by that same Spirit, sons of God from the virgin Church. [Col. 1841C]

We were evil slaves under sin; he served well for us, obeying the Father in righteousness and by his obedience discharging the debt of our service. This is Christ’s life for us. We were children of death because of sin, for “the wages of sin is death”; dying for us, he expiated the guilt of our offense. This is Christ’s death for us. Behold, beloved, all things for you, whose birth was unclean, life perverse, and death perilous, have now through Christ’s grace been changed for the better, as the title of the Psalm has it: “For those who shall be changed” (Ps. XLIV). For birth is now holy, as it is written: “That holy thing which shall be born from you” (Luke I); life is righteous: “My righteous one,” he says, “lives by faith” (Heb. X); death is victory: “But thanks be to God, who gave us [Col. 1842A] victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Cor. XV).

What then, I ask, if so great a bestowal of graces was made upon us in the preceding solemnities, was there need for the gift of today’s celebration? What was lacking to those perfectly reconciled, which needed to be added? He who gave us the Son—“How shall he not with him also give us all things?” (Rom. VIII). Are not Paul, Cephas, and Apollo—all things—ours, if we are Christ’s? Apart from the fact that this visible world with all its elements, and the elements themselves with all their fullness and adornment, serve us, are not all angels ministering spirits, sent to serve for the sake of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation? (Heb. I.) This is too little. God, the Son of God, himself man, the Son of Man, [Col. 1842B] did not come to be served by us, but to serve us and to lay down his beloved soul, which he gave as a redemption for many (Matt. XX). Who ever saw anything like it? Our Lord is everywhere our minister. For us he is born, for us he lives, for us he dies, for us he rises again, for us he ascends, as it is written: “If it were not so, I would have told you: I go to prepare a place for you” (John XIV). For those from whom he takes away a place in the world, he prepares a place in heaven; for us he will come again from heaven: “I will come again,” he says, “to you, and receive you to myself” (ibid.). Truly, he who made us does all things for us: why then do we not do all things for him?

But behold again: what need was there for this solemnity? What more will the other Paraclete do? We wronged God; but, as the common saying goes, we have set matters right with him; we have settled the chief complaint and, as they say, have given a pledge for the offense. We took a man from him and restored to him a better man; we seized a slave and rendered the Son. What more? We entered into the case, heard the complaint, were convicted, and made restitution for everything according to judgment. Might not these things suffice? Certainly: but for redemption, not for grace; for justice, not for friendship. Behold the man who is just as regards the past: what will he do about the future, he who falls seven times a day? Whose inclinations have been bent toward evil from youth—who will preserve him in good? Or, if he falls, who will raise him? “Woe to him who is alone: if he falls, there is none to lift him up.” I dare say it: without the Spirit, Christ is alone. For one who has Christ alone, without the Spirit, [Col. 1842D] is alone. For not without reason is the Spirit sent after Christ: “It is expedient for you,” he says, “that I go away; otherwise the Paraclete will not come” (John XVI).

Let us speak simply, especially for simple and unlearned brethren who do not understand language above the level of the street. A powerful man brings a case against his slave. He convicts him of damage done to himself; he holds the convicted man, rebukes him, presses him hard, until he pays the last farthing and gives judicial punishment for the injury. What then? He is dismissed; he is told: “Go, and sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John V). You are free; but if you fall into my hands, you will not escape in this way: “For it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the Lord” (Heb. X). But how can a slave protect himself from the occasions provided by his master? [Col. 1843A] How can he endure if his master wishes to watch him in everything, grant nothing, and charge everything against him? Wretched is the slave to whom his master charges every sin. Therefore the wise slave, after he has restored everything to his master, thereafter seeks his favor, and henceforth his love and a good peace for the future, lest he be willing to seek occasions against him or readily admit an accuser; and after all this, he does not omit the kiss, as the seal, so to speak, of charity and peace.

This, beloved, is the grace of the present day. We were convicted of robbery, and Christ paid for us what we could not pay. We were made free, but not yet friends; we escaped from the past, but were not secure for the future. And who will again be able to stand against his justice if his charity remits nothing? Who will be able to conceal anything from him if charity does not cover it? Considering all this, which we have treated at such length, the prophet David states it briefly: “Before the face of his cold,” he says—that is, before the inflexibility of his justice, which observes and charges everything—who can endure? “He will send forth his word,” that is, Christ, “and will melt them,” that is, loosen them. For Christ loosens all things, he who came to destroy the works of the devil. “His spirit will blow” (Ps. CXL), as today, when a sound came from heaven as of a spirit—that is, a mighty wind—arriving (Acts II); and the waters loosened by the Word will flow without hindrance into eternal life. [Col. 1843B]

Thus grace is given through the Holy Spirit after justice; and the slave whom the Son dismissed as free is today made a friend through the Spirit. Today, after the justice due for the injury received, the Lord kisses the slave—or rather, friend kisses friend with the kiss of his mouth. For if the Son is rightly understood as the mouth of the Father, the Spirit is rightly called the kiss of the mouth. The kiss, therefore, is the seal of future affection and charity. For “the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.” Charity covers all things, charges nothing, bears all things, excuses all things, pardons all things. The person justified through Christ falls seven times a day through himself; seven times a day he is raised through the Spirit.

Therefore today God has given us, through Christ interceding for us, his charity and love, [Col. 1843C] so that, just as through Christ, in whom God himself was, God reconciled the world to himself, not reckoning its former offenses against it (II Cor. V), so also through the Spirit, in whom he too was, he bound to himself in covenant that which had been reconciled, not reckoning its future offenses against it. Hence it is written: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. XXXI). Through Christ he pardons all things; through the Spirit he imputes nothing. And perhaps he imputes nothing not to all those to whom he pardons everything. Christ, therefore, is in some sense mediator toward justice, the Spirit toward friendship; Christ toward truth, the Spirit toward charity; Christ toward remission, the Spirit toward preservation; Christ toward pardon, the Spirit toward perseverance; Christ toward absolution, the Spirit toward binding together. Yet Christ and [Col. 1843D] the Spirit work all things undividedly. For Father, Son, and Holy Spirit work all things together and alike: they are one without confusion and three without division.

The Son, however, has in some sense his own embassy from the Father, by whom alone he is sent; and the Spirit likewise has, as it were, his own from both. Thus the Son, as it were, appeases the angry Father and dissolves enmities; the Spirit, as it were, tempers the just one, in some manner softens him, and binds him to friendship. Between the iniquity of the defendant and the equity of the Judge, the Son, reconciler and advocate, intercedes, that weakness may be reconciled and majesty appeased; the Spirit, the soothing one and Paraclete, intervenes.

For just as this air is a kind of refreshment and, as it were, a bath for living things—by its own nature’s sweetness and grace tempering for them, from itself and beneath itself, the intolerable heat [Col. 1844A] of the higher element—so also the Holy Spirit is borne over spiritual waters, as it were midway between their numbness and the rigor of supreme equity, protecting, cherishing, and making them fruitful by his charity and grace, lest they be utterly consumed and the earth languish in dryness.

Considering this, the Prophet says: “My soul is like land without water to you” (Ps. CLXII)—to you, that is, to heaven and consuming fire. “Quickly hear me, O Lord,” by sending your Spirit, “for my spirit has failed” (ibid.). And because the Spirit is likened to air, charity is said to be poured forth through the Spirit. Earth, indeed, properly lies below; fire rises upward; water flows; air spreads abroad, as is readily discerned also in odors. They also say that the heaven is movable, and that it, called the *aplanos* (“unwandering” or “fixed”), is carried with such speed from east through west to east, that by its intolerable impetus it would most swiftly overturn all lower things, unless by the Creator’s providence it were slowed by the opposing course of the seven stars called planets—that is, from west through east to west—so that, as air protects lower things from heat, so the planets may be their safeguard and protection against the impetus of the firmament. [Col. 1844B]

All this readily accords with the present assertion; and here the invisible things of God may be perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made. For the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, by which he provides for us and grants consolation, by a kind of opposing movement tempers that equity of divine swiftness which by its fixed motion surveys and examines all things at once. It delays judgment, lest God immediately enter into judgment with his servants, who cannot answer him one thing in a thousand; in whose sight no living being shall be justified; before whom even the heavens are not clean; and who finds perversity in his angels. For the goodness of God alone, which is borne over us sevenfold, tempers his severity toward us, bends his majesty down, and delays vengeance. And while he who is as good as he is great, as merciful as he is strong, in some manner sets himself against himself, the sinner finds time for repentance, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?” (Rom. II).

Considering together this goodness and greatness, the Prophet says: “Great is the Lord, and exceedingly worthy of praise in the city of our God” (Ps. XLII). [Col. 1845A] By reason of his goodness God is praiseworthy and lovable; by reason of his greatness and severity, fearful. Whoever considers severity without goodness despairs; whoever considers goodness without severity, on the contrary sins in hope. Therefore, as the Apostle says, consider the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who perish, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness; otherwise you too will be cut off (Rom. XI).

To your exercise, brethren—who ought to gather much from little and draw great matters from what has been touched or sketched in summary—we leave the task of relating the number and order of the planets to the graces of the Spirit, so that, just as one ascends step by step from the moon to Saturn, so you may ascend from the spirit of fear, which has much likeness to the moon itself, naturally weak and cold, ruling the night, governing the humors, and borrowing its light from another, up to the spirit of wisdom, which is found in elders and makes them mature, weighty, and near to heaven. [Col. 1845B] May that same Spirit of understanding be present, lest you stray from truth; and of counsel, lest you be recalled elsewhere by vanity; and of fortitude, lest you be wearied by your own weakness. May he deign to grant this: he who, with the Father and the Son, from the Father and the Son, in the Father and the Son, is one living, true, omnipotent God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLVI. ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST, I

[Col. 1845C] “Among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. XI).

That testimony, beloved, of our Lord and Savior concerning John his Baptist gives us such certainty concerning the excellence of his glory that we do not doubt that he is inferior to no one. Yet he is not, as some suppose, superior to all; according to this attestation of truth, he is indeed second to none in the kingdom of God, but, so far as this authority goes, not first among all. If he has no greater, who would dare deny—though neither should one presume to affirm—that he also has no equal? For some, clinging to the word “has arisen,” understand the saying to mean only that no saint before him was greater, not that none to come would be greater. We consider this interpretation as novel as it is frivolous. [Col. 1845D] No saint has so expounded it, nor has the Church of Christ heard it until now.

Yet they fortify themselves with blessed Ambrose, who sang in his praise in a hymn: “Greater than the prophets, and less than the angels.” Would that he had added: “than the angels alone.” Yet he did not say “less than the apostles,” but “less than the angels.” “But,” they say, “he is not greater than the apostles, but simply greater than the prophets and simply less than the angels.” The example, therefore, accomplishes nothing, since it settles the dispute by the letter. He is thus extolled with the greatest praise, since among those born of women he is set beneath no one. For while one lives in this corruptible state, which weighs down the soul already lightened by heavenly desire and, as it were, eager to fly away; while an earthly dwelling depresses the understanding from the one thing necessary to the many things that trouble and distract—distract precisely because they trouble—even the greatest of mortals is less than the least of angels. Hence it is said of John himself: “He who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.”

But when the bright and free soul escapes from the bodily mass and the dark prison of flesh to the upper airs, we do not deny that many saints fly beyond many thousands of angels. [Col. 1846A] Blessed Ambrose, however, whom they set against us, explains in our favor the saying, “He who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he,” thus: “He who is least, namely in his own eyes—that is, humbler—in the kingdom of heaven, that is, the present Church, is greater than John in the same sense.” If John is humblest of all, then surely he is also loftiest of all. For everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted; and as much as he humbles himself, so much shall he exalt himself. Therefore, least of all, he is greatest of all; and the greater anyone is among the least, the less he is than the greatest.

Moreover, this nativity is celebrated more than the birthdays of other saints because it is recognized as sacramental and figurative. For as, by preaching, baptism, manner of life, manner of death, and the miracle of his birth, the voice announced beforehand the Word, the forerunner ran before the Lord, the prophet proclaimed him who was to come, the more-than-prophet pointed out him who was present, and the angel identified him whom he had proclaimed in good news—not only to the living in the world, but also to the dead in hell.

[Col. 1846C] Born contrary to nature, therefore, he prefigured him who was to be born above nature. This one was born contrary to nature’s usual course; that one beyond nature’s due; this one wonderfully, that one uniquely. Before this there had been a rare example; of that there had been none at all. Elizabeth’s barrenness prefigured Mary’s virginity: here, barrenness made pregnant; there, virginity made fruitful. The old woman brought forth one because of the one whom the virgin bore. John’s father was old beyond his age; Christ’s Father was absent at every age. For as the silence of Melchizedek’s genealogy in Scripture prefigures the ineffability of Christ’s generation (Gen. XIV; Heb. V), so Zechariah’s old age marks the absence of paternal generation in Christ. Here, then, the old man begot; there, no one did. Here, one who by nature could not beget begot by the gift of grace; there, where the giver of grace, the exactor of nature, alone accomplished the whole, no one begot either by nature or by grace.

It was fitting, indeed, that in the figure less should everywhere be found, and in the truth more everywhere. For morning and evening shadows are longer than their bodies, but at noon shorter. Morning is prophecy; evening, memory; noon, Christ’s presence. Therefore, as Christ increased, John had to decrease; Christ had to be exalted by death and John diminished by the head; Christ to be born as the day increased, John as it decreased. [Col. 1846D]

Further, the marriage of Zechariah and Elizabeth—from which no one is generated by nature but so great a one by grace—which gives birth to John and promises Christ, mystically signifies another and more secret marriage in human beings. For just as outwardly there is the familiar and customary marriage between man and woman, between flesh and flesh, which generates nothing beyond flesh, so inwardly in man and woman there is another between flesh and spirit, generating in flesh through spirit. Still more inwardly, a third is found wholly in the spirit, within the rational soul itself of man and woman: this is called free choice. There reason is Zechariah and will Elizabeth. For what is free choice other than a will free through reason? From reason comes “choice,” from will “free.”

Reason, therefore, ought not only, like a husband, to govern the affection of the heart and every motion of body and soul, but also, as the Lord’s priest, to enter into the holy of holies and contemplate with unveiled face what is not lawful for the people; and while the crowds of senses and imaginations wait outside, it ought to be instructed within by revelation. [Col. 1847A] But the will of the mind, or the affection of the heart, ought to obey reason and, like a wife, be subject to her husband; without his consent it ought to dare nothing among its subjects and presume nothing among strangers; it ought to be made fruitful only by its husband and utterly abhor adulterous embraces. Your inner house is indeed well ordered if affection presumes nothing without consulting reason.

Affection gives the work its name, so that according to it a work is called good or wicked; reason rightly governs affection, as a husband his wife, so that according to it a work is called good or wicked; reason rightly governs affection, as a husband his wife, so that according to reason affection is called bright or dark, legitimate or illegitimate. For those who are wise in doing evil have a disordered conscience, in which [Col. 1847B] reason serves and affection rules; will goes before, reason follows; and the heart’s desire uses reason against reason. Not so this Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth. For both were righteous and advanced in years (Luke I), but without offspring, without fruit. They were the more without offspring because advanced in years; the more barren because old. For newness—whether new or renewed—bears fruit. New newness in the Virgin bears Christ; renewed newness in the barren woman bears John. Yet they were righteous because they were ordered and well composed; but they could not be fruitful by themselves, because from the oldness of old Adam they were still old.

Among the philosophers and sages of this age, the house of the inner human being could once be composed and ordered: the household of domestic motions might neither make a confused clamor, nor the incursion of strangers defile it, nor an impudent wife assail or deceptively entice her husband. But it could not be fruitful unto eternity or bring forth the herald of salvation. For free choice, without which no one is saved, is very powerful in very many respects; but without God’s grace it has no power at all toward salvation. “The Lord will give grace and glory,” because Christ follows John. Grace is given to free choice because it alone is saved; but it is given for this reason: because without grace it is not saved. Free choice receives grace; grace precedes salvation. Free choice receives grace neither when it wishes nor of the kind it wishes; nor does Zechariah generate offspring when he wishes or such as he wishes. [Col. 1847C] Zechariah and Elizabeth, though they strive greatly, beget nothing by themselves, because reason and will in human beings make no progress by any effort, however great, without grace.

Therefore God visits by grace those whom he wills, when he wills, and as he wills; that is, he freely gives grace, which first promises salvation by the hope of holy conduct and afterwards bestows it in the reality of blessed vision. Thus John too was bestowed on those whom God willed, when he willed, and as he willed; and by being born and living he ran before and promised Jesus, and at last pointed him out with his finger. John is begotten of Zechariah and Elizabeth not through their nature, but through God’s operation; likewise good consent is produced from freedom of choice only by God’s generosity, not by its own efficacy.

Elizabeth is at home, or perhaps waiting outside with the people, while Zechariah, having entered the holy of holies, sees the angel (ibid.). Sarah too waits at home while Abraham meets the angels in the heat of the day (Gen. XVIII). The whole people likewise wait below while Moses alone ascends the mountain to the Lord (Exod. XIX and XXIV). [Col. 1848A] But who is so fit for these things? Everywhere men, everywhere priests, everywhere prelates, leaving wives and crowds behind, either enter, meet, or ascend alone toward heavenly and exalted things. Yet in the holy of holies only one angel is seen, and not without great fear; in the heat of day, however, in freedom of air and in the open field, three are met with confidence and joy. On the mountain, indeed, Moses converses with God as a man with his neighbor. I pass over the fact that Jesus himself, even leaving the disciples, ascends the mountain alone to speak with the Father (Matt. XIV).

But if we wished to pursue these matters, neither we would suffice for the discourse nor, as you know, would the hour suffice for the speaker. Therefore, so far as concerns the present solemnity, let us render a few remarks concerning Zechariah. For here we have laid certain foundations, as it were, for meditation, and have given the wise person an occasion to become wiser.

Accordingly, Zechariah sees the angel and is afraid; he hears the promise and distrusts it; therefore he is punished with silence until the time when the promise is fulfilled. For when human reason hears, concerning heavenly mysteries and divine promises, things which it does not comprehend [Col. 1848D], it marvels and hesitates, and investigates how they can be. But because “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him,” even if it believes, it remains mute until the vision; and then, when what we shall be has appeared—for we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be [1 John 3]—it will exult with inexpressible exultation, saying: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and wrought redemption for his people” (Luke 1).

Meanwhile, reason by faith begets what it cannot utter; the will by charity conceives what the eye does not yet see; hope, through long-suffering, carries in the womb of the mind the firstfruits of the Spirit, which it longs to behold. For “the fruit of the Spirit is charity” (Gal. 5). Elizabeth groans while carrying in her womb [Col. 1849A], and labours until the revelation of the glory of the children of God. A woman indeed has sorrow when she gives birth; but when she has borne the child, she rejoices with joy (John 16), and at the birth of such a child many will rejoice. All things belonging to the inward and outward person will rejoice together; they will share in glory and be glorified together.

Meanwhile Zechariah knows in part and prophesies in part; but when that which is perfect has come, then he will know even as he is known. The bond of his tongue will be loosed, and his mouth will be filled with jubilation, so that he may bless God for the grace which now works secretly in nature, but which then will be manifest and known. For all, from least to greatest, will know the grace and truth of God on that day, full of grace and truth, exultation and praise. May God’s grace itself deign to accomplish this in us [Col. 1849B], so that we may rejoice in its manifestation through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLVII. ON THE SAME FEAST, II

“He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the bridegroom’s friend stands and hears, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3).

The abstinence, labours, works of mercy, miraculous powers, or such like outward forms of holiness of other saints, beloved, are validated by their own testimony. But in the case of some, the authority of the Lord and Saviour is proclaimed; as is said of the blessed apostle Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you [Col. 1849C] that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16). Likewise of his fellow-apostle Paul: “This man is a vessel of election for me, to bear my name before nations, kings, and the children of Israel” (Acts 9).

But upon blessed John there are heaped both many oracles of the prophets and the testimonies of Truth itself. For the blessed prophet Isaiah says of him: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord,” and so forth (Isa. 40). The blessed evangelist Mark echoes this at the beginning of his Gospel. Jeremiah likewise says: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the belly, I sanctified you and appointed you a prophet among the nations” (Jer. 1). Nor did the blessed evangelist Luke omit this. But Truth itself, which could neither deceive nor be deceived, said of him: “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” (Matt. 11 [the source misprints “II”]). And elsewhere: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. For this is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face,’” and so forth (ibid.). Elsewhere again: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5). Hence David also says: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Ps. 131). Thus the miracle of blessed John’s birth, the singularity of his life, the character of his death, the prophetic oracles, as we have said, and the testimonies of Truth itself have commended him to Christ’s Church.

As I reflect with you, then, and compare in my heart these and similar things—the lofty testimonies concerning blessed John [Col. 1850A], and his own humble answers concerning himself—I clearly conclude that strength is made perfect in weakness, and that the greater anyone is called by Truth, the lesser he esteems himself. “The greater you are,” says Wisdom, “humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3); and certainly, the more you humble yourself, the greater you will be in all things. O good humility! The Lord indeed is exalted, yet he regards the lowly. O humility beloved by God! “He has regarded,” she says, “the lowliness of his handmaid” (Luke 1). The Holy Spirit likewise rests only upon one who is humble, gentle, and trembling at God’s words.

Therefore this blessed John is blessed, and the more blessed because more humble; and the more humble because more blessed. When he was held in such esteem by people, because of the word of his teaching and the severity of his life, that he was thought to be Christ, he chose, as blessed Gregory says, to stand firmly in himself through humility rather than be emptily carried above himself by the vanity of an empty reputation. For he was not like “the dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth.” Although the wind of vain people’s praise might carry him up even to heaven, nevertheless, humble and weighty, he clung to the earth, mindful of that sentence: “You are earth, and unto earth you shall go” (Gen. 3).

Where are those who are puffed up over nothing and swell greatly over a little, the more vain because the more empty? What do you have, in comparison with John, that makes you boast more than John? Or if you have something, what do you have that you have not received? And why, by swelling with empty glory over what you have received, have you emptied yourself? For one who is puffed up is not truly full, but vainly swollen. Let us therefore hear John, speaking the humbler things the greater he is: “I am not the Christ; I am not Elijah; I am not the prophet. I am a herald; I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord.’ One stronger than I comes after me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to stoop down and untie.”

And when he was much pressed by those who insisted, exulting in the spirit of truth and purity of heart, he said what we have set above:

“He who has the bride is the bridegroom.” As though he said: “I have neither the bride, nor ought I to be called the bridegroom. But the bridegroom’s friend stands and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice.” For this, if you wish to know, is what I am and what I do; and therefore I am, because I do it, and therefore I do it, because I am. The bridegroom, as you know, is Christ; Christ’s bride is the Church. The bridegroom is the Word of God; the bride [Col. 1850D] is the faithful soul.

Therefore, just as the bride has young women and female friends, so also the bridegroom has groomsmen and friends. Speaking of these to the bride, he says: “Let us hear your voice; the friends are listening” (Song 8). Therefore the friend stands, listens, and hears the voice not only of the bridegroom but also of the bride. For one cannot despise the bride if he wishes to hear the bridegroom; he will either hear both or despise both. No one can be a friend of one without being a friend of the other. “What God has joined together, let no one separate” (Matt. 19). “He who hears you,” he says, “hears me; and he who despises you despises me. But he who hears me hears him who sent me” (Luke 10).

See through Christ how we are joined to God: the head of the woman is the man, [Col. 1851A] the head of the man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God. Therefore, if we desire to be friends of the bridegroom, let us hear the bride of God through him and obey those through whom the bride speaks and commands—that is, our prelates and superiors. For we who are subject to them are simply as a woman; while the order of prelates is like our husband, who ought to govern, instruct, feed, make us fruitful, and dispose us in all things and for all things. He is also our head, and Christ is his head, and God is Christ’s head. Therefore, through our superiors we are subject and adhere to Christ and God.

The bridegroom’s friend therefore stands and hears; but the bridegroom sits and teaches. It belongs to teachers to speak and command, while it is fitting for disciples to hear and obey—and to do so cheerfully, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9) [Col. 1851B], and with joy, as this friend of the bridegroom hears and rejoices; and this because of the bridegroom’s voice.

Many rejoice at many things which they hear, but not because of the bridegroom’s voice. Many willingly obey many commands, yet not because of the bridegroom’s voice. For when they hear what they want, they rejoice on their own account, and in this they have already received their reward. And when they are commanded what they desired, they obey willingly, but according to their own desires; and they have nothing to await from the bridegroom. For what is not done for his sake will not be rewarded by him.

Thus every ecclesiastical institution is the bride’s voice; whoever judges or despises it cannot be the bride’s friend. The bride’s voice is the speech and commands of superiors. Whoever despises or neglects these breaks forth into hostility; or, if he carries them out lukewarmly, slowly, with resentment in heart and murmuring of mouth, he has not yet attained friendship, for he does not rejoice because of the bride’s voice.

The bridegroom is the Word of God; his voice is every event. For whatever occurs in time was together, from eternity, in God’s Word. But the book in which angels see and read is closed to us; we read and learn only in the outward realm what is contained in the inward. For what we see happening outwardly, we know to have been ordained inwardly. All things occur as he does or permits them to occur; without his ordering nothing happens. Therefore the outward outcome of a thing is the voice of the Word. One does not murmur at this voice when one loves what has been ordained within. But all things that happen are ordered by the Good [Col. 1851D], occur well in their own manner, and for that reason ought to be loved by the good.

The whole sum of religion and obedience, then, is to love what God loves because God loves it; to hate what God hates because God hates it; to will what God wills because God wills it; and not to will what God does not will. When we learn all these things in outward events, we hear God’s will as though through God’s voice. And if we wish to be friends of the bridegroom, even though we grieve in certain matters for another reason, nevertheless let us rejoice because of the voice which speaks to us the bridegroom’s will.

“One of the bridegroom’s friends,” says, even concerning his own temporal loss, “The word of the Lord is good. He is the Lord; let him do what is good in his own eyes.” Certainly, even when evil befalls evil servants, the word of the good Lord is good. [Col. 1852A] If he destroys the evil man evilly, he is just, and everything just is good; whoever does not love justice is wicked, and this very thing also is good. If he mercifully spares the wicked, he is merciful, and everything merciful is good; whoever does not love mercy is impious, and this very thing also is merciful. If he rewards the good well, he is just; if he tests and chastises them, he is kind. Whoever does not love both is malicious, and this very thing is justly kind and kindly just.

These are all the ways of the Lord—namely mercy and truth—by which he walks among the children of men: killing and making alive, striking and healing, raising up and bringing down, giving and taking away, terrifying and comforting. Nothing happens by chance, or without his knowing, willing, or caring for it. Rather, he governs all things well in time, just as before time he ordered all things well. And in all things, because of his ordering and will, one rejoices with joy who disagrees with him in nothing. That alone is true friendship: with a friend, for the friend’s sake, to will the same thing and not to will the same thing.

The bridegroom’s friend therefore stands beside the bridegroom and listens, ready to obey in all things; and he rejoices with joy in all things because of the bridegroom’s voice, although for another reason he is saddened in many matters. For this also belongs to the bridegroom’s voice: the bridegroom himself sometimes is angry, grieved, weeps, and suffers pain. Yet in all these things one rejoices because of him whose Word he is, who runs with joy the contest set before him.

Where are those who murmur against the course of events and blaspheme God, because they do not love his ordering? Surely, if it is from God, it is good; and if it is good, why do you murmur? “I cannot,” someone says, “love my own loss or the loss of my friend.” But neither ought you to hate God’s justice or discipline. Certainly God does not delight in anyone’s loss. For charity “does not rejoice in iniquity,” but loves its own truth and punishes your iniquity. Charity, however, rejoices together with truth. If you do not rejoice with it, you are without charity, and therefore without God, and with the devil, who hates the justice that condemns his own wickedness. This, indeed, is his everlasting sin, which deserves everlasting punishment.

Therefore, beloved, in the good things which God does, let us love the whole work itself, because it is good from the Good [Col. 1852D], is done well, and tends to good. But in the evil things which the Good permits, also well and for good, let us love not the wickedness which God hates, but the reason why God permits it. For permission belongs to the Creator; wickedness to the creature.

This, dearest friends, is good peace and tranquillity of heart: to stand in equanimity and hear with reverence all things that occur under heaven; in all things to bless him who orders all things; not to wish changed what is done well and accords with the beauty of the universe—while preserving in all things charity, which, as has been said, does not rejoice in iniquity but rejoices together with truth. May he who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages deign to work this in us. Amen.

## SERMON XLVIII. ON THE SAME FEAST, III

[Col. 1853A]

“I have prepared a lamp for my Christ,” and so forth (Ps. 131).

Long ago, beloved, we perceived that you had become more lukewarm than usual, and almost slothful in hearing; hence we too, I confess, have become more lukewarm and weaker in speaking. For the disciple’s attention elicits the teacher’s diligence; and the more devoutly anyone is heard, the more earnestly he speaks.

But you complain that you do not know why we have changed our style. You say that we who used subtly either to devise entirely new things or elegantly renew old ones now tread only common ground and repeat worn-out commonplace discourse. “How,” some of you ask, “has this man sunk so low? How has the gold of his intelligence been darkened [Col. 1853B], and the finest colour of his eloquence changed? He who used wonderfully to say wonderful things, uniquely to devise unheard-of things, luminously to define obscure things, distinctly to divide things entangled, and openly to explain by examples what he had divided—how does he now confuse everything, mix everything together, touch upon everything everywhere, and bring nothing to its expected conclusion? How has his wine been mixed with water, and his silver turned to dross? How is it that he now either is silent or speaks?”

Behold, we shall be silent—but to you; we shall speak—but not to you. You are all inquisitive hearers; and therefore we have changed our manner of speaking because you have set no limit to your curiosity. You seek only novelties; but from where are we continually to mint new ones? You reject with scorn the ancient things, those which may be found in the Scriptures. And why do we copy books? If we say something spoken before us or which can be found written, it stirs nausea or bile in you, not because it is not true, good, and fitting, but because it is not altogether new. If we say what Augustine said, what Ambrose said, or what is read somewhere, you immediately run to the books: what has been said is shown, one to another, to be written elsewhere, and for this one reason alone it is despised by both.

I confess, therefore, that I am in part to blame for this insolence in you. We have trained you in such things and accustomed you to such things that you could scarcely listen to anyone other than us, nor would you now care to hear us in others.

Why then were we formerly inquisitive, pursuing such matters, or why are we now frivolous, abandoning what is customary? The reason for both is ready at hand. There once arose certain men, whose names I suppress, men of notable talent and remarkable learning. Not perverting Holy Scripture as heretics do, but having its legitimate sense less readily at hand, they adapted it most elegantly to their own pursuits; and from authoritative writings, not without the admiration of many and great edification of morals, they discoursed most pleasantly—if we may speak without offending anyone—with trifles. They drew forth nothing against faith and truth, but everything, as you know, to the benefit and honourableness of life and conduct, with a marvellous novelty which you complain that we have abandoned. And—strange to say—they became exceedingly clever through poverty of sense [Col. 1854A].

We followed them because the world followed them; the whole world went after them, and in the judgment of people never had men spoken in such a way. Whoever did not speak thus was mocked, despised, abandoned. Therefore, lest we should be thought to speak otherwise either from envious detraction or from poverty of talent, we applied ourselves; and, as you know, in such matters we were not inferior to all. “For I do not have a heart of horn,” says the poet.

But now we say what we had conceived from the beginning, though, as we said, we have suppressed it until now in order not to be marked as envious or ignorant, adapting ourselves to the times. Perilous times will press in, and subverters of truth will enter, adapting the sayings of Scripture to their own meanings; and our own unrestrained freedom may become for them a pernicious precedent. Why should they not, for the sake of their novelty, abandon the ancient expositions of the Fathers, if the Church had been accustomed to this before them? How will Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, or Gregory be objected to them: “So and so expounded it in this way”? Will they not say: “If this was permitted to others, why will it not be permitted to us? Did we not hear it from these men just as those others will say it?” “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty”; “we are not bound to swear allegiance to the words of a master.”

At almost the same time there arose a new monstrosity of a certain new soldiery, of which, as one man wittily said, “It is an order of the fifth Gospel”: it compels unbelievers to faith with lances and clubs; freely plunders those who do not bear Christ’s name and piously massacres them; and, if any of its members fall while ravaging such people, calls them Christ’s martyrs. Do not these men too nurture for that future son of perdition an authorization of cruelty against Christians? How will Christ’s gentleness, patience, and manner of preaching be set before him? Why should he not willingly do what he finds has been done with licence? How will he fail to say: “Do to them such things as the Church did”?

What then? Do we condemn these men together with the others? We condemn neither group; but we do not praise them in this respect—not because perhaps what they do is altogether evil, but because it can become an occasion for evil. For, lamentably, almost all evils have taken root from good things; virtues nourish vices, and, worn out by the growth of their own foster-children, are swallowed up by them.

[Col. 1854D] Therefore, beloved, very great caution and circumspection are necessary. For all things, whether good or evil, which are to come have before them certain generative causes, as it were, explaining why they come; certain preparers and, as it were, messengers, showing how they arise; and certain signs of their coming, showing when they should occur: “You have prepared their food, because such is its preparation” (Ps. 64). And this text which we have set before you: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Ps. 131).

For nothing is without purpose, nothing confused, nothing sudden; though many things are hidden from mortals and others manifest. Thus the apostles, instructed about the cause and manner of the second coming but concerned about its signs, say: “Tell us when these things will happen, and what will be the sign of your coming” (Matt. 24).

The cause of Christ’s coming in the flesh [Col. 1855A] is human misery; its preparation, Mary’s virginity within marriage; its sign, a star from heaven and an outflow of oil from the earth. The cause of Christ’s coming to baptism is humanity’s union with God; its preparation is John’s baptism. For a lamp was prepared for the coming light, so that many, brought up in darkness, might become accustomed from a small light to behold the great one.

Therefore, in the prophecy concerning John, it is said in the voice of the Father: “There I will bring forth the horn of David” (Ps. 131), that is, I will bring forth the glory of that people whose king David was, as far as the lamp which I have prepared for my Christ. For as Christ himself says: “The Law and the Prophets,” in which lay the glory of that people, “were until John” (Matt. 11). He himself also calls John “a burning and shining lamp”; “upon him,” that is, Christ, for whom the lamp is prepared, “my sanctification shall flourish” (Ps. 131). For he alone is the flower and fruit of holiness, the Holy of Holies; holy and himself sanctifying; born holy, begetting saints.

“His enemies,” that is, the enemies of the lamp, “I shall clothe with shame” (Ps. 131), as though by excessive light, because they neglected to become accustomed to the lamp, so that they might bear the light. For there are two things which confound the eye in seeing: no light and a sudden great light.

But let us hear from the Gospel itself how the Father confounded the enemies of John, Christ, and the Father through Christ. When the Pharisees asked Jesus about his authority, wondering, envying, and indignant, he answered: “And I will ask you one question; if you answer me, I also will tell you by what authority [Col. 1855C] I do these things” (Mark 11). If you receive the lamp, I will show you the light. “Was John’s baptism from heaven or from men?”

And they were confounded—those whom God rejected because they rejected his lamp. Since they were unwilling to confess the truth and did not dare rashly to lie about the lamp, they rightly lied to their own harm, and “iniquity lies to itself.” For they say: “We do not know.” If they had said what was true, “From heaven,” it would have been objected to them why they had not believed him who bore witness concerning the light. But if they had said, “From men,” they would have fallen into the hands of the crowd, who held him, as was true, to be a prophet.

We have spoken little to you today concerning so great a solemnity—for we spent the hour in the preceding apology. At the end, we desire that your charity may be both entreated and admonished: as the prophet says, “Ask for the ancient paths, which is the good way,” worn by the feet of the saints, “and walk in it.” For curiosity is the mother of all vanity (Jer. 6). All truth is solid—not merely ancient, but eternal.

Moreover, our discourse is addressed to the simple, especially on these feast-days, when a crowd of lay people gathers from every direction. Perhaps there will not be lacking a more familiar conference, when we can investigate something more lofty and subtle with you. But these festal sermons are simple for the simple, poured forth in plain speech for those who have not yet taken up wings, but follow on foot the walking Jesus, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit [Col. 1856A], be glory and dominion through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLIX. ON THE FEAST-DAY OF THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

“These are men of mercy, whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten,” and so forth (Ecclus. 44).

Beloved, the feast-day of the apostles Peter and Paul is celebrated; and quite fittingly the death of such persons is called a birthday, since it gives birth to life. Thus the birth by which we are born to death ought more suitably to be called a death than a birthday. For we begin to die when we are born, and to live when we die. Therefore, just as this life is called mortal, so that death ought to be called life-giving. As long as we live here, we are dying; and when [Col. 1856B] we are done with life, we are at the same time freed from death. Hateful is the life which cannot exist without death; desirable is the death which ends life’s falsehood and begins truth.

A marvellous thing: life brings death, death brings life. Life is the birthday of death; death, of life. Just as a torch kindled by fire consumes the fire by which it has been consumed, so this life, kindled from its beginning by death, when it is finally consumed by that same death, consumes death itself. Or just as a flame of fire once introduced into straw consumes itself in devouring the straw, so death, which is sown and conceived together with life, kills life and at the same time destroys itself. For the present life is a vapour and a smoke appearing for a little while. But the life which comes afterward is life alone, without fellowship with death; hence it is in the future life-giving. This life therefore is mortal; that one life-giving.

Furthermore, with regard to the present state, this life gives birth to death, and death itself puts an end to life. According to this: “The wise seemed, in the eyes of the foolish, to die, but they are in peace” (Wis. 3), where, death having already died here, life alone is lived without conflict with it. “The souls of the righteous,” it says, “are in the hand of God, and the torment of wickedness shall not touch them” (ibid.)—that is, Satan’s temptation. Here indeed, while there is conflict with death, it touches everyone, though it does not break the saints. There, however, just as it will not break them, so neither will it touch them; for they have been removed from it by more than a stone’s throw. Therefore the artillery of wickedness will not hurl even a stone as far as them.

See to what the saints arrive from this mortal life, through this life-giving [Col. 1856D] death: namely, to life that gives life, in the hand of living Life. But why do they arrive there? Because they are merciful—first to themselves and, according to this rule, to their neighbour: “Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30), and thereby indeed helping your neighbour. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5); but judgment without mercy awaits the unmerciful. For by the measure by which they have measured, it shall be measured back to them.

Men of mercy, therefore, are manly in mercy. There are three kinds of merciful people. The first assist others from their own resources, not so that they themselves suffer hardship and others receive relief, but so that another’s need is supplied from their abundance. Here Truth measures, according to the intention of the mind, how much is given in proportion to one’s means, rather than the absolute amount. These are those who wipe Jesus’ feet with the hair of their heads, acceptable according to what they have, not according to what they do not have, even to a cup of cold water or merely a good will—which alone sufficiently avails if it finds nothing else.

The second distribute all their possessions; thereafter, just as they acquire in common, so they spend in common. They call nothing their own, but all things are common to all according to reason and need; “he who had much did not abound, and he who had little did not lack.” Here too Truth measures rather what they are unwilling to possess than what they could leave behind. For all leave all things behind who are unwilling to possess anything; each leaves behind as much as he does not desire; and one leaves everything entirely to everyone who obstructs no one in anything. These are those who will receive a hundredfold [Col. 1857B] and possess eternal life.

But the third not only expend all things: they are themselves expended in addition, and give themselves over to the danger of prison, confiscation, and death, in order to call others back from danger to their souls. They are lavish beyond measure with themselves and desirous for others’ good. Truth measures these according to that charity than which no one has greater: that one lay down one’s life for one’s friends. Thus these, manly in mercy, are men of mercy and supreme in mercy.

Such are those glorious princes of heaven and ministers of earth, whose most victorious deaths are celebrated today after long fasts in hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, most severe labours and dangers. Of them the following fittingly continues: “Whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten” (Ecclus. 44). Their righteous deeds have not been forgotten because they did not forget mercy; and as mindful as they were of mercy, so far will they not receive forgetfulness of righteousness.

For some people’s iniquities are forgotten, and the Lord remembers only their righteous deeds; while some people’s righteous deeds are forgotten, and he remembers only their iniquities. But he remembers the righteousness of those who have not forgotten mercy, and he remembers the injustice of those who have not remembered mercy. For only the merciful will find God merciful; those whom mercy does not commend, justice will condemn.

“With their seed good things remain” (ibid.). With people here neither good nor evil things remain, but in turn and as if by blind chance they fall upon good and evil alike. In the future, however, good things alone will remain with the good, and evil things alone with the evil. For this reason it is said, “With their seed,” rather than “with them”; as elsewhere: “His soul shall abide in good things” (Ps. 24), and shall no longer be changed back and forth. “And his seed,” newly gathered from the old, “shall inherit the earth”: that is, the immortal body, which will henceforth not perish. “It is sown a natural body, but shall rise a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15): from old seed, new seed; from mortal, immortal; from corruptible, incorruptible. And good things will remain with that which can endure.

“Their descendants are a holy inheritance” (Ecclus. 44). The children of children are the fruits of works. The works will perish; the fruits will remain unmoved and will be possessed as a holy inheritance—that is, as a firm and eternal inheritance. [Col. 1858A] “Say to the righteous,” whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten because they have not abandoned mercy, “that it is well.” And why is it well? “Because he shall eat the fruit of his devices” (Isa. 3). “He shall eat the labours of his hands, and it shall be well with him.” But “woe unto the wicked in evil, for the recompense of his hands shall be done to him” (ibid.). As he plundered, so shall he be plundered. “Woe to you who plunder; shall you not yourself be plundered?” (Isa. 33). And as he struck, so shall he be struck; as he shut his hand against the beggar, so it shall be shut when he begs.

The inheritance of the greedy man—his descendants—will be malign for him. The inheritance of the greedy will become a hyena’s den for him. The inheritance of the greedy man, who cannot die, will be unquenchable fire for him. But for the merciful “lines have fallen in pleasant places; indeed, their inheritance shall be glorious to them.” May merciful and gracious Jesus deign to lead us to it, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON L. ON THE SAME FEAST, II

We do not wish you, dearest friends, to remain wholly ignorant of the rule of your way of life and the authority behind it. For many, curious about another’s life and unconcerned about their own death, weary the simpler people whom they find with empty questions, taking on the serpent’s voice addressed to the first parent. “Why,” they ask, “have you been commanded [Col. 1858C] to labour thus, to abstain thus, to obey people thus, to keep silence before people thus, to gather separately in assemblies, and to reject the common life of humankind?”

O idle or malicious curiosity! “Why,” says the devil to Eve, “has God commanded you not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil?” (Gen. 3). Cunning malice entered through such a quibble into the simple mind of the little woman, pierced through; and because tender simplicity did not know how to give the reason for the divine command, it could not refute the argument of crafty persuasion.

Therefore, beloved, as the blessed apostle Peter says, we wish you to be ready and instructed to render an answer to everyone who asks you for an account of the way of life and obedience which is in you (1 Pet. 3). Long ago, if you have not forgotten, we addressed you on this matter. But because on this feast-day of the apostles a larger number of brethren than usual has gathered from every side, it will not be burdensome for us to repeat what we believe necessary for you.

Thus, our working the earth with our hands is the pattern of our first parent Adam—not Adam sinning in paradise, but Adam repenting outside it. For in the leisure of paradise and abundance of every kind of thing, sin arose and provoked the Lord. Outside paradise, punishment was accepted, which justly penalized the servant. Better, therefore, is punishment in exile than sin in paradise. Therefore, because we are still sinners and sons in the flesh of a sinner, we do not reject in the flesh the sentence upon condemned flesh; and in the sweat of our face we eat our bread.

But lest the whole labour of a human being be in his mouth [Col. 1859A], we labour more diligently with our hands so that we may have something to give to one who suffers need. Why with silence? Because in much speaking sin will not be avoided; because the Apostle has admonished this; because before the Apostle the prophet said: “I became mute, humbled myself, and kept silence even from good things; and my sorrow was renewed” (Ps. 38). Nothing pours the human heart out of itself more than much speaking; nothing more swiftly incurs idle speech, foolish speech, or even shameful speech than much speaking. Therefore, in order to flee much speaking, we keep silence even from good things, lest an occasion be given to evil things.

[lacuna]

“Hidden fire burns more fiercely.” (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book 4, verse 64.)

Therefore, if the movements of the mind are not poured outward through verbosity, [Col. 1859B] they whirl continually within, like a flame of fire; and, searching through all things of the inner conscience, they encounter those things from which the pain of compunction is beneficially renewed. And because the heart does not evaporate outwardly, but grows hot inwardly from the burning fire of compunction, it produces a shining fire, which it directs upward in meditation. “In my meditation,” he says, “fire shall burn” (Ps. 38). Thus it comes about that one who has learned to be silent outwardly before people begins to speak inwardly to God himself. “I spoke in my tongue,” he says: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end” (ibid.).

Disdaining what is present and forgetting what lies behind, he asks about the end: behold why there is silence. But why in obedience? This “Why?” was first invented by the devil. For the devil was [Col. 1859C] the first to begin questioning the command of obedience: “Why,” he said, “did God command you not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil?” (Gen. III). Before this, the simple man had obeyed simply, not so much because of the reason for the command as because of the authority of the one commanding. For just as faith has no merit when human reasoning supplies it with proof, so obedience is emptied of the virtue of humility when the reason for the command supports it.

Yet do you wish to hear why we either work or rest according to another’s will and authority? Because in this we are imitators of Christ, as most dearly beloved children; and we walk in the love with which he loved us, who became obedient in all things for our sake, not only as a remedy but as an example, so that, as [Col. 1859D] he was, we too may be in this world. For in this, as blessed John says, is confidence. Therefore he became obedient in all things, not only to the Father unto death, but to Mary and Joseph unto prelacy. For when, by the Father’s call saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear him” (Matt. XVII), he was summoned to authority, then for the first time he began to preside over others, having long learned to be subject to others; he began to command, having learned obedience.

Moreover, a just recompense seems fitting: he who in paradise disdained to reign as lord under the Lord should now in exile serve as a servant under a fellow servant. For the condition of nature placed man under the Lord; the transgression of obedience subjected him to the enemy; but grace’s reconciliation [Col. 1860A] made him subject to his brother and fellow servant. Nature subjected him to God, fault to the devil, but reconciliation to a human friend.

“And why,” you ask, “abstain from foods which God created for human use?” Hear this also briefly. Because we have at times used unlawful things freely and lawful things unlawfully; now we never use unlawful things, and use lawful things more sparingly. Because

> “Without Ceres and Bacchus [Liber], Venus grows cold.”  
> (TERENCE, *Eunuch*, act 4, scene 5, verse 6.)

—and because moderation in drink and food wears down the pride of the flesh—we abstain even from permitted things. “All things are lawful,” indeed, “but not all things are expedient.” Paul chastises his body and brings it into slavery; and how do devourers of meat and drinkers of wine—in which is excess—flatter themselves concerning chastity? Surely [Col. 1860B] this is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly; yet we, clothed in soft garments and sunk in down, snore through the whole night.

Do you wish to hear the power of fasting? The most dreadful kind of demons is not cast out except by fasting and prayer. The Savior also, fasting, contends with the devil in the desert (Matt. IV). Hear also, briefly, the threefold fruit of abstinence alone: “By bodily fasting you restrain vices, raise the mind, bestow virtue and rewards” (*Preface of the Mass*). Behold the rationale of our abstinence.

But you say: “If there is such dryness and strictness in food and clothing, why is there such bodily exertion in labors, such business in acquiring things?” Because one who labors much and acquires much in order to eat much serves only his own belly and conducts business for that alone. [Col. 1860C] Rather, it is so that there may be something from which to give to one suffering need, and so that others may be able to enter into our labors, either with us or after us.

Why apart from people? Because evil conversations corrupt good morals. And why several together? Because we are not yet sufficient for solitude; and so that, if anyone falls, he may have someone to raise him up. Likewise, “a brother helping a brother shall be exalted, like a fortified and strong city”; finally, because “it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. CXXXII).

Therefore, that we work with our hands and eat our bread in the sweat of our face is the pattern of penitent Adam; that, besides this, we have a household and livestock is an image of the Patriarchs. “For our fathers,” as someone says, “were shepherds of sheep.”

[Col. 1860D] Thus, to pass one’s life from one’s own labor, household, and the produce of livestock is neither a departure from rectitude nor lacking in authority. What then are certain people doing, who trade and beg, crowding markets and frequenting courts? I answer briefly: “What is beyond this is from evil” (Matt. V).

Yet recently a double kind of religious person has arisen; our fervent times have produced what earlier ages did not know. For just as there are two kinds of those called *trutanni* [vagabonds]—some travel around and traverse the earth, begging everywhere, being false and deceptive through many strange modes of feigning and dissembling; while others pitch tents at crossroads and entrances of churches, surpassing the former in every artifice of feigning and fraud—[Col. 1861A] so some religious, under the pretext of holiness, conduct a very lively commerce in the world to which they are dead, with feigned words: penetrating everything, wandering through everything, leaving nothing unattempted, being among those from whom the world suffers violence and the violent seize it; so that people rise and give more than three loaves, if not because they are friends, then because of their importunity.

These men are always begging and therefore always eating; for what costs them little, they squander easily. Others, seeking a wealthy neighborhood, immerse themselves in little groves near crowded cities and populous towns, surround themselves with ditches, and, taking the utmost care to avoid people, by a marvelous art make themselves more costly the more closely they hide themselves. They work little with their hands, nourish nothing at all, always hanker after others’ hands, and refuse nothing. They are the Gospel birds, which neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and which the heavenly Father feeds. The Lord does indeed feed the birds, beloved; yet they are troublesome to people, whose labors they lie in wait for.

[Col. 1861B] Therefore let us attend more closely to that noble saying of truth: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts XX); and, while we labor with much sweat, let us give with much charity. Let us carefully produce what we may gladly distribute. Let us build for God a temple and for his servants a fitting dwelling from what is ours rather than from what belongs to others; always rejoicing and giving thanks more when we have given than when we have received, and more when we have [Col. 1861C] received others than when we have been received by others. As it is written: “Give alms, and all things shall be clean for you” (Luke XVII). And elsewhere: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and wandering into your house” (Isa. LVIII).

Thus our fathers also, pursuing the grace of hospitality, deserved to receive angels as guests. But that we, having professed chastity, live without wives and children and also without private property, holding all things in common, all obedient to one person and awaiting from him everything according to each person’s need, is beyond doubt the pattern of the blessed apostles and of the primitive Church itself at Jerusalem. With them, along with community of possessions, there was also one heart and one soul. Their inestimable [Col. 1861D] fervor, kindled by the Holy Spirit on the holy day of Pentecost from the furnace in Jerusalem—as it is written, “Whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. XXXI)—has, as charity grew cold and iniquity abounded over a long course of time, evaporated day by day. Yet in such monasteries it still smokes faintly, indicating certain traces, as it were, of an almost extinguished blaze, and displaying some tiny remnants of great coals.

These today, beloved, are “the sharp arrows of the mighty with desolating coals” (Ps. CXIX.4), which we have set before you against “the deceitful tongue” (ibid., 3), which, in all matters, asks with wicked lips and a deceitful tongue, “Why do we do this and that?” but does not care why it itself has come to be. Thus our Order was not built by following presumptuous innovations, but upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets. [Col. 1862A] Its building, constructed almost throughout the whole world as it stands today, has grown into a holy temple in the Lord, in which you also, each in your own place and time, are built together into a dwelling-place of God in the Holy Spirit, through the working of God himself, who works all things in all. To him be honor and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LI. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY

“In all things I sought rest, and in the inheritance of the Lord I shall abide,” etc. (Ecclus. XXIV).

What can properly be said of today’s solemnity—that is, the Assumption of the blessed ever-Virgin—is difficult to determine. For, enclosed within the limits of the Fathers, which we are forbidden to overstep, [Col. 1862B] we dare define nothing else except that on this day—whether with the body or without the body, I do not know; God knows—she was assumed, not for a time, nor merely to the third heaven, if there are several heavens, but to a perpetual and blessed dwelling-place, to the highest heaven of heavens.

She was assumed by him who took flesh from her on earth, to whom alone she would be subject in heaven. For after the fruit of her womb himself, we believe that she is so ordered and placed in heaven—or, if she has not yet risen, is to be placed—that immediately after his beloved soul her own soul is disposed unto wisdom, and after his body her body also unto glory. Therefore she rightly sits first among the generations of the righteous, she who in a proper sense bore the firstborn of all.

[Col. 1862C] For he is the firstborn among many brothers; though by nature only-begotten, by grace he won for himself many who are one with him. For he gave power to those who receive him to become children of God (John I). O lovable and wonderful power! If it were permitted and possible for a poor and low-born person to choose, at will, a wealthy and noble parent, who would not run, who would not hasten to the kings and princes of men? Yet all who wish may become children of God. And why, I ask, except because the Son of God willed to become the son of a poor person, in order by his poverty to make many rich?

But what son of a king and wealthy man would do this: freely empty himself and become for others the son of a needy and low-born person? But once needy, how could he enrich others? Once low-born, how could he ennoble them? Remaining noble, then, he would not wish to descend; made low-born, he could not raise others up. But the love of God is incomparable and his power beyond measure: as it were, he was able to do this because he willed it. For just as “what is foolish of God” and “what is weak of God” is stronger than men, so what is needy of God is richer than men, and what is low-born of God is nobler than men.

Therefore, made the son of a poor person, he made many sons of the rich; made the son of a handmaid, he made many sons of the noble; finally, made the Son of Man, he made many children of God. Thus, as was said, though he is one, by his love and power he won many for himself; and though through carnal generation they are many in themselves, through divine regeneration they are one with him.

[Col. 1863A] For Christ’s head and body are one whole and one sole Christ: one who has one God as Father in heaven and one mother on earth; many children, yet one Son. For as head and members are one son and many sons, so Mary and the Church are one mother and many mothers; one virgin and many virgins. Each is mother; each is virgin. Each conceives by the same Spirit without lust; each brings forth offspring to God the Father without sin. Mary bore the head to the body without any sin; the Church brought forth the body to the head in the remission of all sins. Each is Christ’s mother, but neither brings forth the whole Christ without the other.
