[Col. 1863B] Hence in divinely inspired Scriptures, what is said universally of the virgin mother Church is understood singly of the Virgin Mary; and what is said specially of the virgin mother Mary is rightly understood generally of the virgin mother Church. When discourse is woven concerning either, the meaning is commonly understood of both, mingled together and without distinction. Moreover, every faithful soul, the bride of the Word of God, is in its own manner understood as Christ’s mother, daughter, and sister, both virgin and fruitful. Therefore that which follows is said universally of the Church, specially of Mary, and also singly of the faithful soul, by divine Wisdom itself, which is the Father’s Word.

“In all things I sought rest,” etc. Divine Wisdom is everywhere and in all things; reaching from end to end—that is, from the beginning of all things to their very end—it has impressed its footprints everywhere, by which it may be sought and found. [Col. 1863C] Yet it rests and delights—or labors and is troubled—only in minds endowed with its image and likeness. Thus it complains of some, saying: “I have labored, enduring” (Isa. I); and elsewhere: “Because you are troublesome even to my God” (Isa. VII). But concerning others, with whom it pauses and rests, it says: “Do not trouble me; behold, my children are with me in bed” (Luke XI).

For just as like things naturally rejoice more in likeness found among like things, so they naturally grieve more over likeness found among like things. How, then, could Wisdom be so mistaken as to seek rest in all minds, while finding it fully in few or perhaps none? But what is more marvelous is that that Minerva, born from the subtlety of Jupiter’s brain, became so fat and gross that she even sought fruit on a fig tree—and perhaps not in the season for fruit—and did not find it. For there is a time for every thing under heaven; but above heaven, just as there is nothing temporal, so there is no time.

[Col. 1863D] Therefore Wisdom rests only in the wise. “A desirable treasure,” says the Wise Man, speaking of wisdom, “rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. XXI). But to the fool wisdom is burdensome and contrary; therefore he hates it and, fleeing into a far country, squanders in luxurious living the substance which he might have had, peaceful and abundant, at home with his father and brother.

A person is made wise not merely by knowledge of things, but also by choosing good things and rejecting evil things. Hence it is rightly said of the child nourished with butter and honey: “That he may know to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. VII). Wisdom built for herself such a dining chamber of the rational soul, in which she might dwell and rest: namely, the rational, irascible, and concupiscible powers. By reason it distinguishes friend from enemy, husband from adulterer; by the irascible power it either does not admit the enemy of both reason and desire, or, if carelessly admitted, expels him with strong zeal; and by desire it longs for, receives, and loves only the friend and lawful husband, and grants rest with itself to him alone.

[Col. 1864A] Therefore knowledge springs from reason, rejection from the irascible power, and choice from desire. The wise person, then, who by reason knows good and evil, who by zeal rejects and hates every evil, and who by desire chooses and loves good things alone, builds within himself a house for Wisdom and grants it rest. He also establishes a bridal chamber or prepares a bed in which Wisdom may delight and rest more secretly, according as he shows himself more earnest, fervent, and affectionate in these things.

[Col. 1864B] Therefore Wisdom rightly seeks rest in all, since it created all who could rest in it such as they are. But it by no means finds rest in all, because not everyone remained in what he had received. Why should it not reclaim what it had entrusted? Why should it not demand what it had bestowed? Where it had sown, why should it not reap?

[Col. 1864C] Thus Adam, whom before sin Wisdom had placed in the splendor and light of paradise, sought there after sin. When it did not find him there—for he had fled into hiding because of sin—it pursued him with a cry, saying: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. III). As if to say: You are not where I placed you; and I did not place you where you are. I do not follow into darkness; I do not follow into shadow, one whom I left in light and splendor.

But what are we doing, brothers? Certainly, Wisdom entrusted every deposit not merely to be returned, but to be multiplied with interest; everything it bestowed it justly demands, and what it placed it seeks. Dissoluteness, living luxuriously with harlots, squandered everything. Our strength, weakened in poverty, cannot bring back what was consumed, simply and without gain. Without doubt, those whom justice truly accuses are strictly condemned by judgment unless mercy alone mercifully intervenes. [Col. 1864D] Justice demands all; wickedness has consumed all; weakness restores nothing; judgment remits nothing.

Let mercy therefore come and intervene, meeting justice, for it is the time for mercy; and, since there is a time and season for every thing under heaven, let it overtake wandering Adam like a sheep perishing in the desert—the Adam whom justice once pursued and found hiding beneath a tree in paradise. Let mercy come even near the darkness and shadow of death to seek what was lost; for justice, remaining in the light, rebukes from afar with a cry the lost one hidden in shadow: “Adam, where are you?” Where misery is, let mercy come, because where injustice is, justice cannot come. Finally, let Wisdom itself come to prepare a throne for mercy, Wisdom [Col. 1865A] which once built a house for justice. “In mercy,” it says, “a throne shall be prepared for you” (Isa. XVI). For in justice Wisdom prepared for itself a lofty throne in the holy angels, but in human beings one raised up in mercy. Hence Isaiah beholds the righteous and merciful Lord sitting upon a lofty and exalted throne.

Let mercy therefore come, and from the old and ruined house, open to winds and rain and exposed to the birds of heaven and beasts of the forest—a house in which man does not dare dwell and the Son of Man does not rest—let it renew for itself by a new art a new dwelling, where the Son of Man may lay down his head and pause for a little while. As it is written: “Sleep now and rest”; and immediately: “Rise, let us go from here” (Matt. XVI). For here the saints’ rest is small and brief, but their labor is great and almost unceasing.

[Col. 1865B] Let the eternal One at last come to what is old; and, to renew the old while making all things new, let him in some manner himself grow old. As eternal majesty was, by a new and unheard-of art, bowed down, so that the height of the new head might come upon us and renew the whole body; as light was in some manner darkened and overshadowed, so that a new light might arise for the blind and ancient darkness: so eternity in some manner grew old, so that novelty might be born from it for those who were old. And as by his self-emptying he filled the empty, by his poverty enriched the needy, by his foolishness instructed the foolish, by his weakness strengthened the weak, by his captivity redeemed the captive, by his bonds loosed the bound, and finally by his death gave life to the dead, so by his oldness he renewed the old. For everywhere what is lesser in God is greater in human beings.

[Col. 1865C] Did not the Lord, then, through oldness renew by a new art a new inheritance from the old, in which he might dwell, and a tabernacle in which he might rest—he who previously sought rest in all things and found it nowhere? Hence follows: “And in the inheritance of the Lord I shall abide.” For the inheritance of the Lord is universally the Church, specially Mary, and singly every faithful soul. Christ dwelt nine months in the tabernacle of Mary’s womb; he will dwell in the tabernacle of the Church’s faith until the consummation of the age; and in the knowledge and love of the faithful soul he will abide for ages of ages. Hence follows:

[Col. 1865D] “Then the Creator of all things commanded and said to me,” etc. (Ecclus. XXIV). This is the voice of the inheritance itself. For, when Wisdom had sought rest everywhere, as has been said, and found it nowhere, then it set apart for itself the Jewish people as an inheritance, to whom it commanded and spoke through Moses—that is, it dictated commandments. And he who by this second creation made the Synagogue the mother of the Church rested in his tabernacle, that is, in the tabernacle of the covenant; and likewise now rests in the Church in the sacrament of his body.

Also, after as it were seeking among all women one from whom he might be born, he chose Mary for himself in a special way; hence she is called blessed among women. Then through the Holy Spirit he commanded her inwardly to despise carnal intercourse and love virginity; and through the archangel Gabriel he said to her outwardly that she would conceive Christ by the Holy Spirit, whom she already possessed inwardly. Afterwards Christ, who had created her as a new creature in himself, rested in her womb.

[Col. 1866A] Wisdom also commands and speaks to every faithful soul predestined to salvation, when and how it wills: inwardly through its own reason, by which it enlightens every person coming into this world, and through the inspiration of grace, by which it sets apart voluntary rain for its inheritance; outwardly through teaching and creation, where “the things that are understood are seen through the things that have been made.” Wisdom, which thus creates and forms that soul in Christ Jesus for good works, rests in its conscience.

“And he said to me: Dwell in Jacob, and take inheritance in Israel” (Ecclus. XXIV). This is the Father’s voice to Wisdom, Christ. [Col. 1866B] Wisdom dwells in Jacob, receives inheritance in Israel, but sends down roots only in all and only in the Father’s elect. For every plant which the heavenly Father has not planted, however much it grows or flourishes, will at last be uprooted. Nor is it the Son’s to give the kingdom except to those for whom it has been prepared by the Father (Matt. XX).

Thus Wisdom is not received as an inheritance wherever it dwells, nor does it send down roots wherever it is received as an inheritance. For a thousand will fall from the inheritance and ten thousand from the dwelling, but ruin will not come near the elect, for heavenly generation preserves them as a most strong root. Or, if one prefers, Wisdom dwells in the active persons, who, having supplanted vices, toil in good works; and it is as it were received as an inheritance in the contemplative persons, who have chosen the good part which shall not be taken away from them. [Col. 1866C] But in both kinds of elect Wisdom sends down roots, preserving both against every onset and force of the winds. According to this method the other distinctions also proceed easily, although their order is interchangeable.

Nevertheless, in the Church action and contemplation are two lives; in Mary they are two most complete offices concerning Christ; in each of us, useful alternations and changes are necessary. For what lacks alternating rest is not durable even for a time. May Christ deign to fulfill this in us through the intercession of blessed Mary, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LII. ON THE SAME FEAST, II

[Col. 1866D]

“Who is this, who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song VIII).

Near the beginning of this epithalamium there appears some wondrous figure, I know not what: lying, as it were, in the wilderness, burning and smoking, retaining hidden fire within itself and sending visible smoke upward like a little rod; fragrant also, as though from spices of myrrh and frankincense and every perfumer’s powder. Of her it is said: “Who is this, who comes up through the wilderness like a little rod of smoke?” (Song III).

But later another figure appears—or perhaps the same one because of her progress in virtue—now rising and advancing. She is not at once wholly bright or luminous, but is like the dawn (Song VI), which out of the borderland of night grows into clear light. She is also “fair as the moon,” which is not altogether fair; and “chosen as the sun” (Song VI), which, although wholly luminous, is not wholly gentle. For it shines and scorches: as much as its brightness pleases, so much its heat sometimes harms.

[Col. 1867A] For among natural things there are some that choose the sunlight but flee its heat, and others that are warmed by heat but hurt by light: to them warmth is friendly and brightness hostile, or brightness friendly and warmth hostile. At last she is “terrible as an army set in array” (ibid.), but not yet peaceful. An army may indeed be ordered; but while it is an army, it cannot possibly be secure and wholly peaceful or pacified.

Toward the end, however, a third figure appears, much more wonderful and especially more excellent than the others: neither lying and smoking through the wilderness, nor rising and advancing from the wilderness, but ascending from the wilderness with great strength and wondrous cheerfulness. She is not, I say, merely surrounded or filled with delights, but overflowing and abounding in them; through excessive tenderness unable to support herself, like that Queen Esther who, going up from the women’s banquet hall into the palace of King Ahasuerus (Esther XV), leaned and rested upon her beloved. Perhaps she is that queen of the world who today is delivered from this world and wicked age; who in the banquet hall of the present Church has been washed and adorned above married women, widows, and virgins, and above all these. For although many daughters have gathered riches, this one has surpassed them all.

[Col. 1867B] [Col. 1867C] Today she enters to petition for her people before the King, her Son and Bridegroom. Even the mother herself cannot endure the face of his majesty unless the King extends the golden scepter as a token of mercy. For unless innate and coequal goodness tempers the divine and immeasurable majesty, it is unbearable and inaccessible to every creature. Before it the prophets fall down; and when at length mercy raises them up, they long remain faint and withered. Even the powers of heaven will be moved and tremble at the end.

Yet the mother enters more securely than all others before the Son—not so much because she alone bore him, as because she loved him singularly. “Leaning,” it says, not upon her Son but upon her beloved. For someone may be a son, brother, father, spouse, or anything of that kind, and not be loved; but no one can be beloved without being loved.

[Col. 1867D] Therefore today Mary ascends from the wilderness of this world, not without the admiration of the heavenly powers, who had never before seen anything such as this: someone flying up from this world and taking a seat above all their choirs and thrones. Hence it is said: “Who is this, who ascends from the wilderness, abounding in delights?” Delights are the fruits of virtues. While these are sprouting, flowering, or still forming unripe fruits, they contain some bitterness, difficulty, and sorrow; but by them those trained will finally bear the most peaceful and sweetest fruit of righteousness.

[Col. 1868A] For just as at the time of ripeness, once the husks are rejected and the shells opened, one finally reaches the sweetness and pleasantness of the kernel, and what has long been labored over is gathered with sweetness and joy, so after this life, when every exercise of virtue has wholly ceased, we shall delight in virtues themselves alone, pure and unadorned. Since in this life the blessed Virgin Mary flourished in them beyond all others—whence she deservedly conceived immediately at Nazareth by the Holy Spirit himself—she overflows more abundantly than all with delights in that heavenly abode, as in a house of bread, everywhere leaning upon her beloved, whom she bore more blessedly by faith and love in her heart than in her flesh. Hence it was said: “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke XI).

Meanwhile, until the Bridegroom harvests his ripe myrrh with his spices, may he frequently descend into the garden of nuts, to see whether the vines are flowering and the pomegranates budding.

[Col. 1868B] Moreover, beloved, in ourselves such ascents are not incongruously discovered every day through progress in spiritual conduct, as it is written: “He has disposed ascents in his heart,” etc. (Ps. LXXXIII). And elsewhere: “He made us reign with him and sit with him in the heavenly places” (Eph. II). Thus the rational soul has, as it were, a mystical death, birth, resurrection, ascension, and kingdom; and almost everything celebrated outwardly in history is celebrated inwardly in mystery.

The soul therefore dies to God through disobedience and is born to the devil and the world. Hence: “Cursed be the man who announced to my father, saying: ‘A male child has been born to you’” (Jer. XX). It is evil for a daughter to be born to the devil; worse for a son to be born. The soul also dies to the devil and is born to God through repentance.

[Col. 1868C] Thus, for one dead in sins, the first movement toward life is contrition of heart. While it is pierced by continual consideration of preceding evils and inflamed by sorrow, it creates within itself, as it were, a fire of Gehenna, which smokes upward through confession of the mouth. Since contrition of heart without confession of the mouth is insufficient, so confession of the mouth without amendment of deed is unprofitable. Spices are added so that they may make the smoke smell sweet and show to all that the confessor of sins has been corrected by the sweet fragrance of works—especially myrrh and frankincense, because the most dreadful kind of demons is easily expelled by fasting and prayer; and every perfumer’s powder, because after contrition of heart and confession of mouth, mortification of the flesh and pure prayer to the Lord, generosity in almsgiving must not be neglected. This is like powder scattered little by little from earthly substance that exceeds necessity. “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor” (Ps. CXI). And what follows? “His righteousness endures for ages of ages.”

[Col. 1868D] Therefore such a penitent’s manner of life is followed by righteousness, rising from the valley of tears and advancing as the dawn. The Savior says: “Give alms, and all things are clean for you” (Luke XI). Yet that almsgiving is ordered which does not pass itself by, which first remembers itself, as it is written: “Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX).

[Col. 1869A] Therefore, brother, through contrition, confession, mortification, and prayer, remember yourself and God most diligently; through almsgiving, remember your neighbor devoutly. Through the grace of repentance you restore all things, though by the offense of transgression you had ruined yourself, God, and neighbor. The one whom compunction conceived from the dead unto life in the womb, confession brought forth; whose umbilical cord abstinence cut, reason washed, almsgiving salted with salt, and finally righteousness receives clean, wraps in the swaddling-clothes of virtues, and draws clothed from darkness to light.

For smoke can have something of fragrance but nothing of brightness; dawn has some light, which is the first advance toward the glory of righteousness; the moon, however, is almost wholly bright; the sun has nothing of darkness; and an army set in array also terrifies. Thus the first degree of righteousness is to have in oneself, through innocence, the light of righteousness; the second is, through good works, to give light to others so that they may follow it; the third is to burn with zeal for righteousness toward those who are bright, that they may shine more; the fourth is to appear terrible through one’s incomparable brightness and a certain unbearable majesty.

[Col. 1869B] Yet full and true innocence, which harms neither itself nor anyone else, is scarcely possessed here. Nor does conduct without all disguise readily shine; zeal without all impetuosity hardly burns; and an ordered multitude rarely terrifies with peaceful authority. Hence it was necessary that a third figure should still appear, wholly abounding in delights, scorching no one by day like the sun or by night like the moon—that is, scandalizing no one either by action or by rebuke—but soothing and pleasing all by its gentleness and loveliness. Of such a one it is written: “And he found favor in the sight of all flesh. He magnified him in the sight of enemies, and by his words calmed monsters” (Ecclus. XLII, XLV).

[Col. 1869C] We have nevertheless seen a man who certainly possessed something beyond the human. When some, burned by his action or rebuke, murmured against him in his absence, a certain divine majesty, lovable and reverend, shone in his face with such gentleness and at once such awe, and such grace was poured out upon his lips, that, immediately softened at his appearance, they reproached themselves for having reproached him, and loved, praised, and proclaimed [Col. 1869D] everything belonging to him.

His holy soul truly abounded in delights, as may readily be discerned in his writings, and especially in what he wrote on the Song of Songs. We speak of Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux. Therefore, to those from whom he was absent, he was a sun, a moon, and a terrible army; when present, he flooded them with the delights in which he himself always overflowed. Thus he was terrible to all by love and lovable through awe, so that no one failed through faintheartedness in his word or discipline, was scorched by impatience, or wasted away through envy.

This, therefore, beloved, is the highest degree of righteousness in this life. The first is innocence, which harms no one. The second is generosity, which does good to those whom it can and wishes good to all: beneficent toward those it is able to help, benevolent toward all. [Col. 1870A] For just as a sinner’s almsgiving redeems sins, so a righteous person’s mercy cultivates that person unto greater righteousness, “that the one who is righteous may be made righteous still” (Rev. XXII); but the sinner’s avarice always plunges him downward, “that the one who is filthy may become filthier still” (ibid.).

The third is zeal, in which the bridegroom’s friend, burning with love for the bridegroom, does not permit the bride to grow lukewarm in love. The fourth is authority, which, without any other power, is esteemed venerable by all solely through the grace of virtue and the reputation of holiness. The fifth is charity, which above all is gracious and lovable to all: beautiful through the progress of righteousness and sweet through its supreme abundance in delights. Such was this holy Mother of God in her life, and still more in her death today, as she ascends today to her Son; may [Col. 1870B] she deign to pray to him for us, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LIII. ON THE SAME FEAST, III

“You have held my right hand, and by your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me” (Ps. 72). He said three things: held, led, received. He held, lest she fall; he led, lest she go astray; he received, lest she fail. Thus he held her for stability, led her for progress, and received her for perfection. But who held whom, and how did he lead or receive her? “You held,” he says, “my right hand; you led me in your will; you received me in glory.” He held in faith, led in hope, received in fulfillment.

Meanwhile, this is the voice of the faithful soul rescued from the snare of the hunters, [Col. 1870C] which, once the snare is broken, has been set free and taken up, and gives thanks to its deliverer—until, at the end, the whole Church together sings this, considering where and in what condition it had lain, through what it passed and how, where it has been placed and by whom, into what it had been plunged and why. The contemplation of all these things will indeed strengthen it and continually renew it in thanksgiving. For all divine Scripture, and especially the Psalter, is arranged according to these divisions; and, with two more added—namely, whence it first came into its fall, and in what manner—it is found to be most fully a ten-stringed instrument. “Sing to him upon the psaltery of ten strings” (Ps. 32).

Therefore let the Virgin Mother Mary speak and sing more deeply, she who has surpassed all others, giving thanks [Col. 1870D] to the Son of her flesh; to the brother of her grace, insofar as he is “the firstborn among many brethren”; to the Father of her nature; to the Lord of her life; to the redeemer of her soul; finally, to the holder of her stability, the guide of her progress, and today the receiver of her spirit. Let her say: “You have held my right hand.”

The left hand is the life of the flesh and its prosperity. In a sense, he let this go, who exposed it to poverty, pain, weakness, and death; but everywhere he held the right hand, who in all things preserved the soul, gave patience, and increased merit. For some the Lord holds the left hand and lets go of the right; for some he holds the right and lets go of the left; for some he lets go of both; and for very few indeed he holds both. “You have held my right hand,” she says. Where are those who complain about the left hand? [Col. 1871A] The Mother of Christ glories in the right hand alone; and, because of the sweetness and abundance of the glory into which she has been received, she even counts among her gains the things she suffered. For by experience she has now learned that all things work together for good for those who love God.

A certain judge among the fathers was found who used both hands in the Lord’s battle as his right hand; hence he was called ambidextrous (Judg. 3). Such also was the apostle Paul, who had been instructed everywhere and in all things; who knew how to abound and how to suffer want; who gladly gloried in tribulations and weaknesses; who walked midway through ill repute and good repute, glory and dishonor (Phil. 4; Rom. 5; 2 Cor. 6). John the Baptist likewise was not carried about like a flexible reed by the wind of favor or reproach; and, as he himself testified to the Jews, in their midst stood one whom they did not know—that is, Jesus. For virtues are means, as even the pagan says:

> “Virtue is the mean between vices, removed from either extreme.”
>
> (Horace, *Epistles*, book I, epistle 18, v. 9.)

Those who swell in prosperity and waste away in adversity do not know them.

“And by your will you have led me.” “Yours,” she says, “not mine.” Mary was not led by her own will; and in the Gospel the apostles are taught to pray to the Father: “Your will be done” (Matt. 6). Yet certain fools—especially those who, having renounced their own will, have professed obedience to men—quarrel daily for the sake of their own will, murmur against God in many matters, and resist his ordinance, while rebelling against the authority that is from him [Col. 1871C] and desiring to be the managers of themselves. “We shall do this and this,” they say, “and then this, and then that.” And, what is more foolish still, they wish to instruct everyone else and have everything done according to their own will. “They ought,” they say, “to do this and this.” When something happens otherwise, they murmur, disparage, judge, and condemn.

See into what they have plunged, who ought to do everything under another’s command and yet disdain to be led by others: leaders of themselves, precipitators of themselves. “By your will you have led me,” she says. An insolent man, obstinate in his own will, is rightly reproved by all; yet from this one occasion all controversy arises, every lawsuit and contention is born. For each person contends because he defends, against another who wishes something else, what seems right to himself, pleases him, [Col. 1871D] and is what he wants. Among human beings this may sometimes possess some justice or excuse; but against God every disobedience is sheer impiety. For all must be subject with humble will to this Author, Ruler, and Judge of all; even if they do not wish it, they do so by servile necessity.

“By your will you have led me”: this is piously said by one who piously obeyed and who piously gives thanks to him who led her profitably. For the Lord holds his elect firmly, leads them profitably, and receives them happily. “And with glory you have received me.” He receives into rest one who had served in labor. He receives into heaven one by whom he is received on earth. “I love those who love me,” he says (Prov. 8), “and I receive those who receive me. But those who despise [Col. 1872A] me shall be dishonored” (1 Sam. 2); and those who do not receive me shall be accursed.

Therefore today he receives into heaven that mother who received him, her Son, upon earth; and she who received him in her womb is received by him into the kingdom. And why say more? As each receives, so shall each be received; and as each rejects, so shall each be rejected. Thus, as she received in a singular manner, so she has been singularly received. Martha received him in her house; this woman received him in her womb. Martha served him, I know not with what outward food; this woman nourished her own offspring with her milk. Someone, I know not who, clothed him with a garment; this woman clothed him with flesh. Many sins were forgiven Mary Magdalene because she loved much; very many things were granted to this woman because she loved exceedingly; and she loves exceedingly because she received exceedingly.

[Col. 1872B] Thus, through love a debt is remitted and an undeserved gift is bestowed; by each love increases, and through love each is obtained. Love, therefore, is the sacrifice for sinners and the reward of the blessed. Yet in order that God may be loved by us, God first creates love within us—the love by which he forestalls us, so that we may love him. Hence that blessed disciple whom Jesus loved says: “Not as though we had first loved him, but because he himself first loved us” (1 John 4). Therefore prevenient love seizes and holds our right hand: “His mercy,” he says, “will go before me” (Ps. 58). Helping love leads: “And your mercy,” he says, “helped me” (Ps. 93). Love that follows receives: “And his mercy,” he says, “will follow [Col. 1872C] me all the days of my life” (Ps. 22). The first love reconciles an enemy; the second justifies a friend; the third glorifies a son. For “those whom he predestined, them he also called; and those whom he called, them he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified.”

Thus love, before we were anything, predestined for us that in which we should always be blessed; and those whom it predestined, it seizes, holds, and leads in its will through all things, doing all things in us. For God is he who works in us both willing and being able, for his good will, until he receives us in the glory which the Virgin Mother may obtain for us from her Son, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LIV. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE BLESSED MARY

[Col. 1872D]

“The merciful and compassionate Lord has made a memorial of his wonders” (Ps. 110). In the beginning, beloved, God wondrously made from nothing this world in which we dwell; but at the end he makes it still more wondrously new out of that same world, now grown old and decrepit. For just as the New Testament was contained in the Old Testament—the latter being its shadow and figure, the former its body and truth—so, too, within the old people was the new people; within the old human being, the new human being; within the old world itself, the new world. Everywhere, whatever was wondrously said or done is recapitulated and commemorated still more wondrously in the sacrament.

Accordingly, all things are unfolded again from the head. [Col. 1873A] For all former things are figures of later things, which now begin to be revealed in their appointed times; and these very things are themselves certain coverings and patterns of future things. And as these are truer and more manifest than the former, so those future things are truer and more manifest than these, so that every vanity—every living human being—may always pass away in an image and a kind of vanity, until it comes to the bare, manifest, and stable face of truth. Hence it is written of the consummated and perfect person: “Therefore his goods have been established in the Lord” (Ecclus. 31). Elsewhere: “Until he establishes and makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth” (Isa. 62). The Savior also promises his disciples that in the future he will show himself to them. But Moses, asking this before the time, did not obtain it: “If,” he says, “I have found grace before you, show me yourself” [Col. 1873B] (Exod. 34).

Therefore, in the beginning of the first world God created heaven and earth; in the beginning of the second world he created earth and heaven, and heaven from earth. For Mary, whose nativity is commemorated today, is, according to the origin of her flesh, earthly from earth, and herself earth; but from her is made the fruit of her womb, heavenly from heaven, and himself heaven. And just as there the four elements from which the bodily universe is composed are created, arranged, and adorned historically, so here the bridegroom and bride, as it were heaven and earth, subjects and prelates, or contemplatives and actives, are created, arranged, and adorned sacramentally. And just as there star differs from star in glory, so here one shines by the word of wisdom, to preside over the day, and another [Col. 1873C] by knowledge, to preside over the night.

Others also possess lesser graces for the ministry of signs and times; and each shines in his own place and gift in the new firmament, which shall not be moved. But he strongly separates the upper waters from the lower, lest, when the floodgates have burst, they mingle and make a flood. For the world has its flood, concerning which it is written: “The Lord makes the flood to dwell; and the Lord will sit as king forever” (Ps. 23). There, on the sixth day, humanity was made in the image and likeness of God (Gen. 2); here God becomes, in the sixth age, in the image and likeness of humanity. There humanity is made from earth; here God is made from Mary. There, from earth still incorrupt and virgin, a righteous human being was made, himself a virgin; here, from Mary ever incorrupt and virgin, the just God is made, himself the maker of virgins. [Col. 1873D] There a woman was created from the side of a man without a woman; here a man is begotten from the womb of a woman without a man. There a woman is built from the rib of the sleeping man to be his helper; here the bride is consecrated from the side of the dying Christ. There flesh is supplied in place of a rib; here weakness is assumed in exchange for the power that is given. There two become one flesh; here they are no longer two, but one in one spirit. There, for the sake of his wife, a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to her; here this great sacrament appears in Christ and the Church (Eph. 5), because he, as it were, left Father and mother when he descended from the Father and abandoned the Synagogue in order to cleave to the Church of the Gentiles.

There the human being, created in paradise, is placed in a paradise of delight; here the renewed human being is placed in the Church, rich in spiritual [Col. 1874A] delights and adorned with every kind of flower of graces and sweet fruit of virtues, so that there a human being may work out his salvation with fear and trembling and always carefully guard what he has acquired from his Creator, as it is written: “Let him who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10).

And why say more? Everything that is narrated as having been done there in actuality in that actual and sensible world begins today to be recapitulated in this mystical and spiritual world. God begins to make a memorial of all that he has done, renewing and raising up all things, as it is written: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21); and, “If I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12). For this reason he wished to die aloft in the air, suspended above the earth: that he might raise earthly humanity to a spiritual condition, [Col. 1874B] until finally he might lift it up to heaven and perfect it in a heavenly quality.

Born indeed on earth, he dies in the air and ascends into heaven, because he made the first human being earthly in his earthly world; he made the second spiritual in his spiritual world; and he will make the third heavenly in his heavenly world. The first world is historical, whose creation and government the Old Testament recounts. The second is moral and allegorical, whose condition and government the Gospel recounts. The third is anagogical—that is, leading upward—whose state no one knows except the one who receives it. The Old Testament indeed recounts the creation of the first world and foreshadows the working of the [Col. 1874C] second. But the New Testament announces the reconciliation of the first, which is the creation of the second, and promises the state of the third which it prefigures: “At evening, morning, and noon I shall speak and declare, and he will hear my voice” (Ps. 54).

At evening the earthly and old human being dies in the old world, in the sight of the children of oldness; in the morning the new human being rises and appears in the new world to the children of newness; at noon the heavenly one ascends into heaven and appears before the majesty of the Father, while the holy angels marvel and say, “Who is this who comes from Edom,” and so forth (Isa. 63). There, heard on account of his reverence, he intercedes for us; therefore it is written, “He will hear my voice.” Thus, established and reigning in the third world, he prays to the Father for those whom he draws [Col. 1874D] from the first world and meanwhile places in the second, as it is written: “I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me out of the world” (John 17).

For humanity was created outside paradise, afterwards placed in paradise, and then was to be placed in heaven. But when through the fault of disobedience it withdrew from God, through the justice of vengeance the flesh withdrew from the mind; the flesh itself was cast from paradise, and thus the whole human being lives in exile. For the soul was neither created nor placed in such a body, nor was the body in such a world.

Thus the soul is a pilgrim in such a body, and the body in such a world. The ordered and natural state of humanity was that the spirit was subject to God, the flesh to the spirit, and the world to the flesh; and within the spirit affection was subject to the flesh. This was the first [Col. 1875A] natural world, Saturn’s golden age and the poet’s golden chain. When disobedience broke this chain between the spirit and God, concupiscence between flesh and spirit, and finally the curse between the working of the flesh and the world, there suddenly appeared a certain disordered face of things, rightly called chaos, darkness, and abyss. One who, through grace, had been made a new creation in Christ and placed in the new world recalled that he had been drawn out of it, singing: “How many great and evil tribulations you have shown me! Yet you turned and gave me life, and brought me back from the abysses of the earth” [Col. 1876A] (Ps. 70).

For humanity, taken from earth by nature, placed above by grace, fell below through fault. Thus one now gives thanks and says: “He drew me out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs” (Ps. 39). First created from mud, it is created a second time from mire and drawn from the pit: it was created from earth, fell into the depths, and found no bottom. For the abyss is depth without a bottom: “I am fixed,” he says, “in the mire of the deep, and there is no firm ground” (Ps. 68).

Some material is missing.

[Col. 1875]

## ISAAC OF STELLA: LETTER TO A CERTAIN INTIMATE FRIEND CONCERNING THE SOUL

[Col. 1875B] Brother ISAAC to his beloved ALCHER: himself, and what belongs to him.

You compel me, dearest friend, to know what I do not know and to teach what I have not yet learned. For you wish to be taught by us concerning the soul—but not what we have learned in the divine Scriptures, namely what it was before sin, what it is under sin, or what it will be after sin. Rather, you ask concerning its essence and powers: how it is in the body, how it leaves it, and the rest of what we do not know. Nor do you allow us not to know it. To confess the truth: that very thing which you heard from us in conversation, and which encourages you to hope for something more, escapes, flies away, and in some fashion vanishes from us while we attempt to comply with your prayers and direct our attention to it.

Hence even in this we learn that our soul bears a very great likeness to the divine [Col. 1875C] nature, which restrains an importunate investigator of itself by saying: “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away” (Song 6). There are, therefore, three things: body, soul, and God. But I confess that I do not know the essence of these; and I understand less what body is than what soul is, and less what soul is than what God is. Perhaps you will marvel at this—and do so. Nevertheless, in this corruptible body the soul is weighed down; here earthly habitation presses the mind downward to low things, and earthly limbs and dying members blunt the power of the soul, which works while oppressed.

Of the three things mentioned, the body itself comes first; and it is necessary that the soul, darkened by it, should see it only obscurely. [Col. 1875D] But the higher it rises in vapor from this dark smoke, the more clearly it will see. Therefore it must see the soul itself more clearly and certainly than the body, insofar as understanding is higher and purer than sense; and God himself more clearly than the soul, insofar as intelligence surpasses understanding. For the truth of every essence is in God. In the soul some image of it appears; in the body scarcely a trace of it is found. God alone is truly simple; every body is truly composite; and the soul, in relation to both, can be called either. Or, if any body is simple, the soul is certainly simpler, since it is above every body; but God is most simple, and also highest.

Thus God is all that he has: he is all his own things. But a body can be none of the things it has, since nothing at all belonging to it is itself. The soul, however, as intermediate between these natures, is tempered in an intermediate way: it is some of its own things, and in this respect simple; and it is not some things at all, and in this respect is found not to be truly simple. But, to bind ourselves to a definite [Col. 1876C] assertion, God has neither quality nor quantity. For when it is said what kind or how great he is, nothing other than what he is is predicated of him. But body, though it has both, is neither. The soul has no quantity, because it is not body; nor is it without quality, because it is not God. Yet if it is ever said to possess quantity, or parts, this must be understood from a comparison of analogy rather than from the reality of composition.

For it has natural faculties or powers, according to which it is said to possess virtual or potential parts, such as intelligence, reason, and memory. If these are true parts of the soul according to quantity, they must themselves be souls; and it will be true that it consists of as many souls as it has parts. For every part is found to be of the same nature as its whole. Every part of a body is body. Thus, if the soul has quantitative parts, it is necessarily proved that every part of the soul is another soul. Since, then, intelligence, [Col. 1877A] reason, memory, and such things are parts of the soul and connatural with it, yet are not quantitative, it follows that, since they are the same as the soul itself, they are the same nature, the same essence, wholly the same soul. For reason and soul are not two essences, but one. Their properties are different, but their essence is one. Indeed, according to property, as blessed Augustine says, soul is one thing and reason another; and yet reason is in the soul and the soul is one. But the soul does one thing and reason another: the soul lives; reason understands. And although they are one, the soul alone receives life and reason alone receives wisdom.

See, therefore, how in this respect the image of deity shines in the soul: though there is in it a plurality of natural properties, they are nevertheless one nature; and though none of them is another, none is anything other than another.

The soul, then, is rational, concupiscible, and irascible—its own kind of trinity—and this is the whole of it, neither more nor less. This whole trinity is a certain unity of the soul, and is the soul itself. Therefore the soul has natural attributes, and is itself all of them; for this reason it is simple. It has accidents, and is not itself those; for this reason it is not altogether simple. For the soul is not its own prudence, temperance, fortitude, or justice. Therefore it is its powers, but it is not its virtues. For we must sit in the city until we are clothed, and our powers are clothed from on high. Powers are receptive of gifts which, through habit, become virtues.

Further, just as fire possesses natural [Col. 1877C] heat, warming those who approach it and producing in them accidental heat according to the nature by which they can be warmed; and natural light, illuminating those who approach according to the nature by which they can be illuminated: so in the divine nature there is a natural, fountain-like gift and benefit, illuminating and enkindling, as it were creating wisdom and justice in those who approach, in that part by which they can be kindled and illuminated. Hence: “Approach and be enlightened” (Ps. 33). And: “Draw near to me, and I shall draw near to you” (Jas. 4). And: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5).

Observe, however, that powers are sometimes indiscriminately called virtues, in the sense in which talents are given in the Gospel according to each one’s own capacity (*virtus*) (Matt. 25). Yet people are called virtuous from powers, just as they are called diligent, though indirectly, from virtue. For he who distributes to each as he wills does not fill all the powers of everyone with his grace, but different powers in different persons. Those are more blessed who abound in more powers, provided they abound in better ones, as the Apostle says: “Seek the better gifts” (1 Cor. 12). But the Lord Jesus, whose soul’s powers are all clothed with power from on high, is called full of the Holy Spirit (Luke 4), and full of grace and truth—perhaps uniquely so—from whose fullness we have received.

There are, therefore, natural and accidental properties of body; but none of these is the body. God has neither natural nor accidental properties: rather, all and only and always whatever belongs to God is the one God. The soul, however, has natural properties, which cannot be anything other than the soul itself, and accidental properties, which cannot be anything other than the soul itself. If it should be thought that God also has certain natural properties, since the Father has the Son naturally and the Son the Father naturally, and each has naturally—the one paternity, the other filiation—nevertheless God differs jointly from both body and soul in this: he has no accidental properties; from body, because he is his natural properties; from soul, because he is all his own things, except that one person is relatively spoken of in relation to another. The soul is by no means all its own things; nor does it differ from its accidents by relation or property alone, but by opposition of essence.

[Col. 1878B] Therefore, placed in the middle, the soul must have some affinity with each: with the highest in what is higher in it, and with the lowest in what is lower in it. For, as has been said, according to its properties the soul has a lowest, middle, and highest, although according to essence all are one. The whole essence of the soul is fully and perfectly contained in these three: rationality, concupiscibility, and irascibility. Hence the prophet, wishing to show that Christ would possess a full and perfect human soul, says: “That he may know to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. 7). He first stated similarly of the truth of his body: “He shall eat butter and honey,” as though to say that he will truly experience labor—for butter is extracted from milk only with much toil, fatigue, and repeated beating—and rest, for honey is freely sweet; so that by experience he may know, through rationality, to choose through concupiscibility the good, namely honey, and reject through irascibility the evil, namely butter.

Thus he also feeds us, whom he instructs from himself according to himself, so that by following him we may attain to him: he feeds us with frequent tribulations and softens us with certain consolations, so that from the bitter things we suffer we may learn to flee things more bitter, and from the sweet things we taste beforehand we may desire things sweeter. Therefore, through rationality the soul is capable by nature of being enlightened for the knowledge of something below itself, or even within itself and alongside itself; but through concupiscibility and irascibility it is affected toward desiring or fleeing, [Col. 1878D] loving or hating something.

Thus all the soul’s cognition arises from rationality, and all affection from the other two. Affection is known to be fourfold: concerning what we love, we either rejoice in it when present or hope for it when future; concerning what we hate, we either already grieve or fear what is to be grieved over. Accordingly, joy and hope arise from concupiscibility, while pain and fear arise from irascibility. These four affections of the soul are, as it were, the elements and common material of every vice or virtue. For affection gives every work its name. Since virtue is a settled disposition of a mind rightly formed, the affections of the soul must be formed, composed, and ordered by appropriate reason toward what they ought to seek and in the manner in which they ought to seek it, so that they may advance [Col. 1879A] into virtues; otherwise they easily decline into vices.

When, therefore, love and hatred are formed prudently, moderately, courageously, and justly, they rise into virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice, which are said to be, as it were, the roots or hinges of all virtues whatsoever. For, as blessed Augustine says, what is called fourfold virtue is formed from a certain varied affection of love: temperance is love keeping itself whole and incorrupt for God; fortitude is love readily enduring all things for God; justice is love serving God alone and therefore governing well all things subject to it; prudence is love rightly distinguishing those things which help it toward God from those which hinder it from him.

Accordingly, as was said, every motion of the mind arises from concupiscibility and irascibility, by which it is affected toward choosing or rejecting, loving or hating something above itself, below itself, within itself, or beside itself. From concupiscibility, therefore, come inclination, excitation, delight, and love; from irascibility come zeal, anger, indignation, and hatred. If all these things are well, orderly, and fully formed in the soul, through hatred of the world and of oneself it advances to love of neighbor and God, to contempt for temporal and lower things, and desire for eternal and higher things. But let these brief touches concerning affection, rather than a full treatment, suffice.

Cognition, arising from rationality, varies—or receives various names—because of present, past, and future time: reason, memory, and intelligence. Intelligence is said to be that power of the soul, or attention, which extends and arouses itself [Col. 1879C] for the discovery of things unknown. Intelligence, therefore, searches out unknown things; reason judges what has been discovered; memory stores what has been judged and offers it again for further judgment. Thus intelligence brings what it discovers to reason; memory brings back what it has hidden; but reason moves over them as though present, and, as it were in the mouth of the heart, continually either chews what the teeth of intelligence pluck or ruminates upon what the stomach of memory presents.

For not everything that we know is always at hand, nor is everything known always before the gaze of the knower. Nevertheless, what has been stored in memory is drawn forth temporally and in parts and made present in the mouth of the heart as a word, which externally makes sound in the mouth of flesh. Hence, too, because for God nothing is future and nothing past, all things are, simultaneously, once, always, and as present, in the instantaneous gaze of the one who beholds; and they are said to exist immovably and eternally for him in the Word, as though in *logos*, that is, the reason of the mind, which considers all things simultaneously, once, and always with itself and speaks to itself. Therefore all his cognition of all things is called neither memory nor intelligence, but Word.

Yet reason, memory, and intelligence are three according to their exercise, but one according to essence in the soul, and are what the soul itself is. But just as their exercises vary because of time, although the cognition which is in the soul is one and is what the soul itself is, so also because of the things toward whose knowledge it exerts and directs itself, it is called manifold and receives manifold names.

It is therefore called bodily sense, imagination, reason, [Col. 1880A] understanding, and intelligence. Yet all these things within the soul are nothing other than the soul. They are distinct properties in relation to one another because of their various exercises, but there is one rational essence and one soul. For just as the life of the soul by which it lives—not the manner in which it lives—is nothing other than the living soul, so every cognition of the soul by which it learns—not that by which it is taught—is nothing other than the soul itself perceiving. Nor can the will of the soul, insofar as capacity is concerned, be anything other than the soul itself willing.

Therefore, just as this visible world rises upward through a fivefold distinction—earth, water, air, ether or firmament, and the highest heaven itself, called the empyrean—so there are five advances toward wisdom for the soul journeying in the world of its body: sense, imagination, reason, understanding, [Col. 1880B] and intelligence. For rationality is exercised toward wisdom through five advances, just as affection or will is exercised through four toward love. Thus, as the soul advances in itself through these nine advances, it may, by sense and affection as by certain inward feet, walk in the Spirit, since it lives by the Spirit, as far as cherubim and seraphim—that is, fullness of knowledge and the fire of love. It may possess by exercise the virtues whose capacities it possesses by nature, so that, just as it is called heaven because it is the seat of wisdom, it may likewise be adorned within itself by its quasi-heavenly orders and ordered by virtues. It will be easy for one at leisure to compare these advances, by their names and order, with the orders of angels.

By sense, therefore, it perceives bodies; by imagination, likenesses of bodies; by reason, dimensions of bodies and similar things; and beyond these, the first incorporeal thing, which nevertheless needs body in order to subsist and therefore is in place and time. By understanding it rises above everything which is body, belongs to body, or is bodily in any manner; and it perceives the created spirit, which needs no body for subsistence and consequently no place, though it cannot possibly exist without time, since it is of mutable nature. Finally, by intelligence it somehow sees, and sees as far as nature permits, that one thing which is supremely and purely incorporeal, which needs neither body in order to be, nor place in order to be somewhere, nor time in order to be at some time.

Therefore sense is compared to earth, [Col. 1880D] for it does not transcend body; and every body must be regarded as earth. It is always that power of the soul by which it presents to itself the bodily forms of bodily things. Although it is bodily, it is not a body; and therefore it is called bodily because, as stated, it does not transcend body, or because it is exercised by bodily instruments. Hence, because of the number of its instruments, it is called fivefold, though inwardly it is only one. For just as water received in a lamp sends forth varied rays through many openings, differing according to the quality and position of the openings, though within it is one and uniform, so the inner sense is one and uniform but, according to the quality and position of its instruments, varies and is vigorous in different ways.

For within—not only in the imaginative faculty [Col. 1881A] of the soul, which is the lowest level of spirit, but also in the spirit of animals, which is the highest level of body—sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch are together; yet in their different instruments, as stated, they perform different operations. Fire gleams in the eyes, which are suited to light in position, fire, and composition. Subtle, pure air, contiguous with fire, resounds in the ears, which are suited to air by position and to sound by composition. The rest are evident in the rest: for this thick and, as it were, smoky air, affected by smells or stenches, belongs to the nostrils; and water tastes in the palate. Earth is made firm in touch, especially in the feet and hands, by which we handle earth more directly. Moreover, because the animate body is chiefly earthy matter, touch is active everywhere in it where [Col. 1881B] there is spirit.

From sense, therefore, imagination arises, and according to the diversity of sense it too varies. Imagination is that power of the soul which apprehends the forms of bodily things, though absent. Sense apprehends real bodies through their real qualities when these are present, diversely, as was said, in diverse ways; but imagination apprehends only their likenesses and images, and is therefore called imagination. Since these are neither real bodies nor real qualities of bodies, imagination is a certain removal and evaporation from bodily things, yet not an arrival at the incorporeal: it is an effort of the lowest bodily spirit, but not an attainment of the incorporeal. For it is impossible that what is body should be attenuated into spirit, or that what is spirit should be thickened into body. For whatever is born of flesh is always, by nature and essence, flesh; and what is born of spirit is likewise spirit. Yet there are certain things similar in each: namely, the highest part of body and the lowest part of spirit. In these, without confusion of natures but by personal union, they can readily be joined. For like things delight in like things and easily adhere in union when they do not recoil through dissimilarity. Thus that which is truly spirit and not body, and flesh, which is truly body and not spirit, are easily and suitably united at their extremities: that is, in the soul’s imaginative faculty, which is almost body, and in the sensuality of flesh, which is almost spirit. For just as the highest part of the soul—that is, intelligence or mind, discussed above—bears the image and likeness of its superior, namely God, and could therefore be receptive of him, and was even assumed to personal union, when he himself willed it, without any alteration of nature; so too, since the highest part of flesh, namely sensuality, bears a likeness to the soul, why should it not receive its essence into personal union? Is there not in the sense of an animal a certain image of rationality, in its appetite an image of will, and in the things it shuns an image of rejection?

Thus bodily spirit—which is indeed truly body—distinguishes among many things by natural sense, chooses by the power of desire, and rejects by the nature of irascibility. Yet, although these things are not lacking in minds which are thought to possess nothing at all above bodily nature, the rational soul, through its composition with it, makes the human body a more fitting dwelling-place: as though attuned and harmonized, by the plectrum of the supreme Harpist, to its rational and harmonious motions or measures. As it is written: “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out her seven pillars” (Prov. IX). Although this saying, anagogically, concerns the rational mind, called the dwelling and house of divinity, and allegorically the spiritual building of the Church, yet historically, and as it were at the foundation, it indicates the structure of the human head, the seat of the soul and in some manner the house of reason. For the head—which you know better, since you excel in natural philosophy—is put together from six bones and supported by the seven pillars of the neck. Therefore, if you will not disdain to write us a letter on the composition of the human body, perhaps, with God as author, you will receive from us some reply concerning how the soul gladly receives that instrument for action and delight, guards it anxiously, leaves it unwillingly, awaits it with longing when it has been left, and rejoices exultantly when it is received again, as John says of “harpists playing upon their harps” (Apoc. XIV). Meanwhile, let us pursue what we began; and let what has been said suffice concerning body and soul, natures contrary, as you said, and how they may meet and exist together. For by two most fitting middle terms two discordant extremes may easily and firmly be joined. This may readily be seen in the fabric of the great animal, as some call it, namely this world. The most fitting intermediaries are soul and flesh, as has been said; and more may be assigned: the sensuality of flesh, which is chiefly fire, and the imaginative faculty of spirit, called a fiery vigor. One speaking of souls says:

> “A fiery vigor is theirs, and a heavenly origin.”  
> (VIRGIL, *Aeneid*, VI, 729.)

Perhaps someone will say here: “If the soul is in the body through that sensuality, which is bodily spirit, why does the body not live after the soul’s departure by that spirit which is certainly life?” To this we answer: so long as the integrity and temperance of that sensuality suitable for giving life remain, the soul never departs; but when it is disordered and disrupted, the soul departs unwillingly. It takes all its own things with it—namely, sense, imagination, reason, intellect, intelligence, desire, irascibility—and is affected by these, according to merits, either with delight or pain. But the body, the instrument which before was whole, harmoniously tempered, and disposed so as to contain within itself the melody of music and to sound at a touch, now lies opposite, shattered and useless. The instrument has indeed perished, but the melody or song has not perished—unless you judge mere sound to be the song. For what is not body cannot be local, nor can it locally approach, inhabit, or depart. Rather, as the melody of music is in a musical instrument or on the leaf of an antiphonary while strings or notes are suitably arranged; when they are arranged it arrives, when they are confused it departs: so it is with the soul and its body. And if you ask where the soul is after the body, I ask where the song is after the page or after the sound; where meaning is after a word; where the sense of a statement is after a verse; where number is after what has been numbered. Place four pebbles and three, and there are seven. Remove them: are not three and four still seven? Things capable of being numbered, or things numbered, if you please, are like a body of numbers; verses are the body of meanings; speech is the body of sense; and vocal modulation is the body of song. By all these quasi-bodies incorporeal things are held; at times they arrive and at times they depart. But you will say that this comparison is more fitting for God, who is purely and wholly incorporeal and who is in all things in himself, than for the soul. Let it be so. Yet, as I said before, I can philosophize more certainly, and more easily, about God than about the soul, and about the soul than about the body. Nevertheless, the soul has an image and likeness of the Godhead; and therefore it must be wholly similar in nature.

God, therefore, is everywhere in himself; the soul, wherever it is, is in some fashion in itself. And hence the soul is after the body where it was while acting in the body; God is now where he was before he made the world, and where he would be if the world ceased to exist. But God is infinite and uncircumscribed; therefore, since he is in himself, he is said to be everywhere. The soul is neither infinite nor uncircumscribed; therefore, since it is in itself, it is known to be finite and circumscribed. Yet neither is so by place, but by natural powers and capacities. Its natural capacities and powers are identical with itself. Its essence, therefore, is finite and circumscribed; hence, when it is said to be elsewhere, it is denied to be elsewhere: it is present insofar as it can be, above which it can do nothing. But God is omnipotent. The soul thus remains invisible and non-local; it is seen in the body through the body, as meaning, remaining in a letter, is seen through the letter. And God is wholly invisible, yet in every creature he is seen through the creature itself by those who possess eyes for seeing; but he will be seen more fully and perfectly by spiritual and renewed eyes in the new heaven and new earth. The whole creation is, as it were, the body of the Godhead, and individual creatures are as its individual members. And as God is wholly in the whole and wholly in each individual thing, yet in himself, so the soul is wholly in its whole body and wholly in each member, in itself. This is true of God properly, of the soul by likeness to that truth. Therefore, while the soul is, as stated, incorporeal and consequently non-local, in that part by which it has been called almost bodily it is found also almost local. Hence, as the soul acts through sense upon bodies, so through imagination it acts upon likenesses of bodies and places; and in them—whether waking, sleeping, temporarily withdrawn from the senses, or wholly overwhelmed; whether by itself or through the action of another good or evil spirit—it seems either to act or to suffer something. Yet so far as sense is concerned, it can never rise above body; nor through imagination above bodily likenesses, whether in the body or outside the body, since it has received these powers solely for these operations.

By these powers, therefore, the soul either sees or will see God above itself, an angel beside itself, itself in itself, and even the incorporeal forms of bodies beneath itself. Reason remains, then: the third stage, as was said, in the soul’s progress toward wisdom. Reason is that power of the soul which apprehends the incorporeal forms of bodily things. It abstracts from body those things founded in body, not by action but by contemplation; and, although it sees that they do not actually subsist except in body, it nevertheless apprehends that they are not body. Indeed, the very nature of body, according to which every body is body, is certainly no body. Yet it nowhere subsists outside body, and the nature of body is found only in body; nevertheless it is found not to be body, nor a likeness of body. Hence it is apprehended neither by sense nor imagination. Reason therefore apprehends what neither sense nor imagination apprehends: namely, the natures, forms, differences, and proper accidents of bodily things—all incorporeal, but subsisting only in bodies except in reason. For secondary substances are not found to subsist except in primary substances; much less those whose being consists in being in some subject. Thus we have what above we rightly called the first incorporeal things: since they are not body, they cannot yet be called spirits, because, when the things in which they are have been removed, they in no way subsist in themselves. They need body in order to be, and consequently place in order to be somewhere, and time in order to be at some time. For, as was said, things of this kind subsist only in others, though those others are distinct from them. Secondary substances are in primary substances, but primary substances are not in secondary ones.

The objects with which sense, imagination, and reason concern themselves and flourish have different modes of being: the real and the rational; or, as some prefer, the natural and the doctrinal. Hence the two named disciplines are recognized: natural science and mathematics. *Mathesis* is called teaching, because neither sense knows nor imagination opines the rational mode of things: it subsists wholly in reason and teaching rather than in actuality. Sense and imagination flourish concerning the natural modes of bodily things, but without reason they are not sufficiently effective. They do not ascend to the rational mode, but remaining below it they show it, as if from afar, to reason as it ascends. They can indeed in some measure lead reason itself, but cannot accompany it as far as the incorporeal forms of bodily things. Yet higher still is the discipline called theology, because it reasons concerning divine things. Reason can be aided toward it in a corresponding proportion, but can by no means attain it. For reason has its boundaries and is confined by its own limits. Thus, as the sun rising from underground, languishing amid the misty vapor of waters and marshes, first reddens rather than shines, then, escaping into the freedom of purer air after treading down the mists, shines more serenely; so the soul, arising from the mere animation of flesh into sense, and through sense and beyond it into imagination, still languishes stained by bodily phantasms, until, unfolded into the clarity of reason, it finally rises and flashes forth. Intellect surpasses reason in order and power, as the firmament surpasses air, being wholly free both from the dullness of earth and from the fluidity of water or the moisture of air. Sense, dull and heavy like earth, lies below; imagination surrounds it like water; reason is compared to the subtlety of air, embracing and penetrating all lower things and contemplating from a kind of suspended abstraction. Intellect should be compared to the solidity of the firmament, for it discerns the real mode of spiritual natures. Intelligence seems comparable to the empyrean, the highest fiery heaven, most keen and subtle. Intellect, therefore, is that power of the soul which apprehends the forms of things truly incorporeal. By “truly incorporeal” we mean what does not need body in order to be, and hence does not need place in order to be somewhere, although it is not wholly and purely incorporeal and cannot exist without time. But what is purely incorporeal is simple, wholly sufficient to itself.

Thus, as was said, the soul apprehends body by sense; what is almost body by imagination; what is almost incorporeal by reason; what is truly incorporeal by intellect; and what is purely incorporeal by intelligence. The latter needs neither body in order to be, nor place in order to be somewhere, nor time in order to be at any time, nor cause in order to be from somewhere, nor form in order to be something, nor any genus of subject in which it may subsist, or which it may attend or inhere in. Rather, as was said, it is wholly sufficient to itself: it is through itself and unto itself. Thus there is a certain image and likeness of what is purely and truly incorporeal in that which is truly but not purely incorporeal; of this latter in what we called almost incorporeal; and of this again in what we called almost body. To this is joined, by a certain likeness, the highest body, namely fire; then air to fire, water to air, and earth to water. By this, then, as by a golden chain of the poet, the lower things depend from the higher; or, as by the prophet’s raised ladder, one ascends from the low to the high. Thus wisdom “reaches mightily from end to end,” that is, from highest to lowest, drawing things also from their archetype into their proper states so that they may be what they are, and “ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. VII): moderating and governing through being those things which it draws from non-being into being. So too the soul, an image of that wisdom, if it does not degenerate, gladly follows wisdom everywhere, admiring and loving, investigating and praising in all things both the power that draws all things from non-being into being, the wisdom that orders all things through being, and the goodness that holds all things lest they fall back into non-being. Thus the Psalmist exults: “For you have delighted me, Lord, in your workmanship; and I will rejoice in the works of your hands. How greatly your works have been magnified, O Lord! Your thoughts have become exceedingly profound” (Ps. XCIII). And elsewhere: “I will meditate on all your works, and I will rejoice in your inventions” (Ps. LXXVI). Works belong to creation; inventions, to governance. And elsewhere: “Wonderful are your works, O Lord, and my soul shall know exceedingly” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

The soul therefore has the means by which to investigate and know. Made in the likeness of total wisdom, it bears within itself a likeness of all things. Hence the philosopher defined it as “the likeness of all things.” By sense, therefore, as has often been said, it investigates and knows bodies; by imagination, likenesses of bodies; by reason, bodily dimensions, likenesses of unlike things, and unlikenesses of like things; by intellect, mutable spirit; and by intelligence, immutable God. Since the soul possesses within itself powers by which to investigate all things, and through them is like all things while remaining one—like earth through sense, water through imagination, air through reason, the firmament through intellect, and the heaven of heavens through intelligence; or like metals and stones through essence, plants and trees through life, animals through sense and imagination, human beings through reason, angels through intellect, and God through intelligence—it sings to its Maker with grace and praise, crying: “Your knowledge has become wonderful from me; it has been strengthened, and I shall not attain to it” (Ps. CXXXVIII). This knowledge is said to have been strengthened beyond the soul, so that the soul cannot reach it—as though it has itself been weakened by that which it ought to have contemplated and possessed. Hence elsewhere it laments and mourns: “My iniquities have overtaken me, and I was unable to see” (Ps. XXXIX). And elsewhere: “The light of my eyes—even it is not with me” (Ps. XXXVII). And elsewhere: “My eye has been troubled by fury” (Ps. VI).

Since only the eyes of desire have been illuminated and opened—the eye of the man, that is, the spirit, toward curiosity; and that of the flesh, that is, the woman, toward pleasure—the eye of sense and imagination has been disturbed, so that it sees more obscurely; the eye of reason, so that it scarcely sees; and those of intellect and intelligence, so that they see almost nothing. For who has seen himself? Who has known himself? I mean the image and likeness of God, made in the image and likeness of God. Whoever knows one of two similar things has seen both; and whoever knows neither one nor the other knows neither. Thus the soul, which ought through itself to have known God above itself, has lost the knowledge of itself within itself and of the angel beside itself. Therefore, because angels flourish in intellect, they see one another and our souls; yet we cannot reciprocally see them in their nature, because the soul has been weakened and cannot open its eye to see them. Hence, when angels wish to show themselves to human beings, they either serve the outward sense through an assumed body or the inward imagination through bodily likenesses. But while sense and imagination flourish in natural science, reason in mathematics, and intelligence in theology, intellect does not constitute a discipline of its own. For the incorporeal nature whose incorporeal forms it apprehends is placed, as said, between body and God. It has natural properties, which it is, and these may now be apprehended otherwise through abstraction; it has accidents which, when abstracted and considered in their own nature, fly higher and need intelligence itself, by which God is seen. For natural powers, considered in their highest point and natural source, in essence, are all things: lowest and highest, the principle of all, the nature of natures, and the essence of essences. Hence intellect partly yields to natural science and partly to theology. For what is the essence of justice other than God, participation in whom is called virtue? And as many as are the varieties of participation, so many are the individual forms of justice. Yet there is one essential justice: not a quality, not an accident of the soul, but subsisting in itself, participated in by spirits through participation in the Just One. Such participations are the highest forms of justice, and they are accidental. God is capable of all things, and may be participated in through his natural gift and through the use that follows from that gift. All things participate in him according to essence, according to that essence in a fitting species, and according to both in a fitting use. For all things are: being is the first thing and the principle in every thing. What is not is absolutely nothing; and when something is, it is held in some species, image, or form through which it is distinguished from every other thing, and it naturally has some gift in itself. Nothing is for nothing. These three things are present in everything that subsists, as certain traces of the supreme essence, image, and gift—that is, of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Eternity is in the Father, species in the image, and use in the gift.

Therefore, since everything which subsists by number, measure, and weight is capable of divinity, as said above, one ascends gradually and in different ways, through animation, sensibility, and rationality, from living things to the image and likeness of God which shines in the higher part of the soul. This soul, as God is capable of all things, is capable of all things; and, as has often been said, by the powers that arise from its rationality it is capable of universal knowledge, and by its desiring power it is capable of universal love.
