Whatever it perceives by any sense, it immediately dips, as it were, into the brine of desire, so that it may taste pleasant to it and, as though through taste, may please or displease. Thus within the soul—and indeed identical with the soul—are natural sense, knowing all things and judging among all things, and natural affection, through which it loves all things in their proper order and degree. Yet it has from nature the capacities and, as it were, instruments for knowing and loving; but it has neither knowledge of truth nor the order of love except through grace. For the rational mind, made by God, just as it is the first and only thing to receive his image, so it can receive knowledge and love. Thus the vessels which creating grace forms so that they may exist, assisting grace fills so that they may not be empty. For as the bodily eye, though naturally possessing the capacity to see, and the ear the capacity to hear, never of itself obtains sight or hearing except through the benefit of external light and sound; so the rational spirit, though by the gift of creation fitted to know truth and love good, never obtains the effect of wisdom or charity unless it is suffused by the ray of inward light and inflamed by warmth. For as the eye does not see the sun except in the sun’s light, so intelligence cannot see true and divine light except in that light itself. “In your light,” says the Prophet, “we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV). Therefore, just as that by which the sun may be seen proceeds from it yet does not leave the sun, but remains in it, and, proceeding from it, reveals it; so the light which remains in God and proceeds from him irradiates the mind, so that it first sees the flashing of the light itself, without which nothing is seen, and sees all other things in it. From there intelligence ascends to the fountain of light itself, finds it through its own light, and beholds it.

Thus, as phantasies rise from below into imagination, so theophanies descend from above into intelligence. And as the soul alone does not suffice for life to its own body, so it does not suffice alone for wisdom to itself. Sense is aided externally; imagination from below; reason from the first grace below, according to the saying that every person coming into this world is enlightened; but intellect and intelligence are aided from above. Intelligence, therefore, is that power of the soul immediately subject to God, as the soul’s imaginative faculty is subject to the body, or as the sensuality of flesh is subject to the lowest part of the soul. Yet in God, whom intelligence is nearest to knowing, although distinct properties are found, there is nevertheless nothing lower and nothing unequal. Yet no one knows the Father except through the Son and in the Holy Spirit. The Father does, gives, and forgives all things through the Son in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, although the three persons are coeternal and coequal in their ineffable nature, the Holy Spirit seems in a certain manner closer to creatures, since he proceeds from both and is the gift of both. For all our enjoyment of divinity comes through the gift. In God there is a natural gift, by which he himself is able to be given and enjoyed by every nature, as was said above. For just as bodily light, because it is light, naturally shines—that is, it generates unbegotten light, for “light” signifies light merely existing and unbegotten—and shines forth as proceeding and begotten; and because it shines, it illuminates, that is, supplies light: so in God light is light, in whom there are no shadows at all. Indeed, he himself is inaccessible light, unless he approaches someone by his natural gift, that is, illumination. And because he is light, he certainly shines—that is, emits splendor from himself; and because light shines and emits splendor from itself, it supplies light and illuminates. Thus light, emitting splendor from itself but not losing it, enlightens intelligence from itself to knowledge of truth; and fire, emitting heat from itself while retaining it, inflames affection to the love of virtue. Therefore, although the nature of the coequal Trinity is undifferentiated, nevertheless, as divine things descend to us from the Father through the Son and Holy Spirit, or in the Holy Spirit, according to the saying, “Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII), so human things ascend through the Holy Spirit to the Son and through the Son to the Father. For this reason, when the Son departs, the Paraclete Spirit is sent, to unite the body to its head, that is, to Christ, and Christ himself to God, as it is written: “The head of the woman is the man, of the man Christ, and of Christ God” (I Cor. XI). Thus the Spirit governs, consoles, instructs, and leads the Church to Christ, which Christ himself will at the same time present without spot or wrinkle as a kingdom to God and the Father. May the glorious Trinity deign to accomplish this in us.

These things, brother, amid countless distresses, we have written to you lest we should not obey. For in this year evils of pestilence and famine have come upon our regions such as, it is thought, all former ages have not seen. We saw and noted their signs in the preceding year, knowing that every event has causes from which it proceeds, preparations by which it comes about, signs indicating when it will occur, and final benefits explaining why it happens. For nothing is done by wisdom except wisely; nor by the supreme good except what is good, well done, and directed toward good. Farewell; and pray for us, loving us, because we love you.

[Col. 1889]

## LETTER OF THE SAME ISAAC TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS, ON THE OFFICE OF THE MASS

To the lord and father in Christ, JOHN, by God’s grace bishop of Poitiers, brother ISAAC, abbot of l’Étoile: greeting, service, and obedience.

Behold: what your humility could not obtain despite long and repeated requests, your authority quickly extorted by command. You compel us, from the occasion of a conference—at which we indeed repent of having poured ourselves out so lightly—to bind in writing how we direct our attention to the sacred canon while we celebrate the most holy mysteries. It is a difficult, perhaps inexplicable matter. Nothing is more fleeting than the human heart, nothing more inquisitive; therefore to hold it so long upon one thing is most arduous, and often to direct it uniformly toward a single object—though this comes from the fault of curiosity. Hence divine grace, providing for our weakness, often floods ancient passages with wholly fresh meaning; and when these suddenly shine forth, we marvel beyond all human measure where they had lain hidden and whence they have arisen so suddenly. From this very wonder the heart is enlarged, as it is written; and through that enlargement it is filled with devotion, love, and delight, according to the Psalmist: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX). At other times, when the new sweetness previously seen more clearly than light and tasted more sweetly than honey and the honeycomb hides itself as we pass through the same words, according to the saying, “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. XXX)—that is, in order that they may fear you—for this concealment generates dreadful fear; dread, pain; pain, groans, sighs, and unutterable inward complaints. Thus we mourn the loss of old things no less than we rejoice in finding new ones. And so, through either alternation, as though crushed, ground down, and milled between two millstones, we are transformed into the finest flour of God’s sacrifice. Mixing it with both kinds of tears, namely compunction and devotion, and baking it in the oven of a contrite and humbled heart, we make ourselves into the loaves of presentation which we first of all offer. Therefore, most serene Father, since we are least of all constant even to ourselves, but the Spirit breathes where it wills and what it wills, and we do not know whence it comes or where it goes; and since a person cannot receive anything from himself, nor obtain it from another at will unless it has been given from above, we have until now been wiser in silence before the humility of your request than we can now be in speaking under the command of your authority. But perhaps the question is not what heavenly dew descends upon us, or how clouds rain; rather, how the earth is opened and brings forth the Savior. The question is not how righteousness looks down from heaven, but how truth springs from earth; not how God looks upon us, but how we look upon him.

We, then, to confess simply, direct our attention to each little heading individually, as grace gives it to us; and, as we receive them through the lips like breasts full from heaven, we suck attentively, perfecting from the mouth of an infant and nursing child such praises as we can. Thus, although many things are said and done there in diverse ways, we nevertheless comprehend almost all of them under a threefold action. For three principal actions are distinguished in the sacred canon, served as it were by three altars, attended as it were by a threefold sacrificial priest, and accompanied in a fashion by three sacrifices. Perhaps this is the pattern shown to Moses on the mountain, according to which he was to make the shadow of things to come—that is, the tabernacle in the wilderness. He saw on high what he was to make below; on the mountain he learned what he was to do on the plain; finally, above he learned what he was to teach below; he learned from God what he was to teach human beings. The Apostle speaks according to this pattern: “What I received,” he says, “I have delivered to you” (I Cor. II). O good Father, consider how many today hand on what they have received neither from God nor from the Apostle! Nearly all contemporary traditions serve shameful profit; nearly every penalty imposed for an offense is monetary; nearly every favor bestowed as if freely, even if it does not set its price beforehand, hopes for service afterward. Our graces today are pregnant: under the pretext of a virgin, we give a pregnant woman in marriage. Moses did not teach this deception, nor did Paul teach it. This is not the pattern from the mountain. The tabernacle from the mountain—that is, the tabernacle of God with human beings—was so constructed that in its court it had a bronze altar, where animals were sacrificed; but inside the tabernacle another altar of gold, called the altar of incense, where incense (*thymiama*), frankincense, and other things were placed which, when burned, give off fragrant smoke. Behind this, as though in the innermost and highest place, was set the mercy-seat, which is called not merely holy, but the Holy of Holies.

Between the mercy-seat and the golden altar a veil is spread; in Christ’s Passion it was torn, so that the mercy-seat might be revealed—that is, Christ’s body, which under this mystery was likewise fixed naked to the cross. Between the golden and bronze altars there is the wall of the tabernacle in the wilderness and the dividing wall in the Temple, concerning which the sinner, tending from penitence toward righteousness, says: “In my God I shall pass over a wall” (Ps. XVII). For the first altar signifies the contrite and humbled heart. When upon it we sacrifice through penitence what we lived as if we were beasts of burden, and our irrational deeds, what else do we offer to God but animals of different kinds? In the conversion of a sinner—who through sin is indeed outside, and cannot enter into righteousness except through fitting penitence—compunction of heart slays such animals; confession of the mouth skins them; judgment cuts them into pieces; and fitting affliction burns them. The altar is bronze—that is, dark and resonant—because the penitent is placed within darkness in himself, while his spirit is distressed within him and his heart troubled; and he must cry mightily from the depths, so that his voice may be heard in the heights. Thus he can in his God pass over the wall which divides fault from righteousness, because “a troubled spirit” is a sacrifice acceptable to God, and he does not despise “a contrite and humbled heart.” But the true altar, which is within and golden, signifies the heart purified through penitence, gleaming and bright with the testimony of a good conscience. Likewise, devotion offers the sacrifice of righteousness, oblations, and burnt offerings, when it no longer laments its own offenses but already rejoices in divine things; no longer groans over having committed crimes, but gives thanks for the bestowal of virtues. The third, more properly called the mercy-seat than an altar, is where not merely angels occasionally appear to certain persons, or whoever may appear, but where the mercy-seat itself—and the cherubim, overshadowing it always with outspread wings—signifies the heart lifted above the cloud of phantasms. As it is said: “Man shall approach a lofty heart” (Ps. LXIII). Its citizenship is in heaven, not merely by desire and hope but by continual contemplation, so far as is lawful to a human being; forgetting the things behind, whether good or evil, it always stretches itself toward what lies before, pursuing the prize of the heavenly calling, into which it desires and delights to look with the angels.

First, therefore, is the sacrifice of repentance, which the upright spirit offers upon the contrite heart: that is, compunction. Second is the sacrifice of righteousness, which the Holy Spirit offers upon the pure heart: that is, devotion. Third is the sacrifice of understanding, which the ruling spirit offers upon the exalted heart [Col. 1892B]: that is, contemplation. For compunction corrects the perverse; devotion directs those who have been corrected; contemplation raises up those who have been directed and causes them to dwell with the angels. The contrite heart is tormented over past evils; the pure heart delights in present gifts; but the exalted heart contemplates eternal rewards. Repentance separates from the devil; righteousness joins one to God; understanding delights in God himself.

This is the structure of God’s tabernacle, not so much among human beings as within them. How its image shines forth in the sacred canon is readily apparent, where first the sacrifice of servitude is distinctly offered, afterwards that of freedom, and thirdly that of unity. For through the divine mysteries we are liberated by the Son from the servitude [Col. 1892C] of the devil, in order that we may be united with the Father of the household through the Son. Thus indeed the Son speaks to the Father on behalf of servants: “Father, I will that, as I and you are one, so these also may be one with us” (John 17). Therefore every operation of the heavenly mysteries is known to serve this end: that, united without end to the one God through Christ, we may delight in Christ.

For this reason, though many, we are one bread, one body; yet we have not many heads, but one, whose head is God, so that, many people united through the One and in the One, we may become one spirit with him: wise with wisdom from Wisdom; living with life from Life; powerful with power from Power; fervent with charity from Charity; upright with righteousness; and always glad with gladness from Gladness. But exceedingly eager devotion, yearning especially for the final action [Col. 1892D], anticipated this subject.

Accordingly, once all things belonging to the first action have been duly arranged, and certain prayers or petitions have first been offered with the incense of rams—that is, with the intercessions of apostles and martyrs—the visible priest approaches, still as one born of flesh and therefore flesh, in order to offer visible victims, earthly things from the earth; and he does this upon a visible, material altar, visibly consecrated with material oil. All this is performed, as it were, still outside, since what is done and how it is done can be seen outwardly. Thus it is known to pertain to the servant who does not remain in the house forever.

For this reason it is called an offering of servitude, as it is said: “This offering of our servitude” (canon of the Mass); and it fittingly calls bread and wine the offering of servitude [Col. 1893A]. For when man, taken from the earth by nature, had been established by the grace of the author of nature and giver of grace as lord over the earth, he departed through sin and was condemned by justice beneath the earth. Therefore the earth, which had freely served him by being fertile for his delight, now, coaxed by many strange services and cultivated with labours and sweats most wretched and pitiable, scarcely yields enough for necessity, as it is written: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3).

Since bread and wine are the principal articles of nourishment without which animal life cannot be sustained, the power of animal life is fittingly offered through them when they are offered. For they are its chief portion and represent the whole. What more, then, can a servant who desires reconciliation [Col. 1893B] with his Lord do than offer from his poverty all his sustenance and thereby sacrifice his whole life? Thus, in the first action, while he offers in bread and wine all his sustenance, he kills everything by which he lives as an animal; for one kills life when one takes away its sustenance.

Hence it is wisely said: “You have sat at a great table; carefully observe what is set before you. Set a knife to your throat, knowing that you must prepare such things” (Prov. 23). The great table is the altar of the Lord. There he is set before us for refreshment, he who gave his body and soul for us as our redemption. We must observe that we too must prepare such things for him: that is, we must likewise and together lay down our body and soul for him. Thus, through the spirit of counsel, the Prophet answered himself: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation,” etc. (Ps. 15 [Vulgate numbering]).

But observe the form which he expressed so subtly and elegantly in saying, “Set a knife to your throat.” We set the knife of abstinence and fasting, as it were, to our throat when, having offered all our sustenance to God, we afterwards take from it sparingly and fearfully, as from God’s altar, only for necessity. For the Lord ordained that those who serve the altar should live from the altar. Otherwise, if after such an offering we consume again luxuriously and lavishly, as though it were our own, we take away all that we offer; and we then live, worse still, by plunder. For in that case we no longer live and die for the Lord but for ourselves; and whether we live thus or die thus [Col. 1893D], we belong no longer to the Lord but to ourselves—indeed, not even to ourselves, but to the devil. Therefore, good and prudent man, carefully consider that ours is an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle of their body are not permitted to eat. As the body is defiled by pleasure, so the soul is defiled by vanity and the spirit by ambition.

These indeed are the heads of the dragon whom the Lord gave as food to the peoples of Ethiopia; this is the cup of demons, which it is not fitting to drink together with the cup of the Lord. “For what fellowship has Christ with Belial?” Are you at once pure in spirit because you are pure in body? On the contrary: being pure in body, let the soul be purer and the spirit purest, so that, wholly pure in chastity, purity, and humility, it may need nothing except to wash its feet.

Behold what we aim at when [Col. 1894A] we offer the first oblation; behold what we strive to become while we attend to these things, think upon these things, and handle these things outwardly in word and speech, inwardly, as far as we can, in deed and truth. Yet a higher counsel is needed. In this action the servant does all that he can; but he does not satisfy fully by doing all. He cannot do anything more, yet this entire offering is insufficient. He can kill himself, but he cannot restore himself to life. Therefore he raises himself by prayer and turns to him who can do all things, saying: “Make this offering, O God, in every respect blessed, enrolled, ratified, and acceptable, that it may become for us the Body and Blood” (canon of the Mass).

It is as though he said: “Lord, I have done what I could; supply what I could not do.” And, without wavering in faith, he proceeds to the second action, saying: “Who, on the day before he suffered,” etc. (ibid.); and at those words comes power and efficacy, as it is written: “He will give to his voice a voice of power” (Ps. 67 [Vulgate numbering]). For he speaks and acts: Word and Power: “This is my Body” (canon of the Mass).

Thus, beyond all human reasoning, by divine power and human care, from the old food of the old human being there comes to be new food for the new human being. Therefore the new priest—no longer the old Melchizedek, nor flesh born of flesh—offers not from his own sweat, nor from the earth which he serves wretchedly and in many ways; but the new Jesus, spirit born of the Spirit, offers from divine gifts and endowments, from heaven, a heavenly victim of flesh and blood. He says, no longer timidly as before [Col. 1894C], nor offering a victim of servitude, but with exultation and joy: “[A sacrifice] to your glorious majesty: a pure victim, which purifies; holy, which makes holy; spotless, which makes spotless; namely, holy bread,” not of temporal or animal but of spiritual and eternal life, and a cup able to satisfy and save forever, and therefore “of everlasting salvation” (ibid.).

Moreover, because flesh and blood profit nothing, according to the saying that they are spirit and life, he seeks something still higher; for nothing suffices him until through the Body he is united in heaven to the one God and, through humanity, joined to divinity. Having raised a ladder for himself, he naturally strives to ascend. Therefore through this oblation he girds himself for prayer, saying: “Upon which look with favourable countenance,” etc. (ibid.) [Col. 1894D]. And, as though ascending by the rungs of that ladder, he commemorates the gift of Abel the boy, the sacrifice of Abraham, and the offering of Melchizedek the priest, who expressed an elegant image in bread and wine, just as Abraham expressed the truth in his son and Abel the gift of innocence in the lamb.

Strengthened by this prayer, he approaches the third action with confidence. But because he is not yet able to ascend as he wishes to that highest, sublime altar in the presence of the divine majesty, where the supreme and eternal Priest stands before the Father’s countenance—indeed, this is signified when the visible priest bows beneath the visible altar and, rising, kisses it—he asks that his sacrifice may be carried by the hands of the angel, namely his invisible minister, and united to Christ’s Body in heaven [Col. 1895A]. Thus, just as through it which he sees, we receive bread and wine from the first altar, and in the truth of flesh and blood from the second altar beyond the veil in heaven, through the blessing once promised to Abraham’s seed and the grace brought by Mary, he may share in the power of that sacrament itself: that is, may be united in spirit to the supreme Head. “For the head of Christ is God.”

Behold, most serene Father, how, as the preface admonishes, hearts are raised on high, words on high, works on high. The first oblation separates from the world; the second joins to Christ; the third unites to God. The first mortifies, the second gives life, the third deifies. In the first action is the Passion; in the second, the Resurrection; in the third, glorification. Hence it is said: “Mindful of his blessed Passion and also of his Resurrection from the dead,” etc. (canon of the Mass) [Col. 1895B]. The first is, as it were, outside in the court, the animal life; the second, inside and in the temple, the rational faculty; the third, beyond the veil and in heaven, faith itself now. For just as reason stands above animal perception and faith above reason, so vision stands above faith. “For what a man sees, why does he hope for it?”

Thus the carnal person becomes spiritual, and the spiritual person heavenly or divine; the servant becomes free, and the Son reigns with the Father; the enemy becomes friend and heir. O priest of Christ, persevere while you stand before him! While you do these things, become devoutly mindful of your true servant, who remembers your paternal kindness in every prayer and sacrifice!

But behold: while it pleased us to write these things to you, both because of the subject and because of the recipient, lest we exceed the limits of a letter, your Hugh of Calvin[iac] suddenly fell violently upon our people. He personally beat some of the converts harshly and for a long time; he [lacuna] certain members of the household; [lacuna] injury [lacuna] an absent person with insults and many disgraceful threats. He carried off eight oxen and, as we think, has already [Col. 1896B] sold them; and his hand is still stretched out. From the rooftops he now proclaims that he will take vengeance upon me through all the English. Would that I had either not been an Englishman, or had never seen Englishmen where I live in exile!

[ALCHER OF CLAIRVAUX.]

[Col. 1895]

The book begins. 1075  

CHAPTER I.—How Gerhoh’s statement in his writings, “Christ was born in heaven without a mother, on earth without a father,” is to be understood. He sets forth the doctrine of the new Nestorians, who, under the leadership and instruction of Gisilbert, divide Christ into two sons, man and God: one born of the Virgin, the other begotten by God the Father. They accordingly say that the man, the natural son of man, was adopted by God as a son, and deny that he is in the Father’s glory. 1078  

CHAPTER II.—He teaches that the statement in his letter to Eberhard, Bishop of Bamberg, “Humanity has been supremely glorified in God’s glory,” must be understood not of humanity by which a human being is human, which itself is not a human being, but of humanity which is a human being, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh. He also teaches that it is less correct to say “that the man in Christ was deified.” 1079  

CHAPTER III.—He demonstrates, on the authority of Hilary, Ambrose, the Synod of Sirmium, and Jerome, that it is right to call the man in Christ Most High, and that Paul (1 Cor. 15:25–26) does not oppose this doctrine. 1083  

CHAPTER IV.—Saint Augustine does not conflict with the doctrine in question, nor do insults directed against Christ. The distinction is further established between humanity which is a human being and humanity which belongs to a human being, and humanity by which a human being is human. 1087  

CHAPTER V.—Christ, who is God by divinity and man by humanity, cannot in a true sense be understood as man apart from the Word which was made flesh. 1090  

CHAPTER VI.—The author would prefer, following the example of Saint Hilary, that the definite term “man,” rather than the ambiguous term “humanity,” had been used in those passages of his writings where he says, “Humanity being glorified into God.” In addition, he establishes from the Fathers that Christ the man is to be worshipped not with *dulia* alone but also with *latria*. 1092  

CHAPTER VII.—By the example of the three Magi and the authority of Leo and Augustine, the author confirms that the man in Christ must be worshipped with the worship of *latria*. 1095  

CHAPTER VIII.—The worship of the cross redounds to Christ, who is Son of God according to the man, not according to the humanity by which he is human; nor is he an adopted but a natural Son of God. He teaches that one must distinguish between naturally natural generation and wonderfully natural generation, by which the Son, man-God, was generated. 1098  

CHAPTER IX.—As the Son of God was God through eternity, so Christ, by the unity of the sacrament, existed before his mother [Col. 1898]. Consequently, for the same reason that Nestorius permitted her to be called *Christotokos* (“bearer of Christ”), he could and ought to have permitted her to be called *Theotokos* (“bearer of God”). 1101  

CHAPTER X.—He warns that what he said in his exposition of Psalm XVII, 5 concerning the bridal chamber, kisses, and nuptials of bridegroom and bride must be understood in a spiritual, not a carnal, sense; and that in his exposition of the sixth verse of the same Psalm he intended nothing other than what Augustine and Hilary taught concerning the man assumed into God through grace. 1104  

CHAPTER XI.—What likeness exists between the grace by which God begets his Only-begotten and that by which he regenerates children of wrath into adoption as his own children. Christ is the natural Son of God in both natures: naturally in the divine nature, but wonderfully in the human. What is meant by Psalm XCVIII, 5: “Worship his footstool.” 1109  

CHAPTER XII.—An exposition of the same Davidic verse from Augustine. In worshipping Christ, neither the man must be separated from God nor God from the man. Letter of Bruno, Bishop of Strasbourg, commending Gerhoh’s treatise to Pope Adrian. 1113  

CHAPTER XIII.—Christ is truly present and to be worshipped in the sacrament of the Eucharist; the author pronounces anathema on those who deny that the Lord’s body can be in two places simultaneously, such as Folmar after Berengar, whose blasphemies Gerhoh bitterly laments. 1117  

CHAPTER XIV.—Further material on the vices and heresy of Folmar, who utterly denies that Christ is in the Mass, on the basis of a passage from Augustine misunderstood and corrupted. 1121  

CHAPTER XV.—Folmar must be prevented from correcting and judging his own writings; and the author declares that he will never allow himself to be moved from the judgment of the holy Fathers, who affirm that Christ was exalted to sit beside God the Father Most High. 1125  

CHAPTER XVI.—The author’s doctrine concerning the divine glory of the Son of Man is strengthened by testimonies of both ancient and recent doctors. 1128  

CHAPTER XVII.—While teaching the equality of the glory which human nature possesses in Christ together with the divine nature, he does not in any way confuse the natures with Eutyches. On certain Nestorians at the Synod of Friesach. 1134  

CHAPTER XVIII.—He disputes against scholastic theologians favouring Paul of Samosata, Nestorius, and Photinus, who maintain that the assumed man ought not to receive either the worship of *latria* or love above all things as God. 1139  

CHAPTER XIX.—The Virgin’s Son is truly God, though not from himself, yet through himself; therefore, contrary to Nestorius’s view, the man is not to be co-worshipped with God, but is wholly to be worshipped in one simple act of worship. 1143  

CHAPTER XX.—In the conception and generation of the Son of Man, the true faith holds that what was born in the Virgin by conception and from the Virgin by generation is wholly the Son of the Most High and wholly the son of the Virgin. Thus it is rightly said both that God is the Son of Man and that man is the Son of God. 1147  

CHAPTER XXI.—The same point is further established, and it is shown that the Word was in no way changed in itself by union with human nature, and that the man was born as the only Son of God the Father—something which assumption alone or indwelling could not have conferred upon him. 1152  

CHAPTER XXII.—In Christ’s person man is God and God is man: for God is man through the humanity which he assumed, and man is God through the divinity which he received. 1157

The treatise *On the Building of God*, by a certain unlearned and sinful man, addressed to Chunon, Bishop of Regensburg, begins. 1191  

CHAPTER I.—Who is the author and architect of this Building? What is its material, what its instruments? What is that by which its parts are joined together and remain standing? This building is not overthrown or destroyed by the storms of the ungodly, but is strengthened and raised higher. 1193  

CHAPTER II.—By ecclesiastical resources the spiritual building, like the Lord’s ark, is adorned and fortified with gold and skins. Secular rulers and wicked clerics do not plunder these resources without grave harm to themselves. 1198  

CHAPTER III.—Clerics who shrink from common and apostolic life must be excluded from and punished in the Building of God. Those who defend private property by Louis the Pious’s constitution must not be heard. 1201  

CHAPTER IV.—How greatly Saint Augustine promoted the common and apostolic life of clerics, and how strongly he detested the vice of private property among them. 1205  

CHAPTER V.—How shameful it is that ecclesiastical goods should be granted to soldiers by bishops themselves, who thereby become contemptible among laypeople because they so greatly depart from Saint Ambrose’s example. 1209  

CHAPTER VI.—Those once called defenders of churches were the very people who inflicted the greatest injury upon them; hence their fictitious homage. The property of the Church belongs not to the king but to the poor; bishops who are too weak in defending the Church’s rights are to be condemned. 1215  

CHAPTER VII.—God’s building cannot stand unless bishops cast off the yoke of this world: the pomp of retainers, the services of soldiers, the neglect of evangelical life, and so forth. 1217  

CHAPTER VIII.—How ecclesiastical resources are to be divided and administered by bishops; for example, how a stipend is to be paid to rulers from Church estates and tithes. 1220  

CHAPTER IX.—The goodwill and generosity of rulers toward the Church were very great in the earliest centuries, but not in later times. The election of bishops must be canonical, that is, free. 1221  

CHAPTER X.—What goods may a ruler lawfully give to the Church, and on what grounds? Ecclesiastical offices must be administered by ecclesiastics and secular offices by secular persons. 1224  

CHAPTER XI.—Saint Martin is proposed to bishops as an example: not a lover and companion of soldiers and nobles, but of the poor and monks. 1226  

CHAPTER XII.—On the households, servants, and ministerials of churches, whose condition was once very different from what it is now. It is shameful for a bishop scarcely ever to appear except attended by thousands. 1228  

CHAPTER XIII.—Following the example of Saint Lawrence the martyr, bishops ought to conduct themselves not as owners of ecclesiastical goods, devoted to feeding soldiers, but as their stewards, benevolent toward the poor. 1231  

CHAPTER XIV.—The ancient sacred canons grant no portion of ecclesiastical goods to soldiers, ministerials, or wealthy clerics. 1233  

CHAPTER XV.—The households and estates of churches must not be entrusted or granted to soldiers and other secular officers, but to worthy clerics. 1237  

CHAPTER XVI.—The greatest care must be taken to reclaim the property of churches from secular hands. Therefore bishops should set Abraham before themselves as an example, and clerics should set before themselves his unencumbered, home-born servants. 1239  

CHAPTER XVII.—Bishops, who are in God’s house and building as certain pillars and paintings, must keep their hands from gifts of every kind. 1241  

CHAPTER XVIII.—A bishop acts wisely and beneficially if he avoids things which may indeed be lawful but are not expedient, and thus sometimes refrains even from gifts not otherwise unlawful. 1243  

CHAPTER XIX.—Gifts are sometimes lawfully accepted by bishops, namely when they are distributed to the poor under the witness of their Church; this was done by Peter, Paul, and Martin. 1245  

CHAPTER XX.—Revenues are to be brought into common ownership for clerics living without private property, whom Peter recognizes as his genuine sons and will one day lead to the heavenly Jerusalem. 1247  

CHAPTER XXI.—Pastors of churches are to be appointed from among clerics who have first zealously trained themselves in cloistered and common life. 1248  

CHAPTER XXII.—The objections of powerful persons ought not to deter clerics, especially their prelates, from introducing common life. No one is to be received into a religious community without examination and testing of the spirit. 1250  

CHAPTER XXIII.—On vicars and those who possess canonries in several places at once. 1252  

CHAPTER XXIV.—Punishment for crimes formerly condemned in common by the holy Fathers must not be postponed, even if the multitude of offenders is great, and so forth. 1254  

CHAPTER XXV.—Clerics sunk in the mire of vices must be reformed to apostolic life; Gerhoh rejoices that this has already been done at Rome, Salzburg, and elsewhere. 1257  

CHAPTER XXVI.—Bishops should beware of domineering over the clergy; rather, they should endeavour to show themselves kind to their clerics and generous to the poor. The bishops’ table should be the same as that of clerics, poor people, and so forth. 1261  

CHAPTER XXVII.—May bishops devote themselves to secular business, the courts of rulers, military concerns, and the like? What the apostles and holy doctors of the Church thought concerning this. 1265  

CHAPTER XXVIII.—The life of clerics is not inferior to the life of monks. What garments should a monk made pontiff or bishop wear? 1267  

CHAPTER XXIX.—What the alb and the clerics’ ankle-length tunic signify mystically; by what figures they were prefigured in each Testament; and what their tonsure should be. 1269  

CHAPTER XXX.—The morals of the primitive Church must be expressed in life and virtues by clerics and monks. Bishops should exclude from holy orders those unwilling to do this. 1271  

CHAPTER XXXI.—Why Saint Gregory the Great permitted private property to clerics not in holy orders. 1275  

CHAPTER XXXII.—Saint Augustine composed different rules by which clerics and monks, virgins and widows, and others are to regulate their conduct. 1276  

CHAPTER XXXIII.—On vices and excesses of religious women to be corrected by bishops. 1278  

CHAPTER XXXIV.—Religious persons who do not live religiously are to be expelled from monasteries and excommunicated. 1280  

CHAPTER XXXV.—What sword bishops ought rightly to use. 1281  

CHAPTER XXXVI.—How a bishop should restore religious women living irreligiously to good conduct and regular observance. 1283  

CHAPTER XXXVII.—Before all else a bishop must take care to introduce into the episcopal church regular canons who profess common life. 1285  

CHAPTER XXXVIII.—A fallen cleric is not to be admitted to the functions of office and order except after completing penitence according to the ancient discipline. 1286  

CHAPTER XXXIX.—Why those who relapsed into sin after having once undergone public penitence were formerly no longer admitted to ecclesiastical reconciliation. 1289  

CHAPTER XL.—On the form and distinction of ecclesiastical and secular judgment. For which sins an offender should be struck with anathema, and so forth. 1291
